Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library: complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all extant monuments of Catholic tradition through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, compared with one another and with certain manuscripts, and corrected with the utmost care; continually elucidated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the most extensive editions completed during the three most recent centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text itself, as well as titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated; expanded with both doubtful and apocryphal works that nevertheless possess some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two copious general indexes: one an index of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father wrote on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other an index of Holy Scripture, by which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented upon individual texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in what places in their works.**

**A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others if one weighs: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes—uniform throughout the whole course of the work—the low price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and genre.**

**Second Series**, containing the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or of Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. ## In the Year of the Lord 1166: *The Gregorian Work* of R. P. Garner, Regular Canon and Superior of Saint-Victor in Paris

That is, ready allegorical explanations of nearly all matters contained in the Bible, drawn from all the writings of Pope Saint Gregory; highly necessary for preachers and interpreters of the divine word; recently enlarged with notes from Gregorian writers through the efforts of Brother John Picard, Regular Canon of Saint-Victor in Paris. (Paris: Charles Sevestre, Rue Saint-Jacques, opposite the Mathurins; duodecimo; with royal privilege; 1608.)

[Col. 0009]

## Dedicatory Epistle

To the Reverend Father and Lord in Christ, Lord Denis de Coulomp, most worthy Vicar of the Supreme Prior of Saint-Victor in Paris: greetings.

No one except Carnabas, Ptolemy Philopator, the *Agyrtae*, and the rest of that similarly impious dregs of parricides, would deny that reviving the fading memory of one’s forefathers and, so far as possible and according to one’s ability, repaying the life received from them, is an act of divine filial devotion. Why divine filial devotion? For if we call divine those vows, sacrifices, supplications, entreaties, and all things that pertain to the worship of God, greatest and best, then you will not improperly adorn even the slight honour shown to parents with the title “divine.” For, according to Saint Gregory the Theologian, [Note: [Col. 0009], *To Vitalianus*.] a mortal father, created by the immortal and uncreated God, is in some sense a god, and children ought to regard him in God’s place.

I pass over the splendid praises of the pagans on this subject [Note: [Col. 0009]. Aristotle, *Ethics* VIII, ch. 13, and IX, ch. 2; Plato, *Laws* II; and others.], in order to illuminate words with a striking example. An old proverb, “A wicked Scythian,” bears witness that the Scythian nation was made savage by rustic barbarity; [Note: [Col. 0009]. From Herodotus, *Melpomene*.] yet a certain golden humanity toward their forefathers possessed their iron and inhuman breast so thoroughly that, when Darius king of the Persians reproached them for their womanish daily flights and their refusal of battle, King Idanthyrsus answered boldly through a herald, among other things:

> “There are the tombs of our fathers. Come now: when you have found them, attempt to destroy them; then you will learn whether we shall fight you for the graves or not. But before that, unless reason moves us, we shall not engage in battle with you.”

Holy indeed and supremely praiseworthy was the barbarian ruler’s answer and policy. He wished to begin the contest with the religious defence of ancestral burial-places, as though they were temples consecrated to divine powers; wisely he foresaw that the war would end successfully when devotion toward parents had sounded the trumpet-call.

Yet, as souls surpass bodies, so their honorary tombs—that is, books filled with heavenly teachings—surpass stone or marble sarcophagi, which for the most part contain nothing but ashes. Though bloodless, these books never wither like a living root; rather, through a hidden and life-giving grace of divine discourse, they either restore heavenly life to devout hearts or bring it forth. Therefore, whatever care, goodwill, and humanity we show to graves that preserve paternal bones ought not, it seems, to be withheld from books.

Accordingly Richard Aungerville, an Englishman called Bury from his birthplace, bishop of Durham in England, notable for his reverence and affection toward sacred volumes and theological writings, warned clerics in his *Philobiblon* in these exact words how reverently and carefully books ought to be handled:

> “We render service not only to God by preparing volumes of new books, but also exercise an office of consecrated devotion if we sometimes handle those same books without damage and sometimes entrust them, once returned to suitable places, to unviolated safekeeping, so that they may delight in purity while they are held in the hands and rest securely when stored in their own chambers. Surely, after vestments and vessels consecrated to the Lord’s body, sacred books deserve more honourable treatment; for injury is inflicted upon them as often as anyone presumes to touch them with a foul hand.”

In the preceding chapter he gave, in order to encourage learned persons eagerly to deserve well of the book trade, the title: “How meritorious it is to write new books and renew old ones.” He urged this point especially on the following grounds:

> “But because whatever serves mortals suffers the loss of mortality through the passage of time, volumes worn away by age must necessarily be restored by their renewed successors, so that perpetuity—which is denied to the individual by nature—may be granted by the privilege of the species. For just as the bodies of books, compacted from a mixture of contraries, continually experience the deterioration of their composition, so through the prudence of clerics a remedy must be found by which the sacred book, paying nature’s debt, may obtain an inherited substitute; and like seed may be raised up for its dead brother. Thus may that saying of Ecclesiasticus 30 immediately be fulfilled: ‘His father is dead, and yet as though he were not dead, for he has left one like himself after him.’”

These are Richard’s words, written 250 years ago in praise of the care of one’s library furnishings. Posterity will most deservedly remember and honourably commend the care which you, Reverend Father, have lavished upon our Garner. He lived more than four hundred years ago, and at the beginning of the century just past seemed, through the feeble little work of a languid edition, to have drawn a faint breath anew; now, by your permission and the breath of this livelier typography, he almost breathes a second soul.

Thus it is clear that he returns to you far more welcome and pleasing than Virbius-Hippolytus and Androgeus, son of Minos, returned to Aesculapius—provided, however, that, as Ovid truly sang,

> The fertile freedom of poets extends without limit,  
> And binds its words to no historical truth.

For those men were restored from death, or soon to die, to mortal life—or, as our Adam aptly calls it, to life-giving death [Note: [Col. 0011]. In the prose for the Octave of Christ’s Nativity.]—whereas Garner, through your authority, has been restored to a light that cannot be obscured even by Cimmerian darkness.

But in truth, even if this reason were absent, Garner would still not fail to be most welcome to you. For to whom Pope Saint Gregory is pleasing, could the choicest and most fragrant flowers of Gregory, arranged like cultivated flower-beds through these sixteen little books of Garner, be displeasing? That you are most familiar with Gregory is witnessed by Gregory himself, whom you continually cite in your careful chapter-sermons together with the holy Fathers of both the earlier and middle ages. Not without reason, then, might someone call you their living library: eloquently and abundantly, like the learned evangelical scribe, you bring forth from your treasure things new and old (Matt. 13).

There is also what Saint Jerome, lamenting, declared concerning his Nepotianus: for during table-talk he customarily advanced various opinions of ancient theologians, attributing one to Tertullian, another to Minucius, another to Cyprian, and so forth. With equal right, indeed necessarily and with still greater praise, the same may be said of you, if any observant person who understands how, when, where, and to whom he speaks should arrange it more carefully.

I had almost passed over—but must not pass over—the reason why Garner is now dedicated to you: namely, the burden, lighter than that other burden which you now bear, though envious and unwilling weaker nature resists, yet which you sustain with unbroken courage. How weighty this reason is, comparison with the ancients demonstrates. Aelius Lampridius presented to emperors the lives of Commodus, Antoninus Heliogabalus, and Alexander Severus; Aelius Spartianus those of Hadrian, Aelius Verus, Didius Julianus, Severus, Pescennius Niger; Julius Capitolinus those of Antoninus Pius, Verus, and the two Maximini. They knew well that such works ought to be read with serene eyes by those to whom they offered them, because of the same majesty of the Roman Empire which they themselves bore. I pass over innumerable ecclesiastical writers and biographers, lest I seem ridiculously to light a slender straw in the noonday sun.

Finally, Garner will win your fatherly favour for himself by a final reason, and not an insignificant one: we very often place great value upon the illustrious monuments of our ancestors, indeed even upon the very small things they left behind, because they restore to us their much-desired presence and comfort our most miserable bereavement. But books do this, if anything does, far more happily, more truly, and more naturally; books are happier, more vital, and more genuinely the children of their parents, since they reproduce their parents’ fairer and nobler part: the divine soul and noble intellect. “For children do not resemble their fathers in countenance alone.”

For these reasons, then, receive, Reverend Father, from the hands of him who is your most obedient son in Christ and the last of your canons, Garner restored to life in his *Gregorian Work* by your authority and returning to you.

Brother John Picard.

[Col. 0011]

## To the Candid Reader

I had thought it unnecessary to inform you what had been added to or removed from this edition. But when I discovered that copies of the earlier edition were extremely rare, I turned my mind and hand to the task. First, therefore, know that the work previously printed was so full of errors that one could often scarcely read even two uncorrupted lines; it is now presented to you in a cleaner form.

Yet I do not deny that a number of errors, although relatively slight ones, have crept into this edition: partly through inadvertence, partly through extremely frequent erasures. I was forced to insert these into individual lines by the marks of ancient scribes, retained for almost fifty years by the former printers, but to the later ones more obscure than Platonic numbers. Moreover, in many places the paper was too weak and the ink too uncontrollable: having been applied sparingly, it spread with defective extravagance, obliterating neighbouring letters. All these things, accumulated in the text and margins of the book, created much labour in the work itself.

I mean the recent addition. Its principal feature is the marking of passages drawn from the divine books. To identify them, it was necessary to consult different translations of the Bible; yet I did not always return better informed, since in the passages marked I did not find precisely what I read in Saint Gregory. At times a small word, or a simple component in place of a compound word, had been substituted. And when I applied myself with particular devotion to this devout task, the variety of translations which I repeatedly observed Saint Gregory to have used caused me no little difficulty. Therefore, so that you might read more calmly, whenever a divine saying differing somewhat from the Vulgate edition was cited, I indicated that it was thus found in the Septuagint, Augustine, or Cassiodorus.

Besides this, I added what was the central concern of the whole work: namely, annotations—some of which, while the workers were looking elsewhere, disappeared from your sight and mine—identifying the Gregorian books, homilies, and letters from whose flowering blossoms and branches our Garner constructed his mystical garden. This I completed at last, though with difficulty. I completed it, I say, and at times so painfully that I was on the point of sending both manuscript and pen, as a veteran, to the final reserve rank, had not the thought occurred that it would be unfair to lose the fruit of such protracted labour because of the more tiresome discovery of one or two passages. Therefore, [Col. 0013] if amid these agitations of a mind almost overthrown and precipitated I have stumbled in several places, reader, I ask you—well aware as you are of human weakness—to grant me a more indulgent pardon.

In marking Gregory’s sayings, I used the Nivelles edition; afterward I discovered that it differed from the earlier editions because the divisions in the books on Job had been altered. I therefore gave the first edition’s number first and the latter’s second. You should also observe this: if in a cited location you find a saying occasionally mutilated or interrupted, do not immediately accuse me of falsehood or carelessness. Garner for the most part intentionally omitted quite a few things because they contributed little or nothing to resolving the ambiguity of the expression under discussion. Add also that more than once he altered the order of Gregory’s discourse, taking first what was later and later what was earlier. Whenever this occurs, a marginal note will warn you.

In marking the verses of biblical chapters, I followed the Louvain edition of 1572. You may attribute the not infrequent omission of those verses to the printer, whose mind was elsewhere engaged; if you please, assign the rest to him and to me alike. For I profess that nothing human is alien to me. But I shall speak of the usefulness and delight of this Gregorian anthology after the second part of the preface. Before that, I earnestly beg you not, like Polycrates’ mother, to accuse me of having adorned the father’s labour with a title too distinguished, because I called his work highly necessary for students of heavenly volumes and ecclesiastical persons. This is not my judgment but that of Sixtus of Siena, whose discernment was otherwise exceedingly keen. Farewell; and draw deeply from this treasure of sacred resources, for the greater glory, praise, and honour of the Lord God of knowledge, as the prophetess Anna sings in 1 Samuel 2.

[Col. 0013]

## Commendation of the Excellence and Usefulness of This Work

From Book IV of Sixtus of Siena’s *Sacred Library*.

Garner—for that is how he is styled—subprior of the Victorine monastery near Paris, a man renowned for holiness of life and devout learning, collected and arranged in a most fitting order sixteen books drawn from all the writings of Pope Saint Gregory, concerning the allegorical significations of names and of all matters contained in Holy Scripture. He entitled them *Explanations of the Bible*. It is certainly a work worthy to be welcomed with open arms by students of divine Scripture. It begins: “God sometimes in Holy Scripture.” He flourished under Rupert, Bavarian king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1400.

Thus far Sixtus. The pursuit of truth has compelled me to delete the following matters from his testimony. First, he calls Garner a Parisian, although in the first edition he noticed nothing that would establish this, or give confidence or occasion for conjecture, unless perhaps it was because Garner is called subprior of Saint-Victor in Paris. Yet how feeble such a conjecture is may be inferred, to pass over the rest, from this alone: Saint Bernard would be a native of Clairvaux because he governed the monastery of Clairvaux.

I have removed the title *Explanations of the Bible*, replacing it with the title borne by Garner’s autograph manuscript.

He wrote that Garner flourished in 1400 as a conjecture, not as an assertion, evidently because he saw that the volume had been published in 1518—and indeed through another’s vigilance. My calculation, however, exceeds his by two hundred and some years. For in the uninterrupted register of our canons, beginning with 1300 and extending to our own time, no one of this name and rank occurs. In the third century of his *Writers of England*, Bale lists Nigel Wireker, monk and precentor of the Church of Canterbury, as flourishing in the year of Christ 1200; he states that Wireker drew from Garner’s garden in Book I of the *Flowers*, beginning with the words: “The sublimity of the heavenly powers.” This passage is to be found in Book I, chapter 3, of our Garner’s *Gregorian Work*.

Our canon Absalon—for Arnold Wion, in the *Lignum Vitae*, p. 883, wrongly mixed him in among the Benedictines, as we shall set forth more fully elsewhere if the Lord wills—eventually became abbot of the canons of Sprenckirsbach in the diocese of Trier. A contemporary of Wireker, he produced an alphabetically arranged *Breviary* of this same Garner, which survives in manuscript in our library. Since, then, those two writers left an epitome of Garner to posterity four hundred years later, it is evident that he brought this work of his into public view at the dawn of the eleventh century.

[Col. 0013]

## Preface by Brother John Picard

[Col. 0013A] I do not know whether any of the holy Fathers has been translated, abridged, and excerpted by as many writers as Pope Saint Gregory. The chief among his translators was Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, who, while Gregory was still alive, gave Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule* to Greek ears. For this reason, in Book X of the *Register*, Letter 22, Gregory complains modestly in writing to John, subdeacon of Ravenna:

> “Because Anatolius the deacon, of most beloved memory, gave the book of the *Pastoral Rule* to the Roman emperor when he requested and ordered it, I received this with distress. My most holy brother and fellow bishop Anastasius of Antioch translated it into Greek. And, as has been written to me, it pleased him greatly; but it displeased me greatly, that those who possess better things should occupy themselves with trifles.”

Around the year 870 of human redemption, Alfred, king of the West Saxons, himself both upright and learned, translated the same *Pastoral Rule* into English. As he himself testifies in the prologue—which you will see at the end of the *Life* written by Asser, bishop of Sherborne—he rendered it sometimes word for word, but sometimes sense for sense:

> “As I had learned from Plegmund my archbishop and Asser my bishop, and also from Grimbald and John, my priests. After I had learned the book from them so that I fully understood how I might attain its meaning, I translated it into English. I sent one copy to every episcopal see in my kingdom, and with every book a golden stylus worth fifty mancuses. And I command in God’s name that no one remove the stylus from the books, nor the book from the church, since it is uncertain how long there will be such learned bishops as, praise be to God, are now everywhere.”

Alfred’s work, gift, and decree were indeed magnificent and truly royal. One could then rightly call England blessed, for its king practised philosophy. William of Malmesbury, monk and librarian of the monastery of Malmesbury, mentions that translation nearly five hundred years ago in Book IV, chapter 4, near the end, of *The Deeds of the Kings of England*.

Some three hundred years ago, more or less, our France began to hear the same work speaking French. Our library preserves a manuscript copy of that translation, but the translator’s name is lacking.

[Col. 0015B] Let us turn to the *Dialogues*, rendered into the same number of different languages. For Pope Zacharias gave them to the Greeks to read 140 years after Gregory’s death, as John the Deacon, Book IV of Gregory’s *Life*, chapter 75; Odo of Cluny, flourishing in the year of Christ 920, in his sermon on Saint Benedict; and Sigebert, in the year 742 of his *Chronicle*, attest.

That they were made English by Werferth, bishop of Worcester, during Alfred’s reign was reported by Asser of Sherborne, priest of Alfred himself; Florence of Worcester; and Ingulf, abbot of Crowland, in their chronicles; by William of Malmesbury cited above; by Roger of Hoveden in the earlier part of the *English Annals*; and by Matthew Parker in *Antiquities of the British Church*. Bale alone, a writer of our own age, ascribes them to Alfred in century 2 of his *Catalogue of British Writers*. Two manuscript codices, written with a pen and available to all who inspect our library, attest that they were translated into French, together with forty of the same Gregory’s Gospel homilies.

[Col. 0015C] We judged it worth noting these matters, especially those concerning Gregory’s *Dialogues*, because our Garner drew from them certain passages which would otherwise be open to doubt unless we confirmed their venerable authority and refuted the fabricated conjectures of certain persons. Some doubt the author; others, the events narrated by the author.

Huldrych Coccius, in the dedicatory epistle of his edition of Gregory, published at Basel in 1511, writes in doubt with these words and arguments:

> “Concerning the *Dialogues*, in which he recounts miracles of the Fathers of Italy, I scarcely know what to pronounce, except that I doubt they are Gregory’s; so greatly do they differ from his other writings in character, sequence, gravity of style, and workmanship.”

If the doubt is the offspring of simple ignorance, surely everyone will tolerate it. But if it is feigned hesitation, surely everyone will condemn it. That Huldrych laboured under the latter is evident from the index composed by him, in which he notes that Gregory had the Deacon Peter as his companion. Thus Gregory writes [Col. 0015D] in the prologue to his *Dialogues*:

> “While I sat greatly afflicted and silent for a long time, my most beloved son Peter the deacon was present, one who has been bound to me in close friendship from the first flower of youth and has been my companion in investigating the sacred word.”

Moreover, in the same index he teaches the reader that Gregory delighted greatly in conversing with old men. But in Book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 10, Gregory confesses:

> “For a poor old man was brought to me; and, since conversation with old men has always been pleasing to me, I diligently asked him where he was from.”

Therefore, if Huldrych regarded Gregory’s *Dialogues* as suspect, why did he select these matters from them and gather them into his index? They are small matters, you say. I admit it, and I would think little of them if the most abundant springs of error had not sometimes arisen even from small things. But leaving these aside, I descend to graver matters.

In that same dedicatory epistle he testifies that he read the entire work of Saint Gregory in such a way as to present the reader with a kind of synopsis of Gregory’s teaching. If, then, he read it, where were [Col. 0016A] his eyes when the following testimonies occurred in the *Dialogues*, crying aloud to him that the *Dialogues* belonged to a pope of Rome?

In Book I, chapter 8, there occurs:

> “At the same time the venerable man Anastasius—whom I mentioned above—was notary of the holy Roman Church, which, by God’s ordering, I serve.”

Book III, chapter 3:

> “Agapitus, pontiff of this Roman Church, which, by God’s dispensation, I serve, [sent] to Justinian,” etc.

Again, chapter 8:

> “Constantius was bishop of the city of Aquino; he died recently in the time of my predecessor, Pope John of blessed memory.”

Book IV, chapter 30:

> “Julian, second defender of this Roman Church, which, by God’s ordering, I serve,” etc.

Again, chapter 40:

> “Paschasius, deacon of this Apostolic See,” etc.

Finally, from these matters too it is apparent even to Tiresias that some Roman pope composed the *Thaumatographoi* (Θαυματογράφους), the “writers of miracles,” or *Dialogues*. That Gregory is their genuine author is no less clearly evident from Book II, chapter 31, where he says that Leander, bishop of Seville, had long been joined to him in close friendship. In chapter 32 of the same book he adds:

> “At that same time”—that is, in the days of Emperor Justinian, as he indicates at the beginning of the chapter—“when I was sent to the emperor in order to discharge the Church’s official business.”

And again, in chapter 36:

> “While, by the command of my pope, I was serving the Church’s business in the palace of the city of Constantinople.”

Gregory recalls both the embassy and the friendship he had with Leander, speaking thus in the book on Job:

> “Long ago, most blessed brother, I came to know you in the city of Constantinople, when the affairs of the Apostolic See bound me there, and the embassy imposed upon you by the Visigothic king for matters of faith had brought you thither,” etc.

If anyone asserts that, at that time and under that emperor and bishop, someone other than Saint Gregory undertook an embassy at Constantinople in the name of the Roman Church, he will necessarily invent another person out of his own head.

But lest anyone more zealous for truth should desire fuller testimony, I shall contend once more with Huldrych on the basis of two sealed documents. The first is drawn from nearly the final words of his own epistle:

> “The forty homilies on the Gospels, read to the people on Sundays, contain observations not only on the letter, but also on the best things, together with serious and devout exhortations,” etc.

Since, therefore, he placed Gregory’s homilies beyond all doubt, he at the same time exempted and vindicated the *Dialogues*. For Gregory affirms that he related in his public homilies to the people the histories recounted in Book IV, chapters 14, 15, 16, 19, 27, and 37. He repeats in Homily 15 the first story, narrated in chapter 14, namely that of the paralysed servant; the second, concerning Romula and Redempta in chapter 15, in Homily 40; the third, concerning his aunt Tarsilla in chapter 16, more fully in Homily 38; and the fourth, concerning Abbot Stephen in chapter 19, at greater length in Homily 35. He recounts the fifth, concerning Count Theophanius in chapter 27, more fully in Homily 36; and that of the boy Theodore in chapter 37, in Homilies 19 and 38. It is precisely the same story: when he recounted it in Homily 19, he added that Theodore had been recalled from the threshold of death, not from the pains of illness. But in Homily [Col. 0016D] 38 he says that Theodore died two years earlier after terrible and prolonged sufferings of illness.

I shall add a seventh and eighth story. Though Gregory does not say that he recounted them in his homilies, the same words, persons, places, and other clear features of the narrative plainly show them to be the work of the same writer. The seventh, therefore, concerns Chrysaorius, otherwise Chrysorius—for the name is written in both ways—in chapter 38, and is repeated in Homily 12. The eighth and last concerns Cassius of Narnia: briefly in chapter 56, but described at greatest length in Homily 37.

The second sealed document against Huldrych is taken from letters which he attributes to Gregory. For in Letter 50 of Book II, Gregory directs Maximinianus of Syracuse, among other things:

> “My brothers who live with me are in every way urging me to write briefly something concerning miracles of the Fathers which we have heard were performed in Italy. For this I greatly need the assistance of your charity: please indicate briefly to me those things which come to your memory and which you have happened to learn. For I remember that you told me certain things concerning Lord Nonnosus, abbot near Lord Anastasius of Pentuma, which I have forgotten. Therefore I ask that you set this down, together with anything else of this kind, in your letters and send it to me swiftly.”

By this writing Gregory openly says that he is bringing forth the *Dialogues*, which Huldrych, treating them as illegitimate, rejects after they have been born. Maximinianus of Syracuse, through his replies concerning Nonnosus, Anastasius, and the others, inserted in Book I, chapters 7 and 8; Book III, chapter 36; and Book IV, chapter 32, exposes Huldrych’s hidden malice—or his grossest ignorance.

Finally, let Paterius, disciple of Saint Gregory, and Faustus, pupil of Saint Benedict and an exact contemporary of Gregory, award the prize to this contest. For Paterius, at Gregory’s own urging, fashioned a systematic exposition of Holy Scripture, assembled as a patchwork from excerpts of Gregory’s writings. In it, as I have noticed in passing, he cites Gregory’s *Dialogues*: namely, at 17; in Matthew, 70; in Luke, 33; in John, 12; and in 1 Corinthians. Faustus, moreover, does so in the *Life of Saint Maurus*.

Away with you, therefore, Huldrich: recast your reckoning; and let doubters—or rather, scoffers—take your place as you withdraw. For they treat the miracles recorded in Gregory’s *Dialogues* as so many Sicilian tales and little fables. If you object to the man’s unimpaired character, they retort that he had excessive simplicity and credulity. A fine answer—as though he had not most thoroughly learned the entire discipline of Christian ethics, so that the difference between dove-like simplicity and Arcadian stupidity escaped him. Let them here read what Gregory answered when the Emperor Maurice reproached him with this, drawn from Book IV, Epistle 31:

> In the most serene commands of their lordships, their Piety, while endeavouring to reprove me on certain points, did not spare me even while sparing me. For in them, by the term “urban simplicity,” he calls me foolish. Yet in Sacred Scripture, when simplicity is used in a good sense, it is often joined with prudence or uprightness. [Col. 0017C] Thus it is written also of blessed Job: “There was a man simple and upright”; and the blessed Apostle Paul exhorts us, saying: “Be simple in evil and prudent in good.” And Truth Himself admonishes us, saying: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves,” judging it very useless if prudence be lacking to simplicity, or simplicity to prudence.

How prudent he was, and how richly endowed with prudent simplicity, no one can fail to see. At least, whatever one may require of an approved and trustworthy historian is found in him: namely, the most diligent zeal for truth and a mind freed from every bias, even a particular one. For, as concerns the diligence and trustworthiness of history, nothing can be narrated more diligently or faithfully than what happened in our own province, in our own age, or before our own eyes or those of others. How greatly these small points support Gregory’s *Dialogues* is shown especially by the second book, which contains nothing except what four disciples of Benedict [Col. 0017D] reported. In the other three books you read only of things done either at Rome or in Gregory’s monastery; and if a few external matters are intermingled, they were related by eyewitnesses, worth more than not merely ten—as the comic poet has it—but a thousand hearers.

What, given such fidelity and painstaking, could the most fastidious reader demand that were more certain, more exact, or more carefully composed? Therefore, if henceforth he is to weigh more fairly everything inserted in these *Dialogues*, let him beware of the snare indicated by the author in Book II on Job, when expounding these words: “Do you accept his person, and for God,” etc. “Fools,” he says, “when they observe the deeds of prudent men, see them all as blameworthy; and, forgetful of their own ignorance and weakness, they judge others all the more attentively the more deeply they are ignorant of themselves.”

Gregory speaks admirably indeed. For just as the wicked contemplate or perpetrate nothing which is not only blameworthy but also deserving of public punishment, so they cannot read anything done by holy men, however upright, sound, and undefiled, without fastening upon it their native fault; and the more their impious [Col. 0018A] life differs from such conduct, the more does their judgment differ. Therefore, since they admire and understand earthly things alone, they come to despise with proud minds whatever displays divine power and looks toward heaven.

Would that the four books on the four *Dialogues* of Gregory, written by Ælfric (also called Aluricius), Archbishop of Canterbury, about the eight-hundredth and nine-hundredth year of human restoration, had reached us. From them we should draw abundant material for utterly draining the foolish babblings of Gregory’s scourgers. Yet here we must refrain, lest in a preface we be accused not of prefacing but of speaking at length outright. A controversy of this kind—holy and weighty as it is—is by no means to be debated in so light a skirmish; it deserves a harsher and more vigorous contest. Perhaps God, best and greatest, will someday grant that what I have had occasion here to meditate and foresee may be performed manfully in earnest battle. Therefore, guarding against the most troublesome weariness of the kindly reader, I shall join one thing and another and bring the work to its close.

Our forefathers [Col. 0018B] held these *Dialogues* in such high esteem that from them they took singular incentives to seek and acquire holiness, and the soundest supports for sustaining faith. St. Udalric, bishop of Augsburg in Germany, distinguished by innocence of life, learning, and noble birth, hungered for the handling of these volumes—more than Ambrosian food or nectar—so greatly that, as Berno of Reichenau says in chapter 21 of his *Life*, he often remained fasting while his guests ate and drank. For his food was either the sweet delight of the Psalms or continual attendance upon sacred readings; among these he especially delighted to hear, from the four books of St. Gregory, how many persons, when removed from their bodies, were caught away in spirit.

I do not repeat matters drawn from the same books by Haymo of Halberstadt, who flourished in the year 830, and cited in Book III, chapters 9 and 10, of *On the Variety of Books*. The Council of Mainz—not, indeed, held under Charlemagne in the year of Christ 813, nor under the Emperor Arnulf in 888—instructed by the salutary [Col. 0018C] reading of Gregory’s *Dialogues*, gave this warning in chapter 5 concerning the foulness and gravity of incest committed with one’s own daughter:

> How detestable and execrable a crime it is for any Christian to violate his own little daughter is attested by St. Gregory, pope, in his *Dialogues*, where he recounts that a certain man defiled his own daughter. Since he neglected to do penance, he was suddenly seized by a wretched disease and expired; and after he was buried, an invisible fire consumed not only his body but also the entire tomb.

Gregory, however, narrates the story there summarized in full in *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 32. Moreover, in an ancient penitential entitled *Corrector and Physician*, I found the preceding testimony of the Council of Mainz together with another, whose summary was this: “That penitence can blot out sins even if one repents at the final breath of life.” Therefore either these two canons are lacking from the aforesaid councils of Mainz, or certainly the one I have produced is necessarily different—or rather, intermediate.

There was also canon 17 of the Council of Tribur, held in the year 895, had not the polished hand of Cardinal Baronius corrupted the unskilled pen. In his notes on the tenth day before the Kalends of January in the Roman Martyrology, Baronius brings forward so many grave and hoary authorities that it is evident Melchior Canus’s verdict on Gregory’s scourgers is not merely childish, but downright infantile.

To attack the chief adversaries of the Catholic religion, Jonas, bishop of Orléans, drew weapons from this source as from a most fully furnished arsenal, answering the calumnies of Claudius of Turin, the iconoclast, and adducing the story of the Jew who, though an unbeliever, nevertheless followed the Christians’ example and armed himself against the horrible nocturnal apparitions of demons with the impenetrable breastplate of the cross. Lanfranc of Canterbury, Alger of Cluny, and Guitmund of Aversa, in order to choke the blasphemous and gaping jaws of the barking Berengar, thrust into them a mouthful made up of words from Gregory’s *Dialogues*: the first in his book *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, the second, Guitmund, likewise in Book III of *On the Sacrament of the Altar*. The third, Alger, in Book I, chapter 12, and Book II, chapter 1, of *On the Sacrament*, cites authorities [Col. 0019A] from *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 59.

Many things might usefully be added on this subject, were it not that useful matters, when they abound, generally become unprofitable, and the plan of my work resisted it. Let us therefore gird ourselves with Spartan brevity.

Odo, first abbot of Cluny, enclosed the substance of Gregory’s thirty-five books on Job within the limits of a single volume, about the year 920, as Trithemius in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers and Sixtus of Siena in Book IV of the *Sacred Library* have reported.

Rupert, abbot of Deutz, summarized the same *Morals on Job* in ten books in the year 1114, as he himself testifies in the dedicatory epistle to his work *On the Divine Offices*, saying: “A little commentary on Job in ten books, abridged from the abundance of the thoughts and sayings of blessed Gregory,” etc. Adalber, English by nation, a professed monk of the monastery of Spalding of the Cluniac congregation (according to Bale, *Centuries of British Writers*, century 2), and a deacon by office, composed [Col. 0019B] four books from the more splendid maxims of the *Morals*, preserving in them, however, the continuous numbering; and he called it the *Mirror*, as he himself testifies in the prefatory epistle addressed to the priest Hairmann:

> Meanwhile, to give the reader breathing-space, I decided to divide this little work into four books. And since the life of the human race is there depicted in manifold variety, I was pleased to call it the *MIRROR*.

This writer flourished about the year 1160. A copy of that work rests on the shelves of our library.

Alulf of Tournai, a Benedictine monk, arranged *Collections for the Elucidation of the Entire New Testament* from the writings of St. Gregory; I have seen them printed at Paris in 1515, in quarto. He flourished in the year 1200.

Not long after Alulf, a certain anonymous writer extracted thirty-five little books from the full thirty-five books on Job, at the request of some venerable Father, whom he addresses in this preface:

> You, venerable and most beloved Father, who by reason of your dignity and excellence in holiness ought rather to have commanded than requested, asked [Col. 0019C] that, at the prompting of your charity, I should consider gathering into one work certain authorities from the Bible, uttered by the holy Fathers in various places, for the edification of the inward man, etc.

He called this nocturnal study the *Storehouse of Both Men*, and rightly so by analogy. For, as he writes there, just as a storehouse has prepared in it the things necessary for the body, so in this codex, with careful thought, are prepared whatever things are necessary not only for the outward man in respect of morals, but also for the inward man in respect of virtues. I have placed him after Alulf because he mentions Alulf in his prologue, and the antiquity of the manuscript in our possession plainly shows that he was near Alulf in time.

I shall append another anonymous author to this anonymous one. The company of men sharing a name is usually not unwelcome; and because my discourse has so declined that I mingle jest with serious matters, I shall copy what Robert of Mont-Saint-Michel, continuator of Sigebert, wrote under the year 1173:

> And, that the multitude of those present may appear clearly—he speaks of the first gathering of the court and the splendid banquet to which Henry II, king of England, had summoned all the nobles of his Norman and British dominions—when William of Saint-Jean, administrator of Normandy, and William son of Hamo, seneschal of Brittany, were eating in a certain chamber, they prohibited any knight from eating unless he was called William. After the others had been expelled from the chamber, one hundred and ten knights remained, all called William, besides many others of the same name who ate in the hall with the king.

Our later anonymous author likewise compressed the very extensive commentary of Gregory’s *Morals* into thirty very short books. From our parchment manuscript I have excerpted this opening: “In Sidon is figured the steadfastness of those set under the Law; in the sea, the life of the Gentiles.”

Simon, monk of Affligem—whose monastery at Affligem, a solitude in the district of Brabant [Col. 0020A] bordering Flanders, began in 1083, according to Meyer in his *Chronicle of Flanders*—collected the same Gregorian ethical teaching into ten books three hundred years ago. Yet from such abridgments the reader gains only this advantage of brevity: that he may run through a rather lengthy work in shorter compass and without weariness; but, what I judge more harmful, he loses an ordered treatment of a definite subject, so that it does not satisfy the hunger of the soul that seeks nourishment.

At last, let us smell the ever-green and fragrant flowers of the anthologists, and refresh our failing eyes with their delightful colours.

Paterius, notary of the Holy Roman Church and disciple of Gregory, concerning whom Bede says—for I have found no earlier witness—in the preface to Book VII on the *Song of Songs*: “I have heard that Paterius, disciple of blessed Pope Gregory, gathered from the whole of Holy Scripture whatever Gregory had explained in parts throughout his works and reduced it into a single volume.” If we consult the very extensive indexes of passages of Holy Scripture explained here and there and placed at the end of Gregory’s works, a considerable forest remains which supplies exceedingly abundant material from the other books of the Old Testament: Ecclesiastes, Ecclesiasticus, Wisdom, the Prophets, and the Maccabees. Moreover, in the New Testament the Second and Third Epistles of John and the Epistle of Jude are untouched. Therefore I should judge that Bede’s statement must be understood synecdochically.

Hederic the Italian, a monk of the monastery of St. Gregory the Pope, about the year 840 compiled from the writings of blessed Gregory on Job the first book of *Sentences*, as Arnold Wion writes in Book II, chapter 68, of the *Tree of Life*. Vasaeus reports in his *Chronicle* that St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, extracted three books of *Sentences* from the *Morals*.

Tajus—for that is the form used by the distinguished scholar, not Taio or Tagio, as very many printers have it—surnamed Samuel, bishop of Caesaraugusta, left to posterity five books of selected *Sentences* from the writings of St. Gregory, with a few sayings of St. Augustine intermingled. He presented them to Quiricus, bishop [Col. 0020C] of Toledo, who had requested them, as is evident from this opening period of the dedicatory epistle:

> Mindful of your most kindly request and of my most devoted promise, I have preferred to send to your holiness the text of this little book, marked beforehand with established titles of the sayings.

When he produced this work, I judged it not irrelevant to disclose in his own words, especially since this volume of notable character occupies the shelves of very few people. Tajus therefore says to Quiricus in the preceding epistle:

> Your Blessedness knows well that time when the crooked serpent, with poisonous mouth, scattered the virulent tares of his seed in the minds of certain persons and, by deceitful deception, turned aside from the path of the right way the steps of minds gone astray. At that time a certain pestilent man of mad mind, assuming tyranny, together with perverse supporters of his crime, attacked the orthodox prince Recceswinth, the great worshipper of God; under the pretext of fraudulent plots he strove with proud effort to overthrow the Christian [Col. 0020D] country. Because of this crime, the fierce people of the Vascones, driven from the Pyrenean mountains, ravaged and devastated the land of Iberia in various ways. Alas, alas! The greatness of the calamity interrupts the effort of speech. Yet at last I must come to what speech fears. Innocent blood is shed; some are wounded with claws, others with missiles, very many with various darts; an innumerable multitude of captives is carried away; immense spoils are taken; baleful war is brought against the temples of God; the sacred altars are destroyed; many in clerical office are cut down with swords; and the unburied bodies of many slain are exposed to dogs and birds, etc.

Under this mournful disaster Tajus therefore collected the five books of *Sentences* to lessen grief, as he indicates a little later; and this was about the year 652. This is the Tajus who, in the final year of Chindaswinth, king of Spain, and in the year of Christ 649, went to Rome to seek Gregory’s *Morals* [Col. 0021A] and, after finding them at last by divine aid, brought them back to Spain. This is evident both from the remarkable narrative prefixed to the works of St. Gregory and from the end of the Seventh Council of Toledo. Since that narrative expressly says that Tajus was a devoted student of Augustine as well as Gregory, he did not without reason compose his collections from the sayings of both. I read this opening in them: “God alone is unchangeable in Himself,” etc.

The Venerable Bede, who died in 732, after illuminating the *Song of Songs* with six books and the light of his own genius, compiled Books VII and VIII—according to Trithemius’s reckoning, for the printed copies have only one—from the pithy sayings of Gregory. John of Stuckampton, Bede’s fellow countryman and a man of Winchester, left to posterity sayings drawn from Gregory’s ethical works, arranged in alphabetical order, numbered, and woven into one book. The English centuriator gives their opening as: “Abstinence. Only in unlawful things…” When the Froben printers issued Gregory in 1551, the library of St. Leonard offered six books composed of Gregorian moral sayings; because they were Gregory’s very words, Huldrich Coccius says that he did not omit them without reason. To be sure, that was why they ought to have been omitted. Hanging gardens, woods, parks, thickets, rose gardens, willow groves, and other pleasant places would likewise lack their value because they consist of precisely the same things, merely brought from elsewhere. Yet posterity should repay even the smallest gratitude in thought to learned and highly praiseworthy ancient florilegists, because they collected the selected sayings of learned men verbatim, distributed them among various classes, and left them to us. So powerful indeed is the genius of order that it produces an elegant symmetry even from things lacking symmetry.

Last among the anthologists is Hubert Sculteputaeus, a regular canon of the church called Bethlehem near the walls of Louvain. From all [Col. 0021C] Gregory’s gardens he selected, wove together, and arranged alphabetically a sweet-smelling bouquet of maxims, while, having been received within Louvain in order to escape the raging frenzy of heretics devastating every part of Belgium, he was compelled to suspend the work he had begun *On the True Knowledge of Divine and Human Nature*. These flowers were published with Gregory himself when printed at Paris at the expense of Nivellius.

How far our Garner surpasses all abridgers and anthologists is especially clear from this: the epitomes of great works are composed with such character and flavour that what pleases your palate displeases mine, and scarcely any abridgment can be produced free from some loss.

Moreover, as we have shown, Gregory’s abridgers touched only one of his works; Garner, all of them. But let us grant that they went through everything: their gleanings are nevertheless less welcome because they did not arrange them in suitable and fitting [Col. 0021D] places, but piled them up without any order—order, which one may deservedly call the star of memory and sun of the sciences—like stones or clods of earth. And certainly, even though they may have arranged their material systematically, no one will deny [Col. 0022A] that Garner also carried off from them this chief excellence: he directed both his study and his style toward attaining a clearer light and easier understanding of the divine Scriptures. The more obscure these divine writings are, the more distinguished is the labour expended in dispelling their darkness.

Garner therefore arranged his material so attractively that one would swear a second mind had been added to readers. Intending to explain the mystical significations of almost all things contained in the Bible, he thought it most suitable to begin with their Creator, God best and greatest; to Him he adds the heavenly spirits, then the fabric of heaven and each lamp of the moving spheres; then the manifold alterations of the air, more infinitely changeable than the fabulous Proteus, Prometheus, Vertumnus, or Empusa. Since the index of headings placed before the work presents these things and the rest to eager readers, I pass them over.

[Col. 0022B] Once, while I was conversing with a certain eminent theologian about publishing this work and had explained its summary, he replied that John Benedict, a most distinguished Parisian theologian, had previously done the task more laboriously and more extensively, since in his biblical concordances he had marked not only difficult matters and names but also words. I answered him: “I frankly admit that John Benedict’s labours are most perfect in ingenuity and elaborated with much industry. Yet not everyone can be assisted more quickly by them, since one person has a duller intellect and slower judgment than another, and therefore conceives more slowly and laboriously and expresses what he has conceived more painstakingly. Indeed, it often happens that someone understands correctly but cannot express what he understands elegantly, readily, and copiously. I need not dwell on this. A person may form very many excellent things in rapid thought; nevertheless, unless he is shameless, no one will say that these are to be valued as highly as the heavenly utterances of St. Gregory—or rather, the sayings of the Holy Spirit delivered through Gregory’s mouth.”

For Peter, Gregory’s deacon and interlocutor in the *Dialogues*, left testimony, according to John the Deacon, Book IV of his *Life* of Gregory, chapter 69, that he had frequently seen the Holy Spirit above the head of St. Gregory while he was discoursing. “Hence,” says the same John in the same chapter, “the Holy Spirit is customarily depicted in the form of a dove above Gregory’s head while he is writing.” Finally, to answer my theologian in one word: I do not deny that everyone can read mystical interpretations, but not everyone can convey them as readily, clearly, and copiously as our Garner does from Gregory’s mouth. It is indeed plain that, if preachers wish to linger a little in unfolding the mysteries of a single word, they will have abundant material to say in one sermon for the fruitful instruction of their hearers.

Finally, although we grant some place to anthologists, we do not grant them superiority over Garner. For although he yields to some in antiquity, he is nonetheless not surpassed in labour and industry, since richer fruits can be gathered from him and a more orderly discipline learned.

[Col. 0023]

## The Gregorian Work of the Reverend Father Garner, Regular Canon of Saint Victor at Paris

### Book I

### Chapter I. On God

[Col. 0023A]

[Note: [Col. 0023C] From Homily 8 on Ezekiel I.]

God in Sacred Scripture is sometimes called God by designation and sometimes essentially. He is called so by designation, as it is written: “Behold, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. VII.1). And as Moses says: “If anyone has done this or that, bring him to the gods” (Exod. XXII.8), that is, to the priests. Again he says: “You shall not speak evil of the gods” (ibid., 28), that is, of the priests. And as the Psalmist says: “God stood in the assembly of gods; but in the midst He judges gods” (Ps. LXXXI.1). But God is called essentially, as He says to Moses: “I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. III.6).

Hence the Apostle Paul, wishing to distinguish the appellative name “God” [Col. 0023B] from the essential one, spoke concerning our Redeemer, saying: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. IX.5). He who is called God by designation is God among all things; but He who is called God essentially is God above all things. For every elect person, or one set forth as pre-eminent in an example of righteousness, can be called a god, but among all things, because he is God by designation; whereas Christ is God above all things because He is God by nature.

### Chapter II. On Angels

[Note: [Col. 0024C] Homily 34 on the Gospels.]

We learn from the testimony of Sacred Scripture that there are nine orders of angels: namely angels, archangels, [Col. 0023C] virtues, powers, principalities, dominions, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim. Almost every page of Sacred Scripture testifies that there are angels and archangels. The books of the prophets also frequently speak, as is well known, of cherubim and seraphim. The Apostle Paul likewise enumerates four names of orders in his Epistle to the Ephesians, saying: “Above every principality, power, virtue, and dominion” (Eph. I.21). Writing again to the Colossians, he says: “Whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers” (Col. I.16).

He had already described dominions, principalities, and powers while speaking to the Ephesians; but when he was about to mention these also to the Colossians, he prefaced them with thrones, of which he had not yet spoken to the Ephesians. Thus, when thrones are added to the four mentioned in the Epistle to the Ephesians—principalities, powers, virtues, and dominions—there are five orders expressly named. When angels and archangels, cherubim and seraphim, are added to these, there are beyond doubt nine orders of angels.

Thus the prophet says to the angel who was first created: “Thou art the seal of likeness, full of wisdom, perfect in beauty; thou wast in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. XXVIII.12). Here it must be noted that he is called not “made in the likeness of God,” but “the seal of likeness,” so that, the subtler his nature, the more fully the image of God may be represented in him by resemblance. Immediately afterward the passage adds: “Every precious stone was thy covering: sardius, topaz, and jasper, chrysolite, onyx, and beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald” (ibid., 13). Behold, it names nine stones, which certainly are the nine orders of angels. That first angel was adorned and covered with these orders because, being placed above all the hosts of angels, he was brighter by comparison with them.

It must also be known [Col. 0024B] that the word “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature. For in Greek, *angeloi* means “messengers,” and *archangeloi*, “chief messengers.” Those holy spirits of the heavenly homeland are always spirits indeed, but they cannot always be called angels, because they are angels only when something is announced through them. Hence the Psalmist also says: “He makes His angels spirits” (Ps. CIII.4)—as though he plainly said: “He who always has them as spirits also makes them angels when He wills.” Those who announce lesser things are called angels; those who announce the greatest things are called archangels. Thus it was not just any angel but the archangel Gabriel who was sent to the Virgin Mary (Luke I.26). It was fitting that the highest angel should come for that ministry, because he announced the highest of all things.

They are also designated by individual names, so that their names may indicate what power they possess in their activity. For in that holy city, which perfect knowledge derived from the vision of almighty God fills, they do not receive proper names because their persons could not be known without names. Rather, when they come to minister something to us, they also take among us a name from their ministries. Michael means “Who is like God?” Gabriel, “Strength of God”; Raphael, “Medicine of God.”

Whenever an act of miraculous power is performed, Michael is said to be sent, so that both the deed and the name may make known that no one can do what God is able to do. Hence that ancient enemy, who through pride desired to be like God, saying: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne; I will sit upon the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV.13)—when at the end of the world he is left to his own power and is to be destroyed by final punishment, he is said to be about to fight against the archangel Michael, as John says: “There was a battle with Michael the archangel” (Apoc. XII.7). Thus he who proudly exalted himself to God’s likeness may learn, when slain by Michael, that no one rises to God’s likeness through pride.

Gabriel, whose name means “Strength of God,” is likewise sent to Mary. He came to announce Him who deigned to appear humble in order to overthrow [Col. 0025C] the powers of the air. Of Him the Psalmist says: “Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter in. Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII.7–8). And again: “The Lord of hosts, He is the King of glory” (ibid., 10). Therefore He who was Lord of hosts and mighty in battle, coming to overthrow the powers, was to be announced through the “Strength of God.”

Raphael also, as we have said, is interpreted “Medicine of God.” When he touched Tobit’s eyes, as though in the exercise of a healing office, he wiped away the darkness of his blindness (Tob. XII.13). Therefore, he who was sent to heal was fittingly called the Medicine of God.

The spirits through whom signs and miracles are more frequently wrought are called Virtues. Those are called Powers who have received in their order a greater power than the rest, so that hostile virtues are subject to their dominion and are restrained by their authority, lest they prevail to tempt human hearts as much as they wish. Those are called Principalities who preside even over the good spirits of angels and, directing what must be done while others are subject to them, take precedence in the accomplishment of divine ministries. Those are called Dominions who transcend even the powers of principalities by their lofty distinction. For to rule is to be first among the rest; to dominate is to possess also those who are subject.

Therefore those hosts of angels which excel in wondrous power are called Dominions, because the rest are subject to them in obedience. Thrones are likewise the hosts upon which almighty God always sits in order to exercise judgment. Since in Latin we call thrones “seats,” those are called thrones of God who are filled with such grace of divinity that the Lord sits in them and through them determines His judgments. Hence the Psalmist says: “Thou sittest upon the throne, Thou who judgest righteousness” (Ps. IX.7, 5).

Cherubim means “fullness of knowledge.” Those loftier hosts are called Cherubim because they are filled with more perfect knowledge in proportion as they contemplate the brightness of God more closely; according to the capacity of the creature, they know all things more fully as by the merit of their rank they draw nearer to the vision of their Creator. The hosts of holy spirits called Seraphim [Col. 0026B] burn with incomparable love because of their singular nearness to their Creator. For *seraphim* means “the burning ones” or “those who set aflame.” Since they are so joined to God that no other spirits stand between them and God, they burn the more intensely because they see Him more closely. Their flame, certainly, is love: the more subtly they behold the brightness of His divinity, the more strongly they blaze with love for Him.

But since that heavenly city consists of angels and human beings, and we believe that the human race will ascend there in a number equal to the number of elect angels who remained there, as it is written: “He set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” [Note: [Col. 0025] The Plantin edition reads *constituit* (“he established”) for *statuit* (“he set”), although the Greek word seems to oppose this.] (Deut. XXVI.8, according to the Septuagint), and since, I say, a multitude of human beings equal to the multitude of angels remaining is believed to be destined to ascend there, it remains that those human beings also who return to the heavenly homeland should, in returning, imitate something of those angelic hosts.

For distinct ways of life correspond to the ranks of the several hosts, and by likeness of life men are assigned to their lot. For there are many who grasp little things, yet do not cease devoutly to proclaim even these small things to their brethren. Such persons therefore run in the number of the angels. And there are some who, refreshed by the gift of divine bounty, are able both to grasp and to proclaim the highest secrets of heaven. To what rank, then, are these assigned, if not to the number of archangels? And there are others who perform wonders and work signs mightily. To what lot and number do these run, if not that of the heavenly Virtues? And there are some who even drive malignant spirits from possessed bodies, casting them out by the force of prayer through the power they have received. To what, then, do these receive their merit’s portion, if not among the number of the heavenly Powers? And there are some who, having received virtues, surpass the merits of elect persons; and, being better even than the good, take precedence over their elect brethren. To what rank, then, have these received their lot, if not among the Principalities? And there are some who so rule over every vice and every desire within themselves that, by the very right of their purity, they are called gods among men. Hence it is said also to Moses: “Behold, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. VII.1). To what rank, then, do these run, if not among the Dominations? And there are some who, while governing themselves with watchful care and examining themselves with attentive purpose, ever cleaving to the fear of God, receive this as a gift of virtue: that they are able also to judge others. For divine contemplation is ever present to their minds; and the Lord, presiding in them as upon a throne, examines the deeds of others and wonderfully orders all things from His seat. What, then, are these but thrones of their Creator? And to what, if not to the number of the heavenly Seats, are they enrolled? Through them, while holy Church is governed, even the elect are often judged concerning certain weak acts of their own.

And there are some so full of the love of God and neighbour that they are rightly called Cherubim. For, as we have said, *cherubim* means “fullness of knowledge”; and, as Paul says, “We have learned that charity is the fullness of the law” (Rom. XIII.10). Therefore all who are more abundantly filled than others with love of God and neighbour have received the lot of their merits among the ranks of the Cherubim. And there are some who, kindled by the fires of heavenly contemplation, pant only for the desire of their Creator; they now desire nothing in this world, are fed by love of eternity alone, cast away all earthly things, transcend in mind all temporal things, love and burn, and rest in that very burning. By loving they burn; by speaking they kindle others; and those whom they touch by their word they immediately make burn in the love of God. What, then, should I call these but Seraphim, whose heart, transformed into fire, shines and burns? For they enlighten the eyes of minds toward things above and, by piercing them into tears, cleanse away the rust of vices. Those, therefore, who are thus inflamed with love for their Creator have received the lot of their calling only among the number of the Seraphim.

7. It must further be known that in Sacred Scripture the name “angel” sometimes denotes the Lord Jesus Christ Himself; sometimes His forerunner John; sometimes holy preachers; sometimes the rulers of holy Church; and sometimes the priests of the Church.

[Note: Col. 0027D. From Book XXIV on Job, chapter II.] For Christ is understood by “angel,” as in the book of blessed Job, when Elihu was speaking of the affliction of the human race and added: “If there shall be an angel speaking for him, one like him, to declare man’s uprightness, he will have mercy on him” (Job XXXIII.23). For who is this angel but He who is called through the prophet “the Angel of great counsel”? (Isa. IX.5, according to the Septuagint.) Since in the Greek language “to evangelize” means “to announce,” the Lord, announcing Himself, is called an Angel. And rightly it says: “If there shall be an angel speaking for him,” because, as the Apostle says, “He also intercedes for us” (Rom. VIII.26). But let us hear what He speaks for us: “one like him.”

It is the practice of medicine sometimes to cure like things by like, and sometimes contraries by contraries. For it is often accustomed to treat hot things by hot and cold by cold; but often hot by cold and cold by hot. Therefore our physician, coming down to us and finding us oppressed by such great infirmities, applied to us something like us and something contrary to us. For man came to men, but a righteous man to sinners. He agreed with us in the truth of nature, but differed from us in the power of righteousness. For sinful man could not be corrected except through God. Yet He who corrected had to be seen, so that by offering a pattern for imitation He might change the life of former wickedness; but God could not be seen by man. Therefore He was made man, that He might be seen. Thus the righteous and invisible Lord appeared as visible man, like us, so that, being seen, He might heal as one like us and as one righteous; and, while agreeing with our condition in the truth of our race, He might meet our sickness by the power of His art.

8. Therefore, since the Lord, coming in the flesh, assumed neither our guilt from sin nor our punishment from necessity—for, stained by no defilement of sin, He could not be held under the condition of our guilt—He voluntarily accepted our death when He wished, having trampled down every necessity. Thus it is rightly said that for so great a man this Angel speaks “one like him”:  for He was neither born as others were, nor died as others died, nor rose again as others rose. He was conceived not through intercourse at work, but through the Holy Spirit coming upon. In being born, moreover, He both made His mother’s womb fruitful and preserved it incorrupt. Again, all of us die unwillingly, because we are constrained by our condition to discharge the debt of punishment for our sin. But He, because He was joined to no guilt, yielded to no punishment by necessity: because He subjected our guilt by His lordship, and assumed our punishment in mercy, as He Himself says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again” (John X.18). And He had previously said: “No one shall take it from me, but I lay it down of myself” (ibid.).

Again, He did not rise again as the rest do, because our resurrection is deferred until the end of the age, whereas His was accomplished on the third day. We indeed shall rise through Him, but He by Himself. For He who was God did not, like us, need another in order that He might be raised. In this, therefore, His resurrection differs from ours: we do not rise through ourselves as He did. Because we are simply human, we need higher assistance in order to be able to rise. But He, being God, displayed with the Father and the Holy Spirit the power of that resurrection, though He alone received it in His humanity. Therefore, although the Lord was truly born, truly died, and truly rose again, He nevertheless differs from us in all things by the greatness of His power, while agreeing with us only in the truth of nature. Hence it is well said that this Angel speaks “one like him” for us. For although in all His works He transcends us by immeasurable power, yet in one respect He does not differ from us—that is, in the truth of His form. By this He speaks to the Father for us: by this He shows Himself like us. For His speaking or interceding is His showing Himself, for humankind, to be man.

9. [Note: Col. 0029D. Homily 6 on the Gospel: Matthew XI.7; Luke VII.25 and 27.] John, the Lord’s forerunner and baptist, is also spiritually denoted by “angel,” as the Lord Himself testifies when speaking to the crowds about John in the Gospel: “What went you out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. For this is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel before thy face, who shall prepare thy way before thee” (Matt. XI.7; Luke VII.25; Mal. III.1). For what is called *angelos* in Greek is called *nuntius*, “messenger,” in Latin. He who came to announce the heavenly Judge is therefore rightly called an angel, so that he may preserve in his name the dignity which he fulfills in his work.

[Note: Col. 0029D. From Book XXXIV on Job, chapters VII and XIV.] Again, holy preachers are expressed by the name of angels, as in the book of blessed Job, when the Lord was speaking of the condemnation of the ancient enemy, He added: “When he shall be taken away, the angels shall fear, and, terrified, they shall be purified” (Job XLI.16). What should we understand here by angels but the messengers of the heavenly homeland at the end of time? When the devil is taken away, they will fear, because, at the coming of the strict Judge, the weight of terror then breaks forth so greatly that even the strength of saints and preachers is shaken. For when he is taken away, the angels will fear, because when he is swept away in the whirlwind of judgment, those who may then be found in their bodies—even the messengers of the heavenly homeland—will tremble, shaken by immense dread. For although they are already strong and perfect, yet, because they still dwell in the flesh, they cannot fail to be shaken by some fear amid the storm of so great a terror.

But when this Leviathan is swept away, and all the elements are shaken at his destruction, the hope of the kingdom’s nearness gladdens those holy preachers whom, as we have said, that time will find still in their bodies; bodily weakness troubles them at the manifestation of wrath. There will therefore be in them, in some manner, a joyful trembling and a secure fear: for they are certain that they will be rewarded with the heavenly kingdom, and yet they tremble, because of the weakness of the flesh, at the fear of so great a storm. How, then, will the conscience of the wicked be shaken at that time, when even the life of the righteous is disturbed? What will those who hate the coming of the Judge do, if even those who love Him dread the terror of so great a judgment? But because, in holy preachers, any rust of vices that could have remained in them is burned away by this fear, after it says, “When he shall be taken away, the angels shall fear,” it fittingly adds at once: “And, terrified, they shall be purified” (ibid.).

Hence Paul again says: “Great is the mystery of godliness, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the Gentiles, believed on in this world, taken up in glory” (I Tim. III.16). Since, after saying that the mystery of the dispensation appeared to angels, he adds that it was preached to the Gentiles, he plainly designated by the name of angels holy preachers—that is, messengers of truth. Again, the rulers of churches are denoted by the name of angels. Thus John, writing in his Apocalypse to the seven Churches, speaks to the angels of the Churches—that is, to the rulers of the peoples. Hence the prophet says: “And the angels of peace shall weep bitterly” (Ezek. XXXII.7).

[Note: Col. 0029D. Homily 6 on the Gospel; Book V on Job, chapter XXVIII.] All likewise who bear the title of priest are called angels, as the prophet Malachi testifies, saying: “The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II.7).

[Note: Col. 0030D. St Gregory writes that holy teachers may be understood by “angels.”] But each person also, insofar as he is able and insofar as he has received the grace of heavenly inspiration—if he recalls his neighbour from wickedness, if he seeks to exhort him to good works, if he announces to one who is straying the eternal kingdom or punishment—when he offers words of holy proclamation, has surely become an angel.

## CHAPTER III. ON HEAVEN

In Sacred Scripture, by the name “heaven” is sometimes denoted the order of the heavenly powers; sometimes holy Church; sometimes the soul of any righteous person; sometimes the heavenly judgment; sometimes the divine word; sometimes the exalted life of the saints; sometimes the priesthood of the Jewish people, or the Pharisees or teachers of the Law; and sometimes the heavenly life. When the plural is used, it sometimes signifies angelic spirits; sometimes, spiritually, the holy Apostles; sometimes any righteous preachers; and sometimes any perfect persons.

[Note: Col. 0030D. From Book XVI on Job, chapter VIII.] By the name of heaven is understood the sublimity of the heavenly powers, as Elihu speaks to blessed Job in rebuke: “Look up to heaven and see; contemplate the ether, for it is higher than thou” (Job XXXV.5). Although these words ought by no means to have been said to blessed Job, who knew greater things, nevertheless what is said is true. For by heaven or ether we may understand the heavenly powers, ever fixed upon the divine gaze.

[Note: Col. 0030D. These words occur in the middle of the chapter.] By saying this, he warns us to consider that, when we see angelic spirits still so far distant from us, we may learn how much lower we are than the Creator and ruler of spirits Himself. For even the angels cannot fully contemplate the power of our Creator; yet it is certain that they are higher than we precisely because they have not fallen into the depths as we have. Thus we may gather how far beneath God we are, since we are also subject to creatures sublime indeed, yet far beneath Him. He therefore says: “Look up to heaven and see; contemplate the ether, for it is higher than thou.” As though he said: See how far you are separated from the divine height, at whose power even those powers tremble in humility which surpass you by immeasurable exaltation. And how much lower are you than the Supreme One, when you find yourself lower even than beings lower than He?

[Note: Col. 0031D. From chapter XII, Book XXXII on Job, 113.] Again, by the name of heaven the Church is denoted, as John says in the Apocalypse of the devil under the figure of a dragon: “And his tail drew the third part of the stars of heaven, and cast them to the earth” (Apoc. XI.4). For heaven is the Church, which in this night of the present life shines with the radiant stars above, since it contains within itself innumerable virtues of the saints. But the dragon’s tail casts stars down to earth because that final manifestation of Satan, lifted up through the audacity of the man he has assumed, reveals as reprobate some whom he finds in the Church seemingly elect of God, by gaining possession of them. Thus for stars to fall from heaven to earth is for some, abandoning hope of heavenly things under that leader, to yearn after the pursuit of worldly glory.

Hence it is again said through the same John: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Apoc. VIII.1).

[Note: Col. 0031D. From Book X on Job, chapter XII, 124.] Heaven is called the Church of the elect, which, while it directs itself toward eternal heights through the uplifting of contemplation, suppresses the tumults of thoughts arising from below and makes within itself a certain silence for God. Since this silence of contemplation cannot be perfect in this life, it is said to have occurred for half an hour. For, against the will of the mind, the tumultuous noises of thoughts force themselves in and violently draw the eye of the heart, even when it is already directed toward things above, back again to regard earthly things. “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation depresses the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom IX.15). This silence is therefore rightly described not as an entire hour but as half an hour, because contemplation is by no means perfected here, although it is ardently begun.

[Note: Col. 0031D. From chapter XV, Book XXIX on Job, 20; and Homily 38 on the Gospel, Col. 0032D.] Again, by the name of heaven is understood the soul of the righteous, as it is written: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. VII.49). Elsewhere it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” Paul had previously testified: “We know Christ [to be] the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I.24).
