Therefore, since wisdom is God, and heaven is God’s seat, while the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom, the soul of the righteous is indeed heaven.

[Note: Col. 0032D. From Book XXIX on Job, chapter XVIII, 32.] By the name of heaven is also understood the heavenly judgment, as it is written in the book of blessed Job, when the Lord asks him: “Dost thou know the order of heaven, and wilt thou establish its reason upon the earth?” (Job XXXVIII.33). To know the order of heaven is to see the hidden predestinations of the heavenly arrangements. To establish its reason upon earth is to reveal before human hearts the causes of such secrets; that is, to establish the reason of heaven upon earth is to investigate the mysteries of heavenly judgments in contemplation and to disclose them in speech. Yet no one can do this in this life.

For, to proceed from small matters to greater, who can understand what may be the reason of those secrets: why a righteous man sometimes departs from judgment not merely unvindicated but even punished, while his wicked adversary departs not merely unpunished but victorious? Who can understand why one person lives while laying snares to destroy his neighbours, whereas another dies who would have benefited the lives of many; why one attains the heights of power who studies only to harm, while another desires only to defend the injured and yet himself lies oppressed; why one desires leisure and is entangled in countless affairs, while another desires to be occupied with affairs and is forced into leisure; why one, beginning badly, is led on to worse things until the end of life, while another, beginning well, advances through the length of time to an increase of merits; why one both desires and is able to seek the height of good living; another neither desires nor is able; another desires but is unable; another is able but does not desire? Who, then, can investigate these secrets of the heavenly judgments? Who can understand the discriminating balance of hidden equity?

For no one ascends to know the hidden recesses of judgments. Let it therefore be said to man that he may know himself not to know; that, knowing himself ignorant, he may fear; that he may fear in order to be humbled; that he may be humbled lest he presume upon himself; that he may not presume upon himself in order that he may seek the help of his Creator; and that he who has died by trusting in himself may live by desiring the aid of his Maker. Let the righteous man, therefore, who now knows himself indeed, yet does not know what is above him, hear: “Dost thou know the order of heaven, and wilt thou establish its reason upon earth?”—that is, do you comprehend the hidden orders of heavenly judgments, or are you able to disclose them to human ears? Blessed Job is therefore questioned concerning the investigation of incomprehensible judgments, as though it were openly said to him: All that you suffer you ought to endure the more patiently because, being ignorant of heavenly secrets, you do not know why you suffer this.

[Note: Col. 0032D. Homily 9 on Ezekiel.] Again, by the name of heaven the divine word is denoted, as it is written in the Psalm: “Stretching out heaven like a skin, who coverest its upper parts with waters” (Ps. CIII.3). What is signified by the name of heaven but Sacred Scripture, from which the sun of wisdom, the moon of knowledge, and the stars of examples from the ancient Fathers shine for us? It is stretched out like a skin because, formed through its writers in the language of flesh, it is unfolded before our eyes also through the words of teachers. And what is signified by the name of waters but the most holy choirs of angels? Of them it is written: “And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Dan. III.79; Ps. CXLVIII.4). Therefore the Lord covers the upper parts of this heaven with waters, because the lofty matters of sacred utterance—namely, what it tells of the nature of divinity or of eternal joys—are known in secret only to the angels, while we remain ignorant. This heaven, therefore, is stretched out before us, and yet its upper parts are covered by waters: for some matters of the sacred word are already open to us through the revelation of the Spirit, while others, which can be plain only to angels, are still kept hidden from us.

[Note: Col. 0033D. From chapter XV, Book XXIX on Job, after the middle, 124.] Hence the Lord asks blessed Job: “And who hath begotten the frost from heaven?” (Job XXXVIII.29). For what is expressed by frost but the numbness of unbelief? Heaven, however, is understood as Sacred Scripture, which opens to us the day of understanding and illumines us by the sun of righteousness; and which, while the night of this present life holds us, shines upon us with the stars of the commandments.

15. [Note: Col. 0033D. Ibid., a little after the beginning.] By the name of heaven is also understood the exalted life of the saints, as it is written: “Ascend to heaven, and I will speak” (Deut. XXIII.2, according to the Septuagint). For He was speaking not to an insensible but to a rational creature. Again, it is written in Job, where the Lord asks: “And who hath begotten the frost from heaven?” (Job XXXVIII.29). What do we understand by frost but the hearts of the Jews, cold and bound fast in the numbness of unbelief? And what else should heaven here be understood to mean but the exalted life of the saints? Abraham was heaven; Isaac was heaven; Jacob was heaven. But because the Jewish high priests, persecutors of the Lord and cold with the numbness of unbelief, sprang from the lineage of those Fathers, frost, as it were, came out of heaven: a cold people of unbelievers issued from the lofty offspring of saints. For when Caiaphas was born from Abraham, what else issued from heaven but frost? Yet the Lord is said to have begotten that frost because He Himself created the Jews naturally good, but by His just judgment permitted them, through their own wickedness, to become cold toward Him.

[Note: Col. 0034D. From Book II on Job, chapter XIX, 126.] For the Lord is the author of nature, not of fault. Therefore He begot them by creating them according to nature, while patiently enduring their living in wickedness.

Again, by the name of heaven are denoted the priests of the Jewish people, or the Pharisees, or teachers of the Law, as it is written in the book of blessed Job: “The fire of God fell from heaven, and, striking the sheep and the servants, consumed them” (Job I.16). All who held the office of preaching in the synagogue were rightly called heaven, because they were believed to know heavenly things. Hence Moses also, when he stirred priests and people to heed his admonitory words, said: “Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words of my mouth” (Deut. XXXII.1, according to the Septuagint), signifying by heaven the rank of rulers and by earth the people subject to them.

In this passage, therefore, we may fittingly understand heaven as the priests, Pharisees, or teachers of the Law, because, before human eyes, while serving in heavenly offices, they seemed to shine from above. But because they were deeply stirred up in hostility to our Redeemer, fire, as it were, fell from heaven: while the flame of envy blazed out to deceive the unlearned people even from those believed to teach truth. And what do we understand by the sheep and servants but all innocent persons, though still weak? Because they feared to endure the hostility of the Pharisees and rulers, they were consumed in the burning of unbelief. Therefore let it be said: “The fire of God fell from heaven, and, striking the sheep and servants, consumed them”—that is, the flame of envy fell from the hearts of the rulers and burned up whatever good was arising among the people.

[Note: Col. 0034D. From Book XXV on Job, chapter III.] By the name of heaven is denoted heavenly life, as it is said of the hypocrite in the book of blessed Job: “Though his pride ascend up unto heaven, and his head touch the clouds, yet in the end he shall perish like dung” (Job X.6). The hypocrite’s pride is said to ascend to heaven when his self-exaltation seems to live a heavenly life. His head also touches the clouds when his chief part—namely, his understanding—is believed to equal the merits of the saints who have gone before. But in the end he shall perish like dung, because at death, when he is led to torments, full of the filth of vices, he is trampled by malignant spirits.

For the joys of the present life, which the unrighteous regard as great goods, the righteous reckon as dung. Hence it is written: “The sluggard shall be stoned with the dung of oxen” (Ecclus. XXII.2). For one who refuses to follow the Lord grows sluggish in the love of eternal life. And whenever he is struck by the loss of temporal things, he is excessively afflicted by those things which righteous persons despise as dung. He, therefore, who is crushed by blows involving earthly things is, as it were, stoned with the dung of oxen. And the hypocrite is rightly said to resemble a dung-heap, because while he seeks temporal glory, at one time he swells inwardly with it in thought, at another envies that same glory in others, and even mocks those who truly possess it. Therefore, as many vices as fill him, so many heaps of dung make his breast stink in the sight of the eternal Judge. Let it therefore be said: “Though his pride ascend up unto heaven, and his head touch the clouds, yet in the end he shall perish like dung.” For if he pretends to live a heavenly life and displays his understanding as like that of true preachers, yet in the end he will perish like dung, because his mind will be condemned for the stench of its vices.

[Note: Col. 0034D. From Book XXVII on Job, chapter XXIV.] By the name of “heavens,” moreover, angels are denoted, as Elihu says to blessed Job in mockery: “Hast thou perhaps with him made the heavens, which are most solid, as if cast in bronze?” (Job XXXVII.18). For what is denoted by heavens but those who were created in the heavenly places: the angelic spirits? Of these it is well said that they are most solid, as if cast in bronze. For it is the nature of bronze to be difficult to consume with rust. And those angelic virtues which remained fixed in divine love, when the proud angels fell, received as a gift of recompense that no rust of creeping fault should ever corrode them; that they should remain in the contemplation of their Creator without end of blessedness; and that they should abide with eternal stability in the state in which they were created.

[Note: Col. 0035D. From Book XVII on Job, chapter XIX.] By the name of heavens the holy Apostles are also especially denoted, as it is written in the Psalm: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament showeth the works of His hands” (Ps. XVIII.1). Hence it is again written in Job: “His Spirit adorned the heavens” (Job XXVI.13). For then His Spirit adorned the Apostles, when He filled them. We have learned this from Luke’s account, who says: “And suddenly there came a sound from heaven, as of a mighty wind coming; and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And there appeared to them parted tongues, as it were of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in diverse tongues, according as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts II.2–3).

They received from Him the ornaments of virtue, though they had formerly been possessed by the immense ugliness of fear. For we know that the first of the Apostles—that is, of the heavens—before receiving the grace of this Spirit, as often as he feared death, denied life (Matt. XXVI.69–70). He was overthrown not by punishments, afflictions, or anyone’s dreadful power, but by the mere question of one servant (Luke XXII.35). Indeed, lest the stronger sex should appear formidable, he was tested by the questioning of a maidservant; and again, lest even the weakness of such a sex should be made more contemptible by the lowliness of her office, he was questioned not merely by a maidservant but by a maidservant who was a doorkeeper (John XVIII.17). See how lowly was the person appointed to test him, so that it might plainly be shown how great was the weakness of fear that possessed one who could not stand even before the voice of a serving-girl at the door.

Yet Luke testifies what this man, shortly before timid, became after the coming of the Spirit, and with what authority he preached the Lord against priests and rulers. He who had shortly before been timid now speaks in tongues, shines with miracles, rebukes the unbelief of priests and rulers with a free voice, gives the rest both example and authority for preaching Jesus; he is forbidden by beatings to speak in Jesus’ name, and yet is not restrained (Acts IV, etc.). Strengthened by the power of the Holy Spirit, he trod under the heel of freedom the heights of this world, so that everything that swelled proudly against the grace of the Creator might be seen to lie below him. These are the ornaments of the heavens; these are the gifts of the Spirit, which are wont to be manifested in diverse powers. Of these heavens it is also said in the Psalm: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. XXXII.6). Concerning these ornaments of the Spirit it adds: “And all their power is by the breath of His mouth” (ibid.). Thus it is well said: “His Spirit adorned the heavens,” because holy preachers would have shone with no beauty of strength had they not received the promised gifts of the Paraclete.

[Note: Col. 0035D. Join Gregory’s explanation of the Fourth Penitential Psalm, 13. From chapter X, Book XXX on Job.] By the name of heavens are denoted any holy teachers, as it is written in the Psalm: “Lord, bow Thy heavens and come down” (Ps. CXLIII.5). What do we understand by heavens but holy preachers? For when the heavens are bowed, the Lord comes down, because when holy teachers draw Him down in their preaching, they pour knowledge of divinity into our hearts. God would by no means come down to us if His preachers remained inflexible in the rigor of contemplation.

[Note: Col. 0035D. These words occur before the explanation of the verse cited.] For if, intoxicated by heavenly contemplation, they wished to preach to us those things which they comprehend, and did not rather temper their knowledge with a certain moderation and sobriety, who could receive, in the narrow capacity of understanding, those streams of the heavenly fountain? Therefore the heavens are bent down, so that the Lord may come down and we may be born into the light of the new faith.

19. [Note: Col. 0036D. From Book XXVII on Job, chapter XXIV, about the middle.] By the name of heavens are also denoted the minds of the perfect. Hence Elihu says mockingly to blessed Job: “Hast thou perhaps with him made the heavens, which are most solid, as if cast in bronze?” (Job XXXVII.18). For by heavens may be expressed the minds of the elect, lifted in their inward love above all earthly contagions. Although they dwell bodily in the depths, they already cleave in heart to the heights, and truly say: “Our conversation is in heaven” (Phil. III.20). They are most solid, as if cast in bronze, because no rust of mutability consumes them from the integrity of their begun strength.

## CHAPTER IV. ON THE FIRMAMENT

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of firmament is sometimes denoted our Redeemer, and sometimes the strengthening of angelic nature after the fall of the evil angels.

[Note: Col. 0036D. From Homily 7 on Ezekiel.] Our Redeemer is denoted by the name of firmament, as it is said through Ezekiel: “And the likeness over the heads of the living creatures was a firmament, as the appearance of dreadful crystal, stretched forth over their heads above” (Ezek. I.22). For what is understood figuratively by the firmament but our Redeemer: true God above all things and, among all things, made perfect man, in whom our nature was established before the Father? Of Him it is prophetically said by the Psalmist: “Let Thy hand be upon the man of Thy right hand, and upon the son of man whom Thou hast strengthened for Thyself” (Ps. LXXIX.18).

For before human nature was assumed by the Creator of all, it was earth, not firmament. For sinful man was told: “Thou art earth, and unto earth thou shalt go” (Gen. III.19, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: Col. 0036D. There the common text reads: “thou shalt return.”] But after it was assumed by the Author of all things, lifted up into heaven and raised above angels, that which had been earth became firmament. Yet the likeness of the firmament which is seen—the firmament that had been earth—is then supplied when it says, “as the appearance of dreadful crystal.” Crystal freezes out of water and becomes hard. We know, however, how great is the mobility of water. But the body of our Redeemer, because it was subject to sufferings until death, was in one respect like water: for in being born, growing, being assailed, hungering, thirsting, and dying, it moved through successive moments of time until His Passion. Beholding this course, the Prophet said: “He hath rejoiced as a giant to run the way,” etc. (Ps. XVIII.6). But because, through the glory of His resurrection, He was strengthened from corruption itself into the power of incorruption, He became hard like crystal from water, so that in Him there might remain the same nature, while the mutability of corruption that had existed should no longer remain. Therefore water was changed into crystal when even the weakness of corruption was changed through His resurrection into the firmness of incorruption.

## CHAPTER V. ON THE SUN

In Sacred Scripture, when “sun” is used figuratively, it sometimes means the Lord; sometimes persecution; sometimes the manifestation of a clear vision concerning any matter; sometimes the understanding of the wise; sometimes the brightness of good work or the ardour of the love of God; sometimes the light of truth; sometimes the radiance of preachers; and sometimes the heat of temptation.

[Note: Col. 0037D. From Homily 29 on the Gospel.] The Lord is signified by the name of sun, as it is said through the prophet: “The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in her order” (Hab. III.11, according to the Septuagint). For when the sun is lifted up into its order, the moon is established, because when the Lord ascends into heaven, holy Church is immediately strengthened in the authority of preaching.

21. Again, by the name of sun, persecution is understood, as Truth says in the Gospel: seeds which sprang up without roots withered when the sun rose (Matt. VIII), because the words of life, which flourish in the hearts of earthly persons for a brief temporal moment, are dried up when the heat of persecution comes upon them.

By the name of the sun is denoted the manifestation of clear sight, as the Prophet announces the Lord appearing before the eyes of all, saying: “In the sun he has set his tabernacle” (Ps. 18:6). As though he said: He displayed the mystery of his assumed humanity in the light of manifest vision. And, as the divine voice says through Nathan to the same prophet: “You did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun” (2 Sam. 12:12). For what does “before the sun” suggest but the knowledge of manifest sight? Again, by the name of the sun is expressed the understanding of the wise, as it is written in the Apocalypse: “The fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun, and it was granted him to afflict human beings with heat and fire” (Rev. 16:8). To pour the bowl upon the sun is, plainly, to inflict the sufferings of persecution on persons resplendent with the brightness of wisdom. And it was granted him to afflict people with heat and fire, because, when wise persons, overcome by torments, are touched by the error of evil conduct, all weaker persons, persuaded by their example, burn with temporal desires. For the falls of the strong furnish arguments for the destruction of the weak.

[Note: Col. 0037D. From Book XXII on Job, chapter IV.] Again, by the name of the sun is denoted the brightness of a good work, as blessed Job says: “If I saw the sun when it shone” (Job 31:26). For the sun in its shining is a good work in its manifestation. For it is written: “Let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). And again: “Let your loins be girded, and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:35). What is here denoted by the shining sun is denoted in the Gospel by the burning lamp. For when a good work shines amid unbelievers, a lamp burns in the night; but when it shines within the Church, the sun shines in the day. If a good work is still such that evil persons alone admire it, it is a lamp in the night; but if it advances so far that good and more perfect persons can admire it, it is surely the sun in the day. When a good work shines through the active life of the body, light gleams, as it were, from an earthen vessel in the manner of a lamp. But when it is raised in contemplation through the virtue of the mind alone, light is seen as coming from heaven in the manner of the sun: “If I saw the sun when it shone.”

[Note: Col. 0037D. From chapter V of the Book on Job cited above, far after its beginning.] As though he said openly: Even when my work bestowed upon others the light of an example, I was not kindled into the glory of presumption; for, fearing to be exalted by it, I turned my eyes away from looking upon it.

[Note: Col. 0038D. From Book XXIV on Job, chapter XII.] By the name of the sun is understood the light of truth. Thus the Book of Wisdom reports that the ungodly, on the last day of judgment, once they know their condemnation, will say: “We have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness has not shone upon us, and the sun has not risen for us” (Wis. 5:6). As though they said plainly: The ray of inward light did not shine upon us. Hence the Psalmist, speaking of malign spirits, adds: “The sun rose, and they gathered into their dens,” etc. (Ps. 103:22).

[Note: Col. 0038D. From Book XXVII on Job, chapter XVIV {perhaps XIX}.] For when the light of truth appeared through the flesh, the demons were driven out from the minds of believers and, as it were, returned to their dens, since they held only the hearts of unbelievers.

[Note: Col. 0038D. From Book IX on Job, chapter III.] Again, by the name of the sun is denoted the brightness of preachers, as blessed Job says: “He commands the sun, and it does not rise; and he seals up the stars as under a seal” (Job 9:7). For what is understood by the name of the sun except the brightness of preachers? Hence John says: “The sun became black as a sackcloth of hair” (Rev. 6:12). For at the end of time the sun will appear like a sackcloth of hair, because the resplendent life of preachers is shown as harsh and contemptible before the eyes of the reprobate. They are also figured by the brightness of the stars, because, when they rightly preach to sinners, they illuminate the darkness of our night. Hence, when preachers have been withdrawn, it is said through the Prophet: “The stars of the rains have been withheld” (Jer. 3:3). But because the sun shines by day, and the stars illuminate the darknesses of night, and because in sacred speech the name of day often signifies the eternal country while the name of night signifies the present life, holy preachers become like a sun to our eyes when they open to us the apprehension [variant: contemplation] of the true light; and they shine like stars in darkness when, through the active life, they make provision in earthly matters for our future necessities. They flash like the sun in the day when they raise the gaze of our mind to contemplate the homeland of inward brightness; and they shine like stars in the night because, even when they conduct earthly affairs, by the example of their uprightness they direct the foot of our conduct, which is about to stumble.

But because, after the preachers had been expelled, there was no one to shine upon the Jewish people remaining in the night of its unbelief, either to show the brightness of apprehension [variant: contemplation] or to reveal the light of the active life, Truth itself, which abandoned this people when it rejected her, justly blinded it by withdrawing the light of preaching on account of its perversity. Thus it is rightly said: “He commands the sun, and it does not rise; and he seals up the stars as under a seal.” He did not will the sun to rise for the people from whom he turned away the minds of preachers. And he seals up the stars as under a seal because, when he kept his preachers within themselves through silence, he hid the heavenly light from the blinded minds of the wicked.

[Note: Col. 0039D. From Book X on Job, chapter XXXI.] By the name of the sun is denoted the heat of temptation, as Moses says: “If there is among you a man who has been polluted by a nocturnal emission, he shall go outside the camp, and he shall not return before he is washed with water at evening; and after sunset he shall return to the camp” (Deut. 23:10–11). A nocturnal dream is hidden temptation, when something shameful is conceived in the heart by a dark thought but is not carried out in an act of heart or body. But one polluted by a nocturnal dream is commanded to go outside the camp because it is fitting that one polluted by an unclean thought should judge himself unworthy of fellowship with all the faithful, set the desert of his fault before his eyes, and count himself despicable in comparison with the good. Therefore, for one polluted to go outside the camp is for a person troubled by a shameful assault to regard himself as contemptible in comparison with the continent.

What does it mean that he is washed with water at evening, except that, seeing his failure, he turns to penitential tears, so that with ashes he may wash away everything for which hidden pollution accuses his mind? But after the sun has set he should return to the camp, because, when the heat of temptation has cooled, he must again take confidence toward the fellowship of the good. For after the washing with water, he returns to the camp at the sun’s setting: that is, after penitential lamentation, when the flame of unlawful thought has grown cold, he is restored to confidence in the merits of the faithful, so that he no longer judges himself far removed from others, rejoicing that he is clean through the death of his inward heat.

## Chapter VI. On the Moon

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of the moon are denoted at times the holy Church, at times the reputation of a good work, at times the instability of fools, and at times the mutability of temporal things.

[Note: Col. 0039D. From Book XVII on Job, chapter X.] By the name of the moon is expressed the holy Church, as blessed Habakkuk says: “The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order” (Hab. 3:11, according to the Septuagint). For when the sun is lifted up, the moon is set in its order, because, when the Lord ascended into heaven, the holy Church was immediately strengthened in the authority of preaching. The Psalmist too, beholding the holy Church as destined to remain in everlasting perfection, described it under the name of the moon, saying: “The moon perfect for ever” (Ps. 88:38). Because the Lord’s resurrection confirms it in the hope of resurrection, he rightly adds: “A faithful witness in heaven” (ibid.).

[Col. 0040B. Note: Col. 0040D. From Book XXII on Job, chapter V.] Again, by the name of the moon is understood the reputation of a good work, as blessed Job says: “If I saw the sun when it shone, and the moon moving brightly” (Job 31:26). By the shining sun is understood the brilliance of a good work; by the moon, the good repute of that work. Therefore, after mentioning the sun, he fittingly added the moon “moving brightly,” because commendable reputation follows a good work, through which a celebrated name is possessed in the night of this present life. If it is true, as some think, that the moon receives illumination through its hidden circuit from the ray of the sun, so as to give light in its nocturnal courses, this conjecture too is not foreign to this order of signification. For reputation receives its strength from a good work and spreads the grace of favour like the brilliance of light.

There is another feature of the moon that fittingly corresponds by analogy to a reputation spread abroad: its light shows the way to travellers even in the time of darkness. So too, when the light known to be bright through the reputation of another’s life is displayed, it supplies the one travelling, as it were, with the light of example. Yet sometimes a work adopted from another’s reputation is formed in the mind from a less pure desire. For weak minds, when they hear good things about others, sometimes are stirred to right action not by love of virtue but by love of praise. And it is plainly clear that, just as it is the nature of the sun to kindle and dry whatever it touches, so it is characteristic of lunar fire to burn whatever it touches, yet to make it moist by burning it.

Thus some are inflamed toward a good life by the love of God and the affection for right action, but others by the love of praise. When we are kindled by the desire for right action, we are dried from the moisture of vices as though by the fire of the sun. But one whom the love of praise prompts toward a good work is touched by the desired reputation as by the moon, because it both kindles and dissolves his mind: it kindles him for the exercise of the work, but dissolves him into the desire for favour. Nevertheless, the examples of others often usefully persuade us to perform good works. And when, with a humble mind, we receive the good reputation of another, we either bring our own good deeds to a better state or change evil deeds into good ones. When the splendour of a neighbour’s reputation shines upon us from that neighbour’s life, our mind—as we have said—which directs itself toward attaining the path of virtue, sets its steps as it were in the moonlight.

But just as we profit from another’s reputation, so we are often emptied of virtue if we are inflamed by the praises of our own reputation; for while the mind delights in what it observes to be held about itself externally, it forgets that for which it inwardly longed. But because commendable reputation did not exalt the holy man, the moon moving brightly did not kindle him.

[Note: Col. 0041D. From Book XXXIV on Job, chapter XII.] By the name of the moon is denoted the inconstancy of fools, as Solomon says: “The wise person remains as the sun; the fool changes as the moon” (Ecclus. 27:12).

[Note: Col. 0041D. From Book XXXIV on Job, chapter XII.] Again, by the name of the moon is denoted the mutability of temporal things, as John says in the Apocalypse: “A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet” (Rev. 12:1). In the sun is understood the illumination of truth; but in the moon, which wanes through its monthly changes, the mutability of temporal things. Because the holy Church is covered by the splendour of heavenly light, it is clothed, as it were, with the sun. And because it despises all temporal things, it treads the moon beneath its feet.

## Chapter VII. On the Stars

In Sacred Scripture, when “star” is used in the singular, Christ is understood. But when it is used in the plural, it denotes at times particularly the ancient prophets or the holy apostles and preachers; at times the righteousness of any saints, shining amid the darkness of this life; and at times the pretence of hypocrites, who show the good deeds they do in order to receive praise from people.

By the name of a star Christ is denoted, John bearing witness, by whom he is called “the bright morning star.” Appearing alive after death, he became for us the morning star, because, by providing in himself an example of resurrection, he showed what light follows.

[Note: Col. 0041D. From Book XXVII on Job, chapter V.] By the name of stars too are denoted either prophets or apostles, as it is said of the Lord in the book of blessed Job: “He withdraws the stars of rain, and pours out showers like torrents” (Job 36:27). For there are two kinds of righteous persons in this life: one, those who live well but teach no one; the other, those who live rightly and teach those same right things. Likewise, on the face of heaven some stars appear that no rains follow, while others appear that soak the parched earth with great showers.

Therefore, whenever some persons in the holy Church live rightly but do not know how to preach that same uprightness, they are indeed stars, but born in a dry sky: by the example of good living they offer light to others, but they do not know how to rain the word of preaching. But when some in the Church both live rightly and pour that same uprightness into others by the words of preaching, stars are brought forth into heaven, as it were, to produce rain: they shine by the merits of their life in such a way that they rain in the speech of preaching.

Did Moses not raise up in this heaven a rain-bearing star, who, while he shone from above, poured into the hearts of sinners—as into parched earth below—the rain of holy exhortation for the fruitfulness of growth? Was Isaiah not shown as a rain-bearing star, who, in holding the light of truth which he foresaw, watered the dryness of unbelievers by announcing it prophetically? Were not Jeremiah and the other prophets, placed as it were in heaven, rain-bearing stars? Raised to the height of preaching, while they dared freely to rebuke the perversity of sinners, they pressed down the dust of human blindness by watering it with drops of words. Since the heavenly judgments remove from the present life the souls of these persons, received from this corruptible flesh, the rain-bearing stars are withdrawn from the face of heaven; and the stars return to concealment when, their courses completed, the souls of the saints are hidden in the treasuries of inward providence.

But because the earth would dry up if, when the rain-bearing stars had been withdrawn, the streams from above ceased altogether, it is rightly said: “He withdraws the stars of rain, and pours out showers like torrents.” For when he removed the prophets, the Lord sent the apostles in their place, to rain in the likeness of torrents, after the outward pronouncements of the law had fallen silent with the withdrawal of the ancient Fathers. Therefore he hid the stars of rain and poured forth rains like torrents, because, while he brought the preachers of the Law back to hidden and inward places, a more abundant power of preaching flowed forth through the utterances of those who followed.

[Note: Col. 0042D. From Book XVII on Job, chapter X.] Again, by the name of stars are denoted the souls of all who live well, as it is written in the book of blessed Job: “Behold, the moon does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight” (Job 25:5). For what is signified by the moon except the whole Church together? What by the stars except the souls of those who live well individually, who shine like stars in the darkness of night while they excel in great virtues amid intercourse with wicked people? Hence Paul too says to his disciples: “Among whom you shine as lights in the world” (Phil. 2:15). And again: “Star differs from star in brightness” (1 Cor. 15:41).

Therefore the moon does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight, because neither does the holy Church shine forth in so many miracles by its own power unless the gifts of prevenient grace are poured upon it; nor are the minds of individual persons who live well clean from the stains of sins if they are judged apart from mercy, because, before the eyes of the strict Judge, each person’s own corruptibility defiles that person unless the grace of pardon wipes it away daily.

[Note: Col. 0042D. From Book XXXII on Job, chapter XII, about the middle.] Likewise, by the name of stars is denoted the pretence of hypocrites, as John says of the devil: “The dragon cast its tail and drew down a third part of the stars of heaven, and cast them upon the earth” (Rev. 12:4). For heaven is the Church, which, in the night of this present life, shines through the innumerable virtues of saints that it contains, as through stars radiating from above. But the dragon’s tail casts stars down to earth, because Satan’s end, lifted up through the audacity of the man he has assumed, reveals as reprobate by gaining possession of some whom it finds in the Church as though they were God’s elect. Therefore, for stars to fall from heaven to earth is for some, abandoning hope in heavenly things, to yearn under that leader after the pursuit of worldly glory.

Hence Daniel, under the figure of Antiochus, speaks of this dragon’s tail, saying: “It cast down some of the host and of the stars, and trampled them” (Dan. 8:10). For it casts down from the host and from the stars when it breaks some who are both strong in the virtue of their works and resplendent with the light of righteousness.

## Chapter VIII. On Lucifer

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of Lucifer are understood at times the only-begotten Son of God, or the divine Word, and at times the life of a righteous person.

[Note: Col. 0043D. From Book XXIX on Job, chapter V, 17.] By the name of Lucifer is denoted the only-begotten Son of God, as blessed Job asks concerning his incarnation: “Can you bring forth Lucifer at its time, and make the evening star rise over the children of the earth?” (Job 38:32). For what do we understand by Lucifer except the only-begotten Son of God? The Father brought forth Lucifer in his own time because, as it is written, “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4:4). Born of the Virgin like Lucifer, he appeared amid the darkness of our night, because, driving away the obscurity of sin, he announced to us the eternal morning. He made himself known as Lucifer because he rose from death at daybreak and, by the brilliance of his light, wiped away the foul gloom of our mortality.

[Note: Col. 0043D. From the same Book X, chapter II.] But by the name of Lucifer the divine Word can also be denoted. For the Word of God is one and the same in the preacher’s mouth. When some hear it with joy but others with envy, they turn the brightness of Lucifer into the darkness of evening for themselves. When the former humbly receive the voice of holy preaching, they open the eyes of their heart, as it were, to the light of a star. But when the latter envy one who speaks well and seek not the cause of salvation but the glory of self-exaltation, then, as the evening of their wickedness breaks forth, they close their eyes in the sleep of death. Thus, by a hidden judgment, he who is Lucifer to the elect becomes evening to a reprobate hearer, because by the holy exhortation through which the good return to life, the wicked die more grievously in guilt.

Hence Paul rightly says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some indeed a fragrance of death unto death, but to others a fragrance of life unto life” (2 Cor. 2:15–16). Thus he saw that his Word was both Lucifer and evening for hearers, through which he perceived that some were raised from wickedness while others, conversely, were lulled into wickedness.

[Note: Col. 0043D. From Book X on Job, chapter XII, far after the beginning; Col. 0044D, 20.] Again, by the name of Lucifer is understood the life of a righteous person, as it is said in the book of blessed Job: “When you think yourself consumed, you shall rise like Lucifer” (Job 11:17). And the life of the righteous is rightly compared to Lucifer. For Lucifer, going before the sun, announces it. And what does the innocence of saints proclaim to us except the brightness of the Judge who follows? For in admiration of them we perceive what we should judge concerning the majesty of the true Light. We do not yet see the patience of our Redeemer, but we admire only his power in the conduct of his elect. Therefore, because the good person’s life, by being considered, sets the force of truth before our eyes, a bright Lucifer comes to us before the sun.

Therefore let Zophar say to the tempted person—let him say even to one who seems to despair—“When you think yourself consumed, you shall rise like Lucifer.” [Note: These words have been given above.] For temptations often besiege us in such number that their very multitude almost inclines us to the fall of despair. Hence the mind is often turned to weariness; it scarcely considers the losses of its own virtue, and, grieving altogether, it is broken as though already alienated even from the feeling of pain. It cannot count by how great a tumult of thoughts it is laid waste. It sees itself about to fall moment by moment, and grief itself more gravely hinders it from taking up the weapons of resistance. Darkness besets the eyes wherever they are turned, and although shadows always obstruct its sight, the mind sees nothing but darkness.

Yet before the merciful Judge, these very things that burden even the effort of prayer often plead more subtly for us through justice. For the Creator beholds the gloom of our sorrow and restores the rays of withdrawn light, so that the mind, immediately raised up by gifts, becomes vigorous—the mind which just before the vices warring against it were trampling beneath the foot of pride. It immediately shakes off the burden of the body and, after the darkness of its disturbance, breaks through into the light of contemplation. It is immediately lifted into the joy of progress; and it, which before was compelled to fall amid temptations through despair, despises present things without a struggle of thought and trusts in the future recompense without the obstacle of doubt.

Therefore, when the righteous person thinks himself consumed, he rises like Lucifer, because as soon as he begins to grow dark under the gloom of temptations, he is renewed into the light of grace and displays in himself the day of righteousness—he who shortly before feared that the night of guilt was about to fall.

## Chapter IX. On the Pleiades

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of the Pleiades are denoted all the saints, or the New Testament.

[Note: Col. 0044D. From Book XXIX on Job, chapters XVI, XXVII, XXVIII.] By the name of the Pleiades are denoted the saints. Therefore the Lord asks blessed Job: “Can you bind together the shining stars of the Pleiades?” (Job 38:31). The Pleiades are stars called ἀπὸ τοῦ πλείστου—that is, “from multitude,” or plurality. They were created so close to one another and yet separate that they are together but cannot be joined, so that they are joined by a kind of nearness but separated by contact. What then do the shining Pleiades, which are seven, proclaim but all the saints? Amid the darkness of this present life, they illuminate us with the light of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. Sent to prophesy at different times from the very beginning of the world to its end, they are joined to one another in one respect and not joined in another.

For the Pleiades, as stated above, are joined by nearness and separated by contact; they are situated together, yet emit the rays of their light separately. So holy persons, appearing to preach at one time and another, are separate in the sight of their outward form but joined in the sight of the mind. They shine together because they preach one thing, but they do not touch one another because they endure in different times. How different were the times in which Abel, Isaiah, and John appeared! They were divided in time, certainly, but not in preaching. For Abel, signifying the passion of our Redeemer, offered a lamb in sacrifice; of whose passion Isaiah says: “Like a lamb before its shearer, he shall be silent and shall not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). John too says of him: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

Behold: sent in divided times, yet agreeing concerning the innocence of our Redeemer, John spoke by showing the same Lamb, Isaiah by foreseeing him, and Abel by offering him. The one whom John held forth in showing, whom Isaiah held forth in speech, Abel held in his hands by signifying him. Since we have said how the Pleiades as stars harmonize concerning the Redeemer’s humanity, let us now show how they shine in agreement in manifesting the unity of the Trinity. David, Isaiah, and Paul appeared in this world at different times; yet none of them thinks differently from another, because, though they did not know one another by face, they learned one thing from divine knowledge.

For David, to show God as the author of all things in the Trinity, said: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us” (Ps. 66:7–8). And lest, by naming God three times, he should seem to have spoken of three gods, he immediately added, indicating the unity of that same Trinity: “And let all the ends of the earth fear him” (ibid.). By adding not “them” but “him,” he declared that the three whom he had named were one. Isaiah likewise, when he revealed praise of the unity of the Trinity, expressing the voices of the seraphim, said: “Holy, holy, holy” (Isa. 6:3). And lest, by naming God three times, he should seem to divide the unity of the divine substance, he added: “The Lord God of Hosts” (ibid.). Because he adds not “Lords Gods” but “Lord God,” he indicated that what he had called holy three times is one.

Paul likewise, to show the operation of the holy Trinity, says: “From him, through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. 11:36). And in order to show the unity of that same Trinity, he immediately adds: “To him be glory for ever” (ibid.). Therefore, by adding not “to them” but “to him,” he made known that what he had above called “him” is one by nature and three according to persons. Thus the Pleiades are situated, as it were, in one place because they think in agreement concerning God; yet they do not touch one another because, as has been said, they endure through the different times of this world. Since it belongs to divine power alone to join in the preaching of faith those sent at separate times, and to unite in the brightness of their intention those foretold with unlike gifts, it is rightly said: “Can you bind together the shining stars of the Pleiades?” As though he said: “Can you do as I do, who alone fill all things and, by filling the minds of the elect, join them in a single understanding?”

[Col. 0046B. Note: Col. 0045D. From the Book and chapter cited, far after the middle.] By the name of the Pleiades may also be denoted the grace of the New Testament. For the Pleiades, as we said above, are seven stars. They indicate the grace of the New Testament all the more clearly because all of us plainly perceive that, through it, the Holy Spirit illuminates believers with the light of his sevenfold gift. But when our Redeemer came in the flesh, he bound together the Pleiades, because he possessed in himself, all together and enduringly, all the operations of the sevenfold Spirit. Isaiah says of him: “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root. And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:1–2). Zechariah says of him: “Upon one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. 3:9). And again: “In the golden lampstand are seven lamps” (Zech. 4:2).

No human being has possessed all the operations of the Holy Spirit together except the one Mediator between God and humankind, to whom belongs that same Spirit who proceeds from the Father before the ages. Thus it is rightly said: “Upon one stone are seven eyes.” For this stone to have seven eyes is to retain in operation, all at once, every virtue of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. One person has received prophecy, another knowledge, another powers, another kinds of tongues, another interpretation of utterances (1 Cor. 12:8, 11), according to the distribution of the Holy Spirit; but no one attains possession of all the gifts of that same Spirit.

But our Creator, taking on our weakness, showed that through the power of his divinity he possessed all the virtues of the Holy Spirit at once; he therefore undoubtedly binds together the shining Pleiades. Let blessed Job then hear: “Can you bind together the shining stars of the Pleiades?” As though it were plainly said: “You can possess the lights of certain virtues; but can you exercise all the operations of the Holy Spirit at the same time? Therefore contemplate me, who bind together the Pleiades in every virtue, and restrain yourself from self-exaltation on the basis of your few gifts.”

## Chapter X. On Arcturus

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of Arcturus are denoted at times the whole Church together, and at times the old Law.

[Note: Col. 0047D. From Book IX, chapter XVI, 27.] By the name of Arcturus is understood the whole Church together. Hence the Lord asks blessed Job: “Can you bind together the shining stars of the Pleiades, or can you scatter the circuit of Arcturus?” (Job 38:3 [as printed]). Arcturus illuminates the nighttime hours in such a way that, though placed upon the axis of heaven, it turns through various positions and yet does not set. It does not move by revolving outside its place; rather, remaining fixed in place, it inclines through all regions of the world without ever falling. Therefore, in Arcturus, which illuminates the spaces of night through its circuit without setting, is denoted not the life of saints set forth piecemeal, but the whole Church together: it undergoes whatever weariness comes, but does not incline toward the failure of its own standing. It endures the circuit of labours, but does not hasten to a setting through the passage of time. For Arcturus is not drawn toward the depths of the sky during the night; rather, while it itself turns, the night ends. So, while the holy Church is shaken by innumerable tribulations, the shadow of the present life comes to an end. And while it remains standing, the night passes, because, while it endures in its soundness, the life of this mortality runs its course.

There is also something in Arcturus that we may observe more attentively. It revolves among seven stars, and at one time raises three to the heights and bends four downward; at another it raises four above and presses three below. So too, when the holy Church sometimes preaches to believers the knowledge of the Trinity and sometimes the four virtues—prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice—it alters the appearance of its position, as it were, by the turning of preaching. For when it empties the confidence in their own labour of some who boast of their works, and exalts faith in the Trinity, what else does it do but raise three stars of Arcturus and bend down four? And when it forbids some who lack good works to presume upon faith alone, commanding them instead earnestly to perform what has been prescribed, what else does Arcturus do but raise four stars and lower three?

Let us see how it raises three and lowers four. Behold, through Paul it says against those who pride themselves in works against faith: “If Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before the Lord. For what does Scripture say? Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4:2; Gen. 15:6). Let us see how it raises four and lowers three. Behold, through James it says against those who pride themselves in faith against works: “As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:26).

Therefore Arcturus turns because the holy Church, according to the minds of its hearers, skilfully moves through the various aspects of preaching. Arcturus turns because the holy Church is whirled about amid the tribulations of this night. But at some time the Lord scatters this circuit of Arcturus, because he changes the labours of the Church into rest. Then he binds the Pleiades more completely when he destroys the circuit of Arcturus, because then all the saints are joined even in the likeness of their vision, when at the end of the world the holy Church is released from the labours it now endures. Therefore let him say: “Can you bind together the shining stars of the Pleiades, or can you scatter the circuit of Arcturus?” Understand: “As I do, who then unite the life of the saints even in visible likeness, when I bodily dissolve the circuit of the universal Church.” And what human being does not know that this belongs to divine power alone? But that a human being may know what he himself is, let him continually remember what the Lord alone can do.

[Note: Col. 0047D. From the Book and chapter cited, after the middle.] By the name of Arcturus the old Law may also be understood. Arcturus rises from the northern region. Wherever Arcturus turns in its circuit, it shows the Pleiades; and when the light of day is near, the order of its stars is spread out. Therefore the Law is not unfittingly denoted by Arcturus, which rises in the region of cold. For the Law is revered as though from the north, because it harshly oppressed those subject to it with so great a severity of rigidity. Since it punished some for their faults by having them stoned and others executed by the sword, it was a numbing region, as it were, alien from the sun of charity; the severity of its commandments oppressed more through coldness than it nourished through warmth.

Nor is it surprising that the Old Testament is expressed by the seven stars of Arcturus, because in the observance of the Law the seventh day was held venerable, and vows of prescribed sacrifice extended through the whole week. Wherever Arcturus turns, it displays the Pleiades, which signify the New Testament, because through everything the Old Testament says, the works of the New Testament are announced. For beneath the covering of the letter it conceals the mystery of prophecy. And Arcturus, as it were, bends itself and shows, because, when it is bent toward spiritual understanding, the light of the sevenfold grace signified through it is revealed. And when the daylight draws near, the order of its stars is shown, because, after Truth made itself known to us through itself, it relaxed the commandments of the letter from carnal observances.

## Chapter XI. On Air

[Col. 0048D] In Sacred Scripture, by the name of air is denoted the instability of worldly minds, as Elihu says.

[Note: [Col. 0048D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter 25.] Suddenly the air is condensed into clouds. For air, by its very thinness, is dispersed, so that it is not made solid by any firmness (Job 37:21). Clouds, however, are stronger in proportion as they are denser. What, then, is signified by air except the minds of worldly people, which, devoted to the innumerable desires of this life, are scattered here and there, fluid like air? But air is condensed into clouds when unstable minds are strengthened by the grace of the divine regard with the solidity of virtue, so that, by sound understanding, they gather themselves within the bosom of the heart and do not dissolve into vain thoughts.

## CHAPTER XII. ON CLOUDS

[Col. 0049A]

In Holy Scripture, by the name “clouds” there is sometimes signified Christ’s humanity; sometimes the darkness of ignorance; sometimes the holy prophets; sometimes any holy teachers; sometimes any righteous persons; sometimes unstable people; sometimes firmness of mind; sometimes temporal goods; sometimes a proud heart.

[Note: [Col. 0049D] From Homily 8 on Ezekiel.] By the name “cloud” the flesh of the Redeemer is understood, as the Psalmist says of Him: “Who makes the cloud his ascent” (Psalm 103:3). The Lord made the cloud His ascent because He who is everywhere by divinity ascended to heavenly things in the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0049D] From Homily 21 on Ezekiel, scattered passages.] By the name “cloud” the darkness of ignorance is signified. Hence the prophet Ezekiel, foreseeing the cruelty of the Jews against the Lord, says: “And I saw, and behold, a storm-wind came from the north, and a great cloud” (Ezek. 1:4). For what is understood by the north except the devil, and what is meant by a storm-wind except his temptation? The assault of the evil spirit is rightly called a storm-wind. A whirlwind, by shaking, demolishes the building it strikes. Every temptation of the ancient enemy, which is worked in the mind, is a storm-wind, because by stirring it through desires, it uproots it from the state of its uprightness.

Therefore the storm-wind comes from the north when the evil spirit shakes the life of the Jewish people by temptation; and rightly there is added: “And a great cloud.” For the more anyone burned with cruelty, the more greatly he deserved to be blinded by the darkness of his ignorance. They had awaited with understanding, in the Law and the Prophets, the Redeemer of humankind; yet when they saw Him, they denied Him. Thus their mind was covered with the great cloud of its ignorance, so that afterward, when seeking Him, they might not recognize Him whom before they could both have proclaimed and refused to love. For when they beheld at one time His powers and miracles, and at another His sufferings, a great cloud had come from the north into their unbelieving hearts: because, through the coldness of their sin, they were darkened both by the weakness of His Passion and amid His signs.

[Note: [Col. 0049D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter V.] Again, by the name “clouds” the holy prophets are signified. Thus the Psalmist says: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Psalm 17:14); that is, knowledge was hidden in the prophets, who, before the Lord’s coming, bore immense mysteries pregnant with hidden sacraments, and their meaning was darkened to the eyes of those who looked upon them.

[Note: [Col. 0049D] In the same place.] Again, by the name “clouds” the holy apostles are signified, as the Lord says of them through Isaiah: “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6).

[Note: [Col. 0049D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter XIX, 22.] By the name “clouds” holy preachers are signified, as Elihu says: “The grain desires clouds” (Job 37:11). For what are all the elect except God’s grain, to be stored in the heavenly granaries? Yet grain awaits the rains of clouds in order to grow until it reaches the perfection of fruit; for the mind of the good is watered by the words of preachers, lest it be dried by the sun of carnal desires for want of the moisture of charity.

The heavenly husbandman had seen this grain rising in the world and desiring clouds when He said: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the labourers are few. Pray therefore the Lord of the harvest to send labourers into his harvest” (Matt. 7:37). Thus those who are here called grain are there called harvest; and those who are here called clouds are there called labourers. For holy preachers are indeed both clouds and labourers: clouds by doctrine, labourers by life; clouds, because they pour down through words; labourers, because they do not cease to do what they say. Hence it is added: “And the clouds scatter their light” (Job 37:11). For clouds to scatter their light is for holy preachers to spread examples of life both in speaking and in acting.

[Note: [Col. 0049D] From Book XXI on Job, chapter II.] Again, by the name “clouds” any righteous persons are signified. Thus Isaiah says: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60:7–8). The righteous are said to fly like clouds because they are raised above earthly contagions. They are like doves at their windows because, through the bodily senses, they do not look upon external things with grasping intent, nor does carnal desire draw them outward.

[Col. 0050C] [Note: [Col. 0050D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter V.] By the name “clouds” all unstable persons are expressed. Thus Solomon says: “He who watches the wind does not sow, and he who considers the clouds will never reap” (Eccl. 11:4). By “wind” the evil spirit is signified, who drives the mind by temptations. By the designation “clouds” sinners are expressed, whom the devil drives and calls back now here, now there, as often as he alternates the gusts of his suggestions within their hearts.

[Note: [Col. 0050D] The printed copies read the same sense, though not wholly in the same words.] “He who watches the wind does not sow, and he who considers the clouds will never reap,” because one who fears the temptations of the evil spirit and observes the falls of the wicked despairs of himself: he neither now applies himself to the seed of good work nor afterward is refreshed by the gift of just recompense.

[Note: [Col. 0050D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter XXV.] By the name “clouds” firmness of mind is understood, as Elihu says: “Suddenly the air is condensed into clouds” (Job 37:21). Air, by its very thinness, is dispersed, so that it is not solidified by any firmness; clouds, however, are stronger in proportion as they are denser.

[Note: [Col. 0050D] This was said above in chapter 11.] What, then, is signified by air except the minds of worldly people, which, devoted to the innumerable desires of this life, are scattered here and there, fluid like air? What is meant by clouds except the firmness of the mind? Air is condensed into clouds when unstable minds are strengthened by the grace of the divine regard with the solidity of virtue, so that, by sound understanding, they gather themselves within the bosom of the heart and do not dissolve into vain thoughts.

Peter had been air when, scattered by earthly desires, concern for fishing, passing over him like a breeze, drove him for the sustenance of the flesh. All the apostles, too, had been air: they had already learned lofty things through the Law, but did not yet think firmly through faith. But suddenly air was condensed into clouds, because through the regard of heavenly grace the unstable hearts of fishermen were transformed into the firmness of preachers. Their weak thoughts became dense by thinking strong things; through love of the clouds they received the waters of knowledge; they watered the earth beneath with the words of preaching; and, their ministry completed, they returned to the hidden places of heaven and, their labour finished, came to eternal rest.

[Note: [Col. 0051D] From Book XX on Job, chapter XX, 22.] By the name “clouds” temporal goods are signified, as blessed Job says: “My safety passed away like a cloud” (Job 30:15). A cloud rises high, but a gust drives it onward in its course. Such indeed are the temporal goods of the wicked. They seem to raise themselves high through exalted rank; yet every day they are driven onward in the course of life, as though by certain gusts of their mortality. Safety, therefore, passes like a cloud, because the glory of the perverse, though lofty, is not fixed.

[Note: [Col. 0051D] From Book VIII on Job, chapter X, 114.] By the name “clouds” the hearts of the proud are signified, as blessed Job says: “As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so he who descends into hell does not rise” (Job 7:6). A cloud is suspended aloft, but, thickened, it is driven by the wind to race along; by the sun’s heat it is dispersed and vanishes. So indeed do human hearts become: through the capacity of reason given to them, they rise to high things, but driven by the blast of the evil spirit, they are dragged here and there by the corrupt motions of desire. Yet at the searching regard of the heavenly Judge, they melt as under the heat of the sun; and once handed over to places of punishment, they return no more to the activity of life.

Therefore the holy man, expressing the presumption and ruin of the human race, says: “As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so he who descends into hell shall not rise.” It is as though he said plainly: He who, through pride, hastens toward destruction fails in his ascent. If guilt once drags him to punishment, mercy no longer brings him back to pardon.

## CHAPTER XIII. ON WINDS

In Holy Scripture, when “wind” is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies the devil; sometimes the devil’s temptation; sometimes passing prosperity; sometimes pride; sometimes any transitory thing; sometimes the upheaval of the strict Judge. But when “winds” are spoken of in the plural, the souls of the saints are understood.

[Note: [Col. 0052D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XII, after the middle.] By the name “wind” the evil spirit is signified, as blessed Job says concerning the condemnation of the ungodly: “A burning wind shall carry him away” (Job 27:21). For what is this burning wind except the evil spirit, who kindles the flames of desires in the heart in order to drag it to eternal punishments? Thus any perverse person is said to be carried away by a burning wind, because the plotting evil spirit, who inflames every living person toward vices, drags the dying person to torments.

The mind of every elect person is tempered against the burning of this wind when the heat of vices is extinguished in it and the flame of carnal desires grows cold. Hence Holy Church joyfully cries out in praise of her Bridegroom: “I sat beneath the shadow of him whom I desired” (Song 2:2). But the burning wind carries away the wicked because the evil spirit, having now kindled him with the fire of perverse desire, afterward snatches him away to the flames of Gehenna.

[Note: [Col. 0052D] From Book II on Job, chapter XXVI, at the beginning, 36.] By the name “wind” the temptation of evil spirits is signified, as is said to blessed Job concerning the death of his children: “While your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother, suddenly a violent wind rushed from the region of the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house. It fell and crushed your children, and they died” (Job 1:18–19).

The region of the wilderness is the abandoned multitude of unclean spirits. Because it forsook the blessedness of its Creator, it has, as it were, lost the hand of its cultivator. A violent wind comes from this region and throws down the house because a strong temptation steals in from unclean spirits and overturns the conscience from its state of tranquillity. The house stands upon four corners because the solid structure of our mind is upheld by prudence, temperance, courage, and justice. It rests upon four corners because the whole building of good work rises in these four virtues. Thus too the four rivers of Paradise water the earth, because when the heart is watered by these four virtues, it is tempered against every heat of carnal desire.

Yet sometimes, when sloth creeps into the mind, prudence grows cold; for when it lies numb in weariness, it does not foresee what is to come. Sometimes, when some pleasure steals into the mind, our temperance withers; for insofar as we are led toward present pleasure, we are restrained the less from what is unlawful. Sometimes fear insinuates itself into the heart and disturbs the strength of our courage; and we prove the weaker against adversity insofar as we fear, with excessive love, to lose certain things. Sometimes self-love enters the mind and by a hidden movement diverts it from the rectitude of justice; and insofar as it neglects to surrender itself wholly to its Creator, it resists the law of justice in itself.

Therefore the violent wind shakes the four corners of the house when powerful temptation agitates the four virtues by hidden motions. And the house, as though its corners were shaken, is overthrown when the conscience is troubled as the virtues are assaulted. Within these four corners of the house the children feast, because within the hidden places of the mind—which is chiefly raised to the summit of highest uprightness by these four virtues—the other virtues, like offspring of the heart, nourish one another.

For the gift of the Spirit, which first forms prudence, temperance, courage, and justice in the subject mind, then moderates that same mind in seven virtues so as to give it wisdom against folly, understanding against dullness, counsel against rashness, courage against fear, knowledge against ignorance, and fear against pride.

Yet sometimes, when our mind is supported by the fullness and abundance of so great a gift, if it immediately enjoys security in these gifts, it forgets from whom it has them and thinks that it possesses from itself what it never sees absent from itself. Therefore the same grace sometimes rightly withdraws itself and shows the presumptuous mind how weak it is in itself. We truly recognize the source of our good things when, as though by losing them, we perceive that we cannot preserve them by ourselves.

For the sake of this discipline of teaching humility, it often happens that, when an occasion of temptation rushes upon us, such folly strikes our wisdom that the troubled mind does not know how to meet impending evils or how to prepare itself against temptation. Yet by that very folly the heart is wisely taught: because it becomes foolish for a moment, it afterward becomes wiser in a truer and humbler way; and the wisdom that seems to be lost is thereby possessed more securely.

Sometimes, while the mind raises itself in pride through understanding lofty things, it languishes in grave dullness over low and insignificant matters, so that one who swiftly penetrated the highest things suddenly sees even the lowest things closed to him. Yet this very dullness preserves understanding for us when it withdraws it, because it humbles the heart for a moment and confirms it more truly for the understanding of lofty things.

Sometimes, while we delight in carrying out everything with the weightiness of counsel, when the pressure of an arising situation strikes, we are carried away by sudden rashness; and we who believed that we had always lived with order are suddenly devastated by inner confusion. Yet through the instruction of this same confusion we learn not to attribute our counsels to our own strength; and we are restored all the more maturely to gravity, insofar as we return to it as though it had been lost.

Sometimes, while the mind strongly despises adversities, when events of adversity arise, violent fear strikes it. Yet, shaken by this fear, it learns to whom it should attribute its courage in having stood firmly in certain matters; afterward it retains courage the more strongly because, when fear suddenly came upon it, it saw this courage as though already escaped from itself.

Sometimes, while we rejoice that we know great things, we grow numb through the blindness of sudden ignorance. But insofar as the eye of the mind is closed for a moment by ignorance, it is afterward opened more truly to knowledge, so that, instructed by the scourge of its blindness, it may know from whom it has knowledge itself.

Sometimes, while we arrange everything devoutly and congratulate ourselves that we possess the full inward tenderness of piety, we are struck by a certain hardness of mind. But, as though hardened, we recognize to whom we must attribute the gifts of piety which we have received; and piety, seeming to have been extinguished, is received more truly when, as though lost, it is loved more greatly.

Sometimes, while the mind rejoices that it is subject to divine fear, it suddenly becomes stiff through a moderating pride. Yet it is then greatly afraid because it does not fear; it quickly bends itself once more to humility, and receives it all the more firmly because, by seeming to lose it, it has weighed the value of that virtue.

Therefore, when the house is overthrown, the children die: because, when the conscience is disturbed in temptation, the virtues born in the heart are, for a moment, overwhelmed and deprived of the benefit of their own knowledge. Yet these children live inwardly through the Spirit while outwardly they die in the flesh, because our virtues, though in the time of temptation they fail for a moment from the soundness of their state through disturbance, nevertheless remain whole in the root of the mind through perseverance of intention.

With them three sisters also die, because charity is sometimes troubled in the heart by chastisements, hope is shaken by fear, and faith is assaulted by questions. For we often grow numb, as though estranged from the Creator’s love, when we are wearied by a scourge beyond what we think fitting for us. Often, when the mind fears more than is necessary, it weakens its own confidence of hope. Often, when the mind is stretched by immeasurable questions, disturbed faith grows weary as though it would fail.

Yet the daughters who die when the house is shaken still live, because although this disturbance announces that hope, faith, and charity perish within the conscience, perseverance in right intention keeps them alive before God’s eyes. Hence the servant who brings this news alone escapes, because the discernment of the mind remains unharmed even amid temptations. The servant acts so that Job may receive his children through mourning, when a grieving mind, informed by discernment, preserves in fullness the powers it had begun, as it seemed, to lose.

This, moreover, is wondrously arranged for us by providence: that our mind may never be struck by the assault of sin. For a person would think himself of great strength if he never felt within the hidden places of his mind any failure of those very powers. But when he is shaken by a rushing temptation and is wearied, as it seems, beyond endurance, then the protection of humility is revealed to him against the snares of his enemy; and from that which makes him fear that he will fall feebly, he receives the means of standing strongly.

[Note: [Col. 0053D] From Book XX on Job, chapter XXIV, at the beginning, 25.] By the name “wind” passing prosperity is shown, as blessed Job says: “You lifted me up, and, placing me as it were upon the wind, you dashed me down violently” (Job 30:22). For what is signified by wind except the prosperity of this passing life? But because the glory of the present life is seen as though on high and is secured by no stability, one who delights in temporary prosperity is lifted up and placed, as it were, upon the wind: the breeze of fleeting happiness raises him only in order that it may suddenly cast him down more grievously into the depths.

Since Holy Church, signified by blessed Job, is held in honour by all, what are the weak within her, who rejoice in passing success, except persons apparently lifted up and set upon the wind? For when the breeze of prosperity passes away in a following time of persecution, their elevation immediately collapses; and, suddenly falling, they learn that when previously raised they had been seated upon the wind.

[Note: [Col. 0055D] Alternatively: “had given themselves to the wind.” Thus the printed Gregory has it.] These words, moreover, fit blessed Job’s own person in a special sense—not according to what he was, but according to what he seemed to be. Fleeting prosperity had not raised his mind, for amid so great an abundance of possessions he always kept it low by a wonderful weight of virtue. But according to what could be seen outwardly, he who was humble in his own eyes was elevated in the eyes of others. He was, as it were, set upon the wind and violently dashed down because, supported by external goods, he seemed to fall from that by which he was thought to rise.

Yet the holy man did not suffer this fall in his mind, because no adversity casts down one whom no prosperity corrupts. Whoever clings to truth does not submit in any way to vanity. For since he had fixed the purpose of his thought within by a firm step, all that is outwardly done in changeable fashion did not reach the citadel of his mind.

[Note: [Col. 0055D] From Book XX on Job, chapter XXIX, 28.] By the name “wind” the swelling of pride is understood, as the prophet says concerning malicious people: “They drew in wind like dragons” (Jer. 14:6). For what is signified by dragons except malicious people? Wind signifies the inflation of pride. Thus the perverse draw in wind like dragons when they are puffed up with malicious pride.

[Note: [Col. 0055D] From Book X on Job, chapter XX, 22.] By the name “wind” any transitory thing is signified, as blessed Job says in the person of the weak: “You took away my desire like the wind” (Job 30:15). What is understood by the name “wind” except a transitory thing? Wind takes away desire when any transitory thing destroys the longing for eternity.

[Note: [Col. 0055D] These words occur in the explanation of: “I have been reduced to nothing” (Job 30:15).] The faithful person declares that he suffers what he grieves to see suffered by those whom he loves: they despise heavenly promises and desire earthly things; and if at any time some longing for eternity arises in their mind, it is quickly scattered by the arising pleasure of transient things.

[Note: [Col. 0056D] Gregory has something similar near the end of Homily 18 on Ezekiel.] By the name “wind” the upheaval of the final judgment is understood, as we have learned from the testimony of the prophet Ezekiel, who, contemplating the terror of that judgment, says: “And I saw, and behold, a storm-wind came from the north” (Ezek. 1:4). By “wind” is signified the disturbance of the last judgment; by “north,” the coldness of sinners. Thus the storm-wind comes from the north because the cause of sins requires that the upheaval of the strict judgment disturb all the elements together.

[Note: [Col. 0056D] From Book XIX on Job, chapter IV, at the beginning.] By the speed and loftiness of winds, the souls of the saints are customarily signified, as the Psalmist says of God: “Who walks upon the wings of the winds” (Psalm 103:3), that is, who transcends the powers of souls. Again blessed Job says: “Who gave weight to the winds” (Job 28:25). The Lord gave weight to the winds because, as heavenly wisdom fills souls, He makes them weighty through the maturity bestowed upon them—not with that heaviness of which it is said: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4:3).

For it is one thing to be weighty through counsel, another through sin; one thing to be weighty through constancy, another through guilt. The latter heaviness bears the weight of a burden; the former, the weight of virtue. Souls therefore receive weight so that they may no longer fly apart from their attention to God with a light motion, but stand fixed in Him with the weighty steadiness of constancy.

That people was still lightly moved of whom it is said through the prophet: “He went wandering in the way of his heart. I saw his way and let him go” (Isa. 57:17–18). But the weighty counsel of the heart drives out every instability of wandering. Since there are souls which, through a light movement, now desire this thing and now that, almighty God does not lightly assess those unstable fluctuations of the mind: by leaving it, He judges the wandering of the heart. But when He regards it through grace, He fixes the wandering mind in the steadiness of counsel.
