Therefore it is rightly said: “Who gave weight to the winds,” because when He mercifully deigns to regard the light movements of the mind, He immediately forms it into the maturity of constancy. Or certainly, to give weight to the winds is to temper the glory granted in this life to the elect for their virtues with an admixture of weakness.

## CHAPTER XIV. ON THE SOUTH WIND

In Holy Scripture, by the name “south wind” there is sometimes signified the Holy Spirit; sometimes Judaea; sometimes a lax way of life; sometimes any person fervent in spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0056D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter XXIII, 24; and Book IX, chapter XV, 16: almost the same sense, though the same thing is written in different words.] By the name “south wind” the Holy Spirit is understood, as is said in the Song of Songs: “Arise, north wind; and come, south wind; breathe upon my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song 4:16). By the north wind the evil spirit is understood. By the south wind, which is indeed a warm wind, the Holy Spirit is fittingly signified, for when anyone is touched by Him, he is freed from the torpor of his iniquity.

The north wind is commanded to arise, so that the adversary spirit, which constricts the hearts of mortals, may flee. The south wind comes and breathes upon the garden so that its spices may flow: for when the human mind is filled by the coming of the Holy Spirit, the renown of virtues is immediately scattered from it. Thus the tongue of the saints, like a garden breathed upon by the south wind, may rightly say: “We are the sweet fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2:15).

[Col. 0057A] [Note: [Col. 0057D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter 26.] By the name “south wind” Judaea is understood, as the Lord, speaking through Isaiah of the conversion of the Gentiles, says: “I will say to the north: Give; and to the south: Do not hinder” (Isa. 43:6). As the north signifies the Gentiles, so the south signifies Judaea, which was warmed, as it were, by the noonday sun because, when the Redeemer appeared in the flesh, it was the first to receive the fervour of faith.

Therefore the north is told, “Give,” when the Gentiles are commanded to offer God the gifts of their faith.

[Note: [Col. 0057D] Homily 18 on Ezekiel.] And because, when the Gentiles were converted to faith, Judaea first opposed them, although it was appointed to receive into the recompense of heavenly rewards those who had formerly worshipped idols, Peter was told after the conversion of the Gentiles: “Why did you enter in to men having the foreskin and eat with them?” (Acts 11:4). Therefore the south is commanded not to hinder, because Hebrews standing in the faith are commanded not to condemn the life of the Gentiles by rejecting them.

[Note: [Col. 0058D] From Book VII on Job, chapter XIV, at the beginning, 17.] By the name “south wind” a lax way of life is signified, as Job says: “Consider the paths of Theman, the ways of Saba, and wait a little” (Job 6:19). Theman means “south wind,” and Saba means “net.” What, then, is signified by the south wind, which relaxes limbs stiffened by cold, except laxity in living? And what is shown by the net except the binding force of action? Those who, with an undisciplined mind, desire earthly things do not walk freely toward God, but bind themselves in their disordered undertakings. When they become entangled in the lax actions of their own thought, they set their feet, as it were, in the bonds of a net, where they will remain.

For just as some are drawn back to sins they have already overcome by certain open and unconquered faults, so others return to things they had left behind through certain matters veiled under the name of respectability or the honour of praise. There are many who no longer covet what belongs to others and, having begun to love quiet, separate themselves from the conflicts of this world. Instructed by sacred words, they thirst for them; they long to be free for heavenly contemplation. Yet they do not abandon the land of family possessions with the liberty of a perfect mind. While they often serve it lawfully, they become entangled also in the unlawful conflicts of this world.

While they desire diligently to protect earthly goods, they abandon the rest of heart that they sought. While their fleeing property is protected by continual provision, the word of divine knowledge conceived in the mind is scattered; for, according to the sentence of Truth, thorns choke the seed that has sprung up when the importunate cares of earthly matters drive God’s word from the memory (Matt. 13:7; Luke 8:14). Thus those walk in a net with relaxed steps who, because they do not wholly leave the world, bind themselves as they walk so that they cannot walk.

There are others who not only do not covet what belongs to others, but even leave behind everything that they possess in the world. They cast themselves aside, seek no glory of the present life, separate themselves from the affairs of this world, and trample underfoot nearly every success that smiles upon them. Yet they remain bound by the tie of fleshly kinship; while they serve indiscriminately the love of relatives, they often return through family affection to things which they had already subdued by despising them for their own sake. And while they love their fleshly relatives more than is necessary, being drawn outward they are separated from the parent of the heart.

We have often seen people who, as far as their own purpose is concerned, no longer have desires for the present life and have left the world in deed and profession, but who nevertheless, for the disordered affections of relatives, burst into law courts, occupy themselves with disputes over earthly matters, abandon the freedom of inward quiet, and rebuild within themselves the worldly pursuits they had long ago destroyed.

Where, then, do such persons walk except in a net? A life already begun in perfection had released them from the present age, but disordered love of earthly kinship binds them. Those who pursue the reward of the eternal promise with earnest discipline and steps not relaxed, as they despise themselves for divine love, so they set aside everything by which they perceive themselves hindered. When it is necessary for God’s sake, they serve those whom they are able to serve; but for God’s sake they withhold even private services from relatives.

But undiscerning minds do not know this rule of life; and in proportion as they seek the ways of God laxly, so they foolishly turn back toward the ways of the world. Thus the holy man rightly mentions the paths of Theman after “south wind,” and the ways of Saba after “net,” because those whom the south wind of a reprobate time has relaxed are indeed held fast by the net of entanglement.

In describing the deeds of the wicked, he rightly bids us consider these things, because we love to act perversely, yet judge these actions when we see them in others. What we think should be judged less severely in ourselves, we recognize as shameful in another’s conduct. Thus the mind returns to itself and blushes to do what it reproves; and, as an ugly face displeases when seen in a mirror, the mind sees within itself what is contrary when it beholds a similar life. He says, therefore: “Consider the paths of Theman, the ways of Saba, and wait a little.” It is as though he said plainly: Observe the losses of another’s laxity, and then you will take firmer hope from eternal things if with the right eye of the heart you see what displeases in others.

It is well said: “Wait a little.” For often, while the brevity of the present life is loved as though it would endure for a long time, the mind is broken away from eternal hope and, delighting in present things, is struck by the darkness of despair. When it has supposed that much time remains for it to live, it suddenly leaves life and finds the eternal things that it can no longer avoid. Therefore it is rightly said to wait a little, because what follows without end is immeasurable, while everything that ends is insignificant. What runs the course of its time so as not to exist ought not to seem long to us.

[Note: [Col. 0058D] From Homily 19 on Ezekiel.] By the name “south wind” any person fervent in spirit is signified, as Ezekiel says: “And he led me out by the southern way, and behold, a gate that faced south” (Ezek. 40:24). As sinners are signified by the coldness of the north, so those fervent in spirit are signified by the southern way. Set aflame by the heat of the Holy Spirit, they increase in virtues as though in noonday light.

It should be noted that in the spiritual building one entrance opens to the east, another to the north, and another to the south. By the east are signified beginners; by the north, those who have fallen; by the south, those fervent in spirit. The gate to the east, therefore, is faith, because through it the true light rises in the mind. The gate to the north is hope, because anyone situated in sins utterly perishes if he despairs of pardon. Thus one who has been extinguished through his own iniquity must be revived by hope in mercy. The gate to the south is charity, because it burns with the fire of love. In the southern region the sun is brought high, because through charity the light of faith is raised in love for God and neighbour.

Therefore the gate to the east stands open so that those who have rightly begun the sacraments of faith and afterward have not been plunged into any depth of vice may attain hidden joys. The gate to the north stands open so that those who, after beginning in warmth and light, have fallen away into the coldness and darkness of their sins may return to pardon through penitential compunction and may know the true joy of inward recompense. The gate to the south stands open so that those who burn with holy desires in virtues may daily penetrate, through spiritual understanding, the mysteries of inward joy.

Yet amid these matters one may ask why there are four regions of the world, while this building is described as having not four gates but three. This would rightly be asked if the prophet had seen a bodily rather than a spiritual building. For Holy Church—the spiritual building—has only three gates by which it reaches hidden joys: faith, hope, and charity. Thus one advances toward the inner court through only three gates, because one reaches hidden joys through faith, hope, and charity.

## CHAPTER XV. ON THE NORTH

In Holy Scripture, by the name “north” there is sometimes signified the evil spirit; sometimes the Gentile world; sometimes the coldness of sins.

[Note: [Col. 0059D] From Book XVII on Job, chapter XIV; and especially the Homilies on Ezekiel.] By “the north” the evil spirit is understood, as blessed Job, speaking of the Lord and of that same devil, says: “Who stretches out the north over the void” [Col. 0059D] (Job 26:7). For, since the north wind binds in cold, the numbness of the evil spirit is not inappropriately denoted by the name “north.” Isaiah also attests this, declaring that the devil said: “I will sit upon the mount of the covenant, on the side of the north” (Isa. 14:13). For the evil spirit held the mount of the covenant, because he subjugated through faithlessness the Jewish people who had received the Law. Whenever he possesses the hearts of teachers, the devil presides over the mount of the covenant; and he sits also on the sides of the north, because he possesses the cold minds of human beings. Therefore the devil is rightly said to be stretched out over the void, because [Col. 0060A] he possesses those hearts which are not filled with the grace of divine love.

[Note: [Col. 0059D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter XXVI.] By “the north” the Gentile world is denoted, as Elihu says in the book of blessed Job: “From the north gold shall come” (Job 37:22). For what is denoted by the north except the Gentile world, constricted by the cold of sin? And what is expressed by gold except faithful souls? Hence Jeremiah says concerning certain persons who were growing lukewarm toward good: “How the gold has grown dark; the finest color has changed” (Lam. 4:1). He grieved that the gold had grown dark, because he saw in some persons the brightness of innocence turned into the blackness of guilt. Thus gold is said to come from the north, because, through the regard of the Redeemer’s grace, precious life in the holy [Col. 0060B] Church is multiplied for God from the Gentile world, formerly cold with the numbness of faithlessness. For gold comes from the north when true faith in the Lord shines forth from idol-worshipers themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0060D] From Homily II on Ezekiel I, in the exposition of these words: “And in its midst the likeness of four living creatures.”] By “the north” the coldness of sinners is denoted, as the prophet Ezekiel, beholding the final judgment that will take place for striking sinners, says: “And I saw, and behold, a storm wind came from the north” (Ezek. 1:4). For what else is understood by a storm wind except the disturbance of judgment? And what is understood by the name north except the coldness of sinners? The storm wind comes from the north because, indeed, the cause of sins demands that the shaking of strict judgment should disturb all the elements together. For the terror of the final disturbance is said to come from that source from which it is generated. Since the judgment of final disturbance is brought about to strike the cold [Col. 0060C] minds of sinners, the storm wind is rightly reported to come from the north. This shaking is fittingly called a storm wind, because on that day the hearts of all who are found in mortal flesh will be stirred by exceeding fear.

## CHAPTER XVI. ON LIGHTNING.

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of lightning or thunderbolt are denoted sometimes the arousing of heavenly fear, sometimes the miracles of the saints, and sometimes the sentences of the final judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0060D] From Homily V on Ezekiel.] By “lightning” is understood the arousing of divine terror, as Ezekiel says: “And this was [Col. 0060D] the vision, moving to and fro in the midst of the living creatures: a brightness of fire, and lightning coming forth from the fire” (Ezek. 1:13). For the Holy Spirit is customarily signified by fire, of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12:49). When the carnal mind receives the Holy Spirit, it is kindled with spiritual love and mourns the evil which it has committed. And the earth burns when, with conscience accusing itself, the sinner’s heart is set aflame and burned in the pain of repentance. But divine terror is denoted by the name lightning. Therefore the Holy Spirit, a brightness of fire and lightning coming forth from the fire, is said to move to and fro in the midst of the living creatures because, filling the whole Church, he casts from himself flames of love into the hearts of the elect, so that, in the manner of lightning, he may strike through terror and kindle to his love hearts grown numb.

[Note: [Col. 0061D] These words occur shortly after those above.] A brightness of fire, and lightning coming forth from the fire, moves to and fro among the winged creatures, because the Holy Spirit makes himself present at once to individuals and to all; he kindles those whom he touches, and enlightens those whom he kindles, so that, after their former coldness, once kindled they may burn, and through the fire of love which they have received may give forth flames of example. For lightning coming forth from this fire strikes numb minds; by striking, it awakens and inflames them, so that, burning and shining alike after the love of him, they may run.

55 [Note: [Col. 0061D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter XXI.] By “lightnings” are denoted the miracles of holy persons, [Col. 0061B] as the Lord says to blessed Job: “Will you send forth lightnings, and will they go and, returning, say to you, ‘Here we are’?” (Job 38:35). For what is expressed by lightnings except the miracles of holy preachers? Lightning comes forth from clouds, just as wonderful works are shown through holy preachers. They are customarily called clouds because they both flash with miracles and rain with words. And because human hearts, after they have not been moved through preaching, are disturbed by these flashes of miracles, we learn from the prophet’s testimony, who says: “You shall multiply lightnings and trouble them” (Ps. 17:15).

[Note: [Col. 0061D] All versions read this passage, verse 15, in the third-person present perfect.] As if he said: When they do not hear the words of your preaching, they are troubled through the miracles of preachers. Therefore it is said to blessed Job: “Will you send forth lightnings, and will they go and, returning, say to you, ‘Here we are’?” Understand: “to me.” For lightnings go forth when preachers flash with miracles and, returning, pierce the hearts of hearers with heavenly things. But on returning they say, “Here we are,” when they attribute to God’s power, not to themselves, whatever they know they have accomplished with strength. For what is it to say to God, “Here we are”? A certain obedience is declared in this expression. Thus for holy preachers to say, on returning, “Here we are,” is to ascribe praise to the grace of him from whom they perceive that they have received victory in battle, lest they attribute to themselves what they do. Lightnings can indeed go forth by acting, but they cannot return by being proud.

Let us see lightning going forth. Peter said to a certain lame man: “Silver [Col. 0061D] and gold I do not have; but what I have, this I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, arise and walk.” And, taking him by the right hand, he raised him; and immediately his feet and soles were strengthened, and, leaping up, he stood and walked (Acts 3:6–7). But when the crowd of Jews had been stirred by this deed, let us now see the returning lightning, which says: “Men of Israel, why do you marvel at this, or why do you look at us as though by our own power or ability we had made this man walk? The God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his servant [Col. 0062A] Jesus” (ibid., 12–13); and a little later: “Of whom we are witnesses; and faith in his name has strengthened this man whom you see and know, and the faith that is through him has given him this perfect health in the sight of you all” (ibid., 15–16). Thus the lightning returns when Peter performs a miracle and does not attribute to himself what he does. Therefore lightnings go forth when holy preachers display wonderful works, but in returning say, “Here we are,” when, in what they do, they have recourse to the power of their author.

[Note: [Col. 0062D] From Book XXXIV on Job, chapter V, 13.] By “thunderbolts” are expressed the dreadful sentences of the final judgment, as the Lord, speaking to blessed Job concerning the devil’s condemnation, says: “He will send thunderbolts against him, and they shall not be borne elsewhere” (Job [Col. 0062B] 41:14). For what is denoted by the designation “thunderbolts” except those dreadful sentences of the final judgment? They are called thunderbolts because they burn forever those whom they strike. Paul had seen the thunderbolt come upon the devil when he said: “Whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thess. 2:8). But these thunderbolts which will be sent against him will not be borne elsewhere, because then, while the righteous rejoice, they strike the reprobate alone. For after the threshing of this present life, in which wheat now groans beneath the chaff, the fan of that final judgment will so distinguish between wheat and chaff that neither will the chaff pass into the wheat-storehouse, nor will the grains of the storehouse fall into the fire [Col. 0062C] of the chaff. Therefore those thunderbolts touch no other place, because with their fire they burn not the grains but the chaff.

## CHAPTER XVII. ON THUNDER.

In Sacred Scripture, by “thunder” is understood sometimes the incarnate Lord Jesus Christ, and sometimes the preaching of heavenly terror.

[Note: [Col. 0062D] From Book XXIX on Job, chapter XIII, 15, after the middle.] By “thunder” the incarnate Lord is understood. Brought forth to our knowledge, as though from a meeting of clouds, through the converging prophecy of the ancient Fathers, he appeared visibly among us and sounded forth terribly those things that were above us. Hence the holy apostles themselves, begotten by his grace, were called Boanerges, that is, “sons of thunder.”

[Col. 0062D] [Note: [Col. 0062D] From the passage just marked.] By “thunder” is understood the preaching of heavenly terror. Thus the Lord questions blessed Job, saying: “Who gave a course to the most violent rain, and a way to sounding thunder?” (Job 38:25). For the most violent rain is the immense force of preaching. But the way of thunder is the preaching of heavenly terror. When human hearts receive this terror, they are shaken. But any preacher can give words to the ears; he cannot open hearts. Unless almighty God alone, through inward grace, invisibly grants the words of preachers access to the hearts of hearers, preaching received by the hearer’s ear is received in vain, since a deaf heart prevents it from reaching within [Col. 0063A]. The Lord declares that he gives the most violent rain its course and sounding thunder its way: when he grants words of preaching, he pierces hearts through terror.

The outstanding preacher Paul, while he thundered terribly concerning heavenly mysteries and saw that he could not have this way from himself, exhorted his disciples, saying: “Praying also together for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ” (Col. 4:3). 58 Therefore, though he spoke mysteries, he prayed that the Lord would open in the hearts of hearers a door for those same mysteries. He already had thunder, indeed, but sought that a way for it should be given to him from above. Again he indicated who gives this way, saying: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters; but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3:7).

## CHAPTER XVIII. ON SNOW.

In Sacred Scripture, by “snow” are denoted sometimes the brightness of heavenly life, sometimes the cold hearts of the wicked, sometimes the exalted hearts of saints, and sometimes the visitation of heavenly judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0063D] From Book XXXII on Job, chapter XVII, after the middle, 23.] By “snow” is denoted the brightness of heavenly life, as Jeremiah says concerning the Nazarites: “Her Nazarites were whiter than snow, brighter than milk, redder than old ivory, more beautiful than sapphire” (Lam. 4). For what is denoted by the name Nazarites except the life of those who are abstinent and continent, a life said to be whiter than snow and brighter than milk? Snow freezes from water which comes from above; milk is pressed from flesh nourished in the lower regions. What, then, is shown by snow except the brightness of heavenly life, and by milk except the administration of temporal stewardship? And because continent persons in the Church often perform works so remarkable that many who have maintained a heavenly life, and many who have managed earthly things well, seem to be surpassed by them, they are described as whiter than snow and brighter than milk. Since also by the fervor of their spirit they sometimes seem to surpass the life of the ancient and strong Fathers, it is rightly added: “Redder than old ivory.” For when the term redness is applied, the flame of holy desire is signified. We know that ivory is the bone of large animals. [Col. 0063D] Therefore they are redder than old ivory because, before human eyes, they often appear to possess a more fervent zeal than certain preceding Fathers. To show their whole character together, it is added: “More beautiful than sapphire.” Sapphire is of an ethereal color. And because by their heavenly manner of life they appear to surpass many predecessors who strive toward things above, they are said to have been more beautiful than sapphire.

By “snow” or “hail” are denoted the cold hearts of the wicked, as the Lord asks blessed Job: “Have you entered the storehouses of snow, or seen the storehouses of hail, which I have prepared [Col. 0064A] for the time of the enemy and for the day of battle and war?” (Job 38:22). For what else should be understood in snow or hail except the cold and hard hearts of the wicked? For just as charity is customarily denoted by heat, so malice is customarily denoted in sacred speech by cold. It is written: “As a cistern makes its water cold, so its malice makes the soul cold” (Jer. 6:7). And again: “Iniquity will abound, and the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24:12). Therefore what can more fittingly be understood by the coldness of snow or the hardness of hail than the life of the wicked, which both grows cold through numbness and strikes through the malice of hardness? Yet the Lord tolerates their life, because he preserves them for the testing of his righteous ones. Hence he aptly adds: “Which I have prepared for the time of the enemy and for the day of battle and war,” so that, when our adversary the devil seeks to tempt us, he may employ their manners as weapons of his own against us. For, raging through them, he torments us, but unknowingly purifies us. They become a scourge for our sins; when we are struck through their such life, we are freed from eternal death. Thus it comes about that even the lost life of the reprobate advances the life of the elect, and, while their ruin serves our benefit, it happens by a wondrous dispensation that nothing which perishes should perish for God’s elect.

[Note: [Col. 0064D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter XIV, 17.] By “snow” are denoted the exalted hearts of saints, as Elihu says: “He commands the snow to descend upon the earth” (Job 37:6). Since the Psalmist says: “You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50). [Col. 0064C] What do we understand here by snow except hearts of saints made white by the light of righteousness? Waters are gathered together in the heights so that they may become snow. But when this snow comes down to earth, it is changed again into flowing water. The waters, therefore, are the minds of preachers: as they raise themselves to contemplate things above, they are strengthened by a higher understanding. And when they are carried away in the highest contemplation, they receive the power of steadfastness. But because they are still held on earth by brotherly love, they moderate themselves from their lofty understanding; preaching humbly to the weak, like melting snow they water the hearts of those who are dry. Therefore snow comes from the heavens to the earth when the exalted hearts of saints, already nourished by firm contemplation, descend for brotherly charity’s sake to the humble words of preaching. For as snow covers the earth when it lies upon it, but waters it when it melts, so the strength of saints, through its steadfastness, protects the life of sinners before God; and through its condescension, as though melted, it pours itself upon the dry earth so that it may bear fruit.

And because water is first drawn up from below in order that it may afterward be returned sprinkled from above, all saints, even when they stand on the height of virtue, consider whence they were raised, lest they despise the lowly condition of another’s weakness. Thus the waters return to the lands from which they were lifted, when the righteous, in condescending to sinners, do not cease to remember what they themselves were. Certainly Paul was still water upon the earth [Col. 0065A] when he understood the Law carnally. But, drawn up to heavenly things, he was changed into snow because what he had previously understood weakly he changed into the firmness of true understanding. Yet, condescending to his brethren, he returned, as it were, to the depths as snow, because after the heights of virtue he acknowledges how unworthy he had been, saying: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I received mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. 1:13–14). See how gently he remembers his own weakness, so that he may bear patiently the weaknesses of others. For water, as it were, returned after heaven to the earth from which it had been taken, when Paul, despite the secret things of such great contemplation, remembered that he was a sinner so that he might humbly benefit sinners.

[Col. 0065B] Let us therefore see how this water, destined to be changed into the firmness of snow, is drawn upward. He says: “If we are beside ourselves, it is for God” (2 Cor. 5:13). Let us see how the snow returns to the depths, so that, melting, it may pour itself out. He says: “If we are sober-minded, it is for you” (ibid.). Let us see by what hand it is drawn, so that it may both be lifted while lying low and recalled after being raised up. He says: “The charity of Christ presses us” (ibid., 14). Therefore, since the charity of Christ, which lifts the minds of saints to things above, also shapes them, by a loving moderation, to the humility of condescension for brotherly love’s sake, it is rightly said: “He commands the snow to descend upon the earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0065D] From Book VII on Job, chapter X, 113.] By “snow” is expressed the visitation of heavenly judgment, as blessed Job says: “Upon those who fear frost, snow will fall” (Job 6:16). [Col. 0065C] For what is signified by frost except temporal adversity, and by snow except eternal tribulation coming from above? Frost freezes below, but snow falls from above. And often some people, while fearing temporal adversities, expose themselves to the strictness of eternal visitation. Of them the Psalmist rightly says: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. 13:5). For one now desires freely to defend the truth, but in his very desire, trembling, fears the anger of human power. And when on earth he fears a human being against the truth, he endures from heaven the wrath of that same truth. Another, conscious of his sins, now desires to distribute what he possesses to the needy; yet he fears lest he himself become poor by giving away his goods. And, while tremblingly preparing the supports of the flesh by reserving them, he kills his soul by withholding the nourishment of mercy; and, while he fears earthly want, he cuts himself off from the eternal abundance of heavenly refreshment. Therefore it is rightly said: “Upon those who fear frost, snow will fall,” because those who fear what ought to be trodden underfoot in lowly things suffer what ought to be feared from on high; and, when they refuse to pass through what they could have trampled, they receive a judgment from heaven which they cannot endure.

## CHAPTER XIX. ON HAIL.

[Col. 0066B] In Sacred Scripture, by “hail” are understood sometimes the rebuke of saints, and sometimes the hard and cold hearts of the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 0065D] From Book XXIX on Job, chapter X.] By “hail” is denoted the rebuke of saints, as the Psalmist says: “Before the brightness in his sight the clouds passed, hail and coals of fire” (Ps. 17:13). For clouds pass before the brightness because holy preachers traverse every region of the world through the brightness of miracles. They are also called hail and coals of fire because they both strike through correction and kindle through the flame of charity. The free rebuke of saints is fittingly expressed by the nature of hail itself. Hail, when it comes, strikes; when melted, it waters. But holy men strike the hearts of hearers by threshing them, [Col. 0066C] and pour themselves in by soothing them. For the same Psalmist testifies how they strike, saying: “They shall speak of the power of your fearful deeds; they shall declare your greatness” (Ps. 144:6). And, following this, he adds how they water by soothing: “They shall pour forth the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness, and shall exult in your righteousness” (ibid., 7).

By “hail,” likewise, are denoted the hard and cold hearts of the wicked, as the preceding chapter explains in what we set forth concerning snow: “Have you entered the storehouses of snow, or seen the storehouses of hail?” (Job 38:22).

## THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 0065]

## CHAPTER I. ON BIRDS.

[Col. 0065D]

In Sacred Scripture, by the name “bird” or “flying creature,” when used in the singular, are denoted sometimes our Redeemer, sometimes the devil, and sometimes the human mind; but when used in the plural, sometimes the powers of the air, sometimes the minds of spiritual persons, sometimes proud persons, and sometimes fleeting thoughts.

[Note: [Col. 0065D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter IV, 19, shortly before [Col. 0066D] the end.] By “bird” our Redeemer is denoted, [Col. 0066D] as it is said in Job to the Jewish people: “The bird has not known the path” (Job 28:7). For who is signified here by the name bird except he who, ascending into the heavens, raised up the fleshly body which he assumed? The faithless people of the Jews did not know his paths because they refused to consider the ways of his humility by which he lifted us to the heights.

64 [Note: [Col. 0066D] These matters, in scattered form, are from Book XXXIII on Job, chapter XIV.] By “bird” the devil is denoted, as the Lord says of him to blessed Job: “Will you mock him as a bird?” [Col. 0067A] (Job 40:24). The adversary of the human race is called a bird because of the lightness of his subtle nature. He is a bird because he proudly exalts himself through the subtlety of his nature. He is a bird because he sometimes even pretends, through untamed pride, to be an angel of light. The Lord mocked him as a bird when, in the passion of his only-begotten Son, he showed him the bait of flesh but concealed the snare of divinity.

[Note: [Col. 0067D] These words occur near the end of the chapter.] For he saw what he might take with his mouth, but he did not see what, once seen, his throat would retain. Hence, mocked like a bird, he suffered the snare of Christ’s divinity when he bit the bait of his humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0067D] From Book IX on Job, chapter VII; rather according to St. Gregory’s thought than his words.] By “bird” the human mind is understood, as it is written in the book of blessed Job: “Man is born for labor, and the bird for flight” (Job 5:7). For what is signified by man except our outward human being, that is, the flesh; and what by the designation bird except the inward human being, that is, the mind? Therefore man is born for labor, and the bird for flight: because, in that the flesh is afflicted by scourges, the mind is lifted up to seek higher things, as Paul testifies, saying: “Although our outward human being is corrupted, yet the inward one is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16).

[Note: [Col. 0067D] These words are translated word for word from the indicated passage of Gregory.] Therefore man is born for labor, and the bird for flight, because the mind flies to the heights by the very means through which the flesh labors more harshly in lowly things.

[Note: [Col. 0068D] From Book XIX on Job, chapter I.] By “flying creatures” are denoted the powers of the air hostile to good pursuits, as Truth’s own mouth says in the Gospel that, concerning the seed which fell beside the road, “the birds came and ate it” [Col. 0067C] (Matt. 13:4; Mark 4:4). For evil spirits, besieging human minds, pluck the word of life from memory when they introduce harmful thoughts. Again, to a certain rich man, wise in his pride, it is said: “Foxes have dens and birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8:20; Luke 9:58). Foxes are very deceitful animals, hidden in burrows or caves; and, whenever they appear, they run not by straight paths but by winding turns. Birds, however, as we know, lift themselves into the air on high flight. Thus deceitful and fraudulent demons are denoted by the name foxes, and those same proud demons by the name flying creatures, as though he said: [Col. 0067D] Deceitful and exalted demons find their dwelling in our heart, that is, in the thought of pride; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head, that is, my humility finds no rest in your proud mind.

[Note: [Col. 0068D] From the passage noted above.] By “flying creatures” are denoted the minds of spiritual persons, as the Lord, when he declared the likeness of the kingdom of heaven to a mustard seed, said in the Gospel: “To what is the kingdom of God like, and to what shall I compare it? It is like a mustard seed which a man took and put in his garden, and it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of heaven rested in its branches” [Col. 0068A] (Luke 13:18–19). He himself is the mustard seed, who, planted in the burial-place of the garden, rose up as a great tree. He was a seed when he died, a tree when he rose again: a seed through the humility of the flesh, a tree through the power of majesty. A seed, because “we saw him, and there was no appearance” (Isa. 53:2); but a tree, because he was “beautiful in form beyond the children of men” (Ps. 54). The branches of this tree are holy preachers. And see how widely they spread. What is said of them? “Their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18). Birds rest in these branches because holy souls, which lift themselves above earthly thought by certain wings [Col. 0068B] of virtues, catch their breath from the weariness of this life in the sayings and consolations of these preachers.

[Note: [Col. 0068D] From Book XXVI on Job, chapter XIII, 11.] By “flying creatures” are denoted the minds of the proud, as Elihu says in the book of blessed Job: “Who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth, and instructs us more than the birds of heaven” (Job 3:11). The beasts of the earth are those who, by the practice of carnal life, desire low things. The birds of heaven are those who examine lofty matters through the pursuit of proud curiosity. The former lower themselves below what they are by the way they live; the latter raise themselves beyond what they can attain by their inquiries. The pleasure of the flesh casts the former down among low things; the desire for curiosity lifts the latter up, as it were, among high things. To the former sacred utterance says: “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” [Col. 0068C] (Ps. 31:9); the proud labor of the latter is rebuked when it says: “Do not seek things too high for you, and do not investigate things too strong for you” (Ecclus. 3:12). To the former it says: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and avarice, which is the service of idols” (Col. 3:15). To the latter it says: “Let no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit” (Col. 2:8). Therefore God teaches us above the beasts of the earth and instructs us above the birds of heaven, because, while we recognize what we are, neither the weakness of the flesh casts us down nor the spirit of pride lifts us up. We are neither subjected to low things by sinking down nor puffed up concerning lofty things through pride. Whoever slips through the flesh is laid low by the appetite of beasts; but whoever is exalted in mind is lifted up like birds by a wing of lightness.

[Note: [Col. 0068D] From Book XVI on Job, chapter XIX, 20.] By “birds” are denoted thoughts. Thus, when Abraham offered sacrifice at sunset, birds pressed upon him; he diligently drove them away lest they seize the sacrifice offered (Gen. 15:11). For what do we understand by birds except perverse thoughts? For thoughts which arise often defile even the hearts of the righteous and touch them with the delights of earthly things. But when they are quickly driven away by the hand of holy [Col. 0069A] strictness, there is prompt action lest darkness cover the face of the heart, which unlawful delight had already touched. For intrusive thoughts often press upon us in the very sacrifice of prayer, able to seize or defile what we offer within ourselves while we weep. But when we offer sacrifice to God upon the altar of the heart, let us preserve it, after Abraham’s example, from unclean birds, lest evil spirits and perverse thoughts seize what our mind hopes profitably to offer to God.

## CHAPTER II. ON THE EAGLE.

In Sacred Scripture, by “eagle” are denoted sometimes evil spirits, sometimes the powers of the present age, sometimes, in a spiritual sense, John the Evangelist or the incarnate Lord, sometimes the dignity of the human condition, sometimes the subtle understanding of saints, and sometimes the souls of the elect.

[Note: [Col. 0069D] From Book XXXI on Job, chapter XIX, 33.] By “eagles” evil spirits are expressed, as Jeremiah testifies: “Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven” (Lam. 4:19). For our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of heaven when evil spirits do such great things against us that they seem to surpass even the aerial powers themselves in their inventions of malice.

[Note: [Col. 0069D] From the preceding commentary on Job.] The name “eagle” figures earthly power, as Ezekiel says: “A great eagle, of great wings, with long extension of limbs, full of feathers and variety, came to Lebanon and took the pith of the cedar, and plucked off the top of its branches” (Ezek. 17:3–4). Who is denoted by this eagle except Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon? He is described as having great wings because of the vastness of his army; as having a long extension of limbs because of the length of time; as full of feathers because of his great riches; and as full of variety because of the innumerable adornment of earthly glory. He came to Lebanon and took the pith of the cedar and plucked off the top of its branches because, attacking the height of Judaea, he took away the nobility of its kingdom, as it were the pith of the cedar. And when he carried away into captivity the tender offspring of kings from the summit of their kingdom, [Col. 0069C] he plucked off, as it were, the top of its branches.

By “eagle,” John the Evangelist, in a spiritual sense, or the incarnate Lord is expressed. Thus Ezekiel, [Col. 0069D] describing how he saw the four evangelists under the figure of living creatures, testifies that the faces of a man, lion, ox, and eagle appeared to him in them (Ezek. 1:14, 10), undoubtedly signifying John by the eagle, the fourth creature. For he left the earth in flight because, through subtle understanding, he penetrated the inward mysteries by the living word. John himself also agrees with this prophetic statement in his Revelation, saying: “The first living creature was like a lion; the second living creature like a calf; the third living creature had, as it were, the face of a man; and the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle” (Rev. 4:7).

Although each fittingly applies to an individual evangelist—one setting forth the order of Christ’s human birth, another the death of the calf, as it were, through the slaughter of the world’s sacrifice, another indicating the strength of power as the lion’s roar, and another contemplating the birth of the Word as an eagle gazes upon the rising sun—these four living creatures can nevertheless signify their own head, whose members they are. For he is man, because he truly assumed our nature; calf, because he patiently died for us; lion, because by the strength of his divinity he broke the bond of the death he had assumed; and finally eagle, because he returned to the heaven from which he had come. Thus he is called man in being born, calf in dying, lion in rising again, and eagle in ascending to heaven.

[Col. 0070B] By “eagle” is expressed the dignity of the human condition, as blessed Job says: “My days have passed like an eagle flying toward food” (Job 9:25). The eagle is suspended in very high flight and, by swift exertion, poised in the heavens; but through the appetite of its belly it seeks the earth and suddenly casts itself down from the heights. Thus, thus the human race fell in its first parent from the heights to low things. It had been suspended, as it were, in the freedom of the air through the loftiness of reason, the dignity of its condition; but because it touched forbidden food contrary to the commandment, it came down to earth through the desire of the belly. As it were, it feeds on flesh after flight, because it lost those breathings of free contemplation and delights below in bodily pleasures. Therefore our days pass swiftly like an eagle flying toward food, because the more we seek low things, the more we are prevented from abiding in life.

[Note: [Col. 0070D] In the same place, 1, 2, 3, distinction.] By “eagle” is denoted the subtle understanding of saints, as the Lord asks blessed Job: “Will the eagle rise at your command and make its nest for itself in high places?” (Job 39:30). For what is figured by the eagle except the subtle understanding and exalted contemplation of saints? The keenness of an eagle’s sight surpasses that of all birds, so that no flashing brightness of its own light causes it to close the eyes which it fixes upon the sun’s rays. The eagle rises at God’s command when the life of the faithful, obeying divine commands, is poised in heavenly things. It is said also to make its nest in high places because, despising earthly desires, it is now nourished by hope in heavenly things. It makes its nest in high places because it does not build the dwelling of its mind in an abject and lowly manner of life. Therefore the Lord asks blessed Job, saying: “Will the eagle rise at your command and make its nest in high places?” As if he said: “That to my—[phrase incomplete in source]—I who inwardly inspire, by the grace of hidden generosity, that which I command outwardly.”

[Note: [Col. 0070D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter XXII, §37.] By “eagles” are understood the souls of the elect, as Truth testifies in the Gospel concerning the souls of the faithful as they depart: “Wherever the body shall be, there also the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. XXIV, 28; Luke XVI, 37). As though He plainly said: “Where I, your Redeemer incarnate, preside in the heavenly seat, there, when I free the souls of the elect from the flesh, I shall raise them also to heaven.”

70 CHAPTER III. ON THE DOVE.

In Holy Scripture, the dove sometimes signifies the gentleness of the Lord; sometimes Christ in His entirety, that is, the Head together with the Body; sometimes the Holy Spirit; and sometimes the holy Church.

[Note: [Col. 0071D] From Book XXXII on Job, chapter VII, §6, shortly after the beginning.] By “dove” is understood the gentleness of the Lord, as it is said through the prophet: “The land has been made desolate by the face of the wrath of the dove, and by the face of the wrathful anger of the Lord” (Jer. XXVI, 38). What he had foretold as the wrath of the dove, he then called the anger of the Lord. For the dove is a very simple creature. And because no uneven disturbance of fury enters into God, he called the Lord’s anger “the wrath of the dove.” Thus, in order to show that the force of divine strictness in God is untroubled, he called it both wrath and that of a dove. It is as though he said more plainly: “He who remains gentle inflicts rigorous judgment without being shaken.”

Thus, at the last judgment, remaining in Himself unchangeable, He is altered by no variation or mutability; yet He is by no means manifested to the elect and the reprobate under the same appearance of that unchangeableness. For He will appear calm to the righteous and angry to the unrighteous. For, by the testimony of conscience, they are carried within themselves; hence, though both look upon the one same God, they are not affected in the same way. Their past righteousness shows Him kind to the former, while guilt shows Him terrible to the latter. Therefore, in this passage the Lord’s anger does not mean a disturbance in the divine substance, but the examination of just vengeance upon sinners who are conscious of their own evil. Although they see Him calm in judgment, nevertheless, because they do not doubt that they are to be struck by Him, they imagine Him disturbed according to their own dispositions.

71 This indeed occurs daily in the experience of the present life, so that the hearts of mortals may be taught the character of the coming Judge. When two persons proceed to judgment, one conscious of innocence and the other of guilt, both face the judge while he is still silent, before sentence has been pronounced. Yet the debtor of guilt suspects that the judge’s very silence signifies a grievous wrath against him. This wrath is announced to him not by disturbance in the judge, but by the recollection of his own wickedness. For although sentence does not yet openly declare him guilty, inwardly his conscience already accuses him grievously. On the other hand, the friend of righteousness beholds the countenance of the judge who is to decide; inwardly he rejoices in the testimony of a good recollection, and, because he has nothing within himself to fear, he sees as gracious everything that is within himself.

CHAPTER IV. ON THE TURTLEDOVE.

[Note: [Col. 0072D] From Book VI on Job, chapter XII, §13, far before the end.] By “dove” is signified Christ in His entirety—that is, the Head together with His Body, which is the Church. Hence, in the Law, in the figure of our sacrifice, the throat of a turtledove or dove is commanded to be cut, but not wholly severed (Lev. I, 16), so that after death the head remains attached to the body. For who is our Head except the Redeemer of humankind? Of Him it is written: “He gave Him as Head over the Church, which is His Body” (Eph. I, 22). When the Jews persecuted Him, they sought to blot out His name from the earth. When they saw Him crucified and buried, they believed that they had separated Him from the love of all people.

But the head of the dove or turtledove was cut and yet was not divided from its body. For, because He is the Mediator between God and men—that is, the Head of us all—and because He endured death for us as the sacrifice of true cleansing, He joined all of us to Himself more truly in that very death of His. And by withdrawing Himself visibly from our eyes, He rooted Himself invisibly in our minds. Therefore, after the cutting, the head of the turtledove or dove remains attached to its body, because not even intervening death separates Christ from the Church.

Thus the persecutors accomplished what they had maliciously contrived: 72 they inflicted death in order to cut off from Him the devotion of the faithful. Yet faith grew precisely from the point at which the cruelty of unbelievers believed it had extinguished it. And while they thought that by persecuting His miracles they were cutting them off, they were compelled, without knowing it, to spread them abroad. Therefore the severed head of the dove or turtledove remained attached to the body: our Redeemer indeed suffered for us, but by His Passion He was not separated from us.

By “dove” is signified the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0072C] as is said through Matthew the Evangelist: “Jesus, when baptized, immediately went up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened to Him, and He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and remaining upon Him” (Matt. III, 16). Hence John the Baptist himself also says: “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and He remained upon Him” (John I, 32). Appropriately the reconciling Spirit appeared in a dove, a bird of great gentleness, in order to show, by the appearance of this creature, the simplicity of His own nature. For “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wis. I, 3); and He taught that the one upon whom He descended would be gentle and mild, and would become for the world a herald and minister of heavenly mercy. At the same time, He admonished all who were to be renewed by His grace to approach with simple and pure hearts, according to what is written: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek Him in simplicity of heart; for wisdom shall not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. I, 1).

Appropriately, therefore, the Holy Spirit appeared above the Lord in a dove, for He did not come in order already to strike sins through zeal, but still to bear with them through gentleness. For who could endure His justice, if, before gathering us by gentleness, He had wished to examine our sins with the zeal of uprightness? Therefore, having been made man for men, He showed Himself gentle toward men. He did not wish to strike sinners, but to gather them. He first wished gently to correct them, [Col. 0073A] so that after the world had passed He might have those whom He could save in judgment.

73 By “dove” is signified the holy Church or any elect soul, as the voice of the Bridegroom says to that Church or soul, awaiting the day of the true light as though it were springtime: “Rise up, make haste, my friend, my dove, my fair one, and come; for winter has now passed, the rain has gone and withdrawn; flowers have appeared in our land.” Whether the holy Church or each elect soul, it is the friend of the heavenly Bridegroom through love, a dove through the Spirit, and fair through the beauty of its conduct. When it is now brought forth from the corruption of the flesh, winter has undoubtedly passed for it, because the numbness of this present life departs. The rain likewise has gone and withdrawn, because when it is brought forth to contemplate almighty God in His own substance, drops of words will no longer be necessary, so that the rain of preaching need no longer be poured down: for what it had been less able to hear, it shall see more fully. Then flowers appear in the land, because when the soul begins to taste certain first delights of the life of eternal blessedness, it goes forth fragrant as though already among flowers. After it has gone forth, it will possess them more abundantly in fruit.

CHAPTER V. ON THE COCK.

In Holy Scripture, the cock signifies a holy preacher.

By “cock” is signified the holy preacher, as Solomon says: “There are three things which walk well, and a fourth which proceeds happily: the lion, strongest of beasts, which will fear no encounter; the cock, girded about the loins; and the ram; nor is there a king who can resist him” (Prov. XXX, 29–30). Hence the Lord questions blessed Job, saying: “Who has put wisdom in the inward parts of man, or who has given understanding to the cock?” (Job XXXVIII, 36).

For divinely inspired wisdom is placed in the inward parts of man because, with respect to the number of the elect, it is given not in words alone, 74 but also in their dispositions, so that conscience may live in accordance with what the tongue speaks, and its light may shine more brightly outwardly in proportion as it burns more truly in the heart. Yet it is a matter of great difficulty to examine, by a still subtler exposition, what is added: “Who has given understanding to the cock?”

For who else is signified here but holy preachers, who, amid the darkness of this present life, endeavor by preaching—as it were, by singing—to announce the light to come? For they say: “The night has gone before; but the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII, 12). By their voices they shake off the sleep of our body, crying: “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep” (ibid., 11). And again: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (I Cor. XV, 34). The understanding of teachers ought to be more subtle in proportion as they exercise themselves in penetrating invisible things, as they examine nothing material, and as, while speaking through a bodily voice, they transcend everything that belongs to the body.

Yet such understanding could by no means be fitting for exalted teachers unless the Maker of the highest things Himself supplied it to the singing cock—that is, to the preaching teacher. The cock also receives understanding so that he first discerns the hours of the night and only then utters the cry of awakening. Thus every holy preacher first considers the quality of life in his hearers and only then forms a fitting voice of preaching for their instruction. To discern the hours of the night is, as it were, to judge the deserts of sinners; to discern the hours of the night is to correct the darkness of deeds with an appropriate voice of rebuke.

Thus understanding is bestowed upon the cock from above, because the power of discernment is divinely supplied to the teacher of truth, so that he may know what he should bring to whom, when, and in what manner. For one and the same exhortation is not suitable for all, since an equal condition of character does not bind all alike. Things that benefit some often harm others. Herbs which restore some animals kill others. A light whistle calms horses but excites puppies. A medicine that diminishes one disease adds strength to another. Bread that strengthens the life of the strong kills little children. The speech of teachers must be shaped according to the character of their hearers, so that it may suit each individually and yet never depart from the art of common edification.

For what are the attentive minds of hearers but, as it were, strings stretched [variant: laid out] upon a lyre? The skilled player, in order that they may not produce a discordant song among themselves, strikes them differently. And for this reason the strings render a harmonious melody: though struck by one plectrum, they are not struck with one and the same blow. Therefore each teacher, in order to build up all in the one virtue of charity, must touch the hearts of hearers from one doctrine, but not with one and the same exhortation.

[Note: [Col. 0073D] About the middle of chapter IV these words are read.] We have, moreover, another point which we ought to consider concerning the understanding of this cock: in the deeper hours of night it customarily gives stronger and more prolonged songs; but when morning time is already approaching, it makes altogether lighter and briefer sounds. What does the understanding of this cock indicate to us? It displays the discernment of preachers. When they preach to minds still wicked, they proclaim in loud and lofty tones the terrors of the eternal Judge, because they cry out, as it were, amid the darkness of deep night. But when they recognize that the light of truth is drawing near to the hearts of their hearers, they turn the magnitude of their cry into gentle softness, and set forth not so much the terrible matters of punishments as the pleasing matters of rewards.

Then too they sing with smaller notes, because as morning draws near they preach subtle matters concerning mysteries, so that their followers may hear matters ever more delicate concerning heaven as they approach the light of truth. Those whom the cock’s long cry had awakened while asleep are, when awake, delighted by a shorter song, so that [Col. 0075A] anyone who has been corrected may gladly know, in a subtle manner, the sweet things of the kingdom, though he had formerly feared the adverse things of judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0075D] These words occur near the end of the chapter.] There is yet another point in the cock which must be attentively observed. When it is preparing to utter its song, it first beats its wings and, striking itself, makes itself more wakeful. We see this plainly if we attentively consider the life of holy preachers. For when they set the words of preaching in motion, they first exercise themselves in holy actions, lest, being sluggish in deed within themselves, they awaken others by their voice. Rather, they first shake themselves through exalted deeds and then make others diligent in doing good. They first strike themselves with the wings of their thoughts, because whatever lies uselessly dormant in themselves they discover by vigilant examination and correct by strict rebuke. They first take care to punish their own sins with tears, and then announce the things which must be punished in others.

Therefore they first make a sound with their wings before uttering songs, because before they bring forth words of exhortation, they proclaim in deeds everything that they are to say. And when they are perfectly awake in themselves, then they call others who are sleeping to keep watch. But whence does a teacher possess such great understanding: both to watch perfectly over himself and to call the sleeping to wakefulness by certain stages of his cry; first cautiously to examine the darkness of sins and afterward discreetly to display the light of preaching; to suit each person according to measure and time, and at the same time to show all what they should follow? Whence does he reach to things so great and so subtle, unless he is inwardly taught by Him by whom he was created? Therefore, because praise for such great understanding belongs not to the preacher’s ability but to the Author’s, it is rightly said by that same Author: “Who gave understanding to the cock?” As though He said: “Who but I, who wonderfully created the minds of teachers out of nothing and still more wonderfully trained them to understand hidden things?”

77 CHAPTER VI. ON THE HEN.

In Holy Scripture, the hen sometimes denotes the wisdom of God.

By “hen” is signified the wisdom of God, as it says of itself in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets, how often have I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you would not!” (Matt. XXIII, 37). The name “hen” is not dishonorable. Consider the other birds. Many birds lay eggs before us and warm their young, but no bird grows weak with its chicks as the hen does. We see swallows, geese, and storks away from their nests, and we do not know whether they have young. But we recognize the hen by the weakness of its voice and the looseness of its feathers. It is wholly changed by affection for its chicks; because they are weak, it makes itself weak. Therefore, because we too were weak, the wisdom of God made itself weak, because, as it is written: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. And we saw His glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, [Col. 0076A] full of grace and truth” (John I, 14), so that we may hope beneath His wings.

78 CHAPTER VII. ON THE RAVEN.

In Holy Scripture, the raven sometimes signifies the Gentile world, sometimes the Jewish people, and sometimes any preacher.

[Note: [Col. 0076D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter XVIII, at the beginning, §12.] By “raven” is understood the Gentile world. Hence, when the Lord questions blessed Job, it is said: “Who prepares its food for the raven, when its young cry out to the Lord, wandering because they have no food?” (Job XXXVIII, 41). For what is signified by the raven and its young but the Gentile world, black with sins? Of it the prophet says: “Who gives their food to the beasts, and to the young ravens that call upon Him” [Col. 0076B] (Ps. CXLVI, 9). The beasts receive food when minds once brutish are satisfied with the nourishment of Holy Scripture. Food is given to the young ravens, that is, to the children of the Gentiles, when their desire is refreshed by our manner of life.

This raven was food when the holy Church sought it; but now it receives food because it itself seeks others for conversion. Its young, namely the preachers born from it, do not trust in themselves but in the strength of their Redeemer. Hence it is rightly said: “When its young cry out to the Lord.” For they know that they can do nothing by their own power; and although they hunger, with devout desires, for the gain of souls, they nevertheless pray that this may be accomplished by Him who works all things inwardly. For in true faith they grasp: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (I Cor. III, 7).

The statement, “wandering because they have no food,” means nothing other in this wandering than the desires of preachers burning with zeal. While they yearn to receive peoples into the bosom of the Church, inflamed with great ardor, they direct their desire now toward gathering these, now toward gathering those. For this very agitation of thought is, as it were, a kind of wandering. They pass, as it were, to different places by changing impulses, while in order to unite souls they range with hungry minds through countless ways and diverse regions.

The Jewish people, black through the demerit of unbelief, may also be signified by the raven. Its young are said to cry to the Lord so that food may be prepared by the Lord for that raven, because the holy apostles, born in the flesh from the Israelite people, pour forth prayers to the Lord for their own nation. Thus, as young ravens, they prepare by spiritual understanding the people from which they were carnally born as their parent. Therefore, while its young cry out, food is prepared for the raven: when the apostles pray, the people once faithless are led to knowledge of faith and are satisfied, through the preaching of their children, as though by the voice of fledglings.

Yet in this verse we ought carefully to observe that food is said to be prepared for this raven first while its young cry and afterward while they wander. Food was prepared for the raven while its young cried when, as the apostles preached, Judea heard the word of God and was satisfied with spiritual understanding, at one time in three thousand and at another in five thousand persons. But when, through the multitude of the reprobate, it exercised its cruelty against the preachers and, as it were, killed the life of its young, those same young were scattered throughout all parts of the world. Thus, when their carnal fathers resisted spiritual preaching, they said: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but because you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII, 46), knowing indeed that after the Gentile world believed, Judea too would come to faith. Hence it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in, and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. II, 25–26).

Therefore, because the holy apostles earnestly endeavored both first to preach to those who heard and afterward to show to those who resisted the examples of the converted Gentile world, their young, like hungry chicks, sought food for this raven first by crying and afterward by wandering. For where the young wander, there the raven finds food: when the Jewish people sees, through the labor of the preachers, the Gentile world converted to the Lord, it will someday at last be ashamed of the folly of its unbelief. Then it understands the sayings of Holy Scripture when it realizes that they have previously become known to the Gentiles; and, when the wandering of the young is completed, it opens the mouth of its heart to receive the sacred utterances. For, after the apostles’ journeys throughout the world have been accomplished, it receives spiritually—though late—those things from which, held fast by unbelief, it had long fasted. Because the power of divine might alone works all these things, it is rightly said: “Who prepared food for its raven, when its young cry to the Lord, wandering because they have no food?” Understand: “None but I, who tolerate the unbelieving people while its children exhort it, spare it while they preach, and wait for it to be converted at the end while they wander elsewhere.”

[Note: [Col. 0077D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter VIII.] There is yet another moral interpretation that may be made concerning the raven. After its young are born, it is said to withhold full food from them until they grow black as their feathers develop. It allows them to be afflicted by hunger until, through the blackness of their feathers, its own likeness may be seen in them. They wander here and there in the nest and seek the aid of food with open mouths. But when they begin to grow black, it seeks their food with so much the greater eagerness as it had delayed feeding them for longer.

Certainly the raven is every learned preacher, who cries with a loud voice while bearing, as a kind of blackness of color, the remembrance of his sins and awareness of his own weakness. Disciples are born to him in faith, but perhaps they do not yet know how to consider their own frailty; perhaps they turn their memory away from past sins and therefore do not display the blackness of humility which ought to be assumed against the glory of this world. These open their mouths, as it were, to receive food when they seek instruction concerning exalted mysteries. But their teacher supplies them with the food of more sublime preaching in proportion as he perceives that they are less worthy in grieving over past sins.

He waits and admonishes them first to grow black through the laments of repentance from the brightness of the present life, and then at last to receive the fitting, most subtle nourishment of preaching. The raven beholds the gaping mouths of its young, but first seeks to clothe their bodies with the blackness of feathers. So too the discerning teacher does not administer inward mysteries to the minds of those whom he sees have not yet cast themselves away from this world.

Therefore, in proportion as disciples grow less black outwardly, as it were, through the adornment of this present life, they are filled less inwardly with the food of the word. And the less they empty themselves of bodily glory, the more they fast from spiritual refreshment. But if, in confession of their past life, they produce the groans of their lament as though they were blackening feathers, the teacher immediately flies in contemplation, as a raven considering the refreshment of its young, in order to bring them food from things above. He brings food back to their gaping mouths when, from the understanding he has acquired, he supplies by speech the nourishment of life to hungry disciples. He refreshes them with things above more eagerly in proportion as he knows that they grow black more truly from the brightness of the world through the lamentation of repentance.

Moreover, when the young clothe themselves in the black color of feathers, they promise flight of themselves as well: for the more disciples hold low opinions of themselves and afflict themselves in self-contempt, the more they promise the hope of their own advancement to higher things. Hence the teacher takes greater care to feed quickly those whom he already foresees, by certain signs, may also benefit others. For this reason Paul admonishes Timothy to nourish such feathering young more diligently, saying: “What you have heard from me through many witnesses, entrust to faithful persons who will be fit also to teach others” (II Tim. II, 2).

When this discernment in teaching is cautiously maintained by the preacher, a more abundant supply of preaching is divinely given to him. For when he knows how to sympathize in charity with afflicted disciples, and understands through discernment the suitable time for instruction, he receives greater gifts of understanding, not only for himself but also for those upon whom he expends the efforts of his labor. Hence it is plainly said here: “Who prepares food for its raven, when its young cry out to the day, wandering [Col. 0078D] because they have no food?” For when the young cry in order to be satisfied, food is prepared for the raven: when good hearers hunger for the word of God, greater gifts of understanding are bestowed upon teachers for their refreshment.

82 [Note: [Col. 0077D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XIX, some time [Col. 0078D] after the beginning of §18.] By “ravens” are signified holy preachers, as Solomon says: “The ravens of the torrents shall pluck out the eye that mocks a father and despises the bearing of its mother” (Prov. XXX, 17). All perverse persons mock the Father when they criticize divine judgments. And all heretics, when they despise the preaching of the holy Church and deride its fruitfulness, what else do they do but despise the bearing of their mother? We rightly call that Church their mother too, because those who speak against her go out from her, as John testifies: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us” (I John I, 19).

The ravens come from the torrents when men who are preachers proceed from the streams of the sacred books to defend the holy Church. They too are rightly called ravens, because they do not pride themselves on the light of righteousness, but through the grace of humility confess the blackness of sins in themselves. Hence the Church of the elect also says: “I am black, but beautiful” (Cant. I, 5). And John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (John I, 8). These ravens pluck out the eye of the mocker because they overcome the intention of wicked and obstinate people.

CHAPTER VIII. ON THE OSTRICH.

In Holy Scripture, the ostrich sometimes signifies any hypocrite, sometimes the Synagogue, sometimes the Gentile world, and sometimes hypocrisy.

[Note: [Col. 0079D] From Book XXXI on Job, chapter V, §6.] By “ostrich” is signified the hypocrite, as the Lord says to blessed Job: “The wing of the ostrich is like the wing of the heron and the hawk” (Job XXXIX). Who does not know how greatly the heron and hawk surpass other birds in the speed of their flight? But the ostrich possesses the likeness of their feathers, not the swiftness of their flight. It cannot rise from the ground; it raises its wings in the mere appearance of flight, yet never suspends itself from the ground by flying.

Such indeed are all hypocrites: while they imitate the life of the good, they possess an imitation of holy conduct, but not the truth of holy action. They have wings for flight in appearance, but creep upon the earth in action; for they spread wings in the image of holiness, but, weighed down by the burden of worldly affairs, cannot at all rise from the earth. Hence, rejecting the appearance of the Pharisees, the Lord reproves, as it were, the ostrich’s wing, which performs one thing in deed and displays another in coloring: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly indeed appear beautiful to men, but within are full of the bones of the dead. So also you appear righteous to men, but inwardly you are full of avarice and iniquity” (Matt. XXIII, 27). It is as though He said: “The appearance of the wing seems to lift you up, but the weight of your life presses you down into the depths.” Of this weight the prophet says: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Ps. IV, 3).

We have further reason, in considering this ostrich, to weigh more attentively the hawk and heron. The bodies of the hawk and heron are small but supported by denser feathers; therefore they fly swiftly, because in them there is little to weigh them down and much to lift them. By contrast, the ostrich is clothed with sparse feathers and burdened by a huge body, so that, even if it desires to fly, the scantiness of its feathers cannot suspend in the air the mass of so great a body.

The persons of the elect are aptly signified in the heron and hawk. So long as they are in this life, they cannot be entirely without even a small contagion of fault. Yet because they have little in them that presses them down, they possess an abundant power of good action which lifts them upward. By contrast, although the hypocrite does a few things that lift him up, he commits many things that weigh him down. The hypocrite does not perform no good deeds; rather, he commits many perverse deeds by which he himself presses those good deeds down. Therefore the few feathers and the body of the ostrich do not lift it up, because the multitude of wicked actions weighs down the hypocrite’s small good.

This very feather of the ostrich resembles the feathers of the heron and hawk in color, but not in the likeness of their strength. Their feathers are compact and firmer, and by the strength of their solidity can press down the air in flight. But the ostrich’s feathers are loose, and so unable to take flight, because they are surpassed by the very air which they ought to have pressed down. What, then, do we see in these things except that the virtues of the elect fly firmly so as to press down the winds of human favor? The action of hypocrites, however upright it may seem, is insufficient to fly, because the breeze of human praise passes through the feather of their unstable virtue.

But since we see one and the same outward habit among good and bad alike, since we observe the same appearance of profession in the elect and reprobate, how can our understanding discern, by comprehension, the elect from the reprobate and the true from the false? Yet we recognize this more quickly if we keep uncorrupted in memory the words of our Teacher, who says: “By their fruits you shall know them” (Matt. VII, 20).

[Note: [Col. 0079D] From Book XXXI on Job, chapter X, about the middle.] The Synagogue may also be signified by the ostrich. It had the wings of the Law, but creeping in its heart among low things, it never raised itself from the earth. By the heron and hawk, however, are represented the ancient Fathers, who were able both to fly in life and to perceive by understanding the things which they could discern. Therefore the feather of the ostrich is like the feather of the heron and hawk, because the voice of the Synagogue retained the teaching of its forebears in speech, but did not know it in life. Hence Truth admonishes the people of that Synagogue concerning the Pharisees and scribes, saying: “The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat: therefore do all that they tell you, but do not do according to their works” (Matt. XXIII, 2).

[Note: [Col. 0080D] From Book XXXI on Job, chapter V, §6.] By “ostrich” is signified the Gentile world, which the Lord promises shall be converted when He says through the prophet: “The beast of the field, the dragons and ostriches, shall glorify Me” (Isa. XLIII, 20). The beast of the field—that is, dragons and ostriches—glorifies the Lord when the Gentile world, which had formerly been a member of the devil in this world, exalts the faith which is in Him. He reproaches it by the name of dragons because of its malice, and calls it ostriches because of its hypocrisy. For the Gentile world received wings, as it were, but could not fly: it possessed the nature of reason, but did not know the exercise of reason.

[Note: [Col. 0081] From Book VII on Job, chapter XII, far before the end.] By “ostriches” is signified hypocrisy itself. Hence Isaiah rightly says against the perverse mind under the figure of Judea: “It shall be the lair of dragons and the pasture of ostriches” (Isa. XXXIV, 30). For what is signified by dragons except malice, and what by ostriches except hypocrisy? The ostrich has the appearance of flight but not the use of flight, because hypocrisy presents to all who look upon it an image of holiness, but does not know how to maintain a holy life. Therefore, in a perverse mind the dragon lies down and the ostrich feeds, because hidden malice is cunningly covered and a pretense of goodness is put forward before the eyes of beholders.

CHAPTER IX. ON THE HAWK.

In Holy Scripture, the hawk sometimes signifies any holy person.
