The hawk signifies any holy person. Hence blessed Job is questioned by the voice of the Lord when it is said: “Is it by your wisdom that the hawk grows feathers, spreading its wings toward the south?” (Job 39:26). Almost no one is unaware that, each year, as a new feather grows, the hawk sheds the old one and continually renews its plumage. This does not refer to the time of feathering in the nest, when it is still, of course, a fledgling and cannot spread its wings southward; rather, it describes the yearly renewal of plumage, in which the old feather is cast off and replaced. Domestic hawks are provided with sheltered, warm places so that they may feather better. Wild hawks, however, customarily spread their wings when the south wind blows, so that the warmth of the wind may heat their limbs for shedding the old feathers. When there is no wind, they spread their wings against the sun’s ray and are struck by it, thereby making warm air for themselves. Thus, when their pores are opened, either the old feathers fall out or new ones grow.

What, then, is the hawk’s growing feathers in the south, except that every saint, touched by the breath of the Holy Spirit, is warmed; and, casting aside the practice of his former way of life, takes on the form of the new person? Paul exhorts this when he says: “Putting off the old man with his deeds, and putting on the new” (Col. 3:9). And again: “Though our outer man is corrupted, yet the inner is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16). To cast off the old feather is to abandon inveterate habits of deceitful conduct; to take up the new feather is, by living well, to retain a gentle and simple disposition. For the feather of the old way of life weighs one down, whereas the plumage of new transformation lifts one up, making one lighter for flight in proportion as it is newer.

And rightly does the hawk spread its wings toward the south. To spread our wings toward the south is, at the coming of the Holy Spirit, to lay open our thoughts in confession: no longer taking pleasure in concealing ourselves by self-defense, but making them public by accusation of ourselves. Thus the hawk grows feathers when it has spread its wings toward the south, because each person then clothes himself with the feathers of virtues when, by confession, he lays his thoughts before the Holy Spirit. Whoever does not uncover his old deeds by confession produces no works of new life; whoever does not know how to mourn what weighs him down cannot bring forth what lifts him up. For the very force of compunction opens the pores of the heart and pours forth the feathers of virtues. And when the mind diligently rebukes itself for its sluggish old condition, it is made young by vigorous newness.

Therefore let it be said to blessed Job: “Is it by your wisdom that the hawk grows feathers, spreading its wings toward the south?” That is: Have you given understanding to any chosen person, so that, while the Holy Spirit blows, he may spread the wings of his thoughts, cast aside the burdens of his former way of life, and take up the feathers of virtues for the use of a new flight? Thus he may understand that he does not possess in himself, from himself, the watchfulness of understanding which he is unable to bestow from himself upon others.

## CHAPTER X. ON THE HERON

In Sacred Scripture, the heron signifies the person of the elect.

The heron, or the hawk, signifies the person of the elect. Hence the Lord says to blessed Job: “The wing of the ostrich is like the wing of the heron and the hawk” (Job 39:13). Hawks and herons have small bodies, but are supported by denser feathers. Therefore they fly swiftly through the air, because they have little in them that weighs down and much that lifts up. Thus the person of the elect is fittingly signified in the heron and the hawk; for, so long as they are in this life, they cannot be wholly without even the slightest contagion of sin. Yet, though they have little in them that depresses, they have abundant strength of good action that lifts them to things above. The enclosed feathers of herons and hawks are firmer, and therefore by the strength of their solidity can press the air in flight. So too the solid virtues of the elect fly in such a way as to press down the winds of human favor.

## CHAPTER XI. ON THE KITE

[Col. 0082D]

In Sacred Scripture, the kite signifies the devil.

The kite signifies the devil. We learn this from the testimony of the prophet Zechariah, who, describing his vision, says: “I lifted up my eyes and saw; and behold, two women coming forth, and a spirit was in their wings, and they had wings like the wings of a kite” (Zech. 5:9). What do we understand by the two women except the two principal vices, namely pride and vain glory, which are undoubtedly joined to ungodliness? They are said to have a spirit in their wings because in their actions they serve Satan’s will. The prophet calls him a spirit, of whom Solomon says: “If the spirit of one having power rises up against you, do not leave your place” (Eccl. 10:4); and of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he walks through dry and waterless places” (Matt. 12:43).

The spirit, therefore, is in their wings, because pride and vain glory serve Satan’s will in everything they do. “And they had wings like the wings of a kite.” The kite is always intent on lying in wait for the young of other creatures. These women therefore have wings like the wings of a kite, because their actions are undoubtedly like those of the devil, who is always laying snares for the life of little ones.

## CHAPTER XII. ON THE SPARROW

[Col. 0083B]

In Sacred Scripture, the sparrow signifies Christ.

The sparrow signifies Christ, as the Psalmist says: “Even the sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest where she may place her young” (Ps. 83:4 [Vulgate]). Who else is expressed by the sparrow except our Redeemer, and what else by the turtledove except the holy Church? The sparrow has now found itself a house, because our Redeemer has entered the eternal dwelling-place of heaven. And the turtledove has found a nest, because the holy Church, moved by love of her Creator, employs frequent groanings; and, as though making herself a nest—that is, the most peaceable rest of faith—there she cherishes in the bosom of charity her growing children, like young birds putting forth feathers, warmed until they fly upward.

## CHAPTER XIII. ON THE VULTURE

In Sacred Scripture, the vulture signifies Christ.

The vulture signifies our Redeemer, as it is said through blessed Job concerning the people of the Jews: “The bird has not known the path, nor has the eye of the vulture seen it” (Job 28[:7]). Who is signified here by the name “bird” except him who, ascending to heaven, raised aloft the fleshly body that he assumed? He is also aptly expressed by the designation “vulture.” For when the vulture flies and sees a corpse lying below, it descends to feed upon the corpse. And it is often caught in death because it comes down from the heights to a dead animal.

Thus the Mediator of God and men, our Redeemer, is rightly signified by the designation of the vulture. Remaining in the height of his divinity, he beheld, as in a lofty flight, the corpse of our mortality lying below, and lowered himself from heaven to the depths. For he deigned to become man for our sake. And while he sought the dead animal, he found death among us—he who was immortality in himself. Yet the eye of this vulture was the very purpose of our resurrection, because, having been dead for three days, he freed us from eternal death.

That faithless people of the Jews saw him as mortal, but paid no attention to how he would destroy our death by his own death. They indeed saw the vulture, but did not behold the eyes of the vulture. Since they refused to consider the paths of his humility and the means by which he lifted us to things above, they did not know the path of the bird. For they did not strive to ponder how his humility would raise us to heaven and the purpose of his death restore us to life. Therefore, “the bird has not known the path, nor has the eye of the vulture seen it,” because although they saw him whom they held in death, they refused to see how great a glory for our life would follow from his death.

## CHAPTER XIV. ON THE FLY

[Col. 0084B]

In Sacred Scripture, flies signify importunate cares.

Flies signify the importunate cares of fleshly desires, as it is written: “Dying flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment” (Eccl. 10:1). For superfluous thoughts, which continually arise and fade away in the mind that thinks carnally, destroy the sweetness with which each person is inwardly anointed by the Spirit, since they do not permit him to enjoy its integrity.

Hence Egypt is read to have been struck with a multitude of flies; whereas the people of Israel, by contrast, received observance of the Sabbath as a gift (Exod. 8:24). For what is more laborious in this life than to burn with earthly desires? Or what is quieter here than to desire nothing of this world? The people who follow God, then, received the Sabbath—that is, rest of mind—so that they might not be wearied in this life by any craving of fleshly desires. Egypt, however, which represents the appearance of this world, is struck by flies. For the fly is a most importunate and restless creature; and what else is signified by it except the importunate cares of fleshly desires?

Egypt is therefore struck by flies because the hearts of those who love earthly life are smitten by the unrest of their desires; they are pressed down to the depths by crowds of fleshly thoughts and are not raised to desire inward rest. Hence, when truth comes to the heart by the wondrous help of mercy, it first expels the heat of fleshly thoughts from it, and afterward disposes within it the gifts of virtues. This is well suggested to us by the narrative of the holy Gospel, where, as the Lord was being led to raise the daughter, it is immediately added: “And when the crowd had been put out, he entered, took the girl by the hand, and the girl arose” (Matt. 9:25). The crowd, therefore, is put out so that the girl may be raised; because, unless the importunate multitude of worldly cares is first expelled from the innermost recesses of the heart, the soul that lies dead within does not rise again. For while it disperses itself among innumerable thoughts of earthly desires, it cannot at all gather itself to self-consideration.

# THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0085]

## CHAPTER ONE. ON BEASTS OF BURDEN

[Col. 0085A]

In Sacred Scripture, beasts of burden signify at times the holy Church or a faithful soul; at times anyone placed under discipline; at times carnal persons; at times minds once brutish but converted; at times worldly entanglements; at times those slower in understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0085D] From Homily 17 on Ezekiel.]

The beast of burden signifies the holy Church or a faithful soul. Hence our Redeemer rides upon a beast of burden as he makes his way to Jerusalem. Our Savior makes his way to Jerusalem seated upon a beast of burden when he presides universally over the holy Church and kindles it with desire for heavenly peace. He also makes his way to Jerusalem seated upon a beast of burden when, governing the soul of each faithful person—namely, his own beast of burden—he leads it to the vision of inward peace.

[Note: [Col. 0085D] From Book X on Job, chapter X, §15.]

The beast of burden signifies anyone placed under discipline, as the Psalmist says: “I became like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you” (Ps. 72:23 [Vulgate]). Although man is far better than irrational creatures, he is nevertheless often not permitted what brute animals are permitted. For creatures reserved for some other purpose are certainly not restrained in their movements under discipline. But because man is led toward the life to come, it is indeed necessary that in all his movements he be bound by the ordering of discipline, serve like a domestic animal bound with reins, and live restrained by eternal ordinances.

But whoever seeks to fulfill everything he desires through unbridled liberty longs to be like a wild animal: he does not wish the reins of discipline to hold him, but wishes boldly to run wandering through the forest of desires. Yet divine mercy often breaks those whom it sees going forth into the unrestrainedness of unlawful liberty by the opposition of favorable adversity, so that, crushed, they may learn by what wicked exaltation they had become swollen. Then, subdued by the experience of the lash, they may, like domestic beasts of burden, place the necks of their minds beneath the reins of commandments and proceed along the road of this present life at the will of their ruler.

He knew well that he was bound with these reins who said: “I became like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you.” Thus also that cruel persecutor, brought from the field of faithless pleasure into the house of faith and pricked by the goads of his ruler, heard: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:6).

Beasts of burden signify carnal people, as the prophet says: “The beasts of burden have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1:17). For beasts of burden to rot in their dung is for carnal people to end their lives in the stench of lust.

[Col. 0086A] [Note: [Col. 0086D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter VIII, §12.]

Beasts of burden signify minds once brutish, as the prophet says: “He gives their food to the beasts of burden, and to the young ravens that call upon him” (Ps. 146:95 [Vulgate numbering as printed]). Beasts of burden receive food when minds formerly brutish are satisfied by the pasture of Sacred Scripture.

Beasts of burden also signify worldly entanglements. Hence, when the sons of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, possessing much cattle and many beasts of burden, desired the plains they saw beyond the Jordan, they said to Moses: “The land which the Lord struck down before the children of Israel is a region exceedingly fruitful for feeding animals, and we your servants have very many beasts of burden. We beseech you, if we have found favor before you, give it to us your servants as a possession, and do not make us cross the Jordan” (Num. 32:4–5). Those, therefore, who possess many beasts of burden refuse to cross the Jordan, because those occupied by many worldly entanglements do not seek the dwelling-place of the heavenly homeland.

Beasts of burden signify those slower in understanding, as blessed Job says: “Ask the beasts of burden, and they will teach you; the birds of the air, and they will tell you; speak to the earth, and it will answer you; and the fish of the sea will recount it to you” (Job 12:7–8). What are meant by beasts of burden except those slower in understanding? What by the birds of the air except those who understand lofty and sublime things? Of beasts of burden—that is, those slower in understanding—it is written: “Your animals shall dwell in it” (Ps. 67:11 [Vulgate]). And because those who understand sublime things fly forth in the words of our Redeemer, it is written: “So that the birds of the air come and dwell in its branches” (Matt. 13:32).

What, then, do we understand by the earth except those who think earthly thoughts? Hence the first man, abandoning heavenly things, was told: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19, according to the Septuagint). What are meant by the fish of the sea except the curious people of this age, of whom the Psalmist says: “The fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea” (Ps. 8:9 [Vulgate])? They lie hidden, as though in secret waves, in great inquiries into things.

What all these, when questioned, teach is added in the words: “Who does not know that the hand of the Lord has made all these things?” (Job 12:9). It is as if he were openly saying: Whether you inquire of those slower in understanding, or those who understand sublime things, or those devoted to earthly occupations, or those occupied with the inquiries of this world, all confess God, the Creator of all, and agree concerning his power, although they do not live in agreement under that power. For what every righteous person speaks even by living, the unrighteous person is often compelled to confess concerning God with speech alone. Thus the wicked serve the Author of all things by their testimony, because they cannot deny that he is the Creator of all, though they have dared to oppose his works by their conduct.

## CHAPTER II. ON THE HORSE

In Sacred Scripture, the horse signifies at times the slippery life of the wicked; at times temporal rank; at times this present world itself; at times the preparation of a right intention; at times any holy preacher; at times the bodies of the elect.

The horse signifies the slippery life of the wicked, as it is written: “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31:9 [Vulgate]). And, as another prophet says: “They became lustful and wandering horses; each one neighed after his neighbor’s wife” (Jer. 5:8).

[Col. 0087B]

The horse signifies temporal rank, as Solomon testifies when he says: “I have seen slaves on horses, and princes walking on the ground like slaves” (Eccl. 10:7). For everyone who sins is a slave of sin (John 8:34). Slaves are on horses when sinners are exalted by the dignities of this present life. Princes walk like slaves when no honor raises up many who are full of the dignity of virtues, but the highest adversity presses them down here as though they were unworthy. Hence it is again said: “Those who mounted horses have slept” (Ps. 75:7 [Vulgate]). That is, trusting in the honor of this present life, they closed the eyes of their minds to the light of truth in the death of the soul.

The horse signifies this present world itself, as Jacob says: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path, biting the hoofs of the horse, so that its rider falls backward” (Gen. 49:17). We shall show more clearly what the horse signifies in this testimony if we explain somewhat more carefully the matters surrounding it. Some maintain that Antichrist will come from the tribe of Dan because Dan is here also called a serpent. Thus not without reason, when the people of Israel occupied the land according to the divisions of their encampment, Dan was the first to pitch camp in the north (Num. 2:25), signifying him who said in his heart: “I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13). Of him it is also said through the prophet: “From Dan the snorting of his horses was heard” (Jer. 8:16).

He is not only a serpent, but also a *cerastes*. For *cerasta* means “horns” in Greek, and this serpent is said to be horned. By it the coming of Antichrist is fittingly declared, because against the life of the faithful he is armed both with the bite of pestilential preaching and with the horns of power. Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? Dan therefore becomes a serpent in the way because he entices to walk in the broadness of this present life those whom he flatters as though obeying them. Yet he bites them in the way because he consumes with the venom of his error those to whom he grants liberty.

He becomes a *cerastes* on the path because, when he finds people faithful and constraining themselves to the narrow ways of heavenly commandment, he attacks them not only by the wickedness of crafty persuasion but also crushes them by terror of power. In the anguish of persecution, after the benefits of counterfeit sweetness, he employs the horns of power. Here the horse represents this world, which foams through its pride amid the course of passing times. And because Antichrist strives to seize hold of the last things of the world, this *cerastes* is said to bite the horse’s hoofs. To bite the hoofs of the horse is to strike at the extremities of the age. “So that its rider falls backward.”

The rider of the horse is whoever is exalted in worldly dignities. He is said to fall backward, not upon his face, as Paul is recorded to have fallen (Acts 9:4). To fall upon one’s face is for each person in this life to recognize his own sins and bewail them in repentance. But to fall backward, where one cannot see, is to fall suddenly out of this life and not know to what punishments one is being led. And because Judaea, caught in the snares of its error, awaits Antichrist in place of Christ, Jacob rightly turns suddenly in that same place to speak in the voice of the elect: “I will await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. 49:18). That is, I await not Antichrist like the unbelievers, but, believing faithfully, the true Christ who is to come for our redemption.

The horse signifies the preparation of a right intention, as it is written: “The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but the Lord grants salvation” (Prov. 21:31). For the mind indeed prepares itself against temptation, but unless it is helped from above, it does not fight savingly.

[Col. 0088C]

The horse signifies any holy preacher, as the prophet testifies when he says: “You sent your horses into the sea, stirring up many waters” (Isa. 18:2). The quiet waters lay still because human minds were asleep in the torpor of their vices. But the sea was troubled by God’s horses because, when holy preachers were sent, every heart that had languished in deadly security was terrified by the impulse of saving fear.

Horses signify the bodies of the elect. Hence John the Apostle, contemplating the Lord in the Apocalypse, says: “And the armies which are in heaven followed him on white horses” (Rev. 19:14).

[Note: [Col. 0087D] From Book XXXI on Job, chapter IX, §12.]

He rightly calls an army the multitude of saints that had labored in this battle of martyrdom. They are said to sit on white horses because their bodies shone both with the light of righteousness and with the whiteness of chastity.

## CHAPTER III. ON THE ASS

In Sacred Scripture, asses signify at times the sloth of fools; at times lust; at times the simplicity of the Gentiles; at times any faithful soul or the holy Church; at times one who sustains the needs of others; at times an evil life; at times our flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0088D] From Book I on Job, chapter VI.]

Asses signify the sloth of fools, as Moses says: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together” (Deut. 22:10). It is as though he said: Do not join fools with the wise in preaching, lest, through one who cannot fulfill the task, you hinder the other who has the strength to do so.

[Note: [Col. 0089D] From Book I on Job, chapter VI, after the middle.]

Likewise, the designation “asses” expresses the unrestrained lust of the wanton, as the prophet says: “Whose flesh is like the flesh of asses” (Ezek. 23:20).

[Note: [Col. 0089D] Ibid.]

Asses signify the simplicity of the Gentiles. Hence the Lord, making his way to Jerusalem, is said to have ridden an ass’s colt (Matt. 21:7). What is it for him to come to Jerusalem seated on an ass except, by possessing the simple hearts of the Gentiles, to bring them under his governance and rule to the vision of peace? Hence it is again written: “The ox knew its owner, and the ass the manger of its lord” (Isa. 1:2–3). Who was the ox except the Jewish people, whose neck the yoke of the Law wore down? And who was the ass except the Gentile people, whom any deceiver found like a brute animal, offering no rational resistance, and subjected to whatever error he wished? Therefore the ox knew its owner and the ass the manger of its lord, because the Hebrew people found the God whom they worshipped but did not know, while the Gentiles received the nourishment of the Law which they did not possess.

An ass may also signify any faithful soul or the holy universal Church. Hence our Redeemer, seated upon an ass’s colt, makes his way to Jerusalem.

[Note: [Col. 0089D] From Book XVI on Job, chapter XXI, §22.]

The ass signifies one who sustains the needs of others, as it is said through blessed Job concerning heretics: “They have driven away the ass of the fatherless” (Job 24:3). What do we understand by the fatherless except God’s elect, placed in the tenderness of mind, nourished by the great grace of faith, and not yet seeing the face of their Father, who has already died for them? There are many in the Church who see certain persons longing for heavenly things and holding all earthly things in contempt. Although they themselves labor amid the toils of this world, they nevertheless provide with the possessions they hold in this world the support of life for those whom they see panting after heavenly things. Though they are unable themselves to pursue spiritual works, they render assistance to those striving toward the heights.

For an ass is accustomed to carry human burdens. Thus a person who serves earthly concerns and carries burdens for the use of others is, as it were, an ass of the elect. And often, when heretics turn such a person away from the bosom of the holy Church, they drive away the ass of the fatherless, because, when they draw him over to their unbelief, they remove him from the service of good people.

[Note: [Col. 0090D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter II, §15.]

The ass signifies an evil life, as Moses says: “You shall exchange the firstborn of an ass for a sheep” (Exod. 13:13). Uncleanness is signified by the ass, but innocence by the sheep. To exchange the firstborn of an ass for a sheep, then, is to turn the beginnings of an unclean life into the simplicity of innocence, so that after the sinner has done those things which the Lord rejects as unclean, he may now bring forth by his actions those things which are to be placed upon God’s sacrifice.

[Note: [Col. 0090D] From Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 34.]

The ass signifies our flesh, as it is said in the Book of Judges: “Axa, the daughter of Caleb, sitting upon an ass, sighed. Her father said to her: ‘What do you have?’ And she answered: ‘Give me a blessing, because you have given me dry land; join to it watered land.’ And her father gave her the upper watered land and the lower watered land” (Judg. 1:13–15).

What do we understand by the ass except our body? Axa sits upon the ass when the soul now rules over the irrational movements of its flesh. Sighing, she asks her father for watered land because the grace of tears must be sought from our Creator with great groaning. There are indeed some who have already received the gift of speaking freely for righteousness, defending the oppressed, giving their possessions to the needy, and possessing ardor of faith; but they do not possess the grace of tears. Such people have southern and dry land, but still need watered land, because, though they are engaged in good works, through which they are great and fervent, they must weep also for the evils they previously committed—whether through fear of punishment or love of the heavenly kingdom.

But because there are two kinds of compunction—for the soul that thirsts for God is first pierced by fear and afterward by love—her Father gave her the upper watered land and the lower watered land. The soul receives the upper watered land when, in tears, it afflicts itself through desire for the heavenly kingdom; it receives the lower watered land when it fears the punishments of hell in weeping. In reality, the lower watered land is given first and the upper afterward. But because the compunction of love surpasses the other in dignity, the upper watered land had necessarily to be mentioned first and the lower afterward.

There are, as I have said, two kinds of compunction: the soul is first pierced by fear and afterward by love. It first afflicts itself in tears because, recalling its evils, it fears that it will suffer eternal punishments for them. But when fear has been consumed by a long anguish of sorrow, a certain security born from confidence in pardon arises, and the mind is set ablaze with love for heavenly joys. The person who had first feared being led to punishment then begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom. Thus perfect compunction of fear hands the mind over to the compunction of love.

## CHAPTER IV. ON THE SHE-ASS

In Sacred Scripture, she-asses signify at times persons who live simply; at times wanton movements of the heart; at times simple thoughts of the heart; at times our flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0090D] From Book II on Job, chapter XVII.]

The designation “she-asses” is understood of persons who live simply and devote themselves to carrying the burdens of others. Hence it is written: “The oxen were plowing, and the she-asses were feeding beside them” (Job 1:14). What else do we understand figuratively by the oxen except those who work well, and by the she-asses except certain people who live simply? Since they cannot run in subtle understanding, they walk, as it were, more slowly; and for that reason they carry their brothers’ burdens more gently. They are rightly said to feed beside the oxen, because, even though the minds of simple people cannot grasp lofty things, they are so much the nearer to them as they believe through charity in their brothers’ good things. And since they do not know how to envy others’ understandings, they are not divided from one another, as it were, in feeding. The she-asses and oxen, then, are refreshed together, because those slower in understanding, joined to the prudent, are nourished by their understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] From Book [I] on Job, chapter XIII, §30; the book-number is uncertain in the printed text.]

She-asses signify the wanton movements of the heart, as is said of blessed Job, that “he had five hundred she-asses in his possession” (Job 1:3). We possess she-asses when we restrain the wanton movements of the heart and, whenever something carnal in us seeks to rise up, curb it by the spiritual mastery of the heart.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] From Book II on Job, chapter XXIV, §33, in the middle.]

She-asses also signify simple thoughts of the heart, according to the passage: “The oxen were plowing and the she-asses were feeding beside them; and the Sabeans rushed upon them and took everything away” (Job 1:14–15). What do we understand by feeding she-asses except the simple movements of the heart? When we carefully restrain these from the error of duplicity, we nourish them, as it were, in the field of free purity. But see: while we do this, our enemy carries off the feeding she-asses. For when he sees simple movements of the heart, he often displays the subtle sharpness of his inventions, so that, while praise is sought for subtlety, the simplicity of purity may be lost. And even if he cannot draw a person as far as an evil deed, he nevertheless harms by creeping in through temptation among good thoughts; so that, when he is seen to disturb the good of the mind, he may seem, as it were, to have taken it away utterly.

The she-ass signifies our flesh. Thus it is written that, when Balaam was going to pronounce a curse, he was rebuked by the she-ass upon which he sat. Balaam is making his way toward his purpose, but the animal over which he presides obstructs his intention. Held back by hindrance, the she-ass sees the angel whom the human mind does not see, because our flesh, made slow through suffering, often reveals God to the mind by its affliction—the God whom the mind itself, presiding over the flesh, did not see. Thus it obstructs the anxiety of the spirit desiring to advance in this world, as though it were setting out on a journey, until the invisible one who stands in its way becomes known to it.

Hence Peter rightly says: “He received a rebuke for his madness: a dumb beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s folly” (2 Pet. 2:16). A mad man is rebuked by a dumb beast of burden when a proud mind is reminded by afflicted flesh of the good of humility which it ought to retain. We must therefore consider how great a salvation for the heart bodily suffering is: it restores the mind to knowledge of itself through the recollection of weakness—a recollection which health often drives away—so that the mind, carried outside itself into pride, may be brought back to remembrance by the flesh it endures as wounded. But Balaam did not obtain the gift of this rebuke because, though he was proceeding to utter a curse, he changed his voice but not his mind.

## CHAPTER V. ON THE CAMEL

In Sacred Scripture, camels signify at times the Lord himself; at times the Gentile people; at times the way of life of the Samaritans; at times the administration of earthly things; at times distorted and swollen thoughts.

The camel signifies the Lord, as the same Lord says to the opposing Jews: “Straining out a gnat, you swallow a camel” (Matt. 23:24). The gnat wounds with its buzzing, but the camel willingly bends itself down to receive burdens. The Jews therefore strained out the gnat because they requested that a seditious robber be released. But they swallowed the camel because they tried, by their cries, to destroy him who willingly came down to take on the burdens of our mortality.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] In the same place.]

The camel signifies the Gentile world. Hence Rebekah, coming to Isaac, is brought on the back of a camel (Gen. 24:64), because the Church, hastening to Christ from among the Gentiles, is found amid the twisted and vicious practices of her former way of life.

[Note: [Col. 0092D] Book XXXV on Job, chapter XI; it repeats this.]

When she sees Isaac, she descends, because, upon knowing the Lord, the Gentile people abandoned their vices and sought the lowliness of humility instead of lofty self-exaltation. She covers herself in shame with a veil (ibid., v. 65), because she is ashamed before him of her former life. Hence Paul says to those same Gentiles: “What fruit, therefore, did you then have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21).

[Note: [Col. 0092D] Job, the place cited.]

Camels, which are a mixed-kind animal, may also signify the way of life of the Samaritans. Camels chew the cud but do not divide the hoof. So too the Samaritans chew the cud, as it were, because they receive the words of the Law in part; and they do not divide the hoof, as it were, because they despise it in part. They also bear a heavy burden upon the back of the mind, because everything they do they labor at without hope of eternity: for they do not know the faith of the resurrection. And what can be heavier or more burdensome than to endure the affliction of this passing age and not at all hope for the joyful reward to be revealed to the mind?

[Note: [Col. 0092D] From Book I on Job, chapter XIII, §29.]

Camels, which do not divide the hoof but nevertheless chew the cud, may fittingly also signify good administrations of earthly things. Because these have something of the world and something of God, they must necessarily be signified by a mixed-kind animal. For earthly administration, even when it serves eternal benefit, cannot be carried out without disturbance of mind. Since through it the mind is troubled in the present and a reward is prepared for eternity, it is like a mixed-kind animal: it both has something of the Law and does not have it. It does not divide the hoof because the soul does not wholly separate itself from every earthly work; nevertheless, it chews the cud because, by administering temporal things well, it hopes for heavenly things with the confidence of certainty.

Thus earthly administrations, in the manner of camels, agree with the Law in their head but differ in their foot: for heaven is what those who live justly desire, whereas the things in which they are occupied by their work belong to this world.

Camels may also signify the crooked animal—that is, twisted and swollen thoughts. Hence blessed Job is rightly said to have possessed camels (Job 1:3). We possess camels indeed if, when we think lofty thoughts, we humbly lay them aside. Without doubt we possess camels when we bend our thoughts [Col. 0093B] to compassion for a brother’s weakness and, bearing one another’s burdens in return, know how to show sympathetic condescension toward another’s infirmity.

## 105. CHAPTER VI. ON ANIMALS

In Holy Scripture, by the name *animals* are sometimes meant the holy Evangelists; sometimes the righteous; sometimes the simple within Holy Church; sometimes thoughts somewhat lifted from the earth; sometimes the irrational movements of the soul.

[Note: [Col. 0093D] From Homily 2 on Ezekiel, after the middle.] By the name *animals* the holy Evangelists are denoted, as Ezekiel says: “And in its midst was the likeness of four animals” (Ezek. 1:5). For what is signified by the four animals except the four Evangelists?

[Col. 0093C] [Note: [Col. 0093D] From Book XXIV on Job, ch. VI, after the middle.] By the name *animals* the righteous are denoted, as Ezekiel says: “And I heard the sound of the wings of the animals striking one against another” (Ezek. 3:13). What should we understand by the wings of the animals except the virtues of the saints? For, despising earthly things, they are raised up in flight toward heavenly things. But the flying animals strike one another with their wings, because the minds of the saints, as they seek things above, are stirred up by considering one another’s corresponding virtues. He strikes me with his wing who, by the example of his own holiness, kindles me toward better things. And I strike the neighboring animal with my wing if at some time I show a good work for it to imitate.

[Note: [Col. 0093D] From Book XXXV on Job, ch. XI.] By the name *animals* the simple within Holy Church are denoted, as the Psalmist says of that same Holy Church: “Your animals shall dwell in it” (Ps. 67:11), because Holy Church contains every simple person.

## 106

[Note: [Col. 0093D] From Book XXVI on Job, ch. V.] By the name *animals* are denoted thoughts somewhat raised from the earth, yet still seeking the rewards of earthly recompense, as Ezekiel says: “And I entered and saw: and behold, every likeness of creeping things and the abomination of animals” (Ezek. 8:10). In creeping things, wholly earthly thoughts are signified; in animals, thoughts already somewhat raised from the earth, yet still seeking the rewards of earthly [Col. 0094A] recompense. Creeping things cling to the earth with their whole body; animals, however, are raised above the earth by their belly, though by the appetite of their throat they are always bent toward the earth. Creeping things, therefore, are within the wall when thoughts roll about in the mind which are never lifted from earthly desires. Animals likewise are within the wall when—even though certain just and honorable things are thought—such thoughts nevertheless serve the pursuit of temporal gain and honors. In themselves they are, as it were, raised above the earth; yet through ambition, like the appetite of the throat, they still cast themselves down to what is low.

[Note: [Col. 0094D] From Book XXVII on Job, ch. VII, approximately the middle.] By the name *animals* are denoted the irrational movements of the soul. Thus, when the children of Israel had been brought into the land [Col. 0094B] of promise, the children of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh return to the plains (Num. 31:33), because they slip down from the lofty mountain summits, as it were from the hope of heaven, in order to feed brute animals outside the land of promise. For they labor to nourish the irrational movements of the soul with varied desires. Those blinded by transitory occupations do not know how great is the brightness of eternal light; and, while they pride themselves on earthly things, they shut off the approach of their heavenly light.

## 107. CHAPTER VII. ON THE OX

In Holy Scripture, by the name *ox* are sometimes denoted the Jewish people; sometimes the madness of the lustful; sometimes the labor of the preacher; sometimes a wise person; sometimes the gentleness of teachers; sometimes the devil; [Col. 0094C] sometimes good action.

By the name *ox* the Jewish people are denoted, as the prophet says: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isa. 1:3). See above, Chapter 3, “On the Ass.”

[Note: [Col. 0094D] From Book XXXV on Job, ch. II.] That the madness of the lustful is signified comparatively by the name *ox* is shown by Solomon. Having first described the wantonness of a woman giving evil counsel, he adds: “Immediately he follows her, like an ox led to slaughter” (Prov. 7:22).

[Note: [Col. 0094D] From the book and chapter above.] By the name *ox* the labor of preaching is expressed, as the words of the Law testify: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it treads out the grain” (1 Tim. 5:18). It is as though it said openly: Do not prevent the preacher of the word from receiving his support.

[Col. 0094D] Again, by the name *ox* any wise person is denoted, as it is written: “You shall not yoke an ox and an ass together” (Deut. 25:4), that is, you shall not associate a wise person with a fool in preaching.

By the name *oxen* the gentleness of teachers is denoted, as it is written that in the vessels of the Temple, among crowns and interlacings, oxen, lions, and cherubim were carved (Deut. 22:10). Crowns are indeed a sign of victory; interlacings [§108] signify the unanimity of concord; cherubim, the fullness of knowledge. By oxen, gentleness is understood; by lions, severity. Thus priests and teachers are denoted among crowns and interlacings—that is, among the strength of good work by which they run toward victory, and the concord of charity by which they do not differ from one another—by oxen, lions, and cherubim. For, in the fullness of knowledge which they possess, they must hold both the gentleness of oxen and the ardor of lions, so that in the discipline which they preach they may be inflamed by holy zeal and tranquil through fatherly tenderness.

By the name *ox* the devil is denoted, as Isaiah says: “The lion, like an ox, shall eat straw” (Isa. 11:7); and as the Lord says of him to blessed Job: “He shall eat grass like an ox” (Job 40:10). What is meant by the lion except the devil, and by straw [Col. 0095B] or grass except the life of carnal people? But why is the devil, in eating straw or grass, compared not to a horse but to an ox? This is readily recognized if we consider the difference between the food of the two animals. Horses eat grass however filthy it may be, but drink only clean water. Oxen, however, drink water however filthy it may be, but feed only on clean grass. Why, then, is the devil compared to the ox, which feeds on clean fodder, except because another prophet says of him: “His food is choice” (*esca ejus electa*)? [Note: [Col. 0095D] There the Vulgate edition has “his food is choice” (*cibus ejus electus*) instead.] (Hab. 1:16, according to the Septuagint.) He does not delight in seizing those whom he sees willingly lying with him in the depths, entangled in insolent and filthy actions. Thus he seeks to eat grass like an ox because he seeks to crush, with the tooth of his suggestion, the pure spiritual life [Col. 0095C] of others.

[Note: [Col. 0095D] From Homily 2 on Ezekiel, not far from the beginning.] By the name *ox* good action is denoted, as Moses says: “You shall not plough with the firstborn of an ox” (Deut. 15:15). What do we understand by the firstborn of an ox except good action? We understand the firstborn of an ox as good action in the weak age of our first period of life. Yet one must not plough with it, because, while the first years of our adolescence or youth are still upon us, we must still refrain from preaching, lest the ploughshare of our tongue dare to cut the soil of another’s heart. For as long as we are weak, we must restrain ourselves within ourselves, lest, by displaying tender good qualities too soon, we lose them. Shrubs that have been planted, if they have not first taken root in the ground, quickly wither when touched by hand; but when once they have fixed their root, the hand touches them and yet does no harm, winds buffet them but do not injure them. And walls that have been built, if they are shaken, are overthrown unless they have first dried from their own moisture. Therefore, so long as the mind has not been perfectly dried of the moisture of its perversity, it must not be touched by the hand of another’s tongue, lest, before it has fully received firmness, it lose its solidity; lest, shaken, it fall; lest, like a shrub without roots, when it is shaken more than it can endure, it [Col. 0096A] wither in the blasts.

Therefore, only what is firm should be displayed as an example. For the mind must first be strengthened, and then shown for the benefit of neighbors, when it no longer falls puffed up by praise or wastes away struck by blame. For though Timothy is told, “Command these things and teach; let no one despise your youth” (1 Tim. 4:11–12), it must be understood that his youth was in years, not in character, although in sacred speech adolescence is sometimes called youth. Hence it is written: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Ezek. 2:9).

## CHAPTER VIII. ON THE COW

In Holy Scripture, when *cow* is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies the weakness of the Lord’s Incarnation, [Col. 0096B] sometimes our flesh. When cows are spoken of in the plural, the minds of the faithful are understood.

## 110

By the name *cow* the weakness of the Lord’s Incarnation is denoted, as the Lord says to Moses: “Command the children of Israel to bring you a red cow of full age, in which there is no blemish and which has not borne a yoke. And you shall deliver her to Eleazar the priest, who shall lead her outside the camp and sacrifice her in the sight of the Lord; and he shall dip his finger in her blood, sprinkling it seven times toward the doors of the tabernacle. And he shall burn her in the sight of all—her skin and flesh, blood and dung—you shall commit to the flame” (Num. 19:2–5).

What is prefigured by the cow except the weakness of the Lord’s Incarnation, assumed for sacrifice? Of him it is written that “he [Col. 0096C] died” [Note: [Col. 0096D] Here our edition reads *was crucified* instead of *died*.] “through weakness, yet lives by the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4). This cow is fittingly called red, because his humanity was reddened by the blood of the Passion. Hence in the Song of Songs the bride describes him: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song 5:10): white, indeed, by divinity; ruddy by blood; white by the righteousness of his life; ruddy by the bloodshed of his Passion.

“Of full age, in which there is no blemish.” The age of the Lord’s humanity is complete; all his action is perfect. In that humanity there was no blemish, because it is truly written of him: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” [Col. 0096D] (1 Pet. 2:22). It is fittingly added: “Nor has she borne a yoke.” For it is written: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:35). Since the Lord submitted to no sin, he bore no yoke.

It follows: “And you shall deliver her to Eleazar the priest, who shall lead her outside the camp and sacrifice her in the sight of the Lord.” Why is this cow delivered to the priest to be sacrificed, except because the incarnate Lord, who made himself a sacrifice for our redemption, is delivered into the hands of the Jewish people? He was also sacrificed outside the camp, in the sight of the Lord, because he suffered outside the gate. Hence Paul says: [Col. 0097A] “Let us go forth to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For Jesus, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate. For we have no continuing city here, but seek the one to come” (Heb. 13:13). He suffered outside the gate in order to lead us, as it were, outside the city of this present life’s manner of living, and to persuade us to tear our heart away from earthly dwelling.

It is fittingly said: “He shall sacrifice her in the sight of the Lord.” For our Redeemer was, as it were, put to death in the sight of all, but was sacrificed in the sight of the Father: what was punishment before human eyes was sacrifice before the Father’s eyes. “And he shall dip his finger in her blood.” What is meant by the finger except the discernment of our action? To dip the finger in the cow’s blood is to consecrate our works in the Passion of the Lord’s Incarnation, so that we may imitate the Passion which we know, as it is written: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, that you may follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:2).

Eleazar both sacrifices and dips his finger in her blood, because the Jewish people, on the side of the reprobate, pursued the Lord’s humility even to the Passion; but on the side of the elect, imitated his humility in action [Col. 0097B]. “And he shall sprinkle it toward the doors of the tabernacle.” What is meant here by the tabernacle except the whole Synagogue together? Therefore, whoever has dipped his finger in his blood should sprinkle that same blood toward the doors of the tabernacle; that is, whoever imitates the ways of his Passion should offer to the Synagogue, resisting and not falling away, through good examples and upright conduct, a sign of right living. To sprinkle the cow’s blood toward the doors of the tabernacle is to show the resistant Jewish people, by upright preaching and holy works, examples of his Passion.

It is fittingly said that his finger is to be dipped and sprinkled in the blood seven times. In the number seven, perfection is understood. Thus the whole course of time is completed in seven days, and the Holy Spirit is called sevenfold. To dip the finger in the blood seven times is to imitate the ministry of his Passion by perfect action. And to sprinkle seven times toward the Synagogue is to declare, with perfect preaching, the mysteries of his Incarnation [Col. 0097D] and Passion to unbelievers.

“And you shall burn her before all outside the camp: her skin and flesh, her blood and dung, you shall commit to the flame.” What are signified by the flesh and skin, the blood and dung of the cow, except the carnal sacrifices offered under the Old Testament, which proclaimed the Lord’s weakness? All these, subsequently understood in a special sense by the Fathers according to their outward service, were called dung. Thus Paul, speaking of carnal sacrifices, said: “For whose sake I have counted all things as loss, and reckon them as dung” (Phil. 3:8). They are committed to the flame because, though first offered carnally, they were afterwards consumed [Col. 0098A] by the fire of understanding through the Holy Spirit.

Yet in the same cow—that is, in the very weakness of the Lord’s Incarnation—we may understand the flesh, skin, blood, and dung as his individual works. What is denoted by flesh and skin except outward action? What by blood except the subtle inward power that gives life to outward deeds? What by dung except weariness, thirst, hunger, fear of death, and whatever else he willed to suffer through the humility he assumed? Whatever he possessed through the deficiency of our mortality was, as it were, to be cast away in him. Yet because he undertook all these things from our weakness for our redemption, they are to be burned with fire—that is, understood according to the power of the Holy Spirit—so that all that he did bodily may be recognized as ordered by the incorporeal Spirit of his divinity.

Our flesh may likewise be signified by the cow. We slaughter the cow, therefore, when we destroy the flesh’s indulgence in its own pleasure. But because mortification of the flesh is judged useless without faith, hope, and charity, when the cow is slaughtered in sacrifice it is commanded to be offered with hyssop, cedar wood, and scarlet twice-dyed. What is denoted by hyssop except faith? By cedar wood except hope? And by scarlet except charity? Hyssop is accustomed to cleanse our inward parts. Peter says: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). Cedar wood does not decay, because no end consumes hope [Col. 0098C] in heavenly things. Hence Peter says: “He has regenerated us to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, unto an inheritance incorruptible and undefiled and unfading” (1 Pet. 1:9). Scarlet burns with a red color, because charity both fills and sets ablaze the person whom it possesses. Thus Truth says in the Gospel: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49).

But twice-dyed scarlet is commanded to be offered so that before the eyes of the inward Judge our charity may be colored by love of God and neighbor: so that the converted mind may neither so love quiet for love of God as to set aside care and benefit for the neighbor, nor so serve activity for love of the neighbor as, wholly abandoning quiet, to extinguish in itself the fire of heavenly love. Thus we offer the cow with hyssop, cedar wood, and scarlet when, together with the mortification of the flesh, we kindle the sacrifice of faith, hope, and charity. Whoever, therefore, has already offered himself to God as a sacrifice must, if he desires perfection, take care to extend himself not only toward the breadth of action but also toward the heights of contemplation.

[Note: [Col. 0097D] From Homily 37 on the Gospels, farther from the beginning.] By the name *cows* the minds of the faithful are denoted. Thus, when the ark of the Lord returned from the land of the Philistines to the land of Israel, it was set upon a cart, and cows were yoked to the cart. They are said to have been nursing, and their calves were shut up at home. “The cows went straight along the road which leads [Col. 0099A] to Beth-shemesh; they went by one way, walking and lowing, and did not turn aside either to the right or to the left” (1 Sam. 6:7).

What are cows except the faithful in the Church? When they preserve the commandments of holy speech, they bear the ark of the Lord placed upon them, as it were. Concerning them, it must also be noted that they are said to have been nursing, because there are many people who, though inwardly set upon God’s way, are outwardly bound by carnal affections. Yet those who bear the ark of God in their mind do not turn aside from the straight path. Behold, the cows proceed to Beth-shemesh. *Beth-shemesh* is interpreted “house.” And the Prophet says: “For you who fear the Lord, the sun of righteousness shall arise.” If, therefore, we tend toward the dwelling-place of the eternal Sun, it is surely fitting that we not turn aside from God’s way because of carnal affections.

The whole matter must be considered attentively: the cows, placed beneath God’s cart, proceed and groan; they utter lowing from within, yet do not turn their steps away from God’s path. They feel love through compassion, but do not bend their necks backward. So indeed, so must the preachers of God, and every faithful person within Holy Church, be: they must have compassion upon their neighbors through charity, and yet not stray from God’s way through compassion. To proceed to Beth-shemesh with the ark set upon the cart is to draw near, with heavenly knowledge, to the dwelling-place of inward light. But we truly tend toward Beth-shemesh when, walking the way of uprightness, we do not turn aside to the neighboring sides of error because of affection for our children [Col. 0099C] or loved ones.

Thus, thus must those walk who, placed beneath the yoke of the sacred Law, already bear God’s ark through inward knowledge: by grieving over the needs of their neighbors, they must not turn aside from the path of uprightness which they have received. The plight of others should indeed hold our mind, but should not bend it, lest that same mind be hard if it is untouched by affection, or lax if, being touched too greatly, it is bent.

## CHAPTER IX. ON THE HEIFER

[Note: [Col. 0099D] From Book XX on Job, ch. 16, before the middle.] By the name *heifer* the carnal mind is denoted, as the prophet Hosea aptly describes it under the figure of Ephraim: “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing” (Hos. 10:11). A heifer accustomed to the labors of threshing, once released, often returns to the same work even when not compelled. So the mind of the wicked, given over to the services of this world and accustomed to the weariness of temporal affairs, even if it is permitted to have leisure freely, nevertheless hastens to submit itself to earthly sweats; and through the habit of a miserable manner of life, it seeks the threshing of labor, so that it does not wish to cease from the yoke of worldly servitude even when it may do so.

The Lord was loosing this yoke from his disciples’ hearts when he said: “Take heed to yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34); and immediately added, “and by the cares of this life, and that day come suddenly upon you” (ibid.). And again: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and [Col. 0100A] I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29). What is it for the Lord to call himself meek and humble in teaching, except to set aside the difficulties of striving for self-exaltation and show certain level paths for living rightly? But because the minds of the wicked delight more in the harshness of self-exaltation than in the gentleness of humility and meekness, they think it a pleasure to be under thorns. For love of the world, they are prepared to endure hard things as though they were soft and pleasant, while in this life they seek to attain the heights of worldly possessions. The Lord commands rest from worldly labors and commends the sweetness of holy repose; yet the frenzied mind of the wicked more gladly obtains harsh things carnally than spiritual things. [Col. 0100B] It is fed more by the bitterness of toil than by the sweetness of rest.

## CHAPTER X. ON THE BULL

In Holy Scripture, by the name *bulls* are sometimes understood the Fathers of the Old Testament, sometimes the proud.

[Note: [Col. 0100D] Homily 38 on the Gospels.] By the name *bulls* the Fathers of the Old Testament are denoted, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, I have prepared my dinner; my bulls and fattened beasts have been slaughtered, and all things are ready; come to the wedding” (Matt. 22:4). What do we understand by the bulls and fattened beasts except the Fathers of the New and Old Testaments? For we call fattened animals *altilia*. From *alere*, “to nourish,” we call them *altilia*, as it were *alitilia*.

Now, although it is written in the Law, “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (Matt. 5:43), the righteous had then been granted leave to subdue, with whatever force they could, God’s enemies and their own, and to strike them by the right of the sword. This is unquestionably restrained in the New Testament, when Truth himself preaches: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (ibid., 44). What, then, is signified by bulls except the Fathers of the Old Testament? For, having received from the Law permission to strike their adversaries with the retaliation of hatred, they were, so to speak, bulls, who struck their enemies with the horn of bodily [Col. 0100C] strength.

What, then, is figured by the fattened beasts except the Fathers of the New Testament? Receiving the grace of inward richness, they rise from earthly desires toward the heights of contemplation on wings. To set one’s thought below is nothing but a kind of dryness of mind. But those who, through holy desires, already feed by the understanding of heavenly things upon the inward food of delight from above grow fat, as it were, upon more abundant nourishment. The Psalmist desired to be filled with this richness when he said: “May my soul be filled as with fat and richness” (Ps. 62:6).

Therefore, because the preachers of the Lord’s Incarnation, sent forth, endured persecution from unbelievers—first the prophets and afterwards the holy apostles—it is said to those invited but unwilling to come: “My bulls and fattened beasts have been slaughtered, and all things are ready.” As though it were said more plainly: Accept the deaths of the Fathers who went before, and consider the remedies of our life.

[Note: [Col. 0101D] From Book XXXV on Job, ch. 7.] By the name *bulls* the neck of pride is denoted, as the Lord says to the friends of blessed Job: “Take for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and he shall offer a holocaust for you” (Job 42:8). By bulls, the neck of pride is expressed; by rams, leadership exercised over peoples persuaded by heretics, as it were over flocks led astray. For it is said of proud heretics who corrupt the minds of the weak by evil persuasion: “The assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples” (Ps. 67:31). And because they draw after themselves peoples like flocks, they are sometimes called [Col. 0101B] rams; rams, of course, lead flocks. Hence Jeremiah says reproachfully: “Your leaders are like rams” (Lam. 1:6).

Therefore, when heretics return to Holy Church, they abandon the pride of their exaltation and no longer lead bands of peoples, like following flocks, to destruction. The friends of blessed Job are commanded to offer bulls and rams. To offer bulls and rams in sacrifice is to slaughter proud leadership in the humility of conversion, so that, with the neck of pride subdued, those who once tried to lead may learn to follow in obedience. Their pride is rightly expiated by seven sacrifices, because heretics returning to the Church receive, through the offering of humility, the gifts of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, so that those wasted away by the oldness of their self-exaltation may be renewed by the newness of grace. Therefore let it be said: “Take for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and he shall offer a holocaust for you.” It is as though returning heretics were openly told: Join yourselves to the universal Church through the humility of repentance; and obtain from me, through its prayers, the pardon which you are not worthy to obtain for yourselves. For when through this Church you learn truly to be wise, you erase before me the folly [Col. 0101C] of your former wisdom.

## CHAPTER XI. ON THE CALF

In Holy Scripture, by the name *calf* are sometimes understood Christ or Luke the Evangelist, sometimes a holy preacher.

By the name *calf* Christ or Luke the Evangelist is denoted, as John the Evangelist says in the Apocalypse concerning the four animals: “The first animal was like a lion; the second animal like a calf; the third animal had a face like a man; and the fourth animal was like a flying eagle” (Rev. 4:7). Although each of these may fittingly apply to an individual Evangelist—one indicates the order of his human birth; another, through the slaughter of the world’s sacrifice, the death of a calf; another, the strength of power as the roar of a lion; another, beholding the birth of the Word, looks upon the rising sun as an eagle—these four animals may nevertheless signify their own head, of whom they are members. For he is man, because he truly assumed our nature; calf, because he patiently died for us; lion, because by the strength of his divinity he broke the bond of the death he had assumed; and finally eagle, because he returned to the heaven from which he had come. Thus he is called man in being born, calf in dying, lion in rising again, and eagle in ascending into heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0101D] From Homily 3 on Ezekiel.] By the name *calf* a holy preacher is denoted, as Ezekiel says: “The sole of their foot was like the sole of a calf’s foot” (Ezek. 1:7). In holy preachers the sole of the foot is like the sole of a calf: that is, it walks maturely, strongly, and with a divided hoof. For every preacher possesses dignity in maturity, strength in action, and division of the hoof in discernment. His preaching is not readily accepted if he appears frivolous in character. Nor will there be any display of maturity unless strength of action is present against every adversity. But strength of action itself loses the merit of virtue if there is no discernment in understanding.

## CHAPTER XII. ON DOGS

In Holy Scripture, by the name *dogs* are sometimes understood holy preachers; sometimes flatterers; at other times heretics; at other times Jews; sometimes Gentiles.

[Note: [Col. 0102D] From Homily 40 on the Gospels.] By the name *dogs* holy preachers are denoted, as it is written in the Gospel: “But even the [Col. 0102C] dogs came and licked his sores” (Luke 16:21). What do we understand by dogs except preachers? A dog’s tongue, when it licks a wound, heals it; so too holy teachers, when they instruct us in the confession of our sin, touch the wound of our mind, as it were, with their tongue. And because by speaking they rescue us from sins, they restore us to health, as it were, by touching wounds.

Because the tongue of preachers is signified by dogs, the Psalmist fittingly says to the Lord: “The tongue of your dogs from enemies, by him” (Ps. 67:24). For holy preachers were chosen from unbelieving Jews; by the assertion of truth they gave, so to speak, great barks for the Lord against thieves and robbers who came. Conversely, it is said in condemnation of some: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” [Col. 0102D] (Isa. 56:10). Therefore, because holy preachers condemn sins but approve the confession of sins, saying, “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another that you may be saved” (Jas. 5:16), dogs lick Lazarus’s sores. For holy teachers, receiving the confessions of Gentiles, restore the wounds of minds to health. Hence Lazarus is interpreted “helped,” because those who heal his wounds by the correction of their tongue help him toward deliverance.

But by the licking of dogs may be signified the broad tongue of flatterers. For flatterers lick our wounds when, as they are often wont to do, they praise with shameless favor even the very evils that we condemn in ourselves.

By the name *dogs* heretics are denoted, as it is written: “As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool to his folly” (Prov. 26:11).

By the name *dogs* the Jews persecuting the Lord are denoted, as the Lord says through the Psalmist: “Many dogs have surrounded me” (Ps. 21:17).

By the name *dogs* Gentiles are denoted, as the Lord says to the Canaanite woman in the Gospel: “It is not good to take the bread and throw it to dogs” (Matt. 15:26). It is as though he said: It is not good that the bread of doctrine should be taken away from the children—that is, the Jews, who from the beginning worshiped and adored the Lord—and given to you Gentiles, [Col. 0103B] who served many defilements and idols.

## 120. CHAPTER XIII. ON RAMS

In Holy Scripture, by the name *rams* are sometimes denoted priests; sometimes rational spirits; sometimes leadership over following peoples.

By the name *ram* the first order of priests within the Church is denoted, as Solomon says: “There are three things which walk well, and a fourth which proceeds prosperously: the lion, strongest of beasts, who will fear no encounter; the rooster with girded loins; and the ram; and there is no king who can resist him.” Here the lion is plainly he of whom it is written: “The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” [Col. 0103C] (Rev. 5:5). He is said to be strongest because “what is weak in God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1:25). He fears no encounter, for he says: “The prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

“The rooster with girded loins”: that is, holy preachers announcing the true morning amid the darkness of this night. Their loins are girded because they restrain the loose flow of lust from their members. Lust is in the loins; hence the Lord says to them: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35). “And the ram; and there is no king who can resist him.” Whom else do we understand here by the ram except the first order of priests within the Church? Of them it is written: “Bring to the Lord sons of rams” (Ps. 28:1). By their examples they draw along the people walking behind them like a following flock of sheep. When they live spiritually and rightly, no king is sufficient to resist them, because whatever persecutor opposes them cannot hinder their purpose. For they know both how to run anxiously toward him whom they desire and how to arrive by dying.

Therefore the lion is placed first, the rooster second, and the ram third. Christ appeared first; then the holy preachers, the apostles; and only then the spiritual Fathers set over the Churches—namely, leaders of flocks, because they are teachers of peoples who follow. But because Antichrist will appear after this, Solomon adds him as a fourth: “And he who appeared foolish, after he has been raised on high. If he had understood, he would have put his hand on his mouth” (Prov. 30:32). For he will be raised on high when he falsely claims to be God. But, raised on high, he will appear foolish because, in that very exaltation, he will fail at the coming of the true Judge. Had he understood—had he foreseen his punishment when he began to grow proud—he would not, though well created, have been raised into such boastful pride.

Nor should anyone be troubled because it was said above, “the fourth, which proceeds prosperously.” Solomon said that three proceed well, and the fourth prosperously. For not everything that proceeds prosperously proceeds well; nor does everything that proceeds well in this life proceed prosperously. The lion, rooster, and ram proceed well, but not prosperously here, because they endure the wars of persecutions. The fourth, however, proceeds prosperously but not well, because Antichrist walks in his deceit; yet, during the short span of this present life, that deceit prospers for him. Thus it was said of him through Daniel under the figure of Antiochus: “Strength was given to him against the continual sacrifice because of sins; truth shall be cast down to the earth; and he shall act and prosper” (Dan. 8:12). Thus what Solomon says, “he proceeds prosperously,” Daniel calls, “he shall prosper.”

Rams signify rational spirits, as is said through Moses: “Jacob took green poplar rods, almond rods, and rods from plane trees, and peeled them partly. When the bark had been stripped from the places that were peeled, whiteness appeared; but those that were left whole remained green, and thus a variegated colour was produced. Therefore, when the sheep were mating, [Col. 0104C] he placed them in the water-troughs before the eyes of the rams and sheep, so that they might conceive while looking at them” (Gen. 30:37–38). For what is it to place green rods of almond and plane tree before the eyes of the flock, except to offer to the people, as an example through the course of sacred Scripture, the lives and sayings of the ancient Fathers? These are called rods because they are right according to the test of reason. From some of them he removes the bark, so that in what has been stripped the inner whiteness may appear; and on others he keeps the bark, so that they may remain outwardly green as they were. Thus the rods acquire a varied colour, since the bark is partly removed and partly retained. For the sayings of the Fathers who went before are set before the eyes of our consideration like variegated rods [Col. 0104D]: when we often escape the literal sense, we as it were remove the bark; and when we often follow the literal sense, we as it were preserve the bark. When the bark of the letter is removed from them, the inward brightness of allegory is displayed; and when the bark remains, the green examples of the outward sense are shown. Jacob rightly placed these in the water-troughs, because our Redeemer has set them in the books of sacred knowledge with which we are inwardly filled. As the rams look upon them, they mate with the sheep: our rational spirits, while fixed in attention upon them, mingle with each particular action, so as to produce such offspring of works as they see in the examples of those who preceded them, as expressed in the words of the commandments. And [Col. 0105A] the offspring of good work has a varied colour, because it sometimes considers inward acts after the bark of the letter has been removed, and sometimes, with the covering of history retained, shapes itself in outward matters.

Rams also signify the leadership of peoples who follow. Hence the Lord says to the friends of blessed Job: “Take for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant; and he shall offer a burnt offering for you” (Job 42:8). See the chapter *On the Bull*.

123 CHAPTER XIV. ON SHEEP.

In sacred Scripture, when “sheep” is used in the singular, Christ’s suffering is understood; but when “sheep” is used in the plural, it sometimes means believers from among the Jews, sometimes innocence of thoughts, and sometimes all who are simple.

[Col. 0105B] [Note: [Col. 0105D] From Book I on Job, ch. VI.] Sheep signify believers from among the Jews, as is said figuratively of blessed Job: “His possessions were seven thousand sheep and three thousand camels” (Job 1:3). For what is expressed by seven thousand sheep except the perfect innocence of certain Jews, who came from the pastures of the Law to the grace of perfection? And what is signified by three thousand camels except the whole viciousness of the Gentiles, coming to the fullness of faith? As by sheep we understand Hebrews coming from the pastures of the Law to faith, so nothing prevents us from understanding by camels the Gentile peoples, bent in their ways and burdened with idol-worship. For because they themselves devised gods for themselves to worship, a burden which they had to carry had, as it were, grown upon their backs from themselves. But because the Lord, appearing in the flesh, [Col. 0105C] both filled the Hebrew people with the grace of perfection and, by displaying wonderful works, brought some of the Gentiles to knowledge of the faith, it is rightly said of the shadow that expressed the truth that he possessed seven thousand sheep and three thousand camels.

Morally, however, sheep may signify innocence of thoughts, and camels distorted thoughts. While preserving the truth of the history, we may spiritually imitate what we hear carnally. For we possess seven thousand sheep when, amid ourselves, we feed innocent thoughts upon the sought-for pasture of truth through perfect purity of heart. And three thousand camels will also become our possession [Col. 0105D] if we subject everything lofty and crooked in us to the reason of faith, and willingly bend it under knowledge of the Trinity in the desire for humility. For we possess camels if we humbly lay aside our high-mindedness. We possess camels when we bend our thoughts toward compassion for a brother’s weakness and, bearing one another’s burdens in return, know how to show compassion for another’s weakness by condescending to it.

[Note: [Col. 0105D] From Book XXXV on Job, ch. XI.] Sheep signify all who are simple and innocent, as the Psalmist says to the Father concerning the Son: “You have subjected all things under his feet: all sheep and [Col. 0106A] oxen, and moreover the beasts of the field” (Ps. 8:8). Again the same Psalmist says: “But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Ps. 78:13). Those who neglect to preserve innocence are not satisfied by that refreshment of the inner pasture.

CHAPTER XV. ON THE EWE-LAMB.

[Note: [Col. 0105D] From Book XXXII on Job, ch. IV.] The ewe-lamb signifies the active life, as Moses says concerning one who uttered an oath, whether to do something evil or good, and then forgot the very matter: “Let him offer a ewe-lamb from the flock, or a goat” (Lev. 5:6). To utter an oath is to bind ourselves by a vow to divine service. When we promise good works, we pledge ourselves to act well. But when we vow abstinence and the affliction of [Col. 0106B] our flesh, we swear to treat ourselves badly for the present. Yet because no one in this life, however devoted to God, is so perfect that amid even the smallest of pious vows he does not sin, for sin one is commanded to offer a ewe-lamb from the flock or a goat. For what does the ewe-lamb signify except the innocence of the active life? What does the goat, which feeds hanging upon the highest and most remote crags, signify except the contemplative life? Therefore, whoever sees that he has not fulfilled his promises and purposes ought more zealously to equip himself for God’s sacrifice, either with the innocence of good work or with the lofty nourishment of contemplation. And a ewe-lamb is rightly commanded to be offered from the flock, but a goat is not: the active life belongs to many, the contemplative to few. When we do those things which we see many doing and having done, [Col. 0106C] we give, as it were, a ewe-lamb from the flock.

CHAPTER XVI. ON BEASTS.

In sacred Scripture, when “beast” is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies the devil, sometimes the crowd of Antichrist’s preachers, and sometimes the irrational mind; but in the plural it sometimes signifies demons, sometimes movements of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0106D] From Book XXVII on Job, ch. XVII, 18.] “Beast” means the ancient enemy, who fiercely attacked the first man through deception and tore apart the integrity of his life by evil persuasion. Against him it is foretold, in the prophet’s words, concerning the holy Church of the elect to be restored to its former state: “No evil beast shall pass through it” (Isa. 35:9). Again, in the book of blessed Job it is written: “The beast shall enter its hiding-place and dwell in its den” (Job 37:8). For when, at the end of the world, he has taken possession of that condemned man called Antichrist, what else does he do except enter his hiding-place, in order to remain in his own den? That vessel of the devil is the beast’s den and hiding-place, so that, while lying in wait for people travelling the path of this life, he may hide in him through signs and kill through wickedness.

[Note: [Col. 0106D] From Book XXXIII on Job, ch. XXVI.] “Beast” signifies the crowd of Antichrist’s preachers. Hence John, in the Apocalypse, briefly describing the wickedness of their pretence, says: “I saw another beast rising from the earth, having two horns like a lamb, and it spoke as a dragon” (Rev. 13:11). He had already described the former beast—that is, Antichrist—in the preceding account; after him this other beast is also said to have arisen, because after him the multitude of his preachers glories in earthly power. To rise from the earth is to be proud of earthly glory. It has two horns like a lamb, because through the hypocrisy of holiness it falsely claims for itself the wisdom and life which the Lord truly possessed uniquely in himself. But because under the appearance of a lamb it pours serpentine venom into its reprobate hearers, it is rightly added: “And it spoke as a dragon.” If this beast—that is, the multitude of preachers—spoke openly [Col. 0107B] as a dragon, it would not appear like a lamb; but it takes on the appearance of a lamb in order to perform the work of a dragon.

[Note: [Col. 0107D] From Book VI on Job, ch. XVII.] “Beast” signifies the irrational mind, as Moses says: “If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned” (Exod. 19:12). The mountain is the height of contemplation; the beast is the irrational mind. The beast therefore touches the mountain when the mind, subject to irrational desires, raises itself to the heights of contemplation.
