But it is struck with stones because, unable to bear what is highest, it is killed by the very blows of the heavenly weight.

“Beasts” signify demons, as Job says from the Lord’s mouth: “All the beasts of the field shall play there” (Job 40:15). For what are beasts except unclean [Col. 0107C] spirits? And what is the field except the present age? The beasts of the field play there—that is, in the grasses of the mountains—because demons cast down from the heights delight in this world in the evil deeds of the proud. Beasts play in the grasses when reprobate spirits draw human hearts into unlawful thoughts. Is it not play for unclean spirits to deceive minds made in God’s image now by feigned promise, now to mock them with empty terrors, now to impress transient joys upon them as though they were lasting, now to make lasting punishments seem transient?

[Note: [Col. 0107D] From Book VI on Job, ch. XVI.] “Beasts” signify movements of the flesh, as blessed Job says: “And the beasts of the earth shall be at peace [Col. 0107D] with you” (Job 5:23). For what do beasts mean except movements of the flesh, which rise bestially against us while they provoke our mind by urging irrational things? But when the divine law humbles the heart, even the incitements of the flesh subside, so that, though they murmur in temptation, they nevertheless do not rise as far as the effect of deeds, as if to open rabies of biting. For who, still placed in this corruptible flesh, fully tames these beasts of the earth, when that outstanding preacher, caught up into the third heaven, says: “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and making me captive under the law of sin which [Col. 0108A] is in my members” (Rom. 7:23)? But it is one thing to see these beasts raging in the field of action, another to keep them roaring within the cage of the heart. For when reduced within the enclosure of continence, even if they still roar in temptation, they do not go beyond, as we have said, to the bite of unlawful action. Therefore the beasts of the earth are at peace, because movements of the flesh, though they throb with desires, do not attack us by open contradiction in deed. The beasts of the earth thus make peace with us because, while they provoke us by temptation, movements of the flesh impel us toward love of inward rest.

128 CHAPTER XVII. ON THE LION.

In sacred Scripture, when “lion” occurs in the singular, [Col. 0108B] it sometimes means Christ, sometimes Mark the Evangelist, sometimes the devil, sometimes the confidence of any righteous person, sometimes Antichrist, and sometimes any plunderer; but when “lions” occurs in the plural, it sometimes signifies the severity of teachers and sometimes demons.

The lion signifies Christ, as it is written: “The lion, strongest of beasts, shall fear no encounter” (Prov. 30:36). He is rightly called the strongest of beasts, because “what is weak in God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1:25). He fears no encounter, for he says: “The prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 14:30). Elsewhere it is said: “The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. 5:5).

[Note: [Col. 0108D] From Homily 4 on Ezekiel, at the beginning.] The lion signifies Mark the Evangelist. Hence the prophet Ezekiel, when he described the holy Evangelists under the figure of four living creatures, said: “The likeness of their faces was the face of a man, and the face of a lion at the right side of all four; the face of an ox at the left side of all four; and the face of an eagle above all four” (Ezek. 1:20). That these four winged creatures signify the four Evangelists is shown by the beginnings of the individual Gospel books. Since he began from the human generation, Matthew is rightly signified by a man; because he began with the cry in the wilderness, Mark rightly by a lion; because he began with sacrifice, Luke fittingly by a calf; and because he began from the divinity of the Word, John is worthily signified by an eagle, for he says: “In the beginning was [Col. 0108D] the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Since he fixes his attention upon the very substance of divinity, he has, as it were, fixed his eyes upon the sun in the manner of an eagle.

[Note: [Col. 0108D] From Homily 19 on Ezekiel.] The lion signifies the devil, as the first shepherd of the Church says to the faithful: “Your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). Again Isaiah says: “The lion, like the ox, shall eat straw” (Isa. 11:7).

The lion signifies the confidence of a righteous man, as Solomon says: “The righteous shall be confident like a lion, without terror” (Prov. 28:1). For the lion does not tremble at the encounter [Col. 0109A] of beasts because it knows that it prevails over all of them. Therefore the confidence of a righteous man is rightly compared with a lion: when he sees any persons rise up against him, he returns to the confidence of his mind. He knows that he overcomes all adversaries because he loves him alone whom he cannot lose against his will in any way. Whoever desires outward things, which can be taken away unwillingly, voluntarily subjects himself to alien fear. But unbroken strength is the desire for eternal life and contempt for earthly life; for the mind is set on high when it is lifted away from low things by the judgment of its hope, and it is touched all the less by all adversaries the more safely it is fortified by being placed in things above.

[Note: [Col. 0109D] From Book XXXII on Job, ch. XIV.] The lion signifies Antichrist, as the Psalmist says: “He lies in wait secretly, like a lion [Col. 0109B] in his den” (Ps. 9:9). Antichrist is rightly called both a lion lying in wait: lying in wait through the appearance of miracles, a lion through worldly power. For open power would have sufficed for him to be a lion even if he did not lie in wait. Conversely, secret trickery would have sufficed for him to steal upon people by lying in wait even if he were not a lion. But because this ancient enemy is unrestrained in all his powers, he is allowed to rage in both ways, so that he may be loosed against the elect in contest both by fraud and by strength: by strength through power, by fraud through signs. For then he is not raised up by power alone, but is also supported by the display of signs. To draw those who are openly wicked, he displays worldly power; but to deceive righteous people, he feigns holiness by signs. To the former he recommends the pride [Col. 0109C] of greatness; the latter he deceives by an appearance of holiness.

[Note: [Col. 0109D] From Homily 16 on Ezekiel.] The lion signifies any plunderer, as Isaiah promises concerning the conversion of unbelievers: “The calf, the lion, and the sheep shall dwell together” (Isa. 11:6). For what does the calf mean except one who sacrifices himself to God through contrition of heart? What does the lion mean except one who torments others? And what does the sheep mean except one who is simple and innocent? Yet the calf, lion, and sheep dwell together, because one who prepares himself through a contrite heart for a daily sacrifice to God, another who had raged cruelly like a lion, and another who continues in the simplicity of his innocence like a sheep, have gathered together in the folds of holy Church.

[Col. 0109D] [Note: [Col. 0109D] From Homily 21 on Ezekiel.] The lion signifies the severity of teachers. Hence it is written that upon the vessels of the temple, among the crowns and braided work, oxen, lions, and cherubim were carved; and beneath the oxen and lions hung straps. Crowns signify victory, while braided work signifies the unity of concord. Cherubim, moreover, are said to mean the fullness of knowledge. Priests and teachers, among crowns and braided work (3 Kings 7:29)—that is, between the strength of good work by which they run toward victory and the concord of charity, whereby they do not disagree with one another—are signified by oxen, lions, and cherubim, because in the fullness of knowledge which [Col. 0110A] they possess, they must hold both the gentleness of oxen and the ardour of lions, so that in the discipline they preach they may be aflame with holy zeal and calm with paternal sweetness. Straps should hang below them, so that they may diligently extend to their subjects the restraints of their discipline by which they themselves are bound. For straps to hang below them is to hold the bonds of guardianship over those subject to them. These are then rightly maintained when neither the gentleness of oxen is lost in the ardour of zeal nor the terror of lions is relaxed into gentleness. There must be such discernment that neither discipline is excessive nor mercy lax; otherwise, if guilt is remitted without order, the guilty person is bound more severely in guilt, while if guilt is retained without moderation, the one corrected becomes worse [Col. 0110B] in proportion as he sees that nothing is done toward him from the grace of kindness. Thus harshness must be shown to the wicked outwardly, but charity maintained in the mind, so that stern manifestation may restrain the offender while charity’s safeguard does not lose the reward of gentleness. This is the mastery of discipline: the teacher must know how both to spare sins discerningly and to cut them away mercifully.

[Note: [Col. 0110D] From Book XXVII on Job, ch. XVII, 19.] Lions signify demons of higher power, as it is written in the Psalm: “You appoint darkness, and night comes; in it all the beasts of the forest pass through, the lion cubs roaring in order to seize and to seek their food from God” (Ps. 103:20). The Lord appoints darkness when, repaying judgments for sins, he withdraws the light of his understanding. Night comes because the minds of the wicked [Col. 0110C] are blinded by the errors of their ignorance. In this night all the beasts of the forest pass through, when evil spirits, hidden beneath the darkness of deceit, range through the hearts of the reprobate by carrying out their wickedness. In it also the lion cubs roar, because the ministering spirits of most wicked, though high-ranking, powers rise up in importunate temptations. Yet they ask food from God because they cannot seize souls unless, by a just judgment, they are divinely permitted to prevail.

132 CHAPTER XVIII. ON THE LIONESS.

In sacred Scripture, the lioness sometimes signifies the holy Church, sometimes Babylon, and sometimes the human mind.

[Note: [Col. 0110D] From Book XVIII on Job, ch. XX.] The lioness signifies the Church because it is bold against adversities, as is said through blessed Job concerning the rejection of Judaea: “The sons of merchants have not trodden it, nor has a lioness passed through it” (Job 28:8). We call merchants *institores*, because they are engaged in the work which they pursue. Therefore all who instruct the conduct of the faithful carry on spiritual commerce, so that, when they offer preaching to their hearers, they may receive from them faith and right works; as it is written of holy Church: “She made linen cloth and sold it” (Prov. 31:24). A little later it says of her: “She saw that her trade was good” (ibid., 18). Who then are called merchants except the holy prophets, who laboured by prophesying to instruct the conduct of the Synagogue [Col. 0111A] unto faith? Their sons are called the holy apostles, who were brought forth unto the same faith through the prophets’ preaching, so that they might believe that God is man. Of them it is said to the Church through the Psalmist: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them rulers over all the earth” (Ps. 44:17). But because the apostles, having been rejected, departed from the boundaries of the Synagogue, it is rightly now said: “The sons of merchants have not trodden it.” The sons of the merchants would have trodden it if the holy preachers had crushed the vices of that Synagogue under the foot of virtue. But if we take the merchants to mean the same preachers of the Church, nothing prevents us from understanding the sons of the merchants as the shepherds and teachers who followed the life of the apostles. They did not tread the Synagogue [Col. 0111B] because, when their fathers—that is, the apostles—were rejected by it, they too ceased from its calling. The lioness did not pass through this Synagogue, because holy Church, devoted to gathering the Gentiles, did not occupy herself any longer with that people of Judaea. The Church is rightly called a lioness because it kills those living wickedly in vices with the mouth of holy preaching. Thus the first shepherd himself is told, as if to the mouth of this lioness: “Kill [Note: [Col. 0111D] Here, the common text reads *occide* (‘kill’) instead of *macta* (‘slay’).] and eat” (Acts 10:13). What is slain is killed to its former life; what is eaten is changed into the body of the one who eats. “Kill and eat,” therefore, means: kill them to the sin in which they live, and change them from themselves into your members. And because this Church is the Lord’s body, the Lord himself [Col. 0111C] is called a lion in his own person, and a lioness in relation to his body, when under the figure of Judah it is said to him: “You have gone up to the prey, my son; resting, you have lain down like a lion, and like a lioness” (Gen. 49:9). “Who shall rouse him?” Therefore this lioness is by no means said not to have passed through Judaea, because it did pass through it; but it did not pass entirely through it. For when the apostles preached, first three thousand and afterwards five thousand believed from it. The Church thus passed through the Synagogue but did not pass entirely through it: from it she snatched a few unto the end, yet did not utterly extinguish that people’s unbelief.

[Note: [Col. 0111D] From Book V on Job, ch. XVI.] The lioness signifies Babylon, as Eliphaz says against blessed Job under the figure of the Hebrews: “The roaring of the lion, the voice of the lioness, and the teeth [Col. 0111D] of the lion cubs have been broken” (Job 4:10). The lion signifies the ancient enemy; the lioness expresses the city of this world—that is, Babylon—which is unrestrained in the savagery of its cruelty against the life of the innocent. Joined as it were to the ancient enemy, the most savage lion, it conceives the seeds of his perverse persuasion and bears from itself reprobate children, cruel like lion cubs, in his likeness. The lion cubs are all reprobate persons brought forth to an iniquitous life through the error of evil spirits. Together they all make up the whole worldly city which we have called Babylon; yet individually they are called children of Babylon, as lion cubs not of a lion but of a lioness [Col. 0112A]. For just as the whole Church together is called Zion, while individual holy persons are called children of Zion, so each reprobate person is called a child of Babylon, while Babylon itself is the collective name for all the reprobate. But so long as holy people are in this life, they guard themselves with watchful circumspection, lest the lion walking about secretly steal upon them—that is, lest the ancient enemy kill them under some appearance of virtue; lest the lioness’s voice ring in their ears—that is, lest Babylon’s glory turn their understanding away from love of the heavenly homeland; and lest the cubs’ teeth bite—that is, lest the persuasion of the reprobate grow strong in their heart. Heretics, by contrast, are as though secure because of holiness, since they suppose that by the merits of their lives they have overcome everything. Therefore it is rightly said now: “The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the lioness; [Col. 0112B] the teeth of the lion cubs have been broken.” It is as though it said plainly: We are not worn down by any scourges because we overcome, trampling underfoot through the merits of our life, the strength of the ancient enemy, the desire for earthly glory, and the persuasions of all the reprobate.

The lioness signifies the human mind, as blessed Job says: “And because of pride you will seize me like a lioness” (Job 10:16). Divine providence permits us, even while we serve it with all our intention, to be shaken by attacks of our flesh, lest our mind dare to rise in pride through confidence in its own security. Thus, when shaken, it trembles and plants the foot of hope more firmly in the help of its Creator alone. Hence it is rightly said: “And because of pride you will seize me like a lioness” [Note: [Col. 0112D] From Book IX on Job, ch. XXXIII.]. For when a lioness seeks food for her cubs, [Col. 0112C] she eagerly falls into a trapping-pit. As is reported from certain regions, a pit is made in its path; livestock are placed in it, so that the lioness may be enticed to throw herself in by desire for it. The pit is prepared both narrow and deep, so that she may fall into it by rushing in, but be wholly unable to escape by leaping out. Another pit is also dug adjoining the first, connected to the one containing the livestock by an opening at its far end. A cage is placed in this second pit, so that when the lioness falls and is pressed by terrors from above, she may seek to hide in the more secluded part of the pit and enter the cage willingly. Its savagery is no longer feared, because it is lifted up enclosed in the cage. For the lioness that fell of its own accord into the pit returns to the upper regions surrounded by bars.

Thus, indeed, the human mind was captured. Created in freedom of choice, when it desired to feed the desires of the flesh, it sought food for its cubs like a lioness and fell into the pit of its deception: at the enemy’s urging it stretched out its hand toward the forbidden food. But it immediately found a cage in the pit, because, coming voluntarily to death, it at once underwent the prison of its corruption; yet through intervening grace it is led to the free air. But when it attempts many things and cannot accomplish them, it is bound by the obstacles of its same corruption as by the bars of a cage. It has indeed escaped the pit of damnation into which it fell, because, aided by the Redeemer’s hand, it overcame the punishment of the death to come by returning to pardon. Yet it endures the constraining cage because it is also bound by the fetters of heavenly discipline, lest it wander through fleshly desires. Thus, having fallen of its own accord into the pit, it returns enclosed to the free air: through freedom of choice it fell into sin, yet the Creator’s grace restrains it, unwilling and compelled, from its own impulses. After the pit it therefore endures the cage: raised from eternal punishment, it is bound under the providence of the heavenly Craftsman against the movements of its perverse will. It is rightly said: “And because of pride you will seize me like a lioness,” because man, free though he was, brought death upon himself through food; and, restored to pardon, lives better enclosed under discipline. He was seized like a lioness because of pride, [Col. 0113B] because the discipline of his corruption now humbles him precisely where, unafraid of transgressing the commandment, he boldly leapt into the pit.

But if we turn the gaze of our mind only a little from the fault of the first parent, we find that we too are still daily seized like a lioness by the vice of self-exaltation. For a person often rises, having received virtues, into the boldness of self-confidence; yet by the wondrous providence of mercy some occasion for falling is arranged before his eyes. While through fault he desires something, what does he do except desire prey in a pit? Eager by his own will, he falls, but cannot rise by his own strength. When he sees that he is nothing from himself, he undoubtedly learns whose help he must seek. Yet heavenly mercy lifts him from the pit as one captured, [Col. 0113C] because, once his weakness is recognized, it restores him to pardon. Therefore one returns, like a lioness, through pride to the upper regions in a cage when, after being exalted by virtue, one falls into desires and is bound in humility. Because he had first perished through self-confidence, wondrous mercy brings it about that, knowing his weakness, he now lives enclosed. Since the holy man sees this frequently happen to people, he takes upon himself the voice of our danger, so that, when we recognize his lamentation, we may learn what in ourselves must be lamented.

CHAPTER XIX. ON THE TIGER.

In sacred Scripture, the tiger sometimes signifies any hypocrite, sometimes the devil.

[Col. 0113D] [Note: [Col. 0113D] From Book V on Job, ch. VI, 16.] The tiger signifies any hypocrite. Thus Eliphaz, accusing blessed Job as variegated with the spots of pretence, says: “The tiger has perished because it had no prey” (Job 4:11). Whom does he mark under the name of a tiger, except blessed Job, as bearing the mark of variegation or sprinkled with the spots of hypocrisy? For every pretender, in desiring to appear upright, presents himself as wholly clean. While he assumes certain virtues hypocritically and secretly subjects himself to vices, certain hidden vices suddenly break forth into view; and the skin, as it were, of assumed pretence appears variegated by this admixture, so that it is often astonishing why a person who is seen to possess [Col. 0114A] such great virtues is also defiled by such reprehensible acts. Every hypocrite, then, is a tiger: while a clean colour is produced by dissimulation, it becomes variegated through the interruption of the blackness of vices. Often, while he is exalted by the purity of chastity, he is defiled by the filth of greed. Often, while he appears beautiful through the virtue of generosity, he is stained by the spots of lust. Often, while clothed in the beauty of chastity and generosity, he is darkened by the atrocity of cruelty, as if out of zeal for justice. Often he is clothed with a beautiful appearance through generosity, chastity, and compassion, but is marked by the interspersed darkness of pride. Thus it happens that, amid mingled vices, the hypocrite does not display a clean appearance in himself, as though the tiger could by no means possess one colour. This tiger seizes prey [Col. 0114B] when it usurps for itself the glory of human favour. For one exalted by stolen praise is, as it were, filled with prey. The praise of hypocrites is rightly called prey: prey is what is violently taken away from another. Every hypocrite, since he feigns a life of righteousness and takes for himself the praise of righteous people, plainly takes what belongs to another. Eliphaz, therefore, because he knew that blessed Job had done praiseworthy things while he was in prosperity, believed, after the ensuing blow, that Job had maintained them hypocritically; saying: “The tiger has perished because it had no prey.” It is as though he said plainly: The variegation of your pretence has been destroyed, because flattering praise has been taken away and your hypocrisy now has no prey, since you have been struck by God and lack human favour.

[Note: [Col. 0113D] From ch. XVII of the same book.] The tiger may also signify the devil. [Col. 0114C] Thus Eliphaz, speaking in the person of heretics and puffed up by supposed holiness of life, says: “The tiger has perished because it had no prey.” Satan is not inappropriately called a tiger because of the variety of his manifold cunning. At one time he presents himself to human senses as the lost being that he is; at another he shows himself as an angel of light; at one time he persuades the minds of fools by flattery; at another he draws them to sin by terror; at one time he openly strives to recommend vices; at another he cloaks himself in his suggestions under the hope of virtue. Since he conducts his affairs with such variety, the devil is rightly called a tiger. The heretics, proud in their presumption of holiness, say exultantly: “The tiger has perished because it had no prey.” It is as though they said plainly: The most ancient [Col. 0114D] adversary has no prey in us, because, so far as our efforts are concerned, he now lies defeated.

138 CHAPTER XX. ON THE PANTHER.

[Note: [Col. 0114D] From Homily 16 on Ezekiel, rather far from the beginning.] The panther signifies one variegated with the spots of sins, as Isaiah says concerning sinners who are to be converted: “The panther shall lie down with the kid” (Isa. 2:6). For what do we understand by the panther except one sprinkled with diverse sins? And by the kid except one who humbly recognizes himself as a sinner? The panther lies down with the kid when one who was variegated with the spots of his sins consents to humble himself with one who despises himself and confesses himself a sinner.

CHAPTER XXI. ON THE WOLF.

[Col. 0115A]

In sacred Scripture, the wolf sometimes signifies any plunderer and sometimes the devil.

[Note: [Col. 0115D] From the same homily.] By the name wolf is meant any rapacious person, as Isaiah says: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb” (Isa. XI, 6). For what do we understand by the wolf but one eager for plunder, and by the lamb but any gentle person? The wolf dwells with the lamb because, through the inward compassion of holy charity, those who were plunderers in the world rest in peace with the meek and gentle. Hence it is written in the Gospel: “But the hireling, and he who is not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, and leaves the sheep and flees” (John X, 12).

[Note: [Col. 0115D] From Homily 14 on the Gospels.] A hireling, and not a shepherd, is one who tends the Lord’s sheep not from inward love but for temporal rewards. For a hireling is one who indeed holds the place of a shepherd, but does not seek the gain of souls; he longs for earthly advantages, delights in the honour of preeminence, feeds upon temporal concerns, and rejoices in the reverence bestowed upon him by men. These are the hireling’s rewards: that, in return for the very fact that he labours in governance, he may find here what he seeks, and hereafter be estranged from the inheritance of the flock. Whether someone is a shepherd or a hireling cannot truly be known if an occasion of necessity is absent. For in a time of peace the hireling, like the true shepherd, commonly stands watch over the flock. But the wolf’s coming [Col. 0115C] reveals with what disposition each stood over the flock’s keeping. For a wolf comes upon the sheep when any unjust and rapacious person oppresses the faithful and humble. But he who seemed to be a shepherd was not one: he left the sheep and fled, because, while he fears danger to himself from that man, he does not presume to resist his injustice. He flees, moreover, not by changing his place, but by withholding help. He flees because he saw injustice and was silent. He flees because he hid himself beneath silence. To such persons the prophet aptly says: “You have not gone up to meet the enemy, nor set yourselves as a wall for the house of Israel, that you might stand in battle in the day of the Lord” (Ezek. XIII, 5). To go up against the enemy is to oppose, with the free voice of reason, whatever powers act wickedly. And on the day of the Lord we stand in battle for the house of Israel [Col. 0115D] and set up a wall, if by the authority of justice we defend faithful innocents against the injustice of the perverse. Since the hireling does not do this, when he sees the wolf coming, he flees.

[Note: [Col. 0116D] From the same homily.] There is, however, another wolf, which without ceasing tears to pieces daily not bodies but minds: namely, the evil spirit, which prowls about the folds of the faithful, laying snares and seeking the death of souls. Of this wolf it is said: “The wolf seizes and scatters the sheep” (John X, 12). The wolf comes and the hireling flees because the evil spirit tears the minds of the faithful in temptation, while he who occupies the place of shepherd has no concern of watchfulness. Souls perish, while he rejoices in earthly advantages [Col. 0116A]. The wolf seizes and scatters the sheep when he draws one person into lust, turns another toward avarice, lifts another up in pride, divides another through anger; he pricks this one with envy and trips up that one by deceit. Thus the wolf scatters the flock when the devil destroys the faithful people by temptations. Yet against this the hireling is kindled by no zeal, stirred by no fervour of love, because, while he seeks only outward advantages, he carelessly permits the flock’s inward losses. Hence it is immediately added: “But the hireling flees, because he is a hireling, and does not care for the sheep” (ibid., 13). The sole reason, therefore, why the hireling flees is that he is a hireling. It is as though it were plainly said: he cannot stand in danger for the sheep who, in presiding over the sheep, does not love the sheep but seeks earthly profit [Col. 0116B]. For while he embraces honour and delights in temporal advantages, he trembles to expose himself to danger, lest he lose what he loves.

## CHAPTER XXII. ON THE WILD ASS

In Sacred Scripture, when *onager*—the wild ass—is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies any solitary righteous person; sometimes the incarnate Lord; sometimes one who does all that he desires; sometimes the Gentile people; sometimes one who, placed in the field of faith, is bound by the reins of no ecclesiastical office. When wild asses are spoken of in the plural, they sometimes signify heretics and sometimes Jews.

[Col. 0116C] [Note: [Col. 0116D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter XII.] By the name wild ass is signified any solitary person, as the Lord says to blessed Job: “Who has let the wild ass go free, and who has loosed his bonds?” (Job XXXIX, 8). For the wild ass, which dwells in the wilderness, fittingly signifies the life of those who live apart from popular crowds. It is rightly also called free, because worldly business is a great servitude, by which the mind is severely worn down, even though people toil at it willingly. To lack the condition of this servitude is to desire nothing in the world any longer. For prosperity presses like a yoke of servitude when it is desired; adversity presses when it is feared. But if anyone has once freed the neck of the mind from the dominion of temporal desires, that person enjoys a certain liberty even in this life [Col. 0116D]: he is stirred by no longing for prosperity and constrained by no fear of adversity.

The Lord saw this heavy yoke of servitude laid upon worldly necks when he said: “Come unto me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart; and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. XI, 28–29). For it is a harsh yoke and the weight of hard servitude, as we have said, to be subject to temporal things, to pursue earthly things, to hold fast to what slips away, to wish to stand in things that do not stand, to desire what passes away, yet not wish to pass away with what passes. [Col. 0117A] For when all things flee contrary to their desire, those who first afflicted their minds by longing to obtain them afterward oppress themselves through fear of losing them. Therefore, he is let go free who, having trampled earthly desires, is relieved by security of mind from longing for temporal things. Each person’s bonds are loosed when, by divine assistance, the inward restraints of carnal desires are broken.

For when a devout intention calls one to conversion, but the weakness of the flesh still recalls one from that intention, the soul is hindered as though bound by certain bonds. We often see many people desire the life of holy conduct, but fear now sudden misfortunes, now adversities to come, lest they be unable to attain it. While they cautiously foresee uncertain evils, they are incautiously kept in the bonds of their sins [Col. 0117B]. For they set before their eyes many things which they fear they will be unable to endure if these should happen to them in religious life. Of them Solomon aptly says: “The way of the slothful is like a hedge of thorns” (Prov. XV, 19). For when they desire the way of God, the suspicions of their own fears, set before them like thorns of obstructing hedges, prick them. Since this does not usually hinder the elect, he fittingly added there: “The way of the righteous is without stumbling-block” (ibid.). For whatever adversity meets them in their conduct, the righteous do not stumble, because they leap over the obstacles of temporal adversity by the bound of eternal hope and inward contemplation.

Therefore he says: “Who has let the wild ass go free, and who has loosed his bonds?” Understand: except I. Thus the Lord looses the wild ass’s bonds when he breaks from the mind of each elect person the knots of weak thoughts and immediately scatters everything that formerly bound that person’s mind [Col. 0117C].

[Note: [Col. 0117D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter XV, not far from the beginning.] The incarnate Lord can also be signified by the name wild ass. Nor should anyone judge it unworthy that the incarnate Lord can be figured by such an animal, since it is known to all that in Sacred Scripture he is also set forth figuratively as both worm and beetle. Thus it is written: “But I am a worm, and not a man” (Ps. XXI, 47). And, according to the Seventy Interpreters, the Prophet says: “A beetle cried out from the wood.” Since he is figured by things so abject and lowly, what insulting thing can be said of him [Col. 0117D] of whom it is established that nothing is said literally?

For he is called a Lamb because of innocence; a Lion because of power; and sometimes he is compared to a serpent because of death or wisdom. Therefore he can be spoken of figuratively through all these things, because nothing drawn from any of them can be believed of him essentially. If he were essentially any one of these, he could no longer be called another. If he were properly called a Lamb, he could not be called a lion; if he were properly called a lion, he could not be signified by a serpent. But we call him all these things, so much the more broadly in figure as they are further from his essence.

Thus the wild ass can signify the incarnate Lord [Col. 0118A]. The wild ass is a wild animal; and because the incarnate Lord benefited the Gentiles more than Judaea, by assuming an animal body he came, as it were, not into a house but rather into a field. Of this field of the Gentiles the Psalmist says: “The *species*—appearance—of the field is with me” (Ps. XLIX, 11).

[Note: [Col. 0117D] Our edition here has *pulchritudo* (“beauty”). Cassiodorus, however, in his Psalter reads *species*, with Gregory.]

The incarnate Lord, who in the form of God is equal to the Father, is in the form of a servant less than the Father—and in that respect less also than himself. Therefore let the Father say concerning the Son according to the form of a servant: “Who has let the wild ass go free, and who has loosed his bonds?” (Job XXXIX, 8). For “everyone who commits sin is the servant of sin” (John VIII, 34). Since the incarnate Lord became a participant in our nature but not in our guilt, he is said to have been let go free, because he is not held under the dominion of sin [Col. 0118B]. Of him elsewhere it is written: “Free among the dead” (Ps. LXXXVII, 5). He is said to be let go because, in assuming our nature, he is in no way held under the yoke of iniquity. Although the stain of our guilt did not touch him, the suffering of our mortality nevertheless bound him. Hence, after he has been called free and let go, it is rightly added of him: “And who has loosed his bonds?” His bonds were loosed when the infirmities of his passion were transformed into the glory of resurrection. The apostle Peter bears witness concerning these bonds, saying: “Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of hell, because it was impossible that he should be held by them” (Acts II, 24).

[Note: [Col. 0118D] From Book X on Job, chapter XV.] By the name wild ass is signified one who does whatever he desires, as Sophar says of a vain man: “And he thinks himself born free like a colt of a wild ass” (Job XI, 12). For by the colt of a wild ass every kind of wild creature is expressed: abandoned to the impulses of nature, it is not held by the reins of masters. Wild asses are free both to go where they desire and to rest when they are weary. And although a human being is far better than irrational animals, a person is nevertheless often not permitted what brute animals are permitted. Since they are reserved for no other end, their movements are doubtless not constrained beneath discipline. But because a human being is led toward the life to come, it is certainly necessary that in all one’s movements one serve under the ordering of discipline, like a domestic animal bound with reins, and live according to eternal ordinances [Col. 0118D]. Whoever therefore seeks, through unbridled freedom, to fulfil everything that he desires, desires nothing other than to be like a colt of a wild ass: that the reins of discipline may not restrain him, but that he may boldly roam through the forest of desires.

[Note: [Col. 0118D] From Book VII on Job, chapter IV.] By the name wild ass is signified the Gentile people, as blessed Job says: “Will the wild ass bray when it has grass, or will the ox low when it stands before a full manger?” (Job VI, 5). What is signified by the wild ass—that is, the wild donkey—but the Gentile people? Nature brought it forth outside the stalls of discipline [Col. 0119A], and it remained wandering in the field of its pleasures. What, then, is figured by the ox but the Jewish people? Subjected to the yoke of heavenly dominion, gathering proselytes unto hope, it drew the ploughshare of the Law through the hearts it could reach.

Yet, as the life of blessed Job bears witness, we know that many even among the Gentiles awaited the Redeemer’s coming. And when the Lord was born, we learned from Simeon’s coming in the Spirit into the Temple with what longing holy men from the Israelite people desired to see the mystery of his incarnation. Hence the Redeemer himself says to the disciples: “I tell you that many kings and prophets and righteous persons desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke X, 24).

The wild ass’s grass and the ox’s hay, then, are this very incarnation of the Mediator [Col. 0119B], through which Gentiles and Jews alike are satisfied. Since the prophet says, “All flesh is grass” (Isa. XL, 6), the Creator of all, taking flesh from our substance, willed to become grass, so that our flesh, which is grass, might not remain grass forever. Thus the wild ass found grass when the Gentile people received the grace of the divine incarnation. Then the ox did not have an empty manger, when the Law presented to the Jewish people his flesh, whom it had prophesied to a people long awaiting him. Hence the Lord, when born, is laid in a manger, to signify that the holy animals, found long fasting under the Law, would be satisfied with the hay of his incarnation. For he who was born filled the manger, since he gave himself as food to the minds of mortals, saying: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John VI, 56).

But because the longings of the elect among the Gentiles were delayed for a long time, and all holy persons among the Hebrew people groaned while awaiting their redemption for a long time, blessed Job, recounting the mysteries of prophecy, fittingly indicated the reasons for affliction in both nations, saying: “Will the wild ass bray when it has grass, or will the ox low when it stands before a full manger?” As though he plainly said: The Gentile people groans because the grace of its Redeemer has not yet refreshed it; and Judaea therefore prolongs its lowing because, holding the Law but not seeing the author of the Law, it fasts while standing before the manger [Col. 0119C].

[Note: [Col. 0119D] From chapter VI of the same book.] By the name wild asses may be signified [Col. 0119D] those who, placed in the field of faith, are bound by the reins of no ecclesiastical office. The signification of the ox likewise expresses those upon whom, within holy Church, the yoke of an assumed order presses for the office of preaching. The wild ass’s grass and the ox’s fodder are the necessary refreshment of the faithful people.

For some, like oxen, are held within the Church by the reins of an office they have undertaken; others, like wild asses, know not the stalls of sacred order and dwell in the field of their own will. But when one from secular life burns with desire for inward vision, desires the food of inward refreshment, and, seeing oneself fasting in the blindness of this pilgrimage, refreshes oneself with such tears as one can, that person is like a wild ass braying because it cannot find grass [Col. 0120A]. Another person bears the burden of an assumed order, toils in the labour of preaching, and already desires to be refreshed by eternal contemplation. But because that person does not yet behold the countenance of the Redeemer, that person groans like an ox tied to an empty manger. Since, placed far from inward wisdom, we do not see the inheritance of eternal verdure, we fast from the desired grass like brute animals. Of this grass it is said: “By me, if anyone enters, he shall be saved; and he shall go in and go out and find pasture” (John X, 9).

[Note: [Col. 0119D] From the beginning of chapter XXXII of Book XVI on Job.] By the name wild asses is signified any heretic, as it is written: “Others, like wild asses in the wilderness, go forth to their work” (Job XXIV, 10). There are certain heretics who avoid mingling with people, seeking a more secluded withdrawal of life. Those whom they encounter they frequently infect all the more with the plague of their persuasion because they appear more worthy of reverence through the supposed merits of their life. Of these it is now said: “Others, like wild asses in the wilderness, go forth to their work.” For the wild ass is a wild donkey. Heretics are rightly compared here to wild asses because, abandoned to their pleasures, they are alien to the bond of the faith of reason. Hence it is written: “The wild ass accustomed to the wilderness, in the desire of her soul, has drawn in the wind of her mouth” (Jer. II, 24). The wild ass is accustomed to the wilderness because, while it cultivates the strength of its own heart’s discipline, it dwells where there is no fruit. It draws in the wind of its mouth in the desire of its soul because those things it perceives in its mind from a desire for knowledge have power to puff it up [Col. 0120C], not to build it up. Against such persons it is said: “Knowledge puffs up; charity builds up” (I Cor. VIII, 2). Thus it is fittingly added here also: “They go forth to their work.” For they carry out not God’s work but their own, since they follow not sound doctrines but their own desires. For it is written: “He who walks in an undefiled way ministered to me” (Ps. C, 6). Whoever does not walk in an undefiled way therefore ministers more to oneself than to the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0120D] From Book XXIX on Job, chapter XVIII.] By the name wild asses are signified the Jews, as Jeremiah says: “The wild asses stood upon the rocks; they drew in the winds like dragons. Their eyes failed because there was no grass” (Jer. XIV, 6). What is signified by wild asses and dragons but proud and utterly wicked Jews [Col. 0120D]? They are called wild asses on account of their haughty pride; they are called dragons because of their poisonous thought. They stood upon rocks because they trusted not in God but in the highest powers of this world, saying: “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX, 15). They drew in the winds like dragons because, puffed up with the spirit of pride, they swelled with malicious arrogance. Their eyes failed because their hope fell away from what it had fixed upon: loving temporal things, it neglected to await eternal things; and it lost earthly things because it preferred them to God. For they said: “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” [Col. 0121A] (John XI, 48). They feared that, unless the Lord were killed, they would lose their place—and yet, having killed him, they lost it. But he adds why these things befell those wretches: “Because there was no grass”; that is, the knowledge of eternity was lacking in their hearts, and no teaching as fodder of inward verdure refreshed them.

## CHAPTER XXIII. ON THE ONOCENTAUR

[Note: [Col. 0121D] From Book VII on Job, chapter 12, before the end.] By the name onocentaurs are signified the morally slippery and the proud, as Isaiah says against the perverse mind under the figure of Judaea: “Behold, the lair of dragons and the pastures of ostriches, and demons shall meet with onocentaurs” (Isa. XXXIV, 13). What, indeed, is signified by dragons but malice, and by ostriches but hypocrisy? In a perverse mind, therefore, the dragon lies and feeds, because hidden malice is cunningly concealed, while an imitation of goodness is displayed to the eyes of those who behold it. But what is figured by the name onocentaurs but the morally slippery and the proud? For in the Greek tongue, ὄνος (*onos*) means “ass”; and by the designation ass, lust is signified, as the Prophet testifies when he says: “Their flesh was like the flesh of asses” (Ezek. XXIII, 20). The term bull, however, indicates the neck of pride, as the Lord says through the Psalmist concerning the proud Jews: “Fat bulls have surrounded me” (Ps. XXI, 13).

Onocentaurs, then, are those who, subject to the vices of lust, lift up their necks from that very cause for which they ought to be humbled. Serving the pleasures of their flesh, having cast shame far away, they not only do not grieve that they have lost uprightness, but still even rejoice in the work of their disgrace [Col. 0121C]. Demons meet with onocentaurs because evil spirits readily serve their desires when they see them rejoice in things over which they ought to weep.

## CHAPTER XXIV. ON THE RHINOCEROS

In Sacred Scripture, the name rhinoceros sometimes denotes a person powerful in this world and sometimes the proud Jewish people.

[Note: [Col. 0121D] From Book XXXI on Job, chapter I.] By the name rhinoceros are signified the powerful of this world, as the Lord says to blessed Job: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?” (Job XXXII, 12). The rhinoceros is wholly of an untameable nature, so that, if it is ever captured, it cannot be kept at all.

[Note: [Col. 0121D] Münster nevertheless notes in Book V of his *Cosmography* that one living specimen was brought from India in 1513 to Emmanuel, king of Portugal, who in 1515 presented a combat between an elephant and a rhinoceros in the city of Lisbon.]

Being unable to endure captivity, it is said, it immediately dies. Its name, translated into Latin, means “horn in the nostril.” What is signified in the nostril but foolishness, and in the horn but pride? What, then, is signified in the rhinoceros but the powerful people of this world, or the very highest powers of principalities? Lifted up by the pattern of foolish boasting, while they are outwardly puffed up by false honours, they wretchedly become inwardly empty through real miseries. To them it is fittingly said: [Col. 0122A] “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. X, 9).

At the very beginning of the nascent Church, when the power of the rich raised itself against her and thirsted for her death with such vast cruelty, while she succumbed in anxiety under so many tortures and persecutions, who then could have believed that she would rise up and bring the erect, harsh necks of the proud beneath herself, and that, tamed beneath the yoke of holy fear, they would be bound by the gentle reins of faith? For in its beginnings this rhinoceros’s horn assailed her for a long time, and she was struck as though to be utterly destroyed. But through the dispensation of divine grace, she gained strength, given life through dying; and this rhinoceros, wearied from striking with its horn, bowed it down. What was impossible for human beings was not difficult for God, who broke the rigid powers of this world not by words but by miracles [Col. 0122B].

For behold, we recognize daily that rhinoceroses serve: we now see the powerful of this world, once confounded by foolish pride in their own strength, made subject to God. The Lord spoke as though concerning an untameable rhinoceros when he said: “A rich man shall enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty” (Matt. XIX, 23). When the reply was made, “Who then can be saved?” (ibid., 25), he immediately added: “With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible” (ibid., 26). It is as though he said: This rhinoceros cannot be tamed by human strength, but can nevertheless be subjected by divine miracles.

[Note: [Col. 0122D] From chapter II of the foregoing book.] Therefore here also it is fittingly said to blessed Job, who bears the type of holy Church: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?” Understand: as it will serve me, who endured its resistance to human preaching for a long time, but whom, when I suddenly willed it, I subdued by miracles [Col. 0122C]. Or, more plainly: Are those who pridefully boast in foolish self-exaltation subjected to your preaching without my help? Consider, then, through whom you prevail; and in all that you prevail, bow down the mind’s pride.

[Note: [Col. 0122D] From Book XXXI on Job, chapter XI.] The proud Jewish people can also be signified by the name rhinoceros. The rhinoceros, which is also called *monoceros* in Greek manuscripts, is said to be of such strength that no hunter’s skill can capture it.

[Note: [Col. 0122D] Philesius and other recent writers affirm this.]

But, as those who have laboured in painstaking investigation to describe the natures of animals assert, a virgin girl is placed before it. When it comes, she opens her bosom; laying aside all fierceness, it lays its head in her lap. Thus it is suddenly found powerless by those who seek to capture it. It is described also as being boxwood-coloured. When it enters into conflict with elephants, it is said to strike the bellies of its adversaries with the single horn it bears in its nostril; wounding their softer parts, it easily throws down those attacking it.

[Note: [Col. 0122D] That the rhinoceros and monoceros are different animals is shown both by the designation itself and by Scaliger, *Exercises* 205, and Gesner, Book I, *On Quadrupeds*, under the letter R.]

Thus by rhinoceros—or indeed *monoceros*, that is, unicorn—may be understood that people [Col. 0123A] which, from the Law it received, drew not works but merely pride among men, and so bore a single horn among the other beasts. Hence the Lord, foretelling his passion as the Prophet sings, says: “Deliver me from the mouth of the lion, and my lowliness from the horns of unicorns” (Ps. XXI, 22). For there were as many unicorns—or indeed rhinoceroses—in that nation as there were those who, trusting in the works of the Law with singular and foolish pride, opposed the preaching of truth.

Therefore it is said to blessed Job, who bears the type of holy Church: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?” As though it were more plainly said: Will you bend beneath the rule of your preaching that people whom you see, in its foolish self-exaltation, proudly raging in the slaughter of the faithful? Understand: as I do, who see it exalt itself above me with its single horn, yet, whenever I will, immediately subject it to myself [Col. 0123B].

## CHAPTER XXV. ON BEHEMOTH

[Note: [Col. 0123D] From Book XXXII on Job, chapter X.] By the name Behemoth is signified the devil, as the Lord says to blessed Job: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you” (Job XL, 10). Whom does he indicate under the name Behemoth but the ancient enemy? Behemoth is translated into Latin as “animal.” When its malice is subsequently described, the person is plainly shown. But since it is written of God that “he made all things together” (Ecclus. XVIII, 1), why does he say that he made this animal with man, since it is agreed that he made all things together?

Again, we must ask how God created all things together, when Moses describes created things distinctly, varying according to the succession of days [Col. 0123C]. Yet we recognize this more readily if we closely investigate the causes of origins themselves. The substance of things was created together, but their forms were not fashioned together. What existed simultaneously in the substance of matter did not appear simultaneously in the appearance of form.

[Note: [Col. 0123D] These words have been separated from the preceding passage by the insertion of other material.]

But since we say that all things which we find proceeding one from another were simultaneously created in their substance, in what sense is Behemoth asserted to have been made with blessed Job, when angel and human do not have one substance, nor is a human produced from an angel, nor an angel from a human? If Behemoth is said to have been made with blessed Job for this reason—that every creature is undoubtedly created together by its Maker, who in his activity is not at all extended by the passage of time [Col. 0123D]—why is said spiritually of Behemoth what is common generally to all creatures?

But if we weigh the causes of things by subtle examination, we recognize that angel and human were made together: together, that is, not by unity of time but by kinship of rational nature; together through the image of wisdom bestowed, though not together through an associated substance of form. For it is written concerning man: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26). And Satan is told through Ezekiel: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. XXVIII, 12). Thus, amid all creation, human and angel came forth as made together because they were set apart from every irrational nature. Since, therefore, in the whole creation of things no rational animal exists except angel and human, whatever cannot use reason was not made with man. Let it therefore be said concerning man and angel—who, although he lost the power of his sublimity, by no means lost the subtlety of rational nature—“Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you”: so that, when man sees that he who was made with him in rational nature has perished, he may fear for himself the neighbouring fall of pride from his neighbour’s very ruin [Col. 0124A].

## CHAPTER XXVI. ON THE SERPENT

[Col. 0124B] [Note: [Col. 0124D] From Book IV on Job, chapter XIII.] By the name serpent is signified the devil, as Isaiah says: “Upon Leviathan, the bar-serpent, and upon Leviathan, the twisting serpent, upon the earth” (Isa. XXVI, 1). *Leviathan*, when translated, is said to mean “their addition.” Whose, indeed, but human beings’? It is rightly called their addition because, after it introduced the first sin by suggestion, it does not cease daily to increase it through graver persuasions.

Or it was called Leviathan reproachfully, that is, “the addition of human beings.” For it found them immortal in Paradise; yet, by promising divinity to those already immortal, it promised, as it were, to add something beyond what they were. But while it smoothly declared that it would give what they did not possess, it cunningly took away what they did possess. Therefore this Leviathan, in promising to add something to man, crept into him by twisting coils: while it falsely promises impossibilities, it truly takes away even possibilities [Col. 0124C].

We must ask why, having called it a serpent and then immediately added “twisting,” he inserted “bar”; unless perhaps because the serpent’s strength is yielding softness, whereas a bar has rigid hardness. Therefore, in order to signify it as both hard and soft, he calls it both a bar and a serpent. It is hard through malice, soft through flattery. It is called a bar because it strikes even unto death; but a serpent because it always instils its snares softly.

## CHAPTER XXVII. ON THE DRAGON

[Col. 0124D] In Sacred Scripture, by the name dragons are sometimes signified Antichrist, malice, the ancient enemy, the most wicked leaders of the Jews, demons, and openly wicked persons or Gentiles.

[Note: [Col. 0124D] This is drawn partly from Book IV, chapter XIV, and Book XXXII, chapter XII, section 38; and from Paterius the deacon, *On the Apocalypse*.] By the name dragon is signified Antichrist, as John says in the Apocalypse: “The dragon cast its tail and drew away a third part of the stars” (Apoc. XII, 3). What is understood by the dragon but Antichrist, and by its tail but its final persuasion? What, moreover, is shown by the name stars but the pretence of hypocrites, who display before men the good things they do in order to receive praise [Col. 0125A]? Thus by the dragon’s tail a portion of the stars is dragged down to earth, because by Antichrist’s final persuasion certain persons who seem to shine will be swept away. To drag stars down to earth is to involve, in the love of earthly things and the iniquity of open error, those who appear to adhere zealously to heavenly life.

[Note: [Col. 0125D] From Book VII on Job, chapter XII.] By the name dragon is signified malice, as Isaiah says against a perverse mind under the figure of Judaea: “There shall be a lair of dragons and pastures of ostriches” (Isa. XXIV, 13). What is signified by dragons but malice, and by the name ostriches but hypocrisy? For the ostrich has the appearance of flying but not the use of flight; and hypocrisy suggests to all beholders an image of holiness in itself, yet does not know how to maintain a holy life [Col. 0125B]. In a perverse mind, therefore, the dragon lies and the ostrich feeds, because hidden malice is cunningly concealed while an imitation of goodness is displayed to the eyes of those who behold it.

[Note: [Col. 0125D] From Book IV on Job, chapter XIII.] By the name dragon is signified the ancient enemy, as John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand; and he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss” (Apoc. XX, 1). Yet at the end of the world he calls him back for more open conflicts and lets him loose against us with all his strength. Hence it is again written there: “When the thousand years are completed, Satan shall be loosed” [Col. 0125C] (Apoc. XX, 7).

Jeremiah signifies the most wicked leaders of the Jews by the name dragons, saying: “The wild asses stood upon the rocks; they drew in the wind like dragons” (Jer. XIV, 6).

[Note: [Col. 0125D] From Book XXIX on Job, chapter XIV, before the end.] By the name dragons the prophet signifies demons: “In the lairs where dragons formerly dwelt, there shall spring up the green growth of reed and rush” (Isa. XXXV, 7). What is signified by the reed but preachers? What by the rush, which always grows beside the moisture of water, but the small and tender hearers of sacred speech? What is expressed by dragons but the malice of demons? Thus in the lairs of dragons the green growth of reed and rush will spring up, because among those peoples whom the malice of the ancient enemy possessed, both the knowledge of teachers [Col. 0125D] and the obedience of hearers are amassed.

[Note: [Col. 0126D] From Book XXXI on Job, ch. V.] By the name “dragons” openly evil persons or Gentiles are designated, as the Lord promises through the prophet concerning their conversion: “The beast of the field, dragons and ostriches, shall glorify me” (Isa. 43:20). For what is expressed by the name of dragons except malicious minds, which always crawl upon the ground in lowly thoughts? And what is meant by the name of ostriches except those who pretend to be good? They retain the appearance of a holy life as though it were the feather of flight, but do not put it into practice by their deeds. Therefore the Lord declares that he is glorified by dragon or ostrich, because he often turns both the openly evil and the falsely good to his service from the depths of their thought. Or certainly the beast of the field—namely dragons and ostriches—glorifies the Lord when the Gentile people, which in this world had long been a member of the devil, exalts the faith that is in him. He reproaches it by the name of dragons because of its malice, and marks it by the term ostriches because of its hypocrisy. For the Gentile people, having received feathers, as it were, could not fly, since it did not know the nature of reason.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. CONCERNING THE SERPENT

In Sacred Scripture, by the name “serpent” is understood sometimes the devil, sometimes Antichrist.

[Col. 0126B] [Note: [Col. 0126D] From Book XVII on Job, ch. XVIII.] Antichrist is signified by the name of the serpent, as blessed Job says: “By his travailing hand the twisted serpent was brought forth” (Job 26:13). For who is called by the name of the serpent except the ancient enemy, slippery and twisted, who, in deceiving man, spoke with a serpent’s mouth? Of him it is also said through the prophet: “Leviathan, the twisted serpent” (Isa. 27:1). He was permitted to speak through the mouth of a serpent so that man might know, from the vessel itself, what sort of being dwelt within it.

Moreover, the serpent is not only twisted but slippery. Since he did not stand in the uprightness of truth, he entered a twisted animal; and since, if his suggestion is not resisted at first, he suddenly slips—unnoticed—wholly into the inner parts of the heart, he addressed man through a slippery animal. The hearts of the wicked were the caverns of this serpent. Because he drew them into his own perversity, he rested, as it were, in their dwelling-place.

But through the travailing hand of the Lord, the twisted serpent was driven out of his own caverns: for while divine grace heals us, the ancient enemy who held us is cast out from us, as incarnate Truth says: “Now the ruler of this world shall be cast out” (John 12:31). Thus he no longer possesses all the saints by holding them, but persecutes them by tempting them. Since he does not reign within them, he fights against them from without; and because he has lost dominion within, he prepares wars outside. For he who came to the Incarnation on account of human beings expelled him from the carnal hearts of human beings; and, while he held the hearts of unbelievers, he put forth, as it were, a hand to the serpent’s hiding-place. Rightly, then, when the Lord’s hand acts as midwife, the twisted serpent is said to dwell in the caverns which he had occupied; for he went forth, defeated, from the hearts of the faithful, though he had formerly reigned over them with the sceptre of unbelief.

[Note: [Col. 0126D] Above, ch. II of this book.] Antichrist is designated by the name of the serpent, as it is said in Jacob’s utterance: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path, biting the horse’s hoofs, so that its rider falls backward” (Gen. 49:17). Consult the chapter on the horse.

## CHAPTER XXIX. CONCERNING THE BASILISK

[Col. 0127A]

In Sacred Scripture, when “basilisk” occurs in the singular, it sometimes means the devil and sometimes Antichrist; but when basilisks are mentioned in the plural, demons are signified.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] From Book XVII on Job, ch. XX.] The devil is designated by the name of the basilisk, as it is said through the prophet: “The nursing child shall delight over the asp’s hole, and the child that has been weaned shall put his hand into the basilisk’s cave. They shall neither harm nor kill in all my holy mountain” (Isa. 11:8). Whom does he call the nursing child, or the child once weaned, except the Lord? And what does he signify by the asp’s hole and the basilisk’s caverns except the hearts of the wicked? When the ancient enemy devoted his whole self to their consent, he gathered together the twisting coils of his cunning, as it were, in his own hole. He calls him an asp because he rages secretly, and a basilisk because he strikes openly.

Therefore the Lord put his hand into the basilisk’s and asp’s hole when he took possession of wicked hearts by divine power and drew out from there the captured asp or basilisk—that is, the captive devil—so that he might not harm the elect faithful in his holy mountain, which is the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] From Book XV on Job, ch. IX.] Antichrist is designated by the name of the basilisk, as it is written concerning certain wicked persons: “They have broken the eggs of asps and woven spiders’ webs. Whoever eats of their eggs shall die; and what is brooded over shall break forth into a basilisk” (Isa. 59:5). For wicked people “break the eggs of asps” when they disclose by perverse deeds the counsels of malignant spirits hidden in their hearts. They “weave spiders’ webs” when, out of desire for this world, they perform any temporal works; since these are established by no solidity, the wind of mortal life undoubtedly carries them away.

It is rightly added: “Whoever eats of their eggs shall die,” because one who heeds the counsels of unclean spirits kills the life of the soul within himself. “And what is brooded over shall break forth into a basilisk,” because the counsel of a malignant spirit, concealed in the heart, is nourished toward complete wickedness. For the basilisk is called king of serpents. And who is the head of the reprobate except Antichrist? Therefore, “what is brooded over shall break forth into a basilisk,” because one who has received within himself the asp’s counsels to be nurtured becomes a member of that wicked head and grows into the body of Antichrist.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] From Book XXXIV on Job, ch. X.] Demons are designated by the name of basilisks. Hence, rightly angered by preceding sins, the Lord says through the prophet of those whom he abandons to the hand of the ancient enemy: “I will send against you serpents, basilisks, against which there is no incantation” (Jer. 8:17). This is as though he said: By a just judgment I shall hand such persons over to unclean spirits whom they cannot shake off through the exhortation of preachers, as through the speech of enchanters.

## CHAPTER XXX. CONCERNING THE VIPER

[Col. 0128A]

In Sacred Scripture, when “viper” occurs in the singular, it sometimes means the sudden and violent temptation of the devil, and sometimes, in the contrary interpretation, the gentle and prolonged temptation of that same devil; but when vipers are mentioned in the plural, wicked persons are expressed.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] From Book XV on Job, ch. VII.] By the name of the viper is designated either the violent or the gentle and prolonged temptation of the devil, as is said through blessed Job concerning the hypocrite: “He shall suck the head of asps, and the viper’s tongue shall kill him” (Job 20:16). The asp is a small serpent, while the viper has a longer body. Asps lay eggs, and their young are produced from those eggs. But when vipers have conceived, their young rage in the womb.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] See Aristotle, *History of Animals*, Book V, ch. 34; Pliny, Book X, ch. 62.] Breaking through their mothers’ sides, they emerge from their womb. Hence they are called vipers because they give birth by force (*vi pariant*). Thus the viper is born so as to emerge violently and to be brought forth at the death of its mother.

What, then, is represented by the small asps except the hidden suggestions of unclean spirits, which first creep into human hearts through slight persuasion? And what is designated by the tongue of the viper except the devil’s violent temptation? For at first he steals in gently, and afterward violently as well.

[Note: [Col. 0128D] From ch. VIII.] Therefore the hypocrite sucks the head of asps because the small beginning of a hidden suggestion first arises in his heart; but the viper’s tongue kills him because afterward the captured mind is slain by the poison of violent temptation. Unclean spirits first address the human heart with subtle counsels, and while they persuade gently, they pour out, as it were, the venom of asps. Hence it is written: “They have broken the eggs of asps and woven spiders’ webs. Whoever eats of their eggs shall die, and what is brooded over shall break forth into a basilisk” (Isa. 59:5).

Thus it is said of the hypocrite: “He shall suck the head of asps, and the viper’s tongue shall kill him,” because when he willingly receives the wicked suggestion of the ancient enemy, he will afterward surrender himself, conquered, to his violent temptations. Thus in Paradise too he offered words of gentle persuasion to man while he stood upright; but once he had seized him into consent, he now drags even the resisting man along, and, conquered by the delights of his corruption, he kills him almost by force.

[Note: [Col. 0128D] From the same book and ch. VIII.] But perhaps we can understand the same things also by a contrary interpretation. Since the asp kills swiftly with its venom, while the viper kills more slowly, the asp signifies violent and sudden temptation, and the viper gentle and prolonged temptation. Accordingly, death is said to lie in the sucking of the asp’s head, but in the viper’s tongue, because sudden temptation often kills an unsuspecting mind as soon as it arises; whereas prolonged temptation kills as if by a viper’s tongue, because it continues for longer to suggest what is evil through persuasion.

[Note: [Col. 0128D] From Homily 20 on the Gospels.] Wicked persons are designated by the name of vipers, as John the Baptist says to the Jews: “Offspring of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?” (Luke 3:7). The wrath to come is the visitation of final retribution, from which the sinner cannot then flee if he does not now have recourse to the tears of repentance. It should be noted that evil offspring, imitating the actions of evil parents, are called offspring of vipers: because they envy and persecute the good, repay evil to some, and seek injuries against their neighbors; in all these things they follow the paths of their carnal forebears, and are thus like venomous children born of venomous parents.

## CHAPTER XXXI. CONCERNING THE ASP

In Sacred Scripture, by the name “asp” is understood sometimes the devil, sometimes one who disdains to hear the word of God, and sometimes a flattering and hidden suggestion.

The devil is designated by the name of the asp, as the prophet says: “The nursing child shall delight over the asp’s hole, and in the basilisk’s cave” (Isa. 11:8). Consult the chapter “Concerning the Basilisk.”

By the name of the asp is signified one who disdains to hear the word of God, as the Psalmist says: “Their fury is according to the likeness of a serpent, like that of a deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of enchanters” (Ps. 57:5). When an asp perceives that a Marsian enchanter is suffering it, who summons it forth with certain characteristic chants—as there are many magical practices—listen to what it does. Loving its darkness, in which it is said to hide itself wrapped up, when it wishes to come out but nevertheless refuses to hear the voices by which it feels itself compelled, it presses one ear to the ground and blocks the other with its tail. Thus, avoiding those voices as far as it can, it does not come out to the enchanter.

The Spirit of God declared that certain persons are like this: they do not hear God’s word, not merely failing to do it but refusing even to hear it lest they do it. Or should we seek some meaning in the statement that the asp closes its ears in such a way that it presses one to the ground and stops the other with its tail? What does this mean? By the tail, then, things that are behind are understood. Therefore we must turn our back on what is already past, so that we may give attention to what is promised us.

Nor should we take delight in the present; for the Apostle gives this warning: “What fruit, then, did you have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21). He calls back those who remember past things with delight and with a certain desire to enjoy them, lest we return in heart to Egypt. Consider how he commands even present things to be despised: “Fixing our gaze,” he says, “not on the things that are seen but on the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are unseen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4:18). Therefore he says of the present life: “If in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are more miserable than all human beings.”

Forget, then, the past in which you lived badly; despise the present in which you live only for a time, lest present things, binding you, prevent you from reaching the future. For if the present life delights you, you have placed your ear upon the ground. If you delight in your past things, which are already slipping backward, you have stopped your ear with your tail. You ought therefore to go into the light, to leave the darkness, so that, now walking and rejoicing in the light, you may say: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead.” He did not say, “Forgetting what lies behind and delighting in present things.” When he said, “Forgetting what lies behind,” he did not block his ear with his tail; when he said, “Stretching forward to what lies ahead,” he was not deafened by present things either, nor did he place his ear upon the ground.

By the name of asps are designated the hidden and flattering suggestions, or the strong and sudden temptations, of unclean spirits, as blessed Job says of the hypocrite: “He shall suck the head of asps” (Job 20:16). Consult [Col. 0130B] the chapter concerning the viper.

## CHAPTER XXXII. CONCERNING CREEPING THINGS

[Note: [Col. 0129D] From Book XXVI on Job, ch. V.] Earthly thoughts are designated by the name of creeping things, as the prophet Ezekiel says: “And I entered and saw, and behold every likeness of creeping things and the abomination of animals” (Ezek. 8:1). For in creeping things wholly earthly thoughts are signified; but in animals, thoughts already raised somewhat from the earth, yet still seeking the rewards of earthly recompense. Creeping things cling to the earth with their entire bodies, while animals are raised from the ground by their bellies, yet continually incline toward the earth through the appetite of the throat.

Thus creeping things are within the wall when thoughts revolve in the mind which are never raised from earthly desires. Animals also are within the wall when, even though some just or honorable things are now thought, they nevertheless serve the pursuit of temporal gains and honors. Thus in themselves they are as though raised from the earth, yet through their scheming, as through the appetite of the throat, they still lower themselves to what is beneath.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. CONCERNING WORMS

In Sacred Scripture, when “worm” occurs in the singular, it sometimes means Christ and sometimes human offspring; but when worms are mentioned in the plural, they express sometimes restless thoughts and sometimes carnal cares.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] From Book XXX on Job, ch. XV.] Christ is designated by the name of the worm, as the Psalmist says: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21:7).

[Note: [Col. 0130D] From Book XV on Job, ch. XXIV, 20.] The flesh is designated by the name of the worm, as is said through blessed Job of any sensual person: “The worm is his sweetness” (Job 24:20). These words reveal the extent of the blindness of any sensual person devoted to the pleasures of the flesh, when it is said: “The worm is his sweetness.” For what is flesh except decay and worms? Whoever pants after carnal desires loves nothing but a worm. Tombs testify to the substance of the flesh. What parent or faithful friend could touch the flesh of even a dearly loved person when it swarms with worms?

When flesh, therefore, is desired, let one consider what it is when lifeless, and one will understand what is loved. Nothing is so effective for taming the appetite for carnal desires as for each person to consider what he loves while it is living, and what it is when dead. Once bodily corruption has been considered, it is more quickly recognized that, when flesh is unlawfully desired, decay is loved. Rightly, then, it is said of the sensual person’s mind, “The worm is his sweetness,” because one who burns with desire for carnal corruption pants after the stench of decay.

[Note: [Col. 0131D] From Book XVII on Job, ch. IX.] Human offspring are designated by the name of the worm, as Bildad says in the book of blessed Job: “Behold, the moon does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight. How much more is man decay, and the son of man a worm!” (Job 25:5). What is designated by the moon except the Church as a whole, and by the stars except the souls of individual persons who live rightly? Therefore the moon does not shine and the stars are not clean in his sight, because not even holy Church shines brilliantly with so many miracles by its own power unless the gifts of prevenient grace are poured upon it. Nor are the minds of individual persons who live rightly clean from the stains of sin if they are judged apart from mercy; for, in the eyes of the strict Judge, each person’s own corruptibility defiles him unless the grace of pardon daily wipes him clean.

The mind of the elect strives to advance to the freedom of righteousness, but is still held in the fetter of weakness. It desires perfectly to subdue faults, but, so long as it is bound by the corruption of the flesh, it is tied by the bonds of that corruption even against its will. Let one therefore infer how heavily burdened with sins those are who neglect to struggle against these things, if even those who fight them profitably do not wholly overcome sin. Thus, after it has been said, “Behold, the moon does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight,” there immediately follows: “How much more is man decay, and the son of man a worm!” This is as though it were plainly said: If even those who shine by virtues amid the darkness of the present life cannot be without contagion, how tightly bound by the guilt of wickedness are those who still live carnally? If those who now dwell in heavenly desires cannot be free from sin, what burdens of sin do those bear who, devoted to the pleasures of their flesh, still carry the yoke of decay?

Hence Peter says: “If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where shall the ungodly and sinner appear?” (1 Pet. 4:18). It should be observed, moreover, how faithfully Bildad maintained the order of our condition and birth in his speech: he calls man not a worm but decay, whereas he calls the son of man a worm. For the first parent of the human race was a man, not a son of man. Everyone who came forth from him was not only a man but also a son of man. Therefore, just as the son of man is born from man, so a worm is born from decay. Hence man is rightly called decay and the son of man a worm. The first man was decay, not a worm, because although he decayed through death, he nevertheless did not come through birth from decay. But one who is a son of man is called a worm, because he is now propagated from the corruption of mortal bodies.
