[Note: [Col. 0131D] From Book XIII on Job, ch. XVII.] Restless thoughts are designated by the name of worms, as blessed Job says: “I said to decay: You are my father; to the worms: my mother and my sister” (Job 17:14). What does he mean when he says to decay, “You are my father,” except that every human being descends from an origin already corrupted? Thus he adds, “To the worms, my mother and my sister,” because we plainly come into this world from that very decay and with it. In respect of the material of corruptible flesh, worms are our mother and sister, because we have proceeded from decay and come bearing the decay that we bear.

If this may be understood spiritually, nature may be called mother and custom, not without reason, sister, because we are with the latter from the former. This mother and sister are worms because corruptible nature and perverse custom compel us to be wearied in our minds by restless thoughts, as by certain worms. For the corrupted nature of the flesh and perverse custom generate innumerable cares in the heart of our weakness, and are rightly called mother and sister—worms. Cares bite the mind while they trouble it. Indeed, righteous persons do not cease either anxiously to consider and weigh what they should do, or providently to examine where they are to be led after the present life.

[Note: [Col. 0132D] From Book XV, ch. XXXIII, on Job 25.] Carnal cares are designated by the name of worms, as blessed Job says: “This man dies strong and healthy, rich and happy. His inward parts are full of fat, and his bones are moistened with marrow. But another dies in the bitterness of his soul, without any possessions. Yet together they sleep in the dust, and worms cover them” (Job 21:23–24). If anyone perhaps wishes to take this allegorically, we can explain it briefly.

For it is said of the wicked rich man: “His inward parts are full of fat.” As fat comes from abundant food, so pride is born from an abundance of possessions; it fattens the rich person’s mind while his proud spirit is lifted up. Pride of heart is, as it were, a fatness of thickness. Hence, because many commit sins from abundance, it is said through the Prophet: “Their iniquity came forth as if from fat” (Ps. 72:7).

Lovers of this age have, as it were, bones, because in this world they possess the strength of dignities. But if the earthly riches of their household are lacking alongside outward rank, in their own judgment they indeed have bones, but do not have marrow in their bones. Therefore, because this lover of the world is so supported by outward power that he is also fattened by the inward abundance of an earthly household, it is said: “His bones are moistened with marrow.” Or certainly, the bones of this rich man are wicked and hardened habits; the marrow in the bones is the very desire for evil living, which is never sated by the fulfillment of perversity. This marrow, as it were, moistens the bones when wicked desires preserve their perverse habits in the pleasure of delight.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] From ch. XXXIV, the book above.] There are also some who have no riches in this world but desire to have them. They long to be exalted, although they cannot attain in this world what they desire. For though supported by neither possessions nor honors, they are nevertheless condemned as guilty before the sight of the inward Judge by their conscience because of evil desires. Such a person is often afflicted precisely because he cannot become rich and proud. Concerning him it is added: “But another dies in the bitterness of his soul, without any possessions.” Behold: that from which the rich man, vain in his proud heart, rejoices, another poor man, vain in his proud heart, is afflicted.

It is rightly said of both: “Yet together they sleep in the dust, and worms cover them.” To sleep in the dust is to close the eyes of the mind amid earthly desires. Hence every sinner sleeping in his sin is told: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14). The worms born from the flesh cover them both, because carnal cares weigh upon the proud mind both of the rich and of the poor. In earthly matters, the reprobate poor person and rich person, although they are not supported by equal prosperity, are disturbed by equal anxiety: for what one already possesses with fear, the other desires with anxiety.

But because the latter cannot possess it and is grieved, let it be said: “Together they sleep in the dust, and worms cover them,” because, although they are not together raised up by temporal possessions, they nevertheless together lie asleep in the torpor of the mind amid care for temporal things. And worms cover them together, because carnal thoughts press upon the one that he may obtain what he desires, and upon the other lest he lose what he possesses.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. CONCERNING THE MOTH

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of the moth is understood sometimes temptation of the flesh and sometimes heretical perversity.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] From Book XI on Job, ch. XXV.] Temptation of the flesh is designated by the name of the moth, as blessed Job says in the person of a tempted human being: “I am to be consumed like decay, and like a garment eaten by a moth” (Job 13:28). A human being is consumed like decay while he is worn away by the corruption of his flesh. Since unclean temptation arises not from elsewhere but from himself, temptation consumes the flesh like a moth consumes the garment from which it comes forth. For within himself a human being has the source from which he is tempted. Thus the moth consumes the garment from which that moth itself emerged.

It should also be known that the moth pierces a garment without sound; and often a thought pierces the mind in such a way that the mind itself does not perceive it until it has been pierced by its sting. Rightly, then, it is said that a human being is consumed like a garment by a moth, because sometimes we do not recognize the wounds of our temptations until we have been pierced by them in the mind.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] From Book XVIII on Job, ch. XI, near the end.] Heretical perversity is designated by the name of the moth, as blessed Job says of any heretic: “He has built his house like a moth, and like a watchman has made a shelter” (Job 27:18). The moth builds a house for itself by destroying. No better comparison could have been made for the heretic, who establishes the place of his unbelief only in minds that he has corrupted. He also promises his followers safety from eternal fire and the refreshment of eternal rest. Yet his words have no firmness, because they lack the fullness of truth. Hence it is added: “And like a watchman he has made a shelter.” For the watchman’s shelter is established upon no foundation, but is quickly destroyed when time passes; and the rest promised by heretics is destroyed with time, because after this life it is not found at all.

## CHAPTER XXXV. CONCERNING THE CATERPILLAR

[Col. 0134B]

[Note: [Col. 0134D] From Book XXXIII on Job, ch. XXVII, toward the middle.] Luxury is designated by the name of the caterpillar, as the prophet Joel says: “What the caterpillar has left, the locust has eaten; what the locust has left, the grub has eaten; and what the grub has left, the mildew has eaten” (Joel 1:4). Often the wretched mind sees what sin has already passed from it, but does not see where it is still held fast. It rejoices over certain vices because it is no longer subject to them, and neglects to guard against and grieve over the fact that others have succeeded in their place, to which it perhaps yields more wickedly. Thus, while some vices pass and others continually succeed them, the devil holds the hearts of the reprobate without interruption.

Rightly, therefore, it is said: “What the caterpillar has left, the locust has eaten; what the locust has left, the grub has eaten; and what the grub has left, the mildew has eaten.” For what is signified by the caterpillar, which crawls wholly upon the ground, except luxury, which so defiles the heart it holds that it cannot rise to the love of higher purity? What is expressed by the locust, which rises in leaps, except vainglory, which exalts itself through empty presumptions? What is represented by the grub, whose almost entire body is gathered in its belly, except gluttony? And what does mildew indicate, which burns when it touches, except anger?

Thus the locust eats what the caterpillar leaves, because when the vice of luxury has departed from the mind, vainglory often arrives. Since the mind is no longer cast down through love of the flesh, it takes pride in its chastity as though it were holy. The grub eats what the locust leaves, because when resistance is made to vainglory which seemed to arise from holiness, one often gives oneself too immoderately either to the belly or to any desires of ambition. For a mind ignorant of God is drawn all the more harshly toward every kind of ambition because it is restrained by no love even of human praise.

Mildew consumes what the grub leaves, because when gluttony is restrained through abstinence, the impatience of anger rules more fiercely. Like mildew, it eats the harvest as though by burning it, because the flame of impatience wastes the fruits of virtues. Therefore, while vice succeeds vice, one plague devours the field of the mind while another leaves it. It is rightly added there: “Awake, you drunkards, and weep” (Joel 1:5). Those are called drunkards who, confused by the love of this world, do not perceive the evils they endure. What, then, is meant by saying, “Awake, you drunkards, and weep,” except: shake off the stupor of your insensibility, and, amid the devastation of the heart by so many successive plagues of vices, meet them with watchful lamentation?

## BOOK FOUR BEGINS

[Col. 0135]

## CHAPTER I. CONCERNING MAN

[Col. 0135A]

In Sacred Scripture, when “man” occurs in the singular, it sometimes means God the Father, sometimes the incarnate Word, sometimes the Jewish people, sometimes the faculty of reason, sometimes the devil, sometimes the flesh; sometimes it is used according to nature, sometimes according to fault, sometimes according to weakness. When it occurs in the plural, it means sometimes spiritual persons and sometimes any carnal persons.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] From Homily 38 on the Gospels.] God the Father is understood by the name of man, as it is said in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who was a king, who made a wedding feast for his son” (Matt. 22:2). For who is this man, the king, father of the king’s son, except he to whom the Psalmist says: “Give your judgment, O God, to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71:1)? He made a wedding feast for his son. For then God the Father made a wedding feast for God the Son, when he joined him to human nature in the Virgin’s womb; when he willed God, existing before the ages, to become man at the end of the ages.

Or, to put it more plainly and safely: God the Father made a wedding feast for the Son who is king when, through the mystery of the Incarnation, he joined the holy Church to him. The womb of the Virgin who bore him was this bridegroom’s bridal chamber. Hence the Psalmist says: “He has placed his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Ps. 18:6). For he came forth as a bridegroom from his bridal chamber, when God incarnate went forth from the incorrupt womb of the Virgin in order to unite the Church to himself.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] From Homily 9 on the Gospels.] The incarnate Word is understood by the name of man, as it is said through the prophet: “And he is a man; who shall know him?” Hence it is also written in the Gospel: “A certain man, going abroad, called his servants and entrusted his goods to them” (Matt. 25). Who is this man going abroad except our Redeemer, who went to heaven in the flesh that he had assumed? For the proper place of flesh is the earth; it is, as it were, led abroad when it is placed in heaven through our Redeemer.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] From Homily 11 on the Gospels.] The Jewish people are designated by the name of man, as Luke carefully says in the Gospel concerning the rich feaster: “There was a certain rich man, clothed in purple and fine linen, who feasted splendidly every day. And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus” (Luke 16). Whom does this rich man, clothed in purple and fine linen and feasting splendidly every day, signify except the Jewish people, which outwardly possessed the observance of life, which employed the delights of the law it had received for display rather than benefit? And whom does Lazarus, covered with sores, figuratively express except the Gentile people? Since it did not blush to confess its sins when it turned to the Lord, it bore a wound upon its skin.

But wounded Lazarus desired to be satisfied with the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table, and no one gave them to him, because that proud people disdained to admit any Gentile to the knowledge of the law. Since it had the teaching of the law not for love but for self-exaltation, it swelled, as it were, with its received riches. And since words flowed down from its learning, crumbs, as it were, fell from the table.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] From Book XXIX on Job, ch. XIV, before the end.] The faculty of reason is understood by the name of man, as the Lord says to blessed Job: “Who gave the most violent rain its course, and a way to the sounding thunder, that it might rain upon the land without man in the wilderness, where no mortal dwells, that it might fill the pathless and desolate land and bring forth green plants?” (Job 28:25–27). There are many who are greatly insensitive to the words of God. They are indeed counted by the name of faith; they hear the words of life with their ears, but do not at all allow them to pass into the inner parts of the heart. What else are these but a deserted land? That land has no man because their mind lacks the faculty of reason. No mortal dwells in that land because, even if thoughts of rational understanding sometimes enter their conscience, they do not remain. Perverse desires find a seat in their hearts; but right thoughts, if they ever come, run off as if driven away.

But when the merciful God deigns to give freedom of course to his rain and a way to the sounding thunder—that is, to preaching—they are pierced by inward grace, open the ears of their hearts to the words of life, and the pathless land is filled because, while it gives hearing to the word, it is filled with mystery. It brings forth green plants because it not only gladly receives through the grace of compunction the words of preaching poured into it, but also renders them abundantly. Thus it begins to desire to speak what it had been unable to hear, and, having even inwardly withered through not hearing, it now feeds any hungry persons with its own verdure by speaking what is holy.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] From Book XIII on Job, ch. XII.] The devil is designated by the name of man, as it is said in the Gospel: “An enemy, a man, has done this” (Matt. 13:28). The devil and all the wicked are one body in such a way that sometimes the body is denoted by the name of the head, and sometimes the head is called by the name of the body. For the body is denoted by the name of the head when it is said of a perverse man: “One of you is a devil” (John 6:70). Conversely, the head is called by the name of the body when the statement already cited is made concerning that apostate himself: “An enemy, a man, has done this.”

[Note: [Col. 0137D] From Book VI on Job, chapter VII.] By the name “man” the flesh is signified, as it is said in the book of blessed Job: “Man is born for toil, and the bird for flight” (Job 5:7). For man is born for toil, because one endowed with received reason surely considers that it is quite impossible for him to pass through the time of this pilgrimage without labor. Hence Paul aptly added, when announcing his tribulations to his disciples: “For you yourselves know that we are appointed for this” (1 Thess. 3:5). But while the flesh is afflicted by scourges, the mind is raised up to desire higher things, as Paul testifies when he says: “Although our outward man is being corrupted, yet our inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16). Therefore man is born for toil, and the bird for flight, because the mind flies upward from precisely that source from which the flesh labors more harshly in lowly things.

[Note: [Col. 0137D] From Book IV on Job, chapter XV.] “Man” is used by reason of nature, as it is written: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). “Man” is used by reason of fault, as it is written: “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High; but you shall die like men” (Ps. 81). As though it plainly said: you shall perish as transgressors. Hence Paul also says: “Whereas there is among you jealousy and contention, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to man?” (1 Cor. 3). As though he said: You whose minds are divided by discord, do you not still sin from blameworthy humanity?

“Man” is used by reason of weakness, as it is written: “Cursed is he who puts his hope in man” (Jer. 17:5). That is, in weakness.

By the name “men” spiritual persons are signified, as the Lord says through the prophet to certain persons: “But you, the flocks of my pasture, are men” (Ezek. 34). For the Lord indeed feeds those whom fleshly pleasure does not afflict in the manner of enemies.

[Col. 0137D] [Note: [Col. 0137D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XLII.] By the name “men,” too, those who savor carnal things are signified, as the Apostle says: “For whereas there is among you jealousy and contention, are you not carnal?” (1 Cor. 3:3). And shortly afterward he adds: “Are you not men?” (ibid., v. 4).

173 CHAPTER II. ON MAN.

In Sacred Scripture, when *vir* (“man”) is used in the singular, it sometimes means Christ, sometimes an angel, sometimes any perfect person, and sometimes the ancient enemy. But when *viri* (“men”) is used in the plural, it sometimes signifies perfect men and sometimes the six ages of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0137D] From Book XXII on Job, chapter XIII.] By the name “man” Christ is understood, as Ezekiel says concerning Him: “And behold, one man in their midst, clothed in linen garments, with a scribe’s inkhorn at his loins” (Ezek. 9). For what is understood by the man but the Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus? Since He deigned, according to the flesh, to have parents from the priestly tribe, He is said to come clothed in linen. Or certainly, because linen springs from the earth, whereas wool springs from corruptible flesh, He who took the garment of His body from the Virgin Mother, not from the corruption of sexual union, indeed came to us clothed in linen. And because He, being God, after dying for us, rising again, and ascending into heaven, then wrote the New Testament through the apostles, this man had the inkhorn at His loins. For the loins are the posterior part of the body. Therefore, because He composed the writing of the New Testament after His departure, He bore the inkhorn, as it were, behind Him.

[Note: [Col. 0138D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter II.] Again, “man” sometimes means an angel, as the prophet Daniel testifies when he says: “Behold, the man Gabriel” (Dan. 9:21). By the name “man” any perfect person is signified, as the Lord says to blessed Job: “Gird up your loins like a man” (Job 38:3).

174 [Note: [Col. 0138D] From Book XXVIII on Job, chapter IV.] Sacred Scripture is accustomed to call him a man who follows the ways of the Lord with strong and not slack steps. Hence the Psalmist says: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. 26:14). But to gird one’s loins is to restrain either lust in action or the desire for praise in thought. For the delight of the flesh is in the loins. Hence holy preachers are told: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:35). By the loins, lust is signified; by the lamps, the brightness of good works. They are therefore commanded to gird their loins and hold their lamps. It is as though they plainly hear: First restrain lust in yourselves; then show others examples of good works from yourselves.

But since we know that blessed Job was endowed with such chastity, why, after so many scourges, is he told: “Gird up your loins like a man”? It is so that he who had first conquered the lust of corruption might now restrain the lust of pride, lest, taking pride in his patience or chastity, he should be inwardly more lustful before God’s eyes by as much as he appeared patient and chaste before human eyes. Hence Moses also says: “Cut away the foreskins of your hearts” (Deut. 10:16); that is, after extinguishing lust in the flesh, cut away also the superfluous growths of thoughts.

[Note: [Col. 0138D] From Book IV on Job, chapter II, at the beginning and middle.] By the name “man” the ancient enemy is signified, as Jeremiah, seeing his preaching impeded by his hearers’ obstinacy, said in a curse: “Cursed be the man who announced to my father, saying: A male child has been born to you” (Jer. 20:15). Why did that man who announced the prophet’s birth to his father receive a sentence of curse from the prophet? This is surely filled with a mystery so much the greater within as it is devoid of human rationality outwardly. For if perhaps it had conveyed anything outwardly rational, it would not at all have kindled us to seek its inward meaning. Therefore it intimates something to us more fully within precisely because it displays nothing rational without. For if the prophet came forth from his mother’s womb into the world in order to be afflicted, what offense did the announcer of his birth commit?

What, then, is signified in the person of the wavering prophet, except the changeability of the human race, which comes as a deserved punishment? And what is expressed by his father except the world from which we are born? [Col. 0139B] And who is that man who announces our birth to our father, except the ancient enemy? When he sees us wavering in thought, he incites evil-minded persons who are eminent by the authority of this world to persuade us into deception. And when he perceives us doing weak things, he exalts them with favor as though they were strong; and he speaks as though male children had been born, when he rejoices falsely that we have become corrupters of what is true. He therefore announces to the father that a male has been born when, to this world, he shows that the person whom he has persuaded has become a corrupter of innocence. For when any sinner who is proud is told, “You have acted like a man,” what else is asserted but that a male has been born in the world? Rightly, then, the man who announces that a male has been born is cursed, because by that very announcement the reprobate joy of our deed is made known.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter II.] By the name “men” perfect persons are expressed, as Wisdom speaks in Proverbs, saying: “O men, I cry out to you” (Prov. 8:5). It is as though she plainly said: I speak not to women but to men; those whose minds are unstable cannot at all receive my words. Hence Elihu again says to blessed Job: “Remember that you do not know His work, of which men have sung” (Job 36:24). For men sing of the Lord when either heavenly spirits or whatever perfect teachers make His power known to us. Yet they do not know His work, because even those who preach Him reverently acknowledge that His judgments are impenetrable. Thus they know Him whom they preach, yet they do not know His works: by grace they know Him by whom they were made, but they cannot comprehend His judgments, which are brought about by Him even upon themselves.

The Psalmist testifies that Almighty God is not clearly perceived in His working, saying: “He made darkness His hiding place” (Ps. 17:12); and again: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35:7); and again: “The abyss is His garment” (Ps. 103:2). Hence Solomon also aptly says: “As you do not know what is the way of the spirit, or by what method the bones are formed in the womb of pregnant women, so you do not know the works of God, who is the maker of all” (Eccl. 11:5). Let him therefore say: “Remember that you do not know His work, of which men have sung.” It is as though he plainly said: The works of Him of whom all strong persons have spoken are hidden from the eyes of your mind, because they surpass the measure of your knowledge by the very fact that you are bounded by humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] From Book XXII on Job, chapter XIII, before the end.] By the name “men” the six ages of the world are signified, as it is said through the prophet Ezekiel: “Behold, six men came by the way of the upper gate, which faced north, and each had in his hand a vessel of destruction” (Ezek. 9:2). For what else is signified by the six men coming, except the six ages of humankind? They come by the way of the upper gate because they unfold from the condition of Paradise, as from the entrance of the world and from the higher generations. This gate faces north because, unless the mind of humankind, opened to vices, had abandoned the warmth of charity and sought the numbness of mind, it would not have emerged into this breadth of mortality. And each has a vessel of destruction in his hand because every generation, unfolded through its successive ages, before the Redeemer’s coming had in its own activity that from which it received the penalty of damnation.

CHAPTER III. ON WOMAN.

In Sacred Scripture, when “woman” is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies the wisdom of God, sometimes impiety, sometimes it is used of sex, and sometimes of weakness. But when “women” is used in the plural, it sometimes signifies the minds of carnal persons and sometimes vices.

[Note: [Col. 0140D] From Homily 34 on the Gospels.] By the name “woman” the wisdom of God is understood, as it says in the Gospel: “Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does she not light a lamp, sweep the house, and diligently seek until she finds it?” (Luke 15:8). For what is understood by the woman except Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God? What is signified by the drachma except human nature? Because an image is impressed upon a drachma, man, who was made in the likeness of God, is rightly understood through the drachma. The woman lost the drachma when man, by sinning, withdrew from the likeness of his Creator. But the woman lights a lamp because God’s wisdom appeared in humanity. For a lamp is light in an earthen vessel. Light in an earthen vessel is divinity in flesh, concerning which earthen vessel of His body Wisdom itself says: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21:6). For because a potsherd is hardened in fire, His strength dried up like a potsherd, because through the tribulation of the Passion He strengthened the assumed flesh unto the glory of the resurrection.

Having lit the lamp, she sweeps the house because, as soon as His divinity shone through the flesh, all our conscience was shaken. For the house is swept when human conscience is disturbed by consideration of its guilt. And when the house has been swept, the drachma is found, because when a person’s conscience is disturbed, the likeness of the Creator is restored in that person.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] From Book XIV on Job, chapter XXVI.] By the name “woman” impiety is signified, as it is written in Zechariah: “Lift up your eyes and see. What is this that comes forth? And I said, What is it? And he said: This is an amphora coming forth. And he said: This is their eye in all the earth. And behold, a talent of lead was being carried. And behold, one woman sitting in the midst of the amphora; and he said: This is impiety. And he cast her into the midst of the amphora, and put the mass of lead upon its mouth” (Zech. 5:5–8).

Wishing to show the prophet the human race, God signified through the image of an amphora, as through an open mouth, the avarice by which that race was most deeply destroyed. For avarice is like an amphora, which keeps the mouth of the heart open in a wide circumference. We see many people of dull understanding; yet we see them crafty in evil actions, as the prophet testifies, saying: “They are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good” (Jer. 4:22). Therefore, they are sluggish in understanding, but are stirred by the goads of avarice in the things they desire. Blind to see good things, they become wakeful to commit evils when rewards excite them. Hence it is rightly said of this same avarice: “This is their eye in all the earth.” “And behold, a talent of lead was being carried.” What is the talent of lead except the weight of sin arising from that same avarice? “And behold, one woman sitting in the midst of the amphora.” Lest we perhaps be able to doubt who this woman was, the angel immediately made it known, saying: “This is impiety.” “And he cast her into the midst of the amphora.” Impiety is cast into the middle of the amphora because impiety is always contained in avarice. “And he put the mass of lead upon its mouth.” The mass of lead is put upon the woman’s mouth because the impiety of avarice is weighed down by the burden of its sin. For if it did not reach after things below, it would not be impious toward God and neighbor.

“Woman” is used of sex, as it is written: “God sent His Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4:4).

“Woman” is used of weakness, as a certain wise man says: “Better is the wickedness of a man than a woman doing good” (Ecclus. 42:6). For any strong and discerning person is called a man; but a woman is understood as a weak or undiscerning mind. And it often happens that even a discerning person suddenly falls into fault, while another, undiscerning and weak, performs a good work. Yet the person who is undiscerning and weak is sometimes lifted up all the more by what he has done well, and falls more grievously into fault. But any discerning person, even from realizing that he has acted badly, brings himself more tightly back to the rule of strictness, and advances more highly toward righteousness from that very point at which he seemed for a time to have fallen away from righteousness. In this regard it is rightly said: “Better is the wickedness of a man than a woman doing good,” because even the fault of the strong is sometimes an occasion of virtue, and the virtue of the weak an occasion of sin.

“Women” means the minds of carnal people. Hence blessed Job answered his ill-advising wife: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women” (Job 2:10). For what do we understand by women except carnal persons? Since the elect are told, “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. 30:25), the minds of carnal people, who serve God with an unstable intention, are not improperly called women.

By the name “women,” vices are sometimes signified. Hence the prophet Zechariah, speaking of avarice under the image of an amphora, added: “And I lifted up my eyes and saw: and behold, two women coming forth, and the spirit was in their wings. And they had wings like the wings of a kite, and they lifted it between earth and heaven” (Zech. 5:9). What else do we understand by these two women except the two principal vices, namely pride and vain glory, which are undoubtedly joined to impiety? “And they lifted it between earth and heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0142D] From Book XIV on Job, chapter XXVI.] For pride and vain glory have this characteristic: they exalt in their own thoughts above other people the person whom they have infected. Sometimes by the accumulation of possessions, sometimes by the desire for offices, they raise to a kind of height of honor the one whom they have once held captive. But one who is between heaven and earth leaves the low things behind and does not at all reach the higher. Therefore these women lift the amphora between heaven and earth, because pride and vain glory so raise the mind captured through avarice for honor that, despising all neighbors, such persons seem to abandon low things and glory in seeking high things. Yet while all such persons are proud, they surpass in mind those among whom they live, but are not joined to the citizens above. The raised amphora is therefore aptly said to be between heaven and earth, because all avaricious persons, through pride and vain glory, despise within themselves their neighbors, while they do not at all attain the higher things beyond themselves. Thus they are borne between earth and heaven, because they neither maintain among lowly things the equality of brotherhood through charity nor, in exalting themselves, have the power to reach the heights.

180 CHAPTER IV. ON THE WIFE.

[Col. 0142D]

In Sacred Scripture, by the name “wife” good action is sometimes signified, and carnal thought at other times.

By the name “wife” good action is understood, as Moses says: “If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you six years; in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing. With whatever clothing he entered, with such shall he go out. If he had a wife, his wife also shall go out with him” (Exod. 21:2–3). See the chapter “On the Number Six.”

By the name “wife” carnal thought is signified, as we read in the book of blessed Job: “But his wife said to him: Do you still persist in your simplicity? Bless God and die” (Job 2:9). We should know that in prosperity the mind is often touched by troublesome temptation; but sometimes we suffer adversities outwardly and are wearied inwardly by the impulse of temptation, so that scourges torture the flesh while carnal suggestion floods the mind. Hence, after so many wounds of blessed Job, the words of his ill-advising wife are still added. The ill-advising wife is carnal thought assailing the mind.

For, as we have said, we are often terrified by scourges outwardly and wearied by carnal suggestion inwardly. Thus Jeremiah laments: “The sword kills outside, and within there is death like it” (Lam. 1:20). For the sword kills outside when vengeance striking us outwardly pierces us. But within there is death like it, because although the person undergoes scourges, the conscience is not inwardly clean from the filth of temptation. Hence David says: “Let them be as dust before the face of the wind, and let the angel of the Lord press them hard” (Ps. 34:5). One who is carried away in his heart by the breeze of temptation is like dust lifted up before the face of the wind. And when divine strictness strikes amid these things, what else is happening except that the angel of the Lord afflicts him?

But these things occur differently in the reprobate and in the elect. Their hearts are tempted in such a way that they consent; the elect, however, do receive temptations but resist them. The minds of the former are delightfully captured: even if for a time what is wrongly suggested displeases them, later it pleases them through deliberation. But the latter receive the darts of temptations in such a way that they are continually wearied by resistance. And if a tempted mind is ever carried as far as delight, they quickly blush at the very stealthy onset of their delight and rebuke with stern judgment whatever carnal thing they perceive rising within themselves. Hence it is well added at once: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:10). For it is fitting that a holy mind, by spiritual rebuke, should suppress whatever carnal thing murmurs insolently within it, lest the flesh, speaking harshly, draw it into impatience, or, speaking pleasantly, dissolve it into the loose indulgence of lust. Therefore let manly discipline, rebuking the suggestion of unlawful thought, subdue the lax softness of shamefulness, saying: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women.” And let consideration of gifts restrain the impatience of harsh thought, saying: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?”

CHAPTER V. ON THE WIDOW.

In Sacred Scripture, by the name “widow” the soul is sometimes understood, sometimes the holy Church, and sometimes a people infected by heretical perversity.

By the name “widow” the soul is understood, as it is said through blessed Job concerning any wicked person: “He fed the barren woman, who does not bear, and did not do good to the widow” (Job 24:21). For who is called barren here except the flesh? While it desires only present things, it does not know how to give birth to good thoughts. And who is called a widow except the soul? Since her Creator willed to join her to Himself, He came to the bridal chamber of the virgin womb, as the Psalmist testifies: “And He Himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from His bridal chamber” (Ps. 18:6). She is rightly called a widow because her husband suffered death for her and now lives hidden from her eyes in the inner chambers of heaven, as though in a region elsewhere.

Therefore the wicked person feeds the barren woman and neglects to do good to the widow, because, serving fleshly desires, he despises the care and life of the soul. With all his attention and effort he thinks how the flesh, destined to die, may subsist without any necessities; and he neglects to care for the life of the soul, which undoubtedly lives forever, whether in death or in blessedness. Rightly, however, when it has been said, “He fed the barren woman,” it is immediately added, “who does not bear.” For from sacred history we know that certain women were barren but nevertheless bore children at a final time. But the flesh is called not merely barren, but also one that does not bear, because it cannot give birth to good thoughts from its own understanding, even in its final days. For it already fails in its own strength, yet does not cease to desire transitory things. Already wearied from its former vigor, it is nearly expelled by the very world it loves; yet it still makes an unseemly effort to possess temporal things. It can no longer perform perverse acts, but it nevertheless does not cease to think even of things it does not perform. It is therefore rightly called not merely barren but also not bearing, because, as we have said, even when weakened it is not fruitful from its own understanding in offspring of good thought.

By the name “widow” the holy Church is signified. Thus this too may be understood of heretics. For every preacher of error, while teaching a people placed outside the unity of the Church, surely feeds the barren woman and her who cannot bear, because he expends the use of his labor upon one that does not yield spiritual fruits. Yet he does not do good to the widow because he despises living and serving the holy catholic Church, whose husband suffered the adversities of death. For to do good to the widow is to labor in consolation of her who is consumed in love for her dead husband. Hence this same widow, namely the holy Church, complains in the words of the Psalmist: “I sought one to console me, and I found none” (Nah. 3:7). For she finds a consoler only when, from the death suffered by her husband, she sees many arise to life within herself.

By the name “widows” we understand peoples marked by heretical perversity; likewise it is said through blessed Job concerning a heretic: “And his widows shall not weep” (Job 27:15). For whom do we understand as the widows of heretics except the peoples subject to them, happily deprived by his death? Often, when a preacher of error is carried away to eternal punishments, his subject peoples return to the grace of true knowledge. For a perverse preacher presided over these peoples as a husband, because as a corrupter of the mind he had wickedly cleaved to them. Therefore the widows, or deserted women, do not weep, because through the death of their depraved teacher they find the way of truth, though they might have seemed capable of being afflicted by his destruction. Or certainly the widows do not weep because, remaining in their error while judging their preacher to have been holy, they console themselves with false hope lest they mourn.

CHAPTER VI. ON THE INFANT.

By the name “infant” the Lord is understood, as it is said through the prophet: “The infant shall delight at the hole of the asp” (Isa. 11:8). See the chapter “On the *regulus*,” Book III, chapter 29.

By the name “infant” any person reborn or newly converted is signified, as Peter says to certain converts: “Like newborn infants, desire the rational milk without deceit, that by it you may grow unto salvation” (1 Pet. 2:2).

184 CHAPTER VII. ON BOYS.

[Col. 0145B] In Sacred Scripture, by the name “boys” are sometimes signified those who serve heavenly commands; sometimes the still immature condition of beginners; sometimes persons who are innocent but still weak; and sometimes the watchful discernments of the mind.

By the name “boys” are signified those who serve heavenly commands, as blessed Job says in the person of the afflicted Church: “When the Almighty was with me, and my boys around me” (Job 29:5). Those who serve heavenly commands are of course called boys. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Behold, I and my boys, whom God has given me” (Isa. 8:18). And again the Lord says in the Gospel: “Children, have you anything to eat?” (John 21:5). Thus boys are now around the Church because in almost all nations there are found persons who keep the heavenly commands and obey the rules of spiritual teaching. These servants will surely be absent then, when the wicked who are found despise her spiritual commands.

By the name “boys” the still immature condition of beginners is signified, as the messenger says to blessed Job: “The oxen were plowing and the she-asses were feeding beside them, and the Sabeans rushed in, took everything away, and struck the boys with the sword; and I alone escaped to tell you” (Job 1:14–15). For what else do we understand figuratively by oxen except those who work well? What else by she-asses except certain persons who live simply? The latter are well said to feed beside the oxen, because, although the minds of the simple cannot grasp lofty matters, they are near to great things insofar as they believe their brethren’s good through charity. Since they do not know how to envy others’ understanding, they are not divided from one another in their pasture, as it were. Therefore the she-asses are fed together with the oxen, because slower persons, joined to the prudent, are nourished by their understanding.

But “Sabeans” is interpreted “captors.” And who else are signified by the name of captors except unclean spirits, who lead all whom they subject to themselves captive into unbelief? They also strike the boys with the sword because they grievously wound with the darts of their temptation those whom not yet the steadfastness of youth preserves free. Such persons indeed begin good things, but in the still immature state of their beginning they are brought low by unclean spirits that take them captive. The enemy strikes them with the sword because he pierces them with despair of eternity.

But what does it mean that a messenger comes who says, “I alone escaped”? [Note: [Col. 0145D] From chapter XVIII, Book I above.] Who is this messenger who alone escapes while the others perish, except prophetic speech, which, when all the evils it foretold come to pass, as it were returns alone in health to the Lord? For when it is known to have spoken truly concerning the fall of those who perish, it is shown to have lived among the dead. Hence a boy is sent to bring Rebekah to Isaac in marriage, because prophecy in its intervening service waits upon the betrothal of the Church to the Lord. Therefore, when the Sabeans rush in, the boy alone escapes to report, because while malign spirits lead the minds of the weak into captivity, the utterance of prophecy has prevailed, announcing this same captivity in the words: “Therefore my people has been led captive because it had no knowledge” (Isa. 5:13). Thus prophecy is, as it were, saved when the captivity that it foretold is shown.

By the name “boys” are signified those who are innocent but still weak, as again it is said to blessed Job: “The fire of God fell from heaven and, touching the sheep, consumed the boys; and I alone escaped to tell you” (Job 1:16). See the chapter “On Fire” (Book II, chapter 1).

By the name “boys” the watchful discernments of the mind are signified. This too may be understood morally. For what is signified by sheep except the innocence of thoughts? What by boys except the purity of good hearts? We have explained a little earlier that heaven is called the air; hence we call birds “birds of heaven.” And we know that unclean spirits, fallen from the ethereal heaven, wander in the space between this heaven and earth. They envy human hearts all the more as those hearts rise to heavenly things because they see that they themselves have been cast down from heavenly things by the impurity of their pride.

Since, therefore, from the powers of the air the flame of envy rushes against the purity of our thoughts, fire comes from heaven upon the sheep. For they often set the pure thoughts of our minds aflame with the heat of lust and, as it were, burn up the sheep when they trouble the chaste movements of the soul with the temptation of lust. This is called the fire of God because, though it is not caused by God, it arises by His permission. And because by a sudden impulse they sometimes overwhelm even the mind’s watchful discernments, they kill the boys who serve as guards, as it were, with the sword. Yet one escapes unharmed when persevering discernment carefully observes all that the mind undergoes; it alone escapes the death of the sword because discernment does not succumb even when thoughts are disturbed, so that it may report its losses to the soul and, as it were, summon the Lord to mourning.

CHAPTER VIII. ON THE KING.

In Sacred Scripture, when “king” is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies God the Father, sometimes Christ our Redeemer, and sometimes the ancient enemy. When “kings” is used in the plural, it sometimes means angelic spirits; sometimes the holy apostles or any holy preachers; and sometimes holy men.

187 By the name “king” God the Father is understood, as it says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son” (Matt. 22:2). See the chapter “On Man.”

By the name “king” is signified the Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, as the Psalmist says to God the Father concerning the Son: “O God, give Your judgment to the king, and Your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71:1). Hence, in the person of this same our Redeemer, blessed Job says: “When I sat as a king, with an army standing about me, I was nevertheless a comforter of those who mourned” (Job 29:25). For the Lord sits as a king in the heart because He governs the clamoring motions of the soul in our thought. In the mind which He inhabits, He awakens what is sluggish, restrains what is restless, kindles what is cold, moderates what has been kindled, softens what is rigid, and checks what is unrestrained. From this very diversity of thoughts an army, as it were, stands about Him. Or certainly He sits as a king with an army standing about Him because the multitude of virtues surrounds Him as He presides over the minds of the elect. He is also a comforter of those who mourn, by the promise in which He says: “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5); and again: “I shall see you, and your heart shall rejoice; and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16:22).

By the name “king” the ancient enemy is signified, as the Lord says of him to blessed Job under the name Leviathan: “He sees every lofty thing, and he himself is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41:25). For he sees every lofty thing—that is, he looks down, as if from on high, upon all those placed beneath him. And because he strives in intention against his creators, he disdains to consider anyone his equal. It should be noted that the malignant spirit, signified through a bodily beast, is described as seeing lofty things because pride of heart, when it extends outward even to the body, first displays itself through the eyes. Inflated by the haughtiness of their swelling, they look down as though from on high; and the more they abase themselves, the more highly they exalt themselves.

For unless pride displayed itself through the eyes as through certain windows, the Psalmist would never have said to God: “You will save the humble people, and You will humble the eyes of the proud” (Ps. 17:28). Unless pride poured itself forth through the eyes, Solomon too would not have said of the arrogance of Judea: “A generation whose eyes are lofty, and whose eyelids are raised on high” (Prov. 30:13). Therefore, because the ancient enemy is signified through a bodily animal, and because pride that comes forth even to the body holds clearer sway in the eyes, he is described as seeing all things from on high. It follows: “And he himself is king over all the sons of pride.”

Pride alone struck down the ancient enemy, so that he fell into such great evil. He would not have withered through so many branches of vices unless he had first rotted at the root through this vice. For it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10:14). Through pride he himself fell; through pride he laid low the human being who followed him. He attacked the salvation of our immortality with the very weapon by which he extinguished the life of his own blessedness. But the Lord inserted this matter at the end of His discourse so that, after speaking of all the evils of the ancient enemy, He might show what is worse than all evils: pride. Moreover, by being placed last of all, it is shown to be the root of vices. For just as a root lies hidden below while branches spread outward from it, so pride conceals itself within, but manifest vices immediately spring from it. No evils would come forth publicly unless pride bound the mind in secret. It is this which makes the thought of the ancient enemy boil like a pot. Hence it shakes human minds with a kind of fever of madness, but through outward works shows how it overturns the soul which it has shaken. For what afterward foams outwardly in action first boils inwardly in self-exaltation.

Kings signify angelic spirits, as blessed Job says: “For now, sleeping, I should be silent, and in my sleep I should rest with the kings and counsellors of the earth” (Job 3:13). [Note: [Col. 0147D] From Book IV on Job, ch. 25.] For this end man had been placed in paradise: that, if he bound himself by the bonds of love to obedience to his Creator, he might one day pass to the heavenly homeland of the angels without bodily death. For he was created immortal in such a way that, if he sinned, he could die; and mortal in such a way that, if he did not sin, he could also not die; and, by the merit of free choice, might attain the blessedness of that region in which he could neither sin nor die. Therefore, where the elect pass after the time of redemption, bodily death intervening, our first parents too, had they remained in the state in which they were created, could doubtless have been conveyed even without death of their bodies. Thus man would sleep and rest in his sleep when, led to the rest of the eternal homeland, he found, as it were, a retreat from the outcry of this human weakness. For after sin, he keeps watch as though crying out, since he bears the conflict of his own flesh resisting him. [Col. 0148D] Man already possessed this silence of repose when he was created, receiving freedom of choice against his enemy. But because he voluntarily yielded to that enemy, he immediately found within himself that which made noise against himself; immediately, in the struggle, he encountered the tumult of weakness. And although he had been created by his Maker in the silence of peace, yet, voluntarily subjected to the enemy, he endured the cries of battle.

For the prompting of the flesh itself is a kind of cry against the mind’s repose. Before transgression man did not experience it, because he did not possess that through which he could suffer weakness. But after he voluntarily subjected himself to the enemy, bound by the chains of his own guilt, he even unwillingly [Col. 0149A] serves him in certain respects and suffers cries in his mind, when the flesh resists the spirit. Did not he hear inner cries who endured the words of the law opposed to him, saying: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and leading me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7)? Let the holy man therefore consider in how great a peace of heart he would rest if man had refused to accept the serpent’s words, and say: “For now, sleeping, I should be silent, and in my sleep I should rest”—that is, I should withdraw into the secret place of the mind for contemplation of the Creator—had not the consent of the first sin delivered me outside myself to the tumults of temptations. He adds with whom he would also enjoy the joys of this repose, saying: “With the kings and counsellors of the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0149D] From ch. 26, Book cited above.]

From insensible things we learn what we should think concerning sensible and intelligible things. For the earth is made fruitful by the air, while the air is ordered by the character of heaven. Thus human beings preside over beasts; angels over human beings; and archangels over angels. That human beings preside over beasts we both see by experience and learn from the Psalmist’s words: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet, all sheep and oxen, and besides, the beasts of the field” (Ps. 8:8). That angels preside over human beings, the angel testifies through the prophet, saying: “The prince of the kingdom of the Persians withstood me” (Dan. 10:13). That angels are administered by the powers of higher angels is affirmed by the prophet Zechariah, who says: “Behold, the angel who spoke in me was going out; and another angel was going out to meet him, and said to him: Run and speak to this young man, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls” (Zech. 2:3). For if the highest powers did not order the least even in the offices of holy spirits, an angel could in no way have learned from another angel what he was to say to a human being. Since, therefore, the Creator of all holds all things through himself, and nevertheless governs them, some administering others, in order to distinguish the order of the beautiful universe, we rightly understand the spirits of angels as “kings”: the more intimately they serve the Author of all things, the more powerfully they rule those subject to them. Thus man would sleep with kings, because he would rest with angels if he had refused to follow the tongue of the persuader. They are also rightly called counsellors, [Col. 0149D] because they provide for the spiritual commonwealth while joining us to themselves as companions in the kingdom. They are rightly called counsellors because, when through their announcements we know the will of the Creator, in them we undoubtedly find counsel in this distress of our tribulation.

Under the name of kings, blessed apostles and any holy preachers may also fittingly be understood in these words. Since blessed Job is filled with the holy Spirit of eternity—and eternity has neither “was” nor “will be,” for neither past things pass away from it nor future things arrive, since it sees all things in the present—he can contemplate in the presence of the Spirit the future preachers of the Church, [Col. 0150A] who, after leaving their bodies, are not delayed from receiving the heavenly homeland by intervals of waiting, as the ancient Fathers were. For as soon as they pass from the binding of the flesh, they rest in the heavenly dwelling, as Paul attests: “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5:1). But before our Redeemer by his death paid the penalty of the human race, even those who had followed the way to the heavenly homeland were held after their departure from the flesh by the barriers of hell—not that punishment afflicted them as sinners, but that, resting in more remote places, because the intercession [Col. 0150B] of the Mediator had not yet come, they were prevented by the liability of the first sin from entering the kingdom.

Hence, according to the testimony of that same Redeemer, the rich man who is tormented among the dead beholds Lazarus resting in Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:23). Certainly, if they had not still been in the depths, the man placed amid torments would not have seen them. Thus our same Redeemer, dying for the debt of our guilt, enters the lower world in order to lead to heaven those of his own who had clung to him. But where redeemed humanity now ascends, there indeed humanity would have arrived even without redemption had it refused to sin. Let the holy man therefore consider that, had he not sinned, he would ascend unredeemed to that place which holy preachers [Col. 0150C] after redemption must reach with great labor; and let him indicate with whom he would now rest, saying: “With the kings and counsellors of the earth.” For the holy preachers of the Church are kings: they know both how rightly to order those entrusted to them and how to govern well their own bodies, because, tempering in themselves the movements of desire, they rule over their subject thoughts by the law of virtue. They are also rightly called counsellors of the earth. They are kings because they preside over themselves; counsellors of the earth because, by destroying sins, they offer the counsel of life. They are kings because they know how to govern themselves; they are counsellors of the earth because, by the counsel of their exhortation, they draw earthly minds to heavenly things. Was not he a counsellor of the earth who said: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7:25)? And again: “She will be happier if she remains thus, according to my counsel” (ibid., 40).

Any holy persons are signified by the name of kings, as Elihu says of the Lord in the book of blessed Job: “He does not withdraw his eyes from the righteous, and he sets kings upon the throne for ever, and there they are exalted” (Job 36:7). For perhaps the Lord is thought to have withdrawn his eyes from the righteous because here they are torn by the cruelties of the wicked without vengeance. But the Master then looks upon his servants when the malice of a persecutor unjustly afflicts them. For, seeing what they humbly endure here, he undoubtedly already foresees what he will mercifully repay them there. Therefore, he does not withdraw his eyes from the righteous. Behold, one groans humbly, while another is proud and wickedly prospers. One breaks his heart; the other exalts himself in the glory of wickedness. Which of these, then, is far from the divine gaze: the one who endured injustice, or the one who inflicted it on a patient sufferer? The one who retained heavenly grace amid the darkness of grief, or the one who amid outward joys lost inwardly the light of righteousness? Holy persons are rightly called kings by the testimony of sacred Scripture, because, set over every movement of the flesh, they now restrain the appetite of lust, now temper the heat of avarice, now bend down the glory of pride, now crush the promptings of envy, now extinguish the fire of rage. Therefore, they are kings because they know how not to yield and fall beneath the movements of their temptations by consenting to them, but rather to rule over them. Since they pass from this power of self-government to the power of recompense, it is rightly said: “He sets kings upon the throne for ever.” For in governing themselves they were wearied for a time, but on the throne of eternal royal exaltation they are set for ever. And there they receive the power to judge others worthily because here they do not know how wickedly to spare themselves. Hence it is elsewhere said: “Until righteousness is turned into judgment” (Ps. 93 [Vulgate numbering]). For Paul says of himself and his companions: “That we might become the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor. 5:21). Righteousness, then, is turned into judgment, because those who now live justly and blamelessly then receive the power of judging. Hence the Lord says to the Church of Laodicea: “To him who conquers, [Col. 0151C] I will grant to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat with my Father on his throne” (Rev. 3:21). Therefore let it be said: “He sets kings upon the throne for ever.” By adding “for ever,” he aptly makes plain what he means. For had he spoken of the throne of an earthly kingdom, he would by no means have added “for ever,” because those who seize it are surely set upon it not for ever but temporarily.

## CHAPTER IX. ON COUNSELLORS

Angelic spirits or holy preachers are signified by the name of counsellors, as blessed Job says: “For now, sleeping, I should be silent,” etc. (Job 3:13). See above in the chapter “On Kings.”

## CHAPTER X. ON LEADERS

[Col. 0151D]

In sacred Scripture, the name of leaders sometimes signifies the authors of errors, and at other times the principal vices.

The authors of errors are signified by the name of leaders, as blessed Job says in the person of the Church: “The leaders restrained their voice, and their tongue adhered to their throat” (Job 29:10). For who else can be understood here as leaders except the authors of heretical perversity? But in the time of the Church’s peace the leaders restrain their voice, because those who seek to draw wandering peoples after themselves do not now dare to utter their perversities; they are restrained both by the weight of authorities and by the force of reason. Their tongue adheres to their throat because, although they do not dare freely to speak perversely aloud, they nevertheless conceal within themselves all the falsehoods which they plot to advance against the true faith.

Principal vices are signified by the name of leaders, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the holy man under the designation of a horse: “From afar he smells the battle, the exhortation of the leaders, and the howling of the army” (Job 39:25). To smell battle from afar is to recognize from preceding causes what conflicts of vices will follow. Since a thing not seen is known by smell, to smell battle from afar is likewise to investigate hidden evils, as by the breath of the nostrils, so by the foresight of one’s thoughts. Concerning this sense of smell, the Lord rightly says in praise of his Church: “Your nose is like the tower which is in Lebanon” (Song 7:4). For through the nose we distinguish scents and stenches. And what is signified by the nose but the provident discernment of the saints? A tower of watchfulness is set on high so that an approaching enemy may be seen from far off. The nose of the Church is therefore rightly said to be like a tower in Lebanon, because the provident examination of the saints, set on high as it carefully looks about in every direction, detects sin before it arrives. The more vigilantly it marks it beforehand, the more strongly it avoids it. Hence Habakkuk says: “I will stand upon my watch” (Hab. 2:1). Hence he admonishes the soul of each elect person, saying: “Set up a watchtower for yourself; set up bitter things for yourself” (Jer. 31:21). To set up a watchtower for oneself is to know beforehand from lofty consideration the coming contests of vices. And the mind of the elect sets bitter things before itself when, even established in the peace [Col. 0152C] of virtues, it sees evils lying in ambush and does not consent to rest securely.

In the first place, it considers how to avoid every evil; in the second, how not to perform good things incautiously. And after it has subdued wrongs, it strives to subject even right things to itself, lest, should they pass beyond the mind’s governance, they be turned into the fault of self-exaltation. Since evils often arise from good things through the vice of carelessness, it attentively considers how arrogance may arise from learning, cruelty from justice, laxity from compassion, anger from zeal, and torpor from gentleness. And while it performs these good things, it sees that these enemies may rise against it through them. For when it labors to acquire the pursuits of learning, it carefully prepares the mind against the conflict of arrogance. When it desires justly to punish the faults of sinners, [Col. 0152D] it most shrewdly avoids allowing the cruelty of vengeance to exceed the measure of justice. When it endeavors to preserve itself through compassion, it diligently foresees lest it be overcome by some relaxation of discipline. When it stimulates itself with the impulses of righteous zeal, it takes the greatest care lest it kindle itself with the flame of anger more than is necessary. When it moderates itself with great tranquility of gentleness, it watchfully observes lest it grow cold in torpor.

Since, therefore, every vice is seen by the thought of the spiritual soldier before it can creep in, it is rightly said of God’s horse: “From afar he smells the battle.” He also considers what throng of evils may rush in if he permits many or few of them to enter him. Hence it follows: “The exhortation of the leaders and the howling of the army.” For the tempting vices, which serve pride ruling over them in an invisible battle against us, are in part like leaders going before, and in part like an army following after. Not all faults take possession of the heart by an equal approach. But when the greater and fewer faults get ahead of the neglected mind, the lesser and countless ones pour themselves upon it in troops. For pride itself, the queen of vices, when it has fully seized a conquered heart, immediately hands it over to be devastated by the seven principal vices as by its own leaders. The army follows these leaders, because troublesome multitudes of vices without doubt arise from them. We shall show this more clearly if we set forth, as we are able, a particular enumeration of the leaders themselves and their army.

For pride is the root of every evil. Of it Scripture testifies: “The beginning of every sin is pride” [Col. 0153B] (Ecclus. 10:14). From this poisonous root seven principal vices are produced as its first offspring: namely, vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust. Since he grieved that we had been captured by these seven vices of pride, our Redeemer came, filled with the Spirit of sevenfold grace, to the spiritual battle of liberation. But each of these has its army against us.

From vainglory arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, quarrels, obstinacy, discord, and presumptions of novelty.

From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing at a neighbor’s adversities, and grief at a neighbor’s prosperity.

[Col. 0153C] From anger are produced quarrels, swelling of mind, insults, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies.

From sadness arise rancor, faintheartedness, despair, torpor concerning the commandments, and wandering of mind toward unlawful things.

From avarice arise betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjuries, restlessness, violence, and hardening of heart against mercy.

From gluttony arise foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleanness, much speaking, and dullness of understanding.

From lust are generated blindness of mind, thoughtlessness, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present age, and dread or despair concerning the age to come.

[Col. 0153D] Since, then, the seven principal vices produce so great a multitude of vices from themselves, when they come to the heart they draw after them, as it were, the troops of an army that follows.

Of these seven, five are spiritual and two fleshly. Yet each is joined to the next by so close a kinship that one is produced from another.

For the first offspring of pride is vainglory; and when it corrupts the oppressed mind, it immediately gives birth to envy. For while it seeks the power of an empty name, it wastes away lest another should attain it. Envy in turn gives birth to anger, because the more the mind is wounded by the inward wound of envy, the more it loses the gentleness of tranquility. And because it is touched like an aching limb, the hand of an opposed action is felt as though more heavily pressed.

Sadness also arises from anger, because the disturbed mind, the more disorderly it agitates itself, the more it confuses itself by enslaving itself; and, when it has lost the sweetness of tranquility, nothing but the grief that follows from its disturbance feeds it.

Sadness in turn is carried over into avarice, because when the confused heart has inwardly lost in itself the good of joy, it seeks something outward by which it may be consoled. And it desires to acquire external goods all the more because it has no joy to which it may inwardly return.

After these, the two fleshly vices remain, namely gluttony and lust. But it is plain to all that lust is born from gluttony, since by the very arrangement of the limbs the genital organs appear joined to the belly. Therefore, when one is inordinately fed, the other is undoubtedly aroused to shameful acts. The leaders are rightly said to exhort, but the army to howl, because the first vices insinuate themselves into the deceived mind under a certain appearance of reason; but the innumerable vices that follow, while dragging it into every madness, confound it with a kind of bestial clamor.

Vainglory commonly exhorts a conquered heart under an appearance of reason, saying: “You ought to seek greater things, so that the more you have power to surpass many people, the more you may be able to benefit more people.”

Envy also commonly exhorts a conquered heart under an appearance of reason, saying: “In what respect are you inferior to this person or that? Why then are you not equal or superior? How much are you able to do that they cannot do? Therefore, they ought not to be either superior or even equal to you.”

Anger too commonly exhorts a conquered heart under an appearance of reason, saying: “What is done against you cannot be borne calmly. Indeed, to endure it patiently is a sin, because unless it is resisted with great severity, such things will henceforth be heaped upon you without measure.”

Sadness too commonly exhorts a conquered heart under an appearance of reason, saying: “What do you have by which to rejoice, when you bear such evils from your neighbors? Consider with what grief all those must be regarded who return against you in so great bitterness of gall.”

Avarice likewise commonly exhorts a conquered mind under an appearance of reason, saying: “There is very little blame in desiring to possess certain things, because you do not seek abundance but fear want; and what another person keeps wrongly, you yourself spend better.”

Gluttony likewise commonly exhorts a conquered heart under an appearance of reason, saying: “God created all things clean for food; and whoever refuses to be satisfied with food, what else does he do but oppose the gift granted?”

Lust, moreover, commonly exhorts a conquered heart under an appearance of reason, saying: “Why do you not give yourself free rein in your pleasure, when you do not know what may follow you? You ought not to lose the time given you without satisfying desires, since you do not know how swiftly it may pass. For if God had not willed that man should be joined in the pleasure of intercourse, he would not have made male and female at the very beginning of the human race.”

[Col. 0155A] This is the exhortation of the leaders, which, when heedlessly admitted into the secret place of the heart, persuades evil more intimately. The howling army follows it: once the unhappy soul has been captured by the principal vices and has been turned to madness through multiplied iniquities, it is ravaged by a savage brutality. But because God’s soldier strives prudently to foresee the conflicts of vices, he smells battle from afar: with anxious thought he considers what the evils that go before may be able to persuade the mind; he detects the exhortation of the leaders by the acuteness of his nostrils; and because by foreknowing from afar he perceives the confusion of the iniquities which follow, he comes to know, as it were by smell, the howling of the army.

## CHAPTER XI. ON PRINCES

[Col. 0155B] [Note: [Col. 0155D] From Book XI on Job, ch. 10.] By the name of princes are signified those who, by great judgment of counsel, rule over their own thoughts, as blessed Job says of the Lord: “He pours contempt upon princes, and raises up those who had been oppressed” (Job 12:21). They are rightly called princes who always rule their own thoughts by the great judgment of counsel and restrain all foolish impulses by the power of wisdom. But it often happens that the mind is secretly raised into pride by wisdom itself and falls under those vices over which it rejoiced to have been victorious. It is therefore rightly said: “He pours contempt upon princes.” But because those who appear to lie hidden in vices sometimes run to the lamentation of repentance and raise themselves against the sins under which they lay, it is fittingly added: “And he raises up those who had been oppressed.” [Col. 0156A] For some, illumined by a heavenly gift, see in what foulness of sins they lie; they wash the stains of their deeds with tears, and afterwards press beneath themselves the movements of their flesh by which they were previously pressed. This is done by the great dispensation of almighty God, so that things may be uncertain in this life: no one should be proud because of acquired chastity, since “he pours contempt upon princes”; and no one should despair because of being cast down by his vices, since “he raises up those who had been oppressed.”

[Note: [Col. 0155D] From Book XIX on Job, ch. 11, after the middle.] By the name of princes are signified the authors of heretical perversity, as blessed Job says in the person of the Church: “The princes ceased speaking and placed a finger upon their mouth” (Job 29:9). For who else are understood here as princes but the authors of heretical perversity? Of them the Psalmist says: “Contempt was poured out upon princes, and he made them wander in a pathless place, not in a way” (Ps. 106:40). While they do not fear perversely to interpret God’s dispensation, they indeed draw the peoples subject to them not into the way which is Christ, but into a trackless waste. Contempt is also rightly said to have been poured out upon them because they in turn contradict one another by their arguments. [Note: [Col. 0156D] Gregory has examples of this statement in the same place.] Therefore, when the holy Church is overtaken by the final tribulation, remembering her former authority, let her say: “The princes ceased speaking and placed a finger upon their mouth.” That is, openly: When I was permitted publicly to preach, everyone who did not submit to my truth was afraid. For when the holy Church is oppressed by adversity, liberty of speech is granted to all perverse preachers.

## THE FIFTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0155]

## CHAPTER ONE. ON SPIRIT

[Col. 0155C]

In sacred Scripture, by the name of spirit are understood at one time the soul, at another a spiritual effect, at another the swelling of pride, at another an inward thought, and at another the wind.

[Note: [Col. 0156D] From Book XI on Job, ch. 3.] Spirit signifies the soul, as it is written of our Head himself: “Bowing his head, he gave up the spirit” (John 19:30). For if the Evangelist meant by “spirit” something other than the soul, then when the spirit departed, the soul would certainly have remained.

A spiritual effect is understood from a part of the word, as the Psalmist says of the Lord: “Who makes your angels spirits and ministers” (Heb. 1:7). For angels—that is, messengers—are sometimes called preachers in sacred discourse, as the prophet says: “The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7). Almighty [Col. 0156C] God, therefore, makes his angels spiritual, because he makes his preachers spiritual.

Pride is signified by the name of spirit, as the Psalmist says to the Lord concerning the humiliation of the proud: “You will take away their spirit, and they shall fail and return to their dust” (Ps. 103:29). For what is their spirit called but the spirit of pride? Let their spirit therefore be taken away so that they may fail—that is, when the spirit of pride is removed, they may recognize that they are nothing from themselves—and let them return to dust, that is, be humbled by their weak condition.

An inward thought is signified by the name of spirit, as Elihu says of man: “If he directs his heart toward him, he draws to himself his spirit and breath” (Job 34:14). The heart is crooked when it seeks low things; it is made straight when it is raised to things above. Therefore, if a person directs his heart to the Lord, the Lord draws that person’s spirit and breath to himself. By spirit he means inward [Col. 0157A] thoughts; by breath, which is drawn through the body, outward actions. Thus for God to draw a person’s spirit and breath to himself is to turn our inward and outward selves toward desire for him, so that nothing outward may any longer please the mind, and the flesh may not seek to obtain anything lower, even if it desires it. Rather, all that a person is may both burn inwardly in desire toward him from whom that person is and restrain itself outwardly by self-discipline.

## CHAPTER II. ON THE SOUL

In sacred Scripture, the name of soul sometimes means that which is loved more dearly; at other times, the intention of the mind.

The soul is used for that which is loved more dearly, as the Lord says to Satan concerning our Redeemer under the name of blessed Job: “Behold, he is in your hand; but preserve his soul” (Job 2:6). What else do we understand by Christ’s soul except the life of the elect, which he loves dearly? For when we love rightly, we love nothing among created things more dearly than our own soul; and, as we say that we love as our own soul those for whom we strive to express the weight of our love, the life of the elect is fittingly signified by Christ’s soul. Therefore, when Satan is permitted to strike the Redeemer’s body, he is separated from his soul, because when the body is received for the Passion, Satan loses his right of power over Christ’s elect. And when Christ’s flesh dies on the cross, their minds are strengthened against temptations. [Col. 0157C] Therefore let it be said: “Behold, he is in your hand; but preserve his soul.” That is, plainly: Receive permission against his body, but lose the right of wicked dominion over his elect, whom he possesses with himself before the ages through foreknowledge.

The intention of the mind is understood by the name of soul, as blessed Job says: “Why has my soul chosen hanging, and my bones death?” (Job 7:15). What is signified by the soul except the intention of the mind, and by the bones except the strength of the flesh? Everything suspended is undoubtedly lifted from low things.
