Thus the soul chooses hanging so that the bones may die, because, when the intention of the mind raises itself to things above, it kills within itself every power of outward life. For holy persons know with certainty that they cannot have rest in this life. Therefore they choose hanging, because, abandoning earthly desires, they raise their mind to things above. And being suspended, they inflict death on their bones, because, girded in the pursuits of virtue by love of the heavenly homeland, they subdue by the bond of humility that in which they were formerly strong in the world.

## CHAPTER III. ON THE BODY

The name of body signifies any action of ours, as the voice of Truth says in the Gospel: “The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark” (Matt. 6:22). For what is expressed by the eye except the intention of the heart which precedes its work, which, before it exercises itself in action, already contemplates that which it desires? And what is signified by the designation of body except every action which follows its intention as an eye looking ahead? Thus the eye is the lamp of the body, because the merits of action are illumined by the ray of a good intention. And if the eye is single, the whole body will be full of light, because, if we intend rightly through simplicity of thought, a good work is done even though it may appear insignificant. But if the eye is evil, the body will be dark, because when something—even something right—is done with a perverse intention, although it appears to shine before human beings, it is darkened in the judgment of the inward Judge. He rightly adds: “See, therefore, lest the light that is in you be darkness. If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be?” [Col. 0158B] (ibid., 23). For if we darken by evil intention what we believe we are doing well, how great are those evils which we do not fail to know are evil even as we commit them? And if we see nothing where we hold what seems to be the light of discernment, in what blindness do we stumble in those things which we perpetrate without discernment? Therefore, in all our works our intention must be weighed with vigilant care, so that it may seek nothing temporal in what it does, but may fix itself wholly in the stability of eternity. Otherwise, if the structure of our action is placed outside its foundation, it is dissolved when the ground gives way; and that which follows in the work becomes corrupt because it is not generated from the right intention of thought.

## CHAPTER IV. ON THE HEAD

[Col. 0158C]

In sacred Scripture, the name of head sometimes signifies the highest rank of the Jewish priesthood, sometimes the governing part of the human being, and sometimes the beginning of any matter.

The highest rank of the Jewish priesthood is expressed by the name of head, as it is said of our Redeemer under the name of blessed Job: “And, with his head shorn, falling to the ground, he worshipped” (Job 1). For what is signified by the hair except the subtlety of the sacraments, and by the head except the highest rank of the Jewish priesthood? Thus the prophet Ezekiel is told: “You, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword, a razor for shaving hair; take it and pass it over your head and beard” (Ezek. 5). In this action of the prophet is expressed the judgment of the Redeemer, who, appearing in the flesh, shaved the head because he took away the sacraments of his commandments from the Jewish priesthood. He shaved the beard because, abandoning the Israelite kingdom, he cut off the beauty of its power. What then is signified here by the earth except sinful Gentile humanity? For while Judaea believed itself righteous, it is clear how reprobately it thought concerning the Gentiles, as Paul attests: “We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from among the Gentiles” (Gal. 2:15). Our Mediator, therefore, fell to the ground as though with his head shorn because, abandoning Judaea and taking his sacraments from its priesthood, he came to the knowledge of the Gentiles. He shaved the hairs from his head because he removed the sacraments of the law from that first priesthood of his. He fell to the ground because he gave himself to sinners for their salvation. And while he abandoned those who seemed righteous to themselves, [Col. 0159A] he received those who both knew and confessed themselves to be unrighteous. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). Hence too the pillar of cloud, which went before the people in the wilderness, shone with the splendor of fire not by day but by night (Exod. 13:21): our Redeemer, by the example of his life giving guidance to those who followed him, shone with no light to those confident in their own righteousness, but illumined with the fire of his love those who recognized the darkness of their sins.

Nor should the mind judge that Job’s being said to fall is unworthy of its signification of the Redeemer. For it is written: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell into Israel” (Isa. 9:8). Jacob means “supplanter,” while Israel means “the man who sees God.” And what is signified by Jacob except the Jewish people, and by Israel except the Gentile people? For the one whom Jacob sought to supplant through death of the flesh, the Gentile people undoubtedly saw as God through the eyes of faith. Thus the Word sent to Jacob fell into Israel, because the one whom the Jewish people rejected when he came to them was suddenly found by the confessing Gentile people. It is also written concerning the Holy Spirit in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Spirit of the Lord fell upon them” (Acts 10:44). The Word of God or the Spirit is said to fall in sacred Scripture in order to express the unexpectedness of his coming. For what rushes or falls suddenly comes down to lower things. Thus for the Mediator to have fallen, as it were, to the ground is to have come unexpectedly to the Gentiles, with no signs preceding [Col. 0159C] him. It is rightly said that he worshipped as he fell, because, when he himself assumed the humility of the flesh, he poured into those who believe in him the vows of humility. For he did what he taught should be done, as is said of his Spirit: “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. 8:26). He does not intercede because he is equal [to the Father], but is said to intercede because he makes those whom he fills become intercessors. Yet our Redeemer also showed this in himself, when, as he drew near to the Passion, he prayed to the Father. For what wonder is it if, in the form of a servant, he subjected himself to the Father by prayer, in that same form in which he even endured the hands of sinners unto the extremity of death?

The term “head” signifies the principal part of a human being, that is, the mind, as the Psalmist says: “You have made my head rich with oil” (Ps. 22:5). It is as though he said plainly: “You have watered my mind, dry in its thoughts, with the anointing of charity.” Hence it is also said to others: “Let oil not fail from your head” (Eccles. 9:8). For oil upon the head is charity in the mind. Oil fails from the head when charity departs from the mind. Nor without reason is the mind signified by the head: just as the limbs are governed by the head, so thoughts are ordered by the mind.

The term “head” signifies the fault in any matter, as under the figure of Judaea the prophet Jeremiah says of every soul caught in the snare of a wretched intention: “Her enemies have become at her head” (Lam. 1:5). It must be understood that the ancient enemy assails our good works in three ways, so that what is done uprightly before human beings may be corrupted in the sight of the eternal Judge. Sometimes he pollutes the intention in a good work, so that everything which follows in the action does not emerge pure and clean, because he has disturbed it from its beginning. At other times he cannot corrupt the intention of the good work, but sets snares in the action itself, as though on the road, so that when a person proceeds more confidently in the purpose of the mind, a fault secretly added may destroy him as from an ambush. At other times he neither corrupts the intention nor trips one up along the way, but ensnares the good work at its end. The farther he pretends to have withdrawn, whether from the house of the heart or from the path of the work, the more cunningly he waits for the end of the good action which he means to deceive; and having made a person heedlessly secure by seeming to depart, he sometimes pierces that person more harshly and more incurably with a sudden blow. He pollutes the intention in a good work because, when he sees human hearts easy to deceive, he offers their desires the breeze of passing approval, so that in the upright deeds they perform they may be bent, by a crooked intention, toward the pursuit of low things.

Therefore, under the figure of Judaea, Jeremiah says of every soul caught in the snare of a wretched intention: “Her enemies have become at her head.” It is as though he said plainly: When a good work is undertaken with a bad intention, opposing spirits take command from the very beginning of the thought, and possess the soul the more fully because they hold it by ruling from its outset. But when they cannot corrupt the intention, they conceal snares placed upon the way, so that in what is rightly done the heart, exalting itself, may be diverted sideways into fault, and what it proposed at the beginning may in its execution proceed very differently from how it began. For often, when human praise meets a good work, it changes the mind of the worker. Though that praise was not sought, once offered it delights. And when the mind of one acting well is dissolved by this delight, it is scattered from all the inner strength of its intention. Often anger joins itself, as from the side, to our righteousness well begun; and while it disturbs the mind too immoderately under zeal for rectitude, it wounds the entire soundness of inward peace. Often sadness, as though joined from the side, follows heaviness of heart, and overshadows with the veil of sorrow every work which the mind begins with a good intention. Sometimes it is driven away all the more slowly because it seems to serve the oppressed mind more safely. Often excessive joy attaches itself to a good work; and while it requires the mind to be more cheerful than is fitting, it removes from good action every weight of seriousness. Since the Psalmist saw that snares lie hidden upon the path even for those who begin well, he rightly said, filled with the prophetic Spirit: “In this way in which I walked, they hid a snare for me” (Ps. 141:4). But when the ancient enemy strikes neither at the beginning of the intention nor intercepts along the path of the action, he stretches harsher snares at the end. He besets a person with greater malice the more he sees that this alone remains to him for deception. The Prophet saw these snares set against the end, when he said: “They watched my heel” (Ps. 55:7). Since the heel is the end of the body, what does it signify but the conclusion of an action? Thus evil spirits, or any wicked persons who follow their pride, watch the heel when they desire to corrupt the end of an action. Hence the same serpent is told: “She shall watch your head, and you shall watch her heel” [Note: [Col. 0161D] Ambrose, *On Flight from the World*, book 7; Chrysostom, homily on “I will put enmities between you and the woman”; Cyprian, book I *Against the Jews*, ch. II, would read thus if, instead of *ipsa* (“she”), he did not have *ipse* (“he”).] (Gen. 3:15). To watch the serpent’s head is to observe the faults of his suggestion and utterly root them out from the entrance of the heart by the hand of vigilant consideration. Yet, when he is detected at the beginning, he strives to strike the heel; for even if he does not strike through his first suggestion, he aims to deceive at the end. But if the heart is once corrupted in its intention, the middle and the end of the ensuing action are securely possessed by the crafty enemy, because he sees that the whole tree will bear fruit for him when he has corrupted its root with the tooth of poison. The greatest care, therefore, must be taken lest the mind, while serving good works, be polluted by a depraved intention.

## CHAPTER V. ON THE NECK

In Sacred Scripture, the term “neck” sometimes signifies the uprightness of freedom, sometimes pride.

The term “neck” signifies the uprightness of freedom, as it is said through blessed Job in the person of the Church: “He seized my neck, broke me, and set me up as though for a target” (Job 16:13). As the neck signifies pride among evils, so among goods it signifies the uprightness of freedom. Hence even pride itself is sometimes used in the sense of exalted distinction, as the Lord promises the holy Church through the prophet: “I will make you an everlasting pride” (Isa. 60:15). And because, in a time of persecution, certain weak people do not dare freely to preach the truths they hold, it is rightly said of this enemy: “He seized my neck, broke me.” Or perhaps those are marked by the designation “neck” who, in its time of peace, rise more than is fitting and, under the pretext of defending rectitude, serve the vice of arrogance. In time of persecution they feel adversities more sharply precisely because they are puffed up by prosperity. Of them he rightly says: “He seized my neck, broke me”; that is, “The self-exaltation I had among the weak he bent down by the severity of his blow.” “And he set me up for himself as though for a target.” For clearly a target is set up in order to be struck by the shooting of arrows. Thus the faithful people are set up as a target for their enemy because he continually attacks them with his blows when he afflicts them with his persecutions. Whoever endures continual evils in this life receives the blows of one striking him, as though set up for a target. Hence, when the outstanding preacher endured the evils of persecutions and groaned under the persecution of adversaries, he comforted the tender minds of his disciples concerning his afflictions, saying: “For you yourselves know that we are appointed for this” (1 Thess. 3:3). It is as though he said openly: “Why are you astonished at our wounds in this present time? If we seek eternal joys, we came here for this very purpose: to be struck.”

[Note: [Col. 0162D] From book II on Job, ch. XIV.] The term “neck” signifies pride, as blessed Job says to certain wicked persons: “Your necks shall be reduced to mud” (Job 13:12). As sight is customarily signified by the eye, so pride is customarily signified by the neck. Therefore the neck is reduced to mud when every proud person is humbled in death and exalted flesh wastes away in decay. Let us consider what sort of corpses of the rich lie in tombs: what an image of death there is in extinguished flesh, what putrefaction of corruption. Yet these were the very persons who were exalted by honours, swollen by possessions, contemptuous of others, and rejoicing as though they alone existed. Since they did not consider where they were heading, they did not know what they were. But the neck has been reduced to mud, because those who swelled in vanity lie despised in decay. The neck is reduced to mud because the decay of corruption proves how little the power of flesh avails.

## CHAPTER VI. ON THE CROWN OF THE HEAD

In Sacred Scripture, the term “crown of the head” (*vertex*) sometimes means Christ, sometimes faith.

[Note: [Col. 0162D] From book III on Job, ch. XI, after the middle.] The crown of the head signifies Christ, namely the head of the holy Church, as in the sufferings of blessed Job, under the figure of our same Redeemer, it is said: “So Satan went out from the presence of the Lord and struck Job with a most grievous sore from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head” (Job 2:7). What is understood by the Church’s crown of the head but our Redeemer? What is meant by the sole of the foot but the first holy man, Abel? No one among the elect has come into this life who has not endured the adversities of the ancient enemy. And those who, from the world’s beginning, have lived devoutly and suffered cruel things have been members of our Redeemer. Did not Abel declare himself to be a member of this one, when, by being pleasing in sacrifice and also by dying silently, he represented the death of him of whom it is written: “Like a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent, and he shall not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7)? From the very beginning of the world, therefore, he has sought to assault the body of our Redeemer. Thus he inflicted a wound from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, because, beginning first with human beings, he advanced in his rage even to the very head of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0162D] From book XXV on Job, chapter before the middle.] The crown of the head signifies faith, as Jeremiah says to Judaea: “The sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes have violated you even to the crown of the head” (Jer. 2:16). What else is understood in the crown of the head but the height of faith? For some hold the faith to the marrow, yet take no care at all to live faithfully. They do not follow in their conduct what they venerate by belief. By divine judgment it often happens to these people that through living wickedly they lose what they had believed unto salvation. For they continually pollute themselves with wicked actions, and moreover do not believe that the retribution of a just judgment can be rendered to them. And often, while they neglect to live well, even without anyone persecuting them they slip into unbelief. For those who do not believe that strict judgment is imminent, and think they sin with impunity—how can they be or be called faithful? To have lost faith is to disbelieve that due punishments can be inflicted for uncorrected evil works. Since, therefore, they scorn to preserve the works of faith and lose the faith which they appeared to hold, the prophet rightly says to such persons under the figure of Judaea: “The sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes have violated you even to the crown of the head.” To be violated even to the crown of the head is, after the practice of evil action, to corrupt even the very height of faith. When most wicked spirits roll an individual soul in evil deeds but cannot corrupt the integrity of faith, they defile, as it were, the lower members but do not reach the crown. But whoever is corrupted in faith is already violated even to the crown of the head. For the evil spirit reaches, as it were, from the lower members to the highest, when, by polluting the active life, he corrupts the chaste loftiness of faith with the disease of distrust.

## CHAPTER VII. ON HAIR

In Sacred Scripture, the term “hair” sometimes means the wandering thoughts of the mind, sometimes superabundant earthly wealth.

[Note: [Col. 0163D] From book II on Job, ch. XXVII, after the middle.] Hair signifies thoughts of the mind, as it is said of the holy man: “And, having shaved his head, he fell to the ground and worshipped” (Job 1). What, in a moral sense, do we understand by hairs except thoughts which flow away? Hence elsewhere it is said to the bride: “Your lips, bride, are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet” (Song 4:3). For a ribbon binds the hairs of the head. The lips of the bride, therefore, are like a ribbon, because through the exhortation of the holy Church all thoughts dispersed in the minds of hearers are bound, lest they flow loosely away, scatter themselves among unlawful things, or, scattered, weigh down the eyes of the heart. Rather, they are gathered, as it were, into one intention while the ribbon of holy preaching binds them. And it rightly calls the ribbon scarlet, because the preaching of the saints burns solely with the fire of charity. What is meant by the head but the mind itself, which is the governing principle of every action? To shave the head, therefore, is to cut away superfluous thoughts from the mind. And he fell to the ground after shaving his head, because, having restrained the thoughts of his own presumption, he humbly acknowledges how weak he is in himself.

And observe that he worshipped by falling to the ground. For that person offers true prayer to God who humbly sees himself to be dust, who ascribes no virtue to himself, and who acknowledges that the good things he does come from the mercy of the Creator.

The term “hair” signifies superabundant earthly wealth, as it is written in the Gospel concerning Mary Magdalene: “Standing behind at the Lord’s feet, she began to wet his feet with tears and wiped them with her hair” [Note: [Col. 0163D] From Homily 33 on the Gospels.] What are the Lord’s feet but his least members? The woman therefore wets the Lord’s feet with tears—something we too truly do if we bow in compassionate affection toward any of the Lord’s least members; if we suffer with his saints in tribulation; if we regard their sorrow as our own. The woman wiped with her hair the feet she had wet. Now hair is superfluous to the body. And what takes the appearance of hair but superabundant earthly wealth? Since it exceeds what necessity requires, it is not felt even when cut off. We therefore wipe the Lord’s feet with hair when, to saints with whom we sympathize in charity, we also show mercy from what is superfluous to us—so that the mind may grieve through compassion and the generous hand may show the feeling of grief. For one wets the Redeemer’s feet with tears but does not wipe them with hair if one in some fashion sympathizes with neighbours’ pain but does not show them mercy from what is superfluous to oneself. One weeps and does not wipe when one gives words that seem sorrowful, but does not lessen the force of grief by providing what is lacking.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON A LOCK OF HAIR

[Note: [Col. 0164D] From book XXXI on Job, ch. VII, after the middle.] A lock of hair signifies the gathering of thoughts, as the prophet Ezekiel says: “And a likeness of a hand put forth seized me by the lock of the hair of my head; and the Spirit lifted me up between earth and heaven, and brought me to Jerusalem in a vision of God, beside the inner gate which faced north, where the idol of jealousy stood, provoking jealousy” (Ezek. 8:3). Because the mind of the righteous is constrained by the guard of discipline from the drifting desire for all visible things, it is gathered inwardly to itself and made whole; and it fully sees what it ought to be toward God and neighbour, because it leaves nothing of itself outside. The more it is drawn back and restrained from outward things, the more it is enlarged and inflamed inwardly. And the more it burns, the more brightly it shines for apprehending vices. Hence, when holy persons gather themselves within themselves, they detect even hidden faults of others with marvellous and penetrating keenness. Thus Ezekiel rightly now says: “A likeness of a hand put forth seized me.”

## CHAPTER IX. ON BODY HAIRS

[Note: [Col. 0164D] From book V on Job, ch. XXIII.] Body hairs signify superfluous thoughts belonging to human corruption, or to the old life, as Eliphaz says: “When a spirit passed before me, the hairs of my flesh stood on end” (Job 4:15). The spirit passes before us when we know invisible things, yet see them not firmly but fleetingly. For the mind is not fixed for long in the sweetness of inner contemplation, because it is driven back to itself, struck by the immensity of the light. When it tastes inward sweetness, it burns with love and strives to go beyond itself; but, broken, it falls back to the darkness of its weakness. And though making great progress in virtue, it sees that it cannot see what it ardently loves; nor would it love so ardently unless it saw something of it. The spirit therefore does not remain but passes, because our contemplation both opens the heavenly light to us as we yearn for it and immediately hides it from us in our weakness. And because in this life, however greatly someone may have advanced in virtue, that person still feels the sting of corruption—for “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15)—it is rightly added: “The hairs of my flesh stood on end.” The hairs of the flesh are whatever belongs superfluously to human corruption. The hairs of the flesh are called thoughts of the old life, which we cut away from the mind in such a manner that we are troubled by no grief at losing them. Hence Moses rightly says: “The Levites shall shave all the hairs of their flesh” (Num. 8:7). A Levite is called one who is taken up. Therefore Levites must shave all the hairs of their flesh, because one taken up for divine service ought to appear clean before God’s eyes from every fleshly thought, lest the mind produce unlawful thoughts and make the lovely appearance of the soul ugly, as though with luxuriant hairs.

But however far, as we have said, the virtue of holy conduct raises anyone, something still arises from the old nature which must be endured. Therefore the Levites’ hairs were commanded to be shaved, not plucked out. When hairs are shaved, their roots remain in the flesh and grow again to be cut once more. Thus superfluous thoughts must indeed be cut off with great diligence, but can by no means be entirely eradicated. For the flesh continually produces superfluities, which the spirit must continually cut away with the blade of watchful care. Yet we know these things in ourselves more subtly when we penetrate lofty matters by contemplation. Hence it is rightly said: “When a spirit passed before me, the hairs of my flesh stood on end.” For when the human mind is lifted to the summit of contemplation, it chastises itself more severely for its superfluities in proportion as it sees how exceedingly subtle is that which it loves. And, desiring above itself the beautiful reality which it beholds, it judges strictly whatever weak thing in itself it had formerly tolerated calmly. Thus the hairs tremble when the spirit passes, because superfluous thoughts flee before the force of compunction, so that nothing unstable and nothing lax now pleases; for the severity of inward visitation inflames the afflicted mind even against itself. When what is unlawfully born in the heart is cut away with continuous severity, it often happens that the awakened mind clings somewhat more deeply to the ray of its contemplation and almost fixes the spirit which was passing. Yet even this delay of contemplation does not fully disclose the power of the Godhead, because its immensity surpasses human powers even when enlarged and raised up.

## CHAPTER X. ON THE EYE

In Sacred Scripture, when “eye” is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies the intention of the heart; sometimes one who enlightens by teaching; sometimes the contemplative or active life; sometimes perfect knowledge of God. When “eyes” are used in the plural, they sometimes signify wicked counsellors; sometimes hope; sometimes wicked prelates; sometimes those who possess the light of truth in the holy Church; sometimes the workings of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0165D] From book XIII on Job, ch. IX.] The eye signifies the intention of the heart, as blessed Job says: “My friends are full of words; my eye pours tears to the Lord” (Job 16). It often happens that even good works within us are criticized by careless persons. But one who has a witness in heaven ought not fear human reproaches. Therefore it is rightly said: “My friends are full of words; my eye pours tears to the Lord.” What is signified by the eye but the intention of the heart? Thus the Gospel says: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 6:22). For when something is done with a good intention, the action arising from that intention is in no way darkened before the Lord. Therefore, when friends are full of words—that is, when even those joined with us in faith disparage us—the eye must pour tears, so that our intention may wholly flow out in the compunction of inward love, and may rise more subtly toward inward things in proportion as it is driven from outward things by reproaches, lest it vanish outside.

[Note: [Col. 0166D] From book XIX on Job, ch. IV, after the middle.] The eye signifies one who enlightens by teaching, as it is said through blessed Job concerning the holy Church: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame” (Job 29:15). Blind is the person who does not yet see where to go; lame is the person who cannot go where he sees. The holy Church is therefore an eye to the blind because she gives light through the word; she is a foot to the lame because she supports through help. She enlightens the blind by preaching and sustains the lame by assistance. For sin is frequently committed either through ignorance or through weakness: a person either does not know what to will, or cannot accomplish everything he wills. In contrast, the Psalmist rightly says: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation” (Ps. 26:1). Because the Lord provides both knowledge and strength, he is called illumination against ignorance and salvation against weakness. Hence he also says of the wicked: “Let their way be darkness and slipperiness” (Ps. 36), so that through darkness they may not see where they ought to go; and even if they saw the right things, through slipperiness they could not stand in them. Thus these persons limp amid good things through slipperiness, while those persons are ignorant through darkness of what good things they should follow.

[Note: [Col. 0166D] From book VI on Job, ch. XVII.] The right eye signifies the contemplative life and the left eye the active life. Hence the Gospel says: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into the hell of fire” (Matt. 5:29). It must be carefully understood that people’s dispositions differ greatly from one another. Some people have such inactive minds that, if the labour of an occupation confronts them, they collapse at the very beginning of the work. Others are so restless that, if they lack the activity of labour, they suffer more severely, because they endure disturbances of heart all the worse in proportion as they have freer leisure for thoughts. It is therefore necessary that neither a quiet mind be constrained to the exercise of excessive work, nor a restless mind to the pursuit of contemplation. For people who might have contemplated God in quiet have often fallen when burdened by occupations; and people who could have lived well, occupied in human duties, have often been destroyed by the sword of their own repose. Hence some restless spirits, seeking in contemplation more than they can grasp, break out into perverse doctrines; and, while they neglect humbly to be disciples of truth, become teachers of error. To such persons Truth himself rightly says what we have mentioned: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into the hell of fire.” For while the two lives, active and contemplative, are preserved in the mind, it has, as it were, two eyes in the face. The right eye is the contemplative life, the left the active life. But, as we have said, there are some who cannot discern high and spiritual things with sound judgment, and yet undertake lofty contemplation; consequently, by the understanding of perverse error, they fall into the pit of unbelief. Thus the contemplative life assumed beyond their powers compels them to fall from the truth, though the active life alone could have preserved them humbly in the state of their rectitude. It is therefore rightly said to them: “If your right eye causes you to stumble,” and so forth. It is as though he said plainly: “When you are not equal, by fitting discernment, to the contemplative life, hold fast to the active life alone. And when you fail in what you choose as great, be content with what you regard as small, so that, if you are compelled through the contemplative life to fall from knowledge of the truth, you may at least enter the kingdom of heaven one-eyed through the active life alone.”

[Note: [Col. 0167D] From book XXXII on Job, ch. VI.] The eye of God signifies his perfect knowledge, as the prophet says of him to the Israelites: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. 2:8). Clearly God does not have an eye by nature. But because we see by the eye, God is said to have an eye because he sees all things.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] From book XXXIII on Job, ch. XX.] Eyes signify wicked counsellors, as it is said of the ancient enemy in the Lord’s voice: “His eyes are like the eyelids of dawn” (Job 41:9). The eyes, joined to the head and serving the usefulness of sight, appropriately signify the counsellors of Antichrist. By their perverse schemes they foresee what and how things are to be done, and thus provide his evil agents with a path shown, as it were, to their feet. They are rightly compared to the eyelids of dawn. By dawn’s eyelids we understand the last hours of night, in which night seems to open its eyes as it already reveals the beginnings of the coming light. Therefore the shrewd persons of the world who adhere to the wicked counsels of Antichrist are like the eyelids of dawn, because they call the faith which they find in Christ a night of error, and promise that reverence for Antichrist is truth. For they promise to repel darkness and announce the light of truth by conspicuous signs, since they cannot persuade what they wish unless they profess themselves to be better. Thus, when the serpent himself spoke to the first human beings in Paradise, he opened, as it were, his eyelids by pretending to foresee something better, when he reproved human ignorance in innocent minds and promised the knowledge of divinity. For he seemed to repel the darkness of ignorance and announce the divine morning of eternal knowledge, saying: “Your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:5). So, when he comes in that man then condemned, his eyes are compared to dawn’s eyelids, because his wise men regard the simplicity of the true faith as the darkness of a night already past and display his lying signs as rays of the rising sun.

Eyes signify hope, as Jeremiah says: “Wild asses stood upon the rocks; they drew in the winds like dragons; their eyes failed because there was no grass” (Jer. 14:6). See above, under “wild ass,” book III, chapter 22.

[Note: [Col. 0168D] From book XXV on Job, ch. XVI.] Eyes signify wicked prelates, as the Psalmist says of wicked teachers, in the spirit of prophecy rather than with a wish to curse: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bow down their back always” (Ps. 68:24). The eyes are those set upon the face at the summit of honour who have undertaken the task of seeing ahead along the way. Those who adhere behind them are accordingly called backs. Thus, when the eyes are darkened, the back is bent, because when those who follow lose the light of knowledge, they are certainly bent down to bear the burdens of sins. He therefore says: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bow down their back always.” It is as though he said: “Let those who preside over the actions of human life, as though over paths to be foreseen, lack the light of truth, so that their subjects who follow, bent under the burdens of their iniquities, may lose every posture of uprightness.” We know without doubt that this occurred in Judaea when, at the very advent of our Redeemer, the crowd of Pharisees and priests shut their eyes to the true light, and the people, walking according to the examples of its leaders, wandered in the darkness of unbelief.

[Note: [Col. 0168D] From book XVI on Job, ch. X, §11.] Eyes signify the exaltation of pride, as Eliphaz says: “He who has been humbled will be in glory, and he who has lowered his eyes will be saved” (Job 22:29). This saying plainly does not differ from the utterance of Truth, who says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14). Thus Solomon also says: “Before a man’s heart is crushed, it is exalted; and before it is glorified, it is humbled” (Prov. 18). It is rightly said, “He who has lowered his eyes will be saved,” because, so far as can be detected through the service of bodily members, the first expression of pride is usually in the eyes. Hence it is written: “You shall humble the eyes of the proud” (Ps. 17:12). Hence it is said of the very head of the proud: “He sees every lofty thing” (Job 41:25). Hence it is written of the one who clung to him through unbelief: “There is a generation whose eyes are lofty and whose eyelids are raised on high” (Prov. 30:13). To lower one’s eyes, therefore, is to despise no one by looking upon them, but to judge oneself less than and unequal to all whom one sees. Thus the one who lowers the eyes will be saved, because the one who abandons the false summit of pride ascends to the height of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] From book XIII on Job, ch. XIII, §18.] Eyes signify those who have the light of truth in the holy Church, as the same holy Church laments in the voice of her chosen member, blessed Job: “My eye has grown dim because of indignation, and my limbs have been reduced almost to nothing” (Job 17:7). The eye grows dim because of indignation when even those who possess the light of truth in the Lord’s body—that is, in the Church—see themselves continually despised and scorned by the wicked, and are troubled in amazement at the hidden judgment: they cannot penetrate God’s secret purpose in allowing the perverse to prevail against the good. For who would not be astonished when the dancing of Herodias’s daughter obtains from a drunken king that the head of the Bridegroom’s friend—the prophet and more than a prophet—be brought before the faces of the banquet guests? But when these persons grow dim because of indignation, the weak often fall into weakness. Hence it follows: “And my limbs have been reduced almost to nothing.” By “limbs” the frailty of the weak is expressed. When they see the wicked flourish and the just tormented, they sometimes come to regret having begun good things and so proceed more quickly to do evil—as though the good they began had harmed their lives.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] Book I, ch. IX.] Eyes signify the workings of the Holy Spirit, as the prophet Zechariah says of our Redeemer under the figure of a stone: “Upon one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. 3:9). What is signified by eyes but the gifts of the Holy Spirit? See the chapter on the Pleiades.

## CHAPTER XI. ON EYELIDS

In Sacred Scripture, the term “eyelids” sometimes signifies the prelates of the Church, sometimes the shrewd people of this world, sometimes divine judgments.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] From book XIII on Job, ch. VII.] Eyelids signify prelates, as blessed Job says in the person of the Church: “My eyelids have grown dim” (Job 16:17). For those who keep watch in order to look ahead along the paths of the feet are rightly called eyelids. But when vigilant prelates understand the hidden judgments of God, the eyelids of the holy Church grow dim.

Eyelids signify shrewd people of the world who adhere to Antichrist’s perverse counsels, as the Lord says of the devil through blessed Job: “His eyes are like the eyelids of dawn” (Job 41:9). See the preceding chapter.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] From Book XXVIII on Job, chapter V.] By the name of eyelids the divine judgments are signified, as the Psalmist says of the Lord: “His eyelids examine the children of men” (Ps. 10:5). For the Creator is accustomed to examine us in three ways: either when He strikes us with the chastisement of the scourge and reveals how much patience we possess or lack; or when He commands certain things which we do not wish, and discloses to us our obedience or disobedience; or when He reveals some hidden things to us and conceals others, and makes known to us the measure of our humility.

He examines by the scourge when He assails with afflictions a mind that in prosperity had submitted itself well to Him. Thus blessed Job is praised by the Judge’s testimony, [Col. 0170C] and yet is laid low by the blows of the striker, so that his patience might shine forth all the more truly the more severely it had been tested. The Lord examines us by commanding difficult things, as Abraham is ordered to leave his own land and go where he did not know; to take his only son up a mountain; and to sacrifice the one whom he had received as a consolation in old age. To him, assuredly, answering the examination well—that is, obeying the command well—it is said: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22:12); or, as it is written: “The Lord your God tests you, that He may know whether you love Him” (Deut. 13:3). For God’s testing is His examining us by great commands; and His knowing is making us know our obedience.

Again, by opening certain things to us and closing others, He examines us, [Col. 0170D] as is shown by the Psalmist’s testimony quoted above: “His eyelids examine the children of men.” For when eyelids are open we see, and when they are closed we see nothing. What, then, are God’s eyelids but His judgments? They are closed to human beings in one respect and opened in another, so that those who do not know themselves may become known to themselves. Thus, while they grasp certain things by understanding but are altogether unable to know others, their hearts may secretly examine themselves: whether God’s closed judgments spur them on, [Col. 0171A] or His opened judgments puff them up.

Paul was tested by this examination. After receiving inward wisdom, after the barriers of paradise had been opened, after ascending to the third heaven, after the mysteries of heavenly speech, he says: “I do not reckon myself to have apprehended” (Phil. 3:13). And again: “I am the least, not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. 15:9). And again: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5). Thus, examined by God’s opened eyelids, Paul answered rightly: he attained the heavenly secrets, yet stood exaltedly in humility of heart.

Again, when he investigated God’s hidden judgments concerning the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, and could not arrive at them, [Col. 0171B] he was examined as though by God’s closed eyelids. Yet he gave an exceedingly right answer, knowingly bowing himself to God in his very ignorance, saying: “O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgments, and unsearchable His ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been His counsellor?” (Rom. 11:33). Behold: examined by mysteries concealed, as though by closed eyelids, he answered acceptably and rightly. Knocking at the entrance to the secret, since he could not gain admission to what lay within by knowledge, he stood humbly before the doors by confession; and what he could not comprehend within, he praised without in fear.

## CHAPTER XII. CONCERNING THE NOSE

[Col. 0171C] [Note: [Col. 0171D] Above, Book IV, chapter X.] By the name of the nose, discernment is signified, as the Lord says in praise of the Church: “Your nose is like the tower which is in Lebanon” (Song 7:4). See the chapter “Concerning Leaders.”

## CHAPTER XIII. CONCERNING THE NOSTRILS

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of nostrils are sometimes signified exhaling snares and the instigation of the ancient enemy; sometimes foreknowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0171D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter XXVII.] By the name of nostrils are understood the exhaling snares and instigation of the ancient enemy, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the devil: “Smoke proceeds from his nostrils” (Job 41:11). For the sharpness of the eyes is injured by smoke. Therefore smoke is said to proceed from his nostrils, because from the snares of his miracles a dark uncertainty is generated, for a time, even in the hearts of the elect. Smoke comes forth from Leviathan’s nostrils because, from his lying prodigies, the haze of alarm confounds even the eyes of good minds. For when terrible signs are seen, an obscure thought gathers itself in the hearts of the elect.

Hence Truth Himself says through the Gospel: “False Christs and false prophets shall arise, and shall give great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect might be led into error” (Matt. 24:24). In this matter we must earnestly ask how those who are elect can be led into error, or why “if it were possible” is added as though in doubt, when the Lord, knowing all things beforehand, awaits what must be done. But because the heart of the elect is shaken by trembling thought, while nevertheless their steadfastness is not moved, the Lord embraced both facts in one sentence, saying: “So that, if it were possible, even the elect might be led into error.” For to waver in thought is already, as it were, to err. But “if it were possible” is immediately added, because it certainly cannot happen that the elect should be wholly captured by error.

We are therefore compelled to consider, from the statement that smoke proceeds from his nostrils, [Col. 0172A] what he works daily in human hearts through the smoke of his pestilential exhalation, even before he appears openly. For, as we said above, smoke weakens the sharpness of the eyes; hence smoke is rightly said to proceed from the nostrils of him whose harmful inspirations produce perverse thought in human hearts, by which the mind’s sight is blunted lest it see the light. As though by the breath of his nostrils, he emits darkness: in the hearts of the reprobate, through the breathing of his snares, he accumulates from love of temporal life the heat of manifold thoughts. And he multiplies, as it were, balls of smoke when he heaps up in the minds of earthly people the utterly vain cares of this present life.

This smoke proceeding from his nostrils sometimes touches even the eyes of the elect for a time. The Prophet was suffering this smoke inwardly when he said: “My eye is troubled through anger” (Ps. 6:8). He was oppressed by its flood when he said: “My heart has been troubled within me, and the light of my eyes is not with me” (Ps. 37).

“With stakes He will pierce his nostrils” (Job 40:19).

[Note: [Col. 0172D] From the same book, chapter VIII.] What else do we understand by stakes—that is, sharpened poles, which are of course pointed in order to be driven in—but the keen counsels of the saints? These pierce the nostrils of this Behemoth when they both watchfully observe and victoriously transfix his most crafty snares. Through the nostrils, moreover, scent is drawn in; and by inhaling breath, something even at a distance is recognized. By Behemoth’s nostrils, then, are signified his crafty snares, through which he strives most shrewdly to discover the hidden good things of our heart and to destroy them by most wicked persuasion. [Col. 0172D] Therefore the Lord pierces the nostrils of the ancient enemy with stakes, because, penetrating his crafty snares with the keen perceptions of the saints, He renders them powerless.

[Note: [Col. 0172D] From Book III on Job, chapter XXI.] By the name of nostrils, too, foreknowledge is signified, as the prophet says: “Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, because he is accounted exalted” (Isa. 2:22). For we often perceive by smell things we have not seen, so that even when certain objects lie far away, the fragrance of their quality makes itself known to us; and, while we draw breath through the nostrils, we often foreknow things not seen. Thus the spirit of our Redeemer is said to be in His nostrils, whereby His knowledge [Col. 0173A] is designated as residing in foreknowledge, because whatever He made known that He knew in the nature of His humanity, He assuredly foreknew before the ages by His divinity.

The prophet immediately adds why He has breath in His nostrils, saying: “Because He is accounted exalted” (Isa. ibid.). As if he said: He foreknew from above the things to come below, because He came down to the lowest things from heaven. Holy men also, because they have believed what they heard from Him, themselves likewise now foreknow the things to come; and, as they faithfully serve His commands, they await His coming with certain hope.

## CHAPTER XIV. CONCERNING THE MOUTH

Sacred Scripture uses the name of mouth sometimes for the thought of the heart, sometimes for speech, sometimes for a holy preacher, sometimes for the Only-begotten Son of God, sometimes for the preachers of Antichrist, sometimes for the knowledge of teachers, and sometimes for the suggestions of the ancient enemy.

[Note: [Col. 0173D] From Book XV on Job, chapter V, near the end.] By the name of mouth, the thought of the heart is signified, as Zophar says concerning the hypocrite: “When evil is sweet in his mouth, he hides it under his tongue” (Job 20:12). Evil is sweet in the hypocrite’s mouth because iniquity is pleasant to him in his mind. For the mouth of the heart is thought, of which it is written: “With deceitful lips, in heart and heart they have spoken evil things” (Ps. 11:3). But this evil which is in the hypocrite’s mouth is hidden under his tongue, because the harshness of wickedness hidden in his mind is covered under the veil of pleasing speech. Evil would indeed be on the tongue, [Col. 0173C] and not under the tongue, if the hypocrite in speaking revealed the malice of his perversity.

But just as many of the righteous, when they see some acting perversely and requiring stern rebukes, assume harshness upon their tongue while covering the kindness of their mind beneath their tongue—whence it is said to the Bride of the holy Church in the voice of the Bridegroom: “Honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song 4:11)—so, refusing to disclose to the weak the sweetness of their mind, they strike them in speech with a certain harshness, but emit certain gentle and sweet things by which a saddened mind may be refreshed in them through kindness. So all perverse people have evil not on their tongue but under it: with their words they put sweetness on display, while in their thoughts they devise perversities.

Thus Joab took Amasa’s chin [Col. 0173D] in his right hand, but secretly putting his left hand to the sword, poured out his entrails. To take the chin with the right hand is, as it were, to flatter with kindness; but he puts his left hand to the sword who secretly strikes from malice. Hence it is written also concerning their very head: “Under his tongue are toil and sorrow” (Ps. 9, according to the Hebrew). He does not openly show the evil he thinks; he displays not on his tongue, but keeps beneath his tongue, the toil and sorrow of those whose death he seeks.

[Note: [Col. 0173D] From Book XXXII, chapter II.] By the name of mouth, speech is signified, as blessed Job says: “I will put my hand over my mouth” (Job 39:34). For in the usage of sacred speech, action is usually understood by hand and speech by mouth. To put one’s hand over one’s mouth, therefore, is to cover the faults of careless speech by the virtue of good work. For who can be found, however perfect, who does not nevertheless sin in idle speech? James bears witness when he says: “Do not become many teachers. For we all offend in many things” (Jas. 3:1–2); and again: “No human being can tame the tongue” (ibid., 8). Rebuking its faults, Truth Himself says: “I tell you that for every idle word which people have spoken, they will render an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12:36).

But holy people strive before the eyes of the Lord to cover the faults of the tongue by the merits of their life; they strive to weigh down excessive words by the weight of good works. Therefore, in the holy Church [Col. 0174B] the hand is placed over the mouth, when in her elect the fault of idle speech is daily covered by the virtue of good action, as it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31:1).

But again, since it is written, “All things are naked and open to His eyes” (Heb. 6), how can those things be covered which cannot at all be hidden from the eyes of Him to whom all things are naked? Yet what we cover we place beneath, and that by which we cover we place above, so that we cover what has been put underneath. We are said to cover sins, then, which we place, as it were, beneath us when we reject them. And we lay another thing over them when we subsequently choose the work of good action in order to set it above them. Thus whoever forsakes evil works and afterwards does good ones, [Col. 0174C] by what he adds covers past wickedness, laying the merits of good work over it.

[Note: [Col. 0174D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XX.] By the name of mouth, a holy preacher is signified, as the Lord says through the prophet: “If you separate the precious from the vile, you shall be as My mouth” (Jer. 17:19). It must be understood above all that each soul becomes so much more precious in God’s eyes as, for love of truth, it has become more despised in its own eyes. Hence Saul is told: “When you were little in your own eyes, did I not make you head over the tribes of Israel?” (1 Sam. 15:17). As if plainly saying: You were great to Me because you were despised in your own sight; you have become despised to Me. Hence the prophet says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent before yourselves” [Col. 0174D] (Isa. 5:21).

Accordingly, each person becomes the more vile to God the more precious to himself; and the more precious to God the more vile to himself for God’s sake, because “He regards the lowly and knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. 137:6). Therefore it is rightly said: “If you separate the precious from the vile, you shall be as My mouth.” For the present world is vile to God, while the human soul is precious to Him. Thus the person who separates the precious from the vile is called, as it were, the Lord’s mouth, because the Lord speaks His own words through him: speaking whatever he can, he tears the human soul away from love of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0174D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter X, §13.] By the name of mouth the Only-begotten Son of God is signified, as Elihu says: “He shall hear a hearing in the terror of His voice, and a sound from His mouth” (Job 37:2). It is customary in sacred discourse that, when it indicates that something is heard by hearing, it says that the hearing itself is heard, as Habakkuk says: “Lord, I have heard Your hearing, and I was afraid” (Hab. 3:2). Thus here also it is said: “He shall hear a hearing in the terror of His voice.”

By the mouth of God, the Only-begotten Son may be signified. Just as He is called God’s arm, because through Him He works all things—of whom John says, “And all things were made through Him” (John 1:3)—so He is also called His mouth. Hence the prophet says: “The mouth of the Lord has spoken these things” (Ps. 58:14). Through Him God speaks all things to us, as though the term mouth were plainly used for the Word. We too customarily use “tongue” for words, as when we speak of the Greek or Latin tongue, meaning words in the Greek or Latin language. [Col. 0175B] Therefore we rightly understand the Lord’s mouth to be the Son Himself. Thus the bride says to Him in the Song of Songs: “Let Him kiss me with the kiss of His mouth” (Song 1:1), as though saying: Let the sweetness of the presence of my Redeemer’s Only-begotten Son touch me.

By the sound of the mouth, however, the Holy Spirit of the same Lord God may be signified. Thus elsewhere, in signification of that same Spirit, it is written: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a mighty rushing spirit” (Acts 2:2). Therefore a sound proceeds from the Lord’s mouth when His consubstantial Spirit, coming to us through the Son, breaks through the deafness of our insensibility. Concerning this same uncircumscribed and incorporeal sound, the Lord’s mouth says: “He shall receive of Mine and shall declare it to you” (John 16:14).

Thus by the terror of the voice may be understood the force of strength, and [Col. 0175C] by the sound of the mouth the sweetness of consolation. For those whom the Holy Spirit fills, He first terrifies away from earthly action, and afterwards consoles with hope of heavenly things, so that they rejoice afterward with confidence concerning the former things precisely insofar as they previously feared when beholding punishments alone. Hence Paul says of the Spirit of the Only-begotten, as though of this sound of the mouth: “For you have not received the spirit of bondage again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry: Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15).

Hence Truth Himself says: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20:23). Behold, the terror of those converted is transformed into authority: as they punish their evils by repentance, they ascend even to the exercise of judgment, so that here they receive power in God over what they themselves formerly feared from God. For they become judges who have perfectly feared the heavenly judgment; and those who first feared lest their own sins should be retained now begin to forgive the sins of others.

[Note: [Col. 0175D] From Book XXIII on Job, chapter XXVI.] By the name of mouth, the preachers of Antichrist are signified, as the Lord says of him to blessed Job: “Lamps proceed from his mouth” (Job 41). Just as those who see are called eyes, so those who preach are called a mouth. But lamps come forth from this mouth because they kindle the minds of their hearers to love of perfidy. And by that whereby they seem to shine through wisdom, they undoubtedly burn them up through wickedness.

[Col. 0176A] By the name of mouth, the knowledge of teachers is signified, as it is said in the Apocalypse concerning Antichrist’s preachers, under the name of horses: “The power of the horses was in their mouths and in their tails” (Rev. 9:19). For the knowledge of teachers is represented in the mouth, but worldly power in the tail. By the tail, which is behind, is signified the temporal order of this world, which ought to be set behind us. Of this the Apostle Paul says: “Forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forth to those which are before” (Phil. 3:13). For everything that passes is behind; everything which comes and remains is before. Therefore in these horses—that is, in these most wicked preachers, running everywhere under carnal impulse—there is power in their mouth and tail, because they preach by urging perversities, but, supported by temporal powers, they exalt themselves through those things which are behind.

By the name of mouth, the suggestions of the ancient enemy are signified, as the Lord says of him to blessed Job: “Who shall enter into the midst of his mouth?” (Job 41:4). To enter into the midst of his mouth is to penetrate the words of his craftiness, so as to consider not what they sound like, but what they intend. For he seems to promise good, but draws toward a ruinous end. Adam chose to enter into the midst of his mouth when he neglected cautiously to weigh the intention of that persuasion. For he believed that through the enemy he would receive divinity, and lost the grace of immortality. And because he stood carelessly outside the meaning of the enemy’s words, he thereby wholly offered himself to that mouth to be devoured.

Since the ancient enemy attempts to corrupt the minds of the faithful [Col. 0176C] sometimes by his manifestation and sometimes by suggestion—for he acts now by deed, now by persuasion—it is rightly said: “Who shall enter into the midst of his mouth?” Understand: none but I, who examine the words of his suggestions through the discerning minds of the elect and make manifest that they are not as they sounded.

## CHAPTER XV. CONCERNING THE TONGUE

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of tongue are sometimes signified open speech, sometimes the doctrine of falsehood, and sometimes the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0176D] From Book VIII on Job, chapter II.] By the name of tongue, open speech is signified, as blessed Job says to his friends: “Judge what is just in speaking, and you shall not find iniquity in my tongue, nor shall folly sound in my throat” (Job 6). For one who speaks, while awaiting the author’s judgment upon his words, is, as it were, subjected to the judgment of the one who hears him. Therefore whoever fears being reproved in what he says must first examine what he says, so that a fair and strict judge may sit between heart and tongue, carefully weighing whether the heart offers right words, which, profitably receiving them, the tongue may bring before the judgment of its hearers.

Blessed Job, therefore, disputing against his friends but denouncing for us the heretics, detects the rashness of speakers and recalls their words to their mind, saying: “Judge what is just in speaking.” As if plainly saying: If you do not wish to be reproved in what goes forth from you in the outward act of speech, hold within yourselves the scales of justice, so that what is said outside may please by the weight of truth precisely insofar as the balance of discernment weighs it within.

“And you shall not find iniquity in my tongue, nor shall folly sound in my throat.” As if he said more plainly: If you weigh your own words more subtly, you will judge those of another more truly; and when what you say begins to be right, you will recognize that what you hear is just. For my tongue does not sound folly to you unless it proceeds from your own conscience.

The holy Church strives first to expose the false assertions of her enemies and then to disclose the teachings of truth, because, when they suppose themselves to hold what is right, they stubbornly attack the truths which they hear. Therefore heretics must first recognize their own error, lest they contradict the truth when it is heard. For if the ploughman does not uproot the thorns of the field by the cutting of the ploughshare, the earth does not bring received seed into a crop; and unless the physician expels the corruption by opening a wound, sound flesh can in no way grow together where the corruption is. Therefore, first destroying what is perverse, he says: “Judge what is just in speaking.” Then, introducing what is right, he adds: “And you shall not find iniquity in my tongue.”

Heretics commonly say some things openly and retain others in secret. By the tongue is signified open speech; by the throat, hidden deliberation. Thus neither iniquity in the tongue nor folly in the throat sounds forth from the holy Church, because what she preaches in public speech she also keeps in inward faith. She does not teach one thing openly, but teaches in speech what she thinks, preserves in life what she speaks, and whatever she preaches through the tongue flows from the banquet of heavenly wisdom; while through the throat she tastes it in the silence of expectation.

[Note: [Col. 0177D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter IX.] By the name of tongue, the doctrine of falsehood is signified, as the Lord says to blessed Job under the name of Leviathan: “And will you bind his tongue with a cord?” (Job 40:20). Sacred Scripture is accustomed to signify by a cord sometimes allotted portions of measured land, sometimes sins, and sometimes faith. Thus, concerning hereditary portions obtained by division, it says: “Lines have fallen to me in pleasant places, and a goodly inheritance is mine” (Ps. 15:6). For lines fall in pleasant places when, through humility of life, the allotments of a better homeland receive us.

Again, because sins are signified by a cord, the prophet says: “Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity” (Isa. 5:18). For iniquity is drawn with cords of vanity when it is extended by the increase of guilt. Hence the Psalmist also says: “The cords of sinners have encompassed me” (Ps. 118:61). Since a cord is twisted by adding strands so that it may grow, sin is not unfittingly represented by a cord: it is often multiplied in a perverse heart when defended.

Again, faith is expressed by a cord, as Solomon bears witness when he says: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Eccl. 4:12), because faith—woven from the mouth of preachers out of knowledge of the Trinity—remains strong in the elect but is dissolved in the heart of the reprobate alone. In this place, then, nothing prevents our understanding by “cord” either sin or faith.

For our incarnate Lord bound Leviathan’s tongue with a cord when He appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh and condemned all the teachings of his errors. Hence, as Paul testifies, it is said: “He condemned sin concerning sin” (Rom. 8:3). Therefore He bound his tongue with a cord, because by the likeness of sinful flesh He destroyed all the enemy’s plausible arguments from the hearts of His elect. Behold: when the Lord appeared in flesh, Leviathan’s tongue was bound, because, once His truth was known, those doctrines of falsehood fell silent. Every doctrine of error was now silenced, because the Lord constrained Leviathan’s tongue with the cord of His incarnation.

[Col. 0178B] [Note: [Col. 0177D] From Homily XXX on the Gospels.] By the name of tongue, the Holy Spirit is signified, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles that the same Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples in fiery tongues (Acts 2:3). The Spirit rightly appeared in fire, because from every heart that He fills He shakes off the sluggishness of cold and kindles it into desire for His eternity. He was displayed in fiery tongues because that same Spirit is coeternal with the Son, and tongue has a very close affinity with word. For the Son is the Word of the Father; and because the substance of the Spirit is one, that same Spirit ought to have been displayed in a tongue.

Or certainly, because word proceeds through the tongue, the Spirit appeared in tongues because whoever is touched by the Holy Spirit confesses God’s Word, that is, the Only-begotten Son. Nor can such a person deny God’s Word, because he now possesses the tongue of the Holy Spirit. Or, again, the Holy Spirit appeared in fiery tongues because He makes those whom He fills at once ardent and eloquent. Teachers possess fiery tongues because, while they preach that God must be loved, they set their hearers’ hearts ablaze. A teacher’s speech is idle if it cannot provide an incentive to love.

## CHAPTER XVI. CONCERNING THE TEETH

[Note: [Col. 0178D] From Book XIV on Job, chapters XXIII–XXIV.] By the name of teeth, the holy apostles are signified, as blessed Job says in the person of our Redeemer: “Only my lips were left about my teeth” (Job 19:20). For what is signified by lips but speech, and by teeth but the holy apostles? They are set in the body of the Church in order to bite the life of carnal people with rebuke and break it from the hardness of its obstinacy. Hence the first of the apostles, as a tooth set in His body, is told: “Slay and eat” (Acts 10).

But because at the time of Christ’s Passion these teeth lost, through fear of death, the confidence of strength and the confidence of every effective action—so much so that two of them, walking after His death toward the resurrection, spoke on the road and said: “We hoped that He was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21)—it is now rightly said: “Only my lips were left about my teeth.” They were still conversing about Him, but no longer believed in Him. Therefore only lips remained about His teeth: they had lost the power of good action and retained only words of conversation about Him. They lost the bite of rebuke and had the movement of speech. Thus lips alone were left about the teeth: they still knew how to converse, but already feared to preach Him or to bite the vices of unbelievers.

[Note: [Col. 0179D] From Book II on Job, chapters XV and XVIII.] By the name of teeth, holy preachers generally are signified, as it is said of them to the dispersed holy Church: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing” (Song 4:2). What indeed do we understand by the Church’s teeth but holy preachers, who crush the hardness of sinners by their preaching? They are fittingly compared with shorn and washed sheep because, taking on an innocent life in the washing of baptism, they have laid aside the old fleeces of their former manner of life.

[Note: [Col. 0179D] From the book, etc., above.] By the name of teeth, the inward faculties are signified, as blessed Job says: “Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth, and carry my soul in my hands?” (Job 13). Food is broken by the teeth so that it may be swallowed. Thus we rightly understand by teeth the inward faculties, which, as it were, chew and grind up each thing which they think, and send it on to the stomach of memory. The prophet Jeremiah complains of these, saying: “He has broken my teeth by number” (Lam. 3:16). Teeth are broken according to number because, in proportion to each person’s sin, blindness of understanding is produced in the faculties; and according as each has acted outwardly, so he is stupefied in that which he could have understood concerning inward and invisible things.

Thus it is rightly written: “Every man who eats a sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge” (Jer. 31:29). What is a sour grape but sin? For a sour grape is fruit before its time. Whoever desires to be satisfied with the pleasures of the present life hastens to eat before the time. Therefore the person who eats a sour grape has his teeth set on edge, because he who feeds upon delight in the present world has his inward faculties bound, so that they can no longer chew spiritual things—that is, understand them. For through that in which they delighted outwardly, they become stupefied inwardly. And while the soul feeds upon sin, it cannot eat the bread of righteousness, because teeth bound by the habit of sin cannot eat what is righteous and has savour within.

“Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth?” As if he plainly said: Why do I examine with inward faculties any carnal deeds that may have been done in me, if I cannot benefit those who observe me? He fittingly and truly adds: “And I carry my soul in my hands.” To carry the soul in one’s hands is to show the intention of one’s heart in action. For the righteous have this characteristic: in everything they say or do, they seek not only their own advancement [Col. 0180A] but also the edification of their neighbours. Sometimes they judge themselves in certain matters in order to recall sluggish hearers to consider themselves; sometimes they display good works so that their observers may be ashamed not to imitate what they see. For it is written: “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

Therefore whoever indicates his intention through works carries his soul in his hands. But when any righteous person benefits his neighbours neither by judging himself nor by displaying good works, he returns, by what he has done, to words of sorrow. Hence it is now rightly said: “Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth,” etc.—that is, why do I either judge myself strictly before people, or show in my works what I seek, if I do not benefit my neighbours either by judging evils or by showing goods? [Col. 0180B]

[Note: [Col. 0180D] From Book XIII on Job, chapter V, §6.] By the name of teeth, open persecutors of the good are signified, as blessed Job says: “He has gathered his fury against me; threatening me, he has gnashed against me with his teeth; my enemy has looked upon me with terrible eyes” (Job 16:10). What are all the wicked but members of the devil? Through them, therefore, he does whatever he puts into their hearts for them to do. The devil now has fury against the Church, but his fury is scattered, because he stirs up hidden temptations against individuals. But when he breaks out against her in open persecution, he gathers his fury upon her, because in afflicting her he constrains himself with his whole intention.

The devil’s members do not in this time of peace have gathered fury against the elect because they perceive that they can fulfil their wickedness less fully than they wish. But when they see that an opportunity for perversity is available to them, they strike all the more boldly because they mass together against the Church with unanimity. Thus it is rightly said: “He has gathered his fury against me.” And, to explain this fury more fully, it is said: “Threatening me, he has gnashed against me with his teeth.” Then follows: “My enemy has looked upon me with terrible eyes.”

For that ancient enemy has gnashed at the Church with his teeth and looks upon her with terrible eyes because through some persons he practises cruelties, and through others foresees what he is to practise. The teeth of this enemy are the persecutors and executioners of the good, who tear the Church’s members apart when they afflict her elect through their persecutions. The eyes of this enemy are those who devise evils to commit against the Church and inflame, by their counsels, the cruelties of her persecutors. [Col. 0180D] Thus her ancient adversary gnashes against her with his teeth when he pursues in her the life of the good through cruel reprobates. He looks upon her with terrible eyes because by the counsels of the wicked he never ceases to seek evils through which he may always afflict her more grievously.

[Note: [Col. 0180D] Book III, chapter XVIII.] By the name of teeth, perverse suggestions are signified, as Eliphaz, boasting like heretics, says: [Col. 0181A] “The roaring of the lion, the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of the lion’s cubs are broken” (Job 4:10). See the chapter “Concerning the Lioness.”

[Note: [Col. 0181D] From Book III on Job, chapter XXIII.] By “teeth” corrupt preachers are signified, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning Antichrist: “Terror is all around his teeth” (Job 41). For perverse preachers are teeth, because they break those whom they capture into error away from the firmness of truth. For just as we understand the teeth of holy Church to be those who, by their preaching, crush the hardness of sinners—whence it is said to her through Solomon: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep coming up from the washing” (Song 4:2)—so by the teeth of Antichrist are figured the teachers of error, who tear apart the life of the reprobate by biting, and, having drawn them away from the integrity of truth, slaughter them in the sacrifice of falsehood. Their preaching could indeed easily be despised by their hearers; but the terror of secular powers, joined to it, exalts it before human judgment. Thus it is rightly said: “Terror is all around his teeth”; that is, the perverse powers of this world protect the preachers of Antichrist. For while they seek to seduce people by speech, many powerful persons strive to terrify them by violence. Thus terror is around his teeth: as though it were plainly said, “Perverse preachers crush some by persuasion because others are about them who afflict the minds of the weak by frightening them.”

[Note: [Col. 0181D] From Book IX, chapter XV, 24.] By “teeth” the now open perpetration of sin is signified, as blessed Job says in the figure of the Church: “Formerly I broke the jaws of the wicked man, and from his teeth I took away the prey” (Job 29:17). For who can more truly be called wicked than the devil? We break his jaws whenever, reasoning against his snares, we expose his hidden contrivances; and thus we take prey from his teeth, because we call back to the salvation of life the mind which he had already bitten and broken toward sin. By his jaws, then, his hidden snares are shown; by his teeth, the now open perpetration of sin. Of these jaws and teeth the Psalmist writes: “God will break their teeth in their mouth; the Lord will shatter the jaws of the lions” (Ps. 57). But the holy man declares that he first breaks the jaws, so that afterward he may take prey from the teeth; for we truly take prey from his teeth when we first know how to break his jaws. It is necessary first to expose the hidden contrivances of his counsels, so that afterward we may be able to call our hearer’s soul back from open ruin.

## CHAPTER XVII. ON SALIVA

In Holy Scripture, “saliva” sometimes signifies the savour of contemplation, sometimes wisdom.

[Note: [Col. 0182D] From Book VIII on Job, chapter XVIII.] By “saliva” the savour of inward contemplation is signified, as blessed Job says: “How long will you not spare me, nor let me swallow my saliva?” (Job 7:19). Saliva flows from the head into the mouth, and from the mouth into the stomach when it is swallowed. What, then, is our head except the divinity from which we receive the beginning of our being, so that we are creatures? Paul bears witness, saying: “The head of man is Christ, but the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3). And what is our stomach except the mind, which, when it receives its heavenly food—that is, understanding—being refreshed, undoubtedly governs all the members of our actions? For unless sacred utterances expressed the mind by the name of the stomach, Solomon certainly would not have said: “The lamp of the Lord is the breath of man, which searches all the secrets of the stomach” (Prov. 20:27). For when the grace of the heavenly regard illuminates us, it reveals even to us all that is hidden in our mind.

What, therefore, is understood by “saliva” except the savour of inward contemplation? It flows to the mouth from the head because, while we are still placed in this life, scarcely the taste of revelation touches us from the brightness of the Creator. Thus the Redeemer, when he came, mixed saliva with mud and restored the eyes of the man born blind (John 9), because heavenly grace illumines our carnal thought by the admixture of its contemplation and restores the human being from original blindness to understanding. For, since nature has brought forth humanity in this exile, expelled from the joys of paradise, a human being has, as it were, come forth blind from birth.

But, as the holy man suggests, this saliva indeed flows to the mouth, yet it is not swallowed so as to reach the stomach; because contemplation of the divinity touches the understanding, but does not fully refresh the mind, since no one can perfectly behold what, hindered still by the darkness of corruption, he sees only fleetingly. For behold: the mind of the elect already subdues earthly desires; already it transcends all that it considers transient; already it is withdrawn from delight in outward things, and searches out invisible goods. And while doing this, it is often caught up into the sweetness of heavenly contemplation; it now sees something of the inner things as if through darkness, and with burning desire strives to participate in the spiritual mysteries of angels. It is fed by the taste of unbounded light, and, raised above itself, disdains to fall back upon itself. But because the corruptible body still weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9:15), it cannot long cling to the light which it sees fleetingly.
