The very weakness of the flesh draws back the soul that has transcended itself and brings it, though it sighs, back to thinking upon lowly and necessary things.

Therefore the saliva flowing from the head touches the mouth but does not at all reach the stomach, because our understanding is indeed moistened by the liquid of heavenly contemplation, but the mind is by no means fully satisfied. For taste is in the mouth, satisfaction in the stomach. We cannot therefore swallow the saliva, because we are not permitted to be satisfied with the sweetness of heavenly brightness, which we still taste only at the extremity. But because the very fact that we know something, however little, above ourselves is due to the mercy of the One who spares us, whereas our inability perfectly to perceive it still arises from the punishment of the ancient condemnation, it is rightly said: “How long will you not spare me, nor let me swallow my saliva?” As though it were plainly said: “Then you fully spare a human being when you admit that person to the perfection of your contemplation, so that, caught up inwardly, he may see your brightness, and the corruption of his flesh may not repel him outwardly. Then permit me to swallow my saliva, when you have filled me with the savour of your brightness unto the abundance of satisfaction, so that I may no longer hunger through want with the taste of my mouth, but, made firm in you, may abide with the stomach of my mind abundantly watered.”

[Note: [Col. 0183D] From Homily 10 on Ezekiel.] By “saliva” wisdom is signified, as we read in the Gospel: the Lord spat and touched the tongue of the mute man, and immediately the bond of his tongue was loosened and he spoke rightly (Mark 7:35). For what does it mean that, having spat, he touched his tongue, except that saliva for us is wisdom received from the mouth of the Redeemer in the divine utterance? Saliva flows from the head into the mouth. Therefore, when our tongue is touched by that wisdom which he himself is, it is immediately fashioned for the words of preaching.

## CHAPTER XVIII. ON JAWS

[Note: [Col. 0183D] From Book XIII on Job, chapter 6.] By “jaws” holy preachers are signified, as it is said through Jeremiah under the figure of Judaea: “She wept bitterly in the night, and her tears are upon her jaws” (Lam. 1:2). For in the adversity of the Church, those grieve more deeply who know how to crush the life of the carnal by preaching. Through them holy Church crushes the wicked away from their vices and, as though swallowing them, turns them into her own members. Hence those who are themselves, as it were, the jaws of the Church are told by the first shepherd: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13).

This is also why Samson took up the jawbone of an ass and slew his enemies (Judg. 15): our Redeemer, holding in the hand of his power the simplicity and patience of his preachers, put carnal persons to death as regards their vices. And afterward the jawbone poured forth waters upon the ground, because the bodies of preachers given over to death displayed great miracles to the peoples. Hence holy Church complains in the voice of her blessed member Job: “They struck my jaw; they were filled with my punishments” (Job 16). The perverse strike the jaw of the Church when they persecute good preachers; and because the reprobate then think that they have done some great thing when they kill the lives of preachers, it is fittingly added after the striking of the jaw: “They were filled with my punishments.” For the punishment that chiefly chastens the mind of the Church is what fills them.

## CHAPTER XIX. ON CHEEKS

[Note: [Col. 0184D] From Homily 16 on Ezekiel.] By “cheeks” spiritual Fathers are signified, as it is said to holy Church in the Song of Songs: “Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from your hidden things” (Song 6:6). The cheeks of holy Church are the spiritual Fathers who now shine within her by miracles and appear venerable, as it were, in her face. When we see many performing wonders, foretelling things to come, perfectly abandoning the world, and burning with heavenly desires, the cheeks of holy Church grow red like the rind of a pomegranate. But what is all that we admire in comparison with the matter of which it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. 64:4)? Therefore, when he marvelled at the cheeks of the Church, he fittingly added, “apart from your hidden things,” as though he plainly said: “Those things in you which are not hidden are indeed great; but those which lie hidden are utterly ineffable.”

## CHAPTER XX. ON THE FACE

[Col. 0184B]

In Holy Scripture, “face” sometimes signifies the mind; sometimes the mind’s attention; sometimes any prelate of the Church; sometimes knowledge of the devil; sometimes the presence of a thing; and sometimes the vengeance of divine judgment.

By “face” the mind is signified, as Sophar says: “If you remove from yourself the iniquity that is in your hand, and injustice does not remain in your tent, then you will be able to lift up your face without stain, and you will be steadfast and will not fear” (Job 11:14–15). Every sin is committed either by thought alone or by thought together with deed. Iniquity in the hand, therefore, is fault in action; injustice in the tent is iniquity in the mind. For our mind is not inappropriately called a tent, in which we are hidden to ourselves when we are not seen outwardly in action.

Sophar, therefore, because he is the friend of a righteous man, knows what he says; but because, under the guise of heretics, he rebukes a righteous man, he rightly fails to utter even what he knows. Yet, setting aside what he says arrogantly, let us consider how true his words are if they were rightly spoken. First he urges that iniquity be removed from the hand, and then that injustice be cut off from the tent, because whoever already cuts off outwardly his evil deeds must certainly return to himself and carefully examine himself in the attention of his mind, lest the fault which he no longer has in action should yet remain in thought.

Hence Solomon also rightly says: “Prepare your work outside, and diligently cultivate your field, so that afterward you may build your house” (Prov. 24:27). For what is it to cultivate the field diligently outside after the work has been prepared, except, having plucked up and rooted out the thorns of iniquity, to cultivate our action for the fruit of recompense? And what is it, after the cultivation of the field, to return to the building of the house, except that we often learn from good works how great a purity of life we ought to build in thought? For nearly all good works proceed from thought. Yet there are certain refinements of thought that are born from action. For as action proceeds from the soul, so in turn the mind is instructed by action.

The mind, taking the first beginnings of divine love, commands the good things that are done. But once the things commanded have begun to be done, exercised by its own actions, it learns, having begun to command good things, how much it had previously seen too little. Thus the field is cultivated outside so that the house may afterward be built, because we often learn from outward action what subtlety of uprightness we should maintain in the heart. Sophar rightly endeavoured to preserve this order when he said first that iniquity should be removed from the hands and afterward injustice from the tent; for the mind is by no means fully raised up in thought while it still errs outwardly in action.

If we completely cleanse away these two things, we immediately lift up our face to the Lord without stain. For then we lift up our face to the Lord without stain when we neither commit forbidden evils nor retain, through our own zeal, those evils committed against us by others. For our mind is weighed down by grievous confusion at the time of prayer if it is stained either by its own continuing action or accused by pain preserved from another’s malice. When anyone has cleansed away these two things, he immediately rises freely to what follows: “And you will be steadfast and will not fear.” For the more firmly the mind stands in good deeds, the less it trembles before the Judge. Whoever preserves steadfastness overcomes fear, because, while he studies more carefully to perform what the Creator commands, he also thinks securely of that which the Creator threatens terribly.

[Note: [Col. 0185D] From chapter 22 on Job.] By “face” the mind’s attention is signified, as blessed Job says of any wicked person: “Fatness has covered his face” (Job 15:27). Sight is in the face, which is also the foremost and more honourable part of the body. Thus the mind’s attention is not without reason signified by the face: wherever we turn it, there we see. Fatness therefore covers the face when the desired abundance of earthly things weighs down the eyes of the mind; and it defiles before God’s eyes that which ought to have been honourable in them, because it burdens it with manifold cares. For the powerful and wicked have this characteristic: occupied with deceptive riches, they neglect the true riches of God; and the less they seek what is true, the more they are exalted by false riches. For the manifold care of earthly things, because it occupies, blinds.

[Note: [Col. 0185D] From the end of chapter 6, Book XIII on Job.] By “face” any holy prelate of the Church is signified, as it is said through blessed Job in the person of the Church: “My face swelled from weeping” (Job 16:17). When holy Church draws her weak members back from sins and leads them to the remedy of repentance, she undoubtedly assists them with tears, so that they may grow strong to receive their Creator’s grace. And through the strong she laments what she herself did not do, yet what she, as it were, did in her weak members. Hence it is well now said: “My face swelled from weeping” [Note: [Col. 0185D] From chapter 1 above.]. For the face of holy Church consists of those who appear foremost, placed in positions of governance, so that the faithful people may have honour from their appearance even if something ugly lies hidden in the body. These prelates lament the faults of the weak among the people, and so afflict themselves for the falls of others as well as for their own.

[Note: [Col. 0186D] From Homily III on Ezekiel.] By “face” knowledge is signified, as it is said through Ezekiel of the four evangelists under the figure of the four living creatures: “Each had four faces and each had four wings” (Ezek. 1:6). For what is expressed by a face except knowledge, and what by wings except flight? Each person is known by the face; by a wing, however, the bodies of birds are lifted on high. Thus the face pertains to faith, the wing to contemplation. For by faith we are known by almighty God, as he himself says of his sheep: “I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and my sheep know me” (John 10:11). And again he says: “I know whom I have chosen” (John 13:18). By contemplation, however, we are lifted, as it were, above ourselves; as it were, raised into the air.

Therefore each has four faces, because if you ask what Matthew thinks concerning the Lord’s Incarnation, he thinks precisely what Mark, Luke, and John think. If you ask what John thinks, he thinks without doubt what Luke, Mark, and Matthew think. If you ask what Mark thinks, he thinks what Matthew, John, and Luke think. If you ask what Luke thinks, he thinks what John, Matthew, and Mark think. Each has four faces, because the knowledge of faith by which they are known by God is the same in one as it is in all four together. Whatever you find in one, you will recognize in all four alike. And each has four wings, because all together and harmoniously preach the Son of almighty God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and, lifting the eyes of their minds to his divinity, fly upon the wing of contemplation.

Thus the faces of the evangelists pertain to the Lord’s humanity, and the wing to his divinity, because in him whom they behold as bodily they fix their gaze, as it were, upon a face. But when they proclaim him, in his divinity, to be uncircumscribed and incorporeal, they are lifted into the air, as it were, upon the wing of contemplation. Therefore, since the faith of his Incarnation is one in them all and their contemplation of his divinity is alike in each, it is rightly said: “Each had four faces and each had four wings.”

[Note: [Col. 0186D] From Book XXIV on Job, chapter V.] By “face” the knowledge of God is understood, as Elihu says of the redeemed human being: “And he shall see his face with rejoicing” (Job 33:26). Above, he had said how God affects a person by making himself known; now it is said how, while making himself known, he brings joy. For one person is pierced in one way when, looking inwardly, he is frightened by dread of his evils; another is pierced in another way when, beholding heavenly joys, he is strengthened by a certain hope and confidence. The former compunction produces affliction and sadness; the latter moves joyful tears.

For *jubilum* is said to occur when the mind conceives an ineffable joy that can neither be hidden nor disclosed in words, yet manifests itself through certain movements, although it is expressed by no proper terms. Hence the prophet David, seeing that the souls of the elect conceive in their minds so great a joy as they cannot express, says: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. 7). He does not say, “that speaks,” but “that knows,” because jubilation may indeed be known by the understanding but cannot be expressed in speech. For through it that which is beyond sense is felt. And if the consciousness of the person feeling it scarcely suffices to contemplate it, how can the tongue of one speaking suffice to express it?

Therefore, since the light of truth, making itself present to our hearts, now makes them sorrowful by displaying strict justice, now makes them joyful by opening inner joys, it is fittingly added after the bitterness of temptations and the sorrows of tribulations: “He shall see his face with rejoicing.” For first the fire of tribulation is introduced into our mind through consideration of its blindness, so that all rust of vices may be burned away; and then, once the eyes of the heart have been cleansed, the joy of the heavenly homeland is opened, so that we may first cleanse by mourning what we have done, and afterward more clearly contemplate in joys what we seek. First, as intervening sorrow arises, the darkness of evils is wiped away from the mind’s vision; then it is illumined by the swiftly flashing radiance of the circumscribed light.

Therefore this vision, produced through contemplation, is called the face of God. For since we know anyone by the face, we not inappropriately call the knowledge of God his face. Hence Jacob, after wrestling with the angel, says: “I saw the Lord face to face” (Gen. 32:30), as though he said: “I knew the Lord, because he deigned to make me know him.” Paul testifies that this knowledge will be made most fully at the end, saying: “Then I shall know, even as I am known” (1 Cor. 13:12). Therefore, because after the contests of labours and the waves of temptations, the soul is often suspended in ecstasy so as to contemplate the knowledge of the divine presence—a presence which it can feel but cannot fully encompass—it is rightly said of this tempted person after so many labours: “You shall see his face with rejoicing.”

[Note: [Col. 0187D] From Book XXXIV on Job, chapter XXXII.] By “face” the knowledge of the devil is understood, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning him under the name Leviathan: “Want precedes his face” (Job 41:13). For by “face” knowledge is commonly signified; hence it is written: “My face shall go before you” (Exod. 33:14), that is, “My knowledge shall provide guidance.” It must be known, however, that want in sacred speech is understood differently of the elect and differently of the reprobate.

The want of the elect occurs when the true riches of the heavenly homeland return to their minds and, placed in the wretched exile of this present life, they remember that they are poor. They continually long for those riches, of which Paul says: “That you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints” (Eph. 1:18). And because they do not yet behold these riches diligently, they meanwhile groan in the affliction of this poverty. Jeremiah had undoubtedly seen this when he said: “I am the man who sees my poverty under the rod of his indignation” (Lam. 3:1). For the rod of God’s indignation is the stroke of strict judgment. A person suffered that indignation when, driven from paradise, he lost the true riches of inward joy. But because all the elect continually consider that they have fallen into the want of this present life from the abundance of innate power, it is rightly said: “I am the man who sees my poverty under the rod of his indignation.”

The reprobate now do not know how to consider this poverty, because while they pursue what they see, they neglect to think of the invisible things which they have lost. Hence their condition is properly called want, because while they are filled with vices, they are empty of the riches of virtues. It often happens that, lifted up by the madness of pride, they do not consider the losses of their ruin and do not recognize that they are destitute even of good deeds. Hence the Lord says to the angel preaching to Laodicea: “You say, ‘I am rich and have become wealthy and need nothing,’ and you do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked” (Rev. 3:17). The person who is puffed up by an arrogant claim to holiness declares himself rich, but is rebuked as poor, blind, and naked: poor, certainly, because he lacks the riches of virtues; blind, because he does not see the poverty he suffers; naked, because he has lost the first robe. But worse still, he does not know that he has lost it.

Therefore, since, as we have said, the want of the reprobate is deprivation of merits, it is rightly said of Leviathan: “Want precedes his face.” For no one is joined to his knowledge unless he has first been stripped of the riches of virtues. First the devil takes away good thoughts, and then pours into them a more open knowledge of his iniquity.

[Note: [Col. 0187D] From chapter XVII, Book XX on Job, 119.] By “face” the presence of a thing is signified, as blessed Job says in the person of the Church concerning the wicked: “They abhor me and flee far from me; they do not fear to spit in my face” (Job 30:10). For all wicked persons flee far from holy Church, not by the steps of their feet but by their manner of life. They become far away not in place but in merit, when, as their pride grows, they despise her with open reproach. To spit in her face is not merely to speak ill of the good in their absence, but to refute every righteous person even in his presence. When the perverse openly despise them with mockery, they emit in their insults loose words like flowing saliva.

[Note: [Col. 0188D] From chapter XX on Job, Book XI.] By “face” the vengeance of judgment is signified, as blessed Job says to the Lord: “Only do not do two things to me, and then I shall not hide from your face: remove your hand far from me, and let not your dread terrify me” (Job 13:20). For what should we understand by the face of God here except the exercise of judgment, in which he looks upon sins in order to punish them? From this no righteous person is hidden unless the two things he asks may be removed. Of these he adds: “Remove your hand far from me, and let not your dread terrify me.”

In these two things, what else does he seek through the voice of the prophet except the time of grace and redemption? For the Law held the people under the stroke of vengeance, so that whoever sinned under it was immediately punished with death. Nor did the people of Israel serve the Lord from love, but from fear. Yet righteousness can never be fulfilled through fear, for, according to John’s words, “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). Paul also consoles the adopted children, saying: “You have not received again the spirit of slavery unto fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as children, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:15).

Therefore, speaking for the human race, desiring to pass beyond the harshness of the legal stroke and longing to come from fear to love, he entreats almighty God to remove these two things far from him, saying: “Remove your hand far from me, and let not your dread terrify me”; that is, remove from me the harshness of punishment, take away the weight of fear, but by the shining grace of love infuse the spirit of confidence.

## CHAPTER XXI. ON THE BEARD

In Holy Scripture, “beard” sometimes signifies the beauty of virtue and sometimes confidence in one’s own virtue.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] From chapter XX, Book II on Job, 28.] By “beard” the beauty of virtue is signified. Hence it is said to the prophet Ezekiel: “You, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword used for shaving hair; take it and draw it over your head and beard” (Ezek. 5:1). In this action of the prophet is expressed the judgment of the Redeemer, who, appearing in the flesh, shaved the head because he removed the sacraments of his commandments from the Jewish priesthood; he shaved the beard because, abandoning the Israelite kingdom, he cut off its beauty of virtue.

By “beard” confidence in one’s own virtue is signified, as Jeremiah, while he endeavoured to recount deeds performed outwardly, indicated what is done inwardly within ourselves, saying: “Eighty men came from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria, with shaved beards, torn garments, and in mourning; they had offerings and incense in their hands to offer in the house of the Lord. But Ishmael son of Nethaniah came out from Malpha to meet them, going along and weeping. When he had met them, he said to them: ‘Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.’ And when they had come into the midst of the city, he killed them” (Jer. 41:5 ff.).

For a person shaves his beard when he withdraws from himself confidence in his own powers. They tear their garments who do not spare themselves in the rending of outward adornment. Those come to offer incense and gifts in the house of the Lord who promise to offer themselves in sacrifice through prayer together with works. Yet if they do not know how carefully to watch themselves on this very path of holy devotion, Ishmael son of Nethaniah comes out to meet them. For any malignant spirit, brought forth in the error of pride after the example of his predecessor, namely Satan, places himself before them as a snare of deception.

It is aptly said of him: “He went along and wept,” because, in order to prevail by striking down devout minds, he hides himself, as it were, beneath a veil of virtue. And while he pretends to agree with those who truly mourn, secretly admitted into the inner parts of the heart, he kills what lies hidden within as virtue. He often promises to advance them to higher things. Hence he is said to have declared: “Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.” While he promises greater things, he takes away even lesser things. Therefore it is rightly said: “When they had come into the midst of the city, he killed them.” He killed in the midst of the city the men coming to offer gifts to God, because minds devoted to divine works, unless they guard themselves with great watchfulness, lose life on the very journey while, through the enemy’s stealth, they carry the offering of devotion.

## CHAPTER XXII. ON THE NECK

In Holy Scripture, “neck” sometimes signifies sacred utterance and sometimes the display of pride.

[Note: [Col. 0190D] From Homily 15 on Ezekiel.] By “neck” sacred utterance is signified, as the Bridegroom says to the bride: “Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements. A thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the mighty” (Song 4:4). In the neck is the throat, and in the throat is the voice. What, then, is signified by the neck of holy Church except sacred utterances? When a thousand shields are said to hang upon it, the whole number is expressed through this perfect number, because all our defence is contained in sacred utterance. There are God’s commandments; there are the examples of the righteous.

Therefore, upon the neck of the Church—that is, in the preaching of sacred utterance, which on account of its defence and loftiness is said to resemble David’s tower—a thousand shields hang, because as many commandments as there are there, so many defences are there for our breast. If we wish to fight against spiritual wickednesses, let us seek the armour of the Protector in the neck of the Church—that is, in the divine utterance—so that the strength of assistance against vices may be drawn from discerning the commandment. Behold, we hasten to become strong against the powers of the air; in this tower we find the armour of our mind, so that from it we may receive the commandments of the Creator and the examples of those who went before, by which we may be armed invincibly against our adversaries. For whenever you desire to undertake any virtue and see that it has already been fulfilled there by the Fathers, you find there your armour, by which you are fortified against spiritual wars. Shields hang from it: whoever wishes to fight, let him take one, fortify his breast by that virtue, and send forth the darts of words.

And it should be noted that it is said to have been built with battlements. Battlements do what shields do, for both defend the combatant. Yet there is a difference between them: we move shields, for our own defence, as we wish; but we can be defended by a battlement and cannot move it. A shield is held in the hand; a battlement is not held. What, then, is the difference between battlements and shields, except that in sacred utterance we read both the miracles of the Fathers who went before and hear of the virtues of good works? There we learn that one person could divide the sea, another stop the sun, another raise the dead, another raise a paralytic by a word, another heal the sick by his word, another by his sentence oppose the fevers of the infirm.

Yet all of these were gentle in the long-suffering of patience, fervent in zeal for uprightness, rich in the preaching of the word, and generous in mercy. Their miracles testify how true the things they said concerning God were, because they would not have done such things through him unless they spoke truly concerning God. Their works testify how devout, humble, and gracious they were. If, therefore, we are tempted concerning the faith which we have conceived from their preaching, let us behold the miracles of those who spoke, and we shall be strengthened in the faith received from them. What, then, are their miracles except our battlements? For we can be defended by them, and yet we do not hold them in the hand of our own choice, since we cannot perform such things.

But the shield is in the hand and defends, because the virtue of patience and the virtue of mercy, grace going before us, are both in the power of choice and protect from the danger of adversity. Therefore our tower is built with battlements, upon which a thousand shields hang, because through the miracles of the Fathers we are sheltered by sacred Scripture from the dart of adversity, and we also hold in the hand of good works the defences of holy conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] From chapter II, Book XXXIV on Job.] By “neck” the display of pride is signified, as the Lord says concerning the devil under the name Leviathan: “Strength shall dwell in his neck” (Job 41:13). For what is signified by the neck of this Leviathan except the display of pride, by which, raising himself against the Lord with a pretence of holiness, he is also puffed up by the swelling of sin? That pride is expressed by the neck is attested by the prophet Isaiah, who rebukes the daughters of Jerusalem, saying: “They walked with outstretched neck” (Isa. 3:18). Therefore strength is said to dwell in the neck of this Leviathan because power joined to his pride also supports it.

## CHAPTER XXIII. ON THE SHOULDER

[Col. 0191D]

[Note: [Col. 0191D] From chapter XVI, book XXI on Job.] By “shoulder” is signified the union of life in society. Hence blessed Job, recounting the loftiness of his life, immediately pronounces upon himself a sentence of curse if he has failed to fulfill any of the deeds he has mentioned, saying: “Let my shoulder fall from its joint, and let my arm be crushed with its bones” (Job 31:22). It is plainly evident that the arm is joined to the body through the shoulder. Therefore, as good action is signified by the arm, so the union of social life is signified by the shoulder. Hence the prophet also, seeing the holy peoples of the universal Church serving God in harmony, says: “And they shall serve him with one shoulder” (Zeph. 3:9).

In that blessed Job says, “If I lifted up my hand against the orphan, when I saw myself superior in the gate” (Job 31:21), he declares that he preserved a wonderful virtue of patience: he did not allow himself to be provoked by persons of the lowest rank, nor did he depart from what could justly have been his due. Yet, should he have done this, he adds: “Let my shoulder fall from its joint,” because whoever scorns to preserve patience quickly abandons social life through impatience. For the shoulder falls from its joint when a mind unable to endure some adversity abandons brotherly concord. “And let my arm be crushed with its bones,” because all our activity, however connected it may appear to be with various virtues, is undone unless patience is preserved through the bond of charity. For he who refuses to endure others’ evils will lose his own goods. Anyone wounded by the heat of an angry spirit recoils from love; and when he does not endure outward affliction, he darkens himself inwardly by losing the light of charity. He no longer sees where to direct the foot of good work, because he has lost the eye of love. But the holy man’s shoulder does not fall from its joint, because his love does not withdraw through impatience from the concord of social life; nor is his arm broken, because all his activity is guarded in the joining of the shoulder—that is, in the bond of charity.

By “shoulder” is signified action, as the prophet reproachfully says to the reprobate mind under the figure of Babylon: “Uncover your shame; lay bare your shoulder; reveal your legs; cross the rivers” (Isa. 47:2). See book 7, chapter 5, near the end.

253 CHAPTER XXIV. ON THE ARM.

In Sacred Scripture, by “arm” are signified at one time the only-begotten Son of God, at another the Antichrist, and at another action.

By “arm” is signified the only-begotten Son of God, as the Lord says to blessed Job: “Do you have an arm like God, and do you thunder with a voice like his?” (Job 40:4). Since God wisely draws into himself likenesses that are very unlike, we must observe that such expressions are sometimes used of God because of the effect of his working, and sometimes to judge his substance. For when eyes, wings, and shoulders are named in God, a certain effect of operation is indicated. But when hand, arm, right hand, or voice is said of God, the Son consubstantial with him is shown by these terms. For he himself is both hand and right hand. Of his Ascension the Father speaks through Moses, saying: “I will lift up my hand to heaven, and will swear by my right hand” (Deut. 32). [Note: [Col. 0192D] But none of the extant versions has it exactly thus.] He is the arm, of whom the prophet says: “And the arm of the Lord—to whom has it been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1). He is the voice, because in begetting him the Father uttered him: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). And of him it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). David declares that the Father made all things through this Word, saying: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 148:5). Therefore, for God to have an arm is to beget the Son who works; to thunder with a voice is to reveal to the world in a fearful manner the Son consubstantial with himself. Thus, when the Lord says to blessed Job, “Do you have an arm like God, and do you thunder with a voice like his?”, by a wonderful dispensation of mercy he exalts him even while reproving him, because the one whom he surpasses by comparison with himself he shows to be superior to all others.

254 By “arm” is signified the Antichrist, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning his destruction: “And the lofty arm shall be broken” (Job 38:15). For what else is understood by the lofty arm but the proud exaltation of Antichrist, raised over the reprobate minds of men by the arrogance of worldly glory, so that he, a sinful man, yet scorning to be considered a man, falsely claims to be God above humanity? Hence the Apostle Paul says: “So that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. 2:4). To display his swelling pride more fully, he first added: “Who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God or is worshipped” (ibid.). For a human being may sometimes be called “god,” as it is said to Moses: “See, I have made you a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1). But a mere human being cannot be worshipped as God. Since Antichrist exalts himself both above all holy human beings and above the very power of the Godhead, he attempts, by claiming for himself the name of glory, to surpass even that which is worshipped as God. But this pride of his will be struck down by the coming of the strict Judge, as it is written: “Whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thess. 2:8). Therefore it is rightly said: “And the lofty arm shall be broken.”

By “arm” is signified action, as blessed Job says, after enumerating his virtues: “Let my shoulder fall from its joint, and let my arm be crushed with its bones” (Job 31:22). And again it is said through him of the wicked man: “Let it devour the beauty of his skin, and let the firstborn of death consume his arms” (Job 18:13). The beauty of the skin is temporal glory, which, when desired outwardly, is retained like an appearance in the skin. By “arms,” moreover, actions are fittingly signified, because bodily work is done by the arms. But what is death except sin, which kills the soul from its inward life? Hence it is written: “Blessed and holy is he who has a part in the first resurrection” (Rev. 20:6). For that person will rise happily afterward in the flesh who, while placed in this life, has risen from the death of his mind. Therefore, if sin is death, pride may fittingly be understood as its firstborn, because it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10:15). 255 Thus the firstborn of death devours both the beauty of his skin and his arms, because pride supplants the glory and activity of the wicked.

CHAPTER XXV. ON THE CUBIT.

[Col. 0194A]

By “cubit” is signified action, as Ezekiel the prophet says (Ezek. 40), testifying that, for the measurement of the city hidden on the mountain, he saw in the hand of a man a reed of six cubits and a handbreadth. [Note: [Col. 0193D] From book XXX on Job, chapter XII.] For the Church of the elect is situated upon a mountain, because it is not founded in low desires. What, then, is signified by the cubit except action? And what by the number six except the perfection of action? For it is recalled that on the sixth day the Lord completed all his works. But what does the handbreadth beyond the six cubits indicate except the power of contemplation, which already reveals the beginnings of eternal and seventh rest? Since contemplation of eternal things is not completed here, the measure of the seventh cubit is not filled out. Therefore, because the Church of the elect accomplishes in six cubits all that must be done, it is shown as a city set upon a mountain. But because here it still beholds only the beginnings of contemplation, it touches no more than a handbreadth of the seventh cubit.

CHAPTER XXVI. ON THE HANDS.

In Sacred Scripture, by “hand” are understood at one time the only-begotten Son of God, at another the active life, at another power, at another action, at another strength, and at another the severe rigor of the Law.

By “hand” is signified the only-begotten Son of God, as the Father speaks through Moses concerning his Ascension: “I will lift up my hand to heaven, and will swear by my right hand.” [Note: [Col. 0193D] For the reason for this signification, see chapter XXV above, [Col. 0194D], on Deuteronomy 32.]

[Note: [Col. 0194D] From Homily 3 on Ezekiel, far after the beginning.] By “hand” is signified the active life, as it is said through Ezekiel of the holy living creatures: “And the hands of a man were under their wings, in their four parts” (Ezek. 1). In this place the four parts of the world may be understood: namely, east, west, south, and north, because the preaching of the saints has gone forth, with God as its author, into every part of the world. We may also understand by the four parts the four principal virtues from which the remaining virtues arise: prudence, courage, justice, and temperance. We truly possess these virtues when we preserve their order. Prudence is first, courage second, justice third, and temperance fourth. For what benefit can prudence bring if courage is lacking? To know what one cannot do is more a punishment than a virtue. But if someone wisely understands what he should do and courageously does what he understands, he is undoubtedly just; yet temperance must follow his justice, because justice, if it has no measure, often falls into cruelty. Therefore justice is truly justice when it moderates itself with the bridle of temperance, so that one who burns with zeal may also be temperate, lest by burning too fiercely he lose the justice whose moderation he does not know how to preserve.

There are, moreover, two lives of holy preachers: the active and the contemplative. The active life is earlier in time than the contemplative, because one advances to contemplation through good work. But the contemplative life is greater in merit than the active, because the latter labors in the exercise of present work, while the former already tastes inwardly the rest to come. What, then, is signified by hands except the active life, and by wings except the contemplative life? Thus the hand of a man is beneath their wings: that is, the virtue of action is beneath the flight of contemplation. These two lives are well represented in the Gospel by those two women, Martha and Mary. Martha was busied with much serving, while Mary sat at the Lord’s feet and heard his words (Luke 10). One, then, was intent upon action, the other upon contemplation: one served the active life by outward ministry, the other the contemplative through the elevation of her heart toward the Word. And although the active life is good, the contemplative is nevertheless better, because the former comes more fully to development with mortal life. Hence it is said: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (ibid., v. 42). Therefore, because the active life is greater in merit than the contemplative, it is rightly said: “The hands of a man were beneath their wings” (Ezek. 1:8). For although by the active life we do something good, yet through the contemplative life we fly toward heavenly desire.

Hence also, in Moses, active service is called servitude and contemplation liberty (Exod. 21). Although both lives are gifts of grace, so long as we live among our neighbors, one is necessary for us, while the other is voluntary. For who, after knowing the Lord, enters his kingdom unless he first performs the word well? Those who do not neglect the good works they can perform may enter the heavenly homeland without the contemplative life. But they cannot enter without the active life if they neglect to do the good that they are able to do. Therefore the one is necessary, the other voluntary; the one is servitude, the other liberty. Of this liberty Paul says: “For creation itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:21). For true liberty will then be ours when our adoption attains the glory of the children of God.

[Note: [Col. 0195D] From chapter III, book XI on Job.] By “hand” is signified power, as it is said through blessed Job of the Lord: “In whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and the spirit of all human flesh” (Job 12:10). Power is expressed by hand; the life of the body itself is signified by the soul of every living thing; and the effect of spiritual intelligence is expressed by the spirit of all human flesh. Therefore the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh are in the power of him from whom they have their being, so that he who granted being to what had not existed may provide for how it exists.

[Note: [Col. 0195D] From book XXXII on Job, chapter II.] By “hand” is signified action, as blessed Job says: “I will put my hand over my mouth” (Job 39:34). In the usage of sacred speech, action is commonly understood by hand, speech by mouth. To put one’s hand over one’s mouth, therefore, is to cover the faults of careless speech by the virtue of good work. Blessed Job, then, bearing the type of holy Church and speaking his own words in an allegorical sense, sets forth ours: let him say from himself, let him say from us, “I will put my hand over my mouth”—that is, what I perceive has displeased the strict Judge in me because of my speech, I hide before his eyes beneath the covering of right action.

Hence the same Job says again: “If I have washed myself as it were with waters of snow, and my hands have shone as though most clean, yet you will plunge me into filth” (Job 9:30). [Note: [Col. 0196D] From book IX on Job, chapter XIX, §28.] The waters of snow are the tears of humility. This humility, indeed, because before the eyes of the strict Judge it excels other virtues, shines as if with the brightness of great merit. But what else is signified by hands except works? Hence it is said through the prophet to some: “Your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1:15), that is, of the work of cruelty. It should be noted that the holy man does not say, “My hands shone most clean,” but “as though most clean,” because so long as we are bound by the penalty of corruption, however earnestly we labor in right works, we never attain true cleanness but merely imitate it. Hence it is fittingly added: “Yet you will plunge me into filth.” God is said to plunge us into filth when he shows us to be plunged in filth, because the more truly we rise toward him through good works, the more subtly we recognize the stains of our life, by which we differ from his purity. Thus he says: “If I have washed myself as it were with waters of snow,” and so forth. As if he said more plainly: Although I am steeped in the tears of heavenly compunction, although I exert myself in the pursuit of right action, yet in your purity I see that I am not clean.

[Note: [Col. 0196D] From chapter XI, book XVI on Job, §12.] By “hand” is signified strength, as blessed Job says: “Even now my speech is in bitterness, and the hand of my wound is made heavier upon my groaning” (Job 23:2). In his manner blessed Job begins with plainer words, but completes what he says through a profound unfolding of mystery. The sorrow of the afflicted man ought to have been healed by the consolation of his friends; but because their consolation broke out into the blandishments of falsehood, his grief grew more dreadful. For because Eliphaz did not fear to promise better things to one who was restored, the wound increased as though from harmful medicine. Thus it is rightly said: “Even now my speech is in bitterness, and the hand of my wound is made heavier upon me,” because the intention of disordered consolation multiplied the blow which it ought to have lessened.

In these words, under the type of holy Church, is also expressed the grief of the faithful, who groan all the more when they see evil people speaking flatteringly, people who, in Paul’s words, “by smooth words and blessings deceive the hearts of the innocent” (Rom. 16:18). These words are also properly applied to a closer consideration of the mind of the faithful, who do not know how to be without bitterness, even if they appear to prosper in this world. When adversity comes upon them, it doubles the grief which it finds. Therefore “even now” is rightly said, so that it may be plainly shown that the mind of the elect is not without bitterness even in prosperity.

It is well said: “And the hand of my wound is made heavier upon my groaning.” The hand of the wound is the strength of the blow. For the elect first consider their own blow: that they are separated from the vision of their Creator; that they do not at all enjoy the brightness of inward illumination, but groan as exiles in the present life, as though banished to a place of blindness. Therefore they always have their groaning in this hand of the wound. But when adversities also occur in this life, the hand of their wound is made heavier even upon their groaning. There was groaning for the wound even when the adversities of present life were absent; but the bitterness of the first blow increases through the trial of adversity. Thus let him say: “And the hand of my wound is made heavier upon my groaning.” For adversity has struck every righteous person in this life not joyfully, but by multiplying in him the pain of the wound.

[Note: [Col. 0197D] (297–298) From Homily 34 on the Gospels.] By “hands” is signified the severe rigor of the Law, as it is written in the Law itself: “Moses’ hands were heavy. Therefore they took a stone and put it beneath him, on which he sat. But Aaron and Hur supported his hands” (Exod. 17:12). Moses sat upon the stone when the Law rested in the Church. But this same Law had heavy hands, because it did not bear sinners mercifully but struck them with severe rigor. Yet the mercy of the Redeemer tempered for us the rigor of the Law. For in it is written: “If anyone does this or that, let him surely die. If anyone does this or that, let him be stoned.” [Note: [Col. 0197D] Gregory speaks generally of the rigor of the ancient Law, set out in detail in Exodus 21 and elsewhere.] But our Creator appeared in the flesh and promised not punishment but life to the confession of sins. Therefore he bent the hardness of the Law toward mercy, because those whom it justly condemns he himself mercifully frees.

Hence it is well written: “Aaron and Hur supported the hands of Moses.” Aaron means “mountain of strength,” while Hur is interpreted “fire.” Whom, then, does this mountain of strength signify except our Redeemer, of whom it is said through the prophet: “In the last days, the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared upon the summit of the mountains”? Or who is figured by fire except the Holy Spirit, of whom the same Redeemer says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49)? Aaron and Hur, therefore, support the heavy hands of Moses and, by supporting them, make them lighter, because the mediator between God and men, coming with the fire of the Holy Spirit, showed us as more bearable through spiritual understanding the heavy commandments of the Law, which could not be borne while they were understood carnally. For he made the hands of Moses light, as it were, because he redirected the weight of the commandments of the Law toward the virtue of confession.

CHAPTER XXVII. ON THE RIGHT HAND.

[Col. 0198A]

In Sacred Scripture, by “right hand” are signified at one time eternal life, at another the elect, and at another that which is held in high esteem.

[Note: [Col. 0198D] From Homily 21 on the Gospels.] By “right hand” is signified eternal life, as in the Gospel: “And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting at the right, clothed in a white robe, and they were astonished” (Mark 16:5). For what is signified by the left hand except present life, and by the right hand except eternal life? Hence it is written: “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2). Therefore, since our Redeemer had already passed beyond the corruption of the present life, the angel who had come to announce his everlasting life rightly sat on the right.

[Note: [Col. 0198D] From Homily XXIV on the Gospels, after the beginning.] By “right hand” are signified the elect, as the Lord commands in the Gospel: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find” (John 21:6). We read twice in the Holy Gospel that the Lord commanded nets to be cast for fishing: once before his Passion and once after his Resurrection. But before our Redeemer suffered and rose again, he commanded the net to be cast for fishing, yet did not command whether it should be cast on the right or on the left. But after the Resurrection, appearing to the disciples, he commanded the net to be cast on the right. In that fishing so many fish were caught that the nets were broken; in this one, many were caught and the nets were not broken.

Who does not know that the good are figured by the right hand and the evil by the left? Therefore that fishing, in which it was not specifically commanded on which side the net should be cast, represented the present Church, because it gathers good and evil together. It does not choose those whom it draws, because it does not know whom it is able to choose. But the fishing performed after the Lord’s Resurrection was cast solely to the right, because only the Church of the elect attains the vision of the glory of his brightness, and it will possess nothing of the work of the left. In that fishing the net is broken by the multitude of fish, because now so many reprobate persons enter into the confession of faith together with the elect that they even tear the Church itself apart by heresies. But in this fishing many and great fish are caught, and the net is not broken, because the holy Church of the elect, resting in the peace of its Author, is no longer torn by any dissensions.

[Note: [Col. 0198D] From chapter XVIII, book XX on Job, §20.] By “right hand” is signified that which is held in high esteem. Zechariah aptly indicates this when he says: “And he showed me Jesus the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him” (Zech. 3:1). To show more plainly what he had just said, he adds: “And the Lord said to Satan: May the Lord rebuke you, Satan; may the Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you. Is not this a brand snatched from the fire? And Jesus was clothed in filthy garments” (Zech. 3).

Jesus is said to have been clothed in filthy garments because, although free from all sin, he nevertheless came in the likeness of sinful flesh. Satan stood at the right hand of him who was coming. For by ordinary speech we are said to hold at the right what we regard as important, and at the left what we despise. The Lord seemed to hold the Jewish people as important and the Gentiles as nothing. But after he appeared incarnate, the Gentile world, which had been regarded as left-handed, believed; while the Jewish people turned toward unbelief. Therefore Satan stood at his right hand, because he seized from him the people that had formerly been beloved.

But because this Jewish people, now lost, will at some time believe at the end, as the prophet testifies: “The remnant shall be saved [or: shall return]” (Isa. 10:21), the Lord removed Satan from his right hand, saying: “May the Lord rebuke you, Satan.” Indicating the deliverance of the same people, he added: “The Lord who chose Jerusalem.” Since this people was, under the guidance of unbelief, descending toward the fires of Gehenna, but when brought back to faith is delivered from that same fire of eternal burning, it is immediately added there concerning it: “Is not this a brand snatched from the fire?” (Zech. 3:2).

Again, because by “right hand” is understood that which is held in high esteem, this is plainly demonstrated in the book of Judges, when those who went out to battle with Gideon held trumpets in their right hands and jars in their left (Judg. 7:20). [Note: [Col. 0199D] From chapter XVII, book XXX on Job, §33.] In this battle the patient victory and victorious patience of the holy martyrs are signified. For our leader brought with him into the battle of preaching such men as would overthrow their enemies by dying, despising the safety of their bodies, and would overcome their swords not with weapons and swords but with patience. Our martyrs came armed under their leader for battle—but with trumpets, jars, and lamps. The trumpets signify the cry of preaching, the lamps the brightness of miracles, and the jars the frailty of bodies. They sounded the trumpets while preaching; they broke the jars when they gave up their bodies, which were to be dissolved in their Passion, to hostile swords; and they shone with lamps when, after their bodies had been dissolved, they gleamed with miracles.

It should be observed that they held trumpets in their right hands and jars in their left. For we are said to hold at the right whatever we regard as important, and at the left what we count as nothing. It is fittingly written, therefore, that they held trumpets in the right hand and jars in the left, because Christ’s martyrs count the grace of preaching as great and the usefulness of their bodies as very small. Whoever values the usefulness of the body more highly than the grace of preaching holds the trumpet in the left hand and the jar in the right.

CHAPTER XXVIII. ON THE LEFT HAND.

[Note: [Col. 0199D] From Part III of the Pastoral Rule, chapter 27.] By “left hand” are signified the reprobate, as holy Church is told through Isaiah: “You shall spread out to the right and to the left, and your offspring shall inherit the nations” (Isa. 54:3). [Note: [Col. 0199D] From chapter VIII, book XXVIII on Job, §11.] In so great a multitude of nations the Church extends to the right when it receives some who are to be justified. It also spreads to the left when it admits into itself some who will remain in wickedness.

[Note: [Col. 0200D] From Part III of the Pastoral Rule, chapter 27.] By “left hand” is signified the prosperity of the present life, as the Church says in the voice of the elect in the Song of Songs: “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2:6). For what is signified by the left hand except present prosperity, and by the right except blessedness? Thus God’s left hand—that is, the prosperity of the present life—she places, as it were, beneath her head, pressing it down by the intention of her highest love. But God’s right hand embraces her, because she is wholly held in devotion beneath his eternal blessedness.

264 CHAPTER XXIX. ON THE LEFT.

By “left” is signified the glory of the present life, as Truth says in the Gospel: “When you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matt. 6:3), that is, let the glory of the present life not mingle at all with merciful service, but let the desire for applause be ignorant of the work of righteousness.

CHAPTER XXX. ON THE FINGERS.

In Sacred Scripture, by “finger” are understood at one time the Holy Spirit, at another the gifts of the same Holy Spirit, and at another discernment.

[Note: [Col. 0200D] From Homily X on Ezekiel, before the middle.] By “finger” is signified the Holy Spirit, as the Lord says in the Gospel after casting out a demon: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, then surely the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Luke 11:20). On the same matter another Evangelist records him as saying: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matt. 12:28). From these two passages it is inferred that the finger of God is called the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0200D] From the Homily above on the Gospels.] By “fingers” are signified the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as the evangelist Mark confirms when recounting the Lord’s miracle: “They bring to him one who was deaf and mute, and they begged him to lay his hand upon him” (Mark 7:32). He indicates the order of the healing when he adds: “He put his fingers into his ears, and, spitting, touched his tongue; and looking up to heaven, he groaned and said to him: ‘Ephphatha,’ that is, ‘Be opened.’ And immediately his ears were opened, the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke rightly” (ibid., vv. 33–35).

Why is it that God, the Creator of all, when he wished to heal one deaf and mute, put his fingers in his ears and, spitting, touched his tongue? What is signified by the Redeemer’s fingers except the gifts of the Holy Spirit? To put fingers into the ear, therefore, is to open through the gifts of the Holy Spirit the mind of the deaf person to obedience. And why did he touch the tongue after spitting? What is signified by saliva except wisdom? The saliva received by us from the Redeemer’s mouth is wisdom in divine speech. For saliva flows from the head into the mouth. Thus when our tongue is touched by that wisdom which he himself is, it is immediately formed for the word of preaching.

He looked up to heaven and groaned, not because groaning was necessary for him who granted what was requested, but because he taught us to groan to him who presides over heaven, so that our ears may be opened through the gift of the Spirit and our tongue loosed for words of preaching through the saliva of his mouth—that is, through knowledge of divine speech. He immediately says to him, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened”; and at once his ears were opened and the bond of his tongue was loosed. Here it must be observed that “Be opened” was said on account of the closed ears. But once the ears of the heart have been opened to obedience, the bond of its tongue is undoubtedly also loosed as a consequence, so that it may speak to others both of the good things it has itself done and of the things they ought to do. Hence it is appropriately added: “And he spoke rightly.” For that person speaks rightly who has first done in obedience what he urges others to do in speech.

[Note: [Col. 0201D] From chapter XXII, book XV on Job, §17.] By “finger” is signified discernment, as blessed Job says to his friends when they rebuke him: “Attend to me, and be astonished; put your finger over your mouth” (Job 21:5). Consider what I have done, and marvel at this blow which I suffer. “And put your finger over your mouth.” It is as though he said plainly: Knowing the good things that I have done and considering the evils that I suffer, restrain yourselves too from the fault of speech, and fear your own losses in my afflictions. Or certainly, because we distinguish things by our fingers, discernment is fittingly signified by the finger. Hence the Psalmist says: “Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war” (Ps. 143:1), signifying action by hands and discernment by fingers. Therefore the finger is placed over the mouth when the tongue is restrained through discernment, lest it fall through what it says into the fault of folly. Thus he says: “Put your finger over your mouth”—that is, add the virtue of discernment to your speech, so that in the true things you say against the hypocrite, you may see to whom they ought to be said.

CHAPTER XXXI. ON THE BACK.

[Col. 0201D]

[Note: [Col. 0201D] From the Pastoral Rule, Part I, chapter 1, and chapter 16, book XXV on Job, §23.] By “back” are signified subjects, as the Psalmist says of corrupt teachers, in the manner of one predicting rather than wishing them evil: “Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and bend their back always” (Ps. 68:24). For the eyes are those who, set in the very face of highest honor, have undertaken the office of foreseeing the way. Those who follow them in attachment are called backs. Therefore, when the eyes are darkened, the back is bent, because when leaders lose the light of knowledge, those who follow are surely bent beneath the burden of their sins. Thus he says: “Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and bend their back always.” It is as though he said: Let those who preside over the actions of human life, as over paths that must be foreseen, lack the light of truth, so that their subjects who follow, bent beneath the burdens of their iniquities, may lose every upright posture. We know that this undoubtedly occurred in Judaea when, at the very coming of our Redeemer, the crowd of Pharisees and priests closed their eyes against the true light, and the people, following the examples of their leaders, wandered in the darkness of unbelief.

267 CHAPTER XXXII. ON THE SKIN.

In Sacred Scripture, by “skin” are understood at one time Sacred Scripture; at another any foolish persons or evil subjects; or specifically those women who, cleaving to the Lord, were occupied in outward ministries; at another motions of the flesh; and at another the gross minds of human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0202D] From Homily 9 on Ezekiel.] By “skin” is signified Sacred Scripture, as the Psalmist says: “Stretching out heaven like a skin, who covers its upper parts with waters” (Ps. 103:2). For what is signified by heaven except Sacred Scripture, from which the sun of wisdom, the moon of knowledge, and from the ancient fathers the stars of examples and virtues shine upon us? It is stretched out like a skin because, formed in the language of flesh through its writers, it is unfolded before our eyes through the words of teachers in exposition. But what is signified by waters except the most holy choirs of angels? Of them it is written: “And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148:4).

The Lord covers the upper parts of this heaven with waters because the heights of sacred speech—that is, what it tells us about the nature of the Godhead or eternal joys—are as yet known secretly only to the angels. Thus heaven is stretched out before us, yet its upper parts are covered with waters, because some things in sacred speech are already open to us through the revelation of the Spirit, while others, which can be manifest only to angels, are still reserved from us. Yet of these hidden things we already perceive a part through spiritual understanding; we have already received the pledge of the Holy Spirit. Although we do not yet know them fully, we love them from the depths of our being, and in many spiritual senses that we have already known, we are fed with the nourishment of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0202D] From chapter XVII, book XXXIII on Job, §22.] By “skin” is meant any fool or evil subordinate, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the conversion of unbelievers: “Will you fill nets with his skin, or fish-traps with his head?” (Job 40:26). For what is signified by nets or fish-traps except the churches of the faithful, which make up the one Catholic Church? Hence it is written in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind” (Matt. 13:47). The kingdom of heaven [Col. 0203A], that is, is called the Church: when the Lord raises its manner of life to things above, it already reigns in the Lord through its heavenly way of life.

It is rightly compared with a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind, because, sent into this age of the Gentiles, it rejects none, but catches evil persons with good, proud with humble, angry with gentle, and foolish with wise. In the skin of this Leviathan we understand the fools of his body, but in the head the prudent. Or certainly, by the skin, which is outward, are signified subordinates who serve these lowest concerns, while by the head are signified those set over others. And, preserving the proper order, the Lord well declares that He will first fill these nets or fish-traps—that is, His Church and the aspirations of the faithful—with its skin, and afterwards with its head, [Col. 0203B] because He first chose the weak in order afterwards to confound the strong. For He chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise. He first gathered the unlearned, and afterwards philosophers. He taught not through orators, but through fishermen; yet by marvellous power He subdued orators through fishermen. Let Him therefore say: “Will you fill nets with his skin, or fish-traps with his head?” Understand: as I do, who within the Church of the faithful first gather, as it were, the devil’s skin—the lowest and weakest—and afterwards subdue his head, that is, my intelligent adversaries.

[Note: [Col. 0203D] From chapter XXIII, book XIV on Job.] By “skin” are signified those holy women who, cleaving to the Lord, served the needs of His body through outward ministries, as blessed Job says in the person of the Lord: “My bone has clung to my skin [Col. 0203C], my flesh being consumed” (Job 19:20). For strength is signified by bone, but the weakness of the body by flesh. Since Christ and the Church are one person, what is figured by the bone except the Lord Himself? And what by the flesh except the disciples, who at the time of His Passion entertained weak thoughts concerning Him? But by the skin, which remains outwardly upon the body beyond the flesh, what is figured except those holy women who served the Lord in outward ministries, preparing what was needed for the body?

For while His disciples, although not yet firm, preached the faith of truth to the peoples, the flesh clung to His bone. And while the holy women prepared outward necessities, they remained outward in the body, as skin. [Col. 0203D] But when the hour of the Cross arrived, severe fear arising from the persecution of the Jews seized His disciples; each fled, but the women remained. Thus, with the flesh as it were consumed, the Lord’s bone clung to His skin, because at the time of His Passion His strength found women beside Him when the disciples fled.

Peter indeed stood for a while, but afterwards, terrified, denied Him. John also stood—the one to whom, at the very time of the Cross, it was said: “Behold your mother” (John 19:27)—but he could by no means persevere, because it is written also of him: “A certain young man followed Him, clothed with a linen cloth over his naked body; and they seized him. But he left the linen cloth and fled from them naked” [Col. 0204A] (Mark 14:51–52). Although afterwards he returned at the hour of the Cross in order to hear the words of his Redeemer, he first fled in terror. The women, however, are remembered not merely as having neither feared nor fled, but also as having remained even to the tomb. Let Him therefore say: “My bone has clung to my skin, my flesh being consumed.” That is: those who ought to have clung more closely to my strength were consumed by fear at the time of my Passion; but those whom I assigned to outward ministries, I found faithfully clinging to me in my Passion without fear.

[Note: [Col. 0203D] From chapter XXIX, book X on Job, about the middle, §37.] By “skin” are signified the movements of the flesh, as blessed Job says: “You clothed me with skin and flesh; you bound me together with bones and sinews” (Job 10:11). The inward person is indeed clothed with skin and flesh, [Col. 0204B] because, in that by which he is raised to things above, he is besieged by the assault of carnal movements. Yet the Creator by no means abandons in temptation one who strives after righteousness, because by the infusion of grace He anticipates even the sinner. He both exposes the uplifted mind to battles without and strengthens it within. Hence it is well said: “You bound me together with bones and sinews.” We are clothed with flesh and skin, but bound together with bones and sinews, because, though shaken by temptation attacking from without, we are nevertheless strengthened within by the hand of our Creator, lest we be broken. Therefore, by movements of the flesh He humbles us for gifts, but through the bones of virtues He strengthens us against temptations. Thus he says: “You clothed me with skin and flesh; you bound me together with bones and sinews.” As if to say openly: You leave me exposed outwardly for testing, but nevertheless preserve me inwardly, lest I perish, by securing me with virtues.

[Note: [Col. 0204D] From chapter XVI, book XXVI on Job, §22.] By “skins” are signified the coarse minds of men, as God commands Moses: that he should spread haircloth coverings and skins to protect the tabernacle (Exod. 25:9). Since the authority of governance cannot be exercised without the diligent attention of temporal care, almighty God, by a wonderful dispensation of mercy, sometimes lays the burden of governance upon hard and laborious hearts, so that tender spiritual minds may be separated from earthly care. The more willingly the former labour in earthly anxieties, the more safely the latter may lie concealed from this world.

For, in carrying out their assumed burden, even for the benefit of those subject to them, the paths of worldly servitude are hard. And often, as has been said, almighty God carefully hides from outward actions those whom He tenderly loves. For a householder commonly directs servants to work from which he excuses his delicate children, so that his children may be untroubled and seemly; consequently the servants are soiled in the dust. How rightly this is done by divine ordering in the Church is signified by the very construction of the tabernacle. God commands Moses to weave veils of fine linen, scarlet, and hyacinth-blue for covering the Holy of Holies within; and He commands coverings of haircloth and skins to be spread for protecting the tabernacle. These, of course, endure rain, winds, and [Col. 0205A] dust.

What, then, do we understand by the skins and haircloth with which the tabernacle is covered, except the coarse minds of men, who in the Church are sometimes preferred by the hidden judgment of God although they are hard? Since they do not fear to serve temporal cares, they ought to bear the winds of temptations and the rains arising from this world’s adversities. But what is signified by hyacinth-blue, scarlet, and fine linen except the tender yet bright life of the saints? While this life is cautiously hidden in the tabernacle beneath haircloths and skins, its unspoiled beauty is preserved.

Thus, in order that the fine linen may shine in the tabernacle’s interior, the scarlet gleam, and the hyacinth-blue sparkle with its azure colour, the skins and haircloths above endure rain, winds, and dust. Therefore those who advance in great virtues within the bosom of holy Church [Col. 0205B] ought not to despise the life of their prelates when they see them occupied with outward affairs. For their own secure penetration into inward things is made possible by the assistance of those who labour outwardly against the storms of this age. What loveliness of its whiteness would fine linen retain if rain touched it? Or what brightness and clarity would scarlet or hyacinth-blue display if the dust it had undertaken to bear defiled it? Let the haircloth fabric be above, outwardly exposed to dust; let the hyacinth-blue colour be within, suited to adornment. Let those who devote themselves exclusively to spiritual matters adorn the Church; let those whom bodily labour does not burden cover the Church. Therefore, one who already shines spiritually within holy Church must by no means murmur against his ruler who acts in outward affairs. If you shine securely within like scarlet, why do you accuse the haircloth by which you are protected?

## CHAPTER XXXIII. ON SKIN

In Sacred Scripture, “skin” sometimes means the softness of weakness, sometimes sin of the flesh, and sometimes one who serves outward care.

[Note: [Col. 0205D] Book I, chapter XVIII.] By “skin” is signified the softness of weakness, as Jeremiah says: “Her Nazarites were whiter than snow, brighter than milk, redder than ancient ivory, more beautiful than sapphire. Their face has become blacker than coals, and they are not recognized in the streets. Their skin has clung to their bones; it has dried up and become like wood” (Lam. 4:7–8). Seek the exposition of this passage in the chapter “On Snow.”

[Col. 0205D] [Note: [Col. 0205D] From chapter XVII, book XXXII on Job, §23, near the end.] But often, when an abundance of virtues prospers even beyond what is fitting, the mind is led into a certain confidence in itself; deceived by its own presumption, it is suddenly darkened when sin steals upon it. Hence it is rightly added: “Their face has become blacker than coals.” Those who, having lost God’s righteousness, presume upon themselves and fall into sins which they do not even understand become black after being white. And because, after the fire of love, they come to the coldness of the flesh, they are preferred by comparison with extinguished coals. Sometimes, abandoning the fear of God through self-confidence, they become colder than those whose minds are cold. [Col. 0206A] Concerning them it is rightly added: “They are not recognized in the streets.” For *platea*, “street,” is so called in Greek from its breadth.

What is narrower for the human soul than to break its own wills? Of this breaking Truth says: “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matt. 7:13). And what is broader than to resist none of one’s own wills and, wherever the impulse of one’s choice leads, to spread oneself without restraint? Those, therefore, who through confidence in their holiness follow themselves, setting aside the judgment of better persons, as it were walk through streets. But they are not recognized in the streets, because they had shown something different in their life when, by breaking their own wills, they kept themselves in the narrow path.

And it is well added: “Their skin has clung to their bones.” What is expressed by bone except the hardness of strength, and what by skin except the softness of weakness? Their skin, then, is said to cling to their bones because those who think perversely regard the weakness of vice as the hardness of virtue. What they do is weak, yet, deceived by confidence born of pride, they associate it with strong judgments. And the more highly they think of themselves, the more they disdain correction for their wickedness. Hence it is rightly added: “It dried up and became like wood.” Their fault is rendered more insensitive in proportion as it is considered praiseworthy by them. It is rightly called dry, because it grows green through no reflection upon itself.

[Note: [Col. 0206D] From chapter VI, book XIII on Job.] By “skin” is signified sin of the flesh, as blessed Job says in the person of the penitent: “I sewed sackcloth upon my skin, and covered [Col. 0206C] my flesh with ashes” (Job 16:16). What are sackcloth and ashes except repentance? And what should be understood by skin and flesh except sin of the flesh? Therefore, when some return to repentance after a fall of the flesh, sackcloth is as though sewn upon the skin and flesh covered with ashes, because the guilt of the flesh is covered through repentance, lest it appear for punishment in the examination of the strict Judge.

[Note: [Col. 0206D] From chapter VI, book VIII on Job, §11.] By “skin” is signified one who, in the body of holy Church, serves outward care, as blessed Job says: “My skin dried up and contracted” (Job 7:5). In the body of holy Church, those who serve only outward concerns are fittingly called skin. This skin indeed contracts as it dries, [Col. 0206D] because the minds of carnal people, while they love present things and desire what lies, as it were, close at hand, refuse to stretch toward the future through long-suffering. While they neglect the richness of inward hope, by which they might be drawn out, they dry up. For unless despair dried out their hearts, the heat of faint-heartedness would never draw them together.

The Psalmist had feared this contraction when, dreading dryness of mind, he said: “May my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. 62:6). For the fat of richness fills the soul when the infusion of heavenly hope refreshes it against the heat of present desires. Therefore the skin contracts as it dries when a heart given over to outward matters and dried up through despair is not stretched toward love of its Creator, but folds back upon itself, so to speak, in wrinkled thought. [Col. 0207A] Yet it should be considered that carnal minds love present things because they do not reflect at all how fleeting the life of the flesh is. For if they saw the speed of its passage, they would not love it even when it prospered.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. ON FLESH

In Sacred Scripture, when “flesh” is used in the singular, it sometimes means human nature; sometimes the sensitivity of the heart; sometimes carnal life; sometimes carnal pleasure; sometimes carnality; sometimes the weakness of an action; and it is sometimes used with reference to nature, sometimes with reference to fault. But when “fleshes” is used in the plural, it sometimes means the reprobate; sometimes the disciples of the Lord; sometimes punishments or vices of the flesh; and sometimes movements of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0207D] From chapter III, book XXIV.] By “flesh” is signified human nature, as Elihu says: “His flesh is consumed by punishments; let him return to the days of his youth” (Job 33:25). In that first man, when he departed from the Lord, we were driven from the joys of paradise and fell into the misery of this mortal life; and we experience as the punishment of our retribution the grievous sin which we committed at the serpent’s persuasion. Having fallen here, we found nothing outside the Lord except that by which we might be afflicted. And because through the sight of our eyes we followed flesh, we are scourged by the flesh itself, which we preferred to God’s commandments. In it we suffer daily groaning, in it torment, in it destruction, so that, by a marvellous ordering, the Lord might turn into punishment for us that by which we committed sin. The sentence of punishment would thus arise from no source other than that from which had arisen the cause of sin: that man might be trained for life by the bitterness of that flesh through whose delight of pride he came to death.

Since, therefore, the human race was oppressed by innumerable punishments of carnal life, but, upon the coming of our Redeemer, both the vices of our corruption and its torments were destroyed, let it be said of this redeemed person: “His flesh is consumed by punishments; let him return to the days of his youth.” As though saying: Let one cast down by the punishment of mortality into a kind of old age of decay return to the days of his youth; that is, let him be renewed in the integrity of his former life, so that he may not remain as he fell, but, redeemed, may return to that for which he was created to receive.

[Note: [Col. 0207D] From chapter X, book X on Job, §15.] By “flesh” is signified the sensitivity of the heart, as the Lord says through the Prophet to some persons: “I will take away the heart of stone from your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 36:26). The Lord takes away the stony heart when He removes from us the hardness of pride; and He gives a heart of flesh when He immediately changes that same hardness of ours into sensitivity.
