[Note: [Col. 0207D] From chapter VI, book VIII on Job, after the middle.] By “flesh” is signified carnal life, as blessed Job says: “My flesh is clothed with rottenness [Col. 0208A] and the filth of dust” (Job 7:5). Man voluntarily abandoned his innate soundness and plunged himself into the abyss of corruption. Therefore he now either slips through unclean deeds or is defiled by unlawful thoughts. To put it thus: our nature itself, submitted as punishment to its guilt, has become contrary to nature and, if relaxed, is drawn as far as perverse deeds; but if restrained, it is darkened by the persistent thought of perverse deeds. Thus, by the completion of an unlawful deed, rottenness infects the flesh; but through the fickleness of evil thought, dust as it were rises before the eyes. By consenting to vices, we are worn away by rottenness; by enduring in the heart images of vices, we are defiled with the filth of dust. Therefore he says: “My flesh is clothed with rottenness and the filth of dust.” As if openly to say: [Col. 0208B] The carnal life which I endure is polluted either by the decay of slippery action or oppressed, from the recollection of vices, by the miserable darkness of thought.

[Note: [Col. 0208D] From the end of chapter XVII, book XXIII on Job, §27.] By “flesh” is signified carnal pleasure, as Elihu says of the person under trial: “His flesh will waste away, and the bones that had been covered will be laid bare” (Job 33:21). By the ordering of a hidden dispensation we are permitted to be tried in such a way that those who advance in virtue by divine gift may also remember what we are through our own weakness. And while, from receiving the gift, we perform works of virtue, from remembrance of our weakness we may offer the sacrifice of humility.

Sometimes, after growth in strength, not only do vices tempt, but scourges also chastise. When we are tempted by vices, a merciful dispensation deals with us, lest we be exalted because of the virtues in which we advance. But when we are worn down by scourges, the rebukes of evils warn us lest we be deceived by the world’s flattery. While vices tempt us, they humble the virtues advancing within us; while scourges try us, they uproot from the heart the world’s pleasures as they arise. Through tempting vices we learn what we are in ourselves; through striking scourges we learn what in this world we should flee. By the former we are restrained lest we be inwardly exalted; by the latter we are checked lest we desire anything outwardly.

Therefore, while we are in this life, we must both be worn down by scourges and sometimes be tempted by vices. Whether amid the labours of scourges or in the struggle with vices, we learn not only our own weakness, [Col. 0208D] but also how greatly we have advanced in virtue. [Note: [Col. 0208D] From chapter XVIII.] For no one knows his strength in peace. If wars are absent, proofs of virtues do not appear. The soldier who boasts of being strong in peace is unwise. Since, therefore, the merits of strength are often disclosed through the adversities of scourges, Elihu aptly declares: “His flesh will waste away, and the bones that had been covered will be laid bare.” When every outward pleasure is worn away under the pressure of scourges, the bones of inward strength are uncovered.

What is meant here by “flesh” except carnal pleasure itself? Or what by bones except the virtues of the soul? [Col. 0209A] Therefore flesh wastes away and bones are laid bare, because, while carnal pleasure is diminished by rebuking scourges, the strong things of virtues, formerly hidden as it were beneath flesh, are revealed. No one knows how far he has advanced except amid adversities. For when prosperity is present, the evidence of one’s strength cannot be seen.

[Note: [Col. 0209D] From chapter XI, book XXXIV on Job, §26.] By “flesh” is signified carnality, as Elihu again says: “If he directs his heart to the Lord, He draws to Himself his spirit and breath. All flesh will fail together, and man will return to dust” (Job 34:15). The heart is crooked when it desires low things; it is made straight when raised to things above. If, therefore, a person directs his heart to the Lord, the Lord draws that person’s spirit and breath to Himself. By “spirit” he means inward thoughts; by “breath,” which is drawn through the body, outward actions. Thus, for God to draw a person’s spirit and breath to Himself is to change, into a desire for conversion, both our inward and our outward life: so that nothing outward may now delight the mind, nor may the flesh seek anything below—or, if it does seek it, strive to obtain it—but so that all that a person is may burn inwardly in desire for Him from whom that person is, and restrain itself outwardly by self-discipline.

Hence it is aptly added: “All flesh will fail together, and man will return to ashes.” [Note: [Col. 0209D] From chapter XII.] Flesh fails together when it no longer serves any of its own impulses, because the ruling spirit restrains all its instability and, by a certain sword of its strictness, kills everything that lived wrongly in it. Jeremiah had slain himself with this sword of discipline when he said: “After you converted me, I repented; and after you showed me, I struck my thigh” (Jer. 31:19). What is understood by the thigh except pleasure of the flesh? And what does he mean in saying, “After you showed me, I struck my thigh,” except that, after he spiritually saw the things above, he extinguished everything in himself that was living carnally below, so that the more the highest things were disclosed, the less the low things which had held him might be released? For the more anyone begins to live above, the more that person begins to die below.

According to the inclination of carnal action, all Paul’s flesh had likewise died when he said: “Yet I live—no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). Elihu also rightly added here: “And man will return to ashes.” [Col. 0209D] For everyone remaining in sin forgets his mortality and does not remember that he is earth while he is still swollen with pride. But after the grace of conversion, when touched by the spirit of humility, what else does one remember oneself to be but ashes? David had already returned to ashes when he said: “Remember [variant: he remembered], O Lord, that we are dust” (Ps. 102:14). Abraham had returned to ashes when he said: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am ashes and dust” (Gen. 18:27).

[Note: [Col. 0209D] From chapter XXII, book XV on Job, §18.] By “flesh” is signified weakness of action, [Col. 0210A] as blessed Job says: “And when I remember, I am terrified, and trembling shakes my flesh” (Job 21:6). That blessed Job had not forgotten his deeds is shown by his final speech. Hence it is clear that what he now says to his friends—“And when I remember, I am terrified, and trembling shakes my flesh”—is said ironically. As though he were openly saying: If I remember that I have possessed anything characteristic of a hypocrite, I immediately tremble in tears of repentance. And he declares that, if he remembers, his flesh is shaken with trembling—that is, that weakness of action is wearied by fear of retribution.

[Note: [Col. 0210D] From book XIV on Job, chapter XXIX, §31.] “Flesh” is used with reference to nature, as it is written: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh [Col. 0210B] of my flesh” (Gen. 2:23). But it is used with reference to fault where it is written: “My Spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3). The Psalmist also says: “He remembered that they were flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. 77:39). Hence the disciple Paul said: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Rom. 8:9). They were certainly not without flesh, those to whom he sent his Epistles. But because they had overcome the passions of carnal desires, they were no longer in the flesh, being free through the power of the Spirit.

Therefore, when the same Paul says, “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15:50), he undoubtedly intends “flesh” according to fault, not according to nature. He immediately shows that he speaks of flesh according to fault, adding: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption” (ibid.). Thus, in the glory of the heavenly kingdom, flesh will exist according to nature, but it will not exist according to the desires of passions; for, with death’s sting overcome, it will reign in eternal incorruption.

[Note: [Col. 0210D] From chapter IV, book XXXIV on Job.] By “fleshes” are signified the reprobate, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the devil: “The members of his flesh, clinging together” (Job 41:14). For the devil’s fleshes are all the reprobate, who do not rise by desire to an understanding of the spiritual homeland. The members of the flesh are those who join themselves to those acting perversely and preceding them toward iniquity. Conversely, Paul says of the Lord’s body: “You are the body of Christ, and members of a member.” For one thing is a member of the body, another a member of a member. A member of the body is a part in relation to the whole; but a member of a member is a small part in relation to a part. Thus a finger is a member of a hand and a hand of an arm; but all this taken together is a member of the whole body.

If, therefore, in the Lord’s spiritual body we call “members of a member” those who in His Church are ruled by others, so in that reprobate assembly of the devil, “members of the flesh” are those who, in wicked action, join themselves to certain more wicked persons. But because the malicious enemy is united with himself in perverse work from the first to the last, Scripture speaks of his members of flesh as clinging to one another.

By “fleshes” are signified the disciples of the Lord, as blessed Job says in the person of the same Lord: “My bone has clung to my skin, my flesh being consumed.” See above, chapter 32, “On Skins.”

[Note: [Col. 0211D] From chapter XXIV, book XIV on Job.] By “fleshes” are signified punishments of the flesh or vices, as blessed Job says to his friends: “Why do you persecute me as God does, and are satisfied with my flesh?” (Job 19). It is not foreign to the language of piety that he declares himself persecuted by God. For there is a good persecutor, as the Lord says of Himself through the prophetic voice: “The one secretly slandering his neighbour, him I persecuted” (Ps. 100:5).

When any saint is permitted to be scourged, that person knows that the persecution is suffered by an inward dispensation against committed vices. But when cruel persecutors desire the power to strike, their minds are kindled against the life of the good not by zeal for purification but by the fires of envy. Certainly, they do what almighty God permits to be done; yet although one matter is carried out through them together with God, one will is not retained in the same matter. For while almighty God lovingly provides purification, the perversity of the unjust exercises malice in raging. Therefore the words, “Why do you persecute me as God does?” refer to the outward blow, not to the inward intention. Though persecutors outwardly do what God has ordained to be done, they do not desire in their act what God desires: that the good may be purified through affliction.

And it is well added: “And are satisfied with my flesh?” Those whose mind hungers for the punishments of their neighbours seek, without doubt, to be satisfied with others’ flesh. It should also be known that those who feed upon slander of another’s life are likewise satisfied with another’s flesh. Hence Solomon says: “Do not be at the feast of drinkers, nor eat with those who contribute meats for eating” (Prov. 23:20). To contribute meats for eating is to tell one another, in a conversation of detraction, the faults of neighbours. Concerning their punishment it is immediately added there: “Those given to drinking and contributing a share will be consumed, and sleepiness will be clothed in rags” (Prov. 23:21). Those are given to drink who become intoxicated by the disgrace of another’s life. To contribute a share (*symbolum*) is, as each person is accustomed to contribute food according to his share for eating, likewise to contribute words in a conversation of detraction. But those given to drink and contributing a share will be consumed, because, as it is written, every slanderer will be uprooted (Prov. 24:9). Sleepiness will be clothed in rags, because death finds despised and destitute of all good works the person whom, in this life, the sickness of slander has occupied in seeking the crimes of another’s life.

By “fleshes” are signified movements of the flesh, as blessed Job says: “You clothed [Col. 0212A] me with skin and flesh; you bound me together with bones and sinews” (Job 10:11). See the chapter “On Skin.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. ON BLOOD

In Sacred Scripture, “blood” sometimes means Christ’s Passion, sometimes carnal understanding, sometimes sin, and sometimes the malice of a bloodthirsty mind.

[Note: [Col. 0211D] From chapter XXI, book XXXI on Job, §36.] By “blood” is signified Christ’s Passion, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the holy preacher under the figure of the eagle: “Her young will lap up blood” (Job 39:30). As though openly saying: The eagle herself feeds on the contemplation of divinity; but because her hearers cannot at all receive the mysteries of divinity, they are satisfied with the blood of the crucified Lord. To lap blood is to venerate the lowly matters of the Lord’s Passion.

Thus Paul, who had flown to the secrets of the third heaven, said to his disciples: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and Him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2). As though the eagle openly said: I indeed behold my food, the power of His divinity, from afar; but to you, still little ones, I give only the blood of His incarnation to lap. For he who, through his preaching, instructed weak hearers concerning the silent height of divinity by the blood of the Cross alone, what else did he do but provide blood to the young?

[Note: [Col. 0212D] From chapter I, book XXI on Job.] By “blood” is signified carnal understanding, as Solomon says: “He who presses the udders hard to draw out milk produces butter; and he who milks violently draws out blood” (Prov. 30:33). We press the udders hard when we weigh the words of Sacred Scripture with subtle understanding. By this pressure, while seeking milk, we find butter, because, while seeking to be nourished even by a slight understanding, we are anointed by the abundance of inward richness. Yet this should be done neither excessively nor continually, lest, while milk is sought from the udders, blood follow the milk. For some, when they examine the words of Sacred Scripture more than they should, fall into carnal understanding. One who milks violently draws out blood, because what is understood through such examination becomes carnal.

[Col. 0212D] [Note: [Col. 0212D] From chapter VI, book XIII on Job.] By “blood” is signified sin, as the prophet says: “Cursing and lying and murder and theft and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4:2). Sin is commonly signified by “blood,” as one who desires to be freed from sins cries in repentance: “Deliver me from bloodguiltinesses” (Ps. 50:16). Blood, then, touches blood when one fault heaps up another. Hence blessed Job says: “He tore me with wound upon wound” (Job 16:15). For in the weak members of holy Church, it is torn with wound upon wound when sin is added to sin [Col. 0213A] and guilt is aggravated more severely. For one whom avarice draws into robbery, robbery leads into deceit, and who even defends a committed sin by falsehood—what is such a person except one torn with wound upon wound?

[Note: [Col. 0213D] From chapter XIX, book XV on Job, §15.] By “blood” is signified the malice of a bloodthirsty mind, as the prophet says concerning a persecutor of the righteous: “His blood is in the midst of him. He poured it out upon a most clean rock; he did not pour it out upon the earth, so that it might be covered with dust” (Ezek. 24:7). By earth and dust he signifies sinners; by the most clean rock, the righteous person, who is not embittered by the grievous contagions of sins. Blood, therefore, is poured out upon a most clean rock when the malice of a bloodthirsty mind rages in the affliction [Col. 0213B] of a righteous soul.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. ON FAT

[Note: [Col. 0213D] From chapter XXXIII, book XV on Job, §25.] By “fat” is signified pride, as blessed Job says of a proud rich man: “His entrails are full of fat” (Job 21:24). As fat arises from an abundance of food, so pride arises from abundance of possessions. It fattens the rich person’s mind when the soul of the proud is lifted up. Pride of heart is, as it were, a certain fatness of thickness. Hence, because many commit sins from abundance, the Prophet says: “Their iniquity came forth as though from fatness” (Ps. 7:7).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. ON RICHNESS/FATNESS
[Col. 0213C] [Note: [Col. 0213D] From Job, chapter XXII, book XII.] By “fatness” is meant an abundance of earthly goods, as Eliphaz the Temanite says of any ungodly person: “He is armed with a fat neck; fatness has covered his face” (Job 15:27). For a fat neck is affluent pride, supported, as it were, by much flesh—that is, by abundant possessions. Therefore the powerful wicked person arms himself with a fat neck against the Lord, because, swollen with temporal goods, he rises up against the commands of truth as though lifted by the greatness of his flesh. For what is poverty but a kind of leanness, and what is abundance of possessions but the fatness of the present life? Thus he raises himself against the Lord with a fat neck who turns temporal abundance into pride. For the powerful and wicked have this characteristic: occupied with deceptive riches, they neglect the true riches of God. And the less they seek what is true, the more they are exalted by false riches. For the manifold care of earthly possessions, because it occupies the mind, blinds it. Hence it is aptly added: “Fatness has covered his face.” Sight is in the face, which is also the foremost and more honorable part of the body. Thus the direction of the mind is not undeservedly denoted by the face, since wherever we turn it, there we see. Fatness therefore covers the face, because the desired abundance of earthly things weighs down the eyes of the mind and defiles before the eyes of God that which ought to have been honorable in them, because it burdens it with manifold cares.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. ON SUET

[Note: [Col. 0214D] From chapter V, book cited above.] By “suet” is meant earthly power, as the same Eliphaz says: “Suet hangs from his sides” (Job 15:27). There are some who, attached to greater patrons, grow proud and exalt themselves against the poor through those patrons’ power. Of them it is rightly said: “And suet hangs from his sides.” For since suet is the fatness of flesh, and we commonly call the associates of rich men their “sides,” suet hangs from the sides of the wicked because whoever clings to a powerful and wicked man is himself swollen by that man’s power, as though by the fatness of possessions. Following the iniquity of his perverse patron, he does not fear God; he afflicts the poor whom he can and as much as he can; and he lifts up his heart because of temporal glory. Therefore, when someone of this kind clings to a powerful wicked man, suet indeed hangs from his side.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. ON BONES

In Sacred Scripture, when “bone” is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies Christ and sometimes any strong person in the body of Holy Church. When “bones” are mentioned in the plural, they sometimes signify virtues; sometimes the more wicked and shrewder servants in the body of Antichrist; sometimes the hardness of strength; sometimes bodily strength; and sometimes the strength of secular dignities.

By “bone” Christ is signified, as Job says in the person of Christ: “My bone clung to my skin when my flesh was consumed” (Job 19:20). See above, chapter 32, “On Skins.”

[Note: [Col. 0214D] From Job, book XX, chapters XXI–XXII.] By “bone” is signified any strong person in the body of Holy Church who bears the weak, as blessed Job says in the person of the Church: “By night my bone is pierced with pains, and those who devour me do not sleep” (Job 30:17). If we investigate the mystery of the allegory, what is denoted by the bones but every strong person in the body of Holy Church, who holds together the members, as it were, by his own strength while steadfastly bearing the characters of the weak? But when the heat of the final tribulation rises against him, his bone is pierced with pains in the night, because those who seemed to hold others fast in the faith sometimes, conquered by torments, themselves fall away into unbelief. Therefore he says: “By night my bone is pierced with pains.” As though he plainly said: “Pressed by the darkness of tribulation, they were held fast in affliction, so that those who had within me the vigor of strength now have, as it were, a certain opening of fear.” It is well said: “And those who devour me do not sleep,” because evil spirits, who consume all carnal persons from the Church, know no rest from temptation all the more because they are burdened by no weight of flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0214D] From Job, book XXIII, chapter XVI.] By “bones” virtues are signified, as the Psalmist says of the holy martyrs: “The Lord keeps all their bones; not one of them shall be broken” (Psalm 32:21). This is certainly said not of the bones of the body but of the powers of the mind. For we surely know that the bodily bones of many martyrs were broken; and the persecutors of the Lord broke the legs on the cross of the thief to whom it was said, “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), just as they did those of the other thief.

Likewise, that bones signify virtues is shown by Elihu, when it is said through him of the Lord: “He also rebukes through pain upon the bed, and causes all his bones to waste away” (Job 33:19). For what is meant by the bed except temporal rest? But since in this life every rest that we prepare for ourselves is disturbed, it is rightly said: “He also rebukes through pain upon the bed”—that is, in the repose of the present life he troubles us either by the goads of temptation or by the affliction of the scourge. For often, however short a time the human mind may have been without temptation in good pursuits, it is immediately exalted by the very pursuits in which it exercises itself in repose, and by the very virtues in which it strives to increase, when it feels that it is making progress. Therefore, through the governance of our Ruler, the onset of temptation brings it about that the very exaltation arising from its progress is restrained.

Accordingly, after saying, “He also rebukes through pain upon the bed,” he openly adds, “and causes all his bones to waste away,” because when, in that repose which we prepare for ourselves in this age, we are afflicted by the scourge of temptation, we who might perhaps have become inflated by our virtues are made lean by the weary recognition of our own weakness. For when, as we desire, we advance toward God, if no temptation assailed our progress, we would believe ourselves to possess some strength. But by heavenly dispensation it is so dealt with us that, because in making progress we forget our weakness, we are reminded by temptation—and in our progress we recognize what we are by divine gift, and in temptation what we are by our own powers. This temptation would surely carry us off completely unless heavenly protection preserved us. Yet it strikes without breaking, drives without moving, shakes without casting down, so that through our weakness we may perceive why we are shaken, and through divine gift why we stand.

And because the soul of someone conscious of good in itself is often nourished with a certain delight when it recalls its virtues, and grows fat, as it were, with rejoicing in its own fullness, it is rightly said that the bones waste away when temptation strikes. For when one’s own weakness is recognized under the questioning of temptation, all that rich and flourishing rejoicing in our powers is suddenly dried up by the sorrow of anxiety. And we who, considering our good deeds, believed ourselves to be of some consequence, when somewhat more severely assailed, fear that we are on the point of perishing. Then all joy in our good deeds turns into fear of punishments. Then we discover that we are wicked, though shortly before we believed ourselves holy. The mind wastes away; the eyes grow dull; everything that formerly smiled upon us as prosperity vanishes. Light itself is wearisome, and only the darkness of sorrow pours itself into the soul.

[Note: [Col. 0215D] From Job, book XXXII, chapter XIV.] By “bones” are signified the more wicked and shrewder servants of Antichrist, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning them: “His bones are, indeed, pipes of bronze” (Job 40:13). In the body, bones are what hold the members together and are themselves held together. Antichrist therefore has flesh and bones: for some wicked persons are held in error by others, while others, more wicked, hold others in error. What then are we to understand by the bones of Antichrist except those who are stronger within his body? Since iniquity has hardened intensely in their hearts, through them the entire structure of his body stands firm.

For many in this world appear rich and, supported by possessions and deeds, are made firm as though by strength. But by distributing these very things, through which they are foolish, they draw others into their error. At one time they entice some with gifts to become perverse; at another they bind some with rewards so that they remain perverse. What, then, are these except the bones of Antichrist, who, by retaining the wicked, multiply those whom they bear as flesh in his body? At times they offer the sweetness of speech to deceive their hearers, because thorns also put forth flowers: something fragrant indeed appears in them, but what pricks lies hidden. They mingle sweet things with bitter, agreeable things with harmful ones; they humbly submit themselves, and by speech insinuate of themselves what they deny by their conduct. Thus his bones are rightly compared to pipes of bronze, because, after the manner of insensible metal, they possess the sound of good speech but not the understanding of good life. What they affirm, as it were humbly, by speaking, they despise by living proudly. Hence Paul rightly says: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I have become as sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1). For one who speaks good things but does not follow those same good things through love gives forth a sound like bronze or a cymbal, because he himself perceives the words which he himself does not do.

[Note: [Col. 0215D] From Job, book XXXII, chapter XVII.] By “bones” is signified the hardness of strength, as Jeremiah says of certain persons who presumptuously rely upon their own powers: “Their skin clung to their bones” (Lamentations 4:8). What is expressed by bones except the hardness of strength, and by skin except the softness of weakness? Their skin is therefore said to cling to their bones because those who think perversely regard the weakness of vice as the hardness of virtue. What they do is weak, but deceived by confidence born of pride, they associate it in their imagination with strong things. And the more highly they think of themselves, the more they disdain to be corrected concerning their wickedness.

[Note: [Col. 0216D] From Job, book VIII, chapter XIV.] By “bones” bodily strength is signified, as blessed Job says: “My soul chose hanging, and my bones death” (Job 7:15). What is signified by the soul except the mind’s intention, and by the bones except bodily strength? Whatever hangs is undoubtedly lifted up from low things. The soul therefore chooses hanging so that the bones may die, because when the mind’s intention raises itself to things on high, it kills within itself every strength belonging to outward life. For holy men know with certainty that they cannot possess rest in this life, and therefore choose hanging: abandoning earthly desires, they raise the mind on high. And, being suspended, they bring death upon their bones, because those who had formerly been strong in the world, girded for the pursuit of virtues through love of the heavenly homeland, are subdued by the bond of humility.

By “bones” is signified the strength of secular dignities, as blessed Job says of the proud rich man: “His inward parts are full of fat, and his bones are watered with marrow” (Job 21:24). For just as fat comes from abundant food, so pride is born from abundance of possessions; it fattens the rich man’s mind when the spirit of the proud person is lifted up. For pride of heart is a kind of thick fatness. Hence the Prophet says to those who commit sins out of abundance: “Their iniquity came forth as if from fatness” (Psalm 72:7).

Those who love this world have, as it were, bones when they possess the strength of dignities in this world. But if, in their outward rank, earthly and household riches are lacking in their own estimation, they have bones indeed, but not marrow in their bones. Therefore, because this lover of the world is supported by outward power in such a way that he is also fattened by the inward abundance of his earthly household, it is said: “And his bones are watered with marrow.” Or certainly, the bones of this perverse rich man are his perverse and hard habits; the marrow in his bones is the very desire to live wickedly, which is not satisfied even by the gratification of perversity. This marrow, as it were, waters the bones when perverse desires preserve their own perverse habits in the delight of pleasures.

## CHAPTER XL. ON CARTILAGE

In Sacred Scripture, “cartilage” sometimes signifies the inferiors in the body of Antichrist, and sometimes hypocrisy.

[Note: [Col. 0217D] From the end of chapter XIV, Job, book XXXII.] By “cartilage” are signified the inferiors in the body of Antichrist who desire to appear what they are not, as the Lord says to blessed Job: “His cartilage is like plates of iron.” Cartilage indeed has the appearance of bone, but not bone’s strength. There are some in the body of Antichrist who are distinguished by no honors, supported by no riches, adorned by no appearance of virtues, and skilled in no knowledge of craftiness; nevertheless, they desire to appear what they are not, and therefore become more wicked against the life of the good. His cartilage is therefore aptly compared to plates of iron, because those who are weaker in relation to Antichrist are more wicked in committing evils. For other metals are cut by iron; and Antichrist’s cartilage is said to be like iron because those in his body who are unable to attain an appearance of virtues burn more fiercely against the slaughter of believers. Since they see that they cannot work signs and wonders with him, they prove themselves faithful to him through cruelty. And because they cannot corrupt the hearts of the innocent by persuasion, they boast more than the rest that they can destroy the bodies of the good. Thus it is well said: “His cartilage is like plates of iron,” because in his body the weaker each person believes himself to be, the more wickedly he cuts. They are rightly compared not merely to iron but to plates of iron, because, desiring to spread themselves everywhere through unbelief, they extend themselves, as it were, into plates of iron.

[Note: [Col. 0218D] From the same book, chapter XVII, a little after the middle.] By “cartilage” hypocrisy may be signified. For cartilage displays the appearance of bone but does not have the weakness of bone. There are certain vices that display in themselves the appearance of uprightness but arise from the weakness of perversity. For the malice of our enemy disguises itself with such art that it often makes faults seem virtues before the eyes of the deceived mind, so that a person may expect rewards from the very source from which he deserves to find eternal torments.

Often, in punishing vices, cruelty is practiced and is considered justice; excessive anger is inwardly thought to possess the merit of zeal. And when sinners should be corrected cautiously from distorted habits, they are broken by violent bending.

Often lax indulgence is regarded as gentleness and mercy; and while offenders are spared temporally more than is fitting, they are cruelly reserved for eternal punishments.

Sometimes prodigality is thought mercy; and while it is blameworthy to preserve what has been received wrongly, it is not feared that it is worse to scatter it.

Sometimes stinginess is thought frugality; and while it is a serious vice not to give, keeping what has been received is regarded as a virtue.

Often the obstinacy of the wicked is called constancy; and while the mind refuses to be turned from its perversity, it boasts as though defending what is right.

Often inconstancy is regarded as amenability; and the less a person keeps undivided faith with anyone, the more he thinks himself a friend to all.

Sometimes inappropriate fear is considered humility; and, oppressed by temporal fear, someone keeps silent instead of defending the truth, imagining that in accordance with God’s order he is showing himself subject to those above him.

Sometimes pride in speech is considered true freedom; and when truth is contradicted through arrogance, the insolence of speaking is considered a defense of truth.

Often laziness is regarded as the restraint of quietness; and while it is a grave fault not zealously to do what is right, merely abstaining from perverse action is thought to merit great virtue.

Often restlessness of spirit is called watchful concern; and when a person cannot bear quietness, he thinks that by doing what he desires he is fulfilling the exercise of due virtue.

Because error is more difficult to correct when it is regarded as virtue, it is rightly said: “His cartilage is like plates of iron” (Job 40:3). For the more deceitfully the devil displays his craftiness under the pretext of good, the more harshly he holds the mind in fault. Hence those who seem to be seeking the way of holiness, once they have fallen into error, are sometimes corrected more slowly. They consider right what is being done, and they attach perseverance to vice as though it were a virtue to be cultivated. They consider right what they do, and therefore serve their own judgment more earnestly.

## CHAPTER XLI. ON MARROWS

In Sacred Scripture, “marrows” sometimes signify royal nobility, sometimes subtlety of intellect, sometimes riches, and sometimes intentions of the heart.

By “marrow” royal nobility is signified, as the prophet Ezekiel says of Nebuchadnezzar: “A great eagle, with great wings, long in the extension of its members, full of feathers and variegation, came to Lebanon; and it took the marrow of the cedar and plucked off the top of its branches” (Ezekiel 17:4). See the heading “On the Eagle,” book II, chapter 2.

By “marrow,” moreover, subtlety of intellect may fittingly be signified: for “the marrows strengthen the bones by watering them” (Job 21:24). By the bones are understood the fraudulent counsels of the devil. For just as the body’s arrangement and strength reside in the bones, so the devil raises up all his malice in his fraudulent counsels; and just as marrows strengthen bones by watering them, so the subtlety of intellect, infused through the power of spiritual nature, strengthens his counsel.

By “marrows” riches are signified, as blessed Job says of the perverse rich man: “His bones are watered with marrows” (Job 21:24). Consult book III, chapter 33.

[Note: [Col. 0219D] From Homily XXI on Ezekiel, after the middle.] By “marrows” are signified the intentions of the heart. Thus the outstanding preacher, speaking with subtlety, said: “The word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit” (Hebrews 4:12); and immediately added: “Of joints also and marrows, and a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (ibid.).

For the word of God distinguishes joints and marrows because it discerns thoughts and intentions of the heart. By joints, moreover, bone is joined to bone. Often, when we act with a right thought but suddenly turn toward love of praise, and do for praise what we had first begun to do for truth, thoughts are joined to thoughts and become, as it were, certain joints. But the bones joined in a joint also have marrows. The holy preacher made this clearer when he added: “A discerner of thoughts and intentions of the heart.” For the joints are our thoughts, but the marrows are our intentions. Often we think one thing, while what we intend through our thought is something else.

For if a person defends the case of an orphan or widow for the reward of money, and perhaps, entering a church, says to God in his prayers, “You see that I defend the cause of the orphan and widow,” that person undoubtedly knows what he thinks, but does not know what his thought intends. For he thinks one thing and intends another. He seeks not the defense of the orphan or widow but monetary recompense. For he intends to receive the temporal reward, not to defend the orphan and widow. The word of God, therefore, is a discerner of thoughts and intentions of the heart, because it does not consider what you think within yourself, but what you seek to receive through the marrow of the joint—that is, through the intention of your thought.

It remains, therefore, that a teacher, when speaking, should carefully attend lest he begin speaking with an evil intention, or, having begun well, be seduced by favor and turn aside to another desire. For thus a sinister thought is joined to a good thought, so that scarcely even the mind which generates those thoughts recognizes them.

## CHAPTER XLII. ON SINEWS

[Note: [Col. 0219D] From Job, chapter XXV, book XI.] By “sinew” is signified the strong sentence of strict judgment, as blessed Job says to the Lord: “You have put my foot in the sinew, and have observed all my paths, and considered the tracks of my feet” (Job 13:27). God put the foot of man in a sinew because he bound that person’s perversity with the strong sentence of his strict judgment. He observes all his paths because he judges every detail with subtle discernment. For a path is usually narrower than a road. Since roads signify actions, we not undeservedly understand the paths to be the thoughts belonging to those actions. God therefore observes all paths because in every one of our actions he also weighs our thoughts. And he considers the tracks of the feet because he examines how rightly the intentions of our works are set down, lest even what is done well be done from an unright desire.

## CHAPTER XLIII. ON THE BREAST

In Sacred Scripture, “breast” sometimes signifies a thought of lust, and sometimes the heart.

[Note: [Col. 0219D] From chapter II, Job, book XXI, before the end.] By “breast” is signified a thought of lust, as the Lord says to the serpent: “Upon your breast and belly you shall crawl” [Note: [Col. 0220D] But our text and all editions have otherwise.] (Genesis 3:14). For the evil of lust is committed either in thought or in deed. When our crafty adversary is driven away from the effect of the deed, he endeavors to defile the secrecy of thought. It is therefore well said by the Lord to the serpent: “Upon your breast and belly you shall crawl.” The serpent crawls on its belly when the slippery enemy exercises lust through the bodily members subject to him, to the full accomplishment of the deed. But the serpent crawls on its breast when he pollutes in thought those whom he cannot overcome in the deed of lust. One person therefore already commits lust in action: in his case the serpent crawls from the belly. Another turns over in his mind the lust that he is about to commit: in his case the serpent crawls upon the breast. But because thought leads to the completion of deeds, the serpent is rightly described as first crawling upon the breast and afterward upon the belly.

[Note: [Col. 0220D] From Part II of the *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 1.] By “breast” the heart is signified. Thus the divine voice commands that the rational of judgment be fastened with straps upon Aaron’s breast, so that wandering thoughts may by no means possess the priestly heart, but reason alone may constrain it, lest one set as an example for others think anything indiscreet or useless. By the gravity of his life he must always show how much reason he bears in his breast.

## CHAPTER XLIV. ON BREASTS

In Sacred Scripture, “breasts” sometimes signify Jews and Gentiles, sometimes the words of sacred utterance, sometimes arguments of empty hope, and sometimes holy preachers.

[Note: [Col. 0221D] From Job, book XXIV, chapter VI, section 10.] By “breasts” Jews and Gentiles are signified, as it is said to the Church in the Song of Songs: “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle, feeding among lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline” (Song of Songs 4:5). For what are the two breasts but the two peoples, one coming from Judaism and the other from the Gentiles, fixed in the secret place of the heart within the body of Holy Church through their pursuit of wisdom? From this people, those who are elect are compared to the fawns of a gazelle because, through humility, they recognize themselves as sinners; yet, running in charity, if obstacles from temporal hindrance meet them, they pass over them, and, making leaps of contemplation, ascend to things above.

In order to do this, they look upon the examples of the saints who went before them. Hence they are said to feed among lilies. For what do lilies signify except the life of those who truly say, “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2)? Therefore, in order that the elect may be strong enough to attain the highest things, they are nourished by beholding the fragrant and bright life of the righteous. Already they thirst to see the Lord; already, burning with the ardors of charity, they long to be satisfied by his contemplation. But because, while placed in this life, they are not yet able to do so, they are meanwhile nourished by the examples of the fathers who went before.

Thus the time of their feeding among lilies is fittingly defined when it says: “Until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” We need to be refreshed by the examples of the righteous until, with the eternal day breathing upon us, we pass beyond the shadows of sinful mortality. But when the shadow of this temporality has inclined through the passing away of mortality, because we behold the inward light of that very day, we no longer desire to be inflamed toward its love through others’ examples. But now, because we cannot yet behold him, it is supremely necessary that we be stirred up by looking upon the deeds of those who followed him perfectly.

By “breasts” the words of sacred utterance are signified, as Solomon says: “He who presses the breasts hard to draw out milk produces butter; and he who milks violently brings forth blood” (Proverbs 30:33). See above, chapter 35, “On Blood.”

[Note: [Col. 0222D] From Job, chapter XXV, book IV, section 27.] By “breasts” are signified arguments of empty hope or confidence, or the wretched incentives of despair, as blessed Job says in the person of the human race, or of any penitent: “Why did I not die in the womb? Why did I not perish at once when I came forth from the womb? Why was I received upon knees? Why was I nursed at breasts?” (Job 3:11–12).

Sin is committed in the heart in four ways, and is consummated in deed in four ways. In the heart, it is committed by suggestion, delight, consent, and the boldness of self-defense arising from pride. Suggestion comes through the adversary, delight through the flesh, consent through the spirit, and the boldness of self-defense through pride. For fault, which ought to terrify, exalts the mind and lifts it up by casting it down; but by lifting it up more gravely, it trips it up. Thus the ancient enemy broke the uprightness of the first human being by these four blows. The serpent suggested; Eve took delight; Adam consented. And when questioned, he refused through boldness to confess his fault.

What was done in the first parent of our race, as is well known, occurs daily in the human race. The serpent suggested because the hidden enemy secretly suggests evils to human hearts. Eve took delight because the carnal sense immediately submits itself to delight at the serpent’s words. Adam, who was set over the woman, gave consent because, while the flesh is carried away into delight, the weakened spirit also bends from its own uprightness. And Adam, when questioned, refused to confess his fault because the spirit, in proportion as it is separated from truth through sinning, is hardened more wickedly in the boldness of its fall.

Sin is likewise consummated in deed by these same four modes. First the hidden fault is committed; then the guilt is openly displayed before human eyes without shame; afterward it is brought into habit; and finally it is nourished either by the deceits of false hope or by the obstinacy of wretched despair.

Blessed Job therefore considers these modes of sin, whether they occur secretly in the heart or are openly committed in deed, and laments how many degrees of sin the human race has fallen through, saying: “Why did I not die in the womb? Why did I not perish at once when I came forth from the womb? Why was I received upon knees?” The first womb of conception was the tongue of evil suggestion. But the sinner would die in the womb if a person recognized himself as dying in the very suggestion. Yet he came forth from the womb because, after the suggesting tongue conceived him in sin, delight immediately carried him outward as well. After coming forth, he was received upon knees because, when he emerged into the delight of the flesh, he completed the fault by the consent of the spirit, with all the senses subjected, as it were, beneath supporting knees.

But one received upon knees was also nursed at breasts. For in consenting to fault, with the senses of the spirit added, many arguments of empty confidence followed, which nourished the soul born in sin with poisonous milk and soothed it with flattering excuses so that it would not fear the harsh punishments of death. Thus the first human being, after his fault, became bolder and said: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Genesis 3:12). He had fled in order to hide himself through fear; yet, when questioned, he made clear how greatly he feared even while afraid. For when the present punishment arising from sin is feared but the lost face of God is not loved, fear comes from fear, not from humility. For one is proud who, if he were permitted to escape punishment, would not abandon sin.

But, as has been said, fault committed in the heart is also perpetrated in deed by these four modes. He says: “Why did I not die in the womb?” For the womb is the hidden fault of the sinning person, which secretly conceives the sinner and still conceals its guilt in darkness. “Why did I not perish at once when I came forth from the womb?” A person comes forth from the womb when a sinner is not ashamed to commit openly what he committed in secret. Those of whom the prophet said, “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom” (Isaiah 3:9), had come forth, as it were, from the womb of their concealment.

“Why was I received upon knees?” Certainly, when a sinner is no longer ashamed of his iniquity, he is strengthened in that same iniquity by the supports of a most evil habit. The sinner is cherished, as it were, upon knees in order that he may grow, while fault is strengthened by habits so that it may flourish. “Why was I nursed at breasts?” Because when fault begins to emerge into practice, it nourishes itself either with false hope in divine mercy or with the open misery of despair, so that it does not return to correction—either because it imagines its Maker to be merciful toward itself, or because it fears in a disordered manner what it has done.

The blessed man therefore sees the fall of the human race and considers through what precipices it has been plunged into the pit of iniquity, saying: “Why did I not die in the womb?” That is: In the very hidden commission of sin, why was I unwilling to mortify myself to the life of the flesh? “Why did I not perish at once when I came forth from the womb?” That is: After I emerged into open iniquity, why did I not at least then recognize myself as lost? For he would have perished in his own judgment if he had recognized himself as lost. “Why was I received upon knees?” That is: Even after open fault, why did habit still receive me into it, making me stronger for wicked deeds and fostering me by sustaining my perverse practices? “Why was I nursed at breasts?” That is: After I came into the habit of sin, why did I nourish myself toward more atrocious wickedness, whether with confidence in false hope or with the milk of wretched despair?

[Note: [Col. 0223D] From Job, book XXX, chapter X, section 22.] By “breasts” holy preachers are signified, as the bridegroom says of them in the Song of Songs: “Your breasts are better than wine” (Song of Songs 1:1). These are the breasts fixed in the ark of the Lord’s breast that give us milk to drink, because, cleaving to the secrets of highest contemplation, they nourish us by subtle preaching.

## CHAPTER XLV. ON TEATS

[Note: [Col. 0223D] From Job, book XIX, chapter II, section 15.] By “teats” is signified the preaching of error, as the one who long beforehand foresaw the freedom of speech of perverse preachers under Antichrist testifies, saying: “Even the lamiae have uncovered the teat and nursed their young” (Lamentations 4:3). What does he call *lamiae* except heretics, who indeed bear a human face but hearts made beastly through impiety? Therefore, because at that time—or whenever Holy Church is pressed by adversity—freedom of speech is granted to perverse preachers, it is rightly said: “The lamiae uncovered their teats,” because perverse preachers freely proclaim their error. Then they nurse their young, because, while insinuating perverse things, they strengthen the immature souls of their evil followers by nourishing them toward impiety.

## CHAPTER XLVI. ON RIBS
[Note: [Col. 0224D] From chapter VII, book XIV, on Job.] By “ribs” are signified the faculties of the soul, [Col. 0224B] as in the book of blessed Job Eliphaz says of the wicked man: “Let his strength be weakened by hunger, and let want invade his ribs” (Job 18:12). In the manner of Sacred Scripture, he appears to wish for what he foresees will happen—speaking not with the mind of one cursing, but of one proclaiming. Every human being, therefore, consisting of soul and flesh, is composed, as it were, of strength and weakness. For in the respect in which he is made a rational spirit, he is fittingly called strong; but in the respect in which he is fleshly, he is weak. The strength of a human being, then, is the rational soul, which is able through reason to resist the vices that attack it. But the strength of this wicked man is weakened by hunger, because his soul is fed by no refreshment of inward food. Of this hunger God speaks [Col. 0224C] through the prophet: “I will send a famine upon the land—not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of God.” And it is well added: “Let want invade his ribs.” For each person’s ribs are the faculties of the soul, which protect hidden thoughts. Want therefore invades the ribs when, all spiritual refreshment having been withdrawn, the faculties of the mind fail and cannot govern or guard their thoughts. Want invades the wicked man’s ribs because inward hunger so weakens the faculties of his mind that he cannot govern his thoughts at all. For when the faculties of the mind have become dull, thoughts emerge outwardly; and, as the ribs become weak, the inward parts which could have remained soundly hidden are poured forth outside. Hence it comes about that, when thoughts are scattered outwardly, the soul, deceived by the appearance of outward [Col. 0224D] glory, desires it, and loves nothing except what it sees to be beautiful outwardly.

301 CHAPTER XLVII. ON THE WOMB.

[Note: [Col. 0224D] From chapter XV, book XXIX, on Job, 20.] By “womb” is signified the hidden bosom of God’s grace, as the Lord says to blessed Job in a question: “From whose womb did the ice come forth?” (Job 38:29). For what is understood by the womb except the bosom of grace? And what do we understand by ice except the hearts of the Jews, cold and bound fast in the numbness of unbelief? Once, through receiving the Law, keeping the commandments, and the ministries of prophecy, they were held within the bosom of grace, as though within the womb [Col. 0225A] of their Creator. But when the Lord came, constricted by the cold of unbelief, they lost the fervour of faith and charity; cast forth from the hidden bosom of God’s grace, they came out like ice from the womb of their Creator. For ice comes forth, as it were, from God’s womb when those who had been warmed inwardly by the gift of virtues grow cold.

[Note: [Col. 0225D] These are approximately from the middle.] For when almighty God forms human minds in his fear, he conceives them, as it were; and when he advances them to manifest virtues, he gives them birth. But if they become exalted over the virtues received, he abandons them. We have often known persons pierced by consideration of their evils, growing fervent through dread of divine judgment, and by the beginnings of that fear reaching the heights of virtues. Yet, when they become exalted over those very virtues which they receive, bound in the snare of vain glory, [Col. 0225B] they return to their former numbness. Then, while numb, they desire outward glory from the very cause for which they ought to have burned more ardently in loving inward things. And while one is powerful in signs, another in knowledge, one in prophecy, another in great works, and they seek through these gifts to please human beings, all that had previously been inwardly warm they turn into numbness by loving outward praise. Thus ice comes forth, as it were, from the womb when, after benefits of gifts, they are separated from the inward parts of heavenly mercy.

[Note: [Col. 0225D] This is from chapter XXII, book XIV on Job.] By “womb” is understood God’s counsel, as he himself testifies when he speaks through blessed Job: “And I entreated the sons of my womb” (Job 19:17). In God, who is not circumscribed by bodily form, the members of a body—that is, [Col. 0225C] hands, eyes, and womb—are named in such a way that the effects of his power are signified by the names of members. For he is said to have eyes because he sees all things; he is described as having hands because he works all things; and offspring is conceived in the womb and brought forth in this life. What, then, ought we to understand as God’s womb except his counsel, in which we were conceived before the ages through predestination, so that, created in time, we might be led onward through the ages? Therefore the Lord who abides before the ages entreated the children of his womb, because, coming incarnate, he humbly entreated those whom he had powerfully created through his divinity.

[Note: [Col. 0226D] From chapter XXV, book XXVIII on Job.] By “womb” is signified the mind, as Eliphaz says of the hypocrite: “He conceived pain and brought forth iniquity; and his womb also prepares deceits” (Job [Col. 0225D] 15:35). The hypocrite’s mind conceives pain when he thinks perversely; it brings forth iniquity when it begins to fulfil what it has thought. By envying, it conceives pain; by slandering, it brings forth iniquity. For it is a grave iniquity when a perverse person strives to show that others are perverse, so that he himself may appear holy because he has declared others not to be holy. The mind is rightly understood by “womb,” because just as offspring is conceived in the womb, so thought is generated in the mind; and just as foods are held in the belly, so thoughts are contained in the mind. The hypocrite’s womb therefore prepares deceits, because the more he seeks to appear more innocent than all others, the more he conceives greater malice in his mind against his neighbours. [Col. 0226A] For the hypocrite’s mind is never free from a thought of malice. Whether he seeks earthly things or praise, he envies others for possessing what he longs to have bestowed on himself. And the more he longs to appear holier to people, the more he strives to show others perverse, so that, as others become contemptible, he himself may always appear more worthy of reverence. Hence, before human tribunals, he lays out the snares of his tongue against his neighbour’s reputation, so that he alone may gain the esteem of those whom he seeks to please.

303 CHAPTER XLVIII. ON THE BELLY.

In Sacred Scripture, “belly” sometimes signifies the mind, sometimes avarice, sometimes the act of lust, and sometimes our weakness.

[Col. 0226B] [Note: [Col. 0226D] From Homily 10 on Ezekiel, rather far from the beginning.] By “belly” is signified the mind, as the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, your belly shall eat, and your inward parts shall be filled with this scroll which I give you” (Ezek. 3:3). For what is understood by “belly” except the mind? Hence Jeremiah says: “My belly, my belly, I am in pain” (Jer. 4:19). Since he had said this of a spiritual, not a bodily, belly, he added: “The faculties of my heart are troubled” (ibid.). For it would not have served the salvation of the people if the prophet had proclaimed that his bodily belly hurt. But he whose mind felt affliction suffered pain in his belly. Yet why do we bring forward the prophet’s example when we have a clearer testimony from the Lord? When truth itself speaks [Col. 0226C] through itself, the prophet must be silent, because a lamp has no brightness in the sun. For he says: “He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:38). Because words of holy preaching flow from the minds of believers, rivers of living water run down, as it were, from the bellies of believers. And what else are the inward parts of the belly except the inner things of the mind—that is, right intention, holy desire, a will humble toward the Lord and devout toward one’s neighbour? Thus it is rightly said now: “Your belly eats, and your inward parts shall be filled,” because when our mind receives the food of truth, our inner parts no longer remain empty, but are satisfied by the food of life. Yet many read and are hungry even in their reading. Many hear the voice of preaching, but [Col. 0226D] depart empty after hearing it. Though their belly eats, their inward parts are not filled; for, although they grasp in mind the meaning of the sacred word, by forgetting and not keeping what they have heard, they do not lay it up in the inward parts of the heart. Hence the Lord rebukes some through another prophet, saying: “Set your hearts upon your ways. You have sown much and brought in little. You have eaten and are not satisfied. You have drunk and are not intoxicated” (Hag. 1:6). One sows much in the heart but brings in little who learns many things from heavenly commandments, whether by reading or hearing, but produces few fruits by negligent practice. One eats and is not satisfied who, hearing [Col. 0227A] God’s words, longs for gain or the glory of the age. And he is rightly said not to be satisfied, because he chews one thing and hungers for another. One drinks and is not intoxicated who inclines his ear to preaching but does not change his mind. For by drunkenness the perceptions of those who drink are customarily changed. Therefore one who is devout in knowing God’s word but desires to obtain the things of this age drinks but is not intoxicated. For if he were intoxicated, he would undoubtedly have changed his mind, so that he would no longer seek earthly things and no longer love the vain and transient things he once loved. For the Psalmist says of the elect: “They shall be intoxicated by the abundance of your house” (Ps. 35:9), because they are so filled with love for almighty God that, their mind having been changed, they seem strangers to themselves, fulfilling what is written: [Col. 0227B] “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matt. 16:24). For one denies oneself who is changed for the better, begins to be what one was not, and ceases to be what one was.

[Note: [Col. 0227D] From chapter XII, book XV, on Job.] By “belly” is signified avarice, as Zophar says in the book of blessed Job concerning the wicked man: “Breaking in, he stripped the poor man’s house; he seized it and did not build it, and his belly is not satisfied” (Job 20:19). He breaks into and strips the poor man’s house who is not ashamed, after crushing someone through power, also to despoil him through avarice. “He seizes it and does not build it.” This is as though it were said openly: He who ought to have built it instead seizes it. The Lord, coming to judgment, will say to the reprobate: “I was hungry, and you did not give me drink. I was a stranger, and you did not take me in,” and so forth [Col. 0227C] (Matt. 25:41). From their fault he adds: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.). If, then, one convicted of not having given is punished with so great a penalty, with what penalty must one be struck who is reproved for having taken away? He seized it, then, and did not build it, because not only did he give nothing of his own, but also took what belonged to another. It is well added: “And his belly is not satisfied.” For the wicked man’s belly is avarice, because it gathers into itself whatever is devoured by perverse desire. It is clear that avarice is not extinguished by the things it desires but increases. For, after the manner of fire, when it receives wood to consume, it grows; and from that by which the flame seems for a moment to be compressed, it is soon afterwards seen to spread.

[Col. 0227D] By “belly” is signified the act of lust, as the Lord says to the serpent: “You shall crawl upon breast and belly” (Gen. 3:14, according to the Septuagint). See above, chapter 43, “On the Breast.”

[Note: [Col. 0227D] From Homily 19 on Ezekiel, approximately the middle.] By “belly” is signified our weakness, as the bride says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch” (Cant. 3:4). For my beloved puts his hand through the opening when the Lord, by his power, touches our mind through subtle understanding. And the belly trembles at his touch [Col. 0228A] because our weakness, broken by its understanding of heavenly joy, is troubled by its very exultation. Let fear therefore be joined in the mind with joy, because, although it now perceives what it may love concerning heavenly joy, it nevertheless fears lest what it scarcely and faintly perceives should not perish.

CHAPTER XLIX. ON THE INTESTINES.

[Note: [Col. 0227D] From Homily 22 on the Gospels.] By “intestines” are signified God’s hidden and mystical commandments, as Moses says concerning the eating of the lamb: “You shall devour the head with the feet and intestines” (Exod. 12:9). For what is signified by the lamb except the Redeemer? Our Redeemer is God before the ages and human at the end of the ages. To devour the lamb’s head, then, is to receive his divinity in faith. To devour the lamb’s feet is to seek out, with love and imitation, the footsteps of his humility. [Col. 0228B] And what are his intestines except the hidden and mystical commandments of his words? We devour these when we receive the words of life eagerly.

CHAPTER L. ON THE INWARD PARTS.

[Note: [Col. 0228D] From book XIII on Job, chapter VI, 10.] By “inward parts” are signified those who serve spiritual mysteries in the Church, as blessed Job speaks in the person of the Church: “And he poured out my inward parts upon the ground” (Job 16:14). What else ought we to understand as the inward parts of holy Church except the minds of those who contain within themselves some of her mysteries and serve the innermost sacraments? [Col. 0228C] But when the ancient adversary draws certain faithful persons, who seemed to serve inward mysteries, into secular affairs, he undoubtedly pours her inward parts upon the ground, because he tramples in lowly matters those who previously lay hidden in secret and spiritual things.

CHAPTER LI. ON THE NAVEL.

[Note: [Col. 0228D] From chapter XI, book XXXII, on Job.] By “navel” is signified lust, as the prophet testifies when, censuring Judah’s wantonness under the figure of a prostitute, he says: “On the day of your birth your navel was not cut” (Ezek. 16:4). For to cut the navel on the day of birth is, at the time of conversion, to cut away fleshly lust. Because it is difficult to correct what has begun badly and to reform for the better what has once been formed [Col. 0228D] in ugliness, Judah is reproved for her birth: though born a Jewess, she kept the navel uncut, because she did not cut off the loose excesses of lust. Hence again the Lord says of the devil to blessed Job: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job 40:11). The seeds of intercourse are said to be in men’s loins and in women’s navels. Since, therefore, through the devil’s power the sex of both kinds is greatly laid low by the weakness of lust, his strength against males is said to be in the loins, and [Col. 0229A] his power against females in the navel.

CHAPTER LII. ON THE LOINS.

In Sacred Scripture, “loins” sometimes signify mortal descent, sometimes lust, and sometimes the desire for praise.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] From Homily 8 on Ezekiel, far after the middle.] By “loins” is signified mortal descent, as Ezekiel says concerning our Redeemer: “Like the appearance of fire, inwardly around him, from his loins upward; and from his loins downward I saw something like the appearance of shining fire all around” (Ezek. 1:27). What does it mean that Christ Jesus, the mediator of God and men, is described as having inwardly around him the appearance of fire from his loins upward, [Col. 0229B] but from his loins downward as having the appearance of shining fire all around? We must investigate why he is said to have fire inwardly, yet not shining fire, from his loins upward; whereas from his loins downward he is said to have the appearance of fire, but not said to have it inwardly, because he is described as having it shining and all around. For what is expressed by “loins” except mortal descent? Thus Levi is said still to have been in his father’s loins when Melchizedek met Abraham. But from Abraham’s loins the Virgin Mary came forth, in whose womb the Only-begotten of the Father deigned to be incarnate through the Holy Spirit. Through that incarnation God became known to the whole [Col. 0229C] world, as the Psalmist says: “Gird your sword about your thigh, O mighty one” (Ps. 44:4). The Almighty girded the sword around his thigh because the word of his preaching gained strength from his incarnation itself. What then does this fire signify except the ardour of the Holy Spirit, who sets ablaze the hearts which he fills? Of it Truth himself says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire but that it be kindled?” What, then, does it mean that in this appearance of the man who appeared to the prophet, fire burns inwardly all around above the loins, but below the loins fire does not burn inwardly but shines around him, except that before the incarnation of the Only-begotten, our Redeemer, Judea alone possessed within herself the ardour of his love, while after his incarnation [Col. 0229D] fire shone around him, because he poured out the brightness of the Holy Spirit upon the nations throughout the whole world? First, then, there was fire inwardly, but not brightness, because the Holy Spirit filled Judea indeed in many places, but his light had not yet shone forth to the knowledge of the nations. But from his loins downward fire shines around him, because, after he took flesh from the Virgin, he spread abroad far and wide the gifts of the Holy Spirit among humankind. It should be noted that this fire is described as being around him above the loins, not outwardly but inwardly, because, as has been said, the flame of love filled Judea everywhere within her bounds among the elect and spiritual [Col. 0230A] men. Yet it did not go outward, because it did not spread itself among the multitude of nations. This flame of ardour was afterwards seen to shine all around, because throughout the regions of the world the love of almighty God began to increase among all nations. Thus there was first fire inwardly when Jacob said: “I will await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. 49:8). What we call *salutare* (“salvation”) in Latin is called Jesus in the Hebrew word. In this word blessed Jacob’s mind is shown—how he burned with longing for Jesus, whom he was said to await as he died. Fire burned when Moses said: “If I have found grace in your sight, show me yourself, that I may see you” (Exod. 34:9). Fire burned in the mind when David said: “My soul thirsted for the living God. [Col. 0230B] When shall I come and appear before the face of my God?” (Ps. 41:3). Longing for the incarnation of the Word, he said: “Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and give us your salvation” (Ps. 84:8). Fire burned when Simeon, desiring to depart from the corruption of the present life, heard that he would not see death before he saw 309 the Christ of the Lord (Luke 2:26). But behold, this fire now shines outwardly, as though below the loins, because all the Gentile world is set ablaze by love for God incarnate. And because the elect angels in heaven are his members, and converted human beings on earth are his members, he is one human being who burns inwardly above the loins and sends forth below the loins the brightness of his fire all around: by his divinity he held angels fast in his love, and by his humanity he recalled human beings to desire for his holy ardour.

[Note: [Col. 0230D] From book XIII on Job, chapter VI, in the middle, 19.] By “loins” is signified lust, as blessed Job says in the person of holy Church: “He surrounded me with his spears; he wounded my loins with me” (Job 16:14). Holy Church is surrounded by spears from her enemy when, in her members, she is attacked by the missiles of temptations from the crafty assailant. She is rightly said to be surrounded by spears because the ancient enemy attacks us from every side with the wound of his temptation. And because the crafty enemy suggests every sin, but we commit it by consenting to his suggestions, it is expressly added: “He wounded my loins together with himself.” For lust is in the loins. When, therefore, the ancient enemy draws the faithful people into lust, he undoubtedly strikes them in the loins. It should also be noted that he did not say, “He wounded,” but “He wounded my loins together with himself.” For just as speaking may sometimes belong to one person, while conversing belongs to two, or perhaps many, so the ancient enemy does not drag us into sin without our will. He is not said simply to wound our loins, but to wound them with us, because we ourselves fulfil, of our own will, what he wickedly suggests to us; and we wound ourselves with him, as it were, because together with him we are led by free choice to commit evil.

By “loins” is signified the desire for praise, [Col. 0231A] as blessed Job is told: “Gird your loins like a man” (Job 38:3). See above, book IV, chapter 2.

310 CHAPTER LIII. ON THE REINS.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] From Homily 22 on the Gospels, after the middle.] By “reins” is signified fleshly pleasure, as Moses says concerning the eating of the lamb: “You shall gird your reins” (Exod. 12:11). For what is understood by the reins except the delight of the flesh? Hence the Psalmist asks: “Burn my reins” (Ps. 25:2). For if he did not know that the pleasure of lust is in the reins, he would not have asked for them to be burned. Whoever, therefore, eats the Passover ought to have girded reins, so that one who celebrates the solemnity of resurrection and incorruption may no longer be subject to corruption through any vices, [Col. 0231B] may subdue pleasures, and may restrain the flesh from lust. For one who is still subject through lack of self-control to corruption has not known what the solemnity of incorruption is.

CHAPTER LIV. ON THE THIGH.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] From book XXIV on Job, chapter XII.] By “thigh” is signified fleshly pleasure, as the prophet Jeremiah says: “After you converted me, I did penance; and after you showed me, I struck my thigh” (Jer. 31:19). For what is understood by the thigh except the pleasure of the flesh? And what does he mean when he says, “After you showed me, I struck my thigh,” except that, after spiritually seeing the things above, he extinguished within himself all that lived carnally below, so that the more fully the highest things [Col. 0231C] were revealed, the less he might be held by the lowest? For the more anyone begins to live above, the more that person also begins to die below. In respect of the inclination of fleshly action, all flesh had died in Paul when he said: “I live, yet no longer I; but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). Hence Solomon says: “Each man’s sword upon his thigh because of fears by night” (Cant. 1:8).

[Note: [Col. 0232D] From book XX on Job, chapter V.] For nocturnal fears are the snares of hidden temptation. The sword upon the thigh is vigilant guard, restraining the enticement of the flesh. Therefore, lest nocturnal fear—that is, hidden and sudden temptation—creep in, it is always necessary that the sword of watchfulness laid upon it restrain our thigh. Hence it is that the angel with whom Jacob wrestled took hold of the sinew of his thigh and immediately made it wither. The angel signifies the Lord, and Jacob, who contended with the angel, signifies the soul of every perfect person established in contemplation. This soul, striving to contemplate the Lord, is placed as though in a contest: at one time it seems to prevail, because through understanding and perception it tastes something of the uncircumscribed light; at another it yields, because even while tasting it, it again fails. Thus the angel is conquered, as it were, when God is grasped by inward understanding. But it should be noted that the same conquered angel took hold of the sinew of [Col. 0232A] Jacob’s thigh and immediately made it wither; and from that time Jacob limped on one foot, because almighty God, once he is known through desire and understanding, dries up in us every pleasure of the flesh. Formerly, as though resting on two feet, we seemed both to seek God and to hold the world. But after knowing the sweetness of God, one foot remains sound in us and the other limps, because, as love for the world is weakened, it is necessary for love of God to grow strong. Therefore, if we hold the angel, we limp on one foot, because as the strength of inward love grows in us, the strength of the flesh undoubtedly weakens. For everyone who limps on one foot rests only on the foot that is sound, because one whose earthly desire [Col. 0232B] has dried up supports oneself with all one’s strength on the single foot of love. And one stands upon it, because the foot of love for the world, which one was accustomed to place on the earth, one now bears raised from the earth.

By “thigh” is signified bodily descent, as it is said of the Lord: “He had written upon his garment and upon his thigh, King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19:16). For what is his garment except the body which he assumed from the Virgin? Yet his garment is not one thing and he another. Indeed, our flesh too is called a garment; nevertheless, we ourselves are the flesh with which we are clothed. By the thigh, moreover, is understood bodily descent. Therefore, because through the lineage of the human race, as the genealogical sequences described by Matthew and Luke relate [Col. 0232C] (Matt. 1; Luke 3), he came into this world from the Virgin and, through the mystery of his incarnation, made known that he was king and Lord over all nations, he had written upon his garment and upon his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords.” For where he became known in the world, there he implanted knowledge of election.

CHAPTER LV. ON THE KNEES.

In Sacred Scripture, “knees” sometimes signify works, sometimes the faculties of the spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0232D] From chapter XVII, book XXX on Job.] By “knees” are signified works, as Paul says to some who live laxly: “Lift up your slack hands and feeble knees, and make straight paths for your feet” (Heb. 12:12). Again, by divine admonition Gideon was commanded, upon coming to the river, to remove from the conflict of wars all those whom he saw draw water with bent knees. They were therefore led to the river to drink water, and those who drew water with bent knees were removed from the military enterprise (Judg. 7). For Gideon, coming to battle, signifies the advent of our Redeemer. Of him it is written: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. [Col. 0233A] 23:9). Gideon is interpreted “going around in the womb.” For our Lord, through the power of his majesty, encompasses all things, yet through the grace of his dispensation came by assuming humanity within the Virgin’s womb. Who, then, is “going around in the womb” except almighty God, redeeming us by his dispensation, encompassing all things in his divinity and assuming humanity in a womb? He was incarnate in that womb and was not enclosed, because he was within the womb in the substance of weakness and beyond the world through the power of his majesty. Midian, moreover, is interpreted “from judgment.” For their enemies were to be driven back and destroyed, not because of a fault in the one driving them back, but through the judgment of one judging justly. And therefore they are called “from judgment,” because, alienated from the Redeemer’s grace, they bear even in the meaning of their name the desert of just [Col. 0233B] condemnation. Against them Gideon proceeds to battle. For waters signify the teaching of wisdom, while the upright knee signifies right action. Therefore those who are said to have bent the knee while drinking water withdrew, forbidden from the conflict of wars, because Christ goes to battle against the enemies of faith with those who, while drawing from the streams of teaching, do not bend the uprightness of their works. For all are said to have drunk water, but not all to have stood on a straight knee. Those who bent their knees while drinking water were rejected because, as Paul testifies, “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified” (Rom. 2:13).
