Thus those go forth to battle under Christ’s leadership who show in their works what they proclaim with their mouth; who spiritually draw from the streams of teaching [Col. 0233C] and yet do not bend carnally into perverse works, because, as it is written, “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9).

By “knees” are signified the faculties of the spirit, or habits of sinning, as blessed Job speaks in the person of a penitent: “Why did I not die in the womb? Why, coming forth from the womb, did I not immediately perish? Why was I received upon knees?” (Job 3:12). See again chapter 4 above.

314 CHAPTER LVI. ON THE FEET.

In Sacred Scripture, when “foot” is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies one who sustains by helping, sometimes the holy apostles, sometimes one who runs to the tasks enjoined. When “feet” are used in the plural, they sometimes signify the lowest members of holy Church, sometimes holy preachers or ministers of weak works, sometimes the steps of actions, sometimes the footsteps of Christ, sometimes the two loves—of God and of the world—and sometimes thoughts.

By “foot” is signified one who sustains by helping, as blessed Job says: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame” (Job 29:15). See above, chapter 10, “On the Eye.”

[Note: [Col. 0233D] From book XVIII on Job, chapter XIX, rather far from the beginning.] By “foot” are signified the holy apostles, as blessed Job says: “The torrent divides from the people journeying abroad the stone of darkness and the shadow of death—those whom the foot of the needy man has forgotten, and those without a way” [Col. 0234A] (Job 28:3). For who else is understood here as the needy man except him of whom Paul says: “For our sakes he became poor, though he was rich” (2 Cor. 8:9)? The feet of this needy man were the holy apostles, by whose presence he traversed the whole world, going about among the nations. Of them he says through the Prophet: “I will walk in them” (Lev. 26:12). Was not he his foot who, held in chains, said: “For which I fulfil an embassy in chains” (Eph. 6:20)? But the foot of the needy man forgot those who were the shadow of death and the stone of darkness, because at the very beginning of the Church’s birth, when the holy apostles desired to preach the kingdom of heaven to Judea, seeing [Col. 0234B] that they profited nothing at all among them, they turned aside to preach to the Gentiles, as they themselves say in Acts: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). Of them the Psalmist says: “Mountains shall be transferred into the heart of the sea” (Ps. 45:3), because the apostles, driven away from Judea, were carried over into this sea of the Gentiles. Who, then, are those divided from the pilgrim people of the saints by immense hardness arising from obscurity of heart, like a stone of darkness and a shadow of death, except those whom the foot of the needy man forgot—that is, those whom the Lord’s preachers, through the humility of the poor man, left behind on account of the swelling of their pride, and wholly forgot, [Col. 0234C] while transferring the seeds of their preaching to the fruitfulness of the Gentiles alone? He rightly also calls them “without a way,” because, hardened by their unbelief, they refused to make a path into their heart for the words of life.

[Note: [Col. 0234D] From book XXX on Job, chapter VI.] By “foot” is signified one who runs to the tasks enjoined, as Paul says: “The body is not one member, but many. If the foot should say, ‘Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body,’ it is not therefore not of the body. And if the ear should say, ‘Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body,’ it is not therefore not of the body. If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If it were wholly hearing, where would smell be?” (1 Cor. 12:14–17). And shortly afterward: “If all were one member, [Col. 0234D] where would the body be? But now indeed there are many members, yet one body” (ibid., 19–20). For what is holy Church except the body of her heavenly head? In her, one person, by seeing lofty things, is an eye; another, by doing what is right, is a hand; another, by running to assigned tasks, is a foot; another, by understanding the voice of commandments, is an ear; another, by discerning the stench of evils and the fragrance of goods, is a nose. As bodily members do, they render to one another in turn the offices entrusted to them, and from all of themselves make one body. And while they accomplish different things in charity, they are said to be different in that wherein they are contained. But if all did one single thing, they would not be a body composed of many [Col. 0235A] members, because it would not exist as a manifoldly joined whole if it did not possess this harmonious diversity of members.

[Note: [Col. 0235D] From chapter XIX, book XX on Job, 21.] By “feet” are signified the lowest members of holy Church, as blessed Job has holy Church lament over the overthrow of the weak: “They have overthrown my feet, and have crushed them with their paths as with waves” (Job 30:12). For what is signified by the Church’s feet except her lowest members? Since they serve earthly works, they can be deceived by adversaries all the more readily because they understand lofty things less. The adversaries therefore overthrow these feet because they draw the Church’s lowest members into the error of their doctrine. Overthrown feet cannot keep to the path, because the weak, persuaded by their persecutors’ promises, terrified by threats, or broken by torments, turn aside from the straight way. The paths of adversaries are rightly compared with waves when it is said, “They have crushed them with their paths as with waves,” because the troublesome life of the wicked, with its insolent restlessness, rushes down like a storm to overwhelm, so to speak, the ship of the heart. Of this storm Solomon says: “Like a passing storm, the wicked shall not be” (Prov. 10:25). And when any weak person sees the perverse prospering, the wave of miserable imitation plunges that person into the sea of perversity.

[Note: [Col. 0235D] From Book XIX on Job, chapter X.] By “feet” are meant either holy preachers or ministers of lower duties, as is said through blessed Job: “When I washed my feet with butter” [Col. 0235C] (Job 29:6). Since we have often already said that Christ and the Church are one person—he being the head of this body, and she the body of that head—these words must be understood one way according to the voice of the head, and another according to the voice of the body. Whom, then, do we understand by the Lord’s feet except preachers? Of them he says: “And I will walk in them” (2 Cor. 6:16). The feet, therefore, are washed with butter because holy preachers are filled with the richness of good works. For scarcely can preaching itself occur without some fault being incurred. Any preacher is drawn either to some slight indignation if he is despised, or to some slight vainglory if he is honored by his hearers. Therefore the apostles’ feet too were washed, [Col. 0235D] so that they might be cleansed from every small contagion contracted in preaching itself, like dust gathered on a journey. Blessed James also says: “My brethren, do not become many teachers” (James 3:1); and shortly afterward: “For we all offend in many things” (ibid., 2). The feet, then, are washed with butter because the dust gathered from the glory of preaching is moistened and cleansed by the richness of a good work.

But if we must understand these things according to the voice of the body alone, the feet of the Church are the ministers of lower duties. While they perform outward tasks for necessary uses, they cleave to the earth through their lowly ministry, as feet do. Yet those who preside, who devote themselves diligently to teaching, ought carefully to seek out the hearts of those occupied in such tasks, [Col. 0236A] and by the frequent voice of admonition supply them with the richness they receive through their calling. For since, in one body, the members are mutually concerned for one another, just as we are supported by their ministries, so it is necessary that their inner lives be filled by our efforts. Therefore, when holy teachers preach the anointing of the Lord’s Incarnation to persons devoted to lowly ministries, they wash feet with the butter of speech.

Feet are also usually wounded by the roughness of a journey. Hence it is altogether difficult to travel the path of this life amid earthly affairs and to suffer no wounds from the labor of the road. When vigilant superiors recall to their hearts hearers intent upon outward cares, so that they may recognize the evils they have committed amid even lawful works [Col. 0236B] and mourn what they recognize, they wash feet with butter, because they supply the ointments of repentance for their wounds.

[Note: [Col. 0236D] From Homily 3 on Ezekiel.] By “feet” are meant the steps of deeds, as is said through Ezekiel concerning the holy living creatures: “Their feet were straight feet” (Ezek. 1:7). What, indeed, is denoted by feet except the steps of deeds? Thus the feet of the four living creatures are described as Christ’s, because the works of the holy evangelists 318 and of all the perfect are not bent toward following wickedness. But those do not have straight feet who turn back toward the evils of the world which they left behind. Of them it is written: “The dog has returned to his own vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mire” (2 Pet. 2:22).

The outstanding teacher grieved for certain persons [Col. 0236C] who had bent the straightness of their feet backwards, rebuking them thus: “How do you turn again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you desire to be enslaved anew? You observe days, and years, and seasons; and I fear lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain” (Gal. 4:9–11). He admonishes others, saying: “Lift up the slack hands and the feeble knees, and make straight paths for your feet” (Heb. 12:12).

[Note: [Col. 0236D] In the middle of Homily 38 on the Gospels.] By “feet” are meant Christ’s footprints, as is said in the Gospel of that sinful woman, that she stood behind, beside the Lord’s feet (Luke 7:38). We stand facing the Lord’s feet when, established in sins, we resist his paths. But if after sins we turn to true repentance, we now stand behind, [Col. 0236D] beside the Lord’s feet, because we follow the footprints of him whom we opposed.

By “feet” are meant two loves: the love of God, namely, and the love of the world. Sacred history testifies that blessed Jacob wrestled with the angel: he seized the sinew of Jacob’s thigh, immediately made it wither, and from that time Jacob limped on one foot (Gen. 32). The love of God and the love of the world are, as it were, two feet; and we lean, as it were, upon two feet when we seem to seek God while still holding fast to the world. But when almighty God is already known through desire and understanding, he dries up in us every pleasure of the flesh; and thus, after the recognition of [Col. 0237A] his sweetness, one foot remains sound in us and the other limps, because, as the love of the world is weakened, we must grow strong in the love of God. Therefore, if we hold the angel, we limp on one foot: for while the strength of inward love dries up within us, the strength of the flesh is undoubtedly weakened.

For everyone who limps on one foot leans upon the one foot that is sound. Thus, when earthly desire has already dried up, the person supports himself with all his strength upon the single foot of the love of God, and stands upon it, because he carries suspended from the earth the foot of worldly love which he had been accustomed to set upon the earth.

[Note: [Col. 0237D] This is from the beginning of chapter XIX in Job; it was also incorporated into his rhapsody on John, chapter XXXI, but in the surviving manuscripts of Gregory the passage is not found in so complete a form.] By “feet” are meant thoughts, as we read in the Gospel that, after their preaching, the Lord washed the feet of the holy apostles (John [Col. 0237B] 13). For thoughts are understood by feet, because even in a good work the dust of sin is often contracted; and the footprints of speakers are thereby defiled by that through which the hearts of hearers are cleansed. Rightly, after their preaching, the Lord washed the apostles’ feet, lest the mind be secretly polluted by some contagion of sin arising from the grace of preaching itself; lest it attribute to itself what it did, and, by attributing to itself what it did, lose it.

For some people, when they speak words of exhortation, inwardly exalt themselves, however slightly, because the grace of preaching is conveyed through them. While they wash others’ deeds by their word, they take, as it were, the dust of an evil thought from a good journey. What, then, was it to wash the disciples’ feet after preaching, except to wipe away the dust of thoughts after [Col. 0237C] the glory of preaching and cleanse the steps of the heart from inward pride?

## CHAPTER LVII. ON THE ANKLE

[Note: [Col. 0238D] From chapter XIV, Book XXII on Job, after the middle of section 22.] By “ankles” are meant the first traces of a good work, as Ezekiel declares in a figurative account. Concerning the man whom he sees on a high mountain, he says: “He measured a thousand cubits, and led me through the water up to the ankles. Again he measured a thousand, and led me up to the knees; and he measured a thousand, and led me through the waters up to the loins; and he measured a thousand, and led me through the torrent which I could not cross, because the waters of the deep torrent had risen, which cannot be forded” (Ezek. 47). [Col. 0237D]

What, then, is signified by the number one thousand except the fullness of the gift bestowed? Therefore the man who appeared measures a thousand cubits, and the prophet is led through the waters up to the ankles, because our Redeemer, when we turn to him, grants us the fullness of a good beginning and instills into the first traces of our work the gift of spiritual wisdom. For water coming up to the ankles means that, through wisdom received, we now keep the footsteps of desired uprightness. He measures another thousand and the prophet is led through the water up to the knees, because, when fullness in good work is granted, our wisdom is increased so far that it is not at all bent in evil [Col. 0238A] actions. Hence Paul says: “Lift up the slack hands and the feeble knees, and make straight paths” (Heb. 12:12). The water reaches the knee when received wisdom perfectly binds us to the uprightness of good work.

He again measures a thousand, and the prophet is led through the water up to the loins, because fullness of work then grows in us when received wisdom has extinguished within us, as far as possible, every pleasure of the flesh. For unless pleasure of the flesh were in the loins, the Psalmist would not say: “Burn my loins and my heart” (Ps. 25:2). Water comes up to the loins when the sweetness of wisdom destroys even the impulses of the flesh, so that the fires of love which could burn the mind grow cold.

He still measures a thousand: namely, the torrent which the prophet could not cross, of which he also says, “For the waters of the deep torrent had risen, which cannot be forded.” Once the perfection of work has been received, one arrives at contemplation. In that contemplation, while the mind is raised on high, it sees, being lifted up in God, that it cannot penetrate what it sees; and it touches, as it were, the water of a torrent which it cannot cross, because it beholds in contemplation what delights it and yet cannot perfectly behold that very thing which delights it. Therefore the prophet reaches water which he does not cross, because, when at last we are led to the contemplation of wisdom, its very immensity, which raises a human being above himself, [Col. 0238C] denies to the human mind a full knowledge of itself, so that the mind may love it by touching it, yet never penetrate it by crossing beyond it.

[Note: [Col. 0238D] From chapter XLII, Book I on Job.] By “ankle” is meant the end of life. Thus Joseph, who is described as having persevered righteous among his brothers until the end, is said alone to have possessed a tunic reaching to the ankles (Gen. 37:3). For what is an ankle-length tunic except a completed action? A tunic stretched out, as it were, covers the body’s ankle when a good action directs us before God’s eyes to the end of life.

## CHAPTER LVIII. ON THE HEEL

By “heel” is meant the end of our action, as is said by the Psalmist: “They will watch my heel” [Col. 0238D] (Ps. 56:7). See chapter 4 above.

## CHAPTER LIX. ON THE SOLE

In Sacred Scripture, “sole” sometimes means the first righteous man, Abel; sometimes the action of life; and sometimes the end of life.

[Note: [Col. 0238D] From chapter II, Book III on Job, after the middle.] By “sole” is meant the first righteous man, Abel, as is said of blessed Job in the person of the Lord: “Satan went forth from the presence of the Lord and struck Job with a grievous sore, from the sole of his foot to his crown” (Job 2:7). No one comes into this life among the elect without enduring its adversities; moreover, those who lived piously from the very beginning of the world and suffered cruel things were members [Col. 0239A] of our Redeemer. Did not Abel declare himself to be a member of him whose death, concerning whom it is written, “Like a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent and shall not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7), he signified not only by being pleasing in sacrifice but also by dying silently? From the very beginning of the world, therefore, the adversary tried to assault the body of our Redeemer. Thus he inflicted a wound from the sole of the foot to the crown, because, beginning first with human beings, he reached in his violence even to the very head of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0239D] From Homily 3 on Ezekiel.] By “sole” is meant the action of life, as is said through Ezekiel concerning the holy living creatures: “The sole of their foot was like the sole of a calf’s foot” [Col. 0239B] (Ezek. 1:7). That holy preachers are denoted by the name “oxen” is taught by the holy apostle Paul when expounding the testimony of the law: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain” (1 Tim. 5:18). Therefore, in holy preachers, the sole of the foot is like the sole of a calf’s foot: that is, it moves with maturity, strength, and a divided hoof. For every holy preacher has dignity in maturity, strength in work, and discernment in the division of the hoof. His preaching is not readily received if he appears frivolous in conduct; nor will there be any display of maturity if strength in work is lacking against every adversity. But the strength of work itself admits the merit of virtue only if it is accompanied by discernment in understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0239D] From Book XIV on Job, chapter XI, section 5.] By “sole” is meant the end of life, as Baldad says concerning the [Col. 0239C] wicked person: “His sole will be caught in a snare” (Job 18:9). When the perverse mind sees that it has fallen into sin, it seeks to escape the snares of sin by some superficial device of thought. But fearing either terrors or the reproaches of people, it chooses to die eternally rather than suffer some temporal adversity. Hence it gives itself wholly to the vices by which it knows itself already bound. Therefore, the sole of one whose life remains bound in guilt to the [Col. 0240A] end is held in a snare.

## CHAPTER LX. ON THE NAIL

[Note: [Col. 0239D] From Book XIV, chapter XV, section 26.] By “nail” is meant the end of any matter, as is said through the prophet: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus on a diamond nail” (Jer. 17:1). The nail is, indeed, at the end of the body. The diamond is so hard a stone that it cannot be cut with iron. By the iron stylus is signified a strong judgment, and by the diamond nail an eternal end. Thus the sin of Judah is said to be written with an iron stylus on a diamond nail because the guilt of the Jews is reserved by God’s strong judgment for an infinite end.

## CHAPTER LXI. ON THE HOOF

[Col. 0240B]

[Note: [Col. 0240D] From chapter XIII, Book XXXI on Job.] By “hoof” is meant the perfection of virtues, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the holy preacher under the figure of a horse: “He digs the earth with his hoof.” Strength for labor is customarily recognized in a horse’s hoof (Job 39). What, then, is demonstrated by the hoof except the perfection of virtues in the holy preacher? He digs the earth with his hoof when, by the example of his works, he expels earthly thoughts from the hearts of his hearers. The hoof digs the earth because the good teacher empties the hearts of hearers of worldly cares when he shows by his deeds that he despises the world.

Let us see how Paul digs the earth of his hearers’ hearts with the [Col. 0240C] hoof of displayed virtue. He says to his disciples: “Think upon these things, which you have learned and received and heard and seen in me; do these things, and the God of peace will be with you” (Phil. 4). And again: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 11). Therefore, one who corrects others by the example of his work certainly digs the earth with his hoof. One who also subdues the flesh by strict abstinence digs the earth with his hoof.

## THE SIXTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0239]

## CHAPTER I. ON EARTH

[Col. 0239D]

In Sacred Scripture, “earth” sometimes means the firmness of the heavenly homeland; sometimes the holy Church; sometimes the Synagogue; sometimes the Gentile world; sometimes the soul of a righteous person; sometimes a sinful soul; sometimes flesh; sometimes the human soul; sometimes any sinner; sometimes the subject people; sometimes Christ’s humanity; sometimes hell; sometimes Christ’s flesh; sometimes those occupied with earthly affairs; and sometimes earthly action.

[Note: [Col. 0240D] From Book XII on Job, chapter XXII.] By “earth” is meant the firmness of the heavenly homeland, as is said by the Psalmist: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13); and again: “My portion in the land of the living” [Col. 0240D] (Ps. 141:6). Hence again, in the book of blessed Job, it is written concerning every reprobate person: “He shall not be enriched, nor shall his substance endure, nor shall he cast his root into the earth” (Job 15:29).

That person is enriched with virtues whose mind almighty God inhabits. But because the thought of the proud person is not inhabited by the grace of its Creator, that person is surely not enriched with virtues. Because what is inward is empty, it is said: “He shall not be enriched.” But because outwardly he swells with what is transient, it is rightly added: “Nor shall his substance endure”; as though it were plainly said: What he seems to possess outwardly [Col. 0241A] passes away, while inwardly he does not possess that which could not pass away. Hence it is fittingly added: “Nor shall he cast his root into the earth.” What do we understand by earth except the recompense of eternal life? The root, however, means thought. Therefore the proud person does not cast his root into the earth, because he never plants the thought of his heart in the desire for eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0241D] From Book XIX on Job, chapter XII.] By “earth” is meant the holy Church, as it is written: “Let the earth bring forth green grass yielding seed, and the fruit-bearing tree producing fruit according to its kind” (Gen. 1). This was done truly in such a way as to signify what was to be done. For the Church is figured by the earth: it refreshes us with the food of the word and guards us with the shelter of its protection. It feeds by speaking and protects by aiding, so that it brings forth not only the grass of refreshment [Col. 0241B] but also the tree of protection with the fruit of action.

Hence again, in the book of blessed Job, it is said concerning the Lord: “He stretches out the north over the void; he suspends the earth over nothing” (Job 26). By “north” the devil is commonly meant, who, in order to bind the hearts of the Gentiles with the cold of torpor, said: “I will sit on the side of the north” (Isa. 14). [Note: [Col. 0241D] From Book XVII on Job, chapter XIII.] He is stretched over the void because he possesses hearts not filled with the grace of divine love. Yet almighty God is able to fill with the gift of his grace even vessels of the devil, empty of every virtue, and to establish in them the firmness of divine fear, though he sees that no upright action strengthens them. Hence it is fittingly added: “And he suspends the earth over nothing.”

What, indeed, is meant by earth except the holy Church, [Col. 0241C] which, receiving the words of preaching, yields the fruit of good work? Of it Moses says: “Let the earth hear the words of my mouth; let my speech be expected like rain” (Deut. 32). And what is meant by “nothing” except the Gentile peoples? Of them the prophet says: “All nations are accounted as nothing and vanity” (Isa. 40:17). Therefore the earth is suspended over that nothing which had previously been held empty under the north: that is, the hearts of the Gentiles, formerly oppressed by the devil’s torpor, were filled with the love of God.

[Note: [Col. 0241D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XIX.] By “earth” is meant the Synagogue, as is written in the book of blessed Job: “The earth from which bread sprang in its place was overturned by fire” (Job 28:5). What is meant by earth except Judaea? This land—that is, Judaea—used to give bread, because it brought forth the words of the law. Since the reprobate could no longer understand and expound that law, the prophet Jeremiah laments in Lamentations: “The little children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. 4:4).

But this earth was overturned by fire in its place, because, seeing the signs of the faithful, it burned itself with the torch of envy. Since envy always springs from pride, it perished by fire in its place: it burned with envy because it did not abandon pride. Therefore the earth which formerly had bread [Col. 0242A] was afterwards overturned by fire, because the Synagogue, which had set forth God’s commandments through the law, consumed itself with the torch of envy while persecuting the newborn Church. Did it not burn with the torches of its wakefulness when, seeing the signs of our Redeemer, some of its own said: “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs” (John 11:47)? Or again: “You see that we gain nothing; behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12:19). They saw that by which they ought to have been converted, and became more perverse through it. They sought to destroy him whom they saw giving life to the dead. They held the law in their mouths, but persecuted the Author of the law. Therefore the earth from which bread sprang was overturned by fire in its place, because Judaea first possessed within itself the law that might refresh it, and afterward the envy by which it might burn itself.

[Col. 0242B] [Note: [Col. 0242D] From Book XXIX on Job, chapter XIII, section 16.] By “earth” is meant the Gentile world, as the Lord asks in the book of blessed Job: “Who gave a course to the most violent rain, and a way to the sounding thunder, that it might rain upon earth without human beings, in the wilderness where no human being dwells, that it might fill the pathless and desolate place and bring forth green grasses?” (Job 38:25–27).

What is the most violent rain except the immense power of preaching? Rain is violent when holy preachers urge people to believe in eternal joys. But rain is most violent when they admonish people to abandon possessions for the sake of hope, to despise all visible things for invisible things, and to endure the punishments and torments of the present age for the joys that have been heard of. What, however, is denoted by thunder [Col. 0242C] except preaching about heavenly terror? When human hearts receive that terror, they are shaken. But since any preacher can give words to ears, while he cannot open hearts, the Lord declares that he himself gives both the course of rain and the way of sounding thunder, because, when he grants the words of preaching, he pierces hearts through fear.

Having received its way, what this rain and thunder does is then added: “That it might rain upon earth without human beings, in the wilderness.” What do we understand by earth except the Gentile world? [Note: [Col. 0242D] From chapter XIV.] Because it maintained no worship of the Divinity and showed in itself no form of good work, it was indeed a wilderness. Because it had no lawgiver, and none who sought God rationally, there was, as it were, no human being there; and, occupied only by beasts, it was empty of mortals. To rain upon earth in the wilderness, however, is to preach the word of God to the Gentile world. Of this wilderness earth it is elsewhere said: “He set a way in the wilderness” (Isa. 43:19). Of this preaching granted to the Gentile world the Psalmist testifies: “He set rivers in the wilderness” (Ps. 106:33).

Therefore the Lord gave a course to the most violent rain and a way to the sounding thunder, that it might rain upon earth in the wilderness, fill the pathless and desolate place, and bring forth green grasses: that is, he joined inward inspiration to outward [Col. 0243A] preaching, so that the parched hearts of the Gentiles might grow green, closed hearts might be opened, empty hearts might be filled, and barren hearts might sprout.

[Note: [Col. 0243D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter VI, section 9.] By “earth” is meant the soul of a righteous person, as is written when the Lord himself asks blessed Job: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38:4). What is meant by earth except the soul of a righteous person? For the mind of a sinner is dust, because it rises upon the surface and is carried away by the breeze of temptation. Thus it is written: “Not so the wicked, not so; but like dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:4). Nothing prevents earth from being understood as the soul of the righteous, of which it is written: “For earth, drinking the rain often coming upon it and producing vegetation useful to those by whom it is cultivated, receives a blessing” (Heb. 6:7).

But the foundation [Col. 0243B] of this earth is faith. The foundation of this earth is laid when divine fear, the first cause of steadfastness, is inspired in the hidden places of the heart. One person does not yet believe the eternal things he hears; when faith is given to him, a foundation is now laid for the structure of work which follows. Another already believes eternal things, yet does not fear; he despises the terror of the coming judgment and boldly entangles himself in sins of flesh and spirit. When fear of future things is suddenly instilled in this person, foundations are now constructed so that the building of a good life may rise.

Once the foundation of salutary fear has been laid, when the structure of virtues is raised on high, it is necessary for everyone making progress carefully to measure his own strength, so that, when through divine construction he has begun to be great, he may unceasingly consider what he was; thus, humbly attending to what he was found to be by merit, he may by no means claim for himself what he was made by grace. Therefore blessed Job is now recalled to himself by the heavenly voice; lest he dare glory in his virtues, he is reminded of his former life, and is told: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” As though Truth were plainly saying to the sinner whom it has justified: Do not attribute to yourself the virtues you have received from me. Do not exalt yourself against me because of my gift. Recall where I found you when I made you firm by my fear.

[Note: [Col. 0243D] From Homily 5 on Ezekiel.] By “earth” is meant the sinful soul. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I will except that it should burn?” (Luke 12:49). Fire commonly figures the Holy Spirit, whereas earth means the sinner’s soul. The Lord therefore came to cast fire upon earth so that it might be kindled, because, unless sinners’ hearts received warmth from the fire of truth, they would never burn with love for God. But when the carnal mind receives the Holy Spirit, kindled by spiritual love it mourns the evil it has done; and earth burns when, as conscience accuses itself, the sinner’s heart burns and is consumed in the sorrow of repentance.

[Note: [Col. 0243D] From Book XXXI on Job, chapter XIII.] By “earth” is meant flesh, as the Lord, speaking to blessed Job and describing the strong preacher under the figure of a horse, says: “He digs the earth with his hoof” [Col. 0244A] (Job 39:21). See chapter LI, Book V.

By “earth” in the same passage of Job is expressed earthly thought; for one digs the earth with the hoof when a preacher rigorously examines earthly thoughts within himself.

[Note: [Col. 0244D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XXII, before the middle.] By “earth” is meant the human soul, as is said in the book of Job concerning wisdom: “Man does not know its price, nor is it found in the land of those who live pleasantly” (Job 28:13). What wisdom, indeed, does the holy man contemplate except that of which Paul says, “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24)? Of it Solomon wrote: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9:1); and of it the Psalmist said: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24).

Certainly man does not know the price of this wisdom, because he finds nothing worthy to be valued against it. Yet it is not said that this price of wisdom exists and is unknown; rather, it is said to be unknown because it is absent, according to that manner of speaking by which a person caught in difficulty, finding no remedy for help, is accustomed to confess that he does not know what to do. Thus, not to know the price of this wisdom is not to find a meritorious work worthy to obtain it. For we give a price so that, in exchange for it, we may possess the thing we seek. But what did we give that we might deserve to receive this wisdom, which is Christ? For we have been redeemed by grace. The only works we gave were those done in evil living; if just retribution had been maintained, not Christ but punishments would have been returned to us. [Col. 0244C]

Since, therefore, we were found wicked when wisdom came, what good work did we give by which we might deserve to receive that wisdom? Thus man does not know the price of this wisdom because everyone distinguished from brute animals by rational understanding knows that he has not been saved by his own merits, and recognizes that he gave no good work by which he came to faith. To give a price, as it were, in order to receive wisdom is to anticipate God, who is to be known, by the reward of one’s own action. He knew that there was no price for this wisdom when he said: “Who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?” (Rom. 11:35). Hence it is again written: “By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, but is the gift; not from works, lest anyone [Col. 0244D] should boast” (Eph. 2:8–9). Hence again he says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10).

Since we gave no good work by which we might deserve to receive this wisdom, it is rightly said: “Man does not know its price” (Job 28:13). [Note: [Col. 0244D] This is from the end of chapter XXIII of the said Book on Job.] For everyone who now uses reason despises himself under the understanding of this wisdom all the more deeply as he knows more truly its inward realities, so that he sees himself as unworthy to have attained that wisdom through which it is freely brought about that he becomes worthy. Of it it is rightly added immediately: “It is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly.” [Note: [Col. 0244D] From chapter XXIV, ibid.] What is denoted by “earth” here except the human soul? [Col. 0245A] Of it the Psalmist says: “My soul is like earth without water before you” (Ps. 142:6). This wisdom cannot be found in the land of those who live pleasantly, because whoever is still fed by this life’s pleasures is separated from the understanding of eternal wisdom. Wisdom and prudence, therefore, cannot be found in the earth of those who live pleasantly, because they are truly foolish in proportion as, losing greater things, they rejoice in trivial ones. [Note: [Col. 0245D] From the end of the chapter.] Wisdom cannot be found in the land of those who live pleasantly, because those who live pleasantly in this world are still so foolish that they do not even know the thing from which they have fallen.

[Note: [Col. 0245D] From Book XXXI on Job, chapter XV, after the middle, section 25.] By “earth” is meant any sinner, as is said in the book of blessed Job concerning the holy preacher: “Burning and neighing, he swallows the earth and does not regard the sound of the trumpet” (Job 39:24). What is called earth except a sinner? For to the first human being in sin it was said: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:14, according to the Septuagint). What else is the trumpet, which declares the crisis of battle, than the voice of worldly powers, which, when resisted and despised, prepares a contest of death? Trumpets sound when the powers of this world sternly forbid holy persons to speak. But because the holy preacher, inflamed by the zeal of the Holy Spirit, does not cease, even amid punishments, to draw whatever sinners he can to himself, he surely swallows earth while burning. And because he does not fear persecutors’ threats, he does not regard the trumpet’s sounding blast.

This trumpet had sounded from the chief priests when they forbade [Col. 0245C] the scourged apostles to speak of God, as is written: “They commanded them not to speak in the name of Jesus” (Acts 4:18). But let us see how the sound of the trumpet does not frighten God’s horse. Peter says: “It is necessary to obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). What does he say to other persecutors as well? “For we cannot refrain from speaking of the things which we have heard and also seen” (Acts 4:20). Therefore the horse does not fear the trumpet’s sound, because the outstanding preacher, despising worldly powers, dreads no sounds of threats.

[Note: [Col. 0245D] From Book XXII on Job, chapter XV.] By “earth” are meant the subject people and household. Thus blessed Job says: “If my earth cries out against me” (Job 31:38). Everyone who governs a household under private law and presides, for the common good, over a body of faithful people—inasmuch as he possesses rights of governance over the faithful entrusted to him—holds, as it were, earth to be cultivated. For by divine dispensation each person is set over others so that the mind of those subject to him, like earth laid beneath, may be made fruitful by the seed of his preaching. But the earth cries out against its possessor if either the private household or the holy Church reasonably murmurs against the one set over it on account of some injustice. For earth to cry out is for subjects rightly to grieve at the injustice of their ruler.

[Col. 0246A] [Note: [Col. 0246D] From Book III on Job, chapter XV.] By “earth” is meant Christ’s humanity; hence it is said to Israel: “You shall make me an altar of earth” (Exod. 20). To make God an altar of earth is to hope in the Lord’s Incarnation. For then our offering is received by God, when on this altar—that is, upon faith in the Lord’s Incarnation—our humility places whatever it works. Therefore we lay an offering upon an altar of earth if we establish our actions firmly in faith in the Lord’s Incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 0246D] From Book IX on Job, chapter XXX.] By “earth” is meant hell. Hence blessed Job prays, saying: “Leave me, that I may lament my pain a little before I go and do not return 332 to a dark earth covered with the gloom of death” (Job 10:21). What is denoted by the name “dark earth” except the grim prisons of Tartarus? The gloom of eternal [Col. 0246B] death covers them because it separates forever from the light of life all those who are damned. Nor without reason is hell called earth, because all whom it captures are held fast. For it is written: “One generation passes away and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever” (Eccl. 1:4). Therefore the prisons of hell are rightly called dark earth, because those whom they receive for punishment are not tormented by a passing or phantom imagination, but are reserved by customary retribution for everlasting condemnation. Hell is rightly called earth, then, because it holds those received into it firmly.

But the holy man, whether speaking in his own person or in that of the human race, asks to be left alone before he goes; not because one who mourns sin will go to the dark earth, [Col. 0246C] but because one who neglects to mourn will undoubtedly go there. It is like a creditor saying to a debtor: “Pay the debt before you are bound over for the debt.” Yet the debtor is not bound over if he does not delay paying what he owes. Hence it is rightly added: “I shall not return,” because the mercy that spares never again frees those whom the justice of the Judge has once condemned in places of punishment.

These places are described more subtly still when it is said: “A land of misery and darkness.” Misery pertains to pain; darkness to blindness. Therefore that place which holds those cast out from the sight of the strict Judge is called a land of misery and darkness, because outward pain torments those whom inward blindness darkens, separated as they are from the true light.

[Note: [Col. 0246D] From Book IX on Job, ch. XV, 21.] By “earth” Christ’s flesh is understood, as blessed Job says: “The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; he covers the face of its judges” (Job 9:21). What is expressed by the name “earth” except the flesh of our Redeemer? And what is signified by the designation “wicked one” except the devil? The hands of this wicked one were those who raged in the death of our Redeemer. The earth, therefore, was given into the hand of the wicked, because the ancient enemy was unable, by personally tempting him, to corrupt the Redeemer’s mind; but he was permitted to destroy his flesh through his agents for three days, and, without knowing it, by that very permission served the dispensation of heavenly mercy. For, assailing our Redeemer with three temptations, he could not tempt the heart of God. But when he stirred Judas’s mind to bring about Christ’s death, and supplied him with a cohort and attendants from the chief priests and Pharisees, then indeed this wicked one stretched out his hands against the earth. The judges of this earth were the priests and rulers, Pilate, and the mocking soldiers. Thus this wicked one covered the face of its judges, because he veiled the hearts of the persecutors with the cloud of malice, lest they should recognize their Author. Hence Paul says: “To this very day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart” (2 Cor. 3:15). And again he says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). The face of its judges was thus covered, because the mind of the persecutors, [Col. 0247B] though it could lay hold of him in the flesh, did not recognize him as God even through his miracles.

[Note: [Col. 0247D] From Book XV on Job, ch. XIX.] By “earth” are signified those who, though occupied with earthly affairs, attain eternal life through the aid of almsgiving and tears. Thus the Psalmist says, when the Lord’s coming to judgment is announced: “He summoned the heavens above, and the earth, that he might judge his people” (Ps. 49:4). He summons the heavens above when those who, abandoning all their possessions, maintained the manner of life of heaven are called to sit in judgment and come as judges with him. The earth also is summoned above when those who had been bound in earthly occupations nevertheless sought heavenly rather than earthly gain in them—those to whom it is said: “I was a stranger, and you took me in; naked, and you clothed me” (Matt. 25:35).

Hence again, in the book of blessed Job, concerning the condemnation of any hypocrite, or spiritually of Antichrist, it is written: “The heavens shall reveal his iniquity, and the earth shall rise up against him” (Job 20:27). [Note: [Col. 0247D] The following is excerpted piecemeal from the beginning and middle.] For what do we understand by the heavens except the righteous? And what by the earth except those who, occupied with earthly affairs, seek heavenly rather than earthly gain? The heavens reveal this hypocrite’s iniquity, and the earth rises against him, when both those who come as judges with God and those who are delivered through judgment demand testimony against his wickedness. Therefore nothing that he did is concealed at the time of condemnation; and although many of his deeds are now hidden from human beings by duplicity, on the day of condemnation whatever lay hidden within him will be revealed.

[Note: [Col. 0247D] From Book XIV on Job, ch. IX.] By “earth” earthly action is signified. Hence, under the name of the daughter of Babylon, it is said through the prophet to every mind: “Come down; sit in the dust, daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground.” For although dust is always earth, earth is not always dust. What, indeed, should we understand by dust except thoughts, which, as they roll about importunately and silently in the mind [otherwise, “fly forth”], blind its eyes? And what is signified by earth except earthly thought? But because the mind of the reprobate is cast down first to think evil thoughts and afterwards to perform them, the daughter of Babylon, who has descended from the judgment of earthly uprightness, is rightly told in the striking sentence first to sit in dust and then on earth: unless she had first cast herself down in thought, she would not have clung to evil action.

## CHAPTER II. ON SOIL

[Note: [Col. 0248D] From Book XVII on Job, ch. X, 9.] By “soil” the mind of the elect is signified, as Isaiah says: “Upon the soil of my people thorns and briars shall rise—how much more upon all the houses of joy of the exulting city?” (Isa. 32:13). The Lord calls the soil of his people the mind of all his elect. But the house of joy of the exulting city is the mind of the wicked person who, neglecting to consider the punishments to come, abandons himself to the pleasure of the flesh and rejoices vainly. He says, therefore: “Upon the soil of my people thorns and briars shall rise,” etc. As though he plainly said: If vices oppress the minds of those who afflict themselves out of longing for the heavenly homeland, beneath what sins do those lie who abandon themselves to fleshly pleasure without any fear?

## CHAPTER III. ON CLODS

In Sacred Scripture, “clods” sometimes signify the collections of individual groups in Judaea; sometimes persons united through charity, or the distinct orders of the elect in the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0248D] From Book XVIII on Job, ch. XIX, before the end.] By “clods” are signified the collections of individual groups in Judaea, as blessed Job says of Judaea: “Its clods are gold” (Job 28:6). For what do clods signify except collections and multitudes of individual orders? Clods are compacted from moisture and dust. Therefore all who, sprinkled with the dew of grace, confessed in true knowledge that they were dust by reason of the debt of death, shone with the virtue of life and lay there like golden clods. This land—that is, Judaea—had clods in the prophets, clods in the teachers, clods in the ancient fathers, who were held together, through a great infusion of grace, in unity of confession and conduct. Let him therefore say: “Its clods are gold,” because in it the multitude of spiritual persons shone with a virtue so much greater as it was bound together in greater unanimity toward God and neighbour.

[Col. 0248D] [Note: [Col. 0248D] From Book XXX on Job, ch. VI.] By “clods” are signified those united through charity. Hence the Lord asks blessed Job: “When was the dust founded in the earth, and the clods compacted?” (Job 38:38). Clods are formed from coagulated moisture and dust. Thus in this earth—that is, the Church—the clods were compacted, because sinners, having been called and sprinkled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, are united in the gathering of charity.

These clods were compacted when peoples who had previously thought differently, as though through the dispersal of dust, afterwards, having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, came together in the most peaceable harmony of unanimity, [Col. 0249A] so that, although they were three thousand, or again five thousand, Scripture testifies: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). From one dust, indeed, yet distinguished as though by different masses, the Lord daily compacts these clods in the earth, because, while preserving the unity of the sacrament, he gathers faithful peoples in the Church according to the variety of persons and languages. The Lord already signified these clods when he commanded the people to recline in groups of fifty or a hundred for the eating of the loaves and fishes (Matt. 14).

[Note: [Col. 0249D] From the book and chapter cited.] Clods may also signify, if we consider the diversity of merits in the Church, the distinct orders of believers. For while one order consists of preachers, another of hearers, another and another of subjects, another of married persons, another of the continent, another of penitents, [Col. 0249B] and another of virgins, there is, as it were, a distinct variety of clods from one earth, while diverse merits of those doing good are displayed in one faith and one charity. [Note: [Col. 0249D] This is from the end of the chapter.] But these clods could by no means rise, compacted from dust, unless the dust had first received water and been made solid by the moisture it had absorbed; for unless the grace of the Holy Spirit were poured upon sinners, the unity of charity would not hold them together in works of faith.

## CHAPTER IV. ON FURROWS

[Note: [Col. 0249D] From Book XXII on Job, ch. XV.] By “furrows” are signified those well cultivated by the ploughshare of speech, as blessed Job says: “If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep with it” (Job 31:38). Everyone who either governs a household by private right or presides over many faithful persons for the common good, in possessing the rights of governance over the faithful entrusted to him, holds nothing other than land to be cultivated. For each person is set over others by divine dispensation so that the mind of those subject to him, like the substance of land, may be made fruitful by the seed of preaching.

Land uncultivated by any labour often produces some food for human use; ploughed land, however, bears crops for satiety. So there are some who, though not cut by any ploughshare of speech or exhortation, nevertheless produce from themselves certain gifts, however small, like land not yet ploughed. Yet there are others, ever intent upon hearing and retaining holy preaching, who are cleft from their former hardness of mind as by a ploughshare of speech; they receive the seeds of exhortation and yield the fruits of good works through the furrows of voluntary affliction.

Often, however, those who preside commit some injustice, and thus those who ought to have benefited their subjects harm them instead. When the untrained see this, they are stirred to murmur against their ruler, yet they do not grieve deeply for their neighbours out of compassion. But when those already worn down by the plough of reading and cultivated for the fruit of good works see innocent persons burdened even in small matters, they immediately turn to lamentation through compassion, [Col. 0250A] because they bewail as their own the injustices suffered by their neighbour. For the perfect, continually instructed in spiritual matters, know how to groan over others’ bodily losses precisely insofar as they have learned no longer to grieve over their own. Therefore every ruler who acts perversely toward his subjects has both the land crying out against him and the furrows weeping: against his injustice, the untrained peoples indeed burst forth in murmuring voices, but the perfect afflict themselves with tears over his smallest act. What the inexperienced cry out and grieve over, subjects of more proved life bewail in silence.

## CHAPTER V. ON DUST

[Col. 0250B] In Sacred Scripture, “dust” sometimes signifies earthly understanding; sometimes earthly business or desire; sometimes the subtle examination of our works; sometimes the instability of sinners; sometimes the darkness of earthly thought; and sometimes the frailty of the human condition.

[Note: [Col. 0250D] This is from the end of ch. XII, Book III on Job, 17.] By “dust” earthly understanding is signified, as is written concerning the friends of blessed Job: “When they came to him, they scattered dust upon their heads” (Job 2:12). Although the friends of blessed Job came to him with a good intention, they nevertheless bear the image of heretics, because by speaking indiscreetly they fall into fault. Hence blessed Job says to them: “I desire to dispute with God, first showing you to be fabricators of lies and cultivators of perverse doctrines” (Job 13:3). [Note: [Col. 0250D] From ch. XIV, in the same work.] Heretics, because they wish to teach the holy Church, approach it as though to console it. What, then, is dust except earthly understanding? What is the head except that which is foremost in us, namely the mind? What is heaven except the command of heavenly speech? To scatter dust upon the head toward heaven, therefore, is to corrupt the mind by secular understanding and to entertain earthly meanings concerning heavenly words. They generally scrutinize the divine words more than they comprehend them. Thus they scatter dust upon their heads because, in God’s commandments, they strain beyond the capacity of their minds through earthly understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0250D] From Book XXXII on Job, ch. VII, after the middle.] By “dust” earthly business [Col. 0250D] or desire is signified, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the proud: “Hide them together in the dust, and plunge their faces into the pit” (Job 11). As though he said: “Do as I do.” For the Lord, in righteous judgment, hides the proud and impious in dust, because he permits their hearts to be oppressed by the earthly occupations which they choose, despising love for the Creator. Hence, when at the end he examines their life, he does not acknowledge it as his own, saying: “I do not know who you are” (Luke 13). The life of the wicked is hidden beneath dust because it is weighed down by base and low desires. Whoever still desires the things [Col. 0251A] of the world does not, as it were, appear before the face of the true light, because he lies hidden beneath the dust of earthly thought.

[Note: [Col. 0251D] From Book I on Job, ch. XIX, near the end, 39.] By “dust” the subtle examination of our works is signified. Hence Moses is told: “Take for yourself spices—stacte, onycha, sweet-smelling galbanum, and the purest frankincense; all shall be of equal weight. You shall make incense compounded by the work of the perfumer, carefully mixed and pure. When you have crushed all of them into the finest dust, you shall put some of it before the tabernacle of testimony” (Exod. 30:30). We make incense compounded of spices when, upon the altar of good work, we give forth fragrance through a multiplicity of virtues. It is to be mixed and pure, because the more one virtue is joined to another, the more sincerely the incense of good work is offered. Therefore we crush all the spices into the finest dust when we beat our good deeds, as if in a mortar, by the secret examination of the heart, and scrutinize them subtly to see whether they are truly good. To reduce spices to dust, then, is to examine virtues in reflection and bring them back to the subtlety of hidden judgment. And it should be noted that the public command says: “You shall put some of it before the tabernacle of testimony,” because our good works truly please in the Judge’s sight when the mind crushes them by more subtle reflection and, as it were, produces dust from the spices, lest the good that is done be coarse and hard; unless the mind pulverizes it by strict examination, it does not emit its fragrance with sufficient subtlety.

[Col. 0251C] [Note: [Col. 0251D] From Book XXX on Job, ch. VI, 10.] By “dust” the instability of the sinner is signified, as the Lord says to blessed Job: “When was the dust founded in the earth?” (Job 38:4). What do we understand by dust except sinners, who, not made firm by any weight of reason, are carried away by the breeze of every temptation? Of them it is written: “Not so the wicked, not so; but they are like dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:4). Dust was founded in the earth when called sinners in the Church were made firm by the reasoning of the faith handed down, so that those formerly made unstable and tossed about by the breeze of temptation might afterwards stand immovable against temptations and, clinging steadfastly to God, maintain the fixed weight of good living.

[Col. 0251D] [Note: [Col. 0251D] From Book VIII on Job, ch. VI, after the middle, 11.] By “dust” the darkness of earthly thought is expressed, as blessed Job says: “My flesh is clothed with rottenness and with the filth of dust” (Job 7:5). Since man voluntarily abandoned his innate stability and plunged himself into the abyss of corruption, he is now, by just judgment, afflicted for unclean works. To put it thus: our very nature, made subject to the punishment of its fault, has now become outside nature; abandoned, it is led even to perverse deeds, while restrained from the urgency of perverse deeds it is darkened. Thus, by the performance of unlawful action, rottenness infects the flesh; but, by consenting to vices, dust rises before the eyes as the lightness of wicked thought. We are worn down by rottenness when we consent to vices; by enduring images of vices in the heart, we are beset with the filth of dust. He says, therefore: “My flesh is clothed with rottenness and with the filth of dust.” As though he plainly said: The carnal life that I endure is either defiled by the corruption of slippery conduct or oppressed by the darkness of miserable thought arising from the memory of vices.

If, however, we understand this in the voice of the universal Church, we undoubtedly find her at one time corrupted by the rottenness of the flesh and at another burdened by the filth of dust. For many are in her who, while serving the love of the flesh, rot in the stench of lust. And there are some who abstain from fleshly pleasure but nevertheless lie with their whole mind in earthly pursuits. Let the holy Church, then, speaking in the voice of one of her members, declare what she endures from each sort of person. “My flesh is clothed [Col. 0252B] with rottenness and with the filth of dust.” As though she plainly indicates: Many are my members through faith, yet they are not sound or clean in conduct, because men either sink through shameful desires into the rottenness of corruption, or, devoted to earthly affairs, are sprinkled with the dust of earthly desire. In those whom I endure as licentious, I grieve for flesh that is rotting; in those whom I suffer as seekers of earthly things, what else do I bear but limbs defiled with dust?

[Note: [Col. 0251D] From Book XXIV on Job, ch. XII, 27.] By “dust” the frailty of the human condition is signified. As the prophet says: [Col. 0252C] “Remember, Lord, that we are dust.” [Note: [Col. 0252D] There, in place of “remember,” we have “he remembered.”] Abraham likewise says: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Ps. 102:14). And although death had not yet dissolved their living flesh into earth, they already were in their own estimation what they foresaw without doubt that they would become. Hence elsewhere it is said: “You will take away their spirit, and they will fail, and they will return to their dust” (Ps. 103:29). What is their spirit except the spirit of pride? Let their spirit, therefore, be taken away, so that they may fail—that is, that when the spirit of pride is removed, they may recognize that of themselves they are nothing—and let them return to dust, that is, be humbled by their frail condition. For everyone placed in sin forgets his own mortality while he is still inflated by pride. After the grace of conversion, when he is touched by the spirit of humility, what else does he remember himself to be but dust?

## CHAPTER VI. ON THE MOUNTAIN

[Note: [Col. 0252D] This varied signification is almost the same as that at the beginning of Book XXXIII on Job, ch. I.] In Sacred Scripture, when “mountain” is put in the singular, it is understood sometimes of the incarnate Lord, sometimes of the holy Church, sometimes of the apostate angel, sometimes of any heretic, sometimes of the Jewish people, sometimes of the height of good life, sometimes of the holy mind, and sometimes of the height of contemplation. When “mountains” are spoken of in the plural, [Col. 0253A] they are understood sometimes as the holy apostles, sometimes as the swelling pride of ecclesiastical powers, sometimes as lofty contemplations, sometimes as the virtues of angels, sometimes as the lofty meanings of Sacred Scripture, and sometimes as the ancient Fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] From Homily 13 on Ezekiel.] By “mountain” the incarnate Lord is understood, as Ezekiel says: “And he set me upon a mountain exceedingly high” (Ezek. 40:2). Whom does the high mountain signify except Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings? He is indeed from the earth, but beyond the earth: for the flesh of our Redeemer has its material from below, but pre-eminent power from above. It was not enough to call him high unless “exceedingly” were added, because in the conception of that humanity which he assumed he is not only man but God and man; not merely a man above human beings, [Col. 0253B] but a man made even above angels. Therefore this mountain is high, and exceedingly so: though it is of earth in the substance of its humanity, it is nevertheless incomprehensible by reason of the loftiness of its divinity.

Thus, when the prophet Isaiah, raised by the spirit of prophecy, foresaw that the same Lord would come in the flesh, he said: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established on the summit of the mountains” (Isa. 2:2). The house of the Lord was the Israelite people. Therefore he was called the mountain of the Lord’s house who deigned to be incarnate among the Israelite people. There were, moreover, holy men in that people who might rightly be called mountains, because through the merit of their lives they drew near to heavenly things. But the incarnate Only-Begotten was above these mountains, because by his divinity he transcended the nature, life, and merits of all. Hence he is rightly called a mountain above the summit of the mountains, because by his divinity he was found lofty even above the peaks of the saints, so that those who had advanced greatly in God could scarcely touch his footsteps from the summit of thought. Therefore he who in Isaiah is called a mountain above the summit of mountains is in Ezekiel described as an exceedingly high mountain.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] From Book XXXIII on Job, ch. I.] By “mountain” the holy Church is signified, as it is written: “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion” (Ps. 124:1). For Zion means “watchtower” or “mirror”; through it the Church is figured as beholding the Lord according to contemplation.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] From the same book and chapter.] By “mountain” the Testament of God is expressed, as Habakkuk says: “The Lord shall come from Lebanon, and the Holy One from the shady and dense mountain.” For he who promised through the pages of his Testament that he would come, came, as it were, from the mountain where he had held himself under promise. This Testament is aptly called a shady and dense mountain because it is overshadowed by the thick obscurities of allegories.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] From Book XXXIII on Job, ch. I.] By “mountain” the apostate angel is signified, as, under the figure of the king of Babylon, it is said concerning the ancient enemy to preachers: “Raise the standard upon the dark mountain” (Isa. 13:2). Holy preachers raise the standard upon the dark [Col. 0254A] mountain when, against Satan’s pride, which is often concealed beneath the mist of pretence, they exalt the truth of the cross.

[Note: [Col. 0254D] From the same book.] By “mountain” any heretic is expressed, as the Psalmist says in the voice of the Church: “I trust in the Lord; how do you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’?” (Ps. 10:2). When a faithful soul is urged, after abandoning unity, to put trust in the inflated doctrine of a heretical preacher, it is as though she were being persuaded, having deserted the Lord, to flee to a mountain.

By “mountain” the Jewish people is signified, as the prophet Isaiah testifies, reporting the devil to have said: “I shall sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. 14:13). See again Chapter XV, Book I, distinction 1, [Col. 0254B].

[Note: [Col. 0254D] From Homily 11 on Ezekiel, after the beginning.] By “mountain” the height of good life is signified, as Isaiah says to the preacher: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who proclaim good news to Zion” (Isa. 40:9). What, indeed, is understood by the name mountain except a lofty life? Therefore the one who proclaims the Gospel is commanded to ascend a high mountain, so that whoever takes up the office of preaching may ascend to the height of good conduct. Let him pass to high places and transcend the deeds of those entrusted to him, in order that he may see the life of his subjects more discerningly, insofar as he does not subject his mind to earthly things and matters which he despises.

Hence Ezekiel, who is sent to preach, is called a watchman by the Lord: “Son of man, [Col. 0254C] I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3:17). The person entrusted with care for others is called a watchman, so that he may sit at a height of mind and derive the title of his office from the virtue of his conduct. For one who is low down is not a watchman. A watchman always stands at a height so that he may see from afar whatever is coming. And whoever is appointed watchman over a people ought to stand high in life, so that he may be able to help through foresight.

By “mountain” a holy mind is understood, as blessed Job says: “A falling mountain melts away” (Job 14:18). Evil is wrought in the mind even of a righteous person by a sudden event, so that he is tempted so suddenly that an unforeseen occurrence shakes and casts him down, and he sees his fall only after he has fallen. [Col. 0254D] “A falling mountain melts away” when, by God’s just judgment, temptation is permitted suddenly to dominate a mind seen to stand on high. “And the rock is moved from its place” when a strong mind, whose place was righteousness, is suddenly driven over into sin.

[Note: [Col. 0254D] From Book V on Job, ch. XXVI.] By “mountain” the height of contemplation is signified, fittingly symbolized in the receiving of the Law, when it is said: “Moses went up, and the Lord came down upon the mountain” (Exod. 19:14). The mountain is our contemplation itself, to which we ascend so that we may be raised to behold things beyond our weakness. But the Lord comes down into it because, even when we have advanced greatly, he opens to our minds only a little of himself. To his contemplatives still living in this life, divinity does not reveal itself as it is, but shows its brightness faintly to the bleary eyes of our mind. Yet, if in him one can say “a little” or “something,” though he always remains one and the same, he cannot be understood as divisible; nevertheless he is said to be shared by his faithful, although no part is admitted in his substance.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] From Book XVIII on Job, ch. XIX, and Book IX, ch. II, after the middle.] By “mountains” the holy apostles are signified, as the Psalmist says: “The mountains shall be carried into the heart of the sea” (Ps. 45:3). Mountains were carried into the heart of the sea when the preaching apostles, driven back by Judaea’s unbelief, came to the understanding of the Gentiles. Hence they themselves say in Acts: “It was necessary that the kingdom of God be spoken first to you; but since you rejected it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:26). Of these mountains the book of blessed Job says: “He moved mountains, and they knew it not—those whom he overthrew in his wrath” (Job 9:5). The chosen preachers of the eternal homeland are rightly called mountains, because through the elevation of their life they leave the low places of earth and become near to heaven. But Truth moved the mountains when he withdrew the holy preachers from Judaea’s hard-heartedness. Yet those who were overthrown in the Lord’s wrath did not know this removal of the mountains: when the Hebrews drove the apostles from their borders, they thought they had made a gain, since they had lost the light of preaching. For, struck by the just punishment of God as their deserts required, they were blinded by such an error of understanding that they supposed losing the light to be a joy.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] From Book XXXIII on Job, ch. I.] By “mountains” the fear of secular powers is expressed. Of them the Psalmist says: “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord” (Ps. 96:5). For many who formerly swelled with lofty hardness were melted in great fear through repentance when God appeared in the flesh. Or, as the same prophet says again: “Mountains rise, and plains descend” (Ps. 103:8). Many proud persecutors come against the Lord, but return from him humble: mountains rise through the swelling of power, but plains descend, being made level through recognition of fault.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] From Book XXX on Job, ch. XV.] By “mountains” lofty contemplations are signified, as it is written of anyone devoted to the hidden life, under the figure of the wild ass, in the book of blessed Job: “He surveys the mountains of his pasture” (Job 39:8). The mountains of pasture are lofty contemplations of inward refreshment. For the more holy persons cast themselves down outwardly through self-contempt, [Col. 0256A] the more abundantly they are inwardly nourished by the contemplation of revelations. Hence it is written: “He has disposed ascents in his heart in the valley of tears” (Ps. 83:7). For those whom the valley of humility holds outwardly in tears, the ascent of contemplation raises inwardly.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] From the same book and chapter; but according to the old [Col. 0256D] division it is ch. XXVIII.] The mountains of pasture may also be understood as the lofty virtues of angels. They refresh us here by ministering and helping us, because there they are enriched by the inward dew of contemplation. Since, by the Lord’s gift, they protect us in every conflict, they are rightly said to be surveyed. We perceive them as present around us on every side, for by their defence we are fortified against adversaries from every direction.

[Note: [Col. 0256D] From Book XXX on Job, ch. XV.] By “mountains” are understood the lofty senses of Sacred [Col. 0256B] Scripture. Of them the Psalmist says: “The high mountains are for the deer” (Ps. 103:18). Those who already know how to make the lofty leaps of contemplation ascend the high peaks of divine meanings, as the summits of mountains. Since the weak cannot reach these summits, it is rightly added: “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs” (ibid.), because the weak are not exercised by lofty understanding, but are humbly sustained by faith in Christ alone.

[Note: [Col. 0256D] From Book XXVII on Job, ch. V, 6.] By “mountains” the ancient Fathers are signified, as the Psalmist says to the Lord: “You shine wonderfully from the eternal mountains” (Ps. 75:5). What, indeed, do we understand by mountains except the Fathers who went before? A person unable to look upon the rising sun looks at the mountains illuminated by it and realizes that the sun has risen. Therefore the Lord enlightens us from the eternal mountains because, through the admirable lives of the Fathers who preceded us, he illumines us with the ray of his brightness.

## CHAPTER VII. ON HILLS

[Note: [Col. 0256D] From Homily 20 on the Gospels.] When hills are set in comparison with valleys, they signify the proud, as it is said in the Gospel through John: “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low” (Luke 3:5). What do valleys signify except the humble, and mountains and hills except the proud? At the coming of our Redeemer, therefore, the valleys were filled and the mountains and hills made low, because, according to his saying: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11). A filled valley grows, while a humbled mountain or hill diminishes. Thus, in faith in the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, the Gentiles received fullness of grace, while Judaea through the error of unbelief lost that by which it had swelled.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON THE FIELD

In Sacred Scripture, “field” sometimes signifies the Gentiles, [Col. 0257A] sometimes the present age, sometimes our body, sometimes Sacred Scripture, and sometimes the whole Church.

By “field” the Gentiles are signified, as it is written in the Psalm under the person of the Lord: “The beauty of the field is with me” (Ps. 49). For the incarnate Lord benefited the Gentiles more than Judaea; assuming an animate body, he came as it were not into a house but rather into a field.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] From Book XXXIII on Job, ch. XII.] By “field” the present age is signified, as the Lord testifies in the Gospel when he says: “The field is the world.”

[Note: [Col. 0257D] Not in precisely the same words, but Gregory says this in exactly the same sense, Book X on Job, ch. II, 16.] By “field” our body is signified, as Solomon says: “Carefully cultivate your field, that afterwards you may build your house” (Prov. 24:27).

[Col. 0257B] For what is understood by the field except the body? Therefore the person rightly builds the house of the mind who first clears the field of the body of the thorns of vices, lest, if the briars of desires thrive in the field of the flesh, the whole edifice of virtues within be destroyed by the growth of the famine of good.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] From Book XVI on Job, ch. XXII, 23.] By “field” Sacred Scripture is signified, as blessed Job says of heretics: “They reap a field that is not their own” (Job 24:6). What is signified by the field except the breadth of Sacred Scripture? Heretics reap a field not their own because they take from Sacred Scripture statements far removed from their own meanings.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] From the book, etc., cited immediately before.] The field may also signify the whole Church, which perverse preachers reap, [Col. 0257C] because, in persecuting the grace of our Creator, when they seize from it some who appeared upright, what else do they take but ears of grain or clusters of souls?

## CHAPTER IX. ON THE PLAIN

In Sacred Scripture, “plains” sometimes signify the Gentiles, and sometimes those humbled from the swelling of pride.

[Note: [Col. 0258D] From Homily 12 on Ezekiel, immediately at the beginning.] By “plain” the Gentiles are signified, as the Lord says to the prophet Ezekiel: “Rise, go out into the plain, and there I will speak with you” (Ezek. 3:22). Why is it that the Lord first spoke to his prophet in the midst of the Israelites, and yet afterwards says, “Go out into the plain, and there I will speak with you,” except that he first poured the grace of his prophecy upon Judaea and afterwards deigned to show it in the expanse of the Gentiles? For not without reason are the Gentiles signified by the plain, since they stretch far and wide—that is, throughout the whole world.

Thereupon it is added: “And rising, I went out into the plain, and behold, the glory of God stood there, like the glory which I saw beside the river Chebar.” In the plain the prophet saw the glory of God which he had seen beside the river Chebar in the midst [Col. 0258A] of the Israelites, because that same majesty appeared to the Gentiles which had first revealed itself, through the Spirit’s disclosure, to the elect people of Judaea.

## CHAPTER X. ON VALLEYS

In Sacred Scripture, “valleys” sometimes signify the humble, sometimes the humble sayings of the Fathers, sometimes these earthly lowlands, and sometimes the lowest places of punishment.

Valleys signify the humble, as is said in the Gospel through John: “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low” (Luke 3:5). Hence above, chapter 7, *On Hills*.

[Note: [Col. 0258D] From Book XX on Job, ch. XII, 13.] By “valleys” (*convalles*) are signified the lowly sayings of the Fathers, as is said through blessed Job concerning heretics: “[Col. 0258B] Those who, snatching these things from the valleys, when they found individual ones, ran to them with shouting” (Job 30:5). For valleys are the humble sayings of the Fathers. Therefore, whenever heretics find in sacred discourse certain things that seem, as it were, prudent, which they do not understand and consequently suppose to support their own assertions, they immediately noisily scatter these among their wretched hearers—whose souls they do not seek, but their possessions. Indeed, they snatch these things from the valleys because they gather them from the Fathers’ humble sayings in a proud spirit. And while they boast that they have found them for their own party, they run to them with shouting, because they strive to broadcast to people’s ears everything they think, from a desire for praise.

[Note: [Col. 0258D] From the preceding book, ch. XV, after §14.] Valleys may also signify these lowly [Col. 0258C] earthly things. For those who do not know how to contemplate the heights of mountains—that is, the strong deeds of the saints—always dwell in low places, as though in valleys. And when they find some gain or a small payment, they run with shouting, because they strive to seize it even by quarrelling. For, when particular things have been found in a valley, to run with shouting is, when occasions for lawsuits arise, to litigate even over a small recompense. Very often, moreover, one whom a good action shows to be holy is tested when an opportunity for earthly advantage arises.
