For you may see some already performing lofty deeds, already following the examples of the Fathers who went before them in works of abstinence and teaching; but when they suddenly find the profit of this present life, as it were the fruit of a valley, they run to it with shouting. As though the tranquillity of the holiness assumed by them were broken apart, they leap out toward it.

[Note: [Col. 0258D] From Book VII on Job, ch. X.] By “valleys” are signified the lowest places of punishments, as is said through blessed Job concerning the wicked: “My brothers have passed me by, like a torrent that passes swiftly through valleys” (Job 6:15). Often the reprobate retain the same faith by which we live, receive the same sacraments of faith, and are held within the unity of the same religion; yet they do not know the inward compassion of mercy. They do not acknowledge the power of charity by which we burn toward God and neighbour. Rightly, therefore, these people are called both brothers and those who pass by: for they come forth with us from one mother’s womb through faith, but they are not established with us in the single zeal of charity toward God and neighbour.

Since, moreover, they cannot remain long in this life which they pursue with all their desires, it is well said: “Like a torrent, they pass swiftly into valleys.” For however many days of life they receive, by so many daily steps they hasten, as it were, toward their end. [Note: [Col. 0259D] These words occur before the end of the chapter.] They wish their time to be increased; but since the time granted them cannot stand still, whatever additions to life they receive, they daily lose so much of their span of life. Thus the moments of time which they pursue flee; those which they receive they lose. Therefore they pass swiftly into valleys, because although they prolong the desires of their pleasures over a long time, [Col. 0259B] they are suddenly brought to the gates of hell. For if this time, however extended by length of years, is closed by an end, it is not long: from its end, the wretched discover that what they possessed only to lose was brief. Hence Solomon aptly says: “Though a man live many years and rejoice in all of them, he must remember the dark time and the many days which, when they come, prove the past to be vanity” (Eccles. 11:8). For when a foolish mind suddenly encounters evil that does not pass away, it understands, by enduring it, that it is eternal; and that what was able to pass away was vain.

## CHAPTER XI. ON THE STREET

[Col. 0259C] In Sacred Scripture, “street” sometimes signifies breadth of authority; sometimes freedom of one’s own will; sometimes the expansiveness of the present life.

[Note: [Col. 0259D] From Book XIX on Job, ch. XI.] “Street” signifies breadth, as blessed Job says in the person of holy Church: “When I went out to the gate of the city, and my chair was set in the street” (Job 29:7). What is signified by the gate of the city except every good action through which the soul enters the assembly of the heavenly kingdom? And what is meant by the chair except the authority of teaching? In Greek, moreover, *platea* means “breadth.” Holy Church therefore goes out to the gate of the city because, in order to obtain entrance into the heavenly kingdom, she exerts herself in holy actions. A chair is prepared for her in the street because, in the broad sphere of great authority, [Col. 0259D] she displays the freedom of her teaching. For one who publicly preaches what he rightly believes sits, as it were, upon a chair in the street, when he fears no one on account of his preaching and, pressed by no terrors, hides himself in silence.

“Street” signifies freedom of one’s own will, as Jeremiah says of certain people who, having possessed remarkable abstinence and continence, returned to depravity: “They are not recognized in the streets” (Lam. 4:8). See chapter 33, Book V, distinction 1, in the middle.

[Note: [Col. 0259D] From Part II of the *Pastoral Rule*, ch. 7.] 353 “Streets” signify the expansiveness of the present life, as Jeremiah says: “How the gold has grown dim; the finest colour has changed; the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lam. 4:1). What, indeed, is expressed by gold, which excels other metals, except the excellence of holiness? What by the finest colour except the reverence of religion, lovable to all? What by the stones of the sanctuary except persons of sacred orders? What by streets except the expansiveness of the present life? For in Greek, *πλάτος* (*platos*) means “breadth”; undoubtedly streets were named from breadth.

Thus gold grows dim when a life of holiness is defiled by earthly activities. The finest colour is changed when the former reputation of some who were thought to live religiously is diminished. For when anyone, after taking on the habit of holiness, involves himself in earthly affairs, then, as though his colour had been changed, his once-revered standing grows pale and contemptible before human eyes. The stones of the sanctuary also are scattered through the streets when those who ought to have been occupied with the inner mysteries, as though in the hidden places of the sanctuary, for the adornment of the Church, seek public proceedings in secular lawsuits. For the stones of the sanctuary were made for this purpose: that they might appear within the Holy of Holies on the garment of the high priest. But when ministers of religion demand from their subjects honour for their Redeemer without deserving it by their manner of life, they are not stones of the sanctuary in the adornment of the high priest. Indeed, these stones of the sanctuary lie scattered through the streets when persons of sacred orders, devoted to the expansiveness of their pleasures, cling to earthly business. And note that he does not say they are scattered [Col. 0260C] in the streets, but “at the head of the streets,” because even while they conduct earthly business, they wish to appear eminent: that they may follow broad paths through the pleasure of delight, yet seem, as it were, to stand at the head of the streets through the honour of holiness.

## CHAPTER XII. ON THE WAY

In Sacred Scripture, when “way” is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies Christ; sometimes the passing course of Christ’s humanity; sometimes his particular coming into our heart; sometimes the path of uprightness; sometimes the expansiveness of conduct governed by one’s own liberty. But when “ways” is used in the plural, it sometimes signifies our actions; sometimes God’s actions; sometimes modes of life.

[Col. 0260D] [Note: [Col. 0260D] From Book XXIX on Job, ch. XII.] “Way” signifies Christ, as the Lord says to blessed Job in a question: “By what way is light scattered?” (Job 38:24). For he is himself the way who says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). “Light,” however, is understood as the splendour of preaching. Through this way, therefore, light is scattered, because through the presence of our Redeemer the whole Gentile world is enlightened. He appropriately says “scattered,” because through the voices of the apostles the light of preaching shone forth broadly, not narrowly or in a confined manner.

[Note: [Col. 0260D] From Book XIX on Job, ch. III, 2.] “Way” signifies the passing course of Christ’s humanity, as blessed Job says concerning Wisdom: [Col. 0261A] “God understands her way, and he himself knows her place” (Job 28:23). Wisdom, coeternal with God, has a way in one manner and a place in another; and “place,” if anyone understands it, is not local. For God cannot be confined bodily; rather, as has been said, “place” is understood in a non-local sense. The place of Wisdom is the Father; the place of the Father is Wisdom, as Wisdom herself testifies: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14). Wisdom therefore has a way in one manner and a place in another. She has a way through the course of humanity, but a place through the abiding condition of divinity. For she does not pass from where she is eternal, but she passes from where, for our sake, she appeared in time.

Thus it is written in the Gospel that, as the Lord was leaving Jericho, he was passing by; but two blind men [Col. 0261B] sitting beside the way cried out, saying, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David” (Matt. 20:30). At their cry, as is written there, “Jesus stood still and restored light” [i.e. gave them sight] (ibid.). What does it mean to hear while passing by and restore light while standing still, except that he had mercy on us through his humanity, while by the power of his divinity he banished from us the darkness of our mind? For he who for our sake was born and suffered, who rose again and ascended into heaven, is, as it were, Jesus passing by: for this is a temporal action. But he stood still, touched them, and enlightened them, because eternity does not pass as does that spiritual dispensation; remaining in itself, it makes all things new. For God’s standing still is his arranging all changing things by an unchangeable purpose. Therefore he who heard the voices of those asking while passing by, and restored light while standing still, although he endured temporal things for our sake, nevertheless bestowed light upon us from that source where he knows no passing change. Since, therefore, it was uncertain when he would appear to human beings in the flesh, it is rightly said: “God understands her way, and he himself knows her place.”

[Note: [Col. 0261D] From the same book and chapter.] Yet this may also be understood differently. For her way may fittingly be taken as the very fact that she comes to the heart and pours herself inwardly into us. Her place, however, is the heart in which, having come, she remains. Of this way it is said: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord” (Matt. 3:3)—that is, open in your heart an entrance for Wisdom as she comes. Likewise it is said elsewhere: “Make a way for him who ascends [Col. 0261D] over the setting” (Ps. 67:5). For to ascend over the setting was to overcome in rising again the very death he had endured. Thus it says of him who ascends over the setting: “Make a way,” that is, offer a path in your hearts through faith to the Lord as he rises again. Hence John is told by the Spirit: “You will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke 1:76).

Whoever, by preaching, cleanses the hearts of hearers from the filth of vices prepares a way for coming Wisdom. This Wisdom, then, has a way and has a place: a way by which she comes, a place in which she remains. “If anyone loves me,” he says, “he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” [Col. 0262A] (John 14). But when that which is everywhere comes, Wisdom’s coming is the manifestation, through the enlightenment of our mind, of the presence of her majesty. And because it is uncertain to human beings either into whose heart she comes or in whom, after she has come, she rests by remaining, it is rightly said: “God understands her way, and he himself knows her place.” For it belongs to divine sight alone to perceive both the manner in which understanding of Wisdom comes to the human heart and whose mind does not lose, through deadly thoughts, the understanding of life that it has received.

[Note: [Col. 0261D] From Book XXI on Job, ch. V, 17.] “Way” signifies the path of uprightness, as blessed Job says: “If my step has turned aside from the way!” (Job 31:7). What is the way but the path of uprightness? And our step turns aside from the way as often as our thought abandons the path of uprightness through consent to error. For we place, as it were, as many steps outside the way as we are separated from delight in heavenly life by perverse desires.

“Way” signifies the expansiveness of one’s own liberty, as Truth says in the Gospel: “Enter through the narrow gate; for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many enter through it” (Matt. 7:13). Hence Jacob says: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in [Col. 0262B] the path, biting the horse’s heels so that its rider falls backward” (Gen. 49:17). Read Book III, chapter 2, distinction 3.

“Way” signifies holy conduct, as Truth again says in the Gospel: “How narrow is the gate and constricted the way that leads to life! And few are those who find it” (Matt. 7:14).

[Col. 0262C] 357 [Note: [Col. 0262D] Book XX on Job, ch. IV, 5.] “Ways” signify our actions, as Job says concerning God: “Does he not consider my ways and number all my steps?” (Job 31:4). What does he designate by “ways” except actions? Hence Jeremiah says: “Make your ways and your practices good” (Jer. 7). And what do we understand by “steps” except movements of the mind or advances in merits? By these steps Truth calls us to himself, saying: “Come to me, all who labour and are burdened” (Matt. 11:28). For the Lord commands us to come to him not with steps of the body but with the progress of the heart. For he himself says: “The hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem” [Col. 0262D] (John 4:21). And shortly afterward: “The true worshippers will worship in spirit and truth; for the Father also seeks such as these to worship him” (ibid., 23).

He indicates that there are steps in the heart when he calls us to come, yet declares that we are by no bodily movement to pass over to other places. Thus the Lord considers each person’s ways and numbers their steps, so that not even the most minute thoughts escape his judgment, nor the most trifling words, which have become cheap in our ordinary usage, remain unexamined. Hence he says: “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, *raca*, will be liable to the council; whoever says, ‘You fool,’ will be liable to the hell of fire” (Matt. 5:22). For *raca*, in the Hebrew language, is an interjection that reveals the mind of someone who is angry, but does not yet fully express a word of anger. First, then, anger without speech is rebuked; afterward, anger with a sound but not yet formed into a full word; finally, when “fool” is said, anger is condemned when it is brought to completion by an utterance of excess.

And note that anger without speech is said to make one liable to judgment; anger expressed in the utterance *raca*, liable to the council; and anger expressed in the word “fool,” liable to the fire of Gehenna. For the order of the sentence proceeds according to the degrees of fault: at the judgment, the case is still examined; in the council, the sentence on the case has already been determined; in the fire of Gehenna, the sentence issued by the council is carried out. Since, therefore, the Lord numbers with subtle scrutiny the steps of human actions—anger without speech for judgment, [Col. 0263B] anger in a sound for the council, but anger in a sound and word consigned to the fire of Gehenna—the prophet had seen this subtlety of examination when he said: “Most mighty, great, and powerful, Lord of hosts is your name; great in counsel and incomprehensible in thought, whose eyes are open over all the ways of the children of Adam, to render to each according to his ways and according to the fruit of the devices of his hands” (Jer. 32:19–20).

[Note: [Col. 0263D] Book XXXII on Job, ch. XVIII, 24.] “The ways of God” signify his actions, as he himself says to blessed Job: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40:14). For what do we understand by the Lord’s ways except his actions? Concerning them the Lord himself again says through the prophet: [Col. 0263C] “For my ways are not as your ways” (Isa. 55:8). And the devil is called the beginning of God’s ways because, when God was acting in the creation of all things, he first created this being and made him pre-eminent over the other angels. Thus he is strong enough for so many things because, in creating him, the Creator made him first in the order of created substance.

[Note: [Col. 0263D] From Book XXV on Job, ch. XI, 16.] “The ways of God” signify modes of life, as Elihu says in the book of blessed Job concerning the perverse and proud: “They withdrew from God as though deliberately, and were unwilling to understand all his ways” (Job 34:27). It must be known that sin is committed in three ways: through ignorance, through weakness, or deliberately. Sin through weakness is indeed graver than sin through ignorance, but sin committed deliberately is much graver than sin through weakness. Paul sinned through ignorance when he said: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man; but I received mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. 1:13). Peter, however, sinned through weakness when a single servant-girl’s voice shook all the strength of faith that he had professed to the Lord, and he denied in speech the God whom he held in his heart.

But the fault of weakness or ignorance is the more readily covered because it is not committed deliberately. Paul corrected by knowledge what he had done in ignorance; Peter strengthened the mountain and, as it were, the already withering root of faith by watering it with tears.

Those of whom the Master himself said [Col. 0264A] concerning himself sinned deliberately: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15). And shortly afterward: “They have both seen and hated me and my Father” (ibid.). For it is one thing not to do good things, another to hate the teacher of good things; just as it is one thing to sin through rashness, another through deliberation. For what is committed in rashness is often condemned when it comes to counsel and deliberation. Through weakness it very often happens that a person loves the good but cannot fulfil it. But to sin deliberately is neither to do the good nor to love it. Just as it is sometimes a graver sin to love wrongdoing than to commit it, so it is worse to hate righteousness than not to have done it.

There are, then, some in the Church who not only do not do good things, [Col. 0264B] but even persecute them; and they detest in others what they themselves neglect to do. Their sin is committed not through weakness or ignorance, but through deliberate purpose alone. For if they wished to fulfil good things but could not, they would at least love in others what they neglect in themselves. If they themselves desired these things even by mere wish, they would not hate them when done by others. But because they learn these same good things by hearing, despise them in living, and persecute them when they observe them, it is rightly said: “They withdrew from God deliberately.” Hence it is aptly added: “They were unwilling to understand all his ways.” For he does not say, “They do not understand through weakness,” but, “They were unwilling to understand,” because those who despise doing what they ought often also disdain knowing it.

For it is written: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does things deserving stripes shall be beaten with few stripes; and the servant who knows his master’s will and does not act according to it shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12:48). He regards ignorance as a remedy providing impunity for sinning. Such people are darkened by the mere gloom of pride and therefore do not discern, because not knowing is one thing and refusing to know another. Not knowing is ignorance; refusing to know is pride. And they can have no excuse the more because, even against their will, what they know is set before them all the more.

## CHAPTER XIII. ON THE PATH

In Sacred Scripture, when “path” is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies the purpose of the Lord’s Incarnation; [Col. 0264D] sometimes action; sometimes the narrowness of the regulated life. When “paths” is used in the plural, it sometimes signifies the more stringent commandments of the Lord; sometimes the subtle preachings of holy teachers; sometimes thoughts.

“Path” signifies the humility, or the purpose, of the Lord’s Incarnation, as blessed Job says of the faithless people of the Jews: “The bird did not know the path” (Job 28). See chapter 1, Book II, distinction 1.

[Note: [Col. 0264D] From Book XXXIV on Job, ch. XV, 41.] “Path” signifies action, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning Antichrist: “Behind him his path will shine.” For Antichrist’s path is said to shine behind him because wherever he goes, [Col. 0265A] he leaves a great admiration through the brilliance of his miracles; and whether he comes forth in person or through his ministers, he shines with deceitful signs. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “False Christs and false prophets will arise and give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error” (Matt. 24:24). Therefore the path behind Antichrist shines, because he illuminates the works of those whose hearts he penetrates with wonders, so that he may hold their minds all the more deeply in the darkness of error, the more powerfully he displays outwardly through them, as it were, the light of miracles.

“Path” signifies the narrowness of the regulated life, as Jacob says in blessing his sons: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in [Col. 0265B] the path” (Gen. 49). See chapter 2, Book II, distinction 3.

“Paths” signify the stricter commandments of the Lord, as the Psalmist says to the Lord: “Show me your ways, Lord, and teach me the paths of light” (Ps. 24:4). For by ways are signified common and easier commandments through which one goes to the Lord. By paths, however, which are narrower than ways and lead more directly, are expressed the stricter and more difficult commandments of God. It is well said that the ways are to be shown and the paths taught, because in learning the common commandments, which are broad like ways, not much labour is required; but in learning and keeping the stricter commandments, which are narrow and hidden like paths, the greatest diligence in instruction must be applied.

[Col. 0265C] [Note: [Col. 0265D] From Book XXVII on Job, ch. XXII.] “Paths” signify the subtle preachings of holy teachers, as the Lord says to blessed Job: “Do you know the great paths of the clouds, and perfect knowledge?” (Job 37:16). The clouds, indeed, are holy preachers. These clouds have most subtle paths, namely, the ways of holy preaching. “Narrow is the gate that leads to life” (Matt. 7:14). Holy preachers therefore restrain by paths those who do not wander away from the track of their purpose through the broad desires of the world. For the strict discipline of good living is not a broad way but a path upon which every preacher is diligently confined, and which is carefully made narrow under the guardian care of the Teacher.

Is it not, as it were, a certain narrowness of the journey to live in this world yet have nothing of this world’s desire; not to covet another’s goods, not to retain one’s own; to despise the world’s praise, honour those who despise one, despise flatterers, pursue contempt; for God’s sake to love reproaches and flee glory; from the heart to forgive the evils of those who injure one, and to retain unshaken in the heart the grace of love toward them? All these are paths, yet great ones—great because, the narrower they are in this present life through the watchfulness required for such living, the more widely they are opened in eternal recompense. Hence “perfect knowledge” is also aptly added. For perfect knowledge is to do all these things diligently and to know that one’s merits are nothing.

Thus the clouds themselves are taught this perfect knowledge, when Truth says to them: [Col. 0266A] “When you have done all that was commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants’” (Luke 17:10). Perfect knowledge is to know all things and yet, in a certain sense of knowledge, to know oneself to be ignorant. For although we now know God’s commandments; although we now weigh the force of his words with careful reflection; although we now do the things that we believe we have understood—still we do not know how those same deeds must be examined under the strictness of judgment. We do not yet see God’s face; we do not yet behold his hidden counsels.

“Paths” signify thoughts, as blessed Job says to the Lord: “You have put my foot in the stocks, and you have observed all my paths” [Col. 0266B] (Job 13:29). See chapter 42, Book V.

[Note: [Col. 0266D] From Book XXVIII on Job, ch. III.] “Steps” signify actions or the movements of thoughts, as Elihu says concerning the Lord: “His eyes are upon the ways of men, and he considers all their steps” (Job 34:21). It often happens that, while heavenly mercy waits for sinners, they rush into a greater blindness of heart. Hence it is written: “Do you not know that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Rom. 2:5).

And behold: while a violent person seizes whatever he can, oppresses the weak, and for a long time does every evil thing that he wickedly desires, because he is not struck down at once [Col. 0266C] but his punishment is deferred until the end, he does not believe that his utterly wicked action is seen by God. But Elihu now testifies that this is not so when he says: “His eyes are upon the ways of men, and he considers all their steps.” He did not believe that God considered them when a wicked person perpetrated with impunity every evil he could. God was thought not to see righteous actions because he delayed to condemn justly; and his great patience was thought to be a kind of negligence.

The wicked person also believed himself unseen in his sins as often as he sinned with impunity. To him a certain wise man says: “Do not say, ‘I sinned, and what sad thing happened to me?’” (Eccles. 5:3). He does not wish to amend the wickedness for which he has suffered no fitting punishment. The more mercifully he has been waited for, the more wickedly he has been incited to sin; and, despising the patience of heavenly forbearance, he has accumulated from that source from which he ought to have corrected his fault. Thus it is said through the same Job: “God gave him a place for repentance, and he abuses it for pride” (Job 24:23).

Often, too, because he does not immediately receive the punishment he deserves, he does not think that what he does displeases God. He therefore gives himself up so that, presuming, he may break out into every kind of blasphemy, fulfil the wickedness of his pleasures, seize what belongs to others, glut himself by oppressing the innocent, and, because he is not yet struck down, think that his ways are either not seen by the Lord or, what is worse, approved. Eternal and sudden punishment will certainly come, and then [Col. 0267A] he will know that all things are seen by God when, in an unforeseen end, he finds himself condemned in requital for everything. Then, in his punishment, he will open the eyes that he long kept closed in guilt. Then he will feel that the true Judge has considered all things, when he can no longer escape, by experience, the desert of his evils.

Therefore the wicked person who has long been waited for is suddenly taken away precisely because the Lord’s eyes are upon the ways of men and consider all their steps. As though he said: Because the things he looks upon patiently for a long time, he does not at some point leave unpunished. For behold, he suddenly takes away the violent man and, by punishment, cuts off the evils which he had allowed to grow by waiting. Let no one, then, say that the Lord does not know human deeds when he sees some wicked person freely pile up his iniquities. For the one long endured is suddenly removed. By people’s “steps” he means either the individual actions by which we exert ourselves or the alternating movements of inner thought, by which, as by paces, we either withdraw far from the Lord or draw near to him in devotion. For the mind approaches God by as many steps as it advances through good movements; and, conversely, it grows distant by as many steps as it declines through evil thoughts.

## CHAPTER XV. ON THE PATHLESS PLACE

[Note: [Col. 0267D] From Book XXIX on Job, ch. XIV.] The Gentile world is called “pathless,” as the Lord says to blessed Job: “Who gave a course to the most violent rain, that it might fill the pathless and desolate land and bring forth green herbs?” (Job 38:27). For the Gentile world was formerly pathless, since the way of God’s word [Col. 0267C] had not been opened to it. When our Redeemer came, it received the calling of grace in such a manner that it had previously possessed no way of prophecy. It is also rightly called desolate, being deprived either of reason—that is, counsel—or of the fruit of works. Thus the Lord gave a course to the most violent rain, so that it might fill the pathless and desolate land and bring forth green herbs: that is, he granted inward inspiration to outward preaching, so that the empty hearts of the Gentiles might be filled and the barren made fruitful.

[Note: [Col. 0267D] From the end of chapter 2 of the preceding book.] Any believing mind may likewise be called pathless: it may hear the words of life, yet by no means allow them to pass inward to the depths of the heart. For perverse desires find a dwelling in such a heart; but upright desires, if they ever find entrance and press forward, run away. But when merciful God deigns to give a course to his rain, those pierced by inward grace open the ears of their heart to the words of life. And the pathless land is filled: when it affords entry to the word, it is filled with mystery. And it brings forth green herbs, because it not only gladly receives the words of preaching infused through the grace of compunction, but also pours them forth abundantly, so that it may now desire to speak what it could not hear; and, having formerly withered inwardly even while listening to us, it may now, by speaking holy things, feed with its greenness any who hunger.

## CHAPTER XVI. ON THE WILDERNESS

[Col. 0268A]

In Sacred Scripture, when “wilderness” is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies Judaea, the Gentile world, heaven, the heart of unbelievers, or the multitude of unclean spirits; but when “wildernesses” is used in the plural, it signifies the doctrines of heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0267D] From Homily 7 on the Gospels.] “Wilderness” signifies Judaea, as John the Baptist says: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Luke 3:4). We know that the only-begotten Son of God is called the Word of the Father, as John the Evangelist testifies when he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). And from our own speech we know that the voice sounds first, and afterward the word can be heard. John therefore declares himself to be the voice because he precedes the Word. Thus he is called a voice running before the Lord’s coming, because through his ministry the Father’s Word is heard by human beings. He also cries in the wilderness because he announces the consolation of the Redeemer to Judaea, abandoned and forsaken.

“Wilderness” signifies the Gentile world, as the Lord says to blessed Job: “Who gave a course to the most violent rain and a way to the sounding thunder, that it might rain upon a land without people in the wilderness?” (Job 38:25). See chapter 1 of this book, distinction 4.

[Note: [Col. 0268D] From Homily 34 on the Gospels.] “Wilderness” signifies heaven, as Truth says in the Gospel: “Which of you, having a hundred sheep and losing one of them, does not [Col. 0268C] leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost?” (Luke 15:4). Behold: by a marvellous dispensation of mercy, Truth gave a parable in which a human being could recognize himself, though it properly applies to the very Author of humanity. Because one hundred is a perfect number, he had one hundred sheep when he possessed the substance of holy angels and human beings. But one sheep was lost when humanity, by sinning, left the pasture of life. He left the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness because he left the highest choirs of angels in heaven.

Why, however, is heaven called a wilderness, except because “wilderness” means “abandoned”? For humanity abandoned heaven when it sinned. The ninety-nine sheep remained in the wilderness while the Lord sought the one on earth, because the number of rational creatures—namely angels and human beings—created to behold the Lord, [Col. 0268D] had been diminished by humanity’s loss. And in order that the perfect number of sheep might be restored in heaven, lost humanity was sought on earth. For what this Evangelist calls “in the wilderness,” another calls “in the mountains” (Matt. 18:12), so as to signify “in the heights,” because the sheep that had not been lost remained in the exalted places.

[Note: [Col. 0268D] From Book II on Job, chapter XX.] By “desert” is denoted either the heart of believers or the multitude of unclean spirits, as is said to blessed Job concerning the death of his sons and daughters by a messenger: “While your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother, suddenly a violent wind rushed in from the region of the desert, shook the four corners of the house, and, as it collapsed, crushed your children; and they died. I alone escaped to bring you the news” (Job 1:18–19). By Job we understand our Redeemer; by his sons and daughters, the apostolic preachers and the peoples subject to them. They are said to have been feasting in the house of their eldest brother, because they were feeding on the delights of sacred preaching while still dwelling among the Jewish people. The desert-region is the heart of unbelievers, which, when the Creator abandons it, no inhabitant cultivates. What else is the violent wind but strong temptation? Thus the violent wind rushed in from the region [of the desert], because, at the passion of our Redeemer, a fierce temptation came against his faithful ones from the hearts of the Jews. [Col. 0269B]

[Note: [Col. 0269D] From the same book and chapter.] The abandoned multitude of unclean spirits may fittingly be understood by the name “desert”; from it the wind comes and shakes the house, because temptation proceeded from them and stirred the hearts of the persecutors. But this house, in which the children were feasting, stood upon four corners. For we recognize three orders of rulers in the synagogue: priests, scribes, and elders of the people. If we add the Pharisees to these, we find four corners in that house. Therefore the wind came from the region of the desert and shook the four corners of the house, because temptation rushed in from unclean spirits and aroused the minds of the four orders to the wickedness of persecution. The collapsing house crushed the children, because when Judaea fell into the cruelty of persecution against the Lord, it overwhelmed the apostles’ faith with the terror of despair. [Col. 0269C]

By “deserts” are understood the doctrines of heretics, or the advantages of temporal life, as is said through blessed Job concerning certain followers of those heretics, lovers of the world: “They dwell in the desolate places of torrents” (Job 30:6). See Book VII, chapter 8, distinction 6.

## CHAPTER XVII. ON SOLITUDE

In Sacred Scripture, “solitude” sometimes denotes the secret quiet of the mind, sometimes the Gentile world, and sometimes separation from the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0269D] From Book XXX on Job, chapters XII, XXIII, XXIV.] By “solitude” is understood the secret quiet of the mind, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the solitary man under the figure of the wild ass: “To whom I gave a home in solitude, and dwellings in the land of salt” (Job 39:6). Should we understand here solitude of body or solitude of heart? What good is bodily solitude if solitude of heart is lacking? For one who lives apart in body, but inserts himself in thought into the turmoil of human intercourse and earthly desires, is not in solitude. But if someone is bodily pressed by crowds of people and yet suffers no tumult of worldly cares in his heart, he is not in a city. Thus to those living rightly there is first granted solitude of mind, so that they may suppress the inward-rising din of earthly desires; so that, by the grace of heavenly love, they may restrain the cares of the heart bubbling up from below; and may drive away from the eyes of the mind, with the hand of seriousness, all the movements of frivolous thoughts that offer themselves importunately, like flies buzzing about. Thus they may seek within themselves a secret place with the Lord, where, when outward noise has ceased, they may speak silently with him through inward desires. Of this secret place of the heart it is elsewhere said: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. 8:1). See the heading “On Heaven.”

[Note: [Col. 0269D] Book I, chapter 3, distinction 2.] We should know that we by no means attain the height of contemplation unless we cease from the oppression of outward care. We never look upon ourselves so as to know that one thing in us is rational and governs, while another is animal and governed, unless, retreating into the secrecy of this silence, we lull every outward disturbance to sleep. This silence was aptly also prefigured by Adam while asleep, from whose side woman immediately came forth. For whoever is drawn up to understand inward things closes his eyes to visible things; then, within himself, he distinguishes both what ought manfully to preside and what, being weak, can be subject, so that one thing in him may be capable of governing, as the man, and another may be governed, as the woman. Therefore, while inwardly awake through contemplation in this silence of heart, outwardly we are, as it were, asleep. Since men set apart—that is, removed from carnal desires—inhabit this silence of mind, the Lord gave this wild ass a home in solitude, that it might not be pressed by the crowd of temporal desires. Of this solitude it is again said through blessed Job: “Who build solitudes for themselves” (Job 3:14). [Col. 0270C]

368 bis [Note: [Col. 0270D] From Book IV on Job, chapter XXVIII.] To build solitudes is to drive the tumult of earthly desires from the secrecy of the heart and, with a single intention toward the eternal homeland, to pant in love for inward repose. Had not he driven from himself every tumult of thoughts who said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:4)? The multitude of earthly desires had fled, and he had betaken himself to great solitude, where he might more safely see nothing foreign and therefore love nothing unfitting. Hence he says again: “I fled far away, and remained in solitude” (Ps. 54:8). He flees far away who raises himself from the crowd of temporal desires into the lofty contemplation of God. He remains in solitude who perseveres in the mind’s withdrawn intention. [Col. 0270D]

[Note: [Col. 0270D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter XV, 30.] By “solitude” is denoted the Gentile world. Thus what we set above in the person of the solitary one—“To whom I gave a home in solitude, and his dwellings in the land of salt”—may also be understood in the person of our Redeemer. For among the Gentiles there was no patriarch and no prophet; because there was no one who used reason in order to understand God, there was scarcely a human being. Of this solitude Isaiah says: “The desert and the trackless land shall rejoice; solitude shall exult and blossom like a lily” (Isa. 35:1). Again, concerning the Church it is said: “He shall make her desert like delights, and her solitude like the garden of the Lord” (Isa. 51:3). The “land of salt” is this same solitude, repeated under another name: before it knew the true wisdom of God, it brought forth saltiness, because, producing no greenness of good understanding, it had a perverse wisdom. Therefore the Lord received a home in solitude and a dwelling-place in the land of salt, because, incarnate for humankind, he took possession of the abandoned hearts of the Gentiles. Hence the Father says to him through the Psalmist: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2:8). Insofar as he is God, he gives all things with the Father; insofar as he is man, he receives all things from the Father, as it is written: “He gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:27). And again it is written: “Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands” (John 13:3), 369; or as he himself says: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me” (John 6). [Col. 0271B]

[Note: [Col. 0271D] From Book XX on Job, chapter XI.] By “solitude” is understood separation from the Church, as is said through blessed Job of heretics: “Who gnawed in solitude, worn out by calamity and misery” (Job 30:3). What cannot be eaten is commonly gnawed. Heretics, because they strive to understand Sacred Scripture by their own power, are undoubtedly unable to grasp it. Since they do not understand it, they do not, as it were, eat it. And because, unaided by heavenly grace, they cannot eat it, they gnaw at it, as it were, with certain efforts. They handle it outwardly when they attempt something, but do not reach its inward meaning. Since they are separated from the fellowship of the universal Church, they are said not merely to gnaw, but to gnaw in solitude. Long beforehand Truth warned that false preachers would draw their followers to this solitude, saying: “If they say to you, ‘Behold, he is in the desert,’ do not go out” (Matt. 24:26). They are rightly described as squalid with calamity and misery, because they are despised both for the ruin of their morals and for the perversity of their opinions. [Col. 0271C]

## CHAPTER XVIII. ON THE EARTHWORK

[Col. 0271D]

[Note: [Col. 0272D] From Homily 12 on Ezekiel.] By “earthwork” (*agger*) are denoted masses of temptations, as is said to Ezekiel: “Son of man, take for yourself a brick and place it before you; draw upon it the city Jerusalem; arrange a siege against it; build fortifications; heap up an earthwork; set camps against it; and place battering-rams round about” (Ezek. 4:1–2). Here we must first inquire why Ezekiel the prophet, whenever he beholds sublime things or is commanded to perform mystical actions, is first called “son of man.” He is often lifted up to heavenly things, and his mind is nourished by hidden and invisible realities. It is therefore necessary that, amid the hidden things he penetrates, he should be called son of man, so that he may always recognize what he is and never be exalted by those things to which he is led. For what is the purpose of always saying “son of man” to the prophet lifted up to spiritual things, except to remind him of his own weakness? Thus, conscious of his frail condition, he should not be raised up in self-regard by the greatness of his contemplation. Since this prophet bears the type of preachers or teachers, it is rightly said to him now: “Take for yourself a brick and place it before you.” Every teacher who receives an earthly hearer for instruction in the heavenly word takes up a brick. When he begins to tell him what is the reward of the heavenly homeland and what is the vision of heavenly peace, he draws the city Jerusalem upon the brick. He places it before himself when, with attentive mind, he considers the hearer’s condition—that is, observes his progress or failure—and, according to that person’s understanding, moderates the words of his preaching, so that the city Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace, may be drawn in the hearer’s mind. Let it therefore be said: “Take for yourself a brick,” that is, the tender heart of your neighbour; “place it before you,” namely, that you may attentively guard his life and understanding; “and draw upon it the city Jerusalem,” that you may make known to him the heavenly joys belonging to the vision of heavenly peace. For Jerusalem has already, as it were, been drawn upon the brick when an earthly mind begins truly to know the joys of inward peace and to long for the sight of the glory of the heavenly homeland. The vision of inward peace is drawn, as it were, when a mind that formerly savoured earthly things is now raised by love to contemplate the glory of the kingdom of heaven. [Col. 0272C]

But as soon as the soul begins to love heavenly things, as soon as with all its intention it gathers itself toward the vision of inward peace, that ancient adversary who fell from heaven envies it, begins to plot more fiercely, and brings on sharper temptations than before. Thus he often tempts the resisting soul as he never tempted it when he possessed it. Hence it is written: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). Thus also the demoniac healed by the Lord is torn by the departing demon, as it is written: “Crying out and tearing him greatly, it came out of him” (Mark 5:5). Why did the ancient enemy, on leaving, tear the possessed man whom he had not torn while possessing him, except because, when he is expelled from the heart, he often produces sharper temptations in it than he had stirred up when he possessed it quietly? Hence the Israelites too say to Moses and Aaron: “May the Lord look upon you and judge, because you have made our odour stink before Pharaoh and his servants, and have put a sword into his hand to kill us” (Exod. 5:21). Moses and Aaron signify the Law and the Prophets. The weak soul often murmurs inwardly, as it were, against the sacred utterances, because after it begins to hear and follow heavenly words, the adversity of the Egyptian king—that is, the temptation of the evil spirit—increases. Therefore a teacher ought vigilantly to make known to the progressing soul the temptations that will follow, so that it may make itself wary and prepare against the snares of the evil spirit. Hence, after Jerusalem has been drawn upon the brick, it is aptly said: “Arrange a siege against it; build fortifications; and heap up an earthwork.” When the vision of peace is already drawn in a person, it is necessary that the wars of temptations should be announced to that person. For to reach those eternal joys of peace, that person must undoubtedly endure here many trials of tribulation. Hence it is well said: “Arrange a siege against it.” Preachers arrange a siege against the soul they are instructing when, through forewarning, they show in what ways vices oppose virtues: how lust strikes chastity; how anger disturbs the tranquillity of mind; how much foolish joy relaxes the mind’s vigour; how talkativeness destroys the heart’s fortification; how envy kills charity; how pride undermines the citadel of humility; and how deceit, once it has corrupted truth in speech, corrupts it also in thought, so that one who refuses to speak the truth he understands may no longer understand what he is able to say. Therefore a siege is arranged by the preacher when, through words of holy admonition, it is shown which vices lie in wait for each virtue and in what ways. [Col. 0273B]

[Col. 0273C] It is further added: “And heap up an earthwork.” The more the mind begins to desire heavenly things, the more evil spirits pile up earthly thoughts against it through their temptations. The prophet heaps up an earthwork when the holy preacher declares to good minds how earthly desires commonly steal in. “Set camps against it, and place battering-rams round about.” The preacher, as it were, sets camps against the soul when he points out against it the gathered and united snares of evil spirits, so that they may sometimes tempt not from one vice alone, but from associated vices. For certain vices are, as it were, related to one another: spiritual dissipation, gluttonous appetite, and the impurity of lust; likewise talkativeness, deceit, and perjury. From dissipation of spirit the mind is drawn to the greediness of the belly; and when the belly is stretched with food, the flesh, proudly captive, is drawn into lust. Again, deceit arises from talkativeness, because it is very difficult for one who says much not to lie as well. A lie is often covered by perjury, so that it may be concealed before human courts. Pride also cannot exist without envy and vainglory. Every proud person envies others the honour that he himself seeks; and if perhaps he obtains it, he is lifted up into the exaltation of temporal glory, rejoicing through vainglory that he possesses above others what he sees they have been unable to obtain. [Col. 0273D]

We should also know that some vices do not come to the mind at the same time but are laid underneath one another, so that one succeeds another in temptation. One comes before the face, while another insinuates itself from the side in temptation, so that while one is resisted, the mind may be deceived and captured by the other. The very vices mentioned above often furtively substitute themselves one for another. Thus, when we try to overcome anger in ourselves, gentleness sometimes occupies the mind beyond what is necessary, so that it does not apply the requisite severity to sinners. But when careless gentleness within us displeases us, zeal draws itself into heat and carries the captive mind beyond the bounds of patience. Therefore, because mingled and united vices come against the mind, camps are rightly set against the Jerusalem drawn in the preacher’s discourse; because, while individual vices strike the mind from different sides, battering-rams are arranged round about. The preacher therefore places battering-rams round about when he cautiously declares how smoothly lust strikes, how harshly impatience kills, how laboriously avarice inflames and destroys, and how proudly pride extinguishes. To place battering-rams round about is, by preaching, to show what weapons of vices customarily strike the soul from every side. [Col. 0274B]

## CHAPTER XIX. ON THE PIT

In Sacred Scripture, “pit” (*fovea*) sometimes denotes the rejection of earthly things or the abyss of hell, and sometimes a hiding-place of protection.

[Col. 0274C] [Note: [Col. 0273D] From Book XXXII on Job, chapter VII, somewhat before the end.] By “pit” is denoted either the casting down involved in earthly things or the abyss of hell, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the proud: “Hide them all together in the dust, and plunge their faces into the pit” (Job 40:8). The oppressed mind endures this dust of evil thoughts which the wind of most wicked temptation brings. Hence concerning every soul weighed down by earthly desires, under the figure of Ephraim, it is said through the prophet: “Why has Ephraim become a cake baked in the ashes, which is not turned?” (Hos. 7:8). It is aptly added: “And plunge their faces into the pit.” As though he said: “As I do.” For by a just judgment the Lord plunges the faces of the proud into the pit, because he casts down the intention of their heart that raises itself above other people. He looks upon low things whose face looks toward the pit. It is rightly said of the proud that their faces are plunged into the pit, because they seek what is low while proudly desiring what is higher; and the more they raise themselves by exalting themselves, the more they tend downward by falling. They seek earthly glory, and they behold the lowest things while proudly pursuing lofty ones. Their faces are therefore rightly said to be plunged into the pit, because, pursuing low things, they tend toward the abyss of hell. For by a just judgment, those whom voluntary turning-away blinds here are there hidden from the sight of the true light by the pit of merited punishment. [Col. 0274D]

[Note: [Col. 0274D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter XIX, 32.] By “pit” are denoted hiding-places of protection, as is said through the prophet against Judaea: “There the *lamia* lay down and found rest for herself; there the hedgehog had its pit” (Isa. 34:11). [Col. 0275A]

## CHAPTER XX. ON THE TRENCH

[Note: [Col. 0275D] From Book XXXI on Job, chapter XIII, 22.] By “trench” (*fossa*) is denoted humility, as the Lord says to Isaiah: “Enter into the rock; hide yourself in a trench of earth, from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty” (Isa. 2:20). We enter the rock when we penetrate the hardness of our heart; and we hide in a trench of earth from the face of the fear of the Lord if, casting out earthly thoughts, we are concealed from the wrath of the strict Judge in the humility of our mind. The more earth is cast out by digging, the lower the ground is always revealed. Thus, if we cast out earthly thoughts from ourselves more diligently, we find ourselves lower, so that we may be hidden within ourselves. Behold, because the day of divine judgment is imminent, the very face of his fear now appears, as it were; and each person must fear him more terribly as the glory of his majesty draws nearer. What then must be done, and where must one flee? How can anyone hide from him who is everywhere? But behold, we are commanded to enter the rock and be hidden in a trench of earth, so that, breaking through the hardness of our heart, we may turn aside the invisible wrath in proportion as we withdraw ourselves in our own hearts from the love of visible things; so that, when the earth of wicked thought is cast out, the mind may be hidden within itself more safely to the extent that it is more humbly hidden. [Col. 0275C]

[Note: [Col. 0275D] From Part III of the *Pastoral Rule*, Admonition 10.] By “trench” is denoted patience. Hence a trench is said to be in the altar in Ezekiel, “so that the burnt offerings placed upon it may be preserved there” (Ezek. 43:27). If there were no trench in the altar, every sacrifice found upon it would be scattered by an oncoming breeze. What do we understand by God’s altar but the soul of a righteous person? The more good works it performs, the more sacrifices it lays upon itself before the eyes of God. What is the trench of the altar but the patience of the good? By humbling the mind to endure adversities, it shows that mind, as in a trench, to be set low. Let there therefore be a trench in the altar, lest the breeze scatter the sacrifice laid upon it; that is, let the mind of the elect preserve patience, lest, stirred by the wind of impatience, it lose even that which it has done well. This same trench is aptly said to be one cubit deep, because, if patience is not abandoned, the measure of unity is preserved. Hence Paul says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2). For the law of Christ is the charity of unity, which those alone fulfil who do not overstep its bounds even when burdened. [Col. 0275D]

## CHAPTER XXI. ON THE CAVERN

By “cavern” is understood the wicked heart, as is said through the prophet concerning our Redeemer: “The infant at the breast shall delight over the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand into the cavern of the basilisk” (Isa. 11:8). See chapter 29, Book III, distinction 1. [Col. 0276A]

## CHAPTER XXII. ON THE CAVE

In Sacred Scripture, “cave” (*antrum*) sometimes denotes thought or the heart of the good.

[Note: [Col. 0275D] From Book XVII on Job, chapter XVII, 3.] By “cave” is understood the wicked heart, as Elihu says concerning the devil: “The beast enters its hiding-place and remains in its cave” (Job 37:8). Who else is understood by the name “beast” but the devil? For he now possesses the hearts of all the reprobate before he appears openly; through hidden wickedness he holds them as his own cave and hides himself in the dark places of their minds for every harm that he desires to inflict upon the good. Were not the hearts of the persecuting Jews the cave of this beast, in whose counsels he lay hidden for so long, but suddenly burst forth in the cries: “Crucify, crucify!” (Luke 23:21)? And because by tempting he could not reach the tearing apart of the mind, he thirsted for the death in the flesh of our Redeemer. [Col. 0276B]

[Note: [Col. 0276D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter XI.] By “caves” or “dens” are understood the thoughts or hearts of the good, as the Lord says to Job concerning the apostles: “Will you take the prey for the lioness, or fill the souls of her cubs when they lie in caves and lurk in dens?” (Job 38:39).

## CHAPTER XXIII. ON MUD

[Col. 0276C]

In Sacred Scripture, “mud” sometimes denotes Judaea; sometimes the weakness of our created condition; sometimes a multiplicity of earthly things; sometimes teaching that savours of filth; sometimes the enticement of carnal desire; and sometimes a mind suffused with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0276D] From Book XXIX on Job, chapter III.] By “mud” is understood Judaea, as the Lord says to Job concerning it: “The seal shall be restored like mud, and it shall stand like a garment” (Job 38:14). What else did the Lord find the Israelite people to be but mud, insofar as he found it in Egypt devoted to the service of the nations and enslaved to brickmaking? When he led it by so many miracles into the promised land; when, having led it there, he filled it with the knowledge of himself; when he bestowed upon it so many hidden mysteries through the prophets—what else did he make it but a seal for preserving mystery? It too contained, enclosed in divine prophecy, everything that severity revealed at the end. But after so many divine secrets and so many miracles received, when at the coming of its Redeemer it loved earth more than truth, saying through the priests, “If we let him go on like this, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11:48), it returned, as it were, to the bricks it had left in Egypt. Having already been made God’s seal, it bent itself back toward what it had abandoned and showed itself to be mud after the seal in the eyes of Truth, when, through the wickedness of impiety, it lost the mysteries of the word it had received and chose to savour only earthly things, which defile. [Col. 0277A]

It is aptly added: “And it shall stand like a garment.” Even when coarse and rough garments have been put on, they are said to stand because they do not cling closely to the limbs of the one wearing them. Thus Judaea, when it appears to serve in relation to the knowledge of truth, stands like a garment, because it shows itself to serve God through outward commandments but refuses to cling to him through the understanding of charity. While it held only the letter in God’s commandments and did not join itself through the Spirit to inward meanings, it did not cling, as it were, to him who had clothed himself with it.

[Note: [Col. 0277D] From Book XXIX on Job, chapter VI, at the end, 5.] By “mud” is denoted the weakness of our created condition. Thus what we have already explained can be understood otherwise. Because the Lord made man in his likeness, he made him, as it were, a seal of his own power.

Yet that seal shall be restored as mud, because, although through conversion man escapes eternal punishments, he is nevertheless condemned to the death of the flesh in punishment for the pride he committed. For man, formed from mud and endowed with rational understanding, adorned with the likeness of the divine image, swelled with pride of heart and forgot that he had been formed from the lowest things. Hence, by the Creator’s wondrous justice, it came to pass that, because, though made rational, he swelled with pride through consent, he should through death again become the earth which he had refused humbly to recognize himself as being. And because by sinning he lost God’s likeness, but by dying returns to the material of his mud, it is rightly said: “The seal shall be restored like mud.” Since, when the spirit is summoned from the body, it is stripped, as it were, of the mud of its flesh, it is aptly added concerning that same body: “And it shall stand like a garment.” For our mud standing like a garment means remaining empty and stripped until the time of the resurrection. Blessed Job places this weakness of our condition before the Judge’s mercy when he prays: “Remember, I beseech you, that you have made me like mud, and you will bring me back to dust” (Job 10:9). [Note: [Col. 0277D] From Book XLIX on Job, chapter XXVIII, 36.]

For angelic spirits sinned irredeemably because they could stand so much more firmly as they were not held back by an admixture of flesh. But after sinning, man merited pardon because through his fleshly body he received something by which he was less than himself. Thus this weakness of the flesh itself is an argument for mercy before the Judge’s regard, as the Psalmist says: “But he is merciful and will forgive their sins; he multiplied [his mercy] so as to turn away his wrath, and he did not kindle all his wrath; and he remembered that they are flesh” (Ps. 77:39). Thus man was made as mud because he was taken from clay for his created condition. Mud is made when water mixes with earth. Man was therefore created like mud, because the soul, as water poured in, moistens the dust, that is, the flesh. The holy man aptly urges this before the Judge’s mercy when he says in petition: “Remember, I beseech you, that you have made me like mud.” That is, he plainly says: “Consider the weakness of my flesh and pardon the guilt of my iniquity.” The death of that same flesh is aptly added [f. *attingitur*, “is touched upon”] when he immediately continues: “And you will bring me back to dust.” As though he openly asks: “Remember, I beseech you, that through the flesh I come from earth and through its destruction I tend back to earth. Look upon the material of my origin and the punishment of my end, and more quickly erase the fault of one who passes away.” [Col. 0278A]

[Note: [Col. 0277D] From Book XXXIV on Job, chapter XIII, 9.] By “mud” is denoted a multiplicity of earthly things, as Habakkuk the prophet says: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his! How long does he heap upon himself thick mud?” (Hab. 2:6). He heaps himself down with thick mud who, multiplying earthly things through avarice, confines himself under the oppression of his sin. [Col. 0278B]

[Note: [Col. 0278D] From the same book and chapter.] By “mud” is denoted teaching that savours of filth, as the same prophet says to the Lord: “You made a way in the sea for your horses, in the mud of many waters” (Hab. 3:15). As though he said: “You opened a path for your preachers amid the teachings of this world, which savour of filth and earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0278D] From the same book and chapter.] By “mud” is also denoted the enticement of carnal desire, as the Psalmist says in prayer: “Deliver me from the mud, lest I stick fast” (Ps. 68:15). To cling to mud is to be defiled by the filthy desires of carnal concupiscence.

[Note: [Col. 0278D] From Book IX on Job, chapter XXIX, 37.] By “mud” may also be signified a mind overspread with the grace of the divine Spirit, because what has been explained of the outward person can here be understood of the inward: “Remember, I beseech you, that you have made me like mud, and you will bring me back to dust” (Job 10:9). Our inward person is like mud because the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured into the earthly mind so that it may be raised to understand its Creator. Human thought, dried out by the barrenness of its sin, becomes green through the power of the Holy Spirit, like irrigated earth. Yet often, when we use without corruption the powers received in the heavenly gift, the habitual experience of continued prosperity raises us into private self-confidence. It very often happens, therefore, that the Spirit who had lifted us up leaves us for a little while, in order to show a person to himself. The holy man expresses this when he adds: “And you will bring me back to dust.” When, through the Spirit’s withdrawal, the mind is somewhat abandoned amid temptation, the earth is, as it were, dried from its former moisture, so that, left to itself, it may feel its own weakness and recognize how dry man is without the infusion of heavenly grace. It is aptly said to be brought back to dust because, when left to itself, it is carried away by the breeze of any temptation. [Col. 0278D]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. ON DUNG

In Sacred Scripture, “dung” sometimes denotes a transient thing, sometimes the stench of lust, and sometimes any sin whatever.

Solomon denotes a transient thing by “dung,” saying: “The sluggard shall be stoned with the dung of oxen” (Ecclus. 22:2). See Book I, chapter 3, distinction 8. [Col. 0279A]

By “dung” is understood the stench of lust in Joel. See Book III, chapter 1, distinction 3.

[Note: [Col. 0279D] From Homily 31 on the Gospels.] The evangelist signifies every sin by “dung,” where the cultivator of the vineyard says to his master, who had a fig tree planted in his vineyard and found no fruit upon it, that it should be cut down; but he is said to have answered: “Lord, leave it for this year also, until I dig around it and put a basket of dung [about it]” (Luke 13:8). The tree signifies each person’s soul. Every person, according to his measure and to the extent that he occupies a place in this present life, if he does not produce the fruit of good work, occupies the ground like an unfruitful tree, because in the place in which he himself is, he denies others an opportunity to work. He occupies the ground who burdens other minds; he occupies the ground who does not employ in good works the place he occupies. Yet it is ours to pray for such persons. Therefore the cultivator of the vineyard says: “Lord, leave it for this year also, and I shall dig around it.” What is it to dig around the fig tree except to rebuke an unfruitful mind? Every trench is low, and rebuke, when it reveals a mind to itself, humbles it. Therefore, whenever we rebuke someone for sin, we dig around the unfruitful tree, as it were, in fulfilment of the cultivator’s duty. [Col. 0279B; 0280A]

Let us hear what he says after digging: “And I shall put a basket of dung [about it].” What is the basket of dung but the remembrance of sins? Sins of the flesh are called dung. Whenever, then, we rebuke the carnal mind for its sins, whenever we bring past vices back to its memory, we pour a basket of dung over the unfruitful tree, as it were, so that it may recall the evils it has done and, by dung, become fertile for the grace of compunction. Thus the tree returns from stench to fruit, because through consideration of sin the mind raises itself again to good works. [Col. 0280B]

## THE SEVENTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0279]

## CHAPTER ONE. ON WATER

[Col. 0279B]

In Sacred Scripture, “waters” sometimes denote the infusion of the Holy Spirit; sometimes holy knowledge; sometimes corrupt knowledge; sometimes tribulations; sometimes peoples; sometimes the minds of the good who follow the precepts of faith; sometimes the most holy choirs of angels; sometimes the torments of infernal deprivation; sometimes the once-soft hearts of the Jews; sometimes the historical narrative of Sacred Scripture; sometimes knowledge; sometimes unstable speech; sometimes the slippery hearts of the wicked; sometimes unbelief or the coldness of sluggish actions; sometimes waves of sorrow; and sometimes the laments of humility or heavenly compunction.

[Note: [Col. 0279D] From Book XIX on Job, chapter 4.] By the name “waters” the outpouring of the Holy Spirit is signified, as it is said in the Gospel: “He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers shall flow from his belly like living waters” (John 7:38). The Evangelist then adds: “But he said this concerning the Holy Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive” (ibid., 39). Again, holy knowledge is signified by water, as it is said: “He shall give them to drink of the water of saving wisdom” (Ecclus. 15:3). Water is also customarily used for perverse knowledge, as in Solomon, where the woman who represents heresy flatters with crafty persuasions, saying: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. 9:17).

[Note: [Col. 0279D] From the same work, chapter 2, and above.] By the name “waters” tribulations are sometimes understood, as the Psalmist says: “Save me, O God, for waters have entered even unto my soul” (Ps. 68:2).

[Col. 0280B] [Note: [Col. 0279D] In the same place.] By the name “waters” peoples are signified, as John says: “The waters are peoples” (Rev. 17:15). Peoples are signified by waters because human life has its noise from the tumult of the flesh, and daily flows away in the course of mortality.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] From the end, chapter 4, of the preceding book.] By the name “waters” are signified not only the flowing multitudes of peoples, but also the minds of the good who follow the teachings of faith, as the prophet says: “Blessed are those who sow upon all waters” (Isa. 32:20). And the Psalmist says: “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters” (Ps. 28:35). Job also says of the saints: “He weighs the waters by measure” (Job 28:25). [Note: [Col. 0280D] From chapter 5 of the preceding book on Job.] For the saints themselves, though raised to the heights by the uplifting of their spirit, are nevertheless restrained by certain temptations while they remain in this life, lest they grow proud through any exaltation. Thus they cannot advance as much as they wish; but lest they be lifted up in pride, a certain measure is set upon their very virtues. [Note: [Col. 0280D] This is in the middle of the chapter.] For the flesh draws downward lest the spirit raise itself up, and the spirit draws upward lest the flesh cast one down. The spirit lifts us lest we lie in the depths; the flesh weighs us down lest we be exalted by the heights. If the flesh tempted us without the spirit’s lifting us, it would undoubtedly cast us down into the depths by the full force of its temptation.

By the name “waters” are signified the most holy choirs of angels, as the Psalmist says: “Stretching out heaven like a skin, you cover its upper regions with waters” (Ps. 103:2). See Book I, chapter 3, distinction 5.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter 12.] By the name “water” the anguish of infernal deprivation is expressed, as it is said in Job concerning the condemnation of the wicked rich man: “Want shall seize him like water” (Job 27:20). That deprivation is fittingly compared to water, because in hell it torments; hell, which absorbs those received into its depths, is customarily signified by the name of a lake. Thus the prophet also speaks in the voice of the human race: “My life has fallen into the pit” (Lam. 3:53). But the exultation of those delivered sings: “O Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me. You drew my soul out of hell; you saved me from those descending into the pit” (Ps. 29:3–4).

[Note: [Col. 0281D] From Book XXIX on Job, chapter 15, some distance from the beginning.] By the name “waters” are signified the once-soft hearts of the Jews, as it is written in Job: “The waters are hardened into the likeness of stone” (Job 38:30). In stone, indeed, the hardness of the Gentiles is signified. For they worshipped stones, and concerning them it was said through the Prophet: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 113:8). Hence John, seeing the Jews pride themselves upon the stock of their descent, and foreseeing that the Gentiles would pass into the offspring of Abraham through knowledge of faith, says: “Do not presume to say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3:9). Therefore, by stones he calls the Gentiles hard through unbelief; by waters, however, he signifies the Jews’ hearts, formerly soft. Since Judaea first believed in God while all the Gentile world remained stubborn in its unbelief; but afterwards the hearts of the Gentiles were softened to faith and the unbelief of the Jews hardened, it was rightly said: “The waters are hardened into the likeness of stone.” It is as though he said: Those Jewish hearts, soft and penetrable by faith, are changed into the insensibility of the Gentiles. For when the merciful God drew the Gentiles, in anger he rejected Judaea. Thus it came about that, just as the Gentile world had formerly been hardened against receiving faith, so afterwards, when the Gentiles received faith, the Jewish people hardened in the numbness of unbelief.

[Note: [Col. 0281D] From Homily 6 on Ezekiel VIII.] By the name “water” the historical narrative of Holy Scripture is signified. Thus it is written in the Gospel that the Lord commanded the jars to be filled with water, which he immediately turned into wine (John 2:7). What are the jars but our hearts? What is the water but the history of sacred reading? He who could change water into wine could also have filled the empty jars immediately with wine. Yet he commands the jars to be filled with water because our hearts must first be filled through the history of sacred reading. Water is changed for us into wine when the history itself, through the mystery of allegory, is transformed for us into spiritual understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0281D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter 14.] By the name “water” knowledge is understood, as Solomon says: “Deep water, the words from the mouth of a man; and an overflowing stream, the fountain of wisdom” (Prov. 18:4). The prophet David testifies that knowledge is signified by water, saying: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17:12), that is, hidden knowledge in the prophets. Job knew that knowledge is signified by water, when he said of the Lord: “He binds up the waters in his clouds, so that they do not burst forth together below” (Job 26:8). For what does he call water here but knowledge? And what else does he signify by the name “clouds” except holy preachers—that is, the apostles—who, sent throughout the regions of the world, knew how to rain in words and flash in miracles? [Note: [Col. 0282D] This is in the middle of the chapter.] Water is bound in the clouds because, when the knowledge of preachers speaks to the minds of the weak, it is prevented from teaching as much as it is able to understand. For if they poured out with their mouths the knowledge they had drawn in with their hearts, they would overwhelm rather than water their hearers by its immensity. Thus, knowledge being held back within so that it might not burst forth all at once below, that cloud, nourishing its hearers with a sprinkling of words, said: “I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons; as to little children I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:2).

For who could have borne it if he who had been caught up to the third heaven, caught up into paradise, and had heard secret words which it was not lawful to utter to men, had opened such immense depths of knowledge? Or whose strength as a hearer would not have been overwhelmed if the vastness of this water had flowed outward in all the measure that a tongue of flesh could suffice to express what he could draw inwardly? But so that inexperienced hearers may be warmed not by a flood of knowledge but by the measured sprinkling of preaching, God binds up the waters in the clouds, so that they do not burst forth all at once below. That is, he tempers the preaching of teachers, so that the weakness of their hearers, nourished by the teachers’ dew, may grow strong.

[Note: [Col. 0282D] From Book VII on Job, chapter 18.] By the name “water” unrestrained speech is signified, as Solomon says: “He who lets out water is the beginning of quarrels” (Prov. 17:14). To let out water is to loosen one’s tongue into a flow of speech. Yet Solomon says, in a positive sense: “Deep water from the mouth of a man” (Prov. 18:4). Therefore, he who emits water is the beginning of quarrels, because whoever does not restrain his tongue destroys harmony. For through certain downward steps toward its own ruin, an idle mind is driven into the fall of a pit. When we neglect to guard against idle words, we arrive at harmful ones: first we delight in speaking of others’ affairs; then our tongue wounds with slanders the lives of those of whom it speaks; and sometimes it breaks out even into open insults. From this the goads of anger are sown, quarrels arise, torches of hatred are kindled, and all peace of hearts is extinguished. Hence it is written contrariwise: “He who imposes silence on a fool mitigates anger” (Prov. 26:10).

[Note: [Col. 0282D] From Book VIII on Job, chapter 11, near the end, 16.] By the name “waters” are signified the slippery desires of the wicked, as the Psalmist says: “He set the waters as in a bottle” (Ps. 77:13). Waters are in a bottle when the swollen and frenzied desires of carnal minds, seeking to accomplish the evils they desire, are constrained by the narrowness of their own inability. For the wicked often desire to dominate those better than themselves, but all things are nevertheless withheld from them by divine judgment, which wonderfully orders all things. Though exalted, they desire to harm the good, yet, being subject to them, they hope for assistance from them. Therefore waters are in a bottle when the slippery desires of the wicked, because they find no effect in action, are pressed down beneath the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0283D] From Book XVI on Job, chapter 17, 30.] By the name “waters” are signified either unbelief or the coldness of sluggish actions, as it is written in blessed Job concerning any perverse person: “He shall pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat” (Job 24:19). Iniquity is compared to cold because it binds the sinner’s mind in numbness. Hence it is written: “As a cistern makes water cold, so her malice makes the soul cold” (Jer. 6:7). By contrast, charity is heat, because it inflames the mind which it fills. Of this heat it is written: “Iniquity will abound, and the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24:12). Thus, concerning any perverse person, it is rightly said as a prophetic judgment, not as a wish: “He shall pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat.” It is as though it were said openly: Whoever is not humbly restrained beneath the bonds of discipline falls from his unbelief, or from the coldness of perverse conduct, into error through immoderate wisdom. Hence the eminent preacher, avoiding this excessive heat of refined wisdom in the hearts of his disciples, says: “Do not be wise beyond what is fitting to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety” (Rom. 12:3). Otherwise excessive heat might destroy those whom the waters of snow—that is, unbelief or the coldness of sluggish actions—had formerly held as persons destined to die.

[Note: [Col. 0283D] From Book V on Job, chapter 7.] By the name “waters” are signified waves of sorrow, as blessed Job says: “My groaning is as overflowing waters” (Job 3:24). When waters overflow, they come with force and swell in their ever-growing massed currents.
