Thus, when the elect set divine judgments before the eyes of their minds; when they tremble at the hidden sentence hanging over them; when they trust that they can attain God, yet fear lest they fail to attain him; when they recall their past deeds which they bewail; when they dread things still to come because they do not know them—then certain masses, like waters, are gathered within them and flow away in groanings of sorrow, as upon shores lying beneath. The holy man therefore saw how great are the masses of thoughts in the lamentations of repentance, and called these very waves of sorrow “overflowing waters,” saying: “My groaning is as overflowing waters.”

[Note: [Col. 0284D] From Book IX on Job, chapter 19.] By the name “waters” are signified lamentations of humility, or heavenly compunction, as blessed Job says: “If I am washed as with waters of snow, and my hands shine as though most clean, yet you will plunge me into filth, and my garments will abhor me” (Job 9:30). The waters of snow are lamentations of humility. This humility, since before the eyes of the strict Judge it excels the other virtues, shines, as it were, with the whiteness of great merit. For there are some who have lamentations but lack humility: afflicted, they weep, yet in those very tears either pride themselves against the lives of their neighbours or rise up against the ordinance of their Creator. Such persons have waters, indeed, but not waters of snow, and cannot be clean, because they are not washed with the tears of humility. He had washed himself in waters of snow who confidently said: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50:19). Those afflicted with lamentations but rebelliously murmuring do indeed break their minds, but scorn to humble them.

The waters of snow may also be understood otherwise. Water from a spring or river rises from the earth; water of snow falls from the air. Some afflict themselves by the lamentations of prayers, yet with all the exertion of those laments sweat only for earthly desires: they are moved to compunction in prayer, yet seek the joys of passing prosperity.

Therefore the water of snow does not wash them, because their desire comes from below. They are, as it were, drenched with water from the earth who are moved to compunction in prayer for earthly goods. But those who weep because they desire eternal rewards are washed by the water of snow, because heavenly compunction is poured upon them. For when through lamentations they seek the everlasting homeland and, inflamed by desire for it, weep, they receive from above that by which they are cleansed. But what else is signified by hands except works? It should be observed that the holy man does not say, “My hands shine most clean,” but “My hands shine as though most clean,” because, so long as we are bound by the punishment of corruption, however earnestly we labour in righteous works, we never attain true cleanness but only imitate it. Hence he suitably adds: “Yet you will plunge me into filth.” God is said to plunge us into filth when he shows us to be plunged into filth, because the more truly we rise toward him by good works, the more subtly we perceive the filth of our life by which we differ from his purity. He says, therefore: “If I am washed as with waters of snow,” and so forth. It is as though he said more plainly: Although I am drenched with the lamentations of heavenly compunction, although I am exercised in the pursuit of right action, nevertheless in your purity I see that I am not clean.

## CHAPTER II. CONCERNING THE ABYSS

In Holy Scripture, by the name “abyss” are signified at one time hell, at another a despairing mind, at another the incomprehensibility of divine judgments, at another the depth of the devil’s cunning, at another the hearts of the wicked, and at another the judgment of human reason.

[Note: [Col. 0284D] From Book XXIX on Job, chapter 7.] By the name “abyss” hell is signified, as the Lord, questioning Job, says: “Have you entered into the depths of the sea, and walked in the uttermost parts of the abyss?” (Job 38:16). If, according to the manner of divine speech, the sea ought to be understood as the world, nothing prevents the depths of the sea from being understood as the prisons of hell. The Lord sought this depth of the sea when he entered the uttermost parts of hell to rescue the souls of his elect. Hence it is said through the prophet: “You made the depth of the sea a way, that the delivered might pass through” (Isa. 51:10). Before the coming of the Redeemer, this depth of the sea was not a way but a prison, because it enclosed within itself even the souls of the good, though not in places of punishment. Yet the Lord made the depth a way because, coming there, he granted his elect passage from the prisons of hell to heavenly things. Hence it is expressly added there: “That the delivered might pass through.” What he had called “the depth of the sea,” repeating it in other words, he calls “the uttermost part of the abyss.” For just as the abyss of waters cannot be comprehended by our sight, so the hidden things of hell cannot be penetrated by any faculty of our thought. We see those taken away from here, but we do not see what recompense of punishments awaits them according to their merits. He says, therefore: “Have you entered into the depths of the sea,” and so forth. It is as though he said: Unlike you, I have sought not only the sea—that is, the world—by assuming human flesh and soul, but through that humanity, freely submitting myself to death, I descended even to the uttermost parts of hell.

It must be carefully considered that he declares that he walked in the uttermost parts of the abyss. For walking belongs to one who is free, not confined. The steps of one bound by chains are necessarily impeded. Therefore, because the Lord bore no chains of sin in hell, he walked there. For he came free to those in chains. Hence it is written: “I became as a man without help, free among the dead” (Ps. 87:6). Therefore, for the Lord to walk in the uttermost parts of the abyss is to find nothing in the place of damnation that could hold him, as Peter testifies, saying: “Having loosed the pains of hell, because it was impossible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2:24).

[Note: [Col. 0285D] From the same book, chapter 8, 7.] The abyss may also be understood as a despairing mind, as is evident from Job: “Have you entered into the depths of the sea?” (Job 38:16). For the sea is the human mind, whose depths God enters when, through knowledge of itself, it is stirred from its inmost thoughts to lamentations of repentance, when it recalls the wickednesses of its former life and shakes its wavering soul in confession. God penetrates the depth of the sea when he transforms even despairing hearts. He enters the sea when he humbles a worldly heart; he enters the depth of the sea when he does not disdain to visit minds oppressed even by crimes. Hence the question is fittingly continued: “And have you walked in the uttermost parts of the abyss?” For what is the abyss but a criminal mind which, because it cannot comprehend itself, lies hidden from itself in everything that it is, like a dark abyss? Therefore, for God to walk in the uttermost parts of the abyss is to convert even the hearts of utterly wicked people and, by touching despairing minds with the traces of his vision, wonderfully to restore them. For when, after immense crimes, anyone is moved to compunction, what else appears but God walking in the uttermost parts of the abyss?

[Note: [Col. 0285D] From Book XXXIV on Job, chapter 16.] By the name “abyss” is expressed the incomprehensibility of divine judgments, as the Lord, speaking to the devil, declares: “He will reckon the abyss as growing old” (Job 41:33). The Psalmist testifies that God’s eternal and incomprehensible judgments are customarily signified by the name “abyss,” saying: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35:7). Old age is sometimes used to mean the nearness of an end. Thus the Apostle says: “What is becoming old and aging is near to destruction” (Heb. 8:13). Therefore the devil reckons the abyss as growing old because he so makes the hearts of the reprobate foolish as to instil in them a suspicion that the coming judgment will somehow come to an end. He reckons the abyss to be growing old who believes that the divine punishment in torments will someday be terminated. Thus the ancient persuader, in his members—that is, in the wicked—sets a definite end upon future punishments, in order that they may extend their faults without any limit of correction; and so that they may be all the more unwilling to end their sins here because they suppose the punishments of sins will end there.

[Note: [Col. 0285D] From Book XXIX on Job, chapter 15.] By the name “abyss” is signified the depth of the devil’s cunning, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning him: “The surface of the abyss is bound fast” (Job 38:30). For what should we understand in the abyss but the incomprehensible cunning of the ancient enemy? The surface of the abyss is bound fast because his fraudulent snares cannot be perceived by the people he has deceived. For one thing lies hidden within and another is shown without: he transforms himself into an angel of light, and by the crafty art of deception presents many things highly praiseworthy in order to draw people into what is unlawful. Therefore the surface of the abyss is bound fast because, while the apparent goodness of his persuasion is displayed above like solid ice, his hidden malice in the depths is not seen.

[Note: [Col. 0286D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter 25.] By the name “abyss” are signified the hearts of the wicked, as blessed Job says concerning wisdom: “The abyss says, ‘It is not in me’” (Job 28:14). What does he call the abyss here but the hearts of wicked people, fluid through their fall and dark through the gloom of duplicity? This abyss rightly declares that this wisdom is not in it, because the wicked mind, while desiring to be carnally wise, shows itself foolish in spiritual matters. For, as Paul testifies, “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3:19). The more inwardly foolish anyone becomes, the more he strives to appear outwardly wise.

[Note: [Col. 0286D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter 16.] By the name “abyss” is signified the judgment of human reason, as the Psalmist says: “Abyss calls to abyss at the voice of your cataracts” (Ps. 41:8). For abyss calling to abyss is passing from judgment to judgment. The almighty Creator made humankind a rational creature, distinct from all insensible and irrational beings, so that a person cannot be ignorant of what he has done. By the law of nature one is compelled to know whether what one does is wrong or right. For why does one come to judgment for one’s action if one could not know what one did? Therefore even those who scorn to be instructed by the Lord’s commandments know whether the things they do are good or evil. For if they do not know that they do good, why do they glory ostentatiously in certain deeds? Again, if they are ignorant that they do evil, why do they avert the eyes of others from those same deeds? They themselves are witnesses against themselves that they know evil to be what they do, since they are ashamed for it to be seen by others. For if they truly did not believe it to be evil, they would not fear for it to be seen by others.

Therefore it is rightly said by a certain Wise Man: “Since wickedness is fearful, it bears witness to condemnation; and while fear rebukes, striking the conscience concerning its deed, it itself testifies that what it does is worthy of condemnation” (Wis. 17:10–11). Conversely, John says: “If our heart does not rebuke us, we have confidence before God” (1 John 3:21). Let the wicked flee human eyes; certainly they cannot flee themselves. For they know the evil they do; they have conscience as witness and their own reason as judge. In the sin they commit, therefore, they first find the judgment of their own reason against themselves, and afterward are brought before the severity of the Judge as well. Thus it is rightly said: “Abyss calls to abyss,” because, by the wondrous order of hidden providence, a person is not permitted to be ignorant of the evil he does, and the sinner already condemns himself in conscience by his own judgment; after this self-condemnation he hastens to the sentence of the eternal Judge. Therefore abyss calling to abyss is passing from judgment to judgment.

## CHAPTER III. CONCERNING THE SEA

In Holy Scripture, by the name “sea” are understood at one time the present world, at another the Gentile world, at another the bitter unrest of worldly persons, at another the divine utterance, and at another our heart.

[Note: [Col. 0287D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter 6, 7, 8.] By the name “sea” the present world is signified, as it is written: “If he wills to spread out the clouds as his tent and flash with his light above, he will also cover the bounds of the sea” (Job 36:30). The Lord spreads out the clouds when, opening to his servants the way of preaching, he disperses them throughout the breadth of the world. A tent is customarily set up for a journey. And when holy preachers are sent into the world, they make a way for God. Hence the Psalmist says: “Make a way for him who ascends above the west” (Ps. 67:5). In this journey, the very hearts of the saints are God’s tent; resting in them as if upon the road, he is covered, because, coming through them to human minds, he does what he has determined and is not seen. These clouds—that is, the preachers—are rightly called God’s tent, because God, coming to us through grace, is veiled within the minds of his preachers.

But words alone are by no means sufficient for those same holy preachers to persuade unless miracles are added as well. Therefore, after it has been said, “If he wills to spread out the clouds,” and so forth, it is rightly added, “and flash with his light above.” For what should we understand by flashes of lightning but miracles? Of these the Psalmist says: “You will multiply lightning flashes and throw them into confusion” (Ps. 17:15). Through these clouds the Lord flashes from above with his light because, through holy preachers, he illuminates the darkness of our insensibility with miracles as well. Therefore, when these clouds rain with words and disclose the force of flashing light through miracles, they convert even the furthest bounds of the world to divine love. Hence it is rightly added: “He will also cover the bounds of the sea.” [Note: [Col. 0287D] From Book XVII on Job, chapter 18.] What else is signified by the name “sea” but the present world, in which the hearts of people seeking earthly things swell with the diverse waves of thoughts and, stirred by the arrogance of pride, strike against one another like opposing waves while they attack one another with alternating intent? [Note: [Col. 0287D] From Book XXVII above.] And what do we understand by the bounds of the sea but the furthest limits of the world? Therefore let it be said: “If he wills to spread out the clouds,” and so forth. It is as though he said: If he spreads out his saints in the ministry of preaching and assists their words with miracles, he summons the limits of the whole world to faith. We have heard this to be done in Elihu’s words, but now we see it already accomplished by God as its author. For almighty God covered the bounds of the sea with flashing clouds, because through the shining miracles of preachers he led even the limits of the world to faith. Behold, he has now almost penetrated the hearts of all nations. Behold, in one faith he has joined the limits of East and West.

[Note: [Col. 0288D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter 19.] By the name “sea” the Gentile world is signified, as it is written in the psalm: “The mountains shall be carried into the heart of the sea” (Ps. 45:3). What else do we understand by mountains but the holy apostles, and by the sea but the Gentile world? But at the very beginning of the birth of the holy Church, when the holy apostles wished to preach the kingdom of heaven to Judaea and saw that they made no progress there, they turned to preach to the Gentiles, as they themselves say in Acts: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you; but because you have rejected it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). Hence Isaiah again says: “Blush, Sidon, says the sea.” Sidon signifies the steadfastness of those established under the Law, while the sea signifies the life of the Gentiles. “Blush, Sidon, says the sea” (Isa. 23:4), because the life of worldly people established under the Law is rebuked by the life of the Gentiles, and the conduct of the religious is put to shame: the former do not keep in promise what they hear in the commandments, while the latter keep it in life though they are in no way bound by the commandments of the Law.

[Note: [Col. 0288D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter 25.] By the name “sea” is understood the bitter unrest of worldly people. Hence, when blessed Job sought the dwelling-place of wisdom and saw that it could not be found in minds devoted to this world, he said: “And the sea says, ‘It is not with me’” (Job 28:14). What is signified by the name “sea” but the restlessness of worldly minds? As they assail one another with hostilities in turn, they strike against one another like opposing waves. The life of worldly people is rightly called a sea because, when it is stirred by stormy motions of activity, it is separated from the peace and stability of eternal wisdom. By contrast, the prophet rightly says: [Note: [Col. 0289D] Isaiah 66:2 according to the Septuagint, although both Greek and Latin codices differ somewhat.] “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble, quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:7). The spirit flees all the farther from earthly minds because it finds no rest in them. Hence it is said of certain persons by the Psalmist: “Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace” (Ps. 13:3). From this destructive disturbance the Lord calls us back, saying: “Come to me, all who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28). What in this life is more laborious than to burn with earthly desires? Or what here is more peaceful than to desire nothing of this world? Therefore, knowing that wisdom cannot dwell amid these waves of unrest, blessed Job says: “And the sea says, ‘It is not with me.’”

[Note: [Col. 0289D] From the beginning of Homily 6 on Ezekiel.] By the name “sea” the divine utterance is signified, as Ezekiel says: “The appearance of the wheels and their work was like the appearance of the sea” (Ezek. 1:16). What else do we understand by the name “wheels” but Holy Scripture, which rolls in every direction toward the minds of hearers and is held back from the path of its preaching by no angle of error? It rolls in every direction because it proceeds rightly and humbly amid adversity and prosperity. For the circle of its precepts is now above, now below: what is spoken spiritually to the more perfect suits the weak according to the letter; and those very things which little ones understand according to the letter, learned persons raise on high through spiritual understanding. Thus the wheel is, as it were, drawn along the ground because Holy Scripture accords with little ones in humble speech; yet, pouring spiritual things into the great, it raises its circle as if on high and is lifted upward from there. Therefore let him say: “The appearance of the wheels and their work was like the appearance of the sea.” For sacred utterances are rightly described as resembling the appearance of the sea, because in them are great masses of meanings and heaps of senses. [Note: [Col. 0289D] A little before the middle of the homily cited above.] Nor is Holy Scripture without reason called like the sea, because in it the sayings are confirmed by the sacrament of baptismal washing; or, certainly, it should be considered that we sail ships upon the sea when we journey toward lands we desire.

But what do we desire except that land of which it is written: “My portion is in the land of the living” (Ps. 141:6)? The one who crosses the sea is carried over by wood, as I have said; and we know that Holy Scripture foretells to us through the Law the wood of the cross when it says: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21:23). Paul bears witness that this concerns our Redeemer, saying: “He was made a curse for us” (Gal. 3:13). The wood is also proclaimed through the prophets when it is said: [Note: [Col. 0290D] Thus Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, and Book III *Against Marcion*; Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho*.] “The Lord reigned from the wood” (Ps. 95:10). And again: “Let us put wood into his bread” (Jer. 11:19). In the Gospel, however, the wood of the cross is openly shown, where the Lord’s passion, which was foretold, is declared; and through the Apostle this same cross is embraced in words and deeds, when Paul says: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). And again: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid.). Therefore, for us who journey toward the eternal homeland, Holy Scripture is a sea which proclaims the cross, because by the wood it carries us to the land of the living. If the prophet had not seen Holy Scripture as resembling the sea, he would never have said: “The earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters of the sea cover it” (Isa. 11:9).

[Note: [Col. 0290D] From Book XXVIII on Job, final chapter, middle section, 18.] By the name of the sea our heart is understood. Hence the Lord speaks to blessed Job, saying: “Who shut up the sea with doors, when it burst forth as though coming from the womb?” For what is the sea but our heart: troubled by rage, bitter with quarrels, proud through self-exaltation, darkened by malicious deceit? Whoever recognizes within himself the hidden temptations of thoughts considers how fiercely the sea rages. 396 For behold, we have now abandoned perversities; we now cling to right desires; we have now cut off outwardly evil deeds. Yet we are still secretly wearied by the storm of that old life with which we came here, though we are righteous. Unless the restraints of immense fear—the prospect of judgment and the dread of eternal punishment—held it tight, all the foundations of the work built up within us would utterly collapse. For if what rages inwardly by suggestion burst forth outwardly through consent, the whole structure of our life would lie overturned from its foundation. Conceived in iniquity and brought forth in sin, we bring with us into this life a conflict through the afflictions of an ignorance-born corruption, a conflict which we overcome only with labour. Hence it is rightly said: “When it burst forth as though coming from the womb.” For the womb of evil thought is adolescence. [Col. 0290D] Of it the Lord says through Moses: “For the sense and thought of the human heart is inclined to evil from its youth” (Gen. VIII, 21). The evil of corruption which each of us received from the beginning of carnal desires, he practises as he advances in age. Unless the hand of divine fear quickly restrains it, sin suddenly swallows into the depths every good of created nature.

Therefore, when Truth says, “Who shut up the sea with doors,” and so forth, let no one attribute victory over his thoughts to himself. Unless divine grace restrained the waves of the heart from the very beginning of thought, [Col. 0291A] the raging sea of temptations would undoubtedly have overwhelmed the land of the human mind, so that, washed over by false waves, it might wither away—that is, delighting in the destructive pleasures of the flesh, it might perish. Therefore, lest blessed Job attribute to himself his firm resistance against the storms of the heart, he hears the divine voice: “Who shut up the sea with doors, when it burst forth as though coming from the womb?” It is as though he were plainly told: “You assess yourself vainly by your outward good works if you do not consider me inwardly, who restrain in you the waves of temptation. For your ability to bear the waves in deed comes from my power, which breaks the waves of temptation in the heart.”

397 CHAPTER IV. ON THE RIVER.

In Holy Scripture, by the name of rivers are understood at one time the fire of the final judgment; at another, the course of the human race; at another, the flow of false believers; at another, the sayings of the ancient Fathers; at another, the teaching of an evil spirit; at another, the course of mutability; and at another, the present life.

By the name of a river, the fire of judgment is signified, as the prophet, contemplating the coming of the heavenly Judge, testifies: “A swift, fiery river issued from before him” (Dan. VII, 20). By this fiery and swift river is signified the fire which, proceeding at the final assize from the presence of the terrible Judge, will separate the elect from the reprobate.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter VII.] By the name of a river, the course of the human race is signified, as the Lord, speaking to blessed Job about the devil under the figure of Behemoth, says: “He will swallow up the river and not be amazed; and he is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” (Job XL, 18). For what is signified here by the name of the river except the course of the human race? It rises, as it were, by birth from the source of its origin, but passes away through death as though flowing down to the depths. And who are designated by the name of the Jordan except those who have already been imbued with the sacrament of baptism? Since our Redeemer deigned to be baptized in this river, all the baptized ought to be denoted by its name—the river in which the sacrament of baptism itself began.

Since, therefore, from the beginning of the world the devil drew into himself, as though into a certain river, the human race flowing down into the depths until the time of the Redeemer—with scarcely a few elect escaping—this is rightly said: “He will swallow up the river and not be amazed.” [Col. 0291D] But because even after the Mediator’s coming he seizes some believers who neglect to live rightly, it is rightly added: “And he is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.” It is as if it were plainly said: “Before the Redeemer of the world he swallowed up the world without amazement; but, more grievously, after the Redeemer’s coming he is confident that he can devour some marked by the sacrament of baptism.”

[Note: [Col. 0291D] From the same chapter and the preceding book, middle section.] By “river” may also be designated those whom we said were expressed by “Jordan.” Those who have recognized the faith of truth but neglect to live faithfully may rightly be called a river, because they flow downward. Moreover, Jordan in the Hebrew tongue means “their descent.” [Col. 0292A] And there are some who, pursuing the ways of truth, cast themselves down and descend from the pride of their old life. When they apprehend eternal things, they make themselves very much strangers to this world: not only do they seek what belongs to another realm, but they also leave their own possessions; not only do they not seek glory in this world, but when it presents itself they trample it underfoot. Hence Truth says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke IX, 23). A person denies himself when, having trampled down the pattern of pride, he shows himself before God to be estranged from himself.

But the ancient enemy does not count it a great thing when he holds under the law of his tyranny those who seek earthly things. For, as the prophet testifies, we have learned that “his food is choice” (Hab. I, according to the LXX). He does not regard it as wonderful if he swallows those whom pride raises, avarice wastes away, pleasure expands, malice constricts, anger inflames, discord divides, envy ulcerates, and defiling lust kills. Therefore, “He will swallow up the river and not be amazed,” because he does not consider it a great thing to devour those who run downward through their very pursuits in life.

But he strives most intensely to seize those whom he sees, having despised earthly pursuits, already joining themselves to heavenly things. Hence, after the swallowing-up of the river, it is rightly added: “And he is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth,” because he strives by his snares to seize those whom he knows cast themselves down from the glory of this present life for love of the heavenly homeland. [Col. 0292C] Some indeed leave the world and abandon the emptiness of passing goods; seeking the depths of humility, they transcend the manner of human life by living well, and advance in such skill of endeavour that they already work the powers of signs. But because they neglect to conceal themselves by watchfulness, struck by the weapon of vainglory they fall more disastrously from on high. Hence the eternal Judge, who examines the secrets of the heart, threatens the fall of this same ruin when he says: “Many will say to me on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?’ And then I will confess to them: ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity; I do not know who you are’” (Matt. VII, 22–23). Therefore the ancient enemy is confident that even the Jordan will flow into his mouth, because he sometimes kills by the snares of his cunning even those who are already thought to be elect.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XXI.] By the name of rivers, the sayings of the ancient Fathers are signified, as is said through blessed Job: “He has searched the depths of rivers and brought hidden things forth into light” (Job XXVIII, 11). What else here are called rivers but the sayings of the ancient Fathers? Who can adequately weigh what a mighty river burst from the mouth of Moses when he gave the Law? What a mighty river flowed from David’s heart? What streams of rivers issued from the mouth of Solomon and all the prophets? Yet Judaea held only the outward appearance of these rivers, since it kept the surface of the letter [Col. 0293A] and did not know their depths. But we, who seek within them the inward spiritual meanings in the Lord who has come, search their depths.

The Lord himself is said to do this because, by his gift, we are enabled to do it. Therefore through us, who follow not the letter that kills but the Spirit that gives life, the Lord searches the depths of rivers and brings hidden things into light: the spiritual exposition now illuminates the sayings of the Law which the excessively dark obscurity of history had hidden. Hence Truth, speaking in parables in the Gospel, commanded the disciples: “What I say to you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim from the housetops” (Matt. X, 27). The utterances of interpreters have fittingly made the sayings of the ancient Fathers now visible to us.

Therefore the prophet Isaiah, beholding the plain words of the holy Church’s exposition, not obscured by the darkness of allegories, cried out: “A place of rivers, broad and open streams” (Isa. XXXIII, 21). The sayings of the Old Testament had been like narrow, closed streams, confining the vast meanings of their knowledge in the most obscure compression. By contrast, the teaching of the holy Church consists of broad and open streams, because its utterances are abundant for those who find them and plain for those who seek them. Thus he says: “He has searched the depths of rivers and brought hidden things into light.” For, by pouring the Spirit of understanding into his interpreters, he opened the ancient obscurities of the prophets. And the holy Church now recognizes through the Spirit what the Synagogue had previously been wholly unable to understand through the letter. [Col. 0293C] Hence, when Moses spoke with the people, he veiled his face (Exod. XXXIV, 35), signifying that the Jewish people would know the words of the Law but would by no means see that Law’s brightness. Hence Paul says: “To this very day, when Moses is read, a veil lies upon their heart” (II Cor. III, 15).

[Note: [Col. 0293D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter IX, after the middle.] By the name of rivers, the teaching of an evil spirit is signified, as the prophet, seeing the devil’s teaching destroyed by Christ’s teaching, speaks to the Lord: “Then you broke open springs and torrents; you dried up the rivers of Ethan” (Ps. LXXIII, 15). Ethan means “strong”—the one of whom Truth says in the Gospel: “No one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Mark III, 27). The Lord broke open springs and torrents when he opened streams of truth in the hearts of his apostles. Of these it is again said through another prophet: “You shall draw waters with joy from the springs of the Saviour” (Isa. XII, 3). We go to their teaching as persons who know, and we bring back vessels of our hearts full of truth. But when his own springs flowed forth, our Lord dried up Ethan’s rivers: he made barren the teaching of the strong and evil spirit by displaying the ray of his truth.

[Note: [Col. 0293D] From Book XV on Job, chapter V.] By the name of rivers is understood the course of mutability, as it is said of the wicked in the book of blessed Job: [Col. 0294A] “The river overturned their foundation” (Job XXII, 16). Since the wicked neglect to pass in heart to eternal things and do not see that all present things are fleeting, they fix their mind in love of the present life [printed *fingunt*, perhaps *figunt*], and build for themselves in it, as though for a long habitation, a foundation; for through desire they are made firm in earthly things. Thus Cain is described as the first to build a city on earth (Gen. IV, 17), because, a pilgrim from things above, he laid his foundation in things below, placing the resting-place of his heart in earthly delight.

Hence in his line Enoch, whose name means “dedication,” is born first; but in the line of the elect Enoch is remembered as the seventh, because the reprobate dedicate by building in this life, which is before them, whereas the elect await the dedication of their building at the end of time, that is, in the seventh age. You may see many people thinking only of temporal things, longing for things to acquire, and seeking nothing after this life. What, then, do these persons do except dedicate in the first generation? And you may see the elect seeking no glory of the present life, willingly enduring poverty, patiently suffering the evils of the world, in order that they may be crowned at the end. For Enoch is born in the seventh generation among the elect, because the elect seek the dedication of their joy in the glory of final recompense.

But since, in the daily passing of time, the mortality of this present life itself flows away, and by taking away the reprobate destroys their dedication, it is rightly said of the wicked: “The river overturned their foundation,” because the course [Col. 0294C] of mortality undermines in them the stability of their perverse construction.

[Note: [Col. 0294D] From Book XII on Job, chapter IV, shortly before the end.] By the name of a river, the present life is signified, as it is said in the book of blessed Job: “As waters recede from the sea, and a river is drained and dries up, so a human being, once he has fallen asleep, will not rise again” (Job XIV, 11). The sea is the human mind, and the thoughts of the mind are like waves of the sea: at times they swell with anger, through grace they become calm, and through bitterness they flow with hatred. But when the waters of the sea subside, a human being dies, because, in the Psalmist’s words, “On that day all their thoughts perish” (Ps. CLV, 4). And again it is written of one dying: “Love also and hatred perish together” (Eccles. IX, 6). Therefore the drained river dries up, because when the soul is withdrawn the body remains empty. For the lifeless body is like the empty bed of some river.

In this matter it must be carefully observed that the present life, so long as the soul is in the body, is compared both with sea and river. The water of the sea is bitter, but that of the river sweet. Since while living here we are at one time affected by certain bitterness, at another found calm and gentle through sweetness, the course of the present life is expressed by comparison with sea and river. But in these words what follows seems very hard: “So a human being, once he has fallen asleep, will not rise again” (ibid.). How can it be said that he will not rise, when it is written: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed”? [Col. 0295A] Yet the sentence which follows indicates the distinction hidden in the preceding statement. For it adds: “Until heaven is worn away, he shall not awaken” (Job XIV, 12). It is clear that he will not rise until heaven is worn away, because unless the end of this world comes, the human race will not awaken from the sleep of death to life. It does not say, therefore, that humanity will not rise at all, but that it will by no means rise before heaven is destroyed.

CHAPTER V. ON THE STREAM.

In Holy Scripture, by the name of streams are understood at one time the Holy Spirit; at another, holy preachers; at another, the actions of this world; and at another, the gifts [Col. 0295B] of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] From Book XV on Job, chapter X.] By the name of a stream, the Holy Spirit is signified, as it is said of the hypocrite in the book of Job: “May he not see the rivulets of the stream” (Job XX, 17). For what is understood by the stream except the Holy Spirit? The rivulets of the stream are the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Love is a rivulet of the stream; faith is a rivulet of the stream; hope is a rivulet of the stream. But because every hypocrite fails to love his neighbour while seeking the passing glory of the world, he does not see the rivulets of the stream, because he is not filled with the watering of love. While the hypocrite seeks present gains, he despises future gifts; and, lacking faith, he does not see in his mind the rivulet of the stream, because faith is “the substance of things, but the proof of things not apparent” (Heb. XI, 1) [the supplied text is defective]. [Col. 0295C] While the hypocrite holds fast to what is seen in outward appearance, he neglects what is unseen. Therefore he does not see the rivulet of the stream through desire, because he attends only to visible things. For it is written: “What a person sees, why does he hope for it?” (Rom. VIII, 24). He would have seen the rivulets of the stream had he closed his eyes to the glory of the present life and opened them to love of the heavenly homeland.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter II.] By the name of streams, holy preachers are signified, as Solomon says: “To the place from which streams issue, they return, that they may flow again” (Eccles. I, 7).

[Note: [Col. 0295D] From Book VI on Job, chapter II, after the middle.] By the name of streams, the actions of this world are signified, as the reprobate mind, under the figure of Babylon, is reproached through the prophet: “Lay bare [Col. 0295D] your shame, uncover your shoulder, reveal your legs, cross the streams” (Isa. XLVII, 2). A person thought to possess some merit because he is quiet is sometimes exposed when placed in some activity. Hence it is well added: “Lay bare your shame.” For in the administration of work shame is laid bare when a base and abject mind is recognized in the display of activity—a mind which had formerly been thought quiet. The mind uncovers its shoulder when it displays its work, previously unknown. It reveals its legs because it discloses the steps of desire by which it longs for worldly gain. It also crosses streams [Col. 0296A] because it unceasingly seeks the actions of this world, which daily flow toward their end; leaving some behind and obtaining others, it always seems to move from one stream to another.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] From Book XIX on Job, chapter IV.] By the name of streams, the gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, ‘Streams of living water shall flow from his belly’” (John VII, 38); where the Evangelist adds: “He said this concerning the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (ibid., 39).

404 CHAPTER VI. ON RIVULETS.

In Holy Scripture, by the name of rivulets are signified at one time holy preachers; at another, the books of the Evangelists; at another, the explanations of the interpreters of the holy Church; [Col. 0296B] and at another, the streams of preaching.

[Note: [Col. 0296D] From Homily X on Ezekiel, long after the middle.] By the name of rivulets, holy preachers are expressed, as the Psalmist says of the holy Church: “Watering its rivulets abundantly, multiply its generations; in its raindrops it shall rejoice when it springs up” [Note: [Col. 0296D] Psalm LXIV: Augustine and Cassiodorus read this in the Psalter.]. The Church’s rivulets are holy preachers, who cleave the ground of our heart. But when the rivulets are made drunk, the Church’s generations multiply, because when preachers receive more abundant grace of the Spirit, the number of believers increases.

This holy Church rejoices in its raindrops. In a raindrop water passes from the roof to the earth, having fallen from heaven upon the roof. The roof of the holy Church is its holy preachers, who protect us [Col. 0296C] by interceding and strengthening us through admonitions. Since their heart is divinely filled in preaching, water comes, as it were, from heaven onto the roofs; and since we are watered by their words, water falls, as it were, from the roof onto the earth. Therefore when the holy Church springs up, it rejoices in its raindrops, because, as it grows in faith and good works, it considers the gifts it has received and exults in the words of its preachers.

[Note: [Col. 0296D] From Book XIX on Job, chapter XI; I Cor. X.] By the name of rivulets, the books of the Evangelists are understood. Thus Job, speaking under the figure of the holy Church, says: “And the rock poured out for me rivulets of oil” (Job XXIX). The outstanding preacher understands Christ under the name of the rock, confessing: “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4). This rock now pours forth rivulets of oil for the Church’s use, because the Lord, speaking in it, causes the teachings of inward anointing to flow out. Long ago a rivulet went forth from this rock: the book of Matthew, the book of Mark, the book of Luke, and the book of John. And in the different parts of this world, for as many teachings as this rock has issued through the mouths of all the apostles, so many rivulets it pours forth. This rivulet of oil is still poured from this rock whenever the things said concerning Christ in the ancient books are expounded by the Holy Spirit for anointing the minds of hearers. These are called rivulets [Col. 0297A] of oil because they flow down and anoint. Whoever is anointed in them, whoever is inwardly immersed, is made rich.

By the name of rivulets, the explanations of the interpreters of the holy Church are signified. Hence Isaiah the prophet, seeing the plain words of the holy Church’s exposition, not obscured by the darkness of allegories, cried out: “A place of rivers, broad and open rivulets” (Isa. XXXIII, 21). See above, chapter 4, distinction 4.

[Note: [Col. 0297D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XX, after the middle.] By the name of rivulets, the streams of preaching are signified, as is said of the Lord through Job: “He cut out rivulets in the rocks.” For what do we understand by rocks except the hard hearts of the Gentiles? What by rivulets except the streams of preaching? Therefore the Lord cut out rivulets in rocks, because he opened streams of preaching in the hard hearts of the Gentiles, as is also said through the Prophet concerning the watering of the Gentiles’ dryness: “He made the wilderness into a pool of waters, and waterless land into springs of waters” (Ps. CVI, 35). And in the Gospel the Lord promised: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, streams of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII, 38). What we then heard promised, we now see fulfilled. For behold, in holy preachers not descended from Judaea, streams of heavenly commandments flow abundantly from Gentile mouths throughout the Church spread across the entire world. Thus he cut out rivulets in rocks, because from hard hearts the river of holy preaching flowed forth.

406 CHAPTER VII. ON THE TORRENT.

[Col. 0297C]

In Holy Scripture, when *torrent* is in the singular, it signifies at one time the fire of final judgment; at another, the course of mortal life; at another, the inundation of the Holy Spirit; and at another, those who love transitory things. When *torrents* is plural, it signifies at one time the streams of sacred books; at another, the inventors of perverse doctrines; and at another, holy preachers.

[Note: [Col. 0297D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XVIII, at the end, 17.] By the name of a torrent, the fire of final judgment is signified, as is said through blessed Job: “The torrent separates from the pilgrim people the stone of darkness and the shadow of death” (Job XXVIII).

[Note: [Col. 0298D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter VI.] By the name of a torrent, the course of mortal life is expressed, as the Lord, speaking to blessed Job about the devil, testifies: “The willows of the torrent shall surround him” [Col. 0297D] (Job XL, 17). What is signified by the fruitless willow trees except the barrenness of the reprobate? Hence the Psalmist, speaking in the voice of preachers against Babylon, says: “Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments” (Ps. CXXXVI, 2). Willows are described as standing in the midst of Babylon because the fruitless, alienated from love of the heavenly homeland, take root with the whole inward being of their heart in this worldly confusion. Therefore holy preachers do not play their instruments among these willows but hang them up, because, when they see fruitless and reprobate minds, they do not exercise the power of their preaching but rather keep silence in mourning.

But what is expressed by [Col. 0298A] the torrent except the course of this mortal life? Again, speaking of our Redeemer, the Prophet says: “He shall drink from the torrent in the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. CIX, 7). Our Redeemer touched the punishment of mortal life in passing, and therefore did not remain long subject to that death to which he voluntarily submitted. Hence on the third day, by rising again, he raised the head which he had laid down in dying. What, then, is meant by the statement concerning the devil, “The willows of the torrent shall surround him,” except that lovers of mortal life, being strangers to good actions as fruit, cling to him all the more closely as the delight of passing pleasure more abundantly floods them? For the torrent waters them, as it were, at their roots, while love of carnal life intoxicates them in their thoughts. Like willows, they bear no fruit but grow green in leaves, because they sometimes utter words of decency concerning matters not difficult to speak of, yet display no weight of life in good works. Thus it is rightly said: “The willows of the torrent shall surround him,” because all who are fruitless, while serving love of temporal life, render more familiar obedience to the ancient enemy through perverse habits.

[Note: [Col. 0298D] From Book XV on Job, chapter X.] By the name of a torrent, the inundation of the Holy Spirit is signified, as is said of the hypocrite in the book of blessed Job: “May he not see the rivulets of the stream, the torrent of honey and butter” (Job XX, 17). By the name of the stream the Holy Spirit is understood. By the name of the torrent is likewise signified the inundation of that same Holy Spirit, which is gathered in the mind of one contemplating through overflowing infusion, when the mind is filled beyond its capacity to understand.

It must be known that when the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured into us, it fills us at once with honey and butter. Honey falls from above, whereas butter is drawn from the milk of animals. Honey is therefore from the air, but butter from flesh. The Only-Begotten of the supreme Father, though God above all things, became human among all things. When he filled us with the sweetness of his divinity and the mystery of the Incarnation, he satisfied us at once with honey and butter. Therefore, because the Spirit of Christ gladdens the mind which he fills both by the sweetness of his divinity and by faith in the Incarnation, these rivulets of the torrent, of the stream, are said to be of honey and butter alike: they refresh the mind with lofty sweetness from the knowledge of God, [Col. 0298D] and anoint it through the mystery of the charism of the Incarnation’s grace. But the hypocrite does not see these rivulets, because, given over to outward favour and attending only to visible things, he does not lovingly attend to the gifts of the Spirit.

By the name of a torrent are signified those who love transitory things, as Job speaks in lament: “My brothers passed by me like a torrent, which swiftly passes through valleys.” Read again chapter 10, Book VI, distinction 4.

By the name of a torrent are signified the streams of sacred books, as Solomon says: “Let the ravens of the torrents pluck out the eye that mocks a father and despises the bearing of its mother.” Repeat chapter 7, Book II, distinction 4.

[Note: [Col. 0299D] From Book XX on Job, chapter XIII, at the beginning.] By the name of torrents are signified the inventors of perverse doctrines, as Job, speaking of their followers, says: “They dwell in the deserts of torrents” (Job XXX, 6). We call torrents those streams that are gathered from winter waters and that also dry up at other times. Thus the inventors of perverse doctrines are rightly called torrents, because, cold toward the warmth of love, they swell as though in the numbness of winter weather. They do not flow with enduring fullness but are dried up, as it were, by the sun’s heat—that is, by the arguments of Catholics. The inventors of perverse doctrines who rose against the Church have indeed already been extinguished by the fervour of truth; nevertheless, [Col. 0299B] their disciples do not cease to maintain and defend what those men taught. Therefore those who follow their errors dwell in the deserts of torrents: that is, they put their confidence in the preaching of persons whose words have already been dried up by the Catholic reply and reasoning.

[Note: [Col. 0299D] From the preceding book, chapter XIII, 14.] Torrents may also be understood as holy preachers, who, while in the present life they flow into us with divine words, are gathered, as it were, into a great quantity of water in winter. When the summer sun comes, they withdraw, because when the light of the eternal homeland shines forth, they will cease to preach. The deserts of these torrents are the comforts of temporal life. They leave them and turn themselves to obtaining heavenly gains. This torrent had left all these things, saying: “For whom I have counted all things as loss, and consider them as dung” (Phil. III, 8). But because the minds of the wicked desire in this life to obtain those things which the righteous, despising them, leave behind, they are said to dwell in the deserts of torrents. What is unworthy for the saints to receive, they themselves greatly desire.

CHAPTER VIII. ON THE SPRING.

[Note: [Col. 0299D] From Homily 20 on Ezekiel, before the end.] By the name of a spring our Redeemer is signified, as the prophet says: “On that day there shall be an open spring for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for washing the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. XIII, 1). For what is understood by the name of the spring except our Redeemer? The hidden spring is the Father’s invisible Only-Begotten, God; the open spring is that same God incarnate. This open spring is rightly called the house of David because our Redeemer came forth to us from David’s lineage. Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace.” Those inhabit Jerusalem who fix their mind on the vision of inward peace.

The sinner and the menstruous woman mean either one who sins in deed or a mind that slips into evil thought. For this menstrual pollution does not touch another flesh, but pollutes its own flesh. So also every soul which, although it commits no evil deed, is nevertheless made foul by polluted [Col. 0300A] thought. Hence it is said through another prophet, under the figure of Judaea, concerning a soul occupied by impure desires: “All who seek her shall not fail; they shall find her in her menstruation” (Jer. II, 24). Evil spirits who seek her do not fail when they desire to bring destruction and are not repelled by any good thought of righteousness; they find the soul in its menstruation when they readily draw it, situated in polluted thoughts, to perverse action.

Therefore let it be said: “On that day there shall be an open spring for the house of David,” and so forth. For the spring of mercy, our Redeemer, who deigned to be incarnate in the house of David, is now open to us, in order to wash the sinner from perverse deed and cleanse the menstruous mind from impure thought. The spring lies open: let us run to it, let us wash ourselves with tears in this spring of compassion. David himself washed in this spring when, after the stains of grievous guilt, he returned to the lamentations of repentance. Mary Magdalene was washed in this spring of mercy: once a notorious sinner, afterwards she washed away her stains with tears by reforming her conduct. In this spring open to all, Peter washed away what he had denied, because he wept bitterly. In this spring of mercy, the thief was washed at his end: reproving himself in death, he was cleansed from sin by confession of the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0300D] From Homily 20 on the Gospels.] By the name of springs, the gifts of spiritual grace are signified, as is said of the Lord through the Psalmist: “You send forth springs in the valleys” (Ps. CIII, 6). What do we understand by springs except spiritual gifts, and by valleys except the humble? Almighty God sends forth springs in the valleys because he bestows gifts of spiritual grace upon the humble.

By the name of springs, streams of truth are signified, as the Psalmist says to the Lord: “You broke open springs and torrents; you dried up the rivers of Ethan” (Ps. LXXIII, 15). See above, chapter 4, distinction 5.

411 CHAPTER IX. ON THE WELL.

In Holy Scripture, when *well* is singular, it signifies at one time the depth of sin and at another the depth of the present life; when plural, it signifies at one time the books of Holy Scripture and at another the depths of our hearts.

[Col. 0300D] [Note: [Col. 0300D] From Book XXVI on Job, chapter XXIV, at the beginning.] By the name of a well, the depth of sin is signified. Hence David, under the figure of sinners, prays: “Let not the storm of waters overwhelm me, nor let the deep swallow me, nor let the well press its mouth over me” (Ps. LXVIII, 3). When the iniquity of an evil deed has shaken one from the stability of goodness, it has carried him away like a storm of waters. But if it has not prevailed by long habit, it has not overwhelmed him. Everyone who abandons the way of life and casts himself into the darkness of sins sinks himself, as it were, into a well or pit. But if long habit does not oppress him in these things, [Col. 0301A] the well has by no means narrowed its mouth over him. Yet if by prolonged commission he is oppressed even by a habit of iniquity, so that he cannot draw himself up to higher things, he is constricted as though by the narrow mouth of a well. Therefore he undertakes recovery all the more easily, the less he is bound by habit.

[Note: [Col. 0301D] From Book XXVIII on Job, chapter VII.] By the name of a well, the depth of the present life is signified. Since we are delivered from it with help from the divine mountains and the examples of those who have gone before, Jeremiah the prophet is fittingly recorded as cast into a well; to raise him from the well, ropes and old rags are lowered to him (Jer. XXVIII, 11–12). For what is signified by the well except the depth of this life? What by the ropes except the Lord’s commandments? [Col. 0301B] Because these both convict and rescue us when we are placed in evil action, they bind and draw us, as it were; they constrain and lift us up. And what is understood by the old rags except the examples of the ancient Fathers? But lest someone bound with these ropes—that is, with the Lord’s commandments—be cut while he is drawn up, old rags are also lowered: because, lest divine commandments frighten us, the examples of the ancients strengthen us, and by comparison with them we presume that we can do what we fear, because of our own weakness, to undertake.

[Note: [Col. 0301D] From Book XVI on Job, ch. III, 9.] By “wells” the books of Sacred Scripture are signified, as we learn from Isaac’s action, who is recorded to have dug wells. Yet the Philistines filled these wells with earth. For what are understood by wells except the books of Sacred Scripture? We dig wells when we penetrate deeply into the hidden senses of Sacred Scripture. Yet the Philistines secretly fill them when, as we strive toward heavenly things, unclean spirits introduce earthly thoughts into us and, as it were, take away the water of divine knowledge which has been found. For often, when we devote ourselves to the sacred sayings, we endure the snares of malignant spirits more severely, because they scatter the dust of earthly thoughts over our minds, in order to darken the eyes of our attention from the light of inward vision. The Psalmist had certainly suffered this when he said: “Depart from me, you malicious ones, and I will search out the commandments of my God” (Ps. 118:9); plainly indicating that he could not investigate God’s commandments while he endured in his mind the snares of malignant spirits.

[Col. 0301D] [Note: [Col. 0301D] From Book XXXI on Job, ch. XIII, 22.] Wells may also be understood as the depths of our hearts. Thus Isaac is fittingly described as having dug wells among a foreign people. By this example, we learn that, placed amid the hardship of this pilgrimage, we should penetrate the depths of our thoughts; and that until the water of true understanding answers us, the hand of our inquiry should by no means grow idle in drawing out the earth of the heart. Yet the Philistines are said to have filled these wells by lying in wait, because unclean spirits, when they see us diligently digging the heart, introduce into us heaped-up thoughts of temptation. Therefore the mind must always be emptied and unceasingly dug over, lest, if it is left unexamined, the earth of thoughts accumulate upon us unto the swelling of perverse deeds.

For although we always keep vigilant, with the intent eye of the mind, toward heavenly things; although we tread underfoot with the heel of firm contempt all that passes away below; nevertheless, because of the corruption of the earthly flesh in which we are still entangled, we often endure the dust of thoughts in our heart. And while outwardly we persuade others to seek heavenly things, we ought always inwardly to examine ourselves by subtle inquiry, lest some base thought, lingering long within us, defile us.

## CHAPTER X. CONCERNING THE PIT

[Col. 0302B]

In Sacred Scripture, by the name “pit” sin is sometimes signified, and sometimes hell.

[Note: [Col. 0302D] From Book XVI on Job, ch. XXIV, 30, 31.] By the name “pit” sin is signified. Thus the prophet Jeremiah, when he considers someone to have been buried beneath a long-standing habit of iniquity, laments himself in his Lamentations under that person’s image, saying: “My life has fallen into the pit, and they have placed stones over me” (Lam. 3:53). For what is signified by the name “pit” except iniquity, and what by the name “stone” except the hard habit of iniquity? Life slips into the pit when it is defiled by the stain of iniquity. A stone is laid upon it when the mind is devoured by sin even through hardened habit, so that, even if it wishes to rise, it can now scarcely do so at all, because it is pressed down from above by the mass of evil habit.

[Note: [Col. 0302D] From Book IX on Job, ch. XXXVIII.] By the name “pit” hell is signified, as the prophet testifies when he says of certain ignorant persons: “They carried their ignorance with those who descend into the pit.” Hell is not improperly called a pit, because those whom it has once seized it always swallows up, while they are tossed and terrified by the surrounding torments.

## CHAPTER XI. CONCERNING THE DEEP

[Note: [Col. 0302D] From Book XXXIV on Job, ch. XIV, 10.] By the name “deep” the profundity of thoughts is signified, as the Lord says in the book of blessed Job concerning the final ferocity of the devil: “He will make the deep sea boil like a pot” (Job 41:2). For what is expressed by the sea except the life of worldly people, and by the deep except their lofty and hidden thoughts? The devil makes the deep sea boil like a pot because, as is clear, at the time of the final persecution he strives to stir up the minds of the reprobate against the life of the elect through the flame of cruelty. Then the deep sea will boil like a pot when he kindles the hearts of lovers of the world with fierce heat; and those things which in this time of peace lay hidden, shut up within their own malice, will then bubble up into the heat of a most savage persecution and, through the unrestrained liberty of open cruelty, will breathe forth the hatreds of their ancient envy that they had long suppressed.

[Col. 0303A] By the name “deep” hell is signified, as it is said to the Lord through the prophet: “You made the deep of the sea a way, that the redeemed might pass through” (Isa. 51:10). See above, ch. 2, distinction 1.

## CHAPTER XII. CONCERNING WHIRLPOOLS

[Note: [Col. 0303D] From Book XXVII on Job, ch. V.] By the name “whirlpools” the manifold preaching of the expositors of holy Church is signified, as Elihu says of the Lord: “He draws up the drops of rain and pours out showers in the likeness of whirlpools” (Job 35:27). Indeed, by the drops of rain the holy apostles may be signified, of whom it is said through Jeremiah to rejected Judaea: “The drops of rain from heaven were withheld, and there was no latter rain” (Jer. 3:3).

## CHAPTER XIII. CONCERNING DRIPPINGS

[Col. 0303B]

By “drippings” the words of preachers are signified. See above, ch. 6, distinction 1.

## CHAPTER XIV. CONCERNING CHANNELS

By “channels” the divine books are signified, as it is said through Moses: “Jacob took green poplar rods, almond rods, and rods from plane trees, and partially peeled them; and, with the bark removed, whiteness appeared in the parts which had been stripped, while those parts which remained intact stayed green, and thus the color became variegated.” And it is added: “He placed them in the channels where water was poured out, so that when the flocks came to drink, they might have the rods before their eyes and conceive at the sight of them. And it came to pass that, in the very heat of mating, the sheep looked upon the rods and gave birth to spotted, variegated offspring, sprinkled with diverse colors.” Read ch. 13, distinction 2, Book III.

## CHAPTER XV. CONCERNING WAVES

In Sacred Scripture, by the name “waves” are sometimes understood the tumult of temptations and sometimes the paths of the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 0304D] From Book XXVIII on Job, ch. IX, scattered passages XIX.] By the name “waves” the tumult of temptations is signified. Thus, when the Lord spoke to blessed Job of the cruelty of the wicked under the designation of the sea, he added: “I surrounded it with my boundaries, and set bar and doors, and said: ‘Thus far you shall come, and here you shall break your swelling waves’” (Job 38:10). For if we understand our heart by the sea, we may fittingly understand temptations and the clamour of vices by the waves. Therefore the Lord surrounds this sea with his boundaries, because he humbles our heart, still troubled by the burden of its corruption and care, under the measure of contemplation, so that, although it desires more, it may nevertheless not rise beyond what is granted it.

Or rather, the Lord surrounds this sea with his boundaries because he calms our heart, swollen with temptations, by the hidden distributions of his gifts: now acting so that, at the suggestion of the wicked, it may not come to delight; now so that the delight in wicked things may not break forth as far as consent. He, therefore, who regards the illicit movements of the heart, and in some cases prevents them from proceeding as far as consent, while in others restrains them even from delight, surely sets a limit to the raging sea, so that it may not go forth into action, but the wave of temptation, murmuring within the bosom of the mind, may dash itself to pieces there. And because it is then powerfully restrained when it is opposed by the love of God and by inspired virtues, it is rightly added: “And I set bar and doors, and said: ‘Thus far you shall come and shall proceed no farther’” (Job 38:11), etc.

For what else, morally speaking, are the doors except virtues, and what is the bar except the strength of charity? These doors—that is, the virtues of good works—the raging sea destroys unless charity, set in opposition from the hidden place of the mind, binds them fast. For every good of virtue is easily destroyed when the temptation of the heart rushes in, unless it is made firm by charity fixed in the depths. Hence Paul, when in his preaching he was setting certain doors of virtue against the sea of temptations, immediately joined strength to those same doors, saying: “Above all, have charity, which is the bond of perfection” (Col. 3:14). For charity is called the bond of perfection because every good that is done is bound through it, lest it perish. Any work is more swiftly torn away by temptation if it is found unbound from the bond of charity.

But if the mind is bound by love of God and neighbour, whenever movements of temptation suggest any injustice to it, love sets itself against them as a barrier and breaks the waves of perverse persuasion with the doors of virtues and the bar of inward love. Therefore it is rightly said: “I set bar and doors, and said,” etc. (Job 38:10). For while each of the elect is tempted by vices and yet resists doing what evil suggestions urge, he is held as though a sea shut in. And although this sea strikes the mind within with the tumultuous waves of thoughts, it nevertheless does not pass beyond the shores established for good living. This sea indeed rises in swelling waves, but, when it dashes against the fixed resolve of the heart, it returns broken.

By the name “waves” the paths of the wicked are signified, as it is said through blessed Job in the person of the Church: “They overturned my feet and pressed me down as with waves, by their paths” (Job 30:12). See Book V, ch. 56, distinction 9.

# BOOK VIII BEGINS

[Col. 0303]

## CHAPTER I. CONCERNING GOLD

[Col. 0303D]

In Sacred Scripture, by the name “gold” are sometimes signified the brightness of divinity, the splendor of the heavenly city, charity, the brilliance of temporal glory, the splendor of holiness, natural ability, the understanding of one who acts well, and the faithful soul.

[Note: [Col. 0305D] From Book XXXIV on Job, ch. XIII, at the beginning, 8.] By the name “gold” the very inward brightness of divinity is signified, as the appearance of the Bridegroom is described in the Song of Songs: “His head is the finest gold” (Cant. 5:17). For since the head of Christ is God, and nothing among metals shines more brightly than gold, the Bridegroom’s head is called gold, because his humanity rules over us from the brightness of his divinity.

[Note: [Col. 0305D] From Book XVIII on Job, ch. XXVII, 31.] By the name “gold” the splendor of the heavenly city is understood, as John testifies that he saw it, saying: “The city itself was pure gold, like clear glass” (Rev. 21:18). For since all the saints will shine there in the highest brightness of blessedness, the constructed city is said to be of gold. And because their very brightness is mutually visible to them in one another’s hearts, and when the face of any one person is illuminated, that person’s conscience is also penetrated, this gold is therefore said to be like clear glass. There the physical bulk of the members will not hide anyone’s mind from another’s eyes, but the soul will be open; even the harmony of the body itself will be open to bodily eyes. Thus each person will then be visible to another as no one can now be visible even to himself. That heavenly city, therefore, fittingly consists of gold like glass, because it is known to be bright through the gold and transparent through the glass.

[Note: [Col. 0305D] From Book XXXIV on Job, ch. XIII, at the beginning, 10.] By the name “gold” charity is signified. Thus John saw the angel who spoke to him girded at the breasts with a golden belt, because the breasts of the citizens above, now no longer subject to punitive fear and never separated from one another by any division, bind themselves together through charity alone. To have a golden belt around the breasts is to restrain all movements of changeable thoughts by the bonds of love alone.

[Note: [Col. 0306D] From the same book, the following chapter.] By the name “gold” the brilliance of temporal glory is expressed, as it is said through the prophet: “Babylon is a golden cup” (Jer. 51:7). For what is signified by the name Babylon except the glory of this world? It is called a golden cup because, while it displays temporal things as beautiful, it intoxicates foolish minds with desire for itself, so that they may seek beautiful visible things and despise invisible beauties. Eve first became intoxicated of her own accord by this golden cup, concerning whom the history of truth says that, when she saw the forbidden tree, she saw that it was beautiful to behold and pleasant to the sight, and ate. Therefore Babylon is a golden cup because, while it displays the appearance of outward beauty, it takes away the perception of inward rectitude.

By the name “gold” the splendor of holiness is understood, as Jeremiah laments the Jewish people, changed from the brightness of righteousness into the darkness of wickedness, saying: “How the gold has grown dark; the finest color has changed!” (Lam. 1:1). See Book VI, ch. 11, distinction 3.

[Col. 0306A] [Note: [Col. 0306D] From Book XXII on Job, ch. II, after the middle.] By the name “gold” natural ability is signified, as blessed Job says: “If I have considered gold my strength” (Job 31:24). For what do we understand by gold except the natural ability of distinguished understanding? Nor is it contrary to reason that we say gold signifies natural ability: for just as gold is placed beneath an ornament in order that the arrangement of gems may be set above it, so the clear abilities of the saints are humbly laid beneath divine gifts and receive upon themselves the distinct gifts of graces.

Holy men, however, do not reckon gold as their strength, because, however brightly they may shine in ability, they judge themselves to be nothing through their own powers. And although they are able strongly to perceive all things, they desire first to understand themselves, so that the light of their ability, after the manner of the sun, may first illuminate the place where it arises, and afterward the other things to which it spreads as it proceeds; lest, if they know other things but do not know themselves, the sunbeam be darkened where it arises. Therefore they direct the power of their ability to knowing their own weakness, and are made stronger by a better knowledge of their weakness. Thus gold is not believed to be strength if no confidence is placed in the ability received.

[Note: [Col. 0306D] From Book XXII on Job, ch. V, after the middle, 19.] By the name “gold” the understanding of one who acts well is signified, as Solomon says: “As silver is tested in the refining-pot and gold in the furnace, so a person is tested by the mouth of one who praises” (Prov. 27:21). If silver or gold is counterfeit, it is consumed by fire; if genuine, it is revealed by fire. So it is with the understanding of one who acts: its quality is shown in that for which it is praised. If, upon hearing praise of himself, a person exalts himself, what is he but counterfeit silver or gold, consumed, that is, by the furnace of the tongue? But if, on hearing praise, he returns to consideration of the heavenly judgment and fears lest he be weighed down before the hidden Judge on account of these things, then, as though growing through the fire of purification into greater brightness, he shines more clearly precisely from that source from which he endured the fire of anxiety.

By the name “gold” the faithful soul is understood, as Elihu says in the book of blessed Job: “From the north gold will come” (Job 37:22). See Book I, ch. 15, distinction 2.

## CHAPTER II. CONCERNING FINE GOLD

[Col. 0306D]

In Sacred Scripture, by the name *obryzum*—fine or refined gold—are sometimes signified angelic nature and sometimes the perfect mind.

By *obryzum* angelic nature is understood, as it is said through blessed Job, when he seeks the price of wisdom: “Fine gold shall not be given for it” (Job 28:15). For what is signified by fine gold except the holy angels? They are rightly called both gold and fine gold: gold, because they shine with the brightness of righteousness; fine gold, because they have never had any contagion of guilt.

Righteous human beings, so long as they live mortally in this corruptible flesh, may indeed be gold, but can by no means be fine gold, because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15). For although in this life they shine through a great brightness of righteousness, they are nevertheless not wholly free from the defilements of sins, as the apostle John testifies when he says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8); and as James affirms when he says: “For we all offend in many things” (Jas. 3:2). The prophet also prays, saying: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 143:2 [the printed reference reads Job 31:13]).

Therefore those are called fine gold who, remaining in the innocence in which they were created, shine with the charity of righteousness and are stained by none, even the slightest, of the defilements of guilt. But because no angel was to be sent as redeemer of humankind for the sake of this wisdom, lest anyone should place hope in those angels whom we learn often appeared to assist people, it was said: “Fine gold shall not be given for it.” It is as though it were plainly said: Wisdom herself will be manifested, that the human race may be redeemed from guilt. No angel is sent in her stead, because the creature must be set free by the Creator. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “If the Son sets you free, you shall truly be free.”

By *obryzum* the beauty of the mind is signified. Thus blessed Job says: “If I have considered gold my strength, and have said to fine gold: ‘You are my confidence’” (Job 31:24). For what do we understand by gold except the natural ability of distinguished understanding? And what by fine gold except the human mind which, while it is refined by the fire of love, always preserves in itself the brightness of beauty through the daily renewal of fervor. For the mind that strives always to begin through desire does not know how to grow old through sluggishness. Hence Paul says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. 4:23 [the printed reference reads 4:32]). Hence the Psalmist, who had already attained the summit of perfection, spoke as though beginning: “I said, now I have begun” (Ps. 76:11). For if we do not wish to grow weary of the good things begun, it is very necessary that we believe ourselves to be beginning every day.

Let him therefore say: “If I have considered gold my strength, and have said to fine gold: ‘You are my confidence.’” It is as though he openly confessed: I ascribed neither the things I truly understood to my own ability, nor did I principally credit to my own mind whatever good deeds I happened to perform.

## CHAPTER III. CONCERNING TALENTS

[Note: From the Homilies on the Gospels.] By the name “talents” gifts of grace are signified, as it is said in the Gospel: “A certain man, going abroad, called his servants and handed over his goods to them. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own ability; and immediately he departed” (Matt. 25:14). Who is this man except our Redeemer, who went to heaven in the flesh that he assumed? For the proper place of flesh is earth; and it is, as it were, led abroad when it is placed in heaven through our Redeemer.

But this man, going abroad, handed over his goods to his servants because he granted spiritual gifts to his faithful people. To one he entrusted five talents, to another two, and to another one. For there are five senses of the body: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Therefore, by five talents is expressed the gift of the five senses, that is, outward knowledge; by two, understanding and action; and by the name of one talent, understanding alone.

## CHAPTER IV. CONCERNING MONEY

[Col. 0308B]

[Note: [Col. 0307D] From Book XXII on Job, XXIII, 16.] By the name “money” the ministry of holy teaching is signified, as blessed Job says: “If I ate the fruits of my land without money” (Job 31:39). For by land is understood either a private household or holy Church. Therefore, to eat the fruits of the land without money is to receive sustenance from the Church, yet not to offer that Church the payment of preaching. Concerning this money of preaching, the Author says: “You ought to have entrusted my money to the bankers, and when I came I would certainly have received what was mine with interest” (Matt. 25:27 [the printed reference reads 25:17]).

[Note: [Col. 0307D] From Homily 9 on the Gospels, about the middle.] To give money to bankers is to impart the knowledge of preaching to those who can also put it into practice through works. For even money which was not given is received in interest. When what was received is repaid, something is added beyond what was received.
