Therefore, from the money of the word received, that person pays interest who, from what he has heard, strives also to understand other things which he has not heard, so that, gathering one thing from another, he may learn to do of himself even those things which he has not yet learned from the preacher’s mouth.

[Note: [Col. 0308D] From the preceding book on Job.] Therefore he eats the fruits of the land without money who receives ecclesiastical benefits for the use of his body but does not render the ministry of exhortation. What are we pastors still to say, who, going before the coming Judge, undertake the office of preaching but eat ecclesiastical provisions in silence? We demand what is owed to our body, but do not give what is owed to the hearts of those subject to us. Behold, this holy man, bound in this world by so many children, was free amid innumerable occupations for the study of preaching. He never ate the fruits of the land without money, because he rendered to those subject to him the word of good admonition, from whom he received the fruits of bodily service.

It follows: “And I afflicted the soul of its cultivators.” The cultivators of this land are those who, though placed in a lower rank, cooperate, with whatever zeal and work they can, in the instruction of holy Church through the grace of preaching. Not to afflict these cultivators, therefore, is not to envy their labours, lest a ruler of the Church, while claiming for himself alone the right of preaching, oppose even others who preach rightly, being gnawed by envy.

For the devout mind of pastors, since it seeks not its own glory but that of the Author, wishes to be aided by all. The faithful preacher desires, if it can be so, that the mouths of all may sound forth the truth which he alone is not sufficient to proclaim. Hence, when Joshua wished to prevent two men who had remained in the camp, Moses rightly said to him: “Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the people might prophesy, and that the Lord would give them his Spirit” (Num. 11:29). He wished all to prophesy because he did not envy others the good that he possessed.

## CHAPTER V. CONCERNING TREASURE

[Col. 0309B]

By the name “treasure” heavenly desire is signified, as the voice of Truth says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field; when a man finds it, he hides it, and for joy over it goes and sells all that he has and buys that field” (Matt. 13:44).

[Note: [Col. 0309D] From Homily 11 on the Gospels.] The treasure is heavenly desire. The field in which the treasure is hidden is the discipline of heavenly pursuit. He certainly buys this field after selling all things who, renouncing the pleasures of the flesh, tramples all earthly desires under the keeping of heavenly discipline, so that nothing which flatters the flesh may now please him, and the spirit may not dread anything which destroys the life of the flesh.

In this matter, this too should be noted: the treasure, once found, is hidden in order to be preserved. For one does not sufficiently guard the pursuit of heavenly desire from malignant spirits if one does not also hide it from human praises. For in the present life we are, as it were, on a road by which we journey to our homeland. Malignant spirits lie in wait among us like brigands. Thus the person who carries a treasure openly on the road desires to be plundered.

I do not say this so that our neighbours should not see our works, since it is written: “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). Rather, I say it so that we may not seek outward praise for what we do. Let the work be public in such a way that the intention remains hidden: that through good work we may offer an example to our neighbours, yet through the intention by which we seek to please God alone we may always desire secrecy.

## CHAPTER VI. CONCERNING RICHES

[Note: [Col. 0309D] From Book XXII on Job, ch. III, 4.] By the name “riches” the keen insights of counsels are signified, as blessed Job says: “If I rejoiced over great riches, because my hand found very much” (Job 31:25). For what do we believe is called great riches by figurative meaning except abundant keenness of counsel? The hand of one who seeks finds these when the thought of one who considers brings them forth. Solomon, contemplating these riches of wisdom, says: “The crown of the wise is their riches” (Prov. 14:24). Since he calls not earthly metals but prudence riches, he immediately adds the contrary: “The folly of fools is imprudence.” For if he called earthly riches the crown of the wise, he would undoubtedly have declared the folly of fools to be poverty rather than imprudence. But when he added that the folly of fools is imprudence, he showed that by the riches of the wise he meant prudence.

Therefore we find great riches within ourselves when, by investigating the sacred sayings, we receive the gifts of abundant understanding and perceive many senses in them, yet not senses at variance with one another. But it is not a secure joy to know matters either profound or numerous in the divine pages; it is secure to preserve what has been known. For one who understands well recognizes what ought to be done in accordance with that understanding. The more widely understanding extends, the more earnestly it is bound to works that must be fulfilled. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “To whom much has been given, much will be required; and from him to whom they have entrusted much, they will demand more” (Luke 12:48).

Therefore let us regard understanding given as borrowed money, because the more entrusted to us through generosity, the more we are held debtors in action. Since, then, righteous people do not exalt themselves with secure joy over what they understand vigilantly, it is rightly said: “If I rejoiced over my great riches,” etc. It is as though he plainly said: I did not, in righteousness, deem myself rich because I knew many right things which I ought to do; nor did I lift up my heart through understanding, because consideration of the action owed weighed it down.

[Note: [Col. 0310D] From Book VI on Job, ch. III.] By the name “riches” the divine sayings are signified, as Eliphaz says concerning the Jewish people, or any intellectually gifted fool: “The thirsty will drink his riches” (Job 5:5). The thirsty drink the riches of the Jewish people because the converted minds of the Gentiles are watered by the stream of sacred speech which that people possessed in the display of pride.

Otherwise: often a fool has the liquid of the inward spring but does not drink, because he receives the ability for understanding, yet disdains to know the judgments of truth by reading.

[Note: [Col. 0310D] From ch. V, Book IV above.] The riches of the mind are also the words of sacred speech. But the fool sees these riches with his eyes and does not take them up for the use of his adornment, because, hearing the words of the law, he considers them indeed great but does not labour with any zeal of love to comprehend them. On the other hand, another person is thirsty but has no natural ability. Love draws this person to meditation; dullness of understanding resists. Yet often, through study, he sometimes understands in the instruction of divine law what an able person does not know through negligence. Therefore the thirsty drink the riches of this fool: the dull but loving attain the commandments of God which the able despise and therefore do not know.

## CHAPTER VII. CONCERNING SILVER

[Col. 0311A]

In Sacred Scripture, by the name “silver” are sometimes signified the divine utterance and sometimes the writers of the divine utterance.

[Note: [Col. 0311D] From Book IV on Job, ch. XXVIII, before the end, 35, 36; and Book XVIII, ch. XI.] By the name “silver” the divine utterance is signified, as the Psalmist says: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 11:7). The words of the Lord are fittingly called silver tested by fire, because, if the word of God is fixed in the heart, it is tested by tribulations.

But because some desire to possess the Lord’s utterance not inwardly by practice but outwardly by display, it is fittingly said through the prophet: “All those wrapped in silver have perished” (Zeph. 1:11). These are those who do not fill themselves with God’s words as inward nourishment but clothe themselves with them as outward display. Hence it is said through the Prophet to the Jews who kept the letter alone: “Why do you weigh out silver, and not for bread?” (Isa. 55:2).

[Note: [Col. 0311D] From Book XXIII on Job, ch. XVII.] It is as though he said: You weigh sacred utterances, but not for nourishment; because, while you preserve only the appearance of the letter, you lose the richness of inward refreshment that comes from spiritual understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0312D] From Book XVIII on Job, ch. XXVIII, 15.] By the name “silver” the writers of the divine utterance are signified. Thus, when blessed Job sought the price of wisdom, he said: “Silver shall not be weighed in exchange for it.” Since the divine sayings are often signified by silver, the writers of that same utterance may also be understood by the term “silver”; their life shone amid the crowds of people with the light of virtues.

But because the law could point out sins but could not take them away, none of the ancient fathers, nor Moses the lawgiver, became the redeemer of humankind. Therefore silver is not weighed in exchange for this wisdom, because, although any persons might be holy, in comparison with the only-begotten Son they are judged to be of no merit. Unless they knew themselves to be servants of this wisdom, they could not have been holy at all. For they were sent for this purpose: to prepare in human hearts, through preaching, the way for this wisdom, not to rule peoples subject to them in her place, but through her.

Because it was certain that, as time advanced, the sicknesses of a failing world would increase, eternal divine Wisdom acted so as to come, at the end of the ages, in person to this great sufferer afflicted with excessive weakness—that is, to the human race lying sick throughout the whole world. Preachers had first been sent, as it were, like travellers, so that afterward the physician’s power might be greater in proportion as the patient’s disease had grown. But because the life of no righteous preacher is sent to save us, it is rightly said: “Nor shall silver be weighed in exchange for it,” because the life of righteous preachers, however brightly it may shine with holiness, does not replace for us the coming of heavenly Wisdom by its own presence.

## CHAPTER VIII. CONCERNING ELECTRUM

[Col. 0312A]

[Note: [Col. 0312D] From Homily 2 on Ezekiel, a little after the middle.] By the name “electrum” our Redeemer is signified, as Ezekiel says concerning him: “From the midst of it, as it were, the appearance of electrum, that is, from the midst of fire” (Ezek. 1:4). By the name “fire” is understood the heat of persecution with which Judaea burned against her Author. But what is signified by the appearance of electrum except Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and humankind?

For electrum is composed of gold and silver. When gold and silver are mixed in electrum, the silver increases in brightness, while the gold grows pale from its own radiance. The one advances in brightness; the other is moderated in brightness. Therefore, since in the only-begotten Son of God the nature of divinity was united with our nature, in which union humanity increased into the glory of majesty, while divinity moderated itself before human eyes from the power of its own radiance, silver, as it were, increased through gold because human nature was made brighter. And because divinity was moderated from its radiance before our sight, gold, as it were, grew pale for us through silver.

For that unchangeable nature, which while remaining in itself renews all things, would, if it had wished to appear to us as it is, have burned us by its radiance rather than renewed us. But God moderated the brightness of his greatness for our eyes, so that, while his brightness was moderated for us, our weakness too might shine in his light through likeness to him and, through grace received, might, if one may so speak, change the color of its condition. Therefore God made man is like electrum in the fire of persecution. For the fire of malice which burned from Jewish hearts in persecution exercised itself first upon the Author and Redeemer of humankind before it afflicted the holy apostles by raging against them.

## CHAPTER IX. CONCERNING IRON

In Sacred Scripture, by the name “iron” are sometimes signified the firmness of converts, strength, the dart of preaching, and one who does not abandon the malice of doing harm.

[Note: [Col. 0312D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XV.] By “iron” is signified the steadfastness of converts, as blessed Job testifies, saying: “Iron is taken out of the earth” (Job 28:2). By his hidden counsel, almighty God preserves some innocent from their beginnings and advances them to the heights of virtue, so that as they grow in age, both the number of their years and the loftiness of their merits increase together. Others, however, he abandons in their beginnings and permits them, as vices gush forth, to rush headlong through precipitous paths. Yet often he also looks upon these and kindles them with the fire of holy love to follow him; he changes the ingrained itchings of vice in their hearts into the fervour of virtues. And they burn the more eagerly with desire to seek God’s mercy, the more they blush at the memory of their own iniquity.

Just as it often happens in the contest of battle that a soldier, standing before his commander’s eyes, shamefully yields to the enemy’s strength and, weakly turning his back, is struck. Yet, ashamed of this very shameful surrender, he gathers greater strength from his very shame before his commander’s eyes; and afterward he performs such brave deeds as both accomplish the present glory of courage and wipe away the former disgrace of weakness. Thus, sometimes persons are strengthened more vigorously in God’s service out of their previous weakness; both the desire for things to come draws them toward keeping the commandments, and the memory of past things drives them on: on the one side love summons them toward what is to come, on the other memory spurs them concerning the past.

But when the adversaries of the Church see such persons endowed with the highest virtues, and can find nothing in their present life on which to cast reproach, they endeavour to accuse them concerning their past—as Manichaeus attacks our Moses, seeking by the guilt of a former homicide to defile the grace of his subsequent virtues. In this he does not consider how patient Moses afterward was in enduring, but how rash he had first been in striking. Job therefore, opposing such adversaries with most subtle discernment, says: “Iron is taken out of the earth”: that is, one who was formerly weak and despised amid earthly affairs was afterward made strong for heavenly proclamations.

[Note: [Col. 0313D] From Book XXVI on Job, chapter XII.] By “iron” strength is signified, as the Lord says to Ezekiel: “And you, take for yourself an iron griddle, and set it as an iron wall between yourself and the city” (Ezek. 4:3). By the griddle, then, frying is signified; by iron, strength. What so fries and torments the mind of a teacher and doctor as zeal for the Lord? Indeed, Paul burned with the frying of this griddle when he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29). And because whoever is inflamed with God’s zeal against sinners is fortified with strong and lasting protection, lest he be condemned through negligent care in preaching and governing, it is rightly said: “You shall set it as an iron wall between yourself and the city.”

For an iron griddle and an iron wall are placed between the prophet and the city, because when teachers now display strong zeal, they afterward retain that same zeal as a strong defence between themselves and their hearers, lest they be left without defence for vengeance then if they are lax amid corruption now. The prophet heard that he should take this griddle as a wall between himself and his hearers when the divine voice first said to him: “If you announce it to the wicked man, and he is not converted from his wickedness and from his wicked way, he shall indeed die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your own soul” (Ezek. 3:19). Paul had placed this griddle as a wall between himself and his disciples when he said: “I am clean from the blood of all of you” (Acts 20:26). “For I did not shrink from announcing to you the whole counsel of God.”

Teachers, therefore, must desire to be afflicted by the burning of zeal, lest afterward they be compelled to be tortured by the fire of Gehenna because of the body of negligence. But what we owe to unjust persons who are subject to us is one thing; what we owe to just persons who are not subject to us is another. Fear of having to render an account ought to kindle us toward correcting and guarding the former; consideration of justice itself ought to incline us to reverence for the latter. But arrogant men, because they do not know this form of discernment, show toward just persons who are not subject to them what they see good preachers do toward unjust persons who are subject to them.

[Note: [Col. 0313D] From Book XXXIV on Job, chapter VIII, 5.] By “iron” is signified the dart of preaching. Hence, when the Lord speaks to Job concerning the devil’s violence to be wrought through Antichrist, he says: “He will account iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood” (Job 41:18). Iron is sharpened in order that an adversary may be wounded. Bronze, however, is scarcely consumed at all by rust. Thus by iron is signified the dart of preaching, and by bronze the constancy of long-suffering. Hence, too, Moses says of the holy Church under the figure of Asher: “Its sandal is iron and bronze” (Deut. 33:25). For in Holy Scripture a sandal is understood as the protection of preaching, as it is written: “Your feet shod in preparation for the gospel of peace” (Eph. 6:18).

Therefore, because strength is expressed through iron and bronze is called its sandal, its preaching is fortified both by sharpness and constancy. By iron it pierces opposing evils; by bronze it long-sufferingly preserves the good which it has undertaken. The following words more plainly indicate its perseverance there: “As the days of its youth, so shall its old age be.” But when the devil has taken up Antichrist for the exercise of his iniquity, he will account iron as straw and bronze as rotten wood; for unless divine grace protects them, he will consume the strength of preachers like straw in the fire of his wickedness, and reduce the constancy of the patient to dust like rotten wood. Thus both the sharpness of iron and the strength of bronze fail, when through the violence of his power the meaning of preaching is blunted and the long-suffering of patience is scattered.

[Note: [Col. 0314D] From Part III of the *Pastoral Rule*, chapter XIV.] By “iron” is signified one who does not abandon the malice of doing harm. Thus the Lord reproaches the captive people of Israel, though they have not been converted from iniquity: “The house of Israel has turned to dross for me; all these are bronze, tin, iron, and lead in the midst of the furnace” (Ezek. 22:18). It is as though he openly said: “I wished to cleanse them by the fire of tribulation and sought to make them silver or gold; but in the furnace they were changed for me into bronze, tin, iron, and lead, because even amid tribulation they burst forth not into virtue but into vices.”

Bronze, when struck, gives a sound louder than other metals. Therefore one who, under the blow, bursts out into the sound of murmuring has become bronze in the middle of the furnace. Tin, when skillfully prepared, is cast into the appearance of silver. One who is not free from the vice of pretence in tribulation has become tin in the furnace. Iron is used by one who plots against his neighbour’s life. Thus he is iron in the furnace who does not lose the malice of doing harm in tribulation. Lead also is heavier than the other metals. Therefore he is found to be lead in the furnace who is so weighed down by the burden of his sin that, even when placed in tribulation, he is not raised above earthly desires.

### CHAPTER X. ON BRONZE

In Holy Scripture, by the name “bronze” are signified at times Christ; at times true strength; at times the constancy of long-suffering; at times the resonant voice of preachers; at times the obscure preaching of the Fathers of the Old Testament; at times also the unfeeling heart of the wicked; and at times one who murmurs while under chastisement.

By “bronze” Christ is understood, as Ezekiel says concerning him: “And behold, a man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze” (Ezek. 40:3). For who is understood by the name “man” except Christ Jesus, the man who is mediator between God and human beings? But we must ask why it is said of this man that “his appearance was like the appearance of bronze.” We all know that bronze is a very durable metal and altogether resonant. What, then, does it mean that the appearance of the mediator between God and human beings is compared with bronze, except what we plainly know: that the only-begotten Son of God, taking the form of a servant, transformed the frailty of human flesh, through the glory of his resurrection, into eternity, because in him flesh has now become durable without end. For, having risen from the dead, he dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. 6:4).

And why is his very incarnation compared to resonant metal, except because, through that very assumption of our humanity, the glory of his majesty sounded forth to all? He has, as it were, the appearance of bronze through his body, because God became known to the world through flesh. Let it therefore be said: “His appearance was like the appearance of bronze,” because his preaching is like a certain sound issuing from bronze.

[Note: [Col. 0315D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XVII.] By “bronze” true strength is understood, as blessed Job says: “And stone melted by heat is turned into bronze” (Job 28:2). What is signified by stone but a hard heart, and by bronze but true strength? A stone is melted by heat when a hard heart, cold from the fire of divine love, is touched by that same fire of divine love and melts in the fervour of the Spirit, so that it burns in the heat of desire for the life that follows—a life toward which it had formerly remained insensitive when it heard of it. Through this burning it is softened for love and strengthened for action, so that, just as it was formerly hard in love of the world, it afterward shows itself strong in love of God; and what it previously refused to hear, it now begins both to believe and to preach.

Thus stone melted by heat is turned into bronze, because a hard mind liquefied by the fire of heavenly love is changed into true strength, so that a sinner who had formerly been insensible may afterward become strong through authority and resonant through preaching. Isaiah rightly says: “Those who trust in the Lord shall change their strength” (Isa. 40:31). For we change strength when, converted, we flee the present age with as much vigour as we formerly sought it here.

By “bronze” is signified the constancy of long-suffering, as we have learned from the Lord’s words to blessed Job, speaking thus of the devil’s malice: “He will account iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood” (Job 41:18). Read above, chapter 9, distinction 3.

By “bronze” is signified the resonant voice of preachers, as Ezekiel says concerning them under the figure of living creatures: “And sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze” (Ezek. 1:7).

[Note: [Col. 0315D] From Homily III on Ezekiel, after the beginning.] Bronze is a very resonant metal; rightly, then, the voices of preachers are compared to bronze, “because their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:7). Bronze is aptly called glowing, because the life of preachers resounds and burns: it burns with desire and resounds in speech. Therefore glowing bronze is inflamed preaching. But sparks issue from glowing bronze, because fiery words proceed from their exhortations to the ears of hearers. The words of preachers are rightly called sparks because they set ablaze those whose hearts they touch.

It should also be considered that sparks are very subtle and slight, because when holy preachers speak of the heavenly homeland, they cannot disclose as much in speech as they can burn in desire. From their tongue, as it were, certain sparks come to us, because in their voice scarcely some slight thing concerning the heavenly homeland is known—though they themselves burn for it not slightly. For they are not able either to see heavenly glory as it is and in its full measure, or to speak of it as fully as they see it. Thus glowing bronze casts sparks when a preacher can scarcely speak even slightly of that concerning which he himself burns mightily.

[Note: [Col. 0316D] From Homily 15 on Ezekiel, after the middle.] By “bronze” is signified the obscure preaching of the Fathers of the Old Testament. Hence, in constructing the tabernacle, bronze pegs were commanded to be fixed around the outside, so that silver columns might stand within; the tabernacle was to be held fast by cords tied to them (Exod. 38:31). Thus silver columns are set within, but bronze pegs around the outside, and cords are tied to them so that the tabernacle may remain fixed. This means that, in order that the holy apostles might stand firm in the light of their teaching and the whole tabernacle—that is, the holy Church—might stand in the integrity of faith, the Fathers and prophets of the Old Testament were fixed outside like bronze pegs, binding the minds of preachers in firmness by the cords of their words.

The pegs are therefore outside because they existed before the time of this holy Church; nevertheless, they bind those within it because, by preaching the heavenly mysteries that were to come, they made them credible to all once they had been revealed. Thus, in order that the columns may stand immovable within, the pegs outside hold the cords: the preaching of those who were able to foresee and foretell the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation before it occurred enabled the holy apostles to believe that mystery perfectly.

And it is not without reason that the columns are made of silver but the pegs of bronze. What the apostles now preach plainly, the prophets spoke obscurely under mystical meaning. Therefore those who were not clear in their preaching were rightly signified by bronze. But the holy apostles, because they possessed the mystery of our Redeemer in the light of preaching, were expressed by silver columns. Note that silver resounds and shines, whereas bronze resounds but does not shine: the preachers of the New Testament spoke openly of things that they could also show; but the preachers of the Old Testament, because they uttered obscure sayings about the heavenly mystery through the shadows of allegory, gave forth sound as if without light.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] From Book VII on Job, chapter IX, 10.] By “bronze,” Job speaks of the hard and insensible heart of the wicked: “Neither is my strength the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze” (Job 6:12). For what are signified here by bronze and stones except the hearts of insensible people? They often receive heavenly blows and yet are softened by no stroke of discipline. In contrast, when the Lord promises through the prophet concerning the elect, he says: “I shall take from you the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 11:19). Paul also says: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but have not love, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. 13:1).

We know that struck stones cannot give back a clear sound; but when bronze is struck, a very melodious sound is formed by the blow. Yet, since bronze, like stone, lacks life, it has no understanding in its sound. There are some who resemble stones: they have hardened themselves so much against the commands of piety that, when the stroke of heavenly correction tests them, they give back no sound of humble confession. But others, differing in no respect from bronze, receive the lashes of heavenly chastisement and emit the sound of pious confession; yet, because they do not utter words of humility from the heart, they do not know how to return to the state of salvation which they promised.

Thus, the former, struck in the manner of stones, have no voice; but the latter do not escape in any respect the likeness of bronze, for while under blows they speak good things which they do not feel. The former deny both reverence for the one who strikes and the blows themselves; the latter, promising what they do not fulfil, cry out without life. The holy man, therefore, fleeing the hardness of the reprobate under blows, cries: “Neither is my strength the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze.” It is as though he openly confesses: “Under the lash of discipline I flee the likeness of the reprobate; for I have not hardened like stones so that, under the sting of the blow, I do not resound in the duty of confession and know nothing of the meaning of my voice.” But because, under chastisement, the reprobate are weakly strong while the elect are strongly weak, blessed Job, in denying that he is strong through madness, makes known that he is strong through the state of salvation.

By “bronze” is signified one who murmurs while under chastisement, as the Lord reproaches the captive people of Israel, though not converted from iniquity, saying: “The house of Israel has turned into dross for me” (Ezek. 22:18). “All these are bronze, tin, iron, and lead in the midst of the furnace.” See above, chapter 9, distinction 4.

### CHAPTER XI. ON LEAD

In Holy Scripture, by the name “lead” are signified at times Judaea; at times the sin of avarice; and at times anyone weighed down by the burden of sins.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] From Book XIV on Job, chapters XXV–XXVI.] By “lead” Judaea is signified. Hence blessed Job says: “Who will grant me that my words may be written? Who will give me that they may be inscribed in a book with an iron stylus and a plate of lead, or engraved with a chisel on flint?” (Job 19:24). All that blessed Job endured was recorded with an iron stylus and a plate of lead because that weighty people of Judaea, instructed by the strong teaching of the Fathers, recognized it. But because even the hard hearts of the Gentiles came to know these things, why do we see them engraved upon flint?

Notice that what is written on lead is erased more quickly because of the softness of that metal. On flint, however, letters can indeed be impressed more slowly, but are erased with greater difficulty. Judaea, therefore, is not without reason expressed by the plate of lead: it both received God’s commandments without labour and lost them quickly. The Gentile world is likewise rightly figured by flint: it could scarcely receive the words of sacred speech so as to keep them, but kept them strongly once received. But what else is signified by the iron stylus than God’s strong judgment? Hence the prophet also says: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with a diamond point” (Jer. 17:1).

[Note: [Col. 0318D] From Book XIV on Job, chapters XXVI–XXVII.] By lead also, whose nature is of heavy weight, the sin of avarice is signified, because it makes the mind it infects so heavy that it cannot at all be raised to seek things on high. Thus it is written in Zechariah: “Lift up your eyes and see what this is that comes forth,” etc. (Zech. 5:5).

By “lead” is signified anyone weighed down by the burden of sins, as the Lord reproaches the captive people of Israel, though not converted from iniquity, saying: “The house of Israel has turned into dross for me” (Ezek. 22:18). “All these are bronze, tin, iron, and lead in the midst of the furnace.” See above, chapter 9, distinction 4.

### CHAPTER XII. ON TIN

Tin signifies one who feigns holiness. See the same place.

### CHAPTER XIII. ON WEAPONS

In Holy Scripture, by the name “weapons” are signified at times the miracles of the saints; at times human protections; at times the deceits of the devil; at times the necessities of the present life; and at times the members of our body.

[Note: [Col. 0319D] According to the Septuagint and Jerome, where “flashing” stands in place of “brightness.”] By “weapons” are signified the miracles of the saints, as it is written: “Your arrows shall go forth in the light, in the splendour of the flashing of your weapons” (Hab. 3:4). For God’s arrows go forth in the light when his words resound in open truth. But because people often despise even words of life that they understand, miracles are also added. Hence it is added there: “In the splendour of the flashing of your weapons.”

[Note: [Col. 0319D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter II, 3.] The flashing of weapons is the brightness of miracles. We defend ourselves with weapons; with arrows we destroy things opposed to us. Thus weapons together with arrows are miracles together with proclamations. Holy preachers strike adversaries by their words as by arrows; but by weapons—that is, miracles—they defend themselves, so that through the force of their arrows they may proclaim how much they ought to be heard, and through the weapons of miracles they may shine forth as worthy of reverence.

[Note: [Col. 0319D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter XXIV.] By “weapons” human protections are signified, as the Psalmist says: “He will break the bow and shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire” (Ps. 45:10). The Lord breaks the bow when he dissolves every hidden device of those who lay snares. He shatters weapons when he crushes the human protections raised against him. He burns shields with fire when, by the heat of the Holy Spirit, he kindles to the ardour of repentance and confession the minds of sinners who defend themselves with obstinate hardness.

[Note: [Col. 0320D] From Book XXXI on Job, chapters XVII, 28–29.] By “weapons” are signified the innumerable deceits of the devil, as we learn from the Lord’s own words. Speaking of the holy preacher under the name of a horse, he says: “He digs the earth with his hoof; he exults boldly; he goes forth to meet armed men” (Job 39:24). To dig the earth with the hoof is to subdue the flesh by strict abstinence. The more the flesh is pressed down, the more securely the mind rejoices in heavenly hope. Therefore “he exults boldly” is aptly joined to the earth being dug up. For one who strongly restrains what assaults him boldly exults in those things which he desires in eternal peace; and he is ordered more fittingly toward seeking things above in proportion as the body is more strictly tamed from unlawful things.

Because anyone stationed in the contest of battle sees the enemy’s deceit more easily the more strictly he presses his own body, as though it were an ally of the enemy, the joy of the heart is rightly joined after the crushing of the body: “He goes forth to meet armed men.” The armed enemies are unclean spirits, equipped against us with innumerable deceits. When they cannot persuade us to evil, they set evil before our eyes under the appearance of virtues and conceal themselves, as it were, beneath certain weapons, lest we see them naked in their malice.

We go forth to meet these armed enemies when we foresee their snares from afar. Therefore, to go forth to meet armed enemies after digging the earth is to investigate wonderfully the unclean spirits after the flesh has been subdued. To go forth to meet armed enemies after digging the earth is to enter the contest against spiritual things after conquering carnal wickedness. For one who still fights weakly against himself takes up wars set outside against him in vain. For how can one who is subject to carnal desires resist spiritual vices? Or how can one desire to triumph in the labour of an external contest who succumbs within himself to the domestic war of lust?

Or certainly, we go forth to meet armed enemies when, through the effort of exhortation, we anticipate their snares even in another’s heart. For we proceed, as it were, from the place where we were to another place to meet enemies when, setting aside our own concern in due order, we prevent the approach of unclean spirits to a neighbour’s mind.

[Note: [Col. 0320D] From Book XV on Job, chapter XIV.] By “weapons” are signified the necessities of the present life, as Job says concerning the avaricious person: “He shall flee iron weapons and fall upon a bronze bow” (Job 20:24). What are iron weapons but the necessities of the present life, which harshly press upon and even pursue the life of the poor?

By “weapons” are understood the members of our body, as the prophet says of the damnation of the reprobate: “They descended into hell with their weapons” (Ezek. 32:27). The weapons of sinners are the members of the body by which they carry out the perverse desires they conceive. Hence Paul rightly says: “Do not yield your members as weapons of iniquity to sin” (Rom. 6:13). To descend into hell with weapons, therefore, is to endure the torments of eternal judgment with the very members through which they fulfilled the desires of pleasure, so that then pain may engulf them on every side—those who now, enslaved to their pleasures, fight on every side against the justice of the righteous Judge.

### CHAPTER XIV. ON ARROWS

[Note: [Col. 0320D] From Homily 5 on Ezekiel, near the end.] By “arrows” are signified the words of the saints, as it is written: “Your arrows shall go forth in the light, in the splendour of the flashing of your weapons” (Hab. 3:4). The Lord’s arrows are the words of saints, which strike the hearts of sinners. But these arrows have weapons. You know, brothers, that men who fight in battle cast arrows but are protected by weapons. Therefore, when they add miracles to words, they protect themselves as by weapons lest they themselves be struck.

“Your arrows shall go forth in the light,” because the words of God come forth openly. But because miraculous deeds ought to accompany the utterances of teachers, it is rightly added: “In the splendour of the flashing of your weapons.” For when they add the weapons of miracles, they flash upon the minds of persecutors, so that the latter do not dare to persecute them.

### CHAPTER XV. ON A SHIELD

In Holy Scripture, by the name “shield” are signified at times divine protection and at times human resistance.

[Note: [Col. 0321D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter XXIV, 29.] By “shield” divine protection is signified, where it is said: “Lord, you have crowned us as with a shield of your good will” (Ps. 5:13). The Lord is said to crown us with a shield because those whom he helps by protecting, he crowns by rewarding.

By “shield” human resistance is signified, as the Psalmist says: “There he broke the horns, bow, shield, sword, and battle” (Ps. 75:4).

[Note: [Col. 0321D] In place of “horns,” the common text reads “powers.”] By horns is signified the pride of the arrogant; by the bow, the snares of those who strike from afar; by the shield, the stubborn hardness of defences; by the sword, a blow struck nearby; and by battle, the very movement of a mind against God.

[Note: [Col. 0321D] From the book and chapter above.] All this, indeed, is broken in the holy Church when the minds of those resisting God are tamed beneath the yoke of humility imposed upon them. Hence the same prophet again says: “He will break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire” (Ps. 45:10). Again, the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the devil’s body: “His body is like cast shields. Every cast vessel is usually hard, but fragile when it falls” (Job 41:6). Cast shields are strong in receiving the impact of arrows, but fragile in a fall. They are not pierced by the stroke of those attacking them, yet they break apart through their own fall into fragments.

Thus the body of Leviathan—that is, all the wicked, who are hard through obstinacy but fragile in life—is compared with cast shields. When they hear the words of preaching, they permit no arrows of correction to penetrate them, because in every sin they commit they set before them the shield of proud self-defence. For when one of these persons is accused of the guilt of his iniquity, he does not immediately consider how to correct the fault, but what he may advance to assist his defence. Therefore no arrow of truth penetrates them, because he receives the words of holy correction upon the shield of proud defence. Thus it is rightly said: “His body is like cast shields,” because all the wicked, lest the words of those correcting them should reach them, prepare shields of defence as if against the arrows of opponents.

### CHAPTER XVI. ON A BUCKLER

By “bucklers” is signified the protection of virtues, as the bridegroom says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Your neck is like the tower of David, which was built with battlements. A thousand bucklers hang from it, all the armour of the mighty” (Song 4:4). Read again Book V, chapter 22, distinction 1.

[Note: [Col. 0322D] From Book XXXI on Job, chapter XV, 26.] By “buckler” is signified the devil’s resistance, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the holy preacher under the name of a horse: “Above him the quiver shall sound; the spear and buckler shall be brandished” (Job 39:26). The quiver gives a sound against the horse when, against a holy preacher, the hidden plotting of wicked persons makes known still more deceitfully the scheme it craftily conceals, so that it may terrify him by threats sent beforehand as though by the sound of a quiver, when the preacher of God does not fear open insults like arrows striking at close range.

But when he is not frightened by these, the cruelty of persecutions is immediately brought to manifest punishments. Hence, after it has been said, “Above him the quiver shall sound,” there is immediately added: “The spear shall be brandished.” After the sound of the quiver against the preacher of God, the spear is brandished when, after threats have been displayed, open punishment that now strikes nearby is inflicted. Yet when holy preachers suffer punishments in defence of the faith, they do not cease even under blows from drawing to that same faith those whom they can. And while they patiently receive wounds, they prudently return the arrows of preaching against the hearts of unbelievers.

Thus it sometimes happens that those who rage in persecution grieve not so much because they do not soften the preachers as because they lose others through the preacher’s words. Therefore, since they do not overcome him by striking him, lest perhaps others who hear him should also leave them, they immediately prepare the shield of an answer against the speaker’s words. Hence, after saying, “The spear shall be brandished,” it is rightly added: “And the buckler.” For after the raging persecutor strikes the preacher’s body with punishment, he fortifies the heart of the hearers, as with a shield, by the words of his argument.

Thus the holy man is struck because the spear is brandished; but, lest he may be heard, the buckler is set against him. Let it therefore be said: “Above him the quiver shall sound; the spear and buckler shall be brandished.” For against God’s horse, because the schemes of the wicked make a clamour, the quiver sounds; because open punishment is sought, the spear is brandished; and because he is also resisted in disputation, the buckler is brought forward.

### CHAPTER XVII. ON THE SWORD

In Holy Scripture, by the name “sword” are signified at times the word of God; at times the sentence of the future judgment; at times the punishment of eternal damnation; at times a blow struck nearby; at times temporal tribulation; at times the anger or persuasion of an evil spirit; and at times the pleasing persuasion of the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 0322D] From Book XIX on Job, chapter XVI, 28–29.] By “sword” is signified the word of God, as Paul says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6:17). Hence Solomon, describing the warriors strong in spiritual battle, says: “All holding swords, and most skilled in warfare” (Song 3:8). What is figured by the sword except the word of God? Solomon does not say, however, “all having swords,” but “holding” them, because it is not remarkable merely to know the word of God, but to do it. He has the sword but does not hold it who indeed knows divine speech but neglects to live according to it. Nor can one be skilled for battle who does not practise this spiritual sword. For one who sets aside holding the sword of God’s word by living wrongly is entirely insufficient to resist temptations.

[Note: [Col. 0323D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter VII.] By “sword” is signified the sentence of future judgment, as it is said of the followers of heretics: “If his children are multiplied, they shall be for the sword” (Job 27:14). The children of heretics are their followers, who, in assenting to their errors, are as it were begotten through their preaching. But “multiplied, they shall be for the sword,” because although they now increase in immense numbers in ruinous freedom, they will nevertheless be struck by the sentence of the coming judgment. Hence the Lord says through Moses: “My sword shall devour flesh” (Deut. 32:42). God’s sword will devour flesh because, at the last judgment, his sentence will kill those who think carnally.

[Note: [Col. 0323D] From Book XXIII on Job, chapter XIV, 22.] By “sword” is signified the punishment of eternal damnation, as Elihu says concerning the person who has been delivered: “Delivering his soul from corruption, and his life so that it may not pass into the sword” (Job 33:18). Every sinner, indeed, is compelled to pass from this corruption of vices to that sword of punishments, so that where he was here unrighteously delighted, there he may justly be tormented. But the Lord first delivers from corruption, and afterward from the sword, the one whom he purposes to save; for he rescues there from the vengeance of punishment the life whose mind he here withdraws from delight in sin.

For there is nothing to fear there from the sword of judgment for the person whom, after his amendment here, the pollution of sin has not corrupted. Therefore it is rightly said: “Delivering his soul from corruption, and his life so that the sword may not pass into it.” To pass from corruption to the sword is to arrive at punishments to be endured after sins have been committed.

[Note: [Col. 0323D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter XXIV.] By “sword” is signified a nearby blow, as the Psalmist says: “There he broke the horns of bows, shield, sword, and battle” (Ps. 75:4).

[Note: [Col. 0323D] From Book XXXIV on Job, chapter VIII, 4.] By “sword” is signified temporal tribulation, as it is said to Mary concerning the tribulations that would follow: “A sword shall pass through your own soul also” (Luke 2:35).

[Note: [Col. 0323D] Where the Vulgate edition reads ‘you redeemed.’] By “sword” is expressed the anger or persuasion of the evil enemy, as the Psalmist says: “You who delivered David your servant from the evil sword” (Ps. 143:10). The sword of holy preaching is good, by which we are struck so that we may die to sin. But the sword of diabolical persuasion is evil, by which one is wickedly struck so as to be extinguished from the life of righteousness.

[Note: [Col. 0324D] From Book VI on Job, ch. XIII, 16.] By the name of the sword, the flattering persuasion of the wicked is denoted, as Eliphaz says: “Moreover, he saves the poor from the sword of their mouth, and from the violent hand” (Job 5:15). For poor is anyone who is not exalted in his own estimation. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). Now each person is drawn into sin in two ways: either he is led by pleasure or overcome by fear. The sword of the mouth is the wickedness of persuasion; the violent hand is the adversity of power. But because the one who is truly humble, and who is here called poor, desires none of this world’s prosperity, it is rightly said of him with confidence even amid adversities: “He will save,” etc. As though it were said plainly: God so strengthens within themselves the minds of the humble that neither the enticements of persuasions draw them into committing wickedness nor the pains of punishments break them.

447 CHAPTER XVIII. ON THE BOW.

[Col. 0324B] In Sacred Scripture, by the name of the bow are sometimes denoted the day of the last judgment, sometimes the heavenly judgment, sometimes the snares of the wicked, sometimes Sacred Scripture, and sometimes the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0324D] From Book XIX on Job, ch. XVI, 28.] By the name of the bow, the day of the last judgment is denoted, as it is said: “You have shown your people hard things; you have given us the wine of compunction to drink. You have given those who fear you a sign, that they may flee from before the face of the bow” (Ps. 59:3). For in a bow, the farther the string is drawn back, the more forcefully the arrow flies from it. Thus indeed, the longer the day of final judgment is delayed before it comes, the stricter will be the sentence that proceeds from it when it comes. We are therefore now struck by various disasters, so that, corrected by them, we may then be found more prepared. Hence it was said before: “You have shown your people hard things” [Col. 0324C]—that is, the scourges of this age, which precede the more grievous day of judgment to follow. “You have given us the wine of compunction to drink,” so that earthly joys might be changed into tears. “You have given,” he says, “those who fear you a sign, that they may flee from before the face of the bow” (Ps. 59:6). As though he said: This is the time of mercy; that will be the time of judgment. Therefore, through these scourges of the present time you signify how you will strike then, when you judge without sparing, since you strike so strictly now when you spare.

[Note: [Col. 0324D] From Book XV on Job, ch. XIV, 12.] By the name of the bow, heavenly judgment is denoted, as it is said through blessed Job of any perverse person: “He shall flee from weapons of iron, and shall rush upon a bow of bronze” (Job 20:22).

[Col. 0324D] [Note: [Col. 0324D] From Book XV on Job, ch. XVI, 28.] By the name of the bow, the snares of the wicked are denoted, as the Psalmist says: “They have bent the bow, a bitter thing” (Ps. 63:4). Hence the same Psalmist again says:

448 “There he broke the horns of bows, shield, sword, and war” (Ps. 75:4). And again: “He shall break the bow and shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire” (Ps. 45:10).

[Note: [Col. 0324D] From Book XIX on Job, ch. XVI, 28.] By the name of the bow, Sacred Scripture is denoted, as the Psalmist says: “He bent his bow and made it ready; and in it he prepared vessels of death; he made his arrows for those who burn” (Ps. 7:13). For what is signified by the bow except Sacred Scripture? It is itself the bow of the Church; it is itself the bow of the Lord, from which judgments come to human hearts as arrows which strike and terrify. The Lord bent his bow because through Sacred Scripture he set threats before all sinners. In this bow he prepares vessels of death, because according to the sentence of his word he condemns as reprobate those who now neglect correction. In it too he makes his arrows for those who burn, because he sends blazing pronouncements of his words to those whom he corrects by fear.

[Note: [Col. 0325D] From Homily 8 on Ezekiel.] By the name of the bow, the Holy Spirit is denoted, as Ezekiel says of the vision of fire: “Like the appearance of a bow when it is in a cloud on a rainy day” [Col. 0325B] (Ezek. 19:28). Almighty God placed the bow as a sign between himself and humankind, so that he would no longer destroy the world by a flood, saying: “I will place my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. And when I have covered the sky with clouds, my bow shall appear in the clouds, and I will remember my covenant with you” (Gen. 9:13). Hence in this same bow the color of water and of fire is shown together, because it is partly blue and partly red, so that it may be a witness to both judgments: one yet to be carried out and the other already carried out, though the former is no longer to be carried out in the same way. For the world will indeed be burned by the fire of judgment, but it will no longer be destroyed by the water of a flood.

But what does it mean that the prophet saw the shining fire from the loins of the man presiding on the throne, as he says, “like the appearance of a bow when it is in a cloud [Col. 0325C] on a rainy day”? Since the burning fire signifies the fervor of the Holy Spirit, what resemblance is there between the bow and the Spirit, that the fire which appeared should be said to have appeared like the appearance of a bow? But if we attend to the vision of the bow described above, we see how the bow signifies the Spirit. For, as I have said, water and fire appear in the bow.

449 And after the advent of the Mediator, the power of the Holy Spirit shone forth in the human race precisely in this: that it both washed God’s elect in the water of baptism and set them ablaze with the fire of divine love. Thus a kind of bow in a cloud is set forth for testing, as though water and fire were mingled in its color, when Truth says: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” [Col. 0325D] (John 3:5). This bow is in the cloud on a rainy day, because it is shown in the Lord’s Incarnation and in the outpouring of preaching, so that the hearts of believers may be recalled to pardon through the Lord’s mercy. We fittingly understand the cloud to be the flesh of the Redeemer. Of it the Psalmist says: “Who makes the cloud his ascent” (Ps. 98:7). For the Lord made the cloud his ascent, because he who is everywhere in his divinity ascended to heavenly things in the flesh.

CHAPTER XIX. ON THE QUIVER.

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of the quiver are understood sometimes God’s hidden counsel, sometimes the plotting of the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 0325D] From Book XX on Job, ch. XVII, 19.] By the name of the quiver, God’s hidden counsel is denoted, as blessed Job says in the person of the Church: “He opened his quiver and afflicted me” (Job 30:11). For what is denoted by the quiver except God’s hidden and just counsel? As arrows lie hidden in a quiver, so judgments lie hidden in God’s secret counsel. An arrow, as it were, is drawn from the quiver when an open judgment is shot forth from God’s hidden counsel. Therefore he says: “He opened his quiver and afflicted me”; that is, he disclosed his hidden counsel and wounded me by a public blow.

[Note: [Col. 0325D] From Book XXXI on Job, ch. XIV, 25.] By the name of the quiver, the plotting of the wicked is denoted, as the Psalmist says: “They have prepared [Col. 0326B] their arrows in the quiver,

450 that they may shoot in the dark at those upright in heart” (Ps. 10:2). For when the wicked conceal, by secret contrivances, the deceits which they devise against the good, they prepare arrows, as it were, in a quiver. And in the darkness of this present life they strike the upright in heart as in the dark, because their malicious missiles can be felt through their wound, yet cannot be detected as they approach.

CHAPTER XX. ON ARROWS.

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of arrows are sometimes denoted the pronouncements of sacred utterance, sometimes the words of preaching, sometimes the stroke of divine chastisement, and sometimes the deceits of the wicked.

[Col. 0326C] By the name of arrows, the pronouncements of sacred utterance are denoted, as the Psalmist says: “He bent his bow and made it ready; and in it he prepared vessels of death; he made his arrows for those who burn.” Read again Chapter 18 above, distinction 4.

[Note: [Col. 0326D] From Book VII on Job, ch. II.] By the name of arrows, the words of preaching are denoted, as it is said to the coming Redeemer: “Your arrows are sharp, O most mighty one; peoples shall fall beneath you in their hearts” (Ps. 44:16). The utterances of preaching are rightly compared with arrows, because in striking the vices of those who live wickedly, they pierce their hearts. Of these arrows the same Psalmist again says: “The arrows of little children became their wounds” (Ps. 63:8), because the words of the humble pierced the hearts of the proud.

[Col. 0326D] [Note: [Col. 0326D] From Book XXXIV on Job, ch. X, 5.] By the name of arrows, the stroke of chastisement is denoted, as Elisha says to King Joash: “Shoot an arrow.” And when he had shot it, he said: “You shall strike Syria until you consume it” (4 Kings 13:17). Hence blessed Job says: “My words are full of sorrow, because the arrows of the Lord are in me, and their indignation drinks up my spirit” (Job 67:4). [Note: [Col. 0326D] From Book VII on Job, ch. II, 3.] For the holy man, because he considers the misery of his pilgrimage and groans under the strokes of the Lord’s chastisement, says: “My words are full of sorrow,” etc. As though he said plainly: I do not rejoice in the sentence of my exile, but, set under judgment, I grieve because [Col. 0327A] I recognize the force of the blow. Yet there are many whom torments torture but do not correct. Appropriately, therefore, it is added in contrast: “Their indignation drinks up my spirit.” For what is the human spirit but the spirit of self-exaltation? The arrows of the Lord drink up the human spirit when the judgments of heavenly chastisement restrain the afflicted mind from self-exaltation. The arrows of the Lord drink up the human spirit because they draw inward the mind intent on outward things.

David’s spirit had been drunk up when he said: “When my spirit failed within me, you knew my paths” (Ps. 76:20). And again: “I refused to let my soul be comforted; I remembered God and was delighted; I meditated, and my spirit failed a little” (ibid., 3). Therefore the indignation of the arrows drinks up the spirit of the righteous, because the judgments of heaven, while they wound the elect whom they find in sins, change them, so that the pierced mind abandons its hardness and, from the saving wound, the blood of confession may flow.

By the name of arrows, the deceits of the wicked are denoted. See above, Chapter 19, distinction 1.

CHAPTER XXI. ON THE SPEAR.

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of the spear are sometimes denoted the openly raging persecution of the wicked, sometimes the missile of preaching.

By the name of the spear, the openly raging persecution of the wicked is denoted, as the Lord says of the holy preacher under the name of a horse: “Upon him [Col. 0327C] the quiver shall sound; the spear and shield shall flash.” Read again Chapter 16, distinction 2 above.

[Note: [Col. 0327D] From Book XXXIV on Job, ch. VIII, 4, 5.] By the name of the spear, the missile of preaching is denoted, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the devil’s mighty wickedness, under the figure of Leviathan: “When the sword takes hold of him, it shall not be able to stand, neither spear nor breastplate” (Job 41:17). The sword is that man, then condemned, who is assumed by the ancient enemy for his service; for by his malice he pierces both him and the hearts of the weak. This Leviathan takes hold of the sword when he receives this condemned man as his own. What, moreover, is denoted by the spear except the missile of preaching, and by the breastplate except the strength of patience? For with the spear we strike the adversary, but with the breastplate we are defended from the adversary; with the spear we inflict wounds, while with the breastplate we are covered lest we be wounded.

This Leviathan, then, is said to be taken hold of by the sword because, through the reprobate man whom he assumes, he unleashes rage of every kind of unbridled cruelty. For through the display of his immense power at that time, he manifests whatever evil he is able to do. But neither spear nor breastplate will be able to stand, because the malignant enemy, coming in Antichrist, will appear with such great power that, if heavenly aid is lacking, he will both blunt the keenness of preachers and destroy the long-suffering of the patient. Unless the life of the righteous is strengthened by heavenly grace, the spear does not stand, because the strength of preachers is broken; [Col. 0328A] the breastplate does not stand, because the patience of the steadfast is broken open and pierced.

CHAPTER XXII. ON THE LANCE.

[Note: [Col. 0327D] From Book XIII on Job, ch. VI, 9.] By the name of lances, the missiles of temptations are denoted, as the holy Church complains through Job, saying: “He surrounded me with his lances” (Job 16:14). For the holy Church is surrounded with lances by her enemy when, in her members, she is assailed by the burning attacker with the missiles of temptations. It is well said that she is surrounded with lances, because the ancient enemy attacks us with the wound of his temptation.

453 For often, when gluttony is restrained in order that lust may be subdued, the sting of vain glory strikes the mind. But if the body is not worn down by the affliction of abstinence, the flame of lust kindles itself against the mind. Often, while we strive to preserve frugality, we fall into stinginess. And often, while we lavishly give away what we possess, we are led into avarice, because we seek again to gather what we may give. Therefore, since the missiles of the ancient enemy attack us everywhere, it is rightly said: “He surrounded me with his lances.”

CHAPTER XXIII. ON THE BREASTPLATE.

By the name of the breastplate, the long-suffering of patience is denoted, as it is said in the Lord’s words concerning the devil’s power which he will display through Antichrist: “When the sword takes hold of him, neither spear nor breastplate shall be able to stand” (Job 61:17). Consult the chapter On the Spear, distinction 2.

CHAPTER XXIV. ON TOOLS.

[Col. 0328C]

[Note: [Col. 0328D] From Book XXXIV on Job, ch. X, 7.] By the name of tools, the lesser scourges of the Lord are denoted, as it is said concerning the building of Solomon’s Temple: “Hammer and axe and every tool of iron were not heard in the house when it was being built” (3 Kings 6:7). For what did that house prefigure except the holy Church, in which the Lord dwells in heavenly places? For its building, the souls of the elect are brought as certain polished stones. When they are built up, no blows are heard in heaven, because in the eternal homeland every sound of strokes has now fallen silent. No hammer strikes there, because no chastisement afflicts. No axe cuts there, because no judgment of severity casts outside those received within. No tools resound there, because no scourges, even the least, are felt any longer.

454 CHAPTER XXV. ON THE AXE.

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of the axe are sometimes denoted our Redeemer, sometimes the gift of understanding, sometimes the sentence of strict chastisement, and sometimes rebuke.

[Note: [Col. 0328D] From Homily 20 on the Gospel, Matthew 3.] By the name of the axe, our Redeemer is denoted, as John the Baptist says: “Now the axe is laid to the root of the tree. Therefore every [Col. 0329A] tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3:10). The tree of this world is the human race; the axe is our Redeemer, who is grasped, as it were, by handle and iron through his humanity, but cuts through his divinity. This axe is laid to the root of the tree because, although he waits through patience, he sees what it will do. Yet every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire, because every perverse person swiftly finds the burning of Gehenna prepared for him if he scorns to produce here the fruit of good work.

[Note: [Col. 0329D] From Book XXII on Job, ch. IV, 5.] By the name of the axe, the gift of understanding is denoted, as one reads in the Book of Kings: when the sons of the prophets were cutting timber at the Jordan, one of them lost an axe which slipped from its handle into the depths [Col. 0329B] (4 Kings 6:1). The iron in the handle is the gift of understanding in the heart; to cut timber by it is to rebuke those who act wickedly. Sometimes, when this is done carelessly and the fall into vain glory in the very knowledge received is not avoided, the iron is lost in the water, because understanding is made foolish through a lax work.

By the name of the axe, the sentence of strict chastisement is denoted, as it is said concerning the building of Solomon’s Temple:

455 “The house, when it was being built, was built of hewn and finished stones; and hammer and axe and all tools were not heard in the house when it was being built.” Seek this in [Col. 0329C] the chapter On Tools.

By the name of the axe, rebuke is denoted, as the Lord commands through [Col. 0330A] Moses, saying: “If anyone goes simply with his friend into the forest to cut wood, and the axe slips from his hand, and the iron slips from the handle and strikes his friend and kills him, he shall flee to one of the aforesaid cities and live, lest perhaps the kinsman of him whose blood has been shed pursue him, stirred by grief, and seize him and strike his life” (Deut. 19:5).

For we go with a friend into the forest whenever we turn with any neighbor to consider our own faults; and we cut down timber simply when, with pious intention, we lay open the vices of sinners. But the axe slips from the hand when rebuke carries itself farther than necessary and into harshness; and the iron springs from the handle when the speech of correction exceeds into greater severity and, striking a friend, kills him, because the insult uttered kills the hearer’s spirit of love. For the mind of the reproved person suddenly falls into hatred if immoderate rebuke has imposed upon it more than it should.

But the one who carelessly strikes the timber and destroys his friend must flee to three cities, in order that, defended in one of them, he may live; because, turning to the laments of repentance, he is hidden in the unity of the sacrament under faith, hope, and charity. He is not held guilty of the homicide he committed, and the kinsman of the one slain does not kill him when he finds him. When the strict Judge comes—he who joined himself to us through sharing our nature—he undoubtedly does not exact from him vengeance for the guilt of sin, which faith, hope, and charity hide under his pardon. Therefore a fault which is in no way committed through zeal for malice is more swiftly forgiven.

THE NINTH BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 0329]

456 CHAPTER I. ON WOOD.

[Col. 0329C]

In Sacred Scripture, when *lignum* (“wood,” “tree”) is used in the singular, it sometimes denotes the incarnate Wisdom of God, sometimes the cross of the Lord, sometimes insensibility of mind, sometimes a proud heart, sometimes a righteous person, sometimes an unrighteous person, and sometimes the human soul. [Col. 0329D] When *ligna* (“woods,” “timbers”) is used in the plural, it sometimes denotes the examples of the Fathers and sometimes the strong minds of the Fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0329D] From Book XII on Job, ch. IV, 3; and Book XIX, ch. XVI, 27.] By the name of wood, the incarnate Wisdom of God is denoted, as it is written of her: “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her” (Prov. 3:18). And as the Lord himself says: “If they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?” (Luke 23:31). Hence the Psalmist also says: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water” (Ps. 1:3). For the streams of water are the daily passing away of peoples who fail. Therefore, the tree beside the streams [Col. 0330C] of water is he who, bringing forth for us the fruit and shelter of his shade, appeared as Creator in the flesh, in order through his resurrection to establish firmly the human race which was daily going into death through decay.

[Note: [Col. 0330D] From Homily 6 on Ezekiel.] By wood, the Lord’s cross is figured, as it is said through the Law: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on wood” (Deut. 21:23). Paul bore witness that this was said of our Redeemer: “Having become a curse for us” (Gal. 3:31). And again it is written: “Let us put wood into his bread” (Jer. 11:19). For to put wood into bread is to apply the cross to the Lord’s body.

[Note: [Col. 0330D] From Book XII on Job, ch. IV, 3.] By the name of wood, insensibility of mind is denoted, as Jeremiah says concerning certain persons who, to be sure, presumed upon their abstinence: “Their skin clung to their bones” (Lam. 4:8). Seek this in the chapter On Bones, Book V, Chapter 39, distinction 5.

[Col. 0331A] By the name of wood, a proud heart is understood. Hence, when the sons of the prophets were cutting timber at the Jordan, and one of them lost an axe which slipped from its handle into the depths, Elisha came at once, cast wood downward, and raised the iron to the surface. Seek this in the chapter On the Axe, Book VIII, Chapter 25, distinction 2.

[Note: [Col. 0331D] From Book XII on Job, ch. IV, 3.] By the name of wood, a righteous person is denoted, as blessed Job says: “A tree has hope: if it is cut down, it grows green again, and its branches sprout” (Job 14:7). In this place, when a tree is preferred to a human being, what is meant by “human being” except any carnal person? And what is figured by the name of wood except the life of each righteous person? Therefore a tree has hope: if it is cut down, it grows green again, because when a righteous person suffers in the death of suffering for the truth, he is restored in the greenness of eternal [Col. 0331B] life; and he who was green here through faith will be green there through sight. “And its branches sprout,” because often through a righteous person’s suffering the faithful are multiplied in love for the heavenly homeland and receive the greenness of spiritual life, while they rejoice that he acted bravely here for God.

By the name of wood, an unrighteous man is expressed, as the Lord says through the Prophet: “Therefore the Lord has humbled the lofty tree and exalted the lowly tree” (Ezek. 17:24), because, according to the voice of Truth itself, “everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11). Solomon too says: “If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in whatever place it falls, there it shall be” (Eccl. 11:3). For on the day of his death the righteous person falls toward the south, [Col. 0331C] the sinner toward the north: because the righteous person is led to joys through the fervor of the Spirit, while the sinner is condemned in his cold heart along with the apostate angel who said: “I shall sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the North” (Isa. 14:13).

[Note: [Col. 0331D] From the book on Job, ch. XIII.] In this testimony, however, the human soul may be understood indefinitely by the name of wood: “If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in whatever place it falls, there it shall be.” For at the time of a human being’s fall, whether a holy or an evil spirit receives the soul departing from the confines of the flesh, it will hold it with itself forever without any change: so that neither may one who has been exalted fall into punishment, nor one immersed in eternal punishments rise again to the remedy of deliverance.

[Col. 0331D] [Note: [Col. 0331D] From Book XXV on Job, ch. VII.] By the name of timbers are denoted the examples of the Fathers or the sayings of Sacred Scripture. Thus the Lord says to Moses: “Fire shall always burn on the altar; the priest shall feed it by laying timbers upon it every morning” (Lev. 4). For the altar of God is our heart, in which fire is commanded always to burn, because we must unceasingly kindle from it the flame of charity toward the Lord. Each day the priest is to lay timbers upon it lest it be extinguished. For every person redeemed by Christ’s faith has surely become a member of the High Priest, as the apostle Peter says to all believers: “But you are an elect race, [Col. 0332A] a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9). And as the apostle John says: “You have made us a kingdom and priests to our God” (Rev. 5:9).

Therefore, let the priest who feeds the fire on the altar lay timbers on it daily; that is, let every believer, lest the flame of charity fail within him, not cease to store up in his heart both the examples of those who have gone before and the testimonies of Sacred Scripture. For to give a kind of fuel to the fire is to furnish, for the stirring up of charity, either the examples of the Fathers or the Lord’s commandments. Since our inward newness itself grows old daily through the course of this life, this fire must be fed with added timbers, so that, while it is weakened through the practice of our old nature, it may be revived through the testimonies of Scripture and the examples of the Fathers. It is well commanded there that timbers be gathered every morning [Col. 0332B] each day. For this is done only when the night of blindness is extinguished; or certainly when, in the morning, the first part of the day, thoughts of the present life have been set aside, each believer considers this first: by what exertions he may kindle the zeal of charity which already seems to be failing little by little within him. For this fire on the altar of the Lord—that is, in our heart—is quickly extinguished unless it is restored by diligently applying the examples of the Fathers and the Lord’s testimonies.

[Note: [Col. 0332D] From Homily 15 on Ezekiel, a little before the middle.] By the name of timbers, the strong minds of the Fathers are understood. Thus Solomon is said to have made a litter from the woods of Lebanon (Song 3:9). For the woods of Lebanon are cedar timbers, very resistant to decay. Therefore the litter of our peaceful King is the holy Church, which is constructed from [Col. 0332C] strong Fathers—that is, from incorruptible minds. It is rightly called a litter because it bears souls daily to the eternal banquet of its Creator.

[Note: [Col. 0332D] From Book VIII on Job, ch. XXIV, 35.] By the name of timbers, works are denoted, as Moses says: “When you have entered the land which I shall give you, and have planted fruit-bearing trees in it, you shall remove their foreskins” (Lev. 19:23). “The fruits they produce shall be unclean for you, and you shall not eat of them.” Fruit-bearing trees are works fruitful in virtues. Therefore we remove the foreskins of trees when, suspicious of the weakness inherent in the beginning itself, we do not approve the first beginnings of our works. For the beginnings of a new way of life are often still mixed with the carnal life, and consequently ought not to be made known too soon, lest, when the good things that please are praised, a mind deceived by its praise be unable to detect the evils hidden in them. We regard the fruits which they produce as unclean and do not make them fit for our food, because when the beginnings of a good work are praised, it is fitting that this should not feed the doer’s mind, lest, while received praise is sweetly plucked, the fruit of the work be eaten prematurely. Therefore whoever receives praise from human speech for a virtue only begun is one who eats the fruit of the planted tree before its time.

460 CHAPTER II. ON THE TREE.

[Col. 0333A]

In Sacred Scripture, when *arbor* (“tree”) is used in the singular, it sometimes denotes Christ and sometimes the whole human race; but when *arbores* (“trees”) is used in the plural, it sometimes denotes the sacred books and sometimes those who seek lofty things.

[Note: [Col. 0333D] From Book XIX on Job, ch. I.] By the name of the tree, Christ is denoted, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and put in his garden; and it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of heaven rested in its branches” (Matt. 13:31; Luke 13:3). For he himself is the grain of mustard seed who, planted in the burial-place of the garden, rose up as a great tree.

[Col. 0333B] By the name of the tree, the whole human race is denoted, as John the Baptist says: “Now indeed the axe is laid to the root of the tree. Therefore every tree which does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3:10). Seek this in the chapter On the Axe, Book VIII, Chapter 25, distinction 1.

[Note: [Col. 0333D] From Book XX on Job, ch. XI, 9.] By the name of trees, the sacred books are denoted, as blessed Job says concerning heretics: “They ate herbs and the bark of trees” (Job 30:4). Therefore, because heretics, repelled by the barrier of their self-exaltation, cannot perceive the great and inward matters of sacred utterance, but recognize in it certain tender and external things, they are said to perceive herbs and the bark of trees. Those who desire to know things through which they may seem learned [Col. 0333C] without actually being so, while they do not search out from the depths of sacred volumes the force of charity toward God and neighbor, feed, as it were, on herbs or bark, because these are either low or external things which nourish proud minds. Or certainly, to eat herbs is to observe the lesser commandments from Sacred Scripture while scorning the greater ones. Truth rightly rebukes such persons: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint and dill and cumin, and leave aside the weightier matters of the law” (Matt. 23:23). They also eat the bark of trees: these are certain persons who reverence only the surface of the letter in sacred books and preserve nothing of spiritual understanding, since they suppose that nothing more exists in God’s words than what they hear externally.

[Col. 0333D] [Note: [Col. 0333D] From Book X, preceding chapter.] Trees may also denote those who seek lofty things, while herbs denote the earthly life of those who have still only made a good beginning. Therefore it is well said of perverse people who envy others for being what they themselves are not, and grieve that others attain what they themselves cannot: “They ate herbs and the bark of trees.” For if they happen to see good things springing up in the acts of others, they immediately pluck them out with the hand of deadly reproach. When they see persons beginning rightly, they either oppose them in mockery, as though offering counsel. When they observe that certain persons are accomplishing even the highest things, whose progress they cannot utterly destroy, they divert them from their works by certain devices of their own.

[Col. 0334A] Thus, for them to eat herbs and the bark of trees is, by their deadly persuasions, as with the teeth of their malice, to destroy either the endeavors of those who are making a good beginning or the deeds of those who, like trees, already tend upward. The reprobate eat herbs when they consume the beginnings of the weak by mockery.
