They also eat the bark of trees when, by the hand of perverse counsel, they remove from the life of those who believe rightly the covering of good works. They strip these persons in certain actions as trees; but they consume the others as herbs—that is, as things which, despised, are drawn along and trampled underfoot.

462 CHAPTER III. ON THE CEDAR.

[Col. 0334B]

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of the cedar are sometimes denoted the height of heavenly glory, sometimes hope, sometimes the kingdom of Judaea, sometimes one who, established firmly in the love of God, cannot decay, sometimes the loftiness of the heavenly powers, and sometimes the proud power of the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 0334D] From Book XXXII on Job, ch. XII.] By the name of the cedar, the height of heavenly glory is expressed, as the Prophet testifies, saying: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall be multiplied like a cedar of Lebanon” (Ps. 91:13).

By the name of the cedar, hope is understood. Thus, in Moses, when a heifer is slaughtered in sacrifice, cedar wood and hyssop and scarlet twice dyed are commanded to be offered with it. [Col. 0334C] Seek this in the chapter On the Heifer, Book II, Chapter 8, distinction 2.

By the name of the cedar, the kingdom of Judaea is denoted, as the Prophet says: “A great eagle with great wings, long of limb, full of feathers and variegation, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar and plucked off the top of its foliage” (Ezek. 17:3). Seek this in the chapter On the Eagle, Book II, Chapter 2, distinction 2.

[Note: [Col. 0334D] From Homily 20 on the Gospels.] By the name of the cedar is denoted one who, established firmly in the love of God, cannot decay, as the Lord says through Isaiah to the Gentiles left desolate—that is, to the holy Church—promising the merits of spiritual virtues as shrubs in a desert: “I shall give in the wilderness cedar and thorn” (Isa. 41:19). Since cedar is of great fragrance and of a nature resistant to decay, we rightly understand it in this promise. But concerning the thorn, since it was said to sinful humanity: “Your land [Col. 0334D] shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:18), what wonder is it if that which is multiplied for a sinful person as a punishment is promised to the holy Church?

463 By the cedar are signified those who show forth virtues and signs in their works, and who can say with Paul: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2:15). Their hearts are so strengthened by inward love that no decay of earthly love can now corrupt them. By the thorn, however, are signified men of spiritual teaching who, while discoursing on sins and virtues, at one time threaten eternal punishments and at another promise the joys of the heavenly kingdom; they prick the hearts of their hearers and so pierce their minds with the pain of compunction that tears run from their eyes like a kind of blood of the soul.

The cedar is placed in the Church for this purpose: that whoever draws from a neighbor the fragrance of spiritual virtues may not himself grow dull through delight in earthly life, but may be set aflame for the desires of heavenly goods. The thorn is placed for this purpose: that whoever has been pierced by the word of its preaching may himself learn from it to pierce the hearts of those who follow by the word of preaching.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] From Book XXXII on Job, ch. XVIII.] By the name of cedars, the loftiness of the heavenly powers is denoted. Thus, when the Prophet beheld the eminence of the apostate angel, it is said: “The cedars were not higher than he in the paradise of God” (Ezek. 31:8). For who can be understood by the cedars except those ranks of heavenly powers, lofty in stature and planted in the greenness of eternal joy? Although they were created exalted, they were neither set before nor made equal to him.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] From Book XXXII on Job, ch. XII.] By the name of the cedar, the proud power of the wicked is denoted, as the Psalmist says: “The voice of the Lord breaking cedars” (Ps. 28:2).

464 CHAPTER IV. ON THE PALM.

In Sacred Scripture, by the name of the palm are sometimes denoted any righteous person and sometimes the holy Church.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] From Book XIX on Job, ch. XVI, 26, 25.] By the name of the palm, any righteous person is denoted, as it is said: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” (Ps. 91:13).

The palm signifies the holy Church, as it is said through blessed Job in the person of the holy Church: “And like a palm-tree I shall multiply my days” (Job 29:18). For the palm grows slowly, but remains green for a long time. With many difficulties the holy Church comes to firmness in faith, and for the gathering of very many people she desires to remain long in the glory of that same faith. Therefore she believed that she would multiply her days like a palm, she who, when the crisis of sudden temptation arises, grieves that the grace of her peace—slowly acquired by the faithful—is more swiftly intercepted by unbelievers. Nor without reason is the life of the righteous compared to a palm, since the palm is rough to the touch below, as though wrapped in dry bark, but above is beautiful both in appearance and fruit. Below it is constricted by the wrappings of its bark, but above it spreads out in the height of lovely greenery. Such indeed is the life of the elect: despised below, beautiful above. At its base it is, as it were, wrapped in many layers of bark while it is pressed by innumerable tribulations; but at its summit it is, as it were, spread abroad in leaves of beautiful greenery through the abundance of recompense. Let her therefore say, “And I shall multiply my days.” For she believed that she would multiply her days like a palm, since she supposed that the minds of the faithful would rise ever stronger unto the end. But when the hearts of many begin, wearied by persecutions, to grow weak, she grieves that those whom she admired for having undertaken strong resolves are now in herself tending, as it were, toward weakness.

## CHAPTER V. ON THE FIR-TREE

[Col. 0336A]

In Sacred Scripture the fir-tree sometimes signifies an individual holy contemplative, sometimes contemplation itself, and sometimes the heavenly powers.

The fir-tree signifies a contemplative, as Isaiah says: “I shall place a fir-tree in the desert” (Isa. 41:19). For what is signified by the fir-tree, which in growing is raised very high into the air, except those who, while still placed in earthly bodies within the holy Church, already contemplate heavenly things? Although they came forth from the earth by birth, yet by contemplation they already raise the summit of their mind beside the ethereal heights.

[Note: [Col. 0336D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XII.] The fir-tree expresses contemplation, as the Lord promises through Isaiah: “In place of the saltwort a fir-tree shall rise, and in place of the nettle a myrtle shall grow” (Isa. 55:13). For in place of the saltwort a fir-tree rises when, in the heart of the saints, the height of heavenly contemplation springs up in place of the casting off of earthly thought. The nettle is entirely of a fiery nature; the myrtle, however, is said to possess a tempering power. Therefore the myrtle grows in place of the nettle when the minds of the righteous pass from the itching and heat of vices to the moderation and tranquillity of chastity: when they no longer desire earthly things, and extinguish the flames of the flesh by heavenly desires.

Fir-trees signify the heavenly powers, as the Prophet says of the apostate angel: “The cedars were not higher than it in the paradise of God; the fir-trees did not equal its height” (Ezek. 31:8). But who can be understood by cedars or fir-trees? See in chapter 466, “On the Cedar,” above, distinction 5.

## CHAPTER VI. ON THE ALMOND-TREE

[Note: [Col. 0336D] From Book XXI on Job, chapter XII, 20.] The almond-tree signifies the primitive Church, as Solomon says: “The almond-tree shall blossom, the locust shall grow fat, and the caper-bush shall be scattered” (Eccl. 12:5). For the almond shows its flower before all other trees. And what is signified in the flower of the almond except the beginnings of the holy Church? In her preachers she opened the first flowers of virtue, and, in order to bring forth the fruits of good works, she anticipated the saints who were to come after her, like succeeding shrubs. In her the locust was immediately made fat, because the dry barrenness of paganism was steeped in the richness of heavenly grace. But the caper-bush is scattered, because when paganism, called to faith, attained the grace of faith, Judaea, remaining in its barrenness, lost the order of right living.

## CHAPTER VII. ON WILLOWS

In Sacred Scripture the willow sometimes signifies the verdancy of the good, and sometimes the barrenness of the reprobate.

[Note: [Col. 0336D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter VI.] Willows are indeed fruitless trees, yet of such greenness that they can scarcely wither even when cut off at the roots and cast away. Unless willows expressed the life of the elect through the constancy of their greenness, the Prophet would never have said of the children of the holy Church: “They shall spring up among the grasses, like willows beside flowing waters” (Isa. 44:4). For the children of the holy Church spring up among the grasses like willows, when, amid the withering life of carnal people, they endure both in great number and in the perpetual greenness of the mind. They are well said to spring up beside flowing waters, because each of them receives fruit-bearing abundance from the teaching of the sacred word, which passes by in time.

Again, unless the life of sinners were denoted by the barrenness of willows, the Psalmist would never have said, in the voice of the preachers against Babylon: “On the willows in its midst we hung our instruments” (Ps. 126 [137]:2). See the chapter “On Torrents,” Book VII, chapter 7, distinction 2.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON PLANE-TREES

[Note: [Col. 0337D] From Book XXXII on Job, chapter XVIII.] Plane-trees signify the heavenly powers. Hence, when the Prophet beheld the eminence of the apostate angel, he said: “The cedars were not higher than it, in the paradise of God; the fir-trees did not equal its height; the plane-trees were equal to its branches. No tree of paradise was like it, because he made it beautiful in its many thick branches” (Ezek. 31:8). For who can be understood by cedars, fir-trees, and plane-trees except those companies of lofty heavenly powers, planted in the freshness of eternal joy? Although these were created exalted, they were nevertheless neither preferred nor made equal to him. He is said to have been made beautiful in many thick branches because, being set over the other legions, he was rendered more beautiful in proportion as the multitude of angels placed beneath him adorned him. That tree had as many thick branches in the paradise of God as it had legions of heavenly spirits set beneath it. And for this reason, having sinned, he was condemned without pardon: because he had been created great beyond comparison.

## CHAPTER IX. ON THE OLIVE-TREE

[Note: [Col. 0337D] From Homily 20 on the Gospels, after the middle.] Olive-trees signify the merciful, as the Lord promises through Isaiah: “I shall give in the wilderness the cedar, the thorn, the myrtle, and the olive-tree” (Isa. 41:19). Whom do we understand by the olive except the merciful? For in Greek ἔλεος (*eleos*) is called “mercy,” and the fruit of mercy shines before the eyes of almighty God as the oil of the olive. The olive is set in the Church so that one who recognizes another’s works of mercy may learn how he too ought to show mercy to a needy neighbour.

## CHAPTER X. ON THE ELM

[Note: [Col. 0337D] From the homily cited above.] The elm signifies the secular mind, as the Lord promises the holy Church through Isaiah, saying: “I shall place in the desert the fir-tree, the elm, and the box-tree together” (Isa. 41:19). For what is expressed by the elm except the minds of worldly people, who, while still serving earthly concerns, bear no fruit of spiritual virtues? Yet although the elm has no fruit of its own, it is accustomed to support the fruitful vine. Thus worldly people within the holy Church, although they do not possess the gifts of spiritual virtues, nevertheless, when by their generosity they support holy men full of spiritual gifts, what else do they do but bear a vine with its clusters? The elm is set in the Church so that whoever observes someone unable to possess the fruit of spiritual virtues, but nevertheless supporting those who are full of spiritual gifts, may serve according to the measure of his generosity and, by support, bear the clusters of heavenly goods which he cannot bear by producing them.

## CHAPTER XI. ON THE BOX-TREE

[Note: [Col. 0338D] From the immediately preceding homily.] The box-tree signifies one who, because of the weakness of age, is unable to bear good works, but nevertheless holds the faith of faithful parents, as the Lord says through Isaiah: “I shall place in the desert the fir-tree, the elm, and the box-tree together” (Isa. 41:19). Whom else does the box-tree signify, since it does not grow tall and, although it has no fruit, nevertheless has greenness, except those within the holy Church who, although because of the weakness of age they are not yet able to bear good works, nevertheless, following the belief of faithful parents, hold the faith of perennial greenness? The box-tree is set in the Church so that one who observes the greenness of true faith in many still placed in weakness may himself be ashamed to be unbelieving.

## CHAPTER XII. ON THE SYCAMORE

[Note: [Col. 0338D] From Book XXVII on Job, final chapter.] The sycamore signifies the folly of the world. Thus the words of the Gospel narrative testify that, when Zacchaeus could not see the Lord because of the crowd, he climbed a sycamore tree in order to see him as he passed by (Luke 19:4). For the sycamore is called the “foolish fig-tree.” And what do we understand by the sycamore except the folly of the world? Therefore little Zacchaeus climbed the sycamore and saw God, because those who humbly choose the folly of the world themselves subtly contemplate the wisdom of God.

For the crowd hinders our smallness of spirit from seeing the Lord, because the tumult of worldly concerns presses upon the weakness of the human mind and prevents it from fixing its attention on the light of truth. But we wisely climb the sycamore if we prudently embrace as folly what is divinely commanded. For what is more foolish in this world than not to seek again what has been lost, to let what one possesses go to those who seize it, to return no injury for injuries received, indeed to offer patience when further injuries are added? The Lord commands us, as it were, to climb the sycamore when he says: “From him who takes what is yours, do not demand it back” (Luke 6:30). And again: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5:39).

Therefore the Lord is seen passing by the sycamore, because through this wise folly, even though not yet firmly as he truly is, nevertheless through the light of contemplation the wisdom of God is seen, as it were, in passing. Those who seem wise to themselves cannot see it, according to the words of Elihu, because, caught in the lofty crowd of their own thoughts in order to behold the Lord, they have not yet found the sycamore tree. For those who seem wise to themselves cannot contemplate the wisdom of God, because they are as far from his light as they are not humble in their own eyes.

[Note: [Col. 0339D] What follows precedes the foregoing in the Greek text.] For while the swelling of pride grows in their minds, it closes the gaze of contemplation; and by the very thing through which they consider themselves to shine above others, they deprive themselves of the light of truth. Therefore, if we desire truly to be wise and to contemplate Wisdom itself, let us humbly acknowledge ourselves foolish. Let us abandon harmful wisdom and learn praiseworthy folly. For it is written: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1 Cor. 1:27). And again it is said: “If anyone among you seems wise in this age, let him become foolish so that he may be wise” (1 Cor. 3:18).

## CHAPTER XIII. ON THE THORN

In Sacred Scripture, when “thorn” is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies sin and sometimes the force of spiritual teaching. But when “thorns” are spoken of in the plural, they sometimes signify the prickings of vices, sometimes the stings of temptations, and sometimes riches.

[Note: [Col. 0339D] From Book XX on Job, chapter XII; and explained with reference to this verse in the Penitential Psalms: “is broken.”] The thorn signifies sin, as the Psalmist says in the voice of the penitent: “I was turned in my misery, while the thorn is broken for me” (Ps. 31 [32]:4). Every sin is a thorn, because, while it draws one toward pleasure, it tears the mind as though by pricking. He therefore says, “I was turned in my misery while the thorn is broken for me,” because the mind is turned to lamentation so that the pricking of sin may be broken through repentance. In another translation the thorn is said not to be broken but to be fixed fast. This plainly does not differ in meaning, because the soul of the penitent is led to mourning while the committed fault is held fixed in memory.

[Note: [Col. 0340D] From Book XXII on Job, chapter XVII.] The thorn signifies the sting of punishment. Hence blessed Job, having listed his blessings and binding himself under a curse if he had not acted thus, says: “Let a thistle grow for me instead of wheat, and a thorn instead of barley” (Job 31:40). As though he said openly: If I have acted unjustly toward those subject to me; if I have exacted debts and have not myself paid what I owed; if I have begrudged others the exercise of good work—then, instead of goods that refresh for eternity, let evils that prick be given me in judgment. For a thistle grows instead of wheat and a thorn instead of barley when, in the final recompense in which repayment for labour is sought, the sting of pain is found. Notice that, just as barley differs from wheat although both provide nourishment, so the thorn differs from the thistle although both prick: for the thistle is softer, whereas the thorn is always harder for pricking. He says therefore, “Let a thistle grow for me instead of wheat, and a thorn instead of barley.” As though he said plainly: I know that I have done great goods and lesser ones. But if it is not so, let lesser evils answer for my great goods, and greater evils for my lesser goods.

The thorn signifies a man of spiritual teaching, as the Lord promises through Isaiah: “I shall give in the wilderness the cedar and the thorn” (Isa. 41:19). See [Col. 0340B] the chapter “On the Cedar,” above, distinction 4.

[Note: [Col. 0340D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter IV, 5.] Thorns signify the prickings of vices, as the Lord speaks of a confused mind under the figure of Babylon, saying: “Thorns and nettles spring up in its houses, and the paliurus in its strongholds” (Isa. 33:13). For what do we understand by nettles except the itchings of thoughts, and by thorns except the prickings of vices? Therefore nettles and thorns spring up in the houses of Babylon, because in the confusion of a reprobate mind desires of thoughts arise which irritate, and sins of deeds which prick. But those who do such things also have others still more wicked as their defenders; therefore it is immediately added there openly: “And the paliurus in its strongholds.” The paliurus is so densely surrounded with thorns that, because of its roughness, it can scarcely be touched. Thus thorn and nettle arise within, but both are fortified outwardly by the paliurus: lesser wicked people commit whatever evils they please, but greater and most wicked people protect them.

Thorns signify the stings of temptations, as the Lord testifies through Isaiah, saying: “Thorns and briers rise over the ground of my people—how much more over all the houses of the joyous city exulting?” (Isa. 32:13). See Book VI, chapter II, above.

[Note: [Col. 0340D] From Homily 15 on the Gospels.] Thorns signify riches, as it is said in the Gospel in the voice of Truth concerning the seed: “And another fell among thorns, and the thorns that sprang up with it choked it” (Luke 8:7). Explaining this, he says: “What fell among thorns are those who have heard, and who, going their way, are choked by cares, riches, and pleasures and do not bring forth fruit” (ibid., 14). For riches are thorns that tear the mind with the pricking of their thoughts and, when they draw it on even to sin, make it bloody as though by an inflicted wound. Notice that the Lord, when explaining, says that cares, pleasures, and riches choke. For they choke because with their importunate thoughts they strangle the throat of the mind; and while they do not allow good desire to enter the heart, they kill, as it were, the passage of vital breath. Notice also that he joins two things with riches, namely cares and pleasures, because riches certainly both oppress the mind through care and dissolve it through abundance. Properly, therefore, they make their possessors at once afflicted and unrestrained—opposites. But because pleasure cannot coincide with affliction, at one time they afflict through the concern of guarding them, and at another they soften into pleasures through abundance.

## CHAPTER XIV. ON THE FIG-TREE

[Note: [Col. 0341D] From Book VIII on Job, chapter XXX, 37.] The fig-tree signifies the human mind. Thus, under the figure of a certain nation, signifying the malice of the ancient enemies, Truth says through the Prophet: “I have placed my vine in a desert; he has stripped the bark from my fig-tree, laying it bare, despoiled it, and cast it away; its branches have become white” (Joel 1:7). For when hostile spirits lie in wait, God’s vine is made a desert when the soul, full of fruits, is scattered by desire for human praise. This nation strips the bark from God’s fig-tree because, seizing the deceived mind into a desire for favour, it draws it to display and takes away the covering of humility; and it lays it bare and despoils it, because so long as it is hidden in its good works, it is clothed, as it were, with the bark of its own covering. But when the mind desires that what it has done be seen by others, like a stripped fig-tree it loses the bark with which it covered itself.

It is aptly added: “Its branches have become white,” because its works, displayed to human eyes, grow white: a name for holiness is acquired when right action is made public. But because, when the bark is removed, the branches of this fig-tree wither, we must carefully observe that the deeds of the arrogant, displayed before human eyes, dry out precisely through that by which they seek to please. Thus the mind made known through boasting is rightly called a stripped fig-tree, because it is white through what is seen, and is thereby close to dryness because it is bared of the covering of bark.

The fig-tree signifies human nature, as it is said in the Gospel in the voice of Truth: “A certain man had a fig-tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none,” etc. (Luke 13:6). For what does the fig-tree signify except human nature? It was indeed planted well like a fig-tree, but having fallen into sin of its own will, it does not preserve the fruit of action. For, falling into sin by its own choice, because it refused to bear the fruit of obedience, it lost its state of uprightness. Created in the likeness of God, since it did not remain in its dignity, it despised to preserve what it had been planted to be.

## CHAPTER XV. ON THE VINEYARD

In Sacred Scripture the vineyard sometimes signifies the breadth of Sacred Scripture, sometimes the soul fruitful in good works, sometimes the life of any negligent person, and sometimes the universal Church as a whole.

[Note: [Col. 0341D] From Book XVI on Job, chapter XXII, after the beginning of chapter XXIII.] The vineyard signifies the breadth of Sacred Scripture, as it is said of heretics through blessed Job: “They reap a field that is not their own, and they gather the vintage of the vineyard which they have violently oppressed” (Job 34:6). For the breadth of Sacred Scripture can be signified by the name “field.” Heretics reap a field not their own, because from it they take sentences far different from their own meanings. It is also expressed by the term “vineyard,” because it produces clusters of virtues through the utterances of truth. They violently oppress the Lord of this vineyard, that is, the maker of Sacred Scripture, because they try violently to bend his meaning in the words of sacred discourse—he who says: “You have made me serve in your sins; you have given me labour in your iniquities” (Isa. 43:24). And they gather the vintage of that vineyard because, for the purpose of their own interpretation, they heap together clusters of its utterances.

The vineyard signifies the soul fruitful in good works, as the Lord says through the Prophet, under the figure of a certain nation, signifying the malice of evil spirits: “He placed my vineyard in a desert” (Joel 1:7). For when evil spirits lie in wait, God’s vineyard is made a desert when the soul, full of fruits, is scattered by desire for human praise. See chapter 14, distinction 1.

[Note: [Col. 0341D] From Book XX on Job, chapter XX, 22.] The vineyard signifies the life of any negligent person, as Solomon says: “I passed by the field of the sluggard and by the vineyard of the foolish man; and behold, nettles had filled it all, thorns had covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed” (Prov. 24:30). See the chapter “On the Wall,” Book XIII, chapter 3, distinction 1.

[Col. 0342C] [Note: [Col. 0342D] From Homily 19 on the Gospels.] The vineyard signifies the universal Church as a whole, as it is said in the Gospel in the voice of Truth: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard” (Matt. 20:1). See the chapter “On Morning,” Book XII, chapter 6, distinction 5.

## CHAPTER XVI. ON THE ROOT

In Sacred Scripture the root sometimes signifies the Lord’s incarnation, sometimes holy preaching, sometimes human nature, and sometimes hidden thought.

[Note: [Col. 0342D] From Book XIX on Job, chapter XVI, in the middle of chapter XXVII.] The root signifies the Lord’s incarnation, as blessed Job says in the person of the Church: “My root is laid open beside the waters” (Job 29:10). For what ought to be understood by the root of the Church except the incarnation itself of the Redeemer? It was laid open beside the waters when the invisible Lord became manifest to the sight of our vision by assuming our humanity. For the Creator, who could not be seen in his divinity, assumed from us that by which he could be seen by us. Therefore the root is laid open beside the waters because the Author of the human race is displayed to human beings through his humanity. Hence it is rightly said: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water” (Ps. 1:3). See chapter 1 of this book, distinction 1.

The root signifies holy preaching, as blessed Job says of the righteous man under the designation of a tree: “Though its root grow old in the earth, and its trunk die in the dust, at the scent of water it shall bud and put forth foliage as when it was first planted” (Job 14:9).

[Note: [Col. 0343D] From Book XII on Job, chapter IV, after the beginning of section 3.] For what is the root of the righteous except holy preaching? From it he arises and in it he stands. And what is understood by earth or dust except the sinner, to whom the Creator says: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19); or certainly, as our translation has it, “You are dust, and to dust you shall return.” Therefore the root of the righteous grows old in the earth because his preaching is despised among the hearts of the wicked and is thought exhausted of all strength. And the trunk dies in the dust because his body is tested among the hands of persecutors. For, according to the voice of Wisdom, “They seemed to the eyes of the foolish to die, and their departure was thought an affliction” (Wis. 3:2). But he whose root has grown old in the earth and whose trunk has died in the dust buds at the scent of water, because by the breath of the Holy Spirit he brings forth in the hearts of the elect a germ of virtue through the example of his deed. For the irrigation of the Holy Spirit is often signified by water, as it is written: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. But whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst” (John 7:17).

It follows: “And it shall put forth foliage as when it was first planted” (Job 14:9). To put forth foliage after the trunk has been cut down is, when the righteous man has been killed bodily, to stir up the hearts of many by the very example of his passion and to show the greenness of truth from right faith. It is well said, “as when it was first planted.” For everything done here by the righteous is a second planting, because the first planting lies not in the work of the righteous but in the presence of the Creator. And because all that the elect do is first inwardly beheld and arranged, and then outwardly accomplished, it is rightly said, “It shall put forth foliage as when it was first planted”: that is, it shows in the effect of its deed the greenness which it previously possessed in the foreknowledge of the Creator.

[Note: [Col. 0343D] From the same book and chapter.] The root can also signify human nature itself; hence the foregoing can be understood in this way. This root grows old in the earth when the nature of the flesh fails and is reduced to dust. Its trunk dies in the dust because the lifeless body is dissolved from its form. But it buds at the scent of water because it rises again through the coming of the Holy Spirit, and “it also puts forth foliage,” etc.; that is, it returns to that form for receiving which it was created, if, having been placed in paradise, it had not been willing to sin.

[Note: [Col. 0344D] From Book XII on Job, chapter XXII, in the middle of section 23.] The root signifies hidden thought, as Eliphaz says of the wicked rich man: “His substance shall not be inhabited [variant: enriched], nor shall it endure; nor shall he send his root into the earth” (Job 15:29). In some manuscripts, where it says here “shall not be inhabited,” I find “shall not be enriched.” But the sense does not differ; the wording differs. For he is enriched with virtues whose mind almighty God inhabits. But because the thought of the proud person is not inhabited by the grace of its Author, it is certainly not enriched with virtues. Therefore, because he is empty within, it is said, “shall not be inhabited”; but because he swells outwardly with what is transitory, it is rightly added: “Nor shall his substance endure.” It is as though it were openly said: What he seems outwardly to possess passes away, and inwardly he does not possess what could not pass away. Hence it is aptly added: “Nor shall he send his root into the earth.”

If we understand this to be said of this earth, it is plainly beyond doubt that a tree which has no root in the earth falls when moved even by the lightest breezes. And every proud person, while he stiffens himself against almighty God, while he runs against him with neck erect and raises his fat neck against his Author, seems to stand like a tree; but his standing is without a root, because his life is torn away, as by a gentle breeze, so by the movement of a hidden judgment. But if in this passage we understand “earth” as the recompense of eternal life, of which the Prophet says: “My portion is in the land of the living” (Ps. 141 [142]:7), the wicked man shall not send his root into the earth because he never plants the thought of his flesh in longing for eternal life. For what the root is to a tree, thought is to every human being: in what is seen outwardly, one is held fast by what is not seen within. Hence it is said through the Prophet: “It shall send its root downward and bear fruit upward” (Isa. 37:31). When we direct our thought toward compassion for a needy neighbour, we send our root downward, in order that we may bear upward the fruit of recompense.

## CHAPTER XVII. ON THE STAFF

In Sacred Scripture the staff sometimes signifies the discipline of the law, sometimes the support of consolation, and sometimes pastoral care.

[Note: [Col. 0344D] From Book IX on Job, chapter XXII, 32.] The staff signifies the discipline of the law, as it is written of Elisha that, when he sent his servant with a staff to the dead son of the Shunammite woman, he did not restore the boy’s life; but when he came himself, stretched himself upon the dead body, gathered his limbs to the boy’s limbs, and breathed seven times upon the mouth of the dead child, he immediately gave him life anew through the mystery of compassion (4 Kings 4:30 ff.). For God, the Author of the human race, grieved for us like a dead child when, in mercy, he looked upon us extinguished by the sting of iniquity. And because through Moses he produced the terror of the law, he sent the staff, as it were, to the child. But the child with the staff could not raise the dead, because, as Paul testifies, “the law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7:5). But he himself came in person and, humbly stretching himself upon the corpse, gathered himself to the dead limbs in order to make them equal to himself: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:6–7). He walks back and forth because he calls both Judaea and the nations near and far away. He breathes seven times upon the dead because, through the opening of the divine gift, he grants the sevenfold Spirit of grace to those lying in the death of sin. And immediately the living child rises, because the child whom the staff of terror could not raise returns to life through the Spirit of love.

[Note: [Col. 0345D] From Book XX on Job, chapter VIII, 6.] The staff signifies the support of consolation, as the Psalmist says: “Your rod and your staff, they have consoled me” (Ps. 22 [23]:4). For we are struck with the rod and supported with the staff. Therefore, if rulers possess the strictness of the rod that strikes, let them also possess the consolation of the staff that supports. Let there be love, but not softening; rigour, but not embittering. Let there be zeal, but not raging without moderation; mercy, but not sparing more than is fitting.

[Note: [Col. 0345D] From Homily 22 on the Gospels, at the end.] The staff signifies pastoral care, as Moses says concerning the eating of the lamb: “Holding staffs in your hands” (Exod. 12:4). What does the law signify by the staff except pastoral guardianship? Notice that we are first commanded to gird our loins and afterward to hold staffs, because those should undertake pastoral care who already know how to tame in their own bodies the unruly flow of lust, so that, when they preach strength to others, they themselves may not weakly succumb to soft desires.

## CHAPTER XVIII. ON THE ROD

In Sacred Scripture the rod sometimes signifies uprightness, sometimes a blow, and sometimes the rigour of discipline.

[Note: [Col. 0345D] From Book VII on Job, chapter VII.] The rod signifies uprightness, as the Psalmist says to the Lord: “You shall rule them with an iron rod, and you shall break them like a vessel” (Ps. 2:9). We should know that sometimes our adversary breaks us, and sometimes God breaks us. By the breaking inflicted by the adversary we fail in virtue; but when broken by the Lord, we are strengthened in virtue from our vices. The Psalmist had beheld this breaking when he said: “You shall rule them with an iron rod, and you shall break them like a potter’s vessel.” For the Lord breaks us with a rod because, by the strong, iron uprightness of his ordering, while he restores us inwardly, he afflicts us outwardly. For in the very act by which he humbles the strength of the flesh, he exalts the purpose of the spirit. Thus this same breaking is compared to a potter’s vessel, as Paul also says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4). Expressing both breaking and rigour, he says: “Although our outer man is corrupted, yet the inner is renewed day by day” (ibid., 16).

[Note: [Col. 0345D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter XVI, 31.] The rod signifies a blow, as it is said through the prophet Isaiah of our Redeemer, delivering the Gentiles from the dominion of the ancient enemy: “You have overcome the yoke of his burden, the rod of his shoulder, and the sceptre of his exactor, as in the day of Midian” (Isa. 9:4; printed 9:14). For in delivering the Gentiles the Lord overcame the yoke of his burden when, by his coming, he freed them from that slavery of demonic tyranny. He overcame the rod of his shoulder when the Redeemer restrained from the human race that blow which oppressed it heavily through perverse action. He overcame the sceptre of his exactor when he destroyed the kingdom of that same devil, who was accustomed, for the pestilential commission of vices, to exact from the hearts of the faithful the due tribute of punishments.

[Note: [Col. 0346D] From chapter XV of the preceding book, at the end.] For who else can be understood by the exactor except the devil, who once induced human beings wickedly to sin in paradise and daily exacts from them the punishment for this debt? “He asks.”

[Note: [Col. 0346D] From Book XX on Job, chapter VIII, 6.] The rod signifies the rigour of discipline, as the Psalmist says to the Lord: “Your rod and your staff, they have consoled me” (Ps. 22 [23]:4). Gentleness must be mixed with severity; a certain tempering must be made from both, so that subjects may neither be wounded by excessive harshness nor become lax through excessive kindness. This is surely signified by the ark of the tabernacle, in which, together with the tablets, are the rod and manna: for just as in the breast of a good ruler there is the rod of strictness, so there should also be the manna of sweetness with knowledge of Sacred Scripture.

## CHAPTER XIX. ON BRANCHES

In Sacred Scripture branches sometimes signify holy preachers, sometimes works, and sometimes the words and sayings of the Fathers.

Branches signify holy preachers, as it is said in the Gospel in the voice of Truth: “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and put in his garden; it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of heaven rested in its branches” (Luke 13:19). See the chapter “On Birds,” Book II.

Branches signify works, as the Lord says through the Prophet, under the figure of a certain nation, signifying the malice of evil spirits: “He placed my vineyard in a desert, stripped the bark from my fig-tree and cast it away; its branches have become white” (Joel 1:7). See the chapter “On the Fig-Tree,” above, distinction 1.

[Note: [Col. 0346D] From Homily 17 on Ezekiel.] By “branches” are meant the words or sayings of the Fathers, as, when the Lord rode on the ass into Jerusalem, the Gospel says: “A very great crowd spread their garments on the road; others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road” (Matt. XXI, 8). For our Savior, seated on the colt, makes for Jerusalem when, governing the soul of each believer—his own beast of burden—he leads it to the inward vision of peace. He also sits upon the beast when he presides universally over holy Church and kindles it with longing for heavenly peace. Many spread their garments on the road because they discipline their bodies through abstinence, so that they may prepare for him a way to their mind and provide good examples for those who follow. Others cut branches or leafy boughs from the trees and spread them on the road, because in the teaching of Truth they gather words and sayings of the Fathers from their utterances and lay them humbly upon the way of God through preaching. This is what we too, unworthy though we are, now do. For when we adopt the Fathers’ sayings in a sermon of exhortation, we cut leafy boughs from the trees and spread them on the way of almighty God.

## CHAPTER XX. ON LEAVES

By “leaf” are understood the legions of heavenly spirits, as it is said through the prophet concerning the preeminence of the ancient enemy: “The cedars in the paradise of God were not higher than he; the fir trees did not equal his height; the plane trees were not equal to his leaves” [Col. 0347B] (Ezek. XXXI, 8). See chapter 8 above.

By “leaves” are designated the kings of Judaea, through Ezekiel the prophet (Ezek. XVII). Read book II, chapter 2, distinction 2.

## CHAPTER XXI. ON BARK

In Sacred Scripture, by “bark” are designated sometimes the historical sense, sometimes the outward utterances of the Fathers, and sometimes the covering of humility.

By “bark” is understood the historical sense, as it is said through Moses concerning Jacob: “Jacob took green poplar rods and almond rods, and partly stripped them of bark; and where the bark had been removed, whiteness appeared in the parts that had been stripped,” etc. (Gen. XXX, 37). See [Col. 0347C] the chapter “On Rams,” book III, chapter 13, distinction 2.

By “barks” are designated the outward utterances of the Fathers, the surface of the letter, or the outward works of those making a good beginning, as it is said through blessed Job concerning heretics: “They ate herbs and the barks of trees” (Job XXX, 4). See chapter 2, “On Herbs,” above, distinction 3.

By “bark” is designated the covering of humility. See chapter 14 above, distinction 1.

## CHAPTER XXII. ON THE LEAF

By “leaf” is understood frivolity of mind, through blessed Job. Consult book IV, final chapter.

## CHAPTER XXIII. ON FLOWERS

[Col. 0347D] In Sacred Scripture, by “flower” are expressed sometimes Christ Jesus, the man who is mediator between God and humankind; sometimes the glory of the present life, the favor of human praise; and sometimes souls beginning good works.

[Note: [Col. 0347D] From Book XXIX on Job, chapter XVI, 30.] By “flower” is expressed Christ Jesus, mediator between God and humankind, as it is said through the prophet Isaiah: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. XI, 1).

[Note: [Col. 0347D] From Book XIX on Job, chapter V.] By “flower” is designated the glory of the present life, as it is said through Isaiah the prophet: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. XL, 6).

By “flower” is designated the favor of human praise, [Col. 0348A] as Bildad says concerning the hypocrite under the name of the rush or sedge: “Can the rush flourish without moisture, or can the sedge grow without water?” (Job VIII, 1). While it is still in flower and has not been plucked by the hand, it withers before all other herbs. See the chapter “On the Rush,” below, book XIV, chapter 13.

[Note: [Col. 0348D] From Homily 15 on Ezekiel.] By “flowers” are designated souls beginning good works, as it is said in the Song of Songs in the voice of the bride, deeply loving and longing for the bridegroom: “Sustain me with flowers; surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Cant. II, 5). The mind that is joined through love to the invisible Bridegroom and burns with desire for him no longer desires anything in the world; it counts the length of this present life as a punishment, hastens to depart, and to rest in the embrace of love in the vision of the heavenly [Col. 0348B] Bridegroom. Such a mind receives no consolation from the present life, but sighs, burns, pants, and is troubled from its depths for him whom it loves. The very well-being of its body becomes cheap to it, because it has been pierced by the wound of love, as it says: “I am wounded by love.” Indeed, the mind is evil that does not know the pain of this wound. But when the soul begins to pant in heavenly longing and to feel love’s wound, it becomes healthier through the wound, though it had previously been ill through health.

Yet for a mind loving its Bridegroom so strongly, one consolation regarding its present life is customary: namely, if, because it itself is delayed from his vision, the souls of others may profit through its word and be set ablaze for the heavenly Bridegroom by the torches of love. It grieves indeed because it sees itself delayed; everything it sees is sad to it, because it does not yet see him whom it longs to see. But, as I have said, it is no wrong consolation if the fervent soul is delayed and many are gathered through it, so that it may at last see with many what it wished sooner to see alone. Hence it rightly says: “Sustain me with flowers,” etc. For what are flowers but souls beginning good works and fragrant with heavenly desire? What are apples among flowers but the minds of the good which have come to the fruit of good work from the beginning of their holy purpose? Therefore one who languishes with love seeks to be sustained by flowers and surrounded with apples, because, if he is not yet permitted to see him whom he desires, it is a great consolation to him to rejoice in the progress of others. Thus the holy soul, languishing with love, [Col. 0348D] is sustained by flowers and apples, so that it may rest in the good work of its neighbor while it is not yet able to contemplate the face of God.

## CHAPTER XXIV. ON FRUITS

In Sacred Scripture, by “fruits” are designated sometimes the beginnings of our works and sometimes the fragrant coming of God.

By “fruits” are designated the beginnings of our works, as it is said through Moses: “When you have entered the land which I shall give you, and have planted fruit-bearing trees in it, you shall remove their foreskins. The fruits which they produce [Col. 0349A] shall be unclean to you, and you shall not eat of them” (Lev. XIX, 23). See the chapter “On Trees,” above, chapter 1, distinction 10.

[Note: [Col. 0349D] From Book XVI on Job, chapter XXVI, 22.] By “fruits” is meant the fragrant coming of God, as blessed Job says, in the person of the ancient fathers longing for the coming of the Redeemer, or in the person of the earth representing the whole human race: “My days have been swifter than a runner; they fled and did not see good; they passed by like ships carrying fruits” (Job IX).

## CHAPTER XXV. ON APPLES

[Note: [Col. 0349D] From Book I of the Pastoral Rule, chapter XXIV.] By “pomegranates” is designated the unity of faith, as is read in Exodus: where, on the priest’s garment, pomegranates are joined to bells sounding forth the divine voice (Exod. XXVIII, 33). For by the priest’s garments what else should we understand but upright works? The prophet testifies to this when he says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI, 9). Bells adhere to his garments, so that the priest’s works themselves may proclaim with far-reaching sound the way of life. But what is signified by pomegranates except unity of faith? For just as many seeds are protected within one pomegranate by its outer [Col. 0350A] rind, so the unity of faith covers the innumerable peoples of holy Church, though diversity of merits holds them within.

Therefore, when a ruler prepares to speak, let him consider with how much carefulness he ought to speak, lest, if he is swept rashly into speaking, the wounds of error strike the hearts of his hearers and, while perhaps he desires to appear wise, he foolishly cuts apart the cohesion of unity. For this reason Truth gives warning, saying: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX, 49). By salt is signified the wisdom of speech. Therefore, one who strives to speak wisely must greatly fear lest the unity of the hearers be thrown into confusion by his speech. Hence Paul says: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think soberly” (Rom. [Col. 0350B] XII, 3). Lest a ruler rush incautiously into speaking, Truth itself cries aloud to the disciples what we have already set forth: “Have salt in yourselves and have peace among yourselves”; as though it said figuratively through the priestly garment: “Join pomegranates to the bells” (Exod. XXVIII, 35), so that in all you say you may preserve the unity of faith by watchful care.

## BOOK TEN BEGINS

[Col. 0349]

## CHAPTER ONE. ON THE ROCK

[Col. 0349C]

In Sacred Scripture, when “rock” is used in the singular, it signifies sometimes Christ, sometimes firmness of faith, and sometimes the hardness of insensibility. But when “rocks” are spoken of in the plural, they designate sometimes the exalted powers of heaven and sometimes the hard hearts of the Gentiles.

By “rock” is designated Christ, as the Apostle testifies, saying: “And the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4). See book VII, chapter 6, distinction 2.

[Note: [Col. 0350D] From Book XXXV on Job, chapter VII, 6.] By “rock” is understood firmness of faith. Hence the Lord says to Moses: “There is a place with me, and you shall stand upon the rock” (Exod. XXXIII, 21). And shortly afterward: “I shall take away my hand, and you shall see my back” (ibid., 23). For Truth is seen only from within the Catholic Church; the Lord declares that there is with him a place from which he may be seen. Moses is set upon the rock so that he may contemplate God’s face, because unless one holds firmly to the solidity of faith, one does not recognize the divine presence. Of this firmness he again says in the Gospel: “Upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18).

By “rock” is understood the hardness of insensibility. Hence the Lord says to Isaiah: “Enter into the rock; hide yourself in the pit of the earth from the terror of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty” (Isa. II, 10). See the chapter “On the Pit,” book VI, chapter 20, distinction 1.

[Note: [Col. 0350D] From Book XXXI on Job, chapter XIX, after the middle, 35.] By “rocks” are designated the exalted powers of heaven, as the Lord says to blessed Job, concerning the holy man under the name of the eagle: “It dwells upon the rocks” (Job XXXIX, 1). For what do we understand by rocks except the powers of the heavenly virtues? They are those which the wind of our mutability no longer bends now here, now there, as it does trees; for, like rocks set in high places, they are removed from every movement of changeability and fixed in the solidity of exalted height. They too have become hard through the eternity to which they cling.

Therefore, when a person despises earthly things, like an eagle he raises himself toward higher things; uplifted by the spirit of contemplation, he awaits the everlasting glory of angels; and, a stranger to this world, longing for the things he sees, he is already fixed among the heights. Thus it is rightly said, “It dwells upon the rocks”: that is, in the intention of its heart it dwells among those heavenly virtues which, through the strength of their eternity, are now fixed in unshakable solidity, so that they may not be bent in any part toward fault by the variability of change.

By “rocks” are designated the hard hearts of the Gentiles, as it is said of the Lord through blessed Job: “He cuts out streams in the rocks” (Job XXVIII, 10). See the chapter “On Streams,” book VI, chapter 6, distinction 4.

## CHAPTER II. ON THE STONE

In Sacred Scripture, when “stone” is used in the singular, it signifies sometimes hardness of heart, sometimes a hard thought, sometimes the Church, and sometimes the hardened habit of sin. But when “stones” are spoken of in the plural, they designate sometimes angelic virtues, sometimes the minds of the strong, sometimes the hard hearts of the Gentiles, and sometimes the words of Sacred Scripture.

[Note: [Col. 0351D] From Homily 3 on the Gospels.] By “stone” is designated hardness of heart, as blessed Job says: “And stone, when dissolved by heat, is turned into bronze” (Job XXVIII, 2). See the chapter “On Bronze,” book VIII, distinction 2.

By “stone” is designated a hard thought, in the Gospel where Truth says: “They shall not leave in you one stone that shall not be destroyed, because you did not know the time of your visitation” (Luke XIX, 44). For by “city” the soul is understood. Hard thoughts may fittingly be understood by the signification of stones. For when a perverse mind adds one perverse thought to another still more perverse thought, what else does it do but place stone upon stone? But in the destroyed city one stone is not left upon another, because when the soul is brought to its punishment, the whole construction of its thoughts is scattered. The reason it suffers this is added: “Because you did not know the time of your visitation.” For almighty God is accustomed to visit a perverse soul in many ways. [Col. 0351B] He continually visits it by command, at times by scourging, and at other times by miracle, so that it may hear truths it did not know, and yet, still proud and contemptuous, may return either pierced by grief or ashamed at having been overcome by benefits. But because it does not at all recognize the time of its visitation, it is delivered at life’s end to those enemies with whom it shall be joined in the eternal judgment in the fellowship of everlasting damnation.

By “stone” is designated the Church, as it is written in the law: “But Moses’ hands were heavy” (Exod. XVII, 12). Therefore they took a stone and put it beneath him, and he sat upon it. See the chapter “On Hands,” book V, chapter 26, distinction 6.

By “stone” is designated the hard habit of sin. Thus the prophet Jeremiah, seeing that Judaea had been overwhelmed in iniquities by long habit, laments himself under her figure in his Lamentations, saying: “My life has fallen into the pit, and they have placed a stone upon me” (Lam. III, 53). See the chapter “On the Pit,” book VII, chapter 10.

[Note: [Col. 0351D] From Book XXXII on Job, chapter XVIII, 25.] By “stones” are designated the angelic virtues. Thus the prophet, describing the lofty primacy which the prince of the ancient enemy had received in his creation and lost through pride, says: “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, and jasper; chrysolite, onyx, and beryl; sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald” (Ezek. XXVIII, 13). He mentions nine kinds of stones because there are, indeed, nine orders of angels. The devil is said to have been covered by them because he had them, as it were, as a garment for his adornment; since he surpassed their brightness, he was brighter by comparison with them. Hence the same prophet adds: “You were an outspread and protecting cherub on the holy mountain of God; you walked perfectly in the midst of fiery stones” (Ezek. XXVIII, [Col. 0352A] 14). For *cherub* means “fullness of knowledge”; and therefore the devil is called a cherub, because he is undoubtedly believed to have surpassed all others in knowledge. He is fittingly called “outspread and protecting,” for whatever we protect by spreading it out, we overshadow. Since he is believed to have overshadowed the brightness of the rest by comparison with his own brightness, he is said to have been a covering and protector. For he covered the rest as if by casting them into shadow, since he surpassed their greatness by a greater excellence. He walked perfectly among the fiery stones because, among the hearts of angels kindled with the fire of charity, he shone more brightly in the glory of his created condition.

[Note: [Col. 0351D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XIX, after the middle, 20.] By “stones” are designated the minds of the strong, as Peter says to the saints: “You also, like living stones, are built up into spiritual houses” [Col. 0352B] (I Pet. II, 5). And through the prophet the Lord promises the Church that is to come: “Behold, I shall lay your stones in order and found you upon sapphires. I shall make jasper your battlements, your gates of carved stones, and all your boundaries of desirable stones; and all your children shall be taught by the Lord” (Isa. LIV, 11).

For the Lord sets stones in order in the Church because in it he has distinguished holy souls by the diversity of their merits. He founded it upon sapphires—stones that bear in themselves the likeness of the color of the air—because he established the Church’s strength in souls that long for heavenly things. And because jasper is green in color, he made jasper its battlements, because those placed against adversaries for the defense of holy Church are people who are green with inward longings and do not wither through any dryness of the reprobate body. He made its gates carved stones. For these are the gates of the Church through whose life and teaching the multitude of believers enters it. And because they abound in great works and show in their lives what they affirm in speech, they are described as not merely plain but carved stones. For in the life of those in whom upright action is seen, what they have done is, as it were, carved upon themselves. Then, enclosing the entire number of saints in one comprehensive statement, he adds: “All your boundaries [Col. 0352C] of desirable stones.” And as though we who heard this asked him to identify the stones he meant, he added: “All your children taught by the Lord.”

[Col. 0352D] [Note: [Col. 0352D] From the book and chapter above.] By “stones” are designated the hard hearts of the Gentiles, as John says: “The Lord is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham” (Matt. III, 9). By the name of stones he plainly designates the hearts of the Gentiles, then hard and insensible through unbelief. And through the prophet the Lord promises, saying: “I shall take the heart of stone out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. XI, 19).

[Note: [Col. 0352D] From Homily 19 on Ezekiel.] By “stones” are understood the words of Sacred Scripture, as Ezekiel says: “Four tables for the burnt offering were built of square stones” [Col. 0353A]. For what do we understand by tables except the hearts of holy teachers, by whose teaching the minds of hearers are refreshed? A burnt offering is called a wholly burned offering, and we offer a burnt offering when we renounce everything belonging to this world; we offer a burnt offering when we turn to the Lord in both work and thought. Square stones are the words of Sacred Scripture. Square stones stand upright whichever side they are turned toward. So too do the words of Sacred Scripture stand upright everywhere, because they are found blameworthy from no side. For in everything they narrate as past, foretell as future, preach morally, and resound spiritually, they stand, as it were, on a different side, because they have no fault.

Therefore the hearts of saints are God’s tables for the burnt offering, because they are kindled to their depths either in good work or in holy thought. The hearts of saints are God’s tables for the burnt offering, built of square stones, because while they continually think upon God’s words, they sacrifice themselves to the Lord in thought, putting their carnal life to death. Hence it is written: “The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps shall not be overthrown” (Ps. XXXVI, 31). And again it is said: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. CXVIII, 11).

## CHAPTER III. ON SAPPHIRE

[Col. 0353C] In Sacred Scripture, by “sapphire” are designated sometimes the angelic nature and sometimes any saints whatsoever.

[Note: [Col. 0353D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XXVII, 30.] By “sapphire” is designated the angelic nature, as Job says of the value of wisdom: “It shall not be compared to the most precious sardonyx stone or sapphire” (Job XXVIII, 16). Who does not know that sardonyx and sapphire are precious stones? Yet, since there are other precious stones that far surpass them in greatness of value, why are sardonyx and sapphire particularly called precious, when each stone is comparatively among the cheapest of stones? Unless, recognizing that the stones described as precious are not precious, we seek something else in their meaning. Sardonyx bears the likeness of red earth, while sapphire has an airy appearance. Thus in sardonyx human beings may be signified by earth, and in sapphire angels by the vision of the air.

[Note: [Col. 0353D] Josephus, *Antiquities*, book I, chapter 2: Adam is interpreted “red.”] Since the sardonyx stone bears the appearance of red earth, it not unfittingly designates humankind, because Adam, the first to be created, is called “red earth” in the Latin tongue. What then is meant by the statement that this wisdom is not compared with sardonyx or sapphire, except that he who is the power and wisdom of God—Christ Jesus, the man who is mediator between God and humankind—so surpasses all things in greatness [Col. 0354A] that neither the first human beings on earth nor the angels in heaven can be compared with him? Hence the Psalmist says: “Who among the clouds shall be equal to God, or who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 7).

By “sapphire” are designated any saints who long for heavenly things, as the Lord promises the Church that is to come through the prophet: “Behold, I shall lay your stones in order and found you upon sapphires” (Isa. LIV, 11). See the chapter “On Stones,” above, distinction 6.

## CHAPTER IV. ON JASPER

By “jasper” is designated the verdure of inward longing, as the Lord promises the Church that is to come through the prophet: “I shall make jasper your battlements and your gates of carved stone” [Col. 0354B] (Isa. LIV, 12). See the chapter “On Stones,” above, distinction 6.

## CHAPTER V. ON TOPAZ

[Note: [Col. 0354D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter XXVII, after the middle, 35.] By “topaz” is designated one full of many virtues, as Job says of wisdom: “The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be equal to it” (Job XXVIII, 19). For what do we understand by Ethiopia except the present world? By its black color it signifies a sinful people and the foulness of their merits. At times, however, “Ethiopia” is customarily used in particular to designate the Gentile world, formerly black with the sins of unbelief. The prophet Habakkuk saw it terrified at the coming of the Lord and said: “The tents of the Ethiopians shall be afraid, the tents of the land of Midian” (Hab. III, 7). Likewise David the prophet, seeing that the Lord would come to redeem Judaea but that the Gentiles would believe first and Judaea would follow afterward—as it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in, and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. XI, 25)—said: “Ethiopia shall stretch out her hands first to God” (Ps. LXVII, 32). That is, before Judaea believes, the Gentile people, black with sins, offers itself for salvation to almighty God.

Topaz is a precious stone. Since in Greek *pan* (πᾶν) means “all,” it is called, as it were, *to pandion* (τὸ πανδιὸν), because it shines with every color. When the Gentile world, turned to God, believed, many from it were so enriched by the gift of the Spirit that they shine, as it were, with many colors—that is, with many virtues. But lest anyone be exalted by virtues received, the holy man now says: “The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be equal to it.” It is as though he said plainly: No saint, although full of whatever virtues, yet gathered from the world’s blackness, can be equal to him of whom it was said: “What is born of you shall be called holy, the Son of God” [Col. 0354D] (Luke I, 35).

## CHAPTER VI. ON CRYSTAL

[Note: [Col. 0354D] From Homily 7 on Ezekiel.] By “crystal” is designated the strength of the angelic nature, as Ezekiel says: “And above the heads of the living creatures was the likeness of a firmament, like the terrible appearance of crystal, stretched out above their heads” (Ezek. I, 22). By “firmament” the heavenly powers may be understood. This firmament is rightly called like the appearance of crystal, because it is indeed exceedingly strong, yet is formed from water. When angelic nature was created, it received free choice: whether it wished to persevere in humility and remain in the sight of almighty God, or to fall into pride and fall from blessedness. In this respect it was like water. But when others fell, the holy angels persevered in their blessedness and received as a gift that they could no longer fall at all. Thus their nature, since it can no longer be cast down through mutability, was hardened, as it were, into the firmness of crystal.

This crystal is called terrible and stretched out above the heads of the living creatures because those powers that stand before the presence of almighty God are terrible and awe-inspiring to us who are still placed in this corruption. Their joys now surpass the understanding of our minds; therefore they are said to be above the heads of the living creatures. For who, while placed in corruptible flesh, can comprehend what that ineffable and endless joy of angels is? What is that blessedness: to see the Creator’s face without failure and to remain without change in his delight?

## CHAPTER VII. ON THE DIAMOND

By “diamond” is designated eternity, as the prophet says: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with a diamond point” [Col. 0356B] (Jer. XVII, 1). See book V, chapter 60.

## BOOK ELEVEN BEGINS

[Col. 0355]

## CHAPTER ONE. ON FIRE

[Col. 0355B]

In Sacred Scripture, by “fire” are designated sometimes the zeal of charity, sometimes charity, sometimes the Holy Spirit, sometimes malice, sometimes the heat of lust, sometimes the burning of avarice, sometimes the flame of envy, sometimes the heat of compunction, sometimes the fire of Gehenna, sometimes God, and sometimes the heat of suffering.

[Col. 0355C] By “fire” is designated the zeal of charity. Thus the prophet Jeremiah, when he had imposed silence upon himself concerning preaching, saying, “I shall not remember him, nor shall I speak any longer in his name” (Jer. XX, 9), added: “And it became in my heart like a burning fire, shut up in my bones; and I was worn out, unable to endure it. For I heard the reproach of many” (ibid.).

By “fire” is designated charity, as Moses says: “Fire shall always burn upon the altar, which the priest shall feed, placing wood upon it each morning, day by day” (Lev. VI, 12). See the chapter “On Trees,” book IX, chapter 1, distinction 8.

[Note: [Col. 0355D] See above, book I, chapter 16, distinction 1.] Fire designates the Holy Spirit, as Truth says in the Gospel: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it burn?” [Col. 0355D] (Luke XII, 49). Hence Moses says concerning the eating of the lamb: “If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire” (Exod. XII, 20). [Note: [Col. 0355D] From Homily 22 on the Gospels.] We burn with fire what remains of the lamb when we humbly reserve for the power of the Holy Spirit that which we cannot understand and penetrate concerning the mystery of his incarnation. Thus no one should dare proudly either to despise or to pronounce upon what he does not understand; rather, one gives it over to the fire when one reserves it for the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0355D] Vulgate edition, the Greek, and Chrysostom, Homily 20 on the Epistle to the Hebrews.] By “fire” is designated malice, as Ezekiel says: “And I saw, and behold, a whirlwind came from the north, and a great cloud and enfolding fire” [Col. 0356B] (Ezek. I, 4). For by “fire” malice is understood, as it is written: “And now fire consumes the adversaries” (Heb. X, 27), because the most wicked heart wastes away through its own malice. As the fire of love raises up the mind, so the fire of malice enfolds it. For the Holy Spirit lifts up the heart that he fills, while the heat of malice always bends it down to lower things. Judaea, therefore, blinded by the cloud of her ignorance, because it immediately broke forth into the wickedness of persecution, was enfolded in its own fire; it entangled itself in the bondage of wickedness through the very cruelty with which it burned. A whirlwind came from the north, with a great cloud and enfolding fire, because, from the coldness of its own flesh, it was brought into the darkness of its ignorance and burst forth into the malice of persecution.

[Note: [Col. 0356D] From Homily 30 on the Gospels.] Fire is also understood as God, as it is written: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. IV, 24). [Note: [Col. 0356D] From Homily 22 on the Gospels.] God is called a consuming fire because through him the rust of sins is consumed. God is called a consuming fire because from every heart that he fills he shakes away the torpor of coldness and kindles it with longing for his eternity.

By “fire” is designated the heat of suffering, [Col. 0356D] as Moses says concerning the eating of the lamb: “They shall eat the flesh that night, roasted with fire” (Exod. XII, 8). We eat the lamb at night because now in the sacrament we receive the Lord’s body while we do not yet see one another’s consciences. Yet the flesh must be roasted with fire, because fire dissolves flesh that water has boiled, but flesh cooked by fire without water it strengthens. Thus the fire cooked the flesh of our Lamb because the very force of his suffering made him stronger for resurrection and strengthened him for incorruption. Since he recovered strength from death, his flesh was hardened by fire. Hence the Psalmist also says: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” [Col. 0357A] (Ps. XXI, 16). For what is a potsherd before fire except soft clay? But it is acted upon by fire so that it may become hard. Thus the strength of Christ’s humanity dried up like a potsherd because, through the fire of suffering, it grew into the strength of incorruption.

[Note: [Col. 0357D] From Book XXI on Job, chapter IX.] By “fire” is designated the heat of lust, as Job says: “It is a fire devouring unto destruction and rooting out all offspring” (Job XXI, 30). The difference between a sin and a crime is that every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime. In this life many can be without crime, but no one can be without sin. Hence, when the outstanding preacher described a man worthy of priestly grace, he did not say, “If anyone is without sin,” but “If anyone is without crime” (Tit. I, 6). For who can be without sin, when John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” [the citation as printed also gives I Tim. III, 10], “and the truth is in us” (I John I, 8)?

In this distinction between sins and crimes, it must be considered that some sins pollute the soul, whereas crimes extinguish it. Therefore Job, defining the crime of lust, says: “It is a fire devouring unto destruction,” because the guilt of this offense stains not merely unto defilement but devours unto destruction. And because, whatever other good works there may have been, if the crime of lust is not washed away they are overwhelmed by the enormity of this crime, he adds: “And rooting out all offspring.” The offspring are the soul’s good works. But if the flesh rules in a perverse order, the fire of lust burns up everything good that has been brought forth [Col. 0357C].

By “fire” is designated the heat of avarice, as Eliphaz says: “Fire shall devour the tents of those who gladly receive gifts” (Job XV, 34). See the chapter “On the Tent,” below, book XIII, chapter 7, distinction 3.

By “fire” is designated the flame of envy, as blessed Job says: “The fire of God fell from heaven and consumed the sheep and the servants that had been struck; and I alone escaped to tell you” (Job I, 16). See the chapter “On Heaven,” above, [Col. 0357D] book I, chapter 3, distinction 7.

[Note: [Col. 0357D] From Book III on Job, chapter XVII, 22.] By “fire” is designated the heat of compunction, as it is written in the book of Judges. When Jerubbaal was threshing wheat from chaff, he saw an angel; at the angel’s command he immediately cooked a kid, placed it upon a rock, and poured the broth of the flesh over it. The angel touched these things with a staff, and fire coming forth from the rock consumed them (Judg. VI, 11). For what is it to strike wheat with a staff except, through the uprightness of judgment, to separate the grains of virtues from the chaff of vices? But to those doing this the angel appears, because the more diligently people cleanse themselves from outward things, the more the Lord reveals inward things to them. He commands the kid to be killed—that is, every appetite of our flesh to be sacrificed—and the flesh to be placed upon the rock, and the broth of the flesh poured over it.

For what else does the rock signify except him of whom Paul says, “And the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4)? Therefore we place flesh upon the rock when we afflict our body in imitation of Christ. He also pours the broth of the flesh over it who, in the manner of life of Christ, empties even carnal thoughts. For the liquid broth is poured from flesh onto the rock when the mind is emptied of the flow of carnal thoughts. Yet the angel immediately touches these things with a staff, because the power of divine help does not abandon our intention. Fire comes forth from the rock and consumes the broth and flesh because the Spirit breathed forth by the Redeemer burns our heart with such a flame [Col. 0358B] of compunction that it consumes everything illicit in it, both in deed and in thought.

501 [Note: Col. 0358D. From Book XV on Job, chapter 17, §14.] By “fire” is understood the burning of Gehenna. In the book of blessed Job, Sophar says concerning the condemnation of the wicked: “A fire not kindled shall devour him” (Job 20:26). In a most remarkable way, the fire of Gehenna is expressed in a few words. For bodily fire, in order to be fire, requires bodily fuel. Since it must be maintained by piled-up wood, it is undoubtedly fed thereby; it cannot exist unless kindled, nor continue unless replenished. By contrast, the fire of Gehenna, although incorporeal in itself, burns the reprobate bodily; it is neither kindled by human effort nor fed by wood. Created once for all, it endures unquenchably; it has no need of kindling and does not lack burning. Therefore it is rightly said of the wicked: “A fire not kindled shall devour him,” because the justice of the Almighty, foreknowing things to come, created from the very origin of the world the fire of Gehenna, which would begin to exist once for the punishment of the reprobate, but would never bring its burning to an end, even without wood. We must therefore know that all the reprobate, because they sinned alike in soul and body, are likewise tormented there in soul and body. Hence the Psalmist says: “You shall set them as a furnace of fire at the time of your countenance; the Lord shall trouble them in his wrath, and fire shall devour them” (Ps. 20:10). A furnace burns inwardly; but one devoured by fire begins to be burned from the outer part. Therefore, so that the sacred words might show the reprobate burning both outwardly and inwardly, they testify that they are devoured by fire and set like a furnace: that they may be tormented by fire in the body and burn through pain in the mind.

## Chapter II. On Flame

[Note: Col. 0358D. From Book XII on Job, chapters 22 and 24, scattered passages.] By “flame” is signified the heat of carnal desires, as Eliphaz says concerning any wicked person: “Flame shall dry up his branches” (Job 15:30). Those who cling to another in familiar attachment are called branches; flame is understood as the burning of desires. Thus flame dries up the branches of the wicked man, because those who cling to him pant after earthly advancement through his example, are set ablaze by the torches of avarice, and are burned by the fires of carnal desires. For if he attached to himself persons seeking the eternal homeland, he would have green branches upon him. But because those joined to him also burn with earthly desires, the flame of desire sets alight the minds of his dependents—that is, it dries up his branches—so that they bear no fruit of good work, because through wickedness they pant after lowly things.

## Chapter III. On the Spark

In Sacred Scripture, “sparks” sometimes signify the examples of the righteous, and sometimes the words of preachers.

[Note: Col. 0359D. From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter 3, middle, §4.] By “sparks” are signified the examples of the good, as Wisdom says of the righteous: “The righteous shall shine, and shall run to and fro like sparks among reeds” (Wis. 3:7). By the reed-bed it means the life of worldly people, who, like reeds, seem outwardly to rise to great heights through temporal glory, but inwardly are emptied of the solidity of truth. Yet the righteous run like sparks among reeds, because, while they are mingled with sinners, they set them aflame with the fire of their examples and reduce to ashes everything that glitters. Consumed by the flame of piety, when they behold the frailty of their own condition, they recognize themselves as nothing but ash, so that, softened from the hardness of their pride through repentance, they may say with the Psalmist: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust” (Ps. 103:29).

[Col. 0359C] By “sparks” are signified the flaming words of preachers, as Ezekiel says: “And sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze” (Ezek. 1:7). See the chapter “On Bronze,” Book VIII, chapter 10, distinction 4.

## Chapter IV. On Smoke

In Sacred Scripture, “smoke” sometimes signifies compunction, and sometimes dark uncertainty.

[Note: Col. 0359D. From Book I on Job, chapter 19, §39.] By “smoke” is signified compunction, as it is said in praise of the Bride in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a wisp of smoke, fragrant with myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” (Song 3:6).

[Col. 0359D] By “smoke” is signified dark uncertainty, as God says to Antichrist under the name of Leviathan: “Smoke proceeds from his nostrils” (2 Sam. 22:9). See the chapter “On Nostrils,” above, Book V, chapter 13, distinction 1.

## Chapter V. On Coals

In Sacred Scripture, “coals” sometimes signify hidden saints, sometimes saints in general, and sometimes minds grown cold in sins.

By “coals,” hidden saints are signified in particular, as Ezekiel says: “And the appearance of the living creatures was like burning coals of fire, and like lamps” (Ezek. 1:13). The appearance of the living creatures is fittingly compared to burning coals of fire and to lamps. Whoever touches a coal is burned; so one who cleaves to a holy man receives, through constant sight of him, habitual conversation with him, and the example of his deeds, what kindles him to love of truth. He drives away the darkness of his sins and burns with desire for light, so that he now burns through true love, whereas before he lay in iniquity as dead as he was cold. Lamps, however, spread their light farther: though they are in one place, they shine in another. For the reputation of one endowed with the spirit of prophecy, the word of teaching, and the grace of miracles shines far and wide like a lamp. Those who hear of his good deeds, because through them they rise to the love of heavenly things, shine, as it were, from the lamp’s light when they show themselves in good works.
