Therefore holy men are coals because they kindle certain persons set near them to love of the heavenly homeland, as though by touch. But because they shine for persons far away and guide their paths lest they fall into the darkness of their sin, they become lamps. This is the difference between coals and lamps: coals do indeed burn, but they do not drive away the darkness of the place where they lie. Lamps, however, because they shine with the great light of their flames, put to flight the darkness spread all around. From this it should be noted that many saints are so simple and hidden, concealing themselves in lesser places under profound silence, that scarcely can their lives be known by others. What then are these but coals? Although they have burning through the fervor of the Spirit, they do not possess the flame of example, nor do they overcome the darkness of sins in other hearts, because they wholly refuse to have their life known. They are kindled for themselves, indeed, but are not lights for others by example. But those who both spread examples of virtues and show wanderers, by life and word, the light of good work are rightly called lamps, because through the ardor of desire and the flame of speech they repel from sinful hearts the darkness of error. Thus, one who lives well in secret but does not at all benefit another’s progress is a coal. But one placed forth as an example of holiness, who displays to many the light of uprightness from himself, is a lamp: he burns for himself and shines for others.

505 [Note: Col. 0360D. From Book XXIX on Job, chapter 11.] By “coals” saints in general are also understood, as the Psalmist says: “Before the brightness in his presence the clouds passed, hail and coals of fire” (Ps. 17:47). Clouds pass before the brightness because holy preachers traverse all the regions of the world with the splendor of miracles. They are also called hail and coals of fire: because they strike through correction and kindle through the flame of charity.

By “coals” are signified minds cold in sins, as Jeremiah says concerning the Nazirites: “Their face has become blacker than coals, and they are not recognized in the streets” (Lam. 4:8). See the exposition of these words in Book V, chapter 33, distinction 1.

## Chapter VI. On Live Coals

[Note: Col. 0361D. From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter 28, §40.] By “live coals” are signified minds burning with earthly desire, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the devil: “His breath makes coals burn” (Job 41:12). What does he call coals except the minds of reprobate people kindled in earthly desires? They burn whenever they seek some temporal thing, because desires indeed scorch them and do not permit the mind to remain calm or whole. Thus the ancient enemy kindles someone’s coals as often as his secret suggestion draws human minds toward unlawful pleasures. At one time he inflames them with the torches of pride, at another with those of envy, lust, or avarice. He applied the torch of pride to Eve’s mind (Gen. 3), when he incited her to despise the words of the Lord’s command. He kindled Cain with the flame of envy (Gen. 4), when Cain grieved over his brother’s accepted sacrifice and thereby came as far as the crime of fratricide. He burned Solomon’s heart with the torches of lust, subjecting him to such love for women that, following the pleasure of the flesh, he was led even into the worship of idols and forgot reverence for his Creator (3 Kgs. 11). With the fire of avarice he burned Ahab’s mind when he drove him with impatient desires to covet another person’s vineyard, and thereby drew him into the guilt of murder (3 Kgs. 11). Thus an evil spirit becomes so much more like live coals to someone as, by the pressure of secret suggestion, it inflames human minds toward unlawful things.

## Chapter VII. On Ash

In Sacred Scripture, “ash” sometimes signifies worldly care and sometimes repentance.

[Note: Col. 0361D. From Book XXXII on Job, chapter 7, after the middle, §18.] By “ash” is signified worldly care, as the prophet says, under the figure of Ephraim, concerning any soul burdened with earthly desires: “Ephraim has become a cake baked in ashes which is not turned” (Hos. 7:8). By our well-created nature we possess an intention that rises toward God; but through evil habitual conduct there is in us a will that presses downward toward the present world. A cake baked in ashes is cleaner on the side it hides beneath, and dirtier on the side that bears ash above. Therefore, whoever neglects the intention by which he ought to seek God presses down the cleaner part beneath, after the manner of such a cake; and when he willingly bears the cares of the world, he carries piled-up ash above. The cake baked in ashes would be turned if it drove away the ash of carnal desires and displayed above the good intention which it had long crushed beneath by despising it. But it refuses to turn when the mind, pressed down by love of worldly cares, neglects to cast off the weight of ash imposed upon it; and, because it does not seek to rise to a good intention, it presses its cleaner face beneath.

By “ash” is signified repentance, as Job says in the person of one repenting: “I have sewn sackcloth upon my skin, and covered my flesh with ashes” (Job 16:16). See the chapter “On Skin,” Book V, chapter 24, distinction 2.

# Book Twelve Begins

## Chapter I. On Light

In Sacred Scripture, “light” sometimes signifies Christ; sometimes the brightness of the eternal homeland; sometimes the glory or prosperity of the present life; sometimes knowledge of the Law; sometimes vain joy; sometimes righteousness; and sometimes the brightness of preaching.

By “light” Christ is signified, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the light of the world” (John 6:12).

By “light” is signified the brightness of the eternal homeland, as it is said of perverse people through Job: “Thus they walk in darkness as though in light” (John 3:19). Darkness fittingly expresses the present life, in which the consciences of others cannot be seen. But light is our eternal homeland, where, while we behold faces, we in turn see our own hearts within us. Therefore, because the wicked already love the present life and embrace this time of exile as though they were already reigning in their homeland, it is rightly said: “Thus in darkness as though in light.” They are as glad in their present blindness as though they already enjoyed the light of the eternal homeland.

508 [Note: Col. 0362D. From Book XIV on Job, chapter 4, §3.] By “light” is signified the glory or prosperity of the present life, as Baldad says: “Shall not the light of the wicked be extinguished?” (Job 18:9). For the wicked have their own light in the present—that is, the prosperity of the present life. But the wicked person’s light shall be extinguished, because the prosperity of fleeting life ends more swiftly along with life itself. Yet concerning this light the Lord says to Job: “Their light shall be taken away from the wicked” (Job 38:15). The death of the flesh, which restores the elect to their light, takes their light away from the reprobate. For the light of one who is proud is the glory of the present life; it is taken from him when, through the destruction of the flesh, he is summoned to the darkness of his recompense.

[Note: Col. 0362D. From Book XXIX on Job, chapter 3.] By “light” may be understood knowledge of the Law. Since this was taken away from the Jews because of their pride, it is rightly said: “Their light shall be taken away from the wicked” (Job 38:15), because, while they refuse to believe the truth, they lose the knowledge of the Law forever; and while they are proud of the Law they received, they are surely blinded by the glory of their own knowledge. For it is written: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see” (Ps. 68:24). And again it is written: “Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy” (Isa. 6:10). And again: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

[Note: Col. 0363D. From Book XIV on Job, chapter 4, §3.] By “light” is signified vain joy, as Baldad says concerning one who places his joy in temporal things: “The light shall be darkened in his tent” (Job 18:6). The tent means the conscience. And as we often call sorrow darkness, so we ought not without reason to understand joy as light. Therefore the light in the wicked person’s tent is darkened, because in the conscience where he dwells evilly, the joy that had come from temporal things fails.

[Note: Col. 0363D. From Book XXIX on Job, chapter 9.] By “light” is signified righteousness, as the Lord says to blessed Job: “Tell me, if you know all things: in what way does light dwell, and what is the place of darkness, that you may lead each one to his boundaries, and understand the paths of his house?” (Job 38:20). What is understood by light except righteousness, and what is signified by darkness except iniquity? Hence it is said to some who have turned from the wickedness of sins: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:9). Blessed Job is therefore told: “Tell me, if you know all things: in what way does light dwell, and what is the place of darkness?” (Job 38:4). This is as though he were told: If you suppose that you possess full knowledge, say either in whose heart the innocence now lacking will come, or in whose heart the evil now present will persist. “In what way does light dwell”: that is, whose mind will righteousness fill when it comes? “And what is the place of darkness”: that is, in whom will blind iniquity endure? “That you may lead each one to his boundaries”: that is, that you may judge whether the one now seen as wicked will end his life in wickedness, or whether the one now seen as righteous will conclude the end of his life in the perfection of righteousness. “And understand the paths of his house”: that is, that you may consider and discern either to whom persevering good action will grant an eternal dwelling in the kingdom, or whom evil action, binding him to his end, will condemn to eternal punishment. For “house” is used for dwelling, and “path” for action. Thus the path leads to the house, because action draws one to one’s dwelling.

[Note: Col. 0363D. From the same book, chapter 12.] By “light” may also be understood the brightness of preaching. For he himself is the way, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Through this way light is spread abroad, because through his presence all the Gentile world is enlightened. It is aptly said to be “spread abroad,” because the light of preaching shone forth through the voices of the apostles—not narrow and confined, but shining widely.

## Chapter II. On the Lamp

In Sacred Scripture, “lamp” sometimes signifies Christ; sometimes the brightness of preaching; sometimes the brightness of good works; sometimes the light of Sacred Scripture; and sometimes vain joy.

By “lamp” Christ is signified, as he himself says in the Gospel: “What woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it?” See the chapter at the beginning of Book IV, chapter 4, distinction 1.

[Note: Col. 0363D. From Book XXX on Job, chapter 17, near the end.] By “lamp” is signified the brightness of preaching, as Truth says in the Gospel concerning good teachers: “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand” (Matt. 5:15). The bushel means temporal advantage, and the lamp the light of preaching. To put the lamp under a bushel is to hide the grace of preaching for the sake of temporal gain; surely none of the elect does this. And it is well added: “but upon a lampstand.” The lampstand signifies the condition of the body; the lamp is set upon it when the care of preaching is placed above the body.

[Note: Col. 0364D. This is from Book XXVIII on Job, chapter 47.] By “lamp” is signified the brightness of good works, as Truth says in the Gospel to holy preachers: “Let your loins be girded, and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:35). Lust is signified by the loins, and the brightness of good works by the lamp. They are therefore commanded to gird their loins and hold their lamps: that is, plainly, first restrain lust in yourselves, and then show others examples of good works from yourselves.

[Note: Col. 0364D. From Homily 13 on the Gospels.] Thus two things are commanded: to restrain the loins and to hold lamps, so that there may be purity of chastity in the body and the light of truth in action. Neither is acceptable to our Redeemer without the other: if one who does good deeds has not yet abandoned the defilements of lust, or if one excels in chastity but does not yet exercise himself through good works. For chastity is not great without good work, nor is any good work possible without chastity.

[Note: Col. 0364D. From Book XIX on Job, chapter 8, §9.] By “lamp” is signified the light of Sacred Scripture, as blessed Job says in the person of holy Church set amid the final tribulation: “Who will grant me that I may be as in the former months, according to the days when God guarded me? When his lamp shone over my head, and by his light I walked in darkness” (Job 29:2). For then, under pressure from persecution, she sees many of the weak fall away from herself—those whom she now, as a mother, cherishes as little children in the bosom of peace and holds in the tranquil cradle of faith, because, mingled with the strong, they are nourished by the very tranquility of faith. But then many such persons will fall, and the souls of the perfect grieve, through the depths of charity, that they themselves suffer whatever loss befalls the little ones. For the losses of the weak pass to the hearts of the strong through compassion. Hence Paul says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (1 Cor. 11:29). For a person is perfect to the degree that he perfectly feels the pains of others. Therefore, when holy Church is distressed by the falling away of the weak, remembering these times, she will rightly say: “According to the days when God guarded me.”

And it is well said: “When his lamp shone over my head, and by his light I walked in darkness.” The lamp signifies the light of Sacred Scripture. Concerning it the shepherd of the Church himself says: “We have the more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to give heed, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day should dawn and the day-star arise in your hearts” (2 Pet. 1:19). And the Psalmist says: “Your word, Lord, is a lamp to my feet” (Ps. 118:105). Since our ruling faculty is the mind, the mind is called by the name of “head.” Hence the Psalmist says: “You have made my head fat with oil” (Ps. 22:5), as though plainly saying: You have filled my mind with the richness of brightness. Now, therefore, the lamp shines over the head of the Church, because the sacred words cast rays into the darkness of our mind, so that in this dark place of the present life, receiving the light of God’s words, we may see what ought to be done. Now she walks by light in darkness, because holy universal Church, even though she does not penetrate another person’s hidden thought, as though she does not know a face in the night, nevertheless directs the steps of good work by the light of heavenly speech.

By “lamp” is signified joy in the flesh, as Baldad says of the wicked: “And the lamp that is over him shall be extinguished” (Job 18:5). To speak in the common idiom: a lamp is light in an earthen vessel; light in an earthen vessel is joy in the flesh. Therefore the lamp that is over the wicked person shall be extinguished, because, when the recompense for his evils follows him, carnal joy is scattered from his mind. It is well said of this lamp not that it is “with him” but “over him,” because earthly joys possess the minds of the wicked and absorb them in pleasures, so that they are over the mind rather than with it. Even when the righteous possess the prosperity of the present life, they know how to press it down beneath themselves, so that, although they rejoice inwardly in good things, they rise above them by the counsel of seriousness and the governance of virtue. The wicked person’s lamp, which is over him, is therefore extinguished, because his joy quickly fails—the joy which wholly possessed him in this life. And the punishment of torment afterward constricts the person who now wickedly expands himself in pleasures.

## Chapter III. On Dawn

[Note: Col. 0365D. From Book IV on Job, chapter 13.] By “dawn” is signified holy Church, as it is said concerning the devil, or his body, under the name of night: “He awaits the light and does not see it, nor the rising of the dawn as it rises” (Job 5:9). Christ is called light, as he himself says: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). Therefore that night—that is, the dark enemy in his members—awaits the light and does not see it. For either those who retain faith without works, when they trust that they can be saved in the final judgment because of that faith, will find their hope frustrated, because by living evilly they have destroyed what they held by confessing it; or those who display themselves in good action for human praise await in vain a recompense of good works from the coming Judge, because, as they perform them for the sake of praise, they have already received their reward from human lips. Truth bears witness to this, saying: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2). And it is well added: “Nor the rising of the dawn as it rises.” Dawn means the Church, which is changed from the darkness of her sins into the light of righteousness. Thus the Bridegroom marvels at her in the Song of Songs, saying: “Who is this who goes forth like the dawn rising?” (Song 6:9). The Church of the elect rises like dawn because it leaves behind the darkness of its former perversity and turns itself toward the splendor of new light.

Therefore, in that light manifested at the coming of the strict Judge, the body of the condemned enemy does not see the rising of the dawn as it rises. When the strict Judge comes to render recompense, any wicked person, oppressed by the darkness of his own merits, does not know with what brightness holy Church rises into the eternal light of the heart. For then the minds of the elect are caught up on high, to be enlightened by the rays of Divinity; and the more they are bathed in his regard, the more they are lifted beyond themselves by shining grace. Then holy Church fully becomes dawn, when it utterly loses the darkness of its mortality and ignorance. In judgment, therefore, it is still dawn; but in the kingdom it is day. For although with the restoration of bodies it already begins to see light in judgment, it brings that sight to fuller perfection in the kingdom. Thus the rising of dawn is the beginning of the Church’s growth, which the reprobate cannot see: pressed down by the weight of their evils, they are drawn away from the sight of the strict Judge into darkness. Hence the prophet rightly says: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10). Therefore the Psalmist says of this dawn: “You shall hide them in the hiding-place of your countenance, from the disturbance of men” (Ps. 30:21). For each elect person is hidden in judgment through inward sight in the countenance of Divinity, while the outward blindness of the reprobate is driven into turmoil by the strict visitation of justice.

## Chapter IV. On Daybreak

In Sacred Scripture, “daybreak” sometimes signifies the present Church of the elect, and sometimes knowledge of truth.

514 [Note: Col. 0366D. From Book XXIX on Job, chapter 2, §1.] By “daybreak” or “dawn” is signified the present Church of the elect, as the Lord says to blessed Job: “Have you, after your rising, commanded the daybreak, and shown the dawn its place?” (Job 38:12). Understand: as I have. The rising of his Divinity has neither before nor after. Since his being is always through eternity, and since he encompasses all that passes away, he encloses the courses of time within himself. But the rising of his humility both began and ended, and received from time a before and an after. Yet because, when he assumed the shadows of our temporality, he poured upon us the light of his eternity, dawn rightly came to know in time its own place through that rising which the Creator made for himself in time. Since daybreak or dawn is turned from darkness into light, the whole Church of the elect is not without reason signified by the name daybreak or dawn. For, as it is led from the night of unbelief into the light of faith, it opens into day after darkness, like daybreak or dawn, through the splendor of heavenly charity.

By “daybreak” is signified knowledge of truth, as Job says to the Lord concerning man: “You visit him at daybreak, and suddenly test him” (Job 7:18). Who among us does not know that daybreak is called that time when the hours of night are already changed into the brightness of light? We are oppressed by the darkness of night when we are darkened by committing iniquity. But night is turned into light when the splendor of righteousness illuminates our hearts, which the blindness of guilt had pressed down. Thus the Lord visits us at daybreak, because he illuminates the darkness of our error with the light of his knowledge, raises us through the gift of contemplation, and exalts us to the citadel of virtue. But it must be observed that, after the Lord visits at daybreak, he suddenly tests a person, because he both advances our hearts toward virtue by kindling them and, by withdrawing, permits them to be shaken by temptation. For if after gifts of virtue the mind is shaken by no temptation, it boasts that it possesses them from itself. Therefore, so that it may have gifts of strength and humbly know its own weakness, it is raised to high things by the approach of grace, and is tested as to what it is from itself by grace’s withdrawal.

This is well suggested to us in the account of Sacred Scripture which recalls that Solomon received wisdom from God and yet, after receiving that wisdom, was immediately challenged by the question of the prostitutes. For as soon as he received the grace of so great a revelation, he underwent the dispute of dishonorable women; because often, when the regard of inward generosity illuminates our mind with virtues granted to it, slippery thoughts immediately trouble it, so that the mind which rejoices at being raised by an immense gift may also discover, when assailed by temptation, what it is. Thus Elijah, visited at daybreak, opened the heavens by his word, yet when suddenly tested, fled weakly through the wilderness and feared a single woman (3 Kgs. 19). Thus Paul is led up to the third heaven and, penetrating paradise’s secrets, beholds them; yet, returning to himself, he labors against the warfare of the flesh and bears another law in his members, whose rebellion against the law of the spirit he laments as an exhausting struggle within him (2 Cor. 12). Thus the Lord visits a person at daybreak but suddenly tests him after the visitation: he raises him by the gift bestowed, and, withdrawing it a little, shows the person to himself.

## Chapter V. On Morning

In Sacred Scripture, “morning” sometimes signifies the coming of the Lord’s incarnation; sometimes the coming of the Judge; sometimes the beginning of our life; sometimes the prosperity of the present life; sometimes the beginning of the world; and sometimes the childhood of our understanding.

[Note: Col. 0367D. From Book XVI on Job, chapter 25, §127.] By “morning” is signified the coming of the Lord’s incarnation, as the prophet says: “Morning comes, and also night” (Isa. 21:12). For the beginnings of new light shone forth in the presence of our Redeemer, yet the darkness of their unbelief was not wiped away from the hearts of persecutors.

[Note: Col. 0367D. From Book VIII on Job, chapter 21, §23.] By “morning” is signified the coming of the Judge, as blessed Job says: “Behold, now I sleep in dust; and if you seek me in the morning, I shall not remain” (Job 7:21). To the first man when he sinned it was said: “You are dust, and into dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19). “Morning” means that future manifestation of minds at the coming of the Judge, when thoughts are made open as though after the darkness of night. Of this morning the Psalmist says: “In the morning I shall stand before you and shall see” (Ps. 5:5). God’s seeking a person is his examination by subtle interrogation and his judgment of the person by strict scrutiny. Therefore blessed Job, considering the losses incurred by human lowliness, sees that he is already oppressed by present punishment and will still be more grievously afflicted by future things, and says: “Behold, now I sleep in dust; and if you seek me in the morning, I shall not remain.” He laments, as though more plainly saying: In the present I already suffer the death of the flesh; yet I still dread, in the coming judgment, the more grievous sentence of your strictness.

[Note: Col. 0368D. From Book V on Job, chapter 28.] By “morning” is signified the beginning of our life, as Eliphaz says concerning sinners: “From morning until evening they are cut down” (Job 4:20). For the sinner is cut down from morning until evening when, from the beginning of his life to its end, he is wounded by committing iniquity. At every time the reprobate multiply against themselves the blows of growing wickedness, by which, cut down, they fall into the depths. Of them the Psalmist rightly says: “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days” (Ps. 54:26). To halve one’s days is to divide the time of life spent wickedly in pleasures by the tears of repentance, and to restore it by putting it to good use. But the wicked do not halve their days, because they do not change their perverse mind even at the last moment. By contrast Paul admonishes us, saying: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5:16). We redeem time when we repair by weeping the past life that we lost through self-indulgence.

[Note: Col. 0369D. From Book XVI on Job, chapter 25.] By “morning” is signified the prosperity of the present life, as blessed Job says concerning any perverse person: “At the first morning the murderer rises; he kills the needy and poor; but by night he will be like a thief” (Job 24:14). Since a murderer is usually accustomed to commit violence in the slaughter of neighbors chiefly amid the silence of night, why is he here said to rise at the first morning to kill the needy and poor, while at night he is said to be like a thief? Yet while the literal words agree with one another, we are called back to investigate the secrets of the Spirit. Thus morning signifies the prosperity of the present life, as Solomon says: “Woe to you, O land, whose king is a child, and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccl. 10:16). Since morning is the first part of the day and evening the last, we ought not to feast upon the prosperity of this life which comes first, but upon those things that follow at the day’s end—that is, at the end of the world. Therefore those eat in the morning who exalt themselves in the prosperities of this world and, because they care intensely for present things, do not think about future things. “Everyone who hates his brother,” as Scripture says, “is a murderer” (1 John 3:20). Thus the murderer rises at the first morning, because every perverse person is raised up in the glory of the present life and crushes the lives of those who thirst for the glory to come and seek, as it were, to be satisfied in the evening. Therefore, one who is a murderer against the needy and poor in the morning is hidden like a thief at night, because every perverse person who, in the prosperity of the present life, kills the life of the humble by crushing them, when placed in adversity and humiliation secretly injures them through wicked schemes; and what he cannot accomplish by himself, he carries out by attaching himself to the powerful of this world.

[Note: [Col. 0369D] From Homily 19 on the Gospels.] By “morning” is denoted the beginning of the world, in the Gospel according to the voice of Truth: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard” (Matt. 20:1). Who more rightly bears the likeness of the householder than our Creator, who governs what he created and possesses his elect in this world as a lord possesses subjects in his house? He possesses the whole vineyard, that is, the Church; and, from righteous Abel to the last elect person who is to be born at the end of the world, he has brought forth as many saints as he has sent out shoots.

Therefore this householder hires labourers to cultivate his vineyard in the morning, at the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours: because from the beginning of this world until its end he has never ceased to gather preachers for the instruction of the faithful people. For the morning of the world was from Adam to Noah; the third hour from Noah to Abraham; the sixth from Abraham to Moses; the ninth from Moses to the coming of the Lord; and the eleventh from the coming of the Lord to the end of the world.

## CHAPTER VI. ON THE THIRD, SIXTH, NINTH, AND ELEVENTH HOURS

[Col. 0370A]

[Note: [Col. 0370D] From the preceding homily.] We can also distinguish these same differences of hours in each individual person through the stages of life. The morning of our understanding is childhood. The third hour may be understood as adolescence, because, as it were, the sun has advanced upward while the heat of age increases. The sixth hour is youth, because the sun is fixed, as it were, at its midpoint, while in it the fullness of strength is made firm. The ninth hour is understood as old age, in which the sun descends, as it were, from its high course, because that age has failed from the heat of youth. The eleventh hour is that age called decrepit or very aged. Hence the Greeks call those who are extremely old not γέροντας, “old men,” but πρεσβυτέρους, “elders,” in order to indicate that those whom they call more advanced are more than old men.

Therefore, because one person is brought to a good life in childhood, another in adolescence, another in youth, another in old age, and another in decrepit age, labourers are called into the vineyard, as it were, at different hours.

## CHAPTER VII. ON DAY

In Holy Scripture, by the name “day” are sometimes understood the brightness of the future life, sometimes the delight of sin, sometimes the light of understanding, sometimes a spiritual teacher, and sometimes the brightness of the conduct of our Redeemer in the flesh. When “days” is used in the plural, it sometimes denotes the individual souls of the elect, sometimes angelic spirits, sometimes virtues, sometimes the duration of eternity, and sometimes understanding.

[Col. 0370C] By “day” is denoted the brightness of the future life, as the Bridegroom says to the Church in the Song of Songs: “Your two breasts are like twin fawns of a gazelle, feeding among the lilies, until the day breathes” (Song 10:3 [apparently 4:5]). Consult the chapter on breasts, book V, chapter 44, distinction 1.

[Note: [Col. 0370D] From Book 4 on Job, chapter 17.] By “day” is denoted the delight of sin, as blessed Job says: “Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man has been conceived” (Job 3:3). By day is understood the delight of sin; by night, the blindness of mind through which a person allows himself to be cast down in the commission of guilt. He therefore desires the day to perish, so that everything in which sin is seen to flatter may be destroyed when the force of justice intervenes. He also desires the night to perish, so that what the blinded mind commits even by consent may be extinguished by the correction of repentance.

But we must ask why a person is said to be born in the day and conceived in the night. Certainly, a person is born in the day but conceived in the night, because he is not carried away into sinful pleasure unless he has first been weakened by the voluntary darkness of his mind. For first he becomes blind in mind, and afterwards he subjects himself to reprobate delight. Let him therefore say: “Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man has been conceived.” Let the pleasure that drew a person into sin perish; let the heedless weakness of mind that blinded him as far as the darkness of perverse consent perish. For while a person does not heedfully discern the enticements of pleasure, he also falls into the night of most wicked commission.

[Col. 0371A] Therefore one must watch carefully, so that, when sin begins to flatter, the mind may recognize to how great a destruction it is being drawn.

[Note: [Col. 0371D] From Book 1 on Job, chapter 7, 20.] By “day” is denoted the brightness of understanding, as is said of Job’s sons: “His sons went and held feasts in their houses, each on his own day” (Job 1:4). By the name “sons” the holy apostles are denoted. Thus the sons went to hold feasts in their houses when the apostolic preachers, in the various regions of the world, served banquets of virtues to their hearers, as though to people eating.

Hence it is said to these same sons concerning hungry crowds: “You give them something to eat” (Matt. 14:16); and again: “I do not wish to send them away fasting, lest they fail on the way” (Matt. 15:32). That is, let them receive from your preaching the word of consolation, lest, remaining hungry for the food of truth, they collapse amid the labour of this life. Again it is said to these same sons: “Labour not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life” (John 6:27).

How these feasts were supplied is added when it is said, “each on his own day.” If the darkness of ignorance is undoubtedly the night of the heart, understanding is rightly called day. Hence Paul says: “One judges one day above another; another judges every day” (Rom. 14:5). It is as if he said plainly: one understands certain matters while passing over others; another knows everything that can be understood, as it ought to be seen. Each, then, supplies a feast on his own day, because every holy preacher feeds the minds of his hearers with the feasts of truth according to the measure of his enlightened understanding.

[Col. 0371C] Paul had made a feast on his own day when he said: “They will be happier if they remain thus, according to my counsel” (1 Cor. 7:40). He warned each person to consider his own day when he said: “Let each abound in his own understanding” (Rom. 14:5).

By “day” is denoted a spiritual teacher, as the Psalmist says: “Day pours forth speech to day, and night makes knowledge known to night” (Ps. 18:3), that is, one spiritual person brings forth in abundance to another spiritual person the Word who was God in the beginning with God.

[Note: [Col. 0371D] From Book VI on Job, chapter 13, 14.] By “day” is denoted the brightness of the conduct of our Redeemer in the flesh, as Eliphaz says of the Jews who persecuted him: “By day they will encounter darkness, and at noon they will grope as in the night” (Job 5:14). For one sees clearly by day, but in the night our sight is obscured. Therefore, when the persecutors of our Redeemer saw the miracles of divine power and yet doubted his divinity, they suffered darkness in the day, because they betrayed the sight granted in the light. Thus they encounter darkness by day, because in the very presence of Truth they were blinded by the error of unbelief.

Hence the Light itself admonishes them, saying: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12:35). Hence it is said of Judaea: “Her sun set while it was still day” (Jer. 15). Hence the prophet again assumed in himself the voice of penitents, saying: “We stumbled at noon as in darkness, among dark things as though dead” (Isa. 59:10). Hence again he says: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” (Isa. 21:11). The watchman said: “Morning comes, and also night.”

For the watchman comes from the night because the protector of the human race appeared openly in the flesh, yet Judaea, oppressed by the darkness of its unbelief, did not recognize him. It is rightly added in the watchman’s voice: “Morning comes, and also night,” because by his presence a new light shone upon the world, yet the old blindness remained in the hearts of unbelievers. It is well said: “At noon they will grope as in the night.” For we seek by groping what we do not see with our eyes. The Jews, however, had seen his manifest miracles and were still seeking him as though groping, when they said: “How long do you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10:24).

[Col. 0372B] Behold, the light of miracles stood before their eyes, and yet, offering themselves to the darkness of their hearts, they still groped by seeking.

[Note: [Col. 0372D] From Book IV on Job, chapter 11, 10.] By “days” are denoted the individual souls of the elect, as blessed Job says concerning the night in which he was conceived: “Let it not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months” (Job 3:6). By the year we fittingly understand the preaching of heavenly grace, because just as time is completed in a year by accumulated days, so in heavenly grace a manifold life of virtues is fulfilled.

A year may also be understood as the multitude of the redeemed, because just as a year is made up from a multitude of days, so that innumerable company of the elect is completed from the gathering of all good persons. Isaiah proclaims this year of perfect multitude when he says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to proclaim to the gentle, to heal the broken-hearted, to preach forgiveness to captives and opening to the confined, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord” (Isa. 61:1). For the acceptable year of the Lord is proclaimed when the future people of the faithful, to be enlightened by the light of truth, is foretold.

But what are denoted by days if not the individual minds of the elect? What by months if not their multiplied churches, which make one Catholic Church? Therefore let that night neither be counted among the days nor numbered among the months, because the ancient enemy, who is understood by the night, oppressed by the darkness of his pride, indeed sees the coming of the Saviour but does not return with the elect to pardon. For it is written: “For nowhere does he take hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. 2:16).

[Note: [Col. 0372D] From the same book, chapter 12, 11.] For this reason our Redeemer became not an angel but a human being: because he undoubtedly had to become what he redeemed, so that, by not taking hold of the lost angel, he might leave him behind, while by taking hold of humanity in himself he might restore it.

The days may also be understood as the angelic spirits who remain in eternal light, and the months as their orders and ranks. Each individual spirit, because it shines, is a day; but because they are distinguished by certain ranks—some being thrones, others dominions, others principalities, others powers—they are called months on account of this very distribution of companies. But because the ancient enemy is not restored either to the merit of light or to the order of the heavenly companies, he is not numbered among the months. For the blindness of his accomplished pride weighs him down so that he never returns above to those companies of inward brightness. He is no longer joined to the established ranks of light, because by the desert of his darkness he is always pressed down to the depths.

[Col. 0373B] The individual virtues may also be understood by days. Therefore, because we pursue with weeping what we confidently hope will not be charged against us by the Judge who is to come, it is rightly now said of this night, that is, of the commission of guilt: “Let it not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months.” For the year of our illumination is completed then, when, with the eternal Judge appearing, the life of the holy Church’s pilgrimage is fulfilled. Then it receives the reward of its labour, when, after this time of warfare is completed, it returns to its homeland. Hence the prophet says: “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness” (Ps. 64:12). For the crown of the year is blessed when, after the time of labour has ended, the reward of virtues is bestowed.

The days of this year are the individual virtues, and the months the multiplied deeds of virtue. But behold, when the mind is raised through confidence to hope that it will be rewarded for its virtues when the Judge comes, the evils it has done also come to its memory; and it greatly fears lest the strict Judge, who comes to reward virtues, should also weigh with exact scrutiny those things which were done unlawfully, lest, when he completes the year, he should also say of the night: “Let it not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months.”

It is as if it entreated the strict Judge, saying: When, at the completion of the holy Church’s time, you reveal yourself in the final judgment, reward the gifts you have bestowed in such a way that you do not seek out the evils we have committed. For if that night is counted among the days of the year, everything we have done is confounded by the reckoning of our perversity, and the days of virtues no longer shine if the dark confusion of our counted night obscures them in your sight.

[Note: [Col. 0373D] From Book XVI on Job, chapter 21.] By “days” is denoted the duration of eternity, as blessed Job says: “Times are not hidden from the Almighty; but those who know him do not know his days” (Job 24:17). What do the days of the Lord denote but eternity itself? This is expressed only by the designation of one day, as it is written: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11). Yet sometimes, because of its length, it is denoted by the name of many days, concerning which it is written: “Your years are unto age upon age” (Ps. 101:29).

We are carried about within times because we are creatures. But God, because he is the Creator of all, encompasses our times in his eternity. Therefore he says: “Times are not hidden from the Almighty,” because he comprehensibly beholds our times, while we are utterly unable to comprehend what belongs to him. But since God’s nature is simple, it is very remarkable that it is said: “Those who know him do not know his days.” For he himself and his days are not different things. God is what he has: he has eternity, but he himself is eternity; he has light, but he himself is his light; he has brightness, but he himself is his brightness.

What, then, is meant by saying, “Those who know him do not know his days,” except that those who know him still do not know? For even those who already hold him by faith still do not know him by sight. And although he is himself the eternity in which we truly believe, we do not know how he himself is eternity. Thus it is rightly said: “Those who know him do not know his days,” because, although we already know God through faith, we do not see how eternity exists without a past before the ages, without a future after the ages, without prolonged delay, and without perpetual expectation.

By “days” is denoted understanding, as it is said of Job’s friends: “They sat with him seven days and seven nights” (Job 2:13). For by day we recognize what we see; by night we either see nothing through blindness or are darkened by uncertainty. Therefore understanding is signified by day, ignorance by night. By the number seven the totality of the universe is expressed, for this whole passing age is completed in no more than seven days.

What, then, does it mean that the friends of blessed Job are said to have sat with him seven days and seven nights, except that heretics pretend to sympathize with the infirm holy Church even in matters in which they suffer the darkness of ignorance, and prepare for it deceitful snares under the appearance of flattery? Although, swollen with the disposition of pride even in matters they cannot understand, they consider themselves great in their own estimation, nonetheless they sometimes bow themselves to holy Church merely in appearance; and while they soften their words, they pour in poison. To sit on the ground, therefore, is to display something of the appearance of humility, so that, while they exhibit humble things, they may persuade others of the proud doctrines which they teach.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON EVENING

In Holy Scripture, by “evening” or “eventide” are sometimes understood the end of life or adversity, sometimes the torpor of idleness, sometimes adversity, and sometimes the temptation of sin.

By “evening” is denoted the end of life or adversity, as Eliphaz says concerning the perverse: “From morning until evening they are cut down” (Job 20:26). Consult above, chapter 5, distinction 3, in the chapter “On Morning.”

[Note: [Col. 0375D] From Book VIII on Job, chapter 6, 9.] By “evening” is denoted the torpor of idleness, as Job says: “If I sleep, I say: When shall I rise?” (Job 7:4); and again: “I shall wait for the evening” (ibid., 4:11 [uncertain citation]). For sleep expresses the torpor of idleness, while rising expresses the exercise of action. Again, by the name “evening,” because it accords with sleep, the desire for rest is signified.

Yet as long as holy Church lives the life of corruption, it does not cease to weep over the losses caused by its changeability. For humanity was created so that, with the mind standing firm, it might raise itself to the height of contemplation, and no corruption might turn it aside from the love of its Creator. But when, from the inborn firmness of standing, it moved the foot of its will toward sin, it immediately fell from the love of its Creator into itself. Abandoning the love of God, namely the true height of steadfastness, it could not even remain within itself; for, driven by slippery mutability, falling beneath itself through corruption, it departed even from itself.

Therefore, expressing the instability of the human mind, let it say: “If I sleep, I shall say: When shall I rise?” And again: “I shall wait for the evening.” It is as though it plainly said: Nothing received is sufficient for the mind, because it has lost the One who could truly suffice. In sleep I desire rising; in rising I await evening, because both when at rest I seek the exercise of action, and when active I seek the repose of rest.

[Col. 0375C] [Note: [Col. 0375D] From the preceding chapter and book.] By “evening” adversity may also be denoted; hence these words of Job may be understood otherwise. To sleep is to lie in sins. For if sin were not designated by sleep, Paul would not say to his disciples: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15:34). Hence he admonishes his hearer, saying: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14); and again: “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. 13:21 [apparently 13:11]). Solomon likewise rebukes the sinner, saying: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep?” (Prov. 6:19 [apparently 6:9]).

Therefore, whenever one of the elect is burdened by the sleep of sin, he strives to rise to the watches of righteousness. But often, after he has risen, he feels himself lifted up by the very greatness of his virtues. Hence, after virtues, he desires to be tested by the adversities of this present life, lest he fall more grievously through confidence in his virtues. For if he did not recognize that he is better preserved through temptation, the Psalmist would never say: “Test me, Lord, and try me” (Ps. 25:2).

Thus it is rightly said: “If I sleep, I shall say: When shall I rise?” And again: “I shall wait for the evening.” For in the sleep of sin the light of righteousness is sought; and when the prosperity of virtues raises the mind [variant: “raise”], helpful adversity is desired, so that the spirit, when it is lifted more than it ought to be by delight in its virtues, may be made firm by the sorrow produced through the opposition of present life. Hence he does not say, “I shall fear the evening,” but “I shall wait for it.” We wait for prosperity and fear adversity. Therefore the righteous man waits for evening because, when he must be exercised by this tribulation, adversity itself becomes prosperity to him.

[Note: [Col. 0375D] From the preceding book and chapter.] By “evening” may also be denoted the temptation of sin, which often assails the mind more sharply the more the spirit lifts that same mind higher toward the things above. For sin is not so abandoned in this life through the exercise of righteousness that one remains unshaken in that righteousness. Even if uprightness has now driven guilt from the dwelling-place of the heart, that very guilt which is repelled sits at the doors of our thought and knocks for admission.

Moses too indicates this spiritually when, narrating the temporal sequence of bodily events, he says: “Light was made” (Gen. 1:3), and shortly afterward adds: “Evening was made” (ibid., 5). For the Creator of all, foreknowing human guilt, then expressed in time what now takes place in the mind. Light is brought toward evening because the light of uprightness is indeed followed by the shadow of temptation. But because the light of the elect is not extinguished in temptation, it is said that evening, not night, was made: for temptation often conceals the light of righteousness in the hearts of the elect, but does not destroy it; it draws it, as it were, into pallor, but does not extinguish it utterly.

Therefore, after sleep the elect desire rising; after rising they await evening, because they awaken from sin to the light of righteousness, and, set in that very light of righteousness, continually prepare themselves against the allurements of temptation. They do not fear these, but await them, because they know that even trials contribute to the benefit of their uprightness.

## CHAPTER IX. ON NIGHT

In Holy Scripture, by “night” are sometimes denoted the ancient enemy, consent to sin, the present life, the darkness of ignorance, and sorrow.

[Note: [Col. 0376D] From Book IV on Job, chapter 11, 10.] By “night” is denoted the ancient enemy, as blessed Job says: “Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man has been conceived” (Job 3:3). And again: “Let a dark whirlwind possess that night” (ibid.). For it is written: “God will come manifestly; our God will not keep silence. Fire shall burn before him, and a mighty tempest round about him” (Ps. 49:4). Therefore the dark whirlwind possesses this night because that dreadful tempest carries the apostate spirit from the sight of the strict Judge into eternal punishments. This night is possessed by the whirlwind because its proud blindness is struck by strict judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0376D] From Book IV on Job, chapter 17, 20.] By “night” may also be denoted consent itself to guilt. For just as the joy of perverse pleasure is expressed by day, so consent to guilt is rightly understood by night. For it is a lesser fault when the mind is carnally drawn toward pleasure but nevertheless resists its pleasure through the spirit; it is a graver and complete wickedness not only to be drawn toward the enticement of sin by pleasure, but also to yield through familiar consent.

Therefore the more the mind sees itself fouled by consent, the more closely must it be cleansed from pollution by the hand of repentance. Hence it is well said: “Let a dark whirlwind possess that night.” A certain tempestuous whirlwind is the stirred spirit of sorrow. For when someone recognizes the sin he has committed and carefully considers the wickedness of his perversity, he clouds his mind with sorrow; and, as though the clear air of serenity had been shaken, he devastates within himself every tranquility of heart by the whirlwind of repentance.

If this whirlwind did not crush the self-recognizing mind, the prophet would never have said: “With a mighty spirit you will shatter the ships of Tarshish” (Ps. 47:8). Tarshish is said to mean “the exploration of joy.” But when the mighty spirit of repentance occupies the mind, it disturbs every pursuit of blameworthy joy within it, so that it desires nothing but weeping and considers nothing but what may wear it down. For it sets before its eyes, on one side, the strictness of justice, and on the other, the desert of its guilt; it sees what punishment it deserves if the mercy that spares is absent—the mercy which is accustomed through present lamentations to rescue from eternal punishment.

Thus the mighty spirit shatters the ships of Tarshish when the force of compunction, with salutary terror, confounds our strong minds given over to this world as though to a sea. Let him therefore say: “Let a dark whirlwind possess that night,” that is, let not the commission of guilt be cherished by the blandishments of secure repose, but let the bitterness of repentance break in upon the mind in its merciful severity.

[Note: [Col. 0377D] From Book XXIII on Job, chapter 12, 21.] By “night” is denoted the present life, as the prophet says: “My soul desired you in the night” (Isa. 26:9); for it felt itself oppressed by a certain darkness in seeking to see God. He therefore rightly says: “My soul desired you in the night.” It is as though he said: In this darkness of the present life I desire to see you, but I am still enclosed by the cloud of my weakness.

[Note: [Col. 0377D] From Book XXVI on Job, chapter 28, 35.] By “night” is denoted the darkness of ignorance, as Elihu says to blessed Job: “Do not prolong the night, so that peoples may rise in their place” (Job 26:2 [uncertain citation]). It is as though the arrogant plainly said: Do not act in the darkness of your ignorance, so that you may substitute a multitude of weak persons in the place of the strong. For by “peoples” are denoted those who, devoted as it were to common habits, live indiscriminately in all that they desire.

To prolong the night is for peoples to rise in place of the strong: it is to act negligently so that the ignorant and weak obtain the positions even of strong teachers. Peoples rise in place of the strong when those who have learned to live wickedly obtain the places of shepherds.

[Col. 0378A] [Note: [Col. 0378D] From the preceding book, chapter 28, 38.] By “night” may also be denoted sorrow arising from temptation. For no small tribulation occurs when a tranquil mind is troubled by an assaulting temptation, like a sudden enemy. For the adversity of temptation, as it enters the mind, produces certain darknesses in it and troubles it with the obscurity of its bitterness, though it had long shone within itself through the radiant sweetness of virtues.

Therefore it is well said to one who is tempted: “Do not prolong the night, so that peoples may rise in their place.” The night is prolonged when sorrow that has arisen from temptation is not quickly ended by consolation. The night is prolonged because the grief of the mind is extended by confused thoughts. For while a mind caught in temptation considers that it is being driven from the former firmness of its virtue, it is blinded by griefs brought upon it as though by certain darknesses; and its eye is shut against every light of joy, while it anxiously trembles lest it lose utterly what it had long begun to be.

Hence it is rightly said that in this night peoples rise in place of the strong, because in this sorrow of temptation unworthy and manifold thoughts spring up in the heart in place of strong movements of mind.

## CHAPTER X. ON DARKNESS

In Holy Scripture, by “darkness” are sometimes denoted the gloom of ignorance, the tears of repentance, the hidden judgments of God, adversities, the punishments of eternal damnation, sinners, the present life, and iniquity.

[Note: [Col. 0378D] From Book XXV on Job, chapter 4.] By “darkness” is denoted the gloom of ignorance, as Elihu says: “There is no darkness, nor shadow of death, where those who work iniquity may hide themselves” (Job 34:22). What does he seek to denote by darkness except ignorance, and by the shadow of death except forgetfulness? Of the ignorance of certain persons it is said: “Having their understanding darkened by darkness” (Eph. 4:18). Again, concerning the forgetfulness that occurs in death, it is written: “In that day all their thoughts shall perish” (Ps. 145:4).

Since whatever is thought in life is wholly consigned to forgetfulness through death, forgetfulness is like a certain shadow of death. For just as intervening death causes what existed in life no longer to exist, so intervening forgetfulness causes what existed in memory no longer to exist. It is rightly called death’s shadow because it is, as it were, impressed from death itself, imitating its force by lulling the senses.

But because God neither fails to know the evils people merely think nor forgets those they commit—unless repentance erases them from his sight—it is fittingly said: “There is no darkness, nor shadow of death, where those who work iniquity may hide themselves.” It is as though he said: No one is hidden from his judgment, because he can neither fail to see what we do nor forget what he sees.

[Col. 0379A] [Note: [Col. 0379D] From Book IV on Job, chapter 15, 17.] By “darkness” are denoted the tears of repentance, as Job says: “Let that day be turned into darkness” (Job 3:4). For the day is turned into darkness when, at the very beginning of sinful pleasure, one sees to what end of destruction it draws one. Therefore we turn day into darkness when, strictly punishing ourselves, we torment the very perverse enticements of pleasure through the tears of strict repentance, when by weeping we pursue whatever we sinfully indulge in secretly within the heart.

For every believer knows that thoughts are examined with exactness in judgment, as Paul attests when he says: “Their thoughts accusing or even defending one another” (Rom. 2:15). Examining himself inwardly before the judgment, he investigates himself intensely, so that the strict Judge may come to him now in peace, when he sees the guilt which he desires to investigate already punished as guilt.

[Note: [Col. 0379D] From the preceding book, chapter 17, 20.] By “darkness” are denoted the hidden judgments of God, as it is added shortly afterward: “Let darkness and the shadow of death darken it” (Job 3:5). In light, we recognize what we see; but in darkness we either see nothing with the mind or are dimmed by uncertain vision. Therefore hidden judgments are like darkness to our eyes, because they cannot be searched out. Hence it is written of God: “He made darkness his hiding-place” (Ps. 17:20).

And because we recognize that we do not deserve to be absolved, yet are freed through the hidden judgments of divine grace that goes before us, darkness obscures the day when the unsearchable judgments of righteous correction mercifully conceal from its ray the joy of our pleasure, which must be wept for. Hence it is suitably added: “And the shadow of death.” By the shadow of death is understood the death of the flesh, because, just as true death is that by which the soul is separated from God, so the shadow of death is that by which flesh is separated from soul. Hence the martyrs rightly say: “You have humbled us in the place of affliction, and covered us with the shadow of death” (Ps. 43:20). Those who plainly die not in spirit but only in flesh do not say that they are covered by true death, but by the shadow of death.

What, then, does Job mean when he asks for the shadow of death to darken the day of perverse pleasure, except that he seeks, for the blotting out of sins before God’s eyes, the Mediator between God and humankind, who would take upon himself for us only the death of the flesh and would erase the true death of sinners by the shadow of his own death? For he came to us, who were held in death of spirit and flesh: he brought us his one death and dissolved our two deaths, which he found. If he had taken both upon himself, he would have freed us from neither. But he mercifully received one and justly condemned both. He applied his single death to our double death and, by dying, overcame our double death.

Therefore he lay in the tomb for one day and two nights, because he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our double death. Thus he who accepted for us only the death of the flesh underwent the shadow of death and concealed from God’s eyes the sin we committed. Let it therefore rightly be said: “Let darkness and the shadow of death darken it.” It is as though it were plainly said: Let him come who, in order to rescue debtors from the death of flesh and spirit, pays the death of the flesh though he owes it not.

[Note: [Col. 0380D] From Book XVI on Job, chapter 25, 28.] By “darkness” are denoted adversities, as Job says of heretics: “They break into houses in darkness, as they had agreed among themselves in the day” (Job 24:16). What is denoted here by houses except consciences, in which we dwell while considering what we do? Hence it is said to a certain person who had been healed: “Go into your house to your own, and tell them how great things the Lord has done for you” (Luke 8). That is: now secure from the vice of sin, return to your conscience and rouse it to the voice of preaching.

Therefore, when the righteous shine in the present age, teachers of error are afraid to urge perverse doctrines upon them. Instead, they seek plans and eagerly await the overthrow of their prosperity, so that in the darkness of adversity they may break into their minds by persuasion—minds to which, while they lived prosperously, they had not dared to speak perversely. As soon as they see them in adversity, they rise up and assert that such persons suffer these things only because of their sins; for, loving only the glory of the present life, they regard chastisement as condemnation.

Thus they break into houses in darkness because they attempt to corrupt the minds of the good through adversity itself. It is well said: “As they had agreed among themselves in the day,” because, when they saw the righteous shining in the light of prosperity and could not speak against them, they occupied themselves only with malicious schemes against them.

[Note: [Col. 0380D] From Homily 38 on the Gospels.] By “darkness” are signified the punishments of eternal damnation, as is said of the condemnation of Antichrist: “He shall drive him from light into darkness” (Job 18:18). For he is led from light into darkness when he is condemned from the honor of this present life to eternal punishments. Hence of the man who entered the wedding feast without a wedding garment it is said in the Gospel by the Lord’s voice: “Bind his feet and hands and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22:15). Then, by their own strict judgment, the feet and hands of those are bound who now refused to be bound from wicked works by amendment of life; or rather, punishment then binds those whom guilt now bound from good works. For feet that neglect to visit the sick, and hands that give nothing to the needy, are already bound from good work by their own will. Those, therefore, who now willingly bind themselves in vice will then be bound in punishment. It is well said that they are cast into “outer darkness.” By inner darkness we mean blindness of heart; by outer darkness, the eternal night of damnation. Therefore every condemned person is cast, not into inner, but into outer darkness, because there he is unwillingly cast into the night of damnation who here willingly fell into blindness of heart. There too weeping and gnashing of teeth are said to occur, [Col. 0381A] so that those who here rejoiced in gluttony may then gnash their teeth; there may the eyes weep which here were occupied with unlawful desires, so that every member may be subject to punishment which here served under each particular vice.

“Darkness” signifies sinners, as Paul says to certain converts: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:9). See above, chapter I, distinction 6.

By “darkness” is signified the present life, as the Lord says to Job: “Thus they walk in darkness as in light” (Job 24:17). Consult the chapter on light above, distinction 2.

“Darkness” signifies iniquity, as is said to Job: “Tell me, if you know all things, in what way light dwells,” etc. (Job 38:18). See above, chapter 1, distinction 6.

## CHAPTER XI. ON GLOOM.

In Sacred Scripture, gloom signifies the confusion of error and of the mind.

[Note: [Col. 0381D] From Book IV on Job, chapter 10.] By “gloom” is signified the confusion of error, as blessed Job says of the ancient enemy, under the figure of the day on which he was born: “May gloom seize it, and may it be wrapped in bitterness” (Job 3:5). The ancient enemy, bound by the chains of his wickedness, suffers one thing now and will suffer another at the end. For because he fell from the order of inward light, he now inwardly confounds himself in the gloom of error. But afterwards he is wrapped in bitterness, because by the desert of his voluntary gloom he is tortured by the eternal torment of Gehenna. Let it therefore be said: What does he who lost the serenity of inward light endure before the final punishment? “May gloom seize it”; and the following punishment that ravages him without end is also added: “May it be wrapped in bitterness.” For whatever is wrapped up seems, as it were, nowhere to indicate its end, because, just as it does not show where it begins, so it does not reveal where it ceases. Thus the ancient enemy is said to be wrapped in bitterness, because punishments are prepared for his pride which are not only complete in every respect but also infinite.

[Note: [Col. 0381D] From the book cited above, chapter XVII, toward the middle, section 21.] By “gloom” may also be signified the confusion of mind arising from repentance. For the Lord remits no sin without punishment: either we pursue it here with tears, or he reserves it for judgment; so that the mind may always keep diligent watch for its amendment. Therefore, where anyone desires merciful help for himself, there he must necessarily wipe clean in repentance. Thus it is fittingly said of the delight of sin: “May gloom seize it.” For as the eye is confused by gloom, so that very confusion of our mind through repentance is called gloom. For as cloudy gloom darkens the day by a mass of mist, so confusion clouds the mind by troubled thoughts. Of this it is said by a certain writer: “There is a shame that brings glory” (Ecclus. 4:25). When in repentance we bring evil deeds back before the mind, we are immediately confounded by heavy grief; a crowd of thoughts clamors within the soul, sorrow crushes, anxiety lays waste, the mind is turned to misery and darkened as if by some cloudy gloom. This gloom of shame had salutarily overwhelmed the minds of those to whom Paul said: “What fruit then had you in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21). Therefore may gloom seize this day of sin—that is, may the affliction of repentance trouble the allurements of wickedness with worthy sorrow. Hence it is fittingly added: “May it be wrapped in bitterness.” For the day is wrapped in bitterness when, as the mind returns to self-knowledge, the torments of repentance follow the allurements of sin. We wrap the day in bitterness when we see what punishments follow the joy of wicked delight [Col. 0382B] and surround it with harsh tears. For what is wrapped is covered on every side; thus it is desired that the day be wrapped in bitterness, so that each person may see from every side what evils threaten the uncorrected, and may wipe away the wantonness of his pleasure with the laments of sorrow.

## CHAPTER XII. ON SHADOW.

In Sacred Scripture, when “shadow” is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies refreshment of the mind from heavenly protection; sometimes the Incarnation of the Lord; sometimes the torpor of a cold mind; sometimes the obscurity of allegory; sometimes the instability of the present life; sometimes forgetfulness; sometimes imitation of the devil; sometimes the faithless people of the Jews; sometimes the refreshment of eternal rest. But when “shadows” are spoken of in the plural, all the wicked are understood.

[Note: [Col. 0381D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter III.] By “shadow” is signified refreshment of the mind from heavenly protection, as the Psalmist says: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16:8); or as the bride in the Song of Songs, awaiting the coming of the bridegroom, foretells it, saying: “I sat beneath the shadow of him whom I desired” (Cant. 2:3). As if she said: “Under the protection of his coming, I rested from the heat of fleshly desires.”

[Note: [Col. 0382D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter 12, near the end.] By “shadow,” or “overshadowing,” is signified the Incarnation of the Lord, as the angelic speech testifies, which says to Mary: “The power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). For a shadow is formed from light and a body. God, in his divinity, is light; through the mediation of a soul, he deigned in her womb, in his humanity, to become a body. Therefore, because the incorporeal light was to be made bodily in her womb, she who conceived the incorporeal One unto a body is told: “The power of the Most High shall overshadow you”—that is, the incorporeal light of the Godhead will take in you a body of humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0382D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter III, after the beginning.] By “shadow,” when charity departs, is signified the torpor of a cold mind, as it is written of sinful man that “he followed the shadow.” For, fleeing the warmth of charity, man abandoned the sun of virtue and hid himself beneath the shadow of inward cold. [Col. 0383A] Hence the same Truth says: “Iniquity has abounded, and the charity of many shall grow cold” (Matt. 24:12). Hence the first man after his sin is found hidden among the trees of Paradise in the breeze after midday (Gen. 3:8) [the text has invenit; variant/correction: invenitur, “is found”]. For since he had lost the midday warmth of charity, he was now torpid beneath the shadow of sin, as beneath the chill of a breeze. Hence the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the ancient enemy: “He sleeps beneath the shadow” (Job 40:16). By shadow is understood the torpor of wickedness, in which the devil sleeps, because he watches anxiously against hearts warm with charity, but lies secure in cold minds. For he cannot sleep in the hearts of saints, because even when he places himself in them for a brief moment, the heat of heavenly desires tires him. And, as it were, it pricks him to depart as often [Col. 0383B] as they sigh toward eternal things with inward love. For as many voices awaken him as holy thoughts cry out to heaven from their minds. Hence, terrified by the weapons of good deeds and struck by the darts of their sighs, he flees; and returning to the cold hearts of the reprobate, he seeks the shadow of wickedness that he may possess securely.

[Note: [Col. 0383D] Where Jerome reads Theman instead of Lebanon.] By “shadow” is signified the obscurity of allegory, as Habakkuk says: “God shall come from Lebanon, and the Holy One from the shadowy and dense mountain” (Hab. 2:17). For he who promised that he would come through the pages of his Testament comes, as it were, from the place in which he held himself under promise. [Note: [Col. 0383D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter I.] That Testament is rightly called a shadowy and dense mountain [Col. 0383C] because it is shaded by the thick obscurities of allegories.

[Note: [Col. 0383D] From Book II on Job, chapter XXVI, after the beginning.] By “shadow” is signified the instability of the present life, as is said through blessed Job of man: “He comes forth like a flower and is crushed; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition” (Job 14:2). He comes forth like a flower who shines in the flesh, but he is crushed because he is reduced to decay. For what are human beings born into the world but flowers in a field? Let us stretch the eyes of the heart over this breadth of the present life, and behold: it is full of as many flowers as human beings. Life in the flesh, therefore, is a flower in the hay. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “The days of man are as grass; he shall flourish like a flower of the field” (Ps. 102:15). Isaiah also says: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isa. 40:6). Man, indeed, after the manner of a flower, proceeds from what is hidden and suddenly appears in public; immediately he is withdrawn from public sight by death into concealment. The greenness of the flesh displays us, but the dryness of dust removes us from sight. We appeared like a flower, though we had not been; we wither like a flower, though we appeared for a time. And because man is compelled toward death day by day, it is rightly added: “He flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition” (Job 14:2). But since even the sun unceasingly pursues [Col. 0384A] its course and is never fixed in immobility, why is the course of human life compared to a shadow rather than to the sun, except because, having lost love for the Creator, man has lost the warmth of his heart and remained in the coldness of his iniquity alone? For indeed, according to the voice of Truth: “Iniquity shall abound, and the charity of many shall grow cold” (Matt. 24:12). Thus one who has no warmth of heart in the love of God, and yet does not retain the life he loves, surely flees like a shadow. And it is rightly said, “he never remains in the same condition,” because, as childhood passes into boyhood, boyhood into adolescence, adolescence into youth, youth into old age, and old age passes into death, the course of the present life presses us toward loss by its very increases; and man continually declines from the very point at which he believes himself to be advancing in the span of life. For we cannot have a fixed condition here, where we have come to pass away; and this very living of ours is daily passing away from life.

[Note: [Col. 0384D] From Book IV on Job, chapter XVII, section 20.] By “the shadow,” when it is joined with “death,” is signified forgetfulness, because, just as death causes what it kills not to be in life, so forgetfulness causes what it cuts off not to be in memory. Hence, because John came to preach to the Hebrew people the God whom they had forgotten, it is said through Zechariah: “To give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1:79). For to sit in the shadow of death is to languish in forgetfulness, away from the knowledge of divine love.

[Note: [Col. 0384D] From the book and chapter cited above.] By “the shadow of death” is signified imitation of the devil. [Col. 0384C] For he himself, because he brought in death, is called death, as John testifies when he says: “And his name was Death” (Rev. 6:8). Therefore, by the shadow of death is understood the imitation of the ancient enemy, because, as a shadow is cast according to the quality of the body, so the actions of the wicked are expressed from the form of his imitation. Hence Isaiah, when he saw the Gentile peoples perishing in imitation of the ancient enemy and rising to the dawning of the true sun, recounts as past events what he sees will certainly come, saying: “A light has risen for those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Isa. 9:2).

[Note: [Col. 0384D] See Book XVIII on Job, chapter XVIII, section 17.] By the shadow of death is spiritually signified the faithless people of the Jews, as Job says of the condemnation of that people: “The torrent separates the stone of gloom and the shadow of death from the wandering people” (Job 28:4).

By “shadow” is signified the refuge of eternal rest, as blessed Job says: “As a servant longs for the shadow, and as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work, so I have had empty months, and laborious nights have I counted for myself” (Job 7:2–3). Consult the chapter on months below, distinction 2, chapter XIII.

By “shadows” are signified all the wicked, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning imitators of the devil: “The shadows protect his shadow” (Job 40:27). For the shadows of the devil are all the wicked, [Col. 0385A] because, serving the imitation of his wickedness, they bear, as it were, the likeness of an image from his body. But just as the devil’s shadows in the plural are all the reprobate, so his shadow in the singular is each individual sinner. Yet when evil people oppose the teaching of the righteous, when they do not permit any wicked person to be corrected by them, the devil’s shadows protect his shadow: for sinners defend another sinner precisely in that matter in which they are conscious of their own wrongdoing. Thus shadows protect his shadow when those more wicked defend the deeds of the most wicked by perverse patronage.

## CHAPTER XIII. ON THE MONTH.

In Sacred Scripture, by “months” are understood sometimes perfection; sometimes our actions; sometimes either the multiplied Churches of believers that constitute the one catholic Church, or the orders and ranks of heavenly spirits; sometimes gatherings of souls.

[Note: [Col. 0385D] From Book XIX on Job, chapter VIII.] By “month” is signified perfection, as the prophet says: “And month after month shall be perfection” (Isa. 66:23): that is, from the gathering of souls there will be rest for those whose perfection now consists in action.

[Note: [Col. 0385D] From Book VIII on Job, chapter IV, section 7.] By “months” are signified our actions, as blessed Job says: “As a servant longs for the shadow, and as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work, so I have had empty months, and laborious nights have I counted for myself” (Job 7:2). For the servant’s longing for the shadow is the seeking, after the temptations, heat, and sweat of work, of the rest of eternal refreshment. That servant had desired this shadow who said: “My soul thirsted for the Lord, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord?” (Ps. 41:3). He who is said to long for the shadow is rightly called a servant, because every elect person, so long as he is constrained by the condition of infirmity, is held under the yoke of ruling corruption, as under the anxiety of heat. [Col. 0385C] But when he has been stripped of corruption, then he becomes known to himself as free and tranquil. Hence Paul also rightly says: “Creation itself shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:15). For the punishment of corruption now weighs down the elect, but then the glory of incorruption raises them up.
