And, as regards the burdens of present necessity, nothing of freedom is now displayed in the children of God; nevertheless, when the servant of God has been stripped of the bondage of corruption and received the dignity of freedom, he is transformed into the glory of the children of God, because, united to God through the Spirit, he is shown, as a creature, to have passed beyond and overcome what he was. But because he still longs for the shadow, he is a servant; because, as long as he endures the heat of temptations, he bears the yoke of a wretched condition.

But when a hired laborer sees the work that must be done, he immediately teaches his mind to consider the length and weight of the labor; yet when he calls his wearied spirit back to consider the reward of his work, he immediately renews the vigor of his mind for the exercise of labor, and what he judges heavy in the work he considers light in view of the recompense. So, indeed, when all the elect suffer the adversities of this world—when they endure dishonor, insults, loss of goods, and bodily torments—they consider the trials by which they are exercised to be heavy; but when they direct the eye of the mind to the contemplation of the eternal homeland, they discover, by comparison with the reward, how light is what they suffer. What appears wholly unbearable because of pain is lightened by prudent consideration of the recompense. Thus Paul raises himself, ever more resolute than himself, against adversities, because he awaits the end of his work as a hired laborer does. He judges what he endures to be heavy, but weighs it as light by considering the reward. [Col. 0386B] He himself shows how heavy are the things he suffers, testifying that he was more frequently in prisons, beyond measure in beatings, and often in deaths: that from the Jews he received forty lashes less one five times; that he was beaten with rods three times, stoned once, shipwrecked three times, and spent a night and a day in the depth of the sea; that he underwent dangers from rivers, robbers, his own race, the Gentiles, in the city, in the wilderness, at sea, and among false brethren; that he labored in toil and misery, in many fastings, hunger, thirst, cold, and nakedness (2 Cor. 11:24–30); that he endured conflicts without and fears within (2 Cor. 7:5); and that he said he was burdened beyond his strength: “We were weighed down exceedingly, beyond our power, so that we were weary even of life” (2 Cor. 1:8). But he himself declares how he wipes away the sweat [Col. 0386C] of such great labor with the cloth of recompense, saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:17). Therefore he awaits the end of his work like a hired laborer, who, while considering the gain of recompense, judges cheap the labor under which he nearly fails.

It is fittingly added: “So I have had empty months, and laborious nights have I counted for myself.” The elect serve the Creator of all things and are often straitened by lack of material things; they cling to God through love and yet lack the resources of this present life. Therefore those who do not seek present things by their actions pass empty months without the world’s gains; they also endure laborious nights, because they bear the darkness of adversities not only to the point of poverty [Col. 0386D] but often even to bodily torment. For to endure contempt and want is not laborious for good minds. But when adversity becomes an affliction of the flesh, labor is undoubtedly felt in the pain.

By “months” are signified either the multiplied Churches of believers that make up the one catholic Church, or the orders and ranks of heavenly spirits, as Job says of the night of his conception: “May it not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months” (Job 3:6). Consult the heading on day above, chapter 7, distinctions 6 and 7.

[Note: [Col. 0386D] From Book XIX on Job, chapter VIII.] By “months” are signified gatherings of souls, as blessed Job says in the person of Holy Church placed amid its final tribulations: “Who will grant me that I may be as in former months?” (Job 29:2). Holy Church, pressed by sorrows, will speak many such things. For she will be so hemmed in by tribulations that she will long with deep sighing for these times which we endure with great pain. Let her therefore speak—let her speak in Job’s voice: “Who will grant me that I may be as in former months?” Since a fixed number of days is called months, what does the name “months” signify except gatherings of souls? For days, when gathered into months, are withdrawn from view. So too, in this time, while Holy Church gathers souls shining with the light of virtue, she hides them in her inward places. [Col. 0387B] Let her therefore remember her former perfection; let her call to mind how much gain her preaching brought in through souls gathered, and, straitened by tribulations, say: “Who will grant me that I may be as in former months?”

## CHAPTER XIV. ON THE YEAR.

By “year” is signified either the preaching of heavenly grace or the multitude of the redeemed, as Job says of the ancient enemy under the figure of night: “May it not be counted among the days of the year.” Consult the heading on day above, chapter 7, distinction 6.

## CHAPTER XV. ON THE EAST.

[Col. 0387C] [Note: [Col. 0387D] From Book XX on Job, chapter XVIII, sections 20–21.] By “the East” is signified our Redeemer, as blessed Job says in the person of the Church: “At the right hand of the East my calamities immediately arose” (Job 30:12). For what is signified here by “right hand” except the faithful people of Holy Church? Hence the coming Judge places the goats at his left and the sheep at his right (Matt. 25:33). But when, in a time of adversity, Holy Church is attacked even by those who seemed to be faithful, calamities undoubtedly arise at her right hand. Calamities would arise at the left hand if she endured persecution’s adversities from persons outside religion and openly denying Christ. But when she suffers the trial of torments from persons who seem faithful, calamities arise for her, as it were, at the right hand, because those who serve under Christ’s name attack Christ’s name within her. This same right hand is aptly called the right hand of the East (Zech. 6:12). For it is written of her head himself: “East is his name” (ibid.). Since light rises from the east, he is rightly called East, by the light of whose justice the night of our injustice is illumined. Calamities therefore arise at the East’s right hand because those too burst out into persecution who were believed to be chosen members of our Redeemer. And he rightly says that calamities arise immediately: [Col. 0388A] because, since those who persecute were not strangers, evils come suddenly and at once from them.

## CHAPTER XVI. ON MIDDAY.

[Note: [Col. 0387D] From Book XXVIII on Job, chapter II, section 13.] By “midday” is signified the fervor of charity, as Moses says of Adam: “When he heard the voice of the Lord God walking in Paradise in the breeze after midday, he hid himself among the trees of Paradise” (Gen. 3:8). For what does it mean that after man’s sin the Lord does not stand in Paradise but walks, except that, when guilt rushed in, he showed himself moved away from the human heart? And what does “in the breeze after midday” mean except that the more burning light of truth had departed and the chill of his guilt was binding the sinful soul? Therefore, by walking, he rebuked Adam, so that he might reveal his wickedness to blind minds not only by words but also by realities: so that sinful man might hear through words what he had done, might see through the walking the inconstancy of his mutability after losing the condition of eternity, might perceive through the breeze his torpor after the fervor of charity had been expelled, and might know through the declining sun that he was approaching darkness.

[Note: [Col. 0387D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter XVIII, section 34.] By “midday” is signified the fervor of carnal persons, as the bride says to the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “Where do you pasture? Where do you lie down at midday?” (Cant. 1:7). The Lord is fed when he delights in our deeds. He lies down at midday when, amid the carnal desires of the dry heart of the reprobate, he finds in the breasts of his elect the refreshment of good thought.

## CHAPTER XVII. ON SUMMER.

In Sacred Scripture, by “summer” is signified sometimes the kingdom of heaven and sometimes the day of judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0388D] From Homily I on the Gospels.] By “summer” is signified the kingdom of heaven, as the voice of Truth says in the Gospel, where, after mentioning the signs that will occur at the end of the age, it offers a comparison: “Look at the fig tree and all the trees: when they now put forth fruit of themselves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things happen, know that the kingdom of God is near” (Luke 21:29). These words plainly show that the fruit of the world is its ruin. For it grows in order to fall; it buds in order to consume by disasters what it has budded. It is openly shown, therefore, that as the nearness of summer is recognized from the fruit of trees, so the nearness of the kingdom of God is known from the ruin of the world. The kingdom of God is rightly compared with summer, because then the clouds of our sorrow pass away and the days of life shine with the brightness of the eternal sun.

[Note: [Col. 0388D] From the end of Homily 3 on Ezekiel.] By “summer” is signified the day of judgment, as Solomon says: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow; therefore he shall beg in summer, and it shall not be given him” (Prov. 20:4). For one who now neglects to work well because of fear and the torpor of the mind, when the sun of righteousness shines at judgment as in summer, will beg for life but will not receive it, because he despised to do good works for its sake.

## CHAPTER XVIII. ON WINTER.

[Note: [Col. 0389D] From Book XXVII on Job, chapter XIV, section 19.] By “winter” is signified the present life, as Elihu says of the Lord: “He commands the snow to descend upon the earth” (Job 37:6). The rains of winter. For winter is the present life, in which, although hope now raises us toward heavenly things, the cold torpor of our mortality still binds us, as it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15). This winter has rains: undoubtedly, the preachings of rulers. Of these rains Moses says: “May my speech be awaited like rain, [Col. 0389B] and may my words descend like dew” (Deut. 32:2). These rains suit winter; they will cease in summer, because while heavenly life is now hidden from fleshly eyes, it must needs be bestowed upon us through the preaching of saints. But when the heat of eternal judgment has blazed forth, no one will then need the words of preachers. For when the Judge comes, each will be brought back to his own heart, [Col. 0390A] so that, when he can no longer perform holy deeds, he may recognize them, and may know through the punishment of his torpor the right course which he ought to have followed. Hence the prophet rightly says: “Gather them as a flock for sacrifice, and sanctify them on the day of slaughter” (Jer. 12:3). For on the day of slaughter the reprobate are sanctified, because then they recognize the holy things they ought to have done, when they can no longer escape the punishments deserved by their wickedness.

But because holy preachings will cease along with the present life—that is, rains along with winter—it is rightly said, in the persuading voice of the Bridegroom, to the soul departing and hastening toward the eternal summer: “Arise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come. For winter has now passed; the rain has gone and departed” (Cant. 2:10). For as winter passes, rain withdraws, so, when the present life in which we were bound by the cloud of ignorance and the torpor of corruptible flesh has run its course, every ministry of preaching ceases. For then we shall see more clearly through ourselves what we now hear more obscurely through the voices of saints. Therefore the Lord commands the snow and winter rains to descend upon the earth when, by the breathing of the Holy Spirit, he humbles the hearts of the saints to the ministry of preaching for the correction of sinners.

## THE THIRTEENTH BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 0389]

## CHAPTER I. ON THE CITY.

[Col. 0389C]

In Sacred Scripture, when “city” is used in the singular, it sometimes means the heavenly homeland, sometimes Holy Church, sometimes the human soul. But when “cities” are spoken of in the plural, they sometimes mean the Churches of believers and sometimes the thoughts of the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 0389D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter XV.] By “city” is signified the heavenly homeland, as Solomon says: “Wisdom has built herself a house, hewn out for herself seven columns, sacrificed victims, mixed wine, prepared her table, and sent her maidservants to call to the citadel and walls of the city” (Prov. 9:3). For the Church is rightly called the house of Wisdom. She hewed out seven columns because she raised up the minds of preachers, separated from the love of this present age, to bear the fabric of that Church. Because they are supported by the virtue of perfection, they are signified by the number seven. She sacrificed victims because she allowed the lives of preachers to be slain by persecution. She mixed wine because she preached to us together the mysteries of her divinity and humanity. She also prepared the table because she prepared food for us by opening the Sacred Scripture. She sent out her maidservants too, to call us to the citadel and walls of the city, because she took care to have weak and lowly preachers, who might gather faithful peoples [Col. 0390C] to the heavenly buildings of the spiritual homeland.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] From Book XXV on Job, chapter VIII, section 11.] By “city” is signified Holy Church, as Jeremiah the prophet says: “The city shall be built for the Lord from the tower of Hananel to the gate of the corner, and the measuring line shall go out beyond” (Jer. 31:38). No one is ignorant that the city of the Lord is Holy Church. Hananel is interpreted “the grace of God.” At a corner, moreover, two walls are joined. Therefore the city of the Lord is said to be built from the tower of Hananel to the gate of the corner, because Holy Church, beginning from the height of heavenly grace, is built as far as the entrance and reception of the peoples—namely, Jewish and Gentile. But since, as her multitude increases, the reprobate too are gathered into her, it is fittingly added: “And the measuring line shall go out beyond,” because she extends even to those who pass beyond the rule of justice and are not within the number measured by heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] From Homily 10 on Ezekiel, before the middle.] By “city” is signified the human soul, as the Lord, recounting through the prophet what he did in anger, says: “I rained upon one city, and upon another I did not rain. One part was rained upon, and the part that was not rained upon dried up” (Amos 4:7). When one mind receives the words of holy exhortation and another refuses to receive them, the Lord rains upon one city and does not rain upon another. But when even the person who hears his neighbors corrects himself from some vices and disdains to amend himself from others, surely one and the same city is rained upon in part and remains dry in part, because it repels from itself the rain of preaching. For there are some who do not hear words of exhortation at all: these utterly refuse to receive the rain. And there are some who hear but do not follow it to the depths of their being, because they cut off some vices in themselves but persist grievously in others. We often see certain people repel from themselves, through the word of preaching, the heat of avarice: they no longer seize others’ goods and even generously give their own to the needy; yet they do not tame the stings of anger or keep the safeguards of patience in tranquility of mind. Others often overcome in themselves so much of the impurity of the flesh through exhortation that they preserve their body in chastity, yet do not bend their mind toward their neighbors as they ought; rather, through the rigidity of pride, they exalt themselves in thought. In these, one part was rained upon because it bore fruit, while the part not rained upon dried up because, not fully receiving the word of exhortation, it remained barren of good.

[Note: [Col. 0391D] From Book XVI on Job, chapter XXIII.] By “cities” are signified the Churches of believers, as blessed Job says of heretics: “They made men groan from the cities” (Job 24:12). Since cities are named from peoples living together, the Churches of the true faith, established in the various parts of the world and forming one catholic Church, are not without reason signified by the name “cities”; in that Church all believers, thinking rightly about God, live together in concord. In the Gospel the Lord signified this harmony of peoples living together even by their distribution in places. When he was about to feed the people with five loaves, he ordered them to recline in groups of fifty or a hundred, so that the crowd of believers might have its food while divided in place yet united in manner (Mark 6). The rest of jubilee is contained in the mystery of the number fifty, and fifty is named twice so that it may reach one hundred. Therefore, because rest is first taken from evil action, so that afterward the soul may rest more fully in thought, some recline by fifties [Col. 0391D] and others by hundreds: for there are some who already have rest from wicked deeds, and others who already have rest of mind from perverse thoughts. Therefore, because heretics often ally themselves with the perverse powers of this world and persecute the communal life and concord of the good, it is rightly said here: “They made men groan from the cities.” Blessed Job rightly calls these people “men,” because heretics especially seek to destroy those who run along the way of God with perfect steps, not weakly and feebly, but manfully.

[Note: [Col. 0391D] From Book XII on Job, chapter XXII.] The name “cities” likewise signifies gatherings of the wicked, as is said through Eliphaz concerning a wicked rich man: “He dwells in desolate cities and in deserted houses reduced to heaps” (Job 15). For because a city is so called from the intercourse of those living together, the “desolate cities” are the very retinues of bands of the perverse, by whose cries a wicked man is praised when malice carries him away to evil deeds. Hence it is written: “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and he who commits iniquity is blessed” (Ps. 9:17).

[Note: [Col. 0391D] Where Augustine reads thus.] But the “deserted houses” are evil thoughts, which this wicked man inhabits, because in everything he does he seeks to please the thoughts of the wicked. These “desolate cities” and “deserted houses” are rightly so named, because unless almighty God, on account of their preceding sins, abandoned the conduct and thoughts of such persons, they would by no means advance to committing graver crimes. Well, then, is it said: “Which have been reduced to heaps.” For the collapsing structures of houses and cities make heaps, since, when wicked people join themselves to perverse deeds by their disordered actions, they show beyond doubt that they have fallen from the structure of life.

## CHAPTER II. ON THE WALL

In Holy Scripture, by the name “wall” are understood at one time the incarnate Lord, at another the defence of Christian faith, at another the protection of discipline, and at another an impediment to doing good.

551 [Note: [Col. 0392D] From Homily XIV on Ezekiel.] The incarnate Lord is signified by the name “wall,” as is said of holy Church through the prophet: “A wall and an outer wall shall be set in her” (Isa. 26:1). For he is our wall, who surrounds us on every side by guarding us. The outer wall of our wall, however, was all the prophets, who were sent to build faith before the Lord appeared in the flesh. Of this wall it is again said through Ezekiel: “And behold, a wall outside, all around the house on every side” (Ezek. 40:5). Here it should be noted that the wall of the spiritual building is said to be outside. For a wall built for defence is customarily placed not inside but outside. Why then was it necessary to say “outside,” when a wall is never ordinarily placed within? Because what is placed outside ensures that what is within is defended [*defendat*: “must defend”]. But what is plainly indicated by this word except the Lord’s Incarnation?

For God is a wall within for us; but God-man is a wall without. Hence it is also said through the prophet: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones” (Hab. 3:13).

[Note: [Col. 0392D] According to the Septuagint; see Jerome on this passage.] This wall, namely the incarnate Lord, would not be a wall to us if he were not outside; for he would not protect within if he had not appeared without. Nor should this be carelessly passed over: the same wall is said to have been placed around the house on every side. For the house of God is not only the holy angels, of whom the Psalmist says: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place of the dwelling of your glory” (Ps. 25:8).

[Note: [Col. 0392D] Thus Jerome, according to the Hebrew version.]

[Col. 0393A]

[Note: [Col. 0393D] Thus Jerome, according to the Hebrew version.] We also are that house, whose minds he deigns to inhabit. Therefore the wall is around the house on every side, because the only-begotten of the Father, who is above, is himself the strength of angels and, having become below, the redemption of human beings. To them he is strength lest they fall; to us, help that we may rise after falling.

The defence of Christian faith is signified by the name “wall,” as is said through Job concerning the wicked persecutors of the faithful: “As though a wall had been broken down and a gate opened, they rushed upon me” (Job 30:14). A wall, as it were, is broken down when, through the persuasions of the wicked, the faith that is in our Redeemer is destroyed in the hearts of some. And when power in this life is granted to the perverse, what else is opened but the gate of error? Thus, as though a wall had been broken down and a gate opened, the wicked rush upon the good when, having received temporal power, the perverse also attempt to destroy in the hearts of some the defence of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0393D] From the same book and chapter.] By the name “wall” may likewise be understood the protection of discipline. For the enemy enters as though through a broken wall when the defences of discipline in the heart are destroyed by the crafty persuasion either of malicious spirits or of wicked people.

[Note: [Col. 0393D] From Book XXVI on Job, chapter X.] An impediment to doing good is signified by the name “wall,” as is said in the Psalm: “And in my God I shall pass over a wall” (Ps. 17:30). For a wall is everything placed in the way of our journey so that we may not pass to him whom we love. But we pass over the wall when, for love of the heavenly homeland, we trample underfoot whatever obstacles may have been set before us in this world.

## CHAPTER III. ON THE STONE WALL

[Col. 0393C]

In Holy Scripture, by the name *maceria* (“stone wall”) are understood at one time the protection of discipline, and at another the difficulty of perfection.

[Note: [Col. 0394D] From Book XX on Job, chapter XX, 22.] The protection of discipline is signified by the name “stone wall,” as Solomon says: “I passed through the field of a lazy man and through the vineyard of a foolish man; and behold, nettles had filled it all, thorns had covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed” (Prov. 24:30). To pass through the field of a lazy man and the vineyard of a foolish man is to inspect the life of any negligent person and consider his deeds. Nettles and thorns fill it because in the hearts of the negligent there spring up itching earthly desires and the prickings of vices. For it is written: “Everyone who is idle is given over to desires.” But the stone wall was destroyed—that is, the discipline of the Fathers had been dissolved from his heart. For, seeing that the destroyed stone wall meant discipline dissolved, he immediately added: “When I saw this, I laid it to heart, and I learned discipline by example” (Prov. 24:32).

[Note: [Col. 0394D] From Book XXXIV on Job, chapter II, 1.] The difficulty of perfection is signified by the name “stone wall,” as the Lord says through the prophet, under the figure of each individual soul, concerning Judea weakened and walking in evil paths: “Behold, I will hedge up your way with thorns, and I will enclose it with a stone wall, and she shall not find her paths. And she shall follow her lovers and shall not overtake them; she shall seek them and shall not find them; and she shall say: ‘I will go and return to my former husband, for it was better with me then than now’” (Hos. 2:6–7). For the ways of the elect are hedged with thorns when they find the pain of pricking in that which they desire temporally. And, as it were, a stone wall placed in their way confronts them whose desires the difficulty of perfection opposes.

Certainly, the souls of such people seek their lovers and do not find them, while in following malicious spirits they do not obtain the pleasures of this world that they desire. It is well added that, from this very difficulty, she at once says: “I will go and return to my former husband, for it was better with me then than now.” The former husband is the Lord, who joined the chaste soul to himself through the intervening love of the Holy Spirit. Each person’s mind desires him when it finds manifold bitterness, as though thorns, in the pleasures it temporally desires. For when the soul begins to be wounded by the adversities of the world that it loves, it then understands more fully how much better off it was with its former husband. Thus adversity greatly corrects those whom a perverse will corrupts. Therefore one must greatly fear that prosperity may follow when unjust things are desired, because evil is corrected with greater difficulty when it is even supported by the prosperity of perfection.

## CHAPTER IV. ON THE OUTER WALL

554 [Col. 0394C]

[Note: [Col. 0394D] From Homily XIV on Ezekiel.] The prophets are signified by the name “outer wall,” as is said through the prophet concerning the building of holy Church: “A wall and an outer wall shall be set in her” (Isa. 26:20). For in sacred discourse the incarnate Lord himself is very often called a wall because of the defence afforded by his manifestation. For he is our wall, who prevents the assault of malicious spirits from reaching our hearts. But the outer wall of our wall was all the prophets, who were sent in prophecy to build faith before the Lord appeared in the flesh. Therefore in holy Church the Lord is a wall for us, and his prophets have been set as an outer wall, because the words of the prophets also came to build faith in us whom he himself perfectly protects. Thus the wall is fittingly placed first and the outer wall afterward, because we who were called from the Gentiles would never have received the sayings of his prophets unless we had first known the Lord.

## CHAPTER V. ON THE TOWER

The tower signifies circumspection, as the bridegroom says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Your nose is like the tower that is in Lebanon” (Song 7:1). See the chapter “On Leaders,” Book IV, above, chapter 10, distinction 2.

The tower signifies the height of grace, as is said through the prophet Jeremiah: “The city shall be built for the Lord, from the tower of Hananel to the gate of the angel” (Jer. 31:38). See the chapter “On the City,” above, distinction 2.

## CHAPTER VI. ON THE HOUSE

555 In Holy Scripture, by the name “house” are understood at one time the heavenly Church, at another Christ’s body, at another conscience, at another the dwelling-place of heaven, and at another the structure of virtues.

The heavenly Church is signified by the name “house,” as, when Solomon was building the temple, it is disclosed in these words: “The house, when it was being built, was built of hewn and finished stones; and hammer, axe, and every iron tool were not heard in the house while it was being built” (3 Kings 6:7). See Book VIII, chapter 14.

The body of Christ is signified by the name “house,” as Solomon says: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9:1). For Wisdom built herself a house when the only-begotten Son of God, through the mediation of a soul, created for himself a human body within the Virgin’s womb. Thus the body of the Only-begotten is called the house of God, just as it is also called a temple; yet in such a way that the one and same Son of God and of man is both he who dwells and he who is dwelt in.

[Note: [Col. 0395D] From Homily 12 on Ezekiel.] Conscience is signified by the name “house,” as Ezekiel is told: “Enter and shut yourself up in the midst of your house” (Ezek. 3:24). What is meant by the prophet’s being commanded to go out into the plain, except that everyone who preaches goes out into the plain, because by speaking he corrects and restrains from iniquity those who are outside himself, and there sees the glory of the Lord? But because a preacher must always return to his mind and preserve humility and purity within, after the plain he must return to the house, so that in the things he says he may recognize what kind of person he himself is within his conscience.

556 For if he does not keep what he says, or seeks temporal glory from the things he says, he indeed goes out to the plain in speaking, but in failing to reflect on himself he neglects to return to the house. For when we have received the Spirit, we are shut up in the midst of the house when through his grace we are recalled to examine the hidden places of our mind, so that the soul may rest in God within itself and may no longer run about, through external desires, in the restless movement of thought seeking praise and glory. Of this house of the heart Truth himself says to a man healed by himself: “Take up your bed and go into your house” (Mark 2:9). Hence it is said of the perfect soul: “She considers the paths of her house; she does not eat the bread of idleness” (Prov. 31:27).

[Note: [Col. 0395D] From chapter 1, 25, Book XXXV on Job.] He considers the paths of his house who carefully investigates every thought of his conscience. He does not eat the bread of idleness, because what he has received by understanding sacred discourse, he shows forth in works, presenting it before the eyes of the eternal Judge.

The dwelling-place of heaven is signified by the name “house,” as it is said: “The sparrow found herself a house” (Ps. 83:4). See the chapter “On the Sparrow,” Book II, chapter 12.

The structure of virtues is signified by the name “house,” as Solomon says: “Diligently cultivate your field, that afterward you may build your house” (Prov. 24:27). See the chapter “On the Field,” Book VI, chapter 8, distinction 3.

## CHAPTER VII. ON THE TABERNACLE

In Holy Scripture, by the name “tabernacle” are understood at one time the dwelling of the mind, at another bodily habitation, at another thoughts, and at another the construction of earthly happiness.

[Col. 0396B] 557 [Note: [Col. 0396D] From Book XIX on Job, chapter IX.] The dwelling of the mind is signified by the name “tabernacle,” as blessed Job says in the person of the Church: “Who would grant me to be as I was in the days of my youth, when God was secretly in my tabernacle?” (Job 29:4). The age of holy Church is described as that of an individual person. For she was little when, newly born, she could not yet preach the word of life. Hence it is said of her: “Our sister is little and has no breasts” (Song 8:8). For holy Church, before she advanced through the growth of virtue, could not offer the breasts of preaching to her weaker hearers. But the Church is called grown up when, joined to the Word of God and filled with the Holy Spirit, she becomes fruitful in conceiving children through the ministry of preaching: she bears them in exhorting and gives them birth in converting.

Of this stage of her life it is said to the Lord: “The young maidens have loved you” (Song 1:3). For all the Churches which make one Catholic Church are called young maidens: no longer old through sin, but new through grace; not barren through old age, but, in the age of the mind, suited to spiritual fruitfulness. Therefore, when in the days of Antichrist the Church, weakened as though by a certain old age, is unable to give birth through preaching, she remembers her former fruitfulness, saying: “As I was in the days of my youth, when the Lord was secretly in my tabernacle.” What else do we understand here by “tabernacle” but the dwelling-place of the mind? For in all that we do by thinking, we act in the counsel of the heart. Whoever silently reflects on God’s commandments has God secretly in his tabernacle. He had seen that the dwelling-place of his heart was before God’s eyes who said: “And the meditation of my heart is always before you” (Ps. 48:4). Therefore, to show how greatly the righteous person has advanced, let him speak from himself, let him speak in the person of the universal Church: “When God was secretly in my tabernacle.”

[Note: [Col. 0396D] From Homily 13 on Ezekiel, near the end.] Bodily habitation is signified by the name “tabernacle.” We read that when the Hebrew people had been delivered from Egyptian slavery and saw the pillar of cloud while God was speaking, each person stood in the doorway of his own tabernacle and worshipped. For we stand where we fix the eyes of our mind. Thus Elijah says: “The Lord lives, in whose presence I stand” (3 Kings 17:7). For he stood where he had fixed his heart. What is it for the people to look upon the pillar of cloud, to stand in the doorways of their tabernacles, and to worship, except that when the human mind somehow beholds those higher and heavenly things in an enigma, it already goes out through the barriers of bodily habitation by an uplifted thought and humbly worships him? Although it cannot see his substance, it nevertheless marvels at his power through the illumination of the Spirit.

Likewise, because the body is understood by “tabernacle,” Job teaches this when, speaking of the ungodly man, he says: “He who remains in his tabernacle shall be afflicted” (Job 20:26).

[Note: [Col. 0397D] From Book XV on Job, chapter XVIII, 14.] For, he says, the tabernacle is flesh, because the ungodly man gladly inhabits it and, if it were possible, desires never to leave it. But because the righteous place their joy in hope of heavenly things and their citizenship is in heaven, though they are still in the flesh, they are as though no longer in the flesh, because they feed themselves on no delight of the flesh. Hence some are told: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Rom. 8:1). Certainly those who received their teacher’s letters, words of exhortation, were not without flesh; but to be as though no longer in the flesh is to retain nothing of love for carnal things.

On the other hand, this wicked man, who placed all his joy in bodily life, dwelt in the tabernacle of flesh. When he receives that flesh again at the resurrection, he will burn with it, delivered over to the fires of Gehenna. Then he will desire to be led out of it; then he will seek, if he can, to escape its torments; then he will begin to wish to avoid what he loved. But because he preferred that flesh to God, God’s judgment ensures that he is tortured all the more in fire through it. Here he is unwilling to leave it, yet is drawn away from it; there he desires to leave it, yet is kept in it for punishments. Thus, for the increase of his torment, here he is taken unwillingly from the body, and there he is held unwillingly in the body. Therefore, because in punishment his spirit will wish and be unable to escape the flesh that through evil love it preferred to itself, it is rightly said: “He who remains in his tabernacle shall be afflicted.”

[Col. 0397D] 559 [Note: [Col. 0397D] From Book XII on Job, chapter XXV, 27.] Thoughts are signified by the name “tabernacles,” as Eliphaz says: “Fire shall devour the tabernacles of those who willingly accept gifts” (Job 15:34). For just as the body dwells in a tabernacle, so the mind dwells in thought. But fire devours tabernacles when the heat of avarice devastates thoughts. It very often happens that a hypocrite disdains to receive gold or any temporal goods from people; but because he does not receive these, he seeks to receive greater praise from them. Perhaps he does not think that he has accepted a gift because he refuses to accept temporal goods. Therefore one must know that a gift is sometimes offered from the hand and sometimes from the mouth. He who gives a coin gives a gift from his hand; but he who bestows a word of praise offers a gift from his mouth.

Thus, although the hypocrite refuses to receive external gifts that may perhaps suit earthly necessity, what he desires to be given to himself is greater, when, desiring to be praised beyond his merit, he seeks a gift from the mouth. Therefore, because in this very desire for praise his heart is kindled with excessive heat, it is rightly said: “Fire shall devour the tabernacles of those who willingly accept gifts.” But if by their tabernacles we ought to understand their bodies, in which their souls dwell, fire devours their tabernacles because those who burn here in their minds with the fire of avarice are also burned there in the flesh by the fires of Gehenna.

[Note: [Col. 0398D] From Book VIII on Job, chapter XXXII, 41.] The construction of earthly happiness is signified by the name “tabernacle,” as Bildad says: “The tabernacle of the ungodly shall not endure” (Job 8:22). For a tabernacle is built to protect the body from heat and cold. What therefore is expressed here by the name “tabernacle” except the construction of earthly happiness, by which the reprobate heap up perishable things above themselves, as though to defend themselves from the necessities of the present life, like heat and rain? They seek to grow in honours lest they appear despised. They amass earthly things lest they waste away in the cold of poverty. They scorn to take thought for what follows, and with their whole attention labour that nothing may be lacking in the present. They strive to extend their name lest they go unnoticed; even if all things are available to their desire, they consider themselves secure in everything and happy.

Where, therefore, they construct the dwelling-place of their mind, there without doubt they have fixed their tabernacles. They bear adversity impatiently and rejoice without restraint in prosperity; they think only of what is present and do not draw breath toward longing for the heavenly homeland by any recollection. They rejoice that the goods they desire are available to them; and where they rest in the flesh, there they also bury their mind by extinguishing it. For, struck down by the weapon of worldly care, they always carry inwardly in thought the heap of earthly things that they multiply by seeking them outwardly.

By contrast, the righteous neither regard good things offered here as great, nor greatly fear evils inflicted here. Even while they use present goods, they fear evils to come; and while they groan over present evils, they are consoled by love of the good things that follow. Thus they are supported by temporal aid as a traveller uses an inn: he rests in bed and hastens to depart; he rests in body, but his mind aims elsewhere. It is therefore well said: “The tabernacle of the ungodly shall not endure,” because lovers of this fleeting life, while zealously building themselves up in present things, are suddenly carried away into eternity.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON THE TEMPLE

In Holy Scripture, by the name “temple” are understood at one time the soul of the righteous, at another the body of Christ, and at another the faithful people.

[Note: [Col. 0398D] From Homily 14 on Ezekiel, after the middle.] The soul of the righteous is signified by the name “temple,” as Isaiah, when he confessed that he had seen the Lord, says: “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne”; and he immediately adds: “And the things beneath him filled the temple” (Isa. 6:1). For when King Uzziah, proud and presumptuous, dies, the Lord is seen: when the exaltation of this world is slain from the mind’s desire, then the mind contemplates the Lord’s glory.

It should be noted that the Lord sits upon a high and exalted throne. What is his throne except angelic or human creation, over which he presides through the understanding he has given? This throne is called high and exalted because human nature advances, lifted up to heavenly glory, while angelic creation, since many spirits have fallen, is so established in heaven that it cannot fall, and has been exalted from the very fact that it has been confirmed. But his temple is the same as his throne, because the eternal King dwells where he sits. Therefore we are his temple, in whose minds he deigns to dwell.

But “the things beneath him filled the temple,” because whatever is now seen of him is not yet himself but is beneath him. Thus Jacob saw an angel and confessed that he had seen God, because when we behold his ministers, it is already a great thing that we are raised above ourselves. It should be noted, moreover, that it says “they filled the temple,” because even if an angel appears, he nevertheless satisfies the weak mind, so that, if it cannot yet do more, it may at least marvel at the lesser thing it sees. Therefore the things that are beneath him fill the temple, because when the mind advances in contemplation, it contemplates not what he himself is, but what is beneath him.

[Note: [Col. 0399D] From Book XXIX on Job, chapter VII.] The body of Christ is signified by the name “temple,” as Christ himself says to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). How great a fruit proceeded from the destruction of this temple—that is, from the destruction of his body—Samson long ago aptly expressed figuratively in himself. While living he killed only a few; but when the temple was destroyed, he killed innumerable enemies when he died (Judg. 16). For the Lord indeed destroyed few from the exaltation of pride while he was living, but many when the temple of his body was destroyed; and the elect from among the Gentiles, whom he endured while living, he cast down all together by dying. For few from the Israelite people believed while he preached; but innumerable peoples of the Gentiles followed the way of life when he died. He bore the proud while he still lived a passible life; but having died from that passible life, he overthrew them.

562 [Note: [Col. 0399D] From Homily XXII on Ezekiel.] The faithful people are signified by the name “temple,” as is said through Ezekiel: “And the altar was before the face of the temple” (Ezek. 40:41). For what is the temple except the faithful people, as the apostle Paul says to the disciples: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17)? And what is God’s altar except the mind of those who live well? They remember their sins and wash themselves with tears; they mortify the flesh through abstinence; they involve themselves in none of the affairs of this world; they give what they have to the needy; and they do not desire to have what they lack. Thus the hearts of such people are rightly called God’s altar, where the fire burns from the sorrow of compunction and the flesh is consumed.

Do we not daily see such persons in this holy faithful people as though in the court of the temple? Do we not continually behold their life, set before us as an example? The altar, therefore, is before the face of the temple when many are placed in the sight of holy Church who daily sacrifice themselves to God in the lament of compunction before the eternal judgment. As has been said, they chastise their bodies so that they may fulfil what is said through the teacher of the Gentiles: “That you may present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God” (Rom. 12:1). A sacrifice is killed in order to be offered; but a body afflicted for the Lord is a living sacrifice. It is called both sacrifice and living: living because such persons live in virtues, and killed because it is dead to vices. It is a sacrifice because it has already died to this world in evil deeds; but it is living because it performs every good that it is able to do.

## CHAPTER IX. ON THE FOUNDATION

563 In Holy Scripture, when “foundation” is used in the singular, it signifies at one time the Lord himself and at another the faithful. But when “foundations” are spoken of in the plural, the holy apostles are signified.

[Note: [Col. 0399D] From Book XXVIII on Job, chapter VI, 9.] The Lord himself is signified by the name “foundation,” by whose divine power the hearts of our weakness are made firm, as Paul says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11). For he is the foundation of foundations, because he is both the source of beginners and the steadfastness of the strong.

[Note: [Col. 0400D] From Book XXV on Job, chapter X, 15.] Faith is signified by the name “foundation,” as the Prophet says, recording under the figure of Jerusalem the words of enemies destroying it: “Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation” (Ps. 136:7). For destroying enemies lay Jerusalem bare even to its foundation when perverse spirits, after first destroying the structure of good works in the hearts of the faithful, drain away even the firmness of religion. For as a building is constructed upon a foundation, so works are built upon faith. Therefore to lay it bare even to the foundation is, once the work of good living has been overthrown, also to destroy the strength of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0400D] From Book XXVIII on Job, chapter VI, 9.] The holy apostles are signified by the name “foundations,” as the Lord says to blessed Job: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 28:4). What is signified by the name “earth” except holy Church? And what else do we understand by “foundations” except preachers? Since the Lord placed them first in holy Church, the whole structure of the ensuing building rose upon them. Hence when the priest enters the tabernacle, he is commanded to carry twelve stones upon his breast (Exod. 28:9), because our high priest, offering himself as a sacrifice for us, bore twelve stones beneath his head in the first part of his body when he presented strong preachers at the very beginning.

Thus the holy apostles are stones upon the breast for the first display of adornment, and foundations in the ground for the first stability of the building. Therefore, when David the prophet saw holy Church being set and built upon the lofty minds of the apostles, he said: “Her foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86:1). Since, then, our foundations are those who bore the weights of our iniquities, lest blessed Job should be lifted up into pride by confidence in the power of his virtues, he is examined at the very beginning of the Lord’s discourse through the recollection of holy preachers; so that, the more admirable he saw them to be, the more cheaply he might esteem himself in comparison with them.

This is described by the Lord as though already past because whatever will be outwardly future in action has already been inwardly accomplished in predestination. He is therefore told: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” It is as though he were plainly told: Consider the strength of the mighty, and ponder me as their author before the ages. Behold, you see those whom I made in time to be admirable; consider how greatly you ought to submit to me, whom you know to be the author of wonders and of times.

## CHAPTER X. ON THE WALL

[Col. 0401C] In Holy Scripture, by the name “wall” are understood at one time human nature, and at another the hardness of sin.

[Note: [Col. 0401D] From Homily 13 on Ezekiel, after the middle.] Human nature is signified by the name “wall,” as holy Church, in the voice of the bride, openly desiring now to see the bridegroom, says: “Behold, he stands behind our wall” (Song 2:9). For he who showed to human eyes what he assumed from human nature and remained invisible in himself, stood as though behind a wall to those seeking to see him openly, because he did not offer himself to be seen in manifest majesty. He stood, as it were, behind a wall because he showed the human nature he assumed and hid the nature of divinity from human eyes. Hence it is added there: “Looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices” (ibid.). Whoever looks through windows or lattices is neither wholly hidden nor wholly seen.

So our Redeemer was made before the eyes of those who doubted: if, while working miracles, he had suffered nothing as man, he would have appeared plainly to them as God; and again, if, while suffering human things, he had done nothing as God, he would have been considered merely human. But because he both performed divine acts and suffered human things, he looked upon people as though through windows or lattices, so that he might appear as God through miracles and remain hidden through sufferings, while he was seen as man through sufferings but recognized as more than a human being through miracles.

[Note: [Col. 0401D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter IV, 13.] The hardness of sin is signified by the name “wall,” as it is written: “He was building a wall, but they were plastering it” (Ezek. 13:10). What is understood by the name “wall” except the hardness of sin? To build a wall, therefore, is for someone to construct against himself the obstacles of sin. But those plaster the wall who flatter people committing sins, so that what the latter build by acting perversely, the former make smooth, as it were, by flattery.

## CHAPTER XI. ON THE GATE

566 In Holy Scripture, when “gate” is used in the singular, it signifies at one time Christ, at another a holy preacher, at another knowledge of Holy Scripture, at another faith, at another the day of judgment, at another an action, and at another departure from this life. But when “gates” are spoken of in the plural, they signify at one time departures from this life, at another holy teachers, at another wicked teachers, at another good actions or evil actions, at another hostile powers, and at another evil thoughts.

[Note: [Col. 0401D] From Book VI on Job, chapter II.] Christ is signified by the name “gate,” as Eliphaz says concerning the children of the Jewish people—that is, their wicked followers: “They shall be crushed in the gate, and there shall be none to deliver them” (Job 5:4). For who else ought to be understood by the name “gate” but the Mediator of God and humankind, who says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John 10:9)? Therefore the children of this fool prosper outside the gate and are crushed in the gate, because the wicked offspring of the Jews flourished in observance of the law before the coming of the Mediator; but in the very presence of our Redeemer they fell, repelled from the service of Divinity by the deserts of their unbelief. There is none to deliver them, since, when they attempted through persecution to destroy the Redeemer himself, they hid from themselves the remedy of deliverance offered to them.

567 [Note: [Col. 0401D] From Homily 15 on Ezekiel, after the beginning.] By the name “gate” each preacher may be understood, because whoever opens the door of the kingdom of heaven with his mouth is a gate. Hence twelve gates are described both in John’s Apocalypse and in the final vision of the prophet Ezekiel (Rev. 21).

[Note: [Col. 0402D] In the same place.] By the name “gate” Holy Scripture may also fittingly be understood, since in opening understanding to us it opens the door of the heavenly kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0402D] In the same place.] By the name “gate” we may also understand faith, which we first encounter in order that we may enter into the structures of virtues.

[Note: [Col. 0402D] From Book VI on Job, chapter V.] The day of judgment is signified by the name “gate,” as Eliphaz says above: “They shall be crushed in the gate, and there shall be none to deliver them” (Job 5:4). For as the entrance to a city is called a gate, so the day of judgment is the gate of the kingdom, because through it all the elect enter into the glory of the heavenly homeland. Therefore the children of this fool were exalted before the gate, but they shall be crushed in the gate, because lovers of this world are proud in the present life but are struck by eternal judgment at the very entrance to the kingdom.

It is well added: “And there shall be none to deliver.” For Truth delivers from eternal adversity those whom he presses by discipline amid temporal prosperity. But whoever now refuses to be pressed will then be unable to be delivered, because the wicked, who neglect to have him as a father through discipline, do not find him as a deliverer through help in the time of their affliction.

The good action is signified by the name “gate,” as blessed Job says in the person of the Church: “When I went out to the gate of the city, and they prepared a seat for me in the street” (Job 29:7). See the chapter “On the Street,” Book VI, chapter 11, distinction 1.

[Note: [Col. 0403D] From Homily 13 on Ezekiel, after the middle.] By “gate” is signified the departure from this life, as is said through Ezekiel concerning the man who appeared to him: “He stood in the gate” (Ezek. XL, 5). Whoever stands in a gate is in some respect within and in some respect without, because one part of him is seen outside and another is hidden within. Therefore our Redeemer, who is understood by that same man, mercifully incarnate for our sake, stood before human eyes as if in a gate, because through his humanity he appeared visible, yet through his divinity he remained invisible.

Therefore the man who appeared stood in the gate and spoke thus, because the Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, even at the time of his Passion gave his disciples the commandments of life, so that those who believe in him may look toward the gate and, attentively weighing his Passion, may not turn the eyes of their hearts away from their own departure. We also, when we have begun to despise the barriers of the flesh, to pass beyond the narrowness of our mortality through desire for immortality, to strive for the freedom of the heavenly light, and to long for the joys of our heavenly homeland, keep our eyes upon the gate. For, while we desire to pass from temporal mysteries to eternal things, we have, as it were, already turned our backs on the present life and direct the face of our heart toward the desire for our departure. For it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling oppresses the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. IX, 15). Although, therefore, through contemplation we already stretch the mind beyond the narrowness of the flesh, yet, in the mysteries which we have come to know, we are still held within the gate by that very bodily narrowness. For often the soul is so raised up in divine contemplation that it already rejoices to perceive, through a certain image, something of that eternal freedom which eye has not seen nor ear heard. Yet, struck back by the weight of mortality, it falls again to the depths and is held bound by certain chains of its punishment. Therefore he attends to the gate who beholds the joys of his true freedom and now longs to go forth.

By “gates” are signified holy teachers, as the Lord promises to the Church that is coming, saying through the prophet: “Behold, I will lay your stones in order and found you upon sapphires; and I will make your battlements of jasper, and your gates of carved stones” (Isa. LIV, 12). See [Col. 0404A] the chapter “On Stones,” book X, chapter 2, distinction 6.

[Note: [Col. 0403D] From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter XXIII, §29.] By “gates” are signified wicked teachers, as the Lord, questioning blessed Job concerning the devil under the name Leviathan, says: “Who will open the gates of his face?” (Job XLI, 5). His gates, indeed, are wicked teachers. They are called the gates of his face because through them each person enters, so that this Leviathan—that is, the devil—may appear, as it were, in the primacy of his power. For just as Sacred Scripture is accustomed to call holy men the gates of Zion—Zion is interpreted “watchtower,” and not without reason do we call holy preachers the gates of Zion, because through their life and teaching we enter into the hidden things of heavenly contemplation—so also, by the gates of this Leviathan, teachers of errors are signified. When their perverse preaching is accepted, the way of destruction is opened to their wretched hearers. He says therefore: “Who will open the gates of his face?” Understand: unless I, who make the teachers of error, concealed under an appearance of holiness, plainly manifest to my elect through clear knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0403D] From Book XIX on Job, chapter XI, §13.] By “gates” are signified good or evil actions, as the Psalmist says: “You who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. IX, 14). The gates of death are evil actions, which draw one toward destruction. But because Zion means “watchtower,” we understand the gates of Zion as good actions, through which we enter the heavenly homeland in order to behold the glory of our King.

[Col. 0404C] [Note: [Col. 0404D] From Book XXIX on Job, chapter VII, §6.] By “gates” are signified hostile powers, as the Lord asks blessed Job: “Have the gates of death been opened to you?” (Job XXXVIII, 18). The gates of death are hostile powers, which the Lord, descending, opened because by dying he overcame their strength.

[Note: [Col. 0404D] From the preceding book, chapter VIII.] “Gates” may also be understood as evil thoughts, which we lay open to God when, weeping in repentance, we confess them. He sees them even when unconfessed, but enters them when confessed. For then he opens for himself a way in the gates of death, when, after confession, he comes to us after evil thoughts have been loosed. These are called gates of death because the way to destruction is always opened through wicked thoughts.

## CHAPTER XII. ON THE THRESHOLD

[Col. 0404D]

In Sacred Scripture, by “threshold” are sometimes signified the fathers of the New Testament, sometimes Sacred Scripture, and sometimes each individual person.

[Note: [Col. 0404D] From Homily 14 on Ezekiel.] By “threshold” are signified the Fathers of the New Testament, as it is said through Ezekiel: “And he measured the threshold of the gate beside the vestibule of the inner gate: one reed” (Ezek. XL, 8). Since the threshold now described is said to be beside the vestibule of the inner gate, it is plainly shown that the threshold mentioned earlier was outside. But if the gate is the Lord, let us inquire what the threshold of the gate is within and what it is without. For each person enters the gate by means of the threshold. And what are these two thresholds but the Fathers of the Old Testament and the Fathers of the New Testament? For not only those from whom the Lord deigned to be incarnate, but all the Fathers of the Old Testament were the threshold of this gate, because those who deserved to preach him and to hope in him opened to all who came to him the entrance of faith, so that everyone who believed might now enter the Lord, the gate, through this threshold. But why is the first threshold called outer and the second inner, except because the Fathers of the Old Testament came first and the teachers of the New Testament afterwards? The outer threshold rightly signifies the Fathers of the Old Testament, because by their preaching wicked deeds were punished. But by the sayings of the New Testament Fathers, each person’s soul is restrained even from unlawful thoughts, since guilt is shown to be complete already in the deliberation of the heart. The former took care to forbid the souls of their hearers acts of disgrace, cruelty, and robbery. But the latter, in cutting off not only wicked deeds but also unlawful thoughts, have become for us what else but an inner threshold? Hence Truth itself says: “You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother without cause shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. V, 21). The outer threshold also rightly signifies those Fathers who stood at a greater temporal distance from the very incarnation of our Redeemer. Indeed, from Abel onward the Church’s suffering had already begun, and the Church of the elect who went before and those who followed is one. Yet because it is said to the disciples, “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke X, 14), the ancient Fathers are said, as it were, to have stood outside because they did not see bodily the presence of our Redeemer. They were therefore outside, yet not separated from the holy Church, because in mind, deed, and preaching they already held these mysteries of faith and beheld that loftiness of the holy Church which we too behold, still awaiting it yet already possessing it.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] From the preceding homily.] But if in this place we understand the gate as Sacred Scripture, it too has two thresholds, inner and outer, because it is divided into the letter and allegory. Since we pass through the letter toward allegory, we come, as it were, from the outer threshold to the inner one. And in it are very many things that edify the mind according to the letter, so that through what is done inwardly the hearer’s mind may be drawn inwardly. There we find precepts for conduct and examples of virtue; there we are commanded what we ought to do even bodily. There what is commanded for performance is shown by the deeds of holy and strong men, so that, after the clearer commandments and examples of the righteous have instructed us in good action, we may then, if we can, direct the foot of the mind toward the inner threshold—that is, toward the mystical understanding of inward contemplation. It should be noted that the threshold of the gate is measured by one reed. The reed extends to six cubits and a handbreadth, because in Sacred Scripture are found both the teaching of perfect action and the beginning of heavenly contemplation.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] From the end of the preceding homily.] But if in this place the gate is understood as each preacher, the outer threshold in the gate is the active life, while the inner threshold is the contemplative life. By the former one walks in faith; by the latter one hastens toward sight. The former leads outwardly, teaching how each person ought to live well; the latter leads inwardly, so that from a good life one may attain eternal joys.

## CHAPTER XIII. ON THE LINTEL

[Col. 0406B]

[Note: [Col. 0406D] From Homily 22 on the Gospels, about the middle.] By “lintel” is signified the intention of the mind, which presides over action, as Moses says concerning the eating of the lamb: “They shall take of the blood of the lamb and put it upon both doorposts and upon the lintels of the houses in which they shall eat it” (Exod. XII, 7). We have learned not merely by hearing but by drinking what the blood of the lamb is. This blood is placed on both doorposts when it is received not only with the mouth of the body but also drunk with the mouth of the heart. For the blood of the lamb is placed on both doorposts when the sacrament of his Passion is received by the mouth unto redemption and also considered with an attentive mind for imitation. For he who receives the blood of his Redeemer in such a way that he does not yet wish to imitate his Passion has placed the blood upon only one doorpost; yet it must also be placed upon the lintels of the houses. What else do we understand spiritually by houses but our minds, in which we dwell by thought? The lintel of this house is the very intention that presides over action. Therefore the person who directs the intention of his thought toward imitation of the Lord’s Passion places the blood of the lamb upon the lintel of his house. Or certainly our houses are our bodies themselves, in which we dwell as long as we live; and we place the blood of the lamb upon the lintel of the house because we bear the cross of his Passion on our forehead.

## CHAPTER XIV. ON THE DOOR

[Col. 0406D]

In Sacred Scripture, when used in the singular, “door” sometimes signifies Christ, sometimes faith or the vision of God, sometimes the beginning of divine knowledge, sometimes understanding, and sometimes departure. But when “doors” is used in the plural, it sometimes signifies desires of carnal concupiscence, sometimes holy preachers, sometimes the barriers of divine fear, and sometimes virtues.

By “door” Christ is signified, as he himself testifies in the Gospel: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John X, 1).

By “door” faith or the vision of God is signified, as is said through Ezekiel concerning the man who appeared to him: “And he measured door opposite door” (Ezek. XL, 13). [Col. 0407A] Here “opposite” is not used for opposition but for directness. For door opposite door occurs when one arrives by a straight course from the outer entrance to the inner. In the knowledge of almighty God, our first door is faith, while the second is his appearance or vision, at which we arrive by walking in faith. In this life we enter the former, so that afterward we may be brought to the latter. Thus door is opposite door, because through the entrance of faith the entrance of the vision of God is opened.

[Note: [Col. 0407D] From Book V on Job, chapter XXVI.] By “door” is signified the beginning of divine knowledge, as the words of sacred history show when the prophet Elijah is instructed concerning knowledge of God. When the Lord promised that he would pass before Elijah, saying, “Behold, the Lord passes: a great and strong wind overturning mountains and breaking rocks before the Lord,” he immediately added: “The Lord is not in the wind. And after the wind, an earthquake: the Lord is not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake, fire: the Lord is not in the fire. And after the fire, the whisper of a gentle breeze” (III Kings XIX, 11). The wind before the Lord overturns mountains and breaks rocks because the dread that rushes upon us at his coming both casts down the height of our heart and softens its hardness. But although the Lord is said not to be in the wind, the earthquake, and the fire, he is not denied to be in the whisper of the gentle breeze. For when the mind is raised to the height of contemplation, whatever it can see perfectly is not God; but when it sees something subtle, this is what it hears of the incomprehensible substance of eternity. For we perceive, as it were, the whisper of a gentle breeze when, in sudden contemplation, we subtly taste the savor of unbounded truth. Thus what we know of God is true when we recognize that we cannot know anything of him fully. Hence it is well added there: “When Elijah heard it, he covered his face with his cloak, and entering, stood at the door of the cave” (III Kings XIX, 13). After the whisper of the gentle breeze, the prophet covered his face with his cloak because, in that most subtle contemplation of truth, he recognizes how great is the ignorance that covers humankind. To draw a cloak over the face is to veil the mind, through consideration of its own weakness, lest it dare to seek higher things; so that it may not rashly open the eyes of understanding beyond itself, but may reverently close them before that which it cannot grasp. He who does this is described as standing at the door of the cave. For what is our cave but this habitation of corruption, in which we are still held by the old nature? But when we begin to perceive something of the knowledge of divinity, we stand, as it were, already at the door of our cave. Since we cannot advance perfectly, nevertheless, thirsting for the thought of truth, we now catch something of the breath of freedom. Therefore to stand at the entrance of the cave is, with the obstacle of our corruption restrained, to begin to emerge toward knowledge of the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0407D] From Homily 20 on Ezekiel, about the middle.] The term “door” signifies understanding, [Col. 0408A] as Ezekiel says: “And at each treasury-chamber was a door in the fronts of the gates” (Ezek. XL, 38). The treasury-chambers are the hearts of teachers, which preserve the riches of knowledge. The fronts of the gates are the words and deeds of preachers, by which we recognize outwardly what manner of life they inwardly lead. There is a door at each treasury-chamber in the fronts of the gates when every teacher opens the understanding of the hearer, from his own heart, in the sayings and deeds of the Fathers. For when we examine the preaching of the apostle Peter, search out Paul’s words, investigate John’s Gospel, and from their words draw our hearers toward inward understanding, what else do we do but open a door in the fronts of the gates? Let it therefore be said: “At each [Col. 0408B] treasury-chamber, a door in the fronts of the gates,” because if a teacher does not confirm what he says by the words of the apostles, he has no door in the fronts of the gates. And if he has no door, he cannot be called a treasury-chamber of the spiritual building; for if he does not open understanding, he is not a teacher.

By “door” is signified departure, as it is written: “When Moses went out to the tabernacle, all the people rose, looked upon his back, and each stood at the door of his tent” (Exod. XXXIII, 8). When every holy preacher speaks lofty things concerning God, he enters in some measure already into the tabernacle of the heavenly dwelling. Although weaker hearers cannot fully weigh the power of his preaching, they nevertheless look, as it were, upon his back—that is, they follow by understanding those final things which they are able to grasp. But even in the least things which they can comprehend, they already, as it were, leave their tents and stand in the doors, because they strive to leave the dwellings of the flesh and advance toward those joys of eternal life of which they hear (Isa. XXVI).

By “doors” are understood the desires of carnal concupiscence, concerning which it is said through the prophet: “Enter into your chambers; shut your doors” (Isa. XXVI, 26). We enter our chambers when we enter the secrets of our mind; and we shut the doors when we restrain unlawful desires.

[Note: [Col. 0408D] From Book XXVIII on Job, chapter 8, §15.] By “doors” are signified holy preachers, as the Lord says to blessed Job: [Col. 0408D] “Who shut in the sea with doors, when it burst forth as though proceeding from the womb?” (Job XXXVIII, 8). What else do we understand by the sea but the world, and by the womb but the conception of carnal thought? In this place, “womb” signifies the hidden and malicious thought of carnal persons. This womb conceives not the substance of a body in order to bring forth offspring, but a cause of suffering in order to fulfill wickedness. Of this womb of the hearts of the wicked it is elsewhere said: “He conceived sorrow and brought forth iniquity” (Ps. VII, 15). Through this womb the wicked bring forth what they conceive when they think evil; through this womb they bring forth when they perform the evils that they have thought. Therefore the sea burst forth as though proceeding from the womb [Col. 0409A] when the fruits of worldly miseries, conceived from carnal wickedness, raged for the destruction of the holy Church. But by God’s agency this sea was shut in with doors, because holy men were set in opposition like certain doors against the swelling of persecutors, so that the anger of persecutors might be broken by their miracles and reverence for them. For through them the Lord of humility raised the holy Church above the summit of the world before earthly rulers, and restrained the raging assaults of the sea by the exalted authority of that same Church. [Note: [Col. 0409D] From chapter 9, the book on 16.] Because holy teachers are open by their preaching to those who follow them, but closed by their authority against those who resist, they are not without reason called doors: open, that is, to the conduct of the humble, and closed against the terrors of the proud. They are not without reason called doors, [Col. 0409B] because they open the entrance of the kingdom to the faithful and, in turn, oppose themselves to the faithless lest they enter.

By “doors” are signified the barriers of divine fear, as blessed Job says: “Who shuts in the sea with doors?” (Job XXXVIII, 8). See the chapter “On the Sea,” book VII, chapter 3, distinction 5.

By “doors” are signified virtues, as Job indicates in saying: “And I set doors and bars, and said: ‘Thus far shall you come, and no farther; and here shall you break your swelling waves’” (Job XXXVIII, 10–11). See the chapter “On Waves,” book VII, chapter 15, distinction 1.

## CHAPTER XV. ON WINDOWS

[Col. 0409C]

In Sacred Scripture, “windows” sometimes signify the prelates of the holy Church, sometimes the bodily senses, and sometimes contemplative minds.

[Note: [Col. 0409D] From the end of Homily 11 on Ezekiel.] By “windows” are signified the prelates of the holy Church, as the prophet, seeing the temple in his final vision, relates among other things what he saw in that temple: “The ground up to the windows, and the windows closed” (Ezek. XLI, 16). For the apostle Paul says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (I Cor. III, 17). In this temple the windows are priests and watchmen, who pour forth upon the faithful people the light of preaching. But when the ground reaches up to the windows, the windows are closed, because when earthly thought grows in the hearts of priests, the windows do not emit light: priests fall silent in the office of preaching.

[Note: [Col. 0410D] From Book XXI on Job, chapter 2, at the beginning.] By “windows” are signified the bodily senses, as the prophet Jeremiah says: “Death has climbed through our windows; it has entered our houses” (Jer. IX, 21). Since the soul is invisible, it cannot be touched by delight in bodily things except insofar as, joined to the body, it possesses certain outlets of that body—the senses. Sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch are, as it were, certain paths of the mind, by which it goes outside and desires the substance of things external. [Col. 0410A] Through these bodily senses, as through certain windows, the soul looks out upon all external things; and looking, it desires. It is therefore well said: “Death has climbed through our windows; it has entered our houses.” Death climbs through the windows and enters the houses when concupiscence, coming through the bodily senses, enters the dwelling-place of the mind. Conversely, Isaiah says of the righteous: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. LX, 8). See book I, chapter 12, distinction 6.

[Note: [Col. 0410D] From Book II on Ezekiel, Homily 17.] By “windows” are signified contemplative minds, as Ezekiel says: “And he made slanting windows in the chambers, and in their fronts which were within the gate all around” (Ezek. XL, 16). The chambers signify hearts fervent in the love of God. In slanting windows, the part through which light enters is narrow, while the inner part which receives the light is broad. Thus the minds of contemplatives, although they see within themselves something slight of the true light, are nevertheless expanded with great breadth. They can scarcely grasp even the few things that they behold. Very slight is what contemplatives see of eternity; yet from that very slightness the bosom of their minds is enlarged in the increase of fervor and love. They are thus spacious within themselves precisely because they admit the light of austere virtue, as it were, through narrow openings. Since this greatness of contemplation can be granted only to those who love, slanting windows are said to be in chambers, or in those things which are said to be not outside but within [Col. 0410C] beside the chambers. For concerning these same windows it is added: “And in their fronts, which were within the gate all around.” For there were windows in the chambers and also in their fronts, which had been constructed within the gate all around, because he who has an inward heart also receives the light of contemplation, as is said a little below. It should further be noted that slanting windows are said to be within the gate all around. The grace of contemplation is not given to the highest and withheld from the lowest; often the great receive it, often the lowly, often those far removed from office, and sometimes married persons receive it. Therefore, if there is no office among the faithful from which the grace of contemplation can be excluded, whoever has an inward heart can also be illumined by the light of contemplation. For him slanting windows have been constructed within the gate all around, so that no one may boast of this grace as though it belonged exclusively to himself. Let no one, therefore, suppose that he alone possesses the gift of true light; for in the very thing which he thinks he possesses preeminently, another is often richer, though he is thought to possess no good thing.

## CHAPTER XVI. ON COLUMNS

[Col. 0410D]

In Sacred Scripture, “columns” sometimes signify any person strong against the devil’s temptations, sometimes angelic powers, sometimes the foremost preachers of the Church, and sometimes the evangelists.

[Note: [Col. 0411D] From Book VII on Job, chapter XVII, §14.] By “column” is signified anyone strong against the devil’s temptations, as the Lord says in the Apocalypse: “The one who conquers, I will make him a column in the temple of my God” (Apoc. III, 12). For whoever is strengthened with upright intention in God’s work is raised as a column in the structure of the spiritual building, so that, placed in this temple which is the Church, he may serve both usefulness and beauty.

[Note: [Col. 0411D] In the place cited above.] By “columns” are signified powers or the foremost preachers of the Church, as Job says: “The columns of heaven tremble and are afraid at his nod” (Job XXVI, 11). For what else does he call the columns of heaven but either the most holy angels or the foremost preachers of the Church, upon whom the whole structure of the spiritual building, rising in heavenly things, has been built?
