Job calls them columns of heaven whom the Apostle calls columns of the Church, saying: “Peter and James and John, who seemed to be columns, gave to me their right hands” (Gal. II, 9). [Note: [Col. 0411D] These words occur after the middle.] Yet however great their knowledge may become, it is insufficient to penetrate the manner of judgments by which the Creator governs us. Let him therefore say: “The columns of heaven tremble and are afraid at his nod,” because in many matters even those who see the rewards of his will as they proclaim them cannot attain to the height of that will. As we said above, there is no obstacle to understanding this also of the holy angels, since the very powers of heaven, who behold him without ceasing, tremble in their very contemplation. Yet this trembling is not fear before their eyes, but wonder.

[Note: [Col. 0412D] From Book XXVIII on Job, chapter VI, §9.] By “columns” are signified the evangelists, as the Lord says to Moses: “You shall make four columns, and you shall overlay their bases with silver” (Exod. II, 13). For what else is understood by silver but the brightness of the divine word, as it is written: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested in fire” (Ps. XI, 7). And what else do we understand by bases but the doctrines of the holy Church? Four bases overlaid with silver support the columns of the tabernacle because the preachers of the Church, adorned with the divine word, bear in speech and deeds the sayings of the four evangelists, so as to offer themselves as an example to all.

## CHAPTER XVII. ON BASES

In Sacred Scripture, “bases” sometimes signify teachers of the holy Church, sometimes prophets, and sometimes the intentions of the soul.

[Note: [Col. 0412D] A little before the passages cited.] By “bases” are signified teachers of the holy Church, as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the construction of the holy Church: “Upon what are its bases founded?” (Job XXXVIII, 5). What else do we understand by bases but teachers of the holy Church? For columns are raised upon bases, and upon columns the weight of the entire structure. Thus holy teachers are not without reason signified by the name of bases, because when they preach rightly and conform their lives to their preaching, they sustain the whole weight of the Church by the fixed gravity of their character; they bear harsh temptations from unbelievers; and by examples of their deeds they show to the faithful as easy those things which in God’s commands seem difficult and are feared.

The prophets may also be signified by bases. Since they were the first to speak openly of the Lord’s incarnation, we see them, as it were, rising from the foundation like certain bases and sustaining the weights of the structure built upon them. Hence when the Lord again commanded Moses to set up the boards of the tabernacle, he ordered their [Col. 0412B] silver bases to be cast (Exod. XXVI, 19). What else do the boards signify but the apostles, enlarged throughout the world by the extension of their preaching? And what else do the silver bases signify but the prophets, who, solid and molten, sustain the boards laid upon them? For the life of the apostles, while it is instructed by the prophets’ preaching, is also strengthened by their authority. Nor without reason is it commanded that the bases signifying the prophets should be cast of silver. Silver’s brightness is preserved by use; without use, it turns black. Before the Mediator’s coming, the sayings of the prophets were not in use through spiritual understanding; because they could not be seen for their obscurity, they remained, as it were, black. But after the Mediator came and wiped them before our eyes with the hand of his incarnation, whatever light lay hidden in them became bright, and he put the meaning of the earlier Fathers into use because he explained words by events. Whether, therefore, he signifies prophets or teachers who follow in the last times by the designation “bases,” let him say: “Upon what are its bases founded?” (Job XXXVIII, 5). Understand: unless upon me, who wondrously hold all things together and, inwardly and principally, provide the source for outward goods. For whoever ascribes to himself the fact that he is good is not a solid base, because, not resting upon the foundation, he is hurled to the depths by his own weight.

[Note: [Col. 0412D] In the same place, before the end of the chapter.] The bases may also morally signify the intentions of the soul. With watchful care, we must weigh our intention in all our works, [Col. 0412D] so that it may seek nothing temporal in what it does, but may fix itself wholly in the firmness of eternity; lest, if the structure of our action is placed outside the foundation, it be broken apart when the ground gives way. Hence it is well said: “Upon what are its bases founded?” For the bases of each soul are its intentions. Just as a structure rests upon columns, and columns upon bases, so our life rests in virtues, while virtues themselves stand upon inward intention. And because it is written, “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III, 11), the bases are in the foundation [Col. 0413A] when our intentions are strengthened in Christ. Therefore, because the intentions of every chosen soul rest upon hope in eternity, it is rightly said of the faithful soul: “Upon what are its bases founded?” As though he were plainly saying: unless upon me. When every righteous soul directs itself toward me, whatever it does temporally it surely builds in me not temporally.

## CHAPTER XVIII. ON THE BRIDAL CHAMBER

[Note: [Col. 0413D] From Homily 15 on Ezekiel, considerably before the middle.] By “bridal chamber” is signified either the holy Church or any soul that greatly loves God, as Ezekiel says: “And he measured the bridal chamber, one reed in length and one in breadth” (Ezek. XL, 7). Let us consider what is customarily done in a bridal chamber, and from this infer what is done here in the holy Church. For in the bridal chamber bridegroom and bride are pledged and joined to one another in love. Therefore the bridal chamber of God is rightly called either the holy Church or the perfect soul, which is joined through love to the invisible Bridegroom in such a way that it burns with desire for him, no longer desires anything in the world, counts the duration of its present life as punishment, hastens to depart, and longs to rest in the embrace of love through the vision of its heavenly Bridegroom. A mind now such as this receives no comfort from the present age, but sighs, burns, pants, and is distressed from the depths of its being for those things which it loves. Even the preservation of its body becomes cheap to it, because it has been pierced by the wound of love. Thus it says in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by love” (Cant. II, 4). Consider what a bridal chamber Paul’s mind was, when he said: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. I, 1). How greatly had he joined himself in love to almighty God, who judged Christ alone to be life for himself and death to be gain. Hence he again says: “Having the desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, for that is far better” (ibid., 23). But behold: let us see with what love he languishes, who desires to be dissolved. Although we see him meanwhile delayed, does he not seek to be strengthened, saying, “Strengthen me, I pray, with flowers” (Cant. II, 5)? Certainly he does. For he continues: “But to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. I, 24); and he says to disciples who are making progress: “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before our Lord [Col. 0413D] Jesus Christ?” (I Thess. II, 19). Hence this bridal chamber is said to be measured by one reed in length and one in breadth. Length pertains to the long-suffering of waiting, and breadth to the expansiveness of love. Thus the bridal chamber has as much length as it can have breadth: the mind kindled by heavenly desire displays as much long-suffering in waiting for God as it has love for gathering its neighbor, and it patiently endures the delays of length because the breadth of love expands it in the progress of its neighbor. This length may also signify the long-suffering patience shown toward one’s neighbor. And because breadth signifies love, which opens the bosom of the mind and receives friends and enemies alike into love, the length of love is as great as the breadth of the bridal chamber: the more broad a mind is through love, the more long it will be through long-suffering. For each person bears his neighbor to the degree that he loves. If you love, you bear; if you cease to love, you cease to endure.

[Note: [Col. 0413D] From Homily 38 on the Gospels, after the beginning.] By “bridal chamber” is signified the womb of the Virgin Mary, as the Psalmist says concerning the incarnation of our Redeemer: “He is like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Ps. XVIII, 6). For our Redeemer came forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber when, incarnate in order to join the Church to himself, he came forth [Col. 0414B] from the incorrupt womb of the Virgin.

## CHAPTER XIX. ON TREASURY-CHAMBERS
[Note: Homily 18 on Ezekiel, col. 0414D.] By the term “treasuries” (*gazophylacia*) are denoted the hearts of teachers, as the prophet Ezekiel says: “And he brought me out into the outer court, and behold treasuries, and a pavement paved with stone round about in the court” (Ezek. XI, 5). For in Greek *phylattein* (φυλάττειν) means “to preserve,” and in Persian *gazae* means “riches”; hence a *gazophylacium* is commonly called a place in which riches are kept.

584 What, then, are treasuries from the outset but hearts of teachers full of the riches of wisdom and knowledge [col. 0414C], since, in Paul’s words, “To one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit” (1 Cor. XII, 8)? There are indeed some who, through the gift of grace, understand even matters which they have not heard expounded by teachers. These have plainly received the word of wisdom. And there are some who cannot understand for themselves what they have heard, but retain what they have read in commentators and knowingly set forth what they have learned by reading. Of what, then, are these full, if not of the word of knowledge?

Yet this may also be understood otherwise: wisdom pertains to life, but knowledge to teaching. Therefore, one who lives well and preaches wisely is rightly called a treasury of the spiritual building, because heavenly riches are dispensed from his mouth [col. 0414D]. The same teacher of the nations saw his disciples abound in these riches when he said: “You have been made rich in every utterance and in all knowledge” (1 Cor. I, 5).

[Note: Shortly after, these are the words of St Paul, col. 0414D.] Therefore those who contain these true riches within themselves are rightly called treasuries. And the treasuries have pavement round about, because the humility of their hearers clings to and lies beneath them. This pavement is rightly said to be paved with stone in the court, because faithful souls are joined together reciprocally in the breadth of charity. They are called stones because of the strength of faith, and they are laid in the pavement within the structure of humility.

## CHAPTER XX. ON THE VESTIBULE

[col. 0415A]

In Sacred Scripture, the term “vestibule” sometimes denotes humility and sometimes faith.

By the term “vestibule” humility is denoted, as is said through Ezekiel concerning the gate facing north: “Its windows, vestibule, and carvings were according to the measure of the gate which faced east” (Ezek. XL, 22). By the east, 585 those are signified who have remained in innocence after the conversion in which they were born. By the north, however, those who have fallen into sins are represented. By the gate, moreover, entrance into the kingdom of heaven is understood; by the windows, contemplation; by the vestibule, humility; and by the carving, good action [col. 0415B]. Thus the gate toward the north is said to have all that the gate toward the east has: namely, windows of contemplation, a vestibule of humility, and carvings of good works.

[Note: From Homily 19 on Ezekiel, far from the beginning, col. 0415D.] For all who, through being born into a way of life, have remained in innocence, possess the eastern gate, because entrance into the heavenly kingdom lies open to them from the light which they have received. And all who afterwards have fallen into sins and are cast down by the coldness of their body, but through repentance return to love of their heavenly homeland and grow warm again, possess the northern gate, because after the chill of sin entrance into the kingdom lies open to them also through mercy. The gate toward the north is therefore said to have what the gate toward the east has, because converted sinners are as richly endowed with virtues as those who avoided falling into the penalty of sin [col. 0415C]. Hence the Lord says in the voice of the Psalmist: “I ate ashes as bread” (Ps. CI, 10), because he receives penitents just as he receives the righteous. For it is written of sinners: “Long ago they would have done penance in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. XI, 21). Ashes, therefore, are eaten as bread when through repentance a sinner is restored to his Creator as an innocent person is.

The northern gate, then, has windows, a vestibule, and carvings, because when a sinner is restored to life after his offenses, he often receives the light of contemplation; and from the very remembrance of his wickedness he gains the grace of great humility and the effectiveness of good action, so that everything commanded to be done may seem, as it were, carved in his life [col. 0415D].

[Note: From the preceding homily.] The vestibule may also be understood as faith; hence it is appropriately added: “Its ascent had seven steps, namely, the gate and a vestibule before it” (Ezek. XL, 22). One ascends by seven steps to the gate because, through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, entrance to the kingdom of heaven is opened to us. The vestibule, too, is before the steps and the gate, because we first come to faith and afterwards enter the way to heavenly life through spiritual gifts. One does not come to faith through virtues; rather, through faith one reaches virtues.

For Cornelius the centurion, whose alms before baptism were praised by an angel’s testimony [col. 0416A], did not come to faith through works, but came to works through faith. For an angel says to him: “Your prayers and alms have ascended into the sight of God” (Acts X, 2). For if he had not truly believed in God even before baptism, what was he praying for? Or how had almighty God heard him, if he was not asking to be perfected in good things by God himself? He knew, then, God as the Creator of all things, but was ignorant that his almighty Son had become incarnate. Nor could he do good unless he had first believed. For it is written: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI, 6). Therefore he had faith, since his prayers and alms could please God. By good action, however, he deserved to know God perfectly and to believe the mystery of his incarnation, so that he might attain the sacrament of baptism [col. 0416B]. Through faith he came to works, but through works he was strengthened in faith. The vestibule, therefore, is before the steps, because the person who first believes afterward climbs by the steps of virtues to the entrance of the gate.

## CHAPTER XXI. ON THE COURT

In Sacred Scripture, the term “court” sometimes denotes the breadth of the kingdom of heaven, sometimes the breadth of the present life, sometimes the breadth of charity, sometimes contemplation, and sometimes the breadth of eternal life.

[Note: From the preceding homily, col. 0416D.] By the term “court” is denoted the breadth of the kingdom of heaven, as is said through Ezekiel: “And the gate of the inner court was opposite the northern and eastern gate” (Ezek. XL, 19). By the gate, indeed, entrance is meant; by the inner court [col. 0416C], the hidden place of the heavenly kingdom; by the east, the Jewish people or any righteous person; and by the north, the Gentile people or any penitent sinner. Here, moreover, “opposite” is not used to mean opposition, but direct alignment. For the gate of the inner court was shown as so situated that the northern and eastern gates tended straight toward it by a complete approach.

What, then, does it mean that the gate of the inner court, placed on a direct route, is shown opposite the northern and eastern gates, except that it is plainly given us to understand that entrance to the kingdom of heaven lies equally open to the Jewish and Gentile peoples, or to righteous persons and sinners converted after sin? For the mercy of our Creator is generous. And the inner gate looks not only toward the eastern gate but also toward the northern gate, because the joys of the inner court are opened not only to those who remain in innocence, but also to sinners who condemn their sins by repentance [col. 0416D], so that they may know the ineffable mysteries of the heavenly homeland; knowing, may thirst; thirsting, may run; and running, may arrive. He had come to know these secrets of eternal joy who said: “My soul has thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord?” (Ps. XLI, 3).

By the term “court” is denoted the breadth of the present life, as is said through the same Ezekiel: “He measured the gate of the outer court which faced the way of the north, both in length and in breadth” [col. 0417A] (Ezek. XL, 5). For a gate faces the way of the north when any preacher recognizes the life of a sinner and opens to him the inner realities of life by the word of preaching. This is called the gate of the outer court; for the outer court is the present life, in which everything done bodily is also seen bodily. It is measured both in length and in breadth, because when a sinner is led to faith, it is necessary for his teacher to consider how much, by his admonition, the sinner advances in the length of hope and in the breadth of charity.

For one who is converted to God, if he still hopes for the goods of the present life, has no length, because the life in which he has placed his hope is short. If, through desire for earthly things, he is still narrowed by hatred of his neighbor, 588 he has no breadth [col. 0417B], because he does not know either how to despise transitory things or how to expand himself in love of his neighbor. But when one who has been converted patiently hopes for the joys of eternal life, bears the troubles caused by neighbors in charity, and scorns to desire what he does not possess, the gate has length and breadth, because the preacher’s glory is the progress of his hearer. Hence the great preacher says to some: “My joy and my crown” (Phil. IV, 1), and again: “Behold, now I live, if you stand fast in the Lord” (1 Thess. III, 19); and again: “What is our hope or joy? Is it not you before the Lord?” (ibid.).

The length and breadth, therefore, belong to the gate facing north, because when a preacher converts to faith someone unbelieving and numb in the chill of his sin, he creates his own glory by stretching that person toward the length of hope and expanding him into the amplitude of charity [col. 0417C].

[Note: From Homily 17 on Ezekiel, col. 0417D.] By the term “court” is denoted the breadth of charity, as is said through the same Ezekiel: “And he made frontages sixty cubits long; and at the frontage, a court of the gate round about” (Ezek. XL, 9). We have often said already that the number six signifies the perfection of good work. We do not follow the attempt of the wise men of this world to establish this by saying that six is a perfect number because it is completed by its numerical order when one, two, and three are named; or because it is divided into three parts—one sixth, one third, and one half—namely into one, two, and three. Rather, the number six is perfect because on the sixth day God completed all his works.

And because he gave sinful man the law written in ten commandments, and six multiplied by ten rises to sixty, the perfection of good works is rightly signified by sixty cubits. Thus he made frontages of sixty cubits. For by the number sixty perfection is denoted; but by the frontages of a building, what is denoted but the works themselves which are seen outwardly? To give the word of preaching, to provide food for the hungry, to give clothing to those who are cold, and to endure adversity for a good work’s sake—what else are these but the frontages of the heavenly building? For [col. 0418A] the beauty of outward works adorns 589 the dwelling-place of God which is still hidden within.

But these frontages have a court round about, because great works are great in this: that the breadth of charity expands them in the mind. For it is written concerning charity: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. CXVIII, 25); and again concerning it: “You have set my feet in a spacious place” (Ps. XXX, 9).

[Note: These matters occur a little further below than those copied above, col. 0417D.] Therefore the court before its frontages in the perfection of work is the breadth of love. And notice that it says “round about,” so that in everything he does a person may always expand himself within the breadth of charity, lest fear or hatred narrow him. Thus, if someone speaks the word of God but does not preserve in his mind the charity which he preaches, he has a building’s frontage but has no court before the frontage. If someone gives alms but perhaps is exalted in heart by them, and does not relieve his neighbor’s need out of charity but secretly lifts himself up in pride, he displays indeed a frontage in the building, but has not made a court beside the frontage [col. 0418B].

If someone bears insults inflicted by a neighbor and silently endures evils cast against him, the patience he displays is great if he has no pain in his heart and seeks to win, into the tranquillity of gentleness, even the person who behaved badly. But if, while showing patience outwardly, he retains inward pain and does not love the one he endures, he indeed has a frontage in the building, but has no court before the frontage, because one who has subjected himself to the constriction of hatred has certainly lost the breadth of charity. True patience is patience that loves even the person it bears. For to endure while hating is not the virtue of gentleness but a covering for anger. Our gate, indeed, is entrance to the kingdom; and perfectly to love the Lord and one’s neighbor is already to tend toward entrance into the kingdom [col. 0418C].

[Note: From Homily 18 on Ezekiel, col. 0417D.] By the term “court” contemplation is denoted, as again the same Ezekiel says: “And he measured the breadth from the face of the lower gate to the frontage of the inner court, outwardly, one hundred cubits, toward the east and north” (Ezek. XL, 7). In these words, if we understand the gate by which we enter into knowledge of the Lord, the lower gate is faith, while the inner court is contemplation. The lower gate has breadth in its face because faith, through the extent of its charity, has an action visible to neighbors [col. 0418D]. When we see this action being carried out strongly by more perfect persons, we who are cramped in good deeds receive from them examples of great action. Each holy action becomes for us, as it were, a breadth of the way, whereas previously it was the narrowness of difficulty.

The inner court also has a frontage, because the contemplative life shows by certain signs of desires and groanings how much the righteous person sees of that which he loves so greatly. The number ten multiplied by itself rises to one hundred; hence great perfection is rightly signified by the number one hundred.

[Note: Several periods occur before this in Gregory, col. 0418D.] Therefore the man measured the breadth [col. 0419A] from the face of the lower gate to the frontage of the inner court, outwardly, one hundred cubits, because our Redeemer daily measures, through masters and teachers, the lives of the faithful by the standard of perfection—whether in the form of good work through faith, or in holy desires through contemplation. For many seem to be established in faith and to do great works, but they are not measured by one hundred cubits because by what they do they seek earthly glory. Some seem to torment themselves by abstinence and to persist in groanings, but their measure does not reach one hundred cubits because in what they do they seek favor from human judgment.

Who, then, is measured by one hundred cubits but the person whose good action proceeds with right intention, so that in what he does he is not turned toward seeking earthly gains [col. 0419B] or transient praise? For example, to show mercy to one’s neighbors, to distribute possessions, and to give swiftly to an importunate petitioner—this is the breadth in the face of the lower gate. But if, in giving, you do not seek another’s possessions, and if you do not seek earthly glory from that good work itself, you are rightly measured by the hundredfold number, that is, by perfection.

And because many Jews, and very many Gentiles, attained this height of perfection, it is rightly added: “toward the east and north.” The Jewish people is rightly called the east, for from its flesh was born he who is called the Sun of righteousness. Concerning him the prophet says: “For you who fear God, the Sun of righteousness shall arise” (Zech. VI, 12). By the north, however, the Gentiles are represented [col. 0419C], who long lay numb in the chill 591 of their unbelief, and in whose heart he reigned who, according to the prophet’s testimony, said within himself: “I shall set my seat in the north” [col. 0420A] (Isa. XIV, 23). Therefore, because the incarnate almighty Lord made some from Judaism and others from the Gentiles perfect within the holy Church, he measured one hundred cubits not only toward the east but also toward the north. Yet by east and north the righteous and sinners may also be understood.

[Note: From the beginning of Homily 16 on Ezekiel, col. 0419D.] By the term “courts” the breadth of eternal life is signified in the Psalmist: “Enter his gates in confession, his courts in hymns” (Ps. XCIX, 4). For what is expressed by gates but the narrowness of confession, and what by courts but the breadth of eternal life? When we confess our sins with tears, we enter the narrow gate of life. But when after this we are brought to eternal life, we enter the courts of our confession with praises, because there will then be no narrowness [col. 0420B], when the joy of the eternal feast has received us. On account of the narrowness of our confession, Truth says: “Enter by the narrow gate” (Matt. VII, 13); and when the Psalmist had confidently hoped that the joys of eternity would receive him into breadth, he said: “You have set my feet in a spacious place” (Ps. XXX, 9). Thus one tends through gates to courts, because from the narrowness of confession one arrives at the breadth of the feast.

## CHAPTER XXII. ON THE PAVEMENT

By the term “pavement” is denoted the humility of hearers, as Ezekiel says: “And he brought me out into the outer court [col. 0420C], and behold treasuries, and a pavement paved with stone round about in the court” (Ezek. XL, 17). Consult above, Chapter 19, “On the Treasury.”

# HERE BEGINS THE FOURTEENTH BOOK

[col. 0419]

## 592 CHAPTER I. ON HERBS

[col. 0419C]

In Sacred Scripture, the term “herb” sometimes denotes the flourishing of temporal glory; sometimes the support of preachers; sometimes good action; sometimes the knowledge and doctrine of unfading freshness; sometimes the plainer sayings [col. 0419D] of Scripture; sometimes the words of speakers; and sometimes carnal persons.

[Note: From Book XXIX on Job, chapter XIV, 18, col. 0419D.] By the term “herb” the flourishing of temporal glory is understood, as the Prophet says: “In the morning let him pass away like grass; in the morning let him flourish and pass away” (Ps. XXXIX, 6). To flourish and pass away like grass in the morning is for the splendor of temporal glory to wither swiftly amid the prosperity of this age.

[Note: From the preceding book and chapter, col. 0420D.] By the term “herb” the support of preachers is signified, as the Prophet says: “He brings forth hay on the mountains, and herb for the service of men” (Ps. CLXXIX, 8). Hay upon the mountains and herb for the service of men are produced when the great ones of this world, called to knowledge of the faith, generously provide holy preachers with the transitory sustenance of this life [col. 0420C].

593 By the term “herb” good action is denoted, as it is written: “Let the earth bring forth green herb” (Gen. [col. 0420D] I, 1). Although we hold that this occurred historically in the creation of the world, we may nevertheless fittingly understand the earth to have prefigured the Church, which brought forth green herb when, made fruitful by the word of God, it produced works of goodness.

By the term “herb” are understood knowledge and the teaching of unfading freshness, as Jeremiah says: “The wild asses stood upon the rocks” (ibid. XIV, 6), etc. Consult above, Book III, chapter 22, distinction 7, “On the Wild Ass.”

By the term “herbs” the plainer sayings of Scripture are denoted, as blessed Job says of heretics: “And they ate herbs and trees” (XXX, 4). See Book IX, chapter 2, distinction 3.

[col. 0421A] [Note: From Book XXXI on Job, chapter XII, 20, col. 0421D.] By the term “herb” the words of speakers are denoted, as it is written: “A burning wind brought up locusts, which went up over all the land of Egypt and covered the whole face of the land, destroying everything” (Exod. X, 13). “Thus the herb of the land was devoured, and whatever fruit was on the trees.” What do locusts, which separately are the smallest of living creatures yet harm human crops more than the others, signify but the tongues of flatterers? Whenever they observe that the minds of worldly people produce some good things, they corrupt those things by praising them excessively. The fruit of the Egyptians is the work of vainglorious persons; locusts destroy it when flattering tongues incline the heart of one who prospers toward seeking transient praise. Locusts consume the herb [col. 0421B] when all flatterers exalt the words of speakers with their applause.

[Note: From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter VI, col. 0421D.] By the term “herbs” carnal persons are denoted, as the Prophet says concerning the children of the Church: “They shall spring up among the herbs, like willows beside flowing waters” (Isa. XLIV, 4). What is signified by herbs but the life of carnal persons? Yet the children of the holy Church spring up like willows among herbs, 594 because amid the drying life of carnal persons they endure both in great numbers and in the perpetual freshness of the mind. They are rightly said to spring up beside flowing waters, because each of them receives freedom for fruitfulness from the doctrine of Sacred Scripture, which runs on in time.

## CHAPTER II. ON THE LILY

[col. 0421C]

In Sacred Scripture, the term “lilies” sometimes denotes the brightness of the eternal homeland, and sometimes the sweet fragrance of the saints’ good life.

[Note: From Homily 6 on Ezekiel, somewhat far from the beginning, col. 0421D.] By the term “lily” the brightness of the eternal homeland is denoted. Hence the Lord says to Moses: “You shall make also a candlestick of the purest beaten gold. Its shaft, branches, cups, small spheres, and lilies shall come forth from it” (Exod. XXV, 11). What is denoted by the candlestick except the Redeemer of humankind, in whose human nature the light of divinity shone forth, so that he might become the world’s candlestick and every sinner might see by his light in what darkness he lay? Because he took our nature without sin, the candlestick of the tabernacle is commanded to be made of the purest gold.

Now beaten metal is drawn out by hammering. Likewise, our Redeemer, who was perfect God and man from conception and birth, endured the sufferings of his passion and thus came to the glory of the resurrection. Therefore he was a beaten candlestick of purest gold, because he had no sin and yet his body advanced to immortality through the humiliations of the passion. In respect of the virtues of his soul, he had no need at all to advance through blows. But in his members, which we are, he advances daily through blows [col. 0422A], because, when we are struck and shaped so as to deserve to be his body, he himself advances.

The shaft of the same 595 candlestick must be understood as the Church itself, which is his body, because it stands free amid so many adversities. The branches proceeding from the shaft are the preachers, who have sounded forth in the world a sweet melody, namely, the New Song. Cups are usually filled with wine. What, then, are the minds of hearers except cups, filled with the wine of knowledge by holy preachers? And what is a small sphere but the mobility of preaching? A sphere rolls in every direction. Preaching which can neither be restrained by adversity nor raised up by prosperity is a sphere: strong amid adversities and humble amid prosperity; it has neither the angle of fear nor that of pride [col. 0422B]. It cannot be fixed in its course, because it moves itself fluidly through all things.

To pursue the example we have offered: lilies are fittingly described in the candlestick together with branches, cups, and bowls, because after the grace and mobility of preaching of which we have spoken, there follows that flourishing homeland, which blooms with eternal living beings—that is, eternal flowers. The small spheres, therefore, pertain to labor; the lilies, to reward.

By the term “lilies” the sweetly fragrant life of the saints is denoted. Hence, in the voice of the Bridegroom, it is said to the holy Church in the Song of Songs: “Your two breasts are like two young roe-deer feeding among lilies” (Song IV, 5). Consult above, Book V, chapter 44, distinction 1, “On the Breasts” [col. 0422C].

## CHAPTER III. ON THE MYRTLE

In Sacred Scripture, the term “myrtle” sometimes denotes the disposition of a tranquil mind, and sometimes those who show compassion.

By the term “myrtle” the composure of a tranquil mind is denoted, as the Lord promises through Isaiah: “Instead of the salt-bush the fir-tree shall grow, and instead of the nettle the myrtle shall grow” (ibid. LV, 13). Consult above, Book IX, chapter 6, distinction 2, “On the Fir-Trees.”

596 [Note: Above, Book IX, chapter 3, distinction 4. From Homily 20 on the Gospels, shortly after the middle, col. 0422D.] By the term “myrtle” are denoted those who, by compassion, moderate the tribulations of their neighbors. Hence the Lord promises through Isaiah: “I will give [col. 0422D] in the wilderness cedar, thorn, myrtle, and olive-tree” (Isa. LXI, 19). Consult the chapter “On the Cedar,” and add this: myrtle possesses a moderating power, so that by tempering it binds together limbs that are relaxed. What, then, is signified by the myrtle except those who know how to sympathize with their neighbors’ afflictions and mitigate their tribulation through compassion? This accords with what is written: “But thanks be to God, who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we ourselves may be able to console those who are in every distress” (2 Cor. I).

[Note: Gregory, however, repeats the words, “thanks be to God.”] When they bring a word or aid of consolation to afflicted neighbors, they undoubtedly bind them firmly to a state of uprightness [col. 0423A], lest excessive tribulation dissolve them into despair. Myrtles are set there for this purpose: that one who in the heat of tribulation has received from the word or work of a compassionate neighbor the moderating consolation may himself learn how to offer the moderation of his own consolation to afflicted neighbors.

## CHAPTER IV. ON FRANKINCENSE

In Sacred Scripture, the term “frankincense” sometimes denotes the offering of love, and sometimes the power of prayer.

[Note: From Book I on Job, chapter 19, before the end, §40, col. 0423D.] By the term “frankincense” the offering of love is denoted, as it is said of the Church in the Song of Songs: “Who is this, who comes up through the wilderness like a slender column [col. 0423B] of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense and every perfumer’s powder?” (Song III).

[Note: From Homily X on the Gospels, after the middle, col. 0423D.] By the term “frankincense” the power of prayer is expressed. Thus the Gospel relates that the three Magi offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Matt. II). By gold wisdom is denoted; by frankincense, which is burned for God, the power 597 of prayer is expressed, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL, 2). By myrrh, moreover, the mortification of our flesh is figured. Hence the holy Church says of her workers who strive for God even unto death: “My hands have distilled myrrh” (Ps. LXVII, 6).

We offer gold to the newborn King if we shine in his sight with the brightness of heavenly wisdom [col. 0423C]. We offer frankincense if, by holy zeal in prayer, we kindle thoughts of the flesh upon the altar of the heart, so that by heavenly desire we may be able to breathe forth something sweet to God. We offer myrrh if we mortify the vices of the flesh.

## CHAPTER V. ON MYRRH

[Note: From Book XXXV on Job, chapter XIII, 23, col. 0423D.] By the term “myrrh” the sweetness of virtues is understood, as the Prophet says to our Redeemer at his coming: “Myrrh, stacte, and cassia come from your garments; from ivory steps, from which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor” (Ps. XLIV, 9). What is denoted by myrrh, stacte, and cassia except the sweetness of virtues? What is expressed by ivory steps except an ascent of those making progress, shining with great strength? Therefore the Redeemer, in coming, wears myrrh, stacte, and cassia as a garment because he mercifully clothes himself in his elect and sprinkles upon them the fragrance of myrrh-like virtue. In them this fragrance is drawn from ivory steps, because their reputation for virtue arises not from the display of pretense but from the approval of true and unalloyed work [col. 0423D]. And it is rightly said: “From which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor.” For holy souls, brought forth by the ancient fathers into the knowledge of truth, delight their Redeemer in his honor because, from the good they do, they claim nothing for their own praise.

## CHAPTER VI. ON HYSSOP

[col. 0424A]

By the term “hyssop” faith is denoted. Thus in Moses, when a heifer is sacrificed, it is commanded that hyssop, cedarwood, and scarlet be offered with it. Consult Book III, chapter 8, distinction 2, “On the Heifer.”

## CHAPTER VII. ON NARD

[Note: From Book XXXV on Job, chapter XIII, 22, col. 0424D.] By the term “nard” the sweetly fragrant life of the elect is denoted. Hence the holy Church, having perceived in her elect a certain fragrance of sweetness, says in the Song of Songs: “While the king was at his repose, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song I, 12). As though she said more plainly: So long as the King remains hidden from my sight in the repose of the heavenly secret, the life of the elect is exercised in wondrous fragrances of virtues, so that one who does not yet see him whom he desires may burn ardently with longing [col. 0424B]. For, while the King is in his repose, nard gives its fragrance: while the Lord rests in his blessedness, the virtue of the saints in the Church bestows upon us the grace of great sweetness.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON THE NETTLE

In Sacred Scripture, the term “nettles” sometimes denotes the burning heat of vices, sometimes the itching of earthly desires, and sometimes the itchings of thoughts.

[col. 0424C] By the term “nettle” the burning heat of vices is denoted, as the Lord promises through Isaiah: “Instead of the salt-bush the fir-tree shall grow, and instead of the nettle the myrtle shall grow” (Isa. LV, 13). Consult Book IX, chapter 6, distinction 2, “On the Fir-Trees.”

By the term “nettles” itching earthly desires are denoted, as Solomon says: “Through the field of a slothful man,” etc. (Prov. XXIV). Consult above, Book XIII, chapter 3, distinction 1.

By the term “nettles” the itchings of thoughts are signified, as the Lord, under the figure of Babylon, rebukes the confused mind through the Prophet, saying: “Thorns and nettles rise up in her houses” (Isa. XXXIII, 12). See again Book IX, chapter 13, distinction 4.

By the term “thistle” the piercing of sorrow is denoted. Hence [col. 0424D] blessed Job, listing his good deeds, binds himself under a curse if he has not done this, saying: “Let a thistle spring up for me instead of wheat, and a thorn instead of barley” (Job XXXI, 40). Consult the chapter “On the Thorn,” there, distinction 2.

## CHAPTER X. ON LEEKS OR ONIONS

[Note: From Book XX on Job, chapter XVI, col. 0424D.] By the terms “leeks” or “onions” the hardship of the present life is denoted, as the Israelite people says: “We remember the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic” (Num. XI, 5). The minds of the wicked take more pleasure in proceeding through the rough paths of pride than through the pleasant paths of humility and gentleness [col. 0425A]. For, through love of the world, they are ready to bear hard things as if they were soft and delightful, while in this life they strive to seize the heights of worldly things.

The Lord commands rest from the labors of the world and commends the sweetness of holy repose, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28). Yet the deranged mind of the wicked rejoices more in attaining harsh things carnally than in holding pleasant things spiritually; it is fed more by the bitterness of toil than by the sweetness of repose. The Israelite people plainly shows this in itself: while receiving the refreshment of manna from above, it desired from Egypt pots of meat, melons, leeks, and onions.

What is signified in manna except food of grace, sweet to taste, given from above for the refreshment of those who rightly devote themselves to the inner life? And what are meant by pots of meat except carnal works, which must be cooked, as it were by fires, through the labors of life’s tribulations? What is meant by melons except earthly sweetness? What is expressed by leeks and onions, which those who eat them commonly shed tears, except the hardship of the present life—a life lived by its lovers not without mourning and yet loved with tears [col. 0425B]?

600 Therefore, abandoning manna, they sought leeks and onions along with melons and meat, because perverse minds despise the sweet gifts of repose granted through grace; and, in exchange for carnal pleasures, they desire the laborious paths of this life, even though full of tears. They scorn to possess what might give them spiritual joy and eagerly seek what makes them groan carnally, because by a perverse judgment they prefer disturbance to tranquillity, hard things to gentle, rough things to mild, transient things to eternal, and insecure things to secure [col. 0425C].

## CHAPTER XI. ON THE REED

In Sacred Scripture, the term “reed” sometimes denotes the eternity of the Word; sometimes the skill of teachers; sometimes the splendor of temporal glory; sometimes writers of Sacred Scripture; and sometimes Sacred Scripture itself.

[Note: From Book XXXIII on Job, chapter III, 4, col. 0425D.] By the term “reed” the eternity of the Word is denoted, as the Father says through the Psalmist: “My tongue is the reed of a scribe writing swiftly” (Ps. XLIV, 2). Because what we speak passes away, but what we write remains, the tongue of the Father is called the reed of a scribe, because from him is his Word, coeternal and begotten without passing away.

[Note: [Col. 0425D] From the same book and chapter above.] By “reed” is signified the learning of teachers, as is promised in the prophetic voice to the desolate land when it is said: “In the dens where dragons formerly dwelt, the verdure of reed and rush shall spring up” (Isa. XXXV, 7). For what is signified by the reed except preachers? And what by the rush, which always grows beside the moisture of water, except the little and tender hearers of the sacred word? Therefore, in the dens of dragons the verdure of reed and rush springs up, because among those peoples [Col. 0426A] whom the malice of the ancient enemy possessed, both the knowledge of teachers and the obedience of hearers are gathered in abundance.

[Note: [Col. 0425D] From the same book and chapter above.] By “reed” is expressed the brilliance of temporal glory, as is said through the prophet concerning the Lord appearing in the flesh: “A bruised reed he shall not break, and smoking flax he shall not quench” (Isa. XLII, 3). For what is signified by the reed except the temporal kingdom of the Jewish people—bright indeed outwardly, but empty within? And because in that same people the royal line had already failed and its kingdom was held by a foreigner, he aptly calls that same kingdom a bruised reed. What, moreover, is expressed by flax except the priesthood of that same people? It used linen garments; and because at the Lord’s coming it had lost the ardour of charity, as though it had already lost the fire of faith, it was not burning but smoking. Yet the incarnate Lord did not break the bruised reed or quench the smoking flax, because he did not strike, by the power of judgment, the kingdom of Judaea, which was now nearly destroyed, nor its priesthood, which did not retain the fire of faith; rather, he endured them with the long-suffering of patience.

Hence again the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the devil, under the figure of Behemoth: “He sleeps beneath the shadow, in the hiding-place of the reed” (Job XL, 16). [Note: [Col. 0426D] These words are read before the preceding passage.] By “shadow” is understood the numbness of wickedness, in which this Behemoth sleeps, because he watches anxiously over hearts warm with charity, but lies secure in cold minds. For he cannot sleep in the hearts of the saints, since, even if he places himself in them for a brief moment, the very heat [Col. 0426C] of heavenly desires wearies him. And he is, as it were, pricked as often as he must withdraw, as they sigh through inward love toward eternal things. As many voices awaken him as holy thoughts cry out to heaven from their minds. Hence, terrified by the weapons of good deeds and struck by the darts of sighs, he flees; returning to the cold hearts of the reprobate, he seeks the shadow of wickedness which he may securely possess.

What that shadow is which he finds is shown when it is immediately added: “In the hiding-place of the reed.” For what is designated by the name of reed except minds of worldly people devoted to temporal glory? The more lofty and splendid they appear outwardly, the more they become inwardly empty in themselves; because, while they flow away on the surface toward external glory, [Col. 0426D] they are not made firm by any inner solidity. After the manner of a reed, they are empty within through foolishness, but beautiful outwardly by appearance and display.

[Note: [Col. 0426D] See distinction 2, §5.] By “reed” are signified the writers of sacred discourse, as is said through Ezekiel concerning the man who appeared to him: “And a measuring reed was in his hand” (Ezek. XL, 3). For the Lord promises of holy Church through another prophet, saying: “In her the verdure of reed and rush shall spring up” (Isa. XXXV, 7). [Note: [Col. 0426D] From Homily 13 on Ezekiel.] I remember having explained this elsewhere: by the reed teachers ought to be understood, and by the rush hearers. But since both reed and rush are accustomed to grow beside the moisture of water, and both flourish from one and the same water; and since the reed is taken up for writing, whereas one cannot write with a rush—what ought we to understand by the rush and reed except that there is one doctrine of truth which waters many hearers? Yet, once watered, some make such progress in the word of God that they too become writers, that is, as it were, reeds. Others hear the word of life in good hope and retain the greenness of upright works, but cannot in any way advance to writing. What are these in God’s water except, so to speak, certain rushes? They indeed grow green and advance, but cannot express letters.

Therefore our Redeemer, because he granted that the words he spoke should also be written through the labour of teachers, held a reed in his hand. This reed is called a measuring reed because the labours of writers are governed by a certain hidden dispensation of judgment: they benefit some readers, while they cannot benefit others.

[Note: [Col. 0427D] From the same homily, a little further on.] The measuring reed may also be understood as sacred Scripture, because whoever reads it measures himself within it: either how far he advances in spiritual virtue, or how far he remains removed from the good things commanded; how much he now rises to perform the works of faith, or how much he still lies prostrate in depraved deeds.

## CHAPTER XII. ON THE CANE

[Col. 0427C]

[Note: [Col. 0427D] From Homily 6 on the Gospels.] By “cane” is signified the carnal mind, as the Lord says to the Jewish crowds in praise of John: “What went you out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” (Matt. XI, 7). He states this not affirmatively but negatively. For a cane, as soon as a breeze touches it, bends to the other side. And what is signified by the cane except the carnal mind, which, as soon as it is touched by favour or slander, immediately inclines in whichever direction? If the breeze of favour blows from human speech, it becomes cheerful, exalts itself, and bends itself wholly, as it were, toward approval. But if from the same source from which the breeze of praise came there bursts the wind of detraction, then immediately it bends, as it were, in the opposite direction toward the force of anger.

But John was not a cane shaken by the wind, because neither flattering favour made him gentle nor anyone’s anger made him harsh. Neither prosperity knew how to raise him up nor adversity to bend him down. Therefore he was not a cane shaken by the wind: no variation of circumstances bent him from the uprightness of his steadfastness.

By “cane” is expressed the brilliance of temporal glory, as Wisdom says of the just: “The just shall shine and run to and fro like sparks among reeds” (Wis. III, 7). See the chapter on sparks, Book II, chapter 3, distinction 1.

## CHAPTER XIII. ON THE BULRUSH

[Col. 0428A]

[Note: [Col. 0428D] From Book VIII on Job, chapter XXIV, §27.] By “bulrush” is signified every hypocrite, as Bildad says in the book of blessed Job: “Can the bulrush grow green without moisture, or the sedge grow without water?” (Job VIII, 11). He immediately explains whom he compares to the bulrush or sedge when he adds: “While it is still in flower and is not plucked by the hand, it withers before every herb; such are the ways of all who forget the Lord, and the hope of the hypocrite shall perish.”

Therefore, by bulrush or sedge is signified the life of the hypocrite, which has indeed the appearance of greenness, but bears no useful fruit for human use. Remaining dry through barrenness of works, it grows green only in the colour of holiness. Yet neither the bulrush prospers without moisture [Col. 0428B] nor the sedge without water, because the life of hypocrites receives the outpouring of the heavenly gift for good works; but because in all that they do they seek external praise, they are emptied of the fruit of the grace they have received.

[Note: [Col. 0428D] These words occur a little after the preceding passage.] Thus bulrush or sedge does not live without water, because hypocrites receive the greenness of good action only from the heavenly gift; but because they seize it for the use of their own praise, they are green in the water, yet grow empty. It is well added: “While it is still in flower and is not plucked by the hand, it withers before every herb.” The bulrush in flower is the hypocrite in praise. The sedge, rising with sharp points, is not plucked by the hand, because, with his feelings sharpened through arrogance, the hypocrite disdains to be corrected for his depravity. In his flower he cuts the hand that would pluck him, because when the hypocrite is established in praise, if anyone dares correct him, he immediately cuts down his correctors’ life by his harshness. For he desires not to be holy, but to be called holy; and when perhaps he is corrected, the glory of his reputation is, as it were, lopped off. He is angry that he has been detected in depravity and forbids his reprover to speak to him, because he suffers pain as if touched in a hidden wound.

Therefore it is rightly said: “While it is still in flower and is not plucked by the hand, it withers before every herb.” For, according to the flesh, even the just are herbs, as the prophet testifies when he says: “All flesh is grass” (Isa. XL, 6). But the bulrush is said to wither before every herb because, while the just remain in their goodness, the life of hypocrites dries up from the greenness of the uprightness they had assumed. The other herbs also wither, because the works of the just fail with the life of the flesh; but the bulrush precedes the herbs in withering, because before the hypocrite departs from the flesh, he abandons the deeds of virtue which he had displayed in himself.

“Such are the ways of all who forget the Lord, and the hope of the hypocrite shall perish.” For what does the hypocrite hope for in all his works except reverence of honour, the glory of praise, to be feared by those better than himself, and to be called holy by all? But the hypocrite’s hope cannot endure, because, not seeking eternity, he loses what he possesses. For the intention of his mind is not fixed upon that glory which is possessed without end; rather, while he hungers after transitory favour, he loses, by receiving it, that for which he labours, as Truth testifies: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 1).

## CHAPTER XIV. ON THE PALIURUS

By *paliurus* is signified anyone powerful in malice and defending others in evil, as the Lord rebukes, through the prophet, under the figure of Babylon, the crowd of wicked people or any perverse mind: “Thorns, nettles, and paliurus shall spring up in her houses and strongholds” (Isa. XXXIV, 13). See the chapter on the thorn, Book IX, chapter 13, distinction 4.

## CHAPTER XV. ON LETTUCES

[Col. 0429B]

[Note: [Col. 0429D] Book XI, chapter I, distinction 6.] By wild lettuces is signified the bitterness of penitence, as Moses says concerning the eating of the lamb: “They shall eat the flesh that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread with wild lettuces” (Exod. XII, 8).

[Note: [Col. 0429D] From Homily 28 on the Gospels, somewhat after the middle.] See the chapter on fire, and add this: the sacraments of our Redeemer’s commands alone do not suffice for the true solemnity of the mind unless good works are also joined to them. What benefit is it to receive his body and blood with the mouth, yet oppose him by depraved conduct? Therefore it is fittingly added concerning the eating: “And unleavened bread with wild lettuces.” He eats bread without leaven who performs upright works without the corruption of vain glory, who offers deeds [Col. 0429C] of mercy without an admixture of sin, lest he wickedly seize what he appears to dispense rightly.

Those to whom the Lord said in rebuke through the prophet had also mixed this leaven of sin with their good action: “Come to Bethel, and act impiously” (Amos IV, 4); and shortly afterward: “And sacrifice praise from that which is leavened” (ibid., 5). For he sacrifices from leaven who prepares an offering to God from plunder. Wild lettuces, however, are very bitter. Therefore the flesh of the lamb must be eaten with wild lettuces, so that, when we receive the body of the Redeemer, we may afflict ourselves with weeping for our sins, in order that the very bitterness of penitence may wipe from the stomach of the mind the unhealthy moisture of a perverse life.

## CHAPTER XVI. ON MUSTARD

[Col. 0429D]

By “mustard” Christ is signified, as the voice of Truth himself says in the Gospel: “To what is the kingdom of heaven like, and to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and put in his garden; and it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of heaven rested in its branches” (Luke XIII, 19). See the chapter on birds, Book II, chapter 1, distinction 5.

[Note: [Col. 0429D] Thus Augustine and Cassiodorus read in the Psalter.] By “mustard” is signified the strength of a faithful man, as the voice of Truth says in the Gospel: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you shall say to this mountain, ‘Pass from here,’ and it shall pass” (Matt. XVII, 3; Luke XVII, 5). Unless it is crushed, the strength of the mustard seed is by no means known. For uncrushed it is mild, but when crushed it burns, revealing what sharp power lay hidden within it. So every holy man, when he is not assailed, appears insignificant and gentle; but if the threshing of persecution oppresses him, he immediately displays everything that has the savour of heat and is turned into the fervour of virtue. Whatever had formerly seemed contemptible and weak in him, and whatever he had willingly concealed within himself during times of tranquillity, is forced into view when he is stirred by tribulation.

Hence the prophet fittingly says: “In the day the Lord commanded his mercy, and in the night he declared it” (Ps. XLI, 5). The Lord’s mercy is commanded in the day because it is received by knowing it in a peaceful time; but it is declared in the night because the gift received in tranquillity is made manifest in tribulations. For just as perfumes do not diffuse their scent more widely except when shaken, and aromatics do not spread their fragrance except when burned, so holy men make known in tribulations all that they give forth in the fragrance of virtues.

## CHAPTER XVII. ON WHEAT

In sacred Scripture, when “wheat” is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies any elect soul; sometimes the utterance of sacred doctrine; sometimes the flourishing of eternal recompense, or a spiritual work which refreshes the mind; sometimes the inward understanding of sacred discourse [Col. 0430C]. But when “wheats” is used in the plural, it sometimes signifies virtues and sometimes the words of preaching.

By “wheat” is signified any elect soul, as Elihu says in the book of Job: “The cloud desires wheat” (Job XXVII, 29). See the chapter on clouds, Book I, chapter 12, distinction 5.

[Note: [Col. 0430D] From Homily 20 on the Gospels, somewhat after the beginning.] By “wheat” is signified the utterance of sacred doctrine, as the Psalmist says: “And the valleys shall abound with wheat” (Ps. LXIV, 14). For valleys abound with wheat when the hearts of the humble are filled with the grace of virtues by the utterance of sacred doctrine, in accordance with what is written elsewhere through the same Psalmist: “He sends forth springs in the valleys” (Ps. CIII, 10). Water runs down from mountains because the teaching of truth abandons proud minds. But springs arise in valleys because humble minds receive the word of preaching. Already we see it; already we behold valleys abounding with wheat, because the mouths of those who seemed gentle, simple, and contemptible to this world are filled with the nourishment of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0430D] From Book XXII on Job, chapter XIV, §20.] By “wheat” is understood the perfection of righteousness, as Truth teaches in the Gospel: “So is the kingdom of heaven, as if a man should cast seed into the earth, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should germinate and grow while he does not know it” (Mark IV, 26). Announcing the stages of that seed’s growth, he adds: “For the earth brings forth fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then full wheat in the ear” (ibid., 10). He also supplies the conclusion of its growth, saying: “And when the fruit has brought itself forth, he immediately puts in the sickle, because the time of harvest has come” (ibid., 26).

Behold: by the voice of Truth, the growth of merits is distinguished through the stages of crops. For he says: “First the blade, then the ear, then full wheat in the ear.” Was Peter not still a blade when, at the voice of a maidservant, he was suddenly bent by the mere breath of one question? He was indeed green through devotion, but still tender through weakness (Matt. XXVI; Luke XXII). But he was found to be full wheat [Col. 0431B] in the ear when he resisted the persecuting rulers, saying: “It is necessary to obey God rather than men” (Acts V, 29). He was found to be full wheat in the ear when he endured so many blows in the threshing of persecution and yet was not diminished in the manner of chaff, but remained an intact grain.

For a little while, in every soul, so to speak, the moisture of inward grace overflows, so that the blade may grow into grain. Therefore, when anyone sees his neighbour still as a blade, let him not despair of wheat. For from the leaves of blades, which droop softly here and there, the rising grains of crops are strengthened. Every elect person begins first with the tenderness of his rudiments and afterward gradually grows strong unto robust and mighty things.

By “wheat” is understood the flourishing of eternal recompense or the spiritual work that refreshes the mind, as blessed Job, after enumerating the good things he had done, says that if he had not done so, he would pronounce a curse against himself: “Instead of wheat let a thistle spring up for me,” etc. (Job XXXI, 40). See the chapter on thistles, Book IX, chapter 13, distinction 2.

[Note: [Col. 0431D] From Part III of the *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 25.] By “wheat” is signified the inward understanding of sacred discourse, as the Lord asks through the prophet concerning those who do not rightly understand the words of the sacred law: “I gave them wheat, wine, and oil; I multiplied for them silver and gold, which they made for Baal” (Hos. II, 8). We receive wheat from the Lord when, in more obscure sayings, the veil of the letter being drawn aside, we inwardly perceive the marrow of the law’s spirit. The Lord gives us his wine when he intoxicates us by the lofty preaching of his Scripture. He also grants us his oil when, through plainer commands, he orders our life with gentle mildness. He multiplies silver when he supplies us with utterances full of the light of truth. He enriches us with gold when he illumines our heart with the understanding of supreme splendour.

Heretics offer all these things to Baal because, by understanding everything corruptly in the hearts of their hearers, they pervert them. And from God’s wheat, wine, oil, silver, and gold they offer sacrifice [Col. 0432A] to Satan, because they twist words of peace toward the error of discord. They must therefore be admonished to consider that, while with a perverse mind they make discord out of commandments of peace, by God’s righteous judgment they themselves die from the words of life.

The term “wheats” signifies virtues. See Book XI, chapter 1, distinction 10.

[Note: [Col. 0431D] From Part III of the *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 26.] By “wheats” are signified the words of preaching, as Solomon says: “He who hides wheats shall be cursed among the peoples” (Prov. XI, 26). To hide wheats is to keep to oneself the words of holy preaching. Such a person shall be cursed among the peoples, because by the guilt of his silence alone he is condemned to punishment for the many whom he could have corrected. If famine were crushing peoples and someone kept hidden wheat, he would undoubtedly become the author of their death. Let those therefore consider by what punishment they must be struck who, while souls perish through hunger for the word, do not distribute the bread of grace which they have received.

If persons not ignorant of the medical art saw a wound that needed cutting and nevertheless refused to cut it, they would surely incur guilt for a brother’s death through mere indolence. How great a guilt, then, do those see themselves to incur who, knowing the wounds of minds, have refused to heal them by the incision of words? Hence it is said through the prophet: “Cursed is he who restrains his sword from blood” (Jer. XLVIII, 107). To restrain the sword from blood is to withhold the word of preaching from putting to death the carnal life.

## CHAPTER XVIII. ON BARLEY

[Col. 0432C]

By “barley” is signified the letter of the Old Testament, as the Gospel says: “There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fishes” (John VI, 9). To speak briefly, the five loaves are understood as the five books of Moses. They are rightly not wheat loaves but barley loaves, because they belong to the Old Testament. We know that barley is so made that one can scarcely reach its kernel. For that kernel is clothed in a husk of chaff, and the chaff itself clings firmly and tightly, so that it is stripped off with difficulty. Such is the letter of the Old Testament: it is clothed in the coverings of carnal sacraments, but if one reaches its kernel, it feeds and satisfies.

[Col. 0432D] By “barley” is understood the administration of earthly things, as blessed Job says, after recounting the good things he had done: “Instead of wheat let a thistle spring up for me, and instead of barley” (Job XXXI, 40). See the chapter on thistles, Book IX, chapter 13, distinction 2.

## CHAPTER XIX. ON HARVEST

In sacred Scripture, “harvest” sometimes signifies sacred Scripture and sometimes the gift of right understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0432D] From Book VI on Job, chapter II.] By “harvest” is understood Scripture, as Eliphaz says in the book of Job concerning the Jewish people: “The hungry shall eat his harvest, and the armed man shall seize him” (Job V, 5). The harvest of the Jewish people was the crop of sacred discourse. Certain grains of the ears are the words of the prophets, which the Jewish people possessed but did not eat, because it held the law merely in words, yet through the fastidiousness of foolishness starved itself of its understanding. Therefore the hungry eat that people’s harvest, because the Gentile people eat the words of the law by understanding them, whereas the Jewish multitude laboured over them without understanding.

The Lord foresaw these hungry people of faith when he said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. V, 6). Of these hungry people, Hannah says prophetically: “Those formerly full hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry were satisfied” (I Sam. II, 5). But because it lost its harvest, it is rightly added how that people itself also perished: “And the armed man shall seize him” (Job V, 5). The ancient enemy seized the Jewish people armed, because by the darts of deceitful suggestion he extinguished in it the life of faith, so that from the very source by which it believed itself to cleave to God, it might resist his order. Truth himself warns the disciples of this when he says: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he offers service to God” (John XVI, 2).

[Note: [Col. 0433D] From the same book, chapter 5, §4.] “Harvest” may also be understood not only as the letter of sacred Scripture, but also as the gift of right understanding. Therefore what we have said may here be fittingly understood in a moral sense. For the fool has a harvest when any wicked person receives the gift of right understanding: he is instructed by the sayings of sacred Scripture and speaks good things, but in no way performs what he says; he brings forth God’s words but does not love them; he magnifies them in praise but tramples them in life. Therefore, because this fool both understands and speaks, yet does not love these things by doing them, he fasts while possessing a harvest.

The hungry person eats this harvest: the one who longs for God with holy desires says what he hears and does what he has learned. While he is refreshed by the upright preaching of a wicked teacher, what else does he do but feed upon the fool’s grain? Did Truth not urge his hungry ones to eat the fool’s harvest when, to those burning with holy desires, he commanded concerning the Pharisees: “Do what they say; do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII, 3)? It is as though he openly said: They exalt the harvest of the word by speaking it, but by living badly they do not touch it at all. Let this harvest refresh your hunger, because through the fastidiousness of their foolishness they store it up for you.

It is aptly added: “And the armed man shall seize him.” The ancient enemy is conquered as if unarmed when, by suggesting manifest evils, he tries to destroy all good things in the human mind at once. But he comes armed when, leaving some good things untouched, he secretly corrupts others. For he often does not tempt certain persons in their understanding and does not oppose them in meditation on sacred discourse, yet he supplants their life in action. While they are praised for the power of their knowledge, they do not perceive the damage to their works; and while the mind is led by delight in favour, it does not heal the wounds of its life. Therefore the armed enemy seizes the one whom, concealed by deceit, he has left untouched in one respect but overcome from another side.

## CHAPTER XX. ON FRUITS

[Note: [Col. 0433D] From the beginning of Homily 11 on Ezekiel.] By “fruits” are understood converts, whether Jews or Gentiles, as Ezekiel says: “I came to the captives, to the heap of new fruits, to those dwelling by the river Chobar” (Ezek. III, 11). Though the matter required him to indicate that he came to the captives, what need was there to identify the place also by fruits, saying, “to the heap of new fruits,” unless causes are often signified by places? For many years of captivity had already elapsed when Ezekiel prophesied; and of those who had been led into captivity, many had already died bodily. The prophet came to speak to their children. Hence it is also said to him above: “Son of man, I send you to the children of Israel, to apostate nations which have departed from me. Their fathers have transgressed my covenant even unto this day, and the children are stiff-necked [Col. 0434B] and of an unyielding heart, to whom I send you” (Ezek. XI, 6).

Because many of these would believe and would attain, through obedience, the fruitfulness of good work, they are called a heap of fruits. For another prophet testifies that good souls are called fruits when he says: “Israel was holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his fruits” (Jer. II, 1). The Gentiles converted to faith also afterward became the Lord’s fruits; but because Israel believed the Lord first, the prophet rightly called it the firstfruits of his fruits. Therefore, because the prophet brought words not to the former people but to the children of that same people, he came to the heap of new fruits.

## CHAPTER XXI. ON THE EAR OF GRAIN

[Note: [Col. 0434D] From Homily 15 on Ezekiel, some distance from the beginning.] The ear of grain signifies progress in good work, as the voice of Truth says: “So is the kingdom of God, as if a man casts seed into the earth and sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed germinates and grows while he does not know it. For the earth brings forth fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then full wheat in the ear” (Mark IV, 8). A man casts seed into the earth when he implants a good intention in his heart. After casting the seed, he sleeps because he now rests in hope of good work. He rises by night and day because he advances amid adversity and prosperity. The seed germinates and grows while he does not know it because, while he is still unable to measure his growth, the virtue once conceived is led onward to progress. And the earth brings forth fruit of itself because, grace going before, the human mind spontaneously rises to progress in good work.

But this same earth first brings forth the blade, then the ear, then full wheat in the ear. To bring forth the blade is still to possess the tenderness of a good beginning. The blade reaches the ear when the virtue conceived in the mind draws itself onward to progress in good work. It bears full wheat in the ear when virtue has advanced so far that it can become a work strong and perfect. Therefore, when we conceive good desires, we cast seed into the earth. When we begin to do what is right, we are a blade. When we are established in the perfection of that same work, we bring forth full wheat in the ear.

[Note: [Col. 0435D] From Book XVI on Job, chapter XXIII, §28.] By “ears of grain” are signified the sayings of the Fathers, as Job says concerning heretics: “They took away ears of grain from those naked and walking without clothing, and from the hungry”; that is, by saying “naked,” he repeats this with “without clothing” (Job XXIV, 7). But it is one thing to be naked and another to walk naked. Everyone who does neither good nor evil is naked and idle. But one who does evil walks naked, because he proceeds along the path of wickedness without the covering of good work.

There are, however, some who, knowing the evil of their wickedness, hasten to be satisfied with the bread of righteousness and desire to receive the sayings of sacred discourse. Whenever they turn over in their thoughts the Fathers’ sayings for the edification of their minds, they carry ears of grain, as it were, from a good harvest. Thus heretics take ears of grain from those naked, walking without clothing, and hungry, because whether they are still idle and exercise themselves in no good works, or proceed likewise in shamelessness without the covering of good work, even when they already desire to return to penitence and hunger for the nourishment of the word, the heretics take ears away from them: by pernicious persuasions, they destroy the sayings of the Fathers in their minds.

Nor without reason do we say that ears signify the sayings of the Fathers, because, since they are often expressed in figurative discourse, we remove from them the covering of the letter, as it were the chaff of the awns, so that we may be refreshed by the marrow of the spirit.

## CHAPTER XXII. ON CHAFF

[Note: [Col. 0435D] From Book XVI on Job, chapter XXX, §22.] By “chaff” are understood the wicked, as Job says of their damnation: “They shall be as chaff before the face of the wind, and as ashes which the whirlwind scatters” (Job XXI, 8). When a wicked person is seen in power, when he is utterly unrestrained in oppression and violence, he is judged exceedingly burdensome to the thoughts of the weak, and as though rooted in this world. But when the sentence of the strict Judge comes, all the wicked will be as chaff before the wind, because, so to speak, they are suddenly lifted and carried away to the fire by the blast of wrath. Those whom the tears of the needy could not move here, once lying upon them like a mass of great weight through their unjust judgments, are light before the hand of the Judge who seizes them, because they were heavy to their neighbours through injustice.

“And as ashes which the whirlwind scatters.” Before the eyes of almighty God the life of the wicked is ashes, because although it seems green for a moment, it is nevertheless already seen as consumed by his judgment, since it is destined for eternal destruction. This ash is scattered by the whirlwind, because “God shall come manifestly, our God, and shall not be silent; fire shall blaze before him, and a mighty tempest round about him” (Ps. XLIX, 2). By the whirlwind of this tempest the wicked are snatched away from the sight of the eternal Judge; and those who here had made their minds firm in perverse desire will there appear as chaff and ashes, because the carrying whirlwind bears them away to eternal punishments.

## CHAPTER XXIII. ON AWNS

[Note: [Col. 0436D] From Book XVI on Job, chapter VI.] By “awns” are signified reprobate rich people, as Job says concerning their damnation: “And they shall be crushed like the tops of ears of grain” (Job XXIV, 24). The tops of ears are awns. Awns grow joined together in the ear, but as they grow a little, they separate from one another, becoming bristling and rigid. So indeed do the wicked rich rise to the glory of this world. They are joined by their common nature, but as they grow they divide against one another. One despises another, and one burns against another with the torches of envy.

Those, therefore, who separate themselves from the unity of charity through the swelling of the mind stand rigidly against one another like awns. What, then, shall I call the wicked rich of this world except certain awns of the human race? While they are proud against one another, they oppress the life of the good in concert. They are divided against one another, yet together press the grains downward. Now the awns leap upward and the grains lie hidden: the power of the reprobate stands out, while the glory of the elect is unseen. The former display themselves by the torches of honours; the latter humble themselves. But the time of threshing will come, which will break the rigidity of the awns without crushing the solid grains. Then the pride of the wicked is ground down, when it is disclosed with what integrity the life of the elect shines.

For when the unjust fail, the very crushing of the awns causes the grains that lay hidden to appear. When the awns are broken, the brightness of the grains is shown, because when the wicked fall into eternal punishments, the righteousness of the saints is displayed in the full truth of its brightness. Hence John also rightly says: “His winnowing fan is in his hand; he shall thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor, gather the wheat into his barns, and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matt. III, 12; Luke III, 17). Therefore let blessed Job consider with what judgment the exaltation of the wicked is broken, and, comparing them to perishing awns, say: “They shall be crushed like the tops of ears of grain,” because the rigidity of the proud, which now rises up in contempt of the life of the elect, is broken by fear of the final threshing.

## CHAPTER XXIV. ON THE STALK

[Note: [Col. 0436D] From Book VIII on Job, chapter XXV, §29.] By “stalk” is understood the hypocrite, as the prophet says: “There is no standing stalk in him; it shall not produce meal; and if it should produce it, strangers shall eat it” (Hos. VIII, 7). The stalk does not have a shoot when the life of the hypocrite lacks the merits of virtues. The stalk does not make meal when the person who prospers in this present age understands nothing subtle and yields no fruit of good work. Yet often, even if it does make meal, strangers eat it, because even when hypocrites display good works, the desires of malignant spirits are satisfied by them.
