Since they do not seek by these works to please God, they feed not the Lord of the field but strangers.

## CHAPTER XXV. ON STRAW
[Note: [Col. 0437D] From Book II on Job, chapter XXII, 24.] By the name “stubble” human abjection is understood, as is said through blessed Job: “You display your power against a leaf carried away by the wind, and you pursue dry stubble” (Job XIII, 15). For what is man but a leaf, since he fell from the tree in paradise? What is man but a leaf, since he is carried away by the wind of temptation and lifted by the gusts of desires? For the human mind is moved by as many gusts, as it suffers temptations. It is greatly disturbed in this way: when anger withdraws, foolish joy succeeds. It is pressed by the spurs of lust; by the heat of avarice it is stretched far and wide to acquire earthly things. At one time pride raises it up; at another, disordered fear casts it down among low things. Therefore, because he is raised and driven by the gusts of so many temptations, man is rightly compared to a leaf. Hence Isaiah also aptly says: “We have all fallen like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, have carried us away” (Isa. LXIV, 6). Iniquity carried us away like a wind, because it raised us—unfixed by any weight of virtue—into vain exaltation. Man is also aptly called stubble after the leaf. For he who was a tree in his creation made himself a leaf in temptation; but afterward he appeared as stubble in his abasement. Since the leaf fell from on high, and since through the flesh it was close to the earth even when it seemed to stand, he is remembered also as stubble. But because he has lost the greenness of inward love, he is now dry stubble. Let the holy man therefore consider how great is man’s worthlessness, and how great God’s strictness, and say: “You display your power against a leaf carried away by the wind, and you pursue dry stubble.” As though he openly lamented, saying: Why do you assail with such strict justice one whom you know to be so weak in temptation?

## HERE BEGINS THE FIFTEENTH BOOK

[Col. 0437]

### 618 CHAPTER I. ON UNITY

[Col. 0437C]

In Holy Scripture, by the name of unity is sometimes denoted the beginning of living well, and sometimes Christ God, the Redeemer of the human race.

[Note: [Col. 0437D] Here Garner repeated the words “man” and “God,” in place of the demonstrative pronouns found in Job.] By the name “one” the beginning of living well is denoted, as is said through blessed Job: “If a man should wish to contend with God, he will not be able to answer him one thing out of a thousand” (Job IX, 3). In Holy Scripture the number one thousand is customarily used for universality. Hence the Psalmist says: “Of the word which he commanded for a thousand generations” (Ps. CIV, 8). [Note: [Col. 0438D] From Book IX on Job, chapter II.] Since it is certainly established that from the beginning of the world until the coming of the Redeemer no more than seventy-seven generations are counted by the Evangelist, what is expressed in the number one thousand but the complete universality of the foreknown generation, for the bringing forth of a new offspring? Hence John also says: “And they shall reign with him for a thousand years” (Rev. XX, 2), because the kingdom of the holy Church is made firm by the perfection of universality.

But because the monad, multiplied by ten, is brought to ten; and ten, multiplied by itself, is expanded to one hundred; and this, again multiplied by ten, reaches one thousand—when we begin from one in order to arrive at one thousand—what is designated here by the name “one” but the beginning of living well, and what by the extent of the number one thousand but the perfection of that same good life? To contend with God, however, is not to attribute glory to him, but to arrogate to oneself the glory of one’s own virtue. But let the holy man observe that one who has already received the highest gifts, if he exalts himself over what he has received, loses all that he had received, and say: “If a man should wish to contend with God, he will not be able to answer him one thing out of a thousand.” For one who contends with his Creator cannot answer one for a thousand, because one who raises himself up by reason of perfection shows that he does not possess even the beginning of living well. We cannot answer one for a thousand, because, when we exalt ourselves over the perfection of a good life, we show that we have not even begun it.

[Note: [Col. 0438D] For more on unity see Clicthoveus, *On the Significance of Numbers*, and Odo, Abbot of Morimond, and Federicus Morellus, in the poem *On One*.] By the name “one” our Redeemer is denoted, as is said through Ezekiel, when he was speaking of the threshold and the gate, the border and the panels: “And one cubit was the end of both” (Ezek. XL, 12). “Both” is said, as though it were said, “of the two.” For by the breadth of the threshold and the length of the gate we have said that the Old and New Testaments are denoted. But at the end it is added that one cubit is the end of both, because both the Old Testament announced to us the one mediator between God and men, and the New Testament announces that this same one will come in eternal glory, whom we have already known as incarnate for us. Therefore one cubit is the end of both: because he whom the Law foretold appeared in the flesh; and he whom the New Testament now speaks of in hope will appear in the glory of majesty. And then he will be the end of both, when, seen in the power of his divinity, he has fulfilled all that was foretold. For it is written: “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4).

[Note: [Col. 0439D] From Homily 16 on Ezekiel, after the middle.] He is an end, plainly, not one that destroys, but one that perfects. For then he perfects the Law, when, as the Law foretold, he appeared incarnate. But the New Testament still speaks much about his judgment; it still tells much about his kingdom, things that we do not yet see fulfilled. Therefore he will also then be the end of the New Testament, when he has fulfilled what it promised concerning him. The New Testament will be ended because it will be perfected. For when he of whom it speaks has been seen, the words of that Testament will cease. Therefore one cubit is the end of both, because one is he who said: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. CXL, 10). He alone presides in heaven with the Father and the Holy Spirit, like a solitary sparrow upon a building. And as he fulfilled the Law through the mystery of his Incarnation and perfect humanity, so he will fulfill the promises of the New Testament through the manifested glory of his brightness.

### CHAPTER II. ON THE NUMBER TWO

In Holy Scripture, the number two sometimes denotes the two commandments of charity—namely, love of God and of neighbor; sometimes understanding and action; sometimes those perfected in charity; sometimes the two kinds of compunction; and sometimes the two Testaments.

By the number two are denoted the two commandments of charity, namely love of God and of neighbor, as Ezekiel says: “And he measured the front of the gate by two cubits” (Ezek. XL, 9). [Note: [Col. 0439D] The Vulgate has the pronoun “its” in place of the word “gate.”] The front of the gate is the merit of the present life. For as the inner vestibule ought to be understood as heavenly rest, so by the front of the gate the quality of visible life must be signified.

[Note: [Col. 0439D] From Homily 16 on Ezekiel, somewhat far from the beginning.] Therefore the front of the gate is measured by two cubits, because whoever strives here to keep love of God and neighbor reaches the court of eternity. Thus our life, in order to be measured by two cubits, must daily be stretched through charity toward love of God and neighbor together. For charity is not genuine if it has less than two cubits. Hence Moses, when through the colors of the garments he expressed the virtues of the elect in the priestly ornament, commanded scarlet twice dyed to be used (Exod. XXVIII, 5). For what is denoted by scarlet but charity, which is always kindled with the flame of love? Yet the scarlet is dyed twice when our charity is inflamed not only by love of God but also of neighbor. For whoever loves God in such a way as to abandon care for those entrusted to him still has scarlet dyed only once. And whoever loves his neighbor in such a way as to diminish the desire with which he ought to burn toward God does not yet have the color of double dyeing. Therefore we must both love those with whom we live and pant with all our desires toward him in whom we truly live.

[Note: [Col. 0439D] These matters are somewhat disconnected from the preceding.] Thus scarlet is doubly dyed in us if we love our neighbors here as ourselves and hasten, together with those whom we love, toward the author of all things. Therefore, if our life is twice dyed with perfect charity, the front of the gate in us is measured by two cubits. Whether, then, a teacher, sacred speech, or indeed faith is signified by the name of gate, charity is fittingly understood in the measure of each cubit. For one truly preaches who teaches love of God and neighbor; charity is itself the certain knowledge that builds up; and faith is robust when it exercises itself in delight in God and neighbor.

[Note: [Col. 0440D] From Homily 9 on the Gospels.] By the number two are denoted understanding and action, as the voice of Truth says in the Gospel: “A certain man, going abroad, called his servants and delivered his goods to them; and to one he gave five talents, but to another two, and to another one” (Matt. XX, 14–15). For by the five talents is expressed the gift of the five senses, that is, external knowledge. But by two are denoted understanding and action; by the name of one talent, understanding alone is denoted.

[Col. 0440C] [Note: [Col. 0440D] From Homily 17 on the Gospels.] By the number two are denoted those perfected in charity, as Luke says in the Gospel: “The Lord also appointed another seventy-two and sent them two by two before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come” (Luke X, 1). Our Lord and Savior sometimes admonishes us by words, sometimes by deeds. For his deeds themselves are commandments, because when he silently does something, he makes known what we ought to do. See, then, that he sends them two by two to preach; for there are two commandments of charity, namely love of God and of neighbor, and charity cannot exist between fewer than two. For no one is properly said to have charity toward himself; rather, he stretches himself in love toward another, that charity may exist. The Lord sends disciples two by two to preach, so that he may silently indicate to us that one who does not have charity toward another ought in no way to undertake the office of preaching.

By the number two are signified the two kinds of compunction, concerning which see Book III, chapter 3, distinction 6.

[Note: [Col. 0440D] From Homily 6 on Ezekiel, a little after the middle.] By the number two are denoted the two Testaments, as the Lord says to Moses: “You shall also make two golden cherubim, of beaten work, at each end of the oracle. Let one cherub be at one side and the other at the other side, so that they cover both sides of the mercy-seat, spreading their wings and covering the oracle; and let them look toward one another, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat” (Exod. XXVIII, 18). For what is signified by the mercy-seat but the mediator himself between God and men, of whom Paul says: “Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood” (Rom. III, 23)? And what is signified by the two cherubim, said to be “fullness of knowledge,” but the two Testaments? One of them stands at one end of the mercy-seat and the other at the other end, because what the Old Testament began to promise prophetically concerning the Incarnation of our Redeemer, the New Testament perfectly recounts as fulfilled. The two cherubim are made of purest gold because both Testaments are set forth in pure and simple truth. They spread their wings and cover the oracle because we, who are the oracle of almighty God, are protected from impending faults by the edifice of Holy Scripture. As we attentively consider its sayings, we are veiled by wings from the error of ignorance. The two cherubim look toward one another, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat, because the two Testaments differ from each other in nothing and, as it were, keep their faces turned mutually toward one another, because what one promises, the other presents, while they behold the mediator between God and men placed between them.

[Note: [Col. 0441D] These precede the foregoing.] The cherubim would turn their faces away from one another if one Testament promised what the other denied. But since they speak harmoniously concerning the mediator between God and men, in mutually looking upon one another they direct their attention to the mercy-seat. For what the Old Testament signified, the New Testament displayed. To mention a few things out of many: what does it mean that, while Adam sleeps, Eve is brought forth (Gen. XI), except that, when Christ dies, the Church is formed? What does it mean that Isaac is led to be sacrificed, carries the wood, is laid upon the altar, and lives, except that our Redeemer, led to his Passion, himself carried the wood of his cross, and died for us in sacrifice according to his humanity, while nevertheless remaining immortal according to his divinity?

[Note: [Col. 0441D] These words occur in Gregory some lines before the words from Ezekiel: “they went by their four sides.” For other material on the number two see chapter 2 above of the cited work of Clicthoveus, and Adrianus Turnebus in the poem *On the Number Two*.] What does it mean that a homicide, after the death of the high priest, is released and returns to his own land, except that the human race, which by sinning brought death upon itself, after the death of the true priest—namely our Redeemer—is freed from the bonds of its sins and restored to possession of paradise? Therefore the two cherubim rightly look toward one another, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat, because, as we have already said, what the Old Testament promised, the New Testament displayed; and what the former secretly announces, the latter openly proclaims as accomplished. Therefore the Old Testament is prophecy of the New Testament, and the New Testament is exposition of the Old Testament.

### 624 CHAPTER III. ON THE NUMBER THREE

[Col. 0442A]

In Holy Scripture, the number three sometimes denotes the three principal virtues—faith, hope, and charity; sometimes faith in the Holy Trinity; sometimes the three kinds of sin, namely of deed, speech, and thought; and sometimes the three periods of the present life.

[Note: [Col. 0442D] From Book I on Job, chapter XII, 28.] By the number three are denoted the three principal virtues, as is said of Job: “There were born to him seven sons and three daughters” (Job I, 2). For seven sons are born to us when, through the conception of good thought, the seven virtues of the Holy Spirit arise in us. He enumerates this inward offspring when the Spirit makes the mind fruitful, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI, 2). Therefore, when through the coming of the Holy Spirit wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord are generated in the soul of each one of us, an enduring offspring is, as it were, propagated in the mind. It preserves the stock of our heavenly nobility for life all the longer insofar as it joins it to love of eternity. But the seven sons have their three sisters in us, because whatever manly work these dispositions of the virtues perform, they join to faith, hope, and charity. For the seven sons would not attain the perfection of ten unless everything they do were in hope, faith, and charity.

[Col. 0442C] By the number three is denoted faith in the Holy Trinity, as is said through the prophet Ezekiel: “Moreover, the chambers by the way of the eastern gate were three on this side and three on that” (Ezek. XL). [Note: [Col. 0442D] Clicthoveus and William, Abbot of Albaeripae, manuscript in the Victorine Library, advance some observations on the number three.] For he himself is the way for us who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” He is also the eastern way, of whom it is written: “Behold, the man whose name is the East” (ibid. VI, 12). Those, however, who in the holy Church know how to behold the Lord with love for the grain, and are already joined to him by desire, are called chambers. But what does it mean that it is said, “three on this side and three on that”? The chambers near the eastern way are hearts fervent in the love of God. Whether those who were chosen in the Old Testament or those who followed in the New Testament, it is clearly established that all were kindled with love. For they could not truly love the Lord unless they had received the grace of that Trinity which is God.

[Note: [Col. 0442D] From Homily 16 on Ezekiel, after the beginning.] Therefore, three chambers on this side and three on that are by the eastern way because, while the Lord deigned to become incarnate among the old and new Fathers, the eastern way appeared, as it were, in the midst of the chambers; and these chambers are adorned unto true beauty by knowledge of the Trinity. But if we refer the same number to the virtues of the elect, there are three virtues without which one already able to act cannot be saved: faith, hope, and charity. And because the same hope, faith, and charity were present in the ancient Fathers as in the new teachers, three chambers on this side and three on that are described by the eastern way.

[Note: [Col. 0443D] From Book II on Job, chapter XXV, 35.] By the number three are denoted the three kinds of sins in life, namely of deed, speech, and thought; and a messenger is reported to have said to blessed Job: “The Chaldeans formed three companies, invaded the camels, and took them; and they also struck the servants with the sword, and I alone escaped to tell you” (Job I, 17). By camels, which have something clean because they chew the cud and something unclean because they do not divide the hoof, are understood good dispensations of temporal things.

[Note: [Col. 0443D] These words are separated from the foregoing by several periods.] To form, as it were, three companies against the camels is to lay waste the endeavors of earthly stewardship now by unlawful action, now by superfluous speech, now by disordered thought. Thus, while the mind strives to extend itself effectively outward in service, it is separated from consideration of itself and, the more energetically it works over others’ affairs than is fitting, the less it knows the losses that it suffers in itself. But when a right mind undertakes the cares of stewardship, it considers what it owes to itself and what to its neighbors; it neither neglects its own concerns through excess in concern for another, nor puts aside those of another through watchfulness over its own advantage. Yet often, while the mind vigilantly attends to both, while it gives itself to great circumspection concerning itself and the matters entrusted to it, suddenly disturbed by the unexpected onset of some arising circumstance, it is so swept headlong away that all its precautions are suddenly overwhelmed. Thus the Chaldeans strike the young servants, guardians of the camels, with the sword; yet one returns, because amid these things the principle of discernment comes before the eyes of our mind, and the soul, solicitous for itself, understands what it inwardly loses through the sudden assault of temptation.

[Note: [Col. 0443D] From Homily 31 on the Gospels.] The number three denotes the three periods of the present life, namely before the Law, under the Law, and under grace, as the voice of Truth says in the Gospel: “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. Then he said to the cultivator of the vineyard: Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and find none” (Luke XIII, 7). For what does the fig tree signify but human nature? It was indeed well planted like a fig tree, but having voluntarily fallen into its own fault, it does not retain the fruit of action. For, falling into sin by its will because it refused to bear the fruit of obedience, it lost its state of rectitude. Created in God’s likeness, when it did not remain in its own dignity, it despised to preserve that for which it had been planted. But the Lord of the vineyard comes to the fig tree a third time because, by waiting for, admonishing, and visiting human nature before the Law, under the Law, and under grace, he sought it out. He says to the cultivator of the vineyard: “Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and find none.” For he came before the Law because through natural understanding he made known what each person ought, by his own example, to do toward his neighbor. He came in the Law because he taught by commanding. He came after the Law through grace because, by displaying the presence of his compassion, he made it manifest. Yet he complains that he has found no fruit in three years because the minds of some wicked persons are corrected neither by the inspired natural law, nor instructed by commandments, nor converted by the miracles of his Incarnation.

### CHAPTER IV. ON THE NUMBER FOUR

In Holy Scripture, the number four sometimes denotes the four Evangelists; sometimes the sayings of the Evangelists; sometimes the principal virtues; sometimes the four Gospels; and sometimes the four regions of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0443D] On the number four see again Jodocus Clicthoveus, [Col. 0444D] chapter 4, *On the Mystical Significance of Numbers*, and William, Abbot of Albaeripae.] By the number four are understood the four Evangelists, as Ezekiel says: “And in the midst of it was the likeness of four living creatures” (Ezek. I, 5); and a little later: “And the likeness of their faces was the face of a man, and the face of a lion on the right hand of the four” (ibid. XLI, 19). See the chapter on the lion, Book III, chapter 17, distinction 2.

By the number four are understood the sayings of the four Evangelists. See the chapter on columns, Book XII, chapter 16, distinction 3.

By the number four are denoted the four principal virtues, as may be seen in Book I, chapter 13, distinction 2.

[Note: [Col. 0444D] Gregory, however, repeats the word “face” from the following verse.] By the number four are denoted the four Gospels, as the Lord says to Moses: “You shall make four golden rings, which you shall place at the four corners of the ark: two rings shall be on one side and two on the other. You shall also make bars of setim wood and cover them with gold; and you shall put them through the rings on the sides of the ark, so that it may be carried by them. They shall always remain in the rings and shall never be withdrawn from them” (Exod. XXV, 12–15).

[Note: [Col. 0444D] From Part II of the *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 11.] For what is figured by the ark but the holy Church? Four golden rings are commanded to be joined to it at its four corners because, as it is extended through the four regions of the world, it is undoubtedly proclaimed as girded with the four books of the holy Gospel. Bars are also made of setim wood and inserted into the same rings to carry it, because strong and persevering teachers, like incorruptible wood, must be sought. Always adhering to the instruction of the sacred books, they proclaim the unity of the holy Church and, as it were inserted through the rings, carry the ark. For the bars carry the ark when good teachers convey the holy Church to the untaught minds of unbelievers by preaching. They are also commanded to be covered with gold, so that while they make their speech resound to others, they themselves may shine with the splendor of life. Of them it is aptly added: “They shall always remain in the rings and shall never be withdrawn from them.” For those who keep watch for the office of preaching must never withdraw from the study of sacred reading. The bars are commanded always to remain in the rings so that, when occasion requires the ark to be carried, no delay may arise from having to insert the bars; that is, when a pastor is asked by those under his care about something spiritual, it is highly shameful if he then seeks to learn when he ought to resolve the question. Let the bars therefore always adhere in the rings, so that teachers, always meditating in their hearts upon the sacred sayings, may raise the ark of the covenant without delay and promptly teach whatever is necessary. Hence the first shepherd of the Church admonishes the other shepherds, saying: “Always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks concerning the hope that is in us” (1 Pet. III, 15). As though he openly said: So that no delay may hinder the carrying of the ark, let the bars never withdraw from the rings.

[Note: [Col. 0445D] Here the author referred the reader to chapter 20, Book V, but nothing relevant occurs.] By the number four are understood the four regions of the world: east, west, south, and north.

### 629 CHAPTER V. ON THE NUMBER SIX

In Holy Scripture, the number six sometimes signifies the perfection of the matter under discussion, sometimes the perfection of the active life, and sometimes the six ages of this world.

[Note: [Col. 0445D] From Book XXXV on Job, chapter XI, at the end, §19.] By the number six is understood the perfection of the matter under discussion. Thus, in the restoration of his lost possessions, blessed Job received six thousand camels in place of three thousand (Job XLII, 12). For the number six is considered perfect in secular learning because it is the first number completed by its own parts: namely its sixth, its third, and its half, which are one, two, and three, and which taken together make six. No other number before six is found whose whole sum, when divided, is completed by its own parts. But when we rise above this through the sublimity of Holy Scripture, there we find why six is perfect. For the number six is perfect in Holy Scripture because, at the beginning of the world, the Lord completed on the sixth day the works which he began on the first.

[Note: [Col. 0446D] These matters are far removed from the foregoing.] But the number one thousand is called perfect in sacred speech because by its designation is signified the universality of the matter under discussion. By camels, moreover, we understand those who rise above others’ evils, overflowing with the twisted mass of vices. Therefore blessed Job received six thousand camels because the holy Church received fullness of work in the conversion of those who had formerly perished in the foulness of their sins.

By the number six is denoted the perfection of the active life, as is said to Moses: “If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve six years; in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing. With whatever garment he entered, with the same shall he go out. If he had a wife, his wife shall go out with him. But if his master gave him a wife, and she bore sons and daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master; he himself shall go out with his garment. But if the servant says: ‘I love my master, and my wife and children; I will not go out free,’ his master shall bring him before the gods, and he shall be brought to the door and the doorposts, and his ear shall be pierced with an awl; and he shall be his servant forever” (Exod. XXI, 2–6).

[Note: [Col. 0446D] From Homily 3 on Ezekiel.] “Hebrew” is interpreted “passing over.” And a Hebrew servant is bought when each person who now passes in mind beyond this world is subjected to the service of almighty God. For he truly desires to serve God who has learned to pass beyond this world. Thus Moses passes over in order to see the vision (Exod. III); thus David, when he saw the wicked exalted and raised above the cedars of Lebanon, passed over, “and behold, he was not” (Ps. XXXVI, 35). For perhaps we think the powers of the wicked to be something great unless in mind we pass beyond the enduring world.

The purchased Hebrew servant is commanded to serve six years, so that in the seventh he may go out free for nothing. What, then, is signified by the number six but the perfection of the active life? And what is expressed by the number seven but the contemplative life? Therefore he serves six years and goes out free in the seventh, because through the active life which he has fulfilled perfectly, he passes to the freedom of the contemplative life. And it should be observed that he goes out free for nothing, because after they have done all things, they say that they are unprofitable servants; and without doubt, just as the active life was itself a gift, so also the contemplative life will be by grace.

“With whatever garment he entered, with the same shall he go out,” because it is altogether necessary that each of us persevere, to the end of his work, in that which he begins, and remain in the intention which he has undertaken. For one passes to the contemplative life who has not changed the garment of his intention for worse in the active life. Some, before they are joined in holy conduct to the service of almighty God, already love to perform good works. Others learn good works before they come to the service of almighty God. Therefore the person who strove to have good action before coming to the service of God is bought as a Hebrew servant with a wife. And often such a person can pass to the contemplative life and yet not abandon the active life. Hence it is added there: “If he had a wife, his wife shall go out with him.” For the wife also goes out with him to freedom when one who has attained contemplation does not abandon outwardly the action of a good work by which he may benefit others.

“But if his master gave him a wife, and she bore him sons and daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master; he himself shall go out with his garment.” The master gives a wife to the purchased servant when a preacher joins to good action one whom he has subjected to the authority of almighty God. For preachers too are called masters, as it is said to the prophet Elisha concerning his preacher: “Do you know that your master shall be taken away from you?” (4 Kings II, 5). [Note: [Col. 0446D] In the Vulgate this sentence is presented more concisely.] The wife of the purchased servant bears sons and daughters when good action produces strong or tender fruits. But the woman whom the master gave remains with that same master together with her children, while the servant himself goes out with his garment, because good action and the fruits of that good action are reckoned to the preacher’s reward. He himself, however, continuing in the intention of his desire, goes out free to contemplation through heavenly grace.

“But if the servant says: ‘I love my master, and my wives and children; I will not go out free.’” The servant loves his master when he keeps the preacher’s words in an attentive mind. Loving also his wife and children, he refuses to go out free when, loving the active life and its fruits, he does not wish to pass to the contemplative life, because, seeing that he has good works in the service of his ministry, he refuses to withdraw to the repose of freedom. “But let his master bring him before the gods, and let him be brought to the door and the doorposts, and let his ear be pierced with an awl, that he may be his servant forever.” One who has resolved to remain in the active life is brought by the Lord before the gods when he is instructed by his preacher in the sayings of the ancient Fathers, who were priests to us in the way of almighty God. And he is brought to the door and doorposts of the tabernacle so that he may hear something concerning entrance into the heavenly dwelling and may understand closely the day of dreadful judgment, lest through the good works that he performs he seek to please men. Thus his ear is pierced with an awl when his mind is struck with the penetrating fear of God; pierced by the sharp point of God’s word, through all that he does it knows always to attend to the entrance of the kingdom and, as it were, to bear a pierced ear from the door and doorpost of the tabernacle. He shall be his servant in this age so that after the age he may be free. For he is a servant in this age who has resolved through the active life to serve men, so that after the present age he may be able to attain true freedom, of which Paul says: “Because creation itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. VIII, 21). For then true freedom shall be ours when our adoption has attained the glory of the children of God.

But now not only is the active life in servitude; contemplation itself is also so. For although we are caught up above ourselves, it does not yet perfectly possess freedom of mind, but imitates it, because that inward rest is seen in a mirror, darkly. Yet however narrow contemplation may be, the active life is already much broader and more sublime when it passes to a certain freedom of the mind, thinking not of temporal things but of eternal ones.

[Note: [Col. 0447D] On the number six, see also Clicthoveus in the same place, and William, Abbot of Albaeripae, chapter 4.] By the number six are denoted the six ages of this world, as the prophet Ezekiel says: “Behold, six men came by the way of the upper gate, which looked toward the north, and each had an inner vessel in his hand” (Exod. XXXVI, 25). See again Book III, chapter 2, distinction 5.

### CHAPTER VI. ON THE NUMBER SEVEN

[Col. 0448A]

In Holy Scripture, the number seven sometimes denotes the height of perfection; sometimes the rest to come; sometimes the whole of temporality; sometimes the universality of the holy Church; sometimes the fullness of the operation of the sevenfold Spirit; and sometimes the seven virtues.

633. [Note: [Col. 0447D] From Book XXXV on Job, chapter 7 before the middle, and [Col. 0448D] Book I, chapter 6, §12, excerpted.] By the number seven the height of perfection is signified, as is said of blessed Job: “And there were born to him seven sons and three daughters” (Job 1:2). For among the wise men of this world the number seven is held, by a certain reasoning of their own, to be perfect, because it is completed from the first even and the first odd number: from the first number that can be divided and the first that cannot be divided. [Col. 0448B] For the first even number is four, and the first odd number is three; from these two seven consists, and when multiplied by those same parts it rises to twelve. For whether we multiply three by four or four by three, we arrive at twelve. But we who receive the proclamations of heavenly truth tread these matters underfoot, looking down upon them from the fixed height of doctrine. We hold this without any doubt by unshaken faith: that those whom the sevenfold Spirit of grace has filled, he perfects by granting them not only knowledge of the Trinity, but also the practice of the four virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. In those persons too whom he enters, he is in some manner increased by his parts: both because through knowledge of the Trinity the action of the four virtues is received, and because through the operation [Col. 0448C] of the four virtues one comes even to the manifest vision of the Trinity. Thus among us also there is a seven, but very differently, because it rises fully and expressly to twelve, while through faith it perfects works, and again through works it perfects faith. The holy apostles too, to be filled with the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, were chosen as twelve; for they were sent to make known in the four regions of the world the Trinity which is God. Therefore twelve were chosen, so that even from the rationale of the number itself it might be clear that through the four lower things they preached the three highest things. Whether for this or for any other reason, we know most certainly that Sacred Scripture is accustomed to use the number seven for perfection. Therefore seven sons were born to blessed [Col. 0448D] Job for preaching: namely, the apostles, advancing manfully, who, while carrying out the precepts of perfection, maintained in their conduct, as it were, the strength of the superior sex.

634. [Note: [Col. 0448D] From Book XXXV on Job, chapter 7, §6.] By the number seven the coming rest of eternity is understood, when the seventh day is set apart for the Lord’s rest, and is said no longer to contain an evening, because the rest of eternal blessedness is bounded by no limit. Hence also, when the law was given, the seventh day was commanded to be kept as a festival, that eternal rest might be signified by it. Hence, in the course [Col. 0449A] of years, the number seven, multiplied seven times and with one unit added, is brought to fifty, so that the most sacred rest of Jubilee, signifying perpetual blessedness, may be observed. Hence it is that the risen Lord, appearing frequently, is described at his final meal as having eaten with seven disciples, because those who are now made perfect through him are satisfied by him with eternal refreshment.

[Note: [Col. 0449D] From the same book and chapter.] By the number seven this whole realm of temporality is understood. For it is through seven days that the whole duration of this present life unfolds. Hence also, in the figure of the holy Church which goes around the world at every time in preaching, the ark of the Lord, with trumpets sounding, circled and broke down the walls of Jericho over seven days (Joshua 6:4). Hence the Prophet says: [Col. 0449B] “Seven times a day I have spoken praise to thee” (Ps. 118:164). Indicating again that he had said this throughout the whole and entire time of his prayer, he says: “His praise is always in my mouth” (Ps. 33:2). But that the number seven denotes the totality of the present life is shown still more clearly when the number eight is also introduced after it. For when another follows the seven, the very force of this sequence expresses that temporality is to be ended and enclosed by eternity.

By the number seven the universality of the holy Church is signified. Thus John writes in the Apocalypse “to the seven churches” (Rev. 1:4); but through them what else did he intend to be understood except the universal Church? [Col. 0449C] And in order that this universal Church might be signified as full of the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, Elisha is described as having yawned seven times over the dead boy (4 Kings 4). For when the Lord comes upon the dead people, he, as it were, yawns seven times, since in mercy he breathes into it the gifts of the Spirit’s sevenfold grace.

635. By the number seven the fullness of the operation of the sevenfold Spirit is understood, as it is said through the prophet Zechariah concerning our Redeemer under the figure of a stone: “Upon one stone are seven eyes.” See the chapter on the Pleiades, Book I, chapter 9, distinction 2.

[Note: [Col. 0449D] If you wish, add Clicthoveus to these.] By the number seven the seven virtues are understood which arise in the hearts of believers through the working of the Holy Spirit: namely wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord [Col. 0449D] [Note: William, Abbot of Albaeripae, chapter 8; and Clicthoveus, chapters 7 and 8.]. Hence also what we have said above about Job’s children may fittingly be understood in a moral sense: “There were born to him seven sons and three daughters.” For seven sons are born to us when, through the conception of good thought, the Holy Spirit’s seven virtues arise in us. The prophet enumerates this inner offspring when the Spirit makes the mind fruitful, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and [Col. 0450A] piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:2–3). [Note: [Col. 0449D] From Book I on Job, chapter 2, §28.] Therefore, when through the coming of the Holy Spirit wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord are begotten in the soul of each one of us, a lasting posterity is, as it were, propagated in the mind. It preserves the lineage of our heavenly nobility for life all the more enduringly insofar as it joins it to love of eternity. But these seven sons undoubtedly have their three sisters in us, because whatever manly thing these perceptions of the virtues do, they join to hope, faith, and charity. For the seven sons would not attain the perfection of ten unless all that they do were in hope, faith, and charity.

## Chapter VII. On the Number Eight

[Col. 0450B] [Note: [Col. 0449D] Add William, Abbot of Albaeripae, chapter 9, and Clicthoveus, [Col. 0450D] chapter 7.] By the number eight the day of eternal judgment and the resurrection of the flesh are signified, as is said through Ezekiel: “And he measured the vestibule of the gate: eight cubits” (Ezek. 40:9). And lest we should think this vestibule to be outside the gate, it is added: “But the vestibule of the gate was inward.” What then is signified by the inward vestibule except the spaciousness of eternal life, which is now conceived in hope within the straits of the present life? Of it the Psalmist says: “Enter into his gates with confession, into his courts with hymns of praise” (Ps. 99:1). [Note: [Col. 0450D] From the beginning of Homily 16 on Ezekiel.] For when we confess our sins through tears, we enter the narrow gate of life. [Note: [Col. 0450D] But Augustine reads it thus in the Psalms.] But when after this we are led to eternal life, we enter the courts of our gates with praises of confession, [Col. 0450C] because there will then be no narrowness, when the joy of eternal solemnity has received us. Because of the narrowness of our confession, Truth says: “Enter by the narrow gate” (Matt. 7:13). And when the Psalmist presumed that he would receive the joys of eternal spaciousness, he said: “Thou hast set my feet in a spacious place” (Ps. 30:9). Therefore one advances to the court through the gate, because one comes to the breadth of solemnity from the narrowness of confession. Thus those joys which David calls courts are called by Ezekiel the inward vestibule. Hence this very vestibule is said to be measured by eight cubits. For there all are to be received who now labor in the exercise of works and sigh after eternal joys through the grace of contemplation. Nor without reason is the measure [Col. 0450D] of the vestibule set at eight cubits, because all time unfolds through seven days. For the eternal day which follows the completed succession of seven days is the eighth. Therefore the inward vestibule is measured by eight cubits, because through the light which follows the seven days the spaciousness of eternity is opened to us.

## Chapter VIII. On the Number Nine

[Note: [Col. 0450D] See William, Abbot of Albaeripae, chapter 10, and Clicthoveus, chapter 8.] By the number nine the nine orders of angels [Col. 0451A] are signified, as the prophet, speaking of the fall of the ancient enemy and indicating the loftiness of his condition and the power of his primacy, says among other things: “Every precious stone was thy covering: sard, topaz, and jasper; chrysolite, onyx, and beryl; sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald” (Ezek. 28:13). He named nine kinds of stones, because there are plainly nine orders of angels. For when in the sacred words themselves angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, virtues, principalities, powers, cherubim, and seraphim are mentioned in explicit enumeration as citizens of heaven, the distinctions among the heavenly citizens are shown. [Note: [Col. 0451D] Besides these, read William of Albaeripae.] Yet the ancient enemy is described as having been covered by them, because he had them as a garment for his adornment, and because, while he surpassed their brightness, he was brighter by comparison with them.

## Chapter IX. On the Number Ten

[Note: [Col. 0451D] Here the reader was referred to Book IV, but he will see nothing relevant to the purpose; nevertheless, read Homily 34 on the Gospels.] By the number ten the nature of angels and human beings is signified, as Truth says in the Gospel: “Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it?” (Luke 15:8).

# Book Sixteen Begins

[Col. 0451]

## 638. Chapter I. On Vessels

[Col. 0451B]

In Sacred Scripture, when “vessel” is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies a holy preacher, sometimes any undisciplined person, and sometimes the capacity of our understanding. When “vessels” is used in the plural, it sometimes signifies the holy Fathers, sometimes the souls of believing peoples, and sometimes our consciences.

[Note: [Col. 0451D] Book XII on Job, chapter 12, §11; but Gregory does not expressly interpret it here [Col. 0452D].] By “vessel” a holy preacher is understood, as the Lord says to Ananias in the Acts of the Apostles concerning Paul after his conversion: “He is for me a chosen vessel, to bear my name before the Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel” (Acts 9:15).

By “vessel” any disciplined person is understood, as the Lord says to Moses: “A vessel [Col. 0451C] that has no covering or binding over it shall be unclean” (Num. 19:14). 639. [Note: [Col. 0452D] From Book XXIII on Job, chapter 5, §9.] For the lid’s covering or binding is the restraint of discipline. Whoever is not held down by it is rejected as unclean and defiled. For the person who is exposed through a pursuit of display and is covered by no veil of silence is defiled like a vessel without a lid or binding.

[Note: [Col. 0452D] From Book XXX on Job, chapter 6, §10.] By “vessel” the capacity of our understanding is understood, as Moses says concerning the construction of the tabernacle: “Whatever was necessary for the worship and for the bars, men together with women offered: bracelets, earrings, rings, and ornaments for the right hand. Every golden vessel was set apart as an offering to the Lord. Whoever had blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, fine linen, and goats’ hair” (Exod. 35:22). [Col. 0451D] For men together with women offer gifts for the tabernacle’s adornment, because in fulfilling the worship of the holy Church both the exalted deeds of the strong and the lowly works of the weak are counted. What then is shown by bracelets, which bind the upper arms, except the vigorous works of laboring rulers? And what is expressed by earrings except the obedience of subjects? What is understood by rings except the seal of secret matters? For teachers often seal what they consider cannot be understood by their hearers. And what is shown by ornaments for the right hand except the adornments of foremost action? What is understood by a golden vessel set apart as an offering to the Lord except understanding of the Godhead, which is separated from love of lower things in proportion as it is raised to love only what is eternal? What is understood by blue except hope of heavenly things? By purple, except the bloodshed and endurance of sufferings offered out of love for the everlasting kingdom? And what is shown by twice-dyed [Col. 0452C] scarlet except charity, which is dyed with a twofold perfection because it is adorned by love of God and neighbour? What is understood by fine linen except the spotless incorruption of the flesh? And what is signified by goats’ hair, from which the roughness of haircloth is woven, except the severe affliction of penitents? Therefore, while some perhaps exercise teaching through bracelets and rings; others, through earrings and ornaments for the right hand, offer devoted obedience and upright action; others, through the separate golden vessel, possess a brilliant and more subtle understanding of God; others, through blue, purple, and scarlet, do not cease to hope, believe, and love the heavenly things they have heard, even those which they do not yet know by a more subtle understanding; others offer through fine linen the incorruption [Col. 0452D] of the flesh; others through goats’ hair bitterly lament what they willingly committed: thus from the lowly and equal service proceed the diverse deeds of believers.

[Note: [Col. 0452D] From Book XVIII on Job, chapter 27, §23, excerpted.] By “vessels” the holy Fathers are signified, [Col. 0453A] as is said through Job concerning wisdom: “Lofty and eminent vessels of gold shall not be exchanged for it” (Job 28:18). The lofty and eminent vessels of gold were the Fathers of old. But the wisdom of God, in order to redeem us from carnal conduct, appeared in the flesh; and whoever did not truly acknowledge it thought the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, to be one of the prophets. The eyes of the elect held him by faith to be God when they saw him as man. Hence he says to his holy disciples: “Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16:28). When they immediately answered him, “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets” (ibid., 8:28), they are at once asked for their own judgment: “But whom do you say that I am?” (ibid.). Peter immediately responds [Col. 0453B] in the voice of the whole Church: “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., 16:18). Since, therefore, in Paul’s words, we know Christ as “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24), Peter did not wish to exchange lofty and eminent vessels of gold for this wisdom, because he understood no other thing about it than what it was. John was indeed a great vessel of gold; Elijah or Jeremiah was a great vessel of gold. But whoever believes that the same Lord is any one of them has exchanged a lofty and eminent vessel of gold for wisdom. The Church, however, does not exchange lofty and eminent vessels of gold for this wisdom, because she believes Christ, the Son of God, not to be one of the prophets, but to be the one Lord of the prophets.

[Note: [Col. 0453D] From Book XXIII on Job, chapter 6, §12.] By “vessels” the souls [Col. 0453C] of believing peoples are signified, as Moses says concerning the Levites: “That from the twenty-fifth year they may serve the tabernacle, but from the fiftieth they may become guardians of the vessels” (Num. 8:11). What, indeed, is signified by the twenty-fifth year, in which the flower of youth arises, except the very battles against each vice? And what is expressed by the fiftieth, which also contains the rest of Jubilee, except the inward peace of the mind after the battle has been subdued? What then is figured by the vessels of the tabernacle except the souls of believers? Let the Levites, therefore, serve the tabernacle from the twenty-fifth year and become guardians of the vessels from the fiftieth, so that those who still endure, through consenting delight, the conflicts of attacking vices may not presume to undertake the care of others. But when they have subdued the wars of temptations and are now secure within themselves through inward tranquillity, let them receive the charge of souls. But who can bring these battles of temptation perfectly under his control, when Paul says: “I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind and leading me captive under the law of sin” (Rom. 7:23)? But it is one thing to endure battles bravely, another to be overcome by battles weakly. In the former, virtue is exercised lest it become proud; in the latter, it is utterly extinguished, lest it endure. Whoever, therefore, knows how bravely to bear the trial of conflict, even while shaken by temptation, presides in the lofty citadel of peace, because even within himself he sees below himself the [Col. 0454A] contentions of vices, to none of which he yields through a broken delight. Of these vessels the prophet then says: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52:11). [Note: [Col. 0453D] These things are from Part II of the *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 2.] They bear the Lord’s vessels who receive in the faith of their own conduct their neighbours’ souls, to be brought to the eternal sanctuary. Therefore let those who carry living vessels in the bosom of their own pledged responsibility to the temple of eternity consider how greatly they ought to be cleansed within themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0454D] From Homily 12 on the Gospels.] By “vessels” our consciences are signified, as Truth says: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins, who, taking their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and bride. Five of them were foolish and five prudent. But the five foolish, having taken their lamps, did not take [Col. 0454B] oil with them; whereas the prudent took oil in their vessels with their lamps” (Matt. 25:1–5). We must first ask what the kingdom of heaven is, and why it is compared with ten virgins, who are also called prudent and foolish virgins. For since it is certain that no reprobate enters the kingdom of heaven, why is it said to be like even foolish virgins? But it must be known that in Sacred Scripture the kingdom of heaven often means the Church of the present time, concerning which the Lord says elsewhere: “The Son of Man shall send his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all scandals” (Matt. 13:11). For scandals that may be gathered cannot be found in that kingdom of blessedness, in which supreme peace reigns. What then is understood by the kingdom [Col. 0454C] of heaven in this passage except the present Church? Each person exists in the five senses of the body, and the five doubled make ten. Since a multitude of believers is gathered from both sexes, the holy Church is declared to be like ten virgins. And because the wicked are mingled with the good, and the reprobate with the elect, it is rightly said to be like prudent and foolish virgins. For there are many continent people who guard themselves from outward desire and are drawn by hope to inward things; they mortify the flesh, sigh with all longing after the heavenly homeland, seek eternal rewards, and do not wish to receive human praise for their labours. Such people do not place their glory in human speech, but conceal it within [Col. 0454D] their conscience. And there are many who afflict their body by abstinence, but seek human favour from that very abstinence; they devote themselves to teaching and give generously to the needy. Yet they are surely foolish virgins, because they seek only the reward of passing praise. Hence it is aptly said: “The five foolish did not take oil with them, but the prudent took oil with them in their vessels together with their lamps.” For by oil is signified the brightness of glory. Our little vessels are our hearts, in which we carry all that we think. Therefore the prudent have oil in their vessels because they retain the brightness of glory within their conscience, as Paul testifies when he says: [Col. 0455A] “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:11). But the foolish virgins do not take oil with them, because they do not have glory within their conscience, while they seek it from the speech of their neighbours.

Likewise, by “vessels” our bodies are signified, as Paul says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7).

## 643. Chapter II. On the Ark

[Note: [Col. 0455D] From the final Homily on Ezekiel, before the end.] By “ark” our Redeemer is understood, as it is written in the law, where an altar of gold is commanded to be made before the ark (Exod. 40:5). For two altars are commanded by the law to be made in the tabernacle: one outside, the other inside; one in the court, the other before [Col. 0455B] the ark; one covered with bronze, the other clad with gold. On the bronze altar flesh is burned, while on the golden altar spices are burnt. What is this, dearest brothers, that flesh is burned outside and spices inside, except what we see every day: that there are two kinds of compunction? Some weep from fear, while others are moved to lament by love. For one kind of compunction arises from fear, another from love; for it is one thing to flee punishments, another to desire rewards. Many, remembering their sins and dreading eternal punishments, afflict themselves with daily tears, lament the evils they have committed, and burn away vices with the fire of compunction, though they still endure their promptings in the heart. What are these people but a bronze altar on which flesh burns? For they still lament their carnal works. But others, free from carnal vices or made secure by long weeping, burn with the flame of love in tears of compunction; with the eyes of their heart they gaze upon the rewards of the heavenly homeland and desire to dwell among the citizens above. Their servitude seems harsh to them, and their pilgrimage long; they desire to see the King in his beauty and do not cease daily to weep from love of him. What are these but a golden altar in whose heart spices are burned, because their virtues burn? It is well said of that altar that it is placed before the veil of the ark in the Holy of Holies. For the ark of the covenant is he of whom we know it is written: [Col. 0455D] “In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom” (Col. 2:3). The ark is within the veil: our Redeemer is in heaven. But the golden altar, on which incense is burnt, 644 is before the veil, because the hearts of the saints, kindled in God’s love with great virtues, burn through holy desire for him whom they cannot yet see with unveiled face. For a veil stands between the ark and the altar, because the obstacle of our corruption—which still separates us from the vision of God—has not been removed. But so long as we are before the veil, we must burn, like incense set aflame, with the fire of love. Through tears of compunction [Col. 0456A] we ought to seek nothing earthly, nothing passing away. He alone fulfils our desire who made all things. Let us pass beyond all things through desire, so that our mind may be gathered into one; no longer burning in tears from fear of punishments or remembrance of vices, but kindled by the flame of love with the fragrance of virtues.

[Note: [Col. 0456D] From Homily 16 on Ezekiel, after the middle.] By “ark” the present Church is signified, as the Lord says to Noah: “You shall make for yourself an ark of smoothed timbers. The ark shall be three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. You shall make a window in the ark, and shall bring its top to a cubit” (Gen. 6:14–15). What indeed is figured by the ark except the holy Church, which is broad within [Col. 0456B] and narrow above? It is gathered from three hundred, fifty, and thirty cubits into one cubit, because the breadth which the holy Church has in her members who are still weak, being gradually narrowed and advancing upward, tends toward one. Reason itself requires us to believe that in the breadth of that ark all the beasts, every four-footed creature, and creeping things were below, while human beings and birds were, of course, above. Near the upper part was a window in the side, from which the man sent out the raven or the dove, that he might discover whether the water of the flood had already passed away. Since the same ark was finished in one cubit, the man and the birds were near the cubit. Therefore the universal Church is rightly signified by the ark: she is still broad in her many carnal members [Col. 0456C] and narrow in her few spiritual members. And because she is gathered to the one man who is without sins, she is, as it were, completed in one cubit. For we see many within the bosom of this Church rising in pride, dissolving in fleshly pleasure, craving the acquisition of earthly goods, crossing the sea at the command of avarice, serving anger, engaging in quarrels, and injuring their neighbours when they have the power. But because the holy Church still tolerates them so as to convert them, beasts remain below in the breadth of the ark. We see others who no longer seek what belongs to others, bear injuries inflicted upon them with equanimity, are content with their own goods, and live humbly; but because these are already few, the ark is narrowed. Yet we see others even relinquish what they possess, devote no zeal to earthly goods, love their enemies, subdue the flesh from every pleasure, repress every impulse under the judgment of reason, and are raised by the wing of contemplation through heavenly desire. But because such persons are very rare, they are led in the ark close to the cubit, where human beings and birds are contained. Yet let it be asked whether anyone can be without sin, and no one is found. Who, then, is the human being without sin except he who was born without sin? Therefore the ark is completed in the lowest cubit, because there is one author and Redeemer of the holy Church, without sin, toward whom all who know themselves to be sinners make progress.

## Chapter III. On the Cup

[Col. 0457A]

[Note: [Col. 0457D] From Homily 35 on the Gospels, after the middle, etc., and Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 26.] By “cup” the suffering of the Passion is understood, as the Lord says in the Gospel to the sons of Zebedee: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20:22; Mark 10:39). For there are two kinds of martyrdom: one in the mind, the other in mind and action together. To die at the hands of a persecutor is martyrdom in an outward act; but to endure insults and love one who hates is martyrdom in hidden thought. For that there are two kinds of martyrdom, one in hidden action and the other public, Truth testifies when, as stated above, he asks the sons of Zebedee: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” When they immediately reply, “We can,” [Col. 0457B] the Lord at once answers: “You shall indeed drink my cup” (Matt. 20:23). What, indeed, do we understand by the cup except the suffering of the Passion? Elsewhere he says of it: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:38). Yet the sons of Zebedee—that is, James and John—did not both die by martyrdom; and nevertheless each heard that he would drink the cup. For John by no means ended his life through martyrdom, yet he was a martyr, because he preserved in his mind the passion that he did not undergo in his body. We too, therefore, can by this example be martyrs without the sword, if we truly preserve patience in our mind.

## Chapter IV. On the Lamp

[Col. 0457C]

In Sacred Scripture, by “lamp” are signified sometimes Christ; sometimes those saints who burn for themselves through the fervour of the Spirit and shine for others through the example of good work; and sometimes our works.

[Note: [Col. 0457D] From the end of Book X on Job.] By “lamp” is understood Christ Jesus, the man who is mediator between God and human beings, as Job says: “The simplicity of the just is mocked; a lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich, prepared for the appointed time” (Job 12:4). He truly became a lamp to us, because in dying on the cross for our redemption he poured light through the wood upon our darkened minds. John had seen us enlightened by this lamp when he said: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9). Yet he sees it despised in the thoughts of the rich when he adds shortly afterward: “He came unto his own, and his own did not receive him” (ibid., 11). Herod wished to examine the flames of this lamp when he desired to see miracles, as it is written: “For a long time he had desired to see him, because he had heard many things about him and hoped to see some sign done by him” (Luke 23:8). But this lamp emitted no ray of light before his eyes, because it showed nothing wonderful of itself to one who sought it not devoutly but from curiosity. When questioned, the Redeemer kept silence; when expected to perform miracles, he disdained to do so. Keeping himself hidden within himself, he left outside those whom he found ungrateful for outward things, [Col. 0458A] choosing rather to be openly despised by the proud than to be praised with empty speech by unbelievers. Hence this lamp was immediately despised, as is added there: “Herod with his army despised him and mocked him, clothing him in a white garment” (ibid., 11). But the despised lamp, which endures mockery on earth, flashes more brightly from heaven in judgment. Hence it is aptly added here: “Prepared for the appointed time.” Of that time the Psalmist says: “When I shall have received the time, I will judge justices” (Ps. 74:3). Hence Truth himself declares in the Gospel: “My time has not yet come” (John 7:6). Hence Peter says: “Whom heaven must receive until the time of restoration” (Acts 3:21). Therefore the lamp which is now despised is prepared to come at the appointed time, because he who now bears sinners’ mockery will judge sins on the last day; and then he exercises judgment all the more severely insofar as he now gently extends his patience to summon sinners. For he who long waits for those who must be converted punishes the unconverted without reconsideration. This he briefly indicates through the prophet, saying: “I have kept silence, I have always been silent, I have been patient; like a woman in labour I will speak” (Isa. 42:14). A woman in labour brings forth with pain what she carried within for a long time. Thus he who was always silent speaks like a woman in labour, because the coming Judge, who long bore human deeds without vengeance, will at last, with the fervour of examination, show—as though in pain of mind—the sentence of how great a punishment [Col. 0458C] he had kept within. Therefore let no one despise this lamp when it is hidden, lest, when it has flashed from heaven, it burn up its despisers. He who does not now burn to pardon will undoubtedly then burn to punish.

By “lamps,” when they are set in comparison with coals, are signified those saints who both burn within themselves through the Spirit’s fervour and shine for others with the flame of good example. See Book II, chapter 5, distinction 2.

[Note: [Col. 0458D] Above, chapter 1, distinction 6.] By “lamps” our works are signified, as Truth says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins, who, taking their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and bride” (Matt. 25:1). And shortly afterward: “Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps” [Col. 0458D] (ibid., 7). [Note: [Col. 0458D] From Homily 12 on the Gospels.] See the chapter “On Vessels,” and add this: It should be observed that all have lamps, but not all have oil, because both the elect and the reprobate often display good works in themselves. But only those come to the bridegroom with oil who seek within themselves glory for what they have done outwardly. Hence the Psalmist says concerning the holy Church of the elect: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44:14). When the bridegroom comes, all the virgins arise, because the elect and the reprobate are awakened from the sleep of their death. They trim their lamps because they reckon with themselves the works for which they expect to receive eternal blessedness; [Col. 0459A] but the lamps of the foolish virgins are extinguished, because at the coming of the Judge their works—which had appeared bright outwardly to people—are darkened within, and they find no recompense from God, because for those works they have received from people the praise that they loved.

## Chapter V. On Bowls
[Note: [Col. 0459D] From Homily 6 on the Gospels, after the middle.] By the name of bowls, when they are set in comparison with cups, abundant preaching is understood. Hence in the tabernacle, by the Lord’s command, both bowls and cups were made (Exod. 25:29). For by the tabernacle the holy Church is signified; by bowls, abundant knowledge; by cups, slight and narrow knowledge. One man, filled with the doctrine of truth, intoxicates the minds of his hearers. [Note: [Col. 0459D] This saying occurs in Book XX on Job, ch. II.] Therefore, by what he says, he surely offers a bowl. Another is unable to explain what he understands; yet because he announces it in whatever way he can, he surely offers a taste by means of a cup. Thus, in God’s tabernacle, that is, in the holy Church, both bowls and cups are to be prepared, because in the teaching of sacred utterance there must be presented not only great and hidden things which intoxicate, but also small and subtle things which impart knowledge, as though by a taste. Therefore, he who cannot at all minister bowls through the teaching of wisdom ought, insofar as divine generosity enables him, to give his neighbours cups of good speech. To the degree that he feels himself to have advanced, let him draw others also along the way of God; if he tends toward God, let him desire companions and take care not to come to him alone. Hence it is written: “Let him who hears say, Come” [Col. 0459C] (Rev. 22:17), so that he who has already received in his heart the voice of heavenly love may also utter outwardly to his neighbours a voice of exhortation. Perhaps he does not have bread to offer alms to one in need; yet greater is that which he can bestow if he has a tongue. For it is more to refresh with the nourishment of a word a mind that will live for ever than to satisfy with earthly bread the belly of flesh destined to die.

A bowl also signifies the punishment of persecution, as is written in the Apocalypse: “And the fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun, and it was given to him to afflict men with heat and fire” (Rev. 16:1). To pour out a bowl upon the sun is to inflict the punishments of persecution upon men shining with the splendour of wisdom. [Col. 0459D] “And it was given to him to afflict men with heat and fire,” because, when wise men are overcome by torments and touched by the error of evil conduct, the weak, persuaded by their example, are indeed inflamed with temporal desires. For the falls of the strong bring an increase of ruin to the weak.

## CHAPTER VI. ON POTS

In Sacred Scripture, when a pot is mentioned in the singular, it sometimes signifies the Synagogue, sometimes any carnal heart; but when pots are spoken of in the plural, they sometimes denote carnal works.

650 [Note: [Col. 0459D] From the middle of Homily 2 on Ezekiel.] By the name of a pot the Synagogue is specifically [Col. 0460A] signified, as is said through Jeremiah the prophet: “I see a boiling pot, and its face is from the face of the north” (Jer. 1:13). For what else was the mind of the Jews, raging in persecution and rolling the waves of thought in a faith of wickedness, than a boiling pot? Its face was from the face of the north. For by the name of the north the evil spirit is signified. Thus the face of the pot is rightly said to be from the face of the north, because, if Judaea had not submitted itself through slothfulness of mind to the hostile spirit, it would not have burned so fiercely against the good in such wickedness.

[Note: [Col. 0460D] From Book XVIII on Job, ch. XII, 11; and Book XXXIII, ch. XXVII, 40, after the middle.] By the name of a pot, moreover, any carnal heart is understood generally; hence what we have said specifically concerning the Synagogue may be understood of any perverse person: namely, “I see a boiling pot, and [Col. 0460B] its face is from the face of the north” (Jer. 1:13). For a boiling pot is the human heart seething with the heats of worldly cares and the anxieties of desires. But the pot of the human heart is heated from the face of the north when it is inflamed with unlawful desires through the instigation of the adversary spirit. For he who says, “I will sit upon the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. 14:13), kindles the mind which he has once seized with the malignant gusts of his persuasion, like fires laid beneath it, so that, dissatisfied with present things, it may continually burn with desires: that it may desire some things which ought to be despised, despise others already acquired; now gape after its own advantages, now oppose the benefits of others even to its own loss; now satisfy the enticements of the flesh, now, as though carried away upon a certain summit through [Col. 0460C] the pride of thought, setting carnal care aside, raise its whole self up in the image of arrogance. Therefore, because the heart which is inflamed by the instigation of the evil spirit is drawn away through diverse desires, it is rightly declared to be like a heated and boiling pot; for by as many heats as its conscience, blown upon by his temptations, rises, by so many thoughts does it swell within itself.

By the name of pots carnal works are denoted, as we read of the people of Israel that, while receiving from above the refreshment of manna, they longed for the flesh-pots, melons, and onions of Egypt. See the chapter on leeks or onions, Book XIV, chapter 10.

## CHAPTER VII. ON THE AMPHORA

[Col. 0460D] By the name of an amphora he signifies avarice, as is written in the prophet Zechariah: “Lift up your eyes and see what this is which comes forth.” And I said, “What is it?” And he said, “This is the amphora coming forth” (Zech. 5:5–6). See Book IV, chapter 3, distinction 2.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON THE SKIN-BAG

[Note: [Col. 0460D] From Book XIX on Job, ch. VII, 8.] By the name of a skin-bag the thought of the carnal heart is signified, as is said by the Psalmist concerning the Lord: “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a skin-bag” (Ps. 32:7). For the skin-bag is the thought of the carnal heart. By the waters of the sea, however, the bitterness of a perverse [Col. 0461A] mind is understood. Therefore now the waters of the sea are gathered in a skin-bag when the bitterness of a perverse mind does not burst outward into the speech of depraved licence. Then, as John says, the dragon is held shut in the abyss (Rev. 10:2), because diabolical malice is concealed in the crafty hearts of the wicked. But, as it is written there, “The dragon shall be brought forth from the pit of the abyss” (ibid. 9:2), because he who is now covered through fear will then, against the holy Church, openly pour forth from the hearts of the wicked all the poison of serpents. For now a raging conscience hides itself beneath a flattering tongue, and the malice of cunning covers itself, as it were, with a certain abyss of pretence. The time will surely come when perverse carnal persons will openly proclaim against the holy Church what they now contrive in secret thought. For as the persecution of the last time increases, she is compelled to endure the open voices [Col. 0462A] of heretics, when they disclose in the speech of manifest error the movements of their hearts which they now conceal within the recesses of their thoughts. Concerning this same skin-bag the same Psalmist says elsewhere: “He placed the waters as in a skin-bag” (Ps. 77:13). See the chapter on waters. By the name of skin-bags the hearts of the elect are also signified, as is said in the Gospel: “New wine into new skin-bags” (Matt. 9:17).

## CHAPTER IX. ON THE FLASK

By the name of flasks our bodies are signified, as is represented in Gideon’s battle: his companions went out to battle with flasks, lamps, and trumpets. See Book V, chapter 27, distinction 3.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1169: THE VENERABLE GERHOH, PROVOST OF REICHERSPERG

[Col. 0461]

# PRELIMINARY DISSERTATION ON THE LIFE AND WRITINGS OF GERHOH

(Dom Bernard Pez, Prolegomena to Gerhoh’s Commentary on the Psalms, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, Augsburg, 1728.)

## TO THE MOST REVEREND, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS, AND MOST EMINENT LORD LORD HERCULANUS, MOST VIGILANT PROVOST OF THE MOST CELEBRATED AND FLOURISHING CANONRY OF REICHERSPERG IN BAVARIA, OF THE ORDER OF CANONS REGULAR OF ST AUGUSTINE, ETC., ETC., A MOST DEVOTED LOVER OF SACRED ANTIQUITY AND POLITE LETTERS

It is about nine years, most reverend, most illustrious, and most eminent prelate, since, having confidently addressed you by letter, you did not disdain, with singular kindness and humanity, to send and entrust to my fidelity and diligence eight most choice parchment codices. These contained the unpublished works of your predecessor Gerhoh—most holy as well as most learned—who lived nearly six centuries ago: splendid works long desperately desired by learned men. As soon as we saw them—for who, acquainted with so many matters, would not at once communicate so great a triumph to as many knowledgeable persons as possible?—we could not but immediately extol to the heavens in copious praises so wise a prelate, so generous and liberal toward the more sacred Muses, and warmly congratulate the whole literary world that he so promptly and gladly yielded the nobler and more precious monuments of ancient learning and the more secret treasures of his distinguished library to public light and common use. This was contrary to the custom of not a few persons, who will not allow themselves to be moved even by Periclean outcries and servile entreaties to place even for a time the better remains of ancient writers in the hands of scholars, to the great advantage of the Church.

Accordingly, that I might satisfy your expectation as soon as possible, most reverend patron, since at that time I was intensely occupied and overwhelmed with publishing other works, I immediately looked about for friends who would courageously undertake, if not to copy and publish in print all Gerhoh’s minor works contained in these volumes at once, then at least his chief work on the Psalms. Nor did I have to labour long. For Father Felix Maria Wurtenberger, a most learned man of the celebrated Order of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary, then most worthy prior of the convent of Bellenberg or Schönbüchl, not far from Melk, immediately and vigorously claimed this most beautiful task for himself. He carried it out with such zeal and effort, even amid failing health, that in scarcely two years he completed the whole work: transcribing, correcting, elucidating, and preparing it for the press. By his efforts alone this splendid Commentary of Gerhoh would already then have appeared, had not the delays of men and the changeability and malice of the times intervened against the excellent man’s very good intention. These same inconveniences also caused the work, when later he had freely surrendered to me, at a distance, his enormous labours to be reviewed afresh in their entirety and published, to remain suppressed for so many years in private cabinets, awaiting, that is, a somewhat clearer sky and times more favourable to good letters. Since these now appear to have dawned, by God’s good favour, behold, most eminent prelate: your Gerhoh, in a new form and a new light, disdains longer darkness and flies forth into the theatre of the world, of which he was long most worthy; and, what is the greatest of ornaments, he appears under the most august name of the greatest and wisest of Caesars, Charles VI.
