Moreover, there is no room for doubt that this fruit of your generosity will greatly delight your most religious mind and will readily induce you to believe that your kindness has been bestowed upon a man who, more desirous of another’s praise than of his own, has wished to omit nothing that seemed to concern the adornment of Gerhoh’s memory and the enlargement of his glory among posterity. To establish this more fully, I judge that two tasks are here to be performed, as is customary. First, Gerhoh’s life and the deeds which he performed with distinction must be discussed more fully; second, I must undertake a more careful survey not merely of his one Commentary on the Psalms but also of all the writings of Gerhoh that I have so far been able to discover. If I shall have properly accomplished both, it will plainly appear that I have ascribed to Gerhoh the name “the Great” not from a desire to flatter or to adorn my hero beyond his deserts, but by the very best right.

Now, as regards the first point, it would certainly not be difficult to weave from Gerhoh’s own works—which I published both in the preceding volumes of my *Thesaurus* and shall publish in the present and subsequent volumes—a history of Gerhoh’s life far more exact and richer in particular details than that which exists in the work of the most learned Matthew Rader, S.J. But since lack of time precludes my ready willingness, I should ask the learned reader to rest for the time being in Rader’s dissertation, at least one written elegantly and skilfully, until what I have indicated is carried out either by me, when I have more leisure, or by anyone else. Behold, then, Gerhoh’s eulogy written by Rader in the second volume of *Bavaria Sancta*, though with certain matters removed which might detain the reader too tediously and are not necessarily connected with Gerhoh’s affairs.

> “This luminary of the monastery at Reichersperg is truly illustrious and of the first rank; the brilliance of his intellect, still shining today in books and literary monuments, has not been extinguished, but is all the more kindled by the renown of holiness and the splendour of virtue. Polling, a village of Upper Bavaria, famous for its monastery and not far from the town of Weilheim, gave us Gerhoh. He was a greater glory to his native place than it was to him, as often happens. Stagira would be unknown had it not borne Aristotle as its son. He was born in 1093 and died in 1169, in his seventy-sixth year. Nor should you criticize Gretser in the published life of Gerhoh, where, through transposed figures, 1114 is printed in place of 1094—a shameful error of twenty years. It is the shameful blunder of typesetters or a copyist, not of Gretser. Yet I think III should be read in place of IV.
>
> “He learned the elements of the liberal disciplines on his native soil and gave an indication of his ability almost in the cradle itself, when he showed what a capacious and ample mind he brought to absorb the treasures of learning. He far outstripped his contemporaries in speed of learning, though he readily yielded to them in childish cleverness and cunning of intellect, since he commended himself to nearly all by exceptional openness of spirit—which especially makes that age lovable—and simplicity of character. When he was about to leave boyhood, having entered, or perhaps already passed, his sixteenth year, his head was covered by the most foul scabby eruption of psoriasis—a condition especially hostile to childhood [lacuna; OCR-damaged]—and his companions recoiled from him as from an accursed outcast; at the same time he was tormented by shame at the disfiguring disease, not to mention the torment and pains by which he was continually afflicted. But when the foul eruption of his head had at last been wiped away by a merciful heaven and his health restored, Gerhoh at the same time separated his soul and mind from every impure contagion of Venus, and devoted his whole self to chastity, which has great power to embrace the pursuits of wisdom.

[Col. 0465]

> “Thereafter he went to Freising and Moosburg, well-known Bavarian towns, and consecrated all his time to God and the Muses. Since at that time the youth of the Saxons were being excellently cultivated in letters at Hildesheim, Gerhoh also spent three years there in the cultivation of his mind, returning to his native land not a little more learned. He had already acquired no small reputation for learning when he was summoned to Augsburg and placed in charge of the principal school, which then lacked a teacher. Gerhoh had a gracious face, a serene brow, a pleasing countenance, cheeks blooming with their first down, and a whole bodily bearing, unadorned but arranged by nature itself with grace; his morals were upright. These natural ornaments and advantages were commended by the felicity of his intellect and his reputation for learning. Thus Bishop Hermann of Augsburg turned his eyes toward Gerhoh and admitted him into the council of the sacred Fathers. Gerhoh was then among the deacons of the Church in that place, not yet distinguished by the honour of priesthood. At that time Emperor Henry—whom the Romans count as Henry IV and the Germans as Henry V—and Pope Paschal were divided in their bitterest mutual hostility. Bishop Hermann of Augsburg sided with the emperor against the pope, although by evil and condemned arts he had been advanced to the mitre. He had attempted to draw Gerhoh into his party also; but Gerhoh allowed no force or authority, whether of the emperor or of Hermann, to divert him from the true path. Indeed, he first began secretly to abstain from the bishop’s society—the bishop whom Baronius calls a pseudo-bishop—and then openly to defend the pope’s cause, until peace was restored by Calixtus in 1122, the emperor was received into the bosom of the Church, and those who had been given over to dreadful curses were released from the bonds of anathema. The author relates that Hermann too was restored to favour with the pope: ‘When these matters, as stated, had been concluded and settled, the aforesaid bishop was received into the favour of the Roman Church through his [Gerhoh’s] mediation.’ Thus Gerhoh was already then pleasing and acceptable to the Roman pontiff himself and to the entire Roman curia. . . .
>
> “But Gerhoh had long aspired to the discipline of a stricter life and desired to withdraw into the fellowship of religious men, when concern for his parents and brothers delayed his impulse and zeal for piety. He wished to provide for them before casting aside every concern of human affairs. Having persuaded them also to seek a surer and shorter way to heaven, he enclosed both parents in the monastery of Rottenbuch—which was formerly a double house of women and men—with his twin brothers. He himself soon followed them and, by the example of his life, doctrine, and piety, stirred them to steadfastness, labour, watches and vigils, and continual virtues.
>
> “Rottenbuch is a very ancient monastery in Upper Bavaria, situated between Ettal and Polling, founded in 1085 by Welf IV, the first Bavarian prince of that line. When Gerhoh came there in pursuit of religious life, he was received with immense joy by all, like a new sun about to illumine the dwelling. He laid aside secular adornment in order to put on a more sacred one; he rejected extensive and rich conditions of the priesthood in order, in modest attire and with sober, frugal food, to enter more freely upon the heavenly journey. He placed human riches, honours, and even islands, which he could have hoped for, after poverty, contempt, and humility of life, so that he might one day appear richer, more renowned, and more illustrious among those above. There he laid the foundations of religious life, completed his novitiate, and, in the customary words of his forebears, swore to the rules of the order. Yet it often happened that young men admitted into the sacred fellowship of religious persons swore according to the prescribed formula that they would live according to St Dominic, Francis, Basil, Benedict, Bernard, and other Fathers, although they had never read, seen, or known the prescribed rules of life. [Note: [Col. 0465] We are astonished, and deeply regret, that such words escaped a good and learned man—words in which, as no one ignorant of the history of monasticism from the twelfth century down to more recent times can fail to know, there are almost as many errors, not to say falsehoods, as words.]
>
> “This is all the more astonishing in Gerhoh, since he was thoroughly imbued with letters and flourished in the renown of wisdom. For after he had professed himself among the companions of St Augustine, only then did he ask what rule was that according to which every action of his life ought to be measured by the judgment and law of St Augustine. But nowhere, neither at Rottenbuch nor in neighbouring houses of the same institute, could any so-called Rules be found.
>
> “When I saw these things sincerely written in the Reichersperg volume, I first condemned the negligence of the times and of the people living there, who took vows and bound their faith to God in set formulas that they would follow these or those laws of these Fathers or those, while meanwhile they did not know those very laws: laws unknown there, neither written nor produced for those who were required to profess themselves under them. For hear how the most ancient author of the Annals of Reichersperg testifies concerning Gerhoh at his profession: ‘For in those days he was not satisfied with that marvellous sweetness which he found in reading the *Excerpt on the Sayings of the Saints concerning the Canonical Life*, which his brethren had until then used as a rule; but with all attentiveness he sought how he should live according to the Rule of our holy Father Augustine, or what that rule was according to which he had professed himself to live. For nothing seemed to him sufficient as a rule if it was not that which he had professed. Yet that rule was not then found in those places, nor even in others of the same profession. . . . For this reason he considered it necessary to approach the Roman pontiff with certain brethren from the cloister, so that he might establish in that cloister to which he was bound the rule which he had professed together with all the others in common; and this was done.’
>
> “But when I had reflected, I observed that these were times in which most religious men carried their rules [Col. 0467] not inscribed on wax tablets, tablets, parchment, or paper, but had them in use, practice, mind, heart, manners, and exercise—as the Christian Church of old did before the heralds of the holy Gospel committed their precepts to writing. Thus the same author says a little above concerning Gerhoh: ‘How great the ardour and zeal with which he embraced the way of common life, and how great the zeal for righteousness with which he lived, is attested by that whole Church of Rottenbuch; all near and far to whom the fame of his holy manner of life came are witnesses. They attest, I say, how at the beginning of his conversion his zeal began to burn, namely, that through persistence in prayers and divine readings the Lord’s utterance inflamed him so greatly that his own speech also became exceedingly fiery, and his word, as is written of Elijah, burned like a torch. Therefore he continually urged his fellow brethren, not only in words but also by examples, to preserve the good customs of the stricter life and the ordinances of the holy Fathers. Indeed, he rebuked, entreated, and reproved according to the apostle’s command, presenting himself in all things as an example: in many vigils, frequent meditation and reading of the sacred Scriptures, great patience, chastity, and every exercise of good virtues, and finally in every uprightness of conduct he made himself outstanding. Hence he was greatly loved by all good and religious persons. He proved so vigorous a tamer of his own body that he abstained somewhat immoderately even from necessary food, so that when his flesh had been consumed by hunger, his skin almost clung to his bones. Thus he burned wholly and beyond comparison through the inextinguishable fire of most holy love toward God and through the untiring zeal of his soul for the beauty of common life.’ These are the words of the Reichersperg author concerning Gerhoh.
>
> “Moreover, just as builders and architects, though they judge from the estimation of their eyes, by use and sight, how high, broad, and straight a work may be, nevertheless, if they wish to construct the building itself—a tower, walls, ramparts, or partitions—they employ a plumb-line, by whose angles and straight line they test the rising work daily, indeed almost every hour; so, unless a written rule of life is set forth as discipline gradually declines, it slowly turns aside from the true and straight toward the crooked. This was what Gerhoh pressed for. More religious than the others, he determined from what he had learned here and there in the monuments of the Fathers what had been the ancient discipline of religious persons living in common. When the less zealous denied this and pressed him to establish by authority everything he taught—for certain practices had, as happens, crept into use and custom which did not seem to him to be done according to the law, rule, and authority of the ancient Fathers—he went to Rome and there inquired concerning the true laws of his religious order. When he brought back with him what he had sought, he offended no little the minds of those who had been idle. For although he acted in nothing imperiously, but departed in his actual conduct from the negligent manner of life, they could not endure even this. Like owls and bats, they were dazzled by the light of his virtues; and they interpreted his reformed life—which they ought by every means to have followed, loved, and embraced with both hands—as a rebuke and correction of their own life. Nor did their wickedness stop there. Since he did not praise the faults of his household and hated sloth, idleness, untimely conversations, and, finally, bad habits, he himself began to be hated, harassed, persecuted, and sometimes even endangered in his life by those unlike himself.
>
> “Meanwhile, as the fame stirred up by his virtues spread most pleasing fragrances throughout Germany, Bishop Chuno of Regensburg—who was the first bishop to bear that name—drawn by these fragrances, sought Gerhoh from the common brotherhood at Rottenbuch as a companion in his labours, to use his counsel in visiting the diocese and administering the bishopric. He obtained him and initiated him into the sacred honours of the priesthood. Yet Gerhoh did not enjoy great peace even there, because Conrad disturbed public affairs. After Lothar, duke of the Saxons, an illustrious man, had been designated king of the Romans by the magnates of the German empire, Conrad, brother of Frederick, duke of Swabia—who fathered Emperor Frederick Barbarossa—aspired to the kingdom. He went to Milan, was there hailed king by the archbishop, and received the royal insignia. Bishop Chuno of Regensburg and Gerhoh with him, abhorring Conrad’s faction, followed the rightful prince, King Lothar. Conrad bore this most bitterly, persecuted both men with the bitterest hatred, and often laid snares even for their lives. He especially sought Gerhoh’s death repeatedly because, in a public assembly and supplication addressed to the people, he had called him a tyrant. This caused Gerhoh to be compelled to abandon the parish of Cham, which he had received from Chuno to administer and where he had resolved to establish a monastery, on account of factional men and supporters of Conrad who had uttered the most extreme threats against him.
>
> “Amid these events, after Chuno died at Regensburg in 1130, Conrad, bishop of Salzburg, a most excellent and holy man, took Gerhoh under his protection and more than once sent him in his own name as ambassador to the supreme pontiff at Rome; there Gerhoh successfully conducted the affairs of his bishop. For, because of his exceptional virtue and learning, he possessed great influence with the Roman curia. Meanwhile, the head of the monastery at Reichersperg was hastening toward the end of life and left the torch to be borne by another. Bishop Conrad of Salzburg, judging no one more suitable than Gerhoh to govern that monastery—which looked to the authority and jurisdiction of the bishop of Salzburg—appointed him to it in 1132. He administered, enlarged, and adorned that sacred office for altogether thirty-seven years, with the highest benefit to the commonwealth, so that piety and religion, steadfastness and virtue, overflowed into the use and benefit of all Germany. He dared, with the greatest freedom and despising every danger to his life, when occasion required, to exhort, admonish, and even rebuke in speech princes, kings and emperors, bishops and prelates, the supreme and most extensive council of the Christian world—the cardinals at Rome—and the very father and ruler of the Christian name.
>
> “This freedom in speaking and writing, joined with virtue and religion, gained him such authority that the Gauls marvelled at his virtue, the Bohemians proclaimed it, the Pannonians received it, the Greeks at last revered it, the pontiffs honoured him, and the cardinals venerated him. Thus the records of Reichersperg testify: ‘Therefore, they say, once placed in government, what a man he showed himself to be, and how, strengthened by God, he never failed the Church in all its subsequent tribulations, but most often confessed and defended the truth steadfastly before kings and princes, not without danger to his own life, is attested by all Germany, illuminated by the light of his teaching and reproved by the fervour of his Spirit for many excesses and abuses. All with whom he happened to associate or dwell for some time are his witnesses. Above all, the holy community of his brethren and sisters knows how holily and blamelessly he lived among them for almost forty years. All know how tranquil he was when devoted to reading and prayer, and how he allowed no hours to be free from exercises of piety. For bodily exercise seemed to him, with the Apostle, useful only a little, unless the monastery’s need required it. Indeed, the lamp of his heart and mouth shone even into foreign lands. Neither France, nor Bohemia, nor Hungary, nor even Greece remained without a share in the grace radiating from his heart and mouth. For such grace was poured out upon his lips that he was pleasing even to those whom he rebuked. Hence Roman pontiffs and lord cardinals always loved him, although he rebuked them in many matters. He did not fear kings and powerful persons so as to refrain, whenever an opportunity was offered, from declaring to them what was just and salutary. Great men, persons of middling rank, and common people hung upon the sweet and healthful words of his mouth, whether in public assemblies of the Church or private conversations. For he was so deeply imbued with the divine Spirit that rivers of living water almost always and without failing flowed from his belly, whether he was speaking or writing something for the benefit and instruction of his neighbours.’
>
> “And shortly below: ‘How well known, pleasing, and acceptable this blessed man was to the supreme Roman pontiffs who presided over the Roman see in his time—first Pope Calixtus, mentioned above, and then each of his successors down to Pope Alexander; and how reverently those Roman pontiffs received, praised, and approved his religious fervour, zeal, doctrine, and writings; and how swift an effect he always obtained in all his business whenever it was necessary to appeal to the Roman curia, whether in person, through messengers, or by his letters alone on whatever causes—all this is testified by apostolic letters and by letters of the lord cardinals, frequently sent either on his behalf to others or specially addressed to him; as also by those which he himself, often returning from Rome, brought concerning his own cause or that of others. Copies of all these are still found. How greatly the Roman pontiffs themselves, out of reverence and affection for him and at his request, honoured and maintained under their protection and that of St Peter the place over which he presided, namely the monastery of Reichersperg; how often they defended it against grievous enemies and assailants; and what liberty and right they granted and confirmed in perpetuity to that place by their authority, is shown by the privileges of Pope Innocent and Pope Eugenius, obtained and secured for that place by his efforts. After these, the bishops of Salzburg, the elder Conrad and his successor Eberhard, devoutly imitated them; likewise the princes of the realm—dukes and counts—who, each according to his right, fortified the same place by very many privileges. Similarly other bishops, namely those of Bamberg, Passau, and Freising, confirmed by their privileges to the same monastery the estates and possessions granted to that place, either by themselves or by others, within their bishoprics. Finally, the lord Emperor Frederick himself received the monastery of Reichersperg, with all its appurtenances, under the protection of his imperial majesty and of all succeeding kings and emperors, and by his privilege confirmed its ancient and original liberty, through the intervention of Bishops Eberhard of Bamberg and Hartmann of Brixen, according to the petition of this oft-mentioned father.’
>
> “But the incredible force of the spirit of this most distinguished man, proceeding from the depths of his soul, nourished all this: a force received from heaven, which never failed his noble undertakings. Yet he acts with little prudence who assists the commonwealth abroad while ruining matters at home, since nature herself as teacher instructs every person first to provide for himself and his own, and then for others. Gerhoh did not act thus. Every deed, method of living, and mode of teaching of his flowed from the workshop of domestic virtue and discipline. His first task was to call back the habits of his subjects and household, which had declined and grown weak from the rule of the ancient Fathers, to their former vigour; to uproot the seeds of vices; to restore the sinews of virtue cut away everywhere; and finally to give his community a new face and pattern of life. Thus he was gentle and kindly toward the obedient, ready, modest, and observant of religious life; stern and severe toward offenders, the refractory, and the obstinate. Yet he tempered this severity with such meekness and charity that all could perceive and see that both the salvation of each individual [Col. 0471] and the common good of all lay most deeply in his heart. By this means he brought it about that those corrected did not take it ill, but that all generally loved him.
>
> “Moreover, his manner of correcting was most effective because he himself led the way by the example of his life. His habits were so much laws to his household. Hence it came about that the discipline established at home and the reformed habits within the house showed themselves abroad; and people gradually began, as they contemplated him, to adopt a new and innocent manner of life, in company with those who praised and admired him. This religious devotion of his household invited the generosity of nobles, princes, and bishops, so that they not only restored and enlarged the buildings of the monastery—for Gerhoh had entered a house poorly constructed, cramped, and ruinous—but also that many persons of noble birth gave their names to the religious life itself and brought with them no small wealth, by which he greatly enlarged that house in a short time. Gerhoh also added a new dwelling for consecrated virgins, in which most noble and tender young women dedicated themselves eternally as the possession of their heavenly Bridegroom. So fruitful were Gerhoh’s virtue and eloquence.”

“Meanwhile, while he was building up the house, restoring discipline, and bringing in new settlers for the religious life, he did not allow the hand to be idle which his learned and excellent intellect had compelled to produce many outstanding works and monuments full of piety, religion, and learning. He composed eight volumes of meditations on the most holy psalm-odes of the royal prophet, two of which have been lost, while the rest are still read today. He contended with the pen against the followers of Abelard. He sent other works to Otto, the noble historian of Freising, uncle of Ahenobarbus and brother of King Conrad; others to various princes and pontiffs. Nothing of these has survived except the explanations of David’s poems, the book on Antichrist, on the Virgin assumed into heaven, on Faith, on the Fourth Watch of the Night, and on the order of the gifts of the divine Spirit. In his last years he worked very hard to reconcile the disagreements between Emperor Frederick I and Pope Alexander III, sending them various nocturnal studies on that matter. Yet he always attached himself to the better and sounder side; and, after immense labours and abundant fruits reaped from them, at midnight following the day of St John the Baptist—on which he had spoken at length to the people—having received the Christian sacraments two days earlier, in the year 1169, on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, he flew away to the fellowship of the blessed.

His body was buried two days later at the altar of the Holy Cross, which while alive he had always borne in his heart. The image of Gerhoh at Reichersberg today bears this inscription: ‘In the year of the Lord 1132, Lord Gerhoh, distinguished doctor of sacred theology, was made the third provost of this place. He laboured in correcting the morals of the great, and was the founder of the monastery of religious women of the Blessed Virgin.’ I do not think the empty and false calumnies of Aventinus, by which he tries to defile Gerhoh, as he calls him, worth recording in my work; they were long ago bluntly refuted and crushed by our Gretser. You, holy one, whom we suppliantly venerate, awaken and restore in us the burning and twofold spirit of Elijah which you appear to have possessed, now languishing—or at least growing old—that we may sharpen the blunted edge of Christian virtue.”

Thus far Raderus on the life and deeds of Gerhoh. Since, at the end, he enumerates Gerhoh’s writings more meagrely and sparingly than the services of so great a man to the Church deserve, I thought I should do something worthwhile if I now reviewed more carefully and distinctly, in order, each work that has come to my notice, as I undertook above to do. The literary monuments left by Gerhoh are therefore as follows:

I. *Syntagma concerning Emperors Henry IV and V and Pope Gregory VII*, which, according to Casimir Oudin, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, col. 1427, consisted of various little works; with a refutation of Anna Comnena’s false statements in the *Alexiad*, it was prepared for publication by the Jesuit theologian Jacob Gretser at Ingolstadt, in quarto, in 1611, by Angermaria. I greatly regret that this work is not at hand while I write, and that Oudin did not enumerate those various little works. In that way something more certain might be determined concerning the works soon to be listed, some of which perhaps are not different from those earlier works.

II. *Commentary on Psalm LXIV*, or *On the Corrupt State of the Church*, addressed to Pope Eugenius III. The most learned Étienne Baluze first brought this to light, with a notable encomium, from a manuscript in the Colbert Library in which it is entitled *Treatise on Ecclesiastical Affairs*, in book V of his *Miscellanies*, pp. 63–237, in 1700. Since it could not be separated from the remaining commentary on the Psalms, I have arranged for it to be reprinted here in full.

III. *Treatise against the Simoniacs*, addressed to St Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux. Although headless—that is, lacking its beginning—the most illustrious and indefatigable Fr Edmund Martène, Benedictine of the Congregation of St Maur, judged it most worthy of publication from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Dunes, and published it in vol. V of the *New Treasury of Anecdotes*, from col. 1457.

IV. *Book on the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*, addressed to Hartmann, Bishop of Brixen, and Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg. It appears in vol. I, part II, of this *Treasury*, from col. 165. The Reichersberg chronicler also mentions this work under the title *Little Book on the Glorification of the Son of Man*, under the year 1169.

V. *Book against Two Heresies of His Time*, addressed to Godfrey, Abbot of Admont. You have the work printed in the cited place of the *Treasury*, from col. 283. It is the “helmeted prologue,” as he himself calls it, to the commentary on the Psalms. This Godfrey is the very man whose excellent homilies for Sundays and feasts I have very recently published in two folio volumes.

VI. *Lives of the Blessed Berengar and Wirnto, Abbots of Formbach in Bavaria, of the Order of St Benedict*. They appeared in part III of the same volume of my *Treasury*, from col. 399.

VII. *Book on the Building of God*, or *On the Zeal and Care for Ecclesiastical Discipline*, addressed to Chuno, Bishop of Regensburg. You have it published in vol. II, part II, of the *Treasury*, from col. 223.

[Col. 0473]

VIII. *Dialogue on the Difference between a Secular Cleric and a Regular Cleric*, addressed to Innocent II, Supreme Pontiff. Published there from col. 437.

IX. Two books *On the Investigation of Antichrist and the Schism*, addressed to Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg. From a Reichersberg manuscript, the most reverend Fr Reiner Reitter, my most learned colleague, has prepared these for printing in one of the following volumes of the *Treasury*. Raderus mentions only one book on Antichrist, because he never inspected the work itself; but there are in fact two.

X. *Dialogue against the Errors of the Greeks*, mentioned by the Reichersberg chronicler cited above under the title *Dialogue between Greeks and Latins*. It will shortly appear together with the books on Antichrist, into one of which it is inserted in the same manuscript.

XI. *On the Order of the Gifts of the Holy Spirit*. It survives in Reichersberg manuscript no. 52, from which, through the industry and diligence of that outstanding man, the Venerable Fr Leopold Wydemann, vicar of the Carthusian house at Gaming, I have the work ready for printing together with the following two.

XII. *Dialogue on the Fourth Watch of the Night and the Dangers of the Schism.*

XIII. *Book on Faith*, concerning that passage of Proverbs, “Who shall find a valiant woman?”, addressed to Henry, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. Raderus mentions the former work; the Reichersberg chronicler the latter, testifying in the cited place that the *Little Book on Faith* was written by Gerhoh at the request of Lord Henry, cardinal-priest.

XIV. *Little Book on the Assumption of Holy Mary, Mother of God*, also mentioned by Raderus. This little work has been preserved for us by an almost contemporary manuscript of the celebrated monastery of Mariazell in Austria. From it the distinguished and most learned Johann Friedrich Schannat, historiographer of Fulda, while spending some time here with me, did not hesitate to extract it, for publication in its proper place.

XV. *Commentary on the Canon of the Mass*. This is listed by Martin, canon and librarian of Klosterneuburg, in the catalogue of the books of his monastery made at the end of the fourteenth century, which I once copied from a manuscript in the library of the Viennese canonical house of St Dorothy. But I do not remember seeing this work of Gerhoh among the manuscripts of the Klosterneuburg library, which I examined about twelve years ago.

XVI. *Little Works addressed to Pope Alexander [III], to the lords cardinal, and to Eberhard, Bishop of Bamberg, on the Glorification of the Son of Man.* So says the Reichersberg chronicler, calling “little works,” I think, the more extensive letters addressed to the aforesaid prelates of the Churches. These were copied from an Admont manuscript—apart from the book addressed to Pope Adrian—by the most reverend and learned Fr Godfrey Depisch, our colleague, and left by him for publication in vol. VI of the *Treasury*. To these little works you may rightly add Gerhoh’s lengthy letter to Eberhard, Bishop of Bamberg: *How, according to St Hilary, the Father who is about to glorify the Son is greater, yet the glorified Son is not lesser*, etc. It is printed in vol. I, part II, of the same *Treasury*, from col. 315.

XVII. *Book on the Novelties of This Age*, addressed to Pope Adrian IV. Gerhoh himself acknowledges it at the beginning of the book *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*, writing:

> Likewise, a little book dictated for Pope Adrian was presented to him when he was at Benevento, dealing there with the peace between himself and the Sicilian tyrant. In it I collected to a great extent the novelties of this age, and sought a response from him by which he might either approve or disapprove what I thought and think, being ready to agree with him in every respect; for I never wish to dissent from the holy Roman Church in the doctrine of faith, etc.

Scholars will shortly read the work from the manuscript mentioned under the preceding number, which I owe to the distinguished and excellent Fr Sigismund Munich, librarian and superior at Admont, my indefatigable helper.

XVIII. Writings addressed to Pope Anastasius IV, concerning which Gerhoh himself again says in the cited book:

> But after Eugenius no pontiff like him was found in the Roman Church, one who would look so kindly upon my writings and pour oil over them and lay incense upon them; for those who succeeded him did not know me as he did. Nevertheless, I sent my writings, like most finely ground flour, to Pope Anastasius, and he did not answer them. For what reason, I do not judge.

There is no doubt that these writings of Gerhoh concerned the same subject as the book addressed to Adrian: namely, the glory and honour of the man assumed into God, and the reformation of ecclesiastical morals. Gerhoh is wholly present in them everywhere. Meanwhile, I do not know where these writings lie concealed.

XIX. Very many writings addressed to Daniel, Bishop of Prague. The Reichersberg chronicler attributes these to Gerhoh in exactly these words. Yet nothing of them has hitherto been found in German libraries.

XX. A little work against the disciples of Peter Abelard, addressed to Otto, Bishop of Freising, brother of King Conrad; and various little works and writings addressed to the people of Freising themselves, according to the same chronicler. All these appear to have perished. At least I found no trace of any of them in the manuscripts of the Church of Freising or neighbouring monasteries which I examined.

XXI. Two volumes of letters. For the same author writes:

> How he hungered and thirsted after righteousness, and finally how, in what manner, and how greatly he loved every form of righteousness and hated every way of iniquity, is clear to readers and those wishing to know from his various little works, which he wrote to Pope Innocent and Pope Eugenius and to the lords cardinal, and from other little works written to various persons. It is likewise clear from his letters, written to various persons at various times, which are almost all still found in his register and letter-book, in two volumes.

Eager as I was for this inexhaustible treasure for ecclesiastical history, I indeed wrote to you, most reverend and most illustrious prelate; but I learned with immense grief that nothing more of those volumes survives at Reichersberg. Yet perhaps something from them will return, as it were from the underworld, into the light, if not only every corner and compartment of the library but also those of the archive are searched again and again. One of Gerhoh’s letters, concerning the errors of Folmar, provost of Trieffenstein, survives in print in vol. XIII of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*, p. 346, Cologne edition. You may see four others in vol. I, part II, of my *Treasury*, from col. 329. There, I do not know how, a little letter of A.—that is, of Abbot Adam—has slipped in: not of Egen, as the Reichersberg manuscript expressly has it, but of Ebrach or York, addressed to Gerhoh; it had long before been published in the same *Library* and elsewhere. I shall produce more letters of Gerhoh in the following volume, but they will by no means equal the importance or title of the two volumes so eagerly desired by everyone.

XXII. *Chronicle of the Monastery of Reichersberg*, first printed at Munich in quarto in 1611 through the care of the celebrated Christopher Gewold, and later reprinted by the distinguished Fr Peter Ludewig in vol. II of *Writers on German Affairs*, from col. 129. Aventinus appears to have been the first to ascribe this work to Gerhoh. Among those whom he says he used in composing book VI of the *Bavarian Annals*, he praises “Magnus”—I think Aventinus, according to the usage of his age, translated into Latin the old German name of Gerhoh, whose latter element means “great” or “sublime”—“the Augustinian canon of Reichersberg,” who wrote chronicles under Emperor Henry VI [Col. 0475] Augustus.

Casimir Oudin, in his *Supplement to Bellarmine’s On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 459, and Gottfried Olearius, *Library of Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, p. 283, followed Aventinus. The former, however, acknowledged the error in his *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, col. 1428, where he inferred from the year 1178, to which the Reichersberg Chronicle extends, that Gerhoh, who died in 1169, could not have been its author. Yet another error of the same Oudin concerning Gerhoh remains to be corrected. He writes in his *Commentary*:

> None of the cataloguers known to me mentions this Gerhoh except Charles du Fresne du Cange in the Index of Writers prefixed to his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, col. 102, and Gerard Johannes Vossius, book III *On Latin Historians*, part IV, chapter 6, p. 769 of the latest edition; though he wrongly assigns him to the year 1080.

But these cataloguers were not the only ones to celebrate Gerhoh. So did Aubertus Miraeus in his *Supplement on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 328, and Louis Ellies du Pin in his *New Library of Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. IX, p. 186—though he wrongly makes Gerhoh a monk instead of a regular canon. Both could not have been unknown to Oudin.

As for the Reichersberg Chronicle itself, neither in it nor anywhere else is there any certain trace by which one may know that Gerhoh, rather than any other canon of Reichersberg, was its author. Certainly, if it had been Gerhoh’s genuine offspring, the chronicler—whoever he may ultimately be—would not at all have concealed it in his enumeration of Gerhoh’s works. In that enumeration he lists rather accurately, if not everything, at least works of somewhat greater importance, such as no one would deny that Chronicle to be. But I return to matters more certain.

XXIII. *Commentary on the Psalms.* This is the very work now in your hands, drawn from the Reichersberg manuscripts, deservedly praised at the beginning of this dissertation. There are now seven handwritten volumes of this commentary in all; not two, as Raderus reports, but only one has been lost. I spared no effort to recover it, but in vain. The expositions of the Psalms occur in them in the following order.

The first volume, in what is called large quarto, no. 47, contains the exposition of the first twenty Psalms, together with the *Helmeted Prologue*, or book *On Two Heresies*, discussed above under no. 5.

The second, no. 48, comprises the explanation of Psalm XXI and the following nine.

The third, marked no. 49 on the back, presents the exposition of Psalm XXXI and the remainder through Psalm XLIV.

The fourth, which contained the interpretation of Psalm XLIV and of the Psalms through L, is now nowhere to be found at Reichersberg; it is the very volume whose loss I lamented a little earlier.

The fifth, marked no. 50, begins the expositions with Psalm LI and ends with Psalm LXIV.

The sixth, marked no. LI, begins with the exposition of Psalm LXV and ends with the interpretation of Psalm LXXIV.

The seventh, bearing no. 52, preserves the explanation of Psalm LXXV and those following through Psalm CXVIII. It should therefore be noted that Gerhoh’s more extended and, as usual, more elegant expositions contained in this seventh volume do not proceed beyond Psalm LXXVII. For when the holy man had reached that point, the storm of schism that arose broke the thread of his most beautiful work. On this matter Gerhoh speaks thus in the preface to the exposition of Psalm LXXVIII:

> Having completed Psalm LXXVII, the next Psalm, namely LXXVIII, ought to have been expounded, were it not that now that night is at hand in which no one can work. Therefore, making a leap from here to Psalm CXVIII—which we previously expounded as we were able, God favouring us—and then continuing the exposition to the end of the Psalter, we are now compelled, because the power of darkness is at hand, to cease from exposition. But lest we appear to have passed over the intervening Psalms untouched through negligence, here we give the reason. The spiritual Antiochus now reigns, by whose tyrannical violence the Church is so oppressed, the temple of God so violated, profaned, and defiled, while the danger of schism grows exceedingly grave, that there is abundant material for singing—or rather for lamenting and weeping—according to the words of this Psalm: “O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple.”

These are Gerhoh’s words. As I have said, he does not discuss in full and verse by verse any Psalm from LXXVI through CXVIII. Rather, he explains only the titles of each, chiefly from Augustine, and likewise one or two verses from Gregory the Great, reserving a fuller exposition of them all from his own thought for a more suitable time—which he apparently never obtained.

Therefore, lest we should deprive the reader of a perpetual and continuous exposition of all the Psalms individually, we have supplemented these excerpts from Augustine and Gregory with the hitherto unpublished exposition of Honorius of Autun—of whom a full account was given in the preliminary dissertation in vol. II of this *Treasury*—from the Melk manuscripts, through the work of the distinguished Fr Felix Maria. From the same source we have also filled the lacuna of seven Psalms whose explanation perished with Gerhoh’s fourth volume.

Finally, the eighth volume, marked no. 53, contains again a detailed interpretation, following Gerhoh’s original design, of all the Psalms from CXVIII to the last. In the same volume follow explanations of the Canticles also called Ferial. Since Gerhoh is their author, they did not seem at all separable from the Commentary on the Psalms. So much concerning the parchment manuscripts contemporary with Gerhoh himself, from which the present commentary on the Psalms has been drawn.

Now, as to the inward excellence of this work, it is all the greater because it offers so many distinctive matters: matters bearing both on the formation, according to the precepts of the ancients, of Christian morals—and especially ecclesiastical morals—and on illustrating the history of diverse periods, especially the eleventh and twelfth centuries; and finally matters bearing on a thorough knowledge of the controversies concerning faith and doctrine which most occupied learned men of those times. The holy man’s purpose in this genre was evidently to imitate Blessed Augustine, who likewise interwove and transmitted to posterity many outstanding monuments of ecclesiastical doctrine, discipline, and history in his expositions of the Psalms.

Gerhoh himself should be heard on this point, on Psalm X, verse 3:

> Let learned masters now forgive us if we adapt the words of the Psalms to the course of our own time, just as Blessed Augustine continually noted the course of his own time alongside his exposition of the Psalms. For if heretics of every age have bent their bow—that is, Holy Scripture—toward their own error, and those who are now heretics, Simoniacs and Nicolaitans, do not cease to twist their bow according to their own understanding by corrupting the Scriptures, why should it not be permitted us to use the same Scriptures [Col. 0477] to refute their perverse opinions—not as a bow violently bent crosswise, but as a two-edged and twice-sharpened sword? We do not attempt to turn the Scriptures away from their own meaning; rather, we speak, insofar as it has been granted us, to the glory of the Giver. We do not compare or prefer our writings to the writings of the great masters, but desire to satisfy the pious longing of those who demand this work from us: a certain refreshment from the most abundant pastures of the shepherd David, a consoling dish seasoned with the salt of righteousness. To make it sweeter and more savoury to those hungering and thirsting for righteousness, we do not violently wrench from the Psalms an alien meaning, but by saying what accords with the Fathers and sometimes refuting the heresies of our own time, we preserve the meaning that freely and spontaneously presents itself.

Thus far Gerhoh. By this method he successfully achieved that his Commentary might seem not a mere plundering of the earliest and older writers—as is customary with nearly all medieval authors—but an almost new and distinctive work. His opponents did indeed rebuke Gerhoh on this account, but he admirably answered them in Psalm XXXVIII, verse 4:

> My rivals, unwilling—indeed, disdaining—to believe that I burn with such a fire, rise against me, adding to the fire of ardour the fire of pain. Hence my heart within me not only grew hot but grew hot with a double fire when someone sins and is almost scandalized by me because I write, because in my *Treatise on the Psalms*, gathering certain things from the sayings of the Fathers, I add something further, reckoning it presumption and vain glory. Yet, however they may wish to judge us now, those to come will judge more gently. For, as the illustrious man Blessed Jerome says, while we live and are contained in a fragile vessel, the zeal of friends seems beneficial and the reproaches of rivals harmful. But after the earth has returned to its earth, and pale death has removed both us who write and those who judge us, and another generation has come, and a green forest has grown up while the first leaves fall, then minds alone are judged without regard to the distinction of names. The reader does not consider whose work it is, but what kind of work he is to read—whether its author lies as bishop or layman, emperor and lord, soldier and slave, in purple and silk or in the meanest cloth. He will be judged not by diversity of honours but by the merit of his works.

Indeed, Gerhoh seems to have laboured at nothing in this Commentary more ardently or industriously than the defence, against the more recent schools of his time, of the glory and honour of the man assumed into God and born into God. The Reichersberg chronicler expressly declares that this itself supplied Gerhoh with the occasion and inducement to expound the Psalms:

> For the defence of the opinion concerning the glory of the man assumed into God and born into God—an opinion in which, from his youth throughout his whole life, he had various serious opponents and assailants—he wrote diverse little works and letters. First, for this purpose, by the authority of Roman pontiffs, of the lords cardinal, and of very many other Fathers who seemed at that time to be pillars in the Church, he made an exposition of the Psalms in eight volumes.

In accordance with this opinion, Gerhoh most steadfastly maintains that, because of the most perfect, intimate, and close union of the divine Word with human nature, at least many things that belong to the divine nature in the same Christ by essence also belong and have been communicated by grace and union to that human nature in Christ. Yet the essence of each nature remains intact, and all confusion of the two natures is utterly excluded. This may be seen in very many places in this Commentary, especially on Psalm XV, verse 6, and Psalm XXXV, verse 10 and following; and it is argued expressly in almost the whole book *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*, and in nearly all the remaining little works and letters written on this subject. Eutyches, too, is expressly rejected and condemned more than once.

Yet whatever cautions Gerhoh may have taken, he could not avoid the criticism of the celebrated theologian Stevartius. According to Pinio, *New Library*, vol. IX, p. 186, Stevartius judged that Gerhoh, while refuting one extreme, Nestorianism, had fallen into the other, that is, Eutychianism. Certainly harsh and exceedingly strong are the things he comments and writes concerning Christ’s human nature on Psalm VIII, verse 2; Psalm LVI, verse 4; Psalm XIII, verse 1; and elsewhere throughout.

But if Gerhoh was perhaps carried too far in the heat of debate on a most subtle and perplexing question, he will easily deserve pardon from those acquainted with the circumstances and times. Certainly, in the twelfth century this matter seemed so difficult in Germany, where the conflict raged most fiercely, even to many learned and exceptionally erudite bishops that they did not know to which side they should commit themselves. Indeed, even Rome did not have a sufficiently ready and clear decision to make at once. For when Gerhoh, after a prolonged contest with Eberhard, the most learned Bishop of Bamberg, brought the controversy before Pope Alexander II and hoped that his opinion, which he held most certain, would be confirmed and defined by apostolic judgment, the pope was so far from defining the dispute that, leaving the matter undecided, he even ordered both parties henceforth not to deliver public discourses on this question, since these would bring more disturbance than benefit to the people.

In volume VI, which is now under the press, we shall publish the letters of Gerhoh, Eberhard, and Alexander, lest anyone think that I have introduced these matters here without sufficient investigation. Finally, whatever Gerhoh’s opinion concerning the glory of Christ’s human nature may have been, he certainly never ceased to be Catholic, since he never wished to dissent from the holy Roman Church in the doctrine of faith—as we saw above from his book *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*. Finally, most worthy of notice are the things that Gerhoh himself testifies concerning his opinion in the preface to his exposition of Psalm LXIV:

> It had indeed been our intention to abbreviate in the present work this treatise formerly sent and presented to the Roman pontiff, Eugenius III, and strengthened by his approval. But because some oppose our opinion concerning the glorification of the human substance in the Son of God—which we set before Pope Eugenius in this treatise with the intention and purpose that we might abide by his judgment whether it was to be maintained or not maintained, although we had the ancient Roman pontiffs agreeing with us in the same opinion—we have been compelled now to offer to the reader’s consideration in full what we then offered to the Roman pontiff for judgment. Thus, because he accepted and ratified what we affirm in this treatise, every mouth of those teaching contrary things may be stopped, and the faith of those glorifying the man in God may be strengthened—indeed, those venerating him as supremely glorified by the supreme Father, and worshipping him with the worship with which God alone is to be worshipped, etc.

From this it is clear that Gerhoh, together with so many Roman pontiffs who at least privately praised and approved his teaching, either never departed from Catholic truth, or at any rate departed from it without blame.

But enough now concerning the life and writings of Gerhoh. It will now be yours, most reverend, most illustrious, and most eminent prelate, graciously to admit me with him to your gracious bosom, and, if you still possess any other Gerhohian materials, to enrich my *Treasury* with them. When you have kindly done this, you will have bound and obliged not only me but the whole commonwealth of letters to you in the highest degree. Meanwhile, may God, thrice best and greatest, preserve and prosper your most religious governance with every kind of good and advantage!

[Col. 0479]

## NOTICE FROM FABRICIUS

(*Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. IV, p. 47.)

[Col. 0479A] Gerhoh, Gerohus, Gerochus, of the Order of Regular Canons of St Augustine, provost of Reichersberg in Bavaria from 1132 to 1169. Much concerning his life and praises occurs in the *Chronicle of the Monastery of Reichersberg*, p. 226 ff. This Chronicle ends in 1194 and was recently reprinted, from Christopher Gewold’s Munich edition of 1611, quarto, by the illustrious Johann Peter Ludewig in vol. II of *Writers on Bamberg Affairs*, Leipzig, 1718, folio.

In that Chronicle the following testimony concerning Gerhoh’s writings is read on p. 237 (304):

> How, in what manner, or how greatly he loved every form of righteousness and hated every way of iniquity, is clear to readers and those wishing to know from his various little works, which he wrote to Pope Innocent, Pope Eugenius, [Col. 0479B] and the lords cardinal, and from other little works written to various persons. It is likewise clear from his letters, written to various persons at various times, which are almost all still found in his register and letter-book, in two volumes. Also, for the defence of the opinion *On the Glory of the Man Assumed into God and Born into God*, in which he always had various serious opponents and assailants from youth throughout his whole life, he wrote diverse little works and letters. First, for this purpose, by the authority of Roman pontiffs, of the lords cardinal, and of very many other Fathers who seemed at that time to be pillars in the Church, he made an exposition of the Psalms in eight volumes. He also wrote a little work [Col. 0479C] against the disciples of Peter Abelard, addressed to Otto, Bishop of Freising, brother of King Conrad, and various little works and writings to the people of Freising themselves. Likewise, very many writings to Daniel, Bishop of Prague; a little book on Faith at the request of Lord Henry, cardinal-priest; [Col. 0480A] a little work addressed to Pope Adrian [VI]; a *Dialogue between Greeks and Latins*; a little book *On the Glorification of the Son of Man*, addressed to Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg; and, lastly, little works addressed to Pope Alexander [III], the lords cardinal, and Eberhard, Bishop of Bamberg, on the same subject. Moreover, he wrote many other works addressed to various persons, all of which it would take too long to mention.

Among the published works of this Gerhoh are:

*Book on the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*, or *On the Glorification of Human Nature in Christ*, addressed to Hermann, Bishop of Brixen, in Bernhard Pez, *Anecdotes*, vol. I, part II, pp. 164–280. In this book he mentions his commentaries on the Psalms, pp. 163–331; his little book *On the Novelties of His Time*, [Col. 0480B] p. 169; his little work *On Faith*, concerning “Who shall find a valiant woman?”, p. 170; and his little work addressed to Pope Adrian IV, p. 256.

*Book against Two Heresies: the Nestorians, and Those Who Admit Excommunicated Priests and Their Sacraments*, addressed to Godfrey, Abbot of Admont, pp. 283–314. Inserted into this book, at p. 297, is a letter of Hugh of Rading, undertaking to prove that the sacraments of deposed priests are invalid.

Letter to Eberhard, Bishop of Bamberg, on how, according to Hilary, the Father who is about to glorify the Son is greater. There, pp. 317–326. In the Heilsbronn manuscript [Note: [Col. 0479] Johannes Ludovicus Hockerus, p. 47, manuscripts of Heilsbronn.] the writer of this letter [Col. 0480C] is called Gerhard of Reichersberg.

Four letters, pp. 329–334, in which he mentions his writing *On the Questions of Greeks and Latins*, p. 330.

*Syntagma concerning Emperors Henry IV and V*, [Col. 0481A] and Gregory VII and several subsequent Roman pontiffs, published by Jacob Gretser at Ingolstadt in 1611, quarto, and reprinted in vol. VI of Gretser’s works.

*Lives of the Abbots of Formbach, Berengar and Wirnto*, of the Benedictine Order, in the aforementioned Pez, *Anecdotes*, vol. I, part III, pp. 399–420.

*Book on the Building of God*, or *On the Zeal and Care for Ecclesiastical Discipline, Faith, and Duty, and the Diligence of Bishops and Other Clerics*—teaching that their condition is not inferior to the life of monks—in the same work, vol. II, part II, pp. 225–436; addressed to Chuno, Bishop of Regensburg, and, after his death, to the priest Arno.

[Col. 0481B] Epistolary book addressed to Pope Innocent II, *On the Difference between Secular and Regular Clerics*. There, pp. 439–504.

*Exposition of Psalm LXIV (LXV)*, or *Book on the Corrupt State of the Church*, addressed to Pope Eugenius III, in Baluze’s *Miscellanies*, vol. II, new edition, pp. 197–235, preceded by a letter to Henry, cardinal-priest, written after Eugenius’s death, and followed on p. 236 by letters of Eugenius approving Gerhoh’s writing. Baluze noted that it contains much most worthy of knowledge. Among other things, Gerhoh does not approve that, in place of “the Roman Church,” the name “Roman Curia” had begun to be frequently used.

*Treatise against the Simoniacs*, defective at the beginning, in [Col. 0482A] Edmund Martène, *Treasury of Anecdotes*, vol. V, pp. 1459–1496.

Stevartius notes that in the work *On the Investigation of Antichrist*, Gerhoh attacked the Nestorianism of Folmar, while complaining that Gerhoh himself approached more closely the ubiquity doctrine of the Putherists [reading uncertain]. See vol. XXVI of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, p. 240, and the entry “Folmar.”

Against this Gerhoh, a rather severe assailant of secular clerics, a council was held at Regensburg in 1130; see Marcus Hansiz, vol. II of *Germania Sacra*, p. 228. Nor should one omit here the letter of Eberhard, Bishop of Bamberg, addressed to Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, written against Gerhoh because he taught that the divinity in the sacrament of the altar is invoked by those receiving it, and that Christ as man is equal to the Father; [Col. 0482B] also another letter of the same Eberhard to the provosts of Salzburg, to whom he sends his writings against Gerhoh for examination; likewise another letter of his to an anonymous recipient, in which he weighs Gerhoh’s opinion concerning the glory of the Son of Man. Fr Pez published these three letters in the *Codex Diplomaticus*, p. 444, etc. There are besides certain letters of Gerhoh there not at all indicated by Fabricius. The first is addressed to the Abbot of Windberg and recounts what was done in Gerhoh’s disputation with Bernard of Bamberg. The whole collection consists of twenty-four letters, nearly all of which have Gerhoh as author; some, however, were written to Gerhoh himself.

[Col. 0481]

## LIFE OF GERHOH

(Extracted by Gretser from the Reichersberg Chronicle, *Works*, vol. VI, p. 238.)

[Col. 0481C] In the year 1132, Master Gerhoh received the provostship of the place of Reichersberg from Conrad, Archbishop of the Church of Salzburg. Lord Gottschalk, provost of the same place, had voluntarily resigned that provostship into the hand of the same bishop.

In the year 1169, Master Gerhohus, of holy memory, died in a good old age, on the fifth day before the Kalends of July [27 June], after having governed the community of Reichersberg energetically and faithfully for a little less than thirty-eight years. Since he was found faithful in a little thing, faithfully expending the talent entrusted to him by the Lord, he was set over many things; and there is no doubt that he has now entered into the joy of his Lord, having completed seventy-six years of life, in the second indiction, and forty-three years of priesthood.

### Gerhohus’s childhood and homeland

This Father, worthy of praise, is remembered as having followed the Lord from his earliest childhood. When, by his parents’ decision, he was devoted to the study of letters in his father’s house or native place, called Polling, [Col. 0481D] he seemed to surpass all his contemporaries in quickness of intellect and tenacity of memory. Yet in those things which children are accustomed to do in childhood, he was found simpler than the rest and incapable of guile. Thus in due time he displayed the line of his character in deeds and words, already in childhood drinking what he afterwards poured forth. Accordingly, when he was sixteen years old and was struck by an intolerable illness and pain, he became an imitator of the boy Joseph, [Col. 0482C] filled with virtuous shame. Once healed of that sickness, he directed his mind toward a resolution of chastity, and from then on devoted himself wholly to scholarly exercises in the cities of Freising and Moosburg.

### Gerhohus becomes master of the schools at Augsburg, then canon of Augsburg

Later, having reached adolescence and received a sufficiently honourable education, he turned his course toward the schools in Saxony, at the place called Hildesheim. After completing three years of study there, he returned to his homeland. At that time the principal schools in the city of Augsburg lacked a master. He was therefore called and appointed to that office. His cheeks were already shaded by a modest beard; he was handsome in appearance and, as throughout his life, well ordered in conduct. Consequently he was loved by all, but was especially pleasing and very acceptable to Hermann, bishop of that church; for this reason, with the unanimous assent of the brethren, the bishop made him a canon of that church.

[Col. 0482D]

### Gerhohus withdraws from communion with the schismatic bishop

At that time there was great discord between the royal power and the priesthood under Emperor Henry V the Younger. When this discord was at last settled through God’s grace and peace was restored to the Church under Pope Calixtus, Master Gerhohus, meanwhile, was not idle while these events were occurring. Rather, while that discord still endured, he already began to dare to resist the adversaries of God’s law, namely by withdrawing himself from communion with Hermann, bishop of Augsburg, [Col. 0483A] who had received him while he was still in the order of deacon, because that bishop favoured and communicated with the emperor and his party.

At first he did this not openly, but as though secretly. Afterwards, however, he openly confessed that in that evil time he thought with the Church and for the Church, refusing communion even to certain noble and honoured laymen who stood with the emperor’s party. For this reason nearly the entire city was stirred against him, judging him to be almost mad and rash for daring to provoke Caesar’s wrath against himself and the city.

### Gerhohus considers monastic life

When these matters, as has been said, had ended and been settled, the aforementioned bishop was restored, through Gerhohus’s mediation, to the favour of the Roman Church. Thus Gerhohus was already then pleasing and acceptable to the Roman pontiff himself and to the entire Roman curia. For a long time he had also cherished in his heart the purpose of communal religious life. To make himself freer for this undertaking, [Col. 0483B] he brought not only his brothers, but also his father and mother, to a new and holy manner of life in Christ.

Accordingly, after placing his two brothers, still boys, and likewise his father and mother, under a profession of regular life in the monastery of Rottenbuch; and thus being released from all things pertaining to him, the time had come for the purpose of communal life, long conceived in his mind, to break forth as into birth.

### He dedicates himself to God at the monastery of Rottenbuch

> [Note: [Col. 0483] This is in Bavaria. See Hund, *Metropolis*.]

Leaving behind the very wealthy canonry and the noble city of Augsburg, he turned aside to the aforesaid monastery of clerics at Rottenbuch, choosing rather to lead a poor life with the poor than to dwell in the tents or panelled houses of sinners. There he was received as an angel of the Lord. Having laid aside his costly clothing and the hair of his head, and having exchanged his secular dress, he was conformed and joined to the Lord’s flock.

Then, indeed, with what ardour and zeal he embraced the way of common life, and with what zeal for rectitude he lived, the entire church of Rottenbuch bears witness. All who were near or far, to whom the report of his holy life came, bear witness. They testify, I say, how the zeal of his conversion began to blaze: namely, through persistence in prayer, reading, and the riches of the divine utterance, he was so inflamed that his own speech also became exceedingly fiery, and his word, as is written of Elijah, burned like a torch. Therefore he continually urged his fellow brethren, not only by words but by examples, to observe the good customs of a stricter life and the institutions of the holy Fathers; indeed, he rebuked, exhorted, and reproved them according to the Apostle’s command (2 Tim. 3).

In all things presenting himself as an example, in many vigils, frequent meditation and reading of the Holy Scriptures, much patience, chastity (2 Cor. 6), and every exercise of good virtues, [Col. 0483D] he made himself illustrious; finally, he was conspicuous in all integrity of conduct. Hence he was greatly loved by all good and religious people.

### Gerhohus disciplines his body; diligently investigates and follows the Rule of St Augustine; his fervour arouses others’ hatred

He was also an exceedingly severe disciplinarian of his body, so that he abstained somewhat immoderately even from necessary food. His flesh was consumed by hunger, and his skin almost clung to his bones. Thus he burned incomparably, through the inextinguishable fire of most holy love, toward God and, through the untiring zeal of his mind, toward the beauty of common life.

For in those days he was not satisfied with that wonderful sweetness which he found in reading the excerpt from the sayings of the saints concerning canonical life—the work which his brethren had hitherto used as a rule. Rather, he sought with every attentiveness how he ought to live according to the Rule of our holy Father Augustine, or what that rule was according to which he had professed to live. Nothing seemed sufficient to him as a rule if it was not the rule which he had professed. Yet at that time the rule was not found in those regions, nor in other places of the same profession.

For this reason he judged it necessary to approach the Roman pontiff with certain brethren of the cloister, so that he might establish in that cloister, to which Gerhohus was bound, the rule which he had professed jointly and in common with all; and this was done. Hence he stirred up violently against himself the minds and hatred of certain envious and indolent persons whose manner of life differed from his, so that afterwards he suffered in the same place even to the danger of his life. Since he also rebuked there certain other intolerable abuses, the Lord’s saying could already then fittingly have been applied to him: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake,” etc. (Matt. 5). [Col. 0484B]

### Gerhohus is sought by the bishop of Regensburg. The conflict between Conrad and Lothair brings dangers to Gerhohus. He comes to Salzburg

After some time had passed, he was greatly desired by the venerable Chuno, bishop of the Church of Regensburg, and by the provost and brethren of the monastery of Rottenbuch, and was given to the bishop as an assistant. In due course he was ordained priest by him.

In those days Conrad—afterwards king, but then having seized tyrannical power against King Lothair, whom the princes had by common decree made their king—wished himself to be regarded as king. Because the aforesaid bishop withdrew himself from communion with and recognition of him, and Master Gerhohus did so with the bishop, the tyrant, together with his supporters, retainers, and confederates, was hostile to them, even to the point of laying snares for them more than once. By frequently threatening them with bodily harm and injuries, they intimidated them, so that the life of the aforesaid master was often endangered. [Col. 0484C] For he had denounced Conrad’s tyranny and schism in a public and solemn assembly.

He was therefore forced to leave the parish church entrusted to him by Bishop Chuno, namely the parish called Cham, unable to endure their injuries and attacks. There, with the bishop’s assistance and with certain clerics associated with him in the same purpose, he had intended to establish a community of common life; but, as has been said, he was prevented. After the departure from this life of the aforesaid Bishop Chuno of blessed memory, Gerhohus was received by Conrad the Elder, archbishop of Salzburg, who on several occasions sent him to Rome on his embassy to transact ecclesiastical business before the Apostolic See.

### Gerhohus becomes provost of Reichersberg. His character as ruler. His life is criticized. Gerhohus is welcome even when reproving

Thereafter, in the year 1132, [Col. 0484D] the care and provostship of the monastery of Reichersberg, which belonged to the Church of Salzburg and at that time lacked a governor, was entrusted to him with the consent of all by the aforementioned archbishop. The archbishop rejoiced greatly that a man such as this had been given him by God, one capable of building up the Church in sound doctrine.

What manner of man he proved in authority; how, strengthened by God, he never failed in all the Church’s subsequent tribulations; how he most often confessed and defended the truth steadfastly before kings and princes, not without danger to his own life—the whole of Germany bears witness, itself illuminated by the light of his teaching and rebuked for many transgressions and abuses by the fervour of his spirit. All among whom he happened to live or dwell for any period bear witness. Above all, the holy college of his brethren [Col. 0485A] and sisters knows how holily and irreproachably he lived among them for almost eleven years.

All know how tranquil he was when devoted to reading and prayer, and how he left no hour empty of exercises of devotion. For bodily exercise seemed to him, with the Apostle, useful only a little, unless necessity in the monastery required it. Indeed, the lamp of his heart and mouth shone even into foreign lands. Neither France nor Bohemia nor Hungary, nor even Greece, remained without experience of the grace which radiated from his heart and mouth. Such grace was poured upon his lips that he was welcome even to those whom he rebuked.

### His freedom in rebuke. Gerhohus’s devotion to the sacred books

Thus the Roman pontiffs and the lord cardinals always loved him, although in many matters he rebuked them. He did not fear kings and powerful men so as to refrain from declaring to them what was just and salutary whenever an opportunity presented itself. Great men, persons of middling rank, and common people hung upon the sweet and saving words of his mouth, whether in public assemblies of the Church or in private conversations.

He was so filled with the divine Spirit that rivers of living water almost always and without failing flowed from his belly, whether he spoke or wrote anything for the profit and instruction of his neighbours. He held the holy canonical Scripture of the Old and New Testament in such veneration, as was fitting and just, that he did not doubt its truth and constancy in a single iota. While travelling or engaged in any occupation, he allowed nothing from its reading to pass by without making it good through reading or hearing. He maintained this habit and devotion toward holy canonical Scripture throughout his life.

All know how ready and generous he was in teaching, how eager and effective in exhortation, and how severe in [Col. 0485C] rebuke. He preserved among his own the affectionate kindness of a father and the sternness [reading perhaps *durum*, “harshness”] of a master, so that, although they gave him due reverence, he inspired more love than fear in all. In short, he himself was an example of conduct, a model of religious life, an incentive to progress; and, to speak in a brief word, he was himself the chariot of Israel and its charioteer (4 Kings 3).

### The growth of the monastery of Reichersberg under Gerhohus

It is very evident how greatly the place whose governance he assumed advanced through his labour. Though he found it not very wealthy, through his diligence it was enriched with estates and other possessions: both through the grants and generosity of the pontiffs of Salzburg and Passau, to whom that place belonged—namely through the addition of parish churches, that is, parishes with their tithes, and other estates—and through the gifts of princes and offerings of many nobles [Col. 0485D] and other faithful persons who subjected themselves and all their possessions to his direction and wished to be formed by his holy ordinances and disciplines.

### Discipline of monks and clerics under Gerhohus. Idleness is banished from Gerhohus’s community. Each person’s occupations

How well ordered his entire holy congregation was under him, especially its clergy; what fitting order and discipline there were among the clergy; with what honourableness and patience they shone; what gravity was found in the old, what kindness in the young; what constant zeal, what learning, what beauty in the service of God, and what purity and beauty in the ministry of divine things—what tongue could explain it? No idle or slothful person was found among them. If there was one, he was not tolerated.

Very many of them were considered highly noble. All alike devoted themselves either to God’s service, private prayers, or reading at the appointed hours and times; in their proper time [Col. 0486A] they occupied themselves in copying books or other work. Young men and boys laboured at various crafts; Gerhohus himself frequently applied himself to them, now as a kindly instructor, now as a stern corrector.

Amid these things he considered himself blessed when he saw his disciples, like swarms of bees, fervently engaged in spiritual occupations, with none of them falling away. Rather, he declared that all were striving to advance from virtue to virtue, and that thus, by living in this way, they would at last see the God of gods in Zion. Since all lived soberly, justly, and devoutly, they all laboured together for this: that the divine mysteries might be celebrated and handled fittingly, with purity of mind and body, cheerfulness, and willing devotion. He taught that all, learned and unlearned alike, ought to strive for this, and that this was the one and only work for which they left their own possessions when coming from the world and chose to dwell together.

### Gerhohus’s devout wish

With these and innumerable other instructions he exhorted his brethren in conferences. He frequently rejoiced to recall that he wished and prayed God that his congregation might so set itself against the wicked adversaries—that is, “the rulers of this darkness,” who always war against the soul—that it might be “terrible as an army with banners”; and that it might be like “a flock of shorn sheep coming up from the washing,” concerning whom it is said in the Song of Songs that all bear twins and none among them is barren. [Col. 0486B]

### Gerhohus restores the monastery buildings. Many follow Gerhohus’s example

He restored the internal and external buildings of the monastery itself, and all its workshops. He had found them all wooden, very old, and ruinous; through those brethren whom he found fit and suitable in the congregation for this responsibility, he renewed them to a better condition and arranged them more suitably.

For he laid the burdens of external concerns upon his brethren, so that he might give himself wholly to holy leisure, especially upon faithful and prudent lay brethren. The Lord had given him no small number of these, drawn to him by the reputation of his holy character. Among them were many very noble and distinguished men, and thoroughly religious, like the rest. He permitted nothing disordered or contrary to religious life to remain in his congregation.

He likewise exhorted them in his conferences, especially to obedience, explaining to them the obedience of our father Abraham, the patience of Isaac, and the labour and endurance of Jacob. Thus they too were to labour obediently and patiently, working with their own hands that which is good, and considering the Lord’s end and long-suffering. He added that “no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9). He also warned them to be faithful in what was entrusted to them, and to preserve their manner of life, modesty, and chastity among secular persons, with whom they frequently had to live because of external affairs, so that, seeing [Col. 0486D] their good works, those persons might become their imitators and glorify the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5).

### He establishes a monastery of nuns. Most noble virgins—[the heading’s final phrase is textually uncertain]—in a monastery built through Gerhohus’s work

He was the first to establish in the same place a monastery of religious women living under the Rule of Blessed Augustine. Through his care, their church itself, which he constructed from the foundations, was dedicated by the venerable Romanus, bishop of Gurk, in the presence of Archbishop Conrad, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138. The holy souls whom he had gathered had already then entered there as into an ark and were shut in from without, in honour of God and Saint Mary ever Virgin, to whom the monastery was dedicated.

There those blessed souls, desiring to bring the begun work to completion, now await the coming of the Bridegroom (Matt. 25), so that when the gates of the highest kingdom are opened, they may be brought into the chamber of the eternal King. In contempt of the world they shall receive white robes and shining crowns, together with [Col. 0487A] their other companions gathered there from that time and likewise consecrated by the Lord with the honour of virginity. The good shepherd left behind at his death a considerable number of these women. Among them were daughters of noble and distinguished men, and two daughters of one prince, one of the noblest and greatest princes of the realm.

### Gerhohus is esteemed by the supreme pontiffs. The Roman curia’s favour toward Gerhohus
