Moreover, how well known, beloved, and acceptable this blessed man was to the supreme Roman pontiffs who presided over the Roman See in his time—first to Pope Calixtus, mentioned above, and then to each of his successors down to Pope Alexander; how reverently these Roman pontiffs received, praised, and approved the fervour of his religious life, his zeal, teaching, and writings; and how promptly he always obtained an outcome in all his affairs whenever he needed to appeal to the Roman curia, whether personally, through envoys, or by letters alone, on whatever business—is attested by apostolic letters and by the letters of the lord cardinals, frequently sent on his behalf to others or specifically addressed to him.

It is also attested by the letters which, returning often from the City [Rome] on his own affairs or those of others, he brought back personally. Copies of all these are still found. The privileges of Pope Innocent and Pope Eugenius, secured and obtained for that place by his exertions, show how greatly the Roman pontiffs, out of reverence and affection for him, honoured and protected under their own and Blessed Peter’s protection the place which he ruled, namely the monastery of Reichersberg; how often they defended it against grave enemies and attackers; and what liberty and legal right they granted and perpetually confirmed to that place by their authority. [Col. 0487B]

[Col. 0487C]

### The goodwill toward Gerhohus of various princes and bishops

Afterwards the pontiffs of Salzburg, Conrad the Elder and his successor Eberhard, piously imitated them, as did the princes of the realm, namely dukes and counts, each of whom fortified the same place with many privileges according to his legal authority. Likewise, other pontiffs—the bishops of Bamberg, Passau, and Freising—confirmed by their privileges to that monastery estates and possessions granted to the place, whether by themselves or by others, within their bishoprics.

Finally, the lord Emperor Frederick himself received the monastery of Reichersberg, with everything belonging to it, under the guardianship of his imperial majesty and of all his successors, kings and emperors. By his privilege he confirmed to the place its ancient and original liberty, through the intervention of Archbishop Eberhard of Salzburg, Bishop Eberhard of Bamberg, and Bishop Hartmann of Brixen, in accordance with the petition of this often-mentioned Father. [Col. 0487D]

### His labour to restore peace by removing schism. Gerhohus’s books

How sound and Catholic was his faith and apostolic teaching; how greatly, from his youth, he laboured by speech and writing for various ecclesiastical causes and for obtaining and preserving good customs and disciplines for the canonical order; how greatly he fought against the abuses, abominations, and worst novelties which he grieved to see growing in the Church in his time; how greatly he urged concord between royal power and priesthood in writings sent to the Roman curia and the emperor’s court; how greatly he abhorred and guarded against the schism that arose near the end of his life; how greatly he hungered and thirsted for [Col. 0488A] righteousness; finally, in what way, how, and how greatly he loved all justice and hated every way of iniquity—these things are clear to readers who wish to know from his various little works, which he wrote to Pope Innocent, Pope Eugenius, the lord cardinals, and others.

The same is clear from his letters, written to different persons at different times. Nearly all of them are still found in his register and letter-book, in two volumes.

> [Note: [Col. 0487D] Would that they were found! For they do not appear in the carefully written Reichersberg catalogue.]

In defence also of the teaching concerning the glory of the man assumed into God and born into God—a teaching for which he had from youth throughout his whole life various serious opponents and assailants—he wrote various little works and letters, initially on this subject, by the authority of Roman pontiffs and lord cardinals and of many other Fathers who seemed at that time to be pillars in [Col. 0488B] the Church.

He composed an exposition of the Psalms in eight volumes.

> [Note: [Col. 0487D] The exposition on the Psalms survives in the monastery of Reichersberg, [Col. 0488D] except for two volumes which are lost.]

He also wrote a little work against the disciples of Peter Abelard; various little works and writings to Otto, bishop of Freising and brother of King Conrad, and to the people of Freising themselves; likewise many writings to Daniel, bishop of Prague; a little book *On Faith*, at the request of Henry, cardinal priest; a little work to Pope Adrian; a *Dialogue between Greeks and Latins*; a little book *On the Glorification of the Son of Man* to Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg; finally, little works to Pope Alexander and the lord cardinals, and to Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, on the same matter. Besides these he wrote many other things to various persons, all of which would take too long to mention.

### Gerhohus’s death

Until his very illness—indeed, until the very day of his falling asleep—he preached the word of God in the holy Church unceasingly, eagerly, and vigorously, with sound mind and sound judgment, all the members of his body unharmed and his sight and hearing unimpaired. At last, when the Lord called him, with all the brethren present and praying, he slept with his fathers on the fifth day before the Kalends of July [27 June], at midnight. Two days before, he had been nourished with the divine refreshment and incorporated into Christ, whom, as was fitting, he always loved, believed in, loved, and honoured—that is, on the feast day of Saint John the Baptist.

For on that very day, in the public assembly, as was his custom, he had solemnly celebrated the solemnities of Mass himself, in good health; and he had prolonged at great length his final sermon to the people, as though about to bid farewell to all. He was buried, amid the greatest grief of all, honourably in the monastery beside the altar of the Holy Cross, on the third day before the Kalends of the same month of July [29 June]. [Col. 0488C]

Thus far the Chronicle of Reichersberg. This eulogy was inscribed beneath Gerhohus’s image at Reichersberg:

> [Col. 0488D] “In the year of the Lord 1132, Lord Gerhohus, distinguished doctor of sacred theology, was made the third provost of this place. He laboured to correct the conduct of the great, and was the founder of the monastery of nuns of the Blessed Virgin.”

Furthermore, of the many books written by Gerhohus, none remain at Reichersberg, as is evident from the carefully compiled catalogue of that monastery’s library, except two books *On the Investigation of Antichrist*, a sermon *On the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin*, and commentaries on the Psalter. Yet the third and fifth parts are lacking, through the negligence of persons unknown. To the eighth part of the studies on the Psalms, however, are appended a treatise *On Faith* and another *On the Fourth Watch of the Night*. Finally, a third work is *On the Order of the Gifts of the Holy Spirit*.

[Col. 0489]

# LETTERS OF GERHOHUS

(Extracted from the Reichersberg manuscript codex by R. P. Bernard Pez, *Anecdota*, vol. I, part II, p. 329.)

## LETTER I

[Col. 0489A]

To Master A. he writes that it does not seem necessary for his little works *On the Glorification of Human Nature in Christ* to be submitted anew to the judgment of the Apostolic See, since they had long ago been approved by it. He also sends and commends to him his work against Greek errors, etc.

Brother G. to Master A., greetings.

At our recent conference, brother beloved in God, you said that you thought it desirable for me to send to the Roman curia, there to be approved or disapproved, the teaching concerning the glorification of human nature in Christ—a teaching inserted here and there throughout many of my writings as a sign against which contradiction is made. When you had said this to me, I began to consider whether it was expedient to do as you advised. While considering, I reviewed our work previously presented in the Roman curia to Pope Eugenius of most holy memory, containing the same teaching fully and clearly set forth in the treatise on Psalm 64.

Since that wholly apostolic man considered this teaching pleasing and valid, and retained the little work of our writing as an acceptable gift, it seems superfluous or rash for the same teaching, once received at the Apostolic See, to be brought again for examination—as though there were doubt about the judgment of that most holy and prudent man, who truly was “a great priest in his days,” pleasing to God and found righteous. Your prudence knows how kindly he regarded me and my writings.

But now, with respect to his successor Pope Adrian, since I am unknown to him in person, and writings of my smallness have already been presented to him twice—first through the lord bishop of Bamberg and then through my uterine brother R.—and I have received from him no written answer, it does not seem advisable henceforth to press upon him any writing requiring long examination. For he, being a great man and occupied with great and many matters, may perhaps be unable to find leisure patiently to hear or read at length writings of little people such as ourselves. [Col. 0489C]

Therefore our work *On the Questions of Greeks and Latins* seems to be commended to Lord John, cardinal priest, formerly archdeacon of the Church of Jerusalem. I have found him inflamed with good zeal against Greek errors, so that, according to the prudence given him by God, he may consider it and do with it as he thinks fit: whether by sending it to Master Moses or presenting it to other Greeks who come to the curia. Thus he too will not seem blameworthy for having hidden his lord’s money, should he see that, by his own diligence, it may be put out to profit.

For I, a poor little servant of Christ’s poor, have laboured not a little, as far as I could, to dig this small coin from the field of Scripture. But weakened by old age and illnesses, and unable personally to carry it to the table of Romans or Greeks, I send and entrust it to him whom I do not doubt to be a prudent money-changer. When the Lord comes, he will demand it with interest and render to each of us a reward according to his labour: to me, the little digger; to him, the great steward; to you, the mediator of both.

Read, if you please, the first part on the second fifty of the Psalms, in which you will find the psalm mentioned above as the last. Do not doubt that Pope Eugenius of most holy memory agreed with me in every respect. Consider his letter, sent to our smallness, appended after the end of the aforementioned psalm. [Col. 0490B]

## LETTER II

To Henry, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, to whom he offers and commends his exposition of Psalm 64.

To the venerable Henry, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church, etc. It appears below, prefixed to the aforesaid exposition.

To these items in the same Reichersberg codex is appended the letter of Eugenius III, in which he praises and approves Gerhohus’s aforesaid exposition of Psalm 64. It was published by Baluze in the place cited. (It appears below at the end of this exposition.)

## LETTER III

[Col. 0490C]

To Otto, bishop of Freising.—He submits the first part of his exposition of the Psalms to Otto’s judgment and explains what others have thought of it. Certain matters against schoolmen, theologians, and philosophers, etc.

The chief Psalmist teaches that one must sing psalms “in the sight of angels,” and we desire to be his humble followers. Therefore, what we have gathered together in the treatises on the Psalms from the judgments of the Fathers, we willingly present to the angels of the Churches. For they are the money-changers to whom the Lord’s money must be presented and through whom it must be administered, because stewardship has been entrusted to them.

Yet it is rightly required among stewards that a person be found faithful. Faithful, I say, and prudent (Matt. 24). For one without the other is insufficient: either if the faithful person lacks prudence in discerning, or if the prudent person lacks fidelity in preserving what is entrusted to him. Who, do you suppose, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord appoints over his household? Such a person is rare, and therefore illustrious, because one man is chosen out of thousands who is perfect in both respects.

Nevertheless, so far as human judgment is concerned, I, G., the least of Christ’s poor, judge that neither quality is lacking in you, angel of the Church of Freising. Many experiences, shown to me by divine gift, demonstrate that you are at once faithful and prudent.

Accordingly, I send and entrust to your fidelity and prudence for reading what I have at hand in the first part of my Treatise on the Psalms, so that, wherever I think soundly, I may be supported by the testimony of your authority. But if otherwise—which I do not acknowledge—then, recognizing it piously, I may correct it by your counsel. Indeed, Pope Eugenius, the angel of the Roman Church, encourages me by his letter in pursuits of this kind; and therefore I care little for the objections of certain people against me, who almost know no other wisdom than what they have drunk in scholastic exercises, where the waters of Siloam are not found, which [Col. 0491B] flow quietly; where wine is often lacking at the banquet; where such men continually dispute among themselves, who think it delightful to dwell under thorns.

We do not, indeed, deny that among such men there are masters outstanding in the torrents of eloquence and abounding in fountains of wisdom. And, what is more precious, they possess Jacob’s well, namely Holy Scripture, from which they refresh their disciples—men less devoted to wisdom than curious for knowledge. Some of these, leaving Samaria, come to Jerusalem, and there bless the Lord, not from Jacob’s well but from the springs of Israel; for in holy and religious conduct it is pleasant for them to taste Holy Scripture, not according to the various teachings and contests of the masters, [Col. 0491C] but according to the sound and harmonious teaching of the holy Fathers who see God.

Thus masters are preferred to masters: fishermen to rhetoricians; infants and nursing children to disputatious men, from whose mouths God perfects his praise. Through their milky teaching he draws some men to himself away from the torrents of philosophers. By God’s grace I have experienced this in myself in part, and I hope to experience it more fully when that which is perfect comes, and that which is partial is done away. For I too once drank from the torrents of philosophers on the way, and lowered the pitcher of my curiosity into their springs. But, having at last left that pitcher behind, I listened in simplicity with the Samaritan woman to the Savior’s admonitions, urging my neighbors to do likewise, insofar as I could—those [Col. 0491D] who nevertheless do not believe what I write on account of my own speech.

For they themselves hear and recognize that I endeavor to gather true testimonies of the truth. I am accustomed to fortify these everywhere with the authorities of the holy Fathers, accepting them wherever any contradiction is thought to arise, so that no one may readily dare to condemn me or my statements unless he presumes to inflict injury upon the holy Fathers, under whose guardianship and guidance I proceed in fear, ready to give and receive an account.

The angel of the Church of Salzburg has carefully read this very part, as well as the other, and draws me onward in the cord of charity. [Col. 0492A] While you remained in exile, he was the one angel in this province whom I chose, to whose judgment I might entrust myself, perceiving him to be faithful as well as prudent. But now, since, by God’s gift, we have received you back from the furnace of exile as gold tested by fire, you too, by the assent of divine grace, are to be invoked by me as an angel bearing witness to sound doctrine, so that the word concerning our work may stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses, and may, if it please you, be presented to a third angel, namely the Roman pontiff. His letter concerning certain writings of ours is at hand; whoever wishes to read it can readily understand what that angel thinks of me, so that, through chosen angels, in the sight of the other angels who shall judge our work worthy of reading, there may be [Col. 0492B] commendation of it and, where the matter requires, correction.

[Note: [Col. 0491] The letter of Pope Eugenius mentioned above follows in the manuscript.]

## LETTER IV

**To Sister G.**—He declares that he did not supplant the abbess of Braga, but rightly consented to her canonical deposition on account of her obstinacy; nevertheless, he is prepared to assist her if she behaves modestly, etc.

Brother G., to his beloved sister G. in Christ: devoted prayer and perpetual love in Christ.

I have been told that the former abbess of Braga, who is staying among you, complains bitterly that I was, as it were, the author of her supplanting. If this has been reported among you, I desire and ask that my conscience be regarded by you and by our other beloved sisters in Christ [Col. 0492C] as cleared of the charge of supplanting.

For there is a kind of supplanting which occurs without fault, after the example of him who supplanted his brother in the womb, took his birthright from him, and finally obtained his blessing by the counsel of his prudent mother—would that all my counsels might accord with hers! And, as I hope, such were my counsels concerning the reform of the abbey of Braga, which we would most gladly have carried out through the abbess herself at that time, had we found in her consent to it. Instead, we found such rebellion that she broke out into open defiance of obedience in the presence of the lord cardinal, who was ready to punish every act of disobedience. Since I was present, I was obliged to concur in his just sentence concerning her deposition [Col. 0492D] and to work so that, in the place of disobedient Vashti, obedient Esther might be exalted—not through supplanting, but through canonical election and divine disposition.

Yet, since, thanks be to God, no grave crimes were found in the person who was deposed, my counsel is that she should be helped in her needs, provided that through her humility and kindness the suspicion may be removed which letters lately sent by her to Braga have aroused. In them she speaks as though she were exercising dominion and issuing threats. Therefore, if any kindness were shown to one speaking in that way, it would seem to have been extorted by threats and bestowed from human fear rather [Col. 0493A] than divine love.

If, therefore, she listens to you, dearest sister, and to our other dear sisters, advise her; and, on the basis of your advice, I shall gladly make provision for whatever may relieve her, as far as I can consistently with God’s honor. That is, she should receive some definite consolation from the lady abbess of Braga, who loves this woman even though she speaks ill of her.

If then this woman, by loving the other, returns grateful reciprocity and rejoices that her former negligence is being corrected through her, then both she who was deposed and she who was installed will be worthy—not, I say, of my love, but of God’s love. For, while the one acts and the other favors it, a single work of cloistered discipline is being carried out in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation. This will be reckoned to each of them—that is, both to the one who loves [Col. 0493B] and to the one who acts—for the attainment of the reward of blessedness. Both shall be loved by me in Christ’s love, and my diligence, God inspiring it, shall be ready to serve both.

But if they are hostile toward one another, I shall acknowledge myself bound by the duty of the bridal attendant to her whose Lord, Jesus Christ, the bridegroom and lover, I recognize.

I do not say this as though he loves only virgins or penitents enclosed in seclusion; for he also loves her who speaks to him in the Song of Songs:

> “Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves;  
> I sought him, and did not find him.  
> I will arise and go about the city;  
> I will seek him whom my soul loves.”  
> (Song of Songs 3)

Therefore we do not condemn every going about of the bride, since there is a praiseworthy circuit of the bride in which the beloved is sought and found; and, once found, she remains with him and shows him the bed, saying to him: “Our bed is flourishing,” etc. (ibid.). The bride who shows the bed to the bridegroom clearly indicates that rest, not running, delights her—unless perhaps she runs after him, saying: “Draw me after you; we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments” (ibid.).

I too know certain brides of God who are not enclosed, among whom you are foremost and especially beloved to me. In them I approve chastity, integrity of morals, and honorable conduct under no mastership—or under one that is weak or base. I praise them; yet in this I do not praise them: that they are guarded neither by cloistered enclosure nor, as they themselves call it, [Col. 0493D] prison-like confinement.

For there is also a blessed prison, in which Christ rejoices to be visited, saying: “I was in prison, and you came to me” (Matt. 25). You too, beloved sister in Christ, lately fulfilled the service of this pious visitation when you visited our sisters [Col. 0494A]. Know that it would please me if you do so more often—indeed, it would please him who will say to you: “I was sick and in prison, and you came to me” (ibid.).

And would that you might so come to him who remains in prison that you would no longer seek to wander farther away, even to visit your dearest friends in the world. For it is one thing to go about among foreign daughters after the example of Dinah, and another to go up with haste into the hill country after the example of Mary, to the house of a just man and prophet, in order to greet a prophetess. You ought to regard your sister as like that prophetess: now, thanks be to God, not barren, but free from the reproach of barrenness, since, thanks be to God, she has honorable offspring, in whom the name of John shines through God’s grace.

This, I hope, will bring an increase of grace both to her and to me, so that we may rejoice together: I, singing with Zachariah, “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel” (Ps. 105); she, with Hannah, “My heart exulted in the Lord” (Zach. X); and you also, when visiting her, may be granted to sing with blessed Mary in our house: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoiced in God my Savior” (Luke 1).

## LETTER V

**From A., abbot of Ega, to Gerhoh.**—He relates what happened to the provost of Triefenstein at Bamberg and, rejecting the latter’s teaching, praises Gerhoh’s Catholic writings.

To the venerable lord G., provost of Reichersberg, Brother A., called abbot of Ega: the service of devoted prayer.

You should know that what the provost of Triefenstein lately wrote—that he had set out his faith to us—happened only as we have written below. On one occasion, when a little book had been brought forth in our presence, he said: “This is my faith,” and read from it in our hearing, while we paid no attention and suspected nothing concerning it.

But after we received your writings, which you published in Catholic fashion against him, we acted on the command of the bishop of Bamberg to have him go with us into the bishop’s presence at Bamberg. There, before not a few religious and learned men, while the bishop proceeded against him, he humbly professed that he would henceforth neither think nor write anything of the sort.

Moreover, we agree with what those same writings of yours contain and judge them Catholic. Henceforth we desire and pray that divine mercy may enlighten the eyes of your heart to every knowledge of truth and love of virtue.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTERS

*(PEZ., Anecdota, vol. VI, part I.)*

[Col. 0493]

The letters of Eberhard, the most learned bishop of Bamberg, and Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, are distinguished, weighty, and filled with matters of the highest value. Almost the entire subject of these letters concerns the glory and honor of the Son of Man. Gerhoh asserts **by grace** concerning him many things which are proper to **God by essence**; Eberhard attacks this most vigorously.

A second point of controversy is constituted by the sacraments administered by excommunicated persons. Gerhoh, with several older theologians, attributes scarcely anything substantial to them, while Eberhard and others stoutly maintain the contrary. Moreover, after the matter had been examined and elucidated in many disputations and brought before Alexander III, Roman Pontiff [Col. 0495], Gerhoh asked and pressed him to settle the controversy by his judgment. But a different outcome ensued: the pontiff imposed silence on both parties as regards public disputations. See Alexander’s judgment among his letters.

For this reason I think it worthy of note that the pontiff “considered that no definite answer should be given on these same points, because,” he says, “unless we heard him and the others face to face, it did not seem right to us to pronounce judgment on them so readily, or to condemn one party by a hasty judgment on the grounds advanced by the other party alone, when that party had not been heard or defended.” Admirable equity in Alexander III!

## LETTER VI

[Col. 0495A]

**Letter of Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, to the provosts of Salzburg and Chiemsee.**—He declares his grief at the death of Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg, and sends them his writings against Gerhoh for examination.

[Note: [Col. 0495D] From a contemporary Admont manuscript.]

EBERHARD, by God’s grace the unworthy minister of the Church of Bamberg, to the venerable brothers and friends most beloved in Christ, I., provost of Salzburg, and D., provost of Chiemsee: a crown instead of ashes, oil of gladness instead of mourning, and a garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow.

In remembering our most blessed father and lord, Archbishop Eberhard, there continually comes to mind—indeed, it does not depart from our memory—that, when his lord had been taken from him and borne upward in a fiery chariot, that native and inseparable companion of the prophet cried after him, saying: “My father! My father! The chariot of Israel and its charioteer!” [Col. 0495B] (2 Kings 2).

For was not this great priest of ours one who pleased God in his days and was found righteous? He was a chariot when, with paternal consolation and compassion, he lightened the needs and infirmities of others, especially the burdens of sins and the poverty of the poor. It was as though he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11). Or was he not a charioteer, since he ruled those entrusted to him and directed them into the way of truth by examples as well as instruction? He was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. His hand was not turned away from any poor person; he delighted in jesting with them, in “corrixi” [reading uncertain; thus the manuscript reads], and finally in being overcome by an unresisting hand.

Moreover, in order to become all things to all people, even beyond the law, though not contrary to the law, he did not shrink from the breath of a leper or the touch of leprosy. What more? “He was taken away lest malice should change his understanding, or deceit beguile his soul” (Wis. 4). But, “having been made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled long years” (ibid.). And indeed, as it is written, the wickedness of those who remain deserves that those who might have been helpful be swiftly removed.

That memorable follower of the prophet had the magnificent consolation of a double spirit; but to us, at the passing of this most holy man, nothing has been left beyond mourning—unless perhaps we may be worthy to receive before God such great assistance from his patronage. Such a high priest was fitting for us: one for whom to live was Christ and to die was gain (Phil. 1). We had intended to hasten to see [Col. 0495D] him. But alas! We lament and complain, inconsolably, that through the demands of our sins this final benefit—the receiving of his blessing—has been divinely denied to us.

Finally, compelled by circumstances, we had sent certain writings to that father and lord most dear to us, as your discernment will be able [Col. 0496A] to see and recognize. But since they did not reach him while he still survived in the flesh, God hastening to lead him out from the midst of iniquity, we have therefore sent them especially to you, as those nearest to him by the obligation both of flesh and of spirit. Thus some memorial may at least remain in these writings of our devotion toward him and of his favor toward us.

They are sent under the same rule of examination and correction, and for the same judgment which we ought to have expected from his authority; the letter of Lord Gerhoh, as the prior matter of the following little work, has been prefixed at the beginning. Let us console one another. Our most loving father has entered into the joy of his Lord. May the Father [Col. 0496B] of mercies and God of all consolation himself console you and wipe away every tear from your eyes.

## LETTER VII

**Letter of Gerhoh of Reichersberg to Adam, abbot of Ebrach, against the errors of Folmar, provost of Triefenstein.**

To Lord A., venerable abbot of Ebrach, Brother G. of Reichersberg: devoted prayers with faithful service.

A letter lately came into my hands [Note: [Col. 0495D] The initial of the proper name has been erased. But it was E., or Eberhard, as is clear from what immediately follows.] addressed to the lord of Salzburg, in which your name was also mentioned, as you will be able to see in the answer to the letter. Its text runs as follows:

“To his lord E., venerable archbishop of Salzburg, F., by God’s grace—if he is anything at all: perpetual joy and freedom from every adversity. I have diligently set out in writing my faith concerning the truth of the Lord’s body and blood for Lord A., abbot of Ebrach, and also for other learned and religious men, and I found them in no respect whatever opposed or different,” etc., as above.

Here let your wisdom consider whether one offers rightly and divides rightly who carnally separates what the Lord has joined. For God-man joined flesh and bones in his resurrection when he said to his disciples: “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24). For in his body raised from death there were together not only flesh and bones, but also blood, a human spirit, and a divine Spirit, [Col. 0496D] which he breathed upon his disciples, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20).

Since the separation of the human spirit from the body is the death of that body, and likewise the separation of flesh from bones brings about the death of flesh; and since human blood outside flesh lacks the vital spirit, which is the rational soul, it is evident that those who divide Christ in this manner crucify him anew and expose him to contempt. Such is the teaching in the preceding letter, which was sent to a venerable archbishop so that it might be held in greater authority, and which is represented as approved among you and other learned and religious men—the faith in which Christ is divided contrary to Paul’s teaching.

But we, regarding that faith as the greatest perfidy, believe that in the Church of God the flesh of the Paschal lamb is not eaten in such a way—raw or cooked in water—that his blood or flesh is drunk or eaten separately. Although he is received under distinct species, namely bread and wine mixed with water, he remains in himself undivided and whole: wholly in heaven, wholly [Col. 0497B] on the altar, wholly in the mouth of the person eating his body and drinking his blood; wholly in the heart of the one who believes unto righteousness; wholly in the mouth of the one who confesses unto salvation.

Read Ambrose on Luke, where he expounds the angel’s saying, “He shall be great and shall be called Son of the Most High” (Luke 1:32), and you will find that wherever there is a true Christian, there Christ is. For he is to be worshipped neither in Jerusalem nor on this mountain where the fathers worshipped, as though God were not elsewhere; rather, true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth. Therefore in the truth of Christ’s sacraments God is worshipped, and he is received in the body taken from the Virgin and assumed into heaven.

This body is so eaten by the mouths of the faithful that what was commanded figuratively concerning the Paschal lamb is now truly fulfilled. For it could not, nor ought it, to have been literally done as was there said: “You shall eat the head with the feet and entrails” (Exod. 12). For this conflicts with the saying: “You shall not break a bone of it” (ibid.). How could the head and feet have been eaten without breaking the bones? But now, in the true Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, the head with the feet—that is, divinity with the whole humanity—is eaten; because Christ entire is eaten in the mystery of the altar. Nor will the eater change [Col. 0497C] him into himself—namely, the food of his flesh—but he himself will be changed into Christ, so that he may be a member of his body, which is the one Church, redeemed and made alive through the one body of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0497D] *Manducabit*: “will eat.”]

But as to the statement of the aforesaid divider of Christ, “I confess that I eat not the Son of Man, but the flesh of the Son of Man,” we think he drew it from Christ’s saying: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6).

Nestorius, the heresiarch, also drew the poison of his error from this passage, so that he denied the flesh received on the altar to be life-giving on the ground that it was human flesh, sanctified, as it were, by the indwelling of God, but wholly unable to give life to the person eating it, because, he says, “the spirit gives life; the flesh is of no avail.” Against his error the Council of Ephesus reads:

> “We approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, being made partakers of the holy body and precious blood of Christ, the Redeemer of us all—not as receiving common flesh, God forbid; nor as receiving the flesh of a man sanctified and united to the Word by a unity of dignity, or as possessing a divine indwelling, but as truly life-giving and made the very own flesh of the Word. For, being life by nature as God, because he is personally united to flesh, he declared it life-giving. Therefore, although he says to us, ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood,’ we nevertheless must not regard it as the flesh of one man among us. For how can human flesh be life-giving according to its own nature? Rather, we must regard it as truly made his own—the one who for our sake became and was called Son [Col. 0498B] of Man.”

Likewise:

> “If anyone does not confess that the flesh of Christ is life-giving, as being the flesh of the very Word of God the Father, but regards it as belonging to some other person united to him in dignity, or as life-giving merely because it possessed an indwelling, rather than—as I have said—as life-giving because it was made the own flesh of the Word of God, to whom it is possible to give life to all things: let him be anathema.”

[Note: [Col. 0497D] These words occur in the profession of faith printed at the beginning of the Council of Ephesus in the older edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0498D] This is the eleventh anathema in the older edition.]

This Council of Ephesus is one of the four councils whose solidity, as Blessed Gregory says, whoever does not maintain—even if he appears to be a stone—lies outside the building. He adds: “And whoever thinks otherwise, let him be anathema.”

Therefore, beloved and venerable Father, take care lest, though you are considered and are a precious stone in God’s building, you should be believed, because another falsely publishes it, to hold what you do not hold. For I believe, Father, that you hold one faith with us—indeed, with the whole Church—understanding by the name “flesh of Christ” nothing other than Christ’s flesh.

For Christ himself indicates that his words are to be understood in this way: the flesh of the Son of Man is not to be considered one thing and the Son of Man himself another, when he speaks of this sacrament. For, while commending the flesh of the Son of Man to be eaten, he also said beforehand, among other things: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so he who eats me, he also shall live because of me” (John 6). Therefore, whoever eats the flesh of the Son of Man eats the Son of Man; he eats the bread that came down from heaven, [Col. 0498D] which God the Father sealed—not with a material seal but with the indelible seal of supreme divinity—because “the Word became flesh” (John 1).

Therefore, whoever eats the flesh of the Word eats also the Word in his flesh. Otherwise the flesh would be of no avail if it did not have life and the power to give life within itself. Read Hilary’s eighth book, where he treats of this sacrament, and you will find him holding what I hold concerning the eternal Word eaten in his flesh. The aforesaid Folmar did not believe this possible, for he thinks that the Lord’s body, such as it was in the tomb, must be conceived separately.

[Col. 0499A] For he says: “Wherever Christ is, he is whole, although the whole is not there; just as at one and the same time he was wholly in the tomb and wholly in hell, yet the whole was not there, because something of the three substances that make one person in Christ was absent.”

To this we say that, truly, for a time the soul was absent from the body in the tomb, and the body from the soul in hell or paradise. But now neither his soul can be absent from Christ’s body, nor his body from his soul, nor the life of them both—which is nothing other than supreme divinity—from either of them at any time; because Christ no longer dies: death shall have no more dominion over him (Rom. 6). He does not die; he will not be divided; he will not forever be moved from his seat, where he sits with the Father.

Nevertheless, as the Spirit breathes where and as it wills (John 3), so also the man who is born of the Spirit presents himself where and as he wills, either spiritually or bodily, as the Church believes. Spiritually, as the Apostle says: “That Christ may dwell through faith in our hearts” (Eph. 3). Bodily, as the Church believes herself nourished by his body and blood, while Christ himself sanctifies himself by the hands and prayers of priests throughout the Church as they perform what he commanded, saying: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22).

Thus one of his ministers who performs this says: “The cup which we bless, is it not a communion in the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of the Lord?” (1 Cor. 10). He does not say that Christ presents himself bodily in so many different places at one and the same moment in the service of sacrificing priests, or as the received body in the mouths of faithful eaters, through local division or extension of bodily bulk; [Col. 0499C] rather, that he does so by ineffable power, through the mediation of that faith by which we unhesitatingly believe the word of Truth who says: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22).

I rightly said, “through the mediation of faith,” because “faith comes by hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Rom. 10). And just as a human audible word can be apprehended only through hearing, so that divine Word, made perceptible in human flesh as though in a bodily voice, can be apprehended only through faith. Give faith, and you will perceive the truth of what was said: “Do this in remembrance of me” [Col. 0499D] (Luke 22). Take away faith, and you will see that this Word is not apprehended, since it is apprehended only by faith, just as a human spoken word is not apprehended except through hearing.

Take away hearing, and you speak to a deaf person in vain, because he does not grasp what you say. Yet this is not a defect of the word but of hearing, because the sounds of words strike ears both deaf and stopped-up, and ears that are open. So too the Word of God, through that which is audible in it—its incarnation—and veiled beneath the form of bread, is offered by the hands of priests to believing faithful persons and unbelieving unbelievers alike. The believer is fed and filled by it. The unbeliever is judged and condemned by the same thing, because he does not discern the body of Christ. Whoever believes unworthy things about it receives it unworthily: like this man, who thinks Christ is eaten without his bones, who separates his blood from his flesh, and who thinks that he cannot be wholly and entire at once in heaven and on many altars.

Yet he sees that speech proceeding at once from a human heart and mouth is not divided among the many ears of those hearing it, but reaches each one whole and entire. How much more does the Word of God, proceeding from the heart and mouth of the Most High, yet remaining in him and with him, arrive whole and entire where it is sent, for the salvation of the elect—those loved from eternity in the Word himself.

Although unbelievers, like deaf persons, do not grasp this, those who have ears to hear do grasp it, and taste with that taste required where it is said: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. [Col. 0500B] 33).

## LETTER VIII

**Letter of Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, to Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg, against Gerhoh, asserting that the divinity is devoured by those receiving the sacrament of the altar, and that Christ as man is equal to the Father.**

To the most blessed father and lord Eberhard, archbishop of the holy Church of Salzburg: E. of Bamberg, through God’s patience, whatever he is, the whole of that very thing which is in him, without whom nothing is.

Although I have no leisure to write—I who am scarcely permitted even to breathe because of the innumerable and diverse occupations of worldly business, alas!—yet, necessity having no law and compelling me, I have broken somewhat the silence and resolution of silence which I had imposed on myself against writing. For “he who neglects his reputation is cruel” (Prov. 19).

The little sheets of Lord G., with which almost every corner of this land is now filled, have not passed me by or left me untouched among others—whether also among you, I do not know. Yet there I not only believe, but know and am certain, that nothing contrary to me—indeed, I will not say contrary to the truth—has found or will find a place which your mind could receive; for it is the dwelling-place of charity, truth, and all purity.

[Col. 0500D] Our aforesaid writer, learned in other matters not of this time, wrote to certain brothers, as though he alone were a prophet in Israel, that in a conference held with me he was disturbed in mind because I had compared Christ to a vassal. Saving his peace: though he is sufficiently wise and learned, in this he performed the office neither of a wise nor a learned man, nor even of a good man. He both slandered his neighbor and, by interpreting differently from what was said the things spoken between us, disclosed by his own evidence that he had spoken to me in his heart and with a heart directed not to the building-up of charity but rather to destruction.

For, since it is equally perilous to think either more or less than rightly of Christ, our brother himself, in his teaching, advanced something discordant with what the Catholic Church both holds and sings in the praise of the Creed concerning Christ: “Equal to the Father,” etc. I was astonished and, though less learned and wise, admonished him to spare his words and not thus wean us away both from solid food and from the most loving breast of Mother Church, since the same food is both milk for little children and solid food for the perfect.

But as he labored more and more in his proofs, and as, for disproving the truth, he brought forward the testimony of Truth himself—“All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Luke 10), and similar passages—to deny the conclusion that seemed to follow from this, namely that Christ is equal to the Father insofar as he is man, I proposed the analogy of a vassal [Col. 0501B] and lord. Although they may wholly possess the same thing and neither have less than the other, one is nevertheless less than the other.

I compared Christ to a vassal, and a vassal to Christ, in no other way than, as stated above, to specify in some measure what Bede says: “Whatever the Son of God possesses by nature, he gave the assumed man to possess by grace.” In a certain Apology written against follies of this sort, I also showed him that many things are explained by analogy, although one thing is not thereby made wholly equal to another by comparison. For it is very different to treat something by an illustrative comparison or parable, and to assimilate one thing to another, as equal to it in what it is or is not.

For this reason, what I wrote, I wrote then and write even now to your fatherly discernment, so that you may regard me as excused with respect to such extravagances. I submit these writings, such as they are, above all to your judgment and to that of all who love and understand truth, under fixed conditions of correction. For I know that among human inventions nothing is so perfect that it cannot be more perfect, nor so well said that it cannot be said better—or, by enemies, smeared in some respect with a malicious interpretation not suited to the meaning of the speaker or writer.

As the Apostle says, thanks be to God, “no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3). When he was about to pass from this world to the Father, he finally commended to his disciples the sacrament of his body and blood, the sacrament of all sacraments, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body” [Col. 0501D] (Matt. 26).

Building upon this firm and immovable foundation with examples and teachings—gold, silver, and precious stones—the holy Fathers have instructed and fortified the holy Catholic Church with many authorities, so that in the city of God there is no lack of wall or outer wall, and no other teaching is now further necessary. But if anyone, even an angel from heaven, should teach otherwise—that is, contrary to the Gospel—let him be anathema. Nevertheless, because the enemy does not cease continually to sow weeds among the wheat, and because they must grow until the harvest, the greatest care must be taken lest anyone [Col. 0502A] through ignorance or negligence receive false things as true.

Therefore, not usurping the authority of teacher or corrector, but performing, according to our measure, the office of adviser, we have decided to bring before the judgment of Your Holiness, for weighing and removing, certain matters of this kind—matters which trouble both ourselves and others—recently found in the writings of certain brethren. And this we do not for our own glory, nor for the shame or injury of the brethren whose writings they are. For if recourse is had to you as to a wise architect concerning matters pertaining to the adornment of God’s house, it is truly fitting and just, since God has bestowed upon you, above many of your fellow servants, both merits of life and treasures of learning.

[Col. 0502B] Certain writings addressed to Lord Gerhoh, abbot of Ebrach, have reached us, in which, to confess the truth, we, together with the abbot himself and several other brethren, were very greatly scandalized by the excessively incautious words of a certain brother, whom the abbot himself rightly rebukes. These were the words in a letter sent to you:

> “Thus, in the most holy mystery, I do not doubt that I drink, under the taste and appearance of wine, the utterly unmixed blood of the spiritual grape; but I drink it alone and pure, without flesh. So too I believe that I eat, under the taste and appearance of bread, the flesh of Christ alone and pure, without bones, without bodily limbs—indeed, without the fullness of a human body; and I confess that I eat not the Son of Man, but the flesh of the Son of Man.”

[Col. 0502C] Moreover, concerning the eucharistic pyx—that is, the Lord’s body—and certain other matters in the same sequence of letters which he had sent you, he seemed to have gone too far, as though the Lord’s body could be contained less in the eucharistic vessel than upon a spacious altar. But, having been asked by certain religious persons to write something in reply, at least for the edification of any little ones who need milk rather than solid food, we turned over in our minds that Gospel saying which is specially to be understood concerning the sin of scandal: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone” (Matt. 18:15). And we summoned to us, through Lord A., the venerable abbot of Ebrach, that brother who had written such things, especially because some years ago he had received from us—though we are unworthy—the laying on of hands for the priesthood.

[Col. 0502D] With God as author, and his word running swiftly, that brother was recalled from the error of his way. Returning to himself, he came to his senses to the same degree as he had been out of his senses in dividing, in the Lord’s body, flesh from bones and blood, and blood from bones and flesh. The occasion, he said, was these words: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6). Since the words are divided in the sentence, he had understood, with excessive simplicity, that they must also be received separately in the thing itself.

Moreover, he had found it written, namely in certain Sentences:

> “The whole Christ is received under each species, but that person in whom are those three natures”—namely, divinity, soul, and flesh—“and yet that material bread is changed into the body of Christ alone: just as Christ was whole upon the cross, and yet his flesh alone was wounded.”

[Col. 0503A] How inept this division of Christ’s body and blood by the aforementioned brother is, and how contrary to ecclesiastical truth, blessed Augustine declares most clearly:

> “When Christ is eaten, life is eaten; nor, when he is eaten, do we make parts of him.”

Likewise:

> “Each receives his own portion. He is eaten in portions, and remains whole.”

Therefore, having been fraternally admonished concerning the matters already mentioned, his other absurdities, and the excesses of his writings, the brother was corrected—thanks be to God—especially upon consideration of the authority: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). Yet he did not assume flesh alone, without a soul, but a human soul equally with a body.

[Col. 0503B] Likewise: “Take and eat: this is my body” (Matt. 26), which it is the height of unbelief and absurdity to believe either boneless or bloodless. Likewise, to regard the blood as existing without the body—as blood dripping from a body or flowing from a wound—is an equal madness, because we receive it as it is. What it is like he declared when, after the resurrection, he said: “A spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24).

[Col. 0503C] And the great herald of truth itself, blessed Hilary, cries out in testimony to the truth in this way:

> “Unless we learn from him, we speak foolishly and impiously concerning the natural truth of Christ in us, which we affirm. For he himself says: ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.’ No room for doubt has been left concerning the truth of the flesh and blood. For now, both by the Lord’s own profession and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood; and when received and drunk, these bring about that we are in Christ and Christ in us.”

By these words it is sufficiently shown what the sacrament is, what the reality of the sacrament is, and what the effect of the sacrament itself is. These three are principally to be sought in this sacrament.

[Col. 0503D] Admonished by these and other authorities of the holy Fathers, that brother readily agreed to all that the Catholic Church believes; and, thanks be to God, the word of God, because it fell upon good ground, took root and bore fruit in patience. For before the abbot of Ebrach and other religious persons he promised a retraction, with this correction, of his writing, which could not be recalled: henceforth he would not set his mouth against heaven, and on so lofty a matter would either write nothing further or, if necessity perhaps required it, write more sparingly and cautiously, avoiding these two things: falsity of meaning and novelty of expression. Thus far concerning this.

Nevertheless, I cannot pass over in silence another stumbling block which we found in those same invectives of Lord G., the provost. Having taken an authority from the typical sacrifice of the paschal lamb to convict the man whom he calls a divider of Christ, he says among other things:

> “But now, in the true Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, the head together with the feet—that is, divinity together with the whole humanity—is devoured, because Christ whole is eaten in the mystery of the altar.”

[Col. 0504A] Who devised these things? Who heard such things? How much more rightly he might have said with the Prophet: “Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. 140). Whatever his meaning in these words may be, the words themselves seem excessively uncircumcised and foreign to the usage and custom of the Christian school, when the Apostle says: “Avoid profane novelties of speech” (1 Tim. 6). For if our Lord Jesus Christ took care to commend this sacrament under the species of bread and wine in order to avoid horror, why should we, speaking of so ineffable a matter, not likewise avoid both horror and error of speech?

[Col. 0504B] For these words seem excessively dreadful both to say and to hear: “Divinity and humanity are devoured together.” To believe that Christ is received whole at the altar is to make a right offering; but not to distinguish from one another the properties of the two natures in Christ is not right division. Certainly, what was prefigured in the typical lamb is understood to be fulfilled in those who, understanding in Christ divinity and humanity together with our infirmities, follow in faith and deed the footsteps of Christ himself without dullness of mind, as blessed Gregory says. But the words, namely, “Divinity and humanity are devoured together,” do not appear to be supported by that authority.

[Col. 0504C] One must proceed cautiously in such matters, lest we exceed sobriety both in speaking and in thinking. There are many dangers in speaking, but far more and graver dangers in writing, as blessed Hilary teaches and says:

> “In matters concerning God we must not speak with human or worldly understanding; nor, by a violent or shameless proclamation, must the soundness of heavenly utterances be distorted into an alien and impious interpretation. Let us read what has been written, understand what we have read, and then we shall perform the duty of perfect faith.”

Christ’s body and blood are consecrated, received, and distributed upon the altar according to the sacramental species, so that worthy participants of the same table receive them equally, as regards the reality of the sacrament, just as in the heavenly manna, according to the Apostle: “He who had much did not abound, and he who had little did not lack” (2 Cor. 8:15).

[Col. 0504D] But as regards the effect, each eats as much as he believes, Augustine being the authority: “Why prepare stomach and teeth? Believe, and you have eaten.” Hence at the conclusion we pray, saying: “That what we now perform under the visible species of the sacraments, we may receive in the certain reality of the things themselves.” All this concerns the effect and the spiritual manner of receiving, which belong only to the righteous. But sacramentally and really, according to the truth of Christ’s body—which was born of the Virgin and offered upon the altar of the cross—all, worthy and unworthy alike, receive equally: some unto life, others unto death.

[Col. 0505A] Returning to the point, and searching on every side as far as we can, nowhere do we find: “Divinity together with the entire humanity is devoured.” We indeed read: “God suffered,” not “the Godhead suffered”—that is, the person of the Son of God suffered, not that nature which is one and the same, inseparable and indivisible, with the Father and the Holy Spirit. A ram is sacrificed; Isaac is led away by his father’s sword. What is received under the species of bread is Christ’s body; what is received under the species of wine is Christ’s blood. Yet it is not one thing in the one species and another in the other, but the same Christ in each: true God, I say, and true man; he in whom all the treasures of God’s knowledge and wisdom are hidden; he who is the power of God and the wisdom of God; he in whom all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily.

[Col. 0505B] But because of recurring temptations he is more frequently received under two species, since he himself is the refreshment and redemption of souls and bodies. And this is to smear with the lamb’s blood both the threshold and the lintel, likewise sprinkling the middle of the doorposts in the form of a cross. Nowhere yet do I find: “The Godhead suffered; the Godhead was crucified; the Godhead was offered; the Godhead was devoured.” But because the words of the Wise One are like nails driven deeply in, lest we seem to exalt ourselves above the summit, we wish rather to be taught than to judge another on account of the weakness of our understanding. Nevertheless, we have neither learned from teachers or holy Fathers, nor do we believe that it can be taught, that divinity together with the whole humanity is devoured.

[Col. 0505C] Even blessed Augustine says:

> “Because it is not lawful that Christ be devoured with teeth, the Lord Jesus willed that bread and wine should truly be made, in the mystery, his flesh and blood by the power of the consecration of the Holy Spirit, and that he should be offered daily for the life of the world.”

Let all reasonings—indeed, let all philosophical arguments—be silent, or rather perish, where faith is concerned. Let us believe and follow what Christ himself taught, so that not our own understanding may prevail in us, but his effect may continually come before it. For faith has no merit when human reason furnishes proof. Every human reasoning fails where, through God’s power and God’s efficacious word, so great a change of things occurs that bread becomes Christ’s body and wine Christ’s blood, as blessed Ambrose testifies in his book *On the Sacraments*:

[Col. 0505D]

> “You see how efficacious is Christ’s word. For if there is such power in the word of Christ the Lord Jesus that things which did not exist begin even to exist, how much more efficacious is it so that things which did exist may continue to be and yet be changed into something else! Before consecration it was not the body; but after consecration I tell you that it is now Christ’s body.”

Where, therefore, one thing altogether appears and another thing is, yet there is nothing there of deception or illusion, whether phantom or trickery; rather, all things are true and not feigned. Not only is the weakness of human sense not deceived there, but sense itself, together with reason and understanding, is surpassed. And lest this appear impossible to him who is Almighty, hear Hilary: “He is not subject to the laws of nature from whom all nature receives its law.” Therefore the Apostle does not say without reason: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit according to the elements of this world” (Col. 2).

[Col. 0506A] Likewise, another stumbling block in the same letter is found in what he says about “the word of flesh.” Here surely either the mind erred or the pen. But because he appealed to Hilary on this point, let us turn to Hilary, whose words in Psalm 58, from which he fortifies himself, are these and no others:

> “If the Word truly became flesh, and if we truly receive the Word’s flesh in the Lord’s food, how is he not to be thought to abide naturally in us, he who, being born man, assumed to himself the now inseparable nature of our flesh, and united the nature of his flesh to the nature of eternity under the sacrament of the flesh to be communicated to us?”

Therefore, most evidently, both by the foregoing authority and for this reason, it is fitting to say either “the Word’s flesh” (*verbum carnem*) or rather “the flesh of the Word” (*carnem verbi*), rather than “the word of flesh” (*verbum carnis*), because it was not flesh that assumed the Word, but the Word that assumed flesh.

[Col. 0506B] Thus we believe and confess that the Word of God the Father is that which proceeds from the Father. The flesh of the Word is that which the Word itself, proceeding from the Father, assumed. But in what sense “word of flesh” can be said, when it proceeds from the Father alone and was not assumed from flesh, let him see to it. We do not presume to receive it without weightier authority. Likewise, the Apostle does not say without reason: “Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings” (Heb. 13). For to introduce strange and unfamiliar words where the faith of Christ and his sacraments is concerned is to wrap Christ in swaddling cloths other than Mary’s.

The prophet who was to be sent by the Lord humbly says: “I do not know how to speak, because I am a child” (Jer. 1). Likewise, the Lord’s friend and intimate interlocutor, in the very conference with the Lord and before the Lord, confesses himself slow and impeded in speech. He also, than whom, according to the Lord’s testimony, none greater arose among those born of women, says: “He who comes after me has been made before me; I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (Mark 1).

[Col. 0506C] And whence comes it to these scholastics that they devise their novelties in the forefront and judge all who do not receive them?

For above all, this seems a remarkable dogma and a certain new teaching of our time: concerning the equality of the Son of Man with God—as though Christ, insofar as he is man, were equal to God—because they read: “God gave him the name which is above every name” (Phil. 2), and because of certain corresponding and similar authorities. We should like to know, so that we may briefly address the authors or even defenders of this gospel, in what sense they wish to say: “Christ is equal to God insofar as he is man.”

[Col. 0506D] If, however, in saying that Christ is equal to God insofar as he is man, they mean: “Christ, who is a man, is equal to God,” understanding that he is not equal to God according to his humanity but according to his divinity, then this should have been said otherwise: “Christ is equal to God insofar as he is God.” For no Catholic doubts that Christ is both God and man. But he has equality with God from one thing—namely, that he is God; he does not have it from the other—namely, that he is man. For universally, both the assumed man himself and every other creature do not possess from themselves either existence or any quality, whether of nature or of grace, but from him who is and who says: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3).

[Col. 0507A] Therefore everything which is, is from him; and for that reason what is from him through creation is less. But what is naturally from him who is Father is one with him, consubstantial and equal to him in all things, so that in the persons distinction may be adored, in the essence unity, and in majesty equality. This equality, although it belongs to the Son of Man, does not belong to him because he is Son of Man, but because this Son of Man himself is the Son of God.

And since we have begun, let us press them further on these same points. In every comparison one must see what is compared with what, and in what respect one is compared with the other. Therefore, when Christ is said to be equal to God, either you compare him with God insofar as he is man, or you compare him with God insofar as he is God. If you compare him with God insofar as he is man, so as to say, “Christ is equal to God insofar as he is man,” nothing could be more false. If you compare him insofar as he is God in this way, “Christ is equal insofar as he is God,” nothing could be truer—provided equality of the persons is understood not according to relation but according to substance.

[Col. 0507B] And thus we always return to the same source, saying: “Equal to the Father according to divinity, less than the Father according to humanity.” For the assumption did not diminish the greater one, nor did glorification consume the lesser. But lest we proceed into things great and wondrous beyond us, let us arm ourselves, as it were in a closely arrayed battle line, with authorities joined together like shields.

First, he who is Truth itself says: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14). Let us see what our same Lord Jesus said concerning himself and the Holy Spirit when the book of the prophet Isaiah was given to him: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. 61). And the Prophet says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 45). This is also expressed in the very title “Christ,” that is, “Anointed One.” But the lesser is anointed by the greater.

[Col. 0507C] Therefore, since both the Father and the Holy Spirit anoint, Christ, anointed according to humanity, is less than the Father, God, and the Holy Spirit; and he is less than himself insofar as he is God, according to that whereby he is man. Thus Christ—namely, from the time he was anointed, that is, from the Incarnation—is always God and man. Therefore he is always less than God insofar as he is man. “Christ is always equal to God insofar as he is man” [an evident textual error].

Do you suppose it was said without cause: “He upon whom you see the Spirit of God descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes” (John 1)? Does the Spirit of God not remain upon him today? For this ointment, remaining and not failing upon the head, descends from the head to the beard and from the beard down to the hem of the garment. This is the oil that does not fail, but stood firm when the widow’s vessels failed.

[Col. 0508A] Likewise: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20). Hence Augustine, *Against Maximinus*:

> “God the Father is both God and Father of Christ. But he is Christ’s God according to his humanity”—that is, because Christ is a man and born of a woman. “Thus it is said in the Psalms: ‘From my mother’s womb you are my God,’ showing that the Father is his God because he became man. For man was born from his mother’s womb, and God was born of the Virgin according to his humanity, so that he who begot him from himself might not only be Father to him, but might also be God to him whom he created as man from his mother’s womb.”

Observe that he says “created,” not “begot.” For we too, though we were sinners, he voluntarily begot, but only through the word of truth. Yet for him birth was what rebirth is for us, because he was not conceived in iniquities as we are, but was the Lamb of God, free from every stain, who takes away the sins of the world.

[Col. 0508B] Hence it follows:

> “Therefore, he who is Father to the Son from his own womb is the Son’s God from his mother’s womb, not from his own. Hence the Lord himself says: ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father,’ etc.”

Likewise, in the same work:

> “With the fullest reason Christ the man is less than the Father, and that same Christ the God is equal to the Father.”

The Apostle also speaks well, treating of the sacrament of marriage: “This sacrament is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5). Explaining this more fully elsewhere, he says: “The head of the woman is the man; the head of the man is Christ; but the head of Christ is God” (ibid.). Although the holy Fathers explain this in several ways, blessed Augustine explains it thus in *On the Trinity*:

[Col. 0508C]

> “If ‘God’ is understood here in the same way of all three, how is God the head of Christ—that is, how is the Trinity the head of Christ, when Christ is in the Trinity, so that he is Trinity? Or is it that the Father, together with the Son and Holy Spirit, is the head of him who alone is the Son? For the Father is God together with the Son and Holy Spirit, but the Son alone was made man. According to this humiliation the Father is also greater than he; and according to this, that which is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit becomes the head of the man who is mediator, which he alone is.”

Ambrose, *On the Faith*, addressed to Emperor Gratian, book 4:

> “Let God be the head of Christ according to the human condition. He did not say, ‘The Father is the head of Christ,’ but ‘God is the head of Christ,’ because divinity, being the creator, is the head of the creature. And he rightly said, ‘God is the head of Christ,’ in order to signify both Christ’s divinity and his flesh—that is, the Incarnation—in the name Christ; and, in the term God, the unity of divinity and the greatness of power. So far is God called the head of Christ according to the Incarnation that Christ too is called the head of man according to the Incarnation.”

[Col. 0508D] And below:

> “God is the head of Christ where the form of a servant—that is, of man, not of God—is under discussion. But it does not prejudice the Son of God if, according to truth, he is like men, he who is one with the Father in divinity. For his power is not diminished by this interpretation; rather, his mercy is proclaimed.”

[Col. 0509A] But now I beg all of you who love the Lord: attend, and let the Lord’s name be invoked over us, so that falsehood may not prejudice truth, but the light “which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1) may illuminate the darkness of our hearts to recognize the truth. Foolish indeed is the honor paid by those who inflict this injury upon God—and not upon God alone, but also upon man—in making the Son of Man equal to God insofar as he is man.

He fortifies himself greatly by an authority of Ambrose’s *On the Faith*, addressed to Emperor Gratian, in the chapter which deals with the Son’s subjection. The beginning of that chapter is as follows:

> “Therefore, most august Emperor, let us consider how we ought to understand ‘subjected.’”

But because “the letter kills, while the spirit gives life” (1 Cor. 3), Ambrose’s words, the more obscure because the more divine, are not to be read cursorily by everyone, but require a careful and intelligent reader.

[Col. 0509B] Therefore, for a clearer understanding of so great an authority, the chief intention of the author himself must be considered. Disputing against heretics who asserted that the Son was less than the Father even insofar as he is God, blessed Ambrose explains the Apostle’s authority which they adduced to prove the Son’s subjection insofar as he is God. He proves most forcefully that this authority is to be referred not to the Son’s subjection insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is man.

The order of his discussion and reasoning is this. He collects several kinds of subjection found throughout Holy Scripture; and, by removing all these from the Son of God insofar as he is God, since none of them applies to him in that respect, he concludes that the remaining subjection must be referred to human nature in a twofold way: both in the head and in the members, and both according to flesh and according to soul.

[Col. 0509C] For the edification of the hearers and for greater clarity, we judged it worthwhile briefly to survey the kinds of subjection themselves. A creature is subjected to vanity; a woman to a man; one under authority to the authority; a servant to a master. There is also the charitable subjection, whence: “Be subject to one another in the fear of Christ” (Eph. 5). There is also that execrable subjection which the Sabellians and Marcionites asserted, namely, that the Son is absorbed back into the Father; this he especially refutes. There is likewise the creature’s subjection to the Creator: a subjection of will alone, which is not different in Father and Son but the same.

[Col. 0509D] Having removed all these kinds of subjection from the Son of God according to divinity, he consequently and fittingly concludes that the Apostle’s authority on the Son’s subjection must, as stated above, be referred to the nature of humanity. Blessed Ambrose confirms this subjection by inserting certain remarks among those already cited, and at the end concludes the chapter itself with the proposition that man is subjected to God. For he says:

> “Since he is said to be subjected in the time of the dispensation, that subjection will belong to assumed, not perpetual, weakness—especially since the eternal power of God cannot change its state for a time, lest something be added to the power of God the Father from time.”

[Col. 0510A] Therefore let not those who say that the Lord Jesus was subject to God the Father before the Passion, but now after the Passion and Resurrection is neither subject nor to be subjected, glory against us on the basis of this authority. For Ambrose’s phrase, “that subjection will belong to assumed, not perpetual, weakness,” does not favor their party. It was spoken against heretics who asserted an eternal weakness in the Son of God, as we have explained above; according to them, God’s weakness would be perpetual if subjection were perpetual. “The thief does not come except to steal” (Job 10 [citation as printed]). But let no one so steal this authority as to remove all the preceding material and quote only the words that follow: “that subjection will belong to assumed, not perpetual, weakness,” as though he were subject only when still mortal and not now when immortal and impassible.

[Col. 0510B] Likewise, below:

> “Christ is not yet subjected, since his members are not yet subjected. But when we shall be not many members but one spirit, then he himself also will be subjected, so that through his subjection God may be all in all.”

Likewise, below:

> “Subjection, therefore, is the obedience of death; death belongs to the assumption of humanity; therefore that subjection will belong to the assumption of humanity. It is by no means weakness of divinity, but the dispensation itself of mercy.”

Likewise, below:

> “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. He is cursed because he assumed our curses; he is also subjected because he assumed our subjection, but in the assumption of the form of a servant.”

[Col. 0510C] At the end he sums up the force of the argument in these words:

> “According to the flesh, all things will be handed over as subject to him, according to which flesh he was also raised from the dead. And very many rightly interpret the Lord’s subjection according to the human and rational soul, because it is written: ‘Will not my soul be subjected to God?’ He said ‘soul,’ not ‘divinity.’ And so that we might know that the Lord spoke through the Prophet concerning the assumption of human nature, he added: ‘How long will you attack a man?’ according to that which he says in the Gospel: ‘Why do you seek to kill me, a man?’ And he added: ‘Nevertheless, they planned to cast away my price; I ran in thirst; with their mouth they blessed, but in their heart they cursed.’”

For the Jews, when Judas brought it back, refused to receive the price; running in the thirst of madness, because they refused the grace of the spiritual drink. This is the interpretation of devout subjection. For since this is the benefit of the Lord’s Passion, he will surely be subjected in us in that in which he suffered.

[Col. 0510D] Hence it is clear that, if he suffered in human nature, then in that same nature he is subjected in us, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), that is, in human nature. Hence he is called “the man Christ Jesus, mediator of God and men.” For we shall not be subjected except through his subjection, just as we shall not rise except through his resurrection. He himself became the High Priest of good things to come, through whom we have access to God. Or do we not now, after the Resurrection, have access to God through him?

Therefore he himself is subjected through our subjection, he who is our head; and we who are his members shall be subjected to God the Father through his subjection. And we shall be subjected to him both insofar as he is God and insofar as he is man, because he is our Redeemer; and God has subjected all things under his feet, just as he has made those things which are still to come.

[Col. 0511A] For sometimes what belongs to the members is attributed to the head, and conversely what belongs to the head to the members. Certainly, by the same power of his indwelling in us through unity of nature, we too now sit in the heavenly places through him who sits at the Father’s right hand; as Ambrose says, in the future thrones will also sit in judgment, and we, who are members of that head, shall not only sit but also possess the kingdom prepared for us from the beginning of the world. Hence Ambrose:

> “Thus we shall sit at the Father’s right hand in him, not because we shall sit with him, but because we shall sit in the body of Christ.”

Is not, then, he who is the mediator between the highest and the lowest lesser? Rather, through that wondrous exchange of the Incarnation between God and man, the ineffable fellowship is fulfilled. Pope Leo says:

> “If he were not true God, he would not bring remedy; if he were not true man, he would not provide an example.”

[Col. 0511B] There is yet another proof of the same matter, because it is written: “Who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8). And lest anyone say that the Spirit too “makes request for us with unutterable groanings” (ibid.), the Spirit makes request because he causes us to make request; but the Son intercedes because by the sacrament of his Incarnation he intervenes for us. He is both our judge and advocate, always equal to the Father according to divinity and less than the Father according to humanity.

And he is always Emmanuel, which means “God with us” (Matt. 1): with us in his assumption of our nature, with us in subjection, with us in glorification, because he himself is God and we are gods. But he is God according to the fullness of divinity; we, however, are gods according to participation in blessedness. Blessed Pope Leo continues thus:

[Col. 0511C]
