> “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel, which is interpreted ‘God with us.’ For this wondrous birth of the holy Virgin brought forth in one offspring a nature truly human and truly divine, because neither substance so retained its properties that there could be a distinction of persons in them. Nor was the creature so assumed into fellowship with its Creator that he would be the inhabitant and it the habitation; rather, the one nature was mingled with the other. And although one is that which is assumed and the other that which assumes, nevertheless the diversity of both comes together into such power that one and the same Son says that he is less than the Father insofar as he is true man, and professes himself equal to the Father insofar as he is true God.”

And lest we seem to speak merely from ourselves, hear Hilary:

[Col. 0512A]

> “Let no one make himself equal to the Only-Begotten in the substance of divinity. Let him be for us both brother and participant insofar as, the Word having become flesh, he dwelt among us. Indeed, because the man Christ Jesus is mediator of God and men, let him be for us servants both a common Father and a common God.”

We have endeavored to bring these authorities together into one small body, both that they may more easily be committed to memory and that it may be more difficult for anyone to resist Catholic truth; so that, with all these things as it were set before the eyes and readily at hand, there might be, from abundance, a choice against those who hold down God’s truth in unrighteousness.

If any of Hilary’s sayings, which are above human capacity, seem contrary to the foregoing, we first say that, just as Hilary is far removed from the reading of simpler brethren, as Jerome testifies, so also he is far removed from our interpretation. Nevertheless, because we must be ready to give an account of the faith that is in us to everyone who asks, let us endeavor according to our powers—not to expound Hilary, but to answer objections which may perhaps be raised—holding firmly in mind and desiring, so far as we can and with the Lord’s help, to carry out this teaching of blessed Gregory:

[Col. 0512B]

> “The careful hand of the worker must act so that, while the thorn is removed, the ear of grain is nourished.”

What Hilary says in Book 9 seems strongly contrary to the matters stated above:

> “If the birth as man introduced a new nature, and humility changed the form under the assumption of servitude, now the gift of the name restores equality of form.”

Likewise:

> “The Father, who is going to glorify the Son, is greater; the Son, glorified in the Father, is not lesser. Or how is he lesser who is in the glory of God the Father? Or is the Father not greater? Certainly the Father is greater insofar as he is Father, but the Son is not lesser insofar as he is Son. The Son’s birth establishes the Father as greater; the nature of that birth does not permit the Son to be lesser.”

Likewise, in Book 11:

[Col. 0512C]

> “The nature of our bodily nature has been brought into the Father’s divinity.”

And below:

> “By subjection he is to obtain in all things that which belongs to God, lest he be God only in part, but wholly God. Therefore there is no other cause of subjection than that God may be all in all, with no nature of earthly body remaining outside him.”

And shortly afterward:

> “While he is man and God, now he is wholly God. Finally, the name has been given to him on whom all things depend—the name which is above every name—and [Col. 0512D] Jesus is in the glory of God the Father.”

All these things tend toward one meaning; and therefore an easier way out will be granted by Him who bestows wisdom even upon little ones. For what if Hilary should say: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me”? And what if the Lord should command Paul to answer? He will surely say of Christ: “Who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized” (Phil. 2). For Christ considered that His equality with God was not a seizure. But whence? “Being in the form of God.” Certainly from this, and from no other source. Why do we delay further? “Christ had to suffer, and rise from the dead, and thus enter into His glory” (Luke 24). That great prophet was without honour in his own country: when He came unto His own, His own did not receive Him [Col. 0513A] (John 1). Therefore that grain of wheat, falling into the ground, died; and so, not remaining singular and alone, it brought forth much fruit. “A name above every name was given to Him” (Phil. 2). A name is so called from being known: “Made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man” (ibid.). Before the Passion He was regarded by men as merely a man. Even the disciples, because they did not believe in Him as they later did, abandoned Him and fled. “He was reckoned with those who go down into the pit.” How inglorious He was; how devoid of any name! He rose from death, and immediately, by merit of His Passion, the name above every name was given to Him; and through faith and knowledge of His divinity, lifted up from the earth, He drew all things to Himself.

For from the beginning of the Incarnation [Col. 0513B] the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily in that man; but it was veiled by flesh, and that Sun of righteousness was in some manner obscured in the Passion itself. In the Resurrection He spread abroad the rays of His divinity; the nations were given to Him for an inheritance and the ends of the earth for a possession; and, having received the keys of death and hell, He thus entered by His Passion and Resurrection into His glory: so that He sits at the right hand of the Father, reigning with Him and resting in His greater goods. He has attained not only the honour of this name, namely, that He should be believed to be God, but has also obtained immortality and impassibility according to the flesh, with no nature of an earthly body remaining in Him in any respect, as Hilary says—not because the body was cast off, but because it was transformed from its earlier subjection. And thus now He is wholly God [Col. 0513C], that is, wholly divine, as was stated above. We also summarized this in a certain apology of ours. Behold how great a name that son of the carpenter—yet maker of the whole fabric of the world—has now received: for, when the Apostles were sent out to preach, “their sound went out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world.”

And lest anyone doubt these matters, let him hear Augustine: “In the form in which He was crucified, in that He was exalted; and in that form the name was bestowed upon Him, so that with that very form of a servant the only-begotten Son of God might be named. Hence the name was given to Him as man, which He, being God, already possessed.” This name, therefore, was then given through manifestation; it was not foreign to Him [Col. 0513D], but had already been bestowed, and was confirmed through the Ascension and the coming of the Holy Spirit. Increasing daily in us through faith, it will be consummated at the Last Coming, when at the name of Jesus every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings shall bend, and every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2). Thus Jesus Christ, who is one God with the Father, will then be known by all to possess not a lesser but the same glory as He now possesses in reality. In this order the glory and glorification of His name will be fulfilled: He Himself as man is one God with the Father, of one glory as of one essence.

Do not object here, whoever would oppose sound doctrine, that God too was glorified. For, as Hilary says, He did not glorify Himself, nor God; rather, God was glorified in Him and into God. This is not surprising, since God was also glorified in a man at the raising of Lazarus, though in a far different way. Therefore the complete bestowal restores equality to that form: the glorified one is greater, and the glorified one is not lesser; and the Father, insofar as He is Father, is greater, while the Son, insofar as He is Son, is not lesser. And it was given to this man to be as great as the Father Himself is. All these things, according to their different relations, must be distinguished as they have been stated, so that what belongs to each may be assigned to him: to the Father and Son as glorifying and glorified; as giver and recipient; as God and man. “For,” says Hilary, “all glory was acquired not for the Word but for the man.” Thus authority proper to the one who glorifies and gives—to the Father [Col. 0514B] and God—will be rendered to Him; while to Christ the man will be assigned the humility of subjection according to what belongs to man, and equality with God according to what belongs to God.

Blessed Augustine explains all this from the words of the Lord as follows: “Christ God is equal to the Father: He is as great as He, such as He. He is what the Father is; He is not He who is the Father, because He is the Father. He is the Son, yet He is what the Father is: because the Father is God, and so is the Son; the Father is almighty, and so is the Son; the Father is immutable, and so is the Son; and likewise in other respects.” Therefore He is equal to the Father; yet I say that He is less than the Father—but in His humanity. If anyone wishes, by digging more deeply, to uncover rather than cover over the depth of this cistern, then, if an ox or an ass falls into it, he shall be liable for the price of the animals.

## LETTER IX

[Col. 0514C]

Letter of Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, to N., in which Gerhoh’s opinion concerning the glory and honour of the Son of Man, Christ, is further attacked, and it is shown that the Council of Ephesus does not support it.

Although, overcome both by the importance of the matter and by many other occupations, we had determined to attend to other things and absolutely no longer to you, a letter from Lord G. arrived. After excusing certain expressions in which he seemed to have “set his mouth against heaven,” he replied quite patiently to the letter which necessity had compelled us to send him. Moreover, he assented to certain points that he had not formerly been accustomed to concede, as it seemed to us. For, by God’s working and through the Lord’s words, “I ascend to my Father and your Father” (John [Col. 0514D] 20), and so forth—by these words of the Lord, I say—and by the exposition of blessed Augustine on this passage, speaking in the person of Christ: “My God, under whom I too am a man,” he has been admonished and brought so far toward our position as to concede that Christ, according to His humanity, is a creature and, as a creature, subject to God. Yet he remains far from us; for he does not concede that God is Lord, nor that Christ Himself, according to His humanity, is subject to God as to a lord, but only as a son to a father and a creature to its Creator.

He supports his view on the ground that Christ calls God neither Lord before nor after the Resurrection, but calls Him only God or Father. Having considered these points and the canonical and divine authorities more carefully, these words appeared almost delirious; yet they are not to be neglected or passed over in silence, because of the unwary and less practiced, lest they fall into a snare or pit and, though unknowingly, incur the gravest danger. In such matters ignorance excuses no one, but “he who is ignorant shall be ignored.” For an occasion of disease so great and of such a kind, if it possessed long-lasting peace without contradiction, would produce a most grievous disease; and, fostered in silence, this perversity might perhaps at some time break out into an established rule. Therefore such persons must not be played with; before they grow strong, they must be dashed against the rock like little children.

Although “praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner,” nevertheless, for the sake of fraternal admonition and correction, though what we say is dry and bloodless [Col. 0515B], we have resolved, with that widow who offered two mites, to offer into the treasury what we can. Especially since such stained variations ought to be referred to the judgment of those whose lips preserve knowledge and who meditate on the law of the Lord day and night.

How stable—or rather, how fragile—is the foundation upon which this wise man builds appears from this point. If nothing is authoritative except what the Lord Jesus spoke in His own person before or after the Resurrection, we shall return to the ancient chaos, so as to be without the Law and the Prophets, and without everything written for our instruction apart from the Lord’s own words. No sensible person can fail to see how absurd this is. Therefore, rejecting these frivolous matters, let us follow the authorities of the Old and New Testaments. Although abundance itself makes us poor in material for disproving these claims, let us bring forward a few examples from many.

Moses says: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, like me; him you shall hear” (Deut. 18). But who is that person who speaks, and to whom does the Lord speak in the Prophet: “But thou, O Lord, have mercy upon me, and raise me up, and I shall repay them” (Ps. 40)? Is this John the Baptist who rose from the dead, or Elijah, or Jeremiah, or one of the prophets? Such empty chatter is worthy of mockery rather than answer. But since the speech of such people spreads like a cancer, even these things must be answered. For it is clearer than light that we have now arrived at those dangerous times which the Apostle foretold would come, when men, according to the desires of their own hearts, would heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears (2 Tim. 4). It is more like a monster than likely to be true that God should be almighty over some creature and yet not be its Lord.

Augustine, in a sermon on “Let not your heart be troubled,” says: “Let us acknowledge the twofold substance of Christ: namely, the divine, by which He is equal to the Father; and the human, by which the Father is greater. Yet these two are not two Christs, but one Christ.” And shortly after: “Although we believe one person in Christ, we nevertheless confess two substances, that is, natures: the divine and the human; the assuming and the assumed; the creating and the created. Yet these substances are not confused but united, inseparable in one and the same person [Col. 0516A], and always remaining in their own proper character.” What is clearer than the authority of the prophet Isaiah? “Drop down, ye heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Saviour; I, the Lord, created him” (Isa. 45). It plainly appears that, by reason of His creation, the Lord is Lord of Christ according to His humanity; and if createdness remains in Christ, lordship remains in the Creator.

But that we may proceed more securely, let us use arguments sought elsewhere. In the aforementioned sermons Augustine uses an indirect argument against those who asserted that the Son of God was a creature even according to divinity: “If He is created, then He is also a servant; for everything created must necessarily serve its Creator.” But we, using the same argument directly as regards our purpose, say: If the Son of Man was created, He is also a servant. But He was created, as was said in Isaiah; therefore He is a servant, and must serve, as a creature serves its Creator. With Augustine we confidently say that “our dust, now made incorruptible, sits at the right hand of the Father”; and the Father is certainly both Creator and God, and therefore Lord, of that dust.

As Augustine explains elsewhere on the verse, “And thou, O Lord, make me”: “The Father,” he says, “helps the Son insofar as God helps man, on account of the form of a servant—the man to whom God is God, and to whom, in the form of a servant, the Father is also Lord.” This Lord of His is proclaimed by the angel, who will give Him the throne of David His father. Hence that servant, prefigured in Zerubbabel, as is read in Haggai: “On that day I will take thee, Zerubbabel, son of Salathiel, my servant, and I will set thee as a signet; for I have chosen thee, says the Lord” (Hag. 2). The Book of Wisdom is full on every page of matters of this kind, as in this passage: “O Lord my God, thou hast exalted my dwelling above the earth” (Sirach 51).

He refers not only us, but all who dare say of Christ, “Equal to the Father according to divinity, less than the Father according to humanity,” to the Council of Ephesus. But the Prophet is not deceived when he says: “They dug a pit and fell into it” (Ps. 56). For where he wishes to catch others, there he is caught, as is shown by these words of the holy First Council of Ephesus: “Nor do we assert that the Word of God the Father is God or Lord of Christ, lest we again more openly divide the one Christ, Son and Lord, into two and incur the crime of sacrilege by making Him God and Lord of Himself. For, as we said above, the Word of God, united to flesh according to hypostasis, is God of all and ruler of the universe; nevertheless He is neither servant nor Lord of Himself, for it is foolish—or rather impious—to think or say this. For although He called His Father His God, while He Himself too is God by nature and from the Father’s essence, nevertheless we by no means fail to recognize that, while remaining God, He also became man, existing under God according to the proper law of human nature [Col. 0517A]. But how could He Himself be either God or Lord to Himself? Therefore, as man, insofar as befits the measure of His self-emptying, He declared Himself to be under God together with us. Hence He was also in some manner [Codex: “how”] made under the Law, although He Himself promulgated the Law and existed as Lawgiver in His divinity. The measure of Christ’s self-emptying, discernibly gathered from the three states of man, is not one of necessity but of will alone.”

By these words of the council we are first recalled from the Nestorian error, lest we divide the one Christ, Son and Lord, into two by separating the Word and Christ from one another in person and asserting that the Word of God the Father is God and Lord of Christ. This would be sacrilegiously to make Him God and Lord of Himself, since the Word is God and Christ, according to the truth of faith, is God and man. Then, from the point where it says, “For the Word united,” and so forth, we are strengthened in the Catholic faith, so that we may believe without doubt that there are two natures in the one person of Christ: one of the Word and the other of flesh—that is, of God and man—and that the man exists under God according to the proper law of human nature; that is, that the creature serves its Creator. This dispensation is “not of necessity, but of will,” namely in the way in which the Lawgiver was made under the Law.

Thus, with God’s help, we shall pass unharmed through that deep place where the elephant swims and the lamb walks, unafraid of those sophistical entanglements which deceive the less cautious through differing relations. For however it may be stated, whether negatively or interrogatively, God and Lord—or lord and servant—cannot be the same to Himself; that is, two persons cannot be made out of the one person of Christ, God and man, as Nestorius thought: one person of the Word as it were Lord, and another person of the assumed man as it were servant, whom he called Christ a mere man. This error is destroyed by the authority of the council, and the Catholic faith is strengthened: namely, that the one person of Christ consists in and from two natures, one of which serves the other, as was stated above in the words of the council.

If it pleases our brother and elder, by this reasoning the Athanasian Creed will be supported rather than annulled by the creed of the Council of Ephesus, so that in full concord we may always say: “Equal to the Father according to divinity, less than the Father according to humanity.” It is sufficiently presumptuous to judge and condemn all of us who dare distinguish from one another the two natures of that giant of twofold substance, while “neither confusing the persons nor separating the substance.”

That everything said—whether that Christ now has no Lord higher than Himself according to His humanity, or that He retained only the form of a servant and is no longer servant of His Lord and Creator—is empty, can be proved by many authorities. Augustine, on “Let not your heart be troubled,” says: “The form of a servant was added; the form of God did not depart. The former was assumed, the latter was not consumed. Because of the former it is said, ‘The Father is greater than I’; because of the latter, ‘I and the Father are one.’” And shortly after: “This is the form of a servant, in which God the Son is less not only than the Father but also than the Holy Spirit. Nor only this, but also than Himself; because He Himself, in the form of God, is greater than Himself.” The same writer says in Book I of *On the Trinity*: “Christ also made Himself less than Himself by taking the form of a servant. For He did not so take the form of a servant as to lose the form of God, in which He was equal to the Father; and He Himself is the only-begotten Son of the Father both in the form of a servant and in the form of God.”

Again, the same point is most clearly declared in the Acts of the Apostles, when Peter says: “Let all the house of Israel know most certainly that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2). Therefore, according to that in which He was made Christ, He is less even than Himself considered in the nature of divinity, in which He is equal to the Father, and in which all things were made through Him and without Him nothing was made (John 1). If anyone suffers from such poverty of understanding that these things do not suffice, let him turn to the teaching of blessed Augustine, which spreads most widely, and taste it as an antidote against every poison of heretics.

For Augustine says in Book I of *On the Trinity*, chapter 10: “We shall contemplate God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit when the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, has delivered the kingdom to God and the Father; so that the Son of God and Son of Man will no longer intercede for us as our mediator and priest, but He Himself, insofar as He is priest through the assumed form of a servant for our sake, will be subject to Him who subjected all things to Him; and insofar as He is God, He will have us subject with Him, insofar as He as priest will be subject to Him with us. For since the Son is both God and man, the substance of man in the Son is other than the substance of the Son in the Father, just as the flesh of my soul is another substance in relation to my soul—though in one man—than the soul of another man is in relation to my soul. Therefore, when He has delivered the kingdom to God and the Father—that is, when He has led believers living by faith, for whom He now intercedes as mediator, to that contemplation for the attainment of which we sigh and groan—then, when labour and groaning have passed away, He will no longer intercede for us, the kingdom having been delivered to God and the Father.”

Again, below: “What does ‘I came forth from the Father’ mean, except that I appeared less in the assumed creature in another form, not in that form in which I am equal to the Father? And what does ‘I came into this world’ mean, except that I displayed to the eyes even of sinners who love this world the form of a servant that I took in emptying Myself? And what does ‘Again I leave the world’ mean, except that I shall remove from the sight of lovers of the world what they saw? And what does ‘I go to the Father’ mean, except that I teach My faithful to understand Me as equal to the Father? Those who believe this will be found worthy to be led from faith to sight—that is, to the vision itself; and in leading them there He is said to deliver the kingdom to God and the Father [Col. 0519A]. For His faithful, whom He redeemed by His blood, are called His kingdom, and for them He now intercedes. But then, making them cleave to Himself there where He is equal to the Father, He will no longer ask the Father for them; for, He says, ‘the Father Himself loves you.’ For He asks by reason of that in which He is less than the Father; but by reason of that in which He is equal, He hears with the Father.”

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 13: “Unless He who is the Son of Man because of the form of a servant which He received were Himself the Son of God because of the form of God in which He exists, the Apostle Paul would not have said concerning the rulers of this age: ‘For had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.’ For He was crucified in the form of a servant; and yet the Lord of glory was crucified. For such was that assumption as to make God man and man God. Yet, with the Lord’s help, the prudent, diligent, and devout reader understands what is said on account of what, and according to what. For see: we have said that He glorifies His own according to that in which He is God—certainly according to that in which He is the Lord of glory. And the Lord of glory was crucified, because it is rightly said, ‘God was crucified,’ not through the power of divinity but through the weakness of flesh. Just as we say that He judges according to that in which He is God—that is, through divine power, not human—and yet this same man will judge, just as the Lord of glory was crucified.”

See how plainly and fully the entire question disputed between us and our brother concerning Christ has been decided: how He is equal to the Father; how He is less than the Father, the Holy Spirit, and even Himself; how He is subject to God with us; how He has us subject with God; how according to the nature of divinity He hears; and how, by praying and interceding for us, He renders to God the honour due according to human nature. Yet our learned scribe, in certain writings sent to us, contradicts this under the designation *latria*, a term unusual in this context. He asserts that we and all other wise persons who agree, as stated above, with blessed Augustine introduce a diversity of gods: one to whom *latria*—the worship due to God alone—is owed exclusively; another who both owes *latria* to his superior and to whom *latria* is owed by every other creature [Col. 0519D].

But, following the truth of the Catholic faith, we say: the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; yet the Father is not one God, the Son another God, and the Holy Spirit another God. Rather, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God; yet the Son alone became man. Therefore both things belonging to God and things belonging to man fittingly apply to Him: being crucified, being subject to God, praying, interceding; and, conversely, raising the dead, having us subject, hearing prayer, judging when He comes in His glory with His angels.

Since all these things which we say rest upon so great a truth, it now seems superfluous, and therefore less necessary, to produce still more authorities and arguments against the aforesaid novelty—or rather emptiness—because in letters sent to him we have answered his aforementioned inventions more fully, insofar as the opportunity of time allowed. If we wished to press the matter further, the day would fail us before the abundance of arguments and authorities. Nevertheless, for the clarification of the foregoing, we have thought it worthwhile to append at the end of this little work certain matters that illuminate what precedes. We do not set them forth as though speaking from a chair by our own authority; rather, seated with us in humility of spirit in Christ’s help, we exhort and admonish our fellows, fellow disciples, and fellow workers, so that they may supply a reminder to those who know and some measure of edification toward knowledge to those who do not know.

[Col. 0520B]

Pope Leo to Flavian, Patriarch of Constantinople: “We do not say that the Blessed Virgin Mary conceived a man without deity, who, created by the Holy Spirit, was later assumed by the Word; this is what we condemn Nestorius for preaching.” Likewise, shortly after: “From that beginning when the Word was made flesh in the Virgin’s womb, there never existed any division between the divine and human substance.” The same to Maximus, bishop of Antioch: “The rock of the Catholic faith, from which the blessed Apostle Peter received his name from the Lord, admits no trace of impiety and anathematizes Nestorius, who, separating the nature of the Word and of flesh in the conception of the Blessed Virgin and dividing the one Christ into two, wished there to be one person of deity and another of humanity; whereas He is altogether one and the same: He who according to eternal deity was born from the Father without time, and according to true flesh was born from His mother in time.”

From these passages it plainly appears both how Nestorius divided the one Christ into two—lord and servant—which it was sacrilegious, foolish, impious, and altogether impossible to say. Therefore by the words cited above from the council, the error of Nestorius is condemned and the Catholic faith strengthened.

But many obstacles arise through diverse authorities violently twisted from their proper sense into an alien one. This is like offering strange fire and falling under the condemnation of Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu. Pope Leo clearly states in his letter to Bishop Flavian against Eutyches whence this evil arises in the Church of God: “What is more unjust than to hold impious opinions and not believe persons wiser and more learned? Yet those fall into this folly who, when some obstacle hinders them in recognizing truth, have recourse not to prophetic utterances, apostolic writings, or evangelical authorities, but to themselves; and therefore become teachers of error because they have not been disciples of truth.” What learning from the sacred pages of the New and Old Testaments has he acquired who has not even grasped the beginnings of the Creed itself, and whose heart, even in old age, does not yet understand what is proclaimed throughout the world by the voice of all who are to be reborn [Codex: “to reign”]?

Thus certain brothers, for whom we desire and pray that God may forgive them because they do not know what they do, weave snares for themselves from Sacred Scripture—where its contents are vessels of death—and are caught in their own nets. They do not fully understand the obscurity and subtlety of the writings; they accept doubtful matters as certain, and at times false things as true, and harmful things instead of what would have been beneficial. Ashamed to confess their ignorance, they labour themselves and lead others with them into the same temptation. Pope Celestine reproaches Nestorius—who is always, as it were, “the wolf in the fable” for us—with this fault of evasion and wordiness, in a letter addressed to him, saying among other things: “Having been examined, detected, and caught by us in these matters, you are shown to be shaken by a certain verbosity: you wrap truths in obscurities; again, confusing both, you either confess what you have denied or strive to deny what you have confessed. But in your letters you have passed an open sentence, not so much upon our faith as upon yourself, wishing to reason otherwise concerning God the Word than does the faith of all. Behold the benefits of your novelties.”

In expounding the foregoing matters and distinguishing good from evil, let the name of the Lord be invoked; and let each one abound in his own understanding through Him who bestows wisdom upon little ones. Let this alone suffice as manifest and made clear to us, as though by a hidden faith: whoever wishes to attack or disagree with the Athanasian Creed in its assertion, “Equal to the Father,” cannot be secure behind the shield of the Council of Ephesus. Therefore let us also endeavour to beware of and avoid all novelties, as the authority of all orthodox believers urges.

Father, necessity—the necessity explained by us at the beginning—compelled us to write these things to you, though in a rustic style. Moreover, the zeal of this wish has joined itself to necessity: that your authority, in some degree admonished by our words, may apply the file of its correction to our imperfection, so that in our speech there may not be “Yes and no” (Matt. 5), but only “Yes”; and that we may be able to dwell with one mind in the house of God and be far from that kingdom of which it is written: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste, and house shall fall upon house” (Matt. 12).

For the clarification of the foregoing, beneath the twelve chapters promulgated by the Council of Ephesus under the presidency of Cyril, we have appended the corresponding twelve blasphemies of Nestorius. [They are lacking in the manuscript.]

## LETTER X

Letter of Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, to the abbot of Windberg. It informs him what was done and said in a conference held with Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, concerning Gerhoh’s opinion.

A friend to his friend: most faithful friendship.

It is a common proverb: “A friend is proved in necessity.” Likewise: “He is not a friend of the person but of prosperity, whom kindly fortune retains and harsh fortune drives away.” Therefore, that the friendship hitherto maintained between us may now be proved firm and true in the pressing necessity at hand, I ask you, in the true charity of true friendship, as a friend asks a friend, that if perhaps the lord bishop of Bamberg has made or makes mention of the conference held between us when we were in his house, you may not be ignorant of this also. Know that in my first defence, by which I strove to defend the Catholic faith, no one stood by me; those beside me, though agreeing with me, stood afar off in silence, while those who sought my life did violence.

Yet I did not yield to them even for an hour. By pressing many authorities upon them, I departed from that conflict neither victor nor vanquished, singing my Sext office, then due, whose opening is: “It has failed.” The lord bishop, as if joking, seized upon this against me, as though I had failed in that conflict. But I, on the contrary, glorying in the same psalmody, sang that my soul had failed not away from salvation but “in my salvation.” While I had sung the rest silently because the hour pressed and we were hurrying to the table, I expressly sang this and pressed it upon the ears of my opponents: “The wicked have told me fables, but not according to thy law” (Ps. 11). For I considered and consider it a fable that the man assumed into God, to whom “the name above every name” was given (Phil. 2), so that at His name every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings bends, and every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (ibid.), should be denied equality, in the glory given to Him, with the One who gives it.

For, to pass over more subtle and weightier interpreters who agree with me, the Venerable Priest Bede expressly affirms this very point in his homily on the Gospel, “The feast of the Dedication was held” (John 10). There, expounding the words, “What the Father gave me is greater than all” (ibid. 6), he affirms what I affirm: namely, that to the man was given equality with His Father in all glory, although He must be confessed less than the uncreated Father according to His created humanity, made a little lower than the angels. Read, if you please, that chapter in the homily as well. Read also Hilary, who agrees in every respect with our assertion; in him you will also find a clear solution to the statement which you opposed to me concerning those things which the Father has either in Himself or under Himself. The Son declares that all these things were given to Him by His Father.

When I said this, and cited Christ’s own earlier words, where He says, “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matt. 11), and again, “All things which the Father has are mine” (ibid.), you said, as I recall, that the Father has nothing in Himself which He has given to His Son, since the simple nature of the Father has nothing in itself except itself. But the same holy Hilary, teaching in the eighth book of *On the Holy Trinity* both what the Father is and what He has in Himself, not under Himself, says among other things: “God, the living power of immeasurable might, who is nowhere absent and nowhere lacking, teaches through His own things that He is wholly present, and indicates that His own things are nothing other than Himself; so that, where His own things are present, He Himself is understood to be present. Yet He is not believed, in a bodily manner, to be present in one place and not also everywhere, since through His own things He does not cease to be in all things. For His own things are not other than what He Himself is.” Likewise, in the same work: “God is not composed in a human manner, so that in Him there is one thing which is possessed from Him and another that is Himself who possesses it; rather, all that He is is life—namely, perfect, absolute, infinite nature, not constituted from dissimilar things, but itself living throughout.”

It is clear from these words and other teachings of the Fathers that one may properly say of the Father both “what He is” and “what He has,” since the Son Himself says: “As the Father has life in Himself, so He gave the Son also to have life in Himself” (John 5). Hence I wonder that you contradicted me when I said that the Father gave the Son all things which He has in Himself and under Himself. Speaking of these things, Ambrose, in his exposition of Luke on the words, “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matt. 11), says among other things: “If He gave all things, He poured forth eternity and majesty.” The same writer, in the same work: “What,” he says, “is a clearer indication of divine generation than that, when He was about to speak of Christ’s generation, He first introduced the Father Himself as speaking: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’? When He says, ‘In whom I am well pleased,’ He praises not something alien in the Son, but what is His own.”

As Saint Ambrose says these things, our assertion accords with his: we proclaim that Christ, the man, was begotten divinely both from a human mother and from God the Father, and that He is rich in all the riches of paternal majesty even according to His humanity—not as some vassal is rich, endowed with all his lord’s riches, but as an heir is rich: although he is lord of all his paternal riches, he is nevertheless under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by his father (Gal. 4).

Accordingly, in the aforesaid controversy I was deeply offended that the man assumed into God so as to be God was compared by the lord bishop to a vassal. Yet, yielding to his counsels rather than to his disputations, at the advice of that same lord archbishop, I approved the proposal that I should examine my writings with careful consideration, and recapitulate them after the example of blessed Augustine, who composed the book of *Retractations*, in which [lacuna] he clarified certain things he had said, moderated certain things, and excused certain things. I too promised that I would imitate him—not, however, as certain false speakers say, by acknowledging that anything in my writings had been said with a heretical [Col. 0523D] meaning, even if it can be twisted into a perverse sense by the new Nestorian and Photinian heretics, just as certain words of the holy Gospel are twisted by those same persons into the perverse sense of corrupt dogmas. It is not now necessary to discuss these one by one. Yet we touch upon some of them in the little work [Note: [Col. 0523] He appears to be speaking of his work *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*, to be published below.] which, at the urging of my aforesaid lords the bishops, I began and have not yet finished. But when, with God’s favour, I have completed it, and after it has been examined not only by episcopal but also by apostolic judgment I have proposed it for reading even to those enemies themselves, I believe it will please the good, even if it displeases the wicked.

[Col. 0524A] Bede: “What my Father gave me is greater than all. But what the Father gave to the man Jesus Christ, Mediator between God and humankind, greater than all things, was this: that he should be his only-begotten Son, neither unlike his begetter in nature, nor inferior in power, nor later in time. This equality, namely, which the Lord himself possessed in divinity before the world was made, he received in his humanity from the time of the incarnation.”

## LETTER XI

Letter of Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, to Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg.—He vehemently attacks him because he received and circulated his statements in a harsher sense; and further demonstrates that the man in Christ is lesser and unequal to the Father.

E., by God’s grace the unworthy [Col. 0524B] minister of the Church of Bamberg, to Lord G., provost of Richersberg: “not to think more highly than one ought to think” (Rom. 12).

“As we have heard, so we have seen.” In those things which you wrote to our venerable and beloved brother, the abbot of Windberg, we have perceived with eyewitness certainty that you preach and disseminate every unfavourable thing you can about us, in a manner unbecoming your priesthood; and we cannot pass these over in silence. One of these is that, as though we were blaspheming the Son of God and adulterating the word of God, as some do, we had called our Lord Jesus Christ a vassal of God the Father. By God’s mercy this is far from our mouth, heart, and conscience; and it has always been far from our purpose [Col. 0524C] to introduce any novelty, since the Apostle instructs and commands us to avoid profane novelties of speech (1 Tim. 6).

If it pleased your majesty, you could seek other seasonings and defences for your sayings and writings than inventions of this kind, in which you curse the deaf and set a stumbling-block before the blind. But why have you disparaged words of truth? With words composed for rebuke, you strive to overthrow a friend who loved you, because he judged you worthy of love and believed that he would be loved in return. You also attempt to besmear not only our reputation, but that of others who surpass us in both rank and the merit of a long life; and further, that of those who, although lesser than we in order and office, are nevertheless far superior to us in life and learning. [Col. 0524D] You openly point them out when you say in your letter concerning certain persons: “They stood afar off in silence”; and concerning others: “Those who sought my life used violence.” You would do better and more prudently if you took care that your speech, seasoned with the salt of wisdom and discernment, might build up the weak and be free of the blemish of suspicion, detraction, and mockery.

For if you rightly recall our mutual conversation and friendly discussion, when we treated charitably, without contention or rivalry, the proposition which you are accustomed to state, “Christ is equal to the Father insofar as he is man,” and supported it with your customary citations: because all things [Col. 0525A] were delivered to him by the Father (Matt. 11); because the name which is above every name was given to him (Phil. 2); because all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in him (Col. 2); because he is God’s power and God’s wisdom (1 Cor. 1); and because he is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2). Then, as seemed consequent to you but was not coherently consequent according to the truth, you inferred: “Therefore Christ is equal to God the Father insofar as he is man.”

All these points having been soundly and catholicly defined, and the inference rejected on the authority of many passages from the Gospel and the holy Fathers, we nevertheless refuted your argument by an additional comparison, although it required no refutation because of the evident falsehood and incoherence of the propositions put forward together with that which was inferred. The comparison introduced for the purpose of refutation and argument was this: In civil law, the one in whose name a thing is possessed possesses it; and both the vassal and the lord are possessors of the same thing. Whatever one possesses, the other also possesses. Therefore is the vassal equal to the lord in possession? I speak according to human terms—by no means! For one possessor is principal, the other secondary. One possesses in his own name; the other in another’s name, namely, in the name of him who is the principal possessor. And although he possesses all that the lord possesses, nevertheless the dominion of possession is not equal between vassal and lord. But we said and considered these things then not absolutely or in themselves, but solely by way of explanation and illustration, privately, without public declamation or dispute. And even if you were unwilling to keep faith with what was confidential, still, had you known the law and method of refutation, perhaps you would have judged otherwise. For the method of refutation is such that we do not equate things with things in every respect, but compare reasonings with reasonings and refute opposing assertions through the likeness of unlike things.

Indeed, the propriety of a comparison is one thing, the simplicity of direct speech another. To enumerate one by one all the many and varied kinds of comparisons would be excessively long and superfluous. But, to bring forward some instances for greater clarity: it is written, “The disciple is not above the teacher. It is enough for the disciple that he be like his teacher” (Matt. 10). Therefore will the teacher be a disciple, and [Col. 0525D] the disciple a teacher? By no means. Again: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. 23). Therefore is Christ a hen? Indeed, he is no more a hen than he is a vassal, and conversely. Further: “As lightning flashes from beneath heaven, so shall the coming of the Son of Man be” (Luke 17). Will the Son of Man therefore be lightning? Not at all. Finally, that every mouth may be stopped, let us come to the explicit and chief comparison of all comparisons: “Like Father, like Son.” Therefore is the Father the Son, or the Son the Father? According to you, all these things are incongruous; not according to the truth, nor according to us who follow it. Thus in the Gospel the day of the Lord, or even the Lord himself, [Col. 0526A] coming unexpectedly, is said to be called a thief, because it is written: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (2 Pet. 3).

For it must be understood that, although things are compared to one another on some ground of likeness, names are not thereby transferred from the things to which they belong to other things. Enough has been said on such matters for the wise person.

But let us briefly gather together what has been said. We intend to say nothing else, either then or now, than what all divine authority cries aloud: “What the Son of God has by nature, the son of man has by grace.” From this it necessarily follows that he is not equal to God insofar as he is man, as he himself testifies—whose Gospel and testimony we are not ashamed of: “The Father,” he says, “is greater [Col. 0526B] than I” (John 14). This was before the Passion. But lest any room for evasion remain regarding the ways in which he was made a little lower than the angels, and lest the aforesaid authority be thought no longer to hold after the glory of the resurrection, after that resurrection he said to Mary: “Go to my brothers and say to them: I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20). He calls him Father according to his divine nature, God according to his human nature. Therefore even after the resurrection, as before, “he is his God and his Lord.” Hence also: “Worship his footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. 98). Yet it is also his throne, and he sits at the right hand of Majesty on high. Let whoever has ears to hear, hear how this is so and understand what is said in what respect. For we speak to those who know the law.

But you—unless we are mistaken—did not receive the Gospel which you hand down from a man, nor learn it through a man; whether through a revelation of Jesus Christ, he knows, and you may consider. You made us an object of laughter, and you make sport of Christ’s vassalage in a manner unbecoming your prudence. May this not be imputed to you or required of you: “Let him who curses you be cursed” (3 Kings 2). Nor may that come upon you: “He who mocks shall be mocked” (Ecclus. 13). But to me it is a very small matter that I should be judged by you or by a human day. The laughter of fools is a miserable refuge of ignorance and a consolation, or dissimulation, of incompetence: when they perceive that reason fails them, they bark, fox-like, at what does not serve you. Though foxes have dens, they are nevertheless often caught and perish. Their skin is useful; their flesh deadly. Thus far on this matter.

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself compared himself in the Prophet to a little worm. He also emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in outward appearance as a man. He humbled himself even unto death, and death on a cross (Phil. 2). He is the sheep, he is the lion, he is the rock, and he is called by many other names in the sacred utterance. Nevertheless, far be it from us that, on account of any consideration of his self-emptying, we should dare to attribute to him any invented name from our own conception, whether in figurative or non-figurative speech, [Col. 0527A] or scandalize any one of these little ones who believe in him.

Therefore, excluding and anathematizing the name “vassal,” we believe in our heart and confess with our mouth concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, as we have received it in the creed of regeneration: “Equal to the Father according to divinity; lesser than the Father according to humanity.” Hence blessed Hilary says: “Remaining in the form of a servant, he who had previously remained in the form of God, Christ Jesus the man spoke: ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God’” (John 20). Behold, even after the resurrection Christ is still in the form of a servant according to your Hilary. Or lest you think that we strike you with a figurative encomium and say “ours” and “yours.” So that no scruple of doubt may remain in this matter, hear and understand what Augustine says on the same Gospel passage: “‘Go and say to my brothers: I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’ He did not say, ‘to our Father.’ Therefore mine in one way, yours in another: mine by nature, yours by grace. ‘My God and your God.’ Nor did he here say, ‘our God.’ Therefore here too mine in one way, yours in another: ‘my God, under whom I too am a man; your God, among whom I am also the mediator.’” What is said, “under whom I too am a man,” must not be heard with deaf ears. But even if they should be like deaf asps, hardening their ears, they must hear Christ himself crying, “My God” (Matt. 28), and Augustine joining in the cry in the person of Christ himself: “Under whom I too am a man.” You hear subjection; you hear that the nature remains after the resurrection, with only the weakness of nature absorbed. What more do you desire? Why do we still need witnesses? Yet, because abundant caution does no harm, let blessed Gregory follow Augustine on the same passage, “I ascend to my Father,” etc.: “Because I am man, God is God to me; because you have been freed from error, God is God to you.” Here the same nature and the lesser status of subjection are apparent, because he is not the God of divinity but of humanity subjected to him.

Because we follow these authorities, presuming nothing from ourselves, and because, to avoid the overthrow of others, [Col. 0527D] we accept nothing new without certain authority, you have sharpened your tongue against us like a sharp sword. But consider that whoever takes the sword shall perish by the sword (Matt. 26). He who had no practice with arms felled Goliath with a sling, but cut his throat with his own [so the manuscript] sword. Therefore, to use your own weapons henceforth: although it is difficult to wrench a club from Hercules’ hand, you grant that he is an heir, because you cannot deny it. But he is heir by the Father’s appointment and the prerogative of grace, as the Apostle says: “Whom he appointed heir of all things” (Heb. 1), insofar as he is man; “through whom he also made the worlds” (ibid.), insofar as he is God. For although according to divinity he possesses all things with the Father, yet according to humanity [Col. 0528A] he is an heir appointed in accordance with the words: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2). Hence John Chrysostom says: “In saying ‘heir,’ he showed an indication of humility.”

Finally, what you introduce from Bede to prove that the Son is equal to the Father insofar as he is man plainly stands against you, since it says nothing other than that it was given to the man that he should be God—he who is the only-begotten Son, like his begetter, neither unlike in nature nor inferior in power nor later in time. This could not hold true of Christ insofar as he is man. What follows, namely, “This equality he received from the time of the incarnation,” must likewise be understood thus: the man himself, assumed by God in the unity of person, must altogether be confessed lesser than the uncreated Father, not only according to the created humanity, made a little lower than the angels, as you say in your letter, but also according to that same humanity now glorified after the resurrection and ascension. I say, he must be confessed lesser and, insofar as he is man, no less subject by reason of the advancement bestowed by divinity; otherwise he would seem ungrateful and not to have grace for grace.

Since in matters pertaining to faith it is equally blameworthy to be deceived and to deceive, we exhort, warn, and beseech you in the charity of him whom Charity itself brought down from heaven to earth: provide what is good not only before God but also before men, and so moderate your sayings and writings that no one may be scandalized by any ambiguity, or by a differing reception or transposition of words. Thus, walking in the simplicity of the Christian faith, may we all say the same thing: “Equal to the Father according to divinity; lesser than the Father according to humanity,” confessing one person in Christ and two natures. Blessed Ambrose clearly distinguishes their properties in these words: “I have turned over and turned again the divine Scripture, and nowhere have I found the Son of God to be adoptive. But just as Christ, insofar as he is God, naturally has it that he is the natural Son of God and is God, so insofar as he is man, he has by grace that he is the same natural Son of God.”

If anything more obscure should occur—as there are many such expressions in Hilary—it should be turned toward a sound understanding, so that words may serve realities, not realities words. To specify this at least once, with pardon granted for prolixity on account of those who are still like us, so that they need milk rather than solid food: in Book Eleven, where he treats of subjection, the handing over of the kingdom, and the end, blessed Hilary says, “The briefer, the more obscure: man and God—now God is the whole.” As if one were to say: the one person of God and man, this whole consisting of two natures and in two natures, is God. “Whole,” however, is not to be understood integrally or in any other ordinary manner in which we are accustomed to speak, but uniquely and ineffably. For the two natures so form one person in so great a union, as Pope Leo indicates, that one is said reciprocally of the other, and that both statements are true: “The man is God, and God is man—immortal, impassible.” Pope Leo: “Each, God by the power of the one assuming, each, man by the humility of the one assumed, retains without defect its own property in each nature; and just as the form of God does not remove the form of a servant, so the form of a servant does not diminish the form of God.”

May all the faithful who have not disdained to read or hear these writings, though composed in an uncultivated style, be admonished and fortified, insofar as lies in us, that in every expression in which it is said, “insofar as he is God,” “insofar as he is man,” they may beware and diligently take care to observe to what the statement refers—whether to the person, to the nature, or perhaps sometimes to the cause—and may so define this and other similar expressions that they do not depart from the path and rule of the catholic faith. The same judgment must similarly be made concerning “how much is in this,” or “from this,” and “in him,” or “from him,” and other expressions of this kind. For like things have the same judgment. Let these things, once said, suffice.

## LETTER XII

Letter of Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, to Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg.—He briefly replies to the latter’s previous letter and announces that he has written a complete work upon the disputed question.

To his most serene lord E., bishop of Bamberg, brother G. of Richersberg sends devoted prayers with faithful service.

[Col. 0529C] I received your letter gladly; having received it, I read it carefully; having read it, I committed it to memory all the more attentively because in it I observed that wisdom which orders all things sweetly and mightily. For the strength of rebuke, mingled with the sweetness of discernment, strongly warned my lowliness not to think that the proper meaning of a designation must be assigned to things introduced by way of comparison. For example, because in the Gospel the Lord is compared to a thief or to lightning, he is not therefore to be thought a thief or lightning. Hence, when your prudence compared the name of vassal to Christ in a certain illustration, you did not persuade me that this should be understood as though Christ performs the office of a vassal. Know, therefore, that I was not so wise—indeed, not so foolish—as to suppose that you thought this, although in a fraternal discussion you introduced the name “vassal” for a certain comparison.

But because I understood that some were murmuring on the occasion of that discussion, as though I had there confessed or been convicted of an unquestionable heresy, I wrote certain things to the lord abbot of Windberg, your faithful man, for my own defence, not to defame your honour. In them I also briefly inserted a rejection of “vassal”; I shall gladly take care not to repeat this further in my writings, because I perceive that it is grievous to you. But on the occasion of that discussion of yours, examining my writings more carefully rather than retracting them, I completed a little work addressed to my lord of Salzburg. After he had read it, I sent it to the lord of Brixen to read, intending also to send it to your discernment for consideration and, wherever it may seem appropriate, refinement.

## LETTER XIII

Letter of the same to the same.—He declares false the report that he had defamed him at the emperor’s court. He returns to the disputed question, in which he considers the Council of Ephesus a great support to himself.

To his most serene lord E., venerable bishop of the Church of Bamberg, brother G. of Richersberg sends devoted prayers with faithful service.

Our beloved son John, chaplain of my lord the archbishop, coming from you, informed me that you were deeply angered against my lowliness because certain persons had reported to you that I had spoken unfavourably concerning [Col. 0530B] you before the lord emperor and, what would move you still more, concerning the lord archbishop. I admit that your indignation against me would be just if what was reported to you were true. But lest you suppose true what is false, you may learn from the most clement Augustus himself that I said nothing other or otherwise than what I now confess to you.

When I had been maliciously denounced to him by that Folmar—who, like a bitter bellows, had scattered bitter things about me, and who, like an ill-omened harlot, had suggested to the lord emperor, as to another Solomon, that his dead child was mine and my living child was his—as though in my writings I had disparaged the honour of God and the imperial crown of Augustus, although it is plain to readers of his profane little book, sent to my lord the archbishop, that he himself had done this; and although, conversely, it is clear to readers of my writings that I do not think as he disseminated concerning me, sending his fabrications everywhere, which he says and writes are Gerhoh’s heresies: when, I say, I had been so denounced at the imperial court, a report also went abroad among the chaplains of the court and many other brothers that you had convicted me of manifest heresies and compelled me to confess heresies.

Your piety knows that this was not so. At your exhortation I promised to inspect my writings more carefully and, if I found in them anything that was a stumbling-block, to smooth it out after the example of blessed Augustine. I have endeavoured to do this also in the little work recently completed, which I am prepared to submit to the judgment of my lord the archbishop and of you, and also of the Roman pontiff, when the proper time comes—when, by the Lord’s command, the storm now raging has been calmed.

Therefore, when such things had been sown at court, I was asked whether they were true. I denied it, saying that you were indeed my adversary in opinion, as are many learned men, but not so cruel as to judge me a heretic. Then, when Augustus asked whether my lord the archbishop was with me or against me, I said that he was neither for me nor against me. Therefore I ask that you hold me excused with respect to this accusation; nor should it seem unworthy or grievous to you that I have repelled, and still repel, from myself the charge of heresy. I desire to be and to be called catholic, though poor and insignificant, prepared in Christ’s patience to bear many reproaches apart from the charge of schism and heresy.

For being a heretic and having a demon are almost equivalent; nor should one endure such accusations without refuting them when they are made. Other reproaches must be endured after the example of Christ, who, when he was called a glutton, a drinker of wine, a deceiver, a Samaritan, and a friend of tax collectors, was silent like one who had no rebukes in his mouth, though he could have disproved and denied all these things. But when he was said to have a demon, he did not remain silent, but answered: “I do not have a demon, but I honour my Father, and you dishonour me” (John 8). He gave us an example that we too might act thus, patiently bearing it when we are compared to a deaf asp hardening its ears, or to Goliath struck with his own sword, or even to a fox having dens, and to other monsters; so that we may not be moved to anger, but to compassion for those who believe and say such things concerning us.

But if anyone charges one with heresy—that is, an error in faith defended with obstinate animosity—every person who believes rightly and confesses what he believes may say: “I am not a heretic; I do not have the demon of this pestilence; I honour God, and you dishonour me.” For every catholic, in honouring Christ, honours God, because Christ is God. “You believe in God,” he says, “believe also in me” (John 14). “For,” Augustine says in his commentary on John, “it follows that if you believe in God, you ought also to believe in me; which would not follow if Christ were not God.”

Christ, however, is an anointed man, perfect God and perfect man: even in the form of a servant, the Most High Lord, having no lord higher than himself—although he himself, insofar as he is man, has above himself, or rather in himself, God, to whom he said on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 28). Even after the resurrection he calls him his God (ibid.), signifying by the name “God” the highest Divinity, to whom all created things are subjected and serve, and to whom the creature of humanity also served in Christ, the form of God in him having been emptied—not so that it did not exist, but so that it was hidden, because there his strength was hidden when death went before the face of him who was dying. Hidden, I say, not annihilated.

Likewise, when death was swallowed up in victory, the form of a servant was emptied—not so that it might not exist, but so that it might exist in the best way, namely, no longer by serving but by ruling. Whoever assigns to him a lord higher than himself must see whence he proves this, for it is nowhere found in the Scriptures of truth. For though after the resurrection, and also before it, he calls God his God, he neither before nor after the resurrection says that his God is his Lord: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11). He calls the Father Lord of heaven and earth, not his Lord; and rightly so, because being Lord and being Father-God are not the same thing. One is relative to the Son or sons; the other to a servant or servants.

Therefore, because it is perpetual in Christ that he is Son, God is rightly asserted now and eternally to be his Father. Again, because it is perpetual in Christ that he is a creature, the Creator God is rightly asserted to be his God. But because it is not perpetual in him that he serves, since lordship succeeds his servitude—not just any lordship, but the highest—when the form of a servant has been emptied, not so as not to exist but so as to rule in the entire commonwealth of God the Father: whoever proclaims in Christ either that God is the Lord of the man, or that the servant or man is God’s servant, divides Christ into two, Lord and servant, contrary to the Council of Ephesus. Would that you weighed that council in its entirety, together with the letters, acts, and judgments inserted in it. I believe that, just as you call Hilary both yours and ours, you would call the same council both ours and yours; and, agreeing with both Hilary and the aforesaid council, we would say the same thing and think rightly, interpreting devoutly the subjection by which the Son, though he remains and shall remain subject forever, giving thanks to him according to the human nature gratuitously exalted in him and glorified with divine glory, nevertheless has equal—indeed, the same—lordship with God the Father. He will no longer call or acknowledge him to be his God, as he acknowledges him to be his God and his Father: his God, under whom he is man; his Father, with whom that man himself is one Lord.

It is clear, as we think, that we have not heard with deaf ears Augustine’s words: “My God, under whom I am man.” We little ones likewise admonish your exaltedness that, just as we hear from your admonition “under whom,” so you too may hear “with whom” and “in whom.” For many evangelical and apostolic authorities assert that the assumed man, having completed the obedience of his power, rules most mightily, lives, and reigns forever with his Father and in his Father. For, as the Apostle says, “He sat down at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heights, having become so much better than the angels” (Heb. 1)—doubtless in that nature in which he was made, “as he inherited a name more excellent than theirs” (ibid.).

## LETTER XIV

Letter of Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, to Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg.—The teaching of the Council of Ephesus is explained, together with the words of other doctors and of sacred Scripture which Gerhoh adduced to establish his opinion.

E., by God’s grace called bishop of the Church of Bamberg, to venerable brother G., provost of Richersberg: that you may think the same thing toward one another according to Jesus Christ.

The beginning of your letter, where you excuse yourself concerning curses, is sweet as honey; but its final parts are bitter as wormwood or vinegar mingled with gall, where—saving your charity—you mark us as though opposed to the Council of Ephesus. This, it must be said, is less than brotherly. But, having now wiped off and shaken away this dust, we give many thanks to your goodwill because, although we were somewhat at variance, you admonished us in brotherly charity and strongly invited [Col. 0533A] us to the banquet of your feasts, that is, to the Council of Ephesus. Therefore we approach with cheerful countenance and glad spirit, all the more eager—and, indeed, more secure in respect of faith, which would that it worked through love!—being confident that whatever shall be served or proposed must be for us and not against us.

You have fulfilled Scripture: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head” (Rom. 12). Would that these coals, living, burning, and not consuming, might be heaped upon our heads, so that the fire of charity and the light of truth may burn within us! Therefore let us feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Let us see not merely what the surface of words gives off, but what flavour the inward taste reports to us from within.

Your Council of Ephesus—for it exceeds us to call it ours, except insofar as it was held against Nestorius as our catholic faith is ours in the communion of the faithful—its canon is found as follows: “Here begins the canon of the first holy Council of Ephesus, held against Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who asserted that a mere man was born of the holy Virgin Mary, so that he made one person of the flesh and another of the divinity, and did not acknowledge one Christ in the Word of God and flesh, but preached separately one Son of God and another Son of Man. At this synod Saint Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria, presided in the place of Saint Pope Celestine,” and the remaining acts of the holy council.

But let us now come to those matters which, from the tenor of your letter, we perceived that you marked as if drawn from the creed of the same council against us; and we took this gravely, as was fitting. Their text is appended below, where Nestorius is instructed what he must renounce or abjure:

“But neither do we assert that the Word of God the Father is God or Lord of Christ, lest once again we divide more manifestly into two the one Christ, Son and Lord, and incur the crime of sacrilege by making God himself his God and Lord. For, united to the flesh according to substance, as we have said above, God the Word is God of all things and Lord over the universe. Nevertheless, he is neither servant nor lord to himself. For although he called the Father his God, while he himself is also God by nature and from the Father’s essence, nevertheless we in no way fail to know that, while remaining God, he also became man, who would exist under God according to the law of human nature. But how could he be either God or Lord to himself? Therefore, as man, insofar as befits the measure of self-emptying, he declared to us that he was under God; in this same way he was made under the law, although he himself promulgated the law and stood forth as lawgiver inasmuch as he was God.”

You invited us, as we believe, to these feasts, as though what has been set forth were against us. But we gladly feed on this heavenly manna, so that the dryness [Col. 0534A] of our soul, somewhat nourished, may not call bitter sweet and sweet bitter, having the sure moderation of discernment concerning what ought not to be believed and what ought to be believed. To believe that God the Word is God and Lord of Christ is a Nestorian poison. But whoever believes this most manifestly divides into two the one Christ, Son and Lord, and makes God the Word himself his own God and Lord. But God himself is neither servant nor lord to himself, because every absurdity would follow from that Nestorian error if anyone were to say that God the Word is God and Lord of Christ—that is, of God and man.

That statement, however, must not be passed over with a deaf ear, but firmly retained: “We in no way [Col. 0534B] fail to know that, while remaining God, he also became man,” etc. For it is plainly assigned to the man that he is under God as Lord; whereas above this was excluded of God and it was proved that God cannot be under God, and that God can neither be his own servant nor his own Lord. Therefore the conclusion is apt: “Therefore, as man, insofar as befits the measure of his fitting self-emptying, he declared himself to be under God with us; and in this sense too he was made under the law, although he himself promulgated the law and existed as lawgiver inasmuch as he is God.”

If, therefore, we were to say that the Word of God the Father is the God or Lord of Christ—making two persons out of the Word and the flesh, which is a heretical meaning and condemned in the sixth chapter of the aforesaid council—we should undoubtedly sin most gravely against the Creed and against the Catholic faith, [Col. 0534C] dividing Christ more manifestly into two than those heresies which were there condemned before this passage, article by article and individually. For although all alike divide Christ, nevertheless, according to those earlier articles, after the Incarnation God is not denied to be united to the man in some manner. According to Nestorius, however, a mere man born of the Virgin is asserted to have been afterward assumed by the Word as by his God and Lord, his Creator; and thus Christ, one and the same God and man in person, would according to him be split into two, namely into Lord and servant, and would be both God and Lord to himself. To believe this would be absurd and impious. And if we divided Christ in the same way, we ought without doubt to be cast out [Col. 0534D] outside.

But by God’s grace, neither confusing the persons nor separating the substance, we do not speak as Nestorius spoke: that the person of the Word is one thing, that of Christ another; and that the Word is the God and Lord of Christ. Rather, we say this: the Word coeternal with the Father and the man assumed in time are one person—namely our God and Lord Jesus Christ—“equal to the Father according to divinity, less than the Father according to humanity”; as he himself, who is Truth, says: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14). This is the antiquity of the Christian faith, to lay hands upon which is abominable. For it is certain, according to Pope Celestine, how pernicious are novelties of doctrine that descend from the love of vain glory.

[Col. 0535A] Look therefore, attend, and judge whether we split Christ in two contrary to the Council of Ephesus, when we believe and confess inseparably the one person of the assuming Word and of the assumed man, and distinguish nature from nature in such a way that one is greater, as has been said; and as the whole universal Church both holds and sings in this manner: “Although he is God and man, yet he is not two, but one Christ.” This is a faithful saying. “He who speaks a lie speaks from his own resources.” Do not suppose that we speak from our own resources in what we say. If perhaps you do not possess Nestorius’s blasphemies, seek them and you will find that he thought so perversely and impiously concerning the Father’s Word: that it was the God and Lord of Christ as though of another person, whom it had first created and afterward assumed, [Col. 0535B] so that there would be two persons just as there are two natures—one person assuming, the other assumed.

Accordingly, that accursed and accursing Nestorius concludes that blasphemy—which corresponds in the opposite sense to the foregoing chapter of the Council of Ephesus—with this ending, as though God the Word, remaining in that person afterward assumed, had spoken concerning it as concerning his sanctuary: “Destroy this temple, and after three days I shall rebuild it” (John 2). As though he said: “I, the indweller, shall raise by my own power the dwelling-place, which is powerless in itself.” We do not distinguish the Word and flesh from one another as Nestorius does, so as to call the Word the God, Lord, and Creator of Christ, and Christ himself another in person [Col. 0535C] than the Word, his Lord and Creator. That would most plainly split Christ in two.

Detesting this impious division, we reject with it all those monstrous heresies by which Nestorius is there charged with asserting that Christ is one with God through favor, dignity, authority, an aggregating conjunction, a connection composed as it were of parts, participation, or indwelling. Having cursed all errors, we gather with him and in him who says, “He who does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11), and simply say that the one Christ is always God and man in one and the same person, confessing him less than God according to his humanity, but equal to God insofar as he is God. This is not [Col. 0535D] to divide one and the same person into two, but to distinguish two natures joined in one person by a certain hidden and ineffable divine operation: for “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4).

The apostle Paul did not divide either himself or all human beings into two when he said: “Though our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4); rather, he distinguished from one another the things that were in one man. Thus every human being, according to the inward and outward man, is greater than himself and less than himself in different respects; nor for that reason is he a whole man, but one man of a double nature. What wonder, then, if we too distinguish in Christ those things that belong to Christ—namely, the divine and human natures? This is not [Col. 0536A] to split Christ in two, as has often been said, but to distinguish nature from nature. It is not ours to pull with you a contentious rope over such matters, or to seek anything other than Christ’s glory. Let Christ prevail in us; let righteousness prevail; let the truth of faith prevail, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail. For this is that glorious victory which conquers the world: our faith.

From what has now been said it is evident, we believe, to all who are truly wise that we do not dissect Christ and are not opposed to the Council of Ephesus. May the Angel of Great Counsel inspire you not to depose God the Father Almighty from the throne of his majesty, nor diminish him in relation to himself by saying that he is God but not Lord of his creature—[Col. 0536B] namely, the assumed man—which would altogether be contrary to the Council of Ephesus. Thanks be to God, you agree with us in granting that Christ, now after the resurrection, is subject to God the Father and is a creature insofar as he is man—things which we had not understood you previously to concede in every respect.
