But what value is agreement among us on these points if such great disagreement still persists: that we call the Father the God and Lord of Christ insofar as Christ is man, while you concede only that he is his God and not his Lord? Any, even the smallest, difference produces the greatest discord if it is not proportionate.

First, we say that the Old Testament is a wheel within a wheel in the New, and the New in the Old, because [Col. 0536C] each is contained in the other. These are the two lips of the Bride, sounding in harmony with one another. What then matters whether a thing is found here or there, provided that the sure authority of what we hold and say is found? If Christ did not say everything before or after the resurrection, this does not prejudice the truth and authority of what the prophets, apostles, or their successors uttered; for, as the Apostle testifies, he is the author of both Testaments: “God, who at many times and in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us” (Hebrews 1), etc. And it is always repeated and reiterated: “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isaiah 40), and other similar statements.

The New Testament is properly a testament. The sayings of the prophets are testimonies. By the death of the testator the testament was confirmed, strengthened by witnesses previously brought forward; otherwise the testament would seem defective, having no testimony. “If you believed Moses, you would surely believe me” (John 5), Christ said. We therefore follow the witnesses of truth without fear. Perhaps Truth said everything in the person of Christ himself, but, according to Augustine on John, we either cannot or will not understand it, although Christ himself says: “Everything whatsoever that I heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15). When he said “God,” he sufficiently declared “Lord” as well, though perhaps you refused to notice. Therefore hear what he himself says: “You shall not see me henceforth until you say: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 23). Hear David; hear the children [Col. 0537A] crying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 119). He is both Lord and sent by the Lord. Recognize him whom Simeon recognized as “the Christ of the Lord,” concerning whom he received an answer from none other than the Holy Spirit.

We have indeed seen—and, according to the boastfulness of your letter, have seen well—how well you understood Augustine’s statement: “Under whom I too am a man.” Yet we should have wished you to understand it somewhat better. Since you grant that in his human nature, as a creature, he is subject to his Creator, why not as to his Lord? What did you fear from that business walking in the darkness—the heresy of Nestorius—that he might be God and Lord to himself? There is no longer cause for fear, since that calf’s head has been crushed and reduced to ashes, thanks be to God. Therefore, just as you said to us, if we remember rightly, “See whether we have understood Augustine well,” so we return the measure to you with equal balance, very peaceably: hear and understand Christ speaking in the prophet, confessing of himself: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me” (Psalm 84). “Arise,” he says, “and attend to my judgment, my God and my Lord, to my cause” (Psalm 34). Thus speaks Christ, that Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.

And what does Augustine say? “Arise, and enter into judgment with me, my God and my Lord—not for my punishment, but for my cause; not in that which the thief has in common with me, but in that [Col. 0537C] which belongs to those blessed who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake. It is not punishment, but the cause, that makes the martyr.” Again: “And you, Lord, act with me for your name’s sake.” On this passage Augustine says: “For the Father helps the Son, insofar as God helps man on account of the form of a servant; and God is God to that man, and the Father is also Lord to him in the form of a servant.” Since you have said that this is nowhere found in the Scriptures of truth, see whether this is Scripture of truth.

If you object that the Most High has none higher than himself, because we sing to Christ, “You alone are Lord; you alone are Most High,” you must beware of stumbling upon the rock of offense. For that giant of double substance surpasses the assumed man by the height of his divinity alone, so that he is both his God and Lord; and in this respect Christ alone is Lord, alone Most High, essentially undivided from the Father and the Holy Spirit. As in the passages already cited, so likewise in many others in the same prophet, the Father is found to be called the God and Lord of Christ. Again, in the prophet Isaiah: “Thus says the Lord: Behold my servant, I will uphold him; my chosen one, in him my soul has taken pleasure” (Isaiah 42). In the Gospel this is said with an altered word: “Behold my child” (Matthew 12). Let this disturb no one, because one translation does not prejudice another; the centurion too says, “My child lies paralyzed in the house” (Matthew 8), calling his servant *puer* according to common usage. What more do you seek?

If you say that Christ is not found to have called the Father Lord either before the resurrection [Col. 0538A] or after it, and for that reason deny that he is the Lord of his creature, consider what you are saying. For in calling him God, he confessed him also as Lord, since he cannot be someone’s God without being that person’s Lord. Although “God” and “Lord” are said with different relations, neither exceeds the other; and, when these names are taken properly and singularly, they belong to the one alone from whom, in whom, and through whom are all things. Hence: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matthew 4). Taken otherwise, however, there are many gods and many lords. Indeed, all the pages of sacred Scripture are full of instances showing how God is understood in “Lord,” and Lord in “God.” For example: “Thus says the Lord.” And again: [Col. 0538B] “I am your God” (Leviticus 21). Both God is understood in Lord, and Lord in God.

If you will not believe me, believe at least the prophets and Moses himself; and if you will not believe Moses, believe at least the angel, and you will see that what we say rests upon truth. “Hail, Mary,” says the angel, “full of grace, the Lord is with you” (Luke 1), that is, God. Hence Peter, bishop of Alexandria and condemner of Arius: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, namely from the time when the angel greeted the Virgin, saying: ‘Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.’ Gabriel said, ‘The Lord is with you,’ which means God, showing that he would become flesh, according to what is written: ‘The Holy Spirit shall come upon you’” (Luke 1).

Finally, since Christ’s names in Hebrew are full of mystery, did the Son deprive the Father of all these names because he is not found to have called him by all of them in the Gospel? We marvel, and cannot marvel sufficiently, that when you call him the God of Christ, you do not receive him as the Lord of Christ, although you can plainly weigh the force of these names from *dulia* and *latria*, which are well known to you: *latria* belongs to God, *dulia* to a lord—not only to the Lord who is God, but also, in its own manner, to angels and men, to whom it is due.

By the same reasoning that you use from Christ to the Father, we too could argue analogously from the disciples to Christ, so that we would not call Christ by any terms other than those which the disciples are read to have used in the Gospel, and which the Savior himself summed up: [Col. 0538D] “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am.” Shall he then not be their God and ours because they did not say, “Teacher and God and Lord”? But unless they had understood God in “Lord,” they would surely have been rebuked, as was the man who said to him, “Good Teacher” (Mark 10). Because that man did not believe him to be God and called him merely teacher, while these, in calling him Lord, understood God also in Lord, he rightly accepts their praise, saying, “You speak rightly.” But he rebukes the other, saying: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except the one God” (Mark 10). It is as though he said: “Because you do not believe me to be God, you impiously and incorrectly confess me as a good teacher.”

By this same reasoning our Lord Jesus Christ will be deprived of his special name, which is the Tetragrammaton, interpreted as: “This one is the beginning of the passion of life” [uncertain etymological gloss]. To what purpose, then, will that careful and prophetic enumeration of names fade away: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9)? If you had wished to consider more carefully that authority by which you fortify yourselves—“I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matthew 11)—we would say nothing else than, “Peace be with you!” For in saying “Father,” he confesses himself to be the Son of God; in saying “Lord of heaven and earth,” he confesses his own Lord, insofar as he himself is man and a creature of God. For under the designation heaven and earth the whole creation is comprehended, because “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1), and “He who lives for ever created all things together” [Col. 0539B] (Ecclesiasticus 23).

Therefore either the assumed man is included under the name heaven and earth, or he will not be a creature—unless one says that a new creature was then made by God when the Son of God assumed flesh. May God avert this from the hearts of the faithful, for it would be to revive the heresy of Valentinus. This Valentinus, disciple of Marcion, maintained that Christ assumed nothing bodily from the Virgin, but passed through her as through a pipe. Then the faith of our redemption would be empty, and we ought to await another Messiah. That Christ, insofar as he is man, is of the substance of earth is proved from this: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Psalm 84), and “He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one” (Hebrews 2). Augustine says: “Christ is called Adam, and is called the last Adam, because he is from the same material.”

Likewise, when he says, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Psalm 30), it is a confession of both natures: of the divine, in that he says “Father”; and of the human, in that he commends his spirit into his hands, because he is both his God and his Lord. Hence that very verse, canonized by Jesus Christ himself on the cross, is concluded by the Prophet in his person with these words: “You have redeemed me, Lord God of truth” (ibid.). Remember whose words these are in the Acts of the Apostles: “For David says concerning him: I foresaw the Lord always before my face, because he is at my right hand, lest I be moved” (Acts 2). The whole book of Wisdom is full of testimonies to the same thing. If you reject these because Christ does not say them either before the resurrection [Col. 0539D] or after it, by this you take authority away from our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who says: “It is necessary that all things written concerning me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms be fulfilled” (Luke 24). And again: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16).

Henceforth the form of a servant must be examined, because you say that Christ retained only the form of a servant after the resurrection, as though denying that he serves—while inquiry is made into what he serves. “Christ emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men,” etc. (Philippians 2); yet not so as to assume a form without reality or a likeness without truth. The likeness refers to us, [Col. 0540A] but truth nevertheless exists in him. Hence Augustine: “That God took the form of a servant—that is, the nature of a servant—into his own person, and thus the Maker of men was made in the likeness of men,” etc. The truth of these realities was not abolished in him at the resurrection, except for mortality and other such things, which are the punishment of sin. For then death truly went before his face, as you say, and as the Prophet foretold.

What you introduce concerning the self-emptying of the servile form may, it seems to us, readily be set aside; for self-emptying pertains to humility, whereas the transformation of the servile form pertains to glorification and exaltation. But leaving these matters aside, let us return to this: Christ, having completed the obedience of his dispensation, is exalted through the glory of resurrection and ascension, [Col. 0540B] and sits at the right hand of Majesty on high, true God and true man, equal to the Father according to divinity and less than the Father according to humanity. This we believe and confess; and against this faith, strengthened by the authority of the Roman and universal Church, we receive no novelty, nor even antiquity.

If any question arises, we follow the ordinance of the Apostolic See, the decree of Pope Celestine: “The deeper and more difficult aspects of questions that arise, which those who resisted heretics have discussed more extensively, we do not dare to despise; yet neither are we bound to establish them.” We believe that whatever the writings have taught us according to the aforesaid rules of the Apostolic See sufficiently satisfies us, so that we should not at all judge Catholic anything that must be contrary to the established determinations.

[Col. 0540C] Nor should anyone imagine that we say the bondage of former subjection and obedience still lies upon Christ, since even to the apostles it was said: “I shall no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15); and elsewhere: “He is no longer a servant but a son” (Galatians 4). Here is denoted that servitude of fear which love casts out; this servitude is far from Christ and always has been. But we say only this: released from human laws, he is subject to the law of God alone, which is the eternal law, so that, according to Augustine, every creature may serve its Creator.

That law of temporal obedience indeed came to an end when he said, “It is finished” (John 19), where also our old man was crucified with him. But the law of all creation, which we mentioned before, and which he himself accepted for us—not because he was obliged, but because he willed it—still stands and remains unshaken. Therefore Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall have no more dominion over him. For insofar as he lives, he lives to God (Romans 6): according to Augustine, “After rendering the coin in its time to Augustus, he renders himself, the Head with the members, to God.” Thus he is not subject to the curse which took its beginning from Achan; he is bound neither to Moses nor to Caesar Augustus; nor does he bear the mark of servitude under which he was shorn [or: stripped] and reckoned among the impious; nor is he subject even to his parents. For the Lawgiver who had been made under the law is now released from all human laws, except for that [Col. 0541A] which has been declared: the humility of our condition without sin and without sin’s punishment—he alone free among the dead, who, as Son, remains in the house for ever as Head with the body, while that servant who does not remain for ever is excluded.

Let Christ, therefore, God and man, be adored, and let him serve in his own manner, insofar as a creature serves its Creator. For lifting our eyes to the mountains, whence help comes to us, we always return to this: “When he has delivered up the kingdom to God the Father, then he himself also shall be subject to him who subjected all things to him. He shall be subject insofar as he is man,” as Augustine says, together with his body, which is the Church, to him who subjected both him and all things—that is, to the Godhead.

But if you ask whom or in what respect he serves, receive the answer. What does Peter serve? What [Col. 0541B] does Paul serve? What do the spirits and souls of the righteous serve? What do angels and archangels serve? What do cherubim and seraphim serve? There is no one who says: “I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg” (Luke 16). Do you wish to know what they serve? Hear: “Bless the Lord, all works of the Lord” (Psalm 102). Do you wish to know how? “Let every spirit praise the Lord” (Psalm 150). Looking especially to Christ’s person, the Prophet expressed the same thing in these words: “You have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, that my glory may sing to you: O Lord my God, I shall confess you for ever” (Psalm 29). Augustine: “What is ‘I shall confess you for ever’? ‘I shall praise you for ever.’”

This is the final cause; this is the whole business of that life; this is that holocaust offered on the last day of the feast, and the vow rendered to the Lord in Jerusalem, when Jerusalem shall praise the Lord together—its Head with its body, keeping Sabbath from every servile work in that Sabbath-rest—to him alone who made its borders peace and who satisfies his guests with the fat of wheat, that is, with himself. Do you therefore wish to know this secret: what Christ now serves? He intercedes for us, and the Lord looks upon the face of his Christ. Augustine.

Do you still doubt whether Christ serves? Hear how greatly he serves: he is the footstool of his feet. Hence: “Adore also his footstool, for it is holy” (Psalm 98). Yet all this serving God is reigning. I told you long ago, and you heard it, as blessed Jerome testifies in his commentary on the Psalms: “For he both sits on the throne of majesty and is the throne and is the footstool of the feet.” If you inquire further, I first answer: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm 17). If you press more and more, I tell you with the Prophet: “This is a labor before me, until I enter into the sanctuary of God and understand their latter end” (Psalm 73); and with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11). This is Peter’s confession: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16), with whom, and in whom, and through whom, and with whom, the same our Lord Jesus Christ lives and reigns with the Holy Spirit for ever.

## LETTER XV

Gerhoh’s reply to the preceding letter of Eberhard.—He explains at length how the man in Christ is now not a servant by condition, although he is such by natural kind [*genere naturae*]. Certain matters concerning the manner of worshipping the man in Christ, etc.

To his most beloved lord E., venerable bishop of the Church of Bamberg, brother G. of Reichersberg sends devoted prayers together with faithful service.

The eternal Wisdom of God, playing in the circle of the earth from eternity, then especially delights to be with the children of men when the Church, or indeed any rational or faithful soul, is found to be the bride of the Word of God, full of delights, according to that saying in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights and leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8). Such, undoubtedly, unless I am mistaken, is your soul, intent upon sacred reading and seeking truth in the Scriptures of truth.

Hence comes that patience of yours by which you endure a little of my foolishness, and also bear with me, small as I am, although you are great in the Church and a prince in the realm, a lord of lords. Yet, as I have said, you bear with me as one who seeks what you seek and strives with utmost zeal that, as you urge, we may say and think the same thing. We now rejoice that this is partly happening, since that Ephesian chapter pleases you in which we are forbidden, with Nestorius, to divide Christ into Lord and servant, as though the uncreated Word were Lord of a created man, anointed above his fellows, as the aforesaid Nestorius taught. Against him the aforesaid Ephesian synod thus thunders:

> “If anyone says that the Word of God the Father is the God or Lord of Christ, and does not rather confess the same one to be at once God and man, since the Word was made flesh according to the Scriptures, let him be anathema.”

Since, therefore, this chapter pleases you, it must necessarily please you that the Lord of the Word and of the man united to the Word—the whole of which is Christ—is one and indivisible: one Lord with his Father and the Holy Spirit. For although it has been said concerning the Word, the Son, “The Lord rained from the Lord” (Exodus 9), nevertheless there are not two Lords, Father Lord and Son Lord, just as there are not two Gods, Father God and Son God.

Indeed, as you indicate that you understand—and rightly so—it is not one thing for God to be God and another for him to be Lord when both are said absolutely as designations of the divine substance. But when the name Lord, which is relative, is referred to a servant, we cannot concede that the assumed man, now reigning in the kingdom of God the Father, has a Lord over himself, or ought himself to be called the servant of some Lord—especially now, after he has entered into his glory, into his dominion, when the Father says to him: “Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 109), which is the same as saying: “Reign jointly and hold joint dominion with me.” For it follows: “Rule in the midst of your enemies” (Psalm 109).

Accordingly, when in the prophetic Scriptures Christ is called servant or the Father Lord, this must rightly, we think, be referred to the time when this new man, though Lord of all, was nevertheless under guardians and stewards, differing in no respect from a servant, until the time appointed by the Father (Galatians 4). But when, after service had ended, the eternal kingdom announced by the angel to his mother succeeded, I no longer call him servant but Lord, possessing with his Father an undivided dominion. The essence of the servile form remains in him; yet it no longer bears the yoke of servile obedience in its former mode, but, reigning in God and with God, exercises supreme dominion. That time of his sitting has now passed in which, weary from the journey, he sat by the well, giving living water after first rejecting the water that is not living, of which whoever drinks will thirst again. He did not always sit there, however, but rose, never again to sit thus; because, now greatly exalted, he has no need to say what he said in that weariness: “Arise,” he says, “and attend to my judgment, my God and my Lord, to my cause” (Psalm 35).

Augustine, treating this very passage, as you recalled, refers it to the same time when, weary from the journey, he invoked his God and Lord as a creature invokes its Creator and a servant its lord, being then weary from the journey in service and obedience. But now, sitting and resting at the right hand of God the Father Almighty, he will indeed forever acknowledge him as his God, as his Maker—from whom he was made from David’s seed according to the flesh—and as his Father, as the author of his divine generation and at once the maker and author of his human generation. Yet he will not acknowledge him as his Lord, because, service having passed away, he possesses with his Father undivided supreme dominion in [Col. 0543C] both natures.

Therefore, since you say that you wonder at us, when we call him Christ’s God, why we do not receive him as Christ’s Lord, here you have the reason: what has been made in him will always remain made, acknowledging God as its Maker. But what he observed according to the form of a servant—the commandment, according to the saying, “As the Father gave me commandment, so I do” (John 14)—is now wholly past, since he himself passed to the Father, his form of a servant glorified and made bright with that brightness which he himself, still a servant, requested: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was” (John 17).

As Hilary explains this, it must be understood such that what belonged to time received the brightness of his glory which is without time—namely, that brightness which the Word had before. Clothed with this brightness, the servant’s essence and form has not been emptied so that it should cease to be, or become lower than itself, but has been glorified so that it has become higher than itself. Hence we approve that your prudence censured the statement in our letter that the form of a servant was emptied—not so that it should not exist, but so that it might be in the best possible state, namely no longer serving but ruling. Therefore, since the term “self-emptying” gave you offense, although it did not introduce a perverse meaning, I shall take care not to repeat it further, making use in this respect of your correction or rebuke.

[Col. 0544A] Permit us also, I beg you, modestly to touch upon certain points which offend our humility in your writings addressed to us, or render us doubtful through their ambiguity. You say, and firmly affirm, that God the Father is God and Lord of the assumed man; and you assign this not merely to the temporal period of the economy of humiliation, but even now—that is, you assign to that same assumed man a certain eternal servitude. This, then, is what offends our littleness: for just as we do not find in the canonical Scriptures that God the Father is to be called the God and Lord of the man assumed into God from the time when he sat at the right hand of the throne of Majesty on high, so neither do we find servitude assigned to him now glorified. For where, in the prophetic books, he is found to be called either “Lord” [Col. 0544B] or “servant,” the words themselves and their context indicate that this must be assigned to the time of the economy of humiliation; as in: “Awake and attend to my judgment, my God and my Lord, in my cause” (Ps. XXXV), which undoubtedly suits the time and cause of the Passion.

Let your prudence likewise consider that, since you assert that in God the name “God” and “Lord” are to be understood as one and the same, you say, unless I am mistaken, that the assumed man was also assumed into lordship, so that he is one Lord with the assuming Word—a point which, among you and among all, ought to stand firm, especially since the Apostle unequivocally asserts it, saying: “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we from him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Cor. VIII).

When he testifies that he came in the name of the Lord—as the children also cried, saying, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”—neither he nor the children adds a possessive pronoun, so that it might be said that he came in the name of his own Lord, but only “in the name of the Lord.” Elsewhere he says: “I came in the name of my Father” (II Thess. I). From this it may indeed be understood that the Father is signified by “the name of the Lord,” he who also said in the Law of Moses: “Behold, I send my angel, that he may go before you and always keep you” (Exod. XXXII), and so on down to: “And my name is in him.” Yet because he does not say, “I came in the name of my Lord,” as he says, “I came in the name [Col. 0544D] of my Father” (II Thess. I), those seem to me to have understood more correctly who took “the name of the Lord” to mean the whole Trinity rather than the person of the Father alone.

For that Blessed One came in the name of the Lord in such a way that the name Lord belongs to him equally with the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit. With those three, the assumed man—blessed in the Son—is one Lord, so that he is one of those three, because the assumed man did not increase the number of persons. Therefore he bears the name Lord, and the name Lord is in him—not so that he may be a lord or god among those who are called gods or many lords merely by title, but as Lord Almighty wholly above them, in the supreme dominion of the entire Trinity; because the assumed man and the Word which assumed him are not two lords but [Col. 0545A] one Lord.

Therefore, although he is a giant of twofold substance, it nevertheless seems necessary to beware lest the Word of God, who is God—whom, as you wisely observe, the council denies to be the Lord of Christ Jesus, the anointed man—should somehow be asserted to be the Lord of the assumed man. For the man assumed into God is nothing other than the man anointed into God; for to be assumed was for him to be anointed. He is not believed first to have been assumed and then anointed; rather, his very assumption was for him a royal anointing, by which he was advanced to be King of kings and Lord of lords, so that neither within himself nor above or outside himself does he have a lord higher than himself, who might regard that assumed man in glory as his servant, when he is worshipped by all angels and blessed human beings who serve God.

[Col. 0545B] Far be it from us to judge otherwise concerning your prudence than that you affirm the indivisible lordship of the one who assumes and of the one assumed, just as the lordship and kingdom of the Father and the Only-Begotten are indivisible. Far be it also from us to judge this of you: that, when Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one Lord and their lordship is one and singular, you place the man outside the fellowship of that singular lordship into which he was assumed. For these cannot stand together: that he was assumed into the fellowship of that singular lordship, and that in our faith he should be placed outside or below it.

There can be no doubt that this assumption into the fellowship of singular lordship belongs to the form or nature of our lowliness. For the Word never departed from that singular lordship. This assumption indeed took place by a more hidden mystery in the Nativity; but it was made and celebrated more manifestly in his own assumption into heaven, with ministering angels before the whole heavenly court, as the Evangelist Mark testifies, saying: “And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God” (Mark X). And Luke the Evangelist says: Jesus, he says, “began to do and to teach until the day when, having given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up” (Acts I). And the angels say: “Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will so come as you saw him going into heaven.”

Since, therefore, in your faith and ours alike, he was assumed—in the form of our race, which in him is certainly called the form of a servant—into that one and singular lordship, how can it be fitting that in that same form in which he was assumed into singular lordship he should be a servant eternally? We indeed say that the form of a servant remains in him eternally; but by “form of a servant” we express not the indignity of a servile condition, but the reality in him of our nature, we who are servants by condition. And if the servile condition were eternally in him, eternal servitude would necessarily follow. But far be it from us to disfigure by the abasement of servile condition that great mystery of godliness—“manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit”—so that [Col. 0546A] even when he ministered in the flesh, as he said, “The Son of Man came not to be ministered to, but to minister” (Matt. XX), he did this by servile condition rather than filial love. He himself also acknowledges this when he says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John IV). He does not say, “It is of my servile condition”; rather, “My food,” he says, “is”—as though he were saying: “It belongs to filial love in me to do my Father’s will.”

I consider that your prudence may easily and briefly be persuaded not to place Christ, although he is in the form of a servant—that is, in the nature of our race—under the servile condition by which every creature is bound to its Creator, even in so far as he is man; unless, which God forbid, and which I could not believe of your prudence, you should also wish to take away from him, in so far as he is man, the name and dignity of the only and natural Son. For these cannot coexist: that he is the natural and only Son of the Father in so far as he is man, and that in the same respect he is a servant by condition.

The teachings of the Fathers also instruct us that Christ, even in so far as he is man, is not to be classified under the common designation of “creature.” Chief among them is blessed Ambrose, whose words in the first book *On the Trinity* are these:

> “Let us prove,” he says, “that the Son of God is not a creature. For we have heard in the Gospel that the Lord commanded his disciples: ‘Preach the Gospel to every creature.’ He who says ‘every [Col. 0546C] creature’ excludes none. And where are those who call Christ a creature? For if he were a creature, he would command the Gospel to be preached to himself and would be subject to vanity; for, as the Apostle testifies, ‘Every creature is subject to vanity.’ Therefore Christ is not a creature but the Creator, who entrusts to his disciples the task of teaching the creature. This is recorded to have been Arius’s perfidy: that he confessed Christ to be a creature. Therefore Arius’s entrails were poured out, and, falling headlong, he burst asunder in the middle, his foul mouth polluted by those things through which he had denied Christ.”

Because the words of so great a Father rest alike on evangelical authority and reason, they may serve for us as two or three witnesses that Christ—the man, namely, anointed and assumed into God—although rightly called and indeed a new creature, as a man created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth, nevertheless ought not to be classified under the common designation of creature, lest the Gospel be preached to him and lest he be reckoned subject to vanity, even in so far as he is man.

This reasoning also supports the same conclusion: if Christ—whose name is certainly that of the man anointed into God—were to be classified under the common designation of creature, then the service called *latria*, which is owed to God alone, would not be owed to him. But the Council of Ephesus does not permit the man assumed by the Word to be separated from the one worship of the Word. Augustine likewise says concerning the worship of the footstool: “No one eats the flesh of Christ unless he has first worshipped.” Florus also says in the *Decads*, concerning the worship of the footstool: “That which is joined by unity is not divided from worship.” [Col. 0547A] Many more statements of this kind are found in the Fathers, which indicate the worship of the man and at the same time excuse such worshippers from idolatry, because what is worshipped is not a mere man but a man united to the Word.

There are certain men of our own time—among whom Folmar, that enemy of Christ and of us, is one—who have chosen for themselves the evil side, saying that *latria* is to be rendered to the Word, but *dulia*, albeit a certain greater kind of *dulia*, to the man. But this is to strip that man of his divinity and, with Pilate and the Jews, to say something of the sort: “Behold the man!”

For those Greek terms, namely *latria* and *dulia*, differ from one another, as we have learned from the Fathers skilled in the Greek language, in that *latria* is the service owed to God alone, whereas *dulia* is the service by which human beings serve one another—equals serving equals, inferiors their superiors, or even superiors their inferiors. That this is so is proved from Greek manuscripts. For where we read in Paul’s Epistles, “Fervent in spirit, serving the Lord” (Rom. XII), the Greeks read *latreuontes* (“rendering latria”). But where we read, “Through charity serve one another,” Greek manuscripts have *duleuite* (“render service to one another”). The meanings of these names are as distinct among them—and ought to be among us—as that *latria* should never be applied to signify any service other than that owed to God alone.

For we render *latria* to God by worshipping him not among all things but above all things, loving him above all things, sacrificing and offering incense to him, and believing in him. None of this ought to be rendered to any creature which is nothing but a creature; for no human being, however holy, nor any angel, is to be venerated with such worship that he is either adored as God, loved with all one’s heart and all one’s mind, sacrificed to, offered incense, or believed in—although a truth-teller ought to be believed. Hence the man who says, “You believe in God; believe also in me,” indicates that he is God to be worshipped above all creatures with *latria* rather than *dulia*. For *dulia* is not rightly applied to any service other than that which rational creatures render to one another.

Therefore among those learned in this distinction there is a proverb: “He is a *latreus*, not a *duleus*; he is a *duleus*, not a *latreus*.” In the service in which one is a *latreus*, one cannot be a *duleus*, and conversely, because *latria* is rendered to the Creator and *dulia* to the creature.

[Col. 0547D] I say this grieving for those who, I do not know on what inducement, teach that *dulia*, or a greater kind of *dulia* hitherto unheard of, and not *latria*, should be rendered to the man assumed into God. These men are great and highly trained in scholastic disciplines, yet have less faith than they ought in the divinity of Christ the man. For this is found both in the glosses of Peter Lombard on the Psalter concerning the worship of the footstool and in his *Sentences*; it is appended in the glosses to Augustine’s sayings and continued as though it were Augustine’s own. Yet those who consult Augustine’s treatise on the worship of the footstool readily find that it is otherwise treated there.

We do not say this because we fear that your prudence could be led into such an opinion, but because there is a certain ambiguity in your statements from which some might conceive this view. You say—commendably—that you do not place Christ under the Word as under his Lord, lest God be under God or under a Lord; yet you place the man under God as under his Lord. You also describe a service eternal, to be rendered by him to that same Lord and God of his, as sufficiently divine. But because among us Latins, sometimes poor in words, *servitude* is equivocal and is applied both to the service that is *latria*, owed to God alone, and to the service that is *dulia*, through which we are servants of one another either by condition or by the debt of charity—since we do not possess distinct names for distinct services—this, my lord, is the ambiguity which can leave us and others who read your writings uncertain as to what service you assign to the man assumed into God: namely, whether it is that by which the angels, cherubim, and seraphim serve. For you yourselves introduce them as examples of that service.

Their service indeed is wholly divine: eternally to praise God, their maker and illuminator, who makes and preserves them blessed. Yet since that service is *latria*, it does not seem sufficiently fitting for that man, who is God blessed above all things for ever and to whom [Col. 0548C] *latria* ought rather to be rendered by all of us alike and by the angels, than that he himself should render it to his God or Lord as a mere creature to its Creator.

But if anyone should say—which I judge far from your mind—that he himself, in so far as he is man, owes to his God the *latria* which is rightly rendered to him by us as our God, this too is utterly incongruous. For it would introduce a diversity of gods: one to whom *latria* alone would be owed, and another who would both owe *latria* to a God superior to himself and receive *latria* from every other creature. For it was long ago defined in the aforementioned council that we owe *latria* indivisibly not only to the Word but also to the man. Therefore I judge this meaning very far from your prudence, since that the man-God should owe *latria* to his Father is unheard of until now.

But if you ascribe to the man assumed into God another service, called *dulia*, which equals sometimes render to equals—for one who confesses conditional servitude does not at the same time admit the prerogative of the Father’s and the Son’s throne—then the novelty of the expression is displeasing: that any one of the three persons, whose lordship is one and indivisible, should be the servant of another and serve him, especially since Christ’s economic service was completed when he said, “It is finished” (John XIX). Yet the sense could stand if it were expressed in words consonant with the Gospel. For example, the Son himself says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John IV); he does not say, “To serve my Father.” Likewise: “I always do the things pleasing to him” [Col. 0549A] (John VIII); he does not say, “I will always serve him.” For since the Son is what he is from the Father, it is right that in all things he should do the Father’s will and defer to the Father as his principle. But because the Son is consubstantial, he is not bound by an obligation of servitude—especially now that the sackcloth of his servitude has been torn apart and he has been clothed by the Father with the joy of gladness, so that his glory may sing to that Father eternally. What is it for his glory to sing to the Father except that the Father has so glorious and renowned a Son, who is the Father’s eternal glory? For if, as Solomon says, “a wise son is the glory of his father” (Prov. XV), how much more excellent a glory of God the Father is it to have a Son who is the very wisdom and power of God?

But if you say that, even after he had risen from the dead, he still called the Father his God—concerning which Augustine says, “Under whom I too am man”—let your prudence consider when he said this: namely, while he was still about to ascend to the Father, when he outwardly presented himself to the disciples as he was inwardly among them. For, having completed the Passover by which he had passed from this world to the Father, he was already with the Father in himself; but he had to draw the disciples gradually to the same place, not by some sudden leap, just as an eagle stirs her young to fly and hovers over them. Therefore he did not suddenly break away from them by saying, “I ascend to my Father, your God” (John XX). Rather: “I ascend,” he says, “to my Father and your Father, my God and your God,” presenting himself as mediator and, by making a small distinction between himself and us, eager to draw us with him—just as his resurrection itself was disclosed to the disciples not suddenly but gradually and by stages.

But we ought not to regard one part of the heavenly sayings in such a manner that we neglect those other statements found elsewhere, equally clear, concerning his seat in equality, the glory which he requested as that which he had before the world was, and all power given to him. Let us read them together and hold them together. For the man is still under God by the kind of his nature, not by the servile condition of his kind; but he himself is the Son with the Father by the nature of his birth and by the privilege of singular exaltation granted to our nature. Nor do I think that Augustine divides the man from God when, in the first book *On the Trinity*, he says that that man cannot be understood without God, because the man who is God is one and the same; rather, he intended to express the meaning we have just stated.

Thus, while that living creature of four faces is man and calf under God, it is lion and eagle with God; and so the unshaken article of faith will even now stand among us, in either form of expression: “Equal to the Father according to divinity; less than the Father according to humanity,” with the one lordship of both natures preserved, in which, we believe, there is no division.

We certainly venerate the assertions of the Fathers who say: “But neither do we assert that the Word of God the Father is God or Lord of Christ, lest once again we divide the one Christ, Son and Lord, more manifestly into two.” And [Col. 0550A] shortly afterwards: “By no means, they say, are we unaware that, remaining God, he also became man, who existed under God according to the due law of the nature of humanity. But how could he himself be God or Lord to himself? Therefore, as man, in so far as it fittingly accords with the measure of his emptying, he declared that he was with us under God, just as he was made under the law, although he himself promulgated the law and existed as God its lawgiver.”

You, most reverend lord, cautiously inserted these sayings of the Fathers in your writing, and in them you strongly observed that, remaining God, he also became man, who existed under God and declared himself to be with us under God, where he called his Father his God. Yet we should have wished—and still wish—you to consider more attentively this point also: that he is asserted to have existed under God according to the due law of the nature of humanity in no other way than in the way in which he was also made under the law, though he himself promulgated the law and existed as God its lawgiver; under which law, surely, he was as man not without qualification, but only in so far as was fitting for the measure of his emptying. But the measure of that emptying reached its end when the assumed man entered into his divine glory; in that glory, although he is under God by the kind of human nature, which acknowledges the Creator of its humanity, he is nevertheless not subject to him by a servile condition as angels and blessed human beings are, but reigns with him and shares lordship with him, all power in heaven and on earth having been given to him. Given to him, I say, not in his divinity, in which he always possessed this power, being Almighty with the Father, but in the nature of humanity, in which, having become man, he received the glory which he had with God the Father before the world was.

Let your prudence consider also, if you please, more attentively that for Nestorius “Christ” was not the name of the God-man but the name of a mere man, in whom God dwelt as in his temple and whom the indwelling Word called Lord. Hence he wished blessed Mary to be called not *Theotokos* (“God-bearer”) but *Christotokos* (“Christ-bearer”), lest Nestorius—as it seemed to you—make the Word the Lord of Christ, that is, of God and man. But to the Fathers of the council, for whom it was established that the Word is Christ and Christ is the Word, it seemed foolish and impious to call the same one both servant and lord to himself. Thus, for example, it would be foolish to say of myself: “I am the rational element, which I am; I am the sentient element, which is in me and which [the manuscript reads corruptly: *quodque*]; likewise I am Lord.” For this would be to divide me into two, just as he too divided Christ into two.

Yet those same Fathers knew that Christ called his Father also his God, while the Word, God united to flesh, is God of all and Lord of the universe. This too they say in this way: “Although he called his Father his God, while he himself is God by nature and from that Father’s essence, yet by no means are we unaware that, remaining God, he also became man, who existed under God according to the due law of the nature of humanity.” In these words it appears that they acknowledge God under God—that is, the Son, in so far as he is man, under God the Father by the law due to human nature—but do not think or say that the Word, God, is God to the man-God, since he is rather himself the man than God to the man. Indeed, they rather condemn this meaning when they say: “But how can he himself be either God or Lord to himself?”

But you, my lord, say later in your letter: “That giant of twofold substance exceeds the assumed man by the height of divinity so greatly that he is his God and Lord.” These words, as far as their surface meaning or the sense first conceived from them is concerned, seem to differ little or not at all from the statements or meaning condemned by the Fathers. For what else is the height of divinity in that giant of twofold substance than the Word of God, God and man, and the Word himself in the man? Let your prudence consider whether it has not been forbidden by the Fathers to say that Christ, in so far as he is the Word who is God, is Lord to himself as man.

Indeed, reason does not permit even the whole Trinity to be called the God or Lord of the assumed man. For then he himself would be God and Lord to himself, since the man-Word is one of the three. Yet we believe this meaning to be far from your heart; therefore, if it please your discernment, caution ought to be exercised lest your statements be understood to mean what, we believe, you do not think.

[Col. 0551C] I have written this more confidently to your eminence, my lord, disclosing to you the simplicity of my belief, hoping that in these matters I may agree with you and with the whole Church and think the same as you—except that I do not willingly admit now the bond or name of servitude in my Lord Jesus Christ. For I trust that the thought that he, even in so far as he is man, renders *latria* to the Father is as far from your mind as from mine, because it ought to be far from the mind of all believers.

But if these our views please your holiness, give us some signs of peace and clemency. At the same time, let your prudence consider that, in order to crush the head of the calf of Nestorian heresy, it is not enough to deny two persons in Christ; for many others before and after him did not say this either, yet were his companions in that littleness, because they said that that man was God not substantially but only by God’s indwelling. Therefore let your magnificence turn your sword back to its place; turn it against those who say that that man is God not by nature but by disposition (*habitus*), and likewise that God is called and is man not by nature but by disposition; who do not hesitate to say that nothing assumed is God; who say that that man is to be venerated with *dulia*, not *latria*; and that the love due to him is not included in the command by which we are ordered to love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind, but rather in that by which we are ordered to love our neighbor as ourselves. Let your sword spare citizens and fellow-countrymen, and be turned against adversaries.

[Col. 0552A] For we are, and always desire to be, citizens and members of the household both of God and of yourselves, having together with you great confidence in that intercession of Christ. Although you interpret it as a certain service on his part, it pleases us more to approve and hold the understanding of blessed Gregory, who, in Book XXII of the *Morals*, expounding the Apostle’s words, “Christ Jesus, who died—indeed who also rose again—who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Rom. VIII), says:

> “For the Only-Begotten Son to intercede for man before the coeternal Father is to show himself as man; and to have pleaded for human nature is to have taken that same nature up into the exaltation of his divinity. Therefore the Lord intercedes for us not by voice but by compassion, because what he did not will to be condemned in the elect, he set free by assuming it.”

## LETTER XVI

Response of Eberhard to the preceding letter.—He proves that Christ, as man, is a creature and servant even after his ascension into heaven.—What the measure of Christ’s emptying is, etc.

E., by God’s grace called bishop of the Church of Bamberg, to Lord G., provost of Richersberg: to offer rightly and to divide rightly.

When we received the letter sent to us by you, we were at once unable either to examine or consider it, being troubled and disturbed by many concerns. Afterwards, having considered it, we found in it more quibbling than reason. And although the assertion of truth between us and you has been sufficiently made clear in earlier letters, we have nevertheless taken care to add a few things, because of your obstinacy, in order wholly to dispel, by the aid of him who commanded light to shine out of darkness, whatever mist may still remain. We judged it unsuitable to answer word for word because of the length and superfluity; rather, we address only those points which seem more likely to trouble the mind, so that from certain statements the others which have not been stated may be understood.

We are astonished—and cannot sufficiently wonder—at your teaching and answers, because you alter your statements so often and, as if wavering, now deny and now concede the same things. Moreover, as if you had not read or had not understood our letter, you do not answer the objections put to you, but propose matters quite remote from our words and meaning, and fight the air as though beating it. For now you say that the servile form, now that the essence of the servile form, remained in Christ after the Resurrection and Ascension; now you say of Christ that eternally he will acknowledge the Father as his God; now you appear to deny the same thing when you say: “Let your prudence consider when he said this: ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God’: namely, while he was still about to ascend to the Father, when outwardly he showed himself to his disciples as he was inwardly among them.” Elsewhere likewise you say: “Indeed, reason does not permit even the whole Trinity to be called the God or Lord of the assumed man.” How these writings of yours agree with one another, you must see. It seems to us that “is” and “is not” are both in your discourse—not only in these matters but in very many others.

You apply the prophetic Scriptures and other passages concerning Christ’s humanity and humility only to the time before Christ’s Resurrection. Yet Ambrose testifies in *On the Trinity* that what follows belongs to Christ not merely before the Resurrection but after it; and he whom you think supports you is against you when he expounds thus: “‘You are my God from my mother’s womb’ (Ps. XXI). When he says, ‘You are my God from my mother’s womb,’ he indicates that God is his from the time when he was cast forth from his mother’s womb.” If, therefore, God has been his ever since that time, without limitation of time, he must always render to him what is due to his God and what a creature owes to its Creator.

[Col. 0553B] And lest this name “creature,” as applied to Christ in so far as he is man, offend you, observe, after the passage from Ambrose which you introduce to prove that Christ ought not to be called a creature—observe, I say—what Ambrose says subsequently: “Let the unlearned read the whole and understand.” And he adds: “Let them learn how it was said: ‘The Lord created me.’ He did not say, ‘The Father created me,’ but ‘The Lord created me.’ The flesh acknowledges the Lord; glory signifies the Father; our created nature confesses the Lord; love knows the Father.”

The earlier parts of the same chapter, in which Ambrose proves that the Son of God is not a creature and that Christ is not to be called a creature, do not conflict with this passage. There he deals only with the divine nature against the Arians, who asserted that the Son of God, according to divinity, was a creature; here he deals with the human nature. For “From the womb before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. CXIX) is very different from “The Lord created me” or “possessed me as the beginning of his ways”; likewise, “You are my God from my mother’s womb.” Ambrose himself thus expresses the difference between the two natures in the same context: “We see that there is a great distance between creature and Lord: because servitude is creature, whereas the Lord is Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.”

Augustine also agrees, commenting on “Let not your heart be troubled” (I John XIV), arguing against the Arians in this manner: “If he was created, then he is also a servant, because everything created must necessarily serve its Creator.” He indeed used an indirect line of reasoning to prove that the Son of God, in so far as he is God, is not a creature. Using the same reasoning directly for our purpose, we likewise say: If the Son of Man was created, then he is also a servant; but he was created, as is read in Isaiah: “Drop down, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One,” etc. (Isa. XLV), and shortly afterward: “I, the Lord, created him” (ibid.). Consequently, therefore, he is also a servant and must serve in his own manner, as a creature serves its Creator.

[Col. 0554A] If you please, receive these words of authority and these arguments patiently, and do not recoil at least from them, even if you despise us and what belongs to us. For, humbly following these footsteps, we say of Christ what you disapprove: namely, that Christ, according to what he is as God, is Creator; and according to what he is as made of a woman, is creature; and the remaining conclusions necessarily connected with these by evident reason.

But lest perhaps the saying trouble you: “Preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI), and “The creature was subjected to vanity unwillingly,” as though the Gospel had also to be preached to Christ and Christ were subjected to vanity: concerning the former, we unashamedly have recourse to Gregory, who says, among other things: “The Gospel is preached to every creature when it is preached to man alone.” But if someone pressing the point more sharply should say that, because Christ is man, he commanded the Gospel to be preached to himself as well, let him see that this is a manner of speaking like this: “Christ tasted death for all” (Heb. II). Did he therefore taste it for himself as well? Far be it. For this high priest did not need first to offer for his own ignorance and then for that of the people. A similar manner of expression is: “God created all things” (Eph. III), and “Heaven covers all things”; yet neither did God create himself nor does heaven cover itself.

As for the remaining statement set forth above—“The creature was subjected to vanity unwillingly”—lest one should perhaps have to concede that Christ, in so far as he is creature, is subject to vanity, we answer thus: To be subject to vanity properly belongs to that creature which groans and labors in childbirth until now, and universally to everything under the sun. But Christ, even in so far as he is man, is not under the sun but above the sun and above every creature, although he too “set his tabernacle in the sun” and bore with us the burden of the day and heat, himself remaining the Sun of righteousness, with the sun and before the moon throughout generations of generations, in the glory of the Father, with whom there is no change nor shadow of turning. But angelic spirits and the souls of the righteous also, through God’s grace, are no longer under this vanity.

Accordingly, when you say, “Christ, in so far as he is man, is not reckoned under the common term ‘creature,’” [Col. 0554D] we wish you to understand this rightly of Christ, lest perhaps you hold, as certain heretics do, that Christ’s body was not made from our common material—far be it from us to believe that of you. For this is contrary not only to Ambrose, who says in the passages cited above that it is our creature, but also to Augustine, who says that “our dust, now made incorruptible, sits at the right hand of the Father.” Likewise Bede: “That body which, in being born, he had taken from the earth common to the human race, he might, in rising again, clothe with heavenly power, now exalted above all earthly things.” Boethius also, in *On Nature and Person against Nestorius and Eutyches*, argues this point most forcefully, proving that, on the aforementioned error of the heretics, all prophecies would be false and all promises made to the Fathers [Col. 0555A]—especially to Abraham and his seed—would be void. But if you mean what Gregory says, namely, that after his resurrection Christ’s body was indeed of the same nature, but of a different glory, the meaning is sound; but it ought to have been explained in words other than those you used.

But in that authority of Ambrose which you introduced in these words, “Let us prove that Christ is not a creature,” the matter is not human nature, but the divine nature against the unbelief of the Arians, who asserted that the Son of God was a creature according to his divinity.

You have enlarged your phylacteries concerning *dulia* and *latria*, and magnified your fringes, saying, “He is *duleus* (rendering *dulia*), and not *latreus* (rendering *latria*),” and the like. But because what you say you have received from the Greeks is less authoritative, [Col. 0555B] although the authority of your religious order is great, it is as easily despised as it is approved. We therefore pass it over in silence for the present, as though it deserved an obelus, wishing to be content with what has been handed down to us by the holy Fathers.

Yet we cannot be silent about this: you disparage and mock the scholastic men who have occupied themselves with this question, in a manner unworthy of your religious profession and prudence. For it is the habit of the unlearned either to parade their scanty learning by disparaging others, or to conceal—or rather reveal—their ignorance. Some of those whom you sprinkle with such salt are still alive in the flesh; since they are of age, let them speak for themselves, and, unless we are mistaken, they will speak. Their ignorance is the more easily forgiven [Col. 0555C] because they have shown themselves readier to accept correction. For the cause of error is made worse when it is concealed.

But if Greece is your second home, this is scarcely apparent—unless perhaps you left the Greek school too soon, or entered it much too late. Or how did it happen that that good wine was kept until now and was not also brought to you first, as to the steward of the feast, so that you might know the distinction between nature and person—that is, *ousia* [οὐσία, essence or substance] and *hypostasis* [ὑπόστασις, concrete subsistence or person]? This knowledge is surely most necessary. Yet one arrives at it through proper definitions and subdivisions of terms, in which the Greeks abound more than the Latins.

[Col. 0555D] Nevertheless, let no one here walk in darkness so as to suppose that, in the simple essence of divinity, there is any diversity on this account: for God and Godhead are the same; wise and wisdom, omnipotent and omnipotence are the same. For predicates applied to things are such as their subjects allow them to be. And in every respect, for God to be is the same as for him to be this or that—matters belonging to a higher inquiry.

But if you wished to consider more carefully the matters at issue here—the distinction between nature and person—then surely no cloud of error would entangle anyone in your writings where you treat of Christ’s person as subsisting in two natures and from two natures. Yet this is an obstacle both in your statements and for yourselves and others: you do not distinguish what ought to be followed, said, or understood. For sometimes, when matters belonging to the unity of [Col. 0556A] person are under discussion, you thrust forward nature; and conversely, when diversity of nature is being discussed, you leap to person. Accordingly you wrong us also, attributing to us things which we neither say nor think—as in what we said about the giant of twofold substance and about the Council of Ephesus.

For when it was said that the assumed man is so far surpassed by the height of divinity that God is his God and Lord, the reference in “his” is made not to the person but to the nature. This does not mean that God is outside him. But how could he himself be his own God or Lord? That would be said with respect to unity of person, not diversity of nature. This is plainly shown where it says, “He existed under God according to the due law of human nature.” So too it was previously said: [Col. 0556B] “Remaining God, he was also made man.” Thus he is under God together with us, in so far as he shares our nature.

Likewise, concerning the statement “How was he made under the law?” we prefer to appeal here to the Apostle rather than to your teaching. For he says: “Made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4). Here indeed the measure of his self-emptying is expressed: he took both our nature and the misery of nature in respect of punishment, though not in respect of guilt. And in accordance with this assumption of our misery, the Lawgiver himself was made under the law when he fulfilled the law, leaving nothing undone that the law required—yet voluntarily, not from necessity. This is that measure of self-emptying and that manner of legal subjection which befitted the Son of God, as he himself said to John: “Thus it is fitting for us to fulfil [Col. 0556C] all righteousness” (Matt. 3). Accordingly the Fathers of the council aptly added, on the basis of the Lord’s words, “It is fitting”: “In so far as it fittingly accords with the measure of self-emptying.”

With this diversity of natures preserved in unity of person, according to the authority of the council, the man is even now under God. Yet he is not thereby his own God or Lord, as Nestorius thinks, erring both in substance and in terminology. Nestorius called Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, a mere man in himself; and he divided into two the one Son and Lord, Jesus Christ our Lord, who according to the truth of faith is personally one—namely, into Lord and servant, as though the one were two, one God and [Col. 0556D] the other man. To follow him would be to incur the crime of sacrilege, because in the person of Christ neither God without man nor man without God can or ought to be understood.

Something very similar may be seen in every human being. No human being can be divided into two; rather, the things in a human being from which the human being consists are divided by thought rather than in actuality. Thus, while the soul is in the body, it rules the body. Surely the rational element—which you are, as your writings say—is master; the sensitive element, which is in you and which you are, is not. Yet if reason does not rule sensuality in you, see to it that you have the master of the household in your own house. But although reason is one thing and sensuality another, there is nevertheless one human being, or one soul: rational in one respect and sensitive or sensual in another. [Col. 0557A] Hence someone said: “Rule the mind, which, unless it obeys, commands; restrain it with bridles, restrain it with chains.” Let it be permitted here also to draw gold from the mud.

Concerning the words of the council, we think as we said before, without prejudging the doctors; nevertheless, we do not accept in every respect what you say concerning the measure of self-emptying. For in certain statements there you exceed the measure, mode, and limit prescribed by the holy Fathers, as is clear in these words of yours: “The measure of self-emptying then reached its limit when the assumed man entered into his divine glory.” This is as though the whole measure of self-emptying then came to an end. If that were so, God would no longer be man. May Wisdom, the teacher of all things, teach you what is right.

Now Christ is one perfect [Col. 0557B] God and perfect man, with the property of each nature preserved in every respect, so that we may avoid the error of Eutyches no less than that of Nestorius. The one, Nestorius—as has often already been said—impiously believed that, just as there are two natures in Christ, so there are two persons, God and man. The other, Eutyches, falsely thought that, just as there is one person, so there is one nature confused from two; he said that Christ’s person subsists from two natures, not in two natures. But amid these byways there is a middle road: Christ, simply, uncompoundedly, and ineffably subsisting in unity of person from two natures and in two natures.

Once this distinction between nature and person has been made, we shall, with God’s help, incur no danger concerning him who is the stone of stumbling and rock of offence, according to the teaching of blessed Augustine, who says in the sermon mentioned above: “Let not your heart be troubled. This is the form of a servant, in which the Son of God is less not only than the Father, but also than the Holy Spirit; and not only this, but even than himself.” [Col. 0557C] By this same distinction of the two natures in Christ, we do not introduce a plurality of gods, as you, under the pretext of an objection—which you use excessively—rather uncivilly, not to say hostilely, charge us with doing. Nor do we divide God and man from one another separately in respect of person. Nor do we say that the man is to be co-adored with God as though distinct in person, as we know is forbidden by the Council of Ephesus; [Col. 0557D] for the prefix *co-* suggests distinction. Rather, he is co-adored and co-glorified, just as he co-reigns with God the Father in the unity of person which is the Son—our one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, possessing an undivided and perpetual lordship.

Nor may it be admitted that, because humanity was assumed, the Trinity was enlarged so as to become a quaternity, since, as Boethius says, man is added to perfect God. Rather, it must be devoutly believed that one and the same person completes the number of the Trinity. For when God ineffably clothed the man by assuming human nature, he neither changed his person nor increased the Trinity.

Nor have we ever said that one person in the Trinity serves two; rather, all three persons are coeternal and coequal with one another, [Col. 0558A] while human nature has not been abolished or perished, but remains in the order of its subjection according to the due law of human nature. And in this way, as the Son is equal to the Father according to divinity, so he not only was but also always will be, from the Incarnation onward, less than the Father according to humanity. Whoever believes or teaches otherwise will not have the article of the catholic faith standing unshaken within him.

Therefore, most reverend brother, do not henceforth say this ambiguously, in this or that fashion, but simply in the manner in which the catholic Church holds it: “Equal to the Father according to divinity; less than the Father according to humanity.” Thus Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, book I, chapter 11:

> “Once the rule for understanding the Scriptures concerning the Son of God is known—so that we distinguish [Col. 0558B] what in them sounds according to the form of God, in which he is and is equal to the Father, from what sounds according to the form of a servant, which he received and in which he is less than the Father—we shall not be disturbed as though by contrary and conflicting statements of the holy books. For according to the form of God, the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal to the Father, because neither of them is a creature, as we have already shown. But according to the form of a servant, he is less than the Father, because he himself said: ‘The Father is greater than I.’ He is less than himself, because he emptied himself.”

What more is needed for us and for you? Keep this rule, and all will be safe.

But what you add, “with the undivided dominion of each nature preserved,” is ambiguous and makes the minds of hearers [Col. 0558C] or readers more doubtful. For it may seem to mean either that each nature, divine and human, is equally worthy—which is unbelief—or that the person of Christ, indivisibly subsisting from two and in two natures, is one God and one Lord—which is the mystery of piety and catholic faith. Therefore we venerate and embrace with all devotion the character of catholic faith, but detest the meaning contrary to it.

Moreover, we admonish your charity that, if you do not wish to spare us or others, you should at least spare blessed Augustine, upon whose *Retractations* you impose another retraction concerning what he said of Christ’s person: “Under whom I too am a man,” as though he ought to have said, “Under whom I too was a man.” And when he said, “To whom the Father is Lord even in the form of a servant,” you treat the present as though it had been put for the past. [Col. 0558D] Claim for yourselves only this much: that you ought in the same way to correct Hilary, Ambrose, Gregory, Jerome, Bede, and the other holy Fathers in things similarly said by them—as though more had been revealed to you than to all of them.

Finally, do not prejudge the venerable Fathers of the Council of Ephesus, as though they did not wish, or did not know, to say “so long as” instead of “in what manner,” where they said, “How was he made under the law.” That would be either envy or gross ignorance. Granted, if you please, that you may correct the writings of the holy Fathers and accommodate ambiguous statements to your own meaning: what will you say to the following, which Augustine writes plainly in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*? [Col. 0559A]

> “It is no wonder if the Apostle says that even in the world to come the Son will be subject to the Father, when he says: ‘Then the Son himself also will be subject to him who subjected all things to him,’ since the human form will remain to the Son, in which the Father is always greater.”

Let us therefore be permitted with Augustine to believe and confess what Truth itself said: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14).

What moves us even more is that you invert the words of the Gospel and of the Lord himself, as though Truth had spoken with a double heart when he called the Father his God; according to you, after the resurrection he was not his God, as though either Christ’s humanity had been abolished or the power of divinity in the Father had been weakened. How then would Truth say: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God”? [Col. 0559B] (John 20). In answering our objection to you on this point, you introduced these words:

> “Let your prudence consider when he said this: namely, while he was still about to ascend to the Father, when he showed himself outwardly to the disciples such as he was inwardly among them.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore he did not suddenly sever himself from them so as to say, ‘I ascend to my Father, your God’; rather, he says, ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God.’”

By attaching to these statements talk of the session of equality, the glory requested from the Father, and the bestowal of all power, you strive, it appears, to prove that after the resurrection and ascension the Father was not [Col. 0559C] the God of the assumed man, but was so before, when Christ himself pleaded the cause of the assumed man, saying, “Eloi, Eloi,” and so forth.

To this we first say that our Lord Jesus Christ after the resurrection indeed pretended to be going farther—taking “pretended” in the sense of arranging—and appeared to the disciples on the road, outwardly presenting himself as he was inwardly among them. But let Apella the Jew believe that the fact was otherwise than he said when he said, “My God and your God.” For enough has already been said above against this. Indeed, you heard and could sufficiently understand, when Isaiah was read—“I, the Lord, created him,” and “From my mother’s womb you are my God” (Isa. 49)—how Ambrose pursued the matter.

[Col. 0559D] Hear this too: “Wisdom has built herself a house,” and so forth. Unless the child who was born to us had been created by God, we would not have been re-created; nor would we have been reborn unless he himself had been born of a mother. Yet “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1), because this is the Word made flesh.

Accordingly, in what you add at the final or almost final place in your letter, there is a great chaos fixed between us and you. The sequence of your words is indeed this: “But reason does not allow that the whole Trinity should be called God or Lord of the assumed man,” followed by what you consider a reason, though it is no reason: “For thus he himself would also be his own God and Lord.” Yet since the whole Trinity worked Christ’s incarnation, whose operations are inseparable, it is plain that the whole Trinity is God and Lord of that which it created, though in that creation it was assumed by the Word alone. [Col. 0560A] Yet he does not thereby become his own God or Lord, because above the discussion concerns the assumed nature, whereas here it concerns the person, which cannot be divided into two, as we believe has been sufficiently explained above.

To debate these matters further is to grope at noon in darkness and, as the common saying goes, to seek a knot in a reed. But this final statement of your letter, opposed by the authority of both Old and New Testaments, greatly conflicts with its own beginning, where you say: “He will acknowledge him as his God for ever.”

Therefore, that we may hear the end of the whole discourse, Christ says in the Prophet: “O Lord my God, I shall confess you for ever” (Isa. 12). [Col. 0560B] We recall this to mind because you passed it over—though with what intention we do not know—when you expounded the preceding words thus: “That my glory may sing praise to you” (Ps. 29). You said this not as though the assumed man sang that song to God, but as though the glory of the assumed man sang it—that is, as though it were a song to God, now that the sackcloth of mortality had been torn apart, according to the saying: “The glory of the Father is a wise Son.”

But what follows? “O Lord my God, I shall confess you for ever” (Isa. 12). Augustine expounds this: “I shall praise you for ever.” To destroy the ineffable melody of this praise, this super-celestial harmony surpassing every understanding of angels and human beings, is nothing other than to deny God himself; it is to make earth equal to heaven and to destroy the whole framework of Christ’s body.

[Col. 0560C] We attribute to Christ this most blessed servitude of human nature—which is truly freedom, for “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom”—and no other. Indeed, it is not we, but Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, the other holy Fathers, and the entire authority of both New and Old Testaments who attribute it. As blessed Ambrose briefly explains, introducing and expounding the Prophet’s authority: “You have overthrown the covenant of your servant,” and so forth. “In what sense, indeed, did he call him servant, except in the flesh?” And shortly afterward: “By my assumption he is servant; by his own power he is Lord.” If, then, the flesh remains, the rights of flesh due to the divine majesty remain also.

But lest you seek pretexts for slander in the word “servitude,” this is not that servitude in which, according to the first derivation of the word, those captured by enemies were called servants from being preserved; such persons serve either from fear of punishment or merely for appearance’s sake, and from this arose the manifold servitudes of persons and things. [Col. 0560D] Nor is it that servitude which was completed in the suffering of the cross and death, when, passing through, he ministered even to us.
