Rather, it is that splendid, glorious, and never-ending subjection which the Apostle expressly states and Augustine elegantly explains in his book *Against Maximus*, where it is said: “Then the Son himself also will be subject to him who subjected all things to him.”

For the Holy Spirit, who did not assume any creature into unity with his person, although he deigned visibly to manifest himself through a subjected creature, whether in the appearance of a dove or through tongues of fire, [Col. 0561A] was never said to have adored the Father and was never said to be less than the Father. Those manifestations appeared only for a time. But Christ did not assume a human appearance merely for a time, in which he might appear to people and then that form pass away. Rather, while remaining in the invisible form of God, he took the visible form of man into the enduring unity of his person. And in it he was not only born of a human mother, but also grew in it, ate and drank in it, slept in it, was killed in it, rose again in it, ascended to heaven in it, sits at the right hand of the Father in it, will come in it to judge the living and the dead, and in his kingdom will be subject in it to him who subjected all things to him.

[Col. 0561B] The glorification of that same nature does not prejudice this subjection, though the glorification was completed in act in its own time, just as it was from eternity in predestination. Thus, among his many other statements concerning glorification, blessed Augustine says on John:

> “Some have thought that this should be understood as though the human nature assumed by the Word were changed into the Word and the man were changed into God. Indeed, if we examine more carefully what they thought, the man would perish in God. For no one says that the Word of God is, in the estimation of human beings, either doubled or increased, so that either two should be what was one, or that more should be what was less.”

Where the evidence of authority is so great, why do you spend your money not for bread, and your labour not for satisfaction? [Col. 0561C]

At the end of your letter you return to the beginning of the question, saying something alien both from our meaning, yours, and that of all the faithful: that the assumed man renders *latria* to God. By the startling use of this name in a place where it is unfamiliar, you frighten the feeble-minded with a kind of mask of horror, lead them astray in a pathless place rather than on the way, and cause them not to follow the authorities already cited, which are so certain and so evident.

We know that Christ does not adore God on bended knee, nor is he told, “Come,” and he comes; nor, “Do this,” and he does it, as a servant (Matt. 8). Nevertheless, in a certain respect, that is, “Render to God the things that are God’s.” For, as blessed Augustine says in *On the Trinity* [Col. 0561D]: “As Father is said relatively to Son, so Lord is said relatively to a serving creature.” That secret of the divine mystery exceeds the capacity of human speech. For it is more truly thought than spoken, and is more truly real than thought.

Now we cry to the Lord, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8). There tongues will cease, and yet every tongue will confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. In the present time, in order to distinguish the worship of God from reverence shown by human beings, it is proper to employ this distinction of terms, *dulia* and *latria*. But there, not only in our head, who is Christ, but also in his members, the matter is and will be far otherwise.

The most learned and excellent men, teachers of others, devoutly considering these matters and desiring, so far as permitted, to attain an investigation of truth, have sometimes spoken according to differing opinions and sometimes according to the assertion of truth and authority; they have committed these things to writing for the instruction of others. [Col. 0562A] Indeed Master Peter, whom you judge to hold your view—though he touches briefly in the Psalms upon the adoration of the footstool, where he mentions *dulia* and *latria*—sets the matter out more fully in his *Sentences*. There, first proposing the question and disputing it, whether the same adoration should be offered to humanity as to divinity, he first reports the opinion of some that Christ’s flesh and soul ought to be venerated not with *latria* but with a higher kind of *dulia*. Not approving that view, he then supplies the opinion of others concerning a single adoration of man and God, and confirms it by the authorities of John Damascene and blessed Augustine. [Col. 0562B] We have also taken care to set these down.

Nor should it seem overlong, because it is so necessary, lest anyone derive scandal concerning the writings of so great a teacher from your words rather than his own. You either do not understand his words and those of others, or corrupt them by a troublesome interpretation, preserving no distinction between person and nature.

John Damascene:

> “There are two natures of Christ, differing in account and mode, but united according to hypostasis. Therefore Christ is one, perfect God and perfect man, whom we adore with the Father and the Spirit in one adoration together with his undefiled flesh. We do not call the flesh unadorable; for it is adored in the one hypostasis of the Word, which hypostasis is begotten; [Col. 0562C] we do not offer worship to a creature. For we do not adore it as bare flesh, but as united to divinity in one hypostasis of God the Word, the two natures being brought together into one. I fear to touch the coal because of the fire joined to the wood. I adore both together in Christ my God because of the divinity united to the flesh. For I do not add a fourth person to the Trinity, but confess one person of the Word and his flesh.”

Likewise Augustine:

> “Heretics say that the Son is not God by nature but created. They must be answered thus: if the Son is not God by nature but a creature, then he ought not to be worshipped at all or adored as God, since the Apostle says: ‘They worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator.’ But they will reply and say: [Col. 0562D] ‘Why then do you adore his flesh, which you do not deny is a creature, together with his divinity, and serve it no less than divinity?’ I adore the Lord’s flesh—indeed, the complete humanity in Christ—because it was assumed by divinity and united to divinity, in order that I may confess not another, but one and the same Son of God, God and man. Finally, if you separate the man from God, I never believe in or serve him. It is as if someone found a royal purple garment or diadem lying discarded: would he try to adore them? But when the king has put them on, anyone who scorns to adore them together with the king incurs danger of death. So also in Christ the Lord: whoever scorns to adore humanity, not alone or bare, but united to divinity—namely, the one Son, true God and true man—[Col. 0563A] shall die eternally.”

The same author, on Psalm 98, where it says, “Adore his footstool, for it is holy”:

> “It should be known that in Christ there is earth, that is, flesh, which is adored without impiety. For he took earth from earth, because flesh is from earth, and he took flesh from the flesh of Mary. This flesh, assumed by the Word of God, is adored by us without impiety, because no one eats his flesh unless he first adores. But whoever adores does not look at the earth, but rather at him whose footstool it is, on whose account he adores.”

Therefore, since it is clearer than light from the foregoing both what Christ, in so far as he is man, owes to God and what we ourselves owe to God and man, it is pointless, as already said, [Col. 0563B] to inquire or contend over this name, unfamiliar in this context: whether that aforementioned subjection of the assumed man, and that due reverence by which he acknowledges and loves God as his Creator and Glorifier and intercedes without ceasing for us, is *latria* or is not *latria*. To define or comprehend all this as it is lies beyond humanity. For “we know in part and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 2). Paul too heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak. To know all these things fully belongs to eternal life, in which we shall know as we are known.

Or how could we penetrate that ineffable and inestimable mystery in the Son of God according to divine and human nature, which surpasses all the understanding of angels and human beings, when we cannot even explain that we are now servants of the Son of God and that we still await by grace what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (Eph. 2)?

If anything remains for the fire to consume, we do not wish to quarrel further with you about Christ, because that belongs neither to our leisure nor to our rank or office—especially since he himself says in Jeremiah: “Woe is me, my mother! Why have you borne me, a man of strife and a man of discord in all the earth?” (Jer. 15). That woe will be upon those who dispute everywhere about Christ, establish for Christ the law of birth, death, and resurrection according to their own opinion and judgment rather than according to the rules of faith. Therefore we are persuaded and have resolved in mind neither to write further to you about such matters nor to receive writings from you, lest [Col. 0563D] we appear mad to all sound-minded persons by debating clear matters as though they were doubtful, according to the saying of Emperor Marcian, confirmed by Pope Leo:

> “It is the height of madness to seek an imaginary light in the midst of clear daylight. Whoever investigates anything further beyond discovered truth seeks falsehood.”

From the Council of Ephesus:

> “We forbid anyone to say concerning Christ: ‘Because of the one who assumes, I venerate the assumed one; and because of the invisible one, I adore the visible one.’ It is dreadful also to say this: ‘He who was assumed is jointly named God with him who assumed him.’ Whoever says this [Col. 0564A] divides into two Christs him who is one, separately constituting man in one part and God likewise in another. For he plainly denies the unity according to which one is not co-adored with another or jointly named God, but Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, is understood as one, to be venerated with one worship together with his own flesh.”

From the same council, chapter eight:

> “If anyone should dare to say that the assumed man is to be co-adored with the Word of God, co-glorified, and jointly named God as one other together with another—for the added syllable *co-* always compels this meaning—but does not rather venerate Emmanuel with a single supplication and render him one glorification, in accordance with the Word’s having become flesh, let him be anathema.”

Let the careful reader understand that these things were said against heretics [Col. 0564B] who divided the one Christ into two persons.

## LETTER XVII

Gerhoh’s letter to Pope Alexander III.—He dedicates to him his exposition of Psalm 131, denounces Peter Lombard, and commends the reformation of the Church.

Receive, gracious Father Pope Alexander, this little gift from my hand—I who, by God’s grace, am called provost of the monastery of Reichersberg. I mean a little gift, not gold or silver, for I do not abound in such things, but a small exposition on the thirteenth Song of Ascents. I desire that you agree with its meaning, where it says: “I will clothe his enemies with confusion, but upon him my sanctification shall flourish” [Col. 0564C] (Ps. 131).

Are not your enemies those who corrupt others with evil conversations, especially those who teach against the faith of the apostle Peter, confessing Christ as the Son of the living God? Men held varying opinions of him, some calling him Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets—none of whom was either God Most High or the only Son of the Most High. But this man, anointed above his fellows, is Christ, the Son of the living God; therefore he must be believed and confessed to be true God, so that “man God” and “God man” are truly said, signifying that person who is God and man.

Against this and in opposition to it, enemies destined at last to be confounded commonly object and say to someone who calls that man God: “If person is implied or presupposed, you speak truly; if nature is implied, you speak falsely.” When asked what reality they call “person,” they confine it to the signification of the assuming Word, so as wholly to exclude the assumed man from the natural form and glory of divinity in which he was born, and likewise from the signification of person.

Likewise, those who say that man is God, or conversely, say that they speak truly by a trope of accidentality. When asked what they mean by a trope of accident, they say that they commonly call it a trope of accident where the predicate is not attributed to the cause—for example, if someone says “coloured,” they understand … [Note: [Col. 0563D] Thus wrongly in the printed text.]

[Col. 0565A] But we believe that, with that man—assumed into God and born—set as the subject in an utterance, he is to be predicated and declared simply, properly, and truly to be God, as the Evangelists, Apostles, and Prophets alike taught. No figure is needed to explain what is plain, such as the figures they call the trope of accompaniment, trope of accidentality, or reason of association. For the more tropes one adds to the assertion of our faith, the more one detracts from the simplicity and truth of proper speech.

Likewise another teacher, named the Master, says in his *Sentences*: “Christ, insofar as he is man, we ought to love as ourselves; and love for him according to his humanity is contained in that command by which we are bidden to love our neighbour as ourselves. We ought indeed to love him according to his humanity more than ourselves, but not as much as God, because, insofar as he is man, he is less than God.”

Likewise, the same man, in the glosses on the Psalter, upon this verse, “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship the footstool of his feet, for it is holy” (Psalm 98 [Vulgate]), says among other things:

> It must be considered what he commands us to worship when he says: “Worship the footstool of his feet.” Elsewhere Scripture says that the earth is his footstool, in these words: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet.” Does he therefore command us to worship the earth because it is the footstool of his feet? Yet elsewhere Scripture says: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.” But it must be understood that in Christ there is earth, that is, flesh, which is worshipped without impiety. For he took earth from earth, since flesh is from earth, and he received flesh from the flesh of Mary. This flesh, assumed by the Word of God, is worshipped by us without impiety, because no one spiritually eats his flesh unless he first worships.

These statements, drawn from the words of Augustine, are Catholic statements. To them the aforesaid Master added his own words, determining the mode of adoration:

> “I do not say,” he says, “that Christ’s flesh is to be worshipped with that adoration which is *latria*, and which is due to the Creator alone, but with that which is the more worthy kind of *dulia*. For *dulia* is an adoration also rendered to a creature, and it has two kinds: one rendered without distinction to all creatures, the other rendered to Christ’s humanity alone.”

These things Peter dared to say both in his glosses on the Psalter and in his *Sentences*. [Col. 0565D] But others too have so abused the license of disputing about Christ that they have not hesitated to say that in the statement “The man is God,” no thing is called God, but something united to God. Likewise, they say: “Christ is God,” and “I am the beginning,” are true by synecdoche, the part being taken for the whole. Likewise: “Since Christ is the name of a composite person, he is not the third person in the Trinity, because nothing but what is simple exists in the Trinity.” Others again say that Christ denotes only the name of the assuming Word, who spoke through the man as through an instrument.

We find all these things, and many more of the same kind, in their notes or little works. Nor is it now enough for them to say such things in the disorderly schools during disputations or when delivering opinions; such things are even shouted with impunity in ecclesiastical assemblies, before a multitude of clergy and bishops: namely, that Christ, insofar as he is man, is not the Son of God the Father otherwise than one of us; and therefore, although now glorified in glory, he possesses not glory equal to the Father’s glory, but some lower and lesser glory. And although, even in their faith, he surpasses all human beings and angels in glory, he is nevertheless neither equal to the Father in wisdom, knowledge, power, or any good thing, nor can he ever be made equal to him.

Moreover, an anathema was uttered most proudly and hastily by one of those saying such things—for there were only two who said these things and held these opinions. These statements were heard openly in an ecclesiastical assembly, in the presence of the Archbishop of Salzburg and three other bishops; and no one contradicted them except my two uterine brothers. One is Master Rudiger, formerly dean of the Church of Augsburg and now dean of the monastery of Nienburg; the other is Brother Aaron, then dean in the monastery entrusted to me. [Note: [Col. 0565D] Manuscript: “Aaron toen.”] Hearing Christ’s nativity and glory depreciated, they were greatly grieved and, as the occasion permitted, objected, producing in the midst testimonies of the Fathers which supported them—or rather, supported Christ and spoke for Christ. These things too were heard openly in that assembly, and again no one contradicted them.

Furthermore, in this controversy of faith it was added that the determinations of nonscholastics—that is, schoolmen coming from disorderly schools—ought to be accepted against the orthodox Fathers; whereas, if a question arises, especially concerning the Catholic faith, among Fathers who hold not contrary but at times differing opinions, it must be referred to the successors of Peter, prince of the apostles. For Peter’s faith, that it might not fail, Christ prayed and obtained this; and he so strengthened him in faith to strengthen his brothers that the gates of hell should not prevail against it. Therefore upon Peter himself and his successors will flourish the Lord’s sanctification, by which he is undoubtedly sanctified who is acknowledged as Peter’s lawful successor, lawfully subordinate. The faithful believe this of you, Pope Alexander, hoping for this fruit from your apostolate: that the ark of God’s sanctification—that is, the holy Church—when the Lord rises in you, may through you be brought into its rest, with concord between priesthood and kingship cooperating; and we hope that this will happen soon, if that council which, we have heard from the emperor’s own mouth, is to be held in Lombardy takes place, provided that you, Pope Alexander, and your faithful adherents consent to its assembly.

Then, if God so please, when the imperial majesty has inclined toward good concord, we shall see the ark of God’s sanctification brought through you, as through a lawful and righteous priest, into its rest, while the lord emperor leaps and dances like another David before the ark of the Lord. As I learned from him, he desires it to be brought with joy and the exultation of the whole realm into its rest: liberated, namely, from the Philistines and brought out of the temple of Dagon, with the priests of that Dagon and of Mammon rejected—as happened figuratively when God struck them and their princes upon their hinder parts, giving them everlasting reproach, and entrusted his ark to priests of the Levitical race.

That this may happen the Spirit prays with unutterable groanings whenever the Church sings: “Arise, O Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification. Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your saints rejoice” (Psalm 131 [Vulgate]). Great indeed then will be the rejoicing of the saints who behold these things. Even before they happen, believing that they will occur and rejoicing in hope, they rejoice in their beds; they rejoice in their king. Thus I too, though insignificant, once rejoiced according to my measure in my King Christ, who, by the bishops of the Apostolic See, strengthening me more than once, made me glad. This may be recognized from the letters sent to me and on my behalf by that See, by which I was encouraged while fighting for the law of my God. How Pope Eugenius, of blessed memory, stood by me in my struggle may be seen in his letter, whose text is as follows:

> Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son G., provost of Richersberg: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> We have graciously received the writings of your love and have clearly recognized from inspecting them the fervour of your religious devotion. For your heart grew warm within you, and in your meditation a fire was kindled. Your utterance also is vehemently aflame. Therefore, since we know that, through zeal of charity, you burn against most wicked innovations and also against disturbances arising against the Church of God and ecclesiastical persons, we rejoice with paternal affection and commend your devotion in the Lord. But because it is good to begin, though much better to finish, we exhort your love in the Lord to persevere steadfastly in your good purpose. For we love your person with paternal charity as a learned and religious man, and in such matters as we can according to God, we desire to honour and support you.
>
> Given at Sutri, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July [15 June].

Before him, the Roman pontiffs Honorius, Innocent, Celestine, and Lucius also stood by me manfully, and I possess their writings as testimony of this matter. But after the death of blessed Eugenius no one like him was found to stand by me as he did. For a certain marriage contracted after a vow of widowly continence, which he had annulled upon my report, Pope Anastasius after him confirmed; by this he stirred up many oppositions against me. You were then his chancellor, and, as I heard, you could not entirely restrain him in his impulses, although you were in many respects a helpful staff to his feeble old age, being a gentle and clear-sighted man, and therefore like the gentle David.

Accordingly, among the other works of my labour I chose to offer to your gentleness this song, in which David and all his gentleness are mentioned anew to you several times.

Here begins the exposition of the song: “Remember, O Lord, David,” and so forth to the end of the Psalm.

Having said these things about the exposition of the Psalm, I turn to you, Pope Alexander, and speak with the confidence by which I trust that you have been anointed above many of your companions because you loved righteousness and hated iniquity even before you were thus anointed. How much more, then, now that you are anointed with the oil of gladness, ought you to love righteousness and hate iniquity? Therefore hate this iniquity: that the ark of God’s sanctification now has no rest in its tabernacle, where priests and ministers such as the sons of Eli the priest preside. Scripture reports that they lay with the women keeping watch at the entrance of the tabernacle and, using a three-pronged hook, snatched raw flesh not belonging to them; they became so infamous that men despised God’s sacrifice because of them. Because their father did not rebuke them worthily, the iniquity of his house could not be expiated either by sacrifices or offerings. God’s wrath therefore burned so fiercely against it that he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle, where he had dwelt among men. “He delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hand of the enemy.”

The burning of God’s wrath was further inflamed because they carried the holy ark, which ought to have been kept guarded within God’s sanctuary, out into the camp, where there was disorderly battle, since it lacked a lawful leader and prince such as Joshua, who fought in orderly fashion while Moses prayed for him on the holy mountain, with Aaron and Hur joined to him. But the battle of Eli’s sons was exceedingly disorderly and ended badly for them, although they caused the ark of God, which they had not rightly served, to be brought there.

I do not dare fully to set down in writing how great a likeness to that disorder exists in this time—indeed, in this stormy age—so that the ark of God has no rest now in its most excellent tabernacle, that is, in the Roman Church. Peter the apostle, as another Aaron, presided over it in his own person and in his successors for a long time; the Roman Church has been made purple either by their blood or illustrious through confessors. But after men departed from their teachings and examples so far that the Roman pontiffs raised disorderly wars against Roman citizens and other enemies, the ark of God could not have peace in the city of Rome; and, through its unrest, the whole Church was disturbed.

When I was at Viterbo with Pope Eugenius of holy memory, and he told me in private conversation about his vexation, in which, favouring the people of Tivoli against Roman citizens, he had spent much money and had finally concluded a very miserable settlement of peace, I replied: “Although this peace, bought at so great a price, is miserable, it is nevertheless better than your warfare. For when the Roman pontiff prepares himself for war to be fought through hired soldiers, I seem to see Peter drawing a sword of iron. But when this combatant, or one about to fight, fares badly, I seem to hear Christ . . . [lacuna] saying to Peter: ‘Put your sword into its sheath’” (John 18).

After I had said these things, and that holy pontiff had received them graciously, I did not perceive that he thereafter drew the sword of iron, but rather the sword of the Spirit. By wielding it rightly he was likened to holy Samuel, sparing neither Agapitus nor the other Amalekite enemies of Israel, some of whom, captured in his presence, he cut, as it were, into pieces. All Germany knows this: he humbled two great archbishops, namely those of Mainz and Cologne, rejecting and despising their money. Therefore in his days rest was granted to the Roman Church, though not so full and perfect that the holy Church does not need Samuel’s zeal to bring it to completion; for, with scandals still abounding in it, men still despise the sacrifice of God.

I ask you therefore, with your favour unimpaired: since someone is believed to be raised up in the spirit and power of Samuel against impending evils, are you that man, or is another to be awaited? Although the truth of this matter must in the future be fully known from the fruits that follow, it is now partly known from the flowers that bring forth fruit—if you, being highest in dignity among mortals, do not despise this exhortation addressed to you by me, a little man. I write not from rash audacity—far be it—but from the boldness of that charity which does not rejoice in iniquity but rejoices with truth, and which persuaded me, though small, to write something to you, though great, for truth against iniquity.

My confidence was also increased because you, preceding me and my uterine brothers with blessings of sweetness, commanded in your letters sent to us that greeting and apostolic blessing be given to us. You also promised that the favour of your apostolate would be shown to me as I had been held in favour by your predecessors, as certain lord cardinals who knew me know. Know that I chose to commend Samuel’s example to you now, while writing for truth against iniquity, because I desire that at the end of your apostolate, when you depart from this life into the Lord’s rest, where is the ark of sanctification—that is, he whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world—you may be able truthfully to glory in the Lord as Samuel gloried before the children of Israel, saying:

> “Behold, I stand ready. Speak concerning me before the Lord and before his Christ: whether I have taken anyone’s ox or donkey; whether I have slandered anyone; whether I have oppressed anyone; whether I have accepted a gift from anyone’s hand. Despise it today, and I shall restore it to you.” And they said: “You have not slandered us, nor oppressed us, nor taken anything from anyone’s hand.”

May he grant you, Pope Alexander, that you may thus glory in the Lord—that is, in truth—near the end of your papacy: he who is able to do all things beyond what we ask or understand, to whom be honour and glory now and through everlasting ages. Amen.

## LETTER XVIII

The same writer to Henry, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, to whom he writes that he has sent an exposition of Psalm 64.—Why he could not travel to France. On the multitude and snares of his adversaries, etc.

To Lord H., venerable cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church, of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, Brother G. of Richersberg sends devoted prayers with faithful service.

“Remember your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope.” For when you were at Augsburg, in the house of my brother R., together with Lord Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon, you promised me—as Lord R., then chancellor and now, through the favour of God’s mercy, raised to the summit of the apostolate, can remember—that you would so dispose yourself toward knowing and favouring me that he might look upon me with the same eye of kindness with which his predecessors looked upon me. Encouraged and strengthened by them, I composed certain little works through which not only might Christ’s glory be magnified, while my soul magnified the Lord and my spirit rejoiced in God my Saviour, but also the disgrace of him who now works the mystery of iniquity under a cloak of piety might be exposed.

This I did, as far as I could with God’s help, in the treatise on Psalm 64, which I handed with my own hand to Pope Eugenius of blessed memory and likewise gave to you at Augsburg. I also did this in the little work *On the Praise of Faith*, begun and completed at your exhortation. When Lord Hyacinth was at the court of the lord pope in Anagni, it was entrusted to a messenger who did not find you there, so that he might give it to you as the fruit of your request. For you had earnestly asked me to expound for you that saying of Solomon: “Who shall find a valiant woman?” (Proverbs 31). If therefore you received it from him, well; but if not, either request it from him or require from me by letter a reply concerning it, which you may entrust to the present messenger.

Do not wonder that I did not present my person, weakened by old age, to the lord pope or to the curia. For from the German kingdom to the kingdom of France, even if I could travel, it is not safe for me, since many watch and seek an opportunity to disturb the prince’s favour toward me and provoke his displeasure—wrath which I must avoid insofar as this can be done without prejudice to God’s grace. Recently, indeed, he was enraged against me through the lies of certain persons and was scarcely reconciled to me, when the lord of Freising and his clergy, together with other princes, excused me before him. They showed that I was not, as had been reported to him, an enemy of the imperial glory, nor, as enemies had spread abroad, opposed to Christ’s glory.

For, as though I were another Naboth, blasphemy against God and the king was falsely charged against me; consequently, following Naboth’s example, I was judged to deserve stoning by the imperial chaplains, who did not know the truth of the matter. But when the aforesaid bishop, together with others who knew the truth, sufficiently excused me, the emperor himself, by God’s favour, became so reconciled to me that he discussed many matters with me in private conversation which, if I dared commit them to writing, would, I believe, please you in large part. Yet you will one day hear them, if God so ordains that I may speak with you face to face at that celebrated assembly which we hope will take place, as, I believe, you have already heard from the legates of the lord pope, namely the venerable bishops of Pavia and Troyes.

But I do not wish you to be ignorant—you, I mean, the lord pope, Lord Hyacinth, yourself, and the other cardinal lords gracious toward me—that those who afflict me have greatly multiplied, and many rise against me, saying to my soul: “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Psalm 3; cited as Jer. III). Nor is this adversity new to me. For more than thirty years I have fought against and endured these very beasts opposing me and, if it were possible, desiring to lead me into error, so that in my writings I might call evil good and good evil, light darkness and darkness light, sweet bitter and bitter sweet: approving what they condemn and condemning what they vigorously approve, boasting themselves learned.

But although I had at first been somewhat instructed in scholastic exercises, after I entered upon the practices of ecclesiastical religion I came to dislike many opinions of the masters as muddy waters. Through God’s favouring grace I betook myself to the waters of Siloam, which flow in silence; and, insofar as it was granted me, I offered these waters also to others through my writings. As it were at the waters of contradiction, I had many opponents. Delivered and defended from them through Peter’s successors, I had frequent occasion and reason to sing the Song of Ascents whose words are: “Had the Lord not been with us, let Israel now say” (Psalm 123 [Vulgate]), and so on to: “Blessed be the Lord, who has not given us as prey to their teeth. The snare has been broken, and we have been delivered” (ibid.).

By singing and expounding—and, would that I might also ascend—I came to that step in which is sung: “Remember, O Lord, David and all his gentleness” (ibid., Psalm 131 [Vulgate]). Through you I offer its exposition for Pope Alexander of sweet renown to read, because through it he may learn what I think about restoring the state of the Church to better things; about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation; and about the man assumed into God and born, crowned with the glory and honour of divine power. In these two matters I have especially many opponents, who assert that the man united to God is not God’s only natural Son, and that he is not to be honoured in the glory of God the Father so as to be worshipped with the adoration called *latria*, but rather with that called *dulia*.

Against their assertions I have sought to collect in one place authorities of the Fathers that are contrary to them and consonant with our assertion: first, in a little work composed for Pope Adrian and presented to him at Benevento; then recently in the work *On the Sacrifice Cooked in a Frying-Pan*, sent to Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg. If it has been examined at the Apostolic See, I think it will please those who please God; for I have more than once found there approval for what, by God’s favouring grace, I wrote against evil abuses and perverse innovations. As you know, I have opposed these more than once, and I shall still be prepared to oppose them, as God grants, with all the more readiness as I feel myself more urgently encouraged and strengthened by the successor of blessed Peter.

But someone says: “It is already enough that others, better, holier, and no less learned, have discovered and written. It is unlawful and rash to add anything to what named and Catholic men have said, and thus to weary readers by increasing the multitude of commentaries.”

To this I say: Certainly the spacious field of holy Scripture is common to all confessors of Christ, and no one can rightly be denied permission to treat it, provided that, without prejudice to faith, he speaks or writes what he thinks. Who could rightly be indignant because, on the same estate, after one or two wells dug by preceding Fathers, later sons dig more by their own labour? Finally Isaac dug other wells besides those which the servants of his father Abraham had dug, and which the Philistines had formerly stopped up after Abraham’s death. For after he again dug other wells and called them by the same names his father had previously used, Scripture continues and says: “They dug in the torrent-bed and found living water” (Genesis 26). Likewise: “They dug another.” And then: “Departing thence, he dug another well” (ibid.).

Therefore, according to this rule, let them grant to us also, after those wells which they dug—that is, after those treatises which the Fathers and our predecessors treated—the right to dig other wells with the ploughshare of our own intellect, provided that we too can find living water that harms no drinker and gives neither scandal nor error to any reader, unless perhaps to someone like and equal to the traitor Judas. To him the good fragrance of the good ointment was evil, because he himself was evil. So too things good and well said by us, and pleasing to good readers such as Pope Eugenius of holy memory, appear evil to evil and malicious persons. They say: “Why this waste of parchment and time, when things are written which are not read, or, if read, do not please readers who rage and fume against them?”

May it be granted me to hear, against such persons, Christ’s voice through the mouths of Peter’s successors: “Why do you trouble this woman? She has done a good work for me” (Matthew 26). I would rather be likened to that weak and sinful yet repentant woman, anointing the feet and head of Christ—that is, venerating his humanity with his divinity in equal worship of adoration—than to those proud Rabbis and their disciples, who assign *latria* to the Word abiding in flesh and *dulia* to the flesh itself. For the head of the paschal lamb must be eaten with its feet; no distinction at all may be admitted in the adoration by which man is not to be worshipped for God as one thing for another, as the heresiarch Nestorius wished, but man in God and God in man are to be worshipped with one adoration, as the Council of Ephesus affirmed, saying:

> “If anyone dares to say that the assumed man ought to be co-worshipped with God the Word, and co-glorified, and called God together with him, as though one were alongside another—for the addition of ‘co-’ always compels this meaning—and does not rather honour Emmanuel with one adoration and render to him one glorification, according as the Word became flesh, let him be anathema.”

That your prudence may understand that the aforementioned questions are not lightly stirred, take note of the following letters to two great men, namely my lord the Archbishop of Salzburg and the lord of Bamberg. Thus, if our assertion is approved by the Apostolic See, some exhortation may, if possible, be written to them by the lord pope and the curia, strengthening them to stand by me and resist schoolmen accustomed to raise undisciplined questions, not only in the schools but even in ecclesiastical assemblies.

## LETTER XIX

The same writer to Hyacinth, or Jacinth, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.—That he may make the cardinals attentive to the controversy raised concerning the glory and honour of the Son of Man.

To Lord JACINTH, venerable cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, Brother G. of Richersberg sends devoted prayers with faithful service.

Deign to read what I wrote to the lord pope as though I had written it to you, because, since you are a great member of the Roman Church, I do not think that what I wrote to the head is foreign to you. I ask also that through your diligence the matters under discussion may become known to the other cardinal lords, so that they may attend to them, lest in our days the heresiarchs Photinus, Paul of Samosata, Nestorius, and Bonosus be raised again. Their pestilential teaching has spread so widely in the disorderly schools that many masters, disciples, and undisciplined persons now chatter against the Catholic faith, saying: “God, or the Almighty, assumed nothing. Rather,” they say, “flesh and a rational soul—that is, a human being—were assumed; and although great power was given to this person, omnipotence was not given, nor could it have been given, since no creature contains or can contain omnipotence.”

But we believe the man assumed into God when he says: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28). Likewise: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matthew 11). The holy Fathers expound these Gospel testimonies so that omnipotence and all good things which the Word of God, being God, possessed by nature, he conferred by grace upon the assumed man. That grace, as blessed Augustine says, was made in a manner natural to the assumed man, because he did not merit it by being born but received it in being born—not according to measure, as angels or blessed human beings do. To none of them was grace so given and converted into nature that they never could or can sin. But the man assumed into God received in being born that he could not sin and could do all that he willed. This was and is supreme omnipotence, by which human nature was enriched in the Son of God. Since very many detract from this omnipotence, may divine grace raise up the holy Roman Church against the reproaches of such people. And you, who through God’s grace have great influence in the Roman Church, beware lest you be ungrateful for God’s grace; through that grace resist its enemies.

## LETTER XX

The same writer to Alexander III, supreme pontiff.—He asks him to reply what he thinks in the controversy concerning the glory and honour of the Son of Man. On certain little works sent to the Roman curia, etc.

To ALEXANDER, through the favour of divine mercy gracious pontiff of the Apostolic See, Brother G. of Richersberg: may you conquer with Peter and reign with Peter.

We received most gratefully the writings of your graciousness, by which you kindly greeted me and my uterine brothers through Brother Witer, monk of Morimond. We give great thanks to your graciousness because, although we had not yet written anything to you, you deigned to precede us with blessings of sweetness, promising me in particular that you wished to hold me in the same favour in which your predecessors held me. Therefore, that you may know how they held me, deign to read our writings sent to the curia through the bearer of this letter. When you have read and examined them, assist me where I seem to require assistance; correct me where I need correction—especially in the two chapters now under debate.

Two disputants tear my writings to pieces chiefly because they assert that the assumed man is God, the natural Son of God, and the Most High in the supreme glory of God the Father. Although less than the Father according to the nature of his humanity, he is not less according to the omnipotence given to that same man and the complete glory of the Father’s exaltation. They, on the other hand, contend that the assumed man is not God, not God’s natural Son, not omnipotent, and not the Most High. A third, Folmar, joins them, detracting so severely from both the nativity and glory of the assumed man that he denies he is to be worshipped with the adoration called *latria*. Relying on the Council of Ephesus, we affirm that he is to be worshipped, as the omnipotent only Son of God Almighty: Most High in a nature alike exalted and exalting, glorified and glorifying, sanctified and sanctifying; less than the Father according to the condition of human nature, but not less according to the elevation of that same nature.

Since in this controversy my lord the archbishop has chosen silence, awaiting, namely, the assent of apostolic authority to one side or the other, may your holiness not find it burdensome to write to him and to me what appears right, lest under your apostolate the Apostolic See be torn apart. For that they tear apart my reputation—and, as is reported, have even set it forth to be torn apart in your curia—I would think little of it, if they did not touch Christ, contrary to: “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Psalm 16 [Vulgate]). But they touch his anointed ones—indeed, Christ the Most High himself. How the aforesaid Folmar tears him by touching him may be seen in Folmar’s letter, a copy of which will be shown to you if you wish. Although I have sufficiently answered it, I think it suitable to your apostolate that you too should write something against it, either to my lord the archbishop or to Lord Adam, Abbot of Ebrach, to whom Folmar sent the aforesaid letter.

In another writing sent to my lord of Salzburg, Folmar likewise invented so many profane and horrible lies against my person that, unless the archbishop fully knew me and knew my teaching to accord with that of the saints, he might have been induced to entertain an unfavourable suspicion of me. So Folmar induced the chaplains of the lord emperor and made the emperor seriously angry with me, to such an extent that I had to excuse myself to him against many lies spread in his court. Perhaps they have also been spread in your curia, but in vain, I believe, because that curia is not like a reed shaken by the wind. Until now I had no need of letters of recommendation to it, being known to the pontiffs and cardinal lords and not least in their favour. Now, however, I would gladly have obtained a letter for you from my lord the archbishop, had he not been more than ten days’ journey away and impossible to consult. I did not wish to request letters from others, because, like another Nicodemus, I do what I do by night; but I hope for and await the day.

For the day is near when it will breathe forth and the shadows will decline. There are many signs; this too foretells the dawn of day: report says that legates from your apostolate are being sought for Greece to instruct them in the faith. Therefore, if it pleased your majesty, I would wish these legates to consider our little book *Against the Errors of the Greeks*, which I previously sent to the curia there to be examined and, if it pleased them, published. I have now also sent a copy of it for you and the cardinal lords to inspect, if you so please; and may your and their indignation against me, a little man, in this matter be set aside. Although I am small, I dare to speak and write about great matters, investigate truth in them, and approve the truth once found. So too, in writings, I investigated and approved the truth concerning the beginning of your apostolate, ready to confess that same truth before kings and princes as I know it now, and as I hope yet more perfectly to know it from its fruits.

## LETTER XXI

The same writer to the college of cardinals of the Holy Roman Church.—On the various storms by which he has continually been tossed, and in which he always glories that the Apostolic See has been his protection, etc.

To the lord cardinals, Brother G. of Richersberg sends devoted prayers with faithful service.

In my old age I am compelled to recall some part of the labours of my youth, especially those in which, when my heart was distressed, the Lord set me on a rock by strengthening me in Peter’s faith through Peter’s successors.

First, in the doubtful hazard of a duel, it enters the field.

“Faith is destined to fight,” says a certain wise poet. But I do not doubt that, as the beginning of the conflict belongs to faith, so also does its end: faith will continue to fight until sight succeeds it, and there is no longer a need to walk by faith when the very form is seen. Its vision is now hidden, so that faith itself, exercised more and more thereby, may have merit precisely because human reason does not furnish it with experience.

Yet it is permissible to reason about faith according to the rule of faith—not according to the wisdom of this world, which God has made foolish [Col. 0576B], and against whose deception the Apostle warns us, saying: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human traditions and not according to Jesus Christ; for in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily” (Col. 2). Deceived by this philosophy, many departed from the sincerity of faith before our time; their folly, having been refuted by Catholic teachers, ought not to be recalled for further controversy.

But because the ancient serpent does not rest, he does not disdain to renew his ancient deceits. I have experienced this many times, when my heart was distressed among the enemies of faith. As they distressed me, I was raised up upon the rock, while I was more and more exercised in Peter’s faith, Peter’s successors standing by me to defend and uphold Peter’s faith.

The first to stand by me in such a conflict was Honorius of blessed memory, when Master Luitolf was at his court among the masters of France. This man sought to maintain that Christ, insofar as he is man, is indeed the natural Son of man, but the adoptive son of God the Father. I, on the contrary, maintained that adoption did not belong to the assumed man in respect of his being the Son of God. Pope Honorius mentioned above stood by me, having been stirred to do so by a certain booklet presented to him by a learned canon of the Lateran, which I read. In it, the difference was carefully examined between chosen sons—who are also known to be called proper and natural sons [Col. 0576D]—and adopted sons, who are by no means equal to natural sons.

Therefore, after the term “adoption” had been refuted in relation to Christ, the proper and natural Son of God and man, I was raised upon the rock and strengthened in Peter’s faith through Peter’s successor. I returned from the city with joy, firmly holding as true that Peter himself did not err concerning the Son of Man when men were in error, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16).

Again, on another occasion, when I was in Rome, a certain Lateran canon named Adam, newly come from the schools of Master Peter Abelard, sought to maintain that Christ was partly God and partly man. But I believed him to be wholly God and wholly man; and therefore I spoke, because divinity was innate to the man and humanity was united to God in one subsistence, in one living bread, in one chosen one, in one mediator between God and men. The holy Roman Church stood by me [Col. 0577A] and faithfully approved my faith. So much was this so that, when the aforesaid Adam later became an apostate and went to Apulia, one of the cardinals told me that he had rightly been abandoned by Christ for his perfidy.

I replied: “Blessed be my Lord Jesus Christ, who is wholly God to me, not half God, as he wished. Since he worshipped a half-god, not possessing the true Christ, wholly God and wholly man, he was rightly abandoned to the power of him who is the father of lies. But by his grace my Lord Jesus Christ, wholly God and wholly man, has preserved me [Col. 0577B] in my resolve, and is able also to preserve me blameless unto the end in that faith which Peter confessed, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail.” Behold, a second time, when my heart was distressed, the Lord raised me upon the rock.

A third time, during the schism of Peter Leo, I maintained that priests sacrificing in schism did not possess the body of the Lord. For in the law of the Lord it was forbidden for the flesh of the lamb to be carried outside; it had to be eaten in one house. That one house is the universal Church. Within it, when someone, through a fault demanding it, has been deprived of the priestly office, he cannot consecrate the true sacrifice; if, that is, he sacrifices apart from his office. Much less can one sacrificing outside the Church offer the living bread by which the holy Church lives [Col. 0577C], since those wholly cut off from her are dead, when such a fault requires it—a fault which the Church neither ought nor can tolerate within herself.

How many opponents I had in this judgment! But with Innocent, Roman pontiff of blessed memory, then standing by me, I gained such a victory and was raised upon the rock that the flood striking against my house could not move it.

It would be long to recount how often, when my heart was distressed, the Lord raised me upon the rock through Peter’s successors Honorius, Lucius, and Celestine. At their exhortation and encouragement I strove, not only in speech but also in writing, to resist abuses and perverse innovations. I collected many such matters into one work, first in my Exposition of the Sixty-Fourth Psalm, which I personally gave to Pope Eugenius of holy memory, and which I later also gave to Lord Henry, cardinal of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. It was sufficiently approved by Pope Eugenius himself [Col. 0577D], to whom I also then sent other writings. How acceptable these were to him is attested by his letter, whose text is as follows:

> “Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son G., provost of Richersberg: greeting and apostolic blessing. We have kindly received the writings of your devotion,” etc.

Other letters as well, sent to me and on my behalf by the Apostolic See, agree with this letter. Omitting many of them, I shall append two more, so that in the mouth of two or three pontiffs of the Apostolic See the word of good testimony on my behalf may stand [Col. 0578A]—a testimony which younger scholastics and schoolmen strive to overthrow, wholly like those of whom blessed Job says: “But now those younger than I mock me, whose fathers I would not have deigned to put with the dogs of my flock” (Job 30). Certainly those most excellent dogs, barking well, were the aforesaid pontiffs of the Apostolic See. Their letters are these:

> “Celestine, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son G., provost of Richersberg: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “Concerning the troubles and distresses which, as we have learned from the testimony of our beloved son G., cardinal deacon, you endure for the assertion of truth and justice, we sympathize with you in paternal affection; and in those matters in which we can do so according to God, we willingly offer you assistance and counsel. In these matters you ought to have the greater patience, because it is more certain that your zeal endures these same persecutions in defense of justice. For you know that it is neither new nor unusual that, according to the Apostle, those who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution from the ungodly and unlike-minded. The Lord consoles them in the Gospel, promising them eternal blessedness: ‘Blessed,’ he says, ‘are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake’ (Matt. 5).
>
> “Nevertheless, by the obligation of our office, we wish to oppose your adversaries and restrain them by ecclesiastical censure. Therefore, by this present letter we command you to present yourself before us on the next Sunday [Col. 0578C], on which is read, ‘I am the good shepherd’ (John 11), so that, once the matter has been more fully learned from you yourself, we may provide for your peace and tranquility and give you timely assistance as to a beloved son.
>
> “Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February.”

> “Lucius, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren C., archbishop of Salzburg, and R., bishop of Gurk: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “We received with paternal kindness our beloved son G., provost of Richersberg, when he came to the Apostolic See; and, honoring his person for his religious character and integrity, we sent him back to his own place with the favor of the Apostolic See. Therefore, earnestly commending him to your brotherhood by this present letter, we command that, as you have hitherto done for the sake of his religious character and integrity alone, so henceforth, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, you honor and love him [Col. 0578D], and give him help and counsel in his necessities.”

I also sent Pope Adrian of blessed memory a little work composed against innovations and perverse abuses. Although he made no written reply to it, he nevertheless approved it verbally, and conveyed to me, both orally and in writing, greeting and apostolic blessing; nor did he condemn anything in my writing. Thereupon, encouraged to speak and write against the new Photinians, Paulianists, Nestorians, and Bonosians coming from undisciplined schools, I said and wrote certain things.

And therefore, in response to the darts of truth directed by me against them, they spread many lies against me: partly by perverting what I say, and partly by inventing new and unheard-of calumnies. These have been spread far and wide and carried even to the Apostolic court, as also to the emperor’s court. Some speak and think for me, others against me. Thus, if the blowing winds of windy eloquence coming from the north were now violently troubling me, shaking the house of my faith, unless better winds had come and continued to come from the south [Col. 0579A], I should be gravely disturbed.

For word has reached me that, having been maliciously accused in the Roman court by certain cardinals, I am so condemned that one of them said to a messenger of my lord the archbishop of Salzburg that he greatly wondered how the archbishop could tolerate a man gravely defamed for great errors. But word has also conveyed to me that some cardinals who know me and are well received in the court speak better of me. Likewise, in the court of the lord emperor some speak for me and some against me. Thus, amid opposing utterances like contrary winds, and with danger threatening, I am compelled to cry out and awaken Jesus asleep, that he may rise and command the winds and sea, so that there may be a great calm—not only when this particular storm is removed, but also when the general storm is lifted and the evil of schism is moderated.

Thus may the sailors of the universal Church, of whom you, lords cardinals, are the chief, not err with the disciples who thought Christ walking upon the sea to be a phantom [Col. 0579C]; but, with Peter, may they themselves walk upon the sea in this fourth watch of the night, to which that day is believed to be near: the day of wrath, the day of calamity and misery, the great and exceedingly bitter day, on which the man to whom all judgment has been given will show himself almighty God against those false speakers who deny that he is almighty insofar as he is man.

Because I and the faithful who agree with me confess him to be almighty insofar as he is man—though not from the fact that he is man, but because he has been born into God and exalted by the power and brightness of the supreme Godhead—we are defamed as though erroneous. Rather, those err who deny what the universal Church believes and every tongue confesses: namely, that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. Although he is lesser according to the nature of his created humanity, he is nevertheless not lesser according to the nature of the divinity innate to him, and according to the grant to him of all power, as it is written: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28) [Col. 0579D].

Although this power is uncreated, it has been given so fully to the man born into God and created according to God in justice and holiness of truth that he is almighty equally with his Father, working equally powerfully through the Word incarnate in himself as his Father works through that same Word born from himself. For the Word made flesh was not weakened in flesh; rather, the frail vessel of flesh was so strengthened by the fire of divinity that it is no less strong than the divinity itself, to which it is united by a wondrous union through conception [Col. 0580A] and co-glorified through the Ascension. Thus man has been crowned with the glory and honor of the highest divinity and set over all things, so that he may be above all things—not among all things—God blessed forever.

Concerning the glory and omnipotence of this man, deign, lords cardinals, to read the little works which I have written and which I have now sent to the court for reading, and let me know what I ought to hope from you. This is not because I trust in man, but in the Lord, to whom I also say in song: “In the Lord I trust; how do you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain’?” (Ps. 10), and the rest to the end of the psalm. For behold, the sinners spoken of there have bent their bow against me and prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot me in darkness—that is, to slander me by secret whispering [Col. 0580B], which they suppose prevails with you. For they know that I am weakened by old age and illnesses and cannot attend courts as I once could.

But the word of God is not bound. Where I cannot be presented in bodily presence, by God’s help I shall be present in spirit, praying and singing with mind and spirit. May this be effectually accomplished in me and through me by the man born into God, exalted to the throne of God the Father, and commended by the testimony of God the Father himself.

You know, moreover, lords cardinals, that if we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, because he has testified concerning his Son. “For there are three,” John says, “who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit” (1 John 5) [Col. 0580C]. First, one asks why he did not say “the Father and the Son,” but rather, “the Father,” he says, “the Word, and the Holy Spirit.” The answer is that these three witnesses bear testimony not only to us that we are born of God, as he had proposed in saying, “Everything born of God conquers the world” (1 John 5). And at the end of the chapter: “Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God in himself” (ibid.).

But they also—and indeed principally—bear testimony to the Lord Jesus himself, that he is Christ, or that Christ is truth. He himself testified this concerning himself, saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). The Word himself did not need this testimony, since it was not hidden from the prophets, nor even from philosophers, especially Platonists, that he had been truth and life from eternity. But testimony was necessary for the assumed man, that he might be the life and truth of the assuming Word.

Therefore, so that an occasion might not be given to heretics to say that there are two sons—one the Son of God and the other the son of man—when giving testimony concerning that man who hung on the cross, died, and was buried, John did not wish to say that the Father and Son bear testimony to him. For he is one Son in both substances, divine and human. Rather, he says: “the Father and the Word and the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0580D]. For in truth, it is not Son bearing witness to Son, but the Word bearing witness to the assumed man: that he who was denied and rejected as a false witness when the Jews said, “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true” (John 8)—that he, I say, is the truth, power, and wisdom of God.

The testimony in question is not given by one person of Christ to another person of Christ, but by one substance of Christ to the other. “How,” you ask, “does this Word give testimony to the man united to itself?” To pass over much that exceeds our childish capacity: it gives testimony in this, that the Word proceeding from the mouth of the man united to it was no less effectual in accomplishing whatever it willed than when it formerly proceeded from the mouth of the Father to accomplish whatever the Father said to it, and it was done.

For example, God the Father said: “Let there be light” (Gen. 1), and it was so. Likewise, this man said to men: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5), and it was so. Therefore, with as much power as God the Father spoke and, by speaking, made light shine out of darkness in the creation of the world, so powerfully did this man make light shine out of darkness in the restoration of the world [Col. 0581B].

The Father commanded the waters, saying: “Let the waters be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear,” and it was so (Gen. 1). This man commanded the winds and sea, and they obeyed him. He said to the leper: “Be cleansed” (Mark 1), and it was so. He said to the royal official: “Your son lives” (John 4), and it was so. Similarly, in everything that he willed and said should happen, what he willed and said happened. Nor was, or could the Word proceeding from his mouth ever have been, ineffectual, according to his own testimony: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Luke 21).

Moreover, against his Jewish enemies, who rejected him as though he were a liar, even this should suffice [Col. 0581C]: he said of them, “They shall fall by the edge of the sword and shall be led captive among all nations” (ibid.), and so it happened. Therefore, according to the testimony of the Word, Jesus Christ is almighty, doing all things whatsoever he wills.

By that same Word his Father also made all things that he willed. For the Word made man was not weakened in the man, but bestowed upon the man all fullness of powers, so that this man is more properly called power and wisdom than powerful and wise. Thus the Apostle says: “We preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1). He says “Christ,” not “the Word.” For no one doubts that the Word of God is God’s power and wisdom; but with respect to Christ—the anointed man, the man assumed into God and born into God—it could be doubted that he was God’s power and wisdom. Therefore the Word of God, speaking through the truthful Apostle, bears true testimony concerning his flesh, that is, the man united to himself [Col. 0581D]: he has power and wisdom not as other saints have them by an accidental gift, but by the essential good, according to which no one is good except the one God.

Among all the testimonies of the Word, however, this is sweetest to the Church of God: where he testified that his flesh is living bread, saying: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6). For this bread, as is written, God sealed—without doubt with the seal of his own divinity—so that, just as divinity itself is the food of angels, giving them life and blessedness, so the flesh of the Word bestows life and blessedness upon those human beings who worthily partake of it [Col. 0582A].

Accordingly, the Council of Ephesus rightly judged that the flesh of the Word must be believed and called life-giving, against Nestorius, who denied this and, among other blasphemies, spewed forth the claim that the flesh received at the altar ought not to be called the flesh of the Lord, but of a man. But since elsewhere we have said more against this error of his, let us now be content with the testimony of the Word himself concerning his flesh. Holy Hilary speaks much concerning this in the eighth book of *On the Holy Trinity*. Whoever wishes may read what was said by that orthodox teacher, who there sets forth not only the testimony of the Word but also the testament of the body and blood, confirmed by God through the testator’s death, so that no schoolman or school may be permitted to superimpose another.

For just as “no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3), so no one can establish another testimony besides that which has been made firm by Christ’s blood: “This,” he says, “is the blood of the new covenant, which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26) [Col. 0582B]. This is the blood which, as the Apostle says, “will cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Heb. 9). Since this could not be accomplished by the blood of goats or calves, indeed not even by the blood of all saints, the blood of the Lord was necessary for this purpose. The blood, I say, of the Lord, because the man is Lord; in his blood the whole Church is made purple and purified, redeemed and given drink by it, and likewise made an heir of God and co-heir with Christ through his testament.

But how does the Father bear testimony to him? First, by saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). We have said more about this testimony of the Father in a little work addressed to Pope Adrian of blessed memory, which we do not consider necessary to repeat now. But this must not seem to be passed over: Jesus himself says, “If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me” (John 10). Again: “The Father abiding in me does the works” (ibid.). Again: “If you do not wish to believe me, believe the works” (ibid.). Thus, always heeding him in the performance of great works which no other did, and above all in raising him from the dead, the Father bore testimony to him [Col. 0582D] that what he said concerning himself was true: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (ibid.). Again: “My Father, who gave to me, is greater than all” (ibid.).

Explaining these words, the venerable priest Bede says:

> “What is greater than all, which the Father gave to Jesus Christ, mediator between God and men, is this: that he should be his only-begotten Son, in no respect unlike the begetter in nature, inferior in power, or later in time. This equality the Lord himself possessed in his divinity with the Father before the world existed; in his humanity he received it from the time of the Incarnation.”

Again, on the passage, “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28), the same Bede says:

> “He speaks this not of the divinity coeternal with the Father, but of the assumed humanity [Col. 0583A], which by assuming it he was made a little lower than the angels, and in which, by rising from the dead, he was crowned with glory and honor and set over the works of the Father’s hands.”

Again, when he says, “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matt. 11): “If, speaking this of his Father, he had lied, the power of divine works would not have accompanied him, nor would the Father always have been with him,” as he himself says: “He who sent me is with me and has not left me alone” (John 8), etc.

Likewise the Holy Spirit bears testimony to this man that he is Christ, or that he is the Son of God, the power of God. For, just as he said, “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear testimony concerning me, and you also will bear testimony” (John 16), so it was, is, and shall be until the end of the age. These three witnesses bear testimony in heaven, and these three are one. Not “these three are one person,” but “these three are one” (1 John 5) [Col. 0583B]: three in persons, one in substance; and the testimony of those three is one, namely that the man Jesus, who was thought to be Joseph’s son, is the Son of God, equally almighty with his Father.

For his omnipotence must also be believed on the testimony of those witnesses who bear testimony to him on earth: the spirit, water, and blood (ibid.). For the spirit, namely the rational soul which he laid down upon the cross and took up again when he wished, could in no way have despoiled hell or opened paradise to the thief unless he had been almighty. Nor could the water and blood flowing from his side have drowned, or been able to drown, the invisible Pharaoh with his army had it lacked the omnipotence of divine power.

Photinus paid no heed to these heavenly and earthly testimonies—indeed, the one testimony of the three bearing witness in heaven and the three on earth—he who denied that the man born of the Virgin was God. Paul of Samosata, likewise blinded by the same error, taught that divinity was alien to man and humanity alien to God, so that neither God was truly called man nor man God, though God dwelt more fully in the man whom the Virgin bore than in other saints. Nestorius too, following Photinus, divides the man from God [Col. 0583D], denying that the Virgin bore God.

Against these, blessed Jerome says in his exposition of Jeremiah:

> “If everyone who trusts in man is cursed, and Paul of Samosata and Photinus, although they proclaim the Savior holy and exalted in all virtues, nevertheless confess him to be a man, then those who place their hope in a man will be cursed. But if it is objected to us that we also believe in him who said: ‘Now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth which I heard from God’ (John 8), we shall answer with the apostolic saying: ‘Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer.’ For if death has been swallowed up in victory, why should not the lowliness of the flesh, assumed for human salvation, have passed into the majesty of divinity, so that the two should make one, and we should worship not a creature but the Creator, who is blessed forever?”

Therefore, since Jerome teaches that when Christ is worshipped, not a creature but the Creator is worshipped, let those who teach that the man is not to be worshipped with *latria*—but only, as they say, with *dulia*—be silent. Let them be silent, I say, concerning foolish and undisciplined questions. Opposing these, blessed Ambrose says in his commentary on Luke:

> “Since Paul judged that he knew nothing except Christ Jesus, and him crucified, and Peter thought that nothing else ought to be confessed except the Son of God, when and how he was born do we investigate with the scrutiny of human weakness? Paul knew that in these questions there was more occasion for stumbling than advancement in edification [Col. 0584B], and therefore he judged that he knew nothing except Christ Jesus, and him crucified. Peter knew that all things are in the Son of God; for the Father gave all things to the Son. If he gave all things, he poured forth eternity and majesty as well.”

These are Ambrose’s words.

But those importunate disputants, who know or wish to believe nothing except what they can comprehend by intellect and reason, do not desist from undisciplined questions unless apostolic authority sets them a limit. Your prudence should consider how this ought to be done; it is not for us to instruct you, since we lesser ones ought rather to be instructed by you great ones and bound to the ancient boundaries of faith.

For holding and in no way transgressing those boundaries, we little ones shall fight with all the greater confidence, Christ favoring us [Col. 0584C], in proportion as apostolic authority more evidently stands by us. It has so far stood by me, though insignificant, as appears from the aforementioned letters sent from the Apostolic See and serving in my favor. But in the writings of the Roman pontiffs Leo and Gregory, and of the others now reigning with God, I had and have my firmest refuge, as I expressed in a certain letter, whose text is as follows:

> “To Innocent, by divine favor bishop of the Apostolic See, brother G., however unworthy a servant of your holiness: devoted prayers with obedience. Lord, you have become a refuge for us in the Lord, who, before the mountains were made or the world was formed, predestined you for us as a merciful protector against the violence of the ungodly. For I think that, if we did not have the asylum of the Apostolic See, we should already have been reduced to nothing by the unjust powers of the ungodly.
>
> “But you, blessed man, who are not accustomed to walk in the counsel of the ungodly or sit in the chair of pestilence, but in the chair of apostolic power, through the eminent affection of your mercy have become a refuge for us; indeed, the eternal mercy of Christ, reigning in your heart, has become for us a tower of strength against the face of the ungodly who have afflicted and still afflict us [Col. 0584D].
>
> “When Peter Leo exercised tyranny, we suffered much from his supporters, when we saw the ungodly man exalted and raised like the cedars of Lebanon. ‘But I passed by, and behold, he was not’ (Ps. 36). Yet heresies exist, because, as the Apostle maintains, they must exist. Among them we have labored and still labor. For because we once refuted in writings and speech the heretical opinion of certain people who maintained that Christ’s body is consecrated outside the Church even by excommunicated persons [Note: Elsewhere Gerhoh admits that it is consecrated as to its essence, though not as to its fruit.], unless you, Father, had then been my refuge, heretics would have condemned me as a heretic.
>
> “But because the locust is ready to consume the remnant of the caterpillar, evils succeed evils. For from the smoke of the pit of the abyss, as John foresaw in the Apocalypse, locusts have now come forth: namely, several disciples of Peter Abelard, who affirm that the man taken from the Virgin is not God but God’s unique dwelling-place. Although all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in him, they nevertheless deny that the name ‘Godhead’ properly belongs to him so that he may be called God, except by a figurative mode of speech, in which we name the container for the contained [Col. 0585B], or the contained for the container.
>
> “For figurative speech occurs, if that which has something is named for what it has—as often happens when we call a man-made temple ‘church,’ because it has or contains the Church, that is, the righteous assembled in it. And in the Gospel, where it is said, ‘He himself believed, and his whole house’ (John 4), the household is called ‘house,’ because the household has or contains a house. Thus, they say, it is figurative speech when either we assign the name of God to a man who has God within himself, or call God abiding in a man ‘man.’
>
> “But because we preach God properly as man and man properly as God, lest perhaps we run in vain, Father, we have sent you through the bearer of this letter a treatise on this question. If your authority approves it [Col. 0585C], I shall again sing what I sang before: ‘Lord, you have become a refuge for us’ (Ps. 89)—not because I trust in you as a mortal man, but in Peter, indeed in the rock, against whose strength the gates of hell shall not prevail. May it therefore be granted me even now, and for as long as I live, continually to rejoice in singing: ‘Lord, you have become a refuge for us,’ and the rest to the end of the Psalm.”

## LETTER XXI*

### Letter of Cardinal C. to Gerhoh

He praises his doctrine and warns him not to debate matters of subtler argument before the unlearned.

C., by God’s grace cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, to his most reverend master G.: greeting and affection [Col. 0585D].

The Roman Church has long known your learning and sound doctrine and has approved it in every way as fortified by the authority of the canonical Scriptures. We also, who have conferred with you in frequent discussion, have thought and still think the same. Therefore we were greatly astonished at what was publicly reported concerning your person in our court, and we never brought ourselves to believe it.

But now, because we have seen, read, and examined your writings through your faithful messenger, we consider utterly vain the things said by your adversaries.
