We advise your affection, however, by no means to seek to hold discussions of this kind before a popular crowd, lest, through an occasion supplied to those who speak against you—God forbid—the people be led into error [Col. 0586A].

## LETTER XXII

### Letter of Cardinal Hyacinth to Gerhoh

He writes that, as Gerhoh had desired, the pope is attending to the controversy *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man*; he also teaches that Alexander is held to be the legitimate pontiff by the universal Church, with few exceptions.

Hyacinth, by God’s grace cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, to his friend Master G. of Richersberg, most dearly beloved in Christ: greeting and sincere affection in Christ.

We have received your charitable letter with all kindness; after more carefully considering its contents, we conferred sufficiently with the lord pope concerning them. Although he has many matters to attend to, he nevertheless gave a brief answer to your question. Yet we are [were] not without great astonishment that you wrote so late to both the lord pope and ourselves [Col. 0586B].

For we cannot at all believe that your discerning mind could be persuaded that the intrusion of Octavian—who, without any election, whether by cardinals or non-cardinals, presumed with diabolical audacity to cloak himself in the papal mantle—can invalidate the canonically celebrated election of the lord pope. This is especially so because that election has been approved by all kings bearing the Christian name, with one exception; likewise by all secular and ecclesiastical princes of the kingdoms of France, England, Scotland, Ireland, Spain, Sicily, Hungary, Greece, and the East; and also by the Romans and almost all Italians. If any of these agree with Octavian, they do so not guided by God’s Spirit but rather compelled by fear of the emperor.

Therefore, since our Lord did not take honor to himself but was rather called by his brethren, as Aaron was by his brother Moses, you who are led by the Spirit of God ought to constitute yourselves an impregnable wall for his and the Church’s fidelity. We therefore earnestly urge your charity in the Lord to devote yourselves in every way to the peace of the Church and to disclose your wishes to us confidently, because, insofar as we are able with God’s help, we shall take care to satisfy you [Col. 0586D].

## LETTER XXIII

### The Same to Otto I, Bishop of Freising

He defends Hilary against a certain unnamed author who wished it to have been handed down by Hilary that Christ’s body was not glorified above the bodies of the other saints, nor did the human nature in Christ, in the grace it received, surpass the excellence of any angel.

To the venerable bishop O. of the Church of Freising [Note: From the Admont manuscript], brother G. of Richersberg: devoted prayers with faithful service.

Recently a certain little book addressed to your prudence came into our hands, as though to be examined and approved by you [Col. 0587A]. Since it is woven from the teaching of Master Gilbert, as we have detected it in his glosses and censured it in writings which we previously sent to you and yours, it pours out at its end, like a scorpion’s tail, a poison far more perverse than anything we have ever read in the earlier heresies concerning Christ. For the Arians, Photinians, Apollinarists, Bonosians, and the other heretics who detracted from Christ taught that, although he was subordinate to the Father, he was nevertheless superior to the angels. Indeed, the holy Church believes and celebrates this even concerning his holy Mother: that she has been exalted above the choirs of angels, in which pure humanity is acknowledged to have been glorified. But the novelty of this teaching urges one to believe concerning the man whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world [Col. 0587B] that his body is not glorified beyond the bodies of the other saints, nor does he himself, in the grace which he received, surpass the excellence of any angel.

To confirm the meaning of this pestilential teaching, they think they have great patrons, Hilary and Augustine. For Hilary says in the eleventh book *On the Holy Trinity*:

> “Since, then, this origin of earthly bodies surpasses in the condition of a higher state, and God, found in the form of a servant, becomes conformed to the glory of the Lord’s body, how can he who bestowed upon us the form of his glorified body himself be unable to bestow upon his body anything beyond what is common to us and to himself?”

These words of Hilary, compared with what precedes and follows, have a Catholic meaning and agree in every respect with our assertion [Col. 0587C]. This is plainly clear in our carefully corrected manuscripts, where the preceding statement, when read as a question, is understood without error. Such is the passage in the Apostle where, when it is said, “Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect?” (Rom. VIII), there follows, “God who justifies?” (ibid.). If this is read interrogatively, as it ought to be, and said, “God, who justifies?”, a sound meaning arises for all who grasp it. But if it is read affirmatively, the sense is full of error.

Thus, when Hilary says concerning Christ:

> “How can he who bestowed upon us the form of his glorified body himself be unable to bestow upon his body anything beyond what is common to us and to himself?”

if it is read interrogatively, as it ought to be, it produces [Col. 0587D] a Catholic meaning. For under the form of a question the assertion is denied more sharply: namely, lest Christ be thought so weak that he who bestowed upon us the form of his glorified body could himself bestow upon his body nothing beyond what is common to us and to himself. For who can estimate how great are the things he bestowed upon his own body, things wholly impossible to confer upon the bodies of the saints? What saint’s body is truly food, or is found in several places at one and the same time? What body, however glorified, will ever be comparable in glory to that body of which it is said: “Wherever the body may be, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. XXIV)?

Whether by the eagles you understand the angelic powers or holy souls, they desire to gaze upon the countenance of that body, which, like the body of the sun, gives light to the moon so that it may be perfect for ever when it directly beholds that body’s countenance without the interposition of an earthly shadow—the shadow which commonly causes an eclipse at times to souls remaining in the flesh. Though bodily, that countenance is nevertheless glorified beyond all the bodies of saints [Col. 0588A], whose brightness is compared to the stars, with the brightness which the Word had with the Father before the world came to be. For if, when he appeared transfigured on the mountain, his face shone like the sun, how much more now, on the mountain of the Father’s exaltation, does he shine like the sun in its strength? The countenance shown to John in the Apocalypse openly distinguishes him from the other saints, who “will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.” For of none of them is it written that he shines “as the sun shines in its strength”; for each of them will shine in a strength not his own but that of him who will then be all in all, when the whole Christ will be subject to the Father in all his members.

But the Sun of righteousness alone, in his solar body, with the cloud of mortality wiped away, will shine in his own strength—namely, glorified with the glory of the Father and with his own glory. For he entered into his own glory.

[Col. 0588B] I say “his own,” not another’s, because the glory of divine omnipotence, which Christ received in his humanity, he eternally had and has in his divinity. The eternal, immeasurable glory, power, wisdom, and goodness of the Godhead was not so given to the assumed man as to be taken from the Word; for the Word made flesh so gave the assumed man the whole glory which he had, that he retained it whole. “This is a great mystery,” says the Apostle: “which was manifested in the flesh, believed in by the world, taken up in glory” (I Tim. III) [Col. 0588C]. This glory is the Word’s by nature, but the assumed man’s by grace, since such an assumption itself came about through grace.

Those who read him carefully will readily find that holy Hilary held this view. For one reads in him: “All glory was gained, not for the Word, but for the flesh”; and elsewhere: “Certainly, for him who received it, he demands the brightness which he did not cease to possess”; and again: “So that that which belonged to time might receive the glory of his brightness which is without time.” Other statements of this kind are found in him, by which those may be refuted who presume to establish their error from his sayings [Col. 0588D] by twisting them into a perverse sense. They do this in many places, which it is not now necessary to discuss one by one, since we are weary of repeatedly restating matters already set down and presented to the Roman Church, made known to its pontiffs Innocent and Eugenius, and approved by them as consonant with the ancient teachings of the Roman pontiffs.

And indeed, with respect to Hilary, it is no wonder that they corrupt his words as though obscure. But we greatly wonder at Augustine’s sayings being corrupted by them—whether through imprudence or impudence—so that his opinion has produced error among them, if indeed they conceived this utterly false meaning from him and not rather from the father of lies: that they affirm that the man assumed into the one person of the Trinity [Col. 0589A] does not surpass angelic dignity.

To make this clearer, let us set out the words of the question posed by Peter, the disciple of Bishop Gilbert. Writing against us, he says among other things:

> “It is established that Christ, according to his humanity, is always less than the Father, since in that which we call humanity he does not, as Augustine says, surpass the excellence of the angels in nature; and what has already been bestowed upon his body is common to himself and to us.”

And after a few intervening words he says:

> “Since, I say, the glory which he bestowed upon his body is common to himself and to us, to investigate in what manner his body is equal to God the Father in the same glory is a matter for leisure, not diligence; since Augustine also says in the sermon, chapter seven, on John: ‘The Only-Begotten, since he is Lord of all, is without doubt Lord of the angels by the nature in which he is God—equal not to angels but rather to the Father; but by the grace in which he is man, he does not surpass the excellence of any angel.’” [Col. 0589B]

Taking these words of Augustine as though they were an argument, he continues the course of his reasoning:

> “Let them hear Augustine asserting that Christ, in the grace of his humanity, is not superior to the angels, and that his body, in the grace which it has, is equal to the Father.”

[Note: [Col. 0589D] The manuscript reads “they hear” (*audiunt*).]

> “Now, if he had said, ‘In the nature in which he is man, he does not surpass the excellence of angels,’ perhaps some opportunity for evasion would have been left to them. Yet let them understand that we introduced this for the reason that we think they can at least understand this: that nature, which concerns the authority of creation, is one thing, and grace, which pertains to the bounty of the giver, another. [Col. 0589C] For if ‘the grace in which he is man’ and ‘the assumed nature’ are understood to be the same, the author will seem to have spoken without significance for the point at issue, since in that nature he was previously beneath the excellence of the angels. Certainly, if he were conformed to God in the glory of his body, he would have nothing further that he could bestow upon his body beyond what he has already bestowed.”

In these arguments it matters little to me that I should be judged by those who compress the immeasurable divine glory given to Christ into the measure of angelic dignity, a dignity to which we also believe holy human beings are made equal. Yet, because we cannot bear Augustine’s sayings to be so corrupted by them that he should be thought to agree with their error, I do not grudge inserting his very words here [Col. 0589D]. For in the sermon, chapter seven, on John, distinguishing between the only-begotten Son of God and his members—that is, the adopted sons—he says:

> “In the Son the Father loves us, because in him he chose us before the foundation of the world. For he who loves the Only-Begotten surely also loves his members, whom he adopted into him through him. Nor are we therefore equal to the Only-Begotten Son, through whom we were created and re-created, because it was said, ‘You loved them as you loved me.’ For the one who says, ‘As this, so that,’ does not always signify equality; sometimes it means only that because this is, that also is, or that this is in order that that may be. Thus here also: ‘You loved them,’ he says, ‘as you loved me.’ [Col. 0590A] This means nothing other than: You loved them because you loved me. For he who loves the Son would not fail to love the Son’s members, nor is there another reason for loving his members except that he loves the Son. But he loves the Son according to his divinity, because he begot him equal to himself. He also loves him according to that in which he is man, because that same Only-Begotten Word was also made flesh, and the Word’s flesh is dear to him because of the Word. But he loves us because we are the members of him whom he loves. Therefore the love by which God loves is incomprehensible and unchangeable.”

And after a few intervening words he says:

> “Since therefore he hates none of the things he made, who can worthily express how greatly he loves the members of his Only-Begotten, and how much more he loves the Only-Begotten himself, in whom all things visible and invisible were created, and whom he loves in the most perfect order as those things are ordered in their kinds? For by the bounty of his grace he brings the members of the Only-Begotten to equality with the holy angels. But the Only-Begotten, since he is Lord of all, is without doubt Lord of the angels by nature, because he is God, equal not to angels but rather to the Father; but by grace, because he is man, how does he not surpass the excellence of every angel, since he is one person of flesh and Word?” [Col. 0590B]

Here the theft of the Gilbertines must be noted. For when blessed Augustine says by way of question, “How does he not surpass the excellence of every angel?”, they stole the interrogative adverb from the middle of his words and confidently assert in his words that which [Col. 0590C] he more emphatically denies by means of the question. They say concerning Christ, “He does not surpass the excellence of any angel”—a view that is wholly heretical and a teaching that is devilish. For just as the devil is a liar and the father of lies, so these teachers beget a lie in the hearts of their hearers, especially those to whom, because they did not receive the love of the truth, God sends a working of error, so that they may believe a lie—and such a lie that there is no worse lie: namely, when someone stubbornly teaches falsehood against the truth of the Christian faith.

For what is more false than what they say: that Christ, inasmuch as he is man, or according to the grace in him by which he is man, does not surpass [Col. 0590D] the dignity of any angel? And what is truer than what blessed Augustine teaches in interrogative form, saying: “How does he not surpass the excellence of every angel, since he is one person of flesh and Word?” This is the same as saying: assuredly, he surpasses the excellence of every angel. Do you ask how greatly he surpasses it? Hear the Apostle: “Having become so much better than the angels,” he says, “as he has inherited a more excellent name than they” (Heb. IV). To which of the angels was it said: “A name has been given which is above every name” (Phil. II)?

Concerning this name, given to the man by God the Father and denied to him in Master Gilbert’s glosses on the Apostle under the title of a certain monk Ambrose, surnamed Audbert [Col. 0591A], we previously wrote so extensively to you and to your highly learned clerics that it seems superfluous to repeat the matter here. At that time the aforesaid Bishop Gilbert was, presumably, excused to me by you and yours on the ground that he did not hold the view of that Ambrose, whose opinion he perhaps included because he found it set down in older glosses.

But these disciples of his reduce and compress to the measure of the glory either of holy human beings, by corrupting Hilary, or of holy angels, by corrupting Augustine—as is evident from what has been said—the glory and grace, given without measure, of the human nature assumed into the Son of God. Unless they are checked, they cause the iniquity of their master to be remembered in the sight of the Lord and of the holy Roman Church [Col. 0591B], whose ancient and recent pontiffs are opposed by this teaching of such perverse novelty.

We cannot sufficiently marvel at their arguments, in which we perceive the dogmas of the Arians being revived in part. For they say that the following contribute very greatly to the dignity and glory of majesty: that someone rewards one who obeys, hears one who intercedes, subjects all things to one who asks, places them under his feet, blesses one who offers; and that no one whatever, unless he is uncatholic, ignorant like a gentile, denying like a Jew, or altering the faith like an antichrist, would dare to deny this. For the Father bestowed upon him, as upon a high priest whose origin from the Father is beyond telling, the blessing of all nations. But who is greater: the one who blesses, or the one who is blessed?

[Col. 0591C] These assertions once belonged to the Arians, who maintained that the Son was less than the Father; and the holy Fathers reasonably opposed them, because the voluntary obedience, not forced obedience, offered for the salvation of human beings is reckoned to the glory rather than the disgrace of the man who thus obeyed. In short, for this reason God exalted him and gave him the name above every name (Phil. II); for this reason he subjected all things under his feet (Eph. I). This very obedience was a petition, in which he was worthy to be heard because of his reverence—because of his reverence, I say—in whom there was no fault, and whom no necessity of his own misery compelled to make such a petition. Rather, the compassion of mercy required it, in order that things thus lost might be restored.

Certainly, this work of restoration is not less than the work of creation. Indeed, it is more venerable that through a human being there should be resurrection of the dead, who had deserved life, than that through the Word there should be creation of living beings, who had deserved nothing good. For it is more wonderful for life to be restored to the dead who had deserved everlasting death than for life to be given to those who had deserved nothing.

Nevertheless, grant that, when through his obedience he has subjected all things to the Father, so that God may be all in all, then he himself also will be subject to the Father [Col. 0591D] (which, as Augustine maintains, is said lest the human substance, however glorified, be thought to have been transformed into divine substance by a changeability of nature—a meaning which the holy Church condemned in the heretic Eutyches). Grant, I say, that the God-man, the Son of God, is eternally subject to the Father: must this devout and voluntary subjection therefore be reckoned to him as disgrace? Far from it!

[Col. 0592A] For Saint Ambrose says in the fifth book addressed to Emperor Gratian:

> “Just as the Apostle says that in Christ, through the flesh which is the pledge of our salvation, we sit in the heavenly places—although of course we are not sitting—so he also is said to be subject in us through the assumption of our nature.”

Likewise:

> “It is written that, ‘when we were dead through sins, he made us alive together in Christ, by whose grace you have been saved’ (Eph. II), ‘and raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.’ I acknowledge what is written, but not in such a way as to allow that God suffers human beings to sit at his right hand, but that they sit in Christ, because he is the foundation of all and the head [Col. 0592B] of the Church, in whom our common nature according to the flesh won the privilege of the heavenly seat. Therefore, just as we sit in him through communion in bodily nature, so he who, through assuming our flesh, was made a curse for us—though a curse cannot, of course, fall upon the blessed Son of God—so, I say, he will be subject in us through the obedience of all, when the gentile has believed, when the Jew has acknowledged the one whom he crucified, when the Manichaean has worshipped the one whom he did not believe had come in the flesh, when the Arian has confessed as almighty the one whom he denied; when, finally, in all there shall be the wisdom of God, righteousness, peace, love, and resurrection. Let us therefore gather briefly the conclusion of the whole explanation [Col. 0592C]: unity of power excludes the notion of an injurious subjection.”

The same author says:

> “And if you ask how he is subject in us, he himself shows it when he says: ‘I was in prison, and you came to me; I was sick, and you visited me’—weak in that in which he is subject” (Matt. XXV).

While Ambrose says these things, we should rightly understand that the Son is to be subject to the Father in his members, when the subjection of those members themselves has been completed and brought to perfection. But even if that subjection, by which God will be all in all, is to occur in the humanity of his own person, it must not be regarded as injurious but as glorious. For even in the Godhead we read that the Son is subject to the Father, yet he is not therefore to be thought or held lesser or inferior.

[Col. 0592D] Thus, in the confession of faith written at Sirmium by the Easterners against Photinus, among the other errors this error too was condemned: that the Son was thought either not subject to the Father or, if subject, by no means equal to him. The Fathers of the said council declare:

> “If anyone, because he calls the Son Lord and God, and the Father Lord, should call them two Lords—since he speaks of Lord from Lord—let him be anathema. For we do not so equalize or compare the Son with the Father as not to understand that he is subject. For he did not go down into Sodom without the Father’s will; nor did he rain from himself, but from the Lord, that is, by the Father’s authority; nor does he sit at the right hand by himself, but hears the Father saying: ‘Sit at my right hand.’”

Discussing this synodal statement, Hilary says among other things:

> “The Son is not compared or made equal to the Father while he is subject through the service of obedience; while the Lord rains from the Lord; while he has sat at the right hand of God; while he is sent, while he receives, while in all things he obeys the will of him who sent him. But subjection in devotion is not diminution of essence, nor does the duty of religion make the nature inferior. For through this—that God the Father is unbegotten, and the only-begotten Son of God is God—there is nevertheless one God; and both the Son’s subjection and his dignity are taught, while none but the Son is called subject to him. Though he is of God the Father, he yet has from nature a name not of another but of the one whose Son he is; and he is subject to the Father both in obedience and in name, yet in such a manner that the subjection of the name bears witness to the property of a natural and undiffering essence.”

Thus Hilary speaks of the Son’s subjection in his divinity [Col. 0593B], without diminution through that subjection of the equality in which both he who is subject and he to whom he is subject are worshipped as the one most high God. Following in his footsteps, we likewise affirm in nearly the same words that subjection in devotion is not a diminution of glory, nor does the duty of religion make inferior the human nature in the only-begotten Son of God. For through this—that the unbegotten Father is God, and the son of the Virgin, who is also the Son of God the Father, is God through the divinity of the assuming Word, fully given and innate to the assumed man—he is called and is Son of God the Father not by adoption but by the nature of sonship; and he too is to be called God equally with his Father, having a name not of another but of him whose Son he is, and being subject to the Father both in obedience and in name. Yet the subjection of the name bears witness to the property of the natural and undiffering essence by which the assumed man is God equally with the assuming Word, and with the Father who begets the Word and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Word [Col. 0593C], without a duplication or triplication of the Godhead, which always remains in the highest simplicity. This may be declared either of the man to whom it was fully given, according to Isaiah: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come” (Isa. IX), or collectively of the three persons of the one Trinity.

For as there is one Godhead of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so there is the same one Godhead of the Word assuming the man and of the man assumed into the Word [Col. 0593D], as we recently wrote to the venerable father of the universal Church, Pope Adrian. But when we wrote to him, this teaching which we are now opposing had not yet come to our notice: namely, the teaching concerning the glory in the assumed man being of such a measure that he, who is Lord of the angels not only in the divine essence in which he created the angels, but also in the human essence in which, obeying the Father, he restored their number and filled up their losses, does not surpass the angels. Drinking from the torrent on the way, he shattered heads in the land of many; therefore he lifted up his head. For by oath the Lord caused him to grow in that nature in which he could grow, in which also, in order that he might grow and be God not only of Jews but also of gentiles [Col. 0594A], the blessing of all nations was given to him.

Here the opponent has an occasion for contradiction, as we noted above. “Who,” he says, “is greater: the one who blesses, or the one who is blessed? Is not the one who blesses, according to the Apostle, greater?” Here, lest we appear to wish to philosophize before philosophers wise in their own eyes, we show them simply that, even if the one who blesses is greater than the one blessed, nevertheless the person blessed, once the blessing has been received, is sometimes no longer inferior; indeed, is sometimes greater than the one who blesses.

For if a bishop, with an archbishop’s consent and permission, blesses someone as bishop—for this too may lawfully be done according to the canons—is not the man who was lower before the blessing made equal to the bishop who blesses him when he receives the blessing? Likewise, if someone elected archbishop is blessed by one of the suffragans, the others cooperating, then, though he was lower than the one blessing him before the blessing, once blessed he must be regarded not as lower but as greater [Col. 0594B]. Therefore the Apostle’s foregoing statement must be understood in a manner that does not produce an absurd meaning contrary to sound faith.

For that blessed man who came in the name of the Lord was so blessed by the Father, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, that he is God blessed not among all things but above all things for ever (Rom. IX). Accordingly, when so great a blessing has been received, the blessed man is not lower than God who blesses him in such a way that he is God blessed above all things. By this blessing there was given to him the name which is above every name. Before that gift, human nature truly was lower than divine nature; but in the Son of God it was secretly glorified at the conception and openly magnified at the ascension in the highest name, so that its greatness is immeasurable. This greatness must be weighed not by extension of bulk but by immeasurability of power, especially after there was given to it the name above every name, so manifestly declared to the world that the sound of the apostles testifying to it went forth into all the earth: as his going forth is from the highest heaven, so is his course even to its highest point [Col. 0594C].

Therefore, although the supreme Father was greater than him before the blessing, he who has now advanced through the Father’s blessing and glorification to the highest point is not, in the glory given him, to be considered less than the giver, since every tongue now confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father [Col. 0594D]. Thus Hilary says in the ninth book *On the Trinity*:

> “If the Father is greater by the authority of the giver, is the Son then lesser by the acknowledgement of the gift? The giver, therefore, is greater; but he to whom oneness is given is no longer lesser. If this is not given to Jesus—that he is to be confessed in the glory of God the Father—then he is lesser than the Father. But if it is given to him to be in that glory in which the Father is, you have both that the Father is greater in the authority of the giver, and that they are one in the confession of what is given.”

Likewise:

> “The Father is greater when he is asked to restore glory to the assumed man; the Son is not lesser when he resumes glory with the Father.”

Likewise:

> “The Father who is to glorify the Son is greater; the Son glorified in the Father [Col. 0595A] is not lesser.”

Since holy Hilary says these things, we, holding views consonant with his, may say: the Father who is to bless the Son is greater; the Son blessed by the Father is not lesser—especially by that blessing through which he was so blessed as to come in the name of the Lord. That is, the Lord’s name is his name—not in the manner in which many are called lords, since there are many lords, but in the manner in which the name “Lord” properly belongs to God alone, who reigns and rules over all things with divine dominion. Christ’s divinity always had this dominion, and his humanity received it when blessed by the Father, so that even in the form of a servant it possessed the name Lord and came blessed in the name of the Lord.

He was anticipated from eternity with this blessing of sweetness [Col. 0595B], when the man was predestined to be the Son of God to come. I say “Son,” not as others are sons by the grace of adoption, but in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, by which the Father sanctified him in that very fact that, willing to be called and to be his Father, he gave him the glory of the Only-Begotten and likewise the blessing of all nations: namely, in order that he might be God not only of Jews but also of all nations. He gave this to him and confirmed his covenant upon his head.

For the head of that man thus blessed and sanctified is God—or, if it is preferable to say so, his very divinity. Without it, if anyone understands that man, it is as though he considered some other human being able to be a human being without his head, which is the governing part of his essence. The governing part of the first human being, who was made into a living soul, was the intellectual mind. But when he was in this honor, he did not understand; and, unwilling to understand in order to act rightly, he horribly disfigured his head, because he corrupted his intellectual and rational faculty. So too his imitators still disfigure their own head when they pray with covered head: that is, when in prayer they desire sensible rather than intelligible gifts of God.

Such a covering has been placed over the heart of the Jews, who desire earthly rather than heavenly goods. Therefore they do not perceive the brightness of Christ’s countenance, the Sun of righteousness shining with divine brightness, who is the second man incomparably to be preferred to the first [Col. 0595C]. For the governing part of the second man, who was made into a life-giving spirit, is not an intellectual mind but superintellectual divinity. Without this, if anyone conceives of him, it is as though he imagined another man to be human without his governing principle—which is impossible.

Accordingly, those who think of the man assumed into God’s person apart from his divinity, so far as lies in them deprive him of his head by a false understanding, though this truly cannot be done. Hence Augustine says in the sixth book *On the Trinity*:

> “How is God the head of Christ—that is, how is the Trinity the head of Christ, when Christ is in the Trinity, so that he is Trinity? Or is it that the Father together with the Son is head to him who is the Son alone? For with the Son the Father is God; but the Son alone is Christ, especially because the Word, now made flesh, speaks, and according to this humility the Father is also greater, as he says: ‘Because the Father is greater than I.’ Thus that very being God, which he is one with the Father, is the head of the mediator man, which he alone is. For if we rightly call the mind the governing part of a human being, that is, as it were the head of human substance, since the human being together with the mind is human, why is the Word with the Father, which is simultaneously God, not much more fittingly and much more truly the head of Christ, although Christ cannot be understood as man except together with the Word [Col. 0596A], which was made flesh?”

Likewise, in book two:

> “The man was assumed, in whose form the person of God the Word might be presented—not in order that he might have the Word as other holy wise persons have it, but beyond his fellows, not indeed because he possessed the Word more fully, so as to be of more excellent wisdom than the rest, but because he himself was the Word. For the Word in flesh is one thing; the Word made flesh another—that is, the Word in a human being is one thing; the Word as human being another. For ‘flesh’ is used for ‘human being’ where it says: ‘The Word was made flesh’ (John I).”

Likewise, in book four, explaining the saying of the Wise Man, “Send forth, Lord, wisdom from the throne of your majesty,” he says:

> “It is sent in one way so as to be [Note: [Col. 0595D] The edition reads ‘with.’] in a human being; it was sent in another way so as itself to be human. For it passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets; likewise it fills the holy angels and works through them all things fitting to such ministries. But when the fullness of time came, it was sent not to fill angels, nor to be an angel—except insofar as it proclaimed the counsel of the Father, which was also its own—nor to be with human beings or in human beings, for it had been thus before in the patriarchs and prophets, but so that the Word itself might be made flesh, that is, might become human.” [Col. 0596C]

The same author says in book one:

> “Because the form of God received the form of a servant, both are God and both are human; but both are God because of the God who receives, and both are human because of the human being received. For by that assumption neither of them was converted and changed into the other. The Godhead was not changed into a creature so as to cease to be Godhead, nor was the creature changed into Godhead so as to cease to be a creature.”

With Augustine’s statements carefully considered, it is apparent that [Col. 0596D] humanity is so united with God in the one person of the Trinity, and God with humanity, that this very union of the human being with God is that sanctification by which the Father sanctified him and sent him into the world; and it is that blessing by which the same human being came as the blessed King of Israel in the name of the Lord, whom God the Father blessed for ever, so that his kingdom has no end, just as eternity has no end.

Hence it is that, even before the child born knew how to call father or mother, as is read in Isaiah, while he himself reigned and defended his land, the strength of Damascus was taken away and the spoils of Samaria carried off before the king of the Assyrians. “Call his name, *Hasten to strip the spoil, hurry to plunder*; for before [Col. 0597A] the child knows how to call Father and mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria shall be taken away” (Isa. 8). For, indeed, against the tribe of Judah, from which this child was to be born, Damascus was defended by this child not yet born from those tribes of Judah and Jerusalem; Samaria and Damascus were plundered through the king of the Assyrians, who destroyed Samaria and subjected Damascus to himself, and so humbled it that it could not prevail against the house of David, in which this child reigned before he had an adoptive father and a virgin mother. His name, therefore, was rightly called “Hasten to strip the spoil, hurry to plunder,” because marvelous was the haste, wonderful the swiftness, of this child fighting before his birth and stripping his enemies.

Therefore, through the mystery of unity in the reigning Word [Col. 0597B] over all things, the man then to be assumed—and now assumed—into God, the Son of God, was present. For this reason, as the Apostle testifies, Christ was tempted in the wilderness. “Let us not tempt Christ,” he says, “as some of them tempted him” (1 Cor. 10). He shows that Christ, though not yet born, was already then tempted in the wilderness. Read Jerome, who discusses this mystery of unity at considerable length in his sermon on the Assumption of the Blessed Mary, and who affirms on Scriptural authority that God is made one body with humanity and that humanity is coeternal with God—although humanity is not without beginning, nor can the name or property of body belong to the supreme Spirit. Why do you question me concerning the eternity of the human being eternally assumed into God? Ask Jerome, who affirms that humanity is coeternal with God.

[Col. 0597C] Blessed Ambrose agrees with him, expounding in his commentary on Luke the words, “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matt. 28): “If he gave all things,” he says, “he poured over him eternity and majesty.” Therefore argue as much as you please in order to deny eternity and immensity to the human being to whom all things have been delivered by his Father. I place greater faith in [the words of] the Word himself, who says: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Luke 10). And again: “My Father, what he gave me, is greater than all” (John 10 [printed: 29]). Explaining this saying, the venerable priest Bede says in a homily:

> “But that which is greater than all, which the Father gave to the Mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ, is this: that he should be his only-begotten Son, in no respect unlike the begetting Father either in nature, or inferior in power, [Col. 0597D] or later in time. This equality, which the Lord himself possessed in divinity with the Father before the world existed, he received in humanity from the time of the incarnation.”

Do you hear of equality innate to the Word with the Father and given to the human being whom the Word of God, equal to the Father, united to himself? Do you hear this in an ancient homily, long and publicly circulated and recited in church assemblies, and do you accuse us as though we held a new doctrine, when we teach nothing which we do not show in the writings of the ancient Fathers expounding the Scriptures? Show even one Catholic doctor who agrees with you in your sense, in which you deny that the human being assumed into God was made conformed to God—what you think Hilary taught, though he teaches the contrary.

For he says in Book IX *On the Trinity*:

> [Col. 0598A] “This was acquired for humanity: that it should be God. Yet, once assumed, it could in no way remain in the unity of God unless, through the unity of God, it naturally passed into the unity of God; so that, because the Word was God by nature, the Word also, having become flesh, might again be in the nature of God; and so the man Jesus Christ might remain in the glory of God the Father, if the flesh were united in the glory of the Word, and the Word made flesh might then return, even according to humanity, into the unity of the Father’s nature, when the assumed flesh had obtained the glory of the Word.”

And below:

> “For, in order that he might remain in his unity as he had remained, the Father was to glorify him with himself, because through the obedience of the dispensation he had passed beyond the unity of his glory: namely, in order that through glorification he might again be in that nature in which he had been united by the mystery [Col. 0598B] of the divine birth; and that, glorified by the Father with himself, what he had before with him might remain; nor might the assumption of the nature of a servant estrange from him the nature of the form of God. Rather, he might glorify with himself the form of a servant, so that it might remain in the form of God, because he who remained in the form of God was the same one who was in the form of a servant; and since the form of a servant was to be glorified in the form of God, it was to be glorified with him, in whose form the assumed condition of the servant-form was to be honored.”

From Hilary’s words it is clear that he did not think that the Lord’s body was not conformed to the Lord. For the Lord’s body is so called for no other reason than that the Lord, embodied or incarnate, works life for believing human beings through the body [Col. 0598C] of his flesh, just as his divinity works life for angels who behold the unbounded light. Because human beings cannot see that light, they are saved by believing and will have eternal life through Christ’s flesh—what the holy angels have through his divinity.

Whence, then, does the flesh have life abiding in itself, so as to confer eternal life on the one who eats it, except because it possesses that life as assumed into fellowship with the divine nature? Thus Hilary says in Book VIII concerning the Lord’s body:

> “The Father in Christ, and Christ in us, make us one in them. If, therefore, Christ truly assumed the flesh of our body, and if that Christ is truly human, and if under the mystery we truly receive the flesh of his body, then through this we shall be one, because the Father is in him and he in us. How, then, can a unity of will be asserted, when natural property through the sacrament is a complete sacrament of unity?”

And below:

> “The way in which this unity is natural in us he himself thus testified: ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him’” (John 6). “For he will not be in one in whom he himself is not; nevertheless, that person has within himself the [flesh] assumed from him who assumed his own [flesh].”

Likewise: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats my flesh, that person also shall live because of me” (ibid.). “As he lives through the Father, in the same way we live through the flesh. Therefore this is the cause of our life: that we have Christ abiding in us through the flesh, and shall live through him under the condition [Col. 0599A] in which he lives through the Father. If, then, we naturally live through him according to the flesh—that is, having obtained the nature of his flesh—how does he not naturally have the Father in himself according to the Spirit, since he lives through the Father?

> “These things have been recalled by us because those who falsely maintain that the unity between Father and Son is one of will alone used the example of our unity with God, as though we were united to the Son, and through the Son to the Father, by obedience and will alone, and as though no natural communion were granted through the sacrament of flesh and Spirit. Yet, even through the honor given to us—through the Son abiding carnally in us, and through our bodily and inseparable union with him—[Col. 0599B] the mystery of a true and natural unity must be proclaimed.”

You see, kindly readers, how great a power Hilary proclaims to reside in Christ’s flesh: not only does it live divinely, but it also gives life to those who eat it. This plainly could in no way occur unless the inferior nature had received, in Christ, the power of the superior nature. Hence Hilary again says in *On the Synods*:

> “The dignity of divinity is preserved, so that in the Word’s becoming flesh, the flesh should rather begin to be what the Word is. Otherwise, whence come to the flesh its powers in works, its glory on the mountain, its knowledge of the thoughts of human hearts, its security in suffering, and its life in death?”

The same author, in Book XI *On the Trinity*, says:

> [Col. 0599C] “This is the true faith of human blessedness: to proclaim God as the Word and to confess the flesh; neither does God fail to know that he is human, nor does the flesh fail to know that it is the Word. But when God, while remaining God, is born human contrary to the nature of our perception, it is no longer contrary to the nature of our hope that the human being born should remain God, since the higher nature, born into the lower, gives faith that the lower nature can be born into the higher nature.”

Again in the same work:

> “This was acquired for humanity: that it should be God. Yet, once assumed, it could in no way remain in the unity of God unless, through the unity of God, it naturally passed into the unity of God; so that, because the Word was God by nature, the Word also, having become flesh, might again be in the nature of God; and so the man Jesus Christ might remain in the glory of God the Father. If the flesh were united in the glory [Col. 0599D] of the Word, then the Word made flesh would return, even according to humanity, into the unity of the Father’s nature, when the assumed flesh had obtained the glory of the Word.”

When these words of Hilary are carefully weighed, it becomes clear that what he says elsewhere—“nor does an inferior nature ever attain the power of a nature superior and stronger than itself”—must be understood so as not to conflict with his preceding testimonies concerning the nature and power of divinity, which Christ’s inferior nature fully attained. Let us now examine that chapter of his which is thrown at us as contrary to our position—indeed, as supposedly quite inconsistent with Hilary’s preceding words.

He says in *On the Synods*:

> [Col. 0600A] Heretics, constrained by the authorities of the Scriptures, are accustomed to grant the Son only this: that he is like the Father in power; but they take from him likeness of nature. Foolish and impious men, they do not understand that likeness of power exists only from likeness of nature. For an inferior nature never attains the power of a nature superior and stronger than itself. Or what will those who assert this confess concerning Almighty God the Father, if a power of inferior nature should equal his power? It cannot be denied that the Son of God can do the same things, since he has said: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does.” But likeness of nature follows likeness of power, when he says: “For as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son also to have life in himself.” In “life” there is a signification of nature and essence, which is taught to be given for possession just as it is possessed. [Col. 0600B] Therefore likeness of life maintains likeness of power. For likeness of power cannot be unlike nature. Thus it is necessary that likeness of essence entail likeness of power, because, just as the Son does in like manner the very things which the Father does, so the Father who has life gave the Son likewise to have life. Therefore the rashness of an impious profession is condemned: while confessing likeness of power, it dared to preach unlikeness of nature, although the faith that is the chief principle of our hope is to confess an undifferentiated substance of divinity in Father and Son.

These words were spoken against the Arians, who denied to the Son of God, even according to his higher essence, equality with and likeness to the divine nature, though they admitted that he possessed likeness of power. Against these men, when the Eastern bishops had gathered in synod, this judgment was issued:

> [Col. 0600C] “If anyone, while granting in the Son likeness to the Father only according to efficacy—though the Son himself reveals likeness according to essence by the words: ‘For as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son also to have life in himself,’ and teaches likeness according to efficacy by the words: ‘For whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does’—deprives the Son, in respect of essence, which is the principal matter of our faith, of the knowledge of perpetual life which is in the Father and the Son, as though depriving himself, let him be anathema.”

Confirming this synodal judgment, Hilary says what we set above, without touching on the mystery of the incarnation or on the human nature of the Son of God. In his preceding statements already quoted above, and in many arguments inserted in his books *On the Trinity*, that nature is shown to have been so glorified that its glory is nothing other than divine power and essence. For, just as God the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself; and the Son himself, together with the Father, gave his flesh to have life in itself—yet not from itself, just as the Son himself, possessing life given to him in himself, does not have it from himself.

Hence he confesses that his flesh was given for the life of the world; whoever eats it has eternal life, Truth himself says. Therefore the Council of Ephesus, confessing Christ’s flesh to be life-giving, condemned under anathema those who denied this very point.

[Col. 0601A] “But,” you say, “what does Hilary mean when he says, ‘Nor does an inferior nature ever attain the power of a nature superior and stronger than itself’?” For if the flesh of the Word gives blessed human beings life unto eternity, how does the Word itself give blessed angels life? The power and efficacy of divine operation seem to have been given to the flesh, contrary to Hilary’s statement that this cannot occur.

I answer that these words of Hilary must be understood so as not to conflict with his other statements. For he says in Book IX *On the Trinity*:

> “God, glorified in the Son of Man, glorifies in himself the glorified God: in the Son of Man is the glory of God, and the glory of God is the glory of the Son of Man. God glorifies in himself; the human being is certainly not glorified through himself. Nor, again, is he who is glorified in the human being, though God receives glory, nevertheless something other than God. But when God, glorifying God in the glorified Son of Man, glorifies in himself, I find the nature of the glorified one assumed into the glory of the nature that glorifies.” [Col. 0601B]

Bring forward now, whoever you are, heretic, the shifting questions of your winding doctrine. Though they entangle themselves in their own knots, they contain no difficulty of adherence. For the Son is glorified; God is glorified in the human being; and, glorified in the human being, he glorified him in himself. For God makes glorious in himself Christ, born human. He rendered to Christ in himself the glory which he had with him; and, [Col. 0601C] while the assumption of the servant-form is assumed into the form of God in himself, God who was glorified in the human being is glorified—he who before the dispensation of birth was in himself, united both through the form of God and through the nature of birth. For birth had not made God into a God of a new or alien nature; the natural Son stood before the natural Father by natural generation. And when, through the birth of the human being, he is glorified in the human being into the glory of nature, he again shines forth in himself when God makes glorious, when he is assumed into the glory of the Father’s nature, from which he had been emptied by the dispensation.

But apostolic faith brings your most audacious frenzy of impiety to a conclusion, lest you wander abroad with any license of unfettered interpretation, when it says: “And every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory [Col. 0601D] of God the Father” (Rom. 14). He whom the Father glorified in himself must be confessed in his glory. He whom the Father glorified in himself must without doubt be understood to be in those things in which the Father is, since the Father glorified him in himself and he is to be confessed in his glory. For he is not merely in the glory of God here, but in the glory of God the Father. Nor did glory glorify him with an external glory; rather, glory glorified him in himself, taking him back into the glory that is its own, and by that glory which he had with it, glory glorifies him both with itself and in itself.

Thus he is also understood to be inseparable from this conjunction of faith, even under the humiliation of humanity, when he says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17). [Col. 0602A] Since eternal life does not exist when God the Father alone is known without Christ, and since Christ is glorified in the Father, does it not appear sufficiently in these words of Hilary that the inferior nature in Christ received through grace the power and glory of the superior nature, which it could not attain unless it were graciously assumed, in its own nature, into the power of the superior nature? For it is not within the power of that which is lower to rise to what is above it, or to take its power by itself or from itself. “A human being cannot receive anything of himself unless it has been given him from above” (John 3), says John the Baptist, and John the Evangelist testifies to this.

Therefore the human being in the Son of God could not receive anything from himself unless it had been given him from above. Yet he received from above the name given to him, which is above every name (Eph. 1), and together with the name, the power of that name. [Col. 0602B] Conscious of this power, he himself says: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Luke 10); again, “Father, what you gave me is greater than all” (John 10 [printed: 29]); again, “The Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins” (Matt. 6 [printed; cf. Matt. 9]); again, “No one can snatch [them] from my hand” (John 10); again, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28).

For this was given to the human being which belongs eternally to his Word: for example, that none can snatch from his hand, and that he may be almighty in heaven and on earth through the power given to him. Human nature could not attain that power through its own powers; but God was willing and able to give it to him, he who also enriched his members with divine power, according to his promise: “You shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon [Col. 0602C] you”; and again, “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Acts 1).

This power was distributed among the members according to the measure of Christ’s gift; it was not given by measure to Christ himself, that is, to the anointed human being. As the Apostle Peter says, “God anointed [him] with power” (Acts 10); or as the Psalmist says, “with the oil of gladness above his companions” (Ps. 44 [Vulgate 45]). Thus the likeness of power in the anointed human being and in God who anoints is complete: the lower nature is not taken away but translated into the power and glory of the higher nature. This could not have happened unless the lower nature were capable of the power and nature of the higher, just as gold or iron is capable of fire and fiery power, and an animal body is capable of a sentient soul, while a human body is capable of a rational soul.

[Col. 0602D] But Hilary is cited against us as saying: “Likeness of nature follows likeness of power”; and again: “Likeness of power cannot be unlike nature, and thus it is necessary,” he says, “that likeness of essence entail likeness of power.” Given this proposition of Hilary, his faithful hearer or reader may infer: but the human being through whom, as the Apostle affirms, comes the resurrection of the dead, and that human being’s flesh which gives life, have the efficacy of divine power; therefore it follows that, along with likeness of divine power, they also have likeness of divine essence, without which the flesh could avail nothing toward conferring eternal life.

Moreover, it should be noted that in this place Hilary speaks of distinct persons of one divinity, not of distinct natures of one person. [Col. 0603A] He shows likeness of power and nature to be inseparable, especially in God, where, as he himself says, “likeness is property; property is equality; equality differs in nothing.” Equality of nature, moreover, can only be one. But elsewhere, as has been shown, when dealing with the two natures of one person in the Trinity, he demonstrates that one nature is glorified by the glory of the other—by a glory, as he says, “not external, but with God glorifying the human being in himself.” It is therefore absurd to imagine that the human being is made like God in any respect other than that in which the Father’s Word is at once like and equal to the Father: namely, in the divine essence, or glory, or power, or omnipotence, or goodness, or wisdom. In God all these are one—indeed, they are one simple, [Col. 0603B] immeasurable, eternal whole—which was given, through the name above every name, to the assumed human being in the one person of the Trinity. That human being had this eternally in the divinity given to him; but he received it temporally in the very mystery of the incarnation, when divinity itself was given to the human being by being incarnate, since the Word was made flesh, that is, was made human.

The human being, therefore, received what God had: namely, that he might be God almighty, with so great an equality and likeness of divinity and omnipotence that the equality and likeness of the assuming Word and of the human being assumed to God the Father are wholly identical. Certainly, to use the adversaries’ words, it is necessary that things which are known from elsewhere to be different should be one and the same in that in which they are truly equal.

[Col. 0603C] Since, therefore, Father unbegotten, his only-begotten Son, and the gift of both—and likewise the human being conceived and sanctified by this gift and assumed into one person of the Trinity—have one divinity, by which the Father is called God, the Son God, the Holy Spirit God, and the human being conceived of the Holy Spirit God, equality is rightly proclaimed of them all, whose essence or nature of divinity is known to be one and whose power is the same.

For by the name “flesh” or “humanity,” when the divinity which it received is under discussion, we signify the whole human substance—rational soul and flesh joined together. Thus: “The Word was made flesh,” that is, was made human. And: “All flesh [Col. 0603D] shall see the salvation of God” (John 1), that is, every human being. Thus we do not ascribe this likeness or equality with God to flesh alone, which is not a human being but a part of a human being, as the adversary thinks. He frequently uses—or rather misuses—these names against us; whereas we preach not flesh alone, nor humanity alone, but the human being God: not adopted to God the Father, but born as a natural and consubstantial Son, equal to the begetting Father; equal in the essence and nature of divinity which he received by being born, so as to be God; equal in the power by which he can do all that he wills, as God the Father can; and equal in the brightness which he asked for and received in the flesh, and which he had in divinity before the world existed. “Glorify me,” he says, “with yourself, with the glory which I had before [Col. 0604A] the world existed, with you” (John 17 [printed: 5]). “With you,” he says, not “under you”: this is the right hand of the throne of majesty, in which is equality of brightness.

The adversary objects: “If Christ is equal to the Father in the glory of his body, and if we, as Hilary testifies, are to be conformed to that same glory of Christ’s body, in what way will they prove that we are to become equal to God himself?” We await their answer. We reply: Nowhere have we preached that we shall become equal to God. We neither hope that this will occur, nor does it follow from the promise of likeness and conformity to Christ, because many things are alike and conformed which are not equal.

Thus, the image of a person’s face seen in another person’s pupil [Col. 0604B] is found altogether like that face, yet it is not equal to it. For likeness pertains to quality, whereas equality pertains to quantity. Anyone who knows Aristotle’s categories knows that these differ from one another more widely than the species or genera within a single category. Therefore it does not follow that things which are conformed or alike are equal. We do not, then, wonder that this philosopher is blind in divine and supernatural matters, when even in natural matters he does not perceive what truth contains.

But we shall show from Hilary’s own words, more fittingly than from ours, how falsely it is attributed to Hilary that he maintains such conformity between Christ’s body and ours as must entail coequality. For, shortly after the sentence which falsifiers wrongly think affirms that Christ, insofar as he was glorified in the servant-form, is not conformed to God, and that his body can do nothing beyond what is common to us and to himself, he explains what he meant and says:

> [Col. 0604C] “These are our gains and our advances: that we are made conformed to the glory of God’s body. But the only-begotten God, although he was also born human, is nevertheless, as God, something other than all things in all. For that subjection of the body, through which what is carnal is swallowed up into the nature of Spirit, will establish as God all things in all him who, besides being God, is also human.”

These words of Hilary make it clear that the preceding statement of his has been excessively cut short and corrupted, so that it is thought to affirm what it denies and deny what it affirms. For he affirms that the glorified human being in God is conformed to God, and that we shall be conformed to his body, but not coequal. Therefore the human being does not consider it robbery to be equal to God, since he is in the form of God, which is both given to him and innate in him; in that form he is fairer than the children of men, not among all things but above all things, God blessed for ever. Amen.

## LETTER XXIV

The same author to Henry, duke of Saxony and Bavaria, exhorting him, by the example of saints, kings, and dukes, to undertake the defense of the Church of God.

To the glorious and victorious Duke [Col. 0605A] H. of Bavaria and Saxony, Brother G. of Reichersberg offers devoted prayers together with faithful service.

How long, most noble prince, shall I be deprived both of acquaintance with you and of favor from one so familiar to me as I was in the presence of your father? Though I am insignificant and unworthy of so great a prince’s favor and friendship, he deigned to number me among those dear to him and his friends—not those who loved their own interests rather than him, but those who sincerely loved him himself. Hence came his intimate conversations with me about the salvation of his soul, and about the condition and honor of the holy Church of God. For in secular concerns belonging to him he had advisors in abundance—sons of this age, more prudent in their generation than sons of light—as your own nobility also has noble supporters in abundance, by whose prudent counsel you transact worldly affairs.

[Col. 0605B] But I am prompted to suggest to you something concerning the salvation of your soul and the condition and honor of the holy Church of God by that Spirit, I believe, who suggests to us whatever useful, salutary, and true things we say. For he is the Spirit of truth, who teaches all truth and announces to those who believe in him the things that are to come, so that they too may announce them to those who wish to hear. This Spirit of truth has in the Scriptures of truth announced the good and evil that would befall the Church of God through good or evil kings and dukes. We have already, in part, heard and also seen these things in the city of our God: certain kings and dukes, following the example of King David and the good kings Hezekiah and Josiah, and likewise of the good leaders—the holy Maccabees Judas, Jonathan, and Simon—honored the temple [Col. 0605C] of God, which is the Church. Following Solomon’s example, they built it, or even adorned the face of the temple with golden crowns after spiritual Antiochus’s filth had been removed from it.

Nevertheless, the dregs of that filth have not yet been emptied out. Therefore we desire leaders such as Judas, the outstanding leader of the Maccabees and wholly opposed to the aforesaid King Antiochus. For the latter defiled the temple of God; the former cleansed it and adorned it with golden crowns. The latter sold the priesthood; the former defeated the seller and expelled the buyers from the priesthood. Through the former many fell from the people; through the latter great joy came about among the people.

[Col. 0605D] While you diligently apply yourself to punishing evildoers and praising the good, there is peace among the people. But still more and more perfectly worthy of praise is your effort to establish concord between priesthood and kingship. When you called for this cause to be more diligently pursued, papal envoys came through your mediation, as citizens of the apostles, to enlighten the country, bearing peace. But they did not find peace on the road, because they fell into the hands of cruel robbers. Against these, most noble prince, you must employ the authority which God has entrusted to you for the punishment of evildoers.

Nevertheless, because the wrath of Almighty God is in all things to be feared and avoided, and is altogether inescapable, I most faithfully urge your prudence that, when leading an army, you provide protection for cemeteries and churches consecrated to God; and that you make every effort, as far as you are able, to restrain [Col. 0606A] soldiers and squires from harassing and oppressing the poor. Otherwise the great joy which, by God’s favor, has been brought about among the people through you may be turned into sorrow—may God deign to avert this, he who may always be gracious to you as you exercise just punishments, and an enemy to your enemies. I reserve for a suitable time other matters to be suggested to your highness through my insignificance, if you deem me worthy to hear me in a fatherly manner.

## LETTER XXV

The same author to Arbo or Erbo, abbot of Prüfening, exhorting him to soften the mind of the bishop of Regensburg, who had excommunicated all his citizens because of the crime of certain persons.

To the venerable Abbot A. of the monastery of Bruvinensis—today Prüfening—[Col. 0606B] Brother G. of Reichersberg offers devoted prayers together with faithful service.

The Church of Regensburg, like a city set upon a mountain, cannot be hidden, because it is a lofty lampstand on which a lamp has been placed; whether it shines brightly or not brightly, it will be visible to many. You know that among the vessels of the golden lampstand in the tabernacle of God were the vessels for pouring oil and the snuffers. You also know what these signify. Accordingly, I take upon myself, in writing to you, not the office of a teacher but of a monitor. To that Church, which long nourished me and advanced me to the priesthood, I owe such fidelity that, if anyone is scandalized in it, I too burn; if anyone is weak, I too am weak.

Hearing, therefore, of no small disturbance in that Church, I cannot but be disturbed. [Col. 0606C] If distance of place did not prevent it, I would wish to be personally present with you and the other spiritual men there in order to calm the stumbling-block of this disturbance which has arisen from the lord bishop’s excommunication. It must be softened or moderated in such a way that, where his zeal has been overly kindled or inflamed, you who are spiritual may, like vessels for pouring oil fashioned of the gold of charity, temper its flame by pouring out oil. But where smoking flax obscures the flame too greatly, you should, as golden snuffers, pluck away whatever seems to you to require plucking, acting with the lord bishop himself in a spirit of gentleness.

[Col. 0606D] I truly love and gladly honor him. It is out of love and honor for him that I now write to you, that you may suggest to his nobility that he should not be found, in any respect, to have degenerated from his uncle, a man—as you know—most noble both in virtue and in lineage, by doing anything hastily or without counsel. For, when undertaking so great a matter, he could have consulted his lord and father, the archbishop, and others most faithful to him, if your prudence had advised it; unless perhaps he found insufficient counsel among his own household—which I can scarcely believe, provided he had been willing to trust your counsel and that of his other faithful advisers.

But now, let him not think it burdensome at least to consult at the end those whom he did not consult at the beginning, concerning a good outcome and a discerning judgment. Thus the whole people will not be entangled, but innocent will be justly distinguished [Col. 0607A] from guilty and righteous from unrighteous; and even the guilty will be treated with so much greater mercy as it is more evident that those who dishonored the Church by violently laying hands upon a fraudulent man were poor and severely afflicted by hunger, so that that poetic maxim had befallen them:

> A hungry populace does not know how to fear.

But the more honorable citizens of that city and the great majority of the people are found innocent of the sacrilege committed in the church, although many, after the sacrilege had been committed, joined the few sacrilegious persons in carrying out homicide. Since, therefore, two crimes were perpetrated there—sacrilege and homicide—a suitable judgment could have been rendered concerning the perpetrators of each, after they had been sought out by name, [Col. 0607B] which would not entangle the whole population of that city, unless the people themselves had wished unjustly to defend the guilty. This is like the occasion when the Gibeonites, by defending a few guilty persons, deserved to be involved all together in one judgment of condemnation. But it is not credible that all the citizens of Regensburg are so senseless as openly to oppose justice. Therefore the lord bishop should be advised not to involve the righteous with the wicked.

The remainder seems to be lacking in the manuscript.

## LETTER XXVI  
[Note: From the Monsee manuscript, as is the following letter.]

The same author, apparently, to the nuns of Admont, explaining for them the phrase from Psalm 50 [Vulgate 51], “that you may be justified in your words.”

[Col. 0607C] To the sisters of Admont, most beloved in Christ, Brother G. offers devoted prayer and perpetual love in Christ.

Because I was pressed by haste in setting out, I could not fully satisfy your most welcome inquiries. Yet perhaps God punished that haste: he somewhat delayed my journey and, when I wished to hurry away from you, kept me near you for some time. If, therefore, I was chastised on your account because perhaps I sinned greatly by hastening away from you, I hope that God may be reconciled to me through you if you pray for me. I ask you to do this, and to receive this writing as recompense for having said less than was fitting in response to your most holy inquiries.

You asked, dearest sisters, about those words of the Lord [Col. 0607D] in which God is to be justified, according to the saying: “that you may be justified in your words” (Psalm 50). Know, then, that these words are his promises, as we have touched upon in part. This must be noted with the greatest care, and it was necessary for us to set it before you: some of God’s promises he fulfills, so that he himself may be justified. For it is right that what he who is truthful has promised should never prove false. But there are other promises of his which, even if he does not fulfill them, yet he remains righteous and truthful in those very promises which he does not fulfill. To make what we say clearer, let us distinguish the different kinds of God’s promises. Some things God promises unconditionally; others conditionally. [Col. 0608A] Unconditional was the promise he made to David: “From the fruit of your womb I shall set one upon your throne” (Psalm 131); and again: “I have sworn to David my servant: for ever I shall prepare your throne” (Psalm 88). Conditional, however, was the promise addressed to Solomon: “If you walk in my ways and keep my precepts and commandments, as your father walked, I shall prolong your days” (3 Kings 3). Likewise the Jews were told: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1).

Since this is so, whatever God has promised unconditionally must be fulfilled with such necessity that, just as it is impossible for God to be or become a liar, so it is impossible for any one of God’s unconditional promises to be or become ineffective—even though the things God has promised unconditionally appear wholly [Col. 0608B] contrary to nature. It was contrary to nature that aged and barren Sarah should conceive by aged Abraham; yet, because God had promised it unconditionally, it necessarily had to be fulfilled. Abraham believed God when he made the promise, and this very believing was reckoned to him as righteousness, because he believed that things were possible to God even when they appeared contrary to nature. The Apostle praises this faith when he says that Abraham did not weaken in faith and did not consider his own body as dead, nor Sarah’s womb as dead, knowing that God was able also to perform what he had promised. All who imitate this faith by believing God’s promises are counted among Abraham’s children; and, as the Apostle affirms, because they are [Col. 0608C] of faith, they shall be blessed with faithful Abraham.

Indeed, God alone is so truthful and every human being so false that no promise made under a condition to be fulfilled by a human being is ever found fulfilled; for the condition which a human owed to God has always proved void. This is clear in Solomon, to whom God promised long life on the condition that he should walk in God’s ways as his father had walked. Therefore, since he did not keep the conditional ordinance by walking in David’s ways, God could, without prejudice to his own truth, deny him long days; and this happened. For when he had already grown old, his heart was corrupted by women, so that he followed foreign gods, and his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as the heart of David his father had been. Therefore the Lord said [Col. 0608D] to Solomon: “Because you have had these things within you and have not kept my covenant and my commandments, I shall rend and divide your kingdom,” etc. (3 Kings 11). These words of God plainly signify a shortening of Solomon’s days, although some believe that he was afterward saved through repentance; this, however, has no certain authority in the Scriptures.

Likewise, to the Jews to whom it was said, “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1), the good things of the land were justly denied, because they were unwilling to obey the Lord.

Yet it must be understood concerning promises of this conditional kind that, if the force of the condition is placed not in [Col. 0609A] the human being but in God, the conditional promise itself is bound by as great a necessity of truth as an unconditional promise, so that it is inevitable that it be fulfilled. Such is the saying: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, shall draw all things to myself” (John 12). In these words truthful God promised conditionally, but placed the force of the condition in himself; and so he awaited nothing to be fulfilled by a human being, but himself fulfilled all that he said. For he was lifted up from the earth as he willed, and now draws all things to himself: by grace, namely all his chosen members; and by power, both reprobate and chosen alike, since he now orders all things to his own glory and will judge all things at the end.

Setting aside, then, those promises that are made, as it were, doubtfully under conditions, because through the covenant itself certain works are required from human beings as merits—whereas all human beings are found false in rendering those merits—let us cast the anchor of hope into those promises of God which, we do not doubt, rest solely upon the truthfulness of God who promises [manuscript reading: “to doubt”]. For, since it is impossible for God speaking to lie, it is much more impossible for God swearing to lie. Therefore in himself he is most steadfast truth, to which no falsity can ever happen or attach itself. Wishing to establish us firmly in this most steadfast truth of God who promises, the Apostle says in his Epistle to the Hebrews:

“For human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and an oath is for them the end of every dispute, for confirmation. Therefore God, wishing more abundantly [Col. 0609C] to show to the heirs of the promise the unchangeableness of his purpose, interposed an oath, so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us may have the strongest consolation; a hope which we have as an anchor of the soul, safe and firm, entering into the inner part of the veil, where Jesus has entered for us as forerunner, made a high priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Hebrews 6).

Truly this is the priest for ever, who has made the unshakable truth of his promises a bridge for us from these miseries into his eternity. Since he is to be justified in his words, he must be found truthful in his firm promises.

[Col. 0609D] But, to gather a few out of God’s many promises, we are content to set down those which you can easily retain in memory. When you say to God, “that you may be justified, O Lord, in your words,” there is understood: “Have mercy on me.” These are the words of his most steadfast promises:

“Behold, I myself shall seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock. What was lost I shall seek; what was cast away I shall bring back; what was broken I shall strengthen; and what was fat and strong I shall preserve” (Ezekiel 34).

You will find many desirable promises of this kind at the ends of the prophets.
