We are content to indicate that they should be sought and gathered there [Col. 0610A], because for the present we delight to recall some of the promises which incarnate Truth itself deigned to proclaim with his own mouth. Thus we may have something by which to hold him fast and, following Jacob’s example, wrestle with him until, through the strongest faith by which we believe him truthful in his words and promises, we wrest from him all the blessings which he himself truthfully promised. Jacob said to God: “I shall not let you go unless you bless me” (Genesis 32). This is the same as though he had said: “I shall not cease to believe, to weep, and to ask, until I obtain the blessing which you, who are truthful, promised to Abraham my father.” Thus Jacob, steadfast in the strength of his faith, wept and besought the angel with whom he struggled, [Col. 0610B] as the prophet Hosea testifies. Explaining Jacob’s struggle, he shows that, while wrestling with God, Jacob wept and besought him (Hosea 12).

A wonderful thing! He wept and prayed for the word of blessing to come to pass, though he believed without doubt that it would come to pass, since it was certain to him [note: the manuscript reads, “it was steadfastly certain to him”] that God, the truthful promiser, could not become a liar. Yet, as I said, he wept and prayed, because God wills that the very thing he promises should be demanded from him by the highest prayers and deepest tears, and obtained, as it were, by a certain struggle. Therefore, sometimes, to stir up the prayers and tears of believers, when we hold him through faith in his promises, he acts as a wrestler and in a sense shakes himself loose from our hands, permitting something to happen which seems to oppose and contradict his promises.

This happened in [Col. 0610C] Isaac’s marriage: by God’s ordering, he took a barren wife. Her barrenness indeed seemed to obstruct the fulfillment of the divine promise. Since Abraham’s seed had been promised enlargement through Isaac, Isaac might have slept, as it were, secure in God’s promise and neglected his wife’s fertility. But this was not fitting, since God had ordained that his own promise, indeed also his predestination, should be obtained from him through prayers and desires. Knowing this, Isaac prayed to the Lord for his wife, because she was barren. God heard him and granted Rebecca conception. Without doubt both Isaac and his son Jacob wrestled with God, in a sense wresting from him by prayers the fulfillment of the promise.

Thus, O most beloved daughters of kings, daughters of patriarchs who wrestled with God, wrestle also with Christ by prayers, desires, and tears, drawing from him through faith the fulfillment in our days of whatever still remains to be fulfilled of his promises. For he himself promised, saying: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, shall draw all things to myself” (John 12). And behold, even now we are often drawn by him after our longing. Let us therefore say to him: “Behold, you have been lifted up from the earth; draw us after yourself to yourself, that you may be justified in your words.” Speaking of your sheep, you said: “I came that they [Col. 0611A] may have life, and may have it more abundantly” (ibid.). Grant us to enjoy you, the true life, more abundantly from day to day: that each succeeding fruit of your sweetness may always surpass the preceding one, however abundant the latter may be, and that it may always become more abundant than what preceded it. Thus may you be justified in your words, because you promised your sheep not merely that they should have life, but that they should have it more abundantly. You did not say “abundantly,” but “more abundantly”; by this we understand and hope for an everlasting increase of good and blessed life, until we attain that most abundant good, than which nothing is more abundant. Thus Peter and John and the other saints had life more abundantly, continually receiving increase and ascending from good to better.

The rest is missing in [Col. 0611B] the manuscript, several leaves having been cut out by an unknown hand.

## LETTER XXVII

The same writer to N., his daughter in Christ. He explains to her the words of the same Psalm 50: “that you may prevail when you are judged.”

You ask—and by asking compel me, dearest daughter in Christ—that, just as I wrote something to the sisters of Admont about that justification of God by which he is said to be justified in his words, according to the saying, “That you may be justified in your words,” I should also write something to you about that victory of God of which it is said to God: “And may you prevail when you are judged” (Psalm 50).

Here it is worthwhile to observe the proper character of victory. There is no victory except where an opposing party is overcome. For example, however strong an emperor or soldier may be, he cannot be called a victor as long as no one resists him whom he must conquer. But if someone resists and is conquered and overcome, the conqueror, through the conquered, shall bear the name of victor and obtain the title of victory—with glory all the greater as the opposing party appeared stronger. Let us suppose, then, that such an emperor or soldier had promised to defend some land and wished to remain righteous and truthful in this promise. If a strong armed man came against him, entered that land secretly, and ravaged it, then unless its defender came upon him as the stronger and overcame him, he would not be justified in his words; indeed, he would seem deceitful and unjust so long as that strong armed man prevailed [Col. 0611D].

So God, the most mighty commander, had undertaken the protection and defense of King David, whom he had chosen according to his own heart and to whom he had also sworn that he would set one of the fruit of his womb upon his throne. In this particular oath David desired God to be justified and proved true, saying: “Have mercy on me, that you may be justified in your words” (ibid.). But, according to the rebuke of Nathan the prophet, mentioned in the title of this psalm, the stranger who had come to David like a strong armed man had constructed engines of sin in order that God’s sworn word might be made false, and so that God, who is truth, might in some fashion be conquered by falsehood when the divine promise went unfulfilled because of sin. Thus David, as though more concerned for God’s glory than for his own salvation, desires victory for God himself: victory by which his iniquity might be overcome and the strong armed man excluded, who had guarded his own court there so long as David had not acknowledged his own guilt. But perfect acknowledgement of sin was the conquest and expulsion of that strong one.

Recognition of sins is cautious when, in the confession of sins, God is judged—that is, distinguished. For “to judge” is sometimes used for “to distinguish,” as in: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause” (Psalm 42). Our father Adam, after his sins, was unwilling to judge and distinguish God in such a way as to assign justice to God and blame to himself, and thus to judge and distinguish between the righteous and the unrighteous. Rather [Col. 0612B], he cast back and turned his guilt upon God, to whom he said: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion,” etc. (Genesis 3).

Many children imitate this Adam, blaming in their sins their own frailty, as though it were the woman joined to them by God; and, what is more wicked, after Eve’s example they accuse the serpent—that is, the devil—to excuse themselves. David did not do so. Rather, he acknowledged himself alone guilty and false, while confessing God truthful, saying: “For behold, you have loved truth” (Psalm 50). God therefore rightly appeared the victor and the devil conquered, because the victor was judged and separated by the one who had been conquered, through a truthful judgment. Adam, however, confused God and the devil, truth and falsehood, in one matter [Col. 0612C], when he assigned to God also the blame of which the devil had been the instigator, because God had joined to him the woman through whom he had been deceived. Thus the invincible God in some manner allowed himself to be conquered, when he was driven out through the devil from the paradise into which he himself had placed him.

But now the devil, who gloried in being victor, is conquered anew by God’s triumph through their repentance and confession, and is overcome by those through whom God is judged righteous, truthful, and victorious in his words, since a human being’s sin is in no way attributed to him. O how glorious is that victory in which falsehood and guilt are conquered by triumphant truth as by a two-edged sword, when a human being professes truth not only concerning himself but also concerning God—confessing, that is, himself false and God truthful! David confessed himself false when he said: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (ibid.). He also confessed God truthful when he said: “For behold, you have loved truth.” By such a judgment God, when judged, conquered falsehood; and he who is stronger excluded the strong armed man, delivering from him his court—that is, David’s heart, first chosen by God but later invaded by the devil.

God is also rightly judged—that is, distinguished—in this way: when he who is truth is judged to rebuke sin or falsehood truthfully in a person who rebukes it. Therefore the one who rebukes is loved and honored as God, because, as I have said, [Col. 0613A] God is judged to rebuke in him. Thus David, though a great and illustrious king, reverently listened to Nathan the prophet and humbly obeyed him as God, because he honored in Nathan the one who sent him. So too David patiently listened to Shimei cursing him, because he understood that Shimei had been sent by God to curse him; therefore he judged that the sender should be honored in the one sent, however impious he might be. This was why he rebuked the sons of Zeruiah on Shimei’s account.

The impious and proud King Saul had not acted so. Rebuked by Samuel for not fulfilling the Lord’s command, he proved rebellious, and presumed to make God false and himself righteous in the one rebuking him—indeed, in God who rebuked him—saying: “On the contrary, I have fulfilled the word of the Lord, and have brought King Agag of Amalek,” etc. (1 Kings 15). I think that Saul did not distinguish God in the human being; and thus in God truth did not triumph, but falsehood—that is, sin—triumphed, because he dishonored God in the prophet rebuking him by insolently contradicting his rebuke.

Therefore, whenever any one of us is rebuked for some fault by an adversary on the way—that is, by sacred Scripture—or by a teacher, or by a kindly or even hostile reprover, let him recognize and honor truth. Let him make humble confession, so that truth may prevail when it is judged, and, being judged, may be honored; while falsehood may be conquered and excluded, falsehood which rules most wickedly and especially in excuses and defenses of sins. The Apostle’s saying accords with our meaning: “He who eats unworthily eats judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” [Col. 0613C] (1 Corinthians 11). For just as the Lord’s body brings not salvation but condemnation to the recipient when that body of the Lord is not judged—that is, distinguished or honored—so truth itself, which is God, when it is not judged, does not work the work of victory, but in a sense allows itself to be conquered. I illustrated this above by Adam and Saul, both of whom, in making excuses for their sins, despised the truth that rebuked them. David therefore rightly prays: “Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness, to excuses in sins” (Psalm 140).

Let us imitate this David by humbly repenting, attributing our guilt not to God but to ourselves, and loving the truth that rebukes us, so that truth itself may conquer in us the mist [Col. 0613D] of falsehood which assails us, just as the visible sun conquers a cloud when it breaks through and disperses it with its rays. So it happened in David. God, promising good things to David, was like a rising sun, whose rays David might have enjoyed most delightfully had no cloud of sin intervened. That cloud appeared to obstruct the promise which said: “From the fruit of your womb I shall set one upon your throne” (Psalm 131); and elsewhere: “I have sworn to David my servant: for ever I shall prepare your throne, and I shall build your throne from generation to generation” (Psalm 88). But when the cloud of sin intervened, the splendid promise of the truthful God would have been hindered, had it not been fitting that God should be justified in his words in such a way that he could not be overcome by falsehood. For every sin is rightly called falsehood, as opposed to truth.

Now I mean especially that truth by which truthful God has purposed and foreordained human blessedness, not only in an individual, as in David, but universally, as appears in humanity’s creation, when truthful God said: “Let us make man in our likeness and image” (Genesis 1). This purpose of God embraces the number of all the elect, whom he foreknew and predestined to be made conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Therefore, if he called, justified, and glorified those whom he foreknew and foreordained, with no cloud of sin intervening, he would truly make every human being in the divine image and likeness [Col. 0614B]; and the elect would have the brightest day of the divine promises, the brightness of the divine image and likeness shining in all human beings.

But now, because the sun of righteousness so abhors the cloud of sin covering the whole earth that he appears rightly bound to withdraw his brightness—because he could not form the likeness of his image in the mirrors of human hearts, exceedingly filthy, unless their filth were first cleansed away, a filth so great that it seems able to overcome the diligence of the cleanser—the sinful and penitent human being rightly says: “Have mercy on me, O God, by cleansing away my filth. When it has been cleansed, I shall be capable of your likeness; and so may you be justified in your words, by which you said: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness.’ And if sins produce in me unlikeness to you, then, by working likeness, overcome the magnitude and multitude of my sins. [Col. 0614C] Overcome my sins as a king conquers a tyrant. Overcome as the sun conquers the thickness of clouds. Overcome as a physician conquers by the strength of medicines. Overcome as one conquers the thick encrustation of filth who, by frequent polishing, makes a mirror out of rusty material. Prevail when you are judged. For I judge—that is, distinguish—you to be such a God that, when you will, such almighty power is at hand to you that it cannot be conquered by the magnitude and multitude of our sins, but you will finally establish all chosen human beings in conformity to your image, as you purposed when you said: ‘Let us make man [Col. 0614D] in our image and likeness.’” Amen.

## LETTER XXVIII

The same writer to certain nuns, perhaps those of Admont, concerning the strength and purity of faith, using the example of the centurion in the Gospel.

To the dearest sisters in Christ, Brother G. offers devoted prayers.

When I spoke and wrote to you previously, I shaped and suggested to you, insofar as God deigned to grant it, the words and meaning of prayers which you might send up to God as incense of sweetest fragrance. But afterward, unwilling that you should be of little faith—for littleness of faith greatly obstructs the hearing of prayer—I began, by God’s gift, to instruct you in great faith, by which everything rightly desired can be obtained from God. That centurion proves this, whose great faith the Lord admired, saying: “I have not found such faith in Israel” (Luke 7). The praiseworthy greatness of his faith lay in his not thinking that the one ever and everywhere present, the disposer of all things, needed to come in bodily presence to heal the sick servant. He orders things not as an external craftsman orders a work—for example, a mill or the building of a house—but as their inward, immovable, and sustaining force.

Let our spirit and mind imitate this centurion, having soldiers beneath them rather than above them—that is, various thoughts which serve in good or evil—and let the mind say to this one, namely an evil thought: “Go,” [Col. 0615B] and it goes; and to another, namely a good thought: “Come,” and it comes; and confidently let the mind say to its servant—that is, its body, which it chastises and reduces to servitude—“Do this,” namely some useful work, and it does it. . . . Let the mind also consider, as a discerning centurion, that, being placed under divine authority, it commands its thoughts and body in such a way that it needs no intermediary; for by the silent gesture of the will an evil thought is driven away, a good one summoned, and almost every motion of the body governed by the voluntary command of the mind without any intermediary at all.

But those whom he has under him serve the centurion only when he himself, placed under praetorian and imperial authority [Col. 0615C], obeys his superior. If he is disobedient and rebellious toward that superior, he will also find rebellion in his subjects against himself as long as he himself refuses obedience to his superior. So too our mind, like a centurion subjected to God the eternal King, will be powerful through obeying him and powerless through despising him. Thus, though it says to an evil soldier, “Go,” the soldier may not go; indeed, the mind may not possess even power over itself. But we are speaking of the good centurion, obediently placed under his superior’s authority, and therefore powerful and strong.

Such a mind, well ordered under divine authority, can reason with itself after the example of the Gospel centurion: “If I, the inward person, placed under the authority of the invisible King, so govern the thoughts [Col. 0615D] serving in me and beneath me that this entire government is accomplished by an inward command, which neither a thought nor any bodily motion can resist, how much more does the author of unconquered power, the King of unsurpassable dominion, the ever-glorious triumphant one, by the most secret and inward gesture of his will, restrain the forces of hostile rule and, by driving out harmful things—as I drive out evil thoughts with his help—cause healthful things to be present, as I cause good thoughts to be present when I will them?

“Do I run about by any local movement? No: remaining within myself, I dispose with the greatest ease, without intermediaries, the movements of thoughts, senses, and members. For example, when I wish my foot to move, what I will happens; the foot itself experiences the presence and power of my government by rendering obedience. It is not necessary for me, the mind, to go to or send to my body’s foot, since it perceives the effectual force of my command as present to it and inwardly implanted in it. For I, a spirit, furnish it with life—a life given to me by my superior, who is still more inward, namely you. [Col. 0616A] Is not God, then, remaining wholly stable in himself, in a similar way—and indeed in a far more excellent way—the giver of motion to all things, himself far more present to the most remote creatures than I, a created spirit, am even to the innermost members of my body?

“If I, such as I am, a centurion under his authority, say to my servant—that is, my body—‘Do this,’ and it does it, speaking not with a sound of voice but by a gesture of will, how much more has he done whatever he willed in heaven and earth and in all the abysses, wholly present everywhere as I, mind and soul, am wholly present to each member of my body? And if I am not divided into parts, so that one part of me is in one eye of my body and another in the other, since I have no divisible parts, how much more is he one, indivisible God, so that one part of him is not in heaven and another upon earth, since heaven and earth are full of the glory of his majesty?

“Why, therefore, O Savior present everywhere, do you say to me when I ask for my servant: ‘I shall come and heal him’ (Matthew 8)? Where can you come, who are everywhere? How can you enter beneath my roof, whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain? Perhaps you come according to the carnal presence of flesh? But ‘the flesh profits nothing’ (John 6). It is not so with the divinity inherent in you, which, being everywhere, makes your willing sufficient for me; the silent command of your will is sufficient for me. To make that will known outwardly also, say the word, and my servant shall be healed [Col. 0616C] (Matthew 8). For you are the Word through whom all things were made—not a word which ceases once uttered, but a Word which abides, begotten.

“For your Father spoke, and all things were made. He spoke—that is, he begot the eternal Word—not as a fleshly father begets a son, but as a wise mind begets wise counsel. And just as counsel, existing in and begotten from the mind, cannot be separated from that mind, so you cannot be separated from your Father. For even if counsel clothes itself in spoken language, so that it may go forth to the minds of hearers and understanders, it nevertheless remains in the mind which begot it even while it proceeds by speech to other minds; and although that counsel imparts itself to the understandings of others, it does not leave the one from whom it was begotten.

“Thus you, O Jesus, the eternal Word or counsel of the eternal Father, although by clothing yourself in human substance you have gone forth outwardly, yet remain one and the same with the Father and in the Father; you never depart from him, anywhere or at any time. For you and he are not two gods but one God, of whom it is said: ‘I fill heaven and earth’ (Jeremiah 23). Far be it from me, a human being placed under authority, to confine you, so immense and beyond estimation, beneath my roof. In some sense I would do this [Col. 0617A] if I believed you, in your divinity, to be circumscribed by any form.

“Whatever is extended in length, breadth, and height, having some limit to that length, breadth, and height, is circumscribed. But you, without local measure of length, reach from end to end—that is, from the beginning of creatures to their end; without local breadth, you encompass every place; and without local height, you surpass all things, not visible only but invisible. You have traversed the circuit of heaven without local motion; you contain heaven’s thrones; you look into the abysses; you weigh the mountains; you enclose the earth in your palm; you are enclosed nowhere. And should I judge myself worthy for you to enter beneath my roof? Far be such a thought from me, such an opinion as to consider you circumscribable or formed in any way, since you are God before every formed god, as you say: ‘Before me no god was formed’ (Isaiah 43).

“Rather, I believe that you are the form giving form to every beautiful thing. For this is why the earthly human being whom you assumed is beautiful beyond the children of men: you, eternal form and everlasting beauty, dwell in him beyond all others. You display him as surpassingly fair beyond all, since you unite human nature to yourself so fully that you, in the human being assumed, show yourself as one Christ, one king, one priest—one and the same—visible according to the humanity assumed, while remaining invisible according to divinity, which is everywhere present.

“Say, therefore, the word, and my servant shall be healed. Speak by the mighty command of your will, and pronounce this command in a word, lest the servant’s healing be thought to have happened by chance; so that, when this miracle is heard, you may be glorified, believed to be everywhere present, and your inseparable dominion acknowledged—a dominion no interval of places can interrupt. For as you are everywhere, so you reign everywhere. Nor is your being one thing and your reigning another, as it is with earthly kings, whose existence preceded their power. Your power, however, is nothing other than your essence; and therefore, as your essence gives existence to everything that exists, so your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages and your dominion endures through every generation; nor is there anyone who resists your will in your kingdom.

“For I too am a human being: human, not God; frail human, not immortal God; a human being with a beginning, while you are God without beginning or end. I am human, son of a human being—indeed, of mortal human beings. You are Son of Man, that is, son of an incorrupt mother. I am human, burdened with sins. You are God and human, alone fit to cleanse sins. I am human, born not of an untouched virgin but of a corrupted woman; I am human, I am ashes, [Col. 0618A] I am a worm. I am human, as I said, born of a woman, living for a short time and filled with many miseries; like a flower I come forth and am crushed, and I flee like a shadow, never remaining in the same state.

“And yet I have soldiers beneath me—soldiers and servants—and they obey me, though I am by no means free. For I am placed under authority: I am a centurion, not a king, not even a tetrarch like Herod or Pilate, but a centurion under a tetrarch. Yet I have soldiers beneath me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it (Luke 7). How much more do all things created through you, governed by you until now and to be governed hereafter, subsisting in you, obey your majesty, your will, your command! For if you did not sustain all things, they would fall into nothing, since they were made from nothing, and could not subsist.

“You are above all things, beneath all things, within all things, filling and encompassing all things. You grant being to things that are—which even stones possess; life to living things—which human beings share with trees; sensation to sentient things—which they share with animals; understanding to intelligent beings, human beings and angels. Unchangeable, indivisible, non-local, timeless, invisible, incomprehensible in your divinity, by your word alone you can restore and preserve restored health to my servant, my body, my spirit, and anyone dear to me. Therefore, though you know all things, it is enough briefly to say to you: ‘Lord, my servant lies paralyzed at home and is grievously tormented’” (Matthew 8).

[Col. 0618C] “When Jesus heard this, he marveled” (ibid.). He marvels at the greatness of faith, though he does not marvel at the vastness of the whole world. And because greatness of faith pleased him, he granted the requests, moved to mercy not by a multitude of words but by greatness of faith. “As you have believed,” he says, “let it be done to you” (ibid.). “You have believed magnificently, wonderfully, unshakably: though you see me as a small human being, you profess me God present everywhere and almighty everywhere, since you judge my word alone sufficient to restore the health of your servant. Therefore, as you have believed, let it be done to you” (ibid.).

O Lord Jesus, who sit at the right hand of the Father, interceding for us, made priest for ever: grant us such purity of faith as is sufficient now to behold, in the mirror of Scriptures and creatures [Col. 0618D], the brightness of your majesty. May we who already know you through faith be led on to contemplate the vision of your exaltedness, your good Spirit leading us into the upright land. With that Spirit and the eternal Father, may there be to you glory in your chosen and predestined ones, and victory against all enemies—you who live, reign, and rule through all things and in all things for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0619]

**THE GOLDEN COMMENTARY ON THE PSALMS AND THE WEEKDAY CANTICLES OF THE VENERABLE GERHOH, PROVOST OF REICHERSBERG**

Besides a full and lucid exposition of this divine book, it also contains a large part of the history and controversies of those times. Where he falls short, necessary supplements have been added from the still unpublished Commentary on the same Psalms by the man by far most renowned in that same century, HONORIUS OF AUGUSTODUNUM, of the Order of St. Benedict. All these works now appear for the first time, both jointly with the remaining volumes of the most recent *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, of which this is the fifth, and also separately, from the manuscripts of Reichersberg and Melk, through the labour and study of the Reverend Fathers Bernard PEZ, Benedictine and librarian of Melk, and Felix Maria Wirtenberger, of the Order of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary, preacher.

(Augsburg and Graz, 1728.) (G)*

## PART ONE

## THE LETTER OF GERHOH TO EBERHARD, ARCHBISHOP OF SALZBURG, BEGINS

[Col. 0619A] Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, with Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, joined to him (Exod. XXXVIII, 22–23), filled with understanding and wisdom, made the tabernacle of testimony, at the Lord’s command and with the aid of the people of Israel. For men together with women brought bracelets, earrings, rings, and armlets; every vessel of gold was set apart as an offering to the Lord. Whoever possessed blue cloth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, fine linen, goats’ hair, metals of silver and bronze, offered them to the Lord; likewise acacia wood for various uses. The skilled women also gave what they had spun: they gave blue cloth, purple, scarlet, fine linen, and goats’ hair, freely offering everything of their own accord. The leaders, moreover, offered onyx stones and gems. All the men and women, [Col. 0620A] with devout hearts, brought gifts, so that the works commanded by the Lord might be made (Exod. XXXV, 22 ff.).

Now Bezalel, who made the tabernacle and its furnishings, could not be the dedicator or sanctifier of his own work, because he was not a high priest. But Moses, who discharged the office of an archbishop and could consecrate even his brother Aaron as high priest, was fit to sanctify and dedicate the tabernacle which he himself had not made; for he also set it up, anointed it, and sanctified it with all its vessels.

To what purpose is this? That you, Eberhard, bishop of the holy Church of Salzburg, may show yourself ready to consider what I have devoutly made in obedience to God’s command—although I am least in the tribe of Judah, that is, a participant in those who confess the truth. [Col. 0621A] For God is love (1 John IV, 8), and that love imposed this work upon me; and I desire you, its archbishop, to be its dedicator.

Indeed, men and women helped me in making it, because the leaders before me, interpreters of the Psalms, supplied me with, as it were, onyx stones and precious gems: namely, opinions polished with the highest craftsmanship and carved as though by the work of a jeweller. I inserted these into my composition in such a manner that, now weaving their words together with their meaning, now their meaning with my own words, I have added nothing of my own which does not aptly cohere with what those orthodox leaders supplied—the men who treated the Psalms and the other divinely inspired Scriptures before me. I, a little man following in their footsteps, gather ears of grain with Ruth the Moabite, such as could [Col. 0621B] remain from the hands of those reaping with full sickles as they carried great heaps into the Lord’s barns.

Yet it goes well with me if the Lord of the harvest grants me, and other hungry persons, to rub the ears left by the ancient reapers—this very thing which I, hungry myself, offer to those who hunger and ask—and then to draw out selected grains; or to gather crumbs falling from the table of rich masters, so that we may be delivered from the famine which is to oppress Egyptians who will find no food unless they come to the true Joseph, surrendering themselves and their possessions into royal servitude.

Receive, therefore, this bundle of ears: that is, the first part of the exposition on the Psalter. If in it some ears appear green, as it were, because of novelty, may the Lord not reject them in sacrifice—he who commands in the Law that such things be roasted with fire by the priest who raises such a bundle before the Lord. You also, then, lawful priest, if you find in my writings anything thought to be new, do not immediately reject it. Rather, after applying the fire of the Holy Spirit, let there first be a friendly discussion of it between you and me and the other faithful; and, if needed, let a corresponding correction be made, one which roasts the greenness of the ears without destroying the grains hidden in them.

Thus blessed Augustine is recorded to have acted in his books of *Retractations*, where it seemed necessary. Taught, therefore, by the example of a great man, I do not wish men to swear so absolutely by my words that I will not permit anything in them to be reconsidered. Rather, I myself shall reconsider it if anything is found in them which is judged contrary to sound understanding by those [Col. 0622B] judges alone whose eye is single and well cleansed—among whom you, Bishop Eberhard, appear to me pre-eminent. Your eyes are the eyes of doves.

I do not wish to thrust my work upon the black eyes of ravens, whose beaks are ready for tearing apart, because they do not know the kisses of doves. But I believe that whatever you see and approve as consonant with reason and truth will please your dove-like eyes. Nor do I doubt that the dove’s groaning or song, frequently inserted in the Exposition of the Psalms in accordance with the desires of the faithful who request this work, will also be welcome to reason and truth; for I do not dare deny them anything that I can do in the Lord.

## THE MASTER TO HIS DISCIPLES

[Col. 0621]

[Col. 0621C] The Apostle John, asked by the bishops of Asia and by other rulers of churches to compose an Gospel concerning Christ’s divinity, did not agree to their request unless, by prayer and fasting for three days, they earnestly sought from God that he himself might merit to write things worthy of the subject. If so great an apostle, Christ’s special beloved disciple, did not presume to undertake matters beyond himself without the help of fasting and prayer, what wonder if I—great among sinners, least among saints, or indeed nothing—scarcely, or not at all, dare to do what you ask?

Yet, since all things are possible to one who believes, I do not think it impossible, with the help of true faith, that your hope and love may be satisfied, since you hope and desire together with me such nourishment from the Psalms as may satisfy our desire with good things. For this too is promised in [Col. 0621D] the Psalm where it is said:

> Bless the Lord, O my soul,  
> and all that is within me, bless his holy name.  
> Bless the Lord, O my soul,  
> and do not forget all his recompenses:  
> he who forgives all your iniquities;  
> who heals all your infirmities;  
> who redeems your life from destruction;  
> who crowns you with mercy and compassion;  
> who [Col. 0622C] satisfies your desire with good things.  
> (Ps. CII, 1 ff.)

Therefore, that he himself may satisfy with good things your desire and ours, and that of other faithful people also, to whose knowledge our work may perhaps come: in the Lord’s Prayer, where you say, “Give us this day our daily, or supersubstantial, bread” (Luke XI, 2; Matt. VI, 11), hold this very desire: that the daily and supersubstantial bread contained in daily psalmody and in the supersubstantial understanding of psalmody may abound sufficiently for us, both to relish and to distribute.

For holy psalmody is like the ark of the covenant, covered on every side with most pure and spotless gold. Within it is spiritual understanding, like a golden urn [Col. 0622D] containing manna—that is, bread given from heaven, possessing every delight and every flavour of sweetness. And just as, formerly, the ark of the covenant containing manna was neither to be seen nor touched by the people outside the sanctuary unless it had first been wrapped in blue coverings and other veils, so psalmody seems to me to sound in the Church before [Col. 0623A] the people under a great covering of figures. This veil is not to be entirely removed except within the Holy of Holies, where the God of gods shall be seen face to face. For then, when all figures have ceased, truth will shine forth and appear clearly; and, with the veils of figures removed, every spirit shall praise the Lord.

Meanwhile, it goes well with us if our desire is so satisfied with good things that the honeyed understanding of the Psalms is enough to dispel the weariness of this life. By God’s favour, we long to attain this understanding by clinging to the footsteps of the Fathers and gathering their opinions, inserting among them nothing except what accords with their faith and builds up the faith, hope, and love of readers.

If anyone, however, deigns to read what divine mercy has deigned to reveal to me—the last of his servants—as something to be known in part and prophesied in part, in order to relieve disgust with this life and kindle the desire for eternal life where it exists, and awaken it where it does not yet exist, until that which is perfect comes and that which is partial is done away (1 Cor. XIII, 10): for when God’s glory shall be manifested, not in part but in its entirety, then, as the Psalmist says, “I shall be satisfied” (Ps. XVI, 15), if I now hunger and thirst for righteousness and for God’s glory.

But that satisfaction must be reserved for the homeland. It goes well with us on the way if, in the delight of psalmody, there is for us a provision for the journey and for travel, such as was given to Elijah, who was to walk in the strength of one food for forty days and forty nights until the mountain of God, Horeb. “Forty days and forty nights” (3 Kings XIX, 8) signifies the toilsome time of this life, in which, as our strength fails, we need the strength of that food. Since its strength does not know how to fail, it does not cease to refresh and strengthen us.

[Col. 0624B] Therefore, in the strength of that food, I, lame and weak, shall undertake the course of the journey set before me—not relying on my own strength, which is none at all, but trusting in the strength of the food which can sufficiently strengthen our weaknesses. Amen.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0623]

[Col. 0623C] May my speech be pleasing to you (Ps. CIII, 34), O holy Trinity! May my praise be sweet to you, “the name of the Lord, a most strong tower” (Prov. XVIII, 10): the name expressive of the Triune Unity and the one supreme Trinity, the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

To whose praise, honour, and glory, in this present work, we intend to dedicate our purpose, seeking food in the pastures of the shepherd David. He was the first and chief of all the prophets clearly to proclaim the glorious name of the Holy Trinity. With its threefold savour, this outstanding shepherd fed rational sheep in the Psalms, three times fifty in number, and will feed them until the end of the age. For he is the man of whom it is said in the praises of the Fathers:

> With all his heart he praised the Lord  
> and loved God who made him,  
> [Col. 0623D] and gave him power against his enemies;  
> he stationed singers before the altar,  
> and made sweet melodies in their sound;  
> he gave splendour to the celebrations  
> and adorned the times until life’s consummation.  
> (Ecclus. XLVII, 10 etc.)

Truly this outstanding shepherd, “giving splendour to the celebrations, adorned the times until the consummation” (ibid.). In these celebrations, while his Psalms, seasoned with musical sweetness, resound, the times are richly adorned until their consummation. For temporal occupation in such celebrations is an introduction into eternity, which we believe to be the end and consummation of all times. Thus the sheep of this pasture, entering and going out, find pasture: entering here into the fold of faith, they possess the sweet delight of temporal psalmody; and, when they depart from the narrowness of bodily life into the vast meadow of eternity, flowers of unfading [Col. 0624C] goodness will abound for their everlasting food, as they behold the one triune God. In this life his most sweet name feeds them—the name which, as we have said, this distinguished shepherd first of all the prophets clearly proclaimed. Sacred history most clearly relates that he fed his father’s sheep, and he himself sings in these words:

> And he chose David his servant,  
> and took him from the flocks of sheep;  
> from behind the nursing ewes he took him.  
> (Ps. LXXVII, 70)

With this shepherd, the most savoury thing in the richest pastures—namely, the glorious name of the Holy Trinity—first shone forth in clear distinctions of the persons, as we have said. For he was the first to express God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit. Moses had not done this. Although Moses indicated that God the Creator begot the Son, who is the Word by which he said, “and all things were made” (Ps. XXXII, 9), he nevertheless did not clearly disclose either the begetting God or the begotten Word under the name of Father and Son, or under the titles Begetter and Begotten. Rather, with a thick veil covering his face, he set “God” and “the beginning” as signifying the Father and the Son when he said:

> In the beginning God created heaven and earth.  
> (Gen. I, 1)

Instead, he could have said: “In his Son the Father made heaven and earth” (Gen. I, 2). But in saying, “The Spirit of God moved over the waters” (ibid.), he had almost revealed the third person. Yet because he did not say “God the Spirit” or “the Holy Spirit,” the identity of that Spirit of God remained uncertain and under the veil of his face.

For certain ingenious men, thinking that they had clearly seen the face of Moses, believed that this air was signified there under the name *spiritus* (“spirit” or “wind”), because air too is called *spiritus*, as in “stormy winds” [*spiritus procellarum*] (Ps. X, 7). Such a spirit is borne over the waters by the natural ordering of the elements.

[Col. 0625A] Thus indeed, on account of the carnal people of that time, the name of the Holy Trinity was then veiled in Moses. Although he sometimes suggested God’s threefold name by repeating it three times, as here: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob has sent me” (Exod. III, 15), he kept beneath the veil of his face the relative names which distinguish the three persons.

But with this David—something which ought above all to delight and feed us—we find the nourishment of our faith more plainly expressed: namely, the mystery of the Holy Trinity. In what way more plainly expressed? Surely not only by the threefold substantial name, which is “God,” as with Moses—for example, when he says: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us” (Ps. LXVII, final verse)—but also through the explicit relative names: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

For Christ himself speaks in him:

> The Lord said to me: You are my Son.  
> (Ps. II, 7)

The implied sense is: by nature, not by adoption. For it follows:

> This day I have begotten you.  
> (ibid.)

When he says “this day,” we understand it as though he said, “in eternity,” “in immutability.” For just as his being is, and not having been or being yet to come—whence he said to Moses, “I am who I am” (Exod. III, 14), and to the Jews, “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John VIII, 58)—[Col. 0625C] so in his begetting the understanding of our faith admits neither yesterday nor tomorrow, but only today.

What follows, that the Lord Father said, “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. II, 8), is clearly said with respect to the humility of our nature. For according to this form of a servant, it both befitted him and was necessary for us that he should ask the Father—that is, suffer for our salvation. For here we wish to understand nothing else by the word “asking” except obedience, whose supreme mystery, or sacrifice, is that of his most holy Passion.

Likewise, in another Psalm, when the same God the Father, speaking in a vision to his saints—among whom David rejoiced to be one—says:

> He shall call upon me: You are my Father.  
> And I shall set him as firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth.  
> (Ps. LXXXVIII, 27–28)

When, I say, he speaks thus, he both expresses the relative names of Father and Son and sets forth both natures of the only-begotten Son. For according to his divine nature he says: “He shall call upon me: You are my Father” (ibid.). And according to his human nature: “You are my God and the protector of my salvation” (ibid.).

In accordance with this meaning he says: “This firstborn, now made exalted above the kings of the earth”—that is, now raised from the dead and about to sit in eternal session at the right hand of Majesty on high—says, “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John XX, 17).

The same David was the first to name [Col. 0626A] the Holy Spirit, saying:

> Do not cast me away from your face,  
> and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.  
> (Ps. L, 13)

For until then it had been written, “the Spirit of God” or “the Spirit of the Lord.” But here, in the more resonant phrase, he was the first to name “the Holy Spirit.” Thus he clearly proclaimed the relative names of the Holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—which neither Moses nor any other before him had expressed so clearly.

To him, as to Abraham, the promise of the blessed seed, which is Christ, was made with an oath: that Christ would be born from his seed. Singing the Lord’s mercies, he said from the mouth of the Lord himself:

> Once I have sworn by my Holy One:  
> if I lie to David,  
> his seed shall remain for ever.  
> (Ps. LXXXVIII, 36)

Accordingly, it must be reverently observed that the blessed Trinity, which showed itself to Abraham in three angels for the confirmation of the promise—or because of the greatness and dignity of the thing promised—almost expressed itself in three words to David in the promise of that same seed, namely Christ:

> Thus says the Lord of hosts: I shall give you rest from all your enemies; and the Lord foretells to you that the Lord will make you a house.  
> (2 Kings VII, 11)

For in these words, at the beginning of so great a promise—whose meaning is understood from what follows, when he says:

> When your days are completed and you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed after you, who will come forth from your womb, and I shall establish his kingdom for ever. I shall be his Father, and he shall build a house for my name. And I shall establish the throne [Col. 0626C] of his kingdom for ever. I shall be his Father, and he shall be my Son.  
> (2 Kings VII, 12 ff.)

—in these words, I say, the one Godhead of the supreme and undivided Trinity plainly shows itself by the distinction of persons.

For who, or which person, says, “I shall give you rest from all your enemies,” except the person of the Father? For shortly afterward he continues and says: “I shall be his Father, and he shall be my Son.” The “I” is that person of whom the Lord Father says, “And the Lord foretells to you.” That person is the Lord Holy Spirit, who foretold through the mouth of the holy prophets, just as Zechariah says: “As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old” (Luke I, 70).

But the person of whom he immediately says, “the Lord will make you a house,” is the Lord Son. There are not three Lords, but one Lord. So far as it could or ought, this sacred Scripture both preserved this mystery for those to come and concealed it from those living when it was composed, because they could not bear the distinction of the three persons if it were openly preached to them.

But how much, do you suppose, does the Father have in this one, according to the Gospel saying? For the Son said:

> When the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and declare it to you.  
> (John XVI, 14–15)

And immediately he added:

> All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine [Col. 0627A] and declare it to you.  
> (John XVI, 14)

How much, then, do you suppose the Father has in this one; how much did the Holy Spirit receive from this one and announce to the apostles, so that the Son of God might be glorified?

It gives great delight that, after Christ the Son of God ascended into heaven, even before the Holy Spirit came forth appearing in tongues of fire, the first thing that he uttered, receiving it from this one, he announced to Peter so that Peter might say:

> It is written in the book of Psalms:  
> Let their dwelling become desolate,  
> and let there be none to dwell in it;  
> and let another take his episcopate.  
> (Acts I, 20)

For what the Evangelist John relates had already happened: “When he had said this, he breathed on them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (John XX, 22). And Luke, writing the events of the evening of the same day, says among other things: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke XXIV, 45).

But when the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, and the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the throne of Majesty, rested upon each of them like fire—for divided tongues as of fire appeared to them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in diverse tongues as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance (Acts II, 3–4)—when, I say, this sound occurred, and at the sound the multitude assembled in confusion of mind (ibid., v. 6), did not the Holy Spirit receive from this one what he uttered through the mouth of the apostle Peter?

For after first presenting the testimony of the prophet Joel, that they were not drunk, as those who mockingly said, “These men are full of new wine,” supposed (ibid.), he immediately introduced this argument, having stated the proposition concerning the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ:

> For David says concerning him:  
> I saw the Lord always before my face,  
> for he is at my right hand, that I may not be moved.  
> Therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced;  
> moreover my flesh also shall rest in hope,  
> because you will not abandon my soul in hell,  
> nor give your Holy One to see corruption.  
> You have made known to me the ways of life;  
> you will fill me with joy in your presence.  
> Brothers, permit me to speak boldly to you concerning the patriarch David: that he died and was buried, and his tomb is among us to this very day. Therefore, since he was and knew that God had sworn to him with an oath that one from the fruit of his loins would sit [Col. 0627D] upon his throne, he foresaw and spoke concerning the resurrection of Christ: that he was neither abandoned in hell nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, and we are witnesses of it. Therefore, exalted by the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this which you see and hear. For David did not ascend into heaven; yet he himself says:  
> The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand,  
> until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.  
> (Acts II, 25 ff.)

This, as has already been said above, gives great delight: when we wish to say that the Father has many things in this one which belong to the Son, as do all other things—for all the Scriptures tend toward the Son—we observe that the first things uttered by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of the apostle Peter, on the very day he was given, were received from this one. In him God the Father stored up very many faithful testimonies for his Son.

If anyone is troubled as to why we honour this shepherd as especially eminent among the prophets, or as first among the rest—indeed, before the rest—let him observe this: prophets were not called prophets because of every kind of prediction of future events, but chiefly because they spoke sublimely concerning the kingdom of God, the kingdom of Christ, and the Church.

For Moses, Joshua, and Samuel, who were before the prophets, said openly in words nothing concerning the kingdom of God; nothing, or little, concerning the punishments of hell; nothing, or little, concerning the judgment by which the righteous are to be saved and the impious condemned. This was not because they did not know these things, but because excessively carnal men and lovers of the earth would not receive them. The prophets, however, spoke magnificently about such matters.

David was first, for example:

> For in death there is none who remembers you;  
> but in hell who shall confess you?  
> (Ps. VI, 6)

He first sang of Christ’s kingdom in intelligible words, and also used words belonging to the person of Christ suffering or rising again. He is therefore first among the prophets, although no one should doubt that blessed Job, before him, spoke openly about the resurrection of the flesh.

At this point the matter itself quite fittingly suggests that we ask: for what reason did the Word of the Lord, the Spirit of the Lord, intending to speak of the powers of the age to come, choose for himself a king through whom to speak? Indeed, why did he will that the man through whom he had first determined to speak about the [Col. 0628C] salvation of souls or eternal life should be a king?

It was not because David was king that he chose him and desired to speak through him; rather, because he had chosen him and prepared him for this office, he therefore willed that he should be king. Why, then, did he act so? Why did the Word of the Lord come in this manner? Why did he will first to be heard from tribunals? Why did he send forth his first utterances from a royal throne?

Surely because of our hardness, our vanity, and our pride. Let us attend carefully and knowingly confess that the cause is, or has been, in ourselves. The whole audience of this world had become deaf to God and prided itself on hearing vanity; every living human being was altogether vanity. The populous wantonness of the flesh, devoted to the game of vanity, scorned to know and could not hear the serious concerns of eternal life and impending death.

We see the world, now old and decrepit, still for the most part behaving wantonly, scorning the mature words of Gospel preaching and thus being burdened by the hearing of sound doctrine as by a load or mass of sand. Preachers are sometimes publicly mocked unless they take care, as the Lord commanded them, saying: “Do not cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. VII). How much more, when the world was still fresh and vigorous, exulting in the luxury of youth, would it have scorned to hear the Word of the Lord preached by any person whatsoever?

Therefore the Word of the Lord was foreign to this world. It would have no attentive or favourable hearing among the rich men of the age unless it began its address from the mouth of a rich king, a great king, a king strong in hand and victorious, such as this David was.

[Col. 0629A] Yet it was too little that a powerful person should give the Word of God, already mentioned, authority through his power. Sweetness was needed, so that through bodily senses a necessary goodwill might be instilled into minds alien to it. The wondrous craftsman, the Spirit of the Lord, eager for human salvation, provided this also. He willed that the one whom he was preparing as minister of the divine Word should be a boy musician playing the lyre, so that thereafter, gradually advancing, he might make him in due order a Psalmist: that amid musical sweetness he might both prophesy by singing and sing by prophesying the work of salvation for souls.

Thus both the words, running in metrical feet, and the ringing strings of the psaltery, leaping in turn, might gradually reach the mind through the ears and sweetly implant faith, hope, and love of God.

His instrument was formed in the shape of the Greek letter delta, hollow inside, covered on the outside with the skins of dead animals, having ten strings and sounding from above. Each of these things has a mystical meaning for us. Its inner hollow signifies that we are to be emptied of earthly possessions, as he says: “He has scattered, he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever and ever” (Ps. III, 9). The skins of dead animals signify that we ourselves, with our vices and desires, ought to be mortified, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Mortify your members which are upon the earth” (Col. III, 5). Its ten-stringed arrangement is the observance of the Decalogue. The sending forth of sound from above is the desire for heavenly things alone, the love of God alone, as the same Apostle says: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20).

The sound of the strings is the utterance of voices itself. The distinction of the fingers is the plurality of the gifts of the Holy Spirit; their movement is also the activity of all the righteous. Nor is it without mystery that, as we have said, the psaltery—that musical instrument—was triangular, after the shape of the Greek letter delta. For in it there is not only the mystery of the supreme Trinity, which the Psalms resound, but also suggested a certain trinity of the chief virtues, by which we are to be reconciled to the supreme Trinity.

[Col. 0629D] For there are three things through which a human being is led to God’s likeness, according to his purpose when he said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26). These three are faith, hope, and love. For a human being was created in God’s image insofar as he is rational. But he attains likeness to that same creating Trinity by possessing these three: faith, hope, and love.

The first human being, falling away from them, lost the glory of God’s likeness in this order: he did not admit love, did not maintain hope, and did not possess faith. Love of God was first required of him in that God made him unlike all the living creatures and because no helper like him was found for him. “Let us make,” he says, “a helper like himself” (Gen. II, 18), namely for the propagation of offspring so numerous and of such great blessedness that they might be like angels. “And he took him and placed him in the paradise of delight” (ibid., 15).

[Col. 0630A] For such great benefits he rendered no service of love, no utterance of thanksgiving. Then hope was required of him in the giving of this command: “From every tree of paradise eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat” (ibid., 17). For as a rational human being he ought to have hoped, saying: “If God has bestowed such great things freely, will he not give greater things if I keep the command?” But he did not hope in the Lord. Instead, pleasing himself as though free, he wished thus to be God. For unless he had then possessed inward swelling of pride, he would not so easily have yielded when outwardly tempted.

Faith was required of him: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death” (Gen. I, 18). But he did not place faith in this saying; indeed, he believed the serpent more when it said: “By no means shall you die the death” (Gen. III, 4), and obeyed the credulous woman’s evil voice more than the voice of God.

Thus that old Adam, falling away from love, hope, and faith, defrauded both himself and his posterity and removed them far from the likeness of the blessed Trinity. Conversely, the new Adam, by the reverse stages—through faith, hope, and love—restored us to that same likeness of God.

And all Scripture divinely inspired (2 Tim. III, 16) tends toward this end. Above all, the Psalter itself, of three times fifty Psalms, proclaims and sings a threefold jubilee of faith, hope, and love. The first human being, as has already been said, fell away from these virtues—first losing love, then hope, and finally faith. Without them none of his children recovers salvation, though in the reverse order: first possessing faith, then hope, and finally love.

[Col. 0630C] This faith, moreover, must be possessed in relation to one man; this hope in relation to one and the same man; and this love toward one and the same man, Christ. The first part, namely fifty Psalms, sets forth in seven *periochae* or summaries what we ought to believe. The second part, likewise consisting of fifty Psalms, confirms hope by returning through no fewer than seven *periochae*. The third part also, of fifty Psalms, celebrates love with jubilant blessings and praises, recapitulating it seven times.

Since several matters are customarily investigated at the beginnings of books, four are here not idly sought: the subject matter, the intention, the mode of treatment, and the title of the book. Of these we speak briefly. The subject matter of the book is the whole Christ, [Col. 0630D] that is, the head together with all the members. Its intention is that the members themselves may be urged toward conformity with the head, so that the individual members may be suited to such a head. For the form of a body is grotesque and monstrous if its members do not correspond to its head—for example, if the head appears to be of adult age, while the hands or feet appear as infantile or boyish members. Hence the Apostle also exhorts us to grow “to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13).

Now Christ is indicated at the beginning of this book as a mature man, where it says: “Blessed is the man” (Ps. 1). We must therefore be proportioned to the maturity of this man, insofar as the fitness of each member requires: so that those who are in the great body of Christ, which is the Church—whether hands by working well, or eyes by contemplating, or [Col. 0631A] feet by running in the way of his commandments—may be at the measure of the age of this blessed man. Nothing childish is fitting in his whole body, except perhaps in some member which is growing or beginning to grow, yet stretching itself forward toward the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ. Such little ones, indeed, must be borne in Christ’s body and fed and nourished with the milk of the Psalms or of other holy Scriptures, until they reach the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ. If they refuse to reach it but persist in childhood, boys a hundred years old in no way belong to this blessed man, who does not yield to the counsel of the ungodly so as to tolerate in his body—which is blessed—even one such child, accursed in the Scriptures.

It should be noted, however, that it is not said “to the measure of Christ,” but “to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ.” But what is Christ’s fullness except that of which it is said: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14)? Thus the fullness of grace and truth in Christ has an age, because Christ himself advanced in age, wisdom, and grace before God and men, unto manly antiquity and maturity, while he is believed to have reached even to the Ancient of Days—so strong and wise even in his human nature, which alone advanced in him—that he is not more powerless or weaker than God the Father, the Ancient of Days. He also ran the course of this life so manfully that he did not depart from uprightness in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of pestilence.

Those, moreover, are conformed to him who, according to the measure of grace that forms each member and configures it to the head, themselves willingly and diligently take care not to go in the counsel of the ungodly. And if they have gone—as David went in the counsel of the stranger who came to him and persuaded him to both adultery and murder—yet they imitate that same David by not standing, not persevering, in the way of sinners. Rather, they quickly seek the remedy of repentance, lest by lingering in sin they begin to sit in the seat of pestilence. Even if they have begun to sit there, and to stink, though four days dead, in the corruption of pestilence, it is still possible for that blessed man who did not go, stand, or sit in sin to call such persons also from the tomb of their stinking conscience [Col. 0631D] to the light of confession, saying: “Come forth”—that is, confess what you conceal within. Thus even those who are restored to life from four days’ death are conformed to the same man who is life; those recalled to the path of righteousness are conformed to the same man who is the way; and those by whom their sins are truthfully accused are conformed to the same man who is truth. Yet each person is nearer to blessedness in proportion as he has spent less time going, standing, or sitting in sin. But he alone is the supremely blessed man who never went, stood, or sat in sin, having been conceived without sin. To be conformed to such a one is the chief intention of the Psalms, which treat of Christ and his whole body.

The mode of treatment, moreover, is *miktikon*, for there are [Col. 0632A] three modes of treatment: exagematic, dramatic, and *miktikon*, that is, mixed. The exagematic mode is that in which the author alone speaks, and no one else, unless first mentioned by the author or writer himself—as in the five books of Moses, where Moses speaks, and anyone who is to speak there is first mentioned by him. Thus: “The Lord said to Abraham: Behold, Sarah thy wife shall bear thee a son” (Gen. 17:19); likewise: “Rebecca said to Jacob her son: I heard thy father,” etc. (Gen. 27:6).

The dramatic, however, is the kind of speaking or writing in which various persons speak abruptly, without introductory mention, while the author says nothing in his own person. Thus in the Song of Songs, now the utterances of the bridegroom, now those of the bride, now those of the young women, and of other persons are interwoven; [Col. 0632B] and there the author says nothing in his own person, though he speaks the whole work through the persons of others.

*Miktikon*, that is, mixed, is composed of both modes of discourse, when now the author speaks in his own person and now the introduced persons speak—as in the Apocalypse and in Boethius’s *On the Consolation*. For John speaks in his own person: “I John, your brother and companion in tribulation” (Rev. 1:9), and other such things appropriate to himself alone; and there speak the seven thunders, the seven trumpets, and other diverse persons, though mentioned while he writes, yet suddenly introduced, suddenly heard or seen, in John’s very vision.

The exagematic kind is suited to historians, proceeding in plain style through events, concerning which the author must possess unquestioned truth and the hearer or reader easy belief. The dramatic kind, woven from various persons, is suited to wedding songs, such as the Song of Songs. This was also observed by secular authors in the performance of comedies and tragedies, because that kind of speaking seemed more apt to move the emotions of sorrow, joy, or another disposition of mind. The mixed kind, however, is more suited to investigating mysteries and is more effective for persuading one to believe what ought reasonably to be believed. Hence not only the wise men of the world used this kind when investigating secrets, as we have in Plato’s *Timaeus* and Boethius’s *Consolation*; but the prophets too used the same kind when persuading people to believe [Col. 0632D] things marvelous and difficult to believe. The Psalter is woven in this mode of speaking or writing.

For King David, author of the Psalms and outstanding lyre-player, whose psaltery was pleasant with the lyre (Ps. 80:3), when he was reigning prosperously and wished to magnify the worship of God, chose four thousand men to sing Psalms not only with their voices but also with musical instruments. He set over them Asaph, Jeduthun, Heman, Ethan, or the sons of Korah (1 Chron. 15:19; 23:5; 25:1). They sounded the Psalms in three ways: with the human voice, with musical instruments, or jointly in both ways; and this jointly in two ways—either with an instrument after the voice, or with the voice after the instrument. Hence [Col. 0633A] their names too are inserted among the titles, that they might receive honor from their ministry, especially through the significance of the things denoted.

David himself also struck the lyre with the singers in the house of the Lord and sang God’s praises, inserting certain things in his own person, such as: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy” (Ps. 50:1). A psalm, however, is the sound of an instrument. A canticle is the song of a human voice in praise of God. A “psalm of a canticle” is when the voice follows the instrument. A “canticle of a psalm” is when the instrument follows the voice.

Some, however, think that the mode of treatment itself varies according to the different psalms. The variety of the Psalms encourages this belief. For in some occur frequently dramatic songs, which are [Col. 0633B] characteristic of a wedding poem or a lament. An example of a wedding poem is the psalm: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. 44). For only the introduced persons speak there, and the whole psalm proceeds in praise of the bridegroom and bride. A poem of lament is the psalm: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Ps. 136). In it nothing is said in the author’s person, but the mournful complaint of those weeping is expressed through introduced persons. Psalms of this sort, composed solely through introduced persons, may be assigned to the dramatic kind.

An example of the mixed kind is the psalm: “He who dwells in the help of the Most High shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven” (Ps. 90). For the Prophet-author himself says the first verse, while God the Father says the last. For to whom but God the Father would it belong to say of the man who hopes in him: “Because he will hope in me, I will deliver him and protect him, because he has known my name. He will cry to me, and I will hear him; I am with him in tribulation; I will rescue him and glorify him. I will fill him with length of days and show him my salvation” (ibid.)? But in those Psalms in which history is woven, an example of the third mode of treatment is shown to us, as in: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever,” etc.

However varied the Psalms may have been sung then or may be sung now, and however the persons singing or speaking in the Psalms may vary, we must observe this: in psalmody we must join our own feeling to the feeling of the Psalms. For if it was thought right in comedies and tragedies that one who represented the words of a rejoicing or mourning person in theatrical trifles should imitate the feeling of the rejoicing or mourning person, how much more should we, in the praises of the true Christ, conform ourselves—not pretentiously but with true devotion—to the feelings of those whose words we resound. Thus, with David repenting, may we also say in true repentance: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy” (Ps. 50). With him rejoicing, may we also say in joy: “I will exalt thee, O God my King” (Ps. 144). With him wondering, let us wonder, saying: “O Lord, our Lord, how admirable is thy name in all [Col. 0634A] the earth!” (Ps. 8). With him hoping, may we also say in hope: “In thee, O Lord, I have hoped” (Ps. 30). For David alone represented in himself many persons and the feelings of many persons, when, having become all things to all people, he not only sang beforehand but also prefigured him who now alone sings in those who sing well and wisely, as he himself says to the Father: “I will give praise to thee among the peoples, O Lord; I will sing to thee among the nations” (Ps. 56:10).

This is the true David, the sole Psalmist in all who sing wisely—that is, by understanding the feelings of the Psalms. Since all the power of psalmody and prayer lies in the feelings of devotion, let us enumerate some of them and demonstrate them by examples, so that, since we cannot enumerate them all (for the feelings are infinite), [Col. 0634B] we may infer from some examples what in all is praiseworthy and acceptable to God.

There is the feeling of Love, when the mind perhaps sees or recalls what it loves and is suddenly seized by the fire of love. There is the feeling of Wonder, when it contemplates something new and marvelous and is stirred to amazement. There is the feeling of Rejoicing with Another, when, on seeing something acceptable and pleasing, it is suffused with a certain cheerfulness. There is the feeling of Humility, when, from considering its own weakness, it voluntarily restrains itself from self-exaltation. There is the feeling of Sorrow, when, by considering its evils, it languishes and is weakened, as it were. There is the feeling of Fear, when it is shaken by considering impending punishments. There is the feeling of Indignation, when it is inflamed to hatred of adversaries by the very malignity of their injustice. There is the feeling of Zeal, when sorrowful grief kindles it to a desire for vengeance. There is the feeling of good Confidence, when some new and singular trust gives a person more courage than usual in seeking redress.

Of these feelings, the first three belong especially to that kind of Scripture in which praise is offered. For the feeling of Love arises from recalling goodness; the feeling of Wonder from recalling power and strength; and the feeling of Rejoicing with Another from recalling some prosperous outcome or happy deed. The following three belong to that kind in which [Col. 0634D] misfortune and misery are recalled. For the feeling of Humility arises from recalling one’s own weakness; the feeling of Sorrow from recalling present evils or remembering past ones; and the feeling of Fear from foreseeing future ones. The last three feelings are more suited to that kind of Scripture in which invective and accusation against adversaries are made: namely, we are indignant at their wickedness, zealous against injury, and, because of their malice, have greater confidence in God’s mercy.

Examples of each are these. From the feeling of Love the psalm is sung: “I will love thee, O Lord” (Ps. 17). From the feeling of Wonder the psalm is sung: “O Lord our Lord, how admirable,” etc. (Ps. 8). From the feeling of Rejoicing with Another the psalm is sung: “All nations, clap your hands” (Ps. 46). And in all these there is praise. From the feeling of Humility the psalm is sung: “How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget?” (Ps. 30). From the feeling of Fear the psalm is sung: “O Lord, not in thy fury” (Ps. 6). And in all these the prayer of complaint is intermingled. From the feeling of Indignation the psalm is sung: “Why dost thou glory in malice?” (Ps. 51). From the feeling of Zeal the psalm is sung: “God of vengeances” (Ps. 93). From the feeling of good confidence the psalm is sung: “Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence” (Ps. 25).

It must be understood that not all Psalms possess this characteristic, namely that one feeling extends through the entire sequence. Rather, one often passes from one feeling to another, according as the minds of those praying are accustomed to be affected in different ways. It is not our present purpose to explain how this may be recognized in each Psalm. Yet we wish to demonstrate it in a few examples.

Perhaps I begin to consider how great is the happiness of being with God, how great is the misery now of living in this world, and, finally, how great is the calamity of being tortured forever in hell; and from this meditation, suddenly drawn by a great love of the heavenly homeland, I run, led by that feeling, into these words: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly,” etc. (Ps. 1). If we seek the whole meaning of this Psalm according to the inward feeling of compunction, what else do we find it saying everywhere but this: Happy are those who have never departed from God! Happy are those who have always remained with God! Happy are those who persist faithful and devoted in his service! For unhappy and miserable are those who have removed themselves from him and have refused to persevere with him, or who have not returned to him after first departing. Thanks be to him, insofar as I have remained steadfast. Shame be to me, insofar as I have departed. But now, insofar as I am near, I do not wish to withdraw; insofar as I am far away, I desire to return. Would that I might reach him; would that I might never depart from him! Help me, Lord my God! This, therefore, is the feeling of Love arising from praise.

Likewise, an example of another feeling. I considered with myself how great God’s power is, and then began to wonder at the madness of people who nevertheless do not fear to oppose his will. Therefore, compelled by this wonder, I cried out [Col. 0635D] and said: “Why have the nations raged?” etc. (Ps. 2). It is Wonder mingled with Indignation, because we wonder at madness and are indignant at presumption. Or certainly, in ourselves, when outwardly we behold hostile and importunate assaults of vices, and inwardly put confidence in God’s help, we rebuke the very distress of our temptations with a certain indignation, saying: “Why have the nations raged?” (ibid.). The whole point of the Psalm also tends to this: that, strengthened by God’s power, we may despise insolent adversities and confidently judge ourselves stronger than our adversaries in proportion as we are nearer to God. This is the feeling of Wonder mingled with Indignation arising from praise.

The sequence of the following Psalm is not woven according to one feeling, [Col. 0636A] but often passes from feeling to feeling. For example, being placed in distress, I somehow see myself abandoned by God, and from the feeling of Sorrow I burst out into these words: “O Lord, how are they multiplied?” etc. (Ps. 3); “Many say,” etc. Again, returning from the feeling of Sorrow or from the feeling of good Confidence, I say: “But thou, O Lord, art my protector,” etc., so that I may relieve Sorrow through Trust and chasten Trust through Sorrow. And who can enumerate all the powers of the Psalms, all those fiery compunctions of holy feelings by which the soul is inflamed in prayer and a sacrifice most pleasing to God is offered upon the altar of the heart?

It remains that, while singing Psalms, we should strive to shape [Col. 0636B] our minds according to the senses and feelings of the Psalms. Let us call blessed the friends of our Lord whose sins have been forgiven (Ps. 31), who are undefiled, who search his testimonies (Ps. 118). Let us call blessed all who fear the Lord (Ps. 127), desiring to be admitted to their fellowship. Likewise, let us show him, and recount in the Psalms, our misery and the wickedness of our enemies, demons and human beings, seeking and desiring his consolation and protection against it. Meanwhile, let us praise his power, wisdom, and mercy, so that when we make jubilation to him in the Psalms, we too may remember him, and he may deign to remember us for good.

Let these things have been said not only concerning the mode of treating the subject matter of the Psalms, but also [Col. 0636C] concerning the manner of singing Psalms, for the exercise of our minds and the invocation over us of the help of divine consolation.
