For if Elisha the prophet caused a psalmist to be brought to him so that, by the modulation of psalmody and by calling upon the Spirit of the Lord over himself, he might perform a miracle to refresh an army exhausted by excessive thirst, how much ought we to trust in the power of the Psalms? For behold, now in the Church, throughout many religious monasteries, young men and virgins, old persons together with younger, praise in Psalms and hymns the name of the Lord Sabaoth—that is, of armies drawn up for battle—seeking in psalmody divine help against the powers of evil spirits and human beings (4 Kings 3).

[Col. 0636D] Now let us speak of the title. Some maintain that the first Psalm is the title, and, as it were, the preface, of the whole Psalter; nor is this improbable. For what is proper to a title? Namely, that it contain and indicate the author’s name and the subject matter of the work that follows. We find this in the first Psalm, because that Blessed Man of whom it is written at the beginning of this book is himself the author of the Psalms, and he himself together with his whole body is the subject matter of the Psalms. Therefore, since he is the title, he rightly lacks a title: either because it deals fully with the Blessed Man, of whom the following Psalms partly speak and partly prophesy; or because Ezra, who supplied the titles of the Psalms and arranged them, did not dare to place a title upon this Psalm, seeing that in the following passage Christ had spoken of this Psalm [Col. 0637A] and had, as it were, assigned its title when he said: “At the beginning of the book it is written of me” (Heb. 10:7). Nor is it fitting that this Psalm should have a title, since it is the head and title of the other Psalms. The individual Psalms, however, are found prefixed with their own proper titles, as will appear below.

The book’s name is either the *Book of Hymns* or the *Book of Soliloquies*. A hymn is praise of God with song. It is appropriately called the *Book of Hymns*, in which are many praises and songs of divine mysteries. Or it is the *Book of Soliloquies*, because this prophecy was administered to a human being by the Holy Spirit alone, without human instruction.

Prophecy, moreover, is a divine inspiration which foretells events with unshakable truth, whether through deeds or words. This grace was given in many ways: through human actions, as in Noah’s ark, Abraham’s sacrifice, and the crossing of the Red Sea; through births, as in Esau and Jacob, who signified future things; through angels, as they spoke to Abraham, Lot, and others; through visions, as to Isaiah, Ezekiel, and the rest; through dreams, as to Solomon and Daniel; through a cloud and a voice from heaven, as to Moses; or in yet other ways. But David, not by any of these means, but inwardly instructed by a heavenly inspiration, with the Spirit speaking in him, was fulfilled, as in the book of Kings: “The Spirit of the Lord was directed upon David” (1 Sam. 16:13). And the Lord says: “If David in the Spirit calls him Lord, how is he his son?” (Matt. 22:45).

The Holy Spirit, however, was so given to the prophets that at times it departed because of sins and, being appeased, returned. As Peter says: “Prophecy was not at any time brought by human will; but holy men of God, inspired by the Holy Spirit, often spoke” (1 Pet. 1:21). Nor are those excluded from the gift of prophecy who have been given the ability rightly to understand or interpret the Scriptures, or to expound them wisely in the Church, according to the variety found in psalmody itself. For it sometimes treats simultaneously of the whole—that is, Christ and the Church—and sometimes of each separately, that is, [Col. 0638B] Christ or the Church.

It treats of Christ in three ways. Sometimes it speaks of his divinity, as in: “With thee is the beginning” (Ps. 109:3); sometimes properly of his humanity, as in: “Thou hast granted him the desire of his heart” (Ps. 20:3); sometimes by transference, saying of him what belongs only to the members, as in: “Far from my salvation are the words of my sins” (Ps. 21:2). It treats of the Church in two ways: sometimes according to the perfect, sometimes according to the imperfect. It also sometimes inserts remarks concerning the lost for the sake of the good.

## FIRST PSALM

[Col. 0637]

[Col. 0637C] **VERSE 1.** “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence.” — **VERSE 2.** “But his will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night.”

What does this first voice of the Psalter proclaim to us, except that Christ is without sin? Without sin, I say, which we ought to believe and hold in faith. He was conceived and born of the Virgin Mary. He is the one and only one “chosen from thousands” (Song 5:10), to whom the proclamation of this Psalm applies. For who besides that one is such and so great a man? Indeed, if actual sins are in question—to say nothing for the moment of the greatest and best-known saints—who could count the multitude of innocent little children who have not gone in the counsel [Col. 0637D] of the ungodly, stood in the way of sinners, or sat in the seat of pestilence? But if you consider original sin, there is no one at all except this one. For, as the Apostle says, “In Adam all have sinned” (1 Cor. 15:45). Therefore this is that man, the truly blessed man, whose conception and birth took place through the operation of the Holy Spirit, as is beautifully indicated by this saying.

**VERSE 3.** “And he shall be like a tree planted beside the courses of waters.” For by the plural “courses of waters” we understand the divisions of spiritual graces, all of which were poured out together upon this God-bearing man, or blessed man, from the very beginning of his conception. But these gifts, distributed or apportioned, were given to other people, whoever are worthy of him, not in this way or with such fullness, but far less and incomparably less.

But at his conception so great a power of the Most High overshadowed the Virgin—that is, the Holy Spirit, who in the beginning moved over the waters, cherishing them so that they might possess that spiritual fruitfulness by which there is now regeneration in them whose generation had been defective. That same Spirit, I say, gave the Virgin fruitfulness without taking away her integrity, forming in her a new man. Because his conception was wholly effected beneath the shadow of the power of the Most High, like an intact egg made fruitful by the warmth and brooding of a bird under its shadow, it was wholly clean, just as his mother was intact.

For the Virgin herself, intact, is like the whole egg which, in the holy Gospel, is contrasted with the scorpion, when the Lord says: “Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?” (Luke 11:12). The scorpion flatters with its face but wounds with the curved sting of its tail. Thus the devil, speaking in the serpent to Eve, poisoned her with the venom of pride and incontinence, so that in all her posterity, as in the tail of a scorpion, the cause of death is found down to Mary, protected and overshadowed by the Holy Spirit. Though she herself was conceived in sins according to the manner of other human beings, [Note: [Col. 0639D] Concerning this opinion of Gerhoh, now almost obsolete, I wish the same observation to be noted that I very recently made in Dissertation 16 prefixed to the Homilies of the Venerable Godfrey, Abbot of Admont. (See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIV, beginning.)] nevertheless, like “a garden enclosed” and “a sealed fountain” (Song 4:12), she was inaccessible to actual sins.

Indeed, original guilt itself failed and was consumed in her, as smoke vanishes before the brightness of the sun and wax is consumed before fire, while the Holy Spirit—that is, divine love, the love of God the Father—at once illumined and inflamed her. Filled and warmed by this love, she conceived intact. As in an intact egg a bird is conceived through another bird’s heat, or as a worm is conceived from pure earth through the heat of the sun, so the intact and pure Virgin conceived through the heavenly love of God the Father working in her. Beholding her humility and loving her chastity, he uttered a good Word into her mind and womb; and by the heat of his love, not through carnal but spiritual delight, he drew from her flesh flesh fit to be seed for his seed—that is, for his Word, uttered into the Virgin as we have said—and united it through the mediation of a rational soul divinely created, with such power of union that the man conceived in the Virgin through the love of God the Father became God at the very moment of conception. He did not lose the reality of human nature, but was clothed in the power and strength of divinity, according to: “The Lord is clothed with strength, and has girded himself with power” (Ps. 92:1).

But he is not clothed with divine strength and power as with an accidental and separable form. Rather, in divine form—which [Col. 0639C] is nothing other than divinity itself—he shone forth and shines forth “more beautiful than the children of men,” so that divinity itself is the substantial form, indeed more than substantial, of the man thus conceived. For in the natural connection of substances and substantial forms or differences—for example, of humanity and rationality, or of fire and heat—forms are not predicated of substances except by adjectival names: for example, when one says “a rational human being,” “hot fire,” “cold snow,” and “moist water.” But when we call the man born of the Virgin God, we do not make this name adjectival for him; rather, we understand it wholly substantivally of him: to be God, to be life, and to be truth.

Hence, when asked concerning that man as to person, “Who is he?” we rightly answer: “He is the Son of God, and likewise the Son of Man.” When asked concerning essence, “What is he?” we rightly answer: “He is wholly God, wholly man, wholly almighty, and essentially good and wise.” All these things are predicated substantivally of him, whose whole substance is both truly divine and truly human, generated wholly from God and wholly from man through the working of the Holy Spirit. For just as in human generations the son of a man and a woman is wholly the son of both—for example, Isaac is not the son of Abraham alone nor of Sarah alone, but is the son of both—so Christ also is not the Son of God the Father alone or of the Virgin Mother alone, but the son of both.

Perhaps the hearer readily agrees [Col. 0640A] that Isaac, born from the bloods of father and mother, from the will—that is, the carnal love—of the woman, and from the will—that is, the love—of the man, is the son of both man and woman, having been conceived and born, as it were, from the blood of both. But because Christ was born “not of bloods, nor of the will” (John 1:13), or love, “of a man,” but from female blood or flesh alone, without the admixture of male blood or flesh, he may rightly seem properly to be called the son of the woman, because he drew the substance of his flesh from her flesh alone. But how this son of the virgin woman is also called the Son of God the Father is not easily grasped by the understanding, since that man seems to have been generated from a human being only, and not also from God, insofar as he is human.

Nestorius the heretic was in this error. Dividing the man from God too greatly, he split Christ into two sons, assigning to the Virgin Mother alone the generation of the man alone. Hence he forbade the Mother of the Lord to be called *Theotocon*, that is, “God-bearer” or “mother of God,” assigning to her only the birth of the man. But we believe, and therefore speak, that the woman bore a divine human being—indeed, more truly, the God-Man. For that which was taken from her flesh, conceived in her, and born “is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20), is of the love of God the Father; and therefore not only the Word received from God is the Son of God the Father, but also that seed which, taken from her, was conceived in her and born.

[Col. 0640C] For if Isaac, to use examples from nature, born from bloods, from the will of a man, and from the will of the flesh, is not half but wholly the son of Abraham, and not half but wholly the son also of Sarah, because he was wholly conceived from the love of both, then Christ likewise is wholly the son of the woman and wholly the Son of God the Father, because he was wholly conceived and born from the love of both—not from the will of the flesh nor from the will of a man, but from God (John 1:13), and solely from divine will or love.

For this reason we do not call the Virgin’s will, by which she consented to the angel’s words, a will of the flesh, because her will was not carnal but divine and spiritual. Indeed, she was one spirit with God, as the Apostle says: “He who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). Therefore “that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20). For a woman loving God and burning with divine love received and conceived from him the seed, that is, the eternal Word. God remained what he was and began to be human; he remained immortal as he was and became subject to mortality. For in that conception God did not diminish, but the human being advanced. His human substance was not received from God the Father together with the Word, but was conceived together with it through the working of the love of God the Father. Thus the Virgin both received and conceived the divine seed, that is, the Word; and together with that divine seed conceived human flesh united to it—a flesh which she received from no lover, but conceived through divine love.

Therefore this man is rightly called the Son of God the Father, from whose love he was wholly conceived; and God is rightly called the Son of the woman, who received him from God her lover, conceived him without shame, and bore the true God and true human being without pain. Thus God may properly be predicated of the human being, and the human being of God, and he may be called God-Man and Man-God. For, as Pope Leo maintains in his sermon on the Passion of the Lord, God so assumed humanity, and the human being was so assumed into God, that nothing divine was lacking to the one assumed and nothing human to the one assuming.

To this man, to this blessed man conceived and born of divine love, the likeness of a tree planted beside streams of water is rightly promised. We understand [Col. 0641B] this tree to be the tree of life placed in Paradise, where a fountain rose from the earth and watered Paradise by streams of water—that is, by four rivers. On that tree was fruit that produces indissoluble life; from eating it man was then excluded because he had tasted the death-bringing fruit of the forbidden tree. This life-giving tree in the midst of Paradise is the eternal wisdom of God, set in the midst of rational creation. Holding, as it were, the middle place between angels and human beings, it made itself accessible to both and offered both the eternal sweetness of its fruit, beside streams of water—that is, beside all the delights and graces which water the rational and spiritual Paradise. But rational nature, having transgressed the commandment, was shut out from this tree [Col. 0641C] and driven into exile, so that the sweetness of divine wisdom is not accessible to it in itself, because a revolving sword has been placed between them.

Therefore, since man could not come to wisdom, Wisdom itself deigned to come to man, by assuming a true and pure human being. To him it gave the whole power of its benefit and sweetness, so that, just as wisdom is the tree of life for blessed angels, so the blessed man, united with wisdom, might be a tree of life alike for angels and human beings. Just as the fruit of wisdom produces blessedness for the blessed angels, so may the fruit of Christ’s body and blood confer life and blessedness on those who partake of it.

For Christ’s body is the blessed earth from which the fountain rises through the abundance of four rivers—that is, the four Gospels—and of other waters—that is, many [Col. 0641D] graces—watering Paradise, that is, the Church. Or rather, the very earth which no man cultivated is the Virgin Mary, from whom the fountain rose when she bore Christ, the living fountain, who says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). From there this fountain is divided through the heads of four rivers—that is, the four Gospels, or the four sacraments: namely, the Incarnation, which is suggested in this first psalm; the Passion, which is displayed in the second, where it says, “Why have the nations raged?”; and the Resurrection and Ascension, which are treated in the third psalm, where it says, “I slept,” etc. For the words, “I rose, because the Lord sustained me,” indicate the Resurrection; while the words, “My glory, lifting up my head,” indicate his Ascension [Col. 0642A]. The fourth psalm teaches how earth, watered by these four rivers, bears fruit: “They have been multiplied by the fruit,” it says, “of their grain, wine, and oil.” Was it not therefore most truly said that this blessed man, like a tree planted beside streams of water, will yield his fruit?

But you say to me: If he is the tree of life, why do those who taste his fruit, who eat his body and blood, not immediately become immortal? Here one must note: “he will give his fruit in its season.” For if, remaining in mortal sins, you approach unseasonably and eat his body, it is not he who gives, but you who seize; and therefore you eat judgment. But if you grieve for past sins and willingly guard yourself against future ones, he will give his fruit: life-giving food [Col. 0642B], but in its proper season. For here too he gives life to the soul through faith, according to what is written: “The righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17). And again in its proper season—that is, on the last day—he will give life to the body and make it blessed together with the soul.

He therefore is like the tree of life planted beside streams of water. But when he is called “like a tree,” do not suppose that a likeness is thereby presented to you such that the likeness lacks reality. For in this likeness is the Word made flesh, not half-full but altogether “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). It would be half-full if only the Word as Word were life-giving. But now, because his flesh is life-giving with an efficacy no different from that of his divinity, the whole Christ is the tree of life—indeed, life itself, as he says: “I [Col. 0642C] am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

And therefore, because his flesh gives life as the spirit does, the flesh itself is spirit; for “the spirit is what gives life” (John 7:63). Nor is it absurd to say that a body conceived of the Holy Spirit is spirit. For if what is born of flesh is flesh, as each of us is, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit, as are souls reborn from water and the Spirit, then certainly the body born in her from the Holy Spirit—she who conceived from the Holy Spirit—is spirit because it was born of the Spirit; and nevertheless it is flesh, because it was born from the true flesh of the virgin’s body. This is wonderful in our eyes: that the same thing is flesh and spirit. Yet it is not wonderful to the eyes of faith, because all things are possible to one who believes [Col. 0642D].

Otherwise, it would not be true that “the first man became a living soul,” and the second man “a life-giving spirit” (1 Cor. 15:45). The phrase “a living soul” conveys great poverty, because he could neither live of himself nor give life to others. But the phrase “a life-giving spirit” conveys such fullness of grace and truth that, just as God the Spirit lives of himself and gives life to angels, so the man made a life-giving spirit has power to live of himself and to give life to those who believe in him.

Yet this man lives of himself, not from himself, because “as the Father has life” abiding in himself, “so he gave the Son to have life” abiding in himself (John 5:26). And just as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also does the Son [Col. 0643A]; and, to put it more expressly, the body of the Son too gives life to whom it wills. As the Son says: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 10:15)—that is, eternity, omnipotence, immortality, and the other attributes of divinity—so the man assumed into God can truly say: All that my divinity has is mine, such as the efficacy of giving life and the reality of every power, by which the body born of the Virgin has been so filled that it is full of grace and truth, not merely of truth in an empty likeness.

Thus, when this blessed man is said to be like a tree planted beside streams of water, the promise of likeness signifies the fullness of complete truth, as in the words: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten” (John 1:14). And John saw the Lamb “as though [Col. 0643B] slain” (Rev. 5:6). He is not called “as of the only-begotten” in order that he should not be understood to be truly the only-begotten; nor is he said to be “as though slain” in order that he should be understood not truly to have been slain. So too this man is called like the tree of life, which is wisdom; and here we should observe not so much a likeness as a fullness of truth.

For he who is the power and wisdom of the Father is the same one who is the son of his virgin mother; he who “became a life-giving spirit” (1 Cor. 15:45) is the same one who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh: one Emmanuel in two natures, but not in two ranks of dignity; one giant of double substance, but not of double glory. For the two natures in Christ have one dignity and one glory, especially after, departing [Col. 0643C] from this world for the Father, he obtained for his flesh that brightness which he had in divinity with the Father before the world was made (John 17:15).

He did indeed possess this brightness of divinity from the hour of conception. But for us human beings, born obscurely and in sins, he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7), because he deigned to become mortal, though he owed nothing to death. But after his triumph over death, God the Father so exalted him who had voluntarily humbled himself that, to him to whom at conception he had given the reality of the name “which is above every name,” he gave, through the glory of resurrection and ascension, the very “name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that [Col. 0643D] the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (ibid., 10).

For just as the boy David was first secretly anointed king, and afterwards, having overcome many dangers, also received the name of king, so Christ received the eternal kingdom in the virgin’s womb, the angel saying: “He will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Luke 1:32), which is the kingdom above every kingdom. But he was first named in this kingdom when, after the spiritual Goliath and Saul—that is, death—had been killed, his humanity, now put to death, shone in divine glory. Of this it is said: “You crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands” (Ps. 8:6–7).

Nor is it unfitting that the man who reigns forever should be called the eternal king. For the man indeed had a beginning, but his kingdom has neither end [Col. 0644A] nor beginning; since it is certain that this man, who was not always man, was God eternally and always. This is not unusual even in ordinary matters: a predicate is stated of its subject in this manner. If a man, remaining what he was—namely, a man—begins to be something which he previously was not, for example a bishop, we rightly and truly say, “This bishop nursed at his mother’s or nurse’s breasts,” although he was not then a bishop when he nursed at his mother’s breasts.

But if a man began to be something in such a way that he ceased to be a man, as Lot’s wife became a pillar of salt and ceased to be a human being, it would not be a correct or fitting statement for anyone to say, “This statue ate; this stone nursed at its mother’s breasts.” For the man changed into stone or a statue ceased to be what he was when he ate and when he nursed at his mother’s breasts.

Therefore, when God the Son of God began to be man, remaining what he was, he became high priest and began to possess the office of offering sacrifice, which he did not possess in his divinity; for in his divine essence neither sacrifice nor temple was available to him. Yet, as I have said, remaining what he was—namely God and eternal king—he began to be what he was not: made man, made high priest, possessing both the sacrifice which he might offer and the temple in which he might render propitious his own divinity and that of the Father and Holy Spirit. Made, I say, man and high priest, he did not cease to be what he was [Col. 0644B].

Therefore it is rightly and properly fitting to say of the God-man, alike high priest and king, that this man, this high priest, created the world and reigned before the world, although he was not then a man in actual fact when he created the world or reigned before it. Yet this high priest was then king, and in his kingdom there is no change “or shadow due to variation” (James 1:17). Likewise, in his essence there is no change or shadow of variation, although some change and variation may be noted in the acts or sufferings of that person.

Therefore a qualification is necessary in such cases, to specify in what respect something is said. For example, that he wept for dead Lazarus (John 11) was an act of Christ according to his humanity; that he died while hanging upon the cross was a suffering of the same according to his humanity. But that he raised Lazarus [Col. 0644C], and that he himself rose from death, were acts according to his divinity. Nevertheless, the whole Christ did and suffered all this, though he did not suffer it according to his whole self. So the whole man is said to be sorrowful, although sorrow is in the soul alone; and the whole man is said to see, though sight is in the eyes alone.

Nor is it figurative speech when a human being says, “I see,” as though the whole were put for the part; for through the eyes alone the whole person understands and perceives that he sees wholly. Similarly, when Christ said, “Before Abraham, I am” (John 8:58), the whole man himself knows that he was—indeed, rather, that he is—God before Abraham, because future and past are removed from the essence of divinity, to which all things are present. Thus he did not say, “Before Abraham I was,” nor, “Before Abraham my divinity was,” [Col. 0645A] but, “I am,” he says, because even his humanity was present to his divinity.

Read Jerome’s work to Paula and Eustochium concerning the Assumption of Saint Mary; and when you find there that the man in Christ God is coeternal, understand him as a tree planted together with divinity beside streams of water, so that you may know that this man, while preserving his human essence, exists in the complete glory and omnipotence of divinity. For the distinguished Jerome mentioned above, expounding this psalm, affirms that this tree is to be understood as nothing other than Christ. And in order to lend greater force to the promise that the likeness of this tree is promised to the blessed man—since likeness is normally between different things—he explains that the blessed man is not Christ but any one [Col. 0645B] of the elect, so that the tree may be understood more explicitly to be Christ, some likeness of whom is promised to every one of the elect; lest, if a likeness of a tree, however precious, were promised to Christ, who is supreme, this might seem to detract from his supremacy.

Other great Catholic commentators, however, seeing that no human being except the one and only Christ can be found who did not go, stand, and sit in original sin, firmly affirm that Christ alone is proclaimed here as the blessed man. We, therefore, avoiding absurdity on either side, understand Christ by the blessed Man, and eternal Wisdom by the tree. How this blessed Man is planted together with it is known by the Holy Spirit, the maker of this [Col. 0645C] planting, the fountain of waters flowing from this tree to water the Paradise of the Church. In this Paradise the contemplation of one principal tree has long detained us, as we taste and see that its commerce is good.

Therefore, in the lengthy and elaborate treatment at the beginning of this book, we refuted the view of those who say that the man united to God should not properly be called God, but only figuratively, as though the whole were named for the part. [Note: [Col. 0645D] See below the treatise, “How according to Hilary, etc.”] For although there is a difference between Christ’s acts and sufferings, as stated above, there is no difference in divinity. Rather, just as the Word is properly called God, and the Father is properly called God, so the man assumed into God is properly called God. For the same divinity is predicated, not differently, of the Father who deifies the man and of the man deified—indeed, made God and born into God—when “the man is God” is said, and when “the Father is God” is said.

But because, following the streams of living waters, we have perhaps wandered too far while it pleased us to walk about the tree planted beside streams of water, we now withdraw our foot from the difficult path of this question [Note: [Col. 0646D] You have this also below.], which we have treated more fully, so far as the Lord granted us, in the work *On the Glorification of the Son of Man*. Let us now return to our purpose. For we proposed briefly to demonstrate in this psalm that the most holy humanity of our Lord and God Jesus Christ was without sin, both original [Col. 0646A] and actual. It is now enough to establish this by the following three oppositions:

“He did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, but his will is in the law of the Lord.”
“He did not stand in the way of sinners, but he will meditate on the law of the Lord day and night.”
“He did not sit in the seat of pestilence, but he is, or will be, like a tree planted beside streams of water, which will give its fruit in its season.”

Let us now show the two opposite counsels, whose three effects are greatly contrary. What was the counsel of the ungodly in which the man who was not blessed—that old Adam—walked, that is, departed from God? Surely this: that he who was dust presumed to will to be like God. What, on the other hand, was the counsel of the godly in which this blessed man—the new Adam—stood firm and did not walk, that is, did not depart from God? Surely this: that he who was God by nature deigned to descend into our dust [Col. 0646B]. The former was the counsel of the devil’s spirit; the latter, the counsel of the Spirit of God.

Hence the three oppositions mentioned above: that man, in accordance with the former counsel, walked away; this man’s will, in accordance with the latter counsel, was in the law of the Lord. Indeed, as the Apostle says, he was “made under the law” (Gal. 4:4), although he was Lord of the law. The former stood in the way of sinners, for he manifested in action the evil thought of ambition. This one meditated on the law of the Lord day and night, in order to fulfil by the truth of his passion what had been prefigured by legal ceremonies, for example by the paschal lamb, the calf, and other such things. The former sat in the seat of pestilence, that is, he left to his descendants as an inheritance the pestilence of the twofold death, of soul and body. This one, however, like a fruitful tree, gave this fruit in its season, so that by eating his flesh and blood we might be freed from the guilt of that forbidden food.

This first psalm, then, proclaims faith in Christ’s Incarnation: namely, that in the first Adam this second Adam neither walked, nor stood, nor sat, because he was conceived and born of a virgin. Hence he is free from original sin. The remaining words of the psalm, “But his will is in the law of the Lord,” etc., commend his actual righteousness. Thus, by believing in him, we are rightly freed both from original and actual sins, so that we may be righteous persons whose way the Lord knows. But the way of the ungodly will perish—that is, those who persist in unbelief by opposing this [Col. 0646D] blessed man, though his words deserve to be believed with the firmest faith.

For “his leaf will not fall”: that is, his word will not be void, but is more enduring than heaven and earth, as he himself says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. 24:35). He promised the kingdom of heaven to the poor in spirit. He promised consolation to those mourning for their own sins and those of others. He promised mercy to the merciful. He also promised other rewards of blessedness, differently, to others obedient to him in different ways. These rewards, like fruit, are covered and guarded by words as by leaves, and none of them is found false.

Whence is this? Because it is not one person who promised and another who will fulfil the promises—for that would not be promising but foretelling. Rather, he himself who promised will fulfil the promises, as he says in the prophet: “As rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again, but make the earth drink and cause it to sprout, so will my word be which goes out from my mouth: it will not return empty, but will accomplish whatever I have willed and prosper in the things for which I sent it” (Isa. 55:10–11) [Col. 0647A].

“It will prosper,” he says, because everything that he does will prosper. When Peter was younger, he girded himself, ready to go with Christ both to prison and death; but he did not prosper in doing so, because as often as he presumed upon himself, so often he was permitted to deny. And so long as we attempt to accomplish any good by relying too much on our own strength, [Col. 0647B] we do not prosper. But when, instructed by adverse events, we cease to strive in vain and stretch out our hands in prayers or almsgiving, that he may gird us with his power, or with the girdle of faith through which all things are possible to one who believes, then Christ himself, who promised good things to those who do good, deigns by himself to do in us what he commanded us to do, and what we could not do without him. Then he proceeds prosperously and reigns in us, because not what we do, but whatever he does, will prosper, even if it appears adverse.

The blessed Father Augustine knew this, and so prayed: “Lord, give what you command, and command what you will.” The apostle Paul knew it, who said: [Col. 0649C] “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, those who are called saints according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8:28 ff.) [Col. 0647C].

Therefore, if you have learned, O man, that you could not predestine yourself, that you could not call yourself once predestined, and that you could not, nor will be able to, justify or glorify yourself once called, what remains for you except to stretch out your hands to him who alone will prosper in accomplishing these things? And when he begins to work the work of salvation in you, “honour the Lord,” not yourself, “with your substance” (Prov. 3:9): with your riches, not acquired by you for yourself, but given to you by him. Honour the Lord with the firstfruits of your crops.

What are the firstfruits, and what are the crops? Your crops are the rewards of eternal blessedness laid up and promised for you; but the firstfruits of merits precede those crops of rewards. Therefore honour him with your firstfruits, recognizing and attributing to him the merits and good works which he works in you and with you, while he deigns to make you a partner in his work. He has no need of your good things; yet when he works well with you, you work with him as your hand works with you, though it can do nothing without you.

To speak more expressly: as you work with your tool, and your tool which you hold in your hand works with you, so God uses you as an instrument when you do something good with [Col. 0648A] him. For as a smith first works a hammer or another instrument, and afterward works through the instrument while the instrument works with him, so God first inspires a good will in free choice, and afterward breathes upon that good will so that it may act; and he makes it cooperate with himself as he works in it and through it.

In saying this, we do not destroy free choice, but instruct it, so that it may know that it can do nothing without God: as a branch can do nothing unless it remains in the vine; as a hand can do nothing unless it remains in the unity of the body; as any instrument does nothing unless it is moved by the artisan’s hand. Thus we proclaim that the choice of human reason is free, while at the same time testifying that it needs to be set free still further.

[Col. 0648B] For Scripture notes three freedoms, all of which souls to be made blessed in God and with God require. There is freedom from necessity; freedom from sin; and freedom from misery, which is the punishment of sin. From the first freedom, freedom from necessity, free choice is called free because it is in no way compelled or prevented, whether by fatal, natural, or accidental necessity, from freely willing whatever it wishes, whether good or evil.

Nevertheless, if free choice bears upon itself the burden either of sin or of punishment, it necessarily requires a twofold freedom, or liberation: namely, from sin and from misery, in order that its freedom may be true. Of this the Lord says in the Gospel: “If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free” (John 8:36) [Col. 0648C]. For our first freedom from necessity comes from God the Father, who created us. But because man has abused this freedom, he has remained—and always remains—free from necessity; yet unless the Son frees him from sin and misery, he will not be truly and completely free, because the one freedom of man is weighed down by the twofold slavery of sin and misery.

Of neither can he rid himself by his own power, because between sinful and miserable man and just and blessed God there is such enmity that sinful man cannot approach the Just One, nor miserable man the Blessed One, on account of the great chasm of iniquity and misery fixed between these opposites. But in order that miserable sinners might be reconciled to justice and blessedness, Christ, the mediator of God and men, came between them. Since a mediator is not mediator of one party only, he took on what was fitting to both parties, retaining justice and assuming misery, so that he might be suited to sinful, miserable man through misery voluntarily assumed, and might adhere to God the Father through justice. Thus he freed man not only from misery but also from sin by the obedience through which he himself bore misery without sin [Col. 0648D].

It is therefore certain that unless the Son frees us from the yoke of sin and misery, we shall not be truly free, although by the Father’s creative grace we are always free from necessity. Therefore, when through Christ, who frees us from sin and misery, we perform good works, he performs them in us; and everything that [Col. 0649A] he does in us will prosper for us, provided that we seek not our own glory but the glory of God.

**VERSE 4.** “Not so the ungodly, not so.” Because they do not adhere to God through humility. “But [they are] like dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth.” Through pride and vain glory they are scattered from the face of the earth—that is, from the Church, made firm by the moisture of Christ’s grace. Lacking the moisture of that grace, they are cast away by the wind of pride, which seeks high things and puffs up, from the face of the earth—that is, from eternal stability, which is called the land of the living. For as this land of the dying nourishes and contains the mortal outward person, so that other land nourishes and contains the inward and immortal person. And because the wind casts them away, therefore:

**VERSE 5.** “The ungodly shall not rise in judgment.” That is, what the proud seek is taken away from and denied them: namely, that they should judge, that they should sit as judges in the judgment in which only the poor and humble will be judges and will judge. They can say with Peter: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you.” To them the Lord replies in Peter: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:27–28) [Col. 0649B].

Or, “the ungodly do not rise in judgment” (John 3:18), to be judged, because those who do not believe are judged already. Or the ungodly who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit do not rise in judgment in order to judge and accuse themselves through confession and repentance. For, says the apostle Paul, “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (Rom. 11:31). Or: they do not rise in the judgment by which God judges the ungodly and sinners in this world through rebuke and correction, so that they may not be condemned with this world, if at least they may be found capable of amendment through chastisements. For, as the Apostle says, “when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with this world” (1 Cor. 11:32).

For the saints, to be judged by the Lord in this world so as not to be condemned with this world is desirable. Therefore any one of them says: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause” (Ps. 42). But in this judgment those rise in the first resurrection who grieve that they have deserved God’s chastisements, fear further punishment, and willingly take care, saying of the past: “Forgive us our debts”; and of the future: “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6:12–13). But those who are ungodly or utterly unbelieving—such as pagans, or Christians obstinately apostate from Christ—do not rise in this first resurrection.

“Nor sinners in the counsel of the righteous.” As at the beginning of the psalm he proclaimed blessed the man who did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, so now he shows the unhappy sinners who do not rise in the counsel of the righteous. These counsels are contrary to one another. For the counsel of the ungodly, as stated above, was that dust should be proud and exalt itself to God’s likeness. The counsel of the righteous is not to think high things, but to consent to lowly things, humble oneself under the mighty hand of God, and remember that man is dust and will return to dust [Col. 0650A].

Again, the counsel of the righteous is not only to fulfil a commandment but also to add something by counsel, as the Apostle says concerning virgins: “I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7:25). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor” (Matt. 19:21). Sinners do not rise in such counsel, since they scarcely, or not at all, consent even to obey commandments alone.

Another translation has, “in the counsel of the righteous,” and the Hebrew truth agrees with it, reading: “Nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.” For the righteous have one soul and one heart in God, especially those who dwell with one accord in the house and sing: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132). But sinners who persist in sin do not rise in such an assembly, because when people are gathered together in this unity, they join them either not at all or deceitfully [Col. 0650B]. And if such a person enters, “his heart speaks vanity; he gathers iniquity to himself” (Ps. 40:7). He gathers iniquity there where he ought first to lay down the iniquity already gathered; and at last, burdened by the fellowship of the good, he goes out, either in mind or body, and speaks so as to increase vanity and iniquity (ibid., 8).

It should be understood that this is not said of every ungodly person or sinner. For, as the Apostle testifies, Christ died for the ungodly; he came to seek and save what was lost; and he did not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance. Hence it is certain that many ungodly persons and sinners [Col. 0650C] rise in the assembly of the righteous. But this concerns sinners hardened after the likeness of Pharaoh, for whom no blows and no signs are profitable because of their obstinate hardness of heart, known to God.

**VERSE 6.** “For the Lord knows those who are his, and knows the way of the righteous; nor is the way of the ungodly hidden from him.” He knows the way of the righteous by approval, as he says to Moses: “I know you by name” (Exod. 33:12). But he says to the ungodly: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12); and therefore “the way of the ungodly will perish.”

The way of the righteous and the path of the ungodly are here put for their desire. For as a way or path tends toward a given destination, so a good or bad desire is directed and extended toward obtaining something. If something is desired lukewarmly, the spirit’s movement is as though walking slowly or crawling. But when desire becomes intense, the mind runs swiftly to grasp what it longs for. And indeed, apart from little children and the very foolish, everyone runs, because all desire either good or evil. “All indeed run, but one receives the prize” (1 Cor. 9:24).

All the righteous are reckoned as one, because the desire of all of them is in the One and toward the One: in the one God whom they seek to make propitious to themselves, to contemplate and live with the one God. Therefore the Lord knows—that is, approves—their way, namely the desire of the righteous, being generous to give what each righteous person desires. But the path of the ungodly will perish [Col. 0651A], because it does not tend toward one thing, but is directed in diverse ways and scattered. And their path will perish in this respect: when each of them awakens, he will not have the things he desired, wickedly acquired, or wickedly possessed, according to the saying: “They slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75:6).

In this life they dream when they entertain, with a desire to possess them, phantasms of temporal riches in the dreams of their heart’s thoughts: for example, when they build beautiful houses, meditate upon delicious feasts, devise quarrels, or handle in imagination rather than in reality the precious and beautiful things of this world. Even when they pray outwardly, they dream inwardly, imagining at one moment that they rule or teach others, and at another that they reject another’s rule or [Col. 0651B] teaching. They are altogether like sleepers, because they turn over in their hearts mere forms and images of things, not rejecting and separating them as saints and righteous persons do, but loving them and committing fornication with them as the ungodly do.

For the Lord says: “Whoever looks upon a woman”—that is, upon the beauty of this world—“to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). He is polluted with her too, as in a nocturnal dream; and in that pollution there is no hope of offspring, when he embraces her for the pleasure of thought but will not possess her in reality. But if the desired thing came to him, some hope of offspring might arise from it: bad offspring, if he acted badly from it; or good offspring, if from the mammon of iniquity [Col. 0651C] he made friends for himself who might receive him into eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9).

Therefore, because on the path of perverse and worldly desires they die in such a way that their desires are satisfied neither here nor hereafter, their path will perish. So the path—that is, the desire—of that rich man in hell perished when he could not obtain the drop of water he desired. But the Lord knew Lazarus’s way, that is, what his desire was. Let us consult the Gospel. For when Abraham says, “But now he is comforted, while you are tormented” (Luke 16:25), it is plainly gathered that in his misery and sickness Lazarus had a desire for consolation, which he obtained. Therefore his path did not perish, because through desiring consolation he came [Col. 0651D] to consolation.

Therefore the Gospel says: “Woe to you who are rich, because you have your consolation” (Luke 6:24), because, furnished with this consolation, they desire no other. Lazarus, on the other hand, strongly desired that other consolation, ran to it in strong desire, and reached it, because the goads of poverty, sickness, and excessive desolation compelled him continually and intensely to desire an abundance of consolation. So, I think, when the abomination of desolation appears in the days of Antichrist, the elect, driven by the scourge of desolation and pressed by the strongest desire for consolation, will run until they come together into the perfect man (Eph. 4:13), who did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, did not stand in the way of sinners, and did not sit in the seat of pestilence.

[Col. 0652A] A man is called ungodly with respect to God, a sinner with respect to himself, and pestilent toward his neighbor. These three words—“he went,” “he stood,” “he sat”—are drawn from the analogy of exiles, who are more easily recalled while they are still on the road; more difficult to recall once they are standing in exile; and, finally, most difficult of all when they have become teachers and masters there and occupy chairs of authority. Hence the last times will be more dangerous, when evil people “will heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires, their ears itching” (2 Tim. 4:3). Their way will at last perish, because, contrary to their desires, when their chairs have been overthrown, that blessed man who “did not go,” etc., will reign.

This psalm is customarily sung in veneration of a martyr, a confessor, or many saints, because in them is found a great conformity to [Col. 0652B] the blessed man who did not go. For they too did not go into the counsel of the ungodly—whether demons, men, or carnal suggestions—by consenting; they did not stand in the way of sinners by committing sin; and they did not sit in the chair of pestilence by defending it. Thus Adam went when he consented to the devil’s and Eve’s persuasion; he stood when he bit the fruit; he sat when he excused himself. Or otherwise: Adam went when he departed from God; he stood when he took delight in sin; he sat when, confirmed in pride, he could not return by his own power, unless liberated by this one who had none of these faults.

“But his delight is in the law of the Lord.” There is one will without the law, another under the law, and another in the law. The Apostle speaks of himself according to different states.

[Col. 0652C] For according to the first state he says: “I myself was once alive without the law” (Rom. 7:9). According to the middle state he says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward man. But I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and leading me captive in the law of sin,” and death (Rom. 7:22, 27). Of the third state he says: “Now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

Before Moses the world was without law; but those who received the law given through Moses were under the law. And “the law indeed was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). Therefore those who received his grace were not slaves under the law, but sons of grace. [Col. 0652D] “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12). Sons are not under the law like slaves, who fear to transgress the law and would do so if they dared; rather, the will of sons is in the law, because it does not disagree with the law.

Children still little, so long as no desire tempts them, are without law. Adolescents, however, who are tempted and do not dare to sin, are under the law. But those who are tempted and do not sin, not because they dare not, but because they do not wish for the filth of vices and love the beauty of virtues—their will is not under the law but in the law of the Lord. These are sons, not slaves. “And if sons, then heirs: heirs indeed of God and fellow-heirs of Christ” (Rom. 8:17).

But those tempted by desire, who delight in being tempted [Col. 0653A] and dare to sin, are children of Gehenna. Yet they can become children of grace by resisting temptations and overcoming them. For the more victoriously they conquer them, the nearer they become to the light; and they wholly cease to be children of darkness. They will be children of light in the Lord if, when tempted, they do not consent at all to sin—advancing, by not consenting to temptation, to the place where they may live without feeling temptation.

This peace does not belong to this life, which is full of temptations: for human life upon earth is temptation. But here, by not consenting to temptations, we seek the future life, in which we shall not feel temptations. Yet in this life even saints who through faith conquered kingdoms and worked righteousness were tempted. But because their will was in the law, not under the law—because they maintained their devotion not under compulsion [Col. 0653B] but voluntarily—they were not led into temptation, but brought to temptation. They could not be separated from God’s law; and where they could not display it in deeds, they nevertheless meditated in that law day and night, continuing in prayer what they could not do in action.

Because such a will, meditation, or prayer could not be annulled, they too were like a tree planted beside streams of water, which will give its fruit in its season. For, in likeness to Christ, who bore witness to the truth and died for it, they too produced the fruit of confession and martyrdom, whether hidden or manifest. “And their leaf did not fall away” (Jer. 8:10), because truth was in [Col. 0653C] their words. “And everything they did prospered, because all things worked together for good for those who love God” (Rom. 8:28).

Thus they were separated from the ungodly, whom the wind casts away from the face of the earth, who do not rise in judgment, whose way will perish; and they were found in the counsel and congregation of the righteous, whose way the Lord knows. Therefore, at the end of the psalm, rejoicing in thanksgiving for their salvation and blessedness as we, poor though we are, share their joy in the Lord who has glorified them, and rejoicing in heart in supplication for ourselves, who are to be glorified in the same Lord, while bowing our heads, we sing:

Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. This praise of the Trinity was brought forth by the Fathers assembled at the Council of Nicaea against the Arian plague, because that wicked one, the son of iniquity, denied that glory is coequal to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, preaching that the Son is less than the Father and the Holy Spirit less than both. Against this the Catholic Church sings: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.”

[Col. 0653D] At first it was said: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, unto ages of ages.” But blessed Jerome enlarged the same doxology by inserting: “as it was in the beginning, and now, and always.” The same blessed man obtained through a letter from Pope Damasus that, by apostolic institution, this praise should be recited at the end of the Psalms. It is ordinarily observed thus, unless a reason requires the doxology to be omitted, just as the *Gloria in excelsis* is sometimes omitted.

That “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit” is inserted more frequently into psalmody [Col. 0654A] than into readings from other Scriptures, we do not believe to have become customary without divine providence. For, as we said in the prologue, the glorious name of the Trinity was first clearly declared in the Psalms, though it had been hidden beneath the veil of Moses’ face up to this David. Rightly, therefore, the same gracious and precious name is appended at the end of the Psalms as signifying their final purpose.

For what is the end toward which those who sing psalms wisely tend, except the glorification of the Father, who wonderfully created us from nothing; of the Son, who more wonderfully redeemed us from the dominion or slavery of the devil and sin; and of the Holy Spirit, who illumines and adorns most richly the fabric of our being, which the Father built from nothing and the Son rebuilt when it had been destroyed? He illumines it by knowledge of the truth and adorns it by love of virtue, so that we may be unto the praise of his glory—to him whom we sing.

There is another benefit in this: that at the end of Psalms, and at the end of responsories taken from the Psalms [Col. 0654B] or from other books, the Holy Trinity is commemorated. Since Solomon says, “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower; the righteous runs into it and shall be exalted” (Prov. 18:10), when, by perhaps singing wisely, we gather a treasure of good hope, or, by singing negligently, lose it—do we not possess a necessary and secure refuge, in which we may either preserve safely the treasure we have gathered or recover by grace what we have lost?

“The name of the Lord,” Solomon himself says, “is a most strong tower; the righteous runs into it.” But with the severity of the law removed by divine dispensation, now in the time of mercy and grace we dare to say more than Solomon, because “a greater than Solomon is here” (Matt. 12:42). He said of this most strong tower, which is the triune and one name of the Lord, that the righteous should flee to it. We say that both righteous and unrighteous ought to flee to it: the righteous, that he may be justified still more; the unrighteous, that he may be wholly changed. Therefore, whether we sing wisely or—may God avert it—negligently, it is safe for us to flee to this most strong tower, commemorating the name of the Holy Trinity in thanksgiving for good thoughts, words, and deeds, and in confession [Col. 0654D] and repentance for evil thoughts, words, and deeds.

For speech is generated from thought; and from thought together with speech proceeds the beauty of action. In this very fact there is a fitting likeness of the eternal Trinity, and for this reason glory and thanksgiving are owed to it, if in us a good thought has first gone before, in the heart’s faith unto righteousness; if from this there proceeds the confession of the mouth unto salvation; and if from both proceeds a perfect work. Thus in the faith of the heart that thinks well there is glory to the Father; in good speech there is glory to the Son—namely, to the incarnate Word, the eternal wisdom of God, which proceeded from the mouth of the Most High; and in good works the Holy Spirit is glorified. For “one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11).

[Col. 0655A] Indeed, all goes well with us if not only in the Psalms but in all our movements nothing occurs except for the glorification in us of the supreme Trinity. But “who is wise, and will keep these things?” (Ps. 106:43). And “who can understand transgressions?” (Ps. 18:13). Which mortal can count how many vain thoughts arise while psalms are being sung? “The Lord alone knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain” (Ps. 93:11).

Would that the vain thoughts which arise might at least, at the end of the Psalms, be driven away by this fan of the Holy Trinity! Would that we might perceive them in thought in such a way that we do not consent to them! Would that they might touch us without moving us at all! For this is what we say in prayer: “Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the sinner move me” (Ps. [Col. 0655B] 35:12). This hand so moves some people that they cannot stand or sit to sing psalms, and they wander outwardly not only in heart but also in body, otherwise than is fitting.

Would, then, that vain thoughts might rage in us at least in such a way that they do not rule us. For if useless and vain movements of thought “have not ruled over me, then I shall be immaculate and cleansed from the greatest sin” (Ps. 18:14), which is the deliberate consent to evil thoughts. Why have we mentioned these misfortunes of thought except so that, when Psalms or other actions have ended, in the most strong tower which is the name of the Lord we may seek not only a firm defense, where neither rust, moth, nor thief (Matt. 18:6, 20) can diminish our deposit, but may seek [Col. 0655C] in it a medicine sufficiently saving against the sins of thoughts, words, and actions?

In this way, if one has thought, spoken, and acted well, glory be to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things. But if one has thought, spoken, and acted less well, where iniquity has abounded, may grace abound still more, so that from a greater remedy there may be greater glory to the Trinity that heals.

Again, the aforesaid Solomon, wishing that a person might never be without the companionship or meditation of God’s word, said: “It is better to be two than one, for they have profit from their companionship. Woe to one alone, because when he falls he has no one to lift him [Col. 0655D] up. And if two sleep together, they keep one another warm; but how shall one be warmed? And if someone prevails against one, two resist him” (Eccl. 4:9 ff.). He immediately adds: “A threefold cord is not easily broken.”

Certainly, in praising and commending companionship and the benefit of companionship in two persons sleeping together and warming one another, what else is suggested, what else urged, except that the rational mind should never remain alone, but should always delight with the word of God in the bedchamber of the heart, not without great benefit? For if someone prevails against one, two resist him. If an assault of temptations is going to prevail against a person who is alone, and God’s word is joined to that person in holy faith and meditation, two—that is, the person and the word of God—resist it. If it found the person alone, it would surely prevail over him, just as that David, a stranger, prevailed when he found him alone on the roof.

[Col. 0656A] Here the two, sleeping together, will warm one another. For how shall one—that is, a person alone—be warmed? The word of God and the person warm one another, because the word of God, warm itself and warming, warms the person sleeping with it, resting with it in secret meditation, and unable to grow warm by himself.

But what mortal, conceived in iniquities, is found never to be left alone? The Son of the Virgin alone could say: “He who sent me is with me, and has not left me alone, because I always do the things pleasing to him” (John 8:29). If by his gift we sometimes think what is pleasing to him, do we persist in this always? Is not our Beloved “like a gazelle or a young stag” (Song 2:9), now hidden in the forest of his secrets, now revealing himself through the fields of revelations? Does not “the Spirit breathe where he wills, and you hear his voice, but do not know where he comes from or where he goes?” (John 3:8).

Who, therefore, sleeps with him in so unbroken a sleep of contemplation that he does not withdraw from him for an hour? For although he says concerning the one who loves him: “I and the Father will come and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23), nevertheless, while remaining in them according to the root of faith and charity, in a certain manner he departs from them and leaves them for a time to their weakness, as he left Peter and David, his beloved ones.

What, then, must those thus left do except have [Col. 0656C] their anchor of hope fastened to that threefold cord which is not easily broken? This cord is nothing other than the triune and one God, whose name we invoke over ourselves whenever we sing: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.”

It sometimes happens that Gideon, Israel’s leader and judge—that is, any spiritual combatant in prayer—is deprived, in fighting against the battle-lines of vices, of his entire army, that is, of the whole exercise of his spiritual meditation. Yet, trusting at last in the triumphant name of the Holy Trinity, he triumphs with only three hundred, strengthened or helped through the invocation and name of the Holy Trinity, or even through the saving and victorious sign of the holy cross. Its mystery shines in the number three hundred, because, just as we indicate five by the letter V and ten by the letter X, so the Hebrews indicate three hundred by the letter T; and this letter represents the form of a cross.

[Col. 0656D] By its power also the patriarch Abraham triumphed over four kings, setting out to war with three hundred and eighteen household-born servants against the innumerable army of four kings, who were taking five kings captive along with Lot, his kinsman (Gen. IV [probably Gen. 14]). The history of this battle is well known; let us seek its mysteries.

The patriarch Abraham is the faithful spirit. His kinsman, joined to him, is the sensory life, which functions by means of the five senses as if by kings. Each of these senses, like a king, has an army accompanying it. For example, sight has an army of images, that is, crowds of phantasms, which it has absorbed through the eyes; for we retain inwardly, in the field of memory, images and likenesses of things that we see outwardly. [Col. 0657A] Likewise hearing has in the same field its own army, namely certain representations of words and sounds which entered through hearing. Thus too, in touch, taste, and smell, we perceive in ourselves certain phantasms that entered through the doors of these senses.

All of these, together with sensory life itself, ought to remain in Abraham’s neighborhood—that is, so that they do not wander from the path of reason. Yet sensory life with its phantasms is often so captured, even while we pray, by the four worldly passions—unjust desire, wicked fear, perverse joy, and the sorrow of this age—that sometimes the faithful spirit, resembling faithful Abraham in that it has no approving feeling in such matters, notices this great burden through the sad messenger of recollection.

[Col. 0657B] Therefore the faithful spirit imitates faithful Abraham also in this: through the invocation of the Holy Trinity or the sign of the holy cross it pursues the spoil and seeks it again. For prayer and praise are sometimes made more subtle and more heartfelt when, grieving over what is past, people fortify themselves more attentively with the name of the Trinity and the sign of the cross, when “their infirmities have been multiplied” (Ps. 15:4), and afterward they hasten on.

Again, in the elect themselves such weakness is not unto [Col. 0657C] death, but for the glory of God, for the glory of the physician, so that God the physician may be glorified through it, just as the Son of God was glorified through Lazarus’s four-day death. This glorification will take place more magnificently the more attentively Martha and Mary pray. Mary is love of God in us; Martha is love of neighbor. Or Mary is faith in the divinity; Martha is faith in Christ’s temporal dispensation. In the voice of these sisters it is said: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (John 12 [probably John 11]).

If you had been here, the psalm sung without intention would not have died. But now I know that whatever you will, will be. For by the merit of the devotion of such persons the Psalms that were like dead things to us will rise again, when they passed through our mouths without our attention. [Col. 0657D] For Christ says: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:24): the resurrection, namely, of those for whom Martha and Mary intercede; the life of those sisters themselves, who will not die because charity never fails, and, by its double affection toward God and neighbor, bears the likeness of twin sisters.

But where this twofold charity is absent, “Let the dead,” says the Lord, “bury their dead” (Matt. 8:22). For without charity even faith that moves mountains is dead—how much more so psalmody. As for the phrase inserted in the doxology of which we are speaking:

“As it was in the beginning, and now, and always, and unto ages of ages. Amen.”

We can understand it clearly in this way: let “the beginning” refer to the age of eternity, [Col. 0658A] in which full glory was predestined for the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in their house, which is the Church. For every house is built by someone. Moses indeed, though he was a servant in a house not his own, yet because he was its faithful steward, was so glorious that, because of “the glory of his face, the children of Israel could not look upon his face” (2 Cor. 3:7). How much more gloriously will the Lord of the house and its builder be glorified in his own house by his own household!

Indeed, the whole earth is full of his glory—or rather, heaven and earth are full of his glory. Since this glory is hidden, we desire that it be manifested in the world, as it was most fully predestined in the beginning. Let it be manifested now, that is, as long as “now” is said; and always and unto ages of ages, that is, forever.

That which lacks beginning and end is called eternal, like that beginning in which all things were predestined, from which, as from a fountain, all things flow—things that now, and always, and unto ages of ages, by flowing tend toward that same beginning as to their fountain. These things have perpetual being, not eternal being like the beginning itself, which is *Amen*, that is, Truth. It is placed at the end as a seal never to be corrupted, just as the beginning is incorruptible, in which lie the primordial causes of all things.

[Col. 0658B] So surely the final end of those same things, which is *Amen*, that is, Truth—when every falsehood shall be destroyed—will be and will appear incorruptible. This very thing we desire in the glorification of the supreme Trinity. For when we say, “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,” we must understand: “So may it be now and always and unto ages of ages, Amen”—that is, in the execution and fulfillment of predestination—“as it was in the beginning,” that is, in predestination itself and the preordination of things.

The beginning of things is that wisdom in which God saw that it was good. The end of things is that truth in which at last it will be said: “And it was so” (Gen. 1). We read both in Moses: that God saw that it was good, and that he said, “Let this or that be,” and it was so. What he saw belongs to predestining wisdom; what he said should be made, and “it was so,” belongs to truth at work. He wisely saw that it would be good for it to be made; he mightily [Col. 0658D] and truly said that it should be made, and it was so.

The expression “it was so” is partly history and partly prophecy. For example, when he said, “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven,” and added, “and it was so,” with reference to these visible lights, the sun and moon, it is true history. But with reference to the future it is true prophecy, which will then appear fully accomplished, when all things have been consummated and the righteous shine like the sun; and when, as one star differs from another in glory, so too will be the resurrection of the dead (1 Cor. 15:41–42). Then truly it may be said: “And it was so.” When that has happened, *Amen* will be said eternally, because all will know that God preserved truth in his predestination.

Thus, understanding likewise the other things which God preordained [Col. 0659A] in the beginning and will consummate at the end, when the truth of his predestination is manifested, we rightly desire in the glorification of the Holy Trinity that the end may be like the beginning. Thus *Amen* will be said in praise and glorification of God, when mercy and truth meet one another in the elect: mercy, which was in predestination; truth, which will appear in the fulfillment of that same predestination. Then the bracelet will be complete, and the circle drawn together upon the jaw and nostrils of Leviathan (Job 40), when the end and consummation of fulfillment are joined to the beginning of predestination.

We desire this to happen when we sing “Glory to the Father” in the sense stated above, commemorating there the beginning and *Amen*—that is, predestination and the endless end. Though few say this with understanding, many say it faithfully; for few understand, but many believe true what they sing: namely, that alpha and omega, beginning and end, are glory not unlike one another.

## PSALM II

[Col. 0659]

[Col. 0659B] “Why did the nations rage?” As the first psalm contains faith in the Incarnation, so this second psalm consequently contains faith in the Passion. Yet this psalm is called the first in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 13:33), either because the preceding psalm should be regarded not so much as a psalm as a title for the Psalms, or because this is the first of those psalms to which titles have been prefixed. The title of this psalm is:

## A PSALM OF DAVID

A psalm is the sound made upon the musical instrument called the psaltery by the movement of hand and strings, and it signifies good action. A song, made by the exultation of the mind, signifies heavenly joy. Therefore a psalm which begins by dwelling upon good action and says something [Col. 0659C] in particular exultation is called a “song of a psalm.” But when it begins from exultation, dwelling upon it, and ends by touching briefly on good work, it is called a “psalm of a song.” When it concerns action alone, it is a psalm; when exultation, a song.

Thus in this title we have the name “Psalm,” not “Song,” because nothing is inserted here concerning spiritual exultation. Rather, treating of Christ’s Passion, it begins with astonishment and touches upon the terrible judgment at the end, saying: “When his wrath has been kindled in a short time.” Therefore, because in his Passion Christ himself, singing psalms with his own hands upon the cross, wrought the good work of our redemption, this psalm, containing the Passion of the true David, is rightly called a Psalm of David.

[Col. 0659D] It is also a Psalm of David for every imitator of him who is prepared to die with him and prefers, grieving as though in suffering, to endure the beastly raging either of carnal disturbances within himself or of ungodly people raging against him, rather than by consenting to them to possess this world’s pleasure. Let us first expound this astonishment of the Prophet concerning Christ.

**Verse 1.** “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate vain things?” It is indeed a thing worthy of astonishment that this “Beloved” is “white and ruddy” (Song 5:10): white in his holy and pure conception, and also in that life which the preceding Psalm proclaims; ruddy in that Passion [Col. 0660B] which this following psalm announces: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate vain things?”

For he said to the Jews in a certain place—and what he said to them he said and says to all nations and peoples—“Which of you convicts me of sin? If I speak truth, why do you not believe me?” (John 8:46). What else is meant by this question, “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate vain things?” This is why we join this second psalm to the first, or preceding one: because, according to the argument, in the first we recognize Christ, the Son of God, as conceived, born, and living without sin; and in this second we understand set forth the reason why he suffered—a reason the nations and peoples, meditating vain things, did not recognize.

And herein is the wonder: that “he was reckoned among the wicked” (Isa. 53:12) in his Passion, although his pure conception and holy life are certain. Isaiah expresses a similar astonishment about this Beloved, white and ruddy, when it says: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah—this one beautiful in his robe, advancing in the greatness of his strength?” (Song 5:10; Isa. 63:1). To this question the Beloved himself replies, revealing the whiteness of his life thus: “I, who speak righteousness and am a defender unto salvation” (ibid.). This is as though he had said: I am the blessed man who did not go in the counsel of the ungodly, did not stand in the way of sinners, and did not sit in the chair of pestilence; rather, my will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law I meditate [Col. 0660D] day and night. I am the tree of life planted beside streams of water, giving fruit in season; my leaf shall not fall, and everything I do shall prosper.

Then Isaiah says: “Why then is your garment red, and your clothing like that of one treading the winepress?” (Isa. 63:2)—that is: Why did you suffer, and why were you “reckoned with the wicked” (Isa. 53:12), when you speak righteousness? This accords with the astonishment now expressed: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate vain things?” The Prophet was astonished; let us also be astonished, and be indignant with those enemies of truth to whom he himself said: “If I speak truth to you, why do you not believe me?” (John 8:46).

Truly this is astonishing: although those who speak truth are thereby worthy of belief, you do not believe precisely because truth is spoken to you. Why did the nations rage? We do not wonder that the scribes and Pharisees, whose avarice he frequently rebuked, persecuted him. But why did the nations rage? For he was “delivered to the nations to be mocked, crucified, spat upon, scourged, and killed” (Matt. 20:19). He did not preach to the nations or rebuke their sins. Why, then, did the Gentiles—Pilate’s and Herod’s soldiers—rage against him like irrational beasts?

[Col. 0661B] The Jewish people, that is, the crowds, on the other hand, as though acting with counsel and reason, meditated vain things: desiring and devising to hold him in death, guard him shut in the tomb, and thus prevent the world from going after him, lest the Romans come and take away both their place and their nation. They meditated this vainly, because contrary to their counsel he both returned to life from death and rose from the tomb, appeared in the world to preordained witnesses, and now the whole world has gone after him. “Thus they failed, searching out searches and meditating vain things” (Ps. 63:7), so that their counsel was turned to the opposite result.

For they said: “If we let him go on thus, the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 12:48). Had they let him go, the Romans would not have come to avenge righteous blood; but because they did not let him go, the Romans came and destroyed the city. Because foolish boys mocked the true Elisha as bald in the place of Calvary, two bears—two Roman rulers, Titus and Vespasian—came from the forest of the Gentile people and tore to pieces those boys who mocked Christ. Therefore they meditated vain things, and in vain, because events did not proceed as they had arranged.
