They thought evil against the true Joseph, selling him, but God turned it to good, making him lord of the whole land of Egypt. Worse than the Philistines, they wished the true Samson to be kept shut in hell; but at midnight he carried away the gates of hell and raised the human being upon the mountain of divine exaltation, giving him “the name which is above every name” [Col. 0661D] (Phil. 2:9)—not that the man himself received it, but that he, the same God with God the Father, gave it to his humanity.

Worse than Saul, they devised to fasten the true David to the wall, condemning him as a blasphemer and sinner; but he removed from the midst the wall of enmity, “blotting out the handwriting that was against us” (Col. 2:14). Yet their spear, inflicting an ineffectual wound, reached the wall (1 Sam. 19:4): they did not destroy Jesus as they intended, yet they, the murderers, stored up evil for themselves by saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25).

They truly were the attendants of the Babylonian king—that is, of the devil—and kindled the furnace when they inflamed Pilate, saying: “If [Col. 0662A] you release him, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 12:12). But he, truly the Angel of Great Counsel, descended into the furnace of the Passion in such a way that he made “the middle of the furnace like a wind blowing dew” (Dan. 3:50), not only for himself but also for his servants, whether they suffered before him or were to suffer after him for the name of the Trinity. Thus Christ is always accustomed to be exalted and magnified precisely from that by which he was thought to be annihilated. Therefore they meditated vain things, things contrary to their own designs but found consonant and cooperative with the divine counsels.

The raging of the nations and the meditation of the peoples were vain, as being those of inferiors who did not dare even to begin what they desired by their own authority. But so that authority and boldness might be supplied to those inferiors, Herod [Col. 0662B] and Pilate, at that time tetrarchs and—

**Verse 2.** “The kings of the Jewish land stood,” either mutually favoring each other in assent or giving boldness to their inferiors against Christ—whom “Herod despised with his army” (Luke 23:11) and whom “Pilate, after scourging him, delivered” (Matt. 27) to the will of the utterly wicked.

And so that greater authority might seem to stand behind the condemnation of that righteous blood, not only did the aforementioned kings stand firmly, with delay and deliberation, in their judgment, but the rulers Annas and Caiaphas also came together into one counsel, one agreement in perversity, against the Lord the Father and against his Christ. For those who oppose the Son oppose the Father; those who dishonor the one sent dishonor the sender.

[Col. 0662C] Thus they came together as one against the Father and the Son, saying:

**Verse 3.** “Let us burst their bonds”—that is, their commands, those of the Father and Son, or of Christ and the apostles—“and cast their yoke from us”—that is, their law. Though their burden is light and their yoke sweet, it is not sweet to us. Therefore let us cast their yoke from us. For they sent an embassy after Christ, saying: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19:14). They said among themselves: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance” (Matt. 21:38).

Otherwise: those unbelieving kings and rulers came together as one against the Lord and against his Christ. But we, who, knowing the holy name, cannot utterly deny it, should burst their bonds, reject their counsels, and cast from ourselves their yoke—either the yoke of the old law and ancestral, or rather Pharisaic, traditions, and their dominion. For they are to be despised and mocked not only by human beings but also by God, because “it is too little for them to be troublesome to human beings, when they are troublesome also to God” (Isa. 7:13).

VERSE 4. From this it is evident that the Most High himself, who dwells in heaven—that is, in the good angels and holy people—will mock them, terrifying their guards beside the tomb and rising again while they are unaware; and the Lord himself will deride them, as though breathing indignation through his nostrils, when, through the apostles’ diligence and discerning judgment, the world began to believe in him whom they had denied “before Pilate’s face, when he judged that he should be released” (Acts 3:13). Or he mocks them now by the destruction of their place and nation through the Roman army, and he will deride them in the future judgment, when their sons—that is, the apostles—will be their judges, condemning the twelve tribes of Israel, because, while the apostles believed, those tribes refused to believe (Matt. 19:28). You, Pilate, an ungodly judge, said to Christ the Judge, as he stood silent before you: “Do you not speak to me? Do you not know that I have power to release you and power to crucify you?” (John 19:10). You were astonished and angry that, “like a lamb before its shearer” (Isa. 53:7), so the true Lamb before you, who scourged him, did not open his mouth at your pleasure. But wait a little; wait

[Col. 0663B] until you see him coming in the clouds with great power and majesty:

VERSE 5. Then he will speak to you—then without doubt, when every flesh, every eye, even those who pierced him, shall see him. Then, I say, he will speak to you and to them in his wrath: that is, in just vengeance, which, although he himself remains in his untroubled calm, appears wrath to the ungodly. For just as this visible sun, remaining unchangeable in its own condition, nevertheless appears altered in harshness to eyes once healthy but afterwards injured, so the Sun of righteousness, always the same in himself, appears to people made worse to grow fierce in anger, although he judges in tranquillity and orders

[Col. 0663C] all things with great reverence. To those indeed whom he punishes, he appears, in exacting vengeance, to be angry and to strike enemies in wrath and fury: in wrath as regards present vengeance, in fury as regards eternal punishment. Yet he does this not as one angry or enraged, since he is free from every disturbance; rather, as a just king, he punishes the ungodly as justice requires, since he was appointed by God to this royal office. It is superfluous for us to attest that he was appointed king. This blessed man is of age; let him speak of himself. Let us hear what he says:

VERSE 6. “But I,” he says, “have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his commandment.” I—the one against whom they raged, whom

[Col. 0663D] they refused to have reigning—I, he says, have in my humanity been appointed king. For in my divinity I am the eternal King of all ages. Yet, as a man, anointed by the Holy Spirit, I received royal authority not from a flask, like Saul and Jehu, but from a horn, like David and Solomon (1 Sam. 9:3; 2 Kings 9:1, 6; 1 Sam. 16:13; 1 Kings 1:39). First, in the secrecy of the virginal womb, as David was in his father’s house; then, when the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove and remained upon me, “I was appointed king over Zion, his holy mountain” (Matt. 3:16): over God’s peculiar people, which is Zion because of the visions of the prophets; a mountain because of David’s kingdom; holy because of the Levitical priesthood. At that appointment, while the Holy Spirit remained upon me,

[Col. 0664A] because he had anointed me, the Father’s voice was heard distinctly:

VERSE 7. The Lord said to me: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” For he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Ps. 2:7). The voice also sounded from the cloud upon the mountain, where Moses and Elijah were present with me in my transfiguration, before the chosen disciples. There, when the Lord again said to me, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Luke 9:35), there was added: “Hear him.” It was not said, “Hear them,” lest Moses and Elijah might be thought to have been appointed kings over Zion, his holy mountain; rather, of me alone it was said: “This is my beloved Son; hear him” (Matt. 3:17): that is, obey him;

[Col. 0664B] acknowledge this one as your king and teacher. For I am the prophet concerning whom Moses himself, who was then with me on the mountain, long before foretold: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren; you shall hear him as you hear me, and every soul that will not hear that prophet shall be cut off from his people” (Deut. 18:15). Therefore, rightly agreeing with Moses, the paternal voice said of me: “Hear him.” Likewise, agreeing with David, my father according to the flesh, the Lord Father himself said to me: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” “You are my Son,” he says: not an adopted son, such as those whom I did not beget but adopted. You are my natural Son, the one whom I begot from the womb before the morning star

[Col. 0664C] (Ps. 109 [110]); not at some time past, but today: that is, in eternity, ever present to me. Thus among human beings, in time, “today” is always present, because whenever “today” is spoken, that is, at every time, it is present. Today has this likeness to eternity: it too is always present, though far less simply than eternity, since in today there is something past and something future; but in eternity there is nothing future and nothing past. Rather, there is in it a simple and eternal something: not time, but a present age (*aevum*).

Of this eternal today the Lord said to me, “Today I have begotten you.” My apostle Paul, speaking of me in the Acts of the Apostles, said to the Jews: “And we announce to you that the promise made to our fathers

[Col. 0664D] God has fulfilled for our children by raising Jesus, as it is also written in the first psalm: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Acts 13:33). According to Paul’s meaning, “today” may be understood as the day of my resurrection, on which, as the firstborn from the dead, I opened to many brethren the way of rebirth—that is, resurrection. I, as I have said, am the firstborn: that is, the first raised from the dead; in this present day of my resurrection I am the firstborn among many brethren (Rom. 8:29). But in eternity’s today I am the only-begotten, “like a solitary sparrow” (Ps. 101 [102]:8), because in this begetting no one is my companion. Therefore the Lord, who has me as both only-begotten and firstborn, says to me, whether as to the firstborn

[Col. 0665A] or as to the only-begotten: “Today I have begotten you.” Commended, therefore, by this testimony of the Father, “I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his commandment.” The commandment of love, which is “his commandment,” is also mine, because “all things whatsoever the Father has are mine” (John 16:15). Thus, in saying “proclaiming his commandment,” I confidently said: this is “my commandment, that you love one another” (John 15:12). I taught this commandment “over Zion, his holy mountain,” teaching the apostles, not the Gentiles, because “I was not sent except to the sheep that were lost of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). But that my kingdom might also be extended to the Gentiles, he who begot me today—that is, eternally—said to me:

[Col. 0665B] VERSE 8. “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” In response to this saying of the Father, I, “obedient to the Father unto death, asked” (Phil. 2:8) that he might give me the nations. For on the Mount of Olives I asked not only for those whom he had given me, namely the apostles, but also for those who would believe through their word; and I asked that they might be given to me, “that all may be one” (John 17:21), both the apostles and the Gentiles believing their words. Thus I, the unity; I, the cornerstone, for the union and joining of the two walls, asked that my faithful ones, both from Gentiles and from Jews, might be one, just as “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). I asked this, as I have said, praying on the Mount of Olives while my bloody sweat

[Col. 0665C] ran down to the earth. I asked the same thing while hanging and dying on the cross, offering myself on the altar of the cross as a victim not only living, but life-giving. For this is why blood came from my side there with water: that by the sacrifice of my blood God the Father might be appeased and guilty humanity made alive; while, through the addition of my holy and sacrificed blood, the water was sanctified and made fruitful for the power of baptism, and the people, sanctified through water and reborn through water, might enjoy eternal life. For the eternal life of those who, through baptism into my death, are buried with me is this: that, just as I rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so they too may walk in newness of life. This life, I say, of those who live eternally, is that seed

[Col. 0665D] promised to me in Isaiah as the everlasting reward of my precious death. For it is said there of me: “If he makes his soul an offering for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand” (Isa. 53:10).

Therefore my very crucifixion was a great petition, heard because of its reverence (Heb. 5:7). My very death was not merely a petition but also a forceful demand for obtaining the long-lived seed promised to me, for directing the good will of the Lord in my hand, and for possessing the inheritance promised to me when the Father says in this very psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.” It was the Father’s precept and commandment of love which he said to me:

[Col. 0666A] “Ask of me.” And as the Father gave me commandment, so I did; so I asked, obedient to him unto death. Behold how the lamb which was silent before its shearer and did not open its mouth (Isa. 53:7) now opens its mouth in the Psalm, by its own bleating showing that it was not without cause shorn amid scourges or immolated on the cross, since that very immolation was the petition of which the Father said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession.” An inheritance is so called from the *herus*, the master who holds free dominion over it. But an inheritance is possessed when it is not neglected but cultivated so as to bear fruit. Therefore the kingdom was taken from the Jews and given to “a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21), because the nations are the possession

[Col. 0666B] of him who possessed, made, and created them. He created them out of nothing; he made them from clay in his image. He possessed them when redeemed by his blood through his grace, just as he likewise created the Jewish people out of nothing, made them from clay in his image, and possessed them when they were delivered out of Egypt by the blood of the Passover lamb. Hence Moses says to that people, ungrateful for such great benefits: “Do you thus repay the Lord, foolish and senseless people? Is he not your Father, who possessed you, made you, and created you?” (Deut. 32:6).

If, therefore, that ancient people is reproved as foolish and senseless because it was ungrateful and returned evil to God for such great benefits, how much more must we be reproved if we neglect so great a salvation, acquired for us Gentiles, for us heathen who were far from God’s possession but have been made near in Christ’s blood, not by the blood of a brute animal but by the precious

[Col. 0666C] blood of the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world? We were given to him who asked the Father for us, not that he might hold us negligently, but that, by diligent cultivation, he might possess us as “a people acceptable to himself, zealous for good works” (Titus 2:14), for good fruits, as befits an inheritance so asked for and so given; so that glory may thereby be given both to the Father who promised and gave, and to the Son who asked. For it would not be glorious for so great a promiser to give at any time a barren inheritance to so great a petitioner, especially as the reward of such great petition and obedience.

But having heard so often already the word—or commandment—by which he said,

[Col. 0666D] “Ask of me,” we ought carefully to understand also the manner or quality of the asking. How did he ask, if not by dying? Without doubt, the humility of his most holy Passion was a petition; it was a sacrifice, besides which God desired no other holocaust or sin offering. Thus the meaning is: Therefore I, the blessed man, who owed nothing to death because I did not commit sin, paid the debt of death when the nations raged and the peoples devised vain things; when the kings of the earth stood forth and rulers gathered together against the Lord and against me, his Christ. Therefore, I say, I was silent, continually silent, and patient, though I could at any moment have said what I said once: “I am he”; and they “went backward and fell backward” (John 18:6), because the Lord Father said to me: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your

[Col. 0667A] inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession.” To this saying of the Father belongs also what Isaiah, as was said above, declared among other things: “If he makes his soul an offering for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand” (Isa. 53:10). But why would his death be of such worth or such power, unless the same man who was born in time were God before the ages? Therefore, when the Father was about to say, “Ask of me,” he prefaced it: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” As if he said: Because you are my Son, whom I begot today—that is, in eternity—ask boldly for whatever you wish, for whatever you ask you shall obtain. “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” Ask, I say,

[Col. 0667B] and I will give you the nations—both because you who ask are my Son, and because that for which you ask is your inheritance. For by two considerations—namely, the favour due to the Son who asks humbly, and the right of the lawful heir—it is impossible for me, being just and good, not to be moved. Moreover, the sum of what follows to the end of the psalm is what he said: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). Again he said: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18). This is judicial authority, over those on the right and those on the left, signified by this short verse:

VERSE 9. “You shall rule them with a rod of iron; like a potter’s vessel you shall shatter them.” For the eternal Father to say this to his coeternal Son is nothing other than appointing him king, as the Son himself said above: “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain.” He says therefore: Rule them—that is,

[Col. 0667C] reign over them; do not tyrannize. Reign, but with a rod of iron, an unbending rod, so that it may be “the rod of uprightness, the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. 64 [65]:7). And because from eternity you loved the righteousness of your faithful ones in eternal predestination, now, in the realization of that predestination, rule them with an iron rod by chastening them with a most firm discipline.

Again, because from eternity you have always hated the iniquity of your enemies, you shall shatter them like a potter’s vessel. For you have been set for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel (Luke 2:3), so that you rule those for whose resurrection you have been set, and shatter those for whose fall you have been set. Certainly the breaking of earthen vessels, according to the prophetic sense, is distinguished in two ways. Jeremiah too saw in the potter’s house an earthen vessel broken, and another vessel formed from the same clay at the potter’s pleasure (Jer. 19:11). And Isaiah the prophet foretold an earthen vessel so broken that no fragment of pottery would remain in which a little coal might be carried (Isa. 30:14). Thus there is breaking for correction and breaking for irrevocable condemnation. For soft clay, once broken, can be repaired again, as was shown to Jeremiah in the potter’s house. But hardened clay can indeed be broken, yet it is impossible to form it into another vessel. Thus Pharaoh, hardened and crushed by ten plagues,

[Col. 0668A] was broken but not corrected or formed into another vessel. But “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who” called upon “his name” (Ps. 98 [99]:6), like soft clay amid blows, “called upon the Lord, and he heard them. He spoke to them in a pillar of cloud. They kept his testimonies and the commandment which he gave them. O Lord our God, you heard them; you were gracious to them, while taking vengeance on all their devices” (Ps. 98 [99]:7–8). Therefore, Lord, when you took vengeance, they were broken; because you were gracious to them, they were formed into another vessel. Thus, indeed, the potter has power not only to make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour (Rom. 9:21), but also to form what has been made and broken into another vessel, as suits his justice and mercy. But where clay has become so hardened that its iniquity is altogether obstinate, nothing suits divine justice and mercy except to break utterly the stubbornly hard clay, so that no fragment remains to draw water—to obtain amid the flames of Gehenna a drop of water—or to carry a little coal to mitigate infernal cold, because “they pass from snowy waters to excessive heat” (Job 24:19). Therefore the Gospel foretells for such persons weeping in excessive heat and gnashing of teeth in excessive cold (Matt. 8:12): they will be tormented by extreme cold and heat in hell, where repentance will be far too late and delayed. Therefore:

[Col. 0668C] VERSE 10. “Now, O kings, understand.” For now is “the acceptable time; now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2), in which everyone who asks shall receive and everyone who knocks shall have opened to him. That rich man in hell asked far too late for the drop of water which he had neglected to ask for in this life. Therefore, now, O kings, understand that the king appointed over Zion, the holy mountain, has received the ends of the earth as possession and kingdom. Understand now, while it is the acceptable time; understand—that is, perceive for yourselves.

But if you cannot, “be instructed by others, you who judge the earth.” And although you are kings, whether by holding royal authority in this world or over our body, nevertheless acknowledge that you are servants of the highest King appointed by God the Father, and therefore serve him.

[Col. 0668D] VERSE 11. “Serve the Lord in fear”: not servile fear, but filial fear, which is the beginning of wisdom. Serve, I say; but do not let your service be wretched and burdensome. “Rejoice in him,” not in wantonness, lest you fall into rashness by hoping too greatly in his mercy, but with trembling of mind. Rejoice with trembling of body, because fear belongs to the mind and trembling to the body. It is the nature of the human body that the higher its position, the more greatly it is shaken by trembling so long as falling from there seems possible. Therefore you kings, whether worldly or spiritual, set upon the lofty summit of affairs, rejoice indeed in the Lord because of your exaltation, but with trembling, lest perhaps, while you rule others and preach to others, you yourselves become reprobate. This trembling was in the apostle Paul, who said: “I chastise

[Col. 0669A] my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9:27). Therefore you too, O kings, imitate the Apostle.

VERSE 12. “Lay hold of discipline”: chastise your body and bring it into servitude. Lay hold of discipline, even though it flees from you; embrace the discipline of God who scourges, and receive it gratefully: “for whom the Lord loves he corrects” (Prov. 3:12). Submit yourselves to this discipline, not kicking against the goad, but asking for pardon and clemency.

“Lest the Lord become angry, and you perish from the righteous way,” cut off from Christ, who is the Way, and therefore righteous because he is not only the Way but also the Truth (John 14:

[Col. 0669B] 4). He is the Way in example, the Truth in promise. Therefore he is the righteous Way, because one is led along the way of commandments or examples to the fulfillment of the promises, in which eternal blessedness is promised; there Christ himself, who is now Way in example and Truth in promise, will be blessed Life in reward.

VERSE 13. “Blessed are all who trust in him.” Blessed are not those who trust in their own merit, but those who trust in him, knowing him to be true in his promise, true in his word, by which he promised “that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal [life]” (John 3:15), and may escape the eternal punishment coming upon unbelievers when his wrath burns, when it is fully kindled. Although this may seem delayed, it will happen shortly: either because he will come swiftly and quickly and will not delay, since “the day of destruction is near, and the times hasten to be present” (Deut. 32:35); or because judgment will take place in a brief moment, since human beings are not brought into judgment one by one, nor individual deeds separately and severally, but all things together, “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet” (1 Cor. 15:52). Then indeed miserable will be those who do not believe in Christ, and blessed all who trust in him.

[Col. 0670B] Glory to the Father, who begets the Son today—that is, eternally—appoints him King, and hears his petition as high priest. Glory to the Son, who asks the Father for us and possesses the nations as his inheritance to the ends of the earth. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that blessedness by which all who trust in him are blessed. It is not said “in them,” but “in him,” because Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God.

## PSALM III

[Col. 0669]

[Col. 0669C] “O Lord, why are those who afflict me multiplied?” This is the title of this psalm (VERSE 1):

## A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN HE FLED FROM THE FACE OF ABSALOM HIS SON

It is the custom of prophecy sometimes to begin from history but then to pass over to mystery. The title of this psalm suggests this, because David sang it when he fled from the face of Absalom his son, marveling that his enemies had become so numerous that his own son pursued him, and almost all Israel wholeheartedly followed Absalom. But what follows—“I slept, and took sleep, and rose again”—has no savour if you wish to take it literally. For what weight of meaning or usefulness for the hearer lies in these words, “I slept, and took sleep,” if they are understood literally, as meaning that King David slept and afterwards arose? Understood of Christ, however, they proclaim the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, death, and resurrection, as will become clear in what follows. Therefore this title must be understood not only in the historical but also in the mystical sense, in this way: A Psalm of David—that is, the work of the true David, the strong-handed and beloved king Jesus Christ, is contained here. It is the work in which he laboured when he fled from the face of Absalom—that is, Judas the betrayer, who is likened to Absalom both because of the meaning of the name and because of the similarity of their deaths. Absalom, indeed, is interpreted “the father’s peace,” a name that suits both Judas and Absalom. For that Absalom who persecuted his father had long feigned peace; and Judas, like Absalom, who learned through peace to make war, betrayed the Lord Jesus Christ by kissing and feigning peace—the Father of his disciples, of whom he says: “Can the children of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Matt. 8:15).

Thus each Absalom, persecuting his father by a similar persecution, rightly deserved to perish by a similar death. Absalom perished by hanging, abandoned by the mule; Judas likewise by hanging, abandoned by the Synagogue. For when the rulers said to Judas, as he confessed his crime, “What is that to us? See to it yourself”

[Col. 0670D] (Matt. 27:4), he was abandoned by them, who detested both him and the price of blood thrown down by him and not received by them. For they said concerning the thirty pieces of silver: “It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood” (ibid., v. 6). David, then, fled from the face of his son—and so too did Christ, who is strong-handed against his enemies and beloved by his friends. David fled bodily; Christ, however, both bodily and spiritually. Bodily, he fled from the upper room, lest Judas, arriving, should kill him in secret; for he wished to be seized and die openly. He fled to the Mount

[Col. 0671A] of Olives, so that his prayer might be completed there before he was seized and bound. From there he fled into the garden beyond the torrent Cedron, where he wished to be taken, to expiate the sins of the one who had been cast out of the garden of delights by his own fault. But by spiritual flight he had fled from the face of Absalom—from the face, that is, from the mind, of the betrayer—when, abandoning him in his sin, he said: “What you are doing, do quickly. Then Satan entered into him” (John 13:27). Having now investigated the meaning of the title, let us, by God’s favouring grace, investigate the text of the psalm.

It should be observed that, after the first psalm concerning faith in the Incarnation and the second concerning faith in the Passion, this one consequently treats faith in the Resurrection and Ascension. It may seem here that the Passion is being treated, as in the preceding psalm, but that is not so. The Passion is indeed recalled where it says: “O Lord, why are those who afflict me multiplied?” But the principal narrative and thanksgiving concern the glory of the Resurrection and Ascension. For after the nations raged—Gentiles and Jews—until they killed him, they rejoiced and in many ways, as it were, gloried in turn, taking his death itself as strong proof that he was not from God, that he was a deceiver, and that therefore his name would perish and there was no salvation for him in God. Yet he, dead at that time, spoke after three days; and now, living for ever, he speaks the words contained in the following psalm: “O Lord, why are those who afflict me multiplied? Many rise up against me. Many say to my soul: There is no salvation for him in his God. But you, O Lord, are my protector, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head. With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain. I slept and was overcome by sleep, and I rose again.” Who, unless asleep in the sleep of sin and overcome by the deep slumber of deception, does not recognize this as the voice of one risen, these as words of resurrection? Thus the Son speaks to the Father:

VERSE 1. “O Lord,” he says, “why are those who afflict me multiplied?” There were many who afflicted me in my own person, but that does not suffice them. For even after I slept in the sleep of death and rose again, raised from death, those who afflict

[Col. 0671D] me have still multiplied, by persecuting me in my apostles and other members. The lovers and venerators of my name are few and simple; but my persecutors are many and manifold. They are so many that they have multiplied even from the number of the disciples, because Judas and many other disciples went back, and go back every day. Therefore, marveling, I say: Why—that is, to what extent, how greatly—have those who afflict me been multiplied, just as David, my servant and faithful father, was afflicted when his son persecuted him?

Still marveling at their multitude, I say: “Many rise up against me.” For just as many rose against their lord David, those who attached themselves to Absalom, so many are those who adopted the counsel of Judas the betrayer, or who will attach themselves to Antichrist. Some dare to kill my body; others to deny my name. And indeed they are many. For many were those who killed me and my martyrs; and many were, and are, those who denied to me the name of divinity. Their chief was Arius, whose counsel, like that of another Ahithophel, was made foolish when, by the better and sounder counsel of the Catholics, the name of Divinity was glorified in me in such a way that it is to be believed not accidental or adoptive in my case, as it is in the case of many gods, to whom it is said: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81 [82]:6), but wholly substantial: inasmuch as I, as man, was born “not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God”

[Col. 0672B] (John 1:13). Accordingly, I am natural God, not a false god like the gods of the nations, which have eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear (Ps. 113 [115]:5), for “there is no breath in their mouths” (Ps. 134 [135]:17). I am not an adoptive God, like those to whom participation was granted, not the fullness of divinity; rather, I am wholly natural God, to whom not participation but the fullness of divinity was given, when the Word became flesh, when that same Word was conceived and born in the Virgin by divine love, remaining what he was and becoming what he was not. Therefore, against the many who afflict me, I say:

VERSE 4. “But you, O Lord, are my protector,” in the holy conception. For you received your servant child, “remembering your mercy, as you spoke

[Col. 0672C] to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed for ever” (Luke 1:55). You received your servant child so that I might be your child, your only-begotten and firstborn Son.

Again, against the many who rise against me, I say that you are my glory, raising me from death and saying to me: “Arise, my glory” (Ps. 65 [66]:9). From this it is understood both that I, the Son, am the Father’s glory, and that God the Father himself is my glory. For if “a wise son is the glory of his father” (Prov. 10:1), how much more is the Son, Wisdom, the Father’s glory, as is elsewhere said: “I, Wisdom, came forth from the mouth of the Most High, firstborn before every creature” (Ecclus. 24:6). And if the glory of a son is a sensible and honourable father, how much more is God the Father immortal? Therefore I, the Son, do not say vainly that you, God the Father, are my glory, raising me from the disgrace of death. And against those who say, “There is no salvation for him in his God,” you lift up my head by the glorification of the Ascension. Against the heretics who call me a creature, you lift up my head—that is, me, who am the head of my body—so highly that I am proclaimed not partly but wholly the Most High, the Son of the Most High.

David himself, my father, likewise endured this reproach when his son Absalom persecuted him: it was said of him, “There is no salvation for him in his God.” But you exalted him after Absalom had been slain and Ahithophel hanged, restoring him to his kingdom. Yet far more gloriously you exalted my head in my kingdom and yours, which is one undivided kingdom. In it I am, according to my divinity, above every principality and every creature, and, according to my humanity, exalted: I am no longer to be called a creature, as Arius wished.

[Col. 0673A] For that is properly called a creature which, before it came to be, was nothing. But I was not nothing before I came to be, because before I became man I was eternal God, and, remaining what I was, I became what I was not. Therefore I am not to be numbered among creatures, as Arius wished. Rather, I am to be venerated above every creature and worshipped together with the Father, because I existed before every creature according to my divinity, and have been exalted above every creature according to my humanity—that is, in so far as I am man. Thus, Father, you magnified me, your Holy One, above every name, giving to me as man that which is above every name, lifting up my head, because I, “the stone which the builders rejected,” have become “the head of the corner” (Ps. 117 [118]:22). But before I was thus exalted, I was humbled in the Passion.

VERSE 5. “With my voice [manuscript: loudly] I cried to the Lord.” Many cry out, but neither with their own voice nor to the Lord. Whoever says to God, “Our Father” (Matt. 6:9), while not wishing to be a son himself, cries with another’s voice. Whoever in prayer desires from the Lord something other than the Lord himself does not cry to the Lord. Nor should one be said to cry in prayer who, in praying, does not intensely desire what he asks, because intense desire is a cry—either to

[Col. 0673C] the Lord, if it is good, or against the Lord, if it is evil. Hence: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor” (Ps. 9:16), because desire itself was a great cry worthy to be heard. And Moses, though silent and desiring, was told: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. 14:15). But in evil, shameful desire was a cry against the Lord in the sin of the Sodomites and Gomorrhites. But I cried to the Lord with my own voice when I said: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1). And again on the cross: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46).

“And the Father heard me from his holy mountain”: either from the Mount

[Col. 0673D] of Olives (Luke 22), where I prayed at greater length; or from the height of his mercy, signified by the Mount of Olives; or from myself, who am the Mount of Olives, “the mountain of God, the rich mountain,” “the mountain in which it has pleased God to dwell” (Ps. 67 [68]:16, 18). That I cried to the Lord with my own voice may be recognized from this: that I obeyed him unto death; for in his obedience—
### Verse 6

“I slept”: with the sleep of death upon the cross, and I fell asleep while lying dead in the tomb. That the Lord Father heard me when I cried out may be recognized from this: after I had slept and lain in slumber until the third day, “free among the dead” (Ps. 87:6), at last I rose from the dead by my own power, because the Lord received [Col. 0674A] me—not by any ordinary receiving, but as the Lord received me in my very conception so that I might be Lord, so likewise he received me in the resurrection as immortal and incapable of suffering, so that I too might henceforth be immortal and incapable of suffering, over whom death would no longer have dominion. For the Lord so received me that I too, being Lord, might rule over death, and it might lie beneath me like a winepress which I trod and subjected to myself (Isa. 63:3). For although I, the cluster of grapes from the land of promise, carried upon the beam of the cross, was for a time trodden in that same winepress, nevertheless I too trod the winepress when I rose triumphing over death, because the Lord received me. What follows:

### Verse 7

“I shall not fear thousands of people surrounding me.” This is the voice of one going into heaven to sit at the right hand of God, [Col. 0674B] where thousands of people cannot harm or even touch him. These thousands surrounded either his body in the Passion or the bodies of the saints; but, being unable to kill the soul, they walked about in a circle and could not reach the inmost marrow of life.

Much more, after Christ ascended into heaven, his persecutors, like the most wicked Sodomites struck with blindness, walk about in a circle, unable to find the door (Gen. 19), that is, him who says, “I am the door” (John 10:9). Therefore he now says: “I shall not fear thousands of people surrounding me.”

But because Christ, now established in his security, nevertheless does not cease to intercede for the members of his body, the voice of the intercessor follows:

[Col. 0674C] “Arise, O Lord; save me.” That is, make my people safe. But he who rightly asks for future benefits is not ungrateful for past ones; accordingly, what follows is thanksgiving:

### Verse 8

“For you have struck all those who opposed me without cause: because they hated me gratuitously.” This continuation does not depend upon what precedes, but looks to what follows. For he does not save Christ because he struck those opposing him; rather, because he struck his lying adversaries in their lying mouths with the fist of truth, their teeth were broken—that is, their words of cursing were brought to nothing.

Or the teeth are the rulers, who cut certain persons off from the number of the saints and incorporate them among the wicked. Such teeth were also beneficially broken when, through the preaching of the apostles, a great multitude of priests obeyed the faith; or they were terribly broken when the Romans came and took away both their place and their nation. Demons also came and carried their souls off to hell, according to that saying: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn even to the lowest parts of hell; it shall devour the earth with its increase and burn the foundations of the mountains. I will heap evils upon them and spend my arrows upon them. They shall be consumed by famine, and birds shall devour them with a most bitter bite. I will send upon them the teeth of beasts, with the fury of those that drag themselves upon the earth, and of serpents. Outside the sword shall lay them waste, and within, terror: the young man together with the virgin, the nursing child with the aged man. [Col. 0675A] And I said: Where are they? I will cause their memory to cease from among men” (Deut. 32:22, 23–26).

Thus indeed they were broken, so that their memory no longer remains, because they are forgotten before God. But:

### Verse 9

“Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people.” In this verse either Christ himself, or the prophet, or any psalmist acts in the role of mediator. For a mediator is not the mediator of one person; he is not the patron of one side. Whoever mediates between two parties endeavors to reconcile both into one.

Now there are two parties at odds with one another: an evil people and a good Lord. Therefore, at the end of this psalm Christ, the discerning mediator, speaks words of reconciliation both to the people and to the Lord, urging [Col. 0675B] the people to believe that “salvation belongs to the Lord,” and that “there is salvation in no one else” (Acts 4:12); and praying to the Lord Father that his blessing may be upon the people.

But if a prophet or any psalmist speaks here, he too speaks as a mediator to the people: All of you who wish to be saved, hold this as certain: salvation belongs not to free choice, not to fated necessity, not to human power, but to the Lord—to the Lord Father, the Lord Son, and the Lord Holy Spirit. Salvation belongs to the one, triune, and simple Lord.

Therefore, all you Egyptians—all human beings suffering from famine—“go to Joseph,” the true “lord” of Egypt, because “salvation belongs to the Lord” (Gen. 41:55). For no other name has been given under heaven to you “human beings, by which you must be saved” [Col. 0675C] (Acts 4:12). Go to him who was sold into this Egypt for the salvation of human beings. Now that he has been exalted to be lord of Egypt, give him everything you possess, lest you perish of hunger. Ask him to buy you and receive you into royal servitude, and to provide grain not only for eating but also for sowing. Say to him: “Our salvation is in your hand, O Lord. Let your mercy look upon us, so that we may serve you securely” (Gen. 47:25).

Let these things be said in order to persuade the people that salvation belongs to the Lord.

Now, turning to the Lord, let this mediator say in humble prayer: O Lord, let your blessing be upon your people. For the supreme mediator, Christ, too, must be believed to say and obtain this in his intercession before the Father, with ineffable words and prayers: that the Father’s blessing may be upon the people for whom he himself was sold.

It is also devoutly fitting, in the person of David or of anyone singing the psalm, to wish in these words that the Lord’s blessing may be upon the Lord’s people. A human being blesses God, or blesses God differently from the way God blesses a human being. A human being blesses God when he praises, magnifies, and highly exalts him as acting justly or mercifully in his works and powers—not because human praise adds anything of magnificence to God, but because the human being thereby becomes great and just if he accords with divine justice or mercy, never murmuring against it, but always praising and magnifying it. [Col. 0676A]

But when God blesses a human being, he either changes him from evil or increases him in good things. The blessing of change was that which was spoken to Jacob: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name” (Gen. 32:8). The blessing of increase was that spoken to the first parents before sin: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28). Again, to Abraham: “I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand which is on the shore of the sea,” God says, “and in your seed all tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:17–18). Again: “Walk before me and be perfect, and I will make you increase exceedingly” (Gen. 17:1, 6). Again: “Arise, walk through the land, for I will give it to you and to your seed after you” (Gen. 13:17). All these utterances signify the blessing of increase in good.

Therefore let us say to you, our God, in whose hand is our salvation: Let your blessing be upon your people—that blessing by whose divine working they may be changed from evils, enlarged in goods, and brought to perfection. You blessed five loaves in the wilderness, and from that blessing such an increase came to them that, after five thousand people had been satisfied from them, a greater quantity of fragments remained than there had been of the loaves themselves (John 6).

You blessed bread and wine, and by your blessing changed them into the ineffable sacrament of your body and blood. In this sacrament visible distribution does not multiply the number in fragments, since in all the visible [Col. 0676B] particles there is one indivisible bread, greater than heaven and earth, greater than all creatures, because it is the body of the Creator.

Great indeed is understood to be the power of the divine utterance that gave things their existence: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 148:5). But no less great is the power of the divine blessing which grants things blessed being. For he blesses the material fruit of the earth upon the altar, and by means of this blessed fruit all who receive it are made blessed. For “as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

This is the blessed fruit of the virgin womb, whose blessing we desire for the people of God, saying: O Lord, let your blessing be upon your people, changing them from evil and bringing them to perfection in good. Amen.

There is another reading of this psalm, in which the whole Christ speaks with and in his members as they endure persecution. For every persecutor is especially Absalom if he feigns peace until he finds a suitable time for persecution, as Absalom did. Many such persons say to my soul: “There is no salvation for him in his God.”

My soul, or the animating principle of the whole body of the Church, is the order of orthodox Fathers, through whose strength the body of the Church is animated. But many say to this soul: “There is no salvation for him in his God.” For otherwise they would not hope that the holy Church, spreading widely, could be destroyed, unless they believed that there was no salvation in God for this soul of mine.

“But you, O Lord, are my protector in Christ,” [Col. 0677A] in whom my nature was received by the Word into unity of person. You are also my glory, because it was received into identity of glory, so that rightly “every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:11). You are also “the one who lifts up my head,” that is, Christ himself, “setting” him at his right hand “over all the works of your hands” (Ps. 8:7).

Therefore, since you, most merciful Father, receive, glorify, and exalt my nature in Christ, “I cried with my voice”: for the voice and prayer of Christ were my voice. I cried to you, Lord, and you heard me from your holy mountain, that is, from Christ. In him I slept, having been joined to the likeness of his death, and I lay in slumber, having been buried with him through baptism into death; and I rose, “so that just as he rose, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:4–5), because the Lord himself received me.

Therefore I shall not fear the thousands of people surrounding me; and, that I may not fear these thousands: “Arise, O Lord; save me, my God.” Arise to save me—you who long ago rose from death to live. Arise, O Lord; save me: for as long as you do not do this, you sleep for me; you lie in slumber for me. Arise for me now unto salvation, help, defense, and the breaking of teeth that tear my flesh, because you have already long ago and often arisen for your other members and broken the teeth of those who devoured your people like bread for food.

Pray this, all of you, together with me: that he who rose for himself in order to reign [Col. 0677B] may always arise to save his people forever, because salvation belongs to the Lord alone, and there is salvation in no one else. And because the people called to faith believe this, O Lord, let your blessing be upon your people, granting them such works that they may deserve to hear at your judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34).

Your blessing, Christ, does not differ from the blessing of the Father. Therefore you blessed those blessed of your Father, foreordained before the foundation of the world, when you appeared in the world (Luke 24), as you ascended into heaven and, lifting up your hands, “you have blessed your land, O Lord,” your disciples, with that blessing by which “you forgave the iniquity of your people; you covered all their sins” (Ps. [Col. 0677C] 84:1–2).

And now, Lord, may your blessing remain upon the people: may it forgive and cover past sins; and, by preserving your blessed disciples from future sins, may it not cease to conform to itself the people regenerated through their faith, so that your blessing may be upon not only your disciples but also your whole people.

Again, there is another reading according to which David and Absalom, Christ and Judas, are together in one person. It was said to Rebecca: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your womb, but the greater shall serve the lesser” (Gen. 25:23).

The lesser people is the mind or soul delighting in the law of God. Although it seems alone, it is nevertheless reckoned, like David, as ten thousand. In these ten thousand the lesser people rules the greater people, that is, the tumultuous multitude of carnal desires, when the mind delighting in God’s law does not consent to a wicked suggestion or to the evil motions of thoughts.

These motions, sometimes multiplied beyond measure, say to the mind, though faithful: “There is no salvation for him in his God.” For when temptations multiply, despair of salvation sometimes steals in, and it is said to my soul: “There is no salvation for him in his God.”

“But you, O Lord, are my protector, my glory.” For I do not glory in my own power, knowing that you humble those who glory in their own power. Therefore you are my glory, you who lift up my head, that is, Christ or the soul intent upon divine things. I recognize this from the fact that amid temptations I did not consent to a wicked suggestion, but [Col. 0678A] cried to the Lord with my voice while temptations pressed upon me; and he heard me, either removing or moderating the force of the temptations under which I slept and lay in slumber for a time—namely, becoming forgetful of God and of myself, forgetting truth amid the dreams of fantastic thoughts.

But when divine grace visited me, I was awakened, returned to myself, and rose; and amid the remnants of my thoughts I made a feast day, a day of resurrection, rejecting the suggestions of death. Thus I rose because the Lord received me in the manner of a physician.

Therefore I shall not fear thousands of people, thousands of disturbances—that is, turbulent thoughts—because the Lord received me. He received me, the soul intent upon divine things, into agreement with his own will. Therefore I sometimes do not understand what I do among vain thoughts; for the evil which I hate, this I do in thoughts. Yet it is not I—the mind or reason—who does it. This is equally apparent because I neither understand nor notice it while I do it in thought.

Therefore the sin that dwells in me (Rom. 7:17) performs its own act without me. I, the soul, not approving that act, flee like David from the face of Absalom and his armies. Absalom is, as it were, killed by hanging when reason refuses consent to the wicked suggestion. David’s army pursues him when good and holy thoughts, arising from the mind’s consent, put vain and harmful thoughts to flight.

Lest they ever prevail, “Arise, O Lord; save me, my God,” preserving me henceforth: [Col. 0678B] “for in temptations already overcome you have struck all those who opposed me without cause; you have broken the teeth of sinners.” But victorious reason should not glory because an evil temptation has been conquered, because this salvation belongs to the Lord. This victory belongs to the Lord: the victory of a mind resisting the suggestions of sins and fleeing, as it were, from the face of Absalom.

We recognize this mind, together with its army, with the ordered battle-line of its camps—that is, of rational meditations—as the people of God. Therefore we desire the Lord’s blessing for such a people, saying: O Lord, let your blessing be upon your people.

This threefold reading which we have considered in this psalm may be found in many psalms. We touch upon this threefold sense in some places, but pass over it in many [Col. 0679A] others, in order to open a way of meditation in the psalms and in those expounded for those who wish to meditate for themselves, and to leave an exercise in those not expounded.

As we said concerning the first psalm: although it deals principally with the purity and righteousness of Christ, it is nevertheless also sung in commemoration of his saints. So too, although a sense may be understood in the present psalm and in many other psalms which can apply to any saint, we avoid assigning this in every individual case, fearing to weary the reader by excessive length.

May he who has the key of David, who opens to whomever he wills David himself, shut up by excessive obscurity, and shuts and no one opens, deign so to assist our diligence in this present exposition that we may at least point out the treasures of holy meditations, of which there is a great abyss and inexhaustible abundance in the Psalms, in the manner in which the hidden treasure is pointed out in the Gospel field.

For although the whole treasure is not dug up while it is pointed out as hidden in the field, nevertheless, when it is known that treasure lies hidden in the field, the field is purchased for joy over it. So, under the inspiration of the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is the key of David, we do not intend to dig up the whole treasure of this field. For it is impossible clearly to see what is invisible or to comprehend what [Col. 0679B] is incomprehensible. But we shall gladly show, through the individual psalms, for the glory of the Trinity itself, the glorious face of the supreme Trinity, insofar as it deigns to manifest itself.

This does not mean that the three eternal persons of the Godhead are expressly manifested in every psalm. For just as the capacity of the water jars set there for the purification of the Jews was divided, each holding two or three measures (John 2:6), so in the Psalms, which are set forth for the purification of Christians, there is a diverse manifestation of the persons: in some psalms two persons, and in others three persons of the one Godhead, are expressed and indicated either by their effects or by their names.

Therefore let us say at the end of the present psalm: Glory [Col. 0680A] be to the Father, who, in exalting my head—that is, Christ—is himself glorified in that such a head is exalted above all things by him. Glory be to the Son, who slept, lay in slumber, and rose. Glory be to the Holy Spirit, who is that salvation and that blessing of which it is said: “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people.”

For just as that utterance of God, by which he spoke and all things were made, is God’s Word, God the Son; so that blessing of God, by which created things are sanctified, is the Holy Spirit.

## Psalm IV

[Col. 0679]

[Col. 0679C] “When I called, God heard me.” The title of this psalm is:

### Verse 1

**FOR THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID’S SONG**

[Note: [Col. 0679D] According to the Vulgate it reads: “For the end, in songs, a Psalm of David.” The Greek, however, has: “A Psalm [Col. 0680D] of David.” Jerome: “For the victor, in songs, a psalm of David” — Εἰς τὸ τέλος ἐν ὕμνοις ψαλμός τῷ Δαυίδ.]

“End” is spoken of in two ways: as consumption, when something fails; and as completion, when something is brought to perfection. The end of consumed bread is its very disappearance; the end of a completed war is glorious victory. “End” is understood in this sense in the titles of the Psalms.

Therefore, where we have “for the end,” the Hebrew has *Victori*, “for the victor.” Thus this psalm is entitled “for the end,” or “for victory,” because it concerns the perfecting and victorious work of the great king David, who, after his ascension into heaven treated in the preceding psalm, gave the Paraclete Spirit to the apostles, by whom they were strengthened and made joyful.

Therefore today it is called a “Psalm of Song.” For a psalm, made by movements of the fingers, signifies the discernment and working of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, who appeared over the apostles and strengthened them. But a song, made by the voice, signifies the exultation of the mind by which they were inwardly made joyful, so that from that time no one took their joy from them.

Thus in the first three psalms, in which the prophetic Spirit testified in order to the faith concerning Christ’s Incarnation, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, the apostolic Church now rejoices in the fourth psalm over the reception of the Holy Spirit, saying:

### Verse 2

“When I called upon him, the God of my righteousness heard me; in tribulation you enlarged me.”

Do not these words correspond to the event that occurred and to the utterance of that day when the Holy Spirit came down from heaven and made the praying disciples of the Lord joyful, so that it was fitting for that assembly and for the whole Church following it to say: “In tribulation you enlarged me, when I called upon you, when I prayed”? For “all were persevering unanimously in prayer with the women and Mary, the mother of Jesus, [Col. 0680C] and his brothers” (Acts 1:42).

Therefore that unanimous Church says: “When I called upon him, the God of my righteousness heard me.” He had ascended into heaven and withdrawn from me the desirable sight of his countenance, but had promised the Paraclete Spirit. Therefore, in order that he might be justified in his words and be to me the God of my righteousness, a truthful promiser, he heard me when I not only called him to myself as though absent, but invoked him within myself. Then the God of my righteousness heard me.

For between him who promises and me who believe his promises, both his righteousness and mine are maintained: he is justified in his words by giving what he promised; and because “the just person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17), God is also the author of my righteousness, for which he heard me when I believed. For unless I had believed, unless through belief I had held the righteousness not of works but of faith, the God of my righteousness would not have heard me; nor could that be called my righteousness which disbelieved the promise of truth.

But now the God of my righteousness heard me as a believer. Since I now have him present within me, I turn my words to him and give him thanks, saying:

“In tribulation you enlarged me.” Did it not happen to those upon whom the Holy Spirit came as this utterance of the prophetic Spirit says: “In tribulation you enlarged me”? Until then their heart and mouth had not been wide, but indeed very narrow.

How was their heart narrow? They were unlettered and unlearned persons. [Col. 0681A] How was their mouth narrow? They possessed the rusticity of one language, Hebrew, so that when speaking in the idiom of their own speech they immediately revealed themselves as Galileans. Yet those whose heart and mouth had been so narrow were enlarged so that they understood the Scriptures and spoke in tongues—and, what is greatest, not in peace but in tribulation. For “the apostles went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been deemed worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41).

Great and wonderful was the enlargement of those who, persevering unanimously in prayer, had been heard according to this prophetic utterance:

### Verse 2

“Have mercy on me and hear my prayer,”

so that they possessed constancy both in heart, concerning the Scriptures, and in mouth, concerning languages, and spoke to the rulers; they said both to the people and to the rulers:

### Verse 3

“Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? Know that the Lord has made his Holy One wonderful.”

For what else is the sense of those words: “Men of Israel, the God of our fathers has glorified his Son Jesus, whom you delivered up and denied before Pilate’s face, when he judged that he should be released. But you denied the Holy and Just One and asked that a murderer be granted to you; while you killed the author of life, whom God raised from the dead, of which we are witnesses. And faith in his name made this man, whom you have seen and know, strong through his name; and the faith which is through him gave him this complete healing in the sight of all of you. And now, brothers, I know that you acted through ignorance, as did also your rulers. But God thus fulfilled what he had foretold through the mouth of all the prophets: that his Christ should suffer. Repent, therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be wiped away” (Acts 3).

And how beautifully what is written here in the psalm, “Be angry, and do not sin,” and what the apostle Peter says there, “Repent, that your sins may be wiped away” (ibid., v. 19), signify one and the same thing as what is written here: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?”

How rightly that falsehood is rebuked which, before the day on which the apostles began to preach, had already been spread among the Jews—that falsehood, I say, which they had sought and purchased by giving abundant money to the soldiers, so that they might say: “His disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep” (Matt. 28:12–13).

If falsehood were offered freely and without inducement, it would be fitting and just that it should be rejected and not accepted. But now, by giving money to the soldiers, you sought falsehood, loving vanity and hating truth. You loved place and nation; you loved earthly prosperity, transient and vain happiness. And lest you lose it, you sought falsehood, placed your hope in falsehood, and seemed secure to yourselves under falsehood’s protection. But we proclaim truth to you, saying:

**Diapsalma.** — ### Verse 4

“And know that the Lord has made his Holy One wonderful.”

But the *Diapsalma* inserted here marks a division, not a conjunction continuing the preceding words. For where we have *Diapsalma*, the Hebrews have *Selah*, which is translated “always” and confirms what precedes or follows. When the psalms were sung before the ark, it was customary at places of this kind to make a certain break in the words, so that the following words might be understood as possessing a praise of their own and as containing something other than the preceding words.

Therefore the Septuagint translators, attending more to the sense than to the words, did not wish to translate *Selah* as “always,” but rendered it *Diapsalma*. This word signifies a division of the words. It is certain that where *Diapsalma* is placed there is a change of things or persons. Thus here, after the rebuke of falsehood, Christ is presented as wonderfully exalted and glorified in truth.

We should understand that in this *Diapsalma* the Prophet saw ineffable things, through which he proceeds and continues with things that can be spoken, saying: “And know that [Col. 0682B] the Lord has made his Holy One wonderful; through this Holy One, thus wonderfully exalted and interceding for me, the Lord Father will hear me when I cry to him in the future, just as he already heard me in the past when I called upon him.

“Therefore, because he is especially ready to hear those who repent, you:

### Verse 5

“Be angry with yourselves, grieving over past sins; and do not sin further, guarding yourselves in the future.”

Or: “Be angry,” which is human, “but do not sin” by carrying your anger [Col. 0682C] into action. For anger which is not carried into action is pardonable. This motion of anger is not in our power, since it sometimes rises without our will; yet, with the help of God’s grace, it can be restrained by us. Therefore what cannot be prevented is permitted, but what can be restrained is altogether forbidden, when he says: “Do not sin in deed, although anger rises in your hearts and in your beds.”

You Jews, speaking in the anger of earth and fearing to lose earthly advantages, crucified Christ; and you still rage against the witnesses of truth, loving falsehood. But do not sin; do not persist in falsehood. Rather, be pierced by the goads of repentance concerning the things you say in your hearts—that is, the things you think within yourselves—and concerning the things you turn over in your beds, or couches, or in the wallowings of the flesh.

Otherwise: What you say with your mouths while reading Moses and the Prophets, say also in your hearts; and while reading or singing in your beds, be pierced with compunction, lest the Lord complain further of you, saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. 15:8).

The *Diapsalma* inserted here indicates that one must pass through repentance from the old life into the new life. In that life:

### Verse 6

“Offer a sacrifice of righteousness”—not the old sacrifice, but the new; not in the blood of bulls or lambs, but in a contrite spirit.

“And hope in the Lord,” not in your own merit. But because many distrust future goods, many say, “Who will show us good things?” To them we apostles reply:

### Verse 7

“The light of your countenance has been marked upon us”—marked by the sign of the cross, by the seal of truth, impressed upon your hearts, so that in us, as in the Gospel drachma, the image of truth may shine.

Otherwise, this verse may be read for the glorification of the Holy Trinity: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord; you have given joy in my heart.” For the Lord to whom these words are addressed—“The light of your countenance has been marked upon us”—is the Father himself. The countenance of the Lord is the Son himself. The light of the Lord’s countenance is the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son.

The Son is rightly called the countenance of God the Father because, just as in a human being’s face an emotion of joy or grief may be perceived, so through the Son the will of God the Father became known to the world. We rightly understand the light of the Lord’s countenance to be the Holy Spirit of the Father and Son because, just as the light of a brightly shining object opens the way and the prospect to bodily eyes—for example, just as the brightness of the sun, having driven away the darkness of night, makes day for us—so the Holy Spirit, having driven away the darkness of ignorance, teaches us all truth. For through him we know both the Son and the Father, and we know him himself as proceeding from both.

Who marked this light of your countenance upon us, O Lord; when and where? The Lord Jesus Christ, while your countenance was still hidden in that humanity so that he could be crucified. For unless it had been hidden, unless he had restrained himself and ceased saying, “I am” (John 18:6), they would all have gone backward and fallen to the ground, and could not have seized him.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, I say, while your countenance was still hidden in his flesh, promised that he would mark upon us this light of your countenance; and immediately he marked it, truly acting as supreme priest by the right of his office, whose role it is to mark not merely the forehead of the body but also the forehead of the believing soul.

For on the very night in which he was betrayed he said: “I will send you the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26), and many similar things bearing on the distinction of the three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Then, on the very day on which he rose, standing in the midst of the disciples, after the good announcement of peace which he had made [Col. 0684A] between God and human beings, he breathed on them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit,” namely, for the remission of sins; for it follows: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20:22). And on the day of Pentecost he sent that same Spirit in a distribution of graces, with many miracles shining forth.

Thus, having the light of your countenance sealed upon them, O Lord, on that same day they began to call and bring in others, so that this same light might be sealed upon them through their ministry and the laying on of hands. For on the same day on which they received the word, they were baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; and about three thousand souls were added that day. All of these, together with the apostles, could say: “The light of your countenance has been sealed upon us, O Lord; you have given gladness in my heart” [Col. 0684B]. Oh, that—since we cannot draw out from each individual saying the treasure hidden within it, for this exceeds our capacity—we might at least be permitted to penetrate the meaning of this one saying: “You have given gladness in my heart.” But who can penetrate it except one who has received that same gladness? Meanwhile, this we can know and say: this gladness is the Holy Spirit. Clearly, just as the Holy Spirit is the light of the Lord’s countenance, so he is rightly called, and is, the gladness of the Father and the Son. Where the Holy Spirit dwells, there is everlasting and inexpressible gladness; and he brings no gladness other than himself.

David himself, through whom these very words were spoken, had experienced this gladness. Indeed, he had received it in a full horn, as it is written: “‘Fill your horn with oil,’ the Lord said to Samuel, ‘and come, that I may send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite. For I have provided for myself a king among his sons’” (1 Kings 16:2). “Therefore Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers, and the Spirit of the Lord was directed upon David from that day onward” (ibid., 13), and thereafter. Yet for a time he diminished this gladness for himself; and, to use the Apostle’s words, “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Eph. 4:30): then he himself grieved the Holy Spirit, when he sinned against Uriah the Hittite. Knowing and feeling this, he said: “Restore to me the gladness of your salvation” (Ps. 50:14).

For holy persons, whose breasts are dwelling-places of the Holy Spirit, know how that happens which the Apostle does not wish to happen, when he says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4:30) [Col. 0684D]. There is a certain touch of this same Holy Spirit, by which he sometimes sensibly touches a person when he wishes to awaken him to longing, lest he neglect the grace which the Spirit himself bestowed upon him. If, at such a time, the person proceeds with a quiet mind, or is privately alone with himself, whether yielding to sleep for a while or keeping vigil, he perceives that gentle and most sweet touch as the familiar summons of a present friend. But if it is otherwise—if, for example, an intrusive straw has disturbed the oracle of the mind, and satisfaction has not yet been made for it—then that touch comes both more slowly and more harshly in its effect, so that the conscience does not hesitate to say: “Behold, the Holy Spirit of God has been grieved” [Col. 0685A].

How much more had the Spirit of the Lord been grieved, and how much reason David had to say, “Restore to me the gladness of your salvation” (Ps. 50), because a traveller—namely the devil, far estranged from the kingdom and city of God—came to the rich man David, and he, “sparing to take from his own sheep and oxen to provide a feast for that traveller, took the poor man’s ewe and prepared food for the man who had come to him” (2 Kings 12:4). But because, as it is written, “Be angry, and do not sin,” he was angry with himself through repentance, and was unwilling to sin further—not that he could live in this world entirely without sin, but because he resolved to live in God’s service without any intention of sinning—his “contrite spirit was a sacrifice of righteousness” (Ps. 50:19) [Col. 0685B]. Through this he so recovered and regained the gift of divine gladness that he could say to God in thanksgiving: “You have given gladness in my heart.” You first gave it; afterwards you restored it a second time, as I prayed when I said: “Restore to me the gladness of your salvation.”

See, moreover, how beautifully the prophetic Spirit distinguished believers from unbelievers in the very manner of expression. For of unbelievers he said: “Many say, ‘Who will show us good things?’” But, indicating that a certain unity had been formed from the multitude of believers, after saying, “The light of your countenance has been sealed upon us, O Lord,” he immediately preferred to speak in the singular, in their person: “You have given gladness in my heart” [Col. 0685C]. And rightly so, because the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. This unity of heart and soul is also beautifully expressed by the inserted adverb: “For you, O Lord, have established me alone in hope.” Thus the Holy Spirit makes one out of many. But those who do not possess him are divided into many and diverse opinions, indeed opinions contrary even to themselves, and for the most part into opposing sects.

What, then, does it mean that after saying, “In peace I shall sleep and rest in the selfsame,” he adds this cause or reason, “For you, O Lord, have established me alone in hope,” unless it is as though he said: Therefore, because I now strive for this singleness or unity, concerning which the Apostle also says:

> “For as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another. Having gifts differing according to the grace given to us: whether prophecy, according to the measure of faith; or ministry, in ministering; or one who teaches, in teaching; one who exhorts, in exhortation; one who gives, in simplicity; one who presides, in diligence; one who shows mercy, in cheerfulness. Let love be without pretence: hating evil, cleaving to good; loving one another with brotherly love; outdoing one another in showing honour; not slothful in diligence, serving in spirit, rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; persevering in prayer; sharing in the needs of the saints; pursuing hospitality. Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse. Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep; be of the same mind toward one another; do not set your minds on high things, but agree with the humble.” (Rom. 12:4–16) [Cols. 0685D–0686A]

This unity is made by one Spirit and one faith. Therefore, I say, I hope to arrive there, where I shall sleep and rest in that great peace which this phrase, “in the selfsame,” is meant to convey. On account of such a meaning, the mode of expression varies according to the distinction between singular and plural number: having said in the plural, “The light of your countenance has been sealed upon us, O Lord,” he immediately says in the singular, “You have given gladness in my heart.” Again, having said in the plural, “They have been multiplied by the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil,” he immediately says in the singular, in the person of their whole multitude—whose heart is, or ought to be, one heart and one soul, or one spirit and one faith—“In peace I shall sleep and rest in the selfsame” [Col. 0686B].

This may indeed be understood as spoken of the reprobate, or earthly-minded:

**VERSE 8.** “They have been multiplied by the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil,” so that the sense is one of rebuke: they congratulate themselves because they have been multiplied by earthly riches. Nevertheless, conversely, it is also understood in a venerable sense: the good have been multiplied by that which came from Christ, who, like a grain of wheat falling into the earth, died; and who gave the two gifts of the Holy Spirit, of which we have already spoken often, like the fruit of wine and oil.

[Col. 0686C] This unity or singleness, which speaks in this psalm and in most of the others, is what the Lord Christ himself asked for on the very night on which he was betrayed. “‘Holy Father,’” he said, “‘keep in your name those whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we also are’” (John 17:11). Again he says: “‘I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word: that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us,’” etc. (ibid., 20–21). He concluded thus: “‘That the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them’” (ibid., 26). This love, plainly, must be understood as nothing other than the Holy Spirit.

Together with the apostles, in whose person this psalm was sung, let us too, instructed by apostolic doctrine, join our voices, longing especially that:

**VERSE 9.** In peace we may sleep in the selfsame and rest with them: enlarged in tribulation, not constricted; sealed by the light of the Lord’s countenance; gladdened by joy of heart; multiplied by the fruit of grain, wine, and oil [Col. 0686D]. Of the grain which fell into the earth and died, and brought forth much fruit; of the wine that gladdens the heart of a human being; of the oil by which the face is made cheerful, and with which David was anointed. This is the oil poured out through the true David, by whose anointing we are Christians, called together in peace into the selfsame.
