For the apostles and disciples of Christ were multiplied by the fruit of grain, wine, and oil when, after Christ had been put to death and the disciples scattered because of the word of God in the Hebrew language—a word mortified, as it were, in that language, but multiplied in all languages through the twofold gift of the Holy Spirit, signified by wine and oil—a multitude of men and women believed: on one day, to three thousand men (Acts 2:41); on another day, to five thousand men (Acts 4:4) [Col. 0687A]. All of these, together with their women and children, intoxicated with the wine of the Holy Spirit and sealed upon the foreheads of their souls with the oil of the same Spirit, were made perfect into one by sleeping and resting in peace in the selfsame, because “they had one heart and one soul” in the Lord, and “none of them said that anything which he possessed was his own” (ibid., 32).

So great was the power of the wine, or new wine, with which they were said to be filled; so great was the power of the oil with which they were anointed as kings and priests, that afterwards, when they had been scattered in persecution, the apostle Peter said to them:

> “You are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition, that you may proclaim the excellences of him who called you from darkness into his marvellous light.” (1 Pet. 2:9) [Cols. 0687B–0688A]

From these words of the apostle Peter one may observe that this people for acquisition retained one heart, although scattered by the persecution in which Stephen, the first martyr, was killed, throughout the regions of Pontus, Galatia, Bithynia, and Samaria. So strongly, intoxicated with wine or new wine, did they fall asleep in peace in the selfsame that the violence of persecution could not shake from them their most sweet sleep. Let each one of us therefore say from the innermost longing of his heart: “In peace I shall sleep and rest in the selfsame.”

Glory to the Father, the Lord; glory to the Son, his countenance; glory to the light of his countenance, which is the Paraclete Spirit [Col. 0688B].

## PSALM V

[Col. 0687]

[Col. 0687B] “Give ear to my words, O Lord.” The title of this psalm is (VERSE 1):

## UNTO THE END, FOR HER WHO OBTAINS THE INHERITANCE

We read in Genesis that Abraham begot Ishmael by the slave-woman Hagar (Gen. 16:15), and Isaac by the free woman Sarah (Gen. 21:2). Ishmael, however, the elder by birth, persecuted Isaac; for which reason the slave-woman was cast out with her son, and the free woman with her son “obtained the inheritance.” “But Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines” (Gen. 25:6). Isaac, however, possessed his father’s inheritance, his father’s faith; so that he who was called the God of Abraham was also called the God of Isaac.

This Isaac, possessing with his noble wife Rebecca the inheritance—namely, the inherited faith of Father Abraham—transmitted and entrusted it to his son Jacob. Hence he who was called the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac was also called the God of Jacob. Esau was cast out from this inheritance, although noble according to the flesh, on account of his greed and baseness of mind. “Jacob begot Judah and his brothers” [Col. 0687D], to whom he left the same inheritance of faith, represented by the division among them of the land of promise as their inherited possession. “Judah begot Phares and Zarah; Phares begot Aminadab” (Matt. 1:2–3), and so the remaining faithful fathers begot faithful sons, noble heirs of their paternal faith, as far as “Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born” (ibid., 16): the true Isaac, a noble son, to whom Rebecca was joined—that is, the holy apostolic Church, treated in the preceding psalm. Every Catholic follower and lover of apostolic faith and doctrine is her legitimate son.

To such a beloved son of Isaac and Rebecca the fragrance of garments testifies that the inherited blessing is due: that “the sons of his mother” may “bow down before” him and that he may be “lord of his brothers” (Gen. 27:29) [Col. 0688B]. They do not have the fragrance of garments; they do not have the scent of a full field, since they are empty and Christians in name alone: “For there is no truth in their mouth; their heart is vain; they dealt deceitfully with their tongues” [Col. 0688C].

But just as Ishmael and Esau, who were according to the flesh, persecuted Isaac and Jacob, who were according to the Spirit, so it is now. For the sons of the concubines, to whom the gracious Father has given temporal gifts common to good and evil alike, and fleshly sons excessively occupied with hunting the fleeting desires of the world, desire to rule, dominate, or hold pre-eminence in this world over noble sons, blessed sons. Yet they lack the faith through whose ardour the apostle Peter received the primacy of the Church and of the whole world, and through whose steadfastness the prince of the apostolic senate became prince of the world.

Would that, together with the primacy of domination, they wished to possess faith—the legitimate inheritance of this primacy—so that truth might be in their mouth and their heart not vain. But because they divide what God joined together, they are found like the Israelites who reduced noble Joseph to slavery but would not retain his faith. They are likewise like the Edomites, who sought to take away the land of promise from God’s people in the time of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, yet would not receive the faith by which the children of Israel entered that land. They wish only to rule over the saints, but by their deeds deny the faith which alone is worthy to rule. On account of it they were called patriarchs—that is, princes of fathers, or chief fathers—because they were especially powerful in it, as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were. On account of it, as noted above, the senate of the Apostles was made prince of the whole world [Col. 0689A], to judge the whole world when it shall fully possess the primacy due to its faith.

But now, while those who do not possess the truth of faith rule wickedly, prayer is necessary against that multitude which wickedly seizes the inheritance—namely, judicial authority, due and hereditary to the faithful alone—and for her who will obtain the inheritance: not the multitude, but the small number of faithful, who will obtain the inheritance, that is, primacy and judicial authority. Then it will appear clearly that you are not a God who wills iniquity. It does not yet appear, but it will in the morning, when I shall stand before you and see what I am now unable to see, while you seem to will this iniquity: that unjust persons should have power over the just.

By unjust persons I mean Jews stained with Christ’s blood, pagans devoted to idolatry, heretics who do not have the truth of faith, and false Christians who do not have true charity [Col. 0689B]. Whenever any of these have possessed judicial authority over the faithful, that Church whose inheritance this judicial authority is has been oppressed. Thus the Jews, possessing judicial authority, condemned Christ himself, the head of the Church, though Pilate judged that he should be released. They also brought Stephen, full of grace and strength, before their council and, after hearing witnesses against him, condemned him in a seemingly lawful judgment (Acts 6–7). They likewise expelled the apostles from their borders after they had suffered abuse before their council, and handed over the apostle Paul to the Romans.

After the Jews, acting according to the multitude of their impieties, had been expelled and cast out from the inheritance they had seized, from their usurped judicial authority, the holy Church meanwhile, singing and praying the psalm which we are considering for the confirmation of the faith which alone is worthy to obtain the inheritance, was still oppressed by the unjust and violent judgments of pagan rulers down to the emperor Constantine, who was the first among the emperors openly to obtain legitimate rule. Before him, indeed, the emperor Philip had secretly become a Christian in the thousandth year from the founding of the city; having been converted by Origen’s preaching, he is said to have lived only a short time after his conversion. But, as we said, the Church did not experience a believing empire until Constantine [Col. 0689D]. Then the Church was heard and delivered from pagan tyrants, since they too were cast out from judicial authority, expelled from the inheritance which they had seized according to the multitude of their impieties.

There succeeded them in wickedness heretical emperors: Constantius, son of Constantine; Julian the Apostate, friend of the Arians and enemy of Catholics; Valens, an emperor wholly Arian; and almost all the kings of the Goths, who were Arians. In their times heretics were so powerful against the Catholic faith that Athanasius, a man Catholic in every respect, was driven by them into exile, and no Catholic bishop was permitted to sit in his own episcopal seat. Did not the holy Church then necessarily sing the verse of the present psalm: “Let them fall from their own counsels; according to the multitude of their impieties cast them out, for they have provoked you, O Lord”? [Col. 0690A]

After these persons had been expelled, according to the multitude of their impieties, from the holy Church and from judicial authority, false Christians succeeded them in wickedness. The foremost among these are ecclesiastical and secular judges, who confess the faith in words but deny it by deeds. They are separated from heretics because they profess the Catholic faith, but they are not joined to Catholics because they deny it in practice. Whenever they obtain judicial authority in the Church, they oppress the faithful all the more grievously because they do so more inwardly. It is therefore necessary that the Church cry out against such people and for her who will obtain the inheritance, that God may take judicial authority from them. Because the Church is grievously afflicted by their excessive multitude near the end, this psalm is rightly entitled “unto the end”: although the Church has often been delivered, it has not yet OBTAINED the end or completion of deliverance [Col. 0690B]. Let us now, desiring such an end, sing “unto the end” and say—or rather, let the undefiled mother Church sing and say:

**VERSE 2.** “Give ear to my words, O Lord.” O Lord, who “rule over the power of the sea, and calm the movement of its waves” (Ps. 80:10). O Lord of those who rule, because you rule over every dominion of Jews, tyrants, heretics, and false Christians: give ear to my words. Your ears are the power and mercy by which you can and will show compassion. By these ears receive my words, so that, according to what you will and can do, you may deliver me from strangers [Col. 0690C].

“Understand my cry,” because my words are not without a cry when there is vehemence in the intention of prayer. Thus your servant Moses cried out, though praying silently, because he prayed with great desire for deliverance, seeing Pharaoh’s chariots with their armies draw near and seeing the people of God distressed, fearing captivity and death. Then Moses’ strong attentiveness was a cry, O Lord, before you. Thus now, as the army of false brothers threatens and rushes upon me, your bride, may my distress be a cry which you understand. Observe that these words employ a metaphor from human likeness. For although in God there is no difference between his ear and his heart, he nevertheless says distinctly here: “Receive the words with your ears, and understand the cry,” as though with the heart.

**VERSE 3.** Attend, with a certain application of mind, to the voice of my prayer: a voice which is not grumbling against you or against your judgments, but a prayer for obtaining deliverance—O my King, Christ, Son of the living God, and my God. He has set down three names in this threefold prayer. First, Lord, whom we understand as the Father; then King, whom we understand as Christ; lastly God, whom we understand as the Holy Spirit. Speaking to the Three, he does not say in the plural: “Receive my words with your ears, understand my cry, attend to the voice of my prayer.” Rather, he says “receive,” “understand,” “attend” in the singular, because there are not three lords, or three kings, or three gods. Each of the Three is Lord, King, and God, yet the Three are one: one Lord, one King, one God [Col. 0691A].

Nor does the Father rule separately apart from the Son and the Holy Spirit; nor does the Son reign separately without the Father and Holy Spirit; nor does the Holy Spirit deify holy angels and good people apart from the Father and Son. For those whose essence is undivided have undivided lordship and kingship; and the Godhead of the Three is indivisible, because it is wholly incapable of receiving any accident, and nothing in things can be divided except what can be changed through accidents. Therefore Lord, King, and God are invoked with great ardour of holy longing when the holy Church is oppressed by the wicked lordship and perverse reign of him who, though he is “the man of sin, the son of perdition,” nevertheless sits in the temple of God, “showing himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. 2:3). Indeed, he “is exalted above everything called God or worshipped” (ibid., 4), daring to rule and reign not under God but against God in the Church, which is God’s temple.

Observe the divisions and parts of this psalm. First, as already indicated, she prays for that inheritance with a threefold prayer to the triune God. Then she declares herself heard at, “For I will pray to you.” Next she says that her rival must be excluded at, “Nor shall [the wicked] dwell [near you].” Fourth, she asks for help in conflict, lest enemies impede her on the way, at, “Lord, lead me.” Fifth, she foretells the punishment of the wicked at, “Judge them, O God,” and the reward of the just at, “And let them rejoice.”

It should be noted that in the threefold prayer which he places first, he gives three names: Lord, King, and God. He names Lord absolutely, but in naming King and God adds a possessive pronoun, saying, “my King” and “my God.” Since there is one Lord of all, both good and evil, just as there is one judge of the living and the dead, nothing was to be added to this name, by which his dominion in every generation is signified as equally venerable and fearsome. But he is King specifically of the Jews—that is, of those who confess his name, who can say: “The Lord governs me, and I shall lack nothing” (Ps. 22:2) [Col. 0691C]. For he governs the pliant and breaks the unyielding like a potter’s vessel.

Likewise, he is called God specifically of those for whom, through their faith, it is an inheritance that he himself should be their God: not only an enduring help in the present life but also, after this life, their beatifying reward, when “they shall be his people, and God himself with them shall be their God” (Rev. 21:3) [Col. 0691D]. Therefore let the Church say: “Attend to the voice of my prayer, my King and my God, you who govern me in the present life, so that I lack nothing, and who in the future will deify and make me blessed with no reward other than yourself. You, my King, attend to my voice; attend to my longing, aflame for your rule, that you alone may reign in me and that sin may not reign in my mortal body. May you alone be held King in the whole world, and may your kingdom be a kingdom of all ages, thus filling the whole world as the stone cut out without hands and ‘made into a great mountain’ (Dan. 2:35), filling the whole world after first crushing the gold, silver, bronze, iron, and clay of kingdoms opposed to truth” [Col. 0692A].

“You, my God, attend to my voice; attend to me as I pray this with my heart’s voice: that you alone, my God, may be held God in the world, and that he may be removed from the midst—taken from the midst—who, though he is the man of sin, wishes to be worshipped as God. Indeed, he exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped, raising his throne above the stars of God, exercising dominion over your saints and elect, sitting on the mount of the Testament, while claiming that, as though by authority of the Old and New Testaments, people must serve and obey him. Yet holy people, to whom you alone are God, know that although rulers—kings and bishops—must be obeyed in accordance with you and for your sake, ‘not only the good and gentle, but also the perverse’ (1 Pet. 2:18), no one must be obeyed against you. Indeed, if anyone proclaims a gospel contrary to you and your apostles, your apostle, speaking now in your Spirit and judging in your power, pronounces him accursed.”

Thus I have prayed, and thus I shall pray to you—not to obtain your possessions, but to obtain you yourself. For my psalmody tends unto the end, for the inheritance to be obtained, which is nothing other than yourself. To have you as King and God is to be an heir of God and a co-heir of Christ, and therefore to lack nothing; for you, my King and my God, are most fully sufficient to everyone who has you as King and God.

**VERSE 4.** Because I shall pray in this way in order to obtain you yourself, you will hear my voice—not waiting for noon, but in the morning, that is, when the light of righteousness begins in me, when the night of sin has passed and the day of justification has drawn near (Rom. 13:12) [Col. 0692C].

Alternatively: You will hear me, that is, you will make me understand that I have been heard in the morning, when this world’s night has ended at your manifest coming; when, according to my desire, I shall see only the faithful, only lovers of the faith, as judges of this world and of the devil himself, as your Apostle says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3). Then, in that morning, in that beginning brightness of future serenity everlasting and of serene eternity, ever shining, when perpetual light shall shine upon your saints, O Lord.

**VERSE 5.** In that morning those judges, the most perfect despisers of the world, shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging justly the world by which they were unjustly judged (Luke 22:30) [Col. 0692D]. But I, the Church, for the greater part shall stand at your right hand to be judged. Then I shall see what I do not now see, and, not seeing, believe: that you are not a God who wills iniquity. You now seem to will iniquity because you endure wicked judges in your Church, in your kingdom; but in the morning, when only the perfect shall be judges, then I shall stand and see that you are not a God who wills iniquity.

**VERSE 6.** Nor shall one full of the will to harm dwell near you; nor shall the unjust, to whom you will say, “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matt. 25:42), remain before your eyes. For as soon as you say, “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire,” they shall not remain before your eyes (Matt. 25:41), because “they shall go into eternal punishment” (ibid., 46) [Col. 0693A]. Truly, you are not a God who wills iniquity.

**VERSE 7.** For you hate all who work iniquity. “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity” (Ps. 44:8). You hate all who work iniquity: not those who worked it and now repent, but those who work it deliberately, who are corrupted in their pursuits (Ps. 13:1), because they sin deliberately and so love sin that they desire either to sin willingly or to have sinned with impunity. But penitents, who neither wish to sin nor wish to have sinned with impunity—for they punish their sins in themselves—are not malignant, because they do not wish to sin; nor are they unjust, because they do not wish their past sin to remain unpunished. Nor do they now work iniquity but equity, punishing their own iniquity in themselves; nor do they speak a lie by defending or excusing their sin, but speak truth by confessing their iniquity [Col. 0693B].

But you, the just Judge, will destroy all who speak falsehood by defending or excusing their sin, or by deceiving their neighbour, having one thing in the mouth and another in the heart; or, what is worse, by contradicting with all falsehood the testimony of truth expressed in the Scriptures of truth, as is characteristic of heretics. You will destroy not all who have spoken falsehood, but those who speak falsehood: those who have falsehood in mouth or heart, not those who once had it but of whom it is said, “No falsehood was found in their mouth” (Rev. 14:5).

[Col. 0693C] Some think that lying is useful for some purpose and that saints were sometimes permitted to say what is false, citing Jacob’s example when he falsely claimed to be Esau, the firstborn son. We reply that it is not a lie when truth is signified in word or deed. Jacob, enlightened by the spirit of prophecy, prefigured by figurative words and deeds the truth concerning the rejection of the Jewish people and the election of the Gentile people. Therefore what he said and did was not a lie, because he signified truth.

Likewise, from the lies of the Hebrew midwives in Egypt, who are praised, some think that great usefulness can sometimes excuse a lie. But it should be observed that they were rewarded and praised for the benefit they rendered to the Hebrew infants, not for the lie they told Pharaoh; not because they feared for the Hebrew infants, but because they feared being killed themselves. Had the lie not occurred, the benefit would have been rewarded much more greatly. For they would have become martyrs if, after declaring the truth, they had been killed by Pharaoh for saving the Hebrew infants [Col. 0693D]. Therefore lying did not add to their reward; rather, it greatly diminished the reward prepared for them—not for their lie, but for their kindness.

We may compare the deeds and words of Rahab the prostitute, who concealed Joshua’s messengers and protected them by a lie, with Jacob’s prophetic words and deeds, which we mentioned above. For she too, though lying, prefigured and signified the truth which the Church, now converted from the Gentile people, recognizes as fulfilled in herself and still to be fulfilled: she received the messengers of the true Jesus and hid them in the rooftop chamber of her memory or mind. She most truly says that they returned to Jesus, although she keeps them hidden with herself; for the holy apostles, the first messengers of our salvation, have returned to Christ and reign with him, while also being present to us by faithful patronage. Therefore a great truth was prefigured in the words of Rahab the prostitute, who said that the messengers had departed from her while retaining them with herself [Col. 0694A].

For, as we have said, the apostles have departed from us, yet they are with us through their bodies, which have been buried in peace among us; through the example of their conduct; through the concise creed of their faith; through the writings of their teachings; and through the presence of their benefits. Far be it, then, that we should attribute falsehood to those words in which there was a great proclamation of truth.

Again, some think that, from the Gospel episode in which the Lord pretended to be going farther, it is permissible even for the perfect to feign something false. But this is not so. For the Lord feigned nothing false. We call *fingere* “to compose,” “whence those who fashion clay are called potters”; outwardly he presented and composed himself before the disciples as he inwardly was with them [Note: [Col. 0693D] St Gregory the Great, Homily 23 on the Gospels]. Truth did nothing out of duplicity, but in every respect retained its simplicity, presenting himself to the disciples as a traveller who would go farther—as he was in their hearts: their love had made him near, while their distrust had made him unknown [Col. 0694C].

And indeed, unless they had invited him, he would not have been recognized by them in the breaking of bread, but would have remained unknown; and that would have been to withdraw farther. Let us therefore imitate truth and preserve simplicity in all things. If we feign or arrange something for doing a thing—for example, for going farther—then, unless lodging is offered to us on the way, let it be as we feign; for by such feigning we shall not be liars, when we hold in our will what we feign, unless perhaps an event intervenes, whether one we foresaw or another unforeseen event. If it intervenes, we freely change our plan and yet do not incur falsehood, which is found only in duplicity of heart: when someone speaks with “heart and heart,” so that the hearer is deceived [Col. 0694D].

Thus one who lies is rightly destroyed, because he turns away from truth, which possesses firm being, toward a lie, which is an empty fabrication, having no foundation in an existing thing. Hence in the Apocalypse “falsehood” is called “the pit of the abyss” (Rev. 9:2), that is, a pit without a bottom; for, as we have said, falsehood lacks a foundation, and therefore he in whose mouth falsehood is found will be plunged into destruction and supported by no foundation. Hence we read of the saints: “In their mouth no lie was found; they are without blemish before the throne of God” (Rev. 14:5). “In their mouth,” he says, “no lie was found”; and even if it was once in their mouth, [Col. 0695A] it is not found there, because either charity covered it, as with the lie of the midwives in Egypt and the lie of Rahab the harlot; or the signification of truth excused it, as with Jacob’s lie; or certainly repentance cleansed it, as with the lie of the Apostle Peter, who wept bitterly after his lie. But let those in whose mouth falsehood is found fear what is said: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood.” Yet saints may keep silent about and conceal the truth; they may not speak what is false. For the Lord himself says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). But that it may appear more clearly how cautiously every lie must be avoided, we shall set down here certain extracts from the judgments of the blessed Father Augustine. Though perhaps we burden a weary reader, [Col. 0695B] we believe and desire that a diligent reader may find satisfaction concerning the questions of lies.

Augustine, in the book *On Lying* [Note: [Col. 0695D] ch. 14]:

> “The first kind is a capital lie, to be avoided at all costs: that which is made in teaching religion. No one ought, under any condition, to be brought to such a lie. The second is that which unjustly harms someone: it is such that it benefits no one and harms someone. The third benefits one person in such a way as to harm another, though it does not harm him by bodily uncleanness. The fourth proceeds solely from delight in lying and deceiving; it is a strange lie. The fifth is made in order to please, from a desire for agreeable speech. When all these have been wholly avoided and rejected, there follows the sixth kind: that which harms no one and benefits [Col. 0695C] someone in a temporal advantage—for example, when a person knows where another’s money is, which is about to be unjustly taken, and lies by saying that he does not know. The seventh harms no one and benefits someone by preserving life—for example, when someone who is unwilling to betray a person being sought lies. The eighth kind of lie both harms no one and benefits someone by protecting him from bodily uncleanness.”

> “Therefore one must not lie in the teaching of piety; this is a great crime, and the first kind of detestable lie. One must not lie in the second kind, because no injustice is to be done to anyone. One must not lie in the third kind, because no one is to be helped at another’s injury. One must not lie in the fourth kind for delight in lying, [Col. 0695D] which is vicious in itself. One must not lie in the fifth kind, because not even truth itself is to be uttered with the sole end of pleasing people; how much less a lie, which is certainly shameful in itself precisely because it is a lie. One must not lie in the sixth kind. For not even the truth of testimony may rightly be corrupted for anyone’s temporal benefit or safety. No one is to be led to eternal salvation with the assistance of a kind of lying. Nor must one lie in the seventh kind: no one’s temporal advantage or safety is to be preferred to truth. Nor must one lie in the eighth kind, [Col. 0696A] because among goods chastity of mind is greater than bodily chastity, and among evils what we ourselves do is worse than what we allow to be done.

> “But among these eight kinds, each person sins less in lying the nearer he rises toward the eighth, and more the nearer he sinks toward the first. Whoever supposes that there is any kind of lie that is not a sin will disgracefully deceive himself, while judging himself an honorable deceiver of others.”

The same author [Note: [Col. 0695D] *Against Lying*, ch. 12]:

> “A lie is a false signification with the will to deceive.”

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0696D] *Ibid.*, ch. 17]:

> “Even for the temporal safety of human beings, let a person do what he can. But when he comes to the point at which he cannot provide for such safety without sinning, let him judge that he has nothing left to do when he sees that what remains is something he cannot rightly do.” [Col. 0696B]

The same author, *On the Words of the Apostle*:

> “When you lie out of humility, even if you were not a sinner before you lied, by lying you become what you had avoided being. Truth is not in you unless you call yourself a sinner in such a way that you also know yourself to be one. For truth itself consists in saying what you are. For how can there be humility where falsehood reigns?”

The same author, on the fifth Psalm:

> “Let no one suppose that a perfect and spiritual person ought to lie for this temporal life, by whose death neither his own soul nor another’s is killed. But lying is one thing, concealing the truth another—for saying what is false is one thing, keeping silent about what is true another. If someone perhaps does not wish to betray a person even to this visible death, he ought to be prepared [Col. 0696C] to conceal the truth, not to say what is false, so that he neither betrays nor lies, nor kills his own soul for another’s body.”

The same author [Note: [Col. 0696D] On this Psalm, §7]:

> “There are two kinds of lies in which there is no great fault, though they are not without fault: when we either joke or lie for our neighbor’s benefit. The first, when joking, is not harmful because it does not deceive. The person to whom it is said knows that it was said in jest. The second is milder because it retains some benevolence. But that in which there is no double heart ought not even to be called a lie; for example, if a sword is lent to someone and he promises to return it when the lender asks for it, [Col. 0696D] and if the lender should demand back his sword while enraged, it is plainly not to be returned, lest he kill himself or others, until health is restored to him. Here there is no double heart, because the person to whom the sword was lent, when he promised to return it upon request, did not think that the lender could demand it while mad. It is plainly not blameworthy sometimes to keep the truth silent. But speaking falsehood is nowhere found to be permitted to saints.”

The same author, on the same subject [Note: [Col. 0696D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 18]:

> “Certainly no one is to be judged a liar who says what is false while thinking it true, when, so far as lies within him, he does not himself deceive but is deceived. Therefore one who carelessly believes false things and regards them as true is to be accused, not of lying, but of rashness. Conversely, so far as lies within him, he lies who says what is true while thinking it false. For, as regards his mind, because he does not say what he thinks, he does not speak truth, even though what he says proves true; nor is one in any way free from lying who unknowingly speaks truth with his mouth but knowingly lies in his will.” [Col. 0697A]

The same author [Note: [Col. 0697D] *Ibid.*, shortly afterward]:

> “In considering the things that are said, it matters greatly in what matter a person is deceived or lies. For although, as concerns a person’s will, being deceived is a lesser evil than lying, yet it is far more tolerable to lie in matters separate from religion than to be deceived in matters without faith or knowledge of which God cannot be worshipped.” [Col. 0697B]

The same author [Note: [Col. 0697D] *Ibid.*, ch. 22]:

> “A person ought to say not only what he himself knows to be true, but also, when he himself errs and is deceived, as a human being, what he has in his mind, whether it is true or merely thought to be true and is not. But everyone who lies speaks contrary to what he thinks, with the will to deceive.”

As for benevolent lies, which are made not with a will to deceive but to help, and not from malice but from good will, a certain author says [Note: [Col. 0698D] St Augustine, on this Psalm, §7] that they are not excessively detestable, because those who lie only in this way will, as they say, deserve someday to be delivered from every lie. Nevertheless, even in such cases the habit of lying is very dangerous, because it easily leads to worse lies. Therefore it is safest for a Christian wholly to abstain from and guard against every [Col. 0697C] lie, because of what is written: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood.” I know of a certain virgin devoted to God who, when she interceded for a maidservant whom her mistress wished to discipline with lashes, inserted some kindly lies into her words. The following night she saw the blessed Felicity, mother of seven sons, sharply rebuking her in a vision for the lies she had told, however slight. Felicity imposed this severe penance upon her: just as she guarded her body from every kind of fornication, so she should guard her soul from every kind of lie. For a lie, by which the first woman was corrupted, so deflowers chaste souls in the mind [Col. 0697D] as fornication does the body. This vision is not to be reckoned among empty dreams, because it accords sufficiently with written truth, whose testimony establishes that human bodies would never have become liable to animal-like corruption if our first parents had not been corrupted by the falsehood of the father of lies. But because man, when he was in honor, did not understand truth and did not cling to truth when he received the serpent’s lie, after his mind had been corrupted by falsehood he was also made subject to fleshly corruption: “He was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13). Hence, when the Apostle instructed us in chastity, he said: “Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth” [Col. 0698A] (Eph. 6:14), because “righteousness is the belt of the loins, and faith (fides) the girdle of the reins” (Isa. 11:5). When this belt or girdle of truth was wholly lost by believing the serpent’s lie, our first parents were stirred, in beastly fashion, toward mutual shame and made themselves aprons from fragile leaves. The human race descended from them still imitates them whenever it covers its shameful deeds with the falsehood of empty words devoid of the fruit of truth.

But Christ says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Therefore, if we wish to cling to him, let us beware of the wandering byways that lead through pathless places. Let us beware of lies, with which truth has no friendship. Let us beware the most dreadful death of sinners, so that we may live [Col. 0698B] a right and true life. Let those who call certain lies excusable make their subtleties as much as they please: they cannot leaven the sincere teaching of the Apostle Paul. After saying, “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. 4:23–24), he immediately added: “Therefore, putting away falsehood, let each of you speak truth with his neighbor” (*ibid.*, 25). It is as though he had said: This is the righteousness and holiness of truth: that you both hold truth in the heart and speak it with the mouth, “because,” he says, “we are members of one another” (*ibid.*). Does Paul, when commanding us to speak truth, permit joking lies or those that appear benevolent? By no means. For if lies of that kind occur to a man who is a friend of truth, [Col. 0698C] they should be wiped away by tears and repentance rather than excused or defended. Although such lies may seem venial, if it is maintained that they can be made without any fault, guilt is incurred even in this very defense of them; and such a lie is committed that it is most truly fitting to say of it, “You will destroy all who speak falsehood.” For among other lies a lie is more detestable when, “to excuse excuses in sins” (Ps. 140:4), one deceitfully excuses or defends a lie, or any other unquestionable sin forbidden by prophetic, apostolic, and evangelical teachings. For the Prophet says: “Cursing and falsehood and murder have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4:2). Behold: he who joined falsehood and murder detested both alike. What has already been said is sufficient to show how apostolic writings forbid lying. [Col. 0698D]

But in the Gospel the Lord teaches us to speak simple truth in such a way that “every word” of ours may be “yes, yes; no, no” (Matt. 5:37). This is fittingly observed in simplicity if, when there is affirmation in the heart, there is also affirmation in the mouth; for this is the double “yes”: when what is in the heart is also in the mouth. Likewise, if there is negation in the heart, let it also be in the mouth, expressed by “no, no,” lest “yes” and “no” be contradictory in us [Col. 0699A] while the mouth contradicts the heart. For the Lord Jesus Christ was not “yes and no,” but “yes” was in him, because he spoke outwardly what he had inwardly. “Not so the ungodly, not so” (Ps. 1:5). Hence they are reproved by him when he says: “How can you speak good things, when you are evil?” (Matt. 12:34). Again, he says: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46). Let these testimonies of truth now suffice against lying. Let us continue with the rest.

**VERSE 8.** “A man of blood,” that is, a murderer, whom above we called unjust, and “a deceitful man”: namely, one who, being wicked, “speaks falsehood,” by which he pretends to be good. Such a man the Lord will abhor—that is, disinherit—because, being a man of blood and deceitful, he wished, under an evil and unlucky omen, to be honored as though an heir in the usurped government over the Church; therefore he shall be abominable because of the evil omen. Or the Lord will abhor him when among humankind there shall be no place for him who exalted himself in the temple of God not only above human beings, but also “above everything called God or worshipped” (2 Thess. 2:4). For this is the proper description of Antichrist and of every member of his body: a man of blood and deceitful. After the open tyrants and the servants of tyrants who tortured martyrs—men of blood, malicious, unjust, and workers of iniquity—and after the heretics speaking falsehood, of whom we have already spoken, this man of blood and deceitful is rightly understood as Antichrist: a man of blood by the violence of tyrants, and deceitful by the fraudulence of heretics. [Col. 0699B–C] “And now there are many antichrists” (1 John 2:18), says the Apostle John, looking toward the last hour. If John in his own time said that it was near because of its extreme proximity, much more do we now see it as near, who see many antichrists: men of blood because of tyrannical violence, and deceitful because of heretical and simoniacal fraud. By this twofold impiety they so misuse Christ’s inheritance that, if not in words, yet in deeds, they say: “Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance” (Ps. 82:13); for they possess and sell churches no otherwise than if these were their own inheritance, confident alike [Col. 0699D] in their violence and fraud that no judicial authority can prevail against them. Yet the Lord will abhor such a man of blood and deceit, someday casting him out of his inheritance and destroying him by the brightness of his coming.

Here one should observe the difference among the names and terms, which express, step by step and in proportion to their force of meaning, increasing degrees of guilt and condemnation. First he set down “malicious persons,” harmful in their will; then “the unjust,” harmful by an evil deed for their own advantage; then “workers of iniquity,” that is, those who in doing evil love not so much their own advantage as iniquity itself. Next he marked out heretics, who are to perish because of their falsehood. Finally, he set down “a man of blood and deceitful.” Now the malicious person “will not dwell beside you, O God,” though he may nevertheless seem to be seen as from afar, as that rich man was seen in hell by Abraham: “He saw Abraham from afar, and Lazarus in his bosom” (Luke 16:23). But the wicked will not remain before your eyes, or the eyes of your own, because “the wicked is taken away lest he see the glory of God.” You hate also all workers of iniquity, because you are the righteous King, who have always loved righteousness and hated iniquity. Because they loved it, they hated their own souls; and therefore they shall remain in your hatred, O God. You hate them indeed sharply enough; but you destroy heretics and all who speak falsehood more sharply and terribly. But the Lord not only hates and destroys the man of blood and deceit—one wholly opposed to divine charity and truth—but also abhors and will detest him forever. [Col. 0700A–B]

But I, your bride, your redeemed one, your dove, shall not be excluded from the inheritance, but shall enter your house with my noble offspring. I shall enter, not by just any entrance, but as a lawful bride is customarily brought into her husband’s house, so that she herself, with her lawful children, may possess the inheritance and never be cast out of the house, as the slave-woman and her son are cast out. Rather, she may remain in it in such a way as to possess all the store-rooms of this house with her bridegroom, the eternal King, of whom she now says in hope, but then will be able to say in reality: “The King brought me into his store-rooms” (Song 1:3). For she will enjoy the delights of those store-rooms [Col. 0700C] eternally in her bridegroom and through her bridegroom. Therefore I, the bride, shall enter—not indeed in the righteousness of my own deeds, but in the multitude of your mercy, my King and my God—because you mercifully went before me, that I might will good; and your mercy followed me, lest I fall away from the good will which I conceived from you, my bridegroom, but might always advance from day to day, either by devoutly doing good works or, when I could not perform them, by loving them more devoutly even in others whose works surpassed my own. Therefore I await and hope for entry into your house.

But now, as though keeping watch before the door, I shall worship toward your holy temple. Thus formerly the Jews, wherever in the world they were, prayed and worshipped toward your visible [Col. 0700D] temple. So I shall reverence in worship the invisible sanctuary, the invisible temple—namely, the man exalted above all things and consecrated with the whole fullness of divinity in the heavenly Jerusalem—not only toward God, who is in that temple, but I shall worship toward the temple itself. I shall worship that temple itself, because God dwells in that man, in that temple, in such a manner that he is God-man. Therefore I shall worship toward that holy temple, desiring to be sanctified by it, in it, and toward it, just as priests are sanctified in the temple, toward the temple, through the high priest. But because in this temple he who is high priest is himself also the temple, I shall worship toward the holy temple, desiring to be sanctified in him, through him, and toward him. Yet there are many hindrances and many snares of enemies [Col. 0701A] around the way that leads to the temple.

**VERSE 9.** Lord, you yourself, who are the temple, my King and my God, lead me in your righteousness, which differs from the righteousness of human beings. For human righteousness is to repay good for good and evil for evil. But yours is first to repay good for evil, and then, for those good things, to repay better and greater good things. For example: for sins you give repentance; for that repentance from evils you give works of virtue; and for these you will finally give yourself. Lead me, then, in this your righteousness because of my enemies and yours. Since my enmity and yours against them are shared, let your leading in the way of your righteousness be my protection against their violence and snares. And lest I ever suffer true reproaches from them, direct my way—my conduct—before your sight, which is not deceived, so that it may not be crooked but made straight in the way of uprightness. [Col. 0701B]

Some books have: “Direct your way before my sight,” that is: direct, before my sight and in my conscience, your way—that true love by which you come to human beings according to your promise, in which you say: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). Thus lead me in your righteousness and direct my way before your sight, or your way before my sight. Even if you do not do this because you are my friend, nevertheless, because of the insolence [Col. 0701C] of my enemies and yours, do not delay to do it for the sake of my enemies, nor cease to lead and direct me, taking account of their unjust and false curses and slanders.

**VERSE 10.** “For there is no truth in their mouth.” They will not speak good things about me that they know to be true; and they speak evil things which they do not know to be true. Nor is it surprising that they have falsehood in their mouth, because “their heart is vain,” that is, earthly: it is under the sun, under which there is “vanity of vanities” (Eccl. 1:2), and not in “the sun of righteousness,” in which “the righteous shall shine as the sun” (Matt. 13:43). Their heart is not vain but altogether heavenly, tasting not the things that are under the sun but the things that are above, where Christ is “the sun of righteousness at the right hand of God the Father” (Col. 3:1; Mal. 4:2). There is no truth in their mouth; vanity is in their heart. What shall I say about their throat, which lies between mouth and heart?

**VERSE 11.** “Their throat is an open tomb.” For they are also voracious, “whose god is their belly” (Phil. 3:19); and the stench of death breathes out from there, when, because of gluttony, they became flatterers and dealt deceitfully with their tongues. They dealt deceitfully, indeed, not merely through the effort of their voice, but they intend deception by their conduct.

“Judge them, O God.” I do not desire for them a judgment of condemnation; rather, foreseeing that it will come, I predict it. Or I say it even in prayer: Judge them, O God, in the present for their salvation. Judge them and separate them from the nation that is not holy.

“Let them fall from their thoughts,” their own conscience accusing them and their own thoughts convicting them. Or: let them fall short of their thoughts, so that they may be unable to bring the evils they devise to their malicious effects. [Col. 0702A]

“According to the multitude of their impieties, cast them out, because they have provoked you, O Lord.” According to the multitude of their impieties, you once cast the Jews out from the inheritance they had seized, taking from them kingdom, priesthood, place, and nation because of the blood of the prophets and also your own blood, concerning which they had said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). Hence, by your just judgment, “all righteous blood, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (Matt. 23:35), came upon them, so that they deservedly might be expelled from their seized and unjustly [Col. 0702B] possessed inheritance, because they abused judicial power. From it they were expelled, so that they now sit without king and priest, as is written in Hosea, without temple and sacrifice (Hos. 3:4). According to the multitude of their impieties, you once cast out from the man-made temple Heliodorus, sent by Seleucus, king of Asia, to plunder the treasury (2 Macc. 5:18). Having heard the prayers of Onias the priest, you drove this man, scourged by angelic ministers together with his attendants, out of your man-made sanctuary. And behold, here is one greater than Onias. Heliodorus, indeed, a foreigner entangled in the error of paganism and thus in some measure excusable through ignorance, you scourged only briefly and afterward healed through the intercession of Onias the priest. [Col. 0702C] But King Uzziah of Judah, who presumptuously burned incense in the Lord’s sanctuary, you struck with the incurable plague of leprosy, because, though he was king, he presumptuously intruded himself into the office of priests, which was not permitted to him. Therefore, struck with leprosy on the forehead, he was driven from the sanctuary of God by Azariah the high priest, deprived also of the administration of the kingdom, and lived apart according to the law concerning lepers (2 Chron. 26:20). And behold, here is one greater than Azariah. Moses had the sons of Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, who offered strange fire in the sanctuary and were killed by divine vengeance for it, carried out from the sanctuary (Lev. 10:4). And behold, here is one greater than Moses.

For you, great high priest Jesus, you great priest, who “in the time of wrath became reconciliation” (Ecclus. 44:17), are present [Col. 0702D] in your temple, in your sanctuary, which is the universal Church spread through the whole world. Before your all-seeing eyes, many plunder the sanctuary, taking from it the provisions of your poor, far more wickedly than Heliodorus. Many laymen, and persons of lay manner of life, even unworthy of lay communion, learned or unlearned, apply themselves to service at the altar far more presumptuously than King Uzziah of Judah. Many also among the sons of Aaron, of the tribe of Levi—to whom possession in lands was not granted, because they ought to live under the apostolic rule, especially those who have professed it—nevertheless bear in the censers of their hearts the fire of worldly greed, or, what is worse, the fire of most shameful lust; and thus they approach the altar, daring to handle the Holy of Holies [Col. 0703A] while they themselves are ministers of shameful acts. What, then, ought we to desire for these people and those like them, except that, through truly penitent humility, they may fall away not only from their deeds but even from their thoughts?

But if, voluntarily hardened and always resisting the Holy Spirit, they refuse to be corrected, then you, Lord Jesus, who are greater than Moses and all the saints, having made a scourge of cords, according to the multitude of their impieties cast them out of your sanctuary, from the holy inheritance of ecclesiastical office. “Cast out the slave-woman” (Gen. 21:10) and her sons, so that it may be known that the inheritance, of which the title of this Psalm makes mention and around which the whole intention of this Psalm turns, belongs solely to the free woman and her sons. Cast them out, not because they have sinned, which is human, [Col. 0703B] but because they have provoked you, O Lord, by obstinately loving and defending their sins and perniciously encouraging others to sin, which is altogether devilish.

Another translation has: “They have made you bitter, O Lord,” which is a most grievous sin. For though you are bread descended from heaven, sweet and possessing every delight and every flavor of pleasantness, they have made you bitter to themselves, because by eating the sour grape of sins they have made their teeth so blunt that your sweetness is bitter to them. Likewise, although you are eternal light, pleasing to clear eyes of the soul, they have made you bitter to themselves when by obstinate persistence they made the blearedness caused by sins [Col. 0703C] irremediable for themselves. Therefore, by extending the rays of your power, wisdom, and goodness from the height of heaven to illumine these lowest earthly places with your radiance, cast out into outer darkness those who are voluntarily and obstinately bleary-eyed, where there shall be for them “weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 25:30), according to the multitude of their impieties, by which they provoked—or made bitter—you, O Lord. Yet this we desire: that, having been cast out into outer darkness, where there is weeping, they may even in this life be excommunicated and weep for their sins, and that this expulsion and weeping may be penitential, lest it be penal in hell.

**VERSE 12.** “And let all who hope in you, O Lord, rejoice.” After the punishments of the wicked, he adds concerning the inheritance attained, which is the reward of the good, so that, as punishment terrifies, rewards may invite. It is as though he said: Let those persons fall and be humbled; or, if they refuse to be humbled, let them be cast out. Conversely, let all who hope in you rejoice. Let them rejoice, I say, not in an abundance of temporal riches—for, even if these abound, the heart must not be set upon them—but let those rejoice eternally who hope eternally, burning only with desire for eternal things. This joy will without doubt be theirs and will endure in the gladness of their minds; it will be so abundant for them that rejoicing will be perfected even in their bodies, transformed into the blessedness of incorruption, because they shall exult forever. This will be so because you will dwell in them as in a temple; and because they will have in themselves you, the fountain of all exultation, theirs will be eternal [Col. 0704A] rejoicing. Nor only that: in the exultation of body and joy of heart they will have delightful and secure glorying, because no one shall take their joy from them.

And therefore all who love your name shall glory in you with great security: namely, that name of yours by which you are called their inheritance. No angel or human being gave you this glorious name; you yourself gave it to yourself when you said in friendly speech to Moses your servant: “You shall not give the sons of Levi an inheritance in the land. For I myself shall be their inheritance” (Num. 18:20). Therefore, placing their hope now in this name, in the firm truth of this name as in the foundation of an inheritance, and possessing the reality in the future, all shall glory in you who love [Col. 0704B] this your name, by which you, King and God of all, the inexhaustible fountain of blessedness, are called their inheritance. In its eternal produce and fruits consists the blessedness of life present and future, because “this land of inheritance gave its fruit” (Ps. 84:14): namely, the Holy Spirit, who freely justifies in the present life and freely makes blessed in eternal life, giving grace for grace to the heirs—the children, that is, of her who will obtain the inheritance—when also the unjust man, who said “that he might transgress in himself” (Ps. 35:2), will be cursed, the Judge saying to such: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire”; and the righteous person, freely justified through grace, will be blessed, the same Judge saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, [Col. 0704C] receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34). Then, as was said above, in that judgment, in that dawn of eternal brightness, in that Morning, I shall stand before you, my King and my God, and then shall see that you are not a God who wills iniquity. Nor does it please you that the unjust should rule over the just.

**VERSE 13.** For there you will curse the unjust person, and bless the righteous one, justified by faith in truth rather than by works of the law, and aided toward justification by the freely given will—the will of your goodness—which, through prevenient mercy, predestined and called him before he was justified; and, after he was justified through that mercy’s working, so preserved and fortified him on every side through subsequent mercy that your good [Col. 0704D] will itself might be for him a shield and a crown: a shield in battle, a crown for victory. Therefore let the children of predestining, calling, justifying, and glorifying grace say in eternal thanksgiving: “Lord, you have crowned us as with the shield of your good will.” For a crown is a flowery or golden circle brought back upon itself, in which the beginning is joined to the end, so that what was long is made round and the crown is completed. But in the literal sense a crown is not a shield; in the spiritual sense of this verse, however, shield and crown are understood to be the same when it is said: “Lord, you have crowned us as with the shield of your good will.”

From this we perceive how unconquerable almighty God is in his purpose. According to the purpose of his naturally good will, he began the salvation [Col. 0705A] of the elect in eternal predestination; and by calling, justifying, and glorifying them, he wove, as it were, a long line with the flowers of virtues, or fashioned it from the gold of twofold charity. Nor does he cease from his work before he joins the eternity of the elect’s blessedness to the eternity of predestination. This is the turning of a certain length back upon itself, so that the last is joined to the first. Nor is there distinction or variation between first and last: “Those whom he foreknew, these”—and no others—“he predestined to be conformed to the image of the Son. And those whom he predestined, all these, though not these alone, he called. And those whom he called, these—though not all, yet these alone and no others—he justified. And those whom he justified, these—and they alone, and all of them, and no others—he glorified” [Col. 0705B] (Rom. 8:29), precisely as he predestined them eternally. Thus, just as it was predestined from eternity, so the glorification, or beatification, of the elect may remain eternally; and there may be one and the same eternity, one and the same goodness of eternity, not only the causal and primal beginning but also the final completion of the elect’s blessedness, so that their crown may be wholly eternal—begun from eternity and completed unto eternity, wound round through the long circuit of calling and justification, and at last woven together into itself by the indissoluble knot of eternity.

This is the bracelet of divine action by which Leviathan’s jaw is pierced (Job 40:21). This is the unbreakable ring placed in his nostrils, by which that fool is bound and drawn, so that, willing or unwilling—indeed, wholly unwilling—he nevertheless tirelessly cooperates even in the attestations of the blessed: he wishes to hinder them, but, as we have said, unwillingly he is compelled to serve their salvation. He is himself the hammer and smith of the whole earth, through whom the crown of the elect is fashioned—a crown which without doubt would be destroyed and scattered by that same smith, or hammer, unless this crown of God’s good will itself now protects the elect, like a shield amid the wars of temptations, who are at last to be crowned after the warfare of every danger. Therefore, freed and defended by this unconquerable shield, and all garlanded by this imperishable crown, those “who through faith conquered kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises” (Heb. 11:33) shall render everlasting thanksgivings for ever [Col. 0705D], saying to their deliverer: “Lord, as with the shield of your good will you have crowned us.”

We too, sinners in the dangers of temptations, needing the same shield and seeking the same crown from the divine promise through God’s good will, although within ourselves we tremble with fear and trembling, [Col. 0706A] nevertheless rejoice with the saints already crowned, especially on their feast-days of birth [into heaven]; and, congratulating them on their triumph, let us say: “With the shield of your good will you have crowned them, O Lord.” Likewise, on the feast of one martyr or confessor, let us congratulate him, saying:

> Let all who hope in you rejoice, O Lord, for you have blessed the righteous; with the shield of your good will you have crowned him.

[Note: [Col. 0705D] Certain ancient musical notations have been added in the manuscript to this verse. Since they occur commonly in other manuscripts also [Col. 0706D], we have deliberately omitted them.]

Let no reader mock me for writing these things as though I were intent on the trifles of little songs. For I do not write them, or press them for reading, upon austere and learned masters who are called Rabbi by men. Rather, being hungry myself, and seeking food for those like me who especially need this work, or who deign to read it, I seek nourishment in the exceedingly rich pastures of the shepherd David—also in the flavour of antiphons drawn from the Psalms [Col. 0706B], or of responsories and other chants drawn from the Psalms. In order that these may taste more pleasantly and sweetly, we sometimes set musical signs over them, because David himself, the first utterer of the Psalms and a shepherd, tempered the austerity of words by musical sweetness through singers, through the pleasant psaltery with the harp, and through other musical instruments.

At the end of this psalm, recalling its beginning—where a threefold prayer is first addressed in the name of the Trinity—we render thanks to the same Trinity, saying:

Glory to the Father, to whom it was said: “Hear my words, O Lord.” Glory to the Son, to whom it was said: “Understand my cry.” Glory to the Holy Spirit, to whom it was said: “Give heed to the voice of my prayer.” In this lies glory to the Father: that he hears with his ears the words of the praying Church; for, though he is the Ancient of Days, he nevertheless hears clearly, very unlike the gods of the nations, who “have ears and hear not” (Ps. 113:6). In this lies glory to the Son: that he himself understands the Church’s cry, although the Jews deny that he, a man not yet fifty years old, saw Abraham, and although he appeared to be mad when he said, “Before Abraham, I am” (John 8:57). This cry began with the blood of Abel crying from the earth, and endures until that morning of which it is said: “In the morning I shall stand before you.” Glory belongs to the Holy Spirit because he attends to the voice of the praying Church, which says: “In the morning you shall hear my voice.” In that morning, who will boast that he has a chaste heart? [Col. 0706D] For when the day of judgment dawns, heaven and earth will tremble; indeed, “the powers of heaven shall be shaken” (Matt. 24:29). Therefore follows the sixth penitential psalm, in which we go before the face of the Judge by praying not only for ourselves but also for our enemies.

## Psalm VI

[Col. 0705]

[Col. 0705D] “O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury.” The title of this psalm is (VERSE 1):

[Col. 0706D] **FOR THE END; A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR THE OCTAVE.**

The octave is the coming of the Lord, which some have called the octave because, they say, the Lord will come after seven thousand years; but this time is known to no one. More appropriately, the day of judgment is called the eighth day because the times of this world revolve in the recurring cycle of seven days. That eighth day, set beyond the revolving course of the seven days, has no changeability; for then all mutable things will receive a fixed stability, according to the saying: “Yet once more, and I will shake” not only “the earth” but also “heaven,” says the Lord (Hag. 2:7). Expounding this passage, the Apostle says: “When he says ‘yet once more,’ he signifies the removal of things that are movable, as things made, so that those things which are immovable may remain” (Heb. 12:27).

“Therefore, receiving an immovable kingdom” (Heb. [Col. 0707B] 11:27), let us, in accordance with the counsel of the same Apostle, prepare ourselves for the coming of that day, that eighth light, in which the kingdom of God will appear immovable. Its immovability is fittingly signified by the number eight, which is the first cubic number and a solid square—a fact known to arithmeticians and easily perceived if the number eight is formed from two in this way: twice two makes a square such as is seen in four points. Let us therefore say “twice two, twice,” or let four further points be understood as placed beneath four points set in a plane: in this way the four sides and eight corners of a die are represented, of equal dimension, in which no side is shorter or longer than another. For this number eight is solid and square on every side through the number two. This same solid and perfect square occurs in many other numbers. For example, in a thousand: for ten times ten is such a square as appears in this figure.

[Note: [Col. 0707] With the smaller diagram omitted, we have inserted into the text the latter material from the margin.]

[Col. 0707D] But in the marginal side it appears more clearly how the square is formed by ten times ten, to which ten is fitted on every side. If ten further figures of this kind, equally broad, are placed beneath such a square figure [Col. 0708A]—which cannot be demonstrated in a picture—so that “ten times ten, ten times” is said, a thousand is produced; this is found to be a square number of ten, equilateral, cubic, and solid. Yet although such a very solid square occurs in many numbers, it first occurs in eight, because this is the first equilateral number formed from two and, as has been shown, is cubic, square, and solid. A square body of this sort does not roll, but rests firmly upon any one of its sides. Hence this number is called both cubic and equilateral; by its incapacity for rolling, the perfection of the resurrection is expressed—a resurrection accomplished on the eighth day after the week of the Lord’s Passion in Christ’s body and in those who rose with him, and to be accomplished after every week [Col. 0708B] of our passion, that is, after all the mutable time which proceeds in us—and indeed in all Christ’s members—through seven days. In it, the whole nature of souls and bodies rising in Christ and coming to meet him will be made firm, in the perfect man, into an eight no longer capable of change, but altogether cubic and equilateral. For numbers are called equilateral when they are equal on every side, such as twice two twice—that is, eight.

Other numbers, however, have a form longer on one side, such as twice two three—that is, six. In such an unequal form we exist amid the mutability of these seven days, in which “the whole creation,” made in six days, “groans and travails in pain until now. And not only it, but we ourselves also” (Rom. 8:22–23), [Col. 0708C] “having the first fruits of the Spirit,” says the Apostle, “groan within ourselves, awaiting the redemption of our body; because creation itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God” (ibid., 21). This is the glory promised to Christ’s members: that after resurrection and transformation they may be as the angels of God: “For we shall all rise again, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51). All the dead indeed shall rise incorrupt, that is, whole in all their members; but not all shall be changed. For only the elect—because in this life they have been changed from unbelief to the faithfulness of faith, from malice to goodness—will then be changed into the unchangeable stability and immovability [Col. 0708D] of eternal blessedness. There the nature of body and soul, joined into one, whose form is now longer on one side because the flesh is weaker than the soul—and even in the elect, although the spirit is willing, the flesh is weak—will then, I say, be wholly solid and as it were cubic, subject thereafter to no mutability. For then the flesh will be no less impassible and incorruptible than the soul, when not half but the whole of human creation in the elect shall be freed from the bondage of corruption and wholly ennobled in the liberty of the glory of God’s children.

“And we,” says the Apostle, “shall be changed” (1 Cor. [Col. 0709A] 15:51). How? Certainly through an ascent of eight steps, by which one ascends into the building shown to Ezekiel. What are those eight steps? The eight steps of the Beatitudes, of course. For “blessed are the poor in spirit”: they shall have “the kingdom of heaven.” “Blessed are the meek”: they shall possess the paradisal—and more than paradisal—earth, when “the will of God is done as in heaven, so on earth” (Matt. 5:3–4; 6:11). Blessed are those who mourn: then indeed they shall be comforted. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness: then they shall be filled with the sweetness of righteousness. “Blessed are the merciful”: then “they shall obtain mercy.” “Blessed are the pure in heart”: then they shall see God. “Blessed are the peacemakers”: then “they shall be called the children of God.” Blessed are those who now “suffer persecution [Col. 0709B] for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:8 ff.); then in the kingdom of heaven they shall be crowned with “the crown of righteousness which the Lord, the just Judge, will render to them on that day” (2 Tim. 4:8). On that eighth day he will circumcise them with a circumcision not made by hands, removing from them the foreskin of all corruption—from those in whom the corruption of iniquity was here removed through baptism or another remedy. That circumcision to be completed on the eighth day, the last day, was prefigured by the eighth day on which the Law commanded the sons of Israel to circumcise their males. On this eighth day the flesh of Christ and of those rising with him has been circumcised and cleansed from every corruption. The same is awaited in the whole Church, which, having advanced through eight steps and having here been circumcised by the knife of persecution at the eighth step, will then be circumcised and cleansed still further on the eighth day, when the elect will receive not only the resurrection of their bodies from death, but also a full transformation from mortal corruption—as it were, a full circumcision.

There will be another kind of ascent through eight steps, because human nature is distinguished by five boundaries. It has being together with stones and other bodies devoid of vital force; it has life together with trees and other things possessing the power of growth; it has sensation together with animals; it has reasoning above irrational animals and below angels; it has understanding of recognized truth together with angels. Through those five boundaries, as through certain steps, human [Col. 0709D] nature will be advanced in the resurrection. For when the elect are changed, the natural body will be absorbed by life, not so that it ceases to be, but so that its life is no longer lower or weaker. For that which “was sown an animal body shall rise a spiritual body,” and that which “was sown in weakness shall rise in power” (1 Cor. 15:43–44). Similarly, the life of the body itself will be glorified into what is higher, namely into sensation no longer animal but wholly spiritual. Then spiritual sensation will not be below reason, as sensation now is—fivefold and sometimes opposed to reason—so that something pleasurable sometimes seems good to it which is utterly tasteless and contrary to reason. Thus martyrdom or any dreadful torture seems good to reason for truth’s sake, while the weakness [Col. 0710A] of the five senses utterly recoils from it. But then there will be such a union of sensing and consenting between sensation and reason in the elect, when the whole human being will be spirit or spiritual, that no opposition or difference will ever intervene. For unity will reign in the whole of human nature, when what Christ prayed for the elect is fulfilled: that they may be “perfected into one” (John 17:23). Yet, for this to be accomplished, it is not enough for the body to be united to life, life to sensation, and sensation to reason, unless human reason is aided by the understanding of holy angels, so that blessed human beings may be like God’s angels and there may no longer be any division between angelic and human understanding of truth.

To these five steps of ascent, by which the whole human being is made angelic, there will without doubt [Col. 0710B] be added what Truth promised, saying: “They shall all be taught by God” (John 6:45). For “the Spirit of truth will teach them all truth” (John 16:13), the Son will manifest himself to his beloved, and the Father will love them. This will be their illumination on the eighth day, when the fivefold human nature is made blessed by the manifest vision of the Trinity: for the Holy Spirit, teaching all truth, will lead them to the vision of the Son, who is truth; and the Son, manifesting himself, will manifest the Father in himself, because he is in the Father and the Father is in him. Therefore, when the five distinct boundaries of human nature, as it were five wise virgins, are admitted to the joyful vision of the three Persons [Col. 0710C], the eighth day is attained, because five and three are eight, although the three Persons of the Godhead are one. Indeed, those five virgins will enter into the wedding feast and will be one bride so united to Christ the Bridegroom that the two are not only one flesh, but also one spirit; for, as the Apostle says, “He who cleaves to the Lord is one Spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17).

The door of these nuptials will be shut against the five foolish virgins, because neither the understanding, nor the reason, nor the senses, nor the life, nor the body of the ungodly will be admitted into the delights of the wedding feast. Its preparation is true charity, signified by oil. For just as oil floats above every liquid, so charity is preferred before every virtue. “Though I speak with the tongues of men and [Col. 0710D] of angels,” says the Apostle, “and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal. And though I have prophecy and know all mysteries, and have all faith so as to move mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing. And though I distribute all my possessions to feed the poor, and though I give my body so that I burn, and have not charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:1–4).

And lest anyone be deceived, lest some foolish virgin imagine that she has the oil of charity in the vessel of her heart, the Apostle gives clear signs by which true, sincere, and unfeigned charity may be recognized. “Charity,” he says, “is patient, is kind” (1 Cor. 13:4 ff.): patient amid the adversities it suffers from evil people; kind in returning good for evil, even to evil persons and enemies themselves. Charity does not envy—that is, it does not begrudge another’s goods; it is not puffed up by its own prosperity; it does not act improperly, that is, perversely against the judgment of its own conscience. It is not ambitious, that is, it does not desire to be preferred before others. It does not seek its own things, because it sets common things before private things, not private things before common things. It is not provoked; it thinks no evil: it is strong, that is, not only in refraining from avenging its injuries but even in refraining from remembering them. It does not rejoice at another’s iniquity, but rejoices with the truth—that is, with righteousness. For this truth, or righteousness, if temporal evils arise, it endures all things; and although it does not believe every spirit, nevertheless, having tested a spirit and found that it is [Col. 0711B] from God, it believes everything said by it from the Scriptures, hopes for all the promises made concerning the future, and, if they are delayed, endures all things. Charity never fails, because “many waters cannot quench charity, neither can floods overwhelm it” (Song 8:7), for that which was once loved through true charity will never be turned into hatred.

Such charity is that Gospel oil through which lamps burn in the present life, and much more at the coming of the Bridegroom. He will then lead the five virgins into that bridal dining hall, where the master of the feast is the one and triune God, where the Bridegroom himself is one of the three Persons. There, when the three are united by love with the five, [Col. 0711C] that perfect number eight will be completed: cubic, solid, square, and free from every mutability. In view of this, the day of the resurrection of all—and the beatification not of all virgins, but only of the five wise ones abounding in the oil of charity—is called the eighth day.

But because at that time not only does the saying, “They entered with him into the wedding feast,” etc. (Matt. 25:10), possess great sweetness, but the saying “The door was shut,” and the saying to the foolish virgins, “I do not know you,” possess great terror and bitterness: penitent David, anxious about that eighth day, has the singable justifications of this penitential psalm, so that every person fearing like David may not remain among the five foolish virgins, but may reach the number eight of the wise. No one will reach it except either by true innocence, as baptized infants who die in innocence, or by true repentance—the subject of the seven penitential psalms. This psalm is the first of them and is entitled “for the eighth day,” which perhaps is called the octave for the reasons already stated.

Or, as some interpreters of this psalm maintain, it is called the octave because it is set above the number seven, which pertains to body and soul, in this way. There are two lives: one pertains to the body, namely to the old man, to whom the Old Testament was also given and in whom death reigned; the other pertains to the soul renewed in Christ. The number four pertains to the body [Col. 0712A], because it consists of four elements, is affected by four qualities—dry, moist, hot, cold—and is governed by four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. The number three pertains to the soul: to love God with all one’s heart, with all one’s soul, and with all one’s strength. When the matters belonging to the body have been completed, and the action and exercise of the soul through threefold love have been completed as it were in the number seven, the eighth day of judgment will come, in which each person will be repaid according to his merits. Therefore David—that is, every penitent person, or the whole Church exercising itself in penitence—fearing as the penitent David does, prays in this psalm. It is entitled “Psalm,” because it invites good works; and it is attributed to David, that is, to the penitent Church tending toward the End—that is, toward Christ, who is “the Beginning and the End” (Rev. 1:8), namely the beginning and consummation unto righteousness for everyone who believes and has a righteous concern for the octave which he fears, that is, for the day of judgment.

This is the first of the penitential psalms. They are seven because whatever sin is committed in the week of the world—which revolves through seven days, and in which the labour of penitents also lasts—can be erased by true repentance.
