They are also seven because seven principal means of remission have been set forth: first, baptism; second, martyrdom; third, almsgiving; fourth, forgiving others their sins; fifth, converting others from error; sixth, groaning for sins; seventh, communion of the Lord’s body and blood. Here the subject is the penitent; and the Church speaks in the person of one entangled in grave sins, so that no one may despair of mercy if he repents. In keeping with the pattern of all penitential psalms, it begins with the bitterness of repentance and ends with the certainty of pardon. First comes an exordium, in which it seeks goodwill. So that it may be understood what an exordium is, as we find it in many openings of psalms, something must be said concerning the divisions of rhetorical speech.

For although rhetoric is a secular discipline, it nevertheless accompanies divine wisdom—its mistress—as a kind of handmaid, together with the other liberal arts, in Holy Scripture. If anyone wishes and is able to observe it, he may find all rhetorical figures in Scripture. Likewise the other liberal arts—grammar, dialectic, arithmetic, music, astronomy, geometry—either cooperate as handmaid-servants with practical, that is active, labour, or attend as honourable attendants upon theory, that is divine contemplation, in its solemn leisure. Since there is no opportunity at present to demonstrate this concerning each art, let us now say a few things about rhetorical speech, many characteristics of which are found in the Psalms.

There are six parts of a rhetorical speech: exordium, narration, division, confirmation, refutation, conclusion. The exordium is where the hearer’s goodwill, receptiveness, and attention are sought before the narration. The narration is where the case around which the entire speech turns is related. The division is where the case is distinguished into parts. Confirmation is where the part that is approved is established. Refutation is where the part that is not approved is censured. The conclusion is the artful ending of the speech.

The exordium is divided into the introduction proper and insinuation. The introduction proper is a brief winning of goodwill or attention. Insinuation is a lengthy winning, by winding detours, of goodwill, attention, or receptiveness. The prophets use the introduction proper—that is, brief winning—when before their narrative they preface, “Thus says the Lord.” By these few words the hearer is made receptive, attentive, and favourable, [Col. 0713B] because one should attentively and willingly hear what the prophet says, not from his own spirit, but from the divine Spirit. Likewise, when deacons are about to announce the Gospel narrative, they briefly secure the goodwill and attention of those who desire to belong to the number of disciples by prefacing: “At that time the Lord Jesus said to his disciples” (Luke 20:19). Furthermore, when to that preliminary winning of attention and goodwill they add “a parable” or “this similitude,” they make the hearer receptive to the following narrative, lest what is narrated be believed to have been said or done historically. We have given an example of the introduction proper, which is to be used in that kind of case to which the hearer can readily assent.

[Col. 0713C] But if the hearer’s mind seems far removed from readiness to assent, insinuation is necessary, by which the mind of the hearer is gradually prepared, through a lengthy and deliberate circumlocution, to receive the persuasion of the narrative. Although this can be shown in many cases, let us put forward one chapter of the Gospel as an example, in which the complete division of the six parts of rhetorical speech already indicated is found.

> “A certain Pharisee asked Jesus to eat with him. And entering the Pharisee’s house, he reclined at table. And behold, a woman who was a sinner in the city, when she learned that he was reclining in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster vessel of ointment; and standing behind him beside his feet, she watered his feet with tears and wiped them with her hair. But the Pharisee who had invited him, seeing this, said within himself: ‘If this man were a prophet, he would surely know who and what manner of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner’” (Luke 7:36 ff.).

Let us now consider Simon as hearer and our Lord Jesus Christ as an orator more than rhetorical. Knowing that the hearer’s mind was exceedingly far removed from mercy and compassion, before beginning the narration he gave an exordium by insinuation, as follows:

> “Simon, I have something to say to you.” And he said, “Master, say it.” “There were two debtors to a certain moneylender. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave them both. Which, therefore, loves him more?” He answered, “I suppose the one to whom he forgave more.” He said to him, “You have judged rightly” (Luke 7:41 ff.).

See how long an insinuation, how long a preparation of the irreverent hearer! Immediately after it follows the narration, as the Lord says: “Do you see this woman?” For the present, dutiful, and penitent woman was the matter around which this whole speech turned. We have already heard the part called the exordium by lengthy insinuation; we have also heard the part understood as the brief narration. Let us now hear the part called division, which is set out through antitheses:

> “I entered your house: you gave me no water for my feet, but she has watered my feet with tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss, but from the time she entered she has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment” (ibid., 44 ff.).

See how cautious the division is, how rational the distinction! Once it is carefully considered, one can easily discern what must be refuted and what confirmed. Accordingly, confirmation immediately follows, as the orator, intercessor, and advocate of the penitent woman says:

> “Therefore I say to you: many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (ibid., 47).

The refutation follows: “But he to whom less is forgiven loves less” (ibid., 48). In [Col. 0714C] this refutation, the wise and gentle orator spares the hearer, refuting his position by speaking of him as though he were another person who loves less and seeks pardon less.

Finally, the conclusion follows—that is, the artful ending of the speech—when he says to the penitent woman: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (ibid., 50). For faith saved her: she did not doubt that she could be saved by the Saviour. Does it not seem to you that this woman, though not in words, nevertheless in the affection of her heart and in the outward action of her service, completed a penitential psalm—especially since a psalm pertains to action, because in the ten-stringed psaltery the artful [Col. 0714D] movement of fingers or hands makes a psalm? And what was the psaltery of this most humble woman, wisely making music, but Christ himself? The woman who sang well touched this psaltery not only outwardly with her hands; rather—and this was far more effective for salvation—she touched it inwardly through faith, believing him to be the Saviour who could save even such a sinner, one who had neither a good conscience nor a good reputation. Such is the Church gathered from the Gentiles; such also is the sinner, male or female, whose conscience and reputation alike are defiled. What then remains for such a person, except to flee from inmost faith to the Saviour and say:

**VERSE 2.** O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury.

First he sets forth the exordium, in which he gains goodwill through the Judge’s power, his own weakness, and the Judge’s habit of sparing, because he wishes to be entreated not by the dead but by the living. Second, he relates his distresses, so that he may be known to be afflicted, at the words: “I have laboured” (Jer. 45:3). Third follows correction, when he separates himself from evildoers, at the words: “Depart from me” (Matt. 25:41). Fourth, now freed, he rejoicingly prays for his enemies that they may be converted, at the words: “Let them be ashamed.” His purpose, however, is to stir people to repentance. Therefore he cries: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.” As may be gathered from the Greek text, *fury* and *anger* are the same. Hence Latin copies translated from Greek vary: in some, fury comes first and then anger, as we sing it; in others, anger comes first and then fury, as we sing in the responsory drawn from Roman copies: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger, nor correct me in your fury.” Anger or fury is grave indignation, by which the coming judgment is understood. Thus it is written in the Prophet: “That day is a day of wrath” (Zeph. 1:15). And the Apostle says to the impenitent sinner: “But according to your hardness and your impenitent heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of God” (Rom. 2:5). Again: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness of those people who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness” (Rom. 1:17).

To be rebuked and to be corrected are different. To be rebuked is more severe, like being accused; hence condemnation is feared. To be corrected is less severe: that is, to be amended or instructed. Those are rebuked in judgment who are without the foundation of charity, for they are utterly condemned. But those are corrected—that is, amended and purified—who have indeed had the foundation, but have built upon it “wood, hay, stubble” (1 Cor. 3:12). When these are consumed by the fire of judgment, they themselves shall be saved through fire. Some, possessing charity, build upon it gold of wisdom in the hidden contemplation of the heart; silver of eloquence in the edification of their neighbours; and precious stones in the radiant display of examples, when they show in their conduct and works what they teach in speech. The building of such persons will suffer no loss in the fire. But there are others who build upon [Col. 0715D] the same foundation of charity: stubble of worldly thoughts, hay of worldly speech, wood of worldly—but not criminal—actions. And as wood is quickly consumed by fire, hay more quickly, and stubble most quickly, so in purgatorial fire the pardonable evil deeds, words, and thoughts of those possessing the foundation of charity are punished and destroyed in different and unequal degrees. For those who lack this foundation, the fire of judgment will be not for purification but for condemnation.

Therefore the penitent sinner, knowing that “it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31), does not wish there either to be rebuked unto condemnation or corrected unto amendment. Therefore in prayer he says: [Col. 0716A] “O Lord, in your fury and in your anger—that is, in the future judgment—do not rebuke me, that is, do not convict me as one to be condemned; nor even, which is less, correct me as one to be chastised. Rather, heal me here; apply here the plaster of your grace; grant here the remedy which you know to be fitting. Heal me here with the anointing of your sweetness and mercy, while it is the time of grace, lest there I be found either to be condemned or to be healed by harsh burning, when it is the time of fury and anger.” This is not because there is in you any agitation of fury or anger, but because the vengeance then inflicted upon those enduring it will be so unbearable as though it proceeded from the judge’s anger or fury. “But you, O Lord,” says the Wise Man, “judge in tranquillity, and order all things with great reverence” (Wis. 12:18).

Alternatively: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.” Fury, though grave, is nevertheless a brief agitation in a sensible judge. Anger, when it is just in a just judge, will be long, unless repentance and mercy shorten it. Thus fury may be understood as the Judge’s agitation which, on the eighth day, though grave, will nevertheless seem brief, because the judicial sentence will then be issued without delay, as if in fury, when the impious are told: “Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire” (Matt. 25:41). But the anger of the same Judge, by which they will be held without end in eternal punishment, will be long because no repentance or mercy will shorten it. This is not because the impious will then have no repentance, but because it will be too late and therefore wholly fruitless; nor because the eternal Judge has no eternal mercy, but because that mercy will be bestowed not upon the unmerciful but upon the merciful, according to the saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7). Therefore, while the time of fruitful repentance remains, the penitent man, fearing the eighth day, says: “O Lord, do not correct me in your fury, nor rebuke me in your anger by eternal punishments; nor even, what is less and briefer, correct me in your fury on the eighth day itself, saying to me, ‘Wicked and slothful servant, why did you not put my money to the table?’ [Matt. 25:26]; or, ‘Out of [Col. 0716D] your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant’; or, ‘Wicked servant, I forgave you all the debt because you asked me. Ought you not therefore also to have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?’” (Matt. 18:33). Before that eighth day comes: that day “of wrath,” the day “of fury,” “a day of calamity and misery” (Zeph. 1:15).

**VERSE 3.** Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak both from the sickness of sin and from the sickness of misery, which is sin’s punishment. Therefore, because my weakness is manifold and great, I need a manifold and great remedy, by which I may be healed not only outwardly in my languishing flesh, but also inwardly in my bones—that is, in the natural powers of the rational soul itself—powers troubled not slightly or partially, [Col. 0717A] but wholly and throughout: for all my bones are troubled, that is, the powers and virtues of my soul, so that it cannot govern the flesh by its rational—that is, its bony—strength; rather, as it were, the flesh softens the very vigor of the soul. Therefore I say:

**VERSE 4.** And my soul is greatly troubled. Behold, I confess! Behold, I show my wounds to you, the merciful, omnipotent, and wise Physician!

But you, O Lord, who by mercy will, by omnipotence are able, and by wisdom know how to treat and heal the weak: how long will you delay to hear one crying out, to heal one who is sick? Here the penitent implies that he has long struggled against vices, since the delay of the remedy is so prolonged for him. Yet God’s delay [Col. 0717B] is not cruelty, but serves to persuade the soul that it has plunged itself into great evils and cannot be heard after brief and light prayer. For he does not yet pray so perfectly that God, the hearer of all, may say to him: “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am.’” He delays the one praying somewhat, so that, once heard, the person may thereafter guard himself more carefully, and so that it may be shown what punishment awaits those not converted, if conversion itself is so difficult. Hence: “If the righteous is scarcely saved, where shall the ungodly and sinner appear?” (1 Pet. 4:18).

Otherwise: Heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled; that is, my mind is troubled toward repentance. And my soul—that is, even my sensual nature—is greatly disturbed, resisting the evil habit [Col. 0717C] long implanted within it and scarcely adapting itself to discipline to which it is very unaccustomed. And you, O Lord—how long? How long do you delay to heal?

**VERSE 5.** Turn, O Lord: do not delay, but turn toward me as I have turned, according to: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. 1:3). Or, since he is always ready for our perfect conversion, “turn” seems to mean: make me turn back. For he feels the difficulty of conversion; hence he says: “Deliver my soul,” hindered by many things in its conversion. Or: turn away from vengeance, and so deliver my soul bound by sins; and, by giving virtues, save me—not because of my merits, for the condemnation due to sin is just, but because of your mercy.

[Col. 0717D] **VERSE 6.** For in death there is none who remembers you. Therefore I hasten here to be healed through confession, because after death, in the land of forgetfulness, there is none who remembers you; and in hell after judgment, who will confess to you? No one. Before judgment, the rich man buried in hell was able, by some light, to see Lazarus at rest, and, compelled by the comparison, confessed his evils. But after judgment, in deeper darkness, they will see no light of God to whom they may confess. Or he calls “death” contempt for the divine law, because it leads to death; and “hell,” blindness of mind, which after such death so envelops them that they are given over to a reprobate mind. Neither of these confesses. The speaker who says the following strives to be delivered from them:

[Col. 0718A] “I have labored in my groaning.” He groans when he sees what evils he has done and what evils he has deserved because of them. And, as though groaning without tears had profited too little, he adds: “Every night I shall wash my bed,” weeping in my bed through the nights. Or, “I shall wash my bed,” that is, my body, every night—through every act of wickedness. And if I cannot count the hours and moments of the nights, nevertheless I shall confess the total wickedness of each one.

The bed in which the sick soul rests may also be understood as fleshly pleasure and worldly delight; he washes it with tears who endeavors to draw himself away from it. “With my tears I shall drench my couch.” Couch is the same as bed. Or the couch may be called the heap of sins, as though piled up from a great mass of straw and chaff. Therefore he drenches this couch [Col. 0718B] with tears, and by drenching it turns it into manure, so that it may contribute to future fertility.

The nights, alternating with days, signify that he suffers, as it were, alternately: he experiences nights when he serves the law of sin with the flesh, and days when he serves the law of God with the mind. Therefore, so that night may be changed into day, every night—that is, at every fall—he washes the bed, that is, the conscience, in which the healthy sometimes rest when wearied by worldly labors; but the sick are tortured in that same bed, like the “servant” of whom it was said: “He lies at home paralyzed and grievously tormented” (Matt. 8:6). I shall wash the bed of conscience and drench the couch—that is, sensuality. I shall drench it like a garden, so that, when the shower of tears has been poured out, the dry soil of sensuality may bring forth a new harvest of virtues.

[Col. 0718C] **VERSE 8.** My eye is troubled by wrath. God’s wrath against the old man, the first-created human being, was so great that the disease of sin and punishment became hereditary from him for his descendants, Christ alone excepted, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit. God’s wrath is also present when he gives sinners over to a reprobate mind; it is future when he punishes. He says that his eye is troubled by each wrath. It is as though he said: I shall wash my bed and drench my couch because, when I consider what you did in our first parents, what you threaten also for the future, and what you do even now, my eye—my reason or mind—is troubled by your wrath, because of the judgment which begins here, where inward darkness exists together with some [Col. 0718D] light, where the eye is troubled but not extinguished.

Then the ungodly will be in utter blindness, when they are wholly outside God, who is present everywhere, as a blind person is outside light present to him—namely, when they are cast into outer darkness. But now my eye is not wholly blinded, but troubled; therefore I fear, and in fear flee to you, my illuminator, lest I be joined to the ungodly who are to be completely blinded, deprived of every sight of light, and cast into outer darkness. Rightly do I now, being troubled, fear greater punishments, because “I have grown old among all my enemies.” I have grown old, having become a member of the old man, among my enemies—that is, vices, demons, and evil people; and not merely among some, but among all, because I consented to all and acquired oldness from them all. A lamentable [Col. 0719A] account! But now, because such labor of repentance is not vain, lest anyone despair because of the gravity of sins, he indicates that he has been heard and adds:

**VERSE 9.** Depart from me, all you who work iniquity. Having been corrected, he separates himself from those in whose fellowship and company he sinned. Or it is a prophecy that in the judgment, on the eighth day, they will be told: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity”—the Judge saying this, with every righteous and penitent person consenting.

It should be noted that he does not say, on that eighth day, “you who worked iniquity,” but “you who work iniquity,” because their iniquity will not be past, since no fitting repentance has erased it. Thus in the Gospel the Judge himself pronounces that, on the eighth day, even those who prophesied in his name and performed many [Col. 0719B] miracles, but departed this life without repentance for their sins, are to be condemned and called workers of iniquity. Therefore, if they are judged workers of iniquity there, where, with hands and feet bound and cast into outer darkness, they will no longer be able to work, and where they will remain eternally separated from the society of the good solely because of the malice of their will, it is not surprising that now a person justified through repentance says to the ungodly, openly doing crooked and shameful things: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity.” It is as though he said: I do not want fellowship in your friendship. If not in place, at least in affection I flee your iniquity, lest you seem to me to be pleasing if, while remaining with you, I do not show that you displease me. I do not wish to touch what is unclean by secretly consenting to iniquity; I wish to leave the society of the evil by fitting rebuke of iniquity. Depart from me: I no longer wish to be your companion; I do not wish to be condemned for the iniquities of others, since God has granted that I be washed from my own by tears.

“For the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.” By “voice” I mean the inward compunction of the heart, such as was in the heart of Mary as she wept and said nothing with her mouth, but cried aloud deeply through devout compunction of heart. “The Lord has heard my supplication” for sins to be removed from me, “and has received my prayer” for virtues to be obtained, as an acceptable offering. The frequent repetition proceeds from excessive feeling, because for one rejoicing that he has been heard it does not suffice to say only once, “The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping”; but he adds:

[Col. 0719D] **VERSE 10.** “The Lord has heard my supplication,” and adds: “The Lord has received my prayer.” He places “the Lord” three times because he shows that the Holy Trinity was present to his prayers.

The beginning of the psalm was sorrowful, where under fear of wrath and anger he sought the Judge’s favor. The narrative [Col. 0720A] was mournful, where he recounted that he had grown old among all his enemies. The division was cautious, where he separated himself from the fellowship of the ungodly. The confirmation was rational, where, indicating that he had been heard, he repeated the same sense three times, so that the threefold repetition might be not only confirmation that he had been heard, but also devout thanksgiving to the Holy Trinity. Now at last comes the refutation of the opposing party, when he says:

**VERSE 11.** Let all my enemies be ashamed and greatly troubled. He foretells what will happen to enemies who refuse to be ashamed here, who even mock the converted and make them ashamed. He therefore repays them in kind and says: let them be ashamed in the future for the evils they have done, since they not only did evil in themselves but also mocked the good in others. Let them be troubled, saying: [Col. 0720B] “We fools thought their life madness. Behold how they have been numbered among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints” (Wis. 5:4). Let them be troubled not slightly, but greatly, because they sinned greatly through intense hatred—all my enemies, who wish evil to me. Let these things be said for the refutation of adversaries, in accord with divine justice.

Yet I, having obtained mercy, look more to their misery and pray that, before they are ashamed and troubled in divine judgment, which will occur on the eighth day, while there is time for mercy they may turn to righteousness through true repentance of a contrite heart and be ashamed unto salvation through true confession of the mouth, as I too, having turned, was ashamed. Let them turn, lest they go where they were tending, and let them be ashamed at the remembrance [Col. 0720C] of evils, so that by the sting of shame, once converted, they may be compelled to return to the Savior, lest they have him as judge and condemner on the eighth day—which will come very swiftly upon the ungodly who are slow to conversion—because “when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction shall come upon them.”

Thus, in the final conclusion of this psalm, I pray that before sudden destruction comes upon them, they themselves may first turn and be ashamed very swiftly. Such a prayer, placed at the end of the psalm, is an artful conclusion of the matters set forth in its beginning, narrative, division, confirmation, and refutation. Hence we rightly take what is said here at the end as the conclusion of the whole psalm, by which the Judge is, as it were, bound, so that he may be merciful [Col. 0720D] to one who so prays for the salvation of his enemies; for he can never condemn one who, for his sake, loves his enemies, gladly prays for opponents and slanderers, and gladly does good to those who hate him.

Glory to the Lord Father, who has heard the voice of my weeping. Glory to the Lord Son, who has heard my supplication. Glory to the Lord Holy Spirit, who has received my prayer.

## PSALM VII

[Col. 0719]

[Col. 0719D] “O Lord, my God, in you I have hoped.” In the seventh psalm there is a return to the beginning—that is, to the beginning of our faith—[Col. 0720D] to Christ’s Passion, as he prays in that Passion through which we believe that we are saved. For the Prophet’s purpose [Col. 0721A] in this psalm is to introduce Christ, according to his human nature united to the Word, speaking and praying that he may deliver him, lest the wicked prevail over him, and raise him from death. Then he shows, under a certain concession, the condemnation of the wicked and the glory of the righteous that will result from his resurrection; he also shows that some even among the hostile may obtain pardon if, once converted, they do repentance.

The title of this psalm is (**VERSE 1**):

> UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID, WHICH HE SANG TO THE LORD CONCERNING THE WORDS OF CHUSHI, SON OF JEMINI.

The great Fathers disagree concerning the meaning of this title. Blessed Augustine, with whom Cassiodorus agrees, affirms that the title touches upon the history read [Col. 0721B] in the Second Book of Kings. There we plainly find the name Chushi, who, when David was fleeing from the city before his son Absalom, went over, by David’s own counsel, to Absalom’s side, so that he might discover and report what the son was plotting against his father. Ahithophel advised that Absalom permit his father to be killed unawares. But this plan was changed through Chushi’s counsel: he frustrated Ahithophel’s advice and secretly directed David himself to flee from the plains and save himself and his followers. Because of the words of this Chushi—by which he both frustrated Ahithophel’s counsel and conveyed instructions to King David—they think that David sang this psalm; yet they assign what was said [Col. 0721C] historically to allegory under a higher understanding.

For Chushi is interpreted “silence”; Jemini, “right hand”; Ahithophel, “the brother’s ruin”; Absalom, “the father’s peace.” Therefore, to touch briefly on the mystical sense: Absalom, whose name is interpreted “the father’s peace”—Absalom, I say, son and enemy—is in mystery the apostle Judas and the devil: the false peace of the Father and Master, whom Judas betrayed by a kiss, the sign of peace; into whom Satan entered while he was one of the Twelve, just as Satan stirred Absalom against his father though he was beloved by his father. Accordingly, the punishment of this man greatly delights the lover of justice, because, driven mad in mind by God’s judgment, he hanged himself. In this there is no longer a deep mystery, but the very surface of the event shows Judas and Absalom to be alike in punishment. For Absalom too, hanging from an oak [Col. 0721D] while the mule on which he sat passed on, was immediately abandoned and received the deserved arrows—that is, the sentences of eternal death—in his soul. And lest you think it a small matter that Absalom alone bore the figure of Judas alone, Ahithophel also, his counselor, perished by hanging himself. In accordance with the meaning proper to his name, he contemplated in his wicked counsel the ruin of his brother—that is, David’s death—but was frustrated by Chushi’s saving counsel.

Chushi, however, whose name is interpreted “silence,” signifies the apostle Peter both in name and deed. For just as that Chushi outwardly attached himself to Absalom and seemed to deny David, though in his heart he was David’s intimate friend, so the apostle Peter, for a time joined to the company of evil men, denied with his mouth Christ, the true David, whose friend he nevertheless remained in his heart, as the great Fathers before us have said. His constancy was somewhat shaken when he began to sink amid the raging storm of the Lord’s Passion; but the right hand of divine regard preserved him, and Peter’s charity did not fail, because Christ had not become hateful or wearisome to him, although he had kept silence from confessing him. Through this other Chushi, therefore—namely, through the apostle Peter—the counsel of Judas and the Jews was frustrated, because Christ’s name, which they had wanted to extinguish, was spread abroad through him, with the apostles cooperating. These too are aptly designated by the name Chushi, because, having abandoned Christ and fled, and not professing themselves to be his disciples, they kept friendship and love for him [Col. 0722B] in silence. And although in their silence they refrained from open confession of Christ, nevertheless there were words of prayer and good counsel in their silent expectation of the resurrection, which was undoubtedly more fervent in Peter’s heart after he had wept bitterly over his denial.

Certainly the repentance of Peter, weeping bitterly, may fittingly be understood as expressed in the preceding psalm, since he too prayed concerning the eighth day—that is, the day of resurrection—that when the Lord whom he had denied rose again, he might not be rebuked and reproved for his denial in fury or wrath. His repentance was accepted so completely that, when the angel testifying to the resurrection named him specially and the Lord appeared to him individually—that is, on the eighth day, the Lord’s Day—all [Col. 0722C] his sorrow was changed into joy. The same befell the other apostles, to whom Christ himself had said at his supper: “The world indeed will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful; yet your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 16:20). Whether Chushi is understood as the apostle Peter or as the entire company of apostles, as has been set forth, he is rightly called son of Jemini—that is, son of the right hand—lest, because of their flight and silence during the Passion, they should be thought reckoned to the left.

Nevertheless, because this Chushi is called the son of Jemini in the title, whereas the Chushi mentioned in the history of Kings is called son of Arach, not son of Jemini, blessed Jerome, with whom Remigius agrees, maintains more strongly that this psalm is superscribed with the name of another [Col. 0722D] Chushi, understood to have been from the tribe of Benjamin. Blessed Jerome himself says:

> Very many learned men suppose that this psalm was sung when Chushi, son of Arach, David’s friend, destroyed Ahithophel’s counsel and sent messengers to him that he should flee from the wilderness. But it must be known that they are gravely mistaken. First, because Chushi’s name is written there with *Samech*, here with *Sin*. Then, because that man is called son of Arach, while this one is son of Jemini. Further, David, who had commanded Joab and the other commanders, saying, “Spare the young man Absalom” (2 Kings 18:12), would never speak of his son’s death in this fashion: “He conceived sorrow and bore iniquity; he opened and dug a pit, and fell into the ditch which he made”—especially he who, upon hearing of his death, cried out lamenting, “My son, [Col. 0723A] my son Absalom!” (ibid., 33). Nor would he here call a lion one whom there he had called a boy, as sinning, as it were, through ignorance. It must therefore be known that Chushi is interpreted “Ethiopian,” and that the whole psalm is written against Saul, in whose person the whole psalm may be interpreted; because of his dark character he is called an Ethiopian. He is also rightly called son of Jemini, for in the Book of Kings he is recorded as belonging to the tribe of Benjamin: “There was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, and his name was Cis; and he had a son whose name was Saul” (1 Kings 9:1). The same is also proved through Semei, who was of Saul’s family and whom David calls son of Jemini.

Mystically, Chushi the Ethiopian signifies the devil. Nor is it contrary that he is called son of Jemini—that is, of the right hand. For he was created a son of God, but afterwards through vice became an Ethiopian. That Chushi means “Ethiopian” is indicated by Aquila’s translation: “concerning the words of the Ethiopian,” where Symmachus has “concerning the words of Chushi.” Christ speaks to the Father against the Ethiopian; Augustine agrees in this. For he says: “This psalm too can be understood in Christ’s person, if what is said humbly is referred to our humility.” That it should be referred to Christ’s own person is also suggested by what is read in the title: “Unto the end”; for “Christ is the end unto righteousness for everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). Therefore, when it says, “Unto the end,” it removes us from history and sends us to Christ.

It is a psalm because it contains good action, and it is attributed to David—that is, Christ. Or it is attributed to David—that is, to the penitent Church, now justified through that repentance and translated [Col. 0723C] from injustice to the end, that is, Christ, who is righteousness. For just as the anxious penitent spoke in the preceding psalm, so in this psalm the same person may be understood to speak, now certain of forgiveness and so justified through it that he can confidently say: “Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness and according to my innocence upon me.” Likewise: “My just help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart.”

This David also, looking toward the eighth day, said in prayer concerning enemies: “Let them turn and be ashamed very swiftly.” But now, looking at some enemies for whom he had prayed as so unconvertible that the name Ethiopian may suit them—who does not change the blackness of his skin—he no longer asks for such an enemy but prophesies against him: “His sorrow shall return upon his own head, and his iniquity shall come down upon his crown.” Why? Because “he conceived sorrow and bore iniquity.” Once this cause has been given, the prophecy or imprecation of sorrow against the conceiver of sorrow and deviser of iniquity is found just—especially because the impenitent person is understood by the name Ethiopian, one wholly incapable of turning from his blackness.

Hence there is the passage in the Book of Kings concerning Benaiah, chief among David’s mighty men, who killed an Egyptian man, a man worthy of notice. By the Egyptian or Ethiopian man is understood the utterly wicked Semei, who, because he cursed David, was killed at Solomon’s command by Benaiah son of Joiada (2 Kings 23:21). Thus this Semei, though son [Col. 0724A] of Jemini and an Israelite by birth, is called Egyptian because he was not changed from the blackness of his impiety. So either Saul, the ungodly persecutor of David, or any Antichrist, the unconvertible and incorrigible persecutor of Christ, the true David, may be called an Ethiopian, which is understood by Chushi when it is written with the letter *Sin*. Therefore, whether against Antichrist himself or against any obstinate member of his, Christ rightly prays, in himself or in his members, that he may not fall into the power of such an Ethiopian nor be seized by the teeth of such a lion.

First, therefore, using a beginning—that is, a brief appeal in his opening—he invokes the Lord God, through whom he prays to be delivered, setting forth his merit. Second, [Col. 0724B] he requests the aid of the Lord’s resurrection: “Arise, O Lord, in your wrath.” Third, recalling the future judgment, he treats of things hidden: “The Lord judges the peoples.” Fourth, he treats of things manifest in the future: “God is a just and strong Judge.” Fifth, there follows the joyful conclusion of the confession of praise: “I will confess to the Lord according to his justice, and I will sing praise to the name of the Most High Lord.”

He intends to provoke this praise through the words of Chushi—whether “silence” or “Ethiopian”—because, however the name Chushi is interpreted, the violence and wickedness of the persecution raging against Christ are marked, and at last all of it is turned back upon the head of the persecutor himself who conceived and devised it, where it says: “His sorrow shall return upon his own head, and his iniquity shall come down upon his crown,” as happened to Ahithophel, Absalom, Saul, Semei, and many other persecutors of David.

But we recognize this to have been fulfilled—and to be fulfilled—far more abundantly and strictly in the persecutors of the true David. Therefore all that we have in this psalm concerning the words of Chushi must indeed end in confession of praise; but, in order that the mind may be more vigorously stirred to praise the Judge’s justice, the violence of the persecution must first be set forth. Let David therefore speak; let Christ speak to the Father; let a Christian undergoing persecution cry to Christ against the devil, against some great kind of assaulting temptation or persecution, against Antichrist himself or any most wicked member of his, [Col. 0724D] such as Julian the Apostate. When Julian was killed among the Persians, because his sorrow had returned upon his own head, the confession of those praising the just and victorious Christ resounded not only in Christian churches but even in pagan theaters. For they said: “Utterly foolish, utterly foolish: where are your prophecies? God and his Christ have conquered.”

Let David the righteous—that is, Christ—now speak; let David the sinner, yet healed and justified through repentance and grievously afflicted for righteousness’ sake by an unjust persecutor, speak.

**VERSE 2.** O Lord of all through the power by which you rule everywhere; God of all through creation; my God through love—for those who love you will be your people, and you yourself “will be with them as their God” (Rev. 21:3), their own God, as it were, so that they may have you yourself now as helper, author, and preserver of good merits, and in the future have you as the supreme reward, so that you may be their God. You, O Lord, are my God: the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who love you; and my God too, because I love you and await you as the reward of all my righteous labor.

“In you I have hoped,” not in my own strength. Save me. You, the maker of all, made me so that I might be something, that I might be human, a noble creature. Save me, that I may be your blessed creature. That was the old creation, by which you made me human. Let this be the new creation, by which you willingly begot us through the word of truth, that we may be a certain beginning of your creation, created and made not only [Col. 0725B] that we may be human, but that we may be saved.

“From all who persecute me.” When I did not exist, I could not make myself exist. Likewise, since I am not yet saved from all who persecute me, I cannot save myself. Therefore you, who are able because you are Lord, who know because you are God, and who, because you are mine, must be believed to have good will toward me—in you I have hoped.

Behold, in the three names of the one Lord—“Lord,” “God,” “mine”—a Trinity in unity is intimated, in whose most fertile pastures the devout longing of faith in the shepherd David delights and desires to feed more fully. For when I say, “O Lord, my God,” I invoke the Three and the One, and in them signify three things as one: power, wisdom, and goodness. He who is called Lord is understood to be a powerful ruler. When he is called God, he is understood to be wise—or rather, Wisdom itself—as is more clearly evident in Greek etymology. For **Θεός** (*Theos*), which in Greek means what we call “God,” is derived from the verb **θεωρῶ** (*theōrō*), “I see.” Hence *theory* is called vision or contemplation; and the excellence of the contemplative life lies in this, that human reason becomes a participant in eternal Wisdom, which is none other than the Son of God himself.

Therefore, although the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God properly, substantially, and equally, nevertheless the name *Deus* in Latin, or **Θεός** in Greek, which suggests contemplation of eternal Wisdom, is in some manner specially assigned to the Son. God is invoked by this name, “God,” because by this name he is marked as knowing and seeing all things. Likewise, although the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, and the Holy Spirit is Lord properly, substantially, and equally, nevertheless, because the Son and Holy Spirit possess equal dominion with the Father, Creator and Lord of all, from the Father’s own undivided dominion, lordship is in some manner specially assigned to the Father when the Lord is invoked by this name, “Lord.” Again, although the good person is to be made blessed equally through the vision of the whole Trinity—because the Son says, “He who sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9)—nevertheless the beatification of the human person belongs specially to God’s goodness itself, which is none other than the Holy Spirit. Since he is God and God’s gift, the good person, from such a gift of God, calls God “my God” especially, though he is the God of all generally.

[Col. 0726A] Therefore this man confidently says: “O Lord, my God,” in whom dwells this gift of God, which is God’s goodness and is himself God; for the Holy Spirit, given by Father and Son, is not separated from the giver. O Lord Father; God, Son of the Father; my Paraclete, you Holy Spirit given to me in baptism. Lord and God, to whom belong power and knowledge. Lord, whose power cannot be overcome because it rules over all good and evil; God, whose wisdom cannot be deceived because it sees all good and evil and is not itself seen by evils. You, Lord God, are mine through your goodness, by which goodness alone you will good things and do not will evil.

“In you I have hoped,” because, though you can do all things and know all good [Col. 0726B] and evil, you nevertheless will and love not evil things and good things, but good things alone. Therefore I have hoped in you, that through you I may be delivered from all evils that displease you. For evils cannot stand against your will, since you do not will them to exist at all except insofar as it is good that they exist. Since you are naturally good, you would not permit evil persons to exist unless you saw it was good that they exist, on account of the good things that you work well from evils for the salvation of the elect. You increase their goodness even from the malice of those who persecute them, but at last you deliver the good from evil persecutors. Therefore I have hoped in you, because from recognizing you as my Lord and God I have perceived that you, my God, Three and One, possess this power, wisdom, and goodness: that you can, know how to, and will to deliver those hoping in you.

Therefore save me from all who persecute me, and deliver me. “If the Son sets you free, you shall be truly free” (John 8:36), says the Truth; and elsewhere: “The Truth shall set you free” (ibid., 32). Therefore, that I may remain truly free, deliver me, O Omnipotent One and supreme Truth, over whom falsehood does not prevail, so that I may be truly free from all who persecute me.

**VERSE 3.** Lest the persecutor, the devil or a human being, seize my soul like a lion. And if, by your permission, he seizes my possessions, as he did those of blessed Job, let him not seize my soul—that lion who “goes about roaring, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8)—or the ungodly human being who is like a lion, namely like that lion, the devil.

It should be known that when a person is given over to vices, the devil fights in those vices; once delivered from them, he is likewise free from the devil. He uses words proper to the matter: it belongs to the Lord to deliver and save; to the lion, to seize. Deliver me, O Lord, while there is none to redeem or save. It is as though he said: without you, Redeemer and Savior, who gave the price of redemption and bestow the grace of salvation, there is none to redeem or save. Therefore, if you do not save, he destroys; if you do not deliver and redeem, he seizes.

**VERSE 4.** O Lord, my God, if I have done this. He repeats with delight the name of the triune God, saying, “O Lord, my God,” and adds the merit of his innocence. [Col. 0727A] The order is: “O Lord, my God, if I have done this.” If I, David, first inflicted evils and brought about for myself that which I suffer—Absalom pursuing me, Ahithophel counseling against me, according to what has been reported to me through Chushi’s words; or if I brought about for myself that which I suffer from Saul, who is called Chushi, that is, Ethiopian, and from Semei, who curses me, a man Ethiopian and Egyptian in character—then may I deservedly fall before my enemies, especially if there is iniquity in my hands.

For perhaps there was some iniquity in my hands, through which I did and brought about that which my enemies now plot against me. But because I have repented, because I have already set forth a penitential psalm concerning the eighth day, this iniquity is not now in my hands. Even if it was there, it is there no longer. Therefore I confidently say: “If there is iniquity in my hands,” and:

[Col. 0727B] **VERSE 5.** “If I have repaid those repaying me with evils,” may I deservedly fall. For I trust that there is no longer iniquity in my hands, which either I avoided through the prudence of innocence or washed from my hands by the tears of repentance. I also trust in the merit of patience, because I not only did not inflict evil first, but did not even repay evil to those who repaid me with evil.

The statement “may I fall empty” is not a prayer or an imprecation for a bad outcome, but a concessive prophecy showing what befits those who avenge themselves. For while they raise themselves up by revenge in repaying evils, they fall—defeated by their own anger, filled with malice, and emptied of grace. If they conquered their own anger by putting vengeance aside, they would be stronger and better than conquerors of cities.

[Col. 0727C] Observe that he does not say, “If I repaid those doing evil to me,” but “those repaying me with evil.” It is indeed great patience to endure evil from persons to whom one has done no good; but it is greater to endure evil from persons to whom one has done good, and not repay evils for evils, even to those enemies who repay him evil for good.

David had such enemies in Absalom and Ahithophel, whose counsels and schemes were confounded and frustrated by the words of Hushai. Before them he had had Saul himself as such an enemy; and, as was said above, the name Hushai suitably applies to him. Moreover, the true David, Christ, had such enemies in the Jews, to whom he himself said: “I have done many good works for you” (John 10:32). Yet they repaid good with evil and persecuted him even to death [Col. 0727D], at the prompting of the devil, that most evil Ethiopian; Judas likewise cooperating—devil and Ethiopian alike—against Christ, who was man in relation to his own divinity and that of the Father and the Holy Spirit.

The holy Church still suffers such enemies and such enmities from Antichrist (2 Tim. 3:12), or from any of his members, to whom the name Hushai—that is, “Ethiopian”—may be applied; but those who suffer them appropriately bear the name of the other Hushai, interpreted “silence.” This is especially so when, seeing Truth, which is Christ, oppressed, they lack authority, confidence, or opportunity to speak publicly “upon the housetops” (Matt. 10:27). Yet in their chambers, through prayer and secret converse, they do not lack the words [Col. 0728A] of Hushai—that is, words of silence. For the sake of these words, referred to the End, that is, to Christ, this psalm is composed: a psalm of David, “strong of hand,” and of the unconquerable king against the strong lion, of whom it has already been said, “Lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion,” and of whom he now further says:

**VERSE 6. “Let the enemy persecute my soul.”** As though he said: Above I conceded that, if I am guilty toward my enemies, I should deservedly fall empty. Now I concede even what is more grievous: namely, that the individual enemy, the devil, may persecute my soul by suggesting evil, seize it by drawing it into consent, and trample my life—that is, the faculty of sense by which I live—upon the earth through evil action. Let him trample it into the earth, so that, by savoring and loving earthly things, it may become earth, and the serpent, to whom it was said, “You shall eat earth” [Col. 0728B] (Gen. 3:14), may eat it and incorporate it into himself. And let him bring my glory—that is, my rational mind, upon which the glory of God’s image and likeness has been impressed, since reason itself was made in God’s image—down into dust; let him reduce it to dust, so that my glory, my very reason, becomes dust, which the wind of temptation drives from the face of the earth.

**VERSE 7. “Arise, O Lord, in your anger.”** Here faithful Hushai—for example, Peter, or another apostle, in silence before the Resurrection—prays that the Resurrection itself may be hastened. Or any faithful person, grieved and oppressed, as blessed Peter was after the Passion and before the Resurrection, here asks that the Lord’s Resurrection may be hastened for him. For Christ sleeps and is in a manner dead and [Col. 0728C] buried to those wretched persons who are themselves called Hushai, that is, “silence,” when they have neither authority nor opportunity to speak the truth and to carry out the charity fervent within them; or who are themselves oppressed by the words of Ethiopian Hushai, as Saul persecuted humble David, and as Shimei son of Jemini cursed David while David, on the contrary, was doing good and blessing.

To persons thus oppressed Christ sleeps, when he does not console them, since he hides from them the face of his mercy. He rises when, appearing to them with many proofs, he consoles them by the manifest evidence of his compassion toward humanity and by his open wrath against human vices and errors. Therefore, whether a silent Hushai or someone oppressed by [Col. 0728D] the words of Ethiopian Hushai, let him desire Christ to rise for him, saying: “Arise, O Lord, in your anger”—that is, show yourself in your just vengeance by being angry with sins, not with human beings—and “be exalted,” that is, be magnified and glorified, “at the boundaries of my enemies.”

I do not say, “At the end of prosperous people,” as though their prosperity should come to an end, but, “At the end of enemies.” I ask you, my God, my comforter, to be so exalted that they cease to be enemies to me: let there be an end of those who are hostile, not an end of the prosperous. Let there be an end of enemies, so that they cease to be enemies and become ready to perform and fulfill the commandment of charity which you gave when, in the Law, you said: “You shall love your friend” (Lev. 19:18), and in the Gospel: “Love your enemies” (Matt. 5:44). Again [Col. 0729A] elsewhere you said: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you” (John 13:34); and again: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John 15:12).

To fulfill this commandment—since human weakness does not suffice—you, Lord my God: Lord, ruling over every power; God, ordering all things in the wisdom which you yourself are; mine, because you gave yourself to me when you, God who are charity, gave the gift of charity. Therefore you are Lord of all through power; God of all through providence; and you are mine through the love granted to me. “For the charity of God has been poured forth into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). And that Spirit is love, through whom God, God of all, is my God. So says the Church [Col. 0729B] filled with the Holy Spirit; hers is this voice: “O God, my God, I keep watch for you from the dawn” (Ps. 62:2). Again: “My God, do not be silent toward me” (Ps. 27:1). Again: “My God, look to my help” (Ps. 70:12). And many such expressions occur in Scripture, where God, generally God of all, is called in a special manner the God of his elect alone because the gift of charity has been granted to them.

Therefore any elect person who, through divine grace, has received the gift of charity even to the point of loving enemies may confidently say: “Lord my God, who gave the commandment of charity,

“Arise in the commandment which you commanded.” For it is not as though we loved you first; rather, because you first loved us, your “charity has been poured forth into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who [Col. 0729C] has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). Thus, when you first loved us who were to love you, you yourself rose in the commandment which you commanded, because by your love, which precedes us, you caused your commandment to be kept by us. You first displayed the example of your love and infused into our hearts the affection of that very love. In order to bring it to a fruit-bearing result glorious to you and beneficial to us, arise in the commandment which you commanded: so that you may fulfill in us and utterly complete the commandment which you commanded, which you have in some manner begun in us; and, both beginning and completing that commandment which you commanded, may you first love enemies and make them become your friends and mine, to be perfected and preserved in this friendship.

In your flesh, once dead, you rose once from the dead after conquering death; and now you shall die no more, nor shall death have dominion over you any longer (Rom. 6:9). Likewise arise in the commandment which you commanded, so that, enmities having been conquered, you may be loved in yourself and in your own with such great love not only by us, but also by those who are still enemies and are to become friends; so that this charity may no longer fail, nor hatred thereafter rule or prevail over it, so that we may not be conquered by evil but may conquer evil with good. Therefore, as you rose in flesh once dead for a time, so arise in the commandment of charity, dead in the ungodly. Rise, having won the unconquerable triumph of the Resurrection.

**VERSE 8. “And the assembly of peoples shall surround you.”** The assembly—that is, the congregation—of peoples who love you [Col. 0730A] shall surround you like a garment: “and you shall change them like a cloak, and they shall be changed” (Heb. 1:12), when they surround you.

**VERSE 9. “And because of this assembly, return on high.”** To draw this assembly upward, return on high, where you were before. For you came down from on high into this world, as if naked. You came forth from the most high Father and came into this world; that is, you came into every creature when, in the human being, who is every creature, you assumed every creature, and caused the Gospel to be preached to every creature. By believing and obeying in the human being, every creature became as it were your garment.

Therefore you, who came forth from the Father as if naked, in the world put on the tunic woven from above: namely, the holy Church. It is not the synagogue of one Jewish [Col. 0730B] people, but the assembly of peoples; for the Gospel went out into all the earth, gathering into the unity of faith, hope, and charity an assembly of different nations and diverse peoples, which is the fullness of the Gentiles. For the gathering of this assembly below, arise in the commandment which you commanded. And for drawing it upward to the heights, return on high.

In your flesh, once dead, you rose once and ascended once; but in your own—whether dead through sin or put to death through repentance—you rise with a constant and continual resurrection, while sinners are converted through your working and penitents, having been put to death with you, are clothed with the appearance of the Paschal Resurrection, so that “their appearance” may be “like lightning, and like snow” (Matt. 24:3).

[Col. 0730C] This text is interpreted otherwise, as the words of David himself—that is, Christ—foreknowing his death and speaking of the triumph of the Resurrection, in this way: “Arise, O Lord, in your anger”; that is, exercise this anger of yours “at the boundaries of my enemies.” “Be exalted,” that is, make yourself high, so that they may not understand your anger against them and, thus blinded, crucify you. And, appearing humble, “arise in the commandment which you commanded,” that is, be high, so that they may not understand why you are humble; and thus, the Jews blinded by your humility, while the disciples pass over to the nations, the assembly—that is, not a few persons but a gathering of peoples, namely of the Gentiles—will surround you in faith.

And again, because of this assembly, return on high: because of this assembly, which bears your name, the Christian name, yet denies that very name by its deeds, return on high [Col. 0730D]; cease to be understood. This will happen near the end, when “the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24:12), so that it may truly be said: “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18:8).

“The Lord judges peoples.” This follows in either sense. For after the Ascension, after the universal resurrection of his body, in which “we shall all rise,” as the Apostle says, “but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51), after the transformation of the elect themselves, after the manifestation on high of the Judge himself, the Lord judges peoples. For he will judge the living and the dead. Likewise, after [Col. 0731A] the blinding of false Christians, Christ will come from heaven: “he will come and will not be silent” (Ps. 49:3), but will judge peoples.

“Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness.” He confidently seeks judgment who forestalls the Judge’s face through confession and repentance; who is now weary even of life in the flesh; and whose way of life already in heaven, whose meditation is occupied more with heavenly than earthly things, bears witness to him that forgiveness has been granted. The order is good. For in the preceding psalm, called weak and pierced with compunction unto repentance, he had said, “Save me because of your mercy,” fearing the judgment of justice. But now, because when summoned he has kept the commandment of patience or charity even to the love of enemies, [Col. 0731B] he no longer fears judgment but ventures to pray: “Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness,” which lies in the good things preserved, “and according to my innocence,” which lies in evils avoided. This righteousness and innocence are not from me, but are above me, “coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17).

**VERSE 10. “Let the wickedness of sinners be brought to an end.”** Some manuscripts have “let it be completed,” and the sense is: let the wickedness of sinners be completed, that is, brought to its utmost point, so that “he who is filthy may become filthier still” (Rev. 22:11). And because, as the envy of the wicked increases, there increase [lacuna], he accordingly adds: “You will direct the righteous,” so that, as he who is filthy becomes filthier still, so “the righteous may be justified still more” [Col. 0731C].

But because, on account of hypocrisy, it is not known who is being directed in faith toward righteousness, to be justified still more, and who is being completed in wickedness, whereas the Lord judges all things and himself knows, he rightly adds: “God searches hearts and reins.” By “hearts” thoughts are understood; by “reins,” delights, because the pleasure of generation is in the reins, while in the heart lies the will to generate or to do something else. Therefore the hearts signify the wills of those who think, while the reins signify the final intentions of those same wills, in which the person thinking and generating thoughts takes delight. But God searches hearts—that is, he understands with what disposition thoughts and deeds are done—and reins, that is, the end in which they take delight.

[Col. 0731D] According to the Hebrew truth, however, it should be read: “Wickedness shall be consumed,” so that wickedness is understood to be consumed, not completed. For “God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24). Hence it is now said: “The wickedness of sinners shall be consumed”; and so, sins having been consumed, a righteous person is made from a sinner, and “you will direct the righteous.” He spoke in the plural of sinners—“The wickedness of sinners shall be consumed”—and added in the singular, “You will direct the righteous,” either because sinners are many but the righteous few, or because, from many sinners whose wickedness has been consumed by the fire of charity, one righteous person is made, as all the righteous come together into one perfect man, in the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ. Therefore you, God who search hearts and reins—that is, thoughts and intentions—will direct the righteous.

[Col. 0732A] When thoughts and intentions are in the Lord, he not only directs the righteous but also helps them. Hence he adds:

**VERSE 11. “My righteous help is from the Lord.”** There are two functions of medicine: to heal disease and to preserve health. In accordance with the first, the weak man said in the preceding psalm: “Because I am weak, heal me, O Lord.” In accordance with the second, one now healed and strengthened through repentance says: “My righteous help is from the Lord,” who saves those upright in heart.

There he asks mercy, miserable and without merits; here, because he did not return evil to those repaying him with evil, he asks [Col. 0732B] righteous help from the Lord, who saves those upright in heart. He does not now add anything about the reins, as above; because if thought is right, delight is also right, but the converse does not hold. For in many people delight is right but thought is not right. All human beings delight in blessedness, but right thought does not guide everyone to it. Many are led astray by wandering error: desiring to be blessed, they seek blessedness in deceptive things. But those who seek blessedness through joy which comes from truth alone are upright in heart, just as those have a perverse heart who think themselves blessed through falsehood, which is opposed to truth. God alone is true, “and every human being a liar” (Ps. 115:11). But the evil angel, prince of this world, is a liar and the father of lies.

Therefore the end and fulfillment of blessedness must be established in God’s promises alone. The straight way to attain it is only through God’s commandments. Whoever earnestly intends to walk in their uprightness [Col. 0732C], even if he is not yet upright before people in public action—because perhaps he cannot show in action what he has in his heart—is nevertheless already upright in heart by the mere uprightness of his will. But this is hidden from people unless it proceeds into action, and one’s neighbor receives little help from a good intention existing only in the will. Thus, so that the person upright in heart through good intention may attain good action, he asks righteous help from the Lord who saves those upright in heart.

**VERSE 12. “God is a just judge, strong and patient.”** Above he had said: “The Lord judges peoples.” Now, to commend his judgments, he adds the justice [Col. 0732D] of the Judge, his strength, and his long-suffering: terrifying Ethiopian Hushai—that is, anyone hardened in sins—with fear of future judgment, and consoling anyone reformed from sins. To assure such a person of consolation, he has given his own example: “My righteous help is from the Lord, who saves those upright in heart,” so that every upright person may hope for righteous help by his example.

As if he said: For me, corrected from my perversity through repentance, loving not only friends in God but enemies also for God’s sake, righteous help is ready at hand. You all who have been converted may confidently hope for that same help of God, because God, the just Judge, strong and patient, will not be angry with you every day. To state this more sharply and forcefully [Col. 0733A], he says it in the form of a question: “Will he be angry every day?”—understood: with those who have been converted. But you Ethiopians, marked in this psalm’s title by the name Hushai, should know this:

**VERSE 13. “Unless you are converted,”** that just, strong, and patient Judge will be angry with you; he who is not angry with those who are converted. In Greek, the phrase is more emphatic than “he will be angry”: “you will bring wrath upon yourselves,” because wrath by which he punishes is not in him, but in the angels of wrath through whom he punishes. They delight in human punishment not from justice, in which they do not rejoice, but from malice; for, fiercely envying human beings called to the place from which they themselves fell, they are angry with them. Therefore, whenever they are permitted to punish people, God appears angry because of the vehemence of their own wrath [Col. 0733B], though he works even through angels of wrath in tranquility.

But when those angry spirits are so restrained that they are not allowed to punish except insofar as it pertains to discipline—as the “angel of Satan” (2 Cor. 12:7) buffeting the Apostle Paul, or as Satan harassing blessed Job—God ought by no means to be considered angry. What he permits, he permits graciously, not angrily, although he appears angry to those suffering such things.

Yet even in this manner, in being angry, he will not be angry with his elect every day. He will be angry only until “strength is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9); when it has been perfected, just as “perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18), so perfect strength will cast out and drive far away the angel of Satan. Hence, although the Apostle, asking the Lord three times, was not heard (2 Cor. 12:8), while the tenderness of his strength was still such that the greatness of his revelations could have exalted him unless the angel of Satan buffeted him, it must by no means be believed that throughout every day of his life the great Apostle lay cast down under such buffetings.

For will God, the just Judge, strong and patient, be angry every day? Could or should the just Judge, after the vessel of election had been fully polished by the ways of wrath, have continued to trouble him through such a thorn of the flesh, through such an angel of Satan? He had sent it for no other purpose than the perfection of strength—that is, humility, queen of virtues. Nor is it surprising [Col. 0733D] that, while the Apostle was still young, there could remain in him some tinder of pride on account of the greatness of his revelations. For he himself confesses this concerning himself: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things” (1 Cor. 13:11).

We must therefore grant to the just Judge, who is not angry every day, that during those days in which the Apostle was still a child and inclined toward the fall of pride, he chastised and humbled him through the angel of Satan and the thorn of the flesh, as though angry. But should he have remained angry—or troublesome through an angel of wrath—every day toward that same Apostle when, now made a man, he had put away childish things? Far be this from that Judge, of whom we rightly sing and chant: “God is a just Judge, strong and patient; will he be angry every day?” [Col. 0734A]

Let no one mock me as a man devoted to little songs; rather, let him accept my defense, which I have already given above, where I likewise placed and inserted certain notes customary in the Church upon the text of the Psalms. Perhaps I shall do this more often, in the belief that I do not force what I write upon great teachers, to whom I fear all our work may be distasteful; yet, by God’s favor, nothing will be found inserted in it that departs from the understanding of the holy Fathers or from the edification of charity.

For although the great Fathers before us have maintained that the Apostle was not heard by the Lord when asking that the thorn of the flesh, the angel of Satan, be removed—not once but upon his third [Col. 0734B] request—nevertheless it does not contradict those Fathers that we believe and confidently maintain that the same Apostle, once healed of the sickness of self-exaltation, when he had become a perfect man, was entirely freed from that angel of Satan. It is certain that he was buffeted by it for no other reason than that the strength of humility might be made perfect in weakness (2 Cor. 12:9).

Do you suppose that the Apostle, divinely taught that his threefold petition was not heard because strength had to be perfected in weakness by such continual buffetings, immediately ceased praying? I do not think that he then ceased praying; rather, he changed his prayers and earnestly and unceasingly prayed that the strength of humility might be so perfected in him that such an angel would not be necessary [Col. 0734C] to buffet him. Whoever denies that the Apostle frequently prayed this must, if he can, deny that he frequently used the Lord’s Prayer; he must say that the one who commanded “pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17) acted otherwise than he taught.

Since, then, it is certain that the Apostle often prayed for God’s name to be sanctified in him, for God’s kingdom to come to him—a kingdom in which the angel of Satan has nothing of his own—and for “God’s will to be done as in heaven, so on earth” (Matt. 6:10): by that will, in heaven, that is, in the mind desiring heavenly things, and in the earth of human flesh, the mind, however greatly glorified by the magnitude of revelations, is not exalted, nor does the flesh itself require a thorn to buffet it as though rebellious to the spirit. Finally, since he prayed to be delivered from evil and not led into temptation, who would dare deny that his unceasing prayer was heard in this: that, with Christ’s strength dwelling in him, he was free from the buffetings by which his arrogance had been subdued, once strength had become perfect within him? For will God, the just Judge, strong and patient, be angry, or bring wrath, every day? [Col. 0734D]

Nevertheless, you Ethiopians marked by the name Hushai, know this: this just Judge, strong and patient, will be angry every day while you persist in wickedness, because unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword—indeed, he has already brandished it, because he has decreed that this will happen against you. The sword is Christ, who, in his first coming, was covered by the sheath of humility, but in the second will flash forth: light [Col. 0735A] to his own, terror to the ungodly.

Therefore the just Judge will brandish his sword, his most sharp Word, the two-edged sword (*romphaia*) proceeding from his mouth, when he manifests himself in his glory. By that glory he will distinguish the righteous from the unrighteous as the brightly shining sun distinguishes eagle eyes from the eyes of bats and owls—delighting the former, driving the latter into outer darkness.

But in saying, “Unless you are converted,” he indicates even to the most ungodly that hope of pardon is laid up for them if they are converted. Hear therefore, you ungodly; let every Hushai hear; hear, all who are black in your sins; hear, all Ethiopians: unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword. And although he is patient, do not become lax through his patience. Know that his patience is not lax, because he has already bent his bow [Col. 0735B]. The bow is Scripture, in which, as wood is subdued and bent by a string, so the harshness of the Old Testament is subdued and bent by the grace of the New Testament. He prepared this bow when he established Scripture through the mouths of prophets and apostles; he bent it when he made that same Scripture intelligible through both the evidence of events and the diligence of interpreters.

**VERSE 14. “And in it he prepared”—that is, arranged—“instruments of death”:** certain obscure places, from which death of the soul comes to heretics, not because God drives them to it, but because their own fault deserves it, as they fail to understand the truth of Scripture. From these places, the meanings of the Scriptures, as though stirred by a winnowing-fan, shine out like arrows; by their light we go “in the brightness of a flashing spear” (Hab. [Col. 0735C] 3:11), if we burn with love for knowing truth and holding fast to virtue.

Indeed, he made his arrows not for the lukewarm or slothful but for the burning: burning with the fire which the Lord sent upon the earth and greatly desired to burn. “I came to send fire upon the earth,” he says, “and what do I desire but that it burn?” (Luke 12:49). She who says in the Song of Songs, “I am wounded by charity” (Song 4:9), was struck by these arrows.

Or the apostles themselves are both instruments of death and burning arrows—or arrows for those who burn—according to the text: “To some we are an odor of life unto life; to others, an odor of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:16).

Otherwise: “God is a just judge, strong and patient,” and so forth. For in the three adjectival words by which God the Judge is praised—“just, strong, and patient”—there appears [Col. 0735D] to be an indication of the whole Holy Trinity acting in judgment. “Just,” as he calls him, is God the Son, Truth, to whom the execution of judgment pertains principally and especially, as he himself says: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

Hence also the holy man says: “I do not wish him to contend with me in great strength, nor to press me down with the weight of his greatness; let him set equity before me” (Job 23:7). As if he said: I do not wish the Father to come to judge me, since he has nothing of mine, but is to be feared solely on account of what is his own, and therefore might press me down with the weight of his greatness. But what then? “Let him set equity before me”—that is, let him send the Son to judge me, who has what is mine, in that he is human, and what is his own [Col. 0736A], in that he is God.

To this also belongs what they said to Moses: “Speak to us and we will hear you; let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die” (Exod. 20:19). Therefore God the just and equitable Judge is God the Son himself. God strong is God the Father himself, creator and Lord of all creation. But God patient and kind is God the Spirit himself. Yet the Son alone is not just: the Father and the Holy Spirit, one with the Son, are also just. Likewise, the Father alone is not strong, but the Son and Holy Spirit, one with him, are strong. Nor is the Holy Spirit alone patient and kind, but the Father and Son, one and the same with him, are patient and kind.

And although the Son is specially God the just Judge, the Father will not be absent from judgment [Col. 0736B]; for the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son. That Son rightly possesses all the strength of the Father’s nature, so that he can immediately either save or condemn those whom he justly wills. Before judgment, however, patience—which is the work and office of the Holy Spirit—is granted beforehand. Hence also: “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?” (Rom. 2:4).

Therefore the three adjectival words by which God the Judge is magnified—“just, strong, and patient”—appropriately correspond to the three clauses that follow: “Will he be angry every day? Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword,” and so forth. Because he is patient, he is not angry every day; because he is strong, he has brandished his sword; [Col. 0736C] because he is just, he has bent and prepared his bow, and in it prepared instruments of death, making his arrows for those who burn.

Accordingly, let good Hushai, seeing God’s patience leading sinners to repentance, not fail in the long-suffering of hope; nor let evil Hushai presume to store up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and revelation of righteous judgment. Rather, let each Hushai know that God is not only patient but also strong, able to brandish the sword with so strong a hand that none may resist his strength with impunity. And lest God’s great strength terrify either sinner or righteous person, so that he says, “I do not wish him to contend with me in great strength” (Job 22:6), let each know that God is not only strong but also just: he does not destroy the righteous together with the ungodly, but, like a skilled archer [Col. 0736D] bending and preparing his bow, tempers the strength of Holy Scripture with gentleness, so as to know not only how to restrain the shoulder that withdraws, the lung of pride, the stomach of greed, and the other members of vice, but also how to preserve the new creature in Christ.

**VERSE 15. “Behold, he has conceived iniquity.”** He has just said of the just Judge that he has brandished his sword and bent and prepared his bow. But lest we think that the Judge, tranquil in himself, brings forth that by which the wicked are punished without a preceding cause, he shows that God does not devise a means of punishing; rather, by an equitable judgment he orders that the very pleasures of sin become instruments for God who punishes.

Someone might ask: Why has the just Judge brandished his sword [Col. 0737A] and bent this bow? The answer is: Behold, the cause is plain. For that wicked Ethiopian Hushai, to whom the blackness of sin has become almost natural, first, at the devil’s suggestion, conceived sorrow—that is, love of temporal things.
