The love of these things is called sorrow because they can be lost and must necessarily be taken from those who love them; and they are lost with proportionately greater sorrow as they were desired and possessed with greater love. Thus their love is rightly called sorrow, because the end of possessing them is nothing but sorrow.

For nothing else causes the ungodly in hell sorrow at the loss of temporal things except that even in hell they retain inwardly [Col. 0737B] the love of things which they will then be unable to possess. So that rich man in hell, burning with desire for feasts, could not obtain even a drop of water, because, when full, he had not given crumbs to the hungry poor man. Thus it may rightly be said of that rich man that in this life he conceived sorrow—not in its actual quality, but in its seed. Love is the seed of sorrow when one loves something that cannot be kept and can be taken away against one’s will.

Thus a woman is said to have conceived a human being, not because the seed conceived by her is immediately a human being, but because it will become one if it remains in the womb. Likewise, the person who, at the devil’s suggestion, conceives within the womb of the mind love for temporal things, if he perseveres in it, will have it turned into sorrow when the thing he loves is taken from him against his will. Hence the saints who despise temporal things will be deprived of them without sorrow, because they do not possess them here in love but from necessity. They rejoice when they are freed even from that [Col. 0737C] necessity, to cleave to the vision of Truth alone, which cannot be taken from them, because they loved it in the world and sought it outside the world, above the world, in Christ alone, who is Truth.

Having despised that Truth, wicked Hushai, by conceiving love for temporal things, conceived in seed the sorrow of hell. For behold, he has brought forth iniquity, in order unjustly to take from another what he perversely loves. This occurs because he conceived sorrow, which he brings to birth by planning something wicked and gives birth to by bringing it into action—for example, the act of theft, robbery, or adultery. This act is the devil’s own son, since it is conceived from his seed, which is worldly love. What he understood by the word “conception,” he defines from its result [Col. 0737D], saying:

**VERSE 16. “He opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the hole which he made.”** The pit is earthly covetousness, a deep pit without a bottom, because the more eagerly desired possessions are acquired [Col. 0738A], the more things remain to be desired and acquired, so that covetousness is infinite and deep. The wicked person opened this pit for himself when, through pleasure in possession, he conceived the beginning of fraud or a scheme of shamefulness; he dug it by persisting in the work; and he fell, by giving birth—that is, by completing the work—into the hole he made. For example, while one who defrauds another of money seeks to deceive him, he is first and more grievously harmed in the loss of innocence than the other person is in the loss of money. Why, then, should the Judge be considered cruel when the wicked person is bound only by the cords of his own deeds? In judgment he will not be weighed down by another’s sorrow or another’s wickedness, but rather:

**VERSE 17. “His sorrow, which he conceived, shall return upon his own head, and his iniquity shall descend [Col. 0738B] upon his own crown.”** The head is the mind, and reason is in the crown. The sorrow which the ungodly person conceived and the iniquity which he gave birth to return upon head and crown when the desire to sin suffocates mind and reason and the whole human being becomes the slave of sin ruling over mind and reason. In the future, however, sorrow and iniquity will descend upon the crown from the judgment of God on high, as it were with great force, to crush him in punishment.

But I, little David—that is, the humble penitent—have been freed from the words and counsels of Ethiopian Hushai, or aided by the words and counsels of the other Hushai, who grieves with me and loves me at least in silence.

**VERSE 18. “I will confess to the Lord according to [Col. 0738C] his righteousness.”** This is the joyful conclusion of the whole psalm, in which there sounds not confession of sins but confession of praise: a pleasing and fitting act of praise. The righteous person, justified through faith and repentance, says: “I confess to the Lord according to his righteousness,” by which he destroys the wicked badly and, leasing his vineyard to other laborers, grants righteous help to those whom, being righteous, he justly justifies—not by human but by divine righteousness, by which he freely bestows merits so that he may justly add rewards, giving grace for grace.

I will confess, uttering with my mouth the devotion which I have in my heart; and I will make psalm in deed, so that the psalm may be directed to the End, to the name of the Lord Most High, who is worthy of the confession of praise precisely because he is Most High.

Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, Lord, my God, [Col. 0738D] from whose threefold name the psalm’s opening shines forth, and to whose name confession is also rendered at the end of the Psalm, where the name of the Most High Lord is mentioned.

## PSALM VIII

[Col. 0737]

[Col. 0737D] “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” The title of this psalm is as follows (v. 1):

**FOR THE END: A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR THE WINEPRESSES.**

In the Scriptures, the same reality is often shown under different comparisons. For the Church, which elsewhere is understood through the threshing-floor, is here understood through the winepress, on the same principle. For as grain is separated from chaff on the threshing-floor, so wine is separated from grape-skins in the winepress—though it is necessary that they be born, grow, and come to maturity together. [Col. 0739A] Thus, certainly, in the holy Church good people mingled with evil people are sometimes separated spiritually through the work of God’s ministers, when the good are taught not to consent to evil; and sometimes also bodily, when the winnowing-fan of excommunication casts out those impious persons who persist in their wickedness, lest by their deadly contagion they destroy very many.

Christ himself indicates that evil people must sometimes be spared for the sake of the good, where, discussing the parable of the tares, he teaches that they must be endured for the wheat’s sake. But in this endurance one must note what is said: “Allow both to grow” (Matt. 13:29–30). For as long as the growing tares do not at the same time prevent the wheat from growing, both are deliberately spared on occasion, lest perhaps the wheat also be uprooted together with the tares. But if the tares grow so luxuriantly that they choke the grain, they must no longer be spared; for in enduring them there is no growth of the wheat, but loss. That is, when the tares alone strive so to occupy the Lord’s field, namely this world, that not even the “enclosed garden” (Cant. 4:12) can remain safe from them—the garden which is shut fast by the keys of divine authority, the Lord saying: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not deal maliciously with my prophets” (1 Chron. 16:20). Therefore, when evil persons in the Church malign the good, and do not themselves endure even the fact that they are tolerated, there is no reason why they should be spared—especially if the Church complains against such persons, as Sarah complained against the maidservant’s son in the presence of his father Abraham. [Col. 0739C] It should indeed be noted that this maidservant’s son was allowed to grow in the paternal house with the free woman’s son until such great wickedness was found in him that he persecuted the free woman’s son. But when the persecution was made public, the free mother said: “Cast out the maidservant and her son” (Gen. 21:10).

Yet Isaac, although delivered from domestic persecution, suffered many evils from the foreign Philistines. Envying his successful fortunes, they filled in the wells he had dug and compelled him to flee from place to place. From this we observe that domestic enemies—that is, evil Christians—when Mother Church is able, ought also to be bodily separated from the good. Nevertheless, the good are sometimes compelled by pagans and excommunicated persons to give place to their wrath. [Col. 0739D] Thus, sometimes when good people persecute evil people and expel them from the holy Church, and sometimes when those same good people endure persecution from the evil, there takes place in the Lord’s winepress a separation of wine from grape-skins, and oil from dregs: now in part, but in the future universally. For the Judge will say to the godly: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34); and to the ungodly: “Go, accursed, into eternal fire” (ibid., 41).

In that judgment, since “the heavens will reveal” the ungodly persons’ “iniquity, and the earth will rise up against them” (Job 20:27), it is fitting that in this “Psalm written for the winepresses” the heavens are mentioned: “For I shall behold your heavens, the works of your fingers”; and the earth: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth.” [Col. 0740A] For the heavens are those most perfect saints who, with the Lord, “will judge nations and rule peoples in great steadfastness,” standing “against those who afflicted them in the winepresses” (Wis. 3:8; 5:1). The good and fruitful earth, however, means those who will be saved in judgment because of the fruits of almsgiving, as the Lord says: “I was hungry, and you gave me food,” and so forth (Matt. 25:35).

Alternatively: the Church is called a winepress because in it the divine Word is composed, in sound and meaning, of figures and the things signified by them, as grape-skins and wine, as dregs and oil. When the Word, with the same sound, is conveyed to the ears, or even presented to sight through the figures of letters, pictures, or indeed the entire fabric of the world, the Word itself, apprehended by sight or hearing, is as it were separated in a winepress. The sounds heard and figures seen remain outside, while the meaning flows inward, is carefully received in the pool of memory, and then passes into the disposition of the mind and discipline of character, as it were into a wine-cellar. Of this the bride says: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar; he set love in order within me” (Cant. 2:4).

In this sense, it is rightly said “for the winepresses” that the Lord’s name is wonderful in all the earth: because the earthly creature too wonderfully magnifies the name and praise of its Maker, demonstrating the Creator’s omnipotence by its magnitude, his eternal wisdom by the most ordered arrangement of its condition and motion, and his eternal goodness by the usefulness of its fruits. [Col. 0740C] In these three—omnipotence, wisdom, and goodness—the triune God is indicated, whose wonderful name is proclaimed in all the earth. And the sweetness of this name, understood through visible creation, delights blessed minds as oil pressed from dregs, so that it is pleasant for them to sing: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth.” That earth, as it were a page written in black letters, directs the wise observer to the taste of that wine which makes the human heart glad, and represents that oil of which it is said: “Your name is poured-out oil” (Cant. 1:3). This name is “wonderful in all the earth,” because “the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy” (Ps. 32:5).

But when we behold the heavens and the powers of heaven as works of God’s fingers, and the moon and stars, we read as it were a page written in golden letters, indicating that the Lord’s magnificence is exalted above its own height. [Col. 0740D] Thus John, one of the rational heavens, says: “He who comes after me was made before me; I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal. He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 1:27; 3:30). This was said by the man than whom “among those born of women none greater has arisen” (Matt. 11:11). Likewise, the chief angel of the heavenly host, than whom among angels there is none greater, indicates by his very name that he is less than him whose magnificence is exalted above the heavens. For Michael means, “Who is like God?” And David says: “Who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord?” (Ps. 88:7). Peter, the prince of the apostles, did not wish to be crucified upright, lest he appear to be likened to his crucified Lord.

He alone who wished to be like the Most High, together with his accomplices, has no place in heaven, but in the lowest hell. From his fellowship—or from the most sour grape, as from the foulest dregs—holy human beings and angels, separated far away and strained through the winepress of divine judgment, praise the wonderful name of the Lord, whose magnificence is exalted above the heavens.

Alternatively. The Church is called a winepress because often within her, as in a winepress, through the press of martyrdom the bodies of the good remain on earth like grape-skins and dregs; [Col. 0741B] but their souls flow out into the rest of the eternal cellars. At last, in the resurrection, their bodies too will be joined to them, purified through the winepresses of sufferings in such a way that they too, together with their souls, may be worthy to be received into the eternal dwellings, into the eternal cellars, of which it is said: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14:2).

Therefore, “for the winepresses”—that is, for Churches being established or already established—there is sung “for the end,” that is, for consummation: so that the brightness of the moon, the purity of the stars, and the serenity of the heavens, which the Prophet perceived in the book of eternal predestination, may be found in the Church consummated in the End, that is, in Christ. “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). For this reason this psalm is demonstrative, in commendation of Christ. Speaking of his glory and honour, it aims to exhort its hearers to submit themselves voluntarily to that same Christ, to whom even those unwilling to submit are subject against their will.

To understand fully why we call this psalm demonstrative, or any other psalm of a similar kind of cases, something must be said at somewhat greater length about the kinds of cases distinguished in rhetorical art. Yet these descend from no other art than the art of arts, namely divine wisdom, and display their distinct forms in this book of psalms. There are three kinds of cases: deliberative, demonstrative, and judicial. [Col. 0741D] These involve prosecution and rebuttal, because in every kind of case some persons prosecute and others, in opposition, rebut—that is, refute what has been said against them. Yet these three kinds differ from one another in their respective qualities.

For the deliberative kind concerns the future, aiming to recommend what is useful and dissuade from what is useless; it proceeds entirely through prosecution and rebuttal, because one who advises prosecutes, while one who dissuades rebuts what the other has advised.

Likewise, the demonstrative kind of case, through the prosecution of praise and the rebuttal of blame, aims to commend something honourable and blame something dishonourable. It concerns the present, especially when a person to be chosen for some office of dignity is shown worthy of praise or blame. [Col. 0742A]

The judicial kind of case concerns the past and aims at justice and injustice, when an accuser prosecutes a person as one who ought rightly to be condemned for a deed already done; while the defender, intent on rebuttal, either denies the deed or, conceding the deed, denies that it should rightly be punished.

Of the deliberative kind is what is said in Psalm 12: “How long shall I place counsels in my soul, sorrow in my heart by day?” For it speaks of the future, deliberating in counsel to choose what is found to be useful. Of the judicial kind is what is said in Psalm 93: “Rise up, you who judge the earth; render recompense to the proud.” For it concerns the past, accusing the pride of evil people and teaching that it ought rightly to be punished. This psalm belongs to the demonstrative kind. For it concerns the great King, crowned with glory and honour before the eyes of all, as though present and visible; it proves that voluntary subjection to him is honourable, and shows that refusal to submit is dishonourable, since, willing or unwilling, his enemies cannot escape the dominion under whose feet all things are shown to be subject: whether they serve him in intention and action, or oppose him in intention alone but nevertheless serve him, willing or unwilling, by action or suffering. [Col. 0742B]

This demonstration has the form of a most complete and finished argument, consisting of five parts according to rhetorical art. For among rhetoricians the most finished and perfect argument is that which is divided into five parts. The first part is the proposition, the second the reason, the third confirmation of the reason, the fourth embellishment, and the fifth the conclusion or summary, placed at the end of the discourse and corresponding to its beginning.

The proposition is what this great orator, the expounder of the great King, says: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth.” For in that verse the Prophet briefly shows what he intends to prove. By these words a great and wonderful King is proposed.

The reason is what follows: “For your magnificence is exalted above the heavens. Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and avenger.” [Col. 0742D] By these words the reason is given why this wonderful King is proclaimed as Lord and ruler not in one region of the earth but throughout the whole earth.

The confirmation of the reason is what follows: “For I shall behold your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and stars which you founded.” By these words the reason is confirmed, because what reason has persuaded us to believe—namely, that Christ has been exalted above the heavens of heavens—is also proved by sight, if one considers the beauty of the heavens, that is, the apostles; of the moon, that is, the Church; and of the stars, that is, the lesser saints. After Christ’s exaltation above the heavens, these began to shine through the fire and light of the Holy Spirit sent by him for the illumination of the spiritual heavens, moon, and stars. [Col. 0743A]

The splendid embellishment of the entire discourse, however, lies in the words: “What is man, that you are mindful of him? Or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour; and you set him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and besides these the beasts of the field, birds of heaven, and fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea.” In these verses he notably ennobled and enriched the subject by the abundant adornment of piety, wondering how God had so greatly sought out the human being whom the devil’s envy had cast down so far from eternity.

[Col. 0743B] Finally, the last part of the argument, which is called the conclusion or summary and in which there is also a return to the beginning, is added as follows: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth.” The prophetic spirit, a skilled orator, says as it were: What has been shown true at the beginning of the argument by the reason, confirmation of the reason, and embellishment—returning therefore to the proposition, I make such a summary or conclusion that no sophistical deception of any heretic can weaken it, because repetition is confirmation.

Now let us return to the continuous exposition of the entire psalm. The Prophet begins, therefore, with praise, saying:

**VERSE 2.** Lord of all things by power, our Lord [Col. 0743C] by the worship of rational creatures: “How wonderful is your name in all the earth!” How worthy is your name of the celebration of infinite wonder and praise—the name through which, manifested in flesh, believed in the world, and received up into glory, you who were known as God only in Judaea are now named, celebrated, and renowned in all the earth (Ps. 75:2), not only in Judaea, as the Jews say, nor only in Africa, as the Donatists claim.

He then gives the reason why it is wonderful, as though saying: I call your name wonderful because your magnificence—that is, your Son, or his humanity through which you are magnified—has been exalted in place above the heavens, when he ascended on the fortieth day after the Resurrection. It has also been exalted in glory above the heavens, that is, above all powers of heaven, above all rational creatures, even to the highest co-session with God the Father. For, as the Apostle says, the man assumed into God “sat down at the right hand of the throne of Majesty” of God, equally omnipotent through the omnipotence which he received in time, as the Father is omnipotent through the omnipotence which he possessed from eternity; equally the most high God through the height and divinity which he received in time, as the Father is the most high God through the height and divinity which he has always possessed from eternity. [Col. 0743D] For God the Father had nothing which he did not give to his Son in his humanity.

Thus he himself says: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Luke 10:22), as though saying: In giving me that he might be my Father, he gave me all things which he has—not only that all created things should be subject beneath my feet, but also that all that he himself possesses by his divine nature, for example omnipotence, eternity, and other such things, I too may possess. Thus, just as he is the omnipotent and eternal God, so I too, receiving eternal divinity, am God, omnipotent and eternal—not because I have always been human, but because I have always been God, by that divinity through which I am not only before Abraham, but also before Adam. Christ did not say, “Before Abraham I was,” because it is not proper to divinity to have been, but to be. Nor did he say, “Before Abraham a part of my essence was.”

[Note: [Col. 0743D] The opinion of Hugh of Saint-Victor.]

For the Word is not a part of Christ; rather, Christ himself is the Word, wholly Word just as wholly God: not one half of Christ Word and the other half human, but the whole Christ Word and the whole Christ human, because the same one is God and human. Do you understand what I am saying? If you do not understand, only believe. It can be believed if it cannot be understood. Yet it is true that Christ, the same one, was God and human; nor was the Word a third part, nor was the whole something composed from flesh, soul, and Word as though from parts, because the whole itself was Word. [Col. 0744B] For divinity was not a part, such that the whole would be greater than it; nor was there a part in it, such that something in it would be less than it. In humanity alone we find parts, and the whole consists of parts. For a human being is a certain whole consisting of two parts, soul and body. God assumed this whole; to this whole he gave the whole divinity; and of this whole the whole divinity is proclaimed, so that the whole human being is properly called God.

Hence blessed Augustine says in Book Seven of *On the Trinity*: “Christ in the form of God is equal to the Father; in the form of a servant he is mediator of God and human beings. But because the form of God received the form of a servant, each is called both God and human: each God because of the God who received, and each human because of the human who was received. For by that assumption neither of them was changed into the other: divinity was not changed into a creature, so as to cease to be divinity; nor was creature changed into divinity, so as to cease to be creature.”

[Col. 0744D] Ambrose, moreover, in the book he wrote *On the Trinity*, says: “Therefore we say that he was made human, and that this must be referred to his humanity.” Finally, elsewhere we have: “He who was made to him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:3). Certainly, according to the flesh, he was made from David’s seed. But God was born from God before the ages. Yet “was made” is not always referred to creation. For it is written: “Lord, you have become a refuge to us” (Ps. 89:1). And a little later: “Therefore, if ‘was made’ is frequently referred to something relational, not to nature, then ‘created’ also is not always referred to creaturehood. Hence we understand that what is written concerning the Lord’s Incarnation—‘The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works’—signifies that the Lord Jesus was created from a virgin for the redemption of the Father’s works.”

Likewise in the same work: “Paul,” he says, “forbids me to serve a creature and admonishes me to serve Christ. Therefore Christ is not a creature. ‘Paul,’ he says, ‘a servant of Jesus Christ’ (Rom. 1:1). And he is a good servant who recognizes his Lord; he himself forbids us to serve a creature. How then would he himself serve Christ if he considered Christ a creature? I see therefore how he affirms Christ to have been both made and created in a certain respect, yet denies that he is a creature.” In the same book he likewise testifies that Christ is not an adoptive but a natural Son, saying: “We are called children through adoption; he through the truth of nature. How, then, is he from nothing, who made all things from nothing?” [Col. 0745B]

Thus we must shape the tracks of faith according to the testimonies of Scripture, so that we may join to right belief the purity of sincere confession, and in Christ believe in our hearts and confess with our mouths not only the uncreated divine nature but also the created human nature, exalted above the heavens and the powers of heaven—no longer to be counted among creatures, but to be worshipped above all creatures with the same worship with which God the Father is worshipped. For in the holy Synod of Ephesus we read, under anathema, a prohibition against anyone calling Christ’s humanity “co-worshipped” with the Word of God. The holy Fathers at that same synod proclaim it to be worshipped with a single worship, so that the human being is not distinguished from the Word, but one Emmanuel, God blessed above all, existing from two and in two natures, is worshipped.

His magnificence is exalted above the heavens, that is, above the Scriptures, because the exaltation of humanity into the highest glory of supreme Divinity surpasses the utterances of every language and Scripture. Yet praise of this magnificence is perfected from the mouths of infants and nursing children, when we confess what we believe but cannot utter it, because it is ineffable. Hence follows:

**VERSE 3. “Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise.”** By “nursing children” he means not those young in age, but those simple in disposition, as Peter says: “Like newly born infants” [Col. 0745D] (1 Pet. 2:2). To them the Apostle gave the milk of simple teaching, not solid food. From these the Lord does not merely make but perfects praise, because the human race would not be cared for unless, in the Churches, the least were nourished together with the perfect. They were prefigured by the Hebrew children who praised the Lord as he came to his Passion. Accordingly, the Lord there employs this example, saying: “Have you never read: ‘Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?” (Matt. 21:16.)

The apostles too are called infants, because “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1 Cor. 1:27). Hence this praise is more perfect, because “flesh and blood did not reveal” it, “but the Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:17): divine grace, not human wisdom, kindled them for it, for the destruction of the enemies of grace, heretics and philosophers. Therefore, after saying, “Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise,” he adds, “because of your enemies”—understood: enemies to be destroyed. Hence he adds:

“To destroy the enemy and avenger.” Philosophers are enemies of Christ’s cross; from them God concealed what he revealed to little ones. [Col. 0746A] This enemy is destroyed when any saint glories more truly in the cross of our Lord Jesus than any philosopher could ever glory in this world’s wisdom. For how could anyone glory in that wisdom which God has made and shown to be foolish? Or how ought one not to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to the saints and they are crucified to the world?

He calls the heretic an “avenger,” or defender, who precisely in being avenger and defender is also an enemy. For he attacks the faith which he appears to defend. Similarly, the philosopher, though called a lover and defender of wisdom, is rather an enemy, because, abandoning the Son of God, who is power and wisdom, he urges that the elements be worshipped. The Jew too is an enemy of truth, and an avenger of his own law and defender of ancestral traditions. He destroys some such people by breaking them, because they refuse to bend; others he destroys by bending them, because they themselves yield to the one who bends them—as Saul, enemy and avenger, who, touched by the divine hand, said: “Lord, what do you wish me to do?” (Acts 9:6.)

But Judas, Christ’s enemy and the avenger of the loss which he seemed to think he had suffered in the pouring of the precious ointment over Jesus’ head, because he refused to bend, was broken: “he burst open in the middle, and all his entrails were poured out” (Acts 1:18). [Col. 0746C] Likewise Arius, the heresiarch, because he refused to bend by yielding to catholic faith and truth, was broken and all his entrails were poured out.

What is praised by these words in this demonstrative discourse but Christ, king of unconquerable dominion and ever-glorious victor over every enemy of truth and defender of his own error? Since he alone is able to destroy every enemy and defender, he alone is worthy of dominion, worthy to be crowned with glory and honour, and to be set over the works of the Father’s hands. Indeed, now crowned with glory and honour and set over all things, he is worthy to be acknowledged as the glorious King and to be devoutly served by every nation, tribe, people, and language—for to serve him is to reign. This is the Son of Man whom Daniel saw in the clouds of heaven, because he is present in the holy angels and human beings, who are understood by the clouds. “And there was given to him,” he says, “a kingdom and honour, and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him” (Dan. 7:14). It follows:

**VERSE 4. “For I shall behold your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and stars which you founded.”** We have heard this orator’s demonstrative proposition, where it was said: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” We have also heard the reason for the proposition, where it was said: “For your magnificence is exalted [Col. 0747A] above the heavens. Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and avenger.” Now let us hear the confirmation of the reason, when it says: “For I shall behold your heavens.”

That is as if it said: Truly your magnificence has been exalted above the heavens, because unless you, the sun of righteousness, the brightness of the Father’s glory—the sun who knew your setting—had, after the setting of your death, been raised anew through the Resurrection, neither would the moon have stood in its order nor the stars have overcome the night of ignorance. But now, because the sun has been exalted through the Resurrection and Ascension and the moon has stood in its order, I shall behold heavens illuminated by your splendour; I shall behold prophets formerly obscure but now bright; I shall behold apostles formerly saddened by your death but afterwards “rejoicing” “before the council because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41).

From this I have certainty that your magnificence has been exalted above the heavens: “For I shall behold your heavens,” that is, the apostles, “the works of your fingers.” For your Spirit, understood through finger or fingers, himself strengthened and adorned the heavens, coming upon them in tongues of fire. Through those heavens, as your grace worked, the moon—that is, the Church—was founded together with stars differing in brightness, that is, with certain elect persons possessing diverse gifts of graces. [Col. 0747B]

Alternatively: Truly, Lord our God, you have perfected praise. For you perfected it through the Scriptures. And truly through the Scriptures, because you so illuminated them that I shall “behold,” that is, understand clearly by contemplation, the heavens, that is, the Scriptures themselves from which praise begins when they are pronounced not unfolded but wrapped up. But that praise is perfected when they are unfolded through expositions and bent down to the capacity of infants.

Or: Truly you will destroy enemies, because, beginning from the humility of historical faith—that is, that you were born, suffered, died, and were buried—being confirmed in faith by these and other similar weak things, I shall behold the heavens. That is, advanced to the strength of lofty understanding, as though enlightened by mud made from the spittle of the Lord’s mouth, I shall behold that the heavens declaring your glory are the works of your fingers. By “finger” the Holy Spirit is understood, by whom the law was written (Exod. 8:19). [Col. 0747D] But he says “fingers” in the plural to indicate the operation of the Trinity, as elsewhere it is said: “He measured the mass of the earth with three fingers” (Isa. 40:12); or because of the many and diverse graces which the same Spirit distributes to each as he wills (1 Cor. 10:12).

Alternatively. Truly I said, “Out of the mouths of infants,” because in the Spirit I shall behold your heavens, that is, the apostles: they know nothing from human ingenuity, but whatever they are, they are from grace. Hence all the powers of such heavens are works of your fingers. I shall also behold the moon, namely the universal Church, why it is understood through the moon being explained in Psalm 10. I shall also behold the stars, that is, individual Churches distinguished by places and offices, which you—not they—founded. [Col. 0748A] For neither Peter nor the other apostles founded the Churches, but you, who said: “Upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. 16:18). Peter, or another minister of grace, as a wise architect serves you, the wise human being, the God-human, who builds a house, digs deeply, and lays foundations upon the rock; but he serves you only from what is yours. Therefore you alone founded the Churches, because stability and the authority of the foundation rest in you alone. Hence your apostle Paul, who, laying foundations as a wise architect, laboured more than all, yet thinking humbly of himself says: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

**VERSE 5. “What is man, that you are mindful of him?”** This is said as embellishment, in wonder, so that the Lord’s name may clearly appear truly wonderful—as it is said both in the first proposition of this psalm and in its final summary. It is as though it said: Truly, Lord, your name is wonderful in all the earth, because although your magnificence is exalted above the heavens, yet your mercy looks upon the good and the evil; indeed, it looks upon and seeks the evil in order to make them good. You are mindful of man so as to make from man a son of man, and from the old person a new one; and this is wonderful.

For what is man, that you are mindful of him? What worth does man possess in himself, that you, Lord our God, should be mindful of him? Or what is the son of man, that you visit him? Man is rottenness, and the son of man a worm. Man is mud, and the son of man an earthen vessel. Yet you are mindful of man and visit the son of man. Truly this is wonderful.

He does not say, “What is man and the son of man?” but, “What is man, or the son of man?” By this disjunction a difference between man and son of man is signified. For every son of man is a human being, but not every human being is a son of man. Adam was human, but not a son of man. [Col. 0748C]

Therefore, by the name “man” is signified whoever bears the image of the earthly one; from him, through the travail of penitential sorrow, the new person is born who bears the image of the heavenly one. “The first man is earthly, from the earth; the second man is heavenly, from heaven. As is the earthly one, such also are the earthly ones” (1 Cor. 15:47 and following). Thus the Apostle exhorts us that, as we have borne the image of the earthly one, we should “also bear the image of the heavenly one” (ibid., 49). For we bore the image of the earthly one, made like him in disobedience through disobedience; therefore let us bear the image of the heavenly one, made like him in obedience through obedience.

Whoever bears the image of the old person is in this psalm called “man”; but whoever bears the image of the heavenly one is here called “son of man.” Him you, Lord our God, visit as one of your household and regard as near. For you are mindful of the old person as though he were far away, while he remains in this life, before he descends into hell, where are “the wounded sleeping in the graves, whom you remember no more” (Ps. 87:6), because “your wonders shall not be known in darkness, nor your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness” (ibid., 13).

[Col. 0749A] Yet here you are mindful of man by conferring temporal things. For “you shall save human beings and beasts, O Lord, according as you have multiplied your mercy” (Ps. 35:7–8). You save the old person with that salvation by which you also save beasts; but the new person, who is called son of man, you behold closely and visit when inwardly you illumine his face with the light of your countenance.

Therefore when it says, “What is man?” it must be read in a lowering sense, as though it said: How worthless a thing is man! And therefore it is wonderful that you, Lord our God, are mindful of him. But when it says, “What is the son of man?” it must be read in an elevating sense, as though it said: How precious a thing is the son of man! This is evident from the fact that you, Lord our God, visit him. The son of man was visited in the principal visitation when “the Word was made flesh” (John 1:14), when God was made human. Of him, because of the weakness of the flesh, it is rightly said:

### Verse 6

You made him a little lower than the angels. Man indeed—full of sin and misery, the old man—you greatly lowered beneath the angels, who are free from sin and misery. But this new man, who committed no sin, you made a little lower: for although by the power of righteousness he is above the angels, yet because of the weakness of mortality, from which angels are exempt, he was lower than the angels for a little while—that is, for a short time, namely until death. But after the triumph of death, having through his death destroyed him who held the dominion of death, you crowned him with the glory of the Resurrection and the honour of the Ascension [Col. 0749C]; and with such a glorification of the flesh that the body of weakness which was in him is now a body of glory, like the body of the sun. Hence, having received the Redeemer in a body of weakness, we await that same “Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humility, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:21).—“Then the righteous shall shine like the sun” (Matt. 13:3): the bodies of the saints too shall shine like Christ’s solar body, which illuminates all things by its radiance.

For just as the fullness of ethereal fire rules in such a manner in the solar body that the whole world derives heat and brightness from it, so the whole fullness of the Godhead, dwelling bodily in Christ’s body [Col. 0749D], illumines the knowledge of truth and sets heaven and earth—that is, the heavenly and earthly Church—aflame with love of virtue. Therefore the Son of Man was crowned with glory and honour through the glorification of the Resurrection and Ascension. For that body which was in Christ lower when he was made a little lower than the angels ascended to such a height of eternal Godhead and glory that it is rightly said: “The Son of Man is crowned with the glory and honour of the Godhead.”

For a crown is so called when a golden circle is turned back into itself, so that the sheet of gold, bent back upon itself, has no end; because the end joined to the beginning imitates infinity through the unbroken equality of its roundness. Similarly—and more than similarly—because Christ’s human substance [Col. 0750A] has been raised up to the highest glory of the Godhead, the Godhead not consuming the humanity so that it fails, but bringing it to completion in the end of perfection, so that he is perfect man and likewise perfect God, as it were of rounded and unending glory. Indeed, the Son of Man is said to be crowned with glory and honour when the assumed man is made identical in glory and honour with the Godhead that assumes him. Hence, although Christ truly was made of David’s seed according to the flesh, he is no longer to be counted among the divine works, but is to be adored above all the works of the Father’s hands. For it follows:

### Verse 7

And you set him over the works of your hands, even over the highest choirs of angels, beneath whom you made him, and over all things [Col. 0750B] that are under you. And when he says “all things,” he leaves nothing unsubdued.

### Verse 8

“You subjected all things,” he says, “under his feet.” By the feet Christ’s humanity is understood, just as by his head his divinity. Therefore all things are subjected not only to his head but also to his feet. Hence that same man, now crowned with the glory of the Resurrection, says: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18), because all things in heaven and on earth are subjected to him. What things? Both good and evil things, namely.

“All sheep and oxen, and moreover the cattle of the field.” By setting low things after leaving the higher, he directs us to a mystical meaning. By sheep he understands the innocent; by oxen, prelates, who plough earthly persons with the word of God so that they may bear fruit. Sheep also signify angels [Col. 0750C], because it is written that, leaving the ninety-nine, which are angels, he came to seek the hundredth sheep, that is, man (Luke 15:4). The sense is: you have subjected sheep—that is, heavenly angels, at leisure in heaven—and oxen—that is, evangelists labouring on earth; and moreover the cattle of the field: that is, you subjected to him not only the good but also the evil, who are mixed among the good in the winepresses, as grape pomace with wine and olive lees with oil. For they are cattle of the field, because they live in the flesh, always desiring to satisfy the belly and fleshly lust upon the broad and spacious way which leads to the fields of earthly desires, while avoiding the steep and narrow way that leads to the pastures of righteousness, which are like the mountains of God. Thus Abel too is killed in the field [Col. 0750D] (Gen. 4:8). These are they who say: “I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come” (Luke 14:20).

You also subjected beneath the feet of that same Son of Man (Verse 9) “the birds of heaven,” that is, the proud, who, in order to raise themselves above others in this world, hunger after earthly acquisitions. Once they have acquired them, they think they can fly to heaven, as it were on wings; and, judging other people poor and inglorious in comparison with themselves, they disdain them as though far beneath them. These are they who say: “I have bought an estate” (Luke 14:18), and therefore I cannot come.

You also subjected “the fish of the sea,” that is, the curious, who travel the paths of the sea, seeking temporal things in the deep of this world—things which vanish like paths across the sea. These are inquisitive investigators of other people’s lives [Col. 0751A] and neglectful correctors of their own lives. Or they travel the paths of the sea in that they read the books of poets or secular philosophers, travelling in them as in sea-paths, where the snares and nets of errors can scarcely be avoided. Yet “the net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures” (Prov. 1:17), because the saints do not wander like fish in the paths of the sea, in the shadowy ways of secular learning. Rather, delighted with the beauty of heavenly knowledge, they fly high in the clear heaven; foreseeing from afar the snares of errors, they fly over them in contemplation. Or, if they are caught in them briefly, they tear them apart with the beak of repentance—as Peter, entangled in his threefold denial, did when he wept in bitter repentance, or when, by thrice repeating his confession of love, he expiated his threefold denial [Col. 0751B], as though with a sharp beak he shattered the snares by which he was held.

Hence repentant saints, freed by forgiveness, say: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters. The snare has been broken, and we have been delivered” (Ps. 124:7). But fish entangled in snares or nets, as though seized by deep blindness, become more and more entangled while always striving to plunge themselves into greater depths. Such people do not come to the light of confession, because “everyone who does evil hates the light, so that his works may not be reproved” (John 3:20). These are they who say: “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to test them” (Luke 14:19). In these three faults—pleasure, pride, and curiosity—are contained all the vices enumerated by the apostle John: namely, the lust of the flesh, worldly ambition, which is “pride,” and “the lust of the eyes” (1 John 2:16), through which curiosity has its greatest force.

Another interpretation. The cattle of the field are carnal and bestial, or animal, people, in whom this alone is blamed: that they do not receive the things of the Spirit of God. These things are received in two ways: by faith, through which spiritual things are believed; and by understanding, through which the same things are perceived—not indeed perfectly, but through a mirror and in an enigma. The “natural man does not receive” these spiritual things [Col. 0752A], because he does not relish “the things that are above” (1 Cor. 2:14).

But the birds of heaven are the spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places—that is, situated in the air, which is called heaven. For their guilt is not satisfied by their failing to receive or understand the things of the Spirit of God. They pursue, both directly and through evil people, the things of the Spirit of God. Therefore the people themselves who associate with demons by reason of diabolical wickedness and pride are also called birds of heaven, especially if they not only fail to love spiritual things but persecute them. But those who oppose the good not by open persecution but by secretly laying snares, moving in silence like fish, are not inappropriately called fish of the sea.

Nevertheless, in this great sea, although there are “creeping things without number” (Ps. 104:25) [Col. 0752B], all things are subjected to the sole dominion of him of whom it is said both in the opening proposition of this psalm and in its final conclusion or summary:

### Verse 10

O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!

At the end of this demonstrative discourse, by its conclusion or summary, he returns to the beginning, thereby indicating that good action—from which the word “Psalm” is derived—must be referred back to him from whom it proceeds, who is “Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1:8), the initiator and finisher of every good work.

Glory to the Father, who subjected all things to the Son of Man. Glory to the Son himself, who, though he was the Son of God, deigned [Col. 0752C] to become the Son of Man, deigned to be made lower than the angels, and is now crowned with glory and honour as priest and king: that he, the priest himself, wearing the mitre marked by the line of humanity, and he, the King himself, adorned with the golden crown of divinity, may sanctify and govern us as becomes such a priest and king. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is understood through the fingers, of which it was said in this psalm: “I shall behold the heavens, the works of your fingers.” Glory to the one and triune God, to whom both at the beginning and at the end of the psalm it is said: O Lord, our God, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!

## Psalm IX

[Col. 0751]

[Col. 0751D] “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole heart.” This psalm bears the following title (Verse 1):

### Unto the End, for the Hidden Things of the Son: A Psalm of David

The sense is: this psalm is assigned to David—that is, to the strong of hand, the beloved, and the perfect Church—pressing toward the end, that is, toward Christ, in order to be conformed to him. “For the hidden things of the Son,” that is, for consideration of the hidden judgments that belong to the Son, as it is written: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), who is called “the Son” by antonomasia, as he himself testifies:

“If the Son sets you free, you shall truly be free” (John [Col. 0752D] 8:36).

The Prophet’s purpose in this psalm is to introduce the perfect Church giving thanks to God in every manner for hidden judgments, and through this to instruct its lesser members that nothing in the world is to be believed to occur by random chance, but that all things happen by God’s righteous judgment. Although that divine judgment may sometimes be hidden, it can never be unjust. For example, at Christ’s first coming some thought him merely a man, whereas few—that is, the elect—understood him to be both God and man. Thus even now some Christians do not understand that God is man, or that man is God. This happened and happens by God’s hidden judgment: namely, that then it was disclosed to some and concealed from others, and that now it is disclosed to some and concealed from others: namely, “that the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), that Man is God.

Likewise, concerning the second coming, some unsound-minded people doubt, while the faithful await it as certain; and this too happens by the righteous judgment of God—righteous, I say, but hidden—by which some are chosen and others left behind, according to the saying: “Two shall be in a field: one shall be taken and the other left. Two shall be at the mill: one shall be taken and the other left” (Matt. 24:40–41). “Two shall be in one bed: one shall be taken and the other left” (Luke 17:34).

And indeed, even in this life it can sometimes be known through some indication who are to be taken and who left [Col. 0753B] in the divine judgment, by which the complete separation of good and evil will take place. Yet all alike are ignorant on what day or at what hour that judgment itself will occur, because it is not ours “to know the times or seasons which the Father has put in his own power” (Acts 1:7). This time is so hidden among the other hidden things of the Son that the Son himself says that he does not know at what hour he will come (Mark 13:32).

This is not because he is ignorant of it in himself, he to whom Peter most faithfully says: “Lord, you know all things; you know all things” (Acts 1:24); but because, when the apostles asked about that day, the Son was found as one who did not know. For just as God is said to know for us when he causes us to know—for example, when he says to Abraham, “Now [Col. 0753C] I know that you fear the Lord” (Gen. 22:12), meaning: what has always been known to me, I have now caused you to know—so the Son of God is said for us not to know what he causes us not to know. This is not because he himself is ignorant of anything, since all things are naked and open to his eyes, since he is Wisdom itself, reaching “from end to end mightily, and ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1).

Therefore, if the Son of God, Wisdom, orders all things, he also orders the hidden times of the last day; and he could not order them if he did not know them. Yet he does not know them for us, and neither do the angels, because he reveals to neither people nor angels the hour at which he will come, so that he may always be awaited as near. Even if angels know that hour for themselves, they do not know it for us, because they do not show it to us; for they preserve the hidden things of the Son as servants or as friends who share his secrets [Col. 0753D].

Why some are saved and some rejected, though all come from the same parent, happens by the hidden judgment of God, which is likewise unknown to all. Likewise, the fact that in the present world the evil are exalted and the good oppressed occurs by God’s hidden and righteous judgment: hidden indeed to the evil, but to a great extent manifest to the good. Further, that the son of perdition will, near the end of the world, raise himself so greatly above the Church and afflict it with such severity of persecutions will occur by God’s hidden and righteous judgment. In all these matters the Gentiles, and those who understand wrongly, err and blaspheme God; but the perfect Church not only does not blaspheme God, but praises him attentively with all its strength in everything, saying:

### Verse 2

[Col. 0754A] I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole heart; I will recount all your wonders.

Thus, after the two preceding psalms, which together recapitulate the faith of the Passion and Resurrection necessary for eternal salvation, this psalm fittingly follows. In it the holy Church, confessing the hidden judgments of that same Son, marvels in accordance with the Apostle’s meaning when he says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). For he said this concerning the blindness that happened in part to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in. This blindness, of course, immediately occurred by a hidden judgment when Christ, according to the preceding psalm, was crowned with glory and honour.

The order is good. For since the preceding psalm gave a confirmatory demonstration and rational commendation of the glory and honour of Christ crowned as king and priest, this psalm follows with, alongside praise of that same Christ, a refutation of Antichrist by a demonstration of his impiety and dishonour. Therefore Antichrist himself, along with his members, is to be deprived of glory and honour for his impiety and dishonour, just as Christ, for his piety and honour, is now crowned in himself with glory and honour, and in his members is partly crowned and partly still to be honoured and crowned. Hence, just as on the feast-day of each martyr we repeat in praise of Christ, “You crowned him with glory and honour” (Ps. 8:6), so, at the exaltation of every most wicked person, when “the sinner is praised in the desires [Col. 0754C] of his soul, and the wicked is blessed” (Ps. 10:3), we fittingly say in refutation of Antichrist: “Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail.” Likewise: “Break the arm of the sinner and the evil man,” and so forth (Ps. 10:15). These words are inserted in this psalm for the refutation of Antichrist, as will become clear in the continuous exposition of the psalm, which is divided as follows.

First, the Prophet sings joyfully because the worship of the devil is destroyed by Christ’s coming, and Christ himself reigns, judges, and helps. Second, he exhorts the faithful to sing, setting forth the benefits of the present time and of the future, where he says: “Sing to the Lord, who dwells in Zion,” and so forth. Third, he introduces Antichrist, invoking Christ’s help against him, where he says: “Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail,” and so forth.

[Col. 0754D] He therefore says: O Lord, some, seeing good and evil people afflicted alike and not knowing why this happens, speak against you, thinking that what occurs under divine governance happens through the recklessness of chance. But I, who perceive the hidden reasons for which you do this justly, will give thanks to you—that is, I will praise you—with my whole heart. Others praise with part of their heart: they approve some works of the Lord and blaspheme others. But I will give thanks with my whole heart, because I know that all things are both ordered and done rightly. I shall also tell others that not our works but all your works are wonderful, never blameworthy.

Some marvel at outward deeds, such as Lazarus raised in body, but do not marvel at Paul raised in mind, which is more wonderful. They marvel at some things, but not all. But I shall declare all things, visible and invisible alike [Col. 0755A], and whatever I recount I shall recount as wonderful. And while recounting these things to others, [the syntax is elliptical:] within myself:

### Verse 3

I will rejoice, not in human praise and not in earthly gain, but in you—that is, in the hidden things of the Son—where we are marked by the light of your countenance (Ps. 4:7). And desiring that this joy may always increase, I will exult.

Another interpretation: I will rejoice in mind, and exult in bodily gladness. Or, I will rejoice in soul, according to the saying, “My soul magnifies the Lord” (Luke 1:47); and I will exult in spirit, so that I can confidently say: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has exulted in God my Saviour” (ibid.). And because this joy and exultation, reigning inwardly in the soul, enlivening the five [Col. 0755B] senses, and examining good and evil thoughts in the spirit, ought also to appear outwardly for the edification of neighbours, so that, seeing “our good works,” they may “glorify our Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16)—“not to us, O Lord, not to us, but glory to your name, O Lord” (Ps. 113:1)—ascribing to it every good work, “I will sing to your name, O Most High.”

I will not only rejoice and exult inwardly, but I shall sing outwardly in action, giving glory to your name, which alone is known in this life. O Most High, who by reason of your supreme loftiness are far removed from mortal understanding, as you yourself say to Moses: “No man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20). Therefore I will give thanks, rejoicing and exulting, not in knowledge of your substance but in consideration of your works, most delighted especially in this: that, battling against the devil on our behalf, you appear victorious.

### Verse 4

When my enemy is turned backward. For he used to go before, when almost the whole world followed him. But now he has not indeed been taken away, but has been cast out and thrust behind your back, like another Pharaoh pursuing and persecuting the true Hebrews as they withdraw from him. Or he has been turned backward in this sense: that he, the spiritual Pharaoh, with all his army, who once pursued, now flees, saying: “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them” (Exod. 14:25).

But the righteous, praising your victorious hand in the hidden things of the Son [Col. 0755D], have a secure refuge, because between them and the enemy Pharaoh, or his army, lies the Red Sea: namely, the mystery of Christ’s blood, full of hidden powers. Through these powers all enemies shall be weakened and perish from before your face. How will they be weakened? Because the gates of hell shall not prevail against the Church.

They may indeed seem for a time to grow strong, just as the voices of those who cried, “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke 23:21), grew strong. Yet they shall not prevail, just as those men did not prevail, because they did not accomplish what they wished. For by crucifying Christ they did not cast him down as they intended, but rather exalted him, as Christ himself foretold when he said: “When you have exalted the Son of Man, then you shall know [Col. 0756A] that I am” (Matt. 8:28). Likewise: “As the serpent was lifted up in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14).—“And I,” he says, “if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

Therefore, just as they were then weakened when, as it were, “the wounds they inflicted became the arrows of children” (Ps. 64:9), being unable to extinguish Christ, the eternal sun—who, though through their wounds he descended to the setting of death, nevertheless by his own power returned to the east through the triumph of the Resurrection, for he ascended above the heavens of heavens toward the east (Ps. 68:34)—so now too the ungodly shall be weakened. For when they wish to cast down the righteous and trample the Church of God, they themselves are more deeply cast down and will be trampled underfoot: now in particular instances, but universally at the future judgment.

And they shall perish, either because the ungodly will no longer be ungodly after conversion—as Saul perished when he began to be Paul; as those perished who in rage shed Christ’s blood and afterward drank that same blood for remission of sins by believing in him. Or “they shall perish” as Judas “perished, to go to his own place” (Acts 1:18). They shall perish from before your face, that is, from your memory, because you will remember none of their iniquities. Or, “as wax melts from before the fire” (Ezek. 18:22), so “they shall perish from before your face” (Ps. 68:3), because you, our God, “are a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24). Thus perished he who said: “But now it is no longer I who live” (Gal. 2:20). Therefore demons and evil people shall be weakened and perish from before your face:

### Verse 5

Because you have executed my judgment and my cause. For I, a guilty man, seduced by the devil through the sin of disobedience and having offended God, needed two things: judgment against the devil my seducer, and propitiation with God my Creator. And you, Christ Jesus, mediator between God and men, executed my judgment against the devil, conquering him as he had conquered me, deceiving him with the hook of divinity as he had deceived me, and rendering him the punishment which he deserved by seducing me. And you, the same propitiator, pleaded my cause with the Father, interceding for me and reconciling me through the obedience which you rendered to him on my behalf: thus you executed my cause [Col. 0756D].

Concerning judgment you said: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John 12:31). For by just judgment he had to be cast out who had cast man out of paradise into the miseries of this world, so that the measure by which he had measured should be measured to him in return (Matt. 7:2). But this could not happen by just judgment unless, as he had conquered man, so he was conquered by man. Yet who could conquer him unless he were God? Man had fallen in the conflict while not yet mortal; how could he now stand and triumph, having become mortal and frail? Likewise, the angel had fallen when no one tempted him; how could he now stand in the fiercest conflict? Man alone ought to conquer, but God alone could conquer the devil, and by a just exchange defeat that victor in turn, so that he might justly be cast out.

For although he did not enter justly but crept, by fraud, like a serpent into dominion over the human race, nevertheless, because man suffered justly on account of voluntary consent, it was necessary for his unjust dominion to become the subject of just judgment: he was not to be cast out unless he was first conquered by man. Therefore you, Christ, executed my judgment, overcoming him on my behalf and in my place: first by conquering his temptations in the wilderness, then by destroying through your death him who held the dominion of death.

You also executed my cause before your Father by rendering on my behalf such great humility and obedience that he ought to forgive my pride and disobedience [Col. 0757B], having so great a reason to forgive it that there was not as great a reason for anger. For although it is true that “as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many are made righteous” (Rom. 5:19), nevertheless “the gift is not like the trespass” (ibid., v. 15). The trespass cast human nature down from paradise; but the gift raised it in Christ above the heavens and the powers of heaven.

In that exaltation, O Christ, you sat at the right hand of the Father and sit upon the throne. Though you were judged unjustly, you judge righteousness and equity: now in particular instances, but universally in your final judgment, when all the ungodly shall perish from before your face, because you executed my judgment and my cause.

[Col. 0757C] This may also be referred to the person of the Father as follows: Truly, O Father, your enemies shall perish, because you made my judgment—that is, the judgment by which Christ was judged—mine, that is, beneficial to me. Thus sailors call a wind useful to them “their own.” And you made the cause for which he was condemned mine, that is, beneficial to me. For the fact that he, speaking truth, was condemned for truth as though a blasphemer because he called himself the Son of God was exceedingly beneficial to me, condemned for the lie persuaded upon the first-formed man by the serpent.

From this such great benefit followed that you sat upon the throne—that is, upon the soul of Christ—because you, God, were in Christ reconciling the world to yourself, you who judge righteousness, or, as another translation has it, judge equity.

Now equity is that, as through one offence all human beings came into condemnation, so through one righteousness all may come into justification, except those who reject the remedy prepared and offered to all human beings. Therefore there should be no anxiety that grace may be lacking to anyone who desires salvation; rather, the Apostle—and Christ in the Apostle—warns that no one should be lacking to the grace of God. And he to whom it is now said, “you who declare equity,” is addressed as though it were said: You do not approve the injustice by which anyone would be saved against the obstinate will of his own impiety. For though you sometimes make a willing person out of one unwilling, nevertheless, you who judge righteousness and equity will at last destroy by your rebuke the ungodly person who is voluntarily obstinate in wickedness and always unworthy of your salvation [Col. 0758A], just as those who were stubborn and obstinate in their wickedness have often been destroyed.

For after you sat upon the throne, raised up to the dwelling granted by the eternal Father, you sent the Holy Spirit from heaven; and by that same Spirit, reproving the world through the apostles, you reproved it “concerning sin and righteousness and judgment” (John 16:8).

### Verse 6

You rebuked the nations, and the ungodly man perished. For example: when the nations were rebuked through the apostles and exorcists, the ungodly devil perished from heaven—that is, he was driven out of the heavenly worship rendered to him in idols—and beyond the bounds of the nations believing in you, Christ. When you taught your apostles concerning perfection, you forbade them to be anxious about earthly things for tomorrow, adding: “For all these things the Gentiles seek” (Matt. 6:32). Therefore, those who have undertaken discipleship, or the discipline, of possessing nothing as their own, if they seek those things which the Gentiles also seek, are certainly to be counted among the nations or Gentiles.

You rebuked such nations in Ananias and Sapphira through the apostle Peter, and ungodly Ananias perished with his wife, who agreed with him and knew of his fraud (Acts 5). Thus every ungodly person rebuked by the Holy Spirit shall perish for a similar fraud concerning ecclesiastical property, or also for apostasy after undertaking some holy purpose and afterwards abandoning it.

Another interpretation. You rebuked the nations through the apostles and other heralds of truth, and the ungodly man perished because, with ungodliness destroyed, he became godly. He perished so completely that you blotted out their name—namely, the name of the ungodly—for ever. For whereas they were formerly called vessels of wrath, now, with that name blotted out, they are called vessels of mercy—not for an hour but for eternity, that which is eternal “for age upon age.” For “age of age” is a description of eternity. Other books have “for an age, and for an age of age.”

By “age,” therefore, is understood the entire expanse of times flowing onward and recurring as if in a certain circle. For through the alternation of times it does not wholly cease, but passes in such a way as to return; hence, through the sameness of its own recurrence, it somehow imitates eternity. Yet because of its mutability it departs from eternity. “Age of age” is eternity itself, called the age of age because it will follow after this present age [Col. 0758D]. In this age of age every power of the devil shall perish. For the swords of that

### Verse 7

enemy have failed unto the end—that is, shattered against Christ. For just as swords are destroyed when dashed against solid rock, so the swords—that is, all the engines of impiety and rebellion—have failed, dashed against the end, that is, against Christ. Or they have failed near the end of the present and pilgrim Church: that is, beyond doubt all enemies—the swords of the persecuting Antichrist—shall fail, when Christ, who is the infinite End, destroys him by the brightness of his coming.

And you destroyed their cities. This has more than once happened literally. For Babylon, because it held God’s people captive and afflicted them, was destroyed when the Persians and Medes captured it. Earlier, Gomorrah and Sodom and the other neighbouring cities were destroyed because they served uncleanness and wickedness. And the city of Jerusalem was more than once destroyed for transgression of the divine law: formerly by Nebuzaradan, chief of the cooks (2 Kings 25), and later Antiochus Epiphanes, who destroyed much of it, defiled and profaned its temple through idolatry; and finally, because of the killing of Christ and his disciples, the Roman army destroyed it.

The city of Rome itself is seen so ruined in the secular buildings of its kings that it seems not so much a city as the ruin of a city, because, tyrannizing against the holy apostles and the Church, it sent cruel edicts throughout the bounds of its empire [Col. 0759B]. Nevertheless, by the merits of the apostles and martyrs, with whose blood that city was made purple, although it was destroyed and humbled in secular eminence, it has been set above all the cities of this world by the victorious excellence of spiritual power—not by human authority but by divine authority—as the Lord said to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16:18).

Cities are also destroyed spiritually when one stronger comes upon the armed strong man, the devil, guarding his courtyard, and destroys all his weapons. We see this occur when some person or people, formerly rebellious against God, humbly submits through obedience to the truth which they had opposed through disobedience. Then all the weapons of iniquity “are destroyed, and they shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles” (Isa. 2:4), so that weapons prepared to harm become instruments of virtues. Then members which had been weapons of iniquity become weapons of godliness. Then the strongholds of defences once raised against God fall, and the place becomes like cultivated ground that previously appeared impregnable.

“Go,” says the Lord, “into the village opposite you.” Therefore the village opposed to Christ and his disciples is destroyed when the disciples enter it: that is, when, through the proclamation of truth, a person or people rebellious against God falls [Col. 0759D], either cast down for its own salvation, like Saul, or for its own destruction, like the wicked king Saul. And many tyrants thus perished with the edicts which they made against God’s Church. Hence it follows:

Their memory perished with a sound. The sound of persecution has now perished, and the proclamation of peace has succeeded it. The memory of persecutors also perished with their sound, because, just as the sound of a voice passes swiftly and does not remain in any manner once uttered, so they too swiftly passed away with the passing sound. Or their memory perished “with a sound,” that is, with a great crash, like a huge tree falling from a height to the ground with a crashing sound. Or their memory perished before God, God forgetting that they were ungodly, as he says through the prophet: “I will remember their sins no more” (Jer. 31:34). Likewise, in the fifteenth psalm he says: “Nor will I remember their names upon my lips” (Ps. 15:4). For their memory perished with the sound of good confession: that is, by the sound through which they no longer defended their sins but accused them. Thus the ungodly perished, whether humbled or broken. But

### Verse 8

the Lord remains for ever. Therefore the ungodly raged against God in vain; he will judge them. For already in secret he prepared his throne—that is, judicial power—in the judgment in which he was judged, by the patience through which he gained heaven.

### Verse 9

And he himself, who was unjustly judged, will at last, in manifest judgment [Col. 0760B], judge the world in equity, rendering to each what their merits deserve.

What he said, he still finds himself saying: “He will judge the peoples in righteousness.” The repetition of the expression signifies the certainty and swiftness of its fulfilment; just as Pharaoh’s repeated dream, as Joseph interpreted it, signified the swiftness and certainty of fulfilment. Therefore he will judge swiftly; swiftly he will winnow his threshing-floor and separate the grains from the chaff. But because that judgment is preceded by some delay, however slight, lest in the meantime the enemy, turned back but not yet wholly crushed, should do harm:

**VERSE 10.** The Lord has become a refuge for avoiding evils. For whom? For the poor man, who loves nothing transitory. It is a great thing that the Judge himself should be a refuge and protector [Col. 0760C]. He is also a helper for doing good. When? At fitting times. How? By allowing him for a while to be in tribulations. For a person is not suitably converted away from this world unless pains are mingled with this world’s pleasures. Thus help is the more welcome in proportion as the danger is more grievous.

**VERSE 11.** And therefore, O Lord, let those who know your name hope in you—not in themselves or in the world. A name is known when he whose name it is is known. In declaring his name, however, the Lord says: “I am who I am, and He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. III, 14), that is, the unchangeable One, whose being is above all things, not passing among all things. For even angels [Col. 0760D] have passed away from the state in which they began to be; and man “flees like a shadow and never remains in the same state” (Job XIV, 2); and all things under the sun are vain and transitory. He alone, therefore, is the One who is, to whom no change can happen. Those, then, know his name who, despising mutable things, devoutly serve him alone who is. Let such persons, therefore, hope in you, O Lord, who are, and they shall not be disappointed; for even if they seem to be forsaken for an hour, you nevertheless do not forsake them utterly; nor do you forsake at the fitting time those who seek you, rather than temporal things.

**VERSE 12.** Sing psalms to the Lord who dwells in Zion. Thus far the Prophet has praised God because the enemy has been driven back, the wicked converted, and the Lord made a refuge for the poor. Now he adds what he had not yet stated specifically: the vengeance upon the persecutors [Col. 0761A], and the benefits which he presently bestows upon the good. For such things he urges the faithful to sing psalms, as though saying: He does not abandon you who seek him; therefore sing psalms to the Lord who dwells in Zion. Zion is interpreted “watching-place” and signifies the present Church, which through a mirror and in an enigma, as though from afar, beholds something of the Divinity. Jerusalem is called “vision of peace,” and signifies the future Church, which face to face will behold peace—that is, Christ, who is our peace, dissolving the enmities between God and man. From this Zion one goes to that Jerusalem, but only if the Lord dwells in this one and leads us to that one. Therefore sing psalms to the Lord who dwells in Zion: sing by doing good works, and afterwards proclaim. First [Col. 0761B] do good, and then teach well, as you read: Jesus “began to do and to teach” (Acts I, 1). For when a man’s life is despised, it remains for his preaching also to be held in contempt. Therefore first, “Sing psalms to the Lord who dwells in Zion” (Ps. LXXX, 3). Hold the joyful psaltery with the harp. Take up the psalm and give the timbrel, so that in the psalm there may be good action, and in the harp or timbrel mortification of the flesh.

And thus, prepared to preach the word of God, proclaim among the nations his earnest pursuits. Proclaim by what efforts he himself seeks the salvation of the nations who fear him in every nation; or also by what efforts he is to be sought—he who first seeks us, so that we may afterwards seek him. For the shepherd himself seeks the lost sheep, so that, restored to the fold, the sheep may thereafter seek the shepherd [Col. 0761C] and always desire to cling to him. Many excuse themselves on the ground that they have not been given the means of doing good—for example, having nothing from which to give alms, or being unable to fast because of infirmity. But no one can excuse himself from earnest effort, because every person can strive according to the strength granted him by God. Sometimes effort is most intense without a visible effect in works. Thus every merchant strives to become rich, yet not every merchant becomes rich in proportion to the greatness of his effort toward earthly gains. But if vigorous effort is directed toward divine gains, even though in this life it does not attain a visible result, provided the effort is not relaxed, it shall without doubt attain its result in [Col. 0761D] eternal life. Let us therefore strive in this life for chastity; even if we happen to be wearied by the stimulus of the flesh, let us only not lay aside our pursuit of chastity, and without doubt we shall be adorned with the crown of chastity either in this life or certainly in the life to come. Let us similarly strive after the other virtues.
