Even if the result is for a while denied to our efforts, let us not cease striving; and without doubt, either in this life or in the life to come, we shall attain what we seek. For “everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks” it shall at last “be opened” (Matt. VII, 8), if he does not cease knocking and if, in asking, seeking, and knocking, he makes earnest effort according to his ability.

But whoever neglects earnest pursuit of good endeavours will without doubt be enslaved to evil pursuits, concerning which it is said [Col. 0762A]: “They have become corrupt and abominable in their pursuits.” Nearly every person strives in some fashion. But you who sing psalms, proclaim pursuits worthy of your psalms. Perhaps you say: These pursuits have already often been proclaimed, and those who proclaimed such things have been killed; thus we too may perhaps be killed if we proclaim to people what they do not wish to hear. To this I reply: if you are killed in this way, your death will not be without fruit, just as the death of the holy righteous has fruit—a fruit which they shall enjoy eternally before the Lord.

**VERSE 13.** For he who requires their blood has remembered them. In judgment, he who requires their blood—which he seemed to have consigned to oblivion—has remembered to glorify those slain and to destroy their killers. And lest you suppose [Col. 0762B] that God remembered as though he had wholly forgotten, he adds:

He has not forgotten the cry of the poor. God indeed seems to forget when he long delays doing what he is going to do. This seems so to the disposition of the weak, for whose sake God himself is also said to remember; because Scripture often speaks according to the dispositions of the infirm.

**VERSE 14.** Have mercy upon me, O Lord; see my humiliation. The Prophet sets himself forth as an example in good pursuits, in earnest prayers, because he has spoken of pursuits: so that each person, following his example, may earnestly desire what he desires, and may desire it as he himself desires in his earnest prayer, saying: Have mercy upon me, O Lord; see my humiliation. Have mercy with the inward [Col. 0762C] disposition of mercy; see with the outward and evident effect of compassion. Your gaze is help. Therefore see my humiliation. See how greatly I have been humbled; see how great is my humiliation at the hands of my enemies. For the measure of my humiliation can be weighed from my enemies, who have been exalted through my humiliation and abasement. For just as Christ’s enemies gloried when he was humbled even to death and lay in a lowly tomb, and were exalted as though victors and superiors, so this world now glories in its exaltation over impoverished or even slain believers. Enemies glory over believers who are exalted in this world. But you, O Lord, see my humiliation at the hands of my enemies.

[Col. 0762D] **VERSE 15.** You who raise me up from the gates of death. You do not exalt my enemies in their arrogance, but allow them to be exalted not above, but within the gates of death. Yet you raise me, humiliated by them, from the gates of death—that is, from the desires by which one goes toward death. Their delight is no longer a gate of death but death itself. For desire, which precedes the pleasure of the five senses, leads, as it were by five paths, to the gates and introduces one to death. But the pleasure of those same five senses, which lies in pleasure itself, is consummated death. Hence it is said: “The widow who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (I Tim. V, 6), because the very delight of pleasures is the killing of spiritual life. But you, my God, raise me from the gates of death—that is, from the desires [Col. 0763A] by which one goes toward death, namely, toward carnal delight itself.

That I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion. Zion is the ancient Church, which in the patriarchs and prophets watched from afar for Christ’s coming. The daughter of Zion is the Church of the New Testament, nourished at the breasts of the earlier Church and like her in faith, as a daughter resembles her mother. The gates of this daughter of Zion are hearers of God’s word who are well-disposed, teachable, and attentive; to them and through them the praises of the Lord are rightly proclaimed. For the pearls of the divine word are not given to swine that trample them, nor what is holy to dogs that bark against God’s word; rather, they are given to devout hearers, especially to hearers qualified also to teach others, so that those who hear the discourse from them may enter the Church through them as through gates—that is [Col. 0763B], into the communion of the saints.

Alternatively: the gates of death are bodily senses. Those who seek not the things seen but the things unseen are raised above them. And the gates of the daughter of Zion are the sacraments of the Law and the first elements of faith, opened to those who knock, so that they may arrive at an understanding of the hidden things of the Son, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard” (I Cor. II, 9).

Alternatively: the gates of death are either wicked people or demons, who lead or admit some persons into death. The gates of the daughter of Zion are the angels of the Churches, sent by God visibly or invisibly for the ministry of human salvation. Therefore, when we sing psalms [Col. 0763C] in the presence of angels, whether in silence while invisible angels hear, or openly while visible angels hear—that is, human beings assigned to the fellowship of angels—then we proclaim the praises of the Lord in the gates of the daughter of Zion (Ps. CXXXVII, 1). And because you, God the Father, raise me from the gates of death through the hidden things of your Son, therefore:

**VERSE 16.** I shall rejoice in your salvation. I shall rejoice because your Son, through the hidden mysteries of salvation, brings salvation to me and is gracious toward me, while he is terrible and unwelcome to nations bringing about the destruction of souls or bodies. And therefore those nations themselves have been fixed fast in the destruction which they wrought: when they either killed some in soul by turning them from the faith, or destroyed some established in the faith by bodily torments [Col. 0763D], or even brought their possessions to ruin. In this destruction the nations themselves are fixed fast, because each person’s own iniquity is his punishment and chain, while the wicked man is bound with the cords of his own sins. Hence follows:

In this snare which they hid, their foot has been caught. The hidden snare is deceitful thought; the foot of the soul is love, which, if it is perverse, is called desire, but if upright is called—and is—charity. By that foot the soul moves through certain steps of desires, as if toward the place at which it aims, namely toward good or evil delight. If it reaches it, it rejoices; if it does not reach it, it is saddened; or, if it loses what it has gained, it grieves more than if it had never possessed it. Therefore in the snare which they hid [Col. 0764A]—that is, in fraudulent counsel—the foot, that is, love, is held captive; for carnal delight binds it so tightly that, if it tries to withdraw, pain does not allow it. These are the hidden things of the Son. These are the secret judgments of God, known in this life to few. But at the future coming of the Judge, who will come as lightning:

**VERSE 17.** The Lord shall be known, executing judgments. Then the Judge executing judgments shall be known by all. Then what is now hidden shall be seen: how the sinner has been caught in the works of his hands. By these works they are now separated from the good in disposition, but in the future they shall be separated also by outward punishments, when, separated from the righteous, they are sent into outer darkness, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Note that the character and extent of the punishments [Col. 0764B] by which sinners shall be punished when they are sent into outer darkness proceeds from no source other than the sinners themselves. For external darknesses of punishment shall then envelop them against their will to precisely the extent that the internal darknesses of fault now delight them willingly.

Here the song of the *diapsalma* is inserted because of the hidden joy of the separation that takes place between the good and the evil.

**VERSE 18.** Let sinners be turned into hell. As though he were saying: Let sinners who have been caught in their own works, whose foot is ensnared in the snare which they hid, because they are unwilling to turn to God in this life, at least be turned by tardy repentance, like Judas, who said: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” [Col. 0764C] (Matt. XXVII, 4). Such a conversion will not be from hell to God, but into hell, lest they should always be free to sin and always remain held by deadly delight.

Let all the nations that forget God also be turned into hell; because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, “God gave them over to a reprobate mind, so that they might do what is unfitting” (Rom. I, 28), and so that they might be fixed fast in the destruction they wrought and their foot might be in the snare. But lest they always rejoice in most evil things, at last I grant, and, agreeing with divine judgment, I will and desire that sinners be turned, lest they rejoice in pleasure, at least in hell. This is said openly, lest they suppose they are to be sent elsewhere, lest they await a place in heaven, when a place in hell has been prepared for them [Col. 0764D], to which they shall at last go—as Judas hastened to hang himself with a noose “that he might go to his own place” (Acts I, 28), and leave to another the bishopric which he had unworthily occupied. So it shall happen to the rest who resemble Judas. Nor is this delayed for long.

**VERSE 19.** For the poor man shall not be forgotten forever. Although there seems to be some forgetfulness of the poor while the wicked flourish in wealth, the poor man shall not be forgotten forever. Before the end—before the poor man’s complete failure—the Lord will remember the poor man who bears patiently in his poverty, because the patience of the poor shall not perish forever. This patience is a very great cause of divine compassion. For if the poor man is impatient in his poverty, he shall have either delayed or no consolation from God concerning his poverty [Col. 0765A]. However thoroughly good ground may be ploughed, it shall not bring forth fruit except in patience; without it we shall not even possess our own souls, the Lord saying: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke VIII, 15; XXI, 19).

There is a threefold patience necessary for us. First, toward God: lest, wearied amid his scourges, we murmur. Amid his scourges we owe him nothing other than prayers, praises, and confessions of sins: prayers, that he may spare us; praises, because in this life he chastens every son whom he receives; confessions of sins, by which we have deserved those same scourges. Next, toward our neighbor: lest through impatience we depart from peace with him, or, while he hates us, be provoked to hatred. Finally, patience toward [Col. 0765B] the devil himself is necessary to us. When he assaults us through pleasures of the flesh, patience is necessary lest we consent to him through impatience of lust, or destroy the body by unrestrained self-restraint so that it is unfit for God’s service. Some, through impatience of lust, even after a vow of chastity, have returned to the world, secretly or openly. Some, through impatience arising from intemperate temperance, have castrated themselves with their own hands, or by excessive fasts and vigils have come to such sickness that they could not preserve patience; and thus through impatience they have come to greater impatience. Let us therefore possess our souls in complete patience [Col. 0765C] (Luke XXI, 19), because the patience of the poor shall not perish forever.

**VERSE 20.** Arise, O Lord; let not man be strengthened. In speaking of the end of the world, the Prophet recalls the cruelty of Antichrist, who shall reign near the end of the world. Hence, as though terrified, he cries: Arise, O Lord.

Here it should be noted that, just as the preceding psalm contains the Prophet’s rhetorical argument of confirmation—for it confirms that the Lord’s name is wonderful in all the earth—so this psalm contains an argument of refutation. There he confirmed the exaltation of the new man above the heavens, praised from the mouths of infants and nursing children; here he refutes the hostile man of sin, the son of perdition, as the Apostle says: “who exalts himself above all [Col. 0765D] that is called God or is worshipped” (II Thess. II, 4). For just as there, from the first verse, “O Lord, our Lord,” to the same verse repeated at the end, there is a complete argument of confirmation, divided into five parts—namely proposition, reason, confirmation of the reason, embellishment, and conclusion, of which parts something has been said there—so now, from this verse in which he says, “Arise, O Lord; let not man be strengthened,” to that in which he says, “Arise, O Lord God; let your hand be exalted,” there is likewise, if you consider rightly, a complete five-part argument of refutation. For he proposes, saying: “Arise, O Lord; let not man be strengthened; let the nations be judged in your sight. Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them, that the nations may know [Col. 0766A] that they are men.” By these words he shows in summary that his purpose is to persuade God the Father, or Christ the Judge, not to allow the power of Antichrist and his followers to stand or increase against the Church. It follows: “Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Why do you despise in fitting times, in tribulation? While the wicked is proud, the poor is set on fire; they are caught in the counsels which they devise.” By saying this he gives the reason why the stronger Christ ought to arise against that strong man, Antichrist, and restrain his powers: namely, because help is timely for afflicted righteous persons and for wicked persons who are becoming proud. The confirmation of the reason is what follows: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed.” For he confirms that the wicked man does not without cause grow proud against the poor, since the sinner is praised by flattering tongues precisely in that for which he ought to be reproved—the desires of his soul; and the wicked man is blessed for that for which he ought to be cursed, if there were one to judge rightly between the wicked and the poor [Col. 0766B]. The matters then following from “The sinner has provoked the Lord” to “God has forgotten; he has turned away his face, that he may not see forever,” enumerate the evils of Antichrist, heightening and amplifying the whole case with brilliant embellishment, and thereby call forth the mercy of God to help the poor, whom that wicked man, that son of perdition, oppresses—he who says in his heart: “God has forgotten; he has turned away his face, that he may not see forever.” Then follows the conclusion, in which at the end of the argument he repeats the very thing he proposed at its beginning. There he said: “Arise, O Lord; let not man be strengthened.” Here he says, repeating the same thing: “Arise, O Lord God; let your hand be exalted; do not forget the poor.” Having thus set these things forth in advance and briefly assigned them to the form of a rhetorical argument, let us now return to the continuous exposition of the text.

Arise, O Lord; let not man be strengthened. As though he were saying: The patience of the poor shall not perish forever. But because your frail poor cannot bear the excessive violence of Antichrist, lest perhaps through his immoderate cruelty the patience of the poor should perish, arise, O Lord; let not that man prevail over your poor—a man who is not merely [Col. 0766D] man, but, as your Apostle says, “the man of sin, the son of perdition” (II Thess. II, 3), and yet, sitting in your temple, which is the Church, shall show himself as though he were God, indeed shall also exalt himself above all that is called God or is worshipped. Yet because he is a man and not God—neither natural [a Son] as Christ is, nor adoptive [a son] as a true and catholic Christian is—you, Christ, who are God by nature and have made adoptive gods those whom you willed to be numbered among your members, arise against this not-god, this mere man, or rather impure man. Arise, O Lord—that is, rising against him, “rule in the midst of your enemies” (Ps. CIX, 2). Arise, O Lord, and exercise your dominion, lest that foulest man have leisure to rule for long in your Church. Let not man be strengthened [Col. 0767A]; let him have no strength against your poor, because he is not God, as he pretends, but a mere—or rather impure—man.

I indeed ask that that man not be strengthened; yet, yielding to your ordinance, O God, I consent that he be raised up to such a degree that he does not prevail, but gains some limited strength. As the voices of those crucifying you prevailed, so I am willing that he should prevail, so that the nations may be judged through him. The Jews were judged through Barabbas the robber when, given the choice, they rejected Christ and chose the robber. Let the nations also be judged through Antichrist, as we see happening when, in the election of some bishop either at Rome or in another city, few cry out for a good man, while many cry out for someone like Barabbas the robber [Col. 0767B]. This will happen in a far more magnificent manner in Antichrist himself, the head of evils, insofar as he will be thought not man but God on account of his hypocrisy, by which he will cloak his wickedness. Therefore let him be raised up for so long and to such a degree that, through him, those who are nations may be judged, although they bear the Christian name—which in this very matter they deny, when they approve a man opposed to Christ ruling and being exalted above the Church. Therefore, O Lord Jesus Christ, it is a just judgment that they be judged through him in your sight, where the few saints see within your hidden things. Let them be judged in this way because they did not will to have you and your law.

**VERSE 21.** Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them. Appoint that son of perdition, that promulgator of a perverse law [Col. 0767C], not as a ruler among them but as an oppressor over them, so that at least affliction may give understanding to hearing, and that the nations, instructed by experience, may know that they are men. Because they abandoned the Son of Man and set the man of sin over themselves, they ought rightly to recognize that they are not sons of men belonging to holy newness, but old men, comparable and like to the foolish and senseless old man whom God hates. For, Wisdom bearing witness, there are three things which God hates: “a proud poor man, a lying rich man, and a foolish and senseless old man” (Ecclus. XXV, 4). Men like this old man cannot be called sons of men, but must be called old men, foolish and senseless, delirious old men, and men given over to a reprobate mind [Col. 0767D]. Therefore let the nations adhering to Antichrist know that they are men, so that, knowing this, they may quickly be renewed through repentance; and that those who never wished to repent may no longer have an excuse for their sin, but may perish without excuse with Judas, their forerunner and betrayer, who, knowing what he was and what he had done, openly said: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. XXVII, 4). He knew that he was a sinful man; let the righteous likewise know that they are men.

Thus Antiochus, lifted up against God, when at last struck by a divine plague and tortured as he rotted inwardly, while his army was burdened by his stench and his pains increased at every moment, finally knew himself to be a man inferior to God. Constrained by pain, he said: “It is right for a man to be subject to God, and for a mortal not to think himself equal to God” (II Macc. IX, 12). Likewise, when the Jews who denied and killed Christ, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, acclaimed certain auspicious words to Herod, in which there were voices not of a man but of God—for example, “O King, live forever” [Col. 0768A] (Acts XII, 22), or something of this sort—because he heard praise due to God alone directed toward himself, a mortal, and did not give honor to God, the angel of God struck him; and, bursting with worms, he died. It is reported that, near death, he said: “Behold your god.” Thus he was mocked by those very people who had acclaimed to a mortal man the voice and praises of God. For that fool, at last instructed by affliction, knew well that he was a man, not a god. His flatterers too were forced to know that they were men—that is, liars—not gods—that is, truthful beings. For since it is written, “Every man is a liar,” while God alone is true, all truthful beings who, now above men, cling to the true God are rightly called gods; and liars alone are properly called men, because every man is a liar. Antichrist is to be praised by such men, by such liars. Therefore let these know that they are men. Let him too, wounded like Antiochus or Herod, know that he is a man [Col. 0768B]. Let him be compelled, as they were, to know this: that he is a lying man. Let conscience constrain him, as it constrained his herald Judas, to confess that he sinned in preferring himself to God or consenting to be preferred by others. Judas said: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” [Col. 0768C] (Matt. XXVII, 41). Let this man say: “I have sinned, trampling and causing that same innocent blood to be trampled.” Let the nations that prefer him to you, O Christ, know that they are men, that they are vain and lying.

Those who killed you, O Christ, called good evil when they called you—who went among them doing good—a wrongdoer. Those who prefer Antichrist, or any of his ministers accustomed and ready to do evil, before you or above the Church in a seat of dignity, call evil good when they exalt him with praises. But each, Scripture testifying, is abominable before you: namely, he who calls good evil and he who calls evil good, against the testimony of his own conscience—especially when the life of the person falsely praised or blamed contradicts that praise or blame (Ecclus. XI, 33). Therefore let both kinds—those who praise the evil and those who disparage the good—when the evidence of truth itself becomes clear, know that they are vain and lying, since they are men incorporated into that man of whom it is written, “Man has become like vanity,” and concerning whose like it is said: “Every living man is altogether vanity” (Ps. XXXVIII, 6), and every man is a liar. From the reproach of this vanity and falsehood only those men escape who shall cling as members to that Man who, though he is man, nevertheless truly said: “I am the truth” (John XIV, 6). For vanity and falsehood are opposed to truth; and therefore those who are incorporated into that man who is truth are delivered from vanity and falsehood [Col. 0769A]. Since many have departed from his body while retaining for themselves the Christian name alone, let them know that they are men—that is, vain and false—both in praising evil and in disparaging good. This is especially so when, through false praises, they raise an unworthy man upon the holy Church in the chairs of Moses—indeed, in the chair of Christ—or through false disparagements drive a worthy man from office, lest, if he rules, they should have less liberty to rage madly. Therefore let such persons know that they are men: that they have become like vanity, or even vanity itself [Col. 0770A]; and that they can no longer conceal, hide, or cloak by any means their utterly vain lies uttered, knowingly, for Antichrist against Christ. Let them be compelled to confess it, and let all recognize that they are men.

At this point the inserted *diapsalma* marks the joyful exultation of the praying Prophet on account of the hearing of his prayer which he hopes for—already in part offered and still in part to be spoken—which he begins in this way from a question or complaint.

## PSALM X. According to the Hebrews

> [Note: [Col. 0769D] This title is absent in Gerhoh.]

[Col. 0769]

[Col. 0769B] **VERSE 1.** Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Moved by the excess of evils, he asks, as though in the voice of groaning and complaining persons: Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Then, as though he suddenly understood, he answers it. You have withdrawn, namely, because you despise in fitting times, in tribulation. Although you do not withdraw, since you are everywhere, yet when you do not aid in tribulation, when you delay help, it appears to the nations that you have withdrawn far away, that you despise your own, and have no care for them. But it is not so, because “you have care for all things” (Wis. XII, 13). Rather, as you help your own as a helper in fitting times, helping suitably in tribulation, so sometimes you also despise—or rather, appear to despise—them in fitting times, in tribulation. As you suitably mitigate tribulation [Col. 0769C], so you also suitably allow it to become heavier, with this purpose: that, when they are distressed in tribulation, they may burn more and more with desire for your coming. This is what follows:

**VERSE 2.** While the wicked is proud, the poor is set on fire. He is indeed inflamed both with pain and with love: with pain on account of the evils he sees, and with love and desire for the good things he does not see. He is also inflamed like gold in a furnace, where, while the wood is burned, the gold is purified. Just as heresies had to come so that truth might be sought more fully, tested, and, once tested, loved more greatly, so it is also necessary and fitting that the wicked sometimes be exalted, so that, while their tyranny rages, the good may be sought even by the evil themselves, who are caught in the counsels by which they intend to catch others. What counsels these are, devised against the righteous and in which the wicked shall be caught, is more fully explained from here to: “Arise, O Lord God; let your hand be exalted.” For first a very great storm is described, so that, as though the ship were in danger, the Lord may be awakened by these words: “Arise, O Lord.” Now let us see the streams of storms, stirred up by the blasts of perverse counsels [Col. 0769D]—partly already agitated, partly still to be stirred up against the Church. For this is like a contrary wind: “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked is blessed.” For if the sinner were rebuked for his perverse desires, and the wicked man were cursed and excommunicated for open wickedness, perhaps he would be humbled, just as the wicked Ahab was humbled when Elijah rebuked him. But now:

**VERSE 3.** For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed. Hence the foaming waves of the fierce sea rise against the ship entrusted to Peter. For Antichrist himself, chief among the wicked, or any notable minister of his, is raised up as though he were God when he is praised in the desires of his soul; and he, though a sinner who ought to appease God by repentance, has provoked him by impenitence and arrogance. This is what follows:

**VERSE 4.** The sinner has provoked the Lord. But how does it appear that the Lord has been provoked? Namely from the fact that, according to the multitude of his wrath, that shepherd who seeks the wandering sheep shall not seek the sinner who provokes him—though he seeks the sheep that strays, but does not provoke him. The sinner who provokes God and calls down against himself the multitude of God’s wrath is so deprived of the light of truth that he himself is far from God and God is far from him, because:

**VERSE 5.** God is not before his eyes. He does not acknowledge God; he despises God as though he were nowhere. Therefore his ways are defiled at every time of his life, or at every time—that is, by the iniquity of all times. For just as upon the Jews, the killers of Christ and his disciples, came every righteous blood shed upon earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, so upon Antichrist, the enemy of all the saints, shall come the defilements of all former times [Col. 0771A]; and therefore his ways are defiled at every time.

Your judgments are removed from before his face. For, thinking that you, the judge of the living and the dead, do not judge human actions, he will not be restrained by fear of your judgment; and therefore, without regard for the Lord ruling over him, he himself, as though supreme, will rule over all his enemies, partly through violence and partly through magic and evil arts.

**VERSE 6.** For he said in his heart: “I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil.” That is, without evil arts. He says this in his heart. For with his mouth he pretends to be good and an enemy of evil arts, as Saul, the wicked and proud king, pretended to oppose evil arts in order to win a good reputation for himself, rooting magicians and soothsayers out of the land. Yet how much confidence he had in those same evil arts he disclosed by consulting the woman with a familiar spirit when under pressure, and eating of her calf [Col. 0771B] (I Sam. XXVIII, 8). This calf is believed to have been sacrificed to demons; and therefore Saul was alike defiled by magical art and idolatry. When he thought to advance himself from generation to generation by these evils, while holding cruel hatred against David and his line, he found a swift end to his rule.

Alternatively: He said in his heart, “I shall not be moved”—that is, “I shall not be troubled, but I shall be from generation to generation without evil,” without misfortune, without disturbance. Thus that man of sin prophesies and promises prosperity to himself, but promises and threatens hardships to the Church of God [Col. 0771C].

### Verse 7

His mouth is full of cursing, bitterness, and deceit. His mouth is full of cursing against the good, because he curses them and speaks evil of them; of bitterness, because he threatens them; and of deceit, because he sometimes flatters them. But when he flatters the saints, although a pleasant promise may sound forth on his tongue, yet beneath his tongue—that is, in his heart—are toil and pain, because he devises how to inflict toil and pain upon them: toil by afflicting them, pain by killing them.

Otherwise: “Beneath his tongue are toil and pain.” That is, his tongue is so dangerous that the toil and pain of the saints, which consist in bodily torment, when compared with his most wicked tongue, are beneath his tongue—that is, they involve less danger than his tongue, whose harmful deceit is not easily detected, because he deliberates long beforehand how cunningly to practise his malice. For:

### Verse 8

He sits in ambush with the rich in secret places, that he may kill the innocent. He sits, lingering over his plans; in ambush, like a robber; with the rich, like a tyrant, displaying those whom he himself has enriched; in secret places, so that it may not easily be discovered what is to be chosen among things covertly sought amid ambiguities. He does all this in order to kill the innocent—that is, to make him guilty. For it is one thing to kill a human being, another to kill an innocent person. He kills a human being who tortures the body unto the separation of the soul. But he kills the innocent who takes away his innocence and makes him guilty. Such was the persecution of tyrants in the time of the martyrs: men unwilling to consent to the will of kings were killed. This is the persecution of Antichrist: that innocents may be killed.

Yet even in the time of the martyrs there was a killing of innocents in those who, through fear of punishments, denied Christ and were made guilty from being innocent. Nevertheless, because Antichrist seeks more to kill souls than bodies, he is said to sit in ambush for this purpose, that he may kill the innocent.

### Verse 9

His eyes look upon the poor. Either because he pretends mercy toward anyone poor in spirit, since, when he cannot persecute such persons, he draws them to himself as though pitying their misery; or his eyes look upon the poor because he aims to impoverish anyone who does not consent to him. For while outwardly his eyes look upon the poor either with seeming kindness or with genuine malice and grimness, he himself lies in wait secretly by evil intention, like a lion in his den.

The first persecution against the Church was violent, when martyrs were driven by torments to sacrifice to idols. The second was fraudulent, through heretics and false brethren. The last, through Antichrist and his ministers, will be both fraudulent and violent. Therefore Antichrist himself is compared to a lion lying in wait in a den. By the lion, force is understood; by the den, deceit.

Many such men have already gone before under the name of kings, or even of pontiffs, who have acted wickedly against the purity of the Church by both violence and fraud. Many such will yet follow until the end of the age. But which of them is the chief one, especially marked by the name Antichrist—although, from the time of the apostles, as John testifies, there have been many antichrists—is entirely unknown, until that lawless one is revealed by the brightness of the Lord’s coming, “whom the Lord Jesus himself will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thess. 2:8).

Blessed is that poor person who is not caught by his snares—snares of which we are not free, upon whom the ends of the ages have come—because, daily working the mystery of iniquity, he lies in wait to seize the poor. He repeats the word concerning snares in order both to make us more cautious and to explain the purpose of the one lying in wait: namely, that he may seize the poor. To seize the poor must here be understood as drawing him to consent to his perverse dominion. How is he drawn?

### Verse 10

In his snare—that is, in his deceit, or in his deceitful, ensnaring generosity—he will humble him. For just as a man is said to have humbled a virgin whom he corrupted, so Antichrist is said to humble the poor whom he can corrupt by deceit or gifts. But when he cannot corrupt them so that they will consent to his wickedness, he exercises the dominion of his cruelty against them. Yet in this he will not prosper, because when he has ruled over the poor, he will bend down and fall. He will bend down into the repose of security.

[Col. 0773A] But while thus reclined upon the bed of rest he thinks himself at ease, he will fall by sudden destruction; for when he and his accomplices say, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them, and they will not escape. This will happen to him by a just judgment.

### Verse 11

For he said in his heart: God has forgotten both to save the poor and to punish me. He has turned away his face, so that he may not see me or them unto the end of the age.

Or, because earth is the lowest element, placed at the end of the fabric of the world as though for a foundation, he denies that God sees to the end, so as to see human affairs that are done upon earth, in which nothing takes place except by the ordering of him who sees all things. But because he who sees all things is himself not seen by human beings, this secret is reckoned among the hidden things of the Son, revealed only to the few elect. In the storm of so many dangers, nothing remains for them except to awaken Christ by prayers, for he alone can calm such evils by commanding the winds and the sea, “and there is a great calm” (Matt. 8:26). Hence it follows:

### Verse 12

Arise, Lord; quickly awaken, and make manifest your power. Let your hand be exalted, that it may strike more forcefully, break the horns of sinners, and deliver the poor. Do not forget the poor, as the wicked suppose when they say, “He has turned away his face, that he may not see unto the end” (Ps. 74:11).

Now, assured that his prayer has been heard, he taunts the ungodly who provoke God. This is what follows:

### Verse 13

Why has the wicked man provoked God? What advantage did he gain by provoking God? He truly provoked him, not so much in that he sinned as in that he promised himself impunity for his sins through God’s negligence, believing that God did not care for human deeds. For he said in his heart this, namely: God will not examine individual acts, whether good or evil. He said this, thinking that you do not see his hidden deeds. But you, O God,

### Verse 14

See, in order that you may deliver them up—that is, how you may deliver them up, namely Antichrist and his accomplices, into your hands, that is, into your punishments. You see this and prepare yourself for judgment, because you consider toil and pain—the toil and pain, namely, of which it was said above: “Beneath his tongue are toil and pain.”

Otherwise, Augustine says: “Men are accustomed not to take vengeance because they fear the effort or anger involved; and perceiving this, others sin against them more boldly. Thus this ungodly man said in his heart concerning God: God will not require an account, because he could not punish so many and such great offenses without effort and anger, and would thus be wearied alike by pain and toil.”

Since this seems to be so while God endures evils for so long, the Prophet turns to God as though addressing him upon this matter. “But this meaning requires a particular delivery, in which, if one errs, it is obscured.”

[Note: [Col. 0773D] St Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm IX*, on this passage.]

“He therefore says: O Lord, the ungodly man says in his heart: God will not require an account. And I say: Do you merely see, and not require an account or judge those things which he does, because it is attributed to you that you are unwilling to take the trouble [Col. 0774A] of judging evils so many and so great? Or do you therefore see and endure, because you consider your toil and your anger or pain, being unwilling to labour so much as to deliver them into your hands?

“The hands of God are sometimes called apostate angels. Thus in Job Satan says to the Lord: ‘Put forth your hand and touch his mouth and his flesh’ (Job 2:5). In saying this Satan understood himself to be the hand of God, by which many vessels are fashioned: some are polished that they may shine, others are crushed that they may perish. Hence in Isaiah the hammer of the earth is called Nebuchadnezzar, that is, Satan; and the Lord says of him: ‘I have created the smith blowing coals’ (Isa. 54:16). For the almighty Lord uses him as though he were a smith, or a hammer, or even his own hand, in order to fashion, crush, or polish whatever vessel he wills, according as he himself knows what befits each vessel.

“Since this is so, is it laborious for you, O Lord, who have good angels as your right hand and evil angels as your left hand? Or, seeing your enemies multiplied, do you consider this toil and pain to be yours: that you may deliver them into your hands, that you may deliver them to tormenting angels for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of judgment? Is it laborious for you to send upon them the wrath of your indignation—indignation and wrath and tribulation, a sending forth through evil angels—so that either they may be corrected; or, if they refuse correction, like the Egyptians with their Pharaoh, that is, Antichrist, being scourged, at least the Hebrews, that is, true Christians, may be delivered?

“Far be this from you, God of hosts, who have many armies of angels as though a mighty hand, that you should pass over as burdensome, or long defer, the avenging of the injuries and oppressions of your poor! You subdued Pharaoh, king of Egypt, by certain of your armies serving your will: namely, armies not of lions or bears, but of flies, gnats, locusts, caterpillars, and swelling blisters. Nor did you labour in doing this, but it was accomplished by a word alone, because your servant Moses ‘spoke, and the locust came, and the caterpillar, without number’ (Ps. 104:34). By such an army a great king with his army was scourged, and at last was drowned in the Red Sea by waters serving you, while your people were delivered.

“Herod too, when he swarmed with worms, was overcome and humbled by that very army of worms, so that he might know himself mortal and at last reject the divine praises shouted to him by the foolish people. Is it then, O God of hosts, whom innumerable armies thus serve, that you consider toil and pain, so as to deliver them into your hands? When your ark was formerly captured, you struck your enemies in their hind parts; and when their fields teemed with mice, by the armies of those mice you, God of hosts, achieved a glorious triumph against them.

“Therefore far be it from you that it should be toil to avenge any poor person left to you, who has no protector apart from you! For amid the afflictions of the rich there are many comforters; but the poor man is left to you alone, who, abandoning all things for your sake, has become poor—and so poor that he is an orphan and a fatherless child. His father, the world, is dead, because he finds no paternal or maternal consolations in the world, which hates him for your sake. You will be the helper of such a poor person, such an orphan, such a fatherless child.”

Therefore do not delay your judgments beyond measure, you whose power is ready whenever you will. The whole world fights for you against the senseless and serves you. Do not—do not—leave your poor without your aid and consolation, lest perhaps, constrained by poverty and desolation, when they see the abomination of desolation standing against them—that is, persisting in the holy place, with one ruling there who is not a comforter but the desolator of churches and of the poor—lest, I say, pressed by such desolation, your poor be broken and forced to plead too greatly with their enemies and yours. Hasten to their aid, and:

### Verse 15

Break the arm—that is, the strength—of the sinner and the malicious man: of the sinner, I say, because of his unjust violence; of the malicious man, because of his deceit. Or, a sinner in himself, malicious toward others. Or, a sinner in the act of sinning, malicious in the disposition to persevere.

The apostle Peter was for a time a sinner and a denier of Christ, but he was not a malicious sinner. Therefore his arm was not broken, but through true repentance was so strengthened that “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16:18). But Judas, the most wicked trader, was a malicious sinner. Therefore, rightly broken and shattered, “he burst open in the middle, and all his entrails were spilled out upon the ground” (Acts 1:18). Thus, O God, spare indeed the sinner who is not malicious; but break the arm of the malicious sinner.

Behold, I have prayed and have not poured out my prayers in vain. For, God willing and hearing the prayers of his poor, the judgment for which I long will not be delayed. But his sin will be sought out by judicial examination. It will be sought out what it is, what kind it is, and how great it is, so that judgment may be rendered concerning it. And thus, when the ungodly man has been judged, he will not be found.

So it happened of old, when Pharaoh was judged and was not even found for burial. So, when the ungodly Jezebel, cast down from on high at Jehu’s command, was sought, she was not found: they found only the palms of her hands and the skull as remnants, after dogs had devoured her, but they did not find her. So in the Roman senate, although it was still entangled in the error of paganism, Nero’s sin was sought and he himself was not found; for, as it is reported, when he heard that the senate had judged and condemned him—he who had previously been feared by all—he himself, fearing everyone, fled to forest hiding places and appeared no more, because he perished, either devoured by wolves or, as some suppose, killed by hunger. Likewise therefore, O God, break the arm of Antichrist: let his sin be sought, and let him not be found.

[Col. 0776A] And certainly it will be so. His sin will be sought, and when the sin has been diligently examined, the sinner himself will not be found, because either, having been converted, he will cease to be a sinner, or, having been condemned, he will no longer be found in the height of his condemnation. For although Antichrist himself is believed to be wholly destined for perdition and not to be converted through true repentance, yet a great part of his accomplices will be converted and will not be found in their sins.

Otherwise: since, while the ungodly exalts himself, the poor man is inflamed and thereby purified, his sin will be sought out to determine whether it is still necessary for purging the good. When all these have then been purified, the sin itself will not be found necessary for purging the good, just as, when iron is smooth, a file is unnecessary. This alone therefore remains: that he be removed from the midst and not be found in the midst of the Church, but be shut up in the prison of merited condemnation, so that he may be as though he were not. This is surely a just judgment, because he wished Christ to be as though he were not, intending thus to reign in the Church as though, the kingdom of Christ having been destroyed, his own kingdom ought to endure forever.

But the event will be far otherwise. For Antichrist is the beast “which was, and is not.” Christ, however, is King of all ages, whose kingdom and dominion were without beginning and remain without end. Hence follows:

### Verse 16

The Lord will reign for ever, and unto age upon age. He will reign forever, because his kingdom lacks beginning and end. But because his kingdom does not yet appear clearly, while all his enemies have not yet been placed beneath him to become the footstool of his feet, he will reign manifestly in the age that follows the present age; in that age of ages all those enemies of his, made the footstool of his feet, will lie subject to him.

But you nations, accomplices of Antichrist, will perish from his land, which is the land of the living, because the poor and meek will possess it (Matt. 5:4), because:

### Verse 17

The Lord has heard the desire of those poor persons, by which they longed for the day of the Lord; your ear—that is, your power—has heard the preparation of their heart, namely, the heart prepared to serve you. The desire of the poor is that your judgment may attain victory, O God, righteous Judge, to whose justice and mercy it belongs:

### Verse 18

To judge for the fatherless and humble, that man may no longer continue to exalt himself upon the earth.

The chief fatherless one in this world was Jesus Christ, your Son, having on earth a mother without a father, just as in heaven he had you as Father without a mother. Judgment is sought for this fatherless one, scourged, struck, and condemned to a most shameful death before the eyes of his Mother: namely, that by a just judgment he may appear, appointed by you the Father as Judge of the living and the dead, judging justly though he himself was judged unjustly.

Thus, righteous Father, whom the world did not know, we ask judgment for your Son, fatherless in this world, so that his Mother—and likewise his Bride, the Church—who grieves that he, as a humble fatherless one deprived of inheritance, indeed cast out by evil tenants beyond the vineyard which was his inheritance and killed, may see him raised again; and, seeing and embracing him, may be made glad by abundant consolations according to the multitude of her sorrows in her heart.

The multitude of sorrows was in the heart of our Lady, holy Mary, when she saw her most beloved Son, fatherless and humble in this world, crucified; for she stood by the cross with the beloved disciple. But her sorrow was turned into joy when she saw him crowned with glory and honor through his triumph over death. Thus judgment was rightly given to the fatherless and humble one when his Mother and disciples, sorrowing at his disinheritance and death, were fully gladdened.

For he who was thought disinherited, when his inheritance had been secured to him after the resurrection, himself said: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18). As though saying: My enemies, suspending me upon the cross, deprived me, so far as lay in them, of heaven and earth, when they unjustly judged me, a humble fatherless one. But when God, my God and my Father, judged rightly for me, “all power has been given to me in heaven and on earth,” “that man may no longer continue to exalt himself upon the earth” (ibid.).

Pilate, a human being, exalted himself over the earth, because my earth, my flesh, had been given into the hands of the ungodly; therefore, exalting himself, he said to me: “Do you not know that I have power to release you, and power to crucify you?” (Job 19:10.) But when death was overcome through the victory of the resurrection, Pilate or the Jew, a human being, no longer continued to exalt himself over the earth—that is, over my flesh—because all power was given to me in heaven over angels and on earth over human beings.

Then the desire of the poor disciples was fulfilled, because judgment was rightly given to the fatherless and humble one, that man might no longer continue to exalt himself over the earth, exalted exceedingly above all heavens, when Christ, who descended by humbling himself even unto death, himself also ascended above all heavens, that he might fill all things.

But because the title of this psalm is “Unto the End, for the Hidden Things of the Son,” while his passion, because he suffered in the flesh, was an open passion, something seems to require saying concerning the hidden passions of the same Son, prolonged unto the end, by which Christ is crucified in his members unto the end of the age. What Christ suffered in his own person is contained in the text of the Gospels; but who can recount or write down what he suffered and suffers in his members? Yet, with his help, we shall attempt briefly to touch upon the mystery of his threefold passion, which he first endured in himself and then handed on to his Church as though the remnants of the same fish roasted in three ways, the cup of that threefold passion.

[Col. 0778A] First, he suffered those ministers of death “who sought the life of the child” (Matt. 2), who killed many children at Herod’s command in order to kill him. Herod’s son consented to Christ’s death, completing the measure of his fathers. Therefore, by a just judgment, all righteous blood came upon them, which had been shed from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zachariah.

Such was Christ’s passion, begun in the death of the innocents but consummated in his own death. “When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said: ‘It is accomplished’; and, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit” (John 19:30). Then his Mother and John stood by the cross of Jesus, having this desire: that God the Father might judge for the fatherless and humble one hanging on the cross. And the Lord heard the desire of those poor persons. For “behold, the veil of the temple was torn, the earth shook, the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened” (Matt. 27:51); and the darkness, which had remained over the entire world from the sixth hour until the ninth, departed when Christ died.

When these miracles were seen, the human executioner no longer continued to exalt himself over Christ’s earthly substance, as the centurion cried out: “Truly this was the Son of God” (ibid., v. 54). Nor could the soldiers guarding his tomb exalt themselves over this earth, because, terrified from above and below alike by the lightning-bright appearance of the angel and the earthquake, “they became as dead men” (ibid. 28:4).

Thus judgment was rightly rendered to the fatherless and humble one, dead and buried for the fatherless and humble, “that man might not continue to exalt himself over the earth,” temporarily given into the hands of the wicked insofar as he himself willed, he who set bar and doors to the sea and said: “Thus far you shall come, and here you shall break your swelling waves” (Job 38:11). Therefore the sea-storm of ungodliness could not exalt or magnify itself further over the earth than he appointed, who made the cup of his own passion and that of his people measurable and bearable (1 Cor. 10:13). For if God is faithful, who does not permit his own to be tempted above what they can bear, but will make with the temptation also the way out, that they may be able to endure it, much more must it be believed that in his own passion he so measured the strength of his Mother and disciples that they could endure, being comforted both by the showing of miracles and by the swiftly ripened resurrection through which that humble fatherless one was recognized as the Most High Son of the Most High Father.

The same fatherless and humble one also suffered false witnesses who distorted his words. The first of them were his own countrymen, who mocked his teaching because they knew his mother and relatives. The last were those of whom it is written in the Gospel: “And when many false witnesses had come, at last two false witnesses came, saying: This man said, ‘I can destroy the temple and rebuild it after three days’” (Matt. 26:60 ff.). “And their testimony was not consistent” (Mark 14:59). For he had not said this, but: “Destroy,” he said, “this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

He himself was also punished as a false witness, because he called God his Father. That true testimony of truth was not accepted from him, but the false testimony of those who called him a deceiver and evildoer was accepted. “If this man were not an evildoer,” they say, “we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18:30).

Therefore, just as the first and second Herod, together with Pilate and their associates—the Jews and soldiers who crucified Christ—completed the measure of executioners and butchers by killing in Christ the visible body, so the aforementioned false witnesses completed the measure of falsehood and lies by producing and persuading others of false testimony against Christ, the eternal Word of God, of whom it is said: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). This Word made flesh was not falsified, as those false witnesses wished; rather, it remained and remains true. Hence, just as Christ, though killed, still lives, so, though assailed by false testimony, he remains truthful and Truth, according to this: “For ever, O Lord, your Word remains in heaven”; “your truth” endures “unto age upon age” (Ps. 118:89).

But because this double torture inflicted upon Christ by executioners and false witnesses was so annulled through his resurrection and the manifestation of the risen one in many proofs of truth during forty days that Christ is believed to be living, true, and a faithful witness—so that the human executioner no longer continues to exalt himself over the earth exalted in Christ to the heavens, nor the lying human being to exalt himself over the earth, namely over solid truth believed in the world as the heavens declare it—something must be said concerning the hidden things of the same Son’s passions, according to the title of this psalm.

For the two preceding passions, inflicted upon Christ by executioners and false witnesses, were manifest: his enemies wished to kill life and falsify truth, but did not prevail.

Christ is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6): the way in examples and sacraments; the truth in teaching and promises; the life in the two rewards of the two garments, namely of body and soul. Thus killers persecuted Christ himself as Life. False witnesses persecuted him as Truth. Despisers of his examples and tramplers upon his sacraments persecuted him as the Way. This was the third passion among the hidden things of the Son, which we now pursue more extensively because this psalm treats of the hidden things of the Son.

It is known from Gospel tradition that until his thirtieth year Christ lived privately, subject to his parents and to the ordinances of the Law, giving an example and showing beforehand the way of humility by which sinful human beings ought to be subject to their parents and to the sacramental ordinances of the divine Law. Though God made man was without sin, he nevertheless showed obedience to his parents and obediently observed the sacraments of the old Law: in circumcision, in his presentation at the temple, and in celebrating the three feasts. He also received in himself the sacraments of the new Law, of which he himself is the giver, when baptized in the Jordan. Still more did he confirm those sacraments in his passion, resurrection, and ascension.

But, the Evangelist says, the Pharisees rejected the counsel of God, namely in that they received neither the baptism of John nor that of Christ. Those also rejected the counsel of God who murmured against the sacrament of his body and blood, disputing and saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat and his blood to drink?” (John 6:53). Though such people had first appeared to belong to the number of disciples, they nevertheless went backward, saying: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (ibid. 5:6).

But far more did the wicked Judas reject the counsel of God. Though his feet were sacramentally washed at the Lord’s supper, he remained wholly muddy, far removed from the number of those of whom Christ himself said in the same place: “He who has been washed has no need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean. And you,” he said, “are clean, but not all” (John 13:10). Here you, Judas, most wicked trader, worthless hypocrite, were marked out: remaining in your uncleanness even amid sacraments of cleansing and purification. You ate the Lord’s bread, but alienated the Lord who is the bread far from yourself. You received the washing of feet, but, according to the saying, “Let him who is filthy be filthy still” (Rev. 22:11), you remained in your filth.

Would that you alone had remained in your filth and had not handed it down to your descendants! But now we see and grieve that most wicked traders, hypocrites, heretics, and Simoniacs participate in the divine sacraments and yet are not purified from their uncleannesses. The sacraments of truth and life are indeed a way to life and truth itself. No one passes into the land of promise except through the Red Sea of holy baptism; no one journeys alive through the wilderness of this world toward eternal life unless he has as provision the bread of angels. Whoever neglects to receive it tramples Christ himself in his sacrament.

But whoever receives unworthily is himself “guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:27); so far as lies in him, he rather seizes the Lord’s body in the manner of dogs, to whom that which is holy to the Lord ought not to be entrusted, although he receives it in the manner of the faithful. The faithful receive the body of Christ, judging it worthy of all reception, and, by eating Christ’s body, become Christ’s body. They become what they receive because they do not hear him speaking in vain: “Take and eat: this is my body. Take and drink: this is my blood” (Matt. 26:26).

“Take,” he says: that is, judge it worthy of every reception, and therefore eat and drink with veneration the sacrament that is for you the way, or provision for the journey, to truth and life. Therefore, just as Christ is honored by believers in his sacraments, so he is undoubtedly trampled upon and suffers in those same sacraments at the hands of the ungodly. The worst of these was Judas the trader, the worst despiser of Christ’s sacraments. In them, so far as lay in him, he killed Christ: in the washing of his feet he was neither cleansed nor moved to humility; receiving the morsel from the Lord’s hand, and receiving the good thing wrongly, he remained dead within the banquet of life. Indeed, he went out dead; or rather, as a dead and fetid carcass, he was cast outside. For immediately after the morsel Satan, the overseer of death, entered into him; driven by him even to the noose, he was killed by a fitting death, he who, so far as lay in him, annulled the sacraments of life, in which he inflicted many sufferings upon Christ—openly by adhering to him, but secretly by despising and, so far as lay in him, annulling his examples and sacraments.

[Col. 0781B] Thus Christ himself suffered in three ways: from executioners, from false witnesses, and from despisers of his sacraments. Christ, I say—the fish roasted in three ways—gave to his disciples, and in them to his whole Church, which is his body, the remnants of this threefold roasting.

This Church, then, conformed to the likeness of Christ’s passion, suffered innumerable torments from executioners from the time of Nero, who first proclaimed a universal persecution against the Church, until the conversion of the emperor Constantine. In Constantine’s time peace and tranquility abounded in all the churches. Christ had rebuked the winds and sea, and there was a great calm; and while they were saying, “Peace and security,” sudden destruction came upon the false witnesses.

The greatest of them was Arius, founder of the Arian heresy. While conflict raged on every side against his pestilential teaching, the ship of the Church was endangered by a great storm, so that many were led into error, even persons who seemed elect. Then, when false witnesses had multiplied beyond the number of truthful witnesses, and Constantius, the Arian king, was driving the few remaining truthful witnesses into exile, while the Arian plague infected all the western and eastern churches, the voices of those who assembled against the Catholic faith in the Council of Rimini grew powerful. There they proscribed the faith of the Nicene Council and subscribed to the condemnation of Athanasius, the Catholic pontiff.

To this poison of falsehood was added the innumerable multitude of other false witnesses. Some affirmed that Christ was a mere human being and not God; others that he was God but not truly human, having assumed only a phantom of a human being. Some said that he did not exist before Mary. Others taught that he began from things not existing before the world. Others said that he passed through Mary as through a pipe. Others, with impious mouth, taught that Christ possessed his whole substance from Mary. Many false witnesses uttered many other testimonies of falsehood, by which they did not kill Christ in the flesh, but nevertheless denied him insofar as he is Truth.

Indeed, there is little or no difference in wickedness between killing him and denying him. Certainly, it is less evil to kill him than to deny him. For the person who kills him does not thereby succeed in killing the Father. But the person who denies him as the almighty Son of God the almighty Father necessarily denies the Father also, by denying his Son, concerning whom the Father himself testified: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5).

Yet against this testimony of the Father the voices of false witnesses prevailed, denying Christ as the power of God and the wisdom of God. When Christ was denied by them, his Church too was denied, because the synagogue of Satan then pretended to be the Church and denied that the true Church, preserved at that time in the small number of the elect by God’s provident counsel, was the Church. This happened so that the true and Catholic Church might be conformed to Christ in the likeness also of this passion, which he endured when denied by false witnesses before Pilate and afterwards suffered from heretics denying him.

[Col. 0782B] At last, when all the mists of errors had been driven away by the ray of truth through Catholic teachers, and the Catholic faith was shining throughout the whole world, in this third passion the holy Church suffers with Christ. In his sacraments, he suffered Judas the betrayer and trader; and he still suffers many Judases, many traders, many unclean persons. Their feet are indeed washed sacramentally while they handle Christ’s sacraments or partake of them; but they themselves remain in the filth of their uncleanness—traders, along with Judas the worst trader, and themselves the worst of traders—because in administering God’s sacraments they seek what is their own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ. In them reigns avarice, “which is idolatry” (Col. 3:5), from which Simony is born; and examples of it abound in our own time.

[Col. 0782C] For just as formerly, when Jezebel and her daughter Athaliah tyrannized, the Lord’s prophets were killed and the altars overthrown, so now, while avarice and her daughter Simony reign, the prophets of truth are killed, since they are not permitted to speak the truth, and the altars are overthrown, which are entrusted to simoniacal clerics by simoniacal bishops. Yet the remnant of chosen men, whom the Lord reserved and preserved for himself lest they should bend their knees before Mammon—whom avarice and Simony worship—remain in their purity and suffer with Christ, who endures injuries in his sacraments (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19:18). Some of them, zealous for righteousness with Elijah, are compelled to flee into desert places. And for those who are placed in the cave of the flesh, or who even come forth from the cave

[Col. 0782D] by contemplation, there would be no consolation unless the whisper of a gentle breeze came; for in every holy place the abomination of desolation is seen standing, while the chief and mother Churches are subject to avarice and Simony.

This is the cause of the earthquake, the wind that shatters rocks, and the fire that lays all waste, as was revealed to Elijah. For because of Simony and avarice, rocks—that is, those who seem strong—are shattered; the whole world is shaken; and the fire of covetousness, or the visible fire that avenges evils, grows strong. But because the Church has no consolation in these manifest things, since the Lord is neither in the wind that shatters rocks, nor in the earthquake, nor in the fire, the Church herself prays and sighs for the hidden things of the Son. Therefore

[Col. 0783A] it is said to Elijah: “After the fire, a whisper of a gentle breeze, and there the Lord” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19:11). There consolation, there refreshment, must without doubt be awaited in the hidden things of the Son, in the whisper of the gentle breeze; because Christ’s second coming, though terrifying to the wicked, will be like a whisper of a gentle breeze to the elect. Then the Lord will hear the desire of the poor; O God, your ear will hear the preparation of their heart. Then, according to the desire of the poor, you will so judge the orphan and the humble that man will no longer add to his self-exaltation upon the earth.

And indeed the Lord has already in part heard the desire of the poor, judging on behalf of the orphan and the humble so that the executioner-man may no longer add to his self-exaltation upon the earth. For after the martyrs were killed and their spirits received into heaven, their earthly bodies were glorified through countless miracles in such a way that the executioner-man could no longer add to his self-exaltation over them. These martyrs of Christ became his table-companions not only in the remains of broiled fish, but also in the honeycomb; for through fellowship in Christ’s passion they have also been joined to his glory, so that man may no longer add to his self-exaltation upon the earth—that is, over their bodies, buried in peace, resplendent with miracles, terrible to demons, healing the sick, radiant with manifold power, and awaiting that glory in which we too “await the Lord Jesus, who will refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:20–21).

[Col. 0783B] For in the days of the martyrs, according to Isaiah’s prophecy,

[Col. 0783C] “the yoke of their burden” was removed, and “the sceptre of the oppressor was overcome as on the day of Midian” (Isa. 9:4). For just as Gideon, fighting against Midian amid sounding trumpets, broken pitchers, and flashing lamps, terrified the enemies so that they turned to flight, so Christ, fighting against the ruler of this world amid the sounding apostolic testimonies—when “their sound went out into all the earth” (Rom. 10:18)—and through the breaking of martyrs’ bodies and the miracles thence flashing forth, put the Church’s enemies to flight. Thus man no longer added to his self-exaltation upon the earth—that is, over the bodies of the saints, buried in peace according to the desire of the poor and gleaming with innumerable miracles, just as the lamps flashed on the day of Midian,

[Col. 0783D] by which the camp of Midian was routed. When they were routed, peace was established over Israel and the desire of the poor was heard, because the sceptre of the oppressor was overcome as on the day of Midian.

Foreseeing this from afar, the prophet Isaiah promised the Church this peace, saying: “And it shall come to pass in that day, when God gives you rest from your labor, from your disturbance, and from the harsh servitude in which you formerly served, that you shall take up this parable against the king of Babylon and say: How the oppressor has ceased, the tribute has rested! The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of rulers, which struck the peoples in indignation with an incurable blow, subdued the nations in fury, and cruelly persecuted them. The whole earth has rested and been still; it has rejoiced and exulted. Even the fir trees

[Col. 0784A] and the cedars of Lebanon have rejoiced over you.” Truly, the fir trees and cedars of Lebanon will rejoice when the Church’s persecutions have ceased and the whole earth has rested and been still—that is, the whole Church, in which the lesser saints were like fir trees and the greater like cedars. When the peace of the Churches has been established, all of them are made glad.

Nor did the Lord hear the desire of the poor only in the glorification of martyrs; the Lord also appears glorious in the holy confessors, whom he “made like the saints in glory, and through their words subdued the monsters of heretics” (Ecclus. 45:2). He glorified them in the sight of kings and gave them a crown of glory. He established an everlasting covenant for them, gave them a great priesthood, and made them blessed

[Col. 0784B] in glory to such an extent that the heretical man, the false witness, might no longer add to his self-exaltation over the earth—that is, over the solid and fruitful ground of their teaching. Let us therefore sing in veneration of martyrs and confessors, and rejoice, saying: God has heard the desire of the poor. For according to the desire of the poor, he has so judged on behalf of the orphan and the humble martyr or confessor that man may no longer add to his self-exaltation over earth fertile in the flowers and fruits of virtues, while glorious miracles occur through martyrs’ bodies, and believers’ hearts bear fruit in good habits and works through the teaching of confessors.

But there still burns in the hearts of the poor a most vehement desire which has not yet been fully and sufficiently

[Col. 0784C] heard. For Judas, the worst trader, with his avaricious and simoniacal accomplices, still exalts himself over the earth—that is, over the holy Church—because of the indistinguishable similarity of the sacraments. These are performed with such sameness by Simoniacs as by Catholics that even the elect, if possible, are led into error and suppose that Christ’s sacraments may be received indiscriminately from all persons. Yet the desire of the poor has already in part been heard for the destruction of this evil, because the offices of simoniacal and incestuous clerics have plainly been forbidden by the Apostolic See. This prohibition, however, has not prevailed so completely that man no longer adds to his self-exaltation upon the earth. For although they are forbidden,

[Col. 0784D] the worst Simoniacs and Nicolaitans still glory over the Church because of the similarity of sacramental signs. Thus in Egypt Jannes and Mambres exalted themselves against Moses and Aaron because of the similarity of signs (Exod. 7:11); but after they perceived God’s finger working against them in the signs of Moses and Aaron, they no longer added to their self-exaltation over the earth, over God’s people. So, so, O Lord God, make it manifest that in forbidden offices your finger, the Holy Spirit, works no salvation and no power, whereas in Catholic offices he works salvation and power. Judge this so plainly on behalf of the orphan and humble person, every Catholic, that once the truth of this matter has been disclosed, man may no longer add to his self-exaltation upon the earth—

[Col. 0785A] that the Simoniac or incestuous Nicolaitan may no longer add to his self-exaltation over the earth, over the Catholic and Apostolic Church. Though confined to a small remnant, it is still fruitful. For although, with iniquity abounding, the charity of many has grown cold and almost failed, nevertheless among a few elect that desire burns which, by God’s mercy, is believed to be heard. The preparations of their hearts burn intensely until judgment is rendered on behalf of the orphan and humble Catholic by such a judgment that the worst trader may no longer add to his self-exaltation over the earth—that is, over the Church—or even over his earthly possession and acquisition. Since this is the price of Christ’s blood, namely property offered to ecclesiastics for the support

[Col. 0785B] of those ministering to God and of Christ’s other poor, it is undoubtedly established that this same possession must be expended for the burial-place of strangers, in which Christ’s poor, strangers in this world, may rest, and that provision for their rest must be made from it.

This can happen in certain cases through such repentance of Simoniacs as Judas had, who, moved by repentance, returned the thirty pieces of silver, which we subsequently read were spent on a burial-place for strangers. Thus Judas’s repentance, although it was not fruitful for himself, was fruitful and useful for strangers, when Judas himself no longer added to his self-exaltation over the earth, over the field of blood bought for thirty pieces of silver—the price, that is, of the precious blood—for the burial of strangers.

[Col. 0785C] We have seen with our own eyes certain bishops invested by simoniacal kings who, moved by repentance, whether genuine or false, returned the price of blood—that is, the episcopate itself—to the lord apostolic, renouncing an administration to which they had not been canonically promoted. Having been in some measure purified by this satisfaction, they were again commanded by the lord apostolic to administer the temporal and spiritual goods of bishoprics. They then made from these goods such provision for the field as a burial-place for strangers that they became diligent builders and enrichers of monasteries, for the burial and rest of Christ’s poor strangers.

But the number of those who repent in this manner, whether truly or falsely, is so very small amid

[Col. 0785D] the great number of Simoniacs and others resembling Judas the trader, who exalt themselves over the earth, that the desire of the poor rightly pants and the preparations of their hearts burn vehemently in longing for this: that the number of penitents might be enlarged, bringing forth fruits worthy of repentance for the burial of strangers, and that no man might be found who continued to add to his self-exaltation upon the earth. Then those who truly repent and are truly humbled are saved; while those who repent falsely are strangled with Judas, the worst trader, their entrails poured out upon the ground—that is, their hidden things and uncleannesses disclosed—and they themselves hang between earth and heaven, deprived of both earthly and heavenly honor, because they presume to exalt themselves over the earth against God.

[Col. 0786A] This has happened to a very small extent, but the desire of the poor and the preparation of their heart stretch themselves intensely toward this: that, just as executioners having been humbled and heretics refuted, man no longer adds to his self-exaltation over the earth—that is, over the martyrs’ flesh honored with brilliant miracles and over confessors’ teaching flashing with testimonies of truth—so also, when worst and unclean traders, with Judas the trader, depart from the Lord’s supper, from the table of the Lord’s sacraments, and quickly do what they do—namely, cast away the price of blood and confess their sin—no such man may any longer add to his self-exaltation over the earth, that is, over any ecclesiastical dignity.

But let those alone, and all those, be great in the Church of whom the Apostle says: “Whom God foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. 8:29 ff.).

[Col. 0786B] Those whom, to put it in present terms, he predestined to become priests, bishops, or distinguished in another dignity, he also called by a divine or canonical vocation, as Ambrose, Martin, and men like them. And those whom he thus called he also justified, because he showed them to be righteous judges and men living justly in their dignities. Those whom he thus justified through merits, he also magnified with rewards. Those whom he justified so that they might live praiseworthily, he also magnified so that they might rule others authoritatively. Therefore none of such persons exalted himself over the earth;

[Col. 0786C] rather, while God magnified him, he humbled himself.

The desire of the poor therefore rightly burns for the multiplication of such persons. Rightly, the preparation of their heart is that Christ’s Church should be governed by those same rulers, whom Christ himself left as vicars of his work. If they are established as princes over all the earth, then the desire of the poor will be heard in such a way that man may no longer add to his self-exaltation over the earth. But although this must be fulfilled universally in the manifest judgment of the last examination, when everyone who exalts himself over the earth will be humbled, so that man may no longer add to his self-exaltation over the earth, nevertheless by Christ’s hidden comings—by which he daily visits and examines his Church, casting the mighty down from their seat and exalting the humble,

[Col. 0786D] establishing them as princes over all the earth—the desire of the poor is greatly gladdened. For according to the preparation of their heart, what is expected to occur universally in the approaching manifest judgment now occurs in great measure every day in the hidden judgments of the Son. As the Church sighs for these hidden things of the Son according to the title of this psalm, may the Lord so hear the desire of his poor that man may no longer add to his self-exaltation over the earth.

In Hebrew the title of this psalm is: “For the victor, concerning the death of the Son.” Such a title agrees very well with our meaning, because we bear witness to the victory over the death of the Son.
