For from the death by which he died in the flesh, he rose victorious and now lives, and the life of human beings rose with him.

[Col. 0787A] Again, from the death by which false witnesses crushed him when they refuted him as though he were a false witness, he rose victorious and multiplied witnesses of the truth, who would be witnesses for him in Jerusalem, throughout Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth. Likewise, from the death by which those who judged his flesh and blood to be like the corpse of a dead man put him to death in his sacraments, he prevailed victoriously when he showed himself to be so unlike flesh and blood that, for those who communicate in faith in the sacrament of his flesh and blood, he is the life-giving Spirit, according to the saying: “If, therefore, you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before: it is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:63).

For flesh considered carnally

[Col. 0787B] profits nothing. But because Christ’s flesh gives life—which is the work and office of the Spirit—it is rightly believed and called Spirit according to the power of its operation, because it does what none but the highest and life-giving Spirit can do. For it gives life to the holy Church and will present her alive on the day of judgment, so that man may no longer add to his self-exaltation over her. Nor is what we urge to be believed—that the flesh of the Word is to be believed Spirit—incredible. For if, as the Apostle declares, “he who is joined to the Lord is one Spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17), then much more excellently and divinely the flesh that adhered in God’s Word to the highest Spirit is the highest and one Spirit with him, so powerful to give life to the holy

[Col. 0787C] Church that the carnal man may no longer add to his self-exaltation over her.

In Hebrew it reads thus: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor;

[Col. 0788A] you have prepared their heart, that your ear may hear, and that you may judge the orphan and the oppressed, and that the man of earth may in no way continue to be proud.” Hebrew truth therefore supports our understanding, who desire that the longings of the poor and the preparation of their heart should be so satisfied that, by just judgment, the orphan and oppressed Christ—or Christian—may be exalted, so that the man of earth may no longer be proud. The man of earth is Antichrist. For “the first man is from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. As is the earthly man, such are the earthly; and as is the heavenly man, such are the heavenly. He who comes from heaven is above all” (1 Cor. 15:47 ff.). Hence it is fitting, consequent, and necessary that against him the man of earth should no longer be proud: the man wholly earthly,

[Col. 0788B] and therefore entirely opposed to the heavenly man who comes from heaven. Hence he is also called Antichrist, that is, one opposed to Christ. The blessed poor in spirit desire, according to the preparation of their heart, that he be humbled so that he may no longer add to his self-exaltation over the earth.

Glory to the Father, who begot the Son by a hidden generation. Glory to the Son, who sanctifies and governs his Church by hidden judgments, and who, having emerged victorious after death from his threefold passion, also grants victory over that threefold passion to his Church, which is his body. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who, in order that the hidden things of the Son may be manifested, or that the threefold victory over his death may be brought to completion, inflames the desire of the poor with unutterable groanings and makes it heard. Amen.

## PSALM X

[Col. 0787]

[Col. 0787C] “In the Lord I trust.” The title is as follows (VERSE 1):

**UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID.**

What “unto the end” means, what a psalm is, and how David is to be understood, is clear from the preceding psalms. Here an invective is directed against heretics, who cunningly lie in wait for the simplicity of the Church. Since they are sinners, since the fire of desire and the sulphur of evil works have been the portion of their cup and have intoxicated them, the Lord rains snares upon them, so that through Holy Scripture they may be ensnared in many ways—or rather, may understand it wrongly and interpret it wrongly. The intention is to exhort us to resist heretics in confidence in the Lord’s authority. The method of treatment is twofold. First, he states how heretics strive to draw good people into their perversity. Secondly, he explains what the Lord does to each party: he both rains snares upon sinners and his eyes look upon the poor. The order is inverted: before recounting what the heretics say to him, he answers by saying:

VERSE 2. “In the Lord I trust; how do you say

[Col. 0788C] to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’?” From this answer, then, one understands what the heretics say to the Catholic man, namely, that they urge him to flee to the mountain—that is, to the lofty eminence of their doctrines. The opening of the psalm teaches what should be answered them; it is this: “In

[Col. 0788D] the Lord I trust.” Therefore, however many curses and evil persuasions you bring forward against me, I hope for blessing in return, because I trust in the Lord. For it is written: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence. For he shall be like a tree transplanted beside the waters, which sends its roots toward moisture and shall not fear when the heat comes. Its leaf shall be green; in the season of drought it shall not be anxious, nor shall it ever cease to bear fruit” (Jer. 17:7 ff.). This is the blessing of the man who trusts in the Lord, and, hoping to be blessed in this way, I trust in the Lord.

But you are men. For while jealousy and contention are among you, are you not men? Are you not carnal? Since you are carnal and merely natural men, having jealousy and contention among you, is it not wholly unfitting that we should trust in you or in your doctrines and abandon the Lord’s judgment? The Lord says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat; therefore observe and do everything that they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:2–3). Therefore, although you are men, although you are carnal, I would gladly hear you and gladly obey you if you sat on Moses’ seat, teaching lawfully even though you did not live lawfully.

But now, because you sit “in the seat of pestilence,” blessed is the man “who has not walked in your counsel, nor stood in your way, nor sat in your seat, but trusts in the Lord; whose delight is in the law of the Lord, and who meditates in his law day and night. He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which gives its fruit in its season” (Ps. 1:1–2, 4), and, according to Jeremiah’s prophecy cited above, shall never cease to bear fruit.

[Col. 0789A] “The Lord overturned the seats of those selling doves and cast down the tables of money-changers” (Matt. 21:12). Since, then, I see that you are sellers of doves, who make the Lord’s tables—that is, Christ’s altars—into tables of money-changers for yourselves, how do you say to my soul that, by standing reverently before your seat and partaking at your tables, I should withdraw from the Lord in whom I trust? It is the Lord who says to me through his apostle Paul: “Do not share in the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, rebuke them” (Eph. 5:11). But you urge me to depart from this judgment of the Lord and to communicate indiscriminately at every table, whether of heretics, Simoniacs, or Catholic priests.

And although, trusting in the Lord, I set forth the reasonable decree of the Roman pontiffs, sitting on the chair of Peter and Moses, which severely proscribes as though they were the sin of divination all masses of clerics manifestly guilty of incest and Simony, and forbids anyone to hear them, you nevertheless say to my soul: “Flee to the mountain”—that is, to the eminence of our doctrines. Hold the opinion of learned men, distinguished masters, who subtly maintain that one must communicate indiscriminately at all masses so long as any bishop tolerates in his diocese a priest however openly incestuous and simoniacal.

[Col. 0789B] Christ in Peter, and Peter in his vicar, tells me: Do not hear such men; do not receive the forbidden offices of such men. But some learned master tells me, as though Augustine the Father favored him, that no injury should be done to a sacrament. They think that injury is done to the sacrament if, on account of an unworthy minister, the inviolable sacrament is despised; for though it does not bring salvation to those who administer it wickedly, it nevertheless retains its power for those who partake in simplicity.

Why, then, do they not attend to what that same Father says: Each person’s sin is tolerated in the Church until it either finds an accuser or is defended by an obstinate disposition in a wicked opinion? But the simoniacal and incestuous Nicolaitans, defending with obstinate disposition not so much a wicked opinion as a wicked manner of life, could no longer be tolerated and were canonically forbidden. This judgment indeed concerns manifest cases; God is knower and judge of hidden matters.

But you heretics, greatly dissenting from the Roman Church, summon me to your seat, upon which you sit in the temple of God, exalting yourselves “above every thing that is called God or is worshipped” (2 Thess. 2:4), so that I may rely on the mountainous magnitude of your authority—tolerating everything you tolerate, overlooking what you overlook, and communicating at the forbidden masses at which you communicate. But I trust in the Lord;

[Col. 0790A] and, just as I do not wish to trust in man, in the authority of any human being, so neither do I wish to place my confidence so as to withdraw from the Lord. For it is written: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, makes flesh his arm, and whose heart withdraws from the Lord. For he shall be like a tamarisk in the wilderness and shall not see when good comes, but shall dwell in dryness, in the desert, in a land of salt and uninhabitable” (Jer. 17:5–6). For this reason I do not wish to trust in man in such a way that my heart departs from Christ’s authority.

But you say to my soul—indeed, your persuasion is directed to my soul—because, now that tyrants have been humbled and their cruelty, by which bodies were killed, has been overcome through the triumphs of the martyrs, you heretics seek to kill not bodies but souls. Hence you say to my soul, which you seek to kill: “Flee to the mountain,” that is, to our authority. Or, “Flee to the mountain,” that is, to Christ, who is with us. You say this as though you alone possessed Christ. You say, I mean, “Flee like a bird,” because if I did so I would be like an unstable bird. Or, “like a sparrow,” that is, like a spiritual person having the wings of virtues. In speaking this way and calling me a sparrow, you send arrows into the heart through itching ears.

VERSE 3. “For behold, sinners have bent their bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot the upright in heart in darkness.” In saying this, he makes an apostrophe, turning away from the unbelieving heretics to the faithful. The Apostle teaches that heretics are to be avoided after a first and second admonition (Titus 3:10).

[Col. 0790D] The first admonition, as it were, was his statement, “In the Lord I trust”; the second, his addition, “How do you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’?” Now, having condemned them by their own judgment, as men who defend their evils artfully and thereby shoot the souls of their hearers, he turns away and speaks to the faithful, warning them to beware. “For,” he says, “behold, sinners have bent their bow.” Behold, in public, manifest sinners—manifest Simoniacs and Nicolaitans forbidden because of manifest crimes. Behold, these sinners, flourishing in this world, have obtained bodily and spiritual riches. For they possess churches and know the Scriptures; and thus they have made and bent a bow from the Scriptures of the Old and New Testament, twisting and bending their meaning toward themselves in accordance with their error.

Because this psalm is entitled “unto the end,” it is not absurd to interpret either it or other psalms so entitled in such a way as to adapt the words of the psalms to the things now occurring near the end of the world, for us “upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). This is not done, as heretics do, by bringing the text from its own meaning into our meaning, but by expounding the spontaneous agreement found both in the words of the psalms and in the events of our own times.

[Col. 0791A] Thus Augustine, the august and eminent teacher, while expounding the Psalms in his homilies, observed many matters fitting the events of his own time. In his times, although many heretics had gone out from us who were not of us—Arians, Donatists, and others, whom the same Father taught should be avoided—yet Judas, the worst trader and unclean man, was still within. Concerning him, after the Lord had said to the disciples, “You are now clean,” he added: “But not all. For he knew who would betray him; therefore he said, ‘You are not all clean’” (John 13:10–11).

Therefore this worst trader and unclean man had not yet gone out in the time of the martyrs and holy confessors, because it was day. But after he had been marked by the manifest decrees of pontiffs as the betrayer of Christ—the one who dips his hand in the dish—immediately, when Satan entered him, “he went out” (John 19:5) from hidden lurking-places to open markets. It was night when he went out, because, as darkness prevailed, the worst trader who sold or bought churches and ecclesiastical things was scarcely recognized as such.

[Col. 0791B] The unclean man who had a wife or concubine while in the priesthood was likewise scarcely recognized. But now behold: from the time of the younger Nicholas, through Nicholas himself, Leo IX, Alexander II, Gregory VII, and other Roman pontiffs, Christ has cast his betrayer, the unclean man, out in the Simoniacs and Nicolaitans. Therefore, just as Judas, after he went out, had no fellowship with the disciples in any apostolic ministry, but rather joined Christ’s killers, so, after the manifest condemnation of manifest Simony or sexual incontinence, Simoniacs or Nicolaitans, by celebrating forbidden offices, crucify Christ anew and, so far as lies in them, kill him. Since, therefore, they celebrate their offices through disobedience, which Samuel testifies is the sin of idolatry (1 Kings 15:23), we judge participation in their forbidden offices to be avoided as idolatry. For the Apostolic See has also forbidden any Christian to presume to hear their masses where their Simony, incontinence, and disobedience are manifestly known.

Let the great masters of the schools now go, who in their treatment of this psalm introduce Blessed Augustine, wishing through him to prove that the masses of all priests should be heard indiscriminately. Let them go, I say,

[Col. 0792A] and see to what time the saying of that blessed Father applies. For in his exposition of this verse, “For they have destroyed what you have perfected; but what has the righteous man done?” (Ps. 20:3), according to Blessed Augustine’s own sense it is said: “If heretics have offended, what has the righteous man—that is, Christ—done to you? Did he not leave us peace? Did he not patiently tolerate Judas? Did he not make the thief and betrayer, whom he even called a devil, a preacher with the disciples, in order to show that God’s gifts can reach those who receive in faith through such persons, even if the person through whom they receive is like Judas?”

We rightly commend this meaning of Blessed Augustine as fitted to his own time. For he speaks of Judas before he had been cast out, before he had been strangled by the noose of his own snare. And we, in accordance with this teaching, tolerate thieves, robbers, and unclean persons within the Church in the communion or celebration of sacraments, for the sake of the peace Christ left us. But after we see Judas, on account of such crimes, suspended from office by the noose of prohibition, and his entrails spilled upon the ground—that is, his shameful deeds made manifest—then, avoiding the offices of such persons as a dead, unclean, and foul-smelling corpse, we do nothing contrary to Blessed Augustine. Rather, we imitate him, who carefully abstained from Donatists, Circumcellions, and other heretics of his time after they had been excluded, and did not communicate with them in sacramental celebrations.

[Col. 0792B] Yet he recognized as valid the sacraments of baptism and ordination conferred by them upon persons returning to the Church, because they were healed in those who returned from heresy to the Church either by the same laying on of hands or by reception into Catholic peace.

Let learned masters now pardon us if we adapt the words of the Psalms to the course of our own time, just as Blessed Augustine continually observed alongside his exposition of the Psalms the course of his own time. For if heretics of every age have bent their bow—that is, Holy Scripture—toward their error, and those who are heretics now, the Simoniacs and Nicolaitans, do not cease to twist the bow according to their own meaning by corrupting the Scriptures, why should it not be permitted us to use those same Scriptures to refute their perverse interpretations? We use them not as a bow violently bent crosswise, but as a two-edged and double-sharpened sword.

[Col. 0792C] For we do not endeavor to deflect the Scriptures from their meaning, but speak what has been given to us to the glory of the Giver. We do not compare or prefer our writings to those of great masters, but desire to satisfy the devout longing of those who request this work from us as a certain refreshment from the very rich pastures of the shepherd David, and as a consoling dish seasoned with the salt of justice. To those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, that it may be sweeter and more savory, we do not violently force an alien meaning from the Psalms, but, speaking in harmony with the Fathers and at times refuting the heresies of our own day, we maintain the meaning which voluntarily and spontaneously presents itself.

But heretics have bent the bow—that is, Scripture. Others, who understand it simply, possess it as an unbent bow; heretics are said to bend it when, in their own estimation, they discover in it a subtler meaning. “They have prepared their arrows in the quiver.” From the Scriptures themselves they have prepared revered and poisoned words in the quiver—that is, in their dark heart—so that they may shoot the upright in heart in darkness: concealing themselves in a woodland thicket after the manner of robbers, so that from the very thicket of their most wicked heart, where beasts have their hiding-places, where foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, they may commit robberies and from there shoot those upright in heart—that is, upright in will.

[Col. 0793B] For just as persons of evil will have a distorted heart, so persons of good will are themselves persons upright in heart.

And, to turn our attention to the heretics of our own time: are not those sinners who have been interdicted for manifest simony or incontinence, when they prepare themselves to celebrate forbidden offices—for example, to sing Mass—then, I say, under the name of Mass, drawing the bow from which they shoot poisoned arrows? For if the tree forbidden in Paradise poisoned those who ate its fruits—not because the tree was evil by nature, but through disobedience—how much more do these men, singing in disobedience and communicating in disobedience to those who likewise disobey, because of this twofold disobedience, serve death rather than life in their offices? [Col. 0793C] For when the Lord says of such persons, “I will curse your blessings, and I will bless your curses” (Mal. 2:2), should not their words be regarded as arrows of curses when, in their interdicted Masses, they bless the people? Is not the interdicted Mass itself like a quiver full of poisoned arrows? Hence Pope Innocent says, among other things, in his Letter to Alexander, bishop of Antioch:

> [Note: [Col. 0793D] Cause 1, question 1, chapter *Ventum est*.]  
> “Those ordained by heretics have their head wounded by that imposition of hands. But where a wound has been inflicted, medicine must be applied, by which health may be recovered; and that health which follows the wound cannot be without a scar.”

Does not this Roman Pontiff, by speaking thus, teach that the ordination of heretics is to be avoided as though it were a quiver, or [Col. 0793D] a bow, from which wounds are to be feared?

But since these statements seem to concern Arians and other heretics of that age, let us see whether anything similar is said from the lofty watchtower of the apostolic see against the heretics of our own time, namely Nicolaitans and Simoniacs, by which their bow and quiver are shown to inflict wounds. Pope Nicholas the Younger, presiding over a synod in the church of Constantinople, set as a watchman in a lofty watchtower and seeing the sword, the quiver, and the bow coming, takes care to render every Christian cautious and forearmed against the wounds of Simoniacs, saying among other things:

> “Concerning Simoniacs, we decree that no mercy is to be shown in preserving their rank; rather, according to the sanction of the canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers, we utterly condemn them.”

Likewise:

> “Henceforth, if anyone permits himself to be consecrated by one whom he does not doubt to be a Simoniac, both consecrator and consecrated shall undergo an equal sentence of condemnation; both, having been deposed, shall do penance and remain deprived of their own rank.”

Likewise the notable watchman Pope Urban II, standing in the lofty watchtower, cries to Herman, bishop of Metz:

> “Do not permit those who sell and buy ecclesiastical offices, and priests, deacons, and subdeacons who are married, so long as they remain in their error, to possess any power of their ordination.”

Pope Alexander II, an [Col. 0794B] eminent watchman, says thus:

> “We command by precept that no one hear the Masses of a priest whom he knows beyond doubt to have a concubine or a woman introduced into his household. For the holy synod has deprived such a disgrace—whether deacon or subdeacon—of his office; and let all who are in canonical orders have no wives, and, if they take wives, let them be deposed. Let churches and altars neither be sold nor bought; and those who henceforth sell or buy them shall lie under anathema. Let churches consecrated for a price or by Simoniacs be consecrated anew. Let priests ordained knowingly by Simoniacs from the time of Pope Nicholas until now, and hereafter, know that they are deposed.”

But Gregory VII sounded the trumpet like an angel, because [Col. 0794C] he saw the sword not so much coming as imminent. He says therefore:

> “If there are any priests, deacons, or subdeacons lying in the crime of fornication, we forbid them, on the part of Almighty God and by the authority of Saint Peter, entrance into the Church until they repent and amend their lives. But if any should prefer to persevere in their sin, let none of you dare to hear their office; for their blessing is turned into a curse, and their prayer into sin, as the Lord testifies through the prophet: ‘I will curse your blessings’ (1 Sam. 15:23). But those who refuse to obey this most salutary command incur the sin of idolatry, as Samuel testifies and blessed Gregory teaches: ‘To refuse obedience is the sin of divination, and to refuse compliance is the crime of idolatry.’ Therefore whoever, while calling himself a Christian, despises obedience to the apostolic see incurs [Col. 0794D] the sin of paganism.”

The voice of the watchmen sounded aloud in the decrees set forth above, so that everyone who hears interdicted offices may strive to avoid them as a quiver and a bow—as instruments of death.

Yet these accursed and interdicted men, through their forbidden offices, draw the bow and prepare arrows, in order to shoot in darkness—that is, amid the ambiguous and obscure mystery of iniquity, with their business of impiety and filthiness somewhat veiled. At whom do they shoot? At those upright in heart, upright in will. “The word of God,” they say, “cannot be defiled; the grace of God cannot be prevented [Col. 0795A] from producing its effects, even through ministers like Judas the traitor.” We plainly agree with those who say this, but in the sense defined above, where we showed the distinction between Judas and Judas. For, as has been shown before, no derogation was ever made from the offices of Judas the traitor, tolerated among the apostles. Likewise, no derogation was ever made from the offices of Simoniacs and fornicating clerics while they were still tolerated in their ministry, that is, before they had been interdicted by apostolic commands.

But now, after the heavens revealed the iniquity of Judas and the earth rose up against him; after that most wicked merchant, in some fashion suspended from office, burst asunder in the middle and his entrails were spilled upon the ground: the forbidden offices of him and his like are to be avoided according to [Col. 0795B] the aforementioned decretal commands of the Fathers. Therefore, even if they draw their bow and prepare arrows, even if they thrust their forbidden offices upon us, we, with God’s assent, shall hold forth the shield of apostolic authority and shall not allow their arrows to reach our heart. And knowing this, they avoid us and shoot in darkness—that is, in a darkened meaning, obscured for carnal and unlearned persons—lying in wait, namely, for the simple common people.

Another translation has: “In the dark moon,” by which expression the weak and dark members of the Church are signified. For the Church is figured by the moon, as was noted in the eighth Psalm and must here be explained more fully. There are two opinions about the moon, and which is true cannot be known at all, or can be known only with difficulty. [Col. 0795C] Some say that it has light of its own, but that one half of its globe is bright and the other half dark. When it gradually turns toward the earth the part that shines, so that it may be seen, it appears horned and thus increases until that part is seen in its entirety. When it turns again, the dark part begins to appear, until the whole is again withdrawn from our sight. This is the Church: it shines in its spiritual part and is dark in its carnal part. And the spiritual part is at one time visible to human beings, at another hidden in a conscience known to God alone, though it is seen only in the body.

Others say that it has no light except from the sun; but when it is near the sun, it presents toward us that side which is not seen by the sun and therefore does not shine. But when it withdraws, it is illuminated on that side which it has toward [Col. 0795D] us, until, as the sun sets, it rises full in the east. But when it begins to approach the sun from the other side, the upper part is illuminated and the lower darkened. This too suits the Church, which has no light except from the Sun of righteousness. Perhaps what has been said about the moon will seem too obscure to some. If it is not pleasing, it is enough to observe the moon’s waxing and waning; for when it wanes in order to be renewed, it also signifies the Church, which, when it has failed through dying, shall be raised again. Thus far it has been said how the Church is signified by the moon. Now it must be said how darkness is signified by that same moon, in which heretics shoot.

The moon is darkened in three ways: either when it comes to the end of its monthly [Col. 0796A] course and the new moon has not yet appeared; or when it is obscured by cloud; or during an eclipse, when it appears blood-red. Likewise, the Church was darkened while still new, when, at the beginning of the faith, it had not yet shone greatly upon the earth. Again, when it is reviled by the clouds of blasphemers, it is dark; or when it is bloodied by the slaughter of martyrs. In this darkness heretics shoot, because they know that such times are suitable for deceiving the weak. When these are overthrown, they think that they will draw even the upright in heart to themselves.

Or the ministers of the Church, while they sin, are called the dark moon in which heretics shoot, when they reproach the Church’s sacraments as administered through such persons. By this they deceive some weak people, when they suggest that the merits of ministers should be considered. But the one who trusts in the Lord need fear nothing; let him fear who trusts in a human being. [Col. 0796B] For so great is the power of consecration that it cannot be impeded by evil ministers, provided that consecration is performed through them and not desecration. For as long as someone who possesses the office of consecrating exercises it without the Church’s objection, he consecrates—that is, he makes holy together with the Church, to which Christ has granted the power of consecration.

But if he has been excommunicated or deprived of office by the judgment of his judge—that is, of his bishop, archbishop, primate, or apostolic lord, whose office it is to judge concerning the whole Church and every person—then, if unreconciled, he performs an office forbidden to him, he does not consecrate but desecrates. Therefore one who receives such an office does not trust in the Lord but [Col. 0796C] in a human being, because he thinks that a human being separated from the Lord can accomplish anything, whereas the Lord himself says: “Without me you can do nothing. As” a “branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me” (John 15:5).

But whoever receives a ministry not interdicted through any kind of minister trusts in the Lord, whom he honors in the minister, though unworthy, provided that the minister holds the office of rank without lawful objection. For the holy Church, partly reigning in heaven and partly journeying on earth, there shines as the sun; here it changes, now bright and now dark, like the moon. Indeed, in good prelates it is the full moon, the Paschal moon, the perfect moon, by which the night of this age is illumined as the day of eternity; by which the evening of the Sabbath shines into the first day of the Sabbath; and, as we read in Isaiah, the light of this “moon is like the light of the sun” (Isa. 30:26). For it shines not only through the dignity of offices but also, which is higher, through the dignity of merits; and, as though looking upon the sun along a diameter and directly, it has borrowed full light from it, just as a mirror receives the full image of a person’s face when it is placed directly before that face.

But where there is the dignity of offices alone without the dignity of merits, there is a dark moon. Yet it is a moon: indeed placed far below the sun, but raised above the earth by the eminence of rank. If it is deposed, when it clings to the dragon’s tail which draws down a third part of the stars, and thus also loses the eminence [Col. 0797A] of rank, it is no longer to be called a moon, nor received in offices of lost rank or forbidden office.

Let no one be disturbed because we say that a reprobate minister is to be honored on account of the dignity of his office, although he lacks the dignity of merits. For almost all honor for merits is deferred to the future, as Scripture says: “Do not praise a person during his life” (Ecclus. 11:30). Thus honor is to be rendered in the present life to the dignities of offices. Hence it often happens in the present Church that saints are without honor in this world—needy, distressed, afflicted—though the world is worthy to have them preside over ecclesiastical or secular dignities; while those whom the world deserves are exalted in this world through dignities. But in the future judgment there will be such a reversal that “the last shall be first, and the first last” (Matt. 19:30). For those who, lacking merits, were first in the dignities and honors of the present life will then be last; and those who, possessing the merits for dignities, were regarded in this life as last and almost unworthy of dignities will then be first.

For since divine grace distinguishes its gifts into merits and rewards—excepting infants and others who can merit nothing—among all who are capable of meriting, honor will be rendered in the future according to the degrees of their merits. The Gospel testifies to this, where the Lord answers the good servant who says, “Lord, your mina has made five minas”: “And you, be over five [Col. 0797C] cities” (Luke 19:18–19). Likewise, to another saying, “Lord, your mina has made ten minas,” the answer is: “And you, be over ten cities.” Therefore, as has been said, in the future there will be distinction of rewards and honors according solely to the distinctions of merits.

Yet this comparison of present merits and future honors must be weighed according to quality, not quantity. For regarding quantity it is evident that the quantity of future rewards and honors surpasses the quantity of merits beyond estimation, because “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18), as the Apostle says, when the “eternal weight [Col. 0797D] of glory beyond measure” (2 Cor. 4:17) will be wrought “in us by that which” is now “a momentary and light tribulation.” Through this tribulation, as Peter says, it is necessary that we now suffer a little, “so that the testing of your faith may be found much more precious than gold tested by fire” (1 Pet. 1:7). By this fire the crown of future dignities, to be worthily conferred only upon the worthy, is now fashioned even from this very torment which good persons endure because dignities are conferred in this world upon the unworthy—dignities which ought to be conferred only upon the worthy, were better dignities not reserved for the former in heaven.

But since present dignities sometimes increase and sometimes diminish the merits of future goods—and the former happens rarely, the latter frequently—holy persons, who take the greatest care for the increase [Col. 0798A] of merit, which commonly grows in a low position, and who greatly fear the loss of merits, which commonly occurs in a high position, prefer to be saved humbly in a high place rather than be endangered in a high one. Thus they flee honors in this world, not hypocritically but with their whole heart, although honor itself, well administered, and rank worthily held, sometimes contributes to an increase of merits.

But because this happens very rarely, honor is indeed to be accepted in fear through obedience, should the Lord say, “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14:10); yet it is never to be sought. And when someone desiring the episcopate desires not honor but “a good work” (1 Tim. 3:1), let him nevertheless observe the rule drawn from the saints: one rich in virtues should approach honor under compulsion; one lacking virtues, not even under compulsion. For, as the Apostle affirms, no one takes honor to himself, “but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. 5:4). And if a virtuous person takes honor to himself, according to his own understanding, his honor will not be honor according to the apostolic understanding; rather, he himself will be a dark moon, in whose darkness robbers keep watch in order to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart. For when the moon shines fully, robbers do not dare to come out.

But if a person lacking virtues is advanced to honors even against his will, under compulsion from others, because he has been promoted not by divine but human compulsion, then much more does he, like a dark moon, afford robbers an opportunity to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart. This darkness [Col. 0798C] will befall them by your just judgment, Lord, in whom I trust, because they did not approve of having you in love and knowledge. Therefore they were given up to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting. And those who chose such men and wished them to be set over themselves—because they did not receive you when you came in the name of the Father, nor strove to honor you in your least ones—therefore chose others opposed to you and set them over themselves, blinded by your just judgment and having a darkened heart, shot in their own darkness and subjected to Antichrist, your adversary, as themselves adversaries. For they are adversaries to you.

### Verse 4. For they have destroyed what you perfected.

“You perfected your praise out of the mouths of infants and nursing children” [Col. 0798D] (Ps. 8:4). They destroyed this praise. When the scribes and Pharisees, plotting your death, rejected you, the chosen stone, the children of the Hebrews, like infants and nursing children unaware of what they were doing, carried palm branches as a sign of victory and royal triumph and sang royal praises to you: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; Hosanna to the Son of David. Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that comes; hosanna in the highest” (Matt. 21:9). While those infants and nursing children cried these things in praise of you, you, who stirred them by your Spirit to say them, perfected through the mouths of those infants the divine proclamations of your praise.

But these men destroyed what you perfected, because they both crucified you yourself in your flesh and reviled you in your members by persecuting your least ones; and they praised your enemies and raised them by their praises to royal or priestly dignity. And they always strive to accomplish this: that you may not be praised, that you may not be exalted in your least ones, that you may not administer priesthood or kingship in your least ones. They desire that you should always lie oppressed beneath chief priests like Annas and Caiaphas and beneath judges like Herod and Pilate, as though you were not the king and high priest to whom alone—because you came in the name of the Lord—the honor due from all ought reverently to be rendered.

You also, in some fashion, perfected praise from the mouths of the apostles, who were like infants because they were fishermen and simple persons, when they praised and chose Stephen, a man full of faith [Col. 0799B] and the Holy Spirit. Thus they gave a model for election to ecclesiastical dignities: that those especially should be chosen and praised who were found full of faith and the Holy Spirit. But these men destroyed your institutions, which you perfected through the mouths of the apostles, when they shouted praises for flesh and blood—which shall not inherit the kingdom of God—because of worldly nobility or some other earthly reason, advancing to honors persons resembling Annas and Caiaphas, or Herod and Pilate. Thus they destroyed what you perfected by praising what you do not praise.

But what did the righteous person do? Did the righteous person, trusting in the Lord, agree with the unrighteous who were destroying God’s praise? Far be it! What then did he do when he saw the wicked prevail in promoting some ungodly person or asserting falsehood? What, I say, did that righteous man do, who was unwilling to become unrighteous by praising an unjust person or declaring him righteous for gifts? Since he would not assent to falsehood as though it were truth, in order to remain righteous, what did he do? Hear what he did. He believed in his heart unto righteousness and confessed with his mouth unto salvation. Namely, he believed and confessed that because evil persons rule in the Church, because falsehood is raised up and truth oppressed, the Lord himself does not abandon his Church.

Indeed, he abandons the house of those to whom he says: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate. You shall not see me henceforth until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’” (Matt. 23:38–39). That is: You shall not see me, you shall not have me merciful or [Col. 0799D] propitious, until, in praising me or my own, you say in harmony with those praises which you destroyed when you praised the ungodly for gifts, and which I perfected from the mouths of infants and nursing children who came to meet me with palms and said, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (ibid., 39).

Those who do not agree with this praise and who destroy it, so far as lies in them, because they do not wish him to be exalted or blessed as high priest or king “who comes in the name of the Lord,” shall have “their house left desolate” (Isa. 1:6); for where simony and uncleanness reign, the grace of the Holy Spirit flees. Nevertheless:

### Verse 5. The Lord is in his holy temple,

namely, in the saints, whom he himself makes into his temple. The Lord [Col. 0800A] is in heaven, which heaven is his throne. For the soul of the righteous person is the throne of wisdom, and wisdom itself, which is God, says: “Heaven is my throne” (Acts 7:19). Therefore, in the great saints, as in his temple and as in heaven, the Lord himself sits. And from there his eyes look upon the poor person, that is, upon any faithful person lower than the temple and heaven.

This is what the righteous person says; this is what the righteous person believes to be so; and he receives great consolation from it when the unjust person is exalted by the favor of evil persons. For he knows that, however greatly evil persons may be exalted and multiplied, nevertheless the Lord is in his holy temple, the Lord is in heaven, as has already been explained.

Otherwise: You who destroyed the praise which the Lord perfected from the mouths of infants were unwilling, and still are unwilling, to commend the righteous, because perhaps the righteous offended and offend you. Their unjust works displease the righteous; and, by not joining in them but rather reproving them, the righteous become troublesome to you, perhaps because they exceed due measure in rebuking you. But what did that one righteous person, namely Christ, who is righteous in a unique manner, do? What evil did he ever inflict upon you? How did he provoke your anger against himself, that you should destroy what he perfected? How did he deserve that you should exalt his enemies against him, always striving for this: that his enemy should sit in his holy temple, displaying himself as if he were God?

Nevertheless, whether you wish it or not, the Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord is in heaven. Just as it is true that the Lord is in the temple—the Word in the flesh—so it is true that the Lord, that is, the human being assumed into God, is in heaven. You cannot depose him from there, although in his temple, which is the present Church, you can exalt Antichrist or any one of his ministers to oppress the poor. But since the Lord, protector of the poor, is now in heaven, and his throne is there—for he sits there upon the cherubim and the thrones, judging righteousness—from there his eyes look upon the poor. From that invisible court of eternity, in which all these temporal matters are ordered, the Lord Jesus, whose praise you destroyed, looks upon the poor.

For since nothing occurs in this world which is not either permitted or commanded from there by Christ, to whom “all authority in heaven and on earth has been given” [Col. 0800D] (Matt. 28:18), his eyes look upon the poor person oppressed by you in such a way that he permits nothing to occur in this world except what is good for each one of his poor. “For all things work together for good to those who are called saints according to his purpose” (Rom. 8:28). They are called, namely, by the calling of Christ himself, who says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart; and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29). Upon these poor persons, thus called by Christ who sits in his holy temple—who sits, that is, reigns and judges in heaven—his eyes of mercy always look.

[Col. 0801A] Otherwise: You, God the Father, perfected the praise of Christ your Son from the mouths of infants and nursing children. But those things which you perfected, they destroyed: those who blasphemed, spat upon, and crucified him, or unjustly oppressed any one of his disciples. It is too little for them merely to destroy, or to have destroyed, what you perfected; for they build up and, so far as is in them, perfect what you destroyed. For you perfected royal praise over your Son, our Savior, from the mouths of infants and nursing children so that, when he reigns and saves us, you might “destroy the enemy and avenger” (Ps. 8:3), or defender: the enemy of your law, the defender of his own law; the enemy of righteousness, the defender of his own injustice; and the avenger, always inflicting vengeance with evil intent, although sometimes against his will he serves justice by his vengeance.

Such an enemy, such a defender or avenger, you, God the Father, destroy when you uphold the high priesthood and kingship of your Son. But these men build up, magnify, and exalt that same enemy, when they acclaim as one to be exalted, or proclaim in due order as exalted, as high priest or king, a man known to be an enemy of your just law and a defender of his own unjust law.

But what did the righteous person do? All of you who have ears to hear have heard how evil builders rage by rejecting that stone which God the Father fitted to be placed “as the head of the corner” (Ps. 117:22) and laid beneath in the foundation, so that he who descended and ascended might fill all things. [Col. 0801C] You have heard how they strive to destroy this stone by dissipating his laws and constructing their own unjust laws. The unrighteous indeed acted thus. But what did the righteous God the Father do? Did he too cast down this stone and reject it from himself? Far be it! Rather, the Lord of all is in his temple; the Lord Father is in the Lord Son, as the Son himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10).

Even when this temple, perfected by the Lord, was destroyed through the impious hands of the Jews, nevertheless the Lord was in his temple. For although the soul of Christ left his flesh in the tasting of death, the divinity of the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit did not withdraw the fullness of its indwelling either from Christ’s soul [Col. 0801D] or from his flesh. For the human being made God, born into God and not adopted, remained God before death, in death, and after death, and remains God always; because the Lord is so in this his temple that the temple itself is Lord. The Lord is so in this his heaven, namely in the human being conceived and born from heaven, that heaven itself is Lord. In this heaven is the Lord’s throne, because in him dwells bodily all the fullness of divinity. Hence:

The eyes of the Lord do not see this poor one—Christ, made needy for us and among us—from afar, but look upon him from near; nor do they ever close to him the gaze of their love, because he is the only-begotten in the bosom of the Father. Without any garment of any sin or creature intervening, he is always seen [Col. 0802A] by the Father, and sees the Father ordering all things through him. The Lord sees with eyes open and never to be closed this uniquely poor one for our sake, this singular Son of Man, Son of the Virgin.

But his eyelids test the children of men. The eyelids of God test the children of men—called his children because they have been renewed from the oldness of the ancients. For the Lord has, as it were, closed eyes in the obscure places of Scripture, but open eyes in the plain places. This closing and opening of light in the Scriptures are therefore called the eyelids of God, which test the children of men—that is, prove them—because they are exercised by obscurities and are not puffed up by plain passages. Again, the closing of the eyelids occurs when some heresy grows strong; their opening, when truth is made manifest.

Or the Lord closes [Col. 0802B] his eyelids when he permits the wicked and children of darkness to rule, when he permits sins or the punishments of sins to abound; but he opens those same eyelids when he exalts the good in the holy Church, when, driving away sins and the punishments of sins through the regard of his grace, he makes the sorrow of the elect turn to joy and the night shine as day. Thus he sometimes closes and sometimes opens his eyelids.

### Verse 6. He tests the righteous and the wicked,

because through such alternations both the righteous person is proved and the wicked person reproved: when the righteous person is neither broken by adversity nor exalted or corrupted by prosperity, whereas the wicked person murmurs against God in adversity and in prosperity magnifies not God but himself, expanding in pleasures. Thus also, in the passion of Christ himself, when his eyelids were closed through death, the world rejoiced while the disciples mourned, and were thereby tested. In the resurrection likewise, when the eyelids were opened and the light of immortality shone brightly in Christ, the wicked mourned and the disciples’ sorrow was turned into joy.

And in the Passion Christ’s eyelids were closed to Peter when he denied him; but when the eyelids were opened, the Lord looked upon Peter and he wept bitterly. So also even now his eyelids test the children of men. And he tests not only the good, whom we call children of men, but universally “tests every human being coming into this world, righteous and wicked” (John 1:9); for [Col. 0802D] his light, with the eyelids opened, shines even in darkness. But the darkness—that is, minds friendly to darkness and sins—does not comprehend it (ibid.), does not embrace it, does not love it, because it does not even love itself. This is evident from the fact that it loves iniquity. But whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul, because through the iniquity he loves, the soul is lost.

In the Hebrew truth it is read thus: “The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord, his throne is in heaven. His eyes see; his eyelid tests the children of men. The Lord tests the righteous; but his soul hates the wicked and the one who loves iniquity.” The literal sense is plain, unless perhaps it appears obscure that the soul of the Lord is said to hate the wicked, whereas the Lord, who is wholly spirit, does not have a soul, [Col. 0803A] nor can hatred befall him, to whom it is most truly said: “But you, O Lord, judge in tranquility and order all things with great reverence” (Wis. 12:18).

But this manner of speaking about the Lord is not uncommon: he is said to have anger, fury, or hatred, not because such disturbance occurs in him, but because the wicked person who is tormented thinks that the Lord has anger or fury against him, whereas he does in tranquility what he does when he punishes in the wicked not what he himself made but what they themselves have made. For he hates none of the things which he made, whether in wicked or righteous persons (Wis. 11:25). But because he is eternal goodness, to which wickedness is contrary—and he did not make wickedness; rather, human beings and angels who fell away from goodness made it by their own falling away—God, who is good by nature, punishes and hates it; and his soul, that is, his intention, hates it.

For the soul of God is understood as his intention, just as his arm is understood as his strength, although God, being altogether simple, has neither soul nor arm, nor other human limbs or human affections. For the essence of divinity is simple. Yet human words, assigned metaphorically by means of limbs and affections which they signify, express—or rather obscurely indicate—divine operations: for example, God’s eyes signify that nothing is hidden from him; his hand, that he works all things; and so the divine operation is indicated by other human words and limbs. Therefore it was well said in the Hebrew truth: “The Lord tests the righteous; but his soul hates the wicked [Col. 0803C] and the one who loves iniquity.” Therefore:

### Verse 7. He rains snares upon sinners.

The apostles and prophets are clouds, watering souls with the rain of God’s word. But from these clouds the Lord rains early and latter rain upon the good. From them he also rains snares upon sinners—that is, ensnaring words—so that they are ensnared in many ways through sacred Scripture by understanding it wrongly and interpreting it wrongly. Why is this? Namely because fire, sulphur, and the spirit of storms are the portion of their cup. The fire of lust, the sulphur of evil deeds, and the spirit of storms—that is, the tempest of hellish punishments—are the portion of their cup. Or the spirit of storms is found in their turbulent disputes. Hence, by God’s just judgment, they are ensnared in their expositions [Col. 0804A] by inextricable snares of error.

And all these evils are a portion of their cup, a portion of that punishment given to them by the cup, that is, by measure. For the whole quantity and number of torments which the wicked will receive by the cup of just measure could not be contained in words; therefore a portion of the cup is mentioned here. Yet the whole cup is in some manner signified in the Apocalypse, where it is said of Babylon the harlot: “As much as she glorified herself and lived in delights, so much give her torment and mourning” (Rev. 18:7). For Babylon the harlot so expanded herself in her delights that, if she were permitted always to live, she would wish always to sin. Therefore, by a just measure and a just cup, eternal punishment will be given to her and to those who commit fornication with her. But for the present, fire, sulphur, and the spirit of storms are a portion [Col. 0804B] of their cup.

**VERSE 8.** For the Lord is just: he permits neither his faithful to be tried without the measure of a fitting cup, nor the ungodly to be tortured either here or in hell without measure. For the Lord is just in a primary and singular sense; and he has loved the just acts, variously ordered in the plural, not only in the measure of good rewards but also in the measure of evil punishments. Therefore we rightly proclaim him a just judge, because in all that he ordains for testing the godly and tormenting the ungodly, his countenance has seen equity. His countenance is his Son, through whom he is made known; this countenance is just and sees equity through approval of equity itself. But as the Son is understood through God’s countenance, so the Holy Spirit may be understood through the vision of the countenance; elsewhere he is signified by the seven eyes of the field.

Glory to the Father, who has such a countenance; glory to the Son, the very countenance of the Father; glory to the Holy Spirit, by whom, as it were through the vision of the Son—in whom the Father sees—all the elect are enlightened. Amen. Let the Lord glory that he is our Lord, and that we are his good servants, not servants of sin. Let his countenance glory, because it is expressed in us as in a bright mirror. Let his vision glory, because we are enlightened by its light. Heaven and earth are full of the glory and glorification of this Trinity. Glory is in predestination; glorying is in the execution and completion of predestination. Amen.

## PSALM XI

[Col. 0803]

[Col. 0803D] “Save me, O Lord.” The title is (**VERSE 1**):

> **FOR THE END: A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR THE OCTAVE.**

What the octave is was stated in Psalm VI. There the sinner feared the octave. Here David, penitent and prophet, asks for it, that the iniquity of the age may be destroyed and the truth of the promise to come may appear. First he asks to be freed and saved from the age; secondly, he introduces God promising consolation through the Son, where he says [Col. 0804D]: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord.” The purpose is to call us back from the vanities of this age to the chaste utterances of God, in which salvation lies.

By David, who sings in this psalm “for the end, for the octave,” the whole Church may suitably be understood: both those who preceded Christ’s coming and those who follow it. For the earlier Church [Col. 0805A], which awaited Christ’s coming, kindled by longing for salvation to come, prayed for what the present Church now knows to have been fulfilled by Christ’s advent; yet it still sighs and prays that he may bring to completion in each person not yet fully saved the work of salvation which he accomplished universally in sending the Saviour of the whole world—even in those predestined indeed to salvation, yet still estranged from salvation. For just as, in a body, so long as even one member is not well, the whole body desires a physician, so the Church in heaven, though the Saviour has come and has already saved many, nevertheless cries out for salvation as necessary for herself until the octave. For it says:

**VERSE 2.** “Save me, O Lord”; or, as it is read in Hebrew: “Save me, O Lord, for the holy one has failed.”

[Col. 0805B] First, Adam himself—holy, innocent, and pure, created by you—failed. He was created in order to advance to fellowship with the holy angels. He failed so completely that he was “compared with the senseless beasts” (Ps. XLVIII, 13). In his failure the whole human race fell, in whom, as the Apostle says, “all have sinned” (Rom. III, 23): namely, those who were and are generated from him through concupiscence. In him we too sinned; from him we all derived original sin, which is the death of the soul, together with the mortality of the body. Therefore we long for the octave, each of us saying: “Save me, O Lord,” so that in the octave we may lack not only the most dreadful death of the soul but also bodily mortality—those two plagues by which Adam, created to be holy, failed.

Then, through the multitude of actual sins in all his posterity, truths have been diminished by the children of men.

I do not say that truths have been diminished *for* the children of men, or *in* the children of men, but *by* the children of men; for they themselves, not God, are at fault for the diminution—God, “who makes his sun” of truth “rise upon the good and evil, and rains” the teaching of truth “upon the just and unjust” (Matt. V, 45). But by turning themselves from truth to vanity, they diminish truths by loving vanities. You indeed, O God, are eternal and incorruptible truth, which cannot be diminished in itself. But just as one face has many images in many mirrors, so [Col. 0805D] from you, one truth, come many truths, because many souls are illuminated by love of truth. This is so much the case that no one wishes to be deceived in knowing truth; yet, while unwilling to be deceived, they nevertheless wish to deceive. Thus truths have been diminished by the children of men. If they neither were deceived nor deceived others, they would surely cleave to full truth without any diminution of truth itself. But now, with truth diminished in them, they seek to deceive; as is evident because:

**VERSE 3.** “They have spoken vain things,” that is, false things, every one not merely to a stranger but even to his neighbour, friend, or kinsman. Yet any human being is neighbour to a human being if he shows mercy to him. Hence he is more especially our neighbour who showed mercy to us: the man Jesus Christ. Yet we do not preserve truth even toward [Col. 0806A] this neighbour, when we violate the faith promised to him in baptism. Though many confess that faith in words, they deny it in heart or conduct, possessing deceitful lips—prating, deceitful, and deceptive lips. For by these lips they “have spoken in heart, and heart,” that is, with a manifold or double heart: intending one thing while pretending another. Though inwardly double and manifold, they nevertheless agree in evil.

Truths, I say, have been diminished, not wholly extinguished; for it is itself a spark of truth that they do not wish to be deceived. They do not wish that spark to be extinguished in themselves, yet they so diminish it from its own light that they do not extend its flame to their neighbour, whom they deceive and by whom they do not wish to be deceived.

**VERSE 4.** “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips.” [Col. 0806B] “Destroy”: that is, scatter and destroy—not human beings, but all deceitful lips. Let him destroy the lips, so that they do not speak; destroy their deceitfulness, so that they do not deceive; destroy their totality, so that they may not have unanimity and concord in evil. First let him destroy their collective unity, so that they may not have a multitude united in evil; then destroy their lips, so that they may not have loquacity; finally, destroy in their deceitful lips the deceit itself, so that they may have a simple and good will. May the Lord also destroy the boastful tongue—that is, the proud tongue of heretics, philosophers, and hypocrites.

**VERSE 5.** “Who have said in their boastfulness: We will magnify our tongue.” And if anyone should ask us for authority for what we say, we, wishing to be regarded ourselves as the authority, shall say: “Our lips are our own” [Col. 0806C]; that is, we ourselves, who are teachers, are to be regarded as authoritative, even though our lips are our own and derive authority from nowhere else. “For who is our lord?” That is, who is our master? Thus prophets speaking to Elisha said: “Do you not know that today the Lord will take your master from you?” (IV Kings II, 3). They called Elijah, Elisha’s teacher, his lord. But these boasters, refusing to be disciples of truth, become teachers of errors and acknowledge no master or lord above themselves. Thus they say: “Who is our lord?” We shall submit to no one’s teaching and no one’s rule, for we ourselves are great lords and teachers.

In such desolation, with iniquity abounding everywhere [Col. 0806D] and charity growing cold, what consolation have we unless we understand here the sense of the Apostle: “As through the offence of one came condemnation upon all men, so through the righteousness of one came justification of life upon all men” (Rom. V, 18)? It is of this one that the psalm immediately speaks.

**VERSE 6.** “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord.” The Lord the Father says this: “Now I will arise,” though I seemed to sleep; “now I will arise, now I will awake, now I will show openly in events that I have care for the misery of the poor.” For because of the misery of the needy—who are miserable in themselves and have no help from another—and because of the groaning of the poor, who lack the riches [Col. 0807A] of virtues and even bodily necessities, and therefore do not murmur against me but groan to me: “now I will arise.” This does not mean that I shall appear visibly in my own person, but that against deceitful lips I shall set chaste utterances; against the misery of the needy I shall set silver tested by fire. And I shall set these chaste utterances and this tested silver in the Saviour.

Moreover, so that Jesus himself, the Saviour himself, may not teach before he acts, but so that it may truthfully be said of him that “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I, 1), I shall first act confidently in him. For as he himself says: “The Father abiding in me, he does the works” (John XIV, 10); so I shall act confidently in him, as in my arm. I shall cast out the sellers and buyers from the temple [Col. 0807B] so confidently, with such assurance, that they themselves will marvel and say: “By what authority do you do these things?” (Luke XX, 7). I shall enlighten the blind and heal the lame in the temple; and from that time he himself, my Saviour, will be “teaching daily in the temple” (ibid. XIX, 47). Until the completion of obedience, he will teach in the temple, giving chaste utterances against deceitful lips.

In admiration and reverence for such utterances, the prophet says—and let us say with the prophet:

**VERSE 7.** “The utterances of the Lord are chaste utterances.” For indeed the utterances of the Lord are chaste—that is, without the corruption of pretence—against that of which we complained above when saying: “Every one has spoken vain things.” And they are silver tested by fire, because they have been proved in the furnace of tribulation.

[Col. 0807C] The Hebrew reads: “I will set their help in the Saviour. The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire, separated from earth, refined sevenfold.”

By these words it is made clear that, because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor amid deceitful lips, God the Father sets help in Christ through chaste and pure utterances: through silver tested by fire, purified—or refined—sevenfold; purified of earth, that is, from earth, so that it possesses nothing earthly and promises not earthly but heavenly things.

Purified sevenfold, that is, perfectly. Or sevenfold according to the seven gifts of virtues and the seven degrees of the beatitudes, of which the chaste utterances, the Gospel utterances, speak: “Blessed are the poor; [Col. 0807D] blessed are the meek; blessed are those who mourn; blessed are those who hunger; blessed are the merciful; blessed are the peacemakers” (Matt. V, 3–10; Luke VI, 20). But by the fire of tribulation, which the eighth beatitude contains in those who suffer persecution for righteousness, the silver of God’s utterances itself is purified sevenfold. For those shaped by the Lord’s chaste utterances are purified sevenfold through each of the seven virtues. Or they are purified sevenfold through those seven adversities which the Apostle lists when he says: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” (Rom. VIII, 35).

By this fire of persecution, the poor in spirit are tested, if they truly are poor in spirit. In the same way the meek, mourners, those hungering for righteousness, the merciful, and the peacemakers [Col. 0808A] are tested in the furnace of persecution like earthen or golden vessels. For if, in the fire of tribulation, they break and burst through impatience, they are proved to be earthen vessels. But if, in tribulation, they possess their souls in patience, they are golden vessels, or vessels of silver purified sevenfold. That it may openly appear how great is the benefit in this silver, in these chaste utterances, the Prophet speaks to the Lord; and let us speak with him.

**VERSE 8.** “You, O Lord, will preserve us.” You are our Saviour, whom the Father gave to us, in whom chaste utterances are set. Through these very utterances made known to us and believed by us, you will preserve us, lest we be in the failure in which the holy one failed. For you will renew us from the oldness which we contracted from him, so that, justified through you [Col. 0808B] and regenerated into life, we may be saved, as we asked at the beginning of the psalm.

“And you will guard us from this generation”: from the old generation, the adulterous generation (Mark VIII, 38), which does not receive chaste utterances; from the generation of men in whom truths have been diminished. From this generation you will guard us, leading us into eternity, into the refuge of eternity, where the ungodly shall have no entrance. Why? Because:

**VERSE 9.** “The ungodly walk round about.” And this will be the great distinction: that you will guard us but not them, in whom truths have been diminished, in whom vanities reign. Held fast in the vanities of temporal things, they walk round about: that is, in desire for temporal things, which move and turn with time. These are called circuits because they revolve like a wheel through the repetition of seven days. Therefore they do not attain the stability of the octave, of which this psalm speaks, because they pursue unstable things and turn with the wheel of the unstable world. Of this wheel Solomon says in Proverbs: “A wise king is the winnower of the ungodly; he brings upon them the wheel of evils” (Prov. XX, 26); and another psalm says: “My God, make them like a wheel” (Ps. LXXXII, 11).

Or they walk round about like the donkey that draws the millstone; and at last this donkey’s millstone will be hung about their necks, and they will be plunged into the depths of hell, because they preferred, with the devil, father of lies, to grind out lies with deceitful lips rather than to act confidently and faithfully with the Saviour who acts confidently. Thus, [Col. 0808D] O Lord, the ungodly will perish by your just judgment. And what will become of the children of men? Adam and Eve were human beings, not children of men. Those who remain in their oldness belong to those human beings; but those regenerated and renewed through Christ are rightly called children of men. These children of men you, O Lord, have multiplied, not in temporal things but like the stars of heaven, according to the promise made to Abraham. And this is according to your height, when you make them grow from strength to strength until they behold the form of your loftiness, your height.

Alternatively: O Lord, while many walk in a circuit, few stand upright. We therefore wonder why, among such a great multitude of human beings—of whom few are saved and many perish—all were created. Yet the solution to this question, or wonder, is this: because you, O Lord, according to your height, according to your lofty and profound counsel, have multiplied the children of men. This lofty counsel is not so much to be discussed as to be cried out over with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches, wisdom, and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments!” (Rom. XI, 33).

[Col. 0810A] Glory to the Father, the Lord to whom it is said at the beginning of the psalm: “Save me, O Lord”; glory to the Son, of whom the Father says: “I will set [help] in the Saviour; I will act confidently in him”; glory to the Holy Spirit, the sevenfold Spirit, by whose purification the silver tested by fire and proved from earth has been purified sevenfold.

## PSALM XII

[Col. 0809]

[Col. 0809B] **VERSE 1.** “How long, O Lord, will you forget me unto the end?” The title of this psalm is evident from what has been said before; it is:

> **FOR THE END: A PSALM OF DAVID.**

This psalm shows with what burning charity the ancient saints desired Christ’s Incarnation, through which they understood the Redemption to come; and also with what longing the saints afflicted in this present time desire the second coming. In the first part he complains of delay, saying: “How long, O Lord, will you forget me unto the end?” In the second part he asks to be enlightened, that in the present life he may remain immune and free from every sin, saying: “Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God. Enlighten my eyes, lest at any time I sleep in death” [Col. 0809C]. In the third part, confidently believing himself heard, he gives thanks for God’s mercy and binds himself by a vow that, rejoicing in the Lord in that thanksgiving itself, he is prepared to sing and make melody to him forever. For he says: “My heart shall rejoice in your salvation; I will sing to the Lord who has bestowed good things upon me, and I will make melody to the name of the Lord Most High.” His purpose is to invite us and others to the same longing.

The Prophet, speaking in the person of those who lived before the Incarnation, grieves that he waits so long for the first coming; or, speaking in the person of the saints of this time, he complains of the delay of the second coming.

[Col. 0809D] This psalm aptly accords with the preceding one. For since there he said, “You, O Lord, will preserve us and guard us,” this psalm more earnestly asks Christ for that same thing: namely, that he may not only guard us from every sin in the present life, but also grant that after the failure of this life we may rejoice in himself forever. Therefore David the prophet says—or any person who, with David, perceives that the evils of this world can be removed only through the End, which is Christ. He says, I mean, singing for the End, with his whole desire stretched out toward the End—that is, toward Christ:

“O Lord, you turn your countenance from me because you do not grant my soul the sight of your countenance, your Son, who is your countenance, withholding manifest knowledge of him. And how long will this be? Have you forgotten me? You say in another prophet: ‘Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have pity upon the son of her womb? And even if she should forget, yet I will not forget you’” (Isa. XLIX, 15). You say this to every person who believes in you and is formed in the womb of faith, while he believes with the heart unto righteousness [Col. 0810B] (Rom. X, 10), and is born into the light while with his mouth he confesses you as God unto salvation.

And I believe in the End, that is, in Christ, whom I confess to be not only that Beginning in which God the Father created heaven and earth, but also “the end of every consummation” (Ps. CXVIII, 96), as he himself says: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. I, 8). He is the beginning and source of all things, from whom all things are; he is the end of all things, for whom all things were made. For as “all things were made through him” (John I, 3), so all things were made for him, who was invisible, to be manifested. As a man makes an excellent building to display his skill, so, to make manifest your Son, your Word, the eternal King to be glorified, you made the hosts of angels and men.

Therefore, although he is the end and consummation of all things, he is more particularly the end and consummation of angels and men, whom he completes into one house, having himself become the head of the corner: like a cornerstone completing the whole building, which was made through him and for him—through him as Beginning and for him as End [Col. 0810C] (Ps. CXVII, 22; Eph. II, 20). And I know that I am from him. For unless I were from him, I would not be. This belongs to all alike, good and evil: to be from him, or through him. But not all tend toward him as the end of their course. For because of sins, he so forgets some that he does not fit them to himself, the foundation and supreme cornerstone, either in the wall of the holy angels or in the wall of holy human beings.

I fear that I am in this forgetfulness, in this land of forgetfulness among those “whom you remember no more, and who are cast off from your hand” (Ps. LXXXVII, 6), because I do not yet see the end of my course. In the preceding psalm we said that the ungodly walk in a circuit; therefore they neither find nor seek the end of their course. But I, seeking the end and consummation, fearing lest I be left in forgetfulness and long delayed, say to you, my God:

“How long, O Lord, will you forget me”—understand: *to bring me to the End*, so that I may be your house, completed unto the End “in Christ Jesus, the supreme cornerstone” [Col. 0811A] (Eph. II, XX [sic]), who is the infinite End? Or: “How long, O Lord, will you forget me,” acting as though you had no care for me? Will it be until the end of the second coming, when Christ, who is beginning and end, will be understood? Or until the Incarnation of the Son, when “the fullness of time came” (Gal. IV, 4)—a fullness which is a certain end and a certain consummation?

Will you not at least before the end grant counsels by which I may be directed to the End? For I seek sure and fixed counsels descending from above. For if “every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from” you, “the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of turning” (Jas. I, 17), then a best and perfect counsel also descends “from” you, “the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of turning.” Thus neither in your perfect and best counsel is there “any change or shadow of turning.”

I seek such a perfect and best counsel in my soul and do not find it there, because it is not there. It is above, with you, the Father of lights; it is not in my soul. When I seek in my soul a best and perfect counsel, many imperfect counsels occur in place of that one perfect counsel. In them there is great change and shadow of turning, as I frequently change counsels for counsels, not finding the perfect counsel. Thus, possessing no one best counsel, I place many imperfect counsels in my soul: I place, remove, and replace counsels in my soul [Col. 0811C]. I arrange many things because I do not find the one thing which, once found, would leave me in need of no further counsel. And I have been doing this a long time. But how long shall this change and shadow of turning of counsels remain with me?

**VERSE 2.** “How long shall I place counsels so uncertain in my soul?” Anxiously I seek the best and final counsel and do not find it. Yet I adopt some counsel or other in order to alleviate the feeling of anxiety, but I find no sure consolation, because I have no fixed counsel. Thus I often change counsels in my heart because what I desire is not achieved. For if any counsel were effective, there would be no need to adopt another.

[Col. 0811D] In this the great and unwearied ardour of my soul refreshes itself: it devises so many counsels that it may find the one thing it desires, and yet does not see it. Nor does it on that account cease to desire, certain that one day the one who asks will receive, the one who seeks will find, and to the one who knocks perseveringly it will be opened—if not because he is a friend, then because of his importunity. But because hope is drawn out, desire grows into pain. For just as the heart of one who desires is gladdened and delighted when some counsel appears by which he hopes the desire can be fulfilled, so surely, when that counsel is found ineffective, desire is turned into pain. Therefore, having frequent pains in my heart through frequent changes of counsel, I cry anxiously: “How long shall I place [Col. 0812A] counsels in my soul?” And when those counsels have been frustrated, how long shall I place pain in my heart by day?

Will I be troubled “by day,” that is, daily, by this change? Or rather, “by day” means throughout the whole time of this life, which is a certain “day of wrath, a day of calamity and misery, a great and bitter day” (Zeph. I, 15), heralding the last day. My counsels vary; therefore I would pass beyond this day of changing times into the End, that is, into eternity, where there is no “change or shadow of turning” of counsels (Jas. I, 17); where there is no adversary, and where the enemy is not admitted within the day of eternity. He now attacks during the day of temporal change and is sometimes exalted over me.

For before Christ’s Incarnation, as a “strong man armed” guarding “his own court” (Luke XI, 21), he possessed almost this whole world, while few, in faith, awaited Christ’s coming. And now, with false brethren multiplied in the Church, few walking in truth and sincerity, and carnal affections continually smothering spiritual intention within me, my enemy is exalted over me [Col. 0812B]. And how long, O Lord, will this evil endure?

**VERSE 3.** “How long shall my enemy be exalted over me?” I repeatedly say, “How long?” because I burn with great pains and anxieties, as though delivered over to forgetfulness by you, my Lord.
