To you I say: “How long do you turn your countenance from me? How long shall my enemy be exalted over me?”

[Col. 0812C] **VERSE 4.** “Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God.” You who turned away your countenance, now look upon me; you who seemed to have forgotten me, now hear me praying for my own sake and for myself, that you may send him whom you are to send.

“Enlighten my eyes, lest at any time, through my own sloth, I sleep in death”: that is, in some mortal sin—whether the eyes of my mind, or also the eyes of the whole Church, namely its prelates, weighted down and darkened by the sleep of carnal pleasures. I say: lest I sleep through my own negligence or be overcome by another’s malice.

**VERSE 5.** “Lest at any time my enemy, the devil, should say: ‘I have prevailed against him.’” The enemy of all good says this if he sees my fall. Nor will he alone rejoice over it: all his servants who afflict me will also rejoice if I am moved from the stability of faith [Col. 0812D]. Therefore, O my God, you ought to enlighten my eyes not only for my sake, but also lest my enemy and yours, with his servants who afflict me and desire my ruin, rejoice over me.

**VERSE 6.** “But I have hoped in your mercy”: I have not presumed upon my own strength. For I do not ascribe even my not being moved to myself; for I should already be moved by pride if I attributed to myself what comes from your gratuitous grace. I desire its day; and in desiring, I rejoice. As Abraham, who “saw and rejoiced” in your day—the future day of your Son (John VIII, 56)—rejoiced so that he might see in actuality him whom he had seen in faith, so my heart will rejoice in your salvation, as though already possessing what I desire, because I most certainly believe that what I desire will come to pass.

I will sing to the Lord, who has already bestowed good things upon me in the future reality, by means of most certain hope. So great is the power of faith that what is still future in time is past for it. I will sing in contemplation; I will make melody in action. I will sing and make melody: that is, I will give thanks with joy to the name of the Lord Most High. If, then, the faithful prophet so desired and so served [Col. 0813A] Christ yet to come, with what devotion ought one to serve, sing, and make melody now that he has been received? Therefore let each of us who has now received Christ in the sacrament of the altar say: “I will sing to the Lord who has bestowed good things upon me, and I will make melody to the name of the Most High.”

Glory to the Father, from whom the angel of great counsel is desired amid uncertain counsels; glory to the Son, the Counsellor, of whom it is said: “I shall rejoice in your salvation”; glory to the Holy Spirit, who is the light enlightening human eyes, lest I ever sleep in death. Amen.

## PSALM XIII

[Col. 0813]

[Col. 0813B] “The fool has said in his heart: There is no God.” The title (**VERSE 1**) is:

> **FOR THE END: A PSALM OF DAVID.**

It is clear. This psalm supplies us with words against every fool who says in his heart—whether he is a Jew or a heretic—“There is no God”; understand: *this man Jesus Christ is not God*. For it treats of the profound wickedness of the Jews: the one whom the holy Fathers—their patriarchs and prophets—had desired with intense longing to be given them, and for whom they anxiously longed in the words of the preceding psalm, they saw present in the flesh; yet they rejected not only his words and deeds, but delivered him himself to death. It also treats of their temporal and particular overthrow, their later eternal condemnation, and likewise the glorious and wonderful reward of the saints.

First, because the countenance whose coming the prophet desired in the preceding psalm is here shown to have come, he rebukes its despisers, who did not receive that countenance so long desired. For, as the Evangelist says: “He came unto his own, and his own did not receive him” (John I, 11). Secondly, it threatens them with judgment, where it says: “Will not all who work iniquity know?” Thirdly, the conversion of a remnant from among them is foretold, where it says: “Who will give from Zion the salvation of Israel?” Now let us consider the text.

“The fool has said in his heart: There is no God.” Christ was desired by the patriarchs and prophets as God, the Son of God; as God and man [Col. 0813D], one Emmanuel. But after he appeared in mortal flesh, the foolish Jew, not being wise in things above, said—that is, thought—in his heart: “This man, the ‘carpenter’s son’ (Matt. XIII, 55), whose father and mother we know, is not God.” This, I say, he said in his heart—not like Peter, questioned by the maidservant, who denied Christ with his mouth but not his heart, through weakness rather than impiety, a curable evil. Rather, both in heart and mouth he spoke through impiety, not weakness; through arrogance, not fear: “This man is not God; he is not the Son of God, but the ‘carpenter’s son.’”

And even if he sometimes honoured Jesus openly with the title of divinity—as in: “Good Master, what shall I do to possess eternal life?” (Luke X, 25)—he said this with his mouth and not his heart, plainly contradicting himself by calling good the one whom he denied to be God. For to be substantially good and to be God are equivalent. Therefore the Lord says to him: “Why do you call me [Col. 0814B] good? No one is good save God alone” (Matt. XIX, 17); as though he had said: Why do you call me good with your mouth when in your heart you deny that I am God? Thus, as this single disciple of the Law did, so nearly the whole Jewish people denied Jesus’ divinity in their hearts, even when they honoured him by the title of teacher, good man, or great prophet. Hence the Lord says of them through the prophet: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Mark VII, 6).

Thus clearly, thus the impious and foolish Jew said in his heart: “There is no God.” The fool, unwilling to be wise, said: “There is no God”—he who “would that he were wise and understood and foresaw the last things” (Deut. XXXII, 29).

Or the foolish Gentile said this not only concerning Christ but absolutely: that God does not exist. Yet he said it not in words but nevertheless in his heart. For not even those sacrilegious philosophers who think falsely about God dared say, “There is no God,” or “God is nowhere,” or “God is nothing”; for no one dares to say this, even if he has dared to think it.

Yet the venerable Father Dionysius, disciple of the Apostle Paul, plainly says in his book *On the Divine Names* that God is nothing. In saying this, he is not to be thought foolish, being the disciple of the wise Apostle [Col. 0814D], who did not speak this in a Jewish or Gentile sense. For a Jew is one who confesses the true God but serves him for temporal goods. Unless the things for which he worships God abound to him, he immediately doubts that the God whom he worships exists. Thus the ancient Jews were nursed, as it were, by promises and bestowals of temporal goods so that they might believe God to exist: departing from him, they were scourged; cleaving to him, they were enriched. For this reason they believed that Christ was not God and said in their hearts, “There is no God,” because he disputed against their hardness and taught that poverty ought to be pursued.

Many who bear the Christian name belong to the class of such Jews, serving [Col. 0815A] God for the acquisition of temporal things. All of them reject the poor Christ in their hearts as though he were not God, because they resolve to serve Mammon rather than him, though they cannot serve both alike, as he himself says: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matt. VI, 24).

Pagans differ from Jews in this: they seek temporal things from false and many gods, rather than from the one true God, as Jews do. Therefore, when temporal prosperity does not smile upon them, they blaspheme their gods in their hearts and deny that they possess divine power. For example, they say: “Neptune is not a god, because he did not calm the sea for me but allowed me, though I called upon him, to suffer shipwreck. Jupiter is not a god, because he does not give me the desired rains when I call upon him.” Thus the foolish pagan says in his heart: “There is no God.” Yet he would say this wisely if he thought it of any of his own gods and did not also assert it of our God, the true God. Because he sees that adversities sometimes befall Christians more than pagans, he says in his heart: “The God of Christians is not God.”

But holy Father Dionysius must not be thought to have held the view either of Jews or of pagans. For in his writings he confesses Christ as God and affirms that God himself is superessential: that is, existing not among all things but above all things. In this sense he calls him nothing, because whatever is something has a place among all things. But God is above all things and is not properly said to be something, because neither can he properly be called a substance, since he is not capable of receiving accidents, nor is he in any way called an accident. What is neither substance nor accident may be called nothing, in the sense in which all existing things are understood to be either substance or some thing among the nine categories of accidents [Col. 0815C]. Yet God is beyond and above all things: from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things, and unto whom are all things. But he is nothing among all things, since, remaining in himself above all things that can be understood, he governs all things.

Christ, his Son, is God from God, eternal from the Eternal, omnipotent from the Omnipotent; although not from human nature, yet in human nature God—not among all things, but, as the Apostle says, “God blessed above all” [Col. 0815D] (Rom. 9:5). For the human nature which in him is wholly deified is now, like the Father’s eternal divinity, above all things; nor does it approach by local motion when, in the sacrament of baptism, he is present who baptizes, or in the sacrament of the altar he is present who sacrifices himself, and when the true David is borne in his own hands through the hands of the acting priest. Nor is it now in any way subject either to local movements or to other changeable accidents. Rather, the Son of God, seated as man upon the highest throne—that is, reigning and judging all things with the Father—presents himself everywhere as he wills: not by mobile movement or by local extension of his hands or feet, but wholly, by a total and divine presence, as he wills.

For just as “the Spirit breathes where he wills” [Col. 0816A], and “you do not know whence he comes or whither he goes,” so too does this man “who is born of the Spirit” (John 3:8). Therefore, when Christ God is seen upon the holy altar under the appearance of bread and wine, let no fool, whether in a Jewish or pagan sense, say, “God is not here,” since he himself is God: not only eternal God in the nature of the Word, but also, in human nature supremely deified into eternal God, conceived and born, so that the food of his flesh and the drink of his blood have eternal life in themselves—though not from themselves—and bestow it on those who partake, while he possesses it without measure. Yet he bestows it “according to the measure of his gift” (Eph. 4:7).

For this reason true Christians worship and love him; and because they believe that they receive God within themselves under the appearance of bread and wine, the imperfect dare not, [Col. 0816B] while the perfect do not wish to be subject to the corruptions of earthly pleasures, lest God, whom they have within themselves, be offended. They know that he is God, and they love him whether he chastens through adversities or consoles through prosperities. But those who, with pagans or Jews, savour not heavenly but earthly things are broken by adversities and corrupted by prosperities. For because “they did not approve to have God in their knowledge,” nor do they offer to him their minds and bodies, “God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not fitting for worshippers of the true God” (Rom. 1:28).

Although I have spoken in the singular concerning one fool—“The fool has said”—yet Jews and pagans have multiplied so greatly under the Christian name that I may speak of them in the plural:

[Col. 0816C] They are corrupt and have become abominable. They are corrupt through the passions of carnal desires; and they have become abominable through the turning away of their minds from the love of God to the love of this world. They have become corrupt and abominable not as persons seized or overcome by sins, but as people voluntarily and zealously bent upon sinning in those very sins. Thus, by God’s just judgment, they have become abominable, corrupted not so much in their sins as in their zeal for them, so thoroughly that among the number of such fools there is none who does good—none, I say, not even one—because not one among them is found who says to God from the heart: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge” (Ps. 118[119]:66).

Or I may say this universally: There is none who does good; [Col. 0816D] there is no good person in the entire multitude of humankind, not even one. For “none is good except God alone” (Matt. 19:17). And Christ is indeed God, who, just as he is essentially God, is likewise good—not good through an accidental gift but through essential goodness: fully God, fully good, and alone good, because none is good except God alone. Although angels and human beings are good by participation in him, none is good in comparison with him; just as the moon shines by participation in the sun’s light, yet does not shine in comparison with that same sun.

But in that the foolish are corrupt, abominable, and evil, practising evil pursuits, ignorance does not excuse them, because:

**VERSE 2. The Lord looked down from heaven.** The true Sun first illumined the earth through the prophets, then through [Col. 0817A] himself and through the apostles; indeed, “his invisible things are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity, so that they are without excuse” (Rom. 1:20)—Gentiles and Jews alike. For although the Jews had known God through Scripture and the Gentiles through creation, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; instead, they went astray in their thoughts, or, as was said above, in pursuits altogether inexcusable, because the Lord looked down from heaven by sending his Son.

Or the Son himself, the Lord, looked down from heaven when “he came down from heaven, and was incarnate by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary” [Note: [Col. 0817D] From the Nicene Creed.]. He also looked down from heaven when he gave the Law to the Jews, ordained through the heavenly angels by the hand of a mediator. He looked down [Col. 0817B] also from heaven—that is, from holy souls, whose teaching makes the Church shine like the moon in relation to the sun. He looked down, I say, from heaven upon the children of men: namely, upon the Jews, who, in contrast to men—that is, the Gentiles—are more honorably called “children of men” because of their worship of the one God.

He looked down for this purpose: that he might see—that is, cause human beings themselves to see. Nothing is hidden from him in himself; but he is said to see or know when he causes us to know, as he said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear the Lord” (Gen. 22:12), meaning, “Now I have caused you to know.” He therefore looked down in order that he might see, that is, make us see whether anyone is understanding, with intellect and natural capacity illumined by supernatural light, that the man who speaks God’s words [Col. 0817C] is God—that is, who speaks words fitting only for God, such as: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); likewise, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12); “I am the truth” (John 14:6); “I am the beginning, who also speak unto you” (John 8:23).

If, in speaking these words of God, he had lied, like that liar and father of lies who had said, “I am God, and I have sat in the seat of God, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14)—if, I say, like that one, he had lied while speaking God’s words, since he is neither God nor like the Most High—then this man also would have lied; he would not have been glorified as God through divine miracles, but, like that one, would likewise have been cast down from the height of his heart into hell. But now creation obeyed him speaking thus [Col. 0817D] as it obeyed its Creator, when he made wine from water, fed five thousand with five loaves, and gave sight to the man born blind.

He therefore had a twofold and lawful testimony. “For I,” he says, “am one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John 8:18), so that this word might stand in the mouth of two witnesses: that he who speaks God’s words is God—which is to have one witness—and that the Father works divine works in him—which is to have the other witness. For he says: “The Father dwelling in me, he does the works” (John 14:10). And he himself, in the Father and with the Father, though still mortal, shone forth as [Col. 0818A] God through divine works; but more fully, after obedience unto death, he was exalted so as to sit with princes—indeed, above all the principalities of the heavenly court—with God the Father, holding the throne of divine glory not only in his divinity but also in his humanity. Now every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth bends to him who called himself God, Truth, and Beginning (Phil. 2:9). He would never have been crowned with so great glory and honour unless, in confessing himself to be God, he had spoken truly.

For God Most High is accustomed severely to punish anyone who, though he is not God, confesses himself to be God: as the devil in heaven, and Antichrist sitting in the temple of God and showing himself as though he were God (Rev. 19:20). The former, cast down by Michael, is compelled to know [Col. 0818B] that he is not like the Most High; but Antichrist will be struck by the Spirit of the Lord’s mouth, and thus, when slain, will be known to be less than God. But Christ, calling himself Son of God, glorying that he had God as Father, and proving himself to be God (John 10:36), because he spoke truth, was slain for the testimony of truth, rose through his divine power, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father Almighty, all power in heaven and on earth having been given to him.

He provides many demonstrations of this power through confessors of his name, working such great miracles in the world that it is very remarkable if anyone does not believe him to be God, or if some fool says in his heart, “There is no God.” This is the man who both performed divine works in his own person and performed greater works [Col. 0818C] through his servants, as he himself promised: “He who believes in me shall himself do the works that I do, and shall do greater works than these” (John 14:12). Since this is so evident, it is astonishing that among foolish Jews and pagans there is none who understands of himself that this is God, or who seeks from another teacher this God whom his sayings and works confirm to be God; moreover, they are united in falsehood.

**VERSE 3.** All, both Jews and Gentiles, turned aside from the true God and, as they were led, went together after many images, becoming useless. All became so useless that there is none who does good, not even one, as was explained above. [Col. 0818D] Or “even to one” means: until they arrive at unity. “Their throat is an open sepulchre.”

These three verses are not in the Hebrew; nevertheless, the Apostle introduces them in the Epistle to the Romans against the Jews for their refutation. In the manner of an authoritative teacher, he collected them to confirm his point not from one but from various places in Scripture; following him, the Church still uses the psalm as he arranged it, because she understands him to be of no less authority than the Psalmist. Yet this psalm, when repeated later, does not contain them.

Here it is explained in what way those who turned aside are [Col. 0819A] useless to others. They truly are useless, for their throat is a sepulchre from which the stench of evil persuasion breathes out and corrupts many; it lies open always to voracity and talkativeness, since talkativeness is customarily friendly to and joined with gluttony. Hence the rich man in hell is remembered as having burned in his tongue. Nothing is said of gluttony, because amid excessive feasting, although sin occurs in both ways, namely voracity and talkativeness, there is sometimes greater sin in talkativeness. Therefore, “they dealt deceitfully with their tongues.” For flattery accompanies the voracious and the talkative.

Or, “their throat is an open sepulchre,” because they devour as though dead those whom they corrupt by the stench of their conduct; and beneath their lips—that is, in their heart—is the poison of asps, worse than other [Col. 0819B] poisons because it is incurable. The asp stops its ears lest it hear the enchanter’s voice and lose its poison. So these people stop the ears of their hearts when they disregard the commandments of the Law, lest they lose the poison of their obstinate wickedness. They are so poisonous that they render evil for good. Nor is it surprising that they give what they have in abundance and what fills them.

Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness: of cursing, that is, blasphemies and insults, because they say to the Saviour, “He has a demon,” and, “A gluttonous man and a drinker of wine” (Matt. 11:18–19); and of bitterness, that is, their mouth is full of threats.

Their feet—that is, their affections—are swift because they act without deliberation. Or, swift means headlong and ready to shed the blood of Christ and his people. [Col. 0819C] Therefore destruction and misery are in their ways. For all the ways of the wicked are full of toil and misery. And this is because they have not known the way of peace, concerning which the Lord says: “My yoke is sweet” (Matt. 11:30). Or, with respect to the Jews: destruction and misery are in their ways, because in this life, which is the way to future good or evil, they were crushed by Titus and Vespasian and descended into hell by an unhappy death.

The way of the ungodly is rightly called destruction, because it both grinds down and is itself ground down. It is also called misery, because their destruction benefits them not at all, unlike the holy martyrs, who rose to heaven from present affliction. But the ungodly, crushed by present evils, [Col. 0819D] go to hell; and for this reason they do not return: because they have not known the way of peace, that is, Christ. Just as “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1:16), the initiating cause of good things for the godly, so for these ungodly the initiating cause of evils is that there is no fear of God before their eyes. They close those eyes so as not to see the truth which, whether they wish it or not, they shall know. For the Spirit says to the churches:

**VERSE 4. Shall not all who work iniquity know?** Shall they not know at least amid torments, when affliction alone gives understanding to what is heard? Shall not those who now, as though with closed eyes, work iniquity then acknowledge the truth—this iniquity, namely, that they devour my people by seducing them? Or they also [Col. 0820A] devour my people in this respect as food of bread: because they abuse their ministry in pursuit of gain for their own advantage from my people, rather than for the salvation of people or the glory of God. And this is as sweet to them as bread for food.

Food of dishes, if it is daily, turns to disgust; but bread, though daily food, does not cause disgust, and is more pleasing to a palate accustomed to it than to one unaccustomed. So also these people, whether spiritual or secular rulers over my people, whom they devour like food of bread, delight in their daily profits without weariness; nor do they perceive the hook of iniquity hidden beneath such food. By that hook they will therefore be caught and strangled, because:

**VERSE 5. They have not called upon the Lord.** For those who love sin do not truly invite [Col. 0820B] the Lord into the lodging of their hearts; they love what ought not to be loved and fear what ought not to be feared, as these did:

There they trembled with fear where there was no fear, when they said: “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11:48). Saying this, there they trembled with fear where there was no fear, because either they did not fear in their hearts but pretended fear in order to stir the people whom they devoured into fear; or, if they truly feared, they feared what ought not to be feared. But at last they shall know.

**VERSE 6. For the Lord is in the righteous generation.** When at the judgment the Lord says to the ungodly: “I was hungry, and you did not give me to eat,” and they [Col. 0820C] answer, “When did we see you and not minister to you?” (Matt. 25:42), he will answer: “As long as you did not do it to one of the least of mine, neither did you do it to me” (ibid., 43). When the Judge says this then, shall not all who now “work iniquity” know (ibid., 45) that the Lord is in the righteous generation and among his least ones, to whom he himself promised the kingdom of heaven, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3)?

The Lord is in the righteous generation. But, O miserable Jews, you have not only despised the righteous generation, but also confounded the counsel of the poor Christ: that is, you refused and despised the humble [Col. 0820D] coming of Christ when he came to give counsel, though he is to come to execute judgment. You despised him because the Lord is his hope. You said this mockingly when you cried out to him hanging on the cross: “He trusted in God; let him now deliver him, if he will. For he said, I am the Son of God” (Matt. 27:43). In speaking thus, you confounded him. And because, in confounding the poor man, you rejected the Saviour:

**VERSE 7. Who, coming from Zion, shall give salvation to Israel**, if not he whose counsel as a poor man you confounded? It is understood: no one. For he whom you confounded and killed is at once the Father’s first-born and only-begotten Son, and he has no other whom he may send to you as Saviour. Hence you must mourn over him “as one is wont to mourn at the death of a first-born” (Zech. 12:10), [Col. 0821A] who is at once first-born and only-begotten, saying: “Who shall give salvation to Israel out of Zion?” For another indeed will come in his own name, and you will receive him—or perhaps you have already received him while we sing this psalm. For there have been many antichrists; among them perhaps that singular wild beast has already passed, whom you will receive, or have received, when he comes in his own name.

But he is not the Saviour from Zion; he is the ruler of death from Babylon. I mean Babylon materially, or rather figuratively, as Rome is a city, Peter saying: “The Church gathered in Babylon salutes you” (1 Pet. 5:13), by which name he figuratively designated Rome. He is not, I say, from Jerusalem but from Babylon; not from Mount Zion but the beast ascending from the abyss, such as Julian the Apostate, your deceiver and friend, or another like him, who neither will nor can give you [Col. 0821B] salvation. But this one, whom you confounded as poor, though he can, will not. Who then from Zion will give salvation to Israel, namely carnal Israel? It is understood: no one. For concerning spiritual Israel and the remnants to be converted, he adds prophetically:

“When the Lord shall turn the captivity of Zion, Jacob shall exult and Israel shall rejoice.” You confounded, he says, the counsel of the poor man because the Lord is his hope. You confounded it, I say, by saying, “He trusted in God; let him now deliver him, if he will. For he said: I am the Son of God” (Matt. 27:43). Yet he whom you [Col. 0822A] confounded by speaking thus will save remnants from among you. This is what I, David, prophesying, desire and say; and I suggest that every person wisely singing the psalm should say the same: desiring the salvation of the remnants of Israel, let him say with me, “Who shall give salvation to Israel from Zion?” Who, proceeding from Zion, will give salvation—that is, salvation to Israel—except him whom they despised in humility? No other will give salvation; but he will give himself as salvation to Israel. Therefore, when he himself turns away the captivity of his people, when he condemns the devil who captivates his people, then Jacob—that is, “the wrestler,” signifying active persons—shall exult, and Israel—“the man seeing God,” signifying contemplative persons—shall rejoice.

Note that this is the testimony which the Apostle cites as taken from Isaiah: “There shall come out of Zion one who shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob” (Isa. 59:20; Rom. 11:26). But since David was earlier than Isaiah, Isaiah’s prophecy concerning the Jewish people to be converted in a remnant may be seen as taken from this psalm.

Glory to the Father, the Lord, who looked down from heaven when he sent the Son. Glory to the Son, the Lord, who, sent from heaven, is in the righteous generation. Glory to the Holy Spirit, under whose reigning, justifying, and sanctifying power that generation is righteous, in which God is. Amen.

## PSALM XIV

[Col. 0821]

[Col. 0821C] **VERSE 1. O Lord, who shall dwell in thy tabernacle? Title.**

**A PSALM OF DAVID.**

It is clear. This psalm treats of the unity of the present Church and future rest. For in the present Church the bodily coexistence of evil persons with good does not allow one to know who are truly in the unity of the Church. Some, though unworthy, nevertheless boast that they belong to the Church. The Prophet, therefore, checking their presumption, asks, as though a priest standing before God, who truly serve as soldiers in the present Church and who will rest in eternal blessedness; and he receives an answer containing a complete definition, by which each person may well recognize whether he belongs to the Church. For he sets forth ten notable moral ornaments, arranged as a figure of the Decalogue. Some of these belong to the perfect, some to the imperfect, but all belong to Christ alone; each will be distinguished in its appropriate place. The method of treatment is by question and answer: the first part contains the question, the second the answer.

It may also be understood that Christ himself, the true David, speaks here, definitively showing who shall attain glory under the names Jacob and Israel. Since, therefore, at the end of the preceding psalm it was said, “When the Lord shall turn the captivity of his people, Jacob shall exult and Israel shall rejoice,” lest anyone vainly suppose that faith alone will suffice for this blessedness, he wishes definitively to show who, bearing the meanings of these names, will attain glory. He puts this in interrogative form, not because he removes uncertainty concerning the matter. This psalm is properly an instruction in morals.

Thus, as though standing before the Holy of Holies, before the oracle of the supreme Trinity, Christ, the mediator of God and men, asks as follows; or the Prophet, or any saint seeking the same thing, says: O Lord, I stand before thy face and seek answers from the oracle of thy truth. For I see very many entering thy Church, yet it is not apparent who in it is a servant, who does not remain in the house forever, and who is a son, who remains forever. Therefore I ask:

Who shall dwell in thy tabernacle, or who shall rest on thy holy mountain? Tabernacles belong to those on campaign; we remain in them while we are in this life, which is the warfare of a pilgrim man, labouring under arms. Therefore I do not ask who rests in the tabernacles, where [Col. 0823A] those on campaign and labouring have their dwelling; but I ask, who shall dwell in thy tabernacle, and who shall rest upon thy holy mountain? I see many enter thy tabernacle after taking up the military standard of Christianity or of a stricter religious life; but some go out from us because they were not of us, even before their death. Many more will be taken from us by the angels, the reapers, through their death. These are not to be said to dwell in thy tabernacle as thy soldiers, but to lurk there as enemies.

Who, then, shall dwell in thy tabernacle as an approved soldier, and who shall rest, as a soldier discharged from service, upon thy holy mountain? For the rest which is not complete in thy tabernacle is itself full and perfect upon thy holy mountain. For just as the ark of the covenant was first in the tabernacle made for it by Moses, and was carried from place to place with that tabernacle, but afterwards was placed by Solomon in thy temple upon Mount Zion, thy holy mountain: so every faithful soul, like an ark of the covenant, is carried in the present Church as in a tabernacle, and is transferred from that tabernacle to the Jerusalem above as to a holy mountain, where it shall rest; since no one there will contend in battle. Hence Jerusalem is called “the vision of peace” (Ezek. 13:16), because there will be no action there, but only the vision of peace.

We have heard the cautious question; let us hear the most cautious and entirely sufficient answer. God the Father answers his Son, the true David, or the Prophet David, or any believer asking through the words already stated: You ask who shall dwell [Col. 0823C] in the tabernacle and who shall rest upon my holy mountain. And I tell you that that person shall dwell and rest:

**VERSE 2. He who enters without stain:** namely, one whose stain of original sin is removed upon entering through baptism. This is the first adornment of Christian warfare. Then, secondly, actual righteousness must be in him: he must not remain idle, but must work, because he shall then be accepted if, having entered without stain—whether into the Church, as said above, or into a ministry of some rank conferred upon him without the stain of ambition—he works righteousness.

Of the four cardinal virtues, prudence, justice, temperance, and fortitude, I mention here justice alone in saying, “He who works righteousness,” knowing that all four are comprised in this one virtue, pre-eminent above the rest; for the person who practises justice alone is shown to be prudent, temperate, and strong. But the converse is not so, because a person may be prudent—that is, distinguish evil from good—temperate in pleasures, and strong amid adversities, without justice, by which he renders to all what is due. But if he practises this justice, he is unquestionably prudent, temperate, and strong. In the third place follows:

**VERSE 3. He who speaks truth in his heart.** This is part of practising justice: that he neither knowingly differs from the truth nor speaks otherwise than it, but his speech is “Yes, yes; no, no” (Matt. 5:37): that is, if there is affirmation in his heart, there is affirmation in [Col. 0824A] his mouth, which is meant by “yes, yes”; and if there is negation in his heart, there is negation in his mouth, which is meant by “no, no.” In the fourth place follows:

**He who has not practised deceit with his tongue.** This seems to be the same as the present point, but differs from it, because a person may speak truth deceitfully by adding or subtracting something. Thus deceitfulness of the tongue is prohibited here, just as truth in heart and mouth was commended above.

In the Hebrew the difference is clear. For there it says: “He who is not facile with his tongue.” By these words talkativeness and excessive speech are prohibited, a prohibition very appropriate for avoiding falsehood. And the order is good: after falsehood has been prohibited, excessive speech, which leads a tongue quick to speak easily into falsehood unless guarded against, is consequently prohibited. Thus it is rightly commended: “He who is not facile with his tongue.” After these steps of justice, the fifth follows:

**Nor has done evil to his neighbour:** that is, he has not done to another person what he would not wish done to himself. For every person’s neighbour is another human being; therefore each ought to do for another what he rightly desires to be done for himself. The sixth follows:

**And has not accepted reproach against his neighbours:** that is, it has not been pleasing to him when he hears a reproach against his neighbour. The seventh follows:

**VERSE 4. The wicked person is brought to nothing in his sight.** First, the devil himself, the wicked one, is brought to nothing in that person’s sight when, by evil persuasions and suggestions, he is reduced to nothing because the person does not consent to him but dashes against the rock the little thoughts coming from him, and reduces them to nothing. For example, the wicked one suggests fornication. This suggestion is brought to nothing because the person preserves himself chaste, firmly setting the solid resolve of chastity against the devil as a rock upon which he dashes the devil’s wickedness.

Likewise, a wicked person is brought to nothing in his sight because he regards as nothing the person he recognizes to be wicked. Or, if he is the judge of a case between a wicked man and another who fears the Lord, [Col. 0824D] the wicked man is brought to nothing in his sight—that is, in his judgment. For example, if a thief, wicked and intent on future thefts, has been apprehended, then under his judgment the thief is brought to nothing, because by hanging or another punishment he is prevented from his wickedness. But he glorifies those who fear the Lord, whether innocently free from military service, or truly penitent after abandoning wickedness, because in his judgment he does not cast such persons down but exalts them.

Likewise, if he is an ecclesiastical judge, a person convicted or confessing wickedness is brought to nothing in his sight—that is, in his judgment—because, under his judgment, he is deprived of honour and humbled by suitable punishment, so that his wickedness comes to nothing because it cannot attain its effect. But he glorifies those who fear [Col. 0825A] the Lord, because he honours such persons and judges them worthy of honour. Again, if the promotion of someone to a principality or dignity is being considered with him or before him, and among those to be promoted there is someone wicked, puffed up with ambition for rank, that person is brought to nothing in his sight, because he is judged unworthy of rank and is thus reduced to nothing; but he glorifies those who fear the Lord, because he judges such persons worthy of rank.

Alternatively: He who enters without stain, works righteousness, speaks truth in his heart, has not practised deceit with his tongue, has done no evil to his neighbour, has not accepted reproach against his neighbours, and has reduced the wicked person to nothing in his sight, may now be tempted through pride on account of so many virtues. But lest he lose the virtues he possesses, he does not exalt himself over his merits. Uncertain of his end and always fearing the divine judgment, he fears the Lord; and he does not boast of the virtues granted to him in self-inflation, but in fear glorifies the Lord. In this sense, the plural nominative has been put for the singular, or the singular verb for the plural. For one must say either: “He who fears the Lord glorifies,” or: “Those who fear the Lord glorify.” The eighth follows:

**VERSE 5. He who swears to his neighbour and does not deceive.** This seems to concern vows, in which the perfect person swears—that is, firmly promises obedience to his neighbour, another person for God’s sake—and does not deceive, that is, does not render his vow void. It may happen to a faithful person that he swears and, in swearing, is deceived, because he subsequently discovers in his vow or oath that what he vowed or swore should not have been vowed or sworn, and that it is not expedient for salvation to fulfil it. In this he has been deceived, but he has not deceived; and therefore what he vowed or swore may be changed for the better. Yet such a change must be made not by one’s own judgment, but on the counsel of wise Fathers.

But a person swearing would deceive if he swore something evil, as Herod did. Knowing Herodias to be hostile to John the Baptist, knowing her daughter to be foolish and to agree with her mother, he made a rash and deceptive oath, binding himself to such women, doubtless either through malignant blindness, by which “he was unwilling to understand, that he might do good” [Col. 0825D] (Ps. 35[36]:4), or by a most malicious fraud, in order to find an opportunity to accomplish his cruelty. The holy Evangelist seems to imply this when he says: “And when an opportune day had come” (Mark 6:21). Likewise, if anyone, knowing another person to be imprudent and foolish, makes to that person an oath—that is, a vow—of submission and obedience, he swears to his neighbour and deceives his neighbour, causing him to think himself something when he is nothing; but he deceives himself much more, since he has set a blind eye before himself.

This ninth virtue seems to receive little praise, where it is said: **He has not given his money at interest.** Although spiritual money ought to be given at interest, so that two talents produce two more, five five more, and one mina ten minas, nevertheless to lend temporal money at interest is blameworthy before God and human beings. Nor would abstaining from this seem so very praiseworthy as to deserve the ninth place after the eight moral excellences already set forth: not to be a usurer—especially when this is found excluded in the preceding words, “Nor has done evil to his neighbour.” For one who torments his neighbour with usury does great evil to that neighbour.

Therefore, in order that this step of conduct may be considered worthy of ninth place, we must understand the warning against usury as meaning that not accepting it is highly praiseworthy. Let us suppose, then, that some upright and proven person, already distinguished by the eight aforesaid ornaments of conduct and justice, is promoted in the Church to a dignity in which he must distribute spiritual or temporal goods [Col. 0826B] in the Church. This virtue is very necessary for him: that in the goods which he distributes he should not seek the interest of praise or temporal gain. And if unsolicited lawful gifts are voluntarily offered by devout and faithful people, the tenth and final degree of perfection is that he should not accept gifts against innocent persons.

Indeed, it appears—and it is a great perfection—to accept no gifts at all, as the prophet, describing the blessed man, says: “He casts away avarice arising from extortion, and shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isa. 33:15). Yet far be it from us to think anyone more perfect than Christ, who accepted gifts offered to him by the faithful and also left the apostles an example in this matter. For they, though they were not merely ministers but teachers of perfection and religion, accepted gifts, following Christ’s example, not only permissibly but also laudably; taking the greatest care, of course, not to accept any gifts at the expense of the innocent. Thus, when Simon Magus, full of the gall of bitterness, offered money to the holy apostles in order to obtain the power of miracles at the expense of the innocent, the apostle Peter, shaking his hands free of such a gift, said: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money” (Acts 8:20).

Therefore, although this perfection of righteousness—shaking one’s hands free from every gift—may suit a private individual or a hermit, it is entirely permissible and praiseworthy for a steward, or an assistant to some steward, to receive gifts needed for the use of the poor whom he cares for, provided that he takes care not to receive them at the expense of the innocent. That is, he must not become an oppressor of the innocent because of gifts from wrongdoers, nor honor a guilty benefactor more than an innocent person in need. Above all plagues he must flee simony: giving freely what he freely received; giving to the worthy even though they give nothing; and refusing the unworthy even though they give or promise gifts.

Thus the administrator of the poor sometimes lawfully solicits alms, following the example of the apostle Paul, who made many collections for the poor. Yet he himself was not enriched by those collections; nor, as he himself testifies, was he ever motivated by flattery or an occasion for avarice because of alms (1 Cor. 16:1); nor did he receive gifts at the expense of the innocent—gifts which he received solely for the innocent and poor. At times he even requested them thus: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows in blessings will also reap from blessings. Let each one give as he has resolved in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:6–7).

In these words of the Apostle it may fittingly be noted that the alms which is an acceptable offering is that given not reluctantly or under compulsion, but cheerfully. Therefore, when the wealthy of this age offer their sons or daughters to religious monasteries, whatever is offered with them is very acceptable if each gives as he has resolved in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, but cheerfully. But if anything is extorted from unwilling people, it should be called not so much an offering as a taking-away.

Nevertheless, what people voluntarily promised must sometimes be exacted from them unwillingly; and the one who demands it does not sin, but the one who imposes upon him the necessity of making the demand. Certain monastic stewards carefully endeavor to provide for this: they exact nothing in such cases, but receive voluntary offerings along with children, with such caution that the Church is not burdened. Paul the apostle likewise advises this precaution in receiving widows: the Church should be able to support true widows by avoiding the reception of false ones, especially those who are at once meddlesome and self-indulgent, and those whose necessary needs can be supplied by sons, daughters, or grandchildren, so that the Church may not be burdened.

For this reason the Apostle frightens sons and other relatives who neglect widows, saying: “Whoever does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8). Likewise, we may say that wealthy parents who refuse to care for their children, but, wishing to unburden themselves, endeavor to burden the Church, have denied the faith and are worse than unbelievers. For unbelievers provide necessities for their sons and daughters according to their means; whereas these people, in order to enrich their secular children, give no care, or very little, to those whom they offer.

Nevertheless, because of their stinginess spiritual men ought not to neglect their integrity by seeking to receive gifts at the expense of the innocent. Children are certainly innocent and ought to be received, as many as can suitably be maintained. In receiving them, one must take care that gifts are not accepted at the expense of the innocent—that is, that gifts offered with these innocent children are not valued more highly than the innocent children themselves, of whom it is said: “Let the little children come to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Mark 10:14). One who receives innocent children in this manner does not sin if he receives gifts together with them, but not at their expense, because he does not love the gifts as much as the innocent. This is sufficiently proved if he does not complain unduly about the smallness of the gifts—although the unbelief of the parents is to be regretted, and sound provision must be made lest the Church be burdened beyond measure.

When what we have said has been carefully weighed, it may plainly be recognized that it is no slight but a great virtue in the prudent and faithful steward, “whom the Lord has appointed over his household” (Luke 12:41), to receive gifts in such a way that he never receives them at the expense of the innocent.

All these ten splendid marks of virtues and moral qualities are found principally and fully in Christ; secondarily, they are found in every perfect Christian according to the measure of Christ’s gift. For he alone entered this world without the stain of original fault; apart from that stain no human being except him has come into this world. He worked righteousness, he who, as the Apostle says, “became for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:70 [probably 1:30]). He spoke truth, because he himself is truth, and he speaks of himself when he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). He did not act deceitfully with his tongue by withholding from his hearers anything which he had been sent to proclaim; rather, he made known to his disciples and friends all that he had heard from the Father and was to make known to them.

Nor did he do evil to his neighbor—his Jewish kinsman or his disciple Judas—for which evil they might persecute him. Nor did he accept reproach against those same neighbors. Although he sometimes reproached them for their sins, for example: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who tithe mint, dill, and every herb, who traverse sea and land to make one proselyte” (Matt. 23:23; Luke 11:42)—“you who have taken away the key of knowledge” (Matt. 23:15; Luke 11:52)—yet he did not take pleasure in the fact that there was something in them deserving reproach.

The malicious devil, tempting him in the wilderness, was reduced to nothing in his sight; Christ reduced him to nothing when he opposed to the tempter the authority of Scripture and, having finally refuted him, said: “Depart, Satan” (Matt. 4:10). But he glorified those who fear the Lord; for he chose not proud and presumptuous men as apostles and teachers of the churches, but poor and meek men who feared the Lord. He glorified them so that he “appointed them princes over all the earth” (Ps. 44:17).

He swore—that is, most firmly promised—to his neighbor, the apostle Peter, who is nearest to him, the cornerstone, in the foundation of the Church. He swore, I say—that is, he steadfastly promised—that neighbor: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). Thus he swore to his neighbor and did not deceive him, because what he magnificently promised he magnificently fulfilled, appointing him, together with the whole senate of apostles, to be prince of the world and ruler of kingdoms. In those kingdoms, what he binds is bound, and what he looses is loosed. This authority was given to him over the earth, that is, over the Church.

For concerning those outside—who, precisely in being outside and not believing, have already been judged—the Apostle teaches that the apostles are not to judge. But concerning those within, the senate of apostles judges, and especially the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, because he was especially nearer than the other apostles to the rock from which he was called Peter. Hence he deserved to hear: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16:18).

Thus Christ swore to his neighbor and did not deceive him, because his promise has been fulfilled in great part and is daily fulfilled until the end of the age. With such efficacy does the holy Church triumph against the gates of hell that even to the rulers of hell it is said: “Lift up your gates, O princes” (Ps. 23:7). You princes of hell, lift up your gates; remove your gates from before the prince of the apostles. Remove simony and simoniacs; remove other perversities and perverse persons through whom entrance into hell lies open. Remove these gates from the midst of the Church, so that “the everlasting gates may be lifted up,” through which “the King of glory may enter” (ibid.).

“He has not given his money at interest.” On the contrary, he gave Judas money to distribute to the poor. He indeed accepted gifts from the three magi and from other faithful people, but he did not accept them against the innocent, for whom he laid down his life. Now that the answer to the preceding question has been completed, the Psalm concludes thus:

“Whoever does these things shall never be moved.”

Just as “not everyone who says” to Christ, “Lord, Lord,” “will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of” his Father (Matt. 7:21), so not everyone who sings these things will dwell in my tabernacle or rest on my holy mountain, says the Lord, questioned by the Son himself, or by the prophet, or by any other saint. Therefore, whoever does these things throughout the whole present life, from the time he enters without stain either into the Church, or into a higher observance of holiness, or even, called without the stain of ambition, enters a place of preeminence—whoever, I say, having so entered without stain, does these things in the present time, while it is called today—shall not be moved in the future age of eternity. Rather, he shall rest on your holy mountain, O Lord God, forever, because his rest shall never be disturbed and shall have no end.

“Whoever does these things.” But he does these things not only who preserves an innocence once begun, but also who recovers it when lost through true repentance. For not only is “blessed … the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly” (Ps. 1), but also “blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31:1).

Glory to the Lord Father, who, when questioned, answered well here and explained the stages of merits by which one may attain eternal and unshaken rest. Glory to the Son, who ascended through those same stages and, thus exalted upon the holy mountain, draws all things to himself—namely, his own members. For he himself is the great mountain filling the world, so that his city, set upon this mountain, may rest in him. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is true rest and full rest for those resting in Christ, the holy and exalted mountain. May heaven and earth be full of the glory of this triune God. Amen.

## PSALM XV

[Col. 0829]

[Col. 0829C] “Preserve me, O Lord, because I have hoped in you.” With this psalm the third section now begins, in which there is a recapitulation of that foundation which is especially necessary to faith: namely, the mystery of Christ’s Passion. Its inscription is as follows:

[Col. 0829D] **VERSE 1. An inscription of a title, for David himself.** One must know that in this psalm the same thing should be understood—though it is said in different and fuller words—as is reported to have been written in the title of the Cross. For we read in the Gospel that, when the Lord was crucified, Pilate placed over him this title: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John 19:19). When many Jews objected to this title, Pilate is recorded to have answered: “What I have written, I have written” (ibid.).

There, though through one who did not know, the Holy Spirit signified that the title placed upon the Cross, as upon a triumphal arch, concerning Christ’s kingdom, was inviolable; for the kingdom of Christ acquired by the victory of the Passion would never be destroyed. Ezra, therefore, rightly recalls in this psalm—which concerns Christ’s kingdom—this inscription of that Title which he understood through the Holy Spirit would come to be, and which Pilate was to signify. The sense is this: the kingdom of Christ discussed here, which is signified by the inscription of the title, is attributed to David—not to that son of Jesse, concerning whose title no history tells anything, but to David himself, that is, to the true David understood through him, namely Christ.

For Christ is here shown to be King of the true Jews, that is, of those who confess in every language, while every tongue will confess “that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:11). Therefore that title was in not one language alone, but in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. By this the Holy Spirit signified that Christ’s kingdom was to be extended in this world through his Passion, not only in Judaea but throughout the Roman Empire, then flourishing through Greek wisdom and Latin strength. He had always reigned in heaven through his divinity.

Our King himself speaks in this psalm in the form of a servant. First, according to his humanity, he asks to be preserved and says that all which he suffered was brought to the glory of his inheritance. Second, he gives thanks to the Father for the understanding bestowed on him, for perseverance, resurrection, and session at the right hand of God, where he says: “I will bless the Lord who has given me understanding.” His purpose is to exhort Christ’s members to reign together with their Head.

This psalm is the second among those which treat briefly of the Passion and Resurrection. The first was: “O Lord, why are they multiplied?” (Ps. 3:2). This psalm differs from it because there the prophet treats at length, in Christ’s person, of adversaries—how they attack and are conquered—whereas here he treats at length of the good, and how they are glorified.

Therefore Christ tells us how he first prayed, saying: I, set upon the altar of the Cross as a victim, who am “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John 19:19); I, the same high priest, offering myself upon the altar of the Cross, where I sacrificed and sanctified myself for my own, that they too might be holy in truth; I, worthy to be heard because of my reverence, prayed upon the Cross, cried out with all my heart’s affection, and said to the Lord Father:

“Preserve me, O Lord.”

O Lord Father, preserve me, a man amid dangers. Or, preserve me—that is, preserve my own, for whom I am offered. Preserve them in your name: “Those whom you gave me, while I was with them, I kept. But now,” by the way of obedience, “I come to you,” having become obedient to you unto death, even death on a cross, for my own whom you gave me. “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil.” Therefore I say: Preserve them. Yet I pray “not only for them,” the disciples whom you gave me while I remained in the flesh, “but also for those who will believe in me through their word.”

In all these, preserve me, who “am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 17:11–12 and following). Preserve in them me as the way, that they may not stray; me as truth, that they may neither deceive nor be deceived; me as life, that even if they have died, they may live; and if they have died by some sin, that this sin may not be for them unto death. Rather, everyone who lives and believes in me, the life, may never die; though he dies for a time, he may not die eternally. Thus, Father, preserve me, who am the resurrection and the life, so that even if one of my own has died, he may rise through repentance and live eternally. Therefore, lest none of my own perish, preserve me, O Lord—that is, preserve my own.

And do this by giving grace for grace: for, having been anticipated by your grace, I hoped in you and caused my own to hope in you, which is a great gift of your grace. For that grace, as though for a good merit, I ask this grace: that you preserve me, that is, my own. For they were yours, and you gave them to me; they have kept your word and believed that I came forth from you, and therefore, following my teaching, they have hoped in you. For among other things I told them: “The Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and believed that I came forth from God” (John 16:27). Therefore, Father, they hoped in you, because I, made lower than the angels, proclaimed you to be greater than I and to be my God.

**VERSE 2.** For I said to you, the Lord my Father: “You are my God.” In saying this I spoke truly, because I am a man created by you, though I am also God begotten from you. Therefore I said to the Lord Father, not insofar as I am the maker of all things, but insofar as I was made: “You are my God.” This is evident from the following: “Because you do not need my goods.” For you are naturally rich, possessing “the depth of the riches of wisdom and knowledge” (Rom. 2:33 [probably 11:33]) divine; having every good in yourself, you do not need my goods, because you do not await becoming blessed by my goods or by the goods of my own, just as I, according to my humanity, await being made blessed and enriched by your goods. I need those goods as one poor and hanging on the Cross, and my poor ones need them also.

In the Hebrew it reads: “You are my God, because I have no good without you.” This is rightly said by the man assumed into God, for whom there is no well-being without God, because his well-being is in God his Father—in that God in whom he himself is God. It is likewise rightly said by “man born of a woman, short-lived and full of many miseries” (Job 14:1), for whom life is evil without God and shall never be good unless he cleaves to God, who is the highest good. For human and angelic nature is so noble that it cannot fare well except with, and in, the highest good. To that highest good he says: “You are my God, because I have no good without you.”

Be ashamed, you Pelagian heretics, who say that human beings can be something good by human power through free choice without the assistance of grace. The Son of God, insofar as he is human, assigns all his goods to God the Father. Let us therefore have the mind of Christ, saying to God: “You are my God, because you do not need my goods,” or: “Because I have no good without you.” I, the Son, said all this with my whole heart’s affection to the Lord Father, and the Father heard me; this is evident in its effect, because:

**VERSE 3. He made all my desires wonderful.** Although in my divinity I have one will together with my Father, a will which is neither multiple nor changeable, nevertheless, while still mortal, I had many desires in my human affections. For many times I wished to gather Jerusalem’s children as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and she was unwilling. Many times I wished it, and she was unwilling. Therefore I performed miracles among them and preached, so that, as it were, by the call of a hen I might gather chicks from my people. But because she was unwilling, the fulfillment of my desires was for a time lacking.

But after I rose again, ascended into heaven, and sent the Holy Spirit—not to all the people, but to witnesses preordained by God, namely to the saints who are in his land—those who, laboring amid worldly waves, fixed the anchor of their hope in the land of which it is said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matt. 3:5 [probably 5:5]). Just as the apostles, seeing the earth—that is, flesh—exalted in me above the heavens, were in that land, because in me they hoped that they themselves, or my members, would be exalted to the place whither “the firstfruits of those who sleep” (1 Cor. 15:20) had preceded in me their Head. To such saints, I say, he made all my desires wonderful, beginning in them: for by sending the Paraclete, he strengthened and enlightened my apostles, formerly weak and unlearned; and thus he made all my desires wonderful in them—that is, he fulfilled them wonderfully.

While still mortal, before I had prayed for them on the Cross, I often rebuked them for slowness of understanding. For example, I said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan, for you do not understand the things of God” (Mark 8:33); likewise, to the sons of Zebedee: “You do not know what you ask,” and, “You do not know what spirit you are of.” Elsewhere I said to all: “Are you still without understanding?” And: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me?” (Matt. 20:22; 15:16). In such sayings my desires, by which I wished the apostles to be enlightened, could be recognized. But by speaking and teaching I made little progress in them.

Yet after I prayed on the Cross that they might be preserved by the Father, the Father made all my desires wonderful in those same saints of mine for whom I had prayed: first fulfilling my desires in them, then through them in the other saints who are in his land, namely in the holy Church. For first the apostles themselves, through the power of the Resurrection, the glory of the Ascension, and the coming of the Holy Spirit, received knowledge of the Scriptures and of all languages; and those who had formerly been weak recovered from weakness and became strong in battle. Then through them many children of the city Jerusalem were gathered, whom I wished to gather beneath the wings of grace. And later, when other Jews rejected my word, and for that reason my disciples passed over to the Gentiles to proclaim the kingdom of God, all my desires were made wonderful—those desires concerning the conversion of the Gentiles which I had foretold, “at many times and in many ways speaking in the prophets,” but which “in these last days” I disclosed through myself (Heb. 1:1).

For I spoke of the prodigal son returning to his Father, by whom the conversion of the Gentiles is signified. Elsewhere I said: “The wedding feast is prepared, but those who were invited were not worthy. Therefore go to the crossroads, and invite to the wedding feast whomever you find” (Matt. 22:8–9). Likewise, in another parable it was said to the servant: “Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city.” Again: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel the poor, weak, blind, and lame to enter” (Luke 11:21, 23 [probably 14:21, 23]). By such sayings I disclosed through the Gospel my desires concerning the conversion of Jews and Gentiles.

Therefore, when I came to the Cross, where under the title of this psalm I was to pray, I caused not the donkey alone to be brought to me, but the colt with her (Matt. 21:2), because I was to gather elect persons not only from the Synagogue but also from the conquered Gentile people. I would liken them to my cavalry for crushing Pharaoh’s chariots and submerging them in the waters of baptism as in the Red Sea, because I poured out those waters from my side together with blood under this title’s inscription: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John 19:19).

By that title I was proclaimed King of all who confess: all who believe in their heart unto righteousness and confess with their mouth unto salvation—that I, whom the Jews denied and whose title-inscription they also wished to alter, am rightly entitled Jesus, that is, Savior; Nazarene, that is, holy; King of the Jews: not of those who denied me and still deny me, but of those who confess me before human beings, so that I too may confess them before my Father. For these are they whom I wished to gather from all nations beneath the wings of my arms stretched out upon the Cross.

For long ago I signified that my arms outstretched on the wood of the Cross should be understood as wings, when I caused two cherubim with outstretched wings to be placed within the Holy of Holies; in the spreading of their wings the shape of the Cross is expressed (Exod. 25:37). Likewise, when Isaiah saw me “upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. 6:1)—because, lifted up on the Cross, I was to draw all things to myself through my apostles crucified with me—he also saw seraphim with six wings shaped in the manner of a cross. By this it was plainly signified (ibid., 2) that, through those apostles set aflame by the fire of the Holy Spirit and conformed to me crucified, the whole world redeemed by my blood would be protected beneath the wings of my arms under the mystery of the Cross and borne upward.

[Col. 0834C] Therefore, in these saints of mine he made all my desires wonderful. They renounced their own desires because their desires seemed foul and contemptible to them, whereas mine seemed wonderful and praiseworthy. He made mine wonderful in such a way that they not only burn in the affection of holy desires, but also shine in the effect of good and wonderful works. So that no one may fail to know in what order my desires were made wonderful in my saints, I shall say: before the faith came which justified and made them wonderful, through the yoke of the Law,

**VERSE 4. Their weaknesses were multiplied.** Or their weaknesses were multiplied even through my evangelical teaching, because by my teaching they came to know many weaknesses of their own which they had previously not known. Thus, when I said to them: “You will all suffer scandal because of me this night” (Matt. 26:31), their weaknesses were multiplied according to my word—especially Peter the apostle’s, because he presumed upon his own strength. His weakness was multiplied. This was permitted so that they might run more swiftly to me, the physician; and so it happened.

For after recognizing their own weaknesses, they hastened eagerly to seek a medicine suitable for healing those weaknesses. Peter the apostle, whose weakness was most notably multiplied, swiftly “went out and wept bitterly” (Matt. 26:75). Following his example, every sinner still goes out when he makes known outwardly in confession the sin which he had concealed within. Or he goes out when, as though leaving Caiaphas’s courtyard, he separates himself from the company of evil persons—not merely by an inward disposition but by an evident difference in conduct—while the wicked wonder that good persons do not run with them into the same excess of debauchery.

Vehement repentance knows no slow exertions. Therefore, all who received the physician hastened. For example, Zacchaeus, after his weaknesses had been multiplied, sought Jesus, the true physician; he did not walk slowly, but “ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree in order to see him” (Luke 19:4). And when he heard that Jesus would stay in his house, he did not delay, but “hurried down and received him joyfully” (ibid., v. 5). Likewise Matthew the tax collector, when the physician said to him, “Follow me,” promptly “followed him” (Matt. 9:9). And many others who recognized their multiplied weaknesses promptly received him and still receive him.

“And to all who received him he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:22 [probably 1:12]), and to forget utterly the reproaches of their former weaknesses—those “who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God” (ibid., 14 [probably 1:13]). For they are not chosen because of nobility of blood to be called children of God, and their former names are no longer remembered before God. Therefore he says:

“I will not gather their assemblies from bloods.” That is, I shall indeed gather them into one, but not from bloods; since they are born not from bloods but from God my Father through the regenerating Spirit, so that they may be called children of God and my brothers.

“Nor will I remember their names upon my lips.” I shall no longer remember on my lips those names which they formerly had when they were called children of wrath, children of death, children of Gehenna. By those lips I shall remember their evils, saying in judgment: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:27). Again: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt; ought you not also to have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” (Matt. 18:32). Again: “Wicked and slothful servant, why did you not put my money into the bank?” (Luke 19:23). I shall not remember such names on my lips regarding those who formerly bore the same names, if afterwards they hastened to put them off through repentance and diligence in a better life.

Otherwise: “I will not gather their assemblies from bloods,” because I shall indeed gather, out of the multitude destined for condemnation, assemblies of a few elect; but this will occur not by the legal rite through the bloods of calves, lambs, and goats, but through my own unique blood. Having entered once for all into the Holy of Holies, I shall gather their assemblies; and I shall say to the little flock of such assemblies: “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased my Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32).

“Nor will I remember their names upon my lips”—upon my own lips; or, “upon my lips,” that is, through apostles and prophets, by whom, as by my lips speaking, I shall reproach the impenitent with their names. Or, by my lips, which are the two Testaments, which in harmonious speech condemn the impenitent but forget the former names of the penitent and do not condemn them. Or: “I will not remember their names upon my lips,” as once I used to say in identifying one people: “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel” (Exod. 3:11); or when I commanded that kings be made from the tribe of Judah and priests from the tribe of Levi. At times I was also mindful of names in designating one person, as when I swore to David my servant and when I made an oath to Abraham. But now there is no such regard for names with me, because I am no respecter of persons; rather, in every nation, those who recognized their weaknesses and afterwards hastened to come to me are accepted by me. Nor will I remember their former names, because their transformation is so great that each of them is called:

**VERSE 5. “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.”** That is, the Lord himself is my inheritance and the portion of my cup—that is, the cup of my own. For while others choose earthly and temporal portions, God is the portion of the saints. While others drink deadly pleasures, God is the drink of the saints, who through the intoxication of this cup forget their former pursuits. Therefore I, the Judge of the living and the dead, shall forget their names.

I also, the Son lifted up on the Cross and thereby endowed with a great inheritance—for there I asked my Father, and “he gave me the nations as an inheritance”; I speak of this inheritance (Ps. 7:8 [probably 2:8])—say: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.” The Lord, who was formerly the portion of the Levites, is now the portion of all my inheritance, and he is the portion of my cup; that is, of those who are my inheritance, whom I cultivate, and my cup, which I drink and incorporate into myself. Or, the Lord himself is the portion—that is, the recompense—of my cup, that is, of my Passion.

“You are the one who will restore my inheritance to me.” For my inheritance was lost through sin. But you are—you have true being—you are he who is, who says: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14). All other things run and flow; you are steadfastly. Propitiated by my Passion, you will restore my inheritance to me, so that what was mine in predestination may be subject to me in possession.

For the ordering of predestination was like a certain measuring-cord of distribution, stretched from the beginning of the world to its end. Along this cord of distribution rational creation, both angels and human beings, was apportioned: some are splendid through goodness; others dark and obscure through wickedness. But:

**VERSE 6. “The cords fell to me in splendid places.”** The measuring-line in eternal foreknowledge, or by a certain secret lot, fell to me in the splendid fields of good angels and human beings. But human beings had perished from their predestined brightness. Nevertheless, restored through my Passion, it will appear in that brightness to which it was predestined for me.

For my inheritance, though in part it has darkened itself, is nevertheless splendid to me, because I know to what brightness those whom I sought by my Passion have been foreordained. Even though those who are my inheritance may be as the filth and refuse of all things to this world, nevertheless my inheritance is splendid to me.

Otherwise: “You are the one who will restore my inheritance to me,” that is, “that glory which I had with you before the world was” (John 17:5). For this inheritance, this divine brightness, is hereditary to me because I am your Son. Having for a time emptied myself of that brightness, I now seek it back as something due—not to be bestowed upon my divinity, in which I never lost it, but upon the humanity which I humbled in the form of a servant, so that it might deservedly be exalted into the form of divine brightness. Though it owed nothing to death, it was humbled even unto death.

Therefore I said: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before the world was” (ibid., 1 [probably John 17:5]). Glorify me in my humanity with the glory which I have always had in my divinity. Glorify me not in any ordinary manner, not among the orders of angels, but above all orders of heavenly powers: with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was—*with* you, not beneath you, as Arius wished, but with you in the supreme equality of your glory.

Nor should it seem surprising that such glory is hereditary to me. For when I was conceived by the Holy Spirit, that is, by the love of the most glorious Father, then “the measuring-lines fell to me in splendid places” [Col. 0837C], so that I might be the lawful heir of paternal glory. The Father, acknowledging this concerning me, says: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John 12:28); as though he said: I glorified you when I begot you as the eternal Son in divinity, through whom I created the world—a great proof of your glory, because great wisdom is known through the fact that many great things were wisely made from nothing. And I will glorify you again when, in the nature of humanity, conceived of the Holy Spirit, of my love, and born, I acknowledge you as my Son—not adopted, but conceived and born through the working of my love—through whom, as I created all things, so I shall restore every creature, when the Gospel is preached to every creature, so that [Col. 0837D] everyone who believes in you may not perish but may have eternal life. Thus, having once glorified you, I shall glorify you again, while every creature, wonderfully created through you, the Word, shall no less wonderfully be saved through you as man [hominum; reading uncertain].

Since God the Father says these things to me, it is clear that “the measuring-lines fell to me in splendid places,” because I am the lawful heir of paternal and divine glory, as the natural Son of God—supremely rich not only in my divinity, but also supremely blessed in my humanity—so that both my humanity and my divinity are in highest glory. For “my inheritance is splendid” [Col. 0838A] to me, though it was obscure to Arius the heresiarch, who said that I was less than the Father, whereas I am in highest glory not only according to my divinity but also according to my humanity. I was indeed made lower than the angels through mortality; but now I have received not an angelic but a superangelic and wholly divine immortality, so that, although the integrity of human nature remains in me, that same nature is nevertheless in highest and wholly divine glory.
