But “I will that where I am, there also my ministers may be, that they may see my glory” (John 17:24), and, seeing it, share in it and enjoy it, just as bodily eyes, by seeing the brightness of the sun, become participants in that same brightness and enjoy it all the more delightfully the more clearly they see it. I will all [Col. 0838B] this: that, as I am in glory, so I may be seen in glory by my own, whose eyes of heart are pure and clear; for “the measuring-lines fell to me in splendid places.” For my inheritance is splendid to me, and it has been restored to me through the Passion. Therefore, in thanksgiving:

**VERSE 7.** “I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding,” by which I understand the glory of my inheritance. The first “man, when he was in honor, did not understand” his honor, nor did he give thanks to the giver of that honor, in whom and for whom he was created. Therefore, as one ungrateful, “he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13). But I, the second man from heaven, heavenly, understand the honor and glory of the inheritance bestowed on me. Therefore, “I will bless [Col. 0838C] the Lord, who has given me understanding.” I will bless him also for my members, in whom he has given me understanding, that they may be able to understand the glory of my inheritance.

“Moreover, even unto night my reins rebuked me.” Since one does not bless the Lord perfectly who praises him only for prosperity, I bless the Lord for the prosperity of understanding bestowed upon me and mine; and moreover I shall bless him also because my reins—that is, my kinsmen, from whose loins I have consanguinity—rebuked me with the harsh rebuke of sufferings and taught me obedience, even unto night, that is, unto death.

In the Hebrew it reads: “Moreover, even by night my reins instructed [Col. 0838D] me.” Where it says *instructed*, we have *rebuked*, because instruction comes through rebukes, especially in nights, that is, adversities. Although a foolish person is broken by these, a prudent one is instructed by the same things.

Otherwise: Me—that is, my own—my reins, that is, fleshly passions, rebuked unto night, that is, unto the pleasure of sinning. But I:

**VERSE 8.** “Kept the Lord always before me” [Note: [Col. 0837] The Vulgate has: “I kept the Lord always in my sight.”], so that neither I myself might be moved to impatience through the night of the Passion, nor my own might be moved to deliberate consent to sin through the night of [Col. 0839A] carnal pleasure; because the Lord is at my right hand and stands by me with his help, lest I be shaken.

**VERSE 9.** “Therefore my heart rejoiced” in contemplation, “and my tongue exulted” in speech. For, as Matthew testifies in the Gospel, I exulted in spirit through the joy of my heart, and my tongue uttered exultant words. For I said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25). Likewise: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15). Likewise: “I have power to lay down my life and power to take it up again.” “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down, and I take it up again” [Col. 0839B] (John 10:18). In such sayings my heart rejoiced and my tongue exulted.

“Moreover, my flesh also shall rest in hope.”

Above I had said: “Moreover, even unto night my reins rebuked,” or “instructed,” me. Now I say: “Moreover, my flesh also shall rest in hope,” so that, as it was an addition to my pain that I was rebuked by my relatives, so it may be an addition to my consolation that my flesh rests in the hope of the resurrection, which you, Father, will quickly hasten.

**VERSE 10.** “For you will not abandon my soul in hell,” though it descends indeed to the lower regions for the elect who sit there “in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1:79), awaiting deliverance; [Col. 0839C] yet it will quickly return from there, the pains of hell having been loosed, since it is impossible for it to be held by him. Therefore I say: “For you will not abandon my soul in hell,” which, as soon as it enters, will have with it in paradise the soul also of the confessing thief. Hence it may faithfully be believed that the despoiling of hell and the opening of paradise will happen swiftly, in accordance with the name assigned to me by the Prophet, to whom it was said: “Call his name: Swiftly take away the spoil; hasten to plunder” (Isa. 8:1). I was not called by this name in vain, because, when the despoiling of hell has swiftly been accomplished, you will not abandon my soul in hell; rather, on the day when it has departed from the body, it will be in Paradise with the spoils of many souls. For this reason the holy Evangelist [Col. 0839D] calls the following Sabbath day a great Sabbath day: because the faithful souls freed from hell celebrated a great Sabbath-rest with Christ’s soul, the thief’s soul being joined to them through the power of the Lord’s Passion.

“And you will not give your Holy One to see corruption.” When the archangel Gabriel announced my conception, he said to my mother: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore also that Holy Thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). Thus the angel, speaking, called my body, conceived of the Holy Spirit, *Holy*, not *sanctified*. For that is properly called sanctified to which holiness is accidental. But that to which holiness is wholly substantial is rightly called not so much sanctified as holy [Col. 0840A], as is the body conceived of the Holy Spirit, through which the whole body of the Church is to be sanctified. This Holy One of yours, holy Father, you will not give to see—that is, you will not permit to experience—corruption. For although it can be preserved from the corruption of decay until the swiftly completed resurrection on the third day according to the Scriptures only by divine power, nevertheless, by way of abundance, human care too will be applied to my holy body, by which it would be prevented from decaying if, according to its condition, it tended toward decay as other bodies do. For a sufficient quantity of myrrh and aloes will be applied, aromatic spices which do not allow bodies prepared with them to decay. And it will also be proclaimed throughout the world that Mary Magdalene anticipated anointing my body for burial with the best ointment, which would have delayed the decay of my body if that had been necessary. But it is not necessary, because you will quickly bring the resurrection to completion; nor will you give my body—your Holy One, sanctified for the whole Church—to see corruption. Therefore, rightly, as I said above: “I will bless the Lord who has given me understanding,” because you, Father:

**VERSE 11.** “Have made known to me the ways of life.” You have made known to me that through the obedience of the Passion, through humility, and through love for my neighbors, for whom I die, I go to the Resurrection; and through the Resurrection to the Ascension; and through the Ascension to my sitting at your right hand. There you will fill me with joy, I who [Col. 0840C] now, full of sorrow, say: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Mark 14:34); I who now say to my own: “And you also now indeed have sorrow” (Job 16:22). Then I shall be filled with joy in myself with your countenance, because I, now mortal, shall then be immortal with your countenance—that is, with your Word united to me, which is your countenance, because through it you are known. With that countenance of yours, I, the assumed man—I who am now sorrowful unto death—shall hereafter have joy and delights at your right hand, that is, in your eternal glory, unto the end that has no end; unto the end of which it is elsewhere said: “I have seen an end of every consummation.”

Otherwise: “You have made known to me”—that is, to my own through my examples—the ways of life, concerning which I said: “I have given [Col. 0840D] you an example, that you also may do likewise.” “You will fill me,” that is, my own, “with joy with your countenance,” that is, when they see me, your countenance, alive after death’s triumph.

Or: You will fill them with joy when you send them the Holy Spirit, who is true joy, together with your countenance—with your Son, who am I. For you will send to my desolate disciples the Paraclete in my name, and so you will fill them with joy with your countenance. For he will glorify me, your countenance, because he will take of what is mine and announce it to them. Finally, once the ways of life have been fulfilled in them and they have been filled with joy, when they have passed from this left-hand life, wretched and full of miseries, they will have delights at your right hand, in the glory of eternity, unto the end, unto such a consummation beyond which nothing can be desired.

[Col. 0841A] Glory to the eternal Father, who restored a splendid inheritance to his Son and fills him with joy. Glory to the Son, who is filled with joy not only in himself but also in his members. Glory to the Holy [Col. 0842A] Spirit, who is this same eternal joy, by which Christ, the Head without measure, and the members with measure, are filled—namely, “according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4:7).

## PSALM XVI

[Col. 0841]

[Col. 0841A] “Hear, O Lord, my righteousness.” The title is:

**A PRAYER OF DAVID HIMSELF**

This Psalm and four others are entitled with the name of prayer, because, although prayer is intermingled with the other Psalms [Col. 0841B], in these Psalms prayer alone is contained; and if anything else is inserted into the prayer, it serves the prayer, which is principally intended in these Psalms.

This prayer accords with the subject of the preceding Psalm. Hence it is rightly assigned to David himself, to whom the inscription of the title was also assigned in the preceding Psalm. For Christ himself, just as by weeping at Lazarus’s death he taught us charity in compassion toward our neighbors; just as he fled in order to remove from us the boldness of unconsidered rashness; just as he washed the disciples’ feet to give an example of humility; so he prayed in order to teach us to pray. For in this Psalm the Head himself intends to pray to God for himself and his own, lest they fail. He also treats of his own persecution, of the temporal and everlasting damnation of his enemies, and likewise of his future glorious and complete satiety with his own. For, dying in his obedience, he says to the Father: “You have proved my heart and visited it by night. You have tested me by fire, and no iniquity has been found in me. That my mouth may not speak the works of men: because of the words of your lips I have kept hard ways.” And further on: “My enemies surrounded my soul; they have enclosed their fat; their mouth has spoken pride. Casting me down, they now surrounded me; they fixed their eyes to cast me to the ground. They seized me like a lion ready for prey, and like a lion’s whelp dwelling in hiding.” These things concern his own persecution. But concerning the damnation of enemies, he says: [Col. 0841D] “Arise, O Lord, confront him,” and so forth. Finally, concerning the glorious satisfaction of himself and his own, he says: “But I shall appear before your countenance in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.”

The first part, therefore, concerns prayer; the second, the narrative of the Lord’s Passion; the third, the condemnation of enemies; and the fourth, the glorification of Christ and his own. Thus Christ, showing the true nature of his humanity, prays, saying:

“Hear, O Lord, my righteousness.” O Lord, whom I obey in the form of a servant, and whom I acknowledge as Lord in that same form, hear my righteousness. For as through one person’s disobedience many were made sinners, so it is fitting and just that through one person’s righteousness and obedience many should be made righteous [Col. 0842A]. Of every generous giver of alms it is said: “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever and ever” (Ps. 111:9). And this righteousness is heard before God, because almsgiving itself prays to the Lord. How much more, then, I, who make myself an alms-offering to God for the poor and thereby possess righteousness worthy of being heard, because this almsgiving itself prays—or rather, by righteousness makes a strong claim for mercy to be shown by you, God the Father, to me and mine, for whose good pleasure and command I have performed mercy. For mercy is owed in justice to the merciful. And I am that merciful Samaritan who showed mercy to him whom Aaron, the priest of the Old Testament, passed by, because he could not heal him by the blood of goats or calves. But I poured from my own side wine and oil into his wounds. For my blood is oil and wine, of which it is said in Judah’s blessing: “He shall wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of grapes” (Gen. 49:11). “For I [Col. 0842C] am the true vine” (John 15:1), and a fruitful olive, by whose medicinal blood, as by wine and oil, that man is healed who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers. Therefore, since I have shown mercy to him, “Hear, O Lord, my righteousness,” so that I also, who have now fallen among robbers—crucified by robbers and among robbers—may obtain for myself and mine the mercy which I seek, not unjustly, but by the scales and balance of justice. For if my calamity is weighed in the balance against the sins by which I merited wrath, this calamity itself appears heavier than the sins I have borne upon myself, as the sand of the sea is heavier—namely, the sins of the whole world, for which I suffer and am offered up, I, the Lamb taking away the sins of the world that believes in me, while condemning the sins of the world that does not believe in me. [Col. 0842D] Would that the sins of my own and my calamity might be weighed in the balance of justice! Indeed, because I, already hanging, struggle upon the cross, whose two arms represent the balance, I ask in the presence of the Father and of the whole heavenly court whether my calamity is not sufficiently weighty to outweigh the sins of all who believe in me. If one considers not only what, but who, suffers in this calamity: I, the Son of God, suffer for servants, the just for the unjust. Does not such a sacrifice have a fragrance by which the stench of sins, which the first Adam spread through the human race, may justly be abolished? Does not such a sacrifice have the powerful cry of prayer, worthy to be heard and answered—not only by mercy but also [Col. 0843A] by justice? If a human being only, and not God, suffered calamity on account of human iniquity, the scales would stand with equal pans, holding in one pan, that of judgment, iniquity, and in the other, that of mercy, calamity. But because, on account of the iniquity of humankind alone, I, God and man, suffer calamity—hanging in the balance of the cross, a just man without sins of my own, true God, the fountain of righteousness—hear, O Lord, my righteousness, so that the calamity which I suffer in the pan of mercy may appear the heavier and, like the sand of the sea outweighing a few pebbles—that is, the sins of my own—in the pan of justice, may so raise in judgment that pan of justice with its great weight that whatever sins and evils are in the pan of justice, when that same pan is swiftly and violently lifted in judgment, may all be shaken into the depths of the sea. For if the offering of a lamb against Pharaoh’s wickedness was of such weight that Pharaoh himself was thereby shaken into the depths of the sea, it is just that, when I, the true Lamb, have been offered against the wickedness of the invisible Pharaoh, he himself with his whole army should be cast into the depths of hell, and the true Hebrews be wholly free from his oppression. This is just; this is reasonable: since the greedy robber wished to hold an innocent man, he should lose even the guilty person who wishes to cleave to that innocent one. If this is just—indeed, because it is just—hear, O Lord, my righteousness. Attend to my supplication concerning the removal of evils; with your ears receive my prayer concerning the bestowal of goods. Or: attend in your own heart to the supplication [Col. 0843C] made in the heart; receive with your ears the prayer made with the mouth—for prayer is so called as though it were the “reason of the mouth”—the prayer, I say, uttered not with deceitful lips, as those pray who say, “Lord, Lord” (Matt. 7:21) and do not do the Father’s will, or who judge others without mercy while themselves seeking mercy.

**VERSE 2.** “Let my judgment come forth from your countenance; let your eyes behold things that are equitable.” Behold, ears, eyes, and countenance are ascribed to God the Father, although he is an unbounded spirit, having neither a heart within nor ears or eyes without. But by these human words divine efficacy is signified: for he to whom every will speaks has wondrous ears; and he from whom no secret is hidden has wondrous eyes. Therefore, when it is said to him, “Receive the prayer with your ears,” or “Let your eyes behold equity,” the ears and eyes are to be understood as the Divinity itself, to whom every heart lies open, every will speaks, and from whom no secret is hidden. By his countenance, however, his Son is understood: namely, the Word that was in the beginning, and the wisdom through which all things were made. From this countenance, this Word, this wisdom, the human being assumed in the person of that same Word, countenance, and wisdom receives the ordering of all his judgments. Hence he said: “I can do nothing of myself,” but “as I hear, I judge” (John 5:30), because that assumed [Col. 0844A] man depended upon the oracle of the Word inherent in him. Therefore he prays to the Father, saying: “Let my judgment come forth from your countenance,” that is, let the judgment by which I, appointed judge of the living and the dead, shall judge, come forth from your countenance, from your Word united to me, so that in all my judgment I may judge only and wholly what I hear your Word declaring—the judgment to be exercised invisibly by you through me, the human being, visibly. For you, Father, will judge no one visibly, but you have given to me all judgment that is to be exercised visibly, to me, the Son who will judge manifestly, “because I am the Son of man” (Matt. 27:43).

Likewise, let my judgment, by which I am now unjustly judged under Pontius Pilate, come forth from your countenance, so that nothing may happen to me as man except what is pleasing in your Word united to me.

[Col. 0844B] Similarly, let the judgment by which I shall be judged in my members before kings and governors come forth from your countenance. My elect also, who will sit “upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28), or those likewise who judge angels and worldly matters—of whom one says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more, then, worldly matters?” (1 Cor. 6:3)—exercise my judgment, because I judge in and through them. Therefore I ask that such judgment of mine too may come forth from your countenance, that it may in no respect displease your countenance; but that the world may know that both the judgment by which I judge justly and the judgment by which I am judged unjustly have come into their foreordained effects from your countenance, your will, your voluntary disposition—both for the glorification of myself and my own [Col. 0844C] and for the damnation of enemies—according to the rules of equity by which what is due is rendered to all through my judgment. And if the world will not see these equitable things, at least let your eyes see them: let the most diligent and most clear-sighted discernment that is in you see the equities in this matter, both in the glorification of myself and my own and in the damnation and confusion of enemies. For nothing is more equitable than that those who condemn the innocent should be condemned, and that one innocently and unjustly condemned should be justly glorified.

Otherwise: Let my judgment not come forth “in deceitful lips,” so that I might judge one thing with my mouth and think another in my heart, calling evil good or good evil; but let all judgment of myself and my own come forth [Col. 0844D] from your countenance, from the sincere reason and true understanding which your countenance approves. And lest, through the deceiving obscurity of things, it happen otherwise, let your eyes behold equity—for one translation so reads. Therefore I, judge of the living and the dead, pray this: that my eyes, namely the eyes of my mind made transparent by divine brightness, may see equity; and that my eyes, namely the holy rulers of the Churches, may see equity, lest they at any time stray from justice through blindness. But lest I seem presumptuously to claim my own equity, or vainly to have prayed that my righteousness be heard, I call upon you, searcher of hearts, as witness that I, condemned by an unjust judgment and “reckoned with the wicked” (Mark 15:28), am free from iniquity, as you yourself know—[Col. 0845A] you who, although you know all things, nevertheless, for greater evidence of the truth:

**VERSE 3.** “You have proved my heart and visited it by night.”

When the nocturnal thief, tempting my heart in the wilderness through gluttony, vainglory, and worldly ambition, wished to break into my house, he could not. Afterwards, amid many tribulations—from Jews who slandered, envied, plotted against, blasphemed, and finally crucified me—you tested me, as gold in a furnace, through the fire of the Passion; and no iniquity was found in me, because I was neither drawn by the devil’s nocturnal temptations toward unlawful desire, nor provoked or brought by open persecution to impatience. Thus no iniquity was found in me, though much sought for. “For the prince of this world comes” [Col. 0845B] (John 14:30), seeking something of his own in me, but he found nothing in me. Yet he was permitted, both in himself and through his members, to tempt and afflict me, because through these temptations you, Father, proved me as gold and visited me as a sick man. Although I had no illnesses of my own, I nevertheless truly bore the infirmities of my own, which, when you visited them, had to be healed in this manner. But as regards my own person, no iniquity was found in me; and this, even while I was silent:

**VERSE 4.** “That my mouth may not speak,” you know to be true. Otherwise: “That my mouth may not speak the works of men,” as though human nature in Christ said to God the Father [Col. 0845C]: Lest anyone suppose that I attribute to myself, not to you; to man, not to God; to flesh, not to the Word, the fact that I am free from sin and that no iniquity is found in me, I, the human being, clear myself of such a suspicion by saying: “That my mouth may not speak the works of men.” For the fact that I am free from sin, that neither original nor actual fault is found in me, is not a work of human beings, who by the law of nature beget children and cannot preserve them from sin. It is your work, God my Father, whose Word comes forth into the Virgin’s womb; it is the work of the Holy Spirit, your love, ineffably accomplishing my conception in the Virgin’s understanding beyond all understanding; and it is the work of the Word and Wisdom, building a house for itself, fashioning for itself a dwelling-place of most pure soul and flesh [Col. 0845D], and preserving that same house free from actual sins. These works, I say, are not human but divine. For it is not within a human being’s power that his way should be spotless or that one born of a woman should appear pure.

Or, iniquity was so completely absent from me that I am not found blameworthy even in speech, while keeping my mouth under such great guard that it may not speak the works of men—the things commonly said for boastfulness. Rather, I speak and magnify God’s works for the spread of his glory. For I say: “The Father abiding in me, he does the works” (John 14:10). By this saying no boastfulness accrues to me as man; rather, only his glory is thereby magnified, he who performs the works.

Likewise my mouth—for example, the apostle Paul [Col. 0846A]—carefully takes heed that it may not speak the works of men. When he had said, “I labored more abundantly than all,” lest he seem to speak of a human work, he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10). For one who boasts in himself, speaking the works of men as though he performs his good works by his own strength, is such a servant as does not remain in the house forever: a servant, I say, who does not know what his Lord does in him. But my friend Paul was not such, nor anyone like him who knows well what his Lord does in him; he does not speak the works of men but of God, saying something like this: “Lord, you will give us peace; for you have wrought all our works for us” (Isa. 26:12). Thus, thus is boasting avoided, when divine rather than human power is proclaimed in every good work—[Col. 0846B] whether by my own mouth, sufficiently disciplined in speaking, or by any mouth of mine, namely a minister of my word, desirous not of his own glory but of God’s—so that it may not boastfully speak the works of men but humbly speak the works of God unto God’s glory. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, because he was not my mouth, a divine and truthful mouth, therefore boastfully spoke of a human work, saying: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built as the house of my kingdom, by the strength of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Dan. 4:27). Hence such a useless and evil servant, who neither knew nor cared to know or say what his Lord had done in him and through him, had to be cast out of the house not only of eternity but also of his temporal kingdom [Col. 0846C]; and this happened. For while the speech was still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven: “To you it is said, King Nebuchadnezzar: the kingdom has departed from you, and they will cast you out from among men, until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men” (ibid., 5:28–29). Thus proud boasting was to be humbled through the words of your lips, through which you are known to rule in the kingdom of men, so that my mouth—the truthful mouth which is mine, who am the truth—may not, I say, speak the works of men because of the words of your lips. By them you rebuke not only Nebuchadnezzar but every arrogant person boasting of a great work, as though any good or great work were a work of men rather than of God, who rules in the kingdom of men and works through [Col. 0846D] human beings every good or great work, as was the building of the city of Babylon.

You, God, do not perform sin through angels or sinful human beings, because sin is not properly called a work, but the destruction or deformation of a divine work; thus one who blinds an eye destroys and deforms a divine work. But you, Father abiding in me, performed a divine work when, with you working, I gave sight to the man born blind, raised Lazarus, or performed another divine work, whether through myself or through one of my own. Such works I proclaim through myself or my own, so that my mouth may not speak the works of men and may not attribute any useful or good work to human capacity. Hence Solomon, who was my mouth, after building the great and magnificent Temple, lest he appear to boast because of it as though it had been begun or completed by work of human strength, said among other things: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who spoke with his mouth to David my father and fulfilled it with his hands.” Likewise: “O Lord God of Israel, there is no God like you in heaven above or on earth below, who kept for David my father the things you spoke to him. You spoke with your mouth and fulfilled them with your hands, as this day proves” [Col. 0847A] (3 Kings 8:15, 23, 24). Thus every mouth of mine has been disciplined so that it may not speak your works, God the Father, as though they were works of men, because of the words of your lips, by which you rebuke proud angel and human being. Much more did I, uniquely just, meek, and humble of heart, because the words of your lips—that is, the prophets—were to be kept and fulfilled [Col. 0847B] (for “I have not come to abolish the law or the prophets,” Matt. 5:17), not only restrain my mouth lest it speak the works of men, but also keep the hard ways, the ways of mortality. Therefore I pray:

**VERSE 5.** “Perfect my steps, and those of my own, in your paths.” In the paths of eternity, so that, because I am free from sins yet have been harshly afflicted by the hard ways of mortality for the sake of the words of your lips, this may be my reward: that the steps of my humanity may be perfected in the paths of your divinity, so that my footprints, set upon the solid foundation of eternity, may not be moved. This will finally be accomplished if the stability of eternity is bestowed upon those in whom I walk. Thus, although the waves of the sea upon which I walked were naturally fluid, a certain solidity was bestowed upon them by the impressions of my feet. By this could be signified that solidity of eternity which is to be bestowed upon my footprints in all those subject to me in this great sea of fluid temporality and mortality, and receiving in themselves the footprints of my feet—that is, my examples. Perfect, therefore, my steps in your paths, so that my own footprints may not be moved, firmly established in all my own by perfect solidity. Or also: “That my footprints may not be moved,” that is, those of my own, as Peter’s footprints were moved when he doubted.

In the Hebrew it reads: “Because of the word of your lips I have observed the paths of the robber. Sustain my steps in your tracks, and let not my footprints slip.” [Col. 0847D] Therefore let Christ, who was reckoned with the wicked and robbers, say: “I have observed the paths of the robber,” because, as a robber does not walk upon the public and level road but travels through rocky, trackless, and thorny places, so I, in order to fulfill the words of your lips, did not walk according to the customary traditions of the scribes and Pharisees. Rather, I walked through the path of your commandments, abandoned by them, as in a wilderness; and in their judgment I was like a robber, since they judged me worthy to be crucified with robbers. Indeed, when the robber Barabbas was released, I was, as though a robber, condemned to punishment. Therefore sustain the steps of myself and my own, and let not the footprints of myself and my own slip.

Otherwise: I, in my weak ones, like Peter still timid, have kept hard paths, because for such persons difficulty seems hard in observing [Col. 0848A] the words of your lips. But I now sacrifice myself for them, that they also may be holy in truth. I do not ask that you take them out of the world in such imperfection, but sanctify them in truth, and perfect my steps in them—not only for walking the paths of the general commandments, but also that they may walk rightly in the narrow paths of the most perfect counsels.

**VERSE 6.** “I cried, because you heard me, O God.” Earlier, amid lesser tribulations, I prayed, as it were, less urgently, and then you heard me by performing divine works for me. Therefore, assured of a greater hearing through the great Passion of death, I poured out prayers “with a strong cry” (Heb. 5:7), certain that you would hear this cry because you had previously heard me praying gently, as in Lazarus’s resurrection. Then, in raising one man, you heard me praying only moderately. But I, knowing that you always hear me, cried out and prayed for the raising of the whole human race from the death of souls through my death; and I prayed with a cry that all people might also be raised from bodily death through my resurrection, when, by dying, I destroyed the death of souls and, by rising, restored the life of bodies. What did I cry? Namely this:

“Incline your ear to me, and hear my words.” From the height of supreme Divinity to the sickbed of human weakness, in which I bear the infirmities of many, incline your ear. You are physician to me, the sick one, and to me who truly bears the infirmities of my own; and hear my words, namely these:

[Col. 0848C] VERSE 7. Make your mercies wonderful. Let the veil of the Temple be torn as I die upon the cross; let a great earthquake occur, so that all hell is shaken and captivity is carried away from it; and let the gates of Paradise be opened to that captivity, liberated from hell through me, so that today, after the opening of my side, the soul of the thief to whom I said, “Today you shall be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43), may be joined with me there in Paradise. Make your mercies wonderful also in this: that, as I rise again, many bodies of the saints may rise with me and appear to many as a testimony to my resurrection. Make your mercies wonderful also in this: that you may swiftly comfort the disciples, troubled by my death, through the joy which I promised them when I said: “But I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16:22).

In all these things make your mercies wonderful—mercies which will be still more wonderful if they are present when they are scarcely believed or hoped to be present; and so it will be. For those in hell, now almost despairing, will say: “You have come, O Desired One, whom we awaited in darkness, that you might this night lead the bound from their prison cells. Our sighs called for you; our abundant lamentations sought you. You have become hope to the despairing.” And the disciples also, as though already despairing, will say: “But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). Therefore make your mercies wonderful in this: that you may offer those already foundering in the direction of despair wonderful consolations in the triumphant joy of my resurrection, and such joy as no one may take from them. Thus make your mercies wonderful toward my own before all hope fails within them. For those who say, “We had hoped,” using the imperfect tense of the past, show that they still retain certain remnants of good hope. Therefore, before good hope utterly fails in them, make your mercies wonderful for them, you who save those who hope in you.

Do not, do not delay consolation too long, lest they fall utterly into the abyss of despair; for you do not save those who despair, but those who hope in you. Yet I pray not only for those who will see me on the day of the Resurrection, but also for those who will believe through their testimony and hope in me: let your mercies be made wonderful to all of them. For you save not only those who see me and thereby confess you and believe in you through me, whom they have touched or seen, as Thomas will see and touch me and thus believe; but through me you save all who hope in you, so that I, the Truth, may truly be found to have said: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29).

VERSE 8. Keep me from those who resist your right hand. Your Word, united to me as man, is your right hand; and those who refuse obedience to that same Word resist this Word, this right hand of yours. Therefore keep me, the man, from those who resist your right hand, as the pupil of the eye. Keep me in such a way that it may become known to the whole world that I, the assumed man, in the true light “which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9), am the pupil of your eye. For just as the pupil, though small in the eye, is nevertheless that through which the whole power of sight of the entire eye is directed, so I, the assumed man in divine light, although small in the condition of humanity, am nevertheless so glorified in the brightness of eternal light that you, Father, see no one except through me, your pupil, and no one comes to you, Father, unless enlightened through me. Keep me, therefore, as you ought rightly to keep the pupil of your eye.

Or, “keep me” means: keep all who are mine as you keep me myself, who am the pupil of your eye. For I desire that where I am, there my own may also be, that they too, glorified according to their measure, may see the glory which you gave to me, the most radiant pupil of your eye. With this eye you saw in the beginning all that you had made, and they were very good, before the malice of sin emerged. And now, in the fullness of time, with that same eye and that same light, through me as your pupil—black through the humility of the form of a servant, yet bright through union with that same light—you again look upon your whole creation, while through me and mine the Gospel is preached to every creature.

Keep, therefore, my disciples also, through whom the light of truth must be spread, as the pupil of the eye. Keep as the pupil of the eye all mine who are to be enlightened by their teaching. Keep them, so that, like the pupil of the eye, they may be black through true humility and bright through true charity. For just as everyone “who hates his brother is in darkness,” so everyone “who loves his brother is in the light” (1 John 2:11), and is enlightened as the pupil of the eye. For all of these, praying now upon the cross—or even after the cross and death, remaining at your right hand and interceding—I do not say, “Keep my own,” but I say, “Keep me.” For so long as you do not keep one of the least of mine, you do not keep me; and so long as you give protection to one of the least of mine, whether by angels or by angelic men, whom you set as “watchmen upon the walls of Jerusalem” (Isaiah 62:6), you give protection to me and keep me in my own.

You kept me in mine when, for my sake—since I was to be born from Abraham’s race—you did not allow that race to be exterminated or annihilated: neither by Pharaoh, commanding that every male child, from whom I was believed to be destined to be born, be drowned in the river (Exodus 1:22); nor by the kings of Israel, who hated and persecuted the house of David, from the fruit of whose womb I had been promised, to reign and sit upon the throne of that same David. Your wakeful protection around me, guarding me as the pupil of the eye, also restrained the king of Babylon, lest he utterly destroy my race, either by compelling it to worship the statue he had set up or by killing it (Daniel 3:6). It also restrained the wicked Haman in the Persian kingdom, lest he utterly destroy my race as he wished (Esther 6). Likewise Antiochus, king of the Greeks, was hindered (2 Maccabees 9), enraged by the devil against my race and wishing utterly to destroy it, when my birth was now very near. The devil had wished through the kings and tyrants just mentioned to anticipate this birth, so that, if the stock from which I was to be born were cut down, I, the pupil of your eye, might not come to illumine the whole body of the Church.

But now, as John my beloved testifies, these five kings have fallen (Revelation 17:10): namely, the Egyptian, the Israelite, the Babylonian, the Persian—who is also the Mede—and the last king, the Greek, who fell, overcome by the power of the Maccabees. One remains: the Roman, namely the emperor, under whose governor Pontius Pilate I die in the flesh, and under whose imperial ministers the crown of martyrdom is due to many of my members. Another—that is, Antichrist, who will seek to kill not so much the bodies as the souls of mine—has not yet come, but will come in all the power of Satan, with prodigies and lying signs. He will be so proud that he will sit in my Temple, which is the Church, showing himself as though he were God; indeed, he will exalt himself above everything called God or worshipped. He will spread such clouds of errors throughout the world that, if possible, even the elect will be led into error. They are like the pupil of my eye, chosen so that they may not only avoid error themselves, but also illumine the whole body of the Church against the darkness of errors.

Here, Father, there is need of your protection: you who have kept me in mine as the pupil of the eye against the tyrannies and cunning devices of all past kingdoms, even to this hour, in which there is a power of darkness—but a very brief one. For after the shortest sleep of death I, the pupil of your eye, shall awake again. Indeed, because I am “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5), I shall sleep with watchful eyes. For while my body, having drunk “from the torrent” of death “on the way” (Psalm 109:7), falls asleep in swift passage, like Noah sleeping after drunkenness, I, with my spirit awake and commended into your hands, Father, shall see sufficiently clearly as the pupil of your eye. I shall distinguish between the sons to be blessed and the seed of Canaan liable to a curse because it does not honor my nakedness in this brief, hourly power of darkness.

But in that long power of darkness, the danger will be more serious, when Antichrist reigns in this very respect contrary to me: just as I, the pupil of your eye, am the light of the world, so he, the prince of darkness, with the angels serving him, the rulers of darkness, and all the sons of night and darkness adhering to him, will almost blind the whole world. Therefore, because greater need requires greater help and protection, then, Father, keep me with most diligent protection as the pupil of the eye: lest Arius, a minister of Antichrist, or some other heretic extinguish me in mine; lest he diminish in mine the faith of the divinity by which I, the pupil of your eye, shine most fully; and lest Judas, that worst of merchants, who has now sold me, retain in his successors the power of selling me and possessing “the price at which I was valued” (Zechariah 11:13). Rather, let him be compelled to confess his sin and lose the price, so that it may become a burial-place for strangers, who are the pupil of your eye: that, buried to me in the precious field of eternal inheritance acquired through my blood, they may be kept as the pupil of your eye from every blinding work of Antichrist.

Protect me under the shadow of your wings. For you, Father, have wings: namely, the two Testaments. In one you promise temporal goods to your worshippers; in the other, eternal goods. Under the shadow of these wings protect me, so that, having been given all power in heaven and on earth, I may grant my perfect lovers both assistance in the temporal concerns of this present life and an enduring fruit of everlasting joys in eternal goods. Let none among them lack necessities in temporal matters, but let distribution be made to each according to each one’s need. Yet in the love of eternal things let them have one heart and one soul, so that your left hand, as one wing, may be under the head, and your right hand, as the other wing, may embrace every soul which, by doing your will, Father, and conceiving and bringing forth me, your Word, becomes my mother and your bride. For “whoever does” your will, Father, “is my brother and sister and mother” (Matthew 12:50). And if she is mother to me, your Son, she is therefore your bride. Let every such one, my mother and your bride, then say: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song of Songs 2:6).

Thus protect me, that is, my own, under the shadow of your wings: not so that they suffer no hardship in this world, but lest, cast out beyond your wings, they either fall into or put on avarice through excessive want of temporal things—avarice, a kind of mask and face of the wicked—or, through excessive neglect of eternal things, as charity grows cold among mine, put on the abundance of iniquity as a kind of mask and most hideous face, which is the face of the wicked who afflicted me. For the Jews crucified me chiefly because of avarice, while I disputed against their avarice; especially the Scribes and Pharisees were angry with me because, shortly before my passion, I overturned their tables and seats, drove them from the Temple, and poured their money upon the ground (John 2:15).

Likewise, in the time of Antichrist, as charity grows cold and iniquity abounds, I shall then be afflicted in my poor, who will be oppressed by excessive poverty while the wicked abound. For the wicked, face to face beholding Antichrist and loving him and clothed in his face, will rejoice over the needy, distressed, afflicted, persons of whom the world was not worthy. So too my lovers hear my Apostle saying: “All of you who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27). Therefore, so that my own face, which my poor have put on, may shine clearly as in the purest mirrors under the shadow of your wings—whether understood as stated above, or as mercy and compassion, of which wings one belongs to affection and the other to effect—under the shadow, I say, of these wings, eternal Father, protect them.

VERSE 9. From the face of the wicked. Lest they ever be conformed to the wicked in avarice or some other iniquity. Or: under the shadow of the wings, namely of your love and mercy—of the love by which you loved them before the foundation of the world, and of the mercy by which you call and justify them in the world. Keep my own from the face, that is, the conformity, of the wicked.

My enemies have surrounded my soul. For when “the Dedication was taking place at Jerusalem, and it was winter,” and I was walking “in Solomon’s portico,” “the Jews surrounded” me and said: “How long do you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us openly” (John 10:22–24). Speaking in this way, they surrounded my soul, laying snares in order to take my soul from me. For they craftily brought Caesar’s soldiers, so that, if I had openly said that I was Christ the King, I would at once be seized and killed as an opponent of the Roman king. Therefore I did not then openly say, as they wished, that I was Christ the King; but I said that they were not of my sheep, so that the Roman soldiers, hearing that I designated myself a shepherd rather than a king, might cease to be angry with or lie in wait for me, since they did not understand that my pastoral care possessed royal power. Yet, although I did not speak openly, I was not wholly silent. For I said: “No one can snatch [them] from the hand of my Father” (ibid., 28–29), and no one can snatch them from my hand. And I added: “But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep” (ibid., 26).

By these words, having deceived the Romans, I disputed much with my Jewish enemies, bearing witness to the truth, so that I might graciously do what they had maliciously charged me with failing to do. For they had said: “How long do you keep us in suspense?” (ibid., 24), as though to say: How long do you kill us by not speaking to us as we wish? Therefore, as I said, by graciously speaking the truth I labored to take away their souls, fattened with the grease of malice. But they—

VERSE 10. Have shut up their fat. That is, they closed their fat—their gross heart and their souls fattened—against the truth. And, like fat bulls attacking me, they defended their fat against the sword of my word and teaching, and sought to take my soul from me. Yet no one takes my soul from me; rather, I lay it down and take it up again. In this laying down of my soul, their mouth spoke pride when it said: “Aha! You who destroy the Temple of God and rebuild it in three days—if you are the King of Israel, come down from the cross” (Matthew 27:40). And in many other things their mouth spoke pride against me.

VERSE 11. Casting me out, they have now surrounded me. The wicked tenants, who had previously mistreated my servants, now, seeing and recognizing me as the heir, said: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him” (Matthew 21:38), and the inheritance will be ours. They said this among themselves, and just as they had killed my servants, so now, casting me out of the vineyard and crucifying me outside the city, they surrounded me, gathered as though for a spectacle. Yet because of their excessive cruelty, lest perhaps, by seeing my scourging and crucifixion, they might be moved to some compassion and pity, while I was scourged, spat upon, struck with fists, and tortured in many ways in their presence, they set their eyes to look down at the ground, lest by looking upon my misery they might at least be stirred to a little mercy.

Or: “They set their eyes to look down at the ground.” This alone—and above all—they took care to prevent: that while I lived they might lose the land, the place, the nation, and the other earthly profits which they pursued by trading in God’s house, contrary to my teaching, because I had often disputed against their avarice. Therefore, fiercely enraged against me when the disciple delivered me up, or when Pilate delivered me, after scourging, to their will, or even when you, my Father, delivered me, they—

VERSE 12. Received me like a lion ready for prey, and like a lion’s whelp dwelling in hiding places.

The lion, the devil, was exceedingly eager for the food of my flesh, not knowing that he would be caught by the hook of my divinity. The Jewish leaders also, like that lion, like the devil himself, were eager for my death, not knowing that they too would be overthrown and cast from their land. “And like a lion’s whelp dwelling in hiding places”: that is, the troop of demons, working secretly in hiding with their chief lion, the devil, thirsted for my death. So also the people, like a whelp cooperating with the leaders and thirsting for my blood, cried: “He is guilty of death” (Matthew 26:66). Again: “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke 23:22).

VERSE 13. Arise, O Lord; confront him and overthrow him. Lord God, my Father, who see all these evils but seem not to heed them, as though sleeping: “Arise, awakened like a mighty man overcome with wine” (Psalm 77:65), and strike your enemies on the back. Arise, Lord; watch and see how my enemy runs ahead to block my exit from the tomb. For he says to Pilate: “Lord, we remember that that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will rise.’ Therefore command the tomb to be guarded,” and so forth (Matthew 27:63–64). Thus my enemy feared that I would rise after three days. But you, by raising me not after three days but very early about the beginning of the third day—even at midnight, while darkness still lies over the tomb—anticipate my enemy by a sudden and swift resurrection. And because he wrestles against the most mighty God, overthrow him.

When the patriarch Jacob once wrestled with you in order to extort a blessing from you, you touched “the sinew of his thigh, and immediately it withered” (Genesis 32:25), because this was to come to pass: after the true Israel should be blessed in me, the seed of Abraham who came forth from Jacob’s thigh, immediately Jacob’s race would wither—namely, that part which would not receive the blessing. And behold, this wicked people wrestles not to obtain blessing but against blessing. Therefore overthrow it, so that it may fall, lose the place and nation of which it is proud, and, cast down into hell, pay the penalties it deserves—this people that longs to hold me in hell and death.

Deliver my soul from the wicked man: do not abandon my soul in hell, as pleases the wicked man; but deliver my soul itself from the wicked man—your sword, ready and sharp to wage war against the powers of the air.

In the Hebrew it reads: “Save my soul from the wicked man, who is your sword.” For the wicked man or the devil is God’s sword, just as the king of Babylon was God’s axe and hammer. Therefore, he says, save my soul from such a sword, such an axe, such a hammer.

Or: deliver my soul, your sword, by which your hand—your Word—is armed. Deliver this from the wicked devil and from all—

VERSE 14. Enemies of your hand. And lest, through excessive pride, they further destroy my Church, which is the work of your hand, O Lord, divide them from the few, away from the land. And do not delay this until far off; but what? Lord, divide them from the land while they are still alive, while there remains opportunity for repentance, when even the punishment in this life of the unrepentant may provide an example of your vengeance and judgment. Divide them, I say, from the land for the possession of which they crucified me, saying: “Lest perhaps the Romans come and take away our place and nation” (John 11:48). Divide them from this land by scattering them through the Roman army, so that they may be carried captive into all nations. Divide them from the few, who are my elect and have already been separated.

For it should be known that shortly before the destruction of Jerusalem, certain Jews converted to the faith were warned by the Holy Spirit to leave the city and move into the kingdom of Agrippa, which was allied with the Romans, lest they perish with the wicked. Thus Christ’s prayer was heard when he said: “Lord, divide them from the few, away from the land,” because the wicked, separated from the few elect, were cast out of their own land while alive. Although very many of them were killed by famine and the sword, nevertheless many were carried away captive alive. Thus he says: Lord, divide them from the few, away from the land, in their lifetime.

Divide them also from your hidden things, so that they may not only be driven from their visible earthly riches, but also from your hidden things. For theirs was the covenant and the giving of the law, the worship and the promises; theirs were the fathers, from whom I, Christ, was born according to the flesh; and theirs were the hidden mysteries of offerings and ceremonies. Divide them in their lifetime from all these hidden things of yours, so that among the nations they may be “without king,” without high priest, without Temple, “without altar, without sacrifice” (Hosea 3:4).

But I pray not only against these, but also against those who will imitate them in the time of Antichrist: let them too be separated from the few elect then living, and while still alive divided from the land—that is, excommunicated from the Church—or excluded from the abundance of earthly goods bestowed upon them by Antichrist. Let them be divided from your hidden things, namely from ecclesiastical offices, having from their sect neither bishop nor king; but, like the Jews, let them be without king, without priest, without Temple, without altar, without sacrifice.

Alternatively: Therefore, Lord, divide them from the few, away from the land, while they live, because they did not sin through ignorance. For their belly—that is, their memory, which resembles the belly—has been filled from your hidden things, from the secret matters of the Scriptures, with knowledge of hidden realities as with certain choice foods. And yet moreover—

They are filled with swine-flesh, that is, with the uncleanness signified in the Law by pork; and they have left their remnants to their little ones, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:23).

Alternatively: “They are filled with children,” that is, with evil works, which are understood through children; and when they had been filled with my punishments, they left their remnants to their little ones, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

Alternatively: I prayed that they should be divided from the land; and this will be fulfilled so effectually that, first besieged by the Romans and pressed by hunger, they will eat their children and leave their remnants to their little ones. Josephus relates that this was fulfilled historically: a certain noblewoman named Mary, tormented by unbearable hunger, roasted and partly ate her little son. Other starving persons, smelling the odor of the flesh, violently rushed upon her to take the meat from her; but she brought the remains of the same human flesh into their midst. When they saw the half-eaten child, they were shaken by horror at the deed and filled alike with pity and indignation.

Alternatively: “They are filled with children,” that is, they abounded in children and other prosperous things. They did not kill me, disputing against the profit of avarice, because scarcity compelled them. And although they had many children, scarcely any remnant of them believed among the few elect; and they left these remnants to their little ones, that is, to the humble. For through the apostles, who were saved as though small remnants from the Jewish people, a multitude of little ones was afterward converted, when three thousand believed on one day and five thousand on another (Acts 2; 4). For the sake of such little ones, to be gathered not only from Judaea but also from the Gentiles, I, Jesus, when I was seized for death, said: “Let these go, that my word might be fulfilled,” which I had said: “Of those whom you gave me, Father, I have lost none of them” (John 18:8–9).

And because my word, commanding them to let these go, was in divine power, they, unable to resist my word, let them go. This I so willed because they were not yet fit to die with me, and through them many little ones were to be gathered from Jews and Gentiles. Therefore they let their remnants—that is, the apostles—go, which resulted in salvation for their little ones. Yet they did not intend that salvation; I arranged it when I said: “Let these go.” Therefore, although great benefit came from my death and the release of the disciples, those who killed me and released those remnants are nevertheless guilty on account of their evil intention.

VERSE 15. But I shall appear before your face in righteousness. I, whom they called a deceiver, shall appear in righteousness. I, who have accomplished salvation in the midst of the earth not only from my own good deeds but also from their evil deeds, shall appear just—not only by saving remnants and little ones, that is, the few humble, but also by condemning many proud persons. For it is just that I should cast down “the mighty from their throne” and exalt the humble (Luke 1:52). It is just that my meek disciples should possess the earth (Matthew 5:4) and be made princes over all the earth. It is likewise just that I should utterly destroy the wicked by casting them from that land, for the possession of which they killed me.

Therefore, in all my judgment, by which I shall utterly destroy the wicked tenants and lease my vineyard to other laborers, I shall appear just before your face, righteous Father, whom the world has not known, but whom I have known. Accordingly, just as you are preached as righteous, righteous Father, who, justice demanding it, condemn the world that has not known you but liberate and save me and mine, who know you, so I shall appear as the righteous Son of a righteous Father: condemning those who would not acknowledge me as your Son, and saving those who believed and recognized that “I came forth from you” (John 17:8).

In the Hebrew it reads: “I in righteousness shall see your face; when I awake, I shall be filled with your likeness.” This may be expounded thus: I, who now appear mortal and unlike you, Father, when I awake in the resurrection shall be filled with your likeness. For I shall appear before your face and before those who are yours—whether angels, who desire to look into me, or human beings who see me in such a way as to see in me, the righteous Son, you, my righteous Father—as the just Son of the Just, the eternal Son of the Eternal, the almighty Son of the almighty Father. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst” to see and taste this “righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matthew 5:6); and I shall be filled in them when your glory, God the Father, is revealed in me, the man who is your Son, so that “every tongue may confess that I, Jesus Christ, am in your glory” (Philippians 2:11).

Then I shall be filled in myself and in mine with your glory; then I shall be filled with your likeness, when the ancient counsel you expressed is fulfilled in me and, through me, in mine: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26). For I too, singularly in my own person, beholding you, shall be filled with your likeness when there is no difference of glory between you and me, my humanity having been glorified fully and supremely. When, on the last day, I also refashion the bodies of mine, conforming them to the body of my glory, then I shall be filled with your glory in my members.

At the end of the psalm, let all who hope to be filled with that same glory say, hungering and thirsting for so great a glory: Glory to the Father, whose glory shall be manifested in the Son; glory to the Son, who is now filled with that same glory in his humanity and shall yet be filled with it in his members; glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that fullness of glory or divine likeness which Christ received from the Father without measure and promised to his own according to the measure of his gift.

## PSALM XVII

[Col. 0857]

[Col. 0857B] I shall love you, O Lord, my strength. In this psalm Christ again treats of his death and resurrection, of the benefit resulting from them, and of the persons through whom or the manner in which this came about. He also speaks of the temporal and eternal recompense of the righteous, the outward and inward condemnation of the Jews, and finally the obedience and salvation of the Gentiles. Its title reads as follows (VERSE 1):

**TO THE END, FOR DAVID, THE SERVANT OF THE LORD, WHO SPOKE THE WORDS OF THIS SONG ON THE DAY WHEN HE DELIVERED HIM FROM THE HANDS OF HIS ENEMIES AND FROM THE HAND OF SAUL.**

David himself is Christ, truly strong of hand, truly desirable; he is the servant of the Lord. For he obeyed God the Father as a servant according to the form of a servant. The words of this song are to be attributed to him “unto the end,” that is, to one tending toward perfection in every respect. “On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of his enemies and from the hand of Saul” means nothing other than in contemplation of that day on which he rose from the dead, no longer to die: for, by raising him, the Lord delivered him from the power of his enemies, namely Jews and Gentiles, and from the power of death, which is rightly understood by the name Saul, interpreted as “petition.”

For just as the people asked for Saul as king against the Lord’s will (1 Samuel 8:19), so Adam and Eve asked for death against the Lord’s will. Once its rule was acquired through sin, “death reigned,” says the Apostle, “from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Romans 5:14): either because they were infants and, dying in original sin alone, had not come to the likeness of Adam’s actual transgression; or because they were lovers of righteousness and therefore were not in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, despising righteousness and defending their sin.

To destroy this kingdom of sin and death, this tyrannical kingdom of Saul, since Moses was not sufficient, David, the legitimate king and servant of the Lord, came. Thus it occurred both in the image of shadow and in the reality of the things themselves. For Saul reigned even to the point of Moses’s being despised and, so far as lay in Saul’s power, killed. The Lord had said in the Law: “Amalek is the first of the nations, and in the end they shall perish.” [Note: [Col. 0857D] Vulgate: “His extremities shall perish.”] Again, he said to Moses: “Put this into the ears of Joshua, and write it as a memorial in a book: ‘I shall blot out Amalek from under heaven’” (Exodus 17:14).

When Samuel, in the word of the Lord and according to these ordinances of Moses, commanded Saul to destroy Amalek, Saul spared Agag, king of the Amalekites, and the best of the flocks (1 Samuel 15:3). Rebuked by Samuel for this sin, namely this transgression of Moses, he defended his fault; and by that defense he, as it were, killed Moses, because everyone who defends injustice, so far as lies within him, kills righteousness itself. Immediately after this transgression of the Law and of Moses, he heard: “Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you from being king” (ibid., 23). Again, when he tore the garment of Samuel, who preached the Law, it was said to him: “The Lord shall tear the kingdom from you and give it to your neighbor, who is better than you” (ibid., 28).

Therefore, just as that literal Saul was rejected after his transgression against Moses, so after the complete transgression of the Law, when the kingdom of sin had been rejected, the chosen servant of the Lord, the true David, was raised up. The ministers of death persecuted him just as Saul’s ministers persecuted David. At last Saul died, because death died when Christ, the death of death, rose from the dead. (Then, moreover, the death of death will be completed in full when, in the universal resurrection, the whole force of death is destroyed and no one shall die any longer.) After all this, nothing remains except to love him who before all things and above all things is worthy of love. Therefore Christ, speaking in his own person and for his members, says:

VERSE 2. I shall love you, O Lord. Thus “love is strong as death” (Song of Songs 8:6): for just as no remedy can prevail against death, so that it does not finally come to every mortal human being—it can indeed be delayed, but cannot be wholly averted—so true love, strong as death, may be shaken, but never fails. Therefore, by the verb in the future tense there is declared most certainly that consummation of love which will remain for the elect when Saul’s kingdom—that is, the kingdom of death—has been destroyed.

This is the meaning of what is said through Moses concerning the inextinguishable fire of love, in reference to the altar fire: “This perpetual fire before the Lord, the priest shall nourish by placing wood upon it every morning” (Leviticus 6:12). Therefore, when Christ, the true great priest, says, “I shall love you, O Lord,” a fire is kindled in the temple of the whole Church. To nourish it so that it may never fail, the remembrance of the many graces bestowed through his passion and resurrection is laid beneath it upon the altar of the heart like a pile of wood. Therefore, if we wish to be enlightened and inflamed by this fire, let us not shrink from lingering over meditations on this psalm. It is wholly full, as it were, of sparks of true love, as such benefits and wonders of God are recalled in it, through which faithful persons who faithfully sing the psalm are inflamed toward true and eternal love.

Christ therefore, giving thanks on behalf of himself and his own for his own deliverance and theirs, says: “I will love thee, O Lord.” On that day when Saul shall die—that is, in contemplation of the resurrection by which the dominion of death shall be destroyed—I, in myself and in my members, will love thee. And, that this love may remain consummated for ever, I have great incentives to love, which I now recount: namely, that thou art my Lord and I thy servant, to whom thou sayest: [Col. 0859D] “Behold my servant, whom I have chosen; I have put my Spirit upon him” (Matt. 12:18). Therefore, as an elect servant I will love thee, my lawful Lord.

Moreover, for this reason also I will love thee, O Lord: because, though by the nature of the human condition I was weak, thou didst not give me a strength created by thee, but thou thyself art my strength and firm support. My strength, so that I, thy servant David, might go forth to fight steadfastly against the uncircumcised spiritual Philistine; my firm support, lest I should fail in the battle once begun, but should persevere firmly in it unto victory and cut off his head—that is, “the beginning of all sin, pride” (Ecclus. 10:15). Therefore I will love thee, O Lord, my strength.

[Col. 0860A] VERSE 3. The Lord is my support and my refuge. For when that Philistine, my enemy, was boasting and reproaching the armies of Israel, and Saul’s weapons—the weapons, that is, of the Law, such as the observance of Sabbaths and the offering of carnal sacrifices—were not suitable to me for overcoming Israel’s enemy, the devil, thou wast my refuge in the wilderness as I wrestled against him. For, fleeing from his most wicked suggestions—namely gluttony, vainglory, and avarice—to the streams of thy Scriptures, I found stones of divine and most powerful authority, by which I struck him down, saying to him what is written in Deuteronomy: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. 8:3). Again: “Thou shalt not tempt the Lord [Col. 0860B] thy God” (ibid. 6:16). Again: “Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve” (ibid. 6:13).

Then that uncircumcised tempter left me, and from that time I was delivered and free from suggestions of this kind. Therefore I, having been delivered, will love thee, my Deliverer. Indeed, from the time when the fast of forty days was complete I was free from temptation; but I was not for long rescued from his persecution or from the snares of his evil attendants, the Jews. Against these, God himself—who, insofar as I am man, is my God and my Creator—became my helper, so that I might not yield to adversities but overcome them mightily. Therefore I will hope in him, because from the comparison of past benefits hope of future ones is born: so that, having become a victor in myself, I may also be a victor triumphing [Col. 0860C] in each of my members and elect ones, since he who is my God, mighty to create me, is likewise mighty to help me.

My God and my helper: and I will hope—and will cause my own to hope—in him who is my protector, lest they break a bone in me, the Paschal Lamb. And he is the horn of my salvation, who made me a rhinoceros, possessing the singular horn of divinity and therefore not fearing hunters, that is, evil angels and men; for I have God the Father as the horn of salvation, by whose divine power I was able to scatter and disperse the opposing devil and sin. This is so because he is my receiver, who received me as man into his own [Col. 0860D] Son, receiving me: “He hath received Israel his servant, remembering his mercy” (Luke 1:54). Therefore I shall not boast of my deliverance and victory, but

VERSE 4. Praising, I will call upon the Lord. Praising the Lord for the victory already passed, I will call upon him to help me against future evils or dangers already threatening, which are no small matters. For

VERSE 5. The pains of death surrounded me, and torrents of iniquity troubled me. Since there are two deaths: one by which the soul that sins dies; the other by which all mortal flesh dies. The death of the soul causes inward pains, when joy—which is God himself—is separated from the soul. The death of the body causes outward pains, when the life-giving Spirit is separated [Col. 0861A] from the body. Therefore I, being remote from the most evil and inward death of sins, had in my mortal flesh outward pains of death. These outward pains of death did not fill me inwardly but surrounded me outwardly. And because “I drank of the brook in the way” (Ps. 109:7), torrents of iniquity troubled me.

For the sudden and swiftly passing assault of the wicked upon me troubled me like a torrent, so that I said: “Now is my soul troubled” (John 12:27). Again: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38); “He began to be weary and afraid” (Mark 14:33), because the pains of hell surrounded me. For sorrow and weariness, or fear, are numbered among the punishments of hell. But these punishments and these

[Col. 0861B] VERSE 6. pains of hell surrounded me outwardly, because inwardly I was secure, having power to lay down my soul in hell in order to deliver my own from there, and power to take it up again from hell when the pains of hell had been loosed, since it was impossible for it to be held by it.

Yet although I was, as regards the death of the soul, free among the dead, the snares of death forestalled me in my members, preoccupied through original sin with a double death, namely that of bodies and souls. It was for these that were to be delivered by my passion.

VERSE 7. In tribulation—in the very cross, offering prayers with a strong cry—I called upon the Lord, saying: [Col. 0861C] “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). Thus I cried to my God, because my very passion was a cry worthy of being heard. And from his holy temple he heard my voice. For I was the temple, I the sacrifice, I the priest. Therefore from myself, who am the temple, he heard my voice; and my cry, which was within in his sight, entered into his ears. This became evident in its effect. For while I cried upon the cross and, bowing my head, gave up the spirit (ibid. 27:50),

VERSE 8. The earth was moved and trembled. For a great earthquake took place, because the world cried out that it could not endure my death. The earth [Col. 0861D] was moved and trembled because the earthly centurion himself, seeing this miracle, was moved and trembled, saying: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. 27:54); and many others, moving their heads and “striking their breasts” (Luke 23:48), trembled. Following their example, many both from the Gentiles and from the Jews, through repentance, caused the foundations of the mountains to be shaken by fear and disturbed unto repentance.

The foundations of the mountains—that is, the hearts of proud rulers—were moved, because he was angry with them. “The seven mountains are seven kings,” says the angel in the Apocalypse (Rev. 17:9). By the seven kings are understood all the rulers of this world, because the number seven is accustomed to signify universality. These kings, these mountains, have unstable foundations, because, resting upon the sand of earthly desires, they must necessarily be troubled when the temporal things in which they trust change and are shown, once eternal truth has been made manifest, to be nothing. Therefore through the teaching of Christ’s Gospel the foundations of the mountains were troubled, because he was also angry with them: that is, his wrath became known to them—he who is proclaimed as coming to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

VERSE 9. Smoke went up in his anger, and fire blazed from before his face. The smoke of tearful supplication and heartfelt compunction, like the smoke of spices, rose from the hearts of penitents as from censers, in contemplation of his wrath. And the same censers, previously cold, and coals formerly black and extinguished, [Col. 0862B] were kindled by him. For what are human affections before the coming of divine visitation but certain cold and black coals? For example, fear and love in a human being before knowledge of God are affections, because they strongly move the human heart while things not to be feared are feared and things not to be loved are loved, in a certain dark blindness in which human affections, like black and extinguished coals, give no light, because they have in themselves neither the light of truth nor the warmth of charity.

But if, through God’s breathing upon them, knowledge of truth and love of virtue come to them, then fear, which was formerly disordered in a person, being anxious over things not to be feared, is so ordered that it does not fear things not to be feared, and is inflamed by the terror of divine judgment so as greatly to fear these things. Likewise love, [Col. 0862C] which in a person was disorderly solicitous over things not to be loved, is by divine grace so ordered that it loves only what ought to be loved; and, lest it love these tepidly, it is inflamed by desire for future goods in the kingdom of heaven.

What we have said concerning fear and love may likewise be understood of the other human affections, which, like coals, are kindled when through God’s grace they are rightly ordered: namely, so that a person has no fear except where fear is proper; no sorrow except where sorrow is proper; no joy except where joy is proper. For simply to fear, love, grieve, and rejoice are human affections; but these become vices if one rejoices [Col. 0862D] where one ought not rejoice. They become virtues, however, if things to be feared are feared, things to be loved are loved, things to be grieved over are grieved over, and things in which joy is proper are rejoiced in.

Hence arises a threefold division of these same human affections. Simple affections, like coals still cold, neither burn nor shine. Vicious affections do burn, but do not shine, because the fire of vices, although it produces warmth in the affections, does not remove blackness but increases it. Affections illumined by divine grace, however, both burn and shine together. Thus it is said of John the Baptist that “he was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35). Whence was this, unless because fire blazed from Christ’s face into John at the mutual greeting of Mary and Elizabeth, when, kindled by this fire, he “leaped” while still “an infant in the womb” (Luke 1:41)?

And again fire blazed from his face into John when, by the Jordan, he saw the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove and heard the Father’s voice saying: [Col. 0863A] “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). John, therefore, was a coal so kindled by him that afterwards many were kindled through that burning coal, when, as the Gospel flashed forth, John’s testimony concerning Christ was heard not only in Judaea but throughout the whole world.

Therefore it is truly and rightly said in this psalm concerning David, the servant of the Lord, that coals were kindled by him—whether by coals we understand human affections or human beings themselves. From these, when they burn brightly, the smoke of spices rises: that is, the fragrance [Col. 0863B] of virtues, to the honour of him from whose face, from whose knowledge, fire blazed, by which many coals were kindled. Of this fire the servant of the Lord himself said in the Gospel: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49). He wished, and wishes intensely, that this fire should be kindled, so that each of his own, burning with this fire, may say: “I will love thee, O Lord, my strength,” and so forth. Therefore, in order to spread this fire,

VERSE 10. He bowed the heavens and came down. For though in the form of God he was King of angels and of all heavenly powers, he first bowed the heavens by sending heavenly messengers, Michael and Gabriel, to visit weak humanity. For Michael came to help God’s people, and Gabriel’s ministry is evident both in Daniel’s visions and in the Gospel; and heavenly powers are often read of as having bowed down to visit human infirmities before Christ’s advent. Hence it is now said: He bowed the heavens. For by “the heavens” are understood the powers of heaven.

But because the restoration of human salvation could be accomplished by none of the angels, at last he himself came down. Having gone forth from the highest heaven, he was incarnate in the virgin’s womb; emptying the form of divinity, he put on the form of a servant. He is not said to have come down as though from place to place, since he was in the world and the world was made through him. Rather, from the height [Col. 0863D] of paternal glory to the assumption of flesh from his mother; to the humility of death, to be endured for us dead people, that we might be raised: the Most High, Son of the Most High, humbled himself, becoming obedient for us unto death, through which he descended into hell.
