And there was darkness beneath his feet, because there he walked upon the asp and basilisk, trampling the lion and the dragon—that is, all the princes of darkness. And darkness was beneath his feet, even beneath the least traces of his power and of those whom he delivered from the darkness of hell.

VERSE 11. And he ascended upon the cherubim. For he who descended is also he who ascended above the cherubim, that is, above all the powers of heaven. For, a part being taken for the whole, “cherubim” denotes all the powers [Col. 0864A] of the blessed spirits, above whom he who descended to hell ascended exalted.

Or, in hell itself, where darkness was beneath his feet, there too he ascended above the cherubim—that is, above the elect held there, in whom was the fullness of love signified by “cherubim.” For *cherubim* means “fullness of knowledge,” and fullness of knowledge is fullness of the Law, and “the fullness of the Law is love” (Rom. 13:10). Therefore he ascended above the cherubim when Christ, the true light, poured himself into the elect and beloved in hell; or also when, returning from hell, he ascended toward the East as the true Sun, brightly illuminating his disciples, who are rightly called cherubim because of their fullness of love.

Otherwise: when the cherub stood before Paradise with a flaming sword to forbid entrance to the sinner [Col. 0864B] and to disobedient man (Gen. 3:24), this man, free from every sin, having completed obedience through his death, entered Paradise mightily. He ascended above the cherubim because the angel, guardian of Paradise, reverently humbled himself as though a footstool for the man perfectly obedient and possessing the fullness of divinity—the one who opposed himself to disobedient man perversely desiring divinity.

Therefore the cherub, guardian of Paradise, humbled and placed himself beneath him, not by local submission, since spirit is not contained or moved perceptibly by place, but by spiritual humility, acknowledging the Lord of Paradise. He was able both to enter it powerfully and to bring all the elect into the Paradise [Col. 0864C] of rejoicing, among whom was the repentant thief.

Otherwise: He ascended above the cherubim and flew. For *cherubim* is called the fullness of knowledge, above which the Lord is said to have ascended and flown, because no human knowledge comprehends the height of his majesty. He flew above the wings of the winds, because he bore himself far aloft beyond our understanding into divinity. However greatly anyone may shine with fullness of knowledge, nevertheless he cannot grasp how he who existed came to be conceived; how the Author of humankind before the ages was born as a human being at the end of the ages; how God was flesh and the Word became an infant. Therefore it is rightly added there: He flew above the wings of the winds. He, namely, transcends [Col. 0864D] all understandings of souls; for human souls are not unfittingly understood by the name “winds,” because of their swiftness.

Otherwise: He bowed the heavens—that is, he bowed the heavens, the highest saints, from the height of contemplation to the active ministry of the Word. To one of these it is said: “Peter, dost thou love me?” And when he said, “I love thee,” not once but a third time, so that the great height of heavenly love in him might be understood, immediately he is bowed down from the heights to lowly things when he is told: “Feed my lambs” (John 21:17). Likewise he bowed other heavens, and he himself first came down. Therefore he also says: “I have given you an example, that you also should do likewise” (John 13:15).

And darkness was beneath his feet, because the impious and dark persecutors [Col. 0865A] of his feet—that is, of the apostles—are beneath his feet. For although the elect may seem for a time to be subject to persecutors, yet this world will be judged through them. And he ascended above the cherubim and flew, because he showed himself incomprehensible to those who love him. He also flew by most swift fame, because his fame surpasses winds, than which nothing is swifter. For, born in Judaea, he was immediately revealed in the East to the Magi through a new star. He was dying upon the cross, and the victory of his death was felt in hell. He also flew visibly aloft, raised by his own power in the sight of the disciples, on the day of the Ascension.

VERSE 12. And he made darkness his hiding-place, because “a cloud received him out of their sight” (Acts 1:9). [Col. 0865B] Then he made darkness his hiding-place, because what was visible in him passed into the sacraments, in which he is not seen but is believed to be hidden. For example, in the species of bread and wine his appearance is not manifest but hidden. Thus he rightly made darkness his hiding-place, because in sacraments very obscure to understanding he is hidden from human intellect, though he is not hidden from the right faith of those who fight under him. Hence follows: His tabernacle is round about him.

Otherwise: He made darkness his hiding-place, because through the impious, who are darkness and children of darkness, he secretly accomplishes what he wills. For even if they do not serve him willingly, they nevertheless serve him by necessity; and if his will is not done by them, it is nevertheless done in them and concerning them. But they serve him more happily who, fighting for him in voluntary service, become his tabernacle, concerning which it is said: His tabernacle is round about him.

For those who fight for him are both his soldiers and his tabernacle; and he is in them as in the figurative tabernacle called the Holy of Holies, in which was the ark of the covenant and in which was manna. Thus indeed his tabernacle, called the Holy of Holies, is round about him, because the Church, in which is the true manna, is built from the multitude of saints, in whom Christ, the ark of the covenant, is beheld—yet not clearly in this tent of warfare, spread out and preceded by the pillar of cloud, that is, the obscure doctrine of the prophets, so long as clouds overshadow the tabernacle itself, because carnal and bodily images darken spiritual [Col. 0865D] understanding. Therefore it is said: Dark water is in the clouds of the air; that is, obscure knowledge is in the prophets, or even in the apostles themselves, who fly like clouds, thunder with threats, shed dew with promises, and flash with miracles. Because of these very miracles it is said:

VERSE 13. Before the brightness in his presence, the clouds passed by. For the clouds of prophetic teaching remained in Judaea, and those clouds did not flash with frequent miracles, apart from the miracles of Elijah and Elisha, whose writings are not extant. Therefore the writings of prophets who performed no miracles, or few, remained in Judaea. But the writings of the apostles, flashing with more numerous miracles, could not remain hidden before that brightness or remain confined within the narrow bounds of the Jewish people, [Col. 0866A] because Christ shone in them, he who is the light of the world, the “light” enlightening “every man who comes into this world” (John 1:9). The true Sun of righteousness shone in the deeds and miracles of the apostles. They were clouds so light and so bright that not only were they themselves illumined by the true Sun, but through them the rays of solar splendour were spread far and wide.

Therefore these clouds, bearing Christ’s clear brightness, passed by before his brilliance: unable to remain hidden in Judaea alone, they passed to the Gentiles. Among these Gentiles the apostles themselves were hail, reproving iniquities, and coals of fire through the ardour of charity. In this respect they were hail: because through them,

VERSE 14. The Lord thundered from heaven, threatening dreadful [Col. 0866B] judgment. And in this respect they were coals of fire: because the Most High gave his voice through them, namely the voice of gladness, the voice of exultation in joyful promises. For this reason the apostles are hail and coals of fire: hail to Jews and Gentiles who reject the word of God; coals of fire to those devoted to Christ’s love.

Certainly hail and coals of fire appear contrary because of coldness and heat. Yet this contrariety existed in the apostles because of their different hearers, since they were “to some the savour of life unto life, and to others the savour of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:16). They were hail that freezes in high places and melts in the field, because they terrified the proud and consoled the humble; they crushed the former by the hardness of rebuke and watered the latter, as a garden of delights, by gentle teaching. Some of the former, rejecting this teaching, assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ. Against these Christ himself

VERSE 15. Sent his arrows and scattered them. The apostles themselves, who were hail, were also arrows. For hail appears to fall without rational direction, whereas arrows are directed with a certain rational skill so that they do not strike at random. Thus the apostles were likened to hail because, to the minds of fools, their journeys seemed to be undertaken indiscriminately. But they were arrows rationally directed by the Lord’s hand. Thus the apostle Paul, when a Macedonian man was shown to him in a vision, [Col. 0866D] “was directed into Macedonia” (Acts 16:9); the Spirit of the Lord prevented him from going into Asia; and, when the Jews compelled him to appeal to Caesar, he was directed to Rome.

In this manner Christ himself sent arrows against his enemies and scattered them. Thus through Paul the apostle the Pharisees and Sadducees, previously gathered against the truth, were scattered; and through such arrows among the nations, in one household, children were separated from parents and parents from children, mother was divided from daughter and daughter against mother, daughter-in-law against mother-in-law, and “a man’s foes” became “those of his own household” (Matt. 10:35–36). The true David, to whom this psalm is ascribed, accomplished such divisions because against the impious, previously united in evil agreement, he sent his arrows—that is, [Col. 0867A] evangelists rightly flying with the wings of virtues—and scattered them.

He multiplied lightnings and troubled them. He multiplied the flashes of miracles and troubled them, as on the day of Midian. For just as the camp of Midian was thrown into confusion by the flashing lamps in the hands of the three hundred who were with Gideon, leader of the children of Israel (Judg. 7:21), so Christ, far more greatly, troubled the camp of the impious by powers, wonders, and signs flashing in the works of those sealed by faith in the Trinity, which is denoted by three hundred, or by the sign of the cross, which is likewise denoted by three hundred.

For just as among us the letter V signifies five, X ten, C one hundred, and I one, so among the Hebrews three hundred is signified by the form [Col. 0867B] of the letter *tau*, which has the shape of our letter T, and the figure of the cross is expressed. Therefore Christ, the true David, sent his arrows, hidden in the quiver of his predestination—that is, he sent them into the whole world against the impious—and scattered them. He also multiplied the flashes of signs through faith in the Trinity and through the sign of the holy cross, and troubled them.

For when he sent forth those arrows, he gave them power over all demons and to heal diseases, saying to them: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cast out demons.” Again, he says: “These signs shall follow those who believe: In my name they shall cast out demons; they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents; and if they drink [Col. 0867C] anything deadly, it shall not harm them; they shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall be well.” But they, like flying arrows and flashing spears, directed by the divine hand, “went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16:17–18, 20).

VERSE 16. The fountains of waters springing up unto eternal life appeared. The apostles themselves, drinking these waters from Christ, the highest fountain, had heard: “Whoever drinks” the water that I give “shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up unto eternal life” (John 4:13–14). While Christ still remained in the flesh these fountains of waters lay hidden; but when he had been exalted into heaven and the Holy Spirit poured out upon the apostles, and they spoke [Col. 0867D] the mighty works of God, the fountains of waters appeared in the hearts of believers. Streams of the same waters also appeared in the mouths of those speaking in diverse kinds of tongues.

And the foundations of the world were revealed: that is, the writings of the prophets, upon whose faith the world—the Church spread throughout the whole earth—is founded. Those foundations, formerly veiled and too deeply hidden, were revealed through the apostles. For example, after the outpouring of the Holy Spirit Peter said: “These are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day; but this is” the word “which was spoken through Joel the prophet: I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Acts 2:15–17). [Col. 0868A] The meaning of prophecy, formerly veiled, was revealed through the manifest reality of events.

Likewise, when Matthias the apostle was chosen in place of Judas the apostate, he said: “It is written in the book of Psalms: Let their dwelling become desolate, and let there be none to dwell in it; and let another take his bishopric” (Acts 1:20). When the sayings of the prophets were thus compared with events in the matters mentioned and in many others, then the foundations of the world were revealed.

Indeed, at the beginning of the rising Church, before the full revelation of these foundations, many Jews contended that God was the God of the Jews alone. To them the apostle Paul says: “Is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also” (Rom. 3:29). But which Jew, envying the salvation of the Gentiles, would have conceded this if Paul had not proved it from the prophets’ sayings? He therefore says: “For I say that Christ Jesus was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers; but that the Gentiles might glorify God for mercy, as it is written: Rejoice, ye Gentiles, with his people.” And again: “Praise the Lord, all ye Gentiles; and magnify him, all ye peoples.” And again Isaiah says: “There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the Gentiles; in him shall the Gentiles hope” (Rom. 15:8–12).

Therefore, when the fulfilment of truth in the conversion of the Gentiles to the worship of the one God accorded with such prophetic oracles, it was clearly recognized that the Church was to be gathered and founded from the whole [Col. 0868C] world, “upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone” (Eph. 2:10). Thus the foundations of the world were revealed.

At thy rebuke, O Lord, through the mouths of the preaching apostles. And because the teacher’s tongue labours in vain unless the Spirit, who breathes where he wills, is present, they were also revealed by the inspiration of the spirit of thy wrath. For, while the teacher’s tongue rebuked outwardly, thy Spirit of wrath worked inwardly, humbling the hearts of hearers through grace unto fear, which is the beginning of wisdom and arises from consideration of thy wrath, by which in judgment thou art angry with those who resist truth. [Col. 0868D] For from the moment anyone knowingly resists truth, thy wrath is upon him. Therefore, by the inspiration of the spirit of thy wrath—that is, the spirit of fear by which thy wrath is feared—the prophets’ oracles concerning the holy Church to be spread through the world were made credible; and so the foundations of the world were revealed through thy Spirit.

For this reason I, the Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles, give thanks to him who promised and sent this Spirit. For shortly before this servant of the Lord David, to whom this psalm is ascribed, ascended, he said to his disciples: “You shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea and Samaria, even unto the uttermost part of the earth. And when he had said these things, while they beheld, he was lifted up” (Acts 1:8–9). Therefore, exalted at the right hand [Col. 0869A] of God and having received from the Father the promise, he poured out this gift of the Holy Spirit, whom

VERSE 17. He sent from on high, as he had promised, saying: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth” (John 15:26). Therefore the Son sent from the supreme Father the promised Paraclete. And he received me, his beloved bride, the glorious Church chosen before the ages. He received me: that is, through faith inspired by his Spirit, he made me acceptable to himself. And he took me into his inheritance, that I might be his co-heiress and that all my children, begotten to me his bride by his regenerating Spirit, might be heirs indeed of God and co-heirs of Christ, my bridegroom, who sent the Holy Spirit from on high, received me, and took me up from [Col. 0869B] many waters: that is, chosen and set apart from many peoples, and regenerated from the waters of his baptism.

Or, because there was no salvation in the foods, drinks, and various baptisms of Pharisaic traditions, he took me up from many waters—that is, from various baptisms—by giving his one baptism alone, in which there is salvation. And this was done through his baptism, as it were through a crossing of the Red Sea.

VERSE 18. He delivered me from my most powerful enemies: from the pursuing chariots of the invisible Pharaoh, namely sins, which were overwhelmed in baptism as in the Red Sea. From these enemies, most powerful before I received the grace of baptism against the natural and written Law, because the Law was weakened through the flesh and thus could not remove the wall [Col. 0869C] of enmity—“from these” (Rom. 8:3), I say, “most powerful enemies”—he delivered me by the Holy Spirit given to me in baptism.

He also delivered me from those who hate me, namely evil spirits. For he cast into the sea not only Pharaoh’s chariots, made up of the wheels of sins and vices, but also his army, composed of evil angels and borne in such chariots, drowning them in the water and blood flowing from his side. Therefore he himself delivered me from such enemies, because he knew that my strength had failed against them, whom I could conquer neither through the natural Law nor through the written Law.

For they became strong against me in actual [Col. 0869D] sins and forestalled me in original sin, before I was born into this world—indeed, in my first parents, before I entered the sabbath-rest. For to this end God created and multiplied me in my parents, whom he made good; and, that they might multiply, he blessed them, saying: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28). This, I say, was done on the sixth day so that human nature and its blessed multiplication, after obedience had been fulfilled, might enter on the sixth day into the rest of the seventh day, in which God rested when the works of the world were completed. But I did not then reach the Sabbath day in my parents, because

VERSE 19. They forestalled me in the day of my affliction. The serpent, Eve, and Adam together forestalled me: the serpent by deceiving, Eve by believing his deception, Adam by consenting. They forestalled me in the day of my affliction, because the very day of creation became for me a day of affliction, when in my parents I was expelled from Paradise and subjected to the curse of sins and to the wrath of God, who said to Adam: [Col. 0870A] “Cursed is the earth in thy work; when thou hast tilled the earth, it shall not yield its fruit, but it shall bring forth thorns and thistles to thee” (Gen. 3:17–18). Again, to Eve: “I will multiply thy troubles and thy conceptions,” etc. (ibid. 3:16). Thus they forestalled me in the day of affliction, shutting off from me the Sabbath day, the day of rejoicing, because they did not remain in the Paradise of rejoicing until that day.

And the Lord became my protector, even then establishing enmity between the woman and the serpent, between the woman’s seed and the serpent’s seed, and barring me from the way to the tree of life, lest, if wretched human beings had eaten of it, their wretchedness should be immortal and their immortality wretched—as with the transgressing angels, who, because their miserable life is immortal, find no return to humility and salvation. Lest the same should happen to me, the Lord became my protector by giving me coats of skin, that is, the mortality of bodies, by which there might be for me a remedy against the death of souls.

And in the prison of mortality he chastised me for a long time; but at last, in Christ—in the man without sin who died for sinners, was buried, humbled even to hell, and raised from the dead—God himself, who received me in that same man and took me up from many waters, as has been said, [Col. 0870C] placed the incarnate Word of God, in his flesh now glorified and made resplendent, upon the throne of paternal majesty.

**Verse 20.** He brought me out into the breadth of eternity from the narrowness of temporal mortality. This has already been accomplished in the firstfruits of those who sleep, in the man who is the firstborn of the dead. Therefore, as though I had received in my head the pledge of salvation, I confidently say concerning myself, a new body of the new head: that he has made me safe by conforming the body of my lowliness to the body of his glory. I conceive and believe this from the fact that he willed me before I willed. He first loved me and willed me; preceding me in his gratuitous kindness through many benefits, he made me will him who first willed me. And therefore, because I now have faith in him with a good will—the faith from which the righteous person lives (Rom. 1:17)—I hope this: that the Lord who freely gave this justifying faith, active through good will, himself

**Verse 21.** will repay me with eternal rewards according to my righteousness, which consists in faith and good will; and according to the purity of my hands, which consists in action, he will repay me.

In this passage there is, according to the rationale of faith, a rhetorical discourse argumentatively divided into five parts: (1) proposition; (2) reason; (3) confirmation of the reason; (4) embellishment; (5) conclusion. The proposition is where it is said: “And the Lord will repay you according to my righteousness, and according to the purity of my hands he will repay me.” By these words this is proposed: that a twofold recompense is owed by God, namely, one according to the righteousness of faith and another according to works performed in faith. The reason is what follows: “For I have kept the ways of the Lord, and have not acted impiously against my God.” For these words give the reason why recompense, as though a twofold robe, is rightly due to one who by faith keeps the ways of the Lord in his will and does not criminally offend in deed by acting impiously in any way.

The confirmation of the reason is what follows: “For all his judgments are before my eyes, and I have not cast his righteousnesses away from me.” These words confirm both the watchful goodness of faith toward God—of whom it is said, “All his judgments are before my eyes”—and purity of action, when it is said, “I have not cast his righteousnesses away from me.” The embellishment which follows is brief and splendid: “And I shall be blameless with him, and I shall keep myself from my iniquity.” Nothing adorns rightly spoken and done things of the past more, nothing gives greater honor to the good disposition of faith and the effect of good works, than a good and faithful devotion to persevere and advance to better things in works well begun. This devotion is expressed here when it is said, “And I shall be blameless”—understand, in faith—“and I shall keep myself from my iniquity”—understand, in action.

Finally, after proposition, reason, confirmation of the reason, and embellishment, comes the artful ending of the discourse: by repeating the proposition, a conclusion is made, through which the end of the discourse is joined to its beginning as by an unbreakable bond of argument. For just as he proposed at the beginning, so at the end he concludes, saying: “And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the purity of my hands.” The qualification is what is added: “In the sight of his eyes.” Here the righteousness of faith and the purity of hands—that is, of works—are defined as such righteousness and purity as hypocrites do not possess. They do all their works in order to be seen by people, and they have no concern for that righteousness and purity which are in the sight of God’s eyes, the eyes before which the elect strive to be pleasing. Let us now return to the sequence of the text.

He will make me safe in the future because he willed me in the past [Col. 0871D]. Or: he will make me safe by calling, justifying, and glorifying me, because he willed me by predestining me. Although he does not wholly reveal this predestination to me in this life, nevertheless he indicates it through the fact that he bestowed the righteousness of faith upon me when I neither asked for it nor deserved it. Therefore I know and firmly maintain that he who bestowed the righteousness of faith, the Lord himself, repays me according to my righteousness: he will repay grace for grace, granting pure works for pure faith; and afterward, according to the purity of my hands—that is, my works—he will repay me with the sabbath-rest of eternal blessedness, in which there is no work to be done, but leisure to behold how sweet the Lord is. Yet I claim righteousness and purity of hands for myself not with proud presumption, but with humble and truthful confession.

**Verse 22.** Because, believing in my heart unto righteousness, I have kept the ways of the Lord, holding and following his footsteps, assenting to his commands, and hoping in his promises; nor have I acted impiously against my God by denying him in deeds. Had I done so, I would by no means have possessed purity of hands. But now, believing in my heart unto righteousness, I have kept his ways;

**Verse 23.** for all his judgments are before my eyes; nor have I acted impiously against my God, because I have not cast his righteousnesses away from me. From the time when I believed in him, I held all his judgments before my eyes, knowing that all his ways are mercy and truth, that all his judgments are just. Although I could not attend to them individually [Col. 0872B], nevertheless, since I steadfastly adhered to him, I remembered them universally and generally, and always held his judgments before the eyes of my mind as though written there, believing in my heart unto righteousness that he disposes all things according to the righteousness of his judgments—judgments sometimes hidden, but never unjust: whether rewards for the righteous, punishments for the impious, chastisements for those needing correction, trials for those being tested, or scandals for the reprobate.

I had all God’s judgments before my eyes in such matters because, from the time I was able to understand, I believed them to be just. Even though, seeing the prosperity of sinners, I limped with the feet of my thoughts, when “my feet were almost moved; my steps had almost slipped” (Ps. 72:2), so that I hesitated somewhat as though doubting the justice of God’s judgments, nevertheless I always had this written before me, in the eyes of faith: all God’s judgments are just, and all his ways are mercy and truth. Hence, although I sometimes stumbled with the feet of my thoughts, when “I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (ibid., 3), yet I had his judgments before my eyes and either directed my steps toward their rectitude or corrected them. I directed them through diligence; those distorted through negligence I corrected through repentance.

Alternatively: “All his judgments are before my eyes,” because I considered the divine judgments, both present and future, and saw that they are just; I saw righteousnesses in them. And I did not cast these righteousnesses away from myself. I did not find them burdensome; rather, they pleased me. Even if, through weakness obstructing me, I was sometimes unable perfectly to carry out these righteousnesses, nevertheless I did not reject them as hateful, even when I found them severe as burdens. But even if hitherto I have walked less perfectly and not sufficiently rightly before God in his judgments and righteousnesses, henceforth, with his grace guarding me, I shall remain watchful.

**Verse 24.** And I shall be blameless with him, and I shall keep myself from my iniquity. I shall be blameless, not because I can lack every stain in this life, but because no persuasion of demons shall rule over me: “If they have not ruled over me, then I shall be blameless, and I shall keep myself from my iniquity” (Ps. 18:14). I shall keep myself either by not committing it, or, should it happen contrary to my purpose, by correcting it through swift and fruitful repentance. Therefore, now not only because of the breadth of charity, in which faith works through love, but also because of the long-suffering of perseverance,

**Verse 25.** the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness and according to the purity of my hands. This righteousness of faith and purity of works are in the sight of his eyes. For the righteousness of faith requires this reciprocity: just as I have truly said that all his judgments are before my eyes, so also the purity of my hands should be before his eyes.

Alternatively: “He sent from on high and took me; he made me safe because he willed me.” I, David, servant of the Lord, after Saul’s death—that is, after death died in the Resurrection—delivered from my strongest enemies and brought out from the narrowness of the tomb into the breadth of my Father’s kingdom, adopted as king of my people, now plead their cause. I have become a propitiation for their sins with my Father, whom I know always hears me in the present and in the future; and I establish this from the past.

For before I, as man, had deserved any good thing, the highest Father sent his Word from on high, uttered from his own heart, and took me as man into the unity of the person of his Word, from many waters—that is, as one chosen from thousands of peoples. While I lived in the mortality of the flesh, he delivered me from my strongest enemies, when strong madmen rushed upon me, wishing to destroy me, the physician concerned for the salvation of the human race. And from those who hated me: although they did not lay hands upon me, saying, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death” (John 18:31), yet they hated me with deadly hatred, persuading the people to ask for Barabbas and destroy me.

“For they were strengthened against me,” when my strength was weakened, when my might was hidden. They came before me when I freely wished to die, so that by dying I might destroy death and by rising restore life: they came before me, desiring to take my soul from me on the day of my affliction. And the Lord became my protector, so that no one might take it from me; rather, I laid it down—I, dying in power, commended it into the hands of the Father. But they, striving to forestall my voluntary death, sent soldiers to break my legs and thus force my soul from my body. Yet the Lord became my protector. In the Law he had commanded concerning me, the Paschal Lamb: “You shall not break a bone of it” (John 19:36); and now, before the breaking of my legs, he had received my spirit.

They broke the legs of the thieves, of one repentant and the other unrepentant. But when they came to me in the midst of them, they found me dead, and therefore they did not break my legs. Through unholy persons the Holy Spirit signified by this that, just as the title of my victory placed above my head was not to be erased or corrupted according to the Jews’ desire, so by their will the strength of my legs—that is, the apostles through whom I was to be borne throughout the whole earth—was not to be broken. Therefore the Lord became my protector, and from the narrow people of the Jews, by my strong and tireless legs bearing both me and my Gospel, he brought me out into the breadth of the Gentiles and made me safe because he willed me—that is, because I pleased him.

What follows from these preceding merits of my obedience? Namely this: the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, so that from me, one grain that died, abundant fruit may result. And he will repay me according to the purity of my hands. For, praying and sacrificing myself upon the altar of the cross, I raised pure hands; according to the purity of my hands the Father will repay me, so that those outstretched hands may draw all things to me, as I foretold: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

This is so because I kept the ways of the Lord and did not act impiously against my God, as Adam did. Placed in Paradise to work it and guard it, he did not keep the ways—that is, the commands—of the Lord, and acted impiously against God by obeying the voice of the serpent and his wife more than God. But I kept the ways of the Lord by observing the commandments, and “as the Father gave me commandment, so I do” (John 14:31). Nor did I act impiously against my God by assenting to Satan, who promised me all the kingdoms of the world if I would fall down and worship him, and thus act impiously toward my God. This I did not at all approve, because all his judgments were before my eyes and I did not cast his righteousnesses away from me.

All his judgments were before my eyes. Therefore, when Satan tempted me or the Jews provoked me, I aptly opposed to them the divine judgments expressed in the Scriptures, so that Satan, refuted through the Scriptures, withdrew, and my adversaries said: “How does this man know letters, having never learned?” (John 7:15). And I did not cast his righteousnesses away from me when I was scourged for the sins of my people. God’s righteousness required that guilty man should not escape the penalties due to him unless innocent man, bearing undeserved penalties on his behalf, should be beaten. I, innocent and pure man, did not cast these righteousnesses away from me. I did not turn back, but “I gave my body to those striking me, and my cheeks to those plucking them; I did not turn my face from those reproaching and spitting upon me” (Isa. 50:6).

[Col. 0874D] “And I shall be blameless with him, and I shall keep myself from my iniquity.” For the Jews indeed thought me “a leper, smitten by God, and humbled” (Isa. 53:4), but I shall be blameless from every leprosy of sin with him—with my Father, namely—being righteous as he himself is righteous. “And I shall keep myself from my iniquity”: from the iniquity thought to be mine. Or, “I shall keep myself,” that is, my own people, from the iniquity imputed to me. For they said that I was a glutton, a drinker of wine, and a deceiver (Matt. 11:19). But I am not only innocent and clean from such iniquity; I shall also keep myself—that is, my own—from my iniquity, namely, the iniquity imputed to me.

And the Lord will repay me not only in myself with the glory of Resurrection and Ascension according to my righteousness and the purity of my hands; but also in all my members he will repay me, so that they too may be justified through me and may be pure according to my righteousness and the purity of my hands, made according to their measure conformable to me, their head, before his eyes. By those eyes he himself distinguishes those whom he leaves in filthiness, that they may become filthier still, and those whom he justifies, that they may be justified still further (Rev. 22:11). In this your judgment, God the Father, you will not be an unjust judge, either rejecting one who ought to be chosen or choosing one who ought to be rejected. But:

**Verse 26.** With the holy you will be holy; with the innocent man you will be innocent; with the elect you will be elect; and with the perverse you will be perverse, because you will save the humble people and humble the eyes of the proud.

Therefore let no one accuse you, but rather his own pride, if you have not yet sanctified him; for you will humble the eyes of the proud. Let no one despair of being able to be sanctified if he wishes to be humbled, for you will save the humble people. Therefore, with the holy you will be holy, sanctifying still more the one who through humility and humble repentance and confession of his sins has already begun to be holy. To that holy person—that is, the humble—you appear holy; he does not regard himself as holy, and therefore is accounted holy by you, because you will save the humble people. And with that holy person you will be holy, because you make him holy while his free will cooperates; and he will cling to you as the sanctifier and will not recoil from you through pride.

If you saw pride in him, you would surely make him, perverse in his pride, still more perverse; and as he appeared perverse to you, so you would appear perverse to him. For with the perverse you will be perverse—that is, you appear perverse to the perverse. For they say, “The way of the Lord is not fair”; but “Is not my way fair, and are not rather your ways perverse?” (Ezek. 18:25). You say this, you who will save the humble people confessing their sins and will humble the eyes of the proud who glory in their own strength and presume upon their own righteousness. In doing this you appear perverse to the perverse. Yet with the holy you will be holy, with the innocent man innocent, and with the elect elect; because the person holy through humility says to you: “The Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works” (Ps. 144:13). Thus with the holy you will be holy.

Likewise, one who through humility is innocent with true innocence—by which he harms neither himself nor another—proclaims you innocent, testifying that you are that God of whom Moses, your servant, says: “A faithful God, without any iniquity,” in whom there is no iniquity; the Lord is just and holy, just and upright (Deut. 32:4). Thus with the innocent man you will be innocent. You are proclaimed innocent, whose innocence is so great that you harm absolutely no one; you do not allow those who cause harm to do so without punishment, nor anyone to be harmed unjustly. Such is your innocence that you neither harm nor are harmed, nor do you allow anyone either to suffer unjust harm or to inflict harm with impunity.

Therefore, to those causing harm, whom you punish, you do not appear innocent, because they often cast back upon you the blame of a kind of fated necessity, through which they deserved to be punished, imagining that, since you immutably foreknow all things, they sinned as though by necessity. Likewise, to those whom you allow to suffer harm, though not unjustly, you sometimes do not appear innocent, because they blame your just judgment. But with the innocent man, who harms neither himself nor another, you will be innocent and will be proclaimed innocent.

**Verse 27.** And with the elect you will be elect: that is, you will be chosen by the one whom you choose, and you choose those who choose you, just as you love those who love you (John 14:21). For unless you first chose those whom you foreknew would choose you, there would be none to choose you. Yet in the very fact that from the multitude of humankind you choose so few, you appear perverse to the perverse; and thus, in their estimation, you will be perverse with the perverse. But you are holy, innocent, upright, and elect.

**Verse 28.** Because you will save the humble people and humble the eyes of the proud, so that the humble people may be holy in you who are holy, innocent in you who are innocent, and elect in you, who are the chooser of the humble and chosen by those same humble persons.

Alternatively: just as I, David, above spoke in the person of every elect and perfect person: “And I shall be blameless with him, and I shall keep myself from my iniquity; and the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness and according to the purity of my hands before his eyes”; so also you, whoever you are, who do not yet possess perfect holiness but nevertheless have the will for that same holiness: if you cling to Christ, who is holy, innocent, and elect from among thousands, with that holy one you will be holy, with that innocent man you will be innocent, and with that elect one you will be elect, so that you too may say: “And I shall be blameless with him, and I shall keep myself from my iniquity.” But if you cling to the devil or Antichrist, with that perverse one you will be perverse. This will happen because you, God the Father, will save the humble people who cling and submit to humble Christ, and will humble the eyes of the proud who rebel against that same Christ; and you will save the humble people.

**Verse 29.** For you, Lord, enlighten my lamp: either by opening up the Scriptures of your Word, which Word is “a lamp to my feet” (Ps. 118:104), or by setting upon the lampstand the preachers who are burning lamps. Seeing them enlightened, and asking also for my own enlightenment, I say:

My God, enlighten my darkness, so that my vicious affections, which are darkness, may be enlightened by you and transformed into virtues. For example, may my desire—dark because it desires what ought not to be desired—be so enlightened that, desiring only and wholly what ought to be desired, it itself may be called light by you, who said that “light should shine out of darkness” (2 Cor. 4:6). Likewise, may my anger—dark and worthy of the name of darkness because it sometimes becomes angry even with good things—be so enlightened that, while love for people is preserved, it becomes angry only with their vices, exercising just zeal with love for people and hatred of vices.

May the other excessively dark affections of my mind likewise be so enlightened by you, my God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, “that my whole body may be full of light, having no part dark, but may be wholly full of light; and, like a shining lamp,” may it be enlightened through “the single eye” of my intention. If that eye is perfectly “single” and pure, “my whole body will be full of light” (Luke 11:36); nor, when I am inwardly enlightened, will external temptation be able to prevail against me.

**Verse 30.** For thus enlightened in you, Light of light and source of light, I shall be delivered from external temptation, enjoying inward light; and, strengthened in my God, I shall cross over the wall built from the hardness of my sins between myself and God. Even if I cannot destroy that wall itself, nevertheless, helped by God, I shall cross it. Now between me and God there is, as it were, a dividing wall of my sins, separating me from my God, so that I stand on one side of this wall, I to whom sin still gives pleasure, while God is on the other side, to whom that same sin is displeasing.

Yet God sometimes looks through the lattice and gazes through the windows (Song 2:9), and my face is joined to his face when what displeases him displeases me in part as well. I see him through the windows where the wall of sin is not continuous, where through the lattice of compunction the light of truth is sent into the heart. But this does not suffice for me. I ask to cross over the wall and to stand wholly beside him, accusing and condemning in myself what he accuses or condemns in me, so that only and wholly what pleases him may please me. Let him no longer speak to me through windows, but “let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1), and offer himself for my enjoyment through unbroken love.

But lest anyone think that his love admits the stain of defilement, I say what follows:

**Verse 31.** My God: his way is undefiled. His love is undefiled, by which he comes to me, his Church, his bride. When I have loved him, I am chaste; when I have touched him, I am clean; when I have received him, I am a virgin. Thus his way is undefiled, and his utterances are not shameful; indeed, they cleanse and consume every shamefulness, just as the fiery coal cleansed Isaiah’s lips from defilement (Isa. 6:7).

For the utterances of the Lord themselves are tested by fire. Or the one utterance, the unique Word of God, fused with human nature by the fire of the Holy Spirit into one electrum, not only has no impurity in itself, but purifies every soul that believes in it and assents to it. God indeed consumes sins with such fire as wood, hay, and straw; but he preserves the building of those who hope in him, because they build upon it gold, silver, and precious stones (1 Cor. 3:12): gold of wisdom in thought or contemplation, silver of eloquence in preaching, and precious stones in the splendid practice of virtues.

Therefore God himself is the protector of all who hope in him: protector, namely, in the fire of tribulation in which God’s utterances have been tested. For the incarnate Word of God himself was in tribulation; and the prophets and apostles, holding the Word of God, the Word of life, were themselves tested by the fire of tribulations. Likewise, even to this day all are tested who, holding the Word of life, burn with desire for holiness and shine in word and example. Yet, possessing the good foundation of faith, hope, and charity, they do not build upon this foundation straw of empty thoughts, hay of carnal speech, and wood of worldly actions—unless perhaps so little that it can easily be removed by purgatorial fire. They themselves, because of the noble foundation, may be saved, yet so as through fire: they escape through good hope in God, who is the protector of all who hope in him and alone is God; nor is there another besides him.

**Verse 32.** For who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God? Who is God besides the Lord whom we serve? And besides our God, whom after service we possess as our inheritance and reward? The makers of idols invent many gods for themselves; but who is god besides the Lord, who rules over things? Or who is god besides our God, the God of Abraham and of all Abraham’s children, among whom we too are counted through the faith which we have in our God? (Gal. 3:7). That this our God is the only God I know not only from general benefits, but also from special benefits bestowed upon me, David, because he is

**Verse 33.** God, who girded me with strength. When I had been girded with Saul’s sword, I could not advance so armed against the Philistine; but after laying aside those arms, God girded me with the strength of faith, by which I might believe that “all things are possible to one who believes” (Mark 5:22).

And he made my way blameless, so that I might say to the Philistine: “You come to me with sword and spear and shield; but I come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have reproached today. And the Lord will give you into my hand, and I shall strike you and take your head from you, and today I shall give the corpses of the camp of the Philistines to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth, that all the earth may know that the Lord does not save by sword or spear”; and that the whole Church may know this, “that the Lord is God in Israel—for the battle is his, and he will give you into our hands” (1 Sam. 17:45–47).

As may be understood from these words, the way of the Philistine who came against me with sword and spear in great pride was a defiled and stained way. But my God, of whom I said above, “His way is undefiled,” made my way blameless, cleansing my heart by faith, so that I might come to battle not for my own honor but for his honor, in his name, by an undefiled way, the way of faith. By that faith I believed it possible that, through divine strength and by means of me, a little one, he who exalted himself against God and his armies might be conquered.

**Verse 34.** He made my feet like those of deer, so that, when later fleeing Saul who pursued me, I might flee through woodland and mountainous places like a swift deer. And he set me upon the heights, when in Ramah—which in Latin is interpreted “the heights”—he girded me. For Saul had sent attendants and messengers there to seize and destroy me (1 Sam. 19:20–23). When they came and saw the company of prophets, they too prophesied. When further messengers had been sent and all had joined the company of prophets, Saul himself finally came; joined to the prophets, stripped naked, he prophesied, while my God protected me, who set me upon the heights in Ramah.

**Verse 35.** He teaches my hands for battle. And because he is present with me, turning to him I say: “And you made my arms like a bronze bow,” when with my arms, like a bronze bow most strong, I struck down Goliath with a sling; and with my hands taught by you for battle, I cut off his head with his own sword.

**Verse 36.** And you gave me the protection of your salvation against Saul’s many snares; and your right hand upheld me, because your divine power preserved me amid many dangers, which were provided for me by you not for destruction but for discipline. And amid these same dangers your discipline corrected me unto the end, that is, unto perfect and final completion. And that same discipline will teach me, so that I may be like a humble pupil under the instruction of your discipline.

Finally, Saul having died, you enlarged my steps beneath me, subjecting his kingdom to me; and my footsteps were not weakened by so many persecutions troubling me. Therefore, as my strength remained or was even increased after Saul’s death, when I received royal power, I shall pursue my enemies. I shall pursue the raiders who set Ziklag on fire and carried off my two wives and much plunder (1 Sam. 30:8). I shall pursue and seize them, and shall not turn back until they fail. I shall crush them, and they shall not be able to stand beneath my feet. You girded me with strength for battle; you tripped up beneath me those rising against me; you gave me the backs of my enemies and destroyed those who hated me from Saul’s house. They cried out, and there was no one to save them, because after Abner’s death there was no one to stand for Saul’s house (2 Sam. 3:6). Yet they cried to the Lord, having no foreign god, and he did not hear them. I shall grind them like dust before the wind and wipe them away like street-mud. Even if some of the people of Israel oppose me, like Sheba son of Bichri, who said, “What share have we in David?” you will deliver me from the contradictions of the people.

Thus far the special benefits bestowed upon David, indicated in the literal text of the Psalm, have been set forth. For what follows, “You will appoint me as head of the nations,” and so forth, surpasses the literal history of David and pertains to the true David. That David was never appointed head of the nations, nor was he king of the nations, but only of the Jews. Therefore, compelled here to leave the literal sense and turn to the true David, let us, with God’s help, repeat the special benefits already mentioned in David and gather from them the mysteries of Christ.

Thus Christ, the true David, servant of the Lord, to whom this Psalm is attributed, says: “God, who girded me with strength and made my way blameless.” God the Father, truly my God, girded me as man with the strength of divinity. For unless he were truly God, he could not have conferred upon me the strength of divinity. But now, uniting me as man to his Word, his power, he girded me with strength, so that I, a little man, may be as strong as God himself, my most mighty Father and my God and my power and my strength. To him I said at the beginning of the Psalm: “I shall love you, O Lord, my strength”; or, as another translation has it, “my might.”

Therefore he is the God who girded me with divine power and made my way blameless. Just as his way toward the ancient Church, his bride, whom he loved with chaste love, was undefiled until, through the Virgin conceiving from his undefiled love, I, his Son, was born from that bride and betrothed to myself the new Church of the New Testament as bride; so he also made my way blameless, so that I, conceived and born without stain and living in this world by the undefiled way of love, might continually come to my bride, who bears children for me. Of them I shall say: “The children of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them. Days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast” (Mark 2:19–20). Thus fasting, they too will walk together in the blameless way for the honor of God my Father, who made blameless the way of me and of my own, concerning whom it is said elsewhere: “Blessed are the blameless in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118:1).

“He made my feet like those of deer.” A deer leaps over thorns and gaping places; so I leapt over the pits and thorns of sins, of which it was said to the old man: “When you cultivate the earth, it will not yield its fruit, but it will bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:18). I leapt over thorns of this sort, because, living in this world without sins, I was free among the dead, and free I passed from this world to the Father, seeking the heights like a deer. “And setting me upon the heights,” God my Father himself exalted me and gave me a name above every name (Phil. 2:9), however exalted, whether of dominions, thrones, principalities, or all the heavenly powers. Or, “my feet,” that is, the evangelists, he made like those of deer.

The ancient patriarchs and prophets, who ran before my coming, were deer; I am the fawn of those deer. Those deer desired me who was to be born, just as the deer longs for springs of water. Likewise the apostles and my other feet, children of the ancient deer, desire my second coming; and in those very desires they run to meet bridegroom and bride with swift and strong agility, like deer tending toward the heights, where I am, and where my Father sets me upon the heights.

“He teaches my hands for battle,” so that I may not only be strong and mighty in battle against ancient Goliath, but also prudent and skilled against snares in all the works of myself and my people, through which the strong armed one must be attacked.

And you, Father, made my arms like a bronze bow. You made the prophets and apostles, who are my arms, like a bronze bow, so that they might never tire of shooting the arrows of words of salvation. Or, you made the martyrs, who are my arms, in whom my strength plainly appeared, like a bronze bow; and before kings and governors you enabled them to release the keenest arrows of answers, when, being questioned, they confessed. Even when deprived of their tongues, they still spoke, standing and remaining firm with untiring courage in the testimony of truth. Thus you taught my hands for battle and made my arms like a bronze bow in the time of martyrs drawn up for battle.

And in the time of peace you gave me the protection of your salvation. You gave it to me—that is, to my confessors who lived in peace and died in peace: you gave them the protection of your salvation. Although temporal prosperity smiled upon them like the pleasantness of your left hand, nevertheless your right hand—that is, the delight of eternal and future goods, which is your right hand—upheld me, that is, my confessors, my lovers, my Church, my bride. Thus, adorned in contempt and use of temporal things and in love and enjoyment of eternal things, she could truly say of me, her beloved: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 8:3).

And if, amid those very prosperities, adversities at times befell on account of me—that is, for the disciplining of my own—your discipline did not break me, as dry wood which, if it is crooked, can be broken but cannot be straightened. But because I am the green wood of which I said in my Passion: “If they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?” (Luke 23:31), your discipline then, in my death, corrected me as man, bent away by mortality from the straightness of immortality. It corrected me indeed, since in the end it advanced me to immortality, to the final perfection of every consummation [Col. 0881D]. So also in my members: since I am the green wood in them and they are in me as branches in the vine, your discipline corrected me—that is, those who are mine—unto the end, that is, into conformity with me, who am the end of the law unto righteousness, who “am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1:8). But what shall be done to dry wood not joined to me? Certainly it will not be corrected, but broken and cast into the fire. For under the discipline of tribulation it is not bent toward patience or repentance for sins, but broken toward impatience, giving forth, as it were, the sound of its breaking in words of murmuring amid adversities. Therefore you, Father, are the husbandman who will prune by tribulation or temptation every branch in me that grows green through good will, so that it may bear more fruit [Col. 0882A], that it may bear fruit in patience. “And your discipline itself will teach me”—that is, those who are mine—because through tribulation they are trained as by a rod of discipline, that they may live disciplined lives according to the pattern of sound teaching. But lest, beneath this discipline of tribulations, excessive constriction of anxiety should creep in:

**VERSE 37.** You have enlarged my steps by the breadth of charity, giving, amid tribulations themselves, the gladness of good works, by which one proceeds to heaven as by straight steps. Thus you have enlarged my steps, not only in myself, but also beneath me, in my members. Or “beneath me,” that is, even in temporal things, which are under the sun, that is, under me. For in these too my steps and those of my people are enlarged when the changeable ordering of temporal things is, by a devout intention, referred in the breadth of charity to the pursuit of eternal things [Col. 0882B]. Therefore carnal constrictions do not obstruct, because you have made charity broad, working gladly even from and amid the things beneath me—mortal matters and mortal members.

And my footprints have not been weakened, that is, my paths. For just as I walked mightily in heaven upon the asp and basilisk and trampled the lion and dragon—that is, the poisonous and raging devil—when I saw Satan himself fall like lightning from heaven, unable to resist my ways or lift his head when trampled by me; so my footprints have not been weakened through the weakness of the flesh, because in the wilderness I trod mightily upon the head of the tempter himself, and still tread upon him in my members. In them, though weak, I am strong [Col. 0882C]; and so too in my sacraments, which are not weakened even when they are celebrated through weak ministers, provided that they have not been condemned by God and thus ceased to be ministers, as in the case of manifest simoniacs. Let them only be ministers whose office of ministry has not been forbidden to them, and the footprints of my sacraments will be firm for trampling the ancient serpent with the same power and strength by which he was trampled in heaven and cast down to earth, my strength conquering him through Michael. So now my strength conquers him through the lawful and catholic priesthood, signified by Michael standing before the golden altar with a golden censer (Rev. 8:3). In such a priesthood, designated by the golden altar and golden censer, my footprints have not been weakened [Col. 0882D], because my sacraments are mighty and victorious. In them sure traces of my imitation are found, since sacraments possess a certain likeness to the things whose sacraments they are. Therefore my venerable footprints are in them—I who am the truth. For example, in the form of bread the likeness of my truth is recognized: I am the true bread of angels, who eat me without the veil of sacraments, and of human beings, who eat me under the veil of sacraments. The former eat me as solid bread; the latter eat me through the sacrament of the Incarnation, as though turned into milk; or, certainly, through the sacrament of the Passion, fried in a pan, when I was, as it were, fried in a frying-pan, according to the rite of the legal sacrifice, which was offered hot in a pan from clean flour mixed with oil [Col. 0883A] (Lev. 6:21). In a sacrament of this kind my footprints have not been weakened, for to everyone who worthily eats me, if not in words then in reality, I say: Grow through such milk-like or oily food, and later you shall eat me still more perfectly as solid food. Nor will you change me into yourself, as you change the food of your flesh; rather, you will be changed into me. Therefore my footprints have not been weakened, since that which is celebrated through the frail office of ministers so benefits through the most powerful aid of my divinity that, just as indelible traces of conformity with me are impressed upon angels eating me, so it may be also for human beings eating me in the sacrament of the altar, not changing me into themselves but passing into me as bread, so that they too may be one bread [Col. 0883B], one body, in which the traces of conformity with me are found expressed through works of virtue.

The same understanding applies to the other ecclesiastical sacraments, in which my footprints have not been weakened, although my enemies seek to erase those same footprints. They would rather have me conformed to themselves than themselves to me; they also wish my members, incorporated into me through the power of the sacraments, to be conformed to themselves through malice and incorporated through the mystery of iniquity, which is already at work in the children of unbelief. But I, the most mighty giant of twofold substance, whose footprints have not been weakened, shall pursue the doubled ranks of my enemies, overthrowing the bands of evil spirits and evil human beings.

[Col. 0883C] **VERSE 38.** I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them. Against the invisible suggestions of evil spirits, I shall give the Holy Spirit to my elect, who will remind them of everything whatsoever I have said to them; and thus, through good thoughts in the hearts of my people, I shall pursue evil thoughts and seize them alive. I shall seize the princes of such nations, just as formerly through my servant Joshua I seized the five kings of the foreigners. Joshua caused them, once seized in a cave and shut up for some time, finally to be brought out; and, when brought out, he killed them (Josh. 10:18, 22, 26). Thus I, the true Jesus, shall seize the chief evil spirits and chastise them for a while in the cave of hearts, while I deny them the effects of their wickedness [Col. 0883D]; and at last I shall utterly slay them when they are brought forth through humiliations.

And I shall not turn back until they fail. I shall not turn aside from this pursuit until they fail and lose all their strength. So that they cannot recover it, I shall break them after the manner of the ancients, who first hanged criminals upon a cross and afterward broke their legs, so that, according to the commandment of the law, they might be buried on the same day on which they had been crucified. This was done to the robbers crucified with me. But my legs were not broken, because my footprints have not been weakened; and therefore with unwearied legs I shall pursue not only, as I have said, my invisible enemies, but also the visible ones, and I shall overtake them. I shall catch the crafty in their craftiness, so that, unknowingly and unwillingly, they may serve me [Col. 0884A], and the things they devise against my Gospel may rather advance the progress of the Gospel. And I shall not turn back until they fail, either through repentance or through punishment, as my enemy Saul failed through punishment and became Paul. Likewise I shall not turn aside from pursuing my other enemies until they fail. I shall break them as the legs of the two robbers were broken: one repentant, the other unrepentant. I so ordered it that by such torment the repentance of the one might be completed in this life, while for the other punishment might here begin, to remain for ever. Thus I shall break all my enemies: some unto salvation through the contrition of repentance, others, remaining unrepentant, unto condemnation.

**VERSE 39.** I shall break them, and they shall not be able to stand [Col. 0884B]. Though they resist for a time, they will not be able to stand and endure against me, but shall fall beneath my feet. They shall fall, either cast down by repentance or by punishment. They shall fall beneath my feet—that is, beneath the apostles and other apostolic men whom I shall appoint princes over all the earth. I shall also break invisible enemies by giving power to my elect so that they may crush Satan beneath their feet. Thus the devil and his attendants—desires, lusts, or errors—shall not be able to stand, but shall fall beneath my feet, even beneath my weak members; or beneath my feet, that is, beneath the virtues of my little ones, who, hastening toward me on virtues as on beautiful feet, tread with those same feet upon serpents, scorpions, and every power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm them [Col. 0884C].

**VERSE 40.** And you have girded me with strength for battle. Above I said: “God who girded me with strength”; now, repeating it as in thanksgiving, I say: “And you have girded me with strength for battle,” because as you girded me with strength in my own person, so you have girded me in my own people with strength sufficient for the battle to which I sent them, saying: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (Luke 10:3); again: “Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves” (John 16:33); again: “In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage: I have conquered the world” (ibid.). Thus, by saying these things, I sent and encouraged them for battle. And you, Father, girded me—that is, those who are mine—for battle [Col. 0884D], when you sent them the Paraclete, through whom you gave them the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God. Powerfully girded with this sword upon their thigh, they did not fear the dangers of the world.

And you tripped up beneath me those who rose against me. Those rising against me—that is, against me—and wishing to be above me or above my people, you tripped up, so that both demons and wicked human beings were beneath me. They could prevail neither against me nor against my people, so as to accomplish concerning me or mine what they wished. Rather, I prevailed against them in myself and my people, so that my will was fulfilled either in them, or through them and from them. In them my will was fulfilled if they were converted to good; through them and from them my will was fulfilled if they persisted in their malice, for through them I exercised my own according to my will [Col. 0885A]. At last what I willed was done with them: bound hand and foot, they were sent where I willed; and thus those rising against me are always beneath me.

**VERSE 41.** And you gave me my enemies’ back. In the Hebrew it reads: “You gave me the back of my enemies,” so that they do not dare resist me but either humbly follow me, and thus are a back to me, or flee from me; and you have given me the back of those who flee, so that, pursuing them, I may strike their backs—especially those Jews who killed me and said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). When they have been cast down into hell and tripped up, so that they are beneath me—that is, beneath my judgment, in my prison—I still strike their backs, that is, their descendants and followers, upon whom they called down my blood, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” For my enemies were those Jews themselves who killed me in that person, as though setting their faces against my face; but those count as their back who, joined to them by the same spirit of malice, follow them without seeing me myself and yet hate me. But you gave me the back of my enemies to be wounded by my swords and arrows [Col. 0885B]. The sharpest and final arrows may be understood as these words: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

And you destroyed those Jews who hated me through the Roman army under the commanders Titus and Vespasian. You destroyed them not by a single kind of destruction, as you long ago foreshadowed through the prophet Ezekiel, saying: “And you, son of man, take for yourself a sharp razor for shaving hair, and draw it over your head and over your beard; and take for yourself balances and divide them. A third part you shall burn in the fire in the midst of the city when the days of the siege are completed; a third part you shall take and cut with the sword round about it; and another third you shall scatter into the wind, and I shall draw out the sword after them. And from these you shall take a small number and bind them in the hem of your garment” (Ezek. 5:1–3) [Col. 0885C]. As it was prefigured, so it was fulfilled. For the sharp razor shaving hair was Roman power; by its shaving, the Jews, lacking the vital spirit, were shorn away like superfluous hairs from the living body of the patriarchs and prophets, and from Christ himself, their living head, to whom they adhered outwardly so long as, possessing the Temple of the Lord, they kept the ceremonies of the law. But once the holy city and Temple had been destroyed, so that no stone was left upon another, and the Jews dispersed among all nations, the whole beard was shaved: some was cut by the sword in the city through civil dissensions; some burned in the fire that consumed the city with its Temple; some perished by famine, a sword for them sharper than the sword of the Romans; some was scattered to the wind. And the sword was drawn out after them, because very many were killed by the sword as a spectacle in Caesar’s triumph [Col. 0886A]. That very small portion of the beard which the prophet was commanded to bind in the hem of his garment is the portion of the remnant of which Isaiah says: “The remnant of Israel shall be saved” (Isa. 10:21). Therefore, while the Jews who hated me perished under such diverse disasters, with the rest who did not hate me excepted, you, God the Father, destroyed those who hated me. They thought that by denying me they could have you as God their protector; but it is not so, because everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either. But those fools, because of their confidence in flesh and the blood of Abraham, having lost Abraham’s faith—he who rejoiced to see my day (John 8:26), which they did not gladly see—and because of the beautiful Temple—

**VERSE 42.** They cried out, and there was none to save [Col. 0886B]. For although, possessing the holy Temple, they said, “The Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord is here,” and cried out in that Temple while under siege by the Romans, nevertheless, because they had cast me, the Lord of the Temple, out of the Temple and out of the city to be crucified, there was none to save. For how could those be saved who denied me the Saviour and chose Barabbas for themselves? Almost the same crime is committed down to the present day by those who, when given a choice, refuse to choose good persons for themselves to rule or be bishops, but make bishops or rulers for themselves like Barabbas the robber. Later, when these oppress them, they cry out and there is none to save them. So the Jews who chose the robber and rejected the Saviour, when afflicted—as Josephus relates—by the robbery of the Sicarii within the city and by Roman violence without, cried out and there was none to save [Col. 0886C]. They cried to the Lord whose Son they had killed, and he did not hear them. Those who denied me the Son cried to the Lord, the Father, and he did not hear them. Their followers down to the present day, choosing robbers and rejecting the good, cry to the Lord whose servants they hate; they cry out, and he does not hear them. And I, judge of the living and the dead, shall crush them—I who said to you, God the Father, “You destroyed those who hated me”—that I may show that the things you, Father, do, I your Son likewise do. Now I speak of myself:

**VERSE 43.** And I shall crush them while you destroy them [Col. 0886D]. Because your operation and mine are one, I shall crush them like dust before the wind. For I am its winnower; the winnowing fan is in his hand. I possess judicial power; I shall winnow and cleanse my threshing-floor, and gather wheat into my barn. But those who call themselves Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan; or those who call themselves Christians and are not, but are the synagogue of Barabbas—I shall cast them out like dust before the wind, reckoning them among the nations who worship idols, of whom Isaiah says: “All nations are like a little dust, like a drop from a bucket, and like a grain on the balance; they are reckoned as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. 46:15, 17). Therefore, as the small dust which the wind scatters, so I shall scatter through the winnowing fan of judicial authority [Col. 0887A] those who worship either false gods or me, the true God, falsely.

I shall wipe them away like the mud of the streets. The broad way of this world has mud and is full of the luxurious and unclean. This mud will be wiped away, because the world and its desire shall pass away. Not even the least thing of the mud of worldly desire, or of the filth of muddy uncleanness in which swine roll themselves, shall be found, because the entire world and its desire shall pass away. There will be a new earth and a new heaven, in which righteousness dwells; nothing of the mud of filth will be in it. Rather, from the new earth, in which God’s will shall then be done as in heaven, all mud of uncleannesses shall be removed (1 John 2:17). And then I, the judge, shall wipe away like the mud of the streets those who love mud; to them, as Peter my apostle says, applies the proverb: “A washed sow in a wallow of mud” (2 Pet. 2:22) [Col. 0887B]. For then the wicked, together with wickedness itself, shall perish, swept clean by the broom of judgment, especially from the streets of Jerusalem, which will be paved with pure gold. In those streets there shall no longer be heard such contradiction as was heard in earthly Jerusalem when its citizens opposed me and said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). For you are my Father and my God.

**VERSE 44.** You will deliver me from the contradictions of the people who oppose me and desire Barabbas the robber. And you will set me as head of the nations, that I may be head of the nations, king of the nations and their desired one [Col. 0887C], the cornerstone set at the head of the corner, joining two walls: that is, believing Jews and believing Gentiles, or holy angels and righteous human beings. Thus, Father, you will set me as head of the nations, just as I, the truth, foretell the future. And because of its unquestionable certainty I announce it as though it were already past. For I say that:

**VERSE 45.** A people whom I did not know served me. That is, without doubt the Gentile people whom I did not know, whom I did not visit by bodily presence, will serve me—the people of whom I said to my disciples, “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. 10:5), whom I visited neither through written law nor through the oracles of prophets, to whom I was not sent, since I was sent only “to the sheep which were lost of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24) [Col. 0887D]. That people served me. It did not see me with its eyes, but heard of me through my disciples and obeyed me in the hearing of the ear. For after my resurrection I said to my disciples: “Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature” (Matt. 16:15). Before my death I did not permit this, when I said to them: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (ibid.). For it was necessary that the word of salvation should first be announced to the Jews, to whom I had been promised and sent, because of the truth of God, to confirm the promises to the fathers, and because of the gathering and conversion of those who were sons of the fathers and patriarchs. But after these had been chosen and gathered to me:

[Col. 0888A] **VERSE 46.** Foreign children lied to me. Sons in name alone, but foreign through perversity of conduct, by which they had degenerated from the nobility of their fathers; sons of the patriarchs according to the flesh, but foreigners because they renounced their fathers’ faith. Foreign children, to whom I said: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham”; but “you seek to kill me; Abraham did not do this. You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires. He was a murderer from the beginning” (John 8:39, 40, 44). In saying such things I identified the foreign children who lied to me, saying: “Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God in truth” (Matt. 22:16). They called me teacher, though they did not wish to be my disciples. They called me, “Lord, Lord,” and did not do what I said [Col. 0888B]. Therefore I answered them, among other things: “How can you speak good things when you are evil?” (ibid. 12:34). “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46). It is too little merely to say that they lied to me. Indeed, persisting in hatred of truth and love of falsehood, they not only devised a lie but also, with much money, bought off the soldiers, saying to them: “Say that his disciples stole him while we slept” (Matt. 28:13). To confirm this lie, they persecuted my apostles, the true witnesses of my resurrection, and drove them from their borders. Thus they lied obstinately. With their father the devil, who did not stand in truth, they too did not stand in truth; with that murderer they too became murderers in my death [Col. 0888C], choosing to persist in the lie conceived from their father the devil rather than return through repentance to the truth attested by my apostles. Therefore I say that those foreign children not only lied but also grew old in their lie.

Peter, my apostle, likewise for a time lied by denying that he knew me, but he did not grow old in his lie. For after his threefold denial, when the cock crowed, he went out and “wept bitterly” (Matt. 26:75); afterward he remained firm in witnessing to the truth. When he had grown old in that truth, another girded him, and he was crucified for the truth. Truly venerable was the old age of Peter, who grew old in truth. But foreign children who lied and grew old in their lie are altogether detestable, and by a just judgment were abandoned through me and my apostles. For my apostle Paul, in whom I was speaking, said: “It was necessary for the Word of God to be spoken first to you.
