But because you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46) [Col. 0888D]. This was a just judgment: that deserters of truth should be deserted, and that my words might be fulfilled: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:38). For the apostles did not first desert their own fellow-countrymen, whose perversion greatly grieved them; rather, they themselves cast out the apostles and refused to hold the way of truth and the path of uprightness taught by the apostles [Col. 0889A]. Instead they went astray and limped from their paths. They limped, weak in one foot: holding the Old Testament in carnal observance and rejecting the New; following the letter that kills and not loving the Spirit that gives life; neglecting God’s traditions and keeping their own; invoking the God of Abraham with their mouths and denying him by their deeds; calling God my Father their God, while denying me, his Son, as God. Thus they limped from paths which ought to have been their own: namely, the paths of truth promised to the children of Abraham, such as they ought to have been, and such as they would have been if, as true faithful children, they had been willing to be blessed with faithful Abraham by confessing the truth and saying:

**VERSE 47.** The Lord lives, and blessed be my God [Col. 0889B], and let the God of my salvation be exalted. Yet in their limping they confess that I died but refuse to say of me, “The Lord lives.” Therefore, since those foreign children lied and persist in their lie by denying that I live, the people of the nations—once not my people but now made my people—obeyed me in the hearing of the ear. Once not having obtained mercy but now having obtained mercy, it recognizes the truth; knowing me not only to have died but also to have risen, it says: “The Lord lives.” Without doubt, he whom you Jews call dead now lives, and the life of human beings rose with him. For “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall have no more dominion over him. For in that he died, he died to sin; but in that he lives, he lives to God” (Rom. 6:9–10) [Col. 0889C]. He died as man, but lives as Lord; dead through our mortality, but the Lord lives in his divinity; dead in the form of a servant, but now lives as Lord, holding dominion over all creation. Hence he said: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18). Therefore the man who died and has now risen, having received authority to rule in heaven and on earth, lives as Lord. He lives not in just any manner, but as his Father does, who alone has immortality, which he gave also to the Son, made man and dead for human beings. “For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave to the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26) [Col. 0889D]. The Lord lives and has power to give life as the Father does. For as the Father raises up and gives life to the dead, so the Son gives life to whom he wills. The Lord lives, and now not his divinity alone gives life to the dead, but also his flesh and blood, through communion in which bodies too shall be made alive at the resurrection. Therefore the Lord lives, as is evident from the effect, because he gives life to his Church.

The Lord lives, and blessed be my God. He is God of all generally by creation; he is my God especially by the enlivening and blessing through which he gives life to me, his Church, so that I may live by faith in him, and blesses me so that my faith may bear fruit. He blessed the first human beings, saying [Col. 0890A]: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it; rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and the beasts of earth” (Gen. 1:28). To me, his bride the Church, and to my children—especially those whom he has appointed to be vicars of his work, shepherds and rulers of lesser persons—he now likewise blesses, saying to them not so much in voice as by the efficacy of events: “Increase and multiply.” Increase in the progress of virtues, and multiply by exercises and examples of virtue, converting many. Do not be few. Increase, lest you be small in merit; multiply, lest you be few in number. And fill the earth: that is, spread throughout the whole world, and at last fill the land of paradise, the land of promise, the land of milk and honey—the land from which cursed human beings were expelled in the first parents, and into which the blessed robber was brought by me, the Blessed One, when I said to him: “Amen, I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43) [Col. 0890B]. Fill this land; that is, live in this cursed and thorny land in such a way that, departing from here, you may enter that blessed land, most abundantly rich in the flowers and fruits of eternal joy. Meanwhile, while you are in the cursed land, which has beasts, birds, and fish, rule over them through the power of my blessing, by which I, the Blessed One, have blessed you above all creatures that move upon the earth. For “your citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20), where you profess that I am:

And let the God of my salvation be exalted. What you believe, you desire to be made known also to others. You believe, and therefore speak, that I, your God, am the Most High, Son of the Most High. Therefore you, Church gathered from the nations—of whom, in a figure, one sinful woman, wishing to touch me, heard, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:7)—now touch me on high, because you believe that I, the Most High, reign with the Most High Father. Therefore you say: “Let the God of my salvation be exalted.” May that living and blessed God, who is the God of my salvation because he has given me life, blessed me, and saves me lest his blessing perish in me, be exalted: that is, may he be known to be Most High. For he, the God of my salvation, is the Sun of righteousness, of whom it is written: “For you who fear my name, the Sun of righteousness shall arise, and healing in his wings” (Matt. 4:2) [Col. 0890C]. Because of this healing in his wings—namely, in his mercy and compassion, beneath which wings we hope—he is called the God of my salvation: that is, of the Church gathered from the nations. He chose her not by the debt of promise, as he received Israel his servant, “as he spoke to Abraham and to his seed” (Luke 1:55), but through great mercy and compassion, in which, as in the wings of the eternal sun, is my healing. Therefore I desire that this God of my salvation may be exalted, that this Sun of righteousness may be raised to the height of his zodiac, from which he may make summer days—long and bright days—throughout the whole world, in which we may say: “Winter has passed, the rain is gone and withdrawn; flowers have appeared [Col. 0891A]; the blossoming vines have given forth fragrance” (Song 2:11–13). This Sun of righteousness appears as though lowered in the time of winter, when the storm of persecution threatens. Thus, born into this world to endure the wintry troubles of mortality, as it were in the winter of Herod’s persecution, and indeed literally appearing in a winter season, he did not appear on high; but “a little child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6). But the firstborn of the dead, rising from the dead, dedicated the summer season to the solemnity of his Resurrection and Ascension. From that time, though in his own person free from winter’s hardship, while his people still sometimes labour in this world and their persecutors reign, this Sun of righteousness appears as though lowered amid wintry signs that threaten storms [Col. 0891B]. Therefore either the Church or any faithful soul, desiring better times and longing for Paschal and summer days, says: “The Lord lives, and blessed be my God, and let the God of my salvation be exalted.” Thus I, who came blessed in the name of the Lord, shall be proclaimed living, blessed, and exalted in the Church; and I, recognizing that these praises have been given to me by God the Father, bless him and say to him:

**VERSES 48–49.** God, who gives me vengeance and subjects peoples beneath me, my deliverer from wrathful enemies. And you will exalt me above those who rise against me, and rescue me from the unjust man. For as the holy Church desires my exaltation, so you, God the Father, accomplish it: you give me vengeance against demons and their allied rulers, such as Nero and Decius, or Arius and the other heresiarchs, worthy of no clemency. Therefore severe vengeance was wrought upon them. And when the leaders of persecutions or errors have been mutilated by just vengeance, you subject peoples beneath me, because you will save the humble people and humble the eyes of the proud by the deserved acts of vengeance which you give me; for you judge no one, but give all judgment to me, “because I am the Son of God” (Matt. 27:43) [Col. 0891C]. Therefore, through me, the man merciful to human beings, vengeance given to me by you is so tempered that only the stubborn and those hardened in wickedness are subject to the dreadful penalties of vengeance—vengeance without mercy, because they judged me and mine without mercy. But vengeance against the humble and simple people, although they too deserved vengeance, will be moderated, because they were not without mercy toward me and mine, so that it does not destroy them but subjects them to me. This is merciful vengeance: when the rebel is made subject to me, through your work, Father, who subject peoples beneath me, so that over them I may be exalted—the God of salvation, delivered from my wrathful enemies, exalted above those rising against me, and rescued from the unjust man.

For as the Chaldeans made three bands (Job 1:17) when they plundered my servant Job, so there are three bands of my enemies. One band is the Jews, who, speaking in the wrath of the earth and unwilling to lose their land or earthly gains, were angrily troublesome to me and my apostles. They were filled with wrathful zeal when, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, they saw crowds of Gentiles gathered to hear the word of God: “They were filled with zeal and contradicted the things spoken by Paul, blaspheming” (Acts 13:45) [Col. 0892A]. For the elder brother—that is, the Jewish people—becomes angry with envious zeal at the reception of the younger; and we always find wicked Jews angered by the salvation of the nations. Thus, when in the Gospel I spoke of the salvation of the nations under the example of Elijah sent to a Gentile widow and Elisha healing Naaman the Syrian, a Gentile, those who hated the salvation of the nations were filled with wrath at hearing this (3 Kgs. 17:10; 4 Kgs. 5:14). Therefore my wrathful enemies are the Jews, of whom is composed one band attacking me and my Church. But I have been delivered; my bride the Church, my body, shall likewise be delivered from these my wrathful enemies. Therefore in thanksgiving, praising you, God my Father, I say: “My deliverer from my wrathful enemies.”

The second troop consists of pagan tyrants and open persecutors rising up against me—that is, against me. But from these you, Father, will exalt me and mine; for the more wonderful the surges of the sea, the higher the storms of the flood overflowing above the loftiest mountains beat upon me, the true Noah, in my ark, so much the more do they raise that ark itself above the earth—the holy Church, namely—in which you, Father, will exalt me above those rising up against me. At last, when my ark has been raised to the high mountains [Col. 0892C] and set there, the storms rising against me will subside.

The third troop consists of false brethren who, having an appearance of godliness but denying its power, call themselves Christians and are not; rather, they are the synagogue of Antichrist himself, called Christians in name alone. This troop includes heretics, schismatics, and all wicked and perverse persons who did not come from the troops of Jews or pagans, but went out from us because they were not of us. These are the accursed army of Gog and Magog. For by the name Gog, interpreted “covered,” is signified the host of Antichrist still covered beneath the veil and appearance of godliness in those who have not yet gone out from us, and yet [Col. 0892D] are covered and hidden within, not being of us. By the name Magog, however, interpreted “uncovered,” is signified the host of that same Antichrist, uncovered and revealed in those who have already gone out from us, because they were not of us. For had they been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.

Therefore, just as the Jews were my angry enemies, and the hostile men who rose against me were pagan rulers, so the wicked man is the false Christian: whether he still presses upon the body of the Church while hidden within, like bad food which, unable to be digested and incorporated into the limbs, oppresses the chest until it is expelled by vomiting; or whether, having now gone outside and been uncovered by the removal of his veil of malice, he afflicts the body of the Church externally—for example, some simoniacal bishop already convicted [Col. 0893A] and deposed, or otherwise exposed and uncovered, persecutes the Church, as Simon Magus did. Exposed by the apostle Peter, he became a public enemy of the Church, which he did not cease to persecute and harass until, at the prayers of the apostles Peter and Paul, the Lord delivered his Church from him (Acts 8:20). Therefore the Lord prays prophetically, and prophesies in prayer, to the Father against him and every wicked man like him, whether covered or uncovered, saying: “From the wicked man you will deliver me.”

Accordingly, this chant is a voice of exultation and salvation in the tents of the righteous; it is customarily sung at the entrance of the Mass on the Wednesday preceding Palm Sunday, when the Lord’s Passion is imminent. For Palm Sunday will not be fully celebrated unless the holy Church first obtains complete triumph over all enemies, denoted by these few words, spoken by Christ or by any true Christian: “My deliverer from angry peoples; from those rising up against me you will exalt me; from the wicked man you will deliver me, O Lord.” For in this short chant are denoted the aforesaid three troops: angry Jews, rising pagans, and wicked Christians, whether concealed within or cast out.

In the Gospel of the same office, the Jews express those three troops. For when the Jews surrounded Jesus as he walked in Solomon’s portico, saying, “How long do you take away our life?” (John 4:24), breathing great anger in these words, they expressed their own wickedness. But when “they took up stones to throw at him” (John 8:59), they foreshadowed open persecutors, pagan tyrants. And when, putting forward an appearance of godliness, they said, “We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, and because you, being a man, make yourself God” (ibid., 10:33), they clearly portrayed in these words the wicked man who, under an appearance of godliness, attacks godliness: though opposed to God, he pretends nevertheless to render service to God.

Suitably, therefore, against these three wedges of enemies, the cry to the Lord—the deliverer from angry enemies, rising pagans, and the wicked man—is raised not only in the aforementioned chant before the holy Gospel, but also in the Offertory, the chant after the Gospel. For the Offertory says: “Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and free me, O Lord, from those rising up against me.” Here the enemies, the Jews who did not crucify him with their own hands but handed him over to the Gentiles, and the rising pagans, who laid hands upon him and upon his martyrs, are plainly indicated.

But because “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Micah 7:6) and afflict him more grievously, the following Offertory verse is sung against the wicked man who afflicts more dangerously: “Because you have become my helper and my refuge in the day of my tribulation, deliver me.” By “the day of tribulation” is denoted the time of Antichrist, of which we read that then there will be tribulations such as have not occurred since nations began to exist (Mark 13:19). For there is not one Antichrist only, but many antichrists; and woe to those who are pregnant and nursing [Col. 0894A] in the days of the antichrists, who say that they are Christians or christs—that is, anointed kings and priests—and are not.

“This day is a day of tribulation,” King Hezekiah says to Isaiah; and, as though explaining the greatness of that tribulation, he says: “The children have come to the birth, and there is no strength to bring forth” (Isaiah 37:3). Therefore, as the Lord says, “Woe to those who are pregnant” (Matthew 24:19) in these days, in which children have come to birth and there is no strength to bring forth: for although there are people who gladly hear the truth, those who will speak it are lacking. Thus there is no strength to bring forth, because King Pharaoh prohibits the office of midwifery, except perhaps to those midwives who kill every male child (Exodus 1:16), and thus do not lessen but [Col. 0894B] increase the tribulation of this time, so that the harshly oppressed Hebrew people may cry more earnestly on the day of tribulation with Christ: “My deliverer from my angry enemies, and from those rising against me you will exalt me; from the wicked man you will deliver me.”

**VERSE 50.** Therefore I will confess you among the nations, O Lord, and I will sing a psalm to your name.

I, Christ, because of all the benefits enumerated above, bestowed or yet to be bestowed upon me and my members, “confess you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, because thus it was pleasing before you” (Matthew 11:25–26). Therefore I will confess you among the nations, O Lord, causing the nations themselves to confess you [Col. 0894C] in words; and I will sing a psalm, causing them to sing psalms—that is, to perform works of virtue—not by spreading fame for their own name, but by magnifying your name. For the magnification of that name the true worshippers, worshipping and magnifying you, Father, in spirit and truth, will say this:

**VERSE 51.** Magnifying the salvations of his king, and showing mercy to his Christ David, and to his seed forever.

That is to say: God the Father is rightly magnified by his people, the Christian people, because he magnifies the salvations of his king—that is, he brings about wonderful and magnificent deliverances among his people, deliverances which his king performs and on account of which he is rightly called Savior. “For he shall save [Col. 0894D] his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21).

The Father, who magnifies these deliverances, is also he who shows mercy to his Christ David. To Christ—that is, to the one anointed above his companions with the oil of gladness, the Holy Spirit and power; to David, mighty of hand against enemies and beloved by his friends—God the Father himself shows mercy, since no human merits preceded in order that a human being might thus be assumed into God and thus anointed, so as to be so mighty of hand that no one can snatch from his hand, just as no one can snatch from the Father’s hand.

And the Father of mercies shows mercies forever to his seed—namely, that seed of whom the prophet promised: “If he gives his life as an offering for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed” [Col. 0895A] (Isaiah 53). To this long-lived seed, forever—whether because Christian worship will endure until the end of the age, or because, when the world passes away, the word of Christ, which is his seed, remains forever, especially in good soil—to this seed, I say, which remains forever, the Father will show mercies enduring forever, indeed eternally.

In the Hebrew it stands thus: “Therefore I will confess you among the Gentiles, and to your name I will sing, to him who magnifies the salvation of his king and shows mercy to his Christ David and to his seed forever.” To this verse the final conclusion may be adapted thus:

“Glory to the Father, who magnifies the salvation of his king, who shows mercy to his Christ David and to his seed forever. Glory to the Son, the king, Christ, the true David, who went out to sow his seed. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that mercy which the Father shows to his Christ David and to his seed forever. Amen.”

## PSALM XVIII

[Col. 0895]

The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands.

[Col. 0895B] **VERSE 1. UNTO THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID.**

The title is clear. The sequence is pleasing. For in the preceding three psalms, the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of Christ have been commended—the sum of our salvation, in which the foundation of faith stands established. What happened thereafter this immediately following psalm now declares.

**VERSE 2.** The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands.

These heavens are the apostles. Though previously earthly and weak, after Christ’s Passion, having received the Holy Spirit, they became such that they are rightly called heavens and rightly called the firmament. “There are no speeches,” he says, “nor words, whose voices are not heard.” For on that day the Holy Spirit performed this miracle [Col. 0895C]: that every kind of language came forth from the mouths of them all. The declaration of such heavens did not remain in one region only; rather, “their sound went out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world.”

And what glory of God did these heavens declare? “In the sun,” they say, “he has set his tent, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, has rejoiced as a giant to run his course. His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his return extends to its height; and there is none who can hide himself from his heat.” Then, praising the law of faith written by God’s finger not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts, he says: “The law of the Lord is spotless, converting souls,” and so forth. Near the psalm’s end [Col. 0895D], the Prophet—or anyone who sings wisely—after gloriously praising the heavens, returns into himself, considers himself, and pours out humble prayer. In comparison with the heavens declaring God’s glory, he recognizes himself to be dust and an earthly sinner. Thus he says: “Who understands transgressions?” And adds: “Cleanse me from my hidden sins,” and so forth.

Now that we have briefly surveyed the whole sequence of the psalm, let us return to its beginning, with the Lord’s help to expound its entire meaning more fully.

It is a rule of rhetorical propriety that, when eloquent orators skilled in persuading and advising speak before a public audience, the ring of common people surrounding them should maintain the deepest silence while they speak. But when the speech has ended—especially in the demonstrative kind of oratory—if it has been delivered well and has persuaded the people assembled of its intended point, whether someone worthy of an office is commended or someone unworthy refuted, a great favorable shout rises from the people, by which the skill of the orators who spoke is praised.

Thus not only eloquent orators but simple supporters also deserve one favor from the person chosen, when that person has been commended as worthy of some dignity: some speaking eloquently and persuasively, others assenting and acclaiming with willing hearts. Likewise, before a person unworthy and rejected from office, those who refuted that person in speech and those who assented to the speakers with eager cries incur an equal displeasure. The speakers and the assenting hearers have one and the same favor with the chosen ruler, though there is some difference in honor.

Therefore, if we ordinary people are to find with Christ the King the same favor as the heavenly orators who commend him before the audience of the whole world, let each of us first say with little David: “O Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up; nor have I walked in great things or in wonders above me” (Psalm 130:1–2). That is: I do not presume to count myself among the great and wonderful heavens declaring God’s glory [Col. 0896D]. Yet I acclaim, I assent, and I magnify those great orators; and I show that the glory marvellously, discriminately, eloquently, and praiseworthily declared by them is pleasing and acceptable to me, because I proclaim those preachers to be worthy of praise and worthy of the names “heavens” and “firmament.” For I say: “The heavens declare the glory of God.”

We have heard great orators speaking magnificently in the great rhetorical assembly of this world, commending a great king and recounting his glory. We applaud and accept them, because there is no possibility of contradiction or hiding-place from the force of the demonstration: those who speak demonstratively show what they proclaim. For those who speak are themselves heavens stretched above the whole earth. For the Maker of the world, “stretching out heaven like a skin” (Psalm 103:2), stretched them out when, drawing them as it were like skin from flesh—that is, from carnal desires and fleshly observances of the Law—he made them heavenly. Indeed, he made them heavens, whose manner of life was above, and whose course never strayed, as stray the wandering stars set beneath heaven.

For although the heavens move with however great speed, they nevertheless always preserve the uniformity of their course: they never admit erroneous variation, and the stars fixed in them never become wandering, stationary, or retrograde, as Lucifer, who rose in the morning, [Col. 0897B] became retrograde with the third part of the stars which he drew after himself down to earth. But these heavens have been established by the word of the Lord which they declare. They seek not worldly and vain glory, but God’s glory. Since these heavens move about the globe under desire for God’s glory alone, they declare God’s glory; for the words that thunder within them and the signs that flash within them do not merely relate God’s glory, but declare it—that is, they announce it by relating it perfectly and expressly.

The mute heavens prefigured these rational and eloquent heavens. At Christ’s birth they immediately sent forth a star, and by its extraordinary and new brightness, declaring the glory of God, the Gentile kings were instructed to recognize God’s glory in the child to whose service that same star was assigned. Yet these heavens declared God’s glory more magnificently among all peoples when the apostles themselves sent Paul the apostle, separated from the other apostles, to evangelize the Gentiles. “For he who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked in Paul among the Gentiles” (Galatians 2:8); and they recognized God’s grace and glory because through Paul’s most radiant Gospel the heavens declared God’s glory.

Even to the end of the age the heavens declare God’s glory, because the Church shines through their teaching as the earth is illumined from heaven—or rather, as the moon shines when illuminated by the sun. For if through the insensible heavens “the glory” of the Creator is in some fashion “declared,” while “the invisible things of God are perceived through the things that have been made” (Romans 1:20), how much more through these rational heavens, in whom Christ, the Sun of righteousness, dwells. From the twelve apostles as from twelve signs, blessing the crown of the year of his goodness (Psalm 64:12), and making this season of grace an acceptable year, he caused those same apostles, like the twelve signs of the solar circuit, to represent throughout the world the very Sun of righteousness.

One of these heavens, declaring God’s glory, says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). And another says: “This man was considered worthy of greater glory than Moses, inasmuch as he who built the house has greater glory [Col. 0898A] than the house” (Hebrews 3:3). “Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony to the things which were to be spoken; but Christ as a Son over his house, whose house we are.” Again elsewhere he says: “Now if the ministry of death, engraved in letters upon stones, came in glory, so that the children of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which is being abolished, how shall not the ministry of the Spirit be in still greater glory?” For “if the ministry of condemnation is glory, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory” (2 Corinthians 3:7–9).

Again, John the Evangelist, a magnificent declarer of God’s glory, having himself declared God’s glory in the New Testament as in one hemisphere of heaven, joined to himself, shining from the Old Testament as from the other hemisphere, Isaiah the prophet as a most brilliant star, in order to declare that same glory of God. Having introduced Isaiah’s testimonies concerning the blinding of the Jews, he added: “Isaiah said these things when he saw God’s glory” (John 12:41).

But what glory of God had Isaiah seen when he said these things concerning the Jews: “Blind the heart of this people and make their ears heavy” (Isaiah 6:10)? Clearly, when Isaiah said these things, he saw God’s glory, as John testifies. And this was that glory: “He saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and the whole earth was full of his glory, and the things beneath him filled the temple” (ibid., 1–2). The high throne is the angelic nature, among whose more exalted ranks are the cherubim and thrones. And who is this Lord sitting upon the high throne, if not the God-man sitting at God’s right hand above the cherubim and thrones and every power of heaven—the human being glorified into God, who with God the Father presides over them? Is it not great glory that on this exalted throne we see a man worshipped by a multitude of angels?

By the lifted-up throne we mean the apostolic choir, raised from the depths of earth to fellowship with the highest angels, so that the apostles themselves are heavenly thrones on which Christ sits, exercising his judgments. Thus the whole earth, the whole Church in its entirety, is full of his glory through the apostles’ teaching; for all things serve his glory, while every knee is bent to him—of things heavenly, earthly, and infernal. No heavenly being is unwilling, and no earthly or infernal being is able in any way to impede the advance and consummation of God’s glory, which the heavens declare by thundering words, flashing signs, and pouring down grace. Thus, as is read in Hosea: “The heavens shall answer the earth, and the earth shall answer the grain and wine, and these shall answer Jezreel” (Hosea 2:21–22).

It is pleasing, in this season of the Lord’s Advent, which returns to us annually while we are writing, to recall that the heavens answer the earth when throughout the whole earth, throughout the whole Church, there is a cry to the heavens themselves. What is cried? This: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth open and bring forth [Col. 0899A] the Savior, and let righteousness spring up together” (Isaiah 45:8).

There are many matters in which these heavens declare Christ’s glory: either the glory by which he glorified the Father upon earth, or that by which the Father glorified, or made radiant, him. Both are denoted in the Greek Gospel of John by the one word δοξάσαι, “to glorify.” [Note: [Col. 0899D] The manuscript reads *doxaste* in Latin letters.] The Father therefore glorified, or made him radiant, with himself in the glory and brightness which he had before the world existed, because he now has in his humanity that brightness and glory which he had in his divinity before the world was made.

But because in the declaration of heavenly glory we can scarcely understand the heavens who declare it, on account of the glory of Christ’s countenance—which is not abolished even if it is not understood by us—let us, as though our eyes were wearied by the brightness of Christ’s countenance, turn our gaze aside a little and behold the works of his hands, which the firmament proclaims in more familiar speech.

For not only do the heavens declare God’s glory, but the firmament also proclaims the works of his hands. The firmament is the same persons as the heavens, for “the heavens themselves were established by the word of the Lord” (Psalm 32:6). They take the name “firmament” because “they became mighty in battle and routed the armies of foreigners” (Hebrews 11:34) by proclaiming the works of God’s hands throughout the world. Had they only declared God’s glory, for example by saying, “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), and other such things, they would have had no opponents, or few, in the world because of their declaration [Col. 0899C] of God’s heavenly glory. But because the works of his hands had to be proclaimed through them—above all, the unique work of his hands which he performed on the cross, when, with hands outstretched on that cross, he drew all things to himself—they needed the strengthening of the Holy Spirit, so that they should not be ashamed of Christ’s Gospel in those works of his hands in which it was “a stumbling-block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles” (1 Corinthians 1:23).

“But blessed,” Christ himself says, “is he who is not scandalized in me” (Matthew 11:6). And the firmament declares that the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings and the weakness of God stronger than human beings. The voice of this firmament is like “the voice of thunder in the wheel” (Psalm 76:19), where it says: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3). Again he says: “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” (2 Corinthians 12:10).

This firmament, moving in a circuit from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, filled the world with the thunder of the Gospel’s voice: its mighty circuit like the firmament’s strong, unwavering movement in its wonderful and unimpeded course around the world. Yet the wandering stars appear to resist this course strongly, as is known to astronomers who posit the course of the planets from west through east to west, and the course of the firmament from east through west again to east.

Such was the course of Paul the apostle, running in the likeness of the firmament. Sent by God—not from human beings or through a human being, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ—he hastened to return to God himself, desiring “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23), having completed his course, as it were, through the west—that is, through administration of temporal things—and toward the east, that is, contemplation of eternal light. But ministers of Satan, transforming themselves into angels of light—false apostles and false brethren—seemed to resist his course. They belonged to the western world, spoke from the world, and ran toward the world, because the world heard them. Yet they ran, as it were, through the east toward the west, because by administering spiritual offices they pursued the acquisition of worldly things.

Nevertheless Paul and the other apostles, having completed their course and kept the faith, were considered worthy not only of the name “heavens” but also of the name “firmament.” For they were made perfect not only by the illumination of the Holy Spirit for declaring God’s glory, they and all their adornment; they were also so strengthened by the power of that same Holy Spirit for proclaiming the works of his hands that they were not ashamed of God’s Gospel, even when proclaiming those works of God which seemed like madness to the world. Thus the heavens and all their adornment were made perfect for declaring God’s glory; and God called heaven “firmament” when he chose and strengthened weak things in order to confound the strong.

Let every hearer, then, be teachable, well-disposed, and attentive to these declarers of God’s glory and to this firmament proclaiming the works of his hands. For such declaration and proclamation are made with discrimination, especially since not all things are declared or proclaimed to all persons, but rather according to a distinction of matters.

**VERSE 3.** Day belches forth the word to day, and night indicates knowledge to night.

For day belches forth the word to day when the heavens, speaking wisdom among the perfect, declare God’s glory as it were by displaying the bright and lofty sun in the upper hemisphere, so that between speakers and hearers, as between illuminating heaven and illumined earth, there is clear day. And night indicates knowledge to night when the firmament, giving milk to little ones, proclaims the works of God’s hands as though bending the sun down toward the lower hemisphere, so as to present night. Through the known bending and humiliation of the highest and brightest sun, little and humble persons receive knowledge; and night, as it were, is instructed by night, when it is said to the humble and gentle through the humble and gentle Christ: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29).

Day indeed belches forth the word of wisdom, a good word, when Christ the true light fully illuminates the teachers of the Church, so that they too, like day, make their light shine before human beings, so that God may be glorified; or when, having themselves become day and attained perfection, they disclose to other perfect persons the good word from the fullness of wisdom as though by belching it forth rather than by expounding it. But night indicates knowledge to night when the simple and less perfect contemplate Christ in human nature according to the form of a servant: having not solar beauty or splendor, but a pallor as of the moon. By this brightness, aided by the starlike light of miracles and works, eternal wisdom is not indeed made manifest to everyone; nevertheless, knowledge of Christ’s human life is cautiously indicated—a life which is the highest discipline of character on earth.

Day belches forth to day the word—that is, wisdom concerning the glory of Christ in which he is equal to the Father. Night indicates to night knowledge concerning his temporal life and dispensation, in which he was a human being like us, capable of suffering: his night conformed to our night, his weakness to our weakness. Yet a dark storm of original and actual sins possessed our night, whereas his night was illumined as day, because all his human weakness passed into divine power, and temporal reproach into eternal glory. For it was not his own need but ours that required it; not his but our iniquity which had to be abolished. He became weak for us who are weak, in order to gain us who are weak. Hence the night of his weakness was illumination amid his delights.

For if before worldly ages he “took delight day by day, playing in the circle of the earth” in his foreknowledge, accounting his “delights to be with the children of men” (Proverbs 8:30–31), how much more was that very night, that very weakness of infancy, in which he was born for us dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, an illumination amid his delights when light arose? The night of his birth itself was a great illumination in his delights, when he was then present in the circle of the earth, calling the Gentiles by a star visible to the whole world.

At that birth, when the true Sun was placed beneath the cloud of human flesh, day belched forth the word to day: God’s brightness shone around shepherds illumined by the Law, while an angel said to them, “Behold, I announce to you great joy, which shall be for all people, because today a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke 2:10–11). And night indicated knowledge to night when, not by speaking but by the sign of its novelty and brightness, the star instructed the Magi, situated in the dark error of Gentilism, and led them as far as the Lord’s manger.

Then, as day belched forth the word to day—that is, as the angel announced great joy to the shepherds—“the ox knew its owner” (Isaiah 1:3), that is, the Jewish people knew its Lord. And as night indicated knowledge to night, while the Magi were taught by a mute sign, “the ass knew the manger of its Lord” (ibid.): for the Gentile people, though compared to an unclean animal, was nevertheless in its firstfruits brought to the manger of its Lord.

Further, day still belches forth the word to day when a perfect teacher, who is an angel of the Lord of hosts, announces great joy to perfect hearers, showing Christ the King, Savior of the world, to be in the city of David—that is, in the holy Church. Though wrapped in the swaddling clothes, as it were, of sacraments, he is nevertheless truly to be adored and, together with God the Father, to be glorified as God, as the angel said to the shepherds: “Glory to God in the highest.” And as, after seeing the child, “the shepherds returned, glorifying God in all that they had heard and seen, as had been said to them” (Luke 2:14, 20).

And night indicates knowledge to night when the same perfect teacher, having become weak for the weak, instructs by example those of lesser capacity whom he cannot instruct by word. Thus he offers those to whom he cannot belch forth the word of Wisdom as day to day—as the angel did to the shepherds, around whom God’s brightness shone—a radiant manner of life, like a bright star giving them guidance along the road to the child.

To him, just as the shepherds offered only a sacrifice of rejoicing and glorification, signifying the perfect, who possess no outward goods and offer within themselves a sacrifice of praise, so “the Magi offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh” (Matthew 2:11), signifying those who do not yet know how to glorify God with angels and shepherds, but nevertheless endeavor, with the devout Magi, to adore him and honor him with outward gifts. Yet these same gifts—gold, frankincense, and myrrh—signify the inward gifts which the holy Church offers: myrrh through martyrs, frankincense through confessors, and gold through Catholic rulers; or myrrh through fasting, abstinence, and other disciplines of the flesh; frankincense through the incense of prayer, holy desire, and other devotions of the mind; and gold through works of charity, of which almsgiving is foremost, to be laid up there where neither thieves can dig it out nor rust destroy it.

Night indicates the discriminating knowledge of this matter to night when one who offers such things, after the example of the three Magi, edifies others by that person’s example. But day belches forth the word to day when, after the example of the angels, “Glory in the highest” (Luke 19:39) is sung, and after the example of the shepherds, God made flesh and wrapped in swaddling clothes is praised and glorified. And while others are illumined by this example, they too announce God’s salvation from day to day, so that as day continually belches forth the word to day from day to day, there may be no place at all of darkness except in hell, where no one will confess God.

It is pleasant to meditate upon these things as the festival of Christ’s Nativity approaches and is already imminent while we write. On it “a child is born to us, a son is given to us” (Isaiah 9:6), and is glorified by perfect praisers along with angels and shepherds who praise and glorify God. Let us faithfully desire that our voices too may be commanded to be admitted among theirs; and let us humbly adore him after the example of the three Magi, so that we, the remnant of the Gentiles, may be made participants in that great joy which the firstfruits of Jews and Gentiles had. For great joy was announced to the shepherds by the angel, and, seeing the star, the Magi “rejoiced with exceedingly great joy” [Col. 0903A] (Matthew 2:10).

Behold, we have looked upon and our hands have handled this word of life which day belches forth to day with the highest discrimination. For not all things are given to all persons: the bright declare to the bright the wisdom which lies in the fruit of eternal things; and those same persons, made night, indicate to the dark the knowledge which lies in the course of temporal things. And this occurs with great discrimination, but also most wonderfully and magnificently. Wonderfully, because:

**VERSE 4.** There are no speeches in the diverse kinds of languages, nor words in the differing idioms of each language, whose voices are not heard; so that from every nation which is under heaven some marvel and say: “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how have we each heard our own language, in which we were born?” (Acts 2:7–8).

And while these heavens declaring God’s glory are thus heard wonderfully in one temple or upper room, they are nevertheless heard magnificently throughout the world. Indeed:

**VERSE 5.** Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world.

First, the apostles themselves, shut within a single upper room, “began to speak the mighty works of God in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (ibid., 4). They had been commanded not to speak in this name; but the word of God was not bound, nor could the teaching of the apostles be confined. Rather, through them—and through their disciples—their sound went out into all the earth [Col. 0903C], once the Gospel had been heard throughout the world, both by the report of its fame and by the words of teaching. First indeed, “there came suddenly from heaven a sound as of a mighty rushing spirit” (ibid., 2); and afterwards tongues divided as if of fire appeared. For the Gospel was to proceed in such a way that, with the sound of its fame running beforehand like a mighty spirit, the divided tongues, in every diversity of human speech, would afterwards, like fire, enlighten and inflame the hearts of hearers and believers—struck by the report of its fame and instructed by rational words—which reached the ends of the earth because they penetrated and filled even its furthest corners. And truly, it was a great miracle that, for the spreading of the Word of God [Col. 0903D], one man then spoke in various tongues; but now, when God’s Word has already been spread abroad, there is a greater and more useful miracle: the one Catholic and apostolic Church possesses within itself various languages, so that in the one body of the one universal Church “every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II, 11). What, then, are the words that have reached the ends of the earth? They are the words of the saints, speaking as follows:

**VERSE 6.** “In the sun he placed his tabernacle”: through the mystery of the Incarnation, by assuming the tabernacle of flesh. And he himself, “like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber,” was born of a virgin. Afterwards, “he rejoiced as a giant to run his course,” completing in thirty-three years the course of his obedience; when this was fulfilled through his Passion [Col. 0904A], he rose from death and ascended into heaven, whence he had come, “because his going forth is from the height of heaven unto its height.” From there he shall come to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire; “and there is none that can hide itself from his heat.” These are the words heard throughout the world; this is the Gospel proclaimed in every language.

But let us hear more attentively those things which have been briefly sketched. Let us hear the apostles, like soldiers of the highest king, proclaiming the coming and preaching the victory of their king, who is about to fight against the devil. For they say: Our King Christ, coming to fight for us, “placed his tabernacle in the sun,” because he placed the tabernacle of assumed flesh in the sun—that is, in the Virgin Mary. She is not inappropriately called the sun, because she alone among women shines with a singular blessing: neither has one like her been seen before, nor shall she have a successor; just as this material sun is so called because it alone appears to shine. Although she is called the star of the sea, yet, by conceiving and bearing within herself the Sun of righteousness, she is worthy also of the name of sun. Thus, rightly proclaiming her most worthy of all praise, we say in her veneration: “Who is this that ascends like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun?” (Cant. VI, 9).

In this sun he placed his tabernacle, because God himself—the Word of God, God’s eternal wisdom, the brightness of the Father’s glory—who on the fourth day long ago gathered and united the ethereal fire, widely diffused, into the solar body [Col. 0904C], whence it might send its rays throughout the whole world as from a fountain, likewise as it were contracted himself, the divine and immeasurable fire, into a human, maternal, or proper body taken from the Virgin Mother. Since in this body “all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily,” just as the fullness of ethereal fire remains in the solar body, certainly his divine body is a solar body. In it, as in the sun, the eternal fire himself placed his tabernacle: that is, he made such a body his tabernacle.

He also placed his tabernacle in the sun in this manner: he did not light the lamp of flesh in order to put it in concealment, but upon a lampstand—in the sun, that is, openly. For he wished the military dwelling-place of the Godhead to be seen by all [Col. 0904D], though previously it secretly “was in the world, and the world knew it not” (John I, 10). But he placed his tabernacle in the sun, that is, openly, so that, while fighting against the devil, it might be a great spectacle to angels and human beings allied on opposite sides. And therefore, once his tabernacle had been prepared, he did not wish to remain hidden within, but came forth in public. How? “Like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber.”

“Like,” in this passage, signifies not so much likeness as reality, as in: “And I saw a lamb as though slain” (Apoc. V, 6), and, “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten of the Father” (John I, 14). “As,” which is an adverb of likeness, here signifies reality, because he is truly the only-begotten of the Father. Likewise, he truly came forth as a bridegroom from his mother. By the word declaring his coming forth, all who hear are invited to a spectacle, because a procession is customarily so called when some venerable and impressive person, with a long train of people preceding and following, goes reverently and fittingly, dressed according to the dignity of his rank—for example, in pontifical or royal ornaments—from one place to another, while many venerate and observe such a procession. But if a bridegroom, beautiful in form beyond many men, came forth from his chamber and publicly showed himself in the very solemnity of the marriage, bringing with him a very beautiful bride, what a cry of rejoicing and sound of feasting crowds, do you suppose, would applaud him? [Col. 0905B]

Thus indeed the Son of God, “fair and beautiful,” whose “bed was flourishing” (Cant. I, 15)—the womb of the Virgin—came forth from that very womb, from that very flowering bed, as from his chamber, while the seal of chastity remained closed. Like a bridegroom he came forth from his chamber: God incarnate came out from the incorrupt womb of the Virgin in order to unite the Church to himself. He had, as it were, taken this beautiful bride by the hand through the flesh which God himself, the Word of God, united to himself in his own chamber, where he kissed her with the kiss of his mouth, fulfilling her desire, whereby this bride had said: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Cant. I, 1). A long procession of the bridegroom’s attendants—namely, the patriarchs and prophets—preceded this procession of the bridegroom; and a long procession of the friends of the bridegroom follows [Col. 0905C], who stand, hear, and rejoice because of the bridegroom’s voice (John III, 29). From all these the Church itself, called the bride, consists. Therefore, when this bridegroom thus came forth, “with the voice of rejoicing and confession, the sound of one feasting” (Ps. XLI, 5) was heard from the angelic multitude. For when one angel announced this very procession to the shepherds, “suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host,” an army “praising and saying: Glory to God in the highest” (Luke II, 13). And so that good human beings might share a common rejoicing with the angels, this was added: “And on earth peace to men of good will” (ibid., XIV [an apparent citation error for II, 14]).

What followed? Amid so great a joy of rejoicing angels and human beings [Col. 0905D], the bridegroom himself also “rejoiced as a giant to run his course.” For immediately on the very night of his Nativity he ran by means of the sign of the star, which appeared soon after his birth. He ran, I say, even to the furthest regions of the earth, making the Magi dwelling in the East believe that the king of the Jews had been born; and thus was fulfilled the prophecy which Balaam, their own prophet, had long ago foretold: “A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel, and he shall crush all the princes of Moab, and Idumea shall be his possession” (Num. XXIV, 17–18). Therefore the Magi run with gifts to the royal wedding. “Herod the king was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him” (Matt. II, 3). When he raged against the infants, this giant, by running into Egypt and then running back after Herod’s death, prefigured his course: leaving the Jewish people for a time, he was to run into the Egypt of this whole world, and finally return to the remnant of the Jews after Herod’s death—that is, after the death of Antichrist [Col. 0906A].

Many who run in the course of temporal life do not know whence they come or where they are going; therefore they run with weariness and sorrow, because they do not know the end of their course (Eccl. IX, 12). But this bridegroom, full of love; this giant, full of strength; full of grace and truth—namely, the grace of love and the truth of strength—knowing that he came forth from God and goes to God, not at all uncertain whence he had come or where he was going, was neither sorrowful nor disturbed. Rather, he rejoiced to run his course: the way of temporal dispensation, the way of obedience, which he ran as a giant—strong, untroubled, unturning, unconquerable through the power of his divinity. For he is a giant of twofold substance: though he died through the voluntary weakness of his humanity, yet he rose and lives through his divinity. And although for an hour his “soul was sorrowful unto death” (Matt. XXVI, 38), nevertheless in his spirit he rejoiced to run his course to that place whence he had come. For:

**VERSE 7.** “His going forth was from the height of heaven”—that is, from the Father, God Most High—when he came forth from the Father [Col. 0906C] and entered the world; and “his meeting is unto its height,” when he again left the world and went to the Father. Therefore, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, he rightly prayed, saying: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was” (John XVII, 5). The angels and human beings whom the Father glorified in the Son, he glorifies beneath himself. But his Son, always glorious in the form of divinity, yet in the form of a servant possessing neither form nor beauty in his Passion, the Father so glorified with the glory of Resurrection and Ascension that he is now, not beneath him, but with him: not only glorious in divinity, but also glorified in assumed humanity with that same glory which the Word had before the world was [Col. 0906D], with him rather than beneath him. For the glory of assumed humanity is no longer less than that of the assuming Word with the Father; indeed, it is altogether the same. Moreover, this giant, though now of twofold substance, while the essential distinction between the assuming and assumed natures remains in him, is nevertheless of one and undivided glory with the Father Most High, because “his return is unto its height.” For he obtained most fully for his humanity also the supreme glory which he always possessed in divinity, not beneath the Father but with the Father.

> [Note: [Col. 0905] A different hand, perhaps somewhat later, adds: namely, to the assumed man.]

Accordingly the Church faithfully hymns him, saying [Col. 0907A]:

> His going forth from the Father,  
> His return to the Father,  
> His course even to hell,  
> His return to the throne of God.

The throne of God is not to be understood as corporeal or visible, but as the invisible power of judging and reigning, in which the human being made God has been made equal to God the Father. Thus the human being is believed to sit with God—that is, to reign with him—at the right hand of the throne of majesty, with the honor of undivided power and equality. To signify this, his return to the Father is called a meeting, because those who are equal commonly meet one another while preserving mutual equality of honor.

What do you say to these things, ancient serpent, envious one, greatly envying the glory of the Son of God? Through the heretic Arius you blasphemed, denying that he is equal to the Father [Col. 0907B], even in divinity. Learn now through Hilary, a wholly Catholic man—whose words I shall set before you—that the Son is equal to the Father also in his now glorified humanity. If you were tortured by the torment of envy when the Son was proclaimed equal to the Father in his eternal divinity, envy now bites you far more deeply when this same Son is proclaimed equal to the Most High Father in his now glorified humanity. Though for a time he was made lower than the angels, he is now set above the “angels, being made so much better than they, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they” (Heb. I, 4).

Hear then, wicked dragon, the source of your torment; hear clear testimonies magnifying the glory of the Son of Man, which you diminish through heretics. Hear, I say [Col. 0907C], Hilary, taught not by flesh and blood but by the Father who is in heaven, speaking in Book IX of *On the Holy Trinity* upon these words:

> “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him. If God has been glorified in him, God has also glorified him in himself, and God has immediately glorified him.” I consider, I say, the first meaning of the Lord’s saying to be unambiguous, when he says: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified.” For all glory was acquired not for the Word but for the flesh—that is, not for the nature  
> 
> [Note: [Col. 0907D] Edition: not for the Nativity of God.]  
> 
> of God, but for the dispensation of the man who was born. But I ask what the following means: “And God has been glorified in him.” For I hear that God has been glorified in him, and I do not know, heretic, what you understand this to mean.

God was glorified in him, namely in the Son of Man.

> “And I ask whether the Son of Man is the same as the Son of God. And since the Son of Man is not one thing, nor the Son of God another”  
> 
> [Note: [Col. 0907D] Edition: “another person.”]  
> 
> (for “the Word was made flesh,” John I, 14), “and since he who is Son of God is also Son of Man, I ask: who is the God glorified in this Son of Man, who is also the Son of God? And since God has been glorified in the Son of Man, who is also the Son of God, let us see what this third statement added means: ‘If God has been glorified in him, God has also glorified him in himself.’ What mystery of sacrament, I ask, is this? In the glorified Son of Man, God glorifies in himself God who has been glorified. In the Son of Man is the glory of God, and the glory of God  
> 
> [Note: [Col. 0907D] Edition: “and the glory of God in the glory of the Son.”]  
> 
> is the glory of the Son of Man. God glorifies in himself; the man is certainly not glorified through himself. Nor again, though God who is glorified in the human being receives glory, he is nevertheless nothing other than God. But when, with the Son of Man glorified, God glorifying God glorifies in himself, I find the glory of a nature assumed into the glory of the nature that glorifies nature. For God does not glorify himself, but glorifies in himself God glorified  
> 
> [Note: [Col. 0907D] Edition: “but he glorifies in himself God glorified in the human being” [Col. 0908D].]  
> 
> in man. And what he glorifies in himself, although he does not glorify himself, nevertheless assumes into the glory of his own nature  
> 
> [Note: [Col. 0908D] Edition: “nevertheless, glorifying nature, he assumes the glory of the glorified into the glory of his own nature.”]  
> 
> the glory of the glorified. And when God, glorifying God, because he has been glorified in man, glorifies in himself him whom he glorified [Col. 0908B], he shows that the God whom he has glorified is in himself when he glorifies him in himself.”

The same writer says in Book III:

> “But now what is it that he awaits in glorification with the Father? Surely that which he had with him before the world was. He had the fullness of divinity, and he has it; for he is the Son of God. But he who was the Son of God had also begun to be the Son of Man. For the Word had been made flesh. He had not lost what he was, but had begun to be what he was not. He had not ceased to possess what was his own, but had received what is ours. What he received demands the increase of that glory from which he did not depart.”

The same writer says in Book IX:

> “The Father, who is to glorify the Son, is greater; the Son, glorified in the Father, is not lesser. Or how is he lesser who is in the glory of God the Father? Or is the Father not greater? The Father is indeed greater insofar as he is Father; but the Son, insofar as he is Son, is not lesser. The Son’s birth constitutes the Father as greater; but the nature of that birth does not permit the Son to be lesser. The Father is greater when he is asked to restore glory to the assumed man; the Son is not lesser when he resumes glory with the Father.”

Likewise Pope Leo the Great, in his sermon on the Passion of the Lord:

> “Thus God united humanity to himself, so that nothing human was lacking to him who assumed, and nothing divine was lacking to that which was assumed.”

Likewise, in his sermon on the Ascension of the Lord:

> “After the Passion, the bonds of death having been broken—bonds which had lost their power by being exerted against him who knew no sin—weakness passed into strength, mortality into eternity, and dishonor into glory. The Lord Jesus Christ, by many plain proofs, showed this glory to the sight of many, until he brought into heaven the triumph of the victory which he had won from the dead.”

Likewise Ambrose, on Luke:

> “Although the other apostles know, Peter nevertheless answers before the rest: ‘You are Christ, the Son of the living God’ (Matt. XVI, 61 [an apparent citation error for 16]). He embraced everything, for he expressed both the nature and the name, in which lies the sum of virtues.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Peter knew that all things are in the Son of God; for the Father gave all things to the Son. If he gave all things, he gave the eternity which he possesses, and poured forth majesty.”

Thus the testimonies of truth, like sharp javelins, pierce you, Arius. Although you lie buried in hell and behold, you stink, we still endure the remnants of your stench in new heretics who detract from Christ’s glory, as if he were not whole but only half in the glory of God the Father—he who is wholly the Son of God the Father. If, as the heretic Bonosus blasphemed, the assumed man were a son by adoption and only the assuming Word were the natural Son, Christ might appear to be differently Son and to possess a different glory with the Father. But now, since whole Christ is the Son of God—not adopted but begotten—it consequently follows, and, though it cannot be comprehended, is rightly believed, that whole Christ is in the glory of God the Father, whose natural Son he is. For the Father not only eternally begot him before the ages, but also, at the end of the ages, uttering his own Word into the Virgin’s heart and, by his love—that is, his Spirit—making her womb fruitful, made her the mother of that same Son of whom he himself is Father, and who is his whole, not half, Son. Therefore rightly may every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus himself is wholly in the glory of God the Father [Col. 0909B]. He now sits with the Father on the throne of grace and mercy; hereafter he will sit on the judicial throne of majesty. Now he is ready to forgive, like a mitred priest; then he will be ready to judge, like a crowned king.

“And there is none that can hide itself from his heat.” For now, sitting upon the throne of grace, he has sent fire into the earth [Col. 0909C], which he strongly wills to be kindled. For while the apostles were praying with the women and the mother of Jesus, and were coming boldly to the throne of grace, that they might find grace and obtain mercy for timely aid, “there came suddenly from heaven a sound of a mighty rushing spirit; and it filled all the house where they were sitting, and tongues divided as if of fire appeared to them” (Acts II, 2–3). And none can hide from the heat of this fire. For as fire that burns a forest, and as a flame consuming mountains, so this fire, once sent into the forest of the human race, burns that forest on the side where the soil of this forest is good, and reduces it to woodland clearings; but where the soil is bad, it leaves the same forest for beasts to inhabit [Col. 0909D], so that it may contain dragons’ dens and wild beasts’ hiding places, and foxes may have holes there and birds of heaven their nests. Thus the world, set in evil, is filled with living and wicked spirits, and at last will burn with the devil himself and his angels. This same fire will burn the envious minds of evil angels and human beings, while the saints will burn like lamps—indeed, then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.

This will be a great torment to their envious enemies. Since they would not here burn through love of righteousness, when the righteous then shine in glory they will burn through the torment of envy, which from that time onward shall never be softened for them. For as the fire of divine love, perfectly kindled in the elect in this life, will endure eternally, so, while the saints shine through true knowledge and burn through true wisdom [Col. 0910A]—when night declares knowledge to night and day pours forth wisdom to day—the flame of the reprobate’s envy, stirred up in this life, if it has not been extinguished by repentance before death, will burn without end. For the same fire which melts the saints like gold makes the ungodly harden like clay.

“And there is none that can hide from his heat”: none but must burn, either by loving the good or by envying the good. Yet the heat of both burnings begins in this life and is consummated in the life to come. For of the good it is said: Thus says the Lord, “whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. XXXI, 9). By the fire in Zion is indicated the small and incipient love of the pilgrim Church. By the furnace in Jerusalem is indicated the perfected fire of that same love [Col. 0910B]. It is compared to a burning furnace, within which nothing cold and nothing lukewarm is found, but fire alone rules there, and whatever is cast into it is changed into fire.

Conversely, of the ungodly it is said: “You shall make them as a fiery furnace in the time of your countenance” (Ps. XX, 10). For those in whom love of evil and hatred of good have begun to burn in this life, while the fire of the Holy Spirit shines for some unto good and for others unto evil, will indeed, once dead, burn like blazing firebrands. But at the resurrection, when they have resumed their bodies, God will make them like a fiery furnace in the time of his countenance. At that time the saints also will be like a furnace of fire, when Christ’s love has been perfected in them—Christ who sent the fire of this love into the earth, and none can hide from his heat.

For just as Christ, “the true light,” “enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I, 9), shining even in darkness, although the dark minds of the ungodly do not comprehend it, so the same Christ, being the brightness of glory, by which those who hope in him shall be glorified and shall glory in him, touches by his heat every person coming into this world. He even summons the cold minds of the ungodly to his love, and none can hide from his heat, “for this sun of righteousness rises upon the good and the evil” (Matt. V, 45). But as darkness does not comprehend him shining in darkness, because it repels from itself the light of truth, so the impious minds themselves do not receive him as he warms kindly disposed minds with love of himself [Col. 0910D] and extends the rays of love even to impious minds. Yet to all who receive him, he gives power to become children of God (John I, 12): to those who believe in his name, receiving and keeping his law written by the finger of God and proclaimed by the Holy Spirit. For this reason the Spirit appeared in tongues of fire: he came to expound the law written by that finger of God, working in the apostles so that they might be competent ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the spirit. For the killing letter was like a stained law; but the life-giving Spirit is truly:

**VERSE 8.** “The law of the Lord, undefiled,” because he makes those who receive him undefiled from being stained. The killing letter was burdensome and oppressive to souls, displaying the commandment through which sin revived and increased in strength, while every pupil of the law strove toward what was forbidden. But the life-giving Spirit—that is, the one who makes good things not only known but loved and done—is himself the sweet law of the Lord, converting souls formerly perverse. When love is poured into them by the Holy Spirit, everything that had been perverse in them is turned toward good; water becomes wine, when a mind formerly cold and tasteless, receiving, as it were, the heat and flavor of wine in the stone water-jar of the heart, is so transformed that it is praised by the master of the feast—that is, by the Holy Spirit—and the bridegroom who comes forth from his chamber and celebrates the wedding rejoices and glories in such wine, because good wine is served even at the end of the wedding banquet.

[Col. 0911B] The killing letter was the testimony of the Lord, but not altogether faithful. Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel: “And I gave them commandments that were not good” (Ezek. XX, 25). Certainly, on the tablets of stone there were good commandments, commending love of God and neighbor; but after the guilt of the calf which they had worshipped, commandments that were not good were added to them: many ceremonies and the heavy yoke of diverse observances, “which,” as the apostle Peter says, “neither we nor our fathers were able to bear” (Acts XV, 10). Hence it was not a testimony faithful in every respect, because it contained not only good commandments but also commandments that were not good.

But the law of the life-giving Spirit is the faithful testimony of the Lord [Col. 0911C], because it commands absolutely nothing except what it helps and profits one to keep. Or, in this respect the old law was not a faithful testimony: it promised its observers goods that were unstable and perishable. But the new law, given through the Holy Spirit, is the faithful testimony of the Lord, because it promises its observers eternal goods, enduring forever, faithfully preserved in heaven, where unfaithful thieves cannot take them away, being driven from there by the faithful word of the Lord. The same covenant is called both law and testimony: law insofar as it commands something to be done or not done; testimony insofar as it promises a reward to the one who keeps the commandment, or threatens punishment to the one who does not keep the precept. Thus the New Testament is in this respect the undefiled law of the Lord, because it commands only what is wholesome; and in this respect the New Testament is called the faithful testimony of the Lord, because the reward it promises is eternal. Therefore it is rightly said: “The testimony of the Lord is faithful.”

“Giving wisdom to little ones,” because the promise of eternal goods does not taste sweet to the proud and great in this world, but only to little ones—that is, the humble—whom the Holy Spirit judges worthy of the savor of eternal and future goods. For “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. IV, 6). And in this, that the proud are rejected and the humble admitted to the wisdom and savor of eternal goods, which God has hidden from the wise and prudent while revealing them to little ones:

**VERSE 9.** “The righteousnesses of the Lord are right, making glad [Col. 0912A] the heart.” They are right in respect of the rejection of the proud; they make glad in respect of the reception of little ones. And lest anyone be able to excuse himself through ignorance if, through the Lord’s right judgments, he is saddened in his pride rather than made glad in humility: “the commandment of the Lord enlightens the eyes.” For Moses did not act as Christ, the giver of the new law, acted: Moses put a veil over his face when he gave an obscure commandment (Exod. XXXIV, 33); Christ, I say, spoke without figures and riddles: “This,” he says, “is my commandment, that you love one another” (John XV, 12). Again: “A new commandment I give you, that you love one another” (ibid., XIII, 34). Observance of this clear commandment makes people little, because “love is not puffed up”; it gladdens hearts, because “love is not provoked [Col. 0912B] and rejoices with truth”; it enlightens eyes through right faith and firm hope, because “love believes all things, hopes all things” (I Cor. XIII, 4–5 ff.). And though that clear commandment of the Lord, which clearly commends love, casts out slavish fear through love itself, yet there will be an inseparable companion of that same love:

**VERSES 10 AND 11.** “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever.” For slavish fear, which involves punishment because it fears punishment, will entirely fail when love has been perfected. But filial fear, by which one does not fear the infliction of punishment but the lessening or complete withdrawal of grace already bestowed, will, once grace is perfected and confirmed, be without punishment. Thus, if one may speak so, there will be fear without fear, enduring for ever and ever in complete and supreme security and sweetness, joined to enduring love, which abides in God eternally; for once rooted and firmly founded, it never falls away. Therefore chaste fear joined to it abides eternally.

Worldly fear makes people fearful and unjust; but the holy fear of the Lord makes a human being God-fearing and just, as the old man Simeon is said to have been “a just and God-fearing man” (Luke II, 25). Therefore the judgments of the Lord are true to the just and God-fearing, whereas they sometimes please and sometimes displease the wicked, as though not all were true. To those made God-fearing and justified by holy fear, these judgments please in every respect, because the Lord’s judgments themselves are true: whether he spares or punishes; whether he spares good people or evil; whether he punishes good people or evil; whether “he hardens whom he wills” (Rom. IX, 18); or whether, as he wills, he has mercy on whom he has mercy, as Moses says: “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will be gracious to whom it pleases me” (Exod. XXXIII, 19). All these and similar judgments may indeed be hidden, but they cannot be unjust, though they sometimes appear unjust to the unjust. But to those whom the holy fear of the Lord has filled, and whom the clear commandment of the Lord enlightening the eyes enlightens, the judgments of the Lord are true, reasonable, and praiseworthy—justified in themselves, or, as the Hebrew has it, “in themselves,” because they need no external authorities or testimonies to justify them, possessing in themselves the ground and power of justice [Col. 0913A]. Hence a certain versifier says, no less ecclesiastically than scholastically:

> Whatever human beings do in the world, God orders alike.  
> Saul, Job, Paul, the man born blind, Herod:  
> He corrects Saul, tests Job, helps Paul, raises the man born blind, kills Herod.

To these same just and God-fearing people, the Lord’s judgments, because of the truth and justice contained in them, are dear and:

**VERSE 11.** “More desirable than much gold and precious stone.” Truly, they are much more desirable than much gold and than very precious stone. They are more desirable, I say, than much gold and precious stone: that is, beyond every lust of the eyes, beyond everything beautiful to sight [Col. 0913B], beyond all things pleasing to bodily vision. These are all signified by a part, namely by much gold and precious stone, which among the things desired by the eyes are more precious and beautiful than the rest. Above all these things, the Lord’s judgments are more precious and more beautiful.

“And sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.” Since, as John says, “everything that is in the world” is either “the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, or the pride of life” (I John II, 16), that is, worldly ambition. Among all these there is such a contrary opposition that things which delight eyes serving and fixed upon worldly curiosity—for example, beautiful and rare colors—do not at all delight taste, smell, and touch, the three senses serving the lust of the flesh; nor hearing, which alone among the five senses serves vain glory, the pride of life. Again, the sweetness of tasting, such as is found in honey and the honeycomb; the pleasantness of smelling, such as is found in the bed of a prostitute who has sprinkled her couch with myrrh and aloes; and the pleasure of touching, such as is found in the shameful act of fornication—these do not delight sight or hearing. Nature itself has separated the latter from such things, since no one can see or hear what sweetness belongs to taste in eating, what pleasantness belongs to smell in smelling, or what pleasure belongs to touch in fornication. The shameless eye is indeed the messenger of a shameless heart and the forerunner of shameless touch, but it is nevertheless altogether alien from the pleasure of touching itself. And truly, through shamelessness of sight chastity itself flees from one’s character [Col. 0913D], even if bodies remain untouched by impure violation, unless one guards against the shameless fixation of the eyes; yet the pleasure of the impure violation itself lies not in seeing but in touching.

Likewise, the favor of popular applause, pleasant only to itching ears, when someone is praised or has already been preferred—or is yet to be preferred—above others in some high ecclesiastical or worldly dignity, merely caresses the hearing. The other senses—sight, taste, smell, and touch—feel in that which delights hearing neither usefulness nor pleasantness.
