But the Lord’s true judgments, justified in themselves, are so much more desirable than all beautiful and precious things in this world that they are at once sweeter than all sweet things in this world and worthier than all the world’s dignities. By honey and honeycomb, with a part taken for the whole, is understood everything pleasant to the lust of the flesh; just as by gold and precious stone is understood everything belonging to the lust of the eyes. This figure is called synecdoche, when a part is used for the whole. That these judgments themselves are desirable and sweet, and worthier than the dignities of this world, is inferred from the fact that in keeping them there is “great reward,” or, as the Hebrew reads: “much fruit.”

In guarding gold and precious stones there is no profit, because he who guards and loves riches will derive no profit from them: anxiously guarding them as a servant, not generously distributing them as a master, he remains devoid of their benefit, however full he may be of riches. Rebuking certain persons for the lust of the flesh, the Apostle says: “What fruit, then, did you have in those things of which you are now ashamed? (Rom. 6:21–22).” The implied answer is: none. And indeed those who love pleasure in such things until the end of this life have no fruit from them, but great loss. “For their end is death. But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have,” he says, “your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (ibid.). In dignities sought ambitiously from God there is no profit; thus every ambitious man, like an unfruitful branch, unless cleansed by repentance, is to be cut off and cast into the fire.

[Col. 0914C] But since all things—beautiful, sweet, or glorious—which nourish the lust of the eyes, the lust of the flesh, and worldly ambition are unfruitful where, in acquiring or retaining them, the true judgments of the Lord, justified in themselves, are despised: if the true judgments of the Lord are kept, then, through those true judgments of the Lord, either their use becomes altogether fruitful, as regards the imperfect; or their contempt, as regards the perfect; or both their use and their contempt together, as regards the most perfect—these things being preferred to everything beautiful, sweet, and glorious.

For it belongs to an imperfect and not very good person, by keeping the judgments of the Lord, to use riches in generously giving alms to Christ’s poor. It is the perfection of a very good person, through keeping those same judgments, to despise riches and become poor for Christ. The former, using riches, gladly builds a temple for the Lord; the latter, despising riches, becomes a temple of the Lord. The former, restraining the lust of the flesh from fornication but allowing it scope in the begetting of children, multiplies the heirs of his estate; but the latter, wholly mortifying desire within himself, becomes indeed an heir of God and a co-heir of Christ. The former, using temporal goods, makes for himself “friends from the mammon of unrighteousness, who may receive” him “into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9); the latter, despising temporal things and with all longing desiring eternal things, becomes one who not only possesses eternal dwellings but is also able to receive others into them.

The former, through lawful marriage, begets children of the flesh, doing well in this if he devotes them to divine service. The latter, doing better, by begetting children in Christ Jesus through the Gospel, labors to bring them to birth until Christ is formed in them. [Col. 0915A] The former, by keeping the judgments of the Lord, is a most compassionate comforter of the holy poor; the latter, by keeping those same judgments, is a most ardent lover of holy poverty. The former, worthily administering dignities through keeping the judgments of the Lord, becomes a servant of the servants of God, being worthily set over others because he is worthy. The latter is likewise worthy of dignity, yet willingly lacks every passing dignity in this life for the sake of keeping the judgments of the Lord, which are harder to fulfill among prelates than among subjects, because “to whom more is entrusted, more is required”; or because he is among those “of whom the world is not worthy.” Therefore he willingly lacks dignity in this world, being one whom a worthy prelate is not worthy to govern.

And therefore, whenever the pronouncements of the judgments of the Lord direct it, let one who is worthy willingly lack dignity, because he does not consider himself worthy. By gladly lacking that dignity, he becomes worthier than one who gladly presides over others in dignity; for this very thing makes the latter unworthy if, in order to be set over others, he gave his assent voluntarily and all too readily. For this is the doctrine of the orthodox Fathers: one strong in virtues should come forward under compulsion, while one lacking virtues should not consent to be promoted even under compulsion—especially to a dignity that promises temporal advantage.

For if the temporal disadvantages of persecutions troubled the Church and, in order to avoid such disadvantages, all good persons fled the office [Col. 0915C] of prelacy, then certainly, if someone assured in the Holy Spirit of a martyr’s crown desired the episcopate, wishing in a perilous time to bear before the rest the banner of faith, that man, in desiring the episcopate, would desire a good work. But because it happens to few in this life that they can, truly understanding the true judgments of the Lord as applying to themselves, say with the Apostle Paul: “I am certain that neither death nor life, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God” (Rom. 8:38–39), it remains that those who have dignities in this world should be as though not having them—companions of the good through humility, set over the evil through authority (2 Cor. 6:10); and that those who do not have them should never love to have them in this world, but should love Christ with the Apostle Peter, should love themselves for loving him and for being loved by him. Those who perfectly love Christ, if he commands them to feed his lambs and sheep, should know that an office of service, not of domination, has been imposed upon them, so that they may be servants of the servants of God.

Yet through this service a greater perfection accrues to the perfect, if, while worthily performing the ministry of dignity, they at once retain both contempt for that dignity in their heart and its ministry in their work: set over their subjects in honor before men, but laid beneath their feet in fear before God. The prelate will finally attain this summit of most perfect perfection when he considers himself blessed, not by a power of ruling, but by willingly embracing the happy discipline of serving in charity; imposing fear, [Col. 0916A] yet desiring more to be loved than feared by his disciples. Both, however, are necessary because of the differing dispositions of disciples: some are unruly and some faint-hearted. He should correct the unruly through fear, comfort the faint-hearted through love, and be patient toward all.

By administering dignity in this way until the end, one who came to it worthily and worthily will have become still worthier in that dignity, and will be taken from the present laborious ministry of dignity into the repose of eternal dignity, the Lord saying to him: “Well done, good and faithful servant: because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:23).

But he also will not be deprived of the fullness of this joy [Col. 0916B] who, though worthy of dignity through the true judgments of the Lord justified in themselves, remains in a humble place in this life—whether under a worthy or an unworthy prelate—remaining worthy in himself, yet willingly lacking dignity, provided that he has aided with his tireless prayers the office of dignity which he did not visibly administer.

There were two perfect men, Moses and Joshua. But when war with the Amalekites was impending, Joshua was sent to battle, while Moses prayed on the mountain. And a great miracle took place: when Moses raised his hands in prayer, Joshua prevailed (Exod. 17:11); when he let them fall from prayer, victory in turn went to the Amalekites. This alternation continued until Moses, without letting fall his raised hands in prayer, prayed perseveringly. Thus, Amalek defeated, Israel triumphed: Moses praying, Joshua fighting. To which of the two, do you suppose, ought this victory to be attributed more? Certainly Joshua labored more physically, since a stone placed beneath Moses supported him as he sat, and Aaron and Hur, lifting the arms of Moses as he prayed, did not allow him to become grievously weary. Joshua, however, standing in the perilous contest of battle, endured great bodily toil. Nevertheless, because he possessed no power to conquer except insofar as he was aided by Moses’ prayer, without doubt in this undertaking either the fruit was equal for both, or indeed the greater fruit belonged to Moses, who supplied strength by praying to the man who fought.

Likewise, now in the Church there are two perfect men. One, elected to the episcopate, is assigned, as it were, to battle; [Col. 0916D] the other is left in private life, living for himself and being free for God, content with disciples or companions alone. Like Aaron and Hur, these do not hinder him from prayer but rather make him readier for it; Christ, the stone upon whom he rests with Moses, supports him, while with Jacob he sleeps with his head—that is, his mind—laid upon that same stone. Let the one labor bravely in the ministry of dignity imposed upon him, and let the other pray earnestly for the one who labors. Thus, with both acting—or rather, with one acting and the other being at leisure—through the labor of one and the prayer of the other, may the word of God run strongly and may the cause attain victory through the zeal of two. Will not each of them at the end hear the Lord say to him: “Well done, good and faithful servant,” etc. (Matt. 25:23)?

You hear that goodness and faithfulness are rewarded, while labor is not even mentioned. What then, you say, is meant by the Apostle’s words: “Each shall receive his own reward according to his labor” (1 Cor. 3:8)? To this I say: should one not consider, in the person who prays for one who labors, that he makes the laborer’s labor his own through the goodness and faithfulness by which he aids the laborer with his prayers? Therefore he hears, “Well done, good and faithful servant.” Therefore, as a good and faithful servant, while guarding “five talents” (Matt. 25:15) through the sanctification of his own five senses, and gaining five others by praying for others, he will also receive in addition that talent which will be taken from the slothful and wicked servant, when an unworthy prelate is deprived—through the true judgments of the Lord justified in themselves—of the very dignity by which he had been unworthily honored, although his subjects were worthy. [Col. 0917B]

For the true judgments of the Lord require this: that a good disciple who had a bad prelate, and who, continuing good, prayed for that bad man to become good, and did all that lay in his power, should not have his prelate’s negligence imputed to him in any degree. These true judgments, I say, require that from such a prelate, like a slothful and wicked servant, the talent of the dignity conferred upon him be taken away in the final trial and given to this man who has multiplied his five talents—namely, by living holily himself and striving that others may live holily, whether fighting in preaching with Joshua or being at leisure and praying with Moses on the mountain.

For just as the energetic [Col. 0917C] preacher, so also the energetic man of prayer, doubles and multiplies the talent entrusted to him. Neither is to be preferred to the other according to a difference of labor, but according to a difference of love and affection. This was greater in Moses praying than in Joshua fighting, as was shown by the evident outcome of the battle, whose victory depended not half, but wholly, upon Moses’ prayer. So even now it may happen that love and affection are greater in one secretly praying to God for the conversion of peoples than in one publicly preaching and laboring for the conversion of the same people. But if the affection of both is equal, both that prelate and that subject may hope for an equal fruit of their affection in reward.

The one is “the voice of thunder in the wheel” (Ps. 76:19), in the circuit of the world; the other is the voice of one crying in the wilderness [Col. 0917D] of the heart. Both, like Seraphim, praise God and cry one to another: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6:3). For *Seraphim* means “burning ones” or “those who set aflame.” Those burn in prayer who pray from affection or love for beloved prelates, from compassion for those same persons in tribulation, or indeed from pity, that evil prelates may be changed and the people delivered from their unjust rule and the perilous danger of bad prelacy. Those who thus pray from affection are burning Seraphim. But those are Seraphim who set aflame for whom it is not enough to burn inwardly in prayer unless they also set others aflame by preaching, exhorting, reproving, beseeching, rebuking “in season, out of season” (2 Tim. 4:2), according as place and time for hearing are granted them, whether a small or a great dignity is conferred upon them together with the name and office of priesthood. In exercising this office, they are rightly called angels, because it is written: “The lips of the priest shall preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7).

Yet all those must be reckoned under the name of angels who, placed in whatever rank or condition, strive to imitate the angelic life. Since angels neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matt. 22:30), all who cultivate continence, both women and men—or, what is most precious and wholly angelic, virginal chastity—will be honored with the title of angelic dignity, even if they never [Col. 0918B] obtain in this life the office of prelacy or priesthood. Hence it follows that many persons of the devout female sex will be more highly honored among the angels than many bishops, since they strive more than these to imitate the angelic life.

For the Virgin Mary deserved to be addressed familiarly by an angel because she strove to pursue the angelic life. And for this reason the Angel of Great Counsel chose her as his mother, because he beheld in her such humility as he had never found either among angels or among human beings—a humility that had not appeared to have an equal before it, nor would have one after it.

“Glory,” therefore, “to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14): for without the perilous title of dignity, without the care of prelacy that is full of danger, all people of good will can, through the true judgments of the Lord justified in themselves, attain fellowship with the angels and participation in the Seraphim, who are the highest angels—especially those who cultivate angelic chastity and humility. Their path is so much safer as it is freer from every entanglement of prelacy, which has often tripped up even eminent men, because one who walks on high falls easily. [Col. 0918C]

You therefore say to me: when the care of dignity is more dangerous, the person who administers it worthily is correspondingly more precious. It is true; but remember the example of Moses and Joshua; remember that battle in whose victory more was attributed to the one praying than to the one fighting. Then you will recognize that the worthy administrator of some dignity is helped by the prayers of others. Although he is prelate in honor before men, yet, if he is wise, if his heart is not exalted nor his eyes lifted up, in fear before God he lays himself beneath the feet of those by whose prayers and merit he believes—or knows—that, while sailing or suffering shipwreck, he has not fallen into the abyss of destruction.

Again you say to me: precisely because, when set on high, he thinks so humbly that he lays himself beneath even the least before God, he is great and deserves greater praise, so as to be like a hinge placed beneath a door, among those of whom it is said: “For the hinges of the earth are the Lord’s, and he has set the world upon them” (1 Sam. 2:8). I answer that it is indeed great humility not to think high things while on high, but to agree with the humble. Yet just as the humility of a man exalted and honored in this world is more praiseworthy, because it does not yield to the allurements of pride while charity is not puffed up, however much it is tempted by the windiness of honor and glory, so the charity toward God of a man neglected and despised in this world is more praiseworthy, while it is not provoked, however much he is crushed even by the trampling of utterly insignificant people.

The former’s humility is tested by honors, that it may be inflated, supposing that he has been raised to dignity because God knows him worthier than others. The latter’s charity is tested by contempt from men, that it may be provoked and indignantly resent being without dignities and honors, in which he sees many people more unworthy than himself exalted. As, therefore, it is praiseworthy in the former that charity is not puffed up, so it is praiseworthy in the latter [Col. 0919B] that charity is not provoked. Praiseworthy is the former’s humility, immovable amid the many seductions of exaltation; praiseworthy is the latter’s charity, undisturbed amid the many provocations of contempt and rejection. It is little merely that the former is not puffed up by honors: rather, the more eagerly he is honored among men, the more he humbles himself before God, fearing that passing honors may hinder him from eternal ones. It is little merely that the latter is not provoked by contempt: rather, the more he is rejected and despised in this world, the more he glories in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom he understands both that the world is crucified to him and that he to the world, when he feels that he despises the world and is despised by it.

[Col. 0919C] These are the two Seraphim whom Isaiah, without prejudice to a more sacred interpretation, saw crying one to another, “Holy, holy, holy” (Isa. 6:3), because each glorifies the triune God in the other; each humbles himself in comparison with the other and considers the other superior; and through the one, in the other, the name of God is sanctified. These are the two Cherubim who look upon one another with faces turned toward the mercy-seat, because each attributes to divine propitiation what he perceives as venerable in the other. These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth, namely, keeping their allotted stations. Thus each says in Amos (Hab. 2:1): “I will stand upon my watch, and set my foot upon the fortification, and I will look to see what may be said to me, and what I may answer to him who reproves me.”

The one guards himself lest he be puffed up by honors; the other guards himself lest he be provoked by contempt. The former guards himself by humility in the rank of honor which he did not assume for himself: for no one such as these takes honor for himself, but only one called by God, as Aaron was. Thus Christ too did not glorify himself to become high priest, but he who spoke to him from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 17:5). The latter guards himself by charity in the low and humble place which he himself chose with the Psalmist, saying: “I have chosen to be cast down in the house of my God rather than dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 83:11). [Col. 0920A]

For in this lies a great difference between the two perfect persons: one is chosen to the elevated station of his watch; the other chose the watch of his station on level ground. For if the former, wishing through ambition, raised himself on high, or if the latter, unwilling and resentful, were cast down from on high to the plain while desiring a high place, the name of the perfect would not suit them. Rather, one would be a member of Antichrist, who exalts himself so as to sit in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God; the other would be a member of the devil, who, desiring to reign in heaven, lies cast down in hell because he refused. Antichrist glories that he is held high in this world; the devil resents being kept in hell. Therefore those who are puffed up through vain glory are members of Antichrist, and those who waste away through indignation and anger at their humiliation in this world are members of the devil.

Of the former it is written: “The vain man is lifted up in pride” (Job 11:12); of the latter it is written: “He will look to the right, and hunger; and to the left, and be angry; and he will curse his God and his king” (Isa. 9:20). Likewise of the former it is written: “A generation whose eyes are lofty, and whose eyelids are raised on high” (Prov. 30:13); of the latter it is written: “The sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and waste away” (Ps. 111:10): namely, when he sees himself despised in comparison with others, he will waste away from excessive anger. Sometimes he is angry even with God because he is oppressed too severely by poverty, sickness, or some other burden, and because, while unworthy persons occupy positions of dignity, he lies there as though he were nothing.

Yet for those proud on high and for those angry and wasting away below, there is one true and perfect medicine: let them strive to love and praise the true judgments of the Lord, justified in itself—that is, in themselves. For the translator has used the accusative in place of the ablative, as we gather from the Hebrew truth, where it reads thus:

> The fear of the Lord is clean, enduring for ages;  
> the judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves,  
> more desirable than gold and much precious stone,  
> and sweeter than honey and the overflowing honeycomb.

Clearly, by God’s grace, we are now tasting for a little while the overflowing sweetness in the divine judgments themselves, in this very exposition of those judgments. By chewing them over, we savor through divine mercy that the Lord must alike be loved and feared in all his judgments—by that fear, indeed, of which it is here said: “The fear of the Lord is clean, enduring for ages.” For this fear mingled with love, if it fills the human breast, kindles it through all divine judgments either to praise or to worship: to praise, when the judgments themselves are sweet to us; to worship, when they seem grievous.

In praise there ought to be thanksgiving for the freely given benefit of God’s judgments toward us; in prayer there ought to be supplication and observance, that the judgments of the Lord—true and justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and precious stone in themselves, and sweeter than overflowing honey and honeycomb in themselves—may be in us what they are in themselves. [Col. 0921A]

For it sometimes happens that things sweet in themselves are not sweet to others. For example: “The fathers ate sour grapes, and the teeth of the children,” who imitate their fathers, “were set on edge” (Ezek. 18:2). Thus bread, sweet in itself, did not taste sweet to teeth made bitter; nor was it sweet to those persons, although it remained sweet in itself. Christ, who is the living bread, possessing every delight and every taste in himself, did not possess this taste on the palate of the Jews. His delight was not pleasing to them because they were in their own sins and the sins of their parents, who had eaten sour grapes by transgressing the command through tasting the forbidden tree. The teeth of their children were set on edge, because, transgressing the natural or written law and doing forbidden things, they imitated those same fathers. Therefore bread sweet and pleasant in itself was distasteful to their teeth.

Daylight from the sun is in itself desirable and pleasant; yet it is hateful and painful to diseased eyes. Likewise, the judgments of the Lord—true and justified in themselves, more desirable in themselves than gold and precious stone, and sweeter in themselves than honey and honeycomb—are nevertheless neither true nor justified, neither desirable nor sweet, to hearts that are untrue, unjustified, most vile, and bitter, hearts to which God himself is not pleasing in his judgments. But “how good, O God of Israel, [are you] to those who are upright in heart!” [Col. 0921C] (Ps. 72:1). How pleasant is bread to a healthy palate! How pleasant and lovable is light to eyes healed of inflammation and blindness! “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden” in your judgments, which “you have perfected for those who hope in you!” (Ps. 30:20–21). Therefore let all who know and love your name “hope in you” (Ps. 9:11). Let them hope for the sweetness reserved for them in your judgments, which you have perfected for those who hope in you. Let us now chew over, if only a little, crumbs of these judgments, overflowing in their sweetness beyond honey and honeycomb.

If God gave everyone everything, acting without judgments, he would throw everything into confusion. For example, if he made all people equally rich in this world, no one would need another’s help; nor would riches be useful, since no one could do good by means of them and thereby obtain a reward for himself. Likewise, if all people were equally needy, no one could come to another’s aid; and this would be a wearisome confusion, because neither could the rich person delight in riches that he saw abundant to all, nor could the poor person be aided by anyone, since the magnitude of want would burden all equally.

But now, through the ineffable sweetness of God’s judgments, all things are well ordered: some are rich, others poor, so that the former, if they will, may be justified by works of mercy in comforting the poor, and the latter, if they will, may likewise be justified by patience in their misery, receiving consolation [Col. 0922A] solely from the mercy of the rich. If this is not shown them, they will have a fuller crown in the life to come, while the rich will bear inexcusable guilt and therefore most just punishment.

But you say to me: since God can justify me in either way, I would prefer to be justified through works of mercy rather than through patient endurance of misery. Does God seem perverse to you, being perverse yourself, so that he who knows all things does not attend to what is expedient for each person? “He who planted the ear, shall he not hear” what your intention cries out? “He who formed the eye, shall he not consider” (Ps. 93:9) what is more expedient for each person—whether that person is to become praiseworthy in good or inexcusable in evil? Certainly he knows the deceiver and the one deceived.

If you deceive yourself and suppose it healthy for you to abound in riches by which you may benefit others, he knows you better who has judged that through misery you must either be tested by patience or rejected through impatience. Does he not say: “He who is unjust in little things is unjust also in greater things” (Luke 16:10)? Yet he has left you something small, in which he may test your justice. For as a rich person has a coin that may perhaps be necessary to you, so you have a good word through which, by prayer, you may help the rich person. Be generous in what you have. For, as the Apostle Paul declares, “A ready will is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have” (2 Cor. 8:12).

Hence, if a woman refuses to do good from what she has, she falsely flatters herself that she would do good if she had [Col. 0922C] what she does not have. For true is that pronouncement of Truth: “He who is unfaithful in little things is unjust also in greater things.” Through the true judgments of the Lord this has been discovered in you: that, acting unjustly in little things, you would similarly act unjustly in greater things. Therefore he preferred that you act unjustly in a small matter rather than a great one, so that, sinning in small things, you may daily be cleansed in the furnace of poverty and be joined to that Lazarus who “received evil things in his lifetime,” because they were small evils (Luke 16:25).

For a person, confined in the stocks of infirmity and full of sores, could not commit, or at least intend, great evils. Yet he was not without small ones, for which he received recompense in this life, because they were so small that they could be cleansed by the hardships of the present life. But that rich man who did not give him crumbs received good things in his lifetime, because his good things were so slight that they could be repaid by temporal goods alone.

For the way of the rich is slippery and winding, so that, even if they sometimes wish to walk rightly, they cannot easily do so. The way of the poor is hard and narrow, constricted as though between two hedges. Hence those found “in the highways and hedges” are said to be “compelled” (Luke 14:24): constrained on one side by one hedge, called misery, because they are poor in themselves; on the other by the hedge called want, because they are raised up by no one’s aid. In this, therefore, the true judgments of the Lord are true, justified, desirable, and sweet in themselves: many are placed upon the dry and narrow path of poverty, but few upon the slippery and winding way of riches. [Col. 0923A]

Likewise, the way of prelacy is very steep, with a precipice on either side, to right and left: on the right through glory, on the left through ignobility; likewise on the left through infamy, on the right through good reputation. Many, being overly careful to avoid the precipice of glory and good reputation, have fallen into the muddy pit of ignobility and bad reputation. Others, on the contrary, being overly careful to avoid ignobility and bad reputation, have plunged into the ruin of vain glory through good reputation. To avoid danger on both sides is very difficult and belongs to very few.

But the way of subjection is level, defended on both sides by prelates—not only good and gentle ones, but also harsh ones. [Col. 0923B] The good and gentle stand on the right, that we may love them in Christ; the harsh stand on the left, that we may endure them for Christ’s sake—yet loving the good in such a way that we do not love whatever evils they may have, however tolerable; and enduring the evil in such a way that we do not so despise whatever good they may have, however slight, as not to love it among the many and great evils we hate in them.

Again, the way is level if, with love for people and hatred of vices, we so revere in them the offices of dignities and deeds appropriate to those offices that we avoid their opposites. And if we sin against them, while they rule and we bear their rule, we pay the penalty in this life; but for them there is very often reserved in the future the penalty for their unjust dealings toward their subjects. Therefore the true judgments of the Lord, justified in themselves, deserve praise because they place few upon the steep and perilous way of prelacy, but many upon the level path of subjection, defended on both sides.

Tell me then, you who quarrel with the condition of your station, who resent seeing others exalted and honored while you are despised—persons whom you know, or believe, to be lower and more unworthy than yourself. Tell me, I beg you: what would you wish to do if, with those persons rejected, you happened to rule over them? I know that you imagine yourself ruling either well or badly. If badly, give thanks to God that the occasion for ruling badly has been taken away from you. If well, I do not believe it unless you show it by faithfully acting in that small thing which you have received. Why should I believe that [Col. 0923D] you would act faithfully if you received much? If I see this proof, I judge you blessed in your small thing, even if you receive nothing great through which you might do greater good.

You say that you wish to preserve yourself more perfectly in prelacy: why, then, do you not preserve yourself in subjection? Do you not know that among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist arose, though he baptized only in water? But you, whatever sort of priest you are, are minister of a better baptism, which Christ gives through you—not in water alone, but in water and blood and the Holy Spirit. In a small office he became so great that among those born of women none was greater than he. Though he was the lawful heir of the legal priesthood, born of the course of Abijah, of priestly lineage, nevertheless, while the priesthood was then occupied under the wicked chief priests Annas and Caiaphas, he was as it were a common man in the wilderness, with no one drawing or choosing him for the priesthood due to him by merit and birth.

Thus you also, “if you wish to be perfect, sell what you have and give to the poor, and” follow Christ (Matt. 19:21), having in yourself “that which was also in Christ Jesus, who, although he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and being found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:5–7). He was not found crowned with gold or wearing the mitre of a high priest in the garb of dignity, but in simple clothing, as a human being. It is better for you to be found, following his example, in the garb of a simple person than, following Caiaphas’ example, in the garb of a high priest. [Col. 0924B]

If the summit of perfection delights you, travel toward it by this more level way, without the fetter of dignity, humbling yourself as Christ also humbled himself. Be good under evil judges as he was best under the worst judges. If you are unwilling to travel this level way toward the palm of perfection, you vainly claim for yourself fitness to run by the steep and rugged way of prelacy when you have not yet learned to walk on level ground. But blessed be the Lord, and blessed his true judgments justified in themselves: he does not leave us, while we seek high things, to ourselves, but has set before us on level ground a way to as great a perfection as is attained by those who run well upon steep paths.

There were two brothers, James and John. Both heard the Lord say: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” They say: “We can.” And he says: “You shall drink my cup” (Matt. 20:22–23), signifying his passion, in which each was to share. Yet neither is recorded as having passed to the kingdom through martyrdom, for Herod indeed “killed James, the brother of John, with the sword” (Acts 12:2), but John rested in peace. Where, then, did he drink the Lord’s cup? Certainly not by dying in the Passion, but by suffering with Christ as he died. For he stood beside the cross with the Lord’s mother. As a sword pierced the soul of the mother when her Son, who was God, died, so a sword is believed to have pierced the soul of the beloved and loving disciple when his beloved and loving master hung and died in his sight. [Col. 0924D]

If you, as a lover of perfection, delight in drinking the Lord’s cup, do not presume yourself fit for martyrdom with James, nor rashly expose yourself to a tyrant or to a cruel punishment of death, unless perhaps another girds you and leads you where you do not wish, God so ordaining. He can strengthen you amid torments and will undoubtedly give constancy to one who suffers for righteousness’ sake. But when no persecutor girds you, keep your heart ready for martyrdom, if the Lord should be pleased so to dispose of you. Nevertheless, stand beside the Lord’s cross with his mother and with John, so that, first being united with Christ through love and compassion, you may become fit for suffering.

If the Lord removes from you the cup of that passion, as he [Col. 0925A] removed it from John, your crown will not be diminished in any respect, because the affection of your love—proved by the effect of compassion—will be rewarded, since it was ready for the effect of suffering.

Likewise, if you, a lover of perfection, delight in being of use to many in a position of pre-eminence, do not presume yourself fit for such an office, nor rashly thrust yourself into so great a ministry—unless perhaps you are girded by another, where you do not wish to go, Christ so ordering it. He can strengthen you, once made a prelate, by his own ordering; and without doubt he will strengthen and preserve you for the benefit of many, if he approves your sincere humility and true devotion for preparing for the Lord a perfect people. But if neither clergy elect you, nor people seek you, nor a higher authority whom you ought not resist girds you, have indeed a heart ready [Col. 0925B] to serve the Lord in whatever ministry he may deign to assign. Yet you too stand beside the Lord’s cross, that you may first learn to be humbled before you desire to be exalted.

But if you have been perfectly humbled and are a pupil of charity, then, even if you never hold the mastership of pre-eminence, provided you remain a disciple of truth, when the Lord removes from you the cup of pre-eminence, you will have as great a crown for the disposition of love and humility proved in you as you would have had for the exercise of good pre-eminence—especially if, set upon the mountain of lofty conduct with Moses, you assist by prayer those who fight in the plain with Joshua; if, knowing that they are afflicted by the suffering of some tribulation, you join them through [Col. 0925C] compassion, weeping with those who weep, rejoicing with those who rejoice, thinking the same thing mutually, not aspiring to high things but consenting to the lowly.

But if, while living a private or poor life under authority or under the domination of the rich, the life of masters or rich persons seems for this reason more precious to you, and pre-eminence itself is therefore to be desired—because in it temptation is greater and the occasion for contest greater—and abundance of possessions is therefore to be sought—because abstinence amid abundance of possessions is more precious than poverty—you are greatly mistaken. You desire to sail against the current of the river, ungrateful to God, who is ready to help you, as one not aspiring to high things but seeking humbler ones, by directing your ship with the river’s current as far as the perfect dwelling-place of charity and humility. To this dwelling-place [Col. 0925D] one proceeds, if attempting to go against the river’s current, scarcely and with the greatest difficulty through riches and positions of pre-eminence, because of the great and innumerable temptations which, like foaming storms, have sunk many vessels of rich and honoured persons into the deep. Thus, through the excessive persistence of temptations, they came to despise the fact that they were stained by them; and this was for them to have fallen into the deep, because it is written: “When the sinner comes into the deep, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3).

But perhaps you say in your heart: “I would not wish to despise temptations, but to contend against them, knowing that every virtue is so much more precious as it has been more vehemently assailed and tested by its contraries.” O foolish one, to whom the true judgments [Col. 0926A] of the Lord, justified, desirable, and sweet in themselves—or in itself—do not taste sweet; for in itself their true justice and desirable sweetness overflow. For just as the light of the sun overflows into itself, and therefore always abounds in its own light; just as the overflowings of the sea return into themselves, and therefore always abound: so the Lord’s true judgments, justified, overflow into themselves; and therefore truth, justice, and desirable sweetness always abound in them, even if they do not taste sweet to you.

How great an abundance of sweetness abounds in them! Hence, as mentioned above, in Hebrew they are called “sweeter than honey and the overflowing honeycomb,” because, just as the abyss of the sea overflows through the veins of the earth into springs and rivers, and, when all rivers return [Col. 0926B] into the sea, it itself abounds from itself and in itself, so the Lord’s true judgments, justified in themselves, gather back into themselves the overflowings which they send forth into springs and rivers of graces. Hence they do not fail from the abundance of their truth, justice, and sweetness.

This you, foolish one, do not understand: you judge dangerous temptations to be desirable contrary to their ordering, although the Lord’s true judgments, justified in themselves, judge them to be avoided. For such sweetness is preserved in those judgments that at times a virtue lacking temptation is more precious than virtue struggling amid temptations. For what wise person, tasting the Lord’s true judgments, does not perceive in them that the chastity of the Virgin Mary—who, feeling no incentives of the flesh, burned with the chaste love of the Lord—was more precious than the chastity of the Apostle Paul, who, while enduring the thorn of the flesh, fought manfully against it? [Col. 0926C]

Again, perhaps judging by outward appearance, you consider contempt for this world more precious in one who possessed much to abandon, and by whose delight he might have been held fast to love of the world. But God, seeing in the heart, judges that in this matter affection ought to be weighed rather than wealth. It was indeed precious that the Apostle Matthew left much; yet, by the Lord’s true judgments, Peter was set before him, though Peter left little. Indeed, to use the words of the holy Fathers: that fisherman left much who retained nothing for himself; he left much who, together with his possessed goods, renounced also his desires; he left much who could confidently say: “Behold, we have left all things and followed thee” (Matt. XIX, 27).

Whence came such great confidence to you, Peter, that you, who were poor and had sought food by hand and craft, should firmly say, “Behold, we have left all things”? I know that you left all the implements of your fishing; I know that Matthew left far greater things; and yet, while he is silent, you speak and say: “Behold, we have left all things.” And although twelve thrones are appointed for you twelve who, leaving all things, followed Christ, I see you, Peter, seated before the others at the summit of apostolic dignity. Why is this, except because the Lord’s true judgments, justified in themselves, weighed your affection rather than your wealth?

Likewise, even now, by the Lord’s true judgments, the measure of affection and inward devotion in each person is weighed rather than external activity. Thus we should not be anxious if we cannot outwardly display the effect of a good and great work through great riches or dignities, provided that inwardly we offer God a great disposition of love. [Col. 0927A]

But someone says: “Then can we be made equal in merits to the apostles merely by having a great disposition of faith and love, and not the effect of works?” To this I say: Perfect love of God is never idle. It performs great things if it is present; but if it refuses to act, it is not love. Therefore, those who seem to have a disposition of goodness, unless they also have an effect suited to their times, places, and offices, are shown [Col. 0927B] not to possess the disposition which they think—or others think—they possess.

For example, the places, times, and offices of the prophets were one thing; those of the holy apostles another; those of the martyrs another; those of confessors another; those of pastors and teachers another; and those of persons obedient, and bound to be obedient, to pastors and teachers another. Hence the Apostle says:

> “He who descended is the same also who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. And he gave some indeed as apostles, but some as prophets, others indeed as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all meet in the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, into a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV, 10–13).

“For the perfecting,” he says, “of the saints,” because, just as the Holy of Holies was visibly completed through Moses, so now the Church is completed through Christ. In Christ the faithful people are simply called “holy”; but the Lord’s portion—namely, his inheritance, of which he himself says, “Indeed my inheritance is glorious to me” (Ps. XV, 6)—is called the Holy of Holies. A share and inheritance of that inheritance is the Lord himself, understood in those who perfectly despise this world. This glorious inheritance, I say, is called the Holy of Holies. [Col. 0927C]

In the building of this tabernacle—which, as we have distinguished, in the faithful and subject people is called “the Holy Place,” and in good prelates “the Holy of Holies”—Christ appointed apostles in his own time. Certain prophets were contemporary with them, possessing the grace of tongues, the interpretation of utterances, and revelations of mysteries and future events. One of these was Agabus, who announced the coming of a great famine, which took place under Claudius. Evangelists too were contemporaries of the apostles, but were distinct in their places and offices. In all of them the one love of God worked; one and the same disposition of divine love burned, but it shone forth in diverse effects according to the diversity of places: “he who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision worked” also in Paul the Apostle “among the Gentiles” (Gal. II, 8). It did so also according to the diversity of offices: the word of God which the first apostles proclaimed, prophets after and according to them expounded more fully. [Col. 0927D] Evangelists [Col. 0928A], moreover, not only preached by voice but evangelized also by writing.

Then pastors and teachers filled the world. Each governed and benefited his own place, having, as is read in Job, understanding together with the cock (Job XXXVIII, 36). By this they knew how to observe the proper times: when to stir themselves up with their own wings by acting well, and when to announce beforehand to others the approaching day by speaking and teaching well. Thus they are rightly called pastors and teachers. They are pastors because, by the example of good action, they lead the sheep to the pastures of life, as is written of the good shepherd: “And when he has sent forth his own sheep, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him” (John X, 4). Therefore to go before the sheep by good examples is the mark of a good pastor.

And because Jesus began both to do and to teach, when a person teaches by word what he does in deed, he holds at once the office of pastor and teacher. What, then, is the office of the sheep? Surely to follow their shepherd obediently and their teacher faithfully, so that they do not follow a stranger but flee from him; for they ought not receive the voice of strangers. By “stranger” I mean one alien to the office and name of pastor, who does not feed them with the sweet bread of examples. By “stranger” I mean one alien to the office and name of teacher, who is like a dumb dog unable to bark. The voice of strangers is the doctrine of heretics and of others who teach perversely. [Col. 0928B]

There were also prophets before Christ’s coming, whose office was obscurely to foretell the mysteries of Christ yet to come; [Col. 0928C] these the apostles announced openly as fulfilled in Christ and now past. In accordance with their distinctive manner, the voices of contemporary prophets in the Church cooperated with the apostles, speaking and discerning by parts, as Paul says: “Let two or three prophets speak,” by parts, “and let the others discern” (I Cor. XIV, 29). Therefore the office of prophets preceding Christ’s advent was one thing, and that of the prophets who followed was another. For of the former it is said: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. XVII, 12), that is, obscure knowledge in the prophets. But through the new prophets the secrets of hearts were revealed, while the sacred Scriptures were lucidly expounded by them. Hence the Apostle says:

> “If all prophesy, and some unbeliever or unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all, he is judged by all; [Col. 0928D] the secrets of his heart will become manifest, and so, falling upon his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among us” (I Cor. XIV, 25).

So too, as the times of the blessed martyrs and confessors differed, their offices also were distinct. For when the battle of persecution threatened, it belonged to the former to die patiently, though they willingly lived, desiring with Paul “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I, 23). Yet because their remaining in the flesh was necessary for others, just as it was gain for the martyrs to die, because by the short passage of holy death they quickly came to Christ, so for the blessed confessors—ready to die willingly for Christ, yet bound and imprisoned in the flesh to live patiently for the same Christ—Christ was the reason for living. [Col. 0929A]

Nor does a contemptible or small office rest upon the pastors and teachers of these last times. For just as, in the building of Christ’s body, which is the Church—the tabernacle called “the Holy Place”—the holy apostles were the foundations, and themselves planted and founded the Church upon their own and the prophets’ teaching by their blood, so teachers and pastors are appointed for the perfecting of those same saints, who are founded upon the foundation of apostles and prophets, divine grace at work and the apostles’ own zeal cooperating.

The completion of this true tabernacle, which God fixed and not man, ought not in any way differ from the beauty of its foundation. For concerning that tabernacle which in shadow was called the Holy of Holies it is written: “As it is raised, so shall it be taken down” (Num. II, 17). The covering of the tabernacle was doubled both on the western side and on the eastern side, the likeness of both sides being preserved. By these mystical words and deeds it was prefigured that the final completion of the Church, effected by pastors and teachers, ought to be similar in the same perfection to its original foundation, made by the apostles and prophets—although the grace of no saints preceding or following them was equal to the grace of the apostles. [Col. 0929B]

For Truth himself said to them: “Blessed are the eyes that see [Col. 0929C] what you see. Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke X, 23–24). In this blessedness none among those born of women was greater than John the Baptist, because his blessed eyes too saw, together with the apostles, what was not granted to many kings and righteous persons.

But “all generations shall call the Virgin Mother blessed” (Luke I, 48); her most blessed eyes saw her Son, the God-man, looking upon her. She could say: “Thou art the God who hast seen me,” as Hagar, Sarah’s maidservant, once said at the well named “of the Living and Seeing One” (Gen. XVI, 13). This mistress of the world is not injuriously compared to that maidservant when she says: “For he hath regarded the lowliness of his handmaid” (Luke I, 48); and she gave birth to him who is the living and seeing well. Hence he says: “If anyone thirst, let him come to me and drink” (John VII, 37).

To that former handmaid the angel showed a well named “of the Living and Seeing One.” To this new handmaid the angel Gabriel announced Christ, the living fountain. The former had conceived from Abraham’s seed; this one conceived the divine seed, that is, the Word of God the Father, which, incarnate in her, is called the seed “of Abraham, in whom all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Acts III, 25). Therefore she was seen to have neither an equal before her nor one to follow her.

Again, elsewhere it is said to the apostles: “You are they who have remained with me in my temptations; and I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table [Col. 0930A] in my kingdom, and sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luke XXII, 28, 30).

Therefore, preserving the privilege of the incomparable dignity of the most blessed Virgin Mary—who herself, when the apostles fled, remained with her Son in his temptations—and duly honouring John the Baptist, who was great before the Lord, no saints are equal to the holy apostles. For in them the disposition of love and the effect of activity were greater. The ointment of divine charity “upon Aaron’s head,” though descending from there “unto the edge of his garment” and making blessed the outermost members of the Church, comes nearer and more fully “upon the beard, the beard,” namely, “of Aaron” (Ps. CXXXII, 3): that is, of Christ the great priest, to whom the apostles clung like a beard and upon whose breast they shone like twelve stones in its ornament. [Col. 0930B]

Therefore do not you—whoever you are, however holy, however devout may be your disposition of love toward God—aspire to riches which you cannot possess: you cannot equal the holy apostles, neither in the disposition of love nor in the effect of works. They were the first to follow the Lord and prepared the way for those who came after. In the battle-line of the true David they first bore the banner of the Holy Trinity by proclaiming the Catholic faith. Hence, just as it is read concerning certain mighty men of David that they indeed were mighty, “but did not attain unto the first three” (II Kings XXIII, 1), so we may say of all the mighty persons arrayed after the apostles in the battle-line [Col. 0930C] of the true David: martyrs, confessors, and Catholic and apostolic pastors and teachers were indeed mighty men, but they did not attain unto the first three. For the holy apostles, the first proclaimers of the Holy Trinity, were stronger than the other mighty men—not by their own strength, but by that of which it is said: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. XXXII, 6).

After the apostles, therefore, throughout the whole army of Christ our Lord, the strong and desirable King, when comparison is made between two perfect persons who have the same disposition of divine love, a disparate and dissimilar effect does not prevent equality. For in the unity and simplicity of divine charity itself their hearts meet as though in an indivisible centre: like straight lines from a single central point extending to a circle described about that same point. They cannot touch it together, since they stretch from that point in divergent directions.

So certain people, in whom perfect charity has already cast out servile fear—which is not cast out except through the perfection of charity itself—have indeed one heart and one soul in God, but do not perform one and the same activity. For, as we briefly noted above, the activity of an apostle differs from that of a prophet; that of an evangelist from that of a martyr; that of a confessor from that of a pastor and teacher; and that again from the activity of one who owes obedience to a pastor and teacher. [Col. 0930D]

[Col. 0931A] Among all these, after those mighty men whom the true David had, wished to have, and taught to be held above the rest, all good persons possess the same disposition of goodness. Although one may be a martyr and another a confessor, one rich and another poor, one a prelate and another subject, provided, as was said, that they have an equal disposition of love, they are not distinguished on account of their dissimilar effects, so as not to be equally blessed before God with that blessedness of which it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8).

Certainly equal purity of heart—equal brightness in the eye of the heart—will deservedly have equality in the vision of God which makes all the elect blessed. Hence those unequal in this purity will be blessed differently and unequally; but equals will not be separated, even though one is led to martyrdom and the other is not. For in the suffering of one, the other, if he knows of it, has [Col. 0931B] such strong compassion that the sword which passes through the former’s flesh passes through the latter’s soul. For he would be ready to lay down his life for him, or with him, if he were dragged to punishment—being full, that is, and perfect in that love in which the Apostle teaches us to lay down our lives for our brethren, just as Christ, loving us, laid down his life for us.

Again, if one of two perfect persons is a pastor, and the other is a male yearling lamb from this pastor’s flock, or one of the perfect sheep, who “are all bearing twins, and none among them is barren” (Cant. VI, 5), and persecution occurs in which such a pastor is required to lay down his life for such lambs or sheep: truly, in such a pastor such lambs and such sheep suffer. Perhaps in some sheep there is a stronger and sharper sword of compassion than the sword of bodily suffering raging against the pastor. [Col. 0931C]

Again, if one of two perfect persons is rich and the other poor, and they recognize one another, when such a poor person is sustained by such a rich person, a certain identity will be effected in their righteousness. The Lord says: “He who receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person shall receive the reward of a righteous person” (Matt. X, 41). He does not say “a reward from a righteous person,” but, he says, “shall receive the reward of a righteous person.”

Again, if, as we also illustrated above, one of two perfect persons is at the ready for preaching with Joshua, as if fighting in the plain by the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, and the other, loving him, struggles for him in prayer, as though with hands—that is, with the exercises of works—not wearied, after the example of Moses praying upon the mountain: because of the identity of their good disposition they will receive equality of rewards; nor will they be separated because of a diversity of affections. For each of these persons was ready for the other’s office; but, keeping their distinct stations, they render to one another a discerning honour and service. In their Church, which, as the Apostle says (I Tim. III, 15), is the pillar of the living God, he has set one as a silver base bearing the weight of the pillar, and the other as a likewise silver or golden capital, an ornament on the summit of the same pillar. [Col. 0931D]

This one is supported, that he may be seen on high;

This one sustains the burden, yet is no less good thereby.

[Col. 0932A]

Both shining, both warm with virtue;

Their ardour equal, though their flame is different.

For this one, the voice is of words; for that one, the voice is of desires;

Though their cry is diverse, their love is one.

Since this is so, there is absolutely no reason why a perfect subject should reasonably seek a place of pre-eminence. Indeed, there are several reasons why a perfect prelate may desire a place of subjection, though after his lawful binding he does not dare seek release. For the one who presides is troubled by concern for himself and for the flock entrusted to him. But one who, in cheerful compassion, assists the troubled person by prayer or other aid is free from anxiety, except insofar as he is troubled through compassion, so that he may pour out prayer more attentively for the troubled person—just as Christ was troubled on our account, although in himself he was free from every anxiety.

Hence the title of the one hundred and first Psalm is fitting for him: “The prayer of the poor man, when he was troubled and poured out his supplication before the Lord.” Therefore, just as he, though free among the dead, was troubled in order to pour out prayers before the Lord for others, so good and faithful persons, free from anxieties of this kind, nevertheless pour out prayers before the Lord for those who preside in anxious concern. They do so in the secret place of the heart, where the Lord alone sees and hears what the Spirit desires, since he asks according to God for the saints with unutterable groanings. [Col. 0932B]

But if “the Spirit asks with unutterable groanings” (Rom. VIII, 26) for the saints, so that they may be further sanctified and remain holy—[Col. 0932C]especially those set over others in order to provide examples and instruction of holiness—how much more is the Spirit of the righteous stirred by unutterable groanings to plead for the cleansing of the saints when, according to Jeremiah’s lamentation, it sees “the nations enter into” the Lord’s “sanctuary, concerning whom he commanded that they should not enter into” his “Church” (Lam. I, 10)? Then, with the Spirit of good persons groaning unutterably, though the tongue may at times be silent, it cries continually and almost without ceasing with the Psalmist: “O God, the nations have come into thy inheritance; they have defiled thy holy temple” (Ps. LXXVIII, 1). Or with Daniel it says: “Hear, O Lord, the prayers [Col. 0932D] of thy servant; make thy face shine upon thy sanctuary, which is desolate” (Dan. IX, 17).

Thus the good disposition of good hearts does not grow cold or rest, whether they themselves preside in anxious care or, in cheerful compassion toward prelates, pray for the holy that they may become holier; and for the unholy, that they may be excluded from the sanctuary of God, and thus be corrected by the mercy of God going before them. For after the groaning complaint concerning the pollution of the holy temple follows what good persons say for themselves and for their enemies: “O Lord, remember not our former iniquities; let thy mercies quickly go before us, for we are brought very low,” etc. (Ps. LXXVIII, 8).

Thus, in the perfecting of the saints and of the true tabernacle, which God fixed and not man, while one person walks in the way of God in this manner and another in that, and one has this disposition and another another, through the Lord’s true judgments, justified, a fitting place and fitting office are distributed. In this wonderful manner both the outer tabernacle, called the Holy Place, and the inner tabernacle behind the veil, called the Holy of Holies, are completed. [Col. 0933A]

The outer tabernacle, called the Holy Place, has among its other ornaments a golden lampstand with seven lamps and likewise golden snuffers. Although the lampstand and its snuffers have one material—for both are made of the purest gold—their offices and forms differ greatly. It is not now necessary to discuss each aspect of their difference. For the present it is enough to note, without prejudice to a more sacred interpretation, that in the active life, called the Holy Place, especially insofar as ecclesiastical ministries are concerned—where there is holy occupation—one person shines by word and example like a golden lampstand, while others, cooperating with him, perform lesser offices like certain snuffers of the lampstand. In one disposition of charity, equally pure and clean, yet unequally distributed by the Lord’s true judgments according to diverse offices, they will possess, through the golden purity, as it were, of the one charity, one blessedness of charity. Nor among such stars of heaven does one differ from another in brightness because of the diversity of lesser and greater offices or affections, but because of the difference between greater and lesser affections. [Col. 0933B] [Col. 0933C]

It often happens that greater offices are performed with a lesser disposition of charity, and lesser offices with a greater disposition. For example, when someone supplying the place of an unlearned person responds “Amen” at your blessing or at the celebration of Mass. There is sometimes a great distinction between the devotion of the one blessing and that of the one responding “Amen.” And before God, through the Lord’s true judgments, there is a distinction in rewards according to the difference in devotions, so that sometimes the last become first and the first last.

Likewise, in the contemplative life, called the Holy of Holies, so far as concerns the most holy leisure of most holy rest in the hidden fellowship of the saints, over which the veil of flesh is spread lest it be exposed to human sight, two cherubim are placed facing one another, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat. [Col. 0933D] In this one must consider that the two cherubim were locally distant from one another, yet agreed in material and form, since both were made of the purest gold, and both, spreading their wings equally, inclined their faces equally toward the mercy-seat. By this it is indicated that the hidden fellowship and contemplation of the saints vary in many ways, as though locally distinct, but are made one in Christ’s love, who is the true mercy-seat; for, as the Apostle says, “he is the propitiation for our sins” (I John II, 2).

Hence, even though zeal for God’s house consumes one holy man in the secret place of his heart within the veil, within the Holy of Holies, and love of divine sweetness delights another, neither must be prejudged: neither that the former lacks charity in his zeal, nor that the latter, in his love of divinity, lacks emulation and zeal for righteousness. For both tend toward the mercy-seat, since each by prayer appeases the divine judgment. The one, like Phinehas, appeases the Lord’s wrath by his zeal; the other, like most meek Moses, to appease that same wrath, either fasts or prays upon the mountain with his face turned toward the mercy-seat (Num. XXV, 7). For both desire that God should be gracious and propitious to human beings, even the ungodly: the former by zeal and the latter by prayer. [Col. 0934A]

For the one who prays is not without zeal; otherwise the sacrifice of his prayer would be rejected, because it would not be seasoned with salt, whereas salt is commanded to be offered in every sacrifice. Nor does the zealous person, who offers a sacrifice cooked and hot in a frying-pan over the fire of emulation according to the command of the Law, separate from it—if he offers rightly—the oil of compassion and mercy, which is commanded to be added to such a sacrifice. Otherwise his sacrifice, offered without oil contrary to the Law, would not be acceptable to God. [Col. 0934B]

What then follows from this consideration of the divine judgments, which in the perfecting of the saints so diversely order diverse persons, disposing one in one manner and another truly in another, except that there should be no schism in the body of the whole Church? For all members are embraced under the most eloquent ordering of the divine judgments; yet one person should esteem another superior to himself, whether now or in the future, because of the differing disposition of humility and charity, weighed by the secret and righteous judgments of the Lord alone—not according to greater or lesser external offices, but according to inward foundations of humility and charity, proved in their places, offices, and effects either before God alone or also before human beings.

This proof occurs in such a way that sometimes great charity is proved in great things, sometimes small charity in small things, sometimes great charity in small things, and sometimes small charity in great things—and is made known to itself. For God does not need tests to recognize such matters. [Col. 0934C]

Nevertheless, in order that his judgments, justified in themselves, may appear justified also in outward matters, he sometimes orders certain tests, by which matters known to him are made known also to human beings and angels, whether through small or great trials, as what was previously hidden is disclosed. For example, great charity was proved in great things when the Apostle Peter said to Christ for the third time, “I love thee,” and Christ also said to him for the third time, “Feed my lambs” or “my sheep” (John XXI, 15–17), so that by the great office of pastoral care there might at once be both a judgment and an exercise of great charity.

Small charity was proved in small things when Adam, though every fruit of the trees of Paradise had been granted him and only one tree forbidden, set aside love for God and listened to the woman urging him to eat the prohibited food of that tree. He obeyed her voice more than God’s voice, and did not restrain himself in a small matter, because his love for God was small.

Great charity was proved in small things when the offering of the widow who put two mites into the treasury was more pleasing than the larger and more numerous offerings of the rich (Luke XXI, 2). There also small charity appeared in great things, because the rich persons’ offering, though great, came from what abounded to them. Or, more clearly, charity is proved small or absent in great things when, in a great benefit bestowed by God, the recipient’s ingratitude appears—as when the angel placed in heaven and made more beautiful than the other angels was ungrateful to his Maker and was not moved to love of the giver by so great a benefit. [Col. 0935B]

Many imitate him, enriched above other human beings in this world by divine generosity with either spiritual or temporal gifts. Lacking charity alone, they are ungrateful to the giver of all good things, not serving their fellow servants with what they received, not for themselves, but for those fellow servants.

The divine judgments are found justified in those whom they either save because of great charity or condemn because of small charity toward God not only through God’s great and small benefits, but also through his great and small scourges. For blessed Job was tested by great scourges and proved to have great charity, of which it is written: “Charity is patient” (I Cor. XIII, 4). He did not become impatient toward God, so as to cease from praises and murmur; nor toward the devil, so as in any manner to attribute his scourge to him—for he attributed it to God alone, saying: “The Lord gave, the Lord took away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done: blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I, 21); nor toward his wife and friends who gave evil advice and spoke importunately to him, so as to reply to them impatiently.

By the small scourge endured by the Apostle Peter, his still small charity appeared, when at the voice of one maidservant he denied the truth, which charity always has as its companion, concerning which it is written: “It does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices together with truth” (I Cor. XIII, 6). [Col. 0935C]

By a small scourge, the great charity of King David appeared, when, rebuked for his sin by the moderate reproof of the prophet Nathan, he was immediately moved to repentance and said: “I have sinned against the Lord” (II Kings XII, 13). By a great scourge, small charity appeared in King Uzziah, who, struck with leprosy because of his presumption, is not recorded to have repented but to have remained in his folly. This is indicated by the fact that he remained separated until the day of his death (II Chron. XXVI, 19), and that the glory of God was revealed to the prophet Isaiah not while Uzziah lived, but after he died. Hence Isaiah says: “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne,” etc. (Isa. VI, 1).

The same may be said of the testing of humility: for there is one who is greatly exalted even by small gifts of God, and one who is only slightly exalted even by great gifts of God. But those who are little exalted by small things and greatly exalted by great things are beyond number; and in all of these, who must be humbled according to the measure of their exaltation, [Col. 0936A] “the judgments of the Lord are true and justified,” because by God’s just judgment “everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14:11). Again, there is one who is greatly humbled even by a great gift or honor bestowed on him by God or by human beings; and there is one who is humbled only slightly, even when he himself receives little honor. Of those in the middle there is no number, in whom there is a middling degree of humility. And in all these, who are to be exalted according to the measure of their humility, the judgments of the Lord are true and justified in themselves.

But that they may also be vindicated in outward tests, great humility is sometimes proved in great matters, sometimes slight humility in great matters, sometimes great humility in small matters, and slight humility in small tests. The great humility of King David was proved in great matters: for it was a great trial of humility to be chosen king while his other brothers were despised; to break the mouths of lions, to tear apart the limbs of bears, to strike down Goliath, feared by all; and, when Saul had at last been killed, to reign over all Israel. Since he possessed great humility amid these great things, after all this he said: “I will play, and become still more despised, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 6:22). He said this to Michal, Saul’s daughter, when she despised him because, playing and dancing before the ark of the Lord, he seemed like one of the buffoons.

But in Saul, slightness of humility was proved amid the great honors of the same Israelite kingdom, when the Lord said to him: “Was it not when you were little in your own eyes that I made you head over the tribes of Israel?” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 15:17). For Scripture says: “Saul was the son of one year when he began to reign, and he reigned two years” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 13:1), which is to say: he was simple and humble when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in this humble simplicity. For his slight humility, unable to stand long amid the great honors of kingship, quickly withered away.

Great humility is proved in small things when something lowly and insignificant, or a contemptible office, is imposed upon a humble and worthy person, and that person is not offended by it, nor judges himself worthy, in his own estimation, of a more honorable office—even though before God he may be judged worthy of greater things. Thus the humility of the prophet Isaiah was tested: he was commanded to go “naked and barefoot” (Isaiah 20:2) as a sign to the children of Israel, and he humbly obeyed. Thus [Col. 0936D] the humility of the prophet Ezekiel was tested: he was commanded to cover with human excrement the bread which he was to eat (Ezekiel 4:12). Such a great prophet did not proudly refuse the command, but humbly excused himself to his commander, declaring that it was hard for him if anything defiled and unclean should enter his mouth contrary to his custom. By such a very humble excuse he obtained that this same command should be made more tolerable, human excrement being replaced for him by cow dung.

Slight humility appeared in small things when Naaman the Syrian, commanded by the prophet Elisha to wash seven times in the Jordan, went away indignant (4 Kings [2 Kings] 5:10). His servants said to him: “Even if the prophet had told you some great thing, surely you ought to have done it” (ibid., 13). By these words he was corrected, and was called forth from slight humility to greater humility.

Therefore, when by such outward tests the inward judgments concerning charity or humility become apparent—virtues through which the entrance into the kingdom of heaven is chiefly opened—the judgments of the Lord are true and justified not only in themselves, but also in human and angelic consciences. But when absolutely no outward signs of humility and charity appear, then the judgments of the Lord, rejecting some because of the slight or nonexistent humility and charity which they possessed and gathering others because of their great charity and humility, are righteous in themselves, even if their justification is hidden from human beings and angels. For the judgments of the Lord are true: although they can be hidden, [Col. 0937B] they can in no way be unjust. Therefore they are more desirable than much gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb—not to every people, but to each one of your servants, Lord God.

**VERSE 12. For your servant keeps them.** Even if your servant is gold or precious stone, pure and made firm by every virtue of charity and humility; or if he is honey and honeycomb, wholly delightful in the honey of his mind and in the honeycomb of his flesh—yet he judges your judgments more desirable than much gold and precious stone, that is, more than himself or another saint like himself; and he loves the sweetness of your judgments more than honey and honeycomb, that is, more than himself or another like himself [Col. 0937C]. And he does this not without cause, because in keeping them there is great recompense and abundant fruit.

Your servant not only hopes for recompense after having kept them, but even now in this life, in keeping them, there is great recompense and abundant fruit, with which no fruit of this world can be compared. For the Apostle says: “What fruit had you then in those things of which you are now ashamed? But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Romans 6:21–22). Thus the sanctification of the present life is abundant fruit in keeping the divine judgments; but eternal life is fruit after they have been kept, provided that one perseveres in keeping them without great and mortal sins.

Now I mean mortal sins: if they have not been expiated before death, after death they will be incapable of expiation. Yet some sins can be expiated even after death, although in this life they may not especially have been recognized, or at least understood. For while no sins escape the divine understanding, very many escape human understanding, even that of holy men. For:

**VERSE 13. Who understands transgressions?** *Peccatum* [sin] is properly said when something is done which is forbidden. But *delictum* [a transgression, omission] is when that which ought to be done and has been commanded is not done. Sin is therefore more easily understood, since it is committed by human action preceded by evil intention. But who will understand transgressions? Or who can understand them, when even while sleeping and being idle, whoever refrains from acting multiplies them? Therefore I do not wish to wait until I understand my transgressions, because they are not intelligible to me; although all things are intelligible to you, my God, they are hidden from me. I do not wish, I say, to wait or postpone my petition for pardon until I see my transgressions, which are hidden from me; but I say: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults.”

**VERSE 14. And spare your servant from others’ sins.** I, David—or I, any penitent person like David—acknowledge that “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 50 [51]:7).
