These are my hidden sins, namely original sins, which came to me from the first parents through intermediary parents, as though through the hidden channels of God’s judgments; and they lie hidden in me, in my nature, as though natural. Actual sins afterward came upon them as though accidental and alien. On account of original sins I say: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults.” On account of actual sins I say: “Spare your servant from others’ sins.”

Alternatively: the sins which are in my conscience and proceed from my own intention are my hidden sins; but those which I committed at the persuasion of another person or the devil are, in that respect, alien to me, because they have been brought in from elsewhere. In my hidden sins I have been made like the devil, who sinned in his heart through pride, with no one persuading him; he fell in his sin with no one impelling him. In my alien sins I have been made like the first-created man, who sinned at another’s persuasion and fell into sin, his persuader drawing him on after he consented to the persuasion. Therefore I say: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults,” lest I be found like the devil who deceives; “and spare your servant from others’ sins,” lest I be found like the old man who was deceived. “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults,” lest the foot of pride come upon me; “and spare your servant from others’ sins,” lest the hand of the sinner move me.

O Lord, I tremble altogether from fear of my hidden faults! I, King David, while I was afflicted by Saul’s persecution, could not keep my own wife, whom I had betrothed to myself with a hundred foreskins of the Philistines; for Saul, her father, took her from me and gave her to another (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 3:14). I bore this patiently; I endured this wrong with long-suffering until, when Saul had died, I received my wife again. Yet I perceived that it was a grievous injury if anyone took a man’s own wife. While suffering this injury, I perceived it, and never thought that I myself would do such a thing to anyone. This lesson was so hidden within me that I then scarcely believed that I ought to take another man’s wife. Indeed, concerning this sin I judged Saul himself, and the man to whom my wife had been given, perhaps more harshly than I ought, not knowing that I should fall into a like or greater sin. For I did not understand the hidden incitements of lust then concealed within me, just as fire is sometimes concealed under ashes until, when wind comes and blows, the hidden fire is stirred up.

Thus surely the hidden incentives of lust, cruelty, and faithlessness lay concealed within me, until aliens came and, blowing from without, kindled the inwardly hidden fires, and they came forth. Was not that traveler an alien—the evil tempter, namely—who came to me asking that a feast be made for him, not from my own sheep but from another’s ewe, from the wife of Uriah the Hittite? Thus, driven by others—by that traveler tempting within—and attracted from without by the lovely appearance of another man’s wife, “I was thrust down and overthrown, so that I fell” (Psalm 117 [118]:13). And unless the Lord had received me, he who did not abandon me even in my sins but brought me back to himself through repentance, I would have remained shut out and alien from the fellowship of the saints along with that alien, that traveler: because of adultery, which I offered as a feast to that alien and traveler; and because of the cruelty of murder, by which, faithlessly shedding murderous blood, I gave that traveler drink.

Then, cast down into the pit of so great a sin through the insolence fostered by peace and prosperity, I recognized that the judgments of the Lord were true and justified: those judgments which had kept me long oppressed under Saul’s persecution when my hidden faults were still hidden even from myself, though manifest to God’s judgments. My hidden faults are manifest to those judgments even now; although I do not see them, I am nevertheless compelled to fear them. Therefore, fearing henceforth the lurking places of my hidden faults, the snares of robbers, and the enmities of household enemies; fearing also the approaches of alien tempters, whether human beings or demons, I pray with my whole heart and say: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from others’ sins.”

[Col. 0939C] Much more must I, any sinner like David in frailty and sinfulness, though not likewise like David in strong hand, say: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from others’ sins.” I consider your great servants and behold their hidden faults disclosed by others; and thereby I am compelled to fear my own hidden faults the more.

Your servant the prophet, who came from Judah, sent to King Jeroboam, boldly rebuked the king himself as he sacrificed to idols; by a mighty miracle he restored the king’s withered arm; he despised his gifts; and, as he had been commanded, departed without eating (3 Kings [1 Kings] 13:4, 6, 9). What hidden things do you suppose were in that prophet’s heart, except certain incentives of self-exaltation secretly formed from his good deeds? But these hidden things were not exposed until aliens approached and applied their outward breath. For the alien spirit of falsehood was present, and alien too was the prophet filled with the spirit of falsehood, who turned the good prophet back from his way and deceived him into eating forbidden food. Because of this disobedience he was given over to be killed by a lion—yet not to be devoured by it—because the sin which he contracted inwardly through self-exaltation, and increased outwardly through manifest disobedience, was expiated by death (3 Kings [1 Kings] 13:24).

In this event it must surely be carefully observed that, unless he had first swelled inwardly, when tempted outwardly he would not have yielded so easily. So too our father Adam, unless he had first swelled inwardly with a desire for divinity, would not have bitten that fruit so eagerly, by eating which it was promised to him and Eve that they would be like gods, knowing good and evil [Col. 0940A]. Thus no one is conquered by alien tempters from without unless he has first been conquered by his own hidden foes, lying in wait against him within. Therefore I say: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from others’ sins.”

Your servant the apostle Peter, when he said, “Even if all are scandalized, I shall never be scandalized” (Matthew 26:31), was already being ravaged inwardly by hidden enemies plundering his heart through the spirit of presumption. Yet the fire of that presumption lay hidden within until aliens came from without and blew upon it. The maidservant of the priest, and in her the evil spirit, by their breath revealed how great were the embers of presumption, together with the coldness of charity growing cool, then in Peter’s heart when he stood warming himself beside the coals with alien attendants. Certainly, unless the Lord had looked upon him, and Peter the apostle had extinguished those same embers with abundant and bitter weeping, he would have remained alienated from Christ along with those aliens. He would not have yielded to those aliens so readily if he had not first been overcome by the hidden temptations of presumption.

O Lord! He was an outstanding soldier of your camps, and I, compared with him, am a little speck of dust. If he, secretly ravaged by hidden foes, was openly overcome by aliens, where shall I, wretched as I am, flee from my hidden faults and from aliens, except to you, Lord? To you Peter also finally fled, after he felt that he had been wounded by his hidden foes and by aliens. But I, more wounded than Peter by my hidden faults and by aliens, have even lost the sense of pain, and cannot weep bitterly like him, while many of my hidden and alien enemies still lie in wait for me. Yet lest I lie altogether in hell, where no one shall confess you: behold, I confess to you that, having suffered many grievous wounds from my hidden faults and from aliens, I fear worse ones still. Therefore, fleeing to you, I say to you with penitent David and weeping Peter: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from others’ sins.”

Spare me, I say, from others’ sins, not so that they may not oppose me, but so that they may not rule over me. I grant that they may oppose me, but I pray that they may not rule me: let them oppose me for my exercise, toward the glorious completion of a glorious contest in good victory; let them not rule over me, so that their evil will may in any way be accomplished concerning me. I do not refuse sometimes to experience their wars, but I refuse to consent to their dominion over me. Therefore, Lord, so spare your servant from others’ sins that I may never be subjected to their dominion—those over whom I shall rather rule through your power, if I am perfectly cleansed from my hidden faults.

Therefore I first say: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults,” and then add: “Spare your servant from others’ sins”—your servant, I say, because I now serve you by keeping your judgments. “For your servant keeps them”; and therefore, by keeping those same judgments, I shall be your servant. I shall not rebel against your judgments, but shall always praise them, saying: “You are righteous, Lord, in every judgment of yours, and your judgment is right” (Psalm 118 [119]:137). Therefore spare me, your servant; spare your servant placed beneath the most just scourge of your judgments. Although the truth of your judgments tastes sweet to your servant, that same truth is great severity to me, your servant, unless mercy exalts itself above judgment. I, your servant, fear the weight of your judgments in the scale of justice because of my iniquity, unless grace, outweighing it on the other side in the scale of mercy, raises the scale of justice above it.

Would that all my sins, which I have contracted from my hidden faults and from others’ sins, might be weighed in the balance; and that you, sparing me, might cast them into the depths of the sea, your mercy sparing me and further defending me from their dominion, outweighing them all! For I know that:

**If they do not rule over me, then I shall be spotless.** No stain from them will cling to me if, though I feel their temptations within me, I do not consent to them, and complete freedom from their dominion remains to me—although, for those living in the flesh, there is no complete freedom from their assault. Yet this will be a great good of freedom for me: if my enemies, hidden or alien, do not rule over me, then I shall be spotless, and cleansed from the greatest transgression, that is, pride. For a voluntary consent of the heart to iniquity cannot occur without the greatest transgression, which is apostasy from God; and “pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclesiasticus [Sirach] 10:15). Pride was the first deceiver of those departing from God and is the final resister of those returning to God, taking strength even from rightly performed deeds. Therefore, when I, your servant, am cleansed from this, then I shall be spotless and cleansed from the greatest transgression.

**VERSE 15. And may the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be pleasing in your sight.** Lord, in accordance with the various things said above, I, your servant, either make known by saying: “May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be pleasing in your sight always”; or I do not make it known by a promise, but desire it in prayer—that the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart may be pleasing in your sight.

For I desire, entering and going out through the door which is Christ, to find pasture in this: that the meditation of my heart may always be in the divine sight. Going out through the opening of my mouth, I desire to find pasture in this: that the words of my mouth may be pleasing [Col. 0942A]. Or, that the words of my mouth may be pleasing, let the utterances of my mouth be such as to please the ears of God. Let the meditations of my heart be such as are accepted in God’s sight not merely for an hour, but always—that is, without interruption.

For the full and worthy fulfillment of this vow, Lord, be my helper and my redeemer: helper in bringing good things to completion; redeemer from evils; helper, that I may worthily accomplish what I have vowed and desired; redeemer, lest, sold under sin, I become again a servant of sin. Rather, redeemed through you—Redeemer from hidden and alien sins—may I henceforth remain free from them in your service, my Lord; in your help, my helper; in the freedom of your deliverance, my redeemer. You took the form of a servant so that you might make me your servant; your strength was made weak so that you might help me in my weakness; you gave yourself as the price so that you might redeem me, who had been a servant of sin, oppressed in sin, sold under sin.

But now glory be to you, Lord, my helper and my redeemer, by whose help and redemption I desire to be strengthened and preserved in your service. Lord, my helper as I strive toward you, because you had long ago become redeemer so that I might strive. For I do not wish to ascribe either the beginning or the completion of my course toward you to myself, lest, deceived again by pride, I begin to apostatize from you. Redeemed by you, freed from evils, I began to will the good; helped by you, I strive to reach the good end by running [Col. 0942C]. Yet I know that it does not belong to me who wills to accomplish what I will, nor to me who runs to arrive where I run, but to you who show mercy (Romans 9:16), that I may so will and run as not to will or run in vain, Lord, my helper and my redeemer.

Glory to the Father, who is that highest heaven of whom it was said in this Psalm: “His going forth is from the highest heaven.” Glory to the Son, who went forth through the Incarnation and returned through the Resurrection and Ascension unto its height, from which he had gone forth. Glory to the Holy Spirit, the everlasting warmth and love of Father and Son, of whom it is said: “There is none who can hide himself from his heat.”

## PSALM XIX

[Col. 0941]

[Col. 0941D] **May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation.**

**(VERSE 1.) UNTO THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID.**

The title is clear.

The subject of this Psalm is the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to John. In John’s account, our Lord Jesus Christ prayed at greater length on the Mount of Olives on the day of tribulation, when he had already been betrayed by Judas and was about to be seized by his enemies. Then, being in agony, he was distressed for us, “and his sweat became like drops of blood running down upon the ground” (Luke 22:44). As John relates, “lifting up his eyes to heaven, he said: Father, the hour has come: glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you. As you have given him power over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him. And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. I have glorified you upon the earth: I have completed the work which you gave me to do. And now, Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was. I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. They were yours, and you gave them to me; and they have kept your word. Now they have known that all things which you gave me are from you, because I have given them the words which you gave me; and they have received them and have truly known that I came forth from you, and they have believed that you sent me.

“I pray for them. I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you gave me, because they are yours. And all that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine; and I have been glorified in them. And now I am no longer in the world, yet these are in the world, and I come to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you gave me, that they may be one as we also are. While I was with them, I kept them in your name. Those whom you gave me I guarded, and none of them perished except the son of perdition, that the Scripture might be fulfilled. But now I come to you, and I speak these things in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. I do not pray that you should take them out of the world, but that you should keep them from evil. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. Sanctify them in truth. Your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, I also have sent them into the world. And for them I sanctify myself, that they too may be sanctified in truth.

“Yet I pray not for them only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word: that all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you; that they also may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me. And I have given them the glory which you gave me, that they may be one as we are one. I in them and you in me, that they may be made perfect in one, and that the world may know that you sent me and loved them as you loved me. Father, those whom you gave me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory, which you gave me because you loved me before the foundation of the world. Righteous Father, the world has not known you; but I have known you, and these have known that you sent me. And I have made your name known to them, and will make it known, that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them” (John 17).

Everything which is asked before the Passion in the words of this prayer is sought and demanded from God the Father more forcefully by the loud cry of his Passion and blood. For if Abel’s blood cried to God, much more did Christ’s blood cry to the Father—not, as Abel’s did, seeking vengeance, but seeking pardon even for his enemies who had shed that blood, as the Son himself said to the Father: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Thus the fourth *periocha* [section] now begins with this Psalm, because the supreme matter of faith is plainly treated here: namely, as has already been said, the Passion of Christ, praying through his Church before the cross and sacrificing himself upon the altar of the cross. The prophet, perceiving beforehand the fragrance of this whole burnt offering and hearing his prayer from afar, spoke not in doubt but in benevolent desire:

**VERSE 2. May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation.** And we, now, say to him who sits at God’s right hand and intercedes for us; we say with the prophet, with the saints of old, and do not cease saying until the end of the age: “May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation”—not because we know this to be necessary for his hearing, but because, from excessive longing, we join our prayers, like mute letters, to that vocal and crying prayer.

For just as in grammar mute letters have no sound of their own unless joined with vowels—hence mute or semivocal letters are called consonants, that is, sounding together, because by themselves, when joined without vowels, they do not sound, but when joined to vowels sound with them—so the prayers of all the saints, as though mute and making no sound in the presence of God the Father in the heavenly court, could not be heard unless the Word made flesh, a Word wholly vocal and more than vocal, were found among human prayers or mingled with the consonants. Therefore, not doubting that Christ praying and interceding for us has been heard and will always be heard because of his reverence, we join to him in prayer the desiring vows of our prayers, saying with the prophet:

**May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation.**

May our Lord, your Father, hear your prayer, Christ, which you made on the day of tribulation, on the day of your Passion. Likewise, may the Lord hear the intercessions which you now make in heaven. Yet we know—and the prophet foresaw—that your prayer has already been heard, in that the Lord saved his Christ by raising him from death and placing him at his right hand. But so long as one of your least members is afflicted, prayer is made in the day of your tribulation, both by the Church crying amid tribulations and by you interceding for her in heaven.

Therefore I, David the prophet—or I, any Psalmist, in this Psalm “unto the end,” that is, unto consummation, according to its foregoing title—ask that finally and completely the Lord Father may hear you, Christ, in the day of this tribulation. For you, indeed, this day has been changed into a day of exultation, Christ, to whom we sing on the day of the Resurrection: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Psalm 107 [118]:24). But for us, your least members, it is still a day of tribulation. Therefore the hearing of your prayer on our behalf is most necessary for us. Thus we say: “May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation.”

That is, may he hear you above in heaven so that he may protect you in your members below on earth. May the name of the God of Jacob protect you—that is, all who are yours. May the God of Jacob, who blessed Jacob the younger when his elder brother was supplanted and rejected, protect you, that is, those called from the Gentile people unto blessing through the motherly compassion of the apostles, as though through Rebecca.

May he protect you lest either an external enemy, like Laban pursuing, destroy you in your least members; or—what is more to be feared—lest he who is both brother and enemy, like Esau, kill you in your least members, who are likened to Jacob the younger son, and, following Jacob’s example, are simple, dwelling simply in the tent of the Church with their mother—that is, with the apostolic Church—while the elder brother is occupied in hunting. Therefore, in these simple persons, like Jacob, may the name of the God of Jacob protect you, Christ, lest perhaps wicked Esau, the bad brother, the false Christian, come and strike the mother with her children; strike Leah or Rachel, that is, destroy the virtue of good action and holy contemplation together with their children, that is, their fruits.

For when Jacob came from Syria with his two wives and their maidservants, with their children and very many flocks, he greatly feared Esau his brother. Therefore he prayed and said: “Lord, who said to me, Return to the land of your birth, deliver me from the hand of my brother, for I greatly fear him, lest perhaps he come and strike the mother with her children” (Genesis 32:9, 11). How much more, Lord Jesus Christ, now that a multitude of believers has been gathered among the Gentile peoples—of whom the active and contemplative lives have been instituted like mothers of many children, and who abound in flocks of simple dispositions, as in flocks of sheep—are you to be believed to pray in heaven for such persons, lest, as has been said, the bad brother strike the mother with her children and the companies of flocks advancing in distinct order.

Therefore, while you pray thus, while you have wives, children, and flocks, may the name of the God of Jacob protect you, so that as that Jacob was not injured by his wicked brother—not in himself, his wives, his children, the maidservants and their children, or his flocks—so you too may now be protected, through the name of the God of Jacob, from Esau. That name is in you, because you are the God of Jacob, and it has been invoked over those who are yours. Esau, as Scripture says, meets you with four hundred men (Genesis 33:1).

The four hundred men are those who profess the Decalogue of the law but seek temporal things alone through keeping the law. For forty times ten, or ten times forty, makes four hundred; and the law, consisting of ten commandments, is signified by the number ten. Temporal things, which vary with the four seasons, are signified by the number four. Therefore the four hundred men who accompany Esau, the carnal brother, are all who adhere to Antichrist, whether they are his contemporaries or precede or follow him, because they accompany him in this: that through the profession of the law they pursue temporal gain. These, along with Esau, meet Jacob as he returns to the land of his birth, because such persons, together with Antichrist, oppose Christ as he returns with his own and leads his own to the land of their birth—the land of promise, the land of milk and honey, grain, wine, and oil; that is, the land of paradise—from this land of most wretched sojourn.

But, O Christ! O Jacob, holy shepherd of the sheep! You who greatly love Leah, who bears good children, but love Rachel, who sees clearly, still more: may the name of the God of Jacob protect you together with all your offspring, your flocks, and all the possessions belonging to you!

**VERSE 3. May he send you help from the sanctuary, and defend you from Zion.** May he send help from the sanctuary to you, that is, to all who are yours: from yourself. Or, may the eternal Father send help from the sanctuary—that is, from the Word united to you as man—to you, praying as man on the day of tribulation and agonizing for those who are yours. Or, from the inward secret of the whole Trinity.

Alternatively: may your Father send help from the sanctuary to you, that is, to any of your little ones not yet holy, from some holy and perfect believer of yours, so that there may never fail in the Church a holy man through whom one not holy may receive help. Or, may he send help to you, that is, to your body wandering on earth, from that holy body of yours which reigns in heaven in yourself and in your elect who already reign with you.

“And from Zion defend you.” May the Lord Father defend you in your holy little ones least suited to contemplation, from Zion—that is, from the contemplation of those who are lofty and contemplative, signified by Mount Zion. For the name Zion is interpreted “contemplation,” because Mount Zion signifies the lofty speculative or contemplative life; and through this, with God protecting her, the holy Church is safe against all errors. But I see various dangers to your Church, or body, in the day of your tribulation; and therefore I ask for help against each one.

First, a bloodthirsty man, like Esau, will persecute you, the true Jacob, in the tyrants from Nero to Diocletian, seeking by the slaughter of bodies to extinguish your name. Against such an Esau and all his accomplices, murderers of bodies, may the name of the God of Jacob protect you. For this is the red horse, and, as John says in the Apocalypse, “a great sword was given” to the devil who sits upon it (Revelation 6:4). Against this sword may the name of the God of Jacob protect you, lest it perhaps strike the mother with her children, as was said above. And even if this great sword kills the bodies of the saints, may it nevertheless not kill their souls by separating them from God.

The second danger is the crowd of heretics, who in the Apocalypse are signified by the black horse: “and he who sat upon it had a balance” (ibid., 5). For the lie against the testimony of truth proceeded from a balance, when, although angels and apostles bore witness, abundant money was given to the soldiers concerning the glory of Christ risen from the dead, so that by their lie they might confirm the lie of the Jews who said that Christ had not risen from the tomb but had been stolen away while they slept. Therefore he who sat upon this horse had a balance: because the devil, father of lies, gave abundant money for a lie and persuaded others to give it. Or he held a balance in his hand because, through Arius, his black horse, [Col. 0947A] wholly opposed to the white horse—that is, the Catholic Church—he presumed to introduce between Father and Son, as it were, a different weight by means of a deceitful balance.

Against such a weigher, and his other heretical accomplices—for example Macedonius, who did not weigh Father, Son, and Holy Spirit rightly, since he said that the Father was greater than the Son and the Holy Spirit less than the Son—the Church fought, almost down to the times of Pope Gregory, the great teacher, through holy contemplators of truth. Hence it is said: “May he send you help from the sanctuary, and from Zion may he protect you”; that is to say: unholy and uncontemplative men, sowing their lies craftily and weighing wrongly the three Persons, or Christ’s divinity and humanity, will oppose [Col. 0947B] the truth. Foreseeing them long beforehand, I, David the prophet—or I, any Christian who sees them already imminent or come—ask for the shield of prayer against them, and join my prayer to you, Christ, as you pray, saying: “May he send you help from the sanctuary, and from Zion may he protect you.”

May God the Father send help to you, Christ, to you who are Truth, against falsehood, from the holy company of the apostles; so that against the balance of the Jews, who purchased a lie with their money, the apostles may with great power render testimony to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord; and against the balance either of Arius, or of Macedonius, or of any other heresiarch who does not think and teach rightly concerning the natural co-equality of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; or concerning the true divinity of the man assumed into God; or [Col. 0947C] concerning the true humanity of the incarnate Word.

“From Zion may he protect you”: from the orthodox Fathers, great and lofty in the contemplation of truth, as from Mount Zion, may your Father, the Father of truth, protect you—that is, your simple members—against the devil, father of lies, who in his deceitful balance, through the teaching of heretics, displays weight against weight, greater against lesser: when he blasphemously declares either that the Son is less than the Father, or that the Holy Spirit is subsequent to, or less than, Father and Son; or when, by wrongly weighing the glory of the assumed man and the glory of the Word assuming him, he proclaims in Christ different glories because of the different natures of divinity and humanity; or, because of the one glory of divinity and humanity, confounds Christ’s two natures into one. Whereas “every tongue [Col. 0947D] should confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is in one simple glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:11), while cautious faith nevertheless distinguishes the nature of divinity from the nature of humanity in the one person of Christ. After the glorification of his resurrection and ascension, he, glorified in that glory which he had before the world was made, now has one indivisible glory and one indivisible brightness which he had before the world was made.

But the father of lies, who sits upon the black horse, varies with his balance the weights of glorified humanity and glorifying divinity in Christ, as though another glory had been bestowed upon humanity than that which the Word had with the Father before the world was made. Yet since the testimony of evangelical truth establishes that the glory, or brightness, [Col. 0948A] which the Word has with the Father was bestowed whole, not half, upon the assumed man, it would be the cunning of the wicked weigher [to assert otherwise]; and “every tongue should confess that our Lord Jesus Christ” is not half but whole “in the glory of God the Father.” Thus “the law went forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3), when contemplators of truth and lovers of Catholic peace—Ambrose, Hilary, Leo the Great, whose testimonies we interwove in the preceding psalm—together with the other orthodox Fathers, refuted heretics and schismatics, proclaimed the one glory of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and taught the one glory or brightness of divinity and humanity in Christ.

There followed, therefore, the third horse, “the pale horse [Col. 0948B] (Apoc. 6:8),” of false Christians. They do not rejoice in blood like the red horse, nor do they debate the truth of faith in a deceitful balance like the rider of the black horse; but they confess the truth of faith with their lips and deny it in their deeds. Hence they have pallor, as it were a middle and mixed color between the white horse of truth and the black horse of falsehood. For if they were entirely white, they would be wholly Catholic; if entirely black, they would be regarded as manifest heretics. But now they are colored pale, as it were in a mixed and middle hue, because “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. 10:36): insofar as they are enemies, they have something akin to blackness; but insofar as they are members of the household, they have something resembling whiteness.

The gathering of such persons is “the pale horse; and he who sits upon it, his name is Death, and power was given to him to kill with sword, hunger, death, and the beasts of the earth” (Apoc. 6:8). Through such persons the devil, whose name is Death, wields even the material sword against the devout. Although a sword as great as that given to Nero, Decius, or some other manifest persecutor of the Church—signified by the red horse—has not been given him, nevertheless a false Christian sometimes strikes a true one with a material sword. Or he strikes with that sword of which it is said: “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. 56:5). For evil conversations corrupt good morals.

They also kill by hunger—not so much hunger for bread or other bodily food [Col. 0948D] as hunger for hearing the word of God. For, “turning their hearing indeed away from the truth and turning aside to fables, they shall heap up teachers to themselves, having itching ears” (2 Tim. 4:3–4). When such teachers hold the chairs of doctors and shepherds in the Church of God, neither teaching nor feeding the people, there will be a great famine, like that once in Elijah’s time. Because of such teachers, heaven being shut, there will be no dew or rain of lesser or greater teaching; and when bread fails everywhere, Elijah is compelled to flee into the wilderness, where ravens feed him, and to Zarephath of Sidon, to a widow woman (3 Kings [1 Kings] 17:3, 9).

Give me an Elijah in such a time, and you will certainly see him driven into flight and reduced to waiting to be fed by ravens: scarcely finding a sinner who repents of his sin, which repentance is Elijah’s food, as though brought by ravens. A widow also feeds him—that is, any poor little soul gathering two sticks of the cross. But Jezebel, a rich and impious woman—or rather, the abundant multitude of the impious—persecutes him. In the Apocalypse she is described as one harlot, having fornicated with the devil: “the mother of fornications” (Apoc. 17:5). Certainly, when this Jezebel, the great harlot, persecutes any little one like Elijah, it happens that he sometimes lacks even bodily food, so that he counts it a favor if even a raven—that is, a secular person—offers him alms.

I know such a man, who, compelled by want of bread, was forced to beg bread even among foreigners, while Jezebel persecuted him, the rider of this pale horse chastising him by hunger and withholding from him his due provisions.

But because power was given to him to kill not only by sword and hunger, but also by death—that is, by deadly plague, while sitting in the chair of pestilence—and by the beasts of the earth: who could stand against this pale horse and its rider by human strength? At the beginning of diabolical deception there was one serpent, more crafty than all living creatures and beasts of the earth. Entering into it, the devil corrupted the whole human race with the poison of deception. But now this same devil has many beasts of the earth, creeping like serpents [Col. 0949C] within the paradise of the holy Church, or even of holy cenobitic life. As they spread their poisons, first human sensuality, like Eve in the weaker, is corrupted; then in many who are stronger the mind too is corrupted, becoming consenting to the depravity of the weak, while it either approves the depravity of carnal uncleanness or fails to punish it adequately. Once the judgment of manly justice is lost, in the one person of flesh and spirit—or in the Church or congregation of carnal and spiritual people—there comes to be one wickedness or uncleanness, as though woman and man had been poisoned by evil beasts.

For by the beasts we must understand those who are exceedingly wicked and crafty; by the woman, any who are soft and easily led astray; by men joined to such women, those strong persons who consent to the weak. Through this progression—of beasts to demons, women to beasts, and men to women—a long rope of sins is woven, by which even the strong Samson is sometimes deceived by a woman, bound, and blinded, when a person formerly virtuous becomes at times consenting to the multitude and habit of the wicked (Judg. 16:21).

Since, therefore, the rider of the pale horse harms in so many ways—killing by sword, hunger, death, and beasts of the earth—what remedy is to be used against him, and with what weapons is he to be fought? He does not permit the contests of martyrs, because he does not openly impose idolatrous worship on anyone, as the rider of the red horse did. This rider and driver of false brethren is not to be refuted by the testimonies and teachings of confessors, [Col. 0950A] because, though their mouths are false, they confess that they know God, crying aloud the faith which they attack by their conduct.

What, Christ our King, will become in this day of tribulation of your body, endangered beneath such a multitude? When Edom persecuted you, the true Jacob, in your body and person, the name of the God of Jacob protected you. For when the enraged Herod sought your life—he was Edom, earthly in both conduct and origin, since he is said to have been born of an Idumaean father and an Arabian mother—and was enraged against you, the true Jacob, like that ancient Edom seeking to kill you, then the name of the God of Jacob protected you, the true Jacob. For just as mother Rebecca advised her son Jacob to flee lest he should be killed (Gen. 27:43), [Col. 0950B] so our mother who is above, free, concerned for you while you were still a child, advised you to flee into Egypt. For behold, an angel of the Lord, one of the servants of the heavenly mother, “appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: Arise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt; and remain there until I tell you. For Herod will seek the child in order to destroy him” (Matt. 2:13).

And then indeed “a voice was heard in Ramah” (ibid., 8), Rachel, your beloved wife, weeping for her children. Yet while the name of the God of Jacob protected you, her husband, the true Jacob, although she “would not be comforted” for her children “because they are not” (ibid.), her consolation will at last be completed, when Jeremiah’s entire prophecy concerning Rachel and her children is fulfilled. For after Jeremiah says: “A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be comforted because they are not” (Jer. 31:15), words of comfort immediately follow, the prophet saying: “Thus says the Lord: Let your voice cease from weeping and your eyes from tears, because there is a reward for your work, says the Lord. And they shall return from the land of the enemy; and there is hope for your latter days, says the Lord, and your children shall return to their own borders” (ibid., 16–17).

Therefore, as is evident from this prophecy, beautiful Rachel, who would not receive temporal consolation for the death of her children—a death by which it came about that they are not—received eternal consolation from the resurrection of her children, by which resurrection it shall come about that these same children truly [Col. 0950D] are. Hence it is also said: “Your children shall return to their own borders, and there is hope for your latter days” (ibid., 31:17).

The holy Church imitates this rejection of consolation and subsequent reception of consolation by omitting, on the day of the slaughter of the Innocents, *Gloria in excelsis* and *Te Deum laudamus*, which are songs of joy, as though unwilling to be comforted concerning her children because they are not, having in some sense come through death into non-being. But on the octave of those same Innocents she resumes the songs of joy, because the octave commemorates the resurrection, and by the resurrection it shall come about that Rachel’s children, who now are not, truly are.

For although the souls of Rachel’s slain children are now beneath the altar of God, [Col. 0951A] nevertheless, as long as their bodies do not live, they themselves, as wholes, are in some manner not; but they await the full and complete being of their entire essence in the general resurrection, concerning which the prophet says: “Your children shall return to their own borders, and there is hope for your latter days.”

Therefore, having received the most firm hope of resurrection, let the Church’s voice cease from weeping for her slain children, and let her celebrate with joy this present day, the octave of the slain Innocents. For behold, while we write these things, the day of the octave of the little ones dawns upon us—God, as we believe, ordaining it—so that what we say about the octave of the Innocents may taste more sweetly because today, while the octave is being discussed, their octave itself is also celebrated. Therefore on this day we desire that the consolation of the whole beautiful Rachel, the Church, may increase, [Col. 0951B] and that the Idumaean king may be confounded.

And may the name of the God of Jacob protect you, Christ, supplanter of the prince of this world, in your members, as it protected you in yourself from the persecution of Herod, the Idumaean king. This prayer of the prophet has already, thanks be to God, been answered: in the time of the martyrs, although Rachel’s children were slain, the mother was not slain with her children, since the God of Jacob protected Rachel herself, Jacob’s wife—that is, the holy Catholic Church—which became more fruitful in the children taken from her.

For just as long ago Rachel’s son Joseph, when he was said to have been devoured by a beast (Gen. 37:33) and utterly removed from the land, himself ruled throughout all the land of Egypt and there begot Ephraim and Manasseh, seed-plots of many peoples (Gen. 41:50); so too the blessed martyrs, when they were believed removed from the land, began through miracles to rule throughout all the land of Egypt, that is, throughout the extent of the whole world. Above all, Christ himself, prince of martyrs, ruled more after being killed than while living. For before death he was known in Judaea alone; after death, what does he say? “All,” he says, “power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:28). Therefore, as was said, the psalmist’s prayer, “May the name of the God of Jacob protect you,” has been answered fully.

Likewise, what is said, “May he send you help from the sanctuary, and from Zion may he protect you,” has been sufficiently answered, O Christ. For when lying Pharisees persecuted the truth of your teaching in your own person, God the Father sent you help from the sanctuary. Since you were the living temple of God, in which Divinity was as a sanctuary, from this sanctuary, from this holy oracle, fitting answers were supplied to you, speaking humanly as man, against the malicious arguments of falsehood.

For example, when those wicked plotters said to you: “Master, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar or not?” help immediately came to you from the oracle of the sanctuary of divinity, so that you answered most fittingly: “Show me the tribute coin.” And they offered him a denarius. “And Jesus said to them: Whose image and inscription are these?” They said to him: “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them: “Render therefore [Col. 0952A] to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:16 ff.).

Likewise we venerate the Father protecting you from Zion whenever we fittingly admire those answers which you drew most appropriately from contemplation of the Scriptures. For example, when you said: “Is it not written in your law that the testimony of two men is true?” (John 8:17). Again, it is written, “My house is a house of prayer” (Luke 19:46). Similarly, wherever the matter required it, you answered most fitting testimonies from Zion, that is, from contemplation of the Old Testament. And in the times of heretics, against the assault of falsehood, God the Father sent help from the sanctuary to every divinely illumined intellect of a confessor, and strengthened you from Zion, when he abundantly supplied those confessors and defenders of your truth with appropriate testimonies from their contemplation of the Scriptures. For so it is read in Hebrew: “May he send you help from the sanctuary, and from Zion may he strengthen you.”

It is clear, therefore, that in your person, seated upon the white horse—that is, made a rider by the man assumed and personally united to you—you fought victoriously against the red horse, outwitting Herod by your escape and flight, and outwitting Pilate by your resurrection. No less victoriously you fought against the black horse, outwitting the enemies of truth with most cautious and wise answers. Likewise, in your members you mocked the red horse and its rider through the martyrs; through the confessors you stripped the black horse and its rider of their strength.

[Col. 0952C] But what you did against the pale horse, and what you instruct us to do, must be examined all the more carefully because its rider is named Death. This conflict with the pale horse and its rider threatens deadly wounds, because the rider is called Death inasmuch as, as stated above, he brings death not in one but many ways: by material and spiritual sword; by hunger for the word of God and for due maintenance; by death of body and soul; by beasts of the earth—that is, evil spirits serving him—or even by beasts of the earth under human appearance, concealing bestial ferocity and serpentine crookedness, and performing in the holy Church the office of the beast which in paradise was more crafty than all living creatures, as we mentioned above.

[Col. 0952D] We recognize Judas as such a beast, such a pale horse: under the appearance of an apostle, an enemy and apostate; under the office of Christ’s ministry, a minister of the devil; under the name of a disciple, Christ’s betrayer. Neither the steadfastness of truth in Christ’s teaching, which he heard, nor the steadfastness of patience in Christ’s passion, which he saw, prompted him in any way toward good; but the power of the mystical supper alone expelled him. For when he had received the morsel by which the betrayer was designated, he immediately went out, as Hilary the teacher relates; he was not admitted to the communion of the heavenly sacraments, which the Lord celebrated after Judas’ departure, after he had supped and completed the old Passover.

For holy Hilary says thus in his exposition on Matthew: “After Judas the betrayer is identified, the Passover is performed without him, when the cup has been received and the bread broken; for he had not been worthy of communion in the eternal sacraments. For he is understood to have departed immediately from this point, since he is shown returning with the crowds. Nor indeed could he drink with God, since he was not to drink in the kingdom, when he promised that all those who drank this fruit of the vine would later drink it with him.”

Although others think differently about this matter, from Matthew, Mark, and John it is beyond doubt gathered that Judas was not present at the sacrifice of the New Testament, although the text of Luke’s Gospel seems to imply otherwise. But the agreement of the evangelists is not now under discussion. Rather, the question is how the pale horse—such as Judas was, a household enemy—together with its rider, is to be overcome and expelled from the society of Christ’s true disciples: one whom neither teaching of truth by word nor the steadfast example of the Passion can bend to assent to the good, which even when known he does not find pleasing. Let us see what the Lord did against such a one.

He humbly washed Judas’ feet with those of the other disciples, and lovingly granted him the banquet of his supper; but he excluded him from the sacrament of his body and blood. From this sacrament he now likewise excludes Judas’ like, some of whom, although they communicate sacramentally in the mystical food of the altar, nevertheless remain fasting from that delight of the life-giving bread of which it is said: [Col. 0953C] “You gave us bread containing every delight and every sweetness of flavor” (Wis. 16:20).

Yet if we prepare worthily for the breaking of this bread, washing the feet not only of friends but also of enemies, ready to keep the Scripture’s command: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink” (Rom. 12:20), and if, acting thus toward evil people as Christ acted with Judas, we finally separate those unwilling to be corrected, insofar as we can and ought: then beyond doubt there will be such an expulsion of the impious as befell Judas, who “departing hanged himself” (Matt. 27:5), and, hanging, “burst asunder in the midst, and his entrails were poured out” upon the ground (Acts 1:18), through the power of the saving sacrifice. By this sacrifice Christ first offered himself in the form of bread and wine, a holocaust kindled by the fire of love; then upon the altar of the cross, once more a holocaust wholly consumed not only by the fire of love but also by that of suffering.

For as the sacrifice of the paschal lamb produced different effects for Israelites and Egyptians—deliverance for the former, devastation for the latter—effects respectively of deliverance and devastation, which could not be wrought by all the preceding plagues; so now the perfect deliverance of the good and the perfect humiliation of the wicked, which could not be accomplished by the battles of martyrs and the contests of confessors, are believed to be brought about by the mystical immolation of the sacred victim, especially if those who are to celebrate it hold fast to Christ’s footsteps both in holy love for the good and in prudent zeal [Col. 0954A] against the bad. To make this clearer, let us consider Christ’s own examples in both respects.

Concerning love, the testimony of the holy evangelist is enough for us: “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end” (John 13:1). He loved them with a love so great and of such a kind that none is greater. For no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends. And at the Last Supper nearly his whole discourse concerned the commendation of love alone; setting forth examples of it in himself, he said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 15:12).

But how great was his zeal regarding the false disciple—whether to convert him within, or cast him out before distributing the ineffable sacrament of his body [Col. 0954B] and blood, which he judged fit to be shared only by those who would drink with him in the kingdom—requires careful examination. It is necessary not merely to know this, but also to imitate it, if we wish rightly to approach the celebration of that same sacrament.

On another occasion Christ himself, instructing his followers in the zeal of fraternal correction, said: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone; if he hears you, you have gained your brother.” But “if he does not hear you, take with you one or two” witnesses. “And if he does not hear them, tell the Church. If he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican” (Matt. 18:15–17). Behold, the diligent and prudent exercise of brotherly zeal toward a false brother, to be persistently practiced by every good brother until he is either converted or, if unwilling to be converted, finally treated as a heathen, is described; nor is he to be allowed communion in the divine sacraments.

Not content to have taught this in words, Christ himself taught it by example. For, when about to celebrate the new Passover, he first celebrated the old Passover, the celebration of which was a kind of preparation for the new. In this very preparation he was moved by such zeal toward the false disciple that he first rebuked him privately, between himself and Judas alone, and then with witnesses present. For he said: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. Nevertheless, [Col. 0954D] the hand of him who betrays me is with me at table” (Luke 22:15, 21). Again: “Amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me” (Matt. 26:21).

By so speaking Christ rebuked his betrayer privately, between himself and Judas alone, because no one other than the guilty man himself could understand whose guilt and conscience was touched by such words. Afterwards, so that the word of this rebuke might stand in the mouth of two witnesses, at Peter’s prompting, that disciple whom Jesus loved, who also reclined at supper upon his breast, asked in a somewhat subdued voice: “Lord, who is it that will betray you?” The Lord said to him: “It is he to whom I shall give the dipped bread.” And having dipped the morsel, “he gave it to Judas” (John 13:25–26). Behold, he was rebuked again in the presence of two witnesses, namely Peter and John.

Finally, while the disciples asked one by one, “Is it I, Lord?” Judas too dared to say: “Is it I, Rabbi?” (Matt. 26:22, 25). The Lord replied: “You say it; and indeed the Son of Man goes as has been decreed concerning him. But woe to the man through whom he will be betrayed” (ibid., 24). While the Lord said this, with the apostolic Church as witness, Judas was openly rebuked and counted among heathens and publicans. For what was it to say, “You say it,” except as though he said: You, who are conscious of this crime, speak the truth about yourself? And what was it to say, “Woe to the man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed,” except to excommunicate the betrayer himself?

But lest anyone seem, by this example, to be excommunicated for a crime contemplated but not yet committed, it should be noted that he did not say, “Woe to the man who has resolved to do this,” but, “Woe to the man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed,” so that Judas might understand that he would then be placed under the curse of excommunication if he brought his contemplated crime to effect. For if he had been excommunicated before the crime was committed, he would not have been admitted to kiss Christ himself.

Christ’s final admonition was given when the criminal act was already imminent: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48). Again: “Friend, for what have you come?” (Matt. 26:50). But once the crime had been committed, he was immediately placed under the curse, nor did he thereafter have any communion with Christ’s disciples. As stated above, and attested by holy Hilary, he is understood to have gone out before the distribution of Christ’s body because, immediately after supper was finished and a short interval had passed, he is shown returning with the crowds.

Behold, we have set forth teaching and examples not only of love to be maintained toward the good but also of ardent zeal to be exercised toward the bad, especially by priests diligently attending to preparation for the sacraments which they are to celebrate. If they imitate these examples of Christ, both their sacrifice and their holocaust will be acceptable: a sacrifice worthy to be held in God’s remembrance, and a rich holocaust, overflowing with the fat and richness of a twofold love—first for God, who is honored by such sacrifice; then for one’s neighbor, who is aided by such sacrifice and holocaust, either that he may more quickly be converted or at least more quickly be hindered from his wickedness, lest by sinning long he store up for himself greater punishments on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s righteous judgment.

But because here, for the first time in our exposition of the Psalms, the terms *sacrifice* and *holocaust* occur together, it must be said what difference there is between these two, and we must discuss them at somewhat greater length.

A sacrifice in the Law was called that victim of which one part was burned upon the altar by the holy fire, and another part was set aside—namely, the right shoulder and the breast, “the shoulder of separation and the breast of elevation” (Exod. 29:26). These two portions were assigned for the food of the priest who sacrificed the victim, so that by his own food he might be taught how he himself ought to live and how he ought to instruct others. These things were written especially for the priests of our time, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. Whether in private confession or public instruction, as they deal with different persons placed under Christian discipline and offered, as it were, to the temple of the Lord, they make a sacrifice of some and a holocaust of others.

For a holocaust is called a wholly burned offering, when nothing is separated from the victim but the whole is burned upon the altar. A holocaust is “a virgin who thinks of the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Cor. 7:34) in Christ Jesus our Lord; because nothing in such a holocaust is separated, but all is burned by the fire of divine [Col. 0956B] love into the sweetest fragrance. “But he who has a wife thinks of the things of this world, and is divided” (ibid., 33): partly intent upon pleasing God, and partly concerned with pleasing his wife. Such a man is offered to God as a sacrifice by his priest or confessor, because one part of him is consumed by the fire of divine love and another part is set apart. Yet the sacrifice is not despised on account of the part set apart, since this part is not without reason called the right shoulder “of separation” and the “breast of elevation.”

The right shoulder, also called the separated portion, signifies that the action of such a person in serving his wife or this world should itself be separated from the world which lies in evil, and so regulated that through it he may be numbered among those who will hear from the Judge on the Judge’s right hand: “I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink,” and so forth (Matt. 25:35). Those wholly devoted to divine service and made into a holocaust will not stand in judgment, but will sit beside the holy apostles, for there thrones will be set in judgment, thrones over the house of David. But those who become a sacrifice now feed the high priest in his poor, not only through the right shoulder, through “the shoulder of separation,” but also through “the breast of elevation,” which signifies the cheerfulness of good will, in which “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). For if someone gives alms to a poor person out of sadness or necessity, [Col. 0956D] he does not join the breast of elevation to the right shoulder, because sadness presses the breast down to the depths, whereas cheerfulness lifts it to things above.

Otherwise: the right shoulder, the portion of separation, is given as food to the priest so that he may recognize that he ought to work in such a way that his left hand does not know what his right hand does, lest his action be found associated with the actions of the people, from whom it ought by its excellence to be separated. The breast of elevation is also given to him, so that the power and loftiness of heavenly contemplation may always remain in his breast, lest he say idly, “We have lifted up our hearts to the Lord,” but may be able to say with the Apostle: “But our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

### Another Interpretation

That the right shoulder of the separation-offering, together with [Col. 0957A] the breast of elevation, is not burned upon the altar with the sacred fire signifies that, in the Lord’s sacrifice, separation is necessary when one scandalizes the sacrificer—whether it be the right hand, as it were the right shoulder—who for that very reason is worthy of outward separation or excommunication, because he had already been secretly separated even while seeming to be within the body of the Church. “Many went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.” The breast of elevation may be understood as the person of whom it is said in the Gospel: “If your right eye scandalizes you, tear it out and cast it away from you” (Matt. 5:29). For unless the breast swelled in self-exaltation, the understanding would neither scandalize nor be scandalized in contemplation. Therefore, just as in the [Col. 0957B] Law the breast of elevation is separated from the sacred fire—by which pride, hateful to God and men, is condemned—so in the Gospel the right eye, when it scandalizes, is commanded to be torn out and cast away. By this is condemned the perverse understanding which accompanies pride and is therefore damnable together with it, and must be separated from the sacred fire of the altar.

But where among the assembly of the faithful there is no member worthy of separation, there truly an all-burnt offering is made so much the richer as the faithful people themselves are increased more in merit and in number, and are filled, as it were, with the fat of good will and the richness of devout action. We find examples of both matters in the holy Gospel. For at the Lord’s supper, as was mentioned above, Judas—the most wicked trader—was a right shoulder [Col. 0957C] by office, but left by merit, already separated in spirit from the apostles. He was also a right eye, but a scandalizing one: right by his resemblance to what is good, scandalizing by the purpose of his malice and wickedness. Therefore the High Priest himself, as has been shown beforehand, in order lawfully to complete his sacrifice, separated there the shoulder of separation—though it was right, though it seemed very useful in its office. For when precious ointment was poured over Christ’s head before the Passion, Judas himself said: “Why this waste? For this could have been sold for much and given to the poor” (Matt. 26:8–9). The other disciples agreed with his words as though they were good and useful. But Jesus, who knew his wickedness, separated that shoulder—falsely right, truly left—[Col. 0957D] and that scandalizing eye; and he sanctified the remaining disciples in the mystical sacrifice, as he said in his prayer: “And for them I sanctify myself, that they too may be holy in truth” (John 17:19).

When he says, “I sanctify myself,” it is as if he said: “I sanctify myself by cutting off, namely, a certain member of myself, so that they too may be sanctified,” or “sanctified in truth,” namely by the removal of the deceptive vanity of false brethren. Thus I sanctify, or sacrifice, myself, making of myself an evening sacrifice for all my own, so that they too may be sanctified—entirely separated, namely, from false brethren—and made an acceptable sacrifice in truth without an admixture of falsehood. For unless they first become a sacrifice by the separation of evils, an all-burnt offering could not be made. Thus, in the Lord’s Passion, his disciples became a sacrifice when certain false disciples were separated from their fellowship because of the scandal of the cross.

But once these same disciples had been confirmed in faith in the Resurrection, and the number of the apostles had been completed through the election of Matthias, when they were together in the upper room, numbering as many as one hundred and twenty disciples, among whom there was no false disciple, “suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting; and divided tongues, as of fire, appeared to them” (Acts 2:2–3). Through this fire, of which they saw a certain signification in fiery tongues, their hearts became flaming; melted together into one [Col. 0958B] all-burnt offering, they were thenceforth incapable of any division, because “they had one heart and one soul” in God (Acts 4:32).

Nor was that all-burnt offering lean, but exceedingly rich, abounding in the same richness as that fatted calf which had been slain and made an all-burnt offering for them. For although his individual actions and sufferings throughout thirty-three years are to be counted as many sacrifices, his final immolation itself—whether at the supper, where, after Judas had been removed, he offered himself and gave himself to the disciples under the form of bread and wine; or on the Mount of Olives, where he sacrificed himself in prayer, when before the disciples he began to be afraid and troubled, and “his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground” [Col. 0958C] (Luke 22:44); or on the altar of the cross, where by dying he destroyed our death—must be regarded as a great and rich all-burnt offering.

If he had been sacrificed for few, he would by no means have been a fatted calf. Therefore, while praying on the Mount of Olives, after he had prayed for the disciples, lest the sacrificial calf seem lean when only they were saved—the means by which so depraved a portion of peoples would be saved—he added: “I pray not for these alone, but also for those who will believe through their word, that they all may be one, as we also are one” (John 17:20–21).

See how fatted this calf is; how greatly enfleshed, how rich, how full-bodied, how [Col. 0958D] enlarged in great and many members through the fat of charity: he sacrificed himself not only for the disciples but also for all who would believe through their word. Into their fellowship he admits the multitude of the nations through the faith of a few disciples, not as an assessor of merits but as a lavish giver of pardon. “I,” he says, “pray for them; I pray not for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours” (ibid. 9). See how this priest, who became both priest and victim amid the fires of the all-burnt offering, remained mindful of sacrifice by separating the unbelieving world, which lies in the evil one, from those who would believe through the disciples’ word.

But because enough has now been said, so far as concerns us, concerning the law of sacrifice, something must still be said—with the help of him of whom we speak—about the richness of this all-burnt offering, whose fragrance is most sweet [Col. 0959A].

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1). Just as some great wisdom or art lies hidden within an ingenious mind, so this only-begotten Word was with the unbegotten Father. And just as wisdom goes outward through works wisely ordered in accordance with that wisdom and in some manner becomes visible, though it had been invisible—for example, if the art of music lay hidden in a wise person’s heart, and according to that art great and many musical instruments were made, then music, formerly invisible in the mind, has in a sense become visible and has gone forth through the marvelous work, though without leaving the mind—[Col. 0959B] so the Word was in the beginning with God; but in order to go forth, according to what is written, the Word walked and went out into the fields: “all things were made through him” (ibid. 3).

Therefore, just as the subtle art of music in the capacity of the mind becomes, as it were, coarser and more substantial in musical instruments, so that it can be seen, touched, and heard, and sweetly perceived by the unskilled, so the subtle Word of God is in some manner apprehended as substantial through those things which were made in him and through him, when, as the Apostle says, God’s “invisible things are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made” (Rom. 1:20). His eternal power is likewise perceived even by the impious, so that they are without excuse.

Again, just as the subtle art of music is transferred from the mind onto parchment, when the subtle rules of the musical art are written down, to be observed in small and large musical instruments in measure, number, and weight—as is evident in organs, where the size of the pipes is differentiated and their number and weight vary according to the invisible pattern of the art which is in the mind—so the subtle Word of God, expressed from the Father’s heart through the Scriptures of truth, contains rules by which every creature, and more particularly the whole Church or any faithful soul, ought to be so ordered that its measure, number, and weight visibly and perceptibly accord with the same rules of truth. The Father invisibly dictated these rules in the same Word and displayed them visibly through creation and Scripture, [Col. 0959D] to be subtly seen and read and to be observed in all measure, number, and weight of human works. Thus the subtlety of the eternal Word appears rich, as it were, through a certain substantiality of works ordered according to it—especially when someone makes from them an all-burnt offering by attributing to God everything found to have been well done, while keeping the rule of God’s Word in measure, number, and weight.

For if anything in human actions departs from this rule, a sacrifice must first be made, so that through the sacrifice of repentance a person may ascribe to himself what has been wrongly done, and finally offer as an all-burnt offering to God alone—author of every good and of good alone—the whole and sole good.

And lest fitting richness should be absent from such an all-burnt offering, it was too little that the Word, eternally begotten of the Father, should have gone forth in this way through works and Scriptures. In his mercy he went forth further when he took hold of Abraham’s seed. Indeed, when the very Word of God—the very seed of God, through whose germination all visible and invisible things were made from nothing—willed to become Abraham’s seed, Abraham himself, the father rejoicing in the promise of this event, when he saw three and worshipped one, “ran to the herd and took from it a very tender calf” [Col. 0960A] (Gen. 18:7), baked unleavened bread, and made a feast.

Certainly the discerning patriarch foresaw that the Word of God would be incarnate from his flesh, so that he would be a most tender calf, most delightful to eat. He foresaw him full of grace and truth, as though of fatness and richness; therefore he rejoiced to see his day—a day which John declares that he saw, saying: “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). “And from his fullness,” John the Baptist says, “we have all received” (ibid. 16).

What John calls fullness, then, we may call richness or fatness, because limbs or bodies are called fat when they are full. But when they have been drained of fat or flesh, they are called neither full nor fat but lean. Therefore all “who received him,” to whom he “gave power to become children of God” (ibid. 12), long after him as lean people, as hungry people, as persons severely exhausted by hunger in a distant country. And we, foully wasted by leanness, [Col. 0960C] long with them until we all come to a perfect man, “to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13).

This will be accomplished in two ways: through the separation of evils and through the completion of every good thing belonging to the individual members of Christ’s body according to the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness. The separation of evils occurs through sacrifice; the completion and consummation of goods occurs through the all-burnt offering. Therefore, groaning amid evils which torment us within and press us without, because in ourselves we have no sacrifice acceptable to God, we have recourse to the one unique sacrifice which Christ offered to the Father in himself, [Col. 0960D] when he, though good, lived among the evil: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, sharing in no way in their impieties—indeed, by reproving the impious he became burdensome even to look upon for them. To live among these was for him a great sacrifice, worthy of everlasting remembrance. Therefore, Christ, we say to you:

**VERSE 4.** May the Lord remember all your sacrifice, so that by your living among the evil without the contagion of evils we may be delivered from every evil; and may the all-burnt offering of your immolation at your supper, on the Mount of Olives, and on the altar of the cross become rich for us, so that its sweet richness and rich sweetness may refresh us in such a way that, while awaiting your revelation, we lack nothing in any grace; and that, as you prayed on the Mount of Olives, we may be consummated into one, as you and the Father are one, and the love with which you loved us may be in us, and you in us.

Indeed, the Lord heard you when you prayed there against open persecutors and manifest heretics; but it remains necessary that he should hear you when, in the day of tribulation, you pray against false disciples comparable to Judas the betrayer and most wicked trader. For against persecutors like Herod you asked that your people be preserved in their corruptible bodies, yet in your name and in the name of your Father, so that through torments they might not be compelled to deny your name. And the Lord heard you in the day of tribulation, because in your martyrs the name of the God of Jacob protected you, lest you, the true Jacob, should be without consolation while Rachel your wife wept, with and in herself, for her children [Col. 0961B].

For that Rachel, as has been stated and expounded above, at first refused consolation when she considered her dying children; but she willingly accepted consolation upon considering future goods, among which the resurrection of Rachel’s children is an especially great consolation. Yet this too is a great consolation for Rachel and Jacob concerning their slain children: although they have been cast with Joseph, Rachel’s son, into the old cistern—that is, into the pit of death—and although they seem to have been devoured by a most wicked beast, being slain by most wicked torturers, nevertheless they rule throughout the whole land of Egypt, and even the evil spirits who are Egyptians obey them. The name of the God of Jacob protected you, Christ, the true Jacob, by hearing your prayer and preserving your martyrs in your name [Col. 0961C].

Likewise you prayed for your confessors, who were to be attacked by many errors. You especially regarded these when in your prayer you said: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you; as you have given him power over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him. And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:1–3). Thus, Christ, the Lord heard you when you prayed in the day of tribulation generally for all your people but especially for confessors.

For through their teaching the Father glorified you, his Son, because he gave them the Holy Spirit who illumined them and glorified you. In glorifying you, that Spirit received of what was yours and announced it to them, and taught them, so that while heretics blasphemed you, they might glorify you and teach that you are in the glory of the Father. And because you are the Word of God, they also glorified you in this: they clearly understood Scripture, previously obscure, and set it forth clearly in teaching. Thus they glorified the Word of God, which you are; and, removing the thick veil of figures, they showed Moses’ face to be bright through fellowship with the Word of God—that Word which you are, Christ, Son of God, who shone like the sun while speaking with Moses and Elijah on the mountain. Those two could not shine in comparison with you, although they had been glorified through participation in your brightness. Therefore your disciples who were there, lifting their eyes—having first seen three—at the end [Col. 0962A] of the vision saw no one except Jesus alone. For, as was said, what is bright by participation in your brightness is not bright in comparison with your clarity. Therefore, as the brightness of the stars vanishes in comparison with the sun, so the glory of Moses’ face vanishes before the surpassing glory of your brightness.

Utterly devoid of this brightness, blind heretics, O Father of Christ, have not known you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent. But holy confessors and Catholic men have truly not only believed by faith but also known by understanding that you, and Jesus Christ whom you sent, are the only true God. By demonstrating this with most lucid teachings and dispelling the darkness of heretics, they glorified your very Son. Indeed, you, Father, glorified your Son in them, as you had been asked by him when, praying in the day of tribulation, he said: “Father, glorify your Son.” Then you sent him help from the sanctuary and defended him from Zion, because by the Holy Spirit filling the hearts of the saints and from Zion—that is, from the contemplation of Scripture—the holy confessors triumphed over every assault of heretical perversity. And you, Christ, were glorified as the Son of God in the supreme glory of God the Father, lacking in your now-glorified humanity no brightness that belongs to your glorifying divinity, in which you are no less bright than the Father who glorifies you. Thus we acknowledge that we must confess a unity of brightness not only in the three persons of the one Godhead but also in the two natures of the one Christ. For although the divinity of the Word that assumed humanity glorified the humanity assumed, nevertheless the Word of God did not give it, or obtain for it from the Father, any glory other than that glory in which the Word himself was with the Father before the world was made [Col. 0962C].

It remains now, Lord Jesus Christ, that, for the full hearing of your prayer, God the Father may remember all your sacrifice, which you offered to him by remaining in the world while preserving yourself from evil, just as you desired also for your own when you said to the Father: “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil” (John 17:15). Your Apostle also taught this when he said: “Remove the evil from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5:13). Although this may fittingly be understood to mean that we should remove evil—that is, wickedness—from ourselves when we cannot remove it from others, nevertheless the Greek wording in which the Apostle wrote, commanding us to remove “the evil” from ourselves, signifies an evil man by a masculine accusative.

How we ought to remove this evil man from ourselves so that our sacrifice may be acceptable to God has been sufficiently shown above through Christ’s example: he removed Judas from himself when he offered the sacrifice of the old Passover, by which he prepared himself and his own for the all-burnt offering of the new Passover.
