We have indeed distinguished the differing times of persecutors, heretics, and false Christians, because of the distinctions among martyrs, confessors, and good—or true—Christians endangered in this age under the evil. [Col. 0963A] Yet false Christians were not lacking even in the time of martyrs or confessors, although the Lord’s threshing-floor was winnowed by the great fan of martyrdoms and confessions, and the malignant deceit with which that same floor is now full could scarcely then have lain hidden—as if chaff alone filled all the granaries.

Nor are martyrs or confessors lacking now, though they are rare, because the palm of martyrdom or the crown of confession is not now offered to the saints as it once was, when the glorious king of martyrs, the crown of confessors, conquered in martyrs while sparing confessors. Yet the present struggle is less glorious but no less dangerous, when the Church is harassed by “dangers from my own race, dangers among false brethren,” whereas formerly it was harassed by “dangers among the Gentiles” (2 Cor. 11:26). Therefore, while the Church is a pilgrim upon earth, it must pray against every persecutor to you, Christ, that the name of the God of Jacob may protect you; and against every heretic, that God the Father may send you help from the sanctuary and defend you from Zion. But we especially, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, hemmed in by the scarcity of good Christians and the abundance of evil ones, must under urgent necessity cry to you, Christ, that God the Father may remember all your sacrifice and that your all-burnt offering may become rich [Col. 0963B].

Therefore, instructed by saving precepts and still formed by divine institution, we pray; and, O Christ, we support you as you pray and sacrifice and offer a rich all-burnt offering, saying: May God the Father remember all your sacrifice, and may your all-burnt offering become rich. May he remember all your sacrifice, that we may remove from ourselves every evil as we ought; and may your all-burnt offering become rich for us, that we may possess in ourselves every good of which we have need, and love every good, so that we may have one heart and one soul with him. May he remember all your sacrifice, that we may turn away from evil; and may your all-burnt offering become rich for us, that we may do good. May he remember all your sacrifice, that our loins may be girded—restrained, namely, from every evil desire—while righteousness is the belt of our loins and faith the girdle of our reins; and may your all-burnt offering become rich for us, that the lamps burning in our hands may never be extinguished, while the richness of this all-burnt offering always abounds as fuel [Col. 0963D] for the fire in the vessel of our flesh.

May he remember all your sacrifice, that every Judas may go out and “his days become few” (Ps. 108:8); and may your all-burnt offering become rich, that another may receive his episcopal office—one worthy by the virtue of his merits and by divine election, like Matthias. May he remember all your sacrifice, that those who are not of us may go out from us; and may your all-burnt offering become rich, that their places may be filled by such members of the household as, having one heart and one soul in God, may never disagree with one another but may speak and think the same thing. May he remember all your sacrifice, that every prodigal son who squandered his substance in riotous living may, returning to himself, say: “I will arise and go to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants” (Luke 15:18–19).

Let him set forth all this as a victim to be offered to God the Father. But let this victim not be received as an all-burnt offering, because such a purpose is partly to be approved and partly separated and rejected: namely, his thought of becoming a hired servant though he was a son. Let God the Father therefore receive this sacrifice by recognizing the son, but separate from it as a right shoulder what pertains to the hired servant.

For there is no small difference between a slave, a hired servant, and a son. A slave is one who keeps the commandment solely out of fear of punishments. A hired servant is one who does not delight in service but in its reward. A son is one who delights in keeping the Father’s commandment even without regard to rewards. The hired servant says in his heart: “My food is what I shall receive as a reward when my labor is ended.” But what does the son say? “My food,” he says, “is to do the will of my Father.” The one is fed and delighted by what he awaits as the reward of labor; the other is fed and delighted by this very thing: that he labors according to the Father’s will.

A slave is brought into service through faith, believing that good things await the good and evil things the evil. He fears future evils for himself more than he hopes for future goods, because he does not yet have a good conscience from which he can hope for future goods; and therefore, fearing evils, he serves beneath the rod. But a slave becomes a hired servant when, as fear of evils diminishes, hope for future goods is born because of a good conscience, through which someone is conscious of past sin with sorrow and willingly guards against it in the future. This prodigal son was in such a state when he wished to be a hired servant. But when his father offered him the kiss, a sign full of love, through that very love he suddenly put off the garment of the hired servant and was clothed in the garment of a son—namely, the best robe; he received the ring, the pontifical sign; and, refreshed by the fatted calf, he became a rich son, while the hired servant nowhere appeared.

Thus, Lord, let every prodigal returning to the Father be received as a son, and let the hired servant be separated, so that the son’s return may be a sacrifice from which something is separated and something sanctified. Let him who wished to be a hired servant grow in the Father’s love, that he may be a son. To serve God in hope of future goods is indeed like a right shoulder. But as filial love advances, that shoulder will be separated when the hired servant becomes a son, who can say with Christ and in Christ: “My food is”—my delight is—“to do the will of my Father.”

May the Lord therefore remember, O Christ, all your sacrifice (John 4:34), so that every son still living in a far country may hasten back to the Father, at least driven by hunger, at least for wages. But once he has arrived and laid aside the disposition of a hired servant, then may your all-burnt offering become rich, so that, fully refreshed by the fatted calf after failing from hunger, he may sincerely say: “My food is to do the will of my Father.” By putting off the hired servant, let him offer you a sacrifice; by putting on the son, let him, now wholly made a son, [Col. 0965A] become an all-burnt offering. By rejecting the husks that were food for swine, let him offer a sacrifice; but as he learns to feast and rejoice with the Father, let him, wholly kindled by filial love, become an all-burnt offering. And let this all-burnt offering be rich, seasoned, namely, with the fatness of that fatted calf itself.

May he remember all your sacrifice, that we may be among the virgins who guard against the corruption of this world. Of those virgins a sacrifice will be made, because some are excluded and some admitted, while the bridegroom does not know the foolish virgins but is united in complete love with the wise. Therefore, lest we be excluded with the foolish, who lack the richness of oil, may your all-burnt offering become rich for us; and let our lamps not be extinguished through failing oil. Rather, through the sufficient richness of that oil, may we offer you a rich all-burnt offering not only in the lamps of manifest works but also in the vessels of hidden consciences, and present to you seven lamps burning before the throne. In their light, may we rejoice not merely for the hour of temporal favor but unto the perfect day of eternal blessedness [Col. 0965B].

May he remember all your sacrifice, that there may be many rich persons who retain some things for themselves and offer some things to you for the consolation of your poor; and may your all-burnt offering become rich, so that there may be such a multitude and holiness among the poor in spirit that you may worthily hear them not only for the salvation of the rich who do good to them, or of the poor who sympathize with them and wish them well, but also for the conversion of other rich persons who do them harm, or poor persons who envy them. Thus may a great all-burnt offering be made for you in the hearts of your poor, when not even an enemy is separated from their hearts so as not to be wished and sought good through the fire of charity: by that charity they love friends in you as your members and enemies for your sake, that they may become your members [Col. 0965C].

May he remember all your sacrifice, that perfect may be the renunciation by which, in receiving baptism or in the stricter vow of a holier purpose, we renounced the devil and all his works and pomps. And may your all-burnt offering become rich, that effective and heartfelt may be the profession by which we confessed that we believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord: who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried; descended into hell; rose from the dead on the third day; ascended into heaven; sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty; from there he shall come to judge the living and the dead. I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and everlasting life. Amen.

May your all-burnt offering also become rich in this: that we may fully observe, with love as lovers of spiritual beauty and fragrant with the good odor of good conduct, the profession of the stricter life which we have undertaken; and that we may live not as slaves under the law but as people made free under grace [Col. 0966A].

May he remember all your sacrifice, that he may fully hear and grant these three petitions: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; and lead us not into temptation; but deliver us from evil.” For through these three petitions of the Lord’s Prayer we prepare a sacrifice for God, while we desire our debts, temptations, and all evils to be separated from us. But we prepare an all-burnt offering when in four petitions we say: “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name; your kingdom come; your will be done, as in heaven so on earth. Give us this day our daily bread” [Col. 0966B]. Therefore, that in these four petitions we may be fully heard and answered for you, Christ: May your all-burnt offering become rich for us.

There is no time now to examine the richness of this all-burnt offering through each of these petitions. But concerning the daily or supersubstantial bread for which we ask, we urge this belief: this is the bread spoken of in the blessing of Asher, when Father Jacob blessed his sons. For he said: “Asher’s bread is rich, and he shall provide delicacies for kings” (Gen. 49:20). Rightly this rich bread provides delicacies for kings, because it has in itself every delight, every flavor of sweetness, and all that richness of which Father Isaac said to Jacob: “May God give you from the dew of heaven and from the richness of the earth abundance” (Gen. 27:28). Again, concerning the same one, he says: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 5:27 [probably 27:27]).

The entire fullness of this field is in this bread, which is called supersubstantial and daily. It is supersubstantial insofar as it feeds angels in heaven; daily because beneath heaven man eats the bread of angels. It is supersubstantial because it strengthens the perfect, establishes the human heart, and delights the healthy palate of faith, lest the perfect fail. It is daily because, carefully chewed by the mouths of the perfect—or even made milk in the body of Mother Church—it nourishes and sustains the weak, that they may advance every day. It is supersubstantial because it lifts up the lofty contemplation of the mind, so that minds may go beyond themselves and often be carried in ecstasy to God, while the supersubstantial food of sweetness which they receive in that ecstasy of mind is known to God alone. It is daily because it makes those same saints sober toward others and accommodating even in the daily dealings and conversations of human life [Col. 0966D].

Thus in this bread, both supersubstantial and daily, this very fact tastes sweetly: in the Lord’s Prayer one Evangelist, Matthew, calls it “supersubstantial bread” (Matt. 6:11), while another, Luke, calls it “daily bread” (Luke 11:3). Truly, in either name great richness and great sweetness are signified. Supersubstantial bread feeds Mary, delighting her to sit continuously at the table of that bread, however great the occupation of her sister Martha may be. The same bread, as daily bread, feeds Martha by strengthening her so that she may eagerly busy herself with frequent service, gladly feeding her shepherd in his poor—especially those who devote themselves to the Word, whether by teaching, as Christ did, or by listening, as Mary did. Of this Word there is daily strength for Martha in her labor, and supersubstantial sweetness for her sister Mary in her repose.

Through this bread, so rich and so full of every good richness, every sweetness, and all delights, may Christ the King’s all-burnt offering become rich for us, so that, delighted and satisfied in the most holy breaking and rumination of this bread, we may rejoice fully, and no one may take our joy from us or disturb it; rather, may it always remain unimpaired [Col. 0967B]. Thus, Lord, may your all-burnt offering become rich, giving us joy not for an hour but forever.

For in this place, where the Septuagint placed *diapsalma*, the Hebrews have *selah*, that is, “always.” In both languages the truth is expressed. For here, as though the day of tribulation had ended, the subject of the psalm is divided and a transition is made from the sorrow of the Passion to the joy of the Resurrection. Therefore *diapsalma* is fittingly inserted here. But the Hebrews, who have here *selah*, which is translated “always,” although through the veil placed over their face they do not see the light of eternity signified by “always,” nevertheless, though blind, convey light to others who see by this adverb frequently inserted into the psalms. As has been said, it signifies eternity; and its insertion is fitting here, joined to the all-burnt offering that will burn eternally, offered by that priest according to the order of Melchizedek, who possesses not a temporal priesthood like Aaron’s but an everlasting priesthood like Melchizedek’s. Hence he is able “to save forever those who approach [Note: [Col. 0967D] So the Codex.] God through himself,” always living to make intercession for his own—offering, namely, as an all-burnt offering for human salvation the assumed manhood, kindled with the whole fire of divinity. This all-burnt offering is forever rich in the sight of God the Father.

And indeed you, Christ, great priest, “in the time of wrath became reconciliation” (Ecclus. 44:17), when on the day of tribulation you offered sacrifice and a whole burnt offering. Concerning this we have already said something, as far as we could with your gift; from it still more is to be inferred. But when that day of tribulation had ended, there succeeded to it—the day of tribulation and passion—a joyful day of resurrection, not only for you but also for those whom you freed from hell, many of whose bodies rose and entered the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem. Therefore let us exult and rejoice in it, proceeding through the following words of the psalm, all of which refer to that very day of exultation. For now, while you sit at the right hand of the Father, the hearts of your faithful are joined to you through holy desires; they set their minds not on things upon earth but on things above, where you, already rich in yourself, together with the Father lack many good things in your body still journeying on earth. Among the many things you lack, you particularly—indeed supremely—lack workers for your abundant harvest.

Therefore we humbly entreat you, Lord, that you, eternal Shepherd, do not abandon your flock, but guard it by continual protection through blessed and good workers, so that it may be governed by those same rulers until the end—shepherds whom you have appointed to preside as vicars of your work. We believe this to be pleasing to you and acceptable to your heart. Therefore, with angels and archangels, with thrones and dominions, and with all the host of the heavenly army, we concur with your heart and say:

[Col. 0968B] **VERSE 5.** “May he grant you according to your heart, and confirm all your counsel.”

May the Father himself grant you, Christ, now sitting at his right hand, such workers for your harvest as are according to your heart. Saul was once a king set over your people, chosen and good not according to your heart but according to the heart of the people. When he was removed, King David reigned, chosen and good not according to the heart of the people but according to your heart; and he was found among the number of saints according to your heart. Thus you say: “I have found David my servant, and have anointed him with my holy oil” (Ps. 88:21). Again: “I have found David according to my heart.”

Likewise, therefore, we now pray; and we join our vows to you as you intercede at the Father’s right hand, asking the Father that, when because of their sins the people must be scourged by rulers such as those who are chosen and good according to the heart of the people, he may either make all workers, all princes, and all shepherds such that they are not according to the heart of the people but according to your heart; or, after removing those others, may establish in authority, both secular and ecclesiastical, such princes over all the earth as are not according to the heart of the people, forgetful of your name, but are sons born in place of the fathers of the Church, made princes over all the earth, mindful of your name according to your heart. Through them may God the Father confirm all your counsel: namely, that the whole fullness of the Gentiles may enter in, and thus all Israel may be saved.

Or indeed, when King David—David the shepherd—has been raised up throughout all kingdoms over all the sheep of your pasture, to feed them in the innocence of his heart and guide them by the understandings of his hands, may all your sheep bear twin offspring and let none among them be barren. For your faithful will not be content merely to keep a commandment, as though producing one offspring, but will add counsel to commandment. It will be too little for them merely not to swear falsely, which is a commandment; they will add not swearing at all, which is counsel. It will be too little not to kill, which is a commandment; they will lay down their lives for their brothers, being themselves ready to be killed for their brothers, which is counsel. It will be too little for them not to seize or steal another’s goods, which is a commandment; they will sell all they possess, give to the poor, [Col. 0969A] and follow you, Christ—which is your counsel. For you said to a certain rich man not by commanding but by counselling: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, come, follow me, and you shall have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21).

This counsel of yours has already been fulfilled in part, but in many persons it remains to be fulfilled. Therefore, that all your counsel may be confirmed, so that all flocks of shorn sheep coming up from the washing may bear twins—fruitful with the twin fruits of commandments and counsels—and so that all your counsel may thus be confirmed: you who took your servant David from following the ewes with young, to feed Jacob your servant and Israel your inheritance, now multiply in the Church such shepherds and kings over the imperfect or active, signified by Jacob, and over the contemplative and perfect, denoted by the name Israel, as may rule and feed your people and the sheep of your pasture according to your heart, as David did.

Again: because you are the true Joshua—you are truly called Jesus, not merely nominally, as that ancient Joshua was, but in substance and effect—just as the angel, explaining the reason for this name of yours, Jesus, said: “For he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21). Since, I say, you who are truly called Jesus will lead your people into the true land of promise, flowing with milk and honey, and since you will not do this without the helper Caleb, while you give invisible grace through any visible minister, may God the Father grant you, according to your heart, stewards of the mysteries to whom the name Caleb may truly belong. Caleb is interpreted “as it were, heart,” since they are according to your heart; just as the name Jesus truly belongs to you because you save your people from their sins. Thus may all your counsel be confirmed: salvation being invisibly given through you, Jesus, and the sacraments of salvation visibly administered through each of your ministers, as though through Caleb, your beloved companion, who visibly cooperates according to your heart with you who work invisibly, according to the force of the name Caleb. Let him not die with those whose corpses are laid low in the wilderness outside the promised land; rather, with you, O Jesus, [Col. 0969D] let him enjoy in the land of promise the eternal delights of grain, wine, and oil.

**Otherwise.** The salvation of the predestined is accomplished in such a manner that Jesus works salvation principally “in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 77:12), that is, in the heart, which holds the middle place in the body. Yet free choice cooperates with the Savior working human salvation, if it is disposed according to the heart of Jesus himself and found worthy of the name Caleb, which, as was said, is interpreted “as it were, heart.” Jesus, indeed, is like a prince and, in princely authority, greater than Moses, the one who introduces into the promised land. Yet he seeks a companion according to his heart: namely, our free choice, willing to agree with him.

For just as of all those who, at Israel’s departure from Egypt, were baptized in the cloud and in the sea, only two—Joshua and Caleb—entered the promised land, so now only two out of all the baptized enter the kingdom of heaven: Jesus himself, baptized for our sake in the Jordan or in his own blood; and the faithful people, buried with him through baptism and wholly agreeing with his will and heart. Thus, being according to Christ’s heart in the voluntary consent of free choice, it may rightly be called Caleb.

Our free choice will then be, as it were, God’s heart when it discerns, chooses, and loves rightly. It discerns good from evil; it chooses that good to be grasped; it loves the good once grasped. It discerns what is God’s good will; it chooses that which is pleasing; it loves that which is perfect. Therefore the Apostle says: “Do not become unwise, but understand what the pleasing and perfect will of God is” (cf. Eph. 5:17): so that the good will may be discerned, lest any evil be mixed with it; the pleasing will may be chosen, lest anything improper be preferred to it; and the perfect will may be loved, lest it ever turn to weariness.

For love of a thing will never grow weary when one does not err in cautiously distinguishing it from other things, and when one deliberates well in choosing it. Hence it is that for lovers of this world the world itself will finally turn to weariness, because they did not deliberate cautiously when they preferred the created world to its Creator. But those who discern Christ and choose him to be loved will finally feel no weariness whatever in his love, when their heart has become wholly according to him.

For in those making progress, who have not yet wholly turned their heart to him, Christ himself in some measure condescends according to their heart by showing himself to them. Thus, on the day of the Resurrection, while there was still darkness at the tomb in the heart of Mary, who did not believe that he had risen, he conformed himself to her doubtful heart and appeared to her not in a recognized form but as though he were a gardener (John 20:15). Likewise, to others who loved and doubted he appeared as though a traveler, being disposed toward them according to their heart. But after Mary’s heart was established in faith according to Christ’s heart, all Christ’s counsel was confirmed in [Col. 0970D] her. Likewise, after the disciples, formerly “foolish and slow of heart to believe,” had hearts burning according to Christ’s heart, “they recognized” the Lord “in the breaking of the bread” (Luke 24:35).

Again, his disciples, fishing without discernment and distinguishing neither right from left, saw him on the shore as though he were an unknown man (John 21:4). But after, according to Christ’s heart, they cast the net on the right side of the boat at his command, they immediately recognized the Lord of the sea from the very result of their fishing; and they offered him their heart according to his own heart. Therefore, when the meal there had ended and he said to Peter for the third time, “Do you love me?”, Peter too for the third time answered according to his heart: “I love you” (ibid., 17).

See how Peter’s heart, making itself like Christ’s heart, presents itself to us in Jesus’ company as another Caleb. Jesus says to him: “Follow me” (ibid., 22), as if to say: You, another Caleb, follow me, the true Joshua; accompany me, cooperate with me, so that the faithful people may be led through the Jordan of baptism into the promised land. That this might happen, the prophet David rightly prophesied by praying, and faithfully prayed by prophesying, saying thus to you, Christ: “May he grant you according to your heart, and confirm all your counsel.” Understand: God the Father.

And although we recognize that this has been fulfilled to a great extent, we still perceive in ourselves and others a great discrepancy between our human heart and Christ’s heart, in which all treasures of divine counsels are hidden. It is wholly fitting for us to be conformed to that heart: with Mary through faith; with the disciples who recognized him in the breaking of bread through ardor of heart; and with Peter through sincere love. Thus his resurrection may become manifest in us—a resurrection in which the perfect union of body and spirit occurred.

Let us not suppose, with Mary seeking Christ in the tomb, that he had not yet ascended to equality with the Father, or that his body was without his spirit. Nor again, with the disciples who thought “that they saw a spirit” (Luke 23:37), let us suppose that Christ did not have flesh and bones, when he says to his bride, the holy Church: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. [Col. 0971C] 2:23). Let our heart, then, wholly burn within us while he speaks to us on the way and opens the Scriptures to us, and let no diversity be found between our heart and Christ’s heart that is condemnable and harmful to us.

But because we have in ourselves, or from ourselves, no power to accomplish these things in ourselves, “we have such confidence through Christ toward God, not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:4–5). Though on account of ourselves he owes us no good thing, to whom he owes nothing but punishments, yet he owes this to his Son: that he should conform human beings to him—the Son who, having become obedient to him and having died, was conformed to the human being who had died.

Therefore we do not ask that so great a thing be given to us for our merits; rather, we ask, O Christ, that [Col. 0971D] God the Father may grant you according to what you have deserved, and may so dispose our free choice according to your heart that, like Caleb, it may accompany you, Jesus, in confirming within us not only every commandment of yours but also every counsel of yours. Therefore we say: May he grant you that our heart may be according to your heart; and may he confirm all your counsel, so that human affection may never kick against your divine counsels, but our heart may walk through free choice according to your heart, until in the true land of promise it enjoys you with eternal sweetness of milk and honey. There:

**VERSE 6.** “We shall rejoice in your salvation, and in the name of our God we shall be magnified.”

There, O Father, O begetter of the Savior, established in the land of promise after [Col. 0972A] every day of tribulation, on the day of solemnity and joy, we shall rejoice in your salvation. I, David the prophet, and every faithful psalmist, and the entire company of the faithful, worthy of the name Caleb—or rather, having received this name by divine graciousness—shall rejoice there, not in our own merit but in your salvation, eternal Father.

“And in the name of our God we shall be magnified.” For those whom he predestined before the ages, he calls and justifies at the fitting time, at the acceptable time; those same persons he will magnify after all times in the glory of eternity, which remains forever. I have said these things turned toward the Father. Again, turned toward the Son, I say:

**VERSE 7.** “May the Lord fulfill all your petitions.”

O Christ, Son of the living God, who intercede for us [Col. 0972B] with the Father, worthy to be heard because of your reverence: to you, petitioning for us, we join our prayers and say: May the Lord, the Father, fulfill all your petitions. For you are now our advocate; you will be our judge in the future. But before you judge us, before you summon us to judgment, may God the Father fulfill in us all your petitions, which you, the high priest who entered the Holy of Holies—that is, heaven itself—to appear before the face of God for us, pour forth for us by that very fact that you appear before God’s face for us.

For the continual appearance there of your humanity in divine glory is a continual petition for those who are to be gathered into heaven, into the Holy of Holies: those who are your members, made participants in your divinity because you became a participant in humanity. Therefore, O great High Priest, who penetrated the heavens, who within the Holy of Holies, within the secrets of heaven, make petitions through the presentation of your humanity for the salvation of human beings and for the glorification of your members, we join our petitions to you as you petition, and say: “May the Lord fulfill all your petitions.”

There can be no doubt that such a high priest, pleasing to God in his days, is heard. For even long before his time, I, David the prophet, in my own days said:

“Now I have known that the Lord has saved his Christ.” Now through the spirit of prophecy I have known that God the Father, having anointed Christ his Son with the Holy Spirit and power, has not merely *will save* him—as though that future fact were uncertain to me—but *has saved* him. For what is still future in time concerning the salvation of the whole Christ, that is, the head and all his members, is immovably past in divine foreknowledge. In those members, according to predestination, the Lord Father has already saved his Christ. But in order that predestination itself may appear in effect, and that his whole body may be saved also in those members in whom it is still weak upon earth:

“He will hear him from his holy heaven.” He who heard him in mortal flesh beneath heaven, made lower than the angels, will now much more hear him from his holy heaven, in immortal flesh glorified above the angels. He who heard Jesus, the great priest, praying in filthy garments, as is read in Zechariah, will now much more hear him clothed in such festal garments and crowned with such crowns as are there described: “Behold, I have taken away your iniquity from you and clothed you with festal garments” (Zech. 3:4). Again: “The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Take from the exiles—from Holdai, Tobiah, and Jedaiah—and on that day you shall come and enter the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, who came from Babylon. You shall take silver and gold, make crowns, put them upon the head of Jesus son of Jozadak the great priest, and speak to him, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold the man whose name is the East” (ibid. 6:10–12).

By the name “East” we understand the glory of Christ rising after the setting of [Col. 0973B] his death. Then human nature in Christ, although it was not changed into the other nature, was nevertheless clothed in the festal garments of divine brightness and crowned with the glory of divine splendor. Therefore he will now hear him from his holy heaven, clothed in festal garments and crowned with golden crowns—he who formerly heard him crowned with thorns and defiled by our sins, as Isaiah says: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and there was no man with me from the nations. I trod them in my wrath, and their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I defiled all my clothing” (Isa. 63:3).

If, therefore, on the day of tribulation, wearing filthy garments like the garments of those who tread the winepress, he nevertheless “was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5:7), how much more now, “beautiful in his robe, walking in the multitude of his strength” (Isa. 63:1), is he worthy to be heard. Therefore either I, David the prophet, or any faithful psalmist, affirm without doubt that God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who heard him on the day of tribulation, now hears and will always hear him from his heaven—indeed, from his bosom. For John says: “The only-begotten is in the bosom of the Father; he has declared him” (John 1:18): that is, he declares outwardly nothing other than what he learns in that bosom, in which bosom he also asks as from nearby whatever he knows is expedient for his members. There God the Father will hear him from his holy heaven, that is, from his holy bosom: from the heavenly secret where no garment [Col. 0973D] intervenes between him and the Father, because, he says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Therefore he will hear him from his holy heaven “in the strength of the salvation of his right hand”; for this is how the Hebrew reads in place of what we have: “In the powers is the salvation of his right hand.” He will plainly be heard in attaining the strength of the salvation of his right hand, because the salvation of his right hand consists in powers. For it is written: “Length of days is in her right hand, and in her left hand riches and glory” (Prov. 3:16).

Therefore length of days is the eternity of the eight beatitudes. And thus the salvation of his right hand is said to be in powers, or in strength, because the length, strength, and dominion of that salvation—of those days, of that blessedness—which is in his right hand, his superior hand, by which he distributes and bestows eternal goods, will never fail. But in his left hand, by which he grants temporal riches and the glory of present dignities, there is indeed some slight kind of salvation; yet in that salvation there is no dominion, strength, or length, but great weakness, great instability, great brevity, and brief pleasure.

Therefore Christ does not pray to obtain this salvation for his own, although he sometimes grants it to his faithful, to whom he sometimes dispenses temporal goods from his left hand. But from his right hand he always grants them eternal goods, in which are dominion and the strength of salvation—the salvation which he now prays to obtain for them in heaven. We also, who are called his members, must always be intent on seeking that same eternal salvation, lest, together with [Col. 0974B] the impious, who delight only in things of the left hand, we become people of the left hand and are so exalted with them in this world that we fall with them.

For:

**VERSE 8.** “Some in chariots, and some on horses.”

The greater are carried in chariots, the lesser on horses. For it was ancient custom that when a triumph was displayed after a victory, the greater, crowned with laurel, were carried in chariots, while the lesser, likewise celebrating, were carried on horses; the populace came out with palm branches and loud voices to celebrate the triumphal festival. Thus chariots now stand for greater dignities and horses for lesser, when it is said: “Some in chariots, and some on horses.”

**Otherwise.** Some glory in the chariots of vain dignities and empty glory, and some are carried on the horses of stiff-necked pride or dissolving luxury, along with Pharaoh and his army. But we, fleeing such things with Moses, as though on foot, sing with Moses and call others to sing, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored” (Exod. 15:1). In saying such things, we praise God for past benefits, and in the name of the Lord our God we shall invoke divine help to attain the future goods which are on the right hand. For those who were eager for things of the left hand, and who said in order to retain them, “It is expedient for us that one man should die, lest perhaps the Romans come and take away our place and nation” (John 18:14; 11:48):

[Col. 0974D] **VERSE 9.** “They have been bound and fallen”; they lost their place and nation. They, and all like them, who prefer temporal and left-hand goods to eternal and right-hand goods, although they seem to themselves to stand on the lofty summit of affairs, have nevertheless fallen, bound by the cords of their sins. But we, who by despising temporal things desire eternal things alone, who wish to use temporal things while enjoying eternal things—we Gentiles, I say, who were stones raised up from stones—have risen and been made upright so that we may be children of Abraham. His likeness was shown to him not on earth but in heaven, when the Lord said to him: “Look up to heaven and number the stars, if you can.” He looked up, he who heard said to him: “Thus shall your seed be” (Gen. 15:5). Therefore we also, looking upward with our father Abraham and looking down upon earthly things, have risen and been made upright.

**VERSE 10.** “Lord, save the king, and hear us on the day when we call upon you.”

We have indeed been made upright; but because we neither rose by our own strength nor are able to stand by ourselves, O Lord Father, save the king in his members, whom you have already saved in himself. Save him in us who are still weak, whom you saved in many soldiers fighting bravely for our king; and hear us through that high priest who intercedes for us on the day when we call upon you, asking from you yourself for you yourself—which is to call upon you. For those who desire something other than you call upon that which they desire. But we desire both to be saved through Christ the king in the powers of the salvation of his right hand, and to be heard through that same high priest on the day [Col. 0976A] when we call upon you: on the day, in the bright expectation and clear desire of that promise which the high priest himself made to us, saying: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

Whenever we call upon you in the day and light of this promise, hear us through him—Jesus Christ our Lord, who intercedes with you for us, who lives and reigns with you, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

Glory to the Father, who hears the Son interceding for us; glory to the Son, the salvation in whom we shall rejoice, as has been said in this psalm: “We shall rejoice in his salvation”; glory to the Holy Spirit, who is this very joy by which we shall rejoice in the salvation of God the Father.

## PSALM 20

[Col. 0975]

[Col. 0975B] **“Lord, in your strength the king shall rejoice.”**

**(VERSE 1.) A PSALM OF DAVID, UNTO THE END.**

The title of the psalm is clear. Its arrangement is pleasing. For while the subject of the preceding psalm was Christ’s priestly supplication in his Passion and his high-priestly intercession in confession of the Father, with a few words concerning his royal power near the end, where it was said, “Lord, save the king,” the principal subject of this following psalm is, as it were conversely, his royal power, with a few remarks concerning priestly mercy interposed.

Thus these two psalms sing of mercy and judgment, and in their connection mercy and truth meet one another in a most fitting order. First, the propitiatory high priest mercifully invites all to himself on the throne of grace; afterward, like a king, he displays great power and strength toward those who despise grace. Thus those whom this does not soften into piety—that he is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world—may at least be deterred from impiety by this: that he is the author of invincible strength and King of unconquerable dominion, an ever-magnificent conqueror, who restrains the forces of hostile rule, overcomes by his own strength the savagery of the roaring enemy, and powerfully storms hostile wickedness. No one at all can resist his power and might, because it is necessary, inevitable, and inevitably ordained that every knee of willing and unwilling beings—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—should bow to him (Phil. 2:10).

[Col. 0975D] Therefore this psalm is rightly entitled concerning David “strong of hand.” For just as David’s strength is described in the statement that “he slew eight hundred in one attack” (2 Sam. 23:8)—a deed or mystical saying signifying the great strength of David, strong of hand—so it is most soundly believed of this true David that he slew and overcame innumerable armies of demons in one attack. This occurred amid the shock of the great earthquake when he died on the cross and his soul descended to hell: the gates of hell fell before his face, their guards put to flight.

For when Christ, the King of glory, entered to overthrow hell, and the choir of angels before him commanded that the gates of the princes be lifted up, and he snatched a great multitude from hell and made them participants in his resurrection, the devil and his attendants received the wound of death in that very fact. For when many people, for whose salvation that enemy fiercely envies them, were snatched from hell’s hand, envy tormented him and his own more vehemently and cruelly.

Again our David, as it were, slew eight hundred in one attack when, in the great shock of an earthquake, a great event occurred as he rose, and the guards of the tomb “became as dead men” [Col. 0976C] (Matt. 28:4). This signifies that all his enemies were assigned to eternal death, especially those who wished him always to lie in the tomb and not reign. Finally, at the last judgment, in one attack, “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet” (1 Cor. 15:52), he will, as it were, slay eight hundred, when he says to those at the left: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). From that time, all sadness having been removed from his kingdom, “Lord, in your strength the king shall rejoice, and in your salvation he shall exult exceedingly.”

This psalm may fittingly be sung for any Catholic king, just as the preceding one may be sung for any Catholic priest. For Catholic kings, if they reign well, are members of that king of whom this psalm speaks. And the priests ought to be members of the same king and priest of whom the preceding psalm speaks. But we now speak of the head of kings, priests, and all those to whom the apostle Peter says: “You are an elect race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9). In the name of the Lord, let us enter the most beautiful house of this psalm. In its prologue we have seen a beautiful vestibule, and have read the fine title inscribed upon the front of the house. In that title the Lord of the house is known not only by the name David; the completion of the house is also indicated when this psalm is seen entitled “unto the end.”

By this title we are instructed that the intention of this psalm is directed toward this end, this perfection of all completion: that, once Christ’s kingdom is consummated and his enemies humbled, there may fully come about what is said at the end of the psalm: “We shall sing and make melody of your powers.” There, near the end of the psalm, powers are mentioned in the plural because of the divisions of graces, which the Spirit distributes as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11), to whom he wills. At the beginning of the psalm, however, the single power of the king is treated: he alone glories in the full power of God the Father, because he is rightly called the power of God and the wisdom of God. Him alone, chosen from among thousands, we glorify in this psalm, saying:

**VERSE 2.** “Lord, in your strength the king shall rejoice, and in your salvation he shall exult exceedingly.”

O Lord God the Father: your Son, the same king and priest, whom we have as such a high priest that he can have compassion on our weaknesses, tempted in all things in likeness to us yet without sin—the same one who for us human beings is a human being like us, passible in our weakness—is also in your strength wholly equal to you. Therefore he who from our frailty says, “My strength has been weakened” (Lam. 1:14), that same one shall rejoice in your strength.

For if his saints through him recovered strength from weakness and became mighty in battle, how much more shall he himself, after rising from death and recovering strength from weakness, having become strong and mighty in battle, rejoice in your strength, saying: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18)—and adding: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature; whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16).

This word of faith proclaimed through the mouth of your Son, our Savior, when he said, “Whoever believes shall be saved”—this saving word, I say, which proclaims that the believer who is baptized will be saved—was a cause of great exultation for him. He delighted in this word before the world was made, when he rejoiced “day by day, playing in the inhabited world, and his delights were to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8:30–31). If then he exulted exceedingly in the delights of foreknowledge, how much more does he now exult, and never ceases to exult eternally, when through faith and baptism his dwelling with human beings is accomplished and the delights which he has in being pleased to dwell with human beings are fulfilled, as he desired before the foundation of the world?

Therefore, dwelling with human beings after becoming human, he said with great affection: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you” (Luke 22:15). For “as an eagle provokes her young to fly” [Col. 0978A] (Deut. 32:11), she flies over them so as to provoke them to fly; or “as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings” (Matt. 23:32) with great desire, so he, made human for human beings, was moved by great desire: desiring to be with human beings and desiring human beings to be with him. Therefore he said: “I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24). And you, God the Father of Christ,
VERSICLES 3 and 4. “You have granted him the desire of his heart”: that he might become man among men; “and you have not withheld from him the request of his lips,” when he said: “I will that where I am, they also may be with me.” Truly you granted him the desire of his heart, that he might be with human beings; for in his conception, where he was conceived as man, [Col. 0978B] there you anticipated him with blessings of sweetness, so that original sin—by which we were all forestalled, our mothers conceiving us in sins—might be far removed from the virgin mother conceiving in the blessing proclaimed to her by the angel: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:28).

Thus, O God the Father, by sending the angel to the virgin who was to conceive your Son, you anticipated him with blessings of sweetness, so that he might draw into himself nothing from the root of bitterness, assuming human nature in such a manner as to exclude both radical or original guilt and actual guilt. For the Holy Spirit, coming upon the virgin, took original sin away from her; and the power of the Most High, overshadowing her, kept her pure and safe from every [Col. 0978C] actual sin, and made her fruitful by such a conception that the blessed mother might conceive and bear a blessed son. You, Father, anticipated him with blessings of sweetness, granting him the desire of his heart: that he might be without sin, full of the delight and exultation of every blessing. This delight and exultation you, Father, stored up upon him in the very conception, and endowed him with an everlasting name, giving him the name that is above every name, as the angel said: “Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Jesus. He shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke 1:31–32).

Above this name, Jesus, there is no higher name, because this Jesus is one person of the Trinity, [Col. 0978D] in which there is nothing prior or subsequent, nothing greater or less, nothing higher or lower. The name of one person in the most high Trinity is Jesus and Son of the Most High. By the sweetness of this name you anticipated him with the blessings by which he himself is proclaimed: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 21:9), so that in him, according to the desire of his heart, all the tribes of the earth may be blessed. You granted him this desire of his heart because now, in the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, all tribes of the earth are blessed, while the Gospel is preached to every creature, through which some from every nation on earth are gathered to the end, that is, to Christ himself. It is therefore evident that you, God [Col. 0979A] the Father, granted this desire of his heart to your Son by anticipating him with blessings of sweetness.

That you did not withhold from him the request of his lips, when he said, “I will that where I am, they also may be with me,” is evident in this: that you placed upon his head a crown of precious stone. That is, you joined to him the primitive Church, adorned like a crown with every precious stone; for the twelve apostles, like twelve precious stones, adorn the primitive Church as the crown of the head which is Christ. Moreover, other precious stones adorned Christ, the head of the Church, at the beginning of the Church’s birth; these too were where Christ was. Thus they say: “But our commonwealth is in heaven, from which we await [Col. 0979B] our Lord Jesus, who will refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” (Philippians 3:20–21).

Because of this glory every precious and shining stone is proclaimed in the crown of the head. When the whole body of the Church, gathered from the entire circuit of the earth, is conformed to the glory of this head, that body will be where the head is: namely, in eternal glory. For he who said, “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory which you gave me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world,” will not be denied the request of his lips. Therefore you have “placed upon his head a crown of” every “precious stone” (John 17:24), not only in the primitive Church but also in the universal Church spread through the circumference of the earth, [Col. 0979C] wondrously fashioned from his side through his passion, and glorified: in some stones through a resurrection already accomplished; in others through a steadfast and utterly certain expectation of the Resurrection. For “many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose” (Matthew 27:52) with him. As they rose, he himself shone forth adorned by their glory, as by every precious stone. And when at the end the bodies of all the saints, sown in weakness, rise in glory (1 Corinthians 15:43), then the whole Church, joined to Christ the head as a great crown made of every precious stone, will shine in eternal life.

VERSICLE 5. “For he asked life of you.” He asked eternal life, namely, for himself [Col. 0979D] and for his members, when he said: “Father, glorify your Son”—understand, in the resurrection—“that your Son also may thus glorify you” (John 17:5)—understand, in the resurrection of his members. Your Son will accomplish this, “as you gave him power over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him” (ibid., v. 2). Thus he asked life of you, for himself and his own, and you granted it to him: not life of any sort, but long-lasting life, eternal life, granting him length of days for ever and ever.

The days of his Nativity into this world were, as it were, short, because the days of mortal life in him came to an end. But the days of his resurrection are long and without end, because “having risen from the dead, he dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that [Col. 0980A] he died, he died to sin”—so that sin might die—“but in that he lives, he lives to God” (Romans 6:9–10), so that man may endure for ever; for by dying he destroyed our death, and by rising he restored life. By raising him from the dead, you, Father, granted him length of days, not only that he himself might live eternally, but also that those rising with him might live in their souls through faith during the age—that is, throughout these long periods of this age until the end of time—and then, after the resurrection, might live for ever and ever in body as well as soul, without any end of life and without any fear of death: for ever and ever, that is, eternally.

VERSICLE 6. “Great is his glory in your salvation; glory and great splendor you shall lay upon him.” His life, [Col. 0980B] in which you granted him length of days, will not merely be long; it will also be glorious, not slightly but greatly. For great will be the glory of him—that is, of the man assumed and raised from death—in your salvation, that is, in your Word, since the glory of the assuming Word and of the assumed man, glorified in God, will not differ.

“You shall lay glory and great splendor upon him.” Truly, upon him as upon an immovable foundation you shall lay glory and great splendor: namely, the glorious Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor any such thing. Its glory is that of which Paul says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12). Its splendor lies in manifest and honorable action. [Col. 0980C] Or glory will lie in virtues, splendor in miracles. And this will be without failing, because the blessing given to the first human beings—“Increase and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it” (Genesis 1:28)—will now be fulfilled in Christ, while he, the grain dead in the earth, is multiplied in such a way that all the earth is subjected to him and his members.

VERSICLE 7. “For you shall give him as a blessing for ever and ever”: namely, that he may increase and multiply for ever and ever, that is, eternally. Or: you shall give him as the blessing promised to Abraham, so that in him all the tribes of the earth may be blessed. At last, “you shall make him glad with joy in the presence of your countenance.” You shall make him glad in his members, when each of his own is told: [Col. 0980D] “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25:21). That joy will be with your countenance, that is, with your Son himself, who is your countenance.

VERSICLE 8. “For the king hopes in the Lord, and through the mercy of the Most High he shall not be moved.” The first man, earthly and from the earth, set in paradise, did not stand fast in God’s mercy but was moved through pride. The second man, heavenly and from heaven, set in heaven through the mercy of God the Father most high, was himself made Most High; therefore he shall not be moved, because the King himself hopes in the Lord. While he still lived in the flesh, he hoped in the Lord, presuming nothing upon human power. Even now he hopes in his members, whom he causes to hope in the Lord and not in human strength. Therefore, through the mercy of the Most High he shall not be moved; [Col. 0981A] neither shall the foot of pride come upon him, nor shall the hand of the sinner move him or his own, who are made steadfast in his mercy.

Otherwise: “Through the mercy of the Most High he shall not be moved.” This king has one time of mercy and another of wrath. The time of mercy lasts as long as he now sits, a merciful high priest, on the throne of grace, the propitiator for the sins of the whole world, receiving the confessions and penances of all who approach the throne of grace. Of this throne the Apostle says: “Let us approach with confidence the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help” (Hebrews 4:16). Upon this throne of grace he now sits before judgment, ready, as we have said, to receive the confessions and penances of all people.

But it will come to pass [Col. 0981B] that he will sit upon the seat of his majesty, while the heavens and the powers of heaven tremble in his sight. Then the repentance of no one, being excessively late, will be accepted; rather, each person will be judged by righteous judgment. Then he will appear as an angry king, moved against his enemies in the justice of the Most High. But now, seated on the throne of grace in the mercy of the Most High, he is not moved; rather, he patiently and mercifully awaits human conversions and acts of repentance. Distinguishing these two times, the Apostle says to every person who sins: “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But by your hardness and your unrepentant heart you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Romans 2:4–5).

Therefore now, as the Apostle says, God’s kindness calls and leads to repentance. This kindness is like the hand of divine propitiation, full of medicines and life-giving ointments, which in this great infirmary of the whole world, full of the infirm and sick, offers abundant remedies of mercy to all according to the riches of divine grace, by which he rains upon just and unjust alike. Penitent sinners who confess find this hand and receive healing medicines from it. But proud and arrogant sinners neither find this hand nor seek medicines from it. There will come the “day of wrath, the day of calamity and misery” (Zephaniah 1:15), a great and exceedingly bitter day, when this hand—which is now most gentle, of sweetest touch, [Col. 0981D] tending the wounds and sores of penitents—will be armed against the impenitent with a most sharp, double-edged sword. Then, in the gleam of the flashing spear—that is, of the judicial sentence—there will be none able to hide, for the right hand of the avenging Judge will then find all who hate him and who refused to receive his medicines. Considering this, the Prophet now says:

VERSICLE 9. “May your hand be found by all your enemies; may your right hand find all who hate you.” Let us also, singing with the Prophet and Psalmist from the marrow of our heart, say: O most high King, who are not now moved in mercy, who now extend medicine to all, may your most gentle hand be found by all your enemies, so that by your hand now healing, [Col. 0982A] enemies may become friends. For unless they find it gentle now, they will someday feel your hand striking grievously. For your right hand will find all who hate you and who, when they could, refused to find it.

Thus in prayer we say: “May your hand be found by all your enemies.” Yet, not praying but concurring with your just judgment, we add: “May your right hand find all who hate you.” With the highest desire we ask that your priestly hand, consecrating the oil of the sick, may now be found by all your enemies, so that by that same hand they may be anointed with the same oil and healed. But if, in stubbornness of spirit, they do not admit the laying on and anointing of this hand, we assent to your righteous judgment: that your right hand itself, armed with the sword [Col. 0982B] of judicial sentence, may at last find all who hate you. For your royal hand does not bear the sword without cause, just as your priestly holy hand does not bear chrism and holy oil, or oil of the sick, without cause.

Otherwise: Some are converted to the Lord in such a way that, with Zacchaeus, they seek to see Jesus and, as it were running ahead of him in devout desire, climb a sycamore tree in order to see him (Luke 19:4). Others do not seek Jesus, but with Saul persecute him, blinded by ignorance because they do not know that by persecuting Christ’s members they persecute Christ himself. For both groups prayer is made here, when it is said: “May your hand be found by all your enemies”: namely, by those in whom the desire of your goodness, aroused by prevenient grace, seeks you with Zacchaeus—Jesus, that is, Savior—while fearing you as Judge; and may your right hand now find all who hate you, who with Saul persecute you in your own, showing them by saving strength that “it is hard for them to kick against [Col. 0982C] the goad” of your justice (Acts 9:5). For if your enemies who hate you do not find you now as Savior, neither will they be found by you as Savior. At last they will find you as Judge, and you, judging, will find them as you test the world by fire. In that fire:

VERSICLE 10. “You shall make them as a furnace of fire in the time of your countenance.” In the time of your countenance, that is, of your manifestation of countenance, when your countenance, now propitious, will appear [Col. 0982D] terrible. You shall make them as a furnace of fire, that they may burn wholly within; and that they may also burn without, the Lord in his wrath will trouble them, and fire will devour them.

It must be understood that all the reprobate, who sinned in both soul and body, will there be tormented alike in soul and body. For a furnace burns inwardly; but one who is devoured by fire begins to be burned from the outside. Therefore, so that the sacred utterances might show the reprobate to burn both outwardly and inwardly, they attest both that they are devoured by fire and that they are made like a furnace: so that they may be tormented by fire in the body and burn through pain in the mind. Thus, in the time of the Lord’s countenance, all the unjust are both made as a furnace and devoured by fire. For when the Judge appears, and their multitude is driven away from his [Col. 0983A] sight, conscience burns within through belated repentance, and Gehenna torments the flesh without.

VERSICLE 11. “You shall destroy their fruit from the earth, and their seed from among the children of men.” And this you shall do, O righteous Judge, in the time of your countenance: your earthly enemies—first the Jews, and then all like them, who love earthly things more than you—shall both lose earthly fruits and fail to find heavenly fruits, because you will destroy their fruit sought from the earth. Or you shall destroy their fruit from the land of promise, so that in it they may not find the fruit of blessedness of which you say in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matthew 5:4). But the Jews will be expelled not only from the land of temporal promise, but [Col. 0983B] also from the land of eternal promise. And their seed—that is, all their prosperity, their posterity not through succession of flesh but through imitation of impiety—will be destroyed by the children of men, condemned and excommunicated, and utterly cast out from the fellowship of the children of men: that is, of all the saints. These are called not so much men as children of men, because they are found renewed from the old state of those who were not children of men but merely men, namely Adam and Eve. But the saints, who love the Son of Man and are counted among his members, are rightly called children of men because they have put off the oldness of the first human beings and put on the newness of the Son of Man. Without doubt the seed of the impious Jews will be separated from such children of men, and this will occur by righteous judgment.

VERSICLE 12. “For they turned evils against you,” saying: “He has a demon and is mad; why do you listen to him?” (John 10:20). Again: “If we let him go on thus, the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (ibid. 11:48). Those who are still their imitators and seed likewise turn their evils against you and turn your goods toward themselves. For they are puffed up by your goods as though these were their own, and as though they had not received them; to such people your Apostle says: “What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). But they turn their own evils against you because [Col. 0983D] they blame not themselves but you, as though your unavoidable foreknowledge compelled them to do evil. For they say: “God has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills; and who resists his will?” (Romans 9:18). They say this as though human evils arise from the good will of God.

Thus heretics turned their evils against you; so did astrologers, asserting that human actions are governed by fated necessity or by the disposition of the stars. Thus the first human beings also turned their evils against you, when Adam said: “The woman whom you gave me as companion gave to me, and I ate.” And Eve said: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (Genesis 3:12–13). By saying such things they craftily shifted their guilt onto you, who are the author of all and only good, so that you might seem blameworthy: you who gave such a woman to the man after you had seen that he would be deceived, and permitted such a serpent to speak in paradise, though you foreknew that its speech would seduce the woman.

There are still many imitators of these people who, following Adam’s example, plead the frailty of flesh created by God as though it were their woman, or the craftiness of the tempting devil as though it were their serpent, thereby turning their evils upon God, the creator of the flesh and of that spirit who by sinning became the devil. Of all such people who turn their evils against you, the author of good, the Jews were worst. They turned evils against you not from ignorance but deliberately, devising counsels that were crafty indeed but futile, because they devised counsels which they could not establish. [Col. 0984B] For they assembled a council and said: “What are we doing? This man performs many signs. If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him” (John 11:47–48). Therefore, in that council they devised counsels by which they might prevent all from believing in you, Christ; but they will not be able to establish those counsels.

VERSICLE 13. “For you shall make them a back”: that is, you shall so blind them that they may be as a back and not see you, “the light prepared for revelation to the Gentiles” before the face of all peoples (Luke 2:32). For their eyes will be darkened, and their back will always be bent. Indeed, they themselves will be a bent back, because you shall make them a bent back by first darkening their eyes—that is, by blinding [Col. 0984C] their teachers through envy and hatred of truth. For if everyone “who hates his brother is in darkness, and darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:9, 11), how much more were they in darkness, and how much more did darkness blind those who hated you, Christ, the best of brothers, as you said: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (John 15:22, 24). Therefore you shall make them a back, so that they may not see the light which you prepared before the face of all peoples.

Yet because the remnant of Israel will be saved, in your remnant you will prepare their countenance. Their countenance was clear-sighted in the patriarchs and prophets. [Col. 0984D] You will prepare and represent that countenance in their remnant when, through Elijah and Enoch, the hearts of the children are turned to their fathers, so that, like pure and bright mirrors, they may receive their countenance. That countenance will be visible in the remnant of the Jews themselves, now made yours. Thus in the apostles and other disciples converted from the Jewish people, the clear-sighted and beautiful countenance shone brightly—so brightly that their whole body was full of eyes “round about and within,” and even their backs “are full of eyes” (Revelation 4:8). For they too belong to that blessed remnant in which you, Christ, will prepare a luminous countenance, such as was Moses’ countenance, made radiant through fellowship with God’s word (Exodus 24:29). For if his countenance was glorified by God speaking with him for an hour, [Col. 0985A] how much more did you—God made man, the Word made flesh—through the fellowship of your long converse glorify the countenances of your apostles and disciples, who were your remnant left to you from so great a people, as you say to Elijah: “I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee before Baal” (Romans 11:1).

In remnant such as this, who do not bend the knee before Baal, Mammon, Beelphegor, Antichrist, or any other idol, you prepare and illumine the countenance of the former Fathers, turning the hearts of the children toward them. This has been done in part, and what still remains to be done will be accomplished, Christ, in your power. Hence, at the conclusion of the whole psalm, we say:

[Col. 0985B] VERSICLE 14. “Be exalted, O Lord, in your strength; we shall sing and chant your powers.” You are that “sun” which “knew its setting,” and which, by your setting, “made darkness, and night came to be.” In that night “all the beasts of the forest passed through, the young lions roaring to seize prey and seek their food from God” (Psalm 103:20–21). Thus, after Joseph died in Egypt—in whom you, the sun of justice, shone—a new king arose, like a beast of the forest, who did not know Joseph. This beast, together with its cubs, its most wicked taskmasters, afflicted your people. But when you, sun of justice, were exalted in your servant Moses, those beasts were placed in their dens—indeed, hurled into hell: “The depths covered them; they sank into the deep like a stone” (Exodus 15:5).

There were also other saviors and defenders among your people: Joshua, Othniel [Vulgate: Othoniel], Barak, Jephthah, Gideon, Samson, Samuel, King David, other good kings, and all the valiant chosen from the bravest of Israel. When these fell, O sun of justice, you set in them, and a dark night came, through which the beasts of the forest passed. But when good worshippers of justice again succeeded to their place, you, Sun of Justice, shone as though in the east, until, bending again toward your known setting, you permitted night to come. During such nights all the beasts have now passed through, down to the last beast, Antichrist.

Those beasts which Daniel saw (Daniel 7:3) [Col. 0985D] fighting one another—the first a lion, the second a bear, the third a leopard, the fourth unnamed and more cruel than the rest—passed through in their nights. For the Babylonian kingdom, signified by the lion; the Persian or Median kingdom, signified by the bear; the kingdom of the Greeks, signified by the leopard; and the Roman kingdom, designated by the fourth beast, ruled in their respective nights and yielded to you, Sun of Justice, now reigning. For your soldiers, martyrs and confessors, filled the world with the triumphal titles of your kingdom. And because such soldiers of yours have fallen, and false brethren, satellites of Antichrist, have entered into their places, behold, night has again come, through which the beasts of the forest pass: beasts cruel not to bodies but lying in wait for souls, [Col. 0986A] in order to kill the innocent by making them guilty. While they make them accomplices—if only through silence—in the evils done everywhere, they stop their mouths; in a wondrous way these beasts rage, perpetrating many murders without shedding blood.

Therefore, so that the night of iniquity in which these beasts pass through may be utterly destroyed and day may dawn, be exalted, O Lord, in your strength. Be exalted, O Sun of Justice, high and bright; appear in your strength. John saw your countenance shining in the Apocalypse (Revelation 1:16), like the sun shining in its strength. Longing for this strength, we say to you: “Be exalted, O Lord, in your strength.” When you were transfigured on the mountain before your disciples, then your face shone like the sun. And behold, you are now upon the mountain of paternal [Col. 0986B] height; let your face therefore shine like the sun throughout the whole world, so that through you, the Sun of Justice, there may everywhere be a day of justice.

Restore your face, that the ages may behold the light.

Restore the day which fled from us when you died.

When the laws of hell are overthrown, may light, heaven, fields, and sea,

Rightly praise God, shining above the stars.

Let there be a festal day, venerable throughout the whole age.

Let clouds of sorrow give way to joy.

Let the day be pure; let the light never bring harm.

Let the harmful night perish; let all things be renowned in light.

Let the little beasts that run in baneful night give way.

Let man, light, walk in light, with light as guide.

That all these good things may soon be fulfilled, be exalted, O Lord, in your strength. For you who, in Michael’s strength, crushed the dragon; who, as a great king, crushed many enemies through your soldiers, angels and human beings—you alone will engage Antichrist in your own proper strength. You alone, who are truth, will overthrow the falsehood of false brethren and pseudo-Christians. You, the true David, will meet this Philistine; and you will kill him, not with a material sword but with the spirit of your mouth. You will strike the earth with the rod of your mouth; with the spirit of your lips you will kill the impious one and destroy him by the brightness of your coming.

For before you, Sun of Justice, are thus exalted and appear so high as to exercise final judgment from the throne of your majesty, a certain morning brightness will precede, like a most radiant dawn. By this brightness of your coming we believe that Antichrist, with his pseudo-Christians, will be destroyed: some pseudo-Christians yielding to the most clear truth, others becoming mute. For when truth is fully manifest, there will be no place for contradiction; all iniquity will stop its mouth, and the mouths of those truly praising you, O Lord our God, will be opened.

Among them we too shall sing and chant your powers. We shall sing in contemplation and chant in action. We shall sing with the jubilation of heart and voice; we shall chant through the skilled motion of fingers and hands upon the ten-stringed psaltery, keeping the ten commandments of the Law in action. And in such singing or psalmody, displaying not our own powers, we shall sing [Col. 0987A] and chant your powers. For when your judgments, by which the lies of pseudo-Christians are destroyed, are perfectly manifested, then, as John your beloved prophesied, we shall sing and chant your powers, saying: “Great and wonderful are your works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are your ways, King of the ages. Who will not fear you, Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy; for all nations shall come and worship before you, because your judgments are manifest” (Revelation 15:3–4). Thus mercy and truth shall go before your countenance; and blessed is the people who, knowing jubilation at that time, shall sing and chant your powers, not their own. And we, by your gift, who desire such things before they occur, shall, after they occur, sing and chant your powers.

[Col. 0988A] Glory to the Father, who anticipated his Son made man with blessings of sweetness; glory to the Son anticipated with blessings of sweetness; glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that sweetness in which the Father blessed the man united to his Word. Glory to the Father exalting his Son; glory to the Son exalted in his strength; glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that strength in which Christ was exalted in the resurrection and ascension, and in which he is yet to be exalted through the clear manifestation of his judgments. That manifestation will be a festal and manifest day. But it is preceded by the morning reception, concerning which, God favoring, there will be discussion in the following psalm and in the following part.

SECOND PART.

[Col. 0987]

PROLOGUE. To Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, and Gotescalch, Bishop of Freising.

[Col. 0987B] Now that twenty psalms have been completed in the first part, you, eager banqueters, demand a second part from me: you, Eberhard, chief prelate of the Church of Juvavum [Salzburg], and you, servant of God, Gotescalch, honoring your name by the reality of the thing. For just as it suits the angel of the Church of Juvavum to wish to help those whom it helps or delights to ponder this work of ours—or rather, the sayings of the holy Fathers gathered into one—so it suits the servant of God (for this is the sense of the name *Gotescalch* in common Latin) that, preserving the property of his name, he willingly exercises himself in meditating upon these matters, according to the saying: “But your servant was exercised in your justifications.” And, that you might know the manner of such exercise, he added: “For your testimonies are also my meditation” (Psalm 118:23–24).

Therefore this meditation upon the testimonies [Col. 0987C] of God, in which this work is occupied, fittingly belongs to every servant of God. And it rightly delights God’s servants. One of them, after recently reading what we have written, wisely said in psalmody something like this: “How sweet are your utterances to my palate, O Lord—more than honey and honeycomb to my mouth!” (ibid., v. 103). He had already said this, or something similar, to the Lord in his chanting. Afterwards, when present before me, he turned to me and said: “Your work ought to be called a honeycomb.” I think he perceived in it something of that sweetness of which it is said to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Your lips, bride, drip honey from the comb.” Again: [Col. 0988B] “Honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song of Songs 4:11).

Yes indeed: the eyes of doves, lacking the gall of bitterness, know how to choose white grains even from a poor man’s chest, and do not judge them less valuable because the man who sows or threshes them does not abound in silver and gold. I am almost such a poor man. What I write or dictate I do not judge to be gold or silver.
