I judge it well enough for myself if my writings, whatever their quality, are compared—as I said in the proem to the first part—to wood carried into the house of the Lord to nourish that fire which the Lord Jesus sent upon the earth and vehemently desired to be kindled.

Far, then, be that alien fire offered in the rebellion of Korah, namely heretical opinion. To prevent even a spark of it from being introduced into our writings, wherever we build a new structure we surround it with a flooring of holy authorities. Wherever we dig a new well, we cover it, as the Law commands, with the strong covering of the Fathers’ judgments. Hence I wonder that a certain reader of our work so rushed headlong and fell into a well that he could scarcely be drawn out by the long rope of holy authorities. We wove several of these authorities into the writing addressed to the Abbot of Admont, which we placed as a kind of helmet upon the head of that part; and for this reason we refer to them in other parts near the beginning, [Col. 0989A] so that whoever wishes to read them may return to the helmeted [Note: [Col. 0989] He means the *Book on the Two Heresies*, published in vol. I, part II of the *Thesaurus Novissimus Anecdotorum*.] head of the first part, and from there may recognize the unity of the other [Col. 0990A] parts also, of which this is the second.

PSALM XXI.

[Col. 0989]

[Col. 0989A] “My God, my God, look upon me.” The title of this psalm is:

(VERSICLE 1.) “UNTO THE END, FOR THE MORNING RECEPTION: A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0989B] Its meaning is this: this psalm is to be attributed to the true David, namely Christ, truly strong-handed and truly desirable: strong-handed against enemies, desirable through his glorious Resurrection. Both are treated fully and plainly in this psalm, in the commemoration of this true David tending toward the end—that is, toward the victory which is the end of the course of his obedience. Hence, wherever the Septuagint translators have placed in the titles, “Unto the end, of David,” the Hebrew truth has “To David the Victor.” By this it is indicated that the completion of victory is the end of the whole struggle, to which, as to its final cause, is referred whatever this David, strong-handed and desirable, either shows by word and example ought to be done bravely, or makes known through his promises ought to be desired wisely.

[Col. 0989C] This psalm treats of the morning receiving—that is, of the resurrection—which took place very early, while it was still dark. This is said of the resurrection by comparison with the sun. For as, when it gradually rises, daylight gathers strength—morning light, or the dawn, going before it and preparing human eyes to behold the sun—so, when Christ rose, the minds of the disciples, and through them of many unbelievers, were gradually enlightened. For the fact that those holy women first see the stone rolled away from the tomb, in which they do not find the body of Jesus (Luke 24:2, 4); that they next behold angelic visions, from which, as these establish faith in the resurrection, they receive belief; that thereafter the Lord Jesus himself appeared first to one of them [Col. 0989D], then to one of the men, namely Peter, and then was seen by two travelling to a village (ibid., 13); that the report of these appearances went before them to the disciples, dispelling from their hearts the cloud of sorrow and unbelief—all this was the dawn of the true light, gradually bringing the joys of the radiant resurrection into sorrowful minds, as wisdom required. But when afterwards the conqueror of death himself appeared in the midst of the disciples, visible and touchable; when he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures; and when at last he sent them the Paraclete from heaven, who led them into all truth and filled their hearts with a joy that no one could take from them—this was now no dawn or morning, but [Col. 0990A] the full vision, insofar as it can be seen in this life, of eternal light and of the true sun.

Where we have “For the morning receiving,” or “morning assumption,” the Hebrew text has “For the morning hind” [Col. 0990B], by which the Lord’s resurrection is again signified. For just as it is the nature of hinds and stags to be more lively and agile in the morning, since then they are borne along by a certain natural delight that prompts them to make higher leaps and gladly climb heights, so our Lord Jesus Christ, raised from death, climbed joyfully and eagerly to the heights. He burst the nets of mortality in which he had for a time been entangled for our deliverance; but, raised from death at morning dawn, like a stag released from nets he ran swiftly. Nor was he content to remain confined within the bounds of Jewish narrowness; rather, by running through the breadth of the Gentiles to the ends of the world, he clearly showed himself to be that stag of whom the patriarch Jacob, blessing his sons, said:

> “Naphtali is a released stag, giving words of beauty” (Gen. 49:21).

For Naphtali is interpreted “breadth.” Who is this Naphtali, the released stag, except our Lord Jesus Christ, released from the confinement of the tomb? He gave words of beauty on the very day of the Resurrection, when, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to the disciples the Scriptures concerning himself, and when “he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45). This released stag also sent forth his disciples like stags from the narrow borders of the Jews, to run eagerly through all the earth and to the ends of the world, when he said to them: “Go into all the world.” And so that they too might give [Col. 0990D] words of beauty, he added: “Preach the Gospel to every creature; whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:15–16). See how this released stag longs for the springs of baptismal waters: the spring has been opened not only in Judaea but throughout the whole world.

Those reborn from this spring are also rightly called released stags: released, that is, from the nets of all sins, which are swallowed up like Pharaoh’s entire host in the Red Sea—in most holy baptism and in the sacrament of Christ’s blood. For through baptismal immersion and participation in Christ’s blood, the nets of sins are broken; and those who are, as it were, stags released from nets are made agile and conformed to Christ, the released stag. This conformity [Col. 0991A] is now begun while the old person is put off and the new is put on through faith and good conduct.

But this psalm is entitled, “Unto the end, for the morning assumption or hind,” so that at the end, when all rise in the universal resurrection and the elect alone are changed, this may be believed to be fulfilled: that the whole Church shall then be like a morning hind, released from every net—not only of guilt, but also of punishment. Hence in many manuscripts it is in the feminine: “For the morning hind,” a title by which the whole Church, to be conformed to Christ the released stag, is aptly signified.

The morning hind may also signify Christ’s human nature, which, like a female, had great [Col. 0991B] frailty for our sake during the time of mortality, but now has great fruitfulness in the days of eternity. For as a grain of wheat remains alone before it dies, but, when it falls into the earth and dies, bears much fruit (John 11:24–25), so this hind—that is, Christ’s human nature—though free from sins of its own, was nonetheless burdened by our sins, because God placed in it the iniquities of us all; and it alone bore the sins of many. Wrapped in the nets of human mortality and frailty even unto death, it had great weakness and was like a solitary hind. But in the resurrection, like a released and strengthened hind, it began to have great fruitfulness, producing so great a multitude of stags that it may rightly be said of it:

> “The voice of the Lord prepares the stags [Col. 0991C] and will reveal the thickets” (Ps. 28:9),

so that the same stags may have an open way, as they run to the high mountains, of which it is said:

> “The high mountains are for stags; the rock is a refuge for hedgehogs” (Ps. 103:18).

Did not the apostle Peter run like a released stag and give words of beauty when, freed from the prison of the flesh, he said: “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel,” etc. (Acts 12:11)? Much more truly now, freed from the prison of the flesh, he gives words of beauty before God, praying for the holy Church. Or certainly he gives words of beauty throughout the universal Church, founded upon the rock from which Peter takes his name [Col. 0991D] (ibid., 16:23), through his vicars—the pontiffs of the Apostolic See—and other Catholic shepherds, by sound teaching.

Likewise the apostle Paul, labouring in the Gospel even to bonds as though an evildoer, was confined with respect to the substance of his flesh, which was like a weak hind held in bonds. But because “the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2:9), and his very bonds advanced the Gospel, like a released stag he gives words of beauty, while Paul, in the mouth of all priests, lays down the laws of commandments, teaching Christ crucified and that there is no God besides Christ with the Father, who reigns with the Holy Spirit, of whom Paul is a witness (Acts 28:28).

All Catholic teachers are likewise designated by the title of this psalm as morning stags. Roaming within the holy Church through most abundant pastures, they know [Col. 0992A] how, after the manner of stags, to make leaps of understanding and fearlessly climb the mountains of contemplation, and thus give peoples words of beauty: what they have learned when raised into the height of contemplation, they vigorously minister to those placed below. Let this suffice concerning the title.

The subject of this psalm is the Lord’s passion and resurrection. It treats this subject as follows. David the prophet set forth the Lord’s passion, still future in his own time, as though it were a past history, transferring Christ’s person to his own, so that, while David the prophet seems to speak, Christ speaks in him and through him concerning his own passion and resurrection. He speaks of the passion, as has been said, as though it were past; for example, when he says: “They pierced [Col. 0992B] my hands and my feet,” etc. But he treats the resurrection in words of the future, where he says: “I shall declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I shall praise you,” etc.

The intention is to exhort hearers to die and rise again with Christ. For unless we die with him, we shall not rise with him; unless we suffer with him, we shall not reign with him. But if we have been made one with the likeness of Christ’s death, we shall also be one with his resurrection. Let us therefore hear first Christ himself speaking in this psalm, and then anyone who desires to be united to his death and resurrection. For that Christ himself speaks in this psalm, the Lamb of God who opens the seven seals of the great book made known not merely in some fashion, but by a living voice [Col. 0992C] (Rev. 5:5). For, about to give up his spirit, he immediately cried out: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” The apostle Paul also, speaking of Christ in the Epistle to the Hebrews, says: “For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, ‘I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise you’” (Heb. 2:11–12).

Thus it is manifest that what is said here—“My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?”—must be assigned to Christ suffering and hanging on the cross; and that what is said here—“I shall declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I shall praise you”—belongs to the same Christ risen again and giving words of beauty. Therefore let Christ himself say, hanging on the cross [Col. 0992D] and crying with a loud voice—a voice truly loud, not because of a passing, high-pitched sound that touched the ears of the Jews and soldiers crucifying him without touching their hearts, but because of the great force of that cry, which “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1). For Christ, offering himself as a sacrifice for the whole Church, which reaches to the ends of the earth, complains that he has been forsaken, as though saying: “So long as one of my least members is forsaken, O my God, I feel myself forsaken.” Therefore I say: God of all generally, but my God particularly. My God, because, though I was in the form of God and did not consider equality with you a thing to be seized, I emptied myself, taking the form of a servant, and [Col. 0993A] was found in appearance as a human being (Phil. 2:6). Again, “my God,” because, though I was an innocent and holy human being, I did not exalt but humbled myself, becoming obedient to you, Father, “unto death, even death on a cross” (ibid., 8). Now, hanging upon it for all my own, I cry: “Eli, Eli, lamma sabacthani” (Matt. 27:46), that is:

**VERSE 2.** My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? “Look upon me” is not in the Hebrew, but was inserted by the Septuagint; it serves to express the sense of the doubled invocation, “My God, my God,” as though saying: “O God, you who rejected humankind because of the disobedience of the first transgression, by which man disdained to be under you as God, desiring to become like you—now look [Col. 0993B] upon me because of my twofold humiliation: namely, because, though I was God, I became human, so that you might be my God.

“Likewise, though I was human and owed nothing to death, yet obedient to you, who are my God, I humbled myself unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore I, twice humbled—once to be born and live in the flesh, a second time to die in the flesh—say twice, ‘My God, my God,’ so that you too may look upon me with a twofold regard: once, that you may raise me myself in the morning assumption from the single death, namely that of the flesh alone; a second time, that you may raise my members from the twofold death of bodies and souls—first destroying the death of souls through the death of my body, then restoring the life of bodies through my resurrection. For I desire the death of souls to be destroyed as I die, and the life of bodies to be restored as I rise; so that as soon as I die on this cross, and water and blood flowing from my side become the material from which my bride is to be fashioned, believing souls may immediately live in me, and faithful souls—whether placed on earth or in hell—may immediately perceive that the gate of life has been opened to them. As evidence of this, let the faithful soul of the confessing thief be with me today in paradise (Luke 23:43); and, when I rise in the body as the firstborn from the dead, let the gate of the resurrection of the dead immediately be opened, as evidence of which many bodies of saints may rise with me.

[Col. 0993D] “But although this will come quickly, some souls of the predestined will delay for a while in believing, like my disciple Thomas and my other disciples, whose unbelief and hardness of heart I shall rebuke on the day of my ascension, because they will not believe those who saw me risen unless they themselves also see and touch me.

“Likewise, many of my bodies will not rise before the last day. Therefore I say: ‘Why have you forsaken me, far from my salvation?’ That is: Why have you allowed my own to be delayed far from my salvation? For one of them will say: ‘Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails and put my hand into his side, I will not believe’ (John 20:25). But words of this kind are words of sins; they are not words of faith [Col. 0994A] or righteousness, when people say that they wish to see in order to believe, whereas they ought to believe in order to see. Therefore, in one unbeliever I rebuked such people and said: ‘Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe’ (John 4:48). Such are the Jews, who ask for signs, unwilling to believe invisible things except those which they can infer from visible signs. Such also are the Greeks, who seek wisdom, unwilling to believe anything except what they can grasp by human reason, saying in their hearts what Thomas says alike in heart and voice: ‘Unless I see, I will not believe’ (John 20:25). The Jew says: Unless I see through signs what I ought to believe, I will not believe. The Greek says: Unless I see through reason what ought to be believed, I will not believe. Indeed, everyone inflated by such empty philosophy desires to comprehend by human reason what a devout mind strives to grasp by the vitality of faith. Therefore, turning over in themselves words of sins, they are far from salvation because they are far from faith. But because I, the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, bore their sins, I call their sins my sins, so that my righteousness may become their righteousness. This agrees with what the Apostle says: ‘Him who knew no sin he made sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him’ (2 Cor. 5:21). And it is said in Isaiah: ‘Truly he bore our infirmities, and the Lord placed in him the iniquities of us all’ (Isa. 53:4, 6).

This verse can also be read so that what is said, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” is a question [Col. 0994C]. The solution to the question is what follows: “The words of my sins are far from my salvation.” As though he said: “God of all, and particularly my God, who never forsake me so that I may be separated from you by iniquity—for elsewhere I said, ‘He who sent me is with me and has not left me alone, because I always do what is pleasing to him’ (John 8:29)—why have you forsaken me to the punishment of sin, when you never forsook me for sinning? But I myself understand the answer to this question. I did indeed ask that this cup might pass from me, but the sins of my own required that I should suffer. The words of my righteousness cried out that I should not suffer, and so too did the words from the mouth of the unjust judge, saying: ‘I find no [Col. 0994D] fault in this man’ (Luke 23:14); likewise: ‘I find no cause of death in him’ (ibid., 22). The words of my righteousness also resounded through the judge’s wife, when she said: ‘Have nothing to do with that righteous man; for I have suffered much in a dream because of him’ (Matt. 27:19). But the words of sins pressing upon my own required that I, one man, should die for the people and that the whole nation should not perish. For these and similar words of my sins I have been made far from my salvation. For although it is my salvation that you always hear and heed me—for elsewhere I said: ‘For I knew that you always hear me’ (John 11:42)—yet, because the sins of my own must be cut off by the sword of my passion, and because the words of my sins, written with an iron stylus upon an adamantine nail [Col. 0995A], must be wholly erased, I, like a goat for the sin of my sins, must be sacrificed, made far from my salvation, since I am not heard in the customary way when I ask that the cup of suffering be removed from me. The prophet says: ‘The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus upon an adamantine nail’ (Jer. 17:1). Natural philosophers say that the hardness of adamant cannot be softened in any way except by the blood of a goat. Therefore, the sin written upon an adamantine nail—the words of my sins deeply impressed—must be erased from the adamantine nail by my blood, for I am the goat to be sacrificed for sinners.

“For these words of my sins, my God, you will not hear me crying by day or by night, to free me from the passion or remove this cup; [Col. 0995B] for by the blood of this cup the record full of words of sins must be erased, written in a script so strong upon an adamantine nail that it cannot be washed or effaced without my blood. I shall be sacrificed like a goat for many sinners and like a lamb for the innocent and righteous. Therefore, neither am I heard when crying by day nor by night, because neither the righteous and prophets, who shone in the world like day, nor sinners comparable to night could be saved without the healing antidote of my cup against the poison of sin. Thus, when I cry by day, ‘If it is possible for at least the righteous and prophets to be saved without the antidote of my cup, may I not drink the cup,’ you will not hear me. Still less, when I cry at night, will you hear me concerning my sins, because you will that the words of my sins be blotted out by the blood of the cup you give me, Father; you know that it is impossible for anyone, whether righteous like John the Baptist or unrighteous like the thief, to be saved without my passion. You know this and make me know it. Therefore it is not to my foolishness that I am not heard in the removal of the cup, for I am altogether heard in the removal of the eternal damnation of those for whom I drink that cup, or who shall worthily drink the same cup.

“For if, to any one of my servants asking a third time, you answer, my Father: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is made perfect in weakness’ (2 Cor. 12:9), and so it is not to his foolishness that he is not heard when he is taught [Col. 0995D] why he is not heard, much more is no foolishness introduced in this matter to me, your only-begotten Son, who am Wisdom coeternal with you, when I am not heard pouring forth prayers in weakness for my weak ones, so that their strength may be perfected in my weakness. For if I approached death in my strength without fear, without prayer having first been offered, afterwards my weak members, for whom it is natural to fear and feel dismay when death approaches—though it is in my power, not theirs—might be broken by despair, as though they did not belong to me. But when they read or hear that I, though having ‘power to lay down my life and to take it again’ [Col. 0996A] (John 10:18), nevertheless began to fear and feel dismay when the hour of death drew near, their strength will be perfected in my weakness; for their hope and trust will be strengthened, knowing that, though they have fear, they still belong to me, who first chose to fear and feel dismay for their strengthening.

“Similarly, in another hard obedience besides death, if my servants begin to fear and feel dismay, their strength will be perfected in weakness if, though fearful, they do not murmur against the Lord, but following my example ask, in fear of future temptations, to be delivered from temptations. Therefore, when I prayed a third time, I carefully roused my disciples also to pray in the same way. For I said: ‘Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, [Col. 0996B] but the flesh is weak’ (Matt. 26:4 [probably 26:41]). Therefore it is not to my foolishness that ‘I was not heard,’ when the strength of my own is perfected in my weakness. My own wisdom so orders it that what the folly of others rages against in me may be instruction for my own: that they may know that strength is made perfect in weakness whenever one of my own is not heard according to desire, yet is heard unto salvation. For in the time of her persecution the holy Church stands in faith and cries in longing, yet grieves that she is despised as though unregarded, when she sees her prayers delayed amid tribulations—whether she cries by day, desiring to retain prosperity, or cries by night, desiring adversity to be removed. For by a deep counsel almighty God, when his saints are crushed by the persecutions of adversaries [Col. 0996C] and cry in unceasing prayers to be delivered, is accustomed to delay the voices of petitioners, so that the merits of those who endure may increase, and that they may be heard all the more to their merit because they are not quickly heard according to their desire.”

The Psalmist therefore says:

**VERSE 3.** “My God, I shall cry by day, and you will not hear.” And the very benefit of the delay in hearing is immediately added, when he at once continues: “and it is not to my foolishness.” Therefore, that the wisdom of the saints may be increased, it profits them that they receive their requests slowly: longing grows from delay, and understanding is increased by longing. As understanding is extended, a more ardent affection for God is opened to it. And affection becomes capable of obtaining heavenly things in proportion as it has been patient in waiting. Yet amid these things sorrow presses holy patience into speech; and though people make progress by delay, they fear lest, failing and found empty, they may be rejected as persons despised in respect of blessings. But because strength is perfected in weakness, and because “we have in ourselves the answer of death, that we should not trust in ourselves but in God who raises the dead” (2 Cor. 1:9):

> “Let no one [Note: [Col. 0995D] St Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, book XXVI, ch. 19.] believe, when he is heard more slowly, that he is neglected by heavenly care. For often our desires are heard precisely because they are not speedily fulfilled, and what we urgently seek to have accomplished prospers better through delay itself. Often our voice is fulfilled by being deferred; and when our petition is seemingly neglected at the surface, our desires are fulfilled more deeply at the root of thought. Thus seeds of crops, compressed by frost, are strengthened; and the more slowly they emerge to the surface, the more abundantly they rise to fruit. Therefore righteous desires are stretched by delay so that they may advance, and are exercised in struggle so that they may be strengthened for what they are to receive and enriched with greater rewards in tribulation. The labour of battle is prolonged so that the crown of victory may increase. Thus, when the Lord does not quickly hear his own, he draws those whom he is thought to repel. For he is an inward physician, cutting away the contagions of sins that he rejects as dwelling deep within us. He cuts away the poison of corruption with the blade of tribulation; and the more he seems not to hear the voices of the sick, the more he secures the end of their sickness. Hence the Prophet says: ‘I shall cry by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and it is not to my foolishness.’ As though he said: It is by no means to my foolishness that you do not immediately hear me crying day and night, because from that by which you seem to forsake me in temporal tribulation, you instruct me more fully in eternal wisdom. Hence he also says elsewhere: ‘A helper in due times, in tribulation’ (Ps. 9:10). For, intending to say ‘in tribulation,’ he first put ‘in due times,’ because we are often crushed in tribulation, and yet the time is not yet fitting for us to be helped toward the desire [edition: ‘toward the desire’] of deliverance.”

In the Hebrew it is thus: “The words of my roaring are far from my salvation. My God, I shall cry by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and there is no silence for me.” Roaring [Col. 0997C] is properly the voice of a lion, which, when it sees itself caught in nets or a cage, is accustomed to utter a great roar. Thus the Lion of the tribe of Judah, caught in the nets of our sins, uttered great roars, crying on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Likewise, Job writes of the roaring of hinds (Job 39:3): they bend down to give birth and utter roars. Therefore this morning hind, bent down even to the reproach of the cross in order to give birth to a multitude of stags and hinds, uttered certain roars when, torn by dogs, she cried out in a great roar: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Other hinds also, giving birth to stags and hinds until Christ is formed in them, utter a great [Col. 0997D] roar in prayers and longings, in some manner saying with Christ: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” For the hearing of all these at last, he himself cried on the cross.

But because there he was not heard so as to obtain or preserve the safety of temporal life, he rightly says: “The words of my roaring are far from my salvation. My God, I shall cry by day, and you will not hear.” As though he said: The words of my roaring are far from salvation because they are not heard—whether by day, to obtain temporal prosperity, or by night, to repel tribulation. Yet there is no silence for me, because I know that I shall finally be heard in my roaring. For I indeed have already become a lion’s cub caught and bitten by hell; [Col. 0998A] I have already been swallowed like another Jonah in the belly of the whale; I already seem like Samson, bound and shorn—or rather, like a sheep shorn—by those who scourged me, stripped me of my garments, and hung me upon the cross.

**VERSE 4.** But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel. You dwell in your holy heaven, of which it was said in the preceding psalm: “He will hear him from his holy heaven, in the mighty deeds of salvation of his right hand.” Therefore I am not heard here when I ask that the cup of suffering be removed from me, because in this request there is not the salvation of the right hand, but a condescension to the weak; and thus I indeed seem to be forsaken by you. But you dwell in me, your holy one, and you will not allow your holy one to see corruption. Rather, you will make me see not only in [Col. 0998B] my flesh, but also in the bodies and souls of my own, the glory of incorruption. For though I now sit like another Job on the dung-heap of mortality, scraping the discharge of my flesh with the potsherd of my passion, yet it shall come to pass that in my flesh I shall see incorruption and immortality, and the eternal, divine splendour of incorruption and immortality. I shall show it to those for whom I now suffer, “because I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may behold my glory,” and behold my flesh glorified with that glory “which I had with you before the world was” (John 17:24).

As they behold me, your Son, in you my Father, and you, the Father, in me your Son, you, Father, shall be the praise of Israel—of every man who sees you as God in me as God, together with the Holy Spirit as God, one God—from whose face the first Adam fled through disobedience. But I, the second Adam, I, true Israel, now made obedient unto death, even death on a cross, before the face of the glorious Trinity—before the face of the Father remaining in me, of the Word united to me, and of the Holy Spirit, by whose fire I am at present made a burnt offering—now present myself through obedience, expiating the fault of him who fled from God in Paradise, ashamed through disobedience. He was silent from praise; but I acknowledge and confess that you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel. Therefore, on this day of evils I shall not be unmindful of good things; on this day when you do not hear me in removing the cup of suffering, I shall remember your mercies, by which, in hearing the people [Col. 0998D] Israel, you were the praise of Israel. For:

**VERSES 5 AND 6.** “Our fathers trusted in you; they trusted, and you delivered them. They cried to you and were saved; they trusted in you and were not put to shame.” When our fathers were afflicted in Egypt, they trusted in you; and, striking Egypt with many plagues, you finally delivered them marvellously through the sacrifice of the Passover lamb, prefiguring this passion of mine (Exod. 12:28). Father Abraham trusted in you, and you delivered him from Ur of the Chaldeans (Gen. 11:31). The patriarch Isaac trusted in you, and you delivered him from the Philistines who envied him (ibid., 26:16). Jacob, also called Israel, trusted in you, praise of Israel, and you delivered him from the hand of Laban and from his pursuing brother [Col. 0999A] Esau (ibid., 31:17; 28:5). Moses and Aaron trusted in you when the Egyptians pursued them beside the shore of the Red Sea, and you delivered them by opening a way through the Red Sea (Exod. 14:22). Many other fathers trusted in you, and you delivered them. Through faith they conquered kingdoms, as Moses and Aaron conquered the Egyptian kingdom through faith. Elijah and Elisha conquered the Israelite kingdom through faith, eliminating from it the worship of idols (3 Kings 18:39). Daniel and the three youths conquered the Babylonian kingdom through faith (Dan. 3:95). Mordecai and Queen Esther conquered the kingdom of the Persians and Medes through faith (Esther 17:10). The valiant Maccabees conquered the kingdom of the Greeks through faith (2 Macc. 15:27). These and many like them [Col. 0999B], as well as lesser persons, trusted in you, and you delivered them.

Yet others were stretched out, refusing redemption in order that they might find a better resurrection. Chief among them am I, who now, behold, am stretched out upon the cross and do not find redemption or deliverance, that I may find a better resurrection—not for myself alone, rising as the firstborn from the dead, but also for all who shall rise with me: those who suffer with me in my suffering, die with me in my death, and are despised together with me in this world; those who are found meek and humble, who after my example do not curse when cursed, nor threaten when suffering. For although I could, if I wished, fight more gloriously with more than twelve legions of angels made available and presented to me than my faithful ones, “who put to flight foreign armies” (Heb. 11:34), nevertheless, behold, I do not fight against the Roman empire or its officer Pilate, in order to provide an example of meekness and humility.

The faithful patriarch Abraham overthrew four kings in one day with three hundred and eighteen household servants (Gen. 14:15). Joshua, leader of Israel, defeated five kings in battle at Gibeon while the sun stood still (Josh. 10:10). Gideon, with three hundred men, put many thousands of enemies to flight (Judg. 7:22). Samson struck down a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass (ibid., 15:15). And none of all these mighty men conquered kingdoms or acted valiantly through any other faith than because they believed that I was to come, and in this faith they were strong and invincible.

[Col. 0999D] **VERSES 7–8.** “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the rejection of the people. All who saw me mocked me; they spoke with their lips and shook their heads.” I, I say, am a worm so liable to be trodden underfoot; like a worm, and like the tenderest wood-worm, I am so frail that not, I say, the Roman emperor himself, but his officer Pilate and that officer’s subordinate soldiers dare to trample me. These most contemptible men do not even permit my garments to be given to my mother standing by, to the beloved disciple, or to any others of my own; rather, they divided my garments among themselves and cast lots for my robe. But in their eyes I am a worm—indeed, I am the tenderest wood-worm. Behold, I hang upon wood, and with the fire of suffering brought near me I cry out like a beetle cast from wood into [Col. 1000A] fire; I, who am so basely and contemptuously trampled upon as though I were a worm and not a human being.

Truly, however, in the eyes of those who love me I am a worm and not a man; for just as a worm is born from moist earth, fertilized solely by the sun’s heat, so I, born from virginal flesh—fertilized by the Holy Spirit through the dew of heaven and the heat of the eternal Sun—am fittingly called a worm and not a man. Not because I am not a man, but because I am more than a man. For if John, though he was called by his father Zechariah a prophet of the Most High, and himself knew that he was a prophet sanctified from the womb (Luke 1:76), nevertheless, because he was not merely a prophet but also more than a prophet, when the Pharisees asked whether he was a prophet, replied:

[Col. 1000B] “I am not a prophet” (John 1:21);

how much more truly do I, not merely a man but more than a man, say: “I am a worm and not a man”? And yet, though I am the Most High God, I became the reproach of men and the rejection of the people: the reproach of men in the thorns and disgraceful blows, and the rejection of the people who rejected me, demanding that Barabbas the robber be given them in my place.

Yet none of this happens to me unto folly. For our fathers, though holy, were nevertheless merely human; therefore they hoped for human consolations amid tribulation, and through those consolations they hoped for other, greater, spiritual consolations. Therefore I say twice, “they hoped,” and finally add, “and you delivered them”: first giving temporal consolations, such as victory over enemies, abundance of crops, and other such things [Col. 1000C] in this life, and through these promising the far greater consolations of eternal goods in hope. But I, who am a worm and not a man, do not need human and temporal consolation as they did, who had to be nourished through these temporal comforts so that they might hope for eternal ones. Some carnal persons, serving only for temporal things, were rewarded here through them and wholly deprived of the eternal things for which they had not served.

Here is wisdom. Let him who has understanding reckon, and he will find that among those who serve God there is as great a distance as “the east is from the west” (Ps. 102:12). For he who serves God for earthly things, having received here the reward of his service, is saved—but only in order to perish more completely. But he who serves in warfare for eternal things, with the pay of his service deferred [Col. 1000D] to the future, is punished here in order to rejoice elsewhere. He does not care for a childish reward, that he may receive a perfect one. He grieves little or not at all when, praying for temporal things, he is not heard; for even in this he prays so as to imitate Christ praying, adding or understanding: “Nevertheless, not as I will” (Matt. 26:39), but as God wills, so let it be—provided that whatever is done to me in such matters is not done to me unto folly.

The perfect soldier of God considers this, choosing rather, with the apostle Paul—or even with Christ himself—not to be heard in such matters, than to be heard quickly according to his wish, but not for his benefit, as the demons were. For the legion of demons that asked for the herd of swine was heard quickly. Paul, asking the Lord three times that the thorn of the flesh might depart [Col. 1001A] from him, was not heard according to his wish (2 Cor. 12:8). So too Christ was not heard according to the will of the flesh, but for the benefit and necessity of his own.

For among Christ’s members—among those, that is, predestined from eternity as elect—there were some such persons for whom it was fitting to drink the cup of suffering through martyrdom, so that the Church might be planted by their blood. The first of these was blessed “Stephen, full of grace and power” (Acts 6:8). There were likewise others dear to God, of whom John, Christ’s beloved disciple, was foremost, whom it was expedient to free from martyrdom, so that the Church might be watered and enlightened by their teaching. Corresponding to this difference between them, the times themselves also differ: one is a time of war, another a time of peace.

[Col. 1001B] For in a time of war the holy martyrs drank the Lord’s cup through manifest sufferings and became friends of God. In a time of peace, however, the blessed confessors, serving God through chastity and teaching, experienced the cup of suffering not as removed from them but as transferred: desiring willingly to die, they were compelled patiently to live. This was for them a kind of drinking of the cup, while they mingled their drink with tears and “crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5:24).

Therefore Christ did not say without reason: “Father, if it is possible, transfer this cup from me” (Matt. 26:39); for where this could and ought to occur, this cup, as we have said, was not removed but transferred. Hence, when Christ offered that same cup to Peter to drink, saying, “Follow me” (John 22:19 [i.e. John 21:19]), and Peter wished to know concerning another fellow-disciple whether he too ought to drink the same cup in the same way, he heard Christ say to him:

[Col. 1001C] “Thus I will that he remain until I come. What is that to you? Follow me” (ibid., 22).

Thus this beloved disciple is believed to have obtained the transfer of the cup through that prayer of Christ in which he said to the Father: “If it is possible, transfer this cup from me” (Luke 22:42). Likewise, the disciple, hearing that he would be girded by another and led where he did not wish, could rightly understand that he belonged to that part of Christ’s prayer in which he said in the Passion: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will”; and, “not my will but yours be done, Father” [Col. 1001D] (Mark 14:36).

In us sinners also the differing effect of this twofold prayer is evident. The cup of certain sufferings which the world threatens is transferred from us, because, without harm to God’s grace and to our salvation, this can and ought to happen. But where this cannot happen, we are girded by another and at times led where we do not wish, while we suffer what we would not wish to suffer if, without harm to God’s glory and grace, we could have peace.

Nevertheless, although in our time “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of the saints” (Ps. 115:15), and of the martyrs from whom the ministers of Antichrist seek to take either the possibility of living justly or the possibility of living in peace—lying in wait for the salvation of souls in the former case and of bodies in the latter—yet in the sight of the Church, through the mutilation of members [Col. 1002A] and the plundering of goods which the wicked devise against the godly, evil persons of courage are not so much corrected as weak good persons are disturbed.

We pray, Christ, that your prayer over us may be heard, through which it may be granted to us and to all whom Antichrist persecutes either to remain thus, as John remained when the cup was transferred from him, or to follow you thus, as Peter followed you by drinking the cup; so that, whether we live or die, we may be found such that our life and death bring “joy” not only to the “angels” in heaven, who rejoice “over” every “sinner doing penance” (Luke 15:10), but also to the godly sons and daughters of mother Church, ready to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep.

And because you tempered your drink with our tears when, though in yourself anointed with the unfailing oil of gladness, you nevertheless drank for our sake the vinegar of sorrow, when your soul was sorrowful unto death: through this very sharing in our sorrow, whereby you, the true Isaac—being the laughter and joy of angels—became a sharer in human sorrow, grant us a share in your gladness. Turn our mourning into joy, so that, our sorrow being changed into gladness, no one may take our joy from us. Grant us such grace that we may never grieve the Holy Spirit dwelling in us, nor wish to grieve him; and that there may never arise from us either sorrow for the godly or joy for the ungodly.

For if, crying at some time by day or by night, [Col. 1002C] we are not heard as we wish, it may be that this itself is not unto sorrow for us, provided it is not unto folly—as it was not unto folly for Christ that he was not heard at the Jews’ pleasure when they said to him: “If you are the Son of God, come down” now “from the cross” (Matt. 27:40). Yet he was heard because of his reverence—not according to the will of the mocking Jews, but for the salvation of all his own: whether those from whom, by transferring the cup, he wills them to remain as John the Theologian remained; or those who will drink the cup like Peter. All these things have been ordered hitherto and will still be ordered according to the ineffable wisdom of divine providence. Therefore Christ himself, hanging on the cross, rightly says: “My God, I will cry by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and not unto folly for me.”

[Col. 1002D] And indeed to many the preaching of the cross seemed great folly, when the omnipotence of Christ himself crucified was proclaimed—an omnipotence scarcely, or not at all, believed by those who foolishly looked upon the weakness of the cross. Of them it is said in what follows: “But they looked and gazed upon me.” “But we,” says the Apostle, “preach Christ crucified: to Jews indeed a stumbling-block, but to Gentiles foolishness; but to those called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God; because what is weak in God is stronger than men, and what is foolish in God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1:23–25).

Let the Jews, if they please, recall their brethren among men: for example, victorious Joshua, left-handed Ehud, Gideon armed with the trumpets of three hundred soldiers, most mighty Samson, David strong of hand, and other strong men. We, on the contrary, say with the apostle Paul that “what is weak in God is stronger than men.” For indeed God’s weak body upon the cross is stronger than men, because it accomplished deeds stronger than all the ancient strong men.

There the true Joshua opened the entrance into the land of promise, hitherto closed, when he opened Paradise to the confessing thief and to all who confess him. There the truly ambidextrous Ehud, with hands outstretched, drew all things to himself, as he had foretold: “I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). There the true Gideon gloriously triumphed in the three hundred through the victory of the cross, which is signified by the letter T. There the true Samson killed more by dying than [Col. 1003B] he had previously killed while living. There the true David, with the shepherd’s staff of the cross, slew the lion and the bear, freeing the sheep attacked by the devil. There, against the proud Philistine Goliath, the true David, strong of hand, possessed five wounds—or five stones in the shepherd’s bag, that is, in his mortal body—but with one stone, that is, one wound, he struck down that proud and hitherto unconquerable foe, through the sacrament of blood and water flowing from his side.

Therefore it was truly said against the Jews’ stumbling-block that “what is weak in God is stronger than men,” because whatever deed is read in their books as done valiantly cannot in any way be worthily compared with that strength which is known to have been present in the weakness of Christ dying and having the horns of the cross in his hands; for “there his strength is hidden” (Hab. [Col. 1003C] 3:4). Hidden indeed, not diminished. This is shown by the fact that, while he was dying on the cross, “death went before his face” (ibid.); and, seeing him, the gates of death were shattered. This was plainly attested by the earth’s shaking, the sun’s darkening, the rocks’ splitting, the tombs’ opening, and the veil of the temple’s being torn from top to bottom.

O Jews, if, according to your custom, you seek signs, behold: you see many signs. This is the chief sign, through which, by Moses’ command, you ought to have recognized that great prophet: because every word that he spoke or foretold did not lack fulfillment. He said to Lazarus, dead and lying in the tomb, already stinking: “Come forth,” and he came out (John 11:43–44). He said to the blind man: “See,” [Col. 1003D] and he saw (Luke 18:42–43). He said to the leper: “Be cleansed” (Mark 1:41), and he was cleansed. He said to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house” (Luke 5:24), and he rose. He foretold that his Gospel would be preached throughout the world, and behold, “their sound has gone out into all the earth,” the sound of the evangelists, “and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5). He foretold that you would be driven from your place and led captive among all nations; and behold, you are dispersed and captive, nor can you regain your place, taken from you by Roman rulers—rather, joined to the Roman Church through the princes of the apostles (Luke 21:24).

Recognize, therefore, that “what is weak in God is stronger than men,” whose strength you boast of, when you see so many signs [Col. 1004A] of invincible strength fulfilled through the mystery of the holy cross.

Recognize, by the truth of prophecy, the face of the true prophet, of whom Moses says: “Every soul that will not hear that prophet shall be cut off from his people” (Num. 9:13). And indeed, if he had preached to you a foreign god, however many signs he had performed, Moses forbids you to hear him. For he says:

“If a prophet arises in your midst, or one who says that he has seen a dream, and foretells a sign or wonder, and what he has spoken comes to pass, and he says to you: ‘Let us go and follow foreign gods, whom you do not know, and let us serve them,’ you shall not hear the words of that prophet or dreamer; for the Lord your God is testing you, that it may be made manifest whether you love [Col. 1004B] him or not with your whole heart and with your whole soul. Follow the Lord your God and fear him; keep his commandments and hear his voice. You shall serve him alone and cling to him. But that prophet or fabricator of dreams shall be put to death, because he has spoken in order to turn you away from the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of bondage, in order to make you stray from the way which the Lord your God commanded you; and you shall remove evil from your midst” (Deut. 13:1–5).

Likewise, if he had proclaimed your God and spoken a word which did not come to pass, he would have to be rejected as a false prophet, since Moses says:

“The prophet who, corrupted by arrogance, presumes to speak in my name what I have not commanded him to say, or in the name [Col. 1004C] of foreign gods, shall be put to death. But if you answer in silent reflection, ‘How can I understand the word which the Lord has not spoken?’ you shall have this sign: what that prophet foretells in the name of the Lord, and does not come to pass, the Lord has not spoken; rather, the prophet has invented it through the pride of his own mind, and therefore you shall not fear him” (Deut. 18:20, 22).

But now, since he has not proclaimed to us a foreign God, but the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, and since, in this attestation of your true God, every word that he spoke has not lacked the efficacy of truth—as is clear, behold, in your dispersion which he foretold—why do you not hear this prophet, commended to you by Moses’ testimony? For if, as you suppose, he had lied in calling himself God or the Son of God, such efficacy of signs would by no means have accompanied a false prophet. If he does not perform the works of the Father, or of almighty God, do not believe that he is the Son of God or God. But if he does perform them, believe the works, that you may know that he is in the Father and the Father in him: one Almighty.

Therefore he performed many miracles possible to God alone, not by asking God, as a holy man, but by commanding, as God-Man—a power granted to none but God alone. Your Moses brought it about, not by commanding, but by crying to God, that the Red Sea might be divided into its divisions. But this prophet, greater than Moses, commanded the winds and the sea, and a great calm ensued. “He commands the winds,” that is, evil spirits, [Col. 1005A] “and the sea,” that is, this stormy age, “and they obey him” (Luke 8:25). He commanded the Romans to take away both your place and your nation, and they obeyed him. He commanded those same Romans, when he willed, to cease from persecuting Christians, and there was a great calm. Although for a time he permitted, or permits, his little vessel on this sea—namely, the holy Church—to be shaken, he nevertheless performs the works of his Father in such a way that, just as his Father, when the flood overflowed, saved eight souls in Noah’s ark, so he himself saves through the wood of the cross those who believe and have in it the hope of resurrection.

Likewise, to say it briefly and fully: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5:19). Truly likewise, because he works with equal omnipotence as the Father works; and truly whatever the Father does, the Son also does, because neither the Father without the Son nor the Son without the Father does anything. Although this can be recognized and proved in many ways, let this suffice for you, O Jews, who have denied the Son of God up to the present day: while he hung on the cross and, as it seemed to you, then performed no signs, the power of paternal majesty was present through a great earthquake and other manifest signs, touching even the hearts of Gentiles so that they believed him to be the Son of God—him whose death the world cried out that it could not endure. Hence came the centurion’s cry: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. 27:54).

[Col. 1005C] Whence came this to you, O Gentile centurion, that you confessed him to be the Son of God while the Jew denied him? Whence came this to you? Was it not because you perceived that what is weak in God was stronger than men? You perceived it from this: you saw such great wonders occur while Christ was dying. Though he was reckoned as a worm and not a man, made the reproach of men and the rejection of the people, still it was made clear, by the very power of his dying, that he was the almighty Son of almighty God. For no one took or wrenched his soul from him, as the souls of the thieves were wrenched from their bodies by the breaking of their legs; rather, he himself powerfully laid it down when he wished, saying: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46), and again powerfully took it up when he rose from the dead.

Let these words suffice against the Jew who blasphemes the weakness of the Lord’s Passion: either let him believe that what is weak in God is stronger than men, or, if [Col. 1005D] he will not yield to manifest truth, let him be compelled to be silent.

But what shall we say to the Gentiles, and especially to the Greeks, who seek wisdom, considering it folly that the Almighty should redeem humankind with so much labor when he could liberate it by a word alone? “But we,” says the Apostle, “preach Christ crucified: to Jews indeed a stumbling-block, but to Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1:23). Against the Jews’ stumbling-block it has indeed been proved that what is weak in God is stronger than men. But now, against the Gentiles who mock the tree of the cross as a sycamore—which is called the foolish fig—and stumble at its foolishness, [Col. 1006A] this must be proved: that what is foolish in God is wiser than men; that the apparent folly of the cross surpasses in true wisdom all the sages of Greece.

Since many Greeks are praised for their wisdom, we cannot speak of many of them. Let us put forward for the present matter one whom we know was regarded as wise among both Greeks and Latins: that Ulysses whom Homer commends among the Greeks, Virgil among the Latins, and our Boethius also praises; whom the entire school of poets calls a wise man. He is so called because he could hear the Sirens’ voices unharmed; because he was neither overcome nor deceived by Circe’s potions and enchantments; because, shaken by innumerable toils on land and sea, he remained unconquered, protected everywhere not so much by strength of body as by the prudence of an ingenious mind.

This man, attacking Polyphemus, devourer of his companions, by cunning, overcame him by blinding the one eye which he alone is said to have had. By his ingenious skill, illustrious Troy is said to have been captured more by the shrewdness of counsels than by the strength of arms; and therefore the theatres of Greeks and Latins celebrate this man as wise and ingenious.

But if we compare the folly of the cross with such great wisdom, it is as though we compared the sunlight with a burning torch. Even if those things read about him whom they call wise were believed not invented but accomplished, incomparably greater are the things accomplished—not invented—through the mystery of the cross, and believed without doubt.

[Col. 1006C] They believe their authors and writers, who were free to invent and mingle falsehood with truth. Let us also believe our authors and writers, in whose testimonies the Spirit of truth speaks without any admixture whatsoever of falsehood. They believe that Polyphemus’s eye was pierced and blinded by the wisdom of Ulysses. And we believe—and therefore speak—that the nostrils of Leviathan were pierced by the stakes of the cross and its nails. He could not free the companions devoured by Polyphemus, though he could avenge them. Hence Boethius says:

> The Ithacan wept for his lost companions,  
> whom savage Polyphemus, lying in his vast cave,  
> swallowed in his monstrous belly;  
> yet, raging with blinded face,  
> he repaid sad tears with joy.

[Note: [Col. 1005D] Book IV, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, metre 7.]

[Col. 1006D] But Christ, rescuing his own from Leviathan’s mouth, pierced its jaw with a ring; and he was about to bring his own out from the belly of the whale after three days and three nights there. Thus he came forth victorious with his own, unharmed—though not without injury to the whale itself, which vomited him forth and lost many whom it had long devoured.

It may have been glorious for Ulysses to capture Troy by deceit and cunning; vastly more and more perfectly glorious was it for Christ, through the trophy of the cross, to conquer hell and subject the whole world to his laws, after binding and casting out the strong armed man. That these things were accomplished, not invented, is undoubtedly attested by the temples overthrown and the churches of Christ built [Col. 1007A] throughout the world; nor are human beings alone called as witnesses to our assertion, but demons also, crying out from possessed bodies while they are compelled to depart through the power of the cross.

Whether, therefore, the things which pagan writings report concerning the wise men of the world—of whom the aforementioned Ulysses was chief—are said to have happened or to have been invented, that which in the mystery of the cross is thought foolish by them is infinitely wiser than the prudent and wise human beings in whom Greece glories and over whose wisdom it is vainly inflated. For “God has made foolish the wisdom of this age” (1 Cor. 1:20) and has destroyed the prudence of the prudent, who, while calling themselves wise, became fools, serving the creature rather than the Creator—which was the greatest folly.

[Col. 1007B] Conversely, great wisdom is to worship in the cross the Creator and Redeemer, believing and confessing that he who was crucified is God and, behold, reigns over all things. To know him is life; to serve him is to reign. His burden is light; to bear his yoke is sweet. To submit to his commands and counsels, and to believe his promises, is salvation, true life, and great wisdom.

Since all this is so, I, Christ, do not say in vain: “I will cry by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and not unto folly for me.” For although my being a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and rejection of the people, appears weak to the Jews and foolish and stupid to Greeks and other Gentiles, nevertheless this weakness [Col. 1007C] is stronger than men, and this foolishness is wiser than men.

But because this strength and wisdom are hidden from the eyes of carnal persons, “all who saw me mocked me; they spoke with their lips and shook their heads.” They showed mockery to the mystery of the cross, to which they ought to have shown veneration. They mocked in their heart, spoke with their lips, and shook their heads. For “shaking their heads,” they said: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days” (Matt. 27:39–40, 43): “He trusted in the Lord; let him deliver him now, if he wills.”

**VERSE 9.** “He trusted in the Lord; let him deliver him.” So great is the identity of wording in the psalm and the Gospel that these two cherubim seem to look at one another: namely, the psalmist and the evangelist, with faces turned toward me, the mercy-seat, who upon the cross became propitiation for the sins of all believers.

The Gospel says: “He trusted in God; let him now deliver him, if he wills” (Matt. 27:43). Here the psalm says: “He trusted in the Lord; let him rescue him; let him save him, because he wills him.” Thus they speak; and though unknowingly, they speak the truth, because you will truly save me by raising me from death, since you will me, you love me—as may be established from what has gone before.

**VERSES 10 AND 11.** “For you are he who drew me from the womb; my hope from my mother’s breasts. Upon you I was cast from the womb. From my mother’s belly, you are my God.”

You are he who drew me from the virginal womb, which no man opened, which was closed before [Col. 1008A] childbirth, in childbirth, and remained closed after childbirth. Hence I know that you will also bring me out of the closed and sealed tomb. “My hope from my mother’s breasts.” Before I had a mother, you were my Father to me; but after I had a mother, whose breasts I suckled, you proved to be not merely my Father according to the begetting by which you begot me today—that is, eternally—but also began to be my hope, insofar as you received me as man into true sonship, not by adoption but by that sanctification of which I said to the Jews: “If he called those gods to whom the word of God came, and Scripture cannot be broken, do you say to him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (John 10:35–36).

Therefore, although I am a true man, yet, sanctified into God, the Son of God, I rightly place my hope in you, my Father and my God, who begot me before the ages and now, when the fullness of time came, sanctified me in my virgin mother’s womb; and preserved that holy mother herself, that she might nurse me with breasts full of heaven, virginal breasts. Therefore I say to you, Father: “My hope from my mother’s breasts,” because I, a human being, the son of such a mother and such a Father, may rightly hope for much good.

“I was cast upon you from the womb”: either from the womb of my virgin mother, as a weak man, as a most tender infant, and as an orphan born into this world without a human father. Through the faith of my devout mother, who commended me to you with especial care, I was cast upon you as Father and guardian. Or I was cast from the womb of my mother, the Synagogue, [Col. 1008C] whose womb did not bring me forth but hurled me away. That mother indeed wished, by casting me out, to destroy me as an abortion; but I, “pushed” and “overthrown that I might fall” (Ps. 117:13), “was cast upon you: my hope from my mother’s breasts.”

For because I would not suck from the breasts of that mother of mine, the Synagogue, its carnal customs, it became clear that you are my hope: you who are not flesh but spirit, not a carnal father but a spiritual one. From your spiritual nobility, such nobility is innate in me, your human son, that I could not suck except breasts full of heaven, virginal breasts, “breasts more beautiful than wine” (Song 4:10), fragrant with the finest ointments. Therefore I loathed the carnal breasts of carnal observances, by which “my mother” was corrupted, by which “she who bore me was violated” (Song 8:5)—my mother, the Synagogue.

[Col. 1008D] Seeing that I did not suck her breasts, she said within herself: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9:16). Thus she cast me out as though unworthy of life, as a desperate man. Nevertheless, you are my hope from my mother’s breasts; upon you I was cast from the womb; and from my mother’s belly you are my God.

From the belly of my virgin mother, you are my God. You indeed begot me from your womb before Lucifer, before the world was made, before there were any times marked out by Lucifer and other heavenly signs; and now, when the fullness of time came, you drew me from the womb of my virgin mother. Or you drew me, made man from David’s seed according to the flesh, from the womb of my mother the Synagogue.

[Col. 1009A] But from your womb, to me begotten before Lucifer, you are not my God; in relation to me you are my eternal Father, possessing me as a Son coeternal with yourself. Yet from the belly of my mother you are my God, and I am therefore your creature: by taking flesh from my mother’s womb, I became a man capable of suffering tribulation. And therefore I ask:

**VERSE 12.** “Do not depart from me, because tribulation is near, and there is none to help.” There is man to inflict tribulation, and there is no man to help. Those known to me withdrew from me as strangers, because even all the disciples, abandoning me, fled; and:

**VERSE 13.** “Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls besieged me.” The many calves were common people, wanton and insolent. The fat bulls were proud, fierce, and wealthy rulers, made fiercer by the very fatness of their wealth. The calves surrounded me when they seized me with swords and clubs as though I were a robber, though I was daily teaching among them in the temple and they did not seize me, because my hour had not yet come. But now, after my hour and the power of darkness had come, the calves surrounding me attacked me with sharp little horns, and the fat bulls so besieged me that no place for escape was open to me.

For when Pilate judged that I should be punished and released, they cried: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself king opposes Caesar” (John 19:12).

[Col. 1009C] Again: “We found this man subverting our nation and forbidding tribute to be paid to Caesar” (Luke 23:2).

Again: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:7).

By shouting such things, and by putting forward on every side false testimony as though I had sinned against Caesar and against the law, they besieged me so that no just ground appeared on which I might be judged worthy of release—being thought an enemy of law and king. Therefore they, as faithful zealots for the law and friends of Caesar:

**VERSE 14.** “Opened their mouth against me like a lion ravening and roaring,” with fierce eagerness like beasts—like a lion or hyena, gaping with open jaws to swallow me. They opened their mouth against me, thirsting for my blood. Therefore like a ravening lion they seized me, and like a roaring lion they cried: “He is guilty of death. Crucify, crucify him” (Matt. 26:66; Luke 23:21).

Such a cry was not a human voice; indeed, it was the roar of the lion that formerly raged against me in Pharaoh, when he ordered the male infants of the Hebrews—among whom I was to be born—to be killed. And now, after I had been born, in Herod, as another Pharaoh, thirsting for my blood, he again ordered male infants to be killed, that he might kill me also among them. But since until now the bloody jaws of this lion had been frustrated and utterly unable to devour me, these people now, cooperating with that same lion, that is, the devil himself, opened their mouth against me, desiring to devour me.

At first they wished to devour me in such a manner that I might be incorporated with them, by keeping the Sabbath, without considering that I am Lord of the Sabbath. They also wished me to observe the traditions of the Fathers which they observed and observe, making the divine commandment void. For God said: “Honor your father and mother” (Exod. 20:12); but they, serving their own greed, teach that a gift to be given to father or mother should be brought to the altar. When I rebuked this, and would not be incorporated with them in doing such things, they turned to another device of their wickedness by which to devour me. Therefore they opened their mouth against me like a lion ravening and roaring.

Yet, however they opened their mouth, they could not devour me or incorporate me into themselves. Therefore:

**VERSE 15.** “Like worthless water I was poured out by them, and all my bones were scattered.” Whom they could not devour, they presumed to trample. But wishing to trample me as unclean water, they slipped in the tracks of their own slipperiness. Through me, however, as through heavenly water, as through the early and latter rain, good earth was watered and the whole Church made fruitful. For as water, when it is poured out, washes and waters, so I, poured out, washed away filth and watered minds. Water came forth from the temple of my body at the right side, and all whom this water reached were made whole (John 19:34).

Yet by that same water the enemies’ way became slippery, so that they fell; and likewise the way of my disciples, so that they could not stand, but all [Col. 1010C] fled, abandoning me. Therefore I say: “All my bones were scattered.” For when I was poured out like water, all my bones were scattered, because on that night all my disciples were scandalized in me, so that Peter, who was one of my stronger bones, denied me three times. Hence, through the excessive fire of sorrow:

“My heart became like melting wax in the midst of my belly.” And the apostles themselves, who had formerly been steadfast, as though my heart, failed in all their strength as the fire of the Passion grew intense, like melting wax. And since the proper seat of the heart is within the enclosure of the ribs, they, like soft entrails, were not unconquered within the strength of my ribs, so as to be as bone from my bones; rather, they were like [Col. 1010D] “flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2:23) in the midst of my belly—that is, in the company of the weak, who possess no strength.

Alternatively: My heart, that is, Scripture—formerly hard—has been dissolved like melting wax, and by its melting gives light. Hence, when I was dying on the cross, the veil of the temple was torn, and the secrets of the sanctuary, formerly veiled, were laid open; thereby the Holy Spirit signifying that the way of the saints had been made manifest while the former tabernacle had no standing. The way of the saints is the way leading into the Holy of Holies—namely Christ, who says: “I am the way” (John 14:6). But while the former tabernacle stood, this way was not openly manifest, because Christ lay hidden beneath the veil of figures—for example, in the figure of the paschal lamb [Col. 1011A], or of the red heifer, or of the goat sacrificed for the sin of the multitude. Rightly was the veil of such figures torn when the true lamb was sacrificed to make the guilty innocent, and the true goat to make the impenitent penitent; when the true “high priest, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made by hands, that is, not of this creation, neither through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. 9:11–12).

**VERSE 16.** My strength has dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue has clung to my throat. My apostles, of whom “the spirit indeed was willing, but the flesh weak” (Matt. 26:41), because of the weakness [Col. 1011B] of the flesh were like melting wax in the midst of my belly; but because of the willing spirit, my strength and my tongue were my strength: strength through the faith by which they believed in their hearts unto righteousness; tongue through the confession by which they confessed with their mouths unto salvation. But in the fire of the Passion this my strength became at once soft and hard: soft like melting wax, so that through them the light of faith might be spread abroad; hard like a potsherd, so that from them might be made a lamp to be set upon the lampstand of the whole Church, not beneath the bushel of Jewish narrowness. For a lamp is light within a potsherd; unless the latter had first been hardened in the fire, it could not contain the oil’s richness as fuel for the flame. Mortal, sinful flesh is like a soft potsherd and [Col. 1011C] worthless clay; unless it is dried out in those who must crucify their flesh with its vices and desires, it cannot become a servant of light.

Therefore I, Christ, though free and wholly pure from sin, nevertheless willingly, through the frailty of mortality, being like a soft potsherd enclosed in Judaea as in a potter’s house, and cast out and trampled in the potter’s field, as the Lord himself, the potter, ordained for me, was not yet prepared “before the face of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:31–32). But when my strength dried up like a potsherd—when my flesh did not fail like hay in the fire of suffering, but advanced by receiving strength like a potsherd in the fire—I was immediately set before the face of all peoples as a light [Col. 1011D] for revelation to the Gentiles by him who, before I appeared in the flesh, said to me: “I have set you as a light to the Gentiles, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth” (Isa. 49:6).

Likewise, before my Passion my apostles and other disciples were being formed like soft potsherds in the potter’s house, while they were instructed through my teaching. But strengthened by my Passion and resurrection, they were made fit for their light to shine before people throughout the whole earth. And as I, the true Job, sitting upon the dung heap, scraped away the discharge of assumed frailty with the potsherd of strength—in which, when I willed, I laid down my life, and again, when I willed, I took it up—so too my apostles scraped away the discharge of their sins through faith in my Passion and resurrection [Col. 1012A]. For during forty days, through many proofs, they who had been weak were made firm like a potsherd; and they who, being my tongue, were struck dumb through the scandal of the cross—for then my tongue clung to my throat—afterwards “began to speak in different tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:4).

Yet because I, Christ, now speak as placed in the Passion—in which I myself was mute and did not open my mouth, like a lamb before its shearer (Isa. 53:7), while all the disciples not only kept silent but even fled, leaving me—rightly I now say that my strength, formerly proved by miracles, dried up, that is, became worthless like a fragile potsherd; and my tongue clung to my throat, because when I suffered I did not threaten, and when I was cursed [Col. 1012B] I did not curse in return (1 Pet. 2:23). Thus you brought me down into the dust of death, Father—you who gave me the cup of this Passion—in which I was brought down to the dust of death according to the judgment of the Jews, who thought that I would never rise again but remain in death’s dust.

Yet, by the far better counsel of my mercy, I was brought down into the dust of death, because through my death I, the grain of wheat that died, now multiply and bear much fruit: even among the ungodly, whom the wind casts away like dust from the face of the earth, I bear fruit, raising from this very dust children of Abraham who are bright and lofty like the stars of heaven. Nor is it strange that I should gather kingdoms from both Gentiles and Jews and bring the nations together into Abraham’s bosom, that they may be Abraham’s children, since, in order that this might occur, I first suffered from the Jews and then from the Gentiles. Of the Passion inflicted by the Jews I spoke above: “Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls besieged me,” and so forth, because to them as calves and bulls the yoke of the Law was due. But of the Passion which the Gentiles inflicted I now say:

**VERSE 17.** Many dogs surrounded me, etc. For in the Gospel, where I said, “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs” (Mark 7:27), I designated by dogs the pagans, worshippers of idols. First calves and bulls surrounded me—that is, the lesser and greater Jews—when, in the house of the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, they mocked me all night with fists, [Col. 1012D] blows, spitting, and blasphemies. In the morning they handed me over bound to Pilate, to be scourged, mocked, spat upon, and crucified by the Gentiles. Therefore I now say: many dogs surrounded me, harassing and tearing me as a doe not yet of the morning but still of the evening, wearied by the course of temporal life.

For as, once weary from a journey, I sat by the well so that there the Samaritan and Gentile woman might find me, and draw from me, the living fountain, waters springing up into eternal life (John 4:6), so I, the doe wearied by these dogs harassing me, sat down—that is, humbled myself unto death, even death on a cross—by my sitting pressing down the well of all worldly wisdom and carnal desire, [Col. 1013A] so that the Church gathered from the Gentiles might find me, the fountain of living waters, which flowed from my side together with blood; and whoever drinks of these waters shall not thirst again, because “it shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:14). Therefore he shall not thirst again, because there is nothing beyond thirsting and drinking the water which springs up into eternal life. What can anyone thirst for beyond eternal life?

Nevertheless, one reborn through the sacrament of this water and given to drink of the water of saving wisdom will ardently thirst for eternal life itself until he comes to that life; once he has received it, he will thirst no more, because, as I have said, there is nothing beyond it. Thus, because many stags wounded by the venom of the ancient serpent felt within themselves the burning of that spreading poison through the desire to sin, and could not quench that burning by drinking the waters of worldly wisdom or satisfying the desires of carnal appetite—since whoever drinks such waters will thirst again, when the lust of sin, falsely medicated and temporarily soothed by worldly wisdom or the satisfaction of carnal desires, again burns more fiercely—by the right and sound counsel of mercy, I, the evening doe, wearied among Jewish hunters and Gentile dogs, showed in myself, through my opened side, waters desirable to every stag. Whoever drinks them, not only by partaking of the sacrament of baptism but also by preserving within himself the power of that sacrament, will be healed wholly in soul and body [Col. 1013C] and will become a morning doe.

For even in this present life he will be renewed like a stag, having slain the serpent, cast off the hair of vices, and uprooted the horns of pride. In the world to come he will be conformed to me, the morning doe, becoming a partaker of my resurrection, when the “body” of human “lowliness is transformed into conformity with the body of my glory” (Phil. 3:21).

But because I bear the sins of many, in order to take them away I am now subject to mortality as a weary doe, whose path is blocked by many thorns. To signify this, a crown of thorns was set upon my head. Therefore, behold: in my weariness many dogs have surrounded me, driving me to and fro, because I was sent from Pilate to Herod and again [Col. 1013D] sent back from Herod to Pilate, now in the praetorium and now outside it, wearied by their barking and bites (Luke 23:7). Indeed, then “Herod with his soldiers” despised me—or rather, with his “dogs” (ibid., 11). Yet he agreed with Pilate and his dogs concerning my death, because they “became friends” in the covenant of death against me, though “previously” they had been “enemies of one another” (ibid., 12).
