For this reason I do not simply say, “Dogs surrounded me,” but “many dogs surrounded me”: namely, Herod’s dogs together with Pilate’s dogs. Since they then became friends and assembled as one against the Lord and against me, his Christ, I say:

The council of evildoers besieged me. Not only when the chief priests and Pharisees assembled a council [Col. 1014A] against me, but also now, when the kings of the earth stood forth—namely Herod and Pilate—and the rulers of the Jews assembled as one to kill me. In this council of evildoers I was publicly and most cruelly scourged; finally I was handed over to be crucified, to death, by four soldiers, who received authority, as it seemed to them, from Pilate. Yet Pilate himself could have had no authority whatever against me unless it had been given from above by God the Father; therefore authority was permitted to them.

They dug my hands and feet, fastening me to the cross with four nails. By this outward deed they displayed what was in their most evil intention: by digging my hands they showed that they had no faith or reverence for my works; [Col. 1014B] by digging my feet, that they tore apart my apostles. Into them—my feet, shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace and to bear me throughout the world—the same Jews who delivered me to the Gentiles to be crucified drove the exceedingly sharp nails of tribulations.

I could more properly have used another word, for example by saying: “They wounded,” or “They pierced, my hands and feet.” But because in this fastening of my hands and feet my Father, the farmer, was at work, I rightly say: “They dug my hands and feet.” For “I am the vine, and my Father is the farmer,” who thus “will take away every branch in me not bearing fruit,” as he has now taken away Judas the traitor; while he “will prune the one that bears fruit, that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:1–2). Therefore my Father, the farmer, dug—or undermined—me, the root of fruitful branches, through the hands of these executioners, and applied much manure, because he placed upon me the iniquities of all my own, and I alone bore the sins of many. Thus these executioners, although unaware of it, were servants of my Father the farmer: with an evil intention they served his good intention when they dug my hands and feet.

For they dug my body like a garden fertile in abundant fruits; and I, like a grain of wheat falling into the earth carefully dug—indeed, I myself being both grain and earth—have borne and bear fruit in patience. “Like a vine” well cultivated, “I have borne fruit with the sweetness of fragrance, and my flowers [Col. 1014D] are fruits of honor and uprightness” (Ecclus. 24:23). I bore fruit in sweetness for the penitent and confessing thief, to whom I said: “Amen, I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43); and for Peter, at whom I looked so that he might weep bitterly and, through the bitterness of tears, attain eternal sweetness. My flowers also, fruits of honor and uprightness, were in the virgin mother and virgin disciple standing by my cross, when I said to my mother: “Woman, behold your son” (John 19:26); and to the disciple: “Behold your mother” (ibid., 27).

Truly these two persons standing beside me in my suffering, while my hands and feet were dug through, were flowers of honor and fruits of uprightness, which came forth from this digging [Col. 1015A] as certain praiseworthy first fruits from the cultivation of excellent soil. There followed, and will follow to the end of the age, an exceedingly great harvest of such brothers of mine. Of each of them I can say to my mother: “Woman, behold your son,” because every person who is my brother is her son. And, showing my mother suitably to such a brother of mine as one giving birth and experiencing sorrow in the suffering of my Passion, I say to him: “Behold your mother.”

For not only was my mother then sorrowful, but the primitive Church of all the disciples, sympathizing with me in my suffering, had sorrow like a woman in childbirth when the diggings of my hands and feet reached their hearts; and a sword of sharpest pain pierced the soul of the virgin mother herself. Therefore, foretelling this to them, I had said: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow, because her hour has come” (John 16:21). This hour of sorrow came to my mother and the apostles in my Passion, when the executioners who visibly dug my hands and feet made manifest in my wounds the causes of invisible pain, by which they dug through the soul of my mother and the souls of the disciples.

But my Father, the farmer, cultivated the soil of my flesh still more by such diggings, making good use of evil diggers. One of them, “opening my side with a spear,” dug into it, “and blood and water came forth” (John 19:34): blood for the redemption of the vineyard sold under sin, water for irrigation of that same vineyard, hitherto dry. Hence the prophet [Col. 1015C] Zechariah says to me: “You also, by the blood of your covenant, sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there was no water” (Zech. 9:11).

For the sake of drawing this water necessary for my prisoners from me, the rock, by the two pieces of wood of the cross, I was, as it were, struck twice by wicked peoples, crying not now in murmuring but repeating in a loud cry: “Away, away; crucify, crucify him” (John 19:15). This double striking was prefigured when Moses, in the person of the scribes and Pharisees, struck the rock twice, and waters flowed forth and torrents overflowed. Hence someone says, as elegantly as truly, in his verses:

> Twice with his rod the leader and prophet struck the rock;  
> The leader’s double stroke: the cross’s two pieces of wood.  
> From the rock a fountain was given to the people without measure;  
> From the Lord’s body, abundant salvation for humankind.

Moses may also be understood as God the Father, who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all to be so struck and dug through that he, formerly known in Judaea as a dry rock—not by revealed knowledge but amid the exceedingly obscure enigma of figures—might send forth from himself more broadly a river’s flood to gladden the city built and enlarged throughout the world from two walls, namely Jews and Gentiles. For before his side was opened, Christ was a fountain closed and sealed with the seals of many figures (Song 4:22). Or certainly that book sealed with seven seals [Col. 1016A] was his own, which no human being or angel was worthy to open (Rev. 5:1), until he himself—the lamb, the fountain, the book—opened himself, after his right side had first been opened on the cross by the soldier’s spear. Just as the element of water visibly came out from it joined to blood, so from that time the invisible water of wisdom did not cease to flow from him. Only the faithful drink it, those who are dyed purple with his blood, namely those planted together in the likeness of his death. For those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.

To such persons the water of saving wisdom, whose figure and sign is baptismal water, tastes sweet and refreshes them. It does not cease to flow from the rock which is Christ, because the Holy Spirit proceeds both from him and from the Father. The Spirit is signified by the water from Christ’s side [Col. 1016B] and is divided thence into seven streams: fear, piety, knowledge, fortitude, counsel, understanding, and wisdom. Therefore it was not without divine providence that this earth was dug through by nails and spear, from which so abundant a salvation was to flow, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled which says: “On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David, for washing the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. 13:1).

The thief first felt the outflow of this river, when it was said to him: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Those also felt the rushing force of this river whom the pit in which there was no water held bound in hell. For as soon as water came from Christ’s side, signifying the Holy Spirit, that same Holy Spirit was poured out for the forgiveness [Col. 1016C] of sins upon the elect held in hell, “and there was evening, and there was morning: one day” (Gen. 1:5). For the visible pouring out of water was as evening; the invisible outpouring of the Holy Spirit was as morning. Thus there was evening and morning, one day, because at one and the same moment there occurred the temporal, visible outpouring of water and the invisible outpouring of the Holy Spirit, who eternally proceeds from Christ’s right side—that is, from his divinity, which is the same as the Father’s.

Earlier this Spirit had proceeded not only for the creation of the world, when “the Spirit moved over the waters” (ibid., 2), but also for the enlightenment of the world through holy prophecies and other manifold graces, when the Spirit moved over human minds fluid like waters. But now, for the first time, he was given with the sacrament of waters flowing from Christ’s side for the forgiveness of sins; and he is given daily when that same water washes bodies through baptism, while the Spirit himself at the same time washes the souls of the baptized from the filth of sins.

Luke the Evangelist observed the sacrament of this matter. When Christ had been crucified, water poured from his side, the whole Passion completed, and burial already accomplished—when no one doubts that it was evening on the day of Preparation—he says: “And it was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was dawning” (Luke 23:54). Why does he say, at the evening hour of that very Preparation, that the Sabbath was dawning, when at that evening, according to the customary alternation of day and night, not day but night ought to have begun to grow dark? Surely the holy Evangelist, speaking thus, indicates that for the holy souls in hell, wearied by long expectation, when Christ’s Passion was completed and water for the forgiveness of sins poured from his side, the Sabbath—that is, rest—was dawning. For, baptized through water and Spirit, when Christ’s soul descended to them at the evening of the day of Preparation, that very evening shone for them as Sabbath—that is, as rest. The soul of the thief rested with them, and from then on was with them in paradise, as Christ promised him: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Therefore, as was said, there was evening and morning, one day: the first day of the Sabbath. “And,” as John says (John 19:31), “that Sabbath was a great day,” because on it all who had died in Christ’s expectation and faith, from Abel to the confessing thief, began to rest. Until then every such thirsty and weary person had sung: “As the stag longs for fountains of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:2–3). But once Christ’s side was opened, all the elect were so refreshed by the water flowing from it in the power of the Holy Spirit that they were not only in paradise’s rest, but themselves became paradise, of which it is fitting to say: “The Lord God had planted a paradise [Col. 1017C] of delight from the beginning, in which he placed the man whom he had formed” (Gen. 2:8).

For, having planted from the beginning many elect, whom God “brought forth from the ground” as “every tree beautiful to see and pleasant for food” (ibid., 9), at last, in the sixth age, on the sixth day before the Sabbath, he placed among them the man beautiful in form above the children of men, that he might work—as his Father God works until now—and guard such a paradise. It was not fitting that he should be an inhabitant of it but its Lord; or rather, such a paradise, such a garden of delights, was placed in this man, the second Adam. For his humanity is that earth from which God brought forth, and does not cease to bring forth until the end of the age, every tree beautiful to see and pleasant [Col. 1017D] for food, while all the elect, rooted and grounded in his charity, become fruitful trees full of those fruits which the Apostle enumerates: “But the fruits of the Spirit are charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity” (Gal. 5:22). Yet our earth, assigned and cursed to bear thorns and thistles through the work of the first Adam, would never bring forth these fruits unless it were irrigated by waters flowing from Christ’s right side.

Let us therefore give thanks to God, who provides for our salvation through the opening of Christ’s side. For just as in the earthly paradise a fountain went forth from the place of delight to water the surface of the earth, so from the right side [Col. 1018A] the fountain of living waters, in the power of the Holy Spirit, irrigates the whole Church. Therefore, although ignorant and malicious, those who dug through Christ’s human body with nails and spear performed a ministry of salvation, until spiritual and divine sacraments for human salvation flowed out from it: blood for redemption and water for cleansing. For it would not have benefited us to be redeemed unless it benefited us to be cleansed; since vessels redeemed but remaining in uncleanness and full of filth would not be capable of eternal blessedness.

Therefore, by divine dispensation, just as once the servants of the patriarch Isaac dug in the torrent and did not cease digging until they found living water (Gen. 26:32), so these men, though evil servants, nevertheless serving divine goodness, in the torrent through which Christ’s soul passed in sorrow unto death, dug his hands, feet, and side until, in the torrent of the Passion itself, living and life-giving water was found—water effecting our salvation, with the Holy Spirit working in it and with it. This Spirit moved over the waters at the beginning of the world, and now is given through waters poured out with the blood that is the price of redemption, so that, as has been said, redeemed through blood and cleansed through water, we may be capable of eternal blessedness.

Therefore Christ’s saying, “They dug my hands and feet,” should be understood in such a way that we notice the whole work of the soldiers who dug, or of Isaac’s servants digging in the torrent, until we join, by understanding [Col. 1018C] and the remembrance of faith, the living water flowing from the digging of Christ’s side with the blood streaming from his body. This water works the effect of our salvation not only in baptismal waters, by which the Church is regenerated and cleansed, but also in waters of tears, by which the confession of penitents, if dry, will be well watered and made more fruitful.

The thief’s confession on the cross is not recorded as having tears, but it was watered by the waters poured from Christ’s side; by these the same thief is believed to have been baptized with the whole Church of the elect who went before him. Nor was he defiled after such baptism, since he died at once in the very time of his baptism: with his legs broken he could not live; and immediately after Christ’s side was opened, as we have said, he was baptized with Christ in paradise. But for Peter, to whom it was granted to live long after that baptism, it was profitable for the more abundant fruit of repentance that, “remembering the word of Jesus, he wept bitterly” (Matt. 36:35).

Likewise, if catechumens approach baptism in faith for cleansing, either by themselves or carried by others, and after receiving baptism die before criminal defilements, baptismal water is sufficient for obtaining salvation even without tears. But those to whom it is granted to live long in this world after receiving baptism must weep bitterly with Peter. Or, if they have been so buried in sin with Lazarus that they have no ability to weep, they need the devotion of others who weep for them, groan and intercede for them with Martha and Mary [Col. 1019A]—a devotion especially vigorous in the female sex, whether with Martha in pious works or with Mary devoted to contemplation under Christ’s teaching. Such teaching is that in which Christ speaks, as he spoke in the Apostle Paul, who says: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). Not that the other teachers of the Churches are to be ranked equal to this great teacher and Apostle of the Gentiles; but all ought to resemble him in this: that with Paul they seek “not their own interests, but those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:20).

Furthermore, the universal tears of the whole universal Church, shed amid pious actions and contemplations, benefit those who remain in the confession [Col. 1019B] of Catholic truth and the communion of ecclesiastical peace, for their quickening and resurrection from the death of sins, if with Lazarus they hear Christ’s call to the sinner hidden within the tomb of conscience: “Come forth” (John 11:43), that is, confess what you have within. Thus, for one who repents in heart unto righteousness and confesses with the mouth unto salvation, the universal tears of the universal Church are beneficial. They are living waters made alive by those waters which once visibly flowed, but which continually flow by an invisible channel from the temple of Christ’s body, from the right side—which is Christ’s eternal life, just as his left side was mortal life. Yet that mortal life has now passed into the right, because the whole Christ now sits at the right hand of God the Father: wholly right, wholly life, wholly the fountain of life. Flowing from him through the paradise of the whole Church as from a place of delight, “the rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:5), because they drink from the torrent of his delight.

The place of delight, as stated above, is fittingly understood as Christ’s eternal, heavenly, immortal life. The torrent of delight is understood as the Holy Spirit. Thus from the place of delight the torrent of delight goes forth to irrigate the paradise of delight: that is, the whole Church, or any religious congregation of believers, or even a single soul so likened to a paradise of delight and garden of pleasures that it is rightly said to it in the Song of Songs: “Who [Col. 1019D] is this who comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights and leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8:5). To such a soul, or to a company of such souls, it is said in Isaiah: “And you shall be like a watered garden, and like a fountain of waters whose waters shall not fail” (Isa. 58:11), because “the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (ibid., 14). Again, in the Song: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed. Your shoots are a paradise” (Song 4:12–13). Again, in Ezekiel, after the praise of the tree ever green and bearing fruit each month, when the cause of its unfailing fruitfulness is given, it is added: “Because its waters go forth from the sanctuary” (Ezek. 47:12).

These are the waters which are there said to go forth from the temple at the right side, irrigating the torrent of thorns [Col. 1020A] and entering the Dead Sea to bring marine fish to life (ibid., 2). For the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the throne at Christ’s right side, irrigates earth full of thorns and thistles, makes paradisal flowers from thorns, and in this world, as in a Dead Sea, gives life to bitter people destined for death, like marine fish. Yet they are not brought to life in the shorelands and marshes, because people hardened and obstinate in uncleanness, although touched by the same inundation of the Holy Spirit when they believe and tremble through the gift of divine fear, are not healed or made alive through the gift of divine love. So also demons believe and tremble, but do not love the coming judgment; they would rather it were not to come, because they have no confidence concerning it.

But John, the Lord’s lover and beloved, says of himself and those like him: “In this the love of God is made perfect in us: if we have confidence in the day of judgment” (1 John 4:17). Through this confidence, rejoicing in hope, they themselves feel in their joy the rush of the river which makes God’s city glad: those to whom this saving water has come, which came from Christ’s side when the soldiers dug.

For not only did evil soldiers with evil intention dig Christ’s hands, feet, and side: good soldiers also, with good intention, dug—and still dig—Christ’s hands when they diligently investigate the works of his hands. They also dig his feet as they strive to cling to his footprints. They dig his right side as well, desiring to draw forth from it not only [Col. 1020C] blood by which the cheeks of the whole Church may be adorned, but also water necessary for irrigating the paradise planted with every beautiful tree and growing through the number of the elect. Hence the distinguished soldier, the Apostle Peter, says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21).

Accordingly, for us, the least soldiers and whatever servants we may be of the true Father Isaac, digging in this torrent of the Lord’s Passion, it has not been idle but has seemed necessary, in this present exposition, not to cease digging Christ’s feet, hands, and side until we found a vein of saving water running from Christ’s right side.

[Col. 1020D] For blood of redemption came from Christ’s feet and hands, because through his temporal journeys and deeds—by which the immobility of the eternal Word was moved, when he himself, the good Samaritan, journeying and drawing near the wounded man, was moved with compassion, divinely-human and humanly-divine—through these journeys and deeds, I say, human nature was redeemed. But in the bloody and watery stream of his side we recognize that “this is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ: not in water only, nor in blood only, but in water and blood together” (1 John 5:6), accomplishing together the redemption and cleansing of his own.

For we had been sold under sin; therefore the price of redemption was necessary, namely the precious [Col. 1021A] blood of Christ. We had also been defiled in sin; therefore washing was necessary—not only through visible water, as John too, baptizing in water, could wash only in this manner, but through water visible and invisible together. Thus Christ alone baptizes through any minister: employing visible water through the minister, but employing invisible water—that is, the Holy Spirit—by himself and not through another. The visible element of water testifies to the Spirit’s presence when the word is added to that element and it becomes a sacrament. Visible water of tears also testifies to his invisible presence: when the penitent soul, either pierced by divine fear, descends to the lower irrigation, weeping for its transgressions; or, pierced by divine love, [Col. 1021B] ascends to the upper irrigation, weeping because eternal goods have been delayed so long.

The story of Achsah, Caleb’s daughter, is known: she asked her father for “upper and lower irrigation” (Josh. 15). We too should imitate her by asking God the Father for the fountain of tears flowing either from fear of punishment or love of the kingdom, so that we may have upper and lower irrigation. Or rather, lower irrigation is the outpouring of tears visibly breaking forth; upper irrigation is the invisible flooding of the Holy Spirit flowing into human breasts through the channel of [Note: [Col. 1021D] Thus the Codex.] divine fear or love. These two channels extend to Christ’s right side, in order to draw from there what they pour in here. For since Christ now sits at the right hand of God the Father, from there to come to judge the living and the dead, there is a cause alike of fear and love: the coming Judge is either feared when conscience accuses us, or loved when a good conscience excuses us.

For conscience itself accuses in two ways, and excuses in two ways. It accuses, namely, when the mind knows of itself that it still wishes to sin in the future, or that a sin already committed should remain unpunished; of these, the one concerns willingness toward evil, the other impenitence. In two ways likewise the same conscience reasonably excuses the mind, when the mind itself knows of itself that it grieves for past sin and gladly guards against future sin. Such [Col. 1021D] grief, together with the will to live henceforth cautiously, is true repentance, which the saints define thus: “True repentance is to weep for sins committed, and not to commit those sins that must be wept for.” Where such repentance exists, sins will not remain unpunished, because repentance (*poenitentia*) is so called from punishments (*poenae*), or from punishing (*puniendo*), as though *punitentia*, since by the fire of grief the sinner punishes and burns up the wood, hay, and stubble—that is, deeds, thoughts, words, and vices. For the entire judicial process is conducted in the heart of the penitent: there conscience accuses, reason judges, fear binds, grief tortures; and, through its pricks and wounds, it pours forth tears as though they were a kind of blood of the inner person, shed at peril—tears undoubtedly mingled with and sanctified by [Col. 1022A] those waters which flow from Christ’s right side. For from there, “where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Col. 3:1), the grace of the Holy Spirit reaches even to His lowest members, whether working remission of sins in the font of baptism or bringing about the lower and upper watering-place in the font of tears.

Therefore, to discover such a fountain, we dig into Christ’s hands, feet, and especially His right side—for example, when we say to Him: “By Thy birth deliver us, O Lord; by Thy baptism and Thy fasting; by Thy cross and Thy passion deliver us, O Lord,” and other such things, by which His temporal dispensations are commemorated. But when we have passed beyond all temporal things—[Col. 1022B] beyond the works of His hands and the traces of His feet—we send the lance of our prayer or supplication even to His right side itself, when, burning with blessed love for His eternity, we say with heart or mouth:

> O Christ, Son of the living God, have mercy upon us;  
> Thou who sittest at the right hand of God the almighty Father, have mercy upon us.

Likewise:

> Splendour of the Father’s glory,  
> Bringing forth light from light,  
> Light of light and fountain of brightness,  
> Illuminating day of days,  
> And true sun, enter in,  
> Shining with perpetual radiance;  
> Pour the beam of the Holy Spirit  
> Into our minds.

In these and other such invocations, in which [Col. 1022C] we commemorate not Christ’s temporal dispensation but His eternal and supercelestial graciousness, we surely touch His right side. From it the flood of the Holy Spirit flows to us, either through the channel of fear to bring about the lower watering-place, or through the channel of love to bring about the upper watering-place. We judge, moreover, a field watered above and below to be more precious than one dry, uncultivated, or barren—such as is the land of the Synagogue, which did not receive the water issuing from the Temple on the right side; indeed, it did not even see that water, because, hindered by the veil upon Moses’ face, it does not know how to see but only to envy. But holy Catholic Church, and every faithful person within her, sings with rejoicing: “I saw water issuing [Col. 1022D] from the Temple on the right side, and all those to whom that water came were made whole.” Those who dug Christ’s hands, feet, and side upon the cross did not attend to the power of this salvation. But Mary Magdalene did not err by erring when, seeing Christ in the garden, she supposed Him to be the gardener (John 20:15). For unless He had been a wise gardener, He would not have admitted these diggers to dig the soil of His body. He allowed them to dig into Himself because He, the gardener, knew what great fruit would arise from that digging and what kind of fountain would proceed from His pierced side. Therefore Christ Himself, not only recounting His passion but also signifying most fully [Col. 1023A] the fruit of that passion, fittingly says in His own person to the faithful who sing: “They dug my hands and my feet.”

**VERSE 18.** “They counted all my bones.” For upon the cross’s gibbet they stretched me out and extended me as they pleased, so that they might survey my bones and ribs with curious gaze. And, to glut their malicious eyes more fully upon my sufferings, it did not suffice them to have looked once at me hanging and stretched out on the cross; rather, they considered and gazed upon me [Vulgate: “and inspected me”] with prolonged looking. Yet I was praying for them. But they, unchanged from vanity into that same thing—remaining themselves in that vanity—considered and gazed upon me with cruel eyes, unable to satisfy their cruelty with the scourging and wounds of my flesh. They considered and gazed: that is, with desire and diligence they watched me, the true Samson, mocking me, unaware that I, shorn at Calvary by them—that is, regarded not as holy among the holy, but as a thief among the wicked—though I was the Nazarene, conspicuous with consecrated hair, would overcome more of my enemies by dying than by living. But they, like foolish boys, mocked me, the true Elisha, as bald at Calvary (4 Kings 2:23). Yet the title set above my hair-covered head testifies that I am the Nazarene, so beautiful in my locks that my bride rightly says to me in the Song of Songs: “His head is finest gold, and his locks are like raised palm branches, black [Col. 1023C] as a raven” (Song 5:11). They, however, like an unbelieving Delilah, shaving me according to their own judgment and reckoning me not among the holy Nazirites but among wicked thieves, considered and gazed upon my outward insults alone; and, like foolish boys, cried to me, the true Elisha: “Go up, bald-head; go up, bald-head” (4 Kings 2:23). Therefore they were handed over to be torn by two bears: namely, the Roman rulers Titus and Vespasian. Nor is it enough for their punishment that they were delivered into the hands of the Roman sword; further, they “shall be portions for foxes,” that is, prey for demons (Ps. 61:11), and shall remain with them in hell. And I, the true Samson, when the hair of my head has grown again through the glory of the resurrection, shall exact such vengeance from them that all who, mocking me as blinded and shorn, considered and gazed upon me, and who bent the knee to me in derision and said, “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. 27:29), may know me to be most strong, able at my will to move not only earth but heaven also. For in the great house of the whole worldly fabric, heaven and earth are, as it were, two eminent columns; and I, Samson the strongest, shall move them, as is shown now by the great earthquake and the darkened sun at my death. Hereafter I shall also shake the earthly Roman empire in vengeance for the injuries done me; and at the final judgment, when I appear in my majesty and you see me, “the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty” (Luke 21:27), then I shall move not only earth but also heaven; [Col. 1024A] for “the powers of heaven shall be shaken” (ibid., 28). When then the world’s structure collapses, its columns of heaven and earth having been shaken, I, Samson the strongest, shall triumph completely over my enemies, though slain in the world. But they, not knowing—indeed, refusing to know—that I am Samson, conceived by angelic annunciation and consecrated a Nazarite from the womb, considered and gazed upon me as shorn and stripped of every protection of holiness, my bones now counted.

For whereas formerly, as a truthful teacher working miracles, I had many disciples and innumerable hearers, now, in punishing me as a liar, blasphemer, and false witness, they counted me—that is, reduced my hearers to a very small number. Even from among my twelve chosen disciples they took one away from me and scattered the rest, that the Scripture might be fulfilled: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered” (Matt. 26:31). But after I rise again, I shall gather my scattered bones once more, and multiply and magnify them from their diminished state. Yet they, not believing this, considered and gazed upon me as diminished and weakened in my bones. Nevertheless, I have most strong bones, none of which shall be diminished, as it is written of the Paschal lamb: “You shall not break a bone of it” (John 19:36). And from my side, through the water and blood flowing from my side, there is fashioned for me the woman, the Church: from me, the man, she takes the name of woman; from me, Christ, she receives the name of Christianity. She is so like me that I can truly say to her: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman, because she was taken from her man” (Gen. 2:23).

But they considered and gazed upon me as a weak man, deprived of my own bones and those of my people. For they could see no farther than the veil of weak flesh: because they did not believe me to be almighty God, they had the veil of Moses’ face laid over their heart. Therefore they saw only my nakedness; and these cursed sons, seed of Canaan and not of Judah, maliciously considered it and gazed upon it, imitating in every respect their father Ham, who regarded and mockingly looked upon the naked shame of his father Noah while he slept drunk in his vineyard (Gen. 9:32). The good sons, indeed, reverencing this nakedness in me, the ruler of the ark—that is, of the Church—honoured and covered it with the cloaks of the sacraments. But these evil sons beheld and gazed upon that same nakedness of mine irreverently and mockingly; and it was too little for them to despise and maliciously inspect my nakedness. To crown their condemnation:

**VERSE 19.** “They divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots for my clothing.” For just as four soldiers—or rather, base executioners—“divided my garments among themselves and cast lots for my clothing” (Matt. 27:35), so their far more wicked followers divided among themselves the Scriptures or sacraments with which I am clothed. For I, the Word of God the Father, [Col. 1025A] am clothed with the Scriptures and the figures of the sacraments; these are divided by heretics. For example, the impious Manichaeans receive the New Testament alone and reject the Old; whereas the Jews, conversely, receive the Old in the letter but do not receive the New in the spirit. Many other heretics divide my garments among themselves while attempting to defend their opposing errors as though by the authority of Scripture. Yet they cannot divide or tear my tunic, woven from above throughout: holy Church. And although they may tear counterfeit charity, like a garment sewn from spiders’ threads, through the rents of hatreds, they cannot divide unfeigned charity—the garment “without seam, woven from above throughout” (John 19:23). For it is not drawn together out of the occasion of earthly and lowest advantages, but, as we have said, is woven from above throughout among those who think alike and seek the things above, not things upon earth. Such charity among those who are dear, seamless and incapable in any way of division, malicious schismatics cannot divide, because it is given from above—not by human choice, but by divine lot alone.

Yet those executioners, Pilate’s servants, knowing that my garments were to be sold for a dear price—garments whose fringe, when touched, used to drive away sicknesses—divided my garments among themselves. And the heretics and schismatics who followed them, imitating them, divided my garments among themselves not only by breaking up my Scriptures as though they contradicted one another, but also by diversifying my sacraments, which [Col. 1025C] are the same wherever they are, so that one might say, “I am of Paul,” another, “I am of Apollos,” another, “I indeed am of Cephas,” another, “But I am of Christ” (1 Cor. 1:12)—as if I were so various and divided in my sacraments that a sacrament administered by a holier minister were holier, while one administered by a less holy or reprobate minister were less holy or liable to reprobation. But this is by no means so. Whenever anyone ministers, provided he is a minister, whatever sacrament is celebrated through him according to the rite of the Church remains valid, Christ working through him; nor is there any difference between a sacrament and a sacrament celebrated by different ministers, however great the difference between minister and minister. Even if a minister ordained in the Catholic Church becomes a heretic and remains a hidden heretic—for example, a Simoniac or a Nicolaitan—the sacraments administered through him are altogether valid. But if he has been exposed, after a first and second correction, especially “if he will not hear the Church” (Matt. 18:17), which forbids such persons the celebration of all sacraments, he is not to be heard, but is to be regarded as a heathen and a publican. This is not, however, because the sacraments celebrated through him are not sacraments, but because holy Roman Church judges that the offices of such persons are to be avoided, as having “a form of godliness but denying its power.” Nevertheless, if anyone has been baptized by such people, he may be well saved in the sacrament of baptism received through them, if, once he recognizes their errors, [Col. 1026A] he rejects them and obeys the Catholic Church, which forbids their offices. Likewise, if someone has been ordained a minister of the altar by such persons without knowing their heresies, what he receives through them is valid, if, on later recognizing them, he obediently follows the Church in avoiding them. But one who knowingly allows himself to be consecrated by a Simoniac is involved in equal condemnation with him.

We say these things not in order to divide the sacraments, but because “it is now required among stewards that one be found faithful,” and not heretical (1 Cor. 4:2). But whoever, amid these examinations, is supported by the testimony of a good conscience, and conducts himself outwardly as befits ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries, may regard it as a very small matter if he is judged by men [Col. 1026B] or by a human day, since he does not even judge himself, but reserves judgment concerning himself for Him alone who possesses full knowledge and judges each person (ibid., 3). Therefore, when the holy Fathers teach that the offices of heretics, Simoniacs, and manifestly incontinent clerics are to be avoided, this is not a division of the sacraments but, while the integrity of the sacraments is preserved, an avoidance of leprosy and a repudiation of Antichrist. For in the sacraments of heretics—who have “a form of godliness but deny its power”—“the mystery of iniquity” is already at work (2 Tim. 3:5; 2 Thess. 2:7), until he is removed from the midst, departing from the midst of the Church through the manifestation of the wickedness now concealed, which now lies hidden in secret, in order that it may be revealed in its own time.

Meanwhile, heretics divide Christ’s garments among themselves, [Col. 1026C] as do schismatics and all ministers of Antichrist. For since Christ’s garments are the form and power of godliness, they divide these garments by possessing the form of godliness in sacraments and divine offices while denying the power of godliness. For they, being unworthy, administer the same sacraments unworthily to unworthy persons, and sometimes simoniacally; by doing this they deprive those same sacraments of their power, because sacraments wickedly administered work neither salvation nor the power of godliness for those who give or receive them, though they retain some form of godliness itself. If, however, anyone participates in the forbidden sacraments of heretics while Catholic in mind, excused by ignorance and pious intention, that person will not share their guilt. Nevertheless, we do not dare to affirm against evangelical truth that he gathers grapes from such thorns or figs from thistles, because in the forbidden masses of heretics, schismatics, or all excommunicated persons we do not believe Christ’s body to be present, but, as blessed Jerome affirms, the body of the “dragon,” who was given “as food to the peoples of Ethiopia.”

Nor did only perverse soldiers divide Christ’s garments with perverse intent. Blessed Matthew (27:28) mentions a scarlet “cloak,” which signifies charity, through which Christ descended from heaven to earth. Jacob saw in a dream a kind of ladder of that descent, in the book of the generations from Abraham down to Christ Himself (Gen. 28:12); and we see it [Col. 1027A] when we attend to the beginning of the holy Gospel according to Matthew. Mark (15:17) mentions “purple,” signifying royal power; this is shown by his leonine face and by the wholly commanding style of his Gospel’s text. Luke (23:11) mentions a “white garment,” signifying priestly purity; this he proclaims in the face of the calf, the priestly victim, and in the Gospel narrative composed by him. John the Evangelist (19:2) mentions a “purple garment,” because, just as the lion is king of beasts in Mark, so the eagle is king of birds in John. Thus these good soldiers, Christ says, “divided my garments among themselves,” so that each might bear witness to a different garment of my power, in opposition to the wicked, who with impious Ham mocked my nakedness as I slept upon the cross.

[Col. 1027B] The enemies indeed considered and gazed upon me, taking pleasure in the nakedness of my human body, which seemed to them stripped of every glory of divinity. But friends, both human and angelic, desire to look into me, delighting in the beauty of my priestly and royal garments, with which my body is clothed and adorned—not now dead, but living and life-giving. For I am King of all ages and great Priest, who, behold, sacrifice myself, offered upon the altar of the cross. Therefore, having as it were temporarily laid aside my royal garment by emptying myself, I now appear in priestly dress; indeed, having taken the form of a servant, I tread the winepress alone as the servant of all my servants, whose blood is sprinkled upon my garments. [Col. 1027C] Therefore my clothing is red, and my garments are like the garments of those who tread in the winepress; I have defiled all my garments, and there is no form or beauty in me—no royal form or beauty of priestly honour. Hence friends who suffer with me and enemies who mock me rightly say of me: “Behold, we saw him without form or beauty; his appearance was not in him” (Isa. 53:2). For although I am “fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. 44:3), they saw me “despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows and knowing how to bear infirmity” (Isa. 53:3), because “my strength was weakened” in the hands of my enemies (Lam. 1:14), and “there was hidden [Col. 1027D] my strength where death went before my face” (Hab. 3:5), when I became the death of death and, like another Jonah, was swallowed by hell which bit me, being drawn into its belly; my enemies imagined that I would never return from the belly of the whale.

**VERSE 20.** “But thou, O Lord, do not remove thy help far away.” Thus I prayed from the belly of hell, from the belly of the whale. Therefore, Father, thou didst hear me, not delaying thy help, not postponing my resurrection far off as that of others is postponed for a long time, namely until the last day; rather, thou wilt raise me on the third day. And now meanwhile:

> Look to my defence;

that is, turn the eyes of thy mercy toward the defence [Col. 1028A] of my people, lest, dismayed by my death and burial, they perish through despair—especially those who, as it were, are my soul and ought to govern my body, that is, my Church; and who, as it were, are my bones and ought to support my flesh, that is, the carnal and weak members in my body. For I know that wicked soldiers are to be sent to break my legs and bones as I now hang upon the cross, and thereafter, in public persecutions, to break my chosen ones. But thou, O Lord, look to my defence, as is written in the Law concerning me, the Paschal lamb: “You shall not break a bone of it” (John 19:36). Guard and defend, therefore, my bones and legs now, for no good signification would lie in their breaking (Num. 9:12); and hereafter defend my stronger members, who, like legs, are to support the whole body of the Church. To one of them I said: “Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18). In such legs of mine, guard and defend my strength or solidity—not only bony but also stony—for I am He of whom it is written: “His legs are marble columns founded upon bases of gold” (Song 5:15). For these legs I pray that they may not be broken, even though shaken by the pressure of great suffering or temptation, as the strongest of them was shaken by denying me three times. Yet he was not altogether broken, because, though his constancy was disturbed, his charity was not turned away—the charity by which, even while denying me, he loved me. Therefore [Col. 1028C] this prayer of mine stretches to the defence of him and those like him, that his faith may not fail, but that he, once converted, may strengthen his weaker brethren, fulfilling with the remaining apostles in the Church, my body, the role of legs or marble columns. The enemies wish to break these legs, these columns. But thou, O Lord, look to my defence, and remove from me the sword which thou thyself hast raised against me, so that, though it kills the body, it may harm the soul in no way. For thou sayest in the prophet Zechariah: “Sword, arise against my shepherd and against the man who cleaves to me. Strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered” (Zech. 13:7). That same sword—that is, death, prepared to obey—also says: “I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.” Though struck by this sword even to the separation of body and soul, may the sword of death itself have no power at all over my soul.

**VERSE 21.** “Deliver my soul, O God, from the sword,” so that I too, having triumphed over death, may rise with my soul returned to my body, to live forever; and so that I may obtain this for my martyrs, that, while this sword rages in their bodies, the soul of none of them may be harmed. To them also I said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28). Thus, O God, deliver my soul and the souls of my people from the sword, so that the sword of death, or any other torment whatsoever, may not prevail to injure their souls. Above all, O God, so deliver my soul from the sword [Col. 1029A] that on the third day my body, put to death by this sword, may receive my soul. Deliver my soul and the souls of my people from this sword, which was raised—that is, permitted by thee, O God—to kill bodies.

“And my only one from the hand of the dog.” For the Jewish people, barking against me, is a dog without reason, yelping without discernment; or Pilate the Gentile, or Herod the foreigner, is a dog, into whose hand and power I was delivered so that Pilate himself dared to say: “Do you not know that I have power to release you and power to crucify you?” To him I said: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:10–11). Therefore, God the Father, thou who gavest me into the hand of such [Col. 1029B] a dog, deliver my only one from the hand of the dog: that is, my soul itself, unique and singular, wholly free from every sin.

Otherwise: holy and spiritual men, through whom the body of the Church must be governed, are to my body, which is the Church, as it were its soul, because without their governance my weak members cannot flourish. And the sword—or rather the devil himself, moving this sword by thy permission—strives for this: that, after the stronger members in the Church have been killed, the Church may fail, altogether deprived of spiritual governance, and become as though dead, having no life-giving sacraments. For those in whom the power of the sacraments lives, and through whom the Holy Spirit, dispenser of the sacraments, works life and salvation, would be gone. [Col. 1029C] Therefore, lest my Church wholly fail while this sword rages through tyrants: “Deliver my soul, O God, from the sword,” always preserving in the Church such persons through whom life-giving sacraments may be administered in the Church, and by whose saving teaching the Church may live. This Church is my only one, because she is joined to me as branches to a vine, as a body to its head, as a stream to a fountain—to a living and inexhaustible fountain. For I am the rock struck twice by the two timbers of the cross, from which humans and beasts drink, that is, the stronger and weaker in the Church. On this day the Church is fashioned from the rib of my side, by receiving the most pure and powerful sacraments of blood and water flowing from my side. That the life-giving power [Col. 1029D] of these sacraments may never fail in the Church: “Deliver my soul, O God, from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog.”

Every heretic attacking my only one—that is, the one Church—is also a dog, wishing to split her apart so that she may not be one or only. Such a dog will be the disastrous Arius, whom I foresee will rage with canine barking and tearing against me and mine. Such a dog will have a strong hand, and Constantius Augustus, Julian the impious, and other powerful persons will favour him, through whom my only one—that seamless tunic—will be torn, unless I now sacrifice and sanctify myself upon the altar of the cross, so that she too may be holy in truth and never torn by any falsehood. Therefore I say: “Deliver my soul [Col. 1030A] from the sword of tyrants, and my only one from the hand of the heretical dog,” lest spiritual vigour in the Church fail through tortures, or the Church herself, divided by sects, cease to be one and only.

**VERSE 22.** “Save me from the mouth of the lion, and my humility from the horns of unicorns.” For the prince of this world comes against me as a lion, to devour me; as Leviathan, to swallow me up for the food of my flesh, not knowing that the iron or sting of divinity is hidden beneath it in order to mock him. Therefore deliver and save me and mine from the mouth of this lion, so that, even if one of my people enters his mouth, he may find a way out through his pierced jaw by the remedy of repentance—as, behold, Peter the apostle, who denied me, is now drawn out of his mouth after being cleansed by bitter weeping when I looked at him. The mouth of this lion is also Pilate or another wicked ruler. Therefore I desire to be saved also from such a lion’s mouth, lest he ever be able to incorporate my people into himself. When he cannot incorporate them into himself, he will raise up most savage unicorns to harry and scatter them. Therefore thou, God the almighty Father, whose horn of omnipotence is stronger than all the horns of unicorns, save now and always my humility from the horns of unicorns. For just as the unicorn is a most proud animal, said to die of indignation if held against its will—it is called a unicorn because of the single horn it has on its nose—so the Jews, seeking only earthly things or glorying uniquely in the worship of one God, are most proud, like unicorns. [Col. 1030C] All proud persons are likewise unicorns, who raise themselves singularly and cannot bear a companion. From the horns of all these unicorns I ask that my humility be saved—my humility in myself and in my people, opposed and contrary to their singular pride. For humility does not know how to raise itself on high, as the horn of every unicorn is raised; rather, it always lies low in its own judgment, like him who said to me: “Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest enter under my roof” (Matt. 8:8), and that other who said: “One stronger than I will come after me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie” (Mark 1:7). Such humble persons will be—and now are—those brothers of mine who, when I their shepherd was struck in my passion, were dismayed in their humility. “But after I rise again, I shall go before them into Galilee” (Matt. 26:32), and there, O Father:

**VERSE 23.** “I shall declare thy name to my brethren.” They are brethren because, humble among themselves, they are united in brotherly love. They are mine because they love me and are loved by me, as joined to me by blood-relationship. Magnifying and commending this blood-relationship clearly, Paul, the vessel of election, after introducing in my person, “Behold, I and my children,” adds: “Since therefore the children have shared in flesh and blood, he likewise shared in the same, that through death he might destroy him who had the empire of death” (Heb. 2:13–14). Hence, “he is not ashamed to call them brethren, saying: I shall declare [Col. 1031A] thy name to my brethren” (Heb. 2:11–12). Therefore, as my prophet David foretold and my apostle subsequently sings, I acknowledge as my brethren not only those related to me by adoption, but also those sharing with me in flesh and blood—especially those to whom, at my last supper, I gave and granted communion in my flesh and blood. To these brethren of mine, after the unicorns have been repulsed, I, raised from death, shall declare thy name, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). Receiving this command, they will go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Thus the knowledge of thy name shall be extended, with the Church planted not in Judaea alone but throughout the whole world; and I, Christ, shall praise thee in the midst of this Church—that is, I shall cause thee to be praised. For I shall say, not only to those gathered from Judaea, but in every nation, to those who fear God; speaking through my apostles by my Spirit in them, I shall say:

**VERSE 24.** “You who fear the Lord, praise him.” You who have reverent fear, praise him. For just as human and worldly fear produces disgrace, since the kingdom of God is shut to the fearful and unbelieving (Rev. 21:8), so divine fear, divinely inspired, kindles persons to praise the Lord. Therefore, from every nation, all of you who fear the Lord, praise him. This praise is not in Africa alone, as Donatus wished; for wherever God is feared, there he is praised, [Col. 1031C] and there is the Church, which is the seed of Jacob and Israel, to whom I say:

> “All the seed of Jacob, glorify him.”

Jacob supplanted his elder brother, and the elder served the younger. Therefore the younger people, blessed after supplanting the elder and gathered from every nation, are the whole seed of Jacob. Likewise, since the firstborn is the old person in all who are conceived through carnal desire, and then through regenerating grace the new person is born, who, like Jacob in the womb of the mother grace, supplants the firstborn; and throughout the whole time of this present life struggles with him, so that not without difficulty the younger may wrest from the elder the service due to himself and seize the blessing: rightly, the whole seed of Jacob is understood as the new person in each individual struggling against the carnal life, which is understood through the hairy brother, until he obtains the blessing by which such complete dominion is granted him that the following may rightly be said to the whole seed of Jacob: “Be lord of thy brethren” (Gen. 27:29); and to the whole seed of Esau God the Father may say: “I have established him as thy lord and subjected all his brethren to his service” (ibid., 37). But because this dominion will not be so perfect and complete in this life that, while the elder and hairy brother persecutes him, the younger and gentle brother has no danger under God the Judge, who alone knows the end for which each of these brothers strives:

**VERSE 25.** “Let all the seed of Israel fear him.” For because he is “terrible in his counsels over the children of men” (Ps. 65:5), not only the whole seed of Jacob, which is still in the struggle of action, but also all the seed of Israel, which already, through a foretaste of contemplative grace, can say: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved” (Gen. 32:30)—let it fear him. For by just judgment he sometimes allows even certain contemplatives to relapse into carnal life, as happened to wise Solomon, who, after seeing the Lord as though face to face, relapsed into carnal shamefulness. For “his heart was corrupted by women” to such an extent that he fell into idolatry and sacrificed on the high places, scorning the Temple of the Lord which he himself had built at the Lord’s command, with the command that sacrifice was to be offered nowhere else [Col. 1032B] but there (3 Kings 11:4, 7). Therefore let all the seed of Israel fear him, and let the whole seed of Jacob glorify him.

It might seem more fitting if it were said thus: “Let all the seed of Jacob fear him, and let all the seed of Israel glorify him.” But because humility, which the spirit of fear produces, is necessary even for the highest contemplatives, while consolation, which the glorification of divine mercy pours forth, is necessary for weak active persons struggling against the flesh, rightly the whole seed of Jacob is summoned to glorify God, and all the seed of Israel is humbled by the fear of the Lord imposed upon it. But why is the Lord thus to be glorified? Namely, because:

For he has not rejected or despised the prayer of the poor man. [Col. 1032C] He has not rejected it so as to cast it away altogether, nor despised it so as to judge the poor man’s prayer worthless. To reject is to take no care of something at all; to despise is, as it were, to look down upon something contemptuously from on high, then quickly turn one’s face away from it and care little for it. But the Lord neither rejected nor despised the prayer of the poor man: that is, of Christ hanging on the cross, or likewise of any poor person who places no confidence in himself. It was said above: “My God, my God, look upon me: why have you forsaken me?” Likewise: “I shall cry by day, and you will not hear.” Yet here I, Christ, the most noble seed of Jacob and Israel, teach that my almighty Father God is alike to be glorified and feared, because he has not [Col. 1032D] rejected or despised the prayer of the poor man.

Nor did he turn his face from me; and when I cried to him, he heard me. Therefore he to whom I said above, “My God, look upon me: why have you forsaken me?” never despised me, nor turned his face away from me. But because, in saying this above, I applied to myself the words concerning my sins, I cried by day and was not heard, that the cup might pass from me; I cried by night, submitting myself, that I might recognize and drink the cup which the Father gave me as not given to me foolishly. All this—that I should both dread drinking the cup and nevertheless drink that same cup not without bodily pain and anxiety of soul—belonged to the old man, whose infirmities and pains I assumed in myself. But now that the Passion is ended and accomplished, [Col. 1033A] in which the old man was crucified, after I had received all the vinegar of the Passion and said, “It is finished” (John 19:30), it will now be evident that he did not reject or despise the prayer of my poor self. For the cup of suffering will pass, as I asked, from many of my members: namely, from holy confessors and from many others whom I will to remain thus until I come, as my beloved disciple John remains. Others, however, concerning whose suffering I consented to the Father’s will when I said, “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. 26:39), will follow me in the footsteps of my Passion, just as that other disciple to whom I said, “Follow me” (John 21:22). Thus from this it will be evident that God my Father did not reject or despise [Col. 1033B] the prayer of the poor man, nor turn his face from me; and when I cried to him, he heard me. Therefore, turning to him in thanksgiving, I say to him:

**VERSE 26. My praise is with you in the great Church.** That is: I shall praise you not only with you in the secrecy of contemplation, but also in the great Church through the public manifestation of preaching. I shall praise you—that is, I shall cause you to be praised inwardly through the single-hearted intention of my faithful people, and outwardly in the great Church, spread throughout the world, through the fruitful manifestation of that good intention. Thus my praise will be with you in those who praise you in secret, after the example of him who said, “My secret is mine; my secret is mine” [Col. 1033C] (Isa. 24:16); and my praise will be for you in the great Church in those whose “light shines before men, that they may see” their “good works and glorify their Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

My praise will be with you in those who remain hidden with you within the Holy of Holies and stored beneath the mercy-seat of your compassion, like the ark of the covenant and the things laid up in it, which were placed behind the veil within the Holy of Holies under the mercy-seat and withheld from the common sight of men. And again my praise will be in the great Church through those whom I set forth outside the veil as a table of presentation and as a lampstand of light, for the nourishment of others and as an example of light. For through my great propitiation, I, the giver of the new law, love some of [Col. 1033D] my faithful people in such a way that I do not wish to deprive them of the most sweet secrecy of their rest, which is like the Holy of Holies; and again I say to others what I said to Peter: “If you love me, feed my lambs” (John 21:15). I said this to that one man, and in him the same thing was said to many whom canonical election will draw from their privacy into public life. But of John I said, “Thus I will that he remain until I come” (ibid., 22); and this same thing was said in that one man concerning all those assigned to remain within the Holy of Holies, “as the golden urn containing manna, and Aaron’s rod that had budded, and” the two “tablets of the covenant” were within (Heb. 9:4), neither visible outside nor carried beyond the Holy of Holies, unless the ark in which these things were laid up was covered round about with a veil of hyacinth-blue skins and other coverings [Col. 1034A] (Exod. 36:35).

Because of this distinction among my faithful people, or indeed because of the divided devotion of one and the same person—now contemplating in secret, now preaching and working openly—I, Christ their head, say to you, Father: “My praise is with you in the great Church,” not only in Africa, nor confined to some corner of a sect, but spread throughout the whole world; in this Church my praise will be. In this sense also it is with you:

**I will pay my vows in the sight of those who fear him.** Thus my praise will be fulfilled in the great Church: I, the great priest, will offer, and cause to be offered, the sacrifice of my body and blood, “a living sacrifice, [Col. 1034B] holy, pleasing” (Rom. 12:1) to God my Father. In this sacrifice all the rational vows of myself and of my people will be fulfilled. These vows will be paid to God the Father in the sight of those who fear him. For though these things are hidden from the wise and prudent of this age, nevertheless the holy vows of this sacrifice will be so manifest in the sight of those who fear him that through faith they will know and understand that under the appearance of bread is my true body, which, as it was given for many for the remission of sins, so is daily offered and eaten for many for the remission of sins. Likewise, in the sight of those who fear him, what appears to be wine will through faith be known to be my blood, which, as it was poured out for many for the redemption [Col. 1034C] and remission of sins, so until the end of the age, when devoutly offered and drunk, works remission of sins for many.

And although this sacrifice is one and the same without distinction, it nevertheless produces its effects differently in those who eat and drink it. Some eat and are filled; others eat and are not filled, but are so humbled that they worship the Lord; still others fall to the ground in ruinous downfall, eating and drinking judgment upon themselves. Yet this difference is not in the one sacrifice itself, which is one wherever it is found. Rather, the diversity of those who eat produces in them diverse effects. For among them there are certain poor people, namely perfect despisers of this world; and among them there are certain rich persons in this world and fat ones of the earth, who [Col. 1034D] either suppose themselves to abound in virtues or do in fact abound in earthly riches. The poor hunger and thirst for righteousness in the communion of my body, since it is fitting that the members be conformed to their head; and therefore they will be filled, when both here through humility and hereafter through glory they are conformed to me. Therefore I say—and this is my promise, for as one who promises I do not deceive the believer:

**VERSE 27. The poor shall eat and be filled.** The rich will not be filled, because they do not hunger for righteousness; but the poor, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, will be filled. Out of their great fullness their heart pours forth a good word, praising not themselves or their own merits, but the Lord. The hunger of these poor persons is indicated by the words, “They who seek him shall praise the Lord”; for those who seek him are hungry. But they seek not earthly riches or worldly glory, but the Lord himself, desiring to serve him—for to serve him is to reign—so that, possessing the Lord himself, they may be counted among the faithful servants who serve him alone, as it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 6:13).

In contrast, unbelievers, who serve sins and this world, are servants of as many masters as they have vices ruling over them. Such people do not seek the Lord, but the pleasures of this world, in which they have and desire to have their consolation. To them it is said: “Woe to you rich, who have your consolation” (Luke 6:24). But the blessed poor shall eat and be filled, and they who seek him shall praise [Col. 1035B] the Lord. For the rich seek to fill the ark with earthly riches; the poor seek to fill their heart with God. Therefore, although they die and fail in body, nevertheless:

**Their hearts shall live for ever and ever.** The rich live in this age, but the poor live in the age that follows the present age. Therefore their hearts shall live for ever and ever, because when this present age has passed, another age will follow in which the hearts of the righteous will live—those over whom the second death has no power, because in this age they received the first resurrection. “Blessed are those who have a part in the first resurrection, because over them the second death has no power” (Rev. [Col. 1035C] 20:6). The first resurrection is that in which hearts begin to live through faith and love. Hereafter there will be a second resurrection, when bodies too will live in the kingdom of heaven. But those whose faith is either nonexistent or dead, since their hearts do not live in the present age, will by no means have their bodies rise to life, but to a torment of death that will remain with them without death; for they refused in this life to receive the life of their hearts when they received the sacrament of life.

By contrast, the poor shall eat and be filled, and they who seek him shall praise the Lord; their hearts shall live for ever and ever. Indeed the rich and proud Jews, though according to the promises made to their fathers they ought to be heirs of the kingdom, do not care to come to this banquet where the life of hearts is received. “The wedding indeed” is “prepared” for them, but “those who were invited were not worthy” (Matt. 22:8). Yet the wedding will be filled with guests reclining at table, because, when the Jews are blinded, the fullness of the Gentiles enters.

**VERSE 28. All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.** Those who had forgotten will remember; those who had turned away will turn to the Lord from all the ends of the earth. God will not be known in Judaea alone, nor will the Church be confined to Africa; rather, all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.

**And all the families of the nations shall worship before him.** They shall worship before him where he himself sees, namely in their consciences, where “true worshippers shall worship the Father in [Col. 1036A] spirit and truth” (John 4:23); or before him insofar as they themselves behold him through faith and love. Thus they shall worship in the Spirit, in whom they shall cry, “Abba, Father,” so that the Spirit himself bears witness to their spirit that they are children of God (Rom. 8:15–16). Thus they shall worship in truth, that they may truly be my members, I who am truth. For those who are members of me in my body, they alone worship the Father in truth, because I am truth. “I,” I say, “am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:16): the way in commandments and examples, truth in promises, life in rewards. Hence whoever worships the Father hoping for anything other than what I promised does not worship the Father in truth. But those who run in the way of my commandments, delighting in the truth of my promise, worship the Father in truth, because in truth I promised them eternal life, which is nothing other than that they may know me, the true God, with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Therefore not in vain will all the ends of the earth remember my most true promises and turn to the Lord; and all the families of the nations shall worship before him—that is, certain elect persons from every family of the nations—because “God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation the one who fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10:34).

**VERSE 29. For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule over the nations.** The kingdom belongs not to proud men [Col. 1036C] but to the Lord. Proud tyrants wished to be honored as though they would reign forever. Hence they were customarily greeted with the words, “O king, live forever” (2 Esd. 2:3), though they were mortal and did not truly reign even for a little while, but tyrannized altogether. Such were the kings of Egypt; the Israelite kings separated from the house of David; the kings of the Assyrians or Babylonians; the kings of the Persians and Medes; and, lastly, the Roman emperors, who had not yet received the kingdom but seemed to possess power as kings, though in truth they were tyrants.

There was but one royal line, that of the house of David, to which the kingdom was sworn and secured by divine promise: “For the Lord swore truth to David, and he will not deceive [Col. 1036D] him: ‘Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne’” (Ps. 131:11). From this seed was raised the King who lives forever, whose kingdom is the kingdom of all ages—not in Judaea alone, but among all nations—for the kingdom is the Lord’s; and, confirming this truth, he shall rule over the nations, gathering from all nations not only poor people who may be satisfied from his table, as has already been said above, but also rich people, who may eat and worship: eat as regards the sacrament, worship as regards the outward appearance. Of these it is said here:

**VERSE 30. All the fat ones of the earth have eaten and worshipped.** For the fat ones of the earth—the powerful and rich of this world, made fat by earthly wealth—are not to be excluded from the sacrament of the altar because of their power [Col. 1037A] or wealth. Yet if they have been publicly identified with some manifest crime, they are not to be admitted before public penance. Thus the Catholic emperor Theodosius, because of the murders committed by him against the Thessalonians, was barred by the great man Ambrose not only from the sacrament of the altar but also from entrance into the Church, until he had made public satisfaction through penance. So too other fat ones of the earth are recorded as having been excluded from sacred communion by holy Fathers because of manifest crimes. But where manifest crimes either did not exist or were unknown, all the fat ones of the earth ate and worshipped together with the poor.

The rich and fat ones of the earth also daily eat the Lord’s body with the poor, because, on account of hidden crimes, the ungodly cannot be distinguished from the godly, nor the worthy from the unworthy among the fat ones of the earth, by human judgment. Therefore, when such persons are not implicated in manifest crimes, the steward of Christ’s body must not forbid these exacting fat persons to eat this sacrament merely because they are fat ones of the earth; rather, he must warn them to fear, because the hidden iniquity which escapes human judgment will certainly not remain hidden when the King enters to see those reclining at table.

For in the sight of him who sees hearts and consciences, some will sit at this banquet, to whom it is said: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations; and I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table and sit upon [Col. 1037C] thrones” (Luke 22:29–30). But others will fall to the earth. For:

**Before him all who descend into the earth shall fall.** If they did not descend into the earth, they would not fall into the earth; but because they descended through guilt, they will fall through punishment. Where will they fall? Into the “land of death and misery, where there is no order and everlasting horror dwells” (Job 10:22). He sought to avoid going there when, guarding against it by repentance, he said: “Spare me, Lord; let me bewail a little my sorrow before I go to the dark land, covered with the gloom of death” (ibid., 20–21). But those who, when about to approach the altar of the Lord, refuse first to bewail their sins, but live in this world without mourning, descend into the earth through voluntary wickedness or impurity—though hidden from men, yet naked before the eyes of God. They shall fall before him into the dark land covered with the gloom of death, for bound hand and foot they will be cast unwillingly into outer darkness, since they voluntarily descended into inner darkness, finding the works of light hateful and loving the works of darkness most dearly.

Therefore they do not go up with Rahab the sinful woman [Col. 1037D] (Josh. 2:6), yet repentant, to the upper room, to the upper part of the house, where with the messengers of Jesus they may make for themselves a covenant of peace and salvation through true repentance and conversion. Instead, like foxes, they have holes into which they descend and in which, hiding, they prefer darkness to light. “For everyone who does evil”—I do not say, one who once did evil and has ceased, but one who stubbornly does evil—“hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved” [Col. 1038A] (John 3:20).

They also descend into the earth who, while sharing in Christ’s sacraments or ministering at their celebration, desire to become blessed through earthly gain while despising heavenly things. For them this is a great and profound descent from heaven to earth, from heavenly blessedness to earthly blessedness. For they suppose gain to be godliness. “But godliness with contentment is great gain” (1 Tim. 6:6). Therefore, when gain is preferred to gain, the earthly to the heavenly in their desire, this is for them, as was said, a certain descent to earth from heaven, though hidden from men but visible and manifest to me, who “saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18).

And now I see many falling from heaven like lightning in the administration or reception of the sacraments, because their feigned godliness, even if it appears clearly to men, most swiftly vanishes like lightning in my eyes and in the eyes of my Father. This happens when the lamps even of those descending to earth are extinguished, as they go to buy the oil of flattery from those who sell, and do not possess that which rises high above all liquids: for love of heavenly things floats above every love of earthly things in the heart of the elect, like good and most pure oil. Those abounding in this oil do not descend into the earth [Col. 1038C] for the foul oil of earthly gain when they partake of or minister in the sacraments. “Nevertheless, its dregs have been emptied out,” but “all sinners of the earth who descend into the earth shall drink” them (Ps. 74:9): now through avarice, and in the future they will fall through manifest punishment. Although this punishment is now hidden from men, it is manifest in the sight of him who gave to me, his Son, to me, the Son of Man, all judgment of the living and the dead. Therefore in thanksgiving:

**VERSE 31. My soul shall live to him, and my seed shall serve him.** My soul, which will descend to hell and, in the judgment of those through whom I was counted among the wicked, seemed dead—yet that very soul of mine, namely [Col. 1038D] the Spirit whom, as I gave it up on the cross, I commended to the Father, saying, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46)—that Spirit, I say, free among the dead from death, shall live to him who holds him in his hand as a good deposit and will restore him to me at the Resurrection with the great profit of many souls rescued from hell and living to him together with my soul.

For just as I, having risen, shall die no more and death shall have no more dominion over me, so also many bodies of saints shall rise with me; and the souls of all the faithful, from the soul of righteous Abel to the soul of the thief to whom I say on the cross, “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), shall live to him with me in the paradise of exultation. My soul too lives to him: it knows neither the death of sin nor separation from the divinity implanted in it; and when it has been separated from my dead body, it shall live to him who, having received it commended into his hands, will restore it to my body.

**And my seed shall serve him.** This is what was promised to me in Isaiah, where it is said of me: “If he gives his soul as an offering for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand” (Isa. 53:10). Therefore this seed of mine promised to me, this long-lived seed—namely all who will believe through my Passion, resurrection, and ascension—shall serve him. For although not all who are baptized, that is, visibly washed only as regards the sacrament, serve him, nevertheless all who are reborn and incorporated into me, and made my seed, [Col. 1039B] shall serve him and be his adopted children. For:

**VERSE 32. The generation to come shall be declared to the Lord; and the heavens shall declare his righteousness to the people that shall be born, whom the Lord has made.** There will indeed be undisciplined people and heretics who presume to claim this generation for themselves, saying that their baptism is a sacrament and ascribing to their own name the children regenerated by it: thus, for example, some may be called Donatists, some Arians, some Nestorians, or Eutychians.
