But when such sects fight among themselves and fail, the generation to come shall be declared to the Lord, and they shall be called Christians by me, Christ, sons of God Most High, not sons of any baptizer. For the heavens also shall declare his righteousness, when my apostles teach that confidence concerning the grace of baptism must not be placed in a human being, so that one says, “I am of Paul,” another, “But I am of Apollos,” and another, “But I am of Cephas” [Col. 1039C] (1 Cor. 1:12). Rather, whatever or however the baptizers and ministers may be, provided they baptize lawfully in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the sacrament itself is the same and is neither better through good ministers nor worse through evil ones.

The generation to come shall be declared to the Lord when the fruitfulness of divine grace alone, through water and the Spirit, multiplies the children of God: either regenerated in the holy Church, or baptized outside it and reconciled to that same Church. Between these there will be this difference: some are born of the free woman, others of the slave woman; [Col. 1039D] yet God will be one Father to them, if his Spirit is in their hearts crying, “Abba, Father.”

Alternatively: the heavens shall declare his righteousness, because the heavenly angels will declare either God’s righteousness to men or the righteousness of his people to God. They also offer the prayers of the people before God, not to instruct him, as though they might teach him, but in ministry. [Col. 1040A] For they “are ministering spirits sent for ministry to those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation” (Heb. 1:14). Therefore, whether angels or apostles and evangelists, they together shall declare God’s righteousness to the people who are to be born from water and Spirit through faith.

It must especially be noted that it says, “to the people who shall be born,” because someone may be baptized deceptively, as Simon Magus was, and no righteousness is declared to the Lord concerning such a person, because though baptized he was not reborn or renewed. But righteousness shall be declared to the people who are born into a new offspring. For when I, Christ, was baptized by John and he, fearful of this ministry, refused it, I said to him: “Permit it now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all [Col. 1040B] righteousness” (Matt. 3:15). For it is just that humankind, created from earth yet exalted above the heavens, should recognize its own order; and since water is a higher element than earth, the earthly material of humanity, lowered and humbled beneath the waters according to its proper order, should recover in me, the new Adam humbled beneath the waters, the righteousness it lost in the first Adam when pride lifted him above the heavens.

Thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness; and therefore I suffered the waters to enter even to my soul: “I came into the depth of the sea, and the tempest overwhelmed me” (Ps. 68:3), so that in me the righteousness of humility might be fulfilled. This same righteousness the heavens—namely, the apostles—shall declare to the people who shall be born, whom the Lord has made. That people whom the Lord made shall be born from water and Spirit through regenerating grace: he first made them from nothing, creating that there might be some creature; later he made them by grace, that they might be a new creature. Therefore let that people whom the Lord made give thanks, for he voluntarily begot them “by the word of truth, that they might be some beginning of his creation” (Jas. 1:18).

Glory to the Father, who begets the new people by the word of truth. Glory to the Son, who established the sacrament of this generation in his Passion and poured regenerating water from his side upon the cross. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who makes that same water fruitful through the infusion of his power, so that in time the people may now be born whom the Lord already made before the ages in predestination.

In this same Passion he established two sacraments for us: [Col. 1040D] the washing of regeneration, when, his side having been opened, he poured out blood and water; and the mystery of his body and blood, when, holding bread and wine, he said, “This is my body; this is my blood” (Matt. 26:26–27). Thereupon the Church, made perfect, rejoices in Psalm 22 and says:

## PSALM 22

[Col. 1039]

[Col. 1039D] **VERSE 1. The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me there in a place of pasture.** For, as though you were asking, [Col. 1040D] “In whose place of pasture?” it immediately adds: “He led me out over the water of refreshment; he turned [Col. 1041A] my soul.” And then: “You have prepared before me a table against those who afflict me.” What is the water of refreshment but saving baptism? Over this water of baptism, which is the foundation of good works, the Lord, says the Church, led me out, namely by the milk of preaching, and afterward—for this is the proper order in which it should be read—afterward, I say, “he placed me there in a place of pasture,” that is, he caused me to study the Scriptures. There he rules me, lest I understand wrongly, and I shall lack nothing necessary for understanding.

And what table is this which, you say, “you have prepared before me against those who afflict me,” but your body and blood, the sacrament of which you set before my understanding under other appearances, lest my enemies prevail against me? And because after these things a twofold gift of the Holy Spirit was given, he says: “You have made my head rich with oil, and how excellent is my intoxicating cup!” For when the Holy Spirit was first given, the apostles were sweetly anointed as with oil, when he breathed on them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; and whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 20:22–23). But when they were made drunk, as it were, by the second cup, they became strong and eloquent, so that it was said: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2:13).

By these sacraments that land and world were prepared for the Lord, concerning which Psalm 23 immediately begins: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 23:1). For this earth and this world are the Church. It is called earth for two reasons, both because of stability and because of fruitfulness; but it is called a world because of perfection. And because the visible sacraments mentioned above alone are not sufficient for anyone to dwell in the eternal Church, it indicates this more aptly in the form of a question: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? The innocent in hands and pure in heart,” etc. (ibid., 3). But let us return to the exposition of Psalm 22.

**The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing.** The title, “A Psalm of David,” is clear. Here the Prophet treats of the mercy and benefit of the Lord’s Passion, which he discussed in the preceding psalm. And just as there he spoke in the person of Christ himself, saying: “My God, [Col. 1041D] look upon me: why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21:2), so here he speaks in the person of the whole Church, or of any one of the elect within the Church, giving thanks for the manifold mercy and grace that proceed from Christ’s Passion. The first of these is that the one imbued with the sacraments of the Lord’s Passion is placed in a place of pasture when he is instructed and made a catechumen; the second, that he is led over the water of refreshment when he is regenerated through baptismal water; the third, that through the visible washing of the body in baptism the soul is turned, so that, having been turned away in Adam, it may be turned toward Christ and made holy; the fourth, that he is led upon the paths of righteousness, lest baptismal grace itself be made void if one strays from the ways of righteousness; the fifth, that he fears no evils in the shadow of death; the sixth, consolation given through rod and staff; [Col. 1042A] the seventh, the table of the heavenly banquet prepared; the eighth, the anointing of the head; the ninth, the intoxicating cup; the tenth, mercy that follows and preserves until the end.

In treating these ten graces, he intends, through these freely bestowed provisions for the journey, to exhort us to hope for heavenly and eternal gifts which eye has not seen nor ear heard, but which are laid up within the house of the Lord. Of that house it is said at the end of the psalm: “and that I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days.”

Therefore either the Church or any elect person, with David—strong of hand in action and desirable in contemplation—recognizing in this psalm entitled “A Psalm of David” the gifts of grace poured out through Christ’s Passion, says in thanksgiving: [Col. 1042B] “The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing.”

In the Hebrew it reads: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me there in a place of pasture.” Therefore I, the Church, or I, a member of the Church, give thanks because the Lord rules me and feeds me by ruling, or rules me by feeding—my Lord himself, my shepherd and my king. He is Lord because he gave me existence by creating me; shepherd and ruler because by feeding and ruling me he grants me blessed existence. Therefore, for his feeding and governance, through which he grants me blessedness, I give him more earnest thanks as one redeemed by him than I did formerly as one created by him. For unless, by feeding and ruling, he granted me well-being, it would be altogether better for me not to exist. But lest I exist unhappily, the Lord who created me from nothing became my shepherd and king by this fact:

**VERSE 2. He placed me in a place of pasture, or in a green place.** Therefore I shall lack nothing, because both the Lord who feeds and rules me is rich, and the place of pasture in which he placed me is green. I did not place myself there; he placed me there by prevenient grace, where I am certain of fullness. For the divine word not only instructs beginners in faith, but also nourishes believers, so that by advancing ever more and more in faith, those who already know God by faith may be brought to contemplate the vision of divine majesty. There they shall have fullness without weariness, because desire will remain in fullness and fullness in desire, such that fullness admits no need and desire no weariness.

He placed me in such a place of pasture [Col. 1042D] when he established me, now a catechumen—that is, instructed in knowledge of the Scriptures—in which I find milk for infants and bread for the strong. Strengthened by such foods:

**He led me over the water of refreshment,** when he admitted me to the grace of baptism. I had first been catechized through confession of faith and recognition of truth, but after baptism I found more fully in them the water of refreshment. For I, the Church—whether in those members of mine who, in infancy, are introduced into the place of pasture through the sacrament of salt and the touch of saliva, or in my older members, who are instructed by faith itself in the heart and placed in the place of pasture—I should have no refreshing food in the place of pasture [Col. 1043A] unless I had come to the water of refreshment, grace leading me out and nourishing me like a little child as a mother. This is the water flowing from the right side of the temple, and all to whom this water came were saved. This water is the foundation of human salvation; therefore I say: “He led me over the water of refreshment.”

For the visible water of baptism signifies another, invisible water: namely, the Holy Spirit, who in the beginning was borne over the waters, so that from the fluid and unstable matter of the waters, by the infusion of his power, he might form me, the one and only Church, rooted and founded in charity. This charity is given only through the Holy Spirit. Hence the Apostle, who was certainly led out and founded over the water of refreshment, says: [Col. 1043B] “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). Likewise, to his disciples, whom that same Apostle had faithfully led over the water of refreshment through the cooperation of God’s grace, he wishes that they, “rooted and founded in charity, may be able to comprehend what is the breadth, length, height, and depth; and also to know the charity of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that they may be filled unto all the fullness of God” (Eph. 3:17–19).

Therefore, if we have been led out and founded over this water of refreshment, and have been washed not only with visible water but also refreshed with the invisible water, which is the Holy Spirit, having tasted the charity that the Spirit himself pours in, we rightly say in thanksgiving: [Col. 1043C] “The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me there in a place of pasture. He led me over the water of refreshment,” which administers refreshment to the human soul that has no good powers in itself, first making fruitful what was dry and barren, so that it may not only possess refreshment abundantly in itself but also bring forth refreshment for others. Thus I, any one of us, like David—desirable through good intention and strong of hand through good work—having been brought to the water of refreshment, give thanks to God not only because he has thus led me out, or, as it is read in the Hebrew, nourished me, but also because—
**VERSE 3. He restored my soul.** This was the third grace shown to me: that after baptism my soul should not be turned away from Him, but turned toward Him, as once the Jordan turned back toward its source [Col. 1043D]. For that part of the Jordan which, when the ark of the Lord passed over, was divided from its source, flowed into the Dead Sea, leaving its channel dry and empty; but that part which turned back and held itself to its source rose high, not merely filling, but greatly overflowing, its channel (Josh. 3:16). So among the baptized, some flow down into the deadly bitterness of this world, retaining only the empty and void sacrament of baptism; but others, turned toward their source or beginning, rise upward—not merely to the sufficiency of their own progress, which would be simply to fill the channel, but even to the enlargement of benefit for their brethren. Therefore the grace shown me is not slight, nor is a slight thanksgiving due [Col. 1044A] because the Lord restored my soul. Certainly, after baptism it would have flowed down into the Dead Sea, descending through vices even to hell, had not the Lord been among us—He who, in His goodness, turned my soul, so prone to evil, away from wickedness, sowing within it a good thought and granting and increasing a good will. By this alone is the soul’s conversion made acceptable, even if opportunity and ability for doing good be lacking.

But so that the light of the converted soul may shine not only before people, that they may see good works and glorify God in the person who does good, a fourth grace is added to the preceding graces, when a person is led along paths of righteousness from the hidden place of the will to manifest action.

[Col. 1044B] To some, the order of the graces seems changed and inverted, because the first grace seems third and the third first. For Christ the shepherd first restored the soul which, in Adam, had turned away like a wandering sheep; then He washed it when restored in baptism; and thirdly, setting before it the divine word by which it might be satisfied, He placed it in a place of pasture, so that, delightfully ranging through those pastures, it might walk along paths of righteousness. Had the Psalmist followed this order, it would have been quite satisfactory. But the order he followed is more pleasing for this reason: although it is a great grace to convert before baptism a person ignorant of the knowledge of truth, or to admit to the sacraments of Christian grace one who remains wholly ignorant and, because of infancy, cannot yet know; nevertheless, far more abundant kindness is shown in that conversion [Col. 1044C] by which, after receiving the sacrament of baptism, a person is so turned toward his own beginning that, through the preserving grace of Christ, who is the ark of the covenant, he is not permitted to flow downward into hell.

Therefore I—David of whatever sort, that is, humble like David, or beloved like David, or strong of hand like David, or at least penitent like David, to whom this Psalm is ascribed—give God the greatest thanks for that conversion of my soul by which He restored it after baptism, so that, abandoning an evil will, it might possess a good one.

Again I give thanks to Him who, after granting me a good will, led me along paths of righteousness, so that I might walk in good and righteous work, not for the enlargement of [Col. 1044D] my own name, but for the glorification of His name. For by grace alone and gratuitous kindness He led me forward in good work along paths of righteousness: along narrow paths, upon which few walk—namely, the two commandments of charity. To beginners these are narrow paths; but for those making progress, whose hearts have been enlarged and who run in the way of the commandments, the journey is no longer in narrow paths, but above the paths. Therefore I give thanks to Him who led me not only at the beginning along a narrow track in the paths, but, now advanced beyond the constrictions of the beginning, led me above the paths of righteousness into the great breadth of charity. And He did this not because of my merit, but so that His name might be proclaimed and glorified. And so that this might be done more fittingly through me, He gave me [Col. 1045A] a fifth grace: that, while magnifying God’s name, I should not fear the adversaries of that same name.

**VERSE 4. For though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, because You are with me.** That is truly called death by which the soul is deprived of God, who is its life. This “death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. 33:22); it is greatly to be feared and carefully avoided. But there is a certain image and shadow of this death, by which the body is deprived of its own life. For the likeness between these two deaths is like that between a body and the body’s shadow: just as the human soul does not live unless God dwells in it, so the human body does not live unless the rational soul dwells in it. Hence, just as the body, deserted by the soul in its death, has no sensation but decays [Col. 1045B] and becomes dust, so the soul, deserted by God through the death of grievous sin, loses its perception, decays in its corruption, and becomes unstable, “like the dust which the wind casts forth from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:4).

Therefore the saints, who were often in deaths for righteousness’ sake, knowing that bodily death is only the shadow of death, say to God: “You have humbled us in the place of affliction, and the shadow of death has covered us” (Ps. 43:20). And for those “dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light arose” (Isa. 9:2). Through this light they were defended from the most evil death of sinners, because that light which arose for them was their life, as it is written: “And life was the light of men; and the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:4–5). For [Col. 1045C] in the midst of the shadow of death the souls of the saints lived, and always live, who do not depart from faith in Christ, as He Himself says: “He who believes in me, even if he has died, shall live” (John 11:25). That is: even if in the midst, in the region, of the shadow of death he is deprived of bodily life, he who believes in me shall nevertheless enjoy true life. For “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:16).

Since death, then, and not death’s shadow or image, is to be feared, I, David—though a sinner, yet penitent and believing in You, Christ, who are life—will not fear the evils of death even in the midst of the shadow of death. I will not fear death, that is, the devil, because You, who are life, deign to be with me. For [Col. 1045D] though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, among the ministers of the shadow of death, who kill bodies, and among the ministers of death itself—heretics or even demons—who seek to kill souls, I will fear no evils, because You are with me. You who are life are with me, dwelling in my heart through faith; You are with me through the ineffable sacrament of Your body and blood; You are with me through the seal of Your cross placed upon my heart, so that I may think upon You as placed upon my forehead, may not blush to confess You, but may truly live true life in You, believing with the heart unto righteousness and confessing with the mouth unto salvation. Even if I should die bodily and, walking in the midst of the shadow of death, be led to Your tribunal, I will not fear the evils of eternal condemnation, because then You will be with me by sight, [Col. 1046A] You who are now with me by faith, which works good through love of You and avoids shameful things.

Nor need I fear, so long as You are with me, that the prince of darkness, encountering me either here while I sleep, or there while I walk amid the shadow of death, may prevail. For it is written: “If two sleep, they shall warm one another; and if anyone prevail against one, two shall resist him” (Eccl. 4:11–12), and so forth. For we are two: I, the rational soul, and Your word, O God; but the devil, Your enemy and mine, is one. Therefore, if he sets himself to prevail—whether against me sleeping here in the sleep of rest or even of death, or hastening there through the shadow of death to Your tribunal—we two, namely You and I, shall resist him. Therefore [Col. 1046B] I will fear no evils, because You, stronger than he—that is, the devil—are with me. Your death, undertaken for me, is with me; Your bruises and wounds are with me; the blows of rods and the spittle are with me—all of which You endured not for Yourself but for me.

I will not fear the evils of the judicial sentence either, because You who are my judge are with me as my advocate: my judge, because I have sinned; my advocate, because I have done penance. Nor could I in any way be freed while You, the just judge, judged me, unless I were defended by You, my advocating patron. But because You are with me as advocate and propitiation for my sins, I will not fear the evils of the judicial sentence. But from what shall I gain knowledge, or any experience, of this grace—that You are with me? Namely, from this:

[Col. 1046C] **Your rod and Your staff, they have comforted me.** For You have not dealt with me as You deal with many wicked people, whom You do not touch with the rod of discipline while they now riot unpunished in their wickedness, because You reserve them for greater and eternal punishments. Rather, Your rod—that is, the light discipline by which You chastise the little, fragile, and weak—has continually chastised me; and Your staff, by which You strike those who are greater and stronger, either humbling them by great affliction or buffeting them with grievous temptation so that their greatness and strength may not exalt them, has touched me on several occasions. For, because of pride, lest it should rule over me, those who trouble me have become very numerous; and amid the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes [Col. 1046D] there was given me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me.

That angel would indeed, through such a thorn, lead me to consent to wickedness; but if that happened, these thorns would not be blows for my humiliation but deadly arrows for my destruction. For if a widow “living in pleasures is dead” (1 Tim. 5:6), much more would I be dead if I regarded the deadly pleasures of the flesh as delights. But, thanks be to God, thorns of this kind are for me more a buffeting than a delight. Therefore I discipline my body by fasts, abstinences, and vigils, insofar as health allows and Your grace, O God, grants.

[Col. 1047A] Alternatively: **Your rod and Your staff, they have comforted me**, because, when it was necessary, You chastised me with the rod of discipline, and again, when it was necessary, You sustained me with the staff of mercy, so that I might always have matter for singing to You of “mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100:1): You scourged me through judgment lest I become insolent, and raised me through mercy lest I fail altogether beneath Your excessive blows.

More fully, however, and more perfectly, Your rod and Your staff have comforted me since I came to know through the Scriptures what rod and staff are—those in which there is comfort, not desolation. For there is a rod of consolation and a rod of desolation. The rod of desolation is eternal punishment, concerning which it is said: “The Lord will not leave the rod of sinners upon [Col. 1047B] the lot of the righteous” (Ps. 124:3). Likewise Assyria was a rod, or staff, of desolation, to whom it is said: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my fury; he himself is the staff of my indignation in my hand” (Isa. 10:5). For Israel, chastised or taken captive through that staff or rod, was not corrected (4 Kings 15:29), since its captivity was never released; rather, Israel, carried into Assyria, was wholly alienated from the people of God and from the temple of the Lord.

But King Nebuchadnezzar, who took the tribe of Judah captive (4 Kings 25:7), was like a rod and staff of consolation in God’s hand, because the captivity effected through him was released after seventy years and served for the correction of those who sat and wept there by the rivers [Col. 1047C] of Babylon, when they remembered Zion and set Jerusalem at the beginning of their joy, never being captivated by or delighting in Babylon’s pleasures (Ps. 136:1). Thus, considering in the Scriptures all corrective scourges, I find consolation in them because they are thereby consolatory, although they formerly seemed to be for desolation.

So too human mortality itself and bodily death have been found to be for consolation, though they were thought to be for desolation. For if, after sin, humanity had eaten of the tree of life and lived forever, it would have remained in fellowship with demons, who possess wretched immortality and immortal wretchedness. But now, since, having eaten of the forbidden tree, humanity had already died in soul and was forbidden to eat of the tree of life, we find through the mortality and death of the body such consolation as was once signified through Moses.

For before Pharaoh and Moses two magicians “cast down their rods, and they were turned into dragons” (Exod. 7:10, 12). Moses also cast down his rod, “which” likewise “was turned into a serpent” (ibid., 4:3), and it devoured the two rods of the magicians and was again turned into its own form. What is signified by the serpent or dragon except death, which entered the world through the persuasion of the ancient serpent? That same serpent, now made a red dragon and bloodthirsty with the blood of Hebrew male children, wielded death as though a rod of fury, desiring, by killing the males, wholly to blot out the race of [Col. 1048A] Abraham, in whose seed the hope and promise of salvation and blessing had been laid up. For God said to Abraham: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18).

Accordingly, the two rods of Pharaoh’s magicians were rightly changed into dragons, because, through the devil’s contrivance, two deaths entered the world: one of the soul, the other of the body. Human nature had been created to flourish with the twofold beauty of bodily and spiritual immortality, like a beautiful rod; but now the two rods are found transformed into serpents and dragons because, as the venom of the ancient serpent raged, a twofold death reigned in the human race. Yet our Moses, Christ, giver of the new law, wholly free from the death of the soul, admitted into Himself one death only—the death of the body. By this death, swallowing up the two deaths, He most truly presented Himself to us as a rod and staff of consolation against the two rods of desolation. For both our deaths were swallowed up in the victory of Him who, by dying, destroyed the death of our souls and, by rising again, restored the life of our bodies.

How saving and consoling was the rod of mortality and death through which our correction was accomplished in Christ, as Isaiah says: “The discipline of our peace was upon Him, and by His bruise we are healed” (Isa. 53:5). We sinned and remained always in those very sins. But He, innocent, was scourged for our sins and humbled even to death on the cross. Although He was the rod of power which the Lord sent forth from Zion, nevertheless [Col. 1048C] He was turned into a serpent, receiving in Himself the death which punished our sins. But, laying aside again as it were the form of the serpent, and swallowing up our twofold death in His victory, this rod of power flowered anew through the resurrection, having withered in death. Therefore it is said: “The Lord is my helper and my protector; my heart hoped in Him, and I was helped, and my flesh flowered again” (Ps. 27:7).

How strong is this staff of our consolation, by which the nature of human flesh is raised and sustained in Christ, lifted above all the powers of heaven and set upon the highest throne at the right hand of God the Most High! So great is this staff; so great, that is, is the power of resurrection in Christ.

Indeed, Christ Himself, raised from death, is such and so great a staff that through Him the entire human race is to be raised from the dust of death. “Many of those who sleep in the dust shall awake.” Truly many, because “we shall all indeed rise”; and, sustained by the staff of the Lord’s resurrection, we shall stand before Christ’s tribunal. “But” because there “we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51), this Psalm is ascribed only to penitent David. For only those who now, through the rod of discipline, die with Christ and are changed for the better, as penitent David was changed, shall also then be changed into glory, when Christ Himself—the staff of our old age, by no means a reed, but altogether iron [Col. 1049A] and solid—judging this world with an iron rod, shall refashion the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of His glory.

Therefore let penitent and humble David speak; let anyone like him speak to You, King Christ, who by Your rod of passion and staff of resurrection divinely work consolation for Your people. Let Israel now say it; let the house of Aaron now say it, whose rod flowered for His and our consolation. Let each one of us who believes that You, Jesus Christ, are the true king and priest—while the rods dry and unflowering, and therefore desolatory and excluding from the priesthood—say to You, King Christ, who bear both the priestly and the royal rod: “Let every knee bend and every tongue confess” (Phil. 1:10–11); and let him say to You: **Your rod and Your staff, they have comforted me**, because in Your death, by which You alone among the dead were free, and in Your Resurrection, by which You did not rise alone, “this hope of mine has been placed in my bosom” (Job 19:27): that participation in that same death and resurrection of Yours may profit me; that after bodily death—or even within the enclosure of this mortal body—I may be free from the laws of death, my soul living in You who are life, flourishing in You who are the flowering rod, and my body resting in hope of the resurrection to come.

Alternatively: **Your rod**, by which You crush the guilt committed by humankind, **and Your staff**, by which You sustain the nature created by Yourself, **have comforted me**. For guilt is ended through the rod of death; nature is perpetuated through the staff of resurrection. “For he who has died,” says the Apostle, “has been justified from sin” (Rom. 6:7), provided, however, that he has died in the Lord; for “blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14:13). And this is my consolation: that I hope to die and rise again in You, my Lord, who, so that I may live in You—

**VERSE 5. You have prepared before me a table against those who afflict me.** This is the seventh grace. This table is Your body and blood, O Christ. Such a table is not before the eyes of the ungodly and foolish, who neither understand nor believe to be true what You say concerning the appearance of bread: “This [Col. 1049D] is my body, which shall be given for you” for the remission of sins (Luke 22:19); and concerning the appearance of wine: “This is my blood of the New Testament, which” shall be shed “for you” and “for many, for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26:28). But this table has been prepared before my eyes, while by the eyes of faith I behold the power and truth of this sacrament, hidden from the perception of flesh. “For I know whom I have believed, and I am certain” (1 Tim. 1:12) that Your body, O Christ, which is given upon Your altar—since You, its author, affirm it to be the very same—is that which the Virgin bore and which hung upon the cross. For You say: “Which shall be given for you” (1 Cor. 11:24). Therefore it is the very same, wholly the very same.

But “the fool says in his heart, There is not” [Ps. [Col. 1050A] 52:1] that very same thing. But I say that it is the very same thing which was given on the cross for us. For I know whom I have believed when He says this, and I am certain that Truth did not speak a lie, nor could anything be said by Truth which was not true. But the body born of the Virgin was offered and given on the cross for us. Therefore that which is offered upon the altar is altogether the very same body: the very same in name, the very same in essence, the very same in operation or efficacy.

The identity of the name is indicated when You, Truth, say: “This is my body” (Matt. 26:26). And because Your holy Church also is Your body—a body which was not given for us for the remission of sins—so that You might designate the singular essence of Your own body as it were by a certain individual property, [Col. 1050B] You said: “which shall be given for you.” By this utterance is signified the essence of Your unique body, given for us; and its efficacy or operation is this: that its giving or offering may result for us and for many in remission of sins.

“I believed, therefore I spoke” (Ps. 115:10): because Your body, O Christ, as I have noted beforehand, is the very same in name, essence, and efficacy. For just as that which was crucified under Pontius Pilate between two thieves is truly called and is Your body, so that You might be made known between two living creatures, so likewise that which is now offered upon the ecclesiastical altar, when the mysteries are celebrated in the Church, is truly called and is Your body—whether ministered and received unworthily or worthily. Some of those who receive it, with the thief on the left, eat and drink judgment upon themselves; others, with the thief on the right, receive it for the remission of sins. For just as it availed the thief on the right for the remission of sins that, seeing weakness in Your body, he believed in its power, so now it benefits the elect and faithful that, seeing the appearance of bread in that same body of Yours, they believe in the majesty of divine power.

Nor is this faith diminished by the fact that the same form or appearance is not manifested to the eyes of beholders in that same body; rather, that fact makes the faith more precious. For He appeared to the disciples in another form, and “their eyes were held so that they did not recognize Him” (Luke 24:16); and He appeared to Mary Magdalene as if a gardener (John [Col. 1050D] 20:15). He was manifested in a poor person’s clothing and appearance to Martin, still a catechumen, whom Martin had clothed with his own garment, but this occurred in a dream. Yet to Peter, patriarch of Alexandria, while awake and imprisoned for his defence of the Catholic faith, Christ Himself appeared as a little boy with a torn garment, because at that time the Church was torn by Arius.

Even during the sacred solemnities of the Mass, Christ has been seen by many faithful persons, too many to enumerate, as present in various forms. To some He appeared as a little boy, to others as a lamb. But to blessed Pope Gregory, bread was seen changed into bloody flesh in the form of a finger, as though newly severed from a living body. Yet through every such variety of appearances Christ’s body, always [Col. 1051A] the very same, does not change its identity; but, being the same both in name and essence, it produces the same efficacy—namely, the remission of sins—especially in those before whose eyes this table is prepared, though hidden from the foolish.

Surely this is what is read in Solomon’s parables: “If you sit down to dine at a powerful man’s table, consider and understand what is set before you; and so stretch forth your hand, knowing that you must prepare such things” (Ecclus. 31:19). For what is the powerful man’s table except that from which is received the body and blood of Him who laid down His life for us? And what is sitting at it except approaching humbly? And what is considering and understanding what is set before you except thinking worthily upon so great a grace? And what is [Col. 1051B] stretching forth the hand in such a way that you know you must prepare such things, except what I have already said: that, just as Christ “laid down His life for us,” so “we too ought to lay down our lives for the brethren” (1 John 3:16)?

You will prepare such things as Christ prepared in this way also: if, when about to approach Christ’s table, you subject your will in every respect to the divine will, just as He subjected His human will to the divine, saying to the Father: “Father, not my will but Yours be done” (Luke 22:42). For whoever approaches communion at the Lord’s table while still wishing in any way to have his carnal will, contrary to the divine will, fulfilled, does not desire to be incorporated into Christ. Rather, if it were [Col. 1051C] possible, he would wish to incorporate Christ into himself; and therefore “he is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:17). He is guilty of Christ’s death, whom, so far as lies in him, he kills. Who is wise and will understand these things? For I should not understand them unless this table had been prepared before my eyes.

But now, because You, O God, have prepared a table before my eyes, I see in this table of Yours a great miracle, a great spectacle. For there are some who are incorporated into You at this table in such a way that they are wholly put to death and slain as to their own life, just as when a dove is incorporated into a heron or hawk, the dove itself is altogether killed. One bird could not be incorporated into another bird while its former life remained. But there are very many who refuse to lose their former life; and therefore [Col. 1051D] they cannot be incorporated into Christ, because they will not die with Him who dies, and will not say with Him to the Father: “Father, not my will but Yours be done” (Luke 22:42). If they said this from the heart in truth, they would indeed sacrifice their carnal life to God, unite their will, utterly mortified, to the divine will, and thus pass into Christ’s body, so that with the Apostle Paul they could say: “Now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

But those wicked men said and say: “Let us unjustly oppress the righteous man” (Wis. 2:10), and “let us swallow him alive like hell” (Prov. 1:12). For they know that they can no longer kill Christ; therefore they wish to swallow Him alive like hell, like that whale [Col. 1052A] which swallowed Jonah alive, unable either to kill him or incorporate him into itself. But “He now dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over Him” (Rom. 6:9).

Yet those who were foolish and malicious, hating wisdom, also became guilty in their thoughts. Furthermore, they presumed to approach wisdom’s table as though wishing to swallow it and unite it to their own foolishness. But Wisdom “has built herself a house, hewn out seven pillars, sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine, and set forth her table. She sent her maidservants to call to the citadel and to the city’s walls: ‘If anyone is little, let him come to me.’ And she spoke to the foolish: ‘Come, eat my bread and drink the wine which I have mixed for you. Leave childishness behind, and live, and walk in the ways [Col. 1052B] of prudence’” (Prov. 9:1–6). See how Wisdom calls her guests to the citadel and the city walls.

By the citadel in a city we mean the highest tower, higher than the other buildings. By this we understand either the common life in the holy Church, whose example shines forth in the apostles and their disciples, among whom “there was one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32) in God; or the purpose of the solitary life, whose example appears in John the Baptist, may be understood as the citadel. Thus the little ones who are to feast with Wisdom are called to the citadel—that is, to perfect and excellent conduct. But among these little and humble ones there are some who are weak and cannot ascend to the citadel; these are called at least to the city walls.

[Col. 1052C] The city walls are lower callings in the holy Church—for example, those of married people, or even of continent people who possess property. They are permitted to dwell beneath the height of the citadel at Wisdom’s feast, provided that they strive to subject and unite their own will to Wisdom’s will, so that what is written may come about: “He who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). It should be observed, moreover, that after foolish and malicious people have been excluded from this feast, foolish but humble people are called, as Wisdom itself says: “If anyone is little, let him come to me”; and, “Eat my bread and drink the wine which I have mixed for you” (Prov. 9:4–5). Yet, lest they suppose themselves permitted to partake of such a table unless they first [Col. 1052D] abandon the folly of their foolishness, She adds: “Leave childishness behind” (ibid., 6).

And because it is not enough to cease from evils unless one also strives to maintain some good purpose, whether in the city’s citadel or in the walls near the citadel, She rightly added, after saying, “Leave childishness behind”: “And live, and walk in the ways of prudence” (ibid.). But because foolish, malicious, and proud people hate wisdom when foolish little ones are admitted to Wisdom’s table, and neither hear Wisdom’s invitation nor do anything but oppose and mock it, there rightly follows: “He who instructs a scoffer brings injury upon himself; and he who rebukes the wicked generates a stain for himself. Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you” (ibid., 7–8). Therefore let us cease rebuking such persons, lest, as they quarrel against us, [Col. 1053A] they generate a stain for us.

But let this be impressed upon humble people as though God were exhorting them through us: that they should never approach Wisdom’s holy feast unless they have first chosen a definite purpose of good conduct, either in the city’s citadel or within its walls. In that calling they must mortify their own will, reducing it beneath the divine will, and directing their will to no action whatsoever except one which they understand—or at least believe—to be pleasing to the divine will.

But lest their understanding or belief be open to deception, so that they suppose themselves to render service to God in some act which is against God, the Scriptures of truth must be searched. In them the good pleasure of the divine will is clearly evident. Whoever is ignorant of them shall be ignored; but one who is not ignorant of them and nevertheless acts contrary to them in such a way as to suppose that it does him no harm has been poisoned by that venom of the ancient serpent by which the first woman was wounded. That is, she was so seduced by the serpent’s persuasion that she thought it would not harm but benefit her to eat what was forbidden against God’s command.

[Col. 1053B] But the person who understands the Scriptures, or believes a Catholic teacher in accordance with them, and yet intends to act contrary to them—thinking indeed that it is harmful, but not so displeasing to God that He will severely punish one who acts thus, because of fellowship with companions—is perverted and wounded by the venom through which the first-formed man languished. [Col. 1053C] When Adam obeyed his wife’s voice more than God’s, he did not do what he did believing it useful; rather, he yielded to his wife, whom, because God had given her as his companion, he did not think it a great fault to obey against the divine voice. For he had not been deceived in the transgression in the same manner as the woman, who believed useful what was harmful; nevertheless he was deceived in this, that he considered his guilt excusable because he did not wish to disturb their social unanimity by opposing his wife’s persuasion. He had received her from God as his companion.

Therefore afterwards, reproved by God for his sin, he turned “his heart to words of malice, to make excuses for excuses in sins” (Ps. 140:4), when he said: “The woman whom You gave me as my companion gave me, [Col. 1053D] and I ate” (Gen. 3:12). In this way many of his followers knowingly act against God’s will for the sake of social cohabitation with those among whom they have chosen to live. They ought rather to leave them than yield to their will against God’s will.

When the wills of the first human beings had thus been set—indeed, perverted—against God’s will, that forbidden food was added to confirm so great a wickedness. Eating it, humanity was sold under sin for nothing. Hence the prophet says: “You were sold for nothing” (Isa. 52:3). Humanity was indeed sold for nothing: it lost itself but did not receive the price promised to it by the devil. Therefore redemption is necessary, in which a human being must give his whole self in order to receive the price promised by God. [Col. 1054A] For, Truth says: “He who loses his life for my sake shall find it” (Matt. 10:31).

What is it to lose one’s life for God’s sake except so to mortify the carnal or animal will that a person firmly resolves never to do anything against God: neither by believing the spirit of error more than the Spirit of truth, which was the sin committed by the deceived woman; nor by yielding to human society, as Adam did? Once human wills have been so disposed, when Christ’s body is received, that blessed bread of angels strengthens the human heart. That flesh which is truly food becomes for a person an antidote to the twofold poison of the first parents, and evil belief is purged by good belief—as though one should say to the person:

“You believed the devil concerning what you did not see in the apple: namely, that eating it would make you like God. Now believe the Son of God concerning what you do not see: namely, that participation in the supreme Divinity will come to you in the bread which He calls His body.” For He says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6:57). Again: “If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever; and the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (ibid., 52).

You therefore, human being, who believed the deceiving devil falsely promising you the reward of divinity, and in that belief ate the forbidden food offered you by him, now believe the Savior, who promises you communion in His Divinity; and in this belief eat His flesh and drink His blood. [Col. 1054C] But before you receive such an antidote, first vomit out the poison conceived from the serpent by recognizing and confessing that it was evil whenever you placed your own will above the divine will: whether by believing good to be evil and evil good, like deceived Eve; or by believing evil to be evil and good to be good as they were, but nevertheless yielding to people, so that against your conscience you either admitted an evil which should have been avoided or omitted a good which should have been done. This was Adam’s sin, to which this second Adam is wholly opposed: He did not come to do His own will, but the will of Him who sent Him.

Whenever we eat this body of his, it is worth the effort [Col. 1054D] to hear his voice from on high: “I am the food of the mature: grow, and you shall eat me. Nor will you change me into yourself, as you do the food of your flesh; rather, you shall be changed into me.” Truly, “this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 77:11), because the one who eats is changed into him who is eaten. This transformation is experienced when the human will is so united to the divine will that a person truthfully says to God himself: “Not what I will, but what you will, be done” (Matt. 26:39).

But whoever still desires his own fleshly will to be done against the divine will—whether, deceived with Eve into false belief, he believes good to be evil or evil to be good; or, deceived with Adam, while retaining the belief that evil is evil, believes a great evil to be a lesser evil, thinking it less evil to offend the most high God than to offend a fellow human being—if such a person approaches to eat Christ’s body and drink his blood, he puts new wine into old wineskins: the wine is spilled and the wineskins perish. The wine is spilled, but is not lost. For how can he perish who “came to save that which was lost”? (Luke 19:10). How could his body and blood perish, who is everywhere? Yet those who pour this blood of the grape, pressed out in the winepress of the cross, into old wineskins become guilty of this blood, as though they had destroyed it, because that which did not perish did not remain in them.

Therefore I give thanks to you, Lord, who rule me, whatever kind of servant of yours I may be, as David—that is, “strong of hand” [Col. 1055B] against temptations, desirable in virtues—or at least as David the penitent, singing the penitential psalm, “Have mercy on me, O God.” I give you thanks, I say, because I have your table prepared before me, while with the eyes of faith I behold that, for me who subject my will to your will and thus sit at your table in humility of heart, your “bread,” which “strengthens the heart of man,” supplies great power, strength, and protection “against those who trouble me” (Ps. 103:16).

For from that from which I receive life, they receive judgment to eat. Even by this, your rod and your staff have themselves comforted me: after the rod of discipline, like a supporting staff, you have prepared a table before me. From this table I am no longer nourished with milk [Col. 1055C] like a little child, but, now trained and weaned, I hold a great feast with Isaac on the day of my weaning, receiving stronger, solid foods, which strengthen and comfort me against those who trouble me.

Who are those who trouble me? Surely those indicated by Job’s messenger, who says: “The Chaldeans formed three bands, invaded the camels, carried them off, and also struck the servants with the sword” (Job 1:17). “Chaldeans” is interpreted as “fierce”; by this name the enemies of the Church are rightly denoted, and they are divided into three bands. One band is that of demons, another that of malicious human beings, and the third that of fleshly passions.

These bands trouble me in different ways. Demons fiercely attack me invisibly, sending harmful thoughts against me. Malicious people, likewise fierce, attack visibly: either striving to draw me into likeness with themselves, or persecuting me because I am unlike them. Fleshly passions—by which “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks upon many things” (Wis. 9:15)—also fiercely trouble me like untamed beasts many times, when I will but cannot fully tame them. Against all enemies of this kind, who trouble me, you have prepared a table before me. Your servant Ambrose understood this as well; having your table prepared before him, he prayed thus:

[Col. 1056A] “Supreme priest and true pontiff, who offered yourself to God the Father as a pure and spotless victim upon the altar of the cross for us sinners; who gave us your flesh to eat and your blood to drink; and established this mystery through the power of the Holy Spirit, saying: ‘Whenever you do this, do it in remembrance of me’: I beseech you through your precious blood, the great price of our salvation; and I beseech you through this wondrous and ineffable love by which you deigned so to love us miserable people that you washed us from our sins in your blood.

“Teach me, your unworthy servant, whom among your other gifts you deigned to call also to the priestly office—not through any merits of mine, but solely through the graciousness of your mercy. Teach me, I pray, through the Holy Spirit [Col. 1056B] to handle so great a mystery with that reverence and love, that devotion and fear, which are fitting and proper. By your grace make me always to believe, understand, perceive, firmly retain, say, and think concerning so great a mystery what pleases you and benefits my soul.

“May your good Spirit enter my heart, sounding there without the sound and noise of words, and speaking the whole truth of mysteries so great. For they are exceedingly profound and covered by a sacred veil. Through your great mercy grant me to celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass with a pure heart and clean mind. Free my heart from unclean and wicked, empty and harmful thoughts. Fortify me with the faithful and pious protection of blessed angels, that the enemies of all good things may depart in confusion.

“Through the power [Col. 1056C] of so great a mystery, and through the hand of your holy angel, drive far from me and from all your servants the most harsh spirit of pride and vainglory, envy and blasphemy, fornication and impurity, doubt and distrust. Let those who persecute us be confounded; let those perish who hasten to destroy every good thing.

“King of virgins, God who loves chastity and integrity, by the dew of your heavenly blessing extinguish in my body every tinder of burning lust, so that the constancy of all chastity of body and soul may remain in me. Mortify in my members the impulses of the flesh and every lustful stirring; grant me true and perpetual chastity, together with your other gifts which truly please you, so that with a chaste body [Col. 1056D] and clean heart I may be able daily to offer you a sacrifice of praise.

“For with what contrition of heart and fountain of tears, with what reverence and trembling, with what bodily chastity and purity of soul, must this divine and heavenly sacrifice be celebrated! Lord, where your flesh is truly received, where your blood is truly drunk, where the lowly are joined to the highest, where you are priest and sacrifice, wonderfully and ineffably! Who can worthily celebrate this unless you, almighty God, make the offerer worthy?

“I know, and truly know, and confess this very thing to your goodness: I am not worthy to approach so great a mystery because of my exceeding sins and countless negligences. But I know, truly believe with my whole heart, and confess with my mouth that you can make me worthy—you who alone [Col. 1057A] can make clean what is conceived from unclean seed, and who make sinners righteous and holy.

“Through this your omnipotence I beseech you: grant to me, a sinner, to celebrate this heavenly sacrifice with fear and trembling, with a fountain of tears, with spiritual gladness and heavenly joy. May my mind perceive the sweetness of your most blessed presence, and the watch of your holy angels around me. Mindful of your venerable Passion, I approach your altar, though a sinner, to offer you the sacrifice which you instituted and commanded to be offered in remembrance of you for our salvation.

“I ask your mercy, that the fullness of your divinity may descend upon this bread and chalice. May there also descend, Lord, that invisible and incomprehensible majesty of your Holy Spirit [Col. 1057B] which once descended upon the sacrifices of the Fathers; may it make our offerings your body and blood, and teach me, an unworthy priest, to handle so great a mystery with purity of heart and body, with a fountain of tears, with reverence and trembling, so that you may gently and graciously receive the sacrifice from my hands for the salvation of all, both living and dead.

“I beseech you, Lord, through this very most holy and life-giving mystery of your body and blood, by which we are daily fed and given drink, washed and sanctified in your Church, and made partakers of one supreme divinity: grant me your holy virtues, so that, filled with a good conscience, I may approach your altar, and these heavenly sacraments may become [Col. 1057C] salvation and life to me.

“For you said with your holy and blessed mouth: ‘The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world. Whoever eats me shall live because of me; he also remains in me, and I in him. I am the living bread which came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever’ (John 6:51–52).

“Most sweet bread, heal the palate of my heart, that I may perceive the sweetness of your love; heal it from every infirmity, that I may perceive no sweetness except you. Most white bread, containing every delight and every taste of sweetness, who always refresh us and are never exhausted in yourself: may my heart eat you, and may the inward parts of my soul be filled with the sweetness of your flavor. The angel eats you with a full mouth; may the pilgrim human being eat [Col. 1057D] you according to his measure, lest he fail on the way; may he be refreshed by such provision for the journey.

“Holy bread, living bread, beautiful bread, pure bread, who came down from heaven and give life to the world: come into my heart and cleanse me from every defilement of flesh and spirit. Enter into my soul and sanctify me, heal me inwardly and outwardly. Be the protection and continual salvation of my body and soul. Drive away the enemies lying in wait for me; let them withdraw far from the presence of my repentance, so that, guarded within and without by you, I may arrive by the straight path at your kingdom. There we shall see you not through mysteries, as is done at this time, but face to face, when you have delivered the kingdom to God and the Father, and God shall be all in all. Then you will satisfy me with yourself in wondrous sweetness, [Col. 1058A] so that I shall neither hunger nor thirst for ever. Amen.”

When this prayer of the great Ambrose has been carefully considered, it becomes plain how you, God, have prepared a table before me against those who trouble me: namely, against the three bands of Chaldeans—that is, of the fierce—already mentioned above. For when one prays and hopes, with so great a man, that through the power of so great a mystery the heart of one sacrificing or communicating may be freed from unclean and wicked, empty and harmful thoughts, and from the spirit of pride, vainglory, envy, and other evil spirits, one band of Chaldeans fiercely opposing us—namely, the demons—is driven away by mystical power.

Likewise, when he prays that those who persecute us may be confounded [Col. 1058B] and those who hasten to destroy us may perish, the other band is driven away: namely, malicious people, whom we desire to be confounded unto repentance and to perish in such a way that they cease to be evil, and that sinners may fail from the earth, and the wicked likewise, so that they are no longer wicked.

Finally, against those who trouble us in the third band—the fleshly stirrings that fight against the spirit—your table, O God, is prepared as a most powerful shield. In preparing it, the minister or guest at this table prays thus: “King of virgins, God who loves chastity and integrity, by the heavenly dew of your blessing extinguish in my body every tinder of burning lust, so that the constancy of all chastity may remain in me. Mortify in [Col. 1058C] my members the impulses of the flesh and every lustful stirring; grant me true and perpetual chastity.”

In the encounter with the first band, where prayer is made against the most harsh spirit of pride, the foundation of humility is laid. Like the root of all virtues, it is first planted in the heart when, through the mystical power of the sacrifice, the spirit of pride is put to flight far away, together with six other evil spirits that flee with it, or even with seven other still more wicked spirits, of all of whom it is the leader, advancing with the raised banner of arrogance.

Then, in the encounter with the second band, prayer is rightly offered for the penitential confusion of malicious people, and a wholesome destruction is desired for them. Unless they lose their soul [Col. 1058D] in this age, they will not find it in eternal life. What is thereby accomplished except that, upon the foundation of humility, there rises a temple of perfect love, worthy of Solomon, the peaceful king, “who makes both one” (Eph. 2:14), after the wall of enmities has been destroyed? Outside this temple every sacrifice is void; every prayer not made in this temple is void. For, as the Apostle testifies: “Though I should deliver my body so that I burn,” becoming wholly a burnt offering—than which there is no greater sacrifice—“but have not love, I am nothing; it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

Therefore, most fittingly, just as King Solomon placed the table of the Presence in the temple, so you, God, have prepared a table before me in the edifice of holy love. It is called holy [Col. 1059A] and is outside the veil by which the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies are divided, because however great charity may be in the present Church, which is called holy, it is less than that charity whose inextinguishable fire is within the veil—that is, beyond heaven, in the kingdom of heaven, within the Holy of Holies. There, among the diverse orders of angels, there is no envy over unequal brightness, because unity of love reigns in all.

Of this charity there is some small “fire in Zion,” but “its furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31:9), because charity begins here but will be perfected in the life to come. Here, as though outside the veil, that holy fire is nourished upon the consecrated altar, according to the precept of the Law: “This fire shall be perpetual before the Lord; the priest shall nourish it by placing wood upon it every morning, day by day” (Lev. 12:6). For in the present life, lest the fire of charity fail, it needs much nourishment from good examples and encouragement from exhortations. To supply these sufficiently belongs to the priest’s care; he eats the loaves of the Presence placed upon the table which you, God, have prepared before me against those who trouble me.

But in the kingdom of heaven the blaze of charity will so reign that it will need no nourishment of teaching there, where “no one shall teach his neighbor,” nor shall one say to his brother, “Know the Lord”; for all shall be taught by God, and all shall know the Lord from the greatest to the least (Jer. 31:34).

But in order that I may arrive at that perfection, [Col. 1059C] I see—and in seeing rejoice—that a table has been prepared before me within the temple of charity, whose walls are extended even to love for those who trouble me. Yet, lest the tares of fleshly love be sown among spiritual love, as happened to Solomon, whose heart in old age “was corrupted by women” (3 Kings 11:4), to whom he bowed his knees, the third band requires most vigilant watches and continual prayers, able to fly to heaven with the wings or feathers of fasting and almsgiving. For “this kind” of Chaldean bands “is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. 17:20).

To overcome this band, Saint Ambrose rightly prayed to you as King of virgins and lover of chastity; and every saint will still pray to you [Col. 1059D] at the fitting time, especially before the table which you have prepared before the faithful: that all lustful and unlawful stirrings may be mortified in the bodies of those who partake of your table, and above all of those who minister at it; and that their chastity may be perfect and complete, adorned before you by humility and love. For by these three virtues—humility, love, and chastity—we are to be reconciled to the supreme Trinity: to the most high Father through humility, to the Son through love, and to the Holy Spirit through the mortification in our members of fleshly pleasures. For our members cannot be a temple of the Holy Spirit unless every carnal shamefulness has been renounced.

Therefore you, Jesus Christ, the unique example of humility, love, and [Col. 1060A] chastity, when you prepared a table against those who trouble me, said among other things: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). Therefore, mindful of your Passion, resurrection, and ascension, we approach this table so that through these three we may receive the three virtues: humility, love, and chastity.

For since in your Passion you humbled yourself, becoming “obedient” to the Father “unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8), we rightly trust that through the mystery and remembrance of your Passion the power of true humility will be given to us. And because, when you appeared to the disciples on the day of resurrection, you poured into them, following the Passion of humility, the gift of your love by breathing upon them and saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 20:22–23), we rightly commemorate your resurrection together with your Passion among the sacred mysteries, so that we may join love to humility.

On the day of your resurrection, you, great priest, took care to nourish the fire of that love by adding kindling wood, when, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, you interpreted to your disciples the Scriptures concerning yourself (Luke 24). Certainly, as you spoke in this way and piled much wood into the disciples’ hearts, an abundant fire of love was made in them, so that they said to one another: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (ibid., 32).

Thus, as the commemoration [Col. 1060C] of your Passion leads to humility, so the remembrance of your resurrection forms us in love: namely, so that upon the foundation of humility, by which we are reconciled to the most high Father, “who dwells in the heights” (Ps. 112:5), “looks upon lowly things, and knows lofty things from afar” (Ps. 137:7), there may rise an edifice or temple of love, for covenant with and glory to you, peaceful King, great Solomon. You have become for us the builder of peace and the cornerstone in whom every structure, being built together, grows into a holy temple.

But lest the joints of this building be dissolved by the flooding stream of fleshly love and unclean lust, chastity of mind and body is added as the strongest bond and support of this house. The memorial mystery [Col. 1060D] of your ascension gives this chastity to your faithful, causing them to relish the things above, where you sit at God’s right hand, and to seek the things above, not those upon the earth (Col. 3:2). Therefore, having tasted the delight of heavenly pleasure, they willingly mortify their members which are upon the earth: fornication, lust, evil desire, and greed—lest they lose the purity of chastity once received.

The most holy communion of the Eucharist bestows all this upon us, if we keep the memory of the Lord’s Passion, resurrection, and ascension with a mind devoutly exulting in God and rejoicing through the oil of gladness. Therefore, to the gifts mentioned above, O Lord, who rule me so that I lack nothing, you add for me the oil of gladness, by which I may rejoice in you. For:

[Col. 1061A] “You have made my head rich with oil.” This is for me the eighth grace, abundantly poured out on the eighth day of the Lord’s resurrection. For after the rod of the Passion, when the table of the living bread—baked by the two woods of the cross, which the holy Church gathers with the widow of Zarephath—had been prepared, you, God the Father, through the glory of the resurrection made my head rich: that is, Christ himself, who is my head, the head of the Church.

For then the humanity assumed in Christ, glorified and made bright, which in the Passion had been sorrowful unto death, was so drenched with the oil of gladness that no sorrow can ever again befall it. Indeed, “as ointment upon the head, which runs down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron” (Ps. 132:2), so joy descends from the human being glorified into God upon the apostles, joined to that head in the likeness of a beard. For “the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord” (John 20:20), and no one took their joy from them. From them the same oil of gladness descended even to the hem of the garment, even to the Church’s most remote members; among them I, David, glory in singing and giving thanks to you, God the Father, because you have made my head rich with oil—that is, my mind, or the human being assumed by your Word, who is my head—driving away that dryness or barrenness of which Isaiah the prophet speaks: “He grew up like a shrub before him, and like a root from thirsty ground. He has no form or beauty” (Isa. 53:2).

Thus the man conceived of a virgin and born from virginal earth, produced as from dry ground, displayed in his Passion a humble and servile appearance, having neither form nor beauty. For this reason he was cut down by the judgment of unjust rulers like dry wood, though he himself was green wood. Hence it is also said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me; rather, weep over yourselves. For if they do these things to the green wood, what will be done to the dry?” (Luke 23:28–31).

Therefore in reality he was always the “green tree planted beside streams of water,” of whom it is clearly written at the beginning of this book in the first psalm (Ps. 1:3) that “his leaf shall not fall.” But he emptied himself so that in his death he might appear like dry wood. In the resurrection, however, he flowered again from the most rich root of his divinity, [Col. 1061D] so that, like a fruitful olive tree, he sufficiently supplies material for light and ointments. In the ascension, too, pouring out the Holy Spirit and bearing fruit like a vine, he abundantly brought forth the sweetness of fragrance: “wine that gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. 103:15).

And this is the ninth grace, of which I say in thanksgiving:

“And my cup”—that is, your Spirit poured out in me—[Col. 1062A] “which intoxicates me, how excellent it is!” For it is your cup because you give it, and mine because you give it to me: how excellent it is! It does not intoxicate so as to take away sobriety, but rather increases it, illuminating the senses now of the inward person and afterward also of the outward person, when “the body of our lowliness shall be refashioned in conformity with the body of” your “glory” (Phil. 3:21).

For now, whether it be called your cup or, as another translation has it, “your intoxicating draught,” it intoxicates in such a way as to give its drinkers forgetfulness of earthly vanities. For just as your body, O Christ, incorporates into you those who worthily eat it, so your blood and your good Spirit incorporate into your very inward parts and make alive with you those who worthily drink them, so that each may say: “I now live, yet not I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

**VERSE 6.**—“And your mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.” This is the last and tenth grace, preparing and preserving the preceding graces. For your mercy, O God, which anticipates the bestowal of “every good gift and every perfect gift” (Jas. 1:17) by conferring them, shall follow me in order to preserve what it has bestowed. Your mercy, I say—that is, your Spirit given to me as a pledge—shall follow me, not for an hour but throughout all the days of my mortal life, dwelling within me, but also at times visiting me more particularly and, by its bestowal, awakening me to your work whether I am awake or asleep.

For while I live in mortal flesh, I need most diligent and persevering protection, lest I fail [Col. 1062C] on the way. Rather, may I run well here and, thus finishing the course and keeping the faith, come to the prize: to dwell hereafter without end in the house of the Lord, a house not made by hands but eternal in the heavens—not for an hour, but eternally, for length of days. This final end depends upon all that has gone before. For the gifts mentioned above were granted so that I might dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days, adopted from a servant into a son. For the servant does not remain in the house forever, but the son remains forever.

Glory to the Father, who anointed and made rich with the oil of gladness my head, Christ his Son. Glory to the Son, who is God’s mountain, a rich mountain, made fat [Col. 1062D] like the fattened calf which the loving Father killed for his prodigal son when he returned. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is this richness or oil, by which, as the Father anointed him, the man Christ Jesus was made rich; this Spirit is also my intoxicating cup—how excellent it is! Glory to the one eternity of these three, which is that length of days with which the prophetic spirit concludes this psalm.

## PSALM 23

[Col. 1061]

[Col. 1061D] **VERSE 1.** “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.” The heading is:

[Col. 1062D] **(VERSE 1.) A PSALM OF DAVID, ON THE FIRST DAY OF THE SABBATH.**

The Gentiles named the days after the names of the seven planets, [Col. 1063A] calling the first day of the week the day of the Sun; the second, the day of the Moon; the third, the day of Mars; the fourth, the day of Mercury; the fifth, the day of Jupiter; the sixth, the day of Venus; and the seventh, the day of Saturn. By such names they honored the seven planets—or rather, certain men whom they deemed great, transferring their names to the planets in the false belief that they were thereby conferring divine honor upon those men. They thought that the fates of human life depended on the planets’ courses, risings, and settings. Thus, for example, one born when Mars rose would be warlike, and one born when Venus rose would be lustful; and so, too, whoever began any undertaking while the other planets rose or set was believed to draw some corresponding quality into himself.

But Christian religion wholly abhorred the pagan superstition of this error, and gave the days of the week such names that the first day is called the Lord’s Day, or the first feria; then, in order, the second feria—that is, the second day from the feria—the third feria, fourth feria, fifth feria, sixth feria, and seventh feria, or Sabbath. Or the days are called *feriae* among us for this reason also: Christians ought always to keep festival and to be free from servile work, which is sin.

The Hebrews, however, because of the dignity of the Sabbath, called all the other days by the name of the Sabbath. The first after the Sabbath was called the first of the Sabbath—that is, the first day after the Sabbath; the next, the second [Col. 1063C] of the Sabbath; and thereafter in order, the third of the Sabbath, fourth of the Sabbath, fifth of the Sabbath, sixth of the Sabbath. Sabbath. On the first of the Sabbath the world was made, and light was made and divided from darkness, so that things formerly confused might become clear through light by the distinction of their forms. Thus, in the resurrection Christ, having put away the darkness of mortality, was glorified; humanity, with the gloom of sins removed, was re-formed; and so a new world was founded.

This psalm treats, in a fitting order, of this glorification of the Redeemer, the restoration of redeemed humanity, and the foundation of the whole Church. For after Christ’s Passion had been accomplished and the water of resurrection had flowed from his side, as was treated in the two preceding psalms, it follows that we should discuss [Col. 1063D] how the Church was founded throughout the world by the triumph of the Lord’s resurrection.

It speaks in the manner of a herald who, after the triumph, proclaims the land to belong to the victor, saying: “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.” In the final verses its purpose is clear, where it urges that the victor be received in triumph.

This psalm is divided into three parts. First, it says that the whole world belongs to the Lord, so that, just as no one is excepted from his rule, no one may be alien to faith or faithfulness. Second, it determines with what virtues those who wish to be enrolled in his court and serve in his army must be endowed. The discipline of this court or army is considered where it says: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” Third, it rebukes the adversaries and, like a herald, prepares the way for the Lord, commanding that the gates, formerly closed against the victor and his followers, be removed from the midst.

Therefore, whether Prophet or devout Psalmist, rejoicing in the triumph of the resurrection, addresses the human race, burdened with diverse superstition, and says:

“The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.” By human law, every possessor of fields, vineyards, or houses says, “This field is mine; this vineyard, or this house, is mine.” And wars, lawsuits, and disputes occur because each person desires to enlarge his own possession. Likewise, by legal right, everyone calls his own what he paid a price for in court. But by divine right the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness—not merely in part, but in its entirety—because the world is his, and all who dwell in it.

Truly the world is his, not given to him by another but created by himself. Yet the devil, an unjust usurper of that same world, led this very Lord of the world up a high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms, saying: “All these have been delivered to me, and I give them to whom I will” (Luke 4:6). Truly, when that father of lies said these things, he spoke from what was his own, “because he is a liar and its father” (John 8:44): father of the lie which he himself invented.

But our Lord Jesus Christ, “being in the form of God,” could by the right of his divine majesty have claimed all things as subject to his dominion even before the obedience of death. For he “did not deem equality with God a robbery” even before the triumph of death. Yet he “emptied himself,” displaying in himself “the form of a servant,” being “found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:6–7). In that appearance, after obedience had finally been completed, he was worthy, as a human being, to receive as the reward of obedience the world, to be crowned with glory and honor—especially since, in possessing such honor, he acknowledged it not as belonging by nature to his own humanity but as grace.

Therefore he did not wish, either by himself or through his disciples, to have it publicly proclaimed before the obedience of death that the earth and its fullness were his. Yet he could justly have said this because he, wholly God, was naturally born God and existed even in human nature; on account of this fatherhood he truly said: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matt. 11:27).
