That is: he gave me all things by giving me this, that he himself is my Father—not adoptively but naturally—because he begot me as his own Son and did not adopt me as a stranger.

Nevertheless, the Lord of heaven “humbled himself” upon earth “unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2:8–9). Thus exalted, although he truly could have said it, he neither did say nor wished to say: “The earth is mine, and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it.” Instead, he declared the dominion of his power in a manner that simultaneously made truth manifest, preserved humility, and taught humility.

[Col. 1065A] “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me,” he says (Matt. 28:18). These words contain not a false and boastful vaunting of power, but true and humble thanksgiving. Thus you also, any mere human being who has nothing that you have not received, should not boast either of things not received as though you had received them, or of things received as though you had not received them. Otherwise, exiled into the region of unlikeness from Christ, you may be conformed to him who said in the prophet: “The river is mine; I made myself” (Ezek. 29:3).

Likewise, in the Gospel according to Luke, showing the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, he says: “These have been delivered to me, and I give them to whom I will” (Luke 4:6). He who said this boasted of things not received as though he had received them—or rather, what is worse, of things seized as though he had not seized them. Pilate was his servant, who said: “Do you not know that I have power to release you and power to crucify you?” (John 19:10). For he boasted of things received as though they had not been received. But the teacher of humility recalled him from this pattern of boasting by saying: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (ibid., 11).

He could also have rebuked the devil by saying: “The kingdoms of the world have not been delivered to you, nor can you give them to whomever you wish. Rather, as is written in Daniel, ‘The Most High rules over the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he wills’” (Dan. 4:14). Thus that liar could have been rebuked for his lie. But he who came to teach human beings and condemn demons restrained Pilate’s empty boasting by sound teaching, while in the devil he condemned falsehood, saying: “Begone, Satan” (Matt. 4:10).

This sort of boasting must therefore be avoided, lest anyone boast with the devil of some good that is not his as though it were his own, or of something received as though he had not received it—as Pilate did. For not even the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom all things were subject by the nature of his divinity, wished, before the merit of obedience had been completed, to attribute all power to himself; nor, even after all power over all things had been given to him as the reward of obedience, did he wish to speak of himself as though he possessed it through himself.

And indeed, from the day of his conception, the man, the Virgin’s Son, who is likewise the Son of God, possessed all things through himself, yet not from himself—just as he does not exist from himself, but from the Father who begets him and, through that very begetting, gives him all things. Therefore, whenever he speaks of himself or of his power, he refers all that he has and all that he can do to the glory and thanksgiving of the Father who gives all things.

But his disciples, honouring the Son as he himself honoured the Father, confidently proclaim him Lord of the whole world, whom they had heard saying: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18). Therefore, the apostles, sent throughout all lands, powerfully cast out from the temples of idols and from the hidden places of unbelieving hearts that usurper who had falsely said in the Gospel that all things had been handed over to him, and in Ezekiel, “The river is mine.” [Col. 1066A] They drive him from the world into hell, saying: “Depart, Satan; or flee, unclean spirit, from the whole Church spread throughout the whole world. Flee from the possession you have usurped. Flee, great dragon, from the river of humankind, which you falsely boast to be yours. Flee from the sweet waters, for the fountains of waters have been sanctified when Christ appeared in glory. And, just as in the Gospel you were permitted to enter the swine—that is, unclean people—with whom you are to be hurled into the sea, so flee, banished from the world into the abyss with all your legion, so that, when you and yours have been plunged into the depths, he alone may rule and reign on earth as in heaven, whose lawful possession, acquired by the triumph of his Passion, is all the earth and its fullness.”

For even before he suffered, the earth and its fullness were his, since it was created by him and through him: “all things were made through him,” and when he came into the world, “he came unto his own.” But after the standards of the King went forth, with the mystery of the Cross shining everywhere and its four arms stretched towards the four regions of the world, by a double right the earth and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it, belong to the triumphant Lord himself.

The literal expulsion of the usurper from the earth, where something like divine worship was offered to him through many idols, is evident from the fact that, as the Christian religion increased in the world, pagan shrines were destroyed while churches were built [Col. 1066C] and multiplied. Nor is the devil now permitted to rule anywhere, except insofar as he is allowed to rage among the swine given to him, in order that he may be hurled together with them into the abyss.

But that ancient serpent was cast out from the earth still more decisively in this: “Lord, you have blessed your land” (Ps. 84:2), the virginal land, the fruitful land, to which the angel said: “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:28). Truly this blessed land and its fullness belong to the Lord—the fullness of which she is told: “Hail, Mary, full of grace” (ibid.). By a singular privilege of blessing, this land and its fullness are the Lord’s beloved possession; but, claiming by a certain universal right, she received from God the Father “the nations for her inheritance, and the ends of the earth for her possession” (Ps. 2:8).

Thus we rightly say: “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness”; for the holy Church is no longer an empty and void land lying hidden beneath the waters of paganism. The Lord, its possessor, raised it from the deep and established it above the rivers, when the waters under heaven were gathered into one place, so that dry land might appear and become fruitful earth. For just as, literally, the waters which at the beginning covered the whole earth were driven down into the subterranean recesses of the earth, so that the world might appear, founded and raised above the seas, and yield its fruit: so, after the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead, when the Holy Spirit was poured forth from above—the Spirit who at the beginning also moved over the waters—the Church was raised up, and she is rightly called the *orbis terrarum*, the world of lands: “world” because of her perfection, “lands” because of the abundance of diverse fruits. [Col. 1067A]

For just as wealth abounds in the world because one land is fertile in grain, another in wine, another in oil, another in gems, another in precious metal or rare cloth, and the lands share with one another, so that all possess in common the produce which each has: so in spiritual things the virtues of individual persons become the common fruit of all, when “each, as he has received a gift, strives to administer it to one another as good stewards of the manifold grace of God”; for example, “if anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God; if anyone ministers, let him do so from the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be honoured,” whose “is the earth and its fullness,” whose are “the world and all who dwell in it” (1 Pet. 4:10–11).

The divine evangelist Luke, noting this very point—that the earth and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it belong to the Lord—rightly records at his Nativity that “a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled. This first enrolment was made” at the birth of the Lord, whose are “the earth and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it.” This enrolment, I say, “was first made when Quirinius was governor of Syria” (Luke 2:1–2), because never before had there been such peace that the whole world could have been enrolled in an enrolment under which all went to make declaration. For before Christ’s coming, kings or tyrants scarcely ruled even parts of the world. But when he came into the world, all were enrolled and made declaration under the authority of one king, because Christ is the one emperor and king of all ages. The enrolment and declaration of all are rightly assigned to him, since the pen of the swiftly writing scribe records in his book unto life those chosen from every nation who now confess him unto death.

Therefore let the apostles speak; let all the elect speak and confess that the earth and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it, belong to the Lord. The fruitful earth belongs to the Lord, whose fruit is in virtues; and its fullness belongs to him, because it is not an empty and void land, but, as the Lord cultivates it, is full of crops. [Col. 1067D]

Many enter this land but do not remain in it, because they believe for a time and in time of temptation fall away. But the Lord knows those who are his: namely, those who dwell in that land which is not empty and void, understood as the holy Church spread throughout the world. Only those dwell in her who prove their faith by deeds. For those whose works contradict the faith which they profess are like exiles within her. Rightly, therefore, this land is the Lord’s, and the world of this land with its inhabitants is the Lord’s.

## VERSE 2. For he founded it upon the seas, gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin (Ps. 32:7).

For the sea is, as it were, confined in a wineskin when, bounded by its shores, barred by bolts, and shut by a gate, it does not cover the land founded above the sea and established above the rivers. For while rivers flow down into the sea, the world stands fixed and immovably founded. Much more, then, is the Church founded above the seas of worldly desires and established above the rivers of temptations: by overcoming desires and temptations, she presses on towards eternity, for which the Lord prepared her. For the Lord is the preparer of the kingdom of heaven and of those who are to enter it. Therefore, at the end, when all things are prepared, he will say: “Come to the wedding feast, for behold, all things are now ready” (Matt. 22:4). Likewise: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you” (Matt. 25:34). [Col. 1068B]

## VERSE 3. Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?

O apostles, who proclaim and show the world founded above the seas and established above the rivers; who, speaking thus to us wretches still being shipwrecked upon the sea, show us the world possessing a lofty shore, the shore of eternal stability and firmness: tell us, who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? Who shall ascend from the height of the sea to the height of this lofty shore, this shore which is the mountain of the Lord?

And the prophet Isaiah, speaking of this mountain, says: “In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be prepared upon the summit of the mountains; it shall be exalted above the hills, and all nations shall flow to it. Many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us ascend the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob” (Isa. 2:2–3). Many, therefore, will say, “Let us ascend”; but who among them all ascends the mountain of the Lord? Many will say, “Lord, Lord” (Matt. 7:21); but who will enter the kingdom of heaven? “Many are called” (ibid. 20:16); but who are the chosen? Many strive, as though with great exertion, to ascend; but who will persevere in ascending to the end? Or who will stand in his holy place, so as not to turn back?

## VERSE 4. He who is innocent in hands and pure in heart.

Do you wish to know who ascends? He who is innocent in hands and pure in heart: that is, one who harms no one by deeds and guards against sin even in thought, unwilling to injure anyone. Yet it does not suffice that such a person, innocent in hands and pure in heart, neither harms another by deed nor intends to harm him in heart. Recognising that true innocence harms neither oneself nor another, he also lives usefully for himself.

### Who has not received his soul in vain.

A person who has eyes but does not use them for seeing possesses them in vain. Likewise, a person who has a rational soul but does not use reason, living irrationally, has received his soul in vain. Such a person will not ascend the mountain of the Lord. Rather, it is the one who has not received his soul in vain, whose obedience is rational just as his mind is rational: because he uses reason well and never abuses it; or, if he has abused it, he makes satisfaction by rational amendment.

[Col. 1069A] Otherwise: Ecclesiastes said, “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Ecclus. 1:2). Having carefully enumerated all desirable things under heaven—such as the riches and pleasures of this world and the honours of temporal glory—he came to this conclusion: after all these things have been passed over and despised as vanities, because they have no true, solid, or lasting being, he judges that there is no other true being for a human person than to fear God and keep his commandments. “Fear God,” he says, “and keep his commandments: this is the whole human being” (Ecclus. 12:13).

Therefore, if a person is wholly human in and through fearing God and keeping his commandments, one who does not fear God and neglects his commandments is not human—indeed, ought not even to be said to exist, because he lacks true being. Such a person, vanishing away with the transitory vanity of this world, is far removed from the blessed solidity of eternity. For vain and solid, vanity and truth, instability and stability, are opposites; and each person becomes like that which he chiefly seeks and loves. Whoever chiefly loves these vain and transitory things vanishes with those vanities. But whoever through fear, love, and observance of the law cleaves to the Lord is one spirit with him; and the more he cleaves to the truth which is God, by obeying his commandments and believing his promises, the farther he becomes from deceitful vanity. He becomes unlike the one to whom vanity is reproached in these words: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but trusted in the multitude of his riches and prevailed in his vanity” (Ps. 51:9). [Col. 1069C]

Riches are rightly joined with vanity, because their existence is altogether unstable and vain. Yet there is a person who receives his soul in this vanity, and there is a person who has not received his soul in this vanity. That “rich man who feasted splendidly every day” (Luke 16:19) received and found acceptable his soul—that is, his life—in the vanity of riches and pleasures. But he did not understand that this vanity was vain until he was buried in hell, carrying with him from his riches nothing but a vain memory of past pleasures. He was tormented because what he had loved as lasting was wholly past. Then “affliction alone gave understanding to his hearing” (Isa. 28:19): he understood how vain was that in which he had received his soul, in which it had been pleasing to him to delight his soul or expend his soul—that is, his life.

“Whoever finds his soul” in this vanity “shall lose it; and whoever loses his soul” (Matt. 10:31) in this vanity “keeps it unto eternal life” (John 12:25). Who finds his soul in this world full of vanities except one who does his own will in it? And again, who loses his soul in this utterly vain world except one who mortifies his own will, by not receiving it in vanity?

We must carefully note the words: “Who has not received his soul in vain.” The human soul, a rational soul, was created so as to put on divine eternity. But after Adam, stripped naked of the glory of immortality, put on a garment of skins—a garment surely vain, because liable to decay and instability—many of his descendants receive their soul in this vain clothing. They do not hate “the garment stained by the flesh” (Jude 8, 9), as the apostle Jude teaches, because it is delightful and exceedingly pleasing to them to rest in this garment and to delight there their soul, that is, their animal and carnal will. [Col. 1070A]

By contrast, as the apostle Jude teaches, certain people hate “the garment stained by the flesh” (ibid. 23). Like Abraham, rejoicing to see Christ’s day, they put on Christ and put it off; for the robe of truth and immortality can by no means be put on over one unless the garment of vanity and mortality has first been taken off. Or they are like Lazarus: burdened in that same garment by pains, sores, and poverty, they may, under pressure of necessity, desire to be fed with crumbs—that is, with the rich man’s table-scraps—but they do not wish to live luxuriously with any rich man.

In the wealthy Abraham is commended the desire for eternal light combined with long patience. Therefore he was the more worthy of praise because, though riches flowed to him, he would not set his heart upon them; he would not receive his soul in the vanity of riches. He overcame the vain desire of vanities through the stronger desire by which he burned for Christ’s day, in which he wished his soul to be found, having denied itself. [Col. 1070C]

But in poor Lazarus is commended weariness of this present life joined with good patience. He maintained this patience in his poverty so that he desired only the bare necessities that give relief to wretched life, regarding others’ excess as his own necessity. Nor did he sin in desiring these things, since he did not desire another’s possessions; for the superfluities of the rich are the necessities of the poor.

Thus precious in the Lord’s sight was the death of wealthy Abraham, who was able amid riches to mortify his soul, not granting it the vain pleasures of wealth, because he did not receive his soul in vanity. And if at any time his soul—that is, animal and sensual desire—played upon him, he did not accept it. Rejecting it as a harlot, as the wretched daughter of Babylon, he did not hold it acceptable or dear. Therefore he dashed her and her little ones against the rock, for whose day he rejoiced in longing. In that desire he received his soul: namely, he willingly granted it everything that could avail to awaken or enlarge so holy a desire.

If, therefore, we are children of Abraham, let us do the works of Abraham. Let us not receive our soul in vanity. Let us withdraw from it the pleasures of vanity and offer it the encouragements of truth. And if something vain occurs—if the delight of vanity overcomes the delight of truth in our soul, as often happens even to the elect, whether they commit unlawful acts or, in lawful things, exceed by some excess the bounds of truth and justice—at least after the act it must not be pleasing to us. Let us not so receive our soul in vanity that, by persisting in vanity, we fail to come to the light of truth. In that light vain works must be exposed, and the soul which has embraced vanity must be disciplined, as one polluted by adulterous love. [Col. 1071A]

But the soul that is subjected to vanity unwillingly, using these vain temporal things under the compulsion of necessity, “because of him who subjected it in hope, shall one day be freed from the bondage” of vanity and corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Rom. 12:21). Why? Because it is subjected unwillingly, and for the sake of him who subjected it bears the vanities it does not wish, in order that it may attain the true goods it does wish. Such a soul does not find itself acceptable in the vanity to which it is unwillingly subject, but in the truth of the promiser who truthfully promises true goods.

Before the light of those goods, it is vain for us to rise, since we are still commanded to sit—that is, to humble ourselves—under the yoke of obedience for the sake of him who subjected us. Thus the Lord appeared to Abraham as he sat, because he looked upon his humbled heart amid riches. He appeared to him sitting “at the door of the tent,” which is the lodging of an exile, and sitting “in the valley of Mamre” (Gen. 18:1), that is, in great and manifest humility. For *Mamre* means “manifest”; because it is delightful for Abraham’s children to sit in the humility of manifest truth, as in the valley of Mamre, lest they rise up and be exalted by the smile of this vain worldly prosperity. This prosperity is especially to be despised at the very height of its day by those who, with Abraham, rejoice to see Christ’s day—a day which appeared to Abraham as he sat in the very heat of the day, and showed him beforehand his own day. [Col. 1071C]

For this kind of sitting in perfect humility, it is sometimes very beneficial to suffer in this world, like Lazarus, through poverty or bodily sickness. Though holy Job proved praiseworthy in using riches well, and was praised by the Lord, he advanced to greater humility through the loss of riches and bodily sickness. He, who is not previously said to have sat upon the ground, then sat upon a dung-heap. Therefore his consolation was rightly doubled after he had been so deeply humbled. There is no doubt that riches themselves had been a consolation in this life to the man who was simple, upright, and feared God, rather than a source of corruption. But this consolation would not have been doubled unless, humble and patient, he had sat upon the dung-heap after the loss of his riches and the infliction of a most grievous wound.

Likewise Lazarus was doubly comforted. It would indeed have been great consolation for him there to rest where Abraham rested. Yet his consolation was greater, as it were twofold, because wealthy Abraham cherished poor Lazarus in his bosom as a pious father cherishes a dear little son. Therefore the promise is not unfittingly applied to saints rich in possessions and poor in spirit, such as Abraham, who, though rich and speaking with the Lord, nevertheless considered himself dust: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). [Col. 1072A]

But to those like Lazarus, who was sick and a beggar until death, applies the promise of consolation which the Holy Spirit proclaimed in Isaiah to such poor persons, having no consolation in this world: “You shall be carried at the breasts, and they shall caress you upon the knees” (Isa. 66:12). Who will caress, and whom will they caress? Surely holy rich persons will caress holy poor persons like Lazarus. Indeed, God himself will caress such persons, for he says: “As a mother comforts her children, so will I comfort you” (ibid. 13). Will this not be great and endless consolation: that, like a mother caressing her dear little child after maternal nursing, God himself with his own hand “will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away” (Apoc. 11:4)?

Although the patriarch Abraham was great, one who did not receive his soul in vanity, wealthy and dying without persecutions, afflicted David—tested through many tribulations—was greater than he. Therefore the blessed evangelist Matthew placed David before Abraham in the genealogy of Jesus Christ, “son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1:1). The order is reversed, but necessarily so: the greatly afflicted saint is preferred to the one not afflicted. David also received the promise, as it were, of a double consolation, since the Lord not only promised him but swore that a son would be born from him and would reign. To Abraham a man was promised who would be born, but he was not said to be a future king. [Col. 1072C]

Poor and afflicted David earned the consolation of this great promise because he did not receive his soul in vanity. He neither intended, upon deliberation, to do anything vain, nor approved what was done without deliberation. Contrary to his resolution and purpose, however, he was forestalled by the tempter and became vain when he sinned against Uriah the Hittite. Yet he did not receive his soul in vanity. On account of this very sin he deeply humbled and thoroughly afflicted his soul, even to contrition of heart, because it had for a time become vain by delighting in the unlawful pleasure of lust, until Nathan the prophet came to him and announced the truth against the vanity perpetrated in sin.

Having heard the truth, David did not at all find himself pleasing in his vanity. Rather, hating the seductive vanity of sin, he accepted and held dear the truth and severity of the reproving prophet. Therefore, repenting of his vanity, he rejoices in God’s truth, saying to him: “For behold, you have loved truth” (Ps. 50:8). Thus freed from vanity’s snare and united with truth by concord, he ascended the mountain of the Lord as one wholly innocent in hands and pure in heart. For after repentance there was not imputed to him what he had formerly been: guilty in hands through murder and unclean in heart through adultery. [Col. 1073A]

So greatly did it avail for his salvation that he did not receive his soul in vanity, that he loved the truth of rebuke and reproof more than the vanity of flattery, had anyone offered it to him. Finally, elsewhere he prays for the truth of correction and detests the vanity of flattery, saying: “Let the righteous man correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner make fat my head” (Ps. 140:5). Therefore let David confidently declare what he had experienced in himself: that even after sins have been committed, the person who does not receive his soul in vanity will ascend the mountain of the Lord—the one who loves truth more than vanity and, founded in that truth, strives to be just not only in conduct but also in speech.

### And has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbour.

Even if at times he swore under the compulsion of necessity, he did not swear deceitfully. For although it is praiseworthy not to swear at all, tolerable to swear truthfully, and damnable to swear falsely: just as we are never permitted to swear falsely, so we are sometimes permitted to swear truthfully when grave necessity compels it—not in order to lead someone into error, but to remove a harmful error by a true oath. Therefore the person who carefully strives to avoid causes and necessities that compel swearing does not offend in speech, nor swear deceitfully to his neighbour. For example, under the law one is compelled to swear, if a deposit is lost, that he has not laid his hand upon his neighbour’s goods. If such a necessity of swearing, or a greater one, arises, he swears without deceit. [Col. 1073B]

But he cannot be compelled to swear falsely in any way, or to swear truthfully in order to deceive and injure someone. Therefore “the man is perfect who does not offend in speech” (Jas. 3:2), and blessing is owed to him. Conversely, a curse is owed to the person who calls “evil good and good evil, bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isa. 5:20), upon whom Scripture invokes woe, which signifies eternal damnation. But the one who does not offend in speech, being free from lying and deceit—

## VERSE 5. He shall receive blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Saviour.

For he shall be among those to whom it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34). If, like Abraham, he received angels—that is, good messengers—into hospitality, he received Christ also in them, whom he honoured in his own. But if, like poor Lazarus, he himself needed lodging or any other comfort, being hungry or thirsty, naked or a stranger, sick or in prison, he will worthily be numbered among those least ones of whom it will be said: “As long as you did it to one of these my least ones, you did it to me” (Matt. 5:40). Thus, whether among the good who are judged or among those who judge, he shall receive blessing from the Lord. [Col. 1073D]

Yet far more will that poor and least person receive blessing from the Lord who, by distributing his own goods to the poor, became poor himself. Hence, as has been said before us: “The presbyter who has either distributed his own possessions to the poor or added them to the resources of the Church, and through love of poverty has placed himself in the number of the poor—even if afterward he receives much from ecclesiastical resources, by which he may serve Christ’s least ones and himself live as least among the least—shall not be defrauded of blessing.” Such a person shall possess double goods in the land of the living: he shall be praised with the good ministers of the least, and crowned among the least themselves.

Therefore, on the feasts of martyrs—who were least ones, and who for the benefit and edification of others not only spent what was theirs but spent themselves beyond measure, being themselves poor and ministers of the poor, sometimes having not even the means to live, nor being permitted to live because of that love than which no one has greater, by which they did not hesitate to lay down their lives for their brethren (John 15:13)—on the feasts, I say, of such least ones of Christ and ministers to Christ’s least ones, we recite the verse of this psalm concerning each one of them: “He shall receive blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Saviour.” Likewise on the feasts of confessors, to whom God granted life for the sake of Christ’s least ones, the Church rightly sings this psalm concerning each one: “He shall receive blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Saviour.” And concerning many she says:

## VERSE 6. This is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob.

But lest you suppose that this blessing proceeds from merits without grace, or from grace without merits, observe that merits are required where it was said: “Innocent in hands and pure in heart; who has not received his soul in vanity, nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbour.” Yet God’s mercy is shown to be the cause both of merits and of rewards when it is said: “He shall receive blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Saviour.” God’s mercy, greater than merits, is placed after great merits, so that however great your merits may be, you may know that you need divine mercy. [Col. 1074C]

Again, lest you suppose that God’s mercy is preceded by human merits, hear what is said: “This is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob.” Therefore, if God “of his own will begot us by the word of truth,” not because we were the beginning, but “that we might be a certain beginning of his creation,” that we might be “the generation of those who seek him” (Jas. 1:18), you should know that it must be ascribed to his mercy and grace that, when some were rejected, he chose others—as he chose Jacob but hated Esau—when they had not yet done anything good or evil, when one was chosen and the other rejected (Rom. 9:13).

Therefore, however great the merits that follow, this generation of those who seek God and seek together to know the face of the God of Jacob ought to seek and acknowledge the prevenience of grace. For just as Jacob was preceded by gratuitous goodness before he had done either good or evil, so this whole generation of those who seek the face of the God of Jacob is preceded by the grace of predestination and election. Good merits do not exist except through grace which precedes and follows: preceding, so that they may be done; following, so that they may not perish.

Although every generation of those who seek God seeks the face of the God of Jacob, those seek and find it more especially and excellently who, like Jacob, dwelt simply with his mother, obtained from his father the blessing through her pious counsel, endured persecution from his brother Esau for its sake and went into exile, gained in exile two wives and flocks of many sheep by patiently rendering service, and at last, a patriarch of patriarchs and a father full of days, was gathered to his fathers. [Col. 1075A]

In the same way, they seek the face of the God of Jacob by following examples of Jacob’s virtues: dwelling simply in the Church, through whose pious favour they are blessed by God the Father. So the apostle Peter, when he was kept in prison and prayer was made by the Church to God for him, “received blessing and mercy from God his Saviour” (Acts 12:5), so that he said: “Now I know truly that God has sent his angel and delivered me from Herod’s hand and from all the expectation of the Jewish people” (ibid. 11).

Thereafter, as the Jewish people—the carnal Esau—persecuted him, Peter was directed, through the urgency of preaching, to save the Gentiles. He acquired, as it were, two wives, because he trained teachers of churches in the eminent virtue of contemplation and action. Through them, he, the shepherd of sheep, feeds many flocks, diligently performing the office laid upon him by the Prince of Shepherds, when for the third time it was said to him: “Peter, do you love me? Feed my lambs,” or, “my sheep” (John 20:15–17). [Col. 1075B]

After the apostle Peter, some in this generation of those who seek the face of the God of Jacob likewise imitate Jacob: feeding sheep and lambs, enduring the persecution of their carnal brother, begetting patriarchs—that is, chosen children—through the Gospel, and at last resting with the fathers in a blessed end. Therefore, at the blessed repose of each such father, the Church fittingly sings: “He shall receive blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Saviour.” And lest the number of such persons be thought small, the statement passes from the singular to the plural: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob.”

The *diapsalma* inserted here quite fittingly separates what has been said from what is to be said, because at this point the persons speaking change and vary. For after Christ’s resurrection has been affirmed and the Christian religion set forth, the gates of death are commanded to be removed—first in the words of the angels who went before God descending into hell. For when Christ, the King of glory, entered to conquer hell, and the angelic choir before his face commanded that the gates of the rulers be lifted up, there were first heard commanding voices saying:

### Verse 7. “Lift up your gates, O princes.”

You were accustomed to secure your gates with certain strong arguments of justice, as though with iron bars, so long as you recited the written bond drawn up against humankind, maintaining most firmly that humanity with all its posterity was rightfully subject to your power and dominion: for, though free, it had voluntarily consented to take on the yoke of sins, by which yoke it was to be dragged into hell. But behold, the iron bars are broken, because your arguments, though strong [Col. 1076A] like iron bars, are destroyed by stronger arguments, when it is most truly said: “As through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of one man many shall be made righteous” (Rom. VI, 19).

And the very human beings who have been set free, who resist your rule, most truly say: “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more therefore, now justified in his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, shall we be saved in his life” (Rom. V, 8–10). You had indeed, you evil princes, as it were bronze gates and iron bars, when sin “reigned from Adam to Moses, [Col. 1076B] even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who was a figure of the one to come” (ibid., XIV). But after he who was to come has come, it is now fitting that “they should give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men, because he shattered the bronze gates and broke the iron bars” (Ps. CVI, 16): for he both destroyed the kingdom of sin and raised up the kingdom of righteousness, just as he had long ago promised, saying: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall raise up for David a righteous Branch; and a king shall reign, and shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and righteousness in the earth” (Jer. XXIII, 5).

Behold, this is judgment: that the prince of this world should be cast out from the temples and hearts upon which he broods. And this is righteousness: that, just as through the sin of one man his descendants came into [Col. 1076C] condemnation, so through the righteousness of one man all who are incorporated into him by faith may be free from condemnation—both those who faithfully awaited his coming, and those who received him present in the flesh. “For as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John I, 12). And to all who will receive him until the end of the age, he will give “power to become children of God,” though previously they were children of the transgressor Adam, through whom, when he sinned, the gates of death were raised, and through whom, when he excused and defended his own sins, those same gates were strengthened as though with iron bars. But because this second Adam neither sinned nor, when falsely accused before Pilate, excused himself, [Col. 1076D] the gates of death fell shattered and the iron bars were crushed.

Therefore, O infernal princes, at whose instigation the innocent one suffered unjustly, you must also lose those whom you seemed to possess, as it were, by right. Lift up, therefore, your gates; lift up those alleged grounds of justice which you seemed to have. Be silent when he comes in whom your prince has nothing. And you eternal gates—namely faith, hope, and charity—be raised up (John XIV, 30). For you eternal gates were, as it were, cast down into the depths while those detained in hell, almost despairing, were there; but now, behold, they sing at the coming of our Lord and theirs: “You have come, O Desired One, whom we awaited in darkness, that on this night you might bring the bound forth from their prisons. Our [Col. 1077A] sighs called for you; our abundant lamentations sought you. You have become hope for the despairing.”

They were indeed despairing, yet not without hope: they always hoped for this triumph, but were regarded as desperate by other impious persons likewise placed in hell, who, as in this world, so also in hell, lacked with the devil hope of human salvation. Therefore, in the good who were regarded as hopeless, you eternal gates—faith, hope, and charity—were cast down, when the souls of believers, those who looked toward him, and those who loved him had long been left in hell. But now be raised, eternal gates. Exult, faith of the elect, because behold, he comes whom you believed would come. Accordingly, you, faith, shall no longer be called faith, because you see what you believed; and when the vision of direct sight succeeds faith, by this succession [Col. 1077B] you are not cast down, but rather raised and brought to perfection after the likeness of the dawn, which is perfected as it rises.

But you lay cast down so long as the things you urged people to believe were credible only to a few, and scarcely so, because so long a delay had intervened that they could hardly be believed as future. But now, “Lift yourself up, lift yourself up; arise, Jerusalem” (Isa. LI, 17). Arise, faith, so that from you there may come a vision of peace, and that you may be Jerusalem, who formerly were Zion: you who showed future things through a mirror and in an enigma, now display them in manifest vision, because behold,

> The King of glory shall enter.

O faith, O eternal gate, by whose present vision you are perfected and raised! And you, O hope of the elect, eternal gate, [Col. 1077C] since, when you possess eternal goods, you will not disappoint those capable of possessing them: now rise and rejoice. You lay in the pit of infernal sadness, under darkness, nearly cast down into the abyss of despair. Rise, I say, and rejoice, because behold, the King of glory shall enter to visit those who hope in him; and you, hope conceived and held from the promise of his coming, shall be the eternal gate of joy, when none of the eternal goods hoped and awaited through you is lacking.

Above all, you, charity of the elect placed in hell, are an eternal gate, because, while faith and hope fail, you shall never fail but remain for ever. You were in some manner cast down while that which you loved was separated from you by too long an absence. But now you, eternal gate, rise, while we, the choirs of angels before the face of him [Col. 1077D] whom you love, command the gates of the princes to be lifted up, preparing a level way for his entrance, which is not far to be delayed. For behold, he is present, and the King of glory himself shall enter.

Alternatively: You, faith, an eternal gate, inasmuch as you are possessed concerning eternal goods and evils; and you, hope, an eternal gate, possessed concerning eternal goods alone; and you, charity, an eternal gate, which once rightly grounded shall never fail (1 Cor. XIII, 8): you three eternal gates in the holy apostles and the other disciples of Christ were exceedingly cast down by the storm of persecution. For even the strongest among you would have failed altogether in faith had not the Lord prayed for him that his faith might not fail. And those of your number retained little hope who said: [Col. 1078A] “But we hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke XXIV, 21). In them too charity, because iniquity then abounded, had grown so cold that they could truly be called “foolish and slow of heart” (ibid., 25).

But now, you eternal gates—faith, hope, and charity—cast down in the hearts of the apostles, rise in such a way that whoever had hitherto been almost unbelieving, strengthened in faith after touching and seeing Christ’s body, may faithfully say: “My Lord and my God” (John XX, 28). Let your hope be firm—not that he is still to redeem Israel, but because this same one, who by the pouring out of his blood has already redeemed Israel formerly sold under sins, has now through his resurrection “raised up a horn of salvation” for you [Col. 1078B] “in the house of David his servant” (Luke I, 69), and shall reign in the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end (ibid., 32–33). And you shall be the house of Jacob in which he shall reign for ever.

Therefore you who, through charity grown cold, were foolish and slow of heart, now, with charity grown warm again, be such that you may truly say: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIII, 32). Thus, then, be raised up, eternal gates, who were in the pit of sadness, so that you may exult and be filled from the breasts of your consolation: for to you, O faith, that which you believed shall be present; to you, O hope, that which you hoped for shall be given; and no one shall take your joy from you, O charity, eternal gate. And the King of glory shall enter.

[Col. 1078C] We know that this King of glory came forth from the Father for our sake and came into the world. Again he left the world and shall enter to the Father before your eyes; for while you see, he shall be raised into heaven (Acts I, IX). Therefore, when he is raised, you too be raised with him, eternal gates, so that, reaching upward, you may be clothed with power from on high and filled with the Holy Spirit. When he enters into you, Christ the King of glory himself shall enter with him, together with his Father, as he promised you, saying: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23).

When, in your craving for an earthly kingdom, you said to him, “Lord, if at this time you will restore the kingdom [Col. 1078D] to Israel” (Acts I, 6), hoping for earthly triumphs such as King David had, or great peace such as King Solomon had in the kingdom of Israel, then your faith, hope, and charity were gates more temporal than eternal, since they stood open rather to the acquiring of temporal than eternal goods. But now rise, you gates, in order that you may be eternal: that is, open rather to eternal and heavenly goods than to earthly ones. And the King of glory shall enter, whose entrance you are unworthy of so long as you are not raised up.

Therefore rise upward, to desire and seek the kingdom of heaven, which is not of this world, but whose going forth is from the highest heaven and whose circuit is unto its highest point. Rise up, because the magnificence of the kingdom promised to you has been raised up. [Col. 1079A] Rise up, because the sun has risen and the moon has stood in its order.

“Lift up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter.” O princes of hell, who had raised evil gates which nevertheless would never prevail against faith or the Church, when, while Christ suffered, you pressed them into mistrust, despair, and forgetfulness of charity: now lift up these gates of yours. Let your impiety recoil upon yourselves. And you eternal gates—faith, hope, and charity—be raised up to believe, hope for, and love the things above, not the things upon earth. And the King of glory shall enter.

We princes of hell have until now held dominion over the whole world as over the courtyard of our prince, who, like an armed strong man, guarded this courtyard of his. From this courtyard [Col. 1079B] we dragged whomever we wished into the prison committed to us, namely hell; and once that prison was shut, there was no one able to leave, although its gates stood open to those entering and were closed to those who had entered. We ourselves, guards of the prison, guarded the prison. But behold, the angelic choir is present, and light shines in the dwelling-place of the prison. And it is plainly said to the Church held captive among us—the Church of the patriarchs and other ancient righteous persons, who, however righteous they may have been, were nevertheless bound with two chains, namely actual and original sins—it is said to this Church now so bound: “Rise quickly; lift yourself up, lift yourself up; arise, Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck” (Isa. LI, 17; LII, 2).

And behold, now the chains have fallen from her hands. Her [Col. 1079C] “yoke” has decayed “at the presence of oil” (ibid., X, 12, 27), at the presence of a king anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions. And we indeed know that many kings and prophets, or righteous persons, desiring to see this King of glory, whom they did not see, and to hear him, whom they did not hear, came to us without breaking our gates; rather, they remained chained among us. David and Solomon came to us, illustrious and glorious kings, and other great kings too, but chained with two chains, namely actual and original sins. But this King of glory came not only without chains; he himself, free among the dead, also loosed others from chains. And:

### Verse 8. “Who is this King of glory, at whose coming [Col. 1079D] our gates fall?”

Perhaps he is the one whom many kings and prophets wished to see and did not see. Tell us, you heavenly angels, we infernal angels: who is “this King of glory,” who “has been gloriously magnified,” who has cast “horse and rider” (Exod. XV, 1), and all the chariots of our king, our Pharaoh, into the sea, drowning and killing us by his own blood together with the water that came forth from his side?

> “The Lord strong and mighty is this King of glory.”

This is what we heavenly angels say to you infernal ministers: he whose power you marvel at is the Lord strong and mighty, of whom Isaiah foretold (XL, 10): “Behold, the Lord shall come in strength, and his arm shall rule.” He first came down from heaven to earth [Col. 1080A] in meekness; but behold, now the Lord strong and mighty himself descends into hell with great strength, and here his arm rules, by which arm, behold, hell is plundered.

This is the truly strong Samson. At the place of Calvary he was shorn and weakened by Dalilah herself—that is, by the Synagogue. But now, as the hair of this Nazarene grows again, that is, as his own divine strength displays itself—the strength of which he seemed stripped and shorn upon the cross—he shakes the two pillars of the great house, moving heaven and earth: for both in heaven the sun is darkened, and there is a great earthquake, both at his death and also at his resurrection.

This strong Lord is the true David, strong in hand, who prevailed with the sling and triumphed with the stone upon the cross. In it his pastoral staff was the cross itself, and his shepherd’s bag was his [Col. 1080B] pure flesh, in which, as though five stones, he received five wounds. But through the mystery of one wound—through the water and blood of his side—your uncircumcised prince was cast down, O infernal princes. Therefore this Lord is rightly proclaimed strong and mighty in battle.

This mighty one casts down the mighty from their seat and makes evil powerful persons suffer powerful torments. He “has shown strength in his arm, scattering the proud in the thought of their heart” (Luke I, 51), and there is none able to resist his power and his will, because “all things are placed under” his “dominion” (Esth. XIII, 9). Therefore he is mighty in battle against your prince and against you, who until now held his people captive in Egypt.

But now, victory having been completed [Col. 1080C] through the cross as through Moses’ rod, all of you Egyptians, with your prince, are put to flight and despoiled, because this is the night that despoils the Egyptians and enriches the Hebrews. And because no one can enter the strong man’s house unless he first binds and overcomes the strong man, this strong and mighty one in battle was first bound, in order that he might loose the accomplices of the collapsing world. Yet your prince was bound by his bonds and died by his death, because “death then died, when Life died upon the tree.” Since, therefore, you have been conquered with your prince, we command you again and say:

### Verse 9. “Lift up your gates, O princes.”

Likewise we say: “Be raised up, eternal gates, and [Col. 1080D] the King of glory shall enter.” For repetition is confirmation: what is commanded by the repeated injunction is to be done without delay, your Pharaoh with his ministers, whose princes you are, obeying the repeated command—just as Pharaoh’s repeated vision in sleep was fulfilled without delay, with all Egypt obeying Joseph, who had been sold into it but then exalted over it.

For the true Joseph, though sold, lives and rules over all the land of Egypt—not only in the world, but also in hell. By his authority, therefore, we say to you: “Lift up your gates, O princes.” And to you, eternal gates, who were oppressed beneath the harsh burdens of the Egyptians, we say: now be raised and exalted, because you shall no longer be subject to Egyptian domination, but, baptized through the Red Sea of Christ’s blood, with the Egyptians slain and submerged, you shall come forth—all you elect, from the first righteous person down to the thief confessing on the cross.

That thief indeed had approached as far as these gates, which we command to be lifted up; but through repentance the eternal gates were raised in him: faith, by which he believed to be God the one whom he saw dying; hope, in which he offered the prayer, “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke III, 42); love of neighbour, by which he showed zeal concerning and rebuked the blaspheming thief; and love of God, by which he loved the heavenly kingdom, in which he wished himself to be remembered. Therefore this thief, snatched from the gate of hell and death, with the eternal gates raised in him, shall today be with Christ in paradise. And all of you also shall be with him whose faith did not fail, whose hope [Col. 1081B] proved long-suffering, whose charity did not fail throughout all the ages gone by in the very long expectation of the liberator promised to you, who now, behold, is present.

### Verse 10. “Who is this King of glory?”

Thus you speak and marvel. Hear—or rather, see him present—for great is he, before whom thrones and dominations hasten, and when he rises, “his enemies are scattered, and those who hate him flee from before his face” (Ps. LXVII, 2), because they cannot bear his strength. For he is the Lord strong and mighty in battle; indeed, he is also the Lord of hosts. First, by strongly and mightily defeating and driving out the vices opposed to him, he destroys them; then, as Lord of hosts, he builds and plants virtues. First he now enters, strong and mighty in this battle, in order to defeat hell; then he, the Lord of hosts, [Col. 1081C] shall place his virtuous elect, rescued from hell, in paradise, where, without the thorns of vices and miseries, the delights of virtues alone shall abound for them in the garden of delights, as he himself glorifies them—he who is the King of glory.

All these words, uttered in the persons of angels, can nevertheless suitably be said in the persons of apostles, martyrs, confessors, and pastors. Let the apostles, therefore, to whom it was granted to know the ministry of God’s kingdom, speak. Let the holy apostles, princes of the churches, say to the chief priests: “Lift up your gates, O princes.” O princes and elders of the people, who have the keys of the kingdom, neither entering yourselves nor allowing others to enter; who have made void God’s commandment [Col. 1081D] for the sake of your traditions, by which you closed the gates of heaven and raised your own gates: lift up your gates; remove your Pharisaic traditions. And you, eternal gates—that is, the divine ordinances of heavenly commandments, by whose observance entrance into the kingdom of heaven lies open—be raised up. And the King of glory shall enter, now seeking not the observance of circumcision made by hand or of carnal sacrifices, but only the glory of the Trinity, which is set forth in the eternal gates, to be pursued not for a time, as the Sabbath, circumcision, and other carnal observances, which ought to cease as shadows now that the light of truth is present.

Once the eternal gates have been opened and raised—that is, once wholly heavenly and spiritual commandments have been made manifest—namely commandments concerning charity, [Col. 1082A] which never fails, humility, chastity, obedience, and the observance of other heavenly virtues which shall remain for ever, people will be followers of these enduring virtues just as the angels of God, within heaven’s eternal gates, eternally love God and one another, and are humble, chaste, and obedient—not laboriously in order to serve, but in order to praise him whom the angels praise eternally.

“Who is this King of glory?” This is what we Jews say, who “are Abraham’s seed and have never served anyone” (John VIII, 33), disciples of Moses, of whom we know that God spoke to him. But we do not know whence comes this one whom you apostles proclaim as King of glory. Who, therefore, is this King of glory? Or how is this one to be believed as King of glory, who hung upon the cross like a thief?

To this we apostles answer that this one whom we proclaim is the Lord strong and mighty in battle. For he foretold to you that because of your unbelief you would fall by the edge of the sword, be led captive among all nations, and that wrath would come upon this people. Hence it was that, “seeing” your “city, he wept over it,” saying: “Days shall come upon you, and your enemies shall surround you with a rampart, hem you in on every side, cast you and your children within you to the ground, and shall not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not know the time of your visitation” (Luke XIX, 41, 43–44).

Therefore he is the Lord strong and mighty in battle, who through the Roman army scatters the people hostile to him, none being able to resist in battle [Col. 1082C] so that what this Lord strong and mighty in battle foretold does not come to pass. Is not the strength and power of this Lord wonderful, who defeats you, his Jewish enemies, through other enemies of his, the pagans? He is therefore truly mighty in battle: domestic sedition and external siege served him among you, O Jews, so that your choice, by which you preferred the seditious Barabbas to Christ, should not have empty consequences. Christ is strong and mighty in this very battle, in which the Romans took away both your place and nation.

He is also the Lord of hosts, multiplying virtues in us, who with great power bear witness to his resurrection and perform many mighty works and miracles in his name, giving sight to the blind, [Col. 1082D] cleansing lepers, raising the dead, and granting many other healings. If, therefore, you unbelieving princes of the people ask who this King of glory is whom we preach, recognize in the overthrow of your gates, in the destruction of your nation accomplished by the Romans, that he is the Lord strong and mighty in battle. Recognize likewise in the raising of the eternal gates, in the glorification and magnification of evangelical ordinances, that he is the Lord of hosts, who through his Gospel does not seek the blood of goats or calves, but, feeding us with his flesh through his own blood, brings us into the Holy of Holies—that is, into heaven itself. Having entered there as our forerunner, he has opened to us and to all who believe in him the eternal gates.

[Col. 1083A] Having entered through these gates, we give thanks to our guide and say: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20). He, therefore, who so willed in mercy and was able in power to lift up the gates of death raised by you, and to raise the eternal gates through us weak persons, to the praise of his glory, is truly the King of glory.

Now the words previously spoken in the person of angels and apostles must be repeated in the person of martyrs. Let Christ’s martyrs now say: “You princes of this world, lift up your gates.” Lift up and remove the evil edicts and wicked laws through which you compel people to enter hell, since you forbid the worship of Christ, the true God, while you worship idols and command them to be worshipped in your laws. These laws are, indeed, [Col. 1083B] gates of hell which shall by no means prevail against the holy Church founded upon the rock. Therefore lift up these gates of yours, O princes of this age; and be raised up, you eternal gates—that is, the good laws of Catholic rulers and ecclesiastical enactments favouring peace. You such gates, rise on high, so that, once the gates of hell have been cast down—that is, wicked laws annulled—you good laws may be maintained everywhere. Let Nero’s laws cease; let the laws of Constantine, the Catholic emperor, be maintained. Let the wicked edicts of tyrants proclaimed against Christ cease and perish, and let the good statutes of emperors be observed everywhere. And the King of glory shall enter, because, after demons have been driven from hearts and temples, Christ the King of glory shall enter hearts by faith and temples by true religion.

[Col. 1083C] “Who is this King of glory?” You princes of the world marvel who this King of glory is. But we martyrs and witnesses of this King of glory say to you that he is the Lord strong and mighty in battle. For while we martyrs stand against you, dreadful princes, in battle, this King of glory triumphs so strongly and mightily through us that by no sort of torments can you terrify or overcome us, his soldiers; “but in all these things we overcome because of him who loved us” (Rom. VIII, 37). Hence we boldly testify that he is strong and mighty in battle: he strengthens us in battle, and his love makes his soldiers lavish with holy blood, provided that they may be permitted to behold him at the cost of this present life.

For just as Gideon of old, [Col. 1083D] with three hundred men armed with jars and lamps, who cried out and sounded trumpets with him, smashing the jars while the lamps flashed, conquered the exceedingly strong and powerful camp of Midian (Judg. VII, 19), so our Lord, whom you, O princes of this age, marvel at, armed with our army—that is, the army of his three hundred witnesses, marked by faith with the number of the holy Trinity—shall overcome and put you princes to flight. For though the fragile jars of our bodies are broken by you, nevertheless, from the light of miracles shining from our death and striking your eyes, your conscience is convicted, so that you cannot long oppose manifest truth. Even when you openly oppose it, you nevertheless acknowledge its face secretly; [Col. 1084A] that is, you cannot deny that our Lord Jesus Christ is the true God. Hence it is near at hand that you shall be put to flight, stumble, and be diminished. Therefore, when you ask and say, “Who is this King of glory?”, we his witnesses answer you confidently: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.”

Again you ask and say, “Who is this King of glory?” while, in contempt of you and your commands, your gates are lifted up and the eternal gates are raised. Hear, and perceive in yourselves what we perceive in ourselves: that he is the Lord of hosts, who works miracles in us—not only strengthening us by his power in battle, but also, after the battle, [Col. 1084B] while we rest in peace at our tombs, or otherwise working many miracles through our names and merits. The demons themselves bear witness to this, that “our bodies were buried in peace” (Ecclus. XLIV, 14) and our names live for ever. Unless they lived, the names heard would not torment the demons. This King of glory, therefore, is truly the Lord of hosts, who also works signs of power through our names, tormenting demons and casting them out of possessed bodies or driving them from temples, while glorifying our relics placed there through miracles and mighty works.

The voice of the confessors: “Lift up your gates, O princes.” You heresiarchs, who refused to be disciples of truth and became teachers of error against faith, [Col. 1084C] which is the gate of truth, have raised your gates—that is, false doctrines. For you, Arius, whose name stinks throughout the whole world, were the first to sow abroad in the world concerning the Son of God: “There was when he was not.” You proclaimed him changeable; you blasphemed that he was less than the Father. By teaching such things you raised the gates of death, and you strengthened them, as it were, with certain bars, by plausible arguments and corrupted testimonies of Scripture.

Likewise, you other heretics have raised gates of death against Catholic faith, fortified by the keys entrusted to Peter, since in attacking truth you fashioned false doctrines. But now, since the light of truth has been revealed at the Nicene synod and at other councils and in the writings of orthodox Fathers, proclaiming the Son *homoousios*, that is, consubstantial with the Father, [Col. 1084D] and refuting every false doctrine: lift up your gates, you princes, you heresiarchs—that is, condemn your own wicked doctrines, unless you wish to be subject to condemnation. But if you remain in condemnation, you princes of these darknesses, demons, lift up to yourselves in hell your gates—that is, evil teachers, especially Arius, whom, disembowelled by a shameful death in a privy, you shall drag into hell.

Lift up likewise your other gates, so that no heretical or schismatic perversity remains which has not, together with its author, been anathematized and bound with you in one bundle to be burned in the fire, lest hereafter any gate of heresy stand open to you.

[Col. 1085A] O princes of darkness, lift up, I say, your gates; and be raised up, eternal gates—that is, you Catholic teachers, raise yourselves together with your doctrine. After the apostles, hold the highest authority, and let Christ speaking in you be heard, concerning whom the Father says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. XVII, 5). Let all who wish to be saved hear him in you. As truly eternal gates, open the entrance into the eternal kingdom by preaching the Son coeternal with the eternal Father—which Arius denies—and the Holy Spirit coeternal with Father and Son—which Macedonius denies.

Let these heresiarchs, together with their like-minded fabricators of lies, be removed from the midst and be in hell. But you be raised up, eternal gates, and [Col. 1085B] the King of glory shall enter. Donatus, attempting to confine this King of glory, excluded him, in his own estimation, from the entire world outside Africa alone. Likewise every other sect, saying of Christ, “Behold, here,” or “behold, there” (Mark XIII, 21), has confined him to one part. On the contrary, rise up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter—indeed, through you he shall be shown already to have entered the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world.

Therefore he is rightly proclaimed by you not only the Lord strong and mighty in battle, but also the Lord of hosts, because through your doctrine the party of opponents has been mightily conquered, and burning lamps in your hands reveal in you the wondrous gifts of virtues. For you are angelic in the praise of chastity, exalted through contempt for the world, and orthodox through many [Col. 1085C] merits of righteousness. Among your number shines the glorious Father Augustine, a foremost conqueror of heretics, with his teacher Ambrose, like two olive trees and two lampstands. These two enlighten the south by the noonday brightness, as it were, of their doctrine. But Bishop Hilary with his disciple Martin shine in the west like a bright evening light. Basil with his Gregory, like a very glowing dawn, adorn the east. Severinus of Cologne and Amandus of Maastricht, shining in the north, say: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind” (Song IV, 16). Thus eternal gates are found through all the ends of the earth, to which it is said: “Be raised up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter.”

[Col. 1085D] After the confessors’ triumph in the assertion of faith follows the voice of the pastors, who, striving to feed rational flocks, keep the savage rage of wolves away from the sheepfolds entrusted to them. Therefore they say also to evil rulers: “Lift up your gates, O princes.” O you princes, now no longer pagans but false Christians, who do not openly attack the Church as Nero or Decius did, but introduce wolves, thieves, and robbers into it: disregarding canonical election, you intrude under the names of bishops, abbots, provosts, priests, chaplains, and canons—not through Christ, who is the door of the sheep and the eternal gate, but through simony, which is the gate of hell—thieves, robbers, and ravening wolves, who do not spare the flock entrusted to them but seek their own interests.

These are not gates of heaven, [Col. 1086A] but gates of hell; not gates of God, but your gates, O princes. Therefore through these gates of yours the King of glory shall not enter. Since they are manifest simoniacs, heretics, and persons anathematized—those who by simony and by the violence of lay princes burst into churches—there is no fellowship of light with these darknesses, no agreement of Christ with Belial, and no salvation in their prohibited masses. Therefore lift up these gates of yours, O princes. “Take these things away from here,” says the Lord, “and do not make my Father’s house a house of trade” (John II, 16). For it is written: “My house is a house of prayer” for all nations, “but you have made it a den of robbers” (Luke XIX, 46). Remove simony and those who entered through it. Remove these gates of hell, because [Col. 1086B] they shall not prevail against the Church. Remove them, lest you too be removed along with these your gates—a thing which we see partly fulfilled in our own days: because on account of such simonies Henry IV was deprived of his kingdom, and he himself was anathematized together with his infernal gates. And eternal gates were raised up: namely, Catholic pastors of churches, canonically called and elected and consecrated with the favour of the Holy Spirit, without whom simoniacs were not so much consecrated as execrated.

But since many gates of hell still remain: Remove your gates altogether, O princes! Join yourselves to the Catholic people, so that through your effort the canonical election of priests may take place; and through lawful advancement be lifted up, you everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter. For through your ministries and offices Christ’s presence will be at hand, sanctifying and purifying the whole Church, so that it may be nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven, bearing this title inscribed on its lintels: “This place is awesome; this is the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28:17); it shall be called the court of God. Truly this place is terrible not only to demons, but also to the companions of demons, the ministers of unclean spirits; for wherever in the Church of God the everlasting gates have been lifted up, thieves do not dare approach there. For what ambitious man would dare Simonically offer money to a pontiff known to emulate the apostle Peter, who said to Simon Magus: “May your money perish with you” [Col. 1086D] (Acts 8:20)? What manifestly incestuous priest would dare claim for himself the priestly office when a bishop presides such as Clement, bishop of the city of Rome and disciple of the apostle Peter, who in his decrees absolutely and perpetually forbids a priest who has fallen with his own wife from the priestly ministry of the sacred altar—barely allowing such a man to shut the doors of the church, carry a water-pitcher for the hands of the priests, and perform other lesser duties? Thus every place in the Church of God which is well ordered and fortified with everlasting gates is terrible to those living disorderly lives.

Likewise, well-ordered enclosures of canons or monks, strengthened with everlasting gates, are certainly terrible to those unwilling to live strictly: to the curious and idle, whose god is their belly, whose pursuit is frivolity and wandering, and whose course runs through infernal gates—that is, through wicked rulers—toward hell, while no strictness of discipline restrains them as they live dissolutely or forbids them their own wills. Therefore, that the whole Church may be a terrible place and be called the court of God, remove all your gates—all customs contrary to truth and salvation which you, princes of error and defenders of wickedness, have introduced. For “if they do these things in the green wood, what shall be done in the dry?” (Luke 23:30). If they do these things in cloisters regularly ordered, what shall be done in irregular conventicles?

Therefore, against all princes of malice and wickedness, may the Lord grant us effectively to sing and say: Remove your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O everlasting gates. Let injustice not rule them, but let falsehood always be subject to truth. And now, meanwhile, since it is altogether impossible not to sin—which is a gate of hell—let at least this be granted to the Church, or to every ecclesiastical person: that sin may not reign in his now mortal body, until perfect peace comes, by which it will happen that sin shall not merely fail to reign but shall not exist at all in bodies then immortal, when death has been swallowed up in victory and the gate of death, which is sin, has been altogether destroyed. Then the Church, or any ecclesiastical person, shall not be put to shame “when he speaks with his enemies in the gate” [Col. 1087C] (Ps. 126:5), when “her husband is renowned in the gates” (Prov. 31:23) and wholly exalts her “from the gates of death, that she may proclaim all his praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. 9:15): in the gates of Jerusalem, to which it is said: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion, for he has strengthened the bars of your gates” (Ps. 147:1–2). Then there shall neither be nor reign in Jerusalem the gates of death, namely sins. But now it is well enough if they do not reign, if these gates of hell do not prevail, while they cannot be wholly and altogether removed.

Meanwhile, open to me the gates of righteousness—you who are in the towers; you, I say, who are in the towers; you elect, who reign in heaven. Open everlasting gates to me, the Church still on pilgrimage; to me endangered among enemies with Judith; to me, with Judith, often washed in the fountain of Bethulia through tears of repentance; to me, who have not delighted in the couches and shamelessness of Holofernes; to me, the slayer of that same Holofernes—that is, the conqueror of wicked desire. To such a one, whether Church or person, you who are in the towers, open the everlasting gates, so that, entering them, I may give thanks to the Lord. “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Ps. 117:20).

Through many gates one comes to the one gate, because one thing is necessary. This one gate is the Virgin Mary, the closed gate inaccessible to any man. Yet through her, though closed, all who are incorporated into her Son shall enter the kingdom of heaven; he came forth from her while her womb remained closed. Among all the everlasting gates to whom it is said, “Be lifted up, O everlasting gates,” this one is more highly lifted up, because the holy Mother of God has been exalted above the choirs of angels. This is truly the gate of the Lord, and the righteous shall enter through it. This everlasting gate was first lifted up by faith, when she believed that things beyond human possibility would be accomplished in her. Hence Elizabeth said of her: “Blessed is she who believed, because those things spoken to her by the Lord shall be fulfilled” [Col. 1088A] (Luke 1:45). Then this everlasting gate was lifted up through faith, by believing an incredible thing, and the King of glory entered it. Now she is lifted up above the choirs of angels, and the King of glory reigns in her.

We have, moreover, a unique example of this everlasting and singular gate in the office of the Mass. The Mass itself is assuredly the gate of the Lord, worthy then of his entry when, after the likeness of the most chaste Virgin Mary, it is found to possess uncorrupted faith by which things incredible to human sense are believed to occur there. For the same body conceived in the Virgin is presented on the altar; and without doubt the King of glory shall enter all who worthily partake in communion of that body. At his entry the antiphon, whose heading is *At the Entrance*, is fittingly sung at the beginning of the Mass: “For the King of glory shall enter through it”—provided, however, that this gate has been so lifted up that the King of glory himself may worthily enter through it. For who would suppose that heretics, especially those publicly identified, excommunicated, or placed under interdict, possess Christ in their offices? With them this gate lies low; therefore the King of glory shall not enter through it, unless perhaps in order to exercise judgment there. For those who communicate unworthily without discerning the Lord’s body eat and drink judgment upon themselves [Col. 1088C] (1 Cor. 11:29 [citation printed: 1 Cor. 2:21]). How much more are judgment and condemnation incurred in Masses under interdict, where the office presumptuously performed against God’s prohibition provokes him not to mercy but to wrath. For he himself says to the masters of the churches, his ministers: “Whoever hears you hears me; whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). Therefore, when the masters of the churches forbid Masses to clerics who traffic in the house of the Lord and are manifestly incestuous, Christ, speaking in his own ministers, has forbidden them. And so, because such Masses are sung and heard against his prohibition, they are not Masses that are gates lifted up on high through which the King of glory may enter; and it is greatly to be feared that Masses of this kind are gates of hell to those who presumptuously sing and hear them.

It should be noted that Christ’s entering as King of glory is one thing, and his entering as judge and avenger of sin another. For where the King of glory himself enters, there he rules and glorifies those into whom he enters. But where the judge and God of vengeance enters, there he renders recompense to the proud, as is elsewhere prayed: “Rise up, you who judge the earth; render recompense to the proud” (Ps. 93:2). He rightly says, “to the proud,” because not every sinner is proud, though every proud person is a sinner [Col. 1089A]. But for sinners who repent and are humbled, forgiveness, not recompense, is prepared. Conversely, for the proud, not forgiveness but fitting recompense is prepared. Since they are wholly temporal, seeking temporal things alone, the everlasting gates shall not be opened to them; nor are their Masses, which they sing for temporal gain, everlasting gates for them. Yet if some Catholic, unaware of the interdict, were to hear such a Mass in order to obtain eternal goods, that Mass would, because of his good faith, be for him an everlasting gate. For the more truthfully one says at Mass, “We have our hearts lifted up unto the Lord,” the more highly the everlasting gate is lifted up; and the King of glory shall enter as a more merciful hearer of all things requested in the Mass, insofar as eternal rather than temporal things are more sincerely desired there. For where earthly things are desired through the Mass, this gate is not lifted upward to heaven but cast down to earth.

Does the Catholic Church, then, sin when in the Mass she prays not only for eternal life but also for temporal peace, favorable weather, the fruits of the earth, the salvation of souls and bodies not only eternal but also temporal, and every provision needed by this present life? Far be it from us to think so, since we read that the holiest men requested such things and frequently offered prayers and petitions at the Lord’s altar in which not only eternal goods are desired and eternal evils renounced, but also temporal goods to be obtained and temporal evils to be removed are mentioned [Col. 1089C]. What then shall we do when we see such Masses of men sent by God proving ineffective? Should we suppose either that the saints ask wrongly, or that God refuses to hear those who ask rightly? The apostle James says of those who ask wrongly: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, in order to spend it upon your desires” (Jas. 4:3). Therefore, those who seek temporal things so as to consume them upon their desires resemble the person of whom it is written: “May his prayer become sin” (Ps. 108:7).
