Their prayer itself becomes sin, above all when, amid the sacred solemnities of the Mass, they celebrate the ineffable sacrament of eternity in such a way as to seek from it temporal things to spend upon their desires. In contrast, holy men seek first the kingdom of God and believe that all these things shall be added to them which may serve the need of passing through this present life and attaining eternal life. Thus, whether they ask for these things or do not ask, provided that they earnestly seek the kingdom of God, we must believe that they are given not to serve pleasure but to meet necessity.

Indeed, every perfect man, following the faithful Abraham, embraces as a free wife piety, which has the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come, and from her hopes for a blessing to arise. But when that nobler wife, like Sarah, long delays in barrenness to give birth, the faithful spirit, like Abraham, grows old during so long a delay of the promised offspring; and meanwhile, while he awaits the birth of Isaac for himself—that is, eternal laughter—he grieves that his pilgrimage is prolonged, saying: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged” [Col. 1090A] (Ps. 119:5). In this very pilgrimage, because the spirit needs temporal things to sustain the body, whether its own or another’s, that noble promise of eternal things, by which we are bidden first to seek the kingdom of God, gives and joins to the spirit as husband another promise—that by which the other things are said to be added to us—as though it were her handmaid. From this union Ishmael is born, a name interpreted “the hearing of God”; and while they await eternal things, they receive these temporal things as aid for this present life and, in seeking them, desire to be heard without delay. So Hagar, Sarah’s handmaid, conceived Ishmael from Abraham without delay; as has been said, his name means “the hearing of God,” while his mistress remained barren until old age and almost to the point of despair.

Thus, when Sarah, already ninety years old, heard that she would bear a child by a man of one hundred years, she “laughed” and said: “After I have grown old, and my lord is old, shall I give myself to pleasure?” (Gen. 18:12). How greatly, do you suppose, would this ninety-year-old and barren woman have despaired if her husband had begotten no child even by the handmaid? For she could have thought her husband cold by nature, since he could not beget by a young woman such as Hagar; and therefore this elderly woman, her womb now dead, might perhaps have fallen wholly into distrust, so as not to believe the Lord promising that she would conceive by that man whose nature she considered altogether cold. But now, when the Lord said to Abraham, “Behold, Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call him Isaac” [Col. 1090C] (Gen. 17:19), Sarah laughed; but, reproved for her laughter and repenting of her distrust, she escaped the snare of unbelief and, trusting the Lord’s words, conceived and bore a son to be preferred to the handmaid’s son.

Similarly, when the faithful and perfect spirit hopes that Isaac—that is, eternal laughter—will be born to it from the promise of heavenly goods, and when the womb of that promise seems already dead because of the excessive delay of everlasting joy, it receives some consolation. Its wife Sarah, that is, its faith or expectation of eternal things, will not fall into despair if in the meantime it begets Ishmael, that is, “the hearing of God,” from the promise of temporal goods. And this son is rightly called Ishmael, “the hearing of God.” For the divine hearing which reaches even to outward things is properly called *exauditio*, “hearing granted,” as it were hearing in external matters. Such goods were promised where it was said: “Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or fields for my sake” (Matt. 19:29), and for the Gospel, “shall receive a hundredfold in this life with persecutions, and in the age to come shall possess eternal life.”

The apostle Peter received this hundredfold in this life with persecutions: from the money offered, he fed many thousands of people living together under his direction, so that there was no needy person among them. Previously he himself had been poor and needy, procuring food by his hands and craft, yet sufficient for himself; he did not possess such riches as would have enabled him to supply the want of others. But after leaving for the Gospel’s sake the little that he possessed and all that he might have desired, he later received very many alms for feeding Christ’s poor. He charged his fellow apostle Paul with concern for the poor, and through him received money collected among the Gentiles. He was not deprived of the promise of a hundredfold in this life, though it was full of hardships and persecutions [Col. 1091A].

And because it is better to need less than to have more, the apostle John, exiled on the island of Patmos, possessed that same hundredfold more pleasantly when he had little need there of earthly consolations and riches. He had no poor there whom he was required to feed, no guests whom he expected to receive; refreshed in himself by divine revelations and angelic conversations, he needed no earthly assistance. Being then, as it were, wholly in the spirit, and desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ in eternal laughter and joy—which the name Isaac signifies—he heard the angel who spoke with him say: “You must prophesy again to peoples” [Col. 1091B] (Rev. 10:11). Thus, as though the childbirth of his noble wife, from whom Isaac was to be born to him, had been delayed into his great old age, a handmaid was in some sense placed before him: the promise of temporal support became necessary to one destined to live long and not merely preach but also write the Gospel in this world. Therefore, after Domitian’s death, when the apostle was released from captivity, he received the hundredfold also in this way: having always all sufficiency in everything, he abounded in every good work, as it is written: “He scattered abroad; he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever and ever” (2 Cor. 9:8–9).

If the apostles and other perfect men, possessing the twofold promise—namely, support for the present and future goods—had been frustrated in the promise pertaining to the present life, their faith in future goods could have been endangered. The word of their prayer would then have been like cold seed, sufficient neither for Ishmael’s generation; nor could any such person say: “Blessed be God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who comforts us in all our tribulation, so that we too may be able to comfort those who are in every affliction” [Col. 1091D] (2 Cor. 1:3–4). Again, they say: “As needy, yet enriching many; as having nothing, and possessing all things” (ibid. 6:10). Do they not, in saying this, glory like holy men whose Ishmael has already been born, that they have been heard? And they await the rewards of future blessedness with all the greater confidence because they more certainly know that they have received in the present the preliminary merits of those same rewards. For God “who supplies seed to the sower” (2 Cor. 9:10) and provides bread to eat so increases the fruits of righteousness that they lack nothing in any grace as they await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. Though they now believe in him without seeing, later they shall see him and rejoice with inexpressible joy, “obtaining the end of” their “faith, the salvation of” their souls [Col. 1092A] (1 Pet. 1:8–9), delighted at the great banquet with Abraham and Isaac, as on the day of Isaac’s weaning—or rather, when Isaac has already come to maturity and the handmaid with her son has then been cast out, when no temporal or earthly support will be necessary for the saints.

This will be the day of Christ, the true Isaac, of which this Christ says to the Jews: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56).

But before that wholly solemn day, father Abraham prays for Ishmael, saying to the Lord: “May Ishmael live before you”; and the Lord replies: “I have heard you also concerning Ishmael; I will make him a great nation, because he is your seed” [Col. 1092B] (Gen. 17:18, 20). For every perfect person whose pilgrimage in this life is prolonged desires not only eternal things but also wishes temporal things to abound—not for evil work, which would be a kind of killing of Ishmael, but for good work, which is his life before God. When the Lord hears such a desire of the poor, he says, as it were through the effects of things, to his faithful one: “I have heard you also concerning Ishmael.” The word “also” is not idly used here, because the promise concerning Isaac is primary, while that concerning Ishmael is secondary. Understanding this, perfect men place Jerusalem at the beginning of their joy: they always maintain the primary desire for eternal blessedness and the secondary desire for the supports of this present life.

But for attaining all these goods, the entry of the King of glory into us is necessary. Without it neither good angels could have prevailed against evil angels, nor the apostles against the rulers of the Jewish people, nor martyrs against tyrants, nor confessors against heresiarchs, so as effectively and authoritatively to say to them: Lift up your gates, O princes. Again, this King of glory, mighty in battle, could not have entered either to overthrow hell, humble tyrants, or confute heresiarchs, unless, after the gates of death had been removed, the everlasting gates had been lifted up through which there was entry for the King of glory himself, the strong Lord, the Lord of hosts [Col. 1092D].

Likewise, in this stormy age three evil princes have raised their gates: namely Judas, the sacrilegious thief; Simon Magus; and Nicholas, the fornicator. They are clearly like, in the mystery of iniquity, those three leaders of sedition—Eleazar, John, and Simon—who, at the time of the siege, devastated the city by civil war and countless slaughter and in a sense divided Jerusalem among their own tyrannies. One of them, John, occupied the upper places of the city, that is, the citadel and the Temple mount. Another, Simon, held the circumference of the city. The third, Eleazar, standing between them, occupied the middle of the city [Col. 1093A].

Do you not see even now, at this final time of consummation, Simon Magus occupying the upper heights of typological Jerusalem—that is, holy Church—namely ecclesiastical honors, and occupying them by selling, selling, and buying? Does not Judas, the worst merchant and sacrilegious thief, hold the outer limits or circumference of the city of God in profits drawn from ecclesiastical property, while sacrilegious usurpers, having wickedly squandered justice, claim tithes and the alms of the poor for themselves? Even bishops themselves are not exempt from this sacrilege when they transfer these same provisions of the poor to secular uses or fail to reclaim them when transferred by others [Col. 1093B]. Nicholas the fornicator holds the middle place between these two, while fornicators among the clergy—and especially among the priesthood—look upward to pseudo-bishops, yet in the mystery of iniquity are themselves set above laypeople. These pseudo-priests become gates to hell for laypeople together with pseudo-bishops; or their forbidden offices and Masses, which persons under interdict sing though forbidden, convey them down to hell along with laypeople who hear them contrary to the interdict, as through certain gates.

Oh, how many souls these gates, or these princes through their gates, sent to hell—especially in the time of Henry IV or V—and still do not cease to send there! It must be said to these princes, and has already often been said by the Roman pontiffs: Remove your gates, O princes; that is, remove your Masses, which you perniciously sing and cause to be sung, so that by them, as by gates of hell, you send to hell those who either sing or hear such Masses against the interdict of the Roman pontiffs. The Church ought to hear these pontiffs when they command what is just, as though hearing blessed Peter himself. Remove these gates; and be lifted up, O everlasting gates—namely the Masses of Catholics, in which the desire for eternity principally reigns, joined by faithful prayers for the condition of temporal things, for the use of believers who through these temporal things proceed toward eternal things [Col. 1093C].

There were indeed among the apostles great leaders of the primitive Church, very much opposed to the aforesaid princes: Simon Peter, head of the apostles, condemning Simon Magus; John the theologian, exhibiting the privilege of virginity against Nicholas the fornicator; and the apostle Paul, laboring more than all in the Gospel, holding the circumference of the holy city, since “from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum” he filled up the Gospel of Christ. By his abundance of almsgiving Paul opposed sacrilegious Judas, diligently gathering alms from the Gentiles and being solicitous to carry or send them to the saints in Jerusalem (1 Cor. 15:10 [citation printed]). May God now raise up and multiply in the Church many equals—and better men—of these princes, opening everlasting gates and rightly, in a manner pleasing to God, celebrating the divine sacraments. Thanks be to God, we now rejoice that such gates are being opened and lifted up [Col. 1094A], and congratulate them by saying: Be lifted up, O everlasting gates. You, I say, everlasting gates, be lifted up, so that the gates of hell may not prevail against us, so that forbidden Masses may not have greater power to anger God than you have to appease him.

Indeed, be lifted up to such a degree that God, provoked to wrath by unlawful Masses, may through you be appeased unto the end; and that through you, everlasting and lifted-up gates, a twofold benefit may accrue to the Church: that, because you are everlasting gates, believers may be enriched with the blessedness of eternity; and that, because you are lifted up, that which would sink downward under an external weight, if it were not raised upward through you, the lifted-up gates, may also be raised upward through good use. Through you may the noble promise of eternal things bear for us Isaac, that is, joy or laughter. Through you, receiving in this life the hundredfold reward, may we also receive Ishmael, whose name means “hearing granted,” so that expectation of future things may be firm through the reception of present gifts and, sufficiently aided by God’s present gifts, we may seek eternal things with greater confidence. Through you, everlasting and lifted-up gates, may “every good gift and every perfect gift from above” descend upon us “from the Father of lights” [Col. 1094B] (Jas. 1:17). May the Lord open you, gates of heaven, and rain manna upon us through you, so that we may eat the bread of angels, the sole refreshment of souls; and may he send us provisions in abundance, also to refresh bodies and strengthen them for good works.

There are also other gates of hell, nearly innumerable, sending innumerable souls to hell. For there are as many gates of hell as there are criminal or capital sins in the world lying in the evil one. Pride is indeed a great gate, raised exceedingly high; avarice and lust are broad and excessively wide gates, along with the remaining capital vices of this kind. To these, in our time, another gate has been added: false repentance. Pseudo-priests deceive souls, pronounce alive those who do not live, and so send them to hell under the appearance of piety; they wound souls under the appearance of a remedy—indeed, kill them by a false presumption of pardon. For they do not require of them, as was commanded in the Law, “the breast of elevation” or “the right shoulder of separation” [Col. 1094D] (Lev. 8:34): that is, they by no means require a purpose of will lifted up toward God, or the right shoulder of action separated from the world. Rather, they impose penances upon those who retain hatred in their hearts and concubines, possess unjustly acquired goods or tithes belonging to laypeople, and do not withdraw from harmful office, business, or military service [perhaps *malitia*, “wickedness”]. Yet, on the contrary, the authority of the holy Fathers attests that no one can do penance for one grave sin while failing to withdraw from another. For one “who offends in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2:10), not indeed according to the effect of the deed, but insofar as attaining salvation is concerned.

And concerning these gates we say—or rather, we desire that it may be effectively said through the Holy Spirit by the rulers of the Church: Remove your gates, O princes [Col. 1095A]. O priests, princes of the people—and would that you were good—remove your gates: that is, along with criminal sins, remove also false repentances. And be lifted up, you everlasting gates, opposed to these gates: namely innocence and true repentance. And the King of glory shall enter. Blessed be God, who has fulfilled, and will still more fulfil, our desire also in this regard, so that we may hear with joy such a decree sounding forth against false repentance as was pronounced in a general council by Pope Innocent, distinguishing false from true repentance:

> “Certainly, because among other things there is one which especially disturbs holy Church, namely false repentance, we warn our brother priests not to allow the souls of laypeople to be deceived by false repentances and drawn into hell. It is clear that repentance is false when, while several sins are disregarded, repentance is done for one alone; or when repentance is so done for one sin that the person does not depart from another. Hence it is written: ‘Whoever observes the whole law, but offends in one point, has become guilty of all’: namely, with respect to eternal life. For just as if he were entangled in all sins, so, if he remains in only one, he shall not enter the gate of eternal life. Repentance is also false when a penitent does not withdraw from an office—whether public, administrative, or commercial—which cannot by any means be conducted without sins; or when hatred is harbored in the heart; or when he does not make satisfaction in respect of any obligation; or when one who has been offended does not pardon the offender; or when someone bears arms against justice.”

This decree of Pope Innocent, if anyone uses it lawfully, is truly an everlasting gate; but alas, it is still cast down far too much through negligence. Therefore, that it may be lifted up and that true repentance may be reformed in the Church through it—true repentance itself being, together with Innocent, an everlasting gate—let each of us say, let all of us say: Be lifted up, O everlasting gates.

But for all the everlasting gates, that they may be lifted up, may you be our chief helper, Mother and Virgin Mary, “gate of the high King and radiant gate of light”; praying also that, whenever we gather to sing or hear Masses, the King of glory, your Son, the strong Lord and mighty in battle, may mercifully enter us through those Masses as through truly penitential and lifted-up gates. In that battle may he judge us who are guilty, and overcome those who attack us, whether demons or evil human beings, or every affection opposed to the honor of virtues—virtues loved by the Lord of hosts himself [Col. 1096A]. And because he is the King of glory, may he both rule his Church gloriously in this life and unite it with his glory in the life to come.

But if the word of our prayer is so weak, through the deserving of our sins, and if we are such that we are unworthy of the hearing signified by Ishmael and of the laughter signified by Isaac: you, everlasting gate, through whom the eternal Word, the blessed seed in whom all tribes of the earth are to be blessed, came into the world from the high Father, the true Abraham, while you remained closed—pray for us. By your strong prayers lift up our weak prayers, O lifted-up gate, so that through you what we have done may be pardonable; what we ask, obtainable; what we offer, acceptable. May the useful consolation of being heard never fail us, even in obtaining supports for this miserable life, until the true Isaac, your Son, is born for us. At his birth on earth you, noble mother, rejoiced, and your neighbors rejoiced with you, namely the holy angels singing: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” [Col. 1096B] (Luke 2:14).

May this true Isaac, through you, the noble bride of the high Father, be born in us, grow, reach youth, and mature. And, once the son of the handmaid has been cast out with his mother—that is, once the need for temporal supports has ceased after our death—may he, Isaac wholly desirable, alone possess us as his inheritance in the manifestation of his glory, for he is the King of glory. He, strong and mighty in battle, like David mighty by his hand, shall most strongly and powerfully overcome all his enemies in the final judgment by the two-edged sword. He, the Lord of hosts, after judgment has been completed, like Solomon the peaceful king, shall hold a peaceful dominion among the ranks of heavenly powers; with them he, the Lord of hosts and King of glory, shall unite human beings who love virtue. To him be glory now and unto the ages. Amen.

Glory to the Father, the Lord whose mountain is the mountain of the Lord, of which it is said in the psalm: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” Glory to the Son, himself the mountain of the Lord, who, lifted up to the summit of the mountains—that is, exalted above all choirs of angels—is strong and mighty in battle, the Lord of hosts, the King of glory. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that blessing and mercy of which the psalm says: “He shall receive blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his savior” [Col. 1096D]. Glory to the eternity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, of which the everlasting gates are spoken, gates contrary to the gates of hell.

## PSALM XXIV

[Col. 1095]

[Col. 1095D] “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.” Title:

**(VERSE 1.) A PSALM OF DAVID, UNTO THE END.**

With quite fitting order this psalm is ascribed to David in repentance, because it is wholly the prayer of the Church in repentance. For those who have drawn near even to the gates of death and, after the everlasting gates discussed in the preceding psalm have been lifted up, have acknowledged—or still acknowledge—their sins, speak in this psalm and ask that the sins of their youth and their ignorances may not be imputed to them. In these they sinned either with the Pharisees, making God’s commandment void because of human commandments; or by yielding to idolatrous tyrants; or by assenting to heretics; or by accepting forbidden offices and hearing such persons, of whom the Lord says: “All who came were thieves and robbers, and the sheep did not hear them” [Col. 1097A] (John 10:8); or also by failing to hear him himself in true teachers and pastors, of whom the Father’s voice says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Luke 9:35). Whoever recognizes that he has erred in such ways, repents from the heart, and wishes henceforth to walk in the way of truth, is well suited to say in this psalm: “Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths. Guide me in your truth and teach me.”

[Col. 1097B] For, as though coming from the schools of the devil to the school of Christ, he desires to be taught what are the elementary beginnings of the word of God. And just as children being educated first learn their letters, so that, once these are known, they may come through them to know greater things, so David the penitent in this psalm sets forth certain Hebrew elements to be learned at the beginnings of this psalm’s verses. These elements need not now be discussed one by one; God willing, they will be treated more fully in Psalm 118. For the present, in this psalm and in the other psalms entitled by Hebrew elements, let us be content to say this: psalms of this kind are doctrinal and provide moral instruction, some perfectly and others imperfectly. Those which contain all the letters of the Hebrew [Col. 1097C] alphabet do so perfectly; those which have fewer of these elements do so less perfectly. In this psalm few of these elements are lacking. For its first verse begins among the Hebrews with Aleph, and among the Latins likewise has A, the first letter. For thus it begins: “To thee, O Lord”; but in the Latin language it could not be maintained throughout all the verses that the initial letters should correspond.

But since the first verse among the Hebrews begins with Alpha, and the second with Beth, let us join these two letters and interpret them. Alpha is interpreted “doctrine”; Beth, “house.” And what is the doctrine of the house but the doctrine of the Church, of which “all Scripture divinely inspired is useful for teaching and rebuking” (2 Tim. 3:16)?—for teaching what is right, and rebuking what is [Col. 1097D] wrongly done. Yet where these elements are set out successively in Hebrew through the initial letters of the verses—as, for example, in the Lamentations of Jeremiah and in the praise of the strong woman in Ecclesiastes—there is a clearer and fuller presentation of what concerns the teaching of the house of God, which is the Church, than elsewhere in Holy Scripture. Hence likewise among the psalms, those are more doctrinal which possess these initial letters, the first of which means doctrine and the second house, because in them the instruction concerning conduct belonging to the adornment of God’s house is more evident. But these elements must be discussed more fully elsewhere.

This psalm is against the adversities of the age, as though it were the prayer of a people established in Babylon, where the penitent has experienced his evils after chastisements. It is set before [Col. 1098A] others with this purpose: that they may learn not to murmur but to pray amid the adversities of this world, just as David the penitent prays amid adversities when he says: “The tribulations of my heart are multiplied; deliver me from my necessities.” In the first part, lifted up to the Lord, he asks to be taught the Lord’s ways. In the second, he prays for the forgiveness of sins, where he says: “Remember thy mercies.” In the third, he shows how eternal goods are obtained after temporal adversities, where he says: “Who is the man that fears the Lord? He has appointed for him a law in the way which he chose. His soul shall abide in good things.” Therefore let David the penitent speak; let the Church, a pilgrim in this world, speak; and let every penitent person speak:

**VERSE 2.** “To thee, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul. My [Col. 1098B] God, in thee I trust; I shall not be put to shame.” I no longer trust in the traditions of the Pharisees; I do not trust in idols; I do not trust in the sects of heretics; I do not trust in the forbidden masses of Simoniacs and Nicolaitans. But I trust in thee, O Lord; and therefore, having seen the lifting up of the eternal gates, I too, following the example of such persons, have lifted up my soul to thee, O Lord. My soul, hitherto cast down and trampled upon the earth, I have lifted up by seeking and setting my mind on things above. To thee, O Lord—to lay hold of thee and embrace thee—saying in my soul and in my heart: “My beloved, I will seize thee and lead thee into the house of my mother” (Song 8:2). Again: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (ibid. 1:1). By frequently pondering such things, I have lifted up my soul to thee, O Lord.

[Col. 1098C] “My God, in thee I trust; I shall not be put to shame.” My first parents, who, trusting in themselves, wished to be “as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:5), were ashamed of their nakedness when, having themselves become disobedient to God, they also endured the disobedience of their flesh. But now, instructed by disciplines, I do not trust in myself, nor, like Adam, in vain coverings of leaves—that is, of words—but I trust in thee, my God. Though thou wast in the form of God, thou didst empty thyself in order to redeem me, so that thy descent from the heights might become my ascent to the heights; that by dying thou mightest destroy my death and by rising again restore life. Therefore I trust in thee and shall not be put to shame, as Adam was ashamed when he hid himself from thy face. [Col. 1098D] For I, seeking thy face, have lifted up my soul to thee, O Lord, and therefore I trust that I shall be clothed and adorned with the robe of glory, the robe of joy, the white robe, so that I may not be confounded or ashamed. Those were deservedly ashamed and confounded who, when called by thee to repentance, fled and hid themselves amid the trees of paradise. I come to the light, that my works may be reproved; of my own accord I confess and forestall thy face in confession. Therefore I trust and shall not be ashamed.

Let the unhappy Jew be ashamed, who says that Christ was born from Joseph’s seed. Let the unbelieving pagan be ashamed, who says to an idol made by hands, “Thou art my God.” Let the lying heretic be ashamed, refuted by manifest truth. Let those also “be ashamed whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind [Col. 1099A] earthly things” (Phil. 3:19). But I, who trust in thee, shall not be ashamed, deceived by my own vanity.

**VERSE 3.** “Nor let my enemies mock me,” as one overthrown by their deception. For those enemies—the demons or wicked people—who before the commission of sin are persuaders toward the sin itself, become mockers after it has been committed. Since I despise all their most evil suggestions and choose rather those things which the Holy Spirit suggests, therefore I trust in thee, my God, whose Spirit I obey; I shall not be ashamed, nor shall my enemies mock me. Nor is it strange that I trust grace will come to me—a grace bestowed upon many and denied to none who trust in thee. For all who await thee, patiently bearing the burden of the day [Col. 1099B] and the heat of present tribulation until thou comest, shall not be confounded, whether through themselves or through enemies.

Blessed Job awaited thee while thou didst chastise him, and he was not confounded; for after asking that he might be spared, he was at last graciously heard. The apostles awaited thee while thou wast asleep in the ship amid the raging storm of the sea, and they were not confounded, because at last thou didst arise, command the winds and sea, and there was a great calm; and all marvelled. The holy martyrs awaited thee and were not confounded, but were glorified through many miracles, whether before or after death. The blessed confessors awaited thee and were not confounded, because the heretics did not prevail over them, but they themselves prevailed over the heretics. But those who set themselves against thine apostles, [Col. 1099C] martyrs, and confessors were confounded, because they could not accomplish what they intended.

**VERSE 4.** “Let all who act wickedly in vain now also be confounded.” Let them be confounded with a healing confusion in true repentance; let them submit to the commendable discipline within the holy Church. If they refuse to bear it, even if they do not themselves depart from the Church, still let them be cast out from her fellowship, lest they destroy very many by their pestilential contagion; but let them alone remain in their confusion, like Achar son of Charmi, of the tribe of Judah. Because of the secretly committed anathema, he was at last exposed, full in his excessively late confession and deserving of confusion; because he had troubled Israel, he was troubled and condemned when all the people stoned him at the command of Joshua, leader of Israel, [Col. 1099D] who said to him: “Because thou hast troubled us, may the Lord trouble thee this day. And all Israel stoned him; and all that belonged to him was consumed by fire. They also gathered over him a great heap of stones, which remains to this present day. And the anger of the Lord was turned away from them. And the name of that place was called the valley of Achor until this day” (Josh. 7:25 ff.).

Achan was rightly troubled, whose name means “trouble,” and who by his sin had troubled the people of the Lord. Those too are rightly troubled now who resemble that same Achar in the leaven of malice and wickedness: when from such leaven the whole mass is corrupted; when they do not fear to destroy many by the contagion of their plague; when they are unwilling to be corrected from their malice; and when past malice is not enough for them, but, still acting wickedly, they sin in vain—that is, without fruit or benefit. For what fruit have they in those things of which they are ashamed after the deed? Certainly, not only do they derive no fruit of any benefit from their sins; rather, they incur very great losses through and after those sins. For “their end is death” (Rom. 6:21). Therefore this prayer against them, praying that all who act wickedly in vain may be confounded, is made not cruelly but mercifully, lest, left longer unpunished, they perish more abundantly themselves and destroy others by their wicked example. But lest I, David the penitent, perish with such people:

[Col. 1100B] “Show me thy ways, O Lord, and teach me thy paths.” Show me thy ways in the active life through the most luminous examples of thy conduct on earth; and teach me thy paths in the contemplative life, in which the saints desire to behold thy divine face in heaven. Therefore I ask that thy ways be shown me and thy paths taught me, since the active life has level ways, passable even for the simple and therefore easily shown, of which it is said: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118:1). And the contemplative life has narrow paths, close to errors; against those errors it is necessary for me to be taught through many testimonies of truth, concerning which it is said: “Blessed are they who [Col. 1100C] search his testimonies” (ibid. 2).

Again, because the very ways of righteousness are narrow at their entrance, like excessively strait paths, but broaden as one advances—when, through the good habit of living well, one already runs not merely without constraint but even with delight in the way of God’s commandments, and it becomes more pleasant for a holy person to fast than to feast, to weep than to laugh, to endure wrong done to him than to avenge it, to be subject than to preside over good people, and to be reproached rather than praised by the ungodly—I desire that both ways and paths be shown me, that I may run along the broad ways through the narrow paths. But lest, while running, I proceed by winding turns and become one of those of whom it is said, “The wicked walk round about” (Ps. 11:9), therefore:

[Col. 1100D] **VERSE 5.** “Direct me in thy truth,” that I may run straight toward the prize; “and teach me,” lest I should ever be deceived by some appearance of truth in a perverse doctrine. Direct me and teach me alike.

“For thou art God my Savior, and I have awaited thee all the day.” I have stated two things belonging to good merit, through which I desire to obtain what I ask. One is faith, by which I believe that thou art God my Savior: “and in no other is there hope of salvation for me. For neither is there any other name under heaven given to men,” says thine apostle Peter, “whereby we must be saved” (Acts 4:12), apart from thy name, which is Jesus in Greek, Savior in Latin, Soter in Hebrew. [Note: [Col. 1099] Thus the manuscript. Gerhoh meant to write: “Jesus in Hebrew, Savior in Latin, Soter in Greek.”] [Col. 1101A] Therefore I believe that thou art God my Savior. This faith is one component of good merits, by which I believe thee to be Savior.

The other component of good merits is the patience of good conduct, by which I have awaited thee all the day, bearing the burden and heat of the day. I have been protected on right and left by the weapons of righteousness: amid prosperity, I did not place my salvation in temporal success, but held most firmly to this faith by which I believed, and therefore also spoke to others, that thou art God my Savior; and amid adversities I did not fail, nor did I avenge myself through impatience, but I awaited thee all the day, knowing that thou hast said: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Heb. 10:13). [Col. 1101B] Therefore I not only believed thee to be Savior, but also awaited thee as requiter, especially desiring this: that, since all thy ways are mercy and truth, thou wouldst rather repay good for evil through mercy than evil for evil through justice. Accordingly, when I might at times have returned requital to those returning evil to me for good, I was unwilling to be so harsh a requiter, but awaited thee, the merciful requiter, and waited all the day: not reviling in return those who reviled me, nor striking back those who struck me.

Otherwise: “Show me thy ways, O Lord, and teach me thy paths. Direct me in thy truth and teach me.” Thou sayest: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). This is altogether true, because thou art the way in examples and precepts, truth in promises [Col. 1101C] and threats, life in rewards. Therefore, desiring to be led by thy examples and precepts, I say to thee: “Show me thy ways, O Lord, and teach me thy paths,” understanding by ways thy examples, and by paths thy precepts. Again, because thou truly threatenest eternal punishments to the despisers of those same examples and precepts, and truly promisest the rewards of eternal blessedness to their keepers, I say to thee: “Direct me in thy truth,” that I may escape the evils thou truly threatenest and obtain the goods thou truly promisest.

For I know that the ways of thy examples and the paths of thy precepts are health-giving, because thou art God my Savior. I know also that thy promises are sometimes delayed, but never withdrawn. Therefore I have awaited thee all the day, preparing myself with most certain expectation, patience, [Col. 1101D] and endurance to receive thy promises, which I neither doubted nor doubt will come to those to whom they are known to have been promised. For thou hast not promised all things to all persons, but diverse things to different persons: for example, to the poor thou promisest the kingdom of heaven, to those who mourn consolation, and to the merciful mercy.

Yet, accustomed to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep, when I, David, mourned Saul, whom Samuel also mourned, I did not receive consolation, but endured from him a long persecution of twenty years, and came to such desolation that, barely escaping his hand and forced into exile, I had not even one safe place for concealment in the kingdom which had been allotted to me through Samuel’s anointing [Col. 1102A] (1 Sam. 15:35). In such lengthy persecutions I could have laid aside hope of reigning; but knowing thee to be a truthful promiser, who didst swear to me, thy servant David, saying: “I will establish thy seed forever, and build thy throne from generation to generation,” I “awaited thee all the day” (Ps. 88:4–5), bearing the burden and heat of the day in so long a persecution.

Again, when I could have killed that enemy of mine when he was caught in the cave, or found sleeping, I did not do it. I did not hasten thus to reign, that I should put forth my hand against the Lord’s anointed; rather, I awaited thee all the day, considering within myself that I should prefer to await thy chastening in his persecution rather than, by killing him, become a ruler too hasty [Col. 1102B] to reign. For I knew that “an inheritance gotten hastily at the beginning shall lack blessing in the end” (Prov. 20:21).

Likewise I, the penitent Church—or I, any penitent person in the Church—although under the reign of Saul, that is, of death, I was born in sin, through which man brought death upon himself like a raging king, nevertheless through holy baptism, holy oil, chrism, and the mystical Eucharist I received such an anointing that, after the reign of sin and death in me, like Saul’s kingdom, had been destroyed, David’s kingdom—that is, the kingdom of righteousness—ought to have gained strength in me and prevailed over the kingdom of sin. In this hope of reigning, now through strong-handed righteousness and in the future through desirable glory, [Col. 1102C] I have clung to thee, Christ, Son of David, truly strong-handed and desirable, through the common observance of Christianity or even through the more religious life of a spiritual profession.

But though I am thus appointed and anointed king, nevertheless, after receiving the royal anointing in the sacraments of the Lord, I still feel in my flesh the law of sin like Saul’s tyranny, and I hear thine apostle saying to me and to others: “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. 6:18), which is as though he said: Flee Saul’s persecution. Amid so many perils of sins and temptations, distrust has often lain in wait for me, so that I despaired of being able to escape, just as David despaired of escaping when, betrayed and handed over by the Ziphites, he was surrounded on every side like a crown by [Col. 1102D] Saul’s soldiers (1 Sam. 23:19). Yet I have awaited thee all the day, certain of thy promise: thou who by dying didst destroy the reign of sin and death, and first restored the reign of righteousness in thine own body, in which the power of Saul—that is, of death—has so been abolished that death has no further dominion over him. Then thou didst do the same in thy great body, which is the Church, now partly raised in souls and in the bodies of those whose bodies rose with thee, entered the holy city, and appeared to many.

But I am still oppressed by Saul’s condemnation, that is, death’s, which has often attempted to pierce me with its spear against the wall. Yet because I have awaited thee all the day, trusting in thy protection, the deadly [Col. 1103A] spear has been driven into the wall as though its wound were vain. The devil has not been able by any temptation to bring it about that my soul and life should be extinguished through impatience, although the wall of flesh suffers some harm. I feel the spear of death fixed in it for so long as “I see in my members a law contrary to the law of my mind” (Rom. 7:23). But this spear makes a vain wound in the wall of flesh when the law of the mind does not incline to consent to the law of the members. It then slips away through flight when, withdrawing from the law of sin and death by intention and repudiation, it can say: “My sin is always against me” (Ps. 50:5).

This is truly said when the intention [Col. 1103B] of the mind is directed not toward sin but against sin: first, that it may not be committed; second, that it may not remain. Thus the apostle Peter had directed the intention of his mind against sin: first, having the purpose not to deny Christ; second, after the sin had occurred, to condemn it through repentance. Therefore the spear of deadly iniquity was driven, as though with a vain wound, into the wall, because it could not utterly extinguish in the apostle either apostolic faith or that love by which even in that hour he loved Christ, whom he denied with his mouth but not with his heart. Therefore he recovered his senses not late but very quickly, because in his deliberation he had not intended to commit his sin, nor had he approved it once committed; but he could truly say: “I know my iniquity, and my sin is always against me” (ibid. 5).

[Col. 1103C] Then, after thou, Christ, hadst looked upon him, and he received the remedy of pardon by weeping bitterly, he could sing from his heart: “For thou art God my Savior, and I have awaited thee all the day.” I, Peter the penitent, though not knowing whether my repentance had been accepted, nevertheless believed that thou whom I had denied wast God my Savior, and I awaited thee all the day. I did not hasten through impatience, indignation, or excessive sorrow to the noose, as Judas had done, who did not believe thee to be his Savior and did not await thee. Indeed, seeing that thou hadst been condemned by his own betrayal, “he went away and hanged himself with a noose” (Matt. 27:5).

He becomes like Judas who before and after sin seeks an opportunity to accomplish it without hindrance, just as [Col. 1103D] Judas sought an opportunity to betray thee, Christ, without a crowd; and who after sin is strangled by the noose of impenitence. But I, Peter, awaited thee all the day, remaining in the great sadness of repentance and grief, bearing the burden and heat of the day from the ninth hour of Preparation until the morning of the Lord’s resurrection day. And while I thus awaited thee through the whole Sabbath day, and “at the evening of the Sabbath, which was dawning toward the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb” (Matt. 28:1), then my faith and my endurance received their worthy fruit. Then truly, when I had almost despaired, “at the cock’s crow hope returned.” To me “salvation was restored; the robber’s sword” and Saul’s spear “are sheathed; faith returned to one who had fallen.” This cock, the messenger of light, was the angel who said [Col. 1104A] to the women: “Go, tell his disciples and Peter” (ibid. 7). For when I was thus singled out by name among the disciples, then, O Christ, I delighted and was refreshed by that faith through which I had believed thee to be God my Savior; and I was pleased by the endurance through which I had awaited thee all the day, unwilling utterly to despair of my salvation.

I, the penitent Church, or I, any penitent person in the Church, desire to resemble this penitent Peter: that I too, struck in my flesh by death’s spear—as he had been wounded in his tongue when denying thee—may finally experience the fruit of faith by which I, penitent, believe, O Christ, that thou art God my Savior. And although, believing this, I have long been delayed, yet I have awaited thee all the day and still await thee, O Christ, expecting this reward of my endurance [Col. 1104B] and long repentance: that thou mayest deign to number me among thy disciples and make this known to me by a sure announcement, so that from such a message, as at the cock’s crow, hope may return to me and salvation be restored to me in my sickness. May the robber’s sword—he who often wounds the tongue through loquacity, the throat through gluttony, and has a continual, habitual practice of wounding the whole wall of flesh through the law of the members—may that robber’s sword, I say, or Saul’s, that is, death’s, at the cock’s crow be sheathed so that it is no longer fixed in the wall of my flesh; and may faith be restored to me who have fallen.

Not that this faith has altogether perished in me—the faith for whose failure in Peter Christ prayed—but because this faith remains languid so long as Christ does not appear alive to that faith; rather, he lies before it as though dead and [Col. 1104C] buried, when invoked in prayers but not making himself present through manifest effects of mercies. Therefore I desire that faith be restored to me and roused as though from sleep, so that Christ, dead and buried for me through three days and three nights—that is, through three sorts of temptation, impurity, curiosity, and pride, harassing me through prosperity and adversity—may now at last rise for me and appear alive, just as, risen from the dead, he appeared to Peter and to the other disciples, “who rejoiced when they saw the Lord” (John 20:20). He presented himself not merely to be seen but also to be touched, saying: “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).

For Christ appears to have only spirit and not flesh and bones when he makes the solemn day of his resurrection for us solely in invisible and spiritual benefits. These spiritual benefits could indeed make us abundantly joyful if, immediately upon receiving them, we were granted to depart and be with Christ, which is best. But because for good people living in the flesh here is fruitful labor, and is itself necessary for the improvement of others still needing improvement, we for whom “to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21)—indeed, we for whom life in the flesh is necessary so that, after many fruits of works, death may be gainful rather than harmful—need the twofold consolation of the Lord’s resurrection. Namely, just as on the day of resurrection [Col. 1105A] he breathed his Spirit upon the disciples, and also showed them his hands, feet, side, flesh, and bones for seeing and touching, so, for as long as it is necessary that we remain in the flesh for the fruit of our work, may he never cease to breathe his Spirit upon us, through whom “love may blaze with fire, and ardor kindle our neighbors.” May he also visibly and tangibly show us his hands, feet, side, flesh, and bones through the visible and tangible benefits of his mercy, by which we may be helped worthily to celebrate the paschal joys, comforted and gladdened not only by the invisible but also by the visible and tangible presence of divine mercy in this festival of the Lord. It is to be celebrated by us in white through the seven days of this present life, as through an entire week, [Col. 1105B] so that no dishonorable stain of shame or blackness may be found in us.

When, in the universal resurrection, the whole week of the Lord’s resurrection has been completed, the saints will then have no need of visible or tangible appearances of Christ. Rather, just as Christ himself vanished from the disciples’ eyes after presenting himself to be seen and touched, so then all his visible benefits will vanish, since they will no longer be necessary. But meanwhile, at the cock’s crow and Christ’s visible appearing, “we have become as those comforted; then our mouth was filled with joy and our tongue with exultation” (Ps. 125:1–2), when we have been helped so manifestly that among the nations it would be said of us: “The Lord has done great things with them”; [Col. 1105C] and it was said by us or our people: “The Lord has done great things with us; we have become joyful” (ibid. 3).

For, to turn to my own particular circumstances, did not the cock crow well for me when those who troubled me were multiplied, and many rising up against me said to my soul: “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Ps. 3:3)? By their prejudgments I was condemned as a schismatic and heretic. Among such people, I was as cold as Peter in Caiaphas’s courtyard, surrounded by the servants of Antichrist and with friends standing far off. When my night was thus cold and the enemies’ coals were suspect to me, behold, amid the sorrows of black night, the cock crowed: the Roman pontiff, having heard the persecutions and the causes of the persecutions, [Col. 1105D] sent me letters of consolation containing the following:

> “CELESTINE, [Note: [Col. 1105D] Celestine II, elected pope 25 September 1143; died 8 March 1144.] bishop, servant of the servants, to his beloved son GERHOH, provost of Reichersberg: greetings and the apostolic blessing.
>
> “We have learned, through the testimony of our beloved son G., cardinal deacon, of the tribulations and afflictions which you endure for the defense of truth and justice. We sympathize with you in paternal affection and willingly offer you assistance and counsel in such matters as we can, according to God. You ought to possess so much the greater patience in these matters, as it is more certain [Col. 1106A] that your diligence endures these same persecutions in defense of justice. For you know that it is neither new nor unusual that, according to the Apostle, those who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3:12),” from the wicked and unlike persons, whom the Lord consoles in the Gospel by promising them eternal blessedness: “Blessed,” he says, “are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:10). Yet in fulfillment of our office we desire to oppose your adversaries and restrain them by ecclesiastical censure. Therefore, by this present letter, we command you to appear before us on the next Sunday, on which is read, ‘I am the good Shepherd,’ so that, after learning the case more fully from you in person, we may provide for your peace and tranquility and be able to assist you fittingly as a beloved son.”

Summoned by this letter, I came to the Apostolic See; but I found Pope Celestine already dead. Pope Lucius had succeeded him, [Note: [Col. 1106D] Lucius II, elected pope 12 March 1144; died 25 February 1145.] and by his own consolations he too became for me a morning cock, as may be known from his letter, which reads as follows:

> “LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren CONRAD, archbishop of Salzburg, and Roman, bishop of Gurk: greetings and the apostolic blessing.
>
> “We received with paternal kindness at the Apostolic See our beloved son Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg; honoring his person because of his religious devotion and integrity, we sent him back to his own place with the favor of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1106C] Therefore, earnestly commending him to your brotherhood by this present letter, we ask that, just as until now you have done on the grounds of his religious devotion and integrity alone, so henceforth, for the reverence of blessed Peter and of ourselves, you may honor and love him, and provide him assistance and counsel in his necessities.”

The same venerable Pope Lucius, while he was still a cardinal priest, had been for me a nocturnal cock, who had sent me from the Apostolic See a nocturnal cock-crow in the following terms:

> “Concerning the abuses and abominations that are now committed in the Church of God, reverend brother, you have noted much in writing, and you could have noted more; for, as our sins deserve, far more occurs in this perilous time than in the days of [Col. 1106D] our fathers. These things are committed so much more freely and frequently because there are none, or very few, who rise up against them and stand in battle on the day of the Lord by setting themselves as a wall for the house of Israel. Therefore we believe that Antichrist has either already come or will come soon; as is read in Job, want precedes his face—want, namely, of virtues and virtuous persons—so that he may carry out his will more freely because there is almost no one to oppose him.
>
> “Meanwhile, good brother, your religious devotion, trained from its cradle in sacred letters, does not fail to know what you ought to do. But I see what I myself must do—and would that I may do it!—and I advise you as a most dear brother: with the Lord’s help, let us avoid the abominations that are committed, and grieve over those who commit them, so that the man clothed in linen, of whom Ezekiel speaks, may mark Tau upon our foreheads and we may not be slain.”

We have said these things about our own particular affairs, lest we appear ungrateful for the gratuitous clemency of God, who, as is read in Job, “gave the cock understanding” (Job 38:36) to distinguish between light and darkness. For unless I had been defended through the pontiffs of the Apostolic See or through certain understanding cocks, I should long ago have been proscribed by the Simoniac and Nicolaitan heretics.

But if we look at the great darkness of Antichrist, [Col. 1107B] in which works of darkness were freely done by those who sold and bought ecclesiastical and spiritual things, to whom night was friendly and light hateful, and who worked deeds of darkness in beds and uncleannesses: was not Pope Gregory VII like a nocturnal cock, crowing amid the darkness of persecutions by forbidding lay investitures and the masses of incestuous men? After him many morning cock-crows followed through his successors, announcing the approaching day, as though they said: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast away the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. 13:12). What now remains to be awaited and desired after cock-crows of this kind, [Col. 1107C] except that “the robber’s sword may be sheathed, faith may return to those who have fallen, the day-star may arise, the darkness of the sky may dissolve, the sailor may gather strength, the straits of the sea may grow calm, and the whole chorus of errors may abandon its way of doing harm”?

When all these things have been invisibly and eternally predestined, they will also be visibly and, as it were, tangibly displayed to believers. Just as the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord and exulted when they touched him after the resurrection, so now the faithful may exult who, before these things came to pass, possessed a certain expectation of such consolations, as though awaiting Christ’s resurrection and appearance. Their shepherd, the shepherd of his faithful, is struck as often as his flock is scattered in desolation, as it is written: “I will strike the shepherd, and [Col. 1107D] his sheep shall be scattered” (Matt. 26:31). And, rising again, he goes before them into Galilee as often as they may there see alive him whom they grieved to see struck—as often as his mercy, preceding all human merits, displays itself to them as though to be seen and touched in Galilee, that is, in a completed crossing-over. For Galilee is interpreted “a completed crossing-over.” In this crossing-over the consolation of the Lord’s flock is brought to completion after the striking and resurrection of the Shepherd, when to those who cross over from evils to goods, or from goods to better things, the Shepherd appears alive in that same crossing-over, saying thus: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18). This is to be believed and confessed—that he says this to such an extent, and his disciples hear it to such an extent, as what Christ commands, to whom all power in heaven and [Col. 1108A] on earth has been given, is done on earth as in heaven.

That which the holy apostles experienced magnificently when, sent out into the whole world to preach the Gospel to every creature, they found no power in all creation able to hinder or delay them as they went throughout the world preaching the Gospel. For although one of them might be bound—Peter by Herod, Paul by Nero—the word of God was not bound, but exercised its dominion in every creature. For as Christ, rising from the dead, had gone before his disciples into Galilee, so, once the transfer from the Jews to the Gentiles had been accomplished, the Gospel chariot swiftly outstripped the oxen by which it was to be drawn, with [Col. 1108B] such power in heaven and on earth that even the spiritual powers of wickedness in the heavenly places were terrified and were compelled to depart from possessed bodies or temples, when “your voice of thunder, O God, was in the wheel” (Ps. 76:19).

The Gospel chariot also thundered in places where none of the apostles taught in person, and earthly powers yielded to the flashing forces of miracles, as it were from the fiery chariot of the true Elijah—sometimes unable, sometimes unwilling, to resist the rushing Gospel chariot. Through such most evident displays of power, in the apostles’ transfer to the Gentiles, Christ was then clearly seen in Galilee exercising authority in heaven and on earth: aiding his own by heavenly gifts, so that they lacked nothing in any [Col. 1108C] grace; and by visible miracles, through which the earth was enlightened, so that God, formerly known only in Judaea, is now known throughout the whole world.

Rightly, therefore, the disciples rejoiced at such great evidence of God’s benefits when they saw the Lord. Rightly too do we, disciples of whatever sort, grieve when we do not see the Lord, because, our sins demanding it, he is so hidden from us that, deprived of divine and human help, we are distressed and do not know what we ought to do. Hence we can rightly say with the holy Maccabees: “The nations have gathered in a multitude to fight against us, and we do not know what we ought to do” (1 Macc. 3:17).

When the pillar of fire in the holy martyrs during the night [Col. 1108D] of persecution, and the pillar of cloud in the holy confessors during the day of tranquillity, went before the people through this desert of the world, “when Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people” (Ps. 113:1), believers could not, amid such certainty of events, fail to know what they ought to do against tyrants or against heretics. Now the perils of the Maccabees have been multiplied in the Church, and there is no certain escape from these dangers. For just as “King Antiochus wrote to all his kingdom that all the people should be one” (1 Macc. 1:43), so now, through the efforts of the devil and Antichrist, it is being brought about that all the people should be one and that there should be no distinction between priest and people: but, as the people is, so should the priest be, with no difference preserved between holy and unholy—for example, between the holy, non-interdicted Masses of Catholic priests and the interdicted, and therefore unholy, Masses of hired and incestuous priests. [Col. 1109A] Amid these things, “we do not know what we ought to do.”

And this ignorance is greatly increased because Christ, the conqueror of death, is manifested neither in interdicted nor in non-interdicted Masses, while neither side is overcome by the other. For both those and these hold churches, and both those and these chant Masses. This time seems like that time when Christ lay in the tomb and manifested his presence neither among the Jewish enemies nor among the friendly disciples—although he was present with his enemies to condemn them, and with his friends to preserve them. Yet because [Col. 1109B] this presence of his was hidden, his disciples, astonished and forgetful of the promises by which they had heard that Christ would rise again, did not know what they ought to do.

Thus their faith, which had died before Christ’s death, would not have been revived when he rose unless the visible and tangible flesh of the living Christ had appeared to them and distinguished his disciples from their Jewish enemies: to these he breathed his Spirit, but not to those; to these he offered himself to be seen and touched, but not to those; with these he ate and drank, but not with those; to these he appeared “by many proofs for forty days” (Acts 1:3), but to those he did not appear; these rejoiced on seeing the Lord, those did not; these he blessed as he ascended into heaven, those he did not; to these he sent from heaven the Paraclete, by whose consolation their sorrow was changed into joy, but not to those.

By all these things and the other proofs of the divine appearance, the apostles, Christ’s friends—to whom he himself had said, “I shall no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15)—were made distinct from their Jewish enemies. The friends rejoiced in the presence and manifest evidence of divine mercies appearing over them; conversely, the enemies were tortured by envy, deprived of such benefits of God as they saw, and envied, abounding in the apostles and other Christians.

Therefore, that a like distinction may be made between the ministers of Antichrist—especially those interdicted by the Roman pontiffs—and the ministers of Christ under the obedience of the prince of the apostles, who seek not their own interests but [Col. 1109D] those of Jesus Christ: I, the Church, or I, an ecclesiastical person, believing concerning you, O Christ, that you are God my Saviour, for whom I have waited all day, no longer able to bear the burden of this your overlong burial—the day and its heat—unless I am aided by your mercies and by clear, visible, tangible manifestations of those mercies, now cry to you:

**VERSE 6.** Remember your compassions, O Lord, and your mercies, which are from everlasting.

Above I indeed put forward merits of whatever kind I possess: namely, faith and waiting—faith by which I believed that you are God my Saviour; waiting by which I waited for you all day. But because I distrust the quality of my merits, I flee to your mercy, [Col. 1110A] that by your mercy I may obtain what I did not deserve through my own righteousness—indeed, what I am proved utterly to have forfeited, if you remember my offences and forget your mercy. Therefore I say: “Remember your compassions, O Lord, and your mercies, which are from everlasting.”

I know that you are merciful unto thousands, taking away iniquities and sins. I know that you are just, “repaying the sins of the fathers in the children unto the third and fourth generation” (Deut. 5:9); and again I know that you are merciful, not unto the third and fourth generation, but unto many thousands of generations. Hence holy Moses says to you truly that you are “merciful unto thousands, taking away iniquities and sins” (Exod. 34:7). “Our fathers sinned” [Col. 1110B] in Paradise, “and are no more” (Lam. 5:7).

For, dead through sins in their souls and made mortal in their bodies, they passed from blessed being to miserable being, which is as though not to be; and therefore they are no more. Yet “we have borne their iniquities” (ibid.), since we have imitated them in the third and fourth generation of iniquities: by evil will, evil deed, evil habit, or—what is worst—by the defence of evils.

And you are our Father, through whose love—namely, by the Holy Spirit’s cooperation—we have been reborn in baptism through your blood. You are our Father, the bridegroom who has children, concerning whom you say: “The children of the bridegroom cannot fast while the [Col. 1110C] bridegroom is with them” (Mark 2:19). You are our Father, who say to us: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 33:12). And you have not passed from blessed being into miserable being, or into non-being. Rather, from this world, in which miserable being exists, you passed to the Father, where you remain for ever; and you have prepared eternal dwellings for your own, to whom you yourself said: “If I go and prepare a place for you, I come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, you also may be” (John 14:3).

Therefore you are our Father in eternal and blessed being, where you prepare dwellings for your own. And if we have borne the iniquities of our fathers, who sinned and are no more, much more is it possible—indeed necessary and unavoidable—that we should bear your virtues, O our Father who are in heaven, who together with your Father [Col. 1110D] and the Holy Spirit are one Father to us, your children. For as, while we were sold under sin, the burden of paternal iniquity hung over us, so now, redeemed, your apostle says to us: “You were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your members” (1 Cor. 6:20).

O how different is the bearing by which we formerly bore sin and that by which we are now admonished to bear God, not only in mind but also in our body! We bore sin like a leaden weight pressing us downward; let us now bear God not only in mind but also in body. “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:16). Let us bear love, not like a heavy burden, but [Col. 1111A] like the silvered wings of a dove, so that with the twin wings of love we may not be weighted downward but raised upward, where Christ is our Father, whose children we are and whose hereditary inheritance is ours.

For as we inherited ignobility from an ignoble father through justice, so now we have inherited nobility from a noble Father, likewise through justice—a justice that has truly kissed mercy, because such justice exists only from mercy. For although it is just that a righteous and noble father should confer the inheritance of righteousness and nobility upon his children, yet, because we were by nature children of wrath, mercy and compassion alone brought it about that we are now adopted children of grace: that is, made children through the superabundant grace of your compassions, O Lord, and of your mercies, which are [Col. 1111B] from everlasting. Therefore they suffice to blot out the sins of those who sinned and are no more.

Your compassions, in the bestowal of works, I do not say were, but are from everlasting: they have never failed and never will fail in the world. And because you are compassionate and merciful—compassionate in an outwardly visible effect, merciful in the inwardly hidden disposition of kindness naturally inherent in you—as you are he who is, so your compassions and mercies are what they are. And as “you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101:28), so your compassions, “which are from everlasting,” are not changeable, and their years shall not fail.

Yet there are certain fools who seek from you, the everlasting [Col. 1111C] compassionate one, not everlasting mercy, but merely temporal and brief mercy. The prophet rebukes them, saying: “Your mercy is like a morning cloud, and like dew passing away in the morning” (Hos. 6:4). The Jews sought such mercy for themselves, desiring to prosper in this world; and therefore they rejected Christ, because they did not find in him a giver of that sort of mercy. For he did not promise his disciples worldly prosperity in this world, but said: “In the world you will have tribulation” (John 16:33). Again: “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but now, because you are not of the world, the world hates you” (ibid. 15:19). Again: “You will be hated by all because of my name. For they will hand you over to councils, [Col. 1111D] and flog you in synagogues” (Matt. 10:17).

But you Jews, who said: “Lest perhaps the Romans come and take away our place and our nation” (John 11:48), loving a beautiful place, the beauty of the Temple, and the populous multitude of the nation, exchanged the long mercy of blessedness which Christ offered you for one brief and swiftly passing. For “like dew passing away in the morning and like a morning cloud” (Hos. 6:4), your desirable things, your objects of desire, passed away—things in whose abundance and continuance God appeared merciful to you. But because you preferred such mercy to the eternal mercy and compassions which are from everlasting, you found neither eternal mercy nor were you able long to retain that brief mercy which you loved. For the fear you feared came upon you, and what you dreaded happened, when the Romans came and took away your place and nation: they destroyed your place in a most cruel devastation, leaving not one stone upon another, and killed part of your nation, dispersing the rest as captives among all nations. [Col. 1112A]

But I, the Church—or I, an ecclesiastical person—will sing the mercies of the Lord for ever. Seeking in this psalm of David the sure mercies of David, I say to you, O Christ, giver of eternal mercy: Remember your compassions, O Lord, and your mercies, which are from everlasting. For they did not come with the world, nor will they depart with the world; but they were before all ages, are from everlasting in the age, and after this age will remain through all ages of ages: the riches of your compassions and your mercies, which are from everlasting. For you grant to your elect and beloved ones gifts that are greatest, intermediate, and least.

The greatest are those shared by chosen human beings with the holy angels: love, humility, holiness, obedience, wisdom, and perseverance in all these things. In such gifts, which remain for ever, I shall sing your mercies, O Lord, for ever; and we praise your mercies, which are from everlasting.

Intermediate goods are those which good people may share with angels and wicked people: such as bodily chastity, which is very often [Col. 1112C] found in wicked people; knowledge, which, when it puffs up, plainly has place in evil hearts no less than in good ones, though it puffs up evil hearts, while it does not puff up good hearts because of the edifying love dwelling there. Fasting, much prayer, giving many alms, writing well, or exercising any other human craft, are common to good and wicked alike. But together with these common gifts, the saints possess a gift not shared with the wicked, a gift always good: namely, using good and evil things well. Conversely, wicked people possess this vice, always evil: using good and evil things badly.

The least gifts of God are shared by us even with cattle, such as bodily health, sustained by food and drink in humans no less than in beasts; [Col. 1112D] and strength of the senses, in which many wild animals or domestic beasts surpass even healthy human beings. The lynx and gazelle excel in keenness of sight; dogs in smell; deer and goats in taste; the mole in touch; and many animals in hearing. In bodily clothing too, certain irrational animals are naturally so equipped and adorned that not even Solomon in all his glory was covered as one of them. What royal purple is so adorned as a peacock’s tail?

> And you, who show the night’s downward course  
> with the light of feathers like a shining lamp.

[*hernica*, perhaps an OCR corruption; likely *cernua*, “downward-bending.”]

You surpass not only other birds in the brightness of your white plumage, but you are more splendid even than kings’ garments gleaming with gold. People often glory greatly if they have coverings or garments in abundance made [Col. 1113A] from the grey, mottled, white, or red pelts of foreign mice. Yet in that abundance they do not possess adornment as stable and enduring as these mice possess; for such skins, once stripped from the mice, quickly grow old, whereas they last long upon the mice while nature preserves them.

Abundance in such goods is God’s transient mercy, quickly passing “like a morning cloud and like dew passing away in the morning.” Nevertheless, to use such things well is a great gift of God; to despise them and regard them as little in choosing better things is a greater gift of God; but not to need them at all, and wholly to forget them because of the greatness of eternal joy, is a very great gift of God. And this great, greater, and greatest gift is not from the abundant fountain of your compassions, O Lord, and of your mercies, which are from everlasting; for they are, and will pass away with temporal goods, while those who become great through their use, greater through their contempt, or greatest through their forgetfulness of them.

Therefore, O Lord, you did not ask that your own be taken out of the world, but that they be preserved from evil, so that, living in the world and using the good and evil things of the world well, they might become great; or, despising them, might become greater; or, wholly forgetting them and having their citizenship in heaven and their heart above, might be greatest (John 17:15). [Col. 1113B]

Therefore, when your apostles were thus great, greater, and greatest, they were already to be transferred from the world because of their merits; but through those who were great you wished to gain others who were great [Col. 1113C] (John 21). Thus, when at your command after the resurrection they cast the net on the right side of the boat, one hundred and fifty-three great fish were caught. This was a great consolation to the fishers, who demonstrated by a visible result that you who had told them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat,” were the Lord (ibid., v. 6). Therefore, seeing this miracle, John said to Peter: “It is the Lord.”

For the fishing had first involved great difficulty, so that your appearance, O Lord, might become more welcome, lightening such labour and gathering into one net one hundred fish as though great, fifty as though greater, and three as though greatest. For although the number of those who use temporal good and evil things well is greater, and the number of those who despise those things is smaller, while the number of those who wholly forget them through ecstasy of mind and through the gentle whisper of the thin breeze—which few saints perceive with Elijah, who are transported in mind to God and are caught in contemplation of the supreme Trinity as though three greatest fish—is very small: nevertheless, those who are greater in number are lesser in the quality of their merits. Thus the hundred fish signify good people who use the world well; fewer in number but greater in merit are those represented by the fifty fish, who, despising the world, celebrate the Jubilee consecrated to remission and festive rest. But those who, through the vision of the Trinity, are transported in mind to God—even while remaining in the flesh, though only swiftly and briefly, yet most sweetly receiving an experience of eternal blessedness—are like three fish, fewest in number but greatest in merit. [Col. 1114A]

Accordingly, the apostolic net, cast at the Lord’s command on the right side of the boat, gathered these three classes of great fish, numbering one hundred and fifty-three. For the apostles, having become all things to all people, according to this threefold distinction of fish, were greater with those who despised these things, and greatest with those who are now sober among men and now transported in mind to God. Thus they were most fully enriched with every treasure of your compassions, O Lord, and of your mercies, which are from everlasting. These were manifested after your resurrection, for the consolation of your disciples and the instruction of the whole Church, in the fishing just described and in many other proofs during forty days; and they were consummated on the fiftieth day by the coming of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1114B]

Therefore I, the penitent Church—or I, a penitent ecclesiastical person—fear that I am not, O God, in your remembrance, because, as I lament your death and burial and fish as it were in vain, you do not reveal yourself to me in such a way that the net of my preaching or prayer, cast out, becomes full of one hundred and fifty-three great fish. For I, David—I, the penitent one—I who sing this psalm of David, do not in myself possess such virtues as I understand to be prefigured in those one hundred and fifty-three great fish; nor do I see the holy Church abounding in such persons that the multitude and greatness of one hundred and fifty-three fish may be expressed by their number and merit. But “the fewness of my days comes to an end quickly” (Job 10:20), because I too abound in few or no fruits of virtue, and see few virtuous persons in the net of the Church.

Therefore, because of the magnitude of particular and common miseries, I am compelled to fear, O Christ, lest perhaps we are forgotten before you. Thus we say with Jeremiah: “Remember, O Lord, what has happened to us; look and behold our reproach. Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses to foreigners. We have become orphans without a father; our mothers are like widows. We drink our water for money, and we have bought our wood [Col. 1114D] at a price. We were threatened at our necks; no rest was given to the weary. We gave the hand to Egypt and to the Assyrians, that we might be filled with bread. Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities. Our servants have ruled over us, and there was none to redeem us from their hand.
