In our hands [Vulgate: *in animabus*, ‘in our souls/lives’] we carried our bread for ourselves, because of the sword in the wilderness. Our skin was scorched like an oven because of the storms of famine. They humiliated women in Zion, virgins in the cities of Judah. Princes were hanged by the hand; they did not honour the faces of elders. They abused young men shamefully, and their boys fell under the wood. Elders failed in [Vulgate: ‘ceased from’] the gates, young men from the choir of singers. The joy of our heart has failed; our dance [Col. 1115A] has been turned into mourning. The crown of our head has fallen. Woe to us, because we have sinned. Therefore our heart has become sorrowful in grief; therefore our eyes have grown dark. Because Mount Zion has been laid waste, foxes have walked upon it. But you, O Lord, remain for ever; your throne endures from generation to generation. Why will you forget us for ever, abandon us for length of days? Turn us, O Lord, to yourself, and we shall be turned; renew our days as in the beginning. But in rejecting, you have cast us off; you are exceedingly angry against us” (Lam. 5:1 ff.).

To this lamentation or prayer of weeping Jeremiah, I, the penitent one, add this saying of the Psalmist: Remember your compassions, O Lord, and your mercies, [Col. 1115B] which are from everlasting. I do not ask for light or brief compassions; I do not desire to catch few or small fish in my fishing, when I offer, O Christ, the singular sacrifice of your body and blood, or when I pour out other prayers before you and pray for the acquiring of virtues or the conversion of people, yet gain nothing or little. Nothing remains but to await your consolation and manifestation—you who now stand upon the shore of eternal stability, seeing your own labouring in fruitless fishing. At times you seem as though to despise them because you remember our sins and are forgetful toward us of your compassions, which are from everlasting.

Therefore, so that in the catch of great fish—that is, great virtues and great persons—there may be for us assured [Col. 1115C] and open consolation, and that our sorrow may wholly be turned into joy, our joy made full, and that joy taken from us by no one: Remember your compassions, O Lord, and your mercies, which are from everlasting; they do not pass away with the world. For as you stand upon the firm shore, with you stands the steadfastness of your compassions, O Lord, and of your mercies, which are from everlasting.

But lest such great goods be hindered by my faults, carefully written in the book of your remembrance:

**VERSE 7.** Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances.

I, Peter, when I was younger, girded myself and walked where I wished, because I presumed upon my own strength; therefore, as often as I presumed, so often [Col. 1115D] did I deny you. I presumed three times, and three times, fearing death, I denied you who are life. Indeed, this fear was—or, if it was not, could have been—in the heart of Peter, repenting of the sin of youth in which he had girded himself while young: namely, that the Lord, who formerly said to him when he doubted and was endangered on the sea, “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14:31), might now say to him at that fishing, when, as the Lord appeared, Simon Peter went up and drew the net to land full of great fish: “O you of little faith, why did you deny me?”

Therefore, it was fitting for Peter, repenting and fearing the reproach of his denial before the seven fellow disciples who had been companions in that fishing—when at the meal of broiled fish and bread none of those reclining dared ask Jesus who he was, knowing [Col. 1116A] “that it is the Lord” (John 21:7)—it was fitting, I say, for Peter there, fearing the reproach of his sins, to pray thus: O Lord, who have now made known to us in this great success of fishing that you are the Lord: you whom I denied as Lord and Master when I denied that I was your disciple, remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances. For I acknowledge that through a certain youthful presumption, without the maturity of old age’s deliberation, when I was young I girded myself for a task beyond me, forgetting the proverb which says: “Let not one who is girding himself boast as one who is taking off his armour” (3 Kings 20:11).

For, girded with the sword of youthful presumption, with which I, like a most daring young man, cut off the right ear of the servant named Malchus, I thought myself the bravest among my fellow disciples. But all that strength of mine utterly vanished at the question of a single maidservant; and it then became entirely evident to me that the strength of human presumption is nothing without divine aid. But I had been ignorant of this while I thought myself to be something or capable of something. Thus ignorance was mingled in me with youthful boldness. Therefore remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances, since it is fitting that you should be ready to forgive what was presumed, not through the cunning of impiety, but through a certain youthful ignorance. [Col. 1116B]

What do you say, Peter? Do you wish the sin of threefold denial to be so given over to oblivion that your physician has no remembrance or care for healing your wounds? “Far be this from me,” you say, “but I wish and desire that my sins should not be in the judge’s recollection for vengeance. Yet I earnestly pray that they may be in the physician’s memory for healing; or rather, that such oblivion of my sins may take place before the Lord that before him there may be a merciful remembrance of me, repenting for those same sins.” I believe each to be good for me; therefore, seeking each, I say: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances”—which is one good.

“And according to your mercy remember me, for your goodness’ sake, O Lord.” This is the other good. From consideration of this twofold benefit I am accustomed elsewhere to say: “Turn your face away [Col. 1116D] from my sins,” which is one good; “and do not cast me away from your face” (Ps. 50:11, 13), which is the other good. Therefore, as there I ask that God’s face be turned away from my sins but not from myself, so now I pray that my sins, but not I myself, may be forgotten. Therefore I say: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances,” and add: “According to your mercy remember me, for your goodness’ sake, O Lord.”

And that you may know that the Lord is accustomed to hear the desire of the poor concerning each of these goods, and that his ear hears the preparation of their heart in such matters, observe how he heard the preparation and desire of my heart—he who heard me thinking such things. For when the meal was ended, the Lord rose from the place of the meal, [Col. 1117A] and I, Peter, conscious of my threefold denial, waited fearfully to see what the Lord would say to me. I was indeed ready to follow in his footsteps, yet did not dare presume anything of myself.

Then he, forgetting my sins but remembering me, said: “Follow me” (John 21:22); that is, imitate me. Though I was God most strong, I nevertheless approached my Passion without any presumption, in the contrition of great humility, having first offered prayer that, if it were the Father’s will, the cup of the Passion might pass from me. You therefore, who wished to go before me in your youth when you girded yourself and walked where you wished, now follow me, so that the healing humility of your following may cure the wounds of your presumption.

And because your heart’s desire is that I should be wholly forgetful of your sins but mindful of you, behold, I repay you good for evil. For you, who when I was dying were found weaker than the rest, will now, when I have risen, be stronger than the rest, so that what I foretold you may be fulfilled: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have at last turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). [Col. 1117B]

Nevertheless, because I am accustomed to show mercy in such a manner that I never forget justice, you who denied me three times must confess me three times; and let this threefold confession be just satisfaction for your threefold denial. After the threefold confession, because I have accepted your repentance, I impose a threefold obedience upon you, saying twice: “Feed my lambs,” and a third time: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:15, 16, 17).

For the same distinction that existed among the one hundred and three fish is now understood in the lambs and sheep. I appoint you fisherman and shepherd for them all, so that you may draw them from the sea-like waves of this world as great fish caught on the right side of the boat, and feed them in most fertile pastures as lambs and sheep to be set at the right hand. [Col. 1117C]

O Peter the apostle, how blessed we may judge you when we see the fruit of your repentance! For you chiefly experienced in yourself that the Lord is sweet and upright: sweet, because he graciously forgave you your threefold denial; upright, because after your threefold confession of love for him he rightly promoted you to the episcopate of the whole world. But because in your person the pattern of the penitent Church, or of any penitent person, is prefigured, gracious shepherd, bring it about that the things assigned to you in this Psalm may fittingly apply to us, sheep or lambs entrusted to you.

And you, O Christ, who so faithfully entrusted us, the sheep of your pasture, to so faithful a shepherd, to be fed with a threefold feeding according to the threefold distinction of fish, lambs, and sheep: feed us through him in such a way that, from manifest evidence of events, we may perceive that the prayers of the Church—or of any penitent person saying with penitent David and penitent Peter, “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances”—have been heard. [Col. 1117D]

For “youth” here is used not so much for age as for youthful boldness, by which we often knowingly abandon the way [Col. 1118A] of righteousness and incur many sins of youth. “Ignorance,” however, is called such when we do not know that what we are doing is evil; or when infants do not know that original sin is in them before baptism; or rather, the ignorance intended here is that of which the Apostle says: “What I do, I do not understand” (Rom. 7:15), that is, I do not approve it.

We suffer many such ignorances when, in eating, drinking, speaking, or sleeping, we slip into excess contrary to the purpose of our intention or approval, by not keeping lawful limits in lawful things. Such ignorances, O God, remember not; for “if you should observe” such “iniquities, O Lord, who shall endure?” (Ps. 129:3). Remember not my sins and ignorances, O Lord, according to [Col. 1118B] your wrath; but according to your mercy remember me, that you may say to me what you said to Peter: “Follow me.” Say it, and by saying make me follow you.

Also bring it about that, as he loved you sufficiently and confessed his love a third time to blot out his threefold denial, so I, purified from my iniquity in the fervent ardour of your love and in sincere confession, may be found worthy of that feeding of which it was said to Peter: “Feed my lambs,” or “my sheep.” I do not ask that pastoral care be entrusted to me as it was entrusted to him. But I ask this: that upon those to whom I owe feeding, or to whom I shall ever owe it, I may bestow a sufficient and necessary *passionem* [suffering], so that none of your lambs or sheep may be able or ought to raise against me the bleating of a just complaint; and that the shepherds set over me or yet to be set over me, or preferred to your other lambs and sheep, may feed me, your humble little sheep borne back on their shoulders to the fold, and all the flock entrusted or to be entrusted to them, so that in the Church that threefold feeding may be fully accomplished, of which Peter was told for the third time: “Feed my lambs,” or “my sheep.”

Let continual vigilance in shepherds’ hearts be, as it were, one or the first feeding of lambs and sheep. Let the holy and blameless conduct of shepherds be the second feeding of the flocks entrusted to them. Let a most fitting measure of wheat in preaching likewise be the third feeding.

[Col. 1118D] Otherwise: Let the first feeding nourish the very little lambs in such a way that those “who have” worldly goods may be “as though they had not,” and those “who use this world, as though they did not use it; those who rejoice, as though not rejoicing; those who weep, as though not weeping” (1 Cor. 7:29–31). And because “the form of this world is passing away,” lest they too pass away and perish with it, let them use the world in such a manner that they never misuse it.

Let the somewhat larger lambs be nourished by the second feeding of pastoral care so that, mindful of Lot’s wife, after renouncing the world they may not look back; nor, having put hand to the plough and looking back, may they deserve exclusion from the kingdom of God. Rather, forgetting what lies behind and stretching forth to what lies ahead, let them run for the prize so as to grasp it; let them abstain from everything not expedient, so as to receive the incorruptible [Col. 1119A] crown.

By the third feeding let the sheep, greater both than the larger and the smaller lambs, be nourished in such a way that there is “none barren among them,” but that “all abound in twin births” (Song 4:2), to which they may supply their milk abundantly. For we recognize that sheep of this sort signify in the Church those who are most perfect and most strong from the fact that, in the Song of Songs, the bridegroom says to his bride: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep, which come up from the washing; all have twin births, and none among them is barren” (ibid., 6:5). Therefore, since sheep are compared to teeth, by whose service the whole body is fed—or teeth to sheep—we clearly recognize that by the name of sheep are signified great teachers, nourishers of twin births, who, with Paul, are able to become all things to all, pre-eminent in the double virtue of the wisdom and prudence of Mary and Martha, of life and doctrine. As with twin breasts, they nourish with these twin births the imperfect and the perfect: those who use the world and those who despise the world, lambs and sheep, active and contemplative persons.

The “two breasts” of these sheep are “like two twin fawns of a gazelle, which feed among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows decline” (ibid., 7:3). They must be made rich with most fertile and delightful pastures, because they are often suckled by their twin offspring, who demand either spiritual or bodily nourishment and, with a certain pious importunity, draw by suckling sweet and [Col. 1119C] pleasant milk from those maternal breasts. If they do not find it, they utter the bleating of complaining murmur because of an excessive lack of nourishment for mind or body. And when those breasts are drawn to the milking-place, unless abundance of milk is found in them, those who milk them, pressing the lean breasts too forcefully, draw blood instead of milk.

This cruel torment of breasts, even to the drawing of blood, had nearly happened to the great sheep—that is, the apostles—when a murmuring of the Greeks arose because their widows were not properly provided for in the daily ministry (Acts 6:1). For, in order to quiet such murmuring, the apostles would, as some wished, have been compelled to abandon the word for the ministry of tables; as though, from breasts torn and excessively pressed, [Col. 1119D] not milk but blood had been expressed. For, if the word of God were neglected amid so great a multitude, however diligent the provision for bodily necessities, it would by no means have been acceptable to God; and yet it would have burdened those from whom it had been importunately extracted. No reward would be expected from it, but punishment, because a better and more important good had been neglected.

But because the apostle Peter had been appointed by the Prince of shepherds not only over lambs but also over sheep, he wisely and prudently provided for both. He set lesser ministers of tables over the multitude of lambs, whether male or female; and for himself and the other Apostles, as great sheep full of milk, he chose broadest fields full of lilies in the most fertile pastures, because such sheep feed among lilies “until [Col. 1120A] the day breathes and the shadows decline” (Song 2:17). Thus the apostle Peter himself said: “It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables. Choose from among yourselves men full of wisdom, whom we may appoint over this work. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and the ministry of the word” (Acts 6:2–3).

Indeed, the prayer and preaching of the apostles were most fertile pastures, from which they, like sheep who were mothers of lambs, had breasts full from heaven, abundantly sufficient to nourish twin offspring, supporting and feeding them in both body and soul. For it is said concerning spiritual food that “with great power the apostles bore witness to the resurrection of Jesus Christ, and great grace was upon them all” (Acts 4:33). [Col. 1120B] “Every day, in the Temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and proclaiming Christ Jesus; and the word of the Lord grew, and the number of disciples in Jerusalem greatly multiplied.” Of bodily nourishment it is likewise written that “there was no one needy among them. For all who possessed fields or houses sold them, brought the proceeds, and laid them at the apostles’ feet. Distribution was made to each according as anyone had need” (ibid., 4:34–35).

Then the great sheep fed among lilies, because the holy apostles delighted both in the spiritual sweetnesses of prayers and preaching and in good children, as in beautiful lilies. Their children themselves, like twin offspring—the perfect and [Col. 1120C] the imperfect—received a double nourishment of milk through the sound teaching of the apostles and the generous almsgiving of the rich, whose abundance then supplied the poverty of Christ’s poor according to the teaching of the Apostle Paul (2 Cor. 8:14).

Without doubt, then, you remembered your compassions, Lord, and your mercies, which are from everlasting. You also, as though unaware, overlooked the sins of the youth and the ignorances of your people because of repentance. Therefore, for the shepherds and sheep of your pasture in that primitive Church, the heavens dropped dew from above and the clouds rained down righteousness; the earth opened and brought forth the Savior.

But now the disorder of heaven and air—such as there was through excessive rains when the Flood was impending, or through excessive [Col. 1120D] drought in the days of Elijah—and the extreme barrenness of lands once fertile are signs to us of your wrath impending because of the sins of our youth and our ignorances. Moreover, famine of the word and of saving teaching, and the great scarcity of those worthy to teach and those worthy to hear the holy Gospel, are certain indications of heavenly wrath. For even if there are somewhere people willing to hear God’s word, those to speak it are lacking. Likewise, if there are somewhere those willing to dispense God’s word, they do not have persons who will listen worthily. For only “friends listen” (Song 8:15); enemies, whose number is greater, mock.

And if there are people abounding in spiritual gifts, they lack bodily support; its excessive deficiency frequently becomes an occasion of murmuring or some other [Col. 1121A] disorder. The weak either murmur against God or against their teachers—or, what is worse, cry out—while the stronger, deprived of necessities, beg like Lazarus at the doors of wealthy men clothed in purple and are licked by dogs’ tongues, because they are charged, by the dog-like slanders of the malicious, as though with the crime of avarice. Again, if there are people abounding in bodily support from their own resources or those of the Church, deprived of virtues and spiritual rulers, they live in luxury and give themselves to idleness and impurity.

Amid these desolations and other similar evils, now rampant almost everywhere, you seem, Lord, to have forgotten your compassions and mercies, which are from everlasting. Therefore, I pray: let the cry of the Church reach you, saying: “Remember your compassions, Lord, and your mercies, which are from everlasting. Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances. According to your mercy remember me, for your goodness’ sake, Lord.”

You who looked upon Peter when he wept—indeed, who looked upon him before his tears so that you might give him tears; you who appeared, on the day of the Resurrection, to that same Peter and to Mary Magdalene, repentant and grieving, before the others who grieved less and were less desolate; you who, according to your mercy, received the thief who repented late—remember me, who am also a thief, or rather have become more cruel than a thief in murdering my own soul or my brother’s soul. For while a thief kills not souls but bodies, I have killed souls by a perverse example. Knowing that the repentant thief said to you as you hung upon the cross, “Remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42), I too, a repentant thief, now say to you reigning in heaven: Lord, according to your mercy remember me, making me today to be with you in paradise.

For since paradise is a garden of delights, in which was planted “every tree beautiful to look upon and pleasant for food” (Gen. 2:9), such a paradise is the Church, or a religious community: delightful as a garden of delights because it is full of virtues and virtuous persons, as though possessing every “tree beautiful to look upon and pleasant for [Col. 1121D] food.” For the good examples of good people are beautiful to behold and sweet and pleasant to those who imitate them. In such a paradise, Christ, I desire to hear you say to me: “Amen, I say to you: today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). “Today,” that is, so long as it is called today. Make me, Christ, to be with you in such a paradise, for even in paradise it would not be well with me without you. Therefore, according to your mercy remember me, so that you may say in full to me, a repentant thief, what you said to the thief upon the cross, and that, by your true command, while it is called today, I may be with you in paradise.

There is also a paradise, a kind of delightful garden: one holy man, watered by the four cardinal virtues as by the four rivers of paradise, having within himself every tree beautiful to behold and pleasant [Col. 1122A] for food in his good moral character. For when the beautiful dignity of his conduct, like a tree beautiful to behold, delights those who look upon it, and the precious usefulness of that same conduct is sweet and pleasant to those who feed upon it through imitation. In such a paradise even a solitary and silent man dwells when, not scattered abroad outside himself, he delights inwardly with you, O eternal Wisdom, as with his bride joined to him in paradise by a nuptial covenant, the Lord blessing and saying: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:25). This is that wise woman whom the serpent cannot deceive, and who in union with the rational spirit bears children worthy of the paradisal earth; hence it is said, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.”

Therefore, may it be granted me to hear you, Christ, say to me also concerning such a [Col. 1122B] paradise: “Amen, I say to you: today you will be with me in paradise.”

Wretched me! How often, cast out from such a paradise, wandering outside myself, have I the thief fallen “among thieves,” who “stripped” me and, “having inflicted wounds, went away, leaving me half-dead” (Luke 10:30). But now, Lord, according to your mercy remember me, and make me today—that is, while it is called today—to be with you in paradise. Remember me, not according to the wrath due to me for my merits, but according to your undeserved mercy. I am worthy to receive and endure wrath, like a vessel of wrath fitted for destruction. You are worthy of glory and honor, you who make vessels of mercy out of [Col. 1122C] vessels of wrath according to your mercy. Therefore, according to your mercy remember me, that from me, who am a vessel of wrath and dishonor, you may make a vessel of mercy and glory, for the sake of your goodness naturally inherent in you, as the preceding and effective cause of all things that have been made.

For before you made anything, you saw that it was good for this or that thing to be made, and it was so made. For example, you saw that it was good and said: “Let the earth bring forth green grass bearing seed, and a fruit-bearing tree making fruit according to its kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth”; and it was so (Gen. 1:11). Likewise, you saw that it was good for lights to be made in the firmament [Col. 1122D] of heaven, and it was so. Finally, you saw that it was good for man to be formed from the mud of the earth, and it was so. Therefore, because all things were made at the prompting and prior approval of your goodness, in the end you saw all that you had made, and behold, they were very good.

Nor is it surprising that, once heaven and earth and all their adornment had been completed, those things were found good which, before they were made, had been seen to be good; and for that very reason, because they were seen to be good, they were brought forth from the maternal womb, as it were, of your goodness into the light, so that they might come from non-being into being—and not merely into being, but into good being: namely, so that each thing might be good and all things together very good.

But more particularly and, as it were, more intimately than the other good things, you saw that the light was good, because the rational and angelic nature, insofar as it was capable of your goodness and brightness, was illumined through love of you; and insofar as it was illumined, it shone and appeared good. Therefore you divided the good light from the evil darkness—that is, from the evil angels. And lest, through the fall of evil angels, the number of the good predestined by your goodness should be diminished, your goodness itself suggested to you that man should be created from earth and multiplied in such a way as to fill the earth—that is, that heavenly homeland, which your goodness so enlarged that it can contain human beings together with angels.

If, therefore, man, made and blessed to increase and multiply upon the earth, had not sinned, the number of the elect would quickly have been completed; and, with good persons multiplied in the land of the living, no one could say, “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13). For all would be good, and only good, in the land of the living; they would not believe, but would behold in present reality the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. Nor would there be any misery in that land of the living for which mercy were necessary. But because sinful man did not attain the land of the living, having fallen into this land of the dying, in which “living for a short time, he is filled with many miseries” (Job 14:1), creative and formative goodness does not suffice for him unless recreative and reformative divine mercy is also present.

Therefore, to you, my Creator and Savior, I say: According to your mercy remember me, for your goodness’ sake, Lord. By that goodness which prompted and suggested that you bring me from non-being into being, make me, through your mercy, pass from miserable being to blessed being. By your goodness you saw that it was good for me to be created, and it was so; for I was created in Adam. Now see me in my misery and, according to your mercy, remember me, that you may make me to be recreated in you, who are the better and second Adam. He was made in the image of God, and in him I too was made through your goodness. You are the very image of God. Therefore, that I—the Church, or I David, or I the penitent—may be transformed into that same image from glory to glory, as by your Spirit, according to your mercy remember me, for your goodness’ sake, Lord.

Your goodness is brightness, and your mercy [Col. 1123D] is brightness. For in the creation of creatures your goodness shone forth when you saw all that you had made, and behold, they were very good. But in the restoration of lost creatures shines your mercy, not less than your goodness. Therefore you are Alpha and Omega, beginning and end: Alpha, or beginning, through your goodness, whose fruitfulness brought forth the primordial causes of things; Omega, or end, through your mercy, whose maternal kindness forms the final causes of things. And as your goodness itself is the most primordial cause of all primordial causes, so your mercy is the most final cause of all final causes.

Hence I too shall sing your mercies forever, because you have said: “Mercy shall be built up forever in the heavens; your truth shall be prepared in them” (Ps. [Col. 1124A] 88:3). After this your mercy has been built in heaven out of stones drawn from the mud of misery and has been fully completed, then comes the end, when you deliver the kingdom to God the Father. And indeed not only shall your mercy be built in the heavens, while you save lost human beings, but also “your truth shall be prepared in them” (Ps. 88:3), when you gather back none of the angels cast out from there, and preserve there the angels who stand. And therefore you are:

**VERSE 8. Sweet and upright is the Lord.** Sweet through mercy; upright through truth. But I, fixed in the mud of the deep and sunk into a place of misery, flee to the sole bosom of your mercy, saying to you: According to your mercy remember me, for your goodness’ sake, Lord. Thus, building the eternal edifice of your mercy upon the immovable foundation of creative goodness, remember me; make me to be presented to you as a stone suitable for such a building; and complete and perfect in me, from me, and with me your final mercy, for the sake of your primordial goodness, Lord.

For although before the foundation of the world you foreknew that I, your future prodigal son, would depart from you, you nevertheless gave me, no less than to the angel, the portion of substance that fell to me. For I am a rational and intellectual creature, like the angel, endowed with free will as he is. And although you foreknew that I would depart from you into a far country, nevertheless, at the prompting of your goodness, you gave me [Col. 1124C] an abundant substance. Because I squandered all of it in dissolute living, I now, as my memory recalls your primordial goodness, seek from you final mercy, saying: According to your mercy remember me, for your goodness’ sake, Lord.

For unless you were good, you would not have enriched me when I was ready to depart from you. Therefore, for the sake of this goodness of yours, remember me now. And although I am not worthy to be called your son, yet according to your mercy remember me, now greatly distressed in deep misery, because “I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg” (Luke 16:3), and I waste away and fail through extreme hunger. But considering that many “hired servants” in your house “abound in bread” (ibid., 15:17), I, wretched and hungry, flee to you, through whom “if anyone enters, he shall be saved, and shall go in and go out and find pasture” (John 10:10).

For, refreshed by the food of your body and blood as by the feast of the fattened calf, he shall, entering, find the pastures of delightful contemplation; and, going out, find the pastures of delightful action. Therefore, while this man sings your mercies forever here below and invites others by his example to sing the same mercies, music and dancing will be heard from afar; and on account of this the elder brother—that is, the Jewish people—and every envious person will be tormented with the devil. To that elder brother, when he angrily asks at last, you will give a goat: the goat, that is, Antichrist, according to your wrath. But I, seeking not a goat but the lamb, or the fattened calf, say to you, O Father: According to your mercy [Col. 1125A] remember me, that you may give me the Lamb who takes away sins according to mercy. To you, O God the Son, I say: grant that I may so eat your body and blood that it may not result for me in judgment, but in obtaining mercy. And because your goodness and mercy are nothing other than your good Spirit, so according to your mercy remember me, for your goodness’ sake, Lord, “that your good Spirit may lead me into the right land” (Ps. 142:10).

But an envious brother, conscious, as he supposes, of no great fault, says to me: “You, a sinful man who squandered your substance by dissolute living, with what confidence do you ask such great benefits?” Thus the Pharisee speaks to me, the tax collector, and I shall answer: Because I am a sinner and unworthy of the condescension of divine mercy, I venture to ask for mercy, because sweet and upright is the Lord. Sweet, because through grace, without merits, he forgives all sins. But upright, because even when sins have been wholly forgiven, he permits certain penalties of sin to remain, not to harm. Clearly upright, because even in those baptized or cleansed by repentance he permits certain penalties to remain. Yet sweet, because he does not allow them to harm, but makes them beneficial, either for the preservation of holy humility, for the exercise of mortal life, or for the acquisition of virtue.

Otherwise: “The lawgiver will give a blessing” (Ps. 83:7), because he who gave the law will give blessing; he who commanded humility will lead to truth. But who is this lawgiver except the sweet and upright Lord, who will give a law to transgressors in the way? For those transgress in the way who abandon truth. But will they, even thus, be abandoned by the sweet Lord? He, therefore, is the sweet and upright Lord who gives the law of the way of humility, by which they may return to the knowledge of truth. He gives an occasion for recovered salvation because he is sweet; yet not without the discipline of law because he is upright. Sweet, because he does not permit them to perish; upright, because he does not forget to punish.

Otherwise: Sweet and upright is the Lord. Sweet, because he freely bestows the gifts of his grace; upright, because he distinguishes those gifts into merits and rewards, so that good merits are granted beforehand in the way through the gratuitous sweetness of grace, [Col. 1125D] and everlasting rewards are given in the homeland through gratuitous uprightness. Or: sweet, because he grants merits beforehand; upright, because according to the quality of merits each person will receive from him his own recompense according to his labor. Sweet, because he freely gives good merits; upright, because at judgment he requires those same merits.

Yet his sweetness does not lack uprightness, nor is his uprightness empty of sweetness. For in generously distributing ten minas to each according to his own capacity, he preserves uprightness; and when, in judgment, he requires the gains of merits, he preserves a merciful sweetness by not requiring them cruelly. Therefore, because the Lord is sweet and upright, he will give a law to transgressors in the way. For in this his sweetness shines: out of his own free choice, not under some compulsion of necessity, the Lord will give sinners a correcting law in the way of this life, placing them on the way of discipline, a way enclosed on either side by the barriers of commandments that command good and prohibit evil.

He will also give a law to transgressors in the way: those who, though they transgress in human excesses, nevertheless do not depart from the way of Catholic faith, nor say or believe that evil is good or good evil. For if they said this, or believed others saying so, they would stray from the way of truth. But now, because they transgress while remaining in the way—believing and saying that good is good and evil evil, although many human sins creep in both in avoiding evils and performing goods—precisely because they transgress in the way, the sweet and upright Lord will give a law to transgressors [Col. 1126B] in the way. They do not perish through stubborn defense of their evils, but are saved through truthful confession, the Lord giving them law—that is, charity. For “the fullness of the law is love” (Rom. 13:10); and those who are on the way of divine commandments love the good alone and wholly. Therefore “charity covers a multitude of sins.” This “charity is patient, is kind” (1 Pet. 4:8 [with wording also echoing 1 Cor. 13:4]). Therefore, out of charitable patience, the sweet and upright Lord makes gentle those who were formerly wild and untamed.

**VERSE 9. He will guide the gentle in judgment;** and, out of charitable kindness, he will teach his ways—that is, his commandments—to those made mild who had formerly been harsh. For their neglect of these commandments, he causes them to understand that scourges have come upon them in judgment. He will guide the gentle toward better things. Their voice is: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged. But when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with this world” (1 Cor. 11:31–32). “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the ruler of this world be cast out” (John 12:31).

In this judgment neither the ruler of this world nor this world, which lies in evil, will be guided toward better things, because neither is gentle under blows. And because every person unyielding and distorted through injustice is not so flexible that he may be straightened by the judge’s hand, he must be broken.

The sweet and upright Lord, willing all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth, when he touches those distorted from his uprightness with the rod of correction, in the present life by judgment now hidden, now manifest, but always just, guides in his judgment those whom he finds gentle and pliable toward repentance; but he breaks those who are unyielding and altogether hardened in their own strength. For just as a bent piece of wood, if it has not become hardened in its crookedness, dried out, and old, can be softened and straightened—but otherwise is broken when forced into straightness while its hardness and dryness remain—so great is the difference among human beings between the gentle and the unyielding that, in divine judgment, the former are straightened and the latter broken.

We properly call *mansueti* (“made gentle”) those who, having first been unmanageable, later become tamed and gentle—almost *manu sueti*, “accustomed to the hand”—because through habitual patience they learn to bear with equanimity the hand of grace, whether scourging or caressing; whereas before, like an unbroken horse, they were accustomed to kick; like a dog, to bark; like a solitary wild beast, to bite back. But we properly call mild those whose disposition is naturally sweet and gentle.

The apostles, the sons of Zebedee, sons of thunder, were still unyielding when, after Christ was not received by the Galileans, they said to him: “Lord, do you wish us to say that fire should come down from heaven and consume them,” as Elijah also did? (John 9:54). But the merciful Lord, sweet and upright, summoned them to gentleness, saying: “You do not know of what spirit you are. The Son of Man came not to destroy souls but to save them” (ibid., 55–56).

Likewise the apostle Peter, still unyielding, said: “Lord, shall we strike [Col. 1127B] with the sword?” (Luke 22:49). Not content merely to say this, he drew his sword and cut off the ear of the servant of the high priest. But the sweet and upright Lord, from the sweetness inherent in him, healed the wound inflicted; and from the uprightness inherent in him, gave a law to Peter, transgressing in the way, saying: “Return your sword to its place. For all who take the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:52).

Hence it is expedient for every person possessing Peter’s zeal to keep this law in the way of faith, so that he may return his sword to its place. If he possesses the spiritual sword, he must return it to its place: namely, sheathing it in its proper place and also drawing it in its proper place, according to the character of circumstances that at one time permit silence, at another speech. Likewise, if he is a minister of God bearing the material sword, he ought to return it to its place: namely, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good, restraining the former and defending the latter.

Therefore the greatest caution must be exercised lest, contrary to this law, either the spiritual or material sword be “taken,” that is, seized. For *accipere*, “to take,” is sometimes used for “to seize.” Hence we call certain birds of prey *accipitres*, hawks; and the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “For you endure it if anyone devours you, if anyone takes” (1 Cor. 11:20), that is, seizes. Thus, there are robbers of swords: those who, contrary to justice and mercy, exercise either spiritual or worldly judgment, oppressing the innocent and letting the guilty go free. There [Col. 1127D] they draw the sword where it ought to be sheathed, and sheath it where it ought to be drawn.

Unless such persons receive the law in the way—unless they repent in this present life—they will undoubtedly perish by the sword of judicial sentence on that day when, with the Lord, the holy alone shall be judges, “and two-edged swords shall be in their hands to execute vengeance upon the nations” (Ps. 149:6–7); and the sword sharp on both sides shall then proceed from the mouth of Christ seated upon the throne. Now, in corrective judgment, he will guide the gentle in the way—that is, in the present life. Then, in the final judgment, the unyielding, who took the sword without the judgment of mercy and truth, shall perish by the sword, when mercy and truth pronounce the final judgment: to those on the right it shall be said through mercy, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34); and to those on the left, through the equity of truth, it shall be said: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (ibid., 41).

Otherwise: Sweet and upright is the Lord; therefore the Lord will give a law to transgressors in the way. “Therefore,” that is, in accordance with the fact that he is sweet and upright, the Lord will give a law—that is, he will distinguish the law already given. For on the way of departure from Egypt, to a transgressing people, the sweet Lord gave exceedingly good commandments written with his finger upon tablets. In these he demands nothing else from a true Israelite except that he fear or love God and walk in his ways. But when that same Israel transgressed in the guilt of the calf, he gave them, as he himself speaks through the prophet, “commandments that were not good” [Col. 1128B] (Ezek. 20:25), concerning ceremonial observance.

And accordingly the Lord is upright, who, by such commandments of exercise, made this same people gentle and guided them; then, in the judgment—that is, in punishments—he guided the gentle. Such are these: whoever does this or that shall be killed, stoned, or burned. And through all these things, having made them mild, he taught them to enter his ways under discipline, toward the promised land. Thus we should judge also concerning ourselves, whom, by nearly the same manner of initiation, he will lead obedient to his ways toward the true land of promise.

Therefore the Lord is sweet and upright also in us. For this reason he will give us too, as transgressors in the way of righteousness, the law of charity, so that “charity” in us “may cover a multitude of sins.” He “will guide the gentle” (1 Pet. 4:8 [citation as printed]), and, having made them gentle through the sacraments of exercises, will guide them, I say, in the judgment of ecclesiastical punishments—for example, that saying of the Apostle: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in charity and a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Cor. 4:21). And so he will teach his ways to those made mild—that is, teachable and well-disposed. For:

**VERSE 10. All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.** His ways of incomprehensible judgments are indeed infinite and unsearchable, but they are contained in these two: mercy and truth. Mercy is that by which, in his first coming, being appeasable, he forgives sins not without justice. Truth is that by which, in his future coming, as incorruptible judge, he judges merits not without mercy. He holds to these ways and walks cautiously along them who, seeing himself delivered not by any merits of his own but through mercy alone, lays aside pride and then guards against the severity of truth and the wrath of the true Judge.

Although these ways are not known to others, to whom mercy sometimes seems to lack truth or truth to exist without mercy, it is nevertheless evident that all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.

**To those who seek his covenant and his testimonies.** His covenant is the Gospel, drawn up and ratified concerning the heavenly inheritance for those who, by adoption, are heirs indeed of God and co-heirs of Christ through the grace of their mother. This covenant, confirmed by the blood and death of the testator, is full of truth and mercy, because Christ Jesus, true God and true [Col. 1129A] man, showed himself to humankind full of grace and truth. His testimonies in Moses and the prophets confirm the same thing: they were witnesses of the mercy and truth contained in the covenant.

Likewise, what else are the preachings or writings of the apostles and apostolic Fathers, or the miracles displayed through martyrs and other saints, than manifest testimonies of truth and grace? To those who seek all these testimonies, it is clear and evident that all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. But those who either do not receive these testimonies, like pagans; distort them, like Jews and heretics; or despise them, like false Christians, shall find neither truth, the mother of initial and servile love, nor mercy, the mother of filial love.

[Col. 1129B] It is pleasant here to investigate for a little while in the testament of God and His testimonies whether mercy alone without truth, or truth without mercy, ever operates. For so it seems to very many, among whom this opinion is widespread: the holy Fathers affirm that all the ways of the Lord, considered together, are full of mercy and truth, since some are condemned through truth and others are saved through mercy. But if those same ways are distinguished so that one treats separately of the destruction of the wicked and separately of the salvation of the good, they affirm that the condemnation of the ungodly belongs to truth alone, and the salvation of the good to mercy alone. Therefore, concerning the totality of the Lord’s ways, they rightly say that mercy and truth are proclaimed together; but concerning one particular part they proclaim mercy alone, [Col. 1129C] and concerning another, truth alone. This is indeed a Catholic opinion and not one to be despised: eternal condemnation is fitted and assigned to the wicked by God’s truth and justice alone, while salvation is fitted and assigned to the saints by His grace and mercy alone.

Nevertheless, for those who seek His testament and His testimonies, it becomes apparent that it was not said without reason that all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. According to the sense stated above, it might seem more suitable to say that all the ways of the Lord are mercy or truth. The Holy Spirit joined mercy and truth by the copulative conjunction “and” in all the Lord’s ways; He did not separate them by the disjunctive conjunction “or.” Therefore, “what” [Col. 1129D] “God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Mark 10:9). In human judgment, divinely ordered, mercy without justice is not valuable, nor is justice without mercy; for justice without mercy is called cruelty, and mercy without justice or truth may be called folly. How much more, then, in divine judgment does justice or truth commend mercy, and mercy commend the truth of justice?

For since the simple nature of Divinity is never capable of any division, mercy is not one thing in it and truth another. Rather, as one and the same ray of the sun, unlike nothing in itself, nevertheless produces unlike effects—by one and the same heat softening wax and hardening clay; by one and the same brightness delighting sound eyes and tormenting bleary ones—so the one and same power of Divinity, altogether simple in itself, by one and the same operation softens some and hardens others. Thus in Egypt, by one and the same manifestation of signs, it softened the kindly hearts of the children of Israel and hardened the envious hearts of Pharaoh and the Egyptians. For envy has such a nature that it does not allow hearts which it has preoccupied with benefits to be softened. On the contrary, it hardens itself all the more fiercely against kindness shown either to itself or to others; and, as though with the bleary eye of the mind, it turns the brilliance of outstanding goodness into torment for itself—the very brilliance which a kindly mind enjoys when present and intensely desires when absent.

Thus when the Lord says, “I shall harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 4:21), it is as though He said: I shall display the most splendid benefits to my people in the land of Egypt; by their bright radiance Pharaoh’s envious and proud heart will be tormented and hardened. Likewise, when He says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth” (Exod. 9:16), it is as though He said: I did not make you envious; but, since I knew that by your own free choice you were proud and envious, I raised you up for this very purpose, so that the envy and pride dormant in you might, as it were, awaken when struck by the radiance of my benefits.

[Col. 1130B] For when I bestowed benefits upon you yourself, making you king of all Egypt, you became more and more puffed up against me by the bright radiance of so great a benefit—though you ought to have given thanks to me—and you were cruel to my people living as exiles in your kingdom. But when I bestowed benefits on that same people, consoling them through signs and wonders displayed in your land, you were tormented through your envy at the radiance of so great a benefit and became more and more hardened in your wickedness. Therefore I hardened you in no other way than by doing good both to you, from which you grew proud so that your heart became swollen, and to my people, whom you envied so that through this very envy your heart became hardened. What, then, was I to do to you, whom both your own prosperity exalted and another’s tormented? Nothing remained except that, in one to whom I had shown such great kindness, when you abused that same kindness, I should also show such great power, so that at the manifestation of this power [Col. 1130D] my people might sing to me:

> “Who is like you among the mighty, O Lord? Who is like you, magnificent in holiness, terrible and praiseworthy, working wonders? You stretched out your hand, and the earth swallowed them. In your mercy you were a guide to the people whom you redeemed, and in your power you bore them to your holy dwelling-place” (Exod. 15:11–13).

See how here the people of God sing mercy and judgment, praising mercy and power alike. The song of mercy is what it says: “In your mercy you were a guide to the people whom you redeemed.” The song of judgment, or of truth and power, is what it says: “In your power you bore them to your holy dwelling-place.” Therefore, just as in this history, as though in a brief picture, [Col. 1131A] it is seen that the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, so throughout the whole extent of His judgments “all the ways of the Lord” are found to be mercy and truth by faithful persons seeking His testament and His testimonies.

For Pharaoh himself bears witness to the truth, or justice, of God’s judgments toward Pharaoh, saying: “God is just; I and my people are wicked” (Exod. 9:27). And there is an evident testimony of mercy in the fact that the plagues inflicted upon Pharaoh and his people through justice were remitted or suspended through divine mercy as often as Moses and Aaron interceded for him.

But in God’s people mercy and truth are plainly perceived by all who seek His testament [Col. 1131B] and His testimonies, as Moses himself sings, in the words set out above: “In your mercy you were a guide to the people whom you redeemed, and in your power you bore them.” It was mercy, indeed, that, speaking freely and without any preceding merit to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob concerning the people to be born from them and to receive their faith, God freely promised blessings in Abraham’s seed. But it was strong truth and true power that, though provoked by the many sins of the Hebrews, He did not cease to do them good until the complete fulfillment of His most truthful promise, according to the “oath which he swore to Abraham our father” (Luke 1:73), that He would give them the promised land, “a land flowing with milk and honey” (Deut. 6:3).

[Col. 1131C] Further, the spiritual and universal Pharaoh—the devil, king of all Egypt and prince of this world—is judged through mercy and truth, not through any cruelty, which it is sinful even to conceive in the Lord. Was it not clear evidence of God’s great mercy toward him that He made him beautiful, so that he was “the seal of likeness” to God, “perfect in beauty, full of wisdom” (Ezek. 28:12), whose height the cedars in the heavenly paradise did not equal? But because by free choice he swelled with pride and envy against his Creator, and was unwilling to have angels of the same nature as his fellow servants, he was cast forth from among the fiery stones—that is, the angels burning and shining with the holy fire of divine charity.

Yet, because mercy is not properly spoken of where misery has not preceded, let us say that it was divine goodness that created both the spiritual Pharaoh brighter than the other angels in heaven and the carnal Pharaoh nobler than the other Egyptians in Egypt. From that brilliance or nobility, because they preferred to be proud rather than to give thanks to God, they began, swollen with the plague of pride, to be miserable; but they did not perceive themselves to be miserable. Divine mercy therefore came to these miserable beings, applying to them such a remedy as would compel them to lose some of their swelling. For by doing good in heaven to the humble angels and in Egypt to the humbled Hebrews, He summoned the proud to the grace of humility, when they felt their pride resisted [Col. 1132A] and grace given to the humble. But they, becoming more and more hardened and wasting away through envy, abused God’s mercy: from benefits bestowed upon themselves by God they grew proud against God, and from benefits bestowed upon others they were hardened through envy.

What remains, then, except that God show in them the power of judgment, since they did not receive the medicine of His goodness? Thus, even in the condemnation of the wicked, mercy and truth meet one another: while they reject mercy, the just Judge shows them truth. Therefore at the judgment He will say: “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). Why? Because you abused my temporal mercy; you are unworthy of eternal mercy. Therefore truth will meet you, judging justly and not without remembrance of mercy, so that my faithful prophet may be proved true, who said of me: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Hab. 3:2).

Behold: in the judgment of just wrath I remember the mercy shown to you. Was it not mercy that I made you rich while I was needy among you, so that, softened to mercy by my poverty, you might act kindly toward me and thus, justice dictating it, might receive eternal goods in return for temporal ones? But they say, Lord: “When did we see you” needy “and not minister to you?” They shall be answered: “As long as you did not” do good “to one of” my least ones, “you did not do it to me” (Matt. 25:44–45). You could plead in your own defense that justice alone without mercy had been brought against you in my judgment, were it not that these least ones of mine, who were poor among you, bear testimony against you: you rejected the mercy offered to you when you were unwilling to be merciful through your own resources to them in their need, while they were poor and you were rich.

[Col. 1132C] Moreover, it was also mercy that not even the least goods remained unrewarded to you: for you received your good things in your lifetime, just as these least ones received evils in their lifetime in return for their least evils. If, therefore, I now wished to receive you together with them into the eternal dwellings, that would be unjust mercy—and therefore not mercy at all, since mercy without justice is folly rather than mercy. Likewise, if I sent them, afflicted in the world and chastised for their sins, with you into eternal fire, that would be excessive mercilessness, devoid of all justice. Let it suffice that these least ones receive with them into the eternal dwellings those who made them their friends from the mammon of unrighteousness. To such persons I now say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom promised to you. For I was hungry and you gave me food; for what you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” (Matt. 25:34–35).

Therefore, “Come, blessed of my Father” pertains to mercy; what follows—“For I was hungry and you gave me food”—commends the merit of justice. Likewise, to the ungodly, “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” is a sentence of justice; what is added—“For I was hungry and you did not give me food”—is a recollection [Col. 1133A] of the mercy by which God first did good to them and patiently endured the evils He received from them.

Does it not appear to you, if you consider all these things carefully, even if not clearly, nevertheless as though through a mirror and in an enigma, that all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth? For neither was mercy denied to the ungodly, by which they were anticipated, nor was justice lacking to the godly, by which they were chastised. The saying of the patriarch Abraham to the rich man is therefore just: “Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, while you are tormented” (Luke 16:25).

That rich man experienced mercy when he received good things in his lifetime; he also experienced justice when, for his mercilessness, he was tormented without mercy. In that torment divine mercy worked together with justice, because, just as it belonged to justice that the rich man was punished, so it belonged to mercy that the poor man’s rest and consolation appeared sweeter because of the rich man’s punishment. Likewise, the poor man experienced justice when he received evils in this life; he also experienced mercy when he received consolation in Abraham’s bosom. In that consolation justice worked mingled with divine mercy: it belonged to mercy that the poor man received consolation, and to justice that the rich man’s torments burned all the more fiercely at the sight of his glory.

What we have said of two persons should be said of the whole body of the godly and ungodly. For from the wholly just punishment of all the ungodly the mercy shown to the godly will shine forth [Col. 1133C] clearly; and from the gracious glory of all the godly, the justice observed even in the punishments of the ungodly will shine forth clearly. For “all who desire to live piously in Christ Jesus,” poor either in possessions or in disposition, “suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12) and will be comforted with Lazarus in the future. The way of the ungodly prospers in this world, because the world loves what is its own; but in the future they will be tormented with the ungodly rich man. All those, whether rich in possessions or disposition, who were not merciful toward the godly poor, will be bound with him in one bundle to be burned.

Even in infants removed from this light before baptism, justice does not operate without mercy. [Col. 1133D] Their punishment will be the mildest: through justice they are punished for original sin, but through mercy their punishment is made the mildest of all those who will be outside God’s kingdom. Baptized infants too, although their guilt has been remitted, do not depart from here without the altogether just penalty of weakness and death; but this brief and light penalty will be followed by the eternal consolation of divine mercy.

Thus, if God scourges every son whom He receives, whether little or great—and scourges through justice but receives through mercy—and likewise if He hates none of those things which He himself made in the ungodly, but mercifully has compassion on everything that He himself made, while through justice punishing in the ungodly the sins which He did not make, it is manifest that mercy and [Col. 1134A] truth meet one another in all the works of God. For even in those whom the judge’s justice condemns, mercy preserves nature; and in those whom mercy saves, the truth of God’s promises is manifest. Let us therefore conclude that all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. Although this is not apparent to all, it shines out altogether clearly to those who seek His testament and His testimonies.

**VERSE 11.** *For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will be propitious to my sin, for it is great.* I said a little above: “For you are God my Savior”; and this name, “Savior,” is sweeter to me than honey and the honeycomb. For, set between mercy and truth, I fear the judgment of truth; in this alone is my consolation: that mercy exalts itself over [Col. 1134B] judgment for the sake of your name, which is *Jesus* in Greek and *Savior* in Latin. Therefore, in great hope of compassion, I say: For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will be propitious to my sin, because I myself neither defend nor diminish my sin, but accuse it and reckon it great, as I ought by right.

*For it is great.* At one time my sin seemed small to me, because “when I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child” (I Cor. XI, 13), and every excess of thought, speech, or deed seemed small to me. But now, when I consider that before the Judge who sees all things I have grievously offended in many matters, my sin appears exceedingly great to me—not by a false estimate but by a true examination of truth. [Col. 1134C] For, knowing that all your ways, O God, are mercy and truth, I now deal with truth: with truth as judge I examine myself without flattery. In doing this, I find myself worthy of great condemnation because of my sin; for it is great.

Truly I have sinned greatly, if I consider the number of my sins. They are exceedingly many, because I have sinned repeatedly and greatly beyond the number of the sand of the sea; my sins have multiplied, and I am not worthy to behold the height of my iniquity, because I provoked your anger and did evil before you—not only before I came to know justice, but, what provoked your anger still more, even after I received knowledge of truth and justice. If, however, you consider the duration of my sin, I have sinned greatly and for a long time, from earliest infancy to this very hour. If you weigh the quality of my sin in the balance of truth, I have done great evil: when you, my God, did good to me, I repaid your good things with evil. If you assess the quantity of my sin, the sufferings of this present time are not proportionate to purging it; for it is great. I have deserved infernal sufferings, not those of this present time; eternal sufferings, not transient ones, I have stored up for myself according to my hardness and impenitent heart. Therefore, apart from your name there is no appropriate or sufficient remedy for my sin; for it is great.

But, on the other hand, abundant hope of healing grace overflows in your name, which is Jesus. Explaining the meaning of that name, [Col. 1135A] the angel said to Joseph: “You shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21). For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will be propitious to my sin, for it is great: because I, David, am penitent; I, the Psalmist, am penitent and belong to your people. And I, the Church, am your penitent people, having in my many weak members many iniquities and sins; nor are my greater members so wholly without every stain as the Novatian heretics boast of themselves, who call themselves *Cathari*, that is, “the pure.”

The founder of these was Novatus, a presbyter of the Roman Church. Disputing against Pope Cornelius, he denied that the lapsed could be restored by repentance; and he claimed such purity for himself and his followers that they did not seem to require the medicine of repentance. But when the holy Church received back through repentance those cleansed who had formerly fallen, Novatus and those agreeing with him withdrew from the Church, as though it were defiled by receiving such persons. They called themselves *Cathari*, that is, “the pure,” as though they needed no repentance, preserved and were able to preserve the purity received in baptism, and therefore left no place for repentance in the Church. Therefore, after these Cathari were anathematized because of their contention, I, the Catholic Church—knowing that among my members I have many sinners, male and female—do not reject the remedy of repentance. Rather, I say to you, Lord Jesus, who are the true physician: “For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will be propitious to my sin, [Col. 1135C] for it is great.”

For many persons are cherished within my bosom, liable to many sins and still needing amendment through true repentance; and even in my perfect members I know there to be so many stains that they themselves truthfully say of themselves: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us.” But if we confess, God “is faithful to forgive us our sins.” Likewise, they say: “We all offend in many things” (I John I, 8 and 9). Therefore this too is the voice even of the perfect in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). Therefore, because I, the Church, forgive my debtors and pray for them, you, [Col. 1135D] who said, “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (*ibid.*), in order that you may be justified in your words, will for your name’s sake, O Lord, be propitious to my sin. I neither defend, excuse, nor diminish it, because I cannot—though I may wish to—excuse my sin; for it is great.

Another interpretation: *For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will be propitious to my sin, for it is great.* Because all your ways, O Lord, are mercy and truth, I too unite mercy and truth in my prayer. With regard to your mercy I say: “For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will be propitious to my sin”; and with regard to truth I say: “for it is great.” Indeed, that you will be propitious to my sin belongs to great mercy; and my statement that my sin is great expresses great truth. But because mercy—the propitiation of pardon and remission—never abandons the truth of a true confession, I confidently ask and affirm that propitiation will be shown me, since I do not offer a feigned confession concerning my sin, which I confess to be great and grievous. In this I do not lie: for it is great.

**VERSE 12.** *Who is the man who fears the Lord?* I know that my past sin is exceedingly manifold and great. And if, while I continue living in the flesh from day to day, the heap of my sins should continue increasing, what hope can there be for future goods for one upon whom the weight of evils grows daily? But why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me, [Col. 1136B] as though there were no sure consolation or firm barrier against the sin rushing upon me? Did not God set a boundary, bar, and door to the sea, and say: “Thus far shall you come, and here you shall break your swelling waves”?

The bar set against the stormy and turbulent sea is that holy fear of the Lord which remains for ever and ever, concerning which it is written: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, who greatly delights in his commandments” (Ps. 111:1). Likewise: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord” (Ps. 127:1). Likewise: “It shall be well at the end with one who fears the Lord” (Ecclus. 1:13). When this fear becomes the beginning of wisdom, it is undoubtedly the end of folly; and therefore, like a most powerful barrier, like a most powerful bar, it is set against the old life, and the new life begins from it. In that new life, although one does not live without sin, sin is nevertheless not condemned there, because a person renewed by the fear of the Lord now agrees with God’s law according to the inward person, so that sin does not reign in the mortal body, although it is burdened under the law of the members.

Thus, yes, every person who fears God with holy fear is restrained, so that, even if inclined to sin, he does not dare to sin. For who is the person who fears the Lord and yet dares to do anything against the Lord? Certainly, if anyone fears the Lord with that fear which is the beginning of wisdom and the end of folly, he does not dare brazenly to offend the Lord.

The demons indeed believe and tremble, and the worst human beings are burdened by servile fear; being companions of demons, they will also be joined to them in punishment under such fear, unless repentance frees them. But who is a human being? Who is a rational human being? Who is a human being far removed from demons and the companions of demons? Who is rational and by no means to be called bestial? Do you wish to hear who? Certainly the one who fears the Lord. For another Scripture says likewise: “Fear God and keep his commandments: this is the whole human being” (Eccl. 12:13). If the whole human being consists in fearing God and keeping his commandments, it follows that the person who neither fears God nor keeps his commandments is not a human being. For if fearing God and keeping His commandments makes one truly and blessedly human, it is plain that those who do not fear God and do not keep His commandments are neither blessedly nor truly human. Therefore, to one who asks who is truly human, the fitting answer is: the one who fears the Lord.

[Col. 1137A] But lest you think sin rules over such fear, hear what follows: *He will establish for him a law in the way which he has chosen.* In the way of faith and uprightness, which he himself has chosen by the resolve of his own free will to keep, the Lord whom he fears establishes for him a law, called the law of the mind. Although another law, in the fleshly members, resists it, the Lord nevertheless establishes the inward law for him so firmly, through the mind’s most steadfast resolve which he has chosen, that—even though he feels the law of sin—he does not willingly consent to it. Even if he has been overtaken in some fault, as Peter and I, David, were—he in denying, I in committing fornication—he does not utterly cast away the law of good resolve which the Lord established inwardly in his mind, nor leave it cast away; rather, by bitter weeping and repentance he restores what had been partly deformed.

And therefore:

**VERSE 13.** *His soul shall abide among good things.* It is indeed tempted amid evils and sometimes wounded, but it does not abide in them. Soon, either when Christ looks upon it or when the Spirit of truth rebukes it, it rises from the evils in which prolonged delay is not sweet to it. Such is the person who fears the Lord and for whom the Lord himself establishes a law in the way which he has chosen. And his soul shall abide among good things. For he devotes his chief efforts and greater periods of time to the higher and greater things. Since in this mortal and mutable life he cannot continually maintain the exercise of holy religion, whenever it is interrupted for a short time he strives to repair it in such a way that what cannot be wholly continuous [Col. 1137C] may at least be extended through longer continuance.

He will not return to the fleshpots in Egypt in such a way as to love darkness more than light; rather, through acknowledgment and confession of sin, he freely comes to the light. Thus I, David, when rebuked by Nathan the prophet, came to the light by kindly receiving his rebuke, and did not hide the sin made manifest by the light of rebuking truth.

Adam did not act thus. He fled to hiding places amid the tree of paradise, desiring to remain concealed. Therefore his soul did not long abide amid the delightful goods of paradise, because the Lord cast him out of the paradise of pleasure into a land full of thorns and thistles. But one who does the truth, not excusing sin with his own falsehoods [Col. 1137D] but accusing it by true confession, comes to the light. Though such a person is for a short time pricked by the thorns and thistles of an accusing conscience, he will nevertheless hear Christ saying to him: “Amen, I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

And whoever rejoices in such a promise, his soul shall abide among paradisal goods. For in the present life, as though by the four rivers of paradise, the teachings of the Gospel—which promise God’s kingdom to penitents—water his soul as it abides among good things and gladden it by hope of future goods. Among those goods it will then abide most perfectly, when, admitted to the joy of the morning of the Lord’s Resurrection, it enjoys gladness. Yet first “weeping shall abide at evening,” when it will weep bitterly with Peter, “and joy in the morning” [Col. 1138A] (Ps. 29:6). Enjoying this joy with that same Peter, it will perceive how truly its soul abides among good things among those who rejoiced when they saw the Lord himself; their heart rejoiced, and no one took, or could take, their joy from them.

Another interpretation: *Who is the man who fears the Lord? He will establish for him a law in the way which he has chosen.* Many think or boast that they possess fear of the Lord, but few truly fear the Lord. Therefore it is a matter worthy of inquiry who truly fears the Lord. For there is a fear which makes people timid, and a fear which makes them reverently fearful; the difference between these two fears is recognized from their very effect, because the timid person flees from the Lord, while the reverently fearful person goes to the Lord.

Peter was still timid when, having seen the miracle of the great catch [Col. 1138B] of fish, he said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8). Many like this Peter have no counsel in distress: as they die, they fear life, so timid that they do not dare to enter upon straight paths, although they are fearful upon a pathless one. But you who, with the same Peter, having a conscience that bears witness to great confidence, dare to say: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters” (Matt. XIV, 18)—since you do not flee from the Lord but go to the Lord through many storms of temptation or tribulation—know that you are no longer timid but reverently fearful.

Such a reverently fearful person was the just Simeon, who awaited Christ’s coming with desire and not with anxious fear. Such a person is sought here when it is said: “Who is the man who fears the Lord?” Do you wish to know who is the person fearing the Lord? Without doubt, the one who, constrained by fear of the Lord, has chosen the way of upright conduct, and for whom the Lord himself establishes a law in that very way which he has chosen: namely, the law of most steadfast resolve, or the law of discipline, whose rod scourges every son whom it receives, so that, instructed through repeated experience of scourges, he may know that it is unsafe for him to depart from the law once received in the way which he chose.

This verse may also be connected with the immediately preceding one according to the Hebrew truth, which reads: “For your name’s sake, O Lord, be propitious to my iniquity, because it is grievous.” When this prayer and confession of sin have been heard, there follows an expression of wonder like that in the words: “Who is this that comes up through the wilderness like a wisp of smoke, from spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” [Col. 1138D] (Song 3:6). For just as that was said in wonder at the innocent soul ascending from this world on high with the fragrance of virtues, so now the Holy Spirit marvels at the truly penitent soul, forcing its way into the kingdom of heaven and saying, “For your name’s sake, O Lord, be propitious to my iniquity, because it is grievous.” He says: “Who is this man fearing the Lord, whom He will instruct in the way that he has chosen?”—as though to say: Who is he? How great, how admirable, is this man who fears the Lord and, like another Jacob, wrestles with the Lord in holy fear?

For just as Jacob said, [Col. 1139A] “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Gen. 32:26), so this man says: I will not let you go unless you are propitious to my sin. And just as, at dawn, it was said to Jacob, who wrestled most resolutely in accordance with his name: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name” (*ibid.*, 28), so to this man acting penitently with courage and seeking pardon it is promised that his soul shall abide among good things and his seed shall inherit the land. Truly, his seed—that is, his good work, which reason performs while it diligently cultivates with the ploughshare of discipline the land, that is, the flesh subject to it—that seed, I say, shall inherit the land: it shall cause him to possess, by inheritance, the land of the living.

Another interpretation: His soul, separated from the body, although without that body it does not possess the fullness of the twofold joy which it awaits after the body’s resurrection, shall nevertheless meanwhile abide among good things, joined to angelic spirits. At last, in the resurrection, his seed—that is, his work—shall inherit the land: it shall be the reason why his body, which is earth, is restored in order to possess a secure inheritance. For since the saints “went forth and wept, sowing their seed” amid some hardship of the body, it is surely just that when they come “with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:6), the body itself also—which was sown animal—should rise spiritual; what was sown in weakness should rise in power; what was sown in dishonor should rise in glory; what was sown [Col. 1139C] in corruption should rise in incorruption. But meanwhile—
### Verse 14

**The Lord is a firm support for those who fear him.** The Lord, who is unchangeable and not a changeable human being, is a firm support for those who fear him—that is, for the reverent, who flee to him, not for the fearful, who flee from him. For those who fear him with a divine fear inspired by God, the Lord himself is a firm support; but for the timid and unbelieving, who fear with merely human fear, there is no firm support. For fear of the Lord gives steadfastness; human fear gives distrust.
