And just as, before the firmament was placed in the midst of the waters, there was no division or distinction of the waters, but, once the firmament had been set in place, the upper waters were divided from the lower waters (Gen. 1:6) [Col. 1139D], so, before the fear of the Lord exists in human beings, there is great confusion within them. But the Lord is a firm support for those who fear him, so that within them there comes about a great distinction among desires, as between upper and lower waters.

For desires that are according to God—for example, the desire for wisdom, integrity, and the other virtues—are like the upper waters, which in the highest angels have already been changed into crystal. Ezekiel saw this crystal above the firmament, because they no longer have anything to fear, being confirmed and made secure above the firmament of the fear of the Lord. But a human being still placed in the flesh is, as it were, with a wife; and this wife is undoubtedly the flesh, joined and subjected to the rational spirit so as to bear rational service. Therefore the inward person [Col. 1140A], who is thus with a wife, however faithful he may be, is nevertheless divided: concerned, that is, both with how he may please God by rendering him the service owed, and with how he may please his wife by receiving and requiring from her the service of due subjection, and by rendering to her the office owed of governance and provision.

Accordingly, since within one and the same person there are many waters of various desires, the firmament of the Lord’s fear is necessary, lest those waters which ought to be divided be confused; lest those which ought to be above be below, and those which ought to be below be above. That is, lest either the flesh become rebellious against the spirit, or the spirit against the Lord. Rather, let the flesh, with its desires found in the appetites of the five senses, remain enclosed under the fear of the Lord; and let reason, with its desires found in the appetite for virtues, be established upon the firmament and foundation of the fear of the Lord [Col. 1140B]. Thus the fear of the Lord itself becomes a firmament in the midst of the waters, dividing waters from waters: by it holy desires are supported, fleshly ones restrained and gathered into one place, so that the dry land of human flesh may appear—not excessively watery, but bringing forth green grass yielding seed, and fruit-bearing trees; that is, every kind and species of fruitful virtue. That all this may come about, the Lord is a firm support for those who fear him.

And because the Lord himself and his fear are wholly in secret, the Hebrew text reads thus: “The secret of the Lord is for those who fear him,” in place of our reading, “The Lord is a firm support for those who fear him” [Col. 1140C]. It rightly follows: **And his covenant, that it may be revealed to them.** For the Old and New Covenant is a firm support for those who fear the Lord, most firmly promising them that the Lord himself, who is now hidden in his secret place, will be revealed to them.

Hence the testator himself, in the Old Testament, offering Moses the sight of his back, says: “My face shall not be seen by you” (Exod. 33:23). But in the New Testament, when transfigured on the mountain, he spoke with that same Moses and Elijah and showed them even his face; and he promised the same thing to every one who loves him, saying: “And I will love him, and will reveal myself to him” (John 14:21).

In another sense also, the Lord is a firm support for those who fear him [Col. 1140D], because he so enlightens them in the Scriptures that his covenant is revealed to them. The Hebrew text confirms this interpretation, where it is read: “The secret of the Lord is for those who fear him, and he shows him his covenant.” When this covenant, or testament, has been shown to them, those who fear the Lord are strengthened, because in it they learn that God is no respecter of persons, but that in every nation whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him.

Therefore I, David the penitent, do not fear the snares of the devil; nor, in order to guard against those snares, do I wish to look down upon the ground, but:

### Verse 15

**My eyes are ever toward the Lord, for he will pluck my feet out of the snare.** Since those who do not look before their feet commonly fall into snares and pits, I nevertheless look upward to the Lord [Col. 1141A], whom alone I fear. In every path of my conduct or action, I intend to guard not so much against giving offence to human beings as against giving offence to him.

Nor, while doing this, do I fear the snares of human or diabolical deception, God protecting me lest I fall into them. And if I do fall, while I attend to his fear and love, while I seek his will in his countenance, I shall nevertheless be secure: for he will pluck my feet out of the snare. Therefore I delight to gaze upon his countenance, whether in the Scriptures or in Christ, so that I may become the wise person of whom it is said: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccles. 2:14)—that is, in the heart, which is as it were the head of the soul, and which ought to be lifted upward to the higher head, namely Christ. “For the head of the woman is the man, and the head of the man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (Eph. 5:23) [Col. 1141B]. The evangelical Truth itself indicates that hearts ought to be raised to him when it says: “Look up, and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near” (Luke 21:28).

Therefore, in good hope, my eyes are ever toward the Lord, for he will pluck my feet out of the snare. My feet, that is, the affections by which I touch the earth: when sight is affected by the pleasure of seeing, taste by the pleasure of tasting, hearing by the pleasure of hearing, and when pleasant things delight smell or touch. Such affections, I say, captured by the snares of pleasures, the Lord himself will pluck free, drawing me out of the mire lest I be fixed in it or cling to it. Sustained and helped by his right hand, may I walk with Peter upon the waves of the sea; even if I begin to sink when worldly pleasure, as a violent wind of temptation threatens, takes hold of my affections [Col. 1141C], nevertheless he will pluck my feet out of the snare.

For the water of worldly pleasure is full of snares and nets, while the devil fishes in this great sea, in which are “creeping things without number, small living creatures with the great” (Ps. 103:25–26). We must cross this water as often as some action lies before us that cannot be done without pleasure. For example, we cannot sleep without the agreeable pleasure of sleep; we cannot restore the body without the pleasure of eating and drinking; nor can we travel the course of this life unless we pass through the waters of such pleasures.

Thus, when we cross from the deficiency of hunger or thirst to the harbour of satiety [Col. 1141D], the passage itself is gentle and pleasant in the very act of refreshment. Yet this gentleness contains many snares and nets, in which our affections are readily entangled. Hence it happens that, when we approach the harbour, caught in the snares and nets of pleasures, we grieve that the journey itself is coming to an end, and the sweetness of the journey delights us more than the need fulfilled in the harbour.

The Hebrew text reads: “For he will bring my feet out of the net.” “A net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures” (Prov. 1:17), says Wisdom. Therefore the nets or snares of temptations are not spread openly before the eyes of winged creatures, but are craftily concealed. Thus the snare of wickedness or pleasure is sometimes hidden beneath the covering of virtue or necessity [Col. 1142A]. For example, while the word of God is preached well, or alms are distributed, vainglory lies in ambush. And when the body is supported with necessary food, the business of pleasure is often carried on under the shadow of necessity. For often the pleasure of eating, which ought to follow necessity like a handmaid, eagerly seeks to go before it as a mistress, and draws the soul beyond the bounds due to necessity—willingly captive, gladly ensnared, voluntarily netted, a soul that sometimes rejoices in having been deceived.

So my wretched and pitiable soul has often rejoiced that it was deceived, while thoughts accused one another or even defended an act that appeared doubtful. Yet when the snare about the feet drew itself tighter, and the hard knot constricted my miserable conscience so that it could not dissimulate [dissimulare: conceal] the guilt it had incurred—for example, [Col. 1142B] when an undisciplined belch, abdominal pain, or three days’ indigestion and prolonged dyspepsia testified that I had exceeded the proper measure in eating—then at last, lifting my eyes to the Lord, I perceived that this was most truly said: “For he will pluck my feet out of the snare.”

For unless I had been freed by a very strong plucking from the snare of gluttony, I should already have been lost, and shall still be lost unless my eyes are toward the Lord, who alone is able to pluck my feet out of the snare. Thus, when I act honourably and virtuously, may the net of pride either not capture me, or, if it captures me, not hold me; when I live praiseworthily, may the desire for vain praise not hold me; when I eat, drink, sleep, or in other ways meet the necessities of nature [Col. 1142C], may the snare of pleasure—hidden, certainly, beneath the covering of necessity itself—either not capture me, or, if it captures me, not hold me.

Therefore let this be my firm counsel and fixed resolve: that my eyes may always be toward the Lord, for he will pluck my feet out of the snare. Those feet indeed cling miserably, but the Lord himself will pluck them free mercifully and wonderfully. They cling often, but he will continually pluck them free, if the unceasing attention of my eyes is not turned away from beholding him. Therefore my eyes are ever toward the Lord, for he will pluck my feet out of the snare.

But when my eyes are raised and fixed upon the Lord, I cry:

### Verse 16

**Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am alone and poor.** Look upon me. You who make my eyes be toward you, let your eyes also be toward me [Col. 1142D]. Once, when in Adam you created me as a noble creature, you saw all that you had made in humanity and for humanity, “and behold, it was very good” (Gen. 1:31), being free from the malice of sins and miseries. But when malice and misery arose in human nature, deceived by diabolical persuasion, you justly looked away from me. You who had previously seen me among the other good things justly turned from me the eyes of your mercy.

But now, appeased through true repentance, turn back upon me those eyes long averted. You who, offended by the disobedience of the first Adam, looked away from me, his offspring, now, appeased through the obedience of the second Adam, look upon me, his redeemed one. After a long turning-away, quickly look upon me [Col. 1143A]: upon me, I say, not upon my sins; for if you look upon these, it follows that you, being just, will justly be angry. But now “turn your face away from my sins” (Ps. 50:11), which I have committed, and look upon me, whom you have made.

And, confirming and making manifest that very look of yours, have mercy on me: lighten my burdensome miseries, heal my pestilential ones, and show full mercy, so that my joy may be full—lacking nothing necessary and overflowing in nothing superfluous. You indeed, God, Father of mercies and God of all consolation, have within yourself reasons to show mercy whenever you see the time for mercy. But in me also there are great and many reasons capable of calling forth your mercy: for I am alone and poor [Col. 1143B]. The only child is usually loved more; and greater pity is felt for the poor.

The Christian people, moreover, is one, not divided by heresies or schisms, and poor, separated from the riches and luxuries of the world.

I too, David the penitent, am alone and poor, because my brothers abandoned and despised me. One of them said to me: “Why have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know the pride of your heart: you came down in order to see the battle” (1 Sam. 17:28). Therefore, although I had seven brothers, I was alone, because those who despised me and regarded me as nothing judged me unworthy of their brotherhood. Hence they did not present me to Samuel in their company; only when he compelled them did they at last admit me, as if an untimely birth, into his presence [Col. 1143C]. Nor was I merely alone among them: I was also reckoned poor and of no worth. They deemed me unworthy to go down to the camp, even to see the camp.

Likewise, I, any penitent person, am alone and poor, because all who loved me while I was given to wantonness now abandon and despise me while I am occupied with serious things. And this adds to my misery: among such rich people I am poor, and am sometimes compelled to seek help even from enemies who feast splendidly every day, clothed in purple, the garment of kings, and fine linen, the garment of high priests and priests. For they rule as kings, as it were, and boast of an appearance of holiness as high priests or priests, while both tyrannizing by the sword and performing divine offices as though saints [Col. 1143D].

But I am poor Lazarus, exposed to the tongues of dogs, because the purulence of my sins has burst outward through confession. I seek whatever covering may be found for my sins, that I may belong to the number of those of whom it is said: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31:1). I therefore neither seek nor desire the purple and fine linen of the rich man who feasts splendidly every day.

I see an infant wrapped in swaddling-clothes and laid in a manger. From those cloths I desire a covering, and I long to feed upon the hay of that manger. For although all flesh is hay, and although “the hay which is today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven” is contemptible (Luke 12:28) [Col. 1144A], the hay of that manger is such flesh that it not only did not itself see corruption, but also grants to those who partake of it so great and such incorruption that they remain forever. For that flesh itself is the Word, and “the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40:8); therefore it can grant those who partake of it to remain forever.

And many indeed were made priests under the law, clothed in fine linen; one succeeded another, just as other hay succeeds hay that has been cut, “because they were prevented by death from continuing. But Jesus, because he remains forever, has an everlasting priesthood. Therefore he is able to save forever those who approach God through himself, ever living to intercede for us. We do not, therefore, have a high priest who cannot sympathize with infirmities” (Heb. 7:24–25) [Col. 1144B]—with the infirmities of every “only and poor” person. For he too, though rich, became poor for our sake; and he, the only Son of his Father in heaven and of his mother on earth, was shown to us as one able to have compassion on those who are ignorant and err, because he was surrounded with our infirmity, not with our iniquity.

But the company of Pharisees, clothed in purple and fine linen, despised him as though he were leprous and struck by God. “But he was wounded for our iniquities” (Isa. 53:5). To this only and poor one I flee, because I am alone and poor, and so forth.

### Verse 17

**The tribulations of my heart are multiplied** [Col. 1144C], as iniquity abounds and the love of many grows cold. Among these many my heart is troubled, because I am compelled to mingle with them on account of the many necessities belonging to the present life. Deliver me, Lord, from these necessities, so that I may seldom or never need to beg at the doors of such people or even attend their abundant feasts, where one hears not readings from Scripture or edifying sermons, but tales and silly songs of jesters and actors.

Alternatively: Human nature, well created but fallen through the fault of its own will into weakness, fell into calamity; oppressed by innumerable necessities, it found nothing in this life except that by which it might be afflicted. But when we serve those same necessities of our nature more than is fitting, and neglect the care of the mind, we add the foulness of guilt to the weakness arising from misery.

For natural necessities commonly possess this very dangerous feature: it is often exceedingly difficult to discern what is done with respect to them from concern for usefulness and what from the vice of pleasure [Col. 1144D]. For temptation often enters under cover of deception: while we render what is due to necessity, we serve the vice of pleasure. Our excuse disguises itself before the eyes of discernment under the covering of weakness, and conceals itself as though under the protection of a utility that must be fulfilled.

To indulge the infirmities of our nature through negligence is nothing other than to add misery to calamity and to multiply the foulness of vices from that same misery. Hence holy men discern with attentive purpose everything they do, lest the weakness of their nature demand from them more than is due to it, lest pleasure grow within them under the covering of necessity. For they endure one thing through weakness, another through the suggestion of temptation; and, standing as most upright judges between necessity and pleasure, they relieve the former by attending to it and restrain the latter by pressing it down. Thus, although they endure the calamity of their weakness, they do not descend through negligence into the foulness of misery [Col. 1145A]. For this is precisely to be in the calamity of necessity: to endure the weakness of flesh that is still corruptible.

He wished to escape these necessities when he said: “Deliver me from my necessities.” For he knew that the sins of pleasures often break forth through the occasion of necessities; and, lest he should admit anything unlawful voluntarily, he earnestly sought to be plucked out of that very condition which, against his will, he endured from the root.

By contrast, the wicked delight in these necessities of their corruption [Col. 1145B], because they turn them toward the use of pleasures. When they serve nature by restoring their bodies with food, through the pleasure of gluttony they swell into the gullet of sensual indulgence. When they seek clothes to cover their limbs, they seek not only things that cover them but also things that exalt them; against the numbness of cold they seek not only things that protect through thickness, but also things that delight through softness—not only things that soothe by the touch of softness, but also things that seduce the eyes by colour. To turn the reason of necessity to the use of pleasure [Col. 1145C] is therefore nothing other than to join the foulness of misery to one’s own calamity.

Considering these things, I, a penitent grieving for past evils and willingly desiring to guard against future ones, say in recalling the past: “The tribulations of my heart are multiplied,” because my heart has been wounded by as many wounds as it has been overcome by pleasures. Again, in caution and fear concerning the future, I say: “Deliver me, Lord, from my necessities,” so that there may be little or no occasion of necessity through which the perversity of pleasure may be fulfilled.

I know indeed that I must eat, drink, sleep, and clothe myself if I wish to live. But, in order that I may be free from the bonds of these necessities, for me “to die is gain”; and therefore, desiring to depart [Col. 1145D] and be with Christ, I ask for a blessed death, saying to you, my God: “Deliver me, Lord, from my necessities.”

That rich man who died badly and was buried in hell did not escape the sufferings of these necessities, because, burning in flames, he thirsted for a drop of water. But I desire to die in such a way that I may be with Christ. For if Lazarus, in Abraham’s bosom before Christ’s coming, was free from these necessities, how much more shall I be entirely free from such things if, released, I am with Christ? This too I ask when I say: “Deliver me, Lord, from my necessities.”

But if remaining in the flesh is necessary for some persons, and if thereby the fruit of my work is to be increased, provided that I live so that Christ is the reason for my living: O Lord, so deliver me from my necessities that those things which cannot be absent while I live may not be harmful. Let them be present without doing harm; let them serve, not rule; let them be for use, not abuse. Thus, freed from their dominion but made a servant of God, I may now have good fruit in sanctification, living soberly, justly, and piously; and, hoping with most certain expectation for eternal life, and rejoicing in hope, may I learn by blessed experience that not only the final reward, but even the expectation of the righteous, is joy, when those who live well await what they shall receive by dying well [Col. 1146A].

There are also necessities which people create for themselves, such as the one who said: “I have bought a farm, and I need to go out and see it.” Another said: “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to test them” (Luke 14:18–19) [Col. 1146B], as though that test were so necessary that it ought to, or could, excuse him. Another said: “I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come” (ibid., 20).

Sometimes perverse or heedless persons fall into such necessities that there is no escape from them without sin. For example, Herod, who had sworn to the girl, was constrained by that very oath, when she made her request, either to give John’s head, committing cruel murder, or to incur perjury. But if he had been wise, he would have chosen the lesser and lighter of the two crimes. Yet he would have been happier and wiser if he had guarded himself against bringing that necessity upon himself.

Deliver me, Lord, from such necessities, so that I may never fall into them; or if—God forbid!—I do fall into them, may I escape a greater evil through a lesser one. This is like soldiers shut in by enemy walls who, compelled by necessity to cast themselves over the wall by leaping down, choose to leap out where the wall is lower and the fall is judged less severe [Col. 1146C]. But since every lame, frail, and weak person is known to be endangered even by the smallest falls, I ask to be delivered from such necessities in such a way that I remain entirely free from them, and never use them as an excuse for failing to come to the wedding feast. Rather, so as not to be absent from it, I prefer to be compelled to enter by certain necessities than, excused by necessities, to remain outside.

Thus I effectively ask to be freed from evil necessities, so that I may be compelled to enter the wedding feast, constrained by good necessities, like the one who said: “I am constrained by two things, desiring to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:23) [Col. 1146D]. Again, constrained by necessity to good work, he says: “Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel, for necessity is laid upon me” (1 Cor. 9:16).

And because someone compelled to good work under such necessities may lose the reward of the work as one pressed into service, he accepts these necessities in such a way as to exclude grievous compulsory service; indeed, so that God may love a cheerful giver or worker, he says: “To write the same things to you is not burdensome to me, but necessary for you” (Phil. 3:1). Again: “If I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me” (2 Cor. 9:17).

Following the example of the one who said these things, I desire to be freed from evil necessities and constrained to what is good by good necessities, through the constraint of love powerfully urging me, so that I may say: “The love of Christ urges me” (2 Cor. 5:14) [Col. 1147A]—that is, it draws me by certain strong hands of necessity.

Alternatively: Humanity was so created that, according to its own will, it could sin and not sin, be disturbed and not be disturbed, die and not die. This was humanity’s great freedom, in which there was no necessity. If, after overcoming the first temptation, humanity had not consented to sin when the devil tempted, it would have been so free from every temptation that it could not sin, could not be disturbed, and could not die. This would have been humanity’s angelic blessedness.

But now, because humanity sinned voluntarily, it has fallen into so deep a pit of sin and misery that it cannot but sin, cannot but be disturbed, and cannot but die. These are the miserable necessities of a person living in the flesh and walking according to the flesh [Col. 1147B]. Yet because there is no condemnation for those who, though they live in the flesh, do not walk according to the flesh or wage war according to the flesh, I ask to be delivered from my necessities in such a way that, when I meet the necessity of the flesh, I may not walk according to the flesh or wage war according to the flesh.

That is, may I possess such great love as covers the multitude of sins and excesses in which I cannot but sin; may it be strong as death against the danger of death, because I cannot but die; and may it be, when I am troubled by many things, my one and only consolation, of which it is said: “But one thing is necessary” (Luke 10:42) [Col. 1147C].

Therefore, when I say in this sense, “Deliver me, Lord, from my necessities,” it is the same as saying: “Lord, give me perfect love, which can be abundant consolation to me against every necessity of this miserable life.” But so that the great building of great love may be set not on an empty but upon a solid foundation, I desire to be like the wise man building a house, who digs deep and lays the foundations upon rock. Therefore I humbled myself through repentance and confession of past sins, so that upon my deep humility I may receive the still more excellent building of love.

Nevertheless, because my humility is still suspect even to myself—for I do not judge myself—you:

### Verse 18

**See my humility.** Examine it; test it; by seeing and testing, first establish in me the foundation of true humility [Col. 1147D], upon which the building of perfect love may worthily be laid. Protected by its covering, may I have no condemnation arising from my necessities. And if I have no labour from them, then on account of this very labour I say: “See my humility, and my labour.” Through the visitation of your mercy, see how much labour of misery I endure; and, moved to clemency by considering my misery and labour, forgive all my sins.

Alternatively: See—that is, receive favourably—my humility [Col. 1148A], because I do not tear myself away from the unity of the Church through a boastful claim of my own righteousness, but, while living among the wicked, labour heavily, being subject for your sake to every human creature, whether to the king as supreme or to governors as sent by him. This humility and subjection would indeed be without labour for me if only worthy persons were placed above me in positions of authority. But now, because I am subject not only to good and gentle masters but also to harsh ones, I endure the great burden of the day and the heat.

And, to use your words, Lord: “I have laboured in bearing them,” for “their assemblies” are “iniquitous” (Isa. 1:13–14). Therefore see not only my humility, by which I willingly humble and subject myself not only to good persons set over me but even to those equal or subject to me in human judgment, considering them better and greater than myself in your judgment [Col. 1148B]. See, I say, not only my humility, but also my labour, by which I patiently bear undisciplined persons placed above or alongside me. Regard this humility and this labour of mine as an acceptable sacrifice; and, appeased by this sacrifice, forgive all my offences.

Above I prayed, saying: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances.” But now, offering before your eyes, Lord, the sacrifice of my humility and labour, I venture to pray more boldly: “See my humility and my labour, and forgive all my offences”—all my sins, not merely those incurred in youth through ignorance or inadvertence [Col. 1148C], but also those I have committed up to this very hour, whether unknowingly or knowingly, through sudden temptation or through deliberate calculation.

The Hebrew text reads: “See my affliction and my labour, and bear all my sins.” For you are he of whom it is written: “Surely he himself took away our sicknesses,” and “he bore our infirmities” (Isa. 53:4). You are the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. Therefore bear all my sins in such a way as to take them away—you who bear and take away the sins of the world.

I do not want you to bear them by merely tolerating me as I sin, as you bear those of whom you say: “I have laboured in bearing them” (Isa. 1:14). Rather, bear my sins so as to take them away, carry them out, or cast them into the depths of the sea, just as you once cast Pharaoh’s chariots and army into the sea. Free me from every dominion of sins, as you freed your people from Pharaoh’s hand; and, as you then looked upon the camp of the Egyptians, so now:

### Verse 19

**Look upon my enemies, for they are multiplied, and they hate me with unjust hatred.** Look upon the demons as Pharaoh’s soldiers; look upon the crowds of evil people as the chariots and horses of those demons; look upon the desires implanted in my flesh and senses; look upon their undisciplined movements, of which it is fitting to say: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. 10:36). Look upon all these enemies of mine.

And because I do not know what I ought to ask concerning each one—for, as your Apostle says: “We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings” (Rom. 8:26) [Col. 1149A]—may that good and gracious Spirit teach you what should happen to each of my enemies: whether demons should be turned away, human beings converted, fleshly desires extinguished, or those people who refuse conversion and, like Pharaoh, are hardened in their wickedness, restrained in their evil designs, lest they persecute beyond measure your people departing from Egypt.

A little above I said: “Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am alone and poor.” And now I say: “Look upon my enemies, for they are multiplied, and they hate me with unjust hatred.” Therefore look upon both me and them: look upon me, the one; them, the many; me, the poor; them, inflamed against me with unjust hatred [Col. 1149B].

For they have been greatly multiplied, since I suffer not only the unjust hatred of unbelievers outside, but also that of false brothers within. Nothing is more unjust than the hatred by which evil is returned for good. The hatred by which evil is returned for evil can in some sense be called just, not unjust. But this is unjust hatred: when someone hates one who loves him, persecutes one who prays for him. With such hatred they returned evil to me for good.

But you, Lord Sabaoth, who judge justly and test hearts and inward parts:

### Verse 20

**Guard my soul**, preserving and bringing to perfection within it the love that it has and desires to have even toward those who hate peace [Col. 1149C]. Guard my soul, lest it turn aside to imitate the perverse. And wherever you see it turned aside after evil persons and ensnared by them, rescue it. Wherever you see me surrounded by their perplexities, rescue me from the midst of a crooked and perverse nation. If you see me tossed by a storm and confined in the belly of the whale, rescue me; tell the whale that devoured me through my heedlessness or disobedience to vomit me onto dry land because of my repentance.

If you see me in the furnace of Babylonian fire, fed by wicked desires, rescue me from that fire by sending me an angel who may make for me something like a wind blowing with dew, lest the fire of anger, pride, lust, or any other wickedness envelop or consume me [Col. 1149D]. If you see me in the lions’ den, send your angel to shut the mouths of the lions, and rescue me from their mouths.

**I shall not be ashamed, because I have hoped in you.** Rescue me for this very reason: that I may not be ashamed, because I have hoped in you, not in my own strength. At the beginning of the psalm I also asked this, saying: “To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, in you I trust: I shall not be ashamed.” And because my countenance has not now been changed in different directions, even near the end of the psalm I ask the same thing that I asked at the beginning: namely, that I may not be ashamed, because I have hoped in you.

I should indeed be greatly ashamed if my hope, frustrated, confounded me; if what I hope for did not happen; if my hope perished. “Hope does not confound,” says your Apostle [Col. 1150A]. Why is this? Surely because “the love of God has been poured out in our hearts” (Rom. 5:5). Therefore hope does not confound because love is poured in. What does the love of God, poured out in our hearts, pour in? Certainly the assurance of consolation, by which I am most certainly assured—as far as a human being can be assured in this life—that:

### Verse 21

**The innocent and upright have cleaved to me**, when the harmful and wicked opposed me. Why, then, have the innocent and upright cleaved to me? Clearly because **I waited for you**. The innocent, who do not wish to harm either themselves or others, and the upright, who willingly correct even crooked things by the assent of their hearts, cleaved to me while I was placed among the wicked because I did not fail by following them into evil. Rather, I waited for you, patiently expecting your judgment, by which I hope to be separated from them. Therefore may these innocent and upright persons also not be ashamed, but
**VERSE 22.** O God, deliver all Israel—that is, the people whom you have prepared for the vision of yourself—from all their tribulations, which they suffer within and without: without, conflicts; within, fears afflict them. So too was that Israel afflicted who was first called by this name. For he endured many distresses: his brother Esau persecuted him (Gen. XXVII, 41) and drove him into exile (Gen. XXXIV, 2); his uncle Laban defrauded him; his daughter Dinah acted wantonly (Gen. XXXV, 22); his firstborn Reuben committed fornication; and his most beloved Joseph was sold [Col. 1150C] (Gen. XXXVII, 28). In Joseph’s sale he was tormented alike by ignorance of what had happened and by his long-standing certain knowledge of his brothers’ envy against that same Joseph.

But at last that Israel was delivered from all his tribulations, because you led him, while he was a wanderer, by straight paths, so that he passed through the place formerly called Bethel (Gen. XXVIII) and now called Bethlehem. There, while he rested upon a stone, you showed him the kingdom of God in the vision of a ladder, whose summit reached to heaven, upon which angels ascending and descending honored the Lord leaning upon the ladder. And lest he should derive too little consolation from this vision—as Pharaoh, seeing twice seven cattle and twice seven ears of grain (Gen. XLI), was not gladdened by a vision he did not understand—lest, I say, [Col. 1150D] this Israel, likewise ignorant of the mystery of the vision, should derive little consolation from it, you gave him knowledge of holy things, disclosing to him the mysteries of your wonders to be performed in that very place.

Therefore, when he awoke from sleep, he said: “Truly the Lord is in this place”; and, afraid, he said, “How terrible is this place! This is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. XXVIII, 16–17). It is as though he were openly saying: Truly, the Lord who appeared to me upon the ladder is to be born here. As a figure of him, he set up the stone as a pillar and poured oil upon it, openly signifying that Christ, the “son of oil,” would be born there, as Isaiah says: “A vineyard was made for the beloved on a horn, the son of oil” (Isa. V, 1), he who is anointed and poured over with the oil of gladness.

Certainly such a vision, and such an unveiling of the vision, was great consolation to Jacob in exile. Yet he had not been delivered from all his tribulations, because afterwards, when he came to his uncle Laban and served him for his daughter Rachel, he labored. But you, O God, gave him honor in his labors and brought his labors to fulfillment; you stood by him amid the fraud of those deceiving him, and made him honorable: namely, by allowing him to obtain in marriage Rachel, his desired and beloved one; by giving him worthy sons from his two wives and their maidservants; and by increasing his flocks of sheep and his other riches, through which he became a renowned man in the land of his pilgrimage [Col. 1151A].

Yet, through these many benefits, that Israel was not delivered from all his straits and tribulations. For, when he was returning to the land of his fathers, his enemies pursued him—namely, Laban and his people [Col. 1151B]. But you guarded him from his enemies and protected him from deceivers, when a heap of stones was gathered as a testimony of peace and covenant between him and his father-in-law.

Still, he had not obtained complete deliverance from all tribulations. For an angel wrestled against Jacob; in that struggle he was distressed, weeping and entreating. But you gave him this most strenuous contest, so that he might prevail; and, having wrested a blessing from the angel, he learned that wisdom is mightier than all things. Afterwards you did not abandon his righteous son, sold into bondage, but mercifully stood by him until you brought him the scepter of kingship and power over those who oppressed him. When Israel heard that he lived and ruled [Col. 1151C] throughout the land of Egypt, then for the first time he said: “It is enough for me; I will go and see him” (Gen. XLV, 28). Thus, when he saw his son Joseph in great glory, consolation first became sufficient for him; for then that Israel was delivered from all his tribulations.

So now, O God, deliver all Israel: lead him by straight paths; show him the kingdom of God; give him knowledge of holy things; grant him honor in his labors and bring his labors to fulfillment; stand by him amid the fraud of those who deceive him; make him honorable [Col. 1152A]; guard him from enemies and protect him from deceivers. And, as he wrestles in prayers and tears in a mighty contest, make him prevail and obtain a welcome blessing, so that he may know that wisdom is mightier than all things.

For thus, as the prophet Hosea testifies, that first Israel “in his strength strove and prevailed against the angel” (Hos. XII, 3–4). And, to make clear by what kind of wrestling he prevailed over the angel: “He wept,” he says, “and entreated him” (Hos. IV). Overcome by such wrestling in prayers and tears, the angel blessed him in that place, calling him Israel, who had previously been called Jacob.

In the same way, therefore, O God, you who delivered that Israel, now deliver all Israel. Do not cease to console him by showing him the splendor of the true Joseph, ruling [Col. 1152B] throughout the Egypt of this world, until, having learned and experienced his glory through his gracious gifts, he says: “It is enough for me; I will go and see him before I die” (Gen. XIV, 28). And I shall see him now through a mirror and in an enigma, before I die; but face to face after I die. Now I shall see him ruling throughout the land of Egypt; then I shall see him reigning in heaven, when Egypt’s kingdom has been destroyed. Now I shall see him feeding his brothers in Egypt, distributing grain to all peoples, and subjecting everything to royal service; but then I shall see him as the bread of angels, feeding angels and human beings from his glorious vision, and shining in the splendor of his Father’s majesty.

Therefore, that all Israel may be able to speak such things with a free and joyful mind [Col. 1152C], do you, O God, deliver all Israel from all its tribulations. Remembering now, at the end, that verse joined to the present Psalm, where it was said, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth,” we say:

Glory to the Father, the Lord. Glory to the Son, the Truth. Glory to the Holy Spirit, Mercy. Glory to the one true and merciful Lord: to be feared because of truth, to be loved because of mercy. Amen.

## PSALM XXV

[Col. 1151]

[Col. 1151D] “Judge me, O Lord, for I have entered in my innocence.” The title is familiar, and is as follows (**VERSE 1**):

## A PSALM OF DAVID

[Note: [Col. 1151D] Vulgate: “Unto the end, a Psalm of David.”]

This Psalm is attributed not to Christ, the mediator and true David, but to any perfect person of whom the argument proceeds in this manner. First, though mingled with the wicked, he shows that he is divided from them by the character of his conduct. Second, he asks that in judgment he may also be locally separated from them. Its purpose is to warn us to avoid the company of the wicked and to cleave to the righteous, because character is formed through companionship.

[Col. 1152D] This Psalm may, however, most suitably be assigned to that same penitent David who, in the preceding Psalm, speaks in the person of the penitent Church, or indeed of any one penitent person. For penitent David, the penitent Church, and every penitent person, after the foregoing confession of truth and mercy, fittingly pray that through that same mercy and truth of the Lord they may finally be distinguished from the ungodly. “Judge me, O Lord,” he says, “for I have entered in my innocence.” And so that he may deservedly be distinguished from the ungodly in the future, he distinguishes himself in the present and says: “I have not sat with the council of vanity, [Col. 1153A] and I will not go in with those who work iniquity.” We must now pursue the words of the Psalm more fully.

“Judge me, O Lord.” Judgment is sometimes used for condemnation, as there: “He who does not believe has already been judged” (John III, 18); and sometimes for discernment, as there: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. XLII, 1). I do not ask for the judgment of condemnation, but for the judgment of discernment. For I am now in great confusion, in great Babylon, in great disturbance, seeing the good together with the wicked, grain with chaff, tares in the midst of wheat, so that scarcely any distinction can be observed among these different things—although there is a great difference between the two masters, whom no one can serve together, and between their final rewards.

Therefore, so that, just as there is a manifest difference between [Col. 1153B] the two masters themselves and their final rewards, so there may also be a manifest difference between their diverse servants: you, O better Lord, to whom I have chosen to cleave, judge me—that is, distinguish me from the servants of the other master—so that we may not be confused in one mass, although we have been poured together into the one broad vessel of this world.

“Your name is oil poured out” (Song I, 3), because to you, Lord Jesus Christ, has been given the name above every name. As oil surpasses every liquid—even if a single drop were at the bottom of the sea, it would rise to the surface by its natural movement and float above the whole sea—so, much more, oil mixed with other liquids in a small vessel always holds the highest place and, though poured in with them, does not permit itself to be confused with them. Thus, O Lord, whom of the two masters I have chosen to serve, your name is above every name.

Nor is this surprising, because you are anointed with the oil of gladness; you were conceived by the Holy Spirit, who in the beginning was borne over the waters like oil, already then foreshadowing that his anointing bestows this: that whoever is thereby poured over the waters of the abyss ought not to be confused. And you indeed, Lord Jesus Christ, possess in yourself the gentleness of this oil, and from your fullness your other elect receive that by which they escape the confusion of this abyss over which darkness lies.

And I, the penitent Church—or I, the penitent Psalmist—who in the preceding Psalm employed lamentation and longed to escape everlasting woe, would now like, as though rejoicing over forgiveness received, to exult in a song of joy [Col. 1153D], according to those three things seen in the book: namely, lamentations, song, and woe. But how shall I sing a song or hymn in a foreign land, especially amid such a great disturbance of Babylonian confusion, where I do not know whether I am worthy of hatred or love? Therefore in this Psalm I desire to be distinguished, so that in the following Psalm, distinguished from the ungodly, I may celebrate in a joyful song that the Lord is my illumination, my salvation, and the protector of my life.

For as long as I am so confused and mingled with the perverse that it does not at all appear to me whether I have been anointed with that oil which is your name poured out—though I am called a Christian, named from your name—I do not dare, relying upon the name alone, to claim for myself the voice of song and say, “The Lord is my illumination [Col. 1154A] and my salvation” (Ps. XXVI, 1). Therefore, so that I may dare this with the good confidence of conscience, judge me, O Lord; distinguish me; make the difference between my conduct and that of the wicked evident, certain, and clear. Although I do not refuse to be joined with them in one threshing-floor through bodily communion and occasional local cohabitation, I nevertheless desire a conduct and an intention of conduct different from theirs, through which I may be found distinct from them both now, according to judgments of differing merits, and in the future, according to judgments of differing rewards. Therefore I cry and say: “Judge me, O Lord,” prompted, if not by the merit of my good works, at least by the merit of faith, through which I have been made innocent from being guilty.

“For I have entered in my innocence.” [Col. 1154B] Although I came forth guilty from my mother’s womb because of Adam’s sin, in whom all sinned and in whom I too sinned—although, I say, I came forth guilty from my mother’s womb—I have entered, from the womb of paradisal grace, into the womb of grace through baptism. In it, grace, a mother, bears into one infancy all those whom either sex distinguishes in body or age distinguishes in time, so that all who are cleansed by this washing are reborn into a new innocence, and one who is immersed as a child of sin emerges as heavenly offspring.

Thus I entered baptism in my innocence: not an innocence which I brought there, but one which I received there. For what good thing do I have that I did not receive? And if I received it [Col. 1154C], I do not wish to glory as though I had not received it, seeking my own glory. Rather, I wish to glory in you, O Lord, through whom I received this innocence, of which I now say: “For I have entered in my innocence.”

Thus we call it “our daily bread,” not because that bread of angels is ours by our own merit, but by the gift of grace. Thus we say, “Our Father, who are in heaven,” not because we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as from ourselves (II Cor. III, 5), such that he might be our Father, but because our sufficiency is from him, who adopted us as sons. And so I now say, “For I have walked in my innocence,” not because any innocence comes to me from myself, but because he who suffered for me as an innocent lamb [Col. 1154D] first clothed me in baptism, of water and the Spirit, and then in the baptism of true penitence, with the fleece of his innocence. Therefore, in the confidence of faith, I now say: “Judge me, O Lord, for I have entered in my innocence.” First I entered baptism; afterwards, when I had lost my innocence, I entered again into penitence in my innocence. Truly mine, because it was given me by grace, not because it was acquired by merits.

For we advance toward the Lord by two steps: intention and action. By intention we enter; by action we go forth. It may happen that my going forth harms someone who finds a stumbling-block in my action. But my entering, so far as intention is concerned, devises [Col. 1155A] harm to no person, but correction, amendment, improvement, the prohibition or restraint of vices, and the building up of virtues. Therefore I say that I have entered in my innocence, because I am conscious of no malice in my intention, even when some harm happens to someone through my going forth in action.

The Hebrew truth has: “Judge me, O God, because I have walked in my simplicity.” This sense accords well with what I said concerning the innocence of my intention. It is understood as that single eye which makes the whole body full of light when, in its singleness, it directs the work. I have walked in the singleness of this eye when I have taken care to preserve innocence of intention, even [Col. 1155B] in those steps of action by which someone has been offended.

I wish this statement to be understood of that time when I strove either to preserve myself after baptism in innocence and simplicity or to recover that same simplicity of innocence through penitence, with that zeal for improvement and amendment in which I wish to persevere until death, with divine assistance. For if I trusted in myself, I know that I would fail. But now I trust in the Lord, and hoping in the Lord I shall not grow weak; because those who hope in the Lord shall be changed and shall have strength, shall run and not grow weary, shall take up wings and fly as eagles, and shall not fail (Isa. XL, 31).

Therefore I too, hoping in the Lord, shall not grow weak or be moved like hypocrites or schismatics, who, so that they may seem righteous and holy [Col. 1155C], do not wish to be among the wicked, though they themselves are worse: like light chaff, they are already carried away before winnowing by the wind of pride. But I do not, as a proud man, ask to be separated from the wicked by the wind of self-exaltation so as to appear holier than they in human sight; rather, I ask that I may be found innocent in your sight, O Lord. For although I have said that I have entered in my innocence, nevertheless, since no one understands sins:

**VERSE 2.** “Prove me, O Lord, and try me.” That is, try me by proving, not by rejecting, as you tried Abraham. By trials and testings show me, not to yourself but to myself, so that I too may punish my evils through the hidden remedy of penitence and may not be found [Col. 1155D] an example of depravity to others. Do not allow me to be tempted by that tempter who tempts only in order to deceive. But you yourself, who test in order to prove, prove me and try me. And if you find any rust in me, do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses to you (Ps. LXXIII, 19). But you yourself:

“Burn my reins and my heart.” Delights reign in the reins; thoughts reign in the heart. Therefore burn my reins, lest anything evil delight me, and my heart, lest I think anything evil, intensely with that fire which you sent into the earth and desired to be vehemently kindled. I know that love is strong as death and jealousy harsh as hell; its lamps are lamps of fire and flame. Many waters could not extinguish love (Song VIII, 6–7). Therefore, with this unquenchable [Col. 1156A] burning, burn my reins and my heart, so that nothing may delight me to think except what the fire of charity has approved by testing, so that it may be said of me: “Many sins are forgiven one who loved much.”

But if you judge that my heart and reins must be burned by the fire of tribulation, do not allow me to be tempted beyond what I can bear. Rather, first prove me mercifully, weighing what I can patiently and profitably bear in the testing of tribulation; and then try me, once this merciful proving has preceded, lest perhaps I be found reprobate if I have been overwhelmed by excessive tribulations which I cannot bear with patience. Yet I ask rather to be proved, tried, and burned by the fire of purifying love than by the fire of purgatorial tribulation; for in the one there is a work of mercy [Col. 1156B], in the other a work of justice. Though each work is praiseworthy, the work of mercy is more lovable and desirable. Therefore I especially ask to be burned in the fire of charity according to your mercy:

**VERSE 3.** “For your mercy is before my eyes,” and it is more desirable. Nevertheless, if it should be necessary for certain stains of mine to be cleansed also by the fire of tribulation, I do not refuse to be proved by this fire either, which is a work of truth and justice, because truth pleases me—the truth that pleases you, O God.

“And I have pleased you in your truth.” As long as the truth of justice displeased me, I too displeased you. But as soon as the truth which pleases you began to please me, I likewise pleased you with that truth [Col. 1156C], in which, as in a brilliantly clear mirror, I had displeased myself, disfigured by sin and falsehood. But I pleased myself in truth, when the stains of falsehoods were wiped from the face of my mind through true confession of sins and true conversion from vanity to truth.

Do you wish to know how I became a friend of truth? First hear how I had been an enemy of vanity. Since vanity and truth are contrary to one another, it is fitting first to hate vanity and then to love truth; for love of vanity and love of truth cannot both be contained in the same heart.

And so that you may have knowledge of both things, receive a description of each. Vanity is that which does not remain as it appears, but deceives the gaze of those who see and suddenly vanishes between the eyes of those who see and those who wish to see. Truth is that which remains forever as it is believed or seen to be. But among the many vanities tumultuously present in the world beneath the sun, there is one vanity called “vanity of vanities”: namely, the devil’s lie [Col. 1156D], which is not as it appears, when the devil himself, who is a liar and father of that same lie, either pretends that he is like the Most High or promises that same likeness of divine loftiness to people who wrongly believe him.

For although it was said to the angel, “You are the seal of the likeness of God” (Ezek. XXVIII, 12), and although man was created in the image and likeness of God (Gen. I, 27), each must seek likeness to divine goodness in such a way that neither presumes to claim for himself likeness to divine loftiness. [Col. 1157A] Because the chief angel arrogated this to himself in vain and false glory, he was rightly cast down from heaven’s height and is held bound by the cords of hell until, in the last judgment, he is hurled into hell’s depths. Then it will appear how truly that lie was “vanity of vanities,” or “falsehood of falsehoods,” by which he either claimed God’s loftiness for himself or deceitfully promised it to humankind.

Meanwhile, although cast down from heaven and bound with the cords of hell in this darksome air, he still deceitfully claims likeness to divine loftiness for himself when he persuades people to worship and honor him as God: among pagans, in images made by hands and other creatures; or among Christians, in the likenesses [Col. 1157B] of masses sung by heretics and others under anathema or deprived of office. For, just as pagans honor the devil and dishonor the true God by offering the reverence of divinity to images which do not possess the Spirit—“for there is no spirit in their mouth” (Ps. CXXXIV, 17)—so also perverse and false Christians dishonor Christ the true God and the Holy Spirit by offering divine reverence to the forbidden offices of heretics and schismatics. These indeed possess an appearance of piety in the sacramental signs performed according to ecclesiastical rite, but deny the power of piety, which is the Holy Spirit.

Witnesses of this are Pope Leo, Pope Gregory, Pope Pelagius, Cyprian the martyr, Augustine the bishop, and the illustrious [Col. 1157C] Jerome, together with other orthodox Fathers. We append some of their testimonies, lest we seem to condemn the forbidden offices of heretics or schismatics without authority.

Pope Leo, to Leo Augustus, in the letter beginning: “I have reverently received the letter of your Clemency, full of the strength of faith and light of truth.” “Before a most Christian prince,” he says, “and one worthy to be numbered with due honor among Christ’s preachers, I make use of the freedom of Catholic faith, and confidently exhort you to fellowship with the prophets and apostles: steadfastly despise and reject those who have deprived themselves of the Christian name.”

[Col. 1157D] And shortly afterwards: “Is it not plain whom your Piety should assist and whom it ought to oppose, lest the Church of Alexandria, which has always been a house of prayer, should now become a den of thieves? For it is manifest that, through the most cruel and savage madness, all light of the heavenly sacraments has been extinguished there: the offering of sacrifice has been interrupted; the sanctification of chrism has failed; and the impious have taken away all the mysteries with parricidal hands. It is therefore a great matter for you, that a crown of faith may also be added to your diadem through triumph over the enemies of the Church.

“For this also ought to stir the priestly and apostolic mind of your Piety to righteous vengeance: pestilent persons obscure the purity of the Church of Constantinople, in which certain clerics are found who agree with the opinion of heretics [Col. 1158A] and, within the very body of Catholics, assist heretics by their assertions. If my brother Anatolius, because he spares them too indulgently, is found too negligent in expelling them, may you deign, through your faith, to provide this remedy also for the Church, so that such persons may be driven not only from the order of clergy but even from residence in the city, lest the holy people of God be further polluted by the contagion of perverse persons.”

Pope Gregory, in the *Moralia*, Book XXXV: “It should be noted with great care that Job’s friends are commanded to offer the sacrifice of their conversion to the Lord not by themselves, but through Job. For he says: ‘But Job my servant shall pray for you; I will accept his face, so that your folly may not be imputed to you.’ It is as though he were openly saying to heretics: [Col. 1158B] ‘I do not receive your sacrifices; I do not hear the words of your petitions, except through the intercession of him whose words of profession concerning me I recognize as true.’”

And shortly afterwards: “Seek your salvation through the Catholic Church, which I love. For I wish to forgive her that wherein you sinned against me, so that she, who suffered from your sickness, may obtain your healing. For she alone is the one through whom the Lord willingly receives sacrifice; she alone intercedes confidently for those who err. Therefore the Lord also commanded concerning the offering of the lamb: ‘It shall be eaten in one house, and none of its flesh shall be carried outside’ (Exod. XII, 48). The lamb is eaten in one house: the true offering of the Redeemer is immolated in the one Catholic Church. The divine law forbids its flesh to be carried outside, because it forbids giving what is holy to dogs.”

Pope Pelagius, to John the Patrician: “Do not continually pollute a Catholic mind by any communion with schismatics. It is established that there is one body of Christ, one Church. One divided from unity cannot consecrate the truth of Christ’s body. One divided from the Church’s body and separated from the apostolic sees desecrates rather than consecrates. Do not therefore wish, as though there were no difference between schismatics and the Church, to associate indiscriminately with the sacrifices of both. For, if we are guided by truth, that which a schismatic produces is not Christ’s body.”

[Col. 1158D] Cyprian, to Magnus the presbyter: “We find that in such an offense not only leaders and authors, but also participants, are destined for punishments unless they separate themselves from communion with the wicked. For the Lord commanded through Moses: ‘Separate yourselves from the tents of these most hardened men, and touch none of the things which are theirs, lest you perish together in their sin’ (Num. XVI, 26). And what the Lord had denounced he fulfilled through Moses, so that whoever had not separated himself from Korah, Dathan, and Abiram immediately paid the penalties for impious communion. By this example it is shown and proved that all will be liable to guilt and punishment who, with irreligious recklessness, join themselves to schismatics against their governors and priests. Likewise the Holy Spirit testifies and says through the prophet Hosea: ‘Their sacrifices [Col. 1159A] are like bread of mourning; all who eat it are defiled,’ clearly teaching and showing that all who have been polluted by their sin are altogether joined with its authors in punishment.”

Augustine, in his sermon on blasphemy against the Holy Spirit: “The visible form of a branch can exist even apart from the vine, but it cannot possess the invisible life of the root except in the vine. Accordingly, bodily sacraments, which even those separated from the unity of Christ’s body carry and celebrate, can display an appearance of piety; but the invisible and spiritual power of piety cannot be in them, just as sensation does not remain with a human limb when it is cut off.”

Jerome, in his sermon *On the Paschal Lamb*: “Let us not suppose that this lamb can be eaten everywhere. We are commanded [Col. 1159B] to eat it in one house, that is, not to suppose that it is sacrificed outside the Church. From this it is clear that Jews, heretics, and all assemblies of perverse doctrines, because they do not eat in the Church, eat not the flesh of the lamb but that of the dragon, who was given as food to the peoples of Ethiopia. But we eat the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”

Strengthened by these testimonies, I, a lover of truth, since I have been pleasing in truth, have separated myself from vanity and have become a friend of truth.

**VERSE 4.** “I have not sat with the council of that vanity,” especially the vanity which is vanity of vanities because of the preeminent lie of the devil, by which he pretends that he is made like the Most High. For since, as Samuel testifies, “not to obey is like the crime of idolatry, and unwillingness to submit is like the sin of divination” (I Sam. XV, 23), who does not readily perceive [Col. 1159C] that every cleric who presumes to offer sacrifice contrary to obedience to the Apostolic See, denying the power of piety, performs the mystery of iniquity? Through lying signs the simple people are so deceived in this mystery that, because of the apparent sameness of the signs—that is, of visible sacraments—they believe that no difference exists between the masses of Catholics, which are sung in obedience, and the masses of hired priests, public simoniacs, and openly incestuous priests, which are sung contrary to obedience to the Church that forbids them.

Yet the difference is exceedingly great. For in the masses of Catholics is recognized the Truth of truths, who says: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke XXII, 19). Those to whom this is said obey him beneficially when he says, “Do this.” But it is said to the disciples of truth, not to those who sit in the council of vanity: there sit upon seats of pestilence those who celebrate the sacrament of highest obedience while guilty of stubborn disobedience. In their masses, forbidden under anathema or excommunication, one can recognize vanity of vanities: Antichrist lying that he is like Christ, and the devil lying that he is like the Most High.

For as Pharaoh, through his magicians, competing against Moses and Aaron by the likeness of signs, strove to appear like the Lord, so now Antichrist or the devil [Col. 1160A], through his clerics trafficking in the Church with Simon Magus, committing fornication with Nicholas, and moreover presuming to perform forbidden offices, strives against truth through the likeness of sacraments. Yet in these the finger of God, the Spirit of truth, works no more than it did in the false signs of Pharaoh’s magicians—except, certainly, for the sacrament of baptism, which, even when performed according to ecclesiastical rite by any layperson whatsoever, is without doubt valid.

To this is added that such pseudo-clerics are forbidden only the ministry of the altar and the ecclesiastical benefice owed to ministers of the altar. Therefore, while tolerating them when they baptize or administer certain other lesser offices, I do not wish to communicate with them in the altar ministry forbidden to them, lest I be found sitting in the council of vanity against obedience to the truth, which teaches the prelates of the Apostolic See to abstain from such persons [Col. 1160B].

Whether Christ’s body is made in their masses or not is superfluous to investigate, since it is undoubtedly established that such masses themselves are forbidden under excommunication by Leo IX and Pope Nicholas, as their successor Pope Alexander testifies, saying: “By authoritative command we order that no one hear the mass of a priest whom he knows without doubt to have a concubine or a woman secretly introduced into his household.” Therefore the holy synod also decreed this from the beginning under excommunication, saying:

“Whoever among priests, deacons, and subdeacons, after the decree concerning clerical chastity issued by our predecessor of blessed memory, the most holy Pope Leo, or by Nicholas, has openly taken a concubine or has not dismissed one already taken: by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, we command and altogether forbid him to sing Mass, to read the Gospel or Epistle at Mass, to remain in the presbytery with those obedient to the aforesaid decree during the divine offices, or to receive a portion from the Church.”

These statements concerning incestuous persons suffice, so that no one may doubt that their offices are forbidden under excommunication and that their sacrifices must be rejected outright. Now concerning those who hold ecclesiastical offices by contract, their employers, and all who trade in the house of God: proof might be demanded that they lie under anathema. But it is unnecessary, since this is most fully confirmed by the decretal letter of Pope Paschal addressed to the Milanese, in which he says:

> He incurs the guilt of eternal death who, when able, does not defend his brother from death. We also, having heard of the extreme danger in which your Excellency stands, incur the penalty of the gravest guilt if we keep silence; for the Lord prophesies that he indeed sheds blood who, by silence, conceals the wickedness of the impious. For we have heard, to our great astonishment, that among you sacred orders are sold for money, whereas all who accept anything of this kind are plainly proved to be heretics by the Holy Spirit speaking thunderously through Gregory: “Whoever is ordained through money is advanced for this purpose: that he may become a heretic.”

And, to show that the cause of this little writing of ours was not presumption but fear, the same blessed man continues:

> Whoever does not burn vehemently, according to the station of his office, against the heresy of simony and neophytes, must not doubt that he has a share with him who first committed this sacrilegious crime.

Since in these words the heresy of simony and of neophytes is named, it is declared most plainly that this crime is most worthy of eternal death, as the divine oracle attests through Augustine, saying:

> Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that every heretic or schismatic—even if he gives many alms, or even sheds his blood for Christ—will be consigned to the fires of eternal flame with the devil and his angels, unless before the end of this life he has been incorporated and restored to the Catholic Church. [Col. 1161B]

Hence the Lord drove sellers and buyers from the Temple; the earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram alive; Peter condemned Simon Magus when he made his attempt; and he condemned all simoniacs with the perpetual anathema of ecclesiastical weapons. It is utterly disgraceful that the Church, now established in fullest vigor, should succumb to so deadly an enemy—the enemy over whom, in the beginning of her infancy, she triumphed with such strength.

But if anyone objects that not consecrations, but the things themselves which result from consecration, are sold, he seems indeed to say something, but understands absolutely nothing. For since neither a church, nor a bishop, nor an abbot, nor anything of this kind can prosper at all without bodily and external possessions—just as the soul does not live temporally without the body—whoever sells one of these two, without which the other cannot be possessed, leaves neither unsold. Yet the sacred canon wholly abolishes this objection, when it forbids a procurator or defender of a church, or one subject to a rule, to be appointed by God through money; and so it likewise cuts down the agents of so great a crime with the sword of anathema.

What more need be said? If simoniacs and neophytes, anathematized and excommunicated as true heretics, are separated from the number of the faithful and from the Church, who does not see that the Masses and prayers of such priests or clerics provoke God to wrath against the people—the God whom we believed would be appeased by such things? For it is written: “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23). And again: “The place of a true sacrifice is not outside the Catholic Church.” Hence it is said: “Avoid a heretical man after a first and second admonition.” How, then, do we avoid such bishops, abbots, or other clerics if we hear their Masses, when, if we even pray with them, we incur excommunication?

It is wholly erroneous even to believe that they are priests, since Peter says to Simon: “May your money be with you unto destruction, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money” (Acts 8:20). Where “you thought” is said, it is clear that he is condemned not for what he had done, but because he believed himself able to do it. And we, under anathema, prohibit the same thing concerning the heresy of simony, as the holy synod decreed: that no one sell either the consecration of churches, [Col. 1162A] or an archpriesthood, or the granting of altars, or the handing-over of churches. Whoever leases, sells, or buys these things, let him be anathema. Amen. And all answered for the third time: “So be it, so be it.”

Let clerics who hold offices by contract and those who employ them hear these things; and from what has been said let them plainly recognize that they lie under anathema and therefore ought rightly to be despised in their forbidden offices together with incestuous Nicolaitans. Yet we wish this not to be unknown: the secret trading and fornications of clerics are to be reserved for the future judgment. But those whose sins are manifest, going before them to judgment, and concerning whom, as has already been shown, judgment has already been made—such persons must be avoided in their forbidden offices, lest, while the devil or Antichrist works the mystery of iniquity through their forbidden [Col. 1162B] sacrifices, God Christ be insulted.

For since he is the Most High and is called the Son of the Most High, and alone works the mystery of justice and godliness in lawful, not forbidden, offices, whoever is prohibited and deprived of office yet presumes to offer sacrifice while the holy Roman Church forbids it through her pontiffs—indeed, while the Lord Jesus Christ himself forbids it in them—is found in that same vanity of vanities to make himself equal or superior to the Most High, in which the devil spoke: “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14). Certainly, when forbidden Masses are made equal and similar to Masses not forbidden, there is found in the mouths of those fabricating such a lie a vanity of vanities, or falsity of falsities. This, together with the first lie of the devil, is rightly judged detestable, although it is found forged on the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north—since it appears to some to be supported, as it were, by certain authorities from the New and Old Testaments.

For we are not unaware that many men powerfully learned in letters affirm that forbidden Masses, so long as any bishop tolerates them in his bishopric, may be heard without distinction, even though the Roman Church forbids them. And this assertion of learned clerics has prevailed to such an extent that, if possible, even the elect are led into error (Matt. 24:24). Yet those who are truly elect, if they have been led into this error, repent in this life, or in the future endure purgatorial [Col. 1162D] punishments because they think against the Roman Church.

Far be it from me to believe anyone against the holy Roman Church, even if he speaks with the tongues of men and angels, even if he shines with miraculous powers. For whatever his merit, anyone who thinks against Peter’s faith, and does not agree with his lawful successors in the matter of Catholic faith, shall bear judgment—whoever he may be, even if he belongs to the number of the elect.

Thus blessed Gregory writes in the *Dialogues* concerning Paschasius, a deacon of the Roman Church. Although he was an outstanding servant of God, a guardian of the poor, a despiser of himself, and had composed most eloquent books concerning the Holy Spirit; although he was so holy that a demoniac was freed by touching the bier on which his corpse was carried—nevertheless, after death he paid most grievous penalties because, with Laurentius, he had held an opinion against Pope Symmachus, not in the chief matter of faith but in the election of Pope Symmachus himself. The aforesaid Paschasius would have preferred Laurentius, had he been able to do so without disturbing the peace of the Church. How much more, then, is dissent in the highest sacrament of faith dangerous and ruinous: dangerous to the elect who are led into error; ruinous to wicked persons who lead into the same error those whom they can, and stubbornly defend the error itself? For those who err, and send into error all whom they can, unless they repent, will be eternally damned. But the good who are deceived by them, like the aforesaid Paschasius—who did not bewail in this life a fault which he did not even believe to be a fault—if they are taken from this life in this deception, will be purged in the other life. [Col. 1163B]

But I, poor David, poor and penitent, judging it far better to be corrected in this life than tortured in another, lest I perhaps be found reprobate, pray this: “Test me in this life.” Therefore I say to you, my God, who are Truth of truths, to whom every vanity is displeasing, especially vanity of vanities—to you, I say: Test me in this life, and try me; burn my reins, lest vain things delight me; burn my heart, lest I willingly think vain things or believe vain things to be true—especially forbidden offices and sacrifices, in which the vanity of vanities has been detected by the holy Fathers, whose testimonies we set forth above.

In these testimonies, which reject vanity but commend mercy and truth, [Col. 1163C] “your mercy is before my eyes, and I have been pleasing in your truth”—a truth proclaimed by the testimonies mentioned above. Therefore, assenting to the testimonies of truth after patiently understanding them, I have not sat with the council of vanity, taking care not to participate in the conventicles of those in whose forbidden sacrifices and offices there is not the mystery of truth and mercy, but the mystery of iniquity and vanity.

For even if, as many powerfully learned men who think against the Roman Church insist, Christ’s body is made there, it is in their hands no otherwise than it was in the hands of the Jews who crucified him; and therefore they are guilty of the Lord’s blood and body. Nevertheless, the sounder view in this matter is that held by the Roman Church, which has alike deprived those holding office by contract and incestuous persons of ecclesiastical office and benefice, and has commanded that their offices not be tolerated in the Church of God.

In carrying out her commands, although some bishops are found sluggish, I nevertheless have not sat with the council of vanity—or, as the Hebrew has it, “with men of vanity”—men who hate truth and love vanity. Sitting with them, that is, agreeing with them in their council, does not please me. For even if I sometimes associate bodily with them, I shall not consent to them, nor approve with them what they approve: they consider themselves blessed in temporal and vain things when, for temporal and vain advantages, they celebrate forbidden offices or do other things that appear good but are not. And because this [Col. 1164A] vanity of all vanities is vanity and the root of iniquities, although I am sometimes among those who do wicked things in the Lord’s threshing-floor, where chaff must be borne with the grain, nevertheless:

> I will not enter in with those who do wicked things.

For I shall apply not even the beginning of consent to doing such things; and, with divine grace helping me, I shall take care that the gates of hell do not prevail in me against the faith which I learned from Peter and his successors, whose testimonies I have mentioned above in part. Therefore, through those gates of hell which heretics have opened, or are opening, when they despise the prohibitions of the apostolic see, I will not enter in with those who do wicked things. But:

### Verse 5. “I hated the assembly of evildoers,” that is, the counsels of those who contrive malice against their neighbors. [Col. 1164B]

For if anyone does not give them gifts, or does not love their deeds, they sanctify war against him, wishing to separate from the Church’s fellowship all who dare oppose their wickedness even by a word. Therefore I hated the assembly of evildoers. I do not say simply, “I hated the assembly”; nor do I say that I hate the evildoers themselves. Although elsewhere I have not implausibly said, “I have hated the wicked and loved your law” (Ps. 118), nevertheless on this occasion I do not say that I hate the evildoers themselves, because such hatred would not be good, especially if it were evil against evil; rather, “I hated the assembly of evildoers,” that is, I hated this contradiction in the adjective, this conflict within a divided expression, by which those are called an *ecclesia* who are not the Church but are evildoers.

For since the Church is rightly called the gathering of the righteous, the synagogue of Satan is unworthy of this name, that it should be called Church. Yet when “the assembly of evildoers” is said, it is as though one said “a dead animal”: if it is an animal, it is not dead; if it is dead, it is not an animal.
