Likewise, an assembly of evildoers, because it consists of evildoers, is not the Church; and therefore it is a thing worthy of hatred that it is called “Church.” Therefore I hated the assembly of evildoers, desiring it to be called Church in such a way that it is not an assembly of evildoers but a gathering of the righteous.

The same judgment will stand even concerning a church made by human hands, if it has been consecrated through simony, in agreement with Pope Alexander, who says in his decrees:

> A church which is shown to have been consecrated through an agreement for a price—or, to speak more truly, execrated—must by no means be regarded as a church. [Col. 1164D]

Since the Roman pontiff says this, we too may freely say that this proclamation—by which every Catholic says, “I hated the assembly of evildoers”—strikes with a fitting verdict simoniacally consecrated churches of evildoers, and likewise churches consecrated by schismatics.

> “And I will not sit with the impious.”

Those who are evildoers are themselves impious: evildoers against their neighbor, impious against God; evildoers because they do not maintain brotherly love, impious because they think against truth and the sincerity of faith. In the former, schismatic perversity is evident; in the latter, heretical impiety appears. And truly, “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the impious” (Ps. [Col. 1165A] 1:1); he becomes more blessed if he does not even sit with those impious persons in order to hear their counsels, because “evil conversations corrupt good morals.” Therefore, avoiding a heretical man after a first and second admonition, I will not sit with the impious, lest perhaps such a confession become dangerous, and their speech, which spreads like cancer, even if it cannot make me agree with impiety, should at least make me contentious, to the ruin of those who hear. Therefore, separated from the assembly of evildoers and impious persons:

### Verse 6. “I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will encompass your altar, O Lord.”

The order is good: first turn away from evil, then do good. For what is it not to sit with them except to turn away from evil? And who would doubt that it is good that “I will wash my hands among the innocent”? In this faith, when I wash my hands in preparation for divine service, I am accustomed to say:

> Grant to our senses, almighty Father, that, just as the outward defilements of our hands are washed away, so may the inner pollutions of our minds be cleansed by you, and may there increase in us the growth of all holy virtues.

And, washed and clothed in sacred garments, I will encompass your altar, O Lord, so that in sacred offices I may hear the voice of your praise and recount all your wonders—that is, mercy and truth, which are all your ways. The great and wonderful miracles of these ways I shall recount to willing hearers, not in the assembly of evildoers, but in your house and in the place where your glory dwells. [Col. 1165C] For just as I hated the assembly of evildoers, so, O Lord, “I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place where your glory dwells.” Therefore, O God, do not destroy my soul with the impious, nor my life with men of blood.

By “impious” I mean those in whose hands are iniquities, especially avarice. They suppose gain to be godliness when, from divine service—which ought to be done for eternal life—they seek worldly profit. “And their right hand is full of gifts,” for which they sell even divine service itself, which should be performed solely for the right hand—that is, for eternal reward. But I have walked in my innocence, as I said at the beginning of the Psalm.

In the Hebrew it reads: “But I shall walk in my simplicity,” especially in my entering into contemplation. For when I go out to action, I shall be anxious and troubled about many things. Therefore, that, freed from many disturbances, I may enter into the place where your glory dwells, embracing the best part in my innocence and simplicity, simply loving the one thing necessary and enjoying its sweetness: redeem me and have mercy on me, granting that one thing which is necessary and best, and never taking it away, so that you may say of me: “She has chosen for herself the best part, which shall not be taken away” (Luke 10:43) from him.

For my foot has stood in the straight way. My foot—that is, my affection, which is usually prone to slip—although shaken by stumbling-blocks, yet has stood upright; that is, it has not withdrawn from your justice, while preserving your love, Lord God. And so that I may instill this same love into my neighbors: “In the churches I shall bless you, O Lord.” [Col. 1166A]

Another interpretation: “I will wash my hands among the innocent.” I shall wash my polluted hands—that is, my works—by repentance, which, if perfect, is equal to innocence. For among the innocent true penitents will possess the kingdom of God. “He who is clean and innocent does not need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean” (John 13:10). But I, wholly polluted, because I am a man polluted in lips and hands dwelling among a people with polluted lips, offer not only my feet to be washed, but also my hands and head.

For by washing my hands—that is, my works—through tears, although I am not innocent, I shall nevertheless be among the innocent and shall obtain the kingdom of God as one violent through repentance, doing violence; because “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:22)—something which the innocent do not seize, but enter as into an inheritance without violence. [Col. 1166B]

And in order that I may wash my hands more perfectly, I shall be separated from the guilty and joined to the innocent. For just as Peter denied among the guilty, and is not recorded to have wept while standing among them, but, “having gone outside, wept bitterly” (Matt. 26:75), so I, who as a guilty man among the guilty polluted my hands, will depart from them and, placed among the innocent, will weep bitterly and wash my hands. For, in the sight of another’s innocence, the pollution of my hands will displease me. Thus I shall wash them in a flood of tears and encompass your altar, O Lord: that is, I shall surround my faithful mind, or the faith of the heart itself, by adorning it with a garment of virtues; or I shall encompass the heavenly altar—that is, the human nature of Christ—which Christ himself, the true high priest, raised up as a pillar, pouring oil upon it from above (Gen. 28:18).

I shall encompass, I say, such an altar by joining myself to the number of those to whom the Apostle says: “All of you who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27). “With all these you shall be clothed as with an ornament,” says the prophet (Isa. 49:18). And I, after washing my hands, shall encompass your altar, O Lord, as with an ornament: the altar made of earth and raised above all the heavens, in whose type Jacob raised a stone as a pillar, pouring oil upon it from above.

I shall encompass this altar, that is, this high earth, so that I may hear your voice of praise—the praise by which you are praised by angels and human beings. For in heaven, beside the altar of the Temple, the prince of the heavenly host stands holding a golden censer in his hand; and that host cries: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of your glory.” And likewise on earth, with the Catholic priest standing beside the altar of the Temple, the choir of the ecclesiastical host cries: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; heaven and earth are full of your glory. Hosanna in the highest! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; hosanna in the highest!” [Col. 1166D]

The harmony of the angels in heaven is wholly unison and consonant, because that ancient disturber of heavenly harmony was cast out from there. While the other angels celebrated the Holy Trinity with equal praise, saying, “Holy, holy, [Col. 1167A] holy,” he wished to be a fourth, so like the Most High that no longer the Trinity, but a quaternity, might be praised in heaven—a praise in which he himself would be proclaimed equal and like to the Most High. But as the blessed angels persevered in the praise of the Trinity and rejected that fourth one, that enemy of the Trinity was cast out of heaven.

In the same way, whoever maintains the praise of the Trinity in the holy Church must hold it firmly until that fourth one, called Antichrist because he is contrary to Christ, is removed from the midst. Yet he wishes to appear like Christ in deceitful signs, by which Pharaoh and all Egypt are deceived until the Paschal full moon. When the number of the elect has then been completed, the Church will be whole and perfect like the moon. Then it will appear that the Paschal Lamb is eaten only in one house. Then the Israelites will be distinguished from the Egyptians. Then it will appear how great is the vanity of vanities in the signs of Pharaoh’s magicians. Then, in one harmony, it will be permitted to say to God’s people:

> Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; he has cast horse and rider into the sea. (Exod. 15:1)

And again:

> Who is like you among the mighty, O Lord? Who is like you, magnificent in your holiness, terrible and praiseworthy, working wonders? (ibid., 11)

What wonders? He cast horse and rider into the sea. “Pharaoh’s chariots and his army he cast into the sea” (ibid., 4). His chosen captains were submerged in the Red Sea. I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send; see the affliction of your people in Egypt, and see also my affliction in Egypt among Pharaoh’s magicians. [Col. 1167C] Judge and distinguish me from them, so that, sealed with the blood of the Paschal Lamb:

### Verse 7. “I may hear the voice of your praise,” praising you among the true Hebrews, and also awaiting in certain hope the return of your praise.

For you will commend those who commend you worthily at the end, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world”—namely, through prevenient grace, yet not without the justice of merits—“for I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; you clothed me when naked; you received me when a stranger; you visited me when sick and in prison. For as long as you did these things to one of my least ones, you did them to me” (Matt. 25:34 ff.). [Col. 1167D]

This voice of your praise is delightful: the voice by which you will praise your dearest little ones and those who minister to them.

Therefore I shall not encompass your altar by celebrating divine office for earthly gain, but so that I may hear the voice of your praise in heaven and in the Church celebrating the Trinity together, and the voice of your praise on the day of judgment. Desiring that day, I say: “Judge me, Lord, so that I may hear your voice of praise among two of the least ones or their praiseworthy ministers.” And because you alone are the teacher who teaches man knowledge, grant that at your altar I may hear your voice of praise among those who are taught by God; and, instructed by you, may I, without envy, in the pursuit of charity which builds up, praise not myself but you.

> [Col. 1168A] “And I shall recount all your wonders.”

Your wonders, I say, not mine; because if anything praiseworthy and wonderful is done through me, it must be ascribed to you, not to me, from whom comes every good. Wretched me! What am I doing? Why do I assign myself this office, that I, a wretched little man, should recount all your wonders, Lord? Truly I would be condemned because of the many sins of such presumption, were it not that charity covers a multitude of sins. For charity indeed bears witness to me that in recounting your praise and proclaiming your wonders I have sought not my own glory or earthly gain, but:

### Verse 8. “O Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, [Col. 1168B] and the place where your glory dwells.”

I do not say simply that I have loved your house, but the beauty of your house; nor do I say that I have loved the place of your dwelling, but the dwelling-place of your glory. For though the holy dwelling of a pure breast, or of the Church, in which you, God, dwell as in your house, is very praiseworthy, it is not enough for one who loves you, O Lord, that your house should be firmly built, unless it is also adorned with glorious beauty.

Hence, in the Song of Songs, we have heard the bride who loves you utter such words: “Our bed is flowering; the beams of our houses are cedar; our ceilings are cypress” (Song 1:16). She sings an epithalamium: describing the couch and bridal chamber in beautiful speech, she invites the bridegroom to rest. For it is better to rest and to be with Christ; but it is necessary to go forth for gains, for the sake of those to be saved. Yet now, having found what she thinks is a fitting opportunity, she announces the adorned bridal chamber and, pointing with her finger to the couch, invites her beloved, as I said, to rest. Like those going to Emmaus, unable to bear the burning of her heart, she draws him to the lodging of her mind, compels him to remain overnight with her, and speaks with Peter: “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Matt. 15:4). Let us now inquire what these things contain spiritually.

In the Church, I think the bed on which one rests is the cloisters and monasteries in which one lives quietly, away from the cares of the world and the anxieties of life. That bed is shown to be flowering when the conduct and life of the brethren shine, sprinkled with the examples and institutions of the Fathers as with sweet-smelling flowers. By houses, further, understand the popular gatherings of Christians. Those placed in high positions—namely, Christian rulers of both orders—like beams binding walls tightly by justly imposed laws, lest each person, living by his own law or will, should fall apart from the others like leaning walls and broken-down fences, and so the whole structure of the building collapse in ruins. [Col. 1168D]

The ceilings, which hang securely from the beams and conspicuously adorn the houses, I take to signify the gentle and disciplined character of a well-ordered clergy, together with rightly administered offices. For how shall the orders of clerics and their administrations stand, unless they are sustained by the favor and generosity of rulers as by beams, and protected by their power? [Col. 1169A]

That the beams are described as cedar and the ceilings as cypress undoubtedly accords with the nature of these kinds of wood and their suitability for the aforesaid orders. Cedar, being incorruptible, fragrant, and of lofty height, sufficiently indicates what sort of men ought to be chosen in the place of beams. Those set over others must therefore be strong and steadfast, long-suffering in hope, lifting the summit of their mind toward things above; and, spreading everywhere the fragrance of their faith and conduct, they can say with the Apostle: “For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2:15).

Cypress likewise, being wood both fragrant and incorruptible, shows that every cleric ought to be of an uncorrupted life and faith, so that he may deservedly be assigned to the beauty of the house and the adornment of its ceilings. For it is written: “Holiness befits your house, O Lord, unto length of days” (Ps. 92:5). Here both the beauty of holiness and the explicit perseverance of unfailing grace are present. Therefore the man chosen for the adornment and beauty of the house must be adorned with good morals and, though he is always within, must nevertheless have a good testimony also from those outside. There are other natural properties of these woods suitable to the matters spiritually discussed, but I omit them for brevity’s sake. [Col. 1169B]

It should be noted beautifully that the whole condition of the Church is comprised in one brief verse: namely, the authority of prelates, the beauty of the clergy, the discipline of the people, and the repose of monks or canons. When all these are rightly ordered, holy Mother Church rejoices in contemplating them; and then she also offers them to her beloved for his consideration, since she refers everything to his goodness as to the author of all authority, attributing none of it to herself.

For when she says “our” and “ours,” this is not a mark of usurpation but of love: namely, the confidence of excessive love judges nothing of him whom she loves greatly to be foreign to herself. Nor does she think herself excluded from the bridegroom’s companionship or from sharing his rest, since she is accustomed always to seek, not what is her own, but what is his. This is the reason why she dared to declare both the bed and the houses common to herself and the bridegroom. For she said: “Our bed, the beams of our houses, and our ceilings,” boldly associating herself in a joint possession with him to whom she does not hesitate to join herself in love.

Not so the woman who has not yet renounced her own will: she lies by herself and lives by herself—or rather, not by herself, but lives luxuriously with prostitutes, by which I mean the desires of the flesh, with which she wastes her goods and the share of substance which she had demanded be divided to her. [Col. 1169D]

But you who hear or read these words of the Holy Spirit: do you think that you can apply any of these things which are said to yourself, and recognize in yourself something of the happiness of the bride, who is sung by the Spirit himself in this song of love, lest it be said to you also, because you hear his voice, yet do not know whence he comes or where he goes? (Job 3:8.) Perhaps you too desire the rest of contemplation, and you do well—provided only that you do not forget the flowers with which you read the bride’s bed to be strewn.

Therefore take care also to surround your own bed with the flowers of good works; by the exercise of virtues, let sacred leisure be preceded by its fruit, as a flower. Otherwise, you will wish to sleep in excessively luxurious leisure if you desire rest without prior training, and, neglecting Leah’s fruitfulness, seek delight only in Rachel’s embraces. It is also an inverted order to demand reward before merit and to take food before labor, when the Apostle says: “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3:10).

“I have understood from your commandments,” he says, so that you may know that the taste of contemplation is by no means owed without obedience to the commandments. Therefore do not think, out of love for your own repose, that any prejudice whatsoever should be done to acts of holy obedience or to the tradition of the elders. Otherwise the Bridegroom will not sleep with you in one bed—especially in that bed which, instead of the flowers of obedience, you have strewn with the hemlocks and nettles of disobedience. Therefore he will not hear your prayers and, when called, will not come. For so great a lover of obedience, who preferred to die rather than not obey, will not grant access to himself to one who is disobedient.

Nor does he approve the empty leisure of your contemplation, he who says through the prophet: “I have labored while enduring,” signifying the time in which, exiled from heaven and the homeland of highest repose, he worked in the midst of the earth (Isa. 1:14). [Col. 1170C] Rather, I fear that you too may be caught by that dreadful sentence which thunders thus against the unbelief of the Jews: “Your new moons, Sabbath, and other festivals I will not endure” (Hos. 2:11). Again: “Your calends and solemnities my soul hates; they have become burdensome to me” (Isa. 1:14); and the prophet will mourn over you and say: “Her enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. 1:7). For why should not the enemy mock what the Beloved rejects?

I greatly marvel at the shamelessness of certain persons among us. Though they have disturbed all of us by their singularity, provoked us by their impatience, and defiled us by their disobedience, they nevertheless dare to invite the Lord of all purity to the bed so foully stained by their conscience, with every urgency of prayer. “When you stretch out,” he says, “your hands, I will turn away my eyes from you; and when you multiply prayer, I will not hear” (Isa. 1:15). What then? The bed is not flowering; indeed, it is foul-smelling, and you draw the King of glory there? Do you do this for rest, or for accusation?

The centurion forbids him to enter under his roof because of his own unworthiness, though his faith is fragrant throughout all Israel (Luke 7:6); and do you compel him to enter into you, foul with the filth of so many vices? The Prince of the Apostles cries: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8); and do you say: “Enter to me, Lord, because I am holy”? “Be all of one mind in prayer,” he says; “love the brotherhood” (1 Pet. 2:17). And the Vessel of Election says: “Lifting up pure hands without anger and disputing” (1 Tim. 2:8). [Col. 1171A]

Do you see how the Prince of the Apostles and the Teacher of the Gentiles agree with one another and speak in the same spirit concerning peace and tranquility of mind, which the person who prays ought to possess? Go on: stretch out your hands to God all day long, you who trouble the brethren all day, attack unanimity, and separate yourself from unity. “And what do you want me to do?” you ask. Certainly: first cleanse your conscience from every defilement of anger, disputing, murmuring, and envy; and hasten to cast out from the dwelling of your heart everything whatsoever known to oppose either the peace of the brethren or obedience to the elders.

Then surround yourself with flowers of every good deed and praiseworthy pursuit, and with the fragrances of virtues: that is, whatever things are true, whatever just, whatever holy, whatever lovely, whatever of good report—if there is any praise of discipline, if any virtue—take care to think upon these things and practice them. [Col. 1171B] Then you will safely call the Bridegroom. When you have brought him in, you too will be able truthfully to say, “Our bed is flowering,” because your conscience gives forth the fragrance of godliness, peace, gentleness, justice, obedience, cheerfulness, and humility. And so much concerning the bed.

Let each person who no longer walks according to the flesh but according to the Spirit recognize himself as the spiritual house of God. For, he says, “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3:17). Take care, therefore, brothers, for this spiritual building—which you are—lest, when it begins to rise higher, it totter and collapse for lack of support and binding with strong timbers. Take care, I say, to supply it with incorruptible and immovable beams: namely, that fear of the Lord which endures for ever and ever; patience, of which it is written, “The patience of the poor shall not perish for ever” (Ps. 9:19); and also long-suffering, which, remaining unbent beneath every weight of the structure, stretches into the endless ages of blessed life—as the Saviour says in the Gospel: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Mark 10:22). Above all, moreover, charity, which never fails, because “love is strong as death,” he says, “and jealousy is hard as hell” (Song 8:6).

Then strive to lay beneath and bind to these [Col. 1171D] beams other timber, equally precious and beautiful, provided that the former are ready at hand for the ornamental work of the ceiling of the house: namely, the word of wisdom or of knowledge, prophecy, the grace of healings, interpretation of utterances, and other such things, which are admittedly known to be more suited to adornment than necessary to salvation. Concerning these I have no command, but I give counsel. For it is evident that timber of this kind is sought laboriously, found with the greatest difficulty, and worked dangerously; for our land is found rarely to produce it, especially in these times. I therefore advise and warn that such things should not be sought too eagerly, but that ceilings should rather be prepared from other timbers which, though they appear less splendid, are nevertheless proved no less strong, [Col. 1172A] and are, besides, acquired more easily and more safely.

Would that I had an abundance of the timbers by which the garden of the Bridegroom, the Church, is thickly planted: peace, goodness, kindness, joy in the Holy Spirit, showing mercy with cheerfulness, giving with simplicity, rejoicing with those who rejoice, weeping with those who weep! Would you not judge that house, so far as its ceilings are concerned, sufficiently and abundantly adorned when you saw it adequately and harmoniously embellished and panelled with such timbers? “Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house.” Always give me, I pray, these timbers, by which I may always offer you the adorned bridal chamber of conscience—my own conscience, I mean, and that of another. I shall be content with these; and so will those who wish to acquiesce in my counsel in this matter, because I think that you too are content with them, especially in these last times, [Col. 1172B] in which, because iniquity abounds, the charity of many grows cold.

But in the holy apostles and apostolic men it is enough for me to admire and venerate the greater beauty of your house, shining forth through many virtues and miracles, because I cannot imitate it. It is enough for me to love in them the great beauty of your house, because you have laid glory and great beauty upon them: by crowning some of them through martyrdom, you made them a purple ascent; by making others shine through your utterances—which are silver tried by fire—in confession of the truth, you made them silver columns; and by the best part which they chose for themselves, you made others a golden couch. “Its midst is paved with charity [Col. 1172C] for the daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 3:10). Although these daughters, because of their weakness, cannot attain martyrdom by the purple ascent, too lofty and arduous for them, nor become silver columns or a golden couch, they can nevertheless, through the mediation of charity, venerate and love the purple ascent, the silver columns, and the golden couch. They love as though their own the good things of others: the great beauty of your house which they do not possess in themselves but possess in others through charity, a charity that does not seek its own interests but those of others.

In this very charity, O Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells. I have loved it, and I count it most pleasing that throughout the whole Church, in every congregation professing monastic or canonical religious life, and in my conscience [Col. 1172D] and another’s, there should be, for the beauty of your house, cedar beams, cypress ceilings, a flowering bed, a purple ascent, silver columns, a golden couch, and a floor paved with charity, as befits the place where your glory dwells—where it may be glorious for you to rest as upon a flowering bed or a golden couch.

Although I do not recognize this beauty in myself, nevertheless, O Lord, I have loved in others the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells, desiring your house to be not only firmly built upon you, the firm rock, but also fittingly adorned. For this reason too the zeal of your house has consumed me, while many dishonour your house through simoniacal trading and many other forms of disorder and indiscipline [Col. 1173A] which I saw and see in your house: with Antichrist and his army ruling—that is, the whole company of the ungodly—some drinking in your house with Belshazzar’s concubines, some robbing with Judas, some trading with Simon Magus, and some boasting with the devil, as though none of them ought to be subject to God, but each were like the Most High.

When these ungodly people are indignant with me and malign me because I refuse to agree with them in their wickedness, I have suffered many adversities and still fear many things—above all, lest I perish with the crowd of the ungodly, among whom I am mixed in the Lord’s threshing-floor. But, O most merciful one:

**VERSE 9.** “Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood.”

The ungodly perish in two ways: in the present life they are incorporated into the son of perdition, and at the future judgment they will be cast down with him into hell to perish. But I, who desire to be a member of the Saviour and await the Saviour himself as my reward at judgment, say in fear of destruction and hope of salvation: “Do not destroy, O God, my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood.” Even if the earth is delivered into the hands of the ungodly, who does not torment me in my body or even plunder me of earthly resources, still guard my soul from the twofold destruction by which the ungodly sin against God, and bloodthirsty men rage against their neighbour.

**VERSE 10.** “In whose hands are iniquities” [Col. 1173C]: because their works are wicked, and “their right hand is filled with bribes,” as we have explained above.

**VERSE 11.** “But I have walked in my innocence,” as has been explained above. “Redeem me, and have mercy on me.” Two things oppress me: [Col. 1174A] sin and the punishment of sin. In sin I recognize my guilt; in the punishment of sin I recognize my misery. In sin I have been sold, so that I cannot avoid sinning; in misery I am bound, so that I cannot avoid being troubled. Therefore, my Saviour, redeem me and have mercy on me: let redemption be my remedy against sin, lest by it I become a member of the son of perdition; and let your mercy help me, lest I perish with him in eternal misery. But if I sin in any respect, may I have you as my advocate with the just and merciful Father, and may you be the propitiation for my sins. And if I suffer miseries, may I experience you as my comforter, as indeed I have experienced you many times, when I was thrust down and overthrown so that I might fall, and yet did not fall. For although I was somewhat bent and inclined [Col. 1174B] toward unlawful excesses in speaking, eating, drinking, and other such things, nevertheless:

**VERSE 12.** “My foot stood in the straight way”: it stood so uprightly, and was so firm in holding the right path, that after the repentance for crimes expressed in the preceding psalm, there was thereafter no wavering of will in me. Indeed, such was and is its steadfastness that I would rather be killed than again become entangled in crimes, or even deliberately be defiled by venial faults themselves. And, preaching that others also must preserve this, “in the churches I will bless you, O Lord,” because I attribute my standing in the right way not to my own strength but to yours.

Glory to the Lord the Father, to whom it was said: “Judge me, O Lord.” Glory to the Lord the Son, who is the truth, of whom it was said in the psalm: “I have pleased you in your truth.” Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is mercy, of whom it was said: “For your mercy is before my eyes.” Glory to the one and triune Lord, true and merciful. Amen.

## PSALM XXVI

[Col. 1173]

[Col. 1173D] “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” The title of the psalm is (VERSE 1):

**UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID, BEFORE HE WAS ANOINTED.**

[Note: [Col. 1173D] Vulgate: “A Psalm of David, before he was anointed.”]

This title sends us to the history. We read in the books of Kings that David was anointed three times. First, while still a boy, at Bethlehem, by Samuel in the house of his father Jesse, in designation of his future kingdom; and from that anointing the Spirit of the Lord was directed into him. Secondly, after Saul’s death, he was anointed at Hebron and reigned over the house of Judah for seven years and seven months. Thirdly, later, he was anointed when he received the province of the whole Israelite people, so that he might reign over all Israel; he went up to Jerusalem and reigned thirty-three years, after the whole house of Saul had then been deprived of every hope of reigning.

These anointings signify something mystical for us. For in this, as in a mirror, the entire pattern of Christ’s anointing shines forth. He too was anointed three times. First, when he was conceived by the Holy Spirit. Having received that anointing, this child David did not immediately exercise royal office, but lay hidden, as it were, in himself like a little child. Secondly, when, at his baptism, the Holy Spirit came upon him in the form of a dove and he was manifested; by this second anointing he began to reign over the tribe of Judah. For from then on, by working miracles in Judaea, he showed himself to be King of the Jews—a fact which Pilate, though understanding it not at all, expressed in the title on the cross. Thirdly, when, rising from the dead, he poured upon his faithful such great grace of his anointing as this same anointed king, who was to be his future father, desires to commend in these words: “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity; like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, Aaron’s beard, which descends to the hem of his garment” (Ps. 132:1–2).

For when he rose, on that very day he stood in the midst of his disciples and said, “Peace be with you”; he breathed upon them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). Afterwards, sitting at the right hand of God, he sent the same Spirit and gave the Holy Spirit again. Thus the true ointment descended from the head to Aaron’s beard and to the hem of his garment: the same Holy Spirit descended from Christ, who is our head, first upon those strong and perfect men, Christ’s apostles, and then through their ministry upon the whole Church.

This threefold anointing was celebrated not only in Christ, anointed above his fellow-participants, [Col. 1175B] but must also be especially considered in every Christian. For as David was anointed three times, so every believer ought to share in a threefold anointing: first, in baptism, where they are renewed by the grace of the Holy Spirit; secondly, when through the bishop’s laying on of hands they are increased by the gifts of the same Holy Spirit; thirdly, on the day of judgment, when they attain the perfect sweetness of that same spiritual grace. We should not suppose that David composed this psalm before he was anointed in his father’s house; but whether he composed it immediately after that anointing or after the second is uncertain.

Not only kings but priests too are customarily anointed, as Aaron was, in figure of the one Christ who was to be priest and king and who also made us his members. Thus both priestly and royal anointing pertain also to us, who are Christ in him and, with him, are one Christ: head and members. But just as David was anointed at his father’s house as a figure of the future kingdom, so we, while still in the devil’s house, are anointed into the sacrament of future impassibility. In that state, just as David before attaining the kingdom laboured under enemies and desired the kingdom, so we meanwhile labour and groan, awaiting the adoption as sons, by which we are anointed a second time in the kingdom. Therefore, moving away from the historical account, the title says, “Unto the end.” This end is the consummation, toward which this psalm is directed. It is attributed to David, or to any believer, and treats of what pertains [Col. 1175D] to the things he did before he was anointed a second time and received into the kingdom.

In the first part it is shown how, after the first anointing, he who labours amid the adversities of this world hopes in the Lord, certain of the second anointing. In the other part the labour, groaning, and prayer by which the second anointing may be obtained are explained, at the words, “Hear, O Lord, my voice with which I cried to you”; and through the spirit of prophecy he also promises it at the words, “I believe that I shall see,” and so forth. The final verse reveals the intention: that no one may grow sluggish after the first anointing, but may act manfully while long-sufferingly awaiting the second or third. But now let us return to the beginning of the psalm, which is connected with the end of the preceding one. There he said, “In the churches I will bless you, O Lord”; here he shows [Col. 1176A] the manner of that blessing. Thus I, David, said: “In the churches I will bless you, O Lord.” I pay what I vowed, blessing you as Lord and saying:

“The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?”

In the first parents the snares of death overtook me through two evils. When the eyes of the flesh were opened to see and desire the forbidden tree, which was beautiful to the sight and pleasant to behold, the whole human race, to be begotten through them, was struck in the very root of its sinful origin and sorrowful propagation by both blindness and weakness: blindness, so that it might not see the good; weakness, so that it might desire evil. Therefore, since I, David, was conceived in iniquities, born altogether blind and weak—blind through ignorance of good and weak through desire for evil; blind by not seeing truth and weak by pursuing vanity; blind by not knowing eternal things and weak by desiring temporal things—the Lord sent Samuel, the angel, that is, his messenger; he took me from my father’s sheep and anointed me with the anointing of his mercy; and “the Spirit of the Lord was directed into me from that day and thereafter” (1 Sam. 16:13).

O how much beauty and grace there is in that expression: “the Spirit of the Lord was directed”! It was not said thus, nor ought it to have been said thus, of Saul, my rival, from whom the Spirit of the Lord was to depart; nor of anyone else, whose feigned or double soul that Spirit of love does not deign to honour anywhere with a direct kiss, but from whose pretence he is to flee at once after a slight touch. But in me, through the sacrament of visible anointing, the invisible anointing of the Holy Spirit was directed as though from the mouth of the Lord—not looking upon me obliquely, but caressing my mouth with the straight and faithful kiss of his own mouth.

By what effects, do you think, was it made evident to me that the Spirit of the Lord was directed into me but not into Saul? Namely, by this: although he hated and persecuted me, I looked upon him with upright eyes, loved him though he did not love me, and restrained my soldiers from killing him as he slept. To them I said: “Far be it from me to stretch out my hand against the Lord’s anointed!” (1 Sam. 26:23). Thus I looked upon him with upright and serene eyes, because the Spirit of the Lord had been upright and directed within me, and would not permit me to envy the honour of the enemy who persecuted me. But Saul did not look upon me with upright eyes after he heard the women singing: “Saul struck a thousand, and David ten thousand among his thousands” (1 Sam. 29:5).

Other effects also clearly showed that after the first anointing the Spirit of the Lord had been directed into me. First came prophetic grace, then the work of strength. For from then on, my mind made serene and enlightened, I became the renowned Psalmist, prophesying and playing the cithara of God’s mighty deeds and composing psalms containing mysteries of the Son of God, who according to the flesh was also to be my son. Through that same anointing I was endowed at once with strength and bodily deliverance, just as I said to Saul: “Your servant was feeding his father’s flock; and a lion or a bear would come and take a ram from the midst of the flock. I pursued them and struck them and snatched it from their mouths. They rose against me, and I seized their chins and strangled and killed them. For I, your servant, have killed both lion and bear. Therefore this uncircumcised Philistine too shall be like one of them, because he dared to curse the army of the living God” (1 Sam. 17:34 ff.).

Thus by this effect it was clear that the Spirit of the Lord had been directed into me: he made me, in accordance with the truth of my name, desirable in speech and strong of hand in deed, as a type of Christ my Son—the truly strong-handed and desirable King who was to come and sit upon my throne. [Col. 1177B] He will preach with delightfulness in teaching, so that a faithful disciple will say to him, “You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:69), and his adversaries themselves, in astonishment, will say, “Never has a man spoken as this man speaks.” He likewise, anointed in his father’s house, will proceed from the bridal chamber of a virginal womb both as a desirable bridegroom and as a mighty, desirable giant. By tenderly cherishing his sheep and mightily overcoming the lion, the devil, or the bear, Antichrist, he will strangle them and snatch sheep or ram from their mouths. Rightly therefore I, David, singing “unto the end”—that is, in singing looking ahead to Christ himself, who is the end of the law for righteousness—will bless the Lord in the churches, saying: “The Lord is my light and my salvation.”

It is written that “the law brought no one to perfection” (Heb. 7:19). The law could teach ignorance, but it could not assist weakness. These two evils existed in man, and from them proceeded all other human evils: one was ignorance, the other desire; ignorance of good and desire for evil. From ignorance comes transgression; from desire, sin. These two therefore existed in man from the beginning. But so that man might recognize his disease, he was left wholly to himself, lest he judge grace superfluous if he had not first recognized the defect of his weakness. Thus the time of natural law was appointed, so that nature might act by itself—not because it could accomplish anything by itself, but so that it might recognize that it could not do so.

Nature, therefore, left to itself, began to wander from truth through ignorance and was convicted of blindness; afterwards it was also to be convicted of weakness. The written law was given to enlighten ignorance, but not to strengthen weakness, so that man might be helped in that part in which he recognized his defect, while he might be left unaided where he supposed himself able to stand by himself. Having therefore received knowledge of truth through the law, he began to strive for perfection; but, crushed by desire because he had no helper, he failed in the work of virtue. Thus he was convicted in both respects: he can neither know truth by himself nor accomplish good. Thereafter grace was fittingly given, both to enlighten the blind and heal the weak: to enlighten ignorance and cool desire; to enlighten toward knowledge of truth and kindle toward the love of virtue. For this reason the Holy Spirit was given in fire, that it might have both light and flame: light for knowledge and flame for love.

Therefore I, David, enlightened through the first anointing to the knowledge of truth and kindled to love of virtue, say because of the light of knowledge: “The Lord is my light”; and because of love of virtue I add: “And my salvation.” Thus, I say, I shall speak in the churches to the end of the age, while this psalm resounds through the mouths of many faithful people who say, both in my person and in their own: “The Lord is my light and my salvation.” I cannot enlighten myself; rather, the Lord dwelling in me, who made clay from spittle and anointed my eyes through faith in the incarnation—an incarnation which I, David, believed would come, and which I, any believer, believe has now occurred—he is my light against the darkness of ignorance, so that I can now distinguish good from evil; and he is my salvation against weakness, so that I can now resist sin. For free will within me has plainly been enlightened and strengthened by the helping and indwelling grace which had previously lain blind and weak in the whole of human nature.

Firm and enlightened, therefore, so that I may know and be able to avoid or overcome the enemy, whom shall I fear? Certainly no one but him. For he who by the first anointing enlightened and healed me will by the second or third anointing so protect me against enemies that he who is my light and salvation will also be my defender. Therefore I say to him in thanksgiving:

“The Lord is the protector of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” Of which visible enemies shall I be afraid? The Lord himself, who enlightens and heals me, also protects me, lest the gift of illumination and salvation perish within me. For the Lord is the protector of my life. Although I ought to give him great thanks because he protects my possessions and my body as he wills, I give him still greater thanks because he is the protector of my life. For if “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17), whoever takes righteousness and faith from a person takes life from that person. But the Lord is the protector of my life, so that my adversary Saul, or one like Saul, even if he takes my outward substance, cannot take faith or righteousness from me.

Of whom, then, shall I be afraid? “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. 13:5): my enemies supposed that I was intent on harming them. Saul feared that through me he would lose the Israelite kingdom; his friends and my enemies feared that, when his kingdom ended, they would suffer loss. Thus they trembled because they feared to lose things destined to perish, things that could be taken from them against their will. But because I love righteousness or faith as my life—indeed, as my true life—which cannot be taken from me against my will, of what demon or human being shall I be afraid? Why should I fear, since I know the Lord to be the protector of my life? He is righteous not by an accidental gift but by essential goodness and righteousness; and since my life comes to me from him, the fountain of righteousness, he is the protector of my life.

Even one who cuts off [Col. 1179A] my head cannot take this life from me, because the Lord is the protector of this life of mine, not only before the death of the flesh, when thieves beset me on every side, lest I lose righteousness, but also in the death of the flesh itself, lest I lose the palm of righteousness. For the palm is due to righteousness, because “the righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” (Ps. 91:13). Since, therefore, the protector of my life is almighty, of whom shall I be afraid?

**VERSE 2.** “When evildoers draw near against me, to devour my flesh.”

This is why a great martyr among my fellow-soldiers, a brave soldier of David, taunts the adversary, saying: “I am roasted already; turn me over and eat,” because evildoers thus draw near to me, like wolves desiring to devour my flesh. They draw near, therefore, because nothing is nearer to me than my flesh. They would, as it were, harass me from afar if they plundered only my outward goods; but now, not content with these, they draw near in order to devour my flesh. This may be because they delight in afflicting my flesh; or because God turns their contrivances, devised to hurt me, to good. For although not according to their intention, yet according to their effect, they draw near in order to devour my flesh—that is, to consume in me my carnal desires and utterly devour and consume my carnal sins, which they tear as with teeth by reproaching or slandering me. Once these are consumed, my flesh becomes Spirit.

For God is able to turn their curses into blessings for me, as he himself says to such people: “I will curse your blessings and bless your curses” (Mal. 2:2). I therefore choose rather to bear the curses of such people than to seek their blessings, because “if I were of the world, the world would love what was its own.” But the hatred of this world is now a great testimony to me that he who by the first anointing designated and fitted me for a royal priesthood will also by the second or third confirm and bring to completion in me the grace well begun. Confirm, I say, in me, David your little servant, that I may be a renowned king, the temporal father of the eternal King; or confirm in me, holy catholic Church, that I may be “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Pet. 2:9), proclaiming the virtues of him who called me out of darkness into his marvellous [Col. 1179D] light. Therefore, enlightened by the gift of this light, I say: “The Lord is my light.”

Or rather, may he confirm in me, as an ecclesiastical person, the grace well begun in baptism through the first anointing, by which he granted me remission of sins; and thereafter, through the second anointing, give me the good merits of growth in virtues, and through the third, the everlasting rewards of eternal blessedness. For attaining these goods, all things that I endure, with the Lord’s help or permission, cooperate for my good while evildoers “draw near against me to devour my flesh.” That they have been allowed solely to consume my carnality is evident from this: when, as it were, they had devoured my flesh—when my sins had been consumed through their agency—even as they drew near [Col. 1180A] against me, that is, preferred themselves to me, they gradually grew weak, their strength being frustrated and enfeebled, according to what is written: “There was a long struggle between the house of Saul and the house of David. David grew stronger and stronger, but the house of Saul diminished daily” (2 Sam. 3:1).

Thus, yes, thus they grew weak, and at last perished altogether: not only false friends who wish to seduce by flattery, but also my enemies who openly trouble me through hatred. They themselves grew weak and fell—both malicious spirits and malicious people, and the very malignancies of vices. While I consented to evil, I did not feel their afflictions. But when I resolved and most firmly determined not to consent to them, whenever I experienced their temptations, things that had formerly been a delight to me were immediately turned into affliction and pain; and in those things I had formerly loved, I found affliction and pain.

But this affliction produced patience; patience, testing; testing, hope; and hope does not disappoint, because the charity of God was poured out in my heart through the first anointing so abundantly that I love even the enemies who trouble me and wish them good in return for evil. Therefore they grew weak and fell by the evil fall by which Saul, the greatest of my enemies, and his sons fell on Mount Gilboa. Mourning them, I said: “How the mighty have fallen in battle, swifter than eagles, stronger than lions! Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you” [Col. 1180C] (2 Sam. 1:23–25), where the mighty of Israel fell.

Consider, whoever you are who wisely sing this psalm, the mourning of wise David over the fall of his enemies. For he does not exult over them as they fall. Rather, having already learned through the first anointing to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep, he showed himself worthy of the second and third anointing by grieving for them from the root of love; and here too he laments in the psalm, saying: “My enemies who trouble me, they themselves grew weak and fell!” Elsewhere he likewise says while weeping: “How the mighty have fallen in battle!”

Every carnal person weeps when beloved persons and friends fall, and rejoices at an enemy’s ruin. Even if such a person has been anointed by the first anointing in baptism, unless that joy is cleansed by repentance, by God’s just judgment he will be deprived of the second and third anointing. Thus he will not be counted among the children of the kingdom, enriched either in this present life with good merits or in the life to come with good rewards; rather, he will be a child of wrath, a child of Gehenna, to whom it is said: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke 6:25).

Perhaps when your enemies fall on Mount Gilboa—in the height, that is, of pride—you rejoice in their downfall, singing and saying: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers draw near against me to devour my flesh, my enemies who trouble me themselves grew weak and fell.” Singing thus, like David, you suppose that you have good understanding, so that your psalm is David’s; but you do not know that you are among those [Col. 1181A] of whom the prophet Amos speaks: “They imagined that they had instruments of song like David, and suffered nothing over the affliction of Joseph” (Amos 6:5). “The affliction of Joseph” here means the affliction of any brother who suffers evil, such as Joseph first suffered from his brothers and then from his Egyptian mistress. The present psalm of David does not suit one who does not sympathize even with enemies suffering such things or worse; for David laments his falling enemies, saying in the contrition of his heart: “My enemies who trouble me, they themselves grew weak and fell!” And elsewhere: “How the mighty have fallen in battle!”

But so that you who desire to sing and lament with David may keep before your eyes, in this psalm, his lament more carefully considered, observe more fully [Col. 1181B] what is contained concerning his mourning in the book of Kings, where it says: “David lamented this lament over Saul and Jonathan his son; and he commanded that the sons of Judah should be taught the bow, as it is written in the book of the just: ‘The illustrious of Israel have been slain upon your mountains,’” and so forth (2 Sam. 1:17–18). If you properly consider who lamented, what he lamented, why he lamented, and moreover what mystical meaning it signifies, this lament is rational and brought forth from the treasury of a wise man.

Who lamented? An anointed king, not ignorant of his election, who did not fail to know that Saul’s death had left the royal throne open for him: the fugitive could now return to his homeland and the exile could now reign. Wonderful innocence, then; wonderful restraint against ambition! It had been too little merely to keep his hands from violence, saying: “May the Lord be gracious to me, that I should stretch out my hand against the Lord’s anointed” (1 Sam. 24:7). For even while saying this he might have wished that Saul’s day of death would come or that Saul, going down into battle, would perish. But see how the hidden justice of his heart is demonstrated by a manifest act: he himself laments, and through the punishment or death of the man who brought the news he decrees that none of his own people should exult. Rightly, therefore, may strong David sing, may he sing confidently, and say: “O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands; if I have repaid evil to those repaying me, let me deservedly fall empty before my enemies” (Ps. 7:4–5).

What, then, did he lament? Namely, that Saul, though he was the Lord’s anointed, deserved through his pride both to be cast away from the face of the Lord and, with all Israel, to fall before his enemies, his illustrious men being slain. This certainly was a thing to be lamented by a wise man, who knew that in the utmost humility he must beware of the example of one who, though the Lord’s anointed, deserved through pride to be enslaved to an evil spirit and fell so far that, after consulting a pythonic spirit, he ended his present life by a miserable end, fully condemned for transgression.

And why did he lament? “That they might teach,” he says, “the sons of Judah the bow, as it is written in the book of the just” (2 Sam. 1:18). The bow means the strength of war; and that bow, or strength of war, is assuredly nothing other than the hand or help of the Lord. The whole strength of war is rightly signified here by the bow, because Saul had especially perished through the bow. For it is written above that the archers pursued him and that he was grievously wounded by the archers. This would certainly not have happened if he too had wished to hold or bend his own bow—that is, if he had placed his hope in God, without whom Israel never conquered or acted bravely, “as it is written,” he says, “in the book of the just.”

Although “the book of the just” may be understood by some as a particular book which can nowhere be found today, more certainly it is understood here as the same book of which it is written in Numbers: “Therefore it is said in the book of the wars of the Lord: ‘As he did in the Red Sea, so he will do in the torrents of Arnon,’” and so forth (Num. 21:14). But what is the book of the wars of the Lord except all Holy Scripture, from which without doubt we are taught to wage the wars of the Lord? For before Moses, who spoke those words, nothing of this kind had been written.

Therefore, “that they might teach the sons of Judah the bow, as it is written in the book of the just”—that is, because the sons of Israel had fought badly through their own fault, the sons of Judah, their fellow-tribesmen, should at least learn to make God their helper, as all the just did, whose victories were all accomplished through God’s wonderful cooperation. The Scriptures testify to this; although divided into many books, they were nevertheless written by one Spirit, and for that reason are rightly reckoned as one book, in accordance with the words: “And I saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals” [Col. 1182C] (Rev. 5:1).

By saying in this lament: “The illustrious men of Israel have been slain upon your mountains; how have the mighty fallen in battle—swifter than eagles, stronger than lions! Jonathan has been slain on your heights!” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 1:23)—how, I ask, do the sons of Judah learn the aforesaid bow through such a lament? Namely, this is to be understood: let all who fight learn from this experience that, however mighty and illustrious they may be, however much they possess the swiftness of eagles and the strength of lions, they can by no means achieve victory when God is opposed to them. Let them learn this, I say, from this experience. For behold, upon your mountains, O Saul—upon *your* mountains, I say, that is, because of your pride—the illustrious men of Israel have been slain [Col. 1182D]; the mighty fell with you. Jonathan too was slain upon your heights—your heights, I say, not his. For this son, worthy of a better father, died not because of his own pride but because of his father’s pride.

For what is said stands in opposition: “Jonathan’s arrow never turned backward” (ibid., 22). Jonathan’s arrow was Jonathan’s faith, by which he made a covenant with David; and it never went backward, for he never made that covenant void. In saying “Jonathan’s arrow” in place of “Jonathan’s faith,” he fittingly referred to the event itself. For it is written above: “Jonathan therefore made a covenant with David. And Jonathan further bound David by oath, because he loved him; for he loved him as his own soul. And Jonathan said to him: Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed; for your seat will be sought for until the day after tomorrow. Therefore you shall go down quickly and come to the place where you are to hide on the day when work is permitted, and you shall sit beside the stone called Ezel. And I will shoot three arrows. If I say to the boy, ‘Behold, the arrows are on this side of you; take them,’ then come to me, for there is peace for you,” etc. (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 20:16 ff.). Therefore Jonathan’s arrow never turned backward; that is, Jonathan never annulled the covenant in which he used the sign of the arrows.

While saying these things and mourning such a lament, he nevertheless strengthens Israel and urges it to hope for timely consolation from God. For he says: “Do not tell it in Gath, nor proclaim it in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the sons of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult” [Col. 1183B] (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 1:20). That is to say: although the illustrious men of Israel have been slain, although the mighty have fallen and weapons of war have perished, quickly take up your bow and strengthen your arm with good hope, so that the enemies may not have occasion to think they have won a complete triumph over you, and so tell others that, although the mighty have fallen, you nevertheless still have God, who is most mighty.

But why, he says, “May neither dew nor rain come upon you, mountains of Gilboa; nor may there be fields of firstfruits” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 1:23)? Namely, so that the mountain’s own barrenness, enduring perpetually, might be a necessary lesson for posterity: so that future kings may always have before their eyes a reminder to beware the vice of pride [Col. 1183C], because there the shield of the mighty was cast away—the shield of Saul—so ignominiously, as though he had not been anointed with oil (ibid., 21), as though it had never returned effectually from the blood of the slain and from the fat of the mighty.

“Daughters of Israel,” he says, “weep over Saul”; for he is to be mourned, “because he clothed you delightfully in scarlet, because he provided golden ornaments for your adornment” (ibid., 24)—understand: from the spoils of enemies which he brought home. Now he himself lies naked; now he himself has become spoil to visible and invisible enemies.

What, finally, does this lament signify mystically except the mourning of the true David—that is, Christ the strong-handed—for the ruin of his own people, the Jewish people? Seeing the city, he himself wept over it, saying: “For if you too had known” (Luke 19:41). [Col. 1183D] And through his Apostle he laments its ruin as already accomplished, when that Apostle says—Christ himself undoubtedly speaking in him—“I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that there is great sorrow for me and continual pain in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren,” etc. (Romans 9:1 ff.).

David therefore mourns Saul and those who had fallen, the mighty and illustrious Israelites. Christ, strong-handed or desirable, mourns the pride of carnal Israel and the false strength of the Israelites, concerning which he himself says in the Psalm: “The mighty rushed upon me” (Psalm 58:4): that is, they wished to establish their own righteousness and gloried, as though illustrious, not in God’s grace but in the works of the Law. And woe to those who did not anticipate this lament of David [Col. 1184A] by the tears of their own repentance! In mourning, moreover, he also commands that they teach the sons of Judah the bow: that they teach the sons of his confession—that is, the Christian people drawn from the Gentiles—not to glory as though in their own merits, but, submitting themselves to God’s grace, to hold firmly the true and steadfast bow of heavenly strength.

The Apostle wisely carries out this command of teaching: “But if some of the branches have been broken off, and you, though you were a wild olive tree, have been grafted in among them and become a participant in the root and richness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, remember: you do not bear the root, but the root bears you. Do not be high-minded, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps neither will he spare you” (Romans 11:17 ff.). In saying these things and the rest [Col. 1184B], he certainly teaches the sons of Judah the bow: that, if they wish to act courageously, they should not boast but should stand humbly in God’s grace.

“For the illustrious men of Israel,” he says, “have been slain upon your mountains, and the mighty have fallen.” The illustrious, namely, are the Israelites according to the flesh, “to whom belong adoption as sons, glory, the covenant, the giving of the Law, worship, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen” (Romans 9:4–5). Thus according to these things they truly are illustrious; yet in taking pride in them they are falsely mighty. Therefore they were slain; therefore they fell, above all through the fault of the priests, who devoured the deceived people.

For this reason he says: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor [Col. 1184C] rain come upon you, nor be there fields of firstfruits.” For *Gilboa* is interpreted “devouring” or “descent”; and by this name the Pharisees, or those priests, are not unfittingly denoted—the men whom the Saviour drove out with a scourge from his Father’s house while they committed robbery there and made prey of the people: devourers and gluttons, as the prophetic saying declares, “They eat the sins of my people” (Hosea 4:8).

“Therefore, mountains of Gilboa,” he says, “let neither dew nor rain come upon you, nor be fields of firstfruits”: that is, while the whole valley of humble nations is watered and drenched from above, so that it may abound with grain, so that the poor may eat and be satisfied and praise the Lord, may you, lofty and proud, receive neither dew—that is, the Holy Spirit—nor rain—that is [Col. 1184D], the word of saving teaching. “I will also command my clouds that they rain no shower upon you” (Isaiah 5:6). My clouds, I say—that is, my Apostles—I will command to withdraw themselves from your pride and to rain the preaching of the Gospel upon the Gentiles.

Thus you shall not be fields of firstfruits; you shall not be the first harvest brought at this time from among you into that heavenly granary, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters. Then a remnant from among you will be saved, and there will be no longer an early harvest but a late harvest. Why? Because there the shield of the mighty was cast away, the shield of Saul, as though he had not been anointed with oil. There, I say—that is, in your pride—I was cast away: I who alone am the shield of the mighty, who ought to have been the shield of Saul, that is, the defense or protection of this frenzied or possessed people [Col. 1185A]. For at your urging it denied me before Pilate; it denied me, I say, saying, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). What did it do by this denial except cast away its shield, the shield of the mighty, as though he had not been anointed with oil—as though I were not the Messiah, were not the Christ, were not anointed with the Holy Spirit, having proof from the blood of the slain and from the fat of the mighty, namely evil spirits or impious men—as though I could take no spoil at all from the hands of my enemies?

After these things David consulted the Lord, saying: “Shall I go up into one of the cities of Judah?” And the Lord said to him: “Go up.” And David said: “Where shall I go up?” And he answered: “To Hebron” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] [Col. 1185B] 2:1). Until now a fugitive, until now an exile, he had mourned and wept, intoxicated with much bitterness. But now, ready in obedience to return home and reign, he wishes to sing and make melody in the tabernacle of his God, following the example of him in whose person he himself speaks: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody in my glory” (Psalm 107:2).

Indeed, to this man asking, “Shall I go up into one of the cities of Judah?” he says, “Go up to Hebron”; and to the other, awaiting as it were the Father’s answer in the tomb—since he did not come of himself but performed everything obediently—he says: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Psalm 56:9). And he immediately responds: “I will arise at dawn”; and, gladly accepting as commanded the ascent to Hebron [Col. 1185C], says: “I will confess you among the peoples, O Lord, and sing to you among the nations” (Psalm 109:2).

Hebron was the city of the burial-place of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the great Adam, as is written in the book of Joshua. Hence it was also called Kiriath-arba. “Hebron was formerly called Kiriath-arba,” he says, “which is interpreted ‘city of four.’ Great Adam was buried there among the Anakim” (Job 14:15). Therefore Hebron, the beginning of David’s kingship, signifies the Jewish people because Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were buried there; but because great Adam was likewise laid there, it signifies the whole human race.

Accordingly David is rightly commanded, both in his own person, to go up to Hebron, where he was to be anointed king a second time over the tribe of Judah, whose name means “confessing”; and in the person of Christ he is taught to sing: “I will confess you among the peoples, O Lord, and sing to you among the nations.” Yet, in consulting, he asks to go up only into one of the cities of Judah, because Christ reigns only in the one Church of the one faith. And in this Psalm he says: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.”

As though he said: I rightly asked one thing of the Lord, since I knew myself to possess such charity and unity of mind that I even loved my enemies and mourned their ruin with such unanimous compassion and such an affection of sympathy as was expressed in my lament which has already been discussed and still must be discussed. For it was not without reason that immediately after my lament was completed [Col. 1186A], I asked for and received one city of Judah, in which I received a second and third anointing—*linitio*, or unction—as consolation for my lament and grief.

But this happened in me, David, by the certain purpose and careful ordering of God—or rather in my Son and God, the true David, weeping over the city of Jerusalem and mourning his enemies before his exaltation—so that you, whoever you are, who desire to sing this Psalm of David well in order to obtain a second and third anointing in the merits of virtues and the rewards of blessedness, may know that you must first mourn in charitable compassion for your perishing enemies, and thus ascend into one of the cities, where, through the generosity of divine grace, you receive royal anointing.

Therefore do not be like proud and envious Saul [Col. 1186B], who, without his bow—that is, without divine help—was severely wounded by the archers and finally fell upon his sword and died. Rather, have your bow: the love of truth, rigid like the wood of a bow; and brotherly charity, like a string made from fleshly entrails, by which the rigor of truth may be tempered and bent toward compassion. From this bow send arrows against your enemies by praying and continually pouring out prayers for their salvation. Let your arrows be sharp, and then peoples will fall beneath you—not in bodily death, but “in the hearts of the king’s enemies” (Psalm 44:6): that is, with their hearts humbled, may they become from the king’s enemies the king’s friends, and may they not begrudge the kingdom to any little one anointed as king, as Saul begrudged it to me, little David, anointed king.

But if, while you pray for them, they do not fall in the hearts of the king’s enemies but fall on Mount Gilboa, mourn them in such a way that by your lament you teach the sons of Judah the bow, as it is written in the Book of the Just; for all Scripture inspired by God teaches this: that we should love friends in God and enemies for God’s sake. When you are conscious of this charity; when, unlike Saul, you are not wounded by the arrows of enemies, because their insults and reproaches do not wound you so that you lose the health of charity; indeed, when from the bow of that same twofold charity you send forth continual prayers as sharp arrows for the salvation of your enemies; and when, in the compassion of such charity, seeing your enemies fallen, you say: “My enemies who trouble me [Col. 1186D] themselves have been weakened and have fallen”—then with great confidence you will be able to sing “unto the end” and say:

**VERSICLES 3 AND 4.** “Though camps stand against me, my heart shall not fear. Though battle rise against me, in this I will hope. One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek.”

Therefore I, David—an exile and fugitive from Saul’s presence; I, once anointed king, but driven from the kingdom destined for me, dwelling in little Ziklag under a foreign king—I, David, I say, conscious in myself both of great rejoicing in the prosperity of my enemies and great compassion in their adversities, do not believe that I shall fall before enemies as Saul fell. Rather, “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (below, v. 13).

Therefore, though camps of Philistines—that is, the schemes of any visible or invisible enemies—stand against me [Col. 1187A], my heart, conscious of fraternal charity, shall not fear: for it is neither wounded by foreign arrows through the reproaches of the wicked nor pierced by its own sword through its own anger on Mount Gilboa, because it is not in Satan’s height. And if not merely the plots of conspiracies stand against me, but battle itself rises against me—that is, the open conflict of attacking foreigners—“in this I will hope,” knowing that “all things work together for good to those who love God” (Romans 8:28).

This happened to me, David, historically on many occasions before the second anointing: trained by continual battles, I was found fit for the second and third anointing. But at last battle rose against me when the enemy had burned the city of Ziklag, carried away my two wives, and taken all the spoil, including women and little children captive. Then I consulted the Lord, saying: “Shall I pursue these raiders or not?” And he said: “Pursue; for you shall without doubt overtake them and recover the spoil” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 30:8 ff.). Strengthened by such an answer from the Lord, I said: “Though camps stand against me, my heart shall not fear; though battle rise against me, in this I will hope.”

Nor was I disappointed in this hope. For I victoriously overcame the enemies and took much spoil, concerning which it was said: “This is David’s spoil.” Enriched by this spoil, when I suddenly heard that Saul the king, my rival and lord of many cities, had fallen in battle, I asked one thing of the Lord—I asked for one city only—saying: “Shall I go up into one of the cities of Judah?” And this one thing I will seek [Col. 1187C], so that I may no longer be compelled to live as an exile among Gentiles worshipping idols and going after mute images as they are led, but may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may behold the delight of the Lord and visit his temple.

Otherwise: I, Christ, the true David, while Saul—that is, death—pursued me in that night when I was to be handed over to death, and while I was about to overcome death itself, asked one thing of the Lord and will seek it, ever interceding, I the Unity, for the completion of the union of my own unto the end of the age. For this is my voice: “Father, I will that those whom you have given me may all be one, as we also are one: I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one” [Col. 1187D] (John 17:21).

Thus, when I was about to die for the nation—and not for the nation only, but in order to gather into one the scattered children of God, so that there might be one fold and one shepherd—I asked one thing of the Lord. This one thing, namely union, I asked when dying once; and I will seek it in the daily sacrament of my death, as my priests celebrate it and pray for the holy Church, which, desiring it to be given peace, guarded, united, and governed, they ask and seek as one. Indeed, I who in my own person asked for this one thing, I myself will seek it through the mouths of priests, while my death is proclaimed in the sacrament of the altar until I come at the end of the age, so that I may dwell in the house of the Lord [Col. 1188A], with peace after wars have been stilled on every side, my members perfectly united to me their head, and diverse stones built together upon me, the cornerstone and foundation, and reconciled to God the Father through me, the cornerstone and mediator.

The Apostle says: “A mediator is not of one; but God is one” (Galatians 3:20). For there were two—God and man—different and opposed. God was just; man was unjust: in this, mark their opposition. Man was miserable; God was good: in this, mark their difference. Thus man was opposed to God through injustice and different from God through misery. Therefore man first needed to be justified from guilt in order to be reconciled, and afterwards delivered from misery in order to be restored. In this respect man needed a mediator to God [Col. 1188B], so that he might be reconciled to him and brought back to him.

But no one could suitably undertake the cause of the estranged parties unless, through some bond of fellowship and peace, he stood in a relationship of friendship and kinship with both. Therefore the Son of God became man so that he could be the mediator of reconciliation and peace between God and man. He assumed humanity, through which he might draw near to human beings; he retained divinity, through which he might not depart from God. Made man, he bore punishment to demonstrate affection; he preserved justice to confer the remedy.

The Word, who was one with God the Father through an ineffable unity, became one with assumed manhood through a wondrous union. Unity belongs to nature; union, to person: he is one with God the Father in nature, not in person; one with assumed manhood in person, not in nature. What is more one than unity? What is one by unity is supremely one. The Word and the Father were one by unity because they were one in nature. And the Word willed to become one with us, so that he might make us one in himself and through himself also with him with whom he himself was one.

Therefore he took our nature from us, that he might join it to himself by a union in person, though it was not joined to him by unity in nature; so that by making something of ours one with himself, he might unite us to himself, that we might be one with him through that which of ours had been united to him, and through him might be one with the Father, who was one with him. “Holy Father,” he says [Col. 1188D], “keep in your name those whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we are. But I do not pray for them alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they too may be one in us, and that the world may believe that you have sent me. And I have given them the glory which you gave me, that they may be one, as we are one: I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one, and that the world may know that you have sent me.”

Unity prays for union: the Word, one with the Father in nature; the man, one with the Word in person; the members, one with the head, first in righteousness and afterwards in glory. For that they may be one in righteousness, “may the world know that you have sent me.” But that they may be one in glory: “I will that where I am, they too may be with me, that they may behold my glory which you have given [Col. 1189A] me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John 17:20 ff.).

“This one thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek.” I asked it when I was offered once to take away the sins of many, when by the cross and by blood with water flowing from my side I blotted out the record contrary to peace and unity.
