I will seek it daily, interceding with the Father for the union of my own, now in one righteousness and afterwards in one glory: so that in temporal life they may have one Lord, whom all may serve “with one shoulder” (Zephaniah 3:9), as is also read in Isaiah.

Let them likewise have one faith and one baptism, as they were called in one hope of their calling; so that, having one heart and one soul in goodness, they may while now laboring in the vineyard unanimously await one denarius, and hereafter may be perfected into one in eternal life in the fellowship of holy angels. This fellowship is daily built up, like a city, by those ascending there: “whose participation is into the same thing,” that is, into one. First let them be one, that they may love one another, that there may be no schisms among them, and that all may say and think the same thing. Then, putting off the garment of mortality and cleaving to the Father of spirits, let them be one Spirit; for “he who cleaves to the Lord is one Spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17).

Cleaving to the Father of lights, let them also be one light in the Lord; just as from diverse lamps shining in one house one brightness is produced, so that, themselves made bright, they may behold my glory which you gave me, Father, because you loved me before the foundation [Col. 1189C] of the world, before I was anointed either king or priest. For the eternal brightness of my divinity, in which you loved me before the foundation of the world, preceded every such anointing belonging to the nature of my assumed humanity.

But lest in me, the one mediator of God and men, divinity and humanity should have different glory, I asked one glory for my humanity, which I have always had in my divinity. Therefore I said: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had before the world was made” (John 17:1). Thus I, a man, asked for the one glory which I, God the Word of God, always possessed. I will seek it in my members, who long with longing to behold [Col. 1189D] that same glory of mine; and, beholding it, may they become one bright house, of which I now say, “that I may dwell in the house of the Lord,” and of which it is elsewhere said: “Behold, the dwelling of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3).

Otherwise: I, David; I, a believer with faithful David; I, a penitent with penitent David; I, one enduring persecution with David; I, one mourning the destruction of enemies with David; I, humble with humble David—I, I say, being such and such among the perfect, or at least, still being among the imperfect, desiring to be such, possessing such desire as a first anointing, so that I may have a second and third anointing in the virtue of merits and the blessedness of rewards—“One thing I have asked [Col. 1190A] of the Lord.”

Those who wish to be happy in this life ask for many and varied things. But I, who desire to be blessed after this life, have asked one thing: I have made one petition, for one thing only—namely, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may behold the delight of the Lord and visit his temple. Since this one thing must be sought without ceasing, I will seek it all the days of my life: I will seek it throughout all the days of mortal life, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord throughout all the days of immortal life. Though in that life there is but one day, “better than thousands” (Psalm 83:11), still, for the sake of the one day of unending eternity, I speak in the plural, “days,” so that I may indicate inexhaustible eternity, which I cannot otherwise express, at least by the human plurality of names.

Whether “one” is said in the neuter, as in the Gospel where it is said, “But one thing is necessary,” and as in the Apostle, where, leaving behind the many things which are past, the prize of one heavenly calling is set before us (Philippians 3:14); or whether it is said in the feminine, “I have asked one thing,” the meaning is not different. For I, David, disdaining the many things that lie behind because they are temporal, amid which I am troubled and anxious over many matters, ask that one thing which is necessary: I have made the one petition which, above all my petitions, I desire to be heard—namely, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, behold the delight of the Lord, and visit his temple.

As long as I, frail, dwell in a fragile house of clay, I am far from that one thing which I pursue [Col. 1190C], from that one thing which I have asked. For “man born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries; he comes forth like a flower and is crushed, flees like a shadow, and never remains in the same state” (Job 14:2). Therefore, against the multitude of miseries, I have asked for one blessedness; against the instability of shadowy life, one eternal identity of enduring life. And I will seek it, so that, freed from many miseries, enriched with one everlasting blessedness, and having laid aside the changeability of mortality, conformed to the unity that is always unchangeable, I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life—in the house not made by hands, eternal in the heavens.

“That I may behold the will of the Lord all the days of my life,” when that petition is fully granted by which we say to you, God the Father: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” For here, while we are separated from the one and endangered amid many things, we who are multiple cannot behold the one identity of the simple divine will. Just as a person in motion thinks that immovable towers and mountains are moving, so we, being changeable, think the divine will changes and varies, as though God now wills this and now that. We cannot clearly see what God wills, or which mortal is worthy of hatred or love in his judicial sentence.

Therefore I seek dwelling in that house, where I may fully behold the will of the Lord which I now know only in part. I know that I have been called, but I do not know whether I have been chosen and predestined to blessedness. I have already been anointed with one anointing, because, called to faith [Col. 1191A], I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living (below, v. 13). But because I still do not know whether I am worthy of hatred or love, I have asked for another anointing and will seek it: namely, that through unanimity of charity joined to faith I may so dwell in the house of the Lord that I may sing: “Behold, how good and delightful it is for brothers to dwell together in one, like ointment on the head, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron” (Psalm 132:1–2).

I have asked for this anointing to be performed with such ointment, and I will seek it, so that through it, being assured of God’s good pleasure toward me, I may behold the will of God and visit his temple. “Visit”: that is, I may look upon his temple with longing and continual attention—the heavenly Jerusalem, or his human nature, which is the temple of divinity.

Another translation has: “that I may contemplate the delight of the Lord and be protected by his temple.” The sense is the same, as though he said: I may dwell in the house for this very end, that I may contemplate the delight of the Lord—that the desirable form of God may appear to me face to face—and may be protected; that is, death having been swallowed up, I may be clothed with immortality, not bestowed from elsewhere but by the very protector of his temple, in which he dwells. The idols of the nations are protected by their temples; but our God, dwelling in the temple itself, will protect his temple. These things I ask in this confidence:

**VERSE 5.** “For he has hidden me in his tabernacle.” I, David, when Saul pursued me, fled to the tabernacle; and there, as the priest Abimelech gave them, I received the loaves which only priests were permitted to eat; moreover, I received for my defense and protection the sword of Goliath the Philistine, stored in the tabernacle (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 21). Thus the Lord protected me in the hidden place of his tabernacle [Col. 1191C].

Likewise I, the true David, when death pursued me, was protected in the hidden place of the tabernacle through the divinity concealed in the hidden place of the tabernacle—that is, of my flesh.

Likewise, I, whoever I am—whether innocent with the boy David or penitent with sinful David—am protected in God by trust in the hidden place of his tabernacle. The tabernacle of Deity is Christ’s flesh, in which by faith and hope he hides me, so that I may not be seen by those seeking me, just as David, when he fled Saul, was figuratively hidden in hiding places so as not to be seen. He hides me, I say, in the day of my evils—that is, in the time of temptations, which is the day of this life—or in the day of evils, when evil persons alone prosper. And he protects me in the hidden place of his tabernacle.

He says “in the hidden place,” as though other parts of it were outward and there were an inner sanctuary—and indeed this is so. For we are the outward parts, in whom he dwells by grace. But he himself is priest in the hidden place of God’s tabernacle, because divinity personally united to itself flesh from our tabernacle, in which it lay hidden. Whoever believes in him with the heart unto righteousness is admitted into the hidden place of the tabernacle. Hence the Apostle: “Our life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3) [Col. 1191D].

[Col. 1192A] It may also be said: “that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life,” that is, while I live, may no adversity exclude me from the unity of believers; “that I may behold the will of the Lord,” that is, may I understand his commandments; and, if not with the eyes, at least with the mind, may I visit his temple—that is, Christ’s body—or make myself his temple. I shall indeed be able to do this, “because he has hidden me in his tabernacle.” From there priestly bread is given to me through the sacrament of the altar. From there comes to me the sword, which is the Word of God hidden in the sacrament of bread and wine; satisfied with such bread and armed with such a sword, while Saul—that is, sin—pursues me, I, David, shall courageously climb the sheerest rocks like a roe deer, like a young hart, and shall say in the praises of God:

[Col. 1192B] **VERSE 6.** “He has exalted me upon the rock, and now has lifted up my head above my enemies.” For the rock is Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4), in whom I, David the prophet, believed would come; and I, whoever I am, David innocent or penitent in the Church, believe that he came into the world and again left the world to go to the Father, drawing all things after himself and to himself. Upon this rock, in the firmness of this faith, he has now exalted me, because “upon this rock”—that is, upon myself—“I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18). And now also, in the time of my pilgrimage, while I flee Saul—that is, sin—he has lifted up my head above my enemies.

For in that, by his gift, I believed in my heart unto righteousness, he hid me in the hidden place of his tabernacle; but in that I confessed with my mouth unto salvation [Col. 1192C], he has now lifted up my head upon the rock. For the Rock himself said to one Peter who trusted, and in him to everyone who confesses: “You are Peter, and upon this Rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18). Thus he exalted me upon the rock, and now has lifted up my head above my enemies, which are the gates of hell, concerning which it is promised to the most steadfast faith that “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.”

For neither demons, nor wicked people, nor the vicious stirrings of fleshly desires—all of which may be understood as enemies and gates of hell—will be able to move the Church founded upon this Rock, or the mind of any believer. For though a flood should strike such a house, it cannot move it; for it is founded [Col. 1192D] upon a firm rock (Matthew 7:25). Upon such a rock he exalted me, placing me in the firmness of faith and virtues.

For Saul had resolved to pursue me even over precipitous rocks passable only to ibexes. And I indeed lifted my eyes to many mountains and many rocks, from which help came to me as I fled from Saul’s face—that is, from consenting to mortal sin; for I would have fallen into his hands if I had consented to mortal sin. Therefore in another place I said: “If there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid evil to those repaying me, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies. Let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it” (Psalm 7:5–6).

But among all mountains there is one mountain of mountains from which help comes to me [Col. 1193A]. There is one Rock of rocks, “in which there is refuge for hedgehogs” (Psalm 103:18), in which I too, David, found and have refuge like a little hedgehog. Though I am found altogether covered, like a hedgehog or an urchin, with the small and daily thorns of sins, I nevertheless rest with firmest hope in the clefts of the Rock—that is, in the wounds of Christ, who is the lamb taking away the sins of the world—while, as he did on the cross, I too pray for my enemies and, when they fall on Mount Gilboa, render the lament of compassion.

Therefore I hope not only for the future exaltation after the final royal anointing, which is laid up for the blessed at the end, when in the resurrection the saints shall receive the Spirit’s complete sweetness, so that their joy [Col. 1193B] may be full; but even now he has exalted my head. Even though the body is dead—that is, undoubtedly destined to die—because of sin, nevertheless he has exalted my head, that is, my mind, above my enemies: the mind which delights in and serves the law of God, although it is held captive in flesh serving the law of sin. He has exalted it above all my enemies, that is, above vicious desires, so that not the flesh may rule the spirit, but the spirit the flesh. Or he has exalted my head, that is, Christ, who is the head of man just as man is the head of woman, above all the heavens; and I, David the prophet, knowing without doubt that this will occur, proclaim it as though past. But I, any member of the Church, together with David the faithful one, now knowing it as past, [Col. 1193C] confidently say: “And now he has exalted my head,” that is, Christ, the head of the whole Church, above all my enemies: Jews, heretics, pagans, false Christians, and evil spirits. For all these benefits:

“I shall go round about and sacrifice [Note: [Col. 1193D] Vulgate: ‘I went round about and sacrificed.’] in his tabernacle a sacrifice of jubilation,” in thanksgiving. And because he offers himself to me as leader, I shall offer myself to him as a soldier; and, with him as leader, I shall go round about as a soldier joined to those in whose regard it is elsewhere said: “They shall return at evening; they shall suffer hunger like dogs, and shall go round about the city” (Ps. 58:7).

In the Hebrew it is read thus: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may behold the beauty of the Lord, [Col. 1193D] and attend upon his temple. For he hid me in his shadow; on the evil day he hid me in the secret place of his tabernacle; upon a rock he exalted me. Now also he will exalt my head above my enemies, who are round about me.” The sense of this Hebrew truth has been explained in what was said above, except for the present words: “above my enemies, who are round about me.” This is rightly said, namely, “above my enemies,” because “the wicked walk round about” (Ps. 11:9). Therefore, as great as is the difference between the utterly simple centre and the multitude or extent of circles which surround the centre but nowhere touch it, so great is the difference between [Col. 1194A] my desire and theirs. For I have asked one thing; they ask many things. They toil in a circuit like a wheel, now raised by prosperity and now cast down by adversity. But I, cleaving as it were to the centre of unity, despising alike this world’s prosperity and adversity, have always had one desire and have always asked one thing: “This will I seek, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.”

All who desire what is unlawful, or wish to appear important in this world, are oppressed in their hearts by dense tumults of thought; and while they stir up crowds of desires within themselves, they tread down their prostrate minds beneath the foot of miserable multitude. By contrast, holy men, because they desire nothing of this world, are undoubtedly oppressed by no tumults in their hearts. For they cast out every disordered movement of desire from the bedchamber of the heart by the hand of holy reflection. And because they despise all transitory things, they do not allow insolent thoughts to arise from them. They desire their eternal homeland alone; and because they love none of the things of this world, they enjoy great tranquillity of mind. Had he not expelled every tumult of thought from himself who said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this will I seek, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord”? For he had fled from the crowd of earthly desires into great solitude, namely within himself, where he might all the more safely behold nothing foreign insofar as he loved nothing unsuitable. From the tumult of temporal things he had sought a great retreat, [Col. 1194C] a tranquil mind, in which he might see God all the more purely because there he found him alone, the sole One.

Indeed, secular people who love this shifting age are turned about with it, and in it and with it move in circles. But I, David, once anointed through Samuel with the anointing of divine mercy—or I, any innocent or penitent person, together with David, having received the first anointing, which is forgiveness of sins, and awaiting the second, which lies in the power of merits, and the third, which lies in the blessedness of rewards—giving thanks to God for the anointing already received and offering prayers for the anointing yet to be received, “shall go round about in his tabernacle.” For if, seeking my beloved on my bed by night, I do not find him, “I shall arise and go round about the city,” seeking him whom my soul loves [Col. 1194D] (Song 3:2). For that city itself is his tabernacle, in which I go round about in mind, traversing by inquiry all the orders of the blessed; or even chanting litanies, beginning from the sanctuary—that is, from Christ himself, the Holy of Holies, the oracle of the whole Trinity. Invoking him first, I say: “Saviour of the world, help us.” Then, after invocations have been made through all the orders of the elect, so that my circuit may return to the same point, near the end of the litany I return to Christ himself, who is Alpha and Omega, beginning and end; and in that sanctuary, namely the mystery of his Incarnation, I go round about, saying: “By thy birth, deliver us, O Lord. [Col. 1195A] By thy baptism and fasting, deliver us, O Lord. By thy cross and passion, deliver us, O Lord.” Thus through entreaties, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings offered for all the orders of the Church, I go round about and sacrifice in the tabernacle of the Lord’s Incarnation—or of the whole Church—a sacrifice of jubilation in praises and prayers. These at length give way to so great a jubilation of mind that it cannot be expressed in words, although it cannot be wholly kept silent.

I shall not go round about with this shifting world, so as to be weighed down by its adversities or lifted up by its prosperities, after the manner of a wheel running in mud. Rather, I shall go round about in his tabernacle, that is, in the whole Church, rejoicing with those who rejoice and weeping with those who weep; ascending through rejoicing at another’s or a brother’s happiness, [Col. 1195B] descending through compassion for a brother’s misery, in the motion of the running wheels—not in this world’s mire, but in the tabernacle, or rather in heaven. For of these it is written: “When the living creatures were lifted up, the wheels also were lifted up with them; when they went, they went, and when they stood, they stood; and when they were lifted up from the earth, they too were lifted up. For the spirit of life was in the wheels” (Ezek. 1:19). Thus I shall go round about in his tabernacle in the manner of spiritual wheels.

Or, as Martha was busy with much service, and as Paul “from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum” filled the Gospel in a circuit; or certainly in contemplation of truth, which, like the heavenly wheels, lacks beginning and end and embraces all things. [Col. 1195C] For whatever truly is, is in truth, and that alone is. But whatever subsists neither truly nor in truth is false—indeed, it is nothing. Therefore, whatever is not comprehended within the circle of truth, because it is not true, is nothing. Hence those who flee from truth tend toward nothingness, while iniquity lies to itself, or lies also to others by calling good evil or evil good. But I, established within the circuit of truth, with truth’s light showing me, call good good and evil evil; and in such a judgment of truth I go round about in the tabernacle of God, approving every good and rejecting every evil, first in my own person and then in others who are in his tabernacle. For [Col. 1195D] we are forbidden to judge those who are outside, as the Apostle says: “Do you not judge those who are within? For what is it to me to judge those who are outside? God will judge those who are outside” (1 Cor. 9:12). Therefore we may lawfully judge those who are within. Thus, judging rightly, I shall go round about in his tabernacle and sacrifice in his tabernacle a sacrifice of loud acclamation, or jubilation—that is, praise—through consideration of goods which are truly good.

Otherwise: “I went round about and sacrificed in his tabernacle a sacrifice of loud acclamation.” I considered the examples of the saints; I surveyed all created things, praising their Creator through their diverse forms of beauty as though through diverse voices. I considered the faith of the whole earth, through which the Church has been exalted together with her head. I examined [Col. 1196A] the divine benefits granted particularly to me and universally to the Church; and for all these things, in his tabernacle—that is, in the whole fabric of the world—I sacrificed a sacrifice of loud acclamation, inviting every creature to praise and bless its Creator, as is done in the hymn of the three youths and in the final three psalms.

Likewise, in the whole Church, which is the tabernacle of God, or through contemplation of the tabernacle—that is, Christ’s Incarnation, by which he was sacrificed for us—I sacrificed a sacrifice of loud acclamation in hymns and spiritual songs, or a sacrifice of jubilation in holy meditations, where, speech failing or falling silent, jubilation alone remains. For by such a sacrifice of jubilation for God’s true benefits, eternal Truth itself is delighted—Truth which is praiseworthy in every respect, not falsely but truly, for all that is accomplished in the tabernacle of the entire worldly fabric either through its goodness at work or through its justice disposing that it be permitted to occur. Its action is always good, and its permission always just. Hence, concerning the mercy of this eternal Truth:

“I will sing and chant a psalm to the Lord”: namely, “I will sing of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100:1), believing and confessing with my mouth that the Lord is merciful to the merciful and a judge without mercy to the unmerciful. I shall sing this not only in faith and speech. In this faith I shall also chant to the Lord by the evidence of my works, showing my faith. For because I [Col. 1196C] believed this to be true, I, David, also compassionately mourned my enemies through mercy, mourning them with a great lament. This great lament was like a sacrifice of loud acclamation, acceptable in the sight of the true David, who mourns his enemies not only in the Lamentations of Jeremiah and of the other prophets, but also in his own person. For, seeing the city rebellious against him, he wept over it, saying: “If only you too had known” (Luke 19:41). Finally, after such mourning, I, Christ the true David, hanging upon the cross and dying to reconcile my enemies, offered a sacrifice of loud acclamation and jubilation, my blood crying aloud—or crying out—more effectually than Abel’s blood. Abel’s blood, crying from the earth, demanded vengeance; but my blood, poured into the mouths of the faithful, cries [Col. 1196D] from the earth—that is, from the whole holy Church—asking not vengeance but mercy, pardon, grace, and peace. Therefore I say:

**VERSE 7.** “Hear, O Lord, my voice, with which I cried to thee.” Hear me, as my blood cries to thee from the earth, that is, from the whole Church, which through confession of faith opened its mouth and received—and daily receives—my blood, crying out and praying for that one thing to be obtained, which I asked when once offered to drain away the sins of many. And I still ask for that same one thing which I asked: I ask it in the mystical sacraments; I ask it in my members. Therefore I say: “Hear, O Lord, my voice, with which I cried to thee.” Hear, O Lord, [Col. 1197A] my voice, full of unutterable groanings, for the second and third anointing.

And indeed, between these two anointings there is one which consists in the power of merits; and the other, which consists in the blessedness of eternal rewards, follows the former so inevitably that the preceding one affords undoubted certainty of the latter which follows. Hence a certain man, holding one of these two anointings, declares himself assured of the other, saying: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall render to me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:7). The completion of the good fight is understood as one anointing; the crown of righteousness as the other. But because one depends on [Col. 1197B] the other, as an inevitable consequence upon its antecedent, I, David, rightly asked not two anointings but one from the Lord. For if the one consisting in the power of merits, as “a good gift” descending from above from the Father of lights (James 1:17), has been granted in advance, the other, consisting in the blessedness of rewards, will without doubt follow as “a perfect gift.” For their works inevitably follow those who, having kept the faith and finished the course, die in the Lord, so that they may rest from their labours. “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14:13). Therefore I, David, once anointed in the reception of the sacraments of faith and still awaiting the twofold royal anointing in merits and rewards, rightly asked only one thing and will seek it, since [Col. 1197C] through the one I hope without doubt for the other. For I believe that I shall see the Lord’s good things in the land of the living, if first I am heard concerning this one petition in the land of the dying. Therefore I say: “Hear, O Lord, my voice, with which I cried to thee,” for that one thing: the inward voice which cries to thee not in a noise of words but in the intensity of desires, to thee who hearest purpose and thought. For “the thought of man shall confess to thee, and the remnant of thought shall keep festival for thee” (Ps. 75:11), even while the tongue is silent but the heart cries and says: “Have mercy on me and hear me. Have mercy on me, who am wretched as long as I lack that one thing which I have asked; and therefore, O merciful one, hear me by granting that one thing which I have asked.” I say, “Hear; have mercy”; again I say, “Hear.” Nor does one petition suffice me [Col. 1197D] for the anointing which I have asked, because desires grow and increase when extended; if they decreased, they would not be desires. But now, the more I pray, the more I am kindled to pray inwardly in my heart, where thou hearest and, I believe, hast already heard, namely that which

**VERSE 8.** “My heart said to thee.” What did my heart say to thee? Namely this: “My face sought [Note: [Col. 1197] Vulgate: ‘My face has sought thee; thy face, O Lord,’ etc.] thy face.” The human heart, or rational mind, which is denoted by the name “heart,” has a face; and this face has cheeks, of which it is said to the bride of the Word, namely the rational mind: “Thy cheeks are beautiful [Col. 1198A] as those of a turtledove” (Song 1:10). Do you suppose that the invisible and incorporeal substance of the mind, distinguished neither by bodily limbs nor adorned by visible colours, has visible cheeks? This was the absurdity of the heretic Tertullus, who taught that the soul’s form was visible and circumscribed after the manner of a body. But you, insofar as you can, apprehend spiritual essence through spiritual insight; and, in order to fit the proposed comparison, consider the soul’s face to be the intention of the mind, from which the rectitude of an action is assessed just as bodily beauty is assessed from the face. Further, understand modesty (*verecundia*; the supplied reading appears to have lost the initial *v*) as a colour in the face, because this virtue especially imparts attractiveness and increases grace. “Thy cheeks are therefore beautiful as those of a turtledove.” He could more conventionally have used and described the face as beautiful, as is usual when the beauty of a person is praised: “beautiful in face” or “fair in face.” But I do not know what he intended in thinking it better to speak of cheeks in the plural, unless I should suppose that it is by no means idle. For it is the Spirit of wisdom who speaks, to whom it is not lawful to attribute anything at all, even the least thing, as idle or said otherwise than it ought to have been. There is therefore without doubt some reason, whatever it may be, why he preferred to say “cheeks” in the plural rather than “face” in the singular. And if you have no better explanation, I shall set forth what seems to me.

Two things are necessarily required in the intention which we have called the face of the soul: the object and the cause—that is, what you intend and for what reason. From these two the soul’s beauty or ugliness is judged. [Col. 1198C] Thus, for example, a soul possessing both rightly and chastely may deservedly and truly be told: “Thy cheeks are beautiful as those of a turtledove.” But of a soul lacking either of these, it cannot be said, “Thy cheeks are beautiful as those of a turtledove,” because of the deformity that remains in part. Still less can this apply to one found to possess neither in a praiseworthy form.

This will become clearer in examples. If, for instance, someone directs his mind toward investigating truth, and does so out of love of truth alone, does he not seem to you to possess both an honourable object and an honourable cause, and deservedly to claim for himself the saying, “Thy cheeks are beautiful as those of a turtledove”? For no blemish deserving reproof appears on either cheek. But if he directs himself toward truth not from a desire for truth at all, but under the pretext either of vainglory or of some other temporal advantage, then, although he may seem to have one beautiful cheek, you will not, I think, hesitate to judge him at least partly deformed, since the ugliness of the cause has marred his other cheek. But if you see a person pursuing no honourable studies, but entangled in fleshly enticements and given over to the belly and luxury—such as those whose “god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame,” who set their minds on earthly things—what then? Will you not judge him utterly foul on both sides, since in his intention both [Col. 1199A] object and cause are found reprehensible? Thus, to direct oneself not to God but to the world belongs to a worldly soul, which has no beautiful cheek at all. To direct oneself, as it were, to God, yet not for God’s sake, plainly belongs to the soul of a hypocrite. Although its face seems fair in this—that it looks toward God with some sort of intention—yet the very pretence destroys all beauty in it and instead introduces ugliness throughout. But if it turns its intention toward God solely, or chiefly, for the necessities of this present life, it is not foul with the rottenness of hypocrisy; nevertheless, we call it darkened by the fault of faint-heartedness, and less acceptable.

Conversely, to direct oneself toward something other than God, yet for God’s sake, is not Mary’s leisure but Martha’s business. Far be it from me to call anything about such a soul ugly. Yet I would not affirm that it has attained the perfection of beauty; for, still anxious and troubled about many things, it cannot avoid being sprinkled with at least a fine dust from earthly actions. Yet this will quickly and easily be wiped away, either at the hour of holy falling asleep, by a fruitless intention and the inquiry of a good conscience directed to God. Therefore, to seek God alone for his own sake alone is precisely to have both cheeks of the twofold face of intention most beautiful; and this is the bride’s distinctive and special quality, fittingly entitling her, by singular privilege, to hear: “Thy cheeks are beautiful as those of a turtledove.” Therefore, that the face of my heart may be wholly beautiful, with both cheeks beautiful, my heart said to thee, my God, [Col. 1199C] who art the true and eternal beauty of the citizens above, angels and human beings, whose glory and beauty fill heaven and earth—that is, angelic and human nature in the elect—to thee, I say, “beautiful in form above the sons of men”: “My face sought thy face,” and in this seeking I shall persevere. For

“Thy face,” or “thy countenance, O Lord, I will seek,” so that “my judgment may come forth from thy countenance” (Ps. 16:2), and my face may be conformed to thy face: that, just as thou dost nothing except good and for the sake of good, so my intention before thy face may always be directed toward good for the sake of good, shining and radiant with the twofold beauty of cheeks, whose [Col. 1199D] beauty has already been discussed above. For thou didst see all things which thou hadst made in the beginning, and they were very good, since they were created by thee, the good Creator, for thy goodness; and thou art supremely good with respect to those good things, Alpha and Omega, beginning and end. Therefore, I know that thou who dost good for the sake of good hast a good countenance. I desire my countenance to be conformed to it, so that, as thy face illuminates and likewise conforms my face, I too, wholly directed and intent in my heart upon doing good for the sake of good, may attain according to my measure a likeness to thy countenance, O Lord, so that I may say with all the saints: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us” (Ps. 4:7). For just as a royal seal impressed upon lead or gold forms upon it the king’s countenance or face, so it is possible for thee, almighty one, to conform [Col. 1200A] my face to thy face through the impress of thy form. Or just as a beautiful face directed toward a pure mirror forms in it a likeness of its own beauty, so we now see thee through a mirror; thou wilt present to thyself the well-cleansed face of our mind as a pure mirror, in which thy fair countenance may appear. For thou art the true Elisha, and I am the dead child; nor can I be raised from death unless thou, who art life, comest to me and, by conforming me to thyself, grantest the breath of life to me who am dead. This will occur when thou appliest thy living face to my dead face, when thou, the true Elisha, placest thy eyes upon my eyes, thy mouth upon my mouth, and thy hands upon my hands. Believing this would occur through the mystery of thy Incarnation, I, David the prophet, say in this very psalm: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

But I, David the penitent, now in the Church, after receiving the sacraments of the Incarnation and, after the life-giving anointing in baptism, having died again through sin, now seeking the second anointing, seek thy countenance, O Lord—that is, thy Son, anointed above his companions. That is, I seek again that, laying his eyes upon my eyes, his mouth upon my mouth, and his hands upon my hands, he may make me live the true life which he himself is, so that I may say: “Yet I live; no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). Until now, while death ruled me, my shameless, evil, and proud eye was the messenger of my shameless, evil, [Col. 1200C] and proud heart. Henceforth the Spirit says: “Let my eyes, together with my other senses, rest from their labours”; and let my eye be chaste, kindly, and humble, the messenger of a chaste, kindly, and humble heart, so that from such a look thy countenance, O Lord, may shine forth in my face. Likewise, because grace is poured forth upon thy lips, may grace abound upon my lips when the mouth of thy countenance is set upon my mouth, so that they may never be opened uselessly, but always profitably, to praise thee and build up my neighbour. May thy hands likewise work in my hands, so that through good works it may become plain and manifest to holy Mother Church that thy countenance, set upon my face, has made me live. In this faith and hope, when I impress the sign of the cross upon my face, I think upon thy countenance on that very cross, which I desire to be applied to my face, and I say: “Thy countenance, O Lord, I will seek.” With such desire I shall burn fervently, having this verse often on my lips and more often in my heart: “May God have mercy upon us and bless us; may he cause his countenance to shine upon us, and have mercy upon us” (Ps. 66:1). Likewise: “Make thy face shine upon thy servant” (Ps. 30:17). Likewise: “Make thy face shine upon thy servant, and teach me thy ordinances” (Ps. 118:135). Yet however bright a mirror may be when formed by a beautiful face, it will remain shapeless if the beautiful face turns away from it. Thus I ask to be conformed to thee, O eternal wisdom and beauty, and made like the countenance of thy goodness, so that I may remain in this conformity to thy face [Col. 1201A] for ever—not rejoicing for an hour in thy light, but unto the endless end.

Can the human mind, however, possess from itself this beauty of its inward face and invisible cheeks? The Apostle contradicts this and says: “What hast thou that thou hast not received?” (1 Cor. 4:7). And John says: “A man can receive nothing from himself unless it has been given him from above” (John 3:27). Another witness of truth says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration” (James 1:17). For I, created in thine image and likeness, am indeed, in the noble condition of creation, a mirror; but through sin and misery I am exceedingly darkened. Therefore, against sin’s rust I seek thy ordinances, by which my heart may be made bright like a pure mirror, capable of thy beauty and thy love—the love by which thou lovest not only beautiful minds but even ugly ones, in order to make them beautiful. But that I may obtain what I ask:

**VERSE 9.** “Turn not thy face away from me.” And if at any time thou turnest it away because thou art incomprehensible, and sayest to me what thou saidst to Moses: “My face shall not be seen by thee; for no man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:23), this I earnestly ask: “Decline not in anger from thy servant.” For just as one who asks temporal goods from thee, the giver of good things, thinks [Col. 1201C] that thou art angry with him only when thou refusest or takest them away, so I, who have asked one thing and sought thy countenance, then think and feel thee angry with me when thou turnest away from me thy desirable countenance, “into which angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1:12). Thus I grant that other goods may sometimes be present and sometimes absent: by bestowing them thou showest thy presence, and by withdrawing or refusing them thou signifyest a kind of absence of thy mercy, in order to test thy servant Job, Tobias, or another such person. But in the withdrawal of thy countenance or face I fear thy anger. Therefore I say: “Decline not in anger from thy servant.”

For thou declinest not in anger when thou turnest thy face from my sins to blot them out, as I, David, am accustomed to say to thee: “Turn thy face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities” (Ps. 50:11); or when thou allowest a person to fall, that he may become more cautious after falling. But, as has been said, thou declinest in anger when, behind the wall of enmity built from sins, thou so hidest thy countenance—desirable to the holy and pious—from a human being or rational soul, thy bride, that thou dost not show thy face even for a brief view, though not for kissing, by looking through the lattices or windows [Col. 1201D] (Song 2:9), or for seeking counsel concerning thy will in confessions or prayers. Lattices adhere externally to a house as ornament and provide, by arched columns inside, an opening for looking out from the house or into it. Windows, however, are joined to a house so as to illuminate it with the sunlight admitted through themselves. We therefore fittingly understand by lattices the fathers of the Old Testament, or also the patriarchs and righteous under the law of nature; and by windows the apostles and other apostolic men, by whose teaching the Church shines as the moon shines through the sun. Therefore, when the wall of our sins is so dense that, as our faults deserve, we are wholly in darkness, our sight cut off from the face of the true light, then, as we chant litanies and ask the ancient and modern saints to pray for us, the face of divine mercy is sometimes granted to be seen as it were through lattices and windows, so that, when its anger has been removed, mercy may shine upon us from the sight of that face. This mercy [Col. 1202B] I, David—I, innocent or penitent, always desiring as David did—say to thee, my God, my mercy, my illumination, and my salvation: “Decline not in anger from thy servant.” But rather,

“Be thou my helper.” For although thou hast granted me free will, yet that will, just as it is wholly free from every necessity, so that no necessity of fated disposition, constellation, or anything else compels it into the inevitability of sinning, is nevertheless wretched and weak with every kind of misery. Thus, even to think, will, or do the least good whatever, it requires thy help. To thee now I say: “Be thou my helper.” And because, when thy help ceases, every effort of human power is immediately found either nonexistent or vain, just as for the beginning and advancement of a good work I say to thee, “Be thou my helper,” so for its perseverance and completion I say: “Forsake me not,” that is, do not interrupt or abandon what thou hast begun.

“Nor despise me”: that is, do not disdain that I, mortal and weak, dare to invoke thee, eternal and most strong, as my helper. For not presumption but faith encourages this confidence, because I believe most firmly and do not at all doubt that thou art, O God, my saviour [Col. 1202D] (Ps. 24:5). Thou who art my Creator art also my Saviour. Thou, Creator, didst make for me a will free from every necessity compelling it to sin. But because through abuse of freedom I fell into the snare of guilt and misery, and because through sin and sin’s punishment a most grievous weakness came upon me, thou who wast my Creator hast become my Saviour, so that thou mayest save from both the freedom of the will—noble enough by its own created condition, but languishing in sin and punishment—by granting forgiveness of sins in this life and, in the future, the blessedness of eternal joys. This anointing is twofold; but I have asked one thing: either, as stated above, I have asked that one anointing which comes first in the power of merits, whose beginning and completion is the forgiveness first of original sins and then of actual sins; or, certainly, I have asked the other one anointing which will follow at the end, by which, when it is accomplished, the faithful [Col. 1203A] soul will be led like David into Jerusalem, the royal city and blessed vision of holy everlasting peace.

For these two anointings are so joined to one another that, when either one is obtained, the other is necessarily possessed. To be sure, for infants, who have never had a time for acting, the former anointing is forgiveness of original sin. For when death comes first, without the intervening anointing of merits, such persons attain the anointing of everlasting joys. Concerning this anointing the apostles, still ignorant, heard Truth say to them: “Until now you have asked nothing. Ask, that your joy may be full” (John 16:24). As though he said: Unless you make this one petition, by which through the anointing of the Holy Spirit you attain complete [Col. 1203B] joy, whatever you ask is nothing; and therefore until now you have asked nothing, because you have not asked this one thing, by which your joy may be full. Oh, how beautiful and delightful it is to understand or imply this one petition in all prayers: “that our joy may be full.” For example, when we pray: “Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come; thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth,” and so forth, we fittingly understand in each of the seven petitions: “that our joy may be full.” For what benefit is it to us that God’s name is undoubtedly hallowed, that God’s kingdom will come, and that God’s will shall be done in heaven [Col. 1203C] and on earth, unless we receive this one petition, that our joy may be full, as we rejoice fully in the fulfilment of such petitions? But demons and wicked men, when God’s kingdom comes, in which his name is hallowed and his will is done, have not the joy of rejoicing with others but the torment of envy. Therefore, lest we be numbered among such people, let us understand this one petition in all our petitions: that our joy may be full, admitting no torment of malice, according to what is written of the saints: “The torment of malice shall not touch them” (Wis. 3:1). Wicked angelic and human spirits are touched and anguished by the excessive torment of malice and envy: by malice in their own wickedness, by envy at another’s happiness. [Col. 1203D] All the wrathful and proud are tormented by the excessive torment of impatience when something occurs contrary to their will. But charity, which “does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices together with truth” (1 Cor. 13:6), frees from many torments and confers full joy upon tranquil minds. Let us ask this one thing, that our joy may be full. “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek,” that my joy may be full. Therefore, lest anyone take that joy from me: “Be thou my helper, O Lord; forsake me not, nor despise me, O God my Saviour.” Do not forsake me,

**VERSE 10.** “For my father and my mother have forsaken me.” The intensification of human misery moves divine mercy to compassion. For one who recognizes and confesses his own misery merits God’s pity through the confession of that misery.

But this is not a new misery which I, David, endure; it is an ancient one: “For my father and my mother have forsaken me.” My father Adam and my mother Eve were blessed by God, who said to them: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it; and have dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and every living creature that moves upon the earth” (Gen. 1:28). Had my parents thus blessed remained in faith and obedience, all their posterity, multiplied through the blessings and power of divine grace, would have been blessed—and I too would have been blessed in it. But when sin arose, it was said to my father Adam: “Cursed is the earth because of your work. When you cultivate the earth, it shall not yield its fruits; rather, it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:17–18). And to my mother Eve God likewise said: “I shall multiply your hardships and your conceptions; in pain you shall bear your children” (Gen. 3:16). From such a curse come the thorns of sins and the thistles of punishments in the human race, in which, through the multiplication of a woman’s hardships and conceptions, the children of men have been multiplied beyond the number of the predestined. Therefore my father and mother forsook me when my first parents exposed me to sins and miseries.

But the Lord received me by assuming flesh for me from the holy Virgin. [Col. 1204C] This had already then been ordained in the divine predestination, when it was said to the serpent: “I shall place enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She herself shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. 3:15).

Also in the literal sense, my father and mother forsook me, little David, because I was the least of my brothers, lowly and despised before them, so that, when Samuel sought me, I was scarcely admitted among the number of my brothers. But the Lord received me, because, setting aside my seven elder brothers, he anointed me through Samuel with the first anointing—the anointing of his mercy—in my father’s house, while those very brothers of mine watched and envied. That first anointing [Col. 1204D] I, David, did not seek; for the Lord forestalled me with the blessings of sweetness when I neither asked nor expected it, and received me as king over Israel. Afterwards, however, when Saul had died, I made one request, saying: “Shall I go up into one of the cities of Judah?” (2 Sam. 2:1). And the Lord received me, calling me to go up to Hebron, where, anointed again as king, I glory in God and say: “The Lord received me.”

Another interpretation: My father is the devil, and my mother Babylon, from whom I was born in unbelief. They forsook me when I sought you and despised them. For to all conceived and born in the sin introduced through the devil, Truth can say: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44). But the Lord received me into [Col. 1205A] his Church, to which he says: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44:11 [45:10]). By this call, proceeding from the mouth of God who calls the holy Church daughter and acknowledges himself as the Father of this his daughter, I, little David—I, whatever sort of son I may be of mother Church herself—dare to say: “For my father the devil, father indeed of the proud, or rather their king, forsook me when I was made humble and adopted into the sonship of God; and my mother, the city Babylon and mother of the impious, forsook me when I forsook her. But the Lord received me,” adopting me as a son through the one man whom he assumed to himself as his natural Son. The Lord, I say, received me, becoming a good father to me in place of an evil father; for as a father [Col. 1205B] he chastens me with the rod of discipline, just as he chastens every son whom he receives. That same Lord is also a mother to me, cherishing and nourishing me with maternal consolations, lest I fail, broken by paternal corrections.

Another interpretation: I, Christ, the true David, have as my father the Jewish people, from whom I sprang according to the flesh, and as my mother the Synagogue. While still a child, I observed her rites: I was circumcised on the eighth day and presented in the Temple with the legal sacrifice. But when, now grown, I began to disregard legal traditions, healing the sick on the Sabbath, I was forsaken by such a father and mother, the Scribes and Pharisees saying against me: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9:16). At last my father and mother most cruelly forsook me when, delivering [Col. 1205C] me to death, they said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). But the Lord, the Word of God, received me; for he who at my conception had assumed me into the unity of his person, so that I, the true David, might be true man and true God, himself received me at the Resurrection into the identity of royal glory. Thus, as victor over death, crowned with glory and honour, I could say as an illustrious king: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18). I did not say this before my death, when I was still made lower not only than God the Father but also than the angels. But after I had triumphed over death, crowned with glory and honour, and ascended to the right hand of the Father—the king who rules all things and has dominion everywhere—I may rightly [Col. 1205D] sing and say through the mouths of my people: “For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has received me.” The Lord, I say, received me, so that I, the man received into the Lord, might be Lord: the Lord God who assumed me as man has now united me not merely in person but also in every dominion. For not some particular authority, but universally all authority, has been given to me—that is, in heaven and on earth. I, the true David, have always had this authority in my divinity; but it was given to me in my humanity, humbled even unto death on the cross—this whole authority which my divine majesty has always possessed together with my omnipotent Father. For my Father and I are not two Lords, but one Lord. Likewise I, true man [Col. 1206A] and also Son of Man, am one Lord in such a way that in my two natures there is no duality whatsoever of lordship. Rightly, therefore, I say: “The Lord received me.” To this Lord, who receives me into natural sonship and through me receives my own into the adoption of sons, I, the true singer, say:

**VERSE 11. “Set a law before me, O Lord, in your way.”** Set a law before me—that is, before my people—in your way, that is, in me, who am “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). “And direct me”—that is, my people—“in a straight path,” through the straits of tribulations, because of my enemies, who blaspheme my name in my people, where they have strayed from the way and straight path. Therefore, not only for your goodness’ sake but also because of my enemies lying in wait for me and mine, do not hand me—that is, my people—over to [Col. 1206B] the souls of those who afflict me. If you hand over the outward possessions or even the bodies of my people into the hands of their persecutors, nevertheless do not hand me—that is, my people—over to the souls of those who afflict me, so that the souls of my people may be conformed to the souls of their persecuting enemies. This would certainly happen if a martyr, by denying me, the Truth, passed over to the will and disposition of the persecutor afflicting him.

I, the true David, know how prone my enemies are to blaspheme my little ones. For I too suffered such things: “For unjust witnesses rose against me, and iniquity lied to itself” (Ps. 26:12 [27:12]). They were indeed fully conscious that they spoke falsely against me when they said: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Luke 11:15). Again: “He has a demon and is mad; why do you listen to [Col. 1206C] him?” (John 10:20). Finally, when two false witnesses stood against me, saying: “This man said, ‘I can destroy this Temple made with hands, and in three days I shall build another’” (Matt. 26:61), then indeed iniquity lied to itself, because their testimony did not agree (Mark 14:59). For I had not spoken of the Temple made with hands, although it would have been possible for me to destroy it and rebuild it in a moment; rather, I spoke of the Temple of my body: “Destroy this Temple, and after three days I shall rebuild it.” Finally, iniquity also lied to itself when they bribed the soldiers and said: “Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep” (Matt. 28:13).

[Col. 1206D] While the true David—who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found—thus prays, I, David the sinner, trusting in the prayer of such a David, made for me a sinner, believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. I believe that, through the power of his prayer, I shall be heard as I pray and say in him and with him: “Set a law before me, O Lord, in your way.” You set a law for created things when, by a fixed law and circuit, you enclosed the abysses and set a law for the waters and the sea, lest they pass their bounds. With this law established, “waters shall pass between the midst of the mountains,” and the sea feels the law set for it when you say: “Thus far you shall come, and no farther; here you shall break your swelling waves” (Job 38:11). Therefore it is possible for you also to set a law before me in your way, that is, in Christ, [Col. 1207A] who is the way, so that I may not pass the limits appointed for those walking in that way. “And direct me in a straight path,” so that, whether I walk in the broad way of the active life or proceed along the narrow path of the contemplative life, I may not wander from justice or truth, nor ever be found outside the way of righteous action and the path of true contemplation, wandering “in a trackless place, and not in a way” (Ps. 106:40 [107:40]).

Direct me thus, always stretching forward and forgetting the things behind, because of my enemies following from behind and wishing to draw me back into Egypt. Direct me in the way, with him speaking who is the way, and who is a pillar of fire because of the strength and uprightness of his shining and burning divinity, and a pillar of cloud because of the strength and uprightness of his bright [Col. 1207B] and gentle humanity (Exod. 13:21). Or he is a pillar of fire because of zeal for truth and justice, and a pillar of cloud because of the gentleness of grace and mercy. For thus “we saw him full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Let us believe that his guidance is sufficient for us through the day of prosperity and the night of adversity. Direct me, lest, having put my hand to the plough, I look back and become unfit for the kingdom of God. Direct me, lest, having gone out from Sodom, I look back like Lot’s wife. Direct me, lest I imitate those who said in the Gospel, “This saying is hard,” and went back, no longer willing to walk straight onward with him who is the way (John 6:61, 67). Direct me in a straight path, lest I travel through winding ways [Col. 1207C] like a twisting and slippery serpent, or walk through the labyrinthine circuits of worldly cares.

“Set a law before me, O Lord, in your way,” which your commandments show, “and direct me in a straight path,” which your counsels show, so that I may in no way turn aside from the straightness of way or path, either to the right or to the left: to the right through evil covered over with the appearance of good; to the left through naked and open evil. Direct me, so that in a straight course I may hasten to reach the prize, running so as to attain it. Direct me always forward because of my enemies, who follow and pursue from behind, lie in wait on the right and left, and place a stumbling-block beside the way. If I deviate even a little from the straightness of the way or path, I shall fall among robbers, like [Col. 1207D] the man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho (Luke 10:30). Those robbers are ready to strip, wound, or kill every person going down from Jerusalem. They strip him by taking away the gifts of grace, such as faith, hope, and charity, and the other perfect gifts added to nature; with wounds inflicted, they damage those excellent natural gifts which they cannot take away, such as memory, reason, and will. And they do this to the person descending from Jerusalem to Jericho.

But I, David anointed as king, knowing that Jerusalem is the royal city formerly inhabited by King Melchizedek, seek to go up to Jerusalem, that there I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life; for when Saul pursued me, I long lived in exile among nations worshipping idols. Therefore, as one wishing to go up to [Col. 1208A] Jerusalem and not down from Jerusalem to Jericho, direct me in the straight path—one wholly directed upward toward Jerusalem—among those to whom the true David says: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all things written through the prophets concerning the Son of Man shall be fulfilled” (Luke 18:31). And if, as I thus ascend to Jerusalem, I am to be handed over to the Gentiles for mockery, spitting, and scourging, then I pray:

**VERSES 12–13. “Do not hand me over to the souls of those who afflict me, that they may accomplish in me what their malice desires.”**

For unjust witnesses—Doeg the Edomite and other liars—rose against me. They lied when they said that Ahimelech the priest had given me counsel against Saul and that the other priests had conspired [Col. 1208B] with me against him.

In the Hebrew it reads: “Show me, O Lord, your way, and lead me in a straight path because of those who lie in wait for me. Do not hand me over, O Lord, to the soul of those who afflict me, for false witnesses have risen against me, and manifest falsehood. But I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.” Therefore, by manifest falsehood iniquity lied to itself against its own conscience: to itself, not to me, whom it did not move. Hence I have greater hope and faith, by which I believe that I shall see the true good things of the Lord in the land of the living, in return for the false evils charged and reproached against me in the land of the dying. Had I endured false accusations, slanders, and iniquity lying to itself impatiently, [Col. 1208C] I would hope for no good from them. But now, because I endured them patiently, I believe through the merit of patience preserved amid lies, with true faith, that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living, where iniquity and falsehood have no place.

But in the land of the dying, because falsehood and iniquity have a place, iniquity itself lied to itself, because the wicked man is both pleased and tormented by his own lie. He is pleased when he persuades those like himself that falsehood is truth; he is tormented when the manifest lie which iniquity told itself is exposed by good people. For every sin returns upon its own author and harms him rather than his innocent neighbour. But I, David—David penitent—amid so many and such great dangers, supported by a good conscience concerning patience maintained, or even by ensuing repentance concerning patience not maintained, and relying upon the testimony either of a good conscience or of true repentance, believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord, not in the land of the dying, where the small number of good grains lies hidden beneath a multitude of bad chaff, where evil days are many and the few good days end quickly; [Col. 1208D] but in the land of the living, where one day is better than thousands, after the chaff and tares have been winnowed from the Lord’s threshing floor and the good grain gathered into the Lord’s barn.

I, David, was indeed anointed once in my father’s house before I was anointed a second or third time. While I was an exile in Ziklag, driven out from the land of Israel and possessing no city of my kingdom, I asked one thing of the Lord: “Shall I go up into one of the cities of Judah?” And, commanded to go up to Hebron, I was long delayed from entering the city Jerusalem, in which I was to have the throne of my kingdom. There was a long struggle between my house and the house of Saul, and I was not permitted to reign in Jerusalem over all Israel while Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, reigned over Israel. In that long delay, during which I was prevented from reigning over the whole kingdom of Israel destined for me while Saul or his sons lived, I was not broken by the vice of faint-heartedness or turned away from the long-suffering expectation of the divine promise, by which Samuel had said concerning me that, once Saul was rejected, I should reign. Most certainly believing that this would happen, I waited long-sufferingly and patiently for the Lord to fulfil his promises, knowing that [Col. 1209B] there is no falsehood in his predictions and promises, because whatever he promises, he also does.

Therefore, while I, David, long served as a soldier—whether in military service under King Saul, who sent me into many dangers, or when that same king drove me out of the land of Israel—I did not fail through distrust, but acted courageously, having great certainty of faith in God’s promise. Therefore, as it is said, I acted courageously and my heart was strengthened. I considered God to be a truthful and powerful promisor, and debtor of his own promise; I waited for him long-sufferingly, humbly, and patiently, until he fulfilled for me what he had promised, not scantily but so magnificently that he not only established my kingdom, but also bound himself by oath that in the future a line descending from me [Col. 1209C] should succeed me: that from the fruit of my womb he would raise up upon my throne such a king as would reign without end, whose throne would endure for ever and ever, and whose royal sceptre would be a sceptre of equity.

I have given you an example, whoever you are that have been anointed in baptism into a royal priesthood and are not [Col. 1210A] immediately delivered from all the violence of Saul—that is, of death. Do not fail under the Lord’s discipline, nor grow weary when you are reproved and chastened by him, even through the agents of impious Saul—that is, death. Though they afflict you and sometimes drive you from the kingdom due to you, so that you can scarcely find a place in which to remain in secure expectation, nevertheless:

**VERSE 14. “Wait for the Lord,”** who does not deceive. In your waiting, act not sluggishly but courageously—not with carnal strength, because there are strong men who fight against you, but with the strength of a good and excellent heart. For those who retain the word of God in a good and excellent heart, loving what it commands and awaiting what it promises, possess praiseworthy spiritual strength. In order that you may have this strength, even if the flesh grows weary, [Col. 1210B] let your heart nevertheless be strengthened more and more from day to day through faith and hope, and wait for the Lord. Do not suppose that what you feel delayed has been denied. Do not fail through despair, but await long-sufferingly what you believe and endure patiently what you suffer. Be one of the crowd that waited for the Lord for three days, so that you may deserve to hear the Lord—or, if you do not hear with bodily hearing, may perceive in the effect of divine mercy that he says of you: “I have compassion on this poor man, because he has now waited for me three days” (Mark 8:2). Endure the Lord when he chastens, and without doubt you will at some time experience him when he consoles.

Glory to the Father, who most fully anointed the true David so that he might reign over all Israel. To him be glory in the providence of such a kingdom. Glory to the Son, the true David, anointed above his companions. May he be glorious not only in himself but also in his companions and participants. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is the royal and priestly anointing; to him be glory in the holy and anointed Church, now and for ever. Amen.

## PSALM 27

[Col. 1209]

[Col. 1209D] **VERSE 1. “To you, O Lord, I shall cry. My God, do not be silent toward me, lest at any time you keep silence,” etc.** From this twenty-seventh psalm begins the fifth *periocha* [section], when the discussion returns to its head, to the summit of the faith which we believe and know rests upon Christ’s Passion and Resurrection. “To you,” he says, “O Lord, I shall cry. My God, do not be silent toward me,” etc. These are the words of our head, praying for his Resurrection so that he may not be like those who go down into the pit, while also inserting a condemnation of his enemies under the form of a concession when he says: “Give them according to their works and according to the wickedness of their devices,” etc. For the saying, “The Lord is my helper and my protector; my heart hoped in him, and I was helped, and my flesh blossomed anew,” is the most certain proclamation of the Resurrection after prayer, in which, namely, his flesh blossomed anew. Though it had flowered from the root of Jesse, it had seemed under scourges [Col. 1210D] and reproaches to have been stripped of its flower. The title is:

## A PSALM FOR THIS DAVID

It is certain that David signifies Christ in the person either of the head or of the members. But when the title has “for this” or “for him,” it is then assigned to Christ, as here, where Christ speaks throughout the psalm. This psalm is the third among those which briefly commemorate the Passion and Resurrection.

First he prays that he may be heard in the time of the Passion and of persecutors, whose punishments he seems to desire but rather declares—not from a spirit of malevolence, but as an attestation of vengeance. Secondly, he gives thanks for his glorification at the words, “Blessed be the Lord.” He declares the salvation of believers at the words, “The Lord is their strength.” By his purpose he exhorts those who desire to be glorified [Col. 1211A] with Christ to endure adversities. He proposes himself to the righteous as an example by trusting in God, since he himself, though worthy before God, asks all things from God and says:

O Lord my God, I, a man, shall cry to you; but do not keep silence so as to separate your Word from me—that is, from that which I am as man. Lest at any time you keep silence from me and I become like those who go down into the pit. My Passion is a cry, because I expire crying out; and with a loud cry I offer prayers and supplications, to be heard because of my reverence. Therefore you, God the Father, do not be silent toward me, but answer me through the manifest proof of your protection in the Passion, preserving me from the breaking of my legs and from other things which ought not to happen to me and are not written concerning me. Do not at any time keep silence toward me; rather speak to me when I have been laid in the tomb: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” [Col. 1211B] (Ps. 107:3 [108:2]). For unless you thus speak to me through the manifest fact of resurrection from the tomb, while I, your psaltery, lie in the tomb, I shall not sound with your Word, which, although not separated from me, will nevertheless be silent in my dead and buried body. By such exceedingly long silence I shall become like other people going down into the pit, none of whom has a body united to your Word, although very many of them, such as the patriarchs and prophets to whom your Word came, were called gods. Nevertheless, when they died, that very Word which had come to them while they lived was silent in them in such a way that, bound by original sin, they descended through death into hell and their mouths kept a long silence in the tomb. To these you said: “You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” [Col. 1211C] (Ps. 81:6 [82:6]). If, then, you called gods those to whom your word came, and from the name of Deity gave them faith and hope of divine immortality, how much more is it fitting that you, Father, glorify me—whom you sanctified and sent into the world—by a swift and speedy resurrection, so that I, your most resonant psaltery, I, your incarnate Word, I, the pleasant psaltery with the harp, I, your Word harmonized with human nature in me by the plectrum and operation of the Holy Spirit, may not long remain silent in the tomb beneath the stone and guard of soldiers? For, since my enemies ordered the tomb guarded until the third day, unless my Resurrection is made manifest on the third day, I shall be made like other persons descending into the pit in the judgement of [Col. 1211D] those very enemies, and perhaps even of friends. Therefore, O Father, do not be silent toward me.

For you are the mightiest lion, and I am a lion’s cub, your son. It is the nature of a lion to restore its dead cubs to life by the sound of its roar. Since, therefore, I am a lion’s cub, the son of a lion—you, my Father, the lion—do not keep silence toward me as I lie in the tomb; but awaken me by the roar of your Word, me, a man so united to your very Word that I myself am your Word, your wisdom, your Son, of whom it is said in the blessings of Judah: “Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son. Resting, you have lain down like a lion and like a lioness. Who shall awaken him?” (Gen. 49:9). Behold, this blessing, in order to distinguish me from the other dead who go down [Col. 1212A] into the pit, says to me in your voice, Father: “You have gone up to the prey, my son.” And truly, in accordance with the prophecy of this blessing, I myself, who went down to plunder hell, ascended victoriously with that prey from hell into paradise, of which I said to the thief: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Yet although in my soul I ascended victoriously from hell into paradise, unless my body rises on the third day according to the Scriptures, I shall become like those who go down into the pit. Therefore, Father, do not be silent toward me; call me quickly from the tomb, and I shall answer you. Call me, saying: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp”; and I shall answer you: “I shall arise at daybreak.”

In the Hebrew it reads: “To you, O Lord, I shall cry, my strong one; [Col. 1212B] do not become deaf to me, lest perhaps, when I am silent, I be compared to those who descend into the pit.” Properly, the father-lion is called the strong one, and I, the lion who is his son, say to him: “To you, O Lord, I shall cry, my strong one; do not become deaf to me, as though you did not hear me, or become deaf because of the filth of sins which I, the innocent lamb, have taken upon myself.” For one is called deaf when, because filth has collected in the openings of the ears, one does not have open ears. And although I committed no sin and no deceit was found in my mouth, nevertheless I bear upon myself the sins and infirmities of those who say of me: “We considered him as it were a leper, struck by God and humbled. But he was sold over because of our iniquities, crushed because of our crimes, and the Lord placed in him the iniquities [Col. 1212C] of us all” (Isa. 53:4, 6). Lest this be thought to have happened rather by the force of the Father’s command than by my own voluntary goodwill, it is likewise most truly said of me: “He was offered because he himself willed it, and he himself bore our sins” (Isa. 53:7).

Therefore I, the strong Son, cry to you, my strong Father: do not become deaf to me. Do not, on account of the filth of others’ sins, delay in hearing me as though you were deaf. Rather, by the linen cloth of the Passion with which I am girded, and with which I wiped the feet of the disciples, cleansing them of filth, I now will the filth of sins—which hindered your ears from hearing—to be removed from the midst, so that when I cry, whether in my own person or in my members, there may be no delay in being heard. [Col. 1212D] Henceforth be a ready hearer for me and mine; and on whatever day I call upon you, hear me swiftly. Do not remember the filth which I remove from your ears, I who take away the sins of the world. Do not become deaf to me. I indeed knew that you always hear me; but I say, “Do not become deaf to me,” for the sake of my people, because as long as you are deaf to one of my least ones, you are deaf to me. Do not become deaf to me, Father, lest, as I lie in the tomb, I perhaps be compared with those who descend into the pit, as explained above.

Another interpretation: It often happens that faint-hearted people praying, unless quickly heard, fall silent in a kind of tomb of distrust. Therefore I, Christ, pray not only for my strong ones, who—as the preceding psalm urged—wait for me three days as though I lay in the tomb and do not appear to them through manifest benefits, until I stand in their midst and say: “Peace be with you” (John 20:19); [Col. 1213A] but I pray also for those who will believe through their word and are not as strong as my disciples, whom I personally instructed in perseverance in prayer. For even if, when one of these knocks at a friend’s door at midnight, the friend himself says: “Do not trouble me; I cannot rise and give to you” (Luke 11:7), he will nevertheless persist in knocking until he receives however many loaves he needs.

But the faint-hearted, like women weeping at the tomb, when they are saddened because benefits hoped for from you, Father, through me the mediator, are denied them, think that I am dead to them and that you are deaf. Such persons need this prayer, because in this psalm I say: “To you I shall cry, my strong one; do not become deaf to me, lest, when I am silent, I be compared to those who descend into the pit.” For through me they send their prayers to you, Father, saying: “Hear us, Father, through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son.” And therefore, unless you hear and answer them quickly, they will consider me mute and you deaf: me mute, as unable to intercede for them; you deaf, [Col. 1213B] as not hearing the prayers offered to you through me. Worn down by such distrust and sorrow, they say concerning me in their hearts: “But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel.” O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! You hoped in the past and do not hope in the present? “Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and so enter into his glory” (Luke 24:21, 25–26), disappearing for a time and then appearing again to his own?

Must not believers likewise be tested in this way until the end of the age, to see whether they are long-suffering in faith and hope: for a little while not seeing Christ, and then for a little while seeing him? For they do not see him for a little while, so that faith may concern what one does not see; for if you see, it is no longer faith. And again, for a little while they see him through some manifest benefit of his grace, so that faith may have merit, being given experience not by human reasoning but by divine manifestation. O foolish and slow of heart to believe! In saying, “We had hoped,” you indicate by the imperfect past tense that [Col. 1213C] your hope has not yet altogether failed. Had it failed in every respect, I would not say that you had a foolish and slow heart, but an unbelieving or faithless one. But now walk while you have some little light of hope, lest the darkness of faithlessness overtake you (John 12:35). Say to the light which converses and walks with you: “Stay with us, because evening is drawing near” (Luke 24:29). Indeed, evening then draws near in your heart when the light of faith and hope inclines toward extinction.

Thus, after reproving the disciples who doubted and almost despaired, I, David, performing the office of mediator between the disciples and you, Father, again pour out prayer for them after reproving them and others like them, and say:
