**VERSE 2. “Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication.”** Earlier I said, “Do not become deaf to me”; now I say, “Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication.” This was, indeed, the twofold supplication: “Do not be silent toward me,” and “Do not at any time keep silence toward me”; or, as the Hebrew truth has it: “Do not become deaf to me, lest, when I am silent, I be compared to those who descend into the pit.” “Lest, I say, when I am silent, I be compared to [Col. 1214A] them.” For it happens that, while I am not silent to myself—for I am the eternal Word and admit no silence in myself—I am silent to others, especially enemies, as to Herod and Pilate, who said to me: “Do you not speak to me?” (John 19:10). I do not reject this silence by which I am silent to enemies until that day of which it is said: “God shall come manifestly and shall not be silent” (Ps. 49:3 [50:3]). I permit this silence by which I am silent to this world, which considers me mute and you, Father, deaf, while it sins so irreverently before my sight and blasphemes in your hearing, as though what it says in its heart were true. What does it say? “God has forgotten; he has turned away his face lest he see forever” (Ps. 9:11 [10:11]). Thus does this foolish world speak.

And I pray not for the world, but for those whom you have given me from the world (John 17:9), lest, while I am silent to myself—that is, in myself or in my people—from the prayer or intercession by which I pray and intercede for them with you, you, by hearing slowly, should be compared to the handmade idols of the Gentiles, which have ears [Col. 1214B] but do not hear, and I likewise be compared to those descending into the pit who worship those idols, whose prayer and sacrifice have no effect for salvation. Lest this evil occur, “Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication.” Do not be silent, do not keep silence, do not become deaf; rather, hear swiftly, O Lord, the voice of my supplication, while I pray before my betrayal on the Mount of Olives, while I lift my hands upon the cross.

What the difference is between supplication and prayer has already been stated above. When Christ prays, he raises his hands, signifying that the works of those who pray ought not to be cast down but lifted upward, according to the saying: “The lifting up of my hands is the evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2 [141:2]). He speaks according to the custom of the Jews, who prayed facing the Temple in Jerusalem wherever they were, as Daniel did in Babylon, though in his time there scarcely remained even the meagre ruins of the city and small remnants of the Temple’s foundations. The Holy Spirit thereby signifies that even when the worship of Christian faith has been almost entirely annihilated and the Temple which is Christ has been destroyed in many hearts, while the Babylonian king—that is, the devil or Antichrist—reigns, or rather tyrannizes, prayer must nevertheless still be made toward the holy Temple, so that every believer may say with Daniel: “Hear, O Lord, the prayers of your servant; make your face shine upon your sanctuary, which is desolate” [Col. 1214D] (Dan. 9:17).

Moreover, Christ, seeing that the Temple of his body was to be dissolved by death and pierced with nails on the cross, which he himself had promised to rebuild in three days, rightly says as he prays on the cross: “Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication, while I pray to you, while in the arms of the cross I lift my hands toward your holy Temple.” I, still a mortal man and soon to die, ask you, Father—ask your divinity and mine—for help quickly to rebuild your holy Temple: namely, the Temple of my body. Unless, after being destroyed, it is rebuilt after three days, my saying—far be it!—by which I said to the Jews, “Destroy this Temple, and after three days I shall rebuild it” (John 2:19), will prove false. For I said this concerning the Temple of my body.

Likewise, if at any time, when iniquity abounds and the charity of many grows cold, with scarcely a few small remnants of the foundation of faith remaining, the abomination of desolation shall stand in a holy place laid waste, annihilated, and deserted, let this then be a great consolation to my little ones: that now, praying, I lift up my hands toward thy holy temple—namely, wishing and obtaining by the lifting up of my hands that the whole Church, which shall endure throughout the whole world until the end of the age, may itself be thy holy temple. For just as this temple of my body shall be destroyed, yet quickly rebuilt, when by a swift resurrection thou wilt not give thy Holy One to see corruption in flesh that dies but does not in the least decay; so the whole Church also, itself a temple, will at times, when persecution grows strong or iniquity abounds, seem diminished from the beauty of its condition, and, as though the structure of its walls had been loosened by schisms and heresies, will be thought destroyed. But because I now, on the cross, praying for my own, lift up my hands toward thy holy temple—that is, that these my own may be one house, one fold, one body, one holy temple of thine, founded upon me, the solid Rock—the gates of hell shall not prevail to destroy it utterly; for I shall rebuild it in three days, while I strengthen my own by faith, hope, and charity, lest they utterly fail.

For I now, praying and lifting up my hands on the cross toward thy holy temple, pray not only for Peter, that his faith may not fail, but also for the whole Church and for every believer in the Church, that his faith may not fail but may advance: so that to the foundation of faith may be added the height of hope, and that height may be perfected in the breadth of charity. For these three—faith, hope, and charity—are that three-day period in which the holy temple is rebuilt: while God is believed omnipotent to do what he wills; hoped for as truthful in fulfilling what he promises; and loved because he freely performs good works in his elect, to whom he has freely promised the eternal rewards of blessedness.

In his works acknowledge God as omnipotent, and hold him in fear, against whose wrath you find no protector more powerful than he himself. In his promises believe him truthful; and, rejecting the vain promises—indeed, the seductions—of the world, hold fast to the truth of the divine promise alone. In his benefits know him to be gracious, and love him for his spontaneous grace. Thus fear, truth, and love, like the light of three days, shall illuminate your heart, so that you may endure the Lord for three days, that you may depart from Egypt by a three-days’ journey, and await the rebuilding of the Lord’s temple after three days.

Again, if you consider that the whole fabric of this world was created for humankind, it plainly appears that humanity ought to have served its Creator in this world as a priest in a temple, using creatures rightly in the service of the Creator. For the first man is that priest of whom the Law says: “If the priest sins, causing the people to offend, he shall offer a calf for sin” (Lev. 4:3). Truly, this priest caused the people to fall away in his sin, because his actual sin became original sin for all people born and to be born from him, except that one alone who, like a calf, was to be offered for the abolition of that very sin. His is this voice:

> To thee, O Lord, will I cry, O my God; be not silent toward me, lest, if thou keep silence from me, I be made like those who go down into the pit. Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication, while I pray to thee, while I lift up my hands toward thy holy temple.

For if the first man, with all his posterity, had remained in God’s service, the whole world would have been his temple; and in this temple, firmly founded by divine power, adorned by divine wisdom through varied forms, fitted by divine goodness for many uses, and dedicated to the long festival of a Sabbath to be celebrated without evening and without end, in the most spacious temple of this world, pure service acceptable to God would have been a sacrifice. But now, because the priest of this temple sinned and, causing the people to offend, violated the whole temple, so that sin might reign throughout this whole temple—that is, throughout the whole world—I, Christ, the spotless calf, for the abolition of that very sin and for the imminent restoration and cleansing of the temple itself, now lift up my hands toward thy holy temple, God the Father: that thou who through me, the Word, didst create the world, may now through me, the crucified man, through me, the sacrificed calf, restore the world, so that the world itself may become and remain thy holy temple.

Let us now consider how widely the meaning of this prayer extends, in which the coeternal Son, made man, says to the eternal Father:

> To thee, O Lord, will I cry, O my God; be not silent toward me, lest, if thou keep silence from me, I be made like those who go down into the pit. Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication, while I pray to thee, while I lift up my hands toward thy holy temple.

For in these words there is understood not only the voice of the Son praying to the Father, but also that of the assumed man calling upon his own Divinity. The meaning is: “I, the assumed man, shall cry to thee, O my God; be not silent toward me.” That is: thou art my Godhead, in whom I, the Son of David and Son of God, am God equally with God the Father and God the Holy Spirit. Thou art my Godhead; since thou art the Father’s Word, be not silent toward me, the man whom thou, the Word, hast personally united to thyself. Thou, the Word who art God, be not silent toward me. From the twelfth year of my age, according to which I was born as man from the Virgin, thou, God the Word, hast sounded forth through me. For then I was found in the temple in the midst of the teachers, listening to them, questioning them, and answering so wisely that those who heard marvelled at my understanding and my answers [Col. 1217A].

Afterward I began to do and teach, even to this hour of passion and crucifixion, in which the power of darkness is so great that not only is my chief disciple to deny me three times this night, but I myself also, like a lamb made dumb before its shearer, shall not open my mouth before unjust judges, who would have no power over me unless it had been given them from above. Yet although the earth is given into the hands of the wicked one, to whom power has been permitted to crucify my flesh, thou nevertheless, God the Word personally united to me as man, be not silent toward me; lest at any time thou keep silence from me.

Even when unjust judges shall think that silence has been imposed upon thee, God the Word, because thou shalt not speak through my mouth, closed by their condemnation—or by my very death—be not silent toward me; lest at any time thou keep silence from me. Rather, through the voice of my blood crying from the earth, do thou, the Word, sound forth then most powerfully, so that thou mayest be heard even in hell, when my soul descends there and says and does such things there as make manifest to the princes of darkness that I shall not be made like those who go down into the pit, whom the weight either of original or of actual sins draws there.

For I, lacking every sin, shall be in hell “alone, free among the dead” (Ps. 87:5), so that I may also free others from it and may mock death itself, saying: “Where is thy victory, O death? Where is thy sting, O death?” (1 Cor. 15:55). Behold, thy prince and ruler comes, seeking in me something that is thine or his; and in me he has nothing.

[Col. 1217C] Rightly, therefore, though unjustly, O death that art bitten, I shall be thy death; and, like another Jonah swallowed here into thy belly, I shall be thy death. For although, when thou didst bite, it came to pass that my body lay buried in the belly of the earth for three days and three nights, and my soul was in the belly of hell as in the belly of a whale, nevertheless, O death, I shall be thy death. For I shall be vomited forth by thee in such a way that Nineveh—that is, the world—shall be converted through my teaching, after thy vital parts have been wounded and slain.

To convert this Nineveh I had first wished to go, when I said to my disciples: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles.” Again: “I am not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). By saying such things I fled, like another Jonah, from the road to the city of Nineveh. But during that flight, while the tempest of Jewish persecution raged because of me, I fell asleep in the heavy sleep of death according to the body, and according to the soul descended into hell as into the belly of a whale. Therefore, raised from the dead on the third day—for it is impossible that I should be held in the belly of a whale or of hell—I shall say to my Apostles: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth; going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature” (Matt. 28:18–19). And they, going forth, shall preach everywhere throughout all Nineveh, while I cooperate and confirm the word through the signs that follow. Thus I, who in my own person declined to preach in Nineveh—indeed, in all the cities of the Gentiles—shall myself, speaking and working in my Apostles, preach repentance throughout the world [Col. 1218A].

If, while my human voice was silent as I lay in the tomb, the Word also united to my humanity likewise kept silence, no such great benefit would result from my death. Therefore I, dying as man, say to thee, immortal God the Word united to me: “Be not silent toward me; lest at any time thou keep silence from me.” Do what thou hast promised in the prophet, saying: “For Zion’s sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest, until her righteousness go forth as brightness, and her Savior be kindled as a lamp” (Isa. 62:1–2).

Behold, although I am a righteous man, and the centurion confesses and says, “Truly this man was righteous” (Luke 23:47); although the traitor himself acknowledges the same when he says, “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27:4); and Pilate agrees, saying, “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matt. 27:24), and his wife had said to him, “Have nothing to do with that righteous man” (Matt. 27:19)—although, I say, I am so righteous a man that even my righteousness has testimony from the unjust, I am nevertheless to be shut in a sepulchre beneath a great sealed sepulchral stone.

Again, although I am the lamp of which Job says, “A lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich is prepared for the appointed time” (Job 12:5), despised by the rich chief priests, behold, in my death I shall be extinguished in such a manner that I shall have neither form nor beauty, and my appearance shall not remain in me—I who, like a lamp, gave sight to others when I enlightened the blind and performed other visible works. But thou, Word of God the Father, united to me as man, before thou didst descend into flesh, foreknowing the sufferings of thy flesh, didst say, as was set forth above: “For Zion’s sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest, until her righteousness go forth as brightness, and her Savior be kindled as a lamp” (Isa. 62:1–2).

Therefore, that thou mayest be justified in thy words and appear righteous and truthful, thou, God the Word united to my human nature, be not silent toward me until I, the righteous one, go forth from the enclosure of the tomb. Lest at any time thou keep silence from me, until I, the lamp extinguished through death, am kindled again in the glory of the resurrection, and through my ascension thou settest me upon the candlestick of the whole Church—both that reigning in heaven and that journeying on earth—above thrones, above cherubim, and above all principalities and powers.

[Col. 1218D] Be not silent toward me, nor keep silence from me; but in the cry of my blood, do thou, the Word, cry from the earth; and in the cry of my soul, cry from the belly of hell as from the belly of a whale. Do not keep silence from this twofold cry until thou raisest me and, by the glory of the resurrection, makest most plainly known that I shall not be made like those who go down into the pit, but rather shall ascend into heaven, never thereafter to be silent, as this world lying in wickedness desires.

For of this world are those who say to my disciples: “We strictly commanded you not to speak in this name, and behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching” (Acts 5:28). Is your envy, O Jews, so tormenting you because the incarnate Word, whose fleshly mouth you thought had been shut by death, sounds forth in Jerusalem through the mouths of the Apostles? Wait a little: you shall soon see what will torment you still more, when “their sound shall go forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Rom. 10:18). You are to be provoked to jealousy and cast down, so that his blood, which you invoked upon yourselves and your children, saying, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25), may cry from the earth—that is, from the holy Church—against you, imitators of Cain the fratricide, until the end of the age.

Nor shall that cry ever admit silence, until complete judgment is passed upon you and all like you, all the wicked wasting away in fraternal hatred. In that judgment it shall appear that Christ, Son of David and likewise Son of God, altogether like the eternal Father, was falsely made by you like those who go down into the pit, when you numbered him with the wicked by such craft, lest his teaching rather than that of a wicked man should be considered authoritative. Thus you devised among yourselves, saying: “When shall he die, and his name perish?” (Ps. 40:6). For that he should die while the good fame of his name remained was too little for you; therefore he was numbered with the wicked, so that his name and reputation might perish.

You have many counterparts among the imitators of your wickedness, who wish and endeavour to close the mouths of the righteous by contriving and spreading many reproaches and accusations against the defenders of truth, so that either they may be silent, or, when they speak, possess no authority. O Jews, you and your followers are driven by vain madness in thinking it possible that the eternal Word should fall silent, or that he should lose his name to whom has been given “the name which is above every name” (Phil. 2:9). Though the mouth of his flesh was silent for an hour in the tomb, nevertheless the prayer he offered in his passion and agony was heard, when he, a mortal man, said of the Word dwelling within him: “My God, be not silent toward me; lest at any time thou keep silence from me, and I be made like those who go down into the pit.”

Indeed, such is the power of this prayer that the Word of God is sounding not only in himself eternally but also perpetually in his instruments—that is, in chosen human beings. And not only God the Man himself, but also his members are found unlike those who go down into the pit. For it is manifest that he himself has ascended to heaven, indeed above the heavens of heavens [Col. 1219D], and draws all his members to himself, according as he himself said: “And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). Again: “Father, I will that where I am, there also my servant may be” (John 17:24).

Let us now return to his prayer, in which, after invoking the Father and the Word united to him, human nature in Christ also invokes the Holy Spirit, saying: “Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication, while I pray to thee, while I lift up my hands toward thy holy temple.” I, the true David, praying to my Father, said: “To thee, O Lord, will I cry.” Praying also to the Godhead of the eternal Word implanted and united in me, I said: “My God, be not silent toward me; lest at any time thou keep silence from me, and I be made like those who go down into the pit.”

Now, so that my threefold prayer may render the whole Trinity propitious and reconciled to human nature, I say to the Holy Spirit: “Hear, O Lord, Holy Spirit, the voice of my supplication, while I pray to thee”—that is, while I pray to the Father to obtain thee, not for myself, who always possess thee, because thou restest eternally in me. For I am the flower sprung from the rod of Jesse, upon whom thou restest with everlasting rest, Spirit of the Lord, who until now hast found no secure resting-place in the whole forest of the human race.

I pray not, I say, to obtain thee for myself, but for my own, for whom thou as Paraclete art necessary for the remission of sins and the acquisition of virtues. Neither of these is necessary for me, since I committed no sin, nor was deceit found in my mouth, for which forgiveness might be necessary. And since I am not so much a virtuous man as I am to be called the very power of God, to which power no further power can be added for its increase. For when the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin Mother and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, then I, the new man, was so conceived that I derived nature from Adam but not guilt; and, clothed with strength and girded with the power of divinity, I can free from sins and adorn with virtues those who believe in me and confess me as Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24).

Accordingly, not for my own sake but for my people’s sake I say to thee, Holy Spirit: “Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication,” by freeing my own from sins and punishments. While I pray to thee for virtues and other goods to be obtained, not for myself but for my own, hear me praying and entreating for my own.

And that the power of action may make the voice of my entreaty or prayer audible, I perform a work of great obedience, great humility, patience, and charity, while I lift up my hands on the cross. Thus the sin of Adam, stretching forth his hands to eat the fruit of the forbidden tree, shall be expiated, while I, the new Adam, a strong man making satisfaction for the old man, decrepit and weak, lift up my hands. Natural law permits this: a strong son may fight a duel for his decrepit and infirm father. And I, according to the justice of this law, fight manfully against the prince of death for the human race growing weak, whose son I am—for I am the Son of Man—while I lift up my hands on the cross [Col. 1220D].

Toward what do I lift them? Toward thy holy temple. O whole holy Trinity!

For principally the temple of my body is the temple of the whole Trinity, in which “all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily.” For I am in the Father and the Father is in me (John 14:10–11), and in both is one Spirit, one charity, one goodness, one will. For I am the eternal wisdom of God, in whom eternal and paternal omnipotence is present together with loving-kindness, which is the Spirit of God. Therefore the temple of my body is the temple of the whole Trinity: in this temple whoever sees me sees also my Father (John 14:9), and likewise the Holy Spirit.

And although in a certain sense I, Wisdom, have specially built for myself this house or temple not made with hands, since I alone, the wisdom of God, am incarnate, not the Father or the Holy Spirit, nevertheless, since eternal power and eternal goodness—that is, the Father and the Holy Spirit—are believed consubstantial with me, eternal Wisdom, the temple of my body, which I, Wisdom, I, the Word, I, the Son, inhabit through assumption in the Incarnation, is also inhabited by the Father and the Holy Spirit through the fullness of their and my divinity: a divinity which embraces, contains, governs, and sustains every creature, and yet bodily inhabits the temple of my body. This does not mean that the eternal Trinity and threefold Godhead is bodily, but that I, Wisdom, one person in the Trinity, am embodied or incarnate—not changed into flesh, but united to flesh [Col. 1221B].

Accordingly, while I lift up my hands toward thy holy temple, O eternal Trinity, I, one of the number of three who are one (John 5:7), I, I say, am both temple, priest of the temple, sacrifice, God, maker, and author of the temple. I am the temple, outside of which no sacrifice is acceptable; I am the priest; I am the everlasting sacrifice through which alone remission of sins is made. I am God, to whom alone, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, the evening sacrifice ought to be offered, so that the temple in which sacrifice is made may be destroyed.

Therefore I now pray and lift up my hands not only concerning the temple already built, but this my prayer also looks toward the temple to be rebuilt anew, while I lift up my hands toward thy holy temple: that is, that this my body, raised from death, may henceforth be a living temple never to be dissolved by any death. Let it be holy, sanctified by that consecration concerning which, after mentioning my own, I say: “And for them I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth” (John 17:19). Let it also be thine, according as I say to thee, Father: “All mine are thine, and thine are mine”; or rather, according to the manner in which thou sayest to me: “Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee” (Ps. 2:7). Again, in the Gospel thou sayest of me: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

For thou callest me thy Son, and I call thee my Father, in such a way that this possessive pronoun is altogether foreign to all adopted sons. I too distinguish them from myself, thy only-begotten Son, saying: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17). I do not say, “I ascend to our Father,” because I alone am thy only-begotten consubstantial Son, which cannot fittingly be said of other sons. Nor do I say, “our God,” but carefully distinguish, saying, “my God and your God.”

Thus thou art God of my own—namely, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, or God of Israel—so that it is their great and full joy that after the labours of their good contests thou wilt give thyself to them as the reward of blessedness, to whom thou hadst first given thyself as help in their labour. But thou art my God because I am thy Son as man, consubstantial with thee according to my divinity, just as I am consubstantial with the Virgin Mother according to my humanity [Col. 1222A]. I am thine in such a manner that thou art in me and I in thee. For thou and I are one God. Neither art thou found outside me, thy temple, thy Son, thy sanctuary, “which thy hands have established” (Exod. 15:17); nor am I found outside thee, my Father. The Jews seek thee outside me, and therefore do not find thee. The Arians separate me from thee, and therefore find neither me nor thee.

But, benevolent reader, are you willing to allow a small digression by which it may be shown to you that in the temple which is Christ the whole Trinity dwells—that is, eternal power, eternal wisdom, eternal goodness? By these three names we have already indicated the eternal Trinity: not because the Father alone is power, the Son alone wisdom, or the Holy Spirit alone loving-kindness or goodness; but because, although each of the three is substantially and equally powerful, wise, and good, this distinction is nevertheless observed among the three. Thus in the Catholic faith we confess the Father alone as omnipotent, although it is equally established that the Son and Holy Spirit are omnipotent, and although we know that there are not three omnipotent beings but one omnipotent God in three persons.

We confess, I think, that we believe in God the Father Almighty in order that a human thought may not enter in, imagining the eternal Father weakened by excessive old age because he is said in Daniel to appear as the Ancient of Days with a grey and aged head (Dan. 7:9). But lest the Son of Man, who is there said to have come to the Ancient of Days, should be thought, on account of his youth, to possess less wisdom than his ancient Father, he is rightly called Wisdom, although the Father and the Holy Spirit are no less Wisdom. Human thought, moreover, might imagine the Holy Spirit as excessively austere, since austerity is customarily feared even in spiritual persons. Therefore, lest God’s Spirit be thought austere, he is called gracious.

And in these three—eternal power, eternal wisdom, and eternal loving-kindness—the whole holy Trinity is understood, or, if it cannot be understood, is soundly believed. It dwells in Christ as in its temple not made with hands, so that there is no confusion or division of the three. For the Father loves the Son not outside himself but in himself. Who indeed does not love within himself his own wisdom, which he sees and possesses in himself? Similarly, the Son loves the Father in himself, because he sees himself powerful and wise in the all-powerful Father. The love by which Father and Son mutually love one another is rightly understood to be the Holy Spirit.

Hear whether the voice of the Father agrees with what we are saying: “This,” he says, “is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). He did not say separately, “I am pleased with myself”; nor did he say separately, “I am pleased with him”; nor indeed did he say jointly, “I am pleased with myself and I am pleased with him.” Rather, he said: “I am pleased with myself in him.” That is: what is pleasing to me about myself is in him; it is not outside him. He is what I am, because I am nothing other than what he is; I cannot be pleasing to myself outside him. Therefore, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

Whatever pleases me pleases in him and through him. For he is the wisdom through which I made all things; in him I eternally arranged whatever I made in time. And I love each of my works all the more as I see it more perfectly conform to its first ordering. Do not think that he is mediator only in the reconciliation of humankind, since through him the condition of all creatures also becomes commendable and pleasing to my sight. In him I love all my works that I make, and I cannot fail to love what I see to be like him whom I love. He alone offends me who withdraws from his likeness.

[Col. 1223B] Therefore, if you wish to please me, be like him; hear him; and if perhaps by acting wickedly you have withdrawn from his likeness, return by imitating him. In him command is given, and in him counsel is given: command, that you may remain steadfast; counsel, that you may return. Would that you had kept the command! But since you have transgressed it, at least hear the counsel. Hear him. The Angel of Great Counsel is sent to you, that he who was given to those created for glory may come to those lost for healing. Hear him. He is Creator; he is Redeemer; he, God, created you with me, he who came among you as man alone. Hear him. He is the form; he is the medicine; he is the example; he is the remedy: hear him.

It would have been happier always to have retained his likeness; but now it will be no less glorious to return to his imitation. Hear him. Recognize, O man, in him the Father’s omnipotence by which you were made from nothing; venerate in him the wisdom of the Word, through whom you were made and according to whose image you were formed as rational. In him, your one Savior, worship the whole Trinity. Worship power with filial and chaste fear. Worship wisdom by a chaste pursuit of truth and a vigorous rejection of falsehood. Worship loving-kindness by voluntary and ready imitation. For just as divine loving-kindness made and makes all things for usefulness, so “to each is given the Spirit for usefulness” (1 Cor. 12:7).

Do not be insolent and proud, lest you offend Christ’s power. Do not be foolish, lest you offend his wisdom. Do not be malicious or useless, lest you offend his goodness. Be a humble, prudent, and kindly worshipper of him, and thus you are not called a Christian by Christ unto your condemnation. Hear him, O Christians, teaching you the worship of the Trinity. For that you may be humble, subject to the Most High Father, and that none of you may say in his heart, “I will be like the Most High,” hear him saying: “Learn of me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). That you may be prudent in honour of the divine wisdom that enlightens you, and kindly through imitation of his goodness, hear him saying: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16).

In your humility you shall be worshippers of the Most High Father, to whom the proud angel refused to submit, saying in his heart: “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14). In serpentine prudence you shall be worshippers of the Son, who, as the serpent was lifted up in the wilderness, was likewise lifted up upon the wood, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life (John 3:16). In dovelike simplicity you shall be worshippers of the Holy Spirit, who appeared in the form of a dove where the Father’s voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.”

Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Father’s voice cries from heaven concerning Christ: “Hear him.” “No one has ever seen God, but the Only-Begotten who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him” (John 1:18): hear him. Hear him instructing you through the manifest works and words which he began “to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1), from the baptism of John until the day when, after giving commands through the Holy Spirit to the Apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up. Hear him teaching you through the sending forth of the Holy Spirit, by whom the Apostles, set aflame, spoke in diverse tongues the mighty works of God. Hear him speaking to you in the holy Gospel, in each of his Apostles. “Do you seek a proof of Christ who speaks in me?” says one of the Apostles (2 Cor. 13:3). Truth speaks every word of truth. Even in his enemies speaking truth, Christ the Truth speaks: hear him.

Through everything that is truly truth, Christ discloses himself, just as artistic ingenuity discloses itself through a wonderful work. “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat; therefore do what they say, but do not do what they do,” says Christ (Matt. 23:2–3). Hear him. He is truth; he is the door of truth; he is the doorkeeper; he opens himself, and no one closes: hear him.

O man, why do you plead your ignorance? Behold, your very nature rebukes you; it convicts you. You know what you are, whence you come, what maker you have, what mediator you need, and do you still shamelessly cry out in defending yourself against God? You know that you are evil, and that you were not made evil by a good craftsman; and yet you cease and do not cry to him who made you, that he may come and restore you—who created, that he may redeem? Do not doubt his power: see how great his works are. Do not doubt his wisdom: see how beautiful his works are. Do not doubt his goodwill: see how his works serve for your benefit.

Therefore in his work he shows you how much he can accomplish in your redemption. The same work shows you what a fearful judge you may expect if you refuse to have a Redeemer. No one can resist him, because he is omnipotent. No one can deceive him, because he is most wise. No one can corrupt him, because he is good to all. No one can avoid him, because he is everywhere. No one can endure him when angry, because he is eternal. No one can bend him, because he is unchangeable.

If therefore we do not wish to experience such a judge, let us love him who prays for us and says:

> To thee, O Lord, will I cry, O my God; be not silent toward me; lest, if thou keep silence from me, I be made like those who go down into the pit. Hear the voice of my supplication, while I pray to thee, while I lift up my hands toward thy holy temple.

For I lift up my hands on the cross not for my own guilt, but for others: namely, that they may become thy holy temple, to be built together and incorporated with me, who am thy holy temple. To this end I lift up my hands toward thy holy temple: that the whole Church together, firmly built and well founded upon me, the Rock, may be thy holy temple. Let each particular Church also—for example, the Roman, Antiochene, Jerusalemite, or any other whatever which remains in the Catholic faith—be thy holy temple; and let it not become a den of robbers, but be called the house of God, having this title written upon its threshold: “This place is terrible; this is the house of God and the gate of heaven, and it shall be called the court of God” (Gen. 28:17). Again: “O how fearful is this place! Truly, this is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven.”

I also lift up my hands on the cross to this end: that each individual Catholic, signed with my cross and, with all the saints, comprehending what is the breadth, length, height, and depth of that cross, may be thy holy temple—broad, long, lofty, and deep: broad through charity; long through the long-suffering of faith; high through the elevation of hope; deep through the profound fear of divine judgments, which makes a person righteous and God-fearing.

Finally, I lift up my hands to this end not in the temple made with hands, polluted by the crimes of the Jews, but outside the gate under the open sky: that my cross may be the altar not of one Jerusalemite temple but of the whole world; and that the world itself, in which, while idolatry prevailed, sacrifices were offered to demons, may henceforth be a temple, not an idol.

Let it be a temple in which children may praise the name of the Lord from the rising of the sun to its setting. Let it be a temple in which, once the defilements of idols have been cast aside, a pure offering may be offered—not to many gods, of whom it is said, “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. 95:5), but to the one God. Let it be a temple adorned by divine power through the varied forms of things, as through many pictures and sculptures; illumined by the grace of divine loving-kindness through “every good gift and every perfect gift” descending from above from the Father of lights (Jas. 1:16), so that the earth may rejoice, irradiated by such splendors, and, enlightened by the brightness of the eternal King, may perceive that it has lost the darkness of the whole world.

Let Mother Church also rejoice, adorned with the splendors of so great a light. [Note: [Col. 1225D] “Let Mother Church rejoice, adorned with the splendors of so great a light”: in the blessing of the Paschal candle.] Let the elect shine everywhere throughout the whole world, so that the terrified princes of darkness may flee into the abyss—now individually and in particular instances, but universally at the universal judgment—when “the righteous shall begin to shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father,” when “those who are learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many unto righteousness, as stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. 12:3). Then the eternal light, the blessed Trinity and the supreme Unity, which is now seen “as through a mirror and in an enigma,” shall be seen openly [Col. 1226A].

Before the altar of the cross was raised in the temple of this world, there were most dense darknesses, because they worshipped and served creatures rather than the Creator—even those who were thought wiser in this world. For pagan philosophers praised Jupiter for the great structure of heaven; for the ordering of the seasons they praised Saturn; to calm the stormy sea they prayed to Neptune; for abundance of crops they offered sacrifice to Ceres. When wine, created by God, made human hearts glad, they praised not God, the Creator of wine, but some vintner, Bacchus. Orators, warriors, boxers, physicians [Col. 1226B], hunters, and fornicators worshipped and served Mercury, Mars, Hercules, Asclepius [Aesculapius], Diana, Venus, or Beelphegor respectively. By these defilements of idolatry they even polluted your holy temple, Lord, which was in Jerusalem, so that there was not even one temple in the whole world in which sacrifice was offered to you, the true God, in purity.

But I, Christ, the true high priest, now lift up my hands on the cross toward your holy temple—that is, toward this end: that this world, cleansed of the defilements of idols, may become your holy temple. Now true religion is growing everywhere; hereafter there will follow so great a purification of the world through fire that in the new heaven and new earth divine brightness may shine, and the whole fabric of the world may be holy and clean, like [Col. 1226C] your holy temple, into which nothing defiled shall ever again enter. When the unclean have been expelled from the world, then purity alone shall reign in the world; and in the whole world thus renewed, as in a rebuilt temple, the Threefold Godhead will shine forth in such a way that there will be no rebellion against God’s reigning power, no contradiction of his reigning wisdom, and no evil appearing to oppose his reigning goodness.

But now, before this universal cleansing of the temple—that is, of the whole Church—this much will be accomplished by my lifting up my hands toward your holy temple: the world itself will become your holy temple. In it, although your power finds rebellion, your wisdom contradiction, and impiety affronts your goodness, nevertheless your mighty and gracious wisdom will overcome malice, “reaching mightily from end to end and [Col. 1226D] ordering all things sweetly,” so that the sin of idolatry, or of any other wickedness, may not reign in the mortal body of those who throughout the world become your holy temple through this sacrifice of mine, which I now offer and which I institute for my own to offer, saying to them: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19).

Therefore let those to whom I said, “Do this,” do it. I said this to my disciples, and in them to their Catholic faithful followers: let them do it, and no others. For if others, remaining in schism or any heresy, presume to do this, they shall perish with Nadab and Abihu when they offered strange fire, or [Col. 1227A] with the two hundred and fifty men who, in Korah’s rebellion against Moses and Aaron, burned incense—unless they repent and observe the rite of sacrifice lawfully instituted through me and mine.

Catholic believers observe this rite; and, with such purity as they can, offer the sacrifice of my body and blood. When they do this, not to acquire earthly profit but in remembrance of me, I sacrifice myself in them and through them; through them and in them I bless and sanctify the people; in them and through them I lift up my hands toward your holy temple. Even if those who immolate me on the holy altar are such as those executioners who, by an office given them from above, slaughter me on the altar of the cross, though they themselves eat and drink judgment upon themselves [Col. 1227B], I nevertheless do not cease, through their ministry, to sanctify my people with that sanctification which the power of the sacrifice confers, not the minister’s merit.

But if they have been deprived of office by a lawful prohibition, as manifest simoniacs and manifest incestuous persons, I do not lift up my hands toward your holy temple through them; for all sacrifice which they offer against the prohibition is defiled and wholly alien from me—especially if that prohibition has been promulgated under excommunication or anathema, as was clearly demonstrated above in another psalm concerning the prohibition imposed on simoniacs and Nicolaitans. The forerunner of such persons is Judas, that most wicked [Col. 1227C] merchant, who hands me over to the scribes, Pharisees, and chief priests. They too are robbers, who had made my house a den of robbers. Veiling their robbery in a certain fashion, they say, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death,” while handing me over to Pilate the governor, so that, while he judges me, they may appear innocent, although they are the worst of robbers (John 18:31). They hand me over to be numbered with the wicked and crucified among robbers, so that my name may be destroyed. But you, Lord God the Father, do not spare me, your own Son, but hand me over for the deliverance of sinners.

**VERSE 3.** “Do not hand me over [Note: [Col. 1227D] Vulgate: “Draw me.”] with sinners.”

Do not hand me over with the intention for which they hand me over. And because those who hand me over think to destroy me: do not destroy me [Col. 1227D] with those who work iniquity. Do not these work iniquity who speak peace with their neighbour while evils are in their hearts? By a kiss, which is a sign of peace, they accomplish murder, even while they said to me: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth.” Thus speaking peace with their mouths, they devised evils in their hearts against me, who was their neighbour: born from their own stock, and who did not pass by as the priest and Levite did, but, as a true neighbour moved by compassion, drew near in order to show mercy to the one wounded by robbers (Luke 10:31–32).

But evils were in their hearts because their intentions contained deliberate hatred. “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin. But now they have no excuse for their sins. If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would have no sin. But now they have both seen and hated me,” the truth, “and my Father” (John 15:22, 24): they hated me, the truthful one reproving their sins, and the Father who begot me, who am truth, the Son of the truthful Father. As I hear, I judge truthfully, calling and judging good good and evil evil—not like false and deceptive teachers, who call or judge good evil or evil good. Therefore, once truth had become known through me, it was fitting that they should assent to truth and repent of the evils reproved by me.

[Col. 1228B] And they would indeed do this if they had evils only in their hands or deeds, and not in their hearts—that is, in their intentions. Matthew and Zacchaeus the tax collectors, Mary Magdalene, and the Canaanite woman did not have evils in their hearts, although they had had them in their deeds. Once they heard the truth, they promptly repented and loved the truth that reproved them. For example, when the Canaanite woman heard herself compared to dogs because of the error of paganism, she gratefully accepted the truth she heard. Thus she deserved to hear: “O woman, great is your faith.” But evils are in the hearts of those who choose rather to hate than to hear truth speaking of their sins—like these people, who sin not through ignorance but, wasting away in hatred of the good, [Col. 1228C] love the evils in their hearts because the evils already committed, or yet to be committed, please them inwardly. They are so far from true repentance, by which committed evils are mourned and are not again committed so as to require mourning, that, on the contrary, they rejoice in utterly evil deeds already perpetrated and are glad when they have done evil.

In such joy they say to me: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days!” (Matthew 27:40). In such joy both they and their followers will say to my servants: “Where is their God?” Since they rejoice that I do not appear, as it were, from the tomb—while I allow my servants to be distressed by the prosperity of Mammon’s servants—these servants of Mammon, visibly displaying their master Mammon, insult my servants afflicted and distressed in this world, saying: “Where is their God?” Therefore, because they are evil and evils are in their hearts, I, agreeing with your justice, God the Father, say:

**VERSE 4.** “Give them according to their works,” which they have done, “and according to the wickedness of their devices,” which they bear in their hearts. I say “according to their works” and “according to their wickedness,” because I, who am truth, love true justice even in punishments. It is justice that their manifest evil works receive manifest vengeance, so that others may have fear; and that secret wickedness be punished by a secret penalty.

A fitting penalty according to their works will be this: because they crucify me, as though for the sake of place and nation, through the ministers of impious Rome, the Romans will come and take away both their place and nation, leaving not one stone upon another that shall not be destroyed. Then, because of and according to their outward and manifest works, the sword will openly devastate them outwardly; and inward terror will torment their conscience according to the inward wickedness of their devices [Col. 1229A]. For they did not truly fear; rather, trembling there where no fear was, indeed pretending alarm, they said: “If we let him go on thus, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11:48). They devised this fear, scheming craftily so that the simple people, hearing it, might consent to their wickedness against me. Therefore, righteous Father, give them according to their works and according to the wickedness of their devices.

And indeed, though their intention is evil, their action is and will be good for many. Therefore reward them not according to the good outcome, but according to the works of their hands; in recompensing their works, weigh not the good that has resulted, but the evil which they themselves intended. Although salvation has come to others from their deed, nevertheless repay them according to their own hand. For in my sufferings their work is one thing, the divine work another. Their work consists in what they wickedly intend when they say in their heart concerning me: “When will he die, and his name perish?” (Psalm 40:6). But the divine work [Col. 1229C] is that my name will grow from that very event through which they thought it would be destroyed. Their work is that I, the grain of wheat, fall into the earth through their murderous hands, having tasted death; but the divine work is that, rising from the dead, I bear much fruit.

Therefore you, who judge justly and distinguish their most wicked work from my good work—or yours—repay them their recompense. I repay them good for evil, but they repaid me evil for good (Psalm 34:12). Therefore you, who judge justly, repay them their recompense, so that by their own deceit, through which they think to deceive, they may themselves be deceived and caught in their own craftiness, according to the works of their hands. I call the evil deeds committed against me “the works of their hands” because they deliberately carried through what they had begun [Col. 1229D], lest they excuse themselves by means of the Gentile soldiers who crucify me, and wish to seem innocent of the murder committed against me. Yet they are the authors of the crime done through the soldiers, and in that deed repay evil for good to me, the author of all human salvation. Therefore you, righteous Judge, repay them their recompense.

**VERSE 5.** “For they have not understood the works of the Lord.” Granted that, while they do evil, a work useful for human salvation results from their evil works through the Lord’s action: although they did not intend to do it, they could at least have understood and loved it once done and attested by the Apostles’ preaching. For Peter says: “Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree, God has exalted at his right hand as Leader and Saviour, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins” (Acts 5:30–31). And: “Now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. But what God foretold through the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ should suffer, he has thus fulfilled. Repent therefore, and turn, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3:17 ff.).

When Peter said this and proclaimed that good works of the Lord had resulted from the evil works of the Jews, some of them understood the Lord’s good works, repented of their own evil deeds, and through the Lord’s good works were delivered from their evil deeds. But those who loved their own evil works did not understand the Lord’s good works, loving darkness rather than light. From this it is clear that they persisted obstinately in the evil works which they obstinately loved [Col. 1230B], and therefore hated the light. “For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved” (John 3:20). For “everything reproved by the light is made manifest” (Ephesians 5:13).

I do not say, “Everyone who has done evil hates the light,” because many—from the number of Jews defiled by Christ’s blood, as well as from the numerous multitude of Gentiles who worshipped idols or performed the pleasures of the flesh—did evil; yet, reproved for their evils by the light of truth, they loved that light itself, which is truth, and recognized and hated their evils when they had been reproved by the light. Nor again do I say, “Everyone who does evil hates the light”; but I say that everyone who does evilly hates the light and [Col. 1230C] does not come to the light. For such a person does not wish to be reproved by the light.

The distinction of the words must be carefully noted. Every person who acts wickedly does evil things, but not conversely: not everyone who does evil things acts wickedly. For the Lord himself, who does nothing wickedly, does many things which are evil to many people. Thus it is written: “I am the Lord, making good things and creating evils, making light and creating darkness, making peace and creating war” (Isaiah 45:7). Likewise good people do many things which are evil to evil persons; yet they themselves do not act wickedly, when they do what they do with a good intention, even if what they do is evil to someone. For if the eye of intention is single, the whole body of action will be full of light (Matthew 6:22).

Mary Magdalene did a good work well in anointing Christ with a good intention [Col. 1230D] and holy devotion. But that good work was evil to the man who said: “Why this waste?” (Matthew 26:8).

Likewise the Jews did an evil work wickedly in crucifying Christ with malicious intention. Yet that evil deed is good to believers, and it would become good even to them if the malice by which they acted wickedly came to an end. For because malice remains in unrepentant evildoers, it is not said, “Everyone who does evil things,” but “everyone who acts wickedly hates the light.” Such is the power of intention that, when it is changed, it makes good for you the work which was previously evil for you. Likewise, if you gave alms, fasted, or prayed with the intention of gaining eternal life, but then, with intention altered and changed, seek human glory from it, a good work becomes evil for you [Col. 1231A]. If, therefore, the light of a good work is darkened by an evil intention and becomes darkness, how great will that darkness be when evil people perform an evil work with an evil intention? I do not say “they did,” in the past tense, but “they do,” in the present tense, because, through the evil intention persisting in their malice, the evil work which is past in act remains present in guilt.

Such was the sin of the Jews who killed Christ with malicious intention and rejected his teaching. Like evil tenants, they killed the heir so that they themselves might possess his inheritance, claiming for themselves the authority to teach and judge. From this authority, promised to them by God under the law, they ought, like good cultivators, to have produced this fruit: when truth preached, they should judge good to be good and evil to be evil. But they judged evil good and good evil so obstinately that they asked for the robber Barabbas to be released as good, and killed Jesus as evil [Col. 1231B].

After the coming of the Holy Spirit, who convicts the world concerning sin and righteousness through the holy Apostles, some Jews repented of this crime; others persisted in their malice and loved their evil work, but were unwilling either to understand or to love the good work of God resulting from it.

Of these and their followers the psalm now says: “Give them according to the works of their hands; repay them their recompense, because they have not understood [Col. 1231C] the works of the Lord.” Even when wonderful works were done among and in them—dead persons raised, lepers cleansed, lame persons healed, blind persons given sight, and many other miracles performed—they did not understand the works of the Lord bearing witness to Christ, as he himself said: “The Father remaining in me, he does the works” (John 14:10). Again: “The works which I do in my Father’s name bear witness concerning me” (John 10:25). Again: “If I had not done among them the works which no one else did, they would have no sin” (John 15:24). Again: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5:17). Again: “If you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works, that you may know and believe that I am in my Father and the Father is in me” (John [Col. 1231D] 10:38).

But they did not understand God’s works. They did not, I say, understand what they ought and could have understood through the reason given to them, if they had been willing to read and observe God’s works as truly significant letters. “For his invisible things, understood through the things that have been made, are clearly seen from the creation of the world, even his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse” (Romans 1:20): all who were unwilling, through visible works, to understand those invisible things of God which were made intelligible by these visible things themselves.

The heavens indicated him as their Lord when they declared his glory through the star seen and understood by the Magi in the east. The earth indicated itself to be his work when, at his death or resurrection, it trembled. He commanded the winds and sea as their Lord and Creator, and they obeyed him as their maker. No one else did such works by commanding; Moses and Elijah, for example, worked wonders in the elements of the world by praying, not commanding. So too did many others. But this one commanded the winds and sea as Lord, and they obeyed him as their Lord. Therefore his works were works of the Lord: such works, and done in such a manner, as his servants, however holy, cannot do and could not do [Col. 1232A]. None of them works miracles by his own power; rather, when invoked by prayer, he who alone does great wonders works them through them.

“But,” you say, “Jesus himself prayed when he raised Lazarus.” True; but when you noticed this, you should also have observed that while praying he says: “Father, I thank you because you always hear me. I knew that you always hear me; but I said it because of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me” (John 11:41–42). If he gave thanks or prayed because of the people standing around, he did not do this for himself. He prayed and gave thanks not from need of his own, but out of love for us: to teach us that the Father’s person is one and his own another; and that, when we contemplate doing great things, we should first offer prayers through him to the Father, since we know that he himself prayed, though he could, if he wished, have done great things without prayer, by the command of his power alone—as he calmed sea and winds by command alone.

By command alone he cleansed leprosy, saying: “I will; be cleansed” (Matthew 8:3). And he commanded that same Lazarus [Col. 1232C] to come out of the tomb, saying: “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11:43); likewise, to the disciples fishing, he said: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find” (John 21:6). What shall I say of command? This Lord who is called Jesus also performed wonders by silent gesture alone. For when, at the wedding, he ordered water to be drawn for wine, nature, sensing his silent gesture, presented water made into wine. Such are the works of the Lord: such as no one else did, and in a manner no one else did or could do. From these works he could be known as Lord of creatures. But they did not understand the works of the Lord, for they were most wicked servants; and such a servant does not know what his lord does (John 15:15).

[Col. 1232D] “And in the works of his hands.” To understand the works and to understand in the works are different things. One understands the Lord’s works who understands that the Lord performs these things, and who understands and loves the Lord working through those works. But one understands in the works of his hands who understands the inward and mystical causes of the works. For example, through the clay made from the spittle of the Lord’s mouth and dust of the earth is understood the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation: wisdom proceeding from the mouth of the Most High united to itself the dusty nature of the human race, in order to heal the blindness of humankind through faith in and love for the Lord’s incarnation.

With this clay the inward eyes of catechumens are most sweetly anointed, and thus they are sent to the pool of Siloam—that is, to baptism. Likewise, through the woman healed from a flow of blood by touching [Col. 1233A] the hem is signified the Church from the Gentiles, healed from the defilements of idolatry through the preacher of the Lord’s incarnation, the apostle Paul. He calls himself, as it were, the hem, the least of the Apostles, since the Apostles themselves are like the Lord’s garment; and the apostle Paul considers himself a small hem hanging from that garment when he says: “For I am the least of the Apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle” (1 Corinthians 15:9).

Whoever understands thus mystically understands not only the Lord’s works, but also understands in the Lord’s works—that is, in outward works, the inward works of the Lord, which are the works of his hands, because he applies himself to their accomplishment more diligently, as though with his own hands. For these visible and outward miracles, by which the garden of the Church is planted and watered, the Lord also does through the hands of ministers and servants; but those inward miracles by which growth is given he works only through himself, with his own hands. Thus the Apostle says: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Through those outward works holiness is sometimes made manifest; through these inward works holiness is begun, increased, and brought to perfection. These are the inward works of the Lord’s hands, which far exceed not only human but even angelic capacity and belong only to the cultivating Trinity. Those who killed me, Christ Jesus, the worker of such deeds, did not direct their understanding through visible works to these works of the Lord’s hands [Col. 1233C]; and, after killing me and after I had been raised from death, they persecuted the disciples who bore witness to and preached these works of mine.

Until the end of the age, both parties have their successors: both Jews who deny divine works and Apostles who preach and praise the same works; and the former persecute the latter because they are opposed to one another. Among those enemies and opponents of the Lord’s works—the first persecutors of the first Church—are numbered not only demons and malicious people, but also fleshly impulses, because these likewise oppose the works of the Lord. Therefore, God the righteous Judge, you will destroy them [Col. 1233D] and not build them up. If I said, “Destroy them and do not build them up,” I might seem to say this as a wish of one desiring and praying. But now I do not so much pray or wish as preach, declaring the punishment they deserve, and I say: “You will destroy them and not build them up.”

It is fitting and just, by the true judgment of truth, that because they destroyed the temple of my body by putting it to death, and did not believe that it could be rebuilt in three days, as I had foretold—indeed, so far as lay in their power, they discouraged belief in its rebuilding already accomplished, bribing the soldiers to lie that I had been secretly taken away by the disciples, lest anyone believe that the temple of my body had been rebuilt—so they themselves may be destroyed by Romans and demons laying waste their bodies and souls, in such a way that they shall never afterward be rebuilt, as they were once rebuilt after being destroyed by the Babylonians seventy years earlier.

It shall not be so for them now after the end of the Roman war: an appointed desolation will not allow them to be rebuilt for the practice of Judaism, lest perhaps, if they practise Judaism in the holy place at Jerusalem, the pure and undefiled religion of Christianity should be hindered. The remnant of them is to be converted, according to Isaiah’s prophecy; but those who remain hardened and are not converted will remain in destruction and desolation. For in this life they shall be “given into the hands of the sword” (Psalm 62:11), the Roman sword; and after this life they shall be portions of foxes—that is, of malicious spirits. Or they shall be given into the hands of the sword, cut off from the body, namely, of the patriarchs, and shall be portions of foxes—that is, of malicious [Col. 1234B] rulers, one of whom was Herod, of whom I said: “Go, tell that fox: for it is not possible that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke 13:32–33). Through such foxes you will destroy them, because through Roman rulers they shall be led captive among all nations and shall never again recover city and temple for the exercise of Judaism or of their customary robbery, by which they made my house a den of robbers.

**VERSE 6.** “Blessed be the Lord, because he has heard the voice of my supplication.” After prayers, thanksgiving rightly follows, especially where the hearing is certain. And I, the only-begotten Son of God, know well that my Father always hears and answers me. Therefore, heard in my prayer—which, according to my humanity, I poured forth not from distrust but [Col. 1234C] from certain foreknowledge of future events—I both heard and answered along with the Father according to my divinity. Now therefore, as true man, I give thanks to true God the Father and say: “Blessed be the Lord, because he has heard the voice of my supplication.”

The difference between the blessing by which a human being blesses God in praise and that by which God blesses a human being in salvation has been discussed in another psalm. But because here the God-man, the Son of God, blesses the Father, this is a special blessing particularly suited to this David, mentioned in the psalm’s title. Thus the sense here is the same as in the Gospel, where this David says: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1). But I, the Son, know that I have been heard and that, as I prayed, I shall be glorified through the glory of the resurrection with such glory of divinity [Col. 1234D] that I shall not be made like those descending into the pit; rather, seen by the disciples in great glory, I shall ascend into heaven to reign eternally. My kingdom will be blessed, as was said from the mouth of infants and nursing children who perfectly praise me: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, and blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David” (Mark 11:9–10).

Thus glorified and blessed, I in turn glorify and bless God my Father, as I said elsewhere: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1). Behold, now heard and wholly certain of my glorification, I glorify and bless, magnify and praise the Father, saying: “Blessed be the Lord, because he has heard the voice of my supplication [Col. 1235A].” By this I know myself to have been heard by God my Father: because he himself is—

**VERSE 7.** “The Lord, my helper and my protector.” He is my helper in doing and completing good works, so that I may truly say to him: “I have glorified you upon earth; I have completed the work which you gave me to do” (John 17:4). For this he is my helper; and he himself is also my protector from all evils. Therefore “my heart hoped in him, and I was helped; and so my flesh blossomed again,” free from sin, though it withered in Adam through sin. Or, having first flowered in freedom from sin, it blossomed again—that is, flowered anew—in the Resurrection. Therefore, when fear of death has been consumed, those in whom I am will confess him; and therefore I will confess him, and this from my own will, not from fear under the law, but freely with the law.

**VERSE 8.** The Lord, of whom it has been said that he is my helper and protector, is also, against the devil, “the strength of his people,” who, trusting in him, does not display or boast of its own righteousness. After their conflict, he is “the protector of the salvations of his Christ”—that is, the salvations accomplished by Christ; in other words, after the conflict he will protect in immortality those made safe through Christ.

**VERSE 9.** “Save, Lord, the people” from the evils of the age—I mean your people, because all that is mine is yours—“and bless your inheritance,” that is, increase it in number and virtues; “and rule them” in temporal life, lest they turn aside to wickedness; “and lift them up above the whole age, forever,” in understanding of the Scriptures [Col. 1235C] and in deed, or above the desire for earthly things. Lift them up forever—that is, to seek and receive eternal things.

Otherwise: “Save your people, Lord, and bless your inheritance.” Although your people are themselves both your inheritance and mine, according to what you say to me elsewhere: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2:8), nevertheless “your people” may rightly be understood as the whole flock of those who say: “We are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Psalm 78:13). But those to whom you yourself will be an inheritance are, by a proper and special grace, your inheritance, as you say to Moses: “You shall give no inheritance to the sons of Levi, for I shall be their inheritance” (Deuteronomy 18:2).

The Apostles and apostolic men, followers of these, did not wish to have an inheritance on earth, so that they might be your inheritance and you theirs. According to this distinction between your people and your inheritance, two kinds of life are discerned at the beginning of the Church: one in which the weakness of the infirm is retained, and another in which the blessed strength of the stronger is perfected; one remaining in little Zoar, the other climbing to the higher places of the mountain; one redeeming daily sins through tears and alms, the other, by daily diligence in spiritual exercise, seeking eternal merits; one lower, the other higher. Those holding the lower way use earthly possessions; those pursuing the higher despise earthly things. The former are the Lord’s people; the latter, his inheritance. Of the former it is said: “A praiseworthy people, whom the Lord of hosts has blessed, saying: You are the work of my hands”; of the latter [Col. 1236A] it is said: “But Israel is my inheritance” (Isaiah 19:25). Therefore, God the Father, hear your Son in this: that you save your people.

“And bless your inheritance.” Save your people with full and everlasting salvation; bless and sanctify your inheritance, so that those who, because of you, have no inheritance on earth and are your inheritance may be blessed and sanctified with such a blessing as excludes every curse, and with such sanctification as, driving away every defilement, presents your own inheritance to you holy and blessed.

Concerning this people and this inheritance you formerly said to me: “Dwell in Jacob, and take inheritance in Israel” (Ecclesiasticus 24:13). Therefore Jacob, struggling in action, is your people, whom I ask to be saved; Israel, resting [Col. 1236B] in the vision of God, is your inheritance, whom I ask to be blessed. “And I took root in an honoured people” (ibid., 16), concerning whom I say: “Save your people”; and “in the portion of my God is his inheritance” (ibid.), concerning whom I say: “Bless your inheritance.”

You once blessed Noah’s sons, saying: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth; and let fear and dread of you be upon all animals of the earth, and upon all birds of heaven, with everything that moves upon the earth” (Genesis 9 ff.). Therefore, since I am the true Noah, who by the wood of the cross overcame the flood of overflowing sins, and from my side—as from the opened doorway in the side of the ark—have brought forth, through water and blood, persons reborn, some little and some great: save the little ones like clean animals come forth from the ark; bless the great [Col. 1236C], that they may increase in merit, multiply in number, and that the fear of their authority may be upon all living creatures and beasts of the earth—that is, upon all earthly human beings, whether brutish and senseless like animals of the earth, or mad and savage like beasts of the earth—so that by fear of them they may either be restrained from the evil they wish to do or governed so as to turn from evil and do good.

And may their fear and dread likewise be upon all birds of heaven, so that spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places may flee groaning and trembling, wounded by the arrows of prayers and terrified by the banner of the cross. With this banner these blessed sons of mine are marked and raised above all things that move upon the earth, so that they may preside over them by the authority of governance.

[Col. 1236D] But since these things too must be governed through them, you, King of all ages, rule them and lift them up forever. Rule them in holy actions, and lift them up in holy contemplation. Rule them, that they may turn from evil; lift them up, that they may do good. Rule them in the present life, and lift them up after this life forever. Rule them, that they may go; lift them up, that they may bear fruit, and that their fruit may remain forever. Thus rule them and lift them up forever, from the present life into eternal life. Behold how the risen one intercedes!

Glory to the Father, whom the Son prays to in this psalm. Glory to the Son, who prays, saying: “To you, O Lord, I shall cry.” Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that salvation and blessing which works on God’s people, where it is said: [Col. 1237A] “Save your people, O Lord, and bless your inheritance.”

When the Prophet heard this cry, he immediately cries out in the following twenty-eighth psalm: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord sons of rams,” etc. By saying this, he exhorts all the faithful together to offer themselves to God by imitating him. He admonishes the perfect, as rams, to persevere and increase; and the others, to advance swiftly, through good works, to the offering of the same sacrifice, even as sons of rams. [Col. 1238A] It bears this title: “A Psalm of David at the completion of the tabernacle.” It directs us to the history: for just as David, after receiving the ark that had been taken away by the Philistines, established a tabernacle for the Lord for prayer and sacrifice, so every believer, after receiving the catholic faith, ought to prepare himself as a tabernacle of sanctification, in which to offer God the sacrifice of praise: namely faith, hope, and love.

## PSALM XXVIII

[Col. 1237]

[Col. 1237B] VERSE 1. “Bring to the Lord,” etc. The title is:

**A PSALM OF DAVID AT THE COMPLETION OF THE TABERNACLE.**

We read in the books of Kings that, in the time of Eli the priest, the Philistines took the ark of the Lord from the place called the Stone of Help to Ashdod, and placed it beside the idol called Dagon (1 Kings 5). The next day they found Dagon lying prostrate before the ark of the Lord, and raised it up; and likewise the following day they found it prostrate and raised it again; and on the third occasion they found it again prostrate before the ark, with its head and the palms of its hands cut off. The ark was in the regions of the Philistines for seven months, and they were struck with a severe plague: mice swarmed in the land and ravaged them, and their protruding *extales*, that is, their buttocks, [Col. 1237C] became putrid. Struck by this plague, they finally returned the ark to Gibeah in the twentieth year; and, for their sin, they sent with the ark five golden hemorrhoids and the same number of golden mice, according to the number of their provinces. When David, after the death of Saul and his son Ish-bosheth, was reigning prosperously, he took the ark from Gibeah to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. After it had been there three months, David brought it to Jerusalem and placed it in its own place, in the midst of the tabernacle which David had stretched out for it, and offered burnt offerings (2 Kings 6).

Alluding, then, to this history, the Prophet deals rather with the tabernacle signified by it, which the Lord completed through sevenfold grace: namely, the Church, brought back [Col. 1237D] from the devil’s jurisdiction. For this psalm suits David the prophet, who speaks of the completion of the tabernacle—that is, in contemplation of the perfected Church, in which warfare is conducted against the devil in this age.

First, he admonishes concerning the sacrifices of those who make offerings. Secondly, he treats of the establishment of the tabernacle, where he enumerates the virtues of the Holy Spirit, at the words: “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters.” Thirdly, he shows what the Lord does for the established Church: how he strengthens it, advances it, and afterwards rewards it, at: “The Lord makes the flood to dwell.”

In the opening verses he makes clear his purpose, as he admonishes the faithful to offer themselves to such a perfecter, [Col. 1238B] saying: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord sons of rams.” But before we enter the text of the psalm concerning the completion of the tabernacle, it seems that something should first be said and investigated about the reason for building and completing the tabernacle.

For we read that a tabernacle was built for the Lord twice: once by Moses in the wilderness, and a second time by David on Mount Zion. But the earlier tabernacle, set up at Shiloh, the Lord rejected, as a figure of the Synagogue which was to be cast off and rejected. The later tabernacle, made by David from skins, is not said to have been rejected by God, although the great Temple subsequently succeeded it, which Solomon, David’s son, built and dedicated when he brought into it the ark of the Lord, for whose sake both tabernacles had been made. The reason for building both tabernacles and the Temple was the ark of the Lord, the ark of the covenant, in which were a golden vessel containing manna, Aaron’s rod that had budded, and the two tablets of the covenant.

This ark signified Christ, or Christ’s body assumed from the Virgin. In it was the golden vessel, that is, the most pure and most divine rational soul, containing manna—that is, the sweetness of divinity which angels live by tasting without satiety, and by which a human being also lives when he eats the bread of angels in the most holy mystery of the altar. This ark was placed in the former tabernacle built by Moses, when, according to the Law of Moses, faith in the Lord’s [Col. 1238D] Incarnation was observed among the Jewish people under the veil of the letter. But the Lord rejected this tabernacle when the Synagogue, rejecting the Lord, itself deserved to be rejected.
