For since the Jews, rejecting the Lord, said, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15), the Lord justly rejecting them, they were handed over into Caesar’s hand—that is, into the power of the Romans, to whom, as though wishing to please them, they crucified Christ as one contrary to Roman laws and as one forbidding tribute to be given to Caesar. Then, when the Romans devastated and carried the Jewish people into captivity, he himself, having been handed over by them into the hands of Roman soldiers, in turn delivered their strength into captivity and their beauty [Col. 1239A] into the enemy’s hands, and shut up his people under the sword (Psalm 77:61–62); and the ark of God was captured by the Philistines—that is, by the Romans themselves (1 Kings 4:11, 17).

For the Romans, who destroyed the Synagogue as though it were the tabernacle of Shiloh, and in this were ministers of God, also captured the ark of God by persecuting Christ and forbidding the faith of Christ to be preached by their decrees. Yet very many Romans and other gentiles were so willing to accept Christ’s worship that the worship of idols remained in this world alongside it; this was like setting the ark of the Lord beside Dagon in a temple. But Dagon fell before the ark of the Lord, because, once Christ’s faith had been received throughout the whole world, Dagon fell and the worship of idols perished. Behold, before the ark of the Lord [Col. 1239B] Dagon lies prostrate, its head and the palms of its hands cut off: because, while Christ’s worship flourished, idolatry perished, having no head—that is, no ruler as its defender—and no palms of hands, because every palm of victory serves Christ, not idols; and Christ himself triumphs everywhere, not only through faithful but also through unbelieving rulers.

The ark was captured in the Philistines’ territory as long as there was no peace or freedom for the worshippers and preachers of the Christian faith, while Roman and pagan rulers persecuted God’s Church. But the captors of the ark were struck with a severe plague when mice—that is, malignant and unclean spirits—ravaged them, and their protruding *extales* became putrid: their disgrace openly appearing, since [Col. 1239C] God handed them over to a reprobate mind to commit shameful sins contrary to natural decency (1 Kings 5). Struck with this plague, they finally let the ark go free, drawn by cows—that is, by preachers—in a new cart composed of the four wheels of the Gospels.

The fact that the Philistines themselves gave golden hemorrhoids and golden mice (1 Kings 5) for their sin signifies that many of the ungodly, after committing foul deeds and wickedness, have covered, or daily cover, their shameful acts by worthy and illustrious fruits of repentance. Of them it is said: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Psalm 31:1). From that time the ark of God was not found in Shiloh, whose tabernacle was destroyed. [Col. 1239D] For, once Christ’s faith has been received, there is no returning to Judaism; rather, through the true David a new tabernacle is made for the same ark, in which the ark itself is placed with such solemnity and joy as ought to be signified by the words of the psalm now under consideration and by David’s mystical deeds prefiguring that same solemnity.

For, when the tabernacle had been completed, King David assembled thirty thousand chosen men from all Israel; and he rose and went, with all the people who were with him, from the men of Judah, in order to bring up the ark of God, upon which the name of the Lord of hosts, who sits above it upon the Cherubim, had been invoked. And they set the ark of God upon a new cart, etc. (2 Kings 6:1–2). What was this festival—let us ask—of a prophet or of a king? [Col. 1240A] Rather, of both prophet and king. For the Spirit of the Lord, who was directed into him, made him a prophet before making him a king; and before allowing him to ascend the throne of the present Israelite kingdom, showed him the mysteries of the future Lord and of his Son, Christ the great King.

What, then, was that great solemnity of prophet and king in bringing up the ark of the Lord? They went, as is written more fully in Chronicles, to carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord from the house of Obed-edom with joy. And when the Lord had helped the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, seven bulls and seven rams were sacrificed. David was clothed in a linen ephod, and all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the Lord amid shouting, the sound of a trumpet, trumpets, cymbals, and clanging harps, [Col. 1240B] etc. (1 Chronicles 15:25 ff.).

Were these things done vainly, or in the absence of the holy Spirit of prophecy? If Elisha awakened the holy Spirit of prophecy in his breast at the playing of one psalmist, as it is written: “Now bring me a psalmist.” And while the psalmist was playing, the hand of the Lord came upon him, and he said: “Thus says the Lord: Make ditches in the bed of this torrent” (4 Kings 3:15 ff.); how much more should that same Spirit, who was also in him, be believed to have awakened amid such great rejoicing, such a sound of trumpets, and such a clatter of trumpets, cymbals, and harps—especially when the king himself, as though forgetful of royal dignity, played and danced with all his strength before the ark of the Lord, so much that he seemed contemptible to his wife Michal? Did that great king, that strong-handed king, [Col. 1240C] play and dance so because of youthful blood running riot—or rather because a humble heart was being broken by the great power of God’s Spirit? He was great and strong in proportion as he was small and contemptible in his own eyes.

Therefore, the fact that, once David’s kingdom over the people of Israel had been confirmed, the ark of the Lord’s covenant was brought up amid such rejoicing of the whole kingdom is a type of that for which the whole world rejoices today: namely, because, after the strong-handed and beloved king, Christ, had risen from the dead and, crowned with glory and honor, had been set over the works of his Father’s hands, the resurrection of that victorious king was immediately preached throughout the world. For, as is written more fully elsewhere, the wonderful ark—the ark containing within itself all the treasures of the whole Godhead—is the structure of the human body, which the Holy Spirit fashioned for the Son of God from the virginal womb; and that ark was its type.

For truly the name of the Lord of hosts, who sits over the Cherubim, was invoked upon this ark. Indeed, because of the fullness of knowledge and of the whole Godhead dwelling bodily in it, the ark itself is called Lord of hosts. Thus the people in Israel sang, and amid the whole multitude of Israel there was a song of praise; David too struck the harp with the singers, and the sound of the singers was heard throughout the whole world. For “there are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard. Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world,” [Col. 1241A] understood as saying: “He has set his tabernacle in the sun,” etc.

The heavens which declare the glory of God (Psalm 18:4), namely the Apostles, are, according to the mystery of the present passage, Asaph, Jeduthun, Heman, and Ethan—that is, “gathering,” “leaping over,” “robust,” and “strong” (1 Chronicles 15). They gather spiritual things, leap over carnal things, are robust in enduring evils, strong in doing good, and with every effort play the harp “for the eighth”: that is, amid every kind of mortification of the flesh, they bear witness to the resurrection, which is called the eighth.

According to the letter, they sang “for the eighth” because they began with the sixth psalm, which has this in its title. The Jews thought “for the eighth” meant for circumcision; we, however, understand it as that better circumcision by which we are to be renewed—namely, the resurrection of the flesh. [Col. 1241B] David stood in their midst, himself holding a psaltery, striking the harp, and leaping with all his strength. For he himself who said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), and, “Behold, I am with you until the end of the age” (Matthew 20:28), struck the breasts of the Apostles with his beautiful fingers—that is, with the gifts of the Holy Spirit—so that they would neither be silent nor fail. In a manner he leapt, that is, he performed through them wonders by which they were aided and their word was confirmed.

“And they placed the ark of God,” he says, “upon a new cart, and brought it from the house of Aminadab” (1 Chronicles 13:7). The new cart upon which this ark of the Lord’s covenant was borne is the new Gospel of Christ, through which, as has been said, his resurrection is proclaimed throughout the whole world. For the cart’s four wheels are the Evangelists. The house of Aminadab, whose name is interpreted “the willing one of my people”—the house, I say, of Aminadab, that is, of Christ, who freely gave himself for his people—was formerly the Synagogue. But now his house is the Church, which, while the Synagogue envied, received faith in Christ’s resurrection. And now indeed she mocks our David as he plays and leaps, sparing no blasphemous utterance—just as Michal, Saul’s daughter, looked out through the window and despised David in her heart as he leapt and danced before the Lord. [Col. 1241D] Yet she will one day say: “I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab” (Song 6:11). “I did not know,” she will say: my soul was troubled by an unexpected change of affairs, and I did not understand the chariots of the Gospel carrying the ark of God, Aminadab.

For when the fullness of the gentiles has entered, that Michal will no longer look through the window and despise the glorious King David; rather, she herself will follow him and indeed receive the ark of the Lord—that is, faith in Christ’s resurrection. Meanwhile she looks through the window because, unwilling to share in such great joys, she lies in wait as though in concealment, devising what or from where she may blaspheme. But let us, having divine help and defense against her snares, follow King David by favoring grace [Col. 1242A] and sing with him:

“Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord sons of rams.” O sons of God—not sons of wrath, not sons of Gehenna, not sons of perdition, but sons of grace; sons by nature of transgressing human beings, whom a fleshly mother conceived in iniquities and bore in sin; but sons of God the Father by adoption, through regenerating grace: you, sons of God, bring to the Lord; bring to the Lord sons of rams.

One offering was required when construction of the tabernacle was begun at the origin of the newborn Church, and another is required now at the completion of the tabernacle near the end of the age. Then it was not little, tender sons of rams, but strong rams, horned with both Testaments, who founded the Church by their blood. Through the horns of their strength they destroyed idols, scattered heresies, and overthrew Jewish and Pharisaic traditions and superstitions. [Col. 1242B] But now, the Church having been firmly founded upon the firm rock, and the foundation of the tabernacle in no way shaken, for the completion of that tabernacle—in which the ark of God, that is, Christ’s body, is to be placed—there is no longer a search for rams equal to the Apostles, strong to endure martyrdoms and robust to destroy idolatry, but only for sons of rams, comparable to the Apostles, whom the Apostles, leaders of the flocks, begot through the Gospel, that they may be new lambs.

Such persons are sought at the completion of the tabernacle, that they may gather together in one within the tabernacle itself, and have one Spirit and one faith, one body, one heart and one soul in God. Of these Christ said to the chief Shepherd: “Feed my lambs.” And because he said twice to him, “Feed my lambs,” and a third time, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:15, 17), we too, singers of the true David, say twice: “Bring, sons of God; bring to the Lord sons of rams,” on account of the tender little lambs; and the third time we say: “Bring to the Lord glory and honor,” on account of the great sheep, on account of the flock of shorn sheep which, having laid aside the fleeces of their possessions, come up from the washing of repentance or innocence, all bearing twin offspring, with none barren among them (Song 4:2). [Col. 1242C] They bear twin offspring because these sheep are not satisfied with keeping the commandment, but have in addition embraced the counsel of perfection. The true David, builder of this tabernacle, says: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19:17). This is the commandment. Again: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (ibid., 21). This is the counsel.

O sons of God, if you offer such sheep—or rather, if you present yourselves as such sheep—you truly offer glory and honor. Therefore I say:

VERSE 2. “Bring to the Lord glory and honor.” And lest you attribute anything to yourselves in this glory, I say again: “Bring glory to his name,” at the completion of the tabernacle, at the completion of every good and perfect work from which glory and honor may arise. Say to him: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, [Col. 1243A] but give glory to your name” (Psalm 113:1). Thus bring to the Lord glory and honor; thus bring glory to his name: whether you bring to God yourselves or others as little and imperfect sons of rams through observance of the commandments, or present yourselves or others as fruitful sheep for God’s glory and honor through observance of the counsel, do all things for God’s glory and not your own.

At the end of every psalm, and especially at the end or completion of the tabernacle, while serving God in this very tabernacle—which is the Church, or the pure flesh of each one of you—say often, say willingly and from the heart: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.” Thus bring glory to his name. I do not say “names,” as though there were many, but “name,” as though it were one—indeed, truly the one name of the Trinity—just as you were baptized not into names, but into the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Bring glory to his name.

Otherwise: O sons of God, regenerated through the Holy Spirit and called to adoption as sons, bring sons of rams, as explained above, to that same Lord, namely the Holy Spirit, through whose operation you have become sons of God; and bring him glory and honor. Bring glory, by believing and declaring that he is not a creature, as Arius and Macedonius blasphemously asserted, but, together with the Father and the Son, is the uncreated, immeasurable, eternal, and almighty Creator. [Col. 1243B] Bring him honor also by believing with the heart unto righteousness and confessing with the mouth unto salvation, preaching that he is to be honored with equal honor together with the Father and the Son by every creature, and worshipped by angels and human beings. And so that you may prove by your works that what you teach is true—you who preach that he must be worshipped—

“Worship the Lord in his holy court,” or: “in his holy hall”: that is, in the heart enlarged and sanctified through love, which is his royal hall, in which true worshippers will worship the Father in Spirit and truth (John 4:23): in spirit, believing with the heart unto righteousness; in truth, confessing with the mouth that very Truth unto the salvation of the hearers.

And if we wish to distinguish the works of the Trinity—which, although inseparable, nevertheless indicate the properties of the persons—one thing is preparation to build the tabernacle, another the construction of the tabernacle itself, [Col. 1243D] and another its completion. For just as David the father prepared abundant resources in gold, silver, bronze, and precious stones for his son Solomon to build the Temple, but Solomon the son built the Temple itself from such resources, so God the Father, in creating rational creatures through his Word on account of his goodness, prepared great resources and made noble material. From this his Son, Christ the peaceful King, made and makes one Church, having himself become the cornerstone by which the wall of angels is joined to the wall of human beings. He has not only been raised as the head of the corner but has also been laid as its foundation. Thus he says of himself as the rock: “Upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matthew 16:18).

Therefore the Father, who created rational creatures and sent his Son into this world, prepared the resources and material of the tabernacle or Temple and laid its immovable foundation. For no one can lay another foundation besides that which was laid by the Father, the Ancient of Days; this is Christ Jesus (1 Corinthians 3:11), who is the solid Rock. Upon this Rock—that is, upon himself—Christ himself builds his Church, which is a tabernacle in Zion and a Temple in Jerusalem: a tabernacle in the time of warfare, a Temple in days of peace. The completion of this tabernacle, which the Father founded and the Son built, is rightly assigned to the Holy Spirit, without whose gift the work of Father and Son is imperfect. For example, [Col. 1244B] the Father created Judas the apostle and the Son chose him as an Apostle; but because he did not receive the grace of the Holy Spirit, he became a devil from being an apostle.

The Apostles too, built by faith upon the Rock which is Christ, would have remained imperfect and incomplete unless, after Christ’s Resurrection and Ascension, they had received the Holy Spirit. Flesh and blood did not reveal the Rock to Peter, but the Father, who laid the Rock, revealed it to Peter and joined Peter himself to the Rock set in the foundation. Yet, because the Holy Spirit had not yet been given, nor had Jesus yet been glorified, Peter was still an incomplete tabernacle when he could not endure the blast of breath from the mouth of one maidservant; rather, as though the cords of faith had been broken and the pegs of hope pulled out, he fell [Col. 1244C] to the ground—and would have fallen utterly into hell, had he not been aided by the gift of the Holy Spirit, to whom the forgiveness of sins specially belongs.

Did not the foundation of faith and the structure of hope also totter in those disciples who, nearly despairing, said: “But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21)? Even the first testimonies of the resurrection seemed like madness to the chosen Apostles. And afterwards, when Jesus stood in their midst and they did not believe, being amazed with joy, he said: “Have you anything here to eat?” They offered him a portion of a broiled fish and a honeycomb (ibid., 41–42); and when he had given them what remained, he breathed on them and said: [Col. 1244D] “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven” (John 20:23).

Then, having received the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit, they began to grow strong in faith. But when, illuminated and inflamed by the fire of that same Holy Spirit, they received from above the best gift and perfect gift, then, in them and through them—as though the tabernacle had been completed, and their sound had gone out into all the earth—that sevenfold voice was heard of which this psalm speaks:

1. “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters.”
2. “The voice of the Lord is in power.”
3. “The voice of the Lord is in magnificence.”
4. “The voice of the Lord breaks the cedars.”
5. “The voice of the Lord cuts through the flame of fire.”
6. “The voice of the Lord shakes the wilderness.”
7. “The voice of the Lord prepares the stags.”

Then the seven thunders uttered their voices (Revelation [Col. 1245A] 10:3), because the writings of the prophets, which until then had a terrifying but by no means intelligible sound, then uttered their voices and gave clear meanings of rational interpretations. Did not the Apostle Peter turn the sound of thunder into an intelligible voice when he said: “Men of Judaea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and receive my words with your ears. For these are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day; but this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:14):

“And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord, that I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams. And indeed upon my servants and upon my maidservants in those days I shall pour out of my Spirit, and they shall prophesy; and I shall give wonders in heaven above and signs on earth below: blood, fire, and vapor of smoke. The sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes. And everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”

When they heard these and other such intelligible utterances, they were cut to the heart and said to Peter and the other Apostles: “What shall we do, brothers?” But Peter said to them: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized for the forgiveness of sins” (Acts 2:37–38).

But not only through the Apostles, but also through [Col. 1245C] their successors—apostolic and catholic men—the completer of the true tabernacle, which God pitched and not man, the Spirit of that same tabernacle, breathes where he wills. You hear his voice through a human being, whatever sort of minister of the word he may be, but do not know where he comes from or where he goes (John 3:8). You do not know the predestination from which he comes; you do not know the end of completion to which he goes. Yet knowing this truly—that you hear his voice whenever you hear, through anyone, the word of truth—do not hear negligently the voice through which God’s tabernacle is completed, whether the whole Church or any ecclesiastical person.

Above all, hear the incarnate Word himself uttering the Holy Spirit’s voices in the Gospel. After him, hear his Apostles; after the Apostles, hear apostolic men. And if anyone preaches to you another gospel than they do, let him be anathema to you. But whoever preaches the same thing that they do, hear them through him, for it is the voice of truth—not the voice of a human being, but the voice of the Lord—whether that voice instils the fear of the Lord over the waters, terrifying wandering minds; or the power of piety, gently soothing the meek; or the magnificence of knowledge, which prepares magnificent consolation for those blessed who mourn; or the gift of fortitude, breaking cedars—that is, presumptuous and lofty people; or the gift of counsel, by which the flame of sin is cut short so that, while it is felt, it may not be consented to; or the gift of understanding, by which the wilderness of Kadesh is shaken, so that a land formerly desert may be broken up, as it were, by the plow of understanding and become a fruitful field, and be Kadesh, [Col. 1246A] which is interpreted “holy”; or finally the gift of wisdom, revealing the hidden things of the Scriptures and preparing the stags.

Whatever of these spiritual gifts the voice of the Lord announces to you, hear it gladly, that you may be a well-disposed hearer; hear intelligently, that you may be teachable; hear obediently, that you may be attentive and carefully observe what the divine voice suggests to you. According to Isaiah’s prophecy, it begins with high notes, placing first the Spirit of wisdom, then that of understanding, and so descending to fear, which sounds most deeply; in this it fittingly represents Christ descending from the highest things to the lowest. But you must ascend from the lowest to the highest, that is, from fear to wisdom; therefore the seven distinctions of the voice must begin for you with the low strings.

Thus first hear the terrifying voice thundering over the waters and sounding deeply; last of all, having passed through the middle strings on this psaltery or harp, you will hear the voice sounding high and revealing the hidden things of the Scriptures—in the present life only in part, for “now we know in part and prophesy in part” (1 Corinthians 13:9). But at the completion of the tabernacle, when our spirit is in fellowship with angelic spirits, there will no longer be anything hidden or obscure. Meanwhile, as has been said, let us hear obediently, gladly, and intelligently what the Spirit says to the Churches through the seven voices which commend the gifts of his sevenfold grace. For:

VERSE 3. “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters.” First, from the oracle of the Lord’s flesh, the voice of the Lord sounded over [Col. 1246C] the waters—that is, over the Jews, who were fluid and unstable. Then, through the Apostles, the God of majesty—that is, the Holy Spirit—thundered over many waters, that is, over the gentiles. For “many waters” are many peoples. Or Christ himself was reckoned insignificant before the Ascension; afterward, raised into heaven, the God of majesty, great and immense, thundered from there not merely over a few waters in Judaea but over many waters throughout the whole world.

I say that he thundered because he instilled fear into such waters: either by thundering to the Jews from the cloud of Christ’s flesh, or by stirring up thunders among the gentiles through the Apostles, who flew as clouds throughout the world. In thundering thus he instilled fear, which is the beginning and the first grace. But after he had terrified them, when some had turned to him, he dwelt upon many waters. Nor did he cease to thunder until that

VERSE 4. voice of the Lord’s thunder became “in power.” This occurred when, with piety added to fear of the Lord, the creature who fears worshipped the Creator; this is power, namely worship directed toward God. To this is added the voice of the Lord “in the magnificence” of works or also of miracles, in which the Spirit of knowledge is given, so that one who worships God may know how to conduct himself in the present life; and God also adds magnificence, which makes people magnificent. This is also:

VERSE 5. “The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars”: that is, in contrition of heart humbling the proud among the gentiles. And the cedars of Lebanon—that is, the taller ones, namely the proud Jews in the last times, when a remnant is saved—he will break; through repentance he will humble them to endure whatever adversities may come, so that in those things which they know through the Spirit of knowledge, they may be strong through the gift of the Spirit of fortitude. The cedar is a very tall tree which is of no use unless it is cut down, because while it remains in its root it bears no useful fruit. Similarly, pride, once cut down, which bears the bitter fruits of sin, gives way to humility, which bears sweet fruit. For it follows: “and, its height having been laid low.”

VERSE 6. “He will crush them like the calves of Lebanon.” In Lebanon calves are customarily fattened for sacrifice, because it is a pasture mountain watered by springs. To this are compared proud persons who have been humbled, because they are prepared, like a calf, to suffer for Christ. Or he will crush them as a calf of Lebanon crushes their branches and shoots, striking with its hooves: that is, once pride and wantonness have been cut away, he will lead them into imitation of his humility—he who was offered as a calf. He is the fattened calf slain for the salvation of the world, who is also called *candidatus* (“white-clad”), because *Libanus* is interpreted “whitening.”

And because he had said, “the Lord will break and crush,” without specifying who this Lord is, he adds: “And the Beloved,” of whom the Father said: “This is my beloved Son” (Luke 9:35). “And he will crush them,” that is, he will humble them by the example of himself, who, although he was in the form of God and higher than all, emptied himself so as to become “like a son of unicorns”: that is, to become a human being, a son of the Jews according to the flesh, in which he suffered as a calf, since the Jews are called unicorns because they raise one horn, whether by taking pride in one Law or by boasting of their own singular righteousness.

Or thus: it is no wonder if they are broken and crushed like a calf. For the Beloved too will himself be crushed, having become a calf of Lebanon—that is, led as a victim by the rulers of this world, whom Lebanon, interpreted “whitening,” signifies. Hence elsewhere: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers assembled together against the Christ of the Lord” (Psalm 2:2). He therefore suffered not as God, according to which he could not be seen, but as a son of unicorns—that is, as a human being, a son of the Jews.

VERSE 7. “The voice of the Lord cutting through the flame of fire.” Fire is the tinder of sin; the flame is consent, action, and habit. The Lord does not remove this flame wholly, but, by giving the Spirit of counsel, cuts it short, so that consent does not proceed as far as action, or action does not become habitual. Repentance also interrupts any such falls when the righteous person falls and rises again. The flame is also cut short when those strengthened by the Spirit of counsel act so that, through idleness, the fire of tinder may not burst out into flame.

This may also, apart from the sequence of the exposition, be understood of the Lord thus: “The voice of the Lord cutting through the flame of fire,” that is, passing through the ardor of persecutors without injury. Or, “cutting through the flame,” that is, dividing their wrath, so as to convert some of them to himself and leave others in their wickedness.

### Verse 8

**The voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness**, etc. By “wilderness” he simply means the Gentiles, who were without law, [Col. 1248A] without God, and without prophets. By “the wilderness of Kadesh” he means the Jews. Kadesh, as is read in Exodus, is a place in the wilderness where water flowed from the rock (Num. 20:1 ff.). Kadesh is interpreted “the holiness of the law,” in which were the Jews, who did not indeed understand the holy and good law spiritually, but nevertheless observed it according to the letter through ceremonies. Therefore, having given the Spirit of understanding, he shakes all these—Gentiles as well as Jews—like a farmer shakes barren soil so that it may bear fruit, and so that, understanding according to anagogy, that is, spiritual understanding, they may believe in the Lord in the Scriptures. This understanding, however, belongs to those whose mind is well disposed by counsel. It follows:

### Verse 9

**The voice of the Lord**, through this understanding, **preparing the deer for the mountain of wisdom**, which concerns [Col. 1248B] the divine essence. Moreover, not only to the Gentiles now, but also to the Jews at the end, he will reveal the things that are concealed concerning the divinity—namely, the shaded coverings of the mysteries—so that they may feed freely; he will open them.

In the Hebrew truth it is read: “The voice of the Lord dividing the flame of fire. The voice of the Lord causing the wilderness to travail: the Lord will cause the wilderness of Kadesh to travail. The voice of the Lord acting as midwife to the deer and uncovering the thickets; in his temple everyone will speak glory. The Lord dwells over the flood, and the Lord will sit as king for ever.”

This is the bracelet by which Leviathan’s jaw is pierced, by which the ring passing through his nostrils is bent back upon itself: for the voice of the Lord, first thundering over the waters, brought down its thunders for this purpose, that the Lord might dwell over the waters, or cause dwelling over them. [Col. 1248C]

For in the first age of the world the voice of the Lord thundered over the waters, when he foretold to his servant Noah, fearing God and righteous, the coming waters of the flood. In the second age, the voice of the Lord sounded in power, commanding Abraham to depart from his land and from his kindred. That voice of power called him to the worship of true piety, leading him out from among ungodly idol-worshippers. In the third age, the voice of the Lord was heard in magnificence—or, as it is read in Hebrew, in beauty—on Mount Sinai, where through knowledge of the law the knowledge of sin was given, and the magnificent glory of God was manifested there upon the summit of Mount Sinai.

In the fourth age the voice of the Lord breaking the cedars resounded, when the word of the Lord came first to Samuel the prophet [Col. 1248D] concerning the breaking of the pride of the sons of Eli, as a figure of the old priesthood to be rejected and a new one to be substituted; and secondly concerning the breaking of Saul’s pride by humble David, who, like a calf of Lebanon, was taken from pastoral places to be king—truly a son of unicorns, that is, of the strong patriarchs who worshipped one God.

In the fifth age the voice of the Lord cutting off the flame of fire sounded in the furnace for the three boys, when the angel of the Lord, dividing the flame of fire, made the midst of the furnace like a wind blowing with dew (Dan. 3:50). The fire did not touch them at all, because divine counsel was with them that they should not worship the golden statue.

Finally, in the sixth age the voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness—or, as it is read in Hebrew, causing the wilderness to travail—brings it about [Col. 1249A] “that the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1). For the virgin earth, tilled by no plough of marital union, but illuminated through faith by the spirit of understanding, bore abundant fruit in giving birth to Christ. And the Gentile world, until then uncultivated and deserted, bore fruit by producing worthy fruits of repentance, illuminated by the gift of divine understanding.

Last of all, the voice of the Lord preparing the deer—or, as it is read in Hebrew, acting as midwife to the deer—is that voice of divine wisdom by which the high mountains are made ready as pastures for deer: while to the saints, who consume serpents, cast off the horns of pride, throw away their old hair, and thirst intensely for living waters, the dense places of Scripture are revealed. From these, by the Lord’s hand acting as midwife, the twisting serpent is cast forth [Col. 1249B] and devoured by them, when they cast away from themselves through confession the poison of sin conceived from the ancient serpent, and afterward bring forth holy offspring through good works.

Indeed, in this sixth age these deer enter the tabernacle, or temple, of the Lord; but in the seventh age, laying aside the mortality of their bodies, they will go forth and find pasture both now and then. For even now the Lord dwells over the flood: he feeds his animals in the ark through the gift of understanding, like another and true Noah, governor of the ark and inhabitant of the flood. After this mortal life he will lead his deer to the pastures of wisdom, where he himself sits as king for ever. See that you understand charity to be associated with the seven gifts enumerated: for it is the foundation of the whole tabernacle.

[Col. 1249C] **And in his temple all will speak glory.** Here he calls it a temple, which in the title he called a tabernacle. Therefore, in this tabernacle thus brought to completion, not only the perfect person but everyone—that is, each according to his own gift—will speak glory to God. Do you wish to know, faithful hearer, what the Lord does with his tabernacle, his temple, thus completed? Hear what follows:

### Verse 10

**The Lord causes the flood to be inhabited.** Truly it is so. For just as formerly, through Noah, he caused the completed ark to remain over the flood, so that not even one of the animals within it might perish, so now he causes the Church, completed by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, to inhabit the flood, lest storms of temptations or [Col. 1249D] persecutions be able to destroy anyone who now remains faithfully in the unity of ecclesiastical peace.

But beware lest you either remain outside as a pagan, or go outside as a heretic, like a raven that will not return to the ark. Beware also lest, while remaining physically inside, you be alien from the Church in spirit, like those of whom it is said: “Natural persons, separating themselves, not having the Spirit” (Jude 1:19). Among these were those to whom Truth said: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46).

Those are to be said to be inside the ark, the tabernacle, or the temple, who, despising outward and worldly pleasures, seek inward and eternal joys. Of such persons, as of smoothed timbers, the Lord makes the completed ark inhabit the flood [Col. 1250A] so that they may remain unharmed amid the dangers of the surging flood, whether of temptations or persecutions.

He also causes his ark, namely his holy Church, to inhabit the flood of baptism, so that, as eight souls were saved in the flood, so in baptism may be saved those to whom belongs the promise of the eight beatitudes, where the Gospel says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit. Blessed are those who mourn,” etc. (Matt. 5:3).

**And the Lord will sit as king for ever.** For when the flood has ceased, when there will no longer be any temptation or persecution, nor will anyone thereafter need baptism, then the Lord will sit as king for ever. The magnificent manifestation of this sitting will be when, at the end of the world, in the sight of good and evil human beings and angels, the King of glory sits upon the throne of his majesty (Matt. 19:28). Then:

### Verse 11

**He will give strength to his people; then he will bless his people in peace.** And then there will be a distinction between people and people, both among the elect and among the reprobate. For even among the reprobate there will be a people not to be arraigned in judgment, because, on account of manifest unbelief, “he who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18; Matt. 25:41). And there will be a people judged in such a way that the Lord says to it: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire,” not because you did not have faith, but because you refused to perform the works of faith. “For I was hungry and you did not give me food; I was thirsty and you did not give me drink” (ibid., 42).

Likewise, among the elect there will be a people not to be judged, [Col. 1250C] namely those who will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel; and there will be a people judged in such a way that the Lord says to it: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you before the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink. For as long as you did it to one of these least brothers of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. 25:34).

Oh, what strength the Lord will then give to the people of his least ones, in whom, being hungry, thirsty, naked, strangers, sick, and imprisoned, he will acknowledge that he himself was hungry, thirsty, naked, a stranger, sick, and imprisoned! But those who fed, gave drink to, clothed, received, and visited such persons—or rather, the Lord himself in such persons—[Col. 1250D] will be granted the magnificent blessing of peace, when the Lord says to them: “Come, blessed of my Father.”

Therefore, since both the people of the perfect and the people of the imperfect are the Lord’s people, the Lord will give strength to his perfect people, in whom he himself is honored or wronged; and he will bless his imperfect people, who both here sow pure alms in blessings and at judgment will reap eternal life from blessings (2 Cor. 9:6), when the Lord himself says to them: “Come, blessed,” etc.

Alternatively: **The Lord will give strength to his people** now in battle, and afterward, once battle has ceased, will bless his people in peace, when he “will wipe every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor any pain any longer, because the former things have passed away” [Col. 1251A] (Rev. 21:4); when “his dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace” (Isa. 9:7).

Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit: to the one Lord, whose is this name, of whom it is said in the Psalm: “Bring to the Lord glory for his name.” This name—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—by whose invocation the tabernacle is built and completed in baptism, was never attributed to any gods, either false or adoptive.

Though every Gentile people, deceived by diverse error, called some false gods “almighty,” as Jupiter, or “terrible,” as Pluto, and transferred every other name of the true God to its false gods, this sole name of the triune and one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—[Col. 1251B] was never attributed to any of the gods, nor was ever heard in this world before the Voice of the Lord thundered over the waters, saying to the disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

Therefore, because it was said in the Psalm, “Bring to the Lord glory for his name,” we bring glory especially to this name, knowledge of which thundered over many waters, through the seven voices set forth in this Psalm, saying at the end of the Psalm: “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.”

Alternatively: Glory to the Father, who thundered over the waters; glory to the Word through whom he thundered, and who assumed the cloud of flesh, so that thunders might sound from that cloud. Glory to the sevenfold Holy Spirit, uttering his voices seven times [Col. 1251C] for the completion of the tabernacle or temple, the dedication of which immediately follows in the next Psalm. For its title reads: “A Psalm of a Song at the Dedication of the House of David.”

This title sends us to history, because just as David built the temple for the Lord at his own expense and with his own provisions, and afterward dedicated it with joy and solemn words to the Lord’s praise, so the body of Christ, built without sin in its unique birth, was dedicated through the Resurrection in the eternal glory of impassibility and immortality. These are the words of the dedicated House—the words of the changed and now no longer dying God-man: “O Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me.” Again: “O Lord, in your favor you gave strength to my beauty”; and afterward: “You tore my sackcloth and girded me with joy” (Ps. 29:3, 8, 12).

It should be noted that the Prophet’s sevenfold voice, calling to dedication, is rightly inserted between [Col. 1252B] two Psalms, of which the former concerns the Passion and the following one the Resurrection. For the Lord’s Passion itself appeared to the Jews, who rejected the cornerstone, to be the dissolution of the temple. Yet through that Passion the house of God, which is the Church, was firmly built: the material flowed from Christ’s side in blood and water, from which material the Church was fashioned, as woman was made from the man’s rib.

Thus, when through Christ’s Passion the tabernacle, temple, or house was built—for it is one thing, called tabernacle in which service is performed, temple in which sacrifice is offered, and house which is inhabited—when, I say, the tabernacle, temple, and house had thus been built, before its dedication was set in place, the Psalmist’s cry sounded: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams.” By such a cry he interrupted the voice of Christ crying in the preceding Psalm for the rebuilding of the temple of his body, [Col. 1252C] and of the same Christ crying in the following Psalm for the dedication of that temple, when he says:

## Psalm 29

[Col. 1251]

[Col. 1251D] **I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me.** Here Christ himself, the head of the Church, treats of his work and eternal reward. He also exhorts his faithful people that, singing psalms to the Lord and confessing by his example, they may deserve to attain the same joy.

Although the title contains:

### A Psalm of a Song at the Dedication of the House of David

David, however, is not recorded to have made or dedicated a house to the Lord, unless perhaps you understand it of the tabernacle in Chronicles, for which he is found to have appointed ministers of different offices. Therefore it must rather be understood according to its signification. The whole Christ is the one house of God: for in the head, which is Christ, the fullness of divinity dwells; and the Church, by certain graces which it receives from his fullness, is his temple.

This house, with regard to Christ, was built at his conception; with regard to the Church, it is always being built while it labors in this life. Its dedication, however, has already occurred in the head, as in the foundation, because Christ, rising again, was confirmed in immortality. With regard to the Church, it will occur in the future, when the righteous, joined to their head, “will stand in great steadfastness” (Wis. 5:1). Since the preceding Psalm concerned the completion of the tabernacle in time of war, this Psalm of a Song—that is, of exultation at the dedication, or confirmation, of David’s house in eternal peace through the renewal of the body—rightly follows.

The whole Christ speaks. First, he presents the song for his dedication, which has occurred in the head, and discloses his intention when, in the same section, he commands the saints to sing psalms. Second, he shows how he deserved to be dedicated, at the words: “But I.” Third, how he received the glory of dedication, at the words: “The Lord heard.” This is a short Psalm concerning the Resurrection, also recalling the Passion, lest the Passion terrify those whom the hope of Resurrection gladdens. He therefore introduces the song for the dedication and says:

### Verse 2

O Lord, I will exalt you—that is, I will praise your exaltedness—because you received me by dedicating me in the glory of impassibility. We understand this dedication also as that of the future house. For what is now said in the person of the foundation, “You received me,” will be said in the person of the whole house.

It follows:

**And you did not delight my enemies over me**—that is, you did not permit them to delight at my dedication, although before you had permitted it: my Jewish enemies, who were confounded when I rose; also the devil and his angels, by whom I could not be held in hell; and all who throughout the world attempted to oppress me through various persecutions.

### Verse 3

**O Lord my God**—he explains this receiving—[Col. 1253B] **I cried to you, and you healed me**, removing the weakness of passibility. And:

### Verse 4

**O Lord, by your power you brought my soul up from hell.** This needs no explanation.

**You saved me from those descending into the pit.** The pit is the deep condition of corruptible flesh; those descending into the pit are those who immerse themselves in earthly lusts. Such persons persecuted Christ, from whom he was saved and removed. Being also free from sin, he was saved from the condition of the flesh’s profound blindness.

It seems contrary either that God should pray, or that enemies should be unable to delight over a human being. To this it must be said that Christ, God and man, prays not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is human and weak; and he is mediator not between the Father and human beings, [Col. 1253C] but between God the Trinity and sinful human beings. For in that he is weak, he draws near to us; but in that he is not iniquitous, he is joined to God.

Moreover, not only according to his divinity, but also insofar as he is human, he presides over us as the head: although the head forms one body with the other members, yet because all the senses are in it, it is more worthy than the other members, in which touch alone is present. Thus Christ, the head of the Church, is, according to his humanity, the mediator full of grace and greater than the members who receive from his fullness. In the Passion his enemies rejoiced over this, but in the dedication he was saved from them.

### Verse 3

**Sing psalms to the Lord, his saints.** You who have noted the title of this Psalm—“A Psalm of a Song at the Dedication of the House of David”—and who know that this dedication has already been fulfilled in the foundation, which is Christ, and hope that it will likewise be fulfilled in yourselves: sing psalms to the Lord by doing good works, [Col. 1253D] and confess to him in songs through the exercises of contemplation, so that you may fulfill the “psalm of a song.” By this psalm or song the Lord is both praised for the dedication already completed in the foundation and entreated for the dedication still to be accomplished in you, who are his saints in faith, not his saints in falsity, like the five foolish virgins, who are regarded as holy because of virginity and burning lamps (Matt. 25 ff.). Yet because, when the bridegroom comes, they are found not to have oil in their vessels, they will not be among his saints.

[Col. 1254A] Do you wish to know, faithful soul betrothed to Christ, with what two arms he embraces you when adorned in true holiness, not only to bring you into the bridal chamber of future blessedness, but also to commend you even now to the angelic companions of the bridegroom and to good prelates? Certainly, leaving aside that “his left hand is under your head, and his right hand will embrace you” (Song 2:6), while in the present life he amasses good merits for you by his helping left hand, and in the future preserves for you, by his beatifying right hand, good rewards proportionate to good merits and even surpassing them—leaving aside, I say, the treatment of such things for now—Christ himself, your bridegroom, is Truth; and he wishes, as it were with two arms, to embrace you by showing you himself and yourself.

Truth, Christ, shows himself and you to you when he enlightens you in truth; when he manifests himself as truth in such a way that first you truly know what you have made yourself to be, when you fell away from truth into falsehoods; and then, through recognizing your own misery, begin to know his true mercy and the merciful truth beloved by his saints. From consideration of yourself conceive fear; from consideration of God conceive hope. If your misery terrifies you, let his mercy console you. But, in order to be capable of mercy, love the truth that reveals your misery. Wherever truth may sound to you in rebuking you, hold fast love for truth itself; and let it be your glory, the testimony of conscience, that you yourself know yourself to be always a friend even of truth when it rebukes you. This glory belongs to all his saints, to whom it is now said: [Col. 1254C] “Sing psalms to the Lord, his saints.”

How many are otherwise! They glory more when they are falsely considered and called holy than when they are truly believed and said to be what they are—namely, unjust and unworthy. Sometimes, indeed, these same persons, not from love of truth but as if by the cosmetic of a feigned humility, themselves admit what they are, not denying that they are unworthy of every dignity, secular or ecclesiastical. But if this truth sounds from another person’s mouth, you would immediately see eyebrows contracted, glances turned aside, sighs drawn, breaths quickened.

And if the inward parts of the breast were open to you, you would see there, as in an idol-shrine, some great image of the devil—or rather the devil himself—saying in his heart, that is, in the human heart which has now become his own: “What does he say? I will sit above the stars of God, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14). For he sets his seat above the stars of God who desires to preside over good people. When he is driven from that seat, jealousy, like an infernal flame, will torment him when he sees someone more worthy than himself exalted. Even a good but imperfect person is sometimes burned by this jealousy when he is judged unworthy of an office and another, as though more worthy than he, is chosen.

Sometimes it happens that such a person seeks for himself a rejection of this kind which has some scent of pride: namely, that he should not be occupied with a lesser dignity, as though reserved for a worthier one, a dignity which he himself disdains to accept because he judges himself worthier than that dignity. Does not such a man have the image of Diana [Col. 1255A] in his heart, hunting and fowling for things higher than himself? The Gentiles worshipped Diana as, so to speak, the goddess of hunting; and this man worships the image of that Diana by fostering within himself the desire of such ambition.

Such a heart, therefore, is not a memorial of holiness; rather, it is a memorial of vanity. The house or church in which a martyr’s body or relics rest is customarily called that martyr’s *memoria*, or memorial. Likewise, the house in which holiness, or its relics, rests is called a memorial of holiness. But in the house or temple of the Lord’s body all holiness rested; in the other elect there are only certain relics of his holiness. Hence, when he had eaten a honeycomb before his disciples, he gave the remains to them (Luke 24:42–43): for good is done to Christians who receive at least the remains of holiness and sweetness, and become a memorial of his holiness worthy of the dedication suggested by this Psalm, which says:

“Sing psalms to the Lord, his saints, and confess to the memorial of his holiness.” O his saints and humble of heart, who alone truly are in the number of his saints, confess to the memorial of his holiness. Confess that you are unjust and unworthy before the memorial of his holiness. Say to the memorial of his holiness—to his body, which is the memorial of his holiness, in which dwells all the fullness of his holiness—say, I say, to that memorial of holiness: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. 8:8). It is your condescension, not my worthiness, that requires this: that you deign [Col. 1255C] to enter beneath my roof, or rather, to receive me beneath your roof. O memorial of holiness, O most renowned holy temple, sanctified and dedicated through the glory of the Resurrection and Ascension.

Alternatively, the dedication of the house has already taken place in Christ, who above says to the Father: “O Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me; you brought my soul up from hell. You saved me from those descending into the pit.” By these words the dedication is explained. Therefore, O his saints, who hold the faith and hope of this dedication, sing psalms to the Lord and confess to the memorial of his holiness, so that by doing good things and confessing your evils you may become fit for the celebration of dedication.

For just as in the handmade temple which Solomon made, first came building, then followed the adornment of the house, and lastly dedication, [Col. 1255D] so it also happened in the unmade temple of the Lord’s body. First, in the virgin’s womb, Wisdom, building for herself, hewed out seven columns, because she established it by the all-sufficient strength of the sevenfold Spirit. Then that house was adorned with the splendid works of miracles and with the grace of his words, when Jesus began “to do and to teach.” Finally, it was dedicated in the resurrection.

The same three things are required in you, O his saints. For through faith you have already been built, having been born again from water and the Holy Spirit in the name of the holy Trinity. You may await with sure hope the dedication in the common resurrection, provided that, during the intervening span of life between building and dedication, you strive to adorn that house with devout works and good confession. Therefore, lest the house already built through faith be found less adorned than is fitting, [Col. 1256A] sing psalms to the Lord, his saints, by doing good works; and when you have done everything commanded you, confess that you are unprofitable servants (Luke 17:10).

Even if the king of this age does not present to you saints outstanding in virtues, in comparison with whom you can consider yourselves unprofitable, return to the memorial of his holiness. In comparison with him, humble yourselves, since he, the Holy of holies, by his own power alone has done and does wonders beyond number. But you have done and do few things, and you do good or speak well not by your own power but by his grace. “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father” (Matt. 10:20). Therefore, when you sing psalms, sing them to the Lord, referring the good work to his glory; and when you speak well, confess to the memorial of his holiness, because, as has already been said, it is not you who speak but the Holy Spirit.

Yet through such works and such confessions the house of God is adorned in you, so that it may be worthy of dedication in the common resurrection of all, when the dead will rise incorruptible. “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51); that is, not all will be dedicated. For only those will then be changed and dedicated in whom the foundation of faith and the building of hope are found adorned by works of charity and confession of truth—provided they had time for working and confessing.

For baptized children who die immediately before the years of discretion are excepted from this sentence. Although they are adorned neither by singing psalms nor by confession, by the grace of baptism alone they are so made white that they are found fit for the solemnity of dedication. Therefore, with these excepted, I say to you, his saints, who have time to work and confess: if you wish worthily to belong to the dedication, strive to be adorned by good works and confession of truth while there is time for working and confessing. For those descending into the pit will have no time after death to work, as Scripture says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it earnestly; for there will be neither work, nor reasoning, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in hell, whither you are hastening” (Ecclus. 9:10). And in this life you, O God, receive confession; but “in hell who will confess to you?” [Col. 1256D] (Ps. 6:6). “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2), because now is the time for singing psalms and confessing. Therefore, sing psalms to the Lord, his saints, and confess to the memorial of his holiness.

If you have a joyful psaltery with a harp, sing psalms to the Lord; if you do not yet have it, at least confess your sins and pray for one another, that you may be saved. But do not confess to scribes and Pharisees, nor to heretics or schismatics, nor to blasphemers of Christ, as the ungodly and despairing Judas did, who said before such people: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27:4). If he had made that confession with a contrite heart to the memorial of Christ’s holiness, whom he had betrayed, such confession would without doubt have been salutary for him.

But he did not go to the memorial of holiness; he did not go to Christ, then hanging upon the cross; he did not confess to him. The thief, however, who hung with him truly confessed to the memorial of his holiness, acknowledging himself a criminal and confessing that Christ had done nothing evil. He said to him: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). It is no wonder that the prayer of righteous Abel has great power, when the prayer of a confessing sinner had such power—not repeated but single—that he immediately heard: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 21:43).

Therefore, following the example of that thief, confess to the memorial of his holiness. At that time, when the dedication of his house was approaching—namely, when the Lord’s Resurrection was now imminent—he purified the thief, though repenting late, [Col. 1257B] and associated him with the feast of his dedication. And even now, to this day, he does the same for those who confess their sins truthfully before the memorial of his holiness. As has already been said, this memorial is understood to be his body, of which he himself said: “Do this in remembrance of me.” Therefore, whenever you eat this bread or drink the cup of his blood, confess to the memorial of his holiness (1 Cor. 11:26).

And confess not only to Christ, the high priest in whom is all fullness of holiness, but also confess your sins to every catholic priest in whom are the relics of his holiness. Confess the truth; confess what the thief also confessed: that you indeed receive what your deeds deserve, however great the evils and sufferings you endure, whereas he did nothing evil, but, bearing our sins, endured a cruel death. Confess to the memorial of his holiness before the day of wrath comes—the day of calamity and misery, great and exceedingly bitter.

### Verse 6

**For wrath is in his indignation, and life in his favor.** Before the wrath of his indignation comes, confess to the memorial of his holiness. That is, confess to the memorial of his holiness for this very reason: because he remembered to sanctify you when you were not mindful of him. Unless he had remembered you, O his saints, he would not have said in his prayer: “And for them I sanctify myself, that they also may be holy in truth” (John 17:19). Again: “Father, sanctify them in truth; [Col. 1257D] your word is truth” (ibid., 17).

Therefore, because he remembered you so that you might be sanctified, you who are his saints, attributing to him the fact that you are holy, confess to the memorial of his holiness. For as “the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine” (John 15:4), so neither can you have holiness from yourselves, nor can you be truly holy in any way unless you receive it from him and have it in him, so that you may be holy. Therefore let us go before his face in confession before the day of wrath comes. **For wrath is in his indignation.**

Since wrath and indignation are motions of a disturbed mind, they are in no way to be thought fitting for God, to whom it is truly said: “But you, O Lord, judge with tranquility and order all things with great reverence; for when you will, power is at your disposal” [Col. 1258A] (Wis. 12:18). Yet his just vengeance, although carried out with the tranquility of one judging, appears to those punished to be wrath and indignation—especially to those who are wrathful and indignant. For just as God appears holy to the holy and chosen to the chosen, so he appears perverse to the perverse, wrathful to the wrathful, and indignant to the indignant, although he himself, as has been said, judges in tranquility, without wrath, indignation, or any disturbance of his mind.

Do you, then, O human being, wish not to feel that God is angry or indignant with you? If you wish this, beware of wrath in yourself, which makes you liable to judgment. For if you do not extinguish wrath, from prolonged wrath bubbles forth “Raca” (Matt. 5:22), which makes you liable to the council. After “Raca” follows indignation, by which you are indignant with your brother as though he were a fool. Blinded by hatred, you then judge and call him a fool even in things that perhaps he simply does or says; for that utterance you will be liable to the fire of Gehenna (ibid.).

In the fire of Gehenna you will feel God’s wrath and indignation, proceeding rather from your own disturbance than from his. Just as Cain, enraged against his brother Abel with such violent wrath that his face fell and wasted away, heard God speaking to him in wrath and saying: “Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen? You have sinned; be still” (Gen. 4:6). “Be still” was aptly said to one exceedingly angry, because he was far from stillness, having quarrels in his heart.

But because he was unwilling to be still or to yield to God’s rebuke, through wrath he came as far as fratricide. By this example we are warned either not to have wrath or to end it as swiftly as possible, lest wrath grow into hatred, make a beam out of a speck, and make our soul a murderer: “For whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

Perhaps here, to excuse excuses in sins, you who are easily angered object to me: “I am not angry with my brother as Cain was, but with my brother’s vice.” You speak well, if it is as you say. For in discovering, judging, and punishing the faults of our brethren, we ought earnestly to act with love for persons and hatred for faults. But in this your conscience bears witness whether you are truly moved by charity: namely, if you are in no way indignant with a sinning brother, but sympathize with him in affection. For true justice has compassion; false justice has disdain. [Col. 1258D] If, therefore, you are moved by disdain, you falsely claim for yourself something like zeal for justice, when you are driven by zeal for wickedness. But how will you prove that you have compassion rather than indignation toward your brother? Clearly, if you take greater pleasure in pouring out to Christ the propitiator words of prayer for him than in pouring out to some conversational companion words of detraction against him. Moreover, if you delight in reproaching, judging rashly, and not praying, know that you are full of indignation and a stranger to compassion. Therefore, because you waste away in anger and indignation against your brother, unless you are corrected by repentance, you too will experience as your judge one who is angry and indignant with you. “For wrath is in his indignation.” But if you are moved by compassion for your sinning brother, so that your will toward him contains a desire for [Col. 1259A] a good life—because you desire and wish him to live blessedly, pleasantly, and prosperously—you too will experience the same from God, because “life is in his will.” Behold what a recompense this is. Your brother’s blessed and honorable life is already in your will; yet you cannot immediately, merely because you will it, confer such a life upon him or obtain from God for him the life you wish. But God, because he is almighty and has power whenever he wills, rewards you with such a recompense that your life is in his will, and that you live only as he wills and as is beneficial for you, because only the life ordained in his will is blessed.

Let us therefore beware of anger and indignation against our brethren, if we fear the anger and indignation of God; for wrath is in the indignation of him who is angry and indignant with the angry and indignant. [Col. 1259B] In the fratricide Cain we have offered an example of original anger, from which many derivative forms of anger afflict every evil person against every good person, while Cain, as it were, still wastes away against Abel. And since we have given a clear example among human beings of original anger—for the devil had been angry with the godly because he had been cast out of heaven—let us also give a clear example of original indignation, from which the derivation of the many indignations afflicting human hearts may be recognized. Eve is found to have been the first among human beings to be indignant because she was forbidden to eat from the tree of knowledge. For unless such indignation had first existed in her breast, the cunning serpent would not have had material with which to tempt her by these words: “Why did God command you not to eat from [Col. 1259C] every tree of paradise?” (Gen. 3:1). But because the shrewd investigator had perceived her indignation at the prohibition of a single tree, he seduced her by tempting her into presumptuously tasting that same forbidden tree, with the false promise that, from that point on, possessing knowledge of good and evil equally with God, she would have no need to learn anything from God or to be subject to him. From this original indignation many indignations have been derived and multiplied among the sons and daughters of Adam and Eve.

Concerning these indignations, it is desirable, for the sake of urging caution, to speak at greater length, beginning with the temptations by which the human breast is provoked to indignation—unless both the serpent’s head is crushed by the woman, [Col. 1259D] that is, by sensuality, and the serpent himself, afterward lying in wait for the woman’s heel, is most carefully guarded against. What is the serpent’s head but the beginning of a perverse and seductive suggestion? For example, he first suggested to the first human beings a covetous appetite for forbidden food, a curious desire for divine knowledge, and a presumptuous desire for divine likeness. By this suggestion, as by the serpent’s head, the woman—that is, human sensuality in the first human beings—was enticed; she was also delighted by the serpent’s belly and bound by his tail. Thus, having conquered the woman through the delight and consent involved in such a suggestion, he drew her as though chained into indignation. For with how great an indignation, do you suppose, was she moved when she who had disdained to be subject to God heard it said to her: “You shall be under your husband’s power, [Col. 1260A] and he shall rule over you” (Gen. 3:16)? Since she was taken from the man’s side, she is rightly understood to have been created as his companion. For if she had been taken from the man’s head, she might have seemed his mistress; if from his foot, his servant. But now, although created as his companion, through fault she was made a servant, so that it was said to her: “You shall be under your husband’s power, and he shall rule over you.”

Yet it is true that where this subjection is adorned by humility, such humiliation of the woman is transformed into humility; as in the Blessed Virgin Mary, who, although knowing no man, nevertheless appeared among men as betrothed to Joseph and subject to him as to a husband. She was so dutiful toward him that he was thought to be Jesus’ father. Nor was that blessed woman so indignant with those who thought this that she herself called him [Col. 1260B] Jesus’ father, saying to her son: “Behold, your father and I have been seeking you in sorrow” (Luke 2:48). It should certainly be noted that she put her husband first under the name of father, and humbly placed herself after him, though she was the lady of the angels. She was so wholly free from every vice of indignation that, although herself undefiled, she did not disdain to observe the discipline appointed for defiled mothers, until, when the apostles were preaching, she was shown to be exalted not only above human beings but even above the choirs of angels. This too we proclaim when we sing: “You have been exalted, holy Mother of God, above the choirs of angels to the heavenly kingdoms.” Therefore this woman, blessed among women, was neither enticed by the serpent’s head through suggestion, nor delighted by its belly through [Col. 1260C] pleasure, nor bound by its tail through consent. Hence she did not fear him lying in wait for her heel.

But because it appears more clearly in the son of this woman how this serpent must be crushed in its head and guarded against in its tail, by which it lies in wait for the heel—that is, for the human being’s end—let us look upon him in whom this serpent, finding nothing of its own, nevertheless presumed to approach with its head through suggestion. It tempted him: first, by the enticement of gluttony after a fast of forty days and nights; second, by the vice of curiosity, saying to him, “Cast yourself down” (Matt. 4:6); third, by ambition, [Col. 1260D] showing him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. But because through these chief temptations the prince of this world found nothing of his own in Christ, he turned to contrary arguments and trials, wishing to bind him with his tail. For to him to whom he had personally suggested a desire for well-flavored bread, he afterward offered through impious men exceedingly bitter gall and vinegar, in order to make him indignant at this. Him whom he had earlier set on the pinnacle of the Temple and urged, by a needless miracle, to become a spectacle for the curious eyes of the Jews, he afterward deprived of sights by veiling his face and covering his eyes, provoking him to a movement of indignation. To him whom he had earlier offered all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, enticing him to eminence, he afterward caused to be rejected by the Jews, who chose [Col. 1261A] rather Caesar as king, or even Barabbas the robber, than him, wishing in this way to provoke him to indignation.

As the malignant serpent did in the Head, so it does also in the members. Those whom it cannot conquer by delights, so that they may indulge lust, it tempts through bitter things, so that they themselves may become bitter and indignant with others. Those whom it cannot conquer by curious things, so as to delight them with a spectacle, it sometimes deprives of every spectacle, so that, while they neither gaze curiously themselves nor are curiously gazed upon by others, they are afflicted with weariness of an obscure life, entertain gnawing cares, and become indignant because they are not conspicuous in this world. Those whom it cannot conquer by ambition, by showing them all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, it provokes to indignation by causing [Col. 1261B] them to be rejected and others to be exalted, whether better than themselves or even worse. Indeed, when better persons are chosen while good persons are rejected, they ought to be no more indignant than Joseph, who was surnamed Justus, was indignant when Barnabas was chosen and he himself rejected (Acts 1:23). Unless such indignation is guarded against in such persons, the soul’s salvation is endangered through God’s indignation and wrath, because wrath is in his indignation. For Dathan and Abiram perished through such indignation when Aaron was chosen. Saul, rejected while David was chosen, perished through such indignation; he did not look on David with right eyes, being indignant because a thousand were ascribed to Saul and ten thousand to David in the women’s song of praise (1 Sam. 18:7). The scribes and Pharisees perished through such indignation when they heard [Col. 1261C] that tax collectors and prostitutes would go before them into the kingdom of God. The Jews, formerly chosen but afterward rejected, perished through such indignation when they were filled with the zeal of indignation against the Gentiles who had been chosen. The apostles themselves were touched by such indignation when they were angry with the good woman for her good work, saying, “Why this waste?” (Matt. 26:8). But because, when the Lord rebuked them, they recognized that the woman had done a good work, they did not perish. On account of such indignation, the evil eye of those who had borne the burden and heat of the day is reproved: they were indignant that the last, who had labored little, should be made equal in reward to themselves, who had labored much, though they had not been equal in labor (Matt. 20:12). The Pharisee puffed up against the tax collector perished through such indignation; and [Col. 1261D] another Pharisee is reproved, indignant at the sinful woman who touched and anointed the Lord’s feet. Although he may have appeared to himself to be moved by zeal for justice, in the Lord’s judgment he was moved by zeal for genuine malice and false justice, because true justice has compassion, while false justice has disdain—even though the just rightly are accustomed to be indignant with sinners (Luke 18:11). But one thing is done through zeal for justice, another through the pattern of pride. The just are indignant, indeed, but not disdainful; they despair, but are not despairing; because, while outwardly they are severe in rebuke, inwardly they love through compassion. Thus they conduct themselves between love for persons and hatred for faults, showing charity toward people and severity toward faults: gladly praying for the salvation of those [Col. 1262A] whose faults they pursue in rebuke. By contrast, those like the Pharisees, moved by anger and indignation without the compassion of love, despise sinners—sinners who are certainly so much better than their despisers as they are gentler under their contempt.

Many nobles perish by such indignation when God chooses the ignoble and contemptible things of the world in order to confound the strong, and the things that are not in order to destroy the things that are. Even one sister began to be indignant with another: Martha with Mary, because Mary, attending to the word of God, had left her alone to serve (Luke 10:40). But when Mary’s portion was praised by divine judgment, Martha’s indignation ceased. Let us therefore recognize that Mary’s portion is praiseworthy, without holding her sister Martha’s portion blameworthy. Let us mutually [Col. 1262B] exhort one another not to be puffed up or become indignant against each other because of the differing dignity of offices pertaining either to action or to contemplation. “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God,” since it is not he himself who speaks, but the Holy Spirit; “if anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength which God supplies” (1 Pet. 4:11), so that in all things God may be honored and one person may not be puffed up or indignant against another. Those to whom it is given to perform good work in one community should not be indignant at those who are profitably at rest. Those to whom it is given to be at leisure and see that the Lord is sweet should not be indignant at brothers or sisters who work well; rather, let them strive to glory not in the dignity of their own spiritual leisure, but in fellowship with their laboring brothers and sisters. [Col. 1262C] And if they cannot do mighty works after the example of the strong woman who “put her hand to mighty things,” let there be in them love, which, if it is strong as death in a mortal and frail body, will never be hateful, even though all the members are weakened through debility or sickness.

Thus, in the homilies of the blessed Pope Gregory, we read of a certain little servant and a certain Romula, gravely ill through the wasting away of all their limbs. Yet, just as the saints through faith conquered kingdoms, did righteousness, and obtained promises, so in these persons, through faith working by love—not through work of the hands but through the work of patience—the kingdom of sin was conquered and the kingdom of justice brought to completion. This [Col. 1262D] was openly shown in their glorious departure from this life. Therefore, where charity is joined with faith and hope, idleness will be far away, because love is never idle. For if it exists, it accomplishes great things; but if it refuses to work, it is not love. The work of the hands sometimes works without ceasing when it is able, but the work of faith works continually. Concerning this, when the Jews asked the Lord in the Gospel what they ought to do, he said: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent” (John 6:29). Again: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which remains” (ibid., 27). We work for this food as often as we meditate on the law of the Lord: gathering divine words like selected grains, winnowing and grinding them, sprinkling them with the waters of tears, and baking them in the oven of the mind through the fire of divine love.
