[Col. 1263A] “Work,” he says, “for the food that remains,” because the charity of truth remains forever, just as truth itself remains forever. We work this charity when, kindled in love of justice by setting ourselves and others aflame with divine words as though with torches, we make progress, so that we may burn and shine after the example of him of whom it was said: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 3:5). Burning, that is, with charity; shining with humility, in which he said that he was not worthy to loose the strap of the divine sandal. Thus, wherever burning charity is found, shining humility will always be its companion. For the flame of charity, wholly free from the smoke of pride, sends forth from itself the purest rays of humility, upon which the Lord looks familiarly, as though close at hand—he who knows lofty things from afar [Col. 1263B] (Ps. 137:6). May the Lord grant that we observe humility and charity, whether we work little or much; for through humility the dignities of others become ours, and through charity the works of others become ours.

But while we learned persons reap temporal benefits from industrious workers and laborers, it is fitting and just that they should reap our spiritual benefits; and Mary’s leisure should be reckoned to Martha’s merit, because Mary could not be at leisure and delight in God’s word without the assistance of her laboring sister, anxious and troubled about many things so that the other sister might have leisure without disturbance. “Be at leisure [variant: Taste],” says the Psalmist, “and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9). Be at leisure—not in restless wanderings, [Col. 1263C] not in vain conversations or most wicked detractions, in which one does not taste that the Lord is sweet—but in readings, prayers, diligent and holy meditations, and other spiritual exercises, especially devout celebrations of Mass and diligent preparations for their celebration. For example: writing books, arranging illuminations, fitting sacred vestments, and preparing other utensils pertaining to the adornment of God’s house or the needs of those who serve in it; or things expressing mystical meanings there and symbolizing invisible grace in visible form. In all these things one tastes that the Lord is sweet. Truly the Lord is sweet and gentle, who by the sweet and pleasant bond of charity causes all the members to agree together as one, so that when one member is glorified all members rejoice together, and if one member suffers all members suffer with it.

May divine mercy therefore strengthen us in holy charity. In holy humility, may he be present with us who possess childlike simplicity: that angel who was with the three boys in the furnace, shook off the flame of the fire, and made the midst of the furnace like a wind blowing with dew. [Col. 1263D] “And the fire did not touch them at all, nor did it grieve them or cause them any distress” (Dan. 3:49). So may the fire of anger, bitterness, and indignation not touch us or cause us any distress, however greatly the king of Babylon may increase its fuel in the furnace of this world. Rather, just as those three praised and glorified God as though with one mouth, so may we also, with concord reigning among us, praise and glorify God as though with one mouth: men with women, learned with unlearned, those who work well with those who are well at leisure—each in his own order singing the hymn of the three boys, which they sang in the fiery furnace while blessing the Lord. Let these inserted remarks on avoiding the vice of anger and indignation suffice for the present, lest by becoming angry or indignant we actually incur the anger and indignation of God, which we contracted originally from Adam. For the wrath, or affliction, or punishment by which God avenged the first sin was in his indignation. For he was, as it were, indignant because they disregarded the warning [Col. 1264A] in which he had said: “On the day when you eat from the tree, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17).

“And life is in [his] will,” that is, in the fulfillment of God’s will, which he alone fulfilled perfectly who, for us, paid to the eternal Father Adam’s debt and wiped away the bond of the ancient offense with his merciful blood. But God’s anger is not without hope of grace, because life follows: it is given, in his will, to you who are unable to return to it—that is, not according to your own powers or merits.

Yet that life will not be given immediately; rather, weeping will remain, and the rest. Individual elements correspond to individual elements. Because wrath is in his indignation, therefore weeping remains until evening. And because life is in his will, therefore joy comes in the morning.

[Col. 1264C] Evening is when the sun declines after noon toward its setting. Then the light of wisdom withdrew from the human being who sinned, and he was condemned to death. From that time weeping lasts as long as the people born from Adam wait in travail for the morning of the future resurrection; and then there will be joy, because then the Lord will wipe every tear from the eyes of the saints. Christ rose in the morning as a sign of that morning joy.

The first resurrection of the soul is also signified by this. For just as Christ, buried in the evening not through fault but through punishment, rose on the morning of the third day, so the human being who sinned in the evening and was, as it were, buried in paradise because he was condemned to death, after the period [Col. 1264D] before the Law and the period under the Law, on the third day—that is, in the time of grace—received the light of faith and rises in soul from the death of sin in this morning. Thus the resurrection that occurred in the morning, by which all are made alive in Christ, is the cause of the joy that remains in the morning; just as the death and burial brought about according to the old Adam, in whom all die, are the cause of the weeping that remains until evening.

For both weeping and joy remain, because neither weeping nor joy ends in a short time, but each lasts for a longer delay. From that most sorrowful evening in which Adam, expelled from paradise, incurred the cause of mourning, all his children went on their way weeping, uttering their first cry of weeping when they were born into this world; and so they departed weeping from this [Col. 1265A] world into hell. If at any time they laughed during the span of this life, their laughter was mingled with pain, and mourning overtook the end of their joy. Hence also that saying in another Psalm: “My tears were my bread by day and by night” (Ps. 41:4). Where days and nights are continued in weeping, does not weeping remain from evening to evening? Does not weeping remain where no interval is granted to laughter? For even if people sometimes laugh in this life full of miseries, the very fact that they laugh, or are able to laugh, is something to be wept over. To remedy this persistent weeping, the finger of God wrote the Law containing the Ten Commandments. Because it showed the wounds of sins but did not heal them, and brought nothing to perfection, it not only did not take away the persistent weeping but increased it. [Col. 1265B] For just as the sick were exposed in the five porticoes beside the sheep-pool but were not healed, so sinners were accused through the five books of Moses but were not cured. Therefore weeping remained until Christ, who showed in himself how great is the cause for weeping in this world because of death and mortality, into which Adam fell after noon toward evening. He himself wept with human feeling over the dead Lazarus, though by divine power he was about to raise him. For weeping and sorrow extended to that evening in which Christ died and was buried for our sins. Descending into hell, where the people of the saints were held captive in death, he was greeted in a tearful voice by those saying: “You have come, O desired one, whom we awaited in darkness, that you might lead forth tonight those bound from their prisons. Our sighs call for you; abundant laments sought you. You have become hope for the despairing, m. c. in torments.” [Uncertain abbreviation or corrupt reading: “m. c.”]

At that time one gate of hell, which is the death of the soul, was already being destroyed, when the dawn of joy shone upon the souls of the saints hitherto mourning in hell. For “a light has arisen for those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death” (Isa. 9:2), when Christ descended through his soul into hell, the life and light of souls. But joy was not yet complete, because the other gate of hell still stood—namely, the death of bodies—for no one had yet risen never to die again. Therefore, in the morning when Christ, the firstborn of the dead, rose [Col. 1265D] from the dead no longer to die, when many bodies of saints rose with him, and the way of resurrection was opened in Christ for all who die in Adam, then, with the other gate of death destroyed, the day of joy shone forth fully. Of it it is elsewhere said: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. 117:24). Let us exult in bodily gesture because of the resurrection of bodies; let us rejoice in the mind’s affection because of the resurrection of souls.

Certainly it may be believed that the true Samson rose at midnight, and at midnight struck Egypt—that is, hell—when all things held deep silence and the night was halfway through its course. Yet until morning there remained the weeping of Mary weeping at the tomb, of the other women weeping with her, and of the apostles themselves mourning and weeping. But as dawn approached morning, the light of joy began to come to them, though there still remained a little darkness of sorrow. For when angels appeared and the Lord was seen by the devout women, and as the report of the resurrection grew more frequent through the testimony of the angels, from that time, with sorrow’s darkness driven away, joy remains until morning. For the resurrection attested to us by angels in the morning is reserved for the end of the world, when all who die with Christ will also rise with him and be made alive in him. Then, after the evening of this dark age, in the clear morning of the age to come, that great dedication of the whole house of David will be completed, [Col. 1266B] which has already taken place in its foundation, Christ’s body raised from the dead. Then weeping will remain at evening for those who will then grieve that the world which they loved has an evening, that is, an end. Then joy will remain in the morning for those who, rejoicing, will see that the future age, which they loved after despising the world, has a beginning. Both will remain—weeping and joy—because those to whom it will then be said in that evening, “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41), will always weep; and those to whom it will be said in that morning, “Come, you blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., 34), will always rejoice. For one and the same judgment will be evening for some, [Col. 1266C] morning for others. “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to eternal life and others to reproach, that they may see forever” (Dan. 12:2). For those who awake to eternal life, the resurrection and judgment will be like morning and a certain beginning of that day of which it is said: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11). But for those who awake to reproach, that they may see forever, the resurrection and judgment will be like a most dark evening: the beginning, namely, of everlasting night and of those darknesses of which it is said, “And the wicked shall be silent in darkness” (1 Sam. 2:9).

This difference in the future resurrection arises from the difference of dissimilar ways of life. For some live [Col. 1266D] in this world in such a way that they establish their own day for themselves in this world’s desire. Such was earthly Jerusalem, over whose destruction the Lord wept, saying: “If only you too had known, and indeed on this your day, the things that make for your peace” (Luke 19:42). The unbelieving soul has its own day here, for whom worldly desire is sweet. But when the world and its desire pass away, then evening will come for it, when it is sent into outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth; and then weeping will remain, when there is a long duration in eternal punishments for most short-lived desires. By contrast, those who do not have their own day in this world, who through the night of anxious temporality desire to come to the day of eternity, when the world and its desire pass away [Col. 1267A] hear the Lord say to them: “But when you see these things happening, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near” (Luke 21:28). When they are told, “Look up,” is not the morning light shown to them, by which the hearts of those whose redemption draws near as the world perishes will be made glad? Then everlasting joy will be shown them in exchange for the temporal and brief sorrow which they endured in this world—a world they did not love—when the day of eternity for which they longed shines forth.

**VERSE 7.** But I said in my abundance, “I shall not be moved forever.” Weeping will remain for those whose house will not be dedicated, because their resurrected body, made to live forever, will not be changed [Col. 1267B] through glory so as to rejoice forever. But I, the true David, merited for myself and my own a solemn dedication—that is, the glorification of resurrected bodies—because I said in my abundance: “I shall not be moved forever.” In others, who have been moved away from God by the foot of pride or by the hand of a sinner that moves them, weeping will remain; but in me weeping will not remain, because I, Christ, in my abundance—that is, in confidence in the divinity abundant in me, whose fullness abounds in me—said this: “I shall not be moved from God, by whom Adam was moved. I shall not be moved,” I say, “forever,” that is, never. And I could say this confidently. For you, Lord, granted strength to my beauty. First you granted [Col. 1267C] my beauty the glory of immunity from sin, when I was conceived by the Holy Spirit. You also granted that beauty of mine the power to work miracles. But that the strength of my flesh was from your will—that is, from the Holy Spirit, who is your will and mine, through whose operation I was conceived—is proved by the fact that my flesh was troubled in itself when, though the spirit was ready for the Passion, it nevertheless was weak. Hence I said: “The spirit indeed is ready, but the flesh is weak” (Mark 14:38). Then I was made troubled, not unto sin, but by the punishment of the flesh: weakness was troubled when I began to be afraid and wearied. No human being has grounds for presumption; even Christ confesses that strength and beauty are given by the Lord. When you turn away, Lord, I am troubled, and therefore, O Lord, I shall cry to you concerning the glory of the flesh, and to you, my God, [Col. 1267D] I shall pray concerning immortality, saying: “What profit is there in my blood,” and so forth.

These words can also be understood in the person of the members, and this is the reason why weeping remains: namely, because I, the people who spoke in Adam, set amid the abundance of delights in paradise, when the Lord said, “On the day when you eat, you shall die,” and the devil, on the contrary, said, “You shall not die by death” (Gen. 2:17), believed the devil rather and said: “I shall not be moved from this good forever, but I shall be like God.” Yet, O Lord, what I was, I was not from myself, but you—

**VERSE 8.** In your will you granted strength to my beauty. From you I was beautiful and strong. This I learned [Col. 1268A] from the fact that, when you turned your face away from me as I sinned, deprived of the light of your knowledge and cast out of paradise, I was made troubled. And I who, enjoying blessings in paradise, praised you, now, O Lord, cast out and groaning, shall cry to you both in myself and in my Head, who, about to die for me, now says:

**VERSE 9.** To you, Lord, I shall cry. What follows, “And to my God I shall make supplication,” means the same thing.

**VERSE 10.** What profit is there in my blood—that is, in the shedding of my blood, which was shed without fault—when I descend into corruption? That is, if I do not rise immediately, if my body is corrupted by decay, if the temple of my body, dissolved by death, is not dedicated through the glory of resurrection, there will be no profit; for I shall be able to gain no one, and thus [Col. 1268B] the confession of you will perish. Therefore I ask that I may not descend into corruption, because “Will dust confess you?” If I remain dust, confession will perish. Proclamation also perishes. For will dust proclaim, for the salvation of others, your truth which you promised for the restoration of the human race? Or will dust—that is, the dead mass of the ungodly, who are to be justified by my Resurrection—remaining dust, confess you, and so forth?

There is a twofold confession without which we should never be: confession of sins and confession of praise. In tribulation let us confess sins; in exaltation, let us confess praise of God’s mercy. But both confessions perish in those to whom the dedication of the house does not belong—that is, that transformation of which the Apostle says: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51). Again: “The dead,” he says, “will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (ibid., 52). All the dead will indeed rise incorruptible—that is, whole, possessing an incorrupt body, with no part of their natural integrity diminished. But not all will be changed into the glory of angelic blessedness, of which the devil and his angels are deprived although their nature remains whole; likewise human beings who are joined to them, though they rise incorruptible—that is, whole—will be deprived of it. Therefore the Apostle says: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed.” But those who are changed will be dedicated, so that they may be a royal hall of such beauty [Col. 1268D] that God himself, who is true beauty, may dwell in them; and of such spaciousness that he whom the whole world cannot contain may walk in them. Hence he says: “For I shall dwell in them and walk among them, and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people” (2 Cor. 6:16). Then God will wipe every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither mourning (Rev. 21:4).

But now, before the time of this dedication, while this house is being built which will then be dedicated, tears are frequent and mourning continual, while weeping always remains until evening and joy until morning. For, without setting aside the higher sense concerning this evening and morning treated above, even amid the changing conditions of daily life, the soul experiences evening as often as it suffers a deficiency in charity; and charity itself, that virtue, is forced toward its setting, contrary to the Apostle’s counsel: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4:26). But when the soul breathes again through repentance, the sun of justice—whose entire brightness and splendor lie in charity—drives away the evening and makes morning, sometimes so brilliant that a person says in his abundance: “I shall not be moved forever.” Thus I, the Apostle Peter, said in my abundance: “I shall not be moved forever.” For when I seemed to myself to abound in Christ’s charity, in that very abundance I said: “Even if I must die with you, I shall not deny you” (Matt. 26:35).

Again: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will not be scandalized” [Col. 1269B] (ibid., 33). Again: “I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death” (Luke 22:33). Thus, speaking in my abundance—that is, presumptuously concerning myself—I said: “I shall never be moved.” But when temptation came through the maidservant, the flood struck against my house and was able to shake it, because it had not yet been founded upon the firm rock through charity, which is strong as death (Song 8:6). Had I then possessed this charity, I should not have been so easily shaken by fear of death, because charity, strong as death, would have cast that fear of death outside.

But because I was shaken in Caiaphas’s courtyard amid the servants of wickedness who mocked and spat upon my Lord, when he himself looked upon me, I went out and wept bitterly. Then weeping lingered with me until evening; and there was for me [Col. 1269C] great lamentation and wailing, grievously increasing toward evening, when I knew my Lord to be dead and buried, and knew myself to be dead in soul. From this twofold sorrow, some small joy consoled me and shone forth in that morning, when the angel remaining at the Lord’s tomb expressly and by name mentioned the disciples—and me in particular—saying: “Go, tell his disciples and Peter” (Mark 16:7), “that the Lord has risen” (Matt. 28:7). But when he appeared especially to me, and this saying became famous among the disciples, so that they said: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Peter,” then indeed I had joy more than morning-joy, now that the sun had risen—not only through Christ’s resurrection made manifest to me [Col. 1269D], but also through my own instruction concerning myself.

For from that time, made wiser, I no longer presumed upon my abundance by saying, “I shall never be moved”; rather, when presumption had passed, I said: “Lord, in your good pleasure you bestowed strength upon my beauty,” making me—not by my merit, but by your will—from a fisherman into a preacher and a worker of miracles. But because in my abundance I presumed, thinking that I possessed an abundance of the strength of charity beyond the other apostles, you turned your face away from me, and I was troubled by denying the truth three times, because I had not yet possessed perfect charity for Truth himself. I did indeed have some charity for the truth, but not yet an abundant charity. For if I [Col. 1270A] had been perfected in charity, I should by no means have denied him.

There are three degrees of charity. If even one of them is lacking, those who have begun to love one another easily recoil from charity. Let us take the example of these degrees from the Son of God himself, who came to us in true and perfected charity. His charity was first sweet, then prudent, and finally strong: so sweet that, for the sake of the human beings whom he loved, he assumed not only human nature but also human misery. So prudent that, although sharing human nature and misery, he in no way shared human guilt; for he was indeed a man, yet “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22). Indeed, though he burned wholly with love [Col. 1270B] for humankind, zeal for God’s house consumed him because of human vices.

Moreover, although his charity was so sweet and prudent—so that he burned wholly with love of people and hatred of vices—he might have been turned from that sweet and prudent love when provoked by the injuries and insults of those whose nature he befriended and whose vices he opposed, unless his love had been strong as death (Song 8:6). But because his love was strong as death, just as death is an incurable sickness, so his love was unconquerable. And as many medicines do not overcome death, so the many waters that entered even into his soul could not extinguish charity in him. Hence upon the cross he prayed for his murderers, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what [Col. 1270C] they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

He assumed their nature through sweet charity; through prudent and wise charity he undertook to instruct their folly; dying for them, and knowing that they had inflicted death upon him, he prayed for them through strong charity. Was not this charity strong as death? Indeed, it might be called stronger than death: death did not overcome it, but it overcame death—except that charity itself, though stronger than bodily death, is the death of vices. It is therefore strong as death, because it is the strongest death of vices: loving a friend in God and an enemy for God’s sake. Unless Christ, suffering torments for his friends, had loved them in God, he would never have prayed for them, saying: “Father, keep in [Col. 1270D] your name those whom you have given me” (John 17:11). For because he knew them to be in God, he rightly asked that they be preserved in him, saying: “Father, while I was with them, I kept those whom you gave me. But now I come to you. I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil” (John 17:13, 15).

Again, unless I had loved my enemies for God’s sake, I should not have said on the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do.” These enemies were not yet in God; therefore they could not be loved in him, but they were loved for God’s sake, when prayer was offered for them that through forgiveness of sins they might come into God. And because strong charity prayed for what it willed, it obtained it. For very many of those who shed Christ’s blood afterward faithfully drank that same blood [Col. 1271A]; and those who had been defiled by blood were cleansed by blood.

We have contemplated Christ’s sweet, prudent, and strong charity in himself, as in its fountain. Let us now see the same charity, as it were, flowing out into the disciples. Wishing them surely to become like himself in charity, after saying to them, “This is my commandment, that you love one another,” he added: “as I have loved you” (John 15:12). It is as though he said: “As I have loved you sweetly, prudently, and strongly, so you too should love one another.” Again: “A new commandment I give you, that you love one another, as I have loved you” (John 13:34).

In Christ, as in the fountain of this love, the whole fullness was infused together and at once from the stream of fatherly mercy and never underwent diminution, [Col. 1271B] remaining at once in the Word and flowing at once into the man united with the Word. But in the disciples it was variable: sometimes they had the sweetness of charity but lacked prudence. At other times, while retaining the sweetness of charity by which they loved what was good, and the prudence by which they hated evil, they lacked the very strength by whose absence charity wavered.

For example, on account of the great sweetness of charity, the apostle Peter says: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:27). But still insufficiently prudent, and not knowing that Christ’s love required following his will in everything, he tried to turn away the Lord who wished to die for us, saying: “Far be it from you,” when Christ had said that he would be scourged and crucified (Matt. 16:22). Again, when Christ came to Peter [Col. 1271C] in order to wash the disciples’ feet, Peter said to him: “You shall never wash my feet” (John 13:8). He spoke thus with affectionate delight, yet imprudently, because Christ was to die according to the counsel of his wisdom, and by his blood, with water flowing from his side, was to wash not Peter’s feet alone but all the elect. Concerning this washing he says to Peter: “Unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me” (ibid.).

He could similarly have said to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—to every human being to be saved—“Unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me,” because no human being enters the kingdom of heaven except through the washing of blood and water flowing from Christ’s side. This washing was also awaited in the underworld by the elect who were to be washed, cleansed, and liberated by it. Therefore the prophet Zechariah, speaking to Christ himself, says: “You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there was no water” (Zech. 6:11). Ignorant of this mystery, Peter said less prudently: “You shall never wash my feet” (John 13:8). And the Lord said: “What I do, you do not know now, but you shall know afterward” (ibid., 7). Again: “Unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me.” By these words Peter, made more prudent, assented to that act of the master which he had first considered almost absurd.

Peter was now established in sweet and prudent love, yet unaware of his own weakness and excessively forward [Col. 1272A] and presumptuous. Therefore he thought that he could not only follow Christ’s death, which he had previously tried to dissuade him from accepting, but even go before him into it, saying: “I will lay down my life for you” (ibid., 37). But because his love still lacked strength, he denied in his failure what he had declared in his abundance: “I,” he says, “said in my abundance: ‘I shall never be moved.’ I said: ‘Even if I must die with you, I shall not deny you’” (Matt. 26:35). Because of this very presumption, you, O God, turned your face away from me, and I was troubled when I feared to die and denied life.

Therefore, in speaking thus, Peter still possessed none of that strength of charity whose sweetness he already possessed. But afterward, strengthened alike in the sweetness, prudence, and strength of charity, when the Lord asked him for the third time concerning his love, he confessed it—as though the Lord had said: “Peter, do you love me sweetly? Do you love me prudently or wisely? Do you love me strongly?”—and he answered: “I love you with sweet love; I love you with prudent love; I love you with strong love” (John 21:17). And the Lord, approving the strength of his charity by which he would overcome death, said: “When you were young, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish” (ibid., 18).

What is shown in Peter alone is evident also in the other apostles: they received first the sweetness of charity, then wisdom or prudence, and finally strength. For while the Son of God still lived in mortal flesh, hearing his [Col. 1272C] preaching and seeing his wondrous works, they sucked honey from the rock—namely, the very sweetness of his love. After he rose from the dead and had become immortal, they again sucked “oil from the hardest rock” (Deut. 32:13), when on the day of resurrection he breathed upon them, gave them the Holy Spirit, and opened their understanding to understand the Scriptures. For their love still lacked wisdom when they did not understand from the Scriptures that Christ had to suffer, thus enter into his glory, and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins had to be preached in his name. But when, as has been said, “he opened their understanding to understand the Scriptures,” and, beginning from Moses and all the prophets, interpreted the Scriptures to them [Col. 1272D] (Luke 24:27), those who had previously been foolish and slow of heart to believe, having abandoned folly and received wisdom, perceived that they had sucked oil from the hardest rock—or from the firm rock—which, while still weak in mortal flesh, had previously nursed them only with the honeyed sweetness of his love. That oil rightly signifies wisdom is sufficiently clear from the fact that those virgins are called wise whose vessels abound with oil, while those are foolish whose vessels lack oil—that is, in their consciences (Matt. 25:4).

See now how little steadfastness there was in apostles enriched in this way by honey and oil—that is, by sweetness of charity and wisdom. Surely they had then already tested the truth of the resurrection by sight and touch, Christ saying to them [Col. 1273A]: “See my hands and my feet.” Again: “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39). As has been said, they had already received honey and oil, and yet they did not dare publicly to confess or preach what they knew. Knowing this weakness of theirs, the Lord himself said to them: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (ibid., 49). The power from on high was the strength of the Holy Spirit, which Christ, ascending on high, sent into that upper room where the apostles had until then been weak. From that time, having received the Spirit of strength, they became through sweet, prudent, and strong charity fit to bear witness to the truth throughout the whole world in every language—those who earlier had not dared to confess Christ even in Judea alone, [Col. 1273B] or in the one Hebrew language.

“The Lord is faithful in all his words, and holy in all his works.” For, as it was faithfully said, so it was faithfully done. It was said of the apostles that they should suck honey from the rock, oil from the hardest rock, and drink the purest blood of the grape (Deut. 32:13). In accordance with the truth of this prophecy, as has been explained, when the apostles had been nourished and fed with honey and oil, and strength alone was lacking, on the day of Pentecost he who, as the rock, had poured out streams of honey and oil for the apostles to drink from the spiritual rock that followed them (1 Cor. 10:4), became for them the grape. Intoxicated by its purest blood, they were thought and said to be [Col. 1273C] full of new wine. Then Peter, explaining this miracle by which those speaking in various languages were thought drunk, said: “These are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day; rather, this is what was spoken through Joel” (Acts 2:15): “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.”

By these words he did not deny that they were altogether intoxicated, but denied that they were intoxicated as the observers supposed, who thought them full of earthly new wine. They were in fact so intoxicated with the spiritual new wine of the Holy Spirit, in the purest blood of the grape, that, forgetting and through excessive intoxication becoming unmindful of concern for worldly things—and, what is more, of their own injuries and insults—they went rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been counted worthy to suffer insult for the name of God [Col. 1273D] (Acts 5:41). From that time, strengthened by grain and wine, they remained strong and unconquerable and were able, like those intoxicated, to rejoice amid adversities.

After the apostles, all who strive for perfection must proceed in such an order: first they too must suck honey from the rock, then oil; finally, strengthened by grain, wine, and oil, they must receive solid bread and wine worthy to be drunk by the beloved, and to be chewed by their lips and teeth. God first inspires in them the sweetness of his love, by which they despise worldly desire; then the prudence or wisdom of that same charity, by which they despise the prudence of the flesh, which is hostile to God. They must not love to be ruled by their own judgment, but by another’s [Col. 1274A], provided that it is according to God. Thus, by renouncing the world and their own judgment, and following another’s decision even in a command that seems absurd to human reason, they become worthy of solid bread and strong wine, through which they may be strengthened in the Lord and in the might of his power, so that they too may now say with Peter to Christ: “I love you sweetly, prudently, strongly.”

But before one reaches this sweet, wise, and strong fullness of charity, an imperfect person often supposes himself to abound in charity and says in his abundance: “I shall never be moved.” But when God turns away his face, he is troubled and, through the most certain experiences of events, is taught that his charity does not abound in sweetness, prudence, or indeed strength. Does it not suit such a person [Col. 1274B] to say in repentance what we are treating in this present psalm, so that he may think and say something like this within himself: “Behold, in my love I do not find so great a delight, wisdom, strength, or constancy as I thought I had. For, thinking myself something when I am nothing, I deceived myself by saying within myself: ‘In my abundance I shall never be moved.’ But you, Lord, in your will, when you willed, for as long as you willed, to what end you willed, and for the reason you willed, bestowed strength upon my beauty; and the strength of my beauty was not in my power but in your will. Yet I said in my abundance: ‘I shall never be moved,’ as though my standing or falling were according to my own [Col. 1274C] disposition and not according to your purpose. I said this in my own abundance, in my own wisdom. But this wisdom proved to be folly; offended by this presumptuous folly, you turned your face away from me, and I was troubled.”

I, King David, before committing sin with Uriah’s wife, said in my abundance: “I shall never be moved,” because I never thought that I would fall through such a shameful lapse. Nor did I think that my house, although not yet dedicated, lay open to the entrance of that stranger who would demand from me such a feast that, sparing my own sheep, I should seize another’s ewe and kill the ewe’s owner. But you, Lord, who bestowed strength upon my beauty not by my will but by yours, seeing in me such proud [Col. 1274D] presumption, turned your face away from me, and I was troubled through the execrable guilt of a twofold crime, namely adultery and homicide.

Likewise, when I commanded the people to be numbered, rejoicing in the multitude of the people, I said in my abundance: “I shall never be moved.” But you, God, who love the humble and those who fear you and resist the proud, turned your face away from me in my pride, and I was troubled. And when I saw the angel striking the people, I said: “It is I who have sinned; I have acted wickedly. What have these sheep done?” (2 Sam. 24:17). Very nearly the same thing is said here: “To you, Lord, I shall cry, and to my God I shall make supplication. What profit is there in my blood, when I go down into corruption? Shall dust confess you, or proclaim [Col. 1275A] your truth?” (Ps. 30:9–10). Thus I cry in my repentance.

**Verses 11, 12, and 13.** “The Lord heard and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper. You turned my mourning into joy for me; you tore apart my sackcloth and surrounded me with gladness, that my glory might sing to you,” etc. To you, I say, I shall confess, because I shall never ascribe my abundance to myself but to you, if I seem to abound in any virtue. And where I do not abound, I shall confess that too to you, as one confesses his sickness to a physician.

Alternatively: I, Christ, the true David, have already above praised my Father for the dedication of my house, and invited others to praise and sing in his praise, saying: “Sing to the Lord, his saints, and confess the remembrance of his holiness.” Now, near the end of the psalm, I shall explain the reasons why my Father should be praised: namely, because I prayed to the Lord, and the Lord heard and had mercy on me. Truly, Lord, you became my helper—that is, you did not give your Holy One to see corruption—because you turned my mourning into joy: that is, you made the apostles who mourned for me rejoice, namely because you tore apart my sackcloth. They had seen me, their teacher and Lord, in the sack of mortality as choice grain. For the sake of the grain dear to them, they would have wished the sack to remain intact, so that I might not die but live in a body that would never die. But I said to them: “Unless a grain of wheat falls [Col. 1275C] into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). Therefore, contrary to their carnal wish but as I willed, the sack of flesh was torn in the Passion, and the grain, falling into the ground, died. Hence the apostles and women mourned, and this was my mourning—that is, mourning undertaken because of me.

But you, Father, turned my mourning into joy for me. For although there was mourning because you tore my sack, through this you turned that mourning into joy: by raising my flesh from the dead, you surrounded me with gladness, so that I should not be pierced any further—as I was formerly pierced on the cross by spear and nails, when soldiers pierced me [Col. 1275D]. At last they shall see in glory him whom they pierced, judging them (John 19:37). Then all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over me; and those who pierced me, whether in my members or even in the sacraments which they handled wrongly, shall then mourn the more. They shall mourn according to Zechariah’s prophecy, as one commonly grieves at the death of a firstborn son (Zech. 12:10).

O Jews, then you too will mourn, because you have lost me, God’s firstborn. God the Father eternally had one Son—at once firstborn and only-begotten—namely me, in his bosom. But for humankind’s salvation I went forth from my Father and came into the world. Yet you rejected me, God’s only-begotten, and waited for another. But my Father has no other besides me. I am at once his firstborn and his only Son; and on the day of judgment you will see this [Col. 1276A], and then mourn over me, the firstborn, when you recognize that you waited for another in vain. Then, as is read in Zechariah: “The families shall mourn, each family separately, and their women separately” (Zech. 12:12).

But my disciples and those like them, whose sorrow shall be turned into joy, will rejoice and exult with completed joy, just as they now rejoiced when they saw me, their Lord, on the day of dedication and resurrection. On that day, having made them glad, you, Father, turned my mourning into joy for me and surrounded me with gladness, when I stood in their midst and said to them: “Peace be with you” (Luke 24:36). For just as, while they wept and mourned, I was surrounded by the sack of sorrow, so, when they were consoled and gladdened through the manifestation of my resurrection, you surrounded [Col. 1276B] me with joy, as they stood around me and rejoiced with the joy described of them in the Gospel: “The disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord” (John 20:20).

Alternatively: You turned my mourning, in which I said, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38), into joy, exchanging the mourning of death for the joy of resurrection. Truly, you tore apart my sack. Sackcloth is a rough garment for use in labor or as a sign of grief; hence the Ninevites, clothed in sackcloth, performed repentance. It is made of goat hair and signifies the mortality which Christ received from sinners. In this sack the divinity was concealed like grain. Hence in another psalm: “I clothed myself in haircloth” (Ps. 35:13), so that divinity might remain hidden in [Col. 1276C] flesh. The sack was torn in dying, and the divinity previously concealed was made manifest by the resurrection, just as an intact sack conceals grain, but one torn open reveals it.

That by the words “You tore apart my sack” I mean the sorrow of mortality is shown by the contrasting statement: “You surrounded me,” or “girded me,” “with the gladness of immortality,” so that my glory may sing to you; that is, so that my Resurrection may be the reason you are praised. And this is because, having suffered once, I shall not be pierced again—that is, I shall die no more.

Alternatively: When Christ has said, “The Lord is my helper,” because he raised me, the Church, having obtained the firstborn from the dead, says: “O Lord, now in your resurrection [Col. 1276D] you have turned my mourning into joy, because you have now torn apart my sack—the veil of my sins and the sorrow of my mortality—and surrounded me with gladness; that is, you have girded me with the first robe, so that before judgment my soul might enjoy its blessedness, so that humility may no longer mourn, but my glory may sing to you. For you have now exalted me from my lowliness, and I shall not be pierced by the consciousness of sin, nor by fear of death or judgment, knowing that the body will rise to glory. Therefore, O Lord my God, I shall confess to you forever—that is, praise you. For this is my glory: to confess that nothing comes to me from myself, but that I must confess to you that all things are from you, who are God, all in all.”

[Col. 1277A] Let what has been said about that dedication of David’s house suffice: in it the foundation, which is Christ, was dedicated and illumined by the glory of the resurrection, and his mourning was turned into joy, as he himself rejoiced and the apostles rejoiced with him on the day of resurrection, the day of solemnity and gladness. But because the universal dedication of the whole house of David—that is, of the whole Church—is expected in the future, in which all the mourning of the elect will be turned into joy when God wipes every tear from their eyes, it seems appropriate to explain more fully the chapter of the prophet Zechariah concerning the mourning of that day: partly to be turned into joy and partly to endure forever.

“And it shall be,” he says, “on that day: I shall seek to destroy all [Col. 1277B] nations that come against Jerusalem. And I shall pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the Spirit of grace and of prayers; and they shall look upon me whom they pierced; and they shall mourn for him as for an only son, and grieve for him as one commonly grieves at the death of a firstborn. On that day there shall be great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo. And the land shall mourn, families by families apart: the families of the house of David apart, and their women apart; the families of the house of Nathan apart, and their women apart; the families of the house of Levi apart, and their women apart; the families of the house of Shimei apart, and their women apart. All the remaining families, families by families apart, [Col. 1277C] and their women apart” (Zech. 12:9 ff.). “On that day,” says the Lord of hosts, “I shall destroy the names of idols from the earth, and they shall no longer be named; and I shall remove the prophets and the unclean spirit from the earth” (Zech. 13:2).

It is clear that these things are spoken of the last day, on which the Lord will destroy all nations that come against Jerusalem—that is, against the Church—whether pagans, Jews, heretics, schismatics, or false Christians. Because, on account of the Christian name with which they are marked, one might have doubted whether these belong to the mourning of that dreadful day, he expressly identifies the more eminent families: namely, the family of the house of David, which was royal; the family of the house of Nathan, which was prophetic; the family of the house of Levi, which was priestly; and the family [Col. 1277D] of the house of Shimei, which was distinguished by scribes and teachers.

He does not name individually the remaining families, which were notable for no dignities; but he names those more worthy ones and assigns them great mourning, such as occurred for Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo, when King Josiah was slain there. In Josiah’s death, which prefigured Christ’s death, there was great mourning in Jerusalem. For the prophet Jeremiah also produced, because of that same death, a fourfold alphabetic lamentation, in which he clearly foretold Christ’s death: “The breath of our nostrils, Christ the Lord, was taken in our sins; of him we said: ‘In your shadow we shall live among the nations’” (Lam. 4:20).

Therefore, just as great mourning then arose even among the more eminent tribes because, their sins requiring it, Josiah the anointed king of the Lord was captured and killed—a famous king, in whom the Jews’ temporal victory and safety then depended—although the wording in the Lamentations, “The breath of our nostrils, Christ the Lord, of whom we said, ‘Under your shadow we shall live among the nations,’” far surpasses Josiah’s person (for he was not the breath of our nostrils, nor did he ever rule among the nations): so also now there is great mourning in Jerusalem when the Lord pours out upon the house of David and Jerusalem’s inhabitants the Spirit of grace and prayers. The more eminent families mourn separately, and their women separately, looking upon him whom they pierced: Jesus Christ, who was captured and died for our sins [Col. 1278B], not his own. Thus we pierced him, because we were the cause for which he was crucified.

This consideration ought to pierce believers’ hearts as often as they behold the wood of the holy cross raised up—whether with bodily eyes or spiritually in their thoughts—like a tall, leafy, fruitful tree, in whose shadow we who believe in the Crucified live among the nations. We live in him all the more blessedly the more attentively we mourn our sins, for which he was crucified.

Families are to mourn, and families separately, and their women separately, so that, according to another prophet, “the bridegroom may come forth from his chamber and the bride from her bridal room” [Col. 1278C] (Joel 2:16). They are to live in such continence as was foreshadowed in the primitive Church, where “the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32) in the Lord; while they repented of their sins, families mourned separately and their women separately. For, as Luke records in the Acts of the Apostles, even women whose husbands were alive then lived in holy widowhood, apart from their husbands and separated from other men. Philo the historian likewise reports that in Alexandria, under Mark, the disciple of the apostle Peter, men separately and women separately led a celibate life in holy conduct.

The world indeed rejoiced because its sins and the punishments of sinners were hidden from its eyes. But the families of David’s house mourned with great mourning. For as David had mourned greatly over Saul, the Lord’s anointed, when he was slain, so many rulers who had assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ later, pierced by repentance, mourned with great mourning. And their women mourned separately, because either they observed complete continence or, following the Apostle’s teaching, “having wives, they were as though they had none” (1 Cor. 7:40). Among these was Prince Constantine, who, like King David, was a famous king. After the killings of martyrs, in which he certainly persecuted Christ, the breath of our nostrils, he was saved through the mourning of repentance. With pious and devout regard he looked upon him whom he had pierced, because he honoured, with every observance of veneration, the Lord’s cross found in his time through his mother Helena; through it he deserved to become victor over the tyrant Maxentius and other enemies—and, more gloriously still, at times over the devil himself.

Likewise the families of the house of Levi mourned separately: those who, living a common life in the clergy and having no inheritance on earth, dwelt far apart from women. Their outstanding guide was Father Augustine. Although the canons permit clerics to live with women whose close kinship removes suspicion, he nevertheless refused to live even with his sister, saying: “Those who are with my sister are not my sisters.” That sister lived separately, governing a community [Col. 1279B] of women established under a rule of common life, after the example of those of whom we read in the Acts of the Apostles that they had one heart and one soul in God, and for whose service the seven deacons are recorded as having been appointed by the apostles to minister to their tables. Similarly, blessed Augustine had assigned to his aforementioned sister a priest as assistant in governance, whose authority might be greater for ruling, together with his sister, those women devoted to God.

If, therefore, you look on this side at blessed Augustine with his clerics living a common and religious life, and on that side at his sister with women devoted to God, no less religiously ordered, does it not seem to you that the prophecy is fulfilled which says: [Col. 1279C] “The families of the house of Levi shall mourn separately, and their women separately”? It would be lengthy to enumerate the families of Levi’s house in the clergy of common life, mourning separately, and their women separately. But since this form of discipline has been handed down from the holy apostles to our own times—that the dwellings of clerics and women devoted to God are distinct from one another—how much more should secular women be kept far from them?

Again, the families of the house of Nathan mourned separately, and their women separately. This Nathan was the prophet who rebuked King David for incest and who, together with Zadok the priest, anointed Solomon as king. Therefore, through him, as through Levi, the clerical order may be understood; its office is indeed not only to rebuke common people [Col. 1279D] but also kings, and, when kings die, to appoint others. If this interpretation is accepted, the rule for the family of Nathan’s house mourning separately and for their women mourning separately is no different from that explained concerning the family of Levi’s house. It need not be expounded again, since clerical continence is equally expressed through Nathan as through Levi in the mourning of their family separately and their women separately.

Nor is it absurd that, in designating a single order, two persons with their families are placed here: one royal and the other priestly—namely Nathan of the royal tribe and Levi of the priestly tribe—since the Apostle commends the same union of royal and priestly dignity when he says to believers: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9). Surely [Col. 1280A] this royal priesthood also includes the order of monks, who through sacred ordinations have been admitted to the clergy by the ministry of the altar and the office of preaching laid upon them.

After Nathan and Levi follows: “The families of the house of Shimei apart, and their women apart”—that is, they shall mourn. This Shimei, being of the tribe of Benjamin, held no distinction in his own person; but his memory is here taken up for good because he was of the chosen tribe, and because the king accepted his repentance after the curse which he had uttered against him. Thus the order of penitents, mourning their sins, may fittingly be signified through this Shimei, so that their women mourn apart. The order of penitents may likewise be signified through the family of the house of David. [Col. 1280B] Nor is it unusual in the divine ordinances that the family of David’s house is placed here before the other tribes, not only on account of the eminence of royal dignity, but also on account of the outstanding repentance which he performed. Thus also in the Gospel the younger son who repents is preferred to the one who said to his father: “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your commandment” (Luke 15:29). And tax collectors and harlots who repent go before Pharisees who presume upon their own righteousness; and, among the Apostles themselves, we see Peter and Paul—who are known to belong to the number of penitents—placed at the summit before all the other Apostles, though all are elect, devout, and holy.

[Col. 1280C] Nor does the Apostle John, whose innocence and purity pleased God, resent that Peter and Paul are set before him—men in whom God was pleased not so much by innocence as by repentance. Thus too “the last shall be first, and the first last” (Matt. 19:30), when there shall be greater joy in heaven over one sinner repenting than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance (Luke 15:7). Great, then, is the dignity of the order of penitents, who, while they mourn apart and their women also apart, increase by their mourning the joy of the angels.

Some of these join monasteries; others do penance outside monasteries under ecclesiastical rules, by which chastity is imposed upon those doing penance for mortal sins. Thus they must either wholly abstain from marriage, or, if penance is granted to persons already married, they must know that continence is also enjoined upon them, so far as they can observe it, while at the same time preserving regard for the weakness of their wives, whom they ought not to deprive except by mutual consent.

But how great care must be taken by those penitents who have been joined to a community living in common and within a cloister, in order that they themselves may mourn apart and their women apart, is taught by the monastic institutions. It would take too long to insert these in full; nevertheless, since the mourning in question is that which, at the Lord’s coming, is to be turned into joy—so that each of us may then be able to say, “You have turned my mourning into joy; you have torn my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness”—let no one concerned for his salvation be unwilling [Col. 1281A] to hear briefly the rule of cloistered and communal discipline, in which almost alone the distinction of fruitful repentance is now preserved.

For those who remain in the world and either retain hatred in their hearts, or possess unjust gains, or so repent of one mortal sin that they remain in another, or, if they have wives, do not have them as though not having them—these persons should not be said to practise repentance, but to feign it. Their mourning is not such as will be turned into joy, nor is their sackcloth such that, when it is torn, they should expect the garment of gladness.

What the institution of monasteries is, Bishop Isidore briefly sets forth in his book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, saying as follows:

[Col. 1281B] “There is this difference between a coenobium and a monastery: a monastery may be called the dwelling of one monk, whereas a coenobium is only that of many. I shall briefly describe their manner of life, as the institution of the Fathers teaches. Having first despised and abandoned the enticements of this world, they gather together for a most holy common life and live jointly in prayers, readings, discussions, vigils, and fasts. They are puffed up with no pride, darkened by no envy; but, modest, reserved, and peaceable, they pursue a life of utmost concord, revealing their thoughts to one another and examining and correcting them. No one possesses a portion of earthly property. They do not wear costly and coloured garments, but the cheapest and plainest. They never use bathing for bodily pleasure, [Col. 1281C] but seldom, because illness makes it necessary. They never go out without the abbot’s permission, nor do they take anything without the signal of their father’s command.

“They work with their hands at things by which the body may receive nourishment and the mind may not be hindered. They sing while working with their hands, and so console the labour itself as though by a divine command. They give their work to those whom they call deans, because they are set over groups of ten, so that concern for his body may hinder none of them from the purpose of his mind—neither in food, nor clothing, nor in anything else needed either for daily necessity or, as often occurs, for mutual infirmity. These deans give the things to the superior; and the superior, arranging everything with great care, supplies [Col. 1281D] whatever their life requires because of bodily weakness. Yet he himself shall render account to him whom they call Father.

“These Fathers, distinguished by understanding, endurance, and discernment, and eminent in every respect without any pride, care for those whom they call sons—with great authority on their own part in commanding, and with willingness on theirs in obeying. At the given signal, all assemble frequently, by night and by day, hastening quickly to the prayer of the canonical hours. They celebrate with fixed attention of heart and persist without weariness until the Psalms are finished. Likewise, every other day, while they are still fasting, they assemble for a conference to hear the Father. They listen with incredible eagerness and profound silence, and, according as those discoursing have moved them, signify the dispositions of their souls by prayer, groaning, or tears through the body.

[Col. 1282A] “Then, in great silence, they take refreshment only so far as health requires, each restraining the greed of his appetite through frugality, lest their hearts be weighed down—even by the very things available to them, which they use sparingly and most plainly. Thus they abstain not only from meat and wine, sufficiently to tame passions, but also from everything that provokes the appetite of belly and throat. Indeed, whatever remains over from the work of their hands and from the restriction of their meals is distributed to the needy with such care that nothing whatsoever is left over.

“Men come to the purpose of this holy soldiery not only from freedom, but also often from servile condition, or rather so that they may thereby be freed. They come also from rural life, from the practice of crafts, [Col. 1282B] and from common labour—indeed, more happily in proportion as they have been more robustly trained. If they are not admitted, it is a grave fault. For many great men, worthy of imitation, have arisen from that number. For this reason God chose the weak things of the world, that he might confound the strong; and he chose the ignoble things, that he might confound the wise, and the ignoble things of the world, and the things which are not, that he might bring to nothing the things which are, so that no flesh may glory before God.

“In like manner there are monasteries of women serving God diligently and chastely. Separated in their dwellings, and removed as far as possible from men, they are joined only by the pious love of holiness and imitation of virtue. No young men have access to them, nor even men who are most grave and fully approved, except as far as the vestibule, for the purpose of supplying necessities of which they are in need. The women who preside over them, each of them most grave and fully approved, are skilled and prepared not only in forming minds and ordering morals, but also in instructing. [Col. 1282C] They exercise and support their bodies by wool-working; they give the garments themselves to the monks, receiving from them in return what is necessary for sustenance. Monasteries of virgins appear to maintain these customs, this life, and this institution, as do those of monks.”

We have inserted these extracts from the words of Isidore in order to show plainly how truly it was foretold in prophecy that the families of men should mourn apart, and their women apart. “All the remaining families,” he says: “families and families apart, and [Col. 1282D] their women apart” (Zech. 12:12). Certainly this prophetic proclamation accords with the Apostle saying: “It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who use this world, as though they did not use it; and those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice” (1 Cor. 7:31), and so forth.

Inviting us to such mourning, the Firstborn himself, who is now mourned as slain, says in the Gospel: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21). Again: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5). Again: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke 6:25). It is therefore necessary to mourn now over this Firstborn, slain as our sins demanded, lest we weep eternally. Those who laugh now, when it is the time for weeping, will weep [Col. 1283A] without hope of consolation when the time for laughter comes. They will weep apart, separated, that is, from the fellowship of holy angels and human beings; and their women apart, because then they will have no leisure to be defiled or to defile others in beds and acts of shamelessness, to be corrupted or to corrupt. Far from them will be women—that is, all enticements and all the splendours of worldly pleasures—when they weep in the darkness, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

On the contrary, the saints, who “have not been defiled with women”—that is, who have been found pure and without stain from carnal enticements signified by the name of women—will then delight in eternal and heavenly joys in the bridal chamber of heavenly marriage, where the whole Church will be bride and Christ bridegroom. Far from it will be cast out not only corruptors and corrupters found in their shamefulness, [Col. 1283B] but even the foolish virgins, then too late mourning bitterly for lack of oil.

Moreover, those who either mourn well now or will mourn punitively in the future will weep and mourn as is customary at the death of a firstborn. For as the firstborn is loved above all children, so Christ, the firstborn of the dead, is loved above all things by those who now mourn well. Therefore, on the day of resurrection and universal dedication, their mourning will be changed into joy; and when the sackcloth of their mortality has been torn, they will be clothed with the gladness of immortality and glory, when their body, sown in dishonour, rises in glory. Then, in that dedication, each such person will be able to sing what is said here in the psalm for the dedication:

“You have turned my mourning into joy for me;  
you have torn my sackcloth  
and clothed me with gladness,

[Col. 1283C] that my glory may sing to you, in which my body, sown in dishonour, has risen; that I may not be pierced with grief, because death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying” (Rev. 21:4).

“O Lord my God, who have thus dedicated my body: I, in that same body, as in a temple dedicated to you, shall confess you for ever, joined to angelic choirs which praise you, and separated from evil spirits and from men who then mourn far too late, when, their firstborn having been taken away, they have no hope of another.”

[Col. 1283D] O Arians, who denied that Christ, the Son of God, is the Firstborn: when, in that festival of dedication, you know him as the Firstborn, you will mourn inconsolably over this Firstborn, because, having rejected him, you will find no other. For there is no other Son of God besides that Firstborn in whom adopted children have any salvation. When God the Father brings this Firstborn into the world, he says: “Let all the angels of God adore him” (Heb. 1:6). But you preached that he is a creature, to be adored neither by angels nor by men as the Father is adored. For you said that he is less than the Father and not begotten of him, but made. We, however, adore this Firstborn as begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father; and we proclaim that he is to be adored and worshipped together with the Father, [Col. 1284A] detesting all the errors of pagans, Jews, heretics, and false Christians who contradict or disobey this Firstborn.

O all you who, though you are sons of Leah or of the handmaids, do not love this Firstborn of Rachel; who envy his dominion; and who, so far as lies in you, hinder him from reigning in the world: while there is still time for fruitful repentance, return to this Firstborn, who now rules over all the land of Egypt—indeed, over heaven and earth—according to his own saying: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18). Mourn before him because you have sinned against him, and he, taking pity on you, will fill your sacks with grain, lest you perish from hunger before you reach him.

And indeed, according to the measure of your fault, he will let you mourn for a while, until you say: “We deservedly suffer these things, because we sinned against our brother, our firstborn” (Gen. 42:21). But at last he will tear your sacks, enriching you so greatly that none of you will need a sack, and he will clothe you with gladness, giving each of you beautiful robes. Clothed and adorned in these, and now freed from the burden of sacks, you will be able to exult, so that each of you may say to that same Firstborn:

“You have turned my mourning into joy for me;  
you have torn my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness,  
that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with grief.”

For even that which was devised for evil has been turned to good, as you, good Joseph, said to your brothers: “You devised evil against me, and [Col. 1284C] God turned it to good” (Gen. 50:20).

“O Lord my God, I shall confess you for ever.” Let us all say this, each one of us, because “not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name” is glory to be given: because we do not perish from hunger; because, carrying empty sacks to you, we bring them back filled with grain, when we eat you, the grain of wheat, sacramentally, until the sack of our mortality is torn and you are no longer possessed in mystery within a sack, but, the sack having been torn, you, the fatness of wheat, satisfy our desire with good things.

Glory to the Father, who festively dedicates the house of David: first in the Firstborn of the dead, raised and glorified as its foundation, and afterwards universally [Col. 1284D] in the general resurrection of the dead and glorification of the good. Glory to the Son, who in this psalm praises the Father for the dedication of his house: now already dedicated in himself, and still to be dedicated in his own people. Glory to the Holy Spirit, whose work this very dedication is.

For just as David the father gave to his son Solomon gold, silver, bronze, and precious stones as expenses for building the house, and therefore the house which Solomon the son built is entitled in this psalm the house of David on account of the material and expenses which David prepared; so God the Father, creating all things from nothing, prepared the material and resources from which his Son—namely, eternal Wisdom—built himself a house. The dedication of this house is rightly attributed to the Holy Spirit, who supports this house on seven [Col. 1285A] pillars, adorns and illuminates it with seven lamps shining before the throne of God, and presents the very human being united to God the Word as a golden lampstand gleaming with seven lights, for the dedication and illumination of the whole house of David—that is, the holy Church. In it may there be glory to the Father, who created its material from nothing through the Word; to the Son, who built it from the material prepared beforehand, together with the Father; and to the Holy Spirit, who has now dedicated it in its foundation and will still dedicate it wholly at the end.

This is to be understood in such a way that the work of creation, assigned to the Father, is not thought foreign to the Son and Holy Spirit; nor is the work of the Son who builds doubted to be also the work of the Father and Holy Spirit; nor is the work of the Holy Spirit who dedicates the house thought foreign to the Father and Son. For, just as the substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is inseparable, so their work is inseparable, although in the distinct work itself, as has been shown above, a distinction of persons is observed—as in this preparing, building, dedicating, or sanctifying of the house.

In consideration of this we say: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit: as it was in the beginning,” when this house was foreordained; “and now is,” while it is being built; “and shall be for ever and ever,” through the eternal feast of its dedication. Amen.

## PSALM XXX

[Col. 1285]

[Col. 1285B] “In you, O Lord, I have hoped.” The title of this psalm is (verse 1):

> **UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID FOR ECSTASY.**

“For ecstasy,” he says—that is, for the consideration of David’s, namely Christ’s, most profound understanding concerning the restoration of the human race, which he ordained through his death and resurrection. This understanding surpasses the understanding of all creatures, so that it may rightly be called ecstasy. *Ecstasy* in Greek is called *excessus* (“going beyond”) in Latin. Now the mind goes beyond itself in two ways: either when it is frightened by earthly things, or when intent on heavenly things it forgets everything else which the concern of ordinary affairs treats. In this psalm, however, ecstasy is understood chiefly as the fear of God’s people, troubled by persecution from the Gentiles and by the failure of faith.

First, against fear, hope and prayer, certainty of deliverance and joy, are set forth. Secondly, the things which disturb, and how great they are, are enumerated, at: “Have mercy.” Against these prayer follows, at: “Deliver.” The third part reveals what he intends, warning us by his example to work rightly with hope and love, at: “Love.” The whole Christ speaks. The first words indeed apply to the Redeemer. Then the redeemed people gives thanks, at: “You have redeemed me.” Afterwards that same people relates at length its disturbance in the second part. But toward the end, and at the end, the Prophet’s voice is interposed, at: “How great,” and at: “Love.”

[Col. 1285D] It should be observed that, despite so great a variety of persons, he does not change person, but, whether speaking in the person of the head or of the members, says, “I,” “of me,” “me,” “to me.” This seems especially marvellous if one considers the unity of Christ and the Church which love has made. For just as the tongue, although it is a different part of the body from the foot, nevertheless assumes the voice of the foot when the foot hurts, saying not, “You tread on the foot,” but, “You tread on me”; so Christ deigns to transform the words of the members [Col. 1286B] into himself, so that we too may speak with his words.

Hence it is that, when dying in what was ours—that is, in the flesh which he had—transforming our ecstasy into himself, he began to fear not in himself but in us. Thus head and members, Christ and Church, become one person. Bridegroom and bride are two in one flesh; therefore they are also one in voice. According to this unity Christ said: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). He did not say, “my people,” but “me,” although it was not he who was in heaven but his own people on earth whom Saul persecuted.

Isaiah likewise commends this unity, in whom Christ speaks and says: “As a bridegroom he bound a mitre upon me, and as a bride he adorned me” (Isa. 61:10). He calls himself, in one flesh, both bridegroom and bride, with one voice, namely: “me” and “me.”

[Col. 1286C] This psalm is the fourth among those which briefly commemorate the Passion and Resurrection. In it are described both the humiliation and exaltation of the martyrs, so that no one who sees himself may be proud, and no one who sees mercy may be afraid. Therefore it begins in the person of the head and says:

**VERSE 2.** “In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be confounded.” That these are his words he himself made heard and known to the whole world when he cried with a loud voice: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). He, then, is the one who, according to the form of a servant, hoped in the Lord that he might not be confounded for ever, as his enemies wished to confound him. According to their judgment, he says, “I became as a perished vessel, [Col. 1286D] because I heard the reproach of many,” for example, saying: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God, save yourself” (Mark 15:30).

Therefore, against reproaches of this kind from enemies wishing to confound him, he prays and says: “In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be confounded”: may I never be confounded while men insult me for having the likeness of sinful flesh.

[Col. 1287A] “In your righteousness deliver me from death. Incline your ear to me”—that is, hear me, humble as I am, drawing near to me through the Word united to flesh. “Hasten to deliver me”—that is, do not delay until the end of the age to separate me from sinners and to deliver souls from hell. In order that this may be so, “be to me a protecting God,” because you are my strength to endure persecutors, and “my refuge” for abandoning them in death. And “for your name’s sake,” to be made known among the Gentiles through me, “you will lead me out,” or “you will be my guide”—that is, in all things I shall follow your will—“and you will nourish me,” gradually gathering saints to me and filling up my body.

“You will lead me out of the snare,” or “out of the trap, which they hid for me”—that is, you will lead me out from the plots which they concealed against me, raising me and lifting me to the things above when the counsels of the Jews have been frustrated. Hence even before the Passion I “commend my spirit into your hands”—that is, I commit it to your power, soon to receive it back. These are the words which he spoke on the cross, and by them he teaches that he himself has spoken in this psalm.

“You have redeemed me,” and so forth. These words apply to the people redeemed by the Passion. For it is fitting not for the Redeemer but for the redeemed people to say: “You have redeemed me.”

The preceding words may also be understood of that same people, which, afraid in ecstasy, nevertheless begins from hope in this manner: “O Lord, I have hoped in you, not in myself.” Fear is not without mercy, because human nature hopes: “I shall not be confounded for ever.” It does not say simply, “I shall not be confounded,” because it is useful to be confounded for a time on account of sins; but it says, “I shall not be confounded for ever.” And because I do not establish my own righteousness, in which you would condemn me, “in your righteousness,” which is mine because given by you, “deliver me.” Behold, I pray:

**VERSE 3.** “Incline your ear to me”—that is, your mercy; in sending the Son, hasten. It signifies that it has been heard, but, fearing delay in the fulfilment of that hearing, says: “Hasten to deliver me from sins. Be to me a protecting God”—that is, protect me—“and be a house of refuge.” A servant flees from an angry lord to a place where his lord is not; but whoever flees from God finds God angry wherever he turns. Yet whoever wishes to escape God finds him appeased by fleeing to him. For he is refuge in the house which is the Church, in which human beings are saved as in Noah’s ark. Hence follows: “That you may save me.” And this is why I seek you, not another:

**VERSE 4.** “For you are”—there is no other—“my strength and my refuge.” And indeed I am not worthy; but “for your name’s sake,” namely, that you may be glorified, “you will lead me,” lest I wander away from you, “and you will nourish me.” There is one food which both father and mother convey into flesh, and which the little child receives as milk when it has become milk, though it will later receive it at table. Thus the Lord, in order to make his wisdom milk for us, put on flesh and nourishes us with this milk, so that at last we may eat the solid food upon which angels feed.

**VERSE 5.** “You will lead me out of this snare which they hid [Col. 1288A] for me.” Here he affirms deliverance. He calls two gates a snare, through which the devil tempts: desire and fear. Through the gate of desire he first tempted the Lord in three ways: gluttony, avarice, and vainglory. When that gate had been closed, he tempted him through fear of the Passion. Through the same gates he tempts all human beings. Therefore the whole body says: “You will lead me out of this snare which they hid for me,” when they said to Christ: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth” (Mark 12:14).
