By speaking so to me, they hid a snare for me: if I denied that tribute ought to be paid to Caesar, they would accuse me as an adversary of Caesar and enemy of the Roman empire; but if I granted that it should be paid, I would incur offence as teaching against the liberty and nobility of God’s particular people.

[Col. 1288B] But I was led out of this snare when I said: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” Again, when they brought to me a woman caught in adultery, they hid such a snare for me that, if I said she should be stoned according to the severity of the law, I would lose the reputation for mercy which had spread concerning me; while if I defended her, I would lose the reputation for justice as a transgressor of the law. But you, God the Father, led me out of this snare which they hid for me. For I said: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her.” And I said to the woman herself: “Has no one condemned you, woman?” And she: “No one, Lord.” “Neither,” I said, “will I condemn you; go, and now sin no more” (John 8:7 and following).

[Col. 1288C] By speaking and acting thus, I was led out of their snare, sinning neither against Caesar nor against God, while preserving both justice and mercy. For what I said, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s,” preserved me from offence against Caesar; what I said, “and the things that are God’s, to God” (Mark 12:17), showed me free from offence against God. Likewise, what I said to the woman, “Has no one condemned you, woman? Neither will I condemn you,” was the proclamation of mercy, which was mediator and reconciler between me, the merciful one, and her, the miserable one. But what I said to the Jews, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her,” and likewise what I said to the woman, “Sin no more,” was the declaration of justice, which otherwise does not pardon past sins unless they are grieved over and caution is maintained against future sins.

[Col. 1288D] Thus the snare of those plotting against me was broken, and I appeared righteous both toward Caesar and toward God, and was found at once righteous and merciful. Nor is it surprising that I escaped their snares. For if “the net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures” (Prov. 1:17), how much more before the eyes of an eagle that sees more keenly? I am the eagle, and my elect are full of eyes before and behind and winged on every side. Therefore, you, Father, who lead me myself out of the snare, will also lead those who are mine, or shall be mine, out of the snare.

In the Hebrew it reads: “And you will lead me out of the net which they hid for me.” Thus they hid either a net or a snare. But you, who see all things and can do all that you will, will lead me and mine out of the snare or [Col. 1289A] net hidden from human eyes, though not from divine eyes. You will so furnish mine with eyes that, knowing how to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and to God the things that are God’s, they will not admit against themselves an occasion for just accusation in courts or councils. Likewise, knowing how to preserve justice with mercy, they will be found prudent as serpents and simple as doves, so that mercy may temper just severity lest it become cruel, and zeal for justice may kindle pious mercy lest it become lax. Thus they may be free both from the snare of excessive cruelty which hates human beings and from the snare of excessive indulgence which fosters their vices. For in them, as just severity is always ready to punish what is wrongly done, so pious love desires that there may be found nothing which ought justly to be punished.

In chastening or cherishing their own bodies, too, a snare or net is sometimes set for them: either, by excessively harsh chastisement of the flesh’s wantonness, they weaken the very nature of the flesh; or, by excessive indulgence in cherishing the nature of the flesh, they foster its wantonness as well. But you will lead me and mine out of this twofold snare which the devil and men have hidden for me. For in the wilderness the devil tempted me by blandishments toward excessive indulgence of the flesh, tempting me through gluttony; afterwards, through men, I was tempted toward excessive severity, when sour wine mixed with gall was offered to me.

[Col. 1289C] But, rejecting both the devil’s blandishment in offering bread and the device of men offering gall, I taught my own people to beware of either snare and to proceed between blandishments and austerities in such a way that a person may not become lax through soothing prosperity nor become despondent amid provoking bitter things. Thus, through the victory of my temptation, you, Father, appeased and propitious—because in those same temptations you are my protector—will lead my people out of the snare of temptations. I, their victor, offer you my spirit on their behalf, saying:

**VERSE 6.** “Into your hands I commend my spirit”—that is, my soul, of which it was said in the prophets: “If he shall set his soul as an offering for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall be directed in his hand” (Isa. 53:10). Therefore, for the sake of the long-lived seed which is to spring from me, the grain cast into the earth, [Col. 1289D] and for the sake of your will, O Lord, to be directed in my hand, I now lay down my soul on the cross to abolish the sin of my people; and into your hands, Father, I commend my spirit—that is, my very soul—knowing that you will soon send it back to my body with the gain of a long-lived seed, after it has first despoiled hell through it and liberated many souls from there.

Indeed, I lay it down and take it up again: I lay it down now in the bosom of your keeping, and thence I take it up again when the redemption of my whole Church has been accomplished. Receiving the grace of redemption, she says to you in thanksgiving: “You have redeemed me, O Lord, God of truth.” For “you have loved truth” (Ps. 50:8) in the very act by which you redeemed me, just as you truly [Col. 1290A] spoke to our fathers, to whom you promised without falsehood what you have bestowed upon me, the Church, without deceit. You promised truly; you performed effectually. Therefore in this thanksgiving I call you God of truth: for if you had not remained steadfast in truth, you would not have sent the promised redemption, though you had been provoked by so many sins of human beings, your servants, that your most beloved Son would by no means have been given for their redemption unless the truth of the one promising had supported this.

It must nevertheless be noted that this truth of promise is maintained in such a way that it destroys the vanity of the contrary promise. For just as it is true that the truthful God promised the obedient man, saying to Abraham after his obedience had been shown: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18), so it is false and utterly vain what the devil, a liar from the beginning and father of lies, promised to the disobedient, saying: “You shall be as gods” (Gen. 3:5).

[Col. 1290B] Some observe the vanity of this false promise to such an extent that, though they remain in their disobedience, they nevertheless think themselves equal to gods—that is, to pious and holy human beings. They would act far more rightly if, with the prodigal son, they returned from vanity to truth and said in truthful confession: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke 15:18–19), no longer worthy to be joined to your saints, to whom you say: “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6). If they said this in truthful confession and were ready thereafter to obey, truth would set them free.

But now, intensely hating the truth of true confession and of a good promise for the future, they love vanity and falsehood—the vain hope of divinity which deceives them. The devil says to them: “Do what I advise; eat what is forbidden—that is, commit the sin forbidden to you—and, through God’s great mercy, you will at length be converted near the end of life and become as gods.” Or: “God, overlooking your iniquity because of the weakness implanted in you, will make you like gods—that is, like holy, chaste, and religious people. For God is not so cruel as to destroy the multitude of human beings lying in sins and dying in them.”

[Col. 1290D] Human weakness, like a deceived woman, sometimes willingly accepts and observes such deceitful whispers of the serpent hissing vanity. But the new Adam does not hear it, because he is Truth itself, to whom vanity and falsehood are hateful. And you, truthful God, Father of truth in your Son himself and in all his members, reject that same vanity; and you do not love those who love it. This is proved by the contrary: since hatred and love are opposites, you do not love lovers of vanity to such an extent that you even hate them. For it is truly said to you:

### Verse 7. “You hate those who heed worthless vanities.”

It might in some way be tolerable if a human being, made like vanity and having vanity within himself, did not heed or defend it. Therefore I do not say to you, God of truth, that you hate those who possess vanities. For what human being, a son of men—of whom it is said, “Every living man is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38:6)—is not, in some respect, deprived of truth and deceived by vanity? Yet where “the creature was subjected to vanity, not willingly” (Rom. 8:20), vanity is neither heeded nor loved; for such a creature groans beneath vanity’s burden and brings forth the fruit of truth even through the use of that very vanity, which all who do not consent to it for evil use for good.

Hence one may still reasonably allow that someone should take heed of a vanity which, although he knows it to be evil, he nevertheless finds useful or necessary in its employment—as with the thorn of the flesh. Though it is a great part of worldly vanity, yet because it was useful to the Apostle Paul, he was eventually taught to take heed of it and bear it, until, as though by a certain cautery, the defect of his capacity for self-exaltation on account of the revelation of truth might be healed by that vanity. Unless, after the first fruits of truth had been granted, certain remnants of vanity had remained in the Apostle, still young, for the preservation of humility, he surely would not have said: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan,” etc. (2 Cor. 12:7). The Apostle, then, was certainly subjected to vanity unwillingly, and not needlessly, but under the necessity of preserving humility. Yet it must beyond doubt be believed that, afterwards perfected in humility, the Apostle no longer needed this thorn, but said in great freedom: “And now I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

Most truly, therefore, and most cautiously it is said to you, God of truth: “You hate those who heed worthless vanities,” because those heed vanity needlessly who do not love truth.

Truth is in things that remain: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one God; and the virtues which stand and remain in him as in a fountain, and from there extend into the chosen rational creature like streams and rays. Thus confess those who say with a true and humble confession: “Lord, with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10).

But vanity is in things that do not remain, but utterly vanish and fail between the hands of those wishing to hold them: all worldly allurements, for “the world will pass away, and its desire” (1 John 2:17). For since “all flesh is grass, and all the glory of flesh is as the flower of grass” (Isa. 40:6), without doubt the grass will soon wither and its flower fall. “But the word of the Lord remains for ever.” This is the Word of which the Apostle John says: “What we have seen and heard, what we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life—and the life was manifested” (1 John 1:1).

Let us too, aided by his grace, handle that Word as a solid pearl: let us handle it in meditation, reading, learning, teaching, and above all prayer. Let us lean upon it as a most firm foundation which will never fall, because the word of the Lord remains for ever. Let us see what this Word promises and to whom it promises; let us discern what it promises and what it commands; and then at last let us hope most firmly for what is promised, when we love what is commanded. For God himself is promised as a reward only to the lovers of his command. If we neglect his commands and hope for his promises, we heed vanity in vain. Vanity, I say, not truth: for we hold an empty hope, conceived not from the truth of the Word that remains for ever, but breathed into the mind that loves vanity from elsewhere. Therefore, Lord, you hate all who heed worthless vanities, because life is hoped for not only vainly but needlessly where truth not only does not promise life, but moreover threatens eternal death.

[Col. 1292B] “But I have hoped in the Lord.”

I, the redeemed people, who lately said, “You have redeemed me, Lord God of truth,” have hoped in the Lord by loving truth and rejecting the vanity opposed to it; for I know that he cannot lie. For, to pass over his other sayings, in all of which I rejoice that there is solid truth, I ponder one saying of his, in whose truth I have great hope. The saying is this: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke 6:37). I shall therefore relinquish vengeance and grant pardon to all who offend me; and, hoping in the Lord’s truth, I shall be secure that I too shall be forgiven as I forgive, and given to as I give. Some perhaps doubt this. But I have hoped in the Lord, who cannot lie.

Yet because truth without mercy would be severity to me, I shall rather exult and rejoice in your mercy, which is truth’s inseparable companion. To exult is to display the mind’s joy with great eagerness of spirit by bodily gesture. To rejoice is to be soothed by a measured disposition of mind. Thus I have great cause for exulting and rejoicing over your mercy.

“For you have regarded my humility.”

It was great that, seeing, you saw the affliction of your people who were in Egypt and came down to deliver them. But it is far greater that you have now regarded my humility with such regard that through it the pride of the old man is expiated—a man whom, together with his posterity, you rightly despised, since you resist the proud. For in saying, “You have regarded,” rather than “You have looked upon,” I indicate that your face had been turned away because of pride, hateful to you.

But I, Christ, humbled myself, becoming obedient to you, the Father, unto death—even death on a cross—upon which, hanging, I said: “Into your hands I commend my spirit.” I also summoned others to learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart. And when human pride was expiated through my humility, you regarded my humility, “and saved my soul from necessities.”

I do not say, “from my necessities,” because my soul—that is, my life—endured human necessities of sleeping, eating, drinking, and the like not by any necessity of its own, but by voluntary choice and power, until that hour when I said: “Father, into your hands I commend [Col. 1293A] my spirit.” You immediately heard and received my spirit, that is, my soul, so that henceforth it is wholly free from the necessities of mortal life. For this reason my soul bore them, apart from sin, in a mortal body: that it might destroy them, so that they should in no way exist in the immortal body of all who die and rise again with me.

For other human beings who are not planted together in the likeness of my death and resurrection will have the sufferings of human necessities even after death: either in punishments, before receiving their bodies, like the soul of the rich man thirsting for a drop of water, though burning outside the body; or those concerning whom, according to the prophecy of the Scriptures, this cry is in hell after judgment: “When shall I again find wines?”; and those to whom it is said in the Gospel: “Woe to you who are full now, for you shall hunger” (Luke 6:25).

But every soul of mine—which, by being conformed to my soul in mortal flesh, becomes mine—after death becomes altogether free from the necessities of human possibility. This is because my soul willingly was subject to these necessities while it sought the creature that was subjected unwillingly to the vanity of such necessities. Therefore I say in thanksgiving not only for my soul and spirit, which I commended into your hands, but also for every soul conformed to that same spirit through faith, humility, charity, and meekness: “For you have regarded my humility; you have saved my soul from necessities.”

[Col. 1293C] Otherwise: I, the redeemed people, who above said, “You have redeemed me, Lord, God of truth,” also now give thanks because I perceive that I am saved, partly in hope and partly in fact, from many necessities under which human frailty lies and cries in another psalm: “Deliver me, Lord, from my necessities.”

There are many necessities which cannot altogether be avoided in this life: suspecting that another’s heart does not think well of what is good, or thinks well of what is not good; not knowing what your own life or another’s will be tomorrow; dying against one’s will; willing a good that one cannot accomplish; being driven toward an evil that one does not will; ascending with difficulty to the newness of a good life; descending easily and following the old habit of sinning. If anyone is drawn toward this habit by the law of the members that makes him captive and opposes the law of the mind, let him cry humbly and supplicantly: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). And so the humble person will be delivered and saved, and will be able to say to you, God, in thanksgiving: “I give you thanks, Lord, for you have regarded my humility; you have saved my soul from necessities.”

The necessity of fear also compelled the soul to serve under the Law and to bear the heavy yoke of ceremonies, which, Peter says, “neither we nor our fathers were able to bear” (Acts 15:10). But now, freed from necessities of this kind, we hear the Apostle Paul say to us: “For you have not received again the spirit of slavery in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry, Abba [Col. 1294A] (Father)” (Rom. 2:15).

Therefore, in that spirit of sonship, each of us, whether approaching death or even lying down to sleep, should say: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit; you have redeemed me, Lord God of truth.” In order to redeem a servant, you delivered up your Son, as you truthfully promised in the Scriptures. Through him you have also saved my soul from the necessities of legal observances, making it free and always having readily available sacrifices which it may offer; whereas formerly, when it could not obtain them, it was at times burdened by guilt, whether it wished to be or not.

For if someone then had to offer for his sin a goat but could not obtain one, or a calf, lamb, turtledoves, young pigeons, a baked offering of fine flour, or a sextary of oil, he remained guilty as long as he could not obtain what was required to be offered for such and such a sin. But now, those necessities having ceased, if you repent after sinning, you can render an acceptable sacrifice in every place and at every time, provided only that you take care to possess a spirit of which you may say: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.”

If your spirit is innocent and devout, it is more acceptable than the legal lamb; if it is without the gall of bitterness amid the sweetness of brotherly love, it is more acceptable than young pigeons; if it loves chastity or mourns chastity lost, it is more acceptable than chaste and mourning turtledoves. It has also slain a calf within itself if it has overcome the arrogance of stiff-necked pride; it has sacrificed a goat within itself if every evil lust has been put to death.

[Col. 1294C] If a person has an abundance of such sacrifices, he may say in respect of each one: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit, which may you deign to receive as an acceptable sacrifice: for innocence, like a lamb; for simplicity, like a dove; for chastity or repentance, like a turtledove; for purity, like fine flour; for mercy, like a sextary of oil, filled, pressed together, and overflowing with the six works of mercy, when the will to show mercy is greater than the means.”

“Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit, because you have saved my soul from the necessity of rendering carnal victims.” You, Father, received in place of many victims one sacrifice offered to you on the altar of the cross, and still offered daily on the holy altar. Standing by it, I—the redeemed person, freed from the necessities of the Law—offer only my spirit and say: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit,” because “in me, not outside me, are your vows, O God, which I shall render to you” (Ps. 115:14): I, the Church; I, the people redeemed and saved from the necessities of the Law, yet devoted to better and easier sacrifices.

Accordingly, one man, speaking metrically of these matters in both a scholastic and ecclesiastical sense, said among other things:

> Whatever is done in the Church, so long as it benefits  
> conduct or faith, is a victim pleasing to God.  
> We offer calves of the tongue; we sacrifice the goat;  
> we reduce incense and the ram of sheep to ashes.  
>
> When we sing or read what restrains evil,  
> what calls the people and ourselves to better things,  
> then too the calf and the goat are sacrificed,  
> when you trample pride and suppress lust.  
>
> The lamb comes from the innocent, the dove from the simple;  
> the turtledove from those who weep, far from the highest rewards.  
> You offer on the altars breads baked in an oven  
> if no scourges shake the strength of your mind.  
>
> If you want them mixed with oil, let piety govern you,  
> and let it please you to be toward the guilty more lenient than is permitted.  
> Offer unleavened things if a purer mind is within you,  
> and let heavenly love bake away the loose impulses of the flesh.  
>
> You also offer fine flour if you gather together those whom error had divided  
> and join them to the faith, and do the same:  
> instructing them as catechumens, you grind them; in baptism you immerse them;  
> forming them into one, you bake them to endure hardships.  
>
> Thus these same things teach morals and figure Christ;  
> thus the other matters of the Law have a double use.

[Col. 1295B] Since, therefore, the necessity of the ancient sacrifices has been removed and the freedom of the new grace exists, let those who have been redeemed by the Lord, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy, now say—let all say, and each say to his Redeemer: “You have saved my soul from necessities.”

### Verse 9. “And you have not shut me up in the hands of the enemy.”

You have not shut me up in the power or desire of life that ensnares, or in the fear of death that binds me; but, by delivering me from the straits of death, you have set my feet—that is, the steps of my righteousness—in a broad place. For I have not received again the spirit of slavery in constricting fear; rather, when the yoke of fear was removed, you made my step easy upon the broad way of charity, which had once been difficult in the narrowness of servile fear, where the terror of death also existed before the glory of the Resurrection was known.

But now, since Christ’s spirit, commended into the hands of the Father, was restored by that same Father to the body and manifested the glory of the Resurrection—accomplished in Christ and to come in his whole body—the fear of death does not constrict. Rather, hope broadens the way of righteousness, by which one must go even through a thousand dangers of death into the broad place: that is, into paradise, or the country of virtues, into the breadth of charity, which is the region of the blessed and a place free from the devil’s power. In that broad place you have set my feet. There the anchor of my hope is fixed in firm ground; there the rope of my ship reaches. Hence, because the future thing is certain, I say that you have already set my feet in a broad place, that is, in the heavenly paradise.

[Col. 1295D] The holy catholic Church itself, extended throughout the world, is likewise a broad place for me to dwell or run in until the prize of the heavenly calling. Yet one runs in it not by the steps of the feet but by the steps of conduct toward that prize. And in that race it must be known from whom, with whom, and to whom one runs. For all run, but only that one receives the prize (1 Cor. 9:24) who runs from this world by quickly turning his love away from it, and runs with his neighbor by joining his love socially to the neighbor whom he recognizes as fleeing the world with him.

But who can contain the whole course of one who thus flees and runs from the world with his neighbor in a broad place, in the stadium of this life, unless he presses toward God alone in the course of charity and says to him: “Be to me a protecting God and a fortified place, and save me”? When he reaches him truly and effectually, he will be able to sing: “You have set my feet in a broad place.”

But now, before one reaches this place, both the world from which I flee by running follows and pursues behind me like another Pharaoh, and the neighbor with whom I wish to run in fellowship is sometimes an adversary to me on the way, about to hand me over to the judge unless I agree with him—especially if he runs well. And while the place of eternal standing to which I flee is sometimes believed to be near, it becomes distant.

### Verse 10. “Have mercy upon me, Lord, for I am troubled.”

I, the Church, already stand in a broad place in my Head, indeed, now glorified, and in certain members glorified together with him. But in my weak members I am troubled by diverse straits: fearing lest the world, either flattering, entice me or mine, or, persecuting, seize us; also fearing lest the companion of my way, disagreeing with me, hand me over to the judge unless I agree with him, either by loving or imitating him if he is good, or by pitying and assisting him with prayers if he is not yet good.

Moreover, I fear him to whom I go, lest perhaps at his judgment I should be found reprobate. Fear behind me, fear at my side, fear before my face: fear of the pursuing world, fear of the accompanying neighbor, fear of God calling me to himself. This fear, so manifold, troubles and distresses me so much that I am compelled to say: “Have mercy upon me, Lord, for I am troubled,” especially in my weak members, not yet established in charity’s peace.

For those who have peace in their mind have a broad place; but for those burdened with the straits of quarrels, the way is narrow which is broad to those who love. Therefore this is now the time for mercy, because I am troubled for many reasons, which I enumerate when I say, “because I am troubled,” not “because I am dying.” For I am no longer alarmed at death, which would be desirable in the cause of righteousness; rather, death having been withheld from me, I fear torments. Thus “my eye has been greatly troubled in your wrath,” or in mine.

The eye is prayer directed toward God. It is disturbed by the wrath of God, in which he permits the saints to be afflicted. My soul also, which holds within memory the notions of things as the belly holds foods, likewise retains how much Christ suffered for us and what he promised to his faithful; it too is disturbed in wrath. Or the soul is sensibility and the belly is flesh, which are disturbed in tribulation. Or the eye means those through whom others see; the soul, those by whose example others live; the belly, the weak within the Church: they are disturbed in the wrath of persecutors.

Or: “in your wrath,” which has not been extinguished through zeal at the sins of the chaff, “my eye has been troubled.” Or brief wrath, by shaking and troubling the mind, disperses contemplation, which exists only in a quiet mind; but wrath that is prolonged and grows into hatred has not zeal but the judgment of condemnation, by which the eye of the mind is blinded. By soul and belly the inward parts may be understood, which are disturbed when, seeing that the wicked cannot be corrected, we are angry inwardly but are not allowed openly to cry out. Christ himself was also troubled, lest saints troubled in tribulations should despair.

### Verse 11. “For my life has failed in sorrow, and my years in groanings.”

The life of the righteous, who desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ unless remaining in the flesh is necessary for the sake of others—the life, I say, of such persons—is the advancement of others. Hence the Apostle: “Now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord” (1 Thess. 3:8). When those for whose sake the righteous live do not advance, their life fails in sorrow; and each of them rightly says: “For my life has failed in sorrow.”

Or life is confessing the Lord, and the confession of the Lord has failed in sorrow. Or literally: life fails in sorrow—that is, strength of mind is weakened by tortures so that one is even weary of living, because human frailty has no good in itself. And my years—the times of this life—are not taken away by death, but are spent in groanings because of unceasing torments; or, when iniquity abounds and one is not permitted to cry out, my years are spent in secret groanings.

“My strength has been weakened in poverty,” or “my vigor in want.” The body lacks health, yet torments are not spared it; it longs for release, but death is spared it. Of this I say: “My strength,” that is, my confidence, “has been weakened.” Or it has been weakened in the poverty of others: because the charity of many will grow cold, my strength has been weakened; and my bones—that is, the strong, who are not troubled by persecutions—have been troubled only by the iniquities of their brethren.

### Verse 12. “Above all my enemies I have become a reproach.”

That is, more than the wicked who are justly tortured for their crimes until confession, I have become a reproach; or I have become a great reproach on account of enemies who are above all my enemies—that is, on account of false Christians and hypocrites, who are worse than pagans, Jews, and tax-collectors. Ezekiel compares such hypocrites to branches cut from a vine, which are worse than wild wood (Ezek. 15:2). Branches remaining in the vine and bearing fruit are indeed better; but once cut off, fire alone awaits them. Wild wood, even when cut, is useful, because it may be put to building.

Then he specifies to whom the Church becomes a reproach because of false Christians: “To my neighbors”—that is, those wishing to believe and already near to faith, but frightened away by the evil life of those burdening the ship. Or, “neighbors,” that is, relatives. “And I became a fear to those who knew me”: I struck fear into them by the dreadful example of tribulations; or this concerns those of whom good had been hoped, who fall into crimes. “I became a fear to those who knew me,” that is, I became doubtful to my familiar associates, who fear lest all my people be such. “Those who see me”—that is, those who know what the Church is and what my invisible hope is—fled from me outward to visible things, or to make schisms and heresies.

### Verse 13. “I am forgotten by them, as though I were dead from their heart.”

Yet I, living for the Lord’s purposes, have become like a lost vessel: that is, I seemed to have perished, gaining no one, or not retaining those gained. And I say this because “I have heard the reproach of many round about”—that is, among those who seek temporal things.

Otherwise: “I am forgotten as one dead from the heart.” I indeed became a great reproach to my neighbors and a fear to those who knew me; and thence a certain temporary recollection of myself struck my heart, as though I were not worthy of such great reproaches before my neighbors and acquaintances. While I wasted away within myself in this way, the grace of God suddenly visited me: I remembered God and delighted in him; and, forgetting myself because of the sweetness of the remembrance of God, “I was forgotten as one dead from the heart”—that is, from self-will. When it was mortified within me, I became like a lost vessel, reckoning myself to be nothing, especially fleeing the ambitions of offices and dignities. Therefore,

[Col. 1298B] “For I have heard the reproach of many dwelling round about”: that is, in the Scriptures I have heard them reproved who seek to become rich and honored in earthly things, and who dwell in such ambition round about like a revolving wheel, falling in its forward motion and rising—or rather dreaming that they rise—in what follows.

Because of certain such people, all Christians are reproached. Their reproachers go around the Church and do not enter it, because they too love the wheel of temporal things. And while they assembled together in that reproach against me, they formed a conspiracy “to take my soul”: namely, to life, so that they might not allow me to die, though I would prefer it. Or they conspired to cast me out of the Church and to take my soul—that is, my consent—into it, that is, into their circuit.

Otherwise: those who saw me, Christ, outwardly—that is, as a mere human being—fled from me because they did not understand the divinity hidden in the man. They fled outward from me, and I was cut off from them as a dead person is cut off from human hearts, since with the body they bury the remembrance also. I became like a lost vessel, because, being dead, I was considered fit to be cast away. For I heard the reproach of many Jews dwelling round about—that is, wandering outside, in the Law, about carnal things and not spiritually understanding the point of truth. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). They killed him, however, by the counsel expressed in the words, “while they assembled together against me,” etc. Thus they took counsel.

### Verse 15. “But I, Christ, knowing that such persons have no power, hoped in you, Father,” etc.

Or I, the Church, understanding that one must not hope in man, “have hoped in you, Lord,” and said: because you, who are unchangeable, are my God, who will save the one whom you correct. And:

### Verse 16. “My lots are in your hands.”

That is, my lots are in your power, not in human merits. One must ask why we are forbidden to use lots in ecclesiastical laws, since Joshua is recorded to have used lots in the distribution of the land. The reply is this: homicide is prohibited by the Law, yet when someone is killed by God’s permission, no sin is committed against the Law, because God is not under the Law but above it. Likewise, when Joshua used lots with the Lord’s permission, he is defended by the authority of the one permitting it.

The Apostles also, by the Holy Spirit’s hidden prompting, chose Matthias by lot before Pentecost (Acts 1:26). But later, more fully enlightened, they sought no signs of lots when choosing Stephen and the other deacons; such a practice had previously been permitted to them as still less perfect. Similarly, when they heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John, not by the selection of lots but by divine authority, Scripture consenting that the Gentiles were to be converted. Therefore, since the shadow of the Law has passed and the true light now shines, in doubtful matters the quality of human conduct must be directed not by lots but by the testimonies and indications of Scripture.

An objection is raised here that Saint Augustine says: “A lot is not something evil, but is a grace which, without merits, chooses whom it wills and in human uncertainty indicates the divine will.” [Note: [Col. 1299D] Augustine, *Expositions on Psalm 30*, verse 16, Exposition IV.]

We reply: nor was the tree in paradise evil because it was forbidden; rather, evil for man was to transgress what had been forbidden. The same must be said of lots. But in this passage, where the Psalmist says, “My lots are in your hands,” the meaning is: although with you there is a just and hidden order of election, yet I, to whom this is hidden, have come by lot to the Lord’s tunic—that is, to charity.

Or “my lots” means: “the times of my life are in your hands,” because we live and die when you will. The Hebrew truth intends this sense, in which it reads: “My times are in your hand.” Another translation likewise has: “My times are in your hands.” Therefore, “deliver me from the hand of my enemies and from those who persecute me.” He calls the devil and his ministers the persecutors.

### Verses 17, 18, 19. “Make your face shine upon your servant.”

For now there is a mingling of evil with good; but let those who belong to you appear—that is, make known to those who think I am neglected that your face is directed toward me and that I serve you. Hence in another psalm: “Judge my cause against an unholy nation” (Ps. 42:1). Since you are true salvation, may my face be illumined by your healing efficacy: “Save me,” not in my own righteousness but “in your mercy,” so that I may not be confounded—that is, mingled with the wicked. May I not be confounded or ashamed before those insulting me because I invoked you—you, I say, and no other.

Or this is the reason why I shall not be confounded: because I invoked you. Or Christ says to the Father: “Make your face shine,” etc.—that is, reveal your good will toward me, so that, as the disciples despair over me dying, they may have confidence in me rising again.

But let the wicked rather, who invoke stones, be ashamed—contrary to what I said, “May I not be confounded.” Let them be led down into hell—that is, joined to the shades—contrary to what I said, “Make your face shine.” And let deceitful, garrulous, false lips, which here do not fear judgment, be made speechless in punishments when your mysteries in me are revealed, so that they may rather say: “We fools thought their life madness,” etc. (Wis. 5:4). I mean lips that speak iniquity against the righteous one—that is, Christ, Head and members—in pride, because the creature acts against the Creator; and in misuse or contempt, because they acted contrary to that manner in which people ordinarily show gratitude for benefits, when they despised as crucified and merely human him who had come for their salvation. In amazement at them the Prophet cries:

### Verse 20. “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord, by which you love those whom you correct!”

But in order that this sweetness may be desired more, and that people, being secure, may not behave negligently, you have hidden the sweetness of your love. Yet in the future it will be open only to those who fear you, not shared with the wicked. You have perfected this sweetness for those who, living according to the Son of God, do not fear with servile fear but hope in you to the end—hope, I say, confessing you in the sight of the sons of men. Hence in the Gospel: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father” (Matt. 10:12). Then he explains the perfection of this sweetness and says:

### Verse 21. “You will hide them from the disturbance of men.”

That is, they may not suffer human disturbance. Or, while the wicked are troubled, they will be in the hiding place of your face, that is, of your knowledge, seeing you. For every elect person is hidden at judgment, through inward sight, in the countenance of divinity, while the outward blindness of the reprobate, repelled by the strict judgment of justice, is troubled.

Therefore holy men do not cease to put themselves to death with the sword of the sacred Word, away from the importunity of temporal desires, the tumult of useless concerns, and the cry of clamorous disturbances; and inwardly they hide themselves before the face of God in the secret place of the mind. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “You will hide them in the hiding place of your countenance from the disturbance of men.” Although this is accomplished perfectly after judgment, even now it occurs to a great extent, when they are carried inward by delight away from the tumults of temporal desires, so that their mind, while it is wholly directed toward the love of God, may not be torn by any empty disturbance.

Thus Paul saw his disciples as dead through contemplation and, as it were, hidden in the secret place of divinity; he said to them: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3). For one who desires to mortify himself greatly rejoices in the repose of contemplation once found, so that, dead to the world, he may remain hidden and conceal himself from all disturbances of external things within the bosom of innermost love.

For when Truth says, “Where your treasure is, there also will your heart be” (Matt. 6:22), just as the heart of a miser who loves his money is stored beside his treasure, either shut in a chest or even buried in the ground, so surely is the heart of the person who perfectly loves true life and true wisdom hidden where he knows the true treasure of wisdom and life that he loves to be stored.

[Col. 1301A] This treasure is hidden in the secret place of the divine countenance. Yet, just as a person’s wisdom shines in his face and outward bearing declares what is hidden within him, so in sacred Scripture the wisdom of God shines forth in the Old and New Testaments as though in the two cheeks of his countenance; and his activity or bearing, made known by both Testaments, declares him to human beings. Therefore sacred Scripture, understood according to its historical sense, is like the surface of God’s face considered outwardly. But the mystical and moral interpretation is the hidden place of this face.

Those who love Scripture’s inward sense and direct their lives according to it, keeping their hearts always fixed beside this treasure, will enter that hidden place. And when men who derive their name from the soil and love earthly things alone are disturbed by the life of these others, thus ordered, thus gilded and adorned with jewels from this treasure, and thus ornamented with little chains of gold studded with silver, these latter are hidden from this disturbance of men in the secret place of your face. They regard it as their greatest protection that they know themselves to be ordered according to your will even in those things which sometimes cause people disturbance.

They are hidden now only in part; but in the future perfectly, when they will feel within themselves no movement outside the good pleasure of your will, O God. [Col. 1301C] But of Cain it is written that he “went out from the face of the Lord” (Gen. 4:16), because he refused to order himself according to God’s good pleasure; rather, he wasted away in his wickedness, and was drawn, for the consolation of that wickedness, solely by delight in earthly things. Therefore he was the first to build a city for himself upon earth, because he placed his defense and consolation in earthly things alone. Those imitate him who defend and fortify the evil deeds they commit by the examples of earthly persons like themselves; trusting in their custom and multitude as though in a fortified city, they consider themselves secure.

O God, who will lead me into this fortified city? Who will grant me to conquer it? Will not you, O God, conquer it—you who drove us back from conquering it, teaching us only to depart from its midst, saying: “Go out from her, my people” [Col. 1301D] (Isa. 52:11)? You also teach us to pray for the peace of this city, so that our peace may be in its peace. Therefore your faithful, desiring to rest in the hiding-place of your countenance and having here no abiding city, knowing that you made the children of Israel dwell in tents and that the holy patriarchs lived in huts, desire, after their example, to dwell rather in your tabernacle than materially in that fortified city: to follow the examples of a few good persons, from whom they may have a tabernacle woven for themselves, rather than the examples of many persons fortified by the authority and multitude of those who do evil.

Therefore, until they are admitted to the hidden place of your countenance, when you say to each one, “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into [Col. 1302A] joy” (Matt. 25:21)—which is the hidden place of your countenance—you will protect them here in your tabernacle, that is, in the present Church, or under the shelter of the sacraments and faith, from the contradiction of heretical, schismatic, deceitful, and wicked tongues. When these sometimes cry out and sometimes whisper, “I heard the reproach of many who dwell round about.”

That is, of those dwelling together in deliberate agreement, while they assembled together against me. For although in other matters they were discordant among themselves, nevertheless, assembling as one against the Lord and against his Christ, they remained and agreed in the counsel which they pursued while they assembled together against me. They agreed among themselves, namely, in those things [Col. 1302B] which were against me—especially where they took counsel to seize, that is, to snatch away, my soul with him “who sits in secret places, that he may kill the innocent. His eyes watch the poor; he lies in wait in secret like a lion in his den; he lies in wait to seize, knowing that he will seize the poor when he draws him” (Ps. 9:9–10) into consent with his perversity.

These men, his henchmen, took counsel to seize my soul—that is, to snatch it away. Hence birds of prey are called *accipitres* [hawks]; and the Apostle, in saying, “If anyone takes” (2 Cor. 11:20), wishes to mean, “if anyone snatches away,” since *accipere*, “to take,” is sometimes used for *rapere*, “to seize”; as also in this place, where I complain of my persecutors or ambushers, who, while they assembled [Col. 1302C] together against me, took counsel to seize my soul.

Alternatively: I, Christ, perfect God and man, subsisting from divinity, a rational soul, and human flesh, truly had—and have—a human soul. The Apollinarians wished to take it from me, that is, to remove it, saying that I did not possess a rational soul but that my flesh lived solely by divinity. These heretics and their followers, while they assembled together against me, took counsel to seize my soul. But I, Father, “commended my spirit into your hands,” that is, this my soul, as has been stated earlier in this very psalm. And you, faithfully preserving what was entrusted to you, stirred up defenders of Catholic truth in defense of my soul, condemning [Col. 1302D] the heretics who asserted that I assumed human flesh alone and not a soul.

Those also who crucified me took counsel to seize my soul. But I hoped in you, Lord; I said, “You are my God; my times are in your hands.” These times were so preordained that no one would take, receive, or snatch my soul from me. Rather, when my appointed times, disposed in your hand, were ended, I placed and deposited it in your hands as a precious trust, commending it to you; and receiving it again from your hand and possessing it, I do not fear those who, while they assembled together against me, took counsel to seize my soul. For death, which ordinarily separates soul from body, will no longer rule over me; and the heresy of the Apollinarians, wishing to take [Col. 1303A]—that is, to snatch or remove—my soul from me, having been condemned by the Catholic Fathers through the authority of the Holy Spirit, will not rise again. Catholics rejoice that I, the author of human salvation, in order to make the whole human being sound, assumed the whole human being into unity of person: namely, a rational soul and flesh taken from the Virgin and conceived by the Holy Spirit.

More wickedly than the rest, however, the Pharisees and scribes wished to seize my soul, attempting to make it conform to their evil traditions, which were contrary to the law of God. But, unwilling to adapt the consent of my soul to such things, I said to them: “Why do you transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? For God said: ‘Honor your father and [Col. 1303B] your mother.’ But you say: ‘Whatever gift is from me will benefit you’; and you have made void the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition. Hypocrites! Isaiah rightly prophesied of you, saying: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men’” (Matt. 15:5 ff.). Against such ravishers of souls, let anyone who has ears hear what the Spirit says to the churches: Hear and understand the traditions which God has given you.

“Deliver me from the hand of my enemies and from those who persecute me.” For my lots, or my times, have been placed and disposed in your hands. But the hand of my enemies is contrary to your hands. [Col. 1303C] This I ask of your mercy: because I have commended my spirit into your hands and my times are in your hands, let the contrary hand—the hand of my enemies—have no power over me. Sometimes, according to what is written, “The earth is given into the hand of the wicked” (Job 9:24), the power and hand of the wicked may do something to our body or even to our earthly possessions. But with a great desire of heart I seek this: that I myself may be wholly delivered and freed from the hand of the wicked and from those who persecute me, just as your servant Moses was once delivered from Pharaoh who persecuted him, so that Pharaoh could harm neither Moses nor the people entrusted to him. Indeed, in persecuting him, Pharaoh was found to have benefited him by driving Moses to the place where you appeared to him: first, in the flame of the bush; secondly, [Col. 1303D] upon the summit of Mount Sinai, where you appeared to him and spoke with him as a friend to a friend. And from fellowship in your speech, when you looked upon him, you so illuminated his face that a mortal eye could not bear its brightness; indeed, the elders of Israel, marveling and astonished as though in ecstasy, were greatly afraid, since they could not look upon his face because of the glory of his countenance. Yet this glory of his face, compared with that glory which Moses and Elijah had with the Lord on the mountain, is eclipsed as the light of a lamp is eclipsed in comparison with sunlight.

Nevertheless, that earlier glory of Moses was preparatory to the later and greater one, and was completed in him in this order. As a child he was nourished in luxury by Pharaoh’s daughter. But when grown up he refused to be called [Col. 1304A] the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasure of temporary sin among the Egyptians. Then, after striking an Egyptian in defense of his brother, a Hebrew man, he fled from Pharaoh; there he became a shepherd of sheep and took Zipporah, one of the seven daughters of the priest of Midian, as wife, by whom he begot two sons. While engaged in this pastoral care, he saw the great vision in the flame of the bush and heard the great commands of God speaking from the flame. He was commanded to undertake an embassy to Pharaoh himself, his persecutor. Coming to him and not fearing his violence, when Pharaoh again pursued him, he crossed the Red Sea with the whole people of Israel and came to Mount Sinai. There, when the Lord appeared and spoke with him, his face shone with the great glory [Col. 1304B] of brightness. This glory and brightness was preparatory and precursory to the other brightness which we recognize in the Gospel, where Jesus was transfigured in the presence of Moses himself and Elijah.

If we consider this order, do we not plainly recognize that, for perfecting and bringing to completion the brightness of Moses’ countenance, both the persecutions of the Egyptian enemies and, amid those adversities, divine appearances, and after the adversities the full consolations of God, cooperated together concerning him? Of these consolations the chief was that his face was illuminated with such brightness both at the receiving of the austere law and at the beginning of evangelical grace that neither the children of Israel under the law nor the apostles in the Gospel could [Col. 1304C] behold it with direct vision. Hence, under the law, a veil was put on to moderate the splendor of his face; and in the Gospel, a bright cloud overshadowed the apostles, still less fitted to see or even to recount such a vision. Therefore it was said to them: “Tell no one of the vision until the Son of Man rises from the dead” (Matt. 17:9).

Thus I principally, Christ, who “did not come to destroy the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17), rightly speak in this psalm of myself to you, God, into whose hands I commend my spirit, concerning all the things prefigured by Moses: I pray to be delivered from the hand of my enemies and from those who persecute me, after the example of Moses once delivered; and, with those very persecutions and your consolations cooperating, to be so illuminated [Col. 1304D] as Moses’ face was illuminated—yet to a degree differing from his as much as my name differs from his, and as the Lord is greater than the servant, God by nature than a god by adoption. For to him God indeed said: “Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1); but to me the Father says: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). Therefore he was made a god by grace over one king; I am God naturally, begotten of God, and set over all the works of his hands.

Yet, to liberate servants, I was humbled in the form of a servant, so that my appearance had no beauty in itself, and friends and enemies saw me as having neither form nor comeliness. Therefore I pray to you, Father: “Deliver me from the hand of my enemies and from those who persecute me,” who would have no power [Col. 1305A] at all over me unless it had been given them from above, and unless I, emptied of the glory of my Lord that was in me, had been humbled in the form of a servant, with neither form nor comeliness in my face. Therefore you, by whose command I appear thus despised—I who am “beautiful in form beyond the children of men”—after the disgrace of death and the cross, illuminate your face upon your servant.

Your most bright and divine face is that true light which enlightens every person coming into this world. But this face was emptied insofar as it was united to the form of a servant. Therefore I, Christ, desiring that the servile form and nature in which I appeared despised should be illuminated by the glory which I had before the world was made, now say to you, Father, in this psalm: “Illuminate your face upon your servant”; [Col. 1305B] and again I say in the Gospel: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5). That is: upon your servant, the man united to me your Word, so illuminate your face that the glory of the assumed man may be the same as that of the eternal Word itself which I am, your Son—who inclined to this servile form so that the glorified man might reign upon the lofty throne, seated at your right hand.

For the salvation and hope of guilty humanity will consist in this: that human nature is believed to reign and sit with you, God the Father, in me your Son, radiant with the light of divine glory, more radiant than Moses’ face was. For if the countenance of him to whom the word of God came rightly shone, how can the supreme light, the blessed Trinity—which does not admit a quaternity—be believed to withhold anything of its highest brightness from human nature so exalted? For the eternal Word itself, [Col. 1305C] namely the Word of God, united that man to itself in one person of the most radiant Trinity, admitting human nature to one person in the Trinity in such a manner that, by doubling the nature in that person, it did not double the person.

But I, Christ, still despised in the form of a servant, after I said what was stated above, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit,” rightly went on, for the glorification even of my servile body, to say: “Deliver me from the hand of my enemies,” who guard my tomb, “and from those who persecute me”—in myself and in my followers—by the lie procured from the soldiers, by which they strive to maintain that my servile body was stolen away and was illuminated by no glory of resurrection. But you, Father, illuminate your face upon your servant, while the apostles bear witness to my resurrection with great power, one of them saying: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God.” Then may the glory of my illuminated face be preached everywhere and made manifest, the Lord cooperating and confirming the word by the signs which follow [Col. 1305D].

Alternatively: I, any Christian whatsoever who has been redeemed—whose voice above was, “You have redeemed me, Lord God of truth”—still placed among enemies and oppressed by their wicked power as by Pharaoh’s tyranny, say to you, Lord God of truth, [Col. 1306A] who redeemed me from Egyptian bondage through the sacrifice of the paschal lamb, so that I should serve you alone: look upon the camp of the Egyptians in this morning watch, when the light that will remain forever draws near. Look also upon me, your servant, so disposed and possessing such a purpose that I may behold without the intervention of a veil both the law shining in the brightness of Moses’ face and grace shining in the brightness of Christ’s face. But this is impossible for me, and the light of both law and grace is wholly inaccessible to me, unless you who redeemed me hear and answer me when I say: “Deliver me from the hand of my enemies and from those who persecute me,” drowning them in the Red Sea and establishing me, your servant, on the mountain of the law and grace.

I do not ask you to drown or destroy in this sea, [Col. 1306B] which the blood of the New Testament has made red, my human enemies who persecute me. For I desire that nothing should be destroyed in them except their being hostile persecutors. Preserve their nature, but destroy their guilt. Heal and restore in them what you yourself made; blot out and wash away in the blood of the New Testament what they themselves do. For they do not know what they are doing, imagining that they render you service by persecuting me, whom they do not judge to be your servant.

But you, Lord, in order to make it evident that I am your servant, first strengthen me in your service, that I may never be able to depart from it; and make this manifest to those who persecute me, lest they be scandalized in me by imagining that they render service to you when persecuting me, whom they do not think your servant—or, if they do [Col. 1306C] think so, pretend to think otherwise, having an occasion for such pretense because you have not yet illuminated your face upon your servant. Hence I myself sometimes waver in your service, not knowing whether I am worthy of your hatred or love. Therefore you, Lord, who “will not give the righteous person to be shaken forever” (Ps. 54:23), illuminate your face upon your servant, approving my service in such a way that it can no more be doubtful that I please you among the number of good servants than it was ever doubtful that Moses was your servant after his face was illuminated.

Likewise, illuminate your face upon every servant of yours, lest anyone sin in ignorance against him, [Col. 1306D] thinking that he renders you service. Illuminate your face upon every servant, that there may be discernment and manifest distinction between one who serves you and one who does not serve you; between Hebrews and Egyptians; between circumcision and slaughter; between the children marked with the name of the Trinity, whom the flame of the Babylonian furnace does not burn, and the king’s ministers who kindle it and suffer punishment from the fire which they increase.

Your Son, O God the Father, is your face. Illuminate this your face upon me, your servant, and upon every other servant of yours. You are like a golden substance; and your Son, being “the brightness of your glory and the figure of your substance,” like a royal or priestly image in the purest gold, presents himself as an incorruptible seal, imprinting himself upon every servant whom he conforms to himself [Col. 1307A]. And you, Father, accomplish this very work of sealing, through him, with him, and in him, in your servants who are to be conformed to the same Son.

But that you may perform this work which you perform very swiftly—not in wrath but in your mercy—I therefore say: “Illuminate your face upon your servant; save me in your mercy.” By your face I understand your Son; by your mercy I understand the Holy Spirit. Therefore illuminate your face, that is, your Son, upon me, so that, planted together in the likeness of his death and resurrection through the mortification of the old man and the newness of a righteous life, I may be found in each of his beautiful faces. For he has the beautiful face of a man, an ox, a lion, and a flying eagle. Conform me to the man, the ox, the lion, [Col. 1307B] and the flying eagle through faith working by love in his incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension.

Through the mystery of the holy incarnation, let me have the face of a man, possessing prudence, which may make my service rational. Through the mystery of the Lord’s passion, let me have the face of a calf or ox—that is, of a sacrificial victim—possessing temperance, by which I may crucify my flesh with its vices and desires. Through the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection, let me have the face of a lion, possessing courage, so that death through sin may no longer rule over me as I live. Through the mystery of the Lord’s ascension, let me have the face of a flying eagle, possessing not my own righteousness, which draws downward, but the righteousness of God, which bears upward.

[Col. 1307C] Thus, Lord, illuminate your face upon me; and, that I may be wholly secure from the four contrary faces—the asp, basilisk, lion, and dragon—preserve me in the hiding-place of your countenance and save me in your mercy, that is, in the Holy Spirit the Paraclete. Confirm the work which you have wrought in me, so that, once separated from fellowship with the faithless and wicked, I may not again be confounded, that is, mixed with them: may I not be confounded and poured together with the wicked into one vessel of destruction, such as they deem me, in whose eyes I have become “like a vessel of destruction.” May I not be with them in one Babylonian confusion.

Or, “may I not be confounded,” that is, may I not be ashamed, because I have called upon you. I called not upon what is yours, but upon you; for I desired you rather than your gifts to come into me. In this invocation I am put to shame whenever, unable to demonstrate that you dwell in me, I hear it said to me: “Where is your God?” [Col. 1307D] (Ps. 41:4). At the beginning of the psalm too I said in my ecstasy, or in my fear: “In you, Lord, I have hoped; let me not be confounded forever”; and now again in my fear I say: “Let me not be confounded, because I have called upon you.” Repetition is affirmation.

In this prayer, by which I ask to be kept safe from confusion—namely, that I may neither be confounded forever nor be confounded because I have called upon you—I do not ask simply not to be confounded, for there is a confusion that brings glory when someone is put to shame unto repentance. Rather, I ask that I may not be confounded forever and may not be confounded in this, namely because I have called upon you. For I have called upon you as helper, comforter, savior, and preserver. Yet you sometimes withdraw the hoped-for and requested help of consolation and salvation, and thereby in some sense make absent the one invoked. Must I not then necessarily be confounded when, having called upon you thus, I am not heard?

But let it be granted that I am sometimes not heard, since I read that the Apostle Paul asked three times and was not heard; and for a time he could therefore have been confounded, not knowing that his not being heard was not unto folly. For he did not yet know how to sing: “My God, I will cry by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and it is not unto folly to me” (Ps. 21:3). Truly the Apostle was for a time confounded because he was not heard; but he was not confounded forever, [Col. 1308B] because he quickly received the divine answer by which he was taught that what was sought was not then useful.

But in the Apostle’s other petitions and prayers, in which eternal salvation was sought, he, asking in the name of the Savior, was so heard that he is never read to have been thereby confounded, as though the eternal helper had been invoked in vain. So I too, crying day and night, if I am not heard, bear such confusion with equanimity, provided that it is not unto folly but unto instruction: namely, that strength may be made perfect in weakness—the strength, that is, of firm humility in the weakness of frail prayer—especially when something is sought which, if granted, would impede eternal salvation.

But where I seek some benefit that can serve eternal consolation, I ask that I may not be confounded [Col. 1308C] forever; let not that be denied me whose denial would harm me forever. “Let me not be confounded, because I have called upon you,” the eternal indweller of good hearts; for if, invoked, you do not come and leave me empty, I shall be confounded forever. But, I pray, let me not be confounded forever because I have called upon you; rather, delivered from such confusion, may I rejoice and exult, not for an hour in the light of an answer harmful to me, but forever in goods that will benefit me from this present time and unto the age—for ever.

Alternatively: You are priest forever; you are the high priest of good things to come, Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, according to your priestly office of future good things which remain forever, I ask that I may [Col. 1308D] not be confounded forever by the denial of good things that endure forever. For Scripture calls the denial of any petition a person’s “confusion”; a proof-text is the passage where Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother, entering to the king, said: “I ask one petition of you; I pray, do not confound my face” (3 Kgs. 2:16), as though she said: “You confound my face unless you do what I ask.” Yet King Solomon then confounded his mother’s face because she did not ask wisely, requesting that Abishag the Shunammite be given as wife to Adonijah; the wise king, understanding that this was not expedient for his kingdom, refused to do it.

So also now the Church, or each faithful soul, is sometimes confounded when not heard, especially in matters which the true Solomon knows would not be expedient if they occurred according to the wishes of a petition relating to temporal goods [Col. 1309A]. But lest they be confounded even in those matters in which eternal blessedness is undoubtedly to be bestowed, it says: “In you I have hoped; let me not be confounded forever.” Likewise: “Let me not be confounded, because I have called upon you.” This means: Let not the effect of petitions seeking eternal goods and calling upon you rather than your gifts be denied me.

In contrast, let the wicked be ashamed and be led down into hell; let deceitful lips be made mute, which speak iniquity against the righteous in pride and abuse. Let them be ashamed in this respect: let them not obtain their desire, their petitions being rendered void and their deceitful lips silenced—lips which speak iniquity against the righteous, asking for temporal goods [Col. 1309B] which they may vainly consume in pride and abuse. To such people it is elsewhere said: “You desire and do not have; you ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, in order that you may spend it upon your desires” (Jas. 4:3).

Wrong desires reign especially through pride and abuse, when earth and ashes pride themselves in the lust of surpassing others and dare to misuse creatures unto the corruption of body and mind, though they should have used them in praise of the Creator. By such pride and abuse they glory as though exalted above heaven and made like the Most High, while they submit to no yoke of obedience. By contrast, those governed under holy obedience do not turn temporal or spiritual gifts granted to them into pride and abuse [Col. 1309C]. In the person of each such individual I said above: “Let me not be confounded forever,” that is, let no gift capable of helping through humility and good use toward the attainment of eternal joy be denied me. But let the wicked be ashamed when your gifts are denied them—gifts by which they desire to corrupt themselves in pride and abuse.

Yet lest such persons perish through obstinate impenitence, let them also be ashamed, being confounded through true repentance, and let them be led down into hell through their own judgment. For, as the Apostle says, “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31). Therefore let them be led down into hell by their own judgment, lest they be deprived of heaven by the divine judgment. Thus the thief, judging himself worthy of penal judgment, was made worthy of paradise.

[Col. 1309D] “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord.” It was sweetness that the confessing thief heard: “You shall be in paradise” (Luke 23:43), even if this were to happen to him after many thousands of years; but the multitude of sweetness was that there was added: “Today.” “Today,” he says, “you shall be with me in paradise.” Truly there is much sweetness in these words, but it would not be great without the abiding presence of him who is the fountain of eternal sweetness. Hence, when he added, “with me,” the declaration in this saying is full of sweetness: “Amen I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise.” Amen—that is, I, the Truth, truly say to you: not after a long time, but today; not with just any angel of mine, but with me; you shall be in paradise, that is, in the true garden of delights, where there is a great multitude of sweetness.

Who can weigh or adequately [Col. 1310A] admire how great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden from those who fear you with servile rather than filial fear? But you have perfected it for those who hope in you in the sight of the children of men. You have hidden from the fearful what you have perfected for those who hope and confess before the children of men. For it is, as it were, a certain hiding of your sweetness when you say: “Whoever is ashamed of me before human beings, I also will be ashamed of him before my Father” (Luke 9:26). But the perfection of sweetness lies in what you say: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I also will confess him before my Father” (Luke 12:8), who is in heaven.

The verse of this psalm, “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit,” was heard upon the cross. Therefore, throughout the sense of this psalm, we gladly remain [Col. 1310B] around the cross, maintaining that the great multitude of sweetness displayed on that same cross to the confessing thief is likewise commended in this psalm, where it is said: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord.” Let this thief alone be a great proof to all that great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden from those who fear you; but you have perfected those who hope in you in the sight of the children of men.

Indeed, this thief confessed the Lord in the sight of the children of men, fearing whom all the apostles fled, leaving him. But they too, later strengthened through the Holy Spirit, confessed the truth in the sight of the children of men, esteeming the terror of human fear as little [Col. 1310C] in comparison with the great multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you hid from those same apostles while still fearful and timid, but perfected for them when strengthened, hoping in you, and confessing you in the sight of the children of men.

Likewise, you hide your sweetness from Christians still timid; but for those same persons who hope in you and confess you in the sight of the children of men, you perfect this sweetness—indeed, you have already perfected it in your predestination. But so that they may attain it and not perish in the disturbance of human beings, you will hide them in the hiding-place of your countenance from the disturbance of human beings. You will protect them in your tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues. We have already, as we were able and with God’s gift, explained above the meaning of this verse. It follows:

[Col. 1310D] **VERSE 22.** “Blessed be the Lord, for he has made his mercy wonderful to me in a fortified city.” I, David the prophet, foreknowing such great benefits of God and seeing them as though accomplished and already past—or I, any psalmist whatever, considering them now fulfilled—attribute none of this to the merit of human virtue. Rather, magnifying in all these things the gratuitous grace of God, I say: “Blessed be the Lord, because he did not weigh human merits according to justice, but, by giving the Holy Spirit, made his mercy wonderful,” that is, made it marvelous. For who am I, or what is my father’s house, that he should deign to have mercy upon me, a human being already condemned in original guilt and not justified by actual virtue—upon me, I say, ashes and dust? Yet in this very fact the mercy of God was made wonderful and marvelous toward me: no good merits provoking grace preceded it, but many evil merits demanding wrath.

He made this mercy wonderful first in the fortified city, that is, Jerusalem—a city fortified by the protection of angels, around which, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, the Lord repeatedly placed a hedge and dug around it [Col. 1311A] (Isa. 34:15). The hedge extending upward was angelic protection, which guards from on high. The trench below was the humility of the patriarchs, prophets, and other righteous, holy, and humble people, of whom it is said in the hymn of the three youths: “Bless the Lord, holy and humble of heart” (Dan. 3:87). Thus the city and people of the Jews were fortified; from them, through the mercy of God made wonderful and marvelous, the primitive Church was chosen. Hers is this voice of praise and thanksgiving: “Blessed be the Lord, for he has made his mercy wonderful to me in a fortified city.”

Likewise, the Church gathered from the Gentiles is a fortified city. Above it angels surround it with a most powerful defense against the powers of the air, against the principalities of this world, the rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. And below, peace on earth to human beings of good will, arising through the battles of the martyrs—indeed, through the banner of the cross fixed in the earth—fortifies this city as a kind of trench. Since this is wonderful in our eyes, each of us rightly says in praise of grace: “Blessed [Col. 1311C] be the Lord, who has made his mercy wonderful to me in a fortified city”; or, as another translation has it, “in a city of surrounding,” that is, a city surrounded, as has just been said, by the protections of angels and saints, so that it is a fortified city.

Or, because throughout the circuit of the world the Church, extended abroad, surrounds each faithful person like a most powerful defense, so that one surrounded by the communion of saints—which each person professes in the Catholic faith—cannot become the prey of demons, let each child of the Church say within himself: “Blessed be the Lord, for he has made his mercy wonderful to me in a fortified city.”

**VERSE 23.** “But I said in the excess of my mind: I am cast away from before your eyes.” In a city indeed well fortified, the divine mercy, made wonderful, guards me. But I, David, when Saul persecuted me, said in the excess of my mind, or in my fear: “I am cast away from before your eyes.” Concerning the excess of mind it was said in the title of the psalm that it occurs in two ways: either when the mind rises above temporal things through contemplation, or when it falls below through excessive fear. But because one translation has, “I said in the excess of my mind,” and another, “I said in my fear,” the excess intended here is rightly understood as that arising from excessive fear. For this is the confession of one greatly afraid: “I am cast away from before your eyes”—that is, when Saul persecuted me and I sometimes despaired of being able to escape. Then I said in my fear: “I am cast away from before your eyes,” [Col. 1312A] knowing and confessing that I had no merit worthy of the regard of your countenance.

“Therefore you heard the voice of my prayer when I cried to you.” Therefore, because, humbled in this way, I cried to you, you heard the voice of my prayer when I cried to you: when I cried not for the obtaining of temporal things, but to you, who are the eternal helper of those who cry to you and love you before all things. Therefore, instructed by my example: “Love the Lord, all you his saints.”

The Hebrew text has: “But I said in my bewilderment: ‘I have been cast out from before the sight of your eyes.’” This utterance may suit Peter when astonishment surrounded him at the sudden catch of fish and he said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” [Col. 1312B] (Luke 5:8). Therefore I, Peter the apostle, chosen by the Lord in the fortified city, set next in place upon the foundational rock and hence named Peter, truly blessing my chooser, say: “Blessed be the Lord, because he has made his mercy wonderful to me, a fisherman, in the fortified city,” saying to me: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:18). Has not mercy been wonderfully made wonderful to me in the fortified city, since there I am Peter, named from the principal rock, and endowed with such power of binding and loosing that whatever I bind upon earth shall be bound also in [Col. 1312C] heaven, and whatever I loose shall be loosed—and this in a fortified city against the gates of hell, which shall not prevail against it, so fortified that no one can lay for it another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus, and no power can break the keys given to it or wrench them from his hand?

But although I, Peter, was so great, nevertheless, seeing the violent wind, I was afraid (Matt. 14:30); and when I began to sink, I said in my fear or bewilderment: “I have been cast out from before the sight of your eyes.” Therefore you heard the voice of my prayer when, thus humbled, I cried to you, saying: “Lord, save me.” For immediately, stretching out your hand, you seized me, knowing that I loved you, as later you tested me, saying: “Peter, do you love me?” (John [Col. 1312D] 21:17).
