You said this three times because I too, in my fear or bewilderment, had denied you three times, so that the threefold confession of love might cleanse, before the sight of your eyes, the threefold denial by which I was cast out from before the sight of your eyes.

Your eyes see all things, as I said to you: “Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you” (ibid.). Yet I was cast out, by my own judgment, from before the sight of your all-seeing eyes, when you knew, saw, and foretold that I would deny you, while I, on the contrary, said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. 26:35). Thus, presuming upon my own constancy, I was cast out from before the sight of your eyes. And therefore, after I had denied you three times among the ungodly, I afterwards went outside and wept bitterly, saying within myself in my fear: “Lord, I have been cast out from before the sight of your [Col. 1313A] eyes.” Therefore you heard the voice of my prayer when I cried to you, weeping bitterly. And from this I know that you heard me: after the threefold denial, you tested me by a threefold confession of love.

Nothing is more pleasant than love or affection, because what is truly and perfectly loved never turns into weariness. In my fear I had chosen bitter weeping for myself, amid the mourning and lamentation of my repentance. But you, Lord—as was sung in the preceding psalm (v. 12)—“You turned my mourning into joy for me; you tore off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness,” granting me, after bitter tears, most sweet delight in your love. Thus, when bitter weeping had now ceased, in great gladness: “May my glory sing to you, and may I not be pierced” (Ps. 29:13) by the sting of a biting conscience [Col. 1313B] because of the threefold denial, since you yourself are witness to my threefold love for you, by which I love you with all my heart, all my soul, all my mind, or all my strength. Desiring by my example to stir up to this love both the lambs and the sheep over whom I have been appointed shepherd, I say: “Love the Lord, all his saints.”

Otherwise: “But I said in the ecstasy of my mind: ‘I have been cast out from before the sight of your eyes.’” In that higher ecstasy of the mind, where the citizenship of the saints is in heaven; where secret words are heard which it is not lawful for a human being to utter; where the whisper of a gentle and delicate breeze is perceived, in which the Lord is—in that ecstasy, I say, raised above myself, I looked down upon myself from on high and despised myself; and recognizing my misery and my exile, I said to you, my God: “I have been cast [Col. 1313C] out from before the sight of your eyes,” because “while we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:6).

Therefore you heard the voice of my prayer: namely, because in the height of contemplation I remembered the humiliation by which, in the first-formed human, I was cast out from before the sight of your eyes. Therefore you heard the voice of my prayer when I cried to you. You did not wait to hear me after my cry; rather, while I cried, in the very act of my crying you heard me crying to you—that is, loving you—for whoever loves you cries to you. For this love is the cry of the heart, not of the mouth, which you gladly hear, just as you heard your servant Moses loving you, to whom, while he loved you and was silent, you said: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. 14:15). Therefore, all of you [Col. 1313D] who wish to be heard by the Lord,

**VERSE 24.** “Love the Lord,” because love itself is the most effective prayer. “Love the Lord, all his saints.” Those who are evil servants and serve only for appearance do not love but fear their master. But you, all his saints, love the Lord, so that you regard his lordship over you as sweet and beloved, and offer him your service not from fear but from love. I shall no longer call you servants, but his saints and friends, because “the servant does not know what his master does” (John 15:15). But you, all his saints, know well what the Lord does in you. For yours is this saying: “We have such confidence through Christ toward God, not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves; but our sufficiency [Col. 1314A] is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5). Therefore, since it is the Lord who works in us both willing and accomplishing for good will, do not be high-minded, as though you had any power from genuine virtue, but agree with the humble: “Love the Lord, all his saints,” because your holiness is his work.

Love the Lord by speaking truth: that is, by attributing your evils to yourselves but your goods to him—accusing yourselves concerning evils and praising him concerning goods. Speak truth, because

“The Lord will seek truth and repay abundantly those who practise pride.” The Lord sought truth from Adam, saying: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9). But he did not speak truth, so as to say: “I am in sin, Lord.” Rather, to the sin of transgression he added [Col. 1314B] the sin of proud self-defence; and then the Lord repaid him abundantly for practising pride, because he cast him out of the paradise of delight into the exile of mortality and many miseries. He will likewise repay abundantly the sons and daughters of Adam who still imitate their father and practise pride.

It would be a sin in some sense tolerable if, in a good and honourable work, one suffered pride—felt it assailing oneself—but did not at all consent to it. For God, who wills no one to perish, overlooks human sins for the sake of repentance; and repentance excludes pride from those sins. But those who practise pride experience through impenitence how truly it has been said of the Lord that he will repay abundantly those who practise [Col. 1314C] pride. For God, who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas. 4:6), humbles not only those who glory and take pride in their sin, but also those who glory and take pride even in their virtue; and conversely he exalts those who humble themselves not only concerning their virtue, but even concerning their sin.

There is one who has pride within himself but does not himself practise it, when he feels it troubling him yet does not consent to it or love it within himself. Again, there is one who practises pride by nourishing it within himself, not accusing his sins but defending them. Yet he does not practise pride abundantly if he soon abandons the proud defence of his sins and flees to the humble remedy of repentance. But the worst kind of sinners are those who persistently [Col. 1314D] and obstinately take pride in their sins. These practise pride abundantly; therefore they shall be repaid abundantly in future punishment, which will never have an end. God also sometimes repays here below, when by punishing some he humbles them. He does this because, if he humbled none now, divine providence would seem not to keep watch; but if he humbled all, divine patience would not be preserved.

**VERSE 25.** “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord.” You have heard what was said: “Love the Lord, all his saints.” But lest love be idle, act manfully. Do not suppose that love is genuine if it refuses to work for the edification of a brother’s salvation. Hence, when Peter said to the Lord, “I love you,” he immediately heard: “Feed my lambs” (John 21:13). Therefore, just as Peter faithfully loved the Lord and acted manfully in feeding the sheep, so you also, fervent in the twofold love—of God, that is, and of neighbour—love the Lord himself with all your heart, all your soul, and all your strength. And, loving your neighbour as yourselves for his edification, act manfully: rebuking, entreating, reproving, and helping him in his needs according to your ability; desiring to help even beyond your ability; and praying for his salvation.

In all these things and other duties of service, as place, time, and opportunity allow, act manfully. And if, while acting, the adversities mentioned above occur, so that you hear the reproach of many [Col. 1315B] dwelling round about—when they gather together against you—trust in the Lord, and let your heart be strengthened, so that, doing good without failure, you may reap in due season, all you who hope in the Lord. This is the hope which you heard at the beginning of the psalm, where it was said: “In you, Lord, I have hoped.” There it was said in the singular: “In you, Lord, I have hoped”; now it is said in the plural: “All you who hope in the Lord,” because the grain of wheat, sown in hope of a plentiful harvest when it said, “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit,” has now borne much fruit. Therefore [Col. 1316A] it now says to many: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord,” and in this hope sing: “In you, Lord, I have hoped; let me never be confounded,” etc.

Thus the end of the psalm is joined to its beginning, so that, with this as it were a ring placed in the nostrils of the king of Assyria, he may be drawn foolishly and led back captive from the assault of those who hope in the Lord and sing with Christ and in Christ, saying: “In you, Lord, I have hoped.” Again: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.” Again: “Make your face shine upon your servant,” etc.

Glory to the Father, whose Son says in this psalm: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.”

Glory to the Son, who says this and who accomplished that redemption of which the Church says: “You have redeemed [Col. 1316B] me, Lord God of truth.”

Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that love and holiness of which it is said to the beloved and holy: “Love the Lord, all his saints”; and also that strength of which it is said: “Let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord.” Glory be to the Father, glorified by him in the Spirit of Christ commended into his hands. Glory be to the Son, glorified by the redeemed people who say: “You have redeemed me, Lord God of truth.” Glory be to the Holy Spirit, glorified by those beloved and holy, and strengthened in him. Amen.

## PART THREE. Supplemented from the as-yet unpublished Commentary of Honorius of Autun.

[Col. 1315]

# PSALM XXXI

[Col. 1315C] **VERSE 1.** “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven,” etc. This psalm is the second of the seven Penitential Psalms and represents the spirit of piety, which is the second rank among the seven spirits. For the first psalm of the seven Penitential Psalms concerns fear and indicates the spirit of fear, by which the sinner turns aside from evil. But this second psalm, which concerns confession, signifies the spirit of piety, by which the penitent does good.

This psalm is counted as thirty-first in order, a number produced by multiplying six and five: whether six times five or five times six, they make thirty. Six signifies the New Law on account of the six works of the Gospel; five signifies the Old Law on account of the Pentateuch of Moses. Unity is added, because all is fulfilled through the worship of the one God.

The subject of the psalm is a people repenting and confessing sins. Its purpose is to exhort us to confession, so that through forgiveness we may attain blessedness.

[Col. 1316C] The words seem to have been taken from the repentance of David, to whom the Lord did not impute the sin concerning Uriah’s wife, because he declared his wrongdoing against himself to the Lord. He made the Lord his refuge when the distress caused by Absalom surrounded him. As a sinner, he endured many scourges; but when penitent, he was surrounded by the Lord’s mercy. He signifies the penitent people, to whom the Lord does not impute sin committed with the flesh, if it declares its wrongdoing against itself through confession; and if it endures scourges, it will find mercy from the Lord. The title of the Psalm is:

## UNDERSTANDING FOR THIS DAVID

That is: understanding belongs to this people, which confesses its sins like David, who speaks here and is understanding—that is, wise. The preceding psalm spoke of the Church’s redemption as accomplished through God’s grace. And because many regarded themselves as righteous through works of the Law and free choice, rather than through divine grace, this psalm is fittingly placed after it, declaring that no one is justified [Col. 1317A] except through forgiveness of sins, which occurs only from God. Thus the person of the Publican confessing sins in the temple is represented here: he is justified by the Lord, while the Pharisee boasting of his merits is rejected. The Publican expresses the voice of the penitent people, confessing its guilt to him in the temple and justified through Christ, while the arrogant person is rejected through false righteousness.

This psalm is divided in four ways by three *diapsalmata*, because the body, consisting of four elements, and the soul, by its three powers, are afflicted through repentance. In the first part is the blessedness of forgiveness; in the second, the penitent’s confession; in the third, the commendation of blessedness; in the fourth, the consolation of the forgiver. Its meaning, then, is this: while the people were hastening toward the royal city, some had strayed from the straight way; having returned to the way, they invite others who are still wandering to it. Those hasten toward the city who walk through faith in Christ to the heavenly Jerusalem. Those stray from the straight path who commit grave sins. Those return to the way who abandon their sins and despair of being saved except through Christ. Justified by grace, these invite other wanderers to righteousness, crying to them:

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven.” Blessedness is immortality. Therefore those called to immortality are blessed. Who are they? “Those whose iniquities have been forgiven.” By what? By baptism, as it is written: “Baptize them for the forgiveness of sins” (Acts 2:38). “And whose sins have been covered.” By what? By [Col. 1317C] works of charity. For “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

**VERSE 2.** “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.” By what? By martyrdom. For sin is not imputed to one who is sacrificed for Christ by the shedding of blood. The Trinity is signified here: iniquities are forgiven through the Holy Spirit; sins are covered through the Son; they are not imputed by the Father. Iniquities are those acts committed before baptism; sins, those committed after baptism. Sins are forgiven through confession and repentance. Yet no one makes confession except one who knows himself to be a sinner. And one knows himself to be a sinner who understands that he is to be saved not by his own merits but through the grace of [Col. 1317D] Christ. Therefore the first understanding is to acknowledge oneself a sinner. Pure confession is to confess, without human shame, what one committed without divine shame. True repentance is both to weep for acts committed and not to commit deeds that must be wept for. Sins are also forgiven through mercy if we forgive those who sin against us. Sins are the foulnesses of the soul, covered by good action. What we are ashamed to have seen, we cover with a garment placed over it. Therefore let sins be veiled by almsgiving, lest they be revealed at judgment. Sin is not imputed if a person confessing God’s grace confesses from the heart, even if time for repentance is lacking because death has forestalled the opportunity, as it is written: “At whatever hour you groan, you shall be saved.”

[Col. 1318A] “And there is no deceit in his spirit,” or, in the Hebrew, “in his mouth.” Deceit is in the spirit of one who, though wicked before God, justifies himself before human beings; who accuses God; who boasts of his righteousness, like the Pharisee; or who confesses himself a sinner in order to be praised by people. But deceit is not in the spirit of one who confesses himself a sinner in heart and mouth; such a one merits God’s grace, like the Publican. The confession follows.

*Diapsalma.*—**VERSE 3.** “Because I kept silent in confession, my bones grew old”: that is, my powers amid sins. What grows old is consumed by age. Those who delay confessing their sins grow old, and they fail from new life. “While I cried out all day long,” transgressing the law at every time. Earlier he said, “I kept silent”; now he says, “I cried out,” because he kept silent from confession, from good preaching, and from good action. But he cried out by boasting of his good works; he cried out by proclaiming evils in words and examples. And this “all day,” that is, throughout his entire life. For while a human being lives, it is as though it were day, because he can do good; night comes, that is, death, when no one can work. Many keep silent with their mouths yet cry out in their hearts all day long, while they think evil or good. Thus God says to Moses, “Why do you cry out?” (Exod. 14:15), although he said nothing with his mouth.

**VERSE 4.** “For day and night your hand was heavy upon me.” That is, the power of your vengeance rested upon me like a heavy weight in prosperity and adversity, and pressed me to confession. Therefore I turned to you from error, “in my misery,” that [Col. 1318C] is, in the wretchedness of punishments, “while the thorn is fixed,” that is, while the conscience of sins pricks me.

Another translation has: “While the spine is broken.” The spinal column, which holds the whole body upright, signifies pride, which raises a person into vanity. This spine is broken when the proud mind is cast down through fear of judgment. Then, understanding itself to be miserable, it turns to confession and merits forgiveness of sin. Hence follows:

**VERSE 5.** “I made my offence known to you, and I did not hide my injustice.” An offence is neglecting a command; injustice is doing what has been forbidden. One makes his offence known to God who, confessing, groans that he has abandoned the command entrusted to him by God. One does not hide injustice who punishes, through repentance, the crimes he has committed.

“I said,” that is, I resolved in my heart: “I shall confess against myself my injustice to the Lord.” That is, I shall accuse not God, fate, or the stars, but myself concerning my injustice; as judge, I shall condemn myself by punishing myself in evils. “And you forgave the impiety of my sin.” When a person punishes guilt, God forgives. When a person conceals through shame, God reveals through punishment. Great grace! While a person is still deliberating whether to confess, God releases sins. The impiety of sin is the defence of sin. Adam’s sin was that he presumed to do what was forbidden; his impiety was that he proudly defended [Col. 1319A] what he had done.

Another translation has: “Of my heart,” namely, the will to conceal and not confess. The commendation of repentance follows.

*Diapsalma.*—**VERSE 6.** “For this every saint will pray to you.” That is: for this forgiveness, or for this impiety, every person who wishes to be holy will pray to you, who alone forgive sins. And he does this “at an opportune time,” that is, in this life, where it is the proper time to pray and the acceptable time; for in hell no one will confess to the Lord.

“Yet in a flood of many waters they shall not come near him.” The flood of many waters is the inundation of the teachings of philosophers or heretics, in which people will not come near to God or be able to become holy. The flood of many waters also signifies the various purifications of the Jews, in which they did not draw near to God, from whom they withdraw far away through superstition. A flood also means judgment, because it will come suddenly, just as the flood came unexpectedly. And as that flood of many waters rose fifteen cubits above all the mountains, so the flood of fiery rivers will swell to the same extent. And as then all perished except those who were in the ark, so on that day all will perish except those who are in the Church. Those who have become holy here through forgiveness will then pass through that fiery flood with the greatest ease and without injury, and will reach God who sanctifies them; but the ungodly, weighed down by the burden of sins, will remain in the fire and will not come near.

[Col. 1319C] **VERSE 7.** “You are my refuge from the tribulation which surrounded me”: whether in the flood of heresies, the flood of temptations, the flood of anxieties, or the flood of torments enveloping the ungodly at judgment. “My exultation,” because I do not rejoice in the world but in you. “Deliver me from those surrounding me”: enemies, sins, or adversities. Thus far the penitent has finished speaking by accusing himself and justifying the Judge; henceforth the Judge’s mercy replies:

*Diapsalma.*—**VERSE 8.** “I shall give you understanding,” so that you may understand both what evils you have done against me or against yourself and what goods you have neglected, and understand what you should do henceforth. The psalm is entitled from this understanding, because the soul is enlightened by understanding. “And I shall instruct you in this way in which you shall walk”: that is, in the way of confession [Col. 1319D] which you have now entered, I shall teach you to live well, so that you may be able to understand my secrets. “I shall fix my eyes upon you.” That is, I shall make you steadfast in the light of my understanding. The Lord’s eyes are mercy and piety. He will fix these upon a converted person when he places one freed from evils in the presence of his vision. A divine admonition follows for those still wandering through the byways of error, that they may be corrected as quickly as possible.

**VERSE 9.** “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding.” Free choice is expressed here. For if a human being did anything compelled by fate or necessity, the Lord would by no means say, “Do not.” But since choice lies in the human will, free from every necessity, whether a person wishes to obey God commanding or consent to the devil persuading, he is rightly told, “Do not.” Moreover, God commands nothing impossible. For if a human being had been created so that he could live only wickedly, it would be impossible for him to avoid evil—indeed, he would necessarily sin—and it would follow that the Lord was unjust if he imputed sin to him. No one is forbidden to do what is impossible. No one is told, “Do not fly from Italy to Africa”; but everyone is told, “Do not sin.” The former is not impossible for a human being; the latter is possible.

By horse and mule are understood the lustful. Therefore the faithful are told: “Do not become like horse and mule,” that is, like those who are borne, not according to God’s will, but according to their own, toward irrational impulses in a beastlike fashion. By the horse, moreover, Gentiles are denoted; by the mule, Jews sluggish in the Law. You Christians, do not be like Jews and Gentiles, luxuriating and committing fornication away from the true God.

Since a dog recognizes its master, and a horse or ox returns to its stall, one may ask how it can be said: “Which have no understanding.” But it should be known that beasts have sensation and memory in imagination, but entirely lack understanding. Through bodily sense, in which some are stronger than human beings, they recognize people; they imagine absent young; through memory birds return to nests and oxen to stalls. But the rational creature alone distinguishes good and evil by reason and perceives virtues and vices through understanding; no beast does this. The voice of those converted [Col. 1320C] to God:

“Constrict their jaws with bit and bridle, those who do not come near to you.” The *camus*, which is heavier, belongs to mules; the bridle belongs to horses. By mules the unclean are signified; by horses, the proud. By the *camus* is understood inward expiration; by the bridle, outward discipline. Or, contrition is meant by the *camus*, preaching by the bridle. Or a forceful attack is meant by the *camus*, measured correction by the bridle. By jaws, with which food is chewed, abundance of provisions is understood. The proud, who devote themselves to luxury and drunkenness, do not approach God. “With bit and bridle, O God, constrict their jaws, those who do not come near to you,” when he removes abundance of goods from the proud, the lustful, and the drunken; oppresses them by adversities; and corrects them through preaching. Therefore, do not [Col. 1320D] become like horse and mule, lest perhaps God constrict you with the bit of tribulation and the bridle of correction, because

**VERSE 10.** “Many are the scourges of the sinner.” These words are drawn from untamed animals, which endure bit, bridle, and scourges until they become accustomed to travel the way along a straight path. So those untamed by vices, kicking against Christ their rider, are scourged by adversities until, overcome by the world’s inconvenience, they submit to the ruler’s command. “But mercy shall surround one who hopes in the Lord.” Those who have faith and hope in God and do not presume upon their merits will receive from God the mercy of forgiveness. On the day of judgment mercy will surround them and will not allow the flood of fire to harm them. After correction of the erring follows an admonition for those walking in righteousness.

[Col. 1321A] **VERSE 11.** “Rejoice in the Lord,” not in earthly things, “and exult, you righteous,” justified not by your merits but through grace. “And glory,” not in your own virtues but in the Lord, “all you upright in heart,” that is, the righteous. Those are called upright in heart to whom all God’s judgments are pleasing, who accuse themselves concerning sins, and praise God in prosperity and adversity. Joy belongs to the soul, exultation to the body, glory to both. The righteous rejoice in soul when they delight in the Lord’s joy; [Col. 1322A] they exult in body when, shining like the sun and equal to angels, they celebrate with sweet harmony the Lord’s benefits. In both they glory when, in every kind of glory, they are satisfied by the vision of God. Therefore this psalm is sung concerning the saints, because everlasting joy, exultation, and glory are prepared for them.

It should be noted that, as some maintain, in ten verses the penitent speaks, accusing himself, and in five verses the Judge replies, because the fivefold passion of Christ removes transgression of the Decalogue.

# PSALM XXXII

[Col. 1321]

[Col. 1321B] **VERSE 1.** “Exult, you righteous, in the Lord; praise befits the upright,” etc. Magnificent delights are brought forth from the storehouse of this book, by which those hungering and thirsting for righteousness are abundantly refreshed. The preceding psalm refreshes those who have been justified; this psalm occupies the thirty-second position in the sequence, a number formed by multiplication by four. For four eights, or eight fours, complete the sum of this number, because all the righteous gathered from the four parts of the world come together in the eight beatitudes. The title of the psalm is:

## A PSALM OF DAVID

That is: this hymn is sung to Christ the desirable one by the faithful people, against vices, with a strong hand. The subject of the psalm is the praise of the righteous who have been justified from sins. [Col. 1321C] Its purpose is to invite us to praise Christ for benefits bestowed.

The words seem to have been taken from Joshua, who is also Jesus, who led God’s people, delivered from the wilderness, into the land of promise. He instructed them to exult in the Lord, at whose shout Jericho fell. And the Lord scattered the plans of the nations which King Balak and the priest Balaam had devised against them; he rejected the thoughts of peoples and the plans of the rulers warring against them; he chose the blessed Israelite nation as his inheritance, upon which he looked down from heaven in signs and miracles, when King Sihon was not saved by his great might and Og the giant, king of Bashan, was not delivered from them by great strength; when he fed them in famine for forty years with heavenly bread.

But he signifies the true Jesus, who delivered a people from error and brought them into the Church; who instructed them to exult because the world’s desire falls at his jubilation; who scattered the plans of the nations against the Church and rejected the counsels of persecuting rulers attacking it; who chose the blessed nation of Christians as his inheritance; who looked down from heaven upon it through his Son, when the king of pride and the giant, the devil, were overcome, and the faithful people were fed with the bread of angels. No one should wonder that the words of the Psalms are drawn from such diverse and chronologically disordered histories, because here [Col. 1322B] the order of events is not sought but that of mysteries. The psalm has two divisions: one, “Exult, you righteous, in the Lord,” in which is the praise of the righteous; the other, “Blessed is the nation,” in which is the gathering of the Church from all nations. It is the voice of the Holy Spirit to those who have been justified.

“Exult, you righteous, in the Lord.” This psalm is connected with the preceding one because the people converted from error are transformed into saints through Christ. At the end of that psalm it is written: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous”; at the beginning of this, the same is repeated: “Exult, you righteous, in the Lord.” There: “Glory, all you upright in heart.” Here likewise: “Praise befits the upright.” The preceding verse is transformed into the following one, because the penitent people have been changed into a justified people. Thus also the Publican, who repented in the temple, went down from the temple justified. The righteous are those who follow in all things not their own will but God’s. Such righteous persons, exult or rejoice in the Lord, not in earthly things. For the exultation of the wicked ends with passing things; the exultation of the righteous never ends. The upright are those who direct their heart according to the rule of truth. Praise befits these upright persons. Praise is the acclaim of many who agree in Christ. But praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner who sins (Ecclus. 15:9).

**VERSE 2.** “Give thanks to the Lord on the harp; sing to him on the ten-stringed psaltery.” The harp is a musical instrument hollowed below and stretched with six strings, which, struck below, give forth a most sweet sound above. Some strings sing well; some murmur. God’s harps are the saints, who, as though struck below, resound above while labouring in earthly things and desiring heavenly ones. The six strings are the six works of mercy: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, receiving the stranger, visiting the sick, and redeeming the captive. These are done on earth but render their sound in heaven. The strings that sing well are spiritual persons who perform these acts cheerfully; the murmuring strings are worldly people pursuing the same acts with some scruple [Col. 1323A] or reluctance. Therefore it is said: “Give thanks to the Lord on the harp,” that is, praise God through works of this kind. We play the harp to God when we crucify our flesh with its vices and desires and give God thanks in prosperity and adversity.

The psaltery is a musical instrument hollowed above and stretched with ten strings, giving forth sound below. The psaltery is the saints instructed from above, who, as though touched above, resound below when they preach heavenly teaching on earth. The ten strings are the ten commandments of the Law. Of these, three concern love of God and seven love of neighbour. The three are these: God is one; you shall not worship a foreign god; you shall not swear falsely by God’s name; observe the Sabbath day. In these the Trinity is worshipped. [Col. 1323B] The following seven concern one’s neighbour: honour father and mother; do not kill; do not commit adultery; do not steal; do not bear false witness; do not covet your neighbour’s property; do not covet his wife and all that is his. In these one’s neighbour is loved. These were written on two tablets because the whole Law and the prophets hang upon the two commandments of love. In this ten-stringed psaltery the saints sing to the Lord when they fulfil the ten commandments in love of God and neighbour. We sing to God on the ten-stringed psaltery when we live commendably in the five bodily and five spiritual senses.

**VERSE 3.** “Sing to him a new song.” The new song is the New Law, namely the Gospel. The new song is “Glory to God in the highest,” which the angels sang when the new man, Christ, was born. He sings a new song who loves his enemy and who leaves all that he possesses. “Sing well to him with a shout,” that is, praise him in song. In the Hebrew it is written: “Sing with jubilation.” Jubilation is joy of heart which cannot be expressed by speech. One sings well who fulfils what he sings. One sings in jubilation who, praising the ineffable God, believes.

**VERSE 4.** “For the word of the Lord is upright,” that is, the Lord’s command is just. “And all his works are in faith,” that is, his works are right, as those who are in faith understand. Or God’s works are those which are done in faith, because “the righteous shall live by faith” (Gal. 3:11), and faith works through love. [Col. 1323D] What are God’s works?

VERSE 5. He loves mercy and judgment. God is love; therefore he does everything out of love. He loves mercy when he bestows mercy on the wretched. He loves judgment when he separates the just from the ungodly. Here he shows mercy; there, judgment. He loves the merciful; he loves just judges. He is merciful when, like David, he spares those who sin against himself; just when, like Phinehas, he punishes those who sin against God. Let the merciful hear: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7). Let judges hear: “With whatever judgment you judge, you shall be judged” (Matt. 7:2). And again: “Judgment without mercy [shall be] for him who has not shown mercy” (Jas. 2:13). It follows: The earth is full of the Lord’s mercy [Col. 1324A], that is, the whole world, because throughout the whole Church the Gospel is preached and sins are forgiven. And he describes mystically how the Church has shone forth as though a new creature through the world’s new creation.

VERSE 6. By the word of the Lord the heavens were established. These words are drawn from the history, when God said: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters” (Gen. 1:6), and called the firmament heaven. And by the breath of his mouth, all their power: when he said, “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven” (ibid., 14), and God made the sun, moon, and stars, and placed them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth.

VERSE 7. Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin [Col. 1324B], when he said, “Let the waters be gathered into one place,” and called the gatherings of waters “seas.” From these coverings the Church is unfolded. First, the Trinity is written most plainly, since in “the Lord” the Father, in “the Word” the Son, and in “the breath of his mouth” the Holy Spirit are expressed. The heavens are the apostles, in whom God’s secrets are hidden. They were established by the Word of the Lord, because through the Son of God they were made firm in faith.

And by the breath of his mouth, all their power: that is, all the apostles’ power was established by the Holy Spirit. For their conversion of the whole world by preaching, and their performance of signs and miracles, they received wholly from the Holy Spirit. The Son is the Father’s mouth, for through him he spoke whatsoever he willed to be made. Therefore it is called the breath of the mouth, because the Holy Spirit [Col. 1324C] is the common power of Father and Son.

I say, gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin: that is, enclosing the sea with shores. The wineskin, made from the hide of a dead animal, is the Church, which puts the flesh to death in its vices. The waters of the sea are peoples fluid in vices and bitter in sins. These waters were gathered in the wineskin when peoples bitter in unbelief flowed together, through the apostles’ power, into the Church’s unity. He not only gathers the waters into a wineskin, but also lays up the deeps in treasuries. The deep is the depth of waters; treasures in the deep are pearls, taken from the shells of the sea. Mystically, the deep is the depth of the Scriptures. God’s treasure, however, is wisdom and knowledge. Therefore the apostles’ power [Col. 1324D] placed the deeps in treasuries when it expounded the depth of the Scriptures through wisdom and knowledge received from the Holy Spirit. And because the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy:

VERSE 8. Let all the earth fear the Lord. That is, let all who inhabit the earth fear the Lord as servants, departing from evil; and love the Father as children, clinging to good. Let all inhabitants of the world be moved by him from unbelief to faith, from injustice to righteousness. Or all creatures are moved by God, since both prosperity and adversity occur at his nod. Or all inhabitants of the world are moved by him when, having attained perfection, they go through him from virtue to virtue. The world is also the Church, set in the circle of the world. Those who inhabit this world [Col. 1325A] are moved by God when Christians, by God’s prompting, turn to repentance. Therefore let all things fear God.

VERSE 9. For he spoke, and all things were made; he commanded, and all things were created. He spoke through the Son; he commanded by authority. By his will he made formless matter out of nothing, and formed matter into diverse kinds. Or Christ spoke what he heard from the Father, and those things which he spoke were accomplished in the Church. He commanded the Law through the prophets and the Gospel through the apostles; and there were created, namely, ecclesiastical institutions and faithful vessels fit for the kingdom of God. Therefore the earth too—that is, earthly persons—fears God, because

[Col. 1325B] VERSES 10 AND 11. The Lord scatters the counsels of the nations. These words are drawn from the tower, when the Lord scattered its builders by dividing them into diverse languages. He rejects the thoughts of the peoples, namely of the Pharisees and Sadducees, who planned to kill Christ. And he rejects the counsels of the rulers Annas and Caiaphas, who took counsel that Christ should be crucified and guarded in the tomb. He destroyed all these things when he rose from death. He also scattered the counsels of the nations against the Church when, destroying idolatry, he subjected them to the Christian religion. He rejected the thoughts of peoples opposed to the Church when through teachers he joined them to the faithful. He rejected the counsels of tyrannical rulers attacking the Church when he bound the persecutors themselves [Col. 1325C] beneath the yoke of faith, as he did Constantine. And because “there is no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. 21:20), the counsel of the Lord remains forever. The Lord’s counsel was that, through the man Christ, the archangel, the devil, should be condemned, and that humanity, deceived from Paradise, should be made equal to angelic dignity. This counsel remains forever, because redeemed humanity has joy and the malignant angel has destruction. The thoughts of his heart are from generation to generation. God’s heart is his wisdom; his thoughts are eternal predestination, in which all things are stored which either have been or are still to be. These thoughts remain from generation to generation because everything he predestined concerning the generation of the righteous or the generation of the wicked will remain fixed. And because [Col. 1325D] the Lord’s counsel concerning human salvation remains forever:

VERSE 12. Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord. The Christian nation has been gathered from all nations into the heavenly Jerusalem: blessed is it, called to eternal blessedness, by which the true God is worshipped and the Lord of all adored. Blessed is the people of believers whom the Lord chose for his inheritance, Jews and Gentiles alike, after rejecting the unbelieving, so that he too might be their inheritance. This inheritance had been lost, but was recovered through Christ. Hence it follows:

VERSE 13. The Lord looked down from heaven. That is, the Father looked mercifully from heaven—that is, from Christ—upon the human race, from which, being angrily offended, he had turned away his face [Col. 1326A]. He saw all the children of men with pity for them.

In the Hebrew it reads: “Upon the children of Adam and Eve,” that is, upon Jews and Gentiles. For through Christ he visited both, and called both to grace through repentance.

VERSE 14. From his prepared dwelling-place he looked upon all who inhabit the earth. The Lord’s body is the tabernacle prepared from eternity for the Godhead. From this body, stretched out on the cross, the Lord looked down, because through Christ’s Passion he bestowed his grace upon all who dwell on earth. Or the tabernacle is the primitive Church, prepared through Christ. From it God looked upon all who dwell on earth when, through the apostles, he converted all to faith [Col. 1326B].

VERSE 15. He fashioned each of their hearts separately. That is, he gives each person his own will. The comparison is drawn from a potter, who easily fashions from soft earth whatever form he wishes. Thus it is easy for God to form good wills in each of the faithful. Or, he gives individual gifts to believers: to one the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another the grace of healings, to another the working of miracles. Or, “he fashioned each of their hearts separately” means: in each person he creates a distinct soul. He understands all their works: with what intention each does good, whether for God or for human praise. Man sees the face, but God sees the heart. And because all have sinned and lack the glory of God, and all are saved through grace:

[Col. 1326C] VERSE 16. A king is not saved by great power, and a giant shall not be saved by the abundance of his strength. Three things are set forth here: king, giant, horse. By the king are understood the powerful of this world; by the giant, the strong; by the horse, the swift. A king is not saved by great power; a giant is not saved by much strength; and a soldier is not saved by the horse’s speed. Rather, all are saved by God, of whom it is written: “Salvation belongs to the Lord” (Ps. 3:9). He is called king who governs his flesh against unlawful impulses. If he presumes upon his own strength, he is not saved; if he trusts in God’s grace, he will be saved. And the giant shall not be saved. This appears to have been drawn from Goliath the giant, who was not saved by his strength but was overthrown by David. A giant [Col. 1326D] is one strong against the devil and vices. He will not be saved if he entrusts himself too greatly to his own strength.

VERSE 17. The horse is deceptive for salvation. He who restrains his body by fasts and chastises it by vigils is called a horse, because he can carry others in virtues. In himself he is deceptive for salvation, because “human salvation is vain” (Ps. 59:13). Yet in the abundance of his strength he shall not be saved. Many hermits were outstanding in many virtues; but because they presumed upon themselves, they were not saved. Why? No one shall be saved in the abundance of his own strength. Whence, then, will salvation come, if neither the king who governs himself, nor the giant strong in warfare against vices, nor the horse carrying others in virtues can be saved by himself? From the Lord. For it follows:

[Col. 1327A] VERSE 18. Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him. The Lord’s eyes are mercy and compassion. These eyes are upon those who fear the Lord and depart from evil, and upon those who hope not in their own merits but in his mercy. For what purpose?

VERSE 19. That he may deliver their souls from eternal death and feed them in famine: with the Word of God, the bread of life. Or he feeds those hungering and thirsting for righteousness with spiritual understanding, lest they fail on the way. This is the salvation of the righteous. Those hoping in God and hungering for righteousness add:

VERSE 20. Our soul waits for the Lord, awaiting his mercy, that it may feed upon incorruptible food [Col. 1328A]. For he is our helper in doing good and our protector against those who hinder our reaching God.

VERSE 21. For in him our heart shall rejoice. That is, our soul dwelling in him shall enjoy eternal joy. And in his holy name—that is, in Christ, who is the Father’s name—we have hoped. The prayer of the righteous follows:

VERSE 22. Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us, according as we have hoped in you. That is, according to the hope we have placed in your mercy, may there be, on the day of judgment, salvation for our body and soul, and glorification with the angels in your vision.

## PSALM XXXIII

[Col. 1327]

[Col. 1327B] “I will bless the Lord at every time,” etc. A door is opened by a key, and what has been shut is seen; by the title a psalm is unlocked and its mysteries disclosed. The title of this psalm is (VERSE 1):

### A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN HE CHANGED HIS COUNTENANCE BEFORE ABIMELECH, WHO DISMISSED HIM, AND HE DEPARTED

The history is as follows. Saul persecuted David, who fled to Achish, king of the Philistines. When the Philistines recognized him, they told the king that he was the man who had killed Goliath, their standard-bearer and ruler (1 Sam. 21). The king ordered that he be brought in and killed. When David learned this, he resorted to a stratagem: he feigned epilepsy, beat a drum at the city gate, was carried in men’s hands, and saliva fell from his mouth onto his beard. Abimelech, judging him possessed, [Col. 1327C] dismissed him, and he departed; and the man [perhaps to be read: “in this way”] sang a psalm to the Lord for his deliverance. Saul signifies the devil; David, Christ; Achish means “how is it?” Abimelech means “the kingdom of my father,” and was a common name for the kings of the Philistines, as Pharaoh was for the Egyptians and Caesar for the Romans. Because of its significance, the common name Abimelech rather than the proper name Achish is placed in the title. David came to Abimelech when Christ came into the kingdom of Israel, which was the kingdom of his Father. He changed his countenance before Abimelech because, though he was in the form of God, he took from the Jews the form of a servant. He changed his countenance when he exchanged Aaron’s old sacrifice for Melchizedek’s new sacrifice, namely, his body and blood. Therefore the change of countenance is [Col. 1327D] the change of the former sacrifice into the new sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood. For the lamb, the goat, and the red heifer signified our sacrifice. When Christ revealed that these signified himself and said before the Jews, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54), seventy disciples, together with a great crowd of Jews who had previously believed, left him, saying: “This saying is hard” [Col. 1328B] (John 6:61). And others said: “Did we not tell you that he is mad and has a demon?” (ibid., 20). The Achishes were those who said: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (ibid., 72). And Christ dismissed them and departed from their hearts to the Gentiles: that is, he withdrew his grace from them and bestowed it upon the Gentiles. David beat the drum. A drum is skin stretched over wood. It signifies Christ stretched out on the cross. Christ beat the drum when he foretold his death to the apostles. He did this at the city gate because the apostles were the gate of the Church, the city of God. Our hearts too are a gate, which Christ opened with the drum of the cross and entered through faith. We beat the drum, as it were, at the city gate for catechumens when, before baptism—which is entrance into the Church—we foretell to them the mysteries of Christ’s Passion [Col. 1328C]. By the saliva is understood the weakness of the flesh; by the beard, the strength of the Godhead. The saliva from his mouth also signifies his words, which appeared childish when he said: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood” (John 6:57). But the saliva fell upon the beard because the apostles, who were strong, declared them to be words of life. David’s being carried in hands signifies that Christ, at the supper, ineffably carried himself in his own hands. David collapsed amid the hands of those seizing him, and Christ died for us amid the hands of those crucifying him. For this mystery the psalm is sung to the Lord. Hence it is counted in the thirty-third place, corresponding to the age in years at which Christ [Col. 1328D] was offered by the Father upon the altar of the cross as the new and true sacrifice. This number, beginning from three, rises to ten and ends truly in three, signifying that the works of the Decalogue must be begun through the Trinity and completed through the Trinity. Therefore Christ wished to die when this number of years had been completed, because he died both for the Jews, who were under the Decalogue of the Law, and for the Gentiles, who awaited the grace of the Trinity.

[Col. 1329A] The subject of the psalm is the Church’s praise for its reception of the new sacrifice. Its purpose is that we may praise Christ, whom we have received as sacrifice. The words are taken from David’s praise when he escaped his enemies’ hands, and they signify the praise of the faithful people for escaping the hands of persecutors. Note that the title concerns the change of sacrifice, while the psalm concerns the Church’s praise for receiving Christ. For Christ dismissed the Jews and went to the Church. Therefore she herself sings in jubilation: “I will bless the Lord at every time.” Likewise observe in other psalms: where the psalm concerns the Resurrection, the title concerns the Passion, as in “Lord, why have they multiplied?”; but where the psalm concerns the Passion, the title concerns the Resurrection, as in “My God.” This figure is called synecdoche, when [Col. 1329B] what precedes is understood through what follows; as when we say “morning,” we understand that night has preceded.

This psalm is written among the Hebrews according to the order of the alphabetic letters, and a great teaching of divine instruction is indicated. The sixth letter—that is, Vau—is absent; it is a perfect number, because perfection is absent from some persons in the Church. It is divided into three or four parts. The first is “I will bless the Lord at every time,” in which is the Church’s praise, woven from four letters. The second is “Draw near to God,” in which is an admonition to believers, comprising six letters. The third is “Come, children,” in which those still wandering are called, connected by four [Col. 1329C] letters. The fourth is “The eyes of the Lord,” in which is the recompense of good and evil, comprising seven letters. Note each point carefully. In the psalm “Blessed are those whose,” there was praise for those turned from error; in the psalm “Rejoice, O righteous,” praise for those justified from sin; in this psalm there is praise of the righteous for receiving the sacrifice by which sinners are cleansed and the rewards of righteousness bestowed. It is the voice of the Church praising God.

### ALEPH

VERSE 2. I will bless the Lord at every time. That is, in prosperity and adversity; or, having received Christ’s sacraments, I shall establish them with praises. His praise shall always be in my mouth. Praise (*laus*) is said to derive from laurel (*laurus*), with which victors were customarily crowned. I shall always praise God the victor [Col. 1329D] with inward and outward mouth: with the mouth of the heart, through faith and devotion; with the mouth of the body, through confession and jubilation. This praise is celebrated in the changed sacrifice; moreover, the Church sacrifices to God a sacrifice of praise. He always praises God who continually bears him in mouth and mind.

### BETH

VERSE 3. My soul shall be praised in the Lord. That is, my life will be praiseworthy and will be praised by those who belong to the Lord. And let the meek hear and rejoice at what I do or say in the Lord. Those who do not wish to be praised in the Lord are not meek, but fierce, harsh, puffed up, and proud. But let the meek—in whom the Lord sits as upon a tamed beast—hear, that is, learn the Church’s sacraments, and rejoice [Col. 1330A] when they see that the soul’s salvation consists in worthily receiving this sacrifice. And after you have understood the Church’s sacraments:

### GIMEL

VERSE 4. Magnify the Lord with me. That is, celebrate the divine sacrifice with me; or, do not praise me alone in the Lord, but proclaim the Lord himself great with me. And let us exalt his name together, that is, in unity or reciprocally. God’s name is exalted in unity when Christ is praised by choirs answering one another.

### DELETH

VERSE 5. I sought the Lord, not gold, and he heard me. If you seek him, seek him not through distances of lands or narrowness of places, but in the heart through faithful love [Col. 1330B]; and seek not money or earthly substance, but the Lord himself; and he will hear you as he heard me. In what respect? He delivered me from all my tribulations, namely famine, thirst, and mortality. Is the Trinity indicated here? In “Magnify the Lord” the Father, in “Let us exalt the name” the Son, and in “I sought the Lord” the Holy Spirit are understood. Having first offered praises and arranged the choirs, the Church now exhorts the people to come to communion itself.

### HE

VERSE 6. Draw near to him in faith and be enlightened in understanding what this sacrament itself signifies. Let not drunkards, adulterers, or proud persons draw near, but the sober, chaste, and humble, who cleanse their conscience by repentance. And your faces shall not be ashamed, as those were put to shame [Col. 1330C] who, not understanding, went backward. Or draw near to him not in place, but approach God through purity of life, and he will approach you through grace; be enlightened by his light through wisdom, and your faces shall not blush on the day of judgment for sins now forgiven. You said that the Lord heard you. From what is this apparent? Because:

### SAI

VERSE 7. This poor man—that is, the Christian people—cried out by believing, understanding, and magnifying. And the Lord heard him. In what? He saved him from all his tribulations. He will do this perfectly when he redeems souls from all the world’s distresses [Col. 1330D] and transfers them from the confused ruin of the age to everlasting security. Or this poor man is Christ, made poor for us: he cried upon the cross, and the Lord heard him by raising him from the dead; and saved him from all his tribulations by establishing him at the right hand of his majesty.

### HETH

VERSE 8. The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him and will deliver them. In the Hebrew it reads: “The angel of the Lord surrounds in a circle those who fear him and will deliver them.” Christ, the Angel of Great Counsel, will place himself around those who fear him and will deliver them from distress. Yet angels are also said to be guardians of each individual believer, lest evil angels harm them, as it is written: “Their angels always see the face of my Father [Col. 1331A] who is in heaven” (Matt. 18:10). They surround the righteous in a circle, station themselves about those who love God, and will deliver them from demons or wicked people. Again he invites them to communion, in which the whole salvation of the soul consists.

### DETH

VERSE 9. Taste—that is, receive the sacrament itself—and see—that is, prove by experience—that the Lord is sweet. That is, he is pleasant food and health-giving. Taste with the palate of the heart and see with understanding that the Lord is sweet to angels and souls, though he seemed bitter to Jews and Gentiles.

It should be known that the Lord is sweet only to Christ’s lovers, and that only the crucified feed upon the flesh [Col. 1331B] of the Crucified One. For those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5:24). This crucifixion concerns not the outward but the inward person. Moreover, that cross is charity. As a cross is joined from two pieces of wood, so charity is joined in genuine love. The three upright arms of the cross are faith in the Trinity; the fourth, supporting the rest, is reverence for unity. The inward person is stretched upon this cross when in all things he obediently submits to Christ’s commands. He stretches himself upward on the cross when he always directs himself toward God by faith and hope, loves him with all soul, all strength, and all mind, and puts nothing before the divine will. He stretches himself across the width of the cross when he loves friends in God and enemies for God’s sake; when, being human, he loves his neighbor—that is, another human—as himself, causing no one to suffer what he would not wish to suffer and granting to all what he wishes granted to himself. He stretches himself along the length of the cross who perseveres in these things for Christ until the end. The nails driven into the feet of the affections are two servile fears: one by which he fears divine judgment because he has neglected the commands laid upon him; the other by which he fears falling into eternal punishment because he has done evil contrary to the Lord’s commandments. The nails driven through the hands of actions are two holy fears: one by which he fears, through negligence or ignorance, doing anything that offends God; the other by which he fears being long delayed from the vision of God. Whoever has thus crucified himself with his vices and desires is refreshed by Christ’s food [Col. 1331D] and, as a co-heir of the Crucified, is brought into the Father’s kingdom. It follows: Blessed is the man who hopes in him, and not in the uncertainty of riches, because here he enjoys eternal blessedness.

### JOD

VERSE 10. Fear the Lord, all his saints. That is, all who have been sanctified through him: fear the Lord by departing from evil; love him by clinging to good. For there is no want among those who fear him. Those serving God often suffer great lack of possessions: outward resources are absent; they lack bodily health; tyrants confiscate their goods; they themselves are sent into exile. How, then, is it true that nothing is lacking to those who fear him? Certainly in the inward person they suffer no want, since they are refreshed with spiritual food, namely the body of Christ or the Word of God [Col. 1332A]. In the future life nothing will be lacking to them, where God, the abundance of every good, will be their reward.

### CAPH

VERSE 11. The rich have lacked and hungered. They have hungered for the highest good, yet they will be in need, that is, deprived, because they do not walk in the right way. There are five things in which the children of this world glory: riches, glory, rank, power, and pleasure. Riches include abundance of goods, secure fortification of buildings, plentiful money, a large household, a multitude and fruitfulness of animals, abundance of fields, and fertility of vineyards. Glory includes renown for reputation, beauty, strength, swiftness, wisdom, and eloquence. Rank includes magistracies, governorships, countships [Col. 1332B], and duchies. Power includes kingship and imperial rule. Pleasure includes beautiful women, handsome children, splendid clothing, and luxuries of food and drink. Those who thirst to possess these things and do not hunger for Christ’s body or the word of life will always be poor. For riches may be taken away by fire, plague, or thieves; glory may be obscured by disgrace and decay with old age; rank may be diminished; power taken away; pleasure embittered. But those who seek the Lord shall not be deprived of any good. They will lack no good when they possess God, who is every good, and whom alone they seek. But now their life is hidden with Christ in God; when Christ, their glory, appears, they will be like him in bodily brightness, because they will see him as he is in his Godhead, face to face. The argument is drawn from opposites [Col. 1332C]. For riches and poverty are opposites. An argument is the judgment of an acute mind. Argument is a reason that gives assurance concerning a doubtful matter. He draws people to love in two ways: by reward and by punishment. Poor people who fear God will abound in every good; rich people who despise God will lack every good. After saying that the poor are refreshed by eating Christ’s body and the rich repelled from this food, the Holy Spirit, or the Church, turns to the children of the kingdom who are still straying and invites them to saving sacraments, saying: I have said, “Fear the Lord.” And, that I may show you what fear of the Lord is:

### LAMETH

[Col. 1332D] VERSE 12. Come, children, whom I have begotten in faith; come through zeal for learning; hear me obediently. I shall teach you the fear of the Lord, by which you may attain wisdom and ascend from slavery to freedom, from exile to the kingdom. After all have gathered and are listening attentively, he says to all:

### MEM

VERSE 13. Who is the person who desires life and loves to see good days? That is, which of you wishes to attain eternal life and enjoy every good? When all answer, “I, I,” he says:

### NUN

VERSE 14. Keep your tongue from evil. Restrain yourself from saying any evil, and let not your lips speak [Col. 1333A] deceit. What you say with your mouth, have also in your heart. For death and life are in the power of the tongue (Prov. 18:21). And whoever thinks himself religious but does not restrain his tongue, that person’s religion is vain (Jas. 1:26). Silence, however, is the guardian of righteousness.

### LAMETH

VERSE 15. Turn away from evil: that is, be innocent; and do good: that is, be righteous. Destroy vices; build virtues. Leave everything the devil prompts, and do what Christ commands. Seek peace and pursue it, that is, follow it eagerly. Have peace and concord with all people; imitate Christ, who is true peace, and you shall have peace in eternal life. To do such things is to fear God. And what, they ask, do those who do these things receive? This:

[Col. 1333B] ### SIN

VERSE 16. The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers. That is, mercy and compassion will overflow upon those who do these things; God’s kindness and generosity will abound in response to their prayers. This is to say: God always looks upon the righteous to see what they desire, and will grant whatever they ask. But what will happen to those who do not do these things? What follows:

### THE

VERSE 17. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil. That is, the vengeance of him who sees all things will come upon sinners. For what purpose? To destroy the memory of them from the land of the living, so that no remembrance and no prayers may be made for them by the saints who will be there. But the righteous [Col. 1333C] are always heard by God.

### SAIN

VERSE 18. The righteous—Abraham, Moses, Joseph, and others in Egypt—cried out, and the Lord heard them and delivered them from all their tribulations.

### SADE

Moreover, the seven Maccabees and very many other martyrs cried out and were not heard in temporal matters, but were consumed by momentary punishments. Yet the Lord heard them in secret, delivering them from the torment of eternal death and crowning them with their desired glory.

### COPH

VERSE 19. The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart. That is, he is close to those who are in tribulation for his sake [Col. 1333D], as he was with Joseph. And he will save the humble in spirit in the heavenly kingdom. For those who humble themselves here are exalted by God.

### RES

VERSE 20. Many are the tribulations of the righteous. Whoever suffers no tribulation [Col. 1334A] is not righteous. For all who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3:12). The righteous endure many troubles in this life, even more than the wicked. And from all these things the Lord will deliver them in the future: from famine, persecutions, and all other things. Then they shall judge nations and rule peoples. The Lord is near to them, because:

VERSE 21. The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them shall be broken. We must consider how this is true. For the bones of many martyrs have been broken, reduced to ashes in blazing fires, some scattered when cast into water, and some strewn in pieces through fields. This book is spiritual and speaks through likenesses to the inward person; it does not speak according to our customary manner [Col. 1334B]. The bones of the saints are the strengths of the soul: patience, gentleness, and the other virtues. The Lord guards these bones in the saints so that not one of them—that is, not even the least virtue—perishes in them. At the end the Lord will save all the righteous. But:

### MEM

VERSE 22. The death of sinners is most evil, although it appears good to fools when they see the funerals of the rich clothed in purple and silk and marble tombs adorned with gold and gems. Yet their souls are shut up in the Tartarean prison and plunged into the sulphurous deep. And those who hate the righteous do wrong. Those who hate Christ the righteous one do wrong—that is, they sin; and those who, hating the righteous because of righteousness, persecute them, are punished for this offense by the worst death, namely eternal death [Col. 1334C]. In the Hebrew it reads: “Wickedness shall kill the ungodly.” And what shall become of the good?

### THAU

VERSE 23. The Lord shall redeem the souls of his servants. Those whom he redeemed from the devil’s power at the price of his blood, he will free from the power of the second death when they serve him. And none of those who hope in him shall do wrong. Those who hate the righteous do wrong; those who hope in God do not do wrong. Therefore the former will have punishments, the latter everlasting joys. Another translation reads: “He shall not abandon any who hope in him”: namely, the good shepherd does not leave the sheep he redeemed [Col. 1334D], but guards them with diligent compassion, feeds them with his body, and will bring them to the promised reward of glory. The apostolic feast claims this psalm for itself because the apostles brought the Church Christ’s new sacrifice.

## PSALM XXXIV

[Col. 1333]

[Col. 1333D] VERSE 1. “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me,” etc., etc. In this work, lilies sometimes grow white, and roses rising from thorns sometimes redden: for at one time joyful things expand the soul; at another, sorrowful things pierce the mind. [Col. 1334D] The preceding psalm treated the institution of the changed sacrifice; this one treats the Church’s imitation of that same sacrifice. The imitation of this sacrifice is the imitation of Christ’s obedience and Passion. Whoever patiently imitates Christ’s obedience truly shares in Christ’s sacraments. Thus so many psalms concerning Christ’s Passion are set before believers as a pattern of patience, because through patience they gain joys. “For if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (Rom. 8:17).

This psalm is placed thirty-fourth in order, and is fittingly adapted to this matter. Thirty arises from three. By three is signified faith in the Trinity; by four, the Church gathered from the four regions of the world; by ten, the reward of eternal recompense. Therefore, if the Church, established under the four Gospels, imitates Christ’s obedience through suffering in faith in the Trinity, it is rewarded with the tenfold number of life. Also, by three the faithful in the active life are signified; by four [Col. 1335B], those founded in the contemplative life upon the four virtues—prudence, justice, courage, and temperance. To those laboring in the vineyard of the Church, Christ will give as their reward the denarius of life. The title is:

### A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF

Where “himself” is added, the person of Christ is understood specifically; but where only “a psalm of David” is written, the faithful people are understood. David is interpreted “strong of hand” or “beloved.” Therefore this psalm—that is, hymn—is sung to Christ, strong of hand and beloved: he who conquered our death and promised us eternal life. He is strong of hand because he conquered death; beloved because he promised life. What hand is stronger [Col. 1335C] than this one, which conquered the world not armed with iron but pierced by wood? What is more beloved than him whom the martyrs, though they did not see him, wished to die in order that they might come to him and see him?

The subject of the psalm is the prayer of the Lord’s human nature concerning the Passion, the Resurrection, the conversion of enemies, and the condemnation of the obstinate. Its purpose is to form us, by Christ’s example, in obedience and patience. All psalms concerning Christ’s Passion have words drawn from the persecution which David suffered from Saul or from others. David suffered persecution in his own land from fellow-countrymen; in a foreign land he was attacked by Gentiles. Against both he sang this song to the Lord. Christ endured persecution from Jews and Gentiles, [Col. 1335D] against whom he poured out this prayer to the Father. The Church is attacked by persecutors and heretics, against whom she is armed by this song. Every believer suffers adversities from neighbours and false brethren, against whom he uses this prayer.

The psalm has three sections. The first is, “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me,” in which there is an imprecation against Christ’s enemies; the second, “But my soul,” in which there is rejoicing over the Resurrection and a narration of the Passion; the third, “I will confess you in the great assembly,” in which there is the confession of one delivered, the confusion of persecutors, and the exultation of the righteous. It is the voice of Christ sweating in the Passion, the voice of the Church labouring in suffering, and the voice of every believer crying to God in tribulation.

[Col. 1336A] “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me.” O Lord, the Word—or O Trinity—judge by judgment: condemn the demons that harm me, a human being, by temptations; defeat, that is, by resisting subject to punishments, the Pharisees and chief priests who attack me by persecutions.

**Verse 2.** “Take hold of weapon and shield.” The weapons are heavenly helps; the shield is divine protection. “Take hold of weapon,” that is, send to me as man angelic defences; “and shield,” that is, defend me by your protection. For while he prayed and, under distress, sweated blood, an angel from heaven appeared strengthening him. The Father furnished him with a shield when everyone wishing to seize him was driven back, as though by a boss on a shield, and fell backward. Or: take hold through me of those who will be weapons against terrible demons and vices, such as [Col. 1336B] the apostles; and of others as a protecting shield, such as Paul. And you who seem to sleep, to the Jews, in my Passion, awake and rise to help me. The Father rose to help Christ when man, through God, conquered the devil and brought back lost humanity.

**Verse 3.** “Draw out the sword,” that is, unsheathe the sword, “and shut in against those who persecute me,” that is, kill them. God’s sword is Christ’s soul; its sheath was human flesh. This sword was drawn out when Christ’s soul was separated from the flesh. By it Christ’s persecutors were shut in: the demons were conquered and the Jews confounded. The Father drew out this sword, cut off from the Church [Col. 1336C] the devil, the head of evils, and slew idolatry, the adversary of the Christian religion. Say to my soul: after you have fought through it and laid low the enemies, put it back into the sheath of the body by raising that body: “I am your salvation.”

**Verse 4.** Let the demons be confounded, and let Jews and Gentiles be put to shame, who seek my soul—that is, who devise to destroy my life. For the demons were confounded when, through Christ’s one soul, they lost many souls; Jews and Gentiles were put to shame when they heard that the man whom they had killed and guarded in the tomb was alive and that many signs were performed through him. Let them be turned back, not forward so as to advance, but backward so as to fall and perish; and let them be confounded in the future judgment, who think evil against me, such as the Pharisees [Col. 1336D] and other Jews. Or let them be confounded in repentance and be ashamed of their sins; let them turn back from idolatry, that is, let them not go ahead in pride but follow Christ behind in humility; and let them be confounded as they repent of their former manner of life. It follows:

**Verse 5.** “Let them become like dust before the face of the wind.” That is, as dust is scattered by the wind, so let Christ’s enemies be driven about by the temptations of demons amid their desires. “And the angel of the Lord,” that is, the devil, “constraining them,” that is, stirring them up still more. Or let them be destroyed by an angel pursuing them in such a manner that absolutely nothing, not even the least thing, remains of them. And since they are dry like dust and empty of the weight of goodness, let them be carried away on the day of judgment by the wind of the storm of God’s wrath, wrapped in a sulphurous [Col. 1337A] whirlwind; and then let the angel of the Lord, namely the devil appointed for God’s vengeance, be constraining them—that is, tormenting them in eternal punishments.

In the Hebrew it reads: “And the angel of the Lord drives away those who are such.” Or otherwise: “Let them become like dust before the face of the wind,” that is, having been converted to faith, let them be lifted by the wind of the Holy Spirit from earthly desires, and, lightened from the burden of sins, be led into heavenly virtues. And let the good angel of the Lord constrain them, binding them to repentance through adversities unto holiness. It follows:

**Verse 6.** “Let their way be darkness and slipperiness,” that is, ignorance and sensuality or instability. Let them not know the light of truth, nor stand in a firm position; [Col. 1337B] but, blind, let them slip from vice into vice with a slippery step, they who rage in my Passion, and let them be afflicted by the angel of the Lord’s brightness. For one who walks in this life is pursued by the devil. Therefore it adds: “And the angel of the Lord pursuing them with eternal torments.” If he is the angel of the Lord, why evil? If evil, why the Lord’s? An angel by nature; the Lord’s by creation; evil by his own will. He is also the Lord’s in this respect: he serves the Lord while punishing the wicked and refining the just in the furnace of tribulation, as a smith purges gold of dross.

Otherwise: let the way of sinners become darkness to those converted, so that, seeing it dark through the light of truth, they may shudder at it; and slippery, so that they may not be able to remain in it any longer. [Col. 1337C] And let the angel of the Lord be Christ, the Angel of Great Counsel—that is, the Father’s messenger—pursuing them by chastising and correcting them away from evils, lest they cling to earthly desires but hasten to the way of salvation. In this manner, as I have said, let my persecutors perish.

**Verse 7.** “For without cause,” that is, without any fault of mine, “they hid from me the destruction of their snare”: they secretly prepared for me the death by which I might be ensnared. I say, their snare, by which they themselves will be ensnared. Or my death was the destruction of their snare, namely sins, which were destroyed by my death. “They reproached my soul in vain.” In vain, that is, they called me a blasphemer when I said, “I am the Son of God”; or they falsely accused me of saying that I could destroy God’s temple and rebuild another not made by hands. [Col. 1337D] Therefore:

**Verse 8.** “Let the snare which he does not know come upon him”: that is, let that death come upon that people, a death which they do not know will come about through my death. And this happened accordingly. For suddenly the Roman army came and surrounded them as they had gathered for the festival. A snare is said to come when someone casts himself headlong into a snare. And because not all were killed, he says what befell the others: “And let the capture which he hid seize him,” that is, let the capture which he secretly prepared for me be the cause of his own capture, and let such a capture seize him. “And let him fall into the snare in it” [variant: “into it”], that is, into Christ—the sudden [snare] which he prepared for me—and let him fall into the pit which he made.

Otherwise: “Let the snare which he does not know come upon him,” that is, [Col. 1338A] let the bond of truth, which he does not know, bind him; “and let the capture which he hid,” that is, Christ’s death contrived through hidden treachery, seize him as he flees from God; “and let him fall into the snare in it,” that is, in Christ: let him fall away from his former life into the bond of love, released from the snare of demonic captivity. Because it is judgment to distinguish between good and evil, all this is understood in both a good and an evil sense. Christ, the true judge, prayed before the Passion for those who loved him, and in the Passion for those who crucified him; and, seated on the cross as though upon a tribunal, he condemned one of the thieves as among those at the left in judgment, while he awarded the other life as one still among those at the right. The rejoicing of the Resurrection follows. Through my death, this will happen to them:

**Verse 9.** “But my soul shall exult in the Lord,” [Col. 1338B] that is, I shall rise, and my soul shall rejoice in the Resurrection brought about by the Lord; “and shall delight in its salvation,” that is, it shall take delight in the salvation which shall occur for others through it—this is its salvation. For the soul of Christ was the salvation of the world; or the salvation of Christ’s soul was the majesty of the Word, from which salvation goes forth and life is bestowed: the fountain of mercy, the remedy of those who plead, the remission of sins.

**Verse 10.** “All my bones shall say,” that is, my strength and power, and all the faculties of my soul, shall cry aloud in jubilation: “Lord, who is like you?” Or Christ’s bones are the apostles, who were carrying the infirmity of the flesh—namely, the Church, still tender in faith. Seeing him raised from death, they cried out in overwhelming astonishment: [Col. 1338C] “Lord, who is like you?” No one. “Delivering the needy from the hand of those stronger than him,” that is, the human race from the power of demons; “the destitute and poor from those who despoil him,” that is, the demons dragging him into various vices and then carrying him off to various punishments.

Note three terms: needy, destitute, poor. Another translation has “beggar” for “poor.” The human race was needy because, having become mortal, it had no help from elsewhere—not from the Law, prophet, or anyone else.
