It was destitute because it sought bread in labour and sweat. It was poor because, cast down from that wisdom and purity, it possessed only a thin and shadowy little faculty of reason. It was also a beggar because it implored help. The demons were stronger [Col. 1338D] than it because they prevailed over it in everything. And because they had it in their power, they dragged it toward everything contrary to God. This is also the voice of Christ giving thanks to the Father: “Delivering me, the needy, from the hand of the stronger,” namely the Jews. Christ became needy for us, that through his neediness we might be rich. Annas, Caiaphas, Pilate, and the Pharisees were stronger than he, since they inflicted bodily death upon him. He was destitute because no one helped him in the Passion; he was poor because he was abandoned by all his own. They despoiled him when they seized him with clubs and swords as though he were a robber. What they did next, he himself relates.

**Verse 11.** “Unjust witnesses rising up questioned me about things I did not know.” Unjust, that is false, witnesses rose up—that is, violently attacked—and questioned me, accusing me concerning things which I did not know [Col. 1339A] in my conscience, that is, things I had not done: “We heard that this man said, ‘I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild another in three days’” (Matt. 26:61). But the Pharisees falsely accused him of many things before Pilate and Herod. And they questioned him: “Do you answer nothing to the things which these bring against you?” (Mark 14:60). But he kept silent as though ignorant, because they were ignorant in their conscience whether he was the Son of God. When he said, “I am,” they tore their garments, saying that he had blasphemed. And why was this? Because they did not know the things concerning which they questioned him. For the Jews believe in God, but do not believe in the Son of God. Therefore, what they do not believe, that they do not know.

**Verse 12.** “They repaid me evil for good.” For [Col. 1339B] miracles, insults and scourges; for life, death. “Barrenness to my soul.” I sowed in them the good seed of God’s word and made them fruitful by good works; they rendered barrenness, when they produced thorns of wickedness. Or they strove to make my soul, fruitful in virtues, barren, so that when dead I might perform no work.

**Verse 13.** “But I, when they troubled me, clothed myself in sackcloth. I humbled my soul in fasting.” The Lord is not read to have put on sackcloth or fasted in the Passion; but because this book is spiritual, it speaks spiritually. Sackcloth, which is customarily spread beneath the dying, signifies mortality. Death is the penalty of sin. But since Christ was conceived without sin [Col. 1339C] and lived without sin, he was naturally immortal. He put on, as it were, sackcloth when he willed to be mortal. For if he had not died, he would not have risen, and thus would not have furnished an example of eternal life. Sackcloth is woven of goats’ hair and is fitting for those in repentance and mourning. As sheep signify the righteous, so goats signify sinners. Therefore, in judgment sheep shall stand on the right and goats on the left. Christ therefore put on sackcloth when, born from sinners, he took mortal flesh and condemned sin through sin. While they troubled me with spitting, blows, and scourges, they clothed me in sackcloth—that is, mortality—under which I lay hidden, unrecognized. “And I humbled my soul in fasting.” Christ’s food is good action. He hungered for their salvation. But while they committed abominable [Col. 1339D] crimes, he remained fasting. In such fasting he humbled his soul when he delivered himself to them there, to satisfy their madness.

“And my prayer shall return into my bosom.” This is drawn from the history. Moses’ hand, brought out of his bosom, appeared leprous; put back into his bosom, it was found whole (Exod. 4:6–7). Moses’ hand is the prophecy of the Law concerning Christ. The bosom is the Father’s hidden mystery. The hand drawn from the bosom appeared leprous when Christ, descending from the Father’s bosom, put on infirm flesh. Hence the Jews said: “We saw him without form or beauty, but as one struck by God and leprous. Therefore we did not esteem him” (Isa. 53:2 ff.). But the hand returned into the bosom was found whole because, when Christ returned to the Father, [Col. 1340A] the God of majesty shone forth. Christ’s bosom is the mystery of the Word, in whose bosom is the Father and he himself in the Father; for “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). Therefore his prayer returned into his bosom when the prayer of his humanity entered the mystery of the Father’s Deity on behalf of the intercession for human deliverance.

**Verse 14.** “As a neighbour and as our brother, so I pleased,” that is, I pleased as though for a neighbour and brother. Another translation has: “As toward a neighbour, as toward our brother, so I walked among them,” that is, I loved them as someone loves his friend and brother. Or I regarded Judas with such affection as a neighbour—that is, a kinsman such as John or James—and as our brother, namely Peter or another apostle. In saying “our” he shows the unity of the Deity; or the unity of the Church because of the sharing of humanity. For according to divinity he is God with God; according to humanity, man with the Church. “As mourning and grieving, so I humbled myself,” that is, I grieved over their destruction as a father grieves over the death of a son. In the Hebrew it is written: “Like a mourning mother, bowed down,” namely when she bows, grieving and sorrowful, over the body of her only son. All this pertains to deliverance as a work; what follows pertains to the evils which they repaid to him.

**Verse 15.** “And they rejoiced against me and assembled.” The Jews indeed assembled to seize him. [Col. 1340C] Having captured him, they rejoiced as though they had taken a cruel robber or savage enemy. “Scourges were gathered against me,” that is, spittings, blows, beatings, and thorns were heaped up together. “And I did not know,” through conscience, any fault for which such things are customarily done.

**Verse 16.** “They were scattered and were not pierced with compunction,” that is, blinded in wickedness and separated from the light of truth; therefore they were not moved to spare him. Or they were scattered by envy and avarice and loosened from the bond of charity; therefore they were not moved to mercy. Or even now they are scattered from their land among all nations and yet are not moved to repentance. “They tested me, saying, ‘Prophesy: who is it that struck you?’” (Luke 22:64). “They mocked me with mockery,” [Col. 1340D] that is, they ridiculed me with great derision when they uncovered my face, struck me with their palms, and moreover spat upon me as unclean (Matt. 26:66). “They gnashed their teeth at me,” saying: “He is deserving of death.”

**Verse 17.** “Lord, when will you look?” That is, they treated me thus; but you, Lord, when will you look upon me suffering in this way? How long do you tolerate these things against your only-begotten, the one who alone pleases you? How long do you not avenge such a cruelly raging nation? “Restore my soul from their wickedness,” that is, from the cruelty of the Jews, and return it, once delivered, to the body, so that I may rise. “From the lions,” that is, from the roaring demons, restore my only one. Christ’s soul was unique—that is, singular, immune from every stain of sin [Col. 1341A]—and therefore the receptacle of Divinity. If you raise me:

**Verse 18.** “I will confess you,” that is, praise you “in the great assembly,” spread throughout the whole world, not the small Synagogue of a few. “Among a weighty people,” namely the Christian people weighty in virtues, I will praise you, not among the Jewish people light in vanities. Having inserted these matters, he returns to the Passion.

**Verse 19.** “Let not those who unjustly oppose me exult over me,” that is, let them not derive joy from killing me unjustly. Another translation has: “Let them not insult me.” If I do not rise, my adversaries will rejoice and will insult me over my death. “Those who hate me without cause,” that is, without fault, but because of good deeds, “wink with their eyes at you.” That is, they used deceits [Col. 1341B] against me. They dealt affectionately with me, while meanwhile signalling to one another by movements of the eyes, as though saying: “He is a deceiver; he is a magician.” Hence follows:

**Verse 20.** “For indeed they spoke peacefully to me,” saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth” (Matt. 22:16). “And, speaking in the anger of the earth, they devised deceits,” that is, angered against me for retaining earthly things, while outwardly speaking these peaceful words they inwardly devised deceits—how to catch, bind, and kill me in speech. And after they seized and bound me:

**Verse 21.** “They opened their mouth wide against me,” that is, they opened it very widely, as though wishing to devour me, crying: “Crucify, crucify him. If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19:6, 12). “If this man [Col. 1341C] were not an evildoer, we would not have delivered him to you” (John 18:30). And on the cross: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. 27:42). Moreover they said: “Aha, aha, our eyes have seen,” that is, “Good, good: we see with our eyes what we desired to see, that the deceiver of the people should hang among robbers.” Now our eyes see what we had previously said, namely that your signs were magical. In the Hebrew it is written: “Vah, vah,” the cry with which they insulted him on the cross.

**Verse 22.** You saw, O Lord Father, their mockeries and my obedience. Do not be silent about vengeance upon them, and do not delay pronouncing sentence upon them for punishment. [Col. 1341D] When a judge is silent, the accused are spared; when he pronounces sentence, they are punished. The Father was, as it were, silent when he did not avenge the Son’s murder in the Passion; as judge he pronounced sentence when he destroyed all of them through the Romans. “Lord, do not depart from me,” that is, give me steadfastness, lest I fail, and let me cling to your right hand until they are punished by worthy vengeance.

**Verse 23.** “Rise to help me, and attend to my judgment,” that is, carefully consider by what unjust judgment they condemned me among robbers. My God, because you created me, and my Lord, because I took the form of a servant, attend to my cause, not to my punishment; for the punishment is equal, but the guilt unequal. For my cause, for which I am judged, is the restoration of the human race.

[Col. 1342A] **Verse 24.** “Judge me according to your righteousness, O Lord my God,” that is, judge me according to what my righteousness demands from your righteousness. Do for me what I deserve, and for them what they deserve. And let them not exult over me because they possess good things while I suffer evil.

**Verse 25.** Let them not say in their hearts: “Behold, aha for our soul,” that is, “It is well for our soul; our desires concerning him have been fulfilled.” Nor let them say: “We have devoured him.” That is, after doing to him everything we wished, we have killed him. They could say this if he had not risen. Then it would be well for their soul, if their soul were satisfied; then they would rejoice over him.

**Verse 26.** Let those who rejoice in my killing be ashamed because of my Resurrection; and let all who consent be seized with reverence together—that is, let those who rejoice in my evils be greatly afraid.

“Let them be clothed with confusion and reverence,” that is, let them be surrounded by blushing and fear, who speak wicked things [Vulgate: “great things”] against me. They spoke wickedly when, after he had been killed and buried, they said: “That deceiver, while he was still alive, promised that he would rise. But since through magical art he appeared great among the common people, this art will no longer be able to benefit him. Guard the tomb, lest his disciples steal him.” After such words they blushed greatly before the soldiers when they heard that he had powerfully come out of the tomb. They were greatly afraid when they offered them money, because they feared that they would shortly perish. They were clothed with confusion [Col. 1342C] when they could not answer the apostles, unlearned men, and moreover saw signs performed through Christ’s name. Those who stirred up the Romans to their own destruction were drenched in reverence—that is, in fear.

Otherwise: let them be ashamed of what they did to me; and let them revere together, that is, let them turn in fear to repentance, who rejoice in my evils. Let those who rejoiced at my death grieve in repentance that they consented, in shame and reverence—that is, in the sackcloth of repentance, as in a mourning garment. Shame opposes the boldness of cruelty; reverence, the shamelessness of falsehood. Reverence is fear of the Lord mixed with love. Let those who spoke wicked things against me—that is, who spoke proudly against me—heal by two virtues what they committed by two crimes.

**Verse 27.** Let the apostles and other believers exult in body and rejoice in soul at my Resurrection, who desire my righteousness—that is, who wish to imitate me in righteousness, or who wish justice to be done me against the Jews. And let them say with mouth and heart: “May the Lord always be magnified,” that is, let the whole world be subject to him for ever, those who desire the peace of his servant—that is, who seek that peace which I, your servant, shall have as a reward because I served you in the Passion of the flesh for the redemption of the human race, so that they may suffer no disturbances either in body or in soul.

[Col. 1343A] **Verse 28.** “And my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness”: namely, my preachers shall diligently set forth to others the truth of your promise; “all the day,” that is, continually they shall proclaim your praise by a good life. Thus far concerning the head; now let us consider the body and members.

The Church’s struggle is not against flesh and blood alone—that is, against the human beings whom we see—but against principalities, powers, and rulers of the world—that is, the devil and his angels whom we do not see. Concerning these it cries:

**Verse 1.** “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me.” That is: O Christ, judge by your judgment the demons harming me with injurious suggestions; defeat by your grace those attacking me with temptations. Or, “Judge those harming [Col. 1343B] me,” that is, separate me from unbelievers who desire to harm me; defeat, by signs and powers, those persecutors and heretics who attack me, by converting them to yourself.

**Verse 2.** “Take hold of weapon and shield.” Weapons are so called because they cover the shoulders, and they signify the virtues by which souls are armed lest the demons’ ambushes prevail against them. A shield is called *sculptum* (“carved”), because in ancient times the deeds of brave men were carved upon shields; and it signifies faith, by which the fiery darts of the most wicked one—that is, burning desires—are repelled. Therefore it is said: “Take hold of weapon and shield,” that is, make me take hold of faith and be armed with virtues against demons, so that I may be able to withstand on the evil day—that is, the day of temptation or tribulation—[Col. 1343C] and overcome vices. And because I cannot do this by myself, rise through grace to help me.

**Verse 3.** “Draw out the sword and shut in against those who persecute me,” that is, let the sword of your wrath fall upon them and confine them, so that they cannot range abroad to harm. Or the sword is the word of God. It is drawn out when evil is resisted through Scripture. The sword is also the soul of a righteous person. It is drawn out by God and the enemy is shut in when, through the soul of a righteous person, a sinner is punished, as Ananias and Sapphira were struck down through Peter’s soul, and companies of fifty were consumed through Elijah’s. Say to my soul, that it may understand you: “I am your salvation; by me you will be made alive after death.” The sword is also drawn out when the holy way of life of a soul is brandished everywhere through its good reputation. [Col. 1343D] Then adversaries are shut in when good works impose silence upon them, so that, pierced by the sword of their holiness, they have nothing bad to say about the good. The Lord will surely be their salvation.

**Verse 4.** Let the demons who seek my soul to destroy it be confounded and put to shame. Demons are confounded when they are conquered by saints. Then they are filled with reverence when they are tormented on account of the saints by God’s judgment. Let the Jews, who by a perverse course go into a precipice, be turned back; and let Gentiles be confounded in idolatry and heretics in their craftiness, who think evil against me—that is, who devise persecutions and tribulations against me in their counsels.

[Col. 1344A] **Verse 5.** “Let them become like dust before the face of the wind.” He says this not as a curse but as a prediction: demons, Jews, persecutors, and heretics will be like dust before the face of the wind on the day of judgment, when they are carried away by the wind of God’s wrath like chaff from God’s wheat—that is, from the assembly of the righteous—and wrapped in the furnace of blazing fire. Then the angel of the Lord, namely Christ, the Angel of Great Counsel, will pursue them as he says: “Depart from me, you wicked, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). Or God’s angels will then pursue them because through those angels they will be cast into the lake of fire and sulphur.

**Verse 6.** “Let their way be darkness and slipperiness,” because they will be cast into outer darkness and whirled about in the unstable vortex [Col. 1344B] of flames; or, according to the variety of their crimes, they will now be tormented by the heat of fire, now by the chill of cold, as it is written: “They shall pass from snowy waters to excessive heat” (Job 24:19). There the angel of the Lord will be constraining them—that is, Christ’s strict judgment pressing upon them.

**Verse 7.** “For without cause they hid from me the destruction of their snare”: without just cause Jews, pagans, and heretics prepared destruction for Christians through secret counsels and ambushes. This was their snare, because they themselves were ensnared in eternal death. In the Hebrew it reads: “They hid the ambushes of their net,” in which they have been caught by demons as fish in the sulphurous torrent, to be cooked as food for the devil. “They reproached my soul in vain,” saying: “You worship a magician, condemned among robbers for his magical acts, and hope for good things from him?”

**Verse 8.** “Let the snare which he does not know come upon him,” that is, upon such a people: let sudden destruction come, which it does not expect; “and let the capture which he hid seize him,” that is, let him be deceived by the fraud through which he wished to deceive; “and let him fall into the snare in it,” that is, let him fall into the pit of death which he dug, be bound hand and foot by the cords of sins, and be cast from the fellowship of saints into eternal fire.

**Verses 9 and 10.** “But my soul shall exult in the Lord” when it sees him face to face as he is; “and shall delight in its salvation,” that is, it shall take delight in Christ, when it has been made like him [Col. 1344D] in glory and beholds him equal to the Father in glory. Then all my bones—that is, all the righteous, firm in heart, strong in persecutions, yielding not to temptations—shall say in rejoicing: “Lord, who is like you?” Here the ineffable joy of the saints is expressed. Lord, whom we have always desired, whom we have always thirsted for, who is like you among the choirs of angels, among the assemblies of saints? “Delivering the needy,” namely the Christian people, from the hand of those stronger than him—that is, tyrants; “the destitute and poor from those who despoil him,” that is, torturers dragging him to various punishments. The people of believers was needy of human aid—that is, bereft of assistance—destitute in necessary things, and poor in spirit for Christ. [Col. 1345A] Therefore it shall be delivered from the hands of its oppressors and from the powers of darkness, and shall be set over all the Lord’s good things.

**Verse 11.** “Unjust witnesses rising up questioned me about things I did not know.” As there were false witnesses against Susanna, so many unjust witnesses rose against the Church and accused Christians of many false crimes, things which they themselves did not know in their conscience.

**Verse 12.** “They repaid me evil for good.” The Church gives temporal goods; persecutors repaid her with punishments. She gave prayers; they repaid persecutions. “Barrenness to my soul.” The Church produced the fruitfulness of faith and good works as a fruitful olive tree; they, like a barren fig tree without the fruit of righteousness, withered and became fit for eternal fire. Moreover, [Col. 1345B] they strove by torments to draw the righteous from the fruitfulness of godliness into their own barrenness.

**Verse 13.** “But I, when they troubled me with threats, rewards, torments, counsels, clothed myself in sackcloth, and humbled my soul in fasting”: that is, I cast away worldly adornment, despised riches, and endured harsh things in body and soul. “And my prayer shall return into my bosom.” The bosom of saints is their conscience. When they pour out prayers for their persecutors but those persecutors continually advance into worse things, then the prayer returns into their bosom, because their good will shall be raised up with full reward. These are the weapons of the righteous: sackcloth, fasting, and prayer, as in the case of Martin and the hermits. The voice in the prayer of the perfect says:

[Col. 1345C] **Verse 14.** “As a neighbour, as our brother, so I pleased,” that is, in the secrecy of prayer I pleased Christ as a brother and co-heir, as a neighbour related to me, as a friend sharing the same hidden counsel. But the voice of penitents in sackcloth and fasting says: “As mourning and grieving, so I humbled myself.” One separated and far removed from God mourns because he does not have what he desires. But one who has in his heart what he desires rejoices because that one pleases him. God is everywhere and is contained in no place. Therefore we do not draw near to him through places, nor are we removed from him through places. We draw near to him through the light of truth; we are made distant through the cloud of flesh. To draw near to God is to become like him; to withdraw from him is to become unlike him. A gold coin and a silver coin are placed together in [Col. 1345D] one place, yet remain far from one another, separated by appearance, quality, and kind. Thus in God we live, move, and are, and yet salvation is far from sinners (Ps. 118:15), while the Lord is near to all who call upon him (Ps. 144:18). I indeed fasted, prayed, and grieved.

**Verse 15.** “And they rejoiced against me and assembled.” Persecutors assembled against Christians; and after plundering their goods and afflicting them with elaborate punishments, they rejoiced. “Scourges were gathered,” that is, multiplied, against me. Truly scourges were gathered against the Church: some were scourged in persecution, some mutilated in their limbs, some burned, some hanged, some thrown into waters, [Col. 1346A] some exposed to beasts, some broken on wheels, some torn apart by untamed horses, some cut asunder by saws, and some killed by the sword. “And I did not know,” that is, I committed none of the crimes for which these punishments are imposed, because I suffered such things for Christ’s cause. Or: I knew no God other than you.

**Verse 16.** My enemies—the Jews, pagans, and heretics—were scattered by wars, crushed by many scourges, and not moved to repentance; rather, hardened in evil, they tested me by threats, terrors, blandishments, and promises. They mocked me with mockery, deriding me with the greatest ridicule, making sport of me, and bringing my life into bitterness. They gnashed their teeth against me, insulting me in many ways and condemning me to various torments.

[Col. 1346B] **Verse 17.** “Lord, when will you look upon me, your bride, labouring under so many evils—me, a desolate widow, crying to you, the just judge? How long will you not avenge me upon those who insult me because of you and heap so many evils upon you?” The just judge, hearing this, delays the salvation of the faithful and vengeance upon the cruel, not through weariness but through love, until the number of the elect is fulfilled; then, by just judgment, a spectacle of the adversaries will be presented to all together. But the afflicted and anxious Church cries: “Restore my soul from their wickedness,” that is, from the cruelty of persecutors. In the Hebrew it reads: “From its calamities,” that is, restore it, delivered from distresses, to the joys of paradise. “From the lions, my only one”: namely, deliver the Church—not manifold through heresies, but one in the integrity of faith—from demons or raging powers, [Col. 1346C] and restore it to your kingdom. If you do this:

**Verse 18.** “I will confess you in the great assembly.” In the heavenly Jerusalem, where there shall be a great gathering of angels and saints; there, among a people weighty in virtues, I shall praise you. The people of believers, which here was not light in its conduct like dust scattered by the wind of temptations through desires, shall not be cast by the wind of God’s wrath into fire, like chaff separated in judgment from grain; rather, like heavy wheat, it shall be stored in the heavenly granary. The Church follows, weeping and imploring divine help.

VERS. 19. Let not those who unjustly oppose me exult over me [Col. 1346D]. The ungodly exult over the good when they see themselves overflowing with an abundance of riches and the latter distressed by lack of everything. Although this is so in this life by your most orderly dispensation, let them not exult over me in that life, so that it should go well with them and ill with me. Those who unjustly oppose me—that is, because they persecute me for righteousness’ sake; who hate me without cause—that is, those whom I have harmed in nothing; and who wink with their eyes—that is, feigned hypocrites, who signify one thing by their face and another in their heart, who do one thing by gestures and another by deeds.

VERS. 20. For heretics or false brethren spoke peaceably to me indeed, in order to deceive me; and, in the wrath of the earth—that is, angry with me, speaking thus only in pursuit of earthly things—they devised deceits in their heart [Col. 1347A], how they might destroy me. And after they prevailed against me,

VERS. 21. They opened their mouth wide over me; that is, they mocked me with loud laughter. They said: “Aha, aha!”—that is, “Good, good! Our eyes have seen what they desired: that you should be afflicted, troubled, tortured—you who worshipped one dead for God; who revered as God a sorcerer crucified with thieves; who promised yourself every good thing from him, while you reproached me with immortal gods and threatened me with eternal punishments.”” In grief he cries out:

VERS. 22. You have seen, O Lord, both their mockery and my affliction. Do not be silent in judgment; rather, bring forth more swiftly against them the sentence of condemnation and of my deliverance. And until judgment comes, [Col. 1347B] O Lord, do not depart from me, as you promised: “Behold, I am with you always, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20). God withdraws from righteous persons who have fallen, yet does not depart: he withdraws when he does not work miracles through them, or permits them to be afflicted by adversaries; he does not depart when he chastises them with scourges as sons, and by cleansing them from filth prepares them as vessels of mercy and heirs of the kingdom.

VERS. 23. Arise, O Lord, for judgment—you who for so long have patiently looked upon my unjust destruction. And attend to my case: how unjustly I have been condemned by them to death, not for crimes but for righteousness, for equity, for your worship. My God, whom I worship, and my Lord, whom I obediently serve: attend to my cause, not to my punishment. For I suffer the same things as thieves and robbers [Col. 1347C]. The punishment is alike, but the cause unlike: they for injustice, I for righteousness.

VERS. 24. Judge me according to your righteousness, O Lord my God. To judge is to distinguish—that is, to separate—the good from the evil. Judge me, that is, distinguish me from those who suffer for crimes things similar to those which I suffer for holy conduct. And do this according to your righteousness, by which you repay evil things to the wicked and good things to the good. And let them not exult over me, so that they may there, as here, enjoy good things, while I there, as here, am afflicted with evils.

VERS. 25. Let them not say in their hearts: “Aha, aha, our souls!” That is, let persecutors not mock me, saying to themselves: “Our souls, rejoice! [Col. 1347D] Your wishes have been fulfilled. You have prevailed over those evil Christians; you have despoiled them and afflicted them with every punishment [Col. 1348A].” Nor let them say, “We have devoured him”; that is, “We have drawn them into our agreement,” or, “We have killed those who would not agree, and have removed their memory from the earth.” Show by my reward and their destruction that they harmed themselves but benefited me.

These words are drawn from the golden calf which the people worshipped in the wilderness, which Moses crushed, burned, and gave to the people to drink in water (Exod. XXXII, 20). The calf made into an idol is the body of the ungodly, worshipping the devil. Moses, whose name means “drawn from water,” is the Christian people drawn from baptism into the kingdom of God. This people crushes the calf, burns it, and gives it in water to drink, when it crushes the devil’s body—that is, the wicked—by the blows of preaching, melts it in the fire of love, and, having steeped it in the water of baptism [Col. 1348B] or in tears of repentance, transfers it into the body of the Church to be consumed. He continues with what will befall the wicked:

VERS. 26. Let those who rejoice in my evils blush on the day of judgment and be ashamed together. Or, as it is written in Hebrew: those who rejoice in my affliction—the demons, Jews, persecutors, heretics—and not only those who act, but also those who consent to those acting. Let them be clothed with everlasting confusion and awe—that is, fear—when you say: “Depart from me, you accursed, into everlasting fire” (Matt. XXV, 41). Those who speak maliciously concerning me after my death say: “Behold, their vain hope has perished; they have been destroyed with Christ the sorcerer; they shall rise no more, as they falsely promised themselves.” But what will befall the good is added:

[Col. 1348C] VERS. 27. Let those who desire my righteousness exult in their mortal body and rejoice in their soul with everlasting happiness; that is, those who love the reward laid up for me because of righteousness. And, rejoicing, let them say: “May the Lord always be magnified”—that is, may God be glorified forever—who desire the peace prepared for his servant, that is, for the Christian people serving God in this world, and seek nothing else.

VERS. 28. And my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness. That is, the tongue of my heart, blessing you with unceasing thought, shall turn over within itself how just you are and how justly you have crowned the righteous. All day it shall jubilantly praise you—that day which has no evening—that is, throughout endless eternity it shall sing your praise with the angels [Col. 1348D] and resound the hymn of jubilation.

## PSALM XXXV

[Col. 1347]

[Col. 1347D] “The unjust man said, that he might sin within himself,” etc. The title of this psalm is taken from the end of the preceding one, where it is written: “Who desire the peace of his servant.” For its title is (VERS. 1):

**UNTO THE END, FOR THE SERVANT OF THE LORD: A PSALM OF DAVID.**  
[Note: [Col. 1347D] Vulgate: “Unto the end, for the servant of the Lord, David himself.”]

[Col. 1348D] A psalm is a good work. The servant of the Lord is the Christian people serving the Lord; this people is David—that is, “strong of hand”—for good works and resistance to vices, persevering unto the end in goodness for the reward of life that shall be given at the end of the world. Therefore this hymn of good work is assigned to the people serving God until the end [Col. 1349A].

This psalm concerns free will and the grace of God, the ungodly and the righteous: the ungodly, who shall blush and be clothed with confusion; the righteous, who shall exult and rejoice. Both parties are described in this psalm, but the title is assigned to the better party. By free choice and God’s righteousness the former advance toward everlasting confusion; by God’s grace and freedom of the will the latter attain perpetual exultation. By the choice of free will the ungodly work iniquity; by God’s righteousness they are blinded in malice, so that from vice into vice, into the depth of sins, they roll down like a wheel in a precipitous plunge from high to low. But by grace the righteous are stirred to willing what is good, and they themselves cooperate with this grace [Col. 1349B] through free will. The former remove themselves from God’s sacrifice by their own choice; the latter draw near to it by grace. Hence this psalm concerning free will is fittingly joined to that in which the unchanging character of the changed sacrifice is discussed.

In the thirty-fifth place stands a number which increases through multiplication by five and seven. For either five times seven or seven times five produces the sum of this number. Five signifies the carnal people serving under the Pentateuch, who withdrew from God by the free choice of the five bodily senses. Seven, however, signifies the spiritual people, who came to faith through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. Thus the latter is begotten from the fountain of life, while the former is darkened away from the true light [Col. 1349C].

The subject of this psalm is the people declining toward evil by free will, and the people adhering to good through grace. Its purpose is that, in doing good, we may not fail, so that, made drunk from the fountain of life, we may see light in the light. Its words seem to be taken from Ahithophel, who devised iniquity in his bed when he plotted David’s destruction. He did not hate malice, and therefore ended his life by the noose. But God extended mercy to David, delivering him from his enemies when those attacking him fell in battle and could not stand against him. Ahithophel signifies Judas, who devised iniquity in the bedchamber of his heart when he plotted Christ’s death. He did not hate malice, and therefore forced out his soul by a noose [Col. 1349D]. But God extended mercy to Christ, whom he delivered in the Resurrection from the persecuting Jews; and those working iniquity fell before the victorious Romans and could not stand against them. He also signifies all the ungodly who devise evils against the righteous and are therefore separated from the fountain and from the true light. The psalm has two parts: one, “The unjust man said,” in which the people of the ungodly is described; the other, “O Lord, in heaven,” in which the people of the blessed is expressed. It is the voice of the Holy Spirit:

VERS. 2. The unjust man said within himself, that he might sin. Righteousness is to love God and one’s neighbor. To possess this righteousness is to be righteous. The unjust person is one who voluntarily abandons it, hates God’s commandments and his neighbor, and loves iniquity. Such an unjust person said within himself [Col. 1350A], that is, he resolved by the choice of his own will that he might sin—that is, that he might do evil. Therefore he deliberates within himself—that is, in his heart—because he feared not God but men. Hence follows: “There is no fear of God before his eyes.” He does not attend with the eyes of his heart to God as present everywhere; and therefore he despises the judgment awaiting transgressors of the law.

VERS. 3. For he acted deceitfully in his sight, that his iniquity might be found unto hatred. In Hebrew it reads: “For he acted deceitfully against him in his own eyes, so as to find his iniquity for hating.” He acts deceitfully in God’s sight who investigates what iniquity is, as though he wished to hate it; and this is what it means for it to be found for hatred. Yet, when found, he does not hate it but loves it; and this is to act deceitfully, because he pretends to know what is good and what evil [Col. 1350B]. Or, iniquity is found for hatred to the person whom God punishes. That iniquity is not found for hatred which is erased through the remedy of repentance. It follows:

VERS. 4. The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit. Iniquity is what he said in his heart, that he might sin. Deceit is his pretence that he knows what is good and does not know what is evil. He was unwilling to understand, that he might do good. It does not say, “He was unable,” but “He was unwilling,” because a human being does evil not under compulsion but voluntarily. God gave man understanding by which he might understand his Creator. But man himself, through free choice, changes good into evil, when, yearning after earthly things, he refuses to know the good. Of such persons it is said: “They are wise to do evil, but to do good they have not known” (Jer. IV, 22). Some desire to understand good [Col. 1350C], but cannot because of the weakness of the flesh, since “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX, 15). Some, endowed with keen intellect, search most earnestly into the fictions of poets and the ravings of philosophers, but are unwilling to understand the mysteries of the divine law, the instruments of eternal life. Some even say in so many words: “It is better for us to be ignorant of good things than knowingly to sin.” These, as is written in Job, say to the Lord God: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways” (Job XXI, 14). And because they drive God from themselves, they shall be driven away by God and punished with a double penalty: because they freely do evil and proudly despise knowing the good.

VERS. 5. He devised iniquity in his bed [Col. 1350D]; that is, in his heart he long pondered the accomplishment of evil. Some have even devised books against the truth, and have sought by writing to destroy not only those present by their example, but also those absent and still to come. He stood in every way that was not good, but did not hate malice; that is, in meditation, counsel, and action he walked every iniquitous way, drew others to himself by word and evil example, and persevered firmly in this pursuit until the end. Moreover, he hated good in others and loved malice.

Observe the body of the ungodly, divided into five members and represented by the number five in the title: they are unjust, fearing not God; deceitful, feigning ignorance of iniquity; iniquitous, unwilling to understand the good [Col. 1351A]; perverse, continually meditating in their bed upon committing iniquity; malicious, persisting in wickedness and, beyond this, embracing malice. It belongs to the wicked to sin of themselves; but the righteous possess good not through themselves but through grace. Some fight against vices and, because they distrust their own strength, commit themselves to God’s grace and conquer the adversary. Others begin to fight, but because they presume upon their own strength, they are overcome and fall in the hour of temptation, returning by their own will to the vomit. Some do not fight, but are led by desires and follow them in everything. Others are not even led by desires, but instead invite demons through incantations or sorceries and, to obtain earthly things or fulfill the desires of the flesh, enslave themselves to their dominion. All this [Col. 1351B] is ascribed to free choice. Concerning grace, however, it follows:

VERS. 6. O Lord, your mercy is in heaven. By freedom of choice some angels fell in heaven; but by God’s grace others were strengthened and did not fall. Therefore the Lord’s mercy is in heaven, by which the holy angels were made strong. Heaven is also called the Church, in which the mystery of Christ is hidden. The Lord’s mercy is Christ, through whom he had mercy on the miserable. Therefore the Lord’s mercy is in heaven—that is, Christ is in the Church—by whose grace the righteous conquer demons, relying upon his mercy. Here is described the manifold grace bestowed upon the pilgrim Church, and the ineffable glory prepared for the Church that shall reign: namely, what eye has not seen [Col. 1351C], because it has no color that it may be seen; nor ear heard, because it has no sound that it may be heard; nor has it entered into the heart of man, because it has no form that it may be imagined—those things which God has prepared for those who love him, namely peace and joy, which are understood by the mind alone (I Cor. II, 9). It follows:

And your truth unto the clouds—understand, “which are to be established,” that is, the teachers. Truth is Christ; the clouds are teachers, because as rain falls from clouds, so teaching flows from them. Thus God’s truth is said to extend unto the clouds because Christ is known to have mercifully aided humankind through teachers. Or, as the Lord’s mercy appeared in heaven to the angels who were strengthened, so in the Church God’s truth, formerly promised through prophets and apostles, shone forth.

[Col. 1351D] VERS. 7. Your righteousness is like the mountains of God. In Hebrew it is written: “Your righteousness is like mountains, O Lord.” Christ is God’s mercy, because through him angels are strengthened in glory and through him human beings are delivered from misery. He is also God’s truth, because whatever was promised through the prophets is established as fulfilled through Christ. He is likewise God’s righteousness, because through him the righteous receive just rewards and the unjust just punishments. Here “righteousness” means the apostles, who were made righteous through Christ and made God’s righteousness known to the world. They were mountains, lofty in virtues, which the rising sun of righteousness illumined; and through them he enlightened the valleys—that is, the humble. All this is said in commendation of grace. First, God’s mercy precedes the human will, so that it wills good [Col. 1352A]. Truth illumines those willing good and shows their choice to be free. When it uses this freely, it is suffused with righteousness. By persevering in this it shall be saved. And because many are called, like Paul, by grace alone without preceding merits, while others are rejected through hidden justice, as that man in the Gospel who wished to follow the Lord, it follows:

Your judgments are a great deep. The abyss is a depth of waters which can neither be measured nor seen through. Three abysses are described: one abyss is the height of God’s judgments; another, the depth of sins; a third, the infinity of punishments. Of the first it is said: “Your judgments are a great deep,” because they are exceedingly hidden. Of the second it is written: “When the sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3). Of the third the demons begged [Col. 1352B] that the Lord would not send them into the abyss (Luke VIII, 31). Whoever voluntarily descends into the middle abyss is pressed by the weight of the abyss hanging above and plunged into the depth of the abyss opening beneath. God’s judgments are rightly called a great deep, because just as we cannot at all see into the interior of a great sea or comprehend its vast extent, so we cannot grasp with the mind or determine by reason the divine judgments: why he does not permit one wishing to follow him, draws another unwilling person; receives to life one grown old in evils, rejects another grown decrepit in good; chooses an infant of an unbeliever but rejects that of a believer; converts one of two persons equally wicked to good while leaving the other in evil. Therefore [Col. 1352C] some, preceded by mercy and illumined by truth, ascend the mountain of righteousness; others, abandoned through justice by God’s hidden judgment, descend into the deep abyss. And although all are his workmanship, he has provided all with the necessities of this life. Therefore it adds:

VERS. 8. You will save humans and beasts, O Lord. That is, you preserve rational and brutish beings by the bodily preservation through which you rain upon the just and the unjust. Hence he exclaims in admiration: How—that is, how wonderfully—you have multiplied your mercy, O God, you who promise forgiveness to sinners and prepare a crown for the righteous! But beasts seek only bodily preservation; the sons of men, however, shall hope in the shelter of your wings. “Humans” without qualification means sinners [Col. 1352D]; “sons of men,” the justified. Adam was a man, but not a son of man. His imitators are called men. But Christ was the Son of Man. The apostles and faithful are sons of men because they are reborn through grace. The shelter of God’s wings is the protection of the Scriptures. The two wings are the two Testaments. The comparison is drawn from birds, whose young hide beneath their mother’s wings. God’s wisdom is our hen, and all believers are her chicks; the two wings are mercy and compassion. Therefore the sons of men hope in the shelter of God’s wings when the faithful do not trust in their own merits but place their hope in Christ’s mercy and compassion; they flee from the hawks of heretics beneath the wings of the twofold law; they seek the wings of twofold love against the hawks of demons; and they shelter themselves beneath the wings of the cross. Such persons

[Col. 1353A] VERS. 9. Shall be made drunk from the abundance of your house. God’s house is the Church, whose abundance is the richness of Holy Scripture. They shall be made drunk from this abundance because the faithful in the Church shall be filled from Scripture’s overflowing plenitude. And you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight; that is, from the overflowing of the Holy Spirit, who waters every soul with spiritual streams, that they may bring forth the fruit of holiness. Thus it is written: “The Spirit, like a torrent, filled the whole house” (Isa. XXX, 28, and Acts II, 2). You shall give the Holy Spirit to the faithful.

VERS. 10. For with you is the fountain of life. That is, you are the fountain and source of every good; you give the font of baptism, which is the fountain of life, through which eternal life is given. Or the fountain of life is God’s teaching, the life of the soul. These words are drawn from Paradise, where there is the tree of life [Col. 1353B] and a fountain flowing like a torrent from the place of delight, watering Paradise’s grove. Paradise is the Church; the tree of life is Christ; the place of delight is the Father; the fountain flowing thence and watering Paradise is the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and making the Church fruitful. Of this Trinity it follows: “And in your light we shall see light”: that is, O Father, in your light, Christ, who is eternal light, we shall see the light, the Holy Spirit.

Observe the body of the devout, described by seven virtues and represented in the title by the number seven. For in them reign mercy, truth, righteousness, judgment, hope, wisdom, and the abundance of the Holy Spirit. These make them merciful, truthful, righteous, judging justly, hoping in God, wise in Scripture, and overflowing with the sweetness of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1353C]. Such persons shall be made drunk from the abundance of your house. The comparison is drawn from those who gorge themselves on excessive wine and, once drunk, forget their afflictions. God’s house is the heavenly Jerusalem. Its abundance is the overflowing plenitude of every kind of glory. Those who are made drunk by this abundance forget every evil. And you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight. The torrent of delight is the mighty inundation of the brightness of the divine vision. Those drink from this torrent who, in full joy, delight in the overflowing abundance of every pleasure. For with you is the fountain of life: that is, O Father, with you is Christ, coeternal with you in deity, wisdom, and the fountain of life, from whose outflow [the text is uncertain: *profundis Verbum*], the Word, the sweetness of every good and the fullness of joys [proceeds].

[Col. 1353D] Concerning this fountain of life and light the rejoicing righteous add: “And in your light we shall see light”; that is, in Christ, who is the brightness of eternal light, we shall see the ineffable light, the Father and the Spirit, not with bodily eyes but with the mind. For one light belongs to the soul and another to the body; likewise, one water is wisdom flowing from the fountain of life, another is water necessary to this life. Bodily light is withdrawn from the world at night, is removed when the eyes are closed, and is seen by certain animals—such as eagles and lynxes—more than by humans. But that light which is called true light, truth, or wisdom is perceived by the gaze of understanding only by pure hearts. Here fountain and light are different: the fountain drives away thirst, light darkness; light mitigates cold, the fountain heat [Col. 1354A]. With God, however, light and fountain are one and the same. He is the fountain of fullness of joys, by whose flood those thirsting for righteousness shall be made drunk. He is the light of eternal brightness, by whose radiance those pure in heart shall be illumined. This is the promise to the blessed. For this hope the saints undergo the labors of life; to attain this glory they restrain the flesh from desires and do not shrink from suffering hardships. The prayer of the righteous follows, that we may arrive there.

VERS. 11. Extend, O Lord, your mercy to those who know you, and your righteousness to those upright in heart. Those who know God are contemplatives, who understand God and spiritual things. Those upright in heart are active persons, who strive in the Lord’s commandments to fulfill his will. Extend your mercy to those who know you [Col. 1354B]. That is: since through you we know good and understand future joys, precede our will with your mercy, so that we may will good; and follow it, so that we may be able to fulfill it by free choice. For thus we shall be upright in heart—that is, of upright will—when we will nothing except what you will. Precede this uprightness by your righteousness: that is, strengthen my choice in good, lest, presuming upon myself as Adam did, I lose the promised rewards. Mercy belongs to grace; righteousness to free will. Therefore, O Lord, extend mercy to us, that by good will we may attain grace and by the righteousness of free action receive the crown. And lest I lose the merits of righteousness:

VERS. 12. Let not the foot of pride come upon me—that is, [Col. 1354C] the inclination toward malice; and let not the hand of the sinner move me from the good—that is, let evil action not cast me down from my station. Pride is private love. He is proud who is excessively pleased with himself, despises God, and scorns his neighbor. The foot of pride is the evil inclination by which a person walks through unlawful things, knowingly transgressing God’s commandments. The foot of pride is the devil’s pursuit; the hand of the sinner is the action of Adam the transgressor. Therefore strengthen me in good through grace, lest I fall from the purpose of holiness through pride, as the devil, growing proud of freedom, fell from heaven, and as man, glorying in free will, fell from Paradise. Hence follows:

VERS. 13. There fell those who work iniquity [Col. 1354D], namely angels and men in the way of pride, who now work iniquity. Whoever acts wickedly outwardly first fell inwardly through pride. For pride is the beginning of every sin. Great indeed is the pride of a servant’s despising his Lord, of a creature’s despising his Creator in his commandments, and of scorning the judgment set before sinners. The devil grew proud when he wished to be like the Most High—that is, to be worshipped as God—and, limping on this foot, fell because he could not stand. Man grew proud when he desired to be as God, and likewise, tottering upon this foot, fell. Concerning them it follows: the demons were expelled from glory, humans from delight, and they could not stand after their fall. First he who did not stand in the truth; then those whom he cast down from Paradise. They could fall by themselves [Col. 1355A]; by themselves they could not rise again.

We must consider what “to stand” means here. To stand is to remain in a state of rest. As the earth is the place of a stone, so God is the place of the soul. And just as a stone released from on high has no rest, but is always falling until it reaches its own place, the earth; so a soul or angel released from God has no rest, but is always falling, namely into the infinite abyss, unless God’s hand receives the falling one and, restoring it to its proper place, gives it rest. Therefore we are accustomed to say for the dead: “May they rest in peace,” that is, in heaven. And therefore, since God is the highest good, God is the kingdom of heaven, peace, and joy; for unless the soul rests in that peace, it labors forever, falling in the great abyss [Col. 1355B].

Let us briefly conclude the sum of the psalm. First it is shown that angel and human being declined toward injustice through free will, and the fivefold body of the ungodly is indicated. Then angels who stood are described as strengthened in heaven by mercy, and human beings as restored not from merits but through grace. The promises of God through the prophets are said to have been fulfilled through Christ, who is truth; rewards are still to be rendered to good and evil through Christ, who is righteousness; and many are called but few chosen by God’s hidden judgment [Col. 1356A]. Humans and beasts—that is, wise and unwise—are said through God’s mercy to possess the necessities of life; but the sons of men—that is, the righteous—are said to hope for future goods. Their sevenfold body is denoted, and an ineffable good is prepared for it: the abundance of God’s house, the torrent of delight, the fountain of life, the light of light. Finally comes the prayer that it may obtain so great a good through the mercy of grace and through the righteousness of its own choice, and may not lose it through pride, by presuming upon its own powers or doing anything wickedly—since both the devil and his angels, and Adam and his descendants, fell through pride, and human beings could return only through grace [Col. 1356B]. Note the four things promised to the righteous in the kingdom: abundance, delight, fountain, and light. By abundance and delight is expressed the ineffable joy of the body; by the fountain of life and light, the inexpressible glory of the soul, which the assembly of the blessed enjoys happily forever.

## PSALM XXXVI

[Col. 1355]

[Col. 1355C] VERS. 1. Do not be vexed by evildoers [Note: [Col. 1355D] Vulgate: “Do not be envious.”], etc. The title of this psalm is:

**A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF.**  
[Note: [Col. 1356D] Vulgate: *ipsi* (“for him”).]

That is: this hymn is ascribed to Christ, desirable to angels and saints. It is also assigned to the faithful people, strong of hand against vices. The subject of the psalm is the correction of those scandalized by wealthy evildoers. Its purpose is to call us away from such scandal, lest we wish to imitate the wicked in order to acquire worldly goods. Its words are thought to be drawn from Saul and David. David, troubled in mind because Saul, proud and malicious, flourished in glory and riches, while he himself, humble and kind, lacked even life’s necessities, is corrected by the Holy Spirit; Saul’s downfall and his own raising up are foretold. For a sword entered Saul’s heart [Col. 1355D] when he died by his own sword. David’s salvation, however, came from the Lord, who protected him in the time of tribulation.

Saul signifies the Babylonian people of this world; David, the faithful people of Jerusalem. In the preceding psalm it was read that God saves humans and beasts, when he supplies worldly goods to good and evil alike; and that, just as certain beasts stronger than others attack, tear, and devour the weaker, so certain bestial human beings, more powerful than others, oppress their inferiors, plunder their goods, and, raging in malice, flourish in worldly possessions, while the righteous languish in hunger, want, and poverty. The imperfect in the Church are scandalized by this confused exchange [Col. 1356C]; they judge themselves unhappy and miserable, but those people fortunate, blessed, indeed worthy of imitation. They are corrected in this song of the Holy Spirit by the perfect, and the punishments of the wicked and joys of the good are proclaimed to them.

This psalm occupies the thirty-sixth place, a number rising from three and ascending to twelve. For three times twelve, or twelve times three, makes thirty-six. Three signifies the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—which the twelvefold teaching of the apostles, or the same number of prophets, corrects from worldly glory to pursuit of things above. Or again, three signifies the three orders of the Church—virgins, widows, and married persons—who through the twelve apostles, judges of the world, are introduced into the heavenly Jerusalem [Col. 1356D]. This number is repeated six times in itself because it exhorts to perfection. For six times six completes this same number and signifies the perfection of both the inner and outer person. It is divided according to the order of the letters of the alphabet, and the sixteenth, *Ain*, which means “fountain” or “eye,” is found lacking, because those who desire earthly rather than eternal things shall not reach the fountain of life nor see light in the light.

It has three sections: first, “Do not be envious,” in which imitation of the wicked is forbidden and which contains six letters; second, “The sinner shall watch the righteous,” in which the envious torment of the wicked is woven through seven letters [Col. 1357A]; third, “I have been young,” in which the condemnation of the wicked and the reward of the good are joined through eight letters. It is the voice of the perfect Church:

*Aleph.*

Do not be envious of evildoers. By “do not” is denoted the choice of free will. To be envious means to imitate, to be indignant, or to be hostile. Evildoers are those who both do evil and hate good. To be zealous is to envy. Those who do iniquity are people occupied with gain, robbery, and fraud. By “evildoers” are understood the more powerful; by “those who do iniquity,” their inferiors. Therefore it says: “Do not be envious of evildoers,” that is, do not wish to imitate wicked rich persons; “nor envy those who do iniquity,” that is, do not begrudge the unrighteous if they abound in riches. Why?

[Col. 1357B] VERS. 2. For they shall quickly wither like hay, and shall soon fall like the green herbs. By hay he means the flowers of the meadow; by green herbs, wild plants. The flowers signify the rich, who here flourish for a time in glory and riches; but because through malice they store up wrath for themselves on the day of God’s wrath, they shall quickly wither when sudden and unexpected destruction overtakes them, “as travail upon a woman with child,” and they shall not escape. The green herbs signify poorer persons committing iniquity, who shall soon fall when sudden and unforeseen death snatches them away. The roots of herbs flourish more in winter, but in summer wither in the sun’s heat. Trees, however, seem dry in winter, but in summer are clothed in blossoms and fruit. Winter is the present life; summer, the life to come. Herbs are lovers of the world, rooted and flourishing here, but withering in the coming summer under the heat of eternal fire. Trees are lovers of Christ: dry amid the world’s goods, firm in the root of love, and blooming in glory and honor in the future summer. Of them it is written: “You have died”—that is, you are dry in this life—“and your life,” that is, the greenness of glory, “is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III, 3) [Col. 1357C]. And when will it bloom? When, after the winter of this world, Christ your life appears like summer, and then you also will appear with him in glory. Therefore do not envy wealthy evildoers, those working iniquity, who hope in the uncertainty of riches and shall be like dry wood, fuel for flames. But:

[Col. 1357D] VERS. 3 and 4. Hope in the Lord, not in riches; and do goodness, not the malice which you see in those wickedly flourishing. And inhabit the land—that is, the Church—which the Father, the husbandman, cultivates, so that you may be a fruitful tree in faith, hope, and the work of love; and you shall feed on its riches—that is, delight in all the Lord’s goods. “You shall feed” pertains to fullness and everlasting sweetness. The riches of the Church here are Holy Scripture and the eternal hope of the life to come. Its riches are the blessed immortality of the soul, the incorruptibility of the body, brightness like the sun, equality with angels, the immediate vision of God, and the enjoyment of every good. Whoever here suffers want for Christ shall feed to fullness upon these riches. Therefore delight in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart. Do not delight in perishable [Col. 1358A] and passing things, but in the Lord; let remembrance of him be sweet to you, not fleshly desire. And he will give you the petitions of the heart, not of the flesh: namely wisdom, understanding, and the fullness of riches already mentioned.

### Verse 5

Reveal your way to the Lord. The density of sins is a kind of veil, and by it our way—that is, our life—is clothed as though in a dark covering. We reveal this way when, by confessing, we lay sins bare. Reveal your way to the Lord: that is, confess your sins to the Lord, and hope in him, not in your own merits; and he himself will grant you pardon. Or: reveal your way to the Lord—that is, tell him what you suffer; open to him what you desire. What do you suffer? “The flesh desires against the spirit.” What do you desire? “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” [Col. 1358B] (Rom. 7:24). Hope in him, because he himself will accomplish this: “the grace of God through Jesus Christ.” And what more will he do?

### Verse 6

“And he will bring forth your righteousness as light”: that is, he will make your righteous life worthy of imitation by all, “that your light may shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify God.” “And your judgment as the noonday.” Noonday is clear light. The Christian’s judgment is to choose rather to follow Christ in poverty than to imitate the wicked in riches. The Lord will bring this judgment forth like the noonday when he sets it before others as an example, like pure light. To bring forth is to draw something from darkness into light.

Righteousness consists in hoping in the Lord, doing good, delighting in the Lord, asking him for eternal goods, revealing sins to him, and seeking pardon. [Col. 1358C] The Lord will bring this righteousness forth from the darkness of this age like light when he leads it into the brightness of the coming judgment, where he will satisfy you from the fountain of life and, in the light—the Son—show you the light, the Father. And he will bring your judgment—by which you judged it better to endure want with Christ’s poor than to flourish amid abundance with evildoers—forth like the noonday, when he makes you bright as the sun at noon, transparent and equal to the angels. In this hope,

### Verse 7

Be subject to the Lord: that is, obey his commands; pray to him concerning present and former sins; and pray that you may attain these goods. Do not [Col. 1358D] envy the one who prospers in his way: that is, do not be indignant against one upon whom prosperity smiles amid evils, in his own way—that is, in injustice, which is his way. And do not imitate a man who commits injustices. Labor in God’s way—that is, in love—for the springtime of sinners will perish. Therefore:

### Verse 8

Cease from anger, and abandon fury. Anger is a brief disturbance of the mind; fury is great indignation. Cease from anger, you who murmur against God; abandon the fury by which you blaspheme God, as though he acted unjustly in allowing the wicked here to abound in riches and the good to languish in want. Do not envy evildoers: that is, do not imitate them by acting wickedly, as though you might then flourish with them for a time.

### Verse 9

For evildoers shall be cut off. [Col. 1359A] A twofold motive is presented—namely, fear and reward—that we may refuse to imitate the utterly wicked. To be cut off is to be cast outside the boundaries: that is, to be disinherited, deprived of the city of God. Therefore, those who act wickedly shall be cut off: that is, wicked people who do evil works are disinherited from the kingdom of God. But those who wait for the Lord—that is, who have patience in poverty and persevere in awaiting the coming of the Lord the Savior—shall inherit the land of the heavenly Jerusalem, a land flowing with milk and honey, that is, filled with every sweetness. This is drawn from those who were cut off in the wilderness because of wickedness, and from those who possessed the land of promise.

### Verse 10

“And yet a little while, and the sinner shall not be.” Something small is called *pusillum*, that which is enclosed in a fist. [Col. 1359B] Do you think your waiting very long? Wait a little, and you will receive without end that for which you wait. The short time still to come will pass just as all that has gone before has passed. And the sinner shall not be, because then no one will sin. And he who sinned here, puffed up by riches—whom you refused to imitate—will not be with you, but will be in punishments. “You will seek his place, and will not find it.”

In a great house, vessels of gold have their place, and earthen vessels have theirs. The golden ones are in a place of honor; the earthen ones in a place of labor. In God’s commonwealth the righteous have their place, and the unrighteous theirs. The righteous are in the place of God’s children; the impious are in the place of servants. Here the children are chastised by their loving Father; the heirs of the kingdom are shaped in character by discipline. The servants serve the Lord while the vessels of mercy—the elect—are refined by God’s craftsmen like gold in the furnace [Col. 1359C] of tribulation. At present they are necessary in this place, while they serve the elect through adversities. But because they will not be necessary there, they will have no place among the elect. Thus, whoever seeks the sinner’s place in God’s kingdom will not find it, because gold refined by fire has no need of it. Evildoers will be expelled from the inheritance.

### Verse 11

But the meek shall inherit the land of the living, the heavenly Jerusalem. The meek are said to be as though “accustomed to the hand” (*manu consueti*); they are gentle and patient, enduring another’s wrongdoing and burdening no one with their own. Because they despise earthly things, they shall inherit the land of the heavenly homeland. “And they shall delight in abundance of peace.” Their delight shall be in enjoying supreme peace and supreme [Col. 1359D] rest, where no fury agitates, no desire inflames, nothing adverse or contrary can exist, but joy, once begun, continues most sweetly in one unchanging manner. And because the life of the righteous torments the wicked, it follows:

### Verse 12

The sinner will watch the righteous person. When a wicked man sees a righteous person distinguished by honorable conduct, he fears that by comparison with him he will seem worthless. Therefore he watches him, to see whether he can rebuke him for some word or deed, so that he may defend his own life; for he thinks that everything is now permitted to him if he sees the righteous man sin in the slightest respect. If he finds nothing, he will gnash his teeth at him, because, when he cannot overthrow his conduct, he at once seeks to take away his very life.

### Verse 13

But the Lord will laugh at him, namely through the saints [Col. 1360A] who mock the threats of the ungodly, as Lawrence mocked Decius; for he foresees that his day will come, namely the day of vengeance, when he will render to each according to his works. And what did the ungodly do to the saints?

### Verse 14

“The sinners have drawn the sword”: that is, they stirred up persecution against them. “They have bent their bow”: that is, they prepared snares for them. For drawing the sword is open assault; bending the bow is hidden treachery. To what end? That they might deceive by snares or counsels the poor and needy—that is, the righteous person, poor in spirit and lacking the resources of this world—and that they might slaughter the upright in heart: that is, kill the innocent with diverse punishments. The Judge’s sentence follows:

### Verse 15

[Col. 1360B] “Let their sword enter into their own hearts”: that is, let vengeance enter their souls. “And let their bow be broken”: that is, let their snares be frustrated. With their swords the wicked tore only the tunics of flesh upon the saints—indeed, they released them from prison bonds and sent their souls to the heavenly palace—but upon themselves they inflicted the death of the soul and plunged themselves into the enclosures of hell. Or: “Let their sword enter into their hearts,” that is, let the outward death of the righteous become their inward death; “and let their bow be broken,” that is, let their deceit be annihilated. Sinners will wither, be cut off, and be slain; but the righteous will inherit the land. Therefore:

### Verse 16

Better is a little for the righteous in this life than the many riches of sinners acquired through injustice. [Col. 1360C] The little possessed by the righteous is also humility; the many riches of sinners are a multitude of crimes and an abundance of offenses. That little leads to the kingdom of heaven; this burden sinks one into Tartarus.

### Verse 17

For the arms of sinners shall be broken: that is, their riches, through which they are strong, shall be annihilated, and their proud deeds crushed. But the Lord strengthens the righteous, saying: “You labor for a time; you will rest forever. Your trouble is brief; your blessedness will be eternal.”

### Verse 18

The Lord knows the days of the blameless: that is, he foreknows what light he has prepared for them in the dwellings of the righteous. He calls innocent those blameless persons who, neither by threats nor rewards, are bent into agreeing with the impious. [Col. 1360D] The Lord knows their days, which have no evening—that is, he has ordained to give them eternity. Hence follows: “And their inheritance shall be forever,” that is, the heavenly Jerusalem. For from little they will come to eternal joy.

### Verse 19

They shall not be put to shame in the evil time. The evil time is the day of judgment, when evils will meet the evil. In that time the blameless shall not be ashamed, while the ungodly, overcome by evils, are punished with eternal disgrace. “And in the days of famine they shall be satisfied.” The days of famine for the righteous are now, because they often suffer bodily hunger when necessities are lacking; nevertheless, they shall be satisfied by the bread of heaven, by the examples of the saints, by the Scriptures, or by the hope of the future promise. The days of famine are also now because they hunger for righteousness, but [Col. 1361A] one day they shall be satisfied by its vision. But the days of famine for the wicked will then come, when they hunger for joys which they cannot possess and with which the righteous will then be satisfied without end.

### Verse 20

For sinners shall perish when they go into eternal fire. But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they have been honored and exalted, shall fail away as smoke fails away. The enemies of the Lord are all who resist truth. Once honored by men and raised to dignities, they immediately fail inwardly like smoke and fall away from the light of truth. Smoke brings dimness to the eyes and, rising on high, vanishes. So worldly honors and dignities obscure the mind’s sight, alienate it from God’s light, and the higher they rise, the more they vanish from the true good. And [Col. 1361B] he adds why they perish:

### Verse 21

The sinner will borrow and not repay, because he has received on loan from the Lord reason, free will, and temporal goods; and he will not repay—that is, he will not expend them for God’s honor. He also borrows when he hears God’s word and does not repay it, when he does not render it back in good works. He borrows when he receives many good benefits and does not repay, when he returns no thanksgiving. But the righteous person has mercy and gives. He has mercy upon himself by living well; he gives to others by teaching well. He also has mercy upon the poor and gives what is necessary. He does this because:

### Verse 22

Those who bless him shall inherit the land: that is, those who praise the Lord for benefits received shall possess the land of the living. But those who curse [Col. 1361C] him shall utterly perish: that is, those who blaspheme God by living wickedly shall perish from that homeland in body and soul.

In the Hebrew it is read thus: “The wicked man borrows and does not repay; but the righteous gives and bestows, because those blessed by him shall inherit the land, and those cursed shall perish.” There the final judgment is plainly described. For the righteous, giving here to the poor, will then be blessed by him when he says, “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34); and then they will inherit the land of the living when they go into eternal life. But the wicked, who receive the world’s goods from the Lord as though on loan and do not return alms, will then perish when cursed by him, when they hear: [Col. 1361D] “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (ibid., 25:41). And because the righteous will inherit the land, lest anyone think that he will attain this by his own merit without grace, he adds:

### Verse 23

By the Lord a person’s steps shall be directed: that is, by the Lord, not by himself, a person is directed toward the good work, namely having mercy and giving; and when he has been directed toward good by grace, then he will desire his way—that is, through free choice he will willingly do righteousness, which is the Lord’s way. Or: by the Lord a person’s steps shall be directed, that is, God will direct human affections, and thus the person will desire the Lord’s way—that is, will love virtues. The Lord does not allow such a person to fail in tribulation, because:

### Verse 24

When he falls into some tribulation [Col. 1362A] or outward distress, the Lord puts his hand beneath him: that is, he gives help and upholds him with consolation, lest he fall. Another translation has: “When he falls, he shall not be disturbed, because the Lord strengthens his hand,” that is, confirms him. Or: when he falls through the frailty of the flesh—because “the righteous falls seven times a day”—he will not be dashed down but will rise again, because the Lord puts his hand beneath him: that is, he extends the hand of mercy to the one doing penance, as he also gave and stretched out his hand to Peter. And, to show that the righteous are not forsaken by God, he adds:

### Verse 25

I, the Church, was young in the first ages of the world; indeed, I have grown old in the last times of the world. And I have not seen the righteous forsaken in soul, nor his seed—that is, those who imitate him—seeking bread, that is, the word of God. But according to the literal sense, many righteous people [Col. 1362B] have been forsaken bodily by God: for example, the Maccabees, who were destroyed by the ungodly through diverse torments. Many also sought bread in a great famine, as Abraham did; and very many, such as martyrs, died from hunger. It follows:

### Verse 26

All day—that is, at all times—he has mercy, distributing alms to the poor; and he lends, granting what is asked to those who seek a loan; and his seed, that is, his offspring, shall be in blessing, that is, in abundance. According to the literal sense, this cannot at all be true: that a person should at all times give freely to some, lend to others, and yet abound. The righteous person has mercy all day, namely throughout the entire time of life, upon his own soul by living righteously; and he lends by imparting teaching to his neighbors, while requiring in return a loan, namely a good work. And [Col. 1362C] his seed—that is, his action—will be in blessing when, through the words “Come, blessed,” they will possess blessing as an inheritance. But his seed is also his imitators, who shall be in eternal blessing. He adds how blessing is to be attained:

### Verse 27

Turn away from evil and do good: that is, depart from every evil and perform good works; and dwell for age upon age: that is, through the good you do, you will reign eternally with God.

### Verse 28

For the Lord loves judgment: that is, the judgment by which [manuscript: *qui*, “who”] you reject evil and choose good. And he will not forsake his saints in the evils of this world or in future punishments; they shall be preserved from evil forever in eternal life. Therefore [Col. 1362D] evil must be avoided, because the unrighteous shall be punished in the future judgment, and the seed of the impious—their followers or their works—shall perish. They will say: “What did pride profit us, or what did the boasting of riches bring us? All things have passed away like a shadow” (Wis. 5:8). The seed of the righteous shall be in blessing; but the seed of the impious shall perish. Therefore good must be done, because:

### Verse 29

But the righteous shall inherit the land of the living and shall dwell upon it for age upon age: that is, they shall reign endlessly in life. This heaven and this earth shall pass away; but a new heaven and a new earth shall stand forever, and the righteous will inhabit them for age upon age in new bodies, immortal and incorruptible. He does not say that they shall dwell [Col. 1363A] “in it,” but “upon it,” because their bodies will then be light—indeed spiritual—and will not cling to the earth by a heavy mass as they do now. What the saints will do in that land follows:

### Verse 30
