The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom. “Mouth” here means the thought of the heart; for wisdom will not then be gathered by reading but by the heart’s most pure vision, and it will be plainly known that God made all things in wisdom. “And his tongue shall speak judgment.” Judgment is called as though *juridicium*, that is, a just utterance. The righteous person’s tongue will then speak judgment because, approving God’s justice in all his judgments, he will rejoice with the angels in praising him. For then they will clearly see how justly God exalted some here, humbled others, enriched some, chastised others with poverty, called some, and rejected others.

### Verse 31

The law of his God is in his heart. He says “his God,” because God delivered him from the ruin of this world. God’s law is love. This will always be in the heart—that is, the soul—of the righteous, who loves God with whole intent for all his judgments and benefits and will sweetly rejoice in this love. “And his steps shall not be tripped up.” To trip up is to set pits before one’s feet. There no one will be able to trip the righteous person’s steps, when original sin will cease and the devil will have no license to deceive. Therefore the righteous, who here meditate wisdom in heart, speak right judgment with mouth, and whose steps—that is, affections—are not tripped up by vices, will inhabit the new land for age upon [Col. 1363C] age. But those who wish to trip them up are next described:

### Verse 32

The sinner considers the righteous: that is, he examines his good life and, out of grief and envy, seeks to kill [Note: [Col. 1363D] Vulgate: “to kill.”] him; that is, he devises how to kill him inwardly in soul or outwardly in body.

### Verse 33

But the Lord will not abandon him in his hands: that is, he will not permit him to be in the sinner’s power, so that he may make him like himself; nor will he condemn him when judgment is rendered to him. Fools think that those who are scourged here are condemned. But the Lord will not condemn in judgment the one who is judged here—that is, who is scourged here by God’s judgment. Or, [Col. 1363D] the Lord will not condemn the righteous in judgment when judgment is rendered to him concerning the impious; because blessedness will receive the righteous, while due punishment will torment the impious. And because tribulation seems long, he strengthens him:

### Verse 34

Wait patiently for the Lord who is coming for judgment, and keep his way: that is, observe his commands. And when he comes, he will exalt you from earth to heaven, so that you may receive by inheritance the land of the living. When sinners perish, you will see that land, your own exaltation, and the destruction of your adversaries. Or, you will see what pleases you: yourself delivered from punishments. Or, when sinners have been condemned, you will see [Col. 1364A] the God for whom you waited, for whose vision you kept his way and endured adversities. He proves that the impious will perish.

### Verses 35 and 36

I saw the impious man exceedingly exalted—that is, greatly raised up, like Nero—and elevated like the cedars of Lebanon: that is, raised above other impious people, like Antiochus. And I passed in mind to his end, and behold, he was not exalted. And if this one was not, much less the others. I sought him by reason, to see whether he had a place for exaltation, and the place of his exaltation was not found.

Lebanon is said to mean “brightness.” Cedars are tall trees, easily thrown down by the wind. The cedars of Lebanon are the powerful people of this age, shining here in glory and riches; the wind of temptation easily uproots them from the mountain of virtues and casts them down to the earth of desires. He who strives toward the summit of virtues will pass beyond these people. The righteous will also pass beyond those who wander on the road of this life when, crossing the sea of the world, he arrives at God’s judgment. There the sinner will not be in the prize of glory, because he did not run here in the stadium. There he will be sought—that is, called to mind—and his place will not be found: that is, the position he holds in human affairs, namely that many obey him, that he gives commands, that he is heard. But this power will not be found when he perishes. Or, the place of sinners is this world, in which they accomplish crimes and abound in riches. But this place is dissolved together with their prosperity when the glory of the whole corruptible world comes to its end. Since this is what awaits the wicked man:

### Verse 37

Keep innocence: that is, do not be angry [Col. 1364C] against those who trouble you, do not hate them, and do not suffer unwillingly. And behold equity: that is, see that it is just, since the Lord commands that enemies be loved. Or, behold God’s equity, who will grant joys to the righteous and inflict punishments on the impious. For there are remnants for the peaceful person: that is, eternal life will belong to the one who loves his enemy. Bodies and the goods of the body are called “remnants,” because they will be left behind by the soul. The peaceful person is one who reconciles those in discord and desires to have peace with all people, so far as lies within him. These have remnants—that is, goods of body and soul—because “the peacemakers shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5:9).

### Verse 38

But the unrighteous shall utterly perish in body [Col. 1364D] and soul alike; the remnants of the impious shall perish with them—the temporal goods that they refused to despise in order to receive eternal goods. Remnants also mean the memory and praise left afterward following death. These will remain for the righteous, who will be in everlasting remembrance; but the impious will perish when they undergo eternal disgrace. Hence the Hebrew has: “Their end shall perish.”

### Verse 39

But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, both now through the redemption wrought by his body and blood, and in the general resurrection, when bodies shall be clothed with the garment of salvation and immortality, and souls shall be clothed with the garment of righteousness and the robe of joy. [Col. 1365A] And he is their protector in the time of tribulation: that is, on the day of judgment, when tribulation and distress shall envelop the impious; then the Lord will protect them from evil.

### Verse 40

And the Lord will help them in good works and in judgment against their adversaries; then he will free them from the devil and punishments, and rescue them from sinners, [Col. 1366A] when he separates grain from chaff, wheat from tares, and lambs from goats. He will save them by bringing them into the everlasting permanence of eternal salvation, because they hoped in him, not in the world. Therefore, when the world perishes with its lovers, they themselves shall inherit heaven—or rather, God—with those who love him.

## Psalm XXXVII

[Col. 1365]

[Col. 1365B] “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury,” etc. The preceding psalm treated the correction of those scandalized by the prosperity of the wicked; this one deals with the repentance undertaken by those who have been corrected, because they were scandalized by fleeting and transitory things. Therefore this psalm is one of the seven penitential psalms, in which the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are marked. In the first, through the Spirit of fear, they turn away from evil; in the second, through the Spirit of piety, they do not cease to do good; in this one, through the Spirit of knowledge, they avoid scandals and reflect upon their sin. This psalm recounts the affliction of penitents, through which forgiveness of sins will be given. Its title is:

### Verse 1. A Psalm of David, for the Remembrance of the Sabbath Day

[Note: [Col. 1365D] Vulgate: “concerning the Sabbath.”]

[Col. 1365C] A psalm is a good work. David means “strong of hand.” Sabbath means rest, because on that day God rested from the works of the world; it prefigures the rest which the Church will have after judgment from the works of this life. This psalm is sung in remembrance of that Sabbath: that is, in expectation of this rest, the faithful people perform a good work in praise of God.

The subject of the psalm is the prayer and affliction of penitents. Its purpose is that through repentance we may flee from coming wrath. Its words are taken from Job, in whom the arrows—that is, the blows—of the Lord were fixed; there was no health in his flesh, no peace in his bones, his soul was filled with delusions, his friends and neighbors stood against him, and they spoke vanity. Yet he was ready for blows, and his pain was before him. God did not abandon him, but, when he was healed, restored everything to him twofold.

But Job signifies Christ, in whom the arrows of our sins were fixed when he was wounded for us. Hence Job is called “suffering,” because Christ suffered for us. There was no health in Christ’s flesh, which was torn by scourges and pierced with nails. His friend Judas and his other false friends and neighbors, the Jews, came against him with swords and clubs and used violence when they seized and bound him. Those near him, the Apostles, stood far off when they fled. Those who sought his soul—that is, sought to take away his life—sought evils for him, that is, the punishments of death. [Col. 1366B] They meditated deceits all day when they plotted to crucify him. But he, as though mute, did not open his mouth; he was ready for blows and was silent for us. His enemies rejoiced over him and spoke great things, saying, “If this is Christ, let him come down from the cross.” After his death, those who repaid him evil for good slandered him as a deceiver and commanded that the tomb of the dead man be guarded. But God did not abandon him, because he raised him and gave salvation to humankind through him.

Job also signifies the faithful people, who are scourged here either for purification or testing and, like Job, worn down by many pains. Therefore, because of the unrest they experience in the affliction of labor, they sing this psalm in remembrance of that Sabbath, the eternal rest.

The thirty-seventh psalm occupies its place and signifies for us the present matter. For four nines together with the unit make this number. Four signifies the Church of humankind gathered from the four regions of the world; nine signifies the multitude of angels, distinguished in nine orders. The fellowship of both will have joy and rest in the one God.

This psalm has a fourfold division. The first is, “O Lord, do not rebuke me in fury,” in which the penitent’s entreaty is marked. The second is, “My scars have become putrid and corrupt,” which contains an account of the twofold calamity of body and soul. [Col. 1366D] The third is, “For I have hoped in you, O Lord,” which contains medicinal consolation. The fourth is, “Do not forsake me, O Lord,” which contains the exultant conclusion. The whole Christ speaks here: first the body involved in sins and miseries, then the head clothed in our sufferings.

### Verse 2

“O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your wrath.” Fury here means dreadful judgment; wrath, final condemnation. To rebuke is by words; to correct is by scourges. The faithful people, understanding the future judgment and remembering the great Sabbath that follows judgment, are terrified because they have been scandalized by the prosperity of the wicked and cry: “O Lord, [Col. 1367A] do not rebuke me in your fury.” That is, do not judge me with those to whom you will say: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” etc. (Matt. 25:42). “Nor correct me in your wrath” with those to whom you will say: “Go into eternal fire” (ibid., 25:41). Rebuke me here in mercy, that you may amend me; correct me with scourges, that you may purify me, lest afterward the purgatorial fire be necessary. Although it differs greatly from the eternal fire in which the impious are to be tormented forever, it will nevertheless be more grievous than anything a human being can suffer in this life.

### Verse 3

For your arrows are fixed in me. God’s arrows are the words of teaching. In the preceding psalm, God’s divinely sent arrows were fixed in the heart of the penitent. These are: “Yet a little while, and the sinner shall not be”; “the arms of sinners shall be broken”; “sinners shall perish”; “the unrighteous shall utterly perish together; the remnants of the impious shall perish” (Ps. 35:10). These arrows clung to them, and therefore they will grieve that they sinned.

One arrow was: “You shall die by death”; another: “In sweat you shall eat bread”; another: “In pain you shall bear children” (Gen. 3:16–19). The arrows, therefore, are mortality and corruptibility, which the human race laments as fixed in itself. “And you have made firm your hand upon me.” God’s hand is vengeance. It is made firm upon a human being when he is weighed down with many miseries and afflictions.

### Verse 4

There is no health in my flesh because of your wrath. God’s wrath is the offense of sins; because of it there is no health in human flesh, which the violence of so many diseases continually ravages. For diseases are hunger, thirst, labor, cold, and heat; while remedies are food, [Col. 1367C] drink, sleep, and clothing. Amid these remedies the flesh is always failing and tending toward destruction. “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins.” That is, my strength fails through weakness and old age, because by sinning it incurred this punishment.

Alternatively: “There is no health in my flesh because of your wrath.” That is, I have understood in the Scriptures your wrath threatening sinners, and therefore I afflict my flesh harshly and subject it to adversities. “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins”: that is, I granted no rest to my bones or limbs until I had purified in repentance the sins I committed.

### Verse 5

For my iniquities have gone over my head, because, as crimes become stronger, the defeated soul succumbs. The head of the soul is reason. Iniquities raise themselves above the head when they claim more for themselves than reason or justice can endure, when the soul is subject to irrational impulses and desires overcome reason. “Like a heavy burden, they weigh upon me,” because sins, like lead, press downward and sink one. For whoever is raised up by iniquities is burdened by the weight of afflictions. The voice follows of those who, after repentance, have relapsed to the vomit.

### Verse 6

“My scars have become putrid and corrupt.” Here the punishments of the body are described through five verses, and the passions of the soul through five. A scar is said to display within itself a hidden wound. The scars of previous wounds are therefore holy traces, [Col. 1368A] and they are known to hurt more grievously whenever one returns to past dangers by touching them. Sins are wounds of the soul. These wounds are healed when sins are corrected. A scar appears when the memory of what was committed remains. Scars become putrid when desires revive in the memory. They are corrupted when crimes are committed again. “Because of my foolishness.” It is foolishness willingly to repeat a danger which one knows one barely escaped. A person incurs this foolishness when he loses true wisdom in Paradise. Hence follows:

### Verse 7

I became miserable, because, losing wisdom and knowledge, I was filled with foolishness and misery. “And I was bowed down unto the end”: that is, I am drawn by pain into death. For because through pride I raised myself up, wishing to be like God, I have therefore been bent down into death. For the body that corrupts weighs down the soul. “All day”: that is, throughout all life I went about grieving both for the sins I committed and for the evils I suffer.

### Verse 8

For my soul is filled with delusions, and there is no health in my flesh: that is, I am afflicted in soul and body—delusions in soul, weaknesses in body. Delusions are the diverse imagined appearances of phantasms that deceive the soul as though true: as when someone imagines in the mind the heavenly Jerusalem as a certain city in which God appears like a king and angels, visible in form and splendid in clothing, like soldiers; or when someone delightfully conceives forms of women in the mind. Weaknesses, moreover, are the various defects and diverse pains that consume the flesh. Another translation reads: “My loins are filled with delusions.” By “loins” is understood carnal pleasure, which the manifold stimulation of the flesh deceives.

### Verse 9

I am afflicted in mind and exceedingly humbled in ashes and sackcloth. I am afflicted by the evils of the world and humbled from the high glory of heaven; therefore I roared from the groaning of my heart. The one who roars from the groaning of the heart, not of the body, is unable to express the intensity of pain in speech, wastes away in tears, and sometimes utters an inarticulate cry. A groan is so called as though a double grief. Bodily groaning is to groan over earthly matters, over death; the groaning of the heart is the Church’s weeping for its own sins or those of others. When a penitent groans, someone says, [Col. 1368D] “Perhaps this or that has happened to him.” Therefore it is added:

### Verse 10

Lord, all my desire is before you. I desire not before human beings, nor earthly things, but heavenly things; I long to see you. I do not desire to flourish in worldly riches with the impious, but to rest in that Sabbath. “And my groaning is not hidden from you,” although it is hidden from human beings. That groaning is not hidden from God which is poured out for the soul’s deliverance. Having set forth the bodily afflictions in mournful sequence, he also proceeds to the soul’s most grievous pains.

### Verse 11

My heart is troubled because I fell in Adam; my strength, which I possessed in free will, has forsaken me; and the light of my eyes—that is, the light of wisdom illuminating reason and understanding—is not with me because of original and actual sin.

### Verses 12 and 13

My friends and neighbors—namely, the angels, familiar to me as friends and neighbors, close in joy—approached against me when the Lord pronounced a mournful sentence over me. They stood against me when he expelled me from Paradise. And those who were near me in the place of pleasure and delight stood far off when the angel received the flaming sword to bar my way of return. The demons used violence, driving me toward vices and harmful desires; they sought my soul, to destroy it. Those who sought evils for me, present and future punishments, spoke [Col. 1369B] vanities—that is, vain and superstitious things—teaching that they themselves should be worshiped as God, urging me to forget eternal things and embrace transitory things. They meditated deceits all day: that is, at every time they surrounded me with deceits and taught deceits through which they drew me into suffering.

### Verse 14

But I, as though deaf, did not hear: that is, I became deaf to the praises of the angels; and like one mute, not opening his mouth: that is, I became silent in respect to divine praises.

### VERSE 15

And I became like a man who does not hear the harmony of the angels, and who has no rebukes—that is, no excuses—in his mouth, because I was deserving of these things. These words are also referred to the Head, whose patience is set before the afflicted body as an example. He became wretched when, for the wretched, he hung upon the cross between thieves. [Col. 1369C] He was bent down unto the end when, in order to raise us up, he bowed himself to death. He went about sorrowful all day when, leaving the supper, he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38).

His soul was filled with mockeries when, in the house of Caiaphas, they mocked him with his face veiled, as though he were a prophet; when before Herod they mocked him, clothed in a white garment, as though he were a high priest; and when in the praetorium, playing with him as a king, they greeted him with a crown of thorns, a purple cloak, and a reed for a sceptre. And there was no soundness in his flesh when the cruelty of the wicked tore it with scourges and nails. He was afflicted according to his humanity when he felt the Passion drawing near. He was greatly humbled when he washed the disciples’ feet. From the groaning of his heart [Col. 1369D] he roared when, troubled in spirit at supper, he said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me” (John 13:21).

Before the Father all his desire was present when he said: “Father, if thou wilt, remove this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will but thine be done” (Luke 22:42). His desire was that the devil should be conquered through the man himself, and that lost man should be redeemed. His desire was that he should rise from death, and that exiled man should receive Paradise. His groaning was not hidden from God: upon the mountain he groaned and prayed because human nature was subject to such calamity, for which he himself had necessarily to die. His heart was troubled when he began to fear [Col. 1370A] and to grow weary. His strength left him when, being in agony, he sweated blood and an angel strengthened him. Or “strength,” that is, his power, left him when nothing adverse happened to those raging against him. The light of his eyes—that is, the splendor of the Godhead—was as though not with him while he endured so many indignities as a sinner.

His friends, namely Judas and the other feigned friends, and his neighbors—that is, the Jews, his kinsmen—approached against him. With torches and lanterns, in order to seize him, they stood against him with swords and clubs, as though to destroy a robber. And those who were close to him, the Apostles, stood afar off, because, leaving him, they fled. And those who sought his soul—that is, sought violently to destroy his life—used force, overcoming him as a thief and dragging him as a guilty man before the judge. [Col. 1370B] And those who sought evils for him—that is, the penalties of death—spoke vanities, that is, false testimonies, and all day devised the deceits by which they might accuse him and hand him over to death.

But he, like a deaf man, did not hear, because he answered nothing. Like one mute, he did not open his mouth, but was silent as a lamb before its shearer. And he became like a man who does not hear because he answered nothing to those accusing and blaspheming him. He had no rebukes in his mouth because he did not rebuke those who falsely accused him. Such things he endured for the sake of his human sharers; but concerning the glory of the Resurrection he adds:

### VERSE 16

For in thee, O Lord, I hoped that thou wouldst raise me up; thou wilt hear, O Lord my God, my humility [Note: [Col. 1369] Vulgate: “For in thee, O Lord, I hoped; thou wilt hear me, O Lord my God.”] for my resurrection and for the redemption of my own.

[Col. 1370C]

### VERSE 17

For I said in prayer: “Let not my enemies ever rejoice exceedingly over me.” They would have rejoiced exceedingly had he not risen. They did indeed rejoice when they killed him; but they did not rejoice exceedingly when they heard that he had risen. And when my feet are moved from the earth onto the cross, they spoke great things over me, saying: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross. He saved others; himself he cannot save” (Matt. 27:42).

In the Hebrew it is written: “When my feet staggered, let them not magnify themselves over me”; that is, let them not long glory because my feet—the Apostles—stumbled in my Passion. But I endured all these things patiently:

[Col. 1370D]

For I am prepared for scourges: that is, I was born for this purpose, to endure scourges, the cross, the lance, gall, and vinegar; and my sorrow is always before me. His sorrow was before his eyes when he saw his mother weeping, the crowd of wicked people insulting him, and the thief reproaching him.

The voice of the Church follows: “You suffered all these things for me.”

### VERSE 19

For I shall declare my iniquity, and I shall be anxious because of my sin.

This voice was expressed by the centurion, who broke forth into confession of God. After Christ’s resurrection, the people, now believing, declared their iniquity when through the Apostles they believed in him whom they had killed. They reflected upon this grave sin [Col. 1371A] when they performed penance for the killing of Christ. The voice of the Head is then added: “You indeed will turn to repentance.”

### VERSE 20

But my enemies live, because they were not immediately punished but flourish; and they have been strengthened over me—that is, have prevailed against me—and those who hate me unjustly have multiplied: namely, on account of good done, teaching, and healing; many, because they are Jews, Pharisees, Sadducees, and pagans. And after my death:

### VERSE 21

Those who repay evil for good—that is, the Jews, who returned death to me for life—spoke evil of me, saying: “That deceiver, while he was still living, said: ‘After three days I shall rise again.’ Therefore command that the tomb be guarded, lest perhaps his disciples come [Col. 1371B] and steal him” (Matt. 27:63–64). This was done because I followed goodness, that is, persevered in love.

### VERSES 22 AND 23

Do not abandon me, O Lord my God, in death; do not depart from me in hell. Give heed to my help while I despoil hell. O God of my salvation, raising me from the dead and giving salvation to humankind through me.

This also suits the Church, whose friends and neighbors approached against her in persecution and stood against her in accusation. And those who were close to her stood afar off, because her own household withdrew from her. Persecutors used force, seeking her soul. And those who sought evils for her spoke vanities, that is, lies, charging [Col. 1371C] her with false crimes. And all day—that is, at all times—either pagans or heretics devised deceits, how they might destroy Christians and plunder their goods.

But the Christian people, like the deaf, did not hear, because they fixed their attention upon future hope. Like the mute, they did not open their mouth, because they did not answer revilings and insults. And they became like one who does not hear and who has no rebukes in his mouth, because, though they could rebuke with true accusations those who deceitfully accused them, they did not do so; rather, after Christ’s example, they kept silent patiently.

Why? Because I hoped in thee, O Lord, not in earthly things. Thou, O Lord my God, wilt hear me, giving me the promised reward and leading me from toil into Sabbath-rest. For I said in prayer: “Let not my enemies ever”—that is, never—“rejoice exceedingly over me.” The enemies of the Church [Col. 1372A] are demons. They rejoice over her if they catch believers in sins. Her enemies are also persecutors and heretics. These rejoice if they draw believers into agreement with themselves. And when my feet are moved, they speak great things over me. The feet of the Church are its affections. If any believers are moved from the state of uprightness into carnal affections, the enemies immediately speak arrogantly, rejoicing over her fall: “This is that holy man, that preacher, that abstinent man, that converter of the whole people!” Such things they hurl at those who have fallen.

But the penitent bears these things patiently, saying: “For I am prepared for scourges.” I endure the scourges of persecutions and the words of those who slander, curse, blaspheme, and insult, because God scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. 12:6)—understand: every penitent son. [Col. 1372B] “And my sorrow is always before me”: the sorrow which I have because I was expelled from Paradise’s joys, because I have offended my God in many matters, and because I remember that Sabbath.

For I shall declare my iniquity in humble confession, and I shall be anxious because of my sin: I shall give alms, pour forth tears, forgive those who sin against me, and withstand those who err. But my enemies—the pagans and heretics—live, that is, flourish in the world’s goods and mock me, oppressed by evils. They are strengthened over me by power and riches, and those who hate me unjustly have multiplied, because of righteousness.

Or otherwise: I am consumed in scourges and sorrows because I am mortal. But my enemies, the demons, live because they are immortal, and they are strengthened over me [Col. 1372C] because they are called immortal gods. Those who hate me unjustly on account of thee multiply, saying that I worship one who died and do not worship immortals.

Those who repay evil for good spoke evil of me—namely, the heretics. The Church gives spiritual gifts; heretics return schisms. The Church gives virtues; they give heresies. The Church gives love; they give detraction. Because I followed goodness, imitating thee through charity. Do not abandon me, O Lord, in adversities; my God, whom I worship, do not depart from me because of what I have committed. Give heed to my help, that I may worthily repent of these things and worthily make satisfaction for them. O Lord God of my salvation, because thou art the Savior, and no other name has been given under heaven to human beings in which they must be saved.

## PART FOUR

[Col. 1371]

## GERHOH’S PROLOGUE BEGINS

[Col. 1371D]

Now that, with God’s help, three parts of the exposition of the Psalms have been completed, eager guests demand a fourth from us. In those three parts they have tasted, and still taste, the sweetness of the Trinity, as Wisdom affects and delights them—the Wisdom which says: “Those who eat me will still hunger, [Col. 1372D] and those who drink me will still thirst” (Ecclus. 24:29). This was said of the guests.

But what is added there in the person of Wisdom concerns the ministers, servers, or cupbearers busy in this feast with their frequent service: “Those who work in me shall not sin, [Col. 1373A] and those who make me clear shall have eternal life” (Ecclus. 24:30–31). Truly, those who work in wisdom—namely by writing or reading—gather these fruits as first-fruits; for those laudably and assiduously occupied in this work have little opportunity to sin grievously. This is the temporal fruit.

But the later fruit will be that whoever makes wisdom clear in words and deeds will have eternal life when he departs from mortal life. Do not work in wisdom and make it clear not only the wise, whose tongue adorns knowledge with sweet and polished eloquence, but also infants and nursing children, from whose mouth God perfects his praise? I, a little one, do not dare count myself among the great teachers [Col. 1373B] who treated the Psalms before me and, like great harvesters, brought great sheaves into the Lord’s barns. Yet, with Christ’s disciples, still small and not yet perfected, when the Spirit had not yet been given because Jesus had not yet been glorified (John 7:39), compelled by hunger I dare, after their example, to pluck and rub ears of grain.

[Col. 1374A]

Doing this in the Lord’s name, I offer you this fourth book as a little bundle of ears gathered from the sayings of the Fathers; and I rejoice to have you as my guests at this table of the Lord. I ask and await from the Lord that this very joy of ours may be full: that then, while feasting, we may rightly rejoice, if the Lord’s mercy grants that such harmony and chorus be present at our banquet as is fitting for a son who was lost and is found, who was dead and has been restored to life. Who do you think that son is? I, I am that young man who was in a far country; but having returned, thanks be to God, to the Father, I received the priestly robe by superabundant grace. From then on, utterly rejecting husks, the food of swine, I gladly remain in the pastures of the Psalms; I love the harmony and chorus, and I pray to the most merciful Father for my envious brother, who is indignant at this.

But I have resolved that I must make no reply to this same brother when he wishes to quarrel. I have said: “I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue. I have set a guard upon my mouth when the sinner stood against me.” From this psalm, therefore, let the beginning of this fourth part be taken.

## PSALM 38

[Col. 1373]

[Col. 1373C]

“I said: I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue.” The title is:

### (VERSE 1) UNTO THE END: A SONG OF DAVID FOR IDITHUN

It is read in the book of Chronicles that David, after bringing back the ark of the Lord from the Philistines into Jerusalem, placed Idithun, Asaph, Heman, and Ethan over the singers. When David had grown old, he appointed Solomon king. Having gathered the princes of the priests and the Levites, he chose twenty-four thousand Levites for the ministry of the house of the Lord; of these he appointed four thousand gatekeepers and an equal number of singers. The rest he divided among the other ministries. He set the sons of Korah over the gatekeepers; over the singers he set the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Idithun with [Col. 1373D] their brothers, who were altogether two hundred and eighty-eight.

Ezra frequently placed these names in the title, both for the honor of the ministry and especially because of the meanings of the names, through which the sense of the Psalms placed under them is opened. Thus the mystery of this psalm is made clear through Idithun, whose name is interpreted “leaping over them.” For this psalm teaches one to leap from the delight of the world to the law of God, and thence to eternity. The title contains “A Song for Idithun” because, although it is burdensome for the flesh to leave worldly life, it is delightful to the mind to leap over human enticements for eternity.

[Col. 1374C]

First, he sets out restraint of the tongue and the prudent avoidance of quarrels among blasphemers, and desires the end where the labor of such prudence is unnecessary. Second, he says that all are subject to vanity, that he waits for the Lord, and asks to be freed from iniquities, at the words: “Nevertheless every living human being is altogether vanity.” Third, amid the evils of the world he asks God to be present to him and to forgive his sins, so that he may depart with a prosperous end, at the words: “Hear my prayer, O Lord, and my supplication.”

This Idithun, leaping over worldly things, incurs envy because of his good; yet because some even corrupt good things, he determines to keep silence among the wicked and says: “I said: I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue.”

[Col. 1374D]

In the preceding psalm Christ prayed for penitents, sympathizing with their weaknesses and pitying those who are ignorant and err, since he was tempted in all things in like manner, yet without sin. But in this psalm, commending his example to innocent righteous persons and justified penitents, he says: “I said: I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue. I set a guard upon my mouth when the sinner stood against me. I became mute, and was humbled, and kept silence from good things,” and so forth.

This example must also be imitated by the righteous. For, according to another prophet [Note: [Col. 1373D] Rule of St Benedict, ch. 6.], “The practice of righteousness is silence” (Isa. 32:17). But if, as blessed Benedict says in his Rule, one must sometimes keep silence even from good and edifying conversation for the sake of silence, [Col. 1375A] how much more must one refrain from evil speech because of its punishment?

Yet, lest we should keep silence obstinately and without discernment, he immediately adds: “And my sorrow was renewed,” and so forth. It is as if he said: “Just as before I sinned excessively by speaking, so now I sin excessively by keeping silence.” Thus the title fittingly says: “Unto the end: A Song of David for Idithun.” Idithun is interpreted “one who leaps over.” The title signifies that this song of David is sung to those who have leapt from vices to virtues, from much speaking to moderation of the tongue, from temporal things unto the end—unto him beyond whom there is no further leap—to eternity itself, which is God. Whoever has attained it seeks nothing further.

It is especially fitting that a person who tends toward this end in singing or psalmody should restrain himself from much speaking. I David, content with and attentive to this end of consummation:

### VERSE 2

“I said: I will guard my ways.” “I said,” that is, I deliberated within myself, as about a difficult matter, that I would guard my ways. “I said,” that is, by my own words I bound myself as by a vow, setting before myself this purpose: “I will guard my ways.” I will guard in silence before God my ways, that is, my fitting works. I will guard my ways, in which it has been decreed that I shall not crawl or creep in the manner of a serpent, but, in the manner of a stag, make leaps and bounds: by silence leaping over the thickets of disputes and the thorns of contention, so that I may not sin with my tongue by returning curses for curses or by answering detractors in an undisciplined manner. [Col. 1375C]

Such things I said to myself in my heart, where a wise person deliberates what, when, to whom, how much, how, and why he should speak or keep silence. I said these things, I say, so that I might not sin with my tongue—a thing exceedingly difficult to avoid, especially among contentious people. For “if anyone does not stumble in word, he is a perfect man” (James 3:2); and a person who does not stumble with the tongue is a rare bird on earth. The tongue, as the common saying goes, “is in the wet” and slips very easily; as James the Apostle says, “no human being can tame it” (ibid., v. 8), although every kind of beast has been tamed by human nature.

Therefore the purpose, “that I may not sin with my tongue,” was difficult. It would be easier simply to keep entirely silent than to speak at the proper time, keep silence at the proper time, and sin in neither. This is precisely what I proposed: that neither in keeping silence nor in speaking I might sin with my tongue. Therefore:

“I set a guard upon my mouth,” so that I might observe in myself a time to keep silence and a time to speak (Ecclus. 3:7); not because I fear the good, who praise what they approve and pardon a slip of the tongue in what they disapprove, but because of the wicked I chose rather to keep silence than to speak, even at that time when silence was difficult: namely, “when the sinner stood against me.” The sinner, not receiving the things that are of the Spirit of God, stood against me, persisting as it were with delay and fixedly in contention, seeking an occasion for calumny.

[Col. 1376A]

The words “when the sinner stood against me” were also said to increase the merit. It is as though he said: “It would not be a great merit if I showed patience when a righteous person rebuked me or spoke against me, according to the words, ‘The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me’ (Ps. 140:5). On the one hand, consciousness of my own sin would command me to silence; on the other, the innocence of the rebuker, whom I would see as superior to me in the case. But now I, superior in the case and innocent, have a sinner standing against me—a sinner against me—against whom I could close a blasphemous mouth by bringing many great and true crimes against his false accusations. Nevertheless, in order to preserve patience and humility, I set a guard upon my mouth, namely, lest I seem, in seeking vengeance, to return curse [Col. 1376B] for curse, while at the same time hoping that the Lord would regard my humility and return blessing to me for cursing.

Thus I too, the true David, became mute as a lamb before the shearer, before Pilate the shearer, and did not open my mouth, so that Pilate marvelled. Speaking also to the disciples, I passed over many things in speaking. Hence I said: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). Indeed, I set a guard upon my mouth to such an extent that:

### VERSE 3

“I became mute and was humbled.” I became mute; that is, I so kept silence that I did not even mutter against those speaking evil of me. And because some people keep silence from pride, disdaining to answer those whom they despise, I not only became mute but was also humbled, so that [Col. 1376C] my silence was pure and humble, not deceitful, proud, or mixed with the leaven of indignation; for I was silent in humility and simplicity.

Or, I was humbled so as to endure reproaches, and I kept silence even from proclaiming good things, lest I give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine (Matt. 7:6). Or, I kept silence even from addressing good hearers while the sinner stood against me among them. Or, I kept silence from good sayings, lest in proclaiming them I fall into the fault of talkativeness and exceed in speech the faults of people, either by exaggerating too greatly or reproving too severely. For I feared the Scripture saying: “A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but that which is immoderate will crush the spirit” (Prov. [Col. 1376D] 15:4).

Therefore I feared lest my immoderate tongue, rebuking without moderation, should crush rather than edify my hearers. Thus I kept silence even from good and edifying conversations, choosing rather, by silent prayer and silence, to leap over the wicked themselves than to leap upon them and contend with them—people so talkative that the saying truly fits them: “A talkative man shall not be guided in the way” (Ps. 139:12). Wishing such people to be avoided, the Apostle instructs his beloved disciple: “Do not contend with words; it is useful for nothing except the overthrow of the hearers” (2 Tim. 2:14). Again he says: “The servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel, but to be gentle toward all” (2 Tim. 2:24). Therefore, that I might be gentle toward all, I sometimes kept silence and became mute.

For “I became mute,” another translation has: “I became deaf,” and [Col. 1377A] its sense is this: I, Idithun, resolving to be silent lest I sin in speaking, sinned by keeping silence, proving true by experience what the pagan says:

> The avoidance of a fault leads into fault, if it lacks skill.

For while fleeing one fault, I fell into another: fearing harmful talkativeness, I fell into harmful silence. Set between the rich Lord and the poor fellow-servant, I run between them, leaping here and there, and passing over the middle: now, by the flight or leap of contemplation, approaching the rich Lord; now, by the condescension of compassion, approaching from there the poor fellow-servant, so that here I may hear the Bridegroom’s voice and there distribute my Lord’s money.

But when I imprudently feared to speak, I kept silence wrongly; and, avoiding prodigality in putting food before the fastidious, I became miserly by not distributing it to the hungry. Sloth also crept into that very miserliness. But the slothful servant is condemned: because he does not distribute, he does not receive; indeed, even what he had is taken from him. This happened to me as well. For, since it is written, “Let him who hears say: ‘Come’” (Rev. 22:17), whenever, by excessive silence, I did not say to my neighbor, “Come,” I too lost my hearing, so that I did not hear the voice of the Lord calling me, because I was unwilling to call others. Thus, becoming mute by excessive silence, I also became deaf by losing hearing, and under such scourges I was humbled—especially because I kept silence from good things, and for that reason my sorrow was renewed.

For whereas at first I grieved that I had said what should have been kept silent, afterward I began to grieve more because I had kept silent about what should have been said. And because there is sorrow in speaking and the zeal of God’s house consuming me in silence, I do not say merely “It grew warm,” but, on both sides:

### VERSE 4

“My heart grew hot”: on the one hand, with the fire of God burning me and with desire for heavenly things, where silence will be safe because no one will speak there after that universal *completorium*—namely, the final judgment completing all divine works—in which thou wilt dismiss every servant of thine, O Lord, according to thy word, in peace (Luke 2:29), and in most peaceful silence. There will be no necessary occupation of teaching or learning, because all will be taught by God (John 6:45), when all the elect see thy salvation, which thou hast prepared then to display before the face of all peoples: “a light for the revelation [Col. 1377D] of the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel” (Luke 2:32).

Since, therefore, the hour of either my life’s or the world’s end has not yet come, in which, as I hope, thou wilt dismiss me thy servant in peace, meanwhile my heart grew hot, while I find neither speaking nor silence safe for myself.

There was once a time—let me confess the truth concerning my own person somewhat more freely—there was a time, I say, when my speech was exceedingly aflame. But because iniquity abounded and the charity of many grew cold, through my own fault my speech too has now begun to grow cold, so that, with nearly all my members as though dead beforehand, scarcely the warmth of life remains in my breast. Yet while that warmth still survives somewhat, my heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire will blaze—as the letters addressed to me from the Apostolic See bear witness while I write this. Their text is as follows:

Eugenius [Note: [Col. 1377] Eugenius III, elected 27 February 1145; died 8 July 1153.] bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have graciously received the writings of your devotion, and from examining them have clearly recognized the fervor of your religious life. For your heart has grown hot within you, and in your meditation a fire blazes. Your speech also is exceedingly aflame. Therefore, because we know that, with the zeal of charity, you burn against the most wicked innovations and also against the disturbances which arise against the Church of God and ecclesiastical persons, we rejoice with paternal affection and commend your devotion in the Lord. Nevertheless, because it is good to begin but far better to bring to completion, we admonish your love in the Lord to persevere steadfastly in this good purpose. For we love your person with paternal charity as a learned and religious man, and desire, in those matters in which we are able according to God, to honor and support you. Given at Sutri, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June [16 May].

It pleased me to insert this letter at this point in the work so that one may observe from it that I, G., servant of this composition, have testimony not only from my own conscience but also from the Apostolic See that I may truthfully say in this psalm not only in David’s person but also in my own: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire will blaze.” There was once a time, as the foregoing letter attests, when my speech was exceedingly aflame. But now, when the flame of my speech has been choked and my mouth is almost entirely shut, because I judge it useless to speak as I used to do and therefore keep silent, the fire once blazing in speech has withdrawn into the inner parts of my heart. Thus my heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire will blaze; because of its greatness I am sometimes unable to contain the word conceived.

For even if I wish to keep silent, I cannot; nor do I know that this is permitted me, and I perceive this well. Rejoicing in this very thing, I shall rejoice because of the Bridegroom’s voice, which I desire to hear even through the mouth of an ass, and how much more through the mouth of a Prophet. By his own grace it has happened to me, desiring to hear this Bridegroom’s voice, that sometimes I have heard it through my own mouth, so that I have felt to be true what he himself said to his disciples: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict” (Luke 21:15). Again: “For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 10:20). Hence one of such persons confidently says: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3).

Far beneath the feet of such persons I lie, a sinner bound with a long and manifold rope. Hence what was said to Ezekiel may in some sense fittingly be said also to me: “And thou, son of man, behold, bonds are placed upon thee”; again: “I will make thy tongue cleave to thy palate, and thou shalt be mute, not as a reproving man, because they are a provoking house” (Ezek. 3:25–26).

Yet I have learned that Job’s friend spoke truly, if he had possessed the virtue of discernment, when he said: “But who can contain the word conceived?” (Job 4:2). Indeed, not to be able to contain a conceived superfluous or evil word is blameworthy and foolish, according to the saying of the wise man: “An arrow fixed in the thigh of a dog, so is a word in the heart of a fool” (Ecclus. 19:12). But, conversely, not to be able to contain a conceived good and necessary word is glorious, just as Jeremiah could not contain it. When he had said: “The word of the Lord has become for me a reproach and derision all day, and I said: ‘I will not remember him, nor speak in his name,’” he immediately added: “And it became in my heart like a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I failed, unable to bear it” (Jer. 20:8–9).

But my rivals, unwilling—indeed disdaining—to believe that I burn with such fire, are stirred against me, adding to the fire of fervor the fire of sorrow. Thus my heart does not merely grow hot but grows hot with a twofold fire within me when someone sins and is almost scandalized by what I write: because, in treating the Psalms, I gather certain things from the sayings of the Fathers and add something of my own; they attribute this to presumption and vain glory. Yet however those now living wish to judge us, those to come will judge more gently.

For, says the eminent man blessed Jerome, while we live and are contained in a fragile vessel, the attentions of friends seem to profit us and the reproaches of rivals to harm us. But after earth has returned to its earth, and pale death has removed both us who write and those who judge us, and another generation has come, and, as the first leaves fall, a green forest has grown up, then intellects alone are judged without regard to the rank of names. The reader does not consider whose work it is, but what sort of work it is that he will read: whether its author lies as bishop or layman, emperor and lord, soldier and servant, in purple and silk or in the poorest cloth. He will be judged not by the diversity of honors but by the merit of his works. Let us now continue what we have begun.

“My heart grew hot within me.” My heart did not merely grow warm, but grew hot, because, as has been said, fire was added to fire. Did that fire, by which the burning disciples say, “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32), warm my heart in love of the truth by illuminating obscure matters? There was added to it the fire of sorrow which wasted me away, so that I said: “I saw transgressors, and I wasted away, because they did not keep thy words” (Ps. 118:158).

Thus, yes, thus my heart grew hot within me with the twofold fire of love and sorrow, where the inward person speaks with his God in a secret soliloquy. And this twofold fire will blaze not with mad or tumultuous heat, [Col. 1380A] but in meditation—that is, kindled prudently by counsel. Therefore my mind was rendered greatly anxious whether I should speak or keep silence. In danger amid this wavering between speaking and silence, I chose this: avoiding the pouring out of speech where there was no hearing, I would speak in secret to God alone, to whom also:

### VERSE 5

“I spoke with my tongue,” so that, after the example of Hannah, I moved tongue and lips, but no voice at all was heard. Therefore I spoke silently with my tongue (1 Sam. 1:13), not to an outward hearer but to an inward one who hears, saying: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end.”

O Lord, ruler of my life: make known to me, who leap over; to me, who have leapt from the delight of the world to a better delight, namely spiritual delight, so that worldly pleasure no longer delights me, but truth, mercy, piety, justice, and purity; to me, for whom wisdom tastes good—not earthly wisdom, but that which is from above; to me, who leap over the things that are seen and desire the heavenly things that are not seen—make known my end. Once I have attained it, there shall be no further leaping. While I run amid scandals, I may continually tend toward it as toward the certain prize appointed for those who run well. When I have received it, I shall leap no further, but rest there, saying: “I have seen the end of every consummation” (Ps. 118:96). I shall rest in that end: “For Christ is the end of the law unto righteousness for everyone who believes.”

[Cols. 1380C–1391A] This end is known to the sheep of whom he himself said: “I know my own, and my own know me” (John 10:14). Peter knew this end when he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). Again: “You have the words of eternal life; and to whom shall we go but to you?” (John 6:69). Paul too knew Christ as “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). Hence, although among the little and weak he preached nothing but Jesus Christ, and him crucified, yet, speaking wisdom among the perfect, he says: “Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16). As though he said: Although he was crucified and died from the weakness which he bore on our behalf, nevertheless he truly says: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25): the resurrection, namely, of human beings revived from the death of soul and body; and the life of holy angels, who live eternally.

Or: “I am the resurrection” of my people who fall and swiftly rise again in this life, according to the saying addressed to the ancients: “The righteous man falls seven times a day and rises again” (Prov. 24:19). But now I do not say, “up to seven times,” but “up to seventy times seven” (Matt. 18:22). I am the resurrection of my people before judgment, and unchanging and endless life after judgment. Again he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Those blessed who are undefiled in the way, who walk in my law, know me as the way (Ps. 118:1). Those blessed who search my testimonies know me as the truth (Ps. 118:2). Those who live in me, the vine, as branches, and bear good fruit, know me as the truest life; and, having me as their root and clinging to me, they will not wither or die in soul, nor will they taste even bodily death until they see the kingdom of God within themselves.

Again he says: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:51). “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). Therefore, only those know this bread who possess a sound palate to taste and savour it. Only those know that he is the sun of righteousness, or the light of the world, who possess a sound eye of the heart to see him in his brightness. For all human beings, even those who pierced him, will see him coming upon a cloud with great power and majesty; but when, after judgment, the cloud of bodily manifestation has been removed, only those whose prayers and desires are now heard will behold and know the sun of righteousness in brightness, saying: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end”—that is, make Christ known to me.

But if you wish to have him known to you, first know yourself. For if you do not know yourself, he will say to you: “Go forth, and follow the tracks of the flocks” (Song 1:7). Again, to such persons—to foolish virgins who, through excessive folly, do not know themselves—he will say: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). Hence blessed Augustine wisely and prudently prayed: “O Lord, may I know myself; may I know you.” This twofold knowledge is so necessary to every person that no other knowledge ought to be preferred to it.

In time or order, it is indeed prior that you should know yourself, and then, singing “unto the end,” know your end, Christ, and say to the Father: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end”; for flesh and blood do not reveal him, but the Father does (Matt. 16:17). Yet this order is reversed, and necessarily so, when this Idithun, wisely singing and leaping over lower things, first seeks knowledge of Christ, which is greater in dignity and fruit, and afterwards knowledge of himself, saying, “that I may know what is lacking to me.” As though he said: First seeking the kingdom of God, I say: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end.” But because I cannot attain it if I do not know myself, before all else: “Make known to me my end.”

“And what is the number of my days, that I may know what is lacking to me?” It should not seem absurd that, in the petition, what is hoped for at the end comes first, when I say: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end.” I am Idithun, whose name means “one who leaps over,” who thus sing; in the ten-stringed psaltery I pass over, as it were leaping beyond, the first and lower strings and strike the highest, saying: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end.” But I return, in accordance with the creatures which went and returned, to the lower things through which there is ascent to the highest; and I say: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, that I may know what is lacking to me.” Leaping toward the highest things, of which I am not yet found capable, I am compelled to return from there to those which are lower.

Thus Isaiah, delighting to cling to the vision of the most high Lord seated upon a lofty and exalted throne, was dazzled by the excess of light and turned his gaze back to those things which were beneath him and filled the temple. “Seraphim,” he says, “stood above it; six wings to one and six wings to another; and they cried: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Isa. 6:1–3). Observe the order of one who leaps over: first, to see the Lord seated upon the lofty throne; then, as though springing back, to contemplate what was beneath him and filled the temple; finally, to cling to the vision of the glory with which not only the temple but the whole earth was full. For the Creator’s glory is visible in every one of his creatures, even the lowest, such as this earth which we tread beneath our feet, to anyone with sound eyes. This is said without prejudice to the higher and more sacred sense in which, mystically, this earthly Church, a pilgrim in the present life, is understood as “the earth”; the holy spiritual persons within it, and life consecrated to sacred orders after the pattern of a temple, as “the temple”; and the Church already reigning in heaven as “the lofty and exalted throne,” consisting partly of angels created and established on high, and partly of human beings raised upward from below by grace.

Therefore this throne is rightly called lofty and exalted: lofty, that is, in angels holy from the beginning; exalted in human beings sanctified by grace and lifted from the lower hell to the heights. If their fellowship delights you, so that in them you may see the Lord seated—that is, resting, reigning, and judging—imitate the creatures that go and return. First exercise yourself in the praises of God upon earth, with heart, mouth, and deed, singing “Holy, holy, holy,” in holy faith, hope, and charity: believing with the heart unto righteousness and confessing with the mouth unto salvation. Through charity, do what is good toward all, especially toward those of the household of faith. Thus trained by godly works, you will be numbered among the hosts of the Lord Sabaoth, which is interpreted “of hosts”; and at last you too will become the lofty and exalted throne of the Lord: lofty in the spirit, coessential and coequal with the angels according to “the measure of a man, that is, of an angel” (Rev. 21:17); exalted in the glorified body, when that which is sown in weakness shall rise in glory.

Do not, therefore, take it badly that, when you leap over lower things and ask for your end to be made known to you, you are not quickly heard. There is something in which you may meanwhile exercise yourself: namely, knowledge of your days. Seek this, that you may receive it and, from such knowledge, be able to say to God: “Behold, you have made my days measurable, and my substance is as nothing before you.” Thus, through knowledge of your measurable days, in which you will know yourself, you will advance toward knowledge of the immeasurable and endless days, in which you will know your end. To know that end now is laborious for you, until you enter the sanctuary of God and understand at the last what your end is, and what is the end of all who sing unto the end, leap unto the end, and now ascend and now descend upon Jacob’s ladder (Gen. 28:12), until they find their end—namely, the Lord—resting upon the summit of the ladder. Of him this one who leaps over also says: “And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?”

There are many examples in Scripture of holy persons ascending and descending on this ladder of Jacob: ascending to the knowledge of God and descending to the recognition of themselves.

[Note: [Col. 1383D] From Sermon 34 of St Bernard on the Song of Songs.]

Thus of old holy Moses, because he presumed much upon the grace and familiarity which he had found with God, aspired to a certain vision, so that he said to God: “If I have found grace in your eyes, show me yourself” (Exod. 33:13). But in place of that vision he received one far inferior, through which he might nevertheless one day attain the very vision that he wished to grasp by leaping over. The sons of Zebedee likewise, walking in simplicity of heart, dared to attempt something great, as though seeking it by a leap. Yet they were brought back to the step by which they had to ascend, when the Lord said to them: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20:21). As though he said: If it delights you to sit with me at the summit of honour, let the contest of labor first train you.

So too the bride in the Song of Songs, because she seems to ask a great thing when she says to the bridegroom, “Tell me, you whom my soul loves: where do you feed, where do you lie down at noon?” (Song 1:6), is restrained, lest she fall by leaping incautiously, by a reply stern indeed but plainly useful and faithful. The bridegroom says to her: “If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go forth, and follow the tracks of the flocks, and feed your kids beside the shepherds’ tents.” For one who strives toward higher things must think humbly of herself, lest, while she lifts herself above herself, she fall away from herself, unless she has first been firmly grounded within herself through true humility. And because the greatest things are obtained especially by the merit of humility, the person to be advanced is humbled by correction and earns advancement by humility. Therefore, when you see yourself humbled, regard it as a sign for good, wholly an indication that grace is drawing near. For, just as the heart is lifted up before ruin, so it is humbled before exaltation (Prov. 16:18). Certainly you read both: that God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Jas. 4:6). Did he not, finally, when he judged that his servant Job’s patience—so great and so proved after a notable triumph—deserved to be rewarded with abundant blessing, first take care to humble him with many severe questions, and thus prepare the way for blessing?

“But it is too little, when God humbles us through himself, if we then accept it willingly, unless we are similarly wise when he does so through another. Therefore receive a remarkable illustration of this in holy David. Once he was cursed, and by a servant. Yet he did not feel even the accumulated injury, because he foresaw grace. ‘What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah?’ he says (2 Sam. 16:10). O truly a man according to God’s heart, who thought that he ought rather to be angry with one taking vengeance upon him than with one reproaching him! Hence he spoke with a secure conscience: ‘If I have repaid evil to those who repaid me, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies’ (Ps. 7:5). Therefore he forbade anyone to stop the reviler who was heaping insults upon him, valuing curses as gain. And he added: ‘The Lord has sent him to curse David.’ Truly according to God’s heart, for he received his judgment from God’s heart.

A cursing tongue raged, but he attended to what God was doing in secret. The voice of the curser was in his ears, while his mind inclined itself to blessing. Was God in the mouth of the blasphemer? Far be it! Rather, he used him to humble David. Nor was this hidden from the prophet, since God had revealed to him the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom. Therefore he says: ‘It is good for me that you have humbled me, that I may learn your ordinances’ (Ps. 118:71). Do you see that humility justifies us? Humility, I said, not humiliation. How many are humbled who are not humble! Some are humbled resentfully, others patiently, others willingly. The first are guilty; the next are innocent; the last are righteous. Although innocence too is a portion of righteousness, its perfection is found in the humble person. But the person who can say, ‘It is good for me that you have humbled me,’ is truly humble. One who bears it unwillingly cannot say this, still less one who murmurs. We promise grace to neither of these merely because he is humbled, although these two are indeed far apart: one possesses his soul in patience, while the other perishes in his murmuring. Yet though one escapes wrath, neither earns grace, because God gives grace not to those who are humbled but to the humble.

The humble person is one who turns humiliation into humility, and it is he who says to God: ‘It is good for me that you have humbled me.’ Nothing which a person bears merely patiently is altogether good for him; it is burdensome. But we know that God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7). Hence, when we fast, we are commanded to anoint our head with oil and wash our face, so that our good work may be seasoned with a certain spiritual joy and our burnt offering may be rich. For only joyful and unreserved humility earns the grace which it displays. Humility that is compelled or forced—as in that patient man who possesses his soul—obtains life through patience, but because of its sadness it will not have grace. For the Scripture, ‘Let the humble man glory in his exaltation’ (Jas. 1:9), does not suit such a person, because he is not humbled voluntarily or gladly.

But do you wish to see a humble person rightly glorying, and truly worthy of glory? ‘I will gladly glory,’ he says, ‘in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may dwell in me’ (2 Cor. 12:9). He does not say that he bears his weaknesses patiently, but that he glories—and gladly glories—in them, thus proving that it is good for him to be humbled. It is not enough at all that he possess his soul as one humbled patiently, unless he also receives grace as one humbled voluntarily. Hear, then, the general rule drawn from this: ‘Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted.’ He plainly signifies that not every humility is to be exalted, but only that which comes from the will, not from sadness or necessity. For conversely, not everyone who is exalted shall be humbled; rather, only the one who exalts himself shall be humbled, namely on account of voluntary vanity. Thus it is not the person who is humbled, but the one who voluntarily humbles himself, who shall be exalted—certainly on account of the merit of his will. For although another may supply the material of humility—for example, insults, losses, or punishments—nevertheless the person who resolves to undergo all these for God’s sake with a silent and joyful conscience is rightly said to be humbled not by another but by himself.

The bridegroom in the Song of Songs also calls the bride back to this humility through knowledge of herself, as we touched on a little above, when he says: ‘If you do not know yourself, go forth.’

[Note: [Col. 1385D] From Sermon 35 of St Bernard on the Song of Songs.]

It is a harsh and severe rebuke when he says, “Go forth.” Servants are accustomed to hear this word from masters who are very angry and indignant, when they have grievously offended them: “Get out of here; get away from me; depart from my sight and from this house.” Thus the bridegroom uses this harsh, bitter, and exceedingly rebuking word against his beloved, but conditionally: if she does not know herself. For he could direct nothing stronger or more effective toward frightening her than to threaten her with going out. You may observe this too, if you attend carefully, by considering from where she is commanded to go out. From where? From what place, do you suppose, unless from spirit to flesh, from the goods of the soul to worldly desires, from the inward rest of the mind to the noise of the world and the disturbance of outward cares? And in all these is there anything but toil, pain, and affliction of spirit?

For any soul which has once learned and received from the Lord how to enter into itself, to sigh after God’s presence in its inmost being, and always to seek his face—for God is spirit, and those who seek him must walk in spirit and not in flesh, so as to live according to the flesh—such a soul, I say, would perhaps judge even the experience of hell itself for a time less horrible and less painful than, after once tasting the sweetness of this spiritual pursuit, again going out to the enticements—or rather, the troubles—of the flesh and returning to the insatiable curiosity of the senses. Ecclesiastes says: “The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear with hearing” (Eccl. 1:25). Hear, then, a person experienced in what we are saying: “You are good, O Lord, to those who hope in you, to the soul that seeks you” (Lam. 3:25). If anyone tried to turn a holy soul from this, I think it would feel no differently than if it saw itself cast down from paradise and from the very entrance to glory.

Hear also another like him: “My heart said to you, my face sought you: I will seek your face, O Lord” (Ps. 26:8). Hence he also said: “But for me it is good to cling to God.” And again, speaking to his own soul, he says: “Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you” (Ps. 114:7). I say, therefore: there is nothing which anyone who has once received this gift fears so greatly as that, abandoned by grace, he may have to go out again to the consolations—or rather, desolations—of the flesh and again endure the uproar of the carnal senses.

Accordingly, the threat is terrible and exceedingly dreadful: “Go forth and feed your kids.” That is: know that you are unworthy of your familiar and sweet contemplation of heavenly things, intelligible realities, and divine visions. Therefore go out from my sanctuary, your heart, where you were accustomed sweetly to draw secret and sacred meanings of truth and wisdom; and, rather like one of the worldly, entangle yourself in feeding and gratifying the senses of your flesh. For by “kids,” which signify sins and are to be placed at the left hand in judgment, he means the wandering and wanton senses of the body, through which sin, like death, entered the soul through the windows. What follows in Scripture also suits this well: “beside the shepherds’ tents.” For kids do not feed above, as lambs do, but beside the shepherds’ tents.

Shepherds—those who are true shepherds—although they possess tents from the earth and upon the earth, that is, their bodies during these days in which they are now on service, nevertheless are accustomed to feed the Lord’s flocks not from the earth but from heavenly pastures. For they preach to them not their own will but the Lord’s. But the kids, which are the bodily senses, seek not heavenly things; rather, beside the shepherds’ tents they take from all the sensible goods of this world—which is the region of bodies—that from which they do not so much satisfy as provoke their desires.

[Note: [Col. 1386D] The text reads *sensilis* (“sensible”); the edition reads *sensibilibus* (“sensible things”).]

What a shameful change of pursuits: that one whose pursuit had formerly been to nourish her pilgrim and exiled soul with sacred meditations as with heavenly goods; to seek God’s good pleasure and the mysteries of his will; to penetrate heaven by devotion and traverse the heavenly dwellings in mind; to greet the Fathers, Apostles, and choirs of Prophets; to admire the triumphs of martyrs; and to marvel at the most beautiful orders of angels—should now, abandoning all these, submit herself to the shameful slavery of the body, obeying the flesh and satisfying throat and belly; begging throughout the whole earth for something from the passing form of this world with which she may in some measure console her ever-hungry curiosity.

“Let streams of waters run down from my eyes” over such a soul, which, having been nourished in saffron garments, at last embraces dung. For, according to the saying of the blessed man, “he fed the barren woman who had no children, and did not benefit the widow” (Job 24:21). And observe that he does not simply say “Go forth,” but “Go forth,” he says, “and follow the tracks of the flocks, and feed your kids.” In this, as it seems to me, he warns us of something very great. What is it? Alas, that a noble creature, once made one of the flock and now miserably plunging into worse things, is not even permitted to remain among the flocks, but is commanded to go after them.

How, you ask? In the way you read: “When man was in honour, he did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13). See how the noble creature was made one of the flock! I think the beasts would say, if it were lawful for them to speak: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us” (Gen. 3:22). “When he was in honour,” it says. You ask in what honour? He lived in paradise, and his dwelling was in a place of delight. He felt no trouble and no want, surrounded by fragrant fruits, strengthened by flowers, crowned with glory and honour, and placed over the works of his Creator’s hands. More especially, he excelled through the distinction of the divine likeness, and he had a share and fellowship with the people of angels and with all the host of the heavenly army.

But he changed this glory of God into the likeness of a calf eating hay. From this it comes that the bread of angels was made hay, laid in a manger and set before us as beasts. “The Word was made flesh” (John 1:14), and according to the Prophet “all flesh is hay.” But this hay was by no means dried up, nor did its flower fall, because the Spirit of the Lord rested upon it. For this reason, at one time, the end of all flesh came about, because the Spirit of life had departed. Thus he says: “My Spirit shall not remain in man for ever, because he is flesh” (Gen. 6:3). Understand that here the name “flesh” denotes vice, not nature. Therefore, on account of vice, all flesh is hay, and all its glory is like the flower of hay. “The hay is dried up,” he says, “and the flower has fallen” (Isa. 40:6). But not that flower which sprang from the rod and root of Jesse, because the Spirit of the Lord rested upon him. Nor is that hay which was made hay, on account of what follows in the prophet: “But the word of the Lord remains for ever.” For if the Word is hay, and the Word remains for ever, then the hay too must remain for ever. Otherwise how does it grant eternal life, if it does not itself remain for ever? For he says: “If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever” (John 6:52). And he makes clear what bread he means when he adds: “And the bread which I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52). How, then, can that through which one lives eternally not be eternal?

But recall with me now the voice of the Son speaking to the Father concerning himself: “You will not,” he says, “give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10). There is no doubt that he speaks of the body which lay lifeless in the tomb. For this is the Holy One of whom the angel who announced to the Virgin also spoke, saying: “And that Holy One which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). How, then, could the holy hay see corruption, springing from the ever-flourishing pasture of an incorrupt womb, and now able to delight the eager eyes of angels fixed upon it, perpetually and without satiety? Let the hay indeed lose its greenness if Mary loses her virginity.

Therefore the food of man changed itself into the fodder of beasts, when man was changed into a beast. Alas, sad and tearful change: that man, inhabitant of paradise, lord of the earth, citizen of heaven, member of the household of the Lord Sabaoth, brother of blessed spirits, co-heir of heavenly powers, should find himself, by a sudden transformation, both lying in a stable because of weakness, needing hay because of likeness to beasts, and bound to a manger because of untamed wildness, as it is written: “Constrain with bit and bridle the jaws of those who do not draw near to you” (Ps. 31:9). At last, O ox, acknowledge your owner; and you, ass, the manger of your Lord, so that God’s prophets may be found faithful who foretold these marvels of God. Know, O beast, him whom you did not know, O man. Worship in the stable him from whom you fled in paradise. Honour the manger whose rule you despised. Eat the hay whom you disdained as bread, as the bread of angels.

But you ask: what was the cause of so great a fall? Surely it was that, when man was in honour, he did not understand. What did he not understand? Scripture does not say; let us say it. Placed in honour, he did not understand that he was mud, delighted by the summit of honour; and immediately he experienced in himself what, so long afterwards, a man among the children of captivity wisely observed and truly declared: “He who thinks himself something, when he is nothing, deceives himself” (Gal. 6:3). Woe to the wretched man: there was no one then to say to him, “Why are you proud, dust and ashes?” (Ecclus. 10:9). This noble creature was mingled with the flock. Hence God’s likeness was changed into beastly likeness. Hence fellowship with beasts was entered into instead of companionship with angels.

You see how this ignorance must be shunned by us: from it so many thousands of evils came upon our whole race. For it says that man was compared to senseless beasts because he did not understand. Therefore ignorance must be guarded against in every way, lest perhaps, if after affliction we are still found without understanding, many evils more numerous and grievous than the former may come upon us, and it may be said of us: “We have treated Babylon, and she has not been healed” (Jer. 51:9). Deservedly indeed, because not even affliction has given understanding to the hearing.

And see also whether perhaps the bridegroom, when he frightened his beloved from ignorance with so great a thunderclap of rebuke, did not say, “Go forth with the flocks,” or “Go forth to the flocks,” but: “Go forth,” he says, “after the flocks of your companions.” Why this?
