Certainly so that he might show the second ignorance to be more fearful and shameful than the first: the first made a human being equal to beasts, but the second makes him lower still. For persons who are unknown—that is, rejected—because of ignorance rightly stand for that dreadful judgment and are handed over to eternal fire; but beasts are not. And there is no doubt that it will be worse for those who are thus condemned than for those who do not exist at all. “It would have been better for him,” I say, “if that man had not been born” (Mark 14:21)—not, indeed, if he had not been born a human being, but if, for example, he had been born a beast or some other creature which, because it has no judgment, would not come to judgment and thus not to punishment.

Let the rational soul, therefore, which blushes for its first ignorance, know that beasts are its companions in enjoying the goods of earth, and that it will likewise have them as companions in suffering the torments of hell. Then at last it will be driven disgracefully even from the flocks of its companion beasts; it will no longer go with them, but plainly after them, when they feel no evil while it is exposed to every evil, from which it will never be delivered, if it has added a second ignorance. For a human being goes out and departs alone after the flocks of his companions when he is shut up alone in the lower hell. Does not one who is bound hand and foot and cast into the outer darkness seem to hold the lower place? And surely the latter condition of that man will be worse than the former, when he who was first made equal to beasts is now even placed after them.

I think that, in the present life, if you attend carefully, you will judge man to go after beasts. Does not a human being, endowed with reason but not living by reason, seem in some way more bestial than beasts themselves? For a beast, if it does not govern itself by reason, has an excuse in nature, from which that gift has been wholly withheld. A human being has none, since it has been granted him by nature as a special prerogative. Therefore a human being is rightly judged, precisely in this respect, to go out and follow behind herd animals: he alone, a rational animal, transgressing the laws of nature by a degenerate manner of life, imitates in habits and affections those devoid of reason. A human being is proved to follow after the flocks: now through the corruption of nature, and later through the extremity of punishment.

See how a human being found to possess ignorance of God is thus cursed—or should I say ignorance of himself? Without doubt, both; for, since each ignorance is condemnable, either one suffices for destruction. Do you wish to know that this is so? You do not doubt it concerning God, if you agree that eternal life is nothing other than knowing the Father as the true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. Hear, then, the bridegroom plainly and openly condemning in the soul ignorance even of itself. For what does he say? Not, indeed, “if you do not know God,” but “if you do not know yourself,” and so forth. It is clear, therefore, that the ignorant person shall be ignored (1 Cor. 14:18), whether it happens that he does not know himself or does not know God. Concerning both kinds of ignorance, if God grants aid, we shall have a very useful discussion.

[Note: [Col. 1389D] From Sermon 36 of St Bernard on the Song of Songs.]

But first I think we must ask whether every ignorance is condemnable. It seems to me that it is not. For not every ignorance condemns. There are many, indeed innumerable, things which may be unknown without any loss of salvation. For example, if you do not know a craft, such as carpentry, masonry, or whatever arts of this kind human beings practise for the uses of the present life, does that hinder salvation? Even without all those arts called liberal, though they are learned and practised by more honourable and useful studies, very many people have been saved, pleasing God in character and works. How many does the Apostle enumerate in the First Epistle to Timothy (1:5) who were made beloved not by knowledge of letters but by a pure conscience and sincere faith? Peter and Andrew, the sons of Zebedee, and all the other fellow disciples were not taken from the school of rhetoricians or philosophers; nevertheless, through them the Saviour worked salvation in the midst of the earth, not through wisdom which was greater in them than in all living beings—as some saint confessed concerning himself—but saved them, and already holy teachers, through their faith and gentleness. Finally, they made known the ways of life not in loftiness of speech or learned words of human wisdom, but, as it pleased God (1 Cor. 2:1), “through the foolishness of preaching he saved those who believe,” because the world did not know him in its wisdom.

Perhaps I seem excessive in disparaging knowledge, as though I were condemning the learned and prohibiting literary studies? Far be it! I do not fail to know how much the Church’s learned people have benefited it and still benefit it, whether by refuting opponents or instructing the simple. For I have read: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I too will reject you, so that you shall not exercise priesthood for me” (Hos. 4:6). I have read: “Those who have been learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto righteousness, like stars for everlasting ages” (Dan. 12:3). But I also know where I have read: “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. 8:1); and again: “He who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccl. 1:18). Do you see what a difference there is among kinds of knowledge, when one puffs up and another causes sorrow?

But I would have you know which of these seems more useful or more necessary to salvation: that which swells, or that which grieves?

[Note: [Col. 1390D] Thus the manuscript.]

But I do not doubt that you will prefer the grieving knowledge to the swelling, because pain seeks the health which swelling only feigns. The one who asks draws near to salvation, for whoever asks receives. Finally, he who heals the broken in heart (Luke 4:18) abhors the puffed-up, as the wise man says that God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Jas. 4:6). And the Apostle said: “I say, through the grace given to me, to all who are among you, not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly” (Rom. 12:3). He does not prohibit wisdom, but thinking more highly than one ought.

What is it to think soberly? To observe with the greatest vigilance what one ought especially, or first, to know; for time is short. Every kind of knowledge is good in itself, provided that it is supported by truth. But you who, because time is short, hasten to work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, take care to know more, and first, those things which you perceive to be nearer to salvation. Do not physicians of the body prescribe a rule of medicine in choosing foods—what should be taken first, what afterwards, in what manner, and what is fitting to take? For although the foods created by God are admittedly good, you make them plainly not good for yourself if you do not observe measure and order in taking them. Therefore, what I say about foods, understand also about forms of knowledge.

But I send you to a better teacher. For this is not our judgment, but his—indeed ours too, because it is truth’s: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8:2). You see that he does not approve the person who knows much if he does not know the manner of knowing. You see, I say, how he places the fruit and usefulness of knowledge in the manner of knowing. What then does he call the manner of knowing? What but knowing in what order, with what diligence, and for what end each thing ought to be known?

In what order? That first which ripens sooner toward salvation. With what aim? Not for empty glory, curiosity, or anything similar, but solely for the building up of yourself or your neighbour. For there are those who want to know only for the sake of knowing, and that is shameful curiosity. There are those who want to know in order that they themselves may be known, and that is shameful vanity. Such persons will certainly not escape the mocking satirist, who sings of one such as this:

> Your knowledge is nothing, unless another knows that you know it.  
> —Persius, *Satires* 1

There are likewise those who want to know in order to sell their knowledge—for example, for money or honours—and that is shameful gain. But there are also those who want to know in order to build up others, and that is charity; and likewise those who want to know in order to be built up, and that is prudence.

Of all these, the last two are not found in the abuse of knowledge. For they wish to understand in order to do good. Hence, “A good understanding have all they that do it” (Ps. 110:10). Let all the rest hear: “To one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” (Jas. 4:17). It is as though he said by comparison: “For one who takes food and does not digest it, it is harmful.” For undigested food, which has not good digestion, produces bad humours and corrupts the body; it does not nourish it. So too, much knowledge taken into the stomach of the soul—that is, the memory—if it is not cooked by the fire of charity and then passed and digested through, as it were, certain limbs of the soul, namely the moral habits, so that life itself may be made good from the good things it has learned, and the habits may become good—will not that knowledge be reckoned as sin, like food converted into corrupt and harmful humours? Is not the sinner a bad humour? Are not bad habits evil humours? Will not one of this sort suffer swellings and torments in the conscience—one, that is, who knows [Col. 1391C] the good and does not do it? Will he not have within himself an answer of death and condemnation as often as the saying comes to mind which God spoke: “That servant who knew his master’s will and did not do it shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12:47)?

And see whether perhaps the Prophet lamented in the person of such a soul when he said: “My belly, my belly, I am in pain” (Jer. 4:19). Does not this repetition seem to suggest a double meaning, so that besides the sense we have given, we should seek another also? For I think the Prophet could have said this in his own person: namely, that, full of knowledge and burning with charity, and altogether desiring to pour it forth, he found no one willing to hear; and so his knowledge was, as it were, a burden to him, because he could not communicate it. Thus the devout doctor of the Church mourns both those who disdain to learn how they ought to live and those who, though knowing it, nevertheless live badly. And this is indicated by the Prophet’s repetition of the same lament.

Do you now perceive how truly the Apostle judged that knowledge puffs up? Therefore I wish the soul, before all else, to know itself: reason requires this both for usefulness and for order. For order, because what we are is first for us. For usefulness, because such knowledge does not puff up but humbles, and is a certain preparation for building up. For unless it stands upon the firm foundation of humility, the spiritual building cannot stand at all. Moreover, nothing can now be more vivid or better fitted for humbling oneself than, if one finds oneself in truth, not to disguise oneself, and not to have deceit in one’s spirit. Let one set oneself before one’s own face and not be drawn away from oneself by turning aside. Does not one who thus looks upon oneself in the clear light of truth find oneself in the region of unlikeness and, sighing miserably, become unable any longer to conceal that one is truly miserable? Will one not cry with the Prophet to the Lord: “In thy truth thou hast humbled me”? For how shall one not be truly humbled in this true knowledge of oneself, when one perceives oneself burdened with sins, weighed down by the mass of this mortal body, entangled in earthly cares, infected by the dregs of carnal desires, blind, weak, bent, involved in many errors, exposed to many suspicions, subject to a thousand necessities, wretched, prone to vices, powerless for virtues? Whence now comes pride of eyes to such a person? Whence the lifting up of the head? Will one not rather be turned in one’s misery while one is pierced by the thorn? (Ps. 31:4.) One will turn, I say, to tears; one will turn to groans and lamentations; one will turn to the Lord and cry in humility: “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against thee” (Ps. 40:4). And when turned to the Lord, one will receive consolation, because he is the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation.

So long as I look into myself, my eye remains in bitterness. But if I look up and lift my eyes to the help of divine compassion, the joy of God will at once temper my bitter sight; and to him I say: “My soul was troubled within me; therefore I was mindful from the land of Jordan” (Ps. 41:7). It is no slight vision of God to experience him as pious and to be entreated, as he truly is: kind, merciful, and abounding over wickedness; whose nature is goodness and whose special property is always to have mercy and to spare. Thus, by such experience and in such an order, God is beneficially made known, when a human being first knows oneself to be placed in need, cries to the Lord, and he hears, saying: “I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me” (Ps. 49:15). And in this way knowledge of yourself will be a step to knowledge of God; and from his image, which is renewed in you, he himself will be seen, while you, with unveiled face, confidently beholding the glory of God, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.

[Col. 1392D] Now at last observe how each knowledge is necessary for your salvation, so that you can lack neither and still possess salvation. For if you do not know yourself, you will not have the fear of God in yourself, nor humility. But whether you presume upon salvation without fear of God and without humility—consider that yourself.

Likewise, if you do not know God, you do not love him; for he will not appear wholly desirable to you unless you taste and see how sweet and gentle he is. Therefore, that you may acquire both kinds of knowledge by God’s gift, become, with the Psalmist, an Idithun, passing over all other forms of knowledge, and say: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, that I may know what is lacking to me.”

“Make known to me, O Lord, my end,” assigned to me because of my fault. For I know that among all the things which I possess or shall possess, nothing is mine except sin and the punishment due for sin. Sin indeed is the way to punishment, yet it delights before punishment. But the Apostle, wishing to make this harmful delight bitter to his disciples, impressed upon their memory the end of such things, saying: “What fruit, then, had you at that time in those things of which you are now ashamed? For their end is death” (Rom. 6:21). Therefore, that the harmful delight which I had in sins may also become bitter to me, make known to me, O Lord, my end: namely, the end due to my sins. Once it is made known, I may know myself and no longer exalt myself above myself. Even if the tongue of flatterers or my own judgment prompts me to think that I am something when I am nothing, by the end made known to me, let me know what is lacking to me of those things falsely attributed to me. Let me know what is lacking to me, who have nothing else as my own but sins and their most evil end. “For their end is death” (Rom. 6:21)—and not death of whatever kind, but the worst death, because “the death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. 33:22).

“Make known to me, O Lord, my end,” so that I may never forget that end which I deserved through my fault, even if, through thy mercy preventing me, I have been appointed to a better end. This latter cannot properly be called mine, because it is gratuitous and given freely, and belongs properly to the grace which gives it. Yet, lest I be swallowed up in excessive sadness by the continual remembrance of my end made known to me, make known also to me, O Lord my God, this end of mine which is to be given freely; and I call it mine in the way that we call ours the bread which we eat daily, saying: “Give us this day our daily bread.”

Make known to me, O Lord, this end of mine—namely Christ, who is Alpha and Omega, beginning and end: beginning without beginning, end without end. Make known to me this end of mine as it was known to those to whom the Apostle truly says: “But now, being freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Rom. 6:22). “And this,” says Truth, “is eternal life: that they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent” (John 17:3). For “Christ is the end of the law unto righteousness for every one that believeth” (Rom. 10:4); and whoever can truly say, “I have seen the end of all consummation” (Ps. 118:96), knows him as this end.

Make known to me, O Lord, both my ends: the one due to my sins and the other hoped for through grace, so that by knowledge of the former I may remain humble and fearful, however many virtues I may hereafter receive; and by knowledge of the latter I may burn with the ardour of holy charity, supported by whose two wings I may be able to pass over all things beneath this end of mine, the Lord Jesus Christ.

Make known also the number of my days: not this number which, although it seems to belong to one clinging to this world, does not belong to one passing beyond all worldly things; but that number which is the number of innumerable days, neither beginning with morning nor ending with evening, of which it is elsewhere said: “I considered the days of old, and I had eternal years in my mind” (Ps. 76:6). The number of these ancient days and eternal years consists in unchangeable permanence. For example, God spoke once: “Let there be light,” and light was made; and that day remains in the luminous substance of the angels. Yet it does not remain unchangeably, since some of them, becoming dark, fell and became princes of darkness; while others advanced because of their fall and still advance, as their number grows through holy human beings joining their fellowship, and through the Church, as the Apostle says, the manifold wisdom of God is made known to them (Eph. 3:10). Therefore, if mutability is found in the work of the first day among heavenly things, how much more does no unchangeable number of days remain among the bodily and corruptible creatures of the remaining days?

All created things, then, must be transcended and passed over by this Idithun, so that he may know the number of days which is, and which he declares elsewhere that he has known, saying: “God hath spoken once; these two things have I heard: that power belongs to God, and unto thee, O Lord, mercy” (Ps. 61:12). These are the two eternal days; and their number, which is, will not be diminished or increased by however great a diversity with which creation varies beneath these two days—namely power and mercy—because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth,” or power and mercy, or justice and peace (Ps. 24:10). These are the two legs of the bridegroom, which the bride commends in the Song of Songs: “His legs are pillars of marble, founded upon bases of gold” (Cant. 5:15). The number of these two days, or legs, or pillars, does not change, because truth remains for ever and ever—truth which is, or rather which itself is, eternal power—and his mercy is from eternity and unto eternity upon those who fear him. Hence I, Idithun, passing over changeable days, call these unchangeable days mine by the gift of grace, because I fear power and hope for and love mercy.

[Col. 1394D] But that I may know what is lacking to me for perfection of fear, hope, and love, make known to me, O Lord, my end and the number of my days, which is unchangeable with thee, though it changes in us, to whom thou now showest power, now mercy: frightening or striking by power, healing and consoling by mercy. To one who is humbled by thy striking, and through humiliation—which is the road to humility—is perfected in humility itself, so that he may be meek and humble of heart, the day of power is made known; and by grace the divine day becomes his own day also. But because thou givest grace to the humble, when such a humbled and humble person is granted that, rooted in charity and humility, he bears the fruit of virtues to the honour of the Giver and the edification of beholders, then he will understand that he has been loved from eternity, through the signs of divine predestination shining forth in such fruits. And since “the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity upon those who fear him” (Ps. 102:17), one who feels oneself loved from eternity in predestination, prevented by God’s grace, loves unto eternity; and thus begins to have one’s end and the number of one’s days made known: that number which is in the eternal power of God and in mercy no less eternal, to be sung for ever. This entire and so great good I, Idithun, seek in a brief prayer when, passing beyond lower things, I direct myself toward the highest good, saying: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end and what is the number of my days, that I may know what is lacking to me.”

[Col. 1395B] And behold, in the midst of my prayers I am heard. Although I do not yet have my end and the number of my days—which is—made known to me, I nevertheless know what is lacking to me of the number of stable and immeasurable days, while I am wholly occupied under unstable and measurable days. Therefore I say:

**VERSE 6.** “Behold, thou hast made my days measurable, and my substance as nothing before thee.” “I considered the days of old, and I had eternal years in my mind” (Ps. 76:6), desiring and longing that my end and the number of my days, which is, might be made known to me. Thus, passing beyond all lower things, I desired the highest good. But that I may know what is lacking to me before I receive the good itself which is lacking, the shortness of my days is here shown to me, so that, seeing how much of the eternity of ancient days is lacking to me, I may become humbler and may not take pride in the glory of present righteousness, which passes away, but may say in true humility: “Behold, thou hast made my days measurable.”

And in Hebrew it reads: “Behold, thou hast made my days short, and my life as though it were not before thee; for every living human being is altogether vanity.” Whether human days are called measurable or short, the sense is the same. The Holy Spirit signifies that the way to immeasurable and eternal days has not yet been brought forth so long as a human being passes through in an image, is troubled in vain, heaps up treasure, and does not know for whom one gathers it. Therefore I say: “Behold, thou hast made my days measurable and short.” For even before sin a measurable and short number of days was assigned to me, after whose passage I was to be transferred to one day, a long day, not closed by any evening. How much more, after sin, will my days be shortened, and only the grave remains to me? (Job 17:1.) For although the inward person is renewed day by day, from the temporal day into the eternal day, yet the outward and old person is corrupted like a garment eaten by moths, so that I may truly say: “Behold, thou hast made my days short, and my substance as nothing before thee.”

My substance, because it quickly passes away in itself, or in comparison with thy substance, or in comparison with thy brightness, is as nothing. That this is true, although it is not visible to human eyes, is nevertheless in some manner inwardly felt where thou seest and art seen by pure hearts. Therefore that which appears great before human beings is as nothing before thee—that is, in thy sight. For anyone powerful in this world and abounding in riches is thought great.

Yet every human being living, however gross and rich, is altogether vanity: every human being living with mortal life is not only vain but vanity itself. Elsewhere it is said: “Man is made like unto vanity” (Ps. 143:4). Here something stronger is said, when every human being is affirmed to be altogether vanity. That is said to vanish which suddenly disappears from between the hands of those handling it or from under the eyes of those looking at it. Thus it is said of the Lord that, after the Resurrection, having appeared to the disciples for a time, he vanished from their eyes (Luke 24:31). Yet although he vanished from their eyes, he did not vanish from their hearts. Thus afterward they said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (ibid., 32). For truth is contrary to vanity. And that man is Truth, as he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). In no way does the saying, “Every living human being is altogether vanity,” apply to him. For the man who is from above, where truth is, not from below, where everything under the sun is vanity, is truth and not vanity. For although “truth sprang out of the earth” (Ps. 84:12), yet he who came from heaven is established above all things—above all things even above the sun, infinitely surpassing all vain things placed under the sun—since he is Truth itself, to which vanity is opposed.

Therefore every human being who clings to him is truthful; every human being who departs from him is false, and consequently vain or vanity, and not merely vanity but altogether vanity. For the whole creation is subjected to vanity in the human being alone, because the human being is every creature. Thus, when the Gospel is proclaimed to the human being alone, it is said to be preached to every creature. Likewise, when the human being alone is said to be like vanity or to be vanity itself, the whole creation is convicted of vanity in the human being, because he vanishes, “coming forth like a flower and being cut down, fleeing as a shadow,” and never remaining in the same state (Job 14:2).

**VERSE 7.** “Yet man passes through in an image.” The human being was indeed created in the image and likeness of God, so that the divine image might shine in human free choice and God’s likeness in human goodness. But, corrupted through the devil’s malice, he came into the far country of unlikeness, being alienated from the likeness of divine goodness. Yet he passes through in the image, whether to eternal blessedness or to endless punishment, because free choice will not be destroyed in him: whether he is made blessed by using it well or condemned by using it badly.

For freedom of choice, by which it is free from necessity, belongs without distinction to God and to every rational creature, good and evil alike. It is neither lost nor diminished through sin or misery; it is not greater in the righteous person than in the sinner, nor fuller in an angel than in a human being. For just as, when the human will turns to good by grace, its consent makes a human being freely good and free in goodness precisely because one becomes voluntary and is not dragged unwillingly; so, when one willingly lapses into evil, that same inclination of one’s own will—not compelled from elsewhere—makes one in evil no less free than spontaneous in being evil. And just as the heavenly angel, or God himself, remains freely good, by his own will and not by any necessity, so certainly the devil falls into evil and persists in it equally freely, by his own voluntary inclination and not by another’s impulse.

[Note: [Col. 1397D] St Bernard, *On Grace and Free Choice*, ch. 4.] Therefore freedom of the will remains even where captivity of mind also occurs: equally full in the evil as in the good, though more ordered in the good; equally entire, in its own measure, in the creature as in the Creator, though more powerful in him.

But when people are accustomed to complain and say, “I wish to have a good will, and I cannot,” this does not at all prescribe a limit to that freedom, as though the will suffered force or necessity in this respect. Rather, they plainly testify that they lack the freedom called freedom from sin. For one who wishes to have a good will has a will; one does not wish to have a good will except by the will. If, therefore, one has will and freedom, one has freedom from necessity but not freedom from sin. Indeed, when one is unable, even while willing, to have a good will, one feels that freedom is lacking—but certainly freedom from sin, by which one grieves to be oppressed, not destroyed. Yet undoubtedly one has a good will in some measure already where one wishes to have it; for what one wills is good. Nor could one will good except by a good will, just as one could not will evil except by an evil will. When we will good, the will is good; when we will evil, the will is evil. In both cases there is will, and in both cases freedom. Necessity yields to the will. But when we cannot do what we will, we feel, in some manner, that freedom itself is captive or miserable through sin, but not lost.

Therefore, from this freedom alone—by which the will is free to judge itself good if it consents to good, or evil if it consents to evil, since it feels that it consents in neither case except by certainly willing—we believe free choice receives its name. For Scripture speaks of freedom in three ways: freedom from necessity, as has already been said; freedom from sin; and freedom from misery.

[Note: [Col. 1397D] St Bernard, *On Grace and Free Choice*, ch. 3; [Col. 1398D] Rom. 6:20; Rom. 6:22.] There is freedom from sin, as the Apostle says: “When you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness. But now, freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life.” But who, while in the flesh of sin, claims freedom from sin for oneself? Therefore I do not think that free choice is so called from this freedom. There is also freedom from misery, of which the Apostle says: “The creation itself shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.” But does anyone presume this freedom for oneself in this mortal life? Accordingly, we rightly deny that free choice receives its name from this freedom as well. There remains, then, the freedom which I judge more fitting for it, which we may call freedom from necessity, because what is necessary seems opposed to what is voluntary, and conversely.

[Note: [Col. 1398D] The same, ibid., ch. 4.] From the freedom called freedom from sin, perhaps “free counsel” might more suitably be named; and from that called freedom from misery, “free delight” might rather be named than free choice. For choice is judgment. Just as it belongs to judgment to discern what is permitted and what is not permitted, so it belongs to counsel to test what is expedient and what is not expedient, and to delight to experience what pleases and what does not please. Would that we consulted for ourselves as freely as we judge about ourselves, so that, just as by judgment we freely distinguish permitted from forbidden things, we might freely choose permitted things as beneficial and reject forbidden things as harmful by counsel. Then we should be not only of free choice, but undoubtedly of free counsel, and thus free from sin. But what if everything which is expedient and permitted also pleased us? Would I not rightly say that we were also of free delight, since we should perceive ourselves to be free from everything that could displease—that is, from all misery? But now, although by judgment we examine and decide that many things ought to be admitted or omitted, we do not choose or reject them by counsel in accordance with the rightness of judgment; and again, we do not gladly embrace as pleasing all the things we prudently observe as right and advantageous, but in addition scarcely persevere in bearing them with equanimity, as though they were harsh and burdensome. It is clear that we possess neither free counsel nor free delight.

But we shall certainly possess them when, through God’s mercy, we obtain what we pray for: “Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matt. 6:10). This will be fulfilled when that which now seems common to every rational creature—the free choice which is free from necessity—will exist also in the elect human beings, as now in the holy angels, both guarded from sin and secure from misery. Then, at last, through the happy experience of triple freedom, they will prove what is the good will of God, pleasing and perfect. Since this has not yet come about, only freedom of choice remains meanwhile full and entire in human beings. Freedom of counsel exists only in part, and this in few spiritual persons, who have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires, so that sin no longer reigns in their mortal body. Yet freedom of counsel makes sin not reign; captivity of free choice means that sin does not wholly cease to be present. But when that which is perfect comes, then that which is in part shall be done away (cf. 1 Cor. 13:10). That is, when freedom of counsel is full, there will no longer be any captivity of choice.

This is what we daily ask in prayer when we say: “Thy kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10). This kingdom has not yet wholly come into us; nevertheless, it comes daily little by little, and day by day gradually expands its boundaries more and more in those alone whose inward person is renewed day by day through God’s help. Insofar as the kingdom of grace expands, the power of sin diminishes. Yet insofar as there is still deficiency because of the body of death, which weighs down the soul, and because of the necessity of earthly habitation, which depresses the mind thinking many things, even those who seem more perfect in this mortal life must confess and say: “In many things we all offend” (Jas. 3:2). And: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and truth is not in us” (1 John 3:8). Therefore they too pray without ceasing, saying: “Thy kingdom come.” It will not be consummated even in them until sin not only does not reign in their mortal body, but neither exists nor can exist at all in their now immortal body.

[Note: [Col. 1399D] The same Bernard, passage cited, ch. 5.] But what shall we say of freedom of delight in this wicked age, where the evil of the day scarcely suffices for itself; where all creation groans and labours in travail until now, subjected to vanity not willingly; where human life is temptation upon earth; where even spiritual persons, who have already received the firstfruits of the Spirit, themselves groan within themselves, awaiting the redemption [Col. 1399C] of their body? Is there any place among these things for freedom of this kind? What freedom will remain for our delight, where misery seems to occupy everything? For neither innocence nor righteousness can be safe from misery as they are safe from sin. Here the righteous person cries: “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24). And again: “My tears have become my bread day and night” (Ps. 41:3). Where days and nights are prolonged in sorrow, certainly no interval of time is left empty for delight. Indeed, those who wish to live godly in Christ suffer persecution all the more (2 Tim. 3:12), because judgment begins with the house of God; and he commanded this when he said: “Begin at my sanctuary” (Ezek. 9:6).

But if virtue is not safe, perhaps vice is safe, and delight can meanwhile have some leisure to avoid misery. Far from it. For those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things do something like what madmen do when they laugh. And there is no truer misery than false joy. Indeed, that which seems happiness in this world is so greatly misery that the wise man says: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. 7:3). There is indeed some pleasure in bodily goods: in eating, drinking, warming oneself, and the other such comforts or coverings of the flesh. But are even these in any degree free from misery? Bread is good, but for one who is hungry; drink delights, but one who is thirsty. Indeed, for one who is full, food and drink are no longer pleasant but burdensome. Take away hunger and one will not care for bread. Take away thirst and one will look upon the clearest fountain as though it were a swamp. Similarly, no one seeks shade except one who is hot; one does not care for the sun except when cold or in darkness. Otherwise none of these will please unless urgent necessity has come first. If this necessity is wholly removed from things, the very pleasure which seems to be in them immediately turns into weariness and annoyance.

We must therefore admit that misery occupies everything belonging to this present life even in this respect, except that, amid common tribulations of more severe labours, lesser consolations of whatever kind occur; and, perhaps as heavy and light things alternately succeed one another according to times and events, experience of a lesser misery seems an interruption of misery, so that when one happens to escape into something less troublesome after experiencing many very grievous things, it is considered happiness.

Nevertheless, we must admit that those not devoid of contemplation, who are sometimes caught up in the spirit and are able to taste, however slightly, the sweetness of heavenly happiness, are free from misery as often as they thus pass beyond themselves. These persons indeed, which cannot be denied, enjoy freedom of delight even in this flesh—though rarely and only in swift rapture—having, with Mary, chosen the better part, which shall not be taken from them. For those who already hold what is not to be taken away experience what is to come; but what is to come is happiness. Happiness and misery cannot exist together at the same time. Therefore, as often as they participate in the former through the Spirit, so often they do not feel the latter. Thus in this life contemplatives alone can in some degree enjoy freedom of delight, and that only partially, in a quite small measure, and on very rare occasions. Freedom of counsel, however, is enjoyed even by any righteous persons, in part indeed but not in a small measure. Freedom of choice, on the other hand, as has plainly appeared above, belongs equally to all who use reason: no less in itself in evil persons than in good, and as full in this age as in the age to come.

[Note: [Col. 1400D] The same Bernard, passage cited, ch. 6.] And I think it has also been plainly shown here that this freedom itself is oppressed for as long as the other two freedoms do not accompany it at all, or accompany it less fully. Nor does our deficiency, of which the Apostle says, “that you do not do the things that you will” (Gal. 5:17), arise from elsewhere. For to will belongs to us by free choice; but to be able to do what we will does not. I do not mean to will good or to will evil, but simply to will. For to will good is progress; to will evil is defect; but simply to will is that very thing which either progresses or fails. Creating grace made it so that it exists; saving grace makes it progress; it itself cast itself down so that it fails. Thus free choice makes us willing; grace makes us well-willing.

For just as it is one thing simply to fear and another to fear God; one thing simply to love and another to love God—for fear and love simply named signify affections, but with an addition they signify virtues—so likewise it is one thing to will and another to will good.

Simple affections belong naturally to us, as though from ourselves; their additions come from grace. Nor indeed is their progress anything else than grace’s ordering of what creation bestowed, so that virtues are nothing other than ordered affections. It is written of some that “they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. 13:5). There was fear, but it was disordered. The Lord wished to order it in the disciples when he said: “I will show you whom you ought to fear” (Luke 12:5). And David says: “Come, children, hear me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 33:12). Likewise, he rebuked people for disordered love when he said: “I am come as light into this world, and men loved darkness rather than light” (John 3:19). Therefore the bride asks in the Song of Songs: “Set charity in order within me” (Cant. 2:4).

Likewise, those who were told, “You do not know what you ask” (Mark 10:38), were reproved for disordered will; but they were taught to bring their crooked will back to the line of rectitude when they heard: “Can you drink the cup which I am to drink?” (Matt. 20:22). At that time he taught them to order the will by word, and afterward by example also, when, praying at the approach of the Passion that the cup might be taken from him, he immediately added: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as thou wilt” (Matt. 26:35 [as printed]). Therefore from God we received the capacity to will, as also to fear and to love, in the creation of nature, so that we might be some kind of creature. But we received the capacity to will good, as also to fear God and to love God, in the visitation of grace, so that we might be God’s creature.

For, created in a certain sense as our own through free will, we become, as it were, God’s through good will. He who made it free makes it good; and he makes it good so that we may be some beginning of his creature, because it is surely better for us not to have existed at all than to remain our own. For those who wished to be their own, “as gods knowing good and evil,” became not only their own but also the devil’s. This concerns the saying: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19). For to those who are not his, he says: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). Therefore, while by an evil will we are the devil’s, in some sense we are meanwhile not God’s; just as, when through a good will we become God’s, we cease to be the devil’s. For no one can serve two masters (Matt. 6:24). Yet whether we are God’s or the devil’s, we do not in the same way cease to be our own. For in each case the freedom of the ungodly remains, by which the ground of merit remains also, so that we may deservedly either be punished as evil, because freely and from our own will we become such; or be glorified as good, because we cannot be so unless we are equally voluntary.

[Note: [Col. 1401D] The same Bernard, ibid., ch. 8.] Free choice therefore remains even after sin—though wretched, yet not impaired; and the fact that a human being is unable by himself to shake off sin or misery does not indicate the destruction of free choice, but the deprivation of the other two freedoms. For it does not belong to free choice, so far as it is in itself, nor did it ever belong to it, either to be able or to be wise, but only to will. It makes the creature neither powerful nor wise, but only willing. Therefore free choice must be judged lost, not if one ceases to be powerful or wise, but if one ceases to be willing. For where there is no will, neither is there freedom. I do not say if a creature ceases to will what is good, but if it ceases to will altogether: it must be confessed without contradiction that, where goodness no longer proceeds from the will, but the will itself wholly perishes, free choice too perishes.

But if it cannot will the good, that is a sign that it lacks, not free choice, but free counsel. If, however, it lacks not the will but the ability to attain the good which it already wills, let it know that it lacks free satisfaction, not that free choice has perished. Therefore, if free choice follows the will everywhere in such a way that it is not lacking so long as the will does not wholly cease to exist, while the will endures alike in evil as in good, then certainly free choice likewise remains whole, both in good and in evil. And just as the will, even when placed in misery, does not cease to be a will, but is called and is a miserable will, just as it is a blessed will: so no adversity or necessity can destroy free choice, or, so far as it is in itself, diminish it in any degree.

Yet although it endures everywhere alike without diminution of itself, it cannot equally, just as it was able by itself to fall from good into evil, also by itself recover breath from evil into good. And what wonder if one lying down cannot rise again unaided, when, even standing, one could not by any effort of one’s own advance to something better? Indeed, while it still possessed to some extent the other two freedoms with it, it could not ascend from their lower stages to the higher—that is, from being able not to sin and able not to be disturbed, to being unable to sin and unable to be disturbed. If, aided in whatever manner by those freedoms, it nevertheless could not extend itself from good to better, how much less, wholly deprived of them, can it now emerge by itself from evil into that good which it formerly possessed.

Humanity therefore necessarily has Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God: so that, because he is Wisdom, he may restore to it true wisdom, for the restoration of free counsel; and, because he is Power, may restore full ability, for the reparation of free satisfaction—so that by the one it may become perfectly good and know sin no longer, and by the other fully blessed and experience nothing adverse. But this perfection must surely be awaited in the life to come, when both freedoms now lost are fully restored to free choice: not as they were granted to any righteous person in this age, however perfect, nor even as they were granted to the first human beings in Paradise, but as angels now possess them in heaven.

Meanwhile, in this body of death and this evil age, it should suffice: by freedom of counsel, not to obey sin in its desire; and by freedom of satisfaction, not to fear adversities for righteousness’ sake. For in this flesh of sin and amid the evil of this day, it is no slight wisdom not indeed to be wholly without sin, but at least not to consent to it; and it is no small ability not yet to experience adversities altogether without suffering, but nevertheless bravely to despise them for truth’s sake.

Meanwhile we must learn, through freedom of counsel, not to misuse freedom of choice, so that one day we may fully enjoy freedom of satisfaction. Thus indeed we repair God’s image in ourselves; thus, by grace, we are prepared to recover that ancient honor which we lost through sin. Blessed is the person who deserves to hear said of him: “Who is he? We shall praise him; for he has done wonders in his life: he could transgress, and did not transgress; he could do evil, and did not do it” (Ecclus. 31:9).

[Note: [Col. 1403D] The same Bernard, ibid., ch. 9.] I think that in these three freedoms is contained the very image and likeness of the Creator, to which we were created: the image indeed in freedom of choice, while in the other two there is marked out a certain twofold likeness. Perhaps this is why freedom of choice alone suffers no complete failure or diminution of itself: because in it there appears to be impressed above all a certain substantial image of the eternal and unchangeable Divinity. For although it had a beginning, it knows no end; it receives neither increase from righteousness or glory, nor loss from sin or misery. What is more like eternity, while not itself eternity?

But in the other freedoms, since they can not only be diminished in part but wholly lost, there is recognized a certain accidental likeness to the divine wisdom and power superimposed upon the image. For we lost them through fault and recover them through grace; and daily some make progress in them more, others less, while others decline in them. They can also be lost in such a manner as to be beyond recovery, and possessed in such a manner as to be incapable in any way either of loss or diminution.

Humanity was created in Paradise in a degree of this twofold likeness to God’s wisdom and power—not the highest degree, but one nearest to it. When, through sin, it fell from that degree—indeed, when we fell in it and with it—we received again through grace, not that very degree, but for its place a certain lower degree. For here we cannot be without sin and misery; nevertheless, with grace helping, we can neither be overcome by sin nor by misery, although Scripture says: “Everyone who is born of God does not sin” (1 John 3:9). But this is said of those predestined to life: not because they do not sin at all, but because sin is not imputed to them, since it is either punished by fitting repentance or hidden in charity. For “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8). And: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31:1). And: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (ibid., v. 2).

The highest angels hold the highest degree of the divine likeness; we hold the lowest; Adam held the middle; but demons hold none. For the spirits above are granted to endure without sin and misery; Adam was granted to be without them, though not also to remain so; while we are not granted even to be without them, yet we need not yield to them. But the devil and his members, just as they never will to resist sin, likewise can never escape sin’s punishment.

Therefore, since these two freedoms—of counsel and satisfaction—through which true wisdom and power are supplied to the rational creature, vary according as God dispenses them, as he wills, for whatever reasons, places, and times, so that they are possessed moderately on earth, fully in heaven, to a middle degree in Paradise, and not at all in hell; whereas freedom of choice is not changed in any degree from the state in which it was created, but, so far as it is in itself, is possessed equally and always in heaven, on earth, and in hell: rightly the former are assigned to likeness, and the latter to image.

And Scripture testifies that in hell both those freedoms have perished—namely, those said to belong to likeness. For that place plainly contains no true wisdom, which is certainly conceived as belonging to freedom of counsel, where we read: “Whatever your hand can do, do it diligently, because there is neither work nor reasoning nor wisdom in hell, whither you hasten” (Eccl. 9:10). Concerning the power bestowed through freedom of satisfaction, the Gospel speaks thus: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. 22:13). For what is the binding of hands and feet except the complete removal of power?

But someone says: How is there no wisdom there, where the evils endured compel people to repent of the evils they committed? Can anyone in torments either fail to repent, or repent of evil without being wise? This objection would be sound if not merely the deed of sin but also the evil will were punished. For no one doubts that a person placed in torments takes no pleasure in repeating the act of sin. Yet if the will remains evil even amid torments, what weight has the renunciation of the act?

And is one therefore thought wise because, now amid the flames, one has no wish to indulge in lust? “Wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wis. 1:4). How, then, shall we prove that the will remains evil even in punishments? Certainly, to omit other matters, they do not wish to be punished at all. Yet it is just that those who have done punishable deeds should be punished. Therefore they do not will what is just. But the will of one who does not will what is just is not righteous. Thus the will is unjust, and thereby evil, insofar as it does not accord with justice.

Two things prove a will unjust: pleasure in sinning, or pleasure in having sinned without punishment. Those, therefore, who took pleasure in sinning while they could, and who, now that they cannot, wish what they sinned to remain unavenged—what appearance is there in them of true wisdom or good will? But suppose they repent of having sinned. If the choice were given, would they not prefer still to sin rather than endure sin’s punishment? Yet the former is unjust and the latter just. How could a good will choose what is unjust rather than what is just? Moreover, those do not truly repent who grieve not so much that they lived for themselves as that they can no longer do so. What happens within is shown without: for as long as the body lives in flame, it is clear that the will persists in wickedness. Thus, of the likeness contained in the freedoms of counsel and satisfaction there is absolutely nothing, nor can there be anything, in hell; yet the image remains even there unmoved through free choice.

[Note: [Col. 1405D] The same Bernard, ibid., ch. 10.] Nor could likeness be found equally anywhere even in this age; rather, the image would still have lain foul and deformed, had not that woman of the Gospel lit a lamp—had Wisdom not appeared in the flesh, overturned the house, and sought her drachma amid the vices, the drachma she had lost, that is, her image. This image, stripped of its native beauty and filthy beneath the skin of sin, lay hidden as though in dust. Having found it, she wiped it clean, lifted it from the region of dissimilarity, restored it to its former appearance, made it like unto the glory of the saints, and indeed will one day render it wholly conformed to herself, when that saying of Scripture is fulfilled: “We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

And truly, to whom did this work belong more fittingly than to the Son of God, who, being “the brightness of glory and the figure of the Father’s substance,” upholding all things by his word, appeared readily equipped from both sources: with that by which to reform the deformed and that by which to strengthen the weak? By the brightness of his figure he drove away the darkness of sins and made the person wise; by the power of his word he made the person strong against the tyranny of demons.

[Note: [Col. 1406D] The manuscript reads: “pressed upon” (*ingruebat*).] The Form itself, therefore, came, to which free choice was to be conformed; for, in order to recover its former form, it had to be reformed from that from which it had been formed.

Now Form is Wisdom; conformity is the effect produced by the image in the body which Form produces in the universe. For “she reaches mightily from end to end and disposes all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1). She reaches from end to end—that is, from the highest heaven to the lowest regions of the earth, from the highest angel to the tiniest worm. And she reaches mightily, not by movement through space, local extension, or merely official administration of a subject creature, but by a certain substantial and everywhere-present power, by which she most powerfully moves, orders, and governs all things. And she is compelled to do none of these things by any necessity in herself; she labors under no difficulty in them, but disposes all things sweetly by a serene will.

Or, indeed, she reaches from end to end—that is, from the beginning of creation to the end appointed by the Creator: whether the end toward which nature presses, the end which a cause hastens, or the end which grace grants. She reaches mightily, because none of these events occurs without her arranging it by powerful providence.

Thus free choice should endeavor to govern its body as Wisdom governs the universe, reaching through it also mightily from end to end: that is, commanding each sense and member so powerfully that it does not permit sin to reign in its mortal body, nor give its members as weapons of unrighteousness, but presents them for service to righteousness. Thus a person will no longer be sin’s slave when he does not commit sin; and, once freed from it, he will begin to recover freedom of counsel and to claim his own dignity, clothing the divine image within himself in a likeness worthy of it—or rather, restoring its ancient beauty.

Let him pursue this no less sweetly than strongly: that is, not from sadness or necessity—which is the beginning, not the fullness, of wisdom—but with a ready and cheerful will, which makes the sacrifice acceptable; for “God loves a cheerful giver” (1 Cor. 9:7). Thus he will imitate Wisdom in every respect, resisting vices mightily and resting sweetly in conscience. Yet we need the help of him whose example summons us to such things, so that through him we ourselves may be conformed to him and transformed into the same image “from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18).

Accordingly, unless a person is helped by the Spirit of the Lord, although he passes along in the image, he is nevertheless troubled in vain. Another translation reads thus.

In the Hebrew, before this verse there is placed a *diapsalma*, signifying a division of what precedes from what follows—and rightly so. For the preceding verse concerns the universal vanity reproved in humankind alone, because human life is a vapor appearing briefly and quickly vanishing. But now there is added concerning that image which will remain unimpaired in the human being—namely, free choice, which admits absolutely no defect—as if it were said: “Every human being is called altogether vanity because human life on earth is unstable. Nevertheless, man passes along in an image”: namely, in an image that remains stable and unmoved so far as concerns the indestructible freedom of choice. Yet if it is not helped by the Spirit of the Lord, it not only grows sluggish in idleness when the Spirit does not stir it; it is also troubled in vain if it is stirred by the Spirit merely to will the good, unless by that same Spirit it is drawn to run strongly.

Therefore strength belongs neither to the one who wills nor to the one who runs, but is a gift of God who has mercy (Rom. 9:16): so that the one who wills may receive the good he wills, and the runner may arrive where he is heading. Otherwise, as I have said, the one who wills and runs is troubled in vain; he strives in vain, whose efforts are nothing unless grace awakens them, and they are fruitless unless the Spirit of the Lord helps them. For the Spirit himself helps our weakness. Accordingly, one who strives without the Spirit of the Lord, by one’s own strength alone, is troubled in vain.

The Hebrew reads: “As much as man walks in an image, so much is he troubled in vain. He heaps up, and does not know for whom he will leave it.” This is the same as saying: As much as a person walks in free choice alone, without assisting grace, so much is he troubled in vain, because with burning avarice—which is the root of all evils—he attends only to temporal and passing things. Avarice thus extinguishes the light of the divine image in a human being, so that he walks in darkness, not knowing where he goes. Hence he heaps up and does not know for whom he will leave it. For he does not know whether his son will possess it—perhaps no son will be born to him; perhaps the son will squander it in dissipation; perhaps he himself will lose it when his final death approaches; perhaps it will even be taken away, so that it does not pass into his son’s possession.

Blessed Gregory, briefly treating this passage in Job, says among other things: “Although man walks in the image of God, he is nevertheless vainly troubled. It frequently happens that a holy man is outwardly troubled yet remains inwardly untroubled; and that which may be vainly troubled belongs to the weakness of the flesh, although he walks in the image of God by the strength of the mind: so that he is strengthened within by divine aid, while outwardly he is still weighed down by the burden of humanity.

“For it is a great security of heart to have no worldly desire. If the heart longs to acquire earthly things, it can by no means be secure and tranquil: either it does not possess them and desires to possess them, or, having gained them, fears to lose them. While it hopes for prosperity in adversity and fears adversity in prosperity, it is rolled hither and thither as by certain waves and is tossed in diverse ways by the changing alternations of things. But if the mind is once fixed with firm stability in the desire for the heavenly homeland, it is less harassed by the disturbance of temporal things. For from all external movements it seeks, as it were, a most secret retreat in the same intention; and there, transcending all mutable things, by the very tranquility of its rest it is in the world yet outside the world. By its intention toward the highest things it rises above all low things, and by a certain freedom it feels itself superior to all things that it does not desire. It does not endure within the tempest of temporal affairs which it sees without, because all earthly things that could oppress the mind through desire lie despised beneath it.”

And now Idithun, placed over earthly things but below heavenly things, seeing beneath himself the vanity which he has crossed over and above himself the truth toward which he stretches, cries out:

**VERSE 8. “And now what is my expectation?”** After I have crossed over all else, what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? I, Idithun, before the Law or under the Law, awaited the Lord Jesus Christ—coming as Redeemer in his first advent and as Judge in his second advent. The delay appeared long to me as I waited and desired him.

The word *exspecto* (“I await”) is compounded from the frequentative verb *specto, spectas* (“I look repeatedly”). For as one who reads repeatedly is said *lectitare*, so one who looks repeatedly is said *spectare*. Those desiring the arrival of their lord or friend commonly look repeatedly toward the places from which the one whom they await is hoped to come. They sometimes also look out through windows or lattices; and thus *exspectatio*, “expectation,” is called the action of those who await—that is, those who repeatedly look outward through windows or lattices.

Thus Abraham the father rejoiced while awaiting the sight of Christ’s day; he saw it from afar and was glad. He who has seen was glad; one who awaits and desires to see may sometimes be wearied by delay, sometimes driven by the desire to see what he awaits. Thus he repeatedly looks at every sound or movement; he looks and awaits, to discover some sign of the one whom he desires to behold. So the holy persons of old awaited Christ’s coming in the flesh as Savior; so I, Idithun, await him as Judge.

The death of saints who await in this manner is rightly called a departure (*obitus*), because in dying they go to meet the one whom they await, desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ. For this is far better; nevertheless, to remain in the flesh for a while is necessary even for saints, whether for themselves and their own improvement, or for others and their edification.

Yet however many examples of goodness a person sees in the image, he still passes on, if, content with the freedom of his own will—called free choice—he walks according to his own pleasure, and, estranged from the likeness of divine goodness, passes into the distant region of dissimilarity. There he dissipates his substance with harlots, that is, by serving seductive pleasures; and he becomes a swineherd, supplying the food of vices to unclean spirits. Even such a person, when he at last returns to himself, sometimes leaps over the swine by a good leap. Then, leaping also over himself, he returns to the father and says: “How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread, while I perish here from hunger! I will arise and go to my father!” (Luke 15:17–18).

For what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? I am not worthy to be called a son, so as to dare await him as a consoling Father. What then is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? Will he not at least receive me among the servants or hired laborers and, as Lord, feed me his servant? For I perish here from hunger, while created in God’s image I indeed walk in an image, but lack God’s likeness as long as I dwell in the region of dissimilarity. Therefore I shall arise and go to my Father—or rather, to my Lord, whom I do not dare call Father. I shall arise and cross over everything that separates me from him and makes me unlike him.

He is holy, and I now desire, with the holy one, to be holy, as he says to his children: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. 11:44). I am weary of remaining any longer in the region of dissimilarity with a people made far from the saints. I judge blessed the person of whom it can truly be said: “He made him like in the glory of the saints” (Ecclus. 45:2). Again Truth says: “Whoever hears my words and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house upon a rock” (Matt. 7:24). One to whom this is said is rightly proclaimed not only formed in God’s image, but also reformed into God’s likeness: for he is holy with the Holy One, elect with the Elect One, and moreover God with God—an adoptive God with God who is God by nature.

To such a person and those like him God says: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6). These are the gods in whose midst God stands, judging gods, according to that saying: “God stood in their midst” (Ps. 81:1), judging gods. [Note: [Col. 1409] The Vulgate: “God stood in the assembly of gods; but in the midst he judges gods.”] Separated from these gods, compared with senseless beasts and made like them, set in the estate to feed swine—what shall I do? I know what I shall do; I know what I shall say. I shall arise, go, and cross over to my father, and say to him: “Lord, my substance is indeed as nothing before you; rather, it has been wholly reduced to nothing and dissipated with harlots. Yet this is my expectation: that, because I am not worthy to be called a son, I may remain among the servants; that you may be called my Lord; and that then my substance may be with you, though it perished with me.

“For what I dissipated in luxurious living, you will restore; you will give better garments than those I lost; you will say to my fellow servants: ‘Quickly bring forth the first robe, clothe him, put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet’” (Luke 15:22). “You will refresh me in my hunger, when the fatted calf has been killed for me.” Therefore I, who lost the substance given to me, but could not lose that substance preserved for me with you—do I not rightly say:

**“My substance is with you”?**

For I know that with you is abundant redemption, to whom we sing: “With the Lord is mercy, and with him abundant redemption” (Ps. 129:7). Thus you too are my Lord, whom I now wish to serve. And my substance is with you. For I am now among those who say: “We were saved in hope” (Rom. 8:24). Yet where the anchor of my hope is, thither I desire to leap in mind, though I am still held back by the heavy chain of my sins. Therefore I say to you, Lord:

**VERSE 9. “Deliver me from all my iniquities.”** For I know that no human being on earth, born from sin, is without sin—however much he may have crossed over sins, resisting sin. Therefore I say: Deliver me from all my iniquities: past, present, and future. From past sins, lest I return to the evils I crossed over; from present sins, lest they rule over me—for “if they have not had dominion over me, then I shall be spotless” (Ps. 18:14); from future sins, so that either they may not come, or, if they come, may find me so fortified and sheltered under your wings that they can do no harm; and so that you may overshadow me with your shoulders, and I may hope beneath your feathers.

My hope in you is also increased because you have made me a reproach to the foolish. For when you caused me to cross over earthly and vain things, then you made me a reproach to the foolish. Oh, how many reproaches and how much mockery I endured because, crossing over the evil customs of evil people, I became unlike those whom I pleased when I was like them! But if I still pleased such people, I should not be Christ’s servant. Since, however, I do not seek to please them, but now desire to please you, my God, and gladly cross over their snares, you who gave me this purpose have made me a reproach to the foolish.

Otherwise: “And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?” The patriarch Jacob said: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49:10). Before he came, Christ promised to the Jews in the Law was their expectation. For I say that Christ Jesus was a minister of the circumcision, to confirm the promises of the fathers, who awaited the Messiah promised to them. But the nations glorify God for mercy, not because Christ was promised to them, but because Christ, rejected by the Jews, was given to them.

“You know,” says the Apostle, “that when you were Gentiles, you went to mute idols as you were led” (1 Cor. 12:2). Therefore they did not then await for themselves the Son of almighty God coming in the flesh, when they went as they were led to mute idols. But now any one of them converted to God says: “What is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?”—as though he said: “I, crossing over mute idols in the time of the martyrs, what should I expect but the Lord Jesus Christ coming from heaven, and even before he comes crowning his martyrs?”

Again, in the time of heretics, I, crossing over their false teachings, what should I expect except the Lord, who will glorify confessors of the Catholic faith? Likewise, now in the last time, whether Antichrist openly reigns or the mystery of iniquity works secretly—especially in the offices of clergy forbidden by synodal decree—when I cross over the forbidden Masses of such persons and gladly hear only the Masses of Catholics, and endure reproaches for this, what amid these things is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? Does not the Lord Jesus himself destroy Antichrist by the brightness of his coming? (2 Thess. 2:8). Will he not slay with the spirit of his lips the one whose working is according to Satan’s operation, in every power and prodigies and lying signs?

Against tyrants, the strong constancy of martyrs prevailed and triumphed. Against heretics, the learned and instructive eloquence of confessors prevailed and triumphed. Against the mystery of iniquity, abundant through Antichrist as the charity of many grows cold, nothing prevails except the Spirit of Christ’s lips and the brightness of the Lord’s coming. And now, therefore, when iniquity abounds, what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? Is it not the brightness of his coming? Is it not the Spirit of his lips, about to slay Antichrist and powerfully triumph over all his impieties by his own piety?

[Col. 1411A] But lest I await such things in vain, I review the faith by which I hold you, Lord God, as guarantor: you who, against the desolations of Antichrist’s abominations, promised such consolations. I have believed your promises; and, as a pledge of certainty, I hold that your substance has been united to my substance through the mystery of the Incarnation. I partly believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation that my substance is with you. For my substance, not my guilt, was assumed by your Son, and this my substance is with you.

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1, 3). But now, at the end of the ages, “the Word was made flesh, and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father” (ibid., v. 4). In this Only-begotten One my flesh, or my substance, is with you. It is indeed less than you in nature, but not less in glory, because the glory of the Only-begotten which my substance possesses in Christ is not less than the glory of the Begetter. Nor have you, who begot this Only-begotten One and made him a little lower than the angels, taken anything of your glory from him: you who begot him in your own substance as Power and Wisdom consubstantial with you, and in my substance gave him your Power and your Wisdom most fully even in the conception according to his humanity—how much more in his exaltation, accomplished through the Resurrection and Ascension?

Therefore I say that, just as the Word was with you in the beginning in the highest glory, so now my substance is with you in the same glory; because the glory of the Word who assumes and of the human being assumed is one and the same, although the nature of Word and human being is not one and the same.

Hence every tongue rightly confesses that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:11), and is with the Father in coequal glory—indeed, in one glory, entirely without difference. Therefore the human being assumed is not to be co-adored or co-glorified with the Word who assumes him, as though one were other than the other; rather, Emmanuel is to be worshipped with one simple act of adoration, in one glory, one omnipotence, and one undivided brightness. This is the brightness which the Sun of righteousness had with the Father before the world existed in his divinity, and which he now has in his humanity, according to his own prayer to the Father: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was” (John 17:5).

Therefore, my God, I rightly say to you that my substance is in your Son with you in the same glory in which the Word was with you. All things were made through the Word (John 1:3); all things have been, or will be, restored through the human being. Without the Word nothing was made; without the human being no one is saved. What was made in the Word was life; what has been, or will be, saved in the human being—who before all things was predestined Son of God in power—was predestined. The Word was the light of human beings; the human being destroyed the death of human beings by dying, he who could truly say of himself: “O death, I shall be your death” (Hos. 13:14).

Therefore one undifferentiated adoration and glorification are rightly due to the Word who assumes and the human being assumed. Considering this, the holy Fathers at the Ephesian synod said near the end of the council:

> “If anyone dares to say that the assumed human being ought to be co-adored with God the Word and co-glorified and called God, as though one were other than the other—for the addition of the one syllable *co-* compels this understanding—and does not rather worship Emmanuel with one reverence and render one glorification, inasmuch as the Word was made flesh: let him be anathema.”

Certain crafty disputants attempt to maintain that Christ’s human nature possesses no divine glory except in the person, because it is believed to have been assumed [Col. 1412B] not into the divine nature but into the divine person. Hence, whatever divine glory is ascribed to Christ, they assign it in such a way to his divine nature and person that they exclude from it the essence of the human nature. They think they have as a patron of this assertion blessed Augustine, whose writing on the Epistle to the Ephesians they invoke at the passage, “He who descended is the same one who ascended” (Eph. 4:10). Here, they say, Augustine teaches what belongs severally to nature and to person. For he says:

> Here it must be said that reason distinguishes between a person and its substance, because one person is often composed of many substances. The substance of each thing is called the form of its substance, as the divinity of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and the bodily nature proper to each body. From these [Col. 1412C] forms, persons, and all things in which those forms exist, are generally called substances; and according to their specific diversity, they are called “this body,” “this spirit.” But something is often compounded out of things so different, as one man from body and spirit; and of him it is fitting to predicate not only the substances of both, but also their proper attributes. For a man is truly said to be both bodily colored and spiritually intelligent. Nor is the logic of truth less sound if the meaning of the words goes beyond the congruity of their proper attribution, as when one says, “the colored man understands,” since it is one and the same person who is colored in body and understands in mind. Thus Christ, since his substance is the divinity by which he is God, and all those things from which man is a substance, is rightly said not only to be [Col. 1412D] God and man, but also to be everywhere according to divinity, and to be contained in a place according to the substance of his human body, and whatever else belongs naturally and properly to it. Nor does the seemingly inconsequent joining of expressions prejudice the truth of the statements. For, because diverse substance often belongs to one person, it is not contrary to the logic of truth that a person, denoted by a name derived from one substance or from a property of it, should be said to be either another substance or a property of that other substance—for example, “God is man,” and “He who is everywhere is contained in a place.” According to this reasoning, therefore, Christ is exalted according to divinity and ascended according to humanity, according to which he who was formerly exalted descended.

In these statements, it must first be noted that, although they are attributed to blessed Augustine, they differ greatly from [Col. 1413A] his style; nor have we been able to find them in his collection of sayings on the Apostolic writings. Hence we reasonably conclude that these words [Note: [Col. 1413D] An extremely ancient hand in the margin notes: “Inserted among Master Gilbert’s glosses on the Apostle, and attributed to Blessed Augustine by his disciples.”] are not his. Yet, if they are his, they must be understood so that they are in no way found contrary to his other pronouncements issued in a Catholic sense.

For whoever thinks that this blessed man held that in Christ the person alone of the man, and not his nature also, possesses the glory of divinity—as though divinity could no more belong to human spirit and body than color belongs to mind or understanding to body, and consequently as though it could no more properly be said that man is God than that the colored man understands, as the foregoing assertion said to be Augustine’s seems to imply—such a person is unquestionably mistaken. This is shown most clearly by other writings of that blessed man.

[Col. 1413B] For in the Treatise [Note: [Col. 1414D] St Augustine, Tractate 78 on Job.] on the words of the Lord, he says: “The man Christ is called the Son of God; indeed, even his flesh alone deserved to be called so in the tomb.” Again: “Christ is God, and a rational soul, and flesh. We confess Christ in all these things and in each one of them.” Again, expounding [Note: [Col. 1414D] The same, ibid., John 14:28.] the words, “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I am going to the Father,” he says:

> Human nature ought to rejoice because it has been assumed by the only-begotten Word, so that it might be established immortal in heaven; and thus earth became exalted, so that incorruptible dust sat at the Father’s right hand. For in this manner he said that he was going to the Father.
