Who would not rejoice at this, if he so loves Christ that he rejoices that his own nature is immortal in Christ, and hopes [Col. 1413C] that this will come to pass for himself through Christ?

Again:

> When divinity came into the womb of the Virgin Mary, by that power by which it formed Adam from clay in Paradise, it fashioned for itself flesh from the substance of Mary herself; and, assuming and uniting it to itself for our salvation, God and man was born.

Again:

> The Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, brought this blessedness: that, once the form of a servant which he received from the virgin’s womb had been removed from the eyes of the flesh, the purified vision of the mind might tend toward the very form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, although he deigned to appear in the flesh; so that the Apostle, filled with that same Spirit, might say: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16). For he knows even Christ’s flesh not according to flesh but according to Spirit: he who, certain by faith rather than inquisitive through touch, recognizes the power of his Resurrection, and does not say in his heart, [Col. 1413D] “Who will ascend into heaven?”—that is, to bring Christ down—or, “Who will descend into the abyss?”—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead. “But the word,” he says, “is near you, in your mouth,” because Christ is God; and if you believe in your heart that the Lord raised him from the dead, you will be saved (Rom. 10:6–7). “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

Again, in the book of the *Retractations* he says:

> I expounded the Apostle’s Epistle to the Galatians not in excerpts, that is, omitting some things, but continuously and in its entirety. I comprised this exposition in one volume. In it, the statement, “Therefore the earlier Apostles were true, who were sent not by men but by God through a man, through Jesus Christ, namely while he was still mortal; and the last Apostle also was true, who was sent through Jesus Christ now wholly God after his Resurrection,” was said “now wholly God” because of the immortality [Col. 1414A] which he began to possess after the Resurrection, not because of the divinity that is always immortal, from which he never departed, and in which he was wholly God even when he was still about to die. The words that follow make this meaning clear. For I added: “The other Apostles were earlier, through Christ still in part man, that is, mortal; the Apostle Paul was last, through Christ now wholly [Col. 1414B] God, that is, immortal in every respect.” I said this in expounding the Apostle’s words: “not from men, nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father,” as though Christ were no longer man. For it follows: “who raised him from the dead” (Gal. 1:1), so that it might thereby appear of whom he said, “nor through a man.” Therefore Christ God is now not man by reason of immortality; but by reason of the substance of human nature, with which he ascended into heaven, even now he is “the man Christ Jesus,” mediator between God and men, because he will come in the same manner as those who saw him going into heaven saw him. The same, on the Epistle to the Philippians (2:9): “He gave the name above every name to the man, not to God, so that the only-begotten Son of God might be named together with the form [Col. 1414C] of a servant.”

Whoever has carefully understood these statements of blessed Augustine by reading them faithfully can plainly understand that so great a teacher never held what these men suppose him to have held in the aforesaid statement, as they call it. For if, as they wish, human nature is no more properly understood to possess divinity when the man is proclaimed God than a colored body is proclaimed intelligent; and if, as they maintain, the elevation and splendor of eternal divinity belong only to the person, and not also to the nature, of the assumed man—how can it stand that blessed Augustine, as we have set forth, says that dust sits at the Father’s right hand? Is not “dust” the name of the lower portion of human substance? If it is placed at the Father’s [Col. 1414D] right hand only in person, as has been said, Augustine speaks vainly and without reason when he says that we ought to rejoice, since the thing for which he advises rejoicing is not true. “Who,” he says, “would not rejoice at this, if he so loves Christ that he rejoices that his own nature is immortal in Christ, and hopes that this will come to pass for himself through Christ?”

Again, he says: “‘Now wholly God’ was said because of the immortality which he began to possess after the Resurrection, not because of divinity, always immortal, from which he never departed, and in which he was wholly God even when he was about to die.” Does not blessed Augustine, by speaking thus, plainly indicate that Christ’s human nature received such immortality that through it it was fully deified, and in such a manner as the Word has been God from eternity?

[Col. 1415A] Far be it that Christ’s human nature should be understood to possess merely such, and not greater, immortality as angels now possess and blessed human beings will possess. For although they are called gods and sons of the Most High on account of the blessed immortality conferred or to be conferred upon them, they nevertheless cannot be called gods by nature or natural sons of God. But this one—to whom, rising from the dead by his own power, eternal divinity, his own divinity, imparted its own immortality—has the name above every name: not adopted as God, but born natural God and Son of God. Therefore he is not wrongfully believed [Col. 1415B] to sit at the right hand of God the almighty Father, with divine omnipotence given to him, so that he may exercise judgment because he is the Son of Man. Divine justice requires that he also judge in the nature in which he was judged, and that he reign in every respect with him at whose right hand he sits.

This is why, before the glorification of his humanity, he declared that his disciples ought to rejoice, saying: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I am going to the Father” (John 14:28). For the highest point of our joy is that the true nature of our flesh, preceding us in that Son of Man, has sat down at God’s right hand. The venerable Ancient of Days, according to Daniel, received him when he came in the clouds of heaven, with thousands upon thousands ministering to him and ten thousand times a hundred thousand standing before him, upon that fiery throne of his; and, according to his father David in the flesh, he pronounced a fitting decree for his hoary head: “Sit at my right hand,” etc. (Ps. 109:1).

But if we do not understand this as the anthropomorphites suppose—namely, that God, like us, has a right hand here and a left hand there, and is circumscribed by human form—or if we think that God’s “sitting” itself means sitting with bent knees, “we fall into that sacrilege,” says Augustine, “in which the Apostle condemns those who exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of corruptible man.” It is wicked to place such an image of God in a Christian temple; it is far more wicked to place it in the heart, where the true temple of God is. Thus God’s being said to sit signifies not a position of limbs but judicial power. And his saying to Christ the Lord, “Sit at my right hand,” means: “Be in equality with me,” which is the same as saying, “Reign with me.” This was said to him according to his human nature, because according to it kingdom and honor were given to him, and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him.

Hence comes the passage: “Sing to the Lord, who ascended above the heaven of heavens toward the East” (Ps. 67:33–34). For Christ’s human nature surpassed the dignity of every virtue and the entire [Col. 1416A] nature of holiness so greatly that it ascended as far as the East—that is, as far as the Word personally united to it—because it left nothing beyond itself except God. It should be noted that it does not say “to the rising” or “to the one who will rise,” but “to the East.” For that ineffable generation is not considered according to past or future: the Son is begotten of the Father in an everlasting present. Nevertheless, this must also be understood locally, because he ascended above the firmament of heaven, toward the eastern region. For the phrase “as far as the East,” that is, as far as the Word personally united to him, is not said with respect to place but to the transformation of human nature—a transformation in which we too, according to the Apostle, shall be transformed according to our measure.

[Col. 1416B] Yet it was not transformed so that the true substance of flesh passed into that substance of the East; rather, glory was added and nature did not depart; passibility was absorbed, impassibility was added; mortality perished, and the immortality of the Word was acquired by the flesh. Thus waters are hardened into the likeness of stone. For crystal is the likeness of a stone, not by its own nature stone; the substance of water, hardened by frost, produces this appearance, as natural philosophers say.

Gregory reports that this comparison suitably applies to the aforementioned transformation of flesh in his exposition of Ezekiel, when he says: [Note: [Col. 1415D] Book I, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, Homily 7.]

> The body of our Redeemer, because until death it was subject to suffering, was in one respect like water: for by being born, growing, becoming weary, hungering, thirsting, [Col. 1416C] and dying, it passed through the moments of time up to his Passion. But because through the glory of his Resurrection it acquired strength from that very corruption unto the power of incorruption, it was hardened from water in the manner of crystal, so that in him there was both the same nature and no longer the mutability of corruption which had been. Thus water was changed into crystal when the weakness of its corruption was made firm through his Resurrection unto the stability of incorruption.

It should be noted that, although crystal is exceedingly beautiful in appearance, it is said in this sense that “the appearance of crystal was terrible,” because our Redeemer, one and the same, will appear serene to the just but terrible to the unjust. Therefore, just as water is hardened into the likeness of a stone without the loss of its substance or [Col. 1416D] quantity of substance, but only by the change of its formerly flowing quality into solidity, so the assumed man to whom we sing ascended, without the loss of substance and with the number and quantity of his members preserved. First, when he rose, he ascended—not locally—to conformity with and immutability of the East, that is, of the Divinity of which we spoke above, with only that flowing quality entirely absorbed by which he feared, could grow weary and be afraid, and said, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38), and other such things. Secondly, [Col. 1417A] he ascended also locally, in the sight of the Apostles, above the firmament of heaven, as stated above, toward the eastern region.

But where and how the Lord’s body is in heaven is, Augustine says in the book *On the Catholic Faith*, an exceedingly curious and superfluous question to ask. One need only believe that it is in heaven. It does not belong to our frailty to investigate the secrets of the heavens. Yet those disputants who, as they suppose, by scrutinizing everything see invisible things and comprehend incomprehensible things, ridicule the simplicity of the Christian faith. In it we sing, and in singing, with Idithun, pass beyond all things placed beneath God; and in the highest glory of his very divinity we venerate human substance, saying: “And now, what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?” What, I say, is my expectation, I who am a servant? Is it not the Lord? Is it not that I may enter into the joy of my Lord? But how comes this to me, a little servant, that the glory or joy of my Lord should come to me? Clearly from this: that, O my Lord, my substance is with you; that in supreme glory, O King of eternal glory, God the Father, my substance is with you. It is beneath you indeed according to essence, but with you according to glory, just as in the beginning the Word was with you—not beneath you according to nature and glory. For what is it to be with you but to be equal in your glory? This was the Word, God, with you in the beginning. But now also, at the end of the ages, propitiation is with you, where the God-man intercedes for me: consubstantial with me [Col. 1417C] insofar as he is man, consubstantial with you insofar as he is God. He is propitiation and propitiator insofar as he is man; he is the giver of propitiation insofar as he is God. Therefore, because in him my substance is with you, appearing before your face for me, Idithun—or for me, the whole Catholic Church—you are appeased through him.

**VERSE 9. Deliver me from all my iniquities.** For though I desire to pass beyond all vanity, my iniquities hinder me like the heaviest fetters. But deliver me from all my iniquities, so that, like a roe or a young stag, I may, with your help, pass beyond the thickets of every vanity. While I passed through the image, content with freedom of choice, I who was made in your image, O God, contracted many iniquities by remaining in the region of dissimilarity, [Col. 1417D] because, having been made in the image of eternal reason, I refused to possess the likeness of eternal wisdom and goodness. Though retaining free choice, I wholly lost free counsel and free good pleasure; for I remained free from necessity indeed, but, fettered by sin and deprived through misery, I lacked the twofold freedom of counsel and good pleasure. But now, wishing to pass beyond all vain things, I perceive that I am weighed down by sins and punishments contracted through free choice. Therefore I cry to you, the all-powerful deliverer: “Deliver me from all my iniquities.”

“Iniquity” is properly spoken of where a human being does not make equal those things which God makes equal. Now God is three and one, in triune unity and unitary Trinity; and in this Trinity there is no inequality, because in the triune God nothing is greater or less, but the Son is equal to the Father, and the Holy Spirit equal to the Father and the Son. Hence Arius was rightly condemned for dogmatically declaring, in his destructive error, the Son unequal to the Father; and Macedonius for declaring the Holy Spirit unequal to the Father and the Son.

This triune God, in his eternal counsel, purposed to form man in his image and likeness: namely, so that the expression of the divine image should be in human free choice, while the twofold likeness of divine wisdom and goodness should be in free counsel and free good pleasure. Thus in man there would be a threefold freedom—of choice, counsel, and good pleasure—from necessity, [Col. 1418B] sin, and misery, in such equality that, as freely as through choice he discerned good and evil, so freely through counsel he would choose good and reject evil, and likewise through the good pleasure of his goodness would lack every burden of misery. Thus he would represent the image of the eternal and supreme Trinity in choice, and its likeness in counsel and good pleasure.

But, made in God’s image, he was to advance at creation itself toward the likeness through the reason present in that image. Had he used it rightly, he would have advanced to God’s likeness without the intervention of iniquity and would have possessed equally the three freedoms already mentioned: as free from sin through counsel and from misery through good pleasure as he had received free choice free from necessity. But because he abused freedom of choice, iniquity thereupon crept in for the sinner, because equality among these three freedoms did not remain. For while freedom of choice remains wholly intact, human beings have little freedom of counsel and good pleasure in this world, and none at all in hell, as was shown above.

Therefore, while there is time in this life for this iniquity or inequality to be destroyed and for the supreme equity and equality of the three human freedoms to come about, one must unceasingly entreat through the continual sacrifice of the heart to be delivered from iniquities and to become as free from sin and punishment as one is free from necessity. Therefore, let one who formerly passed through in the image alone, [Col. 1418D] but possessed the divine likeness less fully, especially in the region of dissimilarity, now recover [Note: [Col. 1417D] The manuscript reads *recapesset*, “let him recover.”] equity by wholly rejecting iniquity or inequality. This inequality is found in the fact that a human being, walking in the image and passing into the region of dissimilarity, has reason intact but does not have wisdom or goodness intact. The Father draws to the Son when, by his gift, reason leads to wisdom. The Father and Son give their gift, namely the Holy Spirit, when wise reason in a human being receives goodness. The more the likeness of divine wisdom and goodness increases in one created in the image of God, [Col. 1419A] the more one is delivered from iniquity, so that likeness may become equal to image. Then man no longer passes in the image alone into hell, but, having advanced into God’s likeness, leaps over hell and leaps over the world like a roe or a young stag—like him of whom it is said in the Song of Songs: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains and skipping over the hills” (Song 2:8).

Let him also become like the wise man building his house upon a rock. In becoming like the wise man, he recovers freedom of counsel; in becoming like the builder, he recovers freedom of good pleasure. For both truly knowing in counsel and being able to do what is good and pleasing in a building founded on rock are signified: one who is likened to a wise man takes good counsel for himself, [Col. 1419B] and one who builds firmly shows that he has understood what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God. But the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God is fulfilled in man when that iniquity is utterly destroyed by which God’s likeness is now found in man to be less than his image. Because there will truly be no equality—or inequality—of image and likeness, let Idithun say: “Deliver me, Lord, from all my iniquities.”

Many iniquities arise from the iniquity already mentioned. Since man passed from Paradise in the image, having lost God’s likeness, there is also this iniquity: even when the spirit is ready to pass beyond all vain things, the flesh is weak—though, had man not sinned, it would be as ready as the spirit. Again, there is another iniquity where equity or equality ought to exist. Just as we presented our members as slaves to impurity and iniquity leading to iniquity, when we were slaves of sin and free from righteousness, so now our members must be presented as slaves to righteousness unto sanctification, that we may serve God free from sin. But insofar as our present zeal for righteousness is less than our former zeal for sinning, there is no equity or equality in our zeal, because our repentance is not as fruitful as our perversity was ruinous. To those already freed from this iniquity the Apostle speaks, saying: “For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. But now, set free from sin and made servants of God, [Col. 1419D] you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Rom. 6:20–22).

Again, when the Lord says in the Law, “You shall not have different weights in your bag; let your measure be fair and your sextary fair” (Deut. 25:13), we commit a great iniquity against such equity when we have weight and weight, greater and lesser, and do not weigh our own case and our neighbor’s upon an equal balance. We desire God to give us a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, yet we do not give such a measure to needy neighbors even when our means suffice; if our means failed, generous intention alone would suffice. Would that there might at least be equity in our intention, so that we should wish to assist a needy neighbor in the same way [Col. 1420A] that we desire God to assist us: with the same measure, the same modius, and the same sextary!

For those who deserve to hear through the six works of mercy, “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you” (Matt. 25:34), have given a good sextary filled with six works of mercy. Therefore they shall receive a full recompense, justice and equity requiring that the same measure be measured back to them by which they measured out to Christ in his least ones: feeding, giving drink, clothing, receiving, visiting, and comforting.

Again, it is worthy and just, equitable and salutary, that we should always and everywhere give thanks to him and show ourselves grateful to him who freely created us when we did not exist, and redeemed us at a great price when we were lost. Since we are purchased servants, bought at a precious price, it is equitable that we should be precious. Therefore we commit a great iniquity against our Redeemer if we do not render an equal return to him who bought us. “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115:12). If I give myself, it is little, because the price given for me was exceedingly great. Yet I know what I shall do: “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (ibid., v. 13). Thus equality will rightly be made between the price given for me and the precious cup offered by me to him. If I do this, I shall in some measure preserve equity, especially if, after receiving the cup of salvation, I call upon the Lord’s name. For “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Acts 2:21).

[Col. 1420C] There is also great iniquity or inequality when we want our debts to be wholly forgiven us, but are unwilling wholly to forgive our debtors. Since, then, there are so many iniquities in human and worldly life, I, Idithun, desiring rightly to pass beyond this, say to you: “My God, deliver me from all my iniquities,” establishing me in supreme equity, so that I may have counsel as free as choice, and flesh and spirit equally ready, according to the words: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Ps. 83:3). Again: “My soul has thirsted for you; how greatly has my flesh also [thirsted] for you” (Ps. 62:2).

Let my modius be fair and my sextary fair, so that equality may come about when [Col. 1420D] my abundance supplies others’ need and others’ abundance mine. Let me also receive the cup of salvation in such a way that, offering it to the Redeemer, I may give thanks, as is worthy and just, equitable and salutary, so that, preserving equity or equality in all things, I may be hindered by no iniquity in passing beyond the world with its vanity.

I confess to you, my God, that I deserved rebuke for my great and many iniquities; and therefore I give you thanks because through the tongues of dogs you healed me, like another Lazarus, grievously ulcerated and full of the sores of sins. Yet he was well off, because dogs came and licked his sores. They licked, not bit, and therefore healed. But my sores were not merely licked by good dogs: evil dogs also tore them with their teeth by reproaching, slandering, and reviling me. At times I could have answered such people; but silently I considered that they could do nothing against me unless you ordained it. Therefore I became altogether mute and did not open my mouth, because you did this. What did you do? You gave me as a reproach to the foolish. Therefore, although in other matters which they said I was ready and prepared to answer and to refute those resisting Catholic truth, when it came to revilings, I observed that you had made me a reproach to the foolish.

**VERSE 10. I became mute and did not open my mouth, because you did it.** By your just judgment, not without mercy, you cut away through their tongues the rottenness of my wounds; for “their tongue is a sharp sword” [Col. 1421B] (Ps. 56:5). By their teeth, like a physician with surgical instruments, you probed the suppurations of my sores; for “their teeth are weapons and arrows” (ibid.). Rightly, therefore, amid these things I became mute, because you did it.

Blessed Gregory, in his exposition of Job, says on this passage: [Note: [Col. 1421D] *Morals on Job*, Book 23, ch. 18.]

> “I became mute and did not open my mouth, because you did it.” A man under the lash, considering that God is greater than himself, submits himself in everything that he suffers to God’s judgment, whose superiority he does not doubt. What he suffers from one better than himself he believes just, even if he does not know the grounds of that justice. Whoever is struck for sin, if he does not resist by murmuring, begins thereby to be more just, because he does not accuse the justice of the one who strikes him. Man was created beneath God, and returns to the order of his condition when he sets before himself the equity of his Judge, even equity which he does not understand; so that, when he considers the Creator’s power, the swelling of his mind subsides through remembrance of his condition. Hence the prophet David, when compelled by the weight of a blow to burst into utterance, recollected himself by considering his condition and said: “I became mute and did not open my mouth, because you made me” (Ps. 38:10). For he weighed the order of his condition and found the justice of the stroke: because he who kindly created him when he did not exist would surely strike him, once he existed, only justly.

Another interpretation: “I became mute,” or “I became deaf,” as another translation has it; I kept silent as though I had not heard the reproaches made against me, guarding myself both from undisciplined contention against men and from murmuring against you, my God, my maker, because you made both me and my scourge—you who “fashion toil in commandment” (Ps. 93:20). You fashion toil, or pain, into a commandment. For by *fingere* we mean to compose; hence we call those who fashion clay *figuli*, potters. And you, our maker or fashioner, who fashioned our substance, still fashion and form the pain of your scourge into a commandment, so that through it you may instruct man as by a commandment. Therefore I became mute from contention and murmuring, but not from prayer: indeed, touched by scourges I pray more attentively and say:

**VERSE 11. Remove your blows from me.** “Your hands, [Col. 1422A] O Lord, made me and fashioned me wholly round about; and do you so suddenly cast me down?” (Job 10:8). “Do not contend with me in great strength” (Job 23:6), because:

**VERSE 12. I have failed under the strength of your hand.** It is written that Moses’ hands were heavy (Exod. 17:12), because the Law, severely striking sinners, was given through him. Under this strength and weight I, Idithun, failed before grace. But now, because “grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17), “Remove your blows from me”; remove, I pray, the heavy hands of Moses, and do not press me down with the weight of your greatness so that I fail utterly, as I have already partly failed under the strength of your hand powerfully striking with rebukes. Whether these are administered through the just or [Col. 1422B] through the unjust, they themselves are altogether just, because:

“You rebuked man for iniquity.” For when, by your ordering, either a just man rebuked me in mercy or an unjust man in malice or harshness, your rebuke, administered through them, was just, because you rebuked man for iniquity. There are sinners who “are not scourged with men”; therefore pride holds them fast (Ps. 72:5). But you rebuked for iniquity the man who passes beyond the heights of pride, so that he might advance more in humility. When humility is perfected, you spare him—for you resist the proud but give grace to the humble.

Therefore, when I say, “Remove your blows from me,” I mean it as though I said: Make me perfectly humble, one to whom you ought to give grace, [Col. 1422C] not proud, one to whom you ought to administer your customary blows; for you always resist the proud, strike those inclined to exalt themselves, bring down the mighty from their seat, and scatter the proud in the imagination of their hearts.

In the Hebrew it reads: “By rebukes for iniquity you rebuked the man.” There is one who is rebuked unto condemnation—namely the devil, and every obstinate person—who is not corrected when rebuked. But you rebuked a man, or human being, using rational counsel, for his corrigible iniquity by rebukes, that is, by instructions, so that through the rebuke he might receive correction.

“And you made his soul waste away like a spider.” This is the manner of instruction: you made waste away like a spider the soul of him whom you rebuked. A spider, while it weaves empty webs to catch flies, dries up, is disemboweled, and dies. So too, while a person labors in gathering temporal possessions, he is wholly disemboweled, dries up from the moisture of virtues, and dies. This is recognized as taking place amid the scourges of divine rebuke. Therefore I say: “By rebukes for iniquity you rebuked man,” and through this he recognized that he himself is the one whom you caused to waste away—that is, whose soul you permitted to waste away like a spider.

Alternatively: In the Hebrew it reads: “And you made his precious things like a moth.” A moth makes precious things and costly clothing worthless; so you have made man, created [Col. 1423A] for the blessed and desirable glory of eternity, worthless through the weakness of corruption and mortality. Or: you have made his desirable things such that they are like a moth to man. For if he is conscious of praiseworthy and desirable deeds or virtues, such consciousness secretly and silently, through the prompting of empty glory, demolishes him like a moth—especially if he has stored up his desirable things on earth, allowing his left hand to know what his right has done; that is, mingling the desire for vain glory with a holy intention or action. Wishing his disciples to beware of such a moth, Truth says: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys” (Matt. 6:20). Again: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matt. 6:3). Heaven [Col. 1423B] is named from concealment, because what is in heaven is hidden from the sight of human beings. Therefore we store up in heaven when we conceal our praiseworthy deeds—not so that our neighbours may not see our works for their edification and God’s glory, but lest we desire them to be known so that we may thereby appear praiseworthy. Otherwise we shall have no reward with God, because the moth of empty glory consumes our desirable things. Since this happens by God’s just judgment, it is rightly said to him: “And you made his precious things like a moth.” Or, “you made his desirable things like a moth”: they are turned into a most harmful moth for the person who seeks, from those desirable things themselves, the empty glory of human praise. This moth, to be sure, does not harm one who lays up treasure in heaven—that is, one who reverently awaits the heavenly, hidden, or secret judgment, not knowing whether there he is judged worthy of hatred or love, especially since divine judgment concerning a good or evil end is still pending, and a person does not perfectly know before his end, even though he may often pray: “Make known to me, Lord, my end.”

Alternatively: “And you made his soul like a spider.” In the constitution of a human being, composed of soul and flesh, the soul is more precious than the flesh. Thus, by that element of a human being which is more precious, one may denote and signify his more precious and praiseworthy manner of life—especially contemplation, or the praiseworthy exercise of spiritual offices. This, like a soul, gives life to lower and earthly works and offices, in whatever person, congregation, [Col. 1423D] or even universal Church it may be joined or adhere through the bond of charity, administering life to them and ordering them according to itself. This soul, however, is made like a spider because, unless precaution is taken, it bites and infuses venom; whence the swelling of empty glory grows violently. And while the wasting sickness of pride lies hidden within, the soul itself accordingly wastes away like a spider, while spiritual exercises too in a person’s life are emptied and vanish through empty and vain glory, so that they serve not as a life-giving soul but as a death-dealing spider. Therefore it is rightly said: “You caused [him] to waste away”; or, as the Hebrew reads: “You made his soul like a spider or a moth.”

The spider, which occurs in the translation of the Seventy Interpreters [the Septuagint], [Col. 1424A] bites quickly, and a person thus envenomed cannot escape swift death unless suitable medicine comes to the rescue. Yet a spider’s venom is not like the incurable venom of an asp, because the sin of self-exaltation or boasting is sometimes healed by a single blow, or is at times easily cured by secret or public satisfaction. But the moth, which occurs in the Hebrew, destroys precious clothing by slow and prolonged ruin unless it is vigorously shaken out. Likewise, a moth-eaten head does not cease to be disfigured once a moth has attacked it, unless perhaps it is washed and scraped with constant combing. Hence the Seventy aptly signified by the spider an evident pride that is easily curable. But the Hebrew truth denotes by the moth a slow and hidden pride, one which does not show itself in the swellings of boastfulness and is therefore [Col. 1424B] less easily healed. Whether it is discovered in the garment—that is, in one’s action—or in the head—that is, in one’s intention—the garment must be vigorously shaken, lest it be harmed by the moth; and such a head must be washed with tears and combed with continual confessions, lest it remain moth-eaten and by its own ugliness make the whole body ugly. Therefore, when you fast, lest you be harmed by this moth, “anoint your head with oil and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. 6:17–18). Oil floats above every liquid; and eternal reward surpasses and is more precious than all the world’s riches, and all things desired in this age cannot be compared with it. [Col. 1424C] Therefore we anoint the head with purest oil when we perform a good work solely with eternal reward in view. And in our head thus anointed no moth has a place among our desirable and praiseworthy works, for which a reward is laid up in heaven.

This is why, when a man’s head is sanctified, it is either shaved or anointed with holy oil, as in the case of priest and king: for the moth rather than the spider lies in wait for strong and manly action. Against its injury, the intention—like a man’s head—is kept sound and beautiful if it is washed with tears: not only the head, but also the bed upon which the head reclines. This happens whenever a holy man can truthfully say: “Every night I shall wash my bed” (Ps. 6:[Col. 1424D] 7). A man’s head is also drenched with priestly or royal anointing when a strong action is performed solely for the honour of the supreme priest and king, and the desire for private glory, like a gnawing moth, is altogether excluded.

But when a woman is sanctified, her head is covered with a sacramental veil; her hair too has been given to her as a covering, because a less strong action requires less protection against pride, which lies in wait for her not as a moth but as a spider. And we know that a spider is shut out by the gentlest covering and driven away by a light touch or even a breath. It lies in wait not for the heel, as a serpent crawling on the ground does, but for the head from above, that is, while hanging down. Therefore a black veil, the sign of humility, is placed upon the head [Col. 1425A] of a consecrated woman. It is by no means appropriate to married women, because, while they experience this sort of tribulation of the flesh—conceiving in distress and giving birth in pain—they need footwear against the serpentine perversity of fornication, which lies in wait for their heel, more than a head-covering against the spider of pride. Since that spider especially lies in wait for holy and good works so that they may perish, it is not married women so much as religious women who fight against it; and they do not wear the veil of humility in vain. A veil is also placed upon married women at their betrothal, certainly not black as a sign of humility but white as a sign of consolation, namely that they may not despair but firmly hope that they can be saved, as the Apostle says, through the bearing of children, if they continue [Col. 1425B] in faith (1 Tim. 2:15). I have chosen to weave these remarks in because of the difference in the assaults represented in the psalm now by the moth, now by the spider. In meditating on this psalm, let the reader take from these differing interpretations what pleases him more, while guarding against both spider and moth.

Alternatively: You rebuked the proud man and through scourges made him humble; this is apparent from the fact that you caused his soul to waste away like a spider. Surely you showed him that his soul is frail like a spider, which is so wasted that, lightly touched, it falls and cannot even stand against a human breath. Hence the wise David, sitting in his seat, who killed eight hundred in a single assault, is nevertheless written to have been like the tenderest little worm of wood (2 Sam. [Col. 1425C] 23:8), namely because you, God, rebuked that man for the iniquity which he committed against Uriah and his wife, and caused his soul to waste away like a spider. Thus, as a spider suspended on high makes fine threads, and in making them expels its own entrails until it is wholly dried out, so a human being touched by divine rebuke and wasting away—because he shrinks in horror from his conscience, as from a wasting discharge resembling a spider’s entrails—expels it through confession and prayer, and is wholly suspended on high, until through true repentance he is dried out and mortified. The Apostle wished his disciples to be mortified in this way, saying: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth: fornication, [Col. 1425D] impurity, lust, evil desire, and covetousness” (Col. 3:5).

“Yet every human being is vainly troubled.” Even if a person dries himself out, disembowels himself, and mortifies himself by every exercise of repentance, while a human being passes through in an image in the land of unlikeness, he is vainly troubled, desiring to fill the belly of his avarice with husks, the food of pigs. He is vainly troubled, I say, because from that from which he wishes to be sated and filled he will never be sated, gathering and not knowing for whom he leaves it. Therefore, because he is then vainly and emptily troubled in avarice—which sometimes does not obtain what it desires and cannot even keep what it has acquired—by a just judgment it comes about that, rebuked for iniquity and wasting away like a spider, he sometimes fears even what need not be feared. And thus he is vainly [Col. 1426A] troubled in his uncertain and as yet unanswered prayer, in which he said above: “Make known to me, Lord, my end.” For however strong he may be in virtues, so long as a person does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or love, he is rightly troubled—sometimes vainly, sometimes not vainly. For one who fears things to be feared is not vainly troubled; but one who fears things not to be feared is vainly troubled. Peter was vainly troubled when amazement surrounded him at the catch of fish, so that he said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:3). He feared what need not be feared: he feared the Saviour’s presence, whereas it is rather the Saviour’s absence that a sinner should fear. For if you consider yourself a sinner, says a certain wise man, you must not drive the Lord away from yourself. If, like a spider, you waste away in the bitterness of a contrite spirit, in [Col. 1426B] the bitterness of your soul, do not be vainly troubled so as to fear what need not be feared—so as to fear undertaking the paths of a stricter life and, as though in confusion, to have no counsel, imitating those who are vainly troubled when they die and fear not death but life. If, melted away by the fear of the Lord, your soul weaves delicate meditations and works from above throughout, after the likeness of the Lord’s tunic woven from the top throughout, like a spider which works bodily on high and not upon the ground, and which is made thin by the discharge of its inner entrails, do not be troubled through distrust of your salvation. Rather, have confidence and say to your soul thus melted away: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” (Ps. 41:12). Many such consolations exist for the soul that is wasting away. [Col. 1426C] “Yet every rational and sensible human being is vainly troubled”—vainly, that is, sometimes without cause, as long as he does not know his end.

A *diapsalma* [musical or textual pause] is inserted here, because there is a transition and leap from the complaint and lament over uncertainty concerning the end to the petition in which Idithun asks, before he departs, that there be made known to him, if not his end, at least his refreshment. Thus he may no longer be vainly troubled, but may, before he departs, be assured of the remission of sins; refreshed after many anxieties and secure of a good end, he may await his end with joy. He therefore says:

**VERSE 13.** “Hear my prayer, O Lord, and my supplication.” Above, while praying, I said: “Make known [Col. 1426D] to me, Lord, my end.” When I prayed this, I received one thing instead of another: for knowledge or certainty of my end, I received knowledge that I am uncertain, knowledge of the frailty of my substance, which is as nothing before you. Thus, yes thus, I had to be instructed through lesser knowledge toward greater knowledge: through knowledge of myself toward knowledge of you, O God, who are my end. Therefore I was not delayed in my first petition without reason, because desire grew through delay; and, increasing and melting into tears, it again bursts forth in prayer when I say: “Hear my prayer, O Lord, and my supplication”—the prayer by which in pious vows I seek a good end; the supplication by which I do not cease to avert an evil end, as long as I fear it. I pray that the good end may come; I deprecate the evil end, lest it come. Therefore you, to whom every will speaks even in silence, whether it prays or supplicates, hear my prayer and my supplication. And because tears too have their own voice before you:

[Col. 1427A] “Hear with your ears my tears.” Although I have passed over many evils, nevertheless, so long as I do not know whether I can pass beyond an evil end, I prefer weeping to laughter. I weep in the night of this ignorance, in which I cannot see my end; and the tears are upon my jaws rather than upon my cheeks. For my cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove, because, since the will or intention is denoted in the cheeks—so that from the clear indication of the will found in the cheeks, that place of the cheeks is itself called the countenance—after I passed beyond the foulnesses of this [Col. 1427B] world, my will and intention are beautiful like those of a turtledove, the most chaste of birds. Having once cut away impurities, I never again will or intend to repeat them, but will and intend to remain chaste, living soberly, righteously, and godly in this age. And thus, as I hope, I have beautiful cheeks, although there is still found in my jaws such ugliness of gluttony that I rightly shed tears on its account whenever I am found to have exceeded far beyond the measure owed to necessity, even to the vice of drunken excess or indigestion. Since this weighs down every person walking in God’s way, it especially hinders me, Idithun, from being able with a lively leap to pass beyond those walking in good action into holy contemplation. Hence tears are sometimes in my jaws, [Col. 1427C] because although willing is present to me—to eat and drink wisely, not as much as appetite demands but as much as necessity reasonably requires—I do not find the power to accomplish it.

Again: as I said at the beginning of the psalm, although I have set a guard upon my mouth, I still do not yet have such discreet restraint of speech that I do not sometimes say what should be kept silent and keep silent what should be said. My jaw is so undisciplined that it moves without discretion in eating or speaking. Hence I have much grief and continual tears, with which I strike at your ears, merciful God. Therefore hear with your ears my tears, especially those which are in my jaws, so that you may grant me to pass beyond the faults of an undisciplined jaw. Restrain my jaws with bit and bridle from gluttony and talkativeness, the two vices that will not draw near to you. Oh, if you, most merciful one, would answer me thus praying with good and consoling words! Oh, if you would say to my soul: “I am your salvation!” (Ps. 34:3). Because I desire your consolation in the exile of this present life, I say:

“Do not be silent, for I am a stranger with you and a sojourner.” Although Joseph’s brothers were strangers in Egypt, they were not altogether sojourners there, where through their brother’s power and mercy they were safe together, he saying to them: “Do not fear; I will feed you and your little ones” (Gen. 50:21). Yet while he was still silent, speaking more harshly through an interpreter, they were truly sojourners and strangers. For though recognized by him, they did not recognize him, when, bearing great anxiety and fearing greater things, they said to one another: “We rightly suffer these things because we sinned against our brother, seeing the distress of his soul when he begged us, and we did not listen; therefore this tribulation has come upon us” (Gen. 42:21). These brothers did not know the outcome of the matter; therefore they were anxious while Joseph was silent and did not reveal who he was. At last Joseph spoke, saying: “I am Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt” (Gen. 45:4). Before he added consoling words to these words, they were indeed somewhat dismayed; but they were immediately cheered when he said: “Do not take it hard that you sold me into these regions; do not fear. You intended evil against me, [Col. 1428B] but God turned it to good, as you see at present” (ibid., 45:5; 50:20).

Therefore, just as those brothers were sorrowful while Joseph was silent, but were cheered when he spoke, so I too, Idithun, when you, great Joseph, who rule throughout the land of Egypt, are silent toward me, am rightly saddened; and because I hope for the consolation of your speech, I say to you: “Do not be silent toward me, for I am a stranger with you and a sojourner in this land of Egypt, with you, the true Joseph.” I am a stranger and a sojourner with you who are merciful, with you who repay good for evils, with you who are utterly forgetful of injuries done to you, if you see a person truly repentant and confessing his sins without deceit, as did those who said: “We rightly suffer these things because we sinned against our brother” [Col. 1428C] (Gen. 42:21). I beseech you, do not be silent, for I am a stranger with you and a sojourner, as all my fathers were. Those fathers and patriarchs were strangers and sojourners in Egypt, whether before they came to know Joseph, or after Joseph’s death, when a new king arose in Egypt who did not know Joseph.

Alternatively: I am a stranger and a sojourner, because “while we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:6), as were all my fathers, for whom this world was exile and heaven their homeland. Or: I am a stranger with you, not with the devil; because I do not wish to be in the company of those strangers who come to the devil and remain with him, but of those who come to you, O God, and wish to remain with you. Thus: I am a stranger [Col. 1428D] with you and a sojourner, as all my fathers were, who were sojourners in this world and therefore departed from it; hence it is certain that I too shall depart. But I fear to depart unless beforehand there is granted to me a full and certain remission of sins. I therefore say:

**VERSE 14.** “Forgive me, that I may be refreshed, before I depart.” I have sinned against you more than Joseph’s brothers sinned against him. Forgive me, therefore, that I may be refreshed, as they were refreshed after forgiveness and pardon, relieved from the heat of their hearts and the heavy burden of their anxieties. Forgive me my debts, as I also forgive my debtors. For them I desire true repentance and generous, swift pardon, seeking no revenge upon them—except perhaps such punishment as is necessary and corrective for them, so that they cannot be corrected and saved without it. Forgive me, that I may be refreshed by the removal of temptations and the giving to me of abundant consolations, before I depart from this life and no longer exist. Some have departed this life so as to return again and be in this life, as we read of those who were raised. But I consider that I shall depart in such a way that I shall not be in this life; therefore I ask to be refreshed before I depart and no longer exist. For if I leave this life with sins, I shall neither be in this life any longer nor in that true being which is being with God. Therefore forgive me, my God, before I depart and no longer exist. This is like a thief conscious that he would receive what his deeds deserve if he were thrust into a prison from which he would never again emerge, saying to the judge before he enters [Col. 1429B] the prison: “O Judge, forgive me before I go into prison and no longer exist, if I go there where there is no good or true being.” Yet the accused would not go into prison if his debt were forgiven. So I also, Idithun, fearing that I may go there in debt, where I shall no longer exist if I arrive there unrefreshed before I depart—or die—ask that full and certain pardon be given me. I know certainly that, if I depart refreshed after receiving forgiveness, I shall go there where I shall henceforth exist eternally in true and blessed being, whence there will be no further need to leap elsewhere. For there the number of days which exists will not pass away but remain stable forever; and the blessed person will know his own end, beyond which he will not wish to pass or ask anything else, having made the happy leap to that place where the end of every consummation will be he himself who says: “I am α and ω [alpha and omega]” (Rev. 22:13).

Glory to the Father, who so created man in his own image that he may pass through in that image and never lose it in any way. Glory to the Son, who is the end of the human being so passing through an image, so that he may fit the divine likeness also to the divine image in himself through conformity to eternal [Col. 1430B] wisdom and the brightness of divine goodness. Glory to the Holy Spirit, whose work is that forgiveness and refreshment desired in the psalm where God is told: “Forgive me, that I may be refreshed, before I depart.” Glory be to the Trinity reigning over all things; may faith in it be most manifest in us through works. Amen.

# PSALM XXXIX

[Col. 1429]

[Col. 1429B] “I waited patiently for the Lord,” etc. The sixth *periocha* [section] in this psalm now has a beautiful heading. Here the Prophet returns to the beginning of our faith, that is, to Christ’s passion, as this verse especially indicates: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you have made ears ready for me. In the head of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will; O my God, I have desired it.” “You did not desire,” he says, “the sacrifice and offering which the Law commanded to be offered; but you have made ears ready for me,” that is, you gave me understanding so that I alone might perfectly understand why you did not desire those things and what you desired more. Then I said: “Behold, I come.” Behold, incarnate, I enter upon the way of obedience, prepared to do your will, as it is written in the head of the book—that is, as it was ordained from eternity in your wisdom, personally united to me, when it was then preordaining the ancient counsel which was to be fulfilled at the end of the ages, namely in the sixth age of the world, which is the end and consummation of times. This end is marked in the title, which is as follows:

**(VERSE 1.) UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID**

Although by “unto the end” the intention of the psalmist is always directed to Christ, nevertheless, speaking in different ways, he now treats Christ’s passion, now his resurrection, now the New Testament given through Christ, now the Catholic faith inspired by him. Here, however, “unto the end” signifies the fullness of time in which the New Testament was given, and into which the Old is shown to have been transformed, with this purpose: that, abandoning the superstitions of idols and [Col. 1430B] of the old Law, which brought nothing to perfection, we may love the New Testament, the Testament that brings to completion.

The whole Christ speaks, first showing that the Church awaited and received God and the New Testament from him. Secondly, he enumerates the wonders performed by God, at the words: “I have proclaimed.” And because it was difficult to recall Jews from their customary ceremonies and gentiles from idolatry to the confirmation of the New Testament, the Prophet employs the authority of the Fathers, who foretold it, such as Abraham and others. He also employs the testimony of Christ and of the universal Church, which he declares to have been fulfilled. Christ therefore speaks in the person of his members:

**VERSE 2.** “Waiting, I waited”: that is, I waited continually in the promises of the prophets, not for the Law, not for a human being who can deceive and be deceived, who also needs a physician, but for the Lord, who, though he delays, nevertheless saves. Hence it fittingly follows: “And the Lord did not turn away, but kindly inclined”—not *upon* me, but *toward* me. Not upon me in order to destroy me, for “his face is against those who do evil,” but toward me in order to benefit me.

**VERSE 3.** And he who hid himself from the prophets heard my prayers, so that in the New Testament that might shine for me which many prophets wished to see and did not see. “And he brought me out of the pit of misery,” that is, out of hell and the depth of carnal desires; “and out of the mire of dregs,” that is, evil works, which foul the feet, stink, plunge one into this pit, hold one there, and are cheap as dregs in comparison with wine. In this pit and mire are idol-worshippers, such as pagans, and lovers of earthly things, such as Jews.

Blessed Pope Gregory, discussing Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 1431D] Book I, Homily 9.], says in this passage: “Whoever among us still exults in pride, yet now sees something of the fear of eternity, ought to fall through repentance. And when, subtly recognizing our weakness, we lie humble, we ought to rise through the consolation of the divine word to stronger works. And when we now stand firm in the solidity of good works, it is necessary that from that by which we correct ourselves we should now, by preaching, call back others also. For one who lies fallen is not commanded to proceed to preaching, lest a weak person destroy in deed what he can build by word. Therefore the Prophet rightly, after asserting that he had been brought out of the mire of dregs [Col. 1431B] and seeing that his feet were set upon a rock, asserts that a new song was put into his mouth. For first he is brought out of the mire of perversity so that his feet may be made firm upon the rock; and after he has fixed the feet and steps of good work upon the rock, then he receives the song of preaching, so that he may sing a hymn to God both in deeds and in words. Thus Saul, while proudly proceeding to Damascus, lay prostrate at the Redeemer’s voice. Although he was to become a preacher, he did not immediately hear that he should preach what he had seen; rather, as he lay there, he was told: ‘Enter the city, and it will be told you what you must do’ (Acts 9:7). Thus, while lying he could hear only this: that, once risen, he might learn; and once risen he learned this: that he might preach what he had learned.”

Alternatively: I, Abraham, waiting, waited for the Lord, who promised me that all tribes of the earth would be blessed in my seed. The Lord himself inclined to me and heard my prayers, and brought me out of the pit of misery, because after bringing me out from Ur of the Chaldeans he made me rich not only in possessions but, what is greater, in blessings, which he spread abroad through my seed. I beheld that seed as a solid rock in the foundation of the Church when I rejoiced to see his day: I saw and rejoiced, giving thanks to him who set my feet upon a rock—that is, who established my faith and hope in Christ. And he directed my steps, not only while I journeyed in Gerar or Egypt because of the severity of famine, but much more gloriously he directed my steps—that is, those of my seed journeying in Egypt and returning from there to the promised land under the leadership of Moses and Aaron. Then indeed

**VERSE 4.** “He put into my mouth,” that is, into the [mouth] of my people, “a new song,” a hymn to our God, with Moses leading the song and saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified” (Exod. 15:1). Again: “Hear, O heavens, what I speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth” (Deut. 32:1). Likewise, when my seed possessed the land promised to me and awaited there the promised blessing by which all nations were to be blessed in my seed, he put into my mouth—that is, into the mouths of my kinsmen—a new song, a hymn to our God, more than once. Hence come those very songs drawn from the ten-stringed psaltery; hence too the *Song of Songs* and other legal songs. These are called old for this reason: they were sung on the occasion of earthly benefits, although they signified spiritual benefits. For example, when it is said in songs of this sort, “Pharaoh’s chariots and his army he cast into the sea” (Exod. 15:4), or, “The barren woman has borne many, and she who had many children has grown weak” (1 Sam. 2:5), heavenly benefits are indeed signified through earthly ones. But because the people of the Old Testament understood only earthly things, those songs are rightly called old for them, upon whom the grace of the New Testament did not shine.

But the evangelical songs are wholly new: for example, the song of Mary, Virgin Mother of God; the song of Zechariah; and the song of Simeon, who, waiting, waited for the Lord, and he inclined to him and heard him, drew him from the mire of dregs and the pit of misery, set his feet upon a rock, and put into his mouth a new song, of this sort: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30). Let not Simeon alone, that righteous and God-fearing man awaiting Israel’s consolation, say now, but every righteous and God-fearing person who likewise awaits Israel’s consolation; let him say, I say: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he inclined to me and heard my prayers.” Let him say this as often as he understands himself to have been heard in some consolation of Israel—as now, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1148, a great consolation has come to Israel. In previous years there had been great desolation, in that kings and princes very often assembled as one against the Lord and against his Christ; but now kings and princes assemble as one to inflict punishment upon nations devastating God’s Church and attacking the city of Jerusalem, where the Lord’s tomb is. Behold, many mighty men from among the mightiest of Israel surround the bed of the true Solomon, all holding swords and highly trained for war, ready to defend and fortify that bed, namely the Lord’s tomb! Each man’s sword is upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night, since the law of continence is enjoined on the Christian army, that God’s camp may be clean and well ordered. Therefore to me, every faithful Catholic, the recollection of past times in this psalm and their comparison [Col. 1432D] with present events is delightful. For I, the Church, in Abraham, as has been said, waiting, waited for the Lord; and he inclined to me and heard my prayers. I, in the many prophets and righteous persons who wished to see Israel’s consolation, waiting, waited for the Lord; and he inclined to me, finally sending him whom he was to send for Israel’s consolation.

Likewise I, in the saints of the New Testament after Christ’s ascension, waiting, waited for the promised Paraclete; and he inclined to me because, while they waited, suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a mighty rushing spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting (Acts 2:2), waiting for the sevenfold Paraclete, the strongest protector against the dragon’s seven heads—that is, the seven chief kingdoms of this world gathered into the Roman empire. There was the kingdom of the Egyptians, which Augustus subjected after defeating Antony and Cleopatra; there the kingdom of the Jews, which through the Maccabees was allied with the Romans and at last under them was broken into tetrarchies. There was the imperial power of the Chaldeans or Assyrians, of the Medes or Persians, and of the Macedonians or Greeks, all assembled in the Roman power then ruling and holding dominion throughout the world. [Col. 1433B] Of these kings, at the birth of the primitive Church five had fallen: the Egyptian king, the Israelite king, the Assyrian or Chaldean king, the Persian or Median king, and the Greek king. The sixth was now the Roman emperor himself, signified by the fourth beast in Daniel’s vision. For from the Chaldean kingdom, under which that vision occurred, after the Persian and Greek kingdoms, the Roman empire itself holds the fourth place. It is rightly compared with a terrible and strong beast, because it terribly and mightily first oppressed God’s Church in the winepress of the Lord’s passion, in which that cluster was pressed which, upon the pole of the cross, we know to have been brought to us through the faith of the two peoples; then in the sufferings of the martyrs, in which that beast was terrible through ten persecutions, repeatedly inflicted from Nero down to Maximian and Diocletian, as though through its ten horns.

[Col. 1433D] Then, when overwhelming pressures were imminent, I, the Church, “waited and waited for the Lord; and he inclined to me and heard my prayers, and put a new song in my mouth,” giving me a spirit of wisdom against the philosophers of the world who resisted Christian simplicity; a life-giving spirit of understanding against the Jews, who held the Law carnally and clung too closely to the letter that kills; a spirit of counsel against the Pharisees, who despised God’s counsel by accepting neither the baptism of John nor that of Christ. The former was a precursor of grace, the latter full of grace and truth; instructed by the spirit of counsel, I, the Church, received both, and now, the office of preparation having ceased, I retain Christ’s baptism alone. There was also given a spirit of fortitude, by whose strengthening the manifold tortures of tyrants could be despised and overcome, with which that beast—placed fourth according to Daniel and sixth according to John—harassed God’s Church. John says: “The seven mountains are seven kings; five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come” (Rev. 17:9–10). For in John’s time five kingdoms had fallen: the Egyptian, which had afflicted God’s people; the Israelite, divided from David’s house and hostile to God’s kingdom; the Chaldean, which had carried God’s people captive; the Persian or Median, which, in Haman the enemy of the Jews, had been hostile to God’s people; and the Greek, which in Antiochus Epiphanes had harassed the Maccabees [Col. 1434A] and other good Jews. These five kingdoms had fallen in John’s time, and the sixth, that of the Romans, then stood. The seventh, which is Antichrist’s, had not yet come, although even then there were already many antichrists.

Heretics were his forerunners. While they raged in the Church and spread the mists of their errors, I, the Catholic Church, “waited and waited for the Lord; and he inclined to me, and heard my prayers, and drew me up from the pit of misery and from the mire of dregs; and set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps,” giving me a spirit of knowledge, by which, triumphing over the errors and falsehoods of heretics, he “put a new song in my mouth.” For then, at the Nicene Synod, I began to sing: “I believe in one God”; and, under Athanasius’s teaching, I began [Col. 1434B] frequently to sing the new song: “Whoever wishes to be saved, before all things it is necessary that he hold the Catholic faith,” etc.

After this, when manifold impiety grew strong and fornicators, robbers, murderers, perjurers, arsonists, and thieves multiplied in the Church and in the world—not only in secular society but also in the house of God, which they made a den of thieves—I likewise, the Church, “waited and waited for the Lord; and he inclined to me and heard my prayers.” For behold: while we write these things against wickedness and impiety, we see in God’s Church a manifest work of the spirit of piety, which we have also touched upon above and which, if the Lord wills, we are prepared to treat more fully elsewhere, with the Lord’s assent, [Col. 1434C] when we have seen the end of this great upheaval, whose beginning we now see: many thousands voluntarily rushing on an expedition against the pagans, enemies of the Lord’s sepulchre.

They hasten competitively to the holy war amid the rejoicing of silver trumpets, under Pope Eugenius II and his envoys, foremost among whom is Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. As their preaching resounds and certain miracles shine forth at the same time, a great earthquake has occurred. Many thousands of Germans with their king, many thousands of Frenchmen with their king, display on their foreheads and helmets, shields and banners, the sign of the most victorious cross. Besides these, great crowds whom no one can number, from diverse tribes, languages, and peoples, hasten into battle-array [Col. 1434D] after taking up the sign and banner of the Lord’s cross. And lest what they do be fruitless, many of them, following Zacchaeus’s example, first restore what they have seized or obtained by fraud. What is greater, following Christ’s example, they offer the kiss of peace to their enemies, forgive injuries, and voluntarily go to battle, where they desire either to be sacrificed for Christ like victims, or to live not for themselves but for Christ, each saying within himself: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21). Is not death gain for him who gains Christ by dying? Is not Christ life for him who has resolved to live not for himself but for Christ? We do not, indeed, doubt that among so great a multitude some serve Christ truly and sincerely, while others do so for various motives, which it is not for us to judge, but for him alone [Col. 1435A] who alone knows the hearts of those who serve rightly or wrongly. Yet we confidently affirm that many are called to this warfare, but few are chosen.

Thus once, at Israel’s departure from Egypt, although a few kept faith with God, many provoked him, and their bodies were overthrown in the wilderness. Likewise, when Gideon led the children of Israel with a great multitude marching to war against the Midianites, few remained with him—only three hundred, while many turned back. Blessed are those who serve God in such a way that they seek God himself as the reward of their service. Blessed are those who live not for themselves but for the Lord. Yet far more blessed are those “who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14:13). Precious in the sight of the Lord is the warfare of his soldiers, [Col. 1435B] and much more precious in the sight of the Lord is “the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15). For who can doubt that those should be counted among the saints who, both fighting and triumphing, gain persons for Christ, and dying, gain Christ? Those who confidently kill the enemies of the Church die more securely at their hands, because they do not make their lives more precious than themselves, provided that they complete the course of their warfare, having with them in battle the true Joshua.

Moreover, the priest Aaron, joined with the whole Levitical tribe, stands with the true Moses praying on high, where he intercedes for us. It is a great spectacle to see soldiers fighting in the field under Joshua’s leadership on the one hand, and on the other blessed Augustine as another Aaron, surrounded by Levites, and Saint Benedict as Hur, surrounded by religious monks, [Col. 1435C] praying and striving on the high mountain—that is, in the ideal which the true Moses set at the beginning of the New Testament, when, having separated his disciples from the crowd, he set before them the beatitudes to be attained, not in a level place but on a mountain, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” etc. (Matt. 5:3).

These are pious spectacles proceeding from the Spirit of piety. To its operation we also ascribe this: in these days there is great freedom for the canonical elections of bishops, abbots, provosts, and other ecclesiastical persons to be advanced to offices of dignity. For many years, almost from the time of Emperor Otto I until Emperor Henry IV, kings and emperors themselves used to sell these offices, [Col. 1435D] while Simony reigned everywhere. Through simoniacal bishops placed in the chair of pestilence, that deadly plague spread down even to the lowest parish priests and chaplains. Through their great multiplication, nearly the whole Church was defiled until Pope Gregory VII, who stood as a wall for the house of Israel by restoring canonical elections in the Church according to the ancient enactments of the canons. Thus, when bishops and the remaining prelates are ordained in the Church through canonical election, the holy whole body of the Christian people is aided by their sound preaching and devout prayers.

Accordingly, after Simony’s long winter, as spring sweetness breathes forth, the Lord’s vineyard blossoms anew. Monasteries and hospices are established, and new songs of praise become frequent [Col. 1436A], so that we see and rejoice at the fulfilment of the saying: “Sing joyfully to the Lord, all the earth; serve the Lord with gladness” (Ps. 99:1). For in monasteries too the new song is celebrated, since from the time of the aforesaid Pope Gregory VII the Office of Blessed Mary has been regularly observed, so that, with God’s service doubled, like the double manna when the great Sabbath and final day of the feast draw near, it may abound for the faithful.

The praise of God also becomes frequent in the mouths of laypeople who serve Christ in warfare. There is no one in the whole Christian realm who dares to sing shameful songs in public; rather, as we have said, the whole earth rejoices in Christ’s praises even through songs in the vernacular, especially among the Germans, whose language is more suited to harmonious song. Among these things this too increases the miracle and the holy [Col. 1436B] spectacle: holy women, devoting themselves to God in monasteries, through continual application to prayers and supplications prepare spices with Mary Magdalene; and married women, whose sons or husbands are going to wage war against the pagans, weep with Rachel and refuse consolation, because their sons or husbands are not to be recalled from such warfare. Therefore Rachel’s very voice, weeping, is heard in Ramah—that is, “on high.”

Last year, from the Lord’s incarnation 1147, much weeping and wailing was heard in our land, while pagans together with Bohemians and Hungarians tyrannized, captured Christians, and cruelly as well as shamefully abused their women. Likewise, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 1436C] 1145, when the city of Edessa, also called Roas, was captured by pagans, much weeping and wailing was heard—and heard on high. Moved by this, Pope Eugenius sent letters to Christian princes and soldiers, that they should assemble “to execute vengeance among the nations.” Therefore there is a hasty rush to arms, because remission of sins is promised by the Apostolic See to those who fight and repent, especially to those who die in so holy a battle, repaying their Saviour, who died for them.

Therefore the faithful Psalmist, who “waited and waited for the Lord,” speaks rightly in singing of the wonderful works of piety to be performed in the order [Col. 1436D] of the seven spirits. Of these, five, as has been stated above, have already worked, as is plainly evident: in the work of wisdom against philosophers; in the work of understanding against Jews; in the work of counsel against Pharisees; in the work of fortitude against the violence of tyrants; and in the work of knowledge against the deceitfulness of heretics. Now, therefore, in the pious works proceeding from the spirit of piety, he can rightly say in song: “I waited and waited for the Lord; and he inclined to me and heard my prayers; and drew me up from the pit of misery and from the mire of dregs; and set my feet upon a rock; and directed my steps; and put in my mouth a new song, a hymn to our God.”

“He set my feet upon a rock,” so that I might hope that Christ, who is the rock, would plainly perform the works of his piety after [Col. 1437A] the manifest works of the five spirits, before the judgment comes, which is to be carried out in the spirit of fear. And therefore “he directed my steps,” because, as I ascend the ladder of seven steps—that is, the seven spirits—after the work of fortitude, which shone forth in martyrs, and the work of knowledge, which shone forth in confessors, I “waited and waited” for the work of piety. In this expectation the Lord “put in my mouth a new song, a hymn to our God.”

In the Office of Holy Mary, in which the hymn to our God is regularly sung, his piety and clemency are invoked when it is continually said:

> Most merciful King Christ,  
> Take possession of our hearts,  
> That we may render to you  
> The praise due at every time.

This is the same as saying: O King of glory, who most powerfully governed the holy martyrs and most wisely the blessed confessors, now most piously and mercifully order the governance of the Church, reigning in it through the clearest works of your piety, that we may render to you the praise due at every time—as the apostles and evangelists, triumphing in their own time through the spirits of wisdom, understanding, and counsel, rendered due praise; and as the martyrs, through the spirit of fortitude, and the blessed confessors, through the spirit of knowledge, acting victoriously in their times, rendered fitting praise—so may we, governed by the clemency of highest piety, render due praise at every time.

[Col. 1437C] Let each of us, from experience of works proceeding from divine piety, say: “I waited and waited for the Lord; and he inclined to me and heard my prayers.” This is apparent in its effect: first, he “drew me up from the pit of misery and from the mire of dregs,” freeing me from evils; then, strengthening me in good things and establishing me in Christ’s commandments and counsels, “he set my feet upon a rock”—that is, my faculties, which formerly were with the devil and wavered in the slippery mire. He set them upon the solid rock, for “the rock was Christ,” and “he directed my steps,” that is, my works, so that, forgetting what lies behind and stretching out toward what lies ahead, I may pursue the prize of the heavenly calling; and, having put my hand to the plough, may not look back like [Col. 1437D] Lot’s wife.

After these two benefits he appropriately added a third: “he put in my mouth a new song,” a hymn or song to our God. The Jew, and every worldly person who desires earthly things, does not so much sing the old song as mutter it with a hoarse throat. Hence Isaiah says to him: “Your voice shall be like that of a python, and your speech shall mutter from the ground” (Isa. 29:4). For the speech of one who is from the earth and speaks of the earth mutters, as it were, from the ground, when in what he says and does—whether in ecclesiastical or secular affairs—he desires earthly things alone.

But the Lord “put a new song in my mouth,” because in everything I say and do I desire to put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new. Therefore [Col. 1438A] I reject all shameful and theatrical songs like rotten rags, and intend to adorn myself with a new song of praise—not singing the old things with Jews who seek earthly things, or with gentiles who worship idols, but I shall sing the pleasant song of the New Testament to our God: to God who clothed himself in our nature, expiated our sins through the mystery of his passion, and transforms us from oldness into newness of life. For when God the Father did not require burnt offering or sin offering but sought only the new sacrifice, then God the Son said to God the Father: “Behold, I come.”

Many shall see that he came who said, “Behold, I come.” They shall see him come in the manifest showing forth of his presence, though in eternal predestination he said, “Behold, I come.” The Jews saw and envied; [Col. 1438B] they saw and hated both him and his Father. Through their hatred the grain died, and it was multiplied in the faith of many peoples from every tribe and language who believe in him. The Pharisees saw and hated; but many from the gentiles, having been converted, shall see and fear. Many imitators of those who have gone before shall see that he was proclaimed as having come, and they shall fear when they hear his preaching, because they will recognize themselves as sinners and dread the coming judgment. Therefore they will leave the broad way of iniquity and strive to enter by the narrow way which leads to life; they will seek it with the greatest care, and yet they will hope in the Lord rather than in their own works or confidence in their own strength. They will hope in the Lord, not without great fruit. For:

[Col. 1438C] **Verse 5. “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord.”**—Blessed is the man, so named from virtue, whose hope is the name of the Lord. In the present passage “the name of the Lord” means the Lord, by which name it is suggested that he rules all things and is above all things. Therefore trust and firm hope must be placed in him alone, because he truly says in the Song of Moses: “I will strike, and I will heal; and there is none who can deliver from my hand” (Deut. 32:39). “I will strike,” by giving a penitent heart; “and I will heal,” by granting forgiveness of sins. Blessed, therefore, is the man whose firm hope is the name of the Lord, ruler of all.
