Therefore, clinging to him, he fears no adversary, because none can prevail against him; and therefore those who trust in the Lord, [Col. 1438D] “like Mount Zion, shall not be moved for ever” (Ps. 124:1); so they too shall not be moved for ever.

When it is said, “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord,” the word *his* is superfluous in the text, since it would have sufficed to say, “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord.” This frequently occurs in translations that differ somewhat from the Hebrew truth: something superfluous is inserted, or something necessary omitted, as here. For in the Hebrew truth it reads thus: “Blessed is the man who has made God his confidence, and has not turned toward pride and the displays of falsehood.” Yet it may be read in such a way that *his* is not superfluous, as follows: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of his Lord.” For, since he [Col. 1439A] is the special servant of his Lord, he who is commonly Lord of all is the special Lord of that man. In the Prophet he says to him: “You are my servant, Israel, because in you I shall be glorified” (Isa. 44:21); likewise: “Do not fear, my servant Jacob” (ibid., v. 2); likewise: “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant.” Blessed, therefore, is the man who is so faithful and special a servant of the Lord of all that the Lord himself is his special Lord; and then, rightly, his Lord—or the name of his Lord—is his trust and hope.

Otherwise: the name of the Lord is Saviour; and therefore, “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord,” who hopes from the Lord not for some temporal thing, but hopes only that the Lord himself will rule him and save him according to his name, by which he is called “Saviour [Col. 1439B] of all people, especially of believers.” Therefore he hopes for salvation from him alone; indeed, he hopes that God himself will be salvation to him, who says: “I am the salvation of the people” (Ps. 24:3). Thus the Lord and Saviour is his firm hope for the future, if, after being drawn through repentance from the pit of misery and the mire of dregs, and being set by the Lord upon the rock through good conduct, and receiving in his mouth a song of praise or preaching, he does not turn his directed feet back to abandoned perversities and does not look toward vanities—that is, earthly things, all of which are vain, as Ecclesiastes says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. 1:1).

Nor does he look toward false madnesses—that is, playful, theatrical, and stage performances. In their spectacles there is indeed real madness, but they are rightly called false because, when either weddings and amorous songs are imitated, as in comedies, or bitter histories, as in tragedies, the masked characters introduced there are not what they are said to be. For example, he who is called Davus or Parmeno there is not what he is called; nor are the courtesan Thais or the soldier Thraso really so named. Everything is done in falsehood—or rather, acted. But those are utterly real madnesses where shameful or cruel acts are seriously committed, no false characters being introduced, but madnesses truly perpetrated there: anger rules—or rather rages—in quarrels and fights, and corrupt lust indulges itself in foul and unclean deeds. Since, then, it is harmful even to look upon the false madnesses of actors, [Col. 1439D] how much more ruinous is it for a Christian either to perform real madnesses in himself and by himself, or to look upon them in others—that is, to love them? For “to look upon” is used in the sense of “to love,” because what is loved is frequently and willingly looked upon. Hence he is rightly proclaimed blessed who, drawn from the pit of misery, standing upon the rock, and singing a hymn to God, has not looked upon or loved false madnesses. Whoever hates these is plainly the more likely to hate the real ones.

But so that those accustomed to spectacles may not be deprived of spectacles, but may, if they wish, have true and salutary spectacles in place of vain and harmful ones:

**Verse 6. “You, O Lord my God, have done many of your wonders.”** O Lord my God, you have done wonders [Col. 1440A] not few but many, both bodily and spiritual. Let him who delights in spectacles and admires remarkable human constructions, charioteers, and tightrope-walkers, rather admire the wonderful construction of heaven and earth. Let him who admires a charioteer guiding horses with bit and bridle rather admire a self-controlled person, rightly directing the varied and wandering impulses of lust implanted within him and restraining them within the narrow limit of chastity. Let him who admires a tightrope-walker rather admire Peter walking upon the sea in sign, and ourselves, together with him, actually treading this great sea—that is, the entire stormy flux of this world, “where there are creeping things without number” (Ps. 103:25).

For these salutary spectacles are more wonderful than those vain ones because a human being learned the latter painstakingly from [Col. 1440B] another human being; but you, O Lord my God, who alone perform great wonders, have no teacher in this matter. Rather, in counsels ordered from eternity and by your own thoughts you performed those many wonders, from which it is known that none is like you even in thought, much less in action.

Blessed Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 1439D] St Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book VI, chapter 15.] says in the sixth book of his exposition of Job:

> “You, O Lord my God, have done many of your wonders.” Who can sufficiently search out the wonders of almighty God? He created all things from nothing; the very fabric of the world is arranged by the marvellous power of his might; heaven hangs above the air and earth is poised above the abyss. From invisible things the whole universe of visible things comes into being. He made man—if one may so speak—gathering together into a small compass another world, but a rational one; and, forming him from soul and flesh, he mingled spirit and clay through an inscrutable arrangement of power. Thus from these things we know one thing and are another; nevertheless, we neglect to wonder, because things wonderful to comprehensible inquiry have become cheap to human eyes through familiarity. Thus, if a dead person is raised, all leap up in amazement. Yet every day a human being who did not exist is born, and no one wonders, although surely everyone agrees that to create what did not exist is greater than to restore what did exist. Because Aaron’s dry rod blossomed, all marvelled; every day a tree is produced from the drying earth and the power of dust is changed into wood, yet no one wonders. Because five thousand persons were filled with five loaves [Col. 1440D], all marvelled that food increased in their teeth; every day scattered grains of seed are multiplied into an abundance of ears of grain, and no one wonders. Seeing water changed once into wine, all marvelled; every day the moisture of earth, drawn into the root of the vine, is changed through the cluster into wine, and no one wonders. Therefore all things are wonderful which people neglect to wonder at, because, as we have said, familiarity dulls them to consideration.”

Likewise, in book twenty-five [Note: [Col. 1440D] Chapter 8.]: “I have proclaimed and spoken; they have been multiplied beyond number.” When the Lord calls, believers are multiplied beyond number, because even those come to faith who do not attain the number of the elect. They are mixed among believers by [Col. 1441A] confession, but because of their reprobate life they do not deserve to be counted there among the lot of believers. Thus the Prophet, seeing so many in this age of the Church believing only in outward appearance—so many as certainly surpass the fixed number and total of the elect—says: “They have been multiplied beyond number,” as though he said: While many enter the Church, there also come to faith in outward appearance those who are excluded from the heavenly kingdom, because by their very multitude they exceed the sum of the elect.

We may also apply to the condition of this age what is said: “Many shall see and fear, and hope in the Lord.” Many shall see the wonders done in former times and those now being done. They shall see the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1441B] almost wholly completed, up to the final testing of deeds. For, as noted above, through the spirit of wisdom the philosophers of this world have been refuted; through the spirit of understanding, the carnal rites of ceremonies have been changed into spiritual ones; through the spirit of counsel, the Pharisees who despised God’s counsel have been rejected and the gentiles received; through the spirit of fortitude, tyrants have been overcome by martyrs; through the spirit of knowledge, diviners and heretics have been throttled by confessors. And now, behold, in our days, as has been shown above, the spirit of piety works manifestly. After it, only the spirit of fear is expected to work the equally terrible and desirable work of the final judgment—terrible to the ungodly, desirable to the devout, indeed terrible and desirable alike even to the saints. [Col. 1441C] For “the powers of heaven shall be moved” (Luke 21:26), by fear together with love: by fear, because they shall see the punishments of the wicked; by love, because they shall see the rewards of the blessed.

Considering such things and judging that the last time is at hand, many shall see and fear; and, pierced and improved by fear, they will afterward hope, proving by experience of their hope that truly blessed is the man who hopes in the Lord, blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and blessed is he who has not looked back—who, once stretched forward and intent upon what lies ahead, has not looked back like Lot’s wife; who has not, I say, looked toward vanities and false madnesses.

Note that it is one thing to see vanities, another to look upon vanities, and another to look *toward* vanities. [Col. 1441D] For one who sees a woman, but not in order to desire her, sees indeed a vanity; and he also looks upon her if the beauty of her flesh and loveliness of skin—like “the flower of grass,” for “all flesh is grass”—delight his gaze. But he does not look *toward* vanity if he is not drawn toward her by deliberate desire, but rather drawn back from her; while even if his eyes are cast upon bodily beauty, they are fixed upon no one (Isa. 40:6). We are not forbidden to see persons with beautiful faces, but it is sinful to desire them or to wish to be desired by them. For while inquisitive and lustful eyes are mutually fixed against one another, even though the bodies remain untouched by unclean violation, chastity itself flees [Col. 1442A] from the mind.

Nor should one who fixes his eye upon a woman, and delights that hers is fixed upon him, suppose that he is seen by no one. He is indeed seen—by those whom he does not suppose see him, namely good and evil angels and perceptive people. And even if seen by no human being, what will he do about that watcher from above, from whom nothing can be hidden? He must not be thought not to see because he sees all the more wisely the more patiently he waits. Therefore let the holy man fear to displease him, lest he take pleasure in vanities when he sees them; let him think upon him who looks upon all things, lest he wish to look toward vanities. For “God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God” (Ps. 52:3): to see whether there is one who understands by himself, or seeks from another teacher, to know the many wonders of which it is here said to you, God: “You, O Lord my God, have done many of your wonders, and none is like you in your thoughts.”

Moses performed wonders. Elisha and Elijah also performed wonders, and many saints performed wonders in their lives; but they did not perform *their own* wonders, because they did not perform them by their own power but by another’s power. Hence Peter, after the lame man had been healed, says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Why do you look at us as though by our own power or piety [Note: [Col. 1441D] Thus the codex.] we had made this man walk? The God of our fathers has glorified his Son, and faith in his name has made strong this man whom you see and know; and the faith which is through him has given him this perfect healing in the sight of you all” (Acts 3:12). If all God’s elect, performing wonders in the name of Christ—whom they either foretold as to come, like the prophets, or announced as having come, like the apostles—recognized that the wonders they performed were not their own but God’s, then you, O Lord my God, performed many wonders of your own through your own power and according to your own thoughts, which foretold them. Therefore none is like you.

I, David, believed this; therefore I spoke and proclaimed it to others, and they were multiplied beyond number, because innumerable are the people—though numberable to God—who received this word, according to that passage in the Apocalypse: “After these things,” he says, “I saw a great multitude which no one could number, from all nations and peoples and tribes and languages, standing [Col. 1442D] before the throne, with palms in their hands” (Rev. 7:9).

Otherwise: “I proclaimed and spoke.” At this point begins the second part of this psalm, in which are enumerated wonders more wonderful than the other wonders: the incarnation of the Word; the preaching of righteousness proclaimed in the great Church; the deliverance of human beings from iniquities; the confounding of enemies; and the joy of those who overcome. For what is more wonderful than the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, which was announced by angels, believed in throughout the world, and taken up in glory? It was announced not only by angels, prophets, and apostles, but—what is worthy of all acceptance—by the incarnate Lord himself, who now says in the psalm: “I proclaimed and spoke.” I not only foretold through prophets, but also personally proclaimed and spoke to the Jews, who, [Col. 1443A] if I had not come and spoken to them, would not have had sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin (John 15:22). For when I called them into one, so that they might have one heart and one soul in God, they were multiplied through the fruit of grain, wine, and oil beyond the number of those few who believed in me and had one heart.

For when I proclaimed and spoke of the new sacrifice, because you, God the Father, did not desire the old sacrifice and old offering, they said: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (John 6:61). [Col. 1443B] And because of this many of my disciples went back. Many went away because the disciples were multiplied beyond the number of the elect and blessed disciples. When they remained with me, I finally explained the hard saying and made it soft and edible, as it were, like bread. Those many broke their teeth, to whom what I proclaimed and spoke was hard. Therefore, offended by its hardness, they went back, because they were beyond number. But Peter, who truly belonged to the number, said to me: “You have the words of eternal life, and where shall we go from you?” (John 6:69).

Afterward, through the same apostles, as the sound of preaching went forth into the whole earth, I proclaimed the same rite of the new sacrifice, and many received the word, so that beyond the fixed number of the predestined [Col. 1443C] false brothers were mixed in: “For many are called, but few chosen” (Matt. 22:14).

Or, the believing gentiles were multiplied beyond the number of Jews who had formerly believed, when they were counted in the wilderness through Moses, as is read in the book of Numbers. Or, they were multiplied beyond number because, though numberable to God, they became innumerable to human beings. But I proclaimed the rite of the new sacrifice to the Jews in person and to the gentiles through my apostles because you, God the Father—

**Verse 7. You no longer desired sacrifice from animals, part of which was burned, and the offering** of bread, oil, incense, and such things, which the Jewish people offered from the fruits of the earth, like another Cain, a cultivator of earth and not a seeker of heavenly things.

It is also clear that you never desired these things, but only permitted them for a time. Thus in Isaiah you say: “What is the multitude of your victims to me? I am full. I did not desire burnt offerings of rams, lambs, and goats. Who required these things from your hands?” (Isa. 1:11–12). Likewise in Jeremiah: “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh; for I did not speak to your fathers or command them, on the day when I led them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But I commanded them this word, saying: ‘Hear my voice, and I will be your [Col. 1444A] God, and you shall be my people; and walk in every way that I have commanded you, that it may be well with you’” (Jer. 7:21 ff.). Likewise elsewhere you say: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 49:13).

Yet you permitted these things to be offered to you, lest the Jewish people, prone to idolatry, should offer the same things to idols or demons, as they did in the wilderness, where “they changed their glory into the likeness of a calf that eats grass” (Ps. 105:20). Sacrificing offerings to it, they said: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” Therefore, as you say in Ezekiel, “You gave them statutes that were not good” (Ezek. 20:25), concerning sacrifices to be offered to you, which you do not love.

Yet because you, supremely good, make good use as you will even of the evil things of evil persons, in the same sacrifices that were displeasing to you, you prefigured the one sacrifice which you love. When it was presented and offered to you, those old sacrifices ought altogether to cease, especially as you protested and said in Isaiah: “My soul has hated your new moons and your sabbaths; they have become burdensome to me; I have laboured in bearing them. Bring incense no more in vain” (Isa. 1:13–14). Whoever in your people had ears to hear heard you rejecting sacrifices of this sort through the prophets, and could truthfully say: “If you had desired sacrifice, I would surely have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings” (Ps. 50:18).

Yet that people, of whom you say in Isaiah: “Bring forth the blind people, who have eyes, and the deaf, who have ears” (Isa. 40:8)—that blind and deaf people, I say—heard neither you in the prophets nor me when I was present and proclaimed and spoke to them.

Strange is the statement that that people had eyes, and yet were blind; they had ears, and yet remained deaf. But it must be understood that they had eyes in that they were able to see the truth, but were blind in that they were unwilling to see. Likewise, they had ears because they were able to hear or obey, but remained deaf because they were unwilling to obey. Therefore, what Zedekiah alone, king of that people, suffered in his body, the whole people, except for the remnant, suffered in mind. For just as the king of Babylon first gouged out his eyes—which he had refused to use rightly—then led him captive into Babylon and imprisoned him, so [Col. 1444D] this people is not merely hindered by the veil over Moses’ face so as not to see, but, having utterly lost its inward eyes, endures captivity under the Babylonian king.

Moreover, what the Spirit speaking in Ezekiel threatened against the harlot Oholah, or Oholibah, is plainly seen to have happened to this sinful nation: “I will stir up against you your lovers, and they shall strip you of your garments; they shall cut off your nose and your ears, and whatever remains shall be cut down by the sword” (Ezek. 23:22). Thus, by your just judgment, God the Father, she lost the ears which she had refused to use well; and her sons likewise stopped up their ears and gnashed their teeth against him (Acts 7:54, 56) who proclaimed to them the good news. They were therefore justly deprived of ears, so that, now wholly hardened, they might have no hearing at all. The right ear of the high priest’s servant, cut off by Peter, was a visible sign of this mutilation of the inward [Col. 1445A] senses. From that time on, even if they hear testimonies concerning Christ from the Scriptures, they can hear only with the left ear, for hatred, not also with the right ear, for love. But I, the new man, have perfect ears. For from them you have indeed taken ears by a just judgment.

“But you have perfected ears for me”: that is, you have made me understand perfectly what you willed. Or, as another translation has it: “You have prepared a body for me,” lest your people, when the old shadowy sacrifice had been removed, should lack the new sacrifice, which surpasses the old as a body surpasses a shadow. For you prepared a body for me, so that, as the sun-like body rises, day may breathe forth and the shadows decline; indeed, when, as its going forth is from the highest heaven, so its course shall be to the height of [Col. 1445B] heaven, the shadows may wholly fail. Then my bride shall desire to be told where I feed, where I lie down at noon, when shadows are shortest and not so dense as the shadows of night.

For certain remnants of shadows will remain as the sign placed upon Cain—that is, upon the fratricidal people—so that no one may kill him. For what are the circumcision and unleavened bread of the Jews scattered throughout the world, except a certain sign made from remnants of the ancient shadows? For the Law had a shadow of things to come, not the very image of the things. But the shadow under the Law was dense and, as it were, nocturnal; now, with the sun-like body of righteousness raised on high, only slight remnants of shadows can scarcely be seen.

[Col. 1445C] In Hebrew it reads: “You have dug ears for me,” which is the same as saying: You bestowed upon me the power and merit of perfect obedience, in that you begot me as God most exalted and as man most humble; namely, so that I, your Son and servant, should not only know your will because I am Son, but should also be ready to obey because I am servant. For I am truly Son, since, as God, I was begotten from your substance, and, as man, I was born through your love. I am also truly servant, since I am the son of your handmaid; nor am I in any respect base because I am the son of a handmaid, but rather wholly free-born, since, as man, I was born from a human being into God.

For you also ennobled my mother by the prerogative of your Spirit, so greatly that by reason of the anointing oil the yoke of [Col. 1445D] servile fear in her rotted away, and she advanced from handmaid to bride. Yet she was not therefore not a handmaid because she was a bride, nor not a bride because she was a handmaid. For she was not therefore not lowly because exalted, nor not exalted because lowly. That she was an exalted bride was the privilege of dignity raising her up; but that she was lowly and a handmaid belonged not only to her natural condition, but also to voluntary devotion, and therefore to virtue. For she remained in her most firmly grounded humility even when, through the spirit of love, she advanced to become the bride of God and queen of heaven.

For she was herself, yet not herself: herself indeed through the lowly condition of human nature, which your overshadowing power preserved in her; but not herself [Col. 1446A] through the dignity of bridal and nuptial love, by which she could say to you, the Lord her God and friend as to the partner of her bed: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” etc. (Song 1:1).

From such exaltation and humility together, you, God the Father, perfected ears for me, a man, and God’s servant, and Son born: that is, you bestowed upon me both perfect understanding of your will and perfect obedience, so that, because I was a human servant, I should will and be obliged to undertake the cause of humankind; and, because I was God and your consubstantial Son, I should know and be able to undertake that cause and to serve your will in its deliverance. For my ears would not be perfect if any one of these things were absent: will or power, obligation or knowledge. But now you have perfected ears for me in that [Col. 1446B] you begot me God and man, Son and servant, one lacking neither obligation, nor knowledge, nor will, nor power to obey you in carrying out the cause of humankind. Thus you, God the Father, perfected ears for me.

You had commanded in the Law of Moses that a victim mutilated by the cutting off of its tail or ears should not be accepted as a sacrifice in payment of a vow. By this command you signified that no sacrifice lacking either obedience, signified by the ears, or perseverance, signified by the tail—which is the end of the body, just as perseverance is the end of a good work well brought to completion—is acceptable to you. Therefore, because the old man had neither ears of obedience under the natural law nor under the written law, and did not persevere in good once begun, you did not desire his [Col. 1446C] sacrifice and offering. But you perfected ears for me, the new man, who, obedient to you unto death, even death on a cross, was a perfect victim, not mutilated in ears or tail, because I lacked neither the virtue of obedience nor that of good perseverance.

Yet I do not attribute this to myself, because I am not from myself, but to you, God my Father, who begot me God and made me man, and who perfected ears for me, God-man: for you gave me the power of perfect obedience, that I might be a fitting victim for abolishing the sins of the whole world in those who believe in me and, through me as mediator, in you. Having once been immolated upon the altar of the cross for them, I shall also be immolated frequently in the ministry of the altar until the end of the age, for the [Col. 1446D] salvation of believers. But of unbelieving Jews:

“You did not require burnt offering and sin offering.” The burnt offering of the red heifer, which was wholly burned, and the sin offering—that is, the scapegoat (Lev. 16:10), upon which sins were laid and which was sent into the wilderness—you did not require. But from me, your Son, you demanded a perfect sacrifice; and I was then paying back “what I did not seize” (Ps. 68:5), because:

**VERSE 8. Then I said: Behold, I come.** I had said this from eternity, in the predestination by which I was predestined as Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, to be conceived not in carnal concupiscence but in the Spirit of sanctification. But I delayed [Col. 1447A] doing what had been predestined until the time of mercy came. When, however, the fullness of time came, I delayed no longer, but then said: “Behold, I come.” When the figures had ceased, I said it not now by predestining but by obeying: “Behold, I come.” “Behold,” openly: I do not speak with a verb of future time, “I shall come,” but without delay I say in the present, “I come.” It is time for the promises to arrive, because the things promising them are being removed.

It should be noted that from this passage the Apostle proves the change of the old Law, saying: “Therefore, when he enters the world, he says: ‘Sacrifice and offering you did not desire’” (Heb. 10:5). It must be understood that the old sacrifices were like words of God making promises. When he said figuratively, “I shall give,” and, “I shall send my Son,” [Col. 1447B] after the reality came, he changed the words and said not, “I shall give,” but, “I have given,” and, “I have sent.” Therefore, when he himself came, he did not desire those things which were his figure.

But if anyone says that the old rite still continues among the Jews and that the figures therefore have not been removed, this is not true. For they have neither king nor priest, and the sacrifices have been removed, although, just as God placed a sign upon Cain so that no one might kill him, so the Jew has retained circumcision, unleavened bread, and things of that sort; having this sign, he is not killed. Yet Cain was cursed by the earth which received his brother’s blood that he himself had shed: that is, the Jew is cursed by the Church, which received Christ’s blood. For this is the earth of which God said: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth” (Gen. 4:10). It cries [Col. 1447C] indeed; but the Jew who shed it, who does not drink spiritually, does not hear, for he has no ears for hearing. Likewise, the gentile who sacrifices to idols does not hear the cry of this blood. The false Christian also, who professes to know God but denies him by deeds, does not hear the voice of this crying blood. For if he heard, he would surely obey.

For what does the sprinkling of this blood cry, speaking better than Abel’s blood, except repentance, obedience, and forgiveness of sins? That blood cried for vengeance against the unrepentant person, against the despairing person who says from despair, “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for” (Gen. 4:13). But this blood, shed in obedience and [Col. 1447D] repentance, asks forgiveness of sins for all who obey and repent—for whom Christ obeyed God the Father, and for whom he also underwent forty days of repentance in the wilderness, which at last he completed through the sufferings of his passion, grieving for us and “wounded for our iniquities,” because he did not feign it but truly himself bore our infirmities and himself carried our sins, and “the chastisement of our peace was upon him” (Isa. 53:4).

A marvelous thing! We ought to have been chastised and disciplined for our sins, so that peace and the grace of God might be restored to us. If all the infernal and temporal punishments were spent in disciplining and chastising us, they would not suffice to complete the chastisement required for our peace. Therefore, while we were being scourged by many miseries, [Col. 1448A] he, innocent, placed himself between us and took upon himself the effective chastisement of our peace. What then was a loving and just Father to do, seeing his innocent Son, equal to himself, humbled for this purpose: not only to intercede in prayer for worthless servants, but also to receive their chastisement by being beaten, and to taste for them the death not owed to himself?

“He, in the days of his flesh, offering prayers with a strong cry, was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5:7): plainly, he was worthy to be heard and answered by the Father, whom he himself heard, as he says: “I can do nothing of myself; as I hear, I judge” (John 5:30). Again: “All things whatever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). Again: “As the Father gave me commandment, so I do” (John 14:31). These are the words [Col. 1448B] of the Son gladly and obediently hearing his Father. It is therefore evident that he who heard in this way had perfect ears. Hence it is now said: “But you have perfected ears for me,” so that I might clearly hear that you did not require burnt offering and sin offering, but willed that I should come into the world and become a sacrifice.

“Then I said: Behold, I come, ready to do your will, my God; I have willed it.” This obedience of mine was perfect, not slow or sluggish, because, when you spoke—indeed, wrote—this in the head of the book, that is, in myself, who am the head of the book, namely of all sacred Scripture, whose head or beginning I am, where I am called the Beginning, Moses saying, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1)—when you wrote, I say, in that head [Col. 1448C] of the book:

**VERSE 9. “To do your will, then I said: Behold, I come.”** The voice saying, “Behold, I come,” indicates the eagerness of obedience with all sluggishness removed. Likewise, the words, “I have willed your will, my God,” denote the gladness of voluntary obedience. For one who patiently endures the will of the commanding God and does what he commands will indeed possess his soul in patience, but does not merit that love by which God loves a cheerful giver; nor can he say, “I have willed your will, my God,” when he can more truthfully say, “I have endured your will.”

But I, Christ, rendering perfect obedience as one for all my own, have willed your will, my God, as is written concerning me in the head of the book: that is, in the divinity inherent in me. I am the book of life; I am your Word coeternal with you; I am the word foretold through the mouth of all the prophets from the beginning of the age and proclaimed through the mouth of the apostles; I am the book written within and without, that is, in my divinity and humanity together. What is written in divinity through eternal predestination is said to be written in the head of the book. Yet upon the skin of humanity, by the pen of a swiftly writing scribe, all the wisdom of divinity is also inscribed.

Moreover, [Col. 1448D] in the head of this book of Psalms, in the first psalm—which is the head and, as it were, title of the others—it is written concerning me, the blessed man, that I should do your will, which I also willed. For you did not give me, against my will, the command to obey unto death; [Col. 1449A] rather I willed your will, because you and I are of one will. Hence, what you, Father, will, I also will: divinely, by the divine will; humanly, by the human will. Thus I also said: “Not what I will, but what you will, be done” (Mark 14:36), subjecting my human will to your divine will and mine, in which you and I differ neither naturally nor actually, because we are one.

But my human will differs from the divine in nature, and before death it differed in action, when it refused the cup of the passion. After the resurrection and ascension, however, although it is of a nature other than the divine, it nevertheless shares fully in divine power without discord, so that I, the new man, may say [Col. 1449B]: “I have willed your will, my God”; that is, by my human will I have wholly consented to the divine will. “And I have your law in the midst of my heart,” as is written of me in the head of the book, that is, in the first psalm, where it says: “But his will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he shall meditate day and night” (Ps. 1:2). For what is said in the head of the book, “His will is in the law of the Lord,” accords with the saying here, “I have willed your will, my God”; and what is said there, “In his law he shall meditate day and night,” is the same as what is expressed here: “And I have your law in the midst of my heart.”

**VERSE 10. “I have proclaimed your righteousness in the great assembly.”** That I had your law in the midst of my heart, and that I willed your will, meant that I was [Col. 1449C] planted like a tree beside streams of water. But that I proclaimed your righteousness in the great assembly meant that I gave fruit in the fitting season, according to what is written concerning me in the head of the book, where it was said of me: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall yield its fruit in its season” (Ps. 1:3).

Alternatively: I, the Christian; or I, David repenting; or the psalmist, who “waited and waited for the Lord,” believed with the heart unto righteousness, because I willed your will, my God, and had your law in the midst of my heart. I also confessed with the mouth unto salvation, because I proclaimed your righteousness in the great assembly. [Col. 1449D] Your righteousness which is from faith, which you inspire—not the righteousness of works that are in the Law. I proclaimed your righteousness in an assembly no longer small, as before, but great, extended throughout the whole world. And:

“Behold, I shall not restrain my lips from speaking the truth,” terrified by the fear of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Amid these things I am at times blasphemed as a pretender; but, O Lord, you knew. You are my witness that, when I am silent, I do not restrain my lips from speaking because of fear, nor do I speak what I speak hypocritically. Or, “you knew” means: from eternity you so ordained that it would be. Hence it is clear that this proclamation of your righteousness is made by authority, not deceitfully but truthfully. You knew this, you who see my heart, whereby I believe unto righteousness precisely what I confess with my mouth unto salvation. You knew, whenever I did not restrain my lips, that I did not speak with “heart and heart,” through doubleness, but in purity of heart through the simplicity of a good intention. For I did not hide in my heart, when I believed it necessary to speak, what I understood to be just.

**VERSE 11. “I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart,”** as those do who are called dumb dogs unable to bark. For, knowing that the just person lives by faith, I held the righteousness of faith in my heart, as I believed it ought to be held; “therefore I also spoke.” What did I speak?

“I have declared your truth and your salvation. I have not hidden your mercy and your truth from the great council.” I declared your truth in the promises partly fulfilled and partly still to be fulfilled through Christ, who is the truth; and I declared your salvation, that is, the same Christ, who is the truth for confirming the promises made to the Fathers, and Savior not only of Jews but also of Gentiles. For I said that Jesus Christ was a minister of circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises of the Fathers, while the Gentiles glorify God for mercy (Rom. 15:8). And therefore I did not hide your mercy and truth from the great council.

I did not hide from the great council—that is, because of the many detractors—your mercy, by which you forgive sins to those who truly repent, and your truth, by which you punish sins in those who do not truly repent or, what is worse, remain in defense of sin and in an attachment to sinning [Col. 1450C]. Thus I declared both, mercy and truth, as I believed expedient. Yet in prayer I entreated, and still entreat, only that mercy might be granted to me or to others, saying:

**VERSE 12. “But you, O Lord, do not put your mercies far from me.”** For just as, when the nocturnal readings in the Church have ended, “But you, O Lord, have mercy on us” is added at the end, so too, when the preachings have ended and the rebukes uttered against the children of night, I who proclaimed truth and mercy desired mercy alone for myself and for my hearers. For righteousness is always awake—the prophet Jeremiah calls it a watchful rod—and prayer is not needed to awaken righteousness, which renders to each his due. But prayer is sometimes needed to awaken mercy, which sleeps even in the disciples’ little boat. Therefore I now say: “But you, O Lord, do not put your mercies far from me.”

I proclaimed both, mercy and righteousness. But you, O Lord, first show mercy alone, forgiving sins and granting fruitful amendment, so that guilty and miserable man may be able to bear your righteousness—such a man as I, David repenting or singing psalms, to whom your righteousness, ready to avenge what I did badly, is of its own accord close at hand.

“But you, O Lord, do not put your mercies far from me.” First show in me, for the instruction of believers and of those hearing me, that I have truthfully testified that you are merciful. Make your mercies [Col. 1451A] appear in me, so that I may say: “A faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance: that Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But I obtained mercy” (1 Tim. 1:15). Thus, so that examples of your mercy may not be sought far away, I ask that you do not put your mercies far from me, so that those who hear me speaking of you may take from me an example of your mercies.

For when I preach you as merciful, saying that you are patient, most merciful, and surpassing in goodness over evil, while on the contrary people seem to see you, as though unmerciful, allowing countless human beings to perish in their malice—for whose conversion the Church prays—I should like to display clear testimonies of your mercy close at hand, lest I be told every day: “Where is your God, whom you preach as merciful?” To those who say this I customarily point out those treasuries of Scripture in which your ancient mercies are stored and sealed. For example, I speak thus: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever. Who alone performs great wonders. Who made the great lights: the sun to rule the day, the moon and stars to rule the night. Who struck Egypt with their firstborn. Who brought Israel out from their midst” (Ps. 135:1 ff.); and he did many other great and ancient wonders, in which he manifested that his mercy is forever.

But such examples of your mercy, O God, seem, as it were, [Col. 1451C] borrowed from far away unless things similar to them, or greater than them, can be shown in the present. Therefore, do not put your mercies far from me, so that I may plainly show close at hand your new mercies, which your ancient mercies prefigured. For example: You who established the earth upon the waters, establish your Church upon the Scriptures. You who made the great lights, sun and moon, cause in our days a great light—priesthood—to shine for rule of the day, namely spiritual holiness and governance; and cause kingship, like a bright full moon, to rule the night, namely temporal warfare and governance. You who struck Egypt with its firstborn, strike hell with its firstborn demons. Strike this world with its firstborn, [Col. 1451D] its evil rulers; and lead Israel, your people, out from their midst with a mighty hand and uplifted arm, so that we may sing to the Lord not so much for ancient mercies as for new, present, and manifest ones: “For he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea” (Exod. 15:1, 21). And let each one of us, now delivered from demons, evil people, or even from Egyptian vices and customs, say for the mercy near to him: “The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation. This is my God, and I will glorify him” (Ps. 114:14).

Therefore, do not henceforth say to me, “Where is your God?” Behold, I say: “This is my God, and I will glorify him,” who makes ancient mercies new for me and makes what was formerly hidden and distant now manifest and near: manifest in my own time, in my own person, and, what is greater and more pleasing to me, in the great assembly contemporary with me, as I proclaimed righteousness in the great assembly, not hiding this mercy from the great council. Therefore I, who first prayed to you, the Lord my God, saying, “Do not put your mercies far from me,” in the midst of my prayers—or in hope, or in fact—graciously and manifestly heard, change the voice of prayer into a voice of thanksgiving, saying:

“Your mercy and your truth have always upheld me.” I give you thanks, Lord, because your mercies, which formerly seemed distant, are now found near to me. For I recognize and feel that your mercy and truth have always upheld [Col. 1452B] me. I formerly observed your mercies in others and considered your works, and I trembled lest perhaps I should remain without a share in your mercies, which I knew in others. But now, through your grace revealing it, I know that your mercy and truth have always upheld me in eternal predestination, as now appears in time.

Alternatively: But you, Lord, cause what I said—“Do not put your mercies far from me,” miserable as I am and in need of mercies—not to lack effect. Complete the works of your mercy, always prepared for me from the foundation of the world, so that at the end of the world I may hear what the blessed will hear, to whom you will say: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you [Col. 1452C] from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34). For always, from the foundation of the world, from the first righteous person onward, your mercy, by which you are good, and your truth, by which you are just, have upheld me, leading me to you. For when I consider your past wonders, I perceive that you are good and love you; I see that you are just and fear you; and thus love and fear lead me onward. Secure in forgiveness, I am converted; secure in the truth of him who promises rewards to one persevering to the end, I strive to persevere to the end. I strive, indeed, according to the strength granted me by you, God; yet I know that I cannot stand unless, by your help, I am delivered and protected from evils surrounding me on every side.

**VERSE 13. “For evils without number have surrounded me.”** When I was a child of wrath, wholly [Col. 1452D] set in the evil one, evils without number filled me. But now, because the prince of this world, cast out, has no place in my heart on account of the peace given to people of good will—of whom I desire to be one—he attacks and assails me from without through the followers of his wickedness, demons and perverse people. Therefore I now say: “Evils without number have surrounded me.”

Alternatively: “Evils without number have surrounded me,” namely sins and diverse kinds of punishments, whose number is unknown to human beings, though it is known to God, who dispenses all things in measure, number, and weight—not only goods but also evils. He who is good inflicts these evils well, when through them he chastises for correction or punishes for condemnation, [Col. 1453A] dealing with each person as he knows, mercifully or justly. I rightly say, evils “without number.” For who could number the sins that are from ourselves and those suggested by others? “Who understands transgressions?” But who can enumerate what he does not understand? “I have sinned beyond the number of the sand of the sea, and my sins have multiplied.” If the tiny grains of sand are innumerable, how much more can I not number sins multiplied beyond the sand, or even, which is less, sufficiently see them? Why is this so? Clearly because:

“My iniquities have overtaken me, and I could not see.” For just as the Chaldeans overtook King Zedekiah and blinded him, first killing his sons while he watched, so my iniquities overtook [Col. 1453B] me and blinded me, first extinguishing the virtues which I possessed while I watched, because my loss of virtues I had possessed did not happen through ignorance. But after losing them I came to such ignorance that, blinded in mind, I cannot see in how great evils I lie, imprisoned under the Babylonian king. Because my sins demand it, even my own body is a prison to me, “which corrupts and weighs down the soul, while the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15).

Alternatively: “My iniquities have overtaken me,” just as the Philistines overtook Samson, blinded him, and made him grind, a woman having deceived him. For, while my own flesh or [Col. 1453C] another’s flesh flatters and entices me, my iniquities have overtaken me, taken away the eyes of my mind, and set me like a donkey at a turning mill, grinding flour—not the flour from which unleavened bread is made to be eaten by Israelites, but flour from which leavened bread is made, fit for Egyptians or even Philistines. For what are the vain thoughts which I sometimes grind, if not the flour of the Philistines, that is, of evil spirits? Unless they had first taken away my inward eyes, I would not, at their suggestion, grind external and useless cares; under their weight I could not see. By no effort could I bring it about that I should see either myself as a sinner or you, God, as the justifier of sinners. From my iniquities such weakness came upon me that those iniquities:

[Col. 1453D] “Have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.” My head is Christ; the hairs of this head are the saints rooted in him, above whom the wicked have multiplied. Or the hairs of this head are all the virtues proceeding from him; above these hairs iniquities have multiplied, because more ranks of vices than battle-lines of virtues are found, since two vices attack each virtue. Thus, for example, humility is attacked by genuine pride and false humility; piety by genuine impiety and false piety. The same is evident in the rest. Hence it is rightly said that iniquities have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head—that is, beyond the virtues which Christ, my head, has rooted in himself.

Alternatively: “My iniquities have multiplied beyond the [Col. 1454A] hairs of my head.” I, a Nazirite, I, like Samson, was strong so long as the hairs of my head were not cut off. But when, deceived and shaven through my own flesh or another’s, as through the harlot Delilah, I lost the holy meditations by which the ruling part of a human being—that is, the rational mind—is adorned as with beautiful hairs. Immediately blinded, I began to grind useless or harmful thoughts, sometimes, while singing psalms, turning one thing in my mouth and another in my heart, because my very heart also forsook me, so that I was very often forgetful of God and of myself, like a dove without a heart. “Ephraim,” says the prophet Hosea, “has become like a dove without a heart” (Hos. 7:11). This reproach therefore rightly applies to me, because my heart forsook me.

[Col. 1454B] Certainly, I was not without a heart like a dove without a heart; but though I had been created rational and endowed with understanding, my heart forsook me. Therefore my condition is worse than that of a dove without a heart and also without gall, because, full of gall and emptied of heart, I am pressed on every side by evils. Nor is there anyone able to rescue me from the hand of these oppressing evils, unless it please you, Lord, to deliver me.

Alternatively: “My heart,” that is, my reason, “has forsaken me”—I, who do not seek what is beneficial and do not even know myself. Thus Peter did not comprehend his own heart when he said: “I will not deny you” (Matt. 26:35). Note that he says: “My heart has forsaken me.” A human being was not naturally created or born without a heart; [Col. 1454C] but what was naturally in humanity before sin, the fault of the first human being forsook both him and his descendants, so that humanity is compared with irrational beasts, which do not have heart or reason. Thus a human being is not blind by nature, but blinded through fault, just as Zedekiah is read to have been blinded by the Chaldeans and Samson by the Philistines through their own fault.

Alternatively: “My iniquities have multiplied,” that is, those of my own people, “beyond the hairs of my head.” For I, Christ, am the head of my body, which is the Church; and my hairs, or my beard, are the elect who cling more closely to me. They are so few that by comparison the wicked are many. I do not speak of the wicked of this world, but of those who are in the Church, concerning whom I said above: “I proclaimed and spoke; [Col. 1454D] they were multiplied beyond number.” Moreover, “my heart has forsaken me”: that is, the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, in whom my heart had confidence, forsook me. This is exceedingly grievous, because nothing is more harmful than to endure as an enemy the one whom you love as your own heart. Thus I loved Judas, so far as lay in me, while he appeared among the apostles. But he forsook me, and left behind him many imitators of his treachery, who were to arise in the Church. From all of these:

**VERSE 14. May it please you, Lord God the Father, to deliver me, your only Son, together with all my members burdened by the treachery of such people; and to cause good and fruitful branches to be grafted into the places of the evil branches that have been cut off; and that not only Matthias, appointed in Judas’ place, may bear fruit, but that apostles like Matthias may occupy the places of every similar Judas, that worst [Col. 1455A] merchant, and bear fruit. You, Lord, look to help me. Look upon me, the true vine, you Father and husbandman; and by your regard help me, cutting off useless branches, because “the time for pruning has come” (Song 2:12), and cleansing the good branches, that they may bear more fruit.**

**VERSE 15. “Let those who seek my soul, to take it away, be confounded and ashamed.”** Let those who seek my soul—not in order to enjoy it in goodness but to take it away—be confounded when I rise again. Yet no one shall take it from me, but I lay it down and take it up again (John 10:17). Therefore, when I take it up again, let those who desire evil for me be confounded and afraid—not only those who do it, but also those who will it.

[Col. 1455B] **VERSE 16. “And let those who say to me, ‘Aha, aha,’ immediately bear their confusion”:** that is, let them repent.

In Hebrew it reads: “Let those who say to me, ‘Aha, aha,’ perish after their confusion.” This is the same as saying: Let those who say to me, “Aha, you who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days” (Matt. 27:40), perish in such a manner that, whether restrained by fear and reverence, they may not dare to utter such mockeries against me and mine, or, bound by love, may not wish to do so.

Alternatively: Let them be confounded—that is, let the miracles shining forth through me and mine trouble them into repentance. And lest their repentance thereafter be fruitless, let them reverence me, and reverently listen to mine, who now, while the power of darkness lasts, wish evil to me, not knowing what they do, being deceived, namely, by those who call me a deceiver and an evildoer. “If he were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18:30), they say to Pilate. Again, to the same man they say: “Lord, we remember that that deceiver said: After three days I shall rise again.” By saying such great evils of me, they wish evil to me and bring it about that others, likewise deceived through them, wish evil to me. But I know both the one deceiving and the one deceived: the deceiver through malice, and the one deceived through ignorance. Therefore I say: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34), praying especially for those who sin against me through ignorance rather than malice. Hence afterward they shall hear from my disciple Peter: “And now, brethren, I know that you acted through ignorance, as did also your rulers” (Acts 3:17). And he will add: “Repent therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out” (ibid., 19).

Alternatively: Let them be confounded and clothed, as with a double garment, in their own confusion; and let them reverence me in the shame and awe of penal fear—unless they are among those who once wished, but have now ceased, or will at some time cease, to wish evil to me. But let this befall those who knowingly and wickedly, persistently and obstinately wish evil to me; to such I also say: “If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, ‘We see’; your sin remains” (John 9:41). Such people wish evil to me even when they say good things to me, for example: “Master, we know that you are true and teach the way of God in truth; is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?” (Matt. 12:16). Thus, while saying good things to me, they wish evil to me, seeking opportunities whereby they may accuse me as an enemy of the kingdom and as contradicting Caesar. Let those who, while speaking good things in this way, wish evil to me and mine be confounded and reverence me. For one often intends evil even while blessing; thus those themselves blinded in mind, while cursing the man born blind who had been given sight, said: “Be his disciple” (John 9:28). They spoke a good thing, but wished evil. Often, too, a sinner is praised with good intention by one who does not know better, concerning the desires of his soul; this is excusable through ignorance. But when it is done deceitfully, the sin is inexcusable. For both of these wish evil to me, Christ: both he who, knowing me to be good, calls me evil, and he who, knowing any adversary of mine to be evil, calls him good. Let both be confounded by the manifest goodness of those whom they call evil, and by the malice of those whom they call good. For the former is wrathful; the latter deceitful. The wrathful man condemns the good; the deceitful man praises the evil. Both are evil and must be guarded against, and prayer must be made against both, that they may be confounded, as was said, and reverence me. Of the wrathful I have already spoken and prayed that they may be confounded. Of the deceitful I still say: “Let them immediately bear their confusion, who say to me, ‘Well done, well done.’” With the wrathful I rightly endure delay, because the abuse of such persons is sometimes advantageous either to me or to mine, just as it was useful to me, David, to hear the curses and reproaches of Shimei. In hope of blessings in return for his curses, I took very seriously the zeal of the sons of Zeruiah on my behalf, and patiently and long-sufferingly endured the reproaches hurled against me, which were useful to me. But delay is harmful when listening to flatterers. Therefore I pray that those who say to me, “Well done, well done,” may without delay immediately bear their confusion.

Alternatively: “May it please you, O Lord, to deliver me.” I do not say, “May it please,” but “May it jointly please you, O Lord,” because I, David the penitent, understand my Lord as three and one. Because of the Trinity of persons I say, “May it jointly please,” desiring that the whole Trinity together consent to my salvation, and that the work in me be manifest not of one person, or of two only, but that it may please all three that I be delivered from evils to be avoided and helped in doing good. Nor again do I say, “May it please you all,” but “you,” on account of the unity of the three, because the three are one. Therefore I say: May it jointly please you, O Lord, to deliver me from evils. And because it is not enough to turn aside from evil unless I do good, according to what elsewhere you say to me: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27), O Lord, look upon me so as to help me in doing good. I call upon you, three and one, for my help according to your good pleasure, because through a mirror and in an enigma I see you alike threefold and one.

The mirror is creation; the enigma is Sacred Scripture. Certainly, in the mirror of creation you appear, O omnipotent Father, who were able to make, and did make, great and many things out of nothing, and thereby showed yourself to be the almighty Creator. Likewise you, Son, the eternal Wisdom of God, reveal yourself in the supremely wise ordering of creatures, “reaching mightily from end to end and disposing all things sweetly.” You also, Holy Spirit the Paraclete, appear in this mirror of the whole creation because you make all things, powerfully created by the Father and wisely ordered through the Son, useful to the saints and elect, for whom all things work together for good. This is a great and evident judgment of your goodness in the mirror of creatures.

Further, in the threefold structure of things—heaven, earth, and sea—you, threefold God, are recognized. For you, Father, are said to be in heaven, although you are everywhere; you, Son, clothed in flesh made from earth, were seen upon earth and dwelt with men; and you, Spirit of both, who in the beginning were borne over the waters and now make the waters fruitful for the quickening of souls, who slay the invisible Pharaoh with his army in the waters of baptism reddened by Christ’s blood, and through that same Red Sea make a passage for God’s people to the promised land; who also, through waters of tears, whiten the life of penitents beyond snow—you are rightly recognized in the element of water familiar to you. Yet, equally with the Father and the Son, you are everywhere, filling all things within and containing all things without; for you are that Spirit of whom it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (Wisdom 1:7).

[Col. 1457C] Therefore, when you turn your eyes to examine the threefold structure of things, as though through a mirror you see its Maker, threefold in unity and one in Trinity: venerating the Father in heaven, the incarnate Son upon earth, and the Holy Spirit in the element of water familiar to him. Yet you, O threefold God, are wholly everywhere in your majesty, by which all things are filled, contained, and governed. “Heaven and earth are full of your glory”; you who say, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24), who contain the thrones of heaven and behold the abysses, encompass the earth in your palm, weigh the mountains, “reaching mightily from end to end and disposing all things sweetly.” You move the world without being moved; you govern visible things without being seen; you contain all things without being contained. Yet in the things which you move, govern, and contain, you are known, just as in a mirror we contemplate the image of the sun, whose brightness our eyes cannot endure to see in itself.

The very globe of the solar body, from which brightness is born and heat proceeds—brightness illuminating the earth, heat making it fruitful—that globe itself, I say, which is the eye of the world, is a kind of mirror of God. In it appears the brightness of the Father’s glory, namely the Son; and from it proceeds the heat of fruitful charity into the whole body of the Church, which is none other than the Holy Spirit. He is especially conspicuous in this: that, having been seen in fire above the apostles, he is still perceived in their fiery tongues whenever we hear them speaking in their Scriptures or epistles.

Further, in the mirror of angelic and human creation, you, Father, show your power by giving them a life so powerful that, whether it remains in eternal blessedness or in eternal punishment, it shall endure forever, subject to no death or failure. For although human bodies die for a time, the rational spirit, whether human or angelic, never loses perpetual life, even when it loses good life. This, in the mirror of rational creation, is a great indication of your omnipotence, O Father, against which absolutely nothing can prevail.

> [Note: [Col. 1457D] The manuscript reads *nullique* (“to no one”) for *nulli* (“to none”).]

Likewise you, Son of God, eternal Wisdom, clearly appear in rational creation, which has no other source for being rational than that you, eternal Reason, illuminate it—you who “enlighten every person coming into this world.” Hence the reason of angel or human distinguishes light from darkness, even in those who loved darkness more than light, because you, unbounded Light, encompass all hearts, whether of those who hate you or of those who love you. Therefore, just as daylight touches alike sound and bleary eyes, yet delights the former and torments the latter, so you, true Light, equally touch all rational minds: some unto aid, that they may become approved; others unto testimony, that they may be without excuse while they love darkness rather than the light shown to them in their distinguishing evil and good by it. Thus Pharaoh said: “The Lord is righteous, but I and my people are wicked” (Exod. 9:27), and yet did not so choose to understand as to act rightly. So also the Jews both saw and hated you, the true Light, and your Father, the Father of lights. What shall I say of the remaining impious children of darkness? Do you not, O unfailing Light, shine even in darkness, though the darkness itself does not comprehend you, while it loves itself rather than you? Will not all workers of iniquity know that you, the true Light, condemn iniquity, whether through the natural law, the thoughts mutually accusing or even defending each one’s life or work, or through the written law, with its plain commandments forbidding evils and commanding goods? Through all these things you, true Light, are recognized in the mirrors of sentient and rational creation.

But those mirrors of minds represent you in themselves more clearly when they have been cleansed of vices and boiled down, as it were, to purity, or filed and polished. But you, Holy Spirit, who flee falsehood in discipline, do not dwell in a body subject to sins, and withdraw yourself from thoughts lacking understanding, inhabit good minds alone. In them, as in transparent mirrors, you manifest yourself as the Spirit of fear, making those who share in you reverent and poor in spirit; as the Spirit of piety, in blessed minds; as the Spirit of knowledge, in the blessed who mourn and recognize their iniquity; as the Spirit of fortitude, in the blessed who hunger and thirst for righteousness; as the Spirit of counsel, in the blessed who are merciful; as the Spirit of understanding, in the blessed pure in heart who see God; and as the Spirit of wisdom, in the blessed peacemakers—as in pure and clear mirrors.

Let what has been said suffice for the moment, by way of illustration, regarding how you, O threefold God, are seen through a mirror. But as to how you, three and one, are known through the enigma of the Scriptures: whoever reads understands, if he prudently observes that not without reason you, one God, said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). Again you say: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; this is my name forever” (Exod. 3:15). The plural number, and the name of God repeated three times, then signify that you are threefold when you say, “Let us make,” and, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” But when you say, “This is my name forever,” you signify that you are one. Otherwise you would say, “These are our names forever,” if by the name of God repeated three times you wished a plurality of gods to be understood; nor would you say, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” but, “We are three gods.”

Again, when you say, “Hear, Israel: your God is one” (Deut. 6:4), you teach faith in unity within the Godhead. But when you say, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Matt. 22:37), you signify that you are threefold, because you show that you are to be worshipped with threefold love. These and other like indications of your threefold majesty, investigated under the veil of the law in a dark enigma, scarcely shine forth. But in the prophets the testimonies of the supreme Trinity shine more fittingly, where the Father is plainly recognized, whose child is asserted to have been born to us and whose Son has been given to us; and there the Son himself speaks of himself: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me. He sent me to proclaim good news to the meek” (Luke 4:18). Behold, in prophecy the clear names of the supreme Trinity are found—or rather, one name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because the three are one. Therefore truth appearing in flesh says in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Again: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:15). And so that the rule of baptism might stand firm and perfect, he says: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). He did not say, “in the names,” lest a plurality of gods be understood in the three; but he said, “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” so that those who wish to preserve the baptism they have received may know that they must worship one God in threefoldness.

O supreme Trinity, how are you to be worshipped, you who, as has been said, are known in the mirror of creation and in the enigma of Scripture? I think—indeed, I most firmly believe and do not doubt in the least—that you must be worshipped as you are proclaimed there to be worshipped, where you are also shown to be known. You are indeed seen there in an enigma; but how you are to be worshipped is seen not so much in the obscurity of the enigma as in the brightness of your light, where it is said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Matt. 22:37). Again: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. 4:10). Why him alone? Hear the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters.” Again: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matt. 6:24). Therefore let us serve the one and threefold God, worshipping him in faith and charity: bound by sincere religion to the Father through faith, to the Son through hope, and to the Holy Spirit through charity.

Let us worship him by diligently imitating, and following the example of, three patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; three righteous men—Noah, Daniel, and Job; three kings—David, Hezekiah, and Josiah; three youths—Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael; three sons of Mattathias—Judas Maccabaeus, Jonathan, and Simon; and three apostles—Peter, James, and John—taken by the Lord up the mountain. Let us worship him by living soberly, righteously, and devoutly: reverencing the Father in sobriety, the Son in righteousness, and the Holy Spirit in piety. Let us worship him by hearing his word obediently, intelligently, and willingly, or delightfully: reverencing the Father, who is to be feared, in obedience; the Son, who is Wisdom, in understanding; and the Holy Spirit, who is the eternal sweetness of God’s Word, in most willing delight. Let us worship him by speaking God’s word so as to move, teach, and delight the hearer, seeking to render the hearer attentive, teachable, and well-disposed: attentive toward the Father, teachable toward the Son, and well-disposed toward the Holy Spirit.

Let us worship him by carefully investigating and understanding what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of that threefold God: good in the worship of the Father, well-pleasing in the worship of the Son, and perfect in the worship of the Holy Spirit. Let us worship him by adding to the image of reason impressed upon us by him the twofold likeness of his wisdom and goodness: so that, just as the unchangeable image of reason in us expresses the Father in us, with whom there is no change or shadow of turning, so wisdom may express the Son and goodness in us may express the Holy Spirit. Let us worship him with a twofold love that is strong, cautious, and sweet: strong as death in honor of the Father’s omnipotence; cautious in avoiding evils in honor of the Son, who is Wisdom; sweet in fulfilling goods in honor of the Holy Spirit, who is eternal Goodness.

[Col. 1460D] Let us worship the threefold God by purifying the memory of our past life through tears of repentance, lifting the affection of the present from earth to heaven, and illuminating our future intention with the single eye of piety: so that a whitened memory may glorify the Father; the heavenly affection arising from it, the only-begotten Son, who came from heaven and is above all; and the simple, pure intention proceeding from both, the Holy Spirit. Let us worship him with pure thought, cautious speech, and kindly action. Let old men, young men, and boys worship him in the choir of men; and in the choir of women, the company of martyrs and virgins, and simple little girls, harmoniously joining their voices in chaste songs: so that in old men and matrons may be honored the gray maturity of the Ancient of Days; in young men and virgins, the vigor of our Savior and defender; and in boys and little girls, the blessed purity and simplicity of the Holy Spirit.

Let us worship him by fasting, praying, and giving alms, without the left hand knowing what the right hand does, so that through these three exercises of Christian religion the favor sought may be not that of this world but of the one threefold God: the unincarnate Father approving our fast, by which we are cleansed from the dregs of fleshly desires; the incarnate Son receiving in the censer of his flesh the incense of our prayer; and the Holy Spirit, who is the charity of both, accepting our alms, given not from sadness or necessity but from cheerful charity.

Let us worship the threefold God alike in our speech and silence. For the Father spoke, and all these things were made which our life upon earth requires. The Son taught the other life, attested by his resurrection, which is not in this world. The Holy Spirit, speaking in the saints, makes intercession with unutterable groanings. Therefore, by speaking of the necessities of this life to be passed in God’s service, we honor the Father, because he knows that we need all these things. By speaking of the glory of the future life prefigured in Christ’s resurrection, we honor the Son. Moreover, in praises, thanksgivings, and prayers the Holy Spirit is honored, because through such private soliloquies or choral harmonies he makes intercession in the saints and for the saints with unutterable groanings, when what is uttered by the mouth is what is occupied in the heart. Let us also worship the threefold God in silence, whereby we restrain lips and tongue from other speech, so that we may always offer these three members unstained to God in the three good kinds of speech noted above.

Let us worship the threefold God by making his cross upon our face with three fingers, under faith in and the name of the Trinity. Let us worship him by writing about him with three fingers. Let women also worship him with three fingers, not only by writing good and holy things, but also by taking and turning the spindle with three fingers, as the strong woman is praised because “her fingers took hold of the spindle” (Prov. 31:19). Again, Ecclesiastes says: “A time to tear, and a time to sew” (Eccles. 3:7), apart, of course, from a more sacred understanding, in which the needle is understood as the sharp, subtle, all-penetrating fear of the Lord, or as Christ himself. Hence in the Gospel an easy passage through a needle’s eye is denied to the rich man, because the narrow gate, which is Christ himself, does not admit one who loves riches (Matt. 19:24). This “time to sew,” I say, may also be applied to the handiwork of the strong woman, who, holding the needle with three fingers while sewing clothes for the poor, performs a work in which the Trinity is glorified among the poor.

But the Trinity is glorified and worshipped not only by three fingers doing good work, but also by the three measures of flour, in the whole substance of a human being, if what the Apostle prays is fulfilled: “May the God of peace sanctify us wholly, so that your whole spirit and soul and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thess. 5:23).

[Col. 1462A] This is what I, David, singing—or repenting—desire to be fulfilled in me. Therefore I invoke not one person of the Trinity but the whole Trinity, saying: “May it jointly please you, O Lord.” “May it jointly please,” that is, may it at once please all three, who are one, to deliver me from evils which are unprofitable, or, what is worse, hinder me from the true worship of the supreme Trinity; and to help me carry out good works and virtues manfully, in honor of that eternal and supreme Trinity. Then my enemies may not mock me as a lazy laborer and useless servant, but, seeing you, supreme Trinity, perfectly worshipped by me, may be confounded and revere you—especially those who wish evil to me and those flattering persons who say to me, “Well done, well done.” Some of these are Gogites, others Magogites, enlarging the army of Antichrist, who is called Gog and Magog.

For those who, pretending with deceitful heart to love my good deeds, say to me, “Well done, well done,” as though applauding my goodness, are Gogites: that is, so covered over that their malice cannot easily be recognized. But those who openly condemn are Magogites, because they are uncovered as enemies, although perhaps they were previously thought friends. These Magogites must be endured for a time, because they exercise patience, purge guilt, and by their wrath often turn away divine wrath; for while desiring to harm, they unwillingly benefit those—especially those for whom all things work together for good—even things intended for their evil. But those Gogites who, feigning friendship, say to me, “Well done, well done,” must immediately bear their confusion when their flattery is exposed. Thus that Gogite who called me, the true David, “good master” with a deceitful heart was immediately rebuked by me when I said: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” (Luke 18:19).

Thus all who say to me—that is, to mine—through flattery, “Well, well done by you,” must immediately bear their confusion, refuted by the clearest evidence of things: no one acts well except God alone. For “all have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:3); and God alone does well or good, because he alone works both willing and accomplishing for good will. Therefore the sober worker says: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10)—understand: “worked.”

Therefore let those who attribute to me, a Christian, a branch, the good that they see in me bear their confusion. For every fruit which the true vine works through me or in me, although it appears in me, is not from me through myself but from Christ the vine and from God, the root of the vine: for God is the head of Christ, from whom through Christ every fruitful branch lives. Indeed, Christ the true vine could not give life to branches remaining in him unless he were also the same one who, being human, is of the same nature and substance as human beings. Hence, for me who remain in him, good thought is like a vine-leaf; good intention, like the flower preceding fruit; good action, like good fruit. When “Well done, well done” is therefore said to me, God’s glory is transferred to me. Let those who say it immediately bear their confusion, struck by such magnificence of good works as no human understanding can or ought to ascribe to me, since the manifest and sole operation of divine grace shines in my works, along with that gracious condescension by which, although I was unworthy, it deigned to work through me and with me its divine work—a work divinely so magnified that, even if I keep silence, anyone who presumptuously attributes to me, a little human being, divine glory due to God alone must bear his confusion.

God alone “does great wonders”; in him alone every saint ought rightly to glory, every saint who works wonders in his life, which he has done from no other source than because he who alone does great wonders has done them in him. In doing these things God has no need of my good works, yet through me he has done, and does, the good which pleases him. Therefore you alone are to be praised and glorified in me: when I appear to do good, you do good through me. But because this is common to good and evil persons—that you, being good, work good things through them—whereas you are said to work only in those whom you make partners in your good work through good intention, therefore more [the text breaks off].

**VERSE 17.** “Let all who seek you exult and rejoice in you, and let those who love your salvation always say: ‘Let the Lord be magnified.’” Let those who love your salvation—who love Christ the true Savior—say this.
