Although you are rich and I am needy and poor, you nevertheless do not abandon the gifts of your grace, but even through me, poor and needy, and with me work such wondrous works that, if anyone should assign them to me in the hearing of any sober listener, he would immediately bear his confusion, and that listener would say to him: “Why do you attribute a work of righteousness, a work of virtue, a work of the Lord, to a sinful man? Why do you assign to a little human being a magnificent work which plainly cannot be done except by God alone?”

Alternatively: “Let them exult and rejoice.” Let them exult in bodily alacrity and rejoice in mental gladness—all who seek you, founded upon you, seeking to glorify you and not me, and glorifying you in me. And let them always say: “Let the Lord be magnified.” Let them say it sometimes with their lips, but continually with the cry of their heart. What are they to say? “Let the Lord be magnified”; or, “Let the Lord always be magnified in his servant,” in whom, by justifying and magnifying him, he shows himself great or magnificent. Therefore let the Lord always be magnified in that the number of his servants is increased; and let each of his servants be magnified, not for an hour but always, by whose regard he himself is magnified and gloried in as being called Lord. For among human beings too it is customary that, when a certain lord’s servant appears honorable and precious, the lord himself thereby appears honorable and magnificent. Therefore, so that the Lord may be magnified in the glorified and magnified virtues of his servants, let those who desire your salvation, O Lord, always say: “Let the Lord be magnified.”

**VERSE 18.** “But I am needy and poor; O God, help me.” Those who say to me, “Well done, well done,” whether through flattery or, as they suppose, through truthful praise, glorify and exalt me by their praises as though I were rich and abounding in many goods, whether spiritual or temporal. But I am needy and poor, in my own judgment, because I know myself better than they do and know that I am needy and poor. I am needy because I need many things; poor because I do not possess the things I need. One person needs many things and has many of the things he needs: though needy, he is not poor. Another needs few things and has the few things he needs; neither is he poor. Indeed, that person is more abundantly supplied than people who need more and possess more, because it is better to need less than to possess more; and that poverty which no want constrains is sufficiently rich. Hence the saying: “Our poverty was sufficient for us, so that it was counted riches” (Tob. 5:25).

But I am needy and poor because I need many things which I do not have. I need many things for my own sake, because I am frail and cannot be content with moderate or few supports in this life. I am also burdensome: “I have become burdensome to myself” (Job 7:20). Nor can I be raised to things above with few or moderate vehicles of virtues, or with sparse wings of holy conduct. Thus, in myself and for my own sake, I need many things; and because I do not have them, I am poor.

Moreover, I also need many things which I do not have, for the sake of helping and consoling others through me. They cry out to me or look to me as though to a rich person able and bound to console or help them. But I am needy and poor. I know that I owe them help and comfort; but my miserable need and poverty consist in this: I am bound by a debt to help others, though I cannot even benefit myself, because I am needy and poor. Yet in this I have my sole hope of salvation and consolation: the Lord is mindful of me.

The Hebrew truth reads: “I am needy and poor,” which has already been explained. Our translation reads: “I am a beggar and poor,” and may be explained thus. When others hear themselves praised, they swell inwardly and say with the Pharisee: “I thank you, God, that I am not like other people” (Luke 18:11). But I am a beggar, saying with the tax collector, who did not lift his defiled eyes to heaven: “What do I say? God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” Thus I am a beggar and poor in my own judgment, even when I am exalted in another’s judgment. I am a beggar seeking forgiveness of sins, though among others I am magnified for an abundance of virtues. I am a beggar, not like a greedy person who asks even for superfluities, but like a poor person asking for necessities. I am a beggar and poor because I ask and have not yet been sufficiently heard. I am a beggar because I ask; and poor because I do not suffice for myself. Therefore, still begging, I say:

“You are my helper and protector; my God, do not delay.” O Lord, you are my helper, who until now have helped me in many good things; you are my protector, who have protected me from many evils; you are my God, who made me. All this is established. But lest I fail on the way, I ask you not to delay in helping me in good things, protecting me from evils, and deifying me in rewards through participation in your Godhead. You are my helper, protector, and God; I say to you: “Do not delay,” because unless you hasten to shorten the evil days, even the elect, if possible, will be led into error—how much more do I fear for myself, who do not know whether I am elect. “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days” (Matt. 24:19), or rather in these evil days, in which I, needy or begging and poor, am pressed on every side, seeing that a great woe hangs over those pregnant and nursing. For woe to those pregnant—that is, swelling with desire for others’ possessions—and woe to those nursing—that is, loving ill-gotten goods and unwilling to restore them.

But I am needy and poor because, while I have given and give to the poor all that I could justly have had and may have, and restore fourfold if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I have become poor and a beggar. By helping the poor I have become poor; by helping beggars I have become a beggar, begging from the rich what I may give to the poor.

I read the saying: “It is better not to have something to give than shamelessly to beg something to give.” Considering this, I did not wish to beg shamelessly, but begged humbly with great shame. But now, lest in begging I be thought to amass shameful gains under the appearance of almsgiving, be my helper, O Lord, so that, with your help and without delay in your assistance, I may be found sufficient and may no longer be bound in beggary and iron, but in all my necessities and those of mine may experience the blessed consoler who understands concerning me, needy and poor. I say “understands,” not merely “hears”: he need not have to hear me begging, but, moved by pity, may himself understand concerning me or another needy, poor, and silent person. Expecting above all such consolation, I waited for you, O Lord, as I said at the beginning of the psalm. Therefore, O Lord, do not delay, but without delay always help me and mine, as I waited in expectation.

Alternatively: Let those who love your salvation always say: “Let the Lord be magnified.” Let them say this while praising and magnifying you, O Lord; but in consideration of himself let each say: “But I am needy and poor.” Let each say this of himself and understand it to be true as he says it, because blessed is the one who understands concerning himself that he is poor and needy. When he calls himself poor or a sinner, let him understand it in such a way that he says: “I understand concerning myself, because I know my poverty and my iniquity.” Hence I also understand that the Lord is mindful of me, from whom I have this understanding, and to whom I say: “You are my helper and protector; my God, do not delay.”

Alternatively: But I am a beggar and poor. When I, the true David who speak in this psalm, had satisfied five thousand men with five loaves, those who had been filled wished to seize me and make me king (John 6:15). But knowing that my kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36), I fled from them to the mountain alone, to pray and to beg; for though I was rich, in order to enrich others I appeared needy and poor in this world, a beggar among men, from whom, either personally or through my own, I begged these temporal things so that I might give them heavenly things. Thus I begged water from the Samaritan woman, so that I might give her to drink of far better water. Yet more abundantly and perfectly I begged by praying to the Father for my own, saying: “Father, keep those whom you have given me”; and I did not ask and beg only for these, but also for those who were to believe in me through their word, that all might be one in me, as I and the Father are one (John 17:11–12). Although he is my Father, because I am God the Son of God, he is also my Lord, because I emptied myself, taking the form of a servant [Col. 1466B], and faithfully serving him; for “as he gave me commandment, so I do” (John 14:31).

Therefore he himself, the Lord in whose service I was humbled, does not forget me or my own, but is mindful of me and my own. To him I also say: “You are my helper and my protector, my God.” A helper in fulfilling obedience; a protector against the evils which arise on the narrow path of obedience itself; the God of me and of my own, to whom I said: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17). I know that you help and protect me and my own; but I ask: “Do not delay.” Rather, work help and protection for my own so swiftly that it may become known to the whole world [Col. 1466C] that your word runs swiftly, through which you help and protect your people. In doing this I ask, Father, do not tarry; do not delay. You indeed, speaking through the prophet concerning me, your servant, said: “Call his name: Hasten swiftly to strip the spoils; hurry to plunder” (Isa. 8:3). And I, according to my name, desiring that my works and those of my own may be completed swiftly, quickly, and hastily in my obedience—with you helping and protecting me in mine—ask: do not delay, do not tarry.

Glory to the Father, the Lord whom I waited for with expectation, and who inclined to me. Glory to the Son, who says in this psalm: “Behold, I come. In the head of the book it is written concerning me, that I should do your will, my God.” Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that union and communion of the paternal and filial will [Col. 1466D], in which God the Son, made man, says to God the Father: “I have willed your will, my God.” For when the Son says to the Father, “I have willed your will,” he signifies that he loves the Father and is loved by the Father; for to will the same thing and to reject the same thing in good matters is firm friendship, even in human agreements. How much more is this so between Father and Son, whose everlasting unity of will is that love which is rightly understood as the Holy Spirit, who, as the Apostle John affirms, is love?

Let the Father glory and be glorified, because, as he inclined to me, I was heard and drawn out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth. Let the Son glory and be glorified by every creature, because he had perfect ears, by which he heard the Father perfectly and obeyed him for us. Let the Spirit of both glory [Col. 1467A] and be glorified, by whose simultaneous kindling and illumination of the apostles righteousness was proclaimed in the great Church of the Gentiles, which before the coming of the Holy Spirit had been enclosed in the small synagogue of the Jews. Let the supreme Trinity glory and be glorified, to whom it is said: “May it please you, Lord, to deliver me”; for salvation would not have come to the world unless the three, who are one, had been pleased together [Col. 1468A]. Therefore it is not said, “May it please you [plural], Lord,” but “May it please you [singular], Lord,” so that unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity may be acknowledged—to whom be honour and glory always and everywhere, without end or failure, in the great Church, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Psalm XL

[Col. 1467]

[Col. 1467A] “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor,” etc. [Col. 1467B] The title is:

**UNTO THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID.**

Or, according to Jerome: “Unto the end; understanding for the sons of Korah.” As is read in the Book of Numbers (26:11), Korah rose up with Dathan and Abiram in rebellion against Moses and Aaron. When they were swallowed up by the earth with all their possessions, Korah, offering incense with two hundred and fifty men, was consumed with them by fire, as a figure of the destruction of those who oppose Christ’s priesthood. Yet certain sons of Korah did not imitate their father’s wickedness. Therefore they were later appointed by David to the ministry of the house of the Lord, and blessed by the Lord with everlasting joy. Accordingly, the psalms inscribed “for the sons of Korah” contain nothing sorrowful. For *Korah* is interpreted “Calvary,” [Col. 1467C] the place of the Resurrection, and whoever are its sons cannot be sorrowful. Indeed, Christ’s Passion itself, signified by Calvary, is our glory. Hence the Apostle says: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14).

This Calvary was prefigured in Elisha. As he went up from Jericho to Bethel, forty-two boys came out of Bethel; when they mocked Elisha, saying, “Go up, bald one” (4 Kings 2:23), Elisha commanded two bears to come out of the forest, and the boys were killed by them. So too, when Christ went up into Bethel—that is, into the house of God, which was the Synagogue—he was mocked by little ones and commanded two bears to come forth: that is, the devil and his angels, or Vespasian and Titus, by whom forty-two were slain [Col. 1467D], because forty-two years after the Resurrection those were destroyed who, though given this number of years for repentance, did not repent.

Therefore those are sons of this Korah who, imitating his humility, accepted the sign of the cross, which had been a mark of disgrace. Their understanding is directed unto Christ, the end: they believe him to be God although poor and suffering. This is the intention of the psalm; and even the Calvary of the Passion is their glory.

Observe that whenever “understanding” is attached to a title, something other than what appears must be understood beyond the surface. Christ himself speaks in this psalm. For who else says: “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my breads, magnified treachery against me. But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise [Col. 1468A] me up, and I will repay them”? Indeed, he who, at the very moment of the Passion, said, “I know whom I have chosen,” immediately added: “But that the Scripture may be fulfilled: He who eats my bread shall lift up his heel against me” (John 13:18), leaves no room for doubt about this [Col. 1468B]. Thus he who, though rich, was made needy and poor for us, and who at the end of the preceding psalm said, “But I am a beggar and poor; the Lord is mindful of me,” says here at the beginning of the next: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor,” etc. He thereby shows both the condemnation and misery of those who are scandalized by him, judging him merely needy and poor—that is, merely human—and the blessedness of those who are not scandalized by him, believing him to be true man and true God.

This psalm is divided into three parts [Col. 1468C]. In the first is heard the voice of the prophet, or of any orthodox teacher, teaching that he is blessed who, seeing Christ’s weakness, understands that his divine power was perfect even in human weakness. The second contains the voice of the Head, speaking of his Passion: “My enemies have spoken evil against me.” The third concerns the Resurrection: “But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up.” Let us explain this text of the psalm more fully.

**VERSE 2. “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor.”** Christ said at the end of the preceding psalm: “I am needy and poor.” But blessed is he who understands concerning this needy and poor one (2 Cor. 8:9). For though he was rich, he became poor for us, that through his poverty we might become rich. For, [Col. 1468D] being in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized (Phil. 2:6). Therefore in his divinity he was always equal in riches to God the Father. He himself, made man, also says: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matt. 11:27). He was therefore rich: in his divinity he always possessed all things, and in his humanity all things possessed by the Father were delivered to him.

The Father has in his power all created things, visible and invisible: thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, the other orders of angels, and everything that can be understood or perceived—or that exceeds angelic and human understanding and is known to God alone—such as his incomprehensible judgments and unsearchable ways, in which no one is his counsellor, and the peace of God which surpasses all [Col. 1469A] understanding. The Father always had and has all these things; and all were at once delivered to the God-man by his Father. For in divinely granting to the man conceived that he should be his Father, not by adoption but by begetting, he at the same time gave him all that the same Son had formerly possessed with himself in his divinity.

What did he possess? Certainly all that the Father possessed: not only in possession but also in the glory in which he was glorious before the ages. The needy and poor man, born of a virgin, possessed this glory fully from conception; but he did not wish it to appear openly, concealing his glory for our salvation. For if men or rulers had known this Lord of glory, they would never have crucified him.

He therefore appeared needy and poor, so that he had nowhere [Col. 1469A] to lay his head, lacking a home of his own in this world. Yet blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor. [Col. 1469B] Simon Barjona was blessed, because flesh and blood did not reveal it to him, but the heavenly Father, enabling him to understand concerning that needy and poor one. Men who said that he was John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets (Mark 8:28), had an understanding not concerning this needy and poor one, but far beneath him. But the blessed disciple, taught by the highest Father, understood concerning this needy and poor one precisely what the Father himself revealed to him. For when God Most High revealed himself as the Father of this needy and poor one, and revealed him not as his adoptive but as his natural Son, [Col. 1469C] this also became known at once: that he was not needy and poor merely as one of the prophets.

For which prophet is in himself so rich that by his own power he can accomplish—not, I say, the greatest goods or all goods, but even a few or the least goods? Which among all the saints can truthfully say, “I can do all things,” unless he adds, “through him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4:13)? And who strengthens the elect except Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, “reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1)? And who or what is this needy and poor one, whom in his poverty we saw mocked by the Jews, having neither form nor beauty, but the power of God and the wisdom of God? [Col. 1469D] John, Elijah, Jeremiah, or any one of the prophets might be called and understood wise and powerful; yet none of them could be called the wisdom or power of God, because none received this height of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge: to be himself the very wisdom of God.

But to this needy and poor one, whom men say is properly the Son of Man and only improperly the Son of God because of the assumed mortality, it was granted altogether as properly to be Son of God as to be Son of Man. Otherwise Peter, when questioned concerning the Son of Man, could not truly have said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” unless he were both Son of Man and Son of God (John 6:70). And if the man is Son of God not by adoption but by generation, he rightly possesses the Father’s riches—not as a needy and poor man admitted solely by grace into an inheritance alien to himself [Col. 1470A], but as a natural son entering his own inheritance, from which he seemed to have gone out for a time, when “his going forth was from the height of heaven” (Ps. 18:7) and made its course even to hell. Having despoiled it and carried off much riches from it, this needy and poor one returned to the Father, receiving for himself the hereditary, everlasting splendour of riches which he had before the world was made.

Indeed, his inheritance was in splendid riches even when he appeared needy and poor in this world. Human nature, not yet assumed into God, was needy and poor while still undifferentiated in its own mass. But once it was set apart by the Holy Spirit and formed in God as the new man, then—separated from needy and poor sinners and [Col. 1470B] made higher than the heavens—it is rightly understood to be rich. Not as one who received a part of God’s riches, but as the one to whom the Father gave all things, and who truthfully says: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father.” Peter acknowledged this; understanding rightly concerning the needy and poor one, he said: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God.”

On this passage Blessed Ambrose says in his commentary on Luke: “Although the other apostles know, Peter nevertheless answered before the rest: ‘You are Christ, the Son of the living God’” (Matt. 16:16). “Thus he embraced all things, who expressed both the nature and the name in which the sum of powers consists.” Again, shortly afterward, he says: “Peter knew that all things are in the Son of God. For the Father gave all things to the Son. If he gave all things, he gave the eternity which he possesses and poured forth majesty as well.”

[Col. 1470C] As Saint Ambrose says these things, we too, thinking in harmony concerning the needy and poor one treated here, understand him thus: we affirm him to be as rich as his Father. Hence, in recalling the extremity of his poverty in humiliation, the Evangelist relates how he washed his disciples’ feet and says among other things: “Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, he rose from supper and laid aside his garments” (John 13:3–4). Behold, he to whom God the Father gave all things lays aside his garments and, girded with a linen cloth, begins to wash his disciples’ feet. For unless he had emptied himself, unless he had been girded with the linen cloth of our passibility, he would not have washed us from sins.

Nevertheless, in that very humiliation of his self-emptying he knew that the Father had given all things [Col. 1470D] into his hands—all things, I say, without any exception. The Father gave all things to him when he granted that he himself should be his Father, to whom he also says: “I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a son” (1 Chron. 17:13). Again: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). He says, “I have begotten,” not “I have adopted,” as with other sons. Therefore this poor and needy one is rightly understood above all sons: the Most High Son of the Most High, the richest Son of the richest Father, enriched with every height of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge in his humanity no less than he was always rich in his own and the Father’s divinity. For the Son of God, born as man into God, cannot lack anything possessed by God the Son, since the Son of Man is the same as the Son of God.

The Son of God has God the Father; likewise the Son of Man has [Col. 1471A] the same Father. The Son of God has divinity, in which he is perfect God; the Son of Man likewise has divinity, in which he himself is perfect God. For although God, in assuming humanity, was not changed into man—he who always remained and remains the same, never less or greater than himself—yet humanity, in receiving eternal divinity, advanced in the Son of God to the majesty of eternal glory in such a manner that the man is not inferior or poorer than God in the complete glory granted to him. Human nature is indeed lesser in divinity; it did not increase in its created condition, but it increased in the confirmation of its glory, in which the Father confirmed him as equal to himself, as it is said of him: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you have strengthened for yourself” (Ps. [Col. 1471B] 79:18).

For human nature was fragile even in the Son of God until it was strengthened by the divinity implanted in it. At the conception, when the Holy Spirit came upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, it was confirmed secretly; just as David was first secretly anointed king and was afterward openly anointed after Saul’s death. Thus also Christ, when by dying he destroyed our death and by rising restored life, was openly confirmed, all fragility which he bore for us having been swallowed up and his glory revealed. This glory was indeed given at the conception, but was made manifest through the Resurrection, the Ascension, and the bestowals of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Father says to him, when he prays for the glorification of his humanity: “I have glorified [Col. 1471C] [you], and I will glorify [you] again” (John 12:28). That is: “I glorified you secretly at conception, and I shall glorify you again openly.”

Then I anointed you king in the chamber of the virginal womb, as the angel said to the Virgin: “The Lord God shall give him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign in the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end.” Again: “He shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke 1:32). Hereafter it shall be manifested to the whole world—not indeed to every people, but to witnesses preordained—that you are he of whom it is written: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. 109:1).

Is not the poor and needy man to whom, or concerning whom, these things were said to be understood concerning the needy and poor—that is, as having surpassed without limit [Col. 1471D] the condition of a needy and poor man? Though he is found in outward appearance as a man and humbled unto death, even death of the cross, he nevertheless has “the name which is above every name” (Phil. 2:7, 9).

Blessed is he who understands this name, whose understanding is concerning the needy and poor one. For in the appearance of a needy and poor man he could not only be understood but also seen and cruelly treated; and blessed was he who was not scandalized in him, understanding the impassible God who endured the Passion in the appearance of a needy and poor man. “We preach Christ crucified,” says the Apostle: “to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:23). Why is Christ crucified foolishness or a stumbling block to some, but God’s power and God’s wisdom to others? Clearly because the former do not understand concerning the needy and poor one. They discern in him nothing beyond what appeared in him, nothing beyond the needy and poor man, nothing beyond man; nor do they believe him to be God when they hear that he was crucified.

But the latter understand that he was not merely made needy and poor for us [Col. 1472A]—for this understanding is also necessary for one approaching God, since, as the Apostle says, he became poor for us that by his poverty we might become rich (1 Cor. 8:9), and “the weakness of God is stronger than men, and the foolishness of God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1:25). They understand, I say, not merely that he was poor, but that in every way he far surpasses this: namely, that he is and was the rich, eternal, omnipotent God. At his death the sun was darkened, the veil of the temple was torn, rocks were split, and the earth trembled. At his Resurrection an earthquake occurred; many bodies of saints rose with him and appeared to many. At his Ascension, and when he sent the promised Spirit to his own, they spoke in diverse tongues of the mighty works of God. Signs, wonders, powers, and distributions of the Holy Spirit jointly testify that he was not merely needy and poor: he who ascended on high led captivity captive and gave gifts to men—gifts which a merely needy and poor person could not give, and which none could give except the infinitely rich God.

Though he was crucified as needy and poor through weakness, he lives by the power of God; nor should he be despised because of the lack belonging to poverty [Col. 1472B], but rather glorified and loved. For he was poor not by necessity but voluntarily; not by condition or the unworthiness of his origin, but by condescension; not through a chance of fortune, but by a rational and most wise choice.

Blessed, therefore, is he who understands concerning the needy and poor—that is, who understands by loving. “What I do,” says the Apostle, “I do not understand”: that is, I do not love it, I do not approve it; “but the evil which I hate, that I do” (Rom. 7:15). If the Apostle rightly says that he does not understand what he does not love, and excuses his inward man by saying that he does not understand but hates the evil which lies close at hand, while good does not dwell in his flesh, then by the same licence we may say [Col. 1472C] that blessed is he who understands—that is, loves—in Christ, the needy and poor one, that which he understands as above the needy and poor one: namely, God Most High, believing with the heart unto righteousness and confessing with the mouth unto salvation. Though rich, for us men and for our salvation he became poor and needy, that through his poverty we might become rich. Blessed is he who understands this—that is, loves it.

For those who saw and hated both him and his Father were not blessed because, although they were wicked tenants, they understood well enough that he was the heir, saying: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Mark 12:7). Therefore he who, by faith working through love, reaches beyond Christ’s humanity, beyond what he was in this world—a needy and poor man—and understands him to be [Col. 1473A] God, and, understanding this, worships him, will be blessed in his deed. “The Lord will deliver him in the evil day.”

In the evil day—that is, the day of judgment, which shall be evil and bitter to the wicked—the Lord will deliver him: the Lord whom he understood as Lord when he saw him, whether on the cross or in the manger, seemingly poor; and whom, seeing him upon the altar under the species of bread and wine, he understood to be the living bread, the true vine, and the Lord of his vineyard. As Lord, he hires labourers in it; in the evil day he shall deliver them, enriching with the denarius of eternal reward those who understood him to be rich when they saw him on the cross as needy and poor, and who laboured in the vineyard when he hired them because they believed his promise of the denarius.

Alternatively: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor.” [Col. 1473B] Christ was exceedingly needy and poor in the Passion; when his own garments had been taken away, he was stripped naked (Gen. 9:21). Then the true Noah, ruler of the ark—that is, of the holy Church—fell asleep in his vineyard, was seen naked, and was mocked by Ham, the accursed son: that is, by the Jewish people. But blessed is the people of the Gentiles who understands concerning this naked, needy, and poor one, whose nakedness they cover with the cloak of most fitting honour. For, in sacred ministries performed in commemoration, they honour him by holy worship and ornamented sacred vestments; and they veil his nakedness, following the example of Noah’s good sons, who covered their father’s nakedness by throwing a cloak over it while turning their faces away.

[Col. 1473C] We turn our faces away from the crime of the Jews who mocked Christ naked when we condemn their deeds. Yet we cover and honour his nakedness in that we celebrate the sacraments of his Passion at the holy altar not only reverently in secret, but sometimes honourably and splendidly, with the people standing around and the choir rejoicing, in the bright and clean adornment of sacred vestments. Even angels delight in this beauty, provided that the ugliness of life and conduct does not contradict the outward beauty of the garments. Otherwise, if, as the pagan says,

> “Foul within, beautiful in the fair skin without,”

we appear fine outwardly but not clean within, it is said to us: “Woe to you, Pharisees, who cleanse the outside of the cup and dish, but within are full of robbery [Col. 1473D] and uncleanness” (Matt. 23:25). But when the Lord says: “Cleanse first what is within, and what is without shall be clean” (ibid., 26), he sufficiently indicates that outward cleanliness of garments and vessels is pleasing to him if the inward purity of those who minister comes first. Then we fittingly stand at the altar in a gold-woven garment or a bright vestment, when, as the Apostle Peter says, “our faith, much more precious than gold which is tested by fire, is found unto the praise and glory of Christ.” Though we now believe in him without seeing, when we see him we shall rejoice with inexpressible joy, receiving the end of our faith, the salvation of our souls (1 Pet. 1:7), when that blessedness shall be fulfilled in us of which it is now said: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor.”

[Col. 1474A] Alternatively: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor,” because, when he understands Christ in any one of his poor as hungry to be fed, thirsty to be given drink, naked to be clothed, a stranger to be received, sick or imprisoned to be visited, he ministers to the poor and needy for Christ’s sake in such a way that, understanding and believing Christ himself to be in them, he makes his good work gracious through sound understanding and holy faith. He ministers reverently and gladly to Christ’s poor as though to Christ himself: either anointing and wiping with hair his feet in his weak members, or pouring precious ointment upon his head by honouring his saints—or Christ himself—through divine, mystical, and faithful services. In both ministries, “good understanding” belongs to all who practise it.

[Col. 1474B] For blessed also is he who understands Christ’s feet in Christ’s poor and anoints them through almsgiving. And blessed three and four times over is he who understands Christ at the altar, who anoints his head, who believes and worships his divinity, or who supports, provides for, or assists his worshippers—that is, holy ministers—so that they may freely devote themselves to serving God in holiness and righteousness before him all their days. Such ministers of the sacred altar, especially those who labour in the word, are those least ones of Christ of whom he himself will say on the day of judgment: “As long as you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. 25:40).

Blessed, therefore, is he who understands concerning such a poor and needy person; he who gives to one asking does well. But one who, understanding the need of one who is silent and does not ask [Col. 1474C], freely shows him charity, helping him according to his ability and desiring to help beyond his ability, does better. For, with no one instructing him, he himself understands concerning the needy and poor, storing up for himself that blessedness by which blessed is proclaimed he who understands concerning the needy and poor. The Lord shall deliver in the evil day the one who faithfully ministered to him in his poor. But before that evil day, the greatest of all evil days, comes, now in this temporal life:

**VERSE 3. “May the Lord preserve him,”** because the days are evil, in which each person needs preservation lest he fear being judged in the final evil day. Therefore may the Lord preserve him who has this good understanding [Col. 1474D] concerning the needy and poor, lest amid the evils of the age he depart from this understanding, but may persevere firmly in it until the end. And, abiding in it, may he give him life and make him blessed upon earth. May he give him life through faith and righteousness, so that the righteous person himself may live by faith and never fall into the death of the soul. May he also give him life in the Resurrection, to be glorified with his poor, to whom he ministered. And may he make him blessed not only then, eternally in heaven, but also now, temporally on earth, so that his blessed life on earth may precede and prepare for the more blessed life in heaven, and temporal salvation on earth may be the forerunner of eternal salvation. Or, may he make him blessed in the land of the living, of which it is said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.”

[Col. 1475A] Alternatively: “May he make him blessed upon earth,” so that the earth—that is, his flesh—may not bring forth thorns and thistles of vices for him, but may sprout green grass, bearing seed and fruit-bearing trees, and every tree beautiful to behold and pleasant for food: delightful in good works to view and sweet in taste to imitate. Thus, both in himself and in his imitators, may the earth yield its fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold. The Prophet fittingly wishes this for the one who understands concerning the needy and poor. But such a wish or prayer is a most certain promise. For the piety exercised in good understanding concerning the needy and poor is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come. The word of promise is this: “The Lord will deliver him in the evil day.”

[Col. 1475B] Therefore, that he may be wholly delivered from all evils in the evil day, the prayer of the Prophet, or of any psalmist, is added when it is said: “May the Lord preserve him, give him life, and make him blessed upon earth.” And let us pray with the one praying; let us prophesy by our wish with the one prophesying, that the Lord may preserve, give life to, and make blessed upon earth that blessed man who understands concerning the needy and poor. Since the words of the one praying or prophesying have been explained above, let us now consider what follows:

“And may he not deliver him over to the desire of his enemies.” Even if he delivers him bodily to be harassed into the hands of enemies who kill or afflict the body, may he nevertheless not deliver him over to their *soul*—that is, to their will—so that their wish concerning him may be done [Col. 1475C]. And should he ever become weak, may strength be perfected in his weakness. In order that this may occur:

**VERSE 4. “May the Lord bring him help upon the bed of his pain.”** The bed of pain is the weakness of the flesh. The paralytic lies on this bed and is grievously tormented when the corruptible body weighs down the soul, which is then grievously tormented when bodily distress presses it toward consent to impatience, murmuring, or some other sin. Should this befall the blessed man, may the Lord bring him help upon the bed of his pain, so that, like the healed paralytic carrying his bed, the healed mind may rule and command the flesh. Then the flesh may no longer be his bed of pain, but rather his most sweet bed of rest, so that he may say: “My flesh shall rest in hope” (Acts 2:26). Again: “In peace I shall sleep and rest together” (Ps. 4:9).

[Col. 1475D] In the Hebrew it reads: “Blessed is he who considers the poor; in the evil day the Lord will save him. The Lord will guard him and give him life, and he shall be blessed upon earth, and He will not deliver him to the desire of his enemies. The Lord will strengthen him on the bed of his sickness.” Therefore, what in our translation are the words of one praying are there the words of one prophesying or promising.

Alternatively: “May the Lord bring him help upon the bed of his pain,” as happened to Hezekiah, to whom fifteen years were added when he prayed (4 Kings 20:6). This number is mystical [Col. 1476A]. For if you proceed by the increments of counting from one to fifteen, you will have one hundred and twenty—the number of those who, remaining and praying in the upper room in the early Church, received the Holy Spirit. Through the consolation of this Paraclete their bed of pain was turned into a bed of rest, when the Church, at first weak in number and merit, grew and was strengthened, walking in the fear of God and being filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit. Blessed was that assembly of Christ’s disciples which rightly understood concerning that needy and poor one whom they recognized as God when they saw him ascending into heaven! “Blessed,” I say, “is the people whose Lord is its God!” (Ps. 143:15). Blessed is he who understood concerning the needy and poor one! Therefore the Lord preserved him, [Col. 1476B] made him blessed upon earth, did not hand him over to the will of his enemies, and brought him help upon his bed of pain.

Yet first he had turned all his bed in his sickness, when, saddened and troubled in the Passion, they all fled, abandoning the Lord, and nearly fell away from that understanding by which they had recognized as rich the needy and poor one whom, through the voice of Peter alone, they had confessed to be the Son of God. But the Lord brought him help upon his bed of pain by adding fifteen years to him, as was said above, when he sent the Holy Spirit upon the one hundred and twenty disciples.

Likewise, by the addition of fifteen years in sickness is signified the promise of the blessings of the life which now is and of that which is to come. For this number contains seven and eight. The number seven [Col. 1476C], on account of the seven days by which the whole course of this present life turns and returns, contains the promise of the life which now is. The number eight, however, on account of the eighth day of the Resurrection, contains the promise of the life to come. Therefore, when it is said concerning the sick man, “May the Lord bring him help upon the bed of his pain,” it may fittingly be understood of the Lord who added fifteen years to Hezekiah laid upon the bed of pain. May he likewise bring such help upon the bed of pain of this blessed man who understands concerning the needy and poor one: that he may obtain the consolation of this present life through daily increases of virtues and merits, and possess the full and solid joy of the life to come, signified by the solid number eight [Col. 1476D], which is found to be the first solid even number. For when one says “twice two,” the first even number multiplied by itself is equal and solid; by it, as was demonstrated in the sixth Psalm, the eighth day of Resurrection is aptly signified.

Blessed Gregory, in his *Morals on Job*, says on this passage:

> [Note: [Col. 1475D] St Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book XXIII, chapter 24.] “You have turned all his bed in his sickness.” What is meant here by “bed” except temporal rest? For when anyone, worn out by worldly cares, is moved by divine grace to abandon the laborious paths of this world, he commonly considers how he may flee the desires of the present life and rest from its labours. He soon seeks for himself an ordered form of the repose he desires, and longs to find, as it were, a bed—a place of withdrawal from every labour [Col. 1477A]. But because, while still placed in this life, he cannot live without temptations even in the hidden retreat of any state of life, a greater pain of temptation is often found precisely in what has been constructed for rest. Thus the Prophet rightly says: “You have turned all his bed in his sickness.” It is as though he said: Everything that he prepared here for his rest, you have, by a hidden judgment, changed into disturbance for him. This is done indeed by a merciful purpose: that the life of the elect may be troubled during the time of this pilgrimage. For the present life is the road by which we make for our homeland; and therefore, by a hidden judgment, we are here worn down by frequent troubles, lest we love the road instead of the homeland. For some travellers, when they happen to see pleasant meadows on their journey, [Col. 1477B] linger as they go and turn aside from the straightness of their intended route; the beauty of the journey delays their steps while it delights them. Therefore the Lord makes the way of this worldly life rough for his elect as they travel toward him, lest anyone, being too greatly fed by the pleasantness of the way of the present life, should delight more in travelling long than in arriving quickly; lest, while pleased by the road, he forget what he desired in the homeland.

In the Hebrew it reads: “You turned all his bed in his thought.” This may be understood as follows: You turned to labour all the bed which he had arranged for himself as rest—not in your thought, but in his own. For if a man governed himself by your thought rather than his own, without doubt he would find rest for his soul, according to your saying: “Take my yoke upon you, and [Col. 1477C] learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart; and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11:29). Therefore, whoever will not be meek and humble in heart beneath your yoke, but swells with pride in his own thought, you turn his bed, devised by him for his own rest, to its opposite end: so that, at last, wearied by his own thoughts and infirmities, when “vexation alone shall give understanding to hearing,” he may understand that he is made weak through his own fault; he may cease to devise vain and presumptuous things; and, by confessing his sins, may learn to pray often and say:

**VERSE 5.** I said: “Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you.”

It should certainly be noted that the blessed man who understands concerning the needy and poor one is troubled upon his bed in the manner stated above [Col. 1477D]. But he who does not understand concerning the needy and poor one is sometimes permitted to possess what seems to him great rest upon his bed in this world, while God reserves him for eternal condemnation. Thus that rich man who “feasted sumptuously every day” (Luke 16:19), supported in his bed by a great heap of straw—that is, earthly resources—rested most softly, receiving his good things in his life; for he was not worthy to be chastened and corrected, having no understanding of mercy concerning Lazarus, needy and poor, lying before his gates.

But that needy and poor man, who had a bed of pain in this life instead of a bed of rest, understood himself, needy and poor, in such a way that in prayer [Col. 1478A] and confession of his sins he continually said something such as is expressed in these words: “I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you.” Hence it is not unfitting that, on the Sunday on which the Gospel of the rich man and poor Lazarus is read, the gradual chant is taken from this Psalm: “I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you. Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor one; in the evil day the Lord shall deliver him.” Likewise, at the introit of that office, when “Lord, I have hoped in your mercy” is sung, the voice of the needy and poor man is represented. Since the rich man gave him no mercy whatever, he hoped all the more in divine mercy as he was abandoned by human mercy, even while the dogs came and licked him.

[Col. 1478B] It sometimes happens that things like ulcers appear upon the skin, when the sins of a poor person revealing himself in confession are laid bare and freely handled by the tongues of detractors or reprovers; through this, the health of the inward person is acquired. But the rich man, ugly within, outwardly clothed as it were in purple and fine linen, lies softly in a bed of rest, while the poor man turns this way and that upon his bed of pain. You, O God, have turned all that poor man’s bed in his sickness, by sending that very sickness upon him or by not delivering him from it. For just as you are said to have hardened Pharaoh’s heart, not by putting hardness into it but by not delivering or protecting him from hardness; and just as you are said to lead into temptation one whom you do not deliver or protect from temptation: so you are not unfittingly said to turn a bed in sickness [Col. 1478C], depriving the sick person of health or rest, so that he cannot lie on one side, but because of the greatness of his pain continually turns from side to side, so that his whole bed, being turned about, is unfit for rest.

When these things occur, truly blessed is the person who understands concerning the needy and poor one, supplying him, according to his ability, with consolation and help upon his bed of pain. For “blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7). But those who deny such persons even crumbs of consolation shall not be delivered in the evil day. Rather, when these receive consolation for the sorrow of their past repentance, those others shall be tormented; for if they had any good merits, they received their good things for them in their lifetime, while the poor man likewise received evils in this life especially for those sins [Col. 1478D] which he cleansed by confession and repentance, saying: “I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you.”

Therefore I, David—or any penitent person—in this pleasant Psalm with the cithara, that is, with the flesh afflicted upon a bed of pain, speak willingly; I speak understandingly, because the vexation of my turned bed gives understanding to my hearing. What do I say? A word of confession and prayer, namely this: “I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you.” I am the one who sinned; I acted wickedly; I sinned against you. This I say, and often said, when, as my bed was turned, innocent persons also happened to be troubled, persons with whom I desired sweetly to rest. I said: “It is I who [Col. 1479A] have sinned; what have these done, who are sheep, who are simple and innocent?” (2 Kings 24:17).

I sinned against you alone when, in secret, with you alone knowing, my God, I committed evils that ought to have been avoided or omitted goods that ought to have been done. For example, when I, David, desired another man’s wife upon the roof, with you alone seeing; or when, delighting in my heart at the number of soldiers, I wished the people to be numbered. Then, before either the lust of the flesh or the pride of the mind had come to effect—so that I might either violate another man’s wife or command the people to be numbered—I ought to have said, and could have said: “Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you.” For I had not yet harmed my neighbours, but had sinned against you in my soul alone—that is, to your injury, my God—because I had done evil before you, which I had not yet done before human beings [Col. 1479B]. But I did not say this then, because I despised the wound of my soul as though it were no wound at all. Therefore you turned all my bed—namely, all my kingdom, in which, after Saul’s death, I ought now to have rested—in my sickness. Thus I, David, mighty of hand, was made grievously weak and, deprived of the strength of my own followers, fled before my son Absalom like a sick man; though earlier I had played with lions as with lambs and laid giants low in war. Then, needy and poor, repenting inwardly not only for manifest deeds but also for unlawful thoughts, I said: “Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you.” Then also:

**VERSE 6.** My enemies spoke evil things against me. Their chief was Shimei, who cursed me and said: “Get out, man of blood,” etc. [Col. 1479C] Yet Shimei was not alone: many other enemies of mine, adhering to Absalom and hating me, said to me and concerning me: “When shall he die, and his name perish?”

**VERSE 7.** If any supporter of my son Absalom entered to see me, his heart spoke vain things, even when his mouth spoke good things. While remaining within, he gathered iniquity to himself. Having gathered it, he went outside and spoke to the same effect.

**VERSES 8 AND 9.** All my enemies whispered against me; against me they thought evil things for me. They established an iniquitous word against me, saying: “This David, now cast down, shall not rise; henceforth he shall not rule.” They said this of me as if I were altogether [Col. 1479D] dead and had no vital spirit remaining in me. But I had indeed slept in the sin either of lust for another man’s wife or of pride in numbering the people. Yet, rebuked through Nathan the prophet and touched by scourges, I opened my mouth in confession of sin and drew in the good Spirit. Thus it appeared that I was not dead in sin—for confession perishes in one who is dead—but asleep and therefore awakened.

For does not one who sleeps—who falls not through an industrious zeal for wickedness but through the stealthy sleep of sin—add that he may rise? But those who pretended to love me when I stood watchful do not believe this. Now that I lie fallen, they not only do not raise me, but trip me up so that I may fall further.

**VERSE 10.** Indeed, the man of my peace in whom I trusted, my counsellor Ahithophel, enlarged his treacherous attack against me, giving counsel that I, driven out from the royal city, should not be permitted to rest even in the forest [Col. 1480A].

**VERSE 11.** But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up, restoring to me the glory of my kingdom; and I shall repay them good for evil, though they repaid me evil for good.

**VERSE 12.** By this I knew that you willed me: because, although my enemy rejoiced for an hour, he shall not rejoice over me long, but shall see cause for grief when it is made manifest why, after rejecting Saul because of his wickedness, on account of

**VERSE 13.** innocence you received me and confirmed me for ever, saying: “I have sworn to David my servant; unto eternity I shall establish your seed” [Col. 1480B] (Ps. 88:4). And I, giving thanks to him who confirms me, shall say:

**VERSE 14.** Blessed be the Lord, God of Israel, from age unto age. Amen, amen.

Alternatively: I, the true David, who was born without original sins and lived without actual sins, nevertheless said: “Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, which is sorrowful unto death.” Heal it from the sickness of sorrow. I have this sorrow because I bore upon myself the sins of many, and for them now say: “I have sinned,” though elsewhere I say: “The words of my offences.” “I have sinned”—that is, I have taken upon myself the sins of my own people—and this is to your honour, to whom I obey even unto death. For my soul, now facing what is imminent, is sorrowful and languid; indeed willing, yet truly grieving, truly sorrowful, not through a conscience tormenting me, but through benevolence and compassion drawing me toward sorrow over the sins of my people. Though innocent of sin, I nevertheless say for them: “Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” [Col. 1480C].

Since I say this for my members, confessing and assigning their guilt to myself so that my righteousness may be bestowed upon them, blessed is he who understands concerning me, needy and poor: I am not burdened by my own sin but by another’s, which I, the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, bore upon myself.

But refusing to understand this, my enemies spoke evil against me. Seeing the people go after me, they called me a deceiver and an evildoer. Thus they said to Pilate: “If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you” [Col. 1480D] (John 18:30). Likewise: “Perhaps the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation. It is expedient that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John 11:48). “Rather,” they say, “it is expedient that one man die and perish than that the whole nation perish.” Thus, greedily longing for my death, my enemies said: “When shall he die and his name perish?” It is not enough for us that he should die, unless even his name be so blotted out that no report of him remains. Therefore they say: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wis. 2:20), because a glorious death commonly produces a good reputation, whereas a most shameful death, such as the death of robbers, is not accustomed to produce a good name. Therefore they hung me between robbers, unjustly condemning me, a just man, so that my reputation might perish together with my life [Col. 1481A].

But this turned out contrariwise: my name did not perish. For just as the grain that is sown does not perish but, cast into good soil, bears much fruit, so my name grew all the more from my death into an abundant harvest of believers confessing my name, which is above every name. Thus at my name every being in heaven, on earth, and under the earth rightly bends the knee, and every tongue confesses that I, the Lord Jesus Christ, am in the glory of God the Father, named and illustrious, and, equally with the Father, glorious above all things (Phil. 2:9, 11). Yet the devil still stirs up persecutions against the Church, that my name may perish even thus. But the bones of the martyrs, sown, sprout forth, so that faith may grow warmer in the earth enriched by their blood. Thus they also say: “As clods of earth are broken upon the ground, our bones have been scattered” (Ps. 140:7).

There is, moreover, another hidden evil more grievous than this open evil: not only open enemies spoke evil against me, but feigned friends also did so. For even if one of them entered to see—that is, to spy out—and his tongue spoke true things, for example, “Master, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth” (Matt. 22:16), nevertheless his heart spoke vain things in calling me Master when he was unwilling to submit to my discipline. This became clear because, when I, the teacher of righteousness, had taught my disciples to abstain from iniquity, he who entered deceitfully, contrary to my teaching, gathered iniquity [Col. 1481C] to himself. “Iniquity lied to itself” (Ps. 26:12), not to me; so too it gathered iniquity to itself, not to me.

After the iniquity gathered within had weighed him down by the rule of equity in the house of equity, he went out with his iniquity and spoke to the same effect, to increase what he had gathered within himself. The feigned friend entered in order to gather iniquity to himself; but the open enemy went outside and spoke to the same effect. Or, while his mouth was silent, his heart gathered iniquity to itself; then, when an opportunity was found, he went outside in speech and spoke to the same effect which he had formerly thought, when his heart spoke vain things while his tongue was silent. Therefore, while one person spoke or cried conspicuously and openly against me [Col. 1481D], the rest whispered against me, pleased by what they heard against me. Thus they themselves whispered secretly to the same effect as that which they had heard openly.

Alternatively: “To the same effect”—that is, together and in agreement—all my enemies whispered against me. Though they had previously been enemies, when action or whispering against me was required they assembled as one, agreeing together to oppose me. Thus the rulers Herod and Pilate, formerly enemies of one another, were reconciled with each other in my death and assembled as one, whispering to the same effect and sending embassies to one another against me. All my enemies did this, always ready and prompt to slander and whisper secretly and insidiously. Therefore [Col. 1482A] I say this universally of all my enemies, because great is the crowd of murmurers and whisperers who, although they do not dare to cry out against the doctrine of truth, nevertheless dare to whisper.

They have some single, special, fierce standard-bearer, of whom I too speak individually: “He went outside and spoke to the same effect.” One spoke openly and many whispered secretly, because few are authors of crime bold enough openly to do wicked things; many agree with them to the same effect by whispering, not daring openly to reveal the counsels of hearts gathering evils to themselves. Truly evils to themselves, not to me: for the things devised against me as evils by their malicious desire are good to me and mine, because of the good effects [Col. 1482B] that have come—and shall still come until the end—from their evils, as this Psalm is inscribed “unto the end.” For they indeed gathered iniquity to themselves, but their iniquity has resulted in great benefit for me and mine.

At last, after all their evil whisperings, they established an iniquitous word against me, intending thereby that my saving name might perish from human memory. They said to Pilate: “Lord, we remember that that deceiver said, while still alive: ‘After three days I shall rise again.’ Therefore command the tomb to be guarded until the third day, lest perhaps his disciples come, steal him, and say to the people: ‘He has risen from the dead’; and the last error shall be worse than the first” (Matt. 27:63–64). They established and confirmed this iniquitous word, devised against faith in the Resurrection, by giving the soldiers abundant money and purchasing from them false testimony: that while they slept, my body was taken away and I did not rise from death.

This is the counsel of the wicked, evil tenant-farmers concerning the son of their lord, the Son of their Lord, the lawful heir. While he lived, they said: “Come, let us kill him” (Mark 12:7); and after he was dead, they added wickedly: “We shall have his inheritance” (ibid.). “We shall have it securely,” they say, “because we have made falsehood our hope and have been protected by falsehood, having spread abroad this report: that he whom we killed did not rise but was carried away by theft by his disciples.” Do you, most wicked tenant-farmers, then suppose [Col. 1482D] that the overwhelming scourge will not touch you, protected by this lie? For you say, as is written concerning you in Isaiah 28:15: “We have made a covenant with death and made an agreement with hell. When the overwhelming scourge passes through, it shall not come upon us, because we have made falsehood our hope and have been protected by falsehood.”

You, most wicked tenant-farmers, are denounced in this prophecy because, as is there written, “you shall be overwhelmed by the scourge and trampled down,” when the Romans come and take away your place and nation. For without doubt your covenant with death shall be annulled and your agreement with hell shall not stand. Neither death nor hell will be able to spare you when God wills that you be scourged, in body through death at the hands of the Romans and in soul in hell [Col. 1483A], after the falsehood by which you thought yourselves protected has been invalidated. Your lie shall not be accepted as truth as you suppose; indeed, what you preach shall be judged unbelievable.

For does not he who sleeps add that he may rise? He who sleeps willingly, and is not so dead as you suppose, shall he not add that he may rise, being soon to awaken? He is said to have slept in death because he willingly laid down his life, soon to receive it again. And just as Adam, who was a figure of him to come, slept so that Eve might be made from his side, so Christ is said to have slept upon the cross, from whose side flowed the sacraments by which his bride, the Church, was formed. Therefore, does he who has power to lay down his life not have power to take it up again? For he himself said both: “I have power,” he says, “to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again” [Col. 1483B] (John 10:18). Behold, he laid down his life. Shall he not add that he may take it again?

But whoever wishes to know how it came to pass that he laid down his life by sleeping upon the cross should hear him himself saying: “The man of my peace,” foremost among those who established the iniquitous word against me, pretended to be a man of my peace. By handing me over with a sign of peace, through a kiss, he accomplished the murder concerning which this prophecy speaks: “He who ate my breads”—that is, my teaching, or the morsel, concerning which there is another prophecy—“in whom I trusted,” that is, whom I allowed my disciples to trust, although I knew that he was a devil. That man, I say, “magnified” [Col. 1483C]—that is, made great—his treacherous attack against me; or “lifted up his heel against me,” that is, raised his foot in order to trample me, with marvellous persistence in treachery. For though I was ready to redeem him, he planned to sell me; and thus he tripped me up, doing with me what he himself wished, refusing to allow himself to be redeemed through me, as I wished—I who will all human beings to be saved. He sold me, the Redeemer, when I wished to redeem him, sold under sin. By selling me, he tripped up the one whom I wished to raise by redeeming him.

In the Hebrew it reads:

> [Note: [Col. 1483D] Thus the manuscript.] “My enemies speak evil against me: ‘When shall he die, and his name perish?’ [Col. 1483D] And if he comes to visit, his heart speaks vain things; he gathers iniquity to himself; going outside, he slanders. All those who hate me murmur together against me; against me they devise evil things for me. They pour into themselves a word of the devil: ‘He who has slept shall not add that he may rise?’ But my peaceful man, in whom I had confidence, who ate my bread, lifted his sole against me.”

Truly he lifted his sole very high, who, seeing me—the Most High—as needy and poor, wished so to trample me that, falling asleep in death, I should not add that I might rise.

**VERSE 11.** But you, Lord, have mercy on me, needy and poor. Have mercy in disposition, and raise me [Col. 1484A], showing in effect that blessed indeed is he who understands concerning me, poor and needy: though I appear poor and needy on the cross, I shall appear rich in the Resurrection; though I ask as a human being, I shall do as God what I ask, as I say elsewhere: “Destroy this temple, and after three days I shall raise it up” (John 2:19). Therefore I shall indeed raise up the temple of my body, because I shall rise by my own power. Yet in order to teach my own people to ask, I too ask, saying: “But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up.”

And I shall repay them, partly through mercy with good for evil, partly through justice with evil for evil. For to my enemies who repent and receive this understanding concerning me, needy and poor—that I am God, rich in mercy toward all who call upon me—I shall forgive sins and repay good for evil, granting them eternal life, though, when they gave me to drink, I drank temporal death from the torrent. But upon my impenitent killers I shall inflict the recompense of justice, taking away from them place and nation in accordance with the vain fear in which they said: “Perhaps the Romans will come and take away our place and nation,” etc. [Col. 1484B] (John 11:48). Therefore I shall chastise all, but some for correction and others for condemnation: making some enemies friends through pardon of sins and gladdening them, while sending others, who persist in enmity, into sorrow and wrath, according to that saying in Isaiah: “I shall provoke you to jealousy by that which is not a nation; against a foolish nation I shall send you into wrath” (Rom. 10:19).

For the sinner who hates me, needy and poor, unto death, shall see my glory spread abroad after the Resurrection, and shall be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and waste away through excessive sorrow—which shall be a cause of joy to me and mine.

For by this I knew that you willed me, because my enemy shall not rejoice over me. My enemy would then rejoice if he saw me always needy and poor, if what he wished should occur when he said: “When shall he die and his name perish?” But because after my Resurrection and Ascension I shall appear rich, and shall also enrich my own people, receiving gifts among human beings and giving gifts to human beings who possess a good understanding concerning me [Col. 1484C]—to those to whom I had formerly appeared needy and poor, who did not have true understanding concerning me—therefore my enemy shall not rejoice over me. This is a cause of joy to me: by this very thing I knew, and made my own people know, that you willed me—that is, that you always loved me—because you shall ordain such things concerning me and mine through the sending of the Paraclete that, once these are seen, my enemy shall not rejoice over me but shall be ashamed when my glorification and that of my people are known.

For, in turning my enemy backward, you repelled him indeed because of his malice; but you received me because of my innocence and confirmed me before you for ever. Me, I say [Col. 1485A], you received—me whom you abandoned for a time when I said to you: “Why have you abandoned me?” (Mark 15:34). For you abandoned me, not by departing from me, since I remain in you and you in me inseparably, but by not sparing me, your own Son, and by handing me over to the hands of the wicked. But because I had committed no sin and no deceit was found in my mouth—indeed, innocent as a sheep led to sacrifice, I did not open my mouth when I, innocent, was offered for the guilty, just for unjust—you received me in the Resurrection because of innocence, though you had abandoned me in the Passion, and confirmed me before you for ever.

You confirmed me not in any manner whatsoever, but for ever: namely, by giving me an eternal name, above every name, so that, once confirmed unto eternal life and exalted above every name, the weakness of mortality might rule over me no more. This confirmation, by which you confirmed me for ever, though hidden from those who do not understand concerning me, needy and poor, is nevertheless manifest before you and before every blessed person who understands concerning me, needy and poor: weakened for a time when my strength was weakened in the hands of my enemies, but now strengthened by that power of which it is elsewhere said: “Let your hand be strengthened, and your right hand exalted” [Col. 1485B] (Ps. 88:14). Likewise: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself” (Ps. 79:18).

For although I was seen needy and poor in my weakness [Col. 1485C], I am nevertheless that rich and mighty one of whom it is written: “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9:6). I am also mighty and powerful in battle: I shall defeat and despoil the armed strong man, being stronger than he, casting him out from his court however strongly fortified; and, taking away his spoils, I shall enrich my own people and make them blessed for that understanding by which they understood concerning me, needy and poor, what they could not see with their eyes. For, seeing me as a needy and poor human being according to the mortality of the flesh, they believed and, through my signs and teachings, understood me to be God almighty, knowing all things.

Thus one of them said to me: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me” (Matt. 8:2). [Col. 1485D] Likewise another: “Lord,” he said, “I am not worthy that you should enter beneath my roof, but only speak the word, and my servant shall be healed” (ibid., 8). They understood concerning me, needy and poor, because they confessed my power—not the kind possessed by my saints, who obtain healings through prayer, but the kind that God alone has, who can do whatever he wills and who commands, and what he commands comes to be. Another, likewise understanding my divine knowledge, said to me: “Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you” (John 21:17). Therefore one who confessed that I, a human being, knew all things thereby understood that I was God, because to know all things belongs to God alone.

Thus you, Father, confirmed me for ever before those who understood divine magnificences concerning me, needy and poor [Col. 1486A], giving effect to their faith or understanding: one was cleansed from leprosy, another’s servant was healed at home. One I healed while present, the other absent—not by prayer but by command—because in those two I prefigured the salvation of two peoples, namely the Jewish and Gentile peoples. One I cured while present through myself; the other I healed while absent, by a word through my apostles. Therefore whoever understands concerning me, needy and poor, if he wishes to express his good understanding in fitting words, let him say:

**VERSE 14.** Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, from age unto age. Amen, amen.

The psalm ends joyfully when, in praise of this poor and needy one, it is said: “Blessed is the Lord,” who [Col. 1486B] is truly Lord, rich toward all who call upon him as Lord, desiring to be his servants; who is the God of Israel—that is, of those who see him. Seeing Christ poor and needy upon the cross, they say within themselves what Israel said: “I have seen the Lord face to face,” he says, “and my soul has been saved” (Gen. XXXII, 30).

That man, seeing the angel so weak that he prevailed against him in wrestling, nevertheless confessed that he had seen the Lord, because he understood in the angel something above an angel. And you, seeing Christ poor and needy upon the cross, confess that you have seen the Lord, understanding, that is, beyond what you see. Understand that the image you behold is neither God nor the man hanging there, but that it surely represents God and man. Therefore, while with your eyes you behold the life-giving image of a poor and needy man [Col. 1486C] hanging upon the cross, understand inwardly in your heart that you see the Lord face to face, when by sound faith you know him to be God whom you behold as man; to be the rich Lord whom you behold needy and poor; to be almighty, whose weakness you see upon the cross; to be the life of the dead, whom you see dead; to be the Savior, whom you see wounded.

Thus, seeing the Lord face to face, you too will deserve to hear: “No longer shall you be called Jacob, but your name shall be Israel” (Gen. XXXV, 10). For Israel is interpreted “a man seeing God.” Therefore, when you understand God in the painted image of Christ crucified, you may be called Israel; and what is said here belongs to you: “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel”—that is, [Col. 1486D] of those who see God: those who see, not those who envy; faithful seers with unveiled face, not the envious Jews, whose heart is veiled. It is the very humility of the needy and poor one in which the supreme height of his divinity does not appear to them.

Nevertheless, that greater people serves the lesser. For the Jews are our book-carriers: they carry the codices for us, by whose testimony both pagans and heretics are refuted whenever they deny what we say concerning Christ or the Church. By the writings of the Jewish enemy, the pagan adversary is convicted, so that he dare not say that the Christian has fabricated the testimonies for himself, when even the Jewish enemy supplies testimony to the Christian’s assertion. For if a pagan raises the question concerning this needy and poor one, unjustly judged under Pontius Pilate, whether [Col. 1487A] he himself is Lord God, the Jew supplies the Christian defender with the document by which he proves to the pagan beyond doubt that it is true: namely, that he who is described as needy and poor at the beginning of this psalm is the blessed Lord God of Israel, as is now said at the end of the psalm: “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel.”

“How,” you ask, “is this man to be understood as God? Is he recent? Does he have a beginning and an end?” Far be it! Rather, he himself is Lord God from eternity and unto eternity: without beginning from the past eternity and without end in the eternity to come. For although this poor and needy one began to be poor and needy, he never began to be Lord God; indeed, he was always Lord God, although he was not always man.

For just as we sometimes truly speak of a “new bishop” who is an old man, because, having newly become bishop, he did not cease to be an old man, [Col. 1487B] so likewise: because he who existed as eternal God became newly man, he remained God as he was. He is rightly called a new man and an ancient God, coeternal with his Father, the Ancient of Days; and, being ancient God and new man, he is blessed from eternity, from which all created things began to be governed, and will be blessed unto the age to come, where, the course of temporality ended, the kingdom of eternity shall stand unmoved, peaceful, and endlessly at rest. “Let it be, let it be.” This repetition signifies that no one should oppose what has been said, but all should assent.

Instead of “Let it be, let it be,” the Hebrew reads: “Amen, amen,” which means “truly” or “faithfully,” because it is truly and faithfully said: “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, from [Col. 1487C] eternity and unto eternity”—he who for our sake was poor and needy in the world for a brief time, and is the rich Lord God from eternity and unto eternity. For by being proclaimed blessed, he is shown to be rich.

Thus Abraham’s servant proved that his master was blessed by God (Gen. XXIV, 34), when, seeking Rebekah in betrothal for his master’s son, he recounted his wealth in silver, gold, livestock, and other possessions. Similarly, blessing his son Isaac, he wished abundant wealth upon him, saying: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed. May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth in abundance; may peoples’ tribes serve you; be lord of your brothers, and may the sons of your mother [Col. 1487D] bow down before you” (Gen. XXVII, 27). Blessing appears in a full field fragrant with many fruits. Conversely, cursed is the land which, when a man works it, does not yield its fruits but produces thorns and thistles. Therefore, when he who was seen as needy and poor in the world is proclaimed blessed from eternity and unto eternity, oh, what a height of riches is signified—riches which are from eternity and will endure unto eternity, because they have neither beginning nor end!

A great, admirable spectacle, venerable to the heavens and to the powers of heaven, appears in the enrichment of this poor and needy one, by which God the Father so enriched him that he gave him all things, as he himself says: [Col. 1488A] “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Luke X, 22)—all things, that is, both what he naturally possesses in himself and what he created under himself by power. This poor and needy one therefore received abundant riches, who even in the days of his poverty could say—and said truly—“All that the Father has is mine” (John XVI, 15).

The Father naturally has within himself the Word born from himself; and that man has this Word incarnate within himself, while the Father brings it forth. The Father has the Holy Spirit proceeding from himself; nevertheless, that man has the Holy Spirit always resting in himself and proceeding from himself.
