For he is the throne of which it is sung: “The Holy Spirit, proceeding from the throne, invisibly penetrated the breasts of the apostles.” For if the soul of a righteous person is the seat of wisdom, much more is the soul of Christ [Col. 1488B] the throne of the divinity bodily dwelling within it.

The Father potentially created beneath himself heaven and earth and all things in them: angels and archangels, thrones and dominions, principalities, powers, virtues, cherubim and seraphim, and the tenth drachma—that is, man. Yet this true man, Christ, united and reconciled all these things in himself; he was set over them all, and all things were made subject beneath his feet. That Father, the Ancient of Days, sits upon the throne; this Lamb, the Son of Man, also sits. Indeed, “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22); and, as is elsewhere said, “He gave him authority also to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (ibid., 27). O height of riches which this needy and poor one received, abundantly enriched by God [Col. 1488C] his Father—not by measure!

Moreover, poor citizens of his receive divisible gifts from the fullness of his riches, and become rich according to their measure by possessing everlasting treasures that do not grow old. Something of this kind is found in the responses of blessed Lawrence. When he had shown the poor to Decius, he said—not of their rags or diseased bodies, but of the gifts of the Holy Spirit which believers had received—“Behold, these are eternal treasures, which are never diminished or decreased, which are sprinkled upon individuals and found in all.”

For Christ’s poor receive divisions of graces and each performs his own office; yet each shares his own particular grace with all. For example, the Spirit of knowledge and the Spirit of godliness are good portions of the heavenly treasure, sprinkled upon Peter and Paul individually, but found in all: for knowledge flows from Paul’s mouth to all hearers according to their capacity, while Peter’s godliness, taught by his own fall, properly opens to all sinners who knock the gates of fitting mercy. [Col. 1488D] Thus both the eye sees and the ear hears for the whole body; nor can the eye say to the hand, “I have no need of your works,” nor the head to the feet, “You are not necessary to me.”

“If you truly desire, brothers, to be rich, love true riches,” says a certain wise man [Note: [Col. 1487D] St. Gregory the Great, Homily 15 on the Gospels]; “for deceptive riches do not remove but increase poverty. If they are distributed, [Col. 1489A] they diminish; but if they are kept, their possessors are vainly troubled and reap no fruit from them.” But true riches are those which, as has been said, are sprinkled upon individuals and found in all; when distributed, they are not diminished; neither moth destroys them, nor thieves dig them out, nor do they grow old like a garment or ever fail. All who receive and preserve them in this present age shall be rich through the merits of virtues, and in the age to come through the glory of blessedness. “Let both goods come to pass, let them come to pass.”

Another interpretation: the Lord God of Israel, who for our sake became needy and poor in the very human nature in which he was poor, is blessed through the divinity of the Father, of himself, and of the Holy Spirit as king and high priest: [Col. 1489B] king of all ages, great priest. A king who is blessed for ruling a people is bound to rule that people; likewise, a pontiff blessed for the pontifical office is bound to bless the people entrusted to him. Therefore Christ also, the king blessed from eternity and unto eternity, [Col. 1490A] that is, king of all ages, is bound to govern his people. Likewise, because the Father gave him the blessing of all nations, making him pontiff not of the Jews only but also of the Gentiles, he is bound, as a blessed pontiff, to bless us who are his people and the sheep of his pasture. “Let it be, let it be.” Let it be that he may rule us so that we do not sin; but if anyone has sinned, let him as high priest be the propitiation for our sins.

Some who divide the Psalter into five books hold that the first book ends here and is secured by this double seal, “Let it be, let it be,” or “Amen, amen.”

Glory to the Father, to whom it is said: “But you, O Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up.” Glory to the Son, who says this while sleeping upon the cross for our sake. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that mercy sought when the incarnate Son says to the Father: “But you, O Lord, have mercy on me.” Glory to the Triune and one God, who is the blessed Lord God of Israel from eternity and unto eternity. Let it be, let it be. Amen. Amen.

## PSALM XLI

[Col. 1489]

[Col. 1489C] “As the stag longs for springs of waters.” The title is:

**(VERSE 1.) UNTO THE END: AN UNDERSTANDING FOR THE SONS OF KORAH**

Its sense is: an understanding is indicated by the following words and is to be ascribed to the sons of Korah—that is, to imitators of our Lord Jesus Christ crucified—who through that very imitation press toward the end, that is, toward the complete and highest good beyond which nothing is to be desired. For *Korah* is interpreted “baldness.” It is used for the very place where the Lord was crucified, which in Hebrew is called *Lithostrotos* [Note: [Col. 1489] Golgotha. For the place where Pilate sat in judgment was called *Lithostrotos* (John XIX, 13).], and in Latin “Calvary,” namely because the skulls of beheaded persons lay scattered there.

Yet the interpretation is more fittingly expressed by the name Korah than by the name [Col. 1489D] of the place itself, because Korah was a person and had many sons. The sons of Korah are called the sons of the bald one; those who mock him are devoured by the devil and his angels, just as boys were devoured by beasts when they mocked Elisha by saying, “Crucify him, crucify him.” To say, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (IV Kings II, 23), was the same thing in childish foolishness.

This psalm treats of longing for the invisible God. It pertains not only to catechumens longing for the font of baptism, but also to those already baptized who, still pilgrims from God in this life, thirst all the more for the fountain of eternal blessedness the more they drink, concerning which it is written: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. XXXV, 10). The Prophet therefore urges them to run to this fountain of baptism or life, leaving idols and putting aside vices.

[Col. 1490C] First he displays his desire; and because the mockery of evildoers confronts it, saying, “Where is your God?” lest they be drawn by the sadness of the world into despair or weariness, in the second part he consoles the sensitive soul. The rational soul does so there: “Why are you sad, O my soul?” Care must be taken that those who have tasted the sweetness of the Lord do not suppose that they alone are addressed in this song, but rather believe this to be the voice of Christian unanimity saying:

**VERSE 2.** “As the stag longs,” etc. After killing a serpent, the stag longs to be healed and refreshed at springs of water; so my soul, with idols abandoned and vices consumed, longs with burning desire all the more for the living God. By a carefully chosen example he depicts his desire. Although believers are compared with stags in many respects, the present [Col. 1490D] passage especially requires the comparison drawn from this: the stag draws the serpent in through its nostrils and, burning more fiercely with its venom, longs for the fountain; after drinking it, it sheds its hairs and antlers. Similarly, when the soul knows itself to burn with the poison of avarice, fornication, idolatry, and other such vices, it runs to Christ, the fountain of waters, who is rightly called a fountain because he is always flowing and whatever flows from him refreshes. Having slain within itself the ancient serpent, the devil; having extinguished vices as though shedding its hairs; and having rooted out the antlers of pride, it again seeks the fountain of water springing up unto eternal life. When it knows that it will pass to that fountain, it burns with still more ardent longing. Therefore, because the stag might long for water either for washing or drinking, he specifies that his own longing is for drinking, saying:

**VERSE 3.** [Col. 1491A] “My soul thirsted”: that is, the rational soul thirsted no longer for dead images, but for God, the living fountain. Therefore the sons of Korah—that is, imitators of the Crucified One and of the needy, poor one mentioned above—who understand, beneath the poverty of his humanity, the riches of his divinity, all say, each says: “As the stag, having consumed the serpent, with utmost swiftness longs to come to springs of water, exceedingly thirsty, so my soul burns with such longing and such haste, having drunk in the devil’s poison through many temptations of the flesh, to come to you, to drink and to share in you; that thus it may become young, made conformed to you, who are the fountain of unfailing cool water, in whom is every fullness of delight.”

For one saying this, it is fitting first to be refreshed by the font of baptism. For he says later in the same psalm: “Therefore I shall remember you from the land of Jordan,” [Col. 1491B] that is, because through baptism I have become the land of Jordan, watered and fruitful, whereas formerly I was dry and barren. Now, with the Lord’s help, let us begin from the beginning as we are about to expound the text of the psalm more fully.

“My mother Eve says: ‘The serpent deceived me’” (Gen. II, 13). She was indeed deceived: she believed the serpent promising divinity, when at his urging she ate the forbidden food and offered it to her husband, my father, to eat. What, indeed, did they gain in that food? Surely, as much poison as if they had eaten the body of that serpent or dragon itself, which was later given as food to the peoples of Ethiopia. Immediately, stripped of the garments of innocence through concupiscence, and through the other vices, they experienced within themselves the force of the advancing poison transmitted into them from the serpent’s body—and transmitted [Col. 1491C] to all their descendants, one of whom am I: I, David, or I, the penitent.

Indeed, when I was merely the son of poison-bearing parents, I did not grieve at concupiscence, pride, and the other poisonous impulses raging in me; rather, I increased the force of the poison when I subjected myself to such impulses by the consent of my mind. But now that I have begun to be a son of Korah, a son of the Crucified One, and have resisted Satan and all his poisonous suggestions—first in the land of Jordan, when I received baptism for the remission of sins; then on the little mountain of Hermon, when, fleeing the fire and destruction of Sodom, I desired to be saved on the little mountain with Lot—from that time onward I, the inward man, or I, a son of Korah, delighting in the law of God according to the inward man, have grievously and painfully borne [Col. 1491D] the poison of sin, feeling the poison of serpents because “good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. VII, 18). For the hairs of vices and the antlers of pride are in my flesh, though washed through baptism in the land of Jordan.

**VERSE 3.** But my soul, delighting in the divine law, thirsted for you, O God, as the stag longs for springs of waters.

[Col. 1492A] For just as a stag, having devoured a serpent, would die from its poison unless it were quickly healed by spring waters, and therefore runs swiftly to springs of water so that, after drinking their waters, the heat of the burning poison that brings death may be cooled within it: so my soul longs for you, O God. For since I am a man born of a woman corrupted by the serpent, filled with many miseries and infected [Note: [Col. 1491D] Codex: “slain” (*interfectus*).] with many poisons, I shall without doubt die unless I receive you, born of an incorrupt virgin—you, the true bread, fruit of the holy land; you, the grain dead in the land of Jordan and multiplied again—as an antidote. Thus, having eaten you, I may not feel the deadly poison and may be free of the antlers of pride and hairs of vices.

For though my flesh languishes and wastes away with many weaknesses, still, because the spirit is willing, my soul thirsts—and has long thirsted—for God, the living fountain.

[Col. 1492B] I once thought that complete restoration and refreshment could be found in this far country; but because I perceive that there is nothing here except food for swine, useless husks, I have now returned to myself. Knowing myself, I stretch beyond myself toward the living God, saying to my Father: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke XV, 18). Again: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light. Extend your mercy to those who know you, and your righteousness to those who are upright in heart” (Ps. XXXV, 10).

While I say such things in prayer, though the flesh is weak, my soul thirsts for you, God, the living fountain, very unlike artificial cisterns. Whoever drinks their waters will thirst again; for one satisfying his desire through the pleasures of worldly wisdom or [Col. 1492C] concupiscence will thirst again, and will never find in such things a stable remedy for his thirst. But whoever finds God, the living fountain, having once drunk from him will thirst no more, because there will come to be within him a fountain of water springing up unto eternal life (John IV, 14). Therefore, rejecting cisterns of worldly wisdom or concupiscence, my soul thirsted for God, the living fountain.

In the Hebrew it reads: “My soul thirsted for God, the strong, living one,” and this may be expounded as follows. Many are called gods, whose divinity is false, whose strength is slight, and whose life is nonexistent, because they are mute images lacking divinity, strength, and life—except that their small degree of strength lies in the fact that some are of stone or metal, which are a little stronger than those of clay or wood; yet fire masters all. [Col. 1492D] But the true God is stronger than all, and he alone can truly say: “I live, for every knee shall bend to me” (Rom. XIV, 11). Again: “No one can snatch from my hand” (John X, 29).

Among the nations it is indeed preached, as they are led to mute images, that their god Hercules was strong and greatly renowned for his strength because he killed the Nemean lion, overcame the Lernaean Hydra, strangled Antaeus in wrestling, and performed many other mighty deeds. Yet womanly love was stronger than he, bending him down to womanly work; and the poison [Col. 1493A] of Nessus’s blood was stronger than he, by which that strong man lost both life and strength, which he could in no way recover, because he did not have authority to lay down his life in such a way as to take it up again by rising from the dead.

Therefore, when my soul thirsts for the living God, I do not desire a god over whom I find death or something else to have prevailed, or to be still able to prevail. I sigh for God strong and living, to whom this invocation truly belongs: “Holy God, holy strong one, holy immortal one, have mercy upon us.” Again: “God, author of unconquered power, king of invincible dominion, and ever-glorious conqueror.” Again: “Almighty everlasting God, who rules alike over the living and the dead, and has mercy upon all whom you foreknow will become yours through faith and works.”

[Col. 1493B] Such eternal and almighty divinity is not found apart from that Korah, apart from that bald one crucified at the place of Calvary, whom the Jews, mocking him for his baldness in childish foolishness, deserved to be given into the hands of beasts. There is no holy God, holy strong one, holy immortal one apart from that poor and needy one of whom we sang above: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor.” For he is the one of whom it is elsewhere sung: “There is none holy as the Lord; indeed, there is no other besides you, and there is no strong one like our God” (I Kings II, 2).

There is indeed another Son, another Father, another Holy Spirit; but there is not another God, another strong one, another immortal one: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, whose divinity, strength, and immortality are one. [Col. 1493C] Nor is there another outside you, poor and needy Korah, equal to you or greater in strength; for the Father, equally strong, equally almighty, equally the living God as you are, is not outside you but in you, as you say: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 10). Again: “He who sees me sees the Father also” (ibid., 9). Again: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30). Therefore you, the Father, and the Holy Spirit are of one divinity, one strength, and one immortality.

For even if I remember you from the land of Jordan, in which you died and were baptized in your own blood; in which, as a sheep before its shearer does not open its mouth, so you did not open your mouth before the judge Pilate or his soldier scourging you, making you bald, and stripping you of your garments, so that you might be mocked not only as bald like Elisha [Col. 1493D] but also naked like Noah: nevertheless, I do not wish to forget that you, in that same land of Jordan, performed divine and mighty works which no one else performed. There you did not have a weakness through which death could be inflicted upon you against your will, but you had the power by which, according to your own will, you laid down your life and took it up again. Though for a time in the land of Jordan you shared our weakness, nevertheless, having there laid aside that weakness, you appeared to your disciples most strong and mighty—or rather, almighty—and after the resurrection said to them: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII, 18).

Before laying aside that voluntary weakness [Col. 1494A] you had also said: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Luke X, 22). Again: “No one can snatch from my hand” (John X, 29). Hence it is clear that in the land of Jordan, especially at Calvary, you, God-man, did not lack divine strength; rather, there your strength was hidden. There, beneath the clothing of our weakness, lay concealed the strength of unconquered Divinity, naturally given to you as man, the Word of God—not so that you might be called God merely by title or adoption, like an angel or a human being who shares in divinity.

For God the Father did not adopt you as his God or Son, but begot you not only from his womb before Lucifer, but also in the Virgin’s womb, bringing forth his Word into her and making her fruitful with his seed through his love, the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1494B] By the Holy Spirit’s operation the seed of God is so united to the virgin’s seed that what is born in her is rightly called the Son of God. Listen, heretic, to the angel if you do not believe me: “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35).

“Therefore,” he says, because the Holy Spirit, the love of God the Father, will come down upon you and make you fruitful; and because the power of the Most High will overshadow you, so that you may not experience the heat of carnal pleasure, in which Eve conceived and in which other women conceive. You alone are blessed among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb—not with a common blessing, but with that blessing in which all tribes of the earth are to be blessed; not with the blessing by which certain persons are blessed among all things, but with the blessing by which the fruit of your womb himself is rightly proclaimed God blessed above all things.

[Col. 1494C] And not only the holy, divine Word which came into you, but also your holy offspring taken from your flesh, which, united to the seed of God, the Word of God, shall be born from you as holy, shall be called the Son of God. This is not because God and man are two Sons, but because there is one Son, God-man, who has natural divinity from the Father and natural humanity from the mother. For divinity has been given to humanity, and humanity has been so united to divinity that the one who is man is God, and the one who is God is man: the same Son of God is Son of the Virgin, and the Son of Man is Son of God the Father.

Few, except the Arians, ever doubted the eternal divinity [Col. 1494D] of the Word. But concerning the divinity of the man united to the Word, not only Nestorius and his accomplices once doubted, but many still doubt even today, asserting that the God-man is so called not properly but figuratively. Against their madness, since, I think, an adequate answer has elsewhere been given by adducing the testimonies of orthodox Fathers who affirm that the man is properly the Son of God and God, and anathematize those who think otherwise, let it now suffice for my soul in its burning desire to satisfy itself in this: that just as a stag poisoned by a serpent longs for springs of water in order to receive healing from living waters, so it may long to come to that Korah, whom, though it knows to be a man mocked at Calvary, it nevertheless knows to be God strong [Col. 1495A] and living.

Let it not say to him, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV, 8), as though he himself were not sufficient; rather, let it place all sufficiency for itself in him, because whoever has the Son has the Father also, and whoever sees the Son sees the Father. Let the antidote made from true humanity and true divinity suffice my soul, intoxicated with serpent poison. Let manna, the food of angels, suffice it, whose taste is like fine flour with honey or like bread made with oil; for the fine flour of most pure humanity is to be tasted with the honey or oil of divinity, so that one bread, Emmanuel, may be understood from and in the two natures.

The angels desire to look into him, not beyond him, because there is nothing beyond him. In him are the Father and the Holy Spirit; he is one God, strong and living, together with his Father, who begot him before the ages and who, at the end of the ages, made the Virgin fruitful through his love, namely the Holy Spirit, so that she might bear a man whose Father was God himself.

[Col. 1495B] Therefore my soul thirsted rightly not beyond him but for him. It can find rest neither below him, nor need it seek anything beyond him. Thus it believes him when he says: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28). Again: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (ibid., [Col. 1495C] 29). Again: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and living waters shall flow from his belly” (John VII, 37).

Hearing these things, my soul, finding rest neither in itself nor in the world, thirsted for God, the living fountain—or for God strong and living. Having found him, it thirsts no further, because there is nothing beyond him; and he alone suffices because he is not alone. For neither is the man alone without divinity, nor is the Son alone without the Father or the Holy Spirit, since the man, with the indestructible essence of his nature preserved, is the Most High God and is called Son of the Most High; and the Son, together with the Father and Holy Spirit, is rightly called one Most High.

For neither are the man and the Word two Most Highs, nor are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit three Most Highs. Rather, there is one Most High, just as not three gods or [Col. 1495D] three almighties but one Almighty is spoken of. The Trinity of divinity or omnipotence did not increase in number of persons because the man became almighty God. Rather, God-man, together with the Father and Holy Spirit, is one Most High, one almighty, one God, one strong one, one immortal one. For as God does not die, so the man, rising from the dead by his divine power, now dies no more, and death shall have no more dominion over him.

As God has immortality—that is, immutability—so the man sitting at God’s right hand has immortality. For everything changed from its own state into another state may not inappropriately be said to die. Thus God alone is properly called immortal, because he alone “has immortality” (I Tim. VI, 16), that is, immutability, [Col. 1496A] which he gave to the man seated at his right hand, exalting him not only above all accidents that produce changeability in things but also above all things subject to changeabilities and capable of receiving accidents.

Therefore my carnal, fragile, mutable, burning soul, thirsting for divinity, strength, and immortality, rightly turns to Korah—that is, to Christ, God strong and living—that it too may be deified, strengthened, and made alive: deified by clinging to its superior; strengthened to govern its inferior well; made alive, lest it ever be changed away from the life it received from above and bestows upon its inferior.

Likewise, the soul of the whole Church—that is, religious life devoted to the divine offices—may itself be deified by clinging to its superior, strengthened to govern its inferior, namely the whole body of the Church, and made alive, lest, having received holy life from above and administered it to its inferior, it lose it at some time through harmful changeability or death.

[Col. 1496B] O my soul, thirsting for God strong and living, behold: you have found the virginal flower full of divinity, strength, life, grace, and truth. Draw from him like an ingenious little bee; draw for yourself, draw for the whole Church, constantly saying in prayer to God strong and living: “Holy God, holy strong one, holy immortal one, have mercy upon us.”

Holy God, to whom incense is offered; holy one, to whom gold is offered; holy immortal one, to whom myrrh is offered: have mercy upon us who offer you incense, [Col. 1496C] because we believe you to be God to be worshiped and honored with sacrifices; gold, because we confess you as a rich and strong king; myrrh, because we proclaim that your once-mortal body was embalmed with the myrrh of immortality and incorruption. Have mercy upon us individually and collectively: individually, that the spirit, soul, and body of each of us may worship you, love you, and thirst for your coming, so that our whole spirit, soul, and body may be preserved blameless for your coming.

Let the whole spirit offer you, O God, incense in the sanctuary of a pure heart, having there an altar of incense ever filled with the fire of love. Let the whole soul also offer you, O most strong King, gold from your gift, rightly ordering its own rule through every bodily member for your praise. [Col. 1496D] Let the whole body also always offer you myrrh, while through hope of immortality it wholly separates itself from mortal sins and corruptions, and, like earth thirsty for the early and latter rain, awaits you, its giver of life, now and in the future. Thus I pray that God strong and living may be merciful to each individual.

But upon all alike—that is, upon the whole Church—do you, holy God, holy Mighty One, holy Immortal One, so have mercy that the entire priesthood of the whole Church may offer you, the true God, most brilliant incense through the purest incense of prayer; and that the entire most Christian kingdom of the whole Church may offer gold to you, the true and mighty King, through the outward adornment of divine worship: such as sacred vestments, golden chalices, temples or churches gilded and richly endowed by royal munificence [Col. 1497A], and likewise made secure by royal protection—after all dross has been purged away from it, smelted through the reign of Antichrist—so that it may no longer be said to the Church: “Your silver has become dross” (Isa. I:22). Rather, may the Church possess both most pure silver and gold—that is, a most Christian kingdom—and most brilliant incense—that is, a most pure priesthood—so that in the gold the power of the King of kings may be displayed; in the incense, the magnificence of the priests’ high priest; and in the myrrh, the Lord’s burial: namely, the whole Church buried with her Lord, who was free among the dead. Thus, just as his body, preserved with myrrh, was free from corruption and anticipated by swift revivification, so may the whole Church, chastened from vices by the myrrh of continence and quickened by virtues, be free from the corruption [Col. 1497B] and stench of sins, even now among the dead, rotten, and foul-smelling members of Antichrist himself, whom the Lord Jesus “will slay with the breath of his mouth” (II Thess. II:8)—not by inflicting death, but by showing him to be dead and wholly alien from true life, and finally by consigning him in his judgment to the everlasting death of punishments.

Of him it is written: “Want shall go before his face” (Job XLI:13), because every miser is always in want. We do not doubt that he will be such a one; in his time, because “iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV:12). What, I ask, is that iniquity through which charity, which “does not seek its own,” grows cold, if not avarice, which does seek its own? Therefore, while this abounds, want shall go before the face of Antichrist, because any miser [Col. 1497C] serving Antichrist, while seeking what is his own, becomes from day to day the richer in himself and, in the same measure, the more avaricious in himself; thus want always goes before his face, through which the charity of many—those who go before the face of this miser—will grow cold. They are indeed needy, yet in their own estimation and pride always rich in spirit, and sometimes in possessions.

By contrast, before the face of the mighty living God proceeds the procession of saints, upon whose brow are set “the blessed poor in spirit” (Matt. V:3), and the remaining orders of the blessed follow in uninterrupted sequence. Among them, in sixth place, are set “the blessed pure in heart, for they shall see God” (ibid., v. 8).—O when shall I come and appear before the face of God? [Col. 1497D] When shall I come through the steps of the beatitudes to that state in which, among the blessed pure in heart, I may see God?

Otherwise: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” That is: when will God’s face so appear to me that I too may gladly appear before him? When shall I be certain that I belong to the number of those of whom the Apostle said: “When Christ, your life, shall appear, then you also shall appear with Christ in glory” (Col. III:4)? When shall I put off the whole old man with his deeds, with his stag’s antlers and hairs grown excessively from the age of sin? When shall I be renewed as a stag, its antlers of pride and hairs of vices cast down, so that I do not flee or hide myself with the old man among the trees of paradise, [Col. 1498A] fearing the face of God?

“When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” My God is true light, and in him there is no darkness at all. But I, having eyes darkened by age and wounded by the blearedness of sin, still fear the light, because “he who does evil hates the light.” Thus I too flee the light, still a child of darkness and night, like a bat willingly fluttering in the dark corner of an evil conscience. But, my God, when shall I have sound eyes, eagle’s eyes, with which I may delightfully appear before the face of my God, the eternal sun and unbounded light, like him who securely came before the face of God, saying: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I:23)?

The old man fled and hid himself from the face of God because he was naked. O when shall I be so clothed in the [Col. 1498B] wedding garment that, not ashamed of my nakedness, I may confidently come and appear before the face of God? Cain likewise, a fratricide, having gone forth from the face of the Lord, was a wanderer and fugitive on the earth; nor did he return before the Lord’s face to appease him through true repentance. He was unwilling even to undertake it, because, immersed in the abyss of despair, he did not seek God’s face. But although I am conscious of sin, as he was, I shall nevertheless come, not despairing as he did. I know that the abyss of sin calls upon the abyss of grace, so that where sin abounded grace may superabound. Therefore, after sin’s great abundance, hoping for abundant grace, I do not say, “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve pardon for” (Gen. IV:13); but I say: When shall I come through [Col. 1498C] true repentance and appear before God’s face, receiving true forgiveness?

I know that the saints who come shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves before God’s face; but first it is necessary that, going forth, they go and weep, scattering their seed (Ps. CXXV:6). Thus the seeds of tears go before; the sheaves of joys to be carried before God’s face follow. Mindful of this order, I too have now wept continually; I have now sown while weeping, watering the field of my heart with those very tears. It is little that I have sown tears, for I have not merely mingled my drink with weeping, but have even eaten tears as though they were delightful bread. For:

**VERSE 4.** “My tears were my bread day and night”: while in my tears there was refreshment for me, not [Col. 1498D] bitterness or deprivation, as for a Christian man and a true son of Core. For one of this sort is instructed by afflictions, nourished by tears, exercised by reproaches, and his soul is fed by its mourning, when it is raised by weeping toward heavenly joys. Within, indeed, it endures the groaning of its pain; yet it is nourished by that food of refreshment through which the force of love here flows out in tears. Thus I too am refreshed by my tears as by bread day and night—that is, at every time, or in the day of prosperity and the night of adversity.

“While it is said to me daily, ‘Where is your God?’” For this continual mockery of the wicked is a cause of tears: while each pagan can point with his finger to his stone, silver, or golden god; or while the miser displays a coin, and the lustful man [Col. 1499A] displays Beelphegor as his god, and mocks me, saying: “Where is your God? Where is the God whom you proclaim as the lover and author of justice, purity, and every propriety of conduct and life, when throughout the whole world the vices of injustice, impurity, malice, wickedness, and every disorder of conduct and life reign and abound exceedingly?”

Otherwise. Those who form separate flocks and gather to themselves disciples separated from the world, because they live quietly for themselves and, having peace with the world, strive to impose no laws upon it; who love both good and bad alike, and accept gifts from both without distinction—these truly can glory in their God and say: “The Lord has magnified his dealings with us” (Ps. CXXV:3). For the Lord has magnified his dealings with them, so that at times even miracles are performed through them; by these miracles they magnify not themselves but their God, through whom they show manifestly that such great works attend them. But you, son of Core, son of the Man mocked upon the cross, are held up to mockery and reproach because you imitate that Core who cursed the foolish children, saying to them:

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men. For you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those who are entering to enter. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who devour widows’ houses while making long prayers. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who traverse [Col. 1499C] sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has been made, you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as yourselves. Woe to you, blind guides. Woe to you who tithe mint, rue, dill, and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy, and faith. These things you ought to have done, and not left the others undone. Blind guides, straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who cleanse the outside of cup and dish, but within are full of robbery and impurity. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to men but within are full of the bones of the dead and every uncleanness. Thus you too outwardly indeed appear righteous to men, but inwardly are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Matt. XXIII:13 ff.).

Because those thus reproved personally were going to persecute the one reproving them and his disciples, he accordingly added, after inserting a few words: “Behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city,” and the rest.

It should certainly be observed in the words of this Core, cursing the foolish children, that he not only execrated vices—for example, impurity, wickedness, and avarice, such things as we too may freely blame without giving offence to people—but, what is more, he named the very persons in whom he rebuked these vices. No teacher can do this [Col. 1500A] without giving great offence to people.

Therefore you who imitate this Core in that you expressly identify vicious persons and strive to alter the customs of the world; who reject the gifts of the wicked, who defend their own iniquities and do not receive the word of God; who even shake the dust from your feet against those who do not hear you; who detest crimes and declare that Christ’s laws are to be observed alike not merely by monks or canons alone but by all Christian peoples—when you act and teach in this manner, I ask, what fruit do you produce in the Church?

Which bishops listen to you, so as to govern according to the canons the Church entrusted to them? Which kings, dukes, or other princes listen to you, so as to exercise their rule purely, without the blemish of avarice, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good? Which clerics listen to you, so as to live clerically, ministering chastely at the altar and living soberly from the altar, content with necessary food and clothing? Which monks listen to you, so as to pursue solitude, flee the crowds of secular people, and never—or only rarely—entangle themselves in the courts of princes? Which consecrated women listen to you, so as to avoid the example of wandering Dinah and preserve the example of Mary sitting at the Lord’s feet? Which soldiers listen to you, so as to extort from no one, make no false accusation, and be content with their wages? Which married men listen to you, so as to love their wives as Christ loved the Church? Which women listen to you, so as to be subject to their husbands in the Lord, as Sarah obeyed [Col. 1500C] Abraham, calling him lord? Which masters listen to you, so as to give their servants what is just? Which servants listen to you, so as to be faithfully subject to their masters, not only to the good and gentle but also to the harsh? Which innocent persons listen to you, so as to preserve their innocence? Which penitents listen to you, so as to bring forth fruits worthy of repentance? Which rich persons listen to you, so as to give one of their two tunics away and do likewise with food? Which poor persons listen to you, so as to possess, with poor Lazarus, the riches of mind?

It would be too long to range through every case and enumerate all classes of people whom you have made and continue to make hostile to yourself by teaching what is least acceptable to them. Therefore I wonder that you do not keep quiet and attend only to yourself [Col. 1500D], or to those who gladly hear and willingly obey you, or to those entrusted to you. What is it to you to rebuke matters which do not concern you? Who entrusted or commanded you to censure the many dwelling round about, while they assemble together against you? At times they have even planned to take your life, desiring your death or contriving the mutilation of your limbs, fearing to be attacked by you.

If your God appeared by confirming your speech with signs following, or if he showed himself hostile to your enemies, it would rightly be endured that you say these things. But now where is your God? Where is the God who execrates what you execrate, who detests what you detest? Where does he show that he wishes the world to have such bishops, kings, clerics, monks, [Col. 1501A] soldiers, and other kinds of people as you commend on the authority of his word? Where is your God? Where is he concealed, that he does not exercise his power in accordance with your—or rather, his own—teaching?

**VERSE 5.** “I remembered these things, and poured out my soul within me.” Because I have often heard these reproaches and the like, I now remembered them while singing the psalm. I did not prepare myself to answer where there is no hearing, nor did I consider returning reproach for reproach; rather, I kept patience and poured out my soul within me. For “my soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song V:6), whether through me or through another, concerning the care of all the Churches; their condition and adornment; the individual orders distinguished within them; the paintings or carvings of palms and cherubim on the temple walls, signifying the Church [Note: [Col. 1501D] The manuscript: “signifying.”]; the lions, oxen, and cherubim represented upon the bases; all the squared and cut stones fitted to a certain rule; the two wonderfully adorned columns, one called Jachim, that is, “firmness,” and the other Booz, that is, “in strength,” prefiguring priestly and royal power, or mercy and justice, which the true Solomon established for the support and adornment of the whole Church; the three storeys of the temple, signifying the three orders, namely, married persons, continent persons, and rulers; and other ornaments of the temple, concerning which it is written:

“All things were of precious stones, cut to a certain rule and measure, both within [Col. 1501C] and without, from the foundation to the summit of the walls, and within as far as the great court. The foundations also were of precious stones, great stones of ten or eight cubits” (III Kings VII:9–10).

These stones, these precious stones, and these foundations are those of whom, or concerning whom, the Apostle says: “Now therefore you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets,” etc. (Eph. II:19). That material building, like every earthly construction, had its foundations below and rose upward. But this spiritual building has its foundations above, as the Psalmist says: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI:1). For the foundation of foundations is Christ. No one doubts that he himself is the Most High Stone, to whom, Peter says, “coming as to a living stone, you yourselves also, as living stones, are built up” (I Pet. II:4–5). Yet the text does not mean that we ought to be raised up upon him.

“They were cut,” it says, “to a certain rule and measure, both within and without.” And afterward: “They were cut to an equal measure” (III Kings VII:9, 11). This must plainly be understood according to the one and same faith. For by faith all these living stones, precious stones, are equal, and are cut both inwardly and outwardly, because they say and think the same both before God and before men. Therefore, being as it were cut or hewn, they can be well joined and adhere to one another. But in operation or power they differ greatly. Thus the Apostle says: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one as he wills” (I Cor. XII:11).

And rightly, “to a certain rule and measure.” For the one and only person who, without any measure, possesses every good gift and every perfect gift is he of whom John the Baptist says: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John III:34). To him the Father gave all things into his hands; but we all have received from his fullness according to measure.

Likewise, it says concerning cedarwood (III Kings VII:12), “both in the greater court and in the inner court of the house of the Lord,” or in the porch of the house, cedarwood is arranged with stones, or upon stones. For in God’s building it is fitting that we should be like stones, stable and firm through patience, and like incorruptible cedar should invite those outside by good examples; and that we should say with the Apostle: “We are Christ’s good fragrance to God in every place” (II Cor. II:15).

Certainly, the court of the house consists of those who, out of charity for those set within, extend themselves toward outward matters, so that, by excluding every importunate thing, they may not disturb the holy leisure of those more suited to religion and holy contemplation. Solomon’s most careful work reaches as far as that court, because whatever Christ works in those who stand before him within benefits those who, as stated above, faithfully labor in outward [Col. 1502C] affairs for their sake. Likewise, in the tabernacle built through Moses, and in its court, there were many ornaments prefiguring the beauty of the Church, of which this is not the time to speak one by one.

For the present, let it suffice me to have said this: my soul, entering into the place of the wonderful tabernacle as far as the house of God, melted with the fire of love, as the beloved spoke of such things; and therefore I poured out my soul within me, since I could not outwardly show in actuality ornaments such as are read of in prefiguration. If at any time I poured out my soul outwardly, seeking externally the things concerning the tabernacle or house of God which I held in memory inwardly, I sought in his work the true Solomon adorning everything wonderfully and visibly—for example, expressing lions, oxen, and cherubim upon the bases of the temple, that is, in its prelates—as in Stephen, the protomartyr, “who was full of grace and power” (Acts VI:8): of the grace, namely, of ox-like gentleness toward the good, to whom he ministered; of the strength of lion-like severity against the wicked, whom he rebuked; and of the wisdom of cherubim, which those disputing with him could not resist. In his outward and manifest work, I say, I sought the true Solomon and did not find him; I called, and he did not answer me.

Moreover, this also melted—or indeed consumed—my soul through the fire [Col. 1503A] of compunction: I saw the house of God destroyed by Babylonian fire and its columns cast down; or, though its walls somehow remained standing, a profane king ruled within it—King Antiochus, sometimes a pretended friend and sometimes an open enemy of the Maccabees, that is, of all Catholics. For just as, when Antiochus sold the priesthood to the impious Jason, the sacrificial fire, which had survived through seventy years of Babylonian captivity, was extinguished, so now, while simony reigns, the house of God has become a den of thieves and a house of commerce; and, to use the words of Pope Leo IV writing to Emperor Leo, “the power of sacrifice has been extinguished.” And blessed Augustine says: “The fire of the Holy Spirit does not shine in their sacrifices, because they have made the house of God a house of commerce.”

Amid all these things it is said to me daily: “Where is your God? Where is he who said, ‘Zeal for your house has consumed me’?” (Ps. LXVIII:12). Where is he who, having made a whip of cords, began to drive those selling and buying out of the temple? Where is he who said to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI:18)? Do you not see the gates of hell, the gates of infernal princes, standing high and raised up? And what use is it that you sing against those very gates and say: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. XXIII:9)? Who or where is this King of glory? Where is this your God? [Col. 1503C]

“I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me,” so that I might silently consider within myself where I could show my God. I meditated as the psalm entitled “Unto the end: understanding for the sons of Core” teaches. Therefore, since “the invisible things of God,” as the Apostle says, “are understood through the things that have been made” (Rom. I:20), I poured out my soul—that is, I expanded it toward understanding—and, illuminating external things through the windows of the senses, distinguished them according to the qualities proper to their various sense-impressions. But I did not know God through these senses, because he is not subject to such qualities. Therefore, leaving behind the instruments of the senses, my mind began by itself to contemplate things not subject to the senses, such as wisdom, itself, and things of this kind. Yet the unchangeable [Col. 1503D] God surpasses even these changeable things. Therefore, that I might in some measure reach him who is above me, I poured out my soul above myself. And why did I do this?

“Because I shall pass over,” or “enter, into the place of the wonderful tabernacle”: that is, through the Church, in which the saints are wonderful, I shall reach the heavenly Jerusalem. The present Church is the tabernacle; whoever seeks God outside it goes astray. This is a wonderful tabernacle because sin does not reign in the body of the faithful; rather, the soul makes the body instruments of righteousness, and the soul, ruling the body, obeys God who rules it. By his help it despises enticements, endures hardships, reaches upward, and passes beyond all transitory things. For this is its voice: “Because I shall pass over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, as far as the house of God,” eternal in [Col. 1504A] heaven. While I, the soul, sigh toward that house and groan in this tabernacle of the present Church, I have many consolations meanwhile.

“In the voice of exultation and confession”: because “the voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous” (Ps. CXVII:15), so harmonious and sweet that not only is the spiritual hearer delighted by it and lifted in heart upward to the house of God, but even one still serving this world in secular life marvels and is moved by the voice of exultation and confession, while the sound of the feasting Church is heard, while the fatted calf is eaten, while symphony and chorus are heard. At this the envious brother wonders—even he who does not desire to eat the calf appointed for the yoke of obedience, but a wanton and foul-smelling kid with his friends; waiting outside, he refuses to enter unless perhaps the Father invites him. We ought to pray for such persons, that, once they too have been brought into the fellowship of the feasting multitude, the Father’s joy may be fulfilled: he wills no one to perish, but all to come to the knowledge of truth.

For then, in the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of the feasting household will be heard more gloriously, when, after the fullness of the Gentiles has first been brought in, the master of the household himself gathers the remnant of the Jews: either by calling carnal and literal Jews from the killing letter to the life-giving Spirit, or by perfectly converting those who profess to know God but deny him by their deeds, so that, as they are called Jews—that is, confessors—only in name, so they may be Jews in truth, not only in words but also in deeds: that is, confessors of Christ. [Col. 1504C]

In the Hebrew it reads: “My tears were my bread by day and night, while it was said to me all day, ‘Where is your God?’ I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me, because I shall come to the shelter; I shall be silent as far as the house of God, in the voice of praise and confession of a multitude celebrating festivals.” Does not he who says, “I shall be silent as far as the house of God,” sufficiently indicate that those remaining outside the house of God cannot be suitably answered while they say to a faithful Christian: “Where is your God?” Let them come into the house of God; let them listen not outside from afar but inside at close range to the Scriptures and divine songs, in the voice of praise and confession of the feasting and festival-celebrating multitude. Let them sing once in truth the Song of Ascents up to the fourteenth and fifteenth Songs of Ascents, lest, always standing outside, they say to me: “Where is your God?” Certainly they will find him there, because “there the Lord commanded blessing, and life for evermore” (Ps. CXXXII:3). There they will perceive the ointment which descends upon the beard, Aaron’s beard, and descends to the hem of his garment, like the dew of Hermon which descends upon Mount Zion (ibid., v. 2).

There, through God’s grace, I, a son of Core, already set “unto the end,” sing the psalm; and, like a stag, I still desire to ascend beyond these steps unto the end, saying: “Because I shall pass over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, as far as the house of God not made with hands, eternal in heaven,” to which I am led in the voice of exultation and confession, while with a spiritual ear is heard [Col. 1505A] the sound of the feasting and festival-celebrating multitude.

This manner of speech is drawn from the analogy of people who, when they celebrate a festival or wedding, introduce organs and other musical instruments serving the pleasure of the ears. If anyone asks what is happening there, so that their songs may not seem frivolous, they say that they are celebrating a wedding or feast-day, veiling an affair of luxury beneath the respectable name of wedding or festival. Thus the sound of the eternal festival delights the ears of the heart; and pleasure in outward hearing is excused if inward pleasure is greater—if, that is, the meaning delights the understanding more than the chant delights the hearing. “For when it happens to me,” says blessed Augustine in the book of the *Confessions*, “that the singing delights me more than the thing sung, I confess that I sin culpably.” [Note: [Col. 1505D] Book X, chapter 33.]

Let singing, then, now sweet and now resounding on high—now of psalms, now of hymns or spiritual songs—delight the hearing; but may spiritual understanding delight the spirit more, while what is uttered by the mouth or received by the ear, understood spiritually, is pondered in the heart. Amid symphonies and psalmody of this sort, the stag—that is, the rational mind—is carried away to the fountains of waters. Drinking from them at times, it is so pierced and drenched that the outward person also receives from them waters of tears. Yet the body, which is corruptible, weighs down the soul: through the weakness of the flesh it relapses into habitual things and endures the phantasms of useless thoughts like troublesome flies. [Col. 1505C] Therefore the mind strengthens the soul, reason the sense-nature, the man the woman, saying:

**VERSE 6.** “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” I, the mind; I, reason; I, the man; I, the inner person created in God’s image—having now entered in hope into the place of the wonderful tabernacle as far as the house of God—wish to draw you with me: you, soul; you, sense-nature; you, woman, held fast by visible and carnal things. But because you are drawn back by the corruptible body weighing you down, you trouble me by not accompanying me, so that invisible things may be pleasing to you: truth, goodness, justice, wisdom, and the other dishes of God’s house—invisible to you indeed, but visible to me, because inwardly I see and apprehend them.

You trouble me greatly in this also: when I eagerly long for such dishes, especially while singing psalms and praying, you, like Eve consenting to the serpent, or weakened through the flesh, importunately introduce into my memory crowds of imagined thoughts, conceived from external sensible things seen, heard, tasted, smelled, and touched. My memory, being to me, the inner person, like a mouth or stomach, when filled with memories of useless things along with recollections of useful things, is so disturbed as your outer fleshly stomach is disturbed when it is filled not only with useful food but also with useless or even poisonous food. [Col. 1506A]

Whenever this happens, you, soul animating the flesh, are greatly disturbed; for since it is your office to animate the flesh and digest its foods in the stomach, much labor falls upon you—not only distributing through the limbs of the body what is useful in the foods, but also expelling the bran through evacuation, and what is especially poisonous through vomiting. Since such disturbance is burdensome to you, soul, why do you trouble me by introducing phantasms of useless and harmful thoughts? I know that you trouble me because you are disturbed by the pleasure of the five bodily senses, as by a serpent suggesting evil and introducing or insinuating unlawful things. Disturbed by this serpent, you disturb me; saddened, you sadden me, by suggesting and introducing useless and harmful things; and what you suffer among things, you compel me to suffer among thoughts.

For just as you are moved and disturbed by things seen through the eyes, heard through the ears, sensed through taste, smell, and touch—grieved when things that delight are removed and when things that offend are imposed—so, through phantasmal images of things, you disturb me, soul, having first been disturbed by things. You, soul, would be blessed if you were undisturbed by things; and I, the mind, would be blessed if I were undisturbed by thoughts. But now, because you are disturbed by things and I am disturbed by thoughts: unhappy man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ (Rom. VII:24): namely, this Core, who suffered for me, the mind, and for you, the soul, in the place of Calvary, and moreover for the liberation of human flesh. Knowing this:

“Hope in God,” because the mighty living God assumed both [Col. 1506C] me, the spirit, and you, the soul, and our flesh—the three measures of meal, that is, of human nature—leavening them into one, so that, through the leaven of divinity hidden sufficiently in these three, there might come to pass what his Apostle says: “May the God of peace sanctify you wholly, so that your whole spirit and soul and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Thess. V:23). Since he assumed these three, he will surely liberate these three.

But the serpent—that is, carnal desire—was not assumed by him; for Eve, infected by lust, did not conceive him, but an inviolate Virgin, overshadowed by the Holy Spirit and wholly free from the heat of carnal concupiscence. Therefore he did not, as an envenomed stag seeking its remedy, desire the fountains of waters, because in him there was no movement or poison of perverse desire. Never through an evil desire of seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling, or touching did he see, hear, taste, smell, or touch anything.

Yet the evil spirit, tempting him in the wilderness, wished to cause him, while speaking to him of bread, to heed him with avidity of taste; and, while suggesting all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, to worship him willingly, as though desirous of seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling, and touching the beautiful and pleasant provocations of the five senses which abound for worldly kings. “All these things,” he said, “I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. IV:9). But he, possessing five most limpid [Col. 1507A] stones in his bag, overthrew the tempter with one of them; for, having in his flesh five senses clean from every desire, he received the devil’s words by simple hearing indeed, but answered the deceiver’s words with words of truth. Thus the true David overthrew the great Goliath.

For what power could that evil one have against this Son of the Virgin’s virtue, he who had deceived the first woman in the serpent by infecting her, when he displayed the forbidden apple, with the desire of seeing and tasting? “For the woman,” Scripture says, “saw the tree, that it was beautiful to behold, pleasing to the sight, and sweet for eating” (Gen. III:6). Thus, delighting in seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling, and touching the fruit of the forbidden tree, she was wholly corrupted and disturbed or saddened; and she made the man likewise corrupted, disturbed, and saddened, so that he together with her might receive the sentence of death. This sentence, propagated to their descendants conceived in the desire of the serpent’s suggestion and born in pain, had nothing of its own in this Core; for although he assumed the spirit, soul, and body of human nature, the vicious desire of the five senses was far from him.

What, then, could the evil spirit gain by tempting him without its instrument—that is, without the desire of the five senses—by which, as through a slippery serpent, it had deceived the first woman and the first man? Certainly, in this temptation the rational spirit, like a man; the fivefold sense-nature of the soul, like a woman subject to the man; were in the most pure flesh, as in a paradisal earth. But the serpent was absent, because carnal desire was not in his flesh. Therefore, in order that he might kill our serpent through the cross in his flesh, our old man was crucified together with him; and he, like the bronze serpent, free from every poison of desire, suspended on the wood, gives the effect of saving medicine to all who look upon him in devout faith and hope in him.

I beheld him—I, the rational spirit—by believing in him, and through him I was set free, partly in actuality and partly in hope: so that, freed from delight in sin, I delight with the law of God; turned away from every deadly will to sin, grieving for past sin and gladly guarding against it in the future. But my freedom from sin will be made perfect when the kingdom of righteousness has been completed in me [Col. 1507D], for which I pray when I say, “Thy kingdom come” (Matt. VI, 10). And because I grieve that you, my soul as it were my wife, and my flesh as earth amid thorns and thistles, are under the curse brought by the serpent, I add, following the teaching of Core, in daily and continual prayer: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth” (ibid.).

I say this vehemently, desiring it as a thirsty stag desires springs of water: that, just as I, the spirit, freed from sin and made a servant of God, delight in the law of God according to the inward power of reason, so you also, sensuality, and you, my flesh, may be freed from sin; and that, serving God, you may feel the divine will being done in you, just as I, the spirit, feel it being done in me. Having attained the effect of this petition, I, desiring as a stag desires springs of water, say continually to you, O strong and living God, for whom I thirst in this psalm: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth” [Col. 1508A].

Why then are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Is it because, as though despairing that you can ascend after me to delight in the law of God, you wish to drag me down after you to lower things, so that, just as you delight in visible things, I, the spirit, may delight in their images, which insinuate themselves secretly into my awareness far more importunately than the visible things themselves insinuate themselves into your five senses? Why do you trouble me through such images, especially in prayer? Or why are you sad, as if despairing that you can ascend after me? Hope in God.

“For I shall yet confess him: the salvation of my countenance and my God.” I shall now confess him as my Savior [Col. 1508B], because I, the spirit, have been saved in hope and am already in part saved in actuality. It still remains for me to confess him anew also for your salvation, O my soul. Concerning it I do not say, “I now confess,” but “I shall yet confess,” because the good of which I speak is future—namely, the salvation of my soul together with the flesh cleaving to it. When that salvation is complete, I shall confess him with full praise: that he himself is the salvation of my countenance, granting full salvation. This will not be while he is absent and appears through a mirror and in an enigma in this wonderful tabernacle, but while he is present and displays himself to us face to face, countenance to countenance. By “us” I mean myself, the spirit, together with soul and flesh.

When this has come to pass, then I shall confess [Col. 1508C] to him: “the salvation of my countenance and my God,” because then his countenance, shining upon my countenance as upon a clean mirror, will be salvation to me, giving my countenance full salvation in the eternal house of God. This is not accomplished in actuality in the tabernacle of the pilgrim Church, but it takes place in spirit. Therefore hope in God, my soul: hope, and by hoping sow now in the tabernacle what you will reap and eat in the house, when my Savior and yours is present, visibly face to face and smiling countenance to countenance. Then sadness will be driven away, in which you are now troubled and sad, my soul. Then will be fulfilled what he himself says: “Blessed are you who now weep, for you shall laugh” (Luke VI, 21).

Accordingly, I dissuade you from sadness, but permit you to weep while it is said daily to me and to you, “Where is your God?” For your sadness wasted me away [Col. 1508D], but your tears repeatedly refreshed me, because my tears—or yours—were bread to me day and night, while it was said daily to me, “Where is your God?” Therefore weep, but without the biting sadness of this world that works death and produces despair of salvation. Weep, but in hope of rejoicing, when Core appears, who is the salvation of my countenance and my God. For by taking my countenance—that is, the form of a servant—he grants salvation to my countenance, and he is the salvation, or Savior, of my countenance. But because he, the same one who is my Creator, breathed into my countenance, in creating me in my first parent, the breath of life which is my countenance, I confess that he is my God.

**VERSE 7.** My God, because he created me; my salvation [Col. 1509A], because by redeeming me he saved me. Hope in God, my salvation, O my soul, so that I also, the spirit, may exult in God my salvation, and you, O soul, may magnify the Lord by hoping and believing in him. Hope, I say, in God, not in me; for there is no salvation for either you or me in me or from me. Rather, my troubled soul is turned back upon myself: I ascribe to myself, to my very self, the fact that my soul is troubled. For I, the rational spirit, have become burdensome to myself, and a cause of trouble to my soul and flesh, because, lifted up in pride, I refused humbly and obediently to be subject to you, my God, the salvation of my countenance, who are above me; and so I could not profitably rule those below me—namely, sensuality and flesh. Justly I lost the dominion granted me over my lower parts [Col. 1509B], because I did not acknowledge you, who are above me, as my Lord. Justly I found my handmaid, sensuality, and my flesh rebellious against me, the spirit, because I myself stood in rebellion against my Lord through pride, thinking high things and not consenting to lowly things.

“Therefore I shall remember thee from the land of Jordan and Hermoniim, from the little mountain.”—Jordan, where you, Lord, the salvation of my countenance and my God, consecrated baptism, is interpreted “descent”; and Hermoniim is the name of a mountain beside the Jordan, interpreted “anathema,” or “curse.” Therefore I, the spirit troubled through pride and justly deprived, because of the fault of my exaltation, of my lordship over sensuality and flesh, shall remember you from the land of Jordan. There, by your humility, when you were baptized by your servant, you provided medicine for me as I swelled with pride [Col. 1509C]. There, descending into the waters, you taught me too to descend and be humbled. There you called back to the order, place, and measure of his condition the human being who had perversely aspired to a likeness of divine height and had neglected the likeness of divine goodness for which he was created.

For right order requires that man, taken from the lowest element, formed from earth, acknowledge himself to be lower even than the element of water; and that he not desire to be like the most high God in height. For not only spiritual or fiery bodies of angels, in which they appear—as the angel in the bush—but even the bodies of birds and fish, created from waters, hold in the order of their condition a place higher than man [Col. 1509D], who was taken from earth, is earth, and will return to earth. Man had not kept to his proper place when, at the devil’s urging, he aspired to be like the Most High.

Against this the Wise Man says: “If the spirit of one having power rise up against thee, do not leave thy place” (Eccles. X, 4). For the evil spirit rises over us, wishing to ride us, whenever he tempts us through pride. Since he always strives upward, he drives his own horses also, as with spurs, by the incentives of pride, that they may raise themselves on high. But the person who does not leave his place, who knows himself to be earth or dust, and who, when that spirit of pride urges him with its spurs, lowers himself—not merely beneath fire or air [Col. 1510A], but even beneath water—is quickly abandoned by the evil and proud rider. And, walking in humility upon the ground, he is ruled as a human being by that Rider who says: “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet and trembling at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 2).

Thus our Core, making for the place of Calvary, rode not a horse accustomed to the leaps of self-exaltation, but a humble ass proceeding humbly. There he gave the clearest example of his humility, gentleness, and patience. There indeed the Jordan flowed as baptismal water: with the stream of precious blood running down, all to whom this water came were saved—those who became humble and learned to maintain their own order, place, and measure. Thus, like well-watered Jordanian soil, they brought forth great fruit. First among them were those whom the primitive Church had as Fathers and teachers; and from them that well-watered and fruitful soil of Jordan itself learned to be such, as it is written: “The Church grew and was strengthened, walking in the fear of God, and was filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit” (Acts IX, 31) [Col. 1510B]. “Walking,” it says, in the fear of God—not flying or leaping in the devil’s swelling pride—it was filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit, so that it might not be empty and void earth, but fruitful Jordanian soil.

“Therefore I shall remember thee from the land of Jordan,” you who “regard the lowly and know the high from afar” (Ps. CXII, 6). By “high” I mean high through self-exaltation, not high through virtue. For just as Mount Hermon lies near the plains, valleys, and channels of Jordan in the literal sense, so steadfastness in virtues is truly near humility. Signifying this, Mount Hermon is called *anathema*, because the virtue of humility anathematizes sins, while the reasoning of discernment takes care that, through excessive preservation of humility, the authority needed for governing is not broken [Col. 1510C]. That authority to govern or rebuke is therefore joined to humility as Mount Hermoniim: it detests and anathematizes vices.

There is also a “little mountain,” or, as it is read in Hebrew, a “very small mountain,” because those reborn through baptism and watered by the Holy Spirit are indeed small, humble, and least in their own judgment through penitence; but they are lofty in virtues before God [Col. 1510D]. Therefore be Jordanian soil: descend, that you may be raised. Be Hermon, anathematizing yourself and displeasing yourself, that you may please God. Blessed Gregory, in his *Morals on Job*, says on this passage:

> [Note: [Col. 1509D] St. Gregory the Great, *Morals*, Book XXXIII, chapter 6.] Hermon is interpreted “anathema,” that is, “alienation.” Therefore he remembers God from the land of Jordan and Hermoniim who, in casting himself down and accounting himself alien from himself, is recalled to the memory of his Creator. Hence the Voice of Truth says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke IX, 23). A person denies himself when, having trampled down the pattern of pride, he shows himself alien before the eyes of God.

Thus David, small in his own eyes but great before God, said: “I will play and become more vile, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (II Kings VI, 12) [Col. 1511A]. Though humble in his own eyes, he was like an immovable mountain in the constancy of government. Likewise John the Baptist, humble indeed like the land of Jordan, did not judge himself worthy to loosen the strap of Christ’s sandal; yet he was accounted great before the Lord and worthy to baptize the Lord in the Jordan. He was therefore not only of the land of Jordan through humility, but also Mount Hermon through the authority with which he anathematized sinners, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?” (Luke III, 7).

Here the foolish humility of some people and the stupid insolence of others comes to mind. There are those who humble themselves so that they are not emulators of the good and do not dare openly to say anything for the correction of vices [Col. 1511B]. Others are so arrogant and ready to rebuke that it burdens them not to have something to criticize. The former possess something of the land of Jordan, but nothing of the little mountain Hermoniim. The latter seem to have something of the mountain, but they are far from Jordan. Safest in the middle are those who, burning equally with love for human beings and hatred of vices, neither exalt themselves over people nor ever submit so much to vices that, by keeping silent about others’ vices, they make those vices their own—which is the greatest cruelty.

For if your brother had a bodily wound that he wished to conceal because he feared being cut, would it not be cruelly concealed by you and mercifully disclosed? How much more, then, ought you to bring it to light by rebuking him [Col. 1511C]: first between yourself and him alone, then before witnesses, and finally before the Church, lest it rot more ruinously in his heart! Such humility pleases God, humility attended by charity that “does not act perversely” (I Cor. XIII, 4): that is, it does not speak perversely against its own conscience by calling good evil or evil good, or by being silent about what ought to be said, or saying what ought to be silent. Charity so little rejoices in iniquity, but rejoices together with truth, that in assailing iniquity and defending truth it often calls adversities upon itself. It is not provoked, but bears all things and endures all things; and amid these things it never so fails as to cease, because of adversities, either from opposing iniquity or defending truth. Among such adversities it is patient [Col. 1511D] and kind: patient, so as not to wish to be conquered by evil; kind, so as to conquer evil with good.

Therefore the virtue of humility is like watered Jordanian soil, because God gives grace to the humble; and the Lord who preserves the little ones says: “Allow the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mark X, 14). Again: “Unless you become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 3). Again: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 3). Again: “Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. XXIII, 12). He regarded the humility of his handmaid (Luke I, 48), like fruitful Jordanian soil without thorns and thistles. He exalted the humble (ibid., 52), like mountains near that land; and among them he himself, the fruit of that earth and lily of the valleys, grew into a high mountain [Col. 1512A], so as to fill the whole world.

For when he was first a small stone cut from the mountain without hands (Dan. II, 34), and was regarded as Mount Hermon, the accursed mountain—made a curse for us in order to free us from the curse of the law—he is now raised above all hills onto the summit of the mountains; and all nations will flow to him in the waters of Jordan by the ship of the holy cross. Most splendid indeed is the virtue of humility, through which one reaches the summit of the mountain. The ardor of charity is beautifully joined to it as the little Mount Hermon: it remains, like an immovable mountain, and never fails; like Hermon, it anathematizes perversities; like the little mountain, it is not puffed up.

[Col. 1512B] Therefore I shall remember you, Lord Jesus, who are the true Core, to whose sons this psalm is ascribed. I shall remember you, I say, from the land of Jordan, in which you gave us an example of supreme humility; and from the little mountain Hermoniim, where, made a curse for us, as though anathematized you hung among thieves, reckoned among the wicked. By this deed you commended to us your greatest love toward us, because “no one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV, 13).

Therefore, because on the night in which you were betrayed you washed the disciples’ feet and, as it were, watered them with Jordanian waters, commending humility to them by saying, “I have given you an example, that you also should do likewise” (John XIII, 15), I shall remember you from the land of Jordan. And because on that same night, throughout the whole supper, you especially taught charity, giving its example in yourself also by laying down your life for your friends—not because they were already friends, but so that from enemies they might become friends [Col. 1512C]—therefore I shall remember you from the little Mount Hermoniim: from Mount Moriah, where Isaac once obeyed his father so as to be sacrificed; where David offered sacrifice on the threshing-floor of Areunah; and where Solomon built the Temple. There finally passion, cursing or anathematization, and mockery consecrated the place of Calvary, because you, our Father Core, suffering, cursed, anathematized, and mocked for us your children, commended to us your love, than which no one has greater.

Therefore I shall remember you by preserving humility from the land of Jordan [Col. 1512D], and by pursuing charity from the little Mount Hermoniim; for humility not commended by accompanying charity is despised in your eyes, and there is no charity which humility forsakes. Therefore I shall remember you not by humility alone—lest, while humility is preserved too much, the authority of ruling be broken—nor by such humility as loves people in such a way that their errors are loved along with them, but by humility wedded to the love of charity, and by love of God and neighbor as it were married to humility. For from such a spiritual marriage of the two chief virtues will come the propagation of many other virtues.
