In it many sons of Core, lest they be mocked as bald, will be adorned through humility as with a white mitre woven of humble material [Col. 1513A], and gloriously crowned through charity as with a golden plate. For the ineffable name of God inscribed upon such a crown—for God is charity (I John IV, 16)—glorifies one mitred beneath by humility and crowned above by charity.

Humility, as I have said, is woven from humble material when both the body is carefully humbled through abstinence lest it grow wanton, and the soul through penitence for past sins or fear of future sins lest it grow proud. It is as though a linen cloth suited to priestly adornment were woven of warp and weft, from which not only a tiara but also the remaining Levitical vestments might be made. Just as such vestments, well woven and diligently whitened, adorn the Levite, priest, or high priest in bodily dress, so, much more, the humbled mind and whitened, likewise humbled flesh honor the dress of the inward human being [Col. 1513B], when before the sight of God one appears humble in mind, as if mitred upon the head, and humble also in one’s entire being, as if clothed and covered in a white, full-length tunic.

Moreover, a golden plate is made from precious material: it is fashioned from gold, the most precious of metals, and the precious name of God is inscribed upon it. So charity is born and grows in the heart from a precious thing; and God’s name is inscribed upon it when we gladly love God because he first loved us and because God himself is charity. Its radiance in the mind resembles a crown, whose circle has no end, because God must be loved with the whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength without end through all ages [Col. 1513C], just as he first loved us without beginning, before all temporal ages, in his Son, in whom he predestined us, as the Apostle says, before the foundation of the world, that we might be holy and without blemish (Eph. I, 4): holy through charity; without blemish through humility of mind and body; holy through the Holy Spirit, who is love; without blemish through the examples of Christ the Son, who for our sake humbled himself unto death, even death on a cross.

If, by dying with him, we mortify our flesh with its vices and desires, carrying such a cross not under compulsion, like Simon of Cyrene, but in voluntary humility, we shall truly be priests of God, clothed in righteousness, according to the saying: “Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI, 9) [Col. 1513D]. For it is just that, as our Core was found humble when crucified in the place of Calvary—he who, though he was God, was found in appearance as a human being, humbling himself and becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross—so we, the sons of Core, may remain humble and obedient unto death, even death on a cross, striving to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth of that cross.

The breadth of the cross is placed before its other dimensions because the broad commandment of charity is imposed upon us before all else, when the Apostle says: “Above all, having continual mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins” (I Pet. IV, 8). You hear that charity not only covers the baldness of the sons of Core upon the head like a golden crown, but also covers the stains inflicted upon the whole body by a multitude of sins, like a golden garment [Col. 1514A]. In such a garment that queen too is adorned who is seen standing at the right hand of her bridegroom, “in golden raiment, clothed round about with variety” (Ps. XLIV, 10), according to what is written: “Charity covers all offences,” and “charity covers a multitude of sins.” Charity is a good garment: not only are the stains of shame covered by it, but in it the adornment of royal beauty is also recognized.

It is fitting that the chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation, people of possession—in other words, all the sons of Core, that is, imitators of the Lord’s passion—be so adorned. To them the understanding of this psalm is assigned; but to the mockers of that same Core it is impenetrable like an abyss whose bottom cannot be found, because the meaning of this psalm is very deep, like an abyss. Yet:

**VERSE 8.** “Deep calls unto deep,” because the deep meaning opens the deep of the cross, and the profound humility of the sons of Core grasps it. For just as the black pupil sees deeply, but the white part does not, so the humble heart understands deeply; because the Holy Spirit, fleeing the proud (*elatos*; the supplied reading *electos* is evidently corrupt) and dwelling in the humble heart, searches all things, even the deep things of God. Thus deep calls unto deep, because profound humility invites into itself the Holy Spirit, who searches the deep things of God and dispenses deep understanding to the sons of Core [Col. 1514C].

Otherwise: “Deep calls unto deep” when the understanding of the sons of Core is helped and illumined by the exposition of the Old Testament through the New. For the two Testaments may be understood as two deeps because of the profundity of their meaning, and deep calls unto deep when the Law agrees with the Gospel. The Law calls the Gospel when it predicts what is fulfilled in the Gospel, as in: “The Lord God will raise up for thee a prophet from among thy brethren, as thou didst ask in Horeb” (Deut. XVIII, 15–16), which we find fulfilled in the Gospel, as the proto-martyr Stephen testifies. Likewise, the Gospel calls the Law because it uses the Law’s testimonies, as in: “You shall not break a bone of it” (John XIX, 36). Likewise: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Matt. XVIII, 16). Likewise the Law says: “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox while it treads out the grain” (I Tim. V, 18; Deut. XXV, 4), which the Apostle teaches was said concerning preachers of the Gospel. This reciprocal calling of the Testaments occurs

“in the voice of thy cataracts.” O God, who sit above the Cherubim and look upon the deeps, in whose hand are the voices of your cataracts—that is, of the prophets, who are aptly called cataracts, meaning hidden openings, such as are said to exist in clouds, through which rain descends, or even in heaven, through which the waters of the Flood are believed once to have poured forth. Hence it is written: “The fountains of the deep were broken up, and the cataracts of heaven were opened” (Gen. VII, 11). Prophets or apostles, from whom the streams of God flow, are therefore rightly called cataracts [Col. 1515A].

For in the voices of such cataracts of yours, Lord, are contained your judgments, which are a great deep. We understand the two principal deeps as two judgments, one present and the other future. The present judgment says to man: “Cursed is the earth in thy work; when thou workest the earth, it shall not give thee its fruits, but shall bring forth thorns and thistles for thee. In the sweat of thy face thou shalt eat thy bread, until thou returnest to the earth from which thou wast taken” (Gen. III, 17 ff.). The future judgment will say to the wicked: “Go, ye cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41). Therefore deep calls unto deep in the voice of cataracts—that is, of prophets or apostles—teaching that unless a person is corrected by the pains of present judgment, he will be handed over to eternal punishments in the future judgment [Col. 1515B].

Considering this, O mighty and immortal God, whom angels praise, dominations adore, and powers tremble before, I tremble wholly, and my troubled soul is turned upon myself. “I feared because of thy judgments” (Ps. CXVIII, 120), knowing that many pass from present punishments to eternal punishments. For when the deep of present and now impending judgment is neglected, it calls forth the other deep, namely the final judgment, by which the incorrigible are sent into the depth of hell. Or deep calls unto deep when the judgment accomplished through the waters of the Flood foretells that judgment by which God will judge the living and the dead, and the world through fire. The rainbow placed in the clouds of heaven testifies to this: by its blue color it signifies the past judgment of water [Col. 1515C], but by its scarlet color the future judgment of fire.

Otherwise: “Deep calls unto deep in the voice of thy cataracts,” O mighty God, when man teaches man from the Scriptures. For a person divinely taught often instructs another person in the voice of prophets and apostles. In this way deep calls unto deep: when, according to profound faith and a profound desire to hear or learn, deep understanding is given to the heart and deep speech to the teacher’s mouth. Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (II Cor. VI, 11). Conversely, where the word of God is neither received nor loved, this deep in the teacher’s mouth is so dried up that even to a good teacher, on account of bad hearers, it is said: “I will make thy tongue cleave to thy palate, and thou shalt be dumb, and not as one rebuking, because they are a provoking house” (Ezek. III, 26) [Col. 1515D]. Where this happens, there deep does not call to deep, but dryness calls to dryness, because there will be either no discourse or dry discourse in the teacher’s mouth, due to the demerit of the undevout hearer.

Otherwise: Deep calls unto deep because either the profound devotion of the teacher calls forth profound devotion in the hearer’s mind, or, conversely, the profound devotion of the hearer calls forth—that is, by its merit demands—profound devotion in the teacher’s mind.

Otherwise. Since Scripture says, “The heart of man is perverse and unsearchable; who shall know it?” (Jer. XVII, 9), the human heart is rightly called an abyss. Hence the Apostle: “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you.” And, to show a deeper abyss, he added: “But neither do I judge myself” (I Cor. IV, 3) [Col. 1516A]. Marveling at this abyss, that one who remembers God from the land of Jordan says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. XI, 33).

Otherwise: “Deep calls unto deep,” that is, man calls man, when he preaches to him some matter of faith and truth. Yet he does not do so in his own voice, but, O God, in the voice of your cataracts—that is, by a voice secretly instilled into him by you through the hidden ways of your Spirit.

Otherwise: “Deep calls unto deep.” Our nature, and especially the substance of the rational soul, which is wholly incomprehensible to itself according to natural reasoning and is, as it were, a certain abyss [Col. 1516B], calls upon the substance and knowledge of divinity within itself. Divinity too—or rather, a greater abyss—is incomprehensible to every creature, though capable of being apprehended by rational creatures. Hence Father Augustine cries to God in his prayers: “May I know myself; may I know thee.”

Otherwise: when someone, like a stag desiring springs of water, desires God, the living fountain, if he is affected by great desire, he will be satisfied by the great abyss of living waters; for to everyone who has a good and great desire, the desired good will be given, but from one who does not have it, even what seems to be possessed will be taken away.

[Col. 1516C] Otherwise: therefore I shall remember you from the land of Jordan and Hermoniim, from the little mountain, preserving, as stated above, humility and charity, because deep calls unto deep: that is, great love obtains forgiveness of many sins, according to the saying, “Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke VII, 47).

Otherwise: therefore my soul is troubled within me, because deep calls unto deep—that is, many sins demand many punishments through your judgments, which are a great deep. At their bidding we are punished in the present life; and unless we are corrected, after death we shall be tormented in soul, and after the resurrection in body and soul together (Ps. XXXV, 7). What your judgments may reserve for me in the abyss of their profundity regarding future punishments, I do not know [Col. 1516D]; I fear them as they are threatened by the voices of your cataracts. But I have already experienced so many present punishments, demanded by my sins, that I can truthfully say:

“All thy heights and thy waves have passed over me.” For I, like disobedient Jonah, was swallowed by the swallowing whale because of disobedience, and descended into the depths of sea and abyss. There, as at the bottom of the sea, as in a far country, returning to myself in penitence, I said: “Thy waves have passed over me. And I said: I am cast out from before thine eyes. Shall I perhaps see thy holy temple? Shall I perhaps pass to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God? How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread, while I here, made the whale’s food in its belly, perish with hunger without food!” I said such things within myself, not despairing of pardon, but reflecting upon future punishments, which I was compelled to fear from my great experience of present ones.

For all thy heights—or, as the Hebrew reads, all thy whirlpools and thy waves—have always passed over me. Thy “heights,” that is, the marvelous surges of the sea in great temptations or tribulations, have passed over me; and thy waves, in lesser punishments or temptations, have come over me. Yet even amid tribulations this is a consolation to me: they have already passed in part, and so I hope that they will pass altogether [Col. 1517A].

Another translation has: “Thy suspended judgments and thy waves have passed over me.” The suspended judgments concern the future abyss which God threatens. For one who threatens does not press us down with the weight of his greatness, nor contend against us with great power; rather, wishing us to be corrected, he suspends before us, as it were with outstretched hand, the blows of the future abyss. The waves which we experience in the present are the first abyss, in which, if we are not purified, the other abyss, now suspended, will afterward come upon us. But if we are purified now, the abyss of future tribulation will indeed come, yet not upon us but upon those who trouble us [Col. 1517B].

Hence, as the Apostle affirms, we now endure tribulations as an example of the righteous judgment of God (II Thess. I, 5). For if, as Peter says, it is now time for judgment to begin with the house of God, and it begins with us, according to the saying, “Begin at my sanctuary,” what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel? And if the righteous person, made righteous by the present scourge, will scarcely be saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear? (I Pet. IV, 17–18). If God now scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. XII, 6), how will one whom he does not now receive be tormented in the future by the scourges of Tartarus? For then, in the final judgment, the wrath of God from heaven will be revealed against all ungodliness of those who hold down the truth of God in unrighteousness. But now, amid the very scourges, he makes his mercy sweet and bright to his own children, who receive paternal discipline with discipline. Of that mercy the following is added:

**VERSE 9.** “By day the Lord commanded his mercy.” Gregory, in his *Morals on Job*, says concerning this passage:

> [Col. 1517D] “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and in the night he declared it.”
>
> [Note: [Col. 1517D] St. Gregory the Great, *Morals*, Book XXXIII, chapter 26.] Each person receives the grace of the heavenly gift in the tranquility of rest; but how much he has received is shown in the adversity of disturbance.
>
> [Note: [Col. 1518D] The same, Preface to Book I of the *Morals*, chapter 2.]

Therefore the Lord’s mercy is commanded by day because it is received through knowledge in a time of tranquility. But it is declared by night because the gift received in tranquility is made manifest in tribulations.

Otherwise: in our translation it is read thus: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night his song.” That is: by day, namely through clear knowledge of the Scriptures, accompanied also by the smiling light of peace and prosperity, the Lord commanded that his mercy be sung in thanksgiving [Col. 1518A]; and by night, that is, in tribulation, he commanded that a song of that same mercy be frequently sung. Hence the Apostle says: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience, patience probation, probation hope, and hope does not confound” (Rom. V, 3). And elsewhere the psalmist says: “I will sing to thee, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. C, 1).

Otherwise: in the day of prosperity the Lord commanded that his mercy be hoped for—namely, that he both mercifully chastises his own in tribulation and delivers them suitably from tribulation, according as he is “a helper in occasions, in tribulation.” But by night he declared it: that is, in tribulation itself he made manifest how true he had been in his promise [Col. 1518B]. Therefore, as the ant gathers in summer what will be useful in winter, so we too must learn in the day of prosperity what mercy of God we ought to hope for in the night of adversity, so that when it comes we may know how to sing his song repeatedly.

Job had learned in prosperity what ought to be sung in adversity. Therefore, like a trained singer, he did not murmur in the night, but sang well, saying: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not also endure evil things? The Lord gave; the Lord took away. As it pleased the Lord, so it has been done: blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job II, 10). Likewise, sailors must provide in calm weather for how a ship is to be steered in a storm; because the instability of winds and variability of seasons always threaten it, nothing remains but to pray without ceasing [Col. 1518C].

Hence in Hebrew it is read: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night his song. With me is prayer to the God of my life. I will say to God: My rock, why hast thou forgotten me?” But our translation has: “Prayer to the God of my life is with me.”

VERS. 10. I will say to God: You are my protector. What, then, shall I do—I, a son of Korah, fearing or enduring the night of tribulation? What shall I offer to my God? Surely incense of prayer—not placed outside myself in a metal censer, but set within me and kindled by the fire of charity—so that my prayer to the God of my life may be offered within me in tribulation in such a way that I do not murmur against God, but say to God: You are my protector. [Col. 1518D]

Why have you forgotten me? Why do I go about grieving while the enemy afflicts me? O God of my life, who gave me life by creating me and breathing into me the breath of life, you are also my protector, because you assumed my nature when you, the Word, became flesh and dwelt in us. You also received me in baptism, buried with you. For, as the Apostle says, we have been buried with Christ through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life (Rom. 6:4). Therefore you received me in baptism, as I said, buried with you, so that just as you rose [Col. 1519A] from the dead through the glory of the Father, so I too may walk in newness of life. And since you have thus received me, why have you forgotten me? Why do you allow me to be overwhelmed by the waves of the sea? Why do you not tell the whale that holds me in its belly to vomit me out onto dry land, as the whale vomited Jonah out? And why do I go about grieving, when I desire to come to you, the true joy, as a deer to springs of water, but am greatly disturbed on my way while the enemy afflicts me? He afflicts me with temptations, tribulations, and scandals. For who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn? (2 Cor. 11:29). But I am especially afflicted as scandals multiply on every side.

VERS. 11. While my bones are being broken—that is, when the strong in the Church yield and turn backward, [Col. 1519B] or when greater virtues fail, because iniquity abounds and charity grows cold, and even the constancy and patience of those who seemed to be pillars fail. Seeing this, my enemies who trouble me reproach me, while they say to me every day: Where is your God? It is as though they said: Your God either does not exist, or does not care to deliver his own, or cannot do so. And because my soul is troubled on this account, what else shall I now counsel it, except what I also counselled above, saying:

VERS. 12. Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Above I said: Hope in God; again I say: [Col. 1520A] Hope in God. Therefore, with repeated encouragement against frequent disturbances, I say to you, my soul, as I have already said: Hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.

Glory to God the Father, whose face I desire, saying: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” Glory to the Son, who is the face of God in his divinity and the salvation of my countenance in his humanity, having deigned to take on the likeness of my countenance. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who, being living water, fills the springs of water for which the deer longs, irrigates the land of Jordan, and makes the Jordan fruitful in baptism, so that grace, a mother, may bear from it sons of Korah. Glory to the one and triune God, who is mighty and living God, and who has made the human being whom he chose to inhabit wholly his own into a mighty, [Col. 1520B] living god; who also deifies, strengthens, and gives life to the sons of Korah in Korah himself, the Lord Jesus Christ, mighty and living God. May he glory in us, the deified, strengthened, and enlivened sons of Korah. May we glory in him who deifies, strengthens, and gives us life. Let us be such—so divine, so strong, and so alive in him—that he himself, mighty and living God, may have glory from us, the sons of Korah. Let his divinity, strength, and vitality be so manifest in us that sufficient grace may be in us and may remain full unto ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM XLII

[Col. 1519]

[Col. 1519C] “Judge me, O God,” etc. Title:

(VERSE 1.) **UNTO THE END: A PSALM OF DAVID.**  
[Note: [Col. 1519D] The Vulgate alone: “A Psalm of David.”]

This is clear. Here any faithful person is speaking, placed among tares and wheat, having to be born and die in common with the wicked, and to share adversities, prosperities, and such things. In the first part he asks to be separated according to cause now and according to place in the future. In the second, he trusts that he will enter blessedness. Therefore amid the troubles of this age he strengthens his soul at the words, “And I shall enter,” where the purpose is clear. Therefore, lest he be dragged down by the pressures of this age, he cries:

“Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation,” etc. Above, those martyrs who suffered tribulations from outsiders spoke, relating their longing. Here, however, all faithful people pray generally, [Col. 1519D] both martyrs and confessors, who are mixed in the threshing-floor with chaff—that is, who suffer reproaches and tribulations from those within the Church, false Christians—and who desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, so that in the future they may be distinguished from the mass of unbelievers with whom they are here mixed in the threshing-floor of the Church, as grains from chaff, and may here quickly be delivered from them. Therefore I—David, I—the Church, [Col. 1520C] or I—the penitent, trusting that what the Apostle said is true: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:39), because I have judged myself by repenting and mourning my sins, when my tears were my bread day and night; now, presuming upon the mercy to be shown me in the divine judgment, I await you, O God, whom I formerly feared as judge, now to judge me. Rightly, as I think. For John, Apostle and Evangelist, says: “If our heart does not reproach us, we have confidence” on the day of judgment (1 John 3:20). I do not dare to compare myself with him who said: “For my heart does not reproach me in all my life” (Job 27:6), because he said this of one to whom Truth testifies that there was none like him on earth. That man, simple, upright, and fearing [Col. 1520D] God, preserving patience amid scourges, could glory in God—that is, in truth—concerning the innocence of his whole life. Not so the ungodly; not so—not so can I, an ungodly person and sinner, say or glory in God, that is, in truth, concerning all my life. Nevertheless, because I believe that remission of sins has come to me from the land of Jordan and Hermonim, from the little mountain, while my tears were my bread day and night, [Col. 1521A] now trusting in your grace, my God, I desire the judgment which I formerly feared to take place, and say: Judge me, O God, by separating me from evil men and angels. I ask that this judgment begin now and be completed at the final assize, so that, while they go into eternal punishment, I may go into eternal life. But now meanwhile, while grain is together with chaff in the threshing-floor, wine together with the grapes in the press, oil together with lees, and wheat and darnel alike have rain and sun in common in the field: distinguish, O God, my cause.

There is a judgment of condemnation, and there is a judgment of separation. A judgment of condemnation is meant when it is said: “Because the prince of this world has already been judged” (John 16:11). Likewise: “Do not judge, and you shall not [Col. 1521B] be judged” (Luke 6:37). The explanation of this saying is added when it continues: “Do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned” (ibid.). This judgment is not to be desired, but is greatly to be feared, not only by sinners but also by those who consider themselves righteous or justified. For “the powers of heaven shall be moved” when that judgment approaches and the whole world trembles before its greatness (Luke 21:26). Therefore, lest I, David, seem to desire the judgment of condemnation, which I rather fear, I indicate that I desire the judgment of separation when I ask to be distinguished from an unholy nation, saying: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation.” Judge me—that is, separate me from an unholy nation, insofar as it is fitting for this to happen both locally and causally. But because local separation is sometimes not useful, I pray in every way that causal separation may always be made and remain: so that, even if my outward action is shared with an unholy nation, the cause may not be shared.

Good and evil alike eat, drink, and sleep; but the cause of eating, drinking, sleeping, or doing anything else is one thing for the former and another for the latter. For the good eat in order to evangelize or otherwise serve God usefully; the evil, on the contrary, evangelize, perform some other useful work—or, worse, an unprofitable work—in order to eat. The wise person eats in order to live; the foolish person lives in order to eat.

Therefore, even if wise and foolish persons have a life similar in act or disposition, their cause is not the same. The wise person orders temporal life so as to obtain eternal life through it, and intends to direct every use of temporal things—using good things well, and even using evil things well—so that from the use of present things there may arise for him a firm expectation of future goods. By contrast, the foolish person, using either evil things badly or even good things badly, while intending to satisfy his own pleasure, curiosity, or avarice, always has an evil cause, even though some action of his may seem to bear a good appearance, similar to the actions of good people, whose intention he does not share.

Therefore I ask to be so separated from an unholy nation that, if certain things are common to me and the unholy, I may nevertheless never have a cause in common with them. [Col. 1522A] And therefore, my God, now meanwhile, while you do not separate me from the wicked by place, while you give temporal goods in common, while you also give gifts of the soul—such as gentleness, mercy, prudence—and exercises of virtue—such as prayers, fasts, and other such things—which, apart from charity alone, are found in common among good and evil alike: while, then, you give such things in common, my God, distinguish my cause from an unholy nation.

I ask that my cause be distinguished in two ways: namely, that neither may my intention resemble the intention of the wicked, nor may your intention toward me, my God, who distributes your gifts to good and evil as you will, be such as your intention toward an unholy nation. For to the wicked, although stubborn and obstinate in wickedness, you nevertheless grant certain good things with this good intention, or for this good cause, [Col. 1522B] that they may be without excuse, when, as you accuse them in your judgment, none of them can say: “I received no talent from which I could gain anything good.” But to the good you bestow lesser goods with this intention, or for this good cause: that, having made good use of them, you may give them greater and more excellent things both in the present and in the future, saying to any such person: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many” (Matt. 21:23). This cause is distinct from that cause for which good things are bestowed on the wicked, as appears in the outcome: the former, by using received goods well, deserve always to receive better things, moving from virtue to virtue, from day to day, forgetting what lies behind and always stretching themselves toward what lies ahead; whereas the latter, like evil tenants, by not cultivating well the vineyard of God’s gifts, deserve that God should destroy them miserably as wicked people and let out his vineyard to other laborers who will render him fruit in its seasons.

But you, my God, distinguish among causes, since, though you do nothing without cause, you behold eternally above time the final causes of temporal things and actions. Likewise, you have before you distinct primordial causes of things, known to you but hidden from human minds except insofar as they can be recognized through manifest movements. For example, you raised up Pharaoh the king for this very purpose, that you might show your power in him. Likewise, you endure with great patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, that you might show [Col. 1522D] the riches of your grace upon vessels of mercy. Yet whether, as is clear in these examples, you show your power through the wicked or your mercy as a primordial or final cause, this does not profit them unto salvation. Therefore I ask that my cause be distinguished from an unholy nation, so that the primordial cause may profit me—the cause for which you created me, that I might exist, and for which you redeemed me, that I might be good—and likewise the final cause toward which you created me, and which the title of this psalm indicates, reading thus: “Unto the end: a Psalm of David.” Therefore judge me, O God, and distinguish my final cause from an unholy nation.

I do not say this as though, like another Balaam, I desired only that my last things should become like those of the good. For he, speaking of the future, said: “Let my soul die [Col. 1523A] the death of the righteous, and let my last things be like theirs” (Num. 23:10). But I speak of the present: Judge—that is, separate me, O God—and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation. Judge and distinguish now my final cause, and also my primordial cause, from an unholy nation, showing by present and evident gifts how unlike the causes of the wicked are both my primordial cause, for which you made me, and my final cause, toward which you made me. An unholy nation, however, contains within its multitude many openly wicked people, and many counterfeit and deceitful good people. Therefore I say:

“Deliver me from an unjust and deceitful man.” As a good and strong shepherd—for example, David of mighty hand—rescues a sheep from the mouth of a bear or lion, so, my God, Jesus [Col. 1523B] Christ, good Shepherd, deliver me from an unjust and deceitful man, lest they ever say, “We have devoured him,” that is, lest they incorporate me into themselves. Rather, may I incorporate them into the holy nation by slaying and eating them, according to what was said to Peter: “Slay, slay, and eat” (Acts 10:13). More than once I opened my mouth in speech or prayer when I desired to eat the unholy nation, saying: “Have mercy, Lord God, upon the sinful nation, the people full of sins.” Likewise: “Let your will be done as in heaven and on earth,” so that, just as the heavenly, whose citizenship is in heaven, so also the earthly, whose heart is on earth, may serve you by breaking their own will and doing yours—you who will all people to be saved. Thus in speaking or praying, I desired to eat the wicked and deceitful and to incorporate them into myself, David the penitent.

But they, like a lion or bear with open jaws, rage against me, either to devour me and incorporate me into themselves, or, if they cannot do this, at least to tear me with teeth and claws by detraction and so disfigure me with the foul spittle of their mouths that my cause may in no way appear similar to the cause of the good. “But you, O Lord, who judge justly and test the reins and hearts, to you I have revealed my cause” (Jer. 11:20). Although before my repentance it was like the cause of the wicked, now, repenting of my sins, I pray that it may become unlike it and that I may be delivered from an unjust and deceitful man: first, lest I myself be unjust or deceitful inwardly through my own wickedness; then, lest I become unjust or deceitful [Col. 1523D] through another’s wickedness. Rightly I say to you, my God: Deliver me, because I do not ascribe to myself the strength by which I may resist injustice or deceit; rather, in the truth of my faith and hope I confess:

VERSE 2. For you, O God, are my strength. You who are my God are also my strength. Without you I can do no good thing; with your help and strengthening I can act courageously, as I once acted courageously with Elijah, zealously zealous for the house of Israel against simoniacs and other unjust and deceitful persons who undermined your altars, killed your prophets, and often sought my life, either to kill or mutilate me or to make me like themselves. Since this is so, why have you rejected me, you who were for a time my strength? Why have you abandoned me while impious [Col. 1524A] Jezebel persecutes me—that is, the pride of this world, queen of vices? Or, because Jezebel is interpreted “dunghill” or “flow of blood,” why have you rejected me, O God, my strength, while carnal uncleanness persecutes me, so that, conscious of my weakness, I dare not resist it at close quarters lest I be conquered, like David, Solomon, and Samson, but hold to the Apostle’s counsel: “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. 6:18). Thus Elijah fled Jezebel; thus Joseph fled his mistress; thus those who have not been defiled with women fled from the unholy nation—for they are virgins, and no lie has been found in their mouth; and if there was one, still no lie has been found, since it has been corrected by repentance that abolishes it. Therefore, fleeing such things too, whether by preserving innocence [Col. 1524B] or by doing penance for such sins with fruits worthy of repentance, I would wish, my God, that you were such strength to me that I did not feel in my members a law resisting the law of my mind. But you have rejected me, because I see another law in my members holding me captive in the law of sin, although in my mind I delight in the law of God according to the inward human being. And why have you thus rejected me? To destroy me, or to exercise me? I do not think it is to destroy me; for if you were destroying me, I would not advance toward what lies ahead, but would fall backward and, abandoning the good I had begun, become an apostate. But now, although

Sad, I nevertheless advance, seeking what lies ahead and forgetting what lies behind. I advance, because I do not turn backward from what was handed down to me, the holy commandment; [Col. 1524C] nevertheless I am sad because I endure many dangers and fear more or worse ones while the enemy afflicts me with innumerable temptations and tribulations. Among these I rightly grieve, because the final cause of the things that happen around me is wholly hidden from me and cannot be investigated by me, because “he has made darkness his hiding-place” (Ps. 17:12), lest it be seen by human perception. Therefore, that the day of joy may dawn or the shadows of sadness decline, you, O God, who dwell in inaccessible light,

VERSE 3. Send forth your light and your truth. Send forth the light of righteousness, which drives away sin, that dense mist and cause of sadness, just as righteousness, conversely, is the cause of joy. Hence it is said: “Rejoice in the Lord, and exult, you righteous” (Ps. 31:11). Likewise: “Exult, you righteous, in the Lord; praise befits the upright.” [Col. 1524D] (Ps. 32:1). Likewise: “Let the righteous feast and exult before God, and delight in joy” (Ps. 67:4). Conversely, Isaiah testifies that sin is the cause of the sadness which I investigate when I say, “Why do I go about sad?” or “Why are you sad, my soul?” saying: “I have made every breath; because of a small sin, why did I grieve him?” (Isa. 54:7). And the Apostle, on account of one man’s sin, urged the entire Church of Corinth to mourning, saying: “And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who has done this deed might be taken away from among you?” (1 Cor. 5:2).

Further, the sadness of those mourning either their own sins or others’ sins is turned into joy if you, O God, send [Col. 1525A] your light and truth into their dark and sad heart. For light is the very manifestation and reproof of sin. For “everything that is reproved is made manifest by the light” (Eph. 5:13), when the person who comes to the light by truthfully accusing his own sins wishes his works to be manifested and reproved. For just as one who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved, so one who has now ceased to do evil and resolves henceforth to act rightly willingly comes to the light, so that his works may presently be reproved. But who, blinded by himself, can come to the light unless you, the true light who enlighten every person coming into this world and shine in darkness, first come to enlighten him? Who among those for whom you, the sun [Col. 1525B] of righteousness, have set because of prolonged anger or another work of darkness, can see the light unless you, the sun of righteousness, rise upon him and send the light of the rays of righteousness into his heart? Therefore I say to you: Send forth your light and your truth. For when you send forth your light and illuminate the sad heart, every harmful sadness will be wholly removed. And because, just as the humility of penitential sadness exalts—for everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted—so the truth of confession liberates, I, David the penitent, who am afflicted inwardly by sadness and outwardly by the enemy, I who go about sad while the enemy afflicts me, seek a twofold consolation against a twofold evil, saying to you, my God: Send forth your light and your truth: light [Col. 1525C] to make me glad in my sadness, truth to free me from the afflicting enemy. That your light, driving away grief, gives joy is attested by what is said elsewhere: “Light has arisen for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart” (Ps. 96:11).

Therefore, Lord God, send your light into my heart as into a dark prison, so that I may first see my sin myself and, by the light of reason and judgment, reprove it and find it grievous. Send also your truth, so that, confessing the truth and not sparing my mouth, I may disclose my sin to faithful ears. For thus you sent your light to Peter, bound in Herod’s prison. For your angel stood by, and “a light shone in the dwelling” (Acts 12:7). You sent forth, I say, your light, to make the sad man glad [Col. 1525D] and to raise the humble man, when the angel said to him: “Rise quickly.” For immediately the chains fell from his hands. You also sent forth your truth through the angel himself, when through the truth of your judgment you brought him, shut in by iniquity, out of confinement, so that the iron gate could not withstand the judgment of your truth. For it was just that the bars of Herod, the enemy who afflicted him, should not hold the one whom the shining Light of truth had chosen as its herald and witness. Thus your soldier was raised and led forth through your light and truth; and that very light and truth led and brought him to your holy mountain, so that, coming into the house of the congregation of saints, he might greatly gladden them by his arrival.

Thus, Lord, lest I long go about sad while the enemy afflicts me, send [Col. 1526A] your light into the dark prison of my heart, and do this through Jesus, the Angel of great counsel, so that I may first see my own foulness and darkness and reprove them by your light. Then, with the two chains falling from my hands—namely, the delight in sin and the habit of sinning—and with the fourfold military watches, namely ignorance, weakness, sin, and misery, put to sleep, may your light, O God, and truth—that is, contrition and confession—lead me out of this prison of Herod, this narrow and dark cavern of an evil conscience, and bring me, through perseverance in good works, to your holy mountain Zion, to the fellowship of your saints in the heavenly kingdom.

Likewise, Light itself, bearing witness concerning itself, says: “Abraham, your father, rejoiced [Col. 1526B] to see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56). Therefore, without light, which restores innocence to those who have fallen and joy to the sorrowful, there is no true joy. Likewise, since it is written, “If the Son sets you free, you shall be truly free” (ibid., 36), and since the Son himself is Truth, who says of himself, “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6), and elsewhere, “You shall know the truth, and the truth shall set you free” (John 8:32), without liberating truth I shall not be free while the enemy afflicts me. Therefore against sadness I ask for light that both justifies and gladdens, and against the afflicting enemy I ask for truth that liberates, saying to you, God the Father, I David: Send forth your light—that is, send him whom you are to send, your Son, [Col. 1526C] who is the true light enlightening every person coming into this world and who is eternal truth. Send forth your light and your truth. May your Son, appearing in flesh, come into the world—he who is light and truth.

Otherwise: Christ, the true light and sun of righteousness, has known his setting; and therefore he sometimes withdraws his light from the world, and night comes, in which all the beasts of the forest pass by, lion cubs roaring in order to seize and seek food for themselves from God. When I, David—I, the penitent—see this happen, I labor throughout such a night and go about sad while the enemy, the devil, prince of darkness, or one of his attendants, afflicts me. Therefore, while I go about sad thus, afflicted throughout the night by the enemy, I too desire to see Christ’s day—which Abraham saw from afar and rejoiced—so that I may be filled with joy when the brightness of the sun is revealed. Of it it is written: “The sun has risen, and they have gathered together and shall be placed in their dens,” namely the beasts of the forest; but “man shall go out to his work and to his labor until evening” (Ps. 103:22). [Col. 1526D] Therefore, as long as it is night, I, going about sad while the enemy afflicts me, continually cry: Send forth your light and your truth. By this I hope that my cause may presently be distinguished from an unholy nation, that my sadness may be turned into joy, and that at last I may be wholly delivered from the unjust and deceitful man, my enemy who afflicts me, so that I may be free with that freedom by which Truth alone, who is Christ, can set free. He now distinguishes the cause of his own, and at the end, sending the angels as reapers, will deliver them from the [Col. 1527A] ungodly and deceitful man. Of this I am certain, because I already possess a pledge through the many gifts of light and truth already bestowed.

They have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles. I asked for two things, because “I have heard these two things,” namely, “that power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, belongs mercy” (Ps. 61:12). These two—mercy and truth—have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed, because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). I ask for these two when I say: Send forth your light and your truth. I call my Lord Jesus Christ, son of oil, by the names light, mercy, and peace, of whom it is written: “A vineyard was made for the beloved on a horn, the son of oil” (Isa. 5:1). [Col. 1527B] Likewise: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1:2). For oil is useful for light, for medicine or mercy; and, when the flood had ceased, the olive branch in the dove’s mouth signified this Son of oil, to be conceived of the Holy Spirit, who is Father of the age to come and Prince of Peace. Therefore, when I say, “Send forth your light,” I understand this Son of oil, whose name is oil poured out, under the name of light, peace, and medicine. Likewise, because he is truth, righteousness, and the power of God, through whom God the Father judges and acts, when I say to you, God the Father, “Send forth your truth,” I ask for that same Son—whether as one to be born for me, David living under the law, or as one to rise for me, David living under grace—as it is written: “For you who fear my name, the sun [Col. 1527C] of righteousness shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings” (Mal. 4:2). He rose once, when, rising above his setting, he rose again after death had been trampled down and conquered. And indeed, having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall have no further dominion over him. For what he lives, he lives to God; having ascended on high, he will no longer descend to the setting of death. Yet he still sets for me many times on account of my anger or another iniquity. When I perceive this has happened, I go about sad while the enemy afflicts me, and it is necessary to cry: Send forth your light and your truth. May your Son come to my aid: the true light, the sun of righteousness rising from on high, to give light to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, to direct [Col. 1527D] our feet into the way of peace. Send forth your light and your truth. May he, the true light, enlighten me, driving away the night of sin and sadness. May he, Truth, set me free, so that the enemy may no longer afflict me; while he afflicts me, he compels me continually to cry to you, my God: Send forth your light and your truth—that is, your Son, who is light and truth.

Otherwise: Through these two gifts of God, signified by the names light and truth, righteousness and peace, power and mercy, we may understand the Son of God, Christ, and the Holy Spirit. For as Isaiah says, “A Son has been given to us” (Isa. 9:6), as though one gift of the Father; and the Apostle says, “The charity of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). These two [Col. 1528A] gifts of God I, David under the law, desired, saying: Send forth your light and your truth. For truth had not yet sprung from the earth. God had not yet sent forth his mercy and truth to deliver my soul from the midst of lion cubs. “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39)—indeed, not yet born into the world—though he was in the world and the world was made through him. Therefore I said to God the Father: Send forth your light—that is, send your Spirit, and they shall be created and at the same time enlightened, those foreordained to life. But so that your Spirit may come to us in fiery tongues, both enlightening and kindling, send forth your truth—that is, your Son, who is Truth.

[Col. 1528B] Otherwise: I, David the penitent, now under grace, ask these two gifts for myself and the Church, saying: Send forth your light and your truth. Send your Spirit, the enlightener and at once the kindler of the faithful. And because your Son, although already born in flesh, having suffered and been glorified, is not doubted—for the testimonies of this fact have been made exceedingly credible—yet because he himself is Truth, with whom Belial has no agreement and with falsehood no communion at all, he is absent from us as often as we are found false, especially in the good promises which we made in baptism or after baptism. Since, when we are given over to falsehood, the Spirit of truth cannot be present unless Truth prepares a way for him—the way whose principal place lies in the true confession [Col. 1528C] of sins, concerning which the following words say, “I will confess to you on the harp, my God,” if the confessor truly grieves over past sins and truly intends to avoid future ones—since Truth flees from us who are false, I, David the penitent, call it back by frequently saying: Send forth, O God, your truth. Make us truthful in good vows and promises, and thus may we rejoice that your Son, your Truth, always dwells in us.

“They shall lead me and bring me to your holy mountain”: the Hebrew truth indicates that this must be understood as future, in which it reads thus: “Send forth your light and your truth; they shall lead me and bring me [Col. 1528D] to your holy mountain and to your tabernacle.” But our translation has the past tense thus: “Send forth your light and your truth; they have led me and brought me to your holy mountain.” Send forth your light, so that, as your Spirit enlightens us, we may clearly see what must be done. Send forth your truth, which sprang from the earth like a grain of wheat and, made bread, so strengthens us that we may not be deceived or tripped up by the deceitfulness of sins. Send forth your light—that is, your Spirit—and your truth—that is, your Son—whose working around me I hope for in the future, and whose past working I have already partly experienced. Therefore I confidently ask for what remains. For these two gifts of yours have led and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles. This has already been accomplished by your grace. It follows:

### Verse 4

“And I shall enter unto the altar of God, unto God who makes my youth glad.” This I still hope and ask may come to pass for me. For past blessings I give thanks; for future ones I offer prayers. I give thanks to you, and to your Son and the Holy Spirit, for your best and perfect gifts, because they led me away from evil and brought me to good, granting me to turn away from evil and do good. They led me from unbelief, from the depth of error, to your holy mountain and into your tabernacles.

Christ, or his body, is this mountain, which according to Isaiah is “raised above the tops of the mountains; and all nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us go up [Col. 1529B] to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths” (Isa. 2:2–3). He himself will teach us the ways of the common commandments; but we, striving toward the perfection of his counsels, shall walk in his paths, not content to keep what was said to those of old: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery,” and such things, but shall add that we do not become angry, do not look upon a woman in order to desire her, do not swear at all, and shall labor to observe the other evangelical ordinances of perfection; or, if we have transgressed them, like Peter swearing and lying, we shall weep bitterly as he did.

For we have been led from the valley of legal commandments to the evangelical mountain, so that there, with the disciples, we may hear [Col. 1529C] that excellent discourse which, beginning with the eight beatitudes, leads and brings willing and attentive hearers from the old things to the new, while Truth speaks thus:

“You have heard that it was said to those of old: You shall not kill. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment.” Likewise: “You have heard that it was said to those of old: You shall not commit adultery. But I say to you that whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. And if your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you; for it is better for you that one of your members should perish than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna. And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you; for it is better for you [Col. 1529D] that one of your members should perish than that your whole body should go into Gehenna. It has also been said: Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce. But I say to you that everyone who dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, causes her to commit adultery; and whoever marries a woman so dismissed commits adultery. Again, you have heard that it was said to those of old: You shall not swear falsely, but shall render your oaths to the Lord. But I say to you: do not swear at all—neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by earth, because it is his footstool; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King. Nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. But let your speech be: yes, yes; no, no. Whatever is more [Col. 1530A] than these is from evil. You have heard that it was said: An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. But I say to you: do not resist evil; but if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also; and to one who wishes to contend with you in court and take your tunic, yield him your cloak also. And whoever compels you to go a thousand paces, go with him another two. Give to one who asks you; and do not turn away from one who wishes to borrow from you. You have heard that it was said: You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy. But I say to you: Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you; and pray for those persecuting and slandering you, that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

[Col. 1530B] After these things, he again leads away and brings in. He leads away from the sad and burdensome fasting of hypocrites, who disfigure their faces, to joyful fasting, when he teaches that the head is to be anointed with the oil of gladness. In that discourse one may readily observe the leading away and bringing in, all the way to the holy mountain, which, according to Daniel, grows from a small stone, so as to crush the kingdoms of the earth and fill the entire face of the earth.

Set upon this mountain, we remain in the tabernacles of God: that is, either in bodies well fitted to serve as soldiers for God, or also in regularly ordered monasteries, where you will see nothing except companies of camps serving as soldiers for God. On this mountain, in these tabernacles, I, David—either “beloved” through innocence, like Mary the virgin mother and John the virgin apostle, or “strong of hand” through penitence [Col. 1530C] like Peter and Paul, whose primacy was exceedingly strengthened through penitence—I say, I, David, established upon the holy mountain, whether beloved or strong of hand, though in the tabernacles I sometimes proceed sadly because of the uncertain danger of battle while the attacking enemy afflicts me, nevertheless, when the battle has been carried through to its end—that is, to victory, because final victory is the purpose of battle—I know that, victory itself completed and my tabernacle at last folded up and put aside through death, “I shall enter unto the altar of God,” that is, unto God who makes my youth glad.

The tabernacle of the present Church has an altar, common to good and evil persons, though only to those sacrificing and communicating within that [Col. 1530D] tabernacle, not outside it. For those who sacrifice outside it neither communicate with the faithful in sacrificing nor do the faithful communicate with them, even if, though excommunicated, they presume to approach the visible altar of God by undertaking forbidden offices.

There is another altar, sublime and invisible, accessible only to the good. Just as only the high priest enters once, and not without sacrifice, into the Holy of Holies, so only the righteous person enters once, body and soul taken up as a whole burnt offering, in order that there he may be wholly renewed in youth and no longer proceed sadly while the old age of the outward person afflicts the inward person; but may wholly and altogether cleave to God, who makes his youth glad. To this altar I, the penitent one, shall at last enter, unto God who makes my youth glad.

[Col. 1531A] I do not say, “will make glad,” but “makes glad my youth,” because my joy has already begun. It grows from day to day the more greatly as I put off the old person and put on the new, he who makes my youth glad while my youth is renewed like the eagle’s. This youth, both by his office and by his appearance, was displayed by that young man of whom the Gospel according to Mark says: “They saw a young man sitting at the right, clothed in a white robe, and they were astonished” (Mark 16:5).

Rightly did the angel, messenger and witness of the resurrection, appear in the guise of a young man, because in the universal resurrection we await the Savior, who, as he now restores our souls by justifying and renewing them, so then will restore the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of [Col. 1531B] his glory, so that we may not be in the old age of sin or punishment, but in the youth and newness of everlasting joy. When this has been fulfilled, I shall no longer proceed sadly, because then the enemy will not afflict me. Indeed, rejoicing, I shall rejoice and confess to you upon the harp, my God, because I shall give thanks for my flesh crucified and well disciplined.

Even now, in some measure, I confess to you, my God, upon the harp, crucifying the flesh with its vices and desires which have clung to it from fellowship with the old person, in whom we all sinned. But then, in full and blessed youth, I shall confess more joyfully and perfectly upon the harp, when no contaminations of old age shall remain, when the body of our lowliness, which [Col. 1531C] “is now sown in weakness, shall rise in power,” which “is sown in dishonor, shall rise in glory,” which “is sown an animal body, shall rise a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15:43–44).

O my soul, still weighed down by the corruptible body: when, desiring to play the harp, you are sometimes hindered by strings that are out of tune or broken, strings which, while the changefulness of corruptible mortality endures, cannot be stretched with perpetual steadiness—do not be sad beyond measure. For I shall yet confess to God upon a harp made firm through the blessedness of immortality and adorned with the eight beatitudes as with eight unyielding strings. For then not the soul alone will enjoy these eight beatitudes; the flesh itself also will be fully made blessed. Therefore, since you await this future without doubt:

[Col. 1531D] **Verse 5.** “Why are you sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him: the salvation of my countenance, and my God.” This has been expounded in the preceding psalm and need not be repeated in a further exposition.

This psalm is customarily sung by the priest when entering to celebrate Mass. Since its sense, already expounded, fittingly applies to him, as it does to every good Christian, there is nevertheless something special for the priest to consider at that time, when he recites this psalm before approaching the altar. For example, he may speak as follows:

I, who am about to intercede for an unholy people so that it may become holy, first ask to be separated—that is, distinguished and set apart in actions and morals—from the unholy people, [Col. 1532A] lest, if I who am unholy presume to intercede for those who are unholy, my intercession be unwelcome and altogether unacceptable. For if I do not please, I shall not propitiate, and shall provoke anger rather than mercy. For the Lord says to me: “Why do you recount my righteousnesses and take my covenant into your mouth? Yet you hate discipline and cast my words behind you. If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you cast your lot with adulterers. Your mouth abounded in malice, and your tongue devised deceit” (Ps. 49:16–19).

Therefore it is not your sacrifice, leavened with so many acts of malice and wickedness, but a sacrifice of praise that will honor me, offered in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Therefore, that I, a priest about to sing Mass, may offer in the unleavened bread of truth and sincerity a sacrifice [Col. 1532B] of praise, judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause, utterly purging out the old leaven. Judge and distinguish me, and distinguish my cause from an unholy people. Among an unholy people priests are not distinguished from the people, but “as is the people, so is the priest” (Isa. 24:2).

When such priests sacrifice for the sake of earthly gain, they do so by seeking their own things, not the things of Jesus Christ. Distinguish, O God, my cause from theirs, so that in sacrificing I may seek above all that which is contained as desirable in the present psalm: namely, that you may be my strength; that you may send forth your light and your truth; and that these, having led and brought me to your holy mountain and into your tabernacles, may finally bring me [Col. 1532C] to the heavenly altar of God, unto God who makes my youth glad. When that youth is complete, may I confess to him upon the harp, continually playing its eight strings: “The salvation of my countenance, and my God.”

Before this visible altar I cannot yet sing, “the salvation of my countenance,” because I do not yet see face to face what I offer and to whom I offer. Rather, in the night I eat the Passover: not the Lamb’s flesh uncovered, but covered by a sacred veil; yet fully possessing without measure the grace of light and truth, and imparting itself in measure to those who eat it. Desiring that the power of this light and truth should go forth from the flesh of the Lamb, who said, “I perceived power to have gone forth from me” (Luke 8:46), I say to you: Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, send forth your light and your truth. Send forth the treasure of light and truth [Col. 1532D] which you possess within, hidden under the appearance of bread and wine. Send it forth into all your members, which are in you as their head, distributing gifts to each one as you know and will.

Glory to the Father, to whom it is said: “Send forth your light,” the Holy Spirit, “and your truth,” that is, your Son, as was explained above. Glory to the Son, the Truth. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is the light whom we shall see in your light—that is, in your Son—when we behold your light, namely your Son, glorified in our countenance. Then each of us too will be able to say: “The salvation of my countenance, and my God.” To him be glory for ever. Amen.

## Psalm 43

[Col. 1533]

[Col. 1533A] “O God, we have heard with our ears; our fathers have declared to us,” etc. The Apostle uses a verse of this psalm as follows: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? As it is written: Because of you we are put to death all day long; we are accounted as sheep for slaughter” (Rom. 8:35–36).

Therefore these words—“O God, we have heard with our ears; our fathers have declared to us the work that you performed in their days and in the days of old”—are the words of perfect martyrs, greatly wondering why he did not quickly destroy the nations, just as, they say, “you once destroyed the nations and planted them; you afflicted peoples and cast them out.” The devout martyrs who were dying desired, indeed, [Col. 1533B] that the same hand of the Lord might quickly destroy the nations—that is, the wicked living as Gentiles—and plant the faithful, so that Christian faith might flourish peacefully throughout the earth.

“But now,” they say, “you have sold your people without price, and there was no multitude in exchange for them.” That is to say: You allowed your own people to be killed and gained no one from them. Certainly, if you gained some, this was still not achieved by an adequate exchange, because “there was no multitude in exchange for them.” Where a thousand were killed, scarcely one or two were converted. But did they groan in vain? Did they desire in vain? Surely not. For when the Lord rose, who had seemed to sleep, the Gentiles with their idols were destroyed, and multitudes of believers, planted through the martyrs, filled the world.

Thus this psalm appropriately bears the following title:

**Verse 1.** “Unto the end, for the sons of Korah, for understanding.” Its meaning is: These words are set before the sons of Korah who strive toward the end—that is, imitators of the Crucified One striving toward the consummate good. They are set before them, I say, for understanding: that they may understand what it signifies that God dealt so kindly with the ancient fathers, yet on the contrary permits these men to be afflicted and to be in every misery.

Before the time of grace he granted temporal goods to many, abundantly, as though to the immature: for example, the children of Israel crossed the sea on dry ground; they were fed with manna and quails in the wilderness; and few often defeated many. But he deprived few, and only rarely, of temporal goods [Col. 1533D] and permitted them to be afflicted. Now, however, in the time of grace, the reverse is true. He bestows prosperity upon few, lest they despair; upon many he brings adversity, thereby summoning the sons of Korah—that is, Christ’s martyrs—to this understanding: that they may desire eternal things alone. One must know that by those things done to the immature people in order that they might believe, these spiritual things were prefigured.

Accordingly, in this psalm he speaks concerning martyrs. First he distinguishes the benefits of God, showing what was given in the world to beginners and what to the perfect in heaven. Second, he shows what martyrs suffer in the world, at the words: “But now you have cast us off.” Third, how they pray for help, at the words: “Arise.” Thus the prophet, marveling in the person of the martyrs that he seems to be abandoned in these times, recalls the past and says:

**Verse 2.** “O God, we have heard with our ears.” O God, who are truly God: because we confess your divinity, rejecting idols, we suffer adversities in the world; because we place your divine laws above the unjust decrees of kings, we endure kings and the friends of kings as enemies; because we prefer your traditions and commandments to the traditions of Pharisees, scribes, and Sadducees, we are held in contempt by them and by people like them. And, as though you neither wished nor were able [Col. 1534B] to defend or deliver us, “for your sake we are put to death all day long.”

Yet we do not doubt in the least your omnipotence, by which you are able to deliver your own when you will. We have not believed it by following unlearned fables, nor invented it for ourselves; rather, relying firmly upon trustworthy authorities testifying to your omnipotence, we have placed faith in it. “Faith is from hearing” (Rom. 10:17), and we have believed the report of those of whom one says: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isa. 53:1).

They heard you inwardly speaking to them with the hearing of the mouth, and we heard them—not through ambiguous intermediaries, but with our own ears, not merely outward but inward ears also, because we weighed inwardly by rational discernment what we heard outwardly. And we know whom we have believed, so that each one of us may say: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain” (2 Tim. 1:12).

For it was not false prophets, but our fathers, who declared this to us: fathers venerable in age, not young men to be despised for frivolity; our fathers, I say, not strangers, who declared it to us as to most beloved sons. Hence it is certain that they said nothing but what was certain, since fathers are not accustomed to deceive their children by offering a stone for bread, a serpent for fish, a scorpion for an egg—or, to speak more plainly, harmful falsehood for useful truth. These fathers, therefore, worthy to be heard by their children, declared to us their children not the fabulous poetic inventions concerning fabricated false gods, but the work which you performed in their days, in the days of old: an excellent work, a divine work, impossible for false gods; a work possible to you alone, the true God; a work which neither human being nor angel could perform without you, but which you yourself performed by your power in their days and in the days of old.

For their days were ancient days, which preceded the new days, as the law precedes grace, as the herald precedes the king, as evening precedes morning in the creation of the world, according to the saying: “And there was evening and there was morning, one day” (Gen. 1:5). Evening is mentioned first, and morning is then added, because day does not dawn unless the shadows first decline; there would be no new days unless the old days had already passed.

[Col. 1535A] We ourselves have seen with our own eyes the work of the new days, and our hands have touched what you performed in us, beginning from your holy temple which is in Jerusalem and proceeding in your working thence to the end of the earth. But the work which you performed in ancient days we ourselves did not see; nevertheless, we have heard it with our own ears, our truthful fathers declaring the work which you performed in their days and in ancient days. For, since they themselves were ancient pupils of the ancient law, their days too are rightly called ancient.

Everything that becomes old and ages is near destruction; and therefore the ancient days passed away and new ones succeeded. Hence it is no wonder if new works succeeded ancient works: works stable, knowing neither destruction nor old age, which you, O God, have performed in us far more salutarily than what you performed in the days of our fathers and in the ancient days.

Alternatively: Our fathers Moses, Joshua, and the others declared to us the work which you performed in their days: in those days you divided the sea, gave manna, drove out strong nations, and placed our fathers themselves in the promised land. They also declared to us “the work which you performed in ancient days”: when you made heaven and earth, placed the firmament amid the waters, gathered the seas together, caused the dry land to germinate, set sun, moon, and stars in the firmament, created birds and swimming creatures from the waters, brought forth walking and creeping creatures from the earth, and made humankind in your image.

These days, in which you made all these things, were more ancient than the days of our fathers; yet our fathers declared the work of those days, however ancient. Moses was first, showing us what you had done even before the creation of humankind; then the other fathers—for example David, saying: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power, gathering the waters of the sea as into a skin” (Ps. 32:6). And shortly afterward: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (ibid., v. 9). And Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Lord: “Who,” he says, “formed all these things? Was it not my hand?” Thus human fathers truthfully declared many things to us even concerning the work of those ancient days, in which there were no human beings. How much more should they be believed concerning those works which you performed in their days, before their eyes. We shall enumerate a few of them—especially those that require understanding from us, the sons of Korah—because they are marvelous in our eyes, since you do not now go forth in our might, but have given us as sheep for food and scattered us among the nations; whereas formerly, in the days of our fathers, you destroyed the nations by assisting our fathers with marvelous and visible triumph.

For:

**Verse 3.** “Your hand destroyed the nations.” Your hand—your power, strength, and might—destroyed, that is, destroyed in various ways by killing [Col. 1536A] or driving out from the promised land, the nations: the Canaanites, Hivites, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, and Girgashites. And in their place you planted them, namely our fathers. You planted them so that, like the paradise of delight which you planted in the beginning, they might grow in number and merit, until the tree of life, Christ Jesus, might stand in their midst, born of a virgin and made under the law.

After our fathers received this law, whenever they neglected it, they were handed over into the hands of the nations, and the nations ruled over them. But when you killed them, they again sought you, turned back, and came to you early in the morning, confessing and repenting of their sins. They remembered that you, O God, are their helper: you who afflicted peoples and [Col. 1536B] drove them out from the promised land, though reserving some to scourge and exercise your servants, our fathers, lest they grow unused to warfare and become presumptuous through excessive security.

This is also what you now do spiritually: planting virtues inwardly, uprooting and exterminating vices, yet leaving certain remnants of vices to preserve humility and to exercise the virtues, which receive growth from such exercise. Truly, your hand both now does that spiritually and then did that historically, working marvelously in both cases: now planting virtues in the holy Church, then planting the fathers in the Holy Land.

**Verse 4.** “For not by their own sword did they possess [Col. 1536C] the land, nor did their arm save them.” Indeed, when, with you offended, they went up to battle despite Moses’ prohibition, their sword was of no use. But once the multitude of those who had disparaged the land had been removed and the Lord’s anger appeased, they began to enter the Holy Land. Without swords, after their circuit for seven days, the walls of Jericho fell. When this miracle was spread abroad and your other miracles were likewise heard, the princes of Edom were troubled; trembling seized the mighty men of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan grew rigid with fear. And, as Moses had sung beforehand in his song, dread and terror fell upon them at the greatness of your arm, until your people passed over—namely our fathers, whom “you brought in and planted upon the mountain of your inheritance, your most firm dwelling-place, which you made, O Lord: your sanctuary [Col. 1536D] which your hands established” (Exod. 15:17).

Truly, therefore, it was said that they did not possess the land by their own sword. They neither gained it by their own power nor held it by their own strength, because their arm did not save them. For their fleshly arm was not stronger than the arms of the nations. But your exalted right hand and your divine arm—your power, a right hand, that is, gracious to them but a left hand hostile and adverse to the nations—saved them; and your arm, that is, your strength, saved them.

For since the nations were far greater in number and stronger than those whom you brought in after driving the nations out, it is clear that the victories were achieved not by human but by divine strength: when one pursued a thousand and two pursued ten thousand; when the enemy itself was killed by hailstones under Joshua’s leadership; when enemies fell by mutual wounds; when Gideon with three hundred put many thousands to flight; and afterward when King Jehoshaphat triumphed through prayers.

In such wars your hand, or right hand, and your arm worked with our fathers, as did the illumination of your countenance: that is, your Son, who is your hand through whom you created all things; your right hand through whom you restore created things to something better; your arm through whom you defeat enemies, as it is said elsewhere: “In the strength of your arm you scattered your enemies” (Ps. 88:11). He is also your countenance, for one who sees him sees you, as he himself says: “Who sees me sees the Father” (John 14:9).

The illumination of your countenance is the Holy Spirit, because “in your light”—that is, in your luminous [Col. 1537B] countenance—“we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10), that is, the Holy Spirit. What is his mercy and consolation toward your people, manifested in some wondrous working, except the illumination of your countenance, through which you and your Son are recognized as merciful and powerful? With our fathers you performed great wonders, not because they deserved this, but because you were pleased in them: that is, your very illumination and that of your countenance pleased you; you were pleased with yourself—that is, you were pleased together—because you displayed in them both work and benevolence of your threefold omnipotence.

Through this you were also pleased in them before other nations which beheld your power, wisdom, and clemency displayed toward our fathers; or, as it is read in the Hebrew: “You were pleased with them,” that is, with the fathers themselves. For it is apparent that the illumination of your countenance was shown to them in your benefits because you were pleased with them. Then, before the other nations that saw your benefits toward those fathers, you were pleased in them, so that they said: “The Lord has magnified his dealings with them.” And truly the Lord is among his people. Likewise: “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he has chosen for his inheritance” (Ps. 32:12). Likewise: “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them against us” (Exod. 14:25).

**Verse 5.** “You yourself are my King and my God.” You yourself, who by ruling them exalted them in temporal things unto eternity, are my King, because I, a son of Korah, according to the title of this psalm, hope by your rule to be governed [Col. 1537D] unto the end for understanding. You are the God of my fathers; you are my God. There shall not be a new God in me; rather, you—the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob—are my God. You are, I say, the God of Jacob, who commands salvations for Jacob, because all things which you command Jacob to observe are salutary.

For Jacob, his brother Esau having been rejected because of gluttony and wickedness, received from his father salvations, that is, saving blessings, as his father said to him: “Behold, the odor of my son is like the odor of a full field,” etc. (Gen. 27:27).
