You commanded that these things should occur, you who loved Jacob but hated Esau, clearly as a type of the younger people, for whom you now continually command salvations. Your apostle Paul says to those whom he addresses as converted from the Gentiles: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father [Col. 1538A] and the Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Thess. 1:2).

Likewise, in the Gospel, you yourself, our Korah, command salvations for Jacob—that is, for the younger people—when you say to your apostles: “Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:15). Thus you say concerning every Jacob: “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved.” Likewise: “Through me, if anyone enters, he shall be saved” (John 10:9).

In the Gospel you command eternal salvations for Jacob; before this acceptable time, before the day of salvation, you commanded temporal salvations—not by giving your presence, but by speaking through creatures, as in the pillar of fire or cloud, and by issuing saving commandments through angels, patriarchs, and prophets.

[Col. 1538B] When the sons of Jacob transgressed these commandments, having lost salvation and prosperity, they were many times delivered into the hands of nations, and the nations ruled over them. But whenever they turned back to him, he immediately sent them saviors and defenders, such as Jephthah, Gideon, Samson, and others like them, through whom you worked salvations in the midst of the earth.

Until salvation came from the Jews—not for the Jews alone, but also for the Gentiles, namely the younger people—you command two salvations: one by which they shall receive a hundredfold in the present life for all things left behind for your sake and for the Gospel’s sake; the other by which, after this life, they shall have eternal life. But carnal Esau, earthly and hairy, while seeking only one salvation in the present life, will lose both salvations, the present and the future. For what fruit does he have in his hunting, pursuing only temporal and fleeting goods, in which he will be ashamed when he understands himself deprived of the blessing of eternal salvation?

But we, sons of Korah, freed from sin and made servants of God, have our fruit unto sanctification, and our end is eternal life. Therefore the sanctification of our life, which we enjoy in the present, is one salvation; eternal life is the other and greater salvation. You command both these salvations for Jacob, whom you love as simple, dwelling with Rebecca—whose name means “patience”—in the tabernacles of churches or regular monasteries. But you hate Esau, occupied in the hunting of the forest of this world.

Yet one salvation is often given to him when he says to his father: “Have you only one blessing?” (Gen. 27:38). Esau asks for one blessing, content to receive, in the fatness of the earth and the dew of heaven from above, abundance of earthly fruits. But Jacob, blessed with a twofold blessing, is understood by the sons of Korah, who indeed understand in the fragrance of the full field which the Lord blessed that fullness of blessing which contains the two salvations commanded for Jacob. For when he is proclaimed established with grain and wine, the stability of eternal fruits is commended in him. Likewise, when it is said to him: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth” (ibid.), abundance of temporal happiness is bestowed upon him, through whose use one comes to the eternal blessing laid up in his seed. Already then the fragrance of Jacob’s garments was a foretoken of this blessing: a twofold salvation of body and soul, not for him alone, but also for us, the sons of Korah, who, according to Jacob’s name, wrestle against vices—not in our own strength, but in yours, O God of Jacob. For in ourselves we are weak and feeble, but strong:

**Verse 6.** “In you we shall winnow our enemies with the horn, and in your name we shall trample down those who rise up against us.” Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made for himself two horns of iron, by which he prophesied that all Syria would be winnowed (1 Kings 22:11). But for us, the sons of Korah—that is, imitators of Christ, humbled for our sake upon Calvary—one horn is sufficient. Fortified by it upon our bald crown, we are accustomed to sing: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and made redemption for his people, and has raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant” (Luke 1:68–69).

This horn is Christ, strong in you, Father, and in us: in you, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; in us, because “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Therefore, possessing the horn in you, by which we are strong, we shall winnow our enemies with the same horn; and in your name—that is, in your Son, through whom you are named and held glorious—we shall spurn those who rise up against us.

Or, in your name, O Christ, by which we are called Christians, we shall spurn those who rise up against us. Those who rise against us are not merely outside us, such as pagans and other external enemies, but also within us, such as false brethren who, though among us, are not of us. Or the goads of vices within us—lust in the flesh and anger in the mind—will not conquer us, the sons of Korah, fortified upon our bald crown by so lofty and strong a horn.

Therefore we shall spurn those who rise up within us, because the enemies of the Church, mockers of our baldness, shall not prevail over us, the sons of Korah. We all alike glory inwardly in this baldness, while we lack the hairs of vices upon the head—that is, in the mind itself—whoever we are among the sons of Korah. Some of us outwardly also are made bald by clerical or monastic tonsure and shaving; while they represent on the head the likeness of Elisha, they rejoice to be mocked with him. Yet they do not curse their mockers as he did, because, knowing that the severity of the law has now passed and the sweetness of grace has come, they instead bless those who mock and curse them. Continually turning to you, the true Korah, they say: “In your name we shall spurn those who rise up against us.”

Although at present we cannot wholly spurn them, while we are fragile and fear falling among enemies, nevertheless we shall spurn them in the future, when we recognize that the time in which they now rise up within us has wholly passed. “For this corruptible nature,” in which we suffer enemies “rising up,” “must put on incorruption, and this mortal nature must put on immortality. But when this mortal nature has put on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying which is written: Death has been swallowed up in victory.” Then we shall spurn those now “rising up within us,” saying: “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death? Now the sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 15:53–57). But far be it from me to glory in victory except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ.

**VERSE 7.** For I shall not hope in my bow, just as my fathers did not hope in theirs, and my sword shall not save me. The bow is understood as lesser strength, the sword as greater strength. Or, by the bow, which strikes at things far off while it is not seen, prayer is signified: by it we fight in secret, sending the darts of entreaty toward friends and enemies situated not only near at hand but also far away, whether by location or by estrangement of mind. But by the sword, which strikes those present at close quarters, is understood the word of truth, convicting [Col. 1540B] the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment. “For the word of God is living and effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit” (Heb. 4:12). Therefore I shall hope in it, and not in my sword or bow; for the bow of my prayer has no taut string by which to shoot effectively the arrows of petitions without your help; nor is my word, but your word, O Lord, compared to a two-edged sword, from whose mouth proceeds a double-edged *romphaea* [sword], powerful alike to condemn and to save. Therefore I, a son of Korah, rightly say that my sword shall not save me, because I have no salvation except from you, the true Savior.

**VERSE 8.** For you have saved us from those who afflict us, and [Col. 1540C] you have put to shame those who hate us. “You have saved” means, without doubt, “you will save us.” For the past is used for the future when an overwhelming certainty of what is future is expressed. You have saved us, I say—that is, you will save us—when you say to us, the sons of Korah: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you” (Matt. 25:34). “And you have put to shame those who hate us,” that is, you will put them to shame, saying: “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (ibid., 41).

Or, by this we know that your sword will save us in the future judgment: because already in this world you have saved us from the unclean spirits that afflict us, which weary us with temptations and afflictions, so that, however much they afflict us by attacking, they cannot draw the consent of our minds after themselves; they are unable to overthrow by assault those whom they attack. [Col. 1540D] And you have put to shame those who hate us, covering their faces with the shame of confusion when they could not accomplish against us what they wished.

In the Hebrew it reads: “You yourself are my king, O God; command the deliverances of Jacob. In you we shall scatter our enemies; in your name we shall trample down our adversaries. For I shall not trust in my bow, nor shall my sword save me; because you have saved us from our enemies and put to shame those who hated us.” The truth of this Hebrew wording differs from the foregoing exposition only in this: where it was said there, “You who command the salvations of Jacob,” here it says, “Command the deliverances of Jacob.” Its sense is this: since you are my king, and are God, neither I nor my fellow soldiers [Col. 1541A] ought to go forth into battle without your royal command; for victory does not attend those who fight without your nod and order, or who ambitiously seize the standard of preeminence.

Therefore, lest the battle be either nonexistent or futile, command, Lord, for the deliverances of Jacob: command the Gospel to be preached; and, as the readers in the Church also daily ask of you, “Bid, bless, send,” and by commanding cast laborers into your harvest. Command them not to go into the way of the Gentiles—that is, not to consent in vices with those who live as Gentiles do—but to labor earnestly for Jacob’s deliverance: to gather from among the Gentiles a younger people, one that supplants vices, and to direct it into the way of eternal salvation. Thus, at your command, we who are your soldiers, your laborers, your fishers—who without [Col. 1541B] your command fought in vain and labored through the whole night, accomplishing or catching nothing—will at last let down the net at your word; strengthened in you, we shall scatter our enemies and trample down our adversaries in your name. And because we shall triumph not in our own strength but in your divine power, therefore not in ourselves or in our strength, but—

**VERSE 9.** In God we shall glory all the day, and in your name we shall confess for ever. Since you scattered my enemies not by my bow and sword but by the strength of your arm; since you saved us from those who openly afflicted us by attacking them, and put to shame those who hated us with concealed hatred, because you did not do to us as they wished—rightly we shall glory not in our own strength but [Col. 1541C] in God all the day.

I use the verb in the future tense, “we shall glory,” lest we be praised before the time; for it is written: “Do not praise a man in his lifetime” (Ecclus. 11:30). Strength valiant in war should be praised, but when victory is complete. The good fortune of a sailor should be praised, but when he has been brought to harbor. Therefore we are not yet praised in the present, but in the future we shall be praised throughout the whole day—a day that will have no evening and to which night will never again succeed. For the perpetuity or eternity of the age in which we shall glory will not be interrupted by nights, but will be one whole day, which, as has been said, is without evening.

And in your name we shall confess for ever. We indeed shall glory, but for ever we shall confess that the whole ground for glory must be ascribed to you; or, as the Hebrew has it, “unto eternity,” because in your name, by which you are called Savior, the completion of our salvation will be accomplished—not while we exult for an hour in the brief joy of temporal safety, but for ever or unto eternity, that is, always and without end.

Here in the Hebrew *Sela* is inserted, interpreted in Latin as *semper*, “always”; in Greek we have *diapsalma*, which we may call a division of the psalm. From here the second part of the psalm begins, which David, skillfully singing, quite clearly distinguishes from the first. For after recounting the good things God did for the fathers and will do for us, he shows what the blessed martyrs suffer between their past and our future, so that he may send the sons of Korah to this understanding worth knowing: that God, by whom a human being was created freely and liberated freely, is to be worshipped freely by the one whom he created and liberated. Yet although God is worshipped and loved with worship and love freely given, he is not loved without reward, though he ought to be loved without regard to reward. For truthfulness cannot be empty or fruitless, and yet it is not mercenary. It does not seek its own interests; it moves of itself and makes people act spontaneously. True love is content with itself: it has a reward, but that which it loves. For whatever you seem to love for the sake of something else, that is what you truly love at which the end of your love is aimed, not that through which it aims. Paul does not preach the Gospel in order to eat; rather, he eats in order to preach the Gospel, because he loves not food [Col. 1542B] but the Gospel. True love does not demand a reward, but deserves one. A reward is certainly proposed to one who does not yet love, owed to one who loves, and rendered to one who perseveres.

Finally, in lower matters we invite unwilling persons by promises or rewards, rather than those who act voluntarily. For who would think a person should be paid to do what he also desires of his own accord? For example, no one hires a hungry person to eat, a thirsty person to drink, or a mother to nurse the little child of her womb. Or would anyone think that someone must be induced by entreaty or payment to fence his own vineyard, dig around his own tree, or erect the structure of his own house? How much more does a soul that loves God seek no reward other than that of its own love! Or, if it seeks something else, it certainly does not yet [Col. 1542C] love that thing.

Some, reading that Christ’s worshippers will receive a hundredfold for things relinquished for his sake, think that he is not to be worshipped freely, since he will give so great a reward. For example, they suppose that one who has now left one house for Christ will receive a hundred houses, and that one who has left one wife for God will in the resurrection receive a hundred wives whose lust he may satisfy. The sons of Korah do not accept such an understanding. Knowing that in eternal life they will be nourished and satisfied with the delights of righteousness alone, for which they now hunger, they do not need to be hired by rewards to desire and seek it, just as no hungry person is hired to eat and no thirsty person to drink. Therefore the sons of Korah, thirsting to see God, worship him freely and urge those who hear them to worship him.

I say “freely,” lest he be worshipped for temporal things or things resembling temporal things. Whoever places the reward of divine worship in temporal things is condemned with the Jews. But whoever seeks in eternal life eternal goods in exchange for temporal goods, yet goods resembling those temporal things—for example, luxurious bedchambers undisturbed by any trouble, bright and tranquil dwellings pleasant to bodily sight and resembling these visible dwellings—is altogether like a dreaming person, of whom it is said: “They slept their sleep, and all men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75:6). For nothing of the kind they dream of will be found in the kingdom of heaven, where God will be all and [Col. 1543A] in all. In that kingdom, among and in all who rejoice, there will be no other cause of rejoicing except God.

Whoever therefore imagines that there he will delight in banquets, adorned garments, or other pleasures placed below God has not yet attained the understanding commended to the sons of Korah in this psalm and conveyed by this fact: that the saints are afflicted in this world, so that their joy may be in God alone.

There were certain heretics, called Cerinthians after their founder Cerinthus, who taught that after the resurrection a thousand years were to be spent in pleasures. Hence among the Greeks they were called Chiliasts, and among the Latins Millenarians. Because they either hoped for themselves or promised to others a thousand years of delights in return for temporal afflictions, [Col. 1543B] they were condemned by the Church. Yet their dregs have not been drained dry: all the sinners of the earth drink them. These would prefer, if the choice were offered, after renouncing temporal and brief pleasures in this world, to receive long or endless pleasures in the world to come, rather than to lack all impurities and pleasures now and eternally and rejoice in the invisible and highest good alone.

For that the highest good is invisible is affirmed not only by divine but also by secular philosophy. The person to whom it is said, “Delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart” (Ps. 30:4), is summoned to the delight of this good. Thus it is the voice of a perfect man: “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. 76:4)—that is, by every enjoyment which is beneath God or can be imagined; if at any time I remember them, I shall be wearied by them. Where, then, holy man, is your delight? In the present life, indeed, the remembrance of God delights me; this I have learned by experience, because “I remembered God and was delighted.” But in the future age the very vision of the invisible God will delight me. For “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

It should certainly be noted that, although the remembrance of the invisible God alone now delights saints who refuse to be consoled by other things, nevertheless visible or intelligible things which, when seen or considered, awaken and increase this very remembrance, become delightful to them in proportion as they feel themselves exercised or preserved by them [Col. 1543D] for keeping God continually in remembrance. For this reason saints love one another: remembrance of God is sweet to them in one another’s company. Hence reading, psalmody, the other divine offices, and spiritual exercises please them, because in them the present remembrance of God grows more frequent and increasingly sweet, preparing them for his future vision.

“My remembrance is through generations of ages,” says Wisdom (Ecclus. 24:28). How true this is the experience of the saints proves: as long as the present world is seen to stand, in which one generation comes and another passes away, the elect will not lack the consolation of remembrance, since full refreshment from the Presence itself is not yet granted them. Thus it is written: “They shall pour forth the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness” (Ps. 144:7), undoubtedly those of whom a little above it had said: “Generation after generation shall praise your works” (ibid., 4). Therefore remembrance belongs to the generations of ages; presence, to the kingdom of heaven. By the former, the elect already taken up are glorified; by the latter, the generation still on pilgrimage is meanwhile consoled.

But it matters what generation receives consolation from the remembrance of God. It is not the perverse and provoking generation, but that which can truly say: “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. 76:3). We believe it entirely if it adds next: “I remembered God and was delighted” (ibid.). For it is just that those whom the present does not delight should have the remembrance of future things at hand, and that those who disdain to be consoled by any abundance of passing things should be delighted by the recollection of eternity. And “this is the generation of those who seek [Col. 1544B] the Lord”: those who seek not their own things, but “the face of the God of Jacob” (Ps. 23:6).

Therefore, for those who seek and long for God’s presence, a sweet remembrance is meanwhile at hand—not one by which they are satisfied, but one by which they hunger all the more for that by which they may be satisfied. The food itself testifies this of itself, saying: “He who eats me will still hunger” (Ecclus. 24:29). And he who has been fed by it says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16:15). Yet blessed even now are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, because someday they themselves, and not others, shall be filled. Woe to you, perverse and crooked generation! Woe to you, foolish and senseless people, who both reject remembrance and dread presence. Rightly so, indeed.

For even now you do not wish to be freed from the snare of hunters, since “those who desire to become rich in this world fall into the snare of the devil” (1 Tim. 6:9); nor then will you be able to escape the harsh word. O harsh Word, O hard saying: “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41)! It is plainly harsher and more severe than that which is repeated daily to us in the Church in remembrance of the Passion: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:55)—that is, he who recalls my death and, after my example, puts to death his members upon earth has eternal life; that is, if you suffer, you shall also reign with me. Yet many recoil from this saying and, even today, go backward, answering not in word but in deed: “This saying is hard, and who [Col. 1544D] can hear it?” (ibid., 61).

Thus the generation that did not direct its heart, whose spirit was not faithful with God, but which rather hopes in the uncertainty of riches, finds it burdensome now to hear the word of the cross and judges the remembrance of the Passion onerous for itself. But how will it bear in the Presence the weight of that word: “Depart, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41)? Whoever falls upon this stone will surely be crushed by it.

But “the generation of the upright shall be blessed” (Ps. 111:2), those who, with the Apostle, whether absent or present, strive to please God. Finally, they shall hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom,” and so forth (Matt. 25:34). Then that generation which did not direct its heart will learn, though too late, how sweet Christ’s yoke and light his burden were in comparison with that pain, although it proudly withdrew its stiff neck from them as from something heavy and harsh. You wretched people cannot serve God and mammon, glory at once in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ and hope in treasures of money, pursue gold and taste how sweet the Lord is. Therefore, the one whom you do not find sweet in remembrance you will without doubt find harsh in presence.

But the faithful soul both longs eagerly for his presence and rests sweetly in remembrance; and until it is fit, with unveiled face, to contemplate the glory of God, it glories in the ignominy of the cross. Thus indeed, thus the bride and dove of Christ meanwhile rests for herself and sleeps between the two inheritances, having already received in the present, from remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord Jesus, silvered wings—the brightness, namely, of innocence and chastity—and hoping further to be filled with joy in your countenance. There also the hinder parts of her back shall become pale gold, when, brought in with joy among the splendors of the saints, she shall be more fully illuminated by the radiance of wisdom. Rightly, therefore, she already glories and says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2:6). By his left hand she understands the remembrance of that love than which none is greater: that he laid down his life for his friends. By his right hand she understands the blessed vision promised to his friends and joy in the presence of majesty.

Rightly that divine and deifying vision, that inestimable delight of the divine presence, is reckoned on the right, of which it is sweetly sung: “Delights are at your right hand unto the end” (Ps. 15:15). Rightly that wonderful love, recalled and always to be recalled, is placed on the left, so that until iniquity passes away the bride may recline and rest upon it. Rightly, therefore, the bridegroom’s left hand is beneath the bride’s head, upon which, reclining, she may support her head—that is, the intention of her mind—lest it be bent and inclined toward carnal and worldly desires, because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15).

What else does such great and utterly undeserved mercy, such free and so proven love, such unexpected condescension, such unconquered gentleness, such astounding sweetness—what, I say, do all these things, when diligently considered, accomplish except to free the mind of the one considering them utterly from every depraved love, wonderfully draw it to contemplation of him who is lovable, affect it powerfully, and by their sweetness cause it to despise whatever cannot be sought or possessed except by contempt and forgetfulness of these things? Accordingly, the bride runs eagerly in the fragrance of these ointments, loves ardently, and thinks that she loves too little when so loved, even when she has bound her whole self in love. Therefore she allows nothing to linger in her breast by which remembrance of him whom she loves may be impeded. Hence her Beloved says: “He shall dwell between my breasts” (Song 1:13), because [Col. 1546A] the remembrance of him whom the lover desires to see face to face in the future now occupies her breast. Everything that increases in her breast the remembrance and love of her Beloved is sweet to her in the present. It will also be sweet to her in the future to see a new heaven and a new earth, in which, since righteousness dwells, the vein or fountain of righteousness will then be visible—the fountain who is God himself.

On this accursed earth, which brings forth thorns and thistles, the bride, set like a lily among thorns (Song 2:2), cannot see clearly and suffers many troublesome pricks; from them come to her many salutary compunctions. For as often as she is pricked by thorns, so often is she pierced inwardly, because it seems to her that she suffers too little, though redeemed by Christ’s Passion—even if she should die a thousand times for him who, though immortal, deigned to die for his sheep. Their bleating is heard in this psalm, saying: “You gave us as sheep for food.”

But to make it clear that, even amid adversities and most bitter torments, the remembrance of God delights the saints, after setting out the hard things they suffer, they add later: “All these things have come upon us, and we have not forgotten you.” Surely the remembrance of God is sweet amid adversities endured for his sake. What are all these things that have come upon you, O martyrs of God—things that could not separate you from the love or remembrance of God? For you say: “All these things have come upon us, and we have not forgotten you; neither have we acted wickedly in your covenant, nor has our heart turned back.” Do you wish to hear, kindly listeners, how great are the things we endure for our God? Listen to what we say to him for whom we suffer, for we say to him:

**VERSE 10.** But now you have rejected and put us to shame. You, Lord our God, who performed great wonders with our fathers, as we have heard with our ears and our fathers have told us; you who reserve many good things in the future for us, their sons, the sons of Korah—in whose coming we shall glory in God throughout the whole day and confess in your name for ever—show us great consolation as regards the past and the future. But now, in the present time, withdrawing the customary helps of old and delaying future consolations, you have rejected us and put us to shame—not indeed in conscience, for this is our glory, the testimony of our conscience: that we suffer evils not for our wickedness but for goodness. Yet you have put us to shame before the face of the wicked, by whom we are considered a reproach here, when it is said of us: “Where is their God?” For they do not think that we have you as a mighty, living, gracious God—or they think you are nowhere—because you do not go forth, O God, in our might; or, as the Hebrew reads, “with our armies,” as you formerly used to do, when, as you went forth with our armies, one of ours pursued a thousand foreigners and two put ten thousand to flight. Then our fathers were stronger than their enemies. But now—

**VERSE 11.** You have turned us backward behind our enemies, so that they are deemed victors and we vanquished: they, supported by dignities, are reckoned first; we, deprived of resources and dignities, last; they are accounted the head, we the tail.

In the Hebrew it reads: “You turned our backs to the enemy”; that is, we who formerly put the enemy to flight are now put to flight by the enemy. And those who hate us because of you plundered for themselves either our possessions or even our bodies for their own slavery; or, what is worse still, they plundered our souls, drawing them into the camp of iniquity, when the love of many from among our number grew cold—those who went out from us because they were not of us. Those who hate us plundered us and our possessions by their own perversity, but not by their own power. For you hold all things in your hand, as is said elsewhere: “In your hand, O Lord, are all the ends of the earth” [Col. 1547B] (Ps. 94:4).

**VERSE 12.** You gave us into the hands of the Gentiles as sheep for food, to whom no mercy is shown in slaughter, as is shown to sheep kept for breeding. Or, like sheep for food, which pass into the bodies of those who eat them. For many among us were, as it were, eaten by the Gentiles: they suffered in such a way that they were transformed into the body of the Gentiles; and the Church mourns them as its own devoured members.

Alternatively, we, the sons of Korah, recount different kinds of martyrs. Of those who endured mockings and scourges, and moreover chains and imprisonment, the voice in this psalm is their voice; and we, the sons of Korah, chanting in their voice, say: “But now you have rejected us and put us to shame, and you do not go forth, O God, in our strength; you have turned us backward behind our enemies, and those who hate us plundered for themselves.” But for those who were stoned, sawn asunder, and died by the slaughter of the sword, we rightly lament, saying: “You gave us as sheep for food.” Or, as the Hebrew reads: “Like a flock for drinking,” because no mercy was shown in the slaughter of such people; or because they died by the slaughter of the sword; or because, like sheep, they were food for lions, bears, and other beasts, being exposed alive to be devoured.

But for those who, overcome by torments, passed over to the rites of the Gentiles, we are not content to say that we were made like sheep for food; rather, we add: “And you scattered us among the Gentiles,” because many of our number [Col. 1547D] were handed over to the Gentiles in slavery. Some of these were scattered from the unity of the Church in such a way that they lived for a time, or even persisted altogether, in the vanities of the Gentiles, deceived by various errors.

**VERSE 13.** You sold your people without a price, handing them over as though freely into the hands of the ungodly. For we see that those whom you gave are great in merit and many in number, while those whom you received for them are sometimes found few in number—“for many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16); and when they are many in number, they are small in merit. For when saints are given to foreigners, whether for testing or correction, either no one is gained from it or only a few who can be compared with those same saints in holiness. Thus we rightly complain that there was no multitude [Col. 1548A] in exchange for them—that is, in compensation for so great a thing.

In the Hebrew it reads: “Their exchange was not great.” Another translation has: “There was no multitude in their rejoicings.” For while idolatrous persecutors were active, a multitude of the faithful did not gather, as was customary, to rejoice before God in churches; rather, they hid in mountains, caves, hollows of the earth, crypts, and other secret places, gathering to lament rather than rejoice. For then “a voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and much wailing” (Matt. 2:18), when devout men buried some of the martyrs and made lamentation over them.

Yet many mourned more for those whom they did not dare to bury, because pagans forbade it, so that the bodies of the saints might be devoured by beasts and birds on land, or by fish in the sea, and in other foul and deep gulfs to which the bodies of the saints were committed to perish. Therefore, as often as the Gentiles so entered God’s inheritance as to defile “the holy temple of God, which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17), says the Apostle, or so as to lay the corpses of God’s servants—whom they could not defile—as “food for the birds of heaven” (Ps. 78:3) and beasts of the earth, so often there was great lamentation and much wailing in the Church, but no rejoicing or only slight rejoicing. Thus it is aptly said: “You sold your people without a price, and there was no multitude in their rejoicings.”

Yet among them there was some rejoicing, since certain of them rejoiced because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for [Col. 1548C] your name. Their voice is: “We glory in tribulation, knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience testing, testing hope; and hope does not put to shame, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:3–5). These, rejoicing in hope and patient in tribulation, when they praised God amid adversities, rejoiced after a fashion; and, as if they felt a breeze of dew blowing in the midst of the furnace of the three boys, they sang a hymn, rejoicing in God their Savior.

But there was no multitude in their rejoicings, because this perfection belongs to few: that they rejoice and are glad when people curse and persecute them. Therefore, although there was perfection in the rejoicing of the saints, there was not a multitude in their rejoicings. For very few, having suffered dishonor, went away rejoicing from the presence of the council; many, however, went forth weeping as they scattered their seed, but shall come again with exultation, carrying their sheaves. Then the rejoicing will belong not to a few but to many, because their sorrow shall be turned into joy—those who now endure reproach for truth. Hence follows:

**VERSE 14.** You made us a reproach to our neighbors, an object of derision and mockery to those who are around us. Affliction and mockery from neighbors are severe because they do not soon pass away. This we, the sons of Korah, lament, exposed with bald Elisha to derision; and would that we were exposed only for an hour to long-lived enemies, rather than set for a long time to be ridiculed by neighboring persecutors. But you, O Lord, at whose judgments we do not dare to murmur, have set us, and fixed us as though immovably, as a sign contradicted and ridiculed by neighbors.

For “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. 10:36), and are sometimes all the more unbearable because they are nearer in place: in one house two are divided against three, and three against two. At other times they are nearer through their manner of life: monks against monks, clerics against clerics, Christians against Christians, religious against religious, false against true, restless against peaceful, imperfect against perfect. They quarrel with so much greater danger because this battle is waged at close quarters. In such contention, those who inflict reproaches, scorn, and mockery belong to the devil’s party; those who endure them belong to God’s party, for whose sake they endure them. To him they say: “You made us a reproach to our neighbors, an object of derision and mockery to those around us.” Derision is made with the nose, mockery with the mouth. Mockery is a confused sound of joy, displaying merriment through excessive taunting; contempt, however, is abject vileness.

**VERSE 15.** You made us among the Gentiles a likeness of Korah, of the crucified Christ, and of the martyrs. For in cursing us, they make us resemble what they detest, saying: “May you die as your Christ did, and as Lawrence or any other.” You also made us a shaking of the head among the peoples. For just as those passing by and insulting you in your Passion shook their heads, so too do they in the passion of the martyrs.

**VERSE 16.** All day my shame is against me. Shame is usually quick to fade. Therefore I, a son of Korah, endured severe shame, which lasts all day and is before me, opposed, that is, to my conscience: either because I did not commit a shameful deed, or because I believe that I have produced fruits worthy of repentance.

Alternatively: “My shame is against me,” that is, ever confronting my face, while I am compelled continually to consider how many, how shameful and dishonoring, troubles the impiety of the wicked inflicts upon the godly. As I consider these, confusion of face has covered me. For a modest person covers his face with a kind of cloak of confusion when his face glows inflamed beneath a cloud of blood. Nature causes this in a modest person: blood, gathered beneath the glass-like skin of the face, makes a person blush. Hence one is said to redden with shame, because the inward redness of blood appears outwardly, even when the conscience inwardly has nothing evil. Hence the bridegroom says to the bride: “Your cheeks are like a fragment of pomegranate, apart from what lies hidden within” (Song 4:3).

It is no great praise when the fault hidden within causes the cheeks to redden like a pomegranate. But when, apart from what lies hidden within—that is, when nothing shameful lies concealed within—and yet amid reproaches the face reddens in the cheeks like a fragment of pomegranate, this is truly praiseworthy and indicates to the bridegroom in his bride a lovable beauty, making her unlike the one to whom it is said: “You have acquired the forehead of a harlot; you do not know how to blush” [Col. 1550A] (Jer. 3:3).

It should be noted, however, that there are two kinds of shame. For, as the Wise Man says: “There is shame that brings sin, and there is shame that brings glory” (Ecclus. 4:25). Shame brings sin when we blush over things that ought not to make us blush—for example, humble service in the needs of the brethren, such as the washing of feet—or when we are ashamed to confess and amend before people a sin whose shameful guilt we are not ashamed to bear in God’s sight.

But shame brings glory when we so blush before God for sin that we are not at all ashamed of whatever purging of sin may be required. Such was Mary, who was not ashamed of the diners when, in order to be washed by the Lord, she washed his feet with tears; in order to dry them, she dried them; in order to anoint them, she anointed them. In the house of the reproachful and indignant Pharisee, she endured his taunts and murmurings, not without the blush of shame. But this shame brought her great glory. For many sins were forgiven her, and, full of shame and modesty, she loved so greatly that she was not ashamed, in the sight of the diners, of the humble service of washing and anointing feet. The man to whom less had been forgiven, and who therefore loved less, did not think to humble himself to this; indeed, in his heart he judged harshly both this woman serving in such a way and the Lord receiving such service.

But this humble service raised her to something high and glorious, for it is subsequently read that [Col. 1550C] she anointed his head with precious spikenard ointment. What service is higher than this? The Baptist, sanctified from the womb, trembled and did not dare touch the holy head of God unless the Lord himself commanded it. But this woman, acting without command—not rashly, but boldly through love and a good conscience cleansed by forgiveness—anointed the head revered by angels. What service is more glorious? Surely, to have ascended from Christ’s feet to his head is great glory: whether one advances through faith in his true humanity to knowledge of his divinity, or, through mercy by giving alms to his least ones on earth, approaches the height of his divinity above the heavens.

If amid such holy services there are heard slanders of those falsely deemed righteous, like Pharisees, or the murmurings of disciples complaining about the wasting of the ointment, the face of one who hears and sees such words or spittle hurled against them cannot fail to be ashamed. But this shame brings glory and stirs the heart of the innocent, or of penitents for sins, to prayer.

In order that the prayer poured forth may be heard more attentively, reproach is interposed among the petitions, and at times the remembrance of mockeries, when the sons of Korah say to God: “You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, a scorn and derision to those who are round about us.” Our mockers might have been neighbors, but so few that, although they pressed close by their mockery, yet, since this came from one side, there would have been elsewhere a place to turn aside, [Col. 1551A] and to avoid their mockeries. Again, they might have been around us, but so distant that there would have been room to breathe among them. But when they are at once neighbors and placed around us on every side, there is nowhere to turn except upward to you, God Most High, who, having granted us to possess in our heart, and utter with our mouth, an understanding fitting for the sons of Korah, have then made us a reproach to our neighbors. For had we been silent among them, we would have been considered philosophers. But now, because by your gift we believe, and therefore also speak, you have made us a reproach to our neighbors, a scorn and derision to those who are round about us. You have made us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples, as was explained above. For as long as I, a son of Korah, either did not possess sound understanding [Col. 1551B] or, possessing it, did not declare it, so long was I pleasing and acceptable to my neighbors placed round about. But when I spoke to them, they assailed me without cause, reproaching and reviling me. Therefore my shame is before me all day long, and confusion of my face has covered me; I do not say my face alone, which would somehow have been bearable, but it has covered me wholly, because I shuddered throughout.

**VERSE 17.** At the voice of one reproaching me with crimes, whether true and corrected, or fabricated through falsehood. I shuddered also at the voice of the slanderer, that is, one contradicting the truth. I say, at the voice, because sometimes the uproar of that dreadful voice against me was so great that I seemed to hear them crying: “Away, away, crucify, crucify [Col. 1551C] him!” (John 19:15). At other times they mingled their voice with such loud laughter, when they multiplied blows with fists behind my back, unseen by me, or slaps even upon my face, striking me with reproaches, that they seemed to me to cry: “Who is it that struck you?” (Matt. 26:68). For I was so struck with fists from behind that both an insult was inflicted and, at times, the perpetrator of the insult was unknown.

Alternatively: Confusion of my face covered me because of the voice of one reproaching me, that is, cursing me to my face, and of the slanderer, that is, one who deceitfully bites at my speech in my absence. It was bearable when friends spoke against me in indignation, because I, like another Job—a son of Korah with shaven head, sitting on a dungheap—dared to speak of the supreme majesty of God, or, though a man of no distinction, concerning the exalted [Col. 1551D] rulers of the Church. But when some notable reviler or debater, like the arrogant Elihu, wholly hostile, rose against me—because such a man wished only to be heard and not to hear, or, if he heard, was unwilling to assent to truth heard or understood—then, beyond measure, beyond what can be said, confusion of my face covered me, not only because of the voice of the reproacher and slanderer, but also because of the face of the enemy and persecutor: a grim face, with gnashing teeth, trembling lips, pallor or redness of the cheeks, and a remarkable and fearful darting of the eyes, even if this were the face of a friend disturbed by anger. But when it was the face of an enemy and persecutor—an enemy through inveterate hatred, a persecutor through the continual utterance of “Raca” or some other manifest act of hidden [Col. 1552A] hatred—who can tell how great was the confusion of my face under the threat of that face, so heavily laid upon me as to cover me? Yet not as those are covered with confusion of whom it is said: “Let them be covered with their confusion as with a double garment” (Ps. 108:29). For a twofold confusion covers them, signified by the double garment: they are confounded inwardly by an accusing conscience and outwardly by a ruined reputation. For although for a time those with an evil conscience may glory in a good reputation, yet the time is near when it may be said of any such person: “See, he already stinks; for he has been dead four days” (John 11:39). This is as if one said: See, he rightly stinks through infamy who, through a long habit of sinning, has a conscience that is dead—indeed, rotten.

[Col. 1552B] But I, a son of Korah, walking the royal road through ill repute and good repute, am neither lifted up by good repute nor cast down by bad. And rightly I refuse to be cast down by ill repute. For I am conscious to myself of no crime that I have not either avoided by God’s protection, or, through his healing, judged in such a way that I hope not to be judged again for it, since, coming before his face in confession, I have already judged myself. For I believe him who said: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31). Yet I do not consent to be exalted by good repute, because although I have been judged, I have not thereby been justified in my own judgment, since I do not even judge myself. Therefore it is a very small thing to me if I am judged by enemies [Col. 1552C] or by a human day; and so I am not covered with a double confusion, inwardly through an evil conscience and outwardly through a bad reputation. Rather, the confusion of my face alone covers me—not from an accusing conscience, but from the voice of the reproacher and slanderer, from the face of the enemy and persecutor.

**VERSE 18.** All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you. All the troubles and adversities enumerated above have come upon us. We neither deserved nor drew them upon ourselves by any crimes or magical arts, as was charged against us. They came of themselves, with the devil alone stirring them up, like a roaring beast or an unbearable torrent. They came upon us in order to crush us and to shake the memory of your goodness, O God, out of our hearts. But we sons of Korah understand [Col. 1552D] that you are not to be worshipped for the sake of attaining this world’s prosperity or avoiding its adversity. We worshipped you freely amid prosperity, and we did not forget you amid adversity. For it is thereby clear that we worshipped you freely when prosperity in passing things abounded: we did not abandon or forget you when it departed and adversity threatened. If the simple and upright man Job had worshipped you because he received good things from your hand, he would not have endured evil things patiently, nor would he have worshipped and praised you amid adversity. Likewise we sons of Korah worshipped you amid prosperity by a free and spontaneous love; therefore we have not forgotten you even amid adversity, because we understand that you are to be worshipped not for earthly things, but for your own sake.

It is also evident that we have not forgotten [Col. 1553A] you amid adversity because we have not acted unjustly in your covenant, that is, in your law, whose precepts we have kept and whose promises we have hoped for; and these we also preached to others as things to be kept and hoped for, though enemies slandered and contradicted us, and persecuted us for this very reason. Or, “we have not acted unjustly in your covenant,” that is, in that compact which we made with you in baptism, where we became children of the New Testament.

**VERSE 19.** And our heart has not turned back, and you have turned our paths aside from your way. Our heart—that is, the reason and intention of the inner person—has not turned back, although the outer person has limped. It has not turned back, I say, so as to go back into apostasy, from the path of righteousness which we entered in baptism or in the resolve of a stricter [Col. 1553B] life. No, I say, our heart has not turned back since, having put our hand to the plough and forgotten what lies behind, we began to stretch forth toward what lies before. For we sons of Korah understood that if one who looks back after beginning to enter the path of uprightness is not fit for the kingdom of God, much less is one fit for God’s kingdom who not only looks back through a perverse will, but also turns back in the steps of perverse action. Therefore our heart has not turned back either to crimes or to idols once perfectly renounced, even though our heart at times turned back in the sense written of the living creatures: “They went and returned” (Ezek. 1:14), when they returned from contemplation’s height to the lowly ministries of action. Thus Peter, having received the apostleship, returned to fishing; and daily the saints return from [Col. 1553C] the lofty contemplation of the heavenly homeland to the care of their own or another’s body. This is not turning back, but stretching forward in such a way as to draw weak companions behind you. This movement is ordered when rational minds, ascending to the heights under God’s drawing, do not leave behind the weak members attached to them. Therefore our heart has not turned back even when we returned from contemplation to action, sometimes setting aside the delightful embraces of most beautiful Rachel and admitting fruitful Leah.

And while these things were to be done, you turned our paths aside from your way: you caused our actions to depend upon your law as streams upon a spring, as branches upon a vine. Or your way, by which you come to human beings and human beings come to you, is Christ, who says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). From this your way you turned our paths aside when, by his example, you taught us to go by narrow and confined paths. For though there is one narrow and confined way leading to life, yet because one person walks in it in one manner and another in another, it has diverse narrow and confined paths, on which you have truly placed us.

**VERSE 20.** Because you have humbled us in a place of affliction. The place of affliction is the frail body, by whose burden we are afflicted; or it is the world lying in wickedness, in which, while we are afflicted by evil people, we are formed toward goodness as by the rod of discipline. And the shadow of death rising up on every side has covered [Col. 1554A] us: that is, those who, dying through ignorance, draw us into the darkness of their own death. Or present mortality is the shadow of harsh death, which is condemnation with the devil.

On this passage blessed Gregory says in his *Morals on Job*: “You have humbled us in a place of affliction, and the shadow of death has covered us.” [Note: [Col. 1553D] St. Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book XXXVI, ch. 28.] “The place of affliction is the present life. Therefore those who are making their way to the eternal homeland now despise themselves for a time in the place of affliction, so that then they may be truly exalted in the place of joy. For the days of affliction now possess the souls of the elect, because days of gladness follow afterwards. For it is written: ‘It shall be well with one who fears God in the end.’ And again it is said of the Church: ‘She shall laugh on the last day.’ For now is the time of affliction [Col. 1554B] for the good, so that rejoicing may follow them, at some time without time.” He continues: “And the shadow of death has covered us.” What is understood in this place by the shadow of death except the death of the flesh? [Note: [Col. 1553D] The same, ibid., book III, ch. 16.] “For as true death is that by which the soul is separated from God, so the shadow of death is that by which the flesh is separated from the soul. Thus the Prophet now speaks in the voice of martyrs: ‘You have humbled us in a place of affliction, and the shadow of death has covered us.’ For those known to die not in spirit but in flesh alone say that they are covered not by true death but by the shadow of death.”

The same author [Note: [Col. 1554D] Ibid., book XXXIII, ch. 3.] says: “What is expressed by shadow, when death is added to it, except the death of the flesh, or any reprobate persons who imitate, through zeal for perverse action, the darkness of the ancient enemy? [Col. 1554C] Hence the Prophet says in the voice of martyrs: ‘You have humbled us in a place of affliction, and the shadow of death has covered us.’ Those who are known to die not in spirit but in flesh alone are oppressed by the shadow of death when the death of the flesh—which is an image of eternal death—separates God’s elect from this life; for as eternal death separates the soul from God, so bodily death separates the body from the soul. Or certainly they are oppressed by the shadow of death because it is written of the ancient enemy: ‘His name is Death’ (Rev. 6:8). Therefore all reprobate people are the shadow of death: they imitate his wickedness of pride and express his image as a shadow, while they draw into themselves a likeness of his malice. They cover God’s elect when they prevail for a time against them in the savagery of persecution. [Col. 1554D]

**VERSE 21.** If we have forgotten the name of our God, and if we have stretched out our hands to a foreign god, will not God search these things out? Above we said—signifying our understanding, we sons of Korah, by which we understand that God must be served freely and that one must not depart from his worship when prosperity ceases and adversity threatens—we said, I say: “All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, nor have we acted unjustly in your covenant.” Again we repeat the same understanding, saying: “If we have forgotten the name of our God, and if we have stretched out our hands to a foreign god,”

**VERSE 22.** “Will not God search these things out?” If, whether through insolence amid abundant prosperity or through impatience amid approaching adversity, [Col. 1555A] we have forgotten the name of our God, in whom we hope for salvation, knowing that no other name under heaven has been given to human beings in which there is any salvation besides the name of our God; if we have forgotten this name, and if we have stretched out our hands to a foreign god—that is, if we have done our works, signified by the hands, in honor of another god, for example Jupiter, Mercury, or another false god—will not God search these things out?

Alternatively: When we sons of Korah, mindful of our Korah crucified at the place of Calvary, pray at times, or sing Mass, as he taught us, in commemoration of himself, or when, apart from Mass, we pray attentively and represent by the gesture of our whole body the cross with which we are signed upon the forehead, we continually stretch out our hands. If, then, we have done this to a foreign god, as many heretics do, will not God search these things out? For heretics have fashioned for themselves a god, not such as he is, but such as they themselves wanted him to be. Some say that the Son is less than the Father; others assert that Christ our God did not exist before Mary; others say that he had a phantom body; others, speaking many untrue things about the true God in other ways, have forged many idols of falsehood, which they worshipped as the true God so long as, ensnared in such falsehoods, they stretched out their hands in prayer. Likewise, those who preach the Gospel or sing Mass in order to eat or to derive other earthly gain from it also stretch out their hands to a foreign god, because what they desire to possess more than God, or love once possessed, is regarded by them as god—or rather, as an idol. [Col. 1555C] Even when praying or singing Mass, they worship not the true God but that transient gain which they covet in a service divinely instituted, yet humanly desired; changing the glory of God not now into the likeness of a calf eating grass—which would be a Jewish sin—but into as many likenesses of idols as they have desires for earthly profits in the service of God, like the Gentiles who go wherever they are led toward mute images. For the conception of earthly gain—for example, of costly clothing, delicate food, gold, or silver—when it occupies the principal desire of one praying or singing Mass, sets up in the sanctuary of the heart, as it were, a certain image fashioned after external things, provided, as I have said, that the principal and final intention of the person praying is to obtain outwardly that gain whose image he holds in his heart, namely, his very conception of such a thing.

Far, far be this understanding from us sons of Korah, even though images of this sort creep in upon us in the outer vestibule of thought! Let it be far from us to place them in the innermost sanctuary of intention. Rather, we must smash them with the hammer of repentance—especially Beelzebub, the god of flies, whom the flies of unclean, wandering, and proud thoughts serve. While praying, these are most powerfully driven away by this understanding of the sons of Korah: they understand that God is to be worshipped only for his own sake. For this [Col. 1556A] understanding works in them so that whatever comes to their minds while praying, other than God himself and what assists in worshipping him, is immediately driven away like a fly or bees, and God alone is retained in memory while that which is spoken by the mouth is being turned over in the heart. For “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession,” or prayer, “is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). And what is our righteousness or salvation but our God? Therefore, when we pray with the intention of living justly in this life and obtaining full salvation in eternal life, our understanding is right—the understanding which this psalm commends to us sons of Korah. Conscious of this understanding, we therefore say in good confidence: if, since we first received the understanding of the sons of Korah, we have stretched out [Col. 1556B] our hands to a foreign god, will not God search these things out?

For he, declaring that he has great zeal against such images, says: “You shall not have foreign gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness that is in heaven above, or in the earth beneath, nor of those things that are in the waters under the earth; you shall not adore them or worship them. I am the Lord your God, a strong and jealous God, visiting the iniquity of fathers upon children unto the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments” (Deut. 5:7 ff.). Therefore, he who called himself the strong and jealous God when speaking against images—will he not search these things out with great zeal if we stretch out our hands to a foreign god after the manner of Gentiles worshipping mute images, or after the manner of false Christians, heretics, or Jews, whose images have already been discussed? Will he not, I say, search these things out, however secretly they may be done?

For he knows the hidden things of the heart. He has no need that anyone should bear witness to him concerning a human being, because he himself knows what is in a human being. He knows what devotion and good intention remain inwardly when lips move, hands are stretched out, knees are bent, or the whole body is outwardly prostrated. He also knows the hidden things of the heart, perfectly discerning for what cause each [Col. 1556D] of the sons of Korah struggles in suffering, approving or disapproving the character of the punishment according to the character of the cause. For it is not punishment but cause that makes a martyr; nor is suffering purgative or corrective when sin is pleasing amid punishments. Only by true innocence or fruitful repentance preserved amid torments does one attain the crown of martyrdom, when suffering is inflicted for righteousness’ sake. I say righteousness either of innocence or of repentance, both of which appear in our Korah. In his own person he maintained the righteousness of innocence, because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22); and, grieving for us and bearing our sins, he fasted forty days and forty nights, and afterwards humbled himself for us under many penitential [Col. 1557A] afflictions, even to death on the cross. For “the Lord placed upon him the iniquities of us all, and the chastisement of our peace was upon him” (Isa. 53:5). Therefore the Jews persecuted him, because he both maintained innocence and taught repentance by word and example. On account of this teaching they said that he stirred up the people: “We found this man,” they say, “subverting our nation” (Luke 23:2). Again: “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judaea, beginning from Galilee even to this place” (ibid.). Therefore whoever intends to preserve the innocence and repentance which Christ displayed in word and example, and suffers adversity for that reason, is planted together with the likeness of Christ’s passion, and therefore shall also be planted together with the likeness of his resurrection, [Col. 1557B] because, as the Apostle says, “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him; if we die with him, we shall also live with him” (2 Tim. 2:11).

It is one thing to suffer; another to suffer with Christ. Not everyone who suffers adversity suffers with Christ, nor does everyone who dies die with Christ. Many suffer adversity, but only those who suffer persecution for righteousness are blessed. We shall all indeed sleep and die, but blessed are the dead who die in the Lord; for God will bring with him only those who have slept through Jesus. The innocent suffer, as Christ was innocent. The penitent suffer, as did the confessing and penitent thief. The impenitent also suffer, as did the blaspheming thief. Therefore, since [Col. 1557C] there is such great diversity among those enduring adversity, and since the benefit or lack of benefit of suffering is weighed according to its causes alone, we sons of Korah have chosen for ourselves the best part among every cause: for your sake we are put to death all day long, O our God. You who know the hidden things of the heart know that we love you. For although you do not question each of us in words as you questioned Peter, saying, “Do you love me?” yet you question us by deeds whether we love you, and each of us says to you, “I love you” (John 21:17). Therefore, as Peter heard, as proof of his love for you, that he would be girded and led by another where he did not wish to go—by which saying you indicated what death would glorify you in him—so we too have, as proof of assured love, the cause for which we suffer: because [Col. 1557D] for your sake we are put to death all day long. For your sake we are put to death by making you known and glorified in the world, either by the voluntary mortification of the flesh or by another’s girding and leading us where we do not wish. For your sake we are put to death all day long, that is, by a long and enduring suffering. Even when we are girded by the command of obedience, we are led by another where we do not wish, because, by breaking our own will, we sacrifice hidden holocausts of the heart. We rightly glory in your cross because, for your sake, we are put to death all day long in obedience, lest the darkness of disobedience overtake us.

Great and rare among our number is one found fit to hear for the third time: “If you love me, feed my lambs,” or “my sheep” (John 21:15). Yet, though not all are shepherds of sheep, [Col. 1558A] without doubt we all, sons of Korah, are sheep of your pasture; and your enemies have reckoned us as sheep for slaughter. Hence the fields have already been drenched with our slaughter, and the sheepfolds sprinkled with our blood, while we sheep are slain together with the shepherds, with no one resisting or bringing help. Therefore, lest we perish amid these dangers, lest a wave stirred against us by the north wind swallow our ship while you sleep—

**VERSE 23.** Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord? Arise, and do not cast us off forever. Arise to strengthen those who stand, lest they fall. Arise to raise those who have fallen. Or arise in order to command the winds, that is, the great spirits. Again, arise in order to command the sea, that is, the bitter hearts of human beings. [Col. 1558B] While you sleep, a great storm has grown terrible through the temptations of unclean and evil spirits, whose blast is a wind contrary to us. The sea, agitated by such a wind, has likewise swelled against us, because the whole world lying in wickedness casts up wonderful swellings and foam in order to crush us—now in our face, now above our head—when we are harassed not only by equals but even by the great rulers of the world.

Amid the dangers of this world, why do you sleep, O Lord? In yourself you neither slumber nor sleep, you who keep Israel; but you sleep for us when you do not aid us in tribulation. You sleep when you do not quickly hear us crying to you. For just as one asleep does not quickly answer when called, nor notice [Col. 1558C] what is said to him until he first awakens, so you, though awake in yourself, sometimes sleep for us, sins demanding it, because you do not show yourself to see our tribulations or hear our prayers. Indeed, justly so: for we receive what our deeds deserve, and in all that we suffer we acknowledge your righteous judgment. Yet because the cause for which we are scourged is sometimes hidden, show us why you judge us so. If it is that strength may be made perfect in weakness, show this, so that we may gladly glory in our weaknesses and your grace may suffice for us. If it is to cleanse sins, make this known also, lest our judgment differ from yours, but, quickly agreeing with it, justify and gladden us. If it is to exercise patience, quickly bring it [Col. 1558D] to perfection in us, so that, as you did for blessed Job, you may restore to us all that Satan’s machinations have taken away. If it is for the manifestation of your glory—that is, if you have sent upon us, through evil angels, the burden of affliction not because we or our parents deserved it—show this also to us, so that as we know without doubt that you have slept for us, so we may also know without doubt the cause of this sleeping of yours. For not only have you been lulled into a deep sleep for us like one “sleeping off drunkenness from wine” (Ps. 77:65), but even when we try to awaken you with prayers and you begin to awake a little by granting us some small measure of saving compunction, you quickly withdraw it and turn away your face, like a powerful person wishing to sleep longer and, by turning away his face, repelling the prayers of those knocking and awakening him. [Col. 1559A] O our God, why do you sleep thus, and—

**VERSE 24.** Why do you turn away your face thus? Did you not once rise of your own accord for our afflicted fathers, like one mighty and roused from wine, and strike their enemies on the back, giving them everlasting reproach? Why then do you now sleep in this way and turn your face from us thus, turning it toward the wall of our sins as though you had no wish to be awakened at all? Turn your face away, we pray, from our sins, and do not turn it away from us. This we cry continually; and yet you turn your face away from us and not from our sins. Why do you do this, O Lord, who do nothing unjustly? Why do you sleep when you forget our poverty and our tribulation? [Col. 1559B] We endure great poverty: we have either unwillingly lost worldly wealth, or willingly left it for your sake, or have refused and still refuse to acquire it. Yet in such poverty we do not find you merciful to us—you who raise the needy from the earth and lift the poor from the dungheap—but you forget our poverty, we who are deprived of your help and human help, and our tribulation, by which our enemies and yours afflict us. Therefore at last arise: perfect the strength for whose perfection in weakness you strike us with blows. Arise by forgiving the sin for whose cleansing you scourge us. Arise by bringing patience to perfection in tribulation, as the Apostle says: “Tribulation works patience; patience, testing; testing indeed hope; [Col. 1559C] and hope does not put to shame” (Rom. 5:3). Arise by manifesting your glory, if our weakness is not unto death but for the manifestation of your glory, as Lazarus’s weakness was. Whatever may be the cause for which, sleeping for us and turning away your face, you forget our poverty and tribulation, at last arise now and do not cast us off forever; but give us patience, of which it is said: “The patience of the poor shall not perish forever” (Ps. 9:19), so that, even if by your just judgment we must be troubled unto death in conformity with you, who said, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38), we may nevertheless not be troubled or sorrowful after death.

[Col. 1559D] Alternatively: For us sons of Korah the resurrection has already been accomplished, because we believe and perceive that you, Christ, died for the putting to death of our offenses and rose again for the raising up of our justification; and accordingly you died for us and also rose for us. But for those who trouble us you have not yet risen, because they do not deny that you died and were buried, but they refuse altogether to acknowledge that you rose as a human being and reign above all things as God together with the Father. For they perceive that we your servants are heard by you no more than if you slept or lay dead. Therefore arise—that is, show yourself to be the good shepherd, who, although slain for your sheep, rose when death was conquered and keeps continual watch over us your sheep. Show your enemies that, although they intend to slaughter [Col. 1560A] us as sheep for the slaughter so that no fruit may come from us, you, good Shepherd, who deigned to die for your flock, so care for us that, although shorn of possessions, we ascend from the washing of baptism or tears, yet none among us is barren. Indeed, we are all sheep of your pasture bearing twin offspring, since in this life we receive a hundredfold benefit of transitory things with persecutions, and in the future expect eternal life. By making this manifest to your enemies, arise, lest they think you sleep so completely that you have no care for us your sheep. Let them perceive in our twin offspring that we are not, as they think, sheep merely for slaughter and not for resurrection; for under you, our Shepherd risen from the dead and no longer to die, we have both our present fruit in sanctification and eternal life as our end. This is not believed among them because—

**VERSE 25.** Now, while you turn away your face, our soul has been humbled into the dust; our belly has been glued to the earth. Our soul, being a rational spirit and owing attention only to heavenly things, while the knowledge of truth illumines it and love of virtue inflames it, has now, deprived of the sight of you, O Sun of righteousness, because your face is turned away, been humbled into the dust—that is, into earthly thoughts, which are compared to dust. And our belly has been glued to the earth, because sensuality, compared to the belly on account of its softness, has wholly adhered to the earth.

Alternatively: Our soul—that is, our life, signified by “soul,” as in, “He who loves his soul shall lose it” (John 12:25)—our soul, I say, has been humbled into the dust because our life has grown old among all its ungodly enemies, who are like dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth. Our belly has been glued or adhered to the earth. As the belly of the body receives foods entering through the mouth, so memory, like the belly of the soul, retains within itself things seen, heard, tasted, smelled, and touched. But when, utterly forgetful of heavenly things, it turns only [Col. 1560D] earthly things over within itself, then our belly adheres to the earth, glued as with most tenacious glue in the pitch of this world. Whoever touches it will be defiled; how much more one who, glued to it, is held in it for a long time?

Alternatively: Our soul has been humbled in the dust—that is, those persons who ought to be spiritual rulers and animators of bodily members have been humbled in the dust, namely, in the society of those who are dust. These rulers do not shake off “the dust of their feet” (Luke 9:5), according to the Gospel command, as a testimony against those who do not receive them and the word of God preached through them; but they dwell in the midst of a defiled people in such a way that they are found to have not only feet defiled with dust, but lips polluted by silence, because they refuse to rebuke what they understand should be rebuked. But our belly has adhered to the earth because those who were wholly carnal in our fellowship, utterly incapable of spiritual understanding, have adhered or [Col. 1561A] been glued to the earth: they are not merely sprinkled with the dust of earthliness, like the spiritual persons signified by the soul, but cling with their entire affection and consent to the earthliness of wicked people, either imitating them or assenting to them.

Alternatively: Our soul has been humbled in the dust by remembrance of sins, either by dust visibly scattered upon the head as a sign of repentance, or invisibly imposed upon the mind, which is the soul’s head, through remembrance of the sentence pronounced upon the first sinful human being: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19). Whenever we retain this inherited sentence in our mind, we have dust, as it were, upon our head; and therefore we truly say: “Our soul has been humbled in the dust,” healed through dust from the wound of that pride by which [Col. 1561B] it rashly lifted itself upward toward likeness to God when the devil said: “You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:5). Therefore, in order that the inward humility of the soul may be fittingly expressed by an outward bodily gesture, our belly has adhered to the earth, than which no gesture of humiliation is greater. For one who bows the head or bends the knees to the ground still has a means of humbling the body further. But when the belly adheres to the earth, the person cannot humble himself further; and he lies or sits beneficially on the dungheap if humility displayed in the body reigns within the soul. The Lord does not sleep for one lying thus, nor does he turn his face away from him. Therefore the humble and humbled penitent sons of Korah do not now say, as above, “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord? Why do you turn away your face?” Rather, without mention of sleeping or turning away, [Col. 1561C] they say in their prayers:

### Verse 26

“Arise, O Lord, help us, and redeem us for your name’s sake.” Arise—that is, display in us the grace and glory of your resurrection, so that we may not only be called and be sons of Korah through imitation of your Passion, but may also be and be called sons of your resurrection, being conformed, that is, to the likeness of your resurrection by eating the honeycomb, just as we had been conformed to the likeness of your Passion by eating a portion of the broiled fish. Then, by drinking the vinegar of bitterness or wine mixed with gall, we tempered our drink with tears; and we ate ashes as though bread [Col. 1561D], because, filled with bitter reproaches, we had little or no sweetness amid all these things, when we were filled and made drunk with bitterness.

But now, as though Good Friday were past and the Paschal solemnity were already at hand for us, with the sun now risen, let Mary, weeping at the tomb, hear: “Do not weep” (John 20:15). Indeed, let the Church gathered from the Gentiles hear how Mary was comforted, how the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord, so that she too, having received consolation, may rejoice with the disciples, drinking now in the kingdom the wine that gladdens the heart of man: that is, with Christ reigning in her, so that all her sorrow may be turned into joy and no one may take her joy from her.

While the children of this Church are still pilgrims in the present life, when the remains of the broiled fish [Col. 1562A]—which she herself fully ate with Christ in the time of persecution—are set before them, let them not distrust divine help, but confidently say: “Arise, O Lord, help us”; which you also did by rising and commanding the winds and the sea, so that great calm came to us when peace was granted to the Churches and those who had clung to the earth were raised up, according to the saying: “Rise up, rise up, Jerusalem; shake yourself from the dust; loose the bonds from your neck” (Isa. 52:2). Therefore let the children of this Jerusalem, gladdened by the sight of peace, say: “Arise, O Lord, help us” to seek good things eagerly and hold them firmly, “and redeem us” from evils, so that through your help we may most blessedly enjoy good things, and through the power of your redemption may be free from evils. “Help and redeem us,” we say, “for your name’s sake.” For we do not lay our prayers before your face on account of our own righteous deeds, but on account of your many mercies, through which you are named and held glorious.

The Hebrew truth suggests this sense, where it reads thus: “For our soul is bowed down in the dust; our belly has clung to the earth.
