Rise, help us, and redeem us for your mercy’s sake.” Therefore, whether we set forth your mercy or your name, O Lord, when we call upon you as helper and deliverer, it is plain that we hope not in our merits but in your mercy, or in your name—you who are Savior and merciful one—to whom we say sometimes with the mouth and often with the heart: “Arise, O Lord, help us, and redeem us for your name’s sake,” or, “for your mercy’s sake.”

[Col. 1562C] Glory to God the Father, of whom we have heard with our ears and of whom our fathers announced to us, as was recalled at the beginning of the psalm. Glory to God the Son, our helper and redeemer, to whom we say at the end of the psalm: “Arise, O Lord, help us and redeem us for your name’s sake,” or “for your mercy’s sake.” Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that mercy which is mentioned at the end of the psalm according to the Hebrew truth, and which in other translations is indicated by the name of God. Glory to the highest Trinity, which is wholly indicated where it is said of the fathers that their own arm did not save them, but “your right hand, and your arm, and the light of your countenance, because you were pleased with them.”

For he to whom “your right hand” [Col. 1562D], “your arm,” and “the light of your countenance” are addressed is God the Father; but his very right hand, arm, and countenance are his Son. The illumination of his countenance is understood to be the Holy Spirit, of whom the Son himself says: “He will glorify me” (John 16:14). May this glory be now and always, and unto ages of ages. As it was in the beginning—when our salvation and redemption were predestined—so may it now be displayed in the experience of manifest help, through which this may plainly appear: “your right hand, and your arm, and the light of your countenance.” Your right hand, most plainly distinguishing and embracing us, separating us from the goats at the left, as the bride says in the Song of Songs: “And your right hand will embrace me” (Song 2:6); your arm, scattering the enemies proud in the thought of their heart [Col. 1563A], putting down the mighty from their seat and exalting the humble, filling the hungry with good things and sending the rich away empty; the illumination of your countenance, by which, being marked, we may say: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us; you have given joy in my heart” (Ps. 4:7). Amen.

## Part Five

[Col. 1563]

## Psalm XLIV

[Col. 1563B] “My heart has poured forth a good word.” This psalm concerns holy nuptials: bridegroom and bride, king and people, Savior and those to be saved. This song is called an *epithalamium*, that is, a praise of the bridal chamber, because it is offered by those invited to the nuptials to the heavenly bridegroom and the bride, the Church. Solomon is said to have taken from this song the subject for writing the Song of Songs.

Three nuptials of the Lord are read of. First, he made nuptials with humankind when, coming from heaven, he joined human nature to divinity. In these nuptials the womb of the Virgin was the bridal chamber from which he came forth as a bridegroom. Second, he celebrated nuptials with the angels when, as a new man ascending into heaven, he joined the angelic multitude to himself. Third, he will celebrate nuptials with angels and human beings when he joins to his glory the Church, led out of the Babylon [Col. 1563C] of the world into heavenly Jerusalem, and reveals himself to them as he is, equal to the Father.

Of the first nuptials it is written: “A certain king made a marriage feast for his son” (Matt. 22:2). Of the second it is said: “Be like men waiting for their master when he returns from the marriage feast” (Luke 12:36). Of the third it is said or written: “Those who were ready entered with him into the marriage feast” (Matt. 25:10). Again, of these it is said: “Blessed are those called to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Rev. 19:9).

At these nuptials the lyres of angels sweetly rejoice; the timbrels of prophets cry aloud in holy exultation; the organs of apostles resound in sweetest harmony; the harps of martyrs [Col. 1563D] harmonize not with strings but with virtues; the cymbals of virgins ring out; and the people of the saints, the choir of all the elect, gently delights the hearing with spiritual pipes and most pleasing melody in sweet-sounding voices. At these nuptials there is such music that every human joy is surpassed by it.

Therefore, while one man sought springs of water like a thirsty stag and, passing through the wondrous tabernacle, sought God in every direction, he heard the sound of this harmony, ran outside, and announced it to others caught amid noise and tumult. And when some acted more sluggishly and only wished to reach that place by prayer, the martyrs, unable to bear delay, raised the banner and burst in companies into the place of contest; having won the victory, clothed in white robes—that is, the wedding garment—crowned with palms and garlands, they forcibly entered these nuptials [Col. 1564B] and earned a triumphal song from those celebrating the feast. Therefore the title of the psalm is:

### Verse 1

**FOR THE END, FOR THOSE WHO WILL BE CHANGED, FOR THE SONS OF KORAH, FOR UNDERSTANDING: A SONG FOR THE BELOVED.**

That is, this nuptial song is set forth for the sons of Korah—that is, imitators of Christ—for understanding, so that they may understand its mysteries concerning the ineffable begetting of the Son of God, the beauty of his humanity, the wondrous union of himself and the Church, and the adornment of the Church. It is a song “for those who will be changed,” from unbelief to faith and from ungodliness to righteousness—those of whom the preceding psalm says, “There was no multitude in their changes”—or for those who will be changed from mortality and the sadness of this world into everlasting joy [Col. 1564C] at the end: that is, from an imperfect change amid every misery into a perfect glory, the equality of angels. And it is for the beloved, the Father’s only Son and the beloved bridegroom of the Church. This psalm is called a song because it treats of the union of bridegroom and bride, where there is only supreme joy, just as at secular weddings there is no sorrow but only gladness.

The subject of the psalm is the bridegroom and bride, and those called to the nuptials: Christ and the Church, and all the elect called to the eternal feast. Its purpose is to admonish us to provide ourselves with a wedding garment, so that we may be able to take part in these nuptials. Its words appear to have been taken from David when he established Solomon in the kingdom [Col. 1564D], spoke to that king of his works concerning the building of the Temple, and the queen of Sheba, named Beroia, stood at his right hand, having come from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom.

The psalm has two parts. The first, “My heart has poured forth,” contains the bridegroom’s praises in four ways: from his appearance, power, the cause of judgment, and the person of the bride. The second, “Hear, daughter,” contains the bride’s praises in four ways: from beauty, power, members, and offspring.

This psalm is forty-fourth in order, a number which is six times seven and two. By six are signified the active, because of the labor of the six works of the Gospel; by seven, the contemplative, because of the rest of the sevenfold Spirit; and by two is signified the twofold love, which is the wedding garment. This number therefore indicates that the active, clothed in love of neighbor [Col. 1565A], and the contemplative, clothed in love of God, are admitted to the nuptials of the Lamb. It is the voice of the Father:

### Verse 2

“My heart has poured forth a good word.” Fullness of the stomach produces bodily belching; fullness of wisdom produces the outpouring of the heart. For God to pour forth from his heart is to beget from the fullness of divinity a Son equal to himself. Thus the bridegroom’s nobility is proclaimed, since he is said to be begotten by the highest God.

The Latin *verbum* (“word”) is formed from *ver* and *bombo*, when it signifies what we speak. But when it signifies the Son of God, it is formed from *vere* (“truly”) and *bono* (“good”), and is called *Verbum*, as though “truly good.” The Father’s heart poured forth that good Word when he begot from himself the Son, who is supreme and true good. Of this Word it is written: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), that is, the Son in the Father.

It is asked by what likeness the Son of God is called the Word. A word is made in three ways: by mouth, heart, and mind. The word of the mouth is a spoken sound, as “man”; the word of the heart is the likeness of the sound “man”; the Word of the mind is the understood substance, “man.” Whatever we wish to do, we first say by the word of the mind, while we arrange in thought what is to be done. And whatever thing we think, we imagine its likeness in the mind. Therefore, when Truth spoke itself just as it is, it begot a Word like itself. Hence the Son is called the Word, image, and likeness of God.

Again it is asked: since Father, Word, and Holy Spirit are one indivisible essence, how is the Word alone incarnate? In one soul there are understanding [Col. 1565C], counsel, and will. Understanding, as it were the Father, begets counsel, as it were offspring; from both proceeds will. Counsel is a word, because when we think out counsel, we say it in the mind; when we make it known to others, we say it with the mouth. Thus the word of counsel remains invisible in the understanding; but in order to appear visibly to others, it puts on the body of sound and proceeds to the ears, audible when spoken, and to the eyes, visible when written.

Therefore, just as neither understanding nor will, but counsel alone, or the word clothed in the body of sound, proceeds, so neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone—who is the Word of God—appeared clothed in humanity, and did not depart from the Father. Hence it is written: “The Word was made flesh” (John [Col. 1565D] 1:14), that is, he put on a human being. And because the Father made all things in this Word, as it is written: “All things were made through him” (ibid., 3), the Father adds: “I speak my works to the king.” The Son is properly called king because through him the Father governs all that he created. Thus he himself says: “But I have been appointed king by him” (Ps. 2:6). The Father spoke his works to this king when, in the wisdom of the Son, he eternally ordered all things to be made. Hence it is written: “What was made in him was life” (John 1:3). For just as a building first exists in the designer’s mind, so every creature, before it is created, was ordered in the Son. For God sees within himself, not outside himself, all that he makes. But what we make, we make after the pattern of things seen outside ourselves, while it is proclaimed that all things were made through him.

Or God the Father says: “My heart has poured forth a good word,” that is, “I have begotten a noble Son”; and the Church adds: “I speak my works to the king,” that is, “Through love I make known works of faith to your Son, my king.” The foregoing concerns the eternity of the Word and the archetypal world; the Father now proceeds to the sensible world.

“My tongue is the pen of a scribe writing swiftly.” The comparison is drawn from a writer, who by writing makes visible what lay hidden in the heart. Thus the Father, through the Son, brought forth by invisible creation whatever he had ordained to be made by invisible wisdom. By the tongue, which brings forth hidden counsel, is understood the Father’s command, by which he spoke and things were made, commanded and things were created [Col. 1566B]. By the pen, through which what is conceived in the mind is written, is understood the Son, through whom was visibly brought forth what had been formed by conception in the mind of God. By the scribe, who dictates what is to be written, is indicated the Holy Spirit, through whom genera, species, forms, and adornments are given to all things being created.

Here the Trinity is indicated in the begetting of the world. Thus it is said: “My tongue is the pen of a scribe,” that is, just as a scribe sets forth through a pen what he dictates, so I, through my Word, brought forth all things which I conceived, and through the Spirit adorned them with forms and figures. “Writing swiftly”: that is, bringing forth swiftly what was thought. No one writes so swiftly that there is no delay in writing. By swift writing is expressed the very swiftness by which all things are created without delay. For in a moment all things were created which were life in the Word of God. Here the bridegroom’s swiftness is proclaimed. Now, with the fabric of the world created and the banquet-house, as it were, prepared, the bridegroom comes forth.

### Verse 3

“More beautiful in form than the children of men.” This is the voice of the Holy Spirit concerning Christ. Why then does it not say, “More beautiful in form than the angels”? Because it says this of Christ’s humanity, which had form; for angels do not have form. But where it is said of Christ, “Being in the form of God” (Phil. 2:6), the equality of the Father is indicated, because in God no form is known.

One is called *speciosus* (“beautiful”) who has a graceful proportion of limbs; *formosus* (“comely”) who has beautiful coloring. *Formum* [Note: [Col. 1565D] Thus the manuscript.] is iron glowing red in fire; hence *formosus* is named from a face reddened with beauty [Col. 1566D].

But it is asked: since the prophet says, “We saw him as having neither beauty nor comeliness” (Isa. 43:2), how is he here called “more beautiful in form than the children of men”? The prophet said that in the person of the Jews, who regarded him as despised in his Passion; but this is said of his natural appearance, because he was naturally such as he appeared on the mountain. Yet, because weak human sight could not endure the brightness of his countenance, he presented himself as he could be seen by human beings. Nor is this remarkable of him who committed no sin, since we also read of Moses that, after converse with the angel, his face shone [Col. 1567A], and the people could not look upon his face. Hence he placed a veil before himself.

But it is asked: since the Lord promises the righteous the brilliance of the sun in the resurrection, why did he not shine like the sun after his resurrection? He was certainly more splendid in body than the sun; but, as has been said, human weakness could not see that glory, and therefore he showed his accustomed form to his own.

The bridegroom, entering, kissed the bride, who had long desired this, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1). Feeling the sweetness of the kiss, she cries in exultation: “Grace has been poured forth upon your lips.” The fullness of grace was poured by the Holy Spirit into Christ’s lips, but flowed out from his lips to humankind when he preached forgiveness and peace. Of this grace it is written: “Your name is ointment poured forth.” Hence in Hebrew it reads: “Grace has been poured forth upon his lips” (ibid., 5:3). For he came to us with the word of grace and the kiss of peace. Therefore—that is, because of that grace by which you promise the kingdom of heaven, which does not pass away but endures—God the Father has blessed you, the beautiful one, forever. For through you he will bless those who believe in him, when at judgment you say: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you” (Matt. 25:34); and this blessing will remain forever.

What follows may be the words of the Father to the Son, but more properly they are the words of the Holy Spirit, in the person of the people invited to the nuptials, praising the bridegroom.

### Verse 4

“Gird your sword [Note: [Col. 1567D] The Vulgate: ‘with your sword.’] upon your thigh [Col. 1567C], O most mighty one.” The metaphor is drawn from a warrior who girds on his sword as he prepares for battle. The sword is Christ’s soul, by which he slew the devil. The sword is also the word of preaching, by which he conquered the rebellious world. Of this it is written in the Song of Songs: “Each man has his sword upon his thigh” (Song 3:8).

By the thigh is indicated assumed humanity, which is generated from Abraham’s thigh. Thus the history is touched on here, when Abraham made his servant swear beneath his thigh—that is, upon the circumcised member—which Abraham regarded as holy because he had received circumcision from God and knew that Christ would proceed from that member (Gen. 24). Note that the servant swore concerning the nuptials of Isaac and Rebekah, which prefigured the union of Christ and the Church [Col. 1567D]. O name most mighty above all, you who, already beautiful as a bridegroom, have come forth from the bridal chamber and bestowed a kiss on the bride when you assumed human nature into divinity: gird on the sword of preaching, make known to the world the mystery of your incarnation, assail with the sword the tyrant who invaded your kingdom, and do this most mightily—that is, very powerfully.

### Verse 5

“In your beauty and your comeliness, look graciously; proceed, and reign.” This is drawn from David, who was beautiful and fair of face, looked upon the people afflicted with Saul in the battle-line, went forth successfully against Goliath, and, having overthrown him, reigned. [Col. 1568A] Thus Christ, beautiful beyond the children of men, mercifully looked upon—that is, regarded—the afflicted people; he proceeded successfully against the devil, and, having overcome him, reigned in the Church.

Beauty refers to humanity; comeliness to divinity. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “His beauty is as the cedar; chosen as Lebanon [Note: [Col. 1567D] The Vulgate: ‘His beauty is as Lebanon, chosen as the cedar,’ etc.], his throat most sweet, and he altogether desirable” (Song 5:15). The sense continues thus: You who, girded with a sword, are beautiful and comely—that is, incarnate in humanity without the stain of sin and comely in the divinity of the Father’s glory—by this beauty and this comeliness look upon humankind; proceed successfully to battle against the cruel enemy; and, having overcome him, reign in us.

“Because of truth,” which you teach, “and meekness” [Col. 1568B], by which you patiently endure adversities, “and righteousness,” by which you perform good works and justify us: “and your right hand shall lead you wonderfully,” that is, your power shall extend you into the breadth of your kingdom by miracles and lead you into the expanse of heaven. By these things the bridegroom’s strength and beauty are praised. Now the power of his preaching, or of his soldiers, is magnified.

### Verse 6

“Your arrows are sharp”: that is, your judgments are effective, penetrating hearts; through them you are led into the breadth of the world. Above he mentioned a sword; now he mentions arrows. A sword is used in close combat; arrows are shot farther away. The sword was his own preaching, by which he pierced the devil, the head of evils; the arrows were the apostles, whom he sent far throughout the world and wounded the hearts of unbelievers with the point of compunction. Hence follows: “Peoples shall fall beneath you.” That is, all peoples shall submit to you and worship you. Where will they fall? “In the heart” [Note: [Col. 1568D] The Vulgate: “into hearts.”]: from pride to humility, from unbelief to faith, from ungodliness to righteousness. “In the heart,” I say, “of the king’s enemies”: that is, those who were enemies of the king, who is Christ, will be changed and will become his friends. Of these it is written in the title: “For those who will be changed.” Of these arrows it is said in the Song of Songs: “All the armor of the strong” (Song 4:4). Here the stability of the King’s kingdom is proclaimed.

### Verse 7

“Your throne, O God, is for ever.” A seat is judgment, a throne, which is also the royal seat of kings. Therefore a throne is ascribed to him because he is judge of the living and the dead. Of this throne it is written: “The Lord God will give him the throne [Col. 1568D] of David his father, and he will reign in the house of Jacob”—that is, in the Christian people—“forever” (Luke 1:32). Note that he described a man who would fight; he calls God the one who will reign. “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever”: that is, your kingdom will be both in this age and in the age to come.

Concerning the king’s equity follows: “The rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom.” By rod he means the royal scepter, and he signifies the rule of justice: that is, you will govern your kingdom by the rule of rectitude and will not suffer anyone unrighteous to remain in it. Hence follows:

### Verse 8

“You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.” Therefore you will join the righteous to yourself in the kingdom, and drive the unrighteous far from the kingdom [Col. 1569A]. There follows the bridegroom’s royal and priestly union. And so that you may give the righteous a kingdom and the unrighteous punishment, therefore God, your God and Father, O Christ, has anointed you with the oil of gladness—that is, with the Holy Spirit—above your companions, that is, above all anointed kings, priests, and prophets. For these were anointed in the Law with visible oil; but Christ was anointed above them because he was anointed with invisible oil, spiritual oil, the oil of gladness. Hence he is called Christ, that is, Anointed One, because he is anointed king and priest by the Holy Spirit, in whose kingdom all believers are anointed with the oil of chrism.

Visible oil is a sign; invisible oil is a sacrament. Through it the faithful are his participants, because they are called Christians from Christ and are his companions—that is, co-heirs of his kingdom. Therefore he is anointed above all [Col. 1569B], because above all he has specially inherited the name of heir and Son of God. There follows the praise of the wedding garment.

### Verse 9

“Myrrh, and stacte, and cassia from your garments.” Bodies of the dead are embalmed with myrrh. Stacte is a herb called ammoniac, which restrains swellings of the flesh. Cassia is an aromatic twig, also called reed, and grows in watery places. Of these it is written in the Song of Songs: “Henna with nard, saffron and reed and cinnamon” (Song 4:13).

The bridegroom’s garment was the Lord’s body, in which the Word of God was veiled. From this garment myrrh gave fragrance: that is, mortality assumed for us. Stacte: that is, humility restraining the swellings of pride. Sweetly fragrant cassia: that is, faith restoring us through baptism to the fragrance of life. Of these ointments it is written in the Song of Songs: “The fragrance of your garments is above all spices” (ibid., 11); “We run after you in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3).

Thus fittingly the Church is Christ’s garment, from which myrrh gives fragrance—that is, virgins mortifying the flesh. Stacte gives fragrance—that is, widows restraining the swellings of pride through humility. Cassia distils—that is, married persons preserving baptism through almsgiving. He says “from your garments” in the plural because many Churches surround Christ in holy devotion. Yet this is also the one garment, the seamless tunic, because it is the one catholic Church. Christ washed this garment in baptism, that it might be without spot; he stretched it out on the cross, that it might be without wrinkle. Such are these species of ointment [Col. 1569D].

“From ivory houses.” Ivory is the bone of the elephant, an animal of the greatest chastity and the coldest nature. Thus it is eagerly sought by the dragon, which is of a hot nature, but the elephant crushes it. The ivory house is the Lord’s body, begotten of a chaste virgin, of which it is said in the Song of Songs: “His belly is ivory” (Song 5:14). The dragon, the devil, avidly assailed this body; but, dying on the cross, it crushed him. Sweet spices give fragrance from this house.

By ivory houses he means spacious, great, and royal houses, by comparison with the elephant, upon which towers are customarily built [Col. 1570A]. Ivory houses, therefore, are chaste souls, polished through many adversities as ivory is by file and saw.

### Verse 10

“From which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor.” The apostles were kings, who ruled the people of God by righteous deeds. The daughters of these kings are faithful souls. They delighted you in your honor: that is, they offered the delights of virtues for your honor. Or, even literally, daughters of kings often left their palaces for Christ’s sake and served the poor for Christ’s honor.

The king having been praised, the queen is introduced with songs; flowers are strewn, sweetest fragrances are supplied, she herself is praised as adorned with precious virtues, and she is placed at the king’s right hand. Thus the guests sing to her:

[Col. 1570B] “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, surrounded with variety.” This queen is the catholic Church, which rules her vices or sins. Of her it is written in the Song of Songs that she is “the most beautiful of women; the daughters of Jerusalem saw her and called her most blessed; queens and concubines praised her” (Song 6:8). And because she does not lie in vices but stands in virtues, she is said to stand not at his left hand but at his right. “In a garment of gold”: that is, in the garment of charity, adorned with the splendor of wisdom; “surrounded” [Note: [Col. 1569D] The Vulgate: “clothed about.”] “with variety”: that is, surrounded, in the praises of God, by the diversity of every language. For she is adorned with the gold of apostles, the silver of prophets, the gems of virgins, the scarlet of martyrs, and the purple of penitents. This is the variety of unity, woven from every nation by a devout manner of life pleasing to the eyes of the Lord [Col. 1570C]. She will stand at the right hand in judgment and will enter with her bridegroom into the joy of the Lord and the heavenly Jerusalem. Now the Father of the bridegroom addresses the bride: the father-in-law admonishes his daughter-in-law.

### Verses 11 and 12

“Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and the house of your father. And the king will desire your beauty.” This means: “Good girl, be subject to my Son, your bridegroom; love him, take no care for the people of your homeland, and I shall make you heir of my kingdom. You will also please my Son, whom I have made heir, and he has need of no other.”

Observe each point. God the Father calls the Church daughter because in baptism he begot her through the grace of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1570D]. “Hear”: that is, obey my Son. “See”: that is, understand what he wills. “Incline your ear” to hear his commandments. “Forget your people”: namely, the pagan, unbelieving, ungodly, idolatrous people. And forget “the house of your father”: that is, the Babylon of the world, the city of the devil.

The father of Gentile religion was the devil, who begot her in the city of Babylon—that is, in the house of the confusion of unclean idolatry—and fed her on the husks of swine, that is, the inventions of poets; but the Son of the king of Jerusalem took her as his bride. Therefore, by abandoning your father the devil, the house of idolatry, and the people of vices, forget them. “And the king will desire your beauty,” which you will possess in virtues, when he says to you: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no spot in you” (Song 4:7), because he—your bridegroom—is the Lord and your God, your creator, who has made you free from a slave, a bride from a captive, a mistress from one cast aside [Col. 1571A]. He is not the one whom you called father, who made you foul, dark, and hideous, but he who bestowed upon you bridal beauty. And all the peoples gathered in you will worship him, because in him are your honor, your blessedness, and everlasting glory.

### Verse 13

“And the daughters of Tyre with gifts”—understand, “will worship him.” Here are indicated those who offer gifts to the bridegroom and bride, namely the daughters of Tyre. Tyre is a city of the Gentiles; its name means “narrowness,” and it signifies the Gentile world set in straits and misery [Col. 1571B]. Its daughters are faithful souls; among them was the Canaanite woman who asked the Lord on behalf of her afflicted daughter (Matt. 15:22).

Another translation has: “And the mighty in gifts,” and signifies those strong in tribulation. Thus those strong men and those daughters will worship the bridegroom with gifts when the faithful give alms to the poor in Christ’s name, or when, amid tribulations, they offer themselves as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God. The three Magi offered gifts at these nuptials, as did those who sold all things and laid the proceeds at the apostles’ feet. The martyrs offered an acceptable sacrifice to God when they presented themselves as an odor of sweetness.

“The rich of the people will entreat your face” [Col. 1571C]: that is, not only will the poor be subject to you, but also the rich—the princes themselves, kings themselves, emperors themselves—will desire to attain your beauty and receive your religion. Now he turns to the guests and praises the bride’s inward adornment.

### Verses 14, 15, and 16

“All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.” Here the Church is called Christ’s daughter because he begot her through the Gospel; she is his bride because he took flesh from her; she is his sister because she will be co-heir of the kingdom. “All glory”: that is, all her beauty. And whose beauty? The beauty of the daughter of King Christ is within, in the soul, in the adornment of virtues. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “How beautiful amid delights is the daughter of the prince!” (Song 7:1). “In golden fringes.” Fringes are the ends of garments [Col. 1571D], and signify perseverance in virtues. “Clothed about with varieties”: that is, surrounded by diverse charisms and different gifts of grace.

Outwardly the queen shines in a garment of gold, that is, in the Christian religion, surrounded by the diversity of languages. Inwardly all her glory gleams in golden fringes, possessing perseverance in every work of love, clothed about with varieties of virtues. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “You are beautiful, my beloved, beautiful and comely; your eyes are doves’ eyes, apart from that which lies hidden within” (ibid., 15). This was signified by Aaron’s garment [Col. 1572A], woven with gold, purple, fine linen, scarlet, and hyacinth, concerning which it is written in the Song of Songs: “The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense” (Song 4:11). There follows praise of the queen’s attendants. She herself will be led into the royal hall, saying: “The king has brought me into his chamber” (Song 1:4).

“Virgins shall be brought to the king after her”: that is, after the queen, the Church, virgins who imitate in their minds either the incorruptible integrity of the Virgin Mary or the integrity of the Church’s faith will be brought to Christ the King through teachers. “Her companions”—that is, widows and chaste women—will be brought to you, O Son, through preachers. All will finally be brought by holy angels amid joy of soul and exultation of body. “They will be brought with singing into the temple of the king” [Col. 1572B]: that is, into heavenly Jerusalem, into fullness of joy.

These are the prudent virgins who, watchful with lamps, welcome the bridegroom and bride; they will enter the nuptials with him, and, after the door is shut against the ungodly, they themselves will exult within forever. Of them it is said in the title: “For those who will be changed.” Now sons are born to the bride, and their praise is now sung:

### Verse 17

“In place of your fathers, sons are born to you.” The fathers of the Church under the Law were prophets, in whose place apostles were born, who were appointed princes over all the earth. The fathers of the Church were apostles, in whose place faithful children were born to the Church, whom he appointed princes over all the earth—namely bishops [Col. 1572C], pastors, teachers, and rulers in the place of the apostles. Or her fathers were worshipers of idols, in whose place children who worship Christ were born to her. And if you forget your people and the house of your Father, these

### Verse 18

“Will remember your name, O Church, in every generation and generation”: that is, they will teach the catholic Church among all peoples. Or these words are those of the Church giving thanks for the sweet admonition of her father-in-law and for union with such a bridegroom. “I shall remember your name, O Lord, my father-in-law”—that is, your Son, who is your name—with intimate love in every generation and generation, that is, through all successions of humankind until the age. Therefore, because I shall remember your name in love and preaching [Col. 1572D], all peoples shall confess you forever and unto ages of ages: that is, they shall praise you until the end of the world, and afterwards without end, when every adversity has ceased and peace and righteousness reign forever.

This psalm is sung at the Nativity of the Lord because both his generations are commemorated in it. Therefore the apostles claim it for themselves, because, appointed princes over all the earth, they invited the people to these nuptials.

## Psalm XLV

[Col. 1573]

[Col. 1573A] “God is our refuge and strength,” etc. The preceding psalm rang out in festive applause for the wedding of the king and queen; this one applauds those invited to the wedding, and sings who they are that have been invited, or through whom they have been called. This is the forty-fifth psalm, a number which is five times nine or nine times five. By the number five are expressed the five prudent virgins, by whom are understood all the elect, who, with lamps of good works, will meet the bridegroom and bride at the judgment and will enter with them into the eternal wedding-feast. By the number nine are expressed the nine orders of angels, who continually sing praises at this wedding. Its title is:

(V. 1.) **FOR THE END; FOR THE SONS OF KORAH; FOR THE HIDDEN THINGS; A PSALM OF DAVID.**  
[Note: [Col. 1573D] The Vulgate omits “David.”]

[Col. 1573B] David is said to mean “strong of hand,” and signifies those faithful persons who remained from the primitive Church in Judaea amid the greatest distress when the apostles passed over to the Gentiles. By them this hymn is sung for the sons of Korah—that is, for imitators of Christ’s passion—that they may persevere patiently unto the end, and thus at the end receive joy without end. It was composed for hidden things—that is, for things concealed: because the Lord of glory lay hidden in the flesh and died at the hands of the ungodly as a thief; and because the Jews, Christ’s kinsmen according to the flesh, were driven away from the banquet, while Gentiles from idolatry were brought in; and because the righteous are oppressed by many tribulations. For few understand why the righteous suffer affliction. But the cross was the key to this mystery, opening for us [Col. 1573C] this secret in Christ’s passion. Hence also the veil was torn which had concealed the hidden things.

The subject of the psalm is the calling of the Gentiles to Christ’s wedding-feast and the rejection of the Jews. Its intention is that we should not fail in tribulation, but flee to the Lord, knowing that he is with us in affliction. Its words are taken from the sons of Israel, whom troubles greatly overtook when the Egyptians grievously oppressed them. Yet they did not fear when the mountains—that is, the Egyptian princes—were cast into the heart of the Red Sea, and the waters roared as they rushed over the fugitives. The rush of the stream drawn from the rock, however, gladdened those who had been delivered, and the Lord sanctified the tabernacle made by Moses. The nations of the Canaanites were disturbed by them, and the kingdoms of the kings Og and Sihon were brought low. [Col. 1573D] This signifies the people of the primitive Church, whom tribulations greatly overtook at the hands of the Jews, when the mountains—the apostles—passed into the heart of the sea of the Gentiles. They were gladdened by the rushing stream of the Holy Spirit, while he sanctified his tabernacle, the Church drawn from the Gentiles, by the stream of baptism.

[Col. 1574A] The psalm is divided into three parts by two *diapsalmata*. In the first is the consolation of those suffering tribulation for Christ; in the second, the gladness of the city and of God; in the third, the removal of wars. The voice is that of one in tribulation for righteousness’ sake:

**V. 2. God is our refuge and the strength of those who labour; a helper in the tribulations which have found us exceedingly.** The world is full of miseries and pressures. In these, Jews and pagans have the help of kings, the strength of powerful men, and the refuges of cities. But the faithful, who are driven by the ungodly from city to city, are permitted to be safe nowhere; they cry: “God is our refuge and strength.” When human beings outwardly afflict us by adversities and demons assail us with temptations, our God—namely Christ, whom [Col. 1574B] we worship—is our refuge. When through patience we overcome torments of the body and through self-restraint the temptations of the soul, Christ, made our God by faith and love, becomes our strength. No tribulation is greater than the conscience of those who love. A person finds tribulation and sorrow when repentance punishes the evils of which conscience accuses him. But tribulations have found him exceedingly when unforeseen torments press upon his cruel conscience. In these God was a refuge for escape, strength for resistance, and help for victory.

**V. 3. Therefore**, because God is refuge, strength, and helper, **we shall not fear when the earth is troubled**—that is, when our flesh is afflicted—**and the mountains are transferred into the heart of the sea**, that is, when the strongest of the saints are thrust into the sea of distresses. The land of Judah too was tilled by the ploughshare of the Law; but the sea was bitter with the unbelief of the Gentiles. This land was troubled when the Wisdom of God came incarnate. For when Herod heard that a new king had been born, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him (Matt. 2:3). It was troubled also when it saw Christ working miracles and the people following him; it was greatly troubled when, after his death, it saw him risen again and many signs performed through the apostles in his name, and wished to destroy all his followers. Then the mountains, the apostles, driven out by them, were transferred into the heart of the sea—that is, into Gentile territory. And then the faithful, who had made God their refuge, did not fear the disturbance of that land.

[Col. 1574D] The apostles were called mountains by comparison, because just as mountains receive the light of the rising sun and pour it down into the valleys, so the apostles, receiving the splendour of the Sun of righteousness, transmitted it to the valleys of the Gentiles. The heart of the sea consists of the princes and philosophers of the Gentiles, from whom the pagans received their established way of life, just as the limbs of the body receive the vigour of life from the heart. The mountains were transferred into the heart of the sea when the apostles were venerated by the very princes and philosophers of the Gentiles. Immediately:

**V. 4. Their waters roared and were troubled.** The comparison is drawn from this. When, in an earthquake, a great mountain is hurled into the bowels of the sea, a mighty sound arises from the crash of the rebounding wave, and the people living around are shaken with terror. So, when the apostles, great mountains, were sent into the heart of the sea of the Gentiles, the stormy waters roared and were troubled. For when they preached a new God to the Gentiles and worked many signs through the sign of the cross, the demons roared, because with dreadful howling they abandoned the images they had inhabited for so long; and, disturbing the waters—that is, the peoples—they stirred them [Col. 1575B] up to persecute Christians. Then the waters were troubled when the peoples, incited by demons, resisted the destroyers of images and wished to kill them. Then the mountains—that is, the rulers—were troubled and enacted laws against Christians. Where were they troubled? In his strength, namely God’s, who was the apostles’ strength and helper: through him they overcame kings and rulers and drew the rebellious world beneath Christ’s yoke.

*Diapsalma.* Demons roared through the counsels of the impious; the waters—that is, peoples flowing in their desires—were disturbed by the novelty of miracles, the destruction of temples, and the prohibition of sacrifices by an unfamiliar rite; the mountains—that is, proud rulers—raged with persecutions. But:

[Col. 1575C] **V. 5. The rush of the river gladdens the city of God**—that is, the overflowing abundance of the Holy Spirit gladdens God’s Church. Of this river it is written: “He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (Job 7:38). This river came with great force from the fountain of life, the Father and the Son, when it filled believers with the knowledge of every language. A city is so called as though from the unity of citizens. The Church is called the city of God because all believers gather in it into one faith and live in the unanimity of love. The rush of this river gladdens it when abundant grace and the consolation of the Holy Spirit cheer it with the joy of eternal life and make it fruitful through the river of baptism. Hence follows: **The Most High has sanctified his tabernacle.**

[Col. 1575D] God’s tabernacle is the Church, so long as it labours on the journey of this life; in this tabernacle martyrs fight against persecutors, and all the faithful fight against vices and demons. The Most High sanctified this tabernacle when he cleansed the Church by baptism, which he dedicated with the blood of his Son. God’s tabernacle is also the Lord’s body, in which the Word of God dwelt. God’s tabernacle also was the virgin’s womb, in which the Son of God remained. Observe that he sanctifies the tabernacle and gladdens the city, because here, amid the dust of carnal persons, he washes the Church like a tabernacle from its defilements; but in the heavenly homeland he will fill with everlasting joy the Church gathered together as the city of God in Jerusalem. Hence it adds:

**V. 6. God is in her midst.** This comparison is drawn [Col. 1576A] from the centre—that is, the point of a circle—which governs the circle and gives it equal form. Just as that which is in the middle is at equal distance from every boundary, so God is said to be in the midst of his city because he provides equally for all, and in the heavenly homeland there will be a joy common to all. Therefore that city will not be moved from that centre by the sound of winds or by the disturbance of waters, because it is founded upon the firm rock, Christ. **God will help her by his countenance**—that is, by his holy inspection—or **at daybreak**, that is, by his illumination; or, as it is read in the Hebrew: **at the morning’s rising**, when, as the morning of the resurrection shines forth, he will grant her, separated from the chaff and freed from all tribulations, eternal blessedness and immortality. And because that city could not be destroyed by any onslaught of adversity:

[Col. 1576B] **V. 7. The nations were troubled in repentance, and kingdoms were bowed beneath the feet of the saints.** For the nations, troubled out of their former error, have now received Christ’s faith; and the kingdoms of the earth, bowed to the Christian religion, serve Christ, the King of kings. This happened because the Lord gave his voice—that is, he gave preaching as a marvellous gift, as a reward-bestowing benefit. And then the earth—that is, the Gentile world—was moved to compunction; it became tillable soil, fit for the seed of God’s word and fruitful in faith and love, saying:

**V. 8. The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector.** That is: the God of angels is with us; the God of the people of Jacob, who is also Israel, is the protector of us Gentiles. The Powers are one of the nine orders, but here all the choirs of angels are understood; by Jacob, the Israelite people is meant. Therefore the Church gives thanks because the God of angels dwelt with her, and because the God of Israel, leaving the Jews, took her up.

*Diapsalma.* **V. 9. Come and see the works of the Lord.** The sons of Korah—that is, imitators of Christ—seem to speak here: “Come, all nations, to the faith; and by understanding see God’s works, the wonders he has wrought upon earth: that a virgin gave birth; that Christ, slain, rose on the third day; that the Holy Spirit granted human beings knowledge of every language.” A wonder is so called because it portends something marvellous.

[Col. 1576D] **V. 10. Removing wars unto the end of the earth.** The wars were impiety and unbelief, which attacked Christ’s faith and contradicted truth. The Lord removed these wars to the end of the earth, because, thanks be to God, the objections of heretics have everywhere ceased, the attacks of pagans have been calmed, and the Christian religion flourishes everywhere. In the literal sense too, the Lord removed wars to the ends of the earth when, at Christ’s Nativity, Augustus reigning, peace prevailed throughout the world; this peace foreshadowed eternal peace.

That wars will cease follows from the fact that the Lord **will break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields in fire**. This is drawn from the history in which David, after defeating Syria, hamstrung the horses and burned the chariots and weapons (2 Kings 8). Bows are the snares of unbelievers, which were shattered by truth when their mad desires were reduced to nothing. Weapons are the public assaults of the wicked, which were broken by the patience of the righteous. Shields are the presumptuous defences of the faithless, which were burned in fire because they were overcome by the Holy Spirit and consumed by manifest reason. Once these poisoned weapons have been broken, the heavenly King will arm his soldiers with the splendid weapons of truth, self-restraint, hope, salvation, faith, and love. There follows the voice of God, warning human beings to understand him.

**V. 11. Be still, and see that I am God.** Since the wars of persecutions have been removed and the weapons of heresies shattered, be free from the tumults of vices and the contradictions of disputes, and see with the eyes [Col. 1577B] of the mind—that is, understand—that I am God, who performed such wonders, removed wars, and shattered weapons; not those whom, deceived, you supposed to be gods, worshipping whom you could have no peace. **I shall be exalted among the nations**, that is, I shall be worshipped as God by all nations. **And I shall be exalted in the earth**, that is, I shall be worshipped in [Col. 1578A] Judaea, namely, and in sea and land. This will occur “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered; then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25). When they receive Christ’s faith through Elijah and Enoch, they will then say in rejoicing:

**V. 12. The Lord of hosts is with us.** Emmanuel is called “God with us,” because the Lord of angels dwelt with us in the flesh, as it is written: “He was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings” (Baruch 3:38). **The God of Jacob is our protector**: that is, Christ, who is the God of our people, supplanter and conqueror of vices, is our protector because he has accepted our conversion and repentance, received into his army those formerly rebellious against him, and invited them to his banquet. This verse was placed above and belongs to the rejoicing of converted Gentiles; here the same order is repeated and belongs to the exultation of converted Jews. The Church sings this psalm at the Epiphany of the Lord because then the river Jordan gladdened the city of God, the Church.

## PSALM XLVI

[Col. 1577]

[Col. 1577C] “All nations, clap your hands,” etc. The title of this psalm is:

(V. 1.) **FOR THE END; FOR THE SONS OF KORAH; A PSALM OF DAVID.**  
[Note: [Col. 1577D] The Vulgate omits “David.”]

That is, this praise of God is sung by the Church for those who believe in the Crucified, that they may be sons unto the end—that is, perfect sons. Korah means “bald,” and the words are taken from the history in which, when Elisha was going up, boys cried: “Go up, bald-head! Go up, bald-head!” (2 Kings 2:23), and two bears came out of the wood and tore forty-two of them apart. Elisha signifies Christ; the boys signify the Jews who, with childish understanding, mocked Christ as he went up upon the cross at Calvary, and perhaps in mockery shouted the same words, “Go up, bald-head!”, as they raised him on the cross. Yet they are read as having said: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” [Col. 1577D] (Matt. 27:40). For they customarily shaved those who were to be crucified, which perhaps they had also done to the Lord. Two bears from the wood devoured forty boys because, after forty years, the two Gentile kings Titus and Vespasian killed the Jewish people, foolish in their wisdom. Fierce demons, too, devoured them. All who mock Christ’s cross share their lot; but those who venerate Christ’s passion are called sons of Korah—that is, sons of the bald one.

The subject of the psalm is the preaching of the apostles, exhorting the Gentiles to praise God. Its intention is also to exhort us to understand the psalms, so that we may attain their promises. The words appear to be drawn [Col. 1578C] from Joshua, who urged the sons of Israel to applaud God, who subjected peoples to them, laid nations beneath their feet, and chose for them Jacob’s promised inheritance. It signifies Christ, who subjected peoples and nations beneath the apostles’ feet and chose the Church as an inheritance.

This psalm is the forty-sixth, the number of years in which the temple at Jerusalem was built, because by this number the Church from the Gentiles builds a temple for the Lord. Forty pertains to the repentance of the Gentiles; six, to evangelical perfection. Moreover, through forty-six days, or six times forty days, the temple of the Lord’s body is built in the virgin’s womb, to which the Church is incorporated.

This psalm is divided into two parts by a *diapsalma*: [Col. 1578D] in one is an exhortation of the Gentiles to God’s praise; in the other, Christ’s ascension is proclaimed. When the mountains were cast into the sea, the sea-waters were troubled: for when the apostles came to the Gentiles, they brought them into the disturbance of repentance; but, once clarified, the waters flowed after their footsteps. For they were those servants sent to call the invited guests to the wedding when the king made a wedding for his son—that is, when God the Father joined human nature to Christ. Therefore, when the Gentiles had been brought into the banquet, the apostles say:

**V. 2. All nations, clap your hands.** The comparison is drawn from those who clap their hands during a feast and sing joyfully. All nations of the whole world, who [Col. 1579A] have entered the royal wedding through faith, clap your hands—that is, rejoice in good works. **Make joyful noise to God with the voice of exultation**: that is, praise in voice, heart, and work him who invited you to his banquet.

**V. 3. For the Lord**, who appeared here humble, is high or supreme above all choirs of angels; and he who was frightened and made ridiculous by the impious is now terrible and to be feared in judgment by all evildoers. He is a great king over all the earth, not only over Judaea, where it was written in the title, “King of the Jews,” but over every people of the earth, because all power in heaven and on earth has been given to him. Or, “a great king over all the earth,” that is, over the whole Church spread through all the earth. Truly he is a great king, because:

[Col. 1579B] **V. 4. He has subjected peoples to us**, fishermen and contemptible men, **and nations beneath our feet.**  
[Note: [Col. 1579D] Vulgate: “and nations beneath our feet.”]  
This is said according to teaching, not according to domination. The feet also signify holy preachings, beneath which all nations have been subjected. But even literally, the whole world hastens to Rome to venerate the footsteps of Peter the fisherman, not to visit the tomb of Nero the emperor. And nations are deservedly subject to Christ’s laws because through grace they have been called to God’s feast. Hence follows:

**V. 5. He chose for us his inheritance**, with “to give” understood. The Father gave him the nations as an inheritance; he chose this beloved form of Jacob for us to be joined to. Here the history is touched upon in which Rebekah was told: “Two peoples are in your womb, and the greater shall serve [Col. 1579C] the lesser” (Gen. 25:23). Of these it is said: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Rom. 9:13). This form—that is, this figure—was a sign of this matter: that the Lord chose the Gentiles through grace and rejected the Jews through justice. Therefore the greater, not in number but because of the pride connected with Law and Prophets, serves the lesser Christian people because of humility.

Another history is also touched upon: Jacob bought Esau’s birthright with food and deserved to be blessed by his father (Gen. 25). Esau sold his primacy for food, and his mother excluded him from his father’s blessing. This form—that is, this figure—was a sign that the Christian people, who forsake carnal things for spiritual things, will possess the inheritance with the blessing expressed in: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25: [Col. 1579D] 34). But the Jewish people, who seek carnal things and despise spiritual things, separated from the blessing, will go with the accursed into punishment.

A third history is noted here. Jacob took two wives: Leah, with weak eyes, and Rachel, beautiful and clear-eyed, whom he loved. Leah is the synagogue, seeing Scripture only carnally with weak eyes; Rachel, however, is the Church, beautiful in virtues and clear-eyed in spiritual matters. The Lord loves this form of Jacob because he chooses the spiritual food of life.

*Diapsalma.* Do not clap only because you have come together for the king’s wedding, but praise also because:

**V. 6. God has ascended amid jubilation.** Jubilation is an immense exultation of the heart, which cannot be contained in letters, syllables, or words, but can scarcely be expressed in a certain wonderful sound, such as is customarily uttered in the Alleluia. Therefore God is said to have ascended in jubilation, because the apostles, amazed at such a miracle, were filled with ineffable joy of heart when they saw him bodily penetrate the heavens whom they had recently seen hanging on the cross with thieves and lying slain in the tomb. **And the Lord at the sound of a trumpet.** This is drawn from the history in which trumpet-sounds were heard on Mount Sinai, and after the Lord gave the Law amid the blast of trumpets and the cry of the jubilant people, he ascended to heaven (Exod. 19:16). But this foreshadowed that Christ ascended to heaven amid the apostles’ jubilation and the clear voice of angels, who sounded like a high-resounding trumpet:

[Col. 1580B] “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 24:7).

They thundered this in heaven; but to the apostles wondering on earth they sounded the trumpet: “Men of Galilee, this Jesus whom you see going into heaven, so you shall see returning for judgment.” The Jews mocked Christ ascending to the cross; they did not see him ascending to heaven. They shall yet see him whom they pierced. And while in the passion he appeared as man, in the ascension he shone forth as God.

**V. 7. Sing psalms to our God; sing psalms to the Father equal with him. Sing psalms to our king, Christ; sing psalms to him who was made man for us.** Sing psalms—that is, celebrate him in good works. By the fourfold “sing psalms,” he indicates the four parts of the world from which the Church of the Gentiles had gathered to [Col. 1580C] the wedding. Sing, you who came from the east; sing, you who came from the west; sing, you who came from the south; sing, you who came from the north, because you ought to recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, while the sons of the kingdom shall be cast out—those who, hearing the music and dancing because the prodigal son had been received into the banquet, refused to enter. And rightly you ought to sing:

**V. 8. For God is king of all the earth.** That is, Christ our God himself has become king of all the earth; therefore sing psalms wisely—that is, intelligently—so that what you sing with your mouth you may understand in your heart. To sing psalms wisely also means to perform good works with discernment: to pray at the proper time, read at the proper time, fast at the proper time, and minister to the poor at the proper time. First he said “sing psalms” four times, thereby indicating boys, youths, young men, and old men from the four parts of the world coming to faith; then he added “sing psalms” once, intending the Church’s unanimity. God, hitherto known in Judaea alone, now henceforth:

**V. 9. Shall reign over the nations**, both presently over the Church converted from the Gentiles, and in the future over the heavenly Jerusalem, gathered from all nations. Hence follows: **God sits upon his holy throne**, that is, upon the Church which he made holy for himself by his blood; or upon the companies of angels, upon the Thrones and Powers. Observe that the king sits on the exalted throne at the right hand of God the Father and presents his presence to the guests, so that they may behold the king in his beauty, they who entered in a wedding garment. And who comes there?

[Col. 1581A] **V. 10. The princes of the peoples**—that is, the apostles—**have been gathered with the God of Abraham**, that is, with Christ born from Abraham’s seed, to judge the world, introduce the elect into the royal banquet, and shut the door against the reprobate; indeed, to cast the chaff away from the grain into the furnace of fire. Or, the princes of the peoples, formerly troubled and persecutors of the apostles and other Christians, have now through the apostles been gathered in faith for the royal wedding with the God of Abraham—not a recent God, but the Ancient of Days. By imitating Abraham’s faith they have become Abraham’s children, and therefore have been brought in to recline with Abraham at the banquet. And why is this? **Because the strong gods of the earth have been greatly exalted** [Col. 1582A]—that is, the apostles, gods of carnal people and strong in good living, have been greatly exalted by miracles, wisdom, and eloquence. For the righteous are called gods in comparison with the wicked. Hence Moses is written “the god of Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1). Or, the Jews, formerly God’s people and the powerful gods of the Gentiles, were excessively lifted up in earthly things into pride against God; therefore they will not be admitted to his banquet, but will be cast into outer darkness.

The Church sings this psalm at the Epiphany of the Lord because through it the Gentiles are introduced to the wedding of Christ and the Church, and the Magi came from the Gentiles to the Bridegroom with gifts. The Ascension of the Lord claims it because Christ ascended into heaven amid jubilation. The feast of the apostles claims it because they, gathered with God as judges, are the princes of peoples.

## PSALM XLVII

[Col. 1581]

[Col. 1581B] “Great is the Lord, and exceedingly praiseworthy,” etc. The preceding psalm recounts how the apostles exhort the Gentiles, brought into the wedding, to praise God; this one presents their praise. This psalm is the forty-sixth. In forty, ten is multiplied four times. The number four expresses all the righteous living in the perfection of the four Gospels; ten, all the righteous observing the Decalogue of the Law. Seven is divided into three and four; three times four, or four times three, is twelve. The number twelve signifies the twelve apostles, filled with the sevenfold Spirit. Since this psalm concerns the Church of both peoples, which is built like a city by the supreme Builder, and through the apostles living stones from Jews and Gentiles alike are carried to this edifice, this psalm is fittingly adorned with such a number. Its title is:

(V. 1.) **A PSALM OF A CANTICLE FOR THE SONS OF KORAH, ON THE SECOND DAY OF THE SABBATH.**

[Col. 1581D] “A psalm of a canticle” is one expression; and so is called a song in which instruments first resound, then the voices of the choir cry aloud. A psalm signifies action; a canticle, joy. The sons of Korah are Christians who imitate the Crucified. The second day of the Sabbath is the second day of the week. On the first day of the Sabbath—that is, Sunday—God made light; on the second, the firmament, that is, heaven. This signifies that on the first day Christ, the true light, rose; and on the second he established the Church as a firm heaven, strengthened it against heresies, and concealed his secrets within it. The second day of the Sabbath is also the entire time from the Lord’s resurrection until the end of the world. On this day the city of God is established like heaven amid the waters of baptism and the streams of the Holy Spirit. The first day of the Sabbath also denotes the synagogue, which observed the Sabbath carnally. The second [Col. 1582B] day of the Sabbath denotes the Church, which will be transferred to the spiritual Sabbath—that is, to eternal rest, which is what “Sabbath” means. This hymn, therefore, is a psalm of a canticle: spiritual praise of the joy of the sons of Korah, that is, sons of Christ’s passion and cross, [Col. 1582C] a joy occurring on the second day of the Sabbath—that is, in this time in which the Church is founded and is completed at the end of the world.

The subject of the psalm is the praise of the Church from the Gentiles, brought into the wedding of Christ the king. Its purpose is to exhort us, the sons of the bridegroom, to praise him, so that we may deserve to be founded in the Lord’s city. Its words appear to be drawn from the history in which the queen of Sheba and others with her came to Jerusalem, and, seeing the temple, said: “Great is the Lord, and exceedingly praiseworthy; as we heard, so we have seen in the city of God. O God, we have received your mercy in the midst of your temple.” It signifies the Church and the faithful who, reaching the heavenly Jerusalem, will say: “As we heard, so we have seen in the city of our God.” Nor should it disturb you that this queen is written to have lived not in David’s time but in Solomon’s. Remember that the author of this book is the Holy Spirit, to whom all past and future things are present, and who at times takes words from the past, at times from the future, weaving by them the mystical work of Christ and the Church.

This psalm has two sections. One begins, “Great is the Lord,” in which the Church’s praise is presented; the other, “We have received, O God,” in which the various ranks of the Church praising God are marked. The nations who have entered the king’s wedding are urged by the apostles to clap and rejoice before God; they begin this applause by rejoicing in this way. It is the voice of the priests:

**V. 2. Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy.** [Col. 1583A] Great, that is, mighty, because he made all things mightily. Praiseworthy, because he made beautiful and wonderful things. “Exceedingly,” or “very,” means beyond what human beings can praise. And where? **In the city**—that is, in the catholic Church—which is the city of our God, namely Jesus Christ, who is our God, the God of us Christians, not of Jews or pagans. In this city he is praiseworthy, not in Babylon, the devil’s city, where he is most execrable. And where is he more praiseworthy? **On his holy mountain**, that is, in Jesus Christ his Son. Christ is called a mountain because he is impregnable, and he upholds the building of this city which Ezekiel saw built on a mountain, whose name was “The Lord is there” (Ezek. 48:35). It is written in Daniel that a stone cut from a mountain without hands grew and filled the whole earth (Dan. 2:34). This was Christ, born from the Jewish people without a man’s seed, who grew through the apostles’ preaching and filled the whole earth through faith. Upon this mountain that city is built, concerning which it adds:

[Col. 1583B] **V. 3. It is founded with the joy of the whole earth: Mount Zion, on the side of the north, the city of the great king.** The Church is called a city because in it the unanimity of faithful citizens comes together. Its great king is called Christ because through him heavenly and earthly things are ruled. Zion is a citadel in Jerusalem and means “watchtower of life”; it signifies the primitive Church, which began on Mount Zion because there the Lord supped, gave his body, and bestowed the Holy Spirit’s knowledge of languages. It is called a mountain because it is lofty in virtues, fortified and strong against heresies. The north is a cold wind and signifies the devil, who said: “I shall set my throne in the north” (Isa. 14:13), that is, in unbelief. Its side is the Gentile world, because it clung to him through unbelief and surrounded him through impiety. For the sides of rulers are called those who cling to and surround them. Therefore, by Mount Zion is understood the primitive Church from the Jews; by the side of the north, the Church from the Gentiles. From these is constituted the one catholic Church, the city of the great king. In its building is laid that precious cornerstone, rejected by people building the wall of iniquity but chosen by God the builder [Col. 1583D] for the joining of the corner; in him the two walls, one coming from circumcision and the other from uncircumcision, meet from opposite sides; and in him the whole joined structure grows into a holy temple, in which the king and priest himself will remain forever.

This verse is construed thus: The city of the great king—that is, Christ’s Church—is founded through the apostles on the side of the north, that is, among the Gentiles, who cling to the devil through idolatry, with the joy of the whole earth—that is, with the great gladness of every people on earth—which belongs to Mount Zion, that is, after the example of the primitive Church from Zion.

Another translation has: **Mount Zion is founded with joy; the sides of the north are the city of the great king.** [Col. 1584A] It is read thus: The Church, which is the city of Christ the great king, which is Mount Zion as consisting of Jews, and which is the sides of the north as consisting of Gentiles, is founded with the joy of the whole earth—that is, it will be gathered into one faith with the highest gladness from every people.

**V. 4. God shall be known in her houses.** Hence he is seen to be great. The houses of this city are its individual churches, such as the Roman Church, the Jerusalem Church, the Alexandrian Church, and others of this kind. The houses of this city also are individual believers, in whom God is known by faith and is magnified as praiseworthy, **when he receives her for protection**, to guard her; or when he receives her for treatment, as a physician receives a sick person. For the physician came to heal the sick, and the sick fell upon the physician.

[Col. 1584B] Another translation has: **God shall be known in her steps**, and the future resurrection is understood, when persons will be assigned, according to the degrees of their merits, to different dwelling-places of joys; and, just as star differs from star in brightness, so each will differ in variety of glory. God will be known in these degrees when he receives her from this world into heaven, when no one will teach his neighbour, saying, “Know the Lord,” because all, from least to greatest, will know him, since they shall see him as he is, eye to eye. The rulers of the world, citizens of Babylon, wished to overthrow this city, but could not, because it was founded upon the firm rock and had God as its defender. Hence follows:

[Col. 1584C] **VV. 5, 6, and 7. For behold**, that is, at present, **the kings assembled to destroy her**; but seeing her firm—indeed, firm as the firmament of heaven, established by God on the second day of the Sabbath—they came together into one, with participation in her understood, and became her citizens though they had been her attackers, like Constantine and his other followers. Seeing that she was so—that is, so firm and so fortified—these kings marvelled, that is, were astonished. They were troubled, fearing punishment for having persecuted her. They were moved as they passed from error to faith. The trembling of the future judgment seized them as they fled from God. There, that is, at the judgment, will be pains like those of a woman in labour. Considering this, they imitated in repentance a woman’s travail: when they conceived a good will, brought forth an excellent work, and, putting off the old human being, were born anew. Therefore the Church’s voice follows in praise of God:

### VERSE 8

With a mighty spirit—that is, by the impulse of the Holy Spirit—you will shatter the ships of Tarshish: that is, the pursuits in which they were accustomed to seek out worldly joys, pursuits through which they acquired riches in which to rejoice. For *Tarshish* is interpreted “the exploration of joy.”

Scholars ask what city was called Tarshish. Some have thought it to be Cilicia, which is called Tarshish from its metropolitan city Tarsus [Col. 1585A]. Others maintain that it is Carthage, formerly called Tarshish, renowned for the ships brought there by Dido and distinguished by commerce. This city is without doubt called Tarshish here, since the interpreters of Isaiah and Ezekiel also render Tarshish as Carthage. It signifies the pride of the nations, which hopes in the uncertainty of riches and is driven about by the wind of desires. But the Lord will shatter the ships of Tarshish by the Spirit when, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, he grants the powerful to despise perishable riches and worldly joys and instead to seek eternal things.

In the Hebrew it is read: “In the wind of the east you will break the ships of Tarshish,” that is, by strong fear you will humble the rich. Tarshish is also interpreted “sea,” and signifies [Col. 1585B] the world. The ships of Tarshish are the cities of the world, which carry their peoples across the salt sea of this age as ships do. Their pilots are their rulers. These ships are shattered by a mighty spirit when cities with their rulers are subjected to Christ through the Holy Spirit, or are overthrown by enemies through the fury of just judgment.

These matters may also be referred to Christ’s Nativity. “God will be known in her dwellings, when he receives her”: that is, God was known in Christ by the faithful when he took flesh from human beings. And how was he known? “For behold, kings”—namely, the Magi—“were assembled and came together in one accord,” with gifts to worship him. Or the Jewish rulers, through Herod, assembled so that he might ask them where [Col. 1585C] Christ was to be born. They came together in one, saying that he would be born in Bethlehem. They “assembled” in order to state what they had read; they “came together in one” when they delivered one judgment. “They themselves, seeing”—that is, the scribes, understanding that it was so written in the prophets—“were amazed” that it had been fulfilled in this way. They were troubled with Herod and disturbed at the arrival of the Magi. Trembling seized them because of the heavenly sign. “There were pains there as of a woman in labour,” because Herod, suspecting a successor to his kingdom, conceived anguish of heart and gave birth to wickedness when he increased the anguish of women in labour by killing their newborn children. Of this it is added: “With a mighty spirit you will shatter the ships of Tarshish,” because in great fury Herod shattered the ships of Tarsus in Cilicia [Col. 1585D], by which he believed that the Magi had been secretly transported into his province. But the Magi, having returned to their own people, say:

### VERSE 9

“As we heard it spoken through Balaam: ‘A star shall arise from Jacob’ (Num. 24:17), so we have seen it in the city of the Lord, Bethlehem.”

The nations invited to the wedding and entering the Church, the city of God, say: “As we heard in the promises, so we have seen in their fulfilment; as we heard in prophecy, so we have seen in the Gospel. As we heard it prophesied beforehand, so in such a manner and in that order we see the whole fulfilled in the city of the Lord of hosts,” that is, of the angels. Or, as another version has, “of armies,” that is, of heavenly and earthly citizens—namely, in the city of our God, that is, Jesus Christ, who [Col. 1586A] is our God. For everything was indeed done in the establishment of the Church just as the prophets foretold. Of it the text continues: “God has founded her to remain for ever.” Babylon will perish; the city of God will stand eternally. And how it is founded is explained.

### VERSE 10

“We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple.”

The temple of God is understood as the synagogue, whose midst is taken to be Jerusalem, where the Temple stood in which God was worshipped by the Jews. The mercy of God was Christ, who was sent to deliver the synagogue. The nations received this mercy in the midst of the Temple when they were accounted worthy to receive by faith Christ, born in the synagogue and offered as a living sacrifice in Jerusalem.

The Virgin Mary was also God’s temple, in whose midst Christ, the mercy of God, lay hidden in the flesh. The Church received him when it believed that he was born of the Virgin. The Church too is God’s temple: its centre is the apostolic order and the other perfect persons; its circumference is the imperfect. The mercy of God is also understood as the Holy Spirit, who is given not as a debt but by grace. This mercy descended into the midst of the temple when the Holy Spirit came in fiery tongues upon the apostles and other believers. The nations received this mercy in the midst of the temple when they were accounted worthy to receive the Holy Spirit through the apostles. The priests also are the middle of this temple, through whose ministry believers today receive the Holy Spirit, or penitents receive the mercy of reconciliation. [Col. 1586C] Hence this psalm is sung in the person of priests.

Nevertheless, every faithful person is God’s temple, as it is written: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3:17). The centre of this temple is understood to be the heart, in which the mercy of the Holy Spirit is received. And that God should everywhere be praised for receiving this mercy is added:

### VERSE 11

“According to your name, O God, so also is your praise unto the ends of the earth”: that is, your name, which is God, is as widely praiseworthy as it is widely worshipped. The name God is worshipped through all the ends of the earth, although it is applied by those ignorant of him to created things, as by pagans. But because the Church is spread through all the ends of the earth, the name of God is everywhere praised. The source from which God’s praise is acceptable follows: “Your right hand is [Col. 1586D] full of righteousness,” that is, your mercy is filled with righteous persons. For you will establish righteous persons throughout the earth, by whom you may be praised. And because through mercy you have separated the righteous from the mass of the lost:

### VERSE 12

“Let Mount Zion rejoice,” that is, the primitive Church; “and let the daughters of Judah exult,” that is, the churches of the nations, daughters of the primitive Church from Judaea, which gave them birth in faith, “because of your judgments, O Lord”: because in justice you have prepared vessels of wrath for dishonour, and in grace have prepared vessels of mercy for glory.

Otherwise: some who live wickedly also speak perversely in this way: “If all who do such things perish, then few will be saved.” To these the Holy Spirit answers: “Your right hand is full of righteousness.” That is, the number of the elect will be so great that God’s right hand at the judgment will be full of righteous people, who will inherit the kingdom of life, while all the ungodly will perish. Then let Mount Zion rejoice—that is, contemplative persons, exalted in virtues and beholding the glory of the Lord—and let the daughters of Judah exult—that is, souls confessing the name of God in the active life—because of your judgments, O Lord. By the winnowing-fan of your judgment you will so separate tares from wheat that not one grain of wheat will fall into the heap of chaff to be burned, nor one ear of chaff pass into the mass stored in the granary. And since this will be so, you daughters of Judah—that is, churches of the nations—

### VERSE 13

“Surround Zion”: that is, imitate the Church from Zion and embrace it, that is, love [Col. 1587B] it. “Tell it in her towers”: that is, preach it to others through the apostles, who are the towers of Zion. Let your preaching not differ from the preaching of the apostles, who were the towers of the city, the Church, and fortified it against heresies.

### VERSE 14

“Set your hearts on her strength,” that is, on her charity. From your heart imitate her in every good manner of life. “Distribute her houses,” that is, divide cities throughout the provinces among yourselves for preaching, as the apostles divided regions among themselves: Peter received Italy, Paul Greece, John Asia, Matthew Ethiopia, and others other provinces.

Another translation has: “Set apart her palaces,” that is, distinguish orthodox preachers from false preachers [Col. 1588A]; recognize who are the towers defending Zion, the city of God, and who are the engines destroying it, “so that you may declare it to another generation”: that is, so that you may tell a generation yet to come to others, and your descendants may in turn declare to others what you told them.

Another translation has: “Distribute her ranks,” that is, arrange freely the distinct offices in the Church, the city of God. In the clergy appoint doorkeepers, readers, singers, acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, priests, and bishops; among the people, prefects, counts, dukes, patricians, kings, and emperors, so that through these ranks the work of the city of God may be completed. “So that you may declare it to another generation.” One generation is that of the Hebrews, the other that of Christians. In this other generation these ranks declare the mighty works of God, saying:

[Col. 1588B]

### VERSE 15

“For this Jesus Christ, who is God and man, is our God, and we worship him. This king, the Lord of this city, is God and our Lord for ever and unto age of ages,” that is, both in this age and in the future one.
