He is not a new god, but God the Creator himself will rule us for ages; that is, this same God will be our king eternally. Through what these ranks declare in this other generation, more and more people hasten separately to this city for the wedding.

This psalm is sung at the Nativity of the Lord because Christ is then received by the world from the virginal temple. The Church also sings it at Pentecost because a mighty spirit then filled the whole house.

## PSALM XLVIII

[Col. 1587]

[Col. 1587C] “Hear these things, all nations; receive them with your ears,” etc. In the preceding psalm the ranks in the Church were commanded to be distributed, so that they might declare the mighty works of God in the other generation. In this psalm they preach to God’s future people, foretell condemnation to lovers of the world, and the reward of life to those who despise it.

This psalm is reckoned forty-eighth, a number produced by multiplying six by eight. It signifies that those who sow seeds of righteousness in the six ages of the world will reap eternal joys in the eight beatitudes. Its title is:

### (VERSE 1) A PSALM OF DAVID FOR THE END, FOR THE SONS OF KORAH

> [Note: [Col. 1587D] In the Vulgate, “David” is omitted.]

David, whose name means “strong of hand,” here denotes the clergy, arranged in various ranks and strong against vices. This hymn is sung for the sons of Korah—that is, for all [Col. 1587D] Christians—that they may be “for the end,” that is, perfect. For “end” here signifies perfection.

The subject of the psalm is those who long for worldly things and refuse to come to Christ’s wedding. Its purpose is to deter us from the pursuit of earthly things and kindle our minds with desire for eternal things. Its words seem to be taken from Balaam, priest of the Gentiles, who “inclined his ear to a parable” when he foretold in parables many things that would happen to the people (Num. 23–24). “The iniquity of his heel surrounded him” when he fell by the sword for his wicked counsel, where the foolish people of Israel and the foolish people of Midian perished, left their riches to strangers, and Balaam himself was compared to irrational beasts when a donkey spoke to him, rebuking the folly of the foolish prophet. The remaining words of this psalm suit those who perished there. He signifies the foolish order of priests, blinded by avarice and deceiving the people by their evil example.

The psalm has four parts. The first is, “Hear these things, all nations,” in which occurs the address of the king and bridegroom. The second is, “The foolish and the senseless shall perish together” [Col. 1588D], concerning the destruction of the wicked. The third is, “Like sheep they are placed in hell,” concerning the condemnation of the evil and the rescue of the good. The fourth is, “Do not fear,” concerning the consolation of the righteous and the desolation of the wicked.

In the psalm “The king has belched forth,” he made a wedding for his son; in the psalm “God is our refuge,” he sent his servants to call those invited; in the psalm “All nations,” the invited gathered together; [Col. 1589A] in the psalm “Great is the Lord,” they sang praises to the Bridegroom; in this psalm the king addresses the guests concerning those who neglected to come to the wedding because of earthly riches, and foretells what will happen to them.

### VERSE 2

“Hear these things, all nations”: hear what I am about to say. “Receive with your ears, all you who inhabit the world.” To hear is to listen to what is said; to receive with the ears is to attend carefully. By “all nations” pagans are understood; by “inhabitants of the world,” Christians. The Church is called the world because, placed in the round world, she is called into the circle of the eternal crown.

### VERSE 3

“You who are earthborn, and sons of men”: that is, the carnal and the spiritual. An earthborn person is one generated from the earth, such as Adam. All imitators of Adam, lovers of the world, are called earthborn. The Son of Man is Christ, born of the Virgin. The sons of men are all righteous imitators of Christ. “Rich and poor together”: that is, slaves or free persons, or humble and proud. Observe that the whole human race is divided here into six classes: nations, that is, unbelievers; inhabitants of the world, that is, believers; earthborn persons, that is, carnal people; sons of men, that is, spiritual people; rich and poor, that is, free and slave. All of you, hear my words obediently with the ears of your heart; fulfil in deeds what you hear, so that you may escape coming evils and receive future goods. First know that here “rich and poor together” means Christ, rich in divinity and poor in humanity.

### VERSE 4

“My mouth shall speak wisdom, and the meditation [Col. 1589C] of my heart understanding.” By the heart faith is signified; by the mouth, confession. “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). Wisdom concerns the explanation of divine mysteries; understanding concerns the instruction of commendable conduct. The hidden mysteries which I conceive in my heart I shall teach you with my mouth.

### VERSE 5

“I shall incline my ear to a parable; I shall open my proposition upon the psaltery.” A parable is a comparative likeness, and the Gospel teaching is understood, since it is for the most part woven from parables. The psaltery, which has ten strings, is understood as the old law on account of the Ten Commandments. A proposition is an enigma set forth for solution. “I shall incline my ear to a parable,” that is, I shall disclose [Col. 1589D] my understanding in Gospel parables. “I shall open my proposition upon the psaltery,” that is, I shall openly resolve the proposed enigmas of the Law. What that proposition is follows:

### VERSE 6

“Why shall I fear in the evil day?” That is, what reason is there why I—or other human beings—should fear on the day of judgment, which is evil for the evil, a day of misery and calamity? This is the reason: “The iniquity of my heel has surrounded [will surround] me.” The heel is the ankle by which we stand, and it signifies the state of the soul. The iniquity of the heel surrounds a person when sin casts him down from the state of good life and binds him. Or the ankle is affection, because as we walk bodily by the ankle, so we walk spiritually by affection. The heel also, being the last part of a person, signifies perseverance [Col. 1590A] in evils until the end. Therefore I and every person ought to fear if “the iniquity of my heel will surround me,” that is, if perseverance in sins seizes me at the end. Thus it was said to the woman concerning the serpent: “You shall crush his head,” that is, you shall suppress the first suggestion of sin, “and he shall lie in wait for your heel,” that is, your end (Gen. 3:15). These people will be able to fear:

### VERSE 7

“Those who trust in their strength and glory in the abundance of their riches.” Those who presume upon their own strength, friends, or riches will fear on the evil day, because on the day of vengeance riches will not profit, nor will friends free friend, nor servants master, from punishments there. For:

### VERSE 8

“A brother will not redeem; will a man redeem?” Christ is the brother of the human race; he made believers brothers and co-heirs, and after rising from the dead he said: “Go, tell my brothers” (Matt. 28:10). This brother will not redeem such persons—and will some sinful human being redeem them? By no means. Christ the brother will not give God his propitiation.

### VERSE 9

“And he will not give the price of the redemption of his soul for such a person.” Christ’s propitiation is his prayer to the Father, by which he intercedes for us. The price of the soul’s redemption is Christ’s sacrifice—namely, his body, which suffered for the salvation of the world and which he continually displays to the Father for the redeemed. Therefore the wicked must fear on the evil day, because neither riches nor any human being will redeem them; nor will Christ himself, the brother of humankind who suffered for them, redeem them or pray [Col. 1590C] for them. Therefore another translation has: “Thus, one redeeming a brother shall not redeem a man; he shall not give God propitiation for him, nor the price of the redemption of their soul.”

Otherwise: “A brother has not redeemed,” that is, Christ has not redeemed the wicked here. Will Adam, a man, redeem them? Or Moses, their brother, did not redeem the Hebrews; Christ, made man, will redeem human beings. Neither Adam for his descendants nor Moses for the Hebrews will give his propitiation or the price of redemption for the soul.

Otherwise: the wicked person will not redeem himself on the evil day, because he did not do so here. He will not then give God his propitiation—that is, repentance, by which God is appeased—nor the price of the redemption of his soul, that is, almsgiving, by which the soul is redeemed in death. Since he neither here performed repentance [Col. 1590D] for his evils nor redeemed his sins by alms, he will therefore labour eternally, that is, he will be in everlasting labour. But what happens here?

### VERSE 10

“He shall still live”: that is, he flourishes for a little while and, as it seems to fools, will live happily to his end; but this end will lead him to perpetual condemnation. Or one who here labours night and day to gather riches on which to place his hope, and does not take care to rest even briefly in God, will labour eternally in punishments and never rest.

If someone were to say, “What harm is it to him when he is dead?”—“And he shall still live unto the end”: that is, whether unwilling or willing, he will live in eternal torment unto the end, that is, without end, where he will seek death and death will flee from him. Yet while he is placed amid delights:

[Col. 1591A]

### VERSE 11

“He will not see destruction, though he sees wise men dying.” Those who lived wisely here do not perish by dying, as he supposed; rather, freed from miseries, they enter into the joy of their Lord. When the impious man sees a person wise in God depart from this world, he says: “What did fasting, chastity, and almsgiving profit this person? Is he not dead? Therefore I shall do myself good while I live.” Thus he does not see destruction, that is, he does not understand that death is impending for him. For he thinks happy only those who flourish here in riches; he judges unhappy those who lack them, and does not think that after death he will be unlike those whom he sees as his equals.

“The foolish and the senseless shall perish together.” The senseless person is one who does not understand future punishments; the fool is one who understands and does not [Col. 1591B] beware. Or the senseless person is one who despises having knowledge of God; the fool is one who hopes in riches rather than in the Lord. They shall perish together, that is, equally.

It is asked how those who do not lose existence can perish. Every soul rests, as it were, either in the friendship of people, in the worldly things it loves, or in a good conscience. But evil people rest not in conscience, which is harsh, but in worldly joys. When these are taken away in death, they find rest neither in outward nor inward things. Therefore those who perish from the goods of body and soul will be in eternal sadness.

It is asked why they are said to be lost. A thing lost is something once possessed and then lost. God possessed human beings in Paradise; he then lost them when, through the devil’s raging, he lost them. He sought and found them in the world. Of those found he lost many, because he does not have them among his possessions. What has been lost and is not sought is forgotten. Once the impious fall into hell, God will seek them no more; therefore they are called lost and consigned to oblivion, because he no longer has them in his estate [Col. 1591C].

The senseless and foolish will perish and leave their riches to strangers. Although they leave them to sons and grandsons so that they may spend them in almsgiving on their behalf, it will benefit them no more than if they left them to strangers who performed no almsgiving.

It is asked, since people leave riches to their sons, how they are said to leave them to strangers. The living are strangers to the dead. Or sons living wickedly have become alienated from their dead parents, because they cannot assist them. That rich man in the Gospel had left his riches to his five brothers, but they were strangers to him because they could not cool him as he burned in the flame (Luke 16:19 ff.).

Otherwise: the Jews were senseless because they did not believe the prophets concerning Christ. Those who refused to receive Christ when he came should be called fools. They will perish together because both those who killed the prophets and those who killed the Lord of the prophets are to be condemned at the judgment. They left their riches to strangers because the Scriptures of the Law and the Prophets passed to the nations. It follows:

### VERSE 12

“And their tombs are their houses for ever; [Col. 1592A] their dwellings from generation to generation.” That is, they laboured to build great houses in which they will not dwell; instead, tombs, not palaces, will be their permanent houses. Their carefully built houses will be tents from which they will migrate to tombs. Or the rich build themselves tombs as though they were eternal houses, at great expense, so that people may remember them after death. But the palaces in which they dwell temporarily are like tents to them, which they will leave to sons and grandsons, as it were from generation to generation, so that after they are dead their names may be invoked in their lands—that is, so that they may be praised by the living. “They called their names in their lands,” that is, they made themselves named and famous. Throughout the whole earth? No, only in lands near their own.

Or rich persons who died wished to be invoked by the living, like Alexander. For pagans feast over the tombs of the dead, drink in the names of those who have died, sing empty songs, and invoke their names. But none of this benefits those placed in hell; rather, it greatly harms those who do it.

### VERSE 13

“And man, though he died while living in honour,” abounding in honours and riches, “did not understand” God, who had granted him the goods of the world. Or he did not understand future goods and evils, so as to correct his life from a beastly life through reason. Therefore he was compared to irrational beasts by seeking earthly things alone and made like them by living without reason. The fierce person is compared to a bear, the rapacious to a wolf, the wanton to a donkey, the quarrelsome to a dog, the unclean to a pig, and the deceitful [Col. 1592C] to a fox.

Or Adam, while he was in the honour of Paradise, did not understand his dignity—namely, that he was formed in the image of God. He was compared to irrational beasts in mortality and corruptibility, and made like them in the miseries of life and sufferings of the flesh. And because riches blind fools and prosperity will destroy them, it follows:

### VERSE 14

“This way of theirs is a stumbling-block to them,” because if they are ever converted to faith, they become hypocrites: when eternal life and contempt for riches are commended to them, they are tortured in their hearts. Therefore the way of riches is a stumbling-block to them, because on it they fall and proceed to destruction. There remains in their mouth a blessing and in their heart a curse. Hence it is added: “Afterwards they will be pleased in their mouth.” For when they fulfil their desires or obtain what they want, they then bless God. Of these it is written: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 19:13). Or, once they themselves have become such, they persuade others also to be such, and will take pleasure in them in their persuasion.

Another translation has: “After them others will run according to their mouth,” that is, others will imitate them in conformity with their persuasion.

Otherwise: “This way of theirs,” that is, the life of beasts which they chose for themselves, “is a stumbling-block to them,” that is, the cause of their future condemnation, because it will lead them from judgment to punishment. Hence the text plainly adds:

### VERSE 15

“Like sheep they are placed in hell.” The comparison is drawn from sheep shorn or fattened. As sheep are shorn of their wool, so these people are stripped of all their riches; and as fat sheep are eaten, so they are consumed by fire. “Death shall feed upon them”: that is, punishment will not consume them so that they come to an end, as sheep when eaten come to an end. Rather, death will feed upon them as an ox does not pluck grass up by the roots but clips off the top: it will not diminish their substance, but will always torture them with anguish.

Another translation has: “Death is their shepherd,” and the devil is understood. For as Christ, the Life, is shepherd of the righteous, so the devil, Death, will be shepherd of the impious.

### VERSE 16

“Nevertheless God will redeem my soul [Col. 1593B] from the hand of hell,” that is, from the power of Tartarus, “when he receives me,” that is, when he receives my nature into his divinity and makes me like himself. The voice of Christ warning us follows:

### VERSE 17

“Do not fear [Vulgate: ‘you will fear’] when a man becomes rich and when the glory of his house is multiplied.” A rich person (*dives*) is so called from *divus*, “a god”: one who after death is regarded as a god and is thought, like God, to lack nothing. “Man” here stands for a sinner, who makes himself feared by others while scorning the laws of justice. Riches here mean money; the glory of a house means honours and dignities. Poor people fear such persons. Or many, when they see wicked people flourish in glory and riches while they themselves [Col. 1593C] are in need, fear that human affairs are neglected by God and that everything happens by chance. To these it is said: do not fear a man because he is rich and glorious, neither because of riches nor because of the manifold power of his household.

### VERSE 18

“For when he perishes, he will not take all things,” that is, he will take none of all his riches with him; “nor will his glory descend with him to hell.” Observe that two things called “as if” are ascribed, one to the unjust and the other to the just. When someone wakes from sleep, he says, “I seemed to myself to be eating; I seemed to myself to be drinking.” So after death it will be for the impious: it will seem as if in dreams they had possessed riches and been in glory and honour. But then they will experience themselves in true misery, and all those things as vanished dreams. The righteous, however, are here as if sorrowful, but there truly always rejoicing; here as if possessing nothing, there possessing all things. The impious person, dying, will take with him none of all that he had here except his sins alone, in which he will be tormented in that country. He who gloried in this world over the poor in costly garments will not have his glory descend with him into the deepest abyss, into which he alone will descend without glory, needy, foul, and naked.

### VERSE 19

“For his soul is blessed in his lifetime,” that is, only in this life which is his own, granted to him: he is exalted, praised by his companions, and blessed by flatterers in his desires. “He will praise you when you do him good,” that is, he will praise you when you give him temporal things. Nor will he merely lack these goods, but he will also undergo punishments. For:

### VERSE 20

“He shall enter unto the generations of his fathers,” that is, he will descend to the place to which the imitators of earlier impious persons descended, those who begot them in sins. The generation of the wicked began with Cain, and daily descends into the dark abyss, until at the last all together are sent into outer darkness. Hence it follows: “For ever he will not see light.” Because the impious flee the light of truth here, they will be in perpetual darkness, where, stripped of reason and without knowledge of God, they will always remain. [Col. 1594C] And rightly so, because:

### VERSE 21

“Man, when he was in honour, did not understand God; he was compared in life to irrational beasts and made like them in death.” Because he lived like livestock and, even in dying, did not know God, the eternal light, he will be in darkness and punishments without end. These are the things which the king wished all nations to hear: the enigma which he set forth in the Law and the Gospel. By this solution he instructed all people to prepare themselves for the wedding of the Church.

## PSALM XLIX

[Col. 1593]

[Col. 1593D] “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken,” etc.

## CONCERNING THOSE CAST OUT OF THE WEDDING

The preceding psalm dealt with those who were unwilling to come to the wedding; this one treats those who entered without a wedding garment, whom the king commanded to be cast out. There it is said that those who trust in riches will fear on the evil day; this day is here described, when God will come openly and fire will blaze before him. The main point of the psalm turns on this hinge: first, Christ’s first coming is foretold as that of a bridegroom instituting a wedding; then Christ’s second coming and the separation of good and evil [Col. 1594D] are described, expressed as though a king were entering among those reclining at table and ordering those without wedding garments to be cast out; finally, Christ’s preaching among human beings is indicated as the king’s address to the guests, teaching what is to be done and what avoided. Its title is:

### (VERSE 1) A PSALM OF ASAPH

Asaph was the master of singers, an excellent musician employed by David for singing psalms. The name Asaph means “assembly,” and signifies the synagogue of the faithful people—patriarchs and prophets—foretelling Christ’s coming. This psalm, that is, this hymn, [Col. 1595A] is ascribed to Asaph, that is, to the synagogue of believers, which foretold both comings of Christ, proclaimed in advance the separation of the two peoples, and anticipated the rejection of the old sacrifice and the institution of the new.

This psalm occupies the forty-ninth position. The number is composed of seven repeated seven times and signifies that those clothed in the sevenfold garment of the Spirit are received to the wedding of the eternal feast. The subject of the psalm is the separation of good and evil and the divine instruction of believers. Its purpose is that we may adorn ourselves with good deeds, so that on the evil day we may imitate the joy of the Lord.

The words seem drawn from the history in which the Lord spoke on Mount Sinai and called the earth—that is, the synagogue—when fire blazed before him and there was a strong storm of lightning and thunder, when he gave the Law and separated his people from the nations (Exod. 19:16). And just as he says here, “Hear, my people, and I will speak,” so there he said, “Hear, Israel: your God is one.” It signifies the day of judgment, when the Lord will speak openly to all, when fire will burn up the impious and a storm will envelop them, when he will separate the righteous from the wicked as chaff from grain.

It has three sections. The first is “The God of gods,” in which both comings of Christ and the division of good and evil are described. The second is “Hear, my people,” in which the rejection of the old sacrifice and institution of the new are expressed. The third is “But God said to the sinner,” in which the reprobation of the wicked is indicated. In [Col. 1595C] the preceding psalm, the ranks in the Church were distributed as though the sons of Korah had sung beforehand to the future people; in this psalm the prophets in the synagogue sang beforehand as Asaph.

“The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken.” In Greek God is called **Θεός** (*Theos*), that is, “seeing,” because he beholds simultaneously all things past, present, and future. God is also called “fear,” because he is to be feared by all. Men chosen by God and made participants in divinity are called gods. Thus it is written: “He called them gods, to whom the word of God came” (John 10:35). Angels are not called gods, because not an angel but a human being was assumed into God, in order to be God: “For he nowhere takes hold of angels, but takes hold of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. 2:16). Hence angels who wished to be called gods and worshipped by human beings were condemned by the highest God.

Therefore the God of gods, who are deified by participation in him, and who is Lord over all things, spoke in his own person—he who formerly spoke through angels, patriarchs, and prophets. “Lord” is used lest a servant dare to object if the Lord chooses to change what he established for a time: just as he exchanged animal sacrifice for his own sacrifice, and forbade carnal marriage to priests of the Church though he allowed marriage to priests of the Law. Christ, who is God with the Father and Lord of all things, spoke when God and man was seen on earth and lived among human beings. What did he speak? That which follows: “Hear, my people,” etc.

After speaking, he called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting: that is, through the apostles he called the whole earth to faith, inviting all who inhabit the earth from east to west to his wedding through his sent servants. He shows the order in which this occurred.

### VERSE 2

“From Zion comes the beauty of his splendour.” That is, from Jerusalem, where the citadel or hill of Zion stands. The beauty of his splendour was the radiance of Gospel preaching, which began from Zion—that is, Jerusalem—and reached the farthest part of the earth. Hence it is written: “Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3), because the law of charity was given in Zion through the Holy Spirit, and the Word of the Lord—that is, the Gospel—was first preached to the peoples in Jerusalem after the Spirit was received.

The beauty of splendour is also the institution of the Lord’s body, performed in Zion in the great furnished upper room; he was beautiful in form beyond the sons of men. Or the beauty of splendour was innocence and the virtues, which went forth from Zion—that is, from the primitive Church—when they called the whole earth. And how does he speak?

### Verse 3

God will come openly: that is, God, who is hidden in his nature, will become man and will come visible to all, speaking in his own person—not another God than our God, that is, our Creator, or he who is our God in a singular manner. And he will not be silent: that is, he will not keep silent that he is God of gods and our God. And when he comes, fire will blaze before him: that is, charity will burn in those who look upon him, that is, who understand him to be God. And around him will be a mighty storm: that is, for those who behold only [Col. 1596C] his surrounding part, namely his humanity, there will be blindness and instability, which will drive them into diverse vices.

### Verse 4

He will summon heaven from above: that is, the apostles, who are heaven, so that he himself may be above them; and through them he will summon the earth. Observe the comparison. Heaven rains upon earth; so doctrine flows from the apostles upon the Church. Why did he summon it? To distinguish his people: that is, to distinguish his own earth from that which is not his. Now the person of Asaph comes forward to exhort those heavens.

### Verse 5

Gather to him his saints: that is, bring to him those who are to become holy through him. Who order his covenant above sacrifices: that is, who reckon the sacrifice instituted by him greater than the [Col. 1596D] sacrifices of the Law. Or, who order—that is, establish—the New Testament upon the Old, in which sacrifices are written.

### Verse 6

And the heavens—that is, the same apostles—will proclaim his justice, namely that justification comes from him. For God is judge: that is, they will also proclaim that he himself is Judge, that he will reward those whom he justifies here, and condemn those unwilling to be justified by him.

This may also be understood concerning Christ’s second coming. “From Zion comes the beauty of his splendor”: that is, he will be born from Zion and appear humble, not exercising power over the wicked in that coming. But at last God will come openly. He is called manifest, as a feast day is called so from the morning [Col. 1597A] onward, because the entire day is devoted to sacrifices. The day of judgment will be a feast day for the good, but a hostile day for the wicked. On that day he will not come hidden, as formerly in humility, but will openly show himself to be God. Our God, the God of Christians, will come and will not be silent in vengeance—he who here was silent in punishment. Fire will blaze before him: that is, in his presence the fire will burn in which the ungodly, burdened by crimes, will remain; this fire, as it is said, will reach as high as the flood rose. And around him will be a mighty storm: that is, angels will be in his service, separating the wicked from among the righteous, as a storm separates chaff from grain. This storm is not made by winds or tempests; rather, by divine power there arises a vehement spirit of angelic ministry, to winnow the Lord’s threshing-floor and separate the wicked from the good [Col. 1597B]. This judgment is called a storm because it will come unexpectedly. It will be mighty, that is, powerful, because with instantaneous swiftness it will distinguish every kind of human being according to merits.

At the judgment there will be four classes, two on the right and two on the left. One class is of the perfect, judging with Christ: such as apostles, martyrs, monks, and virgins. Another is of the imperfect, receiving the kingdom through judgment: such as married persons and penitents. A third class is of the ungodly, perishing without judgment: such as pagans or Jews. The fourth is of the evil, perishing through judgment: such as evil Christians, or Jews before Christ’s coming. Concerning these classes the following is said: “He will summon heaven from above, and the earth, to distinguish his people”: that is, coming from above, he will summon through his angels heaven and earth [Col. 1597C], to distinguish heaven from earth, and his earth from earth that is not his. Heaven denotes the perfect, who will judge; earth denotes those who bear fruit, who will be judged unto life by these words: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning. For I was hungry, and you gave me food,” etc. (Matt. 25:34–35). Thorny earth denotes the unfruitful, barren in good works, who will be condemned through judgment by these words: “Depart from me, cursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” etc. (Matt. 25:41 ff.). The utterly wicked are swallowed up by hell without judgment.

Or: “He will summon heaven from above and earth from below” [Col. 1597D]: that is, he will bring with him from heaven to judgment all the angels; and he will cause all human beings to come from the earth to meet him. Then he will distinguish his people from a people not his own, when he places the righteous as sheep on the right and the ungodly as goats on the left. All this is done through the angels, to whom it is now said: “Gather to him his saints, who order his covenant above sacrifices.” That is: you angels, gather the saints from among the wicked and present them to him—those who understand his promises as surpassing their works and reckon the future reward greater than their works in this life. Then the angels will gather those who do iniquity and cast them into the furnace of fire. And the heavens will proclaim his justice, because God is judge: that is, the righteous will show, not by speech but by their [Col. 1598A] glorification, that he is a just judge, when they go into eternal life and the wicked into eternal punishment. For although the storm is mighty, it removes no grain from the wheat’s portion to the chaff, because it is not any rustic with a fork, but God the Trinity, who with just judgment will winnow, gathering the tares into unquenchable fire and the wheat into the barn.

When those who entered without a wedding garment have been cast out from the wedding feast, the King addresses the invited guests who remained within:

### Verse 7

Hear, my people, and I will speak: that is, my people called by my name, not Pharaoh’s people, hear by obeying, and I will speak by commanding what will benefit you. Israel—that is, “one who sees God”—instructed by the Law and the prophets, be Israel, chosen and blessed through faith and love [Col. 1598B]; and I will testify to you, that is, I will establish by testimonies that I, whom you see as man, am God, and none other than your God. “I am” is fitting for divinity, as both Laws indicate: the Old, which says, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14); and the New, which adds, “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8:58). *Sum* (“I am”) has three letters and one syllable, and sets forth Trinity in unity; the letters themselves also suggest this, since *sator* (“sower”) is found for the Father, *veritas* (“truth”) for the Son, and *munus* (“gift”) for the Holy Spirit. He is *sum* to himself; to us he is called *est* (“is”). It follows:

### Verse 8

I will not rebuke you concerning your sacrifices: that is, I will no longer rebuke you concerning all your sacrifices. He prohibits the sacrifices of the Law in order to establish his own sacrifice, as the master of a household forbids guests [Col. 1598C] to offer cattle and birds for a banquet, so that they may consume what he himself has prepared. “I will not rebuke you concerning sacrifices of the Law. Your burnt offerings are always before me”: that is, if you consume your whole self in my service, this has pleased me and will always please me. He used “burnt offerings” only because of its interpretation, not because of the sacrifice itself, because a burnt offering is called something wholly burned. What he rejects follows:

### Verse 9

I will not take calves from your house: that is, if you possess them, do not offer them; nor offer goats from your flocks. By these two sacrifices he indicates all the other things of the Old Law to be excluded, which had been instituted as signs; nevertheless, they are to be offered as a tithe [Col. 1598D]. For this reason he also promised that the Temple, the place of sacrifice, would be destroyed, because he willed that all things should be offered spiritually. He gives the reason why he will not take them:

### Verse 10

For all the wild beasts of the forests are mine, the cattle on the mountains, and the oxen. As there are domestic beasts, so there are wild beasts; and as there are domestic oxen, so there are wild oxen. All these belong to God, because he created all things.

### Verse 11

I know all the birds of heaven, and the beauty of the field is with me: that is, the birds are mine, and the crops are with me—that is, in my power. God’s knowledge is one thing, human knowledge another. Before they existed, God knew all things as they are today, because if he had not known them, he would not have created them. For all things were life in [Col. 1599A] him, and everything that ever is or will be is always with him, so that, if all things were reduced to nothing, all would be found entire in him. Note that offerings were made from birds and crops. God no longer wishes to receive these sacrifices for sins, but the sacrifice of justice.

This may also be understood otherwise. The wild beasts of the forests signify the nations that wandered among the groves of the world in savage superstition. The cattle on the mountains are the simple persons established in the Catholic Church, known to dwell upon the summit of faith. The oxen signify the apostles and prophets, who labored continually in the Lord’s field. The birds of heaven are the higher powers, such as angelic authorities, who are spiritually moved from place to place with swift motion by holy will. The beauty [Col. 1599B] of the field is the splendor of the Church. All these belong to God, and he knows them all individually, because he has ordered everything in measure, number, and weight. Hence follows:

### Verse 12

If I were hungry, I would not tell you; for the world is mine and its fullness. The Lord neither hungers nor thirsts, but says this in our manner: I ask nothing earthly for your sins, because the earth is mine and all that is in it is mine. And lest anyone suppose that God delights in these things, it is said:

### Verse 13

Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? What madman would believe this? I will not taste it. By these words the faithful are prohibited from legal sacrifice, and directed to distribute such things to the poor as an acceptable sacrifice [Col. 1599C]. He has now said what he does not want from his people; he adds what he wants from Israel:

### Verse 14

Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise: that is, offer to me, your God, devotion of heart, confession of mouth, and persistence in good work—a sacrifice by which God is praised. And pay your vows to the Most High: that is, reckon that you have this from the most powerful God. For we call that “rendering” which we have received from the same person.

### Verse 15

And call upon me in the day of tribulation: that is, if you do this, then you will be able safely to call upon me on the day of your death, and I will deliver you from the tribulation which you will then see, and you will honor me. Thus I will deliver you, so that afterward I will make you praise me always. At the departure of each person from this life, evil spirits immediately come forward [Col. 1599D], accusing the soul; and then a certain judgment of the soul takes place, as it is related that the soul of Moses was met by unclean spirits. Whoever is delivered then will be placed in eternal rest. Whoever lived well is then delivered from the tribulation seen to be imminent; whoever lived badly is handed over to punishments until he pays the last farthing—that is, pays the penalty for the smallest sin. But because many praise God with their mouths and not with works, it follows:

### Verse 16

But God said to the sinner. Asaph presents the words of God. Why do you recount my justice? That is, why do you recount to others the Scriptures in which my acts of justice are contained, by which I justify, advance, and reward? Why do you take my covenant upon your mouth? That is, my Scripture, in which I declare [Col. 1600A] my intentions? It is one thing to expound to others, another to take something up for oneself—as when one sings the hours or makes prayer, which one does only for oneself. The mouth ought to be righteous in matter, which recounts the Lord’s acts of justice, because “praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9). This is understood especially of heretics and of those who speak well but live badly, saying: God will not destroy us, through whose mouth he has willed such great goods to be spoken to his people. Of these it follows:

### Verse 17

But you hated discipline. Discipline is correction. God rebukes and chastises those whom he loves: for he “scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 11:6). When God scourges one who teaches well and lives badly, he hates God’s discipline and murmurs against the merciful punishment inflicted. Hence follows: [Col. 1600B] And you cast my word behind you: that is, you recount it with your mouth, but despise my commandments by your deeds. How?

### Verse 18

When you saw a thief, you ran with him: that is, you consented, by giving counsel, encouragement, or working with him. And with adulterers you placed your portion: consenting to that deed. The same is to be understood concerning all sins. And you despised me not only in deeds but also in words.

### Verse 19

Your mouth overflowed with malice. Openly you spoke every evil thing against your brother who lived rightly, calling him a pretender, hypocrite, and deceiver. And your tongue fashioned deceits. To fashion is to compose skillfully. By artful composition you mixed [Col. 1600C] deceits with good words.

In the Hebrew it reads: “You have let loose your mouth for evil, and your tongue has embraced deceitfulness”; that is, you were malicious in heart and deceitful in words.

### Verses 20–21

Sitting, you spoke against your brother. Sitting is characteristic of one who remains. He wishes every human being to be understood as “brother,” for we are all born from Adam and Eve and are therefore brothers. “Sitting, you spoke”: that is, with deliberate and persevering intent, you heaped malice and deceits upon your neighbor. And against the son of your mother you placed a stumbling-block: that is, against a child of the Church—which you falsely suppose to be your mother—you set an offense by speaking wickedly and deceitfully. You did these and similar things, and I was silent concerning vengeance. And because I did not immediately punish you,

[Col. 1600D] you wickedly thought that I would be like you. If iniquity pleased God, he would be like a human being, who takes pleasure in what he does. You unjustly thought that I was like you in this: that iniquity pleased me as it pleased you, because I did not punish it. But a time will come when I shall appear like you: when I rebuke you, that is, convict you of having lived badly, and set you before your face—you who now place yourself behind your own back.

In the Hebrew it is read thus: “You thought that I would be like you; I will rebuke you and set you before your eyes.” Now sinners cast their sins behind their backs and refuse to look upon them through repentance; at judgment they will see their own foulness before their eyes. Therefore they will grieve in everlasting confusion.

### Verse 22

Understand these things, you who forget God [Col. 1601A]: that is, you who have forgotten that God will judge, observe that I shall rebuke you for sins and set you before your face—that is, I shall convict you through your own selves. Therefore correct yourselves now, lest at some time he seize you and there be none to deliver: that is, lest at last he cause you to be seized by the devil through his judgment, and then none will deliver you, though now you can be delivered from him. And what do you wish us to do? I shall tell you:

### Verse 23

A sacrifice of praise will honor me: that is, I want you to offer me a sacrifice of praise, not of cattle: believe with the heart, praise with the mouth, and perform good works with your hands. And there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God [Col. 1602A]: that is, in that sacrifice is the way by which I shall lead him to the vision of the Son of God; that is, through this sacrifice he will come to knowledge of me.

In the Hebrew it reads: “He who sacrifices confession glorifies me; and he who orders his way, to him I will show the salvation of God.” That is, whoever walks rightly on the way of love, praising God, will come to see God’s face, where he will behold the Son of God in equality with the Father, as it is written: “He who loves me will be loved by me, and I will manifest myself to him” (John 14:21). These are the things which God, the Lord God of gods, spoke to his people Israel.

## Psalm L

[Col. 1601]

[Col. 1601B] “Have mercy upon me, O God, according to …” This psalm is designated the fourth of the penitential psalms, because a person is made perfect through the four virtues—prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. The seven penitential psalms are so arranged because sins are forgiven through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The first is assigned to the Spirit of fear, the second to the Spirit of piety, the third to the Spirit of knowledge, and this fourth to the Spirit of fortitude, which is reckoned one of the four principal virtues. In this psalm humility and prayer are especially emphasized, through which sins are most fully remitted.

It is placed in the fiftieth position because the fiftieth day is written as the number leading to Pentecost, and it signifies the joy which the penitent obtains through pardon. This [Col. 1601C] was expressed by the fiftieth year, called the Jubilee, that is, “full of jubilation,” in which the people recovered their lost inheritance and the person sold returned to lost freedom. Thus, through repentance, the lost inheritance of paradise is recovered and one returns to former freedom. For a person conquered by desire is sold under sin, since everyone who commits sin becomes a slave of sin. In the number fifty, ten is multiplied five times, because after the five ages of the world Christ, the salvation of humankind and the tenfold reward of life, is brought forth; through him the Holy Spirit, who is the forgiveness of sins, is given. The title of this psalm is:

(Vv. 1–2.) **Unto the end, a psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, when he entered in to Bathsheba.**

[Col. 1601D] The story is well known. Uriah, one of David’s commanders, had a beautiful wife. The king, seeing her bathing, desired her, ordered her brought to him, and lay with her. Meanwhile her husband was stationed with the army in the siege of a certain city, but through David’s plan he was killed. After this was done, the Lord sent the prophet Nathan to David. Nathan presented him with the parable of the sheep and the guest, by which he charged him with the sin he had committed. David, recognizing the crime he had committed and terrified by the Lord’s dreadful threat, [Col. 1602B] did penance from the heart, composed this psalm as satisfaction, and obtained again his former grace from the Lord (2 Kings 12).

This psalm, therefore, is ascribed to David the king and prophet, who looked unto the end—that is, to Christ—through whom he saw that his sin would be forgiven, when the prophet Nathan came to him, when he entered in to Bathsheba: that is, when Nathan the prophet reproved him for the adultery committed with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah.

Nathan, who instructed David concerning repentance, is said to mean “he gave,” and signifies the order of teachers who give the faithful people counsel concerning repentance. He presented the parable concerning sheep because the good shepherd laid down his life for the sheep. In the literal sense, moreover, [Col. 1602C] the man who had many sheep was David, who had many wives; the poor man who had one sheep was Uriah, who had only one wife; and the guest for whom the poor man’s sheep was killed is unlawful desire, which is fed by intercourse with the wife. Notice that lust was a guest with David, but held a kingdom with Solomon.

The falls of the saints are written in order that the power of the physician may be commended for the healing of a despairing patient, and that those who have fallen may be encouraged by their example to hope for pardon. But fools take from the saints a model for sinning and reject the model for repenting.

Since David’s sin was imputed to him by God as to other human beings and was even strictly avenged in him, it is asked why he is presented as a figure. But one must know [Col. 1602D] that God chose the Israelite people from the entire human race as a figure; that people was the shadow of the Christian people. For whatever it did, even unknowingly, foreshadowed something that would happen at some time. Yet especially what the Holy Spirit wished to be written through the prophets concerning them or all peoples of former times was a figure of things to come. Hence it is written: “All things happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. 10:11). David, therefore, bore the figure of Christ; Bathsheba, that of the Church; and Uriah, the image of the devil. And just as she, while bathing in the fountain of Kidron [Col. 1603A], stripped of her garments, pleased David and deserved to come to royal embraces, while her husband was also slain by royal command: so the Church—that is, the assembly of the faithful—cleansed from the filth of sins through the washing of sacred baptism, is known to be joined to Christ the Lord; and the devil, through the apostles’ assault, has been brought to nothing. The names themselves also suggest this. David means “beloved”; Bathsheba, “well of the covenant”; Uriah is called “the glory of my God,” and denotes the devil, who claimed for himself the glory of his God, saying: “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14). He is also called, “My light is God,” signifying him who “transforms himself into an angel of light” (1 Cor. 11:14).

Just as Bathsheba did not suffer intercourse with her former [Col. 1603B] husband after she was joined to David, so the Church was not joined to the devil after she came to Christ the Beloved, who was the expectation of the nations. She was the well of the covenant because the depth of the Old Law lay hidden in her. Uriah perished through David’s plan, and the devil lost the Gentile world through Christ’s plan. Do not be surprised that Christ is figured by an adulterer, the Church designated by an adulteress, and the devil signified by a chaste man. There is no addition to ugliness if it is indicated by golden letters; nor is anything taken away from honor if it is denoted by letters in ink.

The subject of this psalm is the prayer of the penitent David. Its purpose is to instruct us by David’s example in repentance and prayer. This prayer brings great benefit to the faithful: so that the righteous person may not [Col. 1603C] trust in his own righteousness when he sees the most righteous David fall, and the sinner may not despair when he hears that so great a sinner obtained pardon.

The words are drawn from David’s own repentance and are fitting for every faithful person who, after falling, has recourse to the Lord with satisfaction and prayer. “For if thou hadst willed” is drawn from the history in which God rejected Cain’s sacrifice because he did not offer righteousness (Gen. 4). Or it is understood from the history in which the Lord despised Saul’s sacrifice because he neglected to render obedience. It signifies that God rejects the offering of one who scorns to offer charity and humility. “Deal favorably” is drawn from the future history when Jerusalem is destroyed by the Babylonians but [Col. 1603D] rebuilt by Zerubbabel and Jesus the priest, and an acceptable sacrifice is offered to God; or from the history in which Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans but rebuilt again by the Emperor Hadrian, in which Christians now offer sacrifices acceptable to God. It signifies that Zion, that is, the Church, is destroyed here by pagans and heretics, but is rebuilt from living stones into the heavenly Jerusalem through Jesus, the high priest and king, Christ.

This psalm is divided into five parts because repentance is performed for the guilt of the five senses. The first is: “Have mercy upon me, O God,” in which is the penitent’s satisfaction. The second is: “Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop,” in which is confidence in mercy. The third: “Turn away thy face,” in which is reverence for the Trinity. The fourth: [Col. 1604A] “I will teach the wicked,” in which is the penitent’s future preaching. The fifth: “Deal favorably,” in which the acceptance of repentance is noted.

In the preceding psalm dreadful judgment is described, and the gentle admonition of the King is added. Therefore, when the sinner hears Jesus say, “Why do you recount my acts of justice?” he is terrified and runs to the Judge with the sacrifice of repentance, saying:

### Verse 3

Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy great mercy. God’s mercy is so great that it brought down the Creator of the world from heaven, clothed him in an earthly body, made him equal to us in mortality though equal to the Father in eternity; imposed the form of a servant upon the Lord of the world, so that the living bread himself might hunger, the fountain of life thirst, strength become weak, and almighty life die. [Col. 1604B] It was great mercy that the Creator should be created for us, the Ruler serve, the Redeemer be sold, the Exalter be humbled, and the Giver of life be killed. According to the measure of this great mercy, have mercy upon me. Christ is the fountain of mercy, in which David, Peter, Zacchaeus, Paul, Mary, the thief, and countless others were washed. Concerning this it follows:

And according to the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my iniquity. The multitude of God’s mercies is greater than the multitude of all sinners. Because thy mercy is manifold and my misery great, according to the measure of thy abundant mercies blot out the greatness of my iniquity. The comparison is drawn from wax upon which an ugly image has been impressed; when that image is erased, the wax is reshaped to receive a beautiful image. [Col. 1604C] For only that person is written in the book of life whose every iniquity is blotted out.

### Verse 4

Wash me yet more from my iniquity. You first washed me in the font of baptism; now wash me yet more in the fountain of tears. And cleanse me from my sin. You washed me in baptism from original sin; now cleanse me from actual sin.

### Verse 5

For I acknowledge my iniquity; therefore forgive me, because I punish it with tears; therefore mercifully spare me. And my sin is always before me: that is, like a horrible image it stands before me, which I always behold, with eyes open or closed, and which I desire to destroy by praying and weeping. Above it is said: “I will rebuke you and set your sins before [Col. 1604D] your face.” The penitent anticipates this and places his sin before himself, always beholding and lamenting it. True repentance is both to grieve for sins committed and not to commit sins that must be grieved for. Therefore I pray to thee, because:

### Verse 6

Against thee alone have I sinned, and done evil before thee, who alone art without sin and alone art good. Note that he addresses Christ himself, the source of mercy. All human beings are held bound by the chains of sins; thou alone art true and just. So that thou mayest be justified in thy words when thou sayest, “Which of you shall convict me of sin?” (John 8:46); and the Prophet says of thee, “He committed no sin” (1 Pet. 2:22); and, “The prince of this world will come to thee and find nothing of his own” (John 14:30). And thou dost surpass [Col. 1605A] all human beings in justice when thou art judged by the unjust, who say: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 26:6); and, “If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to thee” (John 18:30).

Otherwise: Against thee alone, who art King of kings, have I sinned, and done evil before thee, who beholdest all things and promised that thou wouldst be born from my line. But now all the people say: Christ will not be born from David, who committed such a sin; and therefore thy promise is rendered void in human opinion. Therefore forgive my sin, so that thou mayest be justified in thy words by fulfilling thy promise, lest thou appear deceitful rather than true; and prevail when thou art judged by worldly people, who say that because of my many sins thou ought not to fulfill those things. Make it plain that the words concerning the promise made to me will be fulfilled, not because of my merits but through thy justice alone [Col. 1605B]. Thou alone art just in thyself; others are just through thee.

### Verse 7

For behold, I was conceived in iniquities: that is, in original sin, because all sinned in Adam. And in sins my mother conceived me. David was not born from adultery, but from Jesse, a just man, and his wife; nor is marital intercourse sinful. But because a mortal is propagated from mortal parents, he is deservedly said to be conceived in sins. Death is the punishment of sin, possessed from parents as an inheritance but transmitted through the desire of the flesh. Christ, however, who was conceived without desire, was begotten without sin; yet he was mortal not by nature but by will, and thus conquered all things.

[Col. 1605C]

### Verse 8

For behold, thou hast loved truth: that is, confession. Behold, it is apparent that thou didst first love to produce truth in me—that is, knowledge of sin—and repentance, because thou didst first will it in me. Thou hast made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of thy wisdom: that is, thou hast revealed to me the mysteries of thy Son, which indeed thou hast revealed to many, but hast shown surely to me: first, that I might know that thou hast a Son; then, that I might know that he would come from my seed, so that I might foretell his passion and resurrection as though seen. Therefore:

### Verse 9

Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed: that is, thou shalt cleanse me through the blood of the Son of God. The history is alluded to. Blood was sprinkled upon the leper with a bundle of hyssop, and he became clean (Lev. 14). That blood signified the blood of the Son of God, by which lepers in body and soul are cleansed. [Col. 1605D] Hyssop is a small herb that restrains swelling of the lungs. It signifies Christ’s humility, by which he offered himself to God. Hyssop is said to penetrate rock with its root; that rock is Christ.

Thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow: that is, thou shalt purify me through the washing of baptism, and I shall be whiter than snow. The soul has its own brightness, as the body has its own. Among all visible creatures nothing is whiter than snow, beyond which is the soul’s brightness in the body. And after thou hast done this:

### Verse 10

Thou shalt give joy and gladness to my hearing. Above thou saidst, “Hear, my people, and I will speak.” Behold, I hear obediently what thou commandest and do not contradict; [Col. 1606A] and to this hearing of mine thou shalt give joy and gladness. Joy pertains to absolution from sin; gladness, to receiving everlasting life. He will give joy and gladness to hearing when he says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom,” etc. (Matt. 25:34). Upon hearing this voice, the humbled bones—that is, the supports of the soul weakened in repentance—will rejoice. By “bones” are also understood reason and free will, bent down in sins. These will rejoice when thou restorest strength to reason and capacity for free will. For while a person delights in sins, reason is blinded and free will weakened. “That thou mayest give joy and gladness to my hearing.”

### Verse 11

Turn thy face away from my sins. For God to look upon or remember our sins is to will [Col. 1606B] to punish them; to turn his face from sins or forget them is to will not to punish them. Yet God always sees the deeds and thoughts of all people, and never forgets, for all past and future things are present to him. And blot out all my iniquities. Blot out original and actual sins: that is, forgive them, since our committed crime is as though written upon certain tablets while it is held in divine knowledge. And not only forgive sins, but also:

### Verse 12

Create a clean heart in me, O God. Thou who canst do this, cleanse my soul from the darkness of ignorance, so that I may behold and understand thee purely. “Create” is here used for “restore.” Create a clean heart: that is, give a pure understanding. The heart is used for understanding because the source of thoughts [Col. 1606C] is said to be in it. The Lord says, “Thoughts proceed from the heart” (Matt. 15:49). Hence the heart is also cone-shaped, bearing the image of fire, so that it is fittingly formed in such a position as may provide counsel for us. The natural philosophers also teach that the heart is formed first in a human being.

And renew a right spirit in my inward parts. Give again wisdom—that is, give thy Son to my understanding—so that I may be able to act well, because he is the rule of every right action. It is not the spirit but the person who is renewed when reformed from the oldness of sin.

### Verse 13

Cast me not away from thy face. A person is cast away from God’s face when he is scorned as beyond cure. Renew me thus, so that [Col. 1606D] thou no longer cast me away from conformity with him, which is thy face, through whom thou art known; and do not permit me further to transgress thy rule. And take not thy Holy Spirit from me: namely, the Spirit of prophecy or of love.

### Verse 14

Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation: that is, make me possess joy in the salvation of thy Son. He recognizes that he has lost the grace of the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit flees sinners and does not dwell in a body subjected to sins. And strengthen me with a principal spirit, lest I sin again or depart from thee through instability of mind. Here the Trinity is expressly set forth: in the principal Spirit, the Father; in the right Spirit, the Son; and in the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit himself. Yet he is not called the principal Spirit because he is [Col. 1607A] earlier in time or greater, but because the Son and the Holy Spirit are said to be from him, whereas he is not said to be from them. If thou do this and grant me those things for which I have asked:

### Verse 15

I will teach the wicked thy ways: that is, I will instruct other sinners in thy mercy and justice by word and example; and through me the ungodly will turn to thee from error.

### Verse 16

Deliver me from bloods, O God, God of my salvation. In the singular, “blood” is understood as a bodily part, the human being himself, or offspring: a bodily part, as where it says, “Blood came forth from the Lord’s side”; a human being, as where it says, “Flesh and blood has not revealed it to thee” (Matt. 16:17); offspring, as in “of high blood,” that is, born of noble stock. In the plural, “bloods” means sins or deaths. The God of salvation is Christ, through [Col. 1607B] whom salvation is given to believers. O God of all, who art the God of my salvation, deliver me from deaths. He uses “bloods” for deaths because death comes through the shedding of blood. He had incurred many deaths: one by which he killed himself through sinning; another by which he killed Bathsheba in soul; a third by which he treacherously killed Uriah.

And my tongue shall rejoice in thy justice: that is, if thou do this, my tongue will then joyfully declare to others thy justice, by which thou forgivest sins and advance people in good works. Above it is said: “Why do you recount my acts of justice and take my covenant upon your mouth?” (Ps. XVI [as printed]). Now, freed from guilt, he joyfully recounts God’s justice. Hence follows:

[Col. 1607C] **VERSE 17.** “Lord, you will open my lips.” Those lips which guilt had closed you will make fit and clean for proclaiming your righteousness. “And then my mouth will declare your praise,” that is, the praises of your righteousness. Those who sin do not dare to speak, lest they be rebuked and their sins reproached to them. Their lips are opened for speech when, repenting of their sins, they are justified; then, enlivened by the Spirit of God, they despise human glory and hold human praise and reproach equally in contempt, freely rebuking sinners, as Paul did. Their mouths proclaim God’s praise when they declare their sins before people, so that others may take from their salvation an example of conversion. I offer the praise of God as a sacrifice, not animal sacrifice:

**VERSE 18.** “For if you had wished sacrifice, I would have given it.” [Col. 1607D] But I understand that you do not desire sacrifice from sinners, because you said above: “I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks” (Ps. 49:9). Certainly you will not delight in whole burnt offerings, namely those of animals offered. But since such things were offered figuratively, which you now refuse to accept for sins, I know what kind of sacrifice you do accept.

**VERSE 19.** “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God,” that is, a spirit grieved for sins will be an acceptable sacrifice. “A contrite heart,” that is, one afflicted and humbled by repentance—devoted through a pious confession—“you will not despise, O God,” as you do the sacrifices of the Law. I foresee that such a sacrifice will be offered to you by Zion. And therefore:

**VERSE 20.** “Deal graciously, Lord, in your good will with Zion, that the walls of your Jerusalem may be built.” By [Col. 1608A] Zion is denoted the knowledge of God; by Jerusalem, charity. Jerusalem is one city, composed of angels and human beings, a part of which was destroyed through Adam. For it he prays: “Deal graciously,” that is, act generously, giving faith and every good manner of life to those who are to become Zion; and do this “in your good will,” that is, by your grace, “that the walls of Jerusalem may be built” through the elect among humankind, who were destroyed among the apostate angels.

Or: deal graciously with Zion, that is, with the primitive Church from the Jews; and let the walls of Jerusalem be built, that is, through it establish the Church from the Gentiles. Or let the walls of Jerusalem be built from Jews and Gentiles in faith and love; deal graciously with them by granting perseverance and reward.

Zion, which means “watching,” is the present Church; Jerusalem, which signifies “vision of peace,” [Col. 1608B] is the Church reigning in heaven, which is built of living stones. Therefore deal graciously with Zion, that is, with the present Church, by granting sinners pardon and confession, so that through them the walls of Jerusalem may be built: that is, through such stones the number of the elect in the heavenly Jerusalem may be restored to completeness. The walls of Jerusalem are angels and human beings.

**VERSE 21.** “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness.” That is, then the sacrifice of a contrite spirit and broken heart will be especially acceptable to you. “Then you will receive offerings and whole burnt offerings,” namely, believers offering themselves wholly to you and distributing their possessions to the poor.

Or the sacrifice of righteousness is the Lord’s body, sacrificed for us as a lamb; the offerings are confessors, or any believers offering themselves to Christ through faith and [Col. 1608C] works; the whole burnt offerings are martyrs consumed by the fire of suffering or by any bodily torment.

“Then they shall place calves upon your altar,” namely, the priests of the Church. God’s altar is Christ; calves are Christians newly born in faith and renewed in baptism. As calves divide the hoof, so they distinguish good from evil; they chew the cud, that is, they recall to memory the words of God which they have received; and they are armed with horns, that is, strengthened by the mighty examples of the saints. These calves are placed upon the altar when, through the Church’s priests, they are offered to God through Christ; and thus the walls of Jerusalem are restored through this.

[Col. 1608D] Alternatively: now, in the present life, you accept as a sacrifice for sin a contrite spirit; in the future, you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness—praise alone—where those dwelling in your house forever and ever will praise you. For this is the sacrifice of righteousness. Then the righteous will be offering and whole burnt offering, when the divine fire consumes them wholly, and souls are clothed with wisdom, bodies with immortality, and death is swallowed up in victory. The calves will be all the elect, freed from the bonds of the Law and of misery, young in a new age, placed upon Christ the altar, in whom they will rest without end.

This psalm is therefore frequently used by penitents, so that through its calf they may, like David, be built into the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem. Note that the penitent first laments the sins personally committed, then proclaims to others God’s mercy, [Col. 1609A] and finally prays for those who err. It is sung at Lauds in Lent because through repentance one comes to eternal praise. It is also sung at Lauds on ordinary weekdays, [Col. 1610A] because those who escape the darkness of sins come to true light and eternal joy. For this reason it is often repeated at the Hours, so that every believer, a living stone, may, like David, be set in the heavenly building.

## PART SIX

[Col. 1609]

## THE PROLOGUE OF GERHOH BEGINS

[Col. 1609B] In the first fifty psalms, as has been shown far above, the mysteries of faith are sung. In the second group of fifty, hope; in the third, charity is declared. Therefore, having crossed, with God’s help, the first fifty as though they were a shady and dense mountain, and having dealt with the entangled questions customarily raised concerning the mystery of faith—while faith, as the distinguished and divine poet says,

> First seeks the field under the doubtful fortune of battle,

that is, about to fight against heresies and other objections—we descend to plainer, level country. There, unlike above, we wish to proceed not through the winding paths of questions and digressions, but entirely straight ahead, God leading us.

Therefore, reader, do not expect here excursions against the novelties and [Col. 1609C] abuses of this age, or against the cavillers at this work of ours. These have in some measure been answered in the first fifty. Rather, with a favorable mind support the running course of the pen; harden your ears against the Sirens’ songs—that is, disregard the objections of fools, which seem already sufficiently answered—and let us hasten to shore, first invoking the Holy Spirit, that he may deign to be present to us with a favorable wind, lest some spirit of error obstruct or delay our voyage as we hurry toward harbor.

The first fifty psalms instruct a person in faith; the last restore that person, now at peace in charity after the wars, and stir him to the praise of his helper. The middle portion of the psalms—that is, the fifty psalms which, God helping, we are now to sing—especially concerns that intermediate state of the human being of which the Apostle speaks under the person of the weak, still struggling in an uncertain contest: “I delight,” he says, “in the law of God according to the inward human being; but I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind,” etc. (Rom. 7:22–23).

For those reborn and, through faith in Christ, granted remission of past sins, although sprinkled with hyssop, cleansed, and made whiter than snow as they emerge from baptism, are not yet secure, since they enter into battle and conflict with a most savage enemy. Clearly, in such a duel both hope and fear are necessary: the combatant must hope to conquer and fear being conquered, especially in a contest where the heavenly palace lies open to the victor and the [Col. 1610B] infernal prison to the defeated. Accordingly, we rightly recognize that in this middle part of the Psalms we are suitably summoned to hope, which is necessary after faith. Therefore the recapitulations which we call *periochae* begin not, as hitherto, from Christ’s first advent, but from his second, when his wrath is most to be feared and his mercy most to be hoped for; when the defeated hear, “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41), and the victors, “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34). Then the foremost victors will be judges together with God. But those now shamefully defeated through unbelief have already been judged; and therefore the ungodly, who are then to be judged, will not rise in the judgment, because, as was said, they have already been judged.

[Col. 1610C] Look upward at the victors, already crowned in heaven; look likewise at those defeated in battle, now buried in punishment in the Tartarean prison. And you, still standing between them in the battle, arm yourself with both hope and fear; take up and hold weapons on the right and the left, as you are more fully instructed in these middle psalms. For, so that you may plainly recognize that, as the Apostle says, “Tribulation produces patience; patience, testing; and testing, hope” (Rom. 5:3–4), David’s principal tribulations are set forth beforehand in these psalms, comprehended in his seven persecutions.

Here the persecutions endured by David must now be counted. The first was when Saul threw a spear in order to pin him to the wall, and David evaded it and fled [Col. 1610D] (1 Sam. 18:11). The second was when, after he had struck the Philistines with a great slaughter, Saul again attempted to pin David to the wall while he was playing, and, as he evaded it, the spear was driven with an ineffective blow into the wall (1 Sam. 19:10). The third was when David fled and came to Achish king of Gath, and Saul killed the priests of the Lord on his account (1 Sam. 22). The fourth was when the Ziphites reported, saying, “Behold, David is hiding among us,” and Saul rose and pursued David in the wilderness of Maon (1 Sam. 23:19 ff.). When David despaired of being able to escape, a messenger came to Saul, saying, “Hurry and come, for the Philistines have poured over the land” (1 Sam. 24).

The fifth was in the wilderness of En-gedi, when Saul entered a cave to relieve himself, and David rose and silently cut off the edge of his cloak. The sixth was when the Ziphites again reported, saying, “Behold, David is hidden in the valley of Achilah”; Saul rose and went down into the wilderness of Ziph. When Saul slept, Abishai said, “Today God has shut up your enemy into your hands. Now then I shall pierce him once with the spear into the ground, and there will be no need for a second blow.” David said, “Do not kill him” (1 Sam. 26:8). And subsequently: “May the Lord be gracious to me, that I should not stretch out my hand against the Lord’s anointed. Now therefore take the spear which is at his head and the cup of water, and let us go” (ibid., v. 11), and the rest.

The seventh and final persecution was when David said in his heart: “One day I shall fall into Saul’s hands. Is it not better that I flee and save myself in the land of the Philistines, so that Saul may despair and cease seeking me throughout all the territories of Israel? Thus I shall escape [Col. 1611B] his hands.” David rose and went, he and six hundred men with him, to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath (1 Sam. 27:1–2).

By these seven persecutions of David are signified all the persecutions which the devil has stirred up against Christ and his Church. The number seven commonly denotes universality. Thus in Revelation that great red dragon, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, is written to have seven heads, by which are signified all kings who have stirred persecutions against Christ and his holy Church (Rev. 17:7). Moreover, the persecutions endured by Christ in his own person were also seven.

[Col. 1611C] The first was when, according to Matthew, deadly Herod sought his life immediately after his birth and killed infants on his account. The second was when, according to Luke, he came to the place where he had been raised and, already playing the harp—that is, preaching in order to soothe Saul’s fury, namely so that the malignant spirit, possessor or agitator of the Jews, who had already begun to rage against him, might be quieted—“they rose up,” he says, “and cast him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the hill upon which their city was built, so that they might throw him down. But he, passing through their midst, went away” (Luke 4:29–30).

The third was when, according to John, he fled from the face of the mocking Jews. He fled, I say, when he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink [Col. 1611D] his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). For in saying this he truly fled and hid himself from them, according to the title of Psalm 33, inscribed thus: “A psalm of David, when he changed his appearance before Abimelech, and he dismissed him, and went away.”

The fourth persecution was when the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him. When they returned and were asked, “Why did you not bring him?” they answered, “Never has a human being spoken as this man speaks” (John 7:46). But they, persisting in their purpose, brought a woman caught in adultery, testing him so that they might accuse him. The fifth persecution was when he said, “Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am,” and they took up stones [Col. 1612A] to throw at him (John 8:59). The sixth was when he said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and the Jews took up stones to stone him. The seventh and final persecution was when they assembled a council against him and did not cease until they crucified him.

It should indeed be noted that in the persecutions of David as well as in those of Christ, glory always followed tribulation as its companion, which may readily be observed from the acts of both. For example, when Saul first threw the spear, thinking that he could pin David to the wall, there immediately follows: “Saul therefore saw that he was exceedingly prudent, and began to fear him; but all Israel and Judah loved David” (1 Sam. 18:15–16). Likewise, whoever diligently examines David’s other persecutions will always find glory as their companion. In Christ’s persecutions too there is always a glorious end. For example, in his final persecution, in which he humbled himself unto death, even death on a cross, “for this very reason God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name.” It seems useful to observe this here so that anyone in his own struggle against flesh and blood or the devil may be permitted to hope that glory will follow his tribulation.

Further, it should be known that David sang seven psalms corresponding to the number of the aforesaid persecutions: namely Psalms 33, 51, [Col. 1612C] 52, 53, 55 or 56, and 58. This is readily seen from their titles. For the title of the first is: “A psalm of David, when he changed his appearance before Abimelech, and he dismissed him, and went away.” The title of the second: “A psalm of David, when Doeg the Edomite went and reported to Saul, and said: David has come into the house of Abimelech.” The title of the third psalm: “For the end; concerning Amalek; David’s understanding.” This refers to his final flight, when he had taken refuge with Achish son of Maog, king of Gath, and the Amalekites came while David was absent, attacked Ziklag, and burned it with fire.

The title of the fourth: “For the end; in hymns; David’s understanding, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul: Is not David hidden among us?” The title of the fifth: “For the end; concerning the people that was made far from the holy ones; David in an inscription of a title, when the Philistines held him in Gath.” The title of the sixth: “For the end; do not scatter; David in an inscription of a title, when he fled from Saul’s face into the cave.” The title of the seventh: “For the end; do not destroy; David in an inscription of a title, when Saul sent men to guard his house, that he might kill him, and he departed.”

This refers to the second persecution, when, after David had evaded Saul and the spear had struck the wall with a futile blow, Saul sent his agents by night to the house to guard him and kill him in the morning. When they reported this to David, his wife Michal lowered him through a window; he went away, fled, [Col. 1613A] and was saved.
