Above we briefly touched on the mystery of the title of the first psalm: how David, that is, Christ, changed his appearance. In the title of the second psalm, now before us for exposition, Doeg means “motion”; Doeg, I say, the Edomite—that is, “earthly motion”—signifies Antichrist. For his reporting to Saul that David had come into the house of Abimelech, and Saul’s consequent killing of the Lord’s priests, prefigured how Antichrist will rend the Church by persecution even unto death. This psalm is directed against him and says:

## PSALM 51

[Col. 1613]

[Col. 1613A] “Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?” and what follows. “Therefore God will destroy you utterly,” etc. When he has been destroyed, the righteous will see and will say, [Col. 1613B] each one: “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in God’s mercy for ever and unto age upon age. I will give thanks to you forever, because you have acted; and I will wait for your name, for it is good in the sight of your saints.”

David speaks these words in the person of the righteous against Doeg the Edomite, who enacted the mystery of Antichrist. For the title reads:

**(VERSES 1–2). FOR THE END. DAVID’S UNDERSTANDING. WHEN DOEG THE EDOMITE CAME AND REPORTED TO SAUL: “HE HAS COME INTO THE HOUSE OF ABIMELECH.”** [Note: [Col. 1613D] The Vulgate reads: *Achimelech*.] (1 Sam. 22:9).

And the meaning is this: the Prophet’s understanding in this psalm is to speak of the advent of Antichrist, who, stirring many hearts, will persecute and kill Christ’s faithful people. But he wished to refer us to the history so that what is written historically might be shown to require spiritual understanding.

First, therefore, let us consider the history, which is as follows. We read in the first book of Kings that, when David fled from Saul’s face, he came to Nob to the priest Abimelech. When David asked him for a sword and bread, he gave him the loaves of presentation and Goliath’s sword; David departed for King Achish. On that day Doeg the Edomite, Saul’s most powerful chief of shepherds, was there within the tabernacle. But when Saul one day complained that no one told him where David was, Doeg said: “I saw the son of Jesse at Nob with Achimelech, who consulted the Lord for him and gave him provisions and the sword of Goliath.” Therefore the king sent for Achimelech and all the priests [Col. 1613D] who were at Nob. When he commanded his guards to kill them, they refused to stretch out their hands against the Lord’s priests. The king said to Doeg, “Fall upon the priests of the Lord.” Doeg fell upon them and slaughtered on that day seventy-five men clothed in the ephod; he also killed the men who were at Nob, women, little children, oxen, and donkeys. Abiathar alone, son of Achimelech, escaped to David.

Observe that although the history reads *Achimelech*, the psalm title reads *Abimelech*. But, as Jerome says, because the letters *beth* and *caph* differ by a small stroke, the error crept in more easily. Or perhaps, [Col. 1614A] just as in another psalm the title reads not “before Achish” but, with the name changed, “before Abimelech,” so that we may attend not to the history but to the mystery, so here as well.

Therefore *Doeg* means “motion”; *Edomite*, “earthly,” from the same name by which Esau was called, because he sold his birthright for a dish of lentils. *Saul*, “petition,” is the name of death, because sinful people seek death by words and deeds, just as the people extorted a king from God and Saul was given. *Abimelech* means “the kingdom of my Father”; *David*, “strong in hand.” David, chosen to reign permanently, signifies the kingdom of eternal salvation. Before he reigns, Saul persecutes him—the one not chosen to remain—because death, the last enemy to be destroyed, persecutes most fiercely those who are to reign with Christ. For if we were not mortal, the enemy could do nothing to us; he harms immortal angels in no way.

[Col. 1614C] Again, when David received the sacred sword and ate the loaves of presentation, which only priests were permitted to eat, he signified Christ not only as king but also as priest. Therefore David signifies Christ and his body; while Doeg the Edomite signifies the entire body of the wicked along with its head, Antichrist. For the wicked as well as the good are pilgrims here: they are in motion and will indeed depart, but they will remain what they are—earthly, corruptible, and human forever.

This Doeg reported to Saul: “David has come into the house of Abimelech,” because Christ was then delivered over to death when he came to the Jews, for whom the Father established his kingdom. Or, more specifically, Doeg is Antichrist, who, coming before the Judgment through miracles, will stir the whole world and, seeking help from the devil, will report [Col. 1614D] that Christ has come to the Church, which is the Father’s house. David survived the death of the priests whose blood Doeg shed; in this the resurrection was prefigured, just as Isaac was delivered when the ram was sacrificed. Here, however, citizens of the heavenly and earthly kingdoms are intermingled. The Prophet sings in this psalm of these two kinds of human beings.

First he attacks Doeg; second, he reveals his swift end at “Therefore God will destroy you utterly”; third, he states that the righteous, seeing his downfall, will laugh at him, at “The righteous will see and laugh over him”; fourth, he praises the opposing party at “But I, like [Col. 1615A] a fruitful olive tree.” His purpose is to strengthen the faithful, especially those who will live in the times of Antichrist, which will be so dangerous that even the elect, if that were possible, will be led into error.

This psalm is opposed to the first, because just as that psalm speaks first of the blessed man and afterward of the ungodly, this one speaks first of the ungodly and afterward of the good. Therefore the Prophet uses demonstrative rhetoric: he praises the good by the nobility of their end and first censures Doeg by the shamefulness of his end, thus:

**VERSE 3.** “Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?” O Doeg, O Antichrist, to whom the name Doeg the Edomite—interpreted “earthly motion”—is fitting: for you move not upward, like a flame of fire stretching toward heaven, but downward, like earth falling into the depths; because, loving earthly things, you are pressed down toward hell by the very weight of earthly love. Why do you glory, when you move thus in malice, which draws you into hell like lead? What glory did your forerunner Pharaoh gain when, like lead in violent waters, he was drowned with his army? Was it not more fitting for Moses, God’s servant, to sing in glory: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified” (Exod. 15:1)?

So now you too vainly glory with your army, while you are plunged into hell by earthly motion; and the orthodox rightly glory as they sing to the Lord, who is gloriously honored, while you, the devil’s horse, are plunged into hell with your rider, the devil. Your rider, when cast down from heaven and falling like lightning, could in his brief flashing make some sort of boast, since he was still allowed to remain in this dark air and, as a strong armed man, claimed the court of this world for himself by plunder. But now you, his horse, together with your rider, are to fall from this court into hell, dragged there by the leaden weight, as it were, of your malice. Why do you glory in your very malice, which is matter for weeping rather than glorying?

In goodness, which belongs to few and is difficult to preserve in an evil time, glory is not vain when one glories in the Lord, to whom alone glory is due for every good thing, and by whose aid alone, when the days are evil, the good preserve goodness. But in malice, which anyone can easily do, and whose destructive impulse of itself bursts forth into its effects, such glorying is as absurd as if a madman boasted that he was powerful in the strength by which he could kill himself or his own brother. Why then do you glory in malice, you who are powerful not with good power but with evil? For your power is strengthened only by iniquity, whether your own or that of others; power was given to it against the continual sacrifice because of the people’s sins.

Therefore you are powerful with an evil power arising for you from iniquity alone, so as to present your members to serve impurity and iniquity unto iniquity. You are powerful not against iniquity but in iniquity—not only in conceiving it, but also in bringing it forth—as elsewhere is written of you: “He conceived sorrow and brought forth iniquity” [Col. 1616A] (Ps. 7:15). For because you conceived from your father the devil the inward sorrow of malice, you glory in malice; and because in outward deed you gave birth to iniquity, you glory as one mighty in iniquity.

Truly foolish is glorying in such offspring, because, as the Apostle James says: “When desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it has been completed, produces death” (Jas. 1:15). Go now and glory in malice, or desire giving birth to sin or iniquity, because, as the Apostle John says: “Every sin is iniquity” (1 John 3:4). Glory, then, if you can, in sin which, once completed, produces death—not the death precious in the Lord’s sight, but [Col. 1616B] that of which it is said: “The death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. 33:22). Everlasting confusion and endless reproach will undoubtedly follow it. “For many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awaken: some to eternal life, and others to reproach, that they may see forever” (Dan. 12:2). What will they see forever? Surely their shameful disgrace, remaining without end after the exceedingly brief glory or boasting in which they gloried in malice. For when empty and vain glory then ceases, everlasting confusion will remain for them.

For just as an adulterer and seducer of another man’s wife is ashamed when detected and seized by her lawful husband, then dragged in chains by that husband into public judgment and afterwards into a dark prison from which he never hopes to emerge, but where he expects forever to suffer dreadful penalties: so every corrupter of human nature, betrothed to the Word of God when it was created in God’s image and likeness, or when it was restored by the Son of God, will, when seized by that same Son of God at the eternal judgment, be handed over to reproach. Thus the saints judging the world will say to him: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but hoped in the abundance of his riches.” Why do you glory, you who by glorying in malice store up for yourself everlasting confusion on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s righteous judgment? He will disclose the counsels of your most wicked heart, devising wicked thoughts and fashioning them through the tongue. [Col. 1616D] For:

**VERSE 4.** “Your tongue devised injustice all day long.” “All day long,” that is, without interruption, your tongue devised injustice. I do not say, “the mind devised it, and then after some interval the tongue spoke injustice”; rather, I say that your tongue devised injustice, like those of whom it is written: “The heart of fools is in their mouth,” because mind and tongue work together in one and the same headlong fickleness, so that unjust thoughts boil forth in equally unjust words, according to: “The mouth of fools boils forth folly” (Prov. 15:2). Such people, even if they cannot commit injustice, at least speak it. If at times they cannot even speak it, some obstacle intervening, they at least think it. In such wicked thoughts, speech, and actions, you glory, you who are powerful in such things.

But see how your malice benefits you in no way and harms the saints in no way; rather, it works for their good. You indeed practise deceit with the intent to harm; but just as a sharp razor shaves hair and renews the skin, so you, wickedly, in whose hand deceit is directed, are permitted in persecuting the elect to take away their outward goods and sometimes even the limbs of their bodies, as you took away the priests by a swift death, shaving them from the present life as hairs with a razor. Thus you are permitted to rage only against the bodies of the godly; you cannot kill their souls, according to the Truth’s saying: “Do not fear those who kill [Col. 1617B] the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28).

Alternatively: “Like a sharp razor you practised deceit,” that is, as swiftly as a sharp razor, which shaves easily. Thus Job says: “He drinks iniquity like water” (Job 15:16). A thirsty person drinks water easily and deeply; likewise the wicked person commits iniquity easily and boldly. Or, as a sharp razor cuts while promising renewal, so you deceitfully and maliciously promise happiness through outward delights, thereby drawing people toward eternal unhappiness. Though you are miserable, you experienced no corrective punishments when you sinned with impunity and enjoyed that prosperity of which it is written: “The prosperity of fools will destroy them” (Prov. 1:32). It was not enough for you to do evil unless you added the further evil of loving it.

Nor did it seem to you sufficient evil merely to do and love evil, unless, by loving malice above kindness, you exalted it so that malice, raised upward, pressed kindness down into the depths—as though one could raise water above oil or earth above heaven, certainly a futile effort. For the poured-out oil, Christ’s name, always surpasses the vinegar-like name of Antichrist; and “he who is of the earth speaks of the earth, but he who comes from heaven is above all” (John 3:31).

**VERSE 5.** “You have loved malice more than kindness.” With two contrary things placed before you—evil [Col. 1617D] and good—so that you might reach out your hand to whichever you wished and exercise freedom of choice in choosing one or the other, even though kindness touched your mind together with malice, you nevertheless loved malice more than kindness. You rejected in your heart the good suggestion descending upon you from the Father of lights, who rains drops of dew-like grace upon good and evil alike; and you embraced in the arms of approval Babylon the harlot, that is, worldly desire, lustful and frenzied alike, just as Babylonian kings are recorded as having been lustful and likewise frenzied or rabid.

Thus in Daniel the Babylonian kingdom itself is signified by a lioness, which natural philosophers describe as more lustful than the lion and more rabid, especially when she is nursing cubs. Therefore you loved this world’s desire, lustful and frenzied alike, more than kindness, chaste and gentle alike.

And you loved not only to do malice to your own condemnation, but also to speak iniquity rather than equity. You did this wholly intent on the seduction and corruption of others, as it is written: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33).

**VERSE 6.** Nor indeed did you merely love words of iniquity, but, what is worse, every word that hurls downward. For you were unwilling even to conceal your malice by the elegance of composed speech; rather, your heart belched forth nakedly and irreverently evil words, hurling your helpers down with you. Thus that Jezebel of old was cast down, she who spoke words of downfall with a deceitful tongue against Naboth the Jezreelite. Having first used deceitful words, she exposed him to stoning through false witnesses: “Proclaim,” Jezebel said, [Col. 1618B] “a fast; make Naboth sit among the leading men of the people; send in two men, sons of Belial, against him, and let them give false testimony: ‘He has blessed God and the king’; then lead him out and stone him, so that he may die” (3 Kings 21:10).

O hypocrisy hateful to God, even on the surface of the letter! “Proclaim,” she says, “a fast” (ibid., v. 9). For what reason? For a great crime, for monstrous sacrilege: because Naboth cursed God, because Naboth blasphemed God and, moreover, the king. For the Law says: “You shall not curse the ruler of your people,” and “Whoever blasphemes God shall surely die” (Exod. 22:28; Lev. 24:16). Therefore proclaim a fast and say: “Let us all fast, let us all humble ourselves, because we have heard so great an abomination in our days, lest perhaps we be swallowed up from the earth together with the blasphemer.”

Plainly, this is like what the chief priest did when he said, “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.” When He answered, “You have said it,” that great and mighty zealot “tore his garments” and said: “He has blasphemed. What further need have we of witnesses? Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy. What do you think?” And they said: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 26:63 ff.). This, I say, is like that. [Col. 1618D]

But why did they make Naboth sit among the leading men of the people, and only then bring witnesses against him? Surely because Naboth was one of the leading men of the people; and, so that the whole arrangement of the trial might seem decorous, he first sat in his proper rank, in order that, after the witnesses had spoken, he might then be stripped of honour and finally of life. In this way too the wickedness of hypocrisy proceeded, beautifully veiled.

Why say more? They led him outside the city and killed him with stones; indeed, they led Him outside the city and crucified Him. But concerning this the Lord says: “You have killed, and moreover taken possession.” And afterwards He added: “In this place where the dogs licked Naboth’s blood, they shall also lick your blood.” And further: “Dogs shall eat Jezebel in the field of Jezreel,” etc. (3 Kings [1 Kings] 21:19, 23). According to the historical account, these things happened thus. When Jehu entered, Jezebel looked out of the window, her eyes painted with antimony and her head adorned, and said: “Can there be peace for Zimri, who killed his master?” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 9:31.) Clearly, wishing, as far as the moment allowed, to rebuke the murderer and restrain him from killing her by the alarming example close at hand, she spoke thus; and, in the meantime, in order to be pleasing, she adorned her eyes and head. But he said to the eunuchs: “Throw her down.” And they threw her down (ibid., 33). Afterwards, when burial was sought for her because she was a king’s daughter, they found nothing except her skull, feet, and the palms of her hands; for the dogs had eaten the rest. This vengeance for Naboth’s blood was, indeed, a foreshadowing of vengeance for Christ’s blood. [Col. 1619A–B]

This downfall of Jezebel prefigured that downfall which Jeremiah, foreseeing, lamentingly describes under the image of the then-present Babylonian captivity: “The Lord has cast down and has not spared; in His wrath He has destroyed all the beauty of Jacob; He has thrown down to the ground the strongholds of the virgin of Judah; He has defiled the kingdom and its princes” (Lam. 2:2). Again: “The Lord has cast down Israel; He has cast down all its walls; He has filled the daughter of Judah with humiliation and the humiliated” (ibid., 5).

That downfall was heard throughout the whole world. Behold, where is that Synagogue which killed Christ? Certainly, whatever seems to remain is such, or as much, as what remained of Jezebel’s body after the dogs. Its whole kingdom and priesthood are dead; dogs—that is, evil spirits—devour whatever religious service they imagine they render to God by sabbath observance or sacrifice.

But what benefit would it be to the true David who is to reign, persecuted by Doeg the Edomite, that is, Antichrist—what benefit that the Lord cast down all Jacob’s beauty, cast down Israel, or that wicked Jezebel was cast down—if you yourself were not cast down, you evil one, you man of sin, you son of perdition? You who, after the true David has been driven from His kingdom and the priests who favoured Him killed down to the last—that is, reduced to an exceedingly small remnant—will rule as you have planned, sitting in the temple of God, showing yourself as though you were God; indeed, you will even exalt yourself above everything called God or worshipped. [Col. 1619C–D]

What use, I ask, is it that many priests have been killed, while David the king and Abiathar the priest still survive, if you, Doeg, are allowed to rule with Saul the frenzied king in such a way that you, Antichrist, and the frenzied kingdom of sin stand on those heights which you have set up against David the true King? Oh, how many good men too have been killed upon these heights! Hence, in David’s great lament for Saul it is said: “Jonathan was slain upon your heights” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 1:25). Jonathan was indeed a good and faithful man, whose arrow never turned backward, because he never made void the covenant made with David—the covenant in whose making Jonathan is recorded as having used the sign of arrows. Yet, because together with Doeg the Edomite he clung to the frenzied king who persecuted King David, he fell upon Mount Gilboa, upon the heights of his wicked father, the mad king: killed by enemies on account of his father’s pride; a penal death indeed because of the wicked men to whom he adhered, yet also purgative because of the fidelity which he had consecrated to David. [Col. 1620A]

Not by such a death fell that Doeg the Edomite whom the Hebrews suppose to have been Saul’s armour-bearer. Seeing Saul himself fall upon his sword, he too fell upon his sword, as a deserved vengeance hurled them both into hell—the place into which Jezebel was hurled, she who killed Naboth, persecuted Elijah, supported the prophets of Baal, and killed the prophets of the Lord (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 31:5). [Col. 1620B]

Into that place too was hurled the wicked Synagogue, murderer of our Lord Jesus Christ and persecutor of the Lord’s apostles. “Behold,” He says, “I send to you prophets, scribes, and wise men; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city, so that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (Matt. 23:34–35). “All righteous blood,” He says: such as the blood of Abel and that of Naboth, both of whom signify Christ, just as their murderers signify Antichrist.

Since, therefore, the shedders of all righteous blood have been hurled into hell, it is very remarkable that you, most evil one, who will be revealed as the last and chief of all wicked persecutors of the godly, think that you can stand. It will be otherwise. For since you have loved words of casting down, by which you pronounce downfall upon the saints—those like Naboth, defending against you the inheritance of their fathers, lest you turn the vineyard of the Lord of hosts into your vegetable garden, cutting down from it the vines and branches of virtues and virtuous persons and planting, as you desire, vegetables of vices and vicious persons—you will without doubt meet the same fate as wicked Jezebel, who was thrown down. [Col. 1620C]

You, most wicked one, are likened to her because you lavishly feed the priests of groves from your own table, while you are wholly opposed and hostile to Christ’s holy and religious priests. You persecute men like Elijah; like Jezebel, you love dissolute and avaricious prophets or priests unlike him; you kill priests who favour King David, and you persecute David Himself—that is, Christ—in His members, as Doeg the Edomite and King Saul the frenzied did. [Col. 1620D]

**VERSE 7.** Therefore God will destroy you as He destroyed Jezebel, as He destroyed Doeg and Saul, as He destroyed the wicked Synagogue likened to Jezebel, and as He destroyed the assembly of scribes and Pharisees likened to Doeg the Edomite or Saul. He will destroy you as He destroyed them—that is, He will cast you down as He cast Jezebel down. You will fall on Mount Gilboa, that is, in the pride of devouring, as Saul or Doeg fell. For *Gilboa* is interpreted “devouring” or “a running down,” a name signifying the voracity and instability of those concerning whom the true David complains: “Those who devour my people as bread for food” (Ps. 13:4); and again: “They shall come to nothing like water running down” (Ps. 57:8). [Col. 1621A]

In the pride of such men, as on Mount Gilboa, Saul’s kingdom and the power of his armour-bearer Doeg the Edomite were destroyed. But you are worse than they to such an extent that, while any one of them can rightly be called a sinner or a slave of sin, you alone among all sinners are called “the man of sin” (2 Thess. 2:3). This name belongs to you alone, since you are wholly contrary to that Man who among all men is called not only just, but Justice itself, and rightly so. Hence the Apostle says: “Who was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30). [Col. 1621B]

Therefore God will destroy you utterly. He will destroy you then—not in just any way, but utterly, that is, with complete and consummating destruction. When God destroyed Pharaoh’s kingdom, another kingdom nevertheless hostile to His kingdom arose in the tribe of Ephraim against the tribe of Judah; when that was destroyed, the Babylonian kingdom arose. Again, when that was destroyed, the Persian or Macedonian kingdom arose; and when it too was destroyed, the kingdom of the Greeks arose. After this stands the Roman kingdom, which without doubt must also be destroyed, because from Nero’s time to Constantine’s it grievously attacked Christ’s kingdom. Yet it was not destroyed entirely, or utterly, because whenever one tyrant or tyrannical empire was destroyed, a kind of root of tyranny remained in its descendants; nor was there an end to cruelty, even when cruel kings or kingdoms had been destroyed. [Col. 1621C]

Therefore, in order that there may at last be an end to all tyranny, He will destroy you utterly, so that you, the man of sin, who hitherto have reigned—or rather tyrannized—in your members and in your successive forerunners, may have thereafter no successor or heir to your impiety; nor may you yourself ever repent or return to your kingdom.

When Nebuchadnezzar was to be removed from his kingdom, it was said of him by a certain watcher from heaven: “Cut down the tree and cut off its branches; nevertheless leave the shoot of its roots in the earth” (Dan. 4:11–12). By these words it was signified that, though expelled from his kingdom for a time, he would one day return, and would leave the shoot of his posterity in that same kingdom. Accordingly, he was not then to be destroyed utterly, since a son would succeed him. [Col. 1621D]

Likewise Belshazzar, the last of the Babylonian kings, though killed by Darius the Mede and having no successor of his own blood, nevertheless had many successors in his impiety. The whole evil and adulterous generation, the crooked and perverse generation, of all these is to end in you, the man of sin, so that no shoot of your root may remain thereafter either in the line of blood or in the line of perversity. Therefore God will destroy you utterly, so that, with all your generation cut down in you, it may already have an end. [Col. 1622A]

God Himself, I say, will destroy you—not through another king who will succeed you, as Belshazzar was destroyed through Darius succeeding him. No tyrant will destroy you, but God Himself, who will reign eternally. He will not destroy you by setting another like yourself in your place, but by glorifying Himself as the true King David, whom you, Doeg, persecute in His members. He Himself will kill you by the breath of His lips, by the breath of His mouth, and destroy you by the brightness of His coming. He will destroy you utterly, I say, so that at last your cruelty may have an end.

Or “utterly” may mean at the approaching term or end of this world: though He spares you now, while through you He tests His elect. When they have been chastened through you, He will cast you, His rod, into eternal fire, so that your impiety may henceforth produce no shoot harmful to His branches. [Col. 1622B]

For because you, like another Ahab, have presumed to corrupt His vineyard and to plant your own vegetables in it after cutting down the vines, therefore He will not only destroy you but also uproot you with your vegetables. He will utterly uproot you, so that you may never sprout again. For this is He to whom His Father truly said: “Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, destroy, ruin, and scatter; to build and to plant” (Jer. 1:10). Therefore, from the time royal power in heaven and on earth was given to Him—a power which He possessed eternally in His divinity, but received temporally in His humanity—He has uprooted many tares harmful to His wheat and destroyed many structures hostile to His citizens. [Col. 1622C]

But He left some shoot of the worst roots in the earth; and He permitted some structures to remain in the stronghold that was against His citizens, to whom He also said: “Go into the village that is against you” (Matt. 21:2). But now, in the time of harvest, He will say to the reapers: “Gather all the tares,” entirely uprooted, “and bind them into bundles to burn” (Matt. 13:20); for they are no longer to be spared, as I once spared them when I said: “Let both grow together, lest perhaps while gathering the tares you uproot the wheat also.” “Lift up,” He says, “your eyes, and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest” (Matt. 13:29–30; John 4:35). [Col. 1622D]

Therefore, since the harvest is now soon at hand, in which the Lord of the harvest no longer fears for His now mature wheat, He will therefore destroy you utterly, uproot you from among His wheat, and afterwards remove you from your tabernacle. Thus, as you, Doeg, made King David and his fellow-soldiers leave their kingdom, so you, expelled from the kingdom into everlasting exile, may have no tabernacle there.

Some manuscripts read simply “from the tabernacle”; some, “from His tabernacle”; some, “from your tabernacle.” The last reading is supported by the Hebrew text, in which one reads “from your tabernacle.” Let us consider each reading.

[Col. 1623A] “He will remove you from the tabernacle,” so that in your enduring exile you may have no tabernacle at all, just as David, fleeing from your face—or from Saul’s, while you with him persecuted David—had no tabernacle when he hid in woods and mountains.

Alternatively: “He will remove you,” that is, “He will cause you to emigrate from your tabernacle,” in which you served yourself rather than Him, seeking your own gain rather than His, when you were Saul’s armour-bearer—that is, the armour-bearer of death—and the persecutor of King David.

Alternatively: “He will remove you from His tabernacle,” that is, He will cause you, excommunicated and cast out of His tabernacle, which is the Church, no longer to betray David there by plotting, or to kill the Lord’s priests in Saul’s service, in the ministry of death. [Col. 1623B] Even if at times in that very tabernacle you speak what belongs to Jesus Christ, you receive here the earthly reward which you seek, in accordance with your name, by which you are called *Idumaeus*, “earthly.” For you serve earthly things while plotting in this tabernacle against David, who is to reign. Such a servant will not remain in the house forever, because he will be caught in his own snares and pierced by his own sword. Therefore He will remove you from His tabernacle.

“And your root from the land of the living.” Our root is charity, by which we are rooted and founded in the land of the living. Hence your root, Doeg, will be uprooted, because it is not fixed deep down. Like seeds cast upon rock, though they put forth some root, nevertheless, because they have no moisture, they wither when the sun rises; so also you, Doeg: though at times you receive the word with joy and put forth some slight shoot, you are among—and exercise leadership among—those “who believe for a time and in time of temptation fall away” (Luke 8:13). Therefore your root will be plucked up from the land of the living. And you yourself, like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth, will be moved, according to the meaning of your name, by which *Doeg* is called “movement.” [Col. 1623C]

Alternatively: as the root of the elect is charity, which will never wither because “charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13:8), so your root is worldly covetousness, which will wither as the world withers, because “the world passes away, and its desire” (1 John 2:17). Though this root of yours may at times sprout for a while in the land of the living, in elect persons who sin—as King David sinned—it will soon be uprooted through repentance.

Alternatively: the mystery of iniquity which you work through your ministers, in every deception according to Satan’s working, through lying signs, is your root. By it you sprout in the land of the living, that is, in the Church, overthrowing the hearts of the simple with such craft that, if possible, even the elect are led into error. But this root of yours will be uprooted from the land of the living—from the hearts, that is, of saints who disdain your signs as Moses and Aaron disdained the signs of the Egyptian magicians (Exod. 8:18–19). [Col. 1623D–1624A] For although those men performed by their incantations certain signs similar to Moses’ and Aaron’s signs, they were compelled to confess that God’s finger operated in Moses’ signs, whereas it did not operate with, in, or through them or their signs.

Therefore, though Satan’s ministers, cast out from the tabernacle and deprived of ecclesiastical office, possess sacramental signs as though these were their root, by which they sprout and gain temporal advantages while performing forbidden offices contrary to the prohibition of the holy Roman Church, nevertheless “we who live bless the Lord” (Ps. 113:18): He who made us such a land of the living that this root of Antichrist will not be found in it; and if it is ever seen to lurk there, it will quickly be uprooted when its malice, concealed through hypocrisy, is revealed by God. [Col. 1624A–B]

“The heavens will reveal your iniquity” (Job 20:27), so that the righteous may see and know what the unrighteous man refused to understand in order to act well—he who has eyes and does not see. Yet, however many clouds of errors this Doeg, son of night and darkness, may spread abroad,

**VERSE 8.** “The righteous shall see and fear, and shall laugh at him.” Now they shall see and fear in mortal flesh; hereafter they shall see and laugh at him in immortal flesh. Concerning this passage blessed Gregory says in his *Morals on Job*:

> [Note: [Col. 1623D] St Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book VI, ch. 30.] When the righteous man sees all the wicked struck by final vengeance, he rejoices in the glory of due recompense; nor then does he compassionately sympathize, from human feeling, with those already condemned, because, cleaving by vision to divine justice, he is made firm by the unshaken strength of inward strictness. No compassion affects the minds of the elect, raised up in the brightness of heavenly rectitude, because the height of blessedness renders them strangers to miseries. Therefore it is well said: “The righteous shall see and fear, and shall laugh at him.” For the righteous now see the wicked and fear; then they will see and laugh. Since they can now fall into imitation of them, they have fear here; but since they can then be of no benefit to the condemned, they have no compassion there. Thus, judging in the very justice by which they are blessed, they read that eternal punishment is not to be pitied, lest—something which it is unlawful even to suppose—they diminish the quality of their received happiness if, placed in the kingdom, they will what they cannot possibly accomplish. But whoever directs himself to the precepts of life tastes here already, before receiving eternal rewards, the beginnings of that security which is to follow forever: he does not fear the ancient enemy, nor, when the moment of death intervenes, does he in any way dread his violent assaults. For the beginning of recompense for the righteous is often this very security of mind at death. [Col. 1624C–D]

For the righteous see here, and fear for themselves, what evil may come at the end, lest they too fall. For here they walk in the night, attending, as Peter says, “to the prophetic word as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts” (2 Pet. 1:19): that is, until Christ, the true Light, presents Himself to be seen as He is, and also presents His adversary Antichrist to be seen as he is—if indeed he can be said to be, since he has lost true and blessed being. [Col. 1625A]

Certainly both will be seen at the final judgment: Christ will openly sit in judgment, and Antichrist, before the sight of all, will be cast down. Then the righteous, wholly secure, will see him cast down and will laugh at him. Those who now go weeping while sowing their seed will then laugh. Those who now mourn, then made as though comforted from all Antichrist’s assaults, will laugh at him and say:

**VERSE 9.** “Behold the man who did not make God his helper.” Behold the man, not God, who, excessively exalting himself above everything called God, sat in God’s temple as though he were God. Behold the man of sin, the son of perdition, who did not make God his helper, thinking that he could accomplish everything he desired through his own powers and the devil’s aid, whose will he diligently followed. Therefore he did not make God his helper, against whose will he laboured. [Col. 1625B]

“But he trusted in the multitude of his riches.” Certain saints had riches, yet did not trust in them; rather, using them rightly and giving generously, they stored up for themselves a good hope in God. Therefore the man who has riches is not to be blamed if he does not love them by keeping them graspingly, but sows them in blessings by generously dispensing them. Conversely, one who lacks riches is not to be praised while the desire to possess them burns within him. For riches are not condemned, but covetous avarice; nor is poverty, which consists in want, praised if it lacks that poverty which consists in humble and devout patience, of which it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). [Col. 1625B–C]

Such poverty was far from this Doeg the Edomite, who not only possessed riches but heaped them up for himself in a multitude of riches; and, further, trusted in that multitude of his riches. I call them *his* because he accumulated them for himself, not for the poor, and kept them to spend on himself and his pleasures. Against this, Truth instructs His disciples to recognize that all earthly riches are foreign to them: “If you have not been faithful in what is another’s,” He says, “who will give you what is your own?” (Luke 16:12). Therefore the stewardship entrusted to the rich concerns another’s goods; if they are faithful in that stewardship, they will receive as their own eternal riches, which can never be taken from them, in exchange for temporary riches belonging to another. [Col. 1625D]

This Doeg refused to understand, so as to act well with his abundant riches and gain true riches from deceptive ones, and his own riches from those of another. Instead, despising eternal and true riches, he vanished into vain riches and trusted in the multitude of his riches, like that rich man who said: “I will pull down my barns and build larger ones, and there I shall gather all my crops and goods; and I shall say to my soul: Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast” (Luke 12:18–19). These words were not uttered in truth, to be fulfilled in reality, but in vanity devoid of solid being. For God said to him: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (ibid., 20). [Col. 1626A]

Many have thus vanished and gathered riches in vain, from which they had no benefit after death. But this Doeg, this Antichrist, prevailed in his vanity—that is, he was more vain than others. Nothing is more vain than one who loves money more than God. Many were powerful—to their own ruin—in this vanity, that is, strong and mighty. Among such powerful and mighty men were those concerning whom Christ, poor in this world, complains: “The mighty rushed upon me, and the mighty sought my life” (Ps. 58:4; 53:5). [Col. 1626A–B]

The prince of all these mighty men, like a “strong armed man,” guarded his court and long prevailed there, until one stronger than he came and overcame him (Luke 11:21). But this Doeg, as he supposed, surpassed all these—that is, he was stronger—because he dared to oppose himself to the most mighty conqueror of death, whom none ever could or can overcome. Since he did this not upheld by truth but deceived by vanity, he is now rightly mocked when it is said to him: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but trusted in the multitude of his riches and prevailed in his vanity,” deceived himself and deceiving many who believed his vanity rather than God’s truth.

**VERSE 10.** “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in God’s mercy for ever and ever.” Here above all appears that this psalm’s rhetorical declamation belongs to the demonstrative kind of discourse, in which the honourable part is praised and the dishonourable censured. For up to this point Doeg’s blame has been heightened; now the opposite party is praised, when the righteous and good man says: “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in God’s mercy for ever.” [Col. 1626C]

Doeg trusted in the multitude of his riches; but I, like a fruitful olive tree—I, the people of God, being the olive tree from which proud branches were broken off and dried up through pride, while the wild olive was grafted in their place (Rom. 11:17)—I, that olive tree from whose shoot Christ was born, called the son of oil; I, the fertile olive tree which remains green in winter and bears fruit both in adversity and prosperity (Isa. 5:1); I, not a tree to be uprooted like the one to whom it was said above, “Therefore God will destroy you utterly; He will uproot you and remove you from the land,” but abiding as a fruitful olive tree in God’s house, not only serving Him in His tabernacle in the time of war but also praising Him in God’s house in the time of peace—I have hoped not in riches, as Doeg did, but in God’s mercy: not temporary mercy, but mercy enduring forever, of which it is elsewhere said: “Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good, for His mercy endures forever” (Ps. 135:1). [Col. 1626C–D]

There is another mercy of His, brief and slight, in which you, Doeg, became proud. Hence in the Hebrew one reads: “Why do you boast in malice, mighty one, [in] the mercy of God?” In our translation, instead, one reads: “Mighty in iniquity,” because this mercy is understood as the mammon of iniquity, in which Doeg was mighty. Doeg became proud and gloried in such mercy. But even if I sometimes gave thanks for such mercy, using it well either for my own consolation or for that of others, I nevertheless hoped, singing to the Lord forever, not in such mercy but in God’s mercy enduring forever and ever. [Col. 1627A]

When I say “for ever and ever,” it is a repetition—and therefore a confirmation—of the same sense. For when I say, “I have hoped in God’s mercy forever,” in order to confirm that I am founded in the love of the kingdom of heaven which abides for ever and ever, I repeat the same thing and say, “and ever and ever.”

But that I am an olive tree, that I am fruitful, that I am in God’s house hoping in God’s mercy, I do not attribute to myself but to Your grace, O God; and therefore:

“I will give thanks to You for ever, because You have done it.” What have You done? Everything, namely, that I am, and whatever good I ever could or can do. By separating me from the mass of perdition, from the body or members of Antichrist, You joined me to the members of the Church, the branches of the fruitful olive tree. You made me a sharer in the good name, the Christian name. Therefore I too shall await Your name invoked over me and one day to be glorified in me, so that You, O God, may shine forth as all things and in all, and, Doeg having been expelled, You alone may hold sole dominion and grant Your own the most delightful taste of Your name, because it is sweet, because it is good—not in the sight of Doeg and the other enemies, but in the sight of Your saints, who alone taste how sweet the Lord is, how sweet His name is, and how great is the abundance of His sweetness. [Col. 1627B–1628A]

Alternatively: “I will give thanks to You for ever, because You have done” many benefits already in the past against Doeg’s deceits, for the exaltation of David’s kingdom. Even before the judgment, or at the final judgment itself, You will perform many further things glorifying David’s name. Therefore I shall wait and shall not be hasty; I shall await Your name, by which You are called Saviour, so that according to Your name—which is good in the sight of Your saints—you may grant salvation to me as I wait for You patiently. [Col. 1628B]

Glory to God the Father, in whose mercy I have hoped. Glory to God the Son, who will destroy Doeg the Edomite by the brightness of His coming. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that mercy in which one must hope forever. Glory to the one eternity of the Three, which is expressed by the words “for ever and ever.” Amen.

## PSALM LII

[Col. 1627]

[Col. 1627C] “The fool has said in his heart: There is no God.” The title of this psalm is:

**(VERSE 1.) FOR THE END; FOR AMALEK; DAVID’S UNDERSTANDING.**

The history is well known: David, fleeing Saul, came to Achish king of Gath and served under him. Having placed his wives and children in the small city of Ziklag, the Amalekites came, burned the city, and carried off David’s wives and children. Upon hearing this, David pursued those raiders and freed the captives (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 30).

*Amalek* is interpreted “licking the earth,” and signifies a people loving earthly things; *Ziklag*, “conversion,” and signifies the Church. By the wives we understand holy souls; by the children, good works; by David, Christ. [Col. 1627C–D]

It may be believed that David had the same understanding in this psalm that he had when he first composed it. But he repeated it because he understood that what historically befell him at the hands of the Amalekites would spiritually come to pass in Christ and the Church. For Amalek himself is the foolish Jew or heretic, whoever blasphemously says in his heart concerning Christ, “There is no God.” Against him the hope of what is said, “When the Lord restores the captivity of His people, Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad,” strengthens the soul of every wise person, just as it was prefigured in the deed already narrated of David. [Col. 1628C]

Yet this psalm may suitably be distinguished from the thirteenth, so that, although the words of that psalm and this one are the same, their subject matter may be understood as different. This is indicated by their differing titles. For the former has this title: “For the end: a psalm of David.” But this one is called: “For the end; concerning Amalek; David’s understanding.” Augustine reads “concerning Melech” [Note: [Col. 1627] Thus the manuscript; but the printed editions read “concerning Maëlech,” a reading retained also by the Vulgate.], which is interpreted “suffering” or “in labour,” and signifies Christ the Head together with His members; but especially any zealot for charity resembling the Apostle Paul, who grieves when charity grows cold in the last time and labours in birth for little children until Christ is formed in them. [Col. 1628C–D]

Therefore the Prophet, himself also labouring in birth, sings this psalm for the body of Christ in labour, concerning the time of evils, against the foolish people of Antichrist; whereas the psalm above was sung against the foolish Jewish people. Hence in Hebrew both psalms begin thus: “The fool has said in his heart: There is no God.”

It is a beautiful manner of speaking to express a different meaning in the same words and to equate in this passage two foolish or senseless peoples. For that foolish people which, seeing Christ in frail flesh, said in its heart on account of that fleshly frailty, “There is no God,” was rightly rebuked above as blind and stupid, since it was not taught by the miracles it saw to understand that He was God who spoke God’s words and performed God’s works. [Col. 1629A]

And now the people of Antichrist is likewise rightly rebuked: seeing Christian religion fail because iniquity abounds and charity grows cold, it says in its heart: “Christ is not God, whose worship so collapses that a true worshipper of Christ, a true observer of Christian discipline, is scarcely found.” For as the Jewish people were blinded at Christ’s first coming by seeing in Christ the scandal of the cross and the disgrace of death, and therefore denied that He was God, so at the end of time, when the wicked prosper and the good are oppressed and no judge of the living and the dead is perceived, Christ will be thought not to be God by the foolish and senseless people that says in its heart: “There is no God.” [Col. 1629A–B]

In the first part of the psalm is the rebuke of the foolish people; in the second, the threat of judgment, in the words: “Will not all those who work iniquity know?” In the third is the salvation of the Church in labour, strengthened in hope where it is said: “Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion?”

It should certainly be noted that, just as in the preceding fiftieth psalm the whole purpose of the psalm concerned the building up of faith, so in this one the principal purpose is the strengthening of hope, lest the Christian despair when the assault of the flesh or of the wicked multitude becomes powerful against him; for his helper is Christ, Judge of the living and the dead. [Col. 1629C]

For this reason too, in each section the exposition always begins from judgment, whence hope proceeds with fear, so that it may fit together in one heart—or one people, namely the Christian people—fear as the lower millstone and hope as the upper millstone. But because the foolish people receive neither fear nor hope, they do not believe that Christ reigns. Their folly is reproached in the words:

“The fool has said in his heart,” because he does not dare say it with his mouth. What has he said? “There is no God.” This was first said by the foolish Jewish people; afterwards it was said also by that equally foolish people falsely called Christian, because it rejects Christ’s law and loves Antichrist’s laws. Therefore the foolish people which denied Christ and the foolish people which receives Christ are found equal in wickedness. For each has said in its heart: “He whom Mary bore is not God.” [Col. 1629D]

They say this, but their testimony is not to be accepted, both because it is false and because the life of these witnesses is blameworthy. For:

**VERSE 2.** “They are corrupt and have become abominable in their iniquities,” so much so that there is not among them one who does good.

[Col. 1630A] The falsity of their testimony is evident from this: he whom they deny to be God, remaining as God—indeed, truly so—

**VERSE 3.** God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there was one who understood. For who, except God alone, can see the hearts of all human beings or their thoughts? If Christ were not God, Peter would falsely say to him: “Lord, you know all things” (John 16:30). Likewise, after John the Evangelist had said that Jesus did not entrust himself to certain persons, though they believed in him because of the signs they had seen, he added: “because he himself knew all, and had no need that anyone should bear witness to him concerning man; for he himself knew what was in man” (John 2:24–25). Hence Christ frequently answered [Col. 1630B] their thoughts; for example: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9:4). And, appearing to his disciples after his resurrection, he said: “Why do thoughts arise in your hearts?” (Luke 24:38).

For they thought that they saw a spirit, not a body. Jesus, knowing this unspoken opinion of theirs, rebuked and corrected them, offering them flesh and bones to touch, such as a spirit does not possess. He also grants this to his disciples, in whom he himself speaks. Thus Peter the Apostle, speaking in his Spirit, said to Simon: “I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity” (Acts 8:23). Paul likewise affirms concerning prophets speaking in Christ’s name and revealing the hidden things of the heart [Col. 1630C] that God is truly in them—the God who speaks through them. Hence he also says of himself: “Do you seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3).

Is he not therefore truly God, who not only looked down from heaven—that is, from the dwelling-place of his flesh—but also has often looked down, and daily looks down, from any lower heaven, namely from his saint whose citizenship is in heaven, upon the children of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God?

Or, “he looked down” means “he had mercy” upon the children of men, “to see,” that is, to cause to be seen whether there is one who understands in heart or seeks in deed God himself, of whom the fool said in his heart, “There is no God.” And as though he had found what he sought, he delivers the judgment, saying:

[Col. 1630D] **VERSE 4.** All have turned aside; together they have become useless. First they turned aside from the way of truth; and together with that turning aside—or “together,” that is, alike—they became useless. More generally: there is none who does good. Because I speak on behalf of *Melech*, that is, “the woman in labor,” I too, like one in labor and bringing forth conceived words with pain, repeat and say: There is none, not even one.

I said, “There is none who does good”; I say again, “There is none”—so true is this that not even one person is found among the foolish people who does good. Therefore I say: “Not even one.” For if I wished one good person to be understood, I would say, “Except one.” At present, indeed, there is none among them who understands or seeks God. But whether they wish it or not, “the Lord shall be known when he executes judgments” [Col. 1631A] (Ps. 9:17). Long have I kept silence and been still; but now, like a woman in labor, I speak with rebuke and threat to those who hear me concerning those who do not hear me. Therefore I say:

**VERSE 5.** Shall they not know? Shall not all who work iniquity know, shall they not understand, at least in the manifest judgment, Christ, God, rebuking them for his people? “They devour,” he says, “my people like food of bread.” My people are in labor and pain and therefore need consolation and refreshment. But those rich persons who ought to console and refresh them do not feed my people; rather, they devour them—either by plundering and impoverishing them, or indeed, what is worse, by incorporating them into themselves as far as lies in their power—like bread as food. Although bread is eaten every day, it does not so readily become tiresome as any other food, for instance meat, fish, eggs, or such things, which someone eating continually without bread would soon find tiresome.

[Col. 1631B] Therefore they devour my people like bread as food, because such devouring is very savory to them every day. For just as, though one abstains from meat on certain days, one is customarily not to abstain from bread on any day, so all these workers of iniquity, even if they sometimes leave off other sins, never wish to cease from oppressing the people. And this happens because:

**VERSE 6.** They have not called upon God. Even if at times they have cried to God in prayers, nevertheless they have not called upon God himself; for each person calls upon in prayer that which he most eagerly desires to obtain. Therefore, because these people are of the earth and chiefly desire earthly things, even in those offices in which they appear to minister to God, they call upon not God himself but something else that they desire more than him. Thus they in no way possess, or wish to possess, hope in heavenly goods as good sons do.

Nor do they have fear as good servants do. For a good servant is one who, having the beginning of wisdom through fear of the Lord, fears what ought to be feared until he is nourished toward filial nobility, in which he may hope for what ought to be hoped for. But these people, who devour the people in pain [Col. 1631D] and labor—this foolish people who say in their heart, “There is no God,” these foolish rulers of a foolish people—do not themselves wish even to receive the beginning of wisdom, so that by fearing future and eternal punishments they might abstain from the momentary pleasure of vices.

Yet they have another fear, which is not the beginning of wisdom but a sign of folly. For “there they trembled with fear, where there was no fear.” On this passage blessed Gregory says in his *Morals on Job*:

> [Note: [Col. 1631D] Book VII of the *Morals*, ch. 26.] “There are many who already desire to defend Truth freely, yet in that very desire anxiously dread the indignation of human power. And while on earth they fear a man against Truth, they endure from heaven the wrath of that same Truth. There are also some who, conscious of their sins, now desire to give what they possess to the needy; yet they fear that, once they have given their goods, they themselves may lack. And while, in fear, they make provision by keeping the supports of the flesh, they kill their soul by withholding the nourishment of mercy; and while they fear suffering want on earth, they cut themselves off from the eternal abundance of heavenly refreshment. Of these the Psalmist rightly says: ‘There they trembled with fear, where there was no fear’; because surely those who fear things beneath that ought to be trampled underfoot suffer the things above that ought to be feared. And while they wish to pass by what they could tread upon, they receive from above a judgment which they can by no means endure.”

Hence it is rightly said: “Upon those who fear frost, snow shall fall” [Col. 1632B] (Job 6:16). They fear, that is, what ought not to be feared, as did the Jews, who killed Christ because they feared losing their place and their nation.

Alternatively: “They trembled with fear where there was no fear,” because in truth there was no fear in their hearts that the chief priests themselves would lose their place and nation. Yet, in order to incite the simple people whom they devoured to Christ’s death, they trembled by feigning fear where there was no fear. For they said: “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11:48). By speaking thus, they deceived the simple people and incorporated them into themselves, as it were by devouring them, so that all, smaller and greater alike, might agree in Christ’s death.

[Col. 1632C] Those who, having received Antichrist or any leading minister of his, draw the people into his service by feigning and instilling a vain fear are almost like them: they tremble where there is no fear, following the example of the Pharisees who killed Christ. But if this people were not foolish, and if the rulers of this people were wise, understanding, and foresaw the last things, they could more readily be terrified away from evil than encouraged toward evil by the example of the Jews. For by God’s just judgment the fear that they feared came upon them, and what they dreaded happened—not because they let Christ go, but because they did not receive him. For if they had let him go, they would not have lost their place. But because they did not let him go, they lost their place and nation, just as some of them falsely feared and others truly feared.

Nor did it suffice, as vengeance for Christ’s blood, that they were cast out from their place. Worse befell them: God himself, whom they crucified—God himself, I say—scattered their bones through the Roman commanders Titus and Vespasian, when they were delivered into the hands of the sword, exposed in body to slaughtering swords, and made portions for foxes in soul—that is, handed over to malignant spirits. So too it will happen to these ministers of Antichrist [Col. 1633A] that they shall suffer what they fear, whether their fear is real or feigned.

“For God scattered the bones of those who please men.” God, I say—the one of whom they say in their hearts, “There is no God”—proved himself to be God by the manifest punishment of their rejection of him and their acceptance of Antichrist. For just as he scattered those who would not have him reign over them, saying, “We will not have this man reign over us” (Luke 19:14), and chose Caesar instead, so he will also scatter them. Indeed, that the declaration of the future event may be more certain, I use the past tense: “He scattered the bones of those who please men.”

For why, do you suppose, do they hate Christ and Christ’s ministers, and refuse to allow them to be exalted to any dignity, spiritual or secular [Col. 1633B], while rejoicing that Antichrist, or his ministers opposed to Christ, rule in Church or kingdom, unless because they prefer to please human beings rather than God? Just as the Jews wished to please Caesar when they said, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15), so these people wish to please Antichrist or any minister of his when, for example, a wicked pontiff or ruler is exalted, they say: “We have no other but this man.”

They also please human beings in this respect: foolish and wicked as they are, they please themselves, since they too are human beings—that is, carnal people just like their rulers. By contrast, holy and righteous people displease themselves and do not please other human beings. One principal example, the Apostle Paul, says: “If I pleased men, I should not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1:10). “If,” he says, “I pleased men,” that is, carnal persons, “I should not be Christ’s servant.” For of spiritual persons he says elsewhere: “As I also please all” (1 Cor. 10:33); yet he does not add “men,” because he did not care to please carnal persons.

[Col. 1633C] Similar is what the Lord says: “Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16:13). Then, distinguishing his disciples from humanity in general, he adds: “But whom do you say that I am?” (ibid., 15). Likewise, after the Apostle Paul had said of the saints’ reward that eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and it has not arisen into the heart of man, he says: “But to us God has revealed it through his Spirit” (1 Cor. 2:10), distinguishing himself and those like him from humanity in general.

For they have received something beyond human beings, so that they are called angels: they imitate, as far as they can, the angelic life by living chastely like angels or by chastely announcing the word of God like angels. To please such people is not to please human beings but angels. But those who please, and strive to please, human beings—that is, carnal persons, whether themselves or others—are put to shame, because God has rejected them.

It is too little to say that they shall be put to shame in the future; indeed, they already have been put to shame and will henceforth be put to still greater shame. For they have received here a great portion of their shame, because God rejected them—that is, he caused them to be despised [Col. 1634A] even in this life; and in the future they will be more greatly shamed and despised. This is surely a just reciprocity: because wicked people despise the saints, they too are despised by them. Thus “Herod with his army despised” Christ (Luke 23:11), and Christ despised him, because he would neither speak to him nor perform any sign before him.

So Elisha despised Joram king of Israel, saying: “What have I to do with you? Go to the prophets of your father and mother.” Again: “As the Lord lives, before whom I stand, if I did not reverence the face of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not even look upon you or regard you” (4 Kings 3:13–14). Therefore those who please human beings and displease angels and God are put to shame, because God rejected them and has caused, and causes, them to be despised.

[Col. 1634B] **VERSE 7.** Who shall give from Zion salvation to Israel? O Church in labor, do not fail amid so many scandals, but pray and entreat God Christ, whom you believe to be God. And, that the prayer may be more forceful, seize the judge’s attention through an interrogation, thereby gaining hope and a sure expectation of salvation. Thus the Apostle, when he was most grievously pressed by troublesome temptations, said: “Who shall deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). Such a cry of wonder and questioning is the strong prayer of Jacob wrestling with God. But what he afterwards adds—“The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (ibid., 25)—is the joyful exultation of Israel, who sees God and receives the fruit of prayer.

So you also, in labor and without strength to give birth in your travail, continually cry, saying: “Who shall give from Zion salvation to Israel?” (Ps. 13:7). This is nearly the same as saying with the Apostle: “Who shall deliver me from this body of death?” For it is a strong prayer for the conversion of Israel’s remnant, for whom the Holy Spirit prays in many passages of Scripture with unutterable groanings in the saints. Thus Isaiah: “Return, O Lord, for the sake of your servants, the tribes of your inheritance” (Isa. 63:17). Likewise the bride in the Song of Songs says to her bridegroom who has turned away from Israel: “Return, my beloved, return; be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of Bethel” [Col. 1634D] (Song 2:17). She asks for the swift return of the bridegroom, whom she wishes in returning to resemble the agility of a gazelle and a young stag.

And Jeremiah says: “Turn us, O Lord, to yourself, and we shall be turned. Renew our days as at the beginning. But you have rejected us with rejection; you are exceedingly angry with us” (Lam. 5:21–22). Since, therefore, you, Lord, are angry with Israel, who shall give salvation to Israel? Who shall bring the Savior back to Israel? Who shall give me wings like a dove, that I may fly there where I may find salvation for Israel? Who shall deliver me from this body of death, in which I cannot see God face to face as Israel saw him and his soul was saved? Great as the sea is your affliction, O soul or Church in labor: who shall heal you? Who shall give you salvation for Israel?

I say, salvation from Zion, because “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved,” besides [Col. 1635A] that salvation which, conceived by the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, was born in Zion. Hence also: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion, because a man was born in her; the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86:1, 5). Having been born in Zion, he afterward withdrew from that earthly Zion—indeed, from that earthly portion of Zion, namely the Church that is counted as Zion only in name. Who, then, shall give or bring back him who has once turned away? Or rather, who shall turn us back to him, we who have once turned away? For he himself says: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. 1:3). But who shall turn us, turned away and perverted as we are? Surely no one but he himself; no one but his grace.

He was bound, that he might loosen the fetters of the falling world.

> [Note: [Col. 1635D] The manuscript reads *complices*, “accomplices,” apparently for *compedes*, “fetters.”]

He was held captive in Pilate’s praetorium, that he might release the captivity of his people [Col. 1635B].

Therefore you, the portion of the Church in labor and pain—the portion of spiritual persons—who have grieved because Christ’s people have been made captive by Antichrist’s people, as by Amalek, the “licking people” (*populo lingente*), when Amalek captured David’s wives and children, and likewise the wives and children of his soldiers; you, I say, who have thus far been in labor and pain because of adverse events by which the people of Israel have been afflicted by the people of Amalek, the army of Christ by the army of Antichrist: rejoice now and be glad. For behold, your king, King David, comes quickly to your aid and shall set his captive people free, just as in the history David freed the captives whom Amalek had taken at Ziklag.

[Col. 1635C] Therefore, when the Lord restores the captivity of his people, who follow Amalek not by voluntary choice but by forcible captivity, Jacob shall exult and Israel shall be glad: that lesser people to whom the greater serves; that simple and gentle brother who, while his hairy brother was occupied in hunting, received the blessing; that Jacob, I say, who is also named Israel, because he advanced from the struggle of action to the sweetness of contemplation. Then he shall exult with an eager body in God’s service and rejoice with a devoted mind in holy contemplation.

In the Hebrew it is read: “When God shall restore the captivity of his people, Jacob shall exult and Israel shall be glad.” This passage rightly looks to what the title, according to certain manuscripts, has: “for Amalek,” because great joy came to David’s supporters when he brought back from Amalek the captive people with much spoil, having slain the Amalekites and recovered his two wives and all the rest of his own people safe and sound. For the Amalekites had killed none of them, but had only carried them away captive.

[Col. 1636A] By this event is signified that none of the elect shall perish, but all shall be delivered, even if for a time they follow the wicked in body, not in heart, in a pathless place. When all have at last been delivered, there shall be great exultation and joy, so that those who have been saved from Israel shall have full joy.

Jacob, or Israel, especially magnifies this exultation and joy in the deliverance from this captivity because the Amalekites leave behind on the journey an Egyptian boy, whom David refreshes with food, makes the guide of his journey, pursues the Amalekites, finds them feasting, and utterly destroys them. In this deed one may behold the wonderful gift of heavenly grace toward sinners who are to be converted.

> [Note: [Col. 1636D] St. Gregory the Great, *Morals*, Book V, ch. 41.] “For what does it mean that the Egyptian boy of the Amalekite becomes exhausted on the journey, except that the lover of the present age, covered in the blackness of his sin, is often left weak and despised by that same world, so that he cannot run along with it but, broken by adversity, grows numb? But David finds him, because our Redeemer, truly strong in hand, sometimes converts to his love those whom he finds despised by worldly glory. He feeds him with food because he refreshes him with the knowledge of the word; he chooses him as guide of the way because he even makes him his preacher. And he who could not follow the Amalekites becomes David’s guide, because the person whom the world left behind as unworthy not only receives God in his mind when converted, but by preaching also brings him to the hearts of others. With this guide David finds the feasting Amalekite and destroys him, because through the preaching of those whom the world disdained to have as companions, Christ destroys the world’s joy.”

[Col. 1636C] Therefore, when the Lord so restores the captivity of his people that through the weak things of this world he confounds the strong, and through the lowly and despised things of the world works his wonders in converting his people and delivering them from the captivity of the Amalekites, who serve the devil or Antichrist, it is no wonder that Jacob shall exult and Israel rejoice. For “there shall be joy even among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance” (Luke 15:10). Indeed, the heavenly Father himself urges feasting and joy, and he especially rejoices when the son who was lost is found and the one who was dead is seen alive.

Glory to the Father, who enlarges this exultation and joy in Jacob and Israel. Glory to his Son, the true and living God, of whom the fool said in his heart that he was not God, who is also that salvation of which the Psalm says: “Who shall give from Zion salvation to Israel?” Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that exultation and joy in whom Jacob shall exult and Israel shall be glad.

## PSALM LIII

[Col. 1635]

[Col. 1635D] “Save me, O God, in your name,” etc. The title of this psalm is:

**(VERSES 1–2) UNTO THE END, IN SONGS, THE UNDERSTANDING OF DAVID, WHEN THE ZIPHITES CAME TO SAUL AND SAID: “IS NOT DAVID HIDDEN AMONG US?”**

[Col. 1636D] It is read in the First Book of Kings that, when David fled from Saul’s face, he came into the wilderness of Ziph. And the Ziphites came to Saul, saying: “Behold, David is hiding among us. Come down; it is for us to hand him over into the king’s hands.” When Saul heard this, he pursued him into the wilderness of Maon. “Now David despaired of being able to escape from Saul’s face. Thus Saul and his men surrounded David and his men like a crown, in order to capture them. But a messenger came to Saul, saying: ‘Hurry and come, for the Philistines have poured themselves out over the land.’ Therefore Saul turned back from pursuing David and went to meet the Philistines. For this reason they called that place the Rock of Division” (1 Kings 23:19–20 ff.). “David therefore went up from there and dwelt in the most secure places of Engaddi” [Col. 1637A] (1 Kings 24:1). Thus the Ziphites’ treachery did not profit them, and David was not harmed.

The Ziphites, who betrayed David to Saul, signify the Jews, who delivered the true David, Christ, to death. For Ziphites means “flourishing,” a name aptly applied to the Jews, who strove to flourish in temporal goods; and they also flourished in that they were, according to the flesh, descendants of a most noble stock and kinsmen of Christ, who is “the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1).

Likewise, by the Ziphites—that is, the flourishing—may rightly be signified the whole body of the wicked, whose carnal glory, like the flower of hay, grows green for a time and quickly withers. David lies hidden among them—that is, those dead to the world, whose “life is hidden with Christ in God” [Col. 1637C] (Col. 3:3). The Ziphites betray them to Saul, the mad king, when they endeavor to drag them to the death either of soul or body. For the weak envy such people’s peace and almost have their feet moved into stumbling.

But by entering God’s sanctuary through faith, they understand this concerning their end, “unto the end,” as this psalm is entitled: “Unto the end.” They understand, I say, that “they shall quickly wither like hay, and shall soon fall like the green plants of the grass” (Ps. 36:2); that “all flesh is hay, and all its glory like the flower of hay. The hay has withered and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord remains forever” (1 Pet. 1:24; Isa. 40:6). For the Sun of righteousness shall rise, appearing in his bright splendor at the last judgment; and then, when the Ziphites have withered and Saul’s kingdom and death have been utterly destroyed, David, who now lies hidden among the Ziphites, shall be received in glory.

[Col. 1637D] The hidden meaning of this matter is not evident to all. Nevertheless, it is David’s understanding, and it is “in songs,” or hymns, because David, understanding that he is now hidden from Saul’s face but will hereafter reign in glory when Saul is dead—that is, when death is dead—blesses the Lord in hymns and confessions. And since he reads three things in the book of the Lord, namely “lamentations and a song and woe” (Ezek. 2:9), his understanding, after the lamentations of penitence by which eternal woe is escaped, is chiefly occupied with songs—that is, with psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, constant praises, and thanksgivings even amid adversities—according to the saying: “I shall bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” [Col. 1638A] (Ps. 33:1).

It should also be noted that, although David and his men had been surrounded like a crown by Saul’s men, David nevertheless escaped with his companions and, going up from there, lived in the most secure places. Therefore, by this example, whoever sees another law in his members resisting the law of his mind should not despair of being able to escape from the hand of Saul—that is, death, the devil, or Antichrist—from the snares, deceits, and violence of the Ziphites, that is, of flourishing vices, as is understood. Rather, let him frequently pray, saying: “Save me, O God, in your name.” Thus let him by no means cease from the continual, unremitting invocation of the Lord’s name until, delivered from this body of death, he dwells in the most secure places of Engaddi.

Engaddi means “fountain of the kid.” By this name is signified either the grace of the forgiveness of sins, which, given in the font of baptism, makes lambs out of kids; or the fountain of tears, by which, after baptism, grace for the forgiveness of sins is restored to those who have defiled themselves and have been numbered among the kids set at the left hand, so that they may return to the flocks of lambs. To those ascending from such a fountain applies what the bridegroom says to the bride: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep coming up from the washing; all bear twins, and none among them is barren” [Col. 1638C] (Song 4:2).

Therefore David and his men dwell in the most secure places of Engaddi while either they preserve true innocence after baptism, or, if they have lost it, strive to regain it by true repentance: weeping bitterly like Peter (Matt. 26:75), singing “Have mercy on me, O God,” like David (Ps. 50:1), and watering the Lord’s feet with tears like Mary (Luke 7:38). Whoever is neither truly innocent nor truly penitent does not dwell in the most secure places of Engaddi. For those who diligently strive toward these most secure places, the invocation of God’s name should be frequently repeated like a loud and pleasing sailor’s chant.

Therefore let every such person say: “Save me, O God, in your name.” In the first part of this psalm, David—the poor man hidden among the Ziphites, among rich persons who flourish—prays now to be judged and distinguished from them by the dissimilarity of life, and afterwards to be fully delivered in the final examination. The second part shows what shall happen to him and the Ziphites: “For behold, God helps me.” In the third he praises God in hymns or songs: “I shall sacrifice to you willingly.” He begins, therefore, with prayer, saying:

[Col. 1638D] **VERSE 3.** God the Father, “in your name,” that is, in your Son, through whom you are named and held glorious in the world, as he himself says: “I have glorified you upon the earth,” namely because “I have made your name manifest to men” (John 17:4, 6). God the Father, whose name was known only in Judaea, has now become known to the whole world through your Son: save me in your name.

Your name, formerly confined within the narrow limits of Judaea, is now poured-out oil sufficient to heal that wounded man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho (Luke 7).
