I, David; I, the penitent; I, the poor man hidden among rich persons who flourish—not famous or flourishing in riches or virtues; I, wounded by robbers who, after inflicting wounds, departed and left me half-dead—I cry to you, my God, and say: God, who because you are God know all things and can do all things, save me in your name.

As long as your name was enclosed like oil, as long as your Word was not yet incarnate, this sick world was ignorant, although some portion of its sickness was disclosed in the five porticoes. There was no one to say to the sick man who had been infirm for thirty-eight years: “Rise, take up your bed, and walk” [Col. 1639B] (Mark 9:11). But now, because “my eyes,” whether David’s through prophecy or mine as a poor man through the evident fulfillment of events, “have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples” (Luke 2:30), because your name—that is, your Son, humanity’s Savior—has become known to the whole world, save me in that same Son, that same name, that same salvation.

Save me in the manner in which you make the whole person sound on the Sabbath, even the one who has been infirm for thirty-eight years: since neither the present life, whose strength advances only up to thirty years, nor the future life, whose entire hope consists in the eighth resurrection and the eight beatitudes, is found sound or strong.

[Col. 1639C] Such am I: I languish and waste away in the condition of the present life among the strong and flourishing Ziphites, lacking virtues and good morals; and I have only a weak hope of future blessedness. For just as the poor in spirit, the meek, those who mourn, those who hunger for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake rightly have a strong hope in the eight beatitudes promised to them (Matt. 5), so conversely there is a weak hope of those same beatitudes where observance of the virtues named above is weak; and where the vices contrary to these virtues reign, there neither is nor can be any hope of the beatitudes.

For hope is confidence in future blessedness, conceived from the truthfulness of the promiser, who promises it to good merits. Therefore to trust in the Lord without the practice of virtues is not hope but presumption. Hope is sound and strong when the mind is vigorous through the knowledge of the virtues to which blessedness is promised. But because I am sick both in body and mind, having thirty-eight years in infirmity—neither flourishing among the Ziphites in the present life nor hoping for future glory from a good conscience, in which “the righteous shall flourish like the palm tree” [Col. 1639D] (Ps. 93:13)—I, sick as I am, cry out and say: “Save me, O God, in your name,” as the sick man was saved to whom it was said: “Take up your bed and walk” (Mark 2:9).

Alternatively: “Save me in your name,” that is, in your Son, so that I may be in him a strong and sound member. Or save me in your name, so that your name and your glory may be made glorious through my salvation among the Ziphites, who do not know your glory and crave their own. Save me in your name—that is, in your Son. “And in your power,” that is, in the Holy Spirit, who is the power of the Most High, deliver or judge me.

Deliver me by giving me not “the spirit of bondage again in fear,” but the Holy Spirit in freedom. For “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3). Again: “If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law. For those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8), and therefore free; those whom you no longer call your servants but friends, as being clothed with power from on high. In this your power deliver me, so that, set free from sin through your Spirit but made a servant of God, I may now have my fruit in sanctification and eternal life as my end—being now as free from sin as I was formerly free from righteousness.

[Col. 1640B] For when I was a servant of sin, I was free from righteousness; but now, set free from sin, I desire to serve you alone, O God—to serve whom is to reign, and to be whose servant surpasses every glory or flower of the Ziphites flourishing in this world.

Some manuscripts read, “judge me”; others, “deliver me.” But the Hebrew truth reads: “Avenge me in your strength.” The sense is the same. For the person whom God judges—that is, distinguishes from the Ziphites—he delivers; and the one whom he delivers, he avenges. This is the vengeance by which God, the Lord of vengeance, freely acts in rendering recompense: condemning the proud or demons; correcting human beings; or, if they are altogether incurable, condemning them also. He likewise renders vengeance or recompense by annihilating vices, just as those vices, insofar as they prevail, annihilate every good.

Alternatively: O God, Son of God, who art called Savior, and who in the preceding psalm art invoked as the salvation of Israel: save me in thy name, and judge me in thy power; for if I shall have been saved in thy name, which has been preached to the world, I shall not fear to be judged in the power of the judgment to come. To save me, thou camest little and weak, bearing, that is, our infirmities. For truly thou didst take our sicknesses and bear our iniquities, becoming weak for the weak. But to judge me and all men thou wilt come in thy power [Col. 1640D], with great power and majesty. Therefore, anticipating thy face in confession, I confess that I cannot behold thee—the sun of righteousness then shining in thy power—with an unstricken gaze, unless thou now savest me in thy name, while it is the time of mercy. Therefore I say: O God, save me in thy name before thou examinest me; and afterward, when I have been healed, when I have sound eyes, then judge me in thy power. For men shall be judged in thy power as eaglets are judged by the power of this sun shining in its strength.

Natural philosophers report that the eagle examines her young in this manner: whichever of them looks upon the sun shining in its strength with the unstricken keenness of its eyes, her own offspring she recognizes [Col. 1641A], cherishes, and feeds; but whichever, unable to endure the brightness of its light from its rays, turns its eyes away, she casts out as illegitimate. And thou, O Savior, hast a face like that of a flying eagle, judging thy children or young at the final examination; and then thou, the brightness of the Father’s glory, shalt shine in thy power. Yet three other faces, working salvation in the midst of the earth, precede this thy face: the face of a man, an ox, and a lion. In these three faces this thy name, Jesus, is known: since, made man, thou didst visit us; as an ox, thou wast sacrificed for our offenses; as a lion, thou didst rise again for our justification. Thus, having been visited and justified by sins washed away, they shall securely behold thy eagle-like face. In that face thou shalt then appear not as Savior but as Judge. [Col. 1641B]

Hence, when thou didst ascend on high like an eagle, in the sight of the apostles, thy chosen young, “behold, two men stood beside them in white garments, who also said: ‘He shall come in the same manner as ye saw him going into heaven’” (Acts I.10–11). Therefore thou shalt come as “an eagle provoking her young to fly and hovering over them” (Deut. XXXII.11), to whom thou shalt also say: “Come, ye blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you.” And likewise to the illegitimate young: “Depart, ye cursed, into eternal fire.” That voice of the Lord in power, that voice of the Lord in magnificence, shall then be of such strength that none can stand against it, because “these shall go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into life eternal” (Matt. XXV).

[Col. 1641C] Before thou dost thus judge me in thy power, save me in thy name, by which thou art called man, ox, and lion: thou, as man, visiting me upon the bed of sickness; thou, as the sacrificial ox, cleansing me from the leprosy of iniquity; thou, as lion, king of righteousness, Lord of hosts, king of glory, justifying me by virtues bestowed. Afterward, when it pleases thy majesty, judge me in thy power as an eagle judges its young; judge me in thy power, O sun of righteousness, because I hope that I may be able to behold thy face in power, if thy power now proceeds from thee to heal me—as thou art recorded to have said when the woman who touched thy hem was healed: “Someone touched me, for I knew that power had gone forth from me” (Matt. IX.20), thou didst say. To this the holy Evangelist also bears witness [Col. 1641D], that “power went out from him and healed all” (Luke VI.19).

This is what I ask, O Savior: that power may now go forth from thee to heal; and after it has healed me and all sick persons needing thy help, then may that power, formerly saving, become the judge of the saved, separating even locally and bodily at the last judgment those long since spiritually [perhaps: specially] separated in secret. For I also ask for that very hidden judgment which is now being carried out, saying: Judge me in thy power.

The Ziphites—those, that is, who flourish in this world—sometimes have an appearance of godliness, but denying its power, they glory only in the empty flowers of appearance while they are honored, though falsely, for the name of holiness. These are those who distinguish themselves from other men by broadening their phylacteries [Col. 1642A] and enlarging their fringes. But I ask to be distinguished from these flourishing persons, or from those who glory even in the flower of riches, in thy power alone. Therefore I say: Judge me in thy power; that is, distinguish me from those who flourish in this way, so that, as they glory in the display of virtues which they do not possess, or of riches which they do possess, I may gladly glory in my weaknesses, that thy power may dwell in me. From it may come to me not vain or empty glory through boasting, but enduring glory through a good conscience, as to those of whom it is said: “Glory, all ye upright in heart” (Ps. XXXI.11); and who say: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I.12). And wherein do the orthodox—that is, those rightly glorious—rightly glory, unless in thy power dwelling within them?

[Col. 1642B] In contrast, the Ziphites glory in their own power, like that Pharisee (Luke XVIII) who, praying in the temple, despised the publican while reckoning up, as he supposed, the flowers of his virtues; or like the rich man who feasted sumptuously every day, clothed in purple and fine linen, a flowery garment (Luke XVI). But because thou dost humble those who lack thy power and glory in their own, both of them were rejected as not possessing thy power.

At this point there occurs a threefold division of those who flourish. Some flourish in the display of virtues, like that Pharisee; some flourish in abundant riches, like that rich man clothed in purple and feasting splendidly. Between these are those who shall flourish like a palm tree, not here but in the house of the Lord. I call these latter the middle sort because they lie hidden among them, deprived of flowers in this world [Col. 1642C], to whom the Apostle also says: “For ye are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III.3). “Ye are dead,” he says; hence in their lament, or hymn, they customarily say: “In the midst of life we are in death; whom do we seek as helper, save thee, O Lord?” etc.

Some flourish through the excess of their own holiness, being made notable and honorable in men’s sight. Others, through the excess of their own dissipation, flourish and shine in this world’s glory while feasting sumptuously every day. We soldiers of David, avoiding both excesses, live a middle life; and we are, among these and those who flourish, as though dead, because, as the Apostle says, “our life is hidden with Christ in God. [Col. 1642D] But when Christ, our life, shall appear, then we too shall appear with him in glory.” Whom then do we rightly “seek as helper, save thee, O Lord, who art justly angry at our sins, holy God, holy mighty one, holy and merciful Savior: deliver us not to bitter death” (*ibid.*)?

Death would be bitter if we were made more miserable than all men, so as to be deprived both of present glory here and of enduring glory then. Hence the Apostle says: “If in this life only we have hope, we are more miserable than all men” (I Cor. XV.19). For we shall be like autumnal trees, twice dead and uprooted, if we neither flourish in leaves through present glory nor are vigorous with the verdure of virtues in the root, where our life ought to be hidden with Christ. [Col. 1643A] Let our root live now, lest bitter death come upon us, a bitterness which at least no delight of present pleasure may temper with joy. Death is exceedingly bitter when it is a harsh passage from present misery into eternal misery. Holy God, holy mighty one, holy and merciful Savior, deliver us not to this bitter death. Rather, grant that, rooted in charity and founded in humility, we may live inwardly before thee, though without the outward flower of leaves.

Yet we do not reject every flower, but the splendid flower such as we see in hay, and the white or rosy flower such as we behold upon a thorn. We rightly compare the rich man, splendidly dressed and feasting sumptuously every day, to flowering hay; and we compare the boasting Pharisee to a thorn, having envious flowers but bitter [Col. 1643B] fruits. For from thorns of this kind men do not gather figs, nor from such a bramble harvest grapes. There is another kind of flourishing, producing obscure flowers and good fruits, like the vine, the ear of grain, and the palm. Because such flowers bear fruit and yet are not splendid, I ask, Lord, that thou make them sufficiently spring up in me. I do not desire flowers too splendid and fruitless.

Indeed, that Pharisee, adorned, as he supposed, with many flowers of virtues, went up into the temple to pray; but he did not possess humility, which is thy power, and which thou greatly commendest where thou sayest: “Learn of me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI.29). That rich man likewise, not understanding that he was withering [Col. 1643C] in his course, gloried that he was adorned with abundant riches as with flowers. But he did not possess charity toward poor Lazarus, which is thy power, and which thou especially commendest where thou sayest: “These things I command you, that ye love one another” (John XV.17). Again: “By this shall all know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love for one another” (John XIII.35). Again: “This is my commandment, that ye love one another” (John XV.12). Again: “A new commandment I give unto you, that ye love one another” (John XIII.34). And so that you may understand this very love to be Christ’s own proper power, he added: “As I have loved you.” For those who love one another otherwise than his instructions and examples show, have a love that is a vice, not a virtue.

[Col. 1643D] Therefore, O Lord of hosts, King of glory, judge me in thy power by distinguishing me from the Ziphites. I do not seek flowers without fruit, but virtues bearing fruit. I do not seek flowers excessively bright and fruitless, such as the thorn and tares have; rather, I seek flowers lacking brilliance and sheen, yet bearing fruit. Would you know the flowers that bear good fruit? Hear the master of virtues rejecting the bright flowers of the Ziphites and praising the obscure flowers of vineyards: “When,” he says, “thou doest alms, do not sound a trumpet” like the hypocrites. Again: “When ye fast, do not become sad like the hypocrites; for they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to fast. For all their works they do in order to be seen by men” (Matt. VI.2, 16). Behold flowers excessively bright [Col. 1644A] and barren, which Christ does not seek in thee, O David, O penitent, O Christian. Therefore he says to thee: “But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand does” (Matt. III.17). When thou hast fasted, “anoint thy head with oil, that thou mayest not appear to men to fast. When thou prayest, enter into thy chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to thy Father” (*ibid.*, 6).

In such almsgiving, the use of riches; in such fasting, contempt for riches; in such prayer, desire for eternal riches—these are commended as good flowers. But the desire and love of temporal riches are vain and transitory flowers; their use and contempt are counted as fruit and as abiding virtue.

Conscious of this virtue in himself, the Apostle Paul says: [Col. 1644B] “I know how to abound, and how to suffer want; I know how to be full, and how to hunger” (Phil. IV). And so that you may know that his knowing and being able to do these things came not from human but divine power, he says: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (*ibid.*, 13). Where this power abounds, it does a man no harm if he loses the flowers of riches, because divine power itself stands firm within itself. So we read of blessed Job, whose power was evident not only when, possessing the flowers of riches, he was great and praiseworthy before God, but also when those same flowers fell away: then a greater power shone forth in him, by which he knew and was able not only to abound but also to suffer want and misery in him whose power strengthened him for both. This power separated him from all others flourishing in riches [Col. 1644C] so completely that none was like him on earth whose power could be compared with his.

Hence he is significantly called *vir*, as though from *virtus* (“power” or “virtue”); and a man not of any ordinary sort, but “a simple and upright man, fearing God and departing from evil” (Job I.2), retaining his innocence even amid adversities. For neither prosperity’s allurements nor adversity’s provocations diminished his power; rather, it increased more and more. Truly none was like him on earth among men rooted and flourishing in the earth. The worst of these were the Jews, who, loving perishable and earthly things and flourishing in them, mocked Christ, the true Job, as he himself says: “But now those younger than I mock me, whose strength of hands I counted as nothing” (Job XXX.1).

Therefore, lest the strength also [Col. 1644D] of my hands be counted as nothing, do thou, Lord God of hosts, convert me, and judge me in thy power, so that thy abiding power in me may distinguish me from those whose strength of hands is nothing, even though their flower seems great. Their flower shall fall; but may my flower, withered on earth, remain green in the courts of the Lord’s house. I said: “O God, save me in thy name, and judge me in thy power.” I repeat the name of power and say:

**VERSE 4.** O God, hear my prayer, by which I ask from thee not the flowers of the Ziphites but thy power. And hear not only the silent prayer of my heart, but receive also the words of my mouth with thine ears. Receive them with ears, namely of mercy and power, so that thou mayest save me mercifully and powerfully. Do thou receive my words [Col. 1645A]; for although the Ziphites hear them, they do not understand, since they know only temporal things. And this is why I ask:

**VERSE 5.** Because strangers have risen up against me: strangers not by race but by disposition. Ziph was a village of Syria belonging to the tribe of Judah, from which King David sprang. Therefore they were strangers not by city or tribe, but as flourishing and mighty men who betrayed me, David, to Saul; or betrayed me, Christ the true David, to death; or betrayed me, David the penitent Christian, to sin. They sought my soul, not to kill my body meanwhile. The Ziphites seek to betray the saints in a new manner when they provoke them so as to corrupt them through zeal for their own peace and hope of temporal things. And in doing this they did not set God before their sight [Col. 1645B], imagining that God did not know or care what they did. A *diapsalma* occurs here.

**VERSE 6.** For behold, God helps me—not outwardly in flower, but inwardly, where our glory is the testimony of conscience. Yet they do not know this, among whom I lie hidden, and who, as has been said, do not set God before their sight. If they set him before their eyes, they would surely see that God helps me to endure patiently and courageously the things which the Ziphites themselves devise against me. For though bodily strength fails, nevertheless God is the sustainer of my soul. They turn many evils upon me, but thou—

**VERSE 7.** Turn evils from me upon them, so that, as they seek to extinguish my good life, their evil life may be extinguished, and, stripped of its flower, they may no longer be proud. And because they glory in the empty vanity of their flowers, do thou destroy them in thy truth; for it is better for them to be chastised with true punishments than to luxuriate in false and deceptive goods. Destroy them in thy power, whom thou hast endured in thy weakness.

Alternatively: Turn evils upon my enemies, so that they may suffer no evil while remaining in vanity, but, coming to truth, may in that very truth be destroyed from their former intention. Destroy them in thy truth, whom thou hast endured in their vanity. Destroy them—that is, destroy them in diverse ways. For among them are some capable of conversion, such as Saul, who, touched by the divine lash, immediately said: “Lord, what wilt thou have me do?” (Acts IX.6). [Col. 1645D] And when he was told what he must do, he obeyed without delay; and he who had been a teacher of the law became a disciple—not of some great apostle, but of Ananias, disciple of the apostles. Destroy such readily convertible people as thou didst destroy Saul, making Paul out of him.

There are also those who are converted still more easily, because, warned by some revelation without any divine chastisement, they gladly yield to truth, as the centurion Cornelius, who, warned by an angelic oracle, immediately withdrew from the Gentile rite and came to the worship of the Christian religion (Acts X). Destroy these as thou didst destroy the pagan man in him, making a Christian man out of him. There are also those who submit to truth by absolutely no chastisement or admonition, such as Judas the traitor. Lest they vex the Church any longer or beyond what is expedient, [Col. 1646A] destroy them as thou didst destroy Judas. Therefore I say: Destroy them, because they are to be destroyed differently and in dissimilar ways—not insofar as they are human beings and my neighbors, but insofar as they are my hostile, treacherous enemies, Ziphites. Therefore destroy them in diverse ways.

Which “them”? Enemies, that is: let them cease to be enemies and become my friends in the truth which they hate for truth’s sake. Destroy them not away from the truth, but in thy truth, so that they may cease to be adversaries of truth and become, in the truth of thy truth, its friends. But if they absolutely refuse to yield to truth so as to become its friends while they are enemies, then destroy them in thy truth in such a way that, though enemies, they may be as though they were not—that is, unable to do harm. Similar is the saying elsewhere: “Let sinners perish from the face of God” (Ps. LXVII.3). Again: “Let sinners fail from the earth, and the wicked, so that they be no more” (Ps. CIII.35), with “sinners and wicked” understood. Let them be men and not wicked, as it is said in the Proverbs: “Overthrow the wicked, and they shall be no more” (Prov. XII.7).

But I, saved in thy name and freed or judged in thy power, distinguished from the Ziphites both for my own salvation and for the conversion of my enemies—

**VERSE 8.** I will willingly sacrifice to thee, not in the blood of goats or calves, but in the songs of hymns, psalms, and spiritual canticles, in which I will confess thy name, because it is good. I will confess thy name—that is, I will praise thy name willingly, with gratuitous and spontaneous love [Col. 1646C]: not in order to obtain the flowers of the Ziphites, but because of the goodness of thy name itself, because thy name itself is good. For whoever praises thy name for some other reason does not do so freely, but from necessity and desire for some thing which, if he possessed it, he would not praise thee for. But I, in accordance with the title of this psalm, will praise in songs or hymns thy name, of which I said at the beginning of the psalm: “O God, save me in thy name.” And I shall praise it not only because of my need, but much more because of its own goodness, since thy name itself is good. This I have understood and tasted because—

**VERSE 9.** Thou hast delivered me from every tribulation. This tribulation was given so that I might call upon thee [Col. 1646D], thou mightest deliver me, and I, delivered, might honor thee in songs. For elsewhere thou sayest: “Call upon me in the day of tribulation; I will deliver thee, and thou shalt honor me” (Ps. XLIX.15). Thus I, David—I, any poor man desolated among the Ziphites and surrounded on every side by enemies as if by a crown—called upon thee in my tribulation, saying: “O God, save me in thy name,” etc. But thou, invoked by me in my tribulation, hast delivered me from every tribulation, so that by this very deliverance I might understand that thy name is good. Perhaps I should have understood this less had I not been afflicted and called upon thee in tribulation. But now, taught by the experience of things, I well understand thy name, because it is good; and its sweetness tastes good to me, because on account of it and through it thou hast delivered me from every [Col. 1647A] tribulation, establishing me in the most secure places of En-gedi, of which something was said above in the title.

Therefore my eye has looked down upon my enemies. My enemies, the Ziphites, were formerly above me when they betrayed me to Saul. But because, delivered from their midst, I remain in the safest places of En-gedi, now as though from on high my eye has looked down upon my enemies, holding in contempt all the flowers of the Ziphites, who glory far too vainly in the vigor of the flesh, since “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is as the flower of grass” (I Pet. I.24). And if “the grass, which is today and tomorrow is cast into the oven” (Matt. VI.30), loses its flower, in which it is now clothed more gloriously than Solomon in all his glory, so quickly that it exists only today—that is, in the present and momentary time—who does not readily perceive that what cannot endure, however beautiful it may be, should be despised? Therefore my eye has looked down upon my enemies, because unless they are converted and change from enemies into friends, the grass of their flesh shall briefly bloom today and tomorrow—that is, in the everlasting future—shall burn in the infernal furnace. [Col. 1647B]

This entire psalm may fittingly be read in the person of Christ, so that he himself may speak on the day of his tribulation, when his Passion was impending among the Ziphites—that is, the Jews flourishing in the glory of the flesh. God the Father, save me in thy name by glorifying me whom thou hast sent; for I came in thy name, and the Ziphites did not receive me. Another shall afterward come in his own name [Col. 1647C], and him they shall receive; but they who now deliver me to Saul—that is, to death—shall deliver me. Therefore thou, Father, in whose name I came, save me in that same thy name by raising me from death, not as any ordinary dead man, but as thy only Son, who shall reign with thee and sit upon David’s throne, whether my Ziphite enemies will or no. They number and mingle me among other dead persons in my human weakness; but do thou judge me—that is, distinguish me from them—in thy power, showing by my resurrection and ascension that I am thy Son, thy power, thy wisdom, equally omnipotent with thee, O omnipotent Father. O God, hear my prayer. Thou who art my Father, in whose name I, thy Son, came, art also my God [Col. 1647D], because I am man, the Son of the Virgin; and I, who as God hear the prayers of the faithful, as man prayed and intercede for them. Therefore I say: O God, hear my prayer, which upon the Mount of Olives I poured forth for my own, praying at length and shedding a bloody sweat.

Receive with thine ears the words of my mouth for those whom thou hast given me out of the world, because the Jews or Ziphites, neighbors according to the flesh but made strangers in disposition, rose up against me to destroy me. And these strong men, strong with false strength, like madmen opposing me their physician, sought my soul either to draw it into agreement with their own perversity or to take it away from me. Yet I alone, having power at my own will to lay down my soul and take it again [Col. 1648A], showed sufficiently by this very power that I am God: by dying powerfully and by rising powerfully from death. But they did not set God before their sight: they did not conceive that I, a man scourged and slain before their eyes, possessed divinity in such a way as to be believed God. They were unwilling to understand concerning the needy and poor man. For they readily understood that I was needy and poor; above or beyond this they refused to understand anything of my divinity, but judged me deserving of punishment as a false witness and blasphemer of God because I said that I was the Son of God or God.

If, in saying this, I had been a false witness or a blasphemer against God, I surely would not have had God as my helper—as no blasphemer is ever recorded to have been helped by God [Col. 1648B]. For example, Pharaoh made himself equal and opposed himself to God, wishing to retain God’s own people against him. But when he was drowned with his people and God’s people escaped, it was rightly sung in God’s praises: “Who is like unto thee among the mighty, O Lord? Who is like unto thee? Glorious in holiness, terrible and praiseworthy, working wonders” (Exod. XV.11). What wonders? Namely these: thou didst stretch out thy hand against blaspheming Pharaoh and his followers, and the earth devoured them. Likewise Nebuchadnezzar, a blasphemer falsely arrogating divine eminence to himself, was cast out from among men and ate grass like an ox until he acknowledged that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men (Dan. IV). It would take long to recount God’s blasphemers refuted and humbled by God himself. [Col. 1648C]

And so, if I, in calling myself God or Son of God, had been false or blasphemous, then similarly abandoned by God I would not have had—or have—God himself as helper in all that I willed and will, as I have always had him and have him now. For behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the sustainer of my soul, whose spirit or soul I commended into his hands upon the cross. Behold, he now helps me by restoring the soul commended to him, so that, raised from death and exalted at his right hand, I may reign as God, as does God my Father. Hence even now, while my strength has been weakened in the hands of my enemies, I judge among them as a king: sentencing some to eternal death [Col. 1648D], reserving others for pardon. For I say: Turn evils upon my enemies and destroy them in thy truth, so that thou mayest destroy the wicked badly by condemning those obstinate in wickedness, and preserve for repentance those who know not what they do.

For these, praying upon the cross, I will as willingly as for the others whom thou hast given me offer thee the voluntary whole offering of my Passion and death. Likewise through my priests I will willingly sacrifice to thee for such persons, so that no man may perish except wicked men to be wickedly destroyed; these too I excluded in my prayer, saying: “I pray not for the world, but for those whom thou hast given me out of the world” (John XVII.9). Therefore, when these have been saved, in them themselves I will confess thy name, making them praisers of thy name, because thy name is good—not among all good things, but above all good things; or because it is good to confess thy good name. This is clear from the fact that in me and through me thou hast delivered—that is, without doubt wilt deliver—my own from all tribulations; and therefore my eye has looked down upon my Ziphite enemies. [Col. 1649A]

[Col. 1650A] Glory to God the Father, to whom it is said: “O God, save me in thy name.” Glory to the Son, who came in the Father’s name. Glory to the Holy Spirit, that power of God concerning which it is said to God: “And in thy power deliver,” or “judge me.” Amen.

## PSALM LIV

[Col. 1649]

[Col. 1649A] “Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise my supplication,” etc. This psalm is the prayer of our Head, dealing with the present rejection of the Jews, their eternal condemnation, the admission [Col. 1649B] of the Gentiles, and the eternal security of the faithful. It bears this inscription:

**(VERSE 1) UNTO THE END; IN SONGS; UNDERSTANDING OF DAVID HIMSELF.**

And its meaning is: The understanding of this psalm is to be attributed to the true David, that is, to Christ persevering unto the end or completion of his obedience. And this is “in songs,” that is, in joy. Above all, it encourages hope by what is said on behalf of a good combatant: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly away and be at rest?” etc., down to the end where it says: “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days; but I will hope in thee, O Lord.” The title says “in songs” because those rejoicing in hope delight to praise God in songs. It is also called “the understanding of David” because the great David—that is, Christ entire, head and body—speaks here, and his members are warned to understand in what great evil, and how great an evil, they are. Once they understand this, they rightly praise God in hymns or songs, not only when he consoles them in glad and prosperous circumstances, but also when he chastens and disciplines them amid harsh and adverse ones. [Col. 1649C]

But since hope, like an upper millstone, is useless without fear, which is the lower millstone, a righteous and God-fearing man—Peter, for example, still faint-hearted and tossed by the storm—is introduced here lamenting the evils of this age. Since he cannot benefit others, he resolves to separate himself from so many scandals lest they harm him. In figure of this, David, when Saul and his own citizens persecuted him, often fled because of their hostility into the wilderness, hiding in mountains, caves, and hollows of the earth. Hence he says: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude.” No one prefers solitude to villages and cities unless he understands that this land of the shadow of death in which we are is not a place of joy but of sorrow.

Throughout the whole psalm, moreover, the complete character of the servant-form in Christ is described, in whom an example of both patience and humility is given us. For he himself, humbly disposed and maintaining patience, when the Jews wished to stone him, fled into the wilderness and remained there with his disciples. There he awaited him who saved him from faint-heartedness [Col. 1650A] of spirit and from the storm. For while he was there, as John says, in the town called Ephraim near the wilderness, there was a certain sick man, Lazarus of Bethany, which is situated in Judaea and is near Jerusalem, the chief metropolis [Col. 1650B] of the Jews.

When he was summoned by Lazarus’s sisters, as though unmindful of the Jewish storm from which he had shortly before fled as one about to be stoned, and though he knew that shortly afterward he would be crucified, he returned to Judaea and came to Bethany. There, raising Lazarus and preaching openly, and then coming to Jerusalem upon an ass and a colt, he proceeded with such constancy and did all things well, as though he had never known any faint-heartedness. As if he said: “When you Jews wished to stone me, because I did not wish to die by such a death and because my hour had not yet come, I fled far away and remained in solitude, like one faint-hearted and weak. There, praying and instructing my disciples, I awaited him who would save me from faint-heartedness of spirit and storm. This has now occurred, because behold: as I enter openly into the holy city, Hebrew children glorify me as King David; and I, like a mighty king—indeed infinitely stronger than any king—do what no infinite army could have done against you. By this I show that I have been saved from the faint-heartedness of the human spirit: in the strength of the divine Spirit, with zeal for God’s house consuming me, I overturned your tables, poured out the money, and drove sellers and buyers from the temple” (John X and XI). [Col. 1650C]

But let us now return to the psalm, which begins with prayer, as it has in common with the other psalms treating of the Passion; for all these begin with prayer. In the second part it [Col. 1650D] invokes deserved punishments upon its adversaries, saying: “Cast them down, O Lord; divide their tongues.” Thirdly, it declares, proceeding alternately, what God does for him and for his adversaries, where it says: “But I cried unto God, and the Lord shall save me.” Therefore Christ entire, laboring amid the waves of this age, prays, saying:

**VERSE 2.** Hear, O God, my prayer, by which I ask good things necessary and useful for myself and mine; and do not despise my supplication, by which I ask that harmful things be removed. That is, do not regard my prayer as despised or worthless, as thou dost despise the supplication of those whom thou even hearest when they cry to thee only for the acquisition of temporal goods or the removal of temporal evils, merely so that on this day, which smiles upon [Col. 1651A] their peace, nothing distressing may appear to them. Yet, although these things are now hidden from their eyes, they are all kept for the future. Thus their prayers and supplications are despised because they do not seek the highest good or flee the misery of the greatest evil. But I, the true David, because I pray and supplicate for myself and mine against the greatest evils and for the highest goods, rightly ask this of thee, Father: do not despise my supplication. And if it seems to deserve contempt because of my own people, who are still unworthy and for whom I pray that they may become worthy, then while they are unworthy do not attend to them or look upon them; rather, attend to me, Christ thy Son, who am worthy and worthily to be heard because of my reverence.

**VERSE 3.** Attend to me, or unto me, and hear me, helper in due times, in tribulation; for tribulation is near—so near that I am grieved in my exercise, while “my soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI.38). I call this very tribulation my exercise, because I too, like a golden lampstand, am fashioned and perfected amid the frequent fires and hammers of tribulations; and my elect, like the branches of that same lampstand, must be perfected by exercises of tribulation just as I am. Or, “I am grieved in my exercise,” because the earth which I cultivate does not yield its fruits but brings forth thorns and thistles for me, as in my vineyard from which I expected grapes, but it produced wild grapes. I expected it to produce justice, and behold the cry of those saying: “Crucify, crucify him.” Again: “He is guilty of death.” Hence I am troubled.

VERS. 4. From the voice of the enemy crying out against me and crucifying me by voice or tongue alone—that is, the Jewish people—and from the tribulation of the sinner, the Gentile who scourged and crucified me with his hand. For they turned iniquities against me, and in anger they afflicted me. It was not enough for them to kill me unless they also numbered me among the wicked. For this reason they hung me on the cross between two thieves, as though I were an evildoer, as though more wicked than both those wrongdoers. Yet there was no iniquity in my hands, nor did I repay evils to those repaying me; rather, I prayed for them, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” [Col. 1651D] (Luke 23:34). This prayer of mine was offered only for those who sinned against me through ignorance, not for those evil tenants who, knowing me as the heir, cast me out of the vineyard. They were not worthy in any respect to obtain pardon, because they turned iniquities against me not through ignorance; rather, iniquity lied to itself when they said that I cast out demons by Beelzebub and that I had a demon. Thus, by deliberate and contrived falsehood, they turned iniquities against me, and in anger they afflicted me. For malicious anger alone was their motive, so that, speaking in the wrathfulness of the earth, they might afflict me. While they afflicted me—

VERS. 5 and 6. My heart was troubled within me, [Col. 1652A] and the dread of death fell upon me. For, while my soul was sorrowful even unto death, I began to fear and to be weary, because fear and trembling came upon me when the hour of the Passion was at hand—a Passion which human weakness naturally recoiled from, though the willing spirit remained. The voice of weak humanity was: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”; the voice of the willing spirit was: “Father, let your will be done” (Mark 14:36). Indeed, if I had wished, I could have avoided fearing or being weary; but, having become weak for the weak, I willed this: that fear and trembling should come upon me, so that my little ones might thereby hope, even if they trembled amid dangers of this kind [read: of this world], in which I first experienced trembling of body and fear of heart—not through a weak necessity as they do, but through the firm power by which I willed it to be so. For fear and trembling came upon me for as much and as long as I willed.

And darkness covered me: while I hung upon the cross, from the sixth hour until the ninth, the sun being darkened, darkness came over the whole earth (Luke 23:44–45). In this too darkness covered me, the true Samson: my eyes were darkened through death, which extinguished not sight alone but all my five bodily senses at once.

VERS. 7. And I said: Who will give me wings like those of a dove, that I may fly away and rest? Namely, in Paradise, to which I also brought the soul of the thief for rest.

VERS. 8. Behold, fleeing, I went far away and remained in solitude. My soul, alone without the body, rested and kept sabbath in Paradise [Col. 1652C] with the blessed souls alone, including those drawn from hell through me.

Diapsalma. VERS. 9. Thus I awaited him who, by raising my body from death and many bodies of the saints, saved me from faintness of spirit and from the storm, granting me all power in heaven and on earth. Therefore I demand a just judgment against my enemies, saying:

VERS. 10. Cast down, O Lord, those set on high, and divide their tongues, united in evil; for I saw iniquity and contradiction in the city. Formerly I had sent prophets and my other messengers. At last, when my Father said, “They will reverence my Son” (Matt. 21:37), I myself came; and present in person [Col. 1652D] I saw iniquity and contradiction in the city, not merely for an hour but—

VERS. 11 and 12. By day and night; that is, at every time iniquity will surround it upon its walls, and toil and injustice will be in its midst, because it kills the prophets and stones those sent to it. Iniquity and toil are in its midst because, in order to act unjustly, they laboured to fabricate lies; for whoever lies labours. But where iniquity abounds both around and in the middle of a city, what place is there for justice, when both the rulers, like a wall defending the people round about, and the people in their midst all alike devise injustice?

But above all, both rulers and people of this city devote themselves to greed, because usury [Col. 1653A] and deceit have not departed from its streets. Why do I speak of its streets, when they even practised the contrivances of usury in the holy Temple, making God’s house a house of trade? But by casting out those who sold and bought there, I purified the Temple from the filth of avarice, converting from among them some who were worthy of the Temple’s name, since they had from eternity been predestined to holiness. Yet from its streets—reckoned as outside all holiness, like the mud of dregs—usury and deceit did not depart; that is, the intention or effort to profit oneself and deceive one’s neighbours. You too belonged to this street, filled alike with usury and deceit: though you had been called disciple and apostle, because of your greed and deceit you became intolerable to me.

VERS. 13. For if an enemy had reviled me, [Col. 1653B] I would indeed have borne it; and if one who openly hated me had spoken great things against me, perhaps I would have hidden myself from him, just as I hid myself from the foreigner Herod, fleeing into Egypt and remaining hidden there until Herod’s death. Later also, when I was told that Herod, son of the former Herod, wished to kill me—he who also killed John the Baptist—I did not present myself to him, because I did not then wish to be killed by him. He was tetrarch of Galilee and had no authority in Jerusalem, where I was to be killed by that city's judges and high priests. For Pilate himself would have had no authority whatever against me unless it had been given him from above. Therefore the Pharisaic assembly which handed me over to him bears the greater sin.

[Col. 1653C] VERS. 14 and 15. But you, Judas, most wicked merchant—a man of one mind with me, a man of my peace, my guide, my apostle, prince and leader established by me, King David—you who together with me took sweet food even at my last supper, when I earnestly desired to eat the Passover, consummating the Law and inaugurating grace: you, I say, such a man and so received by me, sinned more grievously against me, since it availed me nothing in your regard that we walked together in the house of God in harmony. What, then, shall I say of persons acting so wickedly in such obstinacy that they cannot in any way be softened even by benefits?

VERS. 16. Let death come upon them, and let them go down alive into hell, so that they may become like in punishment those whom they are found like in guilt. It is written that Dathan and Abiram, who rose against Moses, were swallowed alive by the earth with their tents and all their possessions. But Korah, together with the two hundred and fifty who, apart from Aaron, offered incense, was killed by fire that came forth from the Lord. Then a conflagration destroyed fourteen thousand seven hundred of the people, who in the spirit of contention would not repent, although they had seen the punishment of the transgressors; and therefore, by a just judgment, a fire of consumption came upon the fire of dissension. Thus those first schismatics perished: the leaders who sinned knowingly were swallowed alive by the earth, and then upon their followers—who perhaps sinned ignorantly, yet obstinately—came a fire that could in no way be extinguished except by holy fire (Num. 16:31 ff.). For while the conflagration was raging, [Col. 1654A] Aaron, the great and lawful priest, took a censer with holy fire, stood between the living and the dead, and set a limit to the advancing destruction (Num. 16:47–48).

So may it happen to all their followers: let death come upon them, and let them go down alive into hell—except only those for whom I, Christ, the true high priest, offer on the cross the censer of flesh filled with the fire of love. For I do not pray for the world, which lies in the evil one, but for those whom you, Father, gave me out of the world—a world which does not know you. I pray for transgressors, that they may not perish; but for stubborn despisers I do not pray.

For wickedness is in their dwellings, while they live wickedly and shamefully in their private homes; and [Col. 1654B] wickedness is likewise in their midst, while all together devote themselves publicly to injustice. Or “in their midst” means in their heart: there is the seat of wickedness, which, proceeding thence, fills all their dwellings.

VERS. 17. But I cried to God, and the Lord will save me. Kindly hearers, you have heard that I have justly called down punishment on my enemies; now hear also what, praying upon the cross, I obtained for you who are my friends. For they do not cry to God, but against God. But I cried to God, and the Lord will save me. For I said: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). Thus I cried once upon the cross, and the Lord saved me by raising [Col. 1654C] me from death.

But the voice of my blood, crying from the earth, will not cease from its cry for my whole body until all its members are found saved, alike in souls and bodies. For this is what my threefold cry demands: namely, that of my Passion, resurrection, and ascension—three mysteries which

VERS. 18. Were consummated in the evening, morning, and noon. For in the evening I hung dead upon the cross, my Passion being consummated; in the morning I rose; and at noon I ascended in the sight of my disciples. I shall not keep silent about what was thus done; but, when the Paraclete has been sent from heaven to the apostles, I shall through them, instructed in the knowledge of every language, recount and proclaim it, so that their sound may go out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world. [Col. 1654D] I shall recount and proclaim: I shall recount things past and proclaim things future—or rather, the three mysteries themselves. For though they are past in actual occurrence, they are nevertheless future and ever enduring in power and fruit. Nor is this surprising. For if, through the disobedience of one man—though it is past in occurrence yet remains in guilt—many were made sinners, much more through the obedience of my Passion, resurrection, and ascension—though past in occurrence yet abiding in power and fruit—many will be made righteous, having been instructed in these mysteries and united with me by likeness: by the likeness of death, when they have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires; by the likeness of resurrection, when they walk in newness of life; and by the likeness of ascension, when their citizenship is in heaven.

Therefore [Col. 1655A] I shall recount the mysteries of my Passion, resurrection, and ascension, which in the evening, morning, and noon have occurred in fact concerning me; and I shall proclaim how those same mysteries remain in their power and fruit. And God, my Father, to whom I cry, will hear my voice. For the fruit of a prayer heard is this:

VERS. 19. He will redeem my soul in peace; that is, he will redeem it so that it may be in everlasting peace, while both here, among those who hate peace, I shall be peaceable, and hereafter, in the vision of peace—which is the heavenly Jerusalem—I shall rest, wholly freed from those who draw near to me: they honour me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. For they were among many with me: they were with me among the many called, not among the few [Col. 1655B] chosen; among much chaff, not among few grains. Or, they were with me in many things, because they were concerned about many goods common to good and evil alike. Yet in the one thing necessary they were not with me. Or, they were with me in many ecclesiastical observances—namely baptism, confession of faith, reading of the Gospel, celebration of feasts, and such things—but not in charity, without which many good things perish: whether tongues, knowledge, prophecy, or other such things, which, if they alone lack charity, are found wholly useless.

Previously I said, “God, you will hear my voice,” in that he will redeem my soul in peace. Again I say:

[Col. 1655C] VERS. 20. God, who is before the ages, will hear and humble them. This double hearing produces a double fruit, since it works peace for me and mine, and humiliation for enemies. This is what I say: God, who is before the ages, will hear my prayer concerning my enemies and humble them. They have been exalted through familiarity with Caesar or some other mortal ruler; for example, when they say: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). Thus puffed up, they glory in a mortal man who is dust and ashes. But he who is before the ages will humble them. I do not say, “who was before the ages,” because in God’s essence there is nothing past which has ceased to be, nothing future which is not yet; rather, he simply and altogether is before all ages and through all ages.

Those whom a mortal ruler exalts, his successor sometimes humbles after that ruler’s death; and conversely, he exalts those whom the former ruler humbled. But this ruler, who is before the ages and has neither predecessor nor successor, so humbles the proud and exalts the humble (Ps. 124:5) that no one except him can alter his deed.

Here there seems to be a change of speaker, because what follows is more fittingly assigned to the prophet or another elect person than to the person of Christ. For example, David, Peter the apostle, or another principal speaker speaks; and the entire psalm may also be assigned to such a speaker in this manner:

Hear, O God, my prayer for the obtaining of temporal and eternal goods alike. And do not despise [Col. 1656A] my supplication for the averting of temporal and eternal evils alike. For a prayer or supplication made for temporal things alone would deserve to be despised. Yet, lest because of my sins you despise my supplication, do not attend to what I have done against you, but attend to me, or attend in me, whom you made, so that you may extend your right hand to the work of your hands. Forget the evil work I have done and blot it from the book of your remembrance; but attend to me, or in me, whom you made in your image and likeness. With your beauty and loveliness, look upon me as upon a mirror; and do not cease polishing until you see shining in me the beautiful face of your image and likeness. Turn your face toward my face, while nevertheless turning your face away [Col. 1656B] from my sins; and do not turn your face away from me, but attend to me and hear me, so that, heard, I may rejoice in you. For whenever, while praying, I am not heard, I am sorrowful in myself; and this is what I say: “I was saddened in my exercise.”

“Bodily exercise is useful for a little” (1 Tim. 4:8), says the Apostle. It is therefore not surprising if someone is saddened when only slight fruit arises from great bodily exercise. Thus Esau was saddened after the great bodily exertion of hunting, obtaining from it scarcely a small blessing. Though he wept with a great cry, his blessing nevertheless lay only in the fatness of the earth and the dew of heaven above—that is, in earthly prosperity alone. But Jacob, his brother, through the exercise of devotion by which he obeyed his mother, obtained an abundant blessing in heavenly as well as earthly things, his father saying to him: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed,” etc. (Gen. 27:27).

Knowing this, I, David, serving God “unto the end in hymns,” as the title of this psalm has it, set aside bodily exercise, useful only for a little, and obeyed Mother Church, like Jacob dwelling in a tent—that is, ordered by monastic or ecclesiastical disciplines. There, while I applied myself not so much to bodily as to spiritual exercise, not given to hunting like Esau but attentive to hymns and songs like Jacob, who, singing hymns to God, said: “Truly the Lord is in this place” (Gen. 28: [Col. 1656D] 16), this my exercise produced joy in me whenever I felt that my prayer or supplication had been heard.

Even now I labour in the songs of prayers to bring forth joy—not a small joy, but one that consummates well unto the end—saying: “Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise my supplication; attend to me and hear me.” But because I do not have the power to bring forth the joy with which I labour—for if I am not heard, I cannot rejoice unto the end, since I do not know what my strength is or what my end is, so as to act patiently—I am greatly saddened in my exercise.

I have been saddened in the exercise of songs or hymns chiefly in two ways. For it often happens, sins requiring it, that with the exercise of the mind relaxed or interrupted, I am by no means watchful in prayer, as the Apostle exhorts: “Be prudent,” he says, “and watch in prayers” (1 Pet. 4:7). But sometimes I sleep in mind or body in such a way that I do not sing wisely, even if I sing vocally. Thus I have often been saddened in my exercise, saying: “My soul slumbered from weariness” (Ps. 118:28). Likewise: “Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged!” (Ps. 119:5).

Again, when I am in some measure awake and sing wisely, insofar as divine grace inspires me, yet even then sometimes do not feel that I have been heard—while I fear that my prayer, which is not manifestly heard or answered, has been rejected by the ears of divine mercy—I am saddened in my exercise. Hence comes that voice of those who mourn and say in their sorrow: “We waited for peace, and you do not come, O Lord; we sought good things, and behold, disturbance” (Isa. 17:14). [Col. 1657B]

Certainly I, David repenting—or, for example, I, Peter the apostle—was saddened in my exercise when, after weeping bitterly in my exercise, I still could not feel that the voice of my weeping had been heard. Therefore I was troubled by the voice of the enemy, the devil, by whose temptation through the mouth of a maidservant I had fallen; and by the tribulation of the sinner, seeing the mighty wind of the Jewish storm by which Satan, the sinner, afflicted me—he who demanded us in order to sift us like wheat. Such tribulation is indeed a great exercise for the elect, in which the perfect person rejoices, whom no consciousness of an evil cause reproaches. For, enduring sorrows for righteousness’ sake, from those very sorrows he conceives great joy, and, like another Samson, from a strong distress—as though from the mouth of a lion—takes the honey of sweetest consolation, according to the saying of the Apostle James: “Count it all joy, brothers, when you fall into various trials, knowing that tribulation works patience” (Jas. 1:2–3). Likewise Paul says: “We also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience, patience testing, testing hope, and hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:4–5). Thus, rejoicing in hope and patient in tribulation, the righteous and perfect exult.

But I, repenting with David the penitent, walking sorrowfully with Peter still sorrowful, [Col. 1657D] was saddened in my exercise amid those who afflicted and cursed me: either because I perceive that I do not fully love those enemies themselves, or because I fear that I may fail rather than advance among those who afflict me. For I, who neither wish nor ought to be troubled, was nevertheless, against my intention, troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner. This is the exercise in which brief and light anger, like a straw, disturbs the eye. But I pray that my eye may not be put out by the beam of hatred—that anger may not grow into hatred and make a beam out of a straw, so that I become a murderer, as it is written: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

Nor is it surprising that I am tempted to anger against [Col. 1658A] my enemies, since they turned iniquities against me and in anger afflicted me, as explained above. For just as iniquity knowingly lied to itself against Christ, so against me, however insignificant a member of him, it has constructed false calumnies against me. Having no reason other than their anger, in that anger they afflicted me, seeking not to correct me in any respect but only to afflict me.

Therefore, while I struggle with myself, striving to return good to them for evil, and they in turn return hatred to me for love, my heart is troubled within me and the dread of death falls upon me. For because my eye is sometimes troubled by anger, dread of death—that is, dread of hatred, which is the death of the soul, whose life is love—falls upon me; that is, I greatly fear that my long-standing anger may become hatred. And because I perceived the danger to be near, fear of mind and trembling of body came upon me, and darkness covered me.

They covered me, as it were, outwardly, because the spark of love burned and shone within, by which I prayed for my persecutors. Yet, because “whoever hates his brother is in darkness, and darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:11), that very darkness covered me: the excessive hatred of my enemies almost provoked me to hate in return; and though it could not wholly extinguish the fire of charity, since “charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13:8), it nevertheless covered it, as with ashes and dust of its own malice, lest it should shine before people. For it did not permit me to show any kindness [Col. 1658C] to the malicious, since they were too indignant to receive any visible benefit contrary to their evil treatment.

Accordingly, because I could neither edify friends nor gain enemies, I desired the secret of solitude and said: “Who will give me wings like those of a dove, that I may fly away and rest?” For, wishing to live devoutly in Christ, I sometimes endured open persecution and sometimes hidden persecution, of which the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29). Therefore, grieved that I could not correct the wicked and fearing that their company would disturb and worsen me, wearied beyond measure by the present common life and moved by desire for solitude or death, so that I might escape scandals, I desired wings—not those of the raven, which, once sent from the ark, did not return to it, whether lured by corpses or detained by the waters.

Therefore I asked not for the wings of a raven but of a dove. When the dove finds no place outside where its foot may rest, it flees within; and, when sent outside again as need requires, it brings back to those enclosed signs of peace. So the faithful soul, having received the Holy Spirit as a pledge, in order that it may be in that Spirit who is the dove, itself also, as a dove, flees into solitude on the wings of heavenly desires; yet it does not abandon the society of the good, through the office of peace and charity, for whose sake it even endures the proximity of the wicked.

But why does it ask for wings, when the charity of such a soul has two wings? It has them indeed, but perhaps they are bound—not by the birdlime (viscus) of covetousness, but by the care and duty of brotherly [Col. 1659A] concern; and he who loosens them is the one who gives them. But if they are so bound by the duty indispensable for the welfare of the brethren that it cannot fly away and leave them in order to fulfill that duty, merit grows from such a desire; and then one who is in that condition says: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, for it is far better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:23). Thus I, David—I who repent—sought wings; and sometimes, by God’s grace, receiving them, “Behold, fleeing, I went far away and remained in solitude.”

On this passage blessed Gregory says in Job:

[Note: [Col. 1659D] St Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book IV, chapter 30.]

> “One goes far away by flight who raises himself from the crowd of temporal desires into lofty contemplation of God. And one remains in solitude who perseveres in the withdrawn intention of the mind. For the mind that desires unlawful things suffers, as it were, a certain crowd, being ravaged by the insolent tumult of thoughts. By contrast, holy persons, because they desire nothing of this world, are undoubtedly oppressed by no tumults in their heart; but, desiring their eternal homeland alone, they enjoy the tranquillity of mind.”

For great and tranquil is that solitude of the mind in which it alone is with God alone, as a bride with her bridegroom upon the flower-strewn bed of the heart, as she herself says in the Song of Songs: “Our bed is flowery” (Song 1:15). Flowers of this kind abound more in solitude than in a multitude. For all who desire unlawful things or wish to seem something in this world are pressed in heart by dense tumults of thoughts; and when they stir up crowds of desires among themselves, the fallen mind is trampled beneath the foot of miserable thronging and reduced to a plaything. How can the flowers of virtues grow in such a mind, flowers from which a bed fitting for the delights of nuptial flowers may be made?

Therefore, so that I might have flowers upon which I might rest with God and in God, separated, if not in body then in heart, from the tumultuous multitude, I fled and remained in solitude. There, resting on the flower-strewn bed, I awaited him who saved me.

But because, remaining in solitude, I enjoyed some measure of rest while attending to everlasting peace, a diapsalma is rightly inserted here; in Hebrew it is always found as “Forever,” because everlasting peace is tasted beforehand in the solitude of the mind. What follows:

[Col. 1659D] I awaited him who saved me from faintness of spirit and from the storm. For, seeing the mighty wind earlier, I feared as one faint-hearted, as one of little or slight faith. But when I cried, “Lord, save me” (Matt. 14:30), and began to sink amid the danger itself, God, to whom I cried, saved me from faintness of spirit and from the storm. This is what I asked at the beginning of the psalm: namely, that my prayer might be heard. Since I perceive that it has been heard for my salvation, having been saved from faintness of spirit and storm, I now also pray for my enemies, saying: “Cast down, O Lord; divide their tongues.”

There are two principal means by which the wicked prevail against the good: in this world, exalted by honours and powers, they rule; and, by the mutual agreement of many, they are strengthened in falsehood against truth. Thus long ago, among the sons of Adam who were in agreement with one another against God, that tower began to be built. Those who were building it were, as it were, cast down from its height when they were at once divided and confounded by the division of tongues, and prevented from finishing its construction. So now likewise: Cast down, O Lord, all workers of iniquity, and divide their tongues. Cast them down now unto repentance, lest in the future judgment you cast them headlong into eternal punishment; and divide their tongues among themselves now, lest in the future they be divided like goats from the fellowship of the lambs. Let them now be divided among themselves by the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, lest then they be divided by the same sword [Col. 1660B] from the kingdom of God.

On this passage blessed Gregory says in Job:

[Note: [Col. 1660D] St Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book XXXIV, chapter 4.]

> “Just as it is ruinous if unity is absent among the good, so it is more ruinous if it is not absent among the wicked. For the unity of the reprobate obstructs the way of the good all the more harshly insofar as it opposes that way more stubbornly by its collected strength. Paul had observed this harmful unity of the reprobate when, seized in the midst of Sadducees and Pharisees, he said: ‘It is concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead that I am being judged’ (Acts 23:6). By this saying the crowd of hearers, struck at once, broke apart against itself in mutual opposition. And when the multitude in tumult was divided into two parties, a way of escape was opened for Paul, because the crowd of persecutors which had hemmed him in when united gave way when divided. For the righteous are rescued when the unrighteous are divided, and the desires of the elect reach fulfillment when the ranks of the reprobate are confounded by discord.

> “This is also well signified by the dividing of the Red Sea. When the wave is divided into two parts, the chosen people proceed toward the land of promise; for when the unity of the wicked is broken, good minds are led to that which they desire. If the unity of the wicked had not been harmful, divine providence would never have scattered the tongues of the proud in such diversity.”

Therefore, desiring that this unity of the reprobate be scattered, the prophet says of the enemies of holy Church: “Cast down, O Lord; divide their tongues.” They have already been cast down inwardly, because you cast them down within while they were being raised outwardly. In contrast, I pray that they may now be cast down outwardly, so that they may be raised inwardly.

Thus King Nebuchadnezzar was once cast down outwardly from the height of his pride until his heart was humbled. Thus also King Manasseh was cast down from the throne of his kingdom because of his sins, carried to Babylon and put in prison until he was humbled and purified by true repentance. The proud and impious Jezebel too was cast down when Jehu said to the eunuchs: “Throw her down.” This was truly useful to her—not because she was saved by repentance, but because, cast down thus, she could no longer further provoke or store up for herself the wrath of God which she had until then provoked and stored up for herself [Col. 1661A] (4 Kings 9:33).

Since it is altogether useful that persons so exalted be cast down from on high, so that either they may repent or at least be unable to sin further, cast them down, O Lord, while they now live in the flesh, lest, having died in pride and then risen hereafter, you cause them to be cast down into the depths. Cast them down now swiftly by humbling them; this swiftness is indicated by the present-tense word, “Cast down.” For it is certainly true what Truth says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11), that is, whoever exalts himself in the present will be humbled in the future. But because that later humiliation will be too late, penal, and fruitless, I, David, desiring either the conversion of the wicked or at least the deliverance of the good, say: “Cast them down, O Lord,” casting them down swiftly, so that their swift overthrow may benefit either them for conversion [Col. 1661B] or the good for deliverance.

Cast down the exalted, and divide those united in evil. Divide, I say, not their hands or works, because “all things work together for good for those saints who are called according to the purpose” (Rom. 8:28), and who must be perfected through such things. But because unity of tongues in fabricating falsehood or defending sin harms far more, when an unjust and deceitful word seems, for the overthrow of its hearers, to stand firm as though it were true and just, divide, I pray, their tongues, lest the tower of malice which they intend to build rise any higher, and lest their utterly evil conversations corrupt good morals. Divide their tongues [Col. 1661C] so that they may attack and destroy one another, as often occurs among heretics.

Thus Arius and Sabellius destroy one another: the former by dividing the Father and Son too greatly, the latter by uniting them too greatly. Arius says: “The Father is not the same as the Son,” against the saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). But Sabellius says: “The Father is the same person as the Son.” If this were true, the Son could not truly say of himself and the Father, “We are.” Between them Truth triumphs, saying, “I and the Father are one”: by saying “one,” it destroys Arius; by saying “we are,” it destroys Sabellius. So Nestorius and Eutyches were divided against one another: the former divided too greatly, the latter united too greatly, the Word and the man in Christ.

Yet even though the heretics have now been destroyed, many false-speakers and evil-speakers, or grandiloquent speakers, still agree with one another; and many hearers with itching ears agree with them in evil against the good. O Lord, divide their tongues. Their tongues, as the Apostle James declares, “set on fire by Gehenna” (Jas. 3:6), when joined together make a great hellish fire; when separated from one another and scattered, that evil fire fails, just as a fire fails when its material logs are taken away from it. Therefore, so that the fire of greed, which never says “enough,” the fire of lust, pride, envy, and other vices which burns evil hearts, may utterly fail, divide the tongues set on fire by Gehenna; and gather together into one other fiery tongues such as the apostles received, so that under many such tongues there may be one heart and one soul in God—that is, in truth and in charity, which is God. [Col. 1662A]

There is no small reason why I desire the casting down of the exalted and the division of tongues: “For I saw iniquity” of pride “and contradiction” of insolence against humility and obedience in that Babylonian city which intends to build a tower against God. I saw these evils not for an hour but by day and night—that is, continually or without interruption. Nor is it surprising that iniquity is seen in a city where wicked deeds occur not only secretly but also upon the walls, and not merely on some one part of the walls but all around: “Iniquity will surround it upon its walls, and toil and injustice in its midst,” as explained above.

And usury—whether of money, by which anyone lending wishes to receive more, or of vengeance, by which anyone injured wishes to injure more, not satisfied with retaliation—has not departed from its streets. Upon the walls—that is, among the rulers—open iniquity and rapacity appear; but in the streets—that is, among the populace—usury and deceit have not departed, so much does deceit reign or rage that even a friend is deceived by a friend, which is an evil altogether intolerable.

For an open enemy had reviled me. Had he openly heaped insults upon me, I should surely have borne it; for evils inflicted by strangers bring less pain, whereas those torments rage more fiercely within us which we suffer from persons whose disposition gave us confidence, because together with bodily injury we are tortured by the loss of charity. [Note: [Col. 1661D] St Gregory the Great, Book II on Ezekiel, vol. VI.] Hence the Lord says of Judas, His betrayer: “If my enemy had reviled me, I would surely have endured it”; as though He plainly said: I bore his transgression all the more grievously because I experienced it from one who seemed to be mine.

And I, David—every faithful person who, like David, is conformed to the likeness of Christ’s Passion—say: If some manifest enemy of mine, such as the one of whom I spoke above, “I was troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner,” had reviled me with open injuries, I should surely have endured it, because an evil not unforeseen ought to be received more patiently. And if one who hated me openly had spoken great things against me—that is, had proudly insulted me—I might perhaps have hidden myself from him, giving place to mad words so as not to break out into contention, in which there is great patience. Or, “I might have hidden myself” means that I should have thought I could hide myself from one who is outside among those who are within. Yet, since I am troubled even there, it is evident that not without cause did I seek solitude, desiring wholly to escape even the inward assault of false brethren.

Let it be that I patiently endure dangers even from false brethren, who know my life by no sure proof and perhaps think me wicked on the basis of the false testimony of my enemies. But you were of one mind with me: you often agreed wholeheartedly with the good counsels I had found; you were my guide, who sometimes foresaw before me what was to be done and offered me leadership through your counsel; and you were my acquaintance, who dwelt with me for a long time in one Church, where neither your life was unknown to me nor mine to you—whether that life for which repentance was being undertaken by me or by you, or that which thereafter was proposed for practice.

You who together with me received sweet foods—whether bodily foods, which alone taste sweet to evil persons, or spiritual foods, in which it is tasted that the Lord is sweet. Here is displayed a remarkable malice, which could not be softened into gentleness by either bodily or spiritual fellowship, although even hard hearts are commonly softened amid cheerfully offered banquets, especially when by freely given benefits coals of fire are heaped upon the head of one who hates. This, I know, frequently took place between you and me; for at the banquet of the Lord’s table I often remembered you as though you were a good and blessed morsel, stretching out to you the sop: when we walked in the house of God in harmony. From that house you exclude yourself by laying snares for me.

You, I say, such a man—of one mind with me, my guide, my acquaintance, who with me received sweet foods—we walked in the house of God in harmony: it is understood, “you can no longer be endured.” For here the utterance of an agitated mind fails, since no speech can express what punishment such a person deserves. Grammarians call this figure *ellipsis*: sometimes, by withholding a necessary word, it signifies more than it would have signified if the word had been supplied. Therefore, after a kind of silence, by which the agitation of the mind is indicated, the fitting sentence is at last pronounced—not against that one man alone, falsely of one mind but truly discordant, falsely a guide but truly a deceiver—but also against all like him and his imitators:

“Let death come upon them, and let them go down alive into hell, because wickedness is in their dwellings, in the midst of them,” as has been explained above.

On this passage blessed Gregory says in Job: [Note: [Col. 1663D] *Morals*, Book XVIII, ch. 12.] “To increase their guilt still more, holy Church testifies that her enemies both know what they ought to follow and refuse to follow what they know. Therefore it is said of them through the Psalmist: ‘Let them go down alive into hell.’ Those are alive who perceive what is done to them; for the dead know nothing at all and do not feel. Thus the dead, because they do not feel, are commonly put for those who do not know; and the living, because they feel, for those who know. To go down alive into hell is to sin knowingly and consciously.”

For while the living know and feel what is done around them, whereas the dead can feel nothing, they would go down dead into hell if they committed evil through ignorance. But when they know evil and nevertheless do it, they miserably go down alive and conscious into the hell of iniquity. Therefore, that they may recognize how great an evil they are in, let death come upon them and let them go down alive into hell: that is, let a death-bringing punishment come upon them, which may bend them to repentance; or, if they are found wholly unyielding, break them, lest long and prosperous life remain to them for an increase of sin and punishment. And let them go down alive into hell: that is, while still living in the flesh, while there is room for amendment, let them descend into hell—that is, into infernal torment—so that either they themselves may be corrected, or, if they cannot be corrected, other wicked persons may be terrified by their example. Thus we read that it happened to Antiochus, persecutor of the Maccabees, and to Herod, murderer of the children: infernal torment in the torture of their entrails, though it did not avail for their own amendment, nevertheless availed for the consolation of the faithful and the terror of unbelievers.
