Why I should wish such grievous torments upon them under the names of death and hell, let no one wonder, since no devout person delights in such torments inflicted on persons such as these. Behold, I give the reason why so strong a vengeance is required, whether corrective or condemnatory. Their poisonous entrails do not feel a gentle remedy, because wickedness is in their dwellings and in their midst, as though implanted in their marrow; it can be cured or extracted from their dwellings, from their midst, only by the strongest cutting or burning. If wickedness were only in their dwellings and not also in their midst—that is, in their heart or marrow—they could be cured by some mild medicine. But now, since the wickedness ruling in their dwellings most powerfully possesses even their hearts, they must be dealt with severely: so that death may come upon them and they may go down alive into hell.

But I, touched by a light and brief sickness, cried to God, and the Lord saved me. I, like another Job, exposed in possessions and flesh to the tempter and struck by him, cried to the Lord; I did not murmur against the Lord, and the Lord saved me.

This, among His other wonders, I shall recount and proclaim in thanksgiving, for His praise and glory and for the edification of others, “at evening and morning and noon”—that is, at all times. I shall recount and proclaim this great benefit of God not merely by speaking to people in teaching and exhortation, but also to God in thanksgiving for past benefits, often joining prayer for those to come. I shall do this frequently in songs and hymns aptly composed according to the title of this Psalm [Col. 1664D], which themselves demand that the Lord who saved me should not cease still to save me and bring to its end the salvation once begun, as the Psalm-title announces. Thus, while I pray in songs and hymns “unto the end,” the Lord Himself will hear my voice.

It will often happen that people, lacking ears to hear, do not hear me as I recount and proclaim; for only those who have ears to hear hear what the Spirit says to the Churches. Yet, whatever people may do, the Lord Himself will hear my voice, often intensified by the cry of my mouth and continually by that of my heart.

And by this I shall know that He has heard my voice [Col. 1665A], not only for me but also against my enemies: for He will save me and humble them. He will save me in that He will redeem my soul in peace from those who draw near to me, as has been explained above. He will redeem me—namely, the Church, or an ecclesiastical person intent upon songs and hymns—in peace from those who draw near to me, because they were with me among many, as was explained above. Nor do I say simply, “He will redeem me,” but: He will redeem my soul, placing it in peace, so that those who kill the body—sometimes in deed, sometimes by the mere disposition of malice, by which whoever hates his brother is a murderer—cannot kill it. They kill me insofar as they cut away from me the living branches of good action. In cutting these away they draw very near, because they were with me among many, or among a multitude.

For as abundant tares, by their multitude, choke and as it were kill wheat, when in one field they drink the same rain, grow together, and ripen together, though they do not arrive together in one granary: so these enemies of truth, because they were with me among many, occupying by their multitude the most fertile places in the Lord’s field, and fattened, made gross, and enlarged not only by the rain of literal and natural knowledge but also by ecclesiastical resources, have so choked me, holy Church or a holy ecclesiastical person, that scarcely some small spark of living soul remains in me, preserved beneath the altar of God.

There, because the Redeemer of the world will redeem my soul in peace through the sacrifice of His body and blood [Col. 1665C], beyond doubt the voice of that precious blood will be heard, crying better than Abel’s blood. For Abel’s blood sought vengeance; this blood demands pardon even for enemies—yet only if they humble themselves in true repentance and do not, with the fratricide Cain, despair of mercy. Otherwise, if they refuse to humble their souls in true repentance, willing or unwilling they will be humbled by due retribution, because the Lord will hear the voice of the blood which they have shed either in deed or in intention, and He will humble them—He who is before the ages.

Or, as it is read in the Hebrew: “He who is Judge from the beginning.” I do not say “was,” as though anything in His being were past; rather, “He is before the ages” (Ecclus. 42:21). Thus elsewhere He says: “Before Abraham, I am” (John 8:14); likewise: “I am who I am”; and, “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel,” He says, “‘He who is’ has sent me to you” (Exod. 3:14). Therefore He was not like yesterday, which has passed away, but He is today, while “today” is spoken—that is, eternally and always—and He is Judge from the beginning. He Himself will humble those who exalt themselves excessively, placing confidence, I know not in what transitory prince or king. For example, when they say: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15); or as was said to Elijah by the first and second captains of fifty: “The king has commanded that you come down” (4 Kings 1:9). “The king,” they say, “commands,” not considering that this same king, sick in his bed of illness, would not rise from it, as Elijah foretold.

Vain, then, is the confidence of those who glory in such a lord or king against that King and Judge [Col. 1666A] who is before the ages. Speaking in Elijah or in any spiritual person, He saves only that captain of fifty with his fifty who humbles himself in repentance. For he did not speak as the first one did, who said to Elijah, sitting on the summit of the mountain: “Man of God, the king has commanded that you come down”; nor as the other did: “Thus says the king, make haste, come down” (4 Kings 1:11). To say to a man of God, “The king commands that you come down,” or, “Make haste, come down,” is to desire to abase under the dominion of secular power—wholly weak and utterly sick—a perfect man, raised to the summit of righteousness, whose citizenship is in heaven.

This is what the first and second captains of fifty intended: namely, the devil and Antichrist with their attendants, the demons and wicked persons whom they have; all of them alike Gehenna’s fire will envelop, when that king appears with his own at the final judgment—He who is before the ages.

The first captain of fifty may also, quite suitably, be understood as Nero, the first to decree a universal persecution against the Church of God, a worshipper of Accaron’s god Beelzebub, which is interpreted “man of flies,” a name by which the prince of demons is designated in the Gospel. This most filthy and cruel worshipper, Nero, as we have said, was the first in the Roman Empire to kill saints of God like Elijah, and by public and imperial edicts required either that Christ be denied by them or that they themselves be killed bodily.

His accomplices in impiety, men of blood, represent the troop of the first captain of fifty, gathered from the number of those whose “feet are swift to shed blood” (Ps. 13:3). But since it is written of Antichrist that “deceit shall be directed in his hand,” he may be understood as the other captain of fifty, together with all deceivers who are murderers not so much of bodies as of souls.

But the third captain of fifty includes those who, through the truth and sincerity of piety and repentance, take care to separate themselves from men of blood and deceit, and endeavour to honour saints of God like Elijah. When these saints are judging and praying for such persons, they will be spared in the divine judgment, when the world shall be judged by fire.

That judicial fire will indeed envelop those two captains of fifty with their accomplices, for whom there is no change from the malice conceived against Christ, the true Elijah, and His saints. As a type of this, Elijah said to the first and second captain of fifty: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and devour you and your fifty” (4 Kings 1:10, 12). Similar is what is said in the Apocalypse concerning the two witnesses standing before the Lord: “If anyone wishes to harm them, fire will go forth from their mouth and devour their enemies” (Rev. 11:5).

The fire is the fiery utterance of God’s servants, which, as they preach and pray, will devour their enemies: either so that they cease to be enemies and become friends, or else that they may be joined in utterly unchangeable punishment to the devil, the chief captain of fifty among demons, or to Antichrist, the chief captain of fifty among wicked men. [Col. 1667A] But if Nero, the chief man of blood, is understood as the first captain of fifty, then by a just judgment men of blood, his followers, will be bound with him in one bundle to be burned. For their malice and cruelty are obstinate, just as the deceitfulness of Antichrist, the other captain of fifty, and of his false-Christian accomplices is stubborn. For there is no change of their malice through true repentance in this age; therefore there will be no change in infernal punishment in the age to come.

And this is because they did not fear God as that third captain of fifty did, who, bending his knees before Elijah, spoke in prayer: “Man of God, do not despise my life and the lives of your servants who are with me,” etc. (4 Kings 1:13). Therefore Elijah spared this man, because he had been humbled and changed by receiving his own persecution. He did not spare the other two, and rightly so. For there was no change in them, and they did not fear God.

Likewise the true Elijah—whose name means “God the Lord,” and whose proper work is always to show mercy and to spare—will spare only humble and repentant persons. Those stubborn in their wickedness He will not spare, and that by a just judgment. For there is no change in them. This follows because they please themselves in their sin and do not fear God; they do not even possess the servile fear which is the beginning of wisdom. For this reason they ought immediately in the present life to be swiftly cast down from the height of their pride into the pit of everlasting perdition, as was prayed above where we said in songs: “Cast them down, Lord; divide their tongues.” [Col. 1667C] But this Judge, who is before the ages—

**VERSE 21.** “He stretched forth His hand in repaying”: that is, like a patient requiter He waits long, so that He may strike more grievously those long awaited and not changed from their malice. He stretches forth His hand by raising high the axe of judgment and poising it long, that He may strike more forcibly. He stretches forth His hand by drawing His bow with the greatest strength: the farther it is drawn, the more sharply it will strike them, especially those who have defiled God’s covenant. For it was not enough for them not to fear the judgment of Him who is before the ages, or who is Judge from the beginning; they also defiled His covenant, which consists either in the promises made to Abraham and his seed, or in the evangelical precepts and promises.

This covenant, insofar as lay in them, they defiled by contradicting it or by polluting it through contrary deeds, holding their own traditions dearer than divine ones. Hence Truth Himself says to such people: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who have made void the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition” (Matt. 15:6). Therefore:

**VERSE 22.** “They were divided from the wrath of His countenance.” The Jews were divided, scattered throughout the world, and excluded from the land and kingdom given to them. Heretics and schismatics also were divided, mutually opposed to one another by their false doctrines and perverse sects; false Christians too were divided, deprived of the good of that unity and the joy of that unanimity of which it is sung: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1).

Thus these persons are divided now in the present life; more fully in the future they are to be divided from the fellowship of the good, who are not divided because they think the same thing, always striving with one mind to fix their attention upon God’s countenance, which they hope will be gracious to them and wrathful toward their enemies, according to the words: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and His ears unto their prayers; but the countenance of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their remembrance from the earth” (Ps. 33:17).

Therefore they were divided, as we have said, from the wrath of His countenance—the countenance of Him whose covenant they defiled and whose face, always and everywhere present, they did not reverence, unlike him who says: “Whither shall I go from Thy Spirit, and whither shall I flee from Thy face?” (Ps. 138:7). This face or countenance they do not now fear at all; but hereafter “they shall look upon Him whom they pierced” (John 19:37). They shall see Him wrathful whom they now despise as gentle; nor will they be able in any way to hide from the wrath of His countenance when the day of wrath comes: the day of calamity and misery, the day great and exceedingly bitter, the day of whirlwind and tempest, which utterly separates chaff from grain. For then He will chiefly divide them, when appearing openly at the final winnowing, He says to some with the serenity of a gracious countenance: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom,” etc. (Matt. 25:34). But to others, in the wrath of His troubled countenance, He will say: “Go, cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41).

Meanwhile, they should surely be counselled not to remain altogether careless, as though they did not fear wrath coming from afar. He will come, He will come, and He will not delay; and when He is thought to delay, His heart will draw near. For the Lord says in another prophet: “The day of vengeance is in my heart”; and therefore, when that day draws near, “His heart draws near” (Isa. 63:4). “The day of destruction is near, and the times hasten to be present” (Deut. 32:35); and as the times hasten to be present, the heart of Him who is before the ages and will judge all ages will swiftly draw near.

Alternatively: The enemies of Him who is before the ages are divided by the wrath of His countenance; but while they are removed from God by division, and while they attack the Church of God, His truth will shine forth and His heart will draw near, when His formerly secret will becomes manifest. Or “His heart will draw near” means His friends, who are like the heart, knowing His secrets. For when the perverse have been divided at the final judgment by the wrath of the countenance of the Judge whom they do not love, His heart—that is, His friends, drawing near to Him—will judge nations with Him and rule peoples, judging most severely those to whom the word of truth seems hard, and who detest and flee, as though they were poisoned arrows, the most sweet teachings of holiness set forth in hymns and songs.

For truly, for the friends of God, His words have been softened by the clearest expositions, more penetrating than oil, entering the inner parts of flesh and veins even to bones and marrow, healing both the outer and inner human body and mind by medicinal power. And they are arrows: either because God’s words appear harsh to the hard, though they are sweet; or certainly because, though softened, they do not lose the force of their sharp point, of which it is elsewhere said: “Thy arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath Thee” (Ps. 44:6); and again, “Sharp arrows of the mighty” (Ps. 119:4). Therefore God’s soldiers arm themselves with these very words of God, however sweet and softened they may be.

Accordingly, if to you, a little child still needing to be nourished with milk, the word seems hard because you either do not understand it through its obscurity or the slowness of your understanding, or shrink from it because it opposes your wantonness on the way—since you do not dare agree with it because of the austerity of its rigor and the frailty of your infancy—do not be angry with breasts better than wine, nor reject the Word of God; but:

**VERSE 23.** “Cast thy care upon the Lord, and He shall nourish thee.” Cast your care upon the Lord, not upon another. Cast your thought upon the triune and one Lord, who, being almighty, all-wise, and all-good, will powerfully, wisely, and willingly help you as you are tossed by waves. Cast the ship of your mind upon the Lord, as upon the safest harbour of salvation. For if perhaps you cast it upon another, you will find him to be a rock of shipwreck for you.

Cast your care upon the Lord: He will gladly receive it, tend you in that very care, and nourish you; for such care pleases Him, whereas worldly care consumes. Hence Solomon says: “As a worm to wood and a moth to clothing, so a man’s sadness harms his heart” (Prov. 25:20). Therefore, because your care is concerned with how you may please God rather than this world, cast it upon God. He will be able to soften beyond oil for you His word, which is still hard to you but will soon be changed into milk for you, if only you cast your care upon the Lord.

Do not say what those said who, upon hearing Christ’s word about eating His flesh and drinking His blood, went backward, saying: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (John 6:61). Imitate Peter, saying on behalf of himself and his fellow disciples: “Lord, Thou hast the words of eternal life; and to whom shall we go from Thee?” (ibid., 69). Thus he spoke; thus he cast himself upon the Lord when he did not yet understand the words of truth. Therefore he was nourished by the words of grace that gives milk, until the food of the Lord’s flesh and the drink of His life-giving blood delighted him: in these are the solid bread of the perfect and the intoxicating cup—how splendid it is!

Peter shared in such a banquet not merely at the level of the sacrament, but by passing into that body which he ate and becoming a member of that body; now a perfect man, he no longer needed milk. Likewise the Lord will nourish you, if you cling to Him after Peter’s example.

Alternatively: “They are divided”—that is, beyond doubt the enemies of God who defiled His covenant will be divided by the wrath of His countenance. And this will happen when His heart draws near—that is, when the assembly of saints, which is according to His heart, draws near to Him to judge with Him. Yet in this age there will not be a complete division or separation between the righteous and the unrighteous, between the truthful and the liar. For the liar himself, who defiles God’s covenant, so artfully composes his words that his speech is softened beyond oil by the cosmetic of ingenious flattery. Nevertheless, they must be guarded against, because poison lies beneath the oil in such words, and they are arrows.

Despising such words altogether, you who gladly receive truth and carefully dispense it in your truthful words, seasoned with no oil of flattery, cast your care upon the Lord. Do not trust that by your own strength you can stand against deceitful and impious enemies; rather, attribute to Christ whatever strength or knowledge is in you, and urgently ask from Him whatever is lacking. He will nourish you [Col. 1670B] with the bread of life and understanding, so that the enemies of truth cannot resist the Wisdom and Spirit speaking in you, but all who hate you may turn backward, perceiving that the Lord fights for you. Thus they will be forced to say: “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for him” (Exod. 14:25).

He will not give the righteous man to be shaken forever. Though He sometimes allows the righteous to be shaken here, according to the words concerning shaking explained above, where the righteous speaks: “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me,” nevertheless He will not give this shaking to the righteous forever. For from the waves of the surging sea He will bring him, upon the wood of the cross, to the shore of eternal stability, where, established upon the solid ground of promise, he will not fear falling into the pit of the abyss.

**VERSE 24.** “But Thou, O God, shalt bring them down into the pit of destruction”—those who have defiled Thy covenant, the well of living waters, by corrupting the teaching of truth through false words and wicked deeds. Therefore, O God, Thou shalt bring down into the pit of destruction those who now defile Thy covenant, the well of living waters, with the poison of falsehood and do not desist from this pursuit of their warfare. For there is no change in them, and they have not feared God.

This pit is elsewhere called the pit of the abyss, because like the abyss it has no bottom, and there will be in it everlasting agitation. Seeking to avoid it, the righteous prays to Thee, Lord, crying: “Let not the tempest of waters overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me, nor let the pit press its mouth upon me” (Ps. 68:16).

Even in this life Thou wilt bring them down into the pit of destruction, by delivering them over to a reprobate mind, to the desires of their perverse heart, and to much perversity, too deep, after the likeness of an abyss. This abyss of perversity calls upon the abyss of damnation, so that those who have sinned deeply in the world may suffer deeply in hell.

But this will not long be delayed. For men of blood and deceitful men shall not halve their days. Men of blood, who kill the bodies of the saints, such as Nero, and deceitful men, who kill souls by corrupting good morals through the worst conversations, such as Antichrist, shall not halve their days: that is, they will not advance in evil as far as, or for as long as, they wish and imagine. Or they would halve their days in their life if they divided by repentance those whom they have purposed for evil.

On this passage blessed Gregory says: [Note: [Col. 1671D] *Morals*, Book V, ch. 39.] “To halve one’s days is to divide the time of an evil life spent in pleasures by the laments of repentance, and to restore it by apportioning it to good use. But the wicked do not halve their days at all, because they do not change their perverse mind even at the final moment. In contrast, Paul rightly admonishes us, saying: ‘Redeeming the time, because the days are evil’ (Eph. 5:16). We redeem time when we repair by weeping the past life that we have lost through wanton living.”

Thus Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, while he was a man of blood, halved his days when divinely rebuked: he repented that in former days he had been a persecutor of the saints, and thereafter showed himself such a man that he preferred to endure persecution with the saints for Christ rather than inflict it upon the saints. Indeed, this enemy was devoured by the fire going out from the mouth of Stephen, who prayed for those stoning him, among whom Saul was chief; for the witnesses stoning the blessed proto-martyr, that they might be unencumbered, laid their garments “at the feet of a young man called Saul” (Acts 7:57).

Nevertheless, because he halved his days and endured for Christ no lesser torments than he himself had inflicted upon Christians, he was not cast down into the pit of destruction. Rather, even before death he was caught up to the third heaven; and finally, crowned by a victorious death, he obtained what he had desired. Do you wish to know what he desired? “I desire,” he says, “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23).

Whence came such a halving of days to this man of blood? Namely, because, although he had been a man of blood, he was not deceitful as Judas was—the worst of merchants—who accomplished murder by a kiss and learned to make war through peace. Judas indeed knew that the blood he betrayed was innocent, as he himself afterward confessed, moved by late and fruitless repentance: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 7:4). Such deceitful persons rarely, or rather never, are truly converted. For there is no change in them: they sin by a deliberate and deceitful, and exceedingly obstinate, choice of evil will—not through ignorance like Saul, but through persistent malice like the devil.

Therefore one must acquiesce in the divine judgment, that men of blood and deceitful persons of this kind be brought down into the pit of destruction, from which pit no exit will ever again stand open to them.

And indeed, in this their day, which they seek for themselves unto peace—or “in these their days,” that is, it must be recognized that their days are called evil because they are sought by the wicked for peace: for it is not the divine ordinance but the perversity of the evil person himself that makes these days evil, and makes that wickedness of the day of which it is said: “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. 6:34). Let this day in which we were born perish; let that day be turned into darkness, and another, sanctified day shall dawn upon us.

I said above already that fear and trembling came upon me and darkness covered me, because, thanks be to God, my own days have begun to grow dark and displeasing to me. I have taken care, and still take care, to halve them, because I grieve over my past sins and willingly guard myself against future ones, seeking mercy and forgiveness from God, the Father of mercies. Deceitful persons do not hope for this; rather, despairing, they have delivered themselves over to impurity and other crimes.

But I will hope in Thee, Lord. They will be brought by despair into the pit of destruction; but I will hope in Thee, Lord, so that, having been given to drink from the well of living waters springing up into eternal life, I too may be brought into eternal life through the water springing up into eternal life. For just as all rivers return to their source, so this saving water, springing from eternal life, does not cease to run in its springing until it returns to that from which it came. Therefore, springing from eternal life into eternal life, it will not return there empty.

“My word,” says the Lord, “which shall go forth from my mouth shall not return to me empty, but shall accomplish whatever I have willed and shall prosper in the things for which I sent it” (Isa. 55:11). Therefore the water springing from eternal life into eternal life, and the word going forth from the Lord’s mouth and returning to Him, draw with themselves faithful souls that cling to them.

Here, in thanksgiving, I am pleased to recall a certain vision in which water springing from eternal life was represented. A certain brother, of simple and innocent life, long disciplined in holy observance, seemed to see heaven opened before him. And behold, a fiery globe of wonderful size, like glowing, molten gold, appeared in heaven, and around it was a multitude of saints shining with marvellous brightness. Suddenly, as though one of the rivers of paradise, a stream began to flow from that globe to the earth, of such purity that it seemed like liquid gold.

This, I think, is what we have at hand: for beside the sanctuary of Saint Michael, where we are accustomed to write and sit meditating upon the Psalms, this same river seemed to descend. And because “the rush of the river makes glad the city of God,” I confess that through God’s mercy I have sometimes been gladdened by the force of this river, compelling me to write. Thus now, after the long interval during which I stayed in the city of Rome, was greatly wearied in going and returning, and for a long time was kept from writing by other ecclesiastical and monastic occupations, I have returned relying on the apostolic blessing and take up the pen again. I pray divine mercy to make the free offerings of my mouth pleasing to Himself, and to grant that I may write in such a way that in them only that water may have savour—the water which, springing from eternal life into eternal life, may draw kindly readers along with itself to the place toward which it runs [Col. 1673A], lest any of them fall into the pit of destruction prepared for the devil and his angels, and for Antichrist and his followers.

Glory to God the Father, to whom the prayer and supplication of this Psalm is directed when it says, “Hear, O God, my prayer,” etc. Glory to the Son, who, praying to the Father for us, was sorrowful in His Passion, saying: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38). Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that dove whose wings the faithful Psalmist desires, saying: “Who will give me wings like a dove?” Glory to the one and triune God, who will not give the righteous man to be shaken forever, but helps him powerfully, wisely, and mercifully. To Him be praise, honour, and victory through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 55

[Col. 1673]

[Col. 1673B] “Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trodden me under foot,” etc. The title of this Psalm is:

**(VERSE 1.) UNTO THE END, FOR THE PEOPLE WHO HAVE BEEN MADE FAR FROM THE SAINTS, IN THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE; FOR DAVID HIMSELF, WHEN THE PHILISTINES HELD HIM IN GATH.**
The first part of this title is taken from the Gospel, the second from the Old Testament: Pilate placed above the crucified Lord a title which the Jewish people—who refused to have Christ as king—contradicted, and thus became far removed from the saints. Yet the inscription of the title was not erased, because it had been prophesied in another psalm: “Do not destroy the inscription of the title.”

In the First Book of Kings we read that David, when Saul was seeking him, came to Achish king of Gath, a city of the Philistines; but we do not read that he was detained there. Therefore David is better understood as Christ whole and entire, whom the Philistines—that is, foreigners who have become far removed from the saints—held in Gath, which means “winepress.” For formerly the Jews held Christ himself in the winepress, and now the rest of the wicked, who still contradict the title, hold his body there: that is, under pressure. This pressure is not unfruitful, since there the grape flows forth which, before entering the winepress, remains whole yet barren.

Nor is it inappropriate to say that Christ is held in his members, in whom he himself cries: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). Yet the body says in its head: “He raised us up with him and made us sit in the heavenly places” (Eph. 2:6). We already sit there through hope, while he is here with us through love; and this joining makes, as it were, one man in one flesh: bridegroom and bride.

Therefore, on behalf of the people to be saved—or on behalf of the people, that is, against the people who are far from the saints—the Church, while oppressed by the Philistines, prays. First it touches on the tribulations in which it says, through hope, that it is secure. Secondly, it enumerates them more fully at the words, “All day long, attacking”; and, having inserted the conversion of its enemies, it concludes also in this section that through hope it does not fear. Thirdly, at the words, “Your vows are upon me, O God,” it says that, free from the evils of the world, it will sing praise in future blessedness. By the example of its own patience it also urges the simpler faithful to steadfastness.

Temptations are indeed very useful: when a person is tested by them, he is forced to recognize his weakness; and thereafter, no longer presuming upon himself, while he is held in Gath—that is, in the winepress—he is set between hope and fear, and is warned by the example of his head to cry out, saying:

**VERSE 2.** “Have mercy upon me, O God.” For this cry belongs principally to him who, in the inscription of the title, was called King of the Jews—that is, king of those who confess. Then each one of those confessing him, crushed in the winepress of afflictions, ought by the example of his head to utter the same cry.

Let Christ therefore first say: “Have mercy upon me, God the Father, who are my God because I have become man for men. And because I have become not only man but a suffering man in Gath—that is, in the winepress of the Passion—have mercy upon me, my God and Father; for man has trampled upon me”: my servant, indeed my disciple Judas, counted my friend—falsely an apostle and truly a devil [Col. 1674C]. He too is “the enemy man” (Matt. 13:28), who sowed tares among the wheat which I sowed; and, in trampling down my wheat while it was being sown, he trampled me also in my members.

Therefore, O God, have mercy upon me and mine, since the enemy man has trampled me and mine, not merely by casting evil seed into my field, but also by pressing me and mine in the winepress of the Passion. He trampled me like a grape placed in the winepress: invisibly through himself, visibly through human beings. Thus, as wine is pressed from crushed grapes, so devout prayer is pressed from me in tribulation.

A crushed thorn pricks the foot that crushes it: for an evil man, when afflicted, repays evil for evil insofar as he can and has the means. But I am not so, the cluster of Cyprus; nor are my disciples so, themselves clusters clinging to me, the true vine. We do not prick the one who tramples us like a thorn; rather, beneath the trampler’s foot we yield wine, because when we are cursed, we do not curse in return; when we are blasphemed, we entreat; and we pray for those who trample us.

Each one of mine also prays for himself, after my example: “Have mercy upon me, O God, for man has trampled upon me.” Is not such a prayer the finest wine? At times even the one who crushes the grape is so intoxicated by it that he is changed into a grape and suffers for the truth the very things he had inflicted—as Saul, through Stephen’s prayer, became Paul. Thus in such a winepress let Christ’s prayer always sound through the Christian’s mouth: “Have mercy upon me, O God, for man has trampled upon me.”

Have mercy upon me, Christ, that when delivered from the winepress you may exalt me upon the throne of the everlasting kingdom, as you eventually made my father David, long trampled by Saul, sit upon the throne of the kingdom. Have mercy upon me, Christian, that when I too am delivered from the winepress in which man trampled me, you may make me be where my head, Christ, is, who said: “I desire that where I am, there also my servant may be” (John 12:26) [Col. 1675A].

Do you wish to hear, kindly listeners, how man trampled upon me? I tell you: in that all day long, attacking, he afflicted me. It did not suffice him to afflict or attack me for an hour, but he did so all day long—that is, at every time. For all who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus suffer persecution in this world, which is a great winepress: some are crushed, others crush. Yet only those crushed for righteousness’ sake are regarded as grapes.

Although I spoke in the singular—“man has trampled upon me”—so that you may know that many trample upon me, and that this people which has become far from the saints is numerous, being far from the saints, that is, very contrary and unlike them, I now speak in the plural:

**VERSE 3.** “My enemies have trampled upon me all day long,” not because I deserved evil from them, but because they were enemies precisely because I refused to depart with them from the saints. And fittingly I say in the plural, “they have trampled,” because many fighting against me stood there and feared to trample upon me all day long. But I—

**VERSE 4.** “From the height of the day I shall fear.” For the high sun in Cancer makes high and long days, whose height and length are to be feared in the heat of persecution; for unless the evil days are shortened, no flesh will be saved. Being a fragile creature, flesh cannot endure this length or height of days without great peril [Col. 1675C].

But I shall hope in you, my God, that you will shorten the length of this most evil day, from whose height I shall fear until I see it humbled. For at some time the height of this day will be humbled, so that it either will not or cannot raise itself any further. It will not do so in those who are converted from the wickedness of this day, for whom past wickedness is sufficient—indeed seems excessive—and therefore repentance and the everlasting light of a better day will follow. It will be unable to do so in those who, although they remain evil, are nevertheless not permitted by the higher ordering of divine government to exalt themselves as much or as long as they wish.

This I, a combatant set between fear and hope, shall hope: hope nevertheless prevailing and driving away fear in this bitter contest, in which the spirit is willing but the flesh weak; and yet these oppose one another in a most severe conflict, in which the height or length of the evil day is dangerous. But I, who trust not in human strength but in divine strength, shall hope in you, God my helper; and therefore I shall yield neither to the flesh nor to the evil man in this war, in which I hope for victory from divine power.

Alternatively: Height, that is, the fearful pride of this world, cannot last long, but can scarcely be measured by the span of a single day, because it is brief and momentary like the beauty of grass, which is today and tomorrow is cast into the oven. Shall I fear because of the height of a day? Is persecution lasting one day more to be feared than the eternal fire of Gehenna? This is the height of a day, not a long time; and therefore it must be despised. Let those fear such exceedingly brief punishments who do not believe that eternal rewards are laid up for good and evil persons, and whose faith in divine help is uncertain. But I shall hope in you, whom I believe to be my helper in the present battle and, when the war is ended and victory won, my rewarder [Col. 1676A].

Alternatively: “From the height of the day”—that is, from the authority granted from above to those attacking me—I shall fear, because I ought not resist the higher ordering from which all authority comes. Therefore I, Christ, standing with great composure in judgment before the governor of the Roman empire, attributed this height, by which he ruled over me, not to the man but to you, O God, saying: “You would have no authority whatever against me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19:11).

Likewise, I, the humble Christian, submit to every human creature for God’s sake, because the height of human authority depends upon divine ordering. Certainly I shall fear from the height of the day with an ordered fear, so that I may be subject to it in the matters in which I ought; and many fear this height excessively, because they submit in matters in which they ought not. But I shall hope in you, knowing that you are higher than this height of the day and can restrain it when you will.

Alternatively: The Day is Christ, whose twelve hours are the twelve apostles, as he himself says: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” (John 11:9) [Col. 1676C]. The people that became far removed from the saints could not attain the height of this day in the inscription of the title. For the title’s inscription, containing the height of this day, displeased them. He who is written “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John 19:19) is rightly understood to be God Most High through that by which he is properly called Jesus—that is, Saviour—because, as the angel explains, “He shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21).

This name, indeed, was applied equivocally to many who were called saviours not properly but only by designation. But he alone who saved his people from their sins rightly and properly bears this inscription of the title: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.” For he is properly, not adoptively, God, the author of salvation for this people which does not depart from the saints, or which, even if it is far from the saints, has endeavoured to draw near to the saints again.

For those who refuse to draw near to the saints so as to be saved under Jesus the Saviour, holy under the holy Nazarene, and blessed confessors under the King of the Jews, will not see the height of this day. For the darkness which came upon his death on the cross blinded their eyes, so that they could not understand the divine sublimity of him whose human suffering and death upon the cross they saw. Hence they neither fear nor hope in him now in the present, but afterward “they shall look upon him whom they pierced” (John 19:37) [Col. 1677A]. Then they shall see his height, whose humility they now deride; and then they shall fear, when every hope of salvation has then been taken from them.

I too, whom this people, made far from the saints, now tramples like a grape in the winepress, “shall fear from the height of the day,” because “it is dreadful to fall into the hands of God” (Heb. 10:31), and of this most high day, penetrating all things with its brightness and touching all things with its heat. For “there is none who can hide himself from his heat” (Ps. 18:7), since “fire shall go before him and burn up his enemies round about” (Ps. 96:3), in whom there shall be no hope whatsoever of his mercy.

But I shall hope in you, Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews, because I am among the number of those who trust; and when this hope passes into reality, I shall thereafter lack all fear—not as one stupefied who feels nothing because of excessive sickness (for the greatness of stupor excludes awareness of pain and fear, although a sick person who feels pain is better off in that condition), but as one wholly incapable of suffering and incorruptible after the resurrection and judgment. I shall lack pain together with fear. This I shall hope, not in my own power, but in you, whose inscription of the title I acknowledge as utterly true and incorruptible: believing in my heart unto righteousness and confessing with my mouth unto salvation that Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews, “shall save his people” (Matt. 1:21)—not the people whom the last day finds far from the saints, but the people who draw near to the saints, for whom the perpetual light of this most high day, namely Christ, shall shine. Not only is his divinity high beyond every creature, but his humanity too has been exalted into the height of his divinity [Col. 1677C].

I do not merely guard the sound teaching of this faith hidden in secret within myself; because I worship the King of the Jews, I also proclaim it in open verbal confession. And if this discourse is reproached by that people which has become far from the saints—those, namely, who all day long cursed my words because all their thoughts were against me for evil—I, on the contrary, supported by the harmonious testimony of the saints, do not depart from the saints in my discourse. Rather, I preach the very thing which the saints preached. Hence:

**VERSE 5.** “In God I shall praise the word.” If I spoke a lie devised by myself, I would speak from my own resources, as Truth testifies concerning the father of lies: “When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own, because he is a liar and its father” (John 8:44). This applies to heresiarchs, who did not receive from another teacher the lies which they taught, but themselves bore their lies from a lying heart.

But because I teach nothing except what I hold as received from Truth in truth through orthodox teachers, I rightly shall praise the word in God—that is, in truth: a word supported by truth and fortified on every side by the testimonies of truth. But if I now arrogate to myself this word, however true it is, as though I had not received it, vainly glorying, I glory not in God—that is, not in truth—but in falsehood, because I have no good thing which I did not receive.

But, thanks be to God, I have received the true word from the Lord—that is, from Truth. Therefore I rightly shall praise in the Lord, namely in truth, the word of the Lord, because it was given by the Lord; and my word, because it was given to me. Thus in God I shall praise my words as streams flowing from God himself, the fountain of truth, through many most pure channels—the hearts and mouths of the saints—down to me. I too am, in whatever measure, a vessel of truth insofar as I receive the words of Truth itself, and a channel insofar as I pour them out to others through speech or writing. Thus in God, that is, in truth, I shall praise true words as mine in this respect: that I recognize them as given to me [Col. 1678A].

Or I shall praise—that is, make praiseworthy—my words in this: that I fulfil in deeds what I teach in words, according to the saying: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1). For “whoever does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19). By doing what I teach, I shall praise my words—that is, make them praiseworthy.

And because good words are sometimes given to one who does not use them well and turns them to evil, I, which is better, have hoped in God, so that my words, with God’s favour, may be for my benefit, according to the saying that to each of the faithful the manifestation of the Spirit is given for usefulness. Therefore, although I fear from the height of the day, knowing that the Lord is he who judges me and hence that I do not even judge myself, nevertheless, because I am conscious of no deceit or falsehood in my words, I shall not fear what flesh may do to me—that is, the fleshly people who have become far from the saints. Even if they crush me like a grape in the winepress, or like the fruit of the olive, the wine of teaching and the oil of prayer thus pressed from me do not perish; for these tramplers sometimes compel me to speak and pray more than I would if I had peace [Col. 1678C].

They trample, however, not so much with their feet as with their tongues, because:

**VERSE 6.** “All day long they cursed my words,” not because the words are contrary to truth, but because they are found to oppose those people. Thus they too are against me, taking special delight if they can do or say anything against me. When they can neither do nor say anything against me, all their thoughts are for evil, so that if they cannot prevail in doing evil to me, they may at least think it wickedly.

A remarkable wickedness, where all thoughts so tend toward evil that not even one thought is directed toward good. Amid all this, although they may not touch my person with murderous hands, they tear it with the tooth of detraction; and insofar as they can, they so cruelly destroy my way in the esteem of their hearers that they differ little or nothing from murderers—indeed, in truth they are murderers in hating me, because “whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). They do this openly because they have become so far removed from the saints that they rage publicly without shame.

But some from the same people, who have become far from the saints, entered our fellowship deceitfully.

**VERSE 7.** “They shall dwell and hide themselves; they shall watch my heel.” Another translation has: “They shall sojourn and hide themselves.” Sojourners are those who dwell in a country not their own. From this it follows that these false friends remain with us for a time, but are not of us; hence they will at last go out from us. Yet for a while they shall dwell among us and hide in their heart the deceit they have conceived, until they find an opportunity to say or do what they wickedly devise.

Thus Judas, although he was a devil, remained with the apostles, being chosen by Christ, who knew him and joined him to the apostles—not for fruit or good work, as he did the other apostles, to whom he says: “I chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15:16), but as a most necessary example. Thus you, who do not know whom to beware of admitting to companionship or cohabitation, may patiently endure such deceitful brothers after his example, until they are either converted within or go out with Judas; by their departure they will harm no one who remains in the holy people and takes care not to imitate the people who have become far from the saints [Col. 1679B].

Meanwhile, while such pseudo-brothers are within, “they shall watch my heel,” so that if not at the beginning or in the middle, at least at the end of any action of mine they may find something to criticize as wrongly done or wrongly said. For this reason they watch not only my deeds but, as hunters after words and almost counters of syllables, they weigh my speeches and writings for no purpose except to criticize and make my name hateful and burdensome to others. Thus few love me and scarcely anyone can endure me, as these false brothers endured my soul—that is, my life—to whom I was burdensome even to look upon.

When I say that they endured my soul, I sufficiently indicate that they did not love it, but bore it only as a heavy burden. Therefore they watch my heel in order to make me hateful and burdensome to others, just as they themselves endured my soul as burdensome to them: as long as they bore me heavily, they did not love me. Or they watch my heel by secretly laying snares, just as they endured my soul like a heavy burden, feigning love toward me while being false brothers and genuine robbers [Col. 1679C].

Here the wording must be divided, as though the complaint against the people far from the saints were complete. What follows concerning the same people expresses rather the sense of prayer than of complaint. Since many among an unholy people sin through ignorance, as Saul did, many in the holy people rightly pray for such persons and are heard, as Stephen was. Their voice is:

**VERSE 8.** “For nothing you shall save them.” O Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews, to whom alone this inscription of the title properly belongs according to your name, by which you are called Jesus—that is, Saviour. You shall save those who sin through ignorance among the people who, in the inscription of this same title, have become far from the saints, just as you prayed on the cross under that same title, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Likewise Stephen the protomartyr prayed: “Lord Jesus, do not hold this sin against them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Acts 7:59). You, Lord Jesus, shall therefore save such sinners. I, David, trampled by these same persons, pray this prophetically, and while praying prophesy: “For nothing you shall save them.” For you perform the work of your name—you who are called Saviour in the inscription of the title—by saving many who sin in ignorance among the people far from the saints. You work this salvation “for nothing,” that is, without any preceding merit in them, though for a while you permit them to trample you in yourself or in your members.

Or “for nothing” means that it is easy for you to save them, because in such a work you labour not at all. You did labour in enduring them, as you yourself confess in the prophet: “I have laboured in enduring” (Isa. 1:14); yet in saving them you do not labour, because by a word alone, or a silent motion of your will, you accomplish the work of power and salvation [Col. 1680B].

Alternatively: “For nothing you shall save them”: seeking from them no reward necessary to you, but only that it may go well with them. Thus Moses says in the Law: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you except that you fear him, and that it may be well with you at all times?” (Deut. 10:12).

Another translation has: “As my soul endured, save them for nothing.” That is to say: As my soul patiently endured those who were outwardly robbers and inwardly plotters, so do you patiently endure and save them; and do this “for nothing,” that is, grievously or easily [uncertain: the Latin *gravis vel facile* appears corrupt or elliptical].

**The Hebrew truth:** “All day long they afflicted me with words; all their thoughts were against me for evil. They gathered secretly; they watched my footsteps, waiting for my life, because there is no one safe among them. In wrath God will cast down peoples.”

That is to say: because all day long they afflicted me with words, because all their thoughts were for evil, because none among them is safe, since all have turned aside and together become useless, God in righteous judgment will in wrath cast down peoples who have become far from the saints—either into the valley of humility, that they may be saved, or into the depth of destruction, that they may be tormented. “For those who sin willingly, there remains no longer a sacrifice for sins, but the fire of zeal which shall consume the adversaries” (Heb. 10:26–27), says the Apostle.

He calls “adversaries” not those who sin through ignorance or weakness, but those who stubbornly resist truth when it rebukes them, persisting in the love or defense of sin and refusing to submit. This, as Samuel testifies and blessed Gregory explains, is the crime of idolatry. It is one thing not to submit, which sometimes occurs through ignorance or weakness; another to refuse to submit, which happens only through the malice of an obstinate heart.

Therefore “for nothing you shall save them,” because you will convert them for no sacrifice, as being incapable of conversion. For there is no change in them, as was said in the preceding psalm. Therefore you shall save “for nothing” those whom you know to be thus obstinate. Or you shall save them with temporal, bodily salvation, and this “for nothing,” because they make no worthy return of thanksgiving or service for so great a benefit: at times they are clothed in fine linen and purple, feast splendidly, and are full, yet despise needy persons and poor persons like Lazarus. Therefore, after they have been awaited sufficiently and have refused to humble themselves beneath your mighty hand, you will finally break them, as that rich man was broken who was buried in hell after receiving his good things in his lifetime [Col. 1681A].

Alternatively: When I say, “They shall watch my heel,” I do not speak of things unknown or untried; rather, as my soul has endured, often burdened by the perils of such false brothers, you will either save them freely and for nothing when they are converted, or break them in wrath when obstinate, because in wrath you will break peoples who have become far from the saints.

Alternatively: “As they endured my soul,” hating me freely and for nothing, and grievously bearing my burdensome life, so you too will save them freely and for nothing, so that where sin has abounded, your grace may abound beyond measure. Yet however great your grace may be, you do not therefore lack righteous wrath, in which you will break peoples by subduing them through certain scourges, as it is said elsewhere: “Break their jaws with bit and bridle” (Ps. 31:9). For as your right hand once broke the enemy and broke kings in the day of its wrath, so you will still break peoples in wrath: some medicinally, others punitively.

Where we have “you shall break,” another translation has “you shall lead down,” which is the same thing: because those whom you, O God, break from their pride, once humbled you lead to yourself. You do this in two ways in your wrath: either by inflicting your wrath through scourges, so that at least affliction may give understanding to hearing; or by merely displaying the wrath beforehand, so that it may be avoided when foreseen and the sinner, fearing wrath, may be corrected. Then my enemies shall turn backward—namely, when you break peoples in wrath; once broken and changed from enemies into friends, they shall follow, though formerly they were accustomed to go before or oppose, when they watched my heel [Col. 1681C].

**VERSE 9.** “That this might happen, O God, I declared my life to you.” Human life is understood in three ways: the life of nature, by which a human being breathes; the life of grace, by which one lives to God, for whom to live is Christ and to die is gain; and the life of vice, by which one lives to sin while dead to God.

I, the true David, declared to you my life: both that which is of nature and that which is of grace. For I said, O God the Father, that I did not come of myself but that you sent me; that is, when I was invisible, you made me visible. Again I said: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26). Thus I declared to you the life of nature together with that of grace, O God the Father—that is, to your honour.

I did not have the life of sin in myself; nevertheless, I prayed and even wept for sinners. For example, at Lazarus’s death, in which I recognized and lamented the most grievous death of sinners, that is, the death of the soul, as signified there. Again, seeing the sinful city, I wept over it. Or certainly on the Mount of Olives, where, praying concerning my body, I poured out upon the ground a bloody sweat flowing back again, I then shed more abundant tears—tears which in lesser matters I did not restrain—when I prayed not for one dead person to be raised, but for the whole body of the entire Church to be sanctified.

Although the Evangelists are silent concerning these tears shed upon the Mount of Olives, the Apostle is not silent. Speaking to the Hebrews of this great priest, he says: “In the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to him who was able to save him from death, he was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5:7). Of these tears the true Jacob now speaks here: he wept and prayed while struggling most vigorously, in his humanity, with his divine justice, in order to wrest a blessing necessary rather for us than for himself [Col. 1682B].

What then is said in this psalm about these tears? “You have placed,” he says, “my tears in your sight, God the Father,” so that in me, the true Jacob—in me who weep and pray, wrestling by that very weeping and prayer—in me, the true seed of Abraham, you might bestow the blessing so fully, “as is contained in your promise,” where you say to Abraham: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). Therefore, when you have poured out the grace of blessing upon all the tribes of the earth and chosen some from every tribe, then my enemies shall turn backward, as was explained above.

Alternatively: I, David, a sinner and penitent, declared my life to you, O God, giving thanks to you for my natural life: namely, because my soul lives naturally and has the power to enliven the body, a power granted to it by you, the supreme Life. But more fully and more perfectly I declared to you—that is, to your honour—my spiritual life, in which for me to live is Christ and to die is gain.

For I could not live in this spiritual life unless the world had been crucified and made dead to me, and I to the world; unless I had been marked by the inscription of your title; unless, separated from the people made far from the saints, I had been trampled for you among the holy people—that is, crushed together with you in one winepress.

Further, I declared to you, who know all things yet also desire that one who wishes to receive a good life from you should declare his evil life to you, even my old life in which I had grown old in sins among all my enemies. Thus the Apostle Paul says: “I was a blasphemer and persecutor, but I received mercy” (1 Tim. 1:13). In this brief declaration he declared to you, O God, his old life and his new, not only that he might be further purified by such confession, but also that by his example he might urge some to the same course.

Therefore I too, a penitent after his example, declared to you, O God, both my old life and my new. In the one I had the lower watering-place, weeping before you, Lord, in confession of sins; in the other, the upper watering-place, weeping because eternal goods were long delayed. Thus, while I wept, “my tears became bread for me day and night” (Ps. 41:4): by day, as regards the upper watering-place; by night, as regards the lower watering-place [Col. 1683A].

And because, as I complained above, man trampled me like a grape in the winepress, such trampling sometimes pressed tears from me as though wine, and gave them to me to drink with the bread of sorrow instead of wine. Hence “I mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. 101:10) continually, since the people who became far from the saints did not cease from trampling me.

You therefore, who see all things, placed my tears in your sight: you did not despise them but looked kindly upon them, not merely because I wept, but in order that I might weep and be able to weep, and might find weeping itself sweet. If I, Peter, trampled under the feet of the unholy people in the inscription of the title, and thrown down by those tramplers even into triple denial, could not weep until you, Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews, so looked upon me that you gave me tears which you would receive as satisfaction for my sins—certainly you placed those tears in your sight, because they came from your regard.

Likewise I, whatever kind of penitent I may be, pierced with sorrow for my sins, have sometimes had cleansing tears only through your regard; and you too placed them in your sight. For you do not despise tears which you give. Since they flow from you, the fountain of life, they undoubtedly bring life. This too is contained in your promise, by which salvation and life are promised not merely to a weeping sinner, but, what is less, to a groaning sinner. For you say: “At whatever hour the sinner, having turned, shall groan, he shall be saved.”

And because forgiveness of sins is believed in the heart unto righteousness by everyone truly penitent, while confession of sins is made with the mouth unto salvation, salvation is undoubtedly obtained through true confession, “as is written in your promise”; for example, where you say: “He who conceals his crimes shall not be set aright; but he who confesses and forsakes them shall obtain mercy” (Prov. 28:13) [Col. 1683C]. Again, in the Gospel you say: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father” (Matt. 10:32).

For the sinner who confesses himself to be a sinner undoubtedly confesses truth. Therefore, insofar as he confesses truth, he confesses you who are Truth; and if he hates the sins which he confesses and loves you, the Truth by whose illumination he recognizes what he confesses, he merits this blessed reciprocity of confession: that you too confess him before your Father and the holy angels—especially if he is not ashamed to confess and amend before people the evil things he committed before people.

We do not deny that secret sins, even mortal sins, can be cleansed by secret satisfaction, provided that a worthy fruit of repentance follows, insofar as human weakness permits. “I speak humanly because of the weakness of your flesh,” says the Apostle (Rom. 6:19). Do you wish to hear that “human” requirement which is not to be relaxed for any penitent on account of any weakness of the flesh? “Just as,” he says, “you presented your members as servants to impurity and lawlessness unto lawlessness, so now present your members as servants to righteousness unto sanctification” (ibid.).

Is this not sufficiently human, full of condescension and compassion toward human beings? You who, with Zacchaeus, ought in order to attain perfect justification to restore fourfold what you took by fraud in sinning against your neighbour or against God himself, are required only to restore the single equivalent: namely, to present your members for righteousness unto sanctification with no less diligence than formerly you presented those same members for impurity and lawlessness unto lawlessness [Col. 1684A].

But if through your own sloth you wish to remain below this human measure of necessary satisfaction, weighed in the balance of justice and mercy, you can hope for salvation for yourself in no promise of God. Therefore, if you lack the strength to labour as much in God’s service as you laboured in the devil’s service, flee to tears, by which you may extinguish the flames of punishment due to you.

And you, Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews—that is, King of those who confess you—will grant in the world to come laughter to one who now confesses humbly to you and finds weeping sweet, as is written in your promise: “Blessed are those who weep now, for they shall laugh” (Luke 6:21).

**VERSE 10.** Then my enemies shall turn back, as it is also written in your promise, where it is said: “When a man’s ways please the Lord, he will make even his enemies be at peace with him” (Prov. 16:7). My enemies will also turn back in this manner: namely, when it is evident that you have set my tears [Col. 1684C] before you, so that both demons and perverse men who trample upon me may say with the Egyptians: “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them against us” (Exod. 14:25).

For the flood of saving tears possesses such power that, like the Red Sea, it can drown or overwhelm those who pursue us with the invisible Pharaoh, whether visibly or invisibly—provided that these tears are placed before you, O God, and are not despised. Therefore, when you grant such blessed tears, my enemies shall turn back, as was foreshadowed in your promise. For the prior occurrence of ancient benefits is recognized as a preparation and promise of new and future benefits, [Col. 1684D] since all these things happened to the ancients in a figure and were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

Therefore, just as then, in the prefiguration and promise of future goods, the enemies of God’s people turned back when they were hindered from pursuing that people through the waters of the Red Sea, so, because you, O God, have set my tears before you, my enemies turn back through the saving waters of those same tears, reddened by the remembrance and faith of the Lord’s Passion. They turn back, I say, either by a saving conversion, so that they no longer wish to pursue me; or certainly by a judicial conversion, so that, confined by divine judgment, they cannot harm me even if they wish to do so—I who pray continually and entreat conversion both for them and for myself. For example, [Col. 1685A] I frequently say: “Turn us, O God of our salvation, and turn away your wrath from us” (Ps. 34:5). Again: “O Lord God of hosts, turn us; show your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79:8). Again, with Jeremiah I say: “Turn us, O Lord, to yourself, and we shall be turned; renew our days as from the beginning” (Lam. 5:21).

With prayers of this sort: On whatever day—whether in childhood, middle age, or at the end of life—I call upon you, seeking nothing but you, nothing but to please you alone. For if I sought something else, I would call upon not you but that thing. Whenever, therefore, I call upon you, behold, I have known that you are my God. I do not merely say, “that you are God,” but add, “that you are mine.” For although you are generally the God of all, [Col. 1685B] yet you are mine properly and particularly: you who aid me, whom I worship, whom I love, and whom alone I invoke on whatever day I offer vows or prayers. In these I know, either through faith or experience, that you hear me so manifestly that I can say in thanksgiving: “Behold, I have known that you are my God.” Counting this indeed among great riches, I say elsewhere: “The Lord is my portion” (Lam. 3:24).

And you, Lord, truly approving this saying, declare: “I, the Lord, shall be their inheritance” (Ezek. 44:28). Whose, unless those who, not remaining far from the holy things, are themselves the Lord’s inheritance? “You shall give no inheritance,” he says, “to the sons of Levi; I, the Lord, shall be their inheritance.” These are they who keep watch not far from the holy things; indeed, dwelling and weeping between the vestibule and the altar, near and amid the holy things and the Holy of Holies, they pour forth such tears that any one of them may rightly say to you, O God: “You have set my tears before you.”

Some have called that people blessed which is made far from the holy things, for whom the riches are these created things of God: for example, storehouses full, pouring out abundance from one kind into another; fruitful sheep, fat cattle, and the like. But I, David—I, the Psalmist—say that blessed is the people not made far from the holy things, but rather bound by the bonds of obedience within and near the Holy of Holies, so that it has no leisure to withdraw far from the holy things and mingle with an unholy people, like those who “mingled among the nations and learned [Col. 1685D] their works” (Ps. 105:35).

Therefore let no one serving as a soldier of God within the Holy of Holies entangle himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has proved himself, to whom he has credibly dedicated himself to minister within the Holy of Holies, receiving for his ministry a great reward—namely, God himself—so that he may truly say: “Behold, I have known that you are my God.” True, therefore, is the sentence: “Blessed is the people whose Lord is its God” (Ps. 163:15); for however full storehouses may be, they will at some time fail, and however fruitful the sheep and fat the cattle may be, they will at some time perish. But the Lord God, having become the inheritance of his people, will never fail; whenever he is invoked, he will show himself merciful and ready to hear his own.

[Col. 1686A] **VERSE 11.** “In God I will praise the word; in the Lord I will praise the speech,” as was explained above.

Or: In God the Father I shall praise the Word, that is, the Son. For whatever is said of God the Father according to substance—for example, almighty, eternal, immeasurable, and so forth—is likewise predicated of his Word or Son. Thus he himself, together with the Father, to whom he is consubstantial, is without doubt one true God: one almighty, one eternal, one immeasurable, and together with the Father governor and Lord of all creation.

“In the Lord,” in this Word which willed to become flesh, visible and at the same time audible, “I will praise the speech,” that is, the manner of life by which “he began to do and to teach, until the day on which, giving commands through the Holy Spirit to those whom he had chosen, he was taken up” [Col. 1686B] (Acts 1:1–2). This same Spirit, appearing in tongues and making clear the speech previously obscure, is likewise without doubt almighty God, equal to the Father and his Word, because “these three are one” (1 John 5:7).

Alternatively: In God the Father I shall praise the Word, which in the beginning was with him, known to himself alone; and in the Lord—that is, in the Holy Spirit—I shall praise the speech: namely, the manifestation of that same Word through flesh assumed, conceived and born of the Holy Spirit, beautifully formed by his seven fingers and supported upon seven columns, understood as the seven gifts of that same Holy Spirit. Thus the construction of this house is rightly praised in the Lord—that is, in the Holy Spirit—[Col. 1686C] “in whom dwells bodily all the fullness of the Godhead” (Col. 2:9). This speech of the Incarnation does not differ from the eternal Word; rather, it is the same Word made flesh, administering himself to little ones like solid bread turned into milk.

For just as a word or intention of the human heart is hidden before it becomes the speech of the mouth, and is made manifest through that speech, so the eternal Word or counsel of God the Father was secret with him until, as the Apostle says, “he was manifested in the flesh, preached to the world, taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:16). Thereafter, as the Holy Spirit worked through the apostles and other teachers in fiery tongues, the Word previously obscure shone forth in manifest speech. He himself foretold that this would occur, when, speaking of himself, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, he said: “He will glorify me, for he will receive from what is mine and declare it to you” [Col. 1686D] (John 16:14).

Rightly, therefore, “in God I will praise the Word,” because God the Father brought forth from his heart a good and praiseworthy Word; and “in the Lord I will praise the speech,” because the Spirit who was the author and manifestor of that most sacred Incarnation made that same Word, through the mystery of the Incarnation, into speech and clarified it.

Whether, then, you hear that the Word is praised in God or that the speech is praised in the Lord, understand no other than the one and same Son of God. Before the ages he was the Word in the bosom of the Father; at the end of the ages, having become man in his mother’s womb, [Col. 1687A] he who was the word of the heart became the speech of the mouth. Though invisible God, he became visible man—not ceasing to be what he was, but beginning to be what he was not, namely man; and granting to man what he was not, namely God.

Here neither mixture nor division is to be understood. Just as you cannot divide the uttered speech of wisdom from the Word of wisdom, so you cannot divide the man assumed by God from the one assuming him, if you rightly understand that the man is not yet the Son of God; nor can you truly understand the Word of God as not man, since he deigned to be made flesh and born from a human being. Again, these two significations, namely God and man, are not so mixed into some third thing which should be understood as neither God nor man, as flour and water make a third thing which is to be called neither water nor flour.

God, therefore, as we sing, became man without undergoing mixture or division. The two natures, namely divinity and humanity, so came together in one person that, with the natural and substantial distinction of each preserved, he is properly called God-Man and Man-God. This is as when one calls an uttered word “speech,” and calls the speech expressing an uttered word “word.” Hence the prophets use the two in the same sense, so that *word* is understood as *speech* and speech as word: for example, when it is said, “The Word of the Lord came,” or “The speech of the Lord came,” to this or that prophet [Col. 1687C].

And if, through participation in the Word or speech of the Lord, he called gods those to whom the Word of the Lord came or the speech of God came—God himself speaking to them thus: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6)—how much more truly is the man who became the Word or speech of God called God: not adoptive, like those to whom God’s speech came, but natural, since he was born from God and became the Word or speech of God.

Many heretics have detracted from this God, this Word, this speech: Arius, by asserting that the Son is less than the Father; and Nestorius, by dividing the man from God as one divides speech from word. Even now, the people made far from the holy things, wholly irreligious, detract in their disputations from the man assumed into God. Denying that he is properly called God, they say that he is like God’s dwelling-place and is honored improperly with the name of God, just as any saint in whom God dwells participates in some manner in the divine name—for example, when it is said, “I said, you are gods.” And God says to Moses: “Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh” [Col. 1687D] (Exod. 7:1).

Among such adoptive human gods they count the God-Man, who is God blessed above all: God not adopted by God, but born from God as God. Thus the people made far from the holy things diminish the praises of God incarnate and of him honored by the divine inscription of the title through the name Jesus. But I, together with the holy people, shall praise the Word in God and the speech in the Lord. I shall praise God’s humanity and man’s divinity. I shall praise God made man, the mediator of God and men.

Do you wish to hear, against the people made far from the holy things, that holy man whom we know to have been divinely instructed within the Holy of Holies—I mean holy Augustine, hammer of the heretics who have gone far from the holy things? Hear what he says, how, praising the Word in God and the speech in the Lord, he commends the divine humanity and human divinity of the mediator of God and men:

> “If the Son of God had not emptied himself by descending, he would not be the mediator of God and men. But the Son of God became mediator because he lowered his majesty to human things and raised humanity [Col. 1688B] to divine things, so that he might be mediator between God and man: man through God, above men. In this is shown to man how far he had withdrawn from God, when he is recalled through God incarnate; through God-Man an example of obedience is offered to disobedient man; when God assumed the form of a servant, which had previously merited nothing, the fountain of grace is opened; the redemption of the flesh promised in Christ is shown; and through the same nature through which the devil had conquered, he is conquered.”

Again, the same author:

> “Jesus Christ is the mediator of God and men because he is God with the Father and man with men. Behold the mediator: not man as mediator apart from divinity, nor God as mediator apart from humanity. Divinity without humanity is not mediating, nor humanity without divinity; but mediating between divinity alone and humanity alone are Christ’s human divinity and divine humanity.”

Again another holy man, not made far from the holy things but pre-eminent among the saints, Pope Leo, says in his sermon on the Lord’s Passion:

> “The only-begotten of the most high Father entered into such fellowship with human lowliness that, by assuming the substance of our flesh and soul, the one and the same Son of God might remain what he was, increasing what was ours, not what was his own; for weakness, not power, had to be raised, so that when the creature was united with its Creator, nothing divine might be lacking to what was assumed, and nothing human to the one assuming.”

As these holy men and others like them speak against the people made far from the holy things, I—David, I the penitent [Col. 1688D] and singer with David—though not holy, yet not made far from the holy things, because I am joined to them not by holiness but by faith, shall praise in God the incarnate Word. I shall praise the divine humanity and human divinity; I shall praise divinity made human without alteration of itself; I shall praise humanity made divine, or deified, not by a changeability of nature but by a change of qualities. This was signified in the inscription of the title, when the man reckoned among the wicked was named Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.

Therefore, in the Lord I shall praise the speech of this title, so firmly inscribed that it can in no way be corrupted by the people who have become far from the holy things. They do not believe what the saints believe; they will not allow the name of Jesus, which is above every name, to remain so uncorrupted in their hearts that they never doubt that at the name of Jesus every knee must bend and every tongue confess that the man—one person of the Trinity, assumed through divine conception into the full glory of the whole Trinity through divine glorification after death—is to be worshipped in the glory of God the Father.

This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High: that a man should sit upon the exalted throne of paternal majesty, judging all things justly with the Father, though he was unjustly judged before wicked judges.
