This is Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews—that is, of those confessing Jesus Christ and venerating the truth that the meaning of this title belongs to the crucified man as much as it belongs to the impassible God the Father. For the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the whole holy Trinity—are one holy Savior, ruling all things. The whole power of this kingdom, signified in the inscription of the title, was secretly given to the assumed man at his conception, but openly in the glorification of the Resurrection and Ascension, because then his humanity entered into its glory, from which, according to his divinity, he had never departed.

Thereafter the man assumed into heaven—that is, into the secret place of paternal glory—although less than God the Father in his human nature, which in its created condition is neither diminished by misery nor increased by glory, is nevertheless altogether equal to the same Father in the glorification of that same human nature. Otherwise the inscription written above Jesus’ head would be corrupted, if anything of divine glory were taken from the assumed and crucified man, as it is taken from him by the people made far from the holy things. Against them holy Pope Leo thunders thus in his sermon to the people on the Nativity of the Lord:

> “Let the monstrous opinions of heretics and the sacrileges of insane falsehood withdraw far away and fall back into their own darkness. The rejoicing multitude of heaven and the shepherds instructed by angels have taught us that, once the proofs of both natures are known, we should adore both the Word in Christ the man and Christ the man in the Word. For if, as the Apostle says, he who cleaves to God is one spirit, how much more is the Word made flesh one Christ, where there is nothing belonging to one nature that does not belong to both. Though one remains from eternity and the other began in time, yet they came together in unity and can have neither separation [Col. 1689D] nor end; for the one exalting and the one exalted, the one glorifying and the one glorified, adhere so to each other that, whether in omnipotence or in humiliation, neither the divine in Christ lacks the human nor the human lacks the divine.”

Let the unholy people, made far from the holy things, hear this, and cease to deprive the man assumed into God of either divine immensity or eternity. He possesses both through the immense and eternal divinity bestowed upon him, because in God divinity, eternity, and immensity are one and the same. Consequently, just as the man made God has divinity, so he has immensity and eternity. The merely natural man does not grasp this: being far from the holy things, he distinguishes God’s eternity from God’s essence just as he distinguishes a man’s age from a man’s essence [Col. 1690A].

Likewise, imagining immensity, he pictures it in God as the Manichaeans picture it: extended through quantitative length, breadth, height, and depth—an immense thing, a great image—which blessed Augustine reasonably refuted in his *Confessions*. Under his teaching we have also learned what is the breadth of charity, given to the assumed man no less than it is innate to the Word, since he who is charity itself of Father and Son did not receive the Spirit by measure. I mean the Father, who from eternity loves those whom he predestined from eternity in the eternal Son; and this eternity of love is that length which is innate to the Word and given to the assumed man. If he lacked it, he would falsely be named Jesus in the inscription of the title [Col. 1690B]; those who do not believe this corrupt the title, so far as lies within them.

Likewise, the sublimity of divine power and the depth of divine wisdom are recognized in the inscription of the title through the name of King, to whom was given the immeasurable power of governing all things mightily and wisely.

Therefore I too shall praise the Word of God, wholly inscribed upon the skin of humanity; I shall also praise the man honored by such an inscription and properly called Savior-God, not only by Pilate in the inscription of the title, but also by the angel in the announcement of the Lord’s Incarnation: “Behold,” he says, “you shall conceive and bear a Son, and you shall call his name Jesus” (Luke 1:31). And to Joseph: “Do not,” he says, “fear to take Mary your wife; [Col. 1690C] for what is born in her is of the Holy Spirit. She shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he himself shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:20–21). The man, therefore, who saves his people from their sins—a work belonging to God alone—is certainly true God.

In this God I have hoped to be freed and saved from my sins, while I persist in his praises, not made far from the holy things but placed among the holy things by good action and in the Holy of Holies by holy contemplation. Therefore I shall not fear what man may do to me—that man, namely, of whom I said at the beginning of the psalm: “Man trampled me.” For what can such a man do to me except in external matters? Stripped of these as of grapes, in this winepress where I am trodden I shall be purer, and I shall be made like him of whom it is written: “His eyes are more beautiful than wine” (Song 7:9). Or rather, I shall become that wine, worthy for the beloved to drink and to chew with his teeth, which is praised in the Song of Songs. Therefore I shall not fear what man may do to me.

By saying this above I concluded the first part; by repeating it I now conclude the second. There, against many who fought against me, I said: “In God I have hoped; I shall not fear what flesh may do to me,” having God as the safest refuge in whom I have hoped and shall hope. Here, praying for the conversion of the same combatants and giving thanks for their conversion, I likewise say: “In God I have hoped; I shall not fear what man may do to me.” I pray all the more attentively for the hastening of his conversion, the more violently I endure him as an assailant. When he is converted or humbled, I willingly pay vows of thanksgiving all the more devoutly, since that man who trampled or fought against me was a more dangerous enemy and is now a more fruitful friend—perhaps made from Saul into Paul.

For persons of this kind, either to be converted so as to benefit me, or turned away so as not to harm me, I have often promised vows of thanksgiving and praise; and now I devoutly fulfill these vows. For though the man trampling or fighting against me may have taken away certain outward things, his plundering hands have not reached the inner storehouses, namely the wine-cellar in which God, in whom I hope, is able to preserve my deposit. From this inward cell I also endeavor to fulfill my vows to him. Therefore I say:

**VERSE 12.** “In me, O God, are your vows, which I shall render to you as praises.” In me—that is, in my soul—are stored in a pure conscience the vows which I shall offer you: the sacrifice of faith and hope, which charity kindles upon the altar of the heart in praise of your name. In the future, however, when faith and hope cease, charity alone, which remains and never falls away, will pay you praises and vows.

Or, I shall render to you vows of your praise—that is, vows made to you—or *your* vows, that is, vows inspired by you. For what good do I possess, or what praiseworthy thing could I have vowed or can I vow to you, except what comes to me from you? I shall therefore render to you, from your gifts, the sacrifice of jubilation and vows of praise. For the fact that I live is yours: you first gave life and restored it when it was lost, author and restorer [Col. 1691C] of my life. You gave me a soul, which is the life of the body, and your grace, which is the life of the soul.

But my soul, losing your grace through sin, was deprived of its life and fell into death. You, Jesus of Nazareth, destroyed this death of the soul by dying, in the inscription of the title placed above your head on the cross; and by rising you restored bodily life. Therefore, because by your death you have thus rescued my soul from death, “in me, O God, are your vows,” [Col. 1692A] “the vows of praise which I shall render to you” (Ecclus. 17:26). For confession perishes from the dead, and no one in hell will confess you; nor would I praise you if I had remained in death or hell. But now, living in me through your grace, there are vows of praise which I shall render to you.

**VERSE 13.** “For you have rescued my soul from death, and my feet from falling.” Yet this deliverance, begun in this world, will not be completed except in your kingdom, O King of the Jews, whose kingdom remains forever. Into that kingdom you will not call a people made far from the holy things, but your people, sanctified by your Passion in the inscription of the title, as you prayed, saying: “For them I sanctify myself, that they too may be holy in truth” (John 17:19).

You will therefore give your saints a named place in the kingdom of your Father and yours, where neither the soul dies by sinning, nor the eyes will weep their evils, nor the feet—that is, the affections—slip. For there will be no slipperiness of temptation or any danger of death. To that place you have now led me in hope and will still lead me in reality, so that I may please before God your Father when you hand over the kingdom to him. I say, please God alone, not the people far from the holy things; for if I pleased such men, I would not be Christ’s servant, and “those who please” such “men have been put to shame, because God has despised them” (Ps. 52:6).

But “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114:9), in the light of the living. Whoever worships and loves God freely is in this light, a light known to no one but God alone and the person who receives it from God [Col. 1692C]. Therefore it is of little consequence to me if I displease the people made far from the holy things—a people now in hidden and inward darkness, hereafter to be cast into outward, that is, manifest, darkness—provided that I please before God in the light of the living.

Glory to God the Father, in whom I shall praise the Word. Glory to the Son, the Word himself. Glory to the Holy Spirit, the Lord, in whom I shall praise the speech.

## PSALM 56

[Col. 1691]

[Col. 1691D] “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me,” etc. Title:

**(VERSE 1.) FOR THE END: DO NOT DESTROY, OR DO NOT CORRUPT, OF DAVID, IN THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE, WHEN HE FLED FROM SAUL’S FACE INTO THE CAVE.**

We read in the Book of Kings that David, when Saul sought him, fled to the very secure places of Engedi, where he lay hidden in a cave (2 Kings 22:1; 24:4). But he signifies Christ, who lay hidden both veiled by flesh and placed in the tomb, lest God be seen by the Jews. No title, however, was written over David which Saul desired to corrupt. But over Christ, who comes after David, Pilate wrote a title which the Jewish people wished to corrupt. Through the Spirit the Prophet speaks to them, saying: O Pilate, [Col. 1692D] or whoever you are, do not corrupt anything in the inscription of the title made for David himself, that is, Christ, when he fled from Saul’s face—that is, from the knowledge of the devil and the Jews—into the cave of flesh or the tomb. Someone would corrupt it if, because he was incarnate and suffered, he denied him to be King. Pilate, indicating that this prophecy was to be fulfilled, said: “What I have written, I have written” (John 19:22).

This fifth psalm, then, which briefly treats Christ’s Passion and Resurrection, aims to prevent anyone from contradicting Christ’s title, which is the end of our consummation. In this psalm the whole Christ speaks: first, as though hidden in the cave, he prays for his deliverance and briefly touches upon his enemies’ reproaches. [Col. 1693A] Second, he explains how he was delivered and what and by whom he suffered, suitably inserting his Resurrection at the words: “God sent his mercy and his truth.” Third, after his Resurrection he promises to praise God at the words: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready.”

But before we enter the continuous exposition of the psalm, it seems necessary to address that combatant whom, as we said above, these fifty psalms teach to struggle between hope and fear. Therefore, whoever you are who flee from Saul’s face—from the face, that is, of the devil or death—do not corrupt this title: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.” Indeed, do not corrupt yourself by destroying in yourself what is meant by “King of the Jews.” For what is the King of the Jews but the king of confessors? Therefore confess your sins, so that you may be the kingdom of this king; and, hoping in Jesus of Nazareth—that is, your holy saving king—say according to his example: “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, for my soul trusts in you; and in the shadow of your wings I shall hope, until iniquity passes away.”

That is to say, in the Apostle’s sense: I shall fight against the law which is in my members until that comes which delivers me from this body of death, the grace of God. When it comes, I shall say: “God sent his mercy and his truth, and rescued my soul from the midst of lion cubs”—understand: as he rescued my head, my king, from the midst of the sons of men, whose teeth were weapons and [Col. 1693C] arrows. Having briefly prefaced this for the aforesaid combatant, let us return to the beginning of the psalm.

**VERSE 2.** “Have mercy on me, O God.” I, Jesus of Nazareth, declared King of the Jews by the triumphal inscription of an incorruptible title, am burdened by a twofold misery while the impious Saul persecutes me and mine—that is, the devil, ruler of death. I was confined both in the cave of a tiny body and in the narrow tomb; and in my members I have endured and do endure like straits from the first righteous man and the blood of righteous Abel to the last elect person. Therefore, for myself and for them I pray, saying: “Have mercy on me, God the Father,” giving victory in temptation and constancy in suffering to me and mine; and again, “Have mercy on me, God the Father,” giving the glory of resurrection to me and mine.

To me, that I may rise in the body and go forth in great power from the narrow cave of the tomb into the wide glory of my heavenly kingdom; for thus it was necessary for me to suffer and so enter into my glory. But give to mine the glory of resurrection: first in the soul, dead through sin; then in the flesh, to be raised after death. Because of this double resurrection I say twice: “Have mercy on me, have mercy on me”—that is, have mercy on me and mine, or on mine oppressed by a twofold death while Saul, that is, the devil, persecutes them.

I seek mercy not without the merit of justice, because my soul trusts in you. Although it is sorrowful unto death with voluntary sorrow on account of my members, necessarily subject to sorrow, yet it trusts that you will not abandon it in [Col. 1694A] hell or allow its body to see corruption, but will swiftly bring about the Resurrection. Meanwhile, while iniquity reigns and justice is oppressed, while the wicked judge Pilate presides and I, the just judge, am unjustly judged—or while any wicked person rules and some just person is endangered beneath his rule—I shall hope in the shadow of your wings, and shall likewise cause my own people to hope, until this iniquity and perversity passes away and such justice succeeds that the righteous, released from the cave of their narrowness, rightly rule, while the wicked are confined through the just judgments of the righteous within the bounds of justice, like fierce beasts shut up within the cages of their malice by the strongest barriers of laws.

For they are roaring lion cubs, equal in kind to demons, eager to seize their prey, especially when it is the hour and power of darkness and the sun of justice does not appear. When at last it rises, they shall gather together and be placed in their dens; or rather, they shall be confined in the narrow prisons and cages of their own hearts, so that they may not freely go out through manifest deeds of wickedness, nor may the hidden root of wickedness break forth into evil fruits, but may wither while enclosed within. This now indeed occurs partially, insofar as truth rules falsehood and justice rules iniquity; but at the last judgment every iniquity will altogether pass away and come to nothing, like flowing water that swiftly passes.

Until iniquity thus passes away, I—David, I—Christ, or I—a Christian—shall hope in the shadow of your wings. For with the protection of your mercy, as a bird protects its nest or young, you protect the Church and in it your little ones, who need the shade of your protection in the heat of persecution or temptation. Iniquity, which dies now in some and is born in others, will not wholly pass away until every righteous person has been freed from the cave of his narrowness and every unrighteous person, bound by the chains of his obstinacy, has been confined in a penal prison. In order that this may happen swiftly, I shall hope not only in heart but also through other acts and daily groans.

**VERSE 3.** “I shall cry to God Most High,” most high through the sublimity of his essence or the loftiness of his glory, yet near to his own through the mercy of his compassion. I have experienced this in myself through his goodness, he who has done good to me. Do you wish to hear, kindly [Col. 1694D] hearers, in what benefit he has done good to me?

**VERSE 4.** “He sent from heaven and delivered me” from the cave of every narrowness. This was partly fulfilled in the glorious resurrection of the flesh, namely in me, the firstborn from the dead, and in those who rose with me from the caves of their tombs; it remains partly to be fulfilled in the resurrection of all people for judgment, but of the saints for reigning with me, who in the cave of temporal narrowness have been planted together with me in order to die with me. This total and universal deliverance of my own from every narrowness will so certainly occur that I truthfully state it as though past, saying: “He delivered me.” For he has indeed already delivered me, Christ, and will nonetheless still deliver my whole body.

[Col. 1695A] Moreover, he gave to reproach those who trample upon me, namely the Jews, the first tramplers upon me and mine. Because of their wickedness they have been scattered among the nations. As these nations worship me whom they crucified, great reproach hangs over them; their evil conscience inwardly and harsh, shameful insult outwardly torment them. For just as they insulted me crucified and dead when they wished to corrupt the triumphal title written by Pilate, so now, scattered throughout the world, they are insulted as the triumphant banner of my cross is raised before their eyes and against their will, and as the inscription of my title, by which I am signified as true God and great King, is shown to be incorruptible.

For I am the great high priest, upon whose forehead the golden plate shines, and upon whom the ineffable name of God is known to be inscribed in that I am Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews—saving and ruling, that is, my people: the people of the Jews, that is, those truly confessing this title to be true and to signify both my mercy and my power. It signifies my mercy because I am Jesus, that is, Savior of all people, and especially of believers; it signifies my power because I am King of the Jews, holding my kingdom mightily while ruling in the midst of my enemies. No one can snatch anyone from my hand, any more than from the hand of my Father, almighty God.

The fitting likeness is the title placed on the cross above the head of Jesus as he sacrificed himself: “a golden crown engraved with the sign of holiness” (Ecclus. 45:14), upon which, [Col. 1695C] on the head of Aaron while he sacrificed, the name of the Deity was inscribed. Yet the likeness fails in this respect: the golden plate or crown could be removed from Aaron’s head—for example, when he sinned at the waters of contradiction by not sanctifying God there. But upon the mind of the man assumed into God—a mind purer and more subtle than all created spirits—there has been imposed a crown or plate of Divinity, more than golden, such that this mind itself, though human, nevertheless shines in the complete glory of Divinity and divine brightness. Whoever strives to divide it by subtle reasoning, making too great a distinction between the assuming nature and the assumed nature, so far as lies in him corrupts the inscription of the title and the divine name. Not Pilate’s hand, but God’s finger, inscribed it so firmly [Col. 1695D] that no one can corrupt this inscription.

For if the name Jesus—that is, Savior, saving his people from sin, which is a divine work—truly belongs to the crucified man, not figuratively or merely by designation but altogether substantially, then likewise the name of God truly and substantially belongs to him: the ineffable name, the name of eternal wisdom deeply inscribed upon the rational understanding of the human mind. For the golden plate upon the priest’s forehead is the rational intellect in Christ’s human mind. Since that rational intellect was made capable of incomprehensible Divinity, so as to know all that Divinity knows and to be able to do whatever Divinity can do, the inscription of the divine name was, as it were, deeply engraved upon the understanding of the human soul united to God with his flesh—not only personally [Col. 1696A] united, but also naturally joined. For just as pure gold is naturally capable of an inscription made by the sculptor’s art, and neither needs nor retains an inscription made by the painter’s art through colors externally adhering, so Christ’s rational mind, like the purest gold, received inwardly rather than outwardly the inscription of Divinity, made by God’s finger at the conception through the Holy Spirit—that is, through divine love, not human love, effecting this.

For if by God’s finger the divine law was inscribed so firmly upon tablets of stone that this inscription could be erased only by breaking the tablets, how much more does the eternal wisdom of God, inscribed through the ineffable name of Jesus upon the forehead of our high priest and king, display such an inscription of the triumphal title [Col. 1696B] as admits no actual, or even merely intellectual, separation between itself and that plate of human nature upon which it is inscribed—just as we sometimes actually separate an inscription from wax by smoothing it away, or intellectually separate blackness from a raven. His Divinity cannot thus be separated from Christ’s humanity, because both his humanity has been divinized and his Divinity humanized; and from and in the two natures there has come to be one *electrum*, yet of a single golden brightness, because the humanity assumed has been glorified and made bright together with the most radiant Divinity that assumed it.

Indeed, the Word asked this brightness for his flesh, saying: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had before the world was” [Col. 1696C] (John 17:5). But since this question has, I think, been sufficiently treated in the first fifty, it is now enough to venerate with every veneration the man worthy of divine honor: Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews, son of God and of the Virgin—truly God and truly Son of God, truly also man and truly son of man; to be called truly God and truly Savior; truly king of angels and truly king of the Jews, that is, of confessors. For the angels too are among those who confess his divine name, and they themselves, when he was a little child, served him as their God and Lord, according to his will.

Therefore I shall cry to this Jesus, God Most High, [Col. 1696D] ever equally Most High with his Father, the Most High, in his Divinity; yet in his human substance, which for a time was confined in the cave of the virginal womb or also of the tomb, now exalted to the highest height. Thus “his going forth was from the summit of heaven,” that is, from the Father (Ps. 18:7). O how great is my confidence and hope when I cry, from the cave of impending distress, to this God Most High: he who has now been delivered from the cave in which he was for my sake, and sits at God’s right hand, exalted above all things. “And I,” he says, “when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). I shall cry to God Most High that, according to his faithful promise, he may draw me to himself from the cave of impending temptations and tribulations.

Likewise, he says: [Col. 1697A] “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but when I have been taken up, I will send him to you” (John 16:7). He spoke these things to his disciples, still placed in the cave of mortal flesh, while he himself was about to go to the Father—from the cave, namely, of human confinement into the breadth of divine loftiness. And, as he promised, he sent them the Paraclete, consoling the primitive Church—indeed, in the apostles, the whole universal Church. Therefore it is fitting for me, any member of the Church, to sing in thanksgiving and say:

God sent forth his mercy and his truth. A *diapsalma* is appropriately inserted here, because prayer passes into thanksgiving, when I, the Church or an ecclesiastical person, say: God sent [Col. 1697B] forth his mercy and his truth; that is, as he promised, he sent the Spirit of truth, who is the mercy of himself and of the Father. And although he is the Spirit of truth, teaching all truth, he always has with himself, O Christ, you, the supreme truth, coming from the supreme Father. Hence above I said: “He sent from heaven and delivered me,” without specifying what he sent. But now I say openly that God sent forth his mercy and his truth. God the Father sent forth his truth, that is, the Son. God the Father and the Son sent forth their mercy, that is, the Holy Spirit, through the Son’s Passion and the Holy Spirit’s operation.

**VERSE 5.** He delivered, and without doubt will deliver, my soul from the midst of lion cubs. He sent from heaven—that is, from his hidden essence—the Word; and from the secret knowledge of angels, his truth, to be incarnated, and his mercy, to be manifested by a clear work of compassion. For neither the Son sent by God the Father nor the Holy Spirit sent by both came from heaven to earth by local motion. Rather, although each was invisible and remained everywhere, each is said to have come because he deigned to make himself manifest: the one in the human form which he assumed; the other, displaying himself visibly in the form of a dove over Christ or in fire over the apostles. Since God the Father ordained this to occur, it is rightly said to him in thanksgiving: “God sent forth his mercy and his truth” (Ps. 84:12)—namely, the Holy Spirit, by whose operation truth sprang from the earth, [Col. 1697D] because the Son of God was born of the Virgin.

This truth, to confirm the promises of the Fathers, worked a good work in me, the man assumed and united to it, in that it delivered my soul from the midst of lion cubs—that is, from the midst of the people led astray by their rulers. This deliverance was certainly fitting for me as man, because “I slept troubled”: that is, I underwent death after that disturbance of which I said, “Now my soul is troubled” (Ps. 41:7). Likewise: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38). Thus I slept troubled, not by necessity but by my own will, and began sleep, to be awakened and rise from death with greater ease than you, whoever you are, can either shake off sleep yourself or awaken [Col. 1698A] your friend.

In such disturbance and sleep, lion cubs together with lions surrounded me—that is, common people together with rulers, agreeing in the same ferocity. But the mercy and truth of my Divinity delivered my human soul from the midst of lion cubs: for it was neither held in death by wicked men raging against me with leonine ferocity, nor abandoned in hell among greater and lesser demons, resembling lions and lion cubs in bestial ferocity.

David is indeed read to have entered a cave, but not to have slept there. Hence it is clear that this must rather be understood of Christ, who fittingly and properly says, “I slept troubled”: that is, even in that disturbance I did not lose the peace of my heart. For I did not undergo death with conscience beaten and quarreling with itself, as one of the evildoers; rather, with a quiet and silent heart, a well-assured mind preserved patience in the voluntary death by which I freely laid down my soul when I wished and took it again when I wished. And because I named lions and lion cubs, lest anyone suppose that I speak of beasts rather than men, I state it more openly:

The sons of men—that is, the Jews, sons of rational fathers—prepared a snare for my feet and bowed down my soul: not that they crucified me with their own hands, since they said, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death” (John 18:31); but their teeth, with which they gnashed against me, were weapons and arrows—weapons in their counsels and arrows [Col. 1698C] in their words. Or their teeth, that is, the biting detractions with which they bit me and mine through slander, were weapons and arrows: weapons insofar as they defended themselves, arrows insofar as they wounded me. For “weapons” means shield, helmet, breastplate, and every armor of the strong, by which they are protected against their opponents’ blows; but arrows and the other missiles do not defend the fighter, but injure the enemy. Therefore, because these men gnashed against me with their teeth, both protecting themselves and injuring me, I rightly say: “Their teeth were weapons and arrows,” by which they struck me from afar and, perhaps, while absent; “and their tongue a sharp sword,” by striking with which at close quarters they wrought my swift death, saying: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 26:66); likewise, “Crucify, [Col. 1698D] crucify him” (John 19:6); likewise, “We have a law, and according to our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:7).

By saying such things they did not cease until, before the face of Saul—that is, of death—I, the true David, was humbled into the cave of the tomb. They also caused it to be fortified and guarded, lest I should ever rise from the cave and reign. This was the great iniquity of which above I said that I hoped in the shadow of your wings until iniquity should pass away. Although it must be believed to have passed away in part when I rose from this cave and reigned in my kingdom, Saul—that is, death—having been conquered, whose death I shall be, nevertheless the same iniquity remains in part, prolonged. For just as the struggle between the house of David and [Col. 1699A] the house of Saul was long, even after Saul had died, so Saul’s sons, the sons of death, prolonged this iniquity for themselves, desiring to rule unjustly over the righteous.

Therefore, while pestilent sons sit in the seat of pestilence and occupy many seats in the Church, the righteous, oppressed by them, wander in mountains and caves and caverns of the earth: for example, hiding in woods and wildernesses, or inhabiting most impoverished monasteries resembling caves; needy, afflicted, distressed—persons of whom the world, lying in wickedness, was not worthy, that saints should preside over it in secular or spiritual government. Rather, this world was and is worthy of rulers like Herod, Pilate, and Caiaphas. Yet it is not doubted that this iniquity will at some time pass away altogether, when all the wicked have been shut into the caves [Col. 1699B] of due retribution, and the kingdom and every honor are in the hand of Christ, the true David, and of his friends. Therefore I, David, certain that this iniquity will without doubt pass away, shall cry to God Most High until it passes. What shall I cry? This:

**VERSE 6.** Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth. Be exalted by rising from the cave. Be exalted above your “high and lifted-up throne” (Isa. 6:1), and all the earth will be full of your glory; your glory will be over all the earth. Your high throne is the chosen portion of the angels, which remains in the heights when the rest fall into the abyss. Moreover, your lifted-up throne is the human race, crying to you from the depths and, having formerly lain in the lowest place, now raised on high.

Alternatively: your high throne consists in all those who have not fallen grievously, such as John your beloved, illustrious in purity and innocence; your lifted-up throne consists in those people who, having fallen grievously, have been raised by worthy repentance, as the apostle Peter, after his threefold denial, was laudably elevated in the Church of the people upon the elders’ chair.

Alternatively: the spirits and souls of the righteous are your high throne. Since angelic purity and subtlety are in them, you sit in them as in heavenly thrones, O eternal truth and wisdom. And when you work great marvels through their bodies also, you dwell in those bodies as upon a lifted-up throne, sanctified together with its soul. I signify these two thrones by the name “heavens,” when I cry to you, God: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth.” Why do you lie hidden in the cave, my King and my God? For because you are hidden, I am daily told, “Where is your God?” The disciples rejoiced when they saw you, Lord, after you rose from the tomb in your body; while you lay hidden in it, the apostles were sorrowful over the death of their Lord. Thus until the end of the age, whenever you, Wisdom, lie oppressed by fools; you, Justice, by the unjust; you, Truth, by liars—as though in a cave—your disciples grieve and lament as though you were buried.

Therefore, when at last this lamentation is ended, with its great weeping and wailing because of the oppression [Col. 1700A] of you, King of the Jews, let the angelic host of heaven rejoice; let the divine mysteries rejoice. Be exalted above the heavens—that is, above the high and lifted-up throne, namely over the elect angels and human beings—so that, while you order the ministries of angels and the affairs of human beings in praiseworthy and wondrous fashion, every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth may bend to you reigning on earth and in heaven, and every tongue confess that you, Lord Jesus Christ, having come forth from the cave and been exalted above the heavens, are in the glory of God the Father, accomplishing by no lesser power the work of the title’s inscription, by which you are proved to be Savior, than your Father accomplished the work of creation, he who is without doubt the creator of all things.

Alternatively: “Be exalted above the heavens,” that is, above men either innocent or penitent, predestined for the heavenly kingdom, and enrolled through the confession of your praise or of their sins, O Christ, King of the Jews, in the inscription of the title. They do not corrupt this title within themselves, while by pure confession they show themselves true Jews, whose king you are worthily called. When they have been multiplied and exalted from the caves of their distresses, may your glory be made manifest in every land and over all the earth, while your enemies are compelled to enter the hiding places of caves like beasts not daring to come out into the light; while your friends go forth to their work and to their labor until evening—that is, until the end of their life or of this age, in which you, the ancient sun, promised to remain with your friends until the consummation of the age.

Alternatively: “Be exalted above the heavens,” that is, above the souls and bodies of the saints, likened, as stated above, to the high and lifted-up throne: so that in souls illumined by you, the sun of righteousness, peace and the light of good will may shine before you; and in bodies saved through your indwelling there may shine before men the light of good works, so that, seeing their good works, they may glorify you, God, who are in such heavens. May they glorify you, I say, and your Father together with the Holy Spirit so magnificently that your glory may shine over all the earth and, like the splendor of noon and summer, grow so warm that no one may remain hidden and none may hide himself from its heat. For as, when this visible sun is exalted in its zodiac, its splendor and heat are felt over all the earth we inhabit on summer days, so when you, the sun of righteousness, after your setting, in which you lay hidden in the cave, are now exalted above the heavens, your glory will be felt over all the earth we inhabit, in the Church extended throughout the whole world.

For this is your zodiac, through which you, sun of righteousness, travel, and in which you, Jesus of Nazareth, lengthen the day of victory—victorious for your own and ruinous for your enemies—all the more because you inherited the name Jesus in a meaning so different from that earlier Jesus, or Joshua, to whose command the sun stood over Gibeon and prolonged the day, not allowing it to end before vengeance had been executed upon the enemies harassing Joshua’s allies (Josh. 10:13).

[Col. 1701A] In this victory, it should be noted that the five kings of the hostile army, in fear of Israel as Joshua, or Jesus, their leader fought, entered a cave, hoping by hiding there to prolong their lives. But when they had been discovered and seized there, the mouth of the cave was closed by a great stone until the end of the war; and that end was victory, which is noted in the title of this psalm. For where we have, “Unto the end: destroy not; of David,” and so forth, the Hebrew reads, “For victory: do not destroy David.” The battle having thus been completed to its end, or victory, that leader of Israel, called Jesus merely by designation, brought the enemy kings out of the cave for judgment. He made the leaders of Israel tread upon their necks, and then hanged them upon gibbets, to the glory of his victorious [Col. 1701B] name—a name which he possessed only in shadow, since even then hope was placed in the shadow of your wings.

But you, Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews, alone are worthy of this title’s inscription, by which you are proclaimed Jesus—that is, Savior—not in shadow but in truth; and for all your battles there neither was nor ever shall be any end other than victory. Now be exalted; now, having come forth from the cave, make yourself great through the length of your victorious day. Do so as that Jesus son of Nun did, indeed far more than he, as you inherited this name, Jesus, in a far different sense from his. He commanded the sun, and at his command the sun stood in mid-heaven for the span of one day, aiding God’s fighting people until victory was completed. [Col. 1701C] You, O God, command and order your power to strengthen in us the work which you performed in ancient days, when your hand scattered the nations.

Then Michael the archangel, prince of the heavenly powers, was with that Jesus, as he appeared armed to him in the field of Jericho. Now may he be with us, not as he appeared armed then, when it was the time of war, but as he is seen in the Apocalypse, “having a golden censer in his hand, to whom much incense was given, through which” (Rev. 8:3) peace for persons of good will has been and must be obtained. For what is the golden censer but your body, Jesus of Nazareth, assumed from the holy Virgin and fashioned and formed by the fire of the Holy Spirit? Therefore may this censer, offered by the hands of priests with Michael ministering alongside them, now accomplish peace and victory in Israel and compel the hostile leaders to flee into the cave—those who wish you, the true David, to be held in the cave, lest you appear as king upon the throne of your kingdom.

They then fled into the cave of Makkedah, which is interpreted “burning” or “eastern.” Let God now arise, who as man lay hidden in the cave of the tomb; and when he arises, let his enemies be scattered, and let those who hate him flee before his face. Let them flee into the cave of Makkedah, so that, constrained in the cave of burning by fear of Jesus, they may be burned by the fire which you, Jesus, sent into the earth, willing that it be vehemently kindled. Thus may that same cave of burning become for them also the eastern cave, when, purged of sins, [Col. 1702A] they enjoy eastern light. Or certainly, if they do not wish to be converted, may they not be released from the cave that constrains them under the discipline of justice until they are sent into the eternal fire, there to burn with the devil. He falsely pretends to be eastern, boasting that he is like the Most High; yet, confined in the cave of his damnation and bound with the cords of hell, he is now not even equal to the lowest, because redeemed man lives.

Likewise, may all the principal vices which wage war against us within us flee, before the face of Jesus fighting within us for us, into the cave of Makkedah—which, as stated above, is interpreted “burning” or “eastern”—so that in the prison of repentance they may be burned away by the fire of the Holy Spirit until they reach that purity of rational nature which is called, and is, eastern: like him who is the Dayspring from on high and makes eastern those in whom he reforms his likeness according to the ordinance of the first creation, when God said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26).

All this good is sought when it is said to you, O Jesus: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth.” For this is said to you, David the king, as though hidden in a cave and not apparent through the manifest evidence of your rule, while evil rulers like impious Saul dominate unjustly and confine the good in caves of distress. Yet it is fitting rather that, with you David reigning, this iniquity should pass away; and that, with you, Jesus, governing and fighting, your enemies should flee [Col. 1702C] into the caves of Makkedah, from which they should not be permitted to emerge before they are brought to judgment, to be trodden under the feet of the righteous, who rule them justly and judge them justly—either by the present judgment, for the spreading and glorifying of your glory over all the earth, or likewise by the future judgment, for the manifestation of your glory, with which heaven and earth are full.

Take heed, whoever you are who now lie hidden in a cave or mourn that Christ lies hidden, while the impious tyranny of Saul rages: do not destroy this inscription of the title by which Jesus of Nazareth is proclaimed King of the Jews. For if you despair that he can come forth from such a cave and be exalted upon his throne, and do not confess that he, the King of the Jews, is almighty even when he does not show himself to reign, then you too, so far as lies in you, destroy David [Col. 1702D] and corrupt the inscription of the title that can never be corrupted. Pilate did not wish to corrupt it, but replied to those wishing to corrupt it: “What I have written, I have written.” “Do not,” they said, “write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but that he said, ‘I am King of the Jews’” (John 19:21–22). Doubtless, they wanted this to be written: “Jesus of Nazareth, who said, ‘I am King of the Jews,’” as though he were not himself king but falsely claimed to be king. They wanted thus to interrupt and corrupt this triumphal title, but could not.

But their followers, false Christians, saying in words or deeds, “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19:14), corrupt within themselves the inscription of this title, which remains incorruptible for true Jews, because he reigns over them and exalts them with himself from the cave. For if we have been buried with him, we shall also rise with him; if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him. Nor should we be frightened because the cave of the Lord’s tomb is fortified by a sealed stone and guards: for even a very great stone will easily be rolled away by angelic hands, and the wicked guards will be terrified and become as dead men. Not so, not so, with the wicked: they will lie in the cave of Makkedah under a custody far less fragile, because, at Jesus’ command, great stones have been placed at the mouth of that cave. They cannot be removed except when he again commands, judging those enclosed—either now, by the healing judgment which we love and desire, or later, by the punitive judgment which we praise with fear. In both judgments [Col. 1703B] we desire and proclaim the glory of him to whom we sing: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth.” Let your enemies remain on earth and in the earthly cave; but you be above the heavens, judge of the living and the dead. Be exalted, that you may be known to reign in majesty—not that you, who have always been Most High in your Divinity and are now, after your ascension, Most High also in your humanity, might become higher than yourself, but that the glory which you possess in heaven may be manifested throughout all the earth, so that your glory may be known and visible over all the earth.

Alternatively: O God the Father, be exalted in me, Jesus your Son, through my resurrection and ascension. “Glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you, as you have given him power over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him” (John 17:1–2): not in Judaea alone, but in every tribe throughout all the earth, so that your glory may be manifested over all the earth. It is known to few and unknown to many while I lie hidden in the cave of the tomb, or in the lowliness of human nature under the guard of enemies, who—

**VERSE 7.** Prepared a snare for my feet. My feet were rebukes and promises. For I walked, as it were, on these two feet when I rebuked evil people, for example saying, “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who are like whitewashed tombs,” and so forth (Matt. 23:27), and when I promised rewards to the good, for example: [Col. 1703D] “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke 6:20). Therefore they prepared a snare for these feet when they devised traps from my words, as when they brought to me the adulterous woman, intending to bind me in this dilemma: either that I should be held contrary to the law if I said that she should be dismissed, though the law commanded that she be stoned; or that they should deride as deceitful and inconsistent one who preached gentleness yet allowed her to be killed (John 8:3 ff.). By such a deceitful snare they sought to draw me into either destroying the law, which I had come to fulfill, or losing the reputation for mercy which I had come to teach. With such snares they did not cease to pursue me until they bowed down my soul by inflicting death. Yet they did not take my soul [Col. 1704A] from me; rather, I laid it down and took it again. It was bowed down in their own estimation, for they placed me by their judgment in the lower hell; but by my own power it remained free among the dead, not only upright in its own state but also about to raise other souls truly bowed down.

They prepared a snare, indeed, but in vain. For “the net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures” (Prov. 1:17); how much more vainly were snares laid for me, who saw and knew all things and had the wings of Divinity? They could not be hidden from me. For

They dug a pit before my face: that is, while I was present, they cried out the sentence of death. Yet it did not harm me; rather, those who dug it fell into it themselves, for this reason delivered into the hands of the sword [Col. 1704B] of the Romans, which was death of the body for them. They will be the portions of foxes, counted among demons and assigned with them to the pits of hell; and that is death of the soul for them. Thus, blind in their excavated conscience, they dug the pit of Passion and death. I came to endure it, not unwillingly but freely, because:

**VERSE 8.** My heart, O God, was prepared; my heart was always prepared for the work of such obedience. Of it I said, “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover” (Luke 22:15), doubling and repeating the words to express intimate affection. Likewise here I say, “My heart, O God, is prepared,” and again, “My heart is prepared, O God”; and at the Last Supper, “With desire I have desired this Passover.” Or I say twice, “My heart is prepared,” because in the Passion itself I am prepared and devoted to two things: to praise in words, and to make the same praise resound in deeds. Hence I add: “I will sing and recite a psalm,” that is, I will give thanks in words and works. And because I know that a psalm does not resound on a broken psaltery, I do not wish the psaltery and lyre of my flesh, shattered in the tomb, to remain broken for long, as my enemies desire. They broke this psaltery of my flesh, sonorous with divine praises, and this lyre melodious amid adversities with the strings of patience, because they themselves would not dance to my songs—indeed, they grieved that others danced.

**VERSE 9.** Therefore arise, psaltery and lyre: that is, my flesh, performing divine works and suffering humanly. Like a psaltery sounding from above, it had from above the power by which it performed divine works; and like a lyre sounding from below, it had from human mortality the capacity by which it endured Passion and death. Now behold, it lies in the cave of the tomb, making no sound. But it should not remain so long, because after a time of silence follows a time of speaking, which now, now is at hand: the evening of the Sabbath, dawning toward the first day of the week. Therefore arise, my glory—that is, the flesh through which I, Divinity, have been glorified and shall be glorified still more. Arise, psaltery and lyre: that is, flesh so restored through the glory of immortality that you can no longer be broken, and show to be true what our lyre-players and psalm-singers delight to sing: “Christ, rising from [Col. 1705A] the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9).

I, flesh dead for a time, shall arise at dawn. For before the dawn of the third day, which approaches from midnight, the Resurrection ought not to be hastened so as to falsify the Scriptures of truth, which assign it to the third day, as the prophet says: “After two days he will revive us, and on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. 6:3). And it is said in the Law: “Sanctify yourselves, children of Israel, and be ready until the third day” (Exod. 19:14–15). Therefore I must lie in the tomb until the third day; but as midnight approaches, the third day will dawn. For if the evening of the Sabbath dawns toward the first day of the week, much more will midnight be reckoned as a kind of dawn, when I, the true Samson—whose name is interpreted “their sun” or “strength of the sun”—shall carry away the gates of Gaza, that is, destroy the gates of death, and ascend to the summit of the mountain. From that time, I, flesh crucified and dead, after death has been destroyed, shall live again as a joyful psaltery with a lyre, whose sound will be heard throughout all the earth, because:

**VERSE 10.** I will confess you among the peoples, O Lord, and sing a psalm to you among the nations.

> [Note: [Col. 1705D] Vulgate: “I will recite a psalm to you among the nations.”]

That is, I shall be the efficient cause of your praise and confession among all peoples. Indeed, the sound of those who eat me as living and life-giving flesh, and live through me, will go forth into all the earth; and for this they will praise you, because your mercy has been magnified unto the heavens and [Col. 1705C] your truth unto the clouds, in accordance with what I, David, desired above and still desire, saying: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth.”

Alternatively: While the Lord Jesus was struggling in his passion and praying that the Father might glorify him, the Father’s voice was heard saying: “I have glorified, and I shall glorify again” (John 12:28). Likewise here in the psalm, while Christ is struggling and his friends grieve and lament because, buried in a cave and humbled and oppressed by Saul—that is, by death—he does not utter his voice, the voice of power by which he was accustomed to call and raise the other dead, saying, for example, to one dead man: “Young man, I say to you: Arise” [Col. 1705D] (Luke 7:14), and to another: “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11:43), the Father’s fatherly compassion could no longer restrain itself. The Father himself cries out in the cave, calling forth from it the psaltery and harp—that is, the human nature united to his Word, and through and in that Word sounding forth most powerfully. Say therefore: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 107:3).

For if a wise son is his father’s glory, much more are you my glory, my Son, who are my wisdom, my music, my psaltery and harp. For as wisdom or music is first active in the art itself, then is displayed and heard in a psaltery or another instrument intelligently fashioned and perceptible to the senses, so you were in the beginning the Word, full of all [Col. 1706A] art, wholly intelligible to no one except me, who begot you from my heart, and to that Spirit or love by which I loved you as you loved me in the same Spirit, who is our eternal love. Therefore he, the third, understands whatever we two understand. This understanding existed in secret before the world, not yet created through you, my Word; and, when you my Word were uttered in the creation of the world, you, my art or music, still remained profoundly hidden from many.

But when you, the same begotten one, were in the flesh—though formerly invisible—you became visible and audible through the strings of the flesh you assumed. You became psaltery and harp, though formerly you were invisible music, known to me alone in the art itself. But behold: as if the strings of your flesh had been broken, you lie in the cave; and as if the plectrum [Col. 1706B] of your tongue were impeded, you are silent. Yet you had sounded sweetly and rightly: like a psaltery, by promising heavenly things; like a harp, by pacifying and weakening earthly things. Therefore do not remain silent and lie thus for long. Arise from your cave, you psaltery and harp, so that at the sound of your voice the dead may arise. For the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead throughout all the earth shall hear your voice, while your apostles play the harp and sing psalms in you; and those who hear shall live among the living—namely, those first dead through disobedience, but to be raised through hearing and obeying your voice.

Nor is this remarkable in comparison with still more wonderful things, since after this the hour will come in which all who are in the tombs shall hear your voice and come forth: some unto eternal life, others unto reproach, that they may see forever. [Col. 1706C] Therefore, since all human beings are to be summoned by your voice from the caves of their tombs—human beings, I say, who died in the three periods, before the Law, under the Law, and under grace—it is enough that you remain shut in the cave of the tomb until the third day. Therefore, now that the third day is approaching: Arise, psaltery with harp.

To these admonitions of the Father, I, the Son laid in the cave, reply: “I shall arise at dawn.” I indeed foretold that after three days I would raise the temple of my body once it had been destroyed; and, just as Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so I said that I, the Son of Man, would be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights (Matt. 12:40). But [Col. 1706D] because the evil days must be shortened, while truth is nevertheless preserved, this three-day period must somehow be fulfilled; yet it must be shortened in such a way that the final part of Preparation Day and the first part of the first Sabbath are reckoned as whole days, and that the entire three-day period is understood figuratively as complete from the ninth hour, when I gave up my Spirit on the cross, until the dawn of the third day. This figure is called by grammarians synecdoche [manuscript: *synodoche*], in which a part is taken for the whole.

Therefore, this three-day period having been shortened and yet fulfilled, I shall arise at dawn, so that from this shortening of sorrowful days my servants may have hope that the remaining evil days also will be shortened, concerning which I said: “Unless those days were shortened, no flesh would be [Col. 1707A] saved; but for the sake of the elect they shall be shortened” (Matt. 24:22). Then the Scriptures concerning Antichrist’s three and a half years will be fulfilled, just as those concerning the three days of my burial were fulfilled. For he shall reign for “a time, times, and half a time,” that is, for three and a half years, because this was foreshadowed in Elijah’s time, when it did not rain for three years and six months.

Certainly those evil days seemed long to the afflicted persons touched by that plague of excessive drought. Yet for Elijah and for the widow of Zarephath who fed him, they were shortened through the increase of both flour and oil, so that they did not seem long. Likewise, in the days of Antichrist, when every righteous person alike, made like Elijah in zeal for righteousness, shall suffer persecution, and when, heaven being shut, the voluntary rain of saving doctrine has been withdrawn, all the earth [Col. 1707B] shall waste away: flour shall not fail the righteous, from which bread necessary for the salvation of body and soul may be made; nor oil, by which their faces may be made glad, lest the evil days seem excessively long to them.

For as I now arise at dawn when the three days of my burial have scarcely been fulfilled and have been greatly shortened, so then I shall arise for judgment, shortening the time of the wicked. When they say, “Peace and security,” sudden destruction shall come upon them at that dawn: namely, as the great day of the universal resurrection draws near. That day will be preceded as by dawn by the bright illumination of my coming, through which the power of darkness, strengthened through Antichrist, shall be destroyed. I shall kill him with the spirit of my mouth and destroy him by this very illumination of my coming, so that he may know that he shall not rule forever [Col. 1707C] or oppress me and mine in caves, when the dawn of justice shines forth through me, the Sun of Justice, then rising to judge the living and the dead, the righteous and the unrighteous—just as this visible sun, in its rising, distinguishes healthy from bleary eyes.

For surely then those afflicted with the bleary-eyed vision of impiety shall be tormented by seeing and envying, when the law of justice begins to shine at that dawn which will drive away the darkness of injustice through the preaching of your witnesses, who, like two shining lampstands, shall precede my coming.

Alternatively: I shall arise at dawn in every heart that has died with me through fear arising from sound faith; has been buried with me through rest arising from robust hope; [Col. 1707D] and has risen with me through charity as though on the third day, following the two days, namely, of faith and hope. At the dawn of this third day I shall arise, never again to die. For, since charity never fails, its light also remains forever, while the other days pass away together with faith and hope, which will not exist once the thing believed and hoped for has arrived. For “whether tongues shall cease, knowledge shall be destroyed, or prophecies shall be abolished: but now faith, hope, and charity, these three, remain” (1 Cor. 13:8, 13), like the light of three days.

But the day of charity alone shall not fail, because its sun, Christ, shall not set. After the day of faith, on which he hung upon the cross, showing that the old human being must be mortified by the power of faith; and after the day of hope, on which he rested [Col. 1708A] in the tomb, showing that those rejoicing in the hope of renewal must rest; he rose on the day of charity, and breathed that charity, which is his Spirit, upon his disciples, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). Having received him, they say with joy: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). Therefore, as I, Christ, now rise at the dawn of the third day, so I shall always arise at the dawn of charity, which drives away the darkness of hatreds.

Therefore you who wish that I should not sleep for you, but that, as awakened by your prayers, I should arise to help you, know that if you hate your brother, you are in darkness; and you must go and be reconciled to your brother. Then, coming in the bright dawn of charity and offering [Col. 1708B] your gift at my altar, you shall perceive me awakened for you, because, invoked by your prayers, I shall arise at dawn. Therefore, that the dawn of charity may be bright and have no darkness in it, when you stand to pray, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your heavenly Father also may forgive you your sins.

O how often, laboring through the whole night, have we caught nothing because we cast out the net of prayer or preaching before the light of love! And we have proved by experience that it is vain for us to rise before the light, without which we can take hold of no good thing for salvation. O dawn, splendor of eternal light and Sun of Justice, come and illumine those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death! Grant us first dawn, then noonday brightness; grant us to begin and to complete [Col. 1708C] your new commandment, that we may love one another. Thus, in great joy, we who are the bridegroom’s friends shall hear you, the bridegroom, speaking to your Father: “I shall arise at dawn, I, the psaltery and harp,” and the sweet songs of the drama, resounding concerning me and through me among the peoples, shall be heard.

For “I shall confess you among the peoples, O Lord; I shall sing a psalm to you among the nations”: that is, I shall cause among peoples and nations the confessions of sinners, or praises and psalms of good works, to resound. In those who confess, I shall confess you; and in those who sing psalms, I shall sing a psalm to you, because without me they can do nothing. Rather, I work in them, and you, abiding in me, yourself perform the works. Therefore all glory for such [Col. 1708D] works is due to you through me, so that, seeing such works in themselves or in other human beings, they may glorify you, the Father who is in heaven. For I too refer to your glory what I do.

Thus I say: “I shall confess you,” that is, to your praise, among the peoples, O Lord, whom I cause to confess you; and “I shall sing a psalm to you,” to your honor, among the nations. Among the people of the Jews and among the nations of all peoples I shall perform this good work of psalmody and praise, whose chief subject is this:

**VERSE 11.** For your mercy has been magnified unto the heavens, and your truth unto the clouds. Therefore we nations and peoples, confessing and singing psalms, give thanks to you, God the Father, because your mercy has been magnified unto the heavens, and your truth unto [Col. 1709A] the clouds. Your mercy—that is, the Holy Spirit—although immeasurable and incapable of being magnified in itself, has nevertheless been magnified in its operation unto the making of heavens, because “I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8:4): that is, the apostles, brought by the Holy Spirit to perfection and exalted in every brightness of holiness, and made like heavens—that is, like angels.

Yet your truth—that is, your Son—was first magnified in his work through visible flesh unto the making of clouds: that is, unto the formation of those same apostles. For when Christ taught in the flesh by many parables and miracles, intelligible to few—and when not even the apostles understood what was signified by such things—such hearers were formed into clouds, holding in themselves, by a cloudy [Col. 1709B] knowledge, the mystery of the kingdom of God, while concealing it in parables from others. For example, it was said to them: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest, in parables” (Mark 4:11). Likewise: “Tell no one of the vision until the Son of Man has risen from the dead” (Matt. 17:9). Thus, O God the Father, your truth was magnified unto the making of clouds, which afterward, through your mercy, became heavens.

Therefore we peoples and nations, the lesser ones watered by such clouds and illumined by those same heavens—watered by the historical or parabolic knowledge of divine matters, illumined by their mystical or moral understanding—we peoples, I say, gathered into one faith through such clouds; we nations, knowing you, our maker, through such heavens, shall rightly confess you and sing a psalm to your name: that is, to your Son, who places his ascent in such clouds, thundering through commandments and threats, flashing through miracles, and watering the earth with rain through sweet prayers and promises. [Col. 1710A]

Nor are the apostles alone clouds and heavens of this kind; many of their followers also, worthy after the apostles to be revered under the name of clouds and heavens by imitation of them. Therefore, since you have as many heavens, O God, as elect persons predestined to heavenly glory:

**VERSE 12.** Be exalted above those same heavens, O God, and may your glory be over all the earth. Many of such [Col. 1710B] heavens lie hidden as though in the lower hemisphere, because they are either not yet born or concealed in caves and known to you alone. Therefore be exalted above them by exalting them, so that, when all heavens have been exalted—or rather when you, O God, have been exalted in them—heaven and earth may be filled with your glory, and your glory be over all the earth. Then none of these heavens shall lie hidden in a cave or in an underground hemisphere, but, exalted, they shall glorify you, exalted in them and above them.

Glory to the Father, who says to the Son: “Arise, my glory.” Glory to the Son, who is the Father’s glory and truth magnified unto the clouds. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is mercy magnified unto the heavens. Amen.

## PSALM 57

[Col. 1709]

[Col. 1709C] “If indeed you speak justice, judge uprightly, you children of men,” etc. The title of this psalm is clear, and reads thus:

**(VERSE 1.) UNTO THE END: DO NOT DESTROY, OR DO NOT CORRUPT, DAVID IN THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE** [Note: [Col. 1709] Vulgate: “Do not destroy David in the inscription of the title.”]

That is to say: This psalm, looking unto the end—that is, unto Christ—admonishes you, whoever you are, not to destroy David in the inscription of the title. That is, just as the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write: King of the Jews” (John 19:21), so you too must not, so far as lies in you, take Christ’s kingdom away from him by withdrawing yourself from him. This kingdom was indicated in the inscription of the title.

In this psalm the Prophet first speaks concerning justice by reproaching the Jews for judging wrongly, [Col. 1709D] thereby warning us not to do the like. Second, he relates what recompense awaits them at the words, “God shall break their teeth.” Third, he says that the godly and righteous are corrected by the punishment of the ungodly, at the words, “The righteous shall rejoice when he sees vengeance.” But because in these fifty psalms that combatant is instructed who, placed between hope and fear, wrestles not only against the flesh but also, like another Jacob, with God, you, whoever you are who are such a person, must first be warned by me not to destroy in yourself the title “King of the Jews”—that is, king of those who confess—either by failing to confess that you are a sinner or by failing to judge rightly how you are a sinner.

For if you offer rightly but do not divide rightly—confessing sins indeed, but not attributing them to your own fault—you have sinned. What then is expedient, O children of men? I tell you:

**VERSE 2.** “If indeed you speak justice,” he says, “judge uprightly, you children of men.” Do not say: “We are righteous.”

**VERSE 3.** “For in your heart you work iniquities; on earth your hands devise injustices.” Unless you say: “We are sinners and cannot be justified except through the man Jesus Christ,” you have destroyed [Col. 1710D] this title, and the saying “King of the Jews” does not apply to you. Likewise, if you say: “We are indeed sinners, but fate has done this; the stars have done this,” you do not speak justice at all, nor do you judge uprightly, O children of men.

**VERSE 4.** “Sinners of this kind have been alienated from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehoods”—namely [Col. 1711A] when they accuse God and defend themselves. Therefore God shall break their teeth in their mouths. Accordingly, if you who confess sins truly speak justice, let this transferring or removal of guilt be far from you, by which you impute your sins not to yourselves as your own fault but to others.

And because there has been mention of transfer and removal in relation to an accusation—elements of the rhetorical defence which have great force in human judgment, when a person accused of a sin, through artful speech, transfers or removes from himself the blame or cause of sin onto another—lest they perhaps be thought to have similar force in divine judgment, it seems necessary to explain more fully here how one should speak rightly in every class of legal case, not only in human but also in divine judgment.

[Col. 1711B] For among spiritual as well as secular persons there are three classes of cases, distinguished by their occasions and ends: namely, demonstrative, deliberative, and judicial. The demonstrative concerns the present and tends toward the end of honorableness by avoiding dishonor; above we have already shown some psalms to have been composed in this class. The deliberative concerns the future and tends toward usefulness, avoiding and dissuading from what is useless in the deliberation itself. The psalmists likewise sometimes employ this class, for example, saying: “How long shall I take counsel in my soul?” (Ps. 12:2); and: “What profit is there in my blood when I go down into corruption?” etc. (Ps. 29:10).

The judicial, however, concerns the past and tends toward the end of [Col. 1711C] justice by avoiding and dissuading from what is unjust. We are engaged with it in the present psalm, where we are carefully admonished to speak justice and judge uprightly, when it is said to us: “If indeed you speak justice, judge uprightly, you children of men.”

Since secular rhetoricians use these classes of cases before human judges, our own speakers too, endeavoring to speak not so much rhetorically as catholicly in an ecclesiastical or divine court, where God—or even a human being acting in God’s place—presides, fittingly employ the three aforesaid classes of cases and strive toward definite ends to incline the judge’s and hearers’ goodwill and attention. For they do not briefly discuss the praise or blame of one—or indeed very many—particular persons, which are parts [Col. 1711D] of the demonstrative class; for example, when God is praised or the devil blamed. Nor do they seldom or rarely resound with persuasion or dissuasion, which are parts of the deliberative class, recommending what is good and useful and dissuading from what is evil and useless. They also very frequently undertake accusation and defence, which are parts of the judicial class: accusing the unjust and defending the just—as, for example, in the Apostle, where the injustice of one man, through which many were made sinners, is accused, and the justice of one man, through which many are made righteous, is defended.

No secular writer ever has handled, or could handle, as justly and wisely as these holy Scriptures of which we speak the statuses which are called conjectural, legal, and juridical. [Col. 1712A] For the conjectural status arises when there is a dispute concerning whether something was done, in this manner: Someone entrusts to his neighbor for safekeeping a donkey, an ox, a sheep, or any beast of burden, and it perhaps dies, is injured, or is captured by enemies, but nobody sees this. What then shall happen? “An oath,” he says, “shall be between them, that he has not put his hand upon his neighbor’s property; and the owner shall accept the oath, and he shall not be obliged to make restitution” (Exod. 22:11), and many similar things.

The legal status, however, arises when some controversy originates from a written text or texts and there is doubt about the understanding and will, or intention, of the writer. Thus the Jews thought they were faithfully fulfilling the divine Scripture of the holy Law by offering incense [Col. 1712B] and eating the flesh of sacrifice. But what does the Lord say? “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat flesh. For I did not speak with your fathers, nor did I command them, on the day when I led them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices; but I commanded them this word, saying: Hear my voice, and I shall be your God, and you shall be my people,” etc. (Jer. 7:21–23).

But the Apostle writing to the Hebrews dwells especially upon this status, comparing—or preferring—the will of the writer, indeed of God, with the writing or letter upon which the Jew alone relies, and explaining sufficiently intelligibly and persuasively the will of the aforesaid writer. The juridical status occurs when the deed is agreed upon—that is, it is not denied that it was done—but the question is whether it was done lawfully or unlawfully.

[Col. 1712C] This has two divisions: one is called absolute and the other assumptive. The absolute is altogether condemned in the judgments of the Lord. It is called absolute when the very act which was committed is said to have been done rightly, so that nothing external is adduced. Yet the Lord does not inquire into anything done rightly as though it had been done wrongly. Thus this division is blameworthy before him and does not deserve pardon. It is of this kind: Samuel said, “What is this sound of sheep that resounds in my ears, and of herds that I hear?” And further: “Why then did you not obey the voice of the Lord, but turn upon the spoil and do evil in the eyes of the Lord?” And Saul said: “On the contrary, I obeyed the voice of the Lord, and we went on the way by which the Lord sent me; and I brought Agag, king of Amalek, and I destroyed Amalek,” etc. (1 Sam. 15:14, 19, 20).

The other, assumptive division is partly admitted and partly condemned by God in his judgments. It has four parts: concession, removal of the charge, transfer of the charge, and comparison. Concession of guilt is not merely admitted before him; indeed, almost all of us are guilty before him, and this is the whole way of our peace. The most righteous person is the one who concedes most fully and most earnestly asks that he be forgiven, according to the saying: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17).

There are two parts of this concession: one, petition for mercy; the other, exculpation. [Col. 1713A] Petition for mercy occurs when the accused confesses that he acted deliberately and sinned, yet asks that mercy be shown him; for example, David: “Against you alone,” he says, “have I sinned, and have done evil before you.” Exculpation occurs when the accused denies that he acted deliberately with evil intent, but says that he acted through another circumstance: either through ignorance, through fortune—which we more properly call an event—or through necessity.

Through ignorance, in this manner: God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him: “Behold, you shall die because of the woman whom you have taken, for she has a husband.” But Abimelech had not touched her, and said: “Lord, will you destroy an ignorant and righteous nation?” etc. (Gen. 20:3–4). Through chance or event—what they call fortune—in this manner: “Moses, angry [Col. 1713B] with the sons who remained, said: ‘Why have you not eaten the sin offering in the holy place, since it is most holy?’ Aaron answered: ‘Today the sacrifice for sin and the burnt offering have been offered before the Lord. But what you see has happened to me. How could I eat it or please the Lord in the rites with a grieving mind?’” (Lev. 10:16, 17, 19).

Through necessity, in this manner: Why, Jephthah, have you torn your garments? “Alas, my daughter,” he says, “you have deceived me, and you have been deceived. For I have opened my mouth to the Lord, and I cannot do otherwise” (Judg. 11:35). For he is exculpated and excused through the necessity of a vow, since he opened his mouth, saying: “Whoever first comes out of the doors of my house and meets me as I return in peace from the children of Ammon, I shall offer him as a burnt offering to the Lord” (Judg. 11:31). Through the necessity, I say, of the vow, the man who kills his daughter by offering her is exculpated and excused, and deserves to be numbered in the catalogue of the saints who “through faith conquered kingdoms” (Heb. 11:33).

Likewise David received and ate the consecrated bread given by Abimelech the priest; and because he did this through necessity, he is exculpated and excused when the Lord says: “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and ate the loaves of offering, which it was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but for priests alone?” And immediately afterward: “But if you knew what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would never have condemned [Col. 1713D] the innocent” (Matt. 12:3–4). Therefore concession and the parts of concession—petition for mercy and exculpation—are admitted in God’s judgments.

Comparison of the charge likewise occurs in this way: You, Paul, who said, “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2), why did you circumcise Timothy, and why, having taken certain men, did you purify yourself with them and enter the temple, declaring the completion of the days of purification until an offering should be made for each of them? “In order to avoid,” he says, “the danger of a greater charge”—namely, because they had heard about me that I taught apostasy from Moses, which was false, because I am with Moses in spirit and truth. But because this could not be demonstrated by reason, I demonstrated it, though not without some resemblance to guilt.

[Col. 1714A] Transfer or removal of guilt—the two of the four assumptive parts, which is the second division of the juridical status—must everywhere be avoided by the wise in the judgment of God, because from them arises the origin or growth of sin. For God said to Adam: “Who told you that you were naked, unless you ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?” And he said: “The woman whom you gave to be my companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3:11–12). By saying this, he intended to transfer the charge away from himself. For transfer of guilt occurs when we do not deny having acted, but say that we acted under compulsion from the sins of others.
