Likewise, “the Lord said to the woman: ‘Why have you done this?’ She answered: ‘The serpent deceived me, and I ate’” (ibid., 13). By saying this she plainly intended not to remove the charge from herself, but the blame itself—that is, the cause of the charge. For removal of guilt is said to occur when we remove from ourselves not the charge but its cause, and transfer it either to a person or assign it to some thing. But to what sort of person did the woman transfer the blame for the charge, if indeed it deserves to be called a person? To the serpent, whether spiritual—that is, the devil—or earthly—that is, a snake. To what thing? To the serpent’s deception.

But this transfer does not cleanse; it defiles. It does not acquit; it entangles. For what was the serpent’s promise in deceiving? “You shall not die at all,” he says. “For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes shall be opened and you shall be like gods” (Gen. 3:4–5). Let the woman say that the serpent not only persuaded her, but also gave such an argument why she ought to eat. Does she not increase the charge through such removal of the charge? Rightly, therefore, we may say that transfer or removal of guilt ought by no means to be sought from Holy Scripture or instituted between us and God; comparison should scarcely be admitted; but concession should always be admitted, and especially petition for mercy, which is the single and better one of the two parts of concession.

For, as has already been said, there are two parts of concession, one petition for mercy and the other exculpation. Very rarely, or never, in psalms understood in the evangelical sense is exculpation or excuse for sin found. For neither ignorance can excuse anyone after the teaching of Law and Gospel has been made manifest; [Col. 1714D] nor does chance or event excuse one who sins in Christ’s kingdom—marked in the title of the psalm—which stands in ordered stability rather than drifting by chance. By sinning, such a person disturbs, so far as lies in him, the order of this most orderly kingdom, corrupting the title’s inscription concerning Christ’s kingdom.

Likewise, necessity excuses no sinner after mercy and truth, which free persons from necessities, have been given—mercy and truth of which the preceding psalm says: “God sent his mercy and his truth, and delivered my soul from the midst of lion cubs” (Ps. 56:4–5). Since this is so, whether sin occurs through necessity, chance, or ignorance, the necessity, chance, or ignorance itself should be lamented before God rather than offered as an excuse; [Col. 1715A] and what must be lamented is of no value for framing excuses in sins. Yet it has value, if not for excuse or exculpation, at least for some lessening of guilt or reduction of punishment.

For divine and human law do not punish equally homicide committed voluntarily and homicide committed by accident. For example, the Law commands that homicide be avoided altogether, where it says: “You shall not kill” (Num. 35:28). Yet if homicide occurs by accident, the killer is saved in a city of refuge, though not without a slight penalty, because the killer is commanded to live in exile there until the death of the high priest. But one who commits homicide through hatred or deliberate intent is commanded to be torn away even from the altar and killed.

The apostle Paul likewise says that he received mercy—not that he was exculpated or excused through ignorance—because he did ignorantly what the Law, which he had not yet understood, forbade: when he persecuted the Church of God, having zeal for God but not according to knowledge (1 Tim. 1:13). [Col. 1715B] Similarly necessity reduces guilt and the punishment due to guilt, but does not wholly excuse, as is apparent in the examples set forth above. For when the Lord excused King David for eating unlawfully the loaves of offering, and, by his example, excused the disciples who, compelled by hunger, plucked ears of grain on the Sabbath contrary to the prohibition of the Law, he subsequently added at the end, speaking to the Pharisees: “But if you knew what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would never have condemned the innocent” [Col. 1715C] (Matt. 12:7).

By saying this he plainly indicates that some small misery of guilt had preceded, for which the mercy of pardon was necessary. And this mercy, where there is any prior guilt whatever, must be humbly sought by petition for mercy, not demanded as though due by right on the ground of excuse.

Therefore, when God the just judge accuses us, the only necessary element of concession is petition for mercy. By it, conceding and confessing that we are entirely culpable and not excusable through ignorance, event, or necessity, we bend the judge and endeavor to move him to mercy, each of us saying: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Ps. 50:1); likewise: “Have mercy [Col. 1715D] on me, O God, for man has trampled me down” (Ps. 55:2); likewise: “Have mercy on me, because my soul trusts in you” (Ps. 56:2).

Almost all the psalms echo this: by petitioning and devoting themselves to his vengeance while asking for mercy, they urge the judge, ready to take vengeance, to mercy. Yet this mercy of God shall be obtained only by those who truly confess and do not corrupt the title “King of the Jews.” For the others, that vengeance is prepared which is expressed in the psalm in these words: “God shall break their teeth in their mouths; the Lord shall break the molars of lions”—especially if, following Saul’s example, they excuse their sin in such a way as to contend that they acted justly in matters in which those enchanters accuse them. These are the enchanters who, hating vices and loving human beings, wisely and effectively cast their spell where they find hearers teachable, well-disposed, and attentive, who do not stop up their ears like the asp. Against such persons it is said: “He who stops his ears lest he hear the law, his prayer shall be abominable” (Prov. 28:9). [Col. 1716A]

Therefore, if you Jews, who are children of men—that is, of the patriarchs and prophets—wish to be good advocates in the chapel or courtroom of the most righteous Judge, and if indeed you speak justice, judge uprightly. Do not excuse yourselves before the Judge who rebukes your iniquities, whether through ignorance or necessity. For you cannot be excused through ignorance, since you are evil tenants who, recognizing the heir, killed him for this very reason: that you might possess his vineyard. Nor can you be excused through necessity, as though you killed him under the compulsion of necessity because, if he lived, you feared that you would lose your place and nation.

For whenever a necessity of this kind constrains a person so that one of two evils must necessarily be admitted, the lighter, not the graver, must be chosen. This you did not do: in order to preserve your place, you committed a crime surpassing every other crime, and did so in vain. For after you killed the Lord of the place, you lost both place and nation. At least now repent, and do not excuse yourselves through transfer or removal of the charge, saying what you said before Pilate as you cried: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone” (John 18:13); and: “We have a law, and according to our law he must die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:7). [Col. 1716C]

In saying such things, you speak justice indeed, as you suppose—or make others suppose. Yet, because you cruelly pursue the charge of homicide, you transfer it to Pilate or remove it from yourselves onto God’s Law in vain. For “God is not mocked” (Gal. 6:7), nor will he be deceived by your frauds. He knows both the deceiver and the person deceived: namely, that assembly of Pharisees and scribes which deceives the people, and the people itself which has been deceived.

For, contrary to your assertion, he did not sin against God’s law who, being the Son of God, called himself the Son of God—just as you sin by calling yourselves sons of Abraham while not doing Abraham’s works. If he does not do the works of his Father, God Almighty, do not believe him when he says that he is God or the Son of God. But if whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does, [Col. 1716D] then believe—if not his words, at least the works that plainly testify—that this man is God: he not only speaks God’s words but also performs God’s works. “He who is from God speaks the words of God” (John III, 34): that is, such words as no one can truly utter except God—for example, “Before Abraham was, I am” (John VIII, 58); likewise, “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII, 25); likewise, “All that the Father has is mine” (John XVI, 15). In these and other such words of God—words appropriate to God alone—you have the truth as witness, to whom alone you could believe.

But because it is written in your law that “every word shall stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Matt. XVIII, 16), the testimony of works agrees with the testimony of words [Col. 1717A]: by his own power, as God, he makes the dead live, the deaf hear, the mute speak, and performs other wonders which no human beings or angels can imitate. For when wondrous works are performed through angels or human beings, they do not perform them by their own innate power, but by power from above—either freely granted or obtained through prayer. But he commanded the winds and the sea, made the dead live, the deaf hear, and the mute speak, by his own power, in such a way that he required no external aid which he would need to invoke in prayer.

For although he is read to have prayed before raising Lazarus, this was not from any necessity of his own, but for our instruction. Accordingly, in that very place he declares that he is always openly heard; but he prayed before that marvelous work because of the people standing around [Col. 1717B], so that you may know that his praying to the Father, thereby offering others an example, was necessary for the people, not for himself. For even in his humanity he required no external help, since all knowledge and all power were granted to him at once and together in the humanity he assumed—knowledge and power which belong to the divinity assuming it—so that the two natures have one wisdom and one power.

Therefore, if you truly speak justice when you say, “We are sons of Abraham,” judge rightly also concerning him whose day Abraham longed joyfully to see, and saw and rejoiced. Yet you seek to kill him as he rebukes your sins. Abraham did not do this. You seek, I say, to kill the man who spoke the truth to you, testifying both to his divinity [Col. 1717C] and to our iniquity—or rather, disproving your many iniquities and injustices by his single justice.

For you work iniquities in your heart upon the earth; your hands fashion injustices, while you accomplish by action what you intend by sinful thought in your hearts. And you do all this upon the earth: speaking deceit in the earth’s anger and saying, “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come and take away both our place and nation” (John XI, 48). Thus you sin upon the earth, while you allege fear—as though it were solid ground—that you will lose your place and nation if you spare the man who shows himself, by words and works, to be God, Christ, and King of the Jews.

Otherwise: you work iniquities upon the earth, because “the earth [Col. 1717D] is given into the hand of the wicked” (John IX, 24), when through you Christ’s flesh was given into Pilate’s hands. Yet you could not touch his impassible divinity, because you lacked the faith by which the faithful woman touched him, of whom he himself says, “Someone touched me; for I perceived power going forth from me” (Luke VIII, 46).

Otherwise: you work iniquities upon the earth, not only you Jews, but also you prelates of the Churches, who turn the earthly resources entrusted to you in tithes and offerings from works of justice and mercy into works of injustice and impiety. For you Jews also worked iniquity upon the earth when, from the substance of the Temple, you bought Christ from the traitor for death, or bought from the soldiers a lie denying the resurrection, wickedly misusing the earthly substance entrusted to you. [Col. 1718A] And you evil men likewise, from the Church’s wealth entrusted to you for works of mercy, perform works of impiety—raging cruelly against the poor and luxuriating in beds and indecencies.

Do you not know, wretches, that the land you possess is the land of the saints, given either for the use of those who serve God in holiness or for the need of the poor? Yet you luxuriate and tyrannize from it; or at least, you furnish more from it to the luxurious and tyrannical, to assist their impiety, than to the good and holy, to relieve their poverty. Perhaps you say that you are “redeeming the time,” since the days are evil, and that therefore the wicked must sometimes be appeased with gifts, as Jacob appeased his offended brother Esau with gifts. But Jacob appeased the man whom he feared was angry, lest he come and strike mother together with children—he appeased him for himself, his two wives and their children, and also their maidservants and their children. [Col. 1718B] You, however, act very differently.

For you work iniquities in your heart upon the earth, with every effort of your wicked heart, killing your wives Rachel and Leah with their children through evil examples: that is, destroying the contemplative and active lives together with their fruits. You are more wicked than earthly, hairy Esau, who spared such persons once he learned of the gifts prepared for him, which he scarcely accepted even at his brother’s urging. Therefore, if you sometimes procure peace from evil persons by gifts and services, after Jacob’s example—loving the good, contemplative and active persons as Rachel’s and Leah’s children, and enduring, as far as you can, the enemies of both lives—you may in some measure be excused, since you work no iniquities in your heart upon the land of the saints: that is, approve in your hearts nothing that you know to be unjust, although you patiently endure such things until a suitable time.

But if you so work iniquities in your heart upon the earth that, approving in your heart what is unjust, you carry those things out through the abundance of earthly resources, fashioning them by your hands—that is, fitting together the injustices conceived in your heart—so that cords of sins are braided, as it were, from many ropes made up alike of wicked thoughts and deeds, then rightly you are to be driven even here from the Temple by a whip made from such cords, and in the future to be bound with such cords and cast into the fire: first you Jews, then you perverse followers of the Jews, on account of the land of the saints [Col. 1718C] upon which you fashioned injustices [Col. 1718D], sinning alike in desire and deed.

For even the desire to sin, at times without an outward act, is reckoned as sin, Truth saying: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28). Likewise John: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III, 15). How much more detestable is open iniquity, not merely cherished in the heart, but also perpetrated in the land of the saints? Of such a sinner it is said in Isaiah: “In the land of the saints he has acted wickedly, and he shall not see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI, 10). For the wicked shall be removed lest he see the glory of God—the one who sinned in the land of the saints, as has already been said. Or he worked iniquities upon the earth in such a way as to hide his Lord’s money in the earth and not distribute it as he ought.

[Col. 1719A] Therefore, lest you fall into such evils, “love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wis. I, 1). Justice is this: do not do to another what you do not wish done to yourself. Truth wrote this in the heart; and when people did not read it there, that same Truth repeated it on tablets, so that transgressors, confronted with it externally, might return to the heart. Everyone readily speaks this justice. Thus, if someone is asked which is better, gold or faith, he speaks justly in preferring faith to gold; yet he may perhaps intend to deny a loan once the witness is gone, and, when greed excludes truth, choose gold instead. Thus he has not truly spoken justice: he says one thing with his mouth and chooses another in his heart.

Likewise, the Jews spoke justice falsely when they said, “We know that you are truthful” (Matt. XXII, 16), as is clear from the judgment in which they said, [Col. 1719B] “Crucify, crucify” (John XIX, 6). Yet Christ is no less King, as the title of the cross declares. I exhort them to speak and pursue justice both in heart and in deed, but they do neither, being iniquitous alike in heart and deed. Thus, while they speak justice in words, they deny it by their deeds through judging wrongly: first the Jews, and then all false, fleshly Christians who separate themselves from the womb of Mother Church. Nor is this surprising, because:

> Sinners have been estranged from the womb;  
> they have gone astray from the belly;  
> they have spoken falsehood.

For just as Esau, while still remaining in the womb, was rejected, God saying, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I, 2–3), so these men also, still hidden from human beings but manifest to God, are by his secret judgment reckoned alien from the womb—that is, from their origin—because they are children not of that blessing spoken to the first parents, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. I, 18), [Col. 1719C] but of that curse spoken to Eve after sin: “I will multiply your afflictions and your conceptions” (Gen. III, 16). That is: you will be mother not only of blessed children, but with your conceptions multiplied beyond their number, you will bear cursed sons and daughters. Like thorns and thistles sprouting from the earth—that is, from your flesh—they will weigh down the blessed fruit of legitimate and elect children, which is to arise from this same earth.

Thus, estranged from the womb through God’s hidden judgment, they went astray from the belly: that is, having been born from the womb into this world, [Col. 1719D] once their iniquity was revealed they refused to walk in the way of truth, rejecting him who says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6).

Even in recognizing him, some of them—namely Jews and heretics—went astray from the womb, not believing that he is the true God, Son of God the Father, because they knew that he was born from the womanly womb of his mother. Hence they say, “We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy; because you, being a man, make yourself God” (John X, 33). Thus heretics too went astray from the womb by denying that the man whom the woman Mary bore was God, not considering that this same woman, remaining a virgin, conceived in her undefiled womb not from a man but from the Holy Spirit. Since he is divine, not human love, it is rightly said that what was born [Col. 1720A] from her, being holy, shall be called the Son of God.

Nor is this surprising. For if everything that Sarah conceived through Abraham’s love is called Abraham’s son, how should not everything that the Virgin conceived through his love—that is, the Holy Spirit—truly be called the Son of God the Father? For, through the Holy Spirit’s marvelous working, the Word of God was so joined to virginal flesh that the virgin birth itself is rightly believed and called Son as properly of God the Father as of his virgin mother: not by adoption but by birth. For in being born he received both human and divine nature, so as to be Son of the Most High, because the power of the Most High overshadowed his conceiving mother, so that without the carnal heat of lust she might conceive God made man and become the mother of the Son of God.

[Col. 1720B] In vain, therefore, did those go astray from the womb to whom, because of his lodging in the virginal womb, this man did not seem to be God, the Son of God. For he who prepared a virgin’s womb for his body proves himself true God in that same body, since not only his divinity but also his flesh is truly food. Otherwise his flesh would profit nothing for the salvation of souls if, like his very divinity, it did not possess the power to give life; nor would it do in the whole body of the whole Church what each human being’s spirit does in its own body, namely, give life, if it did not, like that divinity itself, possess life abiding in itself. “For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John V, 26).

And as the Son has life in himself, so [Col. 1720C] he gave his flesh to have life in itself. I say “in itself,” not “from itself,” because neither does the Son himself have life from himself, since he has it in himself; nor does he have life any the less because he does not have it from himself. So too his flesh has life none the less because it does not have it from itself, since it has life in itself in such a way that it not only lives eternally and immortally but also grants those who worthily partake of it to live in it, immortally and eternally.

Hence we confess, in the Catholic faith, that we believe in eternal life, we who communicate in his body and blood. For the power of that life-giving sacrament is so great that flesh made divine gives life and makes divine the human beings who worthily partake of it, just as the Word gives life and makes divine the angelic powers [Col. 1720D] that partake of him. In order that man might eat the bread of angels, the Creator of angels became man: “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. And we saw his glory,” John says, “glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I, 14).

“We saw,” they say, “his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten,” because although in Christ human substance is naturally distinct from divine, nevertheless there is one indivisible glory of both natures: one glory, I say, as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, with whom he possesses unity of undifferentiated glory, not only in his ever-glorious divinity but also in his humanity glorified by divinity.

Therefore they were blind who went astray from the womb—Nestorius, namely, and similar heretics—thinking that not God but only a man was born [Col. 1721A] from the virginal womb, without considering that the man divinely conceived and born is God. Nor was it enough for them to go astray in a pathless place and not in the Way; they also spoke falsehood in order to lead others into error. For those estranged from the womb of Mother Church and at the same time wandering from her womb must speak falsehood, since they do not allow Christ, the Truth, to be formed in them and themselves to be made perfect.

They would, however, become perfect if they did not tear open the womb of Mother Church and if, nourished in her bosom with milk, they grew up to receive solid bread. But they will not at all consent to this, because they refuse to hear either maternal caresses or [Col. 1721B] paternal warnings. Thus they are altogether inexcusable. For they do not come to the light of truth because they are unwilling, not because they are unable. Therefore I say:

**VERSE 5.** Their fury is according to the likeness of a serpent: like that of a deaf asp, stopping [Note: [Col. 1721D] Thus consistently in the manuscript.] its ears.

**VERSE 6.** Which will not hear the voice of charmers, nor the spell of the enchanter who charms wisely.

For just as the serpent—that is, the devil—rages by his own will, not through another’s necessity, ever since he deceived humankind in the serpent, so people who imitate him go mad by their own will, not by fatal necessity, and refuse to be recalled from their madness. Likewise, the asp is not naturally deaf, so that it cannot hear; rather, lest it hear the charmer’s voice, it deliberately and purposefully stops its ears. So the brood of vipers, the children of perdition, [Col. 1721C] though they could hear the truth obediently if they wished—for, like other people, they have free will—labor diligently not to hear God’s word obediently.

How? Just as the asp stops its ears with its tail and the earth, lest it hear the charmer’s voice, however skillfully he may charm according to his art, so these do because they refuse to come forth from the caverns of their malice into the light and to lose their poison.

One should know that when a comparison is drawn from something, the thing itself is not thereby praised. The Lord did not praise the unjust judge who refused to hear the widow, nor the lazy man who, overcome by annoyance, gave three loaves to the petitioner; yet he used both as comparisons. So here too the comparison is drawn from the Marsi, who charm an asp in order to draw it from its cavern into the light. But it, unwilling to emerge, presses one ear to the ground and stops the other with its tail; thus avoiding those sounds, it does not come out into the light to the charmer. [Col. 1721D]

Those, then, are said to be like it who either glory in their former life or delight in present things. For if they do not forget the things behind—that is, the past—they stop their ear with the tail. But if they look at the things seen—that is, present things—they press their ear to the earth. Thus they not only do not perform, but do not even hear, the words of preachers by which they might be led from darkness into light.

[Col. 1722A] Another text reads: “Which will not hear the voice of charmers and the medicine prepared by a wise man.” The sense is unchanged, but it indicates what kind of voice of charmers this is. The precepts of the Law and Prophets were indeed a compounded medicine, but a medicine which no one could bear or be healed by. Now, however, it has been medicated by the Lord’s coming, he who fulfilled the Law and the Prophets. Stephen, medicated by this medicine, charmed; against him the Jews shut their ears and stoned their charmer. We suffer such persons now as well; nevertheless, truth is preached in the Church, and the city set upon a mountain and the lamp upon a lampstand have been displayed. For where is Christ’s Church hidden, or Christ’s truth?

The Hebrew reads: “Their fury is like the likeness [Col. 1722B] of a serpent; like that of a deaf basilisk, stopping its ears, so that it may not hear the voice of murmurers, nor the cunning enchantments of an enchanter.” The sense is the same, except that “cunningness” is more literally named than “wisdom” in the enchanter’s art, since it is an evil art, though the comparison is fittingly adapted to good. It is indeed true that such people, like the asp or basilisk, do not receive cunning or wise enchantments. This appears in those who, when Stephen the first martyr charmed them wisely and they could not resist the wisdom and Spirit that spoke, “stopped their ears” (Acts VII, 56), lest they hear the cunning enchantments.

Yet among such people there are some like Saul, concerning whom:

[Col. 1722C] **VERSE 7.** God will break their teeth in their mouth.

Even if, like lions, they thirst greedily for blood, like the man who, still breathing threats and slaughter against the Lord’s disciples, was going to Damascus—which is interpreted “drinking blood”—nevertheless the Lord will break the jaws of lions such as these, making Pauls from Sauls, lambs from wolves, and humble persons from proud ones. This is prophesied in our translation; but in the Hebrew it is requested, where it reads: “God, knock their teeth out of their own mouth; break the jaws of the lions, O Lord.”

Would that you, our God, might knock out in us and in all our friends and enemies alike the teeth of detraction; and, having broken the jaws of voracity, might grant us teeth of the kind you praise in the Song of Songs [Col. 1722D] when you say to your bride: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing; all are bearing twins, and none among them is barren” (Song IV, 2).

By these words there is praised in the bride—apart from the mystery of a higher understanding—moderation in eating and speaking, most dear to the little flock, or to shorn flocks: that is, to lovers and followers of apostolic perfection. By living in unanimity and thinking humbly, they are worthy of the name “flock”; and, having laid aside the fleeces of their possessions, they are likened to shorn sheep coming up from the washing and bearing twins. For, purified by baptism or tears and made fruitful by the fruit of twofold charity, [Col. 1723A] they lack defilement and avoid barrenness.

Alas, how many there are who refuse to have such teeth; and, worse still, who, as far as they can, break teeth of this kind, as the stoners of blessed Stephen did. But after some have been separated from their number, and others who sin through ignorance, like Saul, have been beneficially crushed, God will break their teeth in their own mouth. For Truth will render void words of biting uttered deceitfully and compared to teeth, not in just any manner, but in their own mouth: that is, catching them by their own words.

For example, the Jews wished, like asps, to bite Christ, the supremely good charmer, by saying deceitfully: “Master, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?” (Matt. XXII, 16–17). Behold teeth—not indeed protruding from their mouths through open wickedness like boars’ tusks, but secretly sharpening one another within their mouths for biting amid a simulated kiss. [Col. 1723B] What did Truth do in response? Surely he broke their teeth in their own mouth, when he compelled them to pronounce judgment against themselves. For when he asked whose image and inscription were on the coin, they answered, “Caesar’s.” Thus, after breaking the teeth of calumny, he added: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (ibid.).

Thus God will indeed break their teeth in their own mouth: namely, the deceitful deceits and injuries which they devise like asps abounding in poison, though they lack strength proportionate to that poison. But when great strength accompanies great virulence, they no longer send out a hiss like asps and serpents, but enlarge their roar like lions—for example, saying, “He is guilty of death”; likewise, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend; for everyone who makes himself king opposes Caesar” (John XIX, 12). By speaking in this manner and so favoring Caesar before his deputy Pilate, they exercised rotten teeth with leonine fury. [Col. 1723C]

But the Lord broke the jaws of the lions when he rose from the dead—the one whom they had cried to be guilty of death. As then, so now he breaks, and always, even to the end or victory denoted in the title, he will crush the teeth of asps and break the jaws of lions, while he himself crushes [Col. 1723D] or despises them.

**VERSE 8.** They shall come to nothing like water running away: either, crushed and broken for their salvation, they shall have a contrite heart, as Saul was crushed by divine terror. By that same terror the persecutor Saul was brought to nothing, and Paul began to live. Or else, crushed and broken in punishment, they shall come to nothing—not so as to exist nowhere, but so as to harm nowhere or be able to harm in the kingdom of the King of the Jews, whose title they do not receive in themselves; or, if they receive it, they do not retain its inscription, just as water retains no inscription because of its softness. Therefore they shall come to nothing like water running away.

They are fittingly compared to waters resounding against the rocks of pride and, like a torrent rushing down from a high mountain and drawing everything movable into itself, themselves rushing headlong from the height of exaltation into the depth of perdition and dragging with them all whom they can. [Col. 1724A] But they are to be despised, and sometimes avoided, until they pass away, because they do not last long. Rather, like torrents swollen with snow and winter waters, they will quickly fail when summer approaches and come to nothing. For winter will swiftly pass and depart; flowers will appear, and flowering vines will give their fragrance. Oh, how evil are those shown to be who are compared with so many evils—with serpent, asp, leonine ferocity, and a torrent coming to nothing! And, conversely, oh, how good are those marked out who are purified through such and so many serpents, asps, lions, and torrents!

[Col. 1724B] For the sake of purifying and exercising these people too, the Lord endures them for a while. He does not quickly destroy them; rather, awaiting their conversion and intending, through them, the purification of others, he bends his bow with some delay—that is, he threatens and terrifies them—until they become weak. Thus the madman, mighty in his madness, became weak and at last, as health approached, said, “Lord, what do you wish me to do?” (Acts IX, 6). Behold, as though his own strength had been lost—indeed, truly lost—the sick man cries to the physician, wishing to be taught what he should do and what he should avoid.

Thus he gladly gloried [Col. 1724C] in his weaknesses, in whom power was made perfect in weakness. Had the Lord struck him while he raged in Stephen’s stoning and the slaughter of the other disciples, he would not have made Paul from Saul. In order to make him so, he did not strike him quickly, but bent his bow with delay until he became weak and power was perfected in that very weakness. He does the same in others like Paul, who sin through ignorance yet do not excuse their sins by ignorance, but, together with Paul, accuse themselves vehemently and praise the grace of God by which they are justified.

But those who are strong in evil and refuse to become beneficially weak shall at last, before this King of the Jews whose title they deny,

**VERSE 9.** Be taken away like melting wax, when he [Col. 1724D] judges the world through fire.

For by a just judgment fire has fallen upon them, and they have not seen the sun. That is, without doubt, what I announce as though already past will occur in the future: punitive fire will fall upon those upon whom, in the present life, the fire of lust, pride, anger, envy, and other vices has fallen. Blinded amid these by voluntary blindness and unwilling to understand so as to act rightly, loving darkness more than light, they did not see the sun: namely, the Sun of righteousness, concerning whom they will say amid punishments, “We have strayed from the way of truth, and the sun of righteousness has not shone upon us” (Wis. V, 6).

On this passage blessed Gregory says in Job [Note: [Col. 1723D] St Gregory the Great, *Morals*, Book IX, ch. 65.]:

> “Fire falls upon the wicked, but when the fire falls the sun is not seen, because the flame of Gehenna which devours them blinds them to the vision of the true light [Col. 1725A]; thus the outward pain of burning torments them, while inwardly the punishment of blindness darkens them, so that those who sinned against their Creator in body and heart may be punished alike in body and heart, and may suffer punishments in both, since while they lived here they served their depraved pleasures with both.”

Perhaps you think yourselves asps and lions because, before the fire of that final judgment comes upon you, you meanwhile remain secure and, as it were, at peace. You are indeed permitted to say, “Peace and security,” though peace and security are not truly yours, because:

**VERSE 10.** Before your thorns understand the bramble, [Col. 1725B] you who refused to have the fig tree, or vine, or olive reign over you, but chose the bramble, shall feel the fire coming forth from the bramble and devouring you.

For you are the forest trees which, according to the parable spoken in the Book of Judges and already expounded by us above, chose the bramble as king over yourselves—that is, Antichrist—to rule over you, having rejected the kingdom of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which is figuratively signified by the fruits of the fig tree, vine, and olive. You wish indeed to rest under that bramble’s shade, while your thorns—that is, the prickings of your desires—do not understand how great are the thorns of punishments hidden in the bramble while the bramble is still a plant in the softness of its greenness.

But hereafter those exceedingly harsh thorns will burst forth [Col. 1725C] in the final vengeance, when final tribulation gives understanding to your hearing, so that your thorns—that is, by their exceedingly bitter fruit, they make you understand—what kind of king you have chosen in the bramble, that is, in Antichrist. You have rejected the kingdom—or rather, have been rejected from the kingdom of God—in which gods and human beings, that is, contemplative and active persons, enjoy the sweetness of the fig tree’s, vine’s, and olive’s fruits. It is not now necessary to discuss those fruits individually, because this parable was sufficiently expounded above in Psalm thirty-two. It runs as follows:

> “The trees went to anoint a king over themselves, and they said to the olive tree: Rule over us. And it answered them: Can I forsake my fatness, which gods and human beings enjoy, and come [Col. 1725D] to be moved among the trees [Note: [Col. 1725D] Vulgate: *promovear*, ‘be advanced’]? The trees said to the fig tree: Come and take the kingdom over us. And it answered them: Can I forsake my sweetness and my very pleasant fruits, and go to be moved among the other trees [Note: [Col. 1725D] Vulgate: *promovear*, ‘be advanced’]? The trees also spoke to the vine: Come and rule over us. And it answered: Can I forsake my wine, which makes God and human beings glad, and be moved among the other trees [Note: [Col. 1725D] Vulgate: *promovear*, ‘be advanced’]? Then all the trees said to the bramble: Come and rule over us. And it answered: If you truly appoint me king over you, come and rest under my shade. But if you will not, let fire come forth from the bramble and [Col. 1726A] devour the cedars of Lebanon” (Judg. IX, 8–15).

This parable, as stated, is expounded in the previously mentioned psalm.

Yet something seems to be added here concerning the bramble: although it first appears like a soft plant, afterward it is seen to be a little tree full of very sharp thorns. Therefore those appear to rest under its shade who choose in this life to live softly, serving their own pleasure under the shade and name of some prelate, whose only fruits are thorns, to be understood at last after the soft plants of pleasures and to give understanding through the bitter pricks of torments.

But you who gladly rest under such men surely make their thorns your own, while you consent to their sins either by loving them or by failing, as you ought not, to condemn them. Thus you rest in their shade and bring forth thorns together with them. Although you do not feel them now, at last you will feel them, bitterly piercing you and increasing for you the punitive fire.

But even now you call it “peace and security,” because you are protected neither beneath the fig tree of legal teaching, nor the olive tree of prophetic teaching, nor the vine of evangelical teaching. Like living persons, as [the Vulgate reads] in anger, that just Judge swallows you up—the one who will cause fire to come out from the bramble you chose as your protector, to envelop and swallow you. [Col. 1726B]

For your conduct, neither ordered by the Law, honors God the Father; nor, formed by the Prophets, glorifies the Holy Spirit speaking in them [Col. 1726C]; nor, instructed by the Gospel, honors the Son of God. For the Father planted the fig tree of the Law, from which he expected fruit to be borne by you Jews, but found none. Or rather, you yourselves were planted by him in the field of the Law: that barren fig tree having only leaves and no fruit. Therefore you were so cursed by the Son that you wither from the roots, and no longer may any fruit be expected from you like that which was in the roots of your nation, that is, its first and chief fathers, whom God the Father planted, as it is said elsewhere: “You cast out the nations and planted them” (Ps. LXXIX, 9).

Moreover, the Holy Spirit anointed the Prophets with the oil of gladness and enlightened them; by killing and persecuting them, you always resisted the Holy Spirit, as Stephen the first martyr reproaches you. The Son of God himself, the true vine, announced the Gospel to you by his own mouth and found such fruit among you that, rejecting him, you chose Caesar, saying, “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX, 15). [Col. 1726D] You wished to rest and indulge yourselves under Caesar’s protection as under the bramble’s shade. But the fire of God’s wrath going forth from such a bramble swallowed you up in such a way that it both burned your city and killed you yourselves, according to the saying: “A fire is kindled in my wrath, and shall burn unto the lowest parts of hell; it shall devour the earth with its increase, and shall burn the foundations of the mountains” (Deut. XXXII, 22).

You chose Caesar; through Caesar you were devastated and scattered, even [Col. 1727A] before your thorns understood the bramble: that is, before final tribulation gave understanding to your hearing. Similarly, you false Christians who oppose Christ and favor Antichrist, in whom the mystery of iniquity is already working: before your thorns understand—that is, before the punishments stored up for you make you understand—that Antichrist himself is not a vine but a bramble, before this, I say, fire of heavenly wrath coming forth from the bramble swallows you up, like living persons, in anger.

I rightly call you not living but “like living persons,” because you do not truly live, though you seem to yourselves to live, while you are dead in living. For if “the widow living in pleasures is dead” (I Tim. V, 6), then surely you too, living in pleasures, are dead. Likewise I rightly say of the just Judge that he swallows you up not “in anger,” but “as in [Col. 1727B] anger,” because he judges calmly, without anger. Yet his just retribution appears to be anger, though it ought not to be called anger, either because of the untroubled serenity of divine sweetness or in view of the greater wrath which will appear on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s just judgment. Then too your thorns will understand the bramble: that is, your punishments will make you understand Antichrist.

In the Hebrew it is read thus: “Before your thorns grow into a bramble, as though living, as though in the storm’s wrath, it shall snatch them away.” This means: Before your sins, through the growth of their own wickedness, reveal within you your head, Antichrist, it shall snatch you away as though living, as though in the storm’s wrath. I ought to speak thus directly to you yourselves [Col. 1727C], if I found among you ears open wide. But because your fury is like that of the serpent, and like that of the deaf asp which hardens its ears, there is a change of persons in the middle of the discourse. For when I say to you, “Before your thorns understood the bramble,” suddenly, turning away from you as from deaf persons neither willing nor able to hear, I speak about you to discerning hearers, saying: “As though living, as though in wrath, he swallows them up.” It is as though I said: You who have ears to hear, do not imitate these asps. Their long prosperity will not endure, because divine vengeance swallows them up as though living, as though in wrath; and before the final judgment, that is, before their thorns understand the bramble, divine correction will be so manifest even upon them in this life [Col. 1727D] that the correction of some will result from it. For—

**VERSE 11.** “The righteous man shall rejoice when he sees vengeance; he shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner.” On this passage blessed Gregory says in Job:

> [Note: [Col. 1727D] *Morals*, Book XVIII, chapter 24.] “Many people, when they behold another’s sin, return to their own heart, so as to reflect upon their own. Thus one person is led to torments, while another is thereby delivered from torment. For he sees in another’s punishment what he should fear; and, while he observes the offender thus struck, he binds up his own lax conduct with the strength of justice. Thus it comes about that, because a wicked man while living had drawn many into sin by the pleasure of sin, when dying he recalls some from sin by the terror of punishment; and the righteous man shall wash his hands in [Col. 1728A] the sinner’s blood. The hands of the righteous are washed in the blood of dying sinners, because, when their punishment is seen, the life of the beholder is cleansed.”

Alternatively: The bramble (*rhamnus*) is a plant that is at first soft, but afterwards turns into thorns. It signifies sins which delight in this life and afterwards sting. While they delight, if someone does not think of their future sting, he does not understand the bramble. To understand the bramble is to observe that this softness of pleasure will afterward harden into torments. But the thorns will understand the bramble when the ungodly are taught by their experience of punishments that the present softness now deceives them. Meanwhile, that is, before your thorns understand the bramble—or, as another translation has it, “Before the bramble produces your thorns,” which [Col. 1728B] is the same thing, namely, before the torments of pleasures proceed—even here they are not without punishment. For the fire of vices which has fallen upon them swallows them up, that is, it conceals their evil life, so that they do not see the bramble, that is, so that they do not believe in the future thorns. It swallows them up, I say, not as living, but as though living: namely, those who do not truly live, but seem to themselves to live. It also swallows them up not in wrath, but as though in wrath, either because it is not wrath in comparison with the wrath to come, or because he judges calmly.

“The righteous man shall rejoice.” The third part, in which the correction of the righteous arises from the vengeance upon the wicked, because the fire swallows them up. This is not without profit to the righteous. For the righteous man—certainly because he believes—though there be something in him to be washed away, shall rejoice as righteous in [Col. 1728C] his own good, even if for a time he is saddened under afflictions. Without doubt he shall rejoice when he sees, that is, understands, this present vengeance. For he shall wash his hands in the sinner’s blood: that is, he shall observe the ungodly person perishing and cleanse his works from sins, as Solomon says: “When the fool perishes, the wise man becomes more prudent” (Prov. XIX, 25).

**VERSE 12.** “And man shall say: If indeed there is fruit for the righteous, then indeed there is a God judging them on earth.” Having considered the vengeance upon the ungodly, man—that is, one possessed of rational understanding and not made like horse and mule, which have no understanding—will say, wisely reasoning within himself, that these judgments upon the wicked do not occur by chance, but that there indeed is God judging them upon this earth [Col. 1728D], where they seem to flourish. This is proved by the contrary fact: even for the righteous man, who, seeing vengeance, washed his hands in the sinners’ blood, a judge on this earth where he is oppressed is certainly not lacking. Indeed, God himself the Judge is the fruit of that righteous man: now justifying him, so that he who is righteous may yet be justified, and he who is holy may yet be sanctified; and in the future preserving himself for him as his reward and as the unfading fruit of his complete justification.

In the Hebrew it reads: “And man shall say: Truly there is fruit for the righteous; truly there is a God judging on earth.” This means: Times and temporal things do not truly pass over the earth by fortuitous chance, but there is a God judging and [Col. 1729A] avenging evil and rewarding good. Hence there is fruit here for the righteous man, that he may be justified still more; for the husbandman cleanses every branch that bears fruit in the true vine, so that it may bear more fruit. And, though sparing the bramble for a time, he will finally cut it down with his axe and cast it into eternal fire.

[Col. 1730A] Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit in his kingdom, the kingdom of the bramble brought low. May the kingdom of the Trinity be glorious and fruitful for the righteous; and may the kingdom of Antichrist appear as it is, shameful and harmful to the ungodly. Amen.

## PSALM LVIII

[Col. 1729]

[Col. 1729A] “Deliver me from my enemies.” The title of this psalm is:

[Col. 1729B] **(VERSE 1) FOR THE END: DO NOT DESTROY, OR DO NOT CORRUPT; OF DAVID, FOR THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE, WHEN SAUL SENT AND GUARDED HIS HOUSE IN ORDER TO KILL HIM.**

It is read in the First Book of Kings that Saul sent his guards to David’s house, to watch and kill him in the morning. His wife Michal perceived this, lowered him through a window by night, and thus he escaped (1 Kings XIX, 11). Mystically, David is Christ; David’s house is Christ’s tomb; Saul is the kingdom of the Jews, who sent men to guard the tomb. Yet it is not fitting that Christ’s tomb should have been guarded in order to kill him. Therefore the words “in order to kill him” should rather be referred to his body, which is the Church. To kill Christ was to extinguish, through the guards’ lie, the name and faith of his resurrection [Col. 1729C]; yet the Jews did not accomplish this. For the King lives over Jews and Gentiles alike, as Pilate, signifying this, said: “What I have written, I have written”; and the Prophet foretold: “Do not destroy,” and so forth. This is also the purpose to which the Prophet now exhorts. In vain does anyone attempt to destroy what divine authority has so often forbidden.

Here the whole Christ speaks. First, he prays for his own deliverance and for the salvation of the Gentiles. Second, the visitation and conversion of the Gentiles are declared and prayed for at the words, “They shall return at evening.” Third, the salvation of the Jews is declared; and thanks are given for those gathered from both walls at “They shall return at evening.” Therefore, as a man besieged by enemies, he cries to God, saying: “Deliver me.” Accordingly, that I may first address you, combatant, as we also warned above [Col. 1729D], take careful heed of yourself amid the dangers of this conflict in which you wrestle against vices. Thus, whenever the devil sends in and besieges the house of your body or flesh with as many guards as there are vices, in order to kill you—as he sent the Jews in order to kill Christ—do not, by despairing, destroy the title so often stated; but say according to Christ’s own example: “Deliver me from my enemies, O my God, and free me from those who rise up against me. Deliver me from those who work iniquity, and save me from men of blood; for behold, they have taken my soul and the strong have rushed upon me,” and so forth. For he who, by raising the Head himself, delivered him from those strong men who rushed upon him—indeed, from madmen, who seemed strong to themselves in their insanity [Col. 1730A], though they were weak, and struck the physician—will also deliver you from the power of assailing vices, or of evil spirits and men, [Col. 1730B] so that you may say with this psalm: “But I will sing of your strength, and in the morning I will exalt your mercy, because you have become my protector,” and so forth. Let us now begin to expound more fully the words of the psalm from the beginning, fitting its meaning both to Christ himself and to his members, insofar as he in whose hand we and our words are may deign to grant it.

**VERSES 2–3.** Deliver me—Christ confined in mortal flesh, or even in my body, which is the Church, hemmed in and besieged by the guards of death. These guards, though differing among themselves in four ways, nevertheless unanimously assail me. Some have the will to harm, but do not openly show it; of them I say: “Deliver me from my enemies.” Others reveal by gesture or words the malice conceived against me in their hearts; of them I say: “And free me from those who rise up against me.” Others, with hardened minds, strive also in deed to complete the crime they have conceived; of them I say: “Deliver me from those who work iniquity.” The fourth kind consists of murderers thirsting for blood with bestial cruelty; though wolves, they spare not the sheep. Against them I pray, saying: “And save me from men of blood.” The first belong to that host of Antichrist called Gog, that is, “covered”; the second, third, and fourth belong to Magog, that is, “uncovered.” The first are wicked, the second more wicked, the third most wicked, the fourth more than most wicked. The first do not wish to do good and wish to do harm, yet they keep the poison of impiety hidden within themselves. [Col. 1730D] The second, wishing to do harm, show what they wish, but nevertheless do not attain in deed the effect of evil corresponding to the inward inclination to harm. The third indeed harm openly, but, while harming, do not desire the blood of innocents; the fourth, thirsting for it, rage with bestial cruelty. From these I, Christ, first ask to be saved in myself, then in my whole body, which is the Church.

**VERSE 4.** “For behold, they have taken my soul; the strong have rushed upon me.” Behold, openly pursuing my soul, that is, my temporal life, they took it and led it unto death. Thus elsewhere I complain, saying: “They brought down my life into the pit of death and placed a stone upon me” (Lam. III, [Col. 1731A] 53), desiring, of course, to prevent my body’s resurrection. They lay in wait for my soul; and, to take it in speech, after they had often plotted and been frustrated, at last the strong rushed upon me, seeking no longer by deceit but by violence to seize and hold me once seized. For those seemed strong to themselves who did not make God their helper, but, hoping in the abundance of their riches, prevailed in their vanity. Or they are those who presume upon a righteousness as though it were their own, who insult me for dining with tax collectors and sinners; to whom I answered: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill” (Matt. IX, 12). These are found more harmful, because, seeming strong and righteous through Pharisaic superstition, by their feigned strength they draw almost the whole crowd of false righteousness after the tracks of their flocks [Col. 1731B], which they feed beside the shepherds’ tents. They feed them, I say, not as good shepherds do, who, content with the sheep’s wool and milk, allow them to live; but, since they are men of blood, they slaughter and destroy the shorn sheep. They slaughter the bodies of those who do not agree with them; they destroy the souls of those who favor their malice. Therefore, because they could not make my soul agree with them so as to destroy it, these strong men rushed upon me to slaughter my body, crying before the governor: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. XXVI, 66); likewise: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John XIX, 12).

Thus these madmen, falsely strong and truly weak, [Col. 1731C] neither knowing nor wishing to know that I came as a physician to heal their diseases, shed my blood. Yet from that blood I, the physician, made a medicine also for the salvation of many from their own number: they who, in unbelief and evil strength, shed that same blood, but afterwards, believing and confessing their disease, drank it—grieving and repenting greatly because they killed me, an innocent man who had no cause for death, but walked uprightly and ran in the paths of righteousness, as you know, who are witness and knower of this matter on high—that

**VERSE 5.** “Neither my iniquity nor my sin, O Lord, was the cause” of their rushing upon me as these strong men rushed upon me. Neither the iniquity of ill will [Col. 1731D] nor the sin of wrongful action was found in me, “because without iniquity I ran and directed.” I ran and directed others. I ran through straight paths, and directed toward and along them others whom I found twisted, wandering in trackless ground and not on the way.

Another translation has: “I ran and was directed.” This means: I ran, laboring in my humanity, to which it belonged to run and move in the time of mortality; and I was directed by my divinity, to which it belongs and always belonged to stand upon the height of supreme loftiness. It also directed there the course of mortal flesh united to it, so that, when I am thus exalted, I may draw my whole body to myself with all the framework of my members. Therefore:

**VERSE 6.** “Rise to meet me and see.” O God the Father, who seem to sleep and not to see the miseries [Col. 1732A] and insults threatening me and my own: rise to meet me, so that, just as my going forth is from the highest heaven, so my return to its height may be accomplished and known as accomplished. This is what I ask when I say, “Rise to meet me and see”: accomplish my return through the glory of resurrection and ascension, and make this very thing visible by causing the blind, who do not yet see and deny that I return in equality to the utmost height, to see. Or, “see” means: show that you see what you are thought not to see—namely, how many and how great are the strong guards of death, demons and men, who rushed upon me. I do not pray for the demons, because I nowhere took hold of angels; but I do pray because I took hold of Abraham’s seed, believing in me, in whose seed all nations were to be blessed. You, Lord [Col. 1732B] God of hosts, God of Israel—whom the heavenly powers praise and whom Israel worships, namely, the people who follow Abraham’s faith, who saw my day and deserved to be called father of many nations through my intercession—

Give heed to visit all nations, so that, once all tribes of the earth have been blessed in me, Abraham’s seed, all nations whom you have made may come and worship me before you. For the nations themselves, being greatly weakened by the sickness of sins, cannot come to you at all unless they are first healed by your visitation. You visited the one nation of the Jews through my presence in the flesh; and, having gathered only a very few elect from it, you rejected it. But you know that I, your Word, or your almighty utterance, came from the royal seats, so that those empty seats reserved in heaven might receive human occupants, since demons fell from them. Since, therefore, those royal seats in heaven must be filled by human beings—seats either emptied by angels falling thence or prepared for people who will ascend there—and Jacob’s thigh has so withered that it cannot beget children, give heed to visit all the nations formerly barren. Visit them through the apostles and the apostles’ followers, Catholic men, and also through angels who labor in healing and salvation, as once you visited Sarah daughter of Raguel through the angel Raphael and through Tobias, a righteous and pious man. Thus, by marvellously ordering the ministries of angels and human beings, deign to heal the Gentile world [Col. 1732D], so that, once every demon hostile to human salvation has been entirely put to flight and men unworthy of ecclesiastical dignity have been removed from dignities which they unworthily hold, lawful marriages may take place throughout the world, both among those persons through whose ministry human generation occurs and among those through whom their regeneration occurs.

The former should relax carnal desire only for the begetting of offspring to be lovingly received and disciplinarily nurtured. The latter should wholly restrain the desire of the flesh by continence, and should in no way be occupied with the ministry of generating in the flesh, but with that of regenerating in the spirit. For except in an emergency, when baptism is permitted to laymen and even women, as well as pagans, it is unseemly for one and the same person to exercise the office of generating and regenerating [Col. 1733A]. Therefore carnal marriage is permitted to laypeople and even to clerics outside holy orders who have not taken a vow of continence; but it is altogether forbidden to ministers of the altar and all others who have taken a vow of continence, lest the ministries of generation and regeneration, far distinct from one another, be confused in one person and the people become as the priest. Hence the first ministers of regenerating grace, leaving everything connected with the office of generation, devoted themselves solely to spiritual exercises in the office of regeneration.

Therefore let those who beget children beware of becoming like horse and mule, which have no understanding. Let these, who fit those carnally born to the spiritual ministry of regenerating grace, beware lest, placed in honor, they do not understand [Col. 1733B], and thus be compared to senseless beasts and made like them. Let the former beget sons and daughters in the blessing of Abraham’s seed, or also in that first blessing spoken to the first-created humans: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. I, 28), with the curse entirely removed that was spoken to Eve: “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions” (Gen. III, 16). Let the latter regenerate through baptism so many sons and daughters in Christ that the royal seats still empty in God’s kingdom may quickly be filled, as kings and kingdoms are multiplied in proportion to the multitude of royal seats in heaven.

Even in the holy Church still journeying upon earth, there are as many royal seats as ecclesiastical ranks distinguished in it. Therefore, in order that [Col. 1733C] these royal seats also may be possessed by royal persons—that is, by those justly qualified for just governance—and that the number of the elect predestined for royal seats may very quickly be completed from all nations, you, O God, give heed to visit all nations. Look upon the face of the Church gathered from the Gentiles, and multiply in it the fruitfulness of regeneration, so that the children of her who is deserted may be more numerous than those of her who has a husband, and the wedding feast may be filled with those reclining at table. And when all the wheat, for whose sake you now spare the tares, has been gathered into the barn, spare them no longer and do not have mercy on all who work iniquity. Thus deign to increase the chosen grains both in merit and in number, so that you need not say to your servants: “Let both grow together” (Matt. XIII, 30). But, the wheat preserved, [Col. 1733D] do not have mercy on any tares; do not have mercy on all who work iniquity. I say universally, “Give heed to visit all nations,” and likewise add universally, “Do not have mercy on all who work iniquity,” because “in every nation, whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X, 35), and among all nations “every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. III, 10). Therefore, that the consummation of both universals may be hastened—regarding the elect and predestined, I ask that all nations be visited; regarding the reprobate, I ask that mercy be denied to all workers of iniquity—this may be understood in two ways. Either God leaves no sin unpunished, since repentance itself is called, as it were, *punishment* (*punitentia*), by which God punishes the sins of the elect, with human effort cooperating: either a human being makes satisfaction by repenting, or God takes vengeance. Or there is a certain iniquity such that, if a person commits it, God cannot have mercy on him: namely, blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which is evident when someone stubbornly loves and defends his own sin, which God hates. [Col. 1734A]

Alternatively: “Do not have mercy on all who work iniquity”—that is, with that mercy which does not free them from iniquity, as Isaiah says: “Let us have mercy on the ungodly, and he will not learn to do righteousness” (Isa. XXVI, 10). Therefore there is a harmful mercy which so blinds [Col. 1734B] or hardens the ungodly in his injustice that he does not learn to do righteousness. Of this it is said to the ungodly in Hosea: “Your mercy is like a morning cloud and like dew passing away in the morning” (Hos. VI, 5). For temporal prosperity, which seems to the wicked and foolish to be divine mercy, like a dark cloud or mist hides the sun of righteousness from such people; and, itself passing swiftly away like dew, sends them to eternal punishments. Therefore, O God of hosts, God of Israel, do not have mercy in such a way on all who work iniquity. Though you may have mercy on some, so that those who are in filth may become filthier still, and those who harm may harm still: nevertheless, do not thus have mercy on all who work iniquity. Rather, from their multitude distinguish your elect, not to be deceived by a short-lived mercy [Col. 1734C], but to be chastened and saved according to your great mercy and according to the multitude of your compassions.

Therefore have mercy on all those whom you foreknow will be yours by faith and works—not according to the small mercy of temporal and deceptive prosperity, which sends the ungodly into eternal misery by sparing them now, but according to your great mercy and the multitude of your compassions: wiping out their iniquities by a most mighty and most careful leveling, whereby you leave no sin unwiped out, yet do not break the tablets of Gentile hearts as you broke the stone tablets sent to the stiff-necked people, breaking them punitively as a sign of Jewish hardness. May this not happen to the Gentiles, for whom I pray—not that they be broken, [Col. 1734D] but converted.

*Diapsalma.* And because my prayer cannot be frustrated:

**VERSE 7.** “They shall return at evening, and shall suffer hunger like dogs.”

Now turned away from the light of truth, like bleary-eyed or blind persons, they shall turn to behold it. Though not in the morning, to see how in the beginning was the Word, life and the light of men; though not at noon, to see me, the sun of righteousness, in my supreme height or brightness—a vision reserved for a very few elect who seek me with the bride, asking, “Where do you feed, where do you lie down at noon?”—yet they shall return at evening. For, when the end of the world is already near, they will be moved to repentance by the sight of the dreadful judgment; or, when the end of their own life is near, they will amend their lives. And they shall suffer hunger like dogs. For, not content each with his own salvation, they will suffer the hunger of converting others like dogs: namely, by barking against thieves and enemies and guarding the household goods.

Therefore they will keep watch and go around the city, strengthening the Church against heretical attacks through the teaching of truth. Or, if they are not fit to bark by preaching, they will go around the city by muttering and murmuring in prayer, for example striking at God’s ears with continual prayers: first for every rank of the Church; then for their pastor, flock, brothers and sisters, benefactors, travelers, opponents and slanderers, afflicted persons [Col. 1735B] and captives, and the other members of the Church. As they traverse these in diligent devotion, they treat Lazarus’s ulcerated body like dogs—not wounding its sores with the biting tooth of detraction, but cherishing and healing them with the word of consolation, instruction, admonition, and prayer, like gentle lickings.

They will also be likened to dogs suffering hunger in this respect: driven by the excessive force of hunger, they gather crumbs falling from the table of their masters. For in his great house the Lord of lords has appointed certain lords over his household, to give them their measure of wheat in due season. To them he also said: “You are those who have remained with me in my trials, and I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at [Col. 1735C] my table in my kingdom and sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luke XXII, 29). Those, then, who are such persons do not gather crumbs under the table, but enjoy a full banquet among the friends of God, to whom it is said: “Eat, friends; drink and be intoxicated, beloved” (Song V, 1). But we and those like us, like dogs suffering hunger, find it sweet to gather crumbs falling from the table of such masters. We do not compare our sayings or writings with their sayings and writings, nor do we labor for great hearers or readers; but, little ones for little ones, we set forth crumbs for those suffering hunger, crumbs by no means needed by great masters. For we are not filled, like the man who, belching out his feasts, said: “God, I give thanks to you that I am not like the rest of humankind—robbers, unjust persons, adulterers, and so forth” (Luke XVIII, 11). Rather, we hunger and thirst; and in this work we labor for others afflicted with like hunger and thirst. One such person, apparently hungry, sent me, while I was writing, the following letter as an indication of his hunger:

> “To his lord and father G.—the one title denoting submission, the other affection—brother F. sends himself, not in parts or divided, but wholly, entire in all things and through all things.”
>
> “A book which you composed in eloquent style for guests, namely the venerable Lord Archbishop [Col. 1736A] E. [Note: [Col. 1735D] Eberhard.] and Lord G. [Note: [Col. 1736D] Gottschalk, bishop of Freising.], priest, recently came into my hands. I embraced it with such love that I thought I had found Croesus’s wealth. I read it all the more eagerly because its author is dearer to me. Finally, when I came to that passage in which Ulysses’ cunning is compared with Christ’s folly, I confess that tears burst forth; and, unable to restrain myself, I shamefully stained the page. For your utterances were more desirable to me than much gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Nor without reason. Your utterances are chaste utterances, silver tested by fire, proved in the earth, purified sevenfold. You proceed with ease and purity; that very ease is mingled with wisdom. Blessed are the ears that hear you, and blessed the boys who attend upon you. Oh, if I were permitted to enjoy your conversation, I would rather crawl beneath your table on my hands and lick the crumbs falling from your mouth. So much for this matter. Now, at the end of my little letter, if my advice is not unwelcome, it would surely please me if you sent this exposition itself to Lord Walther, bishop of Cologne. For he has frequently spoken to me in familiar terms of his remembrance of you.”

We have inserted this letter here so that the hunger of dogs, or the longing of the poor, which we intend to satisfy insofar as the Father of mercies deigns to assist us, may be made plainly evident. He not only brings forth from the earth bread that strengthens the human heart, wine that gladdens the human heart, and oil that makes the face cheerful; he also feeds the birds [Col. 1736C] that neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns. Certainly, those who seek bread in the sweat of their faces and bear the burden and heat of the day in the vineyard are those who, through great labor in fastings, vigils, readings, meditations, and other such exercises, reach the marrow of the Scriptures. They have no need for anyone to toss them crumbs as if they were puppies, since the Lord, with their own industry cooperating, has given them abundance of grain, wine, and oil from the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth.

But there are some hungry persons unable to dig and ashamed to beg: that is, neither able to investigate for themselves nor daring to ask others what they do not know. They scarcely understand what is clearly and [Col. 1736D] fully set forth in an exposition; nevertheless, they labor so greatly with hunger to know the meaning of the psalms which they daily chew over that, until they are satisfied, they do not cease murmuring. Rightly it is said of such persons later in this psalm: “They shall be scattered to eat; if they are not satisfied, they shall murmur.” Therefore, to such murmurers, who through the excess of their hunger accept even bitter things as sweet, and who earnestly request this very work which we write, though in a rustic style, we have resolved to minister devoutly, trusting in the help of him in whose hand are both we and our words. He will give great power to those who proclaim the Gospel: whether those converted from Judaism at evening—that is, after the setting of the true Sun, who knew his setting and afterwards, rising, ascended above the setting, drawing to himself the remnant of Israel and the fullness of the Gentiles—or those converted from Gentile paganism itself at evening, as explained above. From both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles, some converts shall suffer hunger like dogs and go around the city, which elsewhere is called the surrounding region—that is, the world which surrounds Judaea on every side, where these things were spoken and where the Lord worked salvation in the midst of the earth; where the Holy Spirit also came upon the disciples in fiery tongues, to whom:

**VERSE 8.** “Behold, they shall speak with their mouth, and a sword is on their lips.” Behold, not only Christ’s first disciples [Col. 1737B], but also the disciples of disciples, succeeding others as they depart, shall speak until the end of the age. Behold, both parties openly—that is, Jews or Gentiles converted—shall speak with their mouths, saying: “Who has heard?” Namely, converted late at evening, they shall suffer hunger like dogs, and, troubled by the unbelievers, they will be indignant at their sluggishness, saying: “Who has heard?” That is: “Who has believed our report?” Thus they speak with their mouths, seeking faithful hearing; and where they do not find it, there is a sword on their lips, ready to avenge all disobedience. “For the word of God is living and effective, and more piercing than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, [Col. 1737C] joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Heb. IV, 12). This sword is to be purchased by selling one’s tunic; it is a sharpened sword, a two-edged sword, the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God. With the edge of both Testaments it strikes enemies and slays the creeping creatures of which Peter was told: “Slay, slay, and eat” (Acts II, 7).

Alternatively: “Behold, they shall speak with their mouth”—not with a heart and a heart, in another’s mouth, that is, with speech not at all corresponding to their heart. They shall speak with their own mouth, namely, in speech suitable to their profession. For when either a good person says evil things or an evil person says good things, each speaks with another’s mouth. But when a person of holy intention and pious profession says good things, he speaks with his own mouth. Thus, behold, the good speak good things with their own mouths and urge the wicked toward good. But because not all obey the Gospel, there is a sword upon their lips for executing vengeance among the nations and rebukes among the peoples. And deservedly, since “Who has heard?” Who among the many hearers has had ears to hear? Almost none, and truly few; and for this reason those who have not heard must be struck with the sword of the Spirit.

Alternatively: “Behold, they shall speak with their mouth” a gracious word full of grace, and likewise a word full of truth. Since the same Word is known to be full of grace and truth, whoever does not receive saving grace shall be struck by avenging truth, as by the two-edged sword of the inescapable Judge, who, after he has killed, can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. Those will deserve this punishment who refused obediently to hear the Word of God [Col. 1738A], but rejected it, judging themselves unworthy of eternal life; and consequently despising the best words, most excellently spoken: “For who has heard such things?” “Never has a man spoken as this man,” who is God and man, and who granted to his disciples that they might speak in every language. Who has ever heard men speaking thus in languages which they had never learned?

Alternatively: “Behold, they shall speak with their mouth, and a sword is on their lips”: that is, they shall have words not only sweet and gentle but also weighty and sharp, because “Who has heard,” or can hear, owing to excessive hardness, things that are sharp like a sword? “This saying,” they say, “is hard; who can hear it?” (John VI, 61). Thus speak certain persons who turn back [Col. 1738B] because of the hardness, as they call it, of sayings which they deny can be endured or even heard.

**VERSE 9.** But you, O Lord, will mock them; that is, you will show that those who speak thus deserve mockery, since more will believe than they themselves believe, and more will hear than they imagine. In this you will mock the unbelievers, either by making them believers or by reducing them to nothing. For you will bring all the nations to nothing, either by converting them now, so that they are no longer nations living as Gentiles, or by condemning them at the last judgment, so that they will be as though they did not exist. For although they will have existence, since in their punishments they will not wholly cease to be, nevertheless, because they will not possess blessed existence, they will be as nothing—even though now, like strong men, they rush upon me, the physician, unwilling to receive the medicine necessary for them. All their strength will be reduced to nothing [Col. 1738C] when, with hands and feet bound, they are cast into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, with fire now and cold now prevailing in their limbs, since, as is written in Job: “From snowy waters they pass to excessive heat” (Job 24:19). They pass, that is, not by their own choice, having power to alter their punishments, but because they then have no strength at all to resist punishment—having previously refused to resist sins. For they would not preserve their strength in that by which, sinning, they withdrew from you, who are true strength. But I, Christ—

**VERSE 10.** “I will keep my strength for you,” Father: I, sent by you, do not withdraw from you. But when [Col. 1738D] I have been lifted up from the earth, from the midst of Saul’s attendants—that is, of death—to the lofty throne of your glory, I shall draw all things to myself, and through myself to you, my God and my Father. For you are my God with respect to my humanity, according to which you are my God. You are indeed my God insofar as you made me, and my Father insofar as you begot me; and I am your work and likewise your offspring—not made in the Godhead, as Arius barked with blasphemous mouth; nor adopted in my humanity, as the heresiarch Bonosus falsely taught, and as certain perverse persons still maintain. They deny, so far as lies in them, to me the man, beset by the attendants of death, natural sonship from God; and they think that I, the Son of Man, should be honored as though I were one of the prophets.
