Leaving them, therefore, in their blindness, I turn to you, kindly hearers, who believe that my God is the same as my Father, saying with Peter: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). And I tell you that your confession, by which you call me the Son of God, is true. For his mercy preceded me once in my own singular person, bestowing upon me, the man, the Son of Man, that I should be the Son of God—not by adoption, but properly; and that same mercy will always precede me in my members. For “who has first given to him, and shall be repaid?” (Rom. 11:35). Certainly not even the human nature assumed in me, the Son of God, merited the glory it possesses before it was assumed; rather, having been preceded by God’s mercy, it received grace greater than which there can be none, [Col. 1739B] and the same—

**VERSES 11–12.** His mercy will precede me in my members, who are to be born from Adam and reborn through me, the second Adam. No one merits any good before grace is received, as the heretic Pelagius asserted; for all good merits come from prevenient mercy. God showed me how great that mercy is in me by contrast with my enemies, whom he made from the same mass vessels of wrath for dishonor. For he endured these vessels of wrath with much patience, in order to show his riches upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory.

Otherwise: “But you, O Lord, will mock them”—that is, the unbelieving Jews [Col. 1739C]—“and will reduce to nothing all nations” lacking charity; without charity all other goods are nothing, as the Apostle says: “If I have prophecy and know all mysteries, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2). How truly the nations without charity are nothing you will then show, when you also drive away from the entrance to the wedding-feast the foolish virgins who have no oil of charity in their vessels, and cast outside the guest who lacks the wedding garment of charity, saying to him: “Friend, how did you enter here without a wedding garment?” (Matt. 22:12).

Why then, O Lord, almighty King, do you now endure such people in your Church? Because I keep within, reserving for you, God the Father—that is, for your good pleasure—my strength, by which I could already destroy them; I do not wield it, like a broadsword laid up in its sheath. When I receive the appointed time from your disposition, I shall judge just judgments and draw my sword, in order to kill all sinners of the earth. But now, before the time of judgment, God shows me over my enemies, so that I may not kill them or allow them to be killed; indeed, I pray for them, saying to God himself, my Father: “Do not kill them”—that is, do not utterly destroy the Jewish people—lest the peoples who are to be converted, or have been converted, to the faith should at some time forget me: that is, consign to oblivion me, Christ, born and suffering among the Jews, and prophesied and foretold in their books before I was born or suffered.

[Col. 1740A] Scatter them by your strength, so that they may carry throughout the world books full of testimonies concerning my birth, death, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and finally my judgment of the world at its end. Let those books not be confined to one corner of the Jewish land, but be borne about over the whole earth; let the Jews be led captive among all nations—not by the strength of the Romans who take them captive, but by your strength, which orders all things, including this: that, just as Cain, a fratricide, wandering, fugitive, and accursed upon the earth, received a sign so that he would not be killed, so these too may be preserved with the sign of circumcision and not wholly killed.

For they are like carriers of book-chests, necessary for this purpose: that they may bear everywhere the books which give testimony to the Christian faith, lest the nations should say that Christians fabricated the testimonies which [Col. 1740B] are found written in the books of their adversaries before the Christian faith had been revealed. For preaching concerning me, Christ born of a Virgin and, after death and resurrection, exalted above all heavens, rests upon an exceedingly strong foundation of truth, since even the opposing party, whether willing or unwilling, supplies in its own books the surest testimonies to these marvels.

For this reason, O Father, not only scatter them by your strength among the nations foreknown for faith, but also cast them down, so that they may possess no priestly or royal dignity. Rather, as is written in Hosea: “They shall sit without king, without priest, without altar, without teraphim” (Hos. 3:4). Let them sit not upon a royal throne or a pontifical chair, [Col. 1740C] but as is read in Isaiah: “Let that daughter of the Chaldeans sit upon the ground” (Isa. 47:1)—that is, the Jewish people, imitators of Chaldean wickedness—lest, if they possessed somewhere a temple, sacrifice, kingdom, or priesthood gloriously ordered according to the Law, they should impede the chariot of the running Gospel, which proclaims a new temple rebuilt in three days; a new sacrifice suited to such a temple; a new kingdom without end; and a new priesthood, not according to the order of Aaron but according to the order of Melchizedek.

Moreover, in the withering branches cut off, the mercy shown to the engrafted branches will be recognized—not that those engrafted should boast against those cut off, but that, by considering them, they may humble themselves more deeply. [Col. 1740D] “For if God did not spare the natural branches, lest perhaps he should not spare them either” (Rom. 11:21). Consideration of this matter restrains pride and produces humility, lest anyone think highly of himself, but rather fear; and, humbled by fear, lest he lose the grace received, but instead be found worthy of greater grace. For as God resisted the proud Jews, so he gives grace to the humble nations. Therefore, since so many goods will result from their life, I beg you, do not kill them—but kill—

**VERSE 13.** “The sin of their mouth,” by which they killed me in the flesh; and likewise kill the utterance of their lips—that is, show it to be unfulfilled by proving false their calling me a deceiver, mad, and possessed by a demon, and their saying that I cast out demons by Beelzebub. Remove from their lips this utterance [Col. 1741A] of theirs, as though killing and blotting it out, so that they may learn not to blaspheme, but at least in their remnant, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, may bless me when converted and recognize as the blessed Son of God him whom, blinded, they did not recognize. For I said to them: “Behold, your house will be left desolate to you. For I say to you: You will not see me henceforth until you say: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 23:38–39). When therefore they say this, when they confess that I came blessed in the name of the Lord, then I shall no longer remember the blaspheming utterance of their lips, as though wholly abolished.

Let therefore what I pray for occur: when their blasphemous speech has been erased and praise has succeeded it, let them be caught [Col. 1741B] in their pride—that is, let them understand that they sinned through hateful pride rather than invincible ignorance, and that therefore they have come, by just judgment, into their impending calamities. And so, humbled, they will be proclaimed from cursing and falsehood—

**VERSE 14.** “In the consummation, in the wrath of consummation, and they shall be no more.” Or, as another translation has it: “From cursing and falsehood they shall proclaim consummations in the wrath of consummation, and they shall be no more.” The sense is the same. For cursing is the same as execration: in it the Jews have become execrable among the nations because of their wickedness; or it denotes the execration by which they cursed Christ, and, by perverting the Scriptures, regarded as accursed according to the Law him who hung on the wood. To that curse they added falsehood by giving money [Col. 1741C] to the guards in order that they might lie.

The order of the words is: “Let them be caught in their pride”; and this is useful to them. For when they are thus humbled, the apostles preaching will proclaim to them, from cursing and falsehood, that at the consummation where the sin of cursing and falsehood abounded, grace may superabound—grace freeing from evils and bringing to completion in goods.

Likewise, many of their followers, though living under the Christian name, are nevertheless execrable and false in this: they live wickedly, although they promised to live well when, receiving baptism, they renounced the devil and his works. They will be proclaimed from cursing and falsehood unto consummation if they too are caught in their pride and if the sin [Col. 1741D] of their mouth is erased: that is, if, abandoning an execrable and shameful way of life, they live soberly, justly, and piously, and truly fulfill the purpose of holy living which they promised either in baptism or afterward. Then, as has been said, freed from cursing and falsehood, they will be proclaimed unto consummation—as Paul, caught in his pride, was afterward beneficially made weak, healed by his weakness, and brought to completion in good. Thus against the swelling of pride the Lord applies the poultice of weakness, as an angel of Satan was given to buffet the Apostle, lest the greatness of his revelations should exalt him.

I observe in Paul two kinds of pride healed by God’s marvelous art: one by which he took pride in evil deeds before conversion, still breathing out and unable to contain within himself the breath of pride; the other, which threatened his salvation because of the greatness of his revelations. The compassionate physician healed the former by speaking from heaven himself to the proud rhinoceros, in order to bind him to his manger, humbling him beneficially not only beneath himself but also beneath Ananias, a disciple. He healed the latter through the angel of Satan who buffeted him, lest it happen that you should understand that pride to be more dangerous which attacks a person because of good deeds, good words, virtues, or revelations.

And because the art of physicians is divided in two ways—namely, into expelling diseases once they arise and preventing them lest they arise—we find the Apostle treated in both ways: caught in his first pride, and preserved from the second, [Col. 1742B] which was worse. This twofold medicine against a very harmful double pride is necessary for all. The former prevents the beginning of a good life, since it does not allow the proud person to bend beneath the instruction of another human being, as we read that Paul was humbled beneath Ananias. The latter impedes the completion of good once begun, which never comes about except through sincere humility, by which a devout person, the greater he is, humbles himself in all things. But this humility, which completes and preserves every good, is possessed very rarely unless the human mind, prone to pride, is restrained and disciplined in the wrath of consummation.

It should be noted that every divine vengeance is called wrath. But sometimes it condemns in evil, as when he will say: [Col. 1742C] “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41); and sometimes it brings to completion in good, as when he scourges every son whom he receives. The first is therefore called wrath of consumption; the second, wrath of consummation. By the former sinners will fail from the earth, so that they are no more; by the latter the humble will advance, so that they may exist well and truly.

Or, in one and the same person, the wrath of consumption does one thing and the wrath of consummation another. Through certain chastisements of God a person is cleansed from sins, so that, his sins consumed by punishment, the person may be found pure; through others he is brought to completion in virtues, so that in God he may rightly now be called a god, according to the saying: “I said: You are gods, and sons of the Most High.” When there follows, however, “But you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes” (Ps. 81:7), [Col. 1742D] it is plainly indicated that death and falling through pride threaten even such gods and sons of the Most High unless they endure discipline in the wrath of consummation until the end of all consummation, of which it is said: “I have seen an end of all consummation; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118:96).

Therefore whoever has advanced to the perfection of most expansive charity, which does not fail, now has less need of the scourge, because through charity, which is not puffed up, he is preserved from every pride. Hence we believe that the Apostle Paul, finally brought to completion in charity, was wholly freed from the angel of Satan buffeting him, counted among the good angels, and entrusted to their continual protection, so that with Elisha he could say: [Col. 1743A] “There are more with us than against us” (4 Kings 6:16). The same may readily be recognized in the other converts from the Jewish people, who were proclaimed from cursing and falsehood unto consummation in the wrath of consummation. “And therefore they shall be no more”: supply, what they had previously been, according to what is written: “Overthrow the wicked, and they shall be no more” (Prov. 12:7).

“And they shall know that God rules Jacob and the ends of the earth.” Formerly, because they were not subject to God’s righteousness but sought to establish their own, they exalted themselves over the Gentiles, whom they considered unclean like dogs. They thought God cared only for the Jews, supposedly justified by the righteousness of the Law. Now corrected in the wrath of consummation and enlightened by grace, they will know that, just as all have sinned—Jews and [Col. 1743B] Gentiles alike—so all need the glory and grace of God. For just as he rules Jacob, saving from Jacob’s offspring those whom he wills, so he also rules the ends of the earth, saving whom he wills, not only in all Judaea and Samaria but even to the uttermost part of the earth. He hears and answers voices crying to him from the ends of the earth, whether Jewish or Gentile; and from all these one Church is perfected, namely, that queen who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom. Hence it has already been said: Jews converted to God will plainly know that God rules Jacob and the ends of the earth. Or, God of Jacob himself rules the ends of the earth, caring for all whom he foreknew and predestined in every nation for blessed life.

[Col. 1743C] For whoever among such persons are not converted in the morning or at midday—as the Apostles, converted to him before the setting of the Sun of righteousness; or those Gentiles who said to Philip, “We wish to see Jesus” (John 12:21); or that Canaanite woman highly praised for her great faith; or that centurion whose faith the Lord admired, saying that he had not found such faith in Israel (Matt. 8:10)—at least they—

**VERSE 15.** “Will return at evening,” that is, late: after the Lord’s death, in which he himself, the true Sun, set, he who also ascends above the setting; or late, at the end of the age, when, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, the remnant of the Jews also will be converted.

Otherwise: “They will return at evening”: those who [Col. 1743D] in the morning—that is, in youth—were perverse with the perverse, hasten all the more to turn to God after their infirmities have multiplied and the day has now declined; that is, when the light of righteousness in them has become darkened. Such people say to Christ: “Stay with us, Lord, for it is toward evening” (Luke 14:29), as though they said: Stay with us, you author and giver of your freely bestowed righteousness, which never grows dark; for all our righteousnesses are known to be as nothing if you judge them without the mercy of pardon.

Those who thus return at evening will suffer hunger, or, as the Hebrew reads, “will bark like dogs”: namely, considering themselves unclean as dogs; or thereafter preserving fidelity like dogs, which are accustomed to be faithful to their masters; or like dogs at their masters’ feast, neglecting not even crumbs. Yet I say, “They will suffer hunger,” which is a sign of health, just as loathing food is an indication of sickness. For no one is more incurable than one who thinks himself healthy and loathes the food through which health is gained and maintained. But those who return at evening, because they regard their conversion as too late and as evening-time or belated—even if they are converted as boys after experiencing wickedness—will, to recover lost innocence, hunger like dogs. Already blessed because they hunger and thirst for righteousness, they desire it to be fulfilled not only in themselves but also in others. Therefore—

**VERSE 16.** “They themselves will be scattered for food.” They [Col. 1744B] will themselves be scattered for this very purpose: to feed, that is, to win others and draw them into their body. But if they are not satisfied by the faith of peoples, they will grieve and murmur—rebuking people, entreating God, or blaming their own sins because their speech finds no place in their hearers and because they do not perceive the desired results in the teaching of obedience or in the answering of prayer.

The prophetic spirit seeks such murmurings in Jeremiah’s Lamentations: “Why,” he says, “has a man murmured, a man for his sin?” (Lam. 3:39). He rightly calls this murmurer a man—that is, a virtuous and rational person—who finds it sweet to murmur, not against God so as to increase sin by his murmuring, but for the removal of his sin, in prayers and confessions directed to God, not against God. This differs from those of whom the Apostle says: “Neither murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by serpents” (1 Cor. 10:10). And Moses says: “Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord” (Exod. 16:8).

For the undisciplined people had murmured against Moses and Aaron because water was lacking in the wilderness. Since they could not obtain it by any human effort, that murmuring was not against them but against the Lord. Yet where the diligence of prelates can and ought to correct such a deficiency or neglect, about which subjects have reason to murmur, the murmuring of subjects is truly against the prelates themselves, if [Col. 1744D] they do not meet their needs insofar as they are able.

Thus, in the Acts of the Apostles, when a murmur of Greeks arose against Hebrews because their widows were not properly provided for in the daily ministry, the Apostles summoned the multitude and first gave an account for themselves: it was not their office, after abandoning the ministry of the word, to serve tables. Then, following the counsel of the multitude, they appointed seven deacons chosen for this work. The foremost of them is read to have been Stephen, the proto-martyr, full of faith and the Holy Spirit; and one of them was afterward rejected (Acts 6:1 ff.). From these events it is plainly understood that, just as undisciplined murmurings directed against God ought to be restrained or even disregarded by teaching or legal authority—as is evident in Moses’ rebukes of wicked murmurers—so disciplined murmurings ought to be quieted by teachers, partly through giving a suitable account and partly by prudently arranging ministries subordinate to them, as is clear in the Apostles’ conduct in Acts, whereby they restrained the murmur.

And lest you perhaps be moved too little by examples of human beings established under God’s authority and having people beneath them, the Lord of all, who is above all, teaches you the same thing. To the people who murmured undisciplinedly against himself and his servants, he terribly sent plagues of fiery serpents and other deaths; but to the Apostle Paul, who murmured in prayer because of the thorn of the flesh, asking that the angel of Satan be taken [Col. 1745B] from him, he mercifully responded. He did so partly by giving the reason why he did not grant his third request, and partly by increasing the grace of strength, which he declared would be perfected in such weakness.

This man was one of those good murmurers of whom it is said here in the psalm: “They themselves will be scattered for food; but if they are not satisfied, they will murmur.” Is it not the voice of one murmuring that the Apostle himself says, in the words of Isaiah, likewise a good murmurer: “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Rom. 10:16). Thus good hungry people murmur, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, and hungering and thirsting, as is fitting, that all righteousness set forth for Jew first and Greek alike, for circumcision together with uncircumcision, may be fulfilled: so that from the two walls joined by one corner-stone one Church may be perfected, one house never to fall. So long as it is not complete, the hungry faith of the saints murmurs; it will then be fully satisfied, when it finds every rightly believed thing fulfilled. Each believer murmurs so long as what he believes is not seen fulfilled.

**VERSE 17.** “But I will sing.” I—the whole holy Church, at last perfected when all my structures have been completed; or I, any member whatever of the already perfected Church—will sing your strength and exalt in the morning your mercy, my God. Why? Because you have become my protector. You who are my God because you created me when I did not exist, are also my protector because, by saving my nature assumed in you, you saved me when I was in destruction. [Col. 1745D] Therefore I shall not boast of my strength, which is nothing, but shall sing your strength, which is invincible; and I shall exalt your mercy, which is ineffable.

The strength of Saul and his attendants, of whom I have said above that strong men rushed upon me, David, was indeed great against me; but the strength of the one who delivered me proved immeasurably greater, so that it could not be overcome. Therefore, my God, my deliverer from enemies rising up, my liberator from those who work iniquity, and my savior from men of blood: wondrously delivered, freed, and saved by your strength, I shall sing that very strength. And because gratuitous mercy was always the inseparable companion and associate of your strength in dealing with me—so that you might strongly crush enemies and mercifully nurture me, ordering all things strongly and sweetly—I shall sing not only the strength that crushes opposing powers, but shall also exalt the mercy that sweetly orders for me all things prosperous and health-giving, as one of our own says: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to his purpose” (Rom. 8:28).

I do not say in the present tense, “I sing your strength; I exalt your mercy,” because it is still a time for weeping and not laughing, so long as those who return at evening hunger like dogs and consequently ought rather to murmur than sing—not [Col. 1746B] against the Lord, however, but to the Lord. This is especially so at evening, because “weeping will linger at evening” (Ps. 29:6). At that evening the true David was buried and beset by the attendants of death, while his friends mourned and his enemies rejoiced. Yet thereafter, “in the morning, joy at dawn” (ibid.) came to his friends and, conversely, grief to his enemies—especially those who guarded the tomb or who bought the falsehood disseminated to suggest that the disciples had stolen him.

They wished to kill Christ, then killed in body, also in spirit: that is, to ensure that no one would believe him alive, and thus that no one would be saved through faith in him. This indeed was the intention of the devil, the governor of death, when, as is noted in the title of this psalm, he “sent and guarded his house in order to kill [Col. 1746C] him,” so that no one would believe in him, as though the triumphal title by which Jesus the Nazarene is glorified as King of the Jews had been erased. But this inscription will not be corrupted. Though, at the onset of the evening in which weeping lingers, it is not at all visible to some, yet when the morning dawn of Christ’s resurrection shines forth—or also that of his whole body at the end toward which this psalm tends—the incorruptible truth of this inscription will be made manifest to all, enemies and friends alike, to the glory of Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews.

Then I, a Jew, now truly confessing both my own misery and his mercy—then, I say, I will sing his strength and exalt his mercy, as I now make this vow, saying: “But I will sing your strength, [Col. 1746D] and exalt in the morning your mercy.”

Or “in the morning,” when the night of every tribulation or temptation has ended, I shall not boast as though freed by my own strength or piety, but shall exalt your mercy and never cease, as it were, to raise it from the depths to the heights in praise. For by raising me on high you received me and became my protector. You, the Maker, became something. What did you become? Certainly, my protector for good through the mystery of your incarnation, and my refuge from evil on the day of tribulation through the sacrament of your passion. On the day, I say, of tribulation—when refuge and consolation are usually most urgently needed—you became for me a refuge, a most secure asylum. In it I might not only remain safe from those rising up against me, but also from it fight bravely in the light of your arrows and the splendor of your flashing spear, praying, disputing, or struggling against enemies in whatever other way; and in overcoming them you became my helper. Hence amid such battles I often said: “The Lord is my helper; I shall not fear what man can do to me” (Ps. 117:6). Again: “The Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon my enemies” (Ps. 117:7). Therefore I shall not only sing praises forever, but now also, while it is time to work—

**VERSE 18.** “I will make music to you” by good works, and deservedly, because you are God my protector, my God, my mercy. Again I call you my protector: because you both received me when I returned from a far country, and at last will receive me after all [Col. 1747B] labors into your rest. Throughout all the days in which I now serve as a soldier, received into your tabernacles, I intend to glorify you as my protector by serving lawfully in your tabernacles. When this warfare is ended, received into your court, I shall sing your mercies forever; I shall remember for eternity that you were merciful to me.

I have said little by calling you merciful. I say more, and more truly declare what is true: you are my mercy. You are that inexhaustible mercy in which all merciful persons participate; but in you there is not participation but fullness of mercy—or rather, you are the very fullness of mercy, the utterly full and highest mercy, with which the earth is full: namely, the holy Church, which continually cries to you, “My God, my mercy.” [Col. 1747C] Many things are said, and many can be said, about your goodness; but all are comprehended in this one thing, when you are called not so much merciful as mercy itself.

Whatever we are, whether by nature as human beings or by profession as believers, is wholly from your gift, O God. Hence your praiser, in thanksgiving, more rightly calls you his mercy than merciful to him, since even the wicked person, when you do him good, will confess to you that you are merciful to him. But one who first considers your mercies over all your works praises you in all things because you are his mercy, since he counts it as done for his consolation that you, eternal mercy, have mercy on all; and he derives matter for praise from the fact that, for his consolation, and even at his prayer, you, eternal mercy, have mercy even upon enemies who show him no mercy.

On this passage blessed Gregory says in Homily 18 [Note: [Col. 1747C] *On the Gospels*]: “Considering in what labors human life is constituted, the Prophet called God a helper; and because he receives us from present tribulation into eternal rest, he also calls him protector. But considering that he sees and bears our evils, tolerates our faults, and nevertheless reserves us through repentance for rewards, he did not wish to call God merciful, but called him mercy itself, saying: ‘My God, my mercy.’ Let us therefore recall before our eyes the evils we have done; let us weigh how great is the kindness by which God tolerates us. Let us consider the inward tenderness of his compassion: that he not only pardons faults, but even promises the heavenly kingdom to penitents after their faults. And from all the depths of our hearts, let each of us say, let all of us say: ‘My God, my mercy.’”

Glory to the strong and merciful Father, whose strength and mercy I shall sing. Glory to the Son, who is [Col. 1748C] the Father’s strength, which I shall sing. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is the mercy of Father and Son, which I have undertaken to sing in this psalm, saying:

> But I will sing your strength,  
> and in the morning exalt your mercy.

## PSALM 59

[Col. 1747]

[Col. 1747D] “O God, you have cast us off and destroyed us,” etc. The title of this psalm is:

(**VERSES 1–2**) **UNTIL THE END: FOR THOSE WHO SHALL BE CHANGED, IN THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE, FOR DAVID HIMSELF, FOR INSTRUCTION: WHEN HE SET MESOPOTAMIA OF SYRIA ON FIRE, AND SYRIA SOBA, AND JOAB TURNED, AND HE STRUCK EDOM IN THE VALLEY OF SALT, TWELVE THOUSAND.**

It is read in Chronicles that, when Nahash king of the Ammonites had died, David sent messengers to console his son Hanun. But when his princes suggested to Hanun that David had sent the messengers more to spy out the land than to do him honor, Hanun shaved David’s servants, cut them close, cut off their garments from the buttocks to the feet, and dismissed them. Then Hanun himself and his people, seeing that they had wronged David, sent a thousand talents and hired chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, Syria, and other places. When David heard this, he sent Joab with an army against them in battle and routed them (1 Chron. 19:1 ff.).

It is also read in the Second Book of Kings that, after Saul’s death, when David was reigning successfully, he struck, among many others, Hadadezer king of Zobah, which is a part of Syria; and Syria became tributary, serving David. After Syria was captured and twelve thousand men of Edom slain, he set guards in Idumaea when he returned, and all Idumaea became subject to David (2 Kings 8:1–10). But we do not read how Joab “turned,” except that, when the king appointed after Saul’s death had taken the citadel of Zion, [Col. 1749A] he said: “Whoever first strikes the Jebusite shall be prince.” And Joab went up first and became prince (1 Chron. 11:6). Or perhaps it refers to the time when men from Judah came to David and David feared them: “But the Spirit clothed Abishai, Joab’s brother, and he said: ‘We are yours, O David; peace be to you’” (ibid. 12:18).

It should also be noted that in the aforementioned slaughter of the Syrians we nowhere read that David set anything on fire. Therefore, as elsewhere, so here too the text departs from history for the sake of its signification when it says, “he set on fire.” And this psalm points forward to Christ, treating of those—that is, for the honor of those—who shall be changed from an old life into a new one, in the inscription of a title made for David himself: that is, by embracing faith in Christ’s kingdom, of which Pilate placed a title above the cross. Or the order is: they shall be changed not for themselves, but [Col. 1749B] for David himself, so that they may live for him, entering into the instruction by which he said: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36).

This change occurred when he “kindled Mesopotamia of Syria,” etc. Mesopotamia is interpreted “an exalted calling”; Syria, “lofty”; Zobah, “vain antiquity”; Joab, “enemy”; Edom, “earthly.” By all these are signified those puffed up by the height of vanity, whom Christ kindles with the fire of charity—which he came to cast upon the earth—in order that they may be renewed. Thus he turns the enemy: either the devil to flight, or the Christian to faith. He struck Edom—that is, he slew the earthly man so that he might live as one made heavenly. He struck twelve thousand of Edom: a perfect number, to which the number of the apostles is assigned, who called people from the four quarters of the world to faith in the Trinity. Hence by this number the whole world struck down is signified. [Col. 1749C] In the Valley of Salt-pits. The valley is humility; the salt-pits, the savor of wisdom. Therefore those were struck in the Valley of Salt-pits who did not suffer vainly, as many heretics do for earthly things, but were wisely humbled for the Lord.

The Prophet speaks of those thus changed, and first recounts the blows inflicted in order that eternal punishments might be avoided. Secondly, he prays for deliverance and, strengthening them by intercession to endure persecutions, confirms them there: “That thy beloved may be delivered.” Therefore, after this slaughter has been accomplished by the fire of charity and the sword of God’s Word, those themselves, changed for the better, will say: “O God, thou hast cast us off.” [Col. 1749D] The first period of the second fifty, which, as we said above, builds toward hope, having ended, this psalm returns to the summit of hope when it says: “O God, thou hast cast us off; thou hast been angry, and hast had mercy on us.” For we say this as those looking forward to Christ’s coming, by which we are to be changed into immortality and impassibility, according to this form of the title: “Unto the end, for those who shall be changed, in the inscription of the title, for David”: for those, he says, who are to be changed unto the end—that is, into immortality and impassibility—because they have received the inscription of the often-mentioned title, which inscription was made for David himself.

It continues: “For instruction, when he kindled Mesopotamia of Syria, and Syrian Zobah, and converted [Col. 1750A] Joab, and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt-pits, twelve thousand.” For this reason he says, “they shall be changed”: because they received his teaching, because by living well and speaking well they became his imitators. And this came not from themselves but from God, who kindled them with the fire of the Holy Spirit, making them Mesopotamia of Syria—that is, calling and raising them on high. For Mesopotamia is interpreted “an exalted calling,” and Syria, “loftiness.” He did this to them when they had previously been Syrian Zobah—that is, the loftiness of vain antiquity. “And he converted,” he says, “Joab.” Joab is interpreted “enemy,” which indeed all of us were; but we have been changed into friends, because through Christ we have been reconciled. “And he struck,” he says, “Edom in the Valley of Salt-pits, twelve thousand.” We too were Edom—that is, earthly and bloody [Col. 1750B] people—but he struck us in the Valley of Salt-pits, making us dead to vices by the two-edged sword of his Word in humility and the seasoning of virtues. And we are, as it were, twelve thousand in number, a number completed by the parts of seven—that is, three and four. For three times four, or four times three, makes twelve. Having the sevenfold gifts of the Spirit, we confess and preach the faith of the Holy Trinity throughout the four parts of the world. At his first coming he kindled believers with penitential fire; but at his second coming, when he comes, he will kindle unbelievers with punitive fire. For the better part, in this psalm we say: “Thou hast given a sign to those who fear thee, that they may flee from the face of the bow, that thy beloved may be delivered,” etc.

[Col. 1750C] Having thus briefly anticipated matters concerning the sense of the whole psalm, let us, God favoring us, begin from the opening in order to consider it more fully.

**VERSE 3. “O God, thou hast cast us off.”** “Thou art just, O Lord, and thy judgment is right, and all thy ways are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10; 118:137). For by thy just judgment thou hast cast us away from that inner rest of Paradise which we possessed in the first parent and lost in him, his sin requiring it. And thou hast destroyed us by imposing the sentence of death, by which thou saidst: “Thou art earth, and unto earth thou shalt go” (Gen. 3:19). Again: “In the sweat of thy face thou shalt eat thy bread. When thou hast worked the earth, it shall not yield its fruits, but shall bring forth thorns and thistles for thee” (ibid., 18). In these words thou hast been angry and hast had mercy on us: angry because of sin, but merciful for thine own sake. [Col. 1750D] Thou hast been angry because of our ungodliness, but merciful because of thy goodness. As a physician is at once angry and merciful to a sick person, cutting and healing his wounds; and as a father is angry and merciful to his son, beating and instructing him: so thou, O God, hast been angry and hast had mercy on us. For if, after sin, we had not been forbidden the tree of life and had tasted its fruit, we should live eternally like angels; and, as with sinning angels, we should have a wretched eternity and eternal wretchedness. But now, because in just anger and gracious mercy thou hast cast us away from the tree of life, lest by taking from it we should live eternally after committing sin, as the transgressing angel lives—who, although he bears the wound of the sword, nevertheless lives, [Col. 1751A] because he cannot die—we give thee thanks, O God, because thou hast cast us away from the tree of life. To heal in us the death of souls, thou hast destroyed us through the mortality and death of bodies: in this judgment thou hast at once been angry and merciful to us, while through the sentence of death—

**VERSE 4. “Thou hast moved the earth and troubled it.”** Thou hast moved it by casting it away from the rest of Paradise; thou hast troubled it by cursing the earth in the work of the sinner. And since for this reason thou broughtest bodily death upon man, that from death itself thou mightest make a medicine, heal its breaches; cure the languors of the earth—that is, of human nature—moved to mercy by this very fact, that it has been moved, made mobile and unstable, although it was created for the immovable stability of eternity inasmuch as it was made in the image and likeness of God. But by going into exile from God’s likeness in the region of unlikeness, it has been so moved that there can be no standing for “man born of woman, living for a short time, filled with many miseries, who comes forth like a flower and is crushed, and flees as a shadow, and never remains in the same state” (Job 14:1–2). Amid all miseries of this kind:

**VERSE 5. “Thou hast shown thy people hard things; thou hast made us drink the wine of compunction.”** And through these very hard things:

**VERSE 6. “Thou hast given a sign to those who fear thee, that they may flee from the face of the bow,”** stretched to strike at the final judgment those who are not corrected by the hard things shown in the present miseries, and who are not at all pierced by the wine of compunction even when they are pierced by miseries.

[Col. 1751C] Otherwise: “O God, thou hast cast us off,” who were Syrian Zobah—that is, the loftiness of vain antiquity through ambition or empty glory; who were Edom—that is, earthly through the concupiscence of the flesh; who were Joab—that is, enemy through the concupiscence of the eyes. For John says: “Everything that is in the world is concupiscence of the flesh, concupiscence of the eyes, and the ambition of the age” (1 John 2:6). Us, I say, such as we were, thou hast in just judgment cast off, and shown us worthy of rejection. And lest, by remaining such, we should always be cast off, thou hast destroyed us, so that we who were Syrian Zobah—that is, lofty, vain, and ancient—might, destroyed from this loftiness, vanity, and antiquity, [Col. 1751D] become humble, stand in truth, and walk in newness of life; that we who were Edom—that is, earthly—might become spiritual; and that we who were Joab—that is, enemy—might become friends of God, to whom thou, O God, who hast destroyed us, mayest say: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15:15).

Before we were thus destroyed, thou wast angry with us, proud as we were, because of our sins. But after thou hadst destroyed us, thou hadst mercy on us humbled. Or: thou wast angry with us in the first Adam; thou hadst mercy in the second. Or: thou wast angry in inflicting a just punishment; thou hadst mercy in making that very punishment not destructive but corrective. Thou wast angry by pouring wine into our wounds; thou hadst mercy by adding the oil [Col. 1752A] of compassion. Thou wast angry with the faults that we made; thou hadst mercy on us whom thou made. Thou wast angry with our work; thou hadst mercy on thy work. Out of this anger and mercy together thou, moved, hast moved the earth with a healing movement toward repentance, and hast troubled it with a disturbance so strong that it is crushed and broken beneath the hammer of tribulation threatening on every side. And because thou dost not despise a contrite and humbled heart, thou who crushest the earth of human flesh so that the spirit may be saved, now heal its breaches by removing the manifold miseries of mortality and death. We do not pray for the world, which lies in the evil one and has no change, but for those whom thou didst foreknow as thine by faith and works, and didst choose out of the world: namely, for those who shall be changed, now by confessing in the inscription of the title, “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews,” [Col. 1752B] and who shall be changed for instruction, namely, by keeping sound doctrine. This doctrine teaches that life must now be changed for the better through goodness, and at the end changed again for the better through impassibility. For those who shall thus be changed, and are foreknown to be changed, we pray that what is to happen may happen sooner; and we desire that the breaches of the earth—that is, of their flesh—may be healed, saying: “Heal its breaches, for it has been moved.” For otherwise it is unworthy to be healed unless it has been moved; nor does it deserve to be healed by impassibility unto eternal blessedness unless it has first been moved by repentance unto godliness. Heal it unto the end indicated beforehand in the title, so that its healing may be complete unto the end—that is, into [Col. 1752C] Christ. For Christ is the end of the law unto righteousness for those who are now changed for instruction; and the same Christ is the end of every consummation for those who shall be changed into glory. For “we shall indeed all rise again, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51) then into glory, because now we are not all changed for instruction by keeping sound doctrine. Weak flesh, moved and troubled, cannot keep that doctrine unless it has been healed by grace. Therefore I pray: “Heal its breaches, for it has been moved.”

And it is no wonder that it has been moved, because thou hast shown thy people hard things. To thy people hurrying toward sweet and pleasant things, thou hast shown hard things. When the sons of Zebedee asked that one might sit at thy right hand and the other at thy left in thy kingdom, thou saidst: “You do not know what you ask”; and thou addedst: “Can you drink the cup that I am to drink?” (Matt. 20:22). By saying this, thou hast shown thy people hard things to be borne before pleasant things are received: first warfare, then reigning; first drinking the cup of suffering, filled from the torrent in the way, then sitting at table in the kingdom. Therefore thou sayest: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 22:28), that is, who have endured hard things, and, made to drink the wine of compunction, have drunk my cup and shall drink it even unto death. Therefore, “I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (ibid., 30). Thus thou hast shown thy people hard things to be suffered before pleasant things. [Col. 1753A] Hence also that saying: “My son, when thou drawest near to the service of God, stand in righteousness and prepare thy soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). These things were said for those who shall be changed. For those who shall not be changed flee the hard things which they see, but afterward they will fall into harder things which they do not see. Thou hast shown thy people even those unseen hard things, which are to be avoided by visible hard things—hard things which seem hard only to the hard-hearted, even to hear of, much less to endure. Hence they say: “This saying is hard” (John 6:61). But for those who shall be changed and are converted through these hard things, this very hardness soon becomes soft; therefore they say: “Thou hast made us drink the wine of compunction.” That is, thou hast made us such that, if at any time severe and harsh torments should come upon us for righteousness’ sake, piercing the body and compuncting [Col. 1753B] the heart, they would please us rather than sadden us, or would so make us drink—that is, intoxicate us—that we should hold them of little account.

Otherwise: “Thou hast made us drink the wine of compunction,” not wine in which is luxury, not wine which overturns the heart, but that which gladdens the heart of man; by it also the sufferer is cleansed as a wound by wine, when the Samaritan tends the wounded man left half-dead, pouring in oil and wine (Luke 10:33). By this wine the wounded person is healed, and the healed person is made to drink; and before the change by which he is changed toward righteousness, he is afflicted, and afterward he is nonetheless afflicted for righteousness’ sake. First, wine as though mingled with myrrh or gall must be tasted briefly; afterward, wine as though excellent, worthy for the beloved [Col. 1753C] to drink, must be long chewed by his lips and teeth. For one must quickly submit to tribulation preparing one for righteousness, and must endure long in tribulation that proves righteousness. Thus Saul, called from heaven and thrown down upon the earth, was made to drink as though wine mingled with myrrh or gall, and was quickly changed so as to say: “Lord, what dost thou wish me to do?” (Acts 9:6). But afterward, afflicted for righteousness’ sake, he was made to drink as though the finest wine; he chewed this same wine for a long time, because he bore long persecutions with patience. In them he even gloried, saying: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience, patience testing, testing indeed hope, and hope does not confound” (Rom. 5:3–5). Again: “Who shall [Col. 1753D] separate us from the charity of God? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword? As it is written: For thy sake we are put to death all day long; we are accounted as sheep for slaughter” (Rom. 8:35–36). Does he not chew good wine who joyfully and gloriously enumerates his own tribulations, and similarly recounts the tribulations of his disciples: “which you endure,” he says, “as an example of the just judgment of God” (2 Thess. 1:4–5)? The Jews wished to make Christ drink wine mingled with gall when they judged that he ought to be put to death as an evildoer; but when he had tasted it, he would not drink, because he was wholly free from the gall of malice. Moreover, that thief on the right, made to drink wine of this sort mingled with gall and thereby changed, is rightly understood [Col. 1754A] to have been one who, suffering not for righteousness but for wickedness, was quickly changed to righteousness by confessing his wickedness. Thus, as though made to drink the wine of compunction, pierced in body and compunct in heart, he became a confessor from a thief, and from an unjust man so great a lover and emulator of righteousness that he firmly rebuked his blaspheming companion and, filled with the faith which justifies the ungodly, cried to Christ: “Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom” (Luke 23:42).

Thus, through the wine administered to thy beloved and elect, thou hast given a sign to those who fear thee, that they may flee from the face of the bow. They know that God’s judgment, begun from the sanctuary, will one day strike like a bow long drawn against those who now afflict the saints, unless [Col. 1754B] they too, fleeing from the face of the bow, become such as not to refuse to suffer with the saints and for the saints what they inflict upon the saints. Thus Saul, who stoned Stephen, was himself afterward stoned; and three times beaten with rods, and afflicted by many dangers of rivers, dangers of robbers, and other dangers, he expiated the guilt contracted by persecuting the saints. Therefore thou hast given a sign to those who fear thee, while thou sparest not those who love thee. For while thou scourgest every son whom thou receivest, thou dost not leave unpunished him whom thou rejectest; while thou rebukest and chastisest those whom thou lovest, thou indicate that thine enemies are to be punished more severely. Therefore let them flee from the face of the outstretched bow; let them flee from the wrath of the future judgment made manifest in the judgment by which God now judges the saints, a judgment which begins with the saints [Col. 1754C] whom he intends to appoint as judges in his own judgment.

This bow is visible in the clouds of heaven, flashing as though with azure and fiery splendor, because the elect—purified through the waters of baptism and tears, and inflamed with the fire of charity—shine forth and will one day judge the world, as it is written: “They shall judge nations, and rule peoples, and their Lord shall reign for ever” (Wis. 3:8). Therefore the bow, prefiguring judgment, is appropriately displayed in the clouds, because judicial power is reserved for the saints, who are denoted by clouds. Hence Isaiah: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isa. 60:8). Christ is rightly believed to be revealed as judge in clouds of this kind, according to the saying: “Behold, the Lord shall come in the clouds of heaven with great power” (Luke 21:27). [Col. 1754D] These clouds now send out the rains of prayers; then they will send out the lightning bolts of judgments. In these clouds the shining bow is seen, because the world will be judged in them and through them. Hence Isaiah: “And behold, he shall come swiftly and speedily; the hoofs of his horses are like flint, and all his bows are stretched” (Isa. 5:26–28). The horses are the same as the clouds in which the Lord will be seen, as it is written: “Behold, the Lord will appear upon a white cloud, and with him thousands of saints” (Rev. 14:14). Because they are to judge with the Lord, it is rightly said: “All his bows are stretched.” The bow of divine judgment is drawn out but does not yet strike; it will strike, and the more powerfully because it is drawn more slowly. For just as in a bow, the farther back the string is drawn, the more violently [Col. 1755A] the arrow is driven forward, so judgment, the longer it delays, will be the more grievous.

A sign of this is given either when the bow is placed in the clouds of heaven, while saints are now judged and will afterward judge; or in the banner of the cross, upon which the Judge of the living and the dead delivered himself to one judging him unjustly, though he would afterward judge justly. Let those who behold that sign flee from the face of the bow by imitating Christ’s passion, because if we are companions in his sufferings, we shall also be companions in his resurrection. “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (Rom. 8:17).

It is one thing to suffer, another to suffer with Christ; for not all who suffer suffer with Christ, nor do all who die die with Christ. Likewise, it is one thing to reign, another to reign with Christ. [Col. 1755B] The blaspheming thief suffered, yet did not suffer with Christ; he died, yet did not die with Christ. Nero reigned, but did not reign with Christ. But the penitent and confessing thief suffered with Christ and died with Christ in that, repenting and confessing, he was justified amid punishments. It would indeed have been much better if, justified before punishments, he had been led to punishment for righteousness’ sake, like Peter. Peter, bound by another and led to the cross for righteousness’ sake, did not expiate faults by his death but glorified God, as Christ had foretold him, signifying beforehand by what death he would glorify God. Surely, when it was signified to Peter by what death he would glorify God, thou, O Christ, in the one Peter gavest [Col. 1755C] a sign to those who fear thee, that they might flee from the face of the bow in the manner in which Peter fled. For because, when he was young, he had girded himself and walked where he wished, the just requital of righteousness required that another should gird him and lead him where he would not wish, for the glorifying of God’s glory.

Nearly similar to this is the case when someone, acknowledging the sins of youth in which he walked where he wished, by a voluntary vow takes upon himself the Lord’s light yoke, is girded through obedience by the bond of the regular life, and is led where he does not wish. For truly precious is that obedience in which self-will is broken: when a wise master wisely commands what serves God’s glory, and the disciple humbly obeys for God’s glory. It is for God’s glory that one obey those seated upon Moses’ chair, not only the good and gentle but also the unruly, provided that they do not command things by which they overthrow the just chair, valuing their own corrupt traditions above God’s holy ones. Thus, to be girded and led without dispute under such persons to some labor by which God may be glorified is to flee from the face of the bow. Indeed, one thus girded need not merely be unafraid, in human judgment, of being struck by the bow of judgment: if he perseveres unto the end, he may also confidently—not in vain hope—trust in Christ’s promise that he will judge with the Lord and will possess in judgment a bow feared by his adversaries. Nor is it surprising, since even in this life the elect are so furnished with bows that, by the light of God’s arrows, they now terrify invisible and visible enemies [Col. 1756A] and at times overthrow them with the sharp arrows either of prayers or of judgments. Hence, in praise of their king, these soldiers continually say: “Thy arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath thee, in the heart of the king’s enemies.” They fall in the heart, certainly, not in the body: they are humbled, and, having previously been enemies of the king, become friends. Or, if they refuse to become friends and persist in being enemies, they will not flee from the face of the bow on the day of judgment, when they shall be struck in body and heart together and cast into the prison of Gehenna’s fire. Yet because mercy and truth shall precede thy face, O dread Judge, in the Scriptures of truth, because of thy mercy thou hast given a sign to those who fear thee, that they may flee from the face of the bow.

A *diapsalma* is inserted here, separating what has been said from what is to be said. [Col. 1756B] For David, who in singing has seemed to assume the person of one judging and threatening with a drawn bow, by a sudden change assumes the person of a petitioner and intercessor, saying to God: “That thy beloved may be delivered.”

**VERSE 7. “Save with thy right hand, and hear me.”**

The order of the words is: “Hear me, and save with thy right hand, that thy beloved may be delivered.” Because there will be a judgment in which those who now wish to flee from the face of the bow, while it is time to flee, will then be struck by an unavoidable bow, I David pray for those who shall be changed in the inscription of the title: that the name Joab, meaning “enemy,” being changed in them, they may become friends and beloved; and thus thy beloved may be delivered. [Col. 1756C] Praying for them, I say: “Save with thy right hand, and hear me.” I do not say, “Hear them,” because they either do not pray or do not pray sufficiently, and are not worthy to be heard so long as they have not been changed in the inscription of the title. But I say, “Hear me praying for those whom thou hast predestined to become thy beloved in thy beloved Son.” Hear me for them, so that what they already are in thine eyes, to whom future things are present, they may also be in human eyes: namely, beloved, openly distinguished from the hated, as Jacob, of whom he says: “Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated” (Mal. 1:2–3). Hear me, that thy beloved may be delivered from the hated, as Jacob, beloved to thee, was delivered from his brother Esau, hated by thee, when Esau pursued him; or as that same beloved man was delivered from his uncle Laban, who pursued him and searched all his possessions in order to find the idols with him, but did not find what he sought. Thus may thy beloved be delivered, so that the prince of this world, signified by Laban, may find nothing of his own among them. Or, as the same beloved man was delivered from the inner discord of his sons when he came to his son Joseph, ruling over all the land of Egypt, so may thy beloved be delivered from the inward ruin caused by discordant subjects, or by thoughts accusing or even defending one another on the day when the Lord shall judge the secrets of hearts. For just as Joseph accused his brothers before his father of a very grave crime and was therefore beloved by his father, whereas his brothers hated him and could not speak any word peacefully to him (Gen. 37:1), [Col. 1757A] so to this day thy beloved are very hateful to criminal brethren for this reason: because they accuse and detest their crimes. Therefore it is necessary that thy beloved be delivered from those who hate them, as Joseph was delivered from his brothers; or rather, as that true Joseph, thy Beloved, was delivered, to whom thou sayest: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). For he too, by accusing his Jewish brethren, especially the scribes and Pharisees, was hated by them and sold, not into slavery but to death. From that death he has been delivered and now rules over all the land of Egypt—indeed, over heaven and earth—as he himself said after his resurrection: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18).

Therefore let the deliverance from all evils which preceded [Col. 1757B] in the Head follow in the members, that thy beloved may be delivered. So long as even one of them has not been delivered, I, being weak with the weak, regard myself as neither delivered nor saved. Therefore, feeling the infirmities of each person within myself through the bowels of compassion and saying with the Apostle, “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11:29), I continually pray for each and for all, saying: “Save with thy right hand, and hear me”; save me with so great a salvation that all thy beloved and elect may be delivered. Save me, not by thy left hand, in which are riches and glory, but by thy right hand, in which is length of days, at which the sheep and lambs to be delivered from the face of the bow shall be set. I do not ask to be enriched or saved by the glory and riches of thy left hand, knowing that “those who desire to become rich” in such things “fall into temptation and the snare of the devil” (1 Tim. 6:9), from which snare thy elect and beloved are to be delivered. Grant me, then, from the left hand, if thou wilt, little; if thou wilt, much; if thou wilt, nothing at all, according as thou knowest it is expedient either for me or for those to whom I must minister such things. But most generously open thy right hand and fill every living thing with the blessing by which thy blessed elect and beloved may be set at thy right hand in judgment and hear: “Come, ye blessed of my Father, and receive the kingdom,” etc. (Matt. 25:34).

Otherwise: “Save with thy right hand,” or, as it is read in Hebrew: “Save with thy right hand, and lift me up,” so that thy left hand may be under my head and thy right hand embrace me, [Col. 1757D] lest either I or any of thy beloved be separated from eternal salvation. May thy right hand, binding us into one and embracing each and all through the love by which we may be thy beloved worthy of thy deliverance, hold us fast. Hear one praying thus not merely by inward affection, but also answer by outward effect.

And lest anyone wonder why I place the hope of my salvation in the right hand rather than in the left, let him know that in the Valley of Salt-pits I have received this savor, by which I relish eternal things more than temporal. A marvelous thing! Those who savor the things above cannot do so unless they are in the valley; for God “looks upon the lowly” as though from near at hand, and “knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. 137:6). Hence, when the Apostle had said, “Savor the things above,” showing that his hearers, called to heavenly things, were [Col. 1758A] in a valley—indeed, in the Valley of Salt-pits—he added: “For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:2). It is a valley, and indeed the Valley of Salt-pits, to imitate the humility of Christ dying, who humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death. One who is unwillingly humbled by another and subjected to others is indeed in a valley, but not in the Valley of Salt-pits, because such humiliation has no savor for him as it has for one who can say from his heart:

> “It is good for me, O Lord, that thou hast humbled me, that I may learn thy justifications” (Ps. 118:71).

See that humility justifies us. I said humility, not humiliation. How many are humiliated who are not humble, and are thereby proved not to be in the Valley of Salt-pits, [Col. 1758B] because it does not taste good—or like a good thing—to them that they are humbled. For some are humbled resentfully, others patiently, and others willingly. The first are guilty; the next innocent; the last righteous. The first, as though in the valley of Gehenna, lose their souls; the second, as though in the valley of tears, possess their souls in patience; but the third, in the Valley of Salt-pits, savoring the things above, exalt their souls. Good is the exaltation of souls which occurs in the Valley of Salt-pits, where whoever humbles himself shall be exalted. Good is the patience that preserves souls in the valley of tears. For patience itself is a part of righteousness and wisdom, but its perfection belongs to the humble person. The humble person is one who can say: “It is good for me that thou hast humbled [Col. 1758C] me.” The one who bears it unwillingly cannot say this, much less the one who murmurs. We promise grace to neither merely because he is humbled, although these two differ greatly from one another. One indeed, possessing his soul in patience, makes progress as though in the valley of tears; the other fails in his murmuring and, unless he repents, perishes utterly in the valley of Gehenna. But although one incurs wrath, neither merits grace, because God gives grace not to the humiliated but to the humble.

There is, however, one who passes from the valley of tears, or even from the valley of Gehenna, into the Valley of Salt-pits when he turns his humiliation into humility, and, from being humiliated, becomes humble. In the Valley of Salt-pits he glories in the things over which he had previously been distressed, either patiently [Col. 1758D] in the valley of tears or impatiently in the valley of darkness. He is the one who says to God: “It is good for me that thou hast humbled me.” To no one is what he bears patiently altogether good; it is burdensome. Yet we know that “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). Therefore, when we fast and humble our souls by fasting, we are commanded to anoint our head and wash our face, so that our good work may be seasoned with a certain spiritual savor of joy, as it were in the Valley of Salt-pits, and our burnt offering may become not only fat with the oil of joy, but also clean through the washed countenance of the mind. For joyous and unreserved humility alone merits the grace which it sets before itself. [Col. 1759A] Humility that is forced or extorted, such as belongs to that patient man who possesses his soul, obtains life indeed through patience; but through sadness it will not possess grace. For the scriptural saying does not suit one of this kind: “Let the humble glory in his exaltation” (Jas. 1:9), since he is not voluntarily humbled and does not willingly bear his cross, but under compulsion; nor does he follow Christ, voluntarily humbled, who was offered because he willed it, and who, being in the form of God, took the form of a servant and humbled himself by his own will and voluntary obedience unto death—unto that inscription of the triumphal title by which, in the Valley of Salt-pits, he struck twelve thousand, conforming the apostles and apostolic men to himself.

Would you hear of one of the twelve thousand struck in the Valley [Col. 1759B] of Salt-pits: a perfect man, perfectly humbled, who, called by Christ from heaven and cast down to earth, was wonderfully joined to the twelve thousand in the apostolic height? I speak of the Apostle Paul: truly Paul—that is, humble—rightly glorying in his humiliation and truly worthy of glory. “Most gladly,” he says, “will I glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12:9). He does not say that he patiently bears his infirmities, but that he glories—and gladly glories—in them, proving that it is good for him to be humbled. Nor is it at all enough for him to possess his soul, as though humbled patiently in the valley of tears, unless, in the Valley of Salt-pits, not savoring high things but consenting to the lowly, seasoned as it were with the salt of wisdom, [Col. 1759C] he receives grace, whose power is made perfect in weakness when weakness itself is willingly borne. Hear then the general rule: “Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11). This plainly signifies that not every humility is to be exalted, but only that which proceeds from the will, not from sadness or necessity. For conversely, not everyone who is exalted will be humbled, but only “he who exalts himself shall be humbled” (ibid.), namely, because of voluntary vanity. Therefore, it is not the person who is humiliated, but the one who voluntarily humbles himself, who will be exalted—surely because of the merit of the will. Granted that another supplies the material of humility—for example, reproaches, losses, or punishments—yet the person who prefers to bear all these with a silent and cheerful conscience rather than depart from the path of righteousness he has undertaken in order to avoid them is rightly said to be humbled not by another but by himself. For it is too little, when God humbles us through himself, that we willingly accept it then, unless, when he does this through another, we likewise savor it in the Valley of Salt-pits. In that valley there is not one salt-pit but many: the person who is to be advanced is humbled by manifold tribulation—now through assaults of the devil, as blessed Job; now through adversities from people, as holy David; now through divine testings, as the patriarch Abraham; now through the weakness of his own flesh, as Lazarus; or through a thorn, as Paul. Many are the tribulations of the righteous besides those we have mentioned. Through all these, arranged like many salt-pits [Col. 1760A] in the Valley of Salt-pits by the ordering of heavenly wisdom, those who are to be exalted in the future must needs be humbled.

Therefore, whenever you fall into various temptations and see yourself humbled by tribulations, regard this altogether as a good sign, an argument that grace is drawing near. For just as “before ruin the heart is exalted” (Prov. 16:18), so before exaltation it is humbled. Certainly you read both that God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. Did he not, finally, take care first to humble his servant Job through many searching and exacting questions, when, after Job’s distinguished triumph and such great and proven patience, he judged him worthy to be rewarded with abundant blessing, thus preparing the way for blessing?

Yet, as I have already said, it is little enough if, when God humbles us by himself, we willingly accept it, unless, when he does this through another, we are equally wise. Therefore receive a remarkable example of this matter in holy David. On one occasion he was cursed even by a servant. But he did not regard the injury as piled upon him, because he foresaw grace. “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah?” he says (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 16:10). O truly a man according to God’s heart, who considered that he should be angered with the avenger rather than with the reproacher! Hence he also spoke with a secure conscience: “If I have repaid evils to those repaying me, let me deservedly fall empty before my enemies” (Ps. 7:5).

He therefore forbade the abusive curser to be prevented, reckoning curses as gain. And he added: “The Lord sent him to curse David” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 16:10). Entirely according to God’s heart was he who drew his judgment from God’s heart. A cursing tongue raged, while he attended to what God was doing secretly. The curser’s voice sounded in his ears, while his spirit bent itself toward blessing. Was God in the blasphemer’s mouth? Far from it! But God used him to humble David. Nor was this hidden from the Prophet, to whom God had revealed the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom, and whom he had placed in the Valley of Salt-pits. Thus he says: “It is good for me that you humbled me, that I might learn your ordinances.”

For, seasoned with the salt of wisdom in the Valley of Salt-pits and introduced into wisdom’s hidden things, he learned also what ought most especially to be sought amid salt-pits such as these: namely, this—that your beloved may be delivered, O God, while your right hand helps, saves, and at the same time delivers them.

Therefore I also—the Church, or an ecclesiastical person—singing in David’s spirit and mind, pray: “That your beloved may be delivered, O God, save with your right hand”; your right hand working in them and through them the virtues and good works concerning which it will be said to those who will stand at your right in your judgment: “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and in prison, and you visited me” (Matt. 25:35–36).

In these words both the sixfold virtue of the least ones who endure hunger, thirst, pilgrimage, nakedness, sickness, and imprisonment for Christ and in Christ, and the sixfold activity of those who minister to Christ in such persons, are so clearly commended in those who will be at his right hand that, for those humbled in the Valley of Salt-pits, nothing seems sweeter than this: that, O God, while your right hand saves them, they may abound in virtues and works of this kind, by which they may be wholly separated from the goats placed on the left and, when you judge, be found among the sheep of your pasture at your right hand. Desiring this intensely, those who wisely sing in the Valley of Salt-pits say for themselves and for the other beloved of God: “That your beloved may be delivered, save with your right hand, and hear me.”

Otherwise: In the blessings with which Moses blessed the children of Israel, it is said among other things: “The Lord appeared from Mount Paran, and with him were thousands of saints. In his right hand was a fiery law. He loved the peoples” (Deut. 33:2–3). To recall these words now might seem superfluous, except that the thousands of saints appearing with the Lord, of whom Moses speaks, are none other than those “twelve thousand slain in the Valley of Salt-pits” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 8:13), with whom the psalm is concerned; and his right hand, in which is the fiery law, is the very hand by which the Psalmist asks to be saved, saying: “That your beloved may be delivered, save with your right hand, and hear me.”

Nor are any other persons rightly understood as God’s beloved in the psalm than those of whom Moses, after first saying, “In his right hand was a fiery law,” immediately added, “He loved the peoples.” Thus you may plainly understand the fiery law in God’s right hand as the most ardent charity expressed in his strongest and best works, by which “he loved the peoples”—the peoples, I say, in the plural, not a people in the singular: not one Jewish people, but all peoples foreordained to blessedness.

Finally, just as at the time when he appeared to Moses in a flame of fire from the midst of the bush and delivered one people, his own special people, from the hand of Pharaoh and the Egyptians with a mighty hand and uplifted arm, so now also, in the fiery law of his right hand—that is, with the burning charity of his omnipotence—he appeared to us in order to deliver us from the hand of the spiritual Pharaoh and his armies: evil spirits together with the whole multitude of vices and vicious persons. With the strong hand by which he conquered the devil himself, he who is stronger overcame that strong man’s courtyard and took away his weapons and abundant spoils—not one people, but many peoples. This was not because the peoples loved him, but because he first loved them. “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his beloved Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. 8:29), among the beloved and more beloved than all the beloved.

Many beloved persons have already been delivered through this one Beloved in spirit and are still to be delivered in body at the final resurrection. Many have been delivered neither in spirit nor in flesh, but are still to be delivered in both; some are not even yet born or known before human beings, yet they are known to him who “loved the peoples” from eternity and foreknew them as his own from eternity. For the full deliverance of all these and their gathering to his people in the kingdom of heaven, the Holy Spirit asks with unutterable groanings in every beloved person who sings and says: “That your beloved may be delivered, save with your right hand, and hear me.”

Save me by your right hand, in which is the fiery law, namely the most ardent charity by which you loved the peoples. Therefore, that all peoples beloved by you may be delivered, and that the full assembly of all tribes ascending to confess your name may come into being—those gathered into one from every people and nation under heaven, whom you loved before the foundation of the world—let your right hand now work salvation in the midst of the earth through the fire of charity so magnificently that there is no one who can hide from its heat. This is what we pray daily when we say:

> Let charity blaze with fire;  
> Let its ardor kindle our neighbors.

And lest anyone wonder with what confidence so great a thing is requested, I say that God has so foreordained and spoken beforehand, “at many times and in many ways formerly through the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us through his Son, through whom he also made the ages” (Heb. 1:1)—“as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and his seed for ever” (Luke 1:55), and “as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old” (ibid., v. 70) concerning the salvation of his beloved. Thus, and far more effectually:

**VERSE 8.** “He spoke in his holy one,” that is, in his Son, by so much more distinctly as he inherited a name more excellent than theirs. After the superscription of the incorruptible title, the triumphal title, he rose from the dead as victor over death and author of salvation. When he appeared to the disciples, he said among other things: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18). And he added: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved; but whoever does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16:15–16).

Since therefore God has thus spoken in his holy one, I, the catholic and apostolic Church, fortified in the Valley of Salt-pits by the twelvefold number of the Apostles, as though by twelve thousand, shall do as God spoke to me in his holy one. For that Holy One is God equally with his Father and is himself God: just as God the Father and God the Son are not two gods but one God, so the holy Father and the holy Son are not two holy ones but one Holy One. And therefore, because he spoke in this his Holy One, who is God no less than the Father himself who speaks—for the Word of God is God, and this Word was made flesh—such an utterance, proclaimed throughout the whole world by God speaking and saying in his Holy One, “Go into all the world,” and so forth, cannot be made void.

Go into all the world, because the whole world is mine, all authority in heaven and on earth having been given to me. And lest anyone doubt that the whole world is mine by a double right—since it was created by me when it did not exist, and redeemed by me when it had been lost—I prove from its parts that, all authority in heaven and earth having been given to me, the whole world is mine. For:

**VERSES 9–10.** “Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is the protection of my head. Judah is my king. Moab is the pot of my hope. Into Idumea I shall stretch out my shoe; foreigners are subject to me.”

That is to say: all peoples, both from among the Gentiles and from among the Jews, foreordained to this end, are mine, so that some of them are Gilead, others Manasseh, Ephraim, or Judah, and so forth. Hence, like a victor after the prince of this world has been cast out, just as victors rejoice in captured booty when they divide the spoils, so I shall rejoice and divide Shechem, and measure out the Valley of Tabernacles: delivering some, rejecting others.

Otherwise: I, the Church, made glad by God speaking in the Holy One and assured of the salvation of every creature, shall rejoice in his utterance; and, according as I am taught by him, I shall divide Shechem and measure out the Valley of Tabernacles. Shechem is the place where Jacob, returning from Laban, made shelters for the sheep and herds, and called it Succoth—that is, “Tabernacles”—where he buried the idols that he had brought from Syria (Gen. 33:17), because faith is not everyone’s. According to interpretation, however, *Sichima* means “shoulders,” which are divided: sins burden some, while others bear Christ’s yoke. “And I shall measure out the Valley of Tabernacles.” The valleys of tabernacles, on account of Jacob’s sheep, signify the Jews; these too are divided, because some believed and others did not. That is, among the Jews I have not a few who serve humbly.

“Gilead is mine.” Gilead is the mountain where Laban caught Jacob fleeing with all that he had acquired in Mesopotamia. There, after disputes, they made a covenant together; gathering stones, they made a mound and ate upon it.
