Laban called it “the Mound of Witness,” while Jacob called it “the Heap of Testimony.” And Laban said to Jacob: “This mound shall be a witness between me and you today: whether I cross it in going toward you, or you pass beyond it intending evil against me. Therefore its name was called Gilead, that is, the mound of witness or heap of testimony” (Gen. 31:48, 52). By it martyrs are understood. This heap was formed in the great tribulation, when this reproach was cast against the Church: that it belonged to Christ.

“And Manasseh is mine.” Manasseh was Joseph’s firstborn, whom he named thus, saying: “God has made me forget my labors and my father’s house” (Gen. 41:51). Hence he is interpreted “forgetful,” and signifies that barren woman to whom Isaiah cried, “Rejoice, barren one who does not bear,” and so forth; then added, “You shall not remember the shame of your youth and the reproach of your widowhood” (Isa. 54:1–4). Or they are called Manasseh because they forget the things behind—that is, their former life.

“And Ephraim is the strength of my head.” Ephraim was Joseph’s other son, whom he named thus, saying: “God has made me fruitful in the land of my poverty” (Gen. 41:52). Hence he is interpreted “fruitfulness” or “abundance.” He signifies the grain which, falling into the earth in the Passion, is multiplied in the Resurrection and yields abundant fruit to the Church. This fruitfulness, says the Church, is the strength of my head, that is, of Christ, of whom the Apostle says: “What is weak in God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1:25).

“Judah is my king.” Judah, Jacob’s son, signifies Christ, in whose figure Jacob, blessing Judah, said: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you,” and so forth (Gen. 49:8). This king says: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10:28).

“Moab is the pot of my hope.” Moab is a people named after Moab, whom Lot’s daughter bore by abusing her drunken father. So also those who misuse the Law produce evil works, through which the pot of tribulations boils in the Church. Jeremiah says of it: “I see a boiling pot, and its face is from the face of the north” (Jer. 1:13). For the devil is the north, who said: “I shall set my seat in the north”; and the Lord says of him in the same Jeremiah: “From the north every evil shall be opened” (Jer. 1:14). Thus Moab is a pot because tribulations against the Church arise from those who misuse the Law. But it is the pot of my hope, because “tribulation produces patience, patience testing, and testing hope” (Rom. 5:3–4). From the fact that Judah is my king, a flame of greater charity is kindled against the pot of iniquity.

Or Moab is the pot—that is, the Gentiles, who are nourishment for my hope—while, through frequent victories amid tribulations or temptations, the rawness of carnal life is boiled away in them and becomes spiritual.

“Into Idumea I shall stretch out my shoe.” Although the world boils with scandals, nevertheless into Idumea—that is, even to people of earthly life—I shall stretch out my shoe: that is, the Gospel, by which the life of those walking in the world is fortified. The humanity in which divinity lay hidden shall also be preached; the Passion, signified by a shoe made from a dead animal, shall be preached. Thus those alien by race, that is, the Philistines, are subject to me. For many worship Christ who will not reign with him—namely, false Christians. Or: because they were strangers, but now are subject. Hence: “I shall call Not-my-people, My-people” (Rom. 9:25).

Otherwise: I, Christ, whose soul was sorrowful unto death under the superscription of the title, raised from death, shall rejoice among the disciples rejoicing at the sight of me as Lord. I shall divide Shechem and measure out the Valley of Tabernacles, distinguishing believers from unbelievers by saying: “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved; but whoever does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16:16). And because unbelievers will persecute believers, especially those fit witnesses of truth, ready to die for the testimony of truth itself, “Gilead is mine”—that is, the heap of testimony, namely the white-robed army of martyrs.

“And Manasseh and Ephraim are mine; Ephraim is the strength of my head.” For just as Ephraim, though younger, was placed before Manasseh when his father Jacob blessed him and was reckoned as if firstborn, so the Gentile people has been preferred to the Jewish people by the judgment of the divinity of my Father and of myself, which is the head of me, Christ. Hence my Apostle says: “The head of the woman is the man, the head of the man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3).

And I, Christ, in the passible affection of my humanity indeed wept over my city and nation because it was to be rejected; but the strength of my head—that is, the judgment of my most powerful divinity—prevailed in the rejection of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles. Yet the primitive Church was first gathered from those very Jews. It heard me calling and saying to it: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44:21). Consequently it is rightly designated by the name Manasseh, interpreted “forgetfulness,” because the Apostles, when Judaea rejected the word of God, forgot their people and the house of their father Abraham and passed to the Gentiles, to raise up from stones other sons of Abraham, better than those carnal ones.

For from the stony, hard Gentiles, worshippers of stones, Ephraim, the strength of my head, was raised up. John the herald wished to raise up this Ephraim, interpreted “fruitfulness,” in Judaea, preaching the baptism of repentance and teaching fruits worthy of repentance. But because he did not find there worthy fruits, as was fitting and just, he said: “Now the axe is laid to the root of the tree. Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3:10). Thus the branch of the olive tree was cut off and the wild olive grafted in, so that, bearing worthy fruits, it might be considered worthy of the name Ephraim. Thus the kingdom was taken from the unfruitful Jews and given to a nation producing its fruits.

Because of fruits of this sort, Ephraim is the strength of my head; or, as has already been said, the strength of my head—that is, of me, who am the head of this Ephraim, namely of the whole Church fruitful in good works.

“Judah is my king,” because I shall appoint rulers from the order of confessors for my body, which is the Church. And when they rightly govern the Church, “Moab is the pot of my hope,” because the good shall be boiled through by the evil. Or Moab itself, which is a pot boiling my elect, is in this respect the pot of my hope: I hope, and at the same time cause my own people to hope and pray for such a Moab, that it may be converted and itself, no less, be cooked by the fire of tribulation by which it cooked others, and become wholesome food.

Or Moab, formerly a pot burning with the fire of earthly desire, may burn more intensely with the fire of charity, which “believes all things, hopes all things”; and thus the pot of my hope may boil with good fire, whereas before it boiled with evil fire. It is not enough for me to gather from Judaea persons such as these: martyrs, worthy of the name Gilead; those who forget what lies behind and stretch forward, worthy of the name Manasseh; penitents producing fruits worthy of repentance, named Ephraim; or even a pot full of foods pleasing to me. Rather, “into Idumea I shall stretch out my shoe.”

[Note: Col. 1765D. St Gregory the Great, *Homilies on the Gospels*, book I, homily 7.] “What is designated by Idumea but the Gentile world, and what by the shoe but assumed mortality? Therefore the Lord declares that he stretches out his shoe into Idumea, because, when through the flesh he became known to the Gentiles, divinity came to us, as it were, shod.” For who does not know that shoes are made from dead animals? Therefore the incarnate Lord appeared as if shod: in his divinity he assumed the dead flesh of our corruption.

It is a sign of prevenient grace that God himself, shod in the skin of our mortality, says that he will stretch out his shoe into Idumea. For he himself goes before his preachers and prepares children of peace in Idumea, which is interpreted “earthly” or “bloody,” a name by which, as has been said, the Gentile world is understood. Thus, as divine grace prepares children of peace there in Idumea, the beautiful feet of those bringing good news of peace may find them, and their peace may rest upon them; but if not, it may return to themselves. For “unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain”—“It is vain for you,” O feet proclaiming peace, “to rise before the light” (Ps. 126:2). It is vain for you to preach peace in Idumea unless the light which enlightens every person coming into this world goes before you and prepares children of peace.

Each of you wisely recognizes this when, about to announce peace in Idumea, he first offers the following prayer:

**VERSE 11.** “Who will lead me even into Idumea? Is it not you, O God, who have cast us off? Who will lead me into the fortified city?—Who will lead me into the stronghold that stands against us? Who will lead me into the courtyard of the armed strong man who possesses his goods in peace, in Idumea not yet completely conquered or despoiled?

For where there is still an evil peace, which you did not come to bring, Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews—who, when the inscription of this title was already close at hand, commanded a tunic to be sold and a sword bought, something very contrary to peace—where, I say, such peace still exists, who will lead me there, into the fortified city, or, as other codices read, ‘into the city of the surrounding region’?

By ‘the city of the surrounding region’ he means the Gentile peoples spread around Judaea, which is called the wheel in the words, ‘Your thunder’s voice was in the wheel’ (Ps. 76:19), that is, the world. Or he calls the future Jerusalem a fortified city. Who will lead me even into Idumea, so that I may reign also among earthly persons, who are not of me but desire to profit from me? Every spiritual person desires earthly persons to be joined to him, so that, once the number of the predestined is complete, they may together attain eternity. Is it not you, O God? Who will lead me?

**VERSE 12.** “Is it not you, O God, who have cast us off?” That is, who allow us to be afflicted? See: this is the same thing I said at the beginning of the psalm. It follows: “And will you not go forth, O God, in our forces?” That is, will you not appear against those who say to us, “Where is your God?” as you formerly showed your power to Moses, Joshua, and the rest, in whose armies you visibly went forth: in the pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night, and in the field of Jericho through an armed angel? Do you not now customarily go forth in our forces—or, as it is read in the Hebrew, “in our armies”? You will work inwardly, and thus lead us better into Idumea, because in this way the accomplishment appears more wonderful, and the battle is waged not for temporal life but for the future. Therefore, since you lead us:

**VERSE 13.** “Give us help out of tribulation”: that is, help us precisely where you are thought to abandon us. “And human salvation is vain.” I do not ask you to give temporal salvation, because the temporal salvation of humanity is vain antiquity.

**VERSE 14.** “In God alone,” inwardly and not by the sword outwardly, “we shall do valiantly,” conquering the devil. And he who is our army and our victory, even though we are of no account, will bring to nothing those who trouble us, so that—understand—we may consider them as nothing. Or he will bring them to nothing by blotting them out of the book of life, where they think themselves written and of great account, although, lacking love of God and neighbor, they are nothing. Hence the Apostle says: “And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2).

Therefore, since by lacking charity they are nothing, to be brought to nothing means nothing other than to be brought to self-knowledge, so that, recognizing themselves, they too may flee from the face of the bow. On this verse blessed Gregory says:

[Note: Col. 1767B. Book XIX of the *Morals*, chapter 30.] “What is signified here by the bow except the day of the final judgment? For in a bow, the farther the string is drawn back, the more forceful the arrow will be. So indeed, the day of final judgment: the longer it is delayed in coming, the more severe the sentence that will proceed from it when it comes. This is why we are now struck by diverse calamities: that, corrected by them, we may then be found more ready. Hence it was said beforehand: ‘You have shown your people hard things’—namely, the scourges of the age, which precede the more grievous coming day of judgment. ‘You have given us wine of compunction to drink,’ so that earthly joys might be turned into tears. ‘You have given a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from the face of the bow,’ as if he said: This is the time of mercy; that will be the time of judgment. Therefore by the scourges of this present time you show how you will strike then, when you judge without sparing, since you strike so strictly now when you spare.”

Glory to the Father, delivering his beloved and saving them by his right hand, according as it is said to him in the psalm: “That your beloved may be delivered, save with your right hand, and hear me.” Glory to the Son, who is his right hand, by which he saves his elect and beloved. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is the very love by which the Father loves his elect in the Son, whom he both chose and loved in him before the foundation of the world.

This glory concerning all his saints belonged to the one and triune God in the beginning, when eternal Wisdom, playing in the world, prepared and predestined delights for itself with the children of men. Therefore, as glory belonged to him in the beginning, so may it belong to him in its fulfillment also now, and always, and unto ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 60

[Col. 1767]

[Col. 1767C] “Hear, O God, my supplication; attend to my prayer,” and so forth. This prayer plainly offers hope to the warrior already mentioned, whose heart is troubled when he sees another law in his members resisting the law of his mind and leading him captive under the law of sin: “You have led me,” he says, “because you have become my hope, a tower of strength from the face of the enemy”—namely, that I may avoid vices and attain virtues. What if my heart is now troubled? Why should I wonder amid the heat of temptation, which happens only for a time? At some point I shall dwell in your tabernacle for ever; I shall be protected in the covering of your wings. And the rest.

This psalm has the following title:

**(VERSE 1) UNTO THE END, IN HYMNS: A PSALM OF DAVID.**

“Unto the end” is fitting, for in this struggle he awaits the final deliverance of God’s grace; and this “in hymns,” because, that he fights and strives to conquer, he ascribes not to his own powers but to God’s praises.

Otherwise: “Unto the end, in hymns, of David,” that is, this psalm, offered to David in praises, points unto the End—that is, Christ—through whom the Church, pressed on every side and laboring upon earth, sighs to God the Father. First it prays to God himself and through him declares that it will persevere toward him. Then, having already been heard, it affirms the future inheritance given to it and promises praises, to which it summons its hearers by the whole intention of the psalm, crying from the ends of the earth and saying:

**VERSE 2.** “Hear, O God, my supplication,” delivering me from evils; “attend to my prayer,” perfecting me in good things. For my supplication is that I may lack sins and the penalties of sins; but my prayer is that, living soberly, justly, and devoutly, I may now have fruit unto sanctification and, at the end, eternal life. Or because three things are written in the book of the Lord—namely, “lamentation and song and woe” (Ezek. 2:9)—my supplication is that through the lamentations of fruitful repentance I may be wholly freed from the eternal woe of perpetual damnation and may enjoy the everlasting joy of song in hymns, indicated beforehand in the title of this psalm.

Hear my supplication in such a way that it may appear outwardly to people that you hear me inwardly, while I pray in my chamber to be delivered from evil. Attend to my prayer by secretly storing within me the hidden treasure to which the kingdom of heaven is compared. Hear my supplication, so that outwardly the lamps may be adorned with bright light and never be extinguished. Attend to my prayer, so that oil concealed in vessels may abound until the bridegroom’s coming. Hear me, the whole Church, so that I may be a city set upon a mountain and cannot be hidden, while the light of my works shines before people. Attend to my prayer, so that through these good works God the Father, the author of all good things, who is in heaven, may be glorified—he whom the heavens of heavens conceal within themselves and do not betray through boastful display.

Otherwise: Hear my supplication, so that, while seeking my bridegroom, your Son, outside, I may not begin to wander after the flocks of his companions.

[Note: Col. 1769D. The manuscript reads: “through the flocks.”]

Attend to my prayer, so that, having found him, I may hold him and not let him go until I bring him into the house of my mother, the synagogue, and into the chamber of her who bore me. Hear my supplication, lest I be idle outside the vineyard. Attend to my prayer, so that, laboring in the vineyard, I may be found worthy to receive the denarius. I hope that this intention of supplication and prayer will be heard, both because it is numerous, coming from the many faces of persons crying from the ends of the earth, and because what is to be attained is nothing other than you, O God, since:

**VERSE 3.** “From the ends of the earth, I, the Church, came”—I, the queen, to hear the wisdom of the true Solomon—“I cried to you, O God the Father, from the ends of the earth.” Or literally, because from every part of the world, from every end of the earth, my cry is heard in hymns and spiritual songs. Or: from the ends of the earth, when an end is put to earthly vices and desires, I cried to you, O God. When? “When my heart was troubled,” after the sign had been given me in the preceding psalm that I might flee from the face of the bow. Seeing that no place of escape was open from the east, west, or desert mountains, my spirit was troubled within me; and in this distress, crying to you, O God, from the ends of the earth, I was heard.

For the understanding heart is troubled amid temptations, through which, nevertheless, our progress is made: provoked by temptations, we struggle; in the struggle we conquer; for victory we shall be crowned; and we shall be exalted upon the rock which is Christ. Since the beginning of future exaltation is now, I—the Church, or any ecclesiastical person—say that when my heart was troubled, refusing to yield to assailing vices and resisting them with continual prayers, you, God the Father, exalted me upon the rock of which it was said to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. 16:18). Upon this rock you exalted me, so that I might not slip on a slippery place but stand firmly upon solid ground.

And because the same rock is the way to himself and to you, the homeland, you led me through it. Thus I hope to come through it to itself: through the way to the homeland itself. “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6): the way in pilgrimage, truth and life in the eternal dwelling. On this way, while you, Father, come to me:

**VERSE 14.** “You have become my hope,” that by the same way I may be led to you, because in it you have led me as far as this security, by which you, mighty God, are to me a tower of strength to which I may flee from the face of the enemy—the evil human being, or the devil himself, who prowls about seeking someone to devour. “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower,” says Solomon; “the righteous runs to it” (Prov. 18:10), namely, by invoking the Lord’s name when his heart is troubled.

In this tower we not only avoid the enemy’s missiles, but also securely hurl from it at him the weapons of prayers or works by which he is crushed. While your name, O God, was still known only in Judaea, I, the Church from the Gentiles, had no access to this tower of your most strong name. But after, through the mystery of your incarnate Word, your name was spread like poured-out oil far and wide even to the ends of the earth, now from the ends of the earth people cry to you and faithfully invoke your name whenever the Lord’s Prayer or another prayer containing your name is spoken, or even silently pondered in thought.

This most strong tower defends not only from the enemy’s attack, so that he may not approach us, but also from the enemy’s face, so that he may not see us hidden within it. For you, O God, “will hide them in the hiding-place of your countenance from the disturbance of men; you will protect them in the hiding-place of your tabernacle from the face of the enemy” (Ps. 30:21), so that, even if they are seen by him for temptation, they are nevertheless not seen for injury.

Alternatively: A tower built on level ground, because it is believed capable of being taken by an enemy, is sometimes besieged in that hope: for its wall, being—as has been said—set upon the plain, is thought liable to destruction either by undermining below or by being surmounted from above. Therefore the face of the besieging enemy is directed against it, whether by shooting missiles upward, constructing engines below, or working against it by subterranean excavation. Hence, as Isaiah [Jeremiah] says: “The very high wall of Babylon shall be utterly undermined by excavation” (Jer. 51:58), being situated on the plain, [Col. 1770D] in the land of “Shinar,” on the plain of “Dura” (Dan. 3:1), whose first tower was destroyed by the confusion of tongues. Such a tower, then, namely one set and situated on level ground, is sometimes safe from the enemy’s attack; yet it is not safe from the enemy’s gaze directed against it, because it can be attacked and perhaps captured by the business that walks in darkness, by the arrow flying by day, or by some other nocturnal or daytime terror.

But he who dwells in the help of the Most High, who can say to that same Most High, when his heart was distressed, “You lifted me up upon a rock; you led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength”—such a one may add: “from the face of the enemy.” For this tower, [Col. 1771A] standing on high above the rock, is completely secure not only from the enemy’s assault but even from the enemy’s face, so much so that the enemy himself flees from the sight of this tower, saying something like: “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them against us” (Exod. 14:25). Its foundation, hewn from the rock, cannot be harmed by undermining; nor can the structure, raised most high by the aid of the Most High and exceedingly exalted, be surmounted. It is a tower of as immeasurable a height as of immeasurable a strength; for its strength and height are God himself.

Rightly, therefore, shall I love you, O Lord, my strength, my support, my refuge, my tower: a tower of strength, secure on every side not only from assault but also from the enemy’s face. When any believer dwells in this most lofty tower, [Col. 1771B] let him believe that these words are spoken to him: “You shall not fear the terror by night, the arrow that flies by day, the business that walks in darkness, the assault and the noonday demon” (Ps. 90:5–6). Here too he can sing in praise of his protector: “When my heart was distressed, you lifted me up upon a rock. You led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength from the face of the enemy.” For the enemy’s face fears the face of this tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus and, by its gaze, puts the enemy to flight, according to the words: “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; and let those who hate him flee from before his face” (Ps. 67:2).

In the Hebrew it reads: “You were my hope, a most strongly fortified tower from the face of the enemy.” Truly it is a most strongly fortified tower, [Col. 1771C] built with battlements through the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation: eternal Wisdom built herself a house, or tower, in which are many battlements, and from which hang a thousand shields—the entire armor of the mighty men who serve Wisdom herself and dwell in her tabernacle. Desiring to be joined to their camp, I say:

**VERSE 5.** “I will dwell in your tabernacle, O God”; or, as another translation has it: “I shall be a sojourner in your tabernacle for ever.” Therefore it is not one individual who cries from the ends of the earth, since one individual cannot be a sojourner for ever. Rather, it is the one Church which, while some depart and others succeed them, dwells in the tabernacle throughout all the days in which they now serve as soldiers, unto the end of the age, [Col. 1771D] and cries to God from the ends of the earth, saying: “I will dwell in your tabernacle for ever. I shall not be uprooted by adversities.” For I would not gather my children unless I were to dwell in your tabernacle unto the end of the age. Yet I shall not serve there by my own strength, but I shall be protected from the heat of the age, from the burning of temptations and tribulations, under the covering of your wings.

Divine protection is rightly compared with the wings of birds warming their tender young or their eggs, because they do not burden them and ward off every injury. Christ uses this comparison in the Gospel, saying: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you: how often I wished to gather your children under my wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. 23:37). That earthly Jerusalem was unwilling [Col. 1772A] to be defended or warmed beneath the wings of divine protection; and therefore it was exposed to every misery, torn by the claws and crushed by the teeth both of demons and of Romans, just as the Lord had threatened it through Moses: “I shall send upon them the teeth of beasts, with the fury of creatures that drag themselves upon the earth and of serpents. Outside the sword shall lay them waste, and within, terror” (Deut. 32:24–25).

But I, the Church from the Gentiles, shall be protected under the covering of your wings—not only so that I suffer no harm, but so that much gain may come to me from the opportunity to flee beneath your wings amid temptations and tribulations, to hide there, and with continual prayers to cry out like chicks demanding food. There, “like a swallow’s young I shall cry; I shall meditate mournfully like a dove” (Isa. 38:14).

[Col. 1772B] Here a *diapsalma* is inserted, for which the Hebrew reads “always,” because whoever has once tasted how good and sweet it is to be protected under the covering of God’s wings always longs for such a covering amid the heat of tribulations. Beneath that covering, such a person finds it sweet to offer or continue prayers and praises constantly, having learned by true experience that, when he cries in this way to God his protector, the divine ears are open. Having experienced this in many things, I—the Church, or the ecclesiastical person—will glorify you, O God, my protector and hearer.

**VERSE 6.** “For you have heard my prayer.” This is clear from the result, because you have given an inheritance—not to just anyone, but to those who fear your name, for whom [Col. 1772C] I prayed and pray. You have given it, I say, in the past tense, either because this bestowal of the inheritance has begun in some persons, or because it is most certainly to come and be accomplished in this order: first, those who fear you are to be adorned with virtues and good conduct; then, from the brightness of merits, they are to come to the brightness of rewards, as from your Spirit, because you—

**VERSE 7.** “You shall add days upon the days of the king; his years unto the day of generation and generation.” The days of Christ the King, the sun of righteousness, are rightly called those who are formed from his splendor. For even in the present time of mortality the king’s days are formed, by which people are instructed in the light of truth; and in the age to come, “days shall be formed, and no one shall be instructed in them” (Ps. [Col. 1772D] 138:16). “I,” he says, “am the light of the world” (John 8:12). Likewise: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (John 9:5). And to those whom he illumines with light he says: “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

Thus are formed the days of the King and sun of righteousness, in which one must walk toward the days and years of eternal life. Hence he also says: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12:35). If, therefore, we walk in the light of the king’s days—which the King himself and sun of righteousness, veiled by the cloud of mortality, made bright by teaching and examples—he will add to us brighter days. These the same sun and King of righteousness forms, once the cloud of mortality has been removed, in the most serene brightness of supreme divinity, [Col. 1773A] in which “the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun” (Isa. 30:26). For the humanity assumed in the Son of God shines with that brightness which the sun of righteousness himself possessed in his divinity before the world was made.

In this day of his power, and likewise amid the splendors of the saints illumined on that day, what we say will be clear: namely, that days shall be added to days by God the Father, to whom I, the Church, singing psalms, say: “You shall add days upon the days of the king.”

The children of night and darkness do not know these days, because everyone who does evil hates the light, which light came into the world; but men loved darkness rather than light. Therefore days of blessedness shall not be added to them, but, because of the inward darkness of vices, they shall be cast into the outward darkness of torments. But you, [Col. 1773B] O God, Father of lights, shall add days upon the days of the king. For to those who now walk in the splendor of righteousness according to Christ’s teaching, and who, if sin befalls them, willingly come to the light so that their works may be reproved, you will give festive days after these laborious days, so that those who labored in the days of the militant King may also keep Sabbath in the days of the King resting from every work. For whoever has entered into the Lord’s rest shall rest from his own works, as God does from his. “From now on,” the Spirit says, “let them rest from their labors; for their works follow them” (Rev. 14:13).

Thus there remains a sabbath-rest for the people of God, the reprobate having been rejected, to whom the Lord swore in his wrath, saying: “They shall not enter into my rest” (Ps. [Col. 1773C] 94:11). Let us hasten to enter that rest of festal days, which are also called years because of their everlasting duration, and one day because of the unchanging identity of that same eternity. Hence elsewhere it is said: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101:11). Likewise: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11). This day—

**VERSE 8.** “Remains for ever before God.” Or rather, the King himself and sun of righteousness, who forms the days of pilgrimage by moving through the south among the innocent and those fervent in his love, and who turns toward the north in summer days so that sinners may be gathered through repentance and illuminated—after the rising of his birth and the setting of his death, ascending anew above the setting, to where he was before—now remains for ever before God. For “having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that he lives, he lives unto God” (Rom. 6:9).

Accordingly, the human being united to God remains impassible and unchangeable before God, crowned with glory and honor in royal days. By daily receiving those who follow him within their brightness, he will add days to days, as has been said; nor will he cease from this work of his. Rather, as he says, “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5:17). This working extends unto the day of generation and generation—that is, of the final regeneration—when the same King shall sit upon the throne of his majesty, making blessed those in whom the days and [Col. 1774A] brightness of generation and generation, that is, regeneration, shall appear.

A crooked and perverse generation is content with one day of only one generation: it is born into this world and celebrates it, as Herod did, and Pharaoh before him, feasting on his birthday. But they give no thought to the other generation, by which those reborn to eternal life, like newborn infants desiring milk, are the blessed offspring of the generation that seeks God, that seeks the face of the God of Jacob. Hence their resurrection will not be called regeneration, since neither are their souls here regenerated to faith nor will their bodies then reign in impassibility.

Therefore only the elect shall then have the day of generation and generation: either because they shall be regenerated and transformed [Col. 1774B] both in body and soul, and conformed to Christ alone, the eternal one; or because they did not merely begin to exist by carnal generation, but also happily received true being by spiritual generation, so as to become heavenly from earthly. Thus, on the day of the scrutinies, holy Church customarily prays for the catechumens, saying: “Almighty everlasting God, increase your Church in spiritual fruitfulness, so that those who are earthly by generation may become heavenly by regeneration.”

When, then, all who are thus regenerated are gathered together into one, when the Lord comes and all his saints with him, the righteous shall shine like the sun; and on that day there shall be great light—the day which shall remain for ever before God through the mercy and truth of God himself.

Would that more people, or all people, [Col. 1774C] sought this mercy and truth in such a manner that they might advance unto the day of everlasting brightness! But who believes our report concerning the testimony of God’s mercy and truth? God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there was one with understanding or one seeking his mercy and truth; but who will seek it? Who will seek his mercy and truth? Mercy is that by which, not on account of our merits but through his goodness, he forgives sins and promises life; truth is that by which he is not deceived but renders what he has promised. Likewise, mercy is that by which we forgive those who sin against us; truth, that by which we keep ourselves from sins insofar as we can.

Another translation has: “Who shall seek his mercy and truth for him?” The words “for him” are not added without purpose. For some seek God’s mercy and truth in the Scriptures and, after learning them, live for themselves, not for him.

Alternatively: “He remains for ever before God”—that is, the King whose days shall be added. So too shall those remain to whom he adds days; and this will be their full and most sufficient blessedness, needing thereafter no addition of days through any gift of mercy or truth. For who will seek mercy there, where no one is miserable? And who will seek truth, where all shall see God “and all shall be taught by God”? (John 6:45). “In that day,” he says, “you shall ask me nothing” (John 16:23).

Alternatively: “You shall add days upon the days of the king,” when someone, following the example of King Hezekiah, laments because he fears, in the middle of his days, to be snatched away and led to the gates of hell. [Col. 1775A] For just as fifteen years were then added to the weeping king’s days, when God cast all his sins behind his back, so now too days, the years of fifteen, shall be added to those who sincerely grieve for their sin. By singing the Song of Ascents, each such person may reach the place where he shall remain for ever before God. It would be sweet to me to proclaim the praises of such mercy and truth of God, if anyone sought them; but who will seek his mercy and truth? Indeed, what is worse, many reject mercy and truth even when freely offered to them. For “they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears; and they will indeed turn away their hearing from the truth and turn aside to fables” (2 Tim. 4:3–4).

Shall I therefore labor in vain, preaching mercy and truth to deaf and irreligious hearers? Rather, I shall obey Scripture, which says: “Do not pour out speech where there is no hearing” (Ecclus. 32:6). Likewise: “In that time the prudent shall keep silence” (Amos 5:13). But shall I, keeping silence among such utterly wicked people and hanging my instruments upon these Babylonian willows, also keep silence toward you, my God? By no means. For although I may cease from teaching, I shall not cease from singing psalms and praying, but—

**VERSE 9.** “Thus I shall sing a psalm to your name for age upon age, that I may pay my vows from day to day.” Thus, by doing good, I shall sing a psalm to your name—that is, [Col. 1775C] for the honor of your name—for age upon age, that is, [Col. 1776A] always, so that I may pay the vows which I made in baptism or in a stricter undertaking. I shall pay them, I say, from day to day: from the day illuminated by the sun of righteousness while veiled by the cloud of mortality. By paying my vows, I shall press onward to the day of everlasting brightness. Or “from day to day” means ascending from virtue to virtue, from brightness to brightness, forgetting what lies behind and stretching toward what lies ahead.

Alternatively: Thus I shall sing a psalm to your name during the age that follows this present age, so that I may pay my vows, lest my psalmody be empty through failure to fulfill my vows. Therefore, that my psalmody may please you, I shall vow whatever is holy, whatever chaste, whatever true, whatever lovely, whatever acceptable to God; and I shall pay my vows from the day of simple intention to the day of luminous completion. Or, by doing good from day to day [Col. 1776B] and joining days to days in works of light, I shall by no means go in the middle of my days to the gates of hell. Rather, seeking the remainder of my years and receiving days added to days, I, like another Hezekiah, shall sing my psalms on every day of my life in the house of the Lord, paying my vows from day to day: from the day of temporality to the day of eternity.

Glory to the Father who lifts me up upon the rock. Glory to the Son, who is the Rock itself. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that mercy of which the psalm says: “Who shall seek his mercy and truth?”

Alternatively: Glory to the Father of mercies, whose are mercy and truth, in which the Holy Spirit and the Son are understood. For the Son is the truth to be proclaimed everywhere, and the Holy Spirit is the mercy [Col. 1776C] to be sung for ever.

## PSALM 61

[Col. 1775]

[Col. 1775C] “Shall not my soul be subject to God?” The title is:

**VERSE 1.** **UNTO THE END; FOR JEDUTHUN; A PSALM OF DAVID.**

Jeduthun means “leaping over them.” He is the faithful person who leaps over the reprobate and those devoted to earthly things, who, [Col. 1775D] pressing toward the end, sings psalms to David himself, that is, to Christ. First, by saying that he is subject to him who is higher than he, he reproaches his persecutors. Second, again saying that he is subject to God, he exhorts others to hope in him, at the words: “Nevertheless, be subject to God, O my soul.” Third, he warns those who go astray to trust in God, not in perishable things, at the words: “Nevertheless, the sons of men are vain.”

This psalm most plainly suits the lawful combatant who struggles between hope and fear in this fiftieth psalm, as was said above. For here, strengthening himself by holy hope, he says: “Shall not my soul be subject to God? O law of sin, law of death, opposed to the law of life of my mind, why do you strive to call me away from hope or expectation of God’s help? Surely in vain: for from him is my salvation.” And further: “In God is my salvation and my glory; God is my helper, and my hope is in God. Hope in him, all assembly of the people,” etc. Thus, by singing unto the end for Jeduthun, he himself also becomes Jeduthun, that is, one leaping over. For he leaps over those to whom he speaks, saying: [Col. 1776D] “How long do you rush upon [a man]?”

Having briefly spoken of the sense of the whole psalm, let us proceed to expound it in order; and, taking the person of the one who leaps over, let us sing thus with God’s help, so that every singer may also become a Jeduthun by leaping over all vain things. But the higher he leaps, the more he may be found subject to God and, in love for him, subject to every human creature for his sake. Yet, standing upon so lofty a citadel of humility, if at any time he is urged by suggestions of demons, human beings, or even his own thoughts to become proud in spirit and mind, let him say in song:

**VERSE 2.** “Shall not my soul be subject to God?” What is it that you suggest to me, who leap over all vain things? You urge me, on account of such leaps, to be proud against him from whom I have both the power and the name of leaping over. But do I remember myself as being above what I am, so that I forget under whom I am? Shall not my soul be subject to God, who is above all things, however great my leaps may be?

Shall I not imitate that centurion who, leaping over the vanity of Gentilism and Judaism, came to the truth, having as his inseparable companion the virtue of holy humility? “For I too,” he says, “am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me” (Matt. 8:9). A good order! First he knew what he was; second, under whom he was; and then, over whom he was. He gave me an example, that I too might leap cautiously in this manner: first toward knowledge of myself, from which, through fitting leaps, I may come to knowledge of God.

“For I am a man born of a woman, living for a short time” (Job 14:1); I am a man made from the ground and destined to return to the ground, according to the truth which says: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). In truth I could say: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8), were it not that I have now learned that I should not speak thus, because the authority under which I have been placed contradicts me and says: rather, if you consider yourself a sinner, you ought not to drive the Lord away from yourself.

Still, I say truly: “I am a sinful man”; but I do not add, “Depart from me, Lord,” because in this also my soul shall be subject to God: consenting to the authority under which I am placed, I shall, according to sound teaching, flee not from the Lord but to him. I shall humbly submit to his holy ordinances in the holy Church, lamenting sins I have committed [Col. 1777C] and guarding against sins that must henceforth be lamented. If I have no strength at all to do this by my own powers, nevertheless, with the help and gift of God—to whom my soul shall be subject—I shall be able. For from him is my salvation.

From God the Father is the Son, who through the flesh he assumed is my salvation. The Son of God is indeed my salvation, from God most high and immeasurable.

**VERSE 3.** For he too is God, equally most high and equally immeasurable as God his Father. Or I call the Son my salvation because he is sufficient to give salvation, as is God his Father. For he too is my God, equally with the Father: God of all by nature; mine by a certain special relation through grace. This grace is plainly recognized in him because he who is my God through the power of creation [Col. 1777D] is also my Savior through the grace of restoration and my defender, when, leaping over worldly vanities, I leave them as it were behind my back.

Therefore, since so great a Savior and defender is mine, and none is stronger than he, I who leap to him and am received by him shall not be moved any more. The hand of the sinner, which moved me in the old Adam, shall not be able to move me now that I am received by the second Adam. And that foot of pride which came upon me while my soul was not yet subject to God shall come upon me no longer, because my soul shall always be subject to God. Thus, though formerly moved by the foot of pride or the hand of the sinner, I shall not be moved any more: founded in the humility of my Savior and to be protected by him for ever.

[Col. 1778A] **VERSE 4.** Since this is so, you rush in vain upon a man—you demons, malicious people, or even you worldly thoughts. Certainly neither winds through evil spirits, nor floods of persecution through ungodly people, nor rain through evil or filthy thoughts can move my house; for it is founded upon the rock of which I said in the preceding psalm: “When my heart was distressed, you lifted me up upon a rock. You led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength from the face of the enemy” (Ps. 80:3–4).

How long, then, enemies of my salvation, do you trouble and harass me? How long do you rush upon the man—that is, the outward man? Since you cannot injure the inward man, like madmen and raging persons you rush upon the outward man. You have no power to injure the soul, which you cannot kill by drawing it into consent with your wickedness; but all of you kill bodies, whether in will through hatred, because “he who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15), or in act through manifest murder: “that upon you may come all righteous blood shed from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zachariah” (Matt. 23:35). That is, from the blood of martyrs killed in the field of this world, of whom Abel was the first, unto the blood of priests teaching between the temple and altar, among whom Zachariah was preeminent.

Although you have personally killed neither of these, you show that you belong to the body of Cain the fratricide or of the Jews who kill the prophets and the Lord of the prophets, because all of you, to the extent of your power, kill all those who, leaping over conformity to you, either display examples of piety in the field of worldly life by making proper offerings and proper divisions, or are devoted to religious observances of eremitic or cenobitic life while teaching between temple and altar, or weeping between porch and altar, doing and teaching the right things which they can. All of you who hate all these kill them, “that upon you may come all righteous blood.”

Or certainly all of you kill yourselves by hating all those whom you rush upon in order to cast them down according to your desire, as though upon a leaning wall which, in your judgment, is about to fall of itself without anyone pushing it, or as upon a demolished fence. [Col. 1778D] Since a fence is a pile of stones without the binding of mortar, it cannot stand against one who pushes or destroys it. How much less can it stand when it has been thrown down and bent from the upright position, even if no one sets engines against it? Therefore, because you regard as such a person, so easily destroyed, the man upon whom you rush in order to destroy him, you do not know that you labor in vain.

Nevertheless, when your engines fail, you shall recognize as immovable the man who truly says: “I shall not be moved any more.” For “those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; he shall not be moved for ever” (Ps. 124:1). Even if a flood strikes the house of this man, it cannot move it, for it is founded upon firm rock. Rather, you are the ones who ought to be compared to a leaning wall [Col. 1779A] and a demolished fence. For behold, I now speak to you as to a leaning wall and a demolished fence, saying: How long do you, who are a whitewashed wall and bent from the state of uprightness, rush upon an upright man? How long do you, who are a demolished fence, not cemented into one and near ruin, rush upon a man who clings most firmly to his most strong foundation with the glue or cement of charity? How long do such destructible persons rush upon a steadfast and by no means destructible man, whose body indeed you may kill, but whose soul you cannot kill?

The Hebrew truth seems to imply this sense, where it reads: “How long do you lie in wait against a man? You kill all, as a leaning wall, [Note: [Col. 1779D] Thus the Codex.] and a falling fence?” Such a wall or falling fence, when it falls, buries only those whom it finds nearby and set behind it—like those impious men who, already near their own ruin, said wrongly within themselves: “Let us unjustly oppress the righteous man, because he is contrary to our works” (Wis. 2:12). Thinking this wrongly within themselves, they spoke in their inward thoughts the deed which they intended; but they could not accomplish what they said. For they themselves fell, delivered to Roman swords and made portions for foxes, that is, for evil spirits.

But the man whom they wished to be oppressed, and whose tomb they sealed so that he might not rise, was not crushed by the death which they inflicted upon him. Rather, for this very reason—because [Col. 1779C] he humbled himself, saying, “Shall not my soul be subject to God?”—or, to express the same sense in Gospel words, because he said to the Father in submission: “Father, not my will, but yours be done” (Luke 22:42); likewise, “not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36); likewise, “I came not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 6:38)—because, I say, his soul was thus subject to God, obeying in all things the divinity of the Father, of himself, and of the Holy Spirit, behold: “God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:9–11).

Thus the human nature assumed [Col. 1779D] into the glory of God the Word who assumed it—which is the glory of God the Father—bestowed this upon his members and left it to his followers who subject their souls to God: even if a whitewashed, leaning wall or a demolished fence should fall against them, it shall not bury any of them. For although the whole city of Jericho fell, Rahab’s hospitable house stood, defended by the messengers of Jesus whom she received; believing their words, she provided well for her house (Josh. 6:25).

The holy Church chosen and gathered from the Gentiles shall stand, because the Catholic and apostolic faith preached by the messengers of Jesus Christ has been received in her. Every faithful soul subject to God and supported by apostolic faith shall also stand. Since this is so, how long do you rush upon the man whose soul is subject to God and cannot be buried, because God is his protector and defender? You accomplish nothing against him; rather, you fail and all of you kill yourselves. Like a leaning wall and demolished fence, you shall fall even though no one rushes upon you; and in no way will you be able to overwhelm the man subject to God his protector, however greatly you strive to rush upon him.

Another reading has: “How long do you set yourselves against a man, to kill all?” When it says “to kill all [the] man,” it is clear that it does not speak of one individual; for one person is not of such extent that he can be killed by all the impious. The one man, therefore, is the one Church: head and members, from Abel to the last righteous person. [Col. 1780B] Upon this man the impious place sufferings as burdens, so that from the beginning to the end each may fulfill in his body what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings. Indicating this span of time, he says: “How long do you add iniquity upon iniquity?” Then, as though mocking them, he adds: “Kill [the Codex reads: ‘to kill’] all that man, and press upon him like a leaning wall and a demolished fence; and thus let us see whether you can erase from the earth the name of him who said: ‘God is my defender; I shall not be moved any more.’”

The enemies themselves perceive that I have the fixed and God-established resolve not to be moved any more; and because of this I await, from afar and from the furthest bounds, the reward of that same resolve, and I long for a death precious in the sight of the Lord. Or, because I consider myself redeemed at a great price, I desire to render precious service and sacrifice to God, so that, even if my life and death appear cheap in the sight of the impious, nevertheless my death may be precious in the sight of the Lord, preceded by a life no less precious—not only in the sight of the Lord, who tests hearts and inward parts, but also in the sight of people who see and do not envy, who see my good works and glorify God and do not envy my salvation and its price. The enemies thought to reject that price, namely that I might lose Christ, who is my price, if he were not laid up in safety so that he could not be taken from me against my will.

**VERSE 5.** “Nevertheless, my enemies thought to reject my price.” They often strove to dishonor me with insults and slanders, in order to reject my price; but they could not do so. Nevertheless, they thought it, and by thought alone became guilty of the deed. Or thus: they perceived that I, subject to God, stood firm and proved that I would not be moved any more; and therefore, being rational beings, they ought to have ceased attacking me. Yet they did not think in this way, but thought to reject my price, seeking to entice me into some apparent concession advantageous to themselves, so that my life, though perhaps not hateful to good people, might at least become less precious.

Thus they thought to cheapen, if not my conscience, [Col. 1781A] at least my reputation, so that, even if I did not turn back by defiling my conscience, I might at least, by seeking what lay ahead more slowly and accommodating myself to sluggish or even backward-moving travelers, lose my reputation. But I preserved the precious treasure of both reputation and conscience in this: while they delayed or even went backward, I ran in thirst. I ran, forgetting what lay behind and stretching toward what lay ahead—in thirst, because with thirst and hunger for righteousness I sought to have all others, enemies as well as friends, as companions or even forerunners in my course. I sought this very thing in continual prayers, desiring to incorporate them with myself in Christ through an easy conversion, just as drink is more easily taken by one who thirsts than food by one who hungers; for eating requires more labor than drinking.

Therefore, just as Christ said on the cross, “I thirst,” wishing to drink in the nations easily converted and incorporate them into himself, so I too ran in thirst, because I wished perverse persons to be converted without difficulty.

But, on the contrary, they blessed with their mouth and cursed in their heart. When they could not overthrow me by harsh means, they attempted it by gentle means, blessing with their mouths and cursing in their hearts, like another Balaam: though blessing sounded in his mouth, cursing was in his heart, God turning the intention to curse into the effect of blessing. Thus they spoke “in heart and heart”; thus they made a distinction with their lips, so that they outwardly presented one thing and inwardly intended another. For in speaking good things they presented human faces, but inwardly they were ravening wolves [Col. 1781C].

Here a *diapsalma* is inserted, for which the Hebrew reads “always,” because everlasting recompense is due to both: to the evil who curse in their hearts, and to the good who patiently endure the same curses for truth’s sake and humbly subject their souls to God. Hence the apostle Peter says: “Those who suffer according to the will of God entrust their souls to the faithful Creator in well-doing” (1 Pet. 4:19). Therefore I, Jeduthun, who above subjected my soul to God in so great a matter, do the same thing, saying:

**VERSES 6–7.** “Nevertheless, be subject to God, O my soul,” bearing his yoke not only patiently but also willingly: patiently, because from him is my patience, by which I possess you, my soul, lest you perish [Col. 1781D] amid so many scandals; willingly, because he is my God, who created me from nothing, and my Savior, who justifies me so that I may live soberly, righteously, and godly. He is my helper, who establishes me in this very righteousness lest I fail amid scandals; therefore I shall not depart—that is, I shall not become a deserter.

Alternatively: God himself, who calls the things that are not as though they were, is my God, who also called me. And because those whom he called, he also justified, he is my Savior by justifying me as well. Again: because those whom he justified, he also magnified, he is my helper by magnifying me as well. For since there are two gifts of the Holy Spirit—one for the remission of sins, the other in the distribution of charisms and virtues—saved by the one and strengthened and helped by the other, I shall no longer depart from the path of uprightness [Col. 1782A]; or, fortified on the way by these two gifts, so that I do not fail on the way, I shall arrive there, where, in blessed permanence, I shall rather not depart thence, as the first-created man departed from paradise and Lucifer from heaven.

**VERSE 8.** For in God is my salvation and my glory. I shall not imitate the devil or Adam, excessively eager for their own glory and wishing to glory as though their salvation came to them from their own power. Rather, in God is my salvation, through which I shall be saved from sins, and my glory, through which I shall be glorified in virtues and in the eternal rewards of virtues. And for this I do not trust that I shall advance by my own powers, but by divine help, because God is the source of my help in holy struggle and endeavor, and my hope is in God, until, hope having been fulfilled, the reality comes [Col. 1782B]. For now faith, hope, and charity—these three—remain; but the greatest of these is charity.

Faith is the assurance of invisible things, conceived from hearing God’s word, placed above opinion and below knowledge. One imbued with this faith, and so grounded in it that he cannot but fear the invisible evils proclaimed in the Scriptures, restrains himself through that fear from the vices for which he does not doubt those evils will be repaid. And immediately hope attends faith: since hope is a good confidence arising from God’s goodness and from human merits, human merits are so slight—or nonexistent—in comparison with divine goodness that I, although by God’s grace conscious of good merits stored up for myself in a soul subject to God, nevertheless, glorying in God alone, say: “My hope is in God” [Col. 1782C].

For although it has first been stated that God is the author of my help by his grace, cooperating with my faith and producing the merits from which hope arises, yet, because those merits are nothing if they are judged strictly and God’s mercy set aside, rightly is my hope in God alone. For I hope from him for the salvation he has begun to be brought to completion also through him, because of his goodness, by which he wills all human beings to be saved, and because of his power, by which he has done everything whatsoever he willed. Therefore, following my example:

**VERSE 9.** Hope in him, every assembly of the people. Be a people, not a crowd: a people gathered in unity, not a crowd thrown into disorder by discord. Be not only a people through civic or popular unanimity [Col. 1782D], but also an assembly of the people, having one heart and one soul in God; and thus hope in him. But in order that such perfect unity of hearts in God, which makes hope in him firm, may be brought to completion in you and perfectly preserved: pour out your hearts before him, first confessing your sins with your whole heart; and then, having received virtues, again pour out your hearts before him, ascribing to him whatever good you do and imputing to yourselves what is evil in you, whether through deficiency in virtues or remnants of vices.

For just as, when the people of Israel entered the promised land and the Canaanites had been conquered, certain remnants nevertheless remained for the instruction and exercise of the Israelite army, lest it become unaccustomed to fighting [Col. 1783A], so also in you, however fully justified you may be in this life, certain remnants of vices will remain for the exercise of your diligence. Nor should you who hope in God fear amid such things; for if you pour out your hearts before him in prayer, weeping, confession, and praise, what you pour out will not perish, and you will be safe, because God is our helper—not for an hour, but forever.

A *diapsalma*, or “always,” is plainly inserted here, because he who is a helper forever never withdraws his everlasting help, but always stands by his own.

**VERSE 10.** Yet the sons of men are vain, although God is a helper forever. Eternity and vanity are wholly opposed; and therefore, once the eternity of God the helper has been shown, vanity ought to be abandoned through his help [Col. 1783B]. Yet vain human beings tend not from vanity to eternity, but from vanity into the same thing—that is, from vanity into vanity. And they do this through lies and deceptions inherited by them; for they, sons of men, descendants of the liar and the deceitful, are likewise liars, deceitful, and crafty: that they may deceive with balances, either literally by means of different weights forbidden in God’s law, defrauding the simplicity of purchasers, or in the exposition of the Scriptures by inserting falsehood into truth.

And they do this all the more effectively the more deceitfully they pretend to weigh all their sayings and judgments in the scale of justice, so that they themselves may deceive. Though they are manifold and various in errors and deceits, they nevertheless present themselves as so concordant from vanity toward the same end [Col. 1783C] that they, who are believed just and upright in the scale of justice, may deceive through vanity. But I, because, as I have already said, I have run in thirst, thirsting for justice and for a scale just in every respect, say in my thirst: you kindly hearers, attend; and thirst with me for what I thirst for, cry out with me what I cry out. What shall I cry?

**VERSE 11.** Do not, I say, hope in iniquity—that is, in riches, which are deemed to bear the name of iniquity and are called the mammon of iniquity because every rich person is either unjust or the heir of an unjust person. The Apostle says: “Command those who are rich in this world not to think proudly, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Tim. 6:17). And I, Idithun, saying the same thing, say to the rich: Do not hope in iniquity. Do not be slaves [Col. 1783D] of unjust mammon.

I say also to the poor: be content with these modest possessions which you have by God’s gift, and do not covet plunder. Poverty is rather to be endured than robbery committed—or even desired, which is less serious—as though out of necessity. Need does not excuse the crime of robbery. The prophet says: “Woe to you who plunder: will you not yourself also be plundered?” (Isa. 33:1). That is: when, having become a plunderer, you seize another’s goods—or, what is less serious, desire them unlawfully—you become prey to the plundering devil: while you plunder, you are plundered; while you hold, you are held.

Take heed, you who plunder, of the enemy who goes about seeking whom he may devour. The prey you wish to seize is in a trap: you catch and are caught; or even [Col. 1784A], while you do not catch it and attempt to catch it, like a ravening wolf you are wounded by a hooked sickle; and, having gained nothing but a wound, you die a death—unless you are healed by the remedy of repentance and become poor in spirit, so thoroughly that even if riches abound, though they must also ebb away, they do not draw your heart downward. Rather, let your heart be above, and send your riches there by storing treasure there, where thieves do not dig through and moth does not destroy them, God guarding them.

If riches abound, do not set your heart upon such abundance, which, by the law of change by which it flows in, flows out far too quickly. For, as the apostle James says, “as the flower of grass, so also the rich man withers in his ways. The grass has withered and the flower has fallen; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Jas. 1:10–11). Therefore you [Col. 1784B], to whom I said above, “Pour out your hearts before him,” pour out your hearts before God in this way also: by storing with him the treasure of your riches, whether bodily or spiritual, store your hearts there likewise, because “where your treasure is, there your heart is also” (Luke 12:34).

He did not pour out his heart well or wisely who, numbering his riches, said: “God, I thank you that I am not like other people—robbers, unjust persons, adulterers—or even like this tax collector” (Luke 18:11). Thanksgiving was like a channel which might have carried the riches of this Pharisee to heaven together with his heart, had it not been leaky through the fissure of pride, by which, despising others, he so gloried [Col. 1784C] that he rejoiced more in another’s failure than in his own progress.

> **[Note: Col. 1783D.]** Thus the manuscript Codex states expressly.

This leprosy of pride is indeed so white that it seems utterly clean, unless it is carefully examined by the judgment of the priest and thereby detected through its difference from the rest of the flesh. Hence it is said in the Law:

> “A person in whose flesh or skin there has arisen a different color, or something like a bright spot—that is, a leprous lesion—shall be brought to Aaron the priest, or to any one of his sons. When he sees the leprosy in the skin, the hairs changed to white, and the appearance of the leprosy lower than the rest of the skin and flesh, it is a leprous lesion, and at his judgment the person shall be separated. But if there is a shining whiteness in the skin, not lower than the rest of the flesh, and the hairs retain their former color, he shall confine him seven days. And he shall examine him [Col. 1784D] on the seventh day; and if the leprosy has not spread farther and has not passed beyond its former boundaries in the skin, he shall confine him another seven days. And on the seventh day he shall inspect him. If the leprosy has become dimmer and has not spread in the skin, he shall pronounce him clean” (Lev. 13:1 ff.).

Does not something like a bright spot show itself in a person’s skin when his life becomes conspicuous through practices of holiness? To determine whether there may be the leprosy of pride in such conspicuousness, such a person must be brought to Aaron the priest—that is, to Christ—or to one of his sons, that is, to imitators who exercise the priesthood. For Christ, who is truth, must be consulted either directly in the Scriptures or through lawful priests [Col. 1785A], whether what pleases human eyes also pleases him.

Seeing—that is, causing us to see—whether the appearance of the leprosy is lower than the rest of the skin and flesh or not, and whether the hairs retain their former color or not, he will pronounce unclean the person condemned by the appearance of shining leprosy differing from the rest of the flesh and by whiteness of the hairs; or clean, if the shining whiteness is not lower than the rest of the flesh and the hairs retain their former color. By these signs a person may indeed be cleared of the leprosy of Pharisaic pride if, when something shining appears in him through an appearance of religion, he does not rejoice or congratulate himself because his life is conspicuous and unlike that of other people.

Thus he does not show himself lower than the rest of the flesh by Pharisaic humility, which always seeks things unlike those of others and capable of display for praise [Col. 1785B]; instead he makes himself equal to other human beings—certainly to his fellow servants—among whom he himself does not know who should be preferred to whom in the judgment of the true and highest priest, in which the first will be last and the last first. Therefore anyone who, pondering this priest’s judgment, prepares himself for it so as to be found there clean from every appearance of leprosy, will be brought to this priest.

The hairs retaining their former color cooperate toward the same end if one’s words and thoughts, after the appearance of holiness has been made manifest, remain in the condition of former humility: that is, if one does not become proud after receiving grace when previously one had not been proud. Otherwise, what profit is there in becoming rich in possessions or virtues, when the wretched soul becomes prouder precisely from that from which it ought to become humbler and more ready to serve its fellow servants [Col. 1785C]?

Therefore, whether bodily or spiritual riches abound, do not set your heart upon them, so as to become proud from them and appear more glorious than other people, when for that very reason you ought to be humbler and, as has been said, more ready to serve—especially if you fear the divine judgment, in which God will speak once and will not repeat the same thing a second time, nor reconsider the word then uttered from his mouth. Though this judgment is future to us, it is to his eyes as though past and wholly fixed.

Therefore, foretelling the same judgment, in which each person will be rendered according to his works, I do not say, “He will speak once,” but:

**VERSES 12–13.** God has spoken once, with an irrevocable utterance [Col. 1785D]. In that utterance I have heard these two things: that power belongs to God, by which it will be said to the wicked: “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41); and that mercy belongs to you, Lord, by which you will say to the good: “Come, blessed of my Father,” and so forth (Matt. 25:34). In both respects, you are rightly to be praised as judge, because you will render to each according to his works.

Alternatively: above I said two things: namely, that one ought not to hope in iniquity, but ought to hope in God. Giving the reason for both, I say: one ought not to hope in iniquity, because God’s power is invincible for the condemnation of the wicked and of iniquity; but one ought to hope in God, because mercy belongs to you, Lord. And truly power and mercy belong to you, because you will render to each according to his works [Col. 1786A].

Let no one wonder that I, Idithun, as though leaping over the other hearers to whom I had hitherto spoken concerning God’s testimonies, now, at the end of the psalm, turning to him who is the end of all things, say: “To you, Lord, belongs mercy, because you will render to each according to his works”—to the good, indeed, a reward from mercy; to the wicked, punishment from power. I have not fabricated from my own heart what I say; rather, I bear witness to what I heard. And I heard not from an uncertain rumor, but from a divine utterance.

For God spoke once, begetting from his heart the one Word. Carried away to that Word, I, Idithun, leaping over all other things, heard in one utterance these two things: that power belongs to God and that mercy belongs to you, Lord [Col. 1786B].

It seems contrary that he says, “God spoke once,” when God “spoke in many portions and in many ways” (Heb. 1:1), indeed both often and in many ways. Likewise, since he spoke once, it seems contrary that two things were heard. To this one may answer that Idithun, leaping above all things, even above the angels, reached the place where the one Father begot the one Word; and by begetting it, he arranged all things, which afterward he ordered in their ranks. Or: within himself he spoke once, but among human beings in many ways.

Or the word “once” should be referred not to number [Col. 1786C] but to the firmness of the decree: by begetting the Word he spoke once, that is, he arranged all things immutably and eternally. But Idithun, carried up to that ordering act, heard, among many things that he heard and need not be stated here, these two concerning power and mercy that pertain to this passage. Or, since he arranged all things once and afterward divided them into their orders, he is said to have heard only these two because nearly all other things are contained in these two. For because of these two came the patriarchs, prophets, Law, Christ, apostles, proclamation, and every celebration of ecclesiastical religion.

Therefore let power be feared, because it is God’s; for no power exists except from him, and every power is just, even if its justice escapes you. But let mercy be loved: power must not be despised because of mercy [Col. 1786D], nor must one despair of mercy because of power.

Glory to God the Father, to whom my soul shall be subject and from whom comes my salvation. Glory to the Son, who is indeed my salvation. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is mercy, inseparably joined to power, by which each will be rendered according to his works. Glory to the triune and one God, my helper, from whom I shall not depart, he preserving me by his help. Amen.

## PSALM LXII

[Col. 1787]

[Col. 1787A] “O God, my God,” etc. The title is:

**VERSE 1. A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN HE WAS IN THE WILDERNESS OF IDUMAEA.**

David hid there when he fled from Saul’s presence (1 Sam. 22:5), signifying the Church, which labors and thirsts in the barrenness of this age; there it does not cease to cry out, teaching how to live rightly amid a depraved nation. In this psalm Christ speaks in the person of head and members. For our voice is his, just as his is ours.

First he sets out his desire, saying: “O God, my God, I watch for you from the dawn.” Secondly, he sets out security here and in the future, while enemies perish and the good reign and rejoice with their king: “But the king shall rejoice in God.” Knowing, however, that those who thirst for righteousness here will be satisfied in the future, while he burns with the necessities of this life he cries: “My God.”

[Col. 1787B] In this psalm the head himself is introduced praying, to show what may be of greatest benefit to one who is still in struggle and danger, fighting against vices: “O God, my God, I watch for you from the dawn.” Bodily vigils also are greatly useful against vices, as is holy meditation, concerning which he says later: “If I have remembered you upon my bed, I shall meditate upon you in the mornings, because you have been my helper, and in the shelter of your wings I shall rejoice,” and so forth.

The head himself speaks this, as the title itself indicates: “A Psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Idumaea,” the sense of which title is this [Col. 1787C]. These words are to be attributed to the true David, Christ, according to the condition in which he lived among the Jewish people, who were a wilderness because they abandoned God’s commandments for their traditions, and Idumaea—that is, earthly or blood-stained—because they loved the earth and thirsted for blood.

In this psalm our Lord intends to show that he was most watchful—that is, attentive and diligent—in fulfilling God’s will, even while he was kept among enemies who always sought to call him away. He does all this to instruct the faithful, lest they too remain in the torpor of night and in unbelief and wicked action; rather, imitating him, they should not sleep amid tribulations, but, doing good in all things, be found at last praiseworthy in him [Col. 1787D], saying thus:

**VERSE 2.** O God, my God, I watch for you from the dawn. God of all generally according to creation; but my God according to special love. For you—that is, for the complete fulfillment of your will—I keep watch and direct my heart most vigilantly, I Christ your Son, wearied in the wilderness of Idumaea [Col. 1788A], both in myself and in my members burdened by the danger of earthliness.

And indeed I, awakened from the sleep of death at early dawn, am already delivered from the wilderness of Idumaea, from the Jewish and earthly people abandoned by God’s grace. Nevertheless, as long as even one of my least ones is wearied in such a wilderness, I reckon myself wearied; for in such least ones I hunger, thirst, am a stranger and naked, sick and in prison, in the wilderness of Idumaea among earthly and bloodthirsty people abandoned by God’s grace. For the unclean persecute the clean through earthly impurity; the impious persecute the godly through murderous wickedness.

But persecution itself brings this benefit: it makes me more watchful and attentive in calling upon you, my God, from the dawn—that is, in the morning. [Col. 1788B] Literally, prayer ought to be more earnest when the hour of resurrection approaches, because then we read that the patriarch Jacob was heard in order to receive a blessing. Likewise, after the apostles had wearied themselves fruitlessly in fishing by night, when morning had come and Jesus stood on the shore, at his command they cast the net on the right side of the boat and caught one hundred and fifty-three large fish; and though they were so many, the net was not torn (John 21:11).

Taught by examples of this kind that in the morning you will hear the voice of one watching from the dawn, I too watch from the dawn—literally, as has been said, or from the light of good intention, my eye being single, so that the whole body of prayer and vigils may be full of light, having no part of darkness through an evil eye [Col. 1788C]. Thus I watch from the dawn because I would not watch unless the sun of righteousness arose for me and by its rays awakened me from the sleep of sloth, which easily steals upon one in the wilderness of Idumaea—as happened to us apostles when the Idumaeans, that is, the earthly Jews, persecuted Christ, the true David, and we could not watch for one hour. For our eyes were heavy when it was the hour and power of darkness, around sunset.

But very early on the first day of the week, once the sun had risen—having ascended above the setting into the east—we began to watch from its light and urged others to watch. One of us said: “Keep watch in the faith; act courageously; let all that you do be done with charity. Therefore let us not sleep as the rest do, but let us watch and be sober” (1 Cor. 16:13–14). Again: “Be sober and watch, because your adversary the devil goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Pet. 5:8–9).

When, in that very hour and power of darkness, it was said to us, “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41), the spirit indeed was willing, but the flesh was weak and sluggish in keeping watch. But now, morning having come and the sun having risen [Col. 1789A], O God, my God, I watch for you from the dawn.
