Finally, the often-mentioned combatant, fighting between hope and fear, perceives that this change and shadowing of alternation—now sleeping, now watching—continually alternate within him as long as he endures the contest in the wilderness of Idumaea against his own flesh or another’s. I too feel this in myself: I am afflicted by the weariness of flesh, and my soul is weary of my life. Therefore my soul has thirsted not to be enriched with gold, silver, or another earthly gain, but for you, in whom is true being, true refreshment, and the fullness of all goods, which is not found in the wilderness of Idumaea. Since my soul finds no refreshment there, it thirsted for you, the fountain of life. And not only my soul, but also my flesh, which is thirsting in many ways because of the many failings it suffers in the wilderness of Idumaea [Col. 1789B].

The Hebrew reads: “O God, you are my strength; from the dawn I shall rise to you. My soul has thirsted for you; my flesh has desired you.” Therefore, because you are my strength, my flesh desires you, subject as it is to manifold variation and weakness: as it changes its stages of life, as it is most easily wearied, so that even prolonged refreshment itself becomes exhaustion, and relief from any weariness becomes weariness. Thus, if we stand long, we grow tired and therefore sit down; and again, sitting long, we grow weary. So also in other respects: while the flesh seeks refreshment from its weariness, it always finds weariness; and thus it thirsts in so many ways.

The more the soul fails in itself, the more it pants for you—that is, for the true immutability which is in you and is not found in the wilderness of Idumaea [Col. 1789C].

Again, the more manifoldly the fragile flesh is worn down, the more ardently it thirsts to cleave to you, who are the fountain of life and are not found

**VERSE 3.** In a desert land, pathless and waterless—in the wilderness, namely, of Idumaea. Its land is desert from the time it was said to the Idumaeans, that is, the Jews: “Behold, your house shall be left desolate to you” (Matt. 23:38). It is pathless, namely, because it does not have Christ, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6); and, lacking that truth and life, it is waterless, having no preachers of truth and life, because the clouds have been commanded not to rain upon it.

Likewise, in every synagogue of Satan a desert, pathless, and waterless land is seen, and the soul’s thirst is not refreshed in it—unless, separated from this desert, pathless, and waterless land by inward desire, it watches for you from the dawn, my God, and thirsts for you, so that through watching and thirsting it may become holy in chaste and holy desire [Col. 1789D].

Thus I appeared before you in the sanctuary, that I might see your power and your glory. Thus I appeared before you—that is, I was first seen by you, that afterward I might see you. For no one sees you unless first seen by you. Therefore you saw me appearing before you in the sanctuary, that is, in holiness, or in holy desire, in holy thirst, so that I too might see your power [Col. 1790A].

For just as the sun by its own light makes us see the power and glory of its brightness, so you, sun of righteousness, anticipated me with your light, so that, enlightened through you, I might see your power and glory: namely, the Divinity in the assumed manhood, invincible in power in battle and immeasurable in glory in triumph. For he could not truly be proclaimed a mighty man in battle, Lord of hosts, or king of glory unless he were also God. Although he bore our infirmities, he did not lose his power and glory; indeed, by the grace of resurrection and ascension he raised his humanity into the glory and power of Divinity, so that whatever power and glory Divinity has by nature, humanity in him has by grace.

Hence his flesh, in the wilderness of Idumaea, in a desert and pathless land, though afflicted in many ways, was glorified and deified in many ways—even to the extent that it may deify those who partake of it, just as Divinity itself deifies blessed angels. “For my flesh,” he says, “is truly food” (John 6:56). Therefore, just as the bread of angels, God’s Word, is food for angels, so the same Word made flesh is bread for all the blessed, both angels and human beings. That flesh, therefore, is truly food which grants perfect satisfaction to those who hunger and thirst in a desert, pathless, and waterless land and say in psalmody: “O God, my God, I watch for you from the dawn” [Col. 1790B].

My soul has thirsted for you; in how many ways my flesh thirsts for you, while my soul desires to be conformed to your soul and my flesh to your flesh, in a desert, pathless, and waterless land. Such is my flesh: not yet sufficiently cultivated by spiritual discipline, not yet marked by the footsteps of the saints, not yet drenched with heavenly dew or rain. In such waterless land, watching for you and thirsting for you, I thus appeared before you in holy desire, that I might see your power and glory; that is: I was known in order that I might know, I was seen in order that I might see your power and glory, lest I assign the power of good merit or the glory of blessed reward to anyone but you, without whom we are capable neither of doing anything virtuous nor receiving anything glorious, and apart from whose mercy our life, however holy, is nothing [Col. 1790C].

**VERSE 4.** For your mercy is better than lives.  
> **[Note: Col. 1789D.]** Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book VIII, chapter 31.

For human action has weak or no power to wash away guilt or to carry out righteousness fittingly, unless the mercy of the one who spares sustains it and the justice of the one who judges rightly does not press it down. Hence it is rightly said: “Your mercy is better than lives,” because, however innocent our life may seem, our life does not free us before the strict Judge unless the kindness of mercy remits the debt of its guilt.

Alternatively: thus I appeared before you in the sanctuary, thirsting and watching, so that through this I might become fit to see your power and glory; because unless someone first thirsts amid this evil which is in a desert, pathless, and waterless land [Col. 1791A], he is not worthy to see the power and glory that are in God and that are God.

Alternatively: in a desert, pathless, and waterless land—that is, in the dwelling-place of the wicked, in the assembly of evildoers, amid a crooked and perverse nation—I thus appeared before you in the sanctuary, that, enlightened by the light of holiness, I might see and make others see your power and glory.

Or I appeared before you, God the Father, in the sanctuary—that is, in your Son, who is called “Holy One” by antonomasia and, having become a member, is the Holy of holies. In him I appeared before you so purely that, with a pure gaze, insofar as it could be done through a mirror and in an enigma, I might see your power, by which you delivered me from the desert, pathless, and waterless land and separated me from it, whether spiritually or even locally; and your glory, by which you glorified and illumined me with virtues in the holy land [Col. 1791B]. This was not demanded by the merit of my own life or my parents’ lives, but was so ordered by the freely purposed design of your mercy, because your mercy is better than lives, however praiseworthy.

Or, “your mercy is better than lives” means that your mercy is more effective in saving than human life is effective in destroying those whom you thus foresee, ordained in your Holy One, your Son, so that they too may see your power and glory.

Alternatively, “your mercy is better than lives” means that the life given in the Holy One through mercy, not because of preceding merits, is better than all human lives, which are many, such as the life of a philosopher, a soldier, or one who follows some other humanly established order [Col. 1791C]. Or your life in reward is better than all lives, however good, reckoned as merit. Or your mercy is better—that is, the life of the merciful, to whom your mercy is due, according to the saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7)—than the lives of the unmerciful, such as the life of the rich man who feasted splendidly every day. What you give those corrected in mercy is better than what the perverse seek for themselves in order to fulfill the desires of their lusts. It was better for ulcer-covered Lazarus than for the luxurious rich man.

For this reason my lips shall praise you: that is, I shall proclaim you praiseworthy to others with lips made pure either by innocence [Col. 1791D] or purified by a burning coal through repentance. For because, dwelling in a desert, pathless, and waterless land—in the wilderness of Idumaea, amid a people with unclean lips—I have been far too silent, it is fitting for me to cry out: “Woe is me, because I have been silent; because I am a man of unclean lips and dwell amid a people with unclean lips” (Isa. 6:5).

The prophet Isaiah did not say this before he saw the Lord of hosts upon a throne high and lifted up. Nor was I accustomed, before I saw your power and glory and mercy better than lives, to devote my lips to your praise; but now my lips shall praise you. They do not yet praise you in actuality, because they are unclean and still need purification.

[Col. 1792A] **VERSE 5.** That they may thus be purified, I shall bless you in my life adorned with good morals, and in glorifying your name I shall lift up my hands: namely, by doing what is good for the sake of heavenly reward, as the fittingness of the praise to be uttered by the lips requires; and then my lips shall praise you. They do not yet praise you, nor are they fit to praise you, but then they shall praise you. Thus, with this intention of praising you and not seeking praises for myself, I shall bless you in my life, and in your name I shall lift up my hands, as has been explained.

Or, I shall bless you in my life as my lips praise you, namely by ascribing whatever is praiseworthy in my life not to my own virtue but to your mercy; and in your name I shall lift up my hands, either by performing good works, as has been said, for the glory of your name [Col. 1792B], or by praying with hands extended in the manner of a cross, following the example of Moses praying on the mountain against the Amalekites, and the example of Christ, who, with hands outstretched on the cross and with a loud cry, was heard because of his reverence.

**VERSE 6.** Thus, with hands lifted up, I pray this: that my soul may be filled as with fat and fatness. Fat (*adeps*) is the fatty substance adhering to the entrails; fatness is the richness nourished by abundant food and seen diffused throughout the whole body. In keeping with this likeness I pray that my soul, which was dry and lean both within and without in a desert, pathless, and waterless land, may be filled as with marrow and fatness. Within, it was lean before divine eyes, having no abundance of good intention. Without, it was lean even before human eyes, having no abundance of good action [Col. 1792C].

But now I pray that, as with fat, my soul may be filled with an abundance of good will and bright intention, and likewise that neighbors may be stirred to the same thing; and that, as with fatness, it may be filled with an abundance of good action visible throughout the whole body and showing by its richness that I, the prodigal son, wasted away through extreme hunger in a far country, in a desert, pathless, and waterless land, but now, fattened on the fatted calf, rejoice in music and dancing.

For, as testimony to a heart rejoicing and exulting because of its inward fatness, my mouth also shall praise with lips of exultation, outwardly expressing by joyous gesture the joy it possesses within—for example, by singing: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). This good will is indeed inward fat, and it extends from hidden entrails to the visible lips of exultation [Col. 1792D].

For the exultation of the lips is hoarse or absent when the heart is still dry and wasted by hunger—or, worse, still stuffed with husks, the food of swine, and not yet emptied through the remedies of confession. “Praise is not fitting—or precious—in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9), unless such a person, coming to the Father, is first received by him, clothed in white garments, admitted to the feast of the fatted calf—that is, to communion in the Lord’s body and blood—and from it receives the fat and fatness sacrificed to God in victims, when a fat offering is immolated [Col. 1793A]; or through the contemplative life, which, wholly aflame with the love of God, is likened to a whole burnt offering.

Alternatively: There is “fatness” in those charisms which we receive for our own salvation and without which we cannot be saved at all: such as love of God and neighbour, faith, hope, chastity, humility, wisdom or knowledge, and other such gifts, by which an inwardly abundantly enriched soul may be saved in private life. But there are other gifts which we receive for others, for example, the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, gifts of healing, kinds of tongues, interpretation of utterances, the working of miracles, and other such things, which the Apostle calls “the manifestation of the Spirit.” “To each one,” he says, “is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness” (1 Cor. 12:7)—understand: for that of one’s neighbours—[Col. 1793B] so that you may understand that the Spirit’s inward power is one thing, and the manifestation of that same Spirit another.

Of the inward power it was said to blessed Mary: “The power of the Most High shall overshadow thee” (Luke 1:35). Of the outward manifestation the bride says to the bridegroom in the Song of Songs, a song of love: “Thy name is oil poured out; therefore the young maidens loved thee” (Song 1:2). Oil poured in through inward gifts and preserved in vessels does not draw the love of the young maidens; but oil poured out in lamps, because it shines outwardly among the young women playing tambourines, draws to the love of the Bridegroom maidens still little in faith, through a word of wisdom or knowledge, or another manifestation of grace poured out for the benefit of others. Thus they may draw near to receive from him first the oil poured secretly into vessels to be preserved, and then the oil poured out to be displayed in lamps.

By oil poured in, understand fat adhering to the vital parts and not appearing outside. By oil poured out, understand richness appearing outwardly and inviting those who see it to the banquet of wisdom. Pray for both, and say: “May my soul be filled as with fat and richness,” so that vessels of conscience, filled with poured-in oil, may abound sufficiently, and lamps of works, filled with poured-out oil, may overflow. “May my soul be filled as with fat,” that I may live soberly, justly, and piously, preserving and day by day storing up for myself the testimony of a good conscience; so that I may truly say: “I am conscious of nothing [Col. 1793D] against myself” (1 Cor. 4:4). But because a minister of God ought also to have a good testimony from those who are outside, may my soul be so filled with richness that I may be one of those who say truly and without pretence: “Let a man so regard us as ministers of Christ” (1 Cor. 4:1). Likewise: “In all things let us show ourselves as ministers of God, so that our ministry may not be blamed” (2 Cor. 6:3–4).

For it does not suffice for Christ’s ministers to possess a good conscience while neglecting their reputation. Yet neither does an outwardly sought reputation make one praiseworthy when conscience is neglected. I know that both are necessary for me as God’s minister: that through the fatness of a good conscience my own salvation may be secured, and through the richness of a good [Col. 1794A] reputation the salvation especially of those committed to me may be shaped. For he who has not the hidden treasure of conscience in the field of his heart is miserable; and “he who neglects his reputation is cruel.” Reputation is not to be sought for empty glory, but neither is it to be neglected, lest our ministry be blamed through some scandal occasioned by our negligence.

On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1793D] St Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book VIII, chapter 10]: “The fatness of richness fills the soul when the infusion of heavenly hope warms it against the heat of present desires.” Therefore the fatness of inward richness signifies the disposition of a good heart filled with good hope; just as, conversely, the disposition of an evil heart is expressed by the name “fatness,” where it is said: “Their iniquity came forth as from fatness; they passed into the disposition [Col. 1794B] of their heart” (Ps. 72:7). And elsewhere: “They have shut up,” he says, “their fatness” (Ps. 16:10), because they refused to disclose the disposition of their evil heart through confession, but endeavoured to shut it up through self-defence, while “their mouth spoke pride” (ibid.) in boasting issuing from such fatness.

Far be from me the richness of such fatness, through which that foolish and senseless people is rebuked as having “grown fat, become thick, and expanded,” and as having “forsaken God its maker and departed from God its saviour” (Deut. 32:15). Likewise in Job that ungodly man is rebuked who runs against God “with fat neck” (Job 15:26), and from whose flanks lard hangs down. Ehud also, the ambidextrous man, killed the exceedingly fat King Eglon with a two-edged sword [Col. 1794C]; and Samuel cut the exceedingly fat Agag into pieces. In these sayings and deeds we are warned to beware the fatness or richness from which iniquity proceeds, but to desire that of which David, singing wisely, says: “May my soul be filled as with fat and richness”; so that, abounding in fatness through the good disposition of a devout heart, and in richness through the good disposition of a holy work, my mouth may praise with lips of exultation the giver of such fatness and such richness. And while I ask this, saying, “May my soul be filled as with fat and richness,” I at the same time make a vow by adding: “And with lips of exultation shall my mouth praise thee.”

Alternatively: I, Christ, the true David, in a land deserted, pathless, and waterless—in the Jewish land, namely—thirsting for [Col. 1794D] the salvation of men, “O God, my God,” watch from the dawn unto thee and pray for my whole body, which is the Church, that it too may not become dry and arid, like a deserted, pathless, and waterless land, fit for no shoot or good fruit; but rather may be rich and abundant, having upper waters for fatness and lower waters for richness. Those who know the ancient history of Achsah, daughter of Caleb, understand what I mean. Having received dry land from her father, she asked, at her husband’s urging, for watered land also: “And her father gave her upper and lower waters” (Judg. 1:15). Or, the rich whole burnt offering is wholly consumed through the active life, which is compared to a victim victorious over lusts.

[Col. 1795A] And so I, Christ, who first received the synagogue from the Father as dry land, ask for watered land too: namely, the holy Church composed both of the small number of Jews and the multitude of Gentiles. Its field may have upper watering through the life of those contemplating things above, and lower watering through the life of those doing good work in earthly matters. Or, let it have upper watering through tears arising from love of heavenly things, and lower watering through tears arising from remembrance of sins and fear of punishments.

And because in my great body, which is the Church, some are for me as flesh, to be cherished in many ways because of their manifold frailty, while others are as the soul enlivening and ruling such flesh, I pray for the soul, for the securing of the flesh’s salvation, that as the soul is filled with fat and richness, the flesh too may become rich through the soul’s richness, according to the saying: “You who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. 6:1). This is the same as saying: You who, as it were, are souls and are fit in spirit to govern carnal and frail people, instruct such persons out of the fatness of kindly affection in a spirit of gentleness, with the spirit of anger far removed—a spirit which does not instruct but destroys.

This spirit of anger reigns in lean souls wasting and growing old through envy or hatred, like the elder son who desired a kid more than the fatted calf, preferring to feast with his friends rather than with his father and his found brother, and preferring to waste away [Col. 1795C] in his envy rather than grow rich in brotherly charity. Therefore, that the leanness of envy may be far from my members, I, Christ—or I, the Church—pray that “my soul may be filled as with fat and richness,” by which my carnal members are to be governed. When they have been made rich, a rich whole burnt offering and a full banquet may be made: namely, with the brother who had perished found through the fullness of the Gentiles and the admission of penitents; and with the elder brother appeased and made peaceful in the converted remnant of the Jews, or even in the remaining persons who keep the Father’s commands and labour well in the vineyard, though they murmur over this and look with a bleary evil eye because the Lord is good in receiving prodigal sons and making the last first.

Therefore, when all these are reconciled into one, let the leanness of envy be far away, and let “my soul be filled as with the fat and richness of the love of God and neighbour”: so that through the fatness of love for God it may love God himself with all its heart, all its soul, and all its strength; and through the richness of brotherly love each person may love his neighbour as himself. Once this richness is perfected, my heart shall exult inwardly in the Lord, and my mouth shall praise outwardly with lips of exultation. The people who honours thee with its lips while its heart is far from thee does not possess lips of exultation, which accompany a pure conscience. But I, David—whether in the person of Christ, or of the Church, or of any faithful person—desire to open lips of exultation in thy praises, O God, my God, unto whom I watch from the dawn; and I thirst for them with that thirst with which [Col. 1796A] my soul thirsts for thee. For the thirst that will have an end comes first; exultation in praise, which will have no end in which to fail, follows: it reaches the end of every consummation, Christ, in whom it now makes progress and shall never fail eternally. Therefore I correctly said above in the past tense: “My soul thirsted for thee,” because this thirst, which now remains in a deserted, pathless, and waterless land, will one day be past; and with a verb in the future tense I offer vows of praise, saying: “And with lips of exultation shall my mouth praise thee,” because “blessed are they who dwell in thy house; for ever and ever they shall praise thee” (Ps. 83:5).

Another reading has: “And lips of exultation shall praise thy name.” The future whole burnt offering of praise of which we speak, in lips of exultation, will then be consummated, and will be as a truly perpetual sacrifice [Col. 1796B] never to be taken away for eternity, when I shall so appear to thee in the sanctuary that, fully enlightened, I may see thy power and thy glory, not through a mirror and in an enigma, as in the desert of Idumaea, but face to face; knowing also not in part, as now, but as I am known, because thy mercy is better than lives. Then, I say, when thirst has ceased, prayer—so necessary now in this deserted, pathless, and waterless place—will cease. “In that day,” says Truth, “you shall ask me nothing” (John 16:23). Prayer, then, will end, but praise will remain, in which I shall sing thy mercies, O Lord, for eternity.

But now all goes well if, though lips of exultation are as yet stopped up by manifold sorrow, at least the heart is [Col. 1796C] watchful.

**VERSE 7.** “I will meditate on thee,” which I also promise when I say: “I will meditate on thee,” believing in thee, thirsting for thee. I will meditate, I say, not against thee like a rebel, but in thee as one obedient and humble. When shall I meditate on thee? “In the mornings”: either literally, watching from the dawn unto thee; or “in the mornings,” that is, in bright works, rightly understood by “morning,” when every labourer customarily begins work, especially he who was hired at the first hour of morning. Morally too, he works in the morning who does good works with Christ as the light showing the way; but, conversely, he works in night who does evil. For “everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3:20). Therefore, casting away the works of darkness, in mornings—that is, in bright works—I shall meditate on [Col. 1796D] thee, provided that, through thy grace going before, I have first remembered thee upon my bed. For if the eye of intention, remembering thee upon the bed—that is, in rest or leisure—is single, desiring nothing besides thee, then the whole body of activity will consequently be bright, or morning-like. And so I truly affirm that if I have remembered thee upon my bed, I shall meditate on thee also in the mornings, giving thanks and ascribing the bright work to thee.

**VERSE 8.** “Because thou hast been my helper”: so that what I contemplated upon my bed, while thou didst sow it, before the dawn of works, might proceed into a bright and morning-like effect, while thou workest not only the willing but also the accomplishing: willing upon the bed, accomplishing in the morning; willing in intention, [Col. 1797A] accomplishing in action. This would be wholly impossible for me in the desert of Idumaea unless thou hadst been my helper, thou who art powerful not only to assist in good things but also to protect from evils.

Therefore, trusting in thy defence, “I shall exult in the covering of thy wings.” I am a chick; and unless thou protectest me with the covering of thy wings, Saul will seize me as a kite: Saul pursuing me David, death pursuing me Christ, sin or the devil pursuing me a Christian. Against the rapacious claws of Saul, death, and the devil, I shall exult securely in the covering of thy wings. I do not yet exult fully in present possession while I labour amid the perils of Idumaea; but in the future I shall exult fully. Yet now my exultation has in some measure begun through this certainty, [Col. 1797B] by which I know that those who kill the body cannot kill the soul, whose life thou art, O my God, unto whom I watch from the dawn. For as the body, clinging to the soul, thereby has life, so:

**VERSE 9.** “My soul has clung after thee,” that it may have life from thee. It has clung, I say, by the glue of charity; “after thee,” I say, by the order of holy humility. Thus the creature’s charity is understood to be ordered toward the Creator, while the lower nature both clings to the higher through charity and shows itself to be beneath—or after—it through humility. “My soul has clung after thee,” so that it loves thee before itself and follows thee in imitation. My soul will not presume to go before thee by giving thee counsel, as Peter did when he dissuaded thee from the humiliations of the Passion, saying: “See that this does not happen to thee [Col. 1797C]” (Matt. 16:22). Rebuked for this by thee, he later learned to follow thee, according to thy saying to him: “Get behind me, Satan”; and elsewhere: “Follow me”; likewise, “Thou, follow me” (John 21:19, 22).

Instructed by these teachings, I, a Christian, no longer wish to go before thee, Christ, by suggesting to thee some new counsel contrary to thy ancient counsel. But, having carefully investigated thy good pleasure as expressed in the Scriptures of truth, it is good for me to cling to thee; to go after thee and acquiesce in thy will through charity and humility is worthy and just, because thy right hand has received me. Thy right hand—that is, thy Son—has received me, that is, my nature, into unity of person. Or thy right hand, thy Son, has received me, that is, my person, into the unity of his body, which is the Church. Rightly, therefore, my soul—that is, my life—clings after thee in such a way as always to love and follow thee, always breaking its own will through love for thee and always following thy will through humility.

Alternatively: “My soul has clung after thee.” I, the true David, have power to lay down and to take up again my soul. Although in the desert of Idumaea it was sorrowful even unto death and, through the frailty of human flesh, wished to avoid the cup of the Passion, saying: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me,” yet it clung after thee, adding: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as thou wilt” (Matt. 26:39). This was indeed for my soul to cling after [Col. 1798A] thee: to break its own will and obediently acquiesce in thine. Having done this, I gave an example to my followers, that they too should do likewise, with similar obedience, though not with similar or equal power; for none of them has power to lay down his soul and take it up again as I do. My soul so clung after thee, God the Father, in me thy Word, that it can do whatsoever it wills in thy power, which is present in it not partially but wholly.

Yet, although exalted into the supreme power of thy and my Divinity, it does not lose the essence of its own condition. For if a small drop of water poured into much wine does not lose the essence of its moisture when conformed to the wine, much more, since my soul has clung after thee, O God—absorbed as it were in the boundless [Col. 1798B] sea of thy Divinity—it does not cease to be, but is most excellently conformed to the Divinity which assumed it. Especially after the death of its body, absorbed into the glory of the resurrection, it retains its own essence, according to which it stands after thee in the order of its condition, although it sits beside thee upon the throne of thy majesty and reigns with thee in the omnipotence of the glorification granted to it. In that glorification thy right hand received me: the entire nature of my humanity, flesh together with soul, now placed and exalted at thy right hand. Such and so powerful is my soul, ruling even in the midst of its enemies.

**VERSES 10–11.** “But they sought my soul in vain.” They—the Jews by name, but truly Idumaeans—sought my soul, not knowing that no one could take it from me against my will. Rather, I laid it down voluntarily and took it up again. Yet they sought to take away my soul, but in vain, because their attempt achieved not what they wished, but what they did not wish. For when they wished me, with my sepulchre guarded, to be held in the lower parts of the earth and under the earth, it did not happen so. My soul could not be held in hell; having loosed the pains of hell, it returned thence with much spoil. Nor could my body be held in the sepulchre; rising in great power after an earthquake, it ascended from the lower parts of the earth above all the heavens to the highest throne of the Father’s exaltedness.

“But they sought my soul in vain; they shall enter into the lower parts of the earth”: both in respect of their souls, to be drawn into hell, [Col. 1798D] and in respect of their bodies, to go into the earth, both by the law of the common condition by which it was said to man, “Thou art earth, and into earth thou shalt go” (Gen. 3:19), and by the privilege of singular condemnation, by which they shall be delivered into the hand of the swords of the Romans and shall become portions for foxes. For even those who survive the sword shall be portions for foxes, by becoming prey to deceitful Roman rulers, such as Herod the tetrarch, concerning whom the Lord says: “Go, tell that fox” (Luke 13:32). And those who die by sword, famine, and pestilence in their perfidy shall be portions for foxes—that is, evil spirits—which shall seize their souls to be drawn into the lower parts of the earth, that is, into hell, and there punished eternally; and, that they may be crushed by a twofold destruction, they shall be clothed again in their bodies at the general resurrection [Col. 1799A] and perish with the devil and his angels on the day of judgment.

Alternatively, God’s peculiar people, whom the Lord set upon high land so that it might eat the fruits of the fields and suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone, because it forsook God its maker and departed from God its saviour by choosing the seditious Barabbas for itself, shall by just judgment be scattered by seditions. Drawn by the rope of captivity from the high land, it shall enter into the lower parts of the earth, so that, throughout all the land which opened its mouth and received Christ’s blood at its hand, it may be cursed according to the imprecation of the Law. It shall not possess the high land, which commonly vomits out such people, but shall enter the lower parts of the earth, scarcely holding among the Gentiles some contemptible outskirts of villages or [Col. 1799B] streets; and it shall always be beneath and not above, since it has no king except Caesar, no ruler of its own nation, but is subject to a foreign power—and, what torments it still more, to Christian rule.

Just as they vainly sought the soul of the unconquered King who came in the name of his Father, God almighty, so they vainly await another who will come in his own name and, as they dream, restore their high land to them. It shall not be so. For when he comes, he must remain a short time; and the Lord Jesus shall kill him with the spirit of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming. He likewise, with the rest of the ungodly, shall enter the lower parts of the earth, to be cast into the lake of fire burning with pitch and sulphur.

He will indeed aspire to set himself upon high land, so as to sit in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God. Indeed, not content with this robbery—he who deems himself equal to God—he will raise himself above everything called God or worshipped, becoming so presumptuous and arrogant as to fear no one. But, whether he wishes it or not, excluded by the high land which vomits out such persons, he shall enter into the lower parts of the earth. He shall be delivered into the hand of the sword, so that, having the wound of the sword, the wound of anathema, he shall, whether willing or unwilling, enter the lower parts of the earth—either deprived of kingdom and life among those who perish, as Julian the Apostate and Constantius the Arian; or certainly humbled to repentance among those who are converted and deprived of their wrongly desired dominion. They shall be compelled to enter into the lower parts of the earth, [Col. 1799D] that they may learn not to be proud; may learn that rulers of churches ought to be far different from the kings of the Gentiles; and may learn to be subject to the one King of kings. Whoever dare to kick against his kingdom and rule shall, willing or unwilling, enter into the lower parts of the earth.

We have also seen in our own days certain pseudo-pontiffs of the Roman city entering the lower parts of the earth in such a manner that, delivered to Satan into the hand of the sword, they swiftly ceased to rule. The latest and chief of these was Peter, son of Leo, set over Pope Innocent II and displayed in the temple of God as though he were God, as though he were a legitimate priest—for priests too are called gods, as are all those to whom the word of God came. But false Christs and false prophets boast falsely in priesthood or in the divine title of prophecy, [Col. 1800A] when they themselves are little foxes and portions for foxes. More rightly they should have dens in the lower parts of the earth than fraudulently or violently occupy the summit of ecclesiastical government.

**VERSE 12.** “But the king shall rejoice in God, and all who swear in him shall be praised.” That King, whose kingdom, though not of this world, is nevertheless in this world, as also in heaven, is Christ the King, King of the Jews. He has written upon his garment and his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Tim. 6:15). He shall reign in the house of Jacob forever, and there shall be no end to his kingdom. This King, I say, crowned with a crown of thorns and made sorrowful even unto death in the desert of Idumaea, now raised from death, “shall rejoice in God.” For in that he lives, he lives unto God, and he himself is God in God, as he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10–11).

Although before his Passion the man truly said this—he who, from the beginning of his conception, remained God in God the Father—nevertheless it was not yet a complete ground for rejoicing, as long as God appeared emptied into man rather than man glorified into God. But now, when the man who was mortal for a time has been glorified into the immortal God with the glory which the Son of God had before the world existed, the man advanced into the glory of Divinity rightly “shall rejoice in God,” having now received authority to reign everywhere, as he says: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18). He always possessed this authority in his divinity; but this King received it from God in his humanity, [Col. 1800C] and therefore rightly “shall rejoice in God.”

“And all who swear in him shall be praised.” I do not say that those are to be praised who swear by him, or by any other oath—an oath which, by the testimony of the King himself, is from evil, and is not so much praiseworthy as tolerable, even when it is true, when it is not evil but is from evil; whereas it is blameworthy when false, and is not only from evil but evil itself. I do not praise, or declare praiseworthy, those who swear in this way; for an oath, though allowed in some manner, is nevertheless not praised by the King himself. But I rightly declare praiseworthy all who swear *in* him, because to swear in him is nothing other than to persevere irrevocably in a good promise made to him, whether in baptism or in a stricter purpose of holiness.

For those who faithfully perform what they have devoutly vowed to him are recognized as his allied friends, as it were by a certain oath, and therefore shall be praised. Conversely, those who deny him in word and deed, or even in deeds alone, are by no means praiseworthy, nor ought they to be heard in the court of this King, whether as praisers of evil or blamers of good.

“For the mouth of those speaking iniquity is stopped”: not only that of the Jews denying this King, but also that of all perverse people who call good evil and evil good, put darkness for light and light for darkness, call sweet bitter and bitter sweet, condemn the just, and justify the ungodly. The mouth of such people is now stopped in part, so that their speech murmurs as though from the ground, [Col. 1801A] and their voice is like that of a Python, so contemptible that it finds no friendly hearers in the midst of the Church, although it whispers secretly in corners.

But when the final judgment has been completed, in which all who swear in him shall be praised by the King himself, when he says, “Come, ye blessed of my Father,” etc. (Matt. 25:34), then the mouth of those speaking iniquity shall be so stopped that profound silence shall be imposed upon them forever. For thereafter “the wicked shall be silent in darkness” (1 Sam. 2:9); with their accursed mouth completely shut, they shall waste away in their torments. In the judgment itself, indeed, they will have some things to say: for example, when “they shall marvel at the suddenness of unexpected salvation, saying within themselves, repenting and groaning for anguish of spirit: ‘These are they whom we once held in derision and as a likeness of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end without honour. Behold, how they are numbered among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints’” (Wis. 5:2 ff.). Likewise: “When did we see thee hungry or thirsty and not minister to thee?” (Matt. 25:44). Likewise the wicked and slothful servant who hid his lord’s money will say something in judgment by way of excuses for sins, when all who have traded well and profitably gained from the money entrusted to them are praised.

But when, as has been said, the judgment is completed, the mouth of those speaking iniquity shall be utterly stopped, and the wicked shall be silent in darkness. For then this King, the universal emperor, shall command the winds and sea; or, as it is read in Mark, rebuking the winds he shall threaten the sea, saying: “Be silent; be muzzled” (Mark 4:39). From that point there shall be a great calm, never disturbed by any sound of sea or waves.

It also happens, through the mercy of this King, that the mouth of those speaking iniquity is stopped as the mouth of blaspheming Saul was stopped and the mouth of Paul was opened: “Formerly,” he says, “I was a blasphemer and persecutor, but now I have obtained mercy” (1 Tim. 1:13). When the apostle Peter preached, the mouth of those speaking iniquity—namely, the Jews stained with Christ’s blood—was likewise stopped, so that three thousand of them were converted in one day and five thousand on another. They openly confessed Christ the King, whom with an iniquitous mouth they had denied; they laid all they possessed at the apostles’ feet and lived not for themselves but for Christ their King, having one heart and one soul in God. Hence those who swear in him shall deservedly be praised among them, because the mouth of those speaking [Col. 1802B] iniquity was commendably stopped when they began—and thereafter ceased not—to speak things pleasing to God and beneficial to their neighbours.

Glory to God the Father, unto whom men watch from the dawn; glory to the Son, who watches in himself and in his members, and by his watchings obtains for his members mercy better than lives. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that very mercy to be exalted in judgment above all lives by which God has distinguished creatures: giving to some that they live and do not feel, to others that they live and feel, and to others that they live, feel, and discern. By these differences trees, beasts, and human beings are distinguished from one another. Human beings alone gather all lives into themselves, because they live with trees, live and feel with beasts, and live and discern with angels. Therefore may God’s glorious mercy be kindly above [Col. 1802C] these lives, so that human nature, which embraces all lives, may be saved in all who are predestined to eternal life. May immeasurable glory be to the triune God, eternally living and by his grace temporally ordering the lives of human beings. Amen.

## PSALM 63

[Col. 1801]

[Col. 1801D] “Hear, O God, my prayer when I make supplication,” etc. Title:

**(VERSE 1.) UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID.**

This is clear. This psalm briefly recounts the Passion and resurrection of Christ. First Christ prays, enumerating the evils which he has suffered as though they had already happened. Secondly, he mocks the savagery of the Jews by recalling that, when the resurrection was announced, they were more disturbed; at the words: “The arrows of little children became their wounds.” Its purpose is to teach us to hope in God when we suffer.

Christ speaks not only from the Head alone but also from the body, and says: “Hear, O God, my prayer when I make supplication; deliver my soul from the fear of the enemy.” By his example that combatant also is admonished to pray who, fighting amid hope and fear, does not know whether the weapons of temptations, like the arrows of little children, are to be repelled from him by the breastplate of righteousness unto the end indicated in the title, or not. For if he himself, who [Col. 1802D] foreknew the future, chose to pray, how much more diligently ought those who are uncertain to devote themselves to prayer, that they may be delivered from fear of a visible or invisible enemy; lest they yield in persecution by an enemy, or fall or despair in the devil’s temptation. For this reason he concludes this prayer with such an end: “The righteous shall rejoice in the Lord and hope in him, and all the upright in heart shall be praised.” But before this happy ending of the psalm, let us run through its tearful text.

**VERSE 2.** “Hear, O God, my prayer when I make supplication.” The distinction between prayer and supplication is clear, although one is customarily used for the other. Thus I, Christ, in my own voice and in the voice of martyrs, praying for goods to be obtained and making supplication for evils to be removed, ask that my prayer may be heard when I make supplication—or, as another translation has it, “when I am afflicted.” Therefore I say: Hear, O God the Father, my prayer by giving good things when I am afflicted amid evils, or when [Col. 1803A] I make supplication asking that these very evils be removed. Hear me more abundantly than I ask, by bestowing goods contrary to the evils by which I am afflicted. And because amid afflicting evils nothing is more harmful than worldly fear opposed to divine fear, thou, O God, hearer of just prayer, “deliver my soul from the fear of the enemy.”

In the Hebrew it reads: “Preserve my life from the fear of the enemy.” For I know that, just as he who loves his soul or life more than thee is not worthy of thee, so too he who fears anything more than thee is not worthy of thee. Therefore preserve my soul, or life, from such fear, lest it fall into its snare; or if perhaps it falls in, deliver it lest it be held fast. Deliver it not so much from the enemy as from fear of the enemy: not that I may have no enemy, but that I may not fear the enemy; not that I may not be killed, but that, fearing thee, I may not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. I do not pray that I may lack an enemy, but that I may not be swallowed up by an enemy.

For whoever, fearing an enemy, knowingly offends thee because of that fear, is swallowed up while living and awake; but if it happens to one who does not know, he is swallowed up dead or asleep. Some are swallowed up living, others dead, in the storm of persecution. Those who knew the truth of the Catholic faith but, overcome by fear or pain of torments, denied it, were swallowed up alive. But those who denied it without knowing the truth were swallowed up dead. Those who feared God more than man—guarding themselves from the wrath of him who can cast soul and body into the hell of fire rather than from the wrath of man, who has power to kill the body alone—could not be swallowed up. Or, if they were swallowed up for an hour, like Peter in denial or Jonah in disobedience, the beast was soon compelled to vomit them forth alive, since, because the remedy of repentance stood in the way, it could not incorporate them into itself.

For because Jonah prayed in the whale’s belly and Peter wept bitterly in the danger of denial, the cruel beast vomited forth both: one visibly, as an example of manifest repentance; the other invisibly, as an example of secret repentance. Since Jonah, rebuked by the sailors, acknowledged his fault, he set forth beforehand the pattern of those who, caught in manifest fashion by the lot of judicial sentence, repent and return to interrupted obedience by willingly bearing the penance imposed upon them. So he, given up by his own judgment to the danger of the sea and deprived of the ship’s help unto the destruction of his flesh, repented; and at last, delivered from the vain fear by which he excessively feared Nineveh’s overthrow and Judaea’s abandonment, he returned in repentance, bearing a hard embassy. “Yet,” he says, “forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 3:4). He would not have spoken thus unless sound fear had driven out vain fear. For sound was the fear by which he feared more to incur God’s offence by keeping silent than that of human beings by speaking.

Moreover, the apostle Peter, pierced not by a man’s rebuke but by Christ’s looking upon him, bore the figure of those who, divinely touched by secret compunction [Col. 1804A], do penance by weeping bitterly because, overcome by human fear or drawn aside by an excessive love of their own life, they have departed from the right path. To return to that path is altogether impossible unless the penitent mind is emptied of fear of the enemy and filled with fear of the Lord. For if it is written of the only-begotten Son of God, humbled in the form of a servant, that “the Spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him” (Isa. XI, 3), how shall we wretches, redeemed from the slavery of sin by his blood and still destined somehow to be judged by him, be—or be able to be—secure enough not to be filled with the Spirit of the fear of the Lord?

But in truth we cannot receive this Spirit of fear and be filled with it unless we are freed from fear of the enemy, as Peter was freed so perfectly that he no longer feared Rome [Col. 1804B], mistress of the world, though he had been terrified by a priest’s maidservant. For, filled with the fear of the Lord, he did not fear to die for confession of the truth which, for a time, he had abandoned by denying it—because he had feared the hostile Pharisaic assembly too much and had loved himself too much. Thus, surely, whoever is possessed by a disordered and excessive fear of the enemy is at the same time possessed by a disordered and excessive self-love. Conversely, whoever lacks disordered fear of the enemy likewise lacks disordered self-love.

Therefore this fear, by which the enemy is feared more than God, must itself be feared, because at the same time the world is loved more than God; and so everyone who wishes to be a friend of the world is made an enemy of God. Conversely, the world hates those whom Christ loves, separating them from the world by the infusion of his own fear and love. “If [Col. 1804C] you were of the world,” he says, “the world would love what was its own. But because you are not of the world, and I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John XV, 19).

See now and consider how many evils disordered fear kindles: by making you a friend of the world, it makes you an enemy of God; while, conversely, ordered fear makes you God’s friend. Therefore, that, filled with ordered fear, you may be free from disordered fear, and may not be cowardly by fearing what ought not to be feared, but reverently fearful by fearing what ought to be feared—like that Simeon “just and devout” (Luke II, 25)—cry to God from your whole heart, saying: “Deliver my soul from fear of the enemy. ‘Pierce my flesh with your fear’ (Ps. CXVIII, 120),” so that, a servant under your fear [Col. 1804D] and free from fear of the enemy, I may be filled with ordered fear and consequently with ordered love. For as a needle or bristle draws in the thread, so ordered fear introduces ordered charity, of which the bride said in the Song of Love: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar; he ordered charity in me” (Cant. II, 4).

Only ordered charity is capable of casting out disordered fear. And therefore, when I say to you, my God, “Deliver my soul from fear of the enemy,” I ask from you ordered charity, which casts out fear. For charity, however fervent it may be, does not build up unless it is ordered. Indeed, the zeal of charity without the virtue of discernment—which distinguishes vices from virtues and sets the virtues themselves in their proper order—is unbearable. Therefore [Col. 1805A] where the emulation of charity is vehement, discernment is especially necessary; and this is the ordering of charity. Zeal without knowledge is always found less effective and less useful, and is very often experienced as more harmful. The more fervent and vehement the spirit, therefore, and the more abundant the charity, the more need there is of vigilant knowledge, to restrain zeal, temper the spirit, and order charity.

Therefore, while praying as Christ that my soul may be delivered from fear of the enemy, I ask that ordered charity may be given to me and my members: charity which combats vices and suitably orders virtues according to the character of their occasions. It could not order them unless it were itself first ordered, after fear of the enemy had been cast out. That fear attacks more fiercely when not one evil man, or a few wicked persons, [Col. 1805B] or even many divided among themselves, but many evildoers united in purpose assail us, as “the kings of the earth stood up and the rulers assembled together against you, O Lord, and against me, your Christ.” But what did they accomplish by the effort of their malice? Nothing whatever. This I, Christ—or I, the Christian—do not ascribe to my own human strength, but to the divine gift, because you, O God—

**VERSE 3.** “You have protected me, a man, from the assembly of evildoers,” that is, of those who devise evil counsels, “and from the multitude of workers of iniquity.” You protected me from an assembly which consisted not of a few but of a multitude, and whose members not only harbored malice in their hearts but also worked iniquity in act. What greater [Col. 1805C] iniquity is there than, out of envy, to persecute and kill a man who does no evil and performs many good deeds? Many martyrs suffered such things. But what they experienced shines forth more clearly in the very chief of martyrs, whom it was insufficient for the Lord to exhort by word unless he also strengthened them by the example of both his passion and his prayer.

He himself suffered affliction from the assembly of evildoers and from the multitude of workers of iniquity, teaching you thereby to suffer likewise. He prayed, and by praying obtained such protection for himself. You too pray to be protected from like persons and in like fashion; and when you perceive that you have been protected, give thanks to God, saying: “You have protected me from the assembly of evildoers, from the multitude of workers of iniquity.” And lest anyone think that those who did not crucify me, Christ, with their hands were called workers of iniquity without cause, [Col. 1805D] I show how they worked iniquity, not with hand, but with tongue:

**VERSE 4.** “For they sharpened their tongues like a sword,” when they openly cried: “We have a law, and according to our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John XIX, 7). Again: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (ibid., 12). Again: “He is deserving of death” (Matt. XXVI, 66). Again: “If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have delivered him to you” (John XVIII, 30).

By saying such things they sharpened their tongues like a sword, accomplishing with their poisonous tongue the murder which the soldiers accomplished with bloody hands. At the third hour they crucified with their tongues him whom, at the sixth hour, the soldiers crucified with wood and nails. Hence, in the Gospel narrative he is said in one place to have been crucified at the third hour [Col. 1806A], and elsewhere at the sixth, in order that the one and same sacrilege of those crucifying by both tongue and wood may be observed in the killing of the supreme priest, free from every stain and praying even for those enemies themselves.

But, repaying evil for good, they bent the bow, not content openly with the sword of the tongue unless they also struck secretly with the bow of deceit. They bent, by their counsels, the bow: a bitter thing painted over with however great a sweetness of words. The bitter thing was hidden by sweetness of speech when they said: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful,” and so forth (Matt. XXII, 16). For they prepared their arrows in the quiver so that, whatever he said, he might be shot at and held, as though guilty either against Caesar if he forbade the payment of tribute, or against the people if he permitted it. They likewise presented the woman caught [Col. 1806B] in adultery in such a way that whatever he should judge concerning her might be judged by them unjust—either against the justice of the law or against the mercy which he himself taught.

But if a net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures, how much more so before the eyes of their leader, Herod? For their laying snares before him who sees all things is as though they wove nooses in the rays of the high noonday sun, to draw it down from heaven to earth, or as though by their breath they attempted to extinguish the fire of the burning sun which by its heat warms the earth. Miserable men! They do not know that they strive in vain. Therefore, as by their counsels they bent the bow—a bitter thing—so also:

**VERSE 6.** “They will shoot at him suddenly, and will not fear.” Suddenly, as if unexpectedly—although he sees all things—[Col. 1806C] they will shoot, bringing the crime they devise to completion, and will not fear. They will shoot at a man and will not fear God; they will shoot at a man who delivers himself to one judging him unjustly and will not fear that same God, who will judge just and unjust persons justly in great majesty, as he himself declared before Pilate, who was judging him unjustly. “Nevertheless,” he said, “from now on you will see the Son of Man coming with great power and majesty” (Matt. XXVI, 64).

Speaking such things, he was their target, and they did not fear, because by this very testimony of truth, condemning him as though a false witness or blasphemer, they “made firm for themselves an evil word.” Their repetition was confirmation: by saying, “Crucify, crucify” (Luke [Col. 1806D] XXIII, 21), they made firm for themselves an evil word. They made it firm not by assertion of truth but by obstinacy in malice. Or they made firm for themselves an evil word by saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25). This evil or malicious saying they made firm for themselves—that is, to harm themselves and their descendants—by such resoluteness of utterance that with that blood there may come upon them all righteous blood shed, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah.

I said that they bent the bow, a bitter thing. Now I say how they bent it, namely thus: “They related [matters] in order to hide snares.” For they assembled a council and said: “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs,” and so forth (John XI, 47). In [Col. 1807A] that assembly of evildoers the snares were hidden in what they said: “If we let him go on like this, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John XI, 48). Since they pretended, under a feigned fear, that he must be killed for loyalty to Caesar and for defense of their eminent place and chosen people, in this they concealed their snares, so that scarcely anyone could understand that they meant to kill him out of envy.

Therefore they said: “Who will see them?”—that is, the snares so hidden. “Let him not be handed over by us,” they say, “but by a disciple. Let him not be killed by us, but by a judge and his soldiers. Let us do all these things through others, so that we may appear to have done nothing. Thus let us hide the snares by saying, ‘It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death’” (John XVIII, 31), so that, when [Col. 1807B] he has been caught and bound in our snares, no one may recognize that the guilt of his death belongs to us, or that we set the snares by which he was detained. For who will see them? Who can guard against them if we act thus?

Thus:

**VERSE 7.** “They searched out iniquities,” that is, how they might destroy the righteous one, lest the world should go after him: so that, counted with the wicked under the appearance of the equity of a reasonable judgment, and hanged among thieves as an evildoer, he might perish in such a way that even his name should perish. “When,” they say, “will he die, and his name perish?” (Ps. XL, 6). They were not content to kill him unless they could also abolish his very name. Therefore a shameful death was devised, so that, condemned by a most disgraceful death [Col. 1807C] and counted among the wicked, he should thereafter have no name in honorable remembrance; nor should anyone believe that he came blessed in the name of the Lord—which the children had acclaimed—when he was seen hanging on the wood, because the law says that one who hangs on wood is cursed.

Thus they pretended to serve the commandment of the law by cursing and calling “deceiver” him who hung upon the wood—as though feigned equity were not iniquity. Yet feigned equity is a double iniquity: when the pretense of equity is joined to iniquity, iniquity is not annulled but doubled, since the pretense itself is a great iniquity, especially when it is used to defend and strengthen another iniquity.

In cleverly searching out all these contrivances, they accomplished nothing; rather, they “failed in searching a search,” that is, in devising bitter counsels which they could not establish. For the more shrewdly such persons think, the more they fail of truth and equity, submerged in darkness, where they do not see God and suppose themselves not to be seen by God. Yet they are seen by God, whom they regard as man and not God, though he is God-Man, voluntarily accepting by his divine counsel the passion of his humanity. Hence:

**VERSE 8.** “Man shall draw near to the high heart,” that is, the human will in him shall be joined and subjected to the divine will, as he says: “Father, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. XXVI, 39). Therefore man shall draw near to the high heart, because the human will is joined to the divine counsel, so that human and divine willing [Col. 1808A] become entirely one in the one and same person of Jesus Christ, God and man. The mutability of the human will is absorbed into the eternal stability of the divine will, in which the high heart of God always hastens, before the heart of most humble man drew near to it. By this approach of voluntary obedience and submission, the whole nature of man deserved to be exalted, according to the saying: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name” (Phil. II, 9). Thus, “man shall draw near to the high heart”: by this phrase the merit of obedience is indicated.

“And God shall be exalted”: by this phrase the reward of supreme height is indicated. For if, by God’s just judgment, “everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke III, 5), it is no wonder that he who, being in the form of God, humbled himself beyond others in the form of a servant, is beyond others exalted in that same form of a servant; and that he is to be glorified and exalted by the confession of every tongue, and venerated in the highest glory of God the Father even in that nature which was humbled by drawing near to the high heart.

Perhaps it would appear more correct for prophecy to say, “Man shall be exalted,” than “God shall be exalted,” since God, naturally the most high Son of the Most High, cannot be exalted higher. But mortal man, now exalted into immortal God, could rightly be proclaimed by the Prophet as one to be exalted. Yet because heretics were to arise who would assign divinity to the Word assuming man in such a way as to strip the assumed man of it—as Nestorius and Bonosus did, one of whom did not allow man to be proclaimed God in any respect, and the other only by adoption—the Spirit of truth, anticipating them and their like, attributes the name of God, which is above every name, not so much to the Word, always most high, as to the man exalted after obedience, saying: “Man shall draw near, and God shall be exalted.”

For this is man’s true and ineffable exaltation: that he should be honored with the supreme name of the supreme God, which is above every name. Other elect persons, who are called gods or sons of God through the grace of adoption, may count it a great benefit of the divine gift that they have received this name according to the measure distributed by the Holy Spirit to each as he wills. But he to whom the same Spirit was not given by measure, and who was conceived of the Holy Spirit—whence he is rightly called Son by generation, not adoption, of the supreme Father, of whom that same Spirit is love—received the name Son of God in a manner so much more distinctive than others that, from the time he was conceived in the Virgin, man possessed the name God in a manner so much more excellent than others.

But because, in drawing near to the high heart, he so humbled himself that the name of God appeared emptied in him, when he who was God was found in appearance as a weak man, not as most mighty God, it is fitting that, as in his drawing near to the high heart we venerate upon the cross humbled man and emptied God, so upon the throne of paternal glory we proclaim exalted God and absorbed man—not because man is no longer man, but because the nature of man remains in the supreme glory of divinity. Hence, as in his passion [Col. 1809A] impassible God was emptied and, as it were, disappeared, so in his glorification man—now impassible with divine impassibility and immortal with divine immortality—is rightly called exalted God, as it were with his humanity emptied; not because his humanity has ceased, but because it remains in divine glory.

Hence Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book IX, no. 6:

> “Although God before man is one thing, man and God another, and, after man and God, the whole man and the whole God another, do not confuse the mystery of the dispensation by times and kinds. For, according to the condition of kinds and natures, there necessarily had to be one manner of speech in the mystery of the man not yet born, another of one still about to die, and another of one now eternal.”

And later (no. 38):

> “For this was acquired for man: that he should be God. But the assumed man could in no way remain in the unity of God unless, through the unity of God, he passed into the unity of God by nature; so that, because the Word was God in nature, the Word made flesh might likewise again be present in the nature of God. And thus Jesus Christ, man, remains in the glory of God the Father if flesh is united in the glory of the Word; and then the Word made flesh returns, even according to man, into the unity of the paternal nature, when the assumed flesh has possessed the glory of the Word. His unity, therefore, had to be rendered to the Father within himself, so that the birth of his nature might again abide glorified in himself; because the novelty of the dispensation had introduced an affront to unity, and unity, as it had formerly been perfect, could no longer exist now unless the assumption of flesh had been glorified within itself.”

The same author, in the same work (no. [Col. 1809C] 40):

> “For all glory was acquired not for the Word but for the flesh; that is, not for the birth of God, but for the dispensation of the man who was born.”

Again, later (no. 41):

> “But when God, glorifying in himself, glorifies God with the Son of Man glorified, I find that the nature of the glorified one is assumed into the glory of the nature of the glorifying one. For God does not glorify himself, but, glorifying God in man, glorifies him in himself.”

Ambrose, *On Luke*:

> “The Father gave all things to the Son. If he gave all things, he communicated the eternity which he possesses and his majesty.”

Augustine:

> “Man passed into God, not by a changeability of nature but by God’s condescension. This passage from this world to the Father, from the form of a servant to the glory of God the Father, from temporality to eternity, is called Pascha [Col. 1809D]. By it man passed over and God was exalted, in fulfillment of the prophecy which says: ‘Man shall draw near to the high heart, and God shall be exalted’; because he who, when God was emptied in suffering, was found in appearance as mortal man, was himself, in the glory of resurrection and ascension, found as immortal God with man glorified.”

Alternatively: “Man shall draw near, and”—thus the codex—“the high heart”; supply, “shall draw near.” For, both obedient as man and disposing by divinity, through highest counsel, all that he was to suffer, he drew near to the passion. Therefore he who before death was God but lay hidden was afterward exalted, crowned with glory and honor, granted by the Father the name of God which is above every name, and made manifest by public vindication.

Alternatively: Those who searched out iniquities failed in searching a search [Col. 1810A]. But those who seek the Lord will not fail, because an understanding man shall draw near to the high heart—that is, to the understanding of the high heart—in order to inquire concerning divine things. In such inquiries, the more man is enlightened, the more God is exalted to him. For no one fails in contemplating divine things; rather, he advances and grows. But God, who does not grow in himself, becomes great in the heart that seeks him, and is thus exalted, as his majesty is found increasingly incomprehensible.

Therefore his enemies deserve ridicule: they failed in their investigations, and did not injure even his garment—the very one whom they wished to kill—because “the wounds inflicted by them became as the arrows of little children.” Indeed, they wickedly inflicted wounds upon his still mortal flesh, but these wounds did no harm. [Col. 1810B] As arrows made of reeds by little children do not wound those whom they strike, but fall back repelled by a light covering, so likewise the wounds or arrows of the Jews touched only the skin of assumed mortality. They could not injure the man united to God; but in shooting at him, they acquired for themselves incurable wounds.

Hence the Hebrew reads: “Therefore God will shoot them with a sudden dart; their wounds shall be brought upon them, and they shall fall by their own tongues.” Thus the arrows which are ineffective against the Lord, but turned back by him against his adversaries, are so effective that deep wounds are inflicted by them, through which they shall fall wounded and slain, condemned by their own tongues. Finally, their arrows were strong only against themselves, weak against the Lord; but:

**VERSE 9.** “And their tongues were weakened against them,” with which they said to the guards of the tomb: “Say that, while you were sleeping, his disciples stole him” (Matt. XXVIII, 13). Truly it is weak and laughable testimony, constructed upon the guarantee of sleeping witnesses. For witnesses are not admitted by a lawful plea except concerning things seen and heard; but if these men slept, they saw nothing. If they saw nothing, how could they be witnesses? Are you so foolish, O Jews, that you think rational people can be made foolish by testimony of this sort? Surely you yourselves slept too deeply when you fabricated testimony from sleeping witnesses by which you intended to strengthen a lie. Hence, because “iniquity lied to itself,” their tongues were rightly [Col. 1810D] weakened against them, not only in this testimony but also in everything they spoke against the truth.

Above it was said that they “made firm for themselves an evil word”; now it is said that their tongues “were weakened against them.” Thus both the strength and weakness of their speech turned to their own contrary. In saying, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25), they made firm for themselves a malicious saying, because there is strength in words by which they condemn themselves. And where they wished to shut the mouths of the disciples so that they might not say to the people, “He rose from the dead” (Jer. XXXII), their tongues were weakened against them, because the apostles proclaimed and told the people that Christ had risen from the dead, never again to die [Col. 1811A], but to live forever and to raise his own members with himself.

Likewise, in their council, when the Pharisees and scribes said: “You see that we accomplish nothing. Look, the whole world has gone after him” (John XII, 19); and again, “It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people” (John XVIII, 14), both strength and weakness are found in their words, to their own harm. In saying, “We accomplish nothing,” they uttered a true and firm statement, because neither they nor other adversaries of truth advance to success; but, like chaff pressing upon fire, they truly accomplished nothing, as they said, unto their own ruin. Their saying in this respect was and will be firm.

But in this their tongues were weakened against them: they judged it expedient that one man should die for the people, whereas by this they were not released but shackled, bound with the rope of captivity, and cast into the prison of hell. Behold how a person speaking against God is cursed, so that both the strength and the weakness of his words turn against him; and it is said to him: “Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant” (Luke XIX, 22).

Thus the wicked tenants perished when they said: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance” (Matt. XXI, 38). “This,” they say, “is the heir.” Nothing truer or firmer could be said of the man whom God appointed heir of all things. But what they add—“We shall have his inheritance”—is so false that it is plainly evident that in this word their tongues were weakened. Such is the work of those who slander Christ or a Christian [Col. 1811C] before the Lord and speak evil against his soul: the strength in part and the weakness in part of such speech are turned to their harm, according to the saying: “Let his prayer become sin” (Ps. CVIII, 7).

Since therefore the tongues of those who made firm for themselves a malicious saying were thus weakened against them, so that whether they proposed things true and firm or false and weak, they found in them contradiction and shame for themselves, while those same things worked together for good to the good, all who saw them condemned by their own mouth were troubled, moved by just reflection. Some of their number, when the apostles preached, saw themselves bound by guilt for the blood of the righteous one [Col. 1811D], and, troubled unto repentance, said to Peter and the other apostles: “What shall we do, brethren?” But Peter said to them: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized for the forgiveness of sins” (Acts II, 37–38). Those who received this word were beneficially troubled.

But those were destructively troubled and perished who, as they had cried that Caesar was their king after rejecting Christ, so, after rejecting the apostles, were delivered bodily into the hands of the Romans and spiritually into the hands of demons, and perished in an exceedingly dreadful devastation. Seeing and prudently observing this, they were troubled.

**VERSE 10.** “And every man feared.” For he who did not fear was not a man, but like horse and mule, which have no understanding [Col. 1812A]. For who, rationally considering that God did not spare the natural branches, can be secure from fear of God, however free he may be from fear of the enemy—from which he asked to be delivered, saying, “Deliver my soul from fear of the enemy”? Thus man fears not the hostile man but God, however gracious God may be.

So the apostles feared not hostile man but God gracious to them, when, after they had been beaten, they were commanded not to speak in the name of Jesus; yet, though scourged and forbidden, they proclaimed the works of God. They were free indeed from fear of the enemy, but watchful under the fear of the Lord. So after them every person worthy of martyrdom in the times of persecuting tyrants, and worthy of confession in the times of deceiving heretics, feared. So until the end of the age every person using human reason will fear, taking care rather to offend God than man, and preferring to die in torments with man offended rather than live in pleasures with God offended, after the example of the apostles, martyrs, and confessors. Disdaining fear of hostile man, they proclaimed the works of God—namely, the resurrection, ascension, and other such things.

“And they understood his works,” because by preaching and proclaiming they were more and more enlightened and understood why he had been born of a virgin and suffered upon the cross. He willed that death, which had entered the world through a woman, should be driven away through a woman; and that he who had conquered upon the wood should also be conquered upon the wood. Likewise, in his other wonders they understood that his works had been ordered [Col. 1812C] not by human but by divine providence. For example, they understood why, when enemies mocked him, he kept silent and did not descend from the cross as they urged: because he had purposed to do something greater, namely to rise after death from the tomb, opening to all who had died and who would die the way of rising again, either to life or to judgment.

That the disciples might understand these and his other works, “he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke XXIV, 45), on the day of the resurrection, breathing upon them and saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX, 20). But they received the gift of understanding more abundantly and perfectly when the Holy Spirit came upon them in tongues of fire and filled their hearts with understanding. From then on [Col. 1812D] they proclaimed Christ’s works with greater constancy and zeal, and understood his deeds with a more capacious sense of reason and faith.

Likewise, until the end of the age, as all the least and greatest sincerely proclaim the works of God, sound understanding increases, so that they may understand that whatever deeds are good and praiseworthy are God’s, not man’s. They must not praise in these things the power of the person through whom, or in whom, they are done, but that of God alone, from whom every good proceeds and to whose praise all praiseworthy deeds are rightly referred, whether done by him alone or through creatures. Hence:

**VERSE 11.** “The righteous shall rejoice in the Lord and hope in him,” not in himself, when all who are upright in heart are praised for this very uprightness; for the righteous rejoices by hoping in the Lord, not in himself [Col. 1813A], and all who are upright in heart, when they are praised, feed not upon their own praise but upon God’s. Otherwise, they would have a heart not upright but crooked and estranged from uprightness, if they claimed for themselves—or, worse, seized—the glory due to God for the works of God, or did not reject it when voluntarily offered.

Accordingly Peter and John, foremost among those who proclaimed God’s works and understood his deeds, when some were filled with amazement and ecstasy at what had happened to the lame man healed through them, and silently attributed God’s deed to human piety or power, said: “Why do you look at us as though by our own power or piety we had made this man walk? The God of our fathers [Col. 1814A] has glorified his Son, and the faith which is through him has given him this complete healing in the sight of us all” (Acts III, 12 ff.).

Therefore these upright in heart will be praised in the Lord all the more because their uprightness of heart was more constant: they courageously rejected from themselves praise due to God alone, themselves praising—and teaching others to praise—in God’s work divine piety and power alone.
