In praise of him, let us also say at the end of this psalm, or of every good work:

Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit: to the Father, whose heart is high; to the Son, who, having become man, drew near to the high heart; and to the Holy Spirit, who is joy, because the righteous shall rejoice in the Lord.

## VENERABLE GERHOH, PROVOST OF REICHERSPERG

Prolegomena. Preliminary dissertation on the life and writings of Gerhoh, 461. Notice from Fabricius, 479. Life of Gerhoh, 481.

### LETTERS OF GERHOH

Letter I.—To Master A.—He writes that it does not seem necessary to him that his little works on the glorification of human nature in Christ should again be submitted to the judgment of the Apostolic See, since they had already once been approved by it. He sends and commends to him his work against the errors of the Greeks, 489.

Letter II.—To Henry, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.—He offers and commends to him his exposition of Psalm 64, 490.

Letter III.—To Otto, bishop of Freising.—He submits the first part of his exposition of the Psalms to his judgment, and explains what others have thought of it, 490.

Letter IV.—To Sister G.—He states that he did not undermine the abbess of Brag, but rightly gave canonical consent to her deposition because of her obstinacy; yet he is prepared to assist her if she is modest, 492.

Letter V.—From A., abbot of Egen, to Gerhoh.—He relates what happened at Bamberg to the provost of Triph, and, rejecting that man’s teaching, praises Gerhoh’s Catholic writings, 494.

Letter VI.—From Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, to the provosts of Salzburg and Kimiss.—He declares his grief at the death of Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg, and sends them for examination his writings against Gerhoh, 495.

Letter VII.—Gerhoh to Adam, abbot of York.—Against the errors of Folmar, provost of Trieffenstein, 496.

Letter VIII.—Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, to Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg.—Against Gerhoh, who asserts that the divinity in the sacrament of the altar is devoured by those who receive it, and that Christ as man is equal to the Father, 500.

Letter IX.—Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, to N.—In this letter Gerhoh’s opinion concerning the glory and honor of the Son of Man, Christ, is further attacked, and the Council of Ephesus is shown not to support it, 514.

Letter X.—Gerhoh to the abbot of Windberg.—He reports what he did and said in the conference held with Eberhard concerning his opinion, 521.

Letter XI.—Eberhard to Gerhoh.—He attacks him severely because Gerhoh took and published his words in an unfavorable sense; he further argues that Christ as man is lesser than and unequal to the Father, 524.

Letter XII.—Gerhoh to Eberhard.—He briefly responds to his previous letter and reports that he has written a full work on the disputed question, 529.

Letter XIII.—The same author to the same recipient.—He denies that he had defamed him at the emperor’s court. The disputed question returns, in which he judges the Council of Ephesus to be a powerful support for himself, 530.

Letter XIV.—Eberhard to Gerhoh.—The teaching of the Council of Ephesus is explained, together with the words of both teachers and Holy Scripture which Gerhoh adduced to establish his opinion, 532.

Letter XV.—Gerhoh to Eberhard.—He replies to the preceding letter and explains at length how the manhood in Christ [Col. 1844] is no longer a servant by condition, although it is such by the genus of its nature, 542.

Letter XVI.—Eberhard to Gerhoh.—He replies to the foregoing letter and proves that Christ as man is a creature and servant even after his ascension into heaven, 552.

Letter XVII.—Gerhoh to Pope Alexander III.—He dedicates to him his exposition of Psalm 131, denounces Peter Lombard, and commends the reform of the Church, 564.

Letter XVIII.—The same author to Henry, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.—He writes that he has sent him an exposition of Psalm 64. Why he was unable to travel to France.—On the multitude and plots of his adversaries, 570.

Letter XIX.—The same author to Hyacinth, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.—That he may make the cardinals attentive to the known controversy concerning the glory and honor of the Son of Man, 573.

Letter XX.—The same author to Pope Alexander III.—He asks him to reply with his opinion in the controversy concerning the glory and honor of the Son of Man. On certain of his little works sent to the Roman Curia, 574.

Letter XXI.—The same author to the college of cardinals of the Holy Roman Church.—On the various storms by which he has continually been battered, and in which he boasts that the Apostolic See has always been his protection, 575.

Letter XXII.—Cardinal C. to Gerhoh.—He praises his teaching and warns him not to dispute before the unlearned about matters of a subtler argument, 585.

Letter XXIII.—Cardinal Hyacinth to Gerhoh.—He writes that the pope is, as Gerhoh wished, attending to the controversy over the glory and honor of the Son of Man; he also teaches that Alexander is regarded as the legitimate pontiff by the whole Church, with few exceptions, 586.

Letter XXIV.—Gerhoh to Otto, bishop of Freising.—He defends Hilary against an unnamed author who wished it to have been taught by him that Christ’s body had not been glorified beyond the bodies of the other saints, and that the human nature in Christ did not surpass in received grace the excellence of any angel, 586.

Letter XXV.—The same author to Henry, duke of Saxony and Bavaria.—He exhorts him to defend the Church of God, setting before him the example of saints, kings, and dukes, 604.

Letter XXVI.—The same author to Arbo or Erbo, abbot of Prüfening.—He urges him to moderate the anger of the bishop of Regensburg, who had excommunicated all his citizens for the crime of certain persons, 606.

Letter XXVII.—The same author to the nuns of Admont.—He explains to them the words of Psalm 50: “That thou mayest be justified in thy words,” 607.

Letter XXVIII.—The same author to N., his daughter in Christ.—He expounds to her the words of the same Psalm: “That thou mayest prevail when thou art judged,” 611.

Letter XXIX.—The same author to certain nuns, perhaps those of Admont.—On the strength and purity of faith, using the example of the centurion in the Gospel, 614.

## GOLDEN COMMENTARY ON THE PSALMS AND THE WEEKDAY CANTICLES

Part One, 619. Part Two, 987. Part Three, 1315. Part Four, 1371. Part Five, 1563. Part Six, 1609.

[Col. 1843] **END OF THE ONE HUNDRED AND NINETY-THIRD VOLUME.**
